7.title: And was there a lesson in all this
7.file: ch07 - And was there a lesson in all this.md
7.relation: Editor James B. South's introduction explains how the Season One finale 'Prophecy Girl' turned him from a skeptic into a viewer who found the show 'worth my thinking about.' He states the book's two-way thesis: philosophy can illuminate BtVS, and the show offers genuine occasions for philosophical reflection on problems like nihilism, human irrationality, friendship, and punishment. Against the intimidation of technical academic philosophy (he cites Rawls's A Theory of Justice), he appeals to Plato's point that we cannot escape popular culture and to Aristotle's distinction between leisure and relaxation, arguing BtVS shows that television-watching can itself become the leisure activity in which philosophy is done.

8.title: Codex 1 - It’s kind of a Slayer thing. Buffy, Faith, and Feminism
8.file: ch08 - Codex 1 - It’s kind of a Slayer thing. Buffy, Faith, and Feminism.md

9.title: The Buffyverse’s Moral Compass
9.relation: Greg Forster argues the Buffyverse's moral structure is neither Christian nor Nietzschean vampire fiction but Platonic eudaimonism: the just person is always happier than the unjust. Faith is the test case — her pleasure-seeking turn to evil with Mayor Wilkins, her body-swap theft of Buffy's life in 'Who Are You?', her self-disgust ('You're nothing! Disgusting, murderous bitch!'), and her begging Angel to kill her in 'Five by Five' enact Plato's Republic examples of the Ring of Gyges and the unjust person mistakenly honored while the just one is punished. Buffy's invisible crime spree in 'Gone' and her 'the work that I have to do' sacrifice in 'The Gift' display the same eudaimonist pattern, with the caveat that the Buffyverse follows a Rousseau-like moral psychology in which compassion, not reason, does the moral work.

10.title: Persuasion As Drama
10.file: ch10 - Persuasion As Drama.md
10.relation: Karl Schudt contends that Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality cannot be refuted by reason (Nietzsche denies reason itself), so drama must persuade where dialectic cannot: a believable story of a Nietzschean life acts as an empathic experiment. Faith is constructed as the Nietzschean ideal — strong, healthy, ruthless ('Find a couple of studs, use them, and discard them'), dismissive of reflection ('You think too much') — serving Mayor Wilkins, whom Schudt reads as a genuine Übermensch sacrificing mankind's mass for his ascension. Watching her world collapse (the accidental killing in 'Bad Girls', her mirror scene in 'Who Are You?', the torture of Wesley and confession on Angel) gives viewers an Aristotelian pity-and-fear warning that the unjust life ends badly, completing her 'leap from Nietzsche to Socrates.'

11.title: “The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self
11.file: ch11 - “The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self.md
11.relation: Jessica Prata Miller reads Buffy through Carol Gilligan's care perspective: Buffy's self is relational (the Scooby Gang, 'Dawn is a part of me' in 'The Gift'), her moral reasoning contextual rather than rule-bound (caging Oz instead of killing the werewolf, rejecting Riley's Initiative 'demons bad' abstraction), and her emotions a moral resource ('My emotions give me power'). She also weighs the criticisms — Buffy's secret harboring of Angel exposed in 'Revelations,' and Faith's utilitarian 'plus column' defense of hiding a killing, which Buffy rejects ('I am' the one who cries over the bystander). Comparing the three Slayers, Miller argues only Buffy attains moral autonomy: Kendra's unquestioning obedience and Faith's hyper-individualistic action-hero isolation both fail, while Buffy's 'I like to think of it as graduation' break from the Watchers' Council shows autonomy achieved within, not against, relationships.

12.title: The Noir Consequences of Sex Eros, Death, and the Possibility of Love
12.file: ch12 - The Noir Consequences of Sex Eros, Death, and the Possibility of Love.md
12.relation: Thomas Hibbs reads BtVS as feminist noir: like classic noir it traps characters in labyrinths where the past bears down on the present (Buffy torn from heaven in 'After Life,' Angel's gypsy curse in 'Innocence,' the psych-ward ending of 'Normal Again'), and it rejects both Enlightenment optimism and the Nietzschean beyond-good-and-evil self-creation Hibbs finds in neo-noir like Body Heat and Thelma and Louise. Sex in Sunnydale always carries noir consequences — Angel losing his soul at the moment of 'true happiness,' Buffy's self-lacerating Spike affair ending in his attempted rape — so the show is skeptical of sexual liberation while recovering a classical eros as longing for wholeness. The Season Six finale locates the 'true essence of magic' in sacrificial love: Xander's yellow-crayon plea in 'Grave' reaches the 'spark of humanity' in Willow where all force fails.

13.title: No Damsel in Distress
13.file: ch13 - No Damsel in Distress.md
13.relation: Mimi Marinucci argues Buffy's violence tracks what agents do, not what they are: souled Angel and chip-enabled Spike receive moral consideration, willing human evildoers like Ford ('Lie to Me') and Ethan Rayne are fought, and Buffy's 'impression of Gandhi' in 'Anne' claims violence can rightly answer injustice. Building on William R. Jones's King–Malcolm X–Mao spectrum and Hannah Arendt's warning that doing violence habituates the agent, she reads the Slayer's fight as symbolic resistance to rape and women's oppression (bloodsucking as rape metaphor in 'Buffy vs. Dracula,' Spike's assault after Buffy ends the affair). The cost is real — 'Restless' reveals the First Slayer's primeval rage and staking with 'Mr. Pointy' mirrors sexualized violence — so she ends by endorsing tempered, appropriate violence (Buffy's Tai Chi training with Angel) over both passivity and aggression.

14.title: Codex 2 - Don’t speak Latin in front of the books Knowledge, Rationality, and
14.file: ch14 - Codex 2 - Don’t speak Latin in front of the books Knowledge, Rationality, and.md

15.title: Smelly Knowledge
15.file: ch15 - Smelly Knowledge.md
15.relation: Andrew Aberdein sorts the Buffyverse's science-supernatural encounters into three grades — reduction to present science, reduction to a future science, and the irreducibly supernatural — illustrated by Sunnydale's rationalizers and Giles's inner skeptic in 'Tabula Rasa,' the Initiative's DNA testing of Oz in 'New Moon Rising,' and the show's characteristic 'creepy mix of magic and science' (Jenny Calendar's 'the divine exists in cyberspace'). He reads 'Normal Again' through Descartes's deceiving-demon skepticism, links Spike's chip and Walsh's Adam to the Phineas Gage case (emotion is needed for rational decision), and maps the grades onto the ancients-versus-moderns quarrel and Feyerabend's methodological anarchism. Giles's 'smelly knowledge' speech about books versus computers anticipates a pluralist, socially sensitive epistemology that enriches rather than rejects science.

16.title: Pals
16.file: ch16 - Pals.md
16.relation: Madeline Muntersbjorn uses Season Four's Initiative-versus-Scoobies conflict to dissolve the Science Wars: Professor Walsh's secret, unfalsifiable Project 314 makes her Karl Popper's bad scientist, while Buffy's gang embodies Feyerabend's pluralism and Peirce-and-James pragmatism — Buffyverse rules are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and the gang welcomes anyone willing to ask questions and do research. Her three ideals — pluralism, pragmatism, pals — culminate in 'Primeval,' where the combo-Buffy enjoining spell (Willow's spirit, Xander's heart, Giles's mind, Buffy's hand) literally enacts James's meliorism: the world may be saved if each agent does their level best, together. Walsh dies alone because she has no pals; Buffy saves the world 'a lot' because she does.

17.title: Conquering the Inner Demon
17.relation: James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.

18.title: Possibilities of Postmodern Education Beyond Control
18.file: ch18 - Possibilities of Postmodern Education Beyond Control.md
18.relation: Toby Daspit reads Season Four as a drama of postmodern education: the Initiative's will to master and dissect — Walsh's Frankenstein-project Adam, who murders a boy to see how he works, fulfilling Wordsworth's 'we murder to dissect' — embodies the Cartesian split and the Hegelian drive to negate the other, while Buffy's world deconstructs fixed identity (Darla reversing the horror-movie opening, the Faith/Buffy body swap in 'Who Are You?', Jonathan's 'Superstar') and thwarts prophecy's metanarrative in 'Prophecy Girl.' Against modernist schooling's 'controlled circumstances' and Freire's banking model (Professor Riegert ejecting Buffy from class, Walsh's transmission lectures), the show models knowledge as collective work — the Scoobies' research sessions in Giles's library, Giles's fluid mentorship versus Kendra's by-the-book training, and the relational magic of 'Primeval' — offering education beyond control in an emergent, postmodern world.

19.title: Making the Pain Go “Poof”
19.relation: James B. South argues Willow's Season Six turn — magic addiction, torturing Warren with a 'bored now,' attempting to end the world in 'Grave' — is tragic precisely because it is unintelligible: against Aristotle's account of tragedy, where pity requires seeing an intelligible mistake, Willow's destruction flows from Freudian depths (via Plato's 'lawless' desires and Jonathan Lear's 'enigmatic signifiers') that cannot be explained, only pointed to. The chapter traces the available evidence — her sidekick insecurity ('I'm not your sidekick!' in 'Fear, Itself'), her 'spurty knowledge' slip, making pain go 'poof' in 'Something Blue' — while insisting these unconscious swerves never add up to a reason for the final break. Xander's yellow-crayon memory in 'Grave' works not as explanation but as a second kind of break that opens space for Willow to regroup.

20.title: Codex 3 - You’re really enjoying this whole moral superiority thing, aren’t
20.file: ch20 - Codex 3 - You’re really enjoying this whole moral superiority thing, aren’t.md

21.title: Buffy As a Watcher (of Sorts)
21.file: ch21 - Buffy As a Watcher (of Sorts).md
21.relation: Jason Kawal tests virtue ethics's 'act as the virtuous person would act' (Hursthouse's criterion) against Xander's 'What would Buffy do?': Buffy qualifies as a moral exemplar with heroic actions (nightly patrols, the 'Gift' plunge) and saintly sacrifices (the 'Doublemeat Palace' McJob for Dawn), but imitation fails — Xander lacks her abilities, tastes, relationships, and pure bravery, and stripping those away one by one turns Buffy into a copy of Xander. Worse, much of what Buffy does is supererogatory (Giles: 'She's a hero... She's not like us' in 'The Gift,' before killing Ben himself), so ordinary people are not morally required to do what she would do. His fix: ask what a fully informed, unimpaired virtuous observer — an 'angelic Buffy looking over our shoulders,' never drugged into 'Beer Bad' cave-Buffy — would deem right for us, given our own abilities and commitments.

22.title: Emotions and Aesthetic Response
22.file: ch22 - Emotions and Aesthetic Response.md
22.relation: Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.

23.title: Erotic Love and Friendship
23.relation: Maps Aristotle's three levels of friendship onto Buffy's three boyfriends: Riley is a utility friendship chosen for the rational goal of a 'normal' boyfriend (echoed by Warren's robot April and the Buffybot, which prove programmed perfection cannot be loved), Spike is a pleasure friendship driven by passion and danger that Buffy ends in 'As You Were,' and Angel is a complete friendship where each values the other for his own sake despite the gypsy curse. This lets the authors solve Aristotle's love paradox (is erotic love chosen or does it choose us?) by adding Augustine's and William of Ockham's third power of the soul, the will: an arational faculty that values the other as an end in himself, neither rationally chosen nor irrationally caused.

24.title: Following the Moral Law
24.relation: Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.

25.title: Codex 4 - That’s the kind of wooly-headed thinking that leads to being eaten
25.file: ch25 - Codex 4 - That’s the kind of wooly-headed thinking that leads to being eaten.md

26.title: Against Fascism
26.file: ch26 - Against Fascism.md
26.relation: Neal King argues the Buffyverse is proto-fascist: Buffy kills demons and vampires on sight within a race-like hierarchy, tempered only by an Augustinian split between natural and moral evil (soulless vampires cannot choose otherwise; soul-bearing humans like Faith, Willow, and Warren can repent), she derives authority from an ancient calling rather than democracy, and the graduation battle of 'Graduation Day, Part Two' stages citizenship forged in mass combat. He imagines a fascist Buffyverse of 'brownskirt' death squads and concludes only the show's secrecy prevents full fascism, finally recommending that the racism be dropped but the ritual sacrifice of evildoers kept — with Willow's flaying of Warren as the model.

27.title: Note to Self Religion Freaky
27.file: ch27 - Note to Self Religion Freaky.md
27.relation: Surveys religion across BtVS and Angel to show it is almost always demonic — the Master's Order of Aurelius, Ethan Rayne's chaos god Janus, the First Evil's eyeless priests in 'Amends,' and Ken's fundamentalist 'Family Home' in 'Anne,' read through Marx's definition of religion as the opiate of the masses — while the heroes use crosses, holy water, and prophecy only instrumentally and never pray. Genuine miracles like the snow that saves Angel are rare and unattributed, prophecies are routinely evaded ('I flunked the written'), and evil is defeated by self-reliance and friendship, as when Xander's unmagical love stops Willow in 'Grave.' The conclusion: the moral center of the Buffyverse is human — neither secularized nor sacralized.

28.title: Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben
28.relation: Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.

29.title: No Big Win
29.relation: Reads sacrifice, salvation, and redemption in the Buffyverse as secular myth: vampires manifest the shadow-side of the human (Liam's resentment becomes Angelus, William's repressed romanticism becomes Spike's rebellion), and the contrast between soulless Spike's genuine moral growth through love of Buffy and human Xander's arrested development shows redemption is measured by 'what have you done with what you've been given.' The Purpose of Evil section argues good and evil must stay in balance because without evil there is no free choice and hence no redemption, and Angel's 'no big win' epiphany — no grand plan, only lessening suffering one kindness at a time — locates life's meaning in the journey of becoming rather than final victory.

30.title: The Superhero As Liberal Reformer
30.file: ch30 - The Superhero As Liberal Reformer.md
30.relation: Jeffrey Pasley traces the show's radical surface — capitalism equated with vampirism (Anya's greed, Glory the über-consumer, the Master's blood factory in 'The Wish'), Big Bads tearing down dimensional barriers exactly as Marx's Communist Manifesto describes the bourgeoisie dissolving feudal ties into free trade, Buffy refusing to commodify slaying into wage labor, and Giles's Magic Box selling mystified junk at inflated margins — but concludes the heroes are not revolutionaries. In the comic-book lineage of Superman and Spider-Man, Buffy and Angel are liberal reformers bound by a superhero code against killing, so Giles must murder the innocent Ben precisely to preserve Buffy's heroic mercy; Angel's 'champions' speech in 'Deep Down' states the incrementalist creed.

31.title: Codex 5 - You’re all slaves to the television Watching Buffy
31.file: ch31 - Codex 5 - You’re all slaves to the television Watching Buffy.md

32.title: The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer
32.file: ch32 - The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer.md
32.relation: Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.

33.title: The Evolution of the Metaphor
33.file: ch33 - The Evolution of the Metaphor.md
33.relation: Tracy Little argues the show takes teenagers' metaphorical speech — 'high school is hell,' 'after we slept together he became a different person,' 'graduation is the end of the world' — and makes it literal: hyena-possessed bullies in 'The Pack,' invisible Marcie whom nobody noticed, Angelus replacing Angel after Buffy and Angel's first night together, and the Mayor's ascension timed to graduation. Invoking Baudrillard's simulacra and hyperreality, the copy becomes more real than the original — the monsters are real but the social horrors they literalize are worse — and the seasons-one-through-three survey traces identity, love gone wrong, and end-of-the-world metaphors as they evolve from monster-of-the-week camp to weighty questions of life and death.

34.title: Psychical Dynamics of Love and Lust
34.file: ch34 - Psychical Dynamics of Love and Lust.md
34.relation: Levine and Schneider apply Freud's 1912 essay on the debasement in love — 'where they love they do not desire and where they desire they cannot love' — to argue that BtVS succeeds not through innovation or moral seriousness but through the conventional 'girl next door': Angel's forbidden-vampire sex is the show's best because forbiddenness heightens desire, Xander's pedestal-placing of Buffy forecloses satisfaction, and Drusilla and Cordelia are already 'debased' sexual objects. Along the way they polemicize against Buffy scholars for projecting their own fantasies onto a show that reinforces, rather than subverts, gender stereotypes and the forbiddenness of sex for young women.

12.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Eric Katz reads Tolkien's One Ring as a modern retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges: Glaucon's challenge in Republic II that no one, given impunity, would remain just. He traces each character's moment of choice - Gollum already corrupted and split into 'Slinker and Stinker', Boromir trying to seize the Ring at Amon Hen and dying redeemed, Galadriel passing the test ('I will diminish, and go into the West'), Tom Bombadil untouched, Frodo finally claiming the Ring at the Cracks of Doom while Sam rejects the vision of 'Samwise the Strong'. Katz argues Tolkien improves on Plato by showing, through living characters, that unlimited power corrupts the soul, and that the answer to 'Why be moral?' is 'to be yourself': those who refuse the Ring are exactly those who know their own limits.

13.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Theodore Schick takes Tolkien's remark that the Ring represents 'potency' externalized beyond its maker's control and applies it to emerging nanotechnology, genetics, and robotics. He sets Bill Joy's call for relinquishment against Eric Drexler's promise of universal assemblers, cell-repair machines, and soldier nanosuits, weighing the 'grey goo' risk against the Rings' own power to heal and preserve (Lothlórien, Bilbo 'well-preserved'). Against the Council of Elrond's solution of destroying the Ring, he argues our situation is disanalogous - Ring-making knowledge is now spread worldwide and there is no single device to destroy - so grass-roots social response, not bans, must tame the new technologies.

14.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Alison Milbank argues we are all in thrall to the Ring because it mirrors our own fetishism: she reads the film's lingering close-ups, Smaug-like hoarding, and Gollum's baby-talking self-division through Freud's theory of the fetish and Marx's commodity fetishism, with Sauron as the emptied idolater who poured his power into the thing. Against this she sets Middle-earth's gift economy - Bilbo's party, Galadriel's gifts, Sam's elven rope - glossed by Heidegger's 'Thinging gathers': Sam praises the rope by restoring it to its elven makers and its use. Tom Bombadil, who treats the Ring as 'a very pretty ring' and nothing more, and Frodo's final sacrifice model the unfetishized life; the chapter closes with Sam's homecoming, where chairs are only chairs and the family circle replaces the Ring.

15.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

16.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Gregory Bassham distills six keys to happiness from Tolkien's hobbits and elves: delight in simple pleasures (Epicurus on natural pleasures, Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles (Sam's star above Mordor, with Marcus Aurelius and Augustine on courage and hope), friendship (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics read against Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo go alone), good character, beauty and creativity (Lothlórien versus Mordor, 'flow'), and wonder (Tom Bombadil, Frodo's 'recovery' of fresh vision at Cerin Amroth). He argues Tolkien thereby becomes a philosophical guide, pointing from the Shire and Rivendell to a richer, more joy-filled life.

17.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
17.relation: Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.

18.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Eric Bronson places Tolkien among the 'sometimes merry' existentialists: Nietzsche's artist who says Yes amid catastrophe and needs 'the power to forget', Jaspers on machines estranging us from our past, and Arendt on Eichmann's obedient inhumanity and the few who create joy in dark times. The elves' songs in Rivendell and Lórien are joy born of sorrow and dispossession - Galadriel suffers because she remembers too much, trying to 'embalm time', while Arwen forgoes immortality for Aragorn. Her refusal of the Ring ('I will diminish, and go into the West, and remain Galadriel') embodies the existentialist affirmation: trust your own light, know what to remember and what to forget.

19.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

20.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.

21.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Scott Davison asks whether Tolkien's world is Manichean - two equal forces of Good and Evil - and answers no: the Ring is not 'altogether evil' in itself but animated by Sauron's infused will, and nothing, not even Sauron, is totally evil, since 'nothing is evil in the beginning'. Developing Augustine's account, he shows evil as parasitic privation - Ringwraiths wear robes 'to give shape to their nothingness', the Eye is 'a window into nothing' - and traces evil to inordinate desire: Sam stays content with his garden while Boromir, Saruman, Denethor, and Sauron reach for more than their place allows. Evil unmakes itself (Saruman dies by Wormtongue's knife), and because goodness is the world's default, there is always hope of overcoming it.

22.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.

23.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

24.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.

25.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings in part as a protest against modernism - the post-WWI mood (Berman, Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', Nietzsche's 'God is dead') that tradition is obsolete and whatever can be done must be done. The heroes win by remembering: Gandalf alone thinks to watch the Shire, Sam's book-learning about elves and the password 'Elbereth' saves the day at Cirith Ungol, while Saruman and Denethor fall into modern despair through the palantír and Pippin's stone dropped in Moria brings Gandalf down. The Ring itself is modernism's false promise of remaking the world, and Tolkien answers it with a fantasy where ancient lore has tangible power - sealed by Pippin's maturing into one of Middle-earth's great librarians.

26.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Andrew Light identifies a distinctive environmental theme he calls 'green time': Tom Bombadil and the ents embody nature's long rhythms and are largely indifferent to the War of the Ring - Tom would simply mislay the Ring, and the ents march to war only after Saruman strips Fangorn. Against readings that make elves or dwarves stand-ins for nature, he argues the text lets nature speak for itself, from a collective, ecosystemic perspective: the ents, 'made of the bones of the earth', decline with their forests and lost the entwives to the tilled land. Deploying Wittgenstein's point that we could not understand a talking lion, he concludes that Tolkien's personified nature trains us in the long view and humility needed for problems like global warming.

27.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

28.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').

29.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.

30.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
30.relation: Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.

31.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
31.relation: John Davenport argues that The Lord of the Rings is neither mere adventure nor Christian allegory but an epic fairy tale whose 'eucatastrophe' - Tolkien's term for the sudden joyous turn, a miraculous reprieve - carries religious hope even though the book contains no churches or prayers. Drawing on Tolkien's 'On Fairy-stories', he makes Sir Gawain and the Green Knight the model for Frodo: Gawain accepts the girdle and is scarred yet reprieved, just as Frodo claims the Ring, loses a finger as Beren lost a hand, and is saved only because the mercy shown Gollum lets the Ring fall into the fire. Gandalf's return, Éowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth extend the pattern; with Kierkegaard the deliverance is grace 'by virtue of the absurd', an echo of the eschaton answering Boethius's question whether our struggles have final significance.

10.title: Rounding Third and Heading Home
10.file: ch10 - Rounding Third and Heading Home.md
10.relation: Joe Kraus uses Gaston Bachelard's Poetics of Space to read baseball's 'home': the batter begins at home yet must leave it, face the pitcher's threat, and return to make scoring meaningful, which is Bachelard's dialectic of shelter versus threat (with Joseph Campbell's monomyth alongside). Freud's uncanny (unheimlich, un-home-like) explains why home plate is both inviting and demoralizing. Bachelard's 'well-determined centers of revery' and Benedict Anderson's shared-news account of nationhood then explain ballparks as communal homes, from Wrigleyville to 'Cardinal Nation' in Quincy, Illinois, and why the Dodgers leaving Brooklyn felt like losing a home.

11.title: The Obligation to Play Baseball
11.file: ch11 - The Obligation to Play Baseball.md
11.relation: Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.

12.title: Second Inning - You Gotta Believe!
12.file: ch12 - Second Inning - You Gotta Believe!.md

13.title: Who Should Be Committed
13.file: ch13 - Who Should Be Committed.md
13.relation: Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.

14.title: Kierkegaard Lays It Down
14.file: ch14 - Kierkegaard Lays It Down.md
14.relation: Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.

15.title: Third Inning - The Umpire’s New Clothes
15.file: ch15 - Third Inning - The Umpire’s New Clothes.md

16.title: The Ambiguous Consolations of Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Ambiguous Consolations of Philosophy.md
16.relation: Ted Cohen shows that 'ties go to the runner' is no convention but follows from Rule 6.05(j) (the runner is out only if tagged before he touches first), then discovers that Rule 7.08(e) contradicts 6.05(j) once 6.09(a) makes a batter who hits a fair ball a runner: on a tie at first the rules say both out and safe. His letters to the National League rules committee get a polite brush-off ('there never are any ties'), and the essay meditates on how players barely know the rules (the 2000 World Series third-strike misplay, cricket's time-wasting law, the spitball rule's gaps) and how rules written 'by journeymen lawyers' charm yet fail. Philosophy's consolation is ambiguous: knowing the rules cost him his teammates' respect, who 'knew the game in some other way.'

17.title: The Integrity of the Game
17.file: ch17 - The Integrity of the Game.md
17.relation: J.S. Russell argues umpires have far more discretion than 'rules are all an umpire has to work with' allows. Via J.L. Austin's performative utterances, a call both creates the out and reports a witnessed event, so it can be false; hence unwitnessed or deceived calls (Ken Burkhart's 1970 World Series missed tag, phantom tags, Bernardo Carbo never touching the plate) should be reviewable to prevent an 'anti-game.' Via Ronald Dworkin's law-as-integrity he then defends Lee MacPhail's reinstatement of George Brett's pine-tar home run and umpire Wes Curry's 1887 interference ruling through a 'first principle of games adjudication': interpret rules to preserve the lusory goal and the excellences the game tests, as umpires' de facto strike-zone management has held league batting averages near .260 for a century.

18.title: Fourth Inning - Fair or Foul
18.file: ch18 - Fourth Inning - Fair or Foul.md

19.title: Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater
19.file: ch19 - Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater.md
19.relation: Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.

20.title: Five Questions about Good Sportsmanship
20.file: ch20 - Five Questions about Good Sportsmanship.md
20.relation: Mark Hamilton asks whether there is lying in baseball (riffing on Jimmy Dugan's 'There's no crying in baseball') and sorts plays of deception by their target. Kant's absolute duty of truthfulness proves too broad for the hidden ball trick, Omar Vizquel's decoys, and faking a tag to fool Manny Ramirez: Aquinas's taxonomy of officious, jocose, and mischievous lies (with Bonhoeffer's situational truth-telling) shows these are jocose falsehoods in an agreed artificial contest, not immoral lies. But deception aimed at umpires is mischievous and immoral, as when Barry Bonds sells a trapped ball as a catch or runners cut bases in the illegal double squeeze; his five questions conclude that tricking opponents is strategy while tricking the officials destroys character and sport.

21.title: Fifth Inning - Baseball and America
21.file: ch21 - Fifth Inning - Baseball and America.md

22.title: Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy
22.file: ch22 - Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy.md
22.relation: Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.

23.title: America’s Game
23.relation: William Morgan answers Richard Rorty's charge that American pop culture breeds only militaristic chauvinism by pointing to baseball's moral self-story: played for love of the game (Whitman) rather than market value. Using MacIntyre's notion of a practice's internal goods, he argues baseball's excellences and fair play are shared, socially constructed goods that resist commodification; through Annette Baier's ethics of trust and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' (saving your wife because she is your wife), the home team extends familial trust into a public moral community. Hence the moral outrage of 'Say it ain't so, Joe' after the 1919 Black Sox scandal and 'Say It Ain't So Sammy' after Sosa's corked bat: fans demand that players justify themselves to the community whose common good the game embodies.

25.title: Crossing the Color Line
25.relation: The Rucks argue that Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism supplied the ideological justification for baseball's color line — blacks were deemed genetically unfit for the game — and that the Negro Leagues disproved it. Rube Foster's Negro National League, and especially Pittsburgh's Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords (Cum Posey, Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige, Cool Papa Bell), displayed black organizational skill and on-field excellence, with Negro League teams beating white major leaguers in barnstorming play. Drawing on Darwin's actual account of cultural evolution and Franz Boas's environmental anthropology, the chapter holds that institutions, training infrastructure, and environment — not genes — explain athletic success, as Jackie Robinson's 1947 crossing of the color line and the later rise of Latin stars like Roberto Clemente confirm.

26.title: The Gift of Baseball
26.file: ch26 - The Gift of Baseball.md
26.relation: McDaniels reads the Negro Leagues through Nietzsche's account of resentment as revolt and Cornel West's tragic philosophy of resistance: excluded from the white majors after Cap Anson's 1887 stand against George Stovey, black players converted resentment into counter-narratives of excellence, with Satchel Paige, Josh Gibson, and Buck O'Neil showboating and clowning in the tradition of plantation dance, gallows humor, and the blues. The call-and-response sermon scene from The Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars & Motor Kings — Bingo Long on the mound answered by the crowd like a black church congregation — shows performance as ritual that sustains community, while bell hooks's 'absence of presence' frames remembering as resistance to hegemonic definitions of race. The chapter closes with the author's grandfather, for whom Robinson, Aaron, Mays, and Paige proved with every pitch 'We're American Too.'

27.title: Seventh Inning - The Japanese National Pastime
27.file: ch27 - Seventh Inning - The Japanese National Pastime.md

28.title: Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment
28.file: ch28 - Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment.md
28.relation: Bassham argues that the core advice of hitting instructors like Ted Williams ('get a good ball to hit') and Charley Lau ('tension is the enemy') echoes Zen Buddhist principles, walking through patience, relaxation, self-knowledge, visualization (Reggie Jackson, Willie Stargell, Barry Bonds's on-deck imagery), practice, Bruce Lee-style kime concentration, and mushin or no-mind. Mickey Mantle going 0-for-30 after over-thinking Ted Williams's hitting tips, and Tony Gwynn's 'see the ball and react,' show how conscious analysis interferes with the muscle memory a half-second fastball demands. If kendo is practiced in a dojo — a 'place of enlightenment' — he concludes, ballparks and batting cages may be dojos too, with the caveat that Cobb, Ruth, and Mantle hardly model egoless humility.

29.title: What’s Wrong with Generalization
29.relation: Brannigan uses Japanese baseball to ask what is wrong with cultural generalization. He presents the Bushido case — samurai-style self-denial, absolute loyalty (Kawakami's Yomiuri Giants), Suisha Tobita's 'training of death,' resolve (konjo), team harmony (wa), and a relational self grounded in Buddhism's no-self and Confucian identity-through-relationships — then tests it against counter-evidence: Sadaharu Oh's flamingo swing owed as much to individual talent and Hiroshi Arakawa's unconventional kendo-and-aikido coaching as to sensei imitation, the 'new breed' (Ochiai, Egawa) flouts the old ways, and William Kelly's 'Whiting problem' warns against polarizing Japanese and American baseball. The chapter's 'three strikes' against the label 'Japanese baseball' conclude that generalizations become dangerous when treated as monolithic nets cast over an entire culture.

30.title: Eighth Inning - Behind in the Count
30.file: ch30 - Eighth Inning - Behind in the Count.md

31.title: Numbers as Players
31.relation: Bennett and Martin argue that the statistics baseball fans treat as objective truth embody far more chance and convention than fans realize. Statistical theory shows luck explains roughly half the spread in 2002 batting averages (Bonds's .370 versus Larry Walker; the 2003 Ramirez–Mueller race decided by one at bat), and Jim Albert's simulation of 1,000 seasons shows about four of five World Series are not won by the most talented team. Drawing on Thomas Kuhn's history of scientific quantification and Theodore Porter's Foucauldian point that numbers 'have agency' and exercise power, they show statistics also act on the game — shaping drafting, salaries, and Hall of Fame election — so Schroeder's stats to Charlie Brown are both indispensable and misleading.

32.title: Softball The Good Is the Enemy of the Best
32.file: ch32 - Softball The Good Is the Enemy of the Best.md
32.relation: Heaphy asks whether softball limits women's potential to be equals on the baseball diamond, using feminist philosophy to explain why women are steered to the 'soft' game. Judith Williamson's analysis of women in mass culture and Simone de Beauvoir's woman-as-invisible-Other explain why female players — the AAGPBL's skirts and charm school, Toni Stone and Mamie Johnson in the Negro Leagues, Ila Borders in the minors — are covered as women first and ballplayers second. Iris Marion Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl' supplies the phenomenology: women throw differently not from anatomy but from experiencing the body as a burden, a socially produced self-fulfilling prophecy. Softball, 'the good,' becomes the enemy of the best — women playing hardball — by letting society postpone hard questions about gender.

34.title: The Moral and Aesthetic Superiority of Baseball
34.file: ch34 - The Moral and Aesthetic Superiority of Baseball.md
34.relation: Kretchmar asks whether the intentional walk of sluggers like Barry Bonds (or Casey at the Bat) is an unfair cop-out. Building an account of games as 'artificial tests' (via Bernard Suits and John Searle's treatment of conventions like 'hello'), he tests the analogy with basketball stalling and finds it fails: walking Bonds shifts rather than avoids the defensive test (the fielding team still owes all its outs), team games legitimately run away from stars as basketball double-teams Shaq, and fans gain new drama — Jeff Kent batting with the tying run after Bonds's walk. He concludes that event-regulated games like baseball, which cannot be shortened, enjoy a moral and aesthetic superiority over time-regulated games, whose endings breed stalling and clock-killing fouls.

35.title: Last Pitch
35.relation: Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.

37.title: 19b
37.relation: A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.

38.title: 20b
38.relation: A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.

39.title: 21b
39.relation: A paired metaphysics debate on whether superstition helps performance. Steven Streeter argues yes: baseball's mystery-rich outcomes breed ritual (Sparky Anderson refusing to step on foul lines, Wade Boggs's chicken, Nomar Garciaparra's glove taps), whose invisible forces — like black holes — can be inferred from their measurable effects on attention, preparation, and focus, with William James's belief-makes-reality as the capstone. Neil Feit counters no: on the counterfactual account of helping, a player cured of superstition would perform the same since his athletic ability is untouched, routines that aid concentration need involve no magical belief, and the burden of proof lies with the believer.

40.title: 22b
40.relation: A paired legal-philosophy debate on whether steroids should be banned. Michael McGrath argues yes from Kant: PED use cannot be universalized and 'the ends do not justify the means,' so the Ken Caminiti, Mark McGwire, and José Canseco confessions stain America's pastime, whose stars are role models and whose users risk devastating health effects — down to wrestler Davey Boy Smith's fatal steroid-related heart attack. Simon Eassom replies no by reframing drugs as Performance Enhancing Technologies: rules merely define the game, enhancers (unlike bat-cannons or netted catcher's gloves) do not de-skill baseball, and banning them because we dislike them is a matter of taste — of aesthetics, not ethics.

41.title: 23b
41.relation: A paired aesthetics debate over the best baseball movie. Vincent Toscano picks The Natural: Robert Redford's Roy Hobbs enacts fall and redemption, Barry Levinson's halo-lit amber cinematography gives the film its mythic beauty, and its Reagan-era warmth answered America's post-sixties malaise. Larry Raful counters with It Happens Every Spring: the best baseball film lets the common man — Ray Milland's chemistry teacher armed with a wood-repelling mystery juice — dream himself into the Show, and he notes we cheer fictional cheating on screen while demanding that the real game stay pure.

42.title: 24b
42.relation: A paired philosophy-of-education debate on whether baseball players were better role models then or now. Edward Sullivan answers 'then' from lived memory: Ted Williams's Korean War service and his 1966 Hall of Fame induction speech demanding Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson be enshrined, and Jackie Robinson enduring Jim Crow spring training under Branch Rickey's pact of 'guts enough not to fight back.' Graham Harman answers 'now,' turning Socrates's Apology complaint that his most dangerous accusers are those safely dead into a diagnosis of nostalgia: the past buried Ty Cobb's and Cap Anson's racism, the Black Sox, and Hal Chase, while today's game is more racially open, physically dedicated, and union-protected.

12.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.

13.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md

14.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Argues Tony misappropriates Sun Tzu's Art of War: he applies tactical precepts like deception, formlessness and 'Balk the enemy's power' (citing the book in 'He Is Risen' after Melfi's jab in 'Big Girls Don't Cry'), but ignores the philosophical core. The chapter contrasts Sun Tzu's monistic one-world view of yin-yang interdependence, harmony and winning without fighting with the Greek two-world dualism of Plato and with the Christianity that lets Tony tell Melfi 'soldiers don't go to hell' in 'From Where to Eternity'. Tony's sausage panic attacks in 'Fortunate Son' show his failure to see how his crimes ripple through his family, and because he lacks the commander's exemplary character and harmony, Tony is 'just a soldier', not a ruler.

15.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Argues ancient ethics explains why Tony, who has 'the world by the balls', still feels like a loser. Plato's Republic diagnoses him as a 'civil war' of unintegrated motivations (loving father and murderer at once, as in 'College'), a condition power over others only worsens; Aristotle teaches that happiness is activity with self-sufficient, integrated desires rather than a list of possessions, and Epicurus's 'sober reasoning' is the therapy Tony never gets. The Hawthorne quotation Tony reads in 'College' and his Gary Cooper ideal from 'The Happy Wanderer' frame the point: Cooper in High Noon is unmesswithable because he does not need vengeance, whereas Tony's compulsive revenge shows the world has the grip on him.

16.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Argues the show's underlying moral vision is Nietzschean passive nihilism filtered through film noir. Tony, unlike the active nihilist who converts value-collapse into self-overcoming, sinks into resentment and life-negation: he wants to rip the throat of the 'happy wanderer', therapy never redeems him, and he quits it with 'I'm a fat fucking crook from New Jersey' in 'Calling All Cars'. The chapter traces the noir lineage (Tony watching White Heat, the Godfather references, Bogart imagery at Satriale's) and reads A.J.'s 'D-Girl' existentialism (Camus's The Stranger, 'There is no God') and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' as the family inheritance of meaninglessness and death-dread.

17.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
17.relation: Argues Tony is at times a practitioner of The Prince and ignores Machiavelli at his peril. He plays the fox with Junior (the figurehead-boss arrangement of 'Meadowlands', the Augustus 'never ate alone' lesson of 'Pax Soprana') and his virtù makes Richie's coup unsellable, but with Richie he seeks love instead of fear, and with Ralph he violates the advice to abstain from subjects' property and women (taking over Pie-O-My and sleeping with his goomah), which ends in Ralph's murder. Fortune, Machiavelli's river, runs through Chris's double-parked car, Janice shooting Richie, Gigi's death on the pishtoon, and the Season Four economic downturn Tony failed to build dykes against.

18.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md

19.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
19.relation: Argues that bracketing his crimes, Tony is an 'ethical manager': against Junior's vanity-driven blunders and Christopher's Scarface-style impulsiveness in 'Meadowlands', Tony shows stakeholder judgment - holding the line on business through Annalisa's sexual provocation in the Naples cave ('Commendatori'), defusing war with Carmine over the Esplanade ('Whitecaps'), and following Melfi's Eldercare advice to give Junior 'the illusion of being in control'. The chapter concedes Tony acts within an egoistic horizon of self, family and crew rather than universal principle, but finds real moral self-restraint in him, invoking Augustine's dictum that 'even robbers take care to maintain peace with their comrades' and Tony's own 'I dunno about morals, but I do got rules'.

20.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
20.relation: Argues Simple Subjectivism ('right for Tony') fails as a reading of the show because it cannot make sense of genuine moral disagreement - Carmela and Tony's adultery battle in 'Whitecaps', Agent Ciccerone versus Tony on extortion - nor ground outrage at the killings of Pussy and the sobbing Matt Bevilaqua. Humean ethical subjectivism, grounded in a common human nature and the sentiment of sympathy (with Berkeley's pin example to explain vice as perception-dependent), fares better: it lets us condemn Tony while explaining his warped sympathy - grieving Pie-O-My more than his human victims - as the product of a mob upbringing that Melfi's alexithymia diagnosis in 'House Arrest' targets.

21.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Argues Tony is a good man and a bad man for the same reason: a moral code of partiality toward family, crew and Italian-Americans ('This family comes before everything else' in 'Fortunate Son', avenging Janice, caring for Livia 'because she's my mother'), whereas morality must ultimately be justified from the impartial point of view (Sidgwick's 'point of view of the universe'). Using the drowning case - save Meadow or two strangers - the chapter shows partiality can receive an impartial justification, then applies this to Dr. Melfi's decision to treat Tony, defensible only while harms to others (her patient's suicide when she is driven into hiding) do not outweigh the good of his treatment.

22.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Answers the title with 'fugheddaboutit' - Carmela is no feminist - but argues she reasons as a Gilligan-style care ethicist. Her moral voice evolves from Church-based justice arguments against Angie's divorce ('Commendatori'), through the justice-tradition confrontation with Dr. Krakower's refusal of 'blood money' ('Second Opinion'), to mature care ethics that balances self with others when she throws Tony out after the Svetlana revelation ('Whitecaps'). Using Noddings on reciprocity and 'total engrossment', the chapter reads the marriage's failure as failed caring, and the Furio romance and the Georgetown ricotta-pie intimidation as care reasoning that defies the submissive female stereotype feminists fear care ethics valorizes.

23.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
23.relation: Argues Tony's self is communitarian - constituted by his roles as father, husband, don and executioner - against the Liberal metaphysics of individualism descending from Descartes's cogito (Livia's 'in the end you die in your own arms') and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract, with the mob boss miscast as a Hobbesian sovereign ('a supreme commander at the top, not the fuckin' Dave Clark Five'). The Naples trip in 'Commendatori' (Paulie discovering he is not really 'Napoletan''), the Columbus Day violence of 'Christopher', and the endless Godfather and Goodfellas mimicry (Christopher's bakery foot-shooting, Tony's Se7en-like murder of Ralphie) show identity as narrative, performed with and through others, not possessed by an isolated self.

25.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
25.relation: Argues the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle - why law-abiding viewers bear a pro-attitude toward Tony while abhorring his real-world counterpart - is genuine, and dismantles three rival explanations: fascination (Richie Aprile is just as oxymoronic yet earns no sympathy), wish fulfillment (Ralph is as incontinent and is hated), and identification (imagining one shares Tony's desires yields absurdities like being jealous of his affair with Valentina). The solution is alliance: within the show's fallen moral world of corrupt cops, blackmailing FBI agents, hypocritical priests and monstrous Livia, Tony is relatively the most moral major character ('I knew his brother; he was worse'), so sympathy for the fictional Tony is consistent with loathing an actual one - and Chase uses our alliance to dramatize the danger of rationalization.

26.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Sopranos and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Argues against Plato's and Tolstoy's worry that art corrupts by infecting audiences with a character's emotions: The Sopranos does get us to identify with a killer (feeling relief when Tony strangles Febby Petrulio in 'College'), and its serial length, psychological intimacy via Melfi's office, and verisimilitude make Tony unusually attractive. But the show supplies alternative moral centers - Melfi's own therapy, the 'House Arrest' shark-and-alexithymia scene, her restraint after her rape in 'Employee of the Month', the 'Funhouse' graduation-versus-crime montage - that let viewers see Tony from outside, so the series invites a complex, reflective moral response rather than imitation and may even be good for us.

27.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
27.relation: Argues Season One is an Aristotelian tragedy: Tony is the 'man in-between' who earns pity and fear, and his tragic flaw is not his sins but his inability to bear his conflicting family roles, manifest in the panic attacks that drive him into therapy. Like Oedipus fleeing Corinth, the cure brings the catastrophe - Livia exposes the therapy to Junior and the hit follows ('Cunnilingus and psychiatry brought us to this') - while the plot maps onto Greek family tragedy, Livia as Medea trying to kill her son and Tony as a failed Orestes. The Green Grove FBI tapes are the recognition scene, the loss of mother and uncle is the reversal, and catharsis is the healthy outward purging of the viewer's own bottled emotion.

29.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
29.relation: Applies Austin's speech-act theory (locution, illocution, perlocution; with Strawson's condition that a listener must recognize the speaker's intention) to the show's language. Analyses include Junior's 'high colonic' insult and 'come heavy' threat in 'Meadowlands', Tony's indirect hit order 'you get him under control?' answered by Gigi's 'with extreme fuckin' prejudice', Tony's conferral of the boss title on Junior, the made-man oath and Paulie's verbal transfer of the sports book in 'Fortunate Son', and Livia's deniable illocutions - advising Junior to tax Hesh, and on the FBI tape permitting (perhaps desiring) Tony's murder - which show how a woman with no power to order exercises power through warning, advising and persuading.

30.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
30.relation: Argues Tony is 'self-blind': against Descartes's claim of infallible self-access and pursuing Socrates's 'know thyself', and using Shoemaker's term, Tony rationally attends to his own mind and still fails to know it. He denies knowing Pussy is a rat despite all the evidence until the 'Funhouse' dead-fish dream tells him 'You knew'; he cannot say whether he foresaw that his 'friendly' loan to Artie would ruin him ('Everybody Hurts'); and he perceives only love for Livia while rage leaks out ('You fucking bitch, that's my mother' in 'I Dream of Jeannie Cusamano'). These cases - with Christopher's unrecognized desire to get caught and Melfi's unnoticed fear of Tony - support the perceptual inner-sense model of self-knowledge over the constitutive model, since brute error about one's own states is possible.

32.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
32.relation: Takes Chase's claim that the show is 'all about people who have made a deal with the Devil' and tours Dante's Inferno to assign Sopranos characters their circles. The goomah arrangement convicts no one of lust because nobody thinks it sinful, but Carmela's knowing complicity ('I have forsaken what is right for what is easy' in 'College') makes her incontinent; the killers fill Circle Seven's boiling blood, with the suicides Vin Makazian and Gloria Trillo among the trees. Fraud is punished below violence, so Silvio the pimp, Janice the lead-cloaked hypocrite, and Hesh the song-thief sink into the Eighth Circle, Melfi faces the false-counselor question via Guido da Montefeltro (absolution does not absolve), Livia and Junior belong in the ninth circle for betraying the heads of the two families, and Tony's 'soldiers don't go to hell' is left for the reader to judge.

33.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
33.relation: Uses the show to argue the problem of evil is evidential rather than logical, and tests each theodicy against Sopranos cases: evil as natural-law by-product (Junior's and Jackie's cancers), punishment for sin (Carmela's cancer scare, Ralph telling Father Phil his hospitalized son is God's payback in 'Whoever Did This'), God's higher morality (rejected as meaningless as 'a triangle with four sides'), long-run goods (Artie's restaurant fire), and character-building (rejected with Melfi's 'How many people have to die for your personal growth?'). The free-will defense also fails - God could have given us Meadow-like dispositions - and Tony's 'You're born to this shit' versus Melfi's insistence on genuine choice dramatizes the debate. The chapter ends with Tony as the Old Testament Yahweh writ small: a jealous, vengeful, tribal ruler whose appeal is no more mysterious than His.

9.title: Act I - Morality, Interpretation, and the Meaning of Life
9.file: ch09 - Act I - Morality, Interpretation, and the Meaning of Life.md

10.title: The Failure of Our Attempts at Meaning
10.file: ch10 - The Failure of Our Attempts at Meaning.md
10.relation: Conard argues that Allen's films converge on one position: life is inherently meaningless because nothing in the universe is permanent, so only something eternal (God) could ground value — and God is a self-deception ('tradition is the illusion of permanence' in Deconstructing Harry; Rabbi Ben's 'blind faith' in Crimes and Misdemeanors). He traces the impermanence argument from Mickey Sachs's mortality panic in Hannah and Her Sisters and young Alvy's dread of the expanding universe in Annie Hall, to Lloyd's 'temporary convulsion' speech in September, Sandy Bates's 'Ozymandias Melancholia' in Stardust Memories, and Louis Levy's suicide. Since real value would require permanence, Conard concludes, Allen's characters' attempts at meaning through romance (Peter's 'I have to sleep alone tonight' in September) and art (Renata's failed faith in posterity in Interiors) are merely distractions and self-deceptions we need 'like we need the air'.

11.title: Why Not to Buy the Porsche
11.file: ch11 - Why Not to Buy the Porsche.md
11.relation: Skoble uses Manhattan's confrontation scene — Isaac telling Yale 'you're too easy on yourself... you'd rather buy the Porsche' over the hominid skeleton — to build an account of integrity as fidelity to correct moral principles, requiring an integrated character in which reason and desire agree. He distinguishes integrity from mere consistency (the 'consistent Nazi') and from stubbornness, and models it on Plato's just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself'. Aristotle's account of habituation defends Isaac's slippery slope: Yale's repeated lies for expediency are forming the kind of character who would inform on friends, so integrity is an objective yardstick of a well-lived life, as Isaac's amends to Tracy at the end confirms.

12.title: From Knowledge to Faith
12.file: ch12 - From Knowledge to Faith.md
12.relation: Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.

13.title: Hope and Despair
13.file: ch13 - Hope and Despair.md
13.relation: Jarvie argues Allen is a 'pragmatic optimist': since dramatizing is not arguing, no character's philosophy (not Sol's 'choose God over truth', not Levy's) can be imputed to Allen, but the ongoing act of filmmaking itself affirms that life is worth continuing. He maps optimism and despair across four films — Mickey's gun and Duck Soup epiphany in Hannah and Her Sisters, the reconstituted couples' self-deceiving rationalizations in Husbands and Wives, Harry's writer's block, and Crimes and Misdemeanors, where Judah literally gets away with murder and Ben's moral-structure faith is shown as naive. Against Sander Lee's hopeful reading of the ending, he develops criteria for interpretation: avoid the biographical fallacy and 'eisegesis', respect authorial statements unless there is overwhelming argument against them.

14.title: Act II - Woody’s Craft
14.file: ch14 - Act II - Woody’s Craft.md

15.title: Interpretive Communities
15.file: ch15 - Interpretive Communities.md
15.relation: Wallace argues Allen's prose is a 'mousetrap' for intellectuals: the dense allusions of 'Sing, You Sacher Tortes', 'The Whore of Mensa', and 'The Kugelmass Episode' invite interpretation, while satires of critics ('Fabrizio's: Criticism and Response', 'The Irish Genius', the Marshall McLuhan scene in Annie Hall) spring on readers who presume to have mastered the text. Using Barthes's 'Death of the Author' (in Allen's persona-shifting essays 'it is the language which speaks, not the author'), Iser's gap-filling implied reader (Allen's non sequiturs make 'the gaps themselves the meaning'), and Fish's 'interpretive communities' (Wallace's own exclusion from Jewish humor like 'No Kaddish for Weinstein'), he concludes Allen demands a 'hermeneutics of modesty' — no single reader or community can exhaust his works.

16.title: Don’t Speak
16.file: ch16 - Don’t Speak.md
16.relation: Holt extracts from Allen's films a theory of aesthetic appreciation as a balance of intellectual and emotional response, neither alone sufficient. Over-intellectualizers fail — Mary's 'marvelous negative capability' patter in Manhattan, Sally dissecting Mahler's Ninth in Husbands and Wives, the McLuhan-scene professor on Fellini, Lester reciting Dickinson by rote — and so do indiscriminate feelers like Dusty, who buys art 'by the yard' in Hannah and Her Sisters. Against skeptics about aesthetic experience he argues all genuine aesthetic experiences are 'resolutive', easing the head/heart conflict Cliff laments, and he reads Allen's terse verdicts ('Great', 'Terrific') through Wittgenstein's Tractatus: 'whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must say little.'

17.title: And There Is No Escape
17.file: ch17 - And There Is No Escape.md
17.relation: Abrams reads Allen through Foucault's panopticon: modern society is unlimited voyeurism in which the medieval God whose 'eyes are on us always' has been replaced by the omniscient gaze of Film — Cliff's exposé documentary forcing Lester to watch his own life in Crimes and Misdemeanors, Tom Baxter stepping off the screen in The Purple Rose of Cairo, and the nested eavesdropping layers of Another Woman, which he counts to infinity via Noël Carroll's 'mass art'. Against Mary Nichols's virtue-ethics reading, he argues Allen's ethics is Nietzschean self-fashioning: Judah lives 'beyond good and evil' where Raskolnikov failed, Allan Felix sheds the Bogart alter ego and 'gives style' to his character in Play It Again, Sam, while Eve in Interiors stages Hegel's master–slave dialectic, the 'master' artist dependent for her identity on those she objectifies.

18.title: “Just What They Say It for I Never Knew”
18.file: ch18 - “Just What They Say It for I Never Knew”.md
18.relation: South argues Allen's signature old recordings from the American songbook are a philosophical device grounded in Aristotle: the Rhetoric's view that emotions carry cognitive orientations that reshape judgment, and the Politics' claim that music forms character, explain why songs comment on the plots they score. He reads Hannah and Her Sisters through 'You Made Me Love You', 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered', and 'I'm in Love Again' — scoring Elliot's inconstancy, Mickey's 'You don't deserve Cole Porter' judgment of Holly, and her growth into someone whose new musical taste signals ethical maturity — and Everyone Says I Love You as a darker cycle where fantasy and finitude ('It's Later Than You Think') drive the compulsion to love again. The happy ending is precisely why Allen called the film a 'cop out': its music says love fades and is out of our control, while the plot pretends otherwise.

19.title: Humor and Philosophy
19.relation: Ascione deploys Schopenhauer's theory of laughter — the sudden, paradoxical subsumption of an object under a heterogeneous concept — as the framework for showing how Annie Hall's gags do philosophical work. The subtitled balcony conversation exposes the self-monitoring deception of new romance, the street-interview 'love fades' scene smuggles in the unpopular thesis that lasting romantic love is mythical (culminating in the dead-shark line), the grammar-school reunion raises questions about what shapes adult character, and the 'dynamite ham' dinner, the pastrami-on-white-with-mayo, and the California scenes diagnose Alvy's own New York provincialism.
