7.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
7.file: ch07 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
7.relation: Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.

8.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
8.file: ch08 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md

9.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
9.relation: McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.

10.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md

11.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Wrathall defends the film's violence by contrasting Fra Angelico's serene Descent from the Cross with Corinth's Red Christ and Gibson's Gethsemane rebuke ('You could not watch even one hour with me'), arguing the gore resists rationalizing Christ's suffering into an economy of exchange, as Camus's Father Paneloux in The Plague insists true faith must not. Drawing on Pascal's instrumental reason, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty, he develops a 'world-disclosive' account of faith: the tall-table scene between Mary and the young carpenter Jesus shows that new practices train new perception, and film reaches the body directly in ways written description cannot. He closes by faulting Gibson for pessimism: Christ's world looks as God-forsaken and demon-haunted as Judas's, closer to Dostoevsky's ascetic Father Ferapont than to a world made new.

12.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.

13.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Taliaferro, writing as a personalist, worries that Gibson's relentless focus on torture eclipses the whole person of Christ: like torture victims losing peripheral vision, viewers lose sight of his teaching, healings, nonviolence, and resurrection, and the satisfaction-theology framing risks relishing redemptive suffering itself. His reconciliation thought-experiment (Patricia's betrayal of Kris and the God-man who resurrects the murdered child) argues that the resurrection, not the passion alone, completes at-one-ment, since no amount of suffering can undo past wrong. He contrasts Gandalf's laughing return in The Return of the King with a Gibson Jesus who could not plausibly laugh after rising, and invokes Scheler's St. Francis, who loves the wholeness behind sickness rather than the sickness, to urge that the film's intensity edges out a life-affirming view of persons as irreducibly valuable in themselves.

14.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Irwin defends the film's violence aesthetically: beauty (Michelangelo's Pietà) distracts from moral truth rather than serving it, and Aristotle's Poetics fits the film neither as tragedy (a flawless Christ cannot fall through hamartia, and a good man's fall from prosperity is 'repulsive', so no catharsis explains why we watch) nor as the Plato-banned spectacle that inflames the passions, since it leaves viewers numb rather than belligerent. Instead he applies Cynthia Freeland's four features of the cinematic sublime, drawn from Burke and Kant: the flogging scenes, the grotesque Satan clutching his deformed child, Judas harried by demon-children to suicide, and even the Aramaic and Latin subtitles produce the pain-pleasure conflict, overwhelming vastness, and jolt from feeling to moral reflection that make the experience sublime. The violence is thus justified as Gibson's deliberate delivery of the sublime, provided viewers leave fear at the gates.

15.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Lawler charges that Gibson's atonement theology, in which the more barbaric the torture the greater the redemption, imprisons Christianity at the stage of Hegel's 'Unhappy Consciousness', where an infinite God is sundered from abject sinful humanity and a priestly mediator is needed. Reading the film through the master-slave dialectic (impotent master Pilate versus the dignified slave Simon of Cyrene; the world of separate egos as Hobbes's war of all against all), he argues that what dies on the cross is the separate ego itself, and that what rises is Geist, the 'I' that is 'We' of the loving human community. Against Tertullian's credo quia absurdum, and using Pascal's 'heart has its reasons' alongside Hegel's dialectical reason, he reads 'you are gods' and the prodigal son as teaching every person's essential divinity, so the film's own art (the Mater Dolorosa, our identification with the flesh-and-blood Jesus) implicitly undermines the separatist theology Gibson intends.

16.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md

17.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
17.relation: Wartenberg recounts a Mount Holyoke panel where a New Testament historian, a scholar of Jewish mysticism, campus ministers, and a film theorist effectively saw different movies, and proposes that the film itself divides into 'The Passion of the Condemnation' (where a humane, tormented Pilate caves to bloodthirsty Jewish crowds, complete with the Matthew 27:25 blood-guilt line left untranslated for American test audiences) and 'The Passion of the Crucifixion' (the two-hour torture that true believers experience as their God's willing sacrifice, overwhelming everything before it). He then explains the split audience through cinema's photographic verisimilitude: just as D.W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation used documentary-style realism to pass Klan apologetics off as history, Gibson's brutally realistic violence lends his slanted, Emmerich-inflected narrative the authority of fact. He rejects the postmodernist consolation that all readings are equally valid, insisting believers were manipulated by the medium's false trustworthiness.

18.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.

19.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
19.relation: Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.

20.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.

21.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md

22.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Irwin takes Pilate's Quid est veritas as a guided tour of theories of truth applied to the film: Gibson's sympathetic Pilate embodies relativism, met with Nietzsche's 'truth is a woman' perspectivism and Baudrillard's postmodern laughter and rejected; Caiaphas and the bad thief demanding Jesus come down from the cross put the correspondence theory to work ('the proof is out there'), though beliefs hang on other beliefs ad infinitum; Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction models the coherence theory, exposed as necessary but not sufficient by Swinburne's case for versus Wells's case against the divinity of Jesus; and Pilate's Barabbas gambit parodies James's pragmatic theory, where working is not enough if there is no corresponding reality. He then retrieves Heidegger's reading of aletheia as uncovering, helped by the Quid est veritas anagram ('Est qui vir adest': it is the man before you) and Gadamer on truth seizing us like beauty, so that Jesus's 'I am the truth' and Claudia's dream-guided warnings point to truth as disclosure. Since disclosure alone cannot decide between inconsistent revealed claims, Irwin ends by leaving the viewer with a leap of faith and a first instinct as final answer.

23.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
23.relation: Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.

24.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.

25.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md

26.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.

27.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
27.relation: Gareth Matthews contrasts Plato's serene Phaedo — Socrates conducting a seminar on immortality, death as the cure for life's ills, 'we owe a cock to Asclepius' — with Gibson's prolonged torture, while noting deep parallels: both men were condemned by large courts on religious charges (impiety, blasphemy) with political subtexts. Socrates in the Apology models facing death through Socratic ignorance ('to fear death is to think oneself wise when one is not'), and Matthews argues Gibson's magnified suffering makes Christ an icon of an atonement nobody could imitate rather than a model for our own deaths; only the Gethsemane prayer and 'why hast thou forsaken me' (read via Cullmann) can actually help a believer face dying.

28.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Bruce Reichenbach reads the film's choreographed pas de deux as three distinct theories of atonement: the conquest dance with Satan in Gethsemane (crushing the serpent of Genesis 3:15, Satan's final scream) enacts the Christus victor view of the Church Fathers; Simon of Cyrene's reluctant co-bearing of the cross illustrates Abelard's moral-influence view, though Gibson shows resilient fortitude rather than the love Abelard's theory requires to transform Simon; and Mary's mirrored 'parallel dance' makes her a co-redemptrix sharing her son's agony. Against this he sets Heidegger — Jesus grasps his death with anticipatory resolve, thrownness, and the 'moment of vision' with Mary, but dies for the Other rather than to authenticate his own life — and faults the film for omitting Anselm's (and Swinburne's) substitutionary atonement entirely: no sin, repentance, reparation, or penance appears, unlike Maximilian Kolbe's real substitution at Auschwitz.

29.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.

30.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md

31.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
31.relation: Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.

32.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
32.file: ch32 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
32.relation: Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.

33.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
33.file: ch33 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
33.relation: Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.

7.title: The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet
7.file: ch07 - The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet.md
7.relation: The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.

8.title: Part I - “May The Force Be with You”
8.file: ch08 - Part I - “May The Force Be with You”.md

9.title: “This One a Long Time Have I Watched”
9.file: ch09 - “This One a Long Time Have I Watched”.md
9.relation: Eberl argues that Anakin and Luke are radically free despite the Chosen One prophecy and Obi-Wan's 'you cannot escape your destiny.' Borrowing Augustine and Aquinas on God's eternity, he holds that foreknowledge (like the Jedi prophecy fulfilled when Vader destroys the Emperor) does not compel events - Anakin's choice makes the prophecy true, not vice versa - and applies Aristotle's tomorrow's-sea-battle to future-contingents like Obi-Wan's self-surrender on the Death Star. Using Locke's locked-room example and Augustine's account of 'inordinate desire,' he concludes that Anakin's fall stems from his own disordered will to control fate ('learn to stop people from dying'), while Han Solo embodies libertarian alternative possibilities ('No mystical energy field controls my destiny').

10.title: “Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”
10.file: ch10 - “Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”.md
10.relation: Stephens reads Yoda as a Stoic sage: Luke's first impressions are blinded by appearance, but Yoda exhibits the Stoic virtues of patience, timeliness, focus on the present, apatheia (freedom from fear, anger, and hate), and ascetic discipline (askesis), living by the dichotomy of control. He reconstructs the contrasting 'logic of the Dark Side' - anger to hatred to aggression to the mastery of others - showing the Emperor as a tyrant who, unlike the self-mastering Stoic (Marcus Aurelius being the counterexample among rulers), seeks to control what is not up to him, so Vader's 'I must obey my master' is servitude to vice. The chapter also marks Stoic limits: the Emperor rightly rejects felt compassion but wrongly refuses beneficence and Stoic cosmopolitanism, and Stoic physicalism cannot accommodate Yoda's 'luminous beings' afterlife.

11.title: “Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”
11.file: ch11 - “Great Warrior Wars Not Make One Great”.md
11.relation: Robinson (a Zen monk) argues the Force is best understood as ch'i and the Jedi path as philosophical Taoism and Zen: the Light and Dark Sides are the yin-yang polarity whose 'balance' Anakin's prophecy restores, and Anakin's fall is the Buddhist three poisons - clinging attachment to his mother and Padme breeding fear, anger, and hate. Yoda's teaching is Zen practice: 'You must unlearn what you have learned' is wu-wei (effortless action), 'Do or do not' rejects the divided mind of trying, and the Dagobah cave parallels the sword master Tesshu's koan insight that the real enemy is one's own mind ('no-enemy'). The chapter also traces Jedi genealogy to Bodhidharma's Shaolin kung-fu, the Korean Hwa Rang and Japanese Sohei warrior monks, and Bushido's samurai code, noting 'Jedi' derives from 'jidai geki'.

12.title: “You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”
12.file: ch12 - “You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”.md
12.relation: Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.

13.title: Part II - “Try Not—Do or Do Not”
13.file: ch13 - Part II - “Try Not—Do or Do Not”.md

14.title: The Jedi Model
14.file: ch14 - The Jedi Model.md
14.relation: Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.

15.title: The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire
15.file: ch15 - The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire.md
15.relation: Brown treats Luke's 'Is the Dark Side stronger?' as the problem of evil: distinguishing natural evils (the wampa, bigger fish) from moral evils (Tarkin destroying Alderaan), he surveys the Platonic craftsman working recalcitrant matter and the Manichean dualism of two gods - the Emperor as would-be 'evil incarnate' - before giving Augustine's answer. On Augustine's free-will defense, no creature is inherently evil; the origin of each moral evil is the creature's own pride and free choice, so Anakin, not the Emperor's seduction, is responsible for his turn ('I'm a Jedi. I know I'm better than this'). The chapter ends on whether evil can ever be finally defeated, arguing the Jedi prophecies of 'balance' fit a world where evil is a permanent possibility that heroism needs.

16.title: Restoring Balance to the Force
16.file: ch16 - Restoring Balance to the Force.md
16.relation: Cooke uncovers an environmental ethic in Star Wars: after surveying anthropocentric resource-management views and Singer's anti-speciesism (Luke blithely shooting womprats, the Geonosian arena's abused beasts), she builds the chapter on Holmes Rolston III's claims that organisms and ecosystems have intrinsic value and that value is systemic and holistic. The 'living Force' - life creates it, midi-chlorians live symbiotically in all cells - makes Jedi training a discipline of respecting nature, exemplified by Yoda's mud hut on Dagobah and the self-sufficient Gungan and Ewok eco-communities that defeat droid armies and stormtroopers. Restoring balance to the Force therefore means restoring symbiotic balance between human culture and the natural world, which the chapter links to Leopold-style land-ethic holism of the biotic community.

17.title: Send in the Clones!
17.relation: Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.

18.title: Part III - “Don’t Call Me a Mindless Philosopher!”
18.file: ch18 - Part III - “Don’t Call Me a Mindless Philosopher!”.md

19.title: Only a Jedi Can Save Us Forgetting and Recollecting
19.file: ch19 - Only a Jedi Can Save Us Forgetting and Recollecting.md
19.relation: Abrams reads the saga through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: the lightsaber Luke learns to feel as an extension of his body is the authentic 'ready-to-hand,' while the Death Star - a massive mechanical eye that enfames Alderaan on its viewscreen before destroying it - embodies the 'present-at-hand' gaze of enframing that converts nature into standing reserve (clone and droid armies, stormtrooper armor). Yoda on Dagobah is perfect attunement, an authentic being-in-the-world who is 'at home' with being, and the Force parallels Heidegger's being: everywhere, easily forgotten. Anakin's slide - slave of Watto, severed hand replaced by cybernetics, final encasement in Vader's armor - is progressive enframing and forgetting of his own being, and Luke's 'the name of your true self... you've only forgotten' is the recollection of being by which the Jedi, not a god, saves us.

20.title: It’s Not Our Lot in Life!
20.file: ch20 - It’s Not Our Lot in Life!.md
20.relation: Arp argues that C-3PO and R2-D2 satisfy the standard functional criteria of personhood - rationality, mental states, language, social relationships, and moral agency - opening with a blind listener who took Threepio's frightened chatter for a man, a Turing-test-style judgment from behavior alone. He catalogues evidence: Threepio's odds-calculating and Wookiee-winning deduction, Artoo's deceptive manipulation of Luke, the droid torture victim's screams at Jabba's palace, and the Chewbacca-Threepio quasi-familial bond on Cloud City. Since droids meet the conditions, their restraining bolts, cantina bans, and forced servitude are slavery, and the Galactic Senate should grant them limited rights - perhaps cheering a droid rebellion against the organic empire - a question the chapter urges on us as robotics approaches Moravec's predictions.

21.title: “May The Force Be with You”
21.file: ch21 - “May The Force Be with You”.md
21.relation: Jones uses the Force's telekinesis (Luke's lightsaber flying to his hand, Yoda raising the X-wing) to probe the metaphysics of causation. Hume shows we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect - only constant conjunction and habit - so Jedi mind-power is no more mysterious than gravity or magnetism; Leibniz's Monadology argues one substance cannot transfer properties to another, so 'how' any cause works is unintelligible; and Hume's problem of induction (will Tatooine's twin suns rise tomorrow? will Vader's officers always choke?) shows law-governed expectations cannot be non-circularly justified. Concurring with Russell that 'cause' is a relic, the chapter concludes the Force qualifies as a kind of cause precisely because our causal concept is too vague to exclude it - and plugs science fiction as a laboratory for sharpening concepts.

22.title: The Force of Love
22.file: ch22 - The Force of Love.md
22.relation: Lawler identifies Hegel's Absolute Spirit with the Force: Hegel's distillation of religious history - divine nature (the Ewoks worshipping C-3PO), the Roman Empire's transcendent Unhappy Consciousness, and Christianity's Consummate Religion - maps onto the saga's movement, with Anakin's virgin birth, prophecy, fall, and Calvary-like redemption fulfilling the pattern differently from the sinless Savior. The Dark Side is the separate ego asserting 'I' against 'We' (Hobbes's war of all against all culminating in the Emperor), and sin is the belief that one is an isolated individual. Against the Jedi's Stoic detachment (Epictetus), the chapter uses Diotima's ladder of love from Plato's Symposium and Hegel's Faust to argue that only passionate, attached love - Anakin's for Padme and Luke's for his father - descends into darkness and brings the Spirit's balance, so 'the Force is with us.'

23.title: Part IV - “There’s Always a Bigger Fish”
23.file: ch23 - Part IV - “There’s Always a Bigger Fish”.md

24.title: An Empire of Fear and Trembling
24.file: ch24 - An Empire of Fear and Trembling.md
24.relation: Cameron reads the Emperor's dominion through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and struggle for recognition: fear is the Empire's currency, from Alderaan's destruction as visible demonstration ('fear will keep the local systems in line') to Vader's deliberately undefined threats ('The Emperor is not as forgiving as I am'), while hatred binds the Sith Master to Maul, Dooku, and Vader. Because the master can never win recognition from an unequal slave, Palpatine's will-to-power rule is a historical dead end, whereas the slave - Anakin laboring in Watto's shop, Luke overcoming his fear in the cave and under Yoda - can transform himself through work and courage. Vader's final turn is thus his achievement of a new self-consciousness, recognizing himself as 'something other than a slave' at the moment Luke's unshakeable faith forces the truth on him.

25.title: Palpatine’s Legacy
25.relation: Decker reconstructs Palpatine's career as a case study in how democracies die: using Aristotle's definition of tyranny and the precedent of Pisistratus and Julius Caesar, he shows Palpatine manufacturing the Separatist threat so the Senate grants him emergency powers - a twist on Machiavelli's loved-versus-feared dictum in which playing the reluctant democrat is itself the means to absolute rule. The Attack of the Clones debate between Anakin ('Someone wise' should make people agree) and Padme becomes a clash between Leo Strauss's philosopher-king ideal of rule by the virtuous few and John Dewey's conception of democracy as a way of life trusting the intelligence of common people, with Rousseau's social contract framing the stakes. The chapter concludes that democratic ends require democratic means and that unaccountable 'watchers' - Straussian statesmen or Anakins - are exactly the path to Empire.

26.title: “Luminous Beings Are We . . . Not This Crude Matter”
26.file: ch26 - “Luminous Beings Are We . . . Not This Crude Matter”.md
26.relation: Donnelly counter-reads The Empire Strikes Back against Aristotle's philosophical realism, in which nature is purposive, form and matter are inseparable, and each person is an irreplaceable primary substance. Lucas 'humanizes technology' - C-3PO reassembled like the Tin Woodsman, AT-ATs as beasts, Han slicing open the tauntaun with a sneer at its flesh, Luke admiring his new bionic hand - blurring Aristotle's art/nature distinction and reducing body to interchangeable machine parts, a Baconian will to power over nature that even Yoda's mind-over-matter training echoes (the chapter opens with Benjamin's remark that the copy eclipses the original). The result, he argues, is dehumanization: preferring the odorless tin heart to creaturely flesh trades the genuinely human for Gulliver's barn of horses.

27.title: “Trust Your Feelings”
27.relation: Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.

28.title: “A New Hope”
28.relation: Long stages William Clifford's ethics of belief against William James's will to believe, with Luke Skywalker as James's exemplar. Clifford's shipowner story condemns faith as 'wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone,' which would convict Luke of immorality when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force; James replies that where a choice is intellectually undecidable and a genuine option - live, forced, and momentous, like Luke's turn to the Jedi life or Obi-Wan's response to Leia's hologram - pragmatic faith is justified and even salvific. Faith can create truths: Han flying into the asteroid field, Luke's unjustified belief that there is good in Vader bringing Anakin back, the author's faith in his students, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s dream - all illustrating 'a new hope.'

29.title: Masters of the Jedi Council
29.file: ch29 - Masters of the Jedi Council.md

5.title: Men in Bright Tights and Wild Fights, Often at Great Heights, and, of Course,
5.file: ch05 - Men in Bright Tights and Wild Fights, Often at Great Heights, and, of Course,.md
5.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the current resurgence of the superhero: Spider-Man's record-breaking opening weekends, 87,000 fans at the San Diego Comicon, and superhero references running through Seinfeld, Scrubs, rock, and rap. It argues that classic superhero stories, like the works of Plato and Aristotle, are here to stay - enduring modern myths that are wildly fun yet thought-provoking, with Superman and Batman now recognized worldwide as cultural icons.

6.title: Superheroes and Philosophy
6.relation: The editors argue that superhero comics, an original American art form like jazz, deserve serious intellectual attention because they dramatize philosophy's deepest questions - ethics, responsibility, justice, personal identity, faith, friendship, and family. They press the point into the near future: genetic engineering and nanotechnology may soon make real the questions comics have long explored, such as whether to genetically supercharge a baby or what to do if you woke up with powers yourself. The volume brings philosophy professors together with comic-book writers and editors to wrestle with these issues.

8.title: Part One - The Image of the Superhero
8.file: ch08 - Part One - The Image of the Superhero.md

9.title: Chapter 1 - The Real Truth about Superman And the Rest of Us, Too
9.file: ch09 - Chapter 1 - The Real Truth about Superman And the Rest of Us, Too.md

10.title: Preparation for a Surprise
10.file: ch10 - Preparation for a Surprise.md

11.title: The One Question I Could Not Answer
11.file: ch11 - The One Question I Could Not Answer.md
11.relation: Comic writer Mark Waid, hired by DC editor Dan DiDio to re-imagine Superman in Superman: Birthright, is stumped by the question 'Why does he do what he does?' He argues that post-9/11 kids see the Big Blue Boy Scout as an ultraconservative protector of a corrupt status quo, making him irrelevant to a generation that knows heroes from metal detectors and assassinated visionaries. Invoking Socrates' claim that the genuine search for wisdom begins with admitting we do not know, Waid resolves to unlearn a lifetime of Superman lore, and locates the key to the character's motivation in Kal-El's utter aloneness: he is the sole survivor of Krypton and 'doesn't belong here'.

12.title: The Need to Belong
12.file: ch12 - The Need to Belong.md
12.relation: Working out Birthright's answer, Waid argues that even the solar-powered Kal-El shares the human need to belong, so he can connect with humanity not by hiding his alien side but by embracing it. Echoing a Marianne Williamson passage about our fear of being 'powerful beyond measure', Waid has Superman wear the S-shield - the banner of his Kryptonian 'tribe' - and use his powers openly, because only by living authentically in service of others does he truly belong. He links this to Aristotle's discovery that happiness is rooted in living with excellence, which Superman 'in his own way' found too.

13.title: The Great Paradox
13.file: ch13 - The Great Paradox.md
13.relation: Waid closes by drawing out the paradox that Superman's shining selflessness is achieved through acting in his own self-interest: in saving others he exercises his distinctive powers and fulfills his authentic destiny, which fulfills him, while embracing his own nature and history puts him in the one activity that most helps others. There is no blanket choice between self and community, he argues - properly fulfilling one's own nature redounds to everyone's benefit - and Superman thereby becomes a mirror for examining the balance of selflessness and self-interest in the reader's own life.

14.title: Chapter 2 - Heroes and Superheroes
14.file: ch14 - Chapter 2 - Heroes and Superheroes.md

15.title: Defining a Hero and a Superhero
15.file: ch15 - Defining a Hero and a Superhero.md
15.relation: Loeb and Morris take on the argument that 'superhero' is an oxymoron - the more super (and invulnerable) a being, the less it risks, so the less heroic it can be, which would disqualify Superman except under Kryptonite. They rebut it by insisting heroism is a moral category: a hero is a person of noble character whose worthy achievements are guided by the good, so a superhero is a person of noble character with superhuman powers or superhumanly developed abilities, which gets Batman and Green Arrow into the fray. They extend heroism to everyday firefighters, nurses, and stay-at-home mothers, and use J. Jonah Jameson's resentment of Spider-Man to show how the hero's sacrifice stands as a standing rebuke to spectators' inertia.

16.title: How to Be a Hero
16.file: ch16 - How to Be a Hero.md
16.relation: Using Superman for All Seasons, the authors argue that Clark's heroic choice required real sacrifice - leaving his family, Smallville, and Lana Lang to serve more people - and that sacrifice and the self-discipline behind it are underappreciated virtues, down payments on great goods attainable no other way, as with Peter Parker and Matt Murdock too. The hero, they say, is a normative concept with a claim on us, and since Plato held that the good is inherently attractive and draws us toward it, well-told superhero stories have genuine moral force, keeping self-discipline, self-sacrifice, and aspiration alive while entertaining us.

17.title: Fear and the Superhero Stories
17.file: ch17 - Fear and the Superhero Stories.md
17.relation: The authors argue superhero stories speak to our fears twice: first by dramatizing external dangers (mad scientists, terrorists, alien menaces), and second by confronting the subtler fear of what using violence will do to our own souls, since habit and a 'rising threshold' of expectations can make once-unthinkable force come to seem necessary. Superheroes like Batman, Spider-Man, Daredevil, and Superman model the answer: they exercise force within strict limits and draw lines they will not cross, fighting evil without becoming evil, and so show that courage, determination, and character can prevail against adversity.

18.title: The Example of the Superhero
18.file: ch18 - The Example of the Superhero.md
18.relation: Quoting Seneca's advice to 'choose for yourself a moral hero' as an ethical pattern and to 'live as if he were watching you', the chapter argues that superheroes can function for us exactly as the Stoic recommended: Superman inspires us, Batman keeps us going when the going is tough, Spider-Man teaches that conscience outranks the crowd's voices, and Daredevil shows that limitations need not hold us back. It closes practically: ask 'What would Superman do?' and go do your version of it.

19.title: Chapter 3 - The Crimson Viper versus the Maniacal Morphing Meme
19.file: ch19 - Chapter 3 - The Crimson Viper versus the Maniacal Morphing Meme.md

20.title: What the Problem Seems to Be
20.file: ch20 - What the Problem Seems to Be.md

21.title: What the Problem Is
21.file: ch21 - What the Problem Is.md
21.relation: In dialogue form, Dennis O'Neil diagnoses the fan's complaint that 'the new Viper sucks' as an attempt to do what Heraclitus said cannot be done - step into the same river twice. He reinforces the point with the I Ching's teaching that things become their opposites (yin into yang, light into darkness) and with Darwin's evolution, arguing that constant change is simply the nature of things, comic-book characters included.

22.title: The One Constant Is Change
22.file: ch22 - The One Constant Is Change.md
22.relation: O'Neil develops two lenses on why the thirty-year-old Crimson Viper cannot stay the same, the first being Jungian archetypes: superheroes are modern incarnations of ancient figures - Superman is, in Jerry Siegel's own words, 'Samson, Hercules, and all the strong men I ever heard of rolled into one - only more so', the Flash a Mercury, Wonder Woman an Amazon, Thor lifted from Norse myth. Myths always mutated as bards adjusted tales to audience feedback around the campfire (Homer included), and modern media markets merely deliver that feedback faster through sales, ratings, and instant web response, so creators reshape characters quickly.

23.title: The Scheme of the Meme
23.file: ch23 - The Scheme of the Meme.md
23.relation: Defining the meme via the OED and Richard Dawkins - a cultural element spread by imitation that mutates like a gene under selection - O'Neil explains why heroes transform: creators get new ideas, markets demand new stories, authors age, new writers arrive, popularity wanes, or an executive has a brainstorm. The evidence ranges over Superman escalating from leaping tall buildings to near-light speed, Batman morphing from 1930s gentleman crime-fighter to Adam West comedian to dark avenger, radio adding Jimmy Olsen and Kryptonite, the Hulk changing color, and Green Lantern changing identity from Alan Scott to Hal Jordan to Kyle Rayner. Gradual change feels organic; the returning fan simply finds the evolved meme unrecognizable.

24.title: What We Want and What We Get
24.file: ch24 - What We Want and What We Get.md
24.relation: O'Neil concludes that fans want writers to 'preserve a part of their childhood', an impossible wish since new stories must change the meme-archetype and somebody will always be outraged. He adds a second Heraclitean twist: the reader has changed too, so you cannot step into the same river twice for two reasons - the Viper is no longer your Viper, and you are no longer his reader. The essay ends with a cosmic flourish about the Viper joining 'the vast, timeless dance of Being', met by the fan's deflating 'Still sucks.'

25.title: Chapter 4 - Superhero Revisionism in Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns
25.file: ch25 - Chapter 4 - Superhero Revisionism in Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns.md

26.title: Crime-Fighters and Vigilantes
26.file: ch26 - Crime-Fighters and Vigilantes.md
26.relation: Skoble frames costumed crime-fighters as vigilantes by definition and tests them against Locke's argument that civil society requires each of us to give up the private right of vengeance to the state - under which superheroes who go looking for trouble are Paul Kersey of Death Wish with a mask. He then reads Miller's The Dark Knight Returns as the first mainstream examination of vigilantism's moral status: Batman tells a congressional committee 'Sure we're criminals... We have to be criminals', breaks laws that shield real criminals, and faces an arrest warrant, TV pundits, and a satirized psychiatrist blaming him for the Joker's crimes.

27.title: Truth, Justice, and the American Way
27.file: ch27 - Truth, Justice, and the American Way.md
27.relation: Contrasting Miller's two icons, Skoble shows Superman becoming a covert government operative on explicitly utilitarian grounds ('I get to save lives - and the media stays quiet'), while Batman insists a badge or flag is neither necessary nor sufficient for justice: 'the world only makes sense when you force it to'. The complications cut both ways - the Sons of the Batman kill indiscriminately in their hero's name, and Batman first regrets not killing the Joker given the hundreds murdered since. Skoble leaves open who is more honest: the vigilante who owns the trade-off, or critics who deplore the protection they depend on.

28.title: A Whole New World
28.relation: Watchmen forces the rethink wholesale by inventing a world where real people donned masks after Superman's 1938 debut, and its heroes are psychologically troubled - Rorschach, driven by the Kitty Genovese murder's thirty-eight silent witnesses, is ruthless yet sincerely committed to justice. Quoting Nietzsche's 'whoever fights monsters' aphorism, Skoble asks whether Rorschach or Batman became monsters, or whether the rest of us are the guilty bystanders; and since Rorschach shows the 'power' to fight crime is a matter of will and choice, Spider-Man's 'great power comes great responsibility' becomes a responsibility that falls on everyone.

29.title: Look On My Works, Ye Mighty
29.file: ch29 - Look On My Works, Ye Mighty.md
29.relation: Ozymandias, Watchmen's smartest human vigilante, kills three million New Yorkers with a staged alien attack to avert nuclear war, and Skoble walks through the question the novel forces: can the end justify the means? The heroes' darkest hour is their acquiescence in his scheme - only Rorschach rejects the utilitarian reasoning ('Never compromise... Evil must be punished') and is killed by Dr. Manhattan to keep the secret. Skoble leaves us asking whether Ozymandias is a misunderstood savior or has 'become a monster', and whether our recoil at his act is moral clarity or weakness.

30.title: Rethinking the Superhero Concept
30.relation: Skoble widens the question to the concept itself: could anyone be trusted as watchman over the world, or is the savior mindset inherently dangerous for a human being to adopt? He reads the embedded Tale of the Black Freighter as the law of unintended consequences - the castaway's vigilante justice destroys the very people he meant to avenge - warning that any hero's limited perspective and fallible beliefs can doom rogue efforts. Moore's move, he argues, is the classic existentialist one of throwing responsibility for meaning and justice back onto ordinary people: if we did our part, no Ozymandias would ever conclude that drastic salvation was needed.

31.title: Who Watches the Watchmen
31.relation: Both novels criminalize independent heroes while co-opting Superman and Dr. Manhattan as state operatives, and Skoble takes up Juvenal's 'Who watches the watchmen?' as a live question of political theory: is the public's resentment of heroes fear (the Comedian's view), envy (Superman's diagnosis), or guilt? He ends by asking whether we should fear unlicensed vigilantes like Batman and Rorschach more than government-owned supermen - and suggests Moore and Miller are making us look into the abyss and use it as a mirror.

32.title: Part Two - The Existential World of the Superhero
32.file: ch32 - Part Two - The Existential World of the Superhero.md

33.title: Chapter 5 - God, the Devil, and Matt Murdock
33.file: ch33 - Chapter 5 - God, the Devil, and Matt Murdock.md

34.title: The Man and His Faith
34.file: ch34 - The Man and His Faith.md
34.relation: Morris argues Daredevil is the rare mainstream hero with a religious interior life: raised nominally Catholic in Hell's Kitchen, his absent mother a nun who calls him 'a servant of God', he prays, thinks in religious categories, and complains to God like King David in the Psalms ('Why do the wicked prosper?'). Distinguishing mere outward religiosity from authentic faith, he proposes his 'Double Power Principle' - whatever has power for ill has equal power for good, religion included - and asks whether faith is blind like Matt Murdock or perceptive like his radar sense: a source of strength or of weakness for a costumed vigilante.

35.title: Faith and Fear
35.relation: Against Quentin Beck's claim that 'a man without fear is a man without faith', Morris argues the fear-based account of religion (Freud's) mistakes superstition for faith: authentic faith is a commitment of the heart rather than intellectual certitude, so the truly fearless are likely people of strong faith, as the martyrs show. He then distinguishes paralyzing self-referential 'fear of' from motivating 'fear that' (better called concern), concluding Daredevil genuinely is the Man Without Fear precisely because his deep-down faithfulness sustains him - he lives 'by faith and not by sight'.

36.title: Daredevil’s Faith as a Source of Strength
36.file: ch36 - Daredevil’s Faith as a Source of Strength.md
36.relation: Testing whether Daredevil's fearlessness is really the vice of rashness, Morris invokes Aristotle's doctrine that every virtue is a mean between two vices, with courage between cowardice and foolhardiness - but since fear is not the only brake on recklessness, prudence can do that work instead, as when Matt calmly backs down from Iron Man's federal authority in Born Again. He concludes that the religious values Matt absorbed - love of neighbor, respect for truth, concern for justice - supply exactly the guidance prudence needs, making faith a distinct form of spiritual strength.

37.title: The Catholic in Spandex
37.relation: Weighing whether Matt Murdock can be a 'good Catholic', Morris catalogs his commandment-keeping and lapses, then argues his real safety net is his mother Maggie's faith: her intercessory prayer over his broken body in Born Again is the force behind his rebirth, on a communitarian view where one person's faith covers another. When Matt's crisis of faith comes in Kevin Smith's Guardian Devil, Maggie's peasant-and-knight fable delivers a version of Pascal's Wager - bet on God, since atheism risks infinite loss for finite gain - and his heart is calmed; Pascal's 'greatness and wretchedness of man' also echoes in Daredevil's own prayer about humanity's 'disparity of magnificence to actions'.

38.title: The Vigilante Man of Faith Hero or Tragic Figure
38.file: ch38 - The Vigilante Man of Faith Hero or Tragic Figure.md
38.relation: Morris answers his title question 'both': Daredevil refuses to kill even Doctor Octopus ('Then I'd be no better than you'), saves the cancer-stricken Bullseye, and tells Typhoid Mary 'You are who you are because of the choices you make', denying that accidents or heritage define a person. To Detective Manolis he gives a law-and-society argument against private killing - 'The moment one man takes another man's life in his own hands, he is rejecting the law... I'm not God - I'm not the law - and I'm not a murderer' - yet his repeated sparing of Bullseye makes him feel complicit in later murders, the tragic cost of his faith, which he nonetheless concludes is strength rather than weakness.

39.title: Chapter 6 - The Power and the Glory
39.file: ch39 - Chapter 6 - The Power and the Glory.md

40.title: From Olympus to Galactus
40.relation: Taliaferro and Lindahl-Urben open with the Greek lesson of Icarus, destroyed by his intoxicated pursuit of glory, and map it onto the Marvel Universe, where a scientific accident made the Fantastic Four 'use their power to help mankind' while their great foes embody a maniacal pursuit of more. The section sets up the two contrasts to come: Dr. Doom, Reed Richards' megalomaniacal classmate, and Galactus, the planet-devourer 'almost beyond good and evil', with the Silver Surfer as his scout.

41.title: A Doomed Pursuit of Power and Glory
41.file: ch41 - A Doomed Pursuit of Power and Glory.md
41.relation: Doom, declaring 'Power has ever been my God', steals the Silver Surfer's cosmic power, and the authors correct Lord Acton: power itself does not corrupt - only the flawed vessel it is poured into, while the uncorrupted are not destroyed by its loss ('Though bereft of my power - I do not crawl!'). The imprisoned Surfer's tranquil equanimity, they argue, is the voice of a Stoic philosopher, and Marvel shares with the best ancient philosophers a faith in a built-in cosmic justice whereby wrongly gotten power destroys its holder - fulfilled when Galactus strips Doom of what was never his.

42.title: Galactus The Power and the Glory
42.file: ch42 - Galactus The Power and the Glory.md
42.relation: Galactus was designed to stand beyond good and evil, yet when the Watcher challenges him he cannot help moralizing, pleading that killing Earth's inhabitants is a merely foreseen and 'regrettable but unavoidable' side effect of his necessary feeding - a move the authors dissect as the same bad rationalization used by greedy executives and corrupt politicians, and one no cosmic being can escape needing. Only when the blind artist Alicia awakens the Surfer's buried compassion, and the Watcher brandishes the Ultimate Nullifier while pleading that humans carry 'the seed of grandeur', does Galactus spare Earth, hailing the 'glint of Glory' in mankind.

43.title: Power and Glory Tests of Virtue
43.file: ch43 - Power and Glory Tests of Virtue.md
43.relation: The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.

44.title: Chapter 7 - Myth, Morality, and the Women of the X-Men
44.file: ch44 - Chapter 7 - Myth, Morality, and the Women of the X-Men.md

45.title: The Demand for Diversity
45.relation: Housel reports film audiences' post-9/11 demand for diverse and female heroes and locates the X-Men - created by Stan Lee in 1963 and almost titled 'The Mutants' - as the comic resource meeting it, richer in strong women than typical superhero teams. She sets up Xavier versus Magneto as mythic duality (good and evil) and introduces Joseph Campbell's three-phase hero cycle of departure, initiation, and return, ending as a 'Master of Two Worlds', as the framework the following sections apply to Storm, Mystique, and Jean Grey.

46.title: The Perfect Storm
46.relation: Storm's journey from being worshipped as a weather goddess in Kenya to joining Xavier's school fits Campbell's heroic cycle, and her bond with the demonic-looking, rosary-carrying Nightcrawler shows strangeness as a bridge to growth - the duality transcended into singularity when she tells him 'I have faith in you'. Housel then grades Storm at Kohlberg's post-conventional level of justice ethics, yet shows her shifting into Gilligan's care ethics when she dashes off to save eight mutant children from a government lab, mastering both 'masculine' justice and 'feminine' care - hence the 'perfect hero'.

47.title: The Shape-Shifting Mystique
47.relation: Mystique, Nightcrawler's abandoned mother, embodies unstable duality - female and male, serpent symbolism, a name rooted in the mystery priesthood - but Housel argues she can never complete the hero cycle because she is a sociopath who abandons her newborn, comas Xavier, impersonates a senator, and joins terrorist attacks. She perverts Kohlberg's rule-governed justice into wicked principles - 'her deeds are rule-governed, but the rules are clearly her own' - and her blanket hatred of humanity ironically betrays the fear and insecurity of a repressed humanity beneath: Storm's perfect anti-hero.

48.title: Phoenix Rising Jean Grey
48.relation: Jean Grey, the self-doubting original X-Man of the Cyclops-Wolverine love triangle, evolves across the films - the phoenix necklace, growing powers, growing confidence - through all three Kohlberg levels to her self-sacrifice that saves the X-Men at the end of X2. Housel rejects reading that act as utilitarian calculation or as the unbalanced self-sacrifice some feminist readings of care ethics would fault: Jean acts not out of duty but out of love and care, beyond the call of duty - what philosophers call supererogation - becoming a female Christ figure whose phoenix image foreshadows resurrection and Campbell's return as 'Master of the Two Worlds'.

49.title: X2, Superhero Myth, Philosophy, and the World
49.file: ch49 - X2, Superhero Myth, Philosophy, and the World.md

50.title: Chapter 8 - Barbara Gordon and Moral Perfectionism
50.file: ch50 - Chapter 8 - Barbara Gordon and Moral Perfectionism.md

51.title: From Librarian to Batgirl to Oracle
51.file: ch51 - From Librarian to Batgirl to Oracle.md
51.relation: South tells Barbara Gordon's two-origin story - librarian turned Batgirl until the Joker's bullet in The Killing Joke, then re-emergent as Oracle, founder of the Birds of Prey - and explains why 'Year One' retellings, which stabilize a character's canon, make such a reading possible. He introduces moral perfectionism as the cluster of themes (the self can become better, exemplars and friends aid the quest, conformity is the danger) found everywhere from Plato's Republic onward wherever narratives trace an individual's moral progress - as Barbara's does.

52.title: Where I Don’t Want to Be
52.file: ch52 - Where I Don’t Want to Be.md
52.relation: South reads Barbara's 'Where I don't want to be' monologue in Batgirl: Year One through Mill's On Liberty passage on people who ask not 'what do I prefer?' but 'what is usually done by persons of my station?' - the pressure to conform Barbara feels as a librarian with a denied police application and a father's expectations. He then argues neither utilitarianism nor Kantianism can guide such a life, since both exclude the question of what I want and who I am becoming; what Barbara needs - and we need - is to make our desires intelligible to ourselves and bridge the gap between who she is and who she wants to be ('Divine my own future... Not a page from someone else's book').

53.title: I Can Become Something More
53.file: ch53 - I Can Become Something More.md
53.relation: Reads Batgirl: Year One as a story of moral perfectionism: Barbara Gordon stumbles into the Batgirl role at a costume ball and resolves that she 'can become something more,' needing Batman as an exemplar in the sense of Nietzsche's 'Schopenhauer as Educator' — not a model to copy but someone farther along who acknowledges the legitimacy of her desire for a higher self. Batman's question 'Why do you want to be one of us?' tests her self-knowledge, and her 'Because I can' wins her a chance; his unmasking at his parents' graves is his acknowledgment of her quest. The chapter stresses that an exemplar's path cannot be duplicated: Barbara's higher self must be rooted in her own unique experience and desire.

54.title: There Is What Could Be
54.file: ch54 - There Is What Could Be.md
54.relation: Argues there is no single final 'best self' in the perfectionist quest: after the Joker shoots Barbara, Oracle: Year One has martial-arts teacher Richard Dragon ask 'Who are you?', and she emerges thinking 'I'm me — more me than I have ever been.' Against the conformity John Stuart Mill warned of, the chapter has Barbara leave Dick Grayson because he has 'managed to turn into Bruce' and keeps 'reminding me of what I once was' — the past acting as a retrograde exemplar and a Millian custom that blocks her next, still-unattained higher self.

55.title: Of Like Minds
55.relation: Concludes the Batgirl study by asking who accompanies Barbara once the exemplar stage is past: friends as equals — Dinah Lance (Black Canary) and Helena Bertinelli (Huntress) — who listen with fresh ears, call her out, and provoke her growth rather than direct her. Barbara's attempt to bench Dinah, and Dinah's response of taking up new training, show friendship as mutual provocation toward a better self, capped by the move to the airborne Aerie One as an image of her 'unattained but attainable self.' Moral perfectionism is offered as a lens through which comics help us calibrate our own progress.

56.title: Chapter 9 - Batman and Friends Aristotle and the Dark Knight’s Inner Circle
56.file: ch56 - Chapter 9 - Batman and Friends Aristotle and the Dark Knight’s Inner Circle.md
56.relation: Opens Matt Morris's chapter by asking whether Batman — more inner-solitary than Spider-Man or Daredevil, whose civilian alter egos enjoy ordinary friendships — could have or be a friend at all. It quotes Ecclesiastes and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics line 'Without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods,' as deployed in Loeb's Hush, to set up the analysis of Batman's inner circle of Robin, Alfred, and the rest.

57.title: From Aristotle to the Bat-Cave
57.file: ch57 - From Aristotle to the Bat-Cave.md
57.relation: Lays out the chapter's analytical tool: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship — utility (mutual practical benefit), pleasure (mutual enjoyment), and complete or virtue friendship between committed, roughly equal good people, 'one soul in two bodies.' Noting that the ancient Greek concept is broader than today's 'friend,' it then turns this threefold taxonomy onto Batman's closest relationships to see whether any rises to the highest form.

58.title: Batman and Robin
58.relation: Applies Aristotle's categories to Batman and Dick Grayson: Robin receives training, gadgets, and a mission (utility) and enjoys the mentorship (pleasure), repaying the huge imbalance with the love and honor Aristotle says the lesser friend owes. Aristotle's claim that the young's pleasure friendships are unstable explains Dick's growth into Nightwing; their later renewed camaraderie as near-equals 'moves in the direction of a complete friendship, but never seems to arrive at quite that high a plateau.'

59.title: The Bat, Harvey Dent, and Two-Face
59.file: ch59 - The Bat, Harvey Dent, and Two-Face.md
59.relation: Treats Batman's bond with District Attorney Harvey Dent as a utility friendship built on shared, extralegal zeal for justice — until acid scarring turns Dent into Two-Face. Using Aristotle's rules that a virtue friendship must end with an incurably vicious person but not be cut off rashly, the chapter argues further that even a utility friendship cannot survive one friend's viciousness when the other is virtuous — 'collaboration with corruption corrupts' — so Batman must bury the friendship despite surgery and therapy aimed at restoring the old Dent.

60.title: The Cop and the Vigilante
60.file: ch60 - The Cop and the Vigilante.md
60.relation: Analyzes Batman and Jim Gordon as Aristotle's friendship of utility: the Bat-Signal and police information serve both men's missions, exactly as Bruce's 'I need an inside man' monologue in Batman: Year One intends. The chapter explains why it never deepens into pleasure — Batman's guardedness about his identity and Gordon's doubts about his unpredictability — and shows its fragility: if Batman ever killed, or Gordon had to arrest him, the reciprocity would end. A rebuffed dinner-party invitation dramatizes that they are colleagues 'ultimately no more.'

61.title: Batman and Catwoman
61.relation: Classifies Batman's attraction to Catwoman as Aristotle's friendship of pleasure: they relish their bat-and-cat chases, she is neither his mentee nor his colleague, and Aristotle's view that romances are pleasure friendships fits what they have. The chapter argues her underlying goodness — she does not kill and often abandons thefts that could harm Batman — explains the attraction and why, after her reform into a neighborhood protector, Batman finally trusted her with his identity as Bruce Wayne.

62.title: The Butler and the Man of the Manor
62.file: ch62 - The Butler and the Man of the Manor.md
62.relation: Examines Bruce and Alfred: real mutual utility (Alfred's lifelong service and quasi-parental role against shelter and income), yet Aristotle's requirement of equality blocks complete friendship — Bruce is always the boss and Alfred always the butler, each bound by an overriding sense of mission. The chapter argues any change, Alfred quitting or Bruce dismissing him, would itself be an alienating act of disloyalty, so this closest of relationships is destined never to ascend higher than it stands.

63.title: The Elusiveness of a Complete Friendship
63.file: ch63 - The Elusiveness of a Complete Friendship.md
63.relation: Argues that Batman himself is chiefly responsible for the elusiveness of complete friendship: the promise to his murdered parents consumes the personal investment such friendship needs, so everyone — Gordon, Dent, the Robins, Batgirl, Alfred — must fit into the mission, as his Hush confession to Catwoman ('I am not very good at this. Having friends.') shows. Aristotle's remark that the good man is a friend to himself lets the chapter cast Bruce and Batman as 'one soul in two personae,' the only virtue friendship left to him. It closes as a cautionary tale: a life of mission can cost the balance — and the friendship — that a good and happy life requires.

64.title: Chapter 10 - The Fantastic Four as a Family The Strongest Bond of All
64.file: ch64 - Chapter 10 - The Fantastic Four as a Family The Strongest Bond of All.md
64.relation: Opens Ryall and Tipton's chapter: where most superhero philosophy focuses on the individual choosing to use power for good or evil, Aristotle's insight that we are essentially social creatures directs attention to the philosophically neglected concept of the family. The Fantastic Four are presented as the rare team whose family bonds are as much a part of their story as their adventures.

65.title: The First Family
65.relation: Contrasts the Fantastic Four's forty years of continuity with teams like the JLA and Teen Titans who proclaim 'they're family' yet inevitably drift apart. The chapter locates the difference in the blood-and-marriage core (Johnny, Sue, Reed) plus Ben Grimm, whose only tie is friendship with Reed — a friendship tested from the start because Reed's hubris caused the accident that disfigured Ben.

66.title: Forming Family Bonds
66.relation: Reads the Fantastic Four's origin through Plato and the 1960s space race: Reed's heedless rush to beat the Russians into space embodies Thrasymachus' Republic claim that the drive for power dominates human life, and Sue shames the reluctant Ben into flying the unshielded ship. Socrates' belief that virtue is its own reward frames the cosmic-ray price each pays — powers eerily matching their personalities — until Ben proposes the team mission statement: 'We've gotta use that power to help mankind, right?'

67.title: A Partnership for Living Well
67.file: ch67 - A Partnership for Living Well.md
67.relation: The chapter's core argument: Aristotle's Politics defines a city as 'a partnership for living well,' and the family is the most intimate such partnership — the Fantastic Four exemplify it. Ben's loyalty to the friend who disfigured him, serving as Reed's conscience, is explained through all three Aristotelian friendships: utility (the belonging he finds nowhere else, from Avengers stints to wrestling), pleasure (the sibling-style war with Johnny he secretly enjoys), and complete friendship — strongest between Reed and Ben, inseparable from Reed's guilt over the one miracle he cannot perform: restoring his friend's human form.

68.title: The Family During Turmoil
68.relation: Surveys the team's turmoil — Ben's walkabouts, Johnny's bids for independence, Reed and Sue's marital strife and suburban experiments, Reed's 'for his own good' secrecy about Ben's cure — to argue that members leave and return not from duty but from a mutual affinity: only within the family do they feel complete and develop their potential best. It also honestly flags the family's dysfunction, reading Ben's departures as a child running away from home and his squabbles with Johnny as sibling rivalry for Reed and Sue's parental attention.

69.title: The Ethos of Teamwork
69.relation: Concludes that the Fantastic Four achieve Aristotle's complete friendship and become 'partners for a greater good': unlike Avengers-style teams whose friendships are mainly self-oriented, the Four's bond is unselfish love aiming at the good of the other. The chapter adds that they turn the family's protective instinct outward, so the world's ordinary citizens live like children under their care.

70.title: Chapter 11 - Comic-Book Wisdom
70.relation: Opens Michael Thau's chapter: at a time when wisdom seems to have vanished from the culture, real wisdom can still be found embodied and enacted in superhero comics. The chapter will show comics both reflecting the general skepticism about wisdom and offering flashes of genuine appreciation of what wisdom is.

71.title: Where Has All the Wisdom Gone
71.file: ch71 - Where Has All the Wisdom Gone.md
71.relation: Argues that although 'philosopher' means 'lover of wisdom,' wisdom has all but vanished from everyday talk — surviving mostly as the jab 'wise-guy' — and even from philosophy departments, where colleagues are praised as 'clever' or 'brilliant' but never 'wise.' The chapter proposes tracing wisdom's disappearance through comic books, cultural barometers in which superheroes' stories once gave wisdom a recognized place.

72.title: The Wisdom of Captain Marvel
72.file: ch72 - The Wisdom of Captain Marvel.md
72.relation: Shows how natural it was in 1940 to list the wisdom of Solomon first among Captain Marvel's Shazam-granted powers, then examines Geoff Johns' JSA retelling as the modern 'but': Billy Batson's transformation is purely physical, so Solomon's wisdom becomes an external advising voice — a device the chapter compares to the personified Philosophy who visits Boethius in prison. The Stargirl romance dilemma reveals wisdom's advice to break up with Courtney as designed to preserve its own authority — fitting to an admirer of wisdom, yet reading to modern eyes as the self-interested calculation of a skeptical age.

73.title: Skepticism and Cynicism about Wisdom
73.file: ch73 - Skepticism and Cynicism about Wisdom.md
73.relation: Contrasts Earth X, where Odin's wisdom is exposed as a fraud — a frail human ruling an alien race under false pretenses — with Johns' Captain Marvel, which is skeptical without full cynicism. The chapter defends wisdom's advice to Billy as genuinely wise: the detached, larger-temporal-perspective counsel characteristic of the wise in both Western and Eastern traditions, while conceding that modern readers, unlike those of 1940, can no longer be sure the larger picture should trump Courtney's tears and Billy's present feelings.

74.title: What Wisdom Requires
74.relation: Explains what wisdom demands: subordinating the loud, here-and-now deliverances of the senses and emotions to reason and the larger picture — as in Plato's wise person contemplating the eternal Forms and the Republic's long course of training, the Bhagavad-Gita's detachment, and Stoic meditative practice. It argues experience is nonetheless central (a sixteen-year-old Captain Marvel could not have it), cites Stick's parting from Matt Murdock in Daredevil over uncontrolled emotion, and uses Casablanca to mark the cultural shift that makes us doubt the larger picture's claims.

75.title: Our Problems with Wisdom
75.relation: Diagnoses why we distrust wisdom: unlike the Epicureans, who trained themselves to discern real pleasure beyond immediate sensation — as Spider-Man's self-discipline wins pleasures Peter Parker could not otherwise know — we equate happiness with pleasant sensory experience; and unlike our ancestors, who saw the passions as external forces undermining freedom (Spinoza's bondage of the emotions), we follow Freud's steam-engine model in treating emotional expression as the true self. Material abundance now satisfies the small picture, making skepticism about the larger picture feasible — though, with Socrates, the chapter doubts it has made us any happier.

76.title: Part Three - Superheroes and Moral Duty
76.file: ch76 - Part Three - Superheroes and Moral Duty.md

77.title: Chapter 12 - Why Are Superheroes Good Comics and the Ring of Gyges
77.file: ch77 - Chapter 12 - Why Are Superheroes Good Comics and the Ring of Gyges.md
77.relation: Opens Jeff Brenzel's chapter: despite philosophers' chatter about Nietzsche's superman, brains in vats, and the trans-human future, academic philosophy has ignored superhero comics — to the loss of a self-declared recovering Silver Age Marvel Maniac. He poses the big question that drives the chapter: why would people with such powers keep choosing to do good and fight evil, at great cost to themselves, for so long?

78.title: Refining the Question
