78.relation: Refines the question by discarding the definitional answer: Watchmen's Rorschach (whose problematic vigilante motives are bound up with Batman-style justice) and Dr. Manhattan (whose godlike powers shape an alien, morally distant consciousness), together with the Dark Knight and Kingdom Come portrayals, show that even subversive comics presuppose heroes must choose to be good rather than be good by definition.

79.title: A Genetic Fallacy and Something Too Simple
79.file: ch79 - A Genetic Fallacy and Something Too Simple.md
79.relation: Disposes of the genetic explanation: the 1954 Comics Code mandated that 'good shall triumph over evil,' but since only a receptive audience kept code-conforming heroes commercially alive, the Code cannot explain why we find super-powered people choosing good plausible and appealing. Stan Lee's reduction of every story to good-guy-vs-bad-guy fights is also too simple — Lee's own humanization of the Fantastic Four and Spider-Man, like Spider-Man 2's near-exclusive focus on Peter's motives, forced the 'extraneous' moral issues to center stage.

80.title: The Problem with Origins
80.relation: Argues origin stories function as signs or interpretations of character, not explanations: Bruce Wayne's parents, the Kents' Smallville virtues, and Xavier's gathering of the X-Men inspire but do not determine their choices. Lex Luthor's ludicrous 1960 origin — swearing eternal vengeance on Superboy for accidentally causing his hair loss — is so bad an explanation that it exposes how no single event, in comics or in our confessional talk-show narratives of genetic makeup and upbringing, fixes what we choose to become.

81.title: Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges
81.file: ch81 - Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges.md
81.relation: The chapter's heart: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges and 'harsh view' of human nature — justice as the weak's compact against the strong, a lineage running from Hobbes to Nietzsche — are powerfully denied by superheroes and by Frodo, who resist the power of the ring. Socrates' tripartite soul and justice-as-psychic-harmony are read as preparation for the Republic's real answer, the ascent to the eternal Form of the Good, which the chapter extends through Aristotle's teleology and virtue ethics: super-powered people, denied any standard social role, must wrestle with what their potential is for — from Kingdom Come's retired Superman and Spider-Man 2's Peter Parker to Astro City's Samaritan, with Uncle Ben's 'With great power comes great responsibility' as the upshot.

82.title: Chapter 13 - Why Should Superheroes Be Good Spider-Man, the X-Men, and
82.file: ch82 - Chapter 13 - Why Should Superheroes Be Good Spider-Man, the X-Men, and.md
82.relation: Opens C. Stephen Evans' chapter by retelling the Republic's Ring of Gyges passage (359c-360d) — the shepherd who uses invisibility to seduce the king's wife, murder him, and seize the kingdom — as the archetype against which the question 'Why should superheroes be good?' will be posed through Spider-Man, the X-Men, and Kierkegaard's double danger.

83.title: Plato and the Question of Why We Should Be Good
83.file: ch83 - Plato and the Question of Why We Should Be Good.md
83.relation: Reconstructs Glaucon's challenge from the Republic: with a ring making injustice cost-free, no one would keep hands off others' possessions, and anyone who stayed just would be mocked as 'a great fool' behind our self-protective praise; Socrates must show that the truly just person 'stripped of the seeming' — enduring the lash, the rack, and the cross — lives better than the honored unjust one. The chapter then turns Plato's thought-experiment on comic-book worlds: why should someone with superpowers care about being good?

84.title: Kierkegaard and the Concept of the “Double Danger”
84.file: ch84 - Kierkegaard and the Concept of the “Double Danger”.md
84.relation: Introduces Kierkegaard's Works of Love: called to universal neighbor-love, we face a 'double danger' — first the inner struggle against selfishness and inertia, then, once we make headway, the world's persecution of genuine goodness, as happened to Socrates, Jesus, and (in his lifetime) Martin Luther King. Genuine self-denial means working unselfishly for the good and then 'being abominated almost as a criminal' for it, a theme the chapter finds explored in Busiek and Ross' Marvels — while Superman, with his undoubting character and public acclaim, faces neither danger.

85.title: Spider-Man’s Struggles
85.relation: Shows Spider-Man living both of Kierkegaard's dangers: the first as his love for Mary Jane collides with his vocation — missing her play in Spider-Man 2, then throwing away the costume — though Peter is tempted to be ordinary, never evil, refuting Glaucon's prediction about the powerful. The second appears in J. Jonah Jameson's newsroom, which spins Spider-Man's good deeds into menace, the discomfort with super-powered goodness Kierkegaard predicted ordinary people would feel.

86.title: The X-Men and the Double Danger
86.file: ch86 - The X-Men and the Double Danger.md
86.relation: Applies the double danger to the X-Men: feared and hated as mutants, with Senator Kelly's registration laws disturbingly recalling Nazi measures against Jews, they are split between Xavier's inclusive peace and Magneto's war on humanity — proof the choice of good is not automatic even for them. Wolverine's growth from rage into Xavier's moral community dramatizes the inner first danger, while their persecution despite unconditional, universal neighbor-love dramatizes the second — including the extra resentment earned by demonstrating their persecutors' irrationality.

87.title: Why Are the X-Men Good
87.file: ch87 - Why Are the X-Men Good.md
87.relation: Systematically rejects candidate explanations of the X-Men's goodness: not self-interested calculation (the world's hostility undercuts it, blunting Magneto's argument), not innate constitution (Magneto chose otherwise, and the Cyclops–Wolverine–Jean Grey triangle shows ordinary desires), not fear of punishment, and not Nietzschean pity or herd resentment — the X-Men are the strong and healthy ones. The chapter's positive account: love of the good is learned through relationships with those who are good to us, from Xavier's loving school that gradually transforms Wolverine and Magneto's Nazi-scarred past to Peter Parker's formative upbringing by Uncle Ben and Aunt May.

88.title: Finding a Strong Basis for the Good
88.file: ch88 - Finding a Strong Basis for the Good.md
88.relation: Argues that loving role models give a motivation but not yet a reason to be good, available to everyone: Plato grounds goodness in a universe whose deep character is just — a metaphysical vision Augustine and C.S. Lewis found religiously congenial — while Kierkegaard grounds the duty of neighbor-love in our relationship to the God who created us out of nothing for eternal life, whose love shown in Christ lets even the persecuted face the double danger with hope. The chapter ends by noting the puzzling absence of religion from the X-Men's world: were its homo religiosus inhabitants to ask what universe they inhabit, they might find in loving the neighbor their deepest connection to the One who perfectly loves them.

89.title: Chapter 14 - With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility On the Moral Duties
89.file: ch89 - Chapter 14 - With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility On the Moral Duties.md
89.relation: Opens Christopher Robichaud's chapter with the midpoint of Spider-Man 2: Peter quits, crime in New York rises seventy-five percent, and unable to walk down the street without meeting someone who needs Spider-Man, he asks 'What am I supposed to do?' — the normative question of what duties, if any, come with great power.

90.title: With Great Power Comes—What
90.relation: Turns Uncle Ben's dictum into normative ethics: the question is not how super-powered people do live but how they ought to, whether they have a duty to take up the hero role, and what obligations follow from it. Two 'hobgoblins' — ethical nihilism and ethical relativism — are dismissed as contrary to our ordinary convictions (Mother Teresa's charity objectively good, Hitler's genocide absolutely bad), clearing the ground for utilitarianism.

91.title: Start Stitchin’ That Costume, Bub. Duty Calls
91.file: ch91 - Start Stitchin’ That Costume, Bub. Duty Calls.md
91.relation: Explains Mill-style utilitarianism — rightness fixed entirely by consequences for overall pleasure and pain, counting every sentient being (a cat may enjoy tuna but not Watchmen) — and applies it: Clark Kent must rescue the failing plane over the Daily Planet press conference, and you must give the jeans money to charity. Since adopting a role is obligated whenever it produces the most overall good, anyone with superpowers has a duty to become a superhero, so Peter Parker's misery in Spider-Man 2 is morally beside the point: utilitarianism says he must remain Spider-Man.

92.title: Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day
92.file: ch92 - Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day.md
92.relation: Presses four objections to utilitarianism through superhero cases: a weakened Jean Grey dying to save Juggernaut's bus victims shows utilitarianism obliterates supererogation — she would be blameworthy whichever way she chose; Ares' demand that Wonder Woman kill an innocent girl to avert global biowar forces her against her character; Batman refusing to let an innocent-of-this-crime Joker die in The Joker: Devil's Advocate shows the theory sacrificing justice; and the Green Goblin accidentally doing great good by dragging a would-be mass shooter down Fifth Avenue shows consequences alone cannot make an intended wrong right.

93.title: I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!
93.file: ch93 - I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!.md
93.relation: Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.

94.title: I Fought the Law and the Law Won
94.file: ch94 - I Fought the Law and the Law Won.md
94.relation: Argues that Batman's warrantless raids, intimidation and evidence-free arrests violate negative duties that bind everyone regardless of role, so producing good (the utilitarian reply) cannot justify them, and superpowers earn no legal exemptions that we would deny police. When Spider-Man evades NYPD warrants, the chapter applies Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito that citizens owe the law their obedience even when wrongly accused, though it concedes that keeping a secret identity safe from villains who would torture or kill loved ones can override the duty to submit, a move consistent with non-Kantian nonconsequentialism since Kant could not abide any lie.

95.title: But It’s Just a White Lie!
95.file: ch95 - But It’s Just a White Lie!.md
95.relation: Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.

96.title: Chapter 15 - Why Be a Superhero Why Be Moral
96.file: ch96 - Chapter 15 - Why Be a Superhero Why Be Moral.md

97.title: The Problem for Spider-Man
97.relation: Sets up the chapter's question through the Spider-Man film: after the promoter cheats him, Peter lets the armed robber go with the taunt "I missed the part where that's my problem," and the robber's escape gets Uncle Ben killed. The scene turns Uncle Ben's "with great power comes great responsibility" into the classic question "Why be moral?" — why not use superpowers for "great personal satisfaction," an egoist's super life, when no payoff for virtue is guaranteed.

98.title: Phony Answers
98.relation: Interrogates the tendency to assume the strongest or overriding reasons always favor doing one's moral duty, imagining an all-powerful malevolent deity who eternally torments the virtuous and rewards the wicked to show that moral reasons could fail to be overriding. Whether morality is rational on this score is left as the live question the Spider-Man narrative will be used to answer.

99.title: Reasons to Be Moral
99.relation: Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.

100.title: In It for the Long Run
100.file: ch100 - In It for the Long Run.md
100.relation: Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.

101.title: Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures
101.file: ch101 - Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures.md
101.relation: Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.

102.title: Swinging from One Idea to Another
102.file: ch102 - Swinging from One Idea to Another.md

103.title: Chapter 16 - Superman and Kingdom Come The Surprise of Philosophical Theology
103.file: ch103 - Chapter 16 - Superman and Kingdom Come The Surprise of Philosophical Theology.md
103.relation: Opens the philosophical-theology chapter by mapping Superman onto Christ: Kal-El sent by his father Jor-El from dying Krypton in a rocket parallels Jesus sent by the Father to Bethlehem, both alien saviors raised as small-town boys. It announces eschatology — final things, ultimate outcomes, whether the hope for justice is an empty utopian dream — as the lens through which the graphic novel Kingdom Come will be read.

104.title: The Background of Kingdom Come
104.file: ch104 - The Background of Kingdom Come.md
104.relation: Explains the Kingdom Come title from the Lord's Prayer and the book's Revelation allusions, then recounts its premise: the retired heroes idle while vicious new "heroes" who "no longer fight for the right" run rampant and Batman rules Gotham by fear. Via Maggin's line "The superhero is Everyman," it turns Superman's despair in the Fortress of Solitude into the reader's own predicament when facing pervasive injustice.

105.title: Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture
105.file: ch105 - Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture.md
105.relation: Argues whether Wonder Woman's "must" really binds Superman — whether he is obliged to leave the Fortress and fight again — depends on one's eschatology or big-picture worldview. It contrasts Christian theism's purposeful culmination with naturalism, whose outlook is fixed by Bertrand Russell's "unyielding despair" passage: accidental collocations of atoms, no preservation beyond the grave, and all human achievement buried beneath the debris of a ruined universe, heroism included.

106.title: Gloom, Doom, and Morality
106.relation: Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.

107.title: Worldviews, Values, and Superheroes
107.relation: Argues that in a naturalist universe of particles and force fields nothing grounds objective good and evil, so a defiant Superman who fights evil just because he wants to prizes sympathy while downplaying truth. Wonder Woman's challenge — "Truth and justice" — raises whether they are in league: Socrates and the classic tradition held truth, beauty and goodness are one, while Nietzsche, godfather of postmodernism, snarls that "Truth is ugly," leaving naturalism a dilemma between believing in ultimate justice or accepting that it is an illusion.

108.title: A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics
108.file: ch108 - A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics.md
108.relation: Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.

109.title: Hope and the Human Challenge
109.file: ch109 - Hope and the Human Challenge.md
109.relation: Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.

110.title: Part Four - Identity and Superhero Metaphysics
110.file: ch110 - Part Four - Identity and Superhero Metaphysics.md

111.title: Chapter 17 - Questions of Identity Is the Hulk the Same Person as Bruce Banner
111.file: ch111 - Chapter 17 - Questions of Identity Is the Hulk the Same Person as Bruce Banner.md
111.relation: Frames the chapter with a San Francisco criminal trial in which Bruce Banner's lawyer argues the Hulk — a large green figure — literally was not the same individual who now stands small and pale before the judge. Ruling requires criteria for "continuity of personal identity over time": what makes you the same person today as ten years ago, applied here to whether Banner should answer for the Hulk's rampage.

112.title: The Hulk’s Bodily Identity
112.relation: Tests the everyday bodily criterion of identity: the Hulk's body contains far more atoms than Banner's, but since all our cells turnover anyway — the "Stan Lee Schooner" has every part replaced yet stays the same boat, the Ship of Theseus problem — and the organ-donor case of "Herb Trimpe" shows a body with greater physical continuity to Kinghorn than to its owner, bodily continuity cannot be what personal identity consists in.

113.title: The Mental Realm of the Hulk
113.file: ch113 - The Mental Realm of the Hulk.md
113.relation: Applies Locke's memory theory: the shape-shifting Martian Manhunter and the irradiated Fantastic Four stay the same people through mental continuity, and the early comics' Banner-minded Hulk meets Locke's criterion — but the later "Hulk smash!" Hulk, who recognizes Betty Ross yet lacks Banner's memories, fails it. The chapter then breaks the criterion itself with Reid's brave-officer objection (the general both is and is not the flogged boy), Alzheimer's and Doc Ock's amnesia attack on Spider-Man, and the circularity of distinguishing genuine from false memory (the deluded fan who "remembers" starring in Adventures of Superman).

114.title: A Causal Account of the Hulk’s Identity
114.file: ch114 - A Causal Account of the Hulk’s Identity.md
114.relation: Proposes that the Hulk is Banner because Banner "Hulks out" — the monster state develops causally from Banner's body and mind through radiation, danger and anger, rather than one person being swapped for another. But a mad scientist's cloning accident that splits Banner into two simultaneous rampaging Hulks breaks the account, since both would be causally derived from Bruce yet could not both be the one person — the fission-style counterexample that afflicts every theory so far.

115.title: Is There No Way to Tell
115.file: ch115 - Is There No Way to Tell.md
115.relation: Presents Derek Parfit's challenge to the whole enterprise: just as there need be no answer to whether a repaired machine is "the same" machine, Parfit's divided-brain case — each half housed in a new body — suggests a person can "survive as two different people without implying that I am these people," so identity questions may lack answers. Kinghorn resists the leap: difficulty finding the truth does not show there is none.

116.title: The Hulk’s Relational Identity
116.relation: Defends a relational account: a person's identity persists through continuing relationships with others (like a marriage or a corporation), against our post-Enlightenment fixation on private attributes. Objections — severed relationships, the castaway, others' biased projections — are answered by positing a God who relates to every person without distortion and guarantees each identity, and who, since divine power cannot do the logically impossible, could not make Banner identical with two numerically distinct Hulks at once.

117.title: What Should We Conclude
117.relation: Renders the verdict in the Banner trial: Bruce is the Hulk, because their relationships continue — when David Banner phones to say Betty Ross will be eliminated, Bruce forms the protective intention the Hulk then executes by destroying the three mutant poodles, and Betty, David and General Ross all relate to the Hulk as Bruce. Physical, mental and causal indicators are mere cues to the deeper continuity of relationships that constitutes who someone is.

118.title: Chapter 18 - Identity Crisis Time Travel and Metaphysics in the DC Multiverse
118.file: ch118 - Chapter 18 - Identity Crisis Time Travel and Metaphysics in the DC Multiverse.md
118.relation: Opens with Sherlock Holmes continuity errors — Watson's war wound migrating from shoulder to leg — and Conan Doyle's forced resurrection of Holmes, defining "corrections": later installments that change what is true of earlier ones. Unlike the finished Holmes serial, comics permit genuine correction across different authors, which is the machinery behind the retcons Crisis on Infinite Earths performs.

119.title: The DC Comics Multiverse
119.relation: Recounts how DC resolved its Silver Age continuity mess: rather than treat Jay Garrick's adventures as a fiction-within-a-fiction, Flash #123 has Barry Allen cross into Earth-2 and meet Garrick — and one cannot meet a merely fictional character — so the multiverse is born. As alternative histories multiplied and heroes routinely world-hopped, the only correction strategy left was postulating yet another world, setting up 1985's Crisis.

120.title: Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds
120.file: ch120 - Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds.md
120.relation: Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.

121.title: Time Travel and Wishful Thinking
121.file: ch121 - Time Travel and Wishful Thinking.md
121.relation: Distinguishes changing the past from affecting it: a fan killing Marv Wolfman in 1984 contradicts what happened, while Superboy #85's failed rescue of Lincoln — Superboy immobilized by time-traveling Lex Luthor's red Kryptonite, so Booth shoots on schedule — is coherent because Luthor only "helped make history." Crisis instead rewrites cosmic history wholesale, and Hanley notes the irony that time-travel theorists usually save coherence precisely by postulating multiple timelines: travelers don't change the world, they change worlds.

122.title: More Things in Heaven and Earth
122.file: ch122 - More Things in Heaven and Earth.md
122.relation: Surveys real multiverse arguments: the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds reading of quantum mechanics, fine-tuning explained by every possible initial condition existing somewhere rather than by God, and David Lewis's modal realism, on which every way the world could have been is a causally isolated world — it was possible to write a shorter chapter because in some world Hanley did. Tegmark's physics multiverses round out the menu before the question: does any of this fit Crisis?

123.title: A Multiversity
123.relation: Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.

124.title: Does Anything Change, or Not
124.file: ch124 - Does Anything Change, or Not.md
124.relation: Argues the superhistory picture still under-delivers: Joe only exchanges histories rather than making Crisis never exist, and the Anti-Monitor may well live on in the not-quite-native hyperhistory. What Crisis's writers really envisaged — Wonder Woman de-aging out of existence to be reborn with a different life — is "dynamic change," making it so no history contains the event, and that, Hanley says, is incoherent.

125.title: Identity in Crisis
125.relation: Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.

126.title: Endurantist Past-Changing
126.relation: Chases the endurantist bullet: if one thing can differ across timelines, one and the same timeline can exist differently in different hyperhistories, letting Joe's murder of Wolfman make 1984 "not the way he remembers it." Yet even this yields only switching, not the dynamic change Crisis dramatizes, so the six-dimensional cosmos stands; Hanley closes with Wolfman's own secret plot device for bringing back the killed Barry Allen Flash.

127.title: Chapter 19 - What’s Behind the Mask The Secret of Secret Identities
127.file: ch127 - Chapter 19 - What’s Behind the Mask The Secret of Secret Identities.md
127.relation: Opens with the Lone Ranger, Zorro and the Princess Bride's masked heroes to ask why superheroes wear masks at all — Tom Morris noting the little raccoon masks fool no one at the office. The puzzle of what the point of disguise could be for heroes doing only admired, nonlethal good deeds sets up the more generic phenomenon of dual identity to be analyzed.

128.title: Dual Identities
128.relation: Lists the classic hero/normal identity pairs (Batman/Bruce Wayne, Spider-Man/Peter Parker, plus Woody Allen's joke alias) and separates costume as role-transition — the Fantastic Four's public uniforms, doctors' scrubs, Bob's garage shirt — from costume as tool, Batman's fear-theater aimed at "a superstitious and cowardly lot" and the female heroes' calculated "gawk factor." What most superheroes do is the distinct third thing, masking: personas from the Latin for mask, keeping Peter's Spider-Man and Matt Murdock's Daredevil secret in both directions.

129.title: Keeping Secrets
129.relation: Takes up the objection that secret identities require the deception superheroes condemn, and answers that skillful deception within a legitimate context — quarterback fakes, a painter's perspective tricks — is acceptable, while even a lie bad in itself can be morally right or obligatory when needed to prevent great harm to the innocent. So Spider-Man's secrecy about being Peter Parker is justified, even praiseworthy, because a slipped secret would hand his enemies leverage over Aunt May and his friends.

130.title: Superman’s Interesting Motivation
130.relation: Argues Superman inverts the usual identity rule: Kal-El's powers precede any civilian persona, so Superman is the real identity and Clark Kent the ruse. Drawing on Pascal's point that celebrity otherness is a function of imagination — a movie star at your cafeteria table changes everything — and on Krishna's disguise as Arjuna's chariot driver in the Bhagavad-Gita and Christ's messianic secret, Morris reads Clark Kent not as operational cover but as Superman's quest to live the human condition from within, loved into humanity by the Kents and refusing to be an isolated "Aristotelian God."

131.title: Switching Identities
131.relation: Maps Superman and Batman onto Plato and Aristotle — the otherworldly philosopher of the heavenly Good versus the this-worldly master of logic and applicable science — then argues that Bruce Wayne's years of intentional self-transformation may have swapped the mask, making Batman the core identity and Bruce the disguise. With Mark Waid, he sees Superman inwardly embracing his alien otherness as the path of authenticity, both cases yielding a fused "heterosis" of identities; Aristotle, Pascal and William James back the closing lesson that who we are is a matter of what we repeatedly do, so every mask may eventually become the face.

9.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
9.relation: The editors' introduction argues that dieting — not just food — deserves philosophical attention, and that the Atkins Diet specifically raises 'chewy' questions about how to decide what to eat, what to believe, and whom to believe, precisely because it defies balanced-diet convention and much expert opinion. It opens with Plato's Republic prescription of roasted meats for campaigning guardians (no pots to carry), cites Nietzsche's Ecce Homo and its 'lengthy disquisition' on his own dietary choices as the rare philosophical treatment of diet, and credits Feuerbach with 'Der Mensch ist was er isst' — you are what you eat. It closes by mapping the volume's sixteen essays across Kant, Hume, Nietzsche, Marx, Dewey, environmental and feminist philosophy, critical race theory, and the philosophy of science.

10.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md

11.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'

12.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Framed by The Onion's 'New Nietzschian Diet Lets You Eat Whatever You Fear Most' and its 'Fat is dead' riff on the death of God, Irwin argues via Nietzsche's Ecce Homo that 'small things — nutrition, place, climate' matter more than philosophy usually admits, and that dieting belongs to giving style to one's character: we are both artists and works of art, so a 'sound mind in an Atkins body' is self-creation. Drawing on his own two years on the diet (187 to 165 pounds, steadier mood, lower cholesterol), he contends Atkins fits some constitutions — Schwarzenegger's carnivorous persona — and not others: Tony Soprano, devouring gabagool amid agita and fainting spells, could not do Atkins without ceasing to be who he is. Nietzsche's 'One has to know the size of one's stomach' becomes the rule of dietary self-knowledge.

13.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.

14.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md

15.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.

16.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
16.relation: O'Connell extracts Brillat-Savarin's 1825 anti-flour-and-starch regimen — clear soup without croutons, shun beer, rye over white bread — as a 'proto-Atkins' and reconstructs its real argument: farmers fatten livestock on starches, so by Humean 'species of Analogy' starches fatten humans, from which abstinence from floury foods is 'deduced.' Hume's Enquiry Section IX, 'Of the Reason of Animals,' supplies the philosophical audit, distinguishing relations of ideas from matters of fact and grading the animal-to-human analogical inference as probable at best. The chapter ends with Hume's fork turned on the diet-book shelf: any volume without experiential reasoning concerning matter of fact deserves the flames — 'nothing but sophistry and illusion.'

17.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
17.relation: In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.

18.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md

19.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
19.relation: Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'

20.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.

21.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Womack tests whether Atkins counts as a Kuhnian paradigm shift, using the Ptolemaic-to-Copernican transition as the model: paradigms define which problems matter, normal science accumulates anomalies, and crisis ends in a new paradigm. Measured against the dieting paradigm's own goals, Atkins flunks — its short-term wins fade by twelve months in the JAMA comparison with the Ornish, Zone, and Weight Watchers diets, with 30–50 percent dropout — so the dieting paradigm itself, which treats obesity as an individual plate problem, is the thing in crisis. Her proposed replacement shifts from the individual to the 'toxic food environment': sidewalks, zoning, food advertising rules, and the French Paradox as the existence proof.

22.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md

23.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
23.relation: Bar On examines the Atkins website's country-by-country packaging and asks what kind of commodity the diet is, answering with Marx's Capital: use-value versus exchange-value, money's erasure of qualitative difference (an Atkins cookbook priced like a tub of supplements), and capitalists who produce use-values only as 'material depositories of exchange-value.' Advertising succeeds not by manipulation but because alienated people — labor sold, selves split to fit the job market — already live in exchange relations, and Atkins mediates even the dieter's relation to herself through purchased bars, supplements, and books. Her conclusion: a weight-loss diet only the relatively privileged can afford, in a world where the poor eat carbohydrates because they are cheap, is itself a symptom of the alienation Marx diagnosed.

24.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Wilkerson borrows the social contract tradition — Hobbes's mutual-restraint founding, radicalized by Pateman's sexual contract and Mills's racial contract — to recast antifat bias as a systematic breach of the social contract enforced by medicine (hallway weigh-ins, weight lectures instead of care), employment, transit seating, and TV fat jokes. Against Atkins's medical discourse of the 'obesity epidemic' she assembles Health at Every Size evidence, trans-fat and high-fructose corn syrup data, and the documented health damage of stigma and dieting itself, concluding that Atkins profits from recasting social problems as individual failings. Atkins for Life's success stories (Kerry Feather's volleyball and new husband, Luann Lockhart's proud daughter) are read as testimony that dieting works as ritual self-abasement purchasing group membership — hence Fat Liberation's 'another world is possible.'

25.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Detmer argues moral vegetarianism follows from principles nearly everyone accepts — cruelty, the infliction of unnecessary or disproportionate suffering, is wrong — and that Atkins, which escalates meat eating without being necessary for weight loss, fails both his necessity and proportion tests. Rebutting human superiority, he deploys Rachels's point that no single feature like language is relevant to every difference in treatment and Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', holds factory-farm castration without anesthetic up against the civet-cat musk trade his students already condemn, and answers Narveson's appeal to intuition and the appeal to tradition. Even granting Atkins maximal health benefits, the margin over a well-planned vegetarian diet (Denmark's WWI blockade, the Framingham data) cannot justify the animal suffering, world-hunger, and environmental costs — most of that case drawn from Singer's Animal Liberation.

26.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Cox and Bender subject Atkins to Kant's universal-law formula — could every one of the billion overweight people on earth adopt it? — in a 'factive' thought experiment: a 25 percent rise in animal-protein output, nearly 250 million additional feed-grain acres, overgrazed ranges, and possibly a tenth of the world's remaining forests cleared for pasture. Calling Atkins reductionism's child (a metabolic switch judged on bathroom scales), they use Marx's 'metabolic rift' — soil nutrients shipped to cities, feedlots severing crops from livestock — and the Cartesian body-as-machine (via Federici) to place low-carb's atomized foods (bungalow subs, soy 'mashed potatoes,' pork rinds) as capitalism's latest rupture in the food system. Their verdict: only plant-leaning regimens could survive universalization, and the deeper fix is Wendell Berry's — eating understood as an agricultural act.

27.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md

28.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Bentley argues Atkins 'masculinized' dieting: since meat is coded male (the hunter's large game, yang, 'strong as an ox') and dieting female, a diet whose emblematic meal is steak, bacon, and creamed spinach let men come out of the dieting closet — Terry Free's competitive wager, business-school professors trading weight charts, and half-male Atkins success stories against Jenny Craig's sixteen men. The symbolism runs both ways: women now order steak openly, while 'white trash' foods like pork rinds ($840 million in 2003 sales) gained middle-class respectability, a class crossing she explains through Bourdieu's Distinction — taste, habitus, and cultural capital.

29.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Parasecoli reads the Atkins program through Lacanian psychoanalysis: the mirror stage explains why dieters invest in the 'you in the picture' Atkins asks them to visualize — an ideal-ego built from others' gazes and shifting cultural body standards (Botticelli's Venus to Jennifer Lopez); hunger, which Atkins treats as an uncontrollable instinct, occupies the place of the Real that resists symbolization; and 'carbs are bad' functions as the upholstery nail that stabilizes the whole symbolic food system. Science plays the external authority whose impenetrable rationale licenses the dieter's leap of faith, while the body that will not slim on schedule — 'your body is not a machine' — is the Real breaking back in.

30.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy.md
30.relation: A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.

10.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Jerry Walls's introduction opens with the film Shadowlands (the Oxford dons teasing Lewis about the fur coats in the wardrobe) to present Lewis as a part-time philosopher who taught philosophy at Oxford and presided over the Socratic Club. It previews the questions the Chronicles raise: truth versus illusion, whether might makes right, why be moral, what may be accepted on faith, whether more than one religion could be true, whether time flows differently in different worlds, and whether Eustace could become a dragon and still be the same person. It reassures Narnia fans that the essays enrich rather than ponderously distort ('gas') stories that should first be enjoyed on their own terms.

11.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md

12.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Stephen Webb argues that Lewis gives hearing, not sight, the fundamental role in knowledge: the Dufflepuds choose invisibility over ugliness, the crew in the Dark Island hear nightmares they cannot see, and in The Magician's Nephew Aslan is heard singing before he is seen. Against A.J. Ayer's logical positivism, Webb develops a 'vocative philosophy of sound' in which meaning lives in voices: Jadis's destructive Deplorable Word versus Aslan's world-creating song, Uncle Andrew's tone-deafness to warranted authority, and Shasta in The Horse and His Boy learning who he is from the voice in the dark that answers 'Myself.'

13.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.

14.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Thomas Senor turns the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (lying, mad, or telling the truth) into a general account of when to believe incredible testimony: weigh the testifier's reliability against how well the claim fits your background beliefs. He shows why Lucy's siblings should have believed her second report of Aslan in Prince Caspian, since by then talking animals and a resurrected Lion no longer clashed with what they knew, and then applies the framework to 'Julia's' report of hearing God, arguing that believing, disbelieving, or withholding rationally depends on the hearer's own background commitments. A footnote explains why Hume on miracles does not fit Lucy's case, since she claims no violation of natural law.

15.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.

16.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.

17.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md

18.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.

19.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
19.relation: Devin Brown uses Eustace, who dodges work on Dragon Island until he wakes as a dragon and discovers he would rather be hungry among human friends than comfortable alone, to contrast Epicurean hedonism and Tom Sawyer's work-avoidance with Mill's higher pleasures and the 'Sherlock Holmes philosophy of work.' Weighing Aristotle's contemplative life against Lewis's love of quests, he reads Father Christmas's tailored gifts and 'everyone must do what he can do best' as an Acorn Philosophy of Vocation with a Marxian 'from each according to his ability' echo, condemns wrong livelihoods like Governor Gumpas's slave trade, and closes on leisure and Aristotle's golden mean, which Lewis turns into 'golden extremes.'

20.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.

21.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.

22.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.

23.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
23.relation: Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.

24.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.

25.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Argues that Narnia is 'unfriendly to the feminine' by reading Susan's exclusion from Aslan's country at the end of The Last Battle ('no longer a friend of Narnia', too interested in nylons and invitations) as the fate of the one heroine who stays stereotypically feminine. It shows that the admired girls (Lucy, Aravis, Jill) succeed only by approximating a masculine standard of adventure, applying Beauvoir's point that measuring women against a male norm implies something wrong with femaleness itself. It further traces how evil in Narnia wears a feminine face: the Green Witch seduces Prince Rilian into Underland, the White Witch tempts Edmund and Digory where the girls resist, and the Witch's Lilith/Jinn lineage ties women to the Fall via 'Daughters of Eve'.

26.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md

27.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
27.relation: Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.

28.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Uses Narnia's magical transformations to probe personal identity, starting with the qualitative/numerical identity distinction illustrated by the look-alike twins Shasta and Corin in The Horse and His Boy. Aristotle's essential/accidental properties frame the question of what Eustace can lose and remain Eustace, including turning into a dragon, and Rabadash into a donkey, showing persons are not identical to their bodies. Descartes's soul argument and Locke's memory theory are tested and rejected, the latter because it cannot handle Rilian's enchanted amnesia, Shasta's forgotten infancy, or Susan's disowned memories without circularity. The chapter defends instead a first-person-perspective theory on which a person is constituted by, not identical to, a body, illustrated by the repeatedly repaired Dawn Treader and by the heroes surviving death in The Last Battle as restored points of view.

29.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Reads Eustace, Uncle Andrew, Experiment House, and Miraz's censored Narnia as Lewis's portraits of modern secularism, which treats the world as mere resource and dismisses the transcendent regardless of evidence. It argues that denying intrinsic value collapses into a Nietzschean master morality of power, visible in Uncle Andrew's use of the children as guinea pigs and the Lone Islands' slave trade, and exposes the secular 'conditioner's' self-exemption as a violation of the Principle of Relevant Difference. Against the Green Witch's debunking of Puddleglum's sun and Aslan as copies of a lamp and a cat, it deploys the Platonic-Cartesian copy/original model of ideas to argue transcendent ideas (eternity, perfection, necessary being) cannot be derived from lower material causes, suggesting instead that the material world is the 'shadowland' copy of a divine original.

30.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
30.relation: Starts from Narnia's time discrepancies (hours in the wardrobe, reigns of years that cost seconds in England, 1303 Narnian years in one) and shows Einstein's relativity makes different time frames plausible before admitting science cannot explain Aslan's 'I call all times soon'. It interprets that claim through Boethius's doctrine of God's timelessness, the eternal present embracing all moments as a simultaneous whole, and defends its compatibility with creaturely free choice: not even Aslan can override the Dwarfs' self-imprisoned perception or force Uncle Andrew to hear him. The chapter closes on the end of Narnian time in The Last Battle, Father Time making an end, and Aslan's timeless country as the fuller reality the temporal world shadowed.

31.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md

32.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
32.file: ch32 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
32.relation: Frames the problem of pain with Hume's Dialogues (Demea and Philo) and reconstructs Lewis's answer as played out on Aslan: pain is God's megaphone that rouses Edmund on the Witch's frozen sledge and strips Eustace's dragon skin in the transforming embrace. Suffering also reveals hidden strengths, as when Aslan's pursuit goads Shasta into unexpected courage, modeled on Augustine's reading of the binding of Isaac as teaching Abraham, not God, what Abraham could endure. Aravis's claw wounds are treated as retributive punishment, tear for tear, exactly proportioned to the drugged slave's whipping, which the chapter defends via Lewis's retributivist theory against purely deterrent punishment. Because divine goodness aims at making creatures good rather than merely happy, Aslan can be both good and terrible, 'not a tame lion', since free will cannot be coerced into perfection.

33.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
33.file: ch33 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
33.relation: Argues that Lewis is an inclusivist about salvation, not a universalist or pluralist: Shift and the self-enclosed Dwarfs are lost, and Aslan explicitly denies being one with Tash, yet Emeth's service to Tash is counted by Aslan as service to him ('all find what they truly seek'). Shasta's providential guidance by a lion he has never heard of, and Jill being saved by drinking from the one stream before knowing whose stream it is, illustrate that the water saves, not knowledge about the water. The chapter supports inclusivism over exclusivism with Lewis's Mere Christianity passages, the 'ought implies can' justice argument against condemning those who never heard the gospel, and Rabadash's healing in Tash's own temple as Aslan working through pagan means.

34.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
34.file: ch34 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
34.relation: Reconstructs Narnian atonement as the early Christian Ransom Theory: Digory's confession, remorse, and 'undoing' of his wrong in The Magician's Nephew, and Aslan giving his life as ransom for Edmund against the Witch's Deep Magic claim in The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe, ending with the Deeper Magic that cracks the Stone Table. It answers John Lucas's four objections (literal Satan, Satan's rights, God negotiating with evil, divine deception) by treating evil as self-chosen bondage whose doors are 'locked on the inside', arguing Aslan's sacrificial identification with wrongdoers displays a love that mere omnipotent force could not, and that wrongdoers like the Witch are not owed full disclosure. It also defends mercy's tension with strict justice, via the example of a deserving prisoner mercifully freed, and finds humor rather than crudeness in Peter Lombard's cross-as-mousetrap image.

35.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
35.file: ch35 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
35.relation: Debunks the 'Anscombe legend' that Lewis abandoned rational apologetics for children's stories after his 1948 Socratic Club defeat by Elizabeth Anscombe over the argument that naturalism is self-refuting. It shows Lewis revised and expanded the argument in the 1960 Miracles, incorporating Anscombe's reasons/causes distinction, and kept writing apologetic essays, while the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (liar, lunatic, or truthful) mirrors the Trilemma of Mere Christianity and shows Narnia using logic, not fleeing it. It rejects A.N. Wilson's identification of the Green Witch with Anscombe and argues the Chronicles teach that prudence and faith are compatible virtues: Edmund's rationalizing, Trumpkin's honest skepticism, and Puzzle's blind trust in Shift all show that fideistic faith is a vice, not what Lewis asks of children.

36.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
36.file: ch36 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy.md
36.relation: Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.
