27.title: 16 - Quantitative and Qualitative Change
27.relation: This edited LibriVox podcast transcript catches three volunteers debating free culture: Wittkower argues copyright is an artificial monopoly justified only when printing presses made reproducing texts capital-intensive — now that consumer gear has put industrial-scale production in everyone's basement ('the working man has wrested the means of production from the big man'), a thirteen-year-old should be free to strip vocals and remix her culture. McGaughey's title thesis — cheap technology means a quantitative change becomes a qualitative change, 'which is by the way from Hegel's Logic' — answers Mowatt's deflation that the Internet merely lowers the bar for things you could always have done locally. Connecting Putnam's Bowling Alone decline of social trust to narrow-casting as a way of rebuilding communities of common concern, they hold up LibriVox's 1,668 free public-domain audiobooks (327 days of audio, volunteers on six continents) as a gift-economy counter-model to a culture we only 'rent' as serfs on branded soil.

28.title: Tools Like Us
28.relation: Arnold coins 'podcrastination' — the voluntary suspension of engagement with reality — and tests podcasting against two poles: Adorno's consciousness industry, under which plugging into an administered device is a 'cyborgian opiate' that deepens our thrall (CBS's listener-programmed KYOU station is still 'administrated'), and Postman's warning that 'we are tools of our tools'. The chapter's spine is Enzensberger's 1970 socialist media theory: podcasting fulfills his eight emancipatory criteria — decentralized programming, each receiver a potential transmitter, interaction, feedback, mobilization, political learning, self-organization — and could coordinate 'smart mobs' like the text-messaging crowds that toppled Estrada at Manila's EDSA plaza. Yet the media's potential is betrayed as much as realized — the Abu Ghraib photos and the 'Macaca' video circulated without catalyzing change — so the prediction is that the podcast will be squandered rather than co-opted: the iPod 'is not going to further a cyborg manifesto. It's only going to create a cyborg lament.'

29.title: Unity in Diversity
29.relation: Lombardo asks whether the podcast, born as an unsanctioned side effect users reinvented out of the iPod (as hip hop reinvented the turntable before corporate co-option made it the hegemonic form), can be a public-sphere institution. Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.

30.title: 19 - The Rhodesian Stranger
30.relation: A comic Socratic dialogue, a pastiche of Plato's Phaedrus, in which a time-lost 'Rhodesian Stranger' wanders in mid-conversation to defend reading against Socrates' retelling of the Thamus-and-Thoth myth — writing as inert painting that gives 'the semblance of truth', summed up in the Stranger's quoting his 'fellow Rhodish' philosopher Schopenhauer: thoughts on paper are footprints in the sand, the path seen but not what was seen along the way. Socrates' elenchus (the ship ticket versus the journey, walking beside a friend and turning back to check on him rather than posting signposts) drives the Stranger into inventing a myth in which gods replace abused speech with pea-pods whose planted seeds become pod-casts gathered by pod-catchers — podcasting imagined as friends dialoguing together toward the true and the good. Socrates closes skeptically, doubting that disconnected pod-communication escapes trivia and universal broadcast, but concedes 'surely beauty is as faithful a guide towards the good as is truth.'

6.title: Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH
6.file: ch06 - Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH.md
6.relation: The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'

8.title: Never Underestimate a TV Writer
8.file: ch08 - Never Underestimate a TV Writer.md
8.relation: Cantor argues the TNG episode 'Darmok' dramatizes Wittgenstein's later philosophy of language: Picard first reads Dathon's 'Temba, his arms wide' as naming objects — the Augustinian picture of language Wittgenstein rejects — then realizes on El-Adrel IV that Tamarian utterances mean through their use in a shared activity, as when he and Dathon fight the beast together. The Tamarians speak entirely in citations of their own myths ('Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra', 'Shaka, when the walls fell'), so language is shown to be embedded in a form of life, exactly Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk' problem. The chapter then ties this to E.D. Hirsch's cultural literacy — Troi's 'Juliet on her balcony' and Picard's Gilgamesh story show communication presupposes shared cultural knowledge — and concludes that the erudite writers Menosky and LaZebnik made a genuinely philosophic episode of television.

9.title: “Logic Without Need Is Sterile”
9.relation: Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.

10.title: “All Good Things Must Come to an End”
10.file: ch10 - “All Good Things Must Come to an End”.md
10.relation: Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'

11.title: Meaning The Final Frontier
11.file: ch11 - Meaning The Final Frontier.md
11.relation: Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.

12.title: “Condemned to Be a Member of This Lowest of Species”
12.file: ch12 - “Condemned to Be a Member of This Lowest of Species”.md
12.relation: Arp uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether unlimited power must corrupt the just: Q's career of meddling ('Encounter at Farpoint', 'Q Who?', 'The Q and the Grey') shows the corrupted case, while Riker given Q-powers in 'Hide and Q' helps his friends instead, a counterexample Glaucon can resist by pleading insufficient time. He then explains the Q's misery — Quinn's bored suicidal plea in 'Death Wish' — through the hedonistic paradox, refining it with Mill's distinction between bodily lower pleasures and mental higher ones and Aristotle's account of the lasting pleasure of completed states like beating the ship's computer at chess. The conclusion is that Q's 'condemnation' to mortality in 'Déjà Q' reveals the human condition as enviable: it is precisely our lacking unlimited power, pleasure, and immortality that drives the striving for truth, justice, goodness, and love.

13.title: Starfleet Directive TWO - Go Boldly, Yet Morally Federation Ethics
13.file: ch13 - Starfleet Directive TWO - Go Boldly, Yet Morally Federation Ethics.md

14.title: “Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”
14.file: ch14 - “Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”.md
14.relation: Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.

15.title: “Make It So”
15.file: ch15 - “Make It So”.md
15.relation: Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.

16.title: “I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”
16.file: ch16 - “I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”.md
16.relation: Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.

17.title: “There’s More to Life than Profit”
17.file: ch17 - “There’s More to Life than Profit”.md
17.relation: Held argues business ethics stalls because it begins from capitalism's presuppositions instead of asking what we fundamentally value, staging the impasse as Quark versus Rom and as Friedman's stockholder theory against Freeman's stakeholder theory ('The Dogs of War', Zek's reforms, 'Profit and Lace'). He recovers Aristotle's Politics distinction between economics serving the household's good and chrematistics — money-making as sheer accumulation, embodied in Quark's 'pure profit' embezzlement — and corrects the libertarian caricature of Adam Smith: the invisible hand works only within commutative justice and virtue, markets serving welfare rather than profit. Through Sen's capability approach and Quark's own defense of greed as promoting human development in 'Prophet Motive', the chapter concludes profit is only a means to freedom and well-being — 'there's more to life than profit' — and the Rules of Acquisition themselves must stand before the ethical judge.

19.title: “Obviously, the Borg Can’t Hold Their Liquor”
19.file: ch19 - “Obviously, the Borg Can’t Hold Their Liquor”.md
19.relation: Decker asks 'What's it like to be a Borg?' and tests whether monist metaphysics justify the Collective: Parmenides's changeless, perfect Being matches the Borg's 'bringing them closer to perfection', Spinoza's one substance (God or Nature) makes assimilationist determinism intelligible and finds truth in Seven of Nine's nostalgia for collective harmony, and Hegel's teleological Geist — the whole 'the world, aware of itself' — most closely mirrors the Borg's galactic quest for an Omega-molecule perfection of 'infinite parts functioning as one.' Yet 'I, Borg' shows Hegelian Spirit working through individuals: Hugh's redemption transforms the Enterprise crew's self-understanding, proving nothing is wholly alien and freedom can coexist with collectivity. Via Haraway's cyborgs and against Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance', the chapter concludes the Borg horrify us because the natural/artificial dualism is already obsolete in our technologized lives — 'if we are the Borg, then resistance truly is futile.'

20.title: “Its Continuing Mission”
20.relation: Argues that Star Trek's real subject is Hegelian recognition: a society is worth living in when every member's claims count as reasons and their talents get developed. It reads 'The Measure of a Man' (Data winning legal personhood), 'The Outcast' (Riker defending the J'naii Soren), and DS9's 'Past Tense' Bell Riots as dramas of winning recognition, and maps the Romulan-Reman and Stratos-Troglyte hierarchies onto Hegel's master-slave dialectic, contrasting Descartes's solipsistic cogito with Hegel's claim that self-awareness needs another. Since recognition requires more than non-interference against Locke-style atomism, the Federation's appeal lies in positive liberties — education, open debate, guaranteed basic needs — even though the shows oddly skip elections and democratic politics, a tension the authors flag through Leonard Nimoy's praise of a world with 'no political agenda.'

21.title: Death on Veridian III
21.file: ch21 - Death on Veridian III.md
21.relation: Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.

22.title: “Something to Believe In”
22.file: ch22 - “Something to Believe In”.md
22.relation: Reads Worf's crisis over the clone 'second coming' of Kahless in 'Rightful Heir' as a live, forced, and momentous option in William James's sense, where 'faith creates its own verification.' Peirce's methods of fixing belief — tenacity, authority, and science — explain why Worf cannot accept Koroth's pious fraud once Gowron's DNA test exposes the clone, while Data's own 'leap of faith' in believing he is more than a machine supplies the Jamesian model of believing without evidence. Worf's compromise — telling the Klingon people the truth but installing Kahless-the-clone as spiritual emperor because 'the words are more important than the man' — is offered as pragmatist truth: what works while staying answerable to hard facts.

23.title: “He’s a Cardassian! That’s Reason Enough”
23.file: ch23 - “He’s a Cardassian! That’s Reason Enough”.md
23.relation: Applies Lyotard's differend and agonistics to the Bajor-Cardassia-Federation triangle around DS9, arguing that 'Duet' dramatizes a dispute where the occupation's horrors are unpresentable in any ruling idiom, so labels like 'Cardassian monsters' and 'Bajoran freedom fighters' frame reality to suit the framer. It follows Aamin Marritza's impersonation of Gul Darhe'el — a guilt-wracked file clerk who wants Bajor's trial to force Cardassia to confess — through Kira's shift from vengeance to forgiveness, and his murder by a Bajoran ('He's a Cardassian! That's reason enough') as proof of totalizing injustice. Federation universalism (Sisko's 'In the Pale Moonlight' compromises, Azetbur's 'Homo sapiens only club' jab, Eddington's 'you assimilate people' speech) appears as one more totalizing standard, with DS9's transgressive characters like Garak pointing past the impasse.

25.title: Tomorrow Is Yesterday
25.relation: Uses the Bajoran Prophets, who experience no linear time ('What is this... time?'), to frame a tour of time's metaphysics: Newton's absolute container versus Leibniz's relationism (the incoherence of a 'temporal vacuum'), Augustine's mind-dependent time (illustrated by 'The Inner Light' and O'Brien's implanted prison years in 'Hard Time'), and McTaggart's argument that neither the A-series nor the B-series can account for change, illustrated by Tasha Yar's death in 'Skin of Evil' and Kirk's Liar-paradox victories over Nomad and Norman. The chapter defends the A-series via tense, then weighs presentism — which would make 'Tomorrow Is Yesterday' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' impossible — against eternalism, whose fatalism Data embraces when his severed head turns up in 'Time's Arrow' ('It has occurred. It will occur.'), and which finally makes sense of prophets who see the future in 'Destiny.'

26.title: “I Feel Exactly What You Feel”
26.file: ch26 - “I Feel Exactly What You Feel”.md
26.relation: Runs Star Trek's transporter and android stories as thought experiments on personal identity: the body theory (Kirk rejecting android Korby — 'Dr. Korby was never here' — and Picard telling the resurrected Rishon Uxbridge 'you do not exist'), the brain theory ('Spock's Brain,' Bashir refusing to replace half of Vedek Bareil's brain), and Locke's memory theory as vindicated by the Trill (Lela Dax's 'a person is but the sum of their memories,' the 'Dax' extradition hearing over Curzon's crimes). Riker's transporter double in 'Second Chances' and the Tuvix fusion then break the memory theory through fission and fusion, prompting Parfit's move that psychological continuity, not numerical identity, is what matters in survival. Memory erasure in 'Dagger of the Mind' and Kurn's rebranding after the failed Mauk-to'Vor in 'Sons of Mogh' count as death if we are our memories.

27.title: Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up
27.file: ch27 - Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up.md
27.relation: Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.

28.title: “Logic Is the Beginning of Wisdom . . . Not the End”
28.file: ch28 - “Logic Is the Beginning of Wisdom . . . Not the End”.md
28.relation: Treats Kirk's computer-killing arguments as logic lessons: his valid syllogism forces Nomad to sterilize itself in 'The Changeling,' while the M-5's trial in 'The Ultimate Computer' models inductive hypothesis testing. The Liar paradox ('Everything Harry tells you is a lie' / 'I am lying') crashes Norman in 'I, Mudd' and, via Tarski's T-sentences and the explosion problem, reveals the concept of truth as inconsistent, with three-valued logic offered as a fix that only relocates the paradox. Gödel's incompleteness theorem then grounds the Lucas-Penrose claim that minds outstrip computer programs like Landru — which Putnam's consistency objection rebuts — leaving Searle's point that computers manipulate symbols without understanding them as the residue of Surak's Vulcan logic being the beginning of wisdom, not the end.

7.title: Setting Up the Game
7.relation: Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction: he argues videogames, and the Zelda franchise in particular, deserve philosophical attention, then frames the book's spirit with Plato's Meno.
