8.file: ch08 - Level 1 - Emotion, Experience, and Thought.md

9.title: Evaluating Zelda
9.relation: Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, or care when Tetra's identity is revealed, though we know none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never suspend disbelief enough to call the police), Carroll's thought theory (fear is too fast and too vivid for mere thoughts), and Walton's pretend theory (involuntary pretending and the uniform way all players see the sail break it). Instead he argues for a multi-level mind, modeled on Plato's divided soul in the Republic and Fodor's mental modules: local unconscious appraisals react to the fire as if real, while a global appraisal of reality-status keeps us in our chairs.

10.title: Game versus Place
10.file: ch10 - Game versus Place.md
10.relation: Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warp sacrifices environmental presence for goal-oriented play: the long, uneventful sails where waves, cloud patterns, and quiet soundscapes dominate are precisely when Hyrule feels like a place, and teleporting turns it into a disposable grid of destinations. Drawing on Castells' spaces of flows versus places, Schivelbusch's 'annihilation of space and time' by the railway (the player becomes a 'human parcel'), and de Certeau's opposition between the panoptic map view and the embodied everyday view, he contends the very existence of the warp option colors all distance traveled. Even panoramic pleasures like hang-gliding over Outset Island, he notes, must be balanced against pure map-grid travel.

11.title: End Game
11.file: ch11 - End Game.md
11.relation: Arp and Milarker use Zelda examples to teach informal logic: Rob's 'all gamers are geeks' is a hasty generalization, the argument that the original Zelda is chronologically first commits equivocation (Earth release order is not Hyrule chronology, since Miyamoto named Ocarina of Time earliest), and debates over banning violent games trade in false dilemmas, ad hominem, and slippery slopes. The chapter sets out premises, conclusions, deductive versus inductive arguments, validity and soundness, strength and cogency, with worked examples from Clawshot reasoning to Best Buy Wii lines. Its point is that fallacious reasoning harms real lives, so readers should audit every argument in the book and in the gaming world.

12.title: Level 2 - Dodongo and Death
12.file: ch12 - Level 2 - Dodongo and Death.md

13.title: Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight
13.file: ch13 - Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight.md
13.relation: Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.

14.title: Game Over
14.file: ch14 - Game Over.md
14.relation: Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.

15.title: Level 3 - Don’t Get Manhandled by Manhandla—or . . . Mind-handled
15.file: ch15 - Level 3 - Don’t Get Manhandled by Manhandla—or . . . Mind-handled.md

16.title: Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil
16.file: ch16 - Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil.md
16.relation: Drzaic and Rauch argue Link is 'good by default' because ludus play (rule-bound, goal-directed, winning the designed story) locks the player into the designers' morality, while paidia play, player-invented goals like the Ocarina of Time flying glitch or the Fierce Deity rampage in Majora's Mask, escapes the story's moral frame entirely. They then map this onto Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil: protagonist Link embodies slave morality (reactive, fear-avoiding, pity, patience, restoring the old Hyrule Ganon disturbed), while the elite paidia player is value-creating like the master, honoring power and secrecy (Huizinga) rather than the protagonist's virtue. The chapter concludes that in videogames the good/evil opposition is welded to ludus, and Zelda fans' naughtiness shows play can go beyond good and evil.

17.title: Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the
17.file: ch17 - Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the.md
17.relation: Robison asks how Link stays the same person through Ocarina of Time's child/adult switches, Twilight Princess's wolf form, and Wind Waker's consciousness-projection into seagulls and mages. Physical-continuity views fail because Link's body changes or is left behind; Locke's memory-based psychological continuity fails because adult Link's past hasn't happened yet when he travels back. After a Ship of Theseus variant (Ganon reassembling Tetra's sunken planks) she proposes that in Zelda's stipulative metaphysics, destiny, the goddess-given roles of courage, wisdom, and power, is the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, fitting videogame universes whose metaphysics are fixed by designers.

18.title: Level 4 - The CDi Games Don’t Count! Timelines and Miyamoto
18.file: ch18 - Level 4 - The CDi Games Don’t Count! Timelines and Miyamoto.md

19.title: Putting Together the Triforce
19.relation: Duncan and Gee study the Nintendo NSider forum threads where fans build Zelda timelines, showing that their marshaling of evidence (Ganon's trident, whether the Master Sword is 'legendary' because of an earlier hero or its sage creators, Hyrule's geography as a marker of time) mirrors scientific argumentation. Using Latour and Woolgar's Laboratory Life, they argue that what 'counts' as evidence, even down to excluding the BS Zelda and CD-i games as non-canon, is socially constructed within a community of practice, not value-free data. David Lewis's plurality of worlds supplies the metaphysics for the split-timeline debate after Ocarina of Time, and the chapter concludes that knowledge in general, in labs and in fandoms alike, is constructed through tools, discourse, and interaction.

20.title: Zelda Is a Communication Game!
20.file: ch20 - Zelda Is a Communication Game!.md
20.relation: Johnson argues that because Zelda has no single authorial vision (teams, outside developers, cryptic Aonuma interviews), the timeline is a 'communication game' fans play together. Interpretation follows the hermeneutic circle of Heidegger and Gadamer (parts inform the whole, as when Wind Waker's references to Ganon's earlier attacks make sense of the series), faces Leibnizian underdetermination since infinitely many theories fit the games, and uses Ockham's razor, whose failures (the y=2x formula) show that simplicity is relative to a community's training, as in Wittgenstein's pupil who suddenly counts '1,004, 1,008'. Hence Miyamoto's own claim that Zelda is a communication game: designers supply puzzle pieces, and the fan community creates the meaning.

21.title: Level 5 - Time and Space in Hyrule
21.file: ch21 - Level 5 - Time and Space in Hyrule.md

22.title: The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future
22.file: ch22 - The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future.md
22.relation: Sherlock reads Majora's Mask's repeating three days as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence from The Gay Science, the demon's demand that we affirm the same life 'innumerable times more', but then shows the Ocarina disrupts the mapping: the Inverted Song of Time and Song of Double Time make each cycle a non-repetition, dissolving the recurrence test's existential weight into a new anxiety about fragmented time. Items that survive the reset and rupees banked in Clock Town give time a material value, while the Deku Scrub transformation scene ('You'll stay looking that way forever') is analyzed as uncanny temporality via Freud's Das Unheimliche, with Derrida's claim that there is no non-metaphysical concept of time framing the conclusion that even game time cannot be separated from its representation.

23.title: Hyrule Regained
23.relation: Through an opening dialogue where a Tax Inspector absurdly appears in Level 9, Siabra-Fraile distinguishes physical from logical space in the NES Zelda: obstacles are chains of conditions (locked door needs key, key needs rupees, rupees need octoroks, octoroks need a sword), and this logical distance, not geometry, is what makes the adventure. Sprites mean what you can do with them (a tree burns, a rock explodes; water is 'the thing that blocks movement and holds zolas'), characters and objects combine like words in semantic fields and like words, phrases, and discourse build screens, levels, and the map. The rules that make Hyrule coherent and playable are, in Wittgenstein's sense, a language game woven into an activity or form of life, so Link can finally prove the inspector out of place.

24.title: Level 6 - Treasures of the Hyrulopolis
24.file: ch24 - Level 6 - Treasures of the Hyrulopolis.md

25.title: A Win for Zelda
25.relation: Cuddy argues that Zelda games can genuinely be art by adapting three aesthetic theories: Walton's make-believe account (art styles are rules for how to 'look', and a novice friend who plays A Link to the Past like a shooter is applying the wrong rules), Rosenstein's transparent/translucent/opaque artwork-worlds (Zelda's avatar, music, terrain, and story make it translucent, while Adventure is mere message and Second Life too close to life), and Panofsky's claim that objective properties demand aesthetic experience. The decisive third property is freeplay, gameplay not tied to beating the game, like exploring with the flippers to find the bottle under the bridge. Some games (Tetris, Super Mario Brothers) fail the test, so some videogames are art and some are not.

26.title: Paradise Found
26.file: ch26 - Paradise Found.md
26.relation: Brown reads The Minish Cap's Hyrule as a working utopia: its Royal Family, guards, and market traders loosely realize Plato's Republic classes from Book V onward, but with fluid social boundaries (Zelda wanders the festival unharassed), no slavery, and relaxed state control that Plato's static order lacked. The town matches Aristotle's polis design (walled, defensible, right-sized, river-powered yet self-sufficient), while the surrounding pastoral landscape embodies Kantian disinterested beauty in nature and the Schillerian idea that through beauty we arrive at freedom. Its vague, prophet-free Picori religion of benevolent Christs-in-miniature needs no Kierkegaardian leap of faith, so unlike Hitler's Germany or Stalin's Russia, Hyrule is utopia actually achieved, and explorable, through Link.

27.title: Level 7 - You are Nearing the End of Your Quest . . . Grumble, Grumble . .
27.file: ch27 - Level 7 - You are Nearing the End of Your Quest . . . Grumble, Grumble . ..md

28.title: A Link to the Present
28.file: ch28 - A Link to the Present.md
28.relation: Compagno argues that the word 'I' in Zelda simultaneously names Link, the virtual body, and the player, the invisible will, and builds this into a 'Schopenhauerian Console': as Schopenhauer held, we have freedom of action but not freedom of will, since the decisions of the unknowable will never appear in consciousness (against Descartes' free mind and Dennett's Cartesian theater critique). Kant's transcendental subject, standing at the border of experience, becomes the player's perspective from which Hyrule exists, what Foucault would call an empirical-transcendental doublet. The payoff: Link's quest is fated and scripted, yet the player wills it in a perpetual present, enacting Schopenhauer's lesson that a determined life is still lived as one's own free act.

29.title: Will You Say Yes
29.relation: Bruce finds Nietzsche's eternal return in the NES Zelda's clockless, endlessly restartable structure: the same game recurs every time you press start, yet since the player changes, each playthrough manifests the forces anew, and the demon's question 'do you desire this once more?' becomes 'do you will to play once more?'. Link's growth through eight dungeons to face Ganon is read as will-to-power, personal strength and self-overcoming rather than mere domination, and saying yes to the struggle is amor fati. Against Plato's two-worlds doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly (both Nietzsche's targets), the original Zelda offers no guide, no Bible, and no linear time to a final judgment: this looped world is the only one, so it must be affirmed.

30.title: Level 8 - The Triforce—Need I Say More
30.file: ch30 - Level 8 - The Triforce—Need I Say More.md

31.title: The Golden Power
31.relation: Dugan reads the Triforce through Lacan's psychology of the dyad and the social symbolic: Link is the player's dyadic anchor ('Miyamoto's Framework' avatar, named because he links us to the system), while the gameworld we progressively master and explore is the social symbolic. Each Triforce piece maps onto the triangle: Courage completes the two-way player-Link bond, Power is the sword/bomb/arrow system consummated in the A Link to the Past final battle, and Wisdom is the realization that these tidy symbolic trinities (Father/Son/Holy Ghost, Brahma/Vishnu/Shiva, the three branches of US government) are simplifications. The 'golden power' is seeing that all such systems are representations posing as totality, offering pre-designed, illusory choice, and inferring who designed the games we are in.

32.title: The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
32.file: ch32 - The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore.md
32.relation: Horn argues the three Triforce pieces are morally neutral: by Kant's Groundwork, only the good will that acts from duty (Link never rescues Zelda for a reward) is good without qualification, so courage, wisdom, and power can each serve evil, and the Triforce would have corrupted Zelda or Link too if fortune had dealt it otherwise. Plato's Ring of Gyges and the Glaucon-Socrates debate explain Ganondorf: he chose to lust for power, and his wealth, status, and fear-based honor are hollow because justice is good for its own sake and his soul is out of balance (which is why the Triforce split at his touch in Ocarina of Time). Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then defines proper use: Link's courage between cowardice and rashness (getting the map, compass, and weapon before the boss), Zelda's internalized prudence, and Ganondorf's power in insatiable excess.

34.title: Rescuing Princess Zelda
34.relation: Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.

35.title: Zelda and Reality
35.relation: Havstad and Jahng inventory every Zelda across the series (royal, wise, resolved, foreseeing, yet passive, imprisoned, even turned to stone in The Minish Cap or asleep through all of Adventure of Link) and read the maiden typology through Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman as Idea, modeled on Plato's Forms, gives men a feminine ideal that real women are then judged against, and 'women are not born, but made' explains how femininity is a male-defined myth serving male interests. Zelda is the glorified yet objectified prize whose passivity lets Link's transcendence happen, and Aonuma's 'reality over realism' design philosophy explains why such stereotypes feel true to players. Sheik and Tetra, who act while disguised as (or turned into) something other than the princess, are the promising cracks in the ideal.

36.title: 20 - Getting to Know the World Next Door
36.file: ch36 - 20 - Getting to Know the World Next Door.md
36.relation: This afterword reflects on the vanishing instruction manual and the blurring boundary between game worlds and the real one: yesterday's games needed booklets for Hurricane Kicks, while Wii-era worlds teach themselves through naturalistic movement, so 'learning the game is the same as playing the game'. Ngim argues games were never utopias but gated communities whose very limitations (impassable rivers, knowable boards) define them, and that game structures now leak into everyday life through loyalty points, serious games, and phones as portals. He closes by urging that game studies become its own discipline rather than being fragmented across sociology, philosophy, and computer science.

39.title: The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy
39.file: ch39 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy.md

40.title: The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy
40.file: ch40 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy.md

3.title: The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy
3.file: ch03 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy.md

5.title: Ideas and Images of Oz
5.file: ch05 - Ideas and Images of Oz.md
5.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Oz endures because it is not one story but a shifting plurality of tales (storyteller Chris Chandler's point, likening it to the Iliad), which each reader can enter through any character, from the Lion to, after Gregory Maguire, the Wicked Witch herself. It models the volume's method with a small logical puzzle about 'there's no place like home'—the phrase is negative because Dorothy herself is part of what home means, so Kansas has a new Dorothy—and previews the book's recurring questions: the Yellow Brick Road as a many-meaninged journey metaphor, the virtues of brain, heart, and courage, evil (why must a little girl kill the Witch?), and the reality-status of Oz versus Kansas.

6.title: The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy
6.file: ch06 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy.md

7.title: I - Are You a Good Witch or a Bad Witch
7.file: ch07 - I - Are You a Good Witch or a Bad Witch.md

8.title: There’s No Place Like Home
8.file: ch08 - There’s No Place Like Home.md
8.relation: Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.

9.title: Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz
9.file: ch09 - Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz.md
9.relation: McCall and Auxier use Aristotle's virtue ethics to unpack the Wizard's claim to be 'a good man but a bad wizard' and to argue that no external token—the diploma, heart watch, or medal—can confer virtue, which is cultivated only through practice and experience. Each companion lacks something specific: the Scarecrow the intellectual virtues and phronesis, the Tin Man the feelings and stable states of character that regulate emotion, the Lion the sophrosyne that balances thinking and feeling into courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice. Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, virtue) frame the companions' bond with Dorothy, and MacIntyre's account of virtues internal to practices explains why the Wizard's public recognition still matters. Dorothy herself begins as the child Aristotle says cannot yet be virtuous—fleeing Miss Gulch in Kansas—but by defending Toto against the Lion and leading the quest she grows into a responsible moral agent, which is what her delayed homecoming requires.

10.title: And Your Little Dog Too!
10.file: ch10 - And Your Little Dog Too!.md
10.relation: Altamura and Fritzman argue the film has the tripartite structure of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit: gray Kansas is a partial truth (thesis), 'somewhere over the rainbow' the antithesis, and the synthesis is Dorothy's discovery that the home she yearned for was Kansas all along—a truth that emerges only through misrecognition, which is why Glinda cannot simply tell her the slippers' power. They read 'Over the Rainbow' through Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and side with Hegel's one world against the Kantian two-worlds reading (Kansas as the knowable island, Oz as the unknowable beyond) that they put in the mouths of heckling 'bullies' and detect in Rushdie. Against Rushdie's line that the companions 'already possess what they seek,' they insist the trio really were hollow men who became brainy, tender, and brave through the journey, the Wizard's trinkets supplying Hegelian public recognition. From the Philosophy of History they cast Dorothy as a world-historical individual whose unintentional destruction of both Witches and exposure of the Wizard advances Oz's freedom—Toto's deliberate pulling of the curtain included.

11.title: Dorothy and the Art of War
11.file: ch11 - Dorothy and the Art of War.md
11.relation: The Bells read Baum's book against Bleeding Kansas and John Brown: 1900 readers, they argue, heard 'Kansas' as the slave-or-free question, making Dorothy the Great Emancipator who frees the Munchkins, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Winkies, and finally herself from the Witch's servitude. They pair her with Socrates, recasting the Republic's opening scene at Cephalus's slave-owning mansion (Thrasymachus's 'injustice on a sufficiently large scale' pays) as an abolitionist confrontation, and quoting the Phaedo's claim that philosophy is practicing for death to explain why vastly outnumbered reformers—Socrates, Brown at Harpers Ferry and Osawatomie, Dorothy facing the Witch's forty wolves, forty crows, bee swarms, and Winkie army—do not fear the odds. The shared moral: the love of wisdom, pursued in a community of inquirers, charms away the fear of death, which is why tyrants and slave-owners, whose own best part is enslaved, live in terror and cannot sleep at night.

12.title: Lessons Learned
12.file: ch12 - Lessons Learned.md
12.relation: Curry argues that The Wiz, the all-Black 1978 remake, dramatizes the acquisition of a distinctively Black 'racial virtue'—a habitual excellence defined in quasi-Aristotelian terms and grounded in W.E.B. Du Bois's picture of races as 'vast families' bound by common history and a divinely rooted race feeling (with Alexander Crummell and William H. Ferris as supporting race theorists). Dorothy, a Harlem kindergarten teacher who has never been south of 125th Street, lacks knowledge of self, and each companion personifies a virtue she must claim: the newspaper-stuffed Scarecrow, whose crows' 'crow commandments' and song 'You Can't Win' embody internalized racist miseducation; the Tin Man's capacity for feeling; and Fleetwood Coupe de Ville's courage outside the New York Public Library, glossed through Ferris's call for 'lion-like men.' Evillene's sweatshop creed that 'suffering is food for the soul' personifies the redemptive-suffering myth and failed-integrationism the chapter rejects, while Glinda's 'believe in yourself' and 'A Brand New Day' make honest admittance of racial reality the precondition of 'co-authoring' the world.

13.title: II - If I Only Had a Mind
13.file: ch13 - II - If I Only Had a Mind.md

14.title: Epilog-Rolling
14.file: ch14 - Epilog-Rolling.md
14.relation: Patton turns the Tin Woodman's backstory—the enchanted axe that costs Nick Chopper his legs, arms, torso and heart, then his head, each replaced by the tinsmith—into a cyborg thought experiment about how much of a person can be swapped out before the person is gone. After a framing nod to Plato's Republic on censoring frightening tales (his father's ban on 'mental violence' fantasy), he brings in Derek Parfit: the R-relation, the 'My Division' brain-split, and the Branch-Line teletransportation case are mapped onto the Woodman (including a hypothetical straw-bodied second Nick) to argue that survival gets different answers from first-person and third-person perspectives. The closing wildcat episode, where the tinned Woodman neatly decapitates a wildcat to save a field mouse, is offered as textual evidence that the tin head failed to preserve moral consistency—so the original Nick Chopper is gone for good, and the Scarecrow's shared brain explains why the two friends later refuse to part.

15.title: “Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”
15.file: ch15 - “Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”.md
15.relation: Tschaepe reads Professor Marvel and the Wizard as skilled givers of 'folk explanations'—stories about desires, beliefs, and feelings that work where logical, scientific, or mechanistic explanations fail—because each explanation is fitted to the pragmatic considerations of its audience and problem. With the companions the Wizard works through a failed dualist argument (a brain is not a mind) for the Scarecrow, an abbreviated Stoic ataraxy pitch for the Tin Man, and Aristotle's discretion-is-valor point for the Lion, settling in each case on folk psychology plus a token (Th.D. diploma, heart-shaped clock, Legion of Courage medal) that supplies the recognition actually needed. Dorothy, whose desire for home is real rather than mistaken, gets no folk explanation from anybody: she must combine the heel-tapping instruction with her own articulated desire—'there's no place like home'—which the chapter treats as pragmatically, not logically, effective.

16.title: III - I’ve a Feeling We’re Not in Kansas Anymore
16.file: ch16 - III - I’ve a Feeling We’re Not in Kansas Anymore.md

17.title: The Loneliest Witch
17.relation: Auxier gives three theories of why water melts the Wicked Witch, one for each register of Oz: as dream (Bergson's account of dreams as memory explains the fire/water effect-swap), as Baum's fairytale (Susanne Langer's presentational symbols make dryness-wickedness versus water-as-life the tale's moral physics), and as Gregory Maguire's possible world, where the philosophy of language takes over. He narrates Frege's sense/reference distinction—mayor of the Munchkins—to explain how fiction can support truth and falsity ('Dorothy melts the Witch' true, 'Dorothy tried to melt her' false), then deploys Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment: 'water' in Oz is XYZ while Kansas water is H2O, so Elphaba's word 'water' does not mean what Dorothy's does, and meanings just aren't in the head. Elphaba—the unique being straddling two worlds, killed by H2O she cannot name and terrified by dreams of oceans—is offered as an even stronger argument for Putnam's semantic externalism than Twin Earth's molecule-for-molecule doppelgangers.

18.title: Conscious Unity “There’s No Place Like Home”
18.file: ch18 - Conscious Unity “There’s No Place Like Home”.md
18.relation: McLachlan maps the whole story onto Schelling's romantic eschatology: gray Kansas is the Ungrund, the boring unconscious unity; the tornado (and Dorothy Gale as 'the gale') is the alienating rupture; and 'there's no place like home' is conscious unity regained through love of concrete, limiting others—richer than the unity she left because it now contains real relationships. Each companion's quest begins in egoism (the Scarecrow as an almost perfect Platonist, all disembodied contemplation like the spider-watching Spinoza; the Tin Man's self-loving imperviousness to pain), while evil in Oz—Miss Gulch's totalizing order, the Witches' slave states, the hidden Wizard—is Schelling's second evil: the attempt to control everything and abolish the freedom of others. Against escape-eschatologies (Plato's shadow-world, Bunyan's Pilgrim who flees his family crying 'eternal life,' Dante turning from Beatrice to the divine light), the Schellingian lesson is that even God becomes personal through relation—which is why the Dainty China Princess's refusal to be a mantel ornament marks the exact point of Dorothy's education in love.

19.title: Roll Credits
19.relation: Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.

20.title: Getting to Oz
20.relation: Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.

22.title: Wait, Did I Hit Pause Where’d the Remote Get to . .
22.file: ch22 - Wait, Did I Hit Pause Where’d the Remote Get to . ..md
22.relation: Seng takes up the fan phenomenon of syncing The Wizard of Oz with Pink Floyd's Dark Side of the Moon and tests the three explanations fans offer: authorial intent (rejected on Pink Floyd's own repeated denials), Jungian synchronicity (rejected as needlessly complex, with the L. Frank Baum coat worn by Frank Morgan as the test case), and pure fluke. He argues the symmetries (the cash-register intro of 'Money' as Dorothy enters Technicolor, 'The Great Gig in the Sky' over the cyclone) are neither objective nor mind-created reality, but meanings made by a third factor in the experience: the viewer whose perceptual habits, in Dewey's and Louise Rosenblatt's sense, supply interpretations like reading the color-splash as prosperity or as the cost of Dorothy's lost innocence. Dorothy's own longing for home becomes the emblem of how habit, not reasoning, governs what we perceive and like.

23.title: Nightmares
23.relation: Auxier asks why the flying monkeys and the shriveling feet of the Wicked Witch of the East give children lifelong nightmares, and answers with a phenomenology of three frightening sequences in escalating duration: the instant shriveling shot, the five-minute cyclone (paired with 'The Great Gig in the Sky' in the Dark Side of the Rainbow sync), and the monkey air-raid. Kierkegaard's Concept of Anxiety supplies the depth psychology: innocence is ignorance, and the child's dreaming spirit projects its own nothing outward, fastening fear onto figures like the monkeys (who are, he notes, played by the Munchkin actors themselves). Merleau-Ponty's lived body versus habit body explains the mechanics: cinema seizes the body's usual 'tour of inspection,' Fleming manipulates active and passive synthesis (the scoreless build-up to the window blow, the barely noticed arsenal of weapons in the Haunted Forest, the dimming lights), and children construct a rigid, inescapable habit body within a single viewing, so the nightmare is the monkey inside our own projected world.

24.title: V - No Place Like Home
24.file: ch24 - V - No Place Like Home.md

25.title: Home Again
25.relation: Flamm and Rea read the Oz story as an existential fable of the appearance-reality distinction in human development: children delight in admitted unrealities while adults live by ideals, and Dorothy's growth is learning to trade the one for the other, dramatized in the China Princess scene where Dorothy must abandon her plan to keep the animated figure frozen on Aunt Em's mantel. The Wizard embodies the American humbug in the P.T. Barnum mold, forcing green spectacles on the Emerald City's citizens so the city only appears green, science as technical illusion without deeper ideals, while the silver shoes reveal that the imaginative escape Dorothy sought was hers all along. Her homecoming is therefore bittersweet and existential: she can never return to the Kansas she left, 'but she can return to herself,' carrying the crayon box of self-chosen ideals with which to color her own reality.

26.title: Must I Repeat Myself
26.file: ch26 - Must I Repeat Myself.md
26.relation: Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.

27.title: A Happy Ending
27.relation: Bickham asks why Dorothy is so eager to leave heroic, Technicolor Oz for the gray, childless, Gulch-dominated farm, and whether, like Hamlet's delay, her rash choice can be evaluated as hers rather than her author's. Aristotle's account of the good life as the exercise of our highest capacities, requiring friends and material goods, makes Oz look like the better home for the competent twelve- or thirteen-year-old he takes Dorothy to be, against the hedonisms of Aristippus, Epicurus, and Bentham and Plato's body-denying dualism. But caring about Dorothy first needs defending from the paradox of fiction, which he works through Currie's simulation theory and Walton's make-believe emotions before dissolving the puzzle: storytelling suspends the reign of logic, so wishing Dorothy well is natural. Finally Heidegger's being-toward-death shows 'happily ever after' is impossible anywhere, and he throws the problem to the reader: write a happy ending for Dorothy in Kansas.

28.title: You Can Go Home Again
28.file: ch28 - You Can Go Home Again.md
28.relation: Fortune stages the movie as a morality play between two conceptions of personhood: the Wizard is an atomist, a self-sufficient ball from the Chuck E. Cheese ball pit who is the same humbug in Omaha or Oz and who reduces heart, brains, and courage to a testimonial, a diploma, and a medal, while Dorothy is a relationalist, a pineapple chunk that belongs on one particular pizza, a person constituted by her web of relations to home. 'There's no place like home' is therefore the relationalist's slogan, an acceptance of home for everything it is, good and bad, with Toto's fate still unresolved under Miss Gulch's law. He closes by suggesting the film's delayed television-era triumph is existential nostalgia: modern, rootless, ear-budded Americans keep watching because the relationalist country it mourns is 'what's in our blood.'

29.title: VI - Something Wicked This Way Comes
29.file: ch29 - VI - Something Wicked This Way Comes.md

30.title: Mirror, Mirror
30.relation: Sailors convicts Dorothy of being the stereotypical female of Baum's and Fleming's versions, disowning responsibility for killing both witches and living to please others, then contrasts her with Elphaba of Wicked as a feminist hero who leaves home, protects Animals, and mixes 'hot' male and 'cold' female anger into a single fury. She reads Elphaba's indeterminate gender through Marilyn Frye's point that easily identifiable groups are the easiest to oppress, through de Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but becomes a woman' and Mill's line that the 'nature of women' is an eminently artificial thing. Singer's liberation logic, together with the Wollstonecraft-Taylor 'Vindication of the Rights of Brutes' episode and the ecofeminist link between the oppression of women and animals, is applied to Elphaba's Animal-rights activism and her position as 'neither man nor beast,' before the Witch's mirror recognition of Dorothy forces the author to soften her verdict.

31.title: As Nasty as I Wanna Be
31.file: ch31 - As Nasty as I Wanna Be.md
31.relation: Greene asks whether Maguire's Elphaba is really wicked, first clearing away her reputation (she adopts the 'Wicked Witch' name because 'it liberates you from convention,' echoing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic about the just person with an unjust reputation and vice versa) and then her nature (the midwife-biting birth, green skin, and witchcraft establish no vampire-like evil essence, since Glinda and Nor are good witches). Following Hume's view that morality is not found in the world but in our assessments, he treats wickedness as a matter of performing actions we judge evil, and weighs Elphaba's life under both headings: good intentions with horrific outcomes (the bees that kill the chef, the icicle that kills Manek, Sarima's family executions) and bad intentions with none (her two failed attempts on Madame Morrible). The verdict is deliberately suspended: if she is wicked at all, it can only be through the consequences of her actions.

32.title: Ineptitude or Wickedness
32.relation: Durand begins from Hume's moral sentiments, the way first impressions (Miss Gulch, the farmer-actors, Professor Marvel) fix our judgments, and shows how Wicked delivers the new information that muddies them, relocating villainy from the green Witch to the green Wizard: an alien despot who scorns Oz's communal moral sense ('I am beyond that lisping childish recital of wrongs and rights'), stations an army of observation at the Witch's borders, and schemes to annex Munchkinland after Nessarose's fall. Marx's 'opium of the masses' frames the religion of Frex and Nessarose as the tool that first pacified, then repressed, the Munchkinlanders, while the Wizard's 'reunification' that is really annexation shows imperial ideology at work. Elphaba's own 'wickedness' comes out as habituated vengeance and an embraced reputation, so the title question is whether she is inept rather than evil, 'a bad witch, but not a wicked one,' and no worse than the Wizard who is merely 'a very bad wizard.'

33.title: Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf
33.file: ch33 - Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf.md
33.relation: Auxier tells the history of matriarchy theory from Bachofen onward, whose stages (Tellurian earth-motherhood, lunar water cults, then Dionysian and Apollonian fire clearing the way for patriarchy) were adapted by Nietzsche in The Birth of Tragedy, quoted by Engels, and developed by Jane Ellen Harrison, Jung, and Gimbutas. He then reads Maguire's Oz myths as survivals of that declining matriarchy: the Kumbric Witch as the Tellurian earth stage, Mother Yackle's Philosophy Club as degraded Dionysian rites, the silver slippers as the totality of feminine power, and the Silver-slippers portrait Boq finds as the earth-to-water transition, noting that Plato's victory of reason over myth is what dragged women's traditional authority down with it. The chapter's payoff is its title claim: Elphaba is Virginia Woolf, her Charmed Circle the Bloomsbury Group, her terror of water and fiery, watery death a repetition of Woolf's drowning 'baptism' under patriarchy.

36.title: The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy
36.file: ch36 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy.md

5.title: 1 Step
5.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Radiohead succeeded The Clash as 'the only band that matters' partly for philosophical reasons: rather than stating abstractions, their music points toward analyses of our actual historical situation, showing 'how it should be possible for pop music to incarnate a particular historical situation' (Greif's question). It reads the laser-data 'House of Cards' video as proof that in our world only the underlying data matters, with Radiohead releasing the source code so fans can re-image it themselves. It then previews the volume's encounters: Heidegger's phenomenology and the manipulation of Yorke's voice on Kid A, Marx on the pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows, and the pathos of Aristotelian tragedy running through the sad songs.

7.title: Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins
7.file: ch07 - Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins.md
7.relation: Reisch asks whether Radiohead is the Pink Floyd of the twenty-first century and answers that the comparison misleads: where Barrett-era Floyd used electronics to escape into psychedelic fantasy, Radiohead's apparent space-rock is phenomenological, giving voice to pre-reflective experience of technological modern life. He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.

8.title: 2. - Radiohead, or the Philosophy of Pop
8.file: ch08 - 2. - Radiohead, or the Philosophy of Pop.md
8.relation: Greif asks how pop music could ever 'incarnate a particular historical situation' and answers with Radiohead's portrait of broadcast culture around 2000: an environing, objectless dread in which each person lives at a knot of shouted messages no one sent and complaining only marks you as a crank. The band's turn to electronica was not avant-garde innovation but the discovery of the sound of that second nature, with Yorke's sampled-and-broken voice alternately absorbed into the machine and reasserting the human, and the lyric 'we' sliding between a scared individual lying that he is not alone, a wished-for collectivity, and the ventriloquized tyrant (as with Brecht's Pirate Jenny). Radiohead's church-tinged sublimity observes the storm from inside it — an internalized, inhuman sublime rather than the tradition's safe vantage on crushing power. Pop, he concludes, neither mirrors us nor preaches: it lets us retain and reactivate knowledge social speech forbids, and its deepest effect is not revolution but defiance — the retention of a private voice, a politics of re-created privacy — epitomized by 'There There' warning 'just 'cause you feel it doesn't mean it's there' inside an art form devoted to making you feel.

9.title: You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World
9.file: ch09 - You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World.md
9.relation: Sylvia argues that the split-screen 'All I Need' video made for MTV's anti-trafficking EXIT project — an American child's comfortable day intercut with a child laborer finishing the very shoes the American takes off — argues against child labor more powerfully than a standard utilitarian argument, because it joins Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos instead of relying on logos alone. Using the cognitive/expressive distinction, he claims the song also argues by turning listeners back on themselves ('I only stick with you because there are no others'). He then deploys Nozick's experience machine: we are all plugged into a Baudrillardian, Matrix-like media hyperreality that can make exploitation fade into background images, and the video's slap in the face 'punctures the hyperreality', showing how emotion can do argumentative work that rigorous argument cannot.

10.title: Are Musical Experiences Universal
10.file: ch10 - Are Musical Experiences Universal.md
10.relation: Slowik uses Radiohead's evolution — from the standard pop structures of Pablo Honey and The Bends to the layered, quasi-classical textures of Kid A and Amnesiac ('In Limbo''s independent melodic lines, the wordless climax of 'Pyramid Song') — to introduce the philosophy of music. He weighs what a musical work is, testing nominalism, idealism, and realism against 'Like Spinning Plates' and its live versions, then pits the emotion theory against formalism in explaining how songs like 'Like Spinning Plates' move us. The chapter closes on whether musical experience is universal and on Hume's 'Standard of Taste': if the test of time validates greatness, then the argument over whether OK Computer or In Rainbows is the better album might actually have an objectively right answer.

11.title: Art and Belief
11.file: ch11 - Art and Belief.md

12.title: Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again
12.file: ch12 - Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again.md
12.relation: Surber proposes Kristeva's 'abject aesthetics' as the new pair of shades that makes Radiohead legible: 'Creep' expresses abjection (the creep excluded even from recognition by the beautiful people), the android of 'Paranoid Android' is a borderline phenomenon neither human nor machine, and the bodily imagery of 'Bones', 'My Iron Lung', and the corpse in 'Knives Out' enacts the eruption of the pre-linguistic, formless abject, as do Donwood's dissolving Kid A letters. He contrasts the Beatles' aesthetics of psychedelic transcendence and Pink Floyd's existentialist aesthetics of alienation — built on Sartre's 'Hell is other people' gaze and the being-for-itself/being-in-itself split — with Radiohead's fluid, boundary-less world where meanings never come into focus and no existential revolt is possible because the embodied self is part of the world. Against the charge of nihilism, he reads Hail to the Thief and In Rainbows ('How come I end up where I started?') as postmodern reconstruction: if boundaries and meanings are fluid, they can also be remade.

13.title: Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins
13.file: ch13 - Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins.md
13.relation: Lott takes up Augustine's puzzle about why we enjoy watching sufferings we would flee, and answers for Radiohead with Aristotle's theory of tragedy: songs like 'Karma Police', 'Exit Music', and 'Fake Plastic Trees' sketch fragmentary characters in breakdown whose undeserved yet partly self-inflicted sufferings — 'Just'''s 'you do it to yourself' is hamartia — evoke pity and fear and then catharsis. Singing along makes identification uniquely intense in pop ('for a minute there, I lost myself' blurs the listener into the character), while music's 'natural sweetness' and its dynamics of build, climax, and release carry the purgation, from the terror of 'Climbing Up the Walls' to the slow ache of 'Videotape'. Because tragedy, unlike history, deals in universals, songs like 'The Bends' and 'High and Dry' open onto reflection on happiness, vulnerability, and the culture that fosters isolation, ending in the thin but real community of listeners who recognize their shared fragility.

14.title: There Are No Unrelated Phenomena
14.file: ch14 - There Are No Unrelated Phenomena.md
14.relation: Dark reads Thom Yorke's solo album The Eraser as an experiment in bearing witness — from Donwood's King Canute 'Gold Cnut' cover to 'Harrowdown Hill', which eulogizes David Kelly, the UN weapons inspector whose inconvenient fact-checking of the Iraq WMD dossier preceded his death ('we think the same things at the same time / we just can't do anything about it'). Drawing on Derrida — religion is responsibility or nothing, a poem is nothing without the risk of meaninglessness, words remain under erasure — he argues that Yorke's pub-table 'collating information' ('Analyze', 'And It Rained All Night'''s 'a million engines in neutral') is a sacred, self-undermining act of attention against officialdom's insistence that this has nothing to do with that. Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged frames the witness, and the chapter closes by hearing 'Reckoner' ('dedicated to all human beings') as the communal fulfillment of that witness.

15.title: Radiohead and the Music Industry
15.file: ch15 - Radiohead and the Music Industry.md

16.title: This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)
16.file: ch16 - This Is Really Happening (So Do Something).md
16.relation: Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.

17.title: C-M-C Music Factory
17.relation: Tate reads Radiohead's career through Marx: the band's standing tension between what they would make of themselves and what their record company would make of them is the worker's plight, and 'We Suck Young Blood' — with its fake 'we want sweet meats' recruitment campaign — literalizes Marx's vampire imagery of capital that 'lives only by sucking living labour'. Yorke's documented unease about money, from the 'six fluffy wee rabbits' mock-interview to 'Meeting People Is Easy'''s confession that money gets a band 'by the balls', maps onto Marx's account of labour degraded into 'a fragment of a man', whose Amnesiac echo is 'Dollars and Cents''' 'we're going to crack your little souls'. The pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows is then read as Marx's C-M-C circuit — selling music to live and make more music rather than M-C-M' accumulation for its own sake — a move that removes the exploitative capitalist middle-man instead of becoming one, and frees the band to make their most human-sounding album, fingers on strings.

18.title: Go Slowly
18.file: ch18 - Go Slowly.md
18.relation: Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.

20.title: Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle
20.file: ch20 - Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle.md
20.relation: Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.

21.title: How to Misunderstand Politics Completely
21.file: ch21 - How to Misunderstand Politics Completely.md
21.relation: Melançon argues Radiohead's real politics lie not in the overt content of Hail to the Thief but in a Camusian movement from absurdity to revolt: 'Exit Music'''s violent shift from Romeo's tender 'you' to the distorted 'we hope that you choke' enacts revolt against imposed rules and wisdom, while the android of 'Fitter Happier' ('a pig in a cage on antibiotics') and the wished-for alien of 'Subterranean Homesick Alien' dramatize absurd life under others' dictates. Following The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel — 'I revolt, therefore we are' — he shows how the songs' 'I' becomes a collective 'we' ('Karma Police', 'Lucky', 'Dollars and Cents') whose revolt, like Sisyphus's conscious walk back down the mountain, affirms life without ever justifying murder. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of expression then explains why the songs are political anyway: artists express a still-unspoken 'fever' (it took years before 'Nude' could be said), creating a public and a common world — politics as unveiling rather than governing, down to 'Electioneering'''s admission that the band too campaigns for our vote.

22.title: Hope at the Door
22.file: ch22 - Hope at the Door.md
22.relation: Sean Burt argues that despite its Orwellian dystopian surface — the internalized mind control of "2 + 2 = 5" ("I'll stay home forever, where two and two always makes five"), the commands of "Sit Down. Stand Up.," the hunted domesticity of "A Wolf at the Door" — Hail to the Thief is genuinely utopian thought in Ernst Bloch's and Fredric Jameson's sense: imagining any different world, even a repressive one, breaks capitalism's "eternal present" and keeps the future open. He traces fleeting glimmers of hope in "Sail to the Moon" and in "I Will"'s move from bunker to "I will rise up," each quickly shut down again by "Backdrifts" and "Where I End and You Begin" yet never fully renounced. The band's denials that the album is political matter because the album rejects both effective protest music (Against Me!'s ironic meta-protest) and ironic critical distance: we are not in on the joke, the joke is on us.

23.title: Rising Up
23.relation: Brandon Forbes uses Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting in concert, rooted in plurality and natality) and violence (instruments that ape power, one against all) to read Radiohead's violent imagery. The "Just" video shows that power lies not in what the prone man says but in everyone's collective act of lying down; "Sit Down. Stand Up." and "2 + 2 = 5" dramatize command backed by weapons and the revolutionary moment when a king's violence breeds the dissent that undoes him; "Life in a Glass House" and "Where I End and You Begin" depict totalitarian terror, the stage where violence has devoured power entirely. "I Will" ("I will rise up," "little babies' eyes") closes the chapter as Arendt's natality — the capacity of new political beginnings the gun can never defeat.

24.title: Thinking in Rainbows
24.relation: Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.

26.title: At Ease
26.file: ch26 - At Ease.md
26.relation: Adam Koehler reads Kid A's disfigured, barely intelligible vocals through Heidegger's account of how enabling technology withdraws into an invisible backdrop of everydayness: Pablo Honey hides its studio machinery behind "natural" rock, but Kid A — the cycled voice of "Everything in Its Right Place," the unintelligible vocoded "Kid A," "How to Disappear Completely" — forces the artifice itself into view, and with it the withdrawn world technology ordinarily conceals. The song is beautiful, he argues, because its willful failure to communicate feels human, enacting the anxiety of living in an information age that traps as much as it connects; John Mayer's lyric-clearing acoustic cover misses the point, since making sense now means risking not making sense, and the album's demand is that we listen to, and understand, everything withdrawn in the background.

27.title: If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . .
27.file: ch27 - If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . ..md
27.relation: Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."

28.title: Knives Out
28.relation: Michael Thompson argues that the much-debated rhythm of "Pyramid Song" — 4/4 with syncopation, 3/3/4/3/3 groupings, or shifting signatures; Yorke says it is only "felt" — is philosophically pointed: by violating ordinary temporal expectations it forces an awareness of time itself, just as Chopin's nocturnes used time-signature changes to voice the nostalgia and melancholy of his Polish exile. Drawing on Gadamer's historically affected consciousness and the embodied, rhythmic daily life described by Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, he reads the lyrics' row-boat to heaven ("all my past and futures") as a synoptic flash in which one sees past, present, and future as one organic whole. Because Yorke's heaven echoes Talking Heads' "Heaven" as a place where nothing happens, the song's consolation is that nothing lies outside our temporal embedding — with past and future united "there was nothing to fear and nothing to doubt."

29.title: A Large Rock Saved My Life
29.file: ch29 - A Large Rock Saved My Life.md
29.relation: Lindsey Fiorelli reads OK Computer as Camus's absurd universe: "Subterranean Homesick Alien" and "Fitter Happier" portray a technological world drained of meaning, where to belong you must become a robotic "pig in a cage on antibiotics" and "Let Down" offers only the "emptiest of feelings." She stresses that Camus demands revolt, not escape — Sisyphus and Meursault embrace the absurd and thereby become happy — whereas Yorke's lyrics keep longing to flee (spaceships, growing wings, the resigned "No Surprises"). Yet the music itself embraces the technology the lyrics curse, and this, she concludes, is Radiohead's real Camusian move: like Camus writing novels about an alienating world, they carve Sisyphus's rock — modern technology, synthesizers and computers — into new and marvelous sounds, overcoming alienation by working within it.

31.title: Today I Woke Up Sucking a Grammy
31.file: ch31 - Today I Woke Up Sucking a Grammy.md
31.relation: Bradley Kaye reads Kid A as an album made under Lyotard's postmodern condition: "Everything in Its Right Place" ("what was that you tried to say?") and the murmured title track bear witness to the differend, something that must be put into phrases but cannot yet be; "The National Anthem" dramatizes incredulity toward the grand narrative of nationalism in favor of little narratives and local justice; "Treefingers" is the painful silence of the inexpressible, and "Optimistic" an ironic micro-political hope. The epigone problem (Yorke to Coldplay, Travis, and Muse: "Good luck with Kid A") and the closing Baudrillard turn — "In Limbo"'s "you're living in a fantasy world," the Marcus Welby and Perry Mason hyperreal, "it's not like the movies" — explain why even labeling the album "Best Alternative Album" Grammy presumes exactly the stable categories Kid A dissolves.

32.title: How to Reappear Completely
32.relation: Tim Footman asks whether a rock band inside the media machine can avoid becoming a simulacrum of itself, tracing Radiohead's attempts to pierce Baudrillard's hyperreality: "Fake Plastic Trees" as the chain from plastic plants to plastic people, "Fitter Happier" as a simulacrum made of training-manual words, the no-singles Kid A campaign and leaked album, and the In Rainbows pay-what-you-want release that stripped away marketing — only to congeal into a new story about the band's anti-commercial perversity, since the free download was really advance publicity for a conventional for-sale album. Even seemingly authentic moments ("How I Made My Millions" recorded at home, the fabled Glastonbury 1997 set, Yorke's Dublin dissociation that became "How to Disappear Completely") are packaged slices of reality, so the band's melancholia is less a defeat of the simulacrum than a way of manifesting within it — "the best you can is good enough."

33.title: How Come I End Up Where I Started
33.file: ch33 - How Come I End Up Where I Started.md
33.relation: Perry Owen Wright applies Baudrillard's Seduction to In Rainbows track by track: the Enlightenment reduced sex to anatomical biology and Natural Law, pornography is its hyperreal simulacrum (the HDTV of sex, played out in "Bodysnatchers"' "pale imitation with the edges sawn off"), and what re-enchants sex is seduction — an endless game of reversible signs, appearance and disappearance, aleatory suspension, and the trompe l'oeil's hypersimulation. "Weird Fishes/Arpeggi" shows the mortal risk of entering the game (the anglerfish's dangling false eyes), "All I Need" personifies Death itself as a stalker-seducer drawn into the loop of signs, "House of Cards" reads infidelity as leaving the game for the Law, and "Jigsaw Falling into Place" reduces seduction to production ending at the orgasm. "Videotape" closes the album at the pearly gates where even death becomes a sign to be seduced — the home movie "in red, blue, green" is the immortal sign we always leave behind.
