6.title: Previews and Coming Attractions
6.relation: The editors' introduction argues that anime — from Akira, Ghost in the Shell, and Neon Genesis Evangelion to My Neighbor Totoro, Nausicaa, and Grave of the Fireflies — is not children's fare but stories about 'monsters, witches, robots, children, and spirits who grapple with questions of societal violence, ethics, morality, justice, heroism, identity, and the soul.' It frames the book's project as finding what lies beneath anime's visual signature of big eyes and giant robots, illustrating the tone with epigraphs from Wolf's Rain ('If life has no purpose, then you're already dead') and Princess Tutu on fate versus defiance. It closes with housekeeping: anime means Japan-originated animation for this book, Western name order will be used, and the contributing artists and industry supporters are thanked.

7.title: Accidental Anime
7.relation: A distributor's memoir, not a philosophical essay: Margo Zimmerman recounts falling into anime at Manga Entertainment via Ninja Scroll and Perfect Blue, and the art-versus-business balance of bringing a niche genre to Western audiences. Its philosophy-adjacent cases are concrete: otaku demanded authenticity over adaptation (fans rejected the Southern-accent dubbing of Mima's country mother in Perfect Blue, and the contested translation of End of Evangelion's final line 'kimochi warui' — 'How disgusting' vs 'I feel sick' — still divides viewers), and she credits anime's serious commentary on mythology, philosophy, nuclear power, and humanity with influencing Western storytelling, citing The Matrix's obvious debt to Ghost in the Shell. No taxonomy philosopher or concept is actually deployed.

9.title: Wave Goodbye from the Catbus
9.file: ch09 - Wave Goodbye from the Catbus.md
9.relation: Heinricy argues anime is the richest medium for posthuman theory because it shows bodies 'in a state of becoming' rather than as grotesque boundary violations: Miyazaki's Catbus and Totoro, Haku's dragon transformation and Chihiro's pig parents in Spirited Away, and the cursed pig-headed aviator of Porco Rosso all treat morphing bodies as possibility, not horror. She sorts anime posthumanism into two valences: a 'Ghost in the Machine' dream of consciousness leaving the body altogether (Motoko merging with the net in Ghost in the Shell), which she rebuts via N. Katherine Hayles's point that consciousness is embodied and would change with any new body, and hybrid configurations like mecha (Gundam, Robotech) where body and machine drive each other. Following Donna Haraway, she contends we are all already cyborgs — vaccines, engineered food, treated water — and credits Japan's nuclear history (via Susan Napier) and its shape-shifting folklore for why anime embraces rather than fears the transformed body.

10.title: Looking Inwards
10.file: ch10 - Looking Inwards.md
10.relation: Barber, Bryce, and Davis test Donna Haraway's emancipatory cyborg thesis against Gunslinger Girl, where the Social Welfare Agency 'adopts' orphaned and abused girls (Henrietta, Rico, Triela, Elsa, Claes), rebuilds their bodies as cybernetic weapons, and drug-conditions them into loyal assassins paired with male handlers. They argue the series realizes none of Haraway's post-gender potential: conditioning erodes memory and autonomy (Rico coolly shoots the porter Emilio who befriended her; Elsa murders her handler Lauro and kills herself; Triela suffers pointless menstrual cramps in a wombless body), while the girls' kawaii styling, teddy bears, and school uniforms make them objects of the male gaze whose cuteness disguises lethal power. The cyborgs' victimization ultimately reinforces traditional gender hierarchy and mirrors conformity-pressured Japanese youth, so the cyborg has 'regressed' from the autonomous heroines of Ghost in the Shell or Battle Angel Alita.

11.title: The Transforming Body
11.file: ch11 - The Transforming Body.md
11.relation: McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.

12.title: Mind
12.file: ch12 - Mind.md

13.title: Is Everybody Disembodied (or, Have We Always Been Posthuman Beings )
13.file: ch13 - Is Everybody Disembodied (or, Have We Always Been Posthuman Beings ).md
13.relation: Stevens uses the film's closing voice-over 'I am Tetsuo' in Otomo's Akira to run the classic identity-and-mind problems: Heraclitus's river and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus ask whether the grotesquely transformed, Akira-absorbed Tetsuo is still the same person, while Descartes's cogito — riffed as 'cogito ergo Tetsuo' — Turing's Test, and Searle's Chinese Room test whether a voice that seems to think proves a thinker behind it (syntax is not yet shown sufficient for semantics, though Edwin Hutchins's distributed cognition reads the Room from the inside out). Weighing embodiment (Pinker's brain-makes-mind, Dennett's self as a 'center of narrative gravity') against disembodiment (Akira levelling Neo-Tokyo from nothing but cryogenically stored remains; Tetsuo's matter teleportation), he concludes through the problem of representation — every utterance is re-presented, as in Augustine's guilty tears over Dido — that we always treat semblances of thinkers as thinkers, so we may have always been decentered, re-presented, posthuman beings no different from Tetsuo and Akira.

14.title: Questioning the Question
14.file: ch14 - Questioning the Question.md
14.relation: Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.

15.title: Spirit
15.file: ch15 - Spirit.md

16.title: In the Palm of Your Hand
16.file: ch16 - In the Palm of Your Hand.md
16.relation: Callis reads Spirited Away as Miyazaki's bid to make audiences feel rather than doctrinally learn Shinto, deploying Thomas Kasulis's distinction between existential Shinto (awe before kami: Chihiro's soot-sprite rescue, cleansing the trash-choked River God, makoto no kokoro purity) and essentialist Shinto (State Shinto's war-era nationalism, visually evoked by the abandoned 1940s train station and the train that haunts the whole film). She argues the drive into the spirit world is a compressed visual history of Shinto — folk shrines, Buddhist guardian statues, torii — and that Chihiro's stolen and recovered name enacts Japan's need to remember its traditions without forgetting how they were abused, supported by Miyazaki's own quotes on rural solstice bath rituals and Tarkovsky-style nostalgia. The three endings (Zeniba's 'Nothing that happens is ever forgotten' vs the Disney dub's memory-will-return line, and Miyazaki's preferred solo train ride) all say the same: the kami spark, like Thich Nhat Hanh's ancestors in the palm of the hand, is carried forward.

17.title: Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes
17.file: ch17 - Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes.md
17.relation: Barkman argues that anime's Christian imagery — the legendary Santa on a cross, Earthian's gay angel lovers, Trinity Blood's bishonen pope and female cardinal, Evangelion's hostile Angels — encodes Japanese religious pluralism rather than orthodox Christianity. He lays out the pluralist position (following Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction and John Hick: Ultimate Reality is only equivocally describable, so doctrine matters less than spiritual mood), contrasts it with exclusivism and inclusivism, and charges pluralism with self-undermining intolerance, then traces Japan's historical demonization of Christianity from the 1637 Shimabara massacre (Ninja Resurrection, Samurai Champloo) to Eva's alien invaders, with Armageddon imagery fueled by the atomic bombs. Because Shinto-Buddhist-Daoist anti-realism dissolves fixed categories, anime dissolves good and evil (Chrno Crusade's I Ching balance) and gender itself, gravitating to the symbol-rich 'jungle' of Catholicism (C.S. Lewis's phrase) — and where Trinity Blood lets some vampires be righteous, Augustine's City of God marks the one nearly orthodox note.

18.title: The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back
18.file: ch18 - The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back.md
18.relation: Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.

20.title: Freeing Clausewitz’s Soul from Gravity
20.file: ch20 - Freeing Clausewitz’s Soul from Gravity.md
20.relation: Melancon tests Just War Theory against Gundam's One Year War: Gihren Zabi's 'Sieg Zeon' funeral oration and Char Aznable's rhetoric show how the vague criterion of comparative justice lets a militarist regime dress aggression — the Three Seconds of Declaration gassing of colonies, Operation British's colony drop on Earth — in just-war language. On the conduct side, Ramba Ral's troops spare civilians and differentiate child targets on White Base, yet Zeon's still-unjust ad bellum position cannot be rehabilitated; and asking whether WMDs are inherently immoral, he uses Anavel Gato's nuclear strike on the Federation fleet review (Operation Stardust) — discriminating, proportional, militarily necessary — to argue weapons are amoral tools judged only by Walzer-style jus in bello criteria. Clausewitz resolves the theory's usefulness: war's inner tendency toward the absolute must stay nested within political goals, and Zeon's drift from fighting for independence into conquering and governing Earth shows exactly how a war that abandons just-war limits loses sight of what victory even is.

21.title: Redemption and Hope for the Future
21.file: ch21 - Redemption and Hope for the Future.md
21.relation: Peters applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of courage — the mean between confidence and fear, shown only in facing an honorable death in war for a noble motive — to Colin MacLeod's two-thousand-year hunt for Marcus Octavius, the Immortal Roman who killed his wife Moya, in Highlander: The Search for Vengeance. Because MacLeod fights from pain and rage, 'like wild beasts,' and secretly seeks death as refuge from grief ('to seek death as a refuge from poverty, or love... is not the act of a brave man'), Aristotle would judge him a coward despite his fearlessness — Amergan the spirit guide diagnoses him the same way. Redemption comes only when Dahlia and the villagers threatened by Marcus's new Rome give him a noble cause and hopefulness: he becomes their general, fights with discipline instead of rage, and turns Marcus's own quickening to destroying the virus, illustrating the chapter's closing thought that for an Immortal dying is easy and living courageously is hard.

22.title: Don’t Be a Vegeta
22.file: ch22 - Don’t Be a Vegeta.md
22.relation: Argues that shonen fighting anime stage a choice between Adam Smith's and Darwin's models of competition: Zoro hunting Mihawk in One Piece, Goku's technique-by-technique training, and Rock Lee's specialization show competition improving people within the limits of a human excellence, while Cell's absorbing evolutions, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's risky hollowification represent limitless 'leveling up' that changes what you are. The chapter concludes that the Darwinian win-at-all-costs model produces the perpetually dissatisfied Vegeta, and that framing competition around being a certain kind of person (a great swordsman, not just a winner) gives life a completable aim — while conceding that Darwinians rightly warn our picture of the 'normal human' has unjustly cast off jinchūriki like Naruto and Gaara and Devil Fruit users like Luffy.

24.title: Alchemic Heroism
24.relation: Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.

25.title: The Sacrificial Lamb
25.relation: Argues Astro Boy re-enacts the sacrificial logic of the atomic age: Atomu is the nuclear-powered copy of the dead Tobio, born from Dr. Tenma's refusal to accept mortality, and his repeated self-sacrifice for humans who discard him (as in 'Save the Classmate,' where the rescued boys' parents still want him removed) shows him functioning as Heidegger's 'standing-reserve' — an object valued only as stored power, with humans themselves next in line. Drawing on Plato's Republic anxiety over originals and copies, Adorno and Horkheimer's dialectic of enlightenment, and Rey Chow's account of mimesis as the sign left by sacrifice, the chapter reads the series as mourning an innocence that became impossible after Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

26.title: The Aftermath of Tragedy
26.file: ch26 - The Aftermath of Tragedy.md
26.relation: Argues that Grave of the Fireflies works as a critique of anime's child-hero convention: Seita acts exactly like a plucky anime protagonist when he defies his not-actually-evil aunt, strikes out on his own with Setsuko, ignores the farmer's advice to apologize and return, and demands a quick fix from the doctor — but these 'heroic' choices kill them both, because he lacks the developed capacity to reason. Against the medieval 'child as little adult' picture that most anime (Dragon Ball, Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!) romanticizes, the chapter deploys Aristotle's view of children as unfinished beings who cannot yet reason or achieve happiness, concluding the film is a cautionary tale about the years of nurture and guidance real children need.

28.title: Equivalent Exchange
28.relation: Reads alchemy's law of equivalent exchange as a parable of capitalism: Locke's labor-mixing argument explains how hours of a life become property and why money is 'distilled life'; Aristotle's attack on limitless wealth-getting (the Midas problem) and Aquinas's capital vices explain how pursuing money for its own sake brings the homunculi — Greed, Pride, and the Sloth the Elric brothers' forbidden act produced — into the world. Marx's 1844 Manuscripts supply the punchline that money performs 'human alchemy' on people, buying their time, esteem, and bodies the way red stones are made from sacrificed humans, so the chapter concludes that capital, like the Philosopher's Stone, profits only by consuming lives and that markets must be held to a promise of fairness and care beyond mere exchange.

29.title: Textually Transmitted Disease
29.relation: Traces hentai from Hokusai's 'Diver and Two Octopi' through the 1920s eroguro journals to the Lolita Anime and Cream Lemon OVAs, then asks whether even this extreme material has value as fantasy. The chapter frames the media-effects debate with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis (revived by Feshbach and tentatively supported by Milton Diamond's finding that Japanese rape rates fell as pornography spread) against Plato's Republic worry that sensational works license irrationality (updated by the Disinhibition, Desensitization, and Cultivation theories), and concludes that hentai's real harm is attitudinal rather than behavioral: its ritual 'breaking' of strong women and sex-as-something-done-to-passive-girls cultivates misogyny and a dehumanizing view of sex.

30.title: 18 - The Devil Within Sara Livingston
30.file: ch30 - 18 - The Devil Within Sara Livingston.md

32.title: Who Wants to Be Human Anyway
32.file: ch32 - Who Wants to Be Human Anyway.md
32.relation: Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.

33.title: Cyborg Goddess
33.relation: Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.

34.title: One Last Anguished Existential Scream
34.file: ch34 - One Last Anguished Existential Scream.md
34.relation: Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.

36.title: ALTERNATE ENDING
36.relation: A closing personal essay arguing that anime's defining gift is the genuinely unexpected — a robot sprouting from Naota's forehead bump in Fooly Cooly, Berserk's catastrophic finale, Samurai Champloo's Edo-meets-hip-hop fusion, Paprika's dream parade — which jolts viewers into noticing and rethinking their expectations, the very opening that philosophic inquiry requires. It also credits anime's sincere, two-way engagement with its audience (the cast-and-crew interviews on DVD extras that won the author over) for the genre's ongoing, unpredictable evolution.

2.title: The Red Sox and Philosophy
2.file: ch02 - The Red Sox and Philosophy.md

3.title: Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch
3.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

5.title: The Red Sox and Philosophy
5.file: ch05 - The Red Sox and Philosophy.md

6.title: Foreword
6.relation: Red Sox official historian Dick Bresciani traces a New England inheritance of endurance from the 1620 Pilgrims through the 1903 first World Series, the fire sale of stars to the Yankees in the 1920s, and the heartbreaks of 1946, 1967, 1975, 1978 and 1986. He argues that the fan virtues of grit, loyalty and cautious optimism mirror the regional character forged by survival, and reads the 2004 ALCS comeback (Millar's walk, Roberts's steal, Ortiz's 12th-inning homer) as the moment fatalism gave way to faith, vindicated again by the 2007 title. The foreword frames the volume as a book by fans for fans that uses the Red Sox to examine faith, morality and community across the history of ideas.

8.title: The Red Sox and Philosophy
8.file: ch08 - The Red Sox and Philosophy.md

9.title: From Professor Thom’s to the “Little Professor”
9.file: ch09 - From Professor Thom’s to the “Little Professor”.md
9.relation: Editor Michael Macomber explains that the book grew from watching Red Sox games at Professor Thom's, a Sox bar in Manhattan's East Village, where exiled fans in Yankee territory fused deep game knowledge with intense passion. He argues that Sox fans display the melding of intellectual and emotional lives that philosophers find so tricky, and pays tribute to Dominic DiMaggio, the 'Little Professor,' whose intelligence (as Ted Williams notes in Halberstam's The Teammates) overcame physical shortcomings. DiMaggio's smart, underrated play is offered as the fitting emblem for a book that examines the Red Sox thoughtfully rather than merely emotionally.

10.title: I - Root Root Root fort Red Sox
10.file: ch10 - I - Root Root Root fort Red Sox.md

11.title: A New Path
11.file: ch11 - A New Path.md
11.relation: Marcus Giamatti narrates his upbringing as an 'Old School' fan under 'Dame Mutability,' his father's personification of the certainty that the Red Sox would always break New England's heart through Bucky Dent, Mookie Wilson, Calvin Schiraldi and Aaron Boone. He argues that being born a Sox fan is an inescapable duty and lifelong quest whose real payoff is not a pennant but the character, faith and perseverance built by enduring, so that when he lay curled up ready to quit during Game Four of the 2004 ALCS, Millar's walk, Roberts's steal and Mueller's single vindicated the whole method. He ends by vowing to pass this philosophy of survival to his unborn daughter Ophelia in Southern California, applying the one-pitch-at-a-time discipline to acting, music and life.

12.title: Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony
12.file: ch12 - Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony.md
12.relation: John McHugh uses his urge to confront Grady Little, who left a spent Pedro Martinez in during Game Seven of the 2003 ALCS, to ask how fans should govern the primal emotions fandom generates. Stoic self-command fails because Epictetus's advice (avoid caring about games entirely, focus only on what you control) would extinguish fandom itself, so McHugh adapts Adam Smith's impartial spectator: the virtuous fan imagines being watched by a sympathetic but emotionally distant fellow fan, settling on a Chicago Cubs fan who gets Bartman the way a Sox fan gets Buckner and Grady. He concludes that we each harbor a team of role-specific inner consciences, and the practical task is harmonizing the Red Sox-fan identity with our other identities rather than suppressing it or being consumed by it.

13.title: The Authentic Red Sox Fan, or The Importance of Turning off NESN and Finding
13.file: ch13 - The Authentic Red Sox Fan, or The Importance of Turning off NESN and Finding.md
13.relation: Corey McCall asks what makes a 'true' Red Sox fan, contrasting the beer-soaked bleacher loudmouth with one-hundred-year-old honorary batboy Arthur Giddon, and treats the nostalgia and resentment around the 2004 bandwagon as the Enlightenment problem of authenticity in miniature. Through Kant's 'Sapere aude' and the ideal of autonomy, he argues the authentic fan is the critical fan who uses reason about the team (questioning Francona's moves, judging whole careers) instead of losing herself in uncritical devotion, reading Jason Varitek's 2004 muzzle of A-Rod as the moment the team's identity crystallized for fans who wanted to be like him. With the Curse gone, fans are freed from fated suffering but inherit Kant's burden of autonomously choosing how fandom will define them, since circumstances no longer decide.

14.title: April 6th, 2009
14.file: ch14 - April 6th, 2009.md
14.relation: David Roochnik interlaces a loss diary (his daughter's soccer defeat and the Sox's 1998 playoff elimination on the same Saturday, the 2003 Grady Little collapse that gave him chest pain, the 2004 comeback) to argue that losing is an art that teaches what winning cannot. The loser's 'if only' imagination transforms the past, the 'it was only a game' rationalization forces honest reflection about what matters, and shared doom forges Red Sox Nation into a community in a way no Yankees nation could exist, since victors never need to think. He applies Plato's Symposium doctrine of Eros, that to love X is to lack X as Socrates lacks wisdom, to explain why eighty-six years of championship-lack made fandom meaningful, and closes fearing that winning in 2004 and 2007 made the Sox 'normal,' eroding the art of losing that glued the Nation together.

15.title: II - Curse Reversed
15.file: ch15 - II - Curse Reversed.md

16.title: If Only . .
16.file: ch16 - If Only . ..md
16.relation: Bryan Pilkington applies Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel's analysis of moral luck, where factors outside an agent's control change how we evaluate the very same act, to Bill Buckner's Game Six error of 1986, alongside constructed cases of Jon Lester skipping the last page of his scouting sheet and a Fenway Franks truck driver who skips his brake check. Drawing on Nagel on negligence, Williams's notion of agent-regret (only Buckner, not Bob Stanley or Rich Gedman, can feel it), and a standard of reasonable expectation for a veteran first baseman, he concludes Buckner can rightly be blamed for the error and even for losing Game Six, though not for the World Series or for the cruel vilification he received. The chapter thus disciplines the fan's 'if only' blame game: a curse is never a satisfying target of blame, but neither is the situation instead of the person.

17.title: The End of a Curse
17.file: ch17 - The End of a Curse.md
17.relation: Erin Flynn argues that 'the Red Sox are cursed' was never an explanation: it commits the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy and an appeal to ignorance, and a curse, to explain anything, would have to be a force over and above the ordinary causes of losing, which no evidence ever identified. Borrowing Nelson Goodman's 'grue' paradox and the new riddle of induction, he coins 'blursed' (cursed-and-blessed relative to Dave Roberts's steal on October 17th, 2004) to show that the same 1920 to 2003 evidence supports the rival description just as well, so the evidence itself never favored 'cursed.' Since curses explain and predict nothing, the choice between descriptions is pragmatic and aesthetic: 'blursed' rightly renders the 1986 choke as the very thing that made the 2004 comeback the singular, bliss-producing event it was, so the Sox turn out never to have been cursed at all.

18.title: Only an Ortiz Can Save Us Heidegger’s Revelation of Being
18.file: ch18 - Only an Ortiz Can Save Us Heidegger’s Revelation of Being.md
18.relation: James Pontuso reads Red Sox history through Heidegger: technology that turns the world into 'standing reserve' breeds the anxious 'everydayness' of the mediocre Pinky Higgins teams, while the run of near-misses from 1967 through Bucky Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986 threw fans into an authentic encounter with tragedy, mortality and the mystery of Being that the Yankees' free-agent 'technology of power' could never teach. Fenway Park, quirky and continuous with the pre-Hitler past, serves as 'home' in Heidegger's homeless age, and the literati's tragic framing of the team (language as the house of Being) made its fate a matter of existential weight rather than mere sport. David Ortiz's 2004 ALCS heroics then function as Heidegger's longed-for revelation of Being, the answer to 'only a god can save us,' after which fans have lived through all three states: everydayness, tragic anxiety, and wonder.

19.title: Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful
19.file: ch19 - Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful.md
19.relation: Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.

21.title: Do You Believe It
21.file: ch21 - Do You Believe It.md
21.relation: Patrick Tiernan argues that Fenway fandom is a genuine religion: William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity) map onto memories of Buckner's error and Dave Roberts's steal, and Peter Berger's 'signals of transcendence' structure the rituals of Truck Day, the hopes of spring training, the damnation of Bucky Dent and Johnny Damon, and the humor of 'Cowboy Up.' He roots the Curse of the Bambino in New England's Puritan-Calvinist legacy of persecution and original sin (Frazee's sale of Ruth), then deploys Hume's account of superstition from 'Of Superstition and Enthusiasm' to deflate the exorcism rituals fans actually performed, from a Sox hat on Everest to dredging for Ruth's piano, as post hoc fallacies. Even so, the rituals reveal the human need for religious practice, and Maslow's peak experience renders the 2004 comeback a brush with the sacred, so the Faithful believe because they have to.

22.title: The Lesson
22.file: ch22 - The Lesson.md
22.relation: Karolina Lewestam and Orla Richardson argue that the Red Sox fan is a moral hero in Kierkegaard's sense: like Abraham in Fear and Trembling, the fan fully accepts that loss is inevitable (the Curse, Aaron Boone, Buckner's grounder) yet refuses the rational course of infinite resignation and keeps believing 'this could be the year.' Where liberal individualism licenses walking away from any loyalty and the modern reflex is to sue luck out of existence, the fan lives at the mercy of fate and thereby enacts Kierkegaard's movement beyond resignation into true faith, the absurd belief against all evidence that Isaac will be spared. Fenway thus becomes the best university for learning to live fully under uncertainty, with Ortiz's 'keep the faith' speech and Schilling's bloody sock as its lessons in perseverance and courage.

23.title: One with the Team
23.relation: Chelsea Harry contends that Red Sox Nation embodies a Confucian rather than Cartesian self: against Descartes's cogito and the egocentric, endorsement-chasing player (A-Rod, the traded Manny), the Sox way treats selfhood as constituted by family, community and mutual sacrifice, from Mike Lowell's hometown discount to Yaz's hospital escape and Schilling's bloody sock. She maps Confucian benevolence (jen) onto Wakefield, Varitek and Ortiz describing how fan love powers their play, filial piety onto the retired numbers honoring franchise elders like Pesky, Doerr and Cronin, and Chung-ying Cheng's 'naturality' onto the fans' claim to be the team's twenty-sixth player, so Johnny Damon's defection reads as the treachery of an ungrateful villager. The 'je ne sais quoi' of team spirit is thus Confucian unity: becoming oneself by subordinating the I to the We.

24.title: Breaking the Eighth Commandment
24.relation: Joel Cade maps baseball's traditionalist-versus-sabermetric war onto the faith-and-reason debate: Joe Morgan's refusal to even read Moneyball repeats Tertullian's fideism, Ted Williams's Science of Hitting exemplifies Augustine's 'faith seeking understanding,' and Wade Boggs's game-day chicken ritual completes his rational hitting exactly as Aquinas says faith completes reason. Theo Epstein's 2004 front office fused the models under the motto 'understanding justifies faith,' using statistics to discover when supposedly obsolete traditional weapons like the stolen base actually work, which is why the seemingly anti-Moneyball Dave Roberts trade paid off in The Steal against Mariano Rivera in Game Four of the ALCS. The chapter closes with the joke that Augustine, who stole pears, would bless stealing second: reconciling faith and reason is how the Sox reversed the Curse, and maybe how faith- and reason-guided people might reconcile.

25.title: Red Sox Future
25.relation: Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.

26.title: IV - The Rivalry
26.file: ch26 - IV - The Rivalry.md

27.title: The Will to Nothingness, or What Happens when the Red Sox Win
27.file: ch27 - The Will to Nothingness, or What Happens when the Red Sox Win.md
27.relation: Nolen Gertz runs the Sox-Yankees rivalry through Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals: the Steinbrenner Yankees are masters whose 'good' simply means strong and winning, while Sox fans are slaves whose 'Yankees suck!' is ressentiment's imaginary revenge, intensified into the most spiritual and poisonous hatred by eighty-six years of impotence. The priestly slaves defeated the masters by cleverness rather than force, mirrored when Epstein's sabermetric 'religion' of prospects and projections terrified the Yankees into converting, building a farm system and embracing the slavish virtues they had scorned. The final twist is Nietzsche's will to nothingness: once the masters fell in 2004 the fans' suffering lost its meaning, breeding bandwagon guilt, pink-hat resentment and nihilistic exhaustion, so freedom requires a transvaluation that lets fans simply enjoy watching baseball.

28.title: A (Bronx) Cheer to the Red Sox “Without Whom, Not as Much”
28.file: ch28 - A (Bronx) Cheer to the Red Sox “Without Whom, Not as Much”.md
28.relation: Writing as a Yankees fan, Konig asks what makes a championship worth wanting: after Schopenhauer's picture of endless striving as suffering, he brings in Richard Taylor (meaning lies in the activity itself, never its completion) and then Nietzsche's will to power, which seeks worthy resistance to overcome. Thought experiments—a childhood 'big game' that turns out to be tee-ball, and the 2004 Sox trouncing the minor-league Atlantic League—show a title without worthy opposition is hollow. Hence the Yankees' twentieth-century dominance would mean nothing without the Red Sox as the sustained, worthy enemy (Bucky Dent, the Pedro-Zimmer melee, the 2004 ALCS collapse included).

29.title: What Makes the Red Sox Great Is More than the Team
29.file: ch29 - What Makes the Red Sox Great Is More than the Team.md
29.relation: Ulatowski argues the 'We Believe' motto is religious: Red Sox fandom is the a priori conviction that Boston is the sports city 'than which none greater can be conceived,' transplanting Anselm's ontological argument—necessary, contingent and impossible objects, existence as a perfection—to the Red Sox via Oliver Wendell Holmes's 'hub of the universe.' He rejects the parallel New York argument because it smuggles a posteriori championship counts into an a priori proof, and answers the fallacy-of-division worry by making Boston's greatness and the Red Sox's greatness an identity rather than a whole-to-part inference.

30.title: Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox
30.file: ch30 - Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox.md
30.relation: Lee casts pre-2004 fandom as a Kierkegaardian leap of faith ('We Believe') and the Curse of the Bambino as Schopenhauer's irrational deterministic will, with the 1918–2004 cycle of spring hope and October collapse as Camus's Sisyphus. But he argues fans are really existentialists: blaming losses on fate or the Curse is Sartrean bad faith that evades responsibility, since fans did hold Bill Buckner (1986 error) and Grady Little (leaving a spent Pedro in during 2003 ALCS Game 7) individually accountable. The 2004 and 2007 champions remain 'our' Red Sox because we freely choose to care about the team's journey, not because it has a fixed essence; a coda borrows Russell's point about ambiguous reference for the word 'Yankee,' and Andy Wasif's appendix runs Yankees-as-evil through relativism, objectivism and subjectivism.

31.title: V - Views from the Grandstands
31.file: ch31 - V - Views from the Grandstands.md

32.title: Missing Numbers
32.relation: Macomber explains fan judgment through Kant's determinate judgment—subsuming sensuous particulars (white sphere, red stitches) under the concept 'baseball'—then warns, with Horkheimer and Adorno's 'disenchantment of the world,' that reducing careers to single concepts (Buckner = 'error,' Dave Roberts = 'The Steal,' Damon = 'traitor') negates everything else a player did, which is why Damon is booed at Fenway while Nomar received a standing ovation. Retired numbers like Jim Rice's 14 invert the process: the harshest reduction becomes an invitation that demands the player's story be told, magnifying rather than erasing him.

33.title: Tie Goes to the Runner
33.file: ch33 - Tie Goes to the Runner.md
33.relation: St. Martin runs the Fenway 'pink hat' controversy through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the virtuous fan is the mean between the deficient bandwagoner who waves at NESN cameras mid-pitch and the excessive diehard who memorizes Dice-K's ERA to belittle others. Terry Francona's courage in sending Dave Roberts in the 2004 ALCS (versus a reckless Ortiz steal attempt) illustrates virtue as the mean between cowardice and foolhardiness, and Aristotle's contrast between the love of honor and the love of contemplation shows both pink hatters and stats-obsessed diehards err by making fandom about themselves. She concludes that accepting fans in any color hat is the truly virtuous mean.

34.title: Evidence Rewarded
34.relation: Goldwater reads Bill James's sabermetric revolution through Quine: science is a continuation of common sense, but mature science replaces the 'animal sense of similarity' (being a Yankee, batting average, RBI) with predictive, league- and park-adjusted categories, turning atomistic box-score tallies into holistic statistics that acquire meaning only from the whole web of data. Because science recognizes only repeatable types, it cannot countenance miracles—Carlton Fisk's 1975 homer greeted by the 'Hallelujah Chorus,' Dave Roberts's steal in 2004—whose meaning lies in happening exactly once. His resolution: GMs like John Henry and Theo Epstein need Quinean prediction, while fans keep the religious language of faith, hope, and redemption.

35.title: Tearing Down Fenway Now That Would Be Offensive
35.file: ch35 - Tearing Down Fenway Now That Would Be Offensive.md
35.relation: Mathis argues fans' contempt for ticket resellers is not about being overcharged, since resellers only charge what Fenway's scarcity market will bear. Following Rawls's A Theory of Justice, he treats access to Red Sox tickets as a public good deliberately sheltered from the free market by the random online waiting room, the five-year season-ticket list, baseball's antitrust exemption, and the 1924 Massachusetts anti-scalping law—all of which promote egalitarian access and a sense of community. Reselling offends because it exploits for private profit a good we collectively protect from market forces, as tearing down Fenway itself would.

36.title: November
36.relation: Auxier's rhapsodic essay channels Bart Giamatti ('the Philosopher') on baseball as sacred leisure and uses Pythagoras—everything is Number, each thing's essence an unnamed ratio—to argue the sacred geometry of Fenway cannot be reduced to the dimensions of mere space. He casts the scorecard-keeping quantifiers (Steinbrenner, the Mathematikoi) against the meaning-seeking true believers (Giamatti, the Akousmatikoi), and claims the Yankees' demolition of their own temple, not the 2004 comeback, is what truly lifted the Curse of the Bambino and guarantees Boston will never tear down Fenway. It ends with circular time: the season, like the Babe finishing his career in Boston, always comes home.

37.title: VI - So Good! So Good! So Good!
37.file: ch37 - VI - So Good! So Good! So Good!.md

38.title: Teddy Baseball
38.relation: Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.

39.title: Manny
39.relation: Santaniello reads five nonconformist Red Sox through ethical theory. Ruth's sale to New York becomes a Kantian case: he tore up his signed three-year contract and demanded a trade while expecting others to keep promises, violating the categorical imperative on promise-keeping. Ted Williams's lifelong war with the 'Knights of the Keyboard' exemplifies existentialist authenticity ('It just wouldn't have been me' tipping his cap), Spaceman Bill Lee embodies Sartre's condemned freedom and existence precedes essence, Jim Rice's Hall of Fame delay is Aristotle's failure to hit the mean between silent deficiency on Boston's racism and excess toward reporters, and Manny's 'Gas is up and so am I' money grab shows Aristotle's point that wealth is an incomplete end pursued for the sake of something else.

40.title: Lester’s Duties and Capabilities
40.relation: Maguire asks whether the Royals did wrong by trying to hit in the late innings of Jon Lester's May 2008 no-hitter, working through Kant's distinction between perfect duties (always binding—playing hard, honoring the codified rules) and imperfect duties (praiseworthy obligations that admit exceptions—respecting the unwritten convention against bunting for a hit in a blowout). Sympathy for Lester's cancer recovery must not enter the calculation, since Jim Abbott's 1993 no-hitter shows the duty must universalize; bunting would be 'bush league' rather than wrong, a lapse in imperfect duty. He extends the analysis to Francona's pitch counts and warns that wanting Ellsbury to bunt against a Yankees no-hitter would treat the pitcher as a mere means to fan pride.

41.title: Where in the World(s) Are We
41.file: ch41 - Where in the World(s) Are We.md
41.relation: Ablondi asks whether fans' 'if only' claims—'If Bob Stanley had struck out Mookie Wilson, the Sox would have won in 1986,' 'if Pesky had hurried his relay in 1946'—can be true when they lack truthmakers in the actual world. He presents David Lewis's modal realism and counterpart theory as the standard solution, then objects: a Fisk counterpart with a different body, birthday and nickname, or a Red Sox made of 1986 Mets counterparts, is not recognizably Fisk or the Red Sox, and nobody cares about a Lonborg counterpart who won Game Seven. He concludes counterfactuals need some other explanation and that we should savor the actual Foulke-to-Mientkiewicz final out of 2004 instead.

5.title: A New Lease of Life for the Undead
5.file: ch05 - A New Lease of Life for the Undead.md
5.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the twenty-first-century zombie and vampire boom (Twilight, True Blood, Zombieland, Fido, Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, zombie walks, Humans Versus Zombies) and asks why the Undead fascinate us when bears would not. Its answer contrasts the vampire, who embodies a Nietzschean super-humanity beyond good and evil still charged with unheeded guilt, with the zombie, a sub-Nietzschean, Spinozan force of decomposition where matter interacts with matter beyond all morality. Zombies thus work as hyperdead memento mori: imagining zombiehood lets us imagine our own annihilation as entry into a condition of liberated power, while the obviously unreal monster helps us shut out the real terrors it reflects.

6.title: PART I - It’s Alive (Sort Of)
6.file: ch06 - PART I - It’s Alive (Sort Of).md

7.title: Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It
7.file: ch07 - Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It.md
7.relation: Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead, and why it seems worse than death, testing vampire and zombie cases against the standard accounts of death's badness. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' sets the experiential-blank frame, but Nagel's deprivation view fails because immortal vampires lose far fewer goods than they gain, and Williams's desire-frustration view fails because zombification replaces desires (scotch for blood) rather than frustrating cancelled ones. Mill's 'better Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied' comparison also falls short since it yields only comparative, not objective, badness; Greene concludes Undeath is dreaded because the Undead do evil things, but no argument shows it is objectively bad, so one might as well make the best of it.

8.title: Dead People
8.relation: William Larkin pits Descartes's res cogitans (the person as psychological continuum, reinforced by Locke's prince-and-cobbler body-switch) against a res corporealis view in which bodily continuity suffices for identity, using Romero's Dead films as intuition pumps. The terror of Roger's 'I don't want to be walking around like that' and Rain's request in Resident Evil only makes sense if we think it would be us rising as zombies, and the tragedy of Karen Cooper devouring her father or Johnny menaging Barbara only lands if the same person persists. Against the 'just dead flesh' scientists and the mall-memory reading of Dawn, he argues zombie psychology is merely residual instinct, so our fear and pity reveal we really believe persons survive as corpses, hence as bodies, not as minds.

9.title: Zombies and Us
9.relation: Hamish Thompson asks what could justify killing zombies, canvassing self-defense, total-brain-death criteria, and release from obligations to a radically altered person, using Shaun of the Dead's mother-killing, Bub's trained shooting in Day of the Dead, White Zombie's piano-playing heroine, and the pod-people substitutions of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He deploys Hume's bundle theory of the self as a fiction of succeeding perceptions and Parfit's graded psychological continuity (with Locke's prince/cobbler case) to argue identity comes in degrees, so zombie termination is never as clean as the genre pretends. The chapter ends by turning the lens around: Shaun's checkout-line beepers and Ed's sofa-and-video-game existence suggest ordinary lives differ from zombiehood only by intermittent acts of imaginative self-direction.

10.title: Resting in Peace
10.file: ch10 - Resting in Peace.md
10.relation: Manuel Vargas asks whether the Undead could really be evil and answers that they are probably less likely to be evil than any random living person. Working from a conceptual analysis of what counts as Undead (ruling out p-zombies and Rob Zombie alike), he distinguishes natural-origin Undead (viruses, seeds) from supernatural ones, then applies the account of evil as acting from non-instrumental desires to harm: classical zombies lack the capacities for evil, and even vampires' black reputation traces less to malice than to the creepiness of needing blood, the Dracula/Vlad the Impaler lineage, and lazy 'creepy equals evil' reasoning.

11.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep
11.file: ch11 - Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.md
11.relation: Larry Hauser reads Blade Runner's replicants alongside the philosophical-zombie thought experiment: like Rachel, who passes as human until a Voigt-Kampff test, zombies are outwardly perfect replicas with 'nobody home' inside. He traces the problem from Descartes's beast-automata and hats-and-coats worry about other minds, through Turing's universal machines and Kripke's necessary identifications (water is H2O), to the way zombie scenarios devour behaviorism, functionalism, and mind-brain identity theory, using Searle's silicon-chip replacement to imagine consciousness shrinking while behavior continues. His own 'familiar' and 'super-smart' zombies (a beloved with no qualia, NEXUS-9 geniuses) argue thought without felt experience is conceivable, before he concludes the phenomenal-zombie conception may self-destruct because a first-person point of view requires the very qualia it strips away.

12.title: PART II - Undead White Males
12.file: ch12 - PART II - Undead White Males.md

13.title: Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners
13.file: ch13 - Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners.md
13.relation: Adam Barrows reads Stoker's Dracula through Being and Time: Stoker's staking of Lucy is framed as liberating the 'true' human from the 'false' Undead, and Mina urges pity on the trapped soul, exactly the structure of Heidegger's claim that only facing one's own death alone makes life a bounded, authentic whole. Dracula emerges as the inauthentic 'they' incarnate, with no reflection in mirrors, no fixed likeness in portraits, and a seduction of tranquilizing delay that mirrors how das Man lulls the dying away from their death, so vampire hunting becomes a philosophical task of forcing authenticity on the deathless. The chapter then reverses the charge: given Heidegger's Nazism, Van Helsing's gleeful 'butcher work' and the hunters' expulsion of 'inauthentic' beings from ontological purity implicate audiences as Dracula's 'willing executioners' in a ritual with chilling fascist overtones.

14.title: “Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place
14.file: ch14 - “Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place.md
14.relation: Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead's survivors, who loot the mall, gorge, grow bored, and degenerate into glitzy despair beside the zombies clawing to get back in, through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. Peter's 'They're us' is glossed by pleonexia, the grasping disposition to want more, which Aristotle roots in being serious about mere living rather than living well, and the quartet's hedonistic 'sweet life' is the life of enjoyment Aristotle dismisses as fit for cattle because it atrophies the rational capacities that make us human. Romero is no Puritan scold: material goods remain instrumentally useful and the mall a sanctuary, but like Aristotle he shows a life of unlimited acquisition is a kind of living death, which is why Peter and Fran must leave empty-handed.

15.title: Fast Zombies
15.file: ch15 - Fast Zombies.md
15.relation: K. Silem Mohammad explains the classic slow zombie via Spinoza's account of bodies defined by ratios of motion and rest, where death is no absolute state but a redisposition of parts, so voodoo zombies at industrial modernity's dawn figure alienated labor and Romero's ghouls an impersonal, relentless compulsion. Through Deleuze's reading of composition and decomposition, zombie feeding becomes an ethological process of absorbing other bodies' relations, and Spinoza's replacement of good/evil with good/bad (anticipating Nietzsche) dissolves the zombie's supposed evil into 'bad encounters' between bodies. The fast zombies of 28 Days Later and the Dawn remake then mark a shift from Freudian uncanny return to full-blown crisis: pure rage without hunger or grievance, bodies in faster motion, leaving us an impossible identification with the composition that will decompose us.

16.title: PART III - Dirty Rotting Scoundrels
16.file: ch16 - PART III - Dirty Rotting Scoundrels.md

17.title: Postmodern Postmortem
17.relation: Dale Jacquette distinguishes Hollywood zombies from Chalmers's philosophical zombies, imagining birthmarked beings whose behavior is run entirely by the brain stem so they speak, run corporations, and bleed like conscios while feeling nothing. He then proposes zombie gladiators: since amoral automata cannot suffer or anticipate death, arena blood sport between them seems morally permissible where Roman games condemned by Seneca were not. The thought experiment turns on itself: shielding conscios from attachments and vicarious suffering cannot cure the institution's symbolic statement that killing human-shaped beings for entertainment is fine, so even if consciousness grounds moral responsibility, how we treat the unconscious still reflects on us, and zombies can be wronged in the only sense left, through what we make ourselves.

18.title: Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans
18.file: ch18 - Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans.md
18.relation: John Draeger argues Romero's catatonic zombies, like plants, lack the cognition and empathy to be blamed, while vampires split: Stoker's narcissistic Dracula resembles Cleckley's amoral psychopath Milt, but Coppola's remorseful Dracula, Anne Rice's guilt-tormented Louis, and the self-deceiving Lestat ('the trick is not to think about it') all grasp consequences, feel others' pain, and can exercise self-control, so they are immoral rather than amoral and accountable for their killings. Accountability brings rights: Van Helsing's summary staking is vigilantism that denies Dracula a fair trial, rehabilitable vampires like Louis might earn civic participation, and a nonviolent, honest vampire suitor cannot be rejected merely for being Undead. The principle generalizes to aliens and robots: whatever can reflect morally must be held responsible and treated with equal dignity.

19.title: Cold Clammy Consistency
19.relation: Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.

20.title: Good Guy Vampires
20.relation: Robert Arp models the vampire's unlife with substance and property dualism (a cursed soul persisting after the staked body in Rice and Stoker versus perishing with it in Blade), then uses Mill's distinction between lower bodily feelings and higher mental pleasures from Utilitarianism to explain how vampires can lament, in higher-pain, their inability to enjoy wind in their hair or wine. The hedonistic paradox dooms Lestat-style pleasure-seekers: seeking pleasure for its own sake yields either the pain of frustration (Louis's dead-twins trick) or boredom across immortal lifetimes ('it's somewhat boring, living forever'), while Aristotle's completed-state pleasures suggest the way out. Good guy vampires from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain escape the paradox by pursuing higher pleasures and activities for their own sake, confirming Mill's closing counsel that only those fixed on objects other than their own pleasure find happiness.

21.title: Deserving to Be a Vampire
21.file: ch21 - Deserving to Be a Vampire.md
21.relation: Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through The Lost Boys, Underworld, Blade, Forever Knight, and Interview with the Vampire. He argues vampirism is not intrinsically immoral: if vampires cannot restrain their feeding we pity rather than blame them, though with Aristotle we still hold people responsible for choosing to become the kind of being that cannot; and feeding need be no worse than mortal carnivory, since consensual feeding (Blade's stored blood, Karen Jenson's donation, Madeleine's offer to Louis) makes the bite more like dentistry with consent than assault. On desirability he weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the Furley-Nussbaum claim that death deprives a life of its long-term projects and relationships, concluding immortality's appeal is rational and that boredom is not inevitable in a changing world. The thought experiment ends in ethics: vampire or mortal, a life's worth depends on choices, so live a life worthy of eternity.

22.title: PART IV - Digging Up the Body Politic
22.file: ch22 - PART IV - Digging Up the Body Politic.md

23.title: Possibilities for Human-Vampire Co-operation
23.relation: Douglas Glen Whitman uses Buffy's vampire brothel (humans paying vampires to feed on willing victims, as Giles concedes) and Blade's mandatory blood bank as two models of human-vampire coexistence to stage the clash between libertarianism (Nozick, Lomasky, Schmidtz) and welfarism (Singer, Unger, G.A. Cohen). He runs vampire personhood through Nozick's criteria from Anarchy, State, and Utopia — sentience, self-consciousness, rationality, free will, moral personality, soul — and argues no standard includes humans while excluding vampires, applying Singer's equal-consideration-of-suffering principle across kinds of beings. He then extends Singer's obligation-to-aid reasoning (rescuing a drowning child vs. donating to UNICEF) to show welfarism would mandate forced blood transfers or 'blood stamps', and argues via Adam Smith's Poor Law settlement rules and modern welfare-based anti-immigration politics that the burden of supporting dependents breeds exclusion. Only the libertarian brothel model of voluntary exchange, he concludes, turns vampire-human relations into a positive-sum game in which humans would actually come to recognize vampires as persons.

24.title: A Political Philosophy of Vampires
24.file: ch24 - A Political Philosophy of Vampires.md
24.relation: Phillip Cole starts from Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof, and argues the panics — like the witch craze Trevor-Roper ties to the Reformation's power struggles — reveal how political authorities constitute borders and power by cultivating fear of imaginary enemies. Freud's uncanny (fear not of death but of the returning dead) and Kristeva's abject (the corpse as the ultimate waste) explain why the Undead horrify and fascinate — Scratchy's ever-watching eyes in Itchy and Scratchy, the drowning corpse in Thérèse Raquin, Six Feet Under's serener dead and its wryly absurdist tone — while the vampire also plays the romantic monster of Coppola's Dracula and Interview with the Vampire. Politically the vampire is the demonized outsider — Stoker's unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's asylum seeker or terrorist — and Buffy blurs the boundary by making demons neighbors and Angel and Spike heroes, while the truly shocking killings (Faith's accidental shooting of a human ally, Warren's gunning down of Tara) are human, all too human. The chapter concludes that we should stop mistaking fear-made borders for moral ones and the constructed outsider for a mortal enemy.

25.title: The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization
25.file: ch25 - The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization.md
25.relation: Simon Clark reads Romero's four Dead films through Freud's repressive hypothesis: the zombie is the return of the repressed, an embodiment of Eros and Thanatos whose bite is at once erotic and regressive (the devouring mouth read as the vagina dentata, via Barbara Creed), and it advances exactly as civilization's authority breaks down — Mr. Cooper's failed patriarchy in Night of the Living Dead, the mall turned domain of lawless pleasure in Dawn of the Dead. Against Freud's conclusion that repression is necessary, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization supplies the hope of a non-repressive order in which liberated instinct turns toil into play, which Clark finds realized in Day of the Dead's beach ending, where Sarah, John, and McDermott survive pleasurably in the absence of zombies. Land of the Dead goes further: the zombies under Big Daddy evolve, use tools, and march on Kaufman's skyscraper, so the Undead martyr becomes the pioneer of Marcuse's gratified civilization — though Sarah's closing nightmare keeps Freud's suspicion alive that every order remains repressive.

26.title: No Way Out
26.file: ch26 - No Way Out.md
26.relation: Leah Murray argues Romero's Dead films stage the American contest between individualism and communitarianism inside the social contract: in Night of the Living Dead, communitarian Ben barricading the farmhouse against every-man-for-himself Mr. Cooper hiding in the basement; in Dawn of the Dead, the Peter-Roger-Fran-Stephen mall commune collapsing when Stephen's 'it's ours, we took it' meets the bikers; in Day of the Dead, Sarah's compassion against the racist, harassing soldiers; in Land of the Dead, Kaufman's Fiddler's Green as a Hobbesian Leviathan born of fear, complete with bread-and-circuses for the poor. Against the Hobbesian fear-born contract (Dawn opens in a full state-of-nature collapse) she sets Rousseau's general will and Tocqueville's civic association, embodied in Riley's freely formed community and in Big Daddy's zombies, who organize, turn from eating humans, and bring down the Leviathan. The films' verdict: fear-based individualist contracts collapse under their own contradictions, while compassionate cooperation — even among the Undead — is the only way out, even if Romero doubts its ultimate viability.

27.title: PART V - Leaving a Good-Looking Corpse
27.file: ch27 - PART V - Leaving a Good-Looking Corpse.md

28.title: The Meta-Fear of Fear
28.relation: Noël Carroll reconstructs Halloween's Undead iconography from the Celtic Samhain and Pope Gregory's absorption of it into All Hallows' Eve, then poses the paradox that people pay to be terrified by corpse imagery they would flee in a real morgue — odd, given Heidegger's point that the Angst of death is so deep we spend our lives denying it. He tests Ernest Jones's Freudian reading of the nightmare — the vampire revenant as a disguised, disavowed incest wish — and rejects it as a Rube-Goldberg apparatus requiring universal incestuous desire and the whole machinery of the unconscious, when sometimes a zombie is just a zombie and The Fog is simply frightening. His own hypothesis: horror films and Halloween give viewers, especially anxious adolescents, a controlled trial run of fear that eases the meta-fear of fear itself, with Bergson's 'anaesthesis of the heart' explaining why Halloween parody and laughter serve the same emotional-control function as the scares.

29.title: The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of
29.file: ch29 - The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of.md
29.relation: Joan Grassbaugh Forry argues the 'vampire aesthetic' both enforces and destabilizes constructed norms of beauty and gender, reading vampire representation through Foucault's made soldier (the body produced by discipline rather than nature) and the Bartky-Bordo feminist analysis of disciplinary beauty practices. Vampires are effortlessly, youthfully beautiful — exempt from the dieting, grooming, and ornamentation that produce femininity — yet their beauty must appear natural, which is exactly the demand beauty culture makes of women; Queen Akasha, Drusilla, and child-vampire Claudia are ultra-feminine femmes fatale whose threat is neutralized by childlike femininity and punished by death or ridicule (Claudia ashes in the sunlight, Drusilla is made to look foolish), while the feminized male protagonists — Louis and Armand in Interview with the Vampire, Angel and nail-polishing, Passions-watching Spike in Buffy, Langella's elegant Dracula — turn beauty, taste, and expressed emotion into audience identification and beautiful martyrdom. The payoff: in the realm of the Undead the male vampire becomes a beautiful martyr while the female vampire becomes a disastrous woman we love to hate.

30.title: Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood
30.file: ch30 - Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood.md
30.relation: Rachel Robison asks why mythology — from Elizabeth Bathory's blood baths to Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, and True Blood's Sookie sensing and desiring Bill and then Eric — credits blood with immortality, youth, erotic compulsion, and shared knowledge, including the vampire's dark inversion of the Eucharist. Her answer runs through the history of philosophy and medicine: Aristotle, Empedocles, and Chrysippus located rationality in the heart and made blood its product, while Galen's humoral theory and bloodletting treated blood as the carrier of health, temperament, and identity — so blood naturally reads as the vehicle of personal identity, free will, and even knowledge, explaining how drinking it could transmit a maker's self to Sookie or Mina. She then asks whether the synthetic 'True Blood' of HBO's show could carry the same powers, concluding it works only if some property is shared with real blood or if the power attaches to the act of drinking what is taken as blood.

31.title: A Meditation on the Word
31.file: ch31 - A Meditation on the Word.md
31.relation: Randall Auxier and Eileen Townsend stage the chapter as fiction: letters, emails, IMs, and texts (1983-2009) between the ancient vampire Étienne Lavec and the newly turned Memphis student Paulie, through which shifting vampire pop culture — Anne Rice, Buffy, True Blood, and Twilight's sparkling, animal-only Cullens — is debated. Lavec's embedded 'Meditation on the Word' recasts the Johannine Logos so that vampires are pure desire, the uncreated darkness at the border of God's light, and his biography enacts the thesis: a Latin Averroist student of Siger de Brabant who drained Aquinas over the Summa's Treatise on Angels writing vampires out of existence, and a collector who hunted or interviewed Royce, Pico della Mirandola, Descartes, Spinoza, Hegel, Kierkegaard, and Nietzsche, whose 'free death' and 'beyond good and evil' he claims as stolen vampire ideas. The running gag and argument is Foucault, whose account of institutions (medicine, psychology, prison) creating their objects Lavec endorses as the order of desire, but who, half-undead after Lavec's failed bite and taunting him anonymously as 'nietzsche26', finally lures him into a trap in the Paris catacombs.

7.title: A Reply to facebook Critics
7.file: ch07 - A Reply to facebook Critics.md
7.relation: Wittkower answers critics who call Facebook broadcast narcissism by way of Sartre: Facebook actions (pokes, the Disney Princess quiz, cats friending cats on Catbook) have no given meaning, so users and their friends create it, which is why there are 'so many different Facebooks'. He takes up Sunstein's 'Daily Me' echo-chamber worry and Hegel's claim that real freedom means choosing within community, arguing Facebook merely makes the dialectic between chosen and unchosen communities explicit. Against the charge that status updates are trivial, he deploys Nietzsche's Last Man and Schopenhauer's cheese-mite microscope to defend caring about a friend's sandwich from the inside of a shared life.

8.title: Who Uses facebook and Why
8.file: ch08 - Who Uses facebook and Why.md
8.relation: Gil de Zuniga and Valenzuela report their 2009 survey of 1,482 Americans on social network site use: 41 percent of adults use them, with women, African Americans, and Hispanics using them more than white men and with use spread across income and education levels. The top motivation is staying in touch with existing family and friends, but users also meet new people, discuss issues, follow news, and join causes. They argue these patterns suggest SNSs may narrow the digital divide and support democratic participation rather than being a teenage fad.

9.title: facebook Itself - The Medium Sent You a Message on facebook
9.file: ch09 - facebook Itself - The Medium Sent You a Message on facebook.md

10.title: 1 - The Privacy Virus
10.file: ch10 - 1 - The Privacy Virus.md
10.relation: Grimmelmann argues the claim that 'kids these days don't care about privacy' gets Facebook users wrong: they untag keg-stand photos, protest the News Feed launch, and reject friend requests because they care about contextual privacy - respect for the rules of distinct social contexts - rather than secrecy. The skeptic's public/private secrecy model mispredicts this, since posting to 300 friends is not broadcasting to the world. But Facebook is still a 'privacy virus': its architecture defeats the everyday 'know your audience' and 'safety in numbers' rules of thumb, so contextual violations like Bono's leaked photo albums and the accidental Christmas-ring announcement happen anyway.

11.title: 2 - It’s Like Talking to a Wall
11.file: ch11 - 2 - It’s Like Talking to a Wall.md
11.relation: Meikle analyzes Facebook as media convergence: status updates and wall posts blur one-to-one communication with the broadcast 'message addressed to nobody in particular', reaching an undifferentiated friend list that mixes intimates, colleagues, and people one dislikes. Cases like the MI6 chief's wife's holiday photos, Amanda Knox's 'Foxy Knoxy' nickname, the Dartmouth professor's Wikipedia lecture note, and the Dunblane survivors story show how private turns instantly public, from Bozeman's password demand to tabloid mining of profiles. He concludes that Facebook demands an ethics of online communication: who gets access to what we generate, and what may they do with it.

12.title: 3 - Ian Became a Fan of Marshall McLuhan on facebook and Suggested You Become
12.file: ch12 - 3 - Ian Became a Fan of Marshall McLuhan on facebook and Suggested You Become.md
12.relation: Bogost applies McLuhan - media as extensions of man, whose form rather than content is what matters - and the tetrad of media effects to Facebook, opening with his own inability to join the UCLA network to show that properties, not gripes, deserve study. He builds a full tetrad: Facebook enhances the directory, the yearbook, and nowness; obsolesces the reunion, memory, and the secret; retrieves the small town, the hang-out, and the diary; and reverses into campus life and high school. The point is that no medium is simply good or bad, and the tetrad itself becomes one more medium Facebook absorbs.

13.title: 4 - With Friends Like These, Who Needs Enemies
13.file: ch13 - 4 - With Friends Like These, Who Needs Enemies.md
13.relation: Losh reads Facebook games (Zombies, Mob Wars, Scrabulous, Parking Wars, PackRat, (Lil) Green Patch, Mafia Wars) through Goffman's 'face' and Brown and Levinson's positive/negative politeness: recruiting friends into an application is a face-threatening imposition that becomes awkward across professor-student and parent-child hierarchies playing as nominal equals. She invokes Derrida on Mauss - 'there is no gift without bond, without bind' - to analyze the reciprocity obligations of gifting games, and finds emergent cooperative norms like PackRat pacts against tit-for-tat stealing. Players revolt when developers monetize asymmetrical play, showing communities negotiate the rules of the magic circle.

14.title: The Profile and the Self - Is the Profile More Like a Door, a Window, or a Painting
14.file: ch14 - The Profile and the Self - Is the Profile More Like a Door, a Window, or a Painting.md

15.title: 5 - Profile Picture, Right Here, Right Now
15.file: ch15 - 5 - Profile Picture, Right Here, Right Now.md
15.relation: Sarachan uses Barthes's Camera Lucida - punctum, studium, and the 'air' of the subject - to argue Facebook profile pictures are all punctum: ephemeral images constantly replaced to strike the viewer instantly, unlike the static yearbook photo. He sorts profile pictures by Barthes's six categories (pose at the webcam, hiding behind objects, Photoshop trick effects, photogenia, aestheticism, syntax) and reads pop-culture avatar images as identity claims. He closes with Benjamin's mechanical reproduction: a webcam image has no original, existing only as infinitely copied bits that paradoxically exist only when someone views the page.

16.title: 6 - You Can’t Front on facebook
16.file: ch16 - 6 - You Can’t Front on facebook.md
16.relation: Marinucci opens with Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic - invisibility licenses injustice because we care about seeming good - and maps it onto Suler's six factors of online disinhibition (anonymity, invisibility, asynchronicity, solipsism, dissociation, minimized authority). Facebook, she argues, lacks all six: real names and offline friends, near-synchronous news feeds, and the integration of every audience from mom to students into one space keep us inhibited. That inhibition is a good thing, since it prevents 'fronting' - presenting a false face to each audience - so Facebook identity integration can foster more authentic self-expression.

17.title: 7 - Why I Am Not a Friend
17.file: ch17 - 7 - Why I Am Not a Friend.md
17.relation: Thalos argues she is not a 'friend' on Facebook because bonding requires credible, fixed self-presentation, and a profile 'can lie like a rug' since everything on it is elective and revisable at whim. Through Sartre's phenomenology of the gaze - being displaced from Subject to object-for-another when caught in another's look - she explains why face-to-face interaction alone builds the mutual bonds and social intelligence we rely on. With Beauvoir she shows how the gaze also carries power, marking woman as the Other, and warns that Facebook's plastic faces offer choice without traction, inhibiting both true bonding and resistance to subjugating looks.

18.title: 8 - Playing Around with Identity
18.file: ch18 - 8 - Playing Around with Identity.md
18.relation: Wandel and Beavers take Groundhog Day's Phil Connors as the model of trying on selves, and apply Goffman's dramaturgical Presentation of Self to see Facebook as a stage where users experiment with identity. Because friends from every part of life watch at once, a 'restraint of accountability' disciplines pretending, much like childhood pretend play or a fraternity's teasing calls members to account for their oddities. Against critics who see fragmentation and narcissism, they argue this dynamic can support becoming who one already is - a more authentic, grounded self - closing with Plato's 'Life must be lived as play'.

19.title: 9 - Spectacle 2.0
19.relation: Vejby and Wittkower ask whether Facebook is Spectacle 2.0 by applying Debord's Society of the Spectacle: on the pessimistic reading, Facebook makes friendship a spectator sport where we alternate between watching friends and performing for them, with corporate owners setting the protocols. They then turn to the Situationist constructive side - situations, dérive, détournement - reading lolcats, rickrolling, and the parody status updates ('Facebook will automatically start plunging the Earth into the Sun') as playful détournement that approaches media as active agents. Their verdict is suspended: the new spectacle co-opts our participation, so the imperative either way is to repurpose, subvert, and play.

20.title: facebook Friends - BBFs, Creepers, That Hawt Guy from Last Night, and Mom
20.file: ch20 - facebook Friends - BBFs, Creepers, That Hawt Guy from Last Night, and Mom.md

21.title: 10 - Why Can’t We Be Virtual Friends
21.file: ch21 - 10 - Why Can’t We Be Virtual Friends.md
21.relation: Condella tests Facebook friendship against Aristotle's three kinds (pleasure, utility, virtue) from Nicomachean Ethics VIII-IX and Cicero's De Amicitia: the average user's 281 friends far exceeds true philia, which needs time, reciprocated goodwill, and shared 'conversation and thought'.
