He grants that Facebook's status updates share conversation and thought and maintain ties across distance, evoking the Seinfeld episode where Jerry refuses Keith Hernandez's too-early request to help him move. But because no one has ever helped a friend move on Facebook, virtual presence cannot make us better people, and Facebook's artificial buoying of dead friendships of utility risks quantity crowding out the few deep friendships that matter.

22.title: 11 - The Friendship that Makes No Demands
22.file: ch22 - 11 - The Friendship that Makes No Demands.md
22.relation: Tedesco sets Facebook's demand-free friendship against the modern moral requirement of impartiality, running from Godwin's burning-archbishop case through Bentham's 'everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one' and Williams's 'one thought too many' objection. He canvasses the escapes - Mill's rarely-demanded public benefactor, Singer's global village where aid is a click away, Jackson's sector plan and Railton's sophisticated consequentialism - and finds each inadequate to friendship's partiality. Facebook friendship looks like a third way that reconciles the two, but it turns out only to be friendship where it supplements a real offline relationship, so the impartiality problem stands.

23.title: 12 - Care Ethics, Friendship, and facebook
23.file: ch23 - 12 - Care Ethics, Friendship, and facebook.md
23.relation: Hamington surveys a hundred Facebook users and argues, through care ethics — Noddings's 'here I am' disposition and her natural versus ethical caring — that Facebook can make us more ethical, because the stream of small particulars about friends supplies the knowledge that is a necessary condition for caring. He uses Benhabib's concrete other to explain how status updates make distant lives 'real' to us, and confesses his own de-friending of a student over a racist comment as a case of Facebook's convenience making it easy not to care. The chapter ends by claiming Facebook dissolves the binary of close friend versus nodding acquaintance into a postmodern range of fluid, mediating friendships, while insisting caring is learned through the body and merely extended, not replaced, in virtual space.

24.title: 13 - What Are Friends For
24.relation: Bloor reads Facebook anxiety through Heidegger's diagnosis of technological nihilism — an efficiency-driven 'being-in-the-world' with no shared arbiter of what matters — borrowing Dreyfus's HAL 9000 example from 2001: A Space Odyssey to show humans enhancing themselves like any other raw material. He argues Facebook's speed lures users into unreflective sharing and standardized behavior where the quirky authentic 'I' dissolves into Heidegger's 'one,' and recruits Aristotle's view that only a few deep friendships morally form us to warn that hundreds of contacts fragment that benefit. Adorno on leisure as mere recuperation between bouts of work frames the therapist who keeps Facebook strictly professional, and the chapter concludes the fault lies in ourselves, not the tools — suggesting a week offline as a test.

25.title: Social Networking - How to Win Virtual Friends and Influence Virtual People
25.file: ch25 - Social Networking - How to Win Virtual Friends and Influence Virtual People.md
25.relation: Written as a breakup letter to Facebook, the chapter first reconstructs the Frankfurt School hope that new media could overcome old mass media's passivity — Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, Althusser's ideology as the form of media — and then tests the site against Ivan Illich's criteria for 'convivial tools.' Briggle finds Facebook fails on Illich's terms: its public walls and News Feed force self-censored persona management before a mixed audience, and its shapeless, undifferentiated flood of updates leaves the user disoriented like Nietzsche's madman after the death of God. Because the site's 'grain' channels users into 'reluctant, hapless exhibitionism' and even imposes the obligation to join, he logs off, concluding that tools reflect our image more than they remake it.

26.title: 15 - Gossip and the Evolution of facebook
26.file: ch26 - 15 - Gossip and the Evolution of facebook.md
26.relation: Cuonzo imports Robin Dunbar's gossip theory — that language evolved to build alliances by replacing primate grooming once groups grew past roughly 150 — to present Facebook as the same efficiency leap in social bonding, where one status update reaches thousands and pokes, virtual flowers, and food gifts revive pre-linguistic bonding gestures. She then argues Facebook is a new form of communication rather than a mere new vehicle: pictorial, non-verbal practices like SuperPoke are not translatable into ordinary language, an inference that assumes meanings are fixed by a community's linguistic practices. The social bonds it forms are correspondingly novel — informational and esteem-building rather than the physical mutual aid that once anchored alliances.

27.title: 16 - facebook as an Excess of Seeing
27.file: ch27 - 16 - facebook as an Excess of Seeing.md
27.relation: Lattimore frames the teacher-student Facebook encounter with Bakhtin's 'excess of seeing' — the viewer always sees more of a person than the person can see of themselves (their face, the world behind their back) and so 'consummates' them — warning against building a 'creepy treehouse' by co-opting students' network for classwork. She explains generational differences in use (her under-25 students' in-joke statuses versus colleagues' quiz posts) through Goffman and Bateson's frames, Granovetter's weak ties, and Strauss and Howe's lifecycle phases, arguing each cohort frames the network differently. Practicing Bakhtin's sympathetic projection into another's profile lets users see themselves as others see them, so that no single photo or quiz consummates a life.

28.title: 17 - Do Status Updates Have Any Value
28.file: ch28 - 17 - Do Status Updates Have Any Value.md
28.relation: Fairweather and Halpern answer the Facebook-skeptic who dismisses status updates as vanity by reading them through Hume's 'natural sympathy' — our disinterested fellow-feeling with any well-presented human sentiment — which they identify with Clive Thompson's 'ambient awareness,' the pointillist portrait assembled from mundane updates. They argue Facebook's structure is a 'great equalizer': because friends need not know one another, no dominance hierarchies or intimacy rituals form, removing offline barriers to sympathy. The first-person, here-and-now grammar of updates invites exactly the quasi-first-personal curiosity that empathy requires, though they concede one-way, unanswered updates may show only that 'the machinery of morality' is revved up, not that users are morally improved.

29.title: 18 - Gatekeeper, Moderator, Synthesizer
29.relation: Butera casts Facebook's three core features as instruments of control: friending is a 'gatekeeper' admitting selected others, the status update a 'moderator' constantly re-authoring the avatar's identity for multiple audiences, and the News Feed a 'synthesizer' that assembles a filtered pseudo-community where friends can be hidden or stalked invisibly. Reading this through Baudrillard's 'promiscuity' of communication networks — the extermination of the interstitial space where the social happens — and Kierkegaard's case that a meaningful life requires openness to the unknown, he weighs unrestricted community as authentic contact against the gated community that keeps exchange meaningful. The defunct no-privacy experiment Buddytown serves as counterpoint, and he concludes that some gatekeeping is essential lest connectivity become an overwhelming flood of nonsense.

30.title: Activity and Passivity - Maybe Se Puede!
30.file: ch30 - Activity and Passivity - Maybe Se Puede!.md

31.title: 19 - facebook, Surveillance and Power
31.relation: Doyle and Fraser open with the Lady Shelley Sawers affair, in which Britain's new MI6 chief was exposed by his wife's public Facebook profile, to ask whether social networks democratize surveillance or perfect it. They read the CIA's social-media monitoring, the Chris Dreyfus promotion case, and Facebook's Beacon advertising scheme through Foucault — Bentham's Panopticon, the carceral continuum, regimes of truth, and the shift to statistically managing populations — arguing that narcissistic self-display makes people 'most controllable,' while Habermas's public sphere frames the hopeful side: Beacon's defeat by user protest, Glassdoor, and Iran's Twitter revolution as diffused power against the centralized state. Foucault's answer is neither utopia nor repression but an ethics of self-management for playing power games with minimum domination.

32.title: 20 - Wall to Wall or Face to Face
32.file: ch32 - 20 - Wall to Wall or Face to Face.md
32.relation: Bar-Tura, a Chicago Jewish social-justice organizer, evaluates Facebook by Habermas's ideal speech situation — equal chances to speak, initiate, and question, aimed at consensus — recounting how Jewish and Muslim teens scheduled to bowl together first met online and shed stereotypes by browsing each other's profiles. Yet face-to-face planning surfaced what wall-to-wall could not: the Shabbat timing question, and Muslim parents' unease about a north-side venue, which revealed socio-economic and racial divides rather than religious ones. Fixed, market-driven profile categories and the 'Daily Me' of niche idea consumption limit Facebook as a public sphere, so profiles must become people and the group must actually gather for social change.

33.title: 21 - facebook as Playground and Factory
33.file: ch33 - 21 - facebook as Playground and Factory.md
33.relation: Scholz argues Facebook is both playground and factory: a space of publics where, in the Arendtian sense he opens with, power is 'the potential to act together,' and a machine that expropriates play as 'interactivity labor' — attention sold to advertisers, ten thousand volunteers translating the interface into sixty-three languages, and data trails aggregated, sold, and locked in a walled garden ('you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave'). Quoting Tim O'Reilly's 'they are participating without thinking that they participate,' he claims users generate surplus value they never see, while 'user uprisings' against the News Feed are mere Debordian spectacles of Internet democracy — enhanced consumer feedback loops. He ends by asking how to secure self-disclosure and meaningful collective action, pointing to non-commercial alternatives like Crabgrass, inside 'the playground that is a factory.'

34.title: 22 - The Proles and Cons of facebook
34.file: ch34 - 22 - The Proles and Cons of facebook.md
34.relation: Morgan and Clulow stage a second-person narrative in which the reader joins a friend's 'Against Corporate Polluters' Cause and receives a manifesto opening with the Communist Manifesto's 'history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles,' updating the proletariat into the internet-era 'iProles' via a mock discussion board voiced by Chomsky, Engels, Luxemburg, and Liebknecht. Facebook's global reach builds real coalitions — the group links up with Iranian environmentalists — but distraction, fragmented duplicate groups, one-click commitment (the 200,000-member 'Obama Grow an Afro' group dwarfing a 57-member Kyoto group), and Facebook's corporate power to silence users (Kieron Bimpson's 'Justice for Francesca' group deleted as spam) blunt its activist promise. Only disciplined uses like Obama's campaign and Carrotmob convert the network into offline change — and elites can play on the same platform.

35.title: 23 - Faking It on facebook
35.relation: Muhr and Pedersen apply Žižek's interpassivity — canned laughter and hired funeral 'weepers' that enjoy or mourn on our behalf — to Facebook, arguing the profile is a surrogate self that enjoys, believes, and suffers for us while being frantically kept alive like a Tamagotchi. The motive, they argue, is escape from the demands of the symbolic order (the Lacanian system of social expectations Žižek works with): our offline identity is 'already a mask,' and Facebook defers rather than removes the duty to be a good, enjoying, authentic person. Since, as in Žižek's comparison of German, French, and American toilets, ideology operates at the level of action rather than belief, users 'fake it till they make it' — performing vibrant, interesting lives until the faked feelings become real.

3.title: Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch
3.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

7.title: Warm-up
7.relation: Editor Ted Richards's introduction strips soccer to its one rule—move the ball into the net without using your hands—and argues that the passions this simple game ignites across every nation, class, age, and gender must spring from the same human wellspring as philosophy itself, so that studying soccer is a study of humanity. He frames the volume's perennial questions (what makes a thing that thing, what is the right thing to do, what makes something beautiful) as arising out of our being rather than academic invention, and previews the book's pairing of philosophers (Kierkegaard, Aristotle, Plato, Nietzsche, Kant, Dewey, Sartre) with players (Pelé, Maradona, Zidane, Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi, Fàbregas, Beckenbauer) across thirty-one chapters by forty authors from fifteen countries.

9.title: FIRST HALF - The Nature of the Game
9.file: ch09 - FIRST HALF - The Nature of the Game.md

10.title: Football as Part of Real Life
10.file: ch10 - Football as Part of Real Life.md
10.relation: Hoyningen-Huene asks why anyone cheers a ball crossing an arbitrarily defined line and answers with his thesis that football re-enacts the drama of life: an unpredictable, fractal mixture of ability and chance—from a bobbling pitch to Manchester United's 1999 injury-time comeback and Maradona's unpunished Hand of God—mirroring the luck, skill, and irreversible injustice of real life. He analyzes the Laws of the Game as having four functions: guaranteeing equal conditions, generating analogies to life's drama, ending the drama at a knowable moment (unlike life's open-ended conflicts), and keeping the game safely distanced from real seriousness, which is why he reads hooligans as people who cognitively mistake the game's drama for a real-life fight. Finally he argues that money, careers, betting, and even the political channeling of Hungary's 1954 World Cup defeat into the 1956 uprising are secondary entanglements parasitic on a primary fascination already present in a nameless village-league match, which no other sport matches in variability of the ability–chance mixture.

11.title: The Good Gossip
11.file: ch11 - The Good Gossip.md
11.relation: Borge weighs Jimmy Sirrel's claim that the best team always wins and the rest is gossip against Alex Ferguson insisting his side played better in a 1–4 defeat to Liverpool, framing the dispute as football Nominalism (only particular matches and results exist) versus football Platonism (an ideal way of playing exists over and above results). He rejects the Platonic ideal as metaphysically impossible—two perfect teams could never both score on every chance while conceding nothing, and style comparisons like catenaccio versus Brazil 1970 collapse without appeal to results—and instead uses possible-worlds counterfactuals: a team can be 'really' best yet unlucky when it creates objective scoring opportunities, like John Terry's slipped 2008 Champions League penalty or Spain's wrongly disallowed golden goal against South Korea in 2002, that go in across the closest possible worlds. Since Liverpool's deeply unfair 2005 comeback in Istanbul is celebrated as a classic, football is fiction and drama rather than a fairness-measuring contest, and the resulting what-if moaning is the good gossip that makes barstool debate worthwhile.

12.title: Oh to Be a Gooner
12.file: ch12 - Oh to Be a Gooner.md
12.relation: Kilpatrick reads Nietzsche's madman's question 'what sacred games shall we have to invent?' as answered by the stadium: after the death of God, soccer has replaced religion as the shared narrative where modern communities make and worship heroes. Using The Birth of Tragedy, he reads a goal as an Apollonian–Dionysian fusion—the scorer's individuated ecstasy merging with the collective joy of teammates and fans—and, on Nietzsche's claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, argues the game is defensible only when played creatively and artistically rather than by negative, win-at-all-costs tactics. Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism (the state as 'the new idol', the 'good European', Zarathustra's 'children's land') means club over country, and Wenger's Arsenal—with its dietary and training laboratory at London Colney cultivating an Overman, its Invincibles season, and its young, passport-blind signings—emerges as the club Nietzsche would support through its very will-to-power.

13.title: Extra Time
13.file: ch13 - Extra Time.md
13.relation: Kent argues soccer is Aristotle's favorite sport because everything in both is organized around the goal: the four causes explain shinguards (plastic, curved shape, Mitre's workers, protection) and the game itself, with the final cause—scoring—defining a thing's identity and goodness, so two differently made balls are both soccerballs if kicked toward a net. Soccer best fulfills sport's three purposes (physical and moral discipline, theatrical imitation with catharsis, recreation): its ninety minutes of uninterrupted continuity force hundreds of renewed acts of self-mastery in Aristotle's sense of courage and the right amount, its single referee with limited powers embodies Aristotle's preferred limited monarchy, and Argentina's sportsmanlike throw-in returning the ball after Cameroon kicks it out for an injured player exemplifies equity—making a rightful exception to the letter of the law. Own goals, where a defender's error harms his own side, supply the hamartia of Aristotelian tragedy, giving fans a healthy catharsis of pity and fear.

14.title: How Beckenbauer and Zidane Practiced the Four Cardinal Virtues
14.file: ch14 - How Beckenbauer and Zidane Practiced the Four Cardinal Virtues.md
14.relation: Coumoundouros explains soccer greatness through three Platonic ideas: the Form of the footballer, which Pelé (1,281 goals, three World Cups, the save by Banks his header 'infected' with greatness and the infamous miss against Uruguay) and Maradona (the Hand of God and the Goal of the Century past five English defenders) approximate as near-perfect imitations, with position-specific Forms like forward Form for Pelé and attacking-midfielder Form for Maradona. Excellence as performing a proper function well (Republic 353a) then accounts for modern players—Ronaldo's evolved winger role, Henry converted by Wenger into a striker, Marta averaging a goal per game proving women's soccer equals the men's. Finally the Republic's four cardinal virtues grounded in the tripartite soul apply off and on the pitch: Beckenbauer playing the 1970 'Game of the Century' with a fractured clavicle and marshaling the 1974 final shows courage, wisdom, and moderation in just balance, while Zidane's 2006 head-butt on Materazzi shows the spirited part overwhelming reason, and with it greatness itself.

15.title: But an FC Bot-celona
15.file: ch15 - But an FC Bot-celona.md
15.relation: Drawing on their RoboCup experience—including the first human-versus-autonomous-robot exhibitions against Osnabrück (2007) and Stuttgart (2009), which the humans easily won—the authors ask whether robots could ever play rather than merely mimic soccer, proposing a modified Turing test: if a robot team's match is recognizable to fans as soccer, robots can play. Since the Laws of the Game tacitly assume human players, they design rules for a human–robot match that preserve soccer's essence—a game of limited, differently capable, fully autonomous players who must pass and move off the ball—banning goal-sized robot walls, wireless communication, software-coach micromanagement, and superhuman speed or size, much as tournament chess had to adapt its rules for Deep Blue versus Kasparov and as Oscar Pistorius's blades raised fairness questions in the Olympics. A robot victory under these 'stacked against the machines' rules, they conclude, could only come from better finesse, teamwork, and vision, and would settle on the pitch whether an FC Bot-celona can genuinely play the beautiful game.

16.title: Added Time
16.file: ch16 - Added Time.md
16.relation: McDermid takes Maradona's cheeky 'a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God' claim literally and asks what would make either 1986 goal against England—the obvious handball or the Goal of the Century—a miracle, using Aquinas's definition of miracles as intentional divine acts beyond the order commonly observed in nature. He explores how God could intervene without breaking natural law, analogizing God to a goalkeeper exempt from the handball rule or a spectator outside the game: in a deterministic world He could only arrange initial conditions (a domino setup requiring fine-tuning at the Big Bang), while in an indeterministic quantum world He could load the chancy micro-events along Maradona's mazy, sensitively balanced run. Hume's empiricist argument against miracles then shows we could never be justified in believing either goal miraculous, since the mundane explanation—Maradona's cheek and skill, lapses of concentration, a missed handball call—always has the whole of past experience on its side.

18.title: Luck as Anathema
18.file: ch18 - Luck as Anathema.md
18.relation: Eylon and Horowitz defend the maligned manager's excuse 'we outplayed them and were plain unlucky' by distinguishing genuine football luck from fluke-luck: unlike sprinting, where outrunning your opponent and finishing fourth is incoherent, football's rules constitute rather than merely measure the skill, and 'almosts'—Roritania City hitting the woodwork eight times while United's one sloppy shot goes in—show ability and success genuinely coming apart. The accusation that football rewards the undeserving then exposes the control condition of moral desert, illustrated by two assassins whose shots differ only by an intervening swallow and by a never-bribed referee who would have taken the money, so that the luck football manifestly displays infects morality and politics generally. Football is anathema to some fans precisely because, unlike life where luck also rules, it displays luck inside an activity explicitly designed to reward merit—yet the authors conclude that 'almosts' and the all-or-nothing scoring are also the source of the game's beauty, and nobody who loves it would have luck removed.

19.title: Does Life Imitate Soccer
19.relation: Minister condemns 'negative soccer'—Sunderland at 28% possession and zero shots at Old Trafford, Stoke's goalless stalemate at Anfield, Bolton's two shots at the Emirates—through Nietzsche's genealogy of morality: teams that recognize superior opponents redefine the game's goal in slave-like resentment, replacing the pursuit of excellence, creativity, courage, and honor with a safety-first legalism of not losing, just as individual diving (Ronaldo's 'superman' dive, Drogba's histrionics) betrays the strong character, while Di Canio catching the ball for the injured keeper and Arshavin protesting his own penalty display honor. Marx then explains why the tactic is structural rather than a personal failing: Premier League revenue gaps, Champions League money, Abramovich's Chelsea billions, and the $55 million cost of relegation economically compel small clubs into what Minister reads as Marxian alienation—players unable to express themselves or flourish because economic forces dictate their play. He ends asking whether life imitates soccer: whether our own financial pressures likewise price excellence, honor, and self-expression out of ordinary lives.

20.title: Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies
20.file: ch20 - Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies.md
20.relation: Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.

21.title: SECOND HALF - The Beautiful Game
21.file: ch21 - SECOND HALF - The Beautiful Game.md

22.title: Why More Beautiful Means Morally Better
22.file: ch22 - Why More Beautiful Means Morally Better.md
22.relation: Durà-Vilà distinguishes narrow on-pitch morality (condemning dives, feigned fouls, and simulation, which no cultural permissiveness justifies) from a broader ethics of how one conducts a fulfilling life, and argues football should be appreciated two-dimensionally—result and aesthetic pleasure together—as shown by Barcelona and Real Madrid fans who grow angry at ugly play even in victory. His positive thesis is that playing beautifully is morally better: the aesthetic tradition of the Brazilian and Dutch schools, Michels and Cruyff's total football flowing into Guardiola's Barcelona, Wenger's Arsenal, and the Spain of Xavi and Iniesta promotes life-enhancing values of creativity, skill, and vision, while results-only football invites the tricks of technically limited players and managers. He concedes a dull team could be narrowly moral and a beautiful team could still dive, but maintains that beauty makes unethical play less sensible and more perverse, and that aesthetic football carries values worth exporting beyond the pitch.

23.title: The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again)
23.file: ch23 - The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again).md
23.relation: Winters celebrates the goalkeeper's fingertip save—Gordon Banks denying Pelé's header in 1970—as football's aesthetic summit, reading the keeper as the lonely, 'stark mad' outsider of existentialist fiction, a lineage he anchors in Camus, the goalkeeper of Algiers who said all he knew of morality he learnt from football. Kant supplies both the dove of the first Critique—needing the air's resistance, just as the tango's strict steps enable the dancer's personality—and the target of critique: against Kantian disinterested contemplation, he adopts Graham's Nietzschean, Dionysiac aesthetics of participation, so spectators proprioceptively feel the keeper twisting in mid-air, as Wittgenstein's question about the galloping horse picture suggests the movement enters our muscles and joints. Understanding a save or a back-heel means seeing it under a general type ('that' free kick, 'that' volley, from Beckham at Wembley back to Garrincha), and Bloch's ruminations in Handke's The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick show the keeper alone at the liminal limit where concession and prevention meet.

24.title: Beyond Picasso and Ronaldo Living Artfully
24.file: ch24 - Beyond Picasso and Ronaldo Living Artfully.md
24.relation: Elcombe asks whether Cristiano Ronaldo, transferred to Real Madrid for $131 million—more than Picasso's Garçon à la Pipe fetched at its record 2004 auction—can be an artist like Picasso. Traditional metaphysics built on Plato's perfect Forms and Aristotle's necessary-and-sufficient conditions locks Art in a special museum realm that soccer, as a purposive sport whose beauty is only a byproduct, can never enter, leaving the game merely 'beautiful', not Art. Dewey's Art as Experience reorients the question from what art is to what art does: artworks are consummations of experience, moments of 'thatness'—that meal, that storm, that Ronaldo free kick—that lift us out of the mundane while remaining within the game's durable rules and history (Ronaldo's artistry grows from Zidane, Maradona, Cruyff, Pelé). On this pragmatist view Ronaldo is an artist in the act, the six-year-old testing a new turn on the pitch lives artfully too, and soccer's artistry becomes groundwork for communication, democracy, and the good life—doing more real work than a painting almost no one ever sees.

25.title: VHS, DVD, YouTube
25.relation: Vargiu seats Kant in the Maracanã grandstand (after the Monty Python philosopher match) to test aesthetic disinterest against football: the judgment of taste is 'merely contemplative' and indifferent to the object's existence—explained through Gadamer's reading of the third Critique—so the gambler, the torcida chanting 'we won', the ultras, and the players themselves (whose attention and struggle preclude contemplation) all fail the test, and Kant stands alone except for the neutral spectator and the Panofsky-style purist. Kant's free versus accessory beauty explains why knowing the offside rule adds an intellectual liking to the aesthetic one (Denilson's inconclusive samba dribbles versus Garrincha's effective ones), and the second feature of taste, general validity—saying 'that Maradona goal is the most beautiful ever' claims everyone's agreement without objective rules—underwrites FIFA's Goal of the Century polls and connects the third Critique to public, communicative reason. Finally, the rewatched match on VHS, DVD, or YouTube, where the result is already known and no bets can be laid, is where fans most often approach genuine disinterested contemplation of the object's mere image.

26.title: Goals for All Ages and All Occasions
26.file: ch26 - Goals for All Ages and All Occasions.md
26.relation: Opening with Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged (and his Sisyphus, invoked to show the intrinsically interested player always wins), the authors force football to face its ugly side—divers, Pepe kicking Casquero on the ground, Catania's mooning free-kick screen, referee Pérez Burrull's robbery of Osasuna, the Heysel disaster, Bilardo pinning opponents and drugging Branco, FIFA's resistance to technology—analyzing it all with MacIntyre's account of social practices: football's constitutive rules and internal goods generate standards of excellence that cheating betrays for extrinsic rewards. Their positive ideal is the Greek Kalon, the noble-and-beautiful they field for Plato and Aristotle, exemplified when De Rossi confesses his handball goal against Messina or opponents return the ball after an injury stoppage—the beau geste uniting aesthetic grace and moral honor, as in the 4–4 Arsenal–Liverpool classic where 'neither side deserved to lose'. The ugly, they conclude, is exactly what lets the beautiful shine, as Eto'o floats over Scholes's tackle to assist a Messi goal.

28.title: So Why Do I Support Aston Villa
28.file: ch28 - So Why Do I Support Aston Villa.md
28.relation: Rose—made a Villan by misreading a 1978 Panini sticker as Aston Villa's claret and blue—asks whether supporting Aston Villa is rational and argues ethics is far more like fandom than philosophers admit. Reasons for supporting Villa (local team, the 1982 European Cup, the colors) explain but never justify his allegiance, and the impartial procedures ethics prizes—the utilitarian benevolent spectator and Rawls's original position behind the veil of ignorance, with its 'sort of Kantian' consent-based alternative—turn out too demanding and too abstract: they would force him to donate his match ticket to charity, forbid the Premiership manager favoring his academy son, and reduce agency to the 'Rose-calcio scale' absurdity of switching to Real Madrid for rational reasons. His positive, communitarian claim is that we are thrown into social traditions whose inherited values—like a team—make moral agency and action possible at all, a 'different kind of rationality' that flirts with relativism yet still needs an exit strategy for cultures that discriminate against women or torture children.

29.title: The Final Whistle
29.relation: Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.

30.title: Don’t Worry, We’ll Be Back Next Season
30.file: ch30 - Don’t Worry, We’ll Be Back Next Season.md
30.relation: Vanhoutte argues the derby is not just a game but a clash of identity, territory and honor: old social and religious oppositions (Protestant Rangers v Catholic Celtic, Asian Fenerbahçe v European Galatasaray, Roma v Lazio's championship coffin parade) make derby loyalty a year-round collective identity in which fans win and lose as a 'we', the twelfth player. He traces this to group-identity formation through boundaries dividing the city into 'us' and 'them', showing how belonging produces both derby joy — hugging strangers, 'You'll Never Walk Alone' — and its dark side, from Figo's burnt Barcelona shirt to the Rangers fan murder of a Catholic man. Divisions only turn lethal when exaggerated, so fans must keep the rivalry a game.

31.title: The Limits of Change
31.relation: Osborne and Coombs turn the Ship of Theseus — every plank replaced, plus Hobbes's reassembled-planks variant — into the 'Aston Villa Paradox': with owner, manager, players, crest and even the shade of claret and blue changed, what makes it the same club fans sing 'Villa till I Die' for? Finding that presentism and Sider's four-dimensionalism cannot say which side on the 2006 pitch was really AVFC, they adopt Lynne Rudder Baker's constitution view: fans create the football-favorable circumstances that constitute a club, so it persists through total replacement of parts as long as supporters keep conferring identity and value — which is why Gareth Barry's value collapsed when he left, and why fans judged Glazer's Manchester United to have stopped existing while welcoming Lerner's Villa.

32.title: SECOND EXTRA-TIME - Soccer and Society
32.file: ch32 - SECOND EXTRA-TIME - Soccer and Society.md

33.title: I Play Therefore I Am
33.file: ch33 - I Play Therefore I Am.md
33.relation: Foster argues football is inescapably mythic: styles of play embody national self-images, from Victorian England's muscular distrust of artistry to Argentina's criolla viveza and the compadrito, to Sebes's 'socialist' Aranycsapat, while clubs become vessels of nationalism like Athletic Bilbao's Basque-only cantera policy and Barça's 'més que un club'. Myth flows both ways — West Germany's 1954 'Miracle of Berne' restarted German patriotism, and FC Start's 1942 'Death Match' grew into a Soviet martyr myth despite its embellishments — so that, as the chapter concludes with Galeano and McNeill, what people believe matters more to a constructed social reality than what is actually true. Tell me how you play and I'll tell you who you are.

34.title: The Moment of Truth
34.relation: Nguyen asks what makes a team great and answers 'passion', analyzed through the philosophy of mind: passion is a dispositional state — like Stoichkov's love of the game, ascribable even while he sleeps — that manifests occurrently and causally raises the probability of success on a probabilistic theory of causation, though it is neither necessary nor sufficient for winning. The case study is Barcelona's 2008–09 treble: after the meltdown and 'madriditis' before the Bernabéu, Guardiola's passion and code of conduct restored unity, producing the 6–2 clásico, Iniesta's stoppage-time equalizer at Chelsea, and the 2–0 Champions League final win over Manchester United. Passion is what separates the great from the good.

35.title: A Little bit of Messi for our Life
35.file: ch35 - A Little bit of Messi for our Life.md
35.relation: The authors cast the contrast between disciplined European and improvisational South American football as Mill's struggle between liberty and authority: the coach's tactical orders are 'rules of opinion' the genius may defy, as Maradona did on his sixty-meter run to the Goal of the Century, while the harm principle marks the line at the 'rules of law' — FIFA's Laws of the Game. The Hand of God goal, which broke even a rule of law yet stood because 'a goal is scored when the referee says so', illustrates Searle's point that football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements, leaving a gap filled only by ethics and fair play. Following Wittgenstein's 'ethics and aesthetics are one and the same', they conclude that a bit of Messi-style rule-breaking — Messi replicated both Maradona goals in 2007 — is what makes football, and life, joyful and beautiful.

36.title: History and Philosophy
36.relation: Imre reads Hungary's Aranycsapat as a political-philosophical event: Sebes's socialist 4–2–4 football was meant to prove that cooperative civil society could flourish under Stalinism, and the 6–3 demolition of England at Wembley, with its self-organizing positional play, became the sporting antithesis to Rákosi's regime — culminating in the 1956 Revolution that Arendt cited as a 'true' revolution of spontaneous councils. The 1954 final loss to West Germany (contrasted with Germany's own rebirth at Berne) entrenched a fatalism that history's organic 'grand narrative' and 'final synthesis' were against Hungary, helping destroy the civil-society possibility the team embodied and pushing Hungarians into anti-politics. His lesson: talent and beauty can be quashed by the contingency of history — igazság, truth-justice, never manifested, and soccer could not overcome history.

37.title: A Season Ahead
37.relation: Borghini and Baldini analyze how a soccer club becomes a metaphorical mirror constructing its patron's public persona: the sport's unpredictability, its win/lose dialectic, and the referee's undisputed authority make it adaptable as a metaphor for life, and value-laden properties flow from club to owner through a three-step mirroring process from bare individual to owner to persona. They contrast the slowly built stile Juve of the Agnelli family with Silvio Berlusconi, who exploits mass media to link himself only to AC Milan's wins — blaming coaches or his own absence for defeats, like Machiavelli's prince overcoming fortuna — and with Maurizio Zamparini, Palermo's self-styled moral 'Leonidas' demanding democratic rules and safer stadiums. Persona construction emerges as deliberate meaning transfer, not mere image-making.

38.title: KICKS FROM THE MARK - It’s Down to Penalties
38.file: ch38 - KICKS FROM THE MARK - It’s Down to Penalties.md

39.title: Choosing the Scapegoat
39.relation: Northcott dissects England's penalty shoot-out misery to ask whether 'bad luck' is objective or a scapegoat: what counts as luck depends on the reasonable standard of preparation, so what was bad luck twenty years ago (no practice) is negligence today, and under Laplace's demon's determinism no sixty-percent chances would exist at all. He rehabilitates objective luck relative to shared standards of reasonableness, concluding that shoot-outs genuinely are more of a lottery than open play — though not a total one. On blame, he uses the deviation-from-default account of causation and Mill's problem of causal selection to argue that singling out a referee over missed open goals or injuries has no objective justification; moral feelings and prejudice pick our scapegoats.

40.title: Double Dutch
40.relation: Krnac explains Holland's five missed penalties against Italy at Euro 2000 — Frank de Boer twice, Kluivert, Stam, Bosvelt — through Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety rather than Cruyff's 'chance' or Vergouw's 'poor preparation'. The self, a synthesis of body, mind and spirit (and of the temporal and eternal), must stake itself on a future-oriented choice, but freedom as 'the possibility to be able' makes every free choice an embrace of the unknown, breeding the anxiety that is 'the dizziness of freedom' — visible in de Boer's slide from a five-out-of-ten miss to a lifeless zero that telegraphed his shot to Toldo. Panenka's 1976 chip shows free action chosen without guarantee, while choosing not to choose is itself an evasion of freedom, in penalties as in life.

41.title: Splitting Hairs
41.relation: Saunders rebuts the complaint that penalty shoot-outs are 'lotteries': unlike the coin toss that decided Liverpool–Cologne in 1965, penalties test skill and nerve, and lotteries are not inherently unfair anyway, since giving two equally deserving kidney patients an equal chance is the fairest resort once relevant grounds run out. Fairness does not demand equal chances of winning — it demands due weight to relevant differences — so the better team should be likelier to win, yet winners are not always the better team, as Liverpool's 2005 Istanbul triumph alongside a fifth-place league finish shows. The point of a match is to decide who wins, not who is better, so penalties are legitimate precisely as a skill-testing, exciting way to separate equally deserving teams.

42.title: Refereeing in the World
42.relation: Crowe uses Sartre to explain why refereeing is existentially anguished: in the moment of decision — Grosso's fall over Neill's outstretched legs at the 2006 World Cup — the referee is radically free and solely responsible, and that anguish drives the six familiar referee types into bad faith. The stickler hides behind the letter of Law 12 as Sartre's student hid behind ethical formulas, the ditherer repeats the woman who leaves her hand inert on her date's, the poseur and frustrated player over-act the café waiter's role, and the postman and tough guy play the 'champion of sincerity' who treats character as fixed. The ideal is the authentic referee 'refereeing in the world' — Collina disallowing his own awarded goal at San Siro and explaining why to Inter — who owns his contingency: 'This is what I have chosen.'

43.title: Football and Religion Don’t Mix
43.file: ch43 - Football and Religion Don’t Mix.md
43.relation: Majeed, writing from Ghana's 2008 Africa Cup of Nations and the Fowl Man affair, argues that 'God is not a referee': a God whose nature is rational, just and good cannot coherently be petitioned to fix match outcomes, so fans who blamed the Fowl Man's bird-charm for the semi-final loss to Cameroon — like players who point skyward à la Kaká — misunderstand both divinity and football. He offers instead an empirical account of winning (strategy, fitness, discipline, fair officiating) topped by irreducible chance, whose illogic even breaks the hypothetical syllogism, since on a lucky day Sheffield United can beat Manchester United. Chance is what keeps football a game at all, and its deeper beauty lies in expressing a common humanity — 'humanity has no boundary' — not in divine intervention.

44.title: A Phenomenology of Reading the Ref
44.file: ch44 - A Phenomenology of Reading the Ref.md
44.relation: Vannatta asks what the rules of soccer are from a player's perspective and tests legal theories: natural law and Rawls's veil of ignorance are too abstract to help on the pitch, and Austin's and Hart's positivism overemphasizes FIFA's top-down commands, so the best account is legal pragmatism — Holmes's bad man treats the law as a prophecy of what the ref will actually call, and Dewey roots the rules in custom and in the whistle itself rather than in prior legislation. Husserl's genetic phenomenology then explains how 'reading the ref' is possible: retention and protention synthesized in passive synthesis let experienced players anticipate play — and the referee's tendencies — without deliberation, replacing the impoverished notion of muscle memory. Playing to the whistle becomes a trainable skill of predicting an indeterminate despot, with lessons for coaching and sportsmanship alike.

45.title: A Funny Old Game
45.relation: Grimwood and Miller ask what makes a footballing cliché ('the boy done good', 'a game of two halves', 'they gave 110 percent') hearably meaningful rather than lazy, using Gadamer's hermeneutics and the later Wittgenstein. Gadamer explains clichés as part of the 'horizon' of prejudices that makes understanding the game possible at all — Ian Holloway's taxi-and-young-lady metaphor baffled because it fell outside that horizon — but Wittgenstein goes further: meaning is what words and gestures do in the language-game, so badge-kissing, like the rain dances Wittgenstein defended against Frazer's reductionism, is an expressive form of life whose sincerity or cynicism settles only in context. Even calling something a cliché is itself a move in the game.

5.title: Fighting Talk
5.relation: The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.

6.title: Enter the Dragon - Traditional Asian Martial Arts
6.file: ch06 - Enter the Dragon - Traditional Asian Martial Arts.md

7.title: Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow
7.file: ch07 - Free Your Mind, and Your Roundhouse Will Follow.md
7.relation: Young argues that dojo courtesy is not the fantasy that good manners win fights (Napoleon and the Karate Kid's Johnny lost on skill, not rudeness) but the framing of a craft within a way of life. He maps Aristotle's techne/ethos distinction onto the Japanese jutsu/do pairing to show founders like Kano, Funakoshi and Ueshiba treated fighting as one part of a whole ethical character, reads his seiza apology to an injured yellow belt through Confucian ren, li, yi and shu, and traces Shinto purity into the sincerity (kime) of committed sparring. His black-belt humiliation by seniors becomes Zen's 'courtesy of brutal': ego-deflating violence that trains no-mindedness (muga, Takuan Soho's fudoshin).

8.title: 2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma
8.relation: Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'

9.title: A Koan
9.relation: Finnigan and Tanaka use the kendo student Kenzo, struck down whenever he thinks 'Now is the time to strike!', to pose the puzzle of intentional action without thought. They set Donald Davidson's causal theory of action (intentions as belief-desire causes) against Takuan Soho's mushin, which warns that wherever you put your mind it stops, then resolve it: training lets a master act 'as Yagyu would', and giving reasons afterwards is how one accepts responsibility for an action no reason was 'in mind' for. The koan dissolves once how-questions (how could I act without thinking?) are distinguished from why-questions (why did you do that?).

10.title: And the Winner Is
10.file: ch10 - And the Winner Is.md
10.relation: Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.

11.title: Knowledge and Mastery
11.file: ch11 - Knowledge and Mastery.md
11.relation: Schubert asks what his own master's certificate actually certified and dismantles two accounts of martial mastery: the 'Secret Knowledge' account (hidden teachings like Crouching Tiger's stolen Wu Dan manual) and the 'Complete Knowledge' account, which absurdly implies mastery is suspended when a new takedown joins the syllabus or his forgetful Iaido master omits a step of a form. Using the distinction between knowing-that, knowing-how and physical ability (he knew how to jump-spin heel-kick with his foot in a cast), he argues mastery is knowing that and how across the essential techniques, principles and strategies a style could have consisted of, by analogy with fluency in a language. Rank, politics and even the ability to perform are at best signs of mastery, not the thing itself.

12.title: The Karate Kid - Character and Education
12.file: ch12 - The Karate Kid - Character and Education.md

13.title: An Enemy Lying in Ambush
13.file: ch13 - An Enemy Lying in Ambush.md
13.relation: Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.

14.title: Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent
14.file: ch14 - Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent.md
14.relation: Cooper and Taylor argue that Kano's judo principles, seiryokuzenyou (maximum efficiency) and jitakyouei (mutual welfare and benefit), echo Bentham's principle of utility: both men swept away archaic rules to reach one efficient ethical goal, and Kano accepted the comparison. They run the hedonic calculus over training bruises versus the joy of a clean throw, use Mill's secondary principles as rule-utilitarian guidelines (release the armbar at the tap rather than calculating each time), and answer the objection that utilitarianism demands too much with Kano's own ethos: like judo, it is about continual improvement, not impossible maximization.

15.title: Living the Absurd Life
15.file: ch15 - Living the Absurd Life.md
15.relation: Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.

16.title: The Last Resort
16.file: ch16 - The Last Resort.md
16.relation: Petersen recounts fighting off a man who threatened to rape and kill her, and argues that karate, not feminist doctrine or therapy, made her a real feminist by rewiring her self-concept, fear responses and relationships. Against the Lara Croft fantasy she sets practical self-defense doctrine ('don't be there'; assertiveness, not aggression, with the bus pest), Australian, US and UN statistics on violence against women, and the Guthrie study of Chicago's feminist Thousand Waves dojo. She frames the transformation with Foucault's 'care of the self': karate's practices of the self give women power through knowledge, so that by black-belt time enduring harassment simply 'isn't who she is'.

17.title: The Way of the Place
17.file: ch17 - The Way of the Place.md
17.relation: Beattie uses Henri Lefebvre's account of the production of space to read the dojo as a 'differential space' practitioners actively create against abstract, conformist space. He shows how bow-ins, founder portraits, Japanese counting, mats, dogi and belt hierarchies mark ownership, bind the school to a lineage, separate 'dojo' from 'street', and shape bodies and safety (with Kendo's door-side seating and MMA's display of physique as hierarchy written into space). Play matters too: Aristotle's point that virtues are built by habit explains how playing at combat in a safe place breeds real courage, and the whole exercise teaches a moving balance between inside and outside.

18.title: The Perfect Weapon - Ethics and Value
18.file: ch18 - The Perfect Weapon - Ethics and Value.md

19.title: Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor
19.file: ch19 - Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor.md
19.relation: Kohn begins with her own response to a serial bin-tipper: practicing iaido sword draws in full view of the neighbours to intimidate an imagined Other. Contrasting iaido's virtual opponent (a mere tool for the self) with aikido's real partners, she deploys Levinas's face of the Other, responsibility without waiting for reciprocity and philosophy as 'the Wisdom of Love', alongside Arendt's shared responsibility for the world's conflicts, to argue that care for even one's attacker comes first, with Kant's categorical imperative as the generalizable counterpart to Levinas's ethics. Her confession: she treated the imagined culprit as an object of hate, when meeting 'the Face' would have demanded an apology and maybe a hug.

20.title: Why It Matters
20.relation: Russell, who at eleven believed practice would let her kill a bull with one blow, argues that martial arts culture systematically breeds epistemic vices: gullibility (ki knockouts, chocolate milk for recovery), closed-mindedness, dojos treated like churches, sunk-cost defence of the side-kick-knifes-from-hands story, and deference to sensei and founders (Funakoshi curing fevers with karate). She diagnoses data-poverty, since lethal techniques cannot be ethically tested, as the enabling condition, and prescribes cautious belief, closing with the Buddha's counsel from Harry Cook's dojo wall: believe nothing on the authority of masters alone. It matters because these are beliefs about what can injure and kill.

21.title: The Moving Shadow of Truth
21.file: ch21 - The Moving Shadow of Truth.md
21.relation: Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.

22.title: What Monkey Should Have Known
22.file: ch22 - What Monkey Should Have Known.md
22.relation: Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.

23.title: Living Beauty
23.relation: Saltzman explains why a flowing Shaolin Kenpo form is beautiful by way of Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Apollonian geometry of square, triangle and circle fuses with Dionysian power and intention, just as yang hardness needs yin softness. She grounds the body's fitness for this in the Golden Ratio known to Pythagoras, answers 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' with Clive Bell's 'significant form' as an objective structure that trained judges can recognize, and locates 'living beauty' in the practitioner's own breakthrough, the moment when, as Nietzsche and Yeats agree, the dancer and the dance dissolve into pure mindless movement.

25.title: Jousting for Virtue
25.relation: Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.

26.title: Boxing, a School for Virtues
26.file: ch26 - Boxing, a School for Virtues.md
26.relation: Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'

27.title: Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art
27.file: ch27 - Is Fencing a Dishonorable Art.md
27.relation: Michaud argues that fencing is the loneliest and most egoistic martial art: alone on the strip, you seek to understand your opponent only in order to deceive them through disengages and parry-feints. He maps the bout onto Hobbes: psychological egoism, the dueling ground as a state of nature of 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', and the referee as the Leviathan whose rules keep the bloodshed out while licensing normative egoism inside them. Testing defenses from Rand, Friedman and Carr's business 'rules of the game', he concludes that fencing kept its soldier's anything-goes ethos after the lethal stakes vanished, making it a 'dishonorable' art: a Hobbesian feast of solitude, egoism and deception.

28.title: The Personality of the Épée
28.file: ch28 - The Personality of the Épée.md
28.relation: Lawrence asks why anyone practices the épée, an 'unmartial martial art' with no self-defense payoff, one-sided exercise value, and only stylized descent from dueling to first blood (unlike foil and saber's artificial targets and right-of-attack rules). His three answers: fencing uniquely rewards psychology, timing and dexterity over strength and pain-endurance (he prefers Odysseus's guile to Ajax's force); it continues a Bronze-Age tradition ('the history of the sword is the history of mankind'); and the named swords of epic, from Excalibur to Sting, point to the weapon's distinctive personality of courage, honor, deadliness, aesthetic fitness for purpose, and an intimacy with the opponent that Housman's saber-duel poem captures.

29.title: Back to Square One
29.relation: Moss concedes fencing's romantic dueling aura, noting that Kant classed a killing in a duel as mere manslaughter, Bentham proposed giving duelists the protection of self-defense for the sake of honor, and Rousseau and Schopenhauer sneered at the whole business. But he argues the sport's uniqueness lies not in honor, psychology or combat origins, which it shares with other martial arts, but in a combination of rules: the blade-set distance between fencers, protective gear that makes them effectively invulnerable, right-of-way, and the return to a neutral start after each point. That combination allows the complex 'phrases' of feint and disengage that make fencing 'physical chess'; what is unique, he concludes, is a matter of rules, not romance.
