5.title: For Crying Out Loud
5.relation: Sharon M. Kaye's introduction recounts the legend that The Onion got its name from an uncle's suggestion while the founders ate onion sandwiches, then argues the dictionary definition of 'onion' fits perfectly: 'bulbous' things are inherently funny and 'pungent' things penetrate and burn. The Onion's satire is therefore philosophical, she concludes, because philosophers have always been critics of the society in which they live—an uncomfortable wake-up call, like heartburn—and the chapters ahead will 'unpeel' the connections.

7.title: Ridicule Is a Survival Strategy
7.file: ch07 - Ridicule Is a Survival Strategy.md
7.relation: Kaye argues that the highest form of ridicule, which The Onion has mastered, targets not stupidity but cheating—specifically 'asscheating,' believing what you want to be true. She reads 'I Believe In Evolution, Except For The Whole Triassic Period' as skewering people who understand Darwin perfectly but exempt humans from evolution because admitting we are just another animal means admitting we die like everything else, the move behind Aquinas-style teleological add-ons that only invite a regress of gods supplying 'extras.' Articles on breast implants, the 'New Nietzschean Diet,' and Tour de France doping all show asscheats artificially inflating their evolutionary fitness; since natural selection stamps every organism with the purpose of survival and reproduction, asscheating is a vice, and ridiculing the asscheats who pollute the gene pool is itself a survival strategy.

8.title: Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory
8.file: ch08 - Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory.md
8.relation: Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.

9.title: Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid
9.file: ch09 - Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid.md
9.relation: Cuddy stages the generational-decline debate between Mark Bauerlein's The Dumbest Generation and Stephen Johnson's Everything Bad Is Good for You, showing that Onion stories can be marshaled for both sides: Aristophanes complaining that today's audiences 'just don't get me' vindicates the perennial declinist, while 'US Students Lead World in Detention' wryly supports Johnson's sleeper curve. Comparing Bauerlein to Aristophanes and the 'Our Dumb World' entry on Aristotle and Plato's schools closing, he concludes every era teems with idiots, so The Onion could have existed in any century. Because induction from earlier generations' failed predictions cannot settle whether Millennials really are dumber, he suspends judgment and toasts The Onion as the smartest perspective around.

10.title: Opinion
10.file: ch10 - Opinion.md

11.title: In All Fucking Seriousness
11.file: ch11 - In All Fucking Seriousness.md
11.relation: Arp asks why well-placed 'fucks' in Onion headlines like 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' are funny, and answers with the golden mean traced to Aristotle and Confucius, who both prized self-control and being a good role model to children: swearing is virtuous when it hits the mean between the vice of too much (gangsta rap's every-other-word profanity, the cemetery gardener's rant, Glengarry Glen Ross) and the vice of too little. He sorts Onion stories into vice tables—'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer' illustrates the vice of cowardice, with courage as the hitting-the-mark mean—and concludes that a well-placed fuck is both funny and virtuous precisely because so many people treat the word as taboo.

12.title: More Asshole Morality
12.file: ch12 - More Asshole Morality.md
12.relation: Hallquist observes that Dan Savage's 'Savage Love' column, syndicated in The Onion, treats 'asshole' not as a mere expletive but as a property that can be discovered, disagreed about, and used to explain behavior—raising exactly the puzzles philosophers raise about morality. He defends an expressivist account modeled on Ayer's: 'Dan Savage is an asshole' expresses an attitude while picking out a range of behavior defined by shared attitudes, and he answers the classic objections (logic requires truth-aptness, moral disagreement seems factual, we ask third parties who the asshole is) by adapting Singer's point that logic applies to commands and attitudes too, and by showing disagreement over assholery is a conflict of attitudes we still have urgent practical reason to resolve. Since the standard arguments against moral expressivism would equally refute this intuitively plausible asshole-expressivism, the objections must fail, giving moral expressivism a modest positive argument.

13.title: Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article
13.file: ch13 - Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article.md
13.relation: Littmann runs Hume's Dialogues argument from evil through Onion headlines: 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy' (Timmy Yu's resounding no), 'God Outdoes Terrorists Yet Again,' 'God Wastes Miracle On Running Catch In Outfield,' and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways As Motive In Killing Of 3,000 Papua New Guineans.' He dispatches the theodicies one by one: limiting God's power or goodness (as Mill's lesser deity would) abandons the God of the tradition; the free will defense fails because police rightly restrain gunmen and no human freedom explains hurricanes; soul-building is pointless for a being who could implant compassion innately or stage fake evils; the 'no best possible world' dodge would excuse the reporter who watches a man burn; and the mystery defense makes reason useless. He concludes no all-knowing, all-good, all-powerful God exists, while insisting readers think it through for themselves.

14.title: Politics
14.file: ch14 - Politics.md

15.title: Area Man And Woman Wonder What They Are Good For
15.file: ch15 - Area Man And Woman Wonder What They Are Good For.md
15.relation: Benatar uses The Onion's 'Area Man' to stage the Hart–Devlin debate: Lord Devlin made the man on the Clapham omnibus's 'real feeling of reprobation' the test for when law may enforce society's morality against private homosexual acts, and H.L.A. Hart replied that shared values can be wicked (Nazi Germany) and that societies transform rather than disintegrate when values change—confirmed by Onion Area Men who hate their gay coworker, have gay sex to dodge the office blood drive, or have spent eight years 'experimenting,' none of which dissolved Britain or America. The chapter adds the feminist complaint that treating the Area Man as the norm erases Area Woman, and closes with Joel Feinberg's crowded-bus thought experiment from Offense to Others: average disgust is relevant to regulating public offense but never decisive, so the ordinary person interests legal philosophy without being its arbiter.

16.title: A Newspaper Gone to the Dogs . . . Enlightened Dogs
16.file: ch16 - A Newspaper Gone to the Dogs . . . Enlightened Dogs.md
16.relation: Bayan traces 'cynic' to the Greek kynikos ('doglike') and the philosophy to Socrates' virtue, poverty, and integrity, through the proto-Cynic Antisthenes to Diogenes of Sinope—the man in the tub, the plucked chicken at Plato's Academy, 'you can step out of my sunlight'—arguing that Cynicism is fierce moral opposition to sham and hypocrisy, which is exactly why the powerful smear cynics. Distinguishing The Onion's cool, Swiftian irony from postmodern 'pseudocynicism,' he concludes the paper is genuinely Cynical: headlines like 'Black Guy Asks Nation for Change' (the Obama reveal), 'God Angrily Clarifies Don't Kill Rule,' and 'Dictator Slays Millions in Last-Minute Push to Be Time's Man of the Year' nuzzle the kind, bark at the greedy, and bite scoundrels, so Diogenes would have read The Onion with paternal fondness.

17.title: Banal Sex
17.relation: Marinucci reads The Onion's sex coverage as 'terminally ambiguous': 'Nation's Gays Demand Right To Library Cards,' 'Massachusetts Supreme Court Orders All Citizens To Gay Marry,' and 'New Bill Would Defend Marriage From Sharks' ridicule the idea that gay marriage threatens straight marriage, while 'Area Homosexual Saves Four From Fire: Heroic Neighbor Praised, Gay' exposes how heterosexism defines gay people sexually while heterosexual men pass as normal, natural, and neutral. Yet the paper also trades in gay stereotypes and mocks the very framework—characters like Amanda Oppel ('Lesbian Identity Ends Abruptly Mid-Junior Year'), the 'Bar Skanks Announce Plans To Kiss,' and Bruce Heffernan of 'Why Do All These Homosexuals Keep Sucking My Cock?' both defy and seem to reaffirm the stability of sexual identity categories. Weighing queer theory (via Jagose) and Golden's fluid 'elective lesbians' against the parody of 'Grad Student Deconstructs Take-Out Menu,' she concludes the paper's stance is deliberately undecidable, perhaps recommending we stop over-thinking sex and treat minority sexual identities as banal, as in 'Gay Couple Has Banal Sex.'

18.title: Scientists Find Anomalies In And Then Go Back and Kill Your Grandparents
18.file: ch18 - Scientists Find Anomalies In And Then Go Back and Kill Your Grandparents.md
18.relation: This chapter is a satirical fake-news 'World' section rather than an essay: 'Vigilante Group Tracks and Kills Storm-Causing Chaos Butterflies' literalizes the butterfly effect of chaos theory, 'Great Thinkers Fired From Canon' mocks citation metrics by crowning 'Ibidem' history's most-cited philosopher, 'University Restructures To Remain Financial: Becomes Bank' parodies corporatized academia as sympathetic magic, and 'ADD Sufferers Fail Cogito: Don't Exist' has distracted patients pop out of existence for failing Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am.' The title story, about physicists whose experiment lets them go back and kill their grandparents, is printed with its sentences scrambled into a reporter's phone-call fragments, enacting its own point that, as Hume noted, causal order is never perceived only imposed—and with quantum time-symmetry and the grandfather paradox, time's arrow jumps wherever it likes, even into loops.

19.title: Funny Newspaper Makes Accurate Prophecy
19.file: ch19 - Funny Newspaper Makes Accurate Prophecy.md
19.relation: Auxier takes the September 28, 2001 Onion issue—'Hijackers Surprised To Find Selves In Hell,' published while late-night TV was still in mourning—to ask what makes some comedy permissible and durable, glancing back at Aristophanes' caricature of Socrates in The Clouds and the circle-men speech Plato puts in his mouth in the Symposium. Hegel supplies the machinery: comedy as a moment of Art within Absolute Spirit may only bring to naught what is already null, while irony that diminishes the noble degrades the ironist—which is why the Warren Commission is fair game for 'Smithsonian Janitor Finds Magic Bullet' but Martin Luther King, a World Historical Individual whose individuality embodies his movement, can never anchor the 'Mrs. Williams Finally Decides Dinner Guest Is Not Going to Show' story. Since 'the news' itself is the great nullity—partial time-slices pretending to explain complex events before their meanings are interpretable—The Onion's rapid 9/11 satire was legitimate and even prophetic, deflating the bullshit of those posing as arbiters of Objective Spirit.

20.title: Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy.md
20.relation: Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.

22.title: World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent
22.file: ch22 - World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent.md
22.relation: Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.

23.title: The Onion’s New Environmental Ethic
23.file: ch23 - The Onion’s New Environmental Ethic.md
23.relation: Matthew Altman reads Onion environmental satire as a staged escape from anthropocentrism: 'New, Delicious Species Discovered' and 'Beauty Of National Forest Enjoyed By Logger' expose that even appreciating nature is just valuing it for us, while the mascara-testing lab rabbit and 'Funny Monkey Tested On' make Singer's speciesism charge vivid against factory farming and animal experiments. He then widens the argument to a biocentric concern for species and ecosystems via 'Stuffed-Animal Biodiversity Rising' and 'Consumer-Product Diversity Now Exceeds Biodiversity,' and to ecofeminism via 'Raped Environment Led Polluters On,' where the forest as flirtatious woman links domination of nature to sexism and victim-blaming. Global stories like the Bush 'national air conditioner' piece show Western overconsumption displacing blame onto Third World overpopulation, and 'I'm Doing My Inconsequential Part' satirizes the self-satisfaction of green consumerism itself — leaving the measure of the Onion's philosophical importance as how dangerous it is.

25.title: The Onion, Sarcasm, and the Good of Mankind
25.file: ch25 - The Onion, Sarcasm, and the Good of Mankind.md
25.relation: Noah Levin recounts how the Onion article 'Area Man Committed To Being Spicy Food Guy' made him recognize his own obnoxious boasting about hot food and quietly change, presenting satire as continuing philosophy's self-help tradition back to Socrates' 'know thyself.' He distinguishes parody, satire, and sarcasm, then formalizes Onion jokes — the RIAA suing radio stations for giving away free music, and 'That Teen-Abstinence Rally Totally Rocked!' — as implicit reductio ad absurdum arguments whose absurd conclusions force rejection of a hidden premise. The sarcastic route beats a direct lecture, he argues, because the target must complete the three-step argument himself: identify the mocked trait, admit having it, and decide whether to change.

26.title: The Guy Is Not Alone. .
26.file: ch26 - The Guy Is Not Alone. ..md
26.relation: Matt Laubenthal confesses he was the philosophy-class windbag and defends Darrin Floen of 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' as heir to Socrates' gadfly role, noting the Athenians also wanted their relentless questioner dead. He teaches Russell's Paradox through a Burger King 's.h.i.t. load' — the set of all sets that are not members of themselves — and reconstructs Darrin's Heraclitean rejoinder that if everything flows and nothing stands still, the static either/or of set membership dissolves the contradiction. Along the way he reads the Onion's Kafka International Airport story ('Are you who you say you are?' repeated for eighty minutes) as existentialist absurdity, and the Star Trek Voyager holographic Doctor as a puzzle about whether a self could be nothing more than mathematical code.

28.title: Get Serious
28.relation: David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.

29.title: Progress
29.relation: Gregory Gilson argues that although The Onion deliberately reports falsehoods, it embodies postmodern theories of truth better than the newspapers it parodies. Lyotard's mercantilization of knowledge and the fragmentation of dominant narratives into separate language games explain headlines like 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity' and 'Astronomer Discovers The Center Of The Universe Is His Beautiful 9-Year Old Son,' which smash incompatible discourses together, while Baudrillard's simulacrum and hyper-reality explain how The Onion — like Disneyworld — is branded fake precisely so mainstream media can seem real. Yet the chapter closes honestly: its own criticism of 'Bush Says He Still Believes Iraq War Was the Fun Thing To Do' assumed some targets were wrong, which assumes a Truth out there — the paradox of a satire whose truthfulness exceeds its own theory of truth.

30.title: Voltaire Lives
30.relation: Douglas Ficek traces The Onion's God stories — 'Lord Under Investigation For Failure To Provide,' God refusing to heal paralyzed little Timmy Yu, and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways' — back through Voltaire's Candide to Leibniz's theodicy, the 'best of all possible worlds' doctrine that Dr. Pangloss keeps reciting through hanging, slavery, and syphilis until Candide concludes we must cultivate our garden. The chapter's sharpest claim is that theodicy works by victim-blaming: Jerry Falwell's 9/11 rant earned the headline-only 'Jerry Falwell: Is That Guy A Dick Or What?' because he excused God by blaming secular Americans, just as Pastor Ellsworth blames heathen tsunami victims. Following theologian Dorothee Soelle, Ficek names this 'theological sadism,' and offers the Bible-drop missionaries of 'Poverty-Stricken Africans Receive Desperately Needed Bibles' as a modern Pangloss who mistakes moral obliviousness for grace.

32.title: Point-Counterpoint Funny versus Really, Really Funny
32.file: ch32 - Point-Counterpoint Funny versus Really, Really Funny.md
32.relation: Andrew Terjesen starts from real cases of Onion satire taken literally — a Michigan sheriff warning about al-Qaida telemarketing, the Beijing Evening News plagiarizing 'Congress Threatens To Leave D.C.', Deborah Norville reporting that 58 percent of American exercise is televised — and explains them through the Problem of Other Minds. Descartes' hats-and-cloaks worry and Russell's analogy solution show how we infer that a straight-faced writer is 'just kidding,' but the analogy fails when cultural context, prejudice (Fred Phelps citing the gay-recruitment story, Christians forwarding the Harry Potter Satanism piece), or wishful thinking breaks the comparison with our own joking behavior. The upshot is that humor is engineered misunderstanding — the Onion works by analogy to real news, and could never warn readers off without destroying the joke.

33.title: Philosophy and Humor
33.relation: Thomas Brommage builds on Wittgenstein's quip that a serious and good philosophical work could consist entirely of jokes: philosophy for Wittgenstein is a therapeutic activity that dissolves pseudo-problems and lays our linguistic practices open to view, never delivering theories. Onion humor works the same way — 'Bill Gates Grants Self 18 Dexterity, 20 Charisma' needs the shared form of life of D&D-style geek culture, the 'Ask a Salmon' advice column breaks the rule that answers answer, and 'Youthful Tendency Disorder' makes the familiar (children running, jumping, and playing pretend) strange enough to skewer ADHD over-diagnosis and pharmaceutical marketing. Since Wittgenstein asks why we feel a grammatical joke to be deep, jokes that expose our conceptual confusions can themselves be serious arguments — which is exactly what a philosophy joke book, and The Onion, deliver.

34.title: Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal
34.file: ch34 - Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal.md
34.relation: Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.

5.title: We’ve Been Abducted by the Doctor, and We Love It!
5.file: ch05 - We’ve Been Abducted by the Doctor, and We Love It!.md
5.relation: The editors' introduction recounts the show's history from its 1963 premiere (the day after the Kennedy assassination) and the Daleks' first appearance through all eleven Doctors, and describes how companions from Ian and Barbara to Rose, Donna, and Amy were 'abducted' by the Doctor's sense of wonder. It argues that the curiosity and love of adventure the TARDIS inspires in viewer-companions is the very same impulse that drives the love of wisdom, and previews the book's six 'episodes' on personal identity, time travel, logic and science, the Doctor's ethics, existentialism and aesthetics, and the show's cultural meaning.

6.title: EPISODE 1 - I’m the Doctor. Who
6.file: ch06 - EPISODE 1 - I’m the Doctor. Who.md

7.title: A Dead End
7.relation: Stokes uses regeneration and the multi-Doctor episodes ('The Three Doctors', 'The Five Doctors', 'The Trial of a Time Lord') to test theories of personal identity: Locke's memory criterion, Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's teleporter and 'branch-line' cases, Nozick's closest-continuer theory, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity. He argues that no objective-continuity account explains why the Fifth Doctor still cares whether he himself survives in 'The Caves of Androzani', and hints that being the Doctor may be a subjective stance in which each incarnation takes ownership of the others as itself.

8.title: Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer
8.file: ch08 - Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer.md
8.relation: Littmann mines Who scenarios as hypotheticals that test identity theories: regeneration, natural doubles like Salamander, impersonating Zygons and Chameleons, bodiless beings like Omega and the Great Intelligence, TARDIS jumps that break spatiotemporal continuity, Cassandra possessing the Doctor and Rose, memory theft by Eldrad and the Daleks, and the Master's year as the unrecognizably good Professor Yana. He argues that sameness of body (including the four-dimensional 'worm' of spatiotemporal continuity), the memory criterion, and psychological similarity each fail, leaving the question of what makes the Doctor the Doctor — and you you — open.

9.title: What’s Persistence Without Identity
9.relation: Hanley first fixes what is true in the Who canon (treating fiction as pretense), then asks how the Doctor persists when regeneration replaces 'every single cell' and when John Smith's amnesia severs memory in 'Human Nature'. Rejecting bodily continuity (the severed hand of 'The Christmas Invasion'), soul 'pellets', and simple memory (Reid's transitivity problem), he defends neo-Lockean mental continuity plus Nozick's closest-continuer schema to explain why Jackson Lake, the regrown Doctor, and DoctorDonna in 'Journey's End' are not the Doctor, and closes with Parfit's claim that psychological continuity rather than identity is what matters in survival, alongside Lewis's space-time-worm alternative.

10.title: I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think
10.file: ch10 - I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think.md
10.relation: Johnson argues that the Platonic-Cartesian soul is refuted by neuroscience (Phineas Gage, Penfield's stimulation studies), and that Locke's memory criterion fails on Reid-style transitivity cases like DoctorDonna and on Bernard-Williams-inspired worry about the amnesiac John Smith, who would still dread the Family of Blood's torture. Parfit's causal-continuity criterion then wrongly makes the meta-crisis Doctor of 'Journey's End' identical with the Tenth, so Johnson defends a four-dimensionalist 'time worm' view on which the Doctors are stages of one person — before a final sorites-style argument (heaps, spin-offs like Torchwood) suggests that 'persons' may not exist at all.

11.title: EPISODE 2 - Wibbly-Wobbly, Timey-Wimey . . . Stuff
11.file: ch11 - EPISODE 2 - Wibbly-Wobbly, Timey-Wimey . . . Stuff.md

12.title: We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel
12.file: ch12 - We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel.md
12.relation: Worley distinguishes logical from empirical possibility (Leonardo's round-square in 'City of Death') and shows that time-travel paradoxes — Leela's self-caused antibodies, the unauthored 'Blink' Easter egg, the Master's Toclafane — can be handled with Zeno-style analysis of contradiction and David Lewis's distinction between external and personal time, under which travelers instantiate rather than rewrite history ('The Visitation', 'The Time Meddler'). He then reads 'Turn Left' and the Doctor's 'alternative time' in 'Pyramids of Mars' through Leibniz's possible worlds and Lewis's actualism about parallel universes, concluding that in 'City of Death' time travel is essential to life on Earth existing at all.

13.title: The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!
13.file: ch13 - The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!.md
13.relation: Goff asks whether the Daleks could genuinely change the past by exterminating the Egyptian pyramid builders, arguing that presentism leaves no past to travel to while eternalism fixes all facts of time so travelers can affect but never change history. He defends the growing block theory — past and present exist, the future does not — and works out that Dalek intervention would generate a new, pyramid-less history replacing the old one no faster than the absolute present advances, so the Doctor could always return to a present still causally continuous with the pyramids.

14.title: Prognosis
14.file: ch14 - Prognosis.md
14.relation: Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' speech in 'Blink' as David Lewis's four-dimensionalism: the universe is one spacetime manifold, time travelers are zig-zag or broken person-stages through it, and in external time effects can precede causes. Lewis's compossibility reading of 'can' dissolves the grandfather paradox and the bilking worry about Sally Sparrow's closed causal chain, and comparison with Horwich and Ismael shows the Doctor agreeing that closed causal loops are possible — indeed, unlike them, he holds they actually happen.

15.title: This Is the Age of Steel
15.file: ch15 - This Is the Age of Steel.md
15.relation: Littmann asks what a genuinely logical creature would do and grades the Cybermen against three accounts of reason: Hobbes's self-preservation and social contract, which the survival-focused Cybermen of 'The Tenth Planet' roughly satisfy but their later wars of conquest betray; Mill's utilitarianism, whose greatest-happiness principle, higher pleasures, liberty, and individuality condemn emotion-stripping, forced 'upgrades', and uniformity; and Hume's claim that reason alone motivates nothing, under which perfectly logical but emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing at all. The upshot is that Cyberman 'logic' is incoherent — no theory of reason makes them rational.

16.title: They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too
16.file: ch16 - They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too.md
16.relation: The chapter reads the Daleks' hunt for the 'human factor' in 'The Evil of the Daleks' and for human DNA in 'Dalek' and 'Daleks in Manhattan' as species essentialism — an Aristotelian picture of a fixed human nature, resurrected as genetic essentialism — set against philosophical alternatives of species as individuals or sets and Mayr's reproductive-isolation criterion applied to Daleks and Thals. It then asks whether the human-Dalek Dalek Sec could count as a person, using Singer's speciesism to argue that rights should track personhood (capacities for pain, intelligence) rather than bare membership in Homo sapiens.

17.title: Doomed to Be Perceived
17.relation: Smithka tests Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived' against two monsters: the Vashta Nerada, whose existence is inferred from indirect evidence (counting shadows, the 'ghosting' of Miss Evangelista) much like Neptune was inferred from Uranus's orbit, and the Weeping Angels, which act only when unperceived and so falsify Berkeley's principle. Working through Locke on substance, Hume's skepticism about unperceivable causes like God, Paley's watchmaker design argument, and scientific realism (Sellars, Churchland) versus van Fraassen's empirically adequate anti-realism, she concludes the Doctor is a realist about unobservables — for whom the Angels are real but 'doomed to be perceived'.

18.title: Aww, . . . Poor Monster. Should We Feel Sorry for the Carrionites
18.file: ch18 - Aww, . . . Poor Monster. Should We Feel Sorry for the Carrionites.md
18.relation: Hewitt treats the Carrionites — word-wielding beings of 'The Shakespeare Code' who do science without numbers — as a test of Hartry Field's Science Without Numbers and hence of the Quinean indispensability argument for Platonism about mathematics: if numbers are unavoidable in our best physics, they exist. Surveying Field's Newtonian case, Balaguer's mathematics-free quantum mechanics, and the objections to each, he concludes that even Carrionite physics would not refute numbers — the Carrionites would merely lack our knowledge of them, so the poor monsters are missing out.

19.title: EPISODE 3 - It’s a Different Morality. Get Used to It, or Go Home!
19.file: ch19 - EPISODE 3 - It’s a Different Morality. Get Used to It, or Go Home!.md

20.title: “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler
20.file: ch20 - “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler.md
20.relation: Decker argues the Doctor's morality resists formula — his motives are private, his timey-wimey perspective complicates consequentialist calculation, and the 'Genesis of the Daleks' child hypothetical breaks rule theories like Kant's and Mill's — so he reads it as an 'ethics of ambiguity' fusing Romanticism (Shelley's imagination, the infinite glimpsed in cups of tea and small beautiful events, Romantic-Gothic divided consciousness) with Sartrean existentialism. Via Sartre's WWII student, bad faith, and Beauvoir's 'adventurer' contrasted with the sub-man and the serious man, he casts the Doctor as a Gallifreyan Prometheus whose gifts of freedom are both dreadful and delightful.

21.title: A Better Way of Living Your Life
21.file: ch21 - A Better Way of Living Your Life.md
21.relation: Akers argues the Doctor follows neither rule deontology, utilitarian calculation, nor virtue ethics, but a relational ethics of care in Noddings's and Slote's sense, expressed as Buber's I-Thou stance — insisting an enslaved Ood is 'a "he," not an "it"' and addressing Donna, Jack, and Rose each as individuals in 'Journey's End'. Linking this to Nussbaum's claim that wonder widens moral concern and to Kant's dynamic and mathematical sublime, she argues the Doctor needs human companions like Rose, Martha, and Donna as a human-scale reference point that renews his wonder — and with it his ethics — while his wiping of Donna's memory shows the care tradition's dangers of power imbalance.

22.title: Toward Caring
22.file: ch22 - Toward Caring.md
22.relation: Sylvia models the Doctor on feminist care ethics: Gilligan's response to Kohlberg's justice-tinged scales and Noddings's distinction between natural caring (for Rose, Martha, Peri in 'The Caves of Androzani') and ethical caring, which explains his forgiveness of the Master and compassion for Dalek Caan after genocides. Against utilitarian impartiality — which cannot say why he should save his companion over a stranger — the relationship itself grounds the obligation, while his vengeful moment facing the lone Dalek in 'Dalek' shows what caring burnout looks like.

23.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
23.file: ch23 - Allons-y into the Starry Heavens.md
23.relation: Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.

24.title: The Dalek Within
24.relation: Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.

25.title: Why the Doctor Is So Special
25.file: ch25 - Why the Doctor Is So Special.md
25.relation: Applying Singer's animal-liberation concept of speciesism — judging moral worth by capacity to feel pain rather than by intelligence or likeness — the authors argue the Daleks are 'super-speciesist' and that Lumic's emotional inhibitors make the Cybermen the same failure, unable to share a universe with unlike beings. Since emotions are judgments that can be educated into fitting responses (Nussbaum, Aristotle), and since Daleks infused with Rose's or Diagoras's DNA collapse into empathetic beings, the chapter concludes that emotion and empathy are why the Daleks will never win and why the Doctor, marked by his companions, is special among Time Lords.

26.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
26.file: ch26 - Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign.md
26.relation: Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.

28.title: Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity
28.file: ch28 - Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity.md
28.relation: Argues that regeneration helps show life after death is logically possible: the successive Doctors (Fourth to Fifth in 'Logopolis') prove identity survives radical personality change, so a perfected heavenly Joe would still be Joe. Testing whether identity lies in body or memory, he contrasts John Smith in 'Human Nature' (same body, so same person) with the 'Journey's End' Doctor-clone whose replicated memories Rose rejects ('But he's not you'), favoring bodily continuity. This leaves the unavailability-of-atoms problem, which he solves with van Inwagen's theory that God removes and preserves our bodies at death like a divine cryonicist, echoing the Fourth Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' tribute in 'The Ark in Space'.

29.title: Love and Doctors
29.relation: Asks whether 'the Doctor' is a Kripkean rigid designator naming one individual or a non-rigid role filled by different people, using the Ninth Doctor's deathbed doubts and the Time Crash memory loop to settle on the rigid reading. He then deploys Locke's body/organism/person distinctions, Parfit's overlapping psychological-connectedness fix to Reid's transitivity objection (Sarah Jane across 1983-1996-2006), and the amnesia-prone regenerations and the Valeyard to show the organism survives regeneration while the person might not. Finally he argues that because DoctorTwo in 'Journey's End' shares all the Doctor's psychologically connected memories of Rose, fission makes them two persons with equal claim, so Rose gets the person she actually loved.

30.title: I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You
30.file: ch30 - I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You.md
30.relation: Reads the Doctor as a Christ-figure and savior (the 'Voyage of the Damned' ascension that drew Christian Voice protests, Martha's year of gospel-telling in 'The Last of the Time Lords'), applying Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideals onto God. But the show under Russell T Davies also distrusts godlike power: Davros's 'you made this' accusation, the Racnoss massacre, and Joan Redfern's question in 'The Family of Blood' show the lonely god's devastation. Against this, companions like Donna embody Nietzsche's Übermensch ('There's no such thing as an ordinary human'), so the chapter concludes the Doctor and ordinary humans need each other, mutually overcoming their weaknesses.

31.title: Life A Celebration
31.relation: Reads John Simm's Master as Nietzsche's most advanced nihilist: having seen the universe die at Utopia, he judges life valueless and converts ressentiment into a joyful will to nothingness, dancing to the Scissor Sisters over his victims. The Ninth Doctor's arc in 'Dalek' mirrors this danger ('What are you changing into?') until he refuses to destroy the last Dalek, beginning his yes-saying to finite life. Following Deleuze's reading, the Doctor defeats the Master not with Martha's gun but with forgiveness ('I forgive you') and her storytelling network, embodying the Übermensch who carries his affirmation into the abyss of the end of the universe.

32.title: Escape to Doctor Who
32.relation: Reads the Master as the personification of Schopenhauer's blind, pointless Will: the Doctor's line 'In many ways we have the same mind' is taken literally, so the Master is the dark noumenal side in everyone, seen in the hypnotized Farrel whose ambition the Master acts out and Colonel Trenchard whose patriotism becomes the Master's weapon in 'The Sea Devils'. Building from Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction, he explains the Will as the inaccessible force we glimpse through inner bodily awareness, evil because purposeless. Watching the Doctor's serial victories is then offered as a light, Schopenhauerian escape through art from the terror of the Will.

33.title: The Master The Slave of the Time-Lord Cunning of Reason
33.file: ch33 - The Master The Slave of the Time-Lord Cunning of Reason.md
33.relation: Uses Hegel's master-slave dialectic to diagnose the Master: his craving to be acknowledged as 'the Master' (Harold Saxon's dominion in 'The Sound of Drums', devouring humans in 'The End of Time') can only win the recognition of inferiors, which is worthless since genuine recognition must come from an equal. As a Hegelian world-historical individual driven by passion, he unknowingly serves the Time Lords' cunning of reason, the four drums being their implanted tool for escaping the time lock. The chapter ends with him finally attaining the slave-consciousness's independence by turning on and killing Rassilon, renouncing the recognition he can never get.

34.title: I Am the Bad Wolf
34.file: ch34 - I Am the Bad Wolf.md
34.relation: Answers Davros's charge that the Doctor fashions companions into weapons by examining his character through virtue ethics: his unifying virtue is Heideggerian 'authentic concern', always offering aggressors like the Nestene or the Sycorax a choice so they become genuinely responsible, as in the fly-swatting thought experiment. Companions instead act from compassion, which lacks impartiality and produces the 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' (Rose's Dalek genocide, Martha's Osterhagen Key, Jack's warp star). Since for Aristotle a friend is 'another himself', the companions' actions are in a sense the Doctor's own yet founded on a distorted disposition, which is why he runs from his past.

35.title: EPISODE 5 - Brilliant! Fantastic! Molto Bene!
35.file: ch35 - EPISODE 5 - Brilliant! Fantastic! Molto Bene!.md

36.title: One More Thing, Don’t Blink!
36.file: ch36 - One More Thing, Don’t Blink!.md
36.relation: Uses Carroll's art-horror theory (monster = threat plus disgust) to ask why the Weeping Angels of 'Blink' terrify despite being beautiful, harmless-seeming statues. The answer: by dumping Kathy and Billy in the past they destroy identity itself, understood through Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity, since everything a person cares about is tied to a time and place. Since the Angels provoke no disgust, the chapter revises Carroll: horror is fear plus impotence, and forcing victims to survive by not blinking makes viewers feel their powerlessness over their own bodies.

37.title: A Beautiful Destiny
37.relation: Asks whether the Dalek casing can literally be beautiful, contrasting Kant's aesthetics (free beauty as the mind's fit with reality versus merely 'dependent' beauty of Davros-designed purpose) with Hegel's claim that beauty is thought embodied in matter, peaking in the human form, and Plato's view (via Nehamas's Phaedrus reading) that beauty begins the desire to care for a thing. Alexander of Hales's beauty-within-the-order and the Fourth Doctor's 'Genesis of the Daleks' echo, then Rosenkranz's aesthetic inferno where ugliness exists only as beauty's negation, show beauty and monstrosity need not be opposites. The conclusion is deliberately open: the puzzle forces us into metaphysics about mind and reality, not mere taste.

38.title: The Odd Thought of Doctor Who
38.file: ch38 - The Odd Thought of Doctor Who.md
38.relation: Maps Leibniz's monadology onto the Whoniverse: the Doctor's individual concept survives each regeneration as a thinking monad while its bodily monads are replaced, parallel Liz Shaws in 'Inferno' show incompossible predicates, and the Time Lords play Leibniz's God permitting minimal evil, which the Doctor accepts in refusing to avert the Daleks' creation in 'Genesis of the Daleks'. The dimensionally transcendental TARDIS illustrates the principle of indiscernibles, the Matrix becomes a failed pre-established harmony haunted by confused perceptions, and the Master hallucinates against the Doctor like Descartes's evil demon. The Valeyard is modeled as an incompossible world on Leibniz's Sextus Tarquinius pyramid and Borges's forking paths, closing with Leibniz's own 'odd thought' academy of wonders.

39.title: EPISODE 6 - Lots of Planets Have a North!
39.file: ch39 - EPISODE 6 - Lots of Planets Have a North!.md

40.title: Bunker Mentality or Love
40.relation: Argues Terry Nation made the Daleks evil by inverting the Socrates-to-Kant tradition equating humanity with rationality: the Daleks of 'The Daleks' (1963) are hyper-rational but feelingless, unable to understand Susan's name or laughter, and Ian's verdict is simply 'They just aren't human'. The chapter situates them in the neutron-bomb panic of the Cuban Missile Crisis era (Skaro's undamaged city, stone trees) and a H.G. Wells lineage of evolution gone wrong (Martians, Morlocks), so the Daleks horrify as the emotionless future we might become after the bomb. Rorty's claim that moral progress comes through enlarged empathy, not reason, explains why Ian teaches the Thals goodness by appealing to love for their captured friend rather than argument.

41.title: The Doctor, Defender of British Dreams
41.file: ch41 - The Doctor, Defender of British Dreams.md
41.relation: Argues the Doctor became Britain's national hero precisely at the moment of post-war imperial decline and decolonization: an anti-imperial Time Lord who still claims Time Lord identity, he personifies the country Britain hoped to be, in Fiske's phrase a mediator between god and man who wins by 'warm humane science' rather than superior force. The chapter traces this through Verity Lambert's anti-establishment design, Tom Baker's 'romantic wanderer', Romana as the ideal modern woman unfettered by gender roles, the Doctor's Big Brother-critiquing in 'The Sun-Makers' against Britain's own CCTV reality, and the spin-offs, concluding the show supplies a national mirror of hope and how Britain thinks it ought to be.

42.title: The Doctor Dances
42.relation: Uses Vico's theory of myth (myths as communal rituals binding passion, decaying into the 'barbarism of reflection') to read the show's myth-versus-science serials: 'The Daemons' dismissively reduces myth to bad science, 'Meglos' shows the Deons' ritual nearly destroying Tigella, while 'Snakedance' shows ancient ritual wisdom, kept by Dojjen, defeating the Mara where decadent scholarship fails. Then Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment grounds the deeper claim that science is itself a limiting myth, so the Doctor's 'laws of time' in 'The Waters of Mars' and 'The Fires of Pompeii' are self-imposed necessity that Donna can puncture. The show's counsel is balance: the Doctor keeps his science humane by respecting myth, dancing rather than shooting.

43.title: Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation
43.file: ch43 - Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation.md
43.relation: Argues Doctor Who is philosophy's ally by way of Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching, which produces justified true belief, and rhetoric, which wins by persuasion: the Master is the master rhetorician whose hypnotic manipulation manufactures unreliable beliefs, while the Doctor is the Socratic teacher who gives information and lets companions decide. Socrates's descriptions of philosophy (the good life, sense of wonder, love of real knowledge) are matched to the show's career as an educational program that teaches viewers to reflect on how they reason, how they treat 'others' like Daleks and Silurians, and to revise their views, that is, to live the examined life.

44.title: Would You Like a Jelly Baby
44.file: ch44 - Would You Like a Jelly Baby.md

45.title: The What, When, and Who of Doctor Who
45.file: ch45 - The What, When, and Who of Doctor Who.md

46.title: The High Council of Gallifrey
46.file: ch46 - The High Council of Gallifrey.md

47.title: The Matrix of Time Lord Bibliographic Sources
47.file: ch47 - The Matrix of Time Lord Bibliographic Sources.md

48.title: Logically Organized Index, for the Cyberman and Dalek in All of Us
48.file: ch48 - Logically Organized Index, for the Cyberman and Dalek in All of Us.md

5.title: Invitation
5.relation: A fictional editor's preface presenting the volume as speeches recovered from the Bene Gesserit Archives and the ruins of Dar-es-Balat, gathered for the ten-thousandth anniversary of Leto II's transformation into the God Emperor. It sets up the book's framing conceit: the essays are in-universe commemorations of Paul, Duncan Idaho, and the Dune-times, written by authors who look back in fascination at 'those legendary philosophies' of ancient Earth.

7.title: The End of the Story
7.file: ch07 - The End of the Story.md
7.relation: Reads the Gom Jabbar test as Herbert's definition of humanity: Paul endures Mohiam's pain box because a human stays in the trap to turn it on the trapper and protect the species, while an animal only chews off its own leg. The Butlerian Jihad's ban on 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' is applied to our own iPod-and-PDA dependence, with Mentat Thufir Hawat showing that losing the machine-crutch 'forced human minds to develop,' in line with Aristotle's phronesis and the politics of the common good (and Plato's contemplation as the core of happiness). The chapter closes by turning the human/animal test on the modern West—Baron Harkonnen-like consumers whose water-hungry beef habit makes us the trap of our own environmental collapse.

8.title: The (Single) Garden Path
8.relation: Compares Herbert's three eugenics programs: the Bene Gesserit's centuries-long Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (explicitly modeled on the communal breeding of the guardians in Plato's Republic, undone when Jessica bears Paul a generation early and he escapes their control), Leto II's Golden Path breeding for Siona's invisibility to prescience, and the Tleilaxu axolotl-tank immortality that collapses when their Face Dancers out-mimic them. Each program is weighed ethically—Leto as the 'ultimate consequentialist' whose species-saving tyranny invokes Mill's utilitarianism and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means, the Sisterhood as shifting toward Kantian duties against using persons as mere means. Herbert's lesson: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics,' whether aimed at a single person, a single result, or a single agenda.

9.title: From the Deserts of Arrakis to the Deserts of Earth
9.file: ch09 - From the Deserts of Arrakis to the Deserts of Earth.md
9.relation: Built entirely on Clausewitz's 'remarkable trinity'—the balance of people, military, and government—as the framework for war in Dune: Duke Leto's plan to win Fremen support on Arrakis, Muad'Dib's defusal of the Stilgar leadership challenge as a model of trinity-balancing in irregular warfare, and the messianic goal-inflation that unbalances the trinity and unleashes the jihad that kills sixty-one billion. The author, a US Army officer writing as a Mentat of Leto II, applies the same lesson to Afghanistan and post-Saddam Iraq: without a clear, achievable political goal, military force produces unintended consequences no Kwisatz Haderach could fully control.

10.title: Intending the Way Out
10.file: ch10 - Intending the Way Out.md
10.relation: Stages the paradox of foreknowledge through Paul's prescient dream of meeting Chani and his futile struggle against the foreseen jihad: since knowledge (on Plato's justified-true-belief account) is factive, a known future seems unalterable. It tests the classic escapes—Boethius's God in ever-present eternity and Aquinas's seeing all time 'under the aspect of eternity,' Laplace's demon, Richard Taylor's fatalism—and finds the Atreides oracles are no gods, only probabilistic predictors whose visions fix the possibilities they see. The way out is Anscombe's Intention: like God knowing creation because He authored it, Paul and Leto know their futures practically, as agents whose intentions help decide which possibilities become actual, so freedom survives as terrific responsibility.

11.title: Politics of Muad’Dib
11.file: ch11 - Politics of Muad’Dib.md

12.title: The Jihadist Way of Life
12.file: ch12 - The Jihadist Way of Life.md
12.relation: Argues the Fremen are 'shockingly American': their Spannungsbogen self-discipline, spiritual self-sufficiency, and endurance of hardship exemplify Emerson's self-reliance, while the jihad's aim of razing the rule of the Great Houses into relations of equals echoes Dewey's democracy as a way of life—faith in the potentialities of every human nature. The parallel runs through the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh and Paul's blind walk into the desert, both acting on values Americans prize. Herbert's remark that people surrender judgment to leaders 'wrapped in the myth fabric of society' grounds the pragmatist point that Fremen myth-making, like America's exceptionalist self-image, works—and Alia's 'my brother is pragmatic' seals it.

13.title: Leto’s Not So Golden Path
13.file: ch13 - Leto’s Not So Golden Path.md
13.relation: Diagnoses the Duniverse's recurring collapse not, as Herbert's 'Dune Genesis' has it, in hero-worship, but in rule conducted entirely through strategic action—Habermas's term for goal-oriented, self-interested rationality—as when even the Atreides council discusses only the appearance of a constitution rather than its legitimacy. Physical stability enforced by threats never becomes normative stability: Corrino, Paul's jihad-empire, and Leto II's 3,500-year tyranny all fail because their subjects are never authors of the law, and Leto's return to Bene Gesserit-style breeding programs ignores humanity's deliberative potential. The proposed remedy is democracy—rule by the people—even against Alia's cry that 'Atreides power must never be marginalized by the chaos of democracy.'

14.title: Spice as the Vehicle of Power
14.file: ch14 - Spice as the Vehicle of Power.md
14.relation: Reads the Duniverse as Hobbes's state of nature at galactic scale: Emperor, Landsraad houses, Guild, Bene Gesserit, and Tleilaxu are rationally self-preserving factions in a war of all against all over scarce spice, where 'justice' names only what enforcement power backs and life for the losers is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' Leto II is the Leviathan—a literal 'mortal God,' half sandworm—whose spice monopoly and fusion of political with spiritual authority impose a forced peace; his assassination then shows split authority re-igniting the conflict in the Scattering and the Honored Matres. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto's hoarding both illustrate that the power to destroy a thing is absolute control over it.

15.title: Ethics of Muad’Dib
15.file: ch15 - Ethics of Muad’Dib.md

16.title: The Spice of Meaning
16.file: ch16 - The Spice of Meaning.md
16.relation: Mines Dune for an account of the meaningful life by contrasting the Harkonnens, who amass power for its own sake and grind Yueh's very identity to dust, with the Fremen, whose rigid rituals give meaning but suffocate anyone who lives entirely inside them—with Duke Leto's abolition of the beggars' water-towel custom as the failure case in between. Following Aristotle's method of starting from 'the views of the wise,' the chapter argues virtue is an open-ended, formulaless skill: rising above inherited identities while repairing the social bonds they sustain, as Paul and Jessica do by breaking selected Fremen rules and leaving the sietch stronger. The worm-rider, feet shifting on sand above a creature that can never be fully controlled, is the closing image of a struggle that never finally resolves.

17.title: Alone into the Desert
17.relation: Audits Duniverse lives by Socrates's standard—the condition of the soul over wealth and power, with justice, courage, temperance, and wisdom—finding Baron Harkonnen utterly wanting, 'Leto the Just' compromised by forgery and concubinage, Paul unjust in his myth-making holy war (though Plato's Republic would smile on ruling myths), and the Fremen admirable in temperance and courage but fatally sure of themselves where Socrates prized knowing that you do not know. Aristotle's function argument and golden mean follow: Paul's first worm-ride is courage between rashness and cowardice, but Paul's and Leto II's extreme, humanity-saving selflessness has no excess to moderate and so breaks the doctrine of the mean. The author concludes Socrates is too harsh and Aristotle closer, yet even he fails: sometimes the best life requires extreme virtue and even injustice, as with the two Atreides emperors.

18.title: The Emergence of Good from Evil
18.file: ch18 - The Emergence of Good from Evil.md
18.relation: Uses David Lynch's film—Baron Harkonnen as evil personified, Paul's prophetic dreams as biblical revelation, 'the sleeper must awaken'—to stage the problem of evil: if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly good, why do Harkonnens and man-eating worms exist? It lays out the free will defense, J.L. Mackie's objection that God could have created beings who always freely choose good, and the moral/natural evil distinction (Feyd's poisoned blade versus the worm destroying the spice crawler), then extracts the film's own alternative theodicy: good is defined against evil, since the Fremen's dormant 'goodness' awakens only in the struggle Paul leads against their enslavers. The chapter ends with John Hick's soul-making thought that spiritual growth comes through response to challenges, while conceding the evidential problem of evil's sheer quantity.

20.title: Long-Term Identity
20.relation: Asks whether the final Duncan Idaho ghola, whose serial memories wake during his encounter with Murbella, is the same person as the original who died holding off nineteen Sardaukar. It tests physical continuity, Locke's memory-based sameness of person (Hayt becomes Duncan only when the original's consciousness reawakens), Parfit's psychological connectedness with its redescription of identity as survival through quasi-memory, Schechtman's narrative self-constitution, Velleman's self-inventing characters, and four-dimensionalist 'space-time worms' on which Leto II's 3,500 years and the Duncans' gappy five millennia are single long selves. Herbert's moral: identity is not fixed—societies and technologies, from the Tleilaxu tanks to the Sisterhood's swift accommodation, keep redrawing what counts as the same person. Same Duncans, same person.

21.title: The Test of Humanity
21.file: ch21 - The Test of Humanity.md
21.relation: Reads the Butlerian Jihad through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: technology is not a device but a way of 'enframing' the world as a standing-reserve, so the Harkonnens see Arrakis, the Fremen, and even Mentat Piter as mere resources, while the Fremen's maker hooks and ecological terraforming show tools absorbed into a lived practice that shapes their users in turn. Paul's prescience becomes the ultimate tool—perfect advice that puts his life on autopilot through Dune Messiah—so Leto II's breeding of Siona-gene humans invisible to oracles completes the Jihad's lesson: self-determination and 'living judgments,' not optimization, are what the Gom Jabbar's test of humanity is for.

22.title: Get Out of My Mind!
22.file: ch22 - Get Out of My Mind!.md
22.relation: Runs Lady Jessica's spice-agony Other Memory through Locke's Essay: if a person is a 'thinking intelligent being' whose identity extends as far as her consciousness reaches, then Jessica—having received the memories of every Reverend Mother back to Raquella Berto-Anirul—must be identical with Raquella, and with Alia who shares the same memories, which is absurd. Thomas Reid's gallant officer is staged as Gurney Halleck, who remembers Rabban's whip but not his sister's eyes, breaking the transitivity of memory-based identity. The chapter closes with three modern paths—psychological continuity, Eric Olson's animalism, and Dennett's selves as 'centers of narrative gravity'—plus a Lockean coda defending the Abomination Alia as a person no fixed class of nature could exclude.

24.title: The Prophet
24.relation: Presents Muad'Dib as Nietzsche's Zarathustra in the Dune universe: the sardonic self-mockery that keeps a great man from believing his own myth, the valuation of life-enhancing 'truths' over correspondence-truth (behind all logic stand 'value judgments,' as Beyond Good and Evil has it), and monumental, mythologized history against Mentat-accurate history that kills religion. Paul's Fremen, first hard and vital, go 'water-fat' under the paradise his jihad built, becoming Nietzsche's 'Ultimate Man'—the last man who has left the places where living was hard and demands 'a little poison now and then'—so Muad'Dib must become the Preacher to destroy the rigid code he created, as Zarathustra came to undo Zoroaster's morality; both prophets preach self-overcoming toward the Superman.

25.title: Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps
25.file: ch25 - Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps.md
25.relation: Argues that Herbert is a genuine philosopher extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra into the twentieth century, via three narrative parallels: the Preacher entering Arrakeen mirrors Zarathustra's first down-going into the town with its tightrope walker and mocking buffoon; Paul's empire of water-fat Fremen and Alia's orthodoxy realizes the 'Ultimate Man' whom the crowd begs for instead of the Superman; and prescience reworks eternal recurrence's gateway 'Moment,' where every timeline ends in Krazilec. Reading Paul's sixty-five-billion-death jihad through Arendt's banality of evil and Herbert's 'superheroes are disastrous' thesis, the chapter concludes Paul is the failed tightrope walker and Leto II the goad—'not lightning, but lightning rod'—pushing humanity beyond man toward the Superman, with Spannungsbogen naming the tension of the drawn bow between animal and Overman.

26.title: In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . .
26.file: ch26 - In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . ..md
26.relation: Continues the earlier defense of oracular freedom ('Curse of the Golden Path'): because an oracle's gaze from a present moment fixes the very set of future possibilities, Paul and Leto are free precisely where they are blind—above all in their 'vision-battle' in the Tanzerouft, which no oracle can foresee, and which Paul's single whispered 'Don't' concedes to his son's Golden Path. Leto's breeding of Siona, invisible to prescience, is read as his deliberate self-blinding—'the price of freedom is an invigilance of eternity'—and the whole affair vindicates heroism as steering probabilities rather than escaping fate. Paul emerges as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense, whose hamartia is his all-too-human refusal to become a monster to save the future.

4.title: Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch
4.file: ch04 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

5.title: Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do
5.file: ch05 - Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do.md
5.relation: The editors' introduction frames Rush as a 'thinking man's band': a cult favorite deliberately outside the mainstream whose fusion of virtuosic, structurally complex music with lyrics on social, scientific, and historical themes triggers both fierce devotion and passionate hatred in listeners. It sketches the band's history from its 1968 Toronto cover-band beginnings through Neil Peart's 1974 arrival and the album-oriented-rock success of Moving Pictures ('Tom Sawyer', 'Limelight'), arguing that Rush's lasting achievements come when thoughtful lyrics and progressive/hard music work together. It invites readers to treat each essay as one voice in an ongoing dialogue and to accept that being different, like Rush, is not a bad thing.

6.title: PART I - To the Margin of Error
6.file: ch06 - PART I - To the Margin of Error.md

7.title: Houston, We Have a Problem, or, What Goes Up Must Come Down
7.file: ch07 - Houston, We Have a Problem, or, What Goes Up Must Come Down.md
7.relation: Auxier interleaves a memoir of sneaking off to Rush's 1977 Memphis concert (the Halloween-weekend ruse with his friend Brice, beers at J-Wags Lounge, the first hangover, and the setlist from 'Bastille Day' through '2112') with a philosophical defense of the band. He rejects the charge that Rush is a vehicle for Ayn Rand's objectivism, arguing Rand was a novelist with 'philosophical moments' whose analogy-built system is not philosophy, and that Peart quickly outgrew her influence by Moving Pictures. Working from Susanne Langer, he claims Rush assimilates lyrics to music (so 'Tom Sawyer' and 'Limelight' need no poetic standard), that music is a 'virtualization' of time creating the illusion of felt life, and that Rush's live processed sounds are second-order virtualizations whose only real test is whether the music is good.

8.title: Coda
8.relation: Bowman surveys the fifty-four recorded Rush tributes of 1996-2005, from the Barenaked Ladies quoting the 'Tom Sawyer' swagger riff in 'Grade 9' to DJ Z-Trip's trip-hop remix, Disarray's death-metal version, Deadsy's industrial take, and string-quartet translations, arguing that Rush's ambiguous genre coding is what lets this 'musicians' music' travel across mutually exclusive fan communities. He builds his own 'scholarly meta-remix' interleaving six versions of 'Tom Sawyer' in different keys and meters, and reads the 7/4 instrumental section's fate in each cover. Borrowing Robert Walser's claim that musical meanings are grounded in an ideological field where institutions enforce preferred meanings, he concludes that tribute artists find 'refractive, distorted, and disruptive' meanings in Rush, and that progressive rock served as 'substitute classical music' for working- and lower-middle-class fans.

9.title: The Heart and Mind United
9.file: ch09 - The Heart and Mind United.md
9.relation: Sheinbaum argues against the assumption that Rush's rhythmic complexity is 'thinking' music opposed to bodily groove, showing through close listening that 'Subdivisions' (7/8 in 2+2+3 groups), 'Limelight' (4/4 and 3/4 bars interleaved), 'Jacob's Ladder' (alternating 5/4 and 6/4), and the 7/8 passages of 'La Villa Strangiato' all groove while the band retains standard eight-bar phrase structures. He treats meter and hypermeter as Western cultural constructions, and reads Rush's metric deviations as a musical image of the individual resisting a 'conformist social order' (citing Chris McDonald on the individualism Rush shares with Ayn Rand's middle-class virtues). His resolution is dialectical: complex and conventional elements operate as simultaneous poles in synthesis, so mind and body, thought and groove, are united rather than opposed, a point he presses against the racialized mind-body binary in writing about rhythm.

10.title: No Heart to Lie
10.file: ch10 - No Heart to Lie.md
10.relation: Reuland uses YouTube drum covers of 'The Body Electric', 'Subdivisions', and 'YYZ' to analyze Rush's 'aesthetic of replicability': songs built as artifacts meant to be reproduced note-for-note, signaled by literal codes like the Morse-code intro to 'YYZ' and the binary '1001001' the android of 'The Body Electric' must crack to become human. He explains why critics deride this anti-expressive virtuosity by way of Amiri Baraka's racial coding of technique, Pierre Bourdieu's account of how 'natural' taste is legitimated while studied learning bears class stigma, and Mary Bucholtz's picture of nerds as hyper-white; the fans' literal meritocracy parodies the information economy's promise that skill converts directly into success. Finally he reads 'Limelight' as Rush's skepticism toward performance as a 'gilded cage' of inauthenticity, so that play-along videos recode performance as self-improvement that cannot be faked.

11.title: He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes
11.file: ch11 - He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes.md
11.relation: Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.

12.title: PART II - The Ebb and Flow of Tidal Fortune
12.file: ch12 - PART II - The Ebb and Flow of Tidal Fortune.md

13.title: Enjoy These Moments
13.file: ch13 - Enjoy These Moments.md
13.relation: Earleywine argues that Rush's lyrics trained a generation in the core moves of cognitive-behavioral therapy, an idea he traces back to Epictetus before Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck rediscovered it against Freudian orthodoxy. He maps specific distortions onto specific songs: 'Witch Hunt' on dichotomous labeling, 'Distant Early Warning' ('black and whites of youth') on all-or-nothing thinking, 'Emotion Detector' on emotional reasoning, 'Vital Signs' and 'Totem' on thoughts altering perception, and 'Subdivisions' ('Conform or be cast out') as realistic critique rather than maladaptive thought. The final step, acting on examined values and savoring the present ('Time Stand Still', 'The Camera Eye', 'Chain Lightning'), makes the songs the incarnation of their own advice: just listen.

14.title: Smashing Critics’ Pumpkins
14.file: ch14 - Smashing Critics’ Pumpkins.md
14.relation: Reisch reconstructs the rock-critical case against Rush ('pretentious', 'ridiculous', Greg Kot's jibe that Peart drums 'like he's working out a calculus formula') as resting on an implicit Platonism: the Forms fix what a 'real' rock'n'roll band is, so a band mixing rock with philosophy, literature, and mathematical precision seems to violate the metaphysical grain of the universe rather than merely disappoint a taste. He explains the Forms through Plato's trees and the Form of the song ('La Villa Strangiato' and 'Happy Birthday'), reads Jack Black's 'one atom' praise of Peart as mathematics-as-highest-knowledge, and treats the 'Aristocrats' joke and UFO mocking Geddy Lee as incongruity humor at kinds illicitly combined. Dropping the Platonic metaphysics of kinds collapses the critics' syllogism into a bare insistence that different is bad, which is the revenge Gene Simmons ('What kind of band is Rush? It's Rush.') and Billy Corgan ('they just don't fit in a neat box') already delivered.

15.title: Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song
15.file: ch15 - Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song.md
15.relation: Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.

16.title: Hope
16.file: ch16 - Hope.md
16.relation: Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.

17.title: Tallying the Total
17.relation: Kreuger applies Derrida's 'Differance' to how Rush gets valued: Hugh Syme's starman, pentagram, and bunnies are signs whose meaning defers down a chain, so no description of Geddy Lee ever touches the thing itself, and the band's twenty-four gold albums (economic value) never settle the contested question of cultural value that critics deny and fans affirm. Time defers value too: 'Time Stand Still' and the concert ticket sell a moment already gone, bootlegs and leaks chase the unrepeatable experience, and radio distance once hid songs like '2112' from value. 'The Spirit of Radio' carries the thesis in its own lyric, 'bearing a gift beyond price, almost free', where 'the words of the profits' on the studio walls measure sold value against integrity, and deferral finally emerges as Derrida's 'condition of possibility' that lets Rush's cultural value recover through Colbert, Rock Band, and I Love You, Man.

18.title: Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love
18.file: ch18 - Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love.md
18.relation: Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.

20.title: A Single, Perfect Sphere
20.relation: Reads Rush's 'Hemispheres' as a correction to Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: Apollo's gifts of reason leave the people joyless, Dionysus's release into passion leaves them starving in winter, and Cygnus is made god of Balance because human nature thinks and feels at once. Against Descartes's two substances and the 'Robots Plus' picture, the author argues feeling is not supernatural icing on a machine but how survival-minded organisms stay in phenomenal contact with the world, so physicalism needs deepening rather than a nonphysical mind.

21.title: “I Want to Look Around Me Now”
21.file: ch21 - “I Want to Look Around Me Now”.md
21.relation: Charts Rush's gradual saturation with synthesizers, sequencers, and electronic percussion from 'Subdivisions' and 'Distant Early Warning' to 'Time Stand Still,' explaining the adoption through Wajcman's gradual-modification model and feminist analyses of technology as a male skill domain — including de Beauvoir's point that technical prowess underwrites virility, which the author applies to Rush fans' valorizing of the trio's chops. It closes by casting the band's handling of music technology as Bourdieu's habitus, granting Rush 'relative autonomy' from the hi-tech pressures of the 1980s.

22.title: Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do
22.file: ch22 - Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do.md
22.relation: A music-theoretic account of how Rush's music signifies only for competent listeners: the vocal pauses of 'Entre Nous' paint separation while its related keys paint unity, the 'Oriental riff' and pentatonics of 'A Passage to Bangkok' and 'Tai Shan' evoke nonspecific otherness, space-music textures open '2112' and 'Cygnus X-1,' and tritones brand evil in 'Witch Hunt,' 'The Necromancer,' and 'YYZ.' It ends by noting the irony that Rush uses its own electric voice to portray the bad guys, concluding with 'Entre Nous' that otherness and difference can be synthesized into a greater whole.

23.title: Does Rush Offer a Way Out
23.file: ch23 - Does Rush Offer a Way Out.md
23.relation: Uses Rush's 1980s lyrics about facades and trust — 'Limelight''s strangers, 'Show Don't Tell''s refusal to take things on faith, 'War Paint''s lying mirror, and the synthesizer as an instrument that can fake any other sound — to stage skepticism about other minds, running from Descartes's cogito through solipsism and behaviorism. Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box and private-language argument dissolve the inner/outer confusion as a grammatical one, and 'Turn the Page' supplies the way out of the fly-bottle: nothing survives a vacuum, and with other people all we can do is be reminded.

24.title: Counterparts Lee’s Voice and Peart’s Drums
24.file: ch24 - Counterparts Lee’s Voice and Peart’s Drums.md
