7.title: Psych and Philosophy
7.relation: Robert Arp's introduction argues Psych is perfect for philosophy because Henry's games train observation and inference exactly as philosophers hone them, while Shawn's ruse shows how clever people abuse those powers to deceive - quoting Machiavelli's line that one who deceives will always find those who allow themselves to be deceived. It sets up the book's recurring ethical question about lying: lies for the liar's profit (Shawn avoiding jail in the pilot), paternalistic lies for the hearer's own good (Henry telling seven-year-old Shawn he 'blacked out' about his mother's death), and lies to benefit many (promising a terrorist freedom to find his bomb). Since Shawn's lies solve cases and save lives, the introduction suggests they may not be so bad in the end, though it admits wishing he would just come clean as a talented honest detective.

9.title: Psych and Philosophy
9.relation: Michaud argues that Shawn's whole psychic career runs on fallacies of relevance - the red herring of claiming to be psychic to dodge arrest, plus ad hominem mockery that deflects Lassiter's fraud accusations - so the show's comedy turns on bad logic being used to lead people to true conclusions. Socrates supplies the opposing voice: like the Sophists who argued any side for money, Shawn reasons for convenience and amusement, and his deception is an inconsistency of the kind Socrates refused in Plato's Crito, where he would not bribe his way out of a death sentence. An invented Platonic-style dialogue has Socrates question Shawn until he concedes that lying breeds more lying and harm - 'her name is Truth!' - before Shawn escapes the elenchus by spotting lipstick on Socrates's collar. The chapter leaves the verdict open: Shawn saves lives and raises the world's happiness, but his trickery also trains Santa Barbara to reason badly and trust con artists.

10.title: Psych and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Psych and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Muniz plays narratologist, arguing that what matters in Psych is not the story but the storyteller: the 1980s prologues, alias gags, pineapples, and Lassie feuds are recurring formula elements, while Shawn's eidetic-memory sequence - the raised eyebrow, the chime, the highlighted detail - is the one necessary element around which every episode's rising action, climax, and denouement are arranged. Asking whether Gus chatting at the aquarium dolphins or the characters' comic pauses break the fourth wall, he answers no: the eidetic sequences only produce a 'projective illusion of cinematic image' that makes viewers feel they see through Shawn's eyes, so the wall is never actually broken - the show simply 'psychs you out in the end.' The chapter even structures itself like a Psych episode, prologue to climax, to prove the point that structure is function.

11.title: Psych and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Psych and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.

12.title: Psych and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Psych and Philosophy.md

13.title: Psych and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Psych and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Yim argues that what onlookers mistake for psychic power is thin-slicing, Gladwell's rapid pattern-recognition, the same skill behind John Gottman's ninety-percent-accurate marriage predictions and Paul Ekman's involuntary micro-expressions, which is how Shawn acquits the telenovela actor in 'Lights, Camera,... Homicidio' by reading genuine surprise on the tape. Criminals deceive by staging a context - a gun by the suicide's hand - that biases investigators the way thinking 'forest' biases us toward 'black bear,' while Shawn's two-stage slice, gut instinct plus conscious interpretation, isolates the telltale detail (a marinated steak in the fridge) that the staging was designed to bury. Henry's flashbacks - the cereal box opened from the bottom, young Shawn reading poker tells in the locker room - are boot camp that trains him to think outside conventional frames, producing the 'tint on the windows to the soul' certitude he invokes in 'Cloudy... with a Chance of Murder.'

14.title: Psych and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Psych and Philosophy.md
14.relation: The Senors use Psych to separate true belief from knowledge: Shawn's hunch that Shabby the sea lion was murdered is true but shabbily evidenced, and his justified, true belief that a Clayton family member sabotaged the plane fails to be knowledge when the killer turns out to be a son-in-law he had no reason to think existed - a textbook Gettier case from 'He Dead.' They then weigh the two main theories of justification, evidentialism (with its base rates and prior probabilities) and reliabilism, and both vindicate the careful, methodical work of Lassiter and Juliet while Shawn's trigger-happy belief-forming habit strikes out twice. Shawn is redeemed only as an evidence-generator whose disregard for priors takes 'impossible' suspects like a murdered sea lion seriously, so that pairing his talents with the detectives' rigor yields the complete detective.

15.title: Psych and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Psych and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Guidry-Grimes treats Chief Vick's hiring of Shawn as a genuine problem in applied ethics rather than a joke: the Psi hypothesis fails Ockham's Razor and no controlled study supports paranormal ability, yet Vick - unlike viewers who know Shawn is a fraud - must weigh her obligations to victims, the department, and taxpayers on the evidence she has. The chapter argues that hiring Shawn is ethically defensible given his record of solving over fifty unsolvable cases, but it catalogues the costs: false hope for distraught families (Marc Klaas's resentment of psychic tipsters), damage to Lassiter's morale, wasted resources, and the fragile public trust bound up with taxpayer money. The conclusion is a compromise: Vick is ethically required to use every tool in the arsenal, including a successful 'psychic,' only in desperate high-stakes cases where the victim's family does not object, and otherwise merely permitted.

16.title: Psych and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Psych and Philosophy.md

17.title: Psych and Philosophy
17.relation: Malloy maps Nietzsche's three metamorphoses onto Shawn's life: the camel who carried Henry's burdensome training and the expectation he become a cop, the lion who slew the dragon 'Thou shalt' by stealing a car at eighteen and ending Henry's dream, and the child who creates his own values of fun, laughter, and silliness - defended as genuinely Nietzschean since the Overman must overcome the 'spirit of gravity.' Gus and Lassiter figure as last men, the herd animals Shawn manipulates and pities (Lassie's literal crap list a study in ressentiment), while only Pierre Despereaux and Mr. Yin count as true rivals because only fellow Overmen, forging values beyond good and evil, can genuinely challenge Shawn. The chapter closes on the Overman's dilemma - loneliness, backsliding into the herd, or trying to make Overmen of others - which explains why Shawn treats his friends and enemies the way he does.

18.title: Psych and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Psych and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Ruiz casts Lassiter as Nietzsche's slave - his worth defined reactively against Shawn, his advice that 'all romance ends in despair or death' reproducing the Judeo-Christian slave revolt in morality that turned weakness into virtue - and Shawn as the master, a self-propelled wheel who bakes a pineapple cake in an Easy Bake oven for nineteen hours whether or not anyone is watching. Shawn's generosity (helping the wrongly accused, the ghost-struck, and the deluded, once even crediting a cat with solving murders in '9 Lives') is read as the noble overflow of superabundant power rather than pity, and his hostage-saving risk-taking as will to power understood as self-mastery. Even the central lie gets a dialectical reading - like art, pretending to be psychic reveals the truth hidden behind appearances - though the chapter concedes Shawn's slavish moments, from daddy issues to his obsession with one-upping Declan in 'Shawn 2.0.'

20.title: Psych and Philosophy
20.relation: McCraw turns the question 'should we trust Shawn?' into the philosophy of testimony: Lassiter's policy of never believing without independent evidence embodies Hume's demand that testimony be backed by evidence of the speaker's reliability, while Buzz McNab's instant faith embodies Reid's innate principles of veracity and credulity, and both extremes fail the department - Lassiter solves too late, McNab chases every early false lead. Juliet's developing, flexible trust - suspicious at first, convinced by results, never naive - models the circumstantial middle path that no hard-and-fast Humean or Reidian rule can capture. The verdict: treat Shawn's testimony as both psychic and psychotic, trusting the track record in some cases and discounting the wilder 'visions' in others, because when to trust is unavoidably vague and case-by-case.

21.title: Psych and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Psych and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Mahon and Ceballos read the pilot through the big-lie principle credited to Hitler and Goebbels: the truth - hyper-observation plus a photographic memory - is too mundane to be believed, so only the biggest possible lie, 'I am a psychic,' saves Shawn from jail, exploiting the reverse psychology by which hearers assume no liar would say something so implausible. The lie's durability is then explained with Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion: like horoscopes and psychoanalysis, Shawn's psychic claim is unfalsifiable, so the ex-con's finger-counting 'tests' in 'Woman Seeking Dead Husband' can confirm it but never refute it - a virtue for a liar, and precisely what makes a claim unscientific. Finally the chapter shifts blame to the victims: like Madoff investors who 'kind of saw it coming,' the SBPD is self-deceived, complicit in a lie it half knows is a lie because the gift horse keeps closing cases.

22.title: Psych and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Psych and Philosophy.md
22.relation: King argues that memory is only generally reliable and hence a limited evidential tool, sorting procedural, episodic, semantic, and flashbulb memory before cataloguing Psych's failure modes: Shawn's source confusion that has him chasing Frenzy when the Yin killer follows Psycho, Abigail's accurate pier memory feeding the false conclusion that Shawn stood her up, and Lassiter's implanted recollections after Shawn feeds him 'remembered' clues in 'From the Earth to the Starbucks.' The fake FBI psychic Lindsey's suggestive questioning of the Home Depot cashier shows how easily vivid 'recovered' memories are manufactured - even though the show conveniently makes them true every time. The upshot: only Henry-trained, near-eidetic recall approaches Shawn's feats, ordinary memory needs physical corroboration before it sends anyone to jail, and everyone else should train recall like a muscle.

24.title: Psych and Philosophy
24.relation: Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue. On Rocha's reading even Kant could endorse the one lie to rule them all - claiming to be psychic - because it respects rationality and human life in a society that irrationally esteems the supernatural, while Shawn's Gus-alias gags and bunny fabrications remain immoral.

25.title: Psych and Philosophy
25.relation: Stephenson tests Shawn's ruse against the major theories of justified deceit and finds it wanting: Plato's Myth of the Metals excuses paternalistic noble lies for social harmony that Shawn's self-aggrandizing motives cannot claim, utilitarianism collapses on the long-term costs of exposure (Gus, Juliet, Henry, and the SBPD condemned by association; clients betrayed; trust in law enforcement eroded), Kant's universalizability test sinks maxims like 'lie whenever a career opportunity is at stake,' and Popper's open society condemns just the deceit on which the psychic brand runs. Even the mutual-deceit analogy to poker and Sissela Bok's reasonable-person publicity test fail, since no public forum of reasonable people would bless duping paying private clients. The escape is extra-moral: Shawn's mischievous hokum is the socially necessary boundary-pusher, whose lesson against unreflective occult belief lands best when delivered with a laugh.

26.title: Psych and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Psych and Philosophy.md
26.relation: The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.

28.title: Psych and Philosophy
28.relation: Ronda Bowen argues that because Shawn delivers true conclusions under a false justification (psychic power), the SBPD's beliefs are Gettier-style justified true beliefs rather than knowledge, using Plato's Theaetetus (perception and true judgment fail as definitions) as the frame and Gettier's Smith/Jones and Ford/Brown cases to model episodes like 'Spellingg Bee,' where the police infer Miklous's guilt from Shawn's staged psychic demonstration. John Hawthorne's lottery propositions explain why Lassiter's 'Shawn isn't a psychic' certainty can never be fully justified, and the chapter closes on internalism versus externalism and the reliability of testimony, concluding the detectives become internally justified only when they re-derive Shawn's conclusions through their own reasoning.

29.title: Psych and Philosophy
29.relation: Amanda Lusky argues Shawn is a model pragmatist in the lineage of Peirce, James, and Dewey: he treats ideas as tools judged by consequences, is tough-minded about facts over theory (James's temperament distinction), and applies the pragmatic maxim from the squirrel-and-tree dispute to his loosely formed but working hunches. His co-operative inquiry with Gus and the SBPD - Gus's safe-cracking knowledge in 'Sixty Five Million Years Off,' passing Lassiter's polygraph in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' - enacts Dewey's democratic community solving problems together, and the chapter reads his tolerance of Gus's paranormal leads ('The Devil's in the Details') as pragmatic openness that enriches Santa Barbara's democratic life.

30.title: Psych and Philosophy
30.relation: Courtland Lewis replays Plato's Theaetetus with Shawn and Henry to show that perception and true judgment fail as accounts of knowledge, then recasts both Gettier cases with Psych material: Chief Vick's justified-but-lucky belief about the chief-of-police job, and Juliet's disjunction 'Shawn is a psychic or Gus is in Mazatlan.' Since justified true belief is not knowledge, he argues Shawn's trained senses fit reliabilism - distinguished from lucky predictors like Leonard Koppett and probed through Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp against Gus's super sniffer - and closes by combining reliabilist-foundationalism (Alston's two levels of knowledge), coherence theory, and Klein's infinitism into Shawn's observe-eliminate-conclude method.

32.title: Psych and Philosophy
32.relation: Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.

33.title: Psych and Philosophy
33.relation: Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.

34.title: Psych and Philosophy
34.relation: Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.

36.title: Psych and Philosophy
36.relation: John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'

37.title: Psych and Philosophy
37.relation: Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.

38.title: Psych and Philosophy
38.relation: C. Scott Sevier argues Henry deliberately recreated Shawn as Aristotle's 'another self' - Lassiter's 'which one?' joke in the kidnapping episode makes the identity explicit - and reads this through Plato's Symposium: via Diotima's ladder of love and the doctrine of forms, Henry achieves immortality by reproducing beauty in his son's educated soul, not just his body. The chapter then frames Shawn's fierce independence against his constant recourse to Henry's voice as the collision between medieval deference to authority and the modern ideal of autonomy in Descartes and Kant, showing that both thinkers quietly borrowed from Augustine (the causal adequacy principle, the good will), so Shawn's 'autonomy' is itself the product of his father's training - an internalized authority indistinguishable from his own.

39.title: Psych and Philosophy
39.relation: Mona Rocha asks whether Psych is sexist given Shawn's eighth-grade-girl caricature of Juliet in 'Spellingg Bee' and the secret knowledge kept from the show's women, then argues it is not: the women's inferior epistemic position is a byproduct of the con, not misogynist gatekeeping, because Shawn works collaboratively and non-hierarchically, shares credit (solving Lassiter's Back Bay Killer case for him in 'From the Earth to Starbucks'), gives the Chief the glory in 'There Might Be Blood,' and confronts the oilrig chauvinist outright. The contrast is The Mentalist, where Patrick Jane's withholding of deductions from Lisbon - going behind her back in 'Red Hair and Silver Tape' and getting evidence thrown out in 'Blood Money' - enacts patriarchal paternalism that undermines female leadership.

40.title: Psych and Philosophy
40.relation: This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.

8.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
8.file: ch08 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
8.relation: The editors introduce the book by contrasting The Good Wife with earlier law shows like Law and Order: for the first time we see lawyers at home, and the central figure is Alicia Florrick, juggling teenagers, a firm in bankruptcy, and a marriage wrecked by Peter's prostitution scandal while keeping up appearances as the 'good wife' and taking lover Will Gardner. They argue the show refuses a single right answer - her choices are selfish, cowardly, vengeful, or simply her being true to herself - and that her growth as a woman, mother, and lawyer challenges preconceived social norms about women and about lawyers. Philosophy enters as the natural sequel: ethics, justice, feminism, privacy rights, epistemology, and social-political philosophy are all sewn into the episodes.

9.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md

10.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Judith Andre uses the show's cases - Alicia's overnight prison visit to Peter for case information in 'Conjugal', snatching evidence before the police in 'Hi', Kalinda's inadmissible but coercive evidence in 'Heart', and Will's advice to use perjured testimony in 'Long Way Home' - to ask whether the profession's zealous advocacy actually serves justice. She explains the adversary system's two-level defense (each side's pursuit of victory supposedly forces truth out, mirroring sport) and its weaknesses: money decides outcomes, and no one in the courtroom is responsible for the truth, as the buried Childs tapes in 'Hybristophilia' show. Individual liberty against state power justifies criminal defense at most, and she endorses David Luban's sober conclusion that the system is justified yet 'cannot mandate lawyers to cut throats', with Alicia remaining the show's uneasy, unreconciled conscience.

11.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Jai Galliott takes the Season Three episode 'Whiskey Tango Foxtrot', in which Nevada-based drone operator Sergeant Elkins kills twelve Afghan civilians and is convicted of murder despite Alicia's scapegoating defense, as a case study in the ethics of drone warfare. Tracing just war theory from the Mahabharata through Augustine to Aquinas's jus ad bellum and jus in bello framework, he applies proportionality and discrimination to the strike and argues that sensor limits and the physical and emotional distance of push-button killing (Grossman's spectrum from knife combat to drones) erode operators' capacity for discriminate targeting. He concludes that drones are a moral hazard but a legitimate asset, and that blame must be apportioned among operator, manufacturer, and commanders rather than dumped on Elkins alone.

12.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Rod Carveth maps Bentham's act-utilitarianism onto Lockhart Gardner's defense-side reasoning and Mill's rule-utilitarianism onto the prosecution's, then tests the pairing on the firm's recurring client Colin Sweeney. Sweeney's cases - the wrongful-death suit in 'Bad' where Alicia says 'Of course' he killed his wife, the manslaughter plea and merger opportunism in 'Hybristophilia', and the perjured testimony Alicia may still use in 'Long Way Home' - show the firm letting the end of client and firm gain justify the means. Sweeney walking free, restored to his company, and a father despite admitting the murder is the counter-intuitive consequence that makes Carveth question whether act-utilitarianism should ground our decisions at all.

13.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md

14.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Celine Morin reads Alicia's love life through the Greek triad agape, eros, and philia as laid out in Plato's Symposium: her unconditional agape for Peter is eroded by his demands for forgiveness ('Stripped', 'Boom'), while the Socratic myth of Eros born from Penia's lack explains why she tells Will their affair is 'romantic because it didn't happen'. She argues Alicia abandons the romantic soul-mate model of her pearl-necklace marriage for Giddens's egalitarian 'pure relationship' with Will, but stays moored to the old family structure, hesitating on the doorstep in the Season Three cliffhanger 'The Dream Time'. Her discovery of feminism through Diane Lockhart is what lets Alicia weigh leaving that structure without destroying her family.

15.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.

16.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md

17.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
17.relation: Mark D. White uses the show's bench - umpire-like Judge Park, the 'cleanse'-addled judge of 'Double Jeopardy', Judge Lessner's 'in my opinion' ritual, liberal Judge Abernathy, and Judge Baxter's sentencing kickbacks in 'Lifeguard' - to ask how far judicial bias infects rulings. He walks through legal formalism's chess-like model, legal realism (Holmes's law as 'prophecies of what the courts will do in fact', Will's lesson to Ms. Cabrini in 'Mock'), Hart's open texture of law, and Dworkin's principles-and-integrity theory, on which Abernathy and Lessner facing the same case would each reach their own 'right answer'. The upshot: judges cannot be neutral umpires, so winning lawyers like Will predict the judge, not just the law.

18.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Lisa McNulty asks what could oblige us to believe someone: Peter's lying fails Kant's Categorical Imperative (a world of universal liars makes lying impossible), while friendship explains Alicia's readiness to believe client Kenny Chatham even before the evidence does. The 'Death Zone' libel trial over an Everest death shows that one's position of power fixes whom one owes presumptive belief - a reader should side with Cardiff, a judge must presume Lambrose innocent - and Pascal's Wager supplies the method of 'behaving like a believer': withholding rumors, withholding conviction, and Alicia publicly playing the wife and sleeping with Peter in a bid to believe in her marriage again. She concludes Peter forfeited any right to be believed, so Alicia has no moral obligation to behave like a good wife.

19.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
19.relation: James Edwin Mahon sorts the show's plots by the gap between deed and motive: Patti Nyholm helps save Marjorie Garnett's liver in 'In Sickness' purely to leverage her firm, Lockhart Gardner sues Chumhum in 'Great Firewall' for the mercenary reason Alicia laments, and the Demorys bribe a juror in 'Fixed' out of altruism. Working through Mill's exchange with Llewellyn Davies and Kant's shopkeeper, he argues motives can be good or bad but never right or wrong, and that no good motive makes a wrong action right - Kant denied even a philanthropic right to lie. Hence Alicia's persuading Shen Yuan to lie about his torture, however compassionate, was wrong.

20.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md

21.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Skyler King and Robert Arp catalogue the excuses cheating men offer - 'my wife let herself go', 'so much eye candy', 'a moment of weakness' - and add evolutionary psychology's parental investment theory to explain why Peter Florrick-types stray while women like Alicia cheat less. The centerpiece is Glaucon's Ring of Gyges story from Book II of Plato's Republic: politicians such as Peter, Bill Clinton, and Eliot Spitzer wear the invisibility ring of power and come to think moral rules no longer bind them. The chapter closes with prudential and moral reasons against infidelity - scorned spouses, broken promises, wounded children - capped by Eli Gold fielding questions about a Brazil-shaped birthmark in 'Anatomy of a Joke'.

22.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Roger Hunt treats Louis Canning, Peter Florrick, and Colin Sweeney as psychiatric cases read through Freud's later drive theory, in which a life drive (Eros) and a death drive (Thanatos) fuse in varying proportions. Sweeney is the purest death-driven type, deriving low-grade sadistic pleasure while feigning personhood to escape punishment; Peter's paranoia assembles a protective barrier of handlers (Eli, Jackie, Alicia, the DNC); Canning may convert self-attack into the very tardive dyskinesia symptoms he weaponizes before juries. The chapter's claim is that the show's evil is not absolute lawlessness but pathology seen from the other characters' perspective, and that the death drive accounts for much of the wickedness on screen.

23.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md

24.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Jennifer Swanson asks whether Alicia can 'have it all', starting from Aristotle: Peter fails the moral virtues (faithfulness, honesty, courage), Jackie's intrusive moments undermine her kindness since Aristotle's unity of the virtues ties them together, and Eli Gold's perfect frankness leaves no room for perfect tact. Following Michael Slote's partial values and impossibility of perfection, she argues career and family are paired values in which gaining one loses the other, as Alicia discovers being pulled between Molly the nanny, Cary's 'she'll have something to fall back on', Diane's partner-track warning, and dumping Will after Grace's twelve butt-dials in 'Parenting Made Easy'. Since perfection is impossible in principle, the answer is balance across all the values of a good life, not Caitlin's retreat into 'I just want to be a mom'.

25.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Karen Adkins argues the show exposes the 'choice' to stay home as neither free nor innocent: Betty Friedan's Feminine Mystique and Linda Hirshman's Get to Work frame how Alicia's more-promising-than-Will-or-Peter career was sacrificed to Peter's ambitions and now constrains her, while Peter's 'thanks for playing the breadwinner', Cary's condescension in 'Fleas', and Jackie's 'we stay in the shadows' speech treat her work as a hobby. The show's feminism goes bland, she contends, when Alicia declines to fight Caitlin's resignation in 'Long Way Home' and endorses choice feminism against her own history. The chapter's evidence runs both ways, though: the 'We're not the cops, honey' double standard, and Alicia's mom skills and lawyer skills flowing productively between nursery and deposition room.

26.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md

27.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
27.relation: John Fitzpatrick asks whether voters should care that Alicia stands beside Peter, from the Season One resignation press conference to the finale's withheld hand. After a rapid tour of right-action theories grounded in the show - Eli Gold's egoism, Peter's 'pitted' evidence tip as consequentialism, Alicia keeping Jonas Stern's dementia secret as deontology, the Florrick-Childs no-children pact as social contract - he turns to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia as a life weaving pleasure, friendship, and practical activity, in which mentors like Will and Diane let us contemplate virtue in others and improve our own character. His conclusion: Alicia's endorsement matters not because she is a good wife but because she is a good person whose judgment reveals Peter's character.

28.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
28.relation: The Azevedos read Plato's Republic Book I as a manual for professionalism: Socrates argues the practitioner - doctor, ruler, lawyer - serves the patient, citizen, and client rather than himself, while Thrasymachus's cynicism that injustice pays and people only seem just is embodied by Eli Gold ('I lie for a living') and by stunt lawyers Nancy Crozier, Patti Nyholm, Louis Canning, and the secretive Jonas Stern. Alicia answers with Aristotle's virtue ethics: professionalism as a cluster virtue cultivated through habituated action, hitting the mean and doing the right thing at the right time for the right reasons. Saint Alicia shows how costly being good all the time is, yet the chapter sides with her striving for virtue over Thrasymachus's goldbrick glory.

29.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Offered as a salute to The Good Wife's female lawyers (Alicia, Diane, Caitlin, Geneva Pine, Dana Lodge, Elsbeth Tascioni), this piece collects good, bad, and memorable real women attorneys: pioneers Bettisia Gozzadini, Arabella Mansfield, Myra Bradwell - barred by Justice Bradley's 'wife and mother' dictum in Bradwell v. Illinois - and Charlotte E. Ray; notorious figures like accused murderer Mary Leonard; and trailblazers Gloria Allred, Sandra Day O'Connor, Constance Baker Motley, and Ruth Bader Ginsburg. The parade of firsts grounds the show's fictional women in the real feminist struggle to enter and practice the legal profession.

30.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
30.relation: This companion piece profiles philosophers who actually practiced law or rhetoric: the sophists Thrasymachus and Protagoras (whose 'man is the measure' relativism was rhetoric for hire and whom Plato and Aristotle despised), Demosthenes, Cicero - called 'the closest thing to a Philosopher King any society has ever seen' - Plutarch with his virtue-and-vice maxims, Cordoba's jurist Averroes, legal-team veteran Francis Bacon, natural-law theorist of war Hugo Grotius, law-degree holders Descartes and Leibniz, Montesquieu of the separation of powers, Bentham (panopticon architect whose utilitarianism lets ends justify means like waterboarding), and legal positivists Hart and Dworkin. Its running joke is that the lawyer-sophist connection is as old as philosophy itself, which is precisely the stereotype The Good Wife plays against.

31.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - The Good Wife and Philosophy.md
31.relation: The book's comic interlude: eleven numbered lawyer jokes, from the vacuum-cleaner dirt bag and the drowning lawyer thrown his partners to 'God doesn't think he's a lawyer' and the closer that 'only three lawyer jokes exist; the rest are true stories'. The list spikes the same lawyers-are-scoundrels stereotype that Judith Andre's opening chapter analyzed seriously and that the editors' introduction answered with Dick the Butcher's 'first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers'.
