10.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
10.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Boardwalk Empire's Prohibition setting - bootleggers, corrupt politicians, G-men, and ordinary citizens at one table against the Volstead Act - puts its characters in philosophically loaded situations that bear directly on real life. It then maps the volume: Littmann reads Nucky as a Machiavellian Prince, Greene casts him as Nietzsche's Superman, Archibald reads Gillian through Plato, Brace and Kingsbury test Aristotle's happiness against Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret, and Robison-Greene treats Jimmy and Richard as war veterans facing existential problems. It closes by previewing chapters on Van Alden's God, the ethics of lying (Fallis), storytelling (Carveth) and deception (Cobb), the body politic (Schwanebeck) and the social contract (Fitzpatrick), causing versus allowing harm (Da Silva), violence (Mellamphy), and a Freudian reading of Jimmy and Gillian (Hirschbein).

11.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md

12.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Littmann tests The Prince against the real bosses behind the show - Nucky Johnson, Capone, Luciano, Rothstein, Torrio - and argues that Prohibition-era history bears out Machiavelli's rules of power. Seizing new opportunities pays (Nucky turning Atlantic City into the World's Playground, Colosimo gunned down for refusing bootlegging, Luciano eliminating Masseria and Maranzano to modernize the Mafia), and harming a rival without crushing him invites revenge (Nucky's fatal leniency toward Jimmy, Maranzano leaving the scarred Luciano alive). A ruler needs good arms, must tailor appearances to each audience (Capone's banquet murder of Anselmi and Scalise, Nucky's respectability and staged generosity), and above all must avoid hatred - the downfall of Nucky, Capone, and Luciano, and of the needlessly arrogant Rothstein, shot over a gambling debt he could easily have paid.

13.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.

14.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Hirschbein has Freud analyze the audience first: like Van Alden, the repressed hypocrite whose true self erupts in drowning Sebso and burning his workplace tormentor, we watch Nucky and Jimmy as avatars of our own repressed aggression and lust. Freud's contest of Eros and Thanatos - his reframing of Plato's tripartite soul as id, ego, and superego - explains why civilization demands renunciation while spectacle like Boardwalk supplies vicarious gratification, with Milgram's and Zimbardo's experiments showing how thin the civilized veneer is. Jimmy's seduction by his mother and killing of the Commodore enact the Oedipus complex writ large, Freud's primal-horde story of the sons' parridical revolt against the father, and the show's catharsis is what lets us live with the sin.

15.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.

16.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md

17.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
17.relation: Carveth argues that the show's historical license is ethically troubling because docudrama viewers - especially those who know nothing of 1920s Atlantic City - absorb 'reel history' as fact. He documents the blend of real and invented: Buscemi's slight Nucky Thompson against the imposing real Nucky Johnson, a fictional military past for Capone, Torrio stripped of his mentor role, and the McGarrigle episodes' misrepresentation of de Valera, Collins, and the Anglo-Irish Treaty. The deepest distortion is violence - the real Nucky ruled through jobs, ostracism, and economic coercion rather than murder, but that would not make good television - and given research showing viewers 'learn' from docudramas they know least about, Terence Winter's ninety-percent-accuracy claim amounts to an unethical misleading of the audience.

18.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Sirvent and Baker take Van Alden's 'strong providential theology' - 'his fate rests in God's hands' at the burned Agent Clarkson's bedside - as a live version of the problem of evil, traced through Augustine and Aquinas to Calvin's all-determining divine omnipotence. The Arminian free-will escape leaves God like a parent watching a child run into traffic, and the 'mysterious ways' reply makes God's moral vocabulary so alien that a God who burns his beloved is 'one-sided' and unworshipable - the same theology that lets Van Alden shift blame for Lucy's pregnancy onto a 'charge from God' before drowning Sebso as 'the judgment of the wicked.' They close with Nucky's God, an inner impetus toward good that asks rather than coerces, and with process theology's persuading God, while Gyp Rosetti's Easter rant at the crucifix shows what believing in the omnipotent alternative costs.

19.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
19.relation: Da Silva asks what Nucky deserves for bringing the thirteen-year-old Gillian to the Commodore and failing to stop the rape, and whether Jimmy - whose very existence depends on that wrong - is entitled to blame him and to ally with the worse man. Working through the doing, enabling, and allowing harm distinction with euthanasia and Good Samaritan cases, degrees of blame, and Parfit's point about collective action, he argues Nucky did wrong but likely less wrong than the Commodore, while Jimmy can blame on his mother's behalf and need not regret a birth that was still good for him - against Benatar's antinatalism. Jimmy's coup fails him, but the moral reason behind it, Nucky's contribution to the rape, was genuine.

20.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
20.relation: Fallis sorts Atlantic City's lies to show which are wrong and why. Kant's and Augustine's absolute bans go too far and Grotius's life-saving exception does not apply - most of these lies get people killed - yet even altruistic lies (Margaret for Madame Jeunet and the ledger), lies told to those who want to be deceived, lies to liars, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that no one believes (Jimmy's flat movie alibi, Rothstein's 'skilled player' whopper) remain wrong: they take informed choice out of the victim's hands, violating the Kantian autonomy that grounds the wrong of lying, and they corrode the trust on which even criminals' co-operation depends.

21.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md

22.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Schwanebeck reads Nucky's fastidious grooming and Prohibition's purity crusade through the body politic metaphor: from Cicero and Seneca's De Clementia, where head and body of the state depend on each other, through Hobbes's bearded Leviathan frontispiece, to temperance propaganda that framed alcohol as poison entering the national bloodstream and wartime posters demanding 'a clean America.' The show exposes the purity ideal as illusion - the true purists are the Klan massacring Chalky's men and the hand-washing Van Alden shouting 'Let these waters wash you clean!' over Sebso's drowning body. Nucky rules less like Seneca's genuinely clement emperor than like Machiavelli's prince who merely appears virtuous, and the gangster genre's kingly tropes ('Et tu, Eli?') crown him head of Atlantic City's body politic.

23.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
23.relation: Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'

24.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
24.relation: Fitzpatrick uses the social contract tradition to explain Prohibition-era Atlantic City. Hobbes's state of nature fits the gang warfare left where no Leviathan is strong enough to enforce federal law against Nucky; Locke's fits a night-watchman government overreaching into Prohibition and thereby breaking the contract, as with Nucky's illegitimate protection 'taxes'; Rousseau's noble savage corrupted by commercial society fits the Klan's pleasure in cruelty and innocent Tommy set against scheming adults. Ethical egoism frames Nucky's framing of Hans Schroeder, consequentialism the Temperance Union's cost-benefit failure, and deontology Margaret's lying campaign speech, while Marx's and Mill's view that human nature is malleable explains the season-spanning transformation of Nucky from half-gangster into 'a gangster and a half.'

26.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Robison-Greene applies Beauvoir to the show's women. Powerful men are the One and women (like Chalky's community under the Klan) are made the inessential Other, and Beauvoir's apparatus - bad faith, the 'appeal' free beings must make to one another, and the happiness that lets women be complicit in their own oppression - frames Lucy, Gillian, and Margaret. Lucy happily performs the role her men write for her, Gillian is so consumed by the fact of her rape that even her apparent freedom keeps her the object of male desire ('just the loneliest person on earth'), while Margaret - Temperance Leaguer, advocate for women's reproductive health, and finally the woman who shuts the door on Nucky's cash - comes closest to making the appeal and to freedom.

27.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
27.relation: Archibald reads Gillian through Plato's Phaedo. The Argument of Opposites - cyclical deaths and rebirths that the immortal soul survives - maps onto the rape at thirteen that killed the child pageant girl and birthed a survivor, her shift into caretaker to control the stroked-out Commodore, and her final drugged regression before Nucky ('Nucky he did something very bad to me'). The Theory of Forms explains her treatment of roles as interchangeable: Jimmy is son, lover, and husband-Form rather than a person to mourn, Angela's death is merely an opportunity for rebirth, and the Jimmy-lookalike Roger can be dressed with his dog tags as 'James' - Forms changing shape while remaining, to Gillian, undamaged.

29.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
29.relation: Mellamphy uses Zizek's Violence to divide the show's bloodshed - Jimmy's hijacking shootout, Eli's wrench murder of O'Neill, Rosetti burning Sheriff Sickels alive - as subjective violence whose spectacle distracts from objective violence: symbolic (the Klan's racism, the language of the Muhammad caricature controversy) and systemic (the capitalism that keeps Nucky untouchable). Zizek's 'chocolate laxative' logic - ruthless exploitation masked by charity - captures 'I'm a philanthropist now' answered by 'You're a gangster. Plain and simple,' and the opening credits' shifting sea shows Nucky's dual roles merging. Critics who complain about gore see only subjective violence and miss the system that produces it, exactly as Zizek predicts, with Marx's self-enhancing circulation of capital as the unseen engine.

30.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
30.relation: Cobb treats the show's storytellers as narrative pedagogues. Nucky's wharf-rat speech is story truth rather than happening truth - Plato's Republic question of true and false tales - and because it allows no dialogue or questioning it fails as full pedagogy; Chalky's story of his father's lynching ties past to present in the interrogation of the Klansman; Rothstein's billiard-ball anecdote for Frankie Yale is episodic memory shaped into identity and threat, a coerced but genuine reasoning exchange ('Do you know what the moral is of this tale, Mr. Yale?'). Measured against Socrates' question-posing inquiry in the Euthyphro, Kant's On Education, and Freire's dialogical 'critical co-investigators,' Nucky, Chalky, and Rothstein all emerge as reflective but deficient pedagogues at large.

7.title: Futurama and Philosophy
7.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Futurama is more than a cartoon: Matt Groening and David X. Cohen built a gold-standard sci-fi show whose storylines engage ethics, time travel, science, normalcy, and the environment. It frames Fry as a twenty-first-century flawed hero in the lineage of Moses, Gilgamesh, Odysseus, Don Quixote, and Frodo, called beyond his inadequacies, and reads his opening 'Space Pilot 3000' musings about the gorilla-throwing-barrels game as a glimpse of life's ups and downs. The chapter presents the show's strategy of making the mundane strange as the backdrop the volume's philosophers will use to examine life and meaning, and jokes that fans' resurrection of the canceled show (wave after wave, like Zapp Brannigan's troops) guarantees Futurama's permanence.

9.title: Futurama and Philosophy
9.relation: In 'A Taste of Freedom,' Zoidberg eats Earth's flag Old Freebie on Freedom Day, is tried by Earth's Supreme Court, and his death sentence triggers a Decapodian invasion that enslaves Earth under the Mobile Oppression Palace. The chapter pits Mill's On Liberty defense of unpopular expression (mankind cannot silence a lone dissenter; unchallenged beliefs are mere 'true opinions' akin to prejudice) against Feinberg's offense principle, mapping the case onto Texas v. Johnson and the symbolic-speech line from Stromberg to Tinker. It ends with Zoidberg burning the flag 'to preserve the freedom it represents': liberty and majority will often conflict (doomsday devices, Proposition Infinity's robosexual marriage ban), so preserving freedom requires tolerating offensive expression.

10.title: Futurama and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Young tests Isaiah Berlin's distinction between negative liberty (absence of external interference) and positive liberty (rational self-government) on three episodes: Fry's super-Slurm compulsion in 'Fry and the Slurm Factory,' human Bender's lethal gluttony in 'Anthology of Interest II,' and the worms whose upgrades win Leela's love in 'Parasites Lost' - each agent is externally unobstructed yet not self-governing. Bender's jacking-on addiction and the Temple of Robotology's threat of Robot Hell in 'Hell Is Other Robots' illustrate Rousseau's 'forced to be free,' the coercion that Berlin warned has licensed totalitarian regimes. The chapter concludes Futurama takes no side, suggesting genuine freedom needs both positive and negative liberty.

11.title: Futurama and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Buchanan reads 'A Big Piece of Garbage' as political ecology: the trash ball Old New York blasted into space in 2000 returns to threaten New New York, showing that even a society that has 'mastered recycling' cannot escape a capitalist economy whose commodities are designed to end as waste. On the trash ball, Fry's nostalgia ('junk isn't garbage... a glorious monument to the twentieth century') debates Leela's 'this stuff was garbage when it was new,' and Fry's rescue plan - building a second trash ball to knock the first into the Sun - merely recreates the disaster, celebrated as 'the twentieth-century spirit' of willful ignorance. Drawing on Bryant and Bailey's political ecology and Rodgers's waste stream, the chapter argues trash unmasks the exploitation of nature crystallized in commodities, so green technology and recycling alone cannot avert ecological crisis.

12.title: Futurama and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Malloy defines war as organized, political, violent conflict and tests Futurama's many invasions against just war theory: Zapp's invasion of Spheron 1 in 'War Is the H-Word' fails just cause ('they stand for everything we don't stand for'), the first Omicronian invasion over the interrupted Single Female Lawyer broadcast fails proportionality and last resort, while the second, over eaten Popplers, passes. Zapp's Hyperdeath laser ribbon-cutting and the Bender suicide-bombing plot against the Brain Balls illustrate discrimination, proportionality, and means evil in themselves, and the postwar demand that Lrrr eat one human - ending with blameless Free Waterfall Jr. - raises war-crimes punishment and restitution. The chapter closes by endorsing Walzer: a state's moral authority hinges on at least acknowledging the rules of war.

13.title: Futurama and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Futurama and Philosophy.md

14.title: Futurama and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Piven argues Zapp Brannigan's 'sexlexia' - his deluded velour-and-spanking seductions of Leela and his relief at finding Lee Lemon is a woman - typifies a whole cast of clueless lovers (Fry coaching Zoidberg's courtship of Edna, Morgan Proctor's mess fetish, Bender coldly dumping the Planet Express ship in 'Love and Rocket'). Kant's condemnation of masturbation as self-abuse that throws away one's personality and violates humanity in one's own person is exposed as unsupported prejudice, and Nietzsche's claim that morality projects fear, envy, and disgust onto the despised other explains why 'perversion' is an arbitrary cultural judgment. Freud, Stoller, and McDougall then recast perversion as unconscious flight from anxiety and death, so the show's kink - up to the Monsterpus of The Beast with a Billion Backs and Amy's 'general sluttiness' - mirrors our own sexlexia and existential dread.

15.title: Futurama and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Jenkins asks what makes Bender Bender when Leela still recognizes him as the walnut-panelled steam robot of 'Obsoletely Fabulous.' Scruffy's progressively repaired conference table stages the Ship of Theseus problem and the same body theory, while the Roboticon 'Soul Detector' (Fry sets it off, robots pass through) rules out Descartes' same soul theory for robots. Episodes from 'Anthology of Interest II' and 'The Honking' to 'The Prisoner of Benda' mind swap and Roberto's instant 1-X re-education support Locke's psychological continuity: Bender persists through an overlapping chain of memories and traits stored on his hard drive - 'Everything that is Bender is right here' - which is why an empathic, ascetic Bender ('The old Bender is gone') threatens his very identity.

16.title: Futurama and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Lewis argues that Futurama's answer to the fear of being forgotten - Zoidberg thriving on negative attention, Bender's billion-cubit statue and the Shrimpkins' forced worship both failing - is to become existentially intertwined with others through friendship, love, and family. Bender's arc in 'A Pharaoh to Remember' is read through Camus's Sisyphus: life itself is meaningless, but our freedom lets us fill it with meaning, which Bender finds not in monuments or worship but in seeing others remember him. Fry's devotion in 'Godfellas' and 'Jurassic Bark' (Seymour waiting outside Panucci's forever), Bender's Big Score, the holophonor opera of 'The Devil's Hands Are Idle Playthings,' and Yancey naming his son after Fry in 'The Luck of the Fryish' show remembrance surviving inside the people we have shaped, including the viewers.

17.title: Futurama and Philosophy
17.relation: Salazar takes Professor Farnsworth's cry that the crew's age regression in 'Teenage Mutant Leela's Hurdles' will end in 'a fate worse than death: pre-life! Then death' as a test of whether death is bad. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' says death cannot be experienced, so the deprivation account of Nagel's 'Death' is needed to explain how death is bad for the one deprived of a valuable future - a dispute staged by Bender's suicide-booth despair in 'Space Pilot 3000' after learning his bending built the booths. The chapter then argues losing one's identity and values can be worse than death (Bender's and Fry's flight from career-chip assignments, the Professor's love of being 161, Leela's frustrated teen redo), closing with Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning and Leela's sacrifice of her regained youth: inner integrity, not erasing the past, makes life worth living.

18.title: Futurama and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Elsby argues Fry's 'brain thing' illuminates how humans form beliefs and adapt to misconceptions: Fry accepts swans as swan boats and deduces 'boat eggs,' romances the radiator woman from the radiator planet, and insists he is in the ruined New York of 4000 rather than L.A. - each time reasoning flawlessly from a false premise before readjusting when corrected. Using Aristotle's incidental perception (seeing the pale thing as Cleon's son), Hume's warning that grouping similar-but-non-identical objects breeds ambiguity, and Mom's grandiose misreading of Fry's anchovy purchase in 'A Fishful of Dollars,' the chapter traces how error enters at each step of identification and inference. The payoff: Fry differs from us only in degree, and our capacity to adapt to overturned assumptions might be inferior to his.

20.title: Futurama and Philosophy
20.relation: Von Gunten asks whether Bender, Calculon, and the robot mafia have moral worth, arguing first that they are sentient: behavioral similarity plus functional equivalence (pain as electric signals in neurons or circuits) defeat both behavior-only objections (the Sphex wasp's preprogrammed loop, knife-avoiding toy robots) and composition-based prejudice - Fry's 'I'm all squishy and flabby' defense at the Hal Institute - which would be 'biologism' analogous to racism. He then distinguishes moral patiency (Nibbler can be harmed but only behaviorally reinforced) from moral agency (deliberation and accountability), concluding that Bender's flexible life - Iron Cook, wrestling, folk music with Beck's head, jacking-on addiction - shows robots transcend their programming as humans transcend evolutionary presets. Limiting moral status to biology or species would be speciesism, so the thirty-first century's robots deserve the full protections and responsibilities humans have.

21.title: Futurama and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
21.relation: The chapter uses 'The Problem with Popplers' to map the real-world ethics of eating meat: Free Waterfall Jr.'s 'You shouldn't eat things that feel pain' restates Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's equal consideration of suffering; Fishy Joe's profits-first stance echoes agro-ecological defenses of meat eating; and Leela's 'eating an intelligent animal is different' voices the common intuition Singer condemns as speciesism. The food-chain justification collapses when the Omicronians claim the apex and demand 198 billion humans in return, and Bender's 'fight to the death and I'll cook the loser' flips the diner's perspective, while Waterfall's orangutan-for-Leela trade sets up Singer's future-directed preferences distinction from Practical Ethics as a possible rescue. The chapter ends on the episode's real target: gluttonous consumption ('stuff the ship!') and the arbitrary sentimentality governing what we will and won't eat.

22.title: Futurama and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Pless asks whether Bender is responsible for his misdeeds given that MomCorp designed him to be an alcoholic kleptomaniac (revealed through Bender Vision in 'Mother's Day') and Planet Express regularly orders him into morally dirty work. Against Asimov's utilitarian Three Laws - embodied by the servile, selfless Robot 1-X of 'Obsoletely Fabulous' - Futurama's 'robot subjectivism' makes every robot a self-interested agent, and Bender's autonomy is proven by his refusal of Mom's 'kill all humans' order and by his fear of punishment in Robot Hell ('Hell Is Other Robots'), which also shows the show's universe is not morally relativist. Because Bender can rewrite his own code - his unprogrammed friendship with Fry, the adoption scam that turns heartfelt in 'The Cyber House Rules' - he sits on the same sliding scale of moral agency as humans, so if Bender can break his programming, we have no excuse for not exercising our own free will.

24.title: Futurama and Philosophy
24.relation: Burkett uses Fry's accidental incest in 'Roswell that Ends Well' - protecting Enos only to cause his death and then becoming his own grandfather via Mildred - to examine backwards time travel through David Lewis's Grandfather Paradox. Killing one's grandfather is shown to be logically impossible (it makes Enos both dead and alive in 1947, so every would-be assassin fails for ordinary reasons like a jammed rifle), while becoming your own grandfather is a consistent causal loop, and branching timelines merely kill a man who is no one's grandfather. The 'paradox-correcting' time spheres of Bender's Big Score fail on Hermes's stolen body, and Bender's year-long loop would spawn infinitely many duplicates were it not for the Globetrotters' Doom Field - so backwards time travel is bizarre but logically possible.

25.title: Futurama and Philosophy
25.relation: DePoe weighs the multiverse against the fine-tuning argument for God's existence: just as Farnsworth's box in 'The Farnsworth Parabox' spills out universe-1's golden Bender plus togas, pirate, and hippie universes, an infinite multiverse would realize every possibility and make our life-permitting constants certain rather than miraculous, while 'Time Keeps on Slippin''s chronoton-disturbed cosmos illustrates what fine-tuning means. He then asks what is metaphysically primitive, staging the 1948 Copleston-Russell exchange ('I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all') and applying Ockham's razor to weigh one infinitely complex God against infinitely many unobservable universes. The chapter concludes in evidential stalemate, closing with the God Entity's counsel in 'Godfellas': 'When you do things right, people won't be sure you've done anything at all.'

26.title: Futurama and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Futurama and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Oschman reads 'Godfellas' as an answer to the problem of evil: Bender, made god of the Shrimpkins, destroys them by meddling too much, and the God Entity explains 'if you do too much, people get dependent. And if you do nothing, they lose hope.' After testing the contrast response (pain makes Slurm sweet) and the Free Will Defense (which covers moral evils like the returning garbage ball of 'A Big Piece of Garbage' but not natural evils or the taste of anchovies), the chapter adopts John Hick's soul-making theodicy: God's epistemic distance - compared to Fry's obsession after tasting super Slurm - keeps creatures uncompelled so they can grow into free moral agents. Fry's slow evolution from delivery boy to 'slightly less lazy slob' is soul-making, and 'The Late Philip J. Fry' wryly confirms life's purpose is 'probably some hogwash about the human spirit.'

27.title: Futurama and Philosophy
27.relation: Williams uses Hermes's slide from chest-harpoon to extendo-arm to Cylon eye to full robot body in 'The Six Million Dollar Mon' - until Zoidberg's 'Monster Mash' surgery restores his brain to Li'l Hermes - to ask what makes a person themselves under voluntary enhancement. The 'Ship of Planet Express' and the seven-year cell-replacement fact recast the Ship of Theseus, exposing our terror of upgrades as inconsistent with our constant physical change, while the therapeutic-versus-enhancement line (medical steroids vs doping, Aimee Mullins's blades) explains why Hermes's chosen upgrades disturb us. Cartesian interactionist dualism predicts Mecha-Hermes stays the same person, yet his personality shifts with his parts, so the chapter turns to physicalism and lands on functionalism: Hermes persists through each swap until the Roberto brain-chip replaces the brain that houses his memories and motivations.

28.title: Futurama and Philosophy
28.relation: Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.

30.title: Futurama and Philosophy
30.relation: Mills-Knutsen reads the Brain Spawn - floating brains whose pain at others' thoughts drives them to dumb life down and finally to hoard all knowledge in the Infosphere ('The Day the Earth Stood Stupid,' 'The Why of Fry') - as Futurama's funhouse mirror of the West's distrust of intellectuals, from Pandora and Eve to Frankenstein and comic-book evil geniuses. Fry, the delta-brainwave-lacking hero made stupid by doing 'the nasty in the pasty,' stabs the Big Brain with Bonfire of the Vanities and later banishes the Brains to another dimension, just as Athens executed Socrates. A close reading of Plato's Apology - Socrates's feigned ignorance exposing everyone else's, his demand of free meals in lieu of exile, and his prophecy of even more annoying successors - maps onto the Big Brain's snobbery and onto universities (Wernstrom's tenure scam in 'A Big Piece of Garbage,' Amy's doctorate in 'That Darn Katz!') as society's way of paying intellectuals to stay out of the way.

31.title: Futurama and Philosophy
31.relation: Onishi argues humor exposes cultural normalcy: Futurama transplants twenty-first-century prejudices into the future, where Leela's one eye still gets her mocked by the blind-and-deaf orphan Kirk ('The Cyber House Rules') and same-sex marriage is unremarkable while robosexual marriage is taboo ('Proposition Infinity,' a parody of California's Proposition 8). Leela's phaser-eye surgery and her self-loathing until 'Leela's Homeworld' reveals she is a mutant show standards of normalcy are cultural rather than natural, and are wielded oppressively. Drawing on Aristotle's habituation, Hume's habit, and Foucault's disciplinary production of subjects, the chapter uses Bender's change of heart after dating the Lucy Liu-bot head in 'I Dated a Robot' to argue habits change through meeting actual people rather than abstract 'ideas' of communities - which is how satire quietly extends what counts as normal.

32.title: Futurama and Philosophy
32.relation: Reitter reads the sewer mutants - banished underground, surviving on what the surface flushes, as in 'The Mutants Are Revolting' where Leela is deported without trial the moment Fry reveals she is not an alien - as philosophy's Other, illuminated by Plato's cave (surface dwellers fear and demonize what they have never seen) and Beauvoir's The Second Sex (Leela passes as an acceptable alien until exposed as a mutant). Mrs. Astor's United Mutant Scholarship Fund film, with its 'noble sewer mutants... uh, people, I guess,' is read alongside Said's Orientalism and racist charity imagery as a third face of Othering. The chapter then adds folklore theory: the mutants are a folk group with their own urban legends (alligators in the sewer, and the 'sub-urban legend' of sub-mutants), ballads like 'The Legend of El Chupanibre,' and freegan-style recycling ethics - a counterculture whose difference the dominant universe-view casts as monstrosity.

33.title: Futurama and Philosophy
33.relation: Taft pairs Fry with Don Quixote: both are media-saturated characters who live as if inside fiction, break the fourth wall, and are dismissed as madmen - Fry scripting a finale for Single Female Lawyer to placate the Omicronians in 'When Aliens Attack,' Quixote blaming enchanters whenever his fantasies misfire. The chapter asks where reality ends and fiction begins, contrasting the Canon's charge that novels merely delight with the Priest's reply that stories display the beauty of a mind - dramatized when Fry's holophoner music, not worm-given strength or the Robot Devil's hands, is what moves Leela in 'Parasites Lost' and 'The Devil's Hands Are Idle Playthings.' Ending with the opera that spills into its own audience until Hermes sings 'Is this really happening or just being staged?,' the chapter argues a life of enchantment can bend reality toward fantasy - Fry authors his own story just as Quixote's neighbors finally beg him to ride again.

34.title: Futurama and Philosophy
34.relation: Micic uses Fry's hundred-cups-of-coffee rescue in 'Three Hundred Big Boys' - a mysterious orange blur to onlookers while Fry calmly watches each cork pop - and the chronoton time skips of 'Time Keeps on Slippin'' as breaks in experience that Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit explains better than Descartes. Against the cogito's inference of a separate thinking 'I,' Hegel treats consciousness as the act of relating subject to object, whose ceaseless repetitions (here1, here2, here3...) we knit into the illusion of a unified self. The identical universes of 'The Late Philip J. Fry' (U1 = U2 = U3...) then model the same collapse of enumeration: the gaps in experience feel abnormal only because we never notice the constant gaps our own consciousness smooths over - including Nibbler's shadow in the pilot's cryogenics lab.

35.title: Futurama and Philosophy
35.relation: Hamer tests sanity against truth using Kierkegaard's asylum anecdote - the escapee intoning 'Boom, the earth is round' proves his insanity precisely by resting it on objective fact - and applies it to 'Insane in the Mainframe,' where Fry, wrongly committed to a robot asylum, is only released once he subjectively believes he is a robot, and to 'The Sting,' where comatose Leela's plan to keep Fry's corpse under her mattress to 'prove I'm not insane' fails the same traitorous way. Pure objectivity cannot certify sanity and pure subjectivity licenses lunacy, so the chapter brings in James's 'The Will to Believe': some beliefs must be held first before their evidence can even count. Fry, who abandons his robot belief the moment his knife-nick bleeds human blood, models the justified believer who pursues the objective truth subjectively.

8.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
8.relation: The editor's introduction surveys the sprawling Frankenstein pop-culture corpus the book will dissect - Whale's 1931 'It's Alive!' scene, the lovable Herman Munster, Mel Brooks's Young Frankenstein, Dean Koontz's Dr. Helios, Boris Karloff's grunting brute, and I, Frankenstein's Adam - insisting the creature now lives in hundreds of films, shows, and novels rather than Shelley's text alone. It frames the book's guiding shocks: whether a re-animated corpse-man has a soul, whether making monsters differs from making babies, and whether Frankenstein's maligned creation would be right to seek to end all of us. It closes by inviting readers to peer into the monster's dull yellow eyes with the lights left on and the door barred.

10.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.

11.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.

12.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Littmann argues that stripped of religious scruple, Shelley's own supreme virtue - kindness, embodied in Victor's family, Elizabeth, Clerval, and the cottagers - actually supports creating artificial life: the monster is benevolent until mistreated, and superior corpse-people would be a race of geniuses rather than a threat we may preemptively suppress. The monster himself invents utilitarianism ('relative as they were, as I applied them, to pleasure and pain alone'), De Lacey nearly lives it by promising the stranger rehabilitation over punishment, but Victor's case against building a mate is exposed as speciesism - he tallies unborn humans' futures while ignoring the joys of unborn cadaver folk, though utilitarians were the first to speak for animal rights. Since intelligent otherness is humanity's only chance at non-human friendship and the risks of Prometheus's fire paid off, the chapter rewrites the modern Prometheus as a blessing and ends with a re-imagined creation scene where the monster says 'I love you' to a Victor who finally names him Nigel.

13.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Jacquette treats Frankenstein as the modern myth of scientific overreach whose two-century grip on pop culture (over a thousand films, Frankenberry cereal) rests on three stitched-together ingredients: Enlightenment faith in applied science, the mortality-awareness of the logician's 'All men are mortal,' and Prometheus-style retribution for challenging nature - while insisting Shelley's tale is science fiction, not supernatural. Victor's real crime is not daring science but abandoning his nameless creation to raise itself, so that 'if he had taken appropriate care of the monster he made, he might not have made such a monster.' The chapter closes with Wittgenstein's remark (Philosophical Investigations §261) that philosophy ends in the wish to 'emit an inarticulate sound,' matched to the Creature's ultimate question 'What was I?' answered only with groans, as Igor's hunting horn fades over the credits of Young Frankenstein.

14.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md

15.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Casetta and Tambolo dissect the 'Frankenfood' metaphor: metaphors map a familiar source domain (the Monster) onto a poorly known target (genetically modified organisms, like the 'Frankenfish' salmon), but the mapping fails because the Monster is a genetically heterogeneous chimera assembled from dead bodies while the engineered salmon is a genetically homogeneous hybrid grown from a single fertilized egg. Framing the question with Aristotle's view of metaphysics as the study of what things ultimately are, and applying Kripke-style origin essentialism and natural-kind essentialism, they show that being a patchwork is no essential property at all - our own symbiotic bacteria outnumber our 'human' cells - so Monster and GMO are not entities of the same kind. The metaphor should be discarded as intellectual junk, yet its allure persists because the living corpse-patchwork disturbs our fantasy of ourselves as pure, unmixed organisms.

16.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Kokotz casts Victor as a pioneer of human 'enhancement' whose eight-foot daemon - stronger, faster, smarter, kinder, and vegetarian - actually achieved his goal of perfecting the human body, yet whose hideous appearance locked him out of society and love, twisting success into catastrophe: the 'Midas problem' of getting exactly what you wished for. Victor's deeper error was trusting Mill's On Liberty test that what people actually desire is thereby desirable; desires come from the human mind rather than nature, so a desired enhancement can make things worse, as the daemon's revenge on William, Henry, and Elizabeth proves. The lesson is institutional as well as conceptual: science must not proceed behind closed doors but under shared ethical oversight, since a Frankensteinian breakthrough carries too much responsibility for any single scientist to bear.

17.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
17.relation: Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'

18.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Fitzpatrick runs Marx's account of alienated labor from the 1844 Manuscripts through the novel: Victor's creature is the product of estranged labor, 'an alien object exercising power over him,' which he cannot name, comes to loathe, and which finally destroys him - the devaluation of the creator tracking the increasing value of the thing made, while workers become commodities producing commodities. The De Laceys' eviction in Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Ingolstadt cholera riots stage class struggle at feudalism's end, and Victor's failure to self-actualize (to 'hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon... criticize after dinner') shows how capitalism turns science into 'a tool of our own destruction.' The chapter closes with 'Frankenstorm' climate change as the alienated externality par excellence - capitalists selling us the rope with which we hang ourselves.

20.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
20.relation: Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.

21.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Pötzsch explains the monster through Rousseau's Émile: innately good ('Everything is good as it comes from the hands of the Author of Nature'), the creature is corrupted because he experienced civilization 'too much and too soon' - the exact inverse of Rousseau's negative education, which shields the heart from vice instead of commanding, and lets the child learn 'through the mere force of things.' Victor knew his parents' model of paternal duty ('a deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life') yet abandoned his offspring and refused the female companion Rousseau deems essential to social development, so that wickedness born of weakness ('if I cannot inspire love, I will cause fear') murders William, Clerval, and Elizabeth. Shelley, a Rousseau admirer, makes Victor's science - an attempt to conquer rather than follow nature, fed by competitive professors at Ingolstadt - the very thing that dooms his parenting.

22.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
22.relation: King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.

23.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
23.relation: Galliott treats Frankenstein as the template for blaming lethal autonomous robots: Victor alone created his creature, but today's 'frankennovation' - Ronald Arkin's 'ethical governor' algorithms, DARPA funding, degree programs in robot warfare, and the South African robotic cannon that killed nine spectators - distributes responsibility across engineers, educators (Victor's father and Professors Krempe and Waldman, who never properly warned him about Agrippa's 'sad trash'), universities, and the military-industrial complex. Yet Shelley's articulate, Paradise Lost-quoting monster is a rational, intentional killer who can be held morally responsible and even punished, as Rob Sparrow demands of machines. Because responsibility does not dilute with numbers - two murderers do not get half a life sentence each - the chapter concludes that everyone in the chain, and all of us who do nothing to stop it, shares the blame for monstrous creations.

25.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
25.relation: Hess asks whether the monster has a soul and makes him the test case between physicalism (Kim, Churchland, van Inwagen) and dualism: recasting Frank Jackson's Mary as a color-blind monster who learns every physical fact about color vision, receives new eyes on Walton's ship, and then learns the 'what it is like' of seeing red for the first time, he argues there are nonphysical mental facts, so physicalism is false. He then runs Plantinga's argument that we are not our bodies or brains through a machine that replaces the monster's parts and hemispheres one by one while he stays conscious, and adds near-death out-of-body evidence like Maria's window-ledge shoe to suggest we can exist disembodied. The upshot is symmetric: whatever we conclude about the monster's soul we must conclude about our own - so be careful about assuming who does and does not have a soul, even monsters.

26.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Frankenstein and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Lopez uses the monster - 'one man made out of many' - to stress-test personal identity: brain-swap and amnesia-torture thought experiments first drive us to identify with our memories (the memory-based psychological criterion) and then, when Victor offers to wipe memory before the pain experiments, with our bodies, yielding inconsistent answers. The monster's own testimony - waking confused, prodding fire like an infant, acquiring language by eavesdropping on Safie's lessons, and building his values from scratch out of Paradise Lost and the cottagers - shows he is a genuinely new person rather than whoever once owned his corpse-parts, since we would not say a memory-wiped torture victim ceases to exist. He concludes the monster satisfies the five listed personhood criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness), with identity riding a continuing stream of consciousness running on a body that is, in the end, secondary 'hardware.'

27.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
27.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues the creature is a person on every serious criterion: it satisfies Kant's rationality test and Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-concept) in both Shelley's novel and I, Frankenstein, and it possesses all ten of Nussbaum's capabilities for flourishing. The twist is that judging the monster a blameworthy murderer already concedes the personhood we deny him, while our exclusion of him is bare Othering and speciesism of the kind Tom Regan attacks in animal ethics. Michaud ends by reversing the question: after humanity's record of crushing minorities, which the creature learns from Volney's Ruins of Empires and weeps over with Safie, what argument could Victor give Adam for sparing us?

28.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
28.relation: Mirko Garasic reads Victor as the Modern Prometheus of the myth Plato tells in the Protagoras: like the Titan punished for stealing fire, Victor's purely technical gift of life fails because, as Zeus tells Hermes, justice and reverence must be shared by all or cities cannot exist. The chapter's real subject is love - Prometheus suffers for loving the humans he made, and the creature asks for a female companion while Victor's hate-filled destruction of her unleashes the second wave of revenge. Tim Burton's Frankenweenie splits this love/hate dualism: young Victor's tear over Sparky makes the experiment work, the classmates' prize-greed and the xenophobic mayor produce the real monsters, and Mr. Rzykruski teaches that science severed from emotion is empty. Via Zygmunt Bauman's liquid modernity, Garasic concludes that our own detached, networked isolation is the danger: scientific progress alone never makes a better society, love and community do.

29.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
29.relation: Spyros Petrounakos reads Frankenstein as a Cartesian narrative whose external events run parallel to the inner worlds of Victor and the creature, from Victor's solitary conception of 'bestowing animation upon lifeless matter' to his imprisonment in a truth nobody would believe when Justine's life is at stake. The monster's acquisition of language at the De Lacey cottage - grasping 'fire, milk, and bread' but not 'good,' 'dearest,' and 'unhappy' - becomes the test case between Descartes's private inner theater (with its evil demon) and Gilbert Ryle's reply, glossing Locke on ideas of reflection, that we learn emotion words by responding directly to behavior rather than by cracking a hidden code. On Ryle's reading the monster's deformity is horror precisely because it is put to Cartesian use, a body that seems to shield its inner life, so the creature only truly comes alive when it behaves like a human being.

30.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
30.relation: Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.

32.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
32.relation: Michael Mendelson rereads James Whale's 1931 Frankenstein as a metaphysics of appearance versus reality: the seemingly monstrous creature killed Fritz only after Fritz tormented him with fire and the whip, killed Dr. Waldman while Waldman was trying to dissect him alive, and drowned Maria in innocent play, expecting her to float like the flowers they had been throwing. The 'criminal brain' was Fritz's accident and explains less than we assume, since the creature spares Henry's fiancée when she screams and faints. The real point is alterity: otherness is a relation, not a property, and individual and social identity are built by excluding an outside where monsters reside - so the horror was inside the well-ordered village all along, the monster is us, and we are its creators.

33.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
33.relation: Mike Kugler argues Shelley's novel tests the radical idealism of her father William Godwin, her mother Mary Wollstonecraft, and her husband Percy: Victor's Promethean project of perfecting humanity in isolation, away from the 'intimate circle' of family and friends, produces a creature whose natural benevolence is destroyed only by repeated exclusion, first by the De Laceys. Drawing on Rousseau's and Wollstonecraft's view that children raised by benevolent parents develop their innate sympathy, the chapter reads the creature as an abandoned child - a new Adam who becomes a Satanic rebel when every community rejects him - and Victor's attempt at reproduction without women and mothers as the novel's deepest violation. The redemptive counterfactual is adoption: what if Victor had raised the creature in his home, as his father did Elizabeth?

34.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
34.relation: Jeff Ewing reads Victor's science through ecofeminist and Marxist critiques: M. Waldman's promise to 'penetrate into the recesses of nature' and 'show how she works in her hiding-places' exemplifies exactly what Val Plumwood condemns - male knowers wringing secrets from a nature pictured as a passive female slave - and Victor studies natural elements 'in their death, not in their life' as raw material for power. Marx and Engels supply the parallel diagnosis: capitalism biases science and technology toward profit, turning tools and knowledge into means of domination rather than human flourishing, just as Victor's knowledge serves only his glory and kills everyone he loves. The chapter concludes that we breed Frankenstein's monsters whenever science treats nature, workers, women, and othered peoples as mere instruments, and only replacing those social relations frees science from power and profit.

35.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
35.relation: Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.

36.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
36.relation: Jessie Dern uses Derrida's Rogues and The Animal that Therefore I Am to show that naming is power: Victor cries 'Devil!' before the creature has done anything, and labels like 'monster,' 'rogue,' and 'animal' are performative verdicts that reveal the labeler, who secures his own goodness by negating the Other, more than the labeled. The novel multiplies the pattern, from Justine's confessor making her 'think that I was the monster that he said I was' to Elizabeth's 'men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other's blood,' while Victor, guarding his self-image, becomes the monster himself. Against the Nietzsche epigraph about fighting monsters, the chapter closes with Derrida's playful self-application ('the animal that therefore I am') as the move the creature never gets to make: contesting the label and claiming a name and a self.

38.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
38.relation: John Karavitis uses Dean Koontz's series, in which Victor Helios/Frankenstein engineers a 'New Race' lacking free will and empathy, to test the bioethics of human enhancement: Michael Sandel's bioconservative Case against Perfection condemns enhancements that bypass effort and agency - performance-enhancing drugs, off-label Ritalin and growth hormone, designer children - as a 'Promethean aspiration to remake nature' that destroys human nature. Allen Buchanan's bioprogressive reply that evolution's blind tinkering can be safely improved upon is challenged by the bonobo/chimpanzee contrast, dogs versus wolves, and Belyaev's tame silver foxes, all showing that small genetic changes cascade into large behavioral and physical ones. Since behavior defines morality, the chapter concludes that genetically remaking ourselves risks remaking morality itself, ending in Koontz's posthuman world where 'efficiency equaled morality' and inefficiency was the only sin.

39.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
39.relation: Joe Slater builds a two-premise anti-natalist argument from Shelley's Paradise Lost epigraph ('Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man?'): since it is wrong to inflict harm on an autonomous being without consent, and every autonomous life inevitably contains harms, creating autonomous beings - Adam in the lab or a baby in the womb - is wrong. He answers the objection from Parfit's non-identity problem via the damaged-brain Adam case, and defends the Harm Premise with Mill's On Liberty: consent matters because autonomous agents must be free to harm themselves, as with the smoker, the drinker, and Frankenstein's stolen kidney. G.E. Moore's 'Moorean shift' and Benatar's genetic, social, and institutional pro-natal biases explain why we resist the conclusion, with a 'Super Adam' incapable of harm as the only escape.

40.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
40.relation: Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.

41.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
41.relation: William Rodriguez argues Branagh's 1994 Mary Shelley's Frankenstein deliberately overturns what Plato's account of art as mimesis that forms character, and Colin McGinn's aesthetic theory of virtue (G-beings versus E-beings), lead us to expect - that beauty of soul shows in beauty of body - since the handsome Victor is the moral degenerate while De Niro's hideous creature is a moral virtuoso whose first words are 'friend' and 'father.' The beautiful Frankenstein family harbors ugliness: Oedipal scenes between Victor and his mother Caroline, the wedding that makes Elizabeth 'brother, sister no more; husband and wife,' and Victor's relish in abandoning his creation. The creature's questions - 'Do I have a soul?', 'Who am I?' - and his secret harvest for the peasant family credit moral worth to the ugly, so the monster fascinates us because the monster is us: evil may be attractive and lurking inside rather than deformed and outside.

5.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
5.relation: Kevin Decker's introduction traces Card's debt to Asimov's Foundation and its 'psychohistory,' and notes the novel's surprising resonance with military readers such as the army helicopter pilot who drew courage from Ender during flight school. It previews the volume's five parts as an escalating set of questions: whether Battle School's engineered childhood can be justified, how empathy and game-playing make a commander, whether the buggers are enemies or misunderstood others, who bears responsibility for xenocide, and how Peter and Valentine's anonymous net politics remakes Earth.

7.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
7.relation: Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.

8.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
8.relation: Jeremy Proulx reads Ender through F.W.J. Schelling's account of evil as a real, positive force rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: Ender's kicks to Stilson and Bonzo, his killing of the Giant in the mind game, and his 'I destroy them' confession all display the 'contraction into the self' Schelling thinks haunts every moral agent. He argues Graff deliberately isolates Ender to force this dark ground to the surface, and that Valentine's 'welcome to the human race' and the hive-queen's forgiveness teach Ender that evil, though never excusable, can be understood and atoned for - his fate also shows freedom tainted by a necessity we neither choose nor control.

9.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
9.relation: Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.

10.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Chad Timm applies Foucault's disciplinary power to the International Fleet: Graff sorts monitored children like 'formless clay,' watches them through a Battle School Panopticon of head monitors and battleroom observation, and uses constant testing and the normalizing gaze to make Ender his own overseer and construct the identity of a commander. He closes by mapping the same sort-examine-discipline circuit onto standardized testing and Race to the Top, noting Ender's flicker of resistance when the children finally see through the adults' game.

11.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md

12.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Andrew Zimmerman Jones argues Ender's genius is empathy cashed out through game theory: from Plato's Laches on courage to Hume's account of sympathy, sizing up the enemy's thinking is the winning strategy, and Ender's love ('in that very moment I also love him') reframes conflicts with Peter and the buggers so they can end rather than merely be won. His one failure is never extending this empathy to Graff and Rackham, so he cannot see that his final battleroom rule-breaking - 'the enemy's gate is down' - is exactly the move the adults' larger game was designed to produce.

13.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. could only get a compassionate child to commit xenocide by presenting war as a game, a framing that neutralizes moral agency just as Milgram's shock experiments and the fake game show The Game of Death did. Using Sunzi's 'know your enemy' to frame the empathy paradox, Walzer's problem of dirty hands for Graff's lesser-evil choices, and Foot's trolley problem alongside drone 'Nintendo warfare' to show how distance makes killing easier, he concludes Ender was likely a willing pawn who let himself be deceived because he endorsed the war's survivalist goal.

14.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Morgan Deane maps Ender's tactics onto Sunzi's Art of War: exploiting Bonzo's hot anger, draining the enemy's martial spirit, Graff's use of 'fatal terrain' to throw students into hopeless situations, and staying 'formless' like water so opponents cannot read his plans. Drawing also on Laozi's Dao as the flow a commander must channel, Confucian role ethics in the general-as-father relation, and Legalist reward-and-punishment systems, he concludes Ender qualifies as a military genius by classical Chinese standards - at the wrenching moral cost both he and Graff pay.

15.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Brendan Shea starts from Wittgenstein's claim that 'game' resists definition and classifies Ender's battleroom fights, buggers-and-astronauts, and the open-ended Giant's Drink, then applies Bernard Suits' definition of games as voluntary attempts to overcome unnecessary obstacles (prelusory goals, constitutive rules, lusory means and attitude). He argues games build Ender's skills and empathy but that Battle School's 'winning is the only thing' ethos endangers moral character - the same rule-breaking that wins the war keeps players from ever questioning whether the buggers needed defeating at all.

16.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md

17.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
17.relation: Cole Bowman explains the human-Formic war through Donald Davidson's critique of the idea of a self-contained conceptual scheme: the buggers' inability to grasp 'father,' 'individual,' or human sentience looks like complete untranslatability, yet Ender donning the bugger mask and the hive-queen's philotic contact show, via Davidson's principle of charity, that translation and a new shared scheme are possible. Kuhn's incommensurable paradigms and Feyerabend's account of how new theories eliminate old meanings frame how both species discard their prior concepts once Ender becomes the single point where the two schemes meet.

18.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Brett Patterson reads Card's philotes and the ansible as an uncanny parallel to Leibniz's Monadology - simple, internally varied, interconnected building blocks whose 'twining' explains instantaneous communication - and reads Ender's bond with the hive-queen through Levinas, for whom the face-to-face encounter with the Other imposes responsibility prior to self-understanding. That bond, formed through the Giant's Drink landscape the buggers built from Ender's own dreams, is why he cannot go home: he becomes Speaker for the Dead to restore the species he destroyed.

19.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
19.relation: Jeffery Nicholas argues Card tries to write Ender as Nietzsche's self-sufficient superman - Graff's isolation program, the will to power, and Rackham's 'humanity does not ask us to be happy' - but the novel actually vindicates Aristotle's claim in the Politics that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Ender's difference from the beast-like Peter and the hive-minded buggers, his longing for Valentine, Alai, and Petra, and his despair in isolation show that friendship, not domination, is what makes him human.

21.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive' against Aquinas' Doctrine of Double Effect and Frankfurt's second-order intentions, arguing Ender's killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail double-effect proportionality because he intends excessive, fear-inducing harm to deter future attackers. He allows that Ender bears only partial responsibility for the xenocide since he could not know the 'simulation' was real, but concludes that, contrary to the Speakers for the Dead doctrine, Ender is not the blameless moral exemplar Card makes of him.

22.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
22.relation: James Cook grades the Third Invasion against the just war principles Ender was never taught: the war is preventive rather than genuinely preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq parallel), proper authority is compromised by deceiving the public, last resort fails since the hive-queen was trying to communicate, and non-combatant immunity condemns destroying the bugger homeworld. He stages Augustine's ban on killing in individual self-defense against Aquinas' permission of it, and uses Kant's humanity formula and Cicero's hostis/perduellis distinction to ask whether the buggers were ever treated as rational beings rather than mere threats.

23.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
23.relation: Danielle Wylie uses Aristotle's conditions for voluntary action - control and knowledge - to argue Ender's planetary strike is one of his 'mixed cases' made under coercion and factual ignorance, so praise and blame attach elsewhere: Graff and Rackham, who foresaw the attack and could easily have stopped it, meet both conditions through culpable omission. Borrowing Rachels' Smith-and-Jones drowning case to show moral responsibility can exist without causal responsibility, she ends with Ender's non-blameworthy 'taking responsibility' as Speaker for the Dead.

24.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
24.relation: Kody Cooper runs Ender's life through classical just war theory: Augustine's axiom that peace is the end of all war explains why even his playground battles aim at a just peace, while the I.F.'s deliberate refusal to protect him from Bonzo's gang throws Ender into the Hobbesian state of nature where each person holds personal authority to use deadly force in self-defense. Sunzi's insistence that a commander must know the enemy grounds Ender's empathic preparation, and Cooper concludes the Third Invasion fails right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality - so the guilt Ender carries is really the I.F.'s and humanity's.

26.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Ender’s Game and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Kenneth Sayles reads Peter and Valentine's net personas through three lenses: John Locke's identity theory to ask whether a consistent virtual persona with no physical anchor deserves our trust, Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask what anonymity does to morality, and Hannah Arendt's account of totalitarianism to warn that nameless, unaccountable influence ('action without a name... is meaningless') paves the way for rule by propaganda and a fictitious world. Real-world parallels - identity theft, the hacker collective Anonymous, YouTube politics - make the Enderverse nets look prophetic rather than fantastic.

27.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
27.relation: Ted Brown and Christie Maloyed read Ender's Game as a Cold War debate between realism and liberalism: Hobbes' state of nature grounds Graff's survival-at-all-costs logic, and Machiavelli's counsel on seizing opportunities and keeping power by force when persuasion fails shapes Peter's insight that 'the right words can change the world.' The human-Formic war becomes a Prisoner's Dilemma neither species can escape without communication, and Ender's postwar practice of governing his colony 'by persuasion rather than fiat' delivers the book's verdict that the power to persuade can outlast the power to destroy.

28.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
28.relation: Greg Littmann reads Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in John Stuart Mill's mold, drawing a detailed parallel between Ender's engineered Battle School childhood and James Mill's grueling raising of his son to be utilitarianism's champion, down to both boys' breakdowns. He argues that although the xenocide was a tragic wrong by Mill's own lights (the hive-queens' happiness counted too), the harm principle permits overriding individual liberty when humanity's survival is at stake - which is why Card's novel, unlike Crime and Punishment or 'The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas,' shows consequentialism at its most troubling rather than its most absurd.
