8.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
8.file: ch08 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
8.relation: The chapter poses the 'Barney Paradox': viewers identify and empathize with a character who is utterly awful (selling a woman, the Scuba Diver con that dupes all his friends), even though we would shun him in real life. Nanay tests and finds insufficient several explanations - Barney is just immature, we only feel schadenfreude at his slap-bet punishments, or his emotions are simply contagious - since none explains why Barney's badness increases our engagement. Using Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table example and Adam Smith's idea of imagining ourselves in another's situation, he argues identification targets the character's situation, which is not itself evil. The appeal is vicarious badness: fiction lets us be 'virtual tourists' in immorality we would never choose for real.

9.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
9.relation: The chapter takes Barney's 'when I get sad, I stop being sad and be awesome instead' as a serious thesis about emotional control. Goffin surveys somatic theories (William James: control the body, fake it till you make it), cognitivist judgment theories (Sartre and Robert Solomon: Ted's rage at Barney for sleeping with Robin is a judgment of betrayal), and Jesse Prinz's 'embodied appraisal' synthesis, concluding emotions are two-stage processes of direct appraisal plus narrative monitoring. Because we partly author the narratives wrapping our appraisals - as Barney did when reinventing himself after Shannon dumped him, and as Lily does by owning her failure as a painter - we can responsibly 'awesomize' our emotions.

10.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
10.relation: The chapter argues Barney is best understood as a committed ethical egoist, distinguishing egoism from egotism, immoralism, and moral skepticism through the Playbook's Scuba Diver scam. Ainsworth rejects psychological egoism (Joey's view in Friends) using evolution and apparent counterexamples like Marshall's Christmas Eve deliveries, then uses Glaucon's ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether anyone would resist injustice with guaranteed impunity. The friendship objection is dissolved via Aristotle's 'a friend is another self': once friends are included in the ego, saving Marshall's relationship or rushing to Ted's hospital bed counts as self-interest, constrained like chess by absolute rules such as the Bro Code's Article 150.

11.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
11.relation: The chapter reads Robin's series-long arc as an argument for non-essentialist feminism against Carol Gilligan's suggestion that all women share fundamental traits and rules. Caught between Lily's Dreamhouse-Barbie domesticity and the Career-Barbie ideal her father forcibly raised her into - mocked by kindergartners at career day, 'called slut' by Marshall for a one-night stand in 'The Naked Man' - Robin keeps trying to live one prescribed path entirely and is miserable both times. Only when she stops choosing between the boxes, marrying Barney while still never wanting children, does the show endorse the non-essentialist feminism of Deborah Rhode and Drucilla Cornell: a woman may custom-tailor her own happy ending.

12.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
12.relation: The chapter uses Sartre to diagnose Barney's fixed persona of suits, womanizing, and Bro Code worship as bad faith: having freely chosen to become the suited businessman who stole Shannon, Barney now acts as if those are his only options, denying his radical freedom. Hardy maps Sartre's own examples onto the show - Wendy the Waitress play-acting a stereotypical waitress, the woman who ignores the knee-touch, Barney tuning out criticism with 'I'm awesome' - and reads emotions, via Sartre's Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, as magical transformations of the world like Marshall's 'best burger' quest and the Bob Barker paternity story. Barney's love for Robin and his secret reunion of Marshall and Lily are the moments he breaks out of bad faith and chooses freely against his persona.

13.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md

14.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
14.relation: The chapter argues the Bro Code's real value lies not in getting laid but in structuring homosocial bonds, listing its best articles (loyalty, equality, generosity) alongside its most sexist ones (the Hot/Crazy Scale, Article 101). Karioris explains men's competitive relations through hegemonic masculinity - the school-bully dominance that forces all masculinities to compete and pushes women out - and invokes Foucault's 'Friendship as a Way of Life' for how bonds between men can escape taboo and emotional distance. Robin as wingwoman ('a better Ted than Ted') and the gang's gender transgressions show the Code can be amended toward equality, with Aristotle's friendship of mutual cooperation and benefit, 'quid pro bro', as the standard.

15.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
15.relation: The chapter reads Future Ted's narration as Hegel's philosophy of history scaled down to one love life: like Hegel's development of freedom, Ted's dating disasters are necessary stages whose rational order appears only retroactively, when the owl of Minerva flies at dusk. Against Marshall and Lily's 'let the universe decide' readings of doppelgangers and apartment signs, Ted's line that 'we only see what we want to see when we're ready to see it' captures belated necessity: the Lucky Penny chain and the Right Place, Right Time walk become one necessary story only through reflection. Meeting the Mother, the final end of Ted's history, redeems the goat beating, the broken engagement, and the lost Chicago interview as contributions to the narrative.

16.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
16.relation: The chapter asks what is true in the fiction of HIMYM, distinguishing explicit 'primitive' truths (Robin is Canadian) from 'derivative' truths (Barney's conquests do not pop in and out of existence; his awesome gland is not real even in the story). Testing candidate accounts - carry over real-world truths, then restrict to shared community beliefs - against the college sub that is obviously a joint, the authors deploy David Lewis's pretense analysis of truth in fiction and Gregory Currie's fictional narrator, which the show's fallible, lying narrator Ted makes both nearly indispensable and insufficient. The upshot: ordinary viewers know exactly what is true in the show (they were smoking dope), while the theories strain to keep up - 'yeah, not so quick.'

17.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
17.relation: The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.

18.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md

19.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
19.relation: The chapter presents Barney as a Humean moral philosopher: reason is the slave of the passions, and norms like the Bro Code are invented conventions that evolve, Adam Smith's invisible-hand style, rather than being designed, revealed, or deduced. The Platinum Rule ('never, ever love thy neighbor') is grounded in Humean reciprocity: the eight-stage arc of attraction to fallout in Barney's Wendy the Waitress disaster, the Gerards' brunch tyranny, and Robin's romance with co-worker Curt shows the retaliation costs that make the norm a rational solution to coordination failures. Against the Golden Rule's painterly elegance, the anatomist's cautious observation of behavior explains why a norm banning neighborly love emerges even in a society of non-saints.

20.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
20.relation: The chapter argues HIMYM offers two complementary feminist icons: Robin embodies personal autonomy and independence - fighting from 'but, um' early-morning shifts to lead anchor, and grieving infertility as stolen autonomy rather than lost motherhood - while Lily, and even more Marshall, exemplify Carol Gilligan's feminist care ethics with its emphasis on emotion over impartiality, cooperation over competition, and partiality toward loved ones. Aristotle's golden mean supplies the test Robin passes by balancing career and love instead of pushing one to an extreme. The twist that a male character best exemplifies care ethics, with Lily bridging the two moral outlooks, is offered as the show's progressive complexity about gender.

21.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
21.relation: The chapter diagnoses the show's identity crises through Heidegger's Being and Time: Marshall's Goliath National Bank drudgery is anxiety over thrownness - the rent, the bills, the situation he never chose - while Lily's prom-night bolt to San Francisco is anxiety over freedom and possibility, and both fail anticipatory resoluteness, the commitment to be yourself while shouldering what you did not choose. das Man ('everybody's doing it') explains the gang's absorbed everydayness. Kierkegaard supplies the problem of time (life understood backwards but lived forwards) and Fear and Trembling's contrast between Abraham's leap of faith into the absurd and the 'demonic': Barney courts legendary moments yet manipulates uncertainty so he never becomes anyone new - the identity crisis that never ends.

22.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
22.relation: The chapter models Ted's annual Slutty Pumpkin vigil as a decision-theory problem: multiplying Ted's subjective probability (0.1) by his utility (9) yields an expected utility of 0.9, beaten by the Victoria's Secret party's 2.5, and two further irrationalities are added - misjudging the objective probability and acting on harmful desires. Yet Ted's impulse purchase of the derelict house in 'Home Wreckers', which becomes his future family home, shows expected-utility reasoning failing when unknowable scenarios multiply. The authors conclude that when the future becomes incalculable, gut feelings are the only remaining and legitimate guides - sometimes it is better to be a happy lunatic waiting on the roof than a rational but unhappy sage.

23.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md

24.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
24.relation: The chapter compares Barney's 'True story' pronouncements with William James's pragmatism, using James's squirrel anecdote and the 'Zoo or False' monkey-mugging to ask when an evidentially undecidable dispute becomes a live practical question. Like James's pragmatic cases for free will and religious comfort, Barney's monkey story and the twenty-eight-year-old 'with some sun damage' are beliefs made true by their practical (mostly entertainment) value, then replaced like outdated theories when new evidence arrives, as James's consistency requirement demands. The divergence: the Barney Stinson (BS) theory of truth is self-serving, engineering unverifiable stories others cannot disprove, while James weighs what works for everyone's experience.

25.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Framed as a sports broadcast with Aristotle as commentator, the chapter tests an evolutionary ethics ('BEES': the good is the naturally desirable, so the Pleistocene Stinson strategy of spreading genes grounds Barney's womanizing) against its classic critics. Hume's is-ought gap and Moore's open question argument are deployed against deriving Barney's right to pursue tail from human nature, while William Casebeer's evolutionary ethics replies that 'good' can be defined by present reproductive success - under which lying and eternal bachelorhood fail, since commitment is what reproduces genomes in urban New York ('BIRDS'). The chapter concludes that evolutionary ethics can support the Bro Code only by contestable redefinition, and the lying objection stands.

26.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
26.relation: The chapter reads the show's storytelling as identity construction through Paul Ricoeur's narrative identity, built on Heidegger's insight that human being is fundamentally temporal: we live in memories and future possibilities, so 'damn you, past Ted!' collisions between selves are structural. Ricoeur's two times - linear cosmological time versus fragmented phenomenological time - explain the show's looped, goat-intruding storytelling, while Giddens's reflexive project of the self (dubbed 'reflexibility') and Turkle's new-media multiple windows explain our fragmented, self-designed identities. Goffman's dramaturgy completes the picture: Barney's womanizer persona is a Goffmanesque masquerade that collapses, the yips, when his first lover reveals the founding story was false.

27.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy.md
27.relation: The chapter defends Barney's 'possimpible' as real philosophy. Aristotle's three formulations of the law of non-contradiction (from the Metaphysics) and Duns Scotus's ex falso quodlibet explosion argument show why classical logic must ban the possible and impossible becoming one - from one true contradiction, 'bimbos love studying formal logic' follows. Hegel's Science of Logic (the limit of the beer, the finite that is itself only by passing into its not-being) and Graham Priest's dialetheism from In Contradiction then argue limits are inherently contradictory, so the possimpible names the real turning point where opposites become each other - lived, the chapter claims, in Barney's transformation from lame hippie into suited bro.

8.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
8.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Crichton was doing philosophy rather than science: he imagined a possibility and probed its range because it could not be tested. It frames the whole book around Malcolm's question of whether we should, not whether we can, and around the gap between what we can do and what we should do with technologies like de-extinction. It connects the film to our illusion of control, insisting there are no ghosts or magic here, only nature, and that forgetting how edible we are turns us into 'bloody smears on the teeth of a T. rex'.

10.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Michaud and Watkins blame Crichton and Malcolm for frightening us away from science, arguing that most life does not 'find a way' and that science is the shield keeping vulnerable humanity a step ahead of extinction by meteors, plagues, and predators. They take up Rousseau's anti-Enlightenment longing to return to nature and reject it, arguing that humility comes from science itself (a 13.72-billion-year-old Earth, Sagan's 'star stuff' making us the universe become conscious of itself), not from abandoning it. Hammond, not science, embodies the real arrogance: he was so certain he could not fail that he tested the park on his own grandchildren.

11.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Littmann surveys real de-extinction efforts (George Church's passenger pigeon, plans to clone a frozen mammoth) and asks when reviving extinct species is morally permissible. He argues that Arne Naess's deep ecology, with its 'equal right to live and blossom', fails because it projects human desires onto organisms like plants that have none, and cannot say whether species or only individuals bear rights. He instead applies Mill's utilitarianism: bring species back when doing so maximizes happiness and minimizes suffering, which permits a Jurassic Park in principle but forbids dinosaur fights and trophy hunts like Roland Tembo's, and rebukes Sattler's claim that only the people we love matter.

12.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Freeman explains why Grant dismisses the clones as 'genetically engineered theme park monsters': a frog-DNA-patched genome is not dinosaur DNA, and nobody knows how much alteration turns a T. rex into something else, so as Wu tells Hammond the park has only reconstructed the past, never re-created it. Behavior cannot vindicate the clones either, since The Lost World's raptors grow up without elders to teach raptor behavior, and the animals must survive an ecosystem of grass, bacteria, and species that did not exist in the Cretaceous. The chapter's running puzzle of how much of an organism can change before it is no longer that organism is a Ship of Theseus problem applied to paleontology.

13.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Shea stages the Wu-Malcolm dispute through Hume's Dialogues: Jurassic Park is an 'intelligent design' so botched that, like Philo's world of needless suffering, it points to ignorant or malicious designers rather than a perfect God, undercutting Richard Owen-style design arguments. He then explains Hammond's folly with Darwinian natural selection and memetics, treating the dinosaur-theme-park as a meme that infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit, fame, and importance. Hammond's fatal errors were assuming evolution 'wants' humans to survive, that complexity means better adapted, and that he could outsmart selection, which the all-female raptors breeding and life 'finding a way' quickly refute.

14.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
14.relation: A pub dialogue applies Aristotle's De Anima, where the soul is the first principle of living things, to cloning: since a living clone must have an emergent, unrepeatable soul, successfully cloning dinosaurs brings new life into existence, which is good, so cloning itself is ethical. It then argues that neither unguided natural selection nor a divine dragon-slayer who nonetheless allowed cloning technology gives us reason not to revive dinosaurs, against Malcolm's 'they had their shot'. But drawing on Plato's forms, it condemns Hammond for controlling rather than merely containing: the lysine contingency and enforced sterility leave the dinosaurs shadows of what they could be, denied their natural flourishing.

15.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md

16.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Billard concedes the Stoic point that we control neither our passions nor nature ('life will always find a way', Sattler's 'you never had control'), as the bucardo cloning failure shows, but argues this proves the park rushed, not that de-extinction is impossible. Dangerousness is subjective, raptor intelligence is a logistics problem rather than a metaphysical objection, and since humans have already caused the sixth mass extinction we may have a duty to bring species back. Because revived animals would be 'neo-dinosaurs' built from fragmentary DNA, de-extinction is creation rather than resurrection, less like playing God than like the transhumanist enhancement humans already practice.

17.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
17.relation: Edwards argues that gene banks assume genes are the essence of a species, which he reads as a modernized Platonism: unchanging forms written in DNA, the same craving Hammond expresses in wanting to show people 'something that wasn't an illusion'. Following Hans Jonas's reading of Darwin, in which conditions rather than essence explain what an organism is, he casts Wu as the Platonist and Malcolm's 'life finds a way' as the evolutionary rebuttal in their debate over breeding control. The moral is that freezing DNA cannot save species, because what makes an animal what it is includes the vanished environment, so we should preserve habitats rather than entrust preservation to 'the hands of engineers'.

18.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Fitzpatrick argues that the awe Ellie feels at the brachiosaurs makes experiencing real dinosaurs so valuable that restoring them may be obligatory, and reads Malcolm's distrust of land managers as sharing Leopold's land ethic, under which firebombing Isla Nublar would be barbarism on the order of Dresden. Invoking Bentham, Mill, and Singer's expansion of the moral community (echoed in the park's dart guns), he weighs Elliot's 'Faking Nature' and Katz's charge that restored nature is a fake and an arrogance against Andrew Light's defense of respectful restoration. He concludes that Jurassic Park failed not because restoration is wrong but because Hammond restored dinosaurs for amusement, and that a careful, land-ethic-respecting de-extinction could one day be justified.

19.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
19.relation: Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.

20.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
20.relation: Michael Muniz argues the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park are real 'in the most important ways' - not cloned in a lab, but real whenever the film runs: they terrify, they occupy our dreams (his T. rex-at-the-window opening), and they re-actualize deep time on screen. He weighs whether the franchise is genuinely horror - preying on fear for a negative response - or something stranger, a tension between fear and excitement in which extinction itself is the source of the scare.

21.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md

22.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.

23.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
23.relation: Kempner argues that the featherless raptors confirm Baudrillard's hyperreal: our dinosaurs are 'a real without origin or reality', like blue raspberry flavor or the never-existent brontosaurus, so the more real the clones pretend to be, the more fake they seem. He reads Wu's 'there isn't any reality here' and The Lost World's fossil-album passage as Crichton's own warnings against mistaking images for reality, while Spielberg's rejection of feathers shows the franchise teaching audiences to prefer the fake. Baudrillard himself used the film's finale, cloned dinosaurs rampaging among their fossilized ancestors in the museum, as the image of our predicament between 'our fossils and our clones'.

24.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
24.relation: Karavitis maps the three films onto the history of animal ethics: Jurassic Park treats dinosaurs as property on Aristotle's ground that only rational humans matter; The Lost World adds Kant's indirect duties, where the sporting rules of Tembo's hunt express duties owed to other humans rather than to the T. rex; and Jurassic Park III moves to Tom Regan, whose 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value fits raptors that remember, plan, and finally choose to spare the humans. The cow and goat fed live to the raptors test how far each view protects animals we treat as mere means.

25.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
25.relation: King charges human exceptionality with being speciesism and asks whether dinosaurs are persons rather than humans, testing Kant's rationality criterion and Descartes' denial of animal thought against the raptor that opens the shed door and the T. rex that spins the Explorer searching for prey. He runs the dinosaurs through Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, then plays his Wittgenstein trump card: animal language would be the language of a different life-form, so the raptors' calls expressing fear and summoning help count as real communication without words. He closes with Regan's rights view, arguing that the cow and goat feeding scenes, like past denials of personhood to Native Americans and women, should shame us into showing a little respect.

26.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Lisa Kadonaga stages a choice between two sealed vials - clone the T. rex or the extinct thicktail chub - and weighs purposes for de-extinction: education and fundraising, Veblen-style prestige and conspicuous consumption, making amends for human-caused extinctions (the chub's wetlands were drained, the tyrannosaur died out before us), and Bentham-style utility of ecosystem function. She argues the chub wins on utility because it could resume a real niche while a top carnivore would wreck modern ecosystems, and questions whether Hammond-style engineering that makes recreated animals dependent on humans (the lysine contingency, terminator genes) violates the animals' right to exist as themselves. Her verdict is 'Pister's Bucket': defer resurrection until habitat and resources exist, and spend the effort saving the species we are killing right now.

28.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
28.relation: Christopher Ketcham writes a mock chronicle in which velociraptors escape to inhabited Nava, deliberately avoid humans, and over decades learn to share a hunting language with a Congo tribe, asking whether we would ever grant such beings equal intelligence and rights. He reads raptor pack behavior and cooperation through Dawkins's selfish gene, and uses Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to argue we can never peer into raptor consciousness, just as we brand human races inferior without looking. Citing Plessy v. Ferguson's whiteness-as-property and Mill's point that mistreating animals belongs in the same category as racial discrimination, he ends with a senate-hearing parody and the Neanderthal precedent: a human 'superiority gene' means coexistence with smart raptors would likely end as it did for them.

29.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
29.relation: Seth Walker asks whether Nick Van Owen - the Earth First! documentarian who monkeywrenches InGen's camp and frees the caged dinosaurs in The Lost World - is a bastard or morally justified. He runs the consequentialist cost-benefit (the escaped T. rex slaughters a cargo ship crew and trashes San Diego; the sabotage costs the team their radio and rescue) against the ecodefense argument built on Arne Naess's deep ecology and biocentric equality, on which Isla Sorna is our 'home' and rescuing the injured baby T. rex Roland Tembo crippled is Self-defense. Singer's principle of equal consideration of suffering - a difference in ability never justifies a difference in consideration - bridges the gap for those who reject biocentrism, and Walker answers the consistency objection (must Nick accept InGen sabotaging him back?) before crediting Nick's defense of his larger home.

30.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
30.relation: Tim Jones argues the films show why Kant's Enlightenment ideal - the courage to use your own understanding without others' guidance, embodied in Hammond's isolated, independently funded genius - has become dangerous now that one man's project can shape the world future people must live in. He tracks Hammond's arc from dismissing Malcolm's review to conceding 'I was wrong', but shows in the sequels that one convert to caution cannot contain a technology: Ludlow ships a T. rex to San Diego and paragliding entrepreneurs land on Isla Sorna anyway, so the damage to future people is done before anyone repents. Against this he proposes Rupert Read's 'Guardians of the Future', a super jury that would veto laws and technologies threatening future people's basic needs - meaning Hammond should have been stopped before he started.

31.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
31.relation: Daniel Kokotz tests Aristotle's border between natural things, moved by inner final causes, and technological artifacts, made for external human purposes, against the park's dinosaurs - and both fit. They hunt, grow, and breed on their own ('life finds a way', the sex-changing frogs-DNA population), yet they exist only because Hammond's scientists cloned them as paying entertainment, exactly like an artifact. Using Grant's different reactions to the incubator versus the wild nest, he shows we blame humans for technologically caused disasters while shrugging at natural ones; his resolution is that nature and technology are not two Aristotelian boxes but extremes of one spectrum, and biotechnology's hybrids prove humans never stood outside nature - we are still just prey in it.

32.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
32.relation: Kenn Fisher reads the franchise as the extinction of the Great Chain of Being: from Plato's humans mid-way between gods and beasts, through Genesis dominion and Descartes's non-conscious animals, to Malcolm's 'God creates man. Man destroys God. Man creates dinosaurs' - with computers (Hammond's control room, Wikipedia, Google) replacing God at the top. He then tracks animals' ascent from property: Francione on welfare versus personhood, Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', and Singer's equality-as-prescription, applied to Dieter Stark tasering a compy (punished by the compys) versus the unexamined electric fences that keep InGen's 'zoo animals' caged. He closes with Carol Adams's meat-masculinity link - Roland Tembo will hunt only a male T. rex, the dinosaurs are all female - and holds up vegetarian Lex as hope that the Chain bends into a Circle.

33.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
33.relation: Roger Hunt argues the films show that whoever assumes human superiority or ownership of created life gets eaten: Dieter Stark zaps a compy and is devoured by a swarm of them, Ludlow claims InGen's patent and becomes a hunting lesson for the baby T. rex. He stages the real debate over dinosaur moral status between the 'value of life' view (Harding and Sattler: experiment on them if enough sentient beings benefit) and Tom Regan's rights view - anything sentient has basic rights from unconditional individual value, and grading lives by usefulness is speciesism like racism or sexism. He then prefers Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach: a T. rex penned in San Diego cannot roam, hunt, or play, so it cannot flourish, and the point is not granting rights but recognizing we have no right to block other beings' flourishing for fun.

35.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
35.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues that when you go extinct you do not come back, dismantling our three hopes: the soul, cloning, and an essential self. Cloning a T. rex yields a new individual 'Rex' with her own perspective, not the original; the soul cannot both be beyond science's reach and record memories and move bodies; and he deploys Gilbert Ryle's view that 'soul' is a language mistake - a mind is just what a functioning brain does, the way 'Jurassic Park' is just buildings, dinosaurs, staff, and money working together, ceasing when the functioning stops. A Hammond stripped by Alzheimer's and atom-replacement of every memory, trait, and particle still gets called John Hammond, so there is no essence over time: we already die constantly and never notice, which is why a second extinction holds no fresh terror.

36.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
36.relation: Jeff Ewing reads the park as Nietzsche's will-to-power in action: Hammond's 'creation is an act of sheer will', resurrecting extinct species because science enables it, is the drive to remake the world godlike in one's own image, and Malcolm's 'so preoccupied with whether or not they could' marks exactly the external mastery Hammond achieved. But the Nietzschean great man also needs internal mastery - control over himself before control over nature - and Hammond failed it: one man (Nedry) held the whole security grid, frog-DNA surprises were foreseeable, raptor intelligence was underestimated, and the storm was ignored. For Nietzsche, lying to yourself about your strength is not arrogance but weakness, so Hammond's disaster was not a moral crime but a failure of self-mastery - a lesson Ewing extends to modern cloning, drones, and weapons pursued without honest reckoning.

37.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
37.relation: Jannelle Poetzsch introduces Hans Jonas's imperative of responsibility - 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life' - through Malcolm's charge that scientists never ask whether they should, since nuclear and genetic power now reach people no old 'love thy neighbor' ethic could imagine. Hammond is Bacon's 'knowledge is power' grown too successful: his 'thintelligence' embodies the gap between the power to act and the ability to foretell, so Jonas demands humility, worst-case rather than optimistic planning, and social institutions strong enough to check people who act merely because they can. Jonas also indicts capitalism's profit motive - Hammond risked his grandchildren and Costa Rican infants to manufacture a need for a dinosaur zoo - closing that the answer is not halting technology but thoughtfully restraining it, because some things cannot be re-caged.

38.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
38.relation: David Morgan unpacks the chaos theory behind Malcolm's 'I hate being right all the time', starting from Newtonian causal determinism and Laplace's demon, according to which the future is fixed and calculable - then showing that non-linear systems like weather and the park show sensitive dependence (Lorenz's butterfly effect), so even a fully determined universe is unpredictable in practice because we can never know initial conditions exactly. He raises the philosophy-of-science question of whether chaos is a property of nature or only of our computer models, and reads 'life finds a way' as Malcolm extending the same contingency to Darwinian evolution: rewind the tape and you get different species. He ends by noting Malcolm's own paradox - a chaos theorist certain of one specific doom - and settles on chaos theory predicting unpredictability: ignore tiny factors and do not be surprised when they bite you.

39.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
39.relation: Michael Stark and A.G. Holdier diagnose the park's collapse as vice rather than accident, using Aquinas's virtue ethics grounded in natural law: Hammond's imprudence (never weighing whether resurrection is right, shrugging off Malcolm's lunch-table warning, still planning 'corrections' over melted ice cream) and Gennaro's intemperance (admissions up to ten thousand dollars a day, 'coupon day', money tunnel-vision), both flowering from pride, the worst vice. Malcolm, despite the flirting and leather, is the only consistently virtuous character: prudence in situational judgment (waving a flare to lure the T. rex away from the kids), temperance about wealth and about Sattler, plus fortitude and justice - even lying to comfort Lex and Tim in the tree reflects character, not rule-breaking. Aquinas's point that virtues are lifelong course corrections, never a finished state, frames the closing Kierkegaard quote about never being finished with life's task.

40.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
40.relation: Trip McCrossin takes Grant's 'they'll just have to evolve, too' as addressed to the audience and asks whether human behavior, not meteors, could cause our extinction, using Malcolm's toolkit: self-organizing life on fitness landscapes, the Red Queen arms race you must run to stay in place, and Gambler's Ruin - once things go bad they cluster and go to hell together. The deepest lens is the Tragedy of the Commons: like herders each adding a sheep to a shared pasture, we do what is best for ourselves without concern for the common good, and the films chart ever-failing 'fences' - the paddock, the coastline, the Navy, the Marines - until pteranodons simply fly off Isla Sorna. Since ours is self-destruction (we run as fast as we can, but really from ourselves), the real fence, he concludes, is daring ourselves to collective restraint.

10.title: The Devil and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Devil and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Robert Arp's introduction opens with Halloween culture and his own seminarian past to ask whether belief in the Devil can survive scrutiny. He lays out a 'just deserts' argument - Hitler, Stalin, and Mao died unpunished while Job, Socrates, and Thomas More died unrewarded, so God, the Devil, Heaven, and Hell must exist to balance the scales - and then answers it with Freud's projection critique (religion as wishful thinking for comfort and moral control) and with the neuroscience tying the mind to a dying brain, which undermines the soul that Hell would punish. The chapter frames the whole book's project: testing devil-belief with arguments and evidence rather than taking it on authority.

11.title: The Devil and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Devil and Philosophy.md

12.title: The Devil and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Devil and Philosophy.md

13.title: The Devil and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Devil and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Nicolas Michaud catalogues the demonic hierarchy - de Spina's goblins, incubi, and familiars, Dante's Malebranche, Binsfeld's seven princes of Hell - through Dungeon Keeper's Dark Mistress, World of Warcraft succubi, Se7en, Hellraiser's Pinhead, Hellboy, and Spawn. His real argument is ontological: names are power, and what we call the Devil fixes how we treat him. Recovering the Hebrew sense of 'satan' as an appointed adversary and 'Lucifer' as light-bringer (compared to Prometheus), he argues the same being could be reframed from tempter to giver of knowledge, much as naming Columbus's invasion a 'discovery' launders atrocity.

14.title: The Devil and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Devil and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.

15.title: The Devil and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Devil and Philosophy.md

16.title: The Devil and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Devil and Philosophy.md
16.relation: James McLachlan splits the Satans of history into 'the Rebel' of Romanticism (Blake, Shelley's turn to Prometheus, the sexy vampires of film) and 'the Asshole' who wants to be God. Using Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the desire to be a complete being, he reads Dracula, Scarface's Tony Montana, and Bond villains as figures who cannot endure the otherness of real persons. With Bohme and especially Schelling's two wills - self-assertion and love of others - he argues evil is a positive, perverted order of pure egoism, and that not even Satan can achieve the total asshole-ness he wants, because selfhood exists only in relation to others.

18.title: The Devil and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Devil and Philosophy.md

19.title: The Devil and Philosophy
19.relation: Elizabeth Butterfield reads The Devil's Advocate through Sartre: Kevin Lomax's 'You set me up!' excuse - after defending the guilty Gettys and Cullen and abandoning MaryAnn - is textbook bad faith, a lie to himself about his own free choices. Milton the Devil plays existentialist, insisting 'I'm no puppeteer... I only set the stage. You pull your own strings,' until Kevin admits his vanity, his drive to win, motivated every choice. Radical freedom entails radical responsibility, and Kevin's final suicide is his last free act, chosen to keep coming out on top, while free will remains the one limit the Devil cannot breach.

20.title: The Devil and Philosophy
20.relation: Jim Berti opens with a dream-fable in which the Devil tempts him with a bank-robbing 'quick fix' for his house-buying cash crunch, then reads the Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil' as the Devil's resume of history's atrocities - Anastasia, the Blitzkrieg, the Kennedys - where he supplies the lighter fluid but never strikes the match. The chapter argues we give God too much credit and the Devil too much blame while omitting ourselves: the Devil is the 'drug dealer of sin,' peddling the seven deadly sins as shortcuts like Rocky IV's steroids, and only effortful virtue refuses them. As the song says, 'it was you and me.'

21.title: The Devil and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Devil and Philosophy.md

22.title: The Devil and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Devil and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Jennifer Baker asks whether the Devil does ethics any good and answers no. Against the tempter hypothesis she sets the traditional virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, where bad behavior traces to habituated vice rather than demons, and the cure is consciously cultivating virtues by hitting the mean between excess and deficiency - Johnny's practiced honesty, the Evangelical cousin's marital vows. She faults the Devil as a one-size-fits-all explanation of evil, a glamour machine (via Postrel and the Romantic Satan of Blake, Byron, and Milton), and a scare tactic the Epicureans warned corrupts character, closing with Plato's divided-soul counsel to aim at long-term goods and a dismissal of Luther's spite-drinking stratagem.

24.title: The Devil and Philosophy
24.relation: John Karavitis (with tongue-in-cheek co-author 'Lucifer') treats The Ninth Gate as an epistemology case study, sorting the characters' beliefs about the Devil - true-believer Balkan, skeptic book-dealer Corso, the occult-tourist Order of the Silver Serpent - and testing them against Plato's Theaetetus definitions of knowledge as perception, true belief, and justified true belief. Balkan's justification is only an internally coherent web of book-learned beliefs, while Corso's external evidence (engravings signed 'LCF,' his journey's experiences) is weighed by the general reliability of his sources. Descartes' dreaming and the deceiving demon then leave the viewer skeptical that the Devil ever appeared at all.

26.title: The Devil and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Devil and Philosophy.md
26.relation: The Bocks use the courtroom frame of The Exorcism of Emily Rose to ask whether anyone could be justified in believing in demon possession, since the same seizures, polyglot voices, and levitations read differently under naturalism and supernaturalism. Kuhn's paradigms explain why neither worldview abandons ship at anomalies, and they weigh Wiebe's 'finite spirits as theoretical entities,' Hume's miracles argument (with Levine's Red Sea thought experiment as rebuttal), and the Cartesian ghost-in-the-machine premise that possession would require. Testing even a Men in Black alien hypothesis against the religiously specific phenomena, they conclude that a witnessed case like Emily's could rationally justify belief in possession.

30.title: The Devil and Philosophy
30.relation: Danny Smith applies Kant's three grades of evil from Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone to The Dark Knight. Batman's saving Harvey over Rachel out of love is normal evil (pathological inclination trumping duty, his 'never kill' rule hardened into moral self-satisfaction), Two-Face's coin is radical evil (outsourcing his freedom and responsibility to chance), and the Joker - burning his own money, making his scarred face the true mask, wanting only chaos - is diabolical evil done for its own sake. Smith then presses Kant's embarrassing problem that evil pursued purely on principle, with no pathological motive, is indistinguishable from the highest good, and half-sympathetically re-reads the Joker as the honest rebel in a corrupt Gotham.

31.title: The Devil and Philosophy
31.relation: George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.

32.title: The Devil and Philosophy
32.relation: Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.

35.title: The Devil and Philosophy
35.relation: A.G. Holdier pits Augustine against Star Wars: South Park's pay-per-view Satan-Jesus boxing match and the Force's balanced light and dark sides picture God and the Devil as equals, but Augustine - drawing on his Manichaean past and Zoroastrianism's Ahura Mazda versus Angra Mainyu - shows this is really two-gods worship, not monotheism. For Augustine the Devil is a derivative creature, created good and freely fallen, and evil is not a positive force but a privation, an absence of God like cold or darkness, so Vader's corruption and redemption both hang on free choice. Mordred's rebellion against Arthur gives the right picture: the Dark Side can never win because it is only diminished goodness.

36.title: The Devil and Philosophy
36.relation: Jonathon O'Donnell reads DmC: Devil May Cry's Limbo City - demon-run banks, the Fox-News parody Raptor News, Virility soda - as the newest stage in the Devil's career. Tracing the shift from Dante's frozen, defeated Satan to Milton's active deceiver and the Black Mass's sacramental counterfeits, he argues the game's demons are both the hiders and the hidden: reality itself is the demonic lie, a counterfeit truth with nothing truer beneath it. When Dante and Vergil's WikiLeaks-style reveal frees humanity, what is unveiled is not God's order but just another contingent world, a secular tale of media institutions manufacturing 'truth' for a conforming public.

37.title: The Devil and Philosophy
37.relation: Ray Bossert reads Tolkien's Silmarillion through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy: elves, being artists, understand Melkor not as tempter but as bad artist, from his rebellious solo in the Music of the Ainur to his botched sub-creations - orcs bred from kidnapped elves - and his covetous collecting of the silmarils. Boethius supplies the machinery: evil seeks a good by unnatural means and only approximates it, wickedness debases its practitioner into a beast, God's foreknowledge embraces free choices without causing them, and Providence is a spinning disc at whose center alone one is steady - so Melkor's rebellion leaves him less free, dragged around the rim. Tolkien's contrast between art (for beauty) and magic (for control) explains why the Devil can only mimic creation, never make anything real.

40.title: The Devil and Philosophy
40.relation: Michael Versteeg and Adam Barkman explain C.S. Lewis's Screwtape doctrine that the Devil conquers minds not by argument but by unreason, since human reason fights on God's side. They unpack Screwtape's tactics as textbook fallacies: jargon like 'religious phase' working as a red herring, dismissing Christianity out of boredom as a non sequitur, the 'Historical Point of View' as the chronological snobbery that cuts generations off from the past, and the endless loop of pride about one's humility as an infinite regress that paralyzes thought. Because reason is, for Lewis, the road toward Heaven, the Devil's highway to Hell is built entirely of bad logic.

41.title: The Devil and Philosophy
41.relation: Thomas Ward reconstructs C.S. Lewis's argument from The Problem of Pain that either demons exist or God doesn't. The free will defense, credited to Augustine, covers the evil humans freely do - freedom being required for love, as the rubber-ducky world shows - but John Perry's baby bat eaten by cockroaches and William Rowe's burned fawn are natural evils no human is responsible for. Given the not-crazy assumptions that God exists and is never morally responsible for evil, something non-human, personal, and wicked must bear that responsibility: hence demons, who like us misused their freedom, stretching the free will defense to cover every evil whatsoever.

44.title: The Devil and Philosophy
44.relation: Eric Swan tours the Devil-song canon - Elvis's 'Devil in Disguise' and 'Devil with a Blue Dress,' the Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil' with its Altamont aftermath, the Grateful Dead's 'Friend of the Devil,' 'The Devil Went Down to Georgia,' Van Halen's 'Runnin' with the Devil,' and Beck's 'Devil's Haircut.' His argument is that these songs chart shifting conceptions of the Devil: from a misogynist shorthand for the betraying woman, to the transpersonal 'you and me' of human atrocity, to a beatable tempter, a party companion in self-destructive excess, and finally a mood of dystopian survival at century's end. The Devil of pop music, Swan suggests, becomes whatever humans need him to be.

45.title: The Devil and Philosophy
45.relation: Steven Neumann reads the sold-my-soul legends around Led Zeppelin ('here's to my sweet Satan' backwards on 'Stairway to Heaven'), Black Sabbath, and bluesman Robert Johnson at the Clarksdale crossroads as a parable of Nietzsche's amor fati: every joy comes bundled with suffering, so greatness means affirming the whole package. He deploys the eternal recurrence thought experiment - would you will your life, Plant's dead son and Bonham's fatal bender included, to repeat eternally? - and contrasts the ascetic denial of pleasure with Nietzsche's claim in Ecce Homo that his own sickness and obscurity made him love fate all the more.

46.title: The Devil and Philosophy
46.relation: Nick Jones asks whether worshipping the Devil and doing evil can ever be good, and answers: artistically yes. Using the transgression that defines extreme metal - blasphemy, church burnings, and Varg Vikernes's murder of Euronymous - he argues Satanic metal's immoral features can enhance its artistic value when they achieve three aims: rebellion, blasphemy, and authenticity. Genuine theistic Satanists who really believe in the Devil they invoke do all three best, though the chapter ends by conceding the cupboard of actual theistic Satanist metalheads is empty.

48.title: The Devil and Philosophy
48.relation: Liz Stillwaggon Swan explains why crime dramas like Criminal Minds, CSI, and Bones are so watchable: Jung's shadow archetype and collective unconscious mean the Devil in human form on screen taps humanity's shared dark layer, while Aristotle's catharsis lets viewers experience pity and fear safely from the couch, identifying with characters like repulsed Garcia or intellectualizing Dr. Brennan. She adds the CSI effect - jurors with warped expectations of DNA and fingerprint work - and argues the shows satisfy a deep need to see devils like Bundy and Dahmer caught within a tidy forty-three minutes.

49.title: The Devil and Philosophy
49.relation: Jeff Ewing reads Faustian bargains - Marlowe's and Goethe's Faust, Dorian Gray's wager with Lord Henry, Tommy Johnson's guitar in O Brother Where Art Thou?, Rosemary's Baby, and Twilight Zone's 'Escape Clause' - through Marx's Capital. The soul becomes a universal commodity with both use value and exchange value, and the Devil a perfect buyer's monopoly who can demand everything, a trade Ewing contrasts with capitalism's effective-demand rule that those who cannot pay go unaided even unto death.

51.title: The Devil and Philosophy
51.relation: Roger Hunt reads Bill Hicks's stand-up as a Socratic comedy exposing Satan's three-point plan: suppress knowledge, breed ignorance, and profit from hypocrisy - from the Waffle House 'readah' scene to Bush-era Gulf War spin ('we looked at the receipts'), JFK-assassination distraction via American Gladiators, and pop stars and marketers who 'suck Satan's cock' (Rick Astley, corporate rock, advertising). Where the Genesis serpent offered knowledge, Hicks's Devil is the force that suppresses it, and Hicks paid a Socratic price - an early death for 'corrupting' his audience - for pointing this out.

52.title: The Devil and Philosophy
52.relation: Jones, Hansmann, and Stachura trace the trope of woman as the Devil's handmaiden - Eve and Lilith, succubae and Sirens, the sixteenth-century witch hunts, down to 'maneater' and 'Poison' rock songs and Blurred Lines - arguing it perpetuates patriarchal power. They apply Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman constructed as the perpetual Other, defined as secondary to man with sexuality at the heart of her Othering, and extend the analysis with Gloria Anzaldua's Borderlands and mestiza consciousness, which rejects the gender binary the woman-as-Devil trope depends on.

55.title: The Devil and Philosophy
55.relation: Aaron Rabinowitz argues that modern Devil stories - Milton's 'Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven', Neil Gaiman's Sandman where Lucifer quits Hell like a two-weeks notice, and Mike Carey's Lucifer building a second creation whose only commandment forbids worship - reveal a Devil whose real motive is free will and autonomy in a predetermined cosmos. Rereading the serpent in Eden, the wager over Job, and the temptation of Jesus through that lens makes Lucifer look reasonable, even commendable, and since we all feel pushed around by obligations, survival needs, and neuroscience, our sympathy for the Devil is inevitable.

56.title: The Devil and Philosophy
56.relation: Tim Jones tests Kundera's thesis that the Devil stands for meaninglessness against the angels' excess of imposed meaning. The Quran's Iblis refuses to bow to Adam but really just wants his own hierarchy with himself on top; the Devil's temptations of Jesus in the desert (stones into bread, the temple leap, dominion in exchange for worship) pick apart the meaning of Jesus's fast only to install his own significance; and Lord of the Flies shows how the conch's collapse into 'just a glorified seashell' lets Jack's hunters turn the island into Hell - so the grinning, meaning-destroying Devil of the pig's head is as terrifying as a plainly evil one.

57.title: The Devil and Philosophy
57.relation: James Edwin Mahon dismantles the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle by testing three accounts of diabolical evil: Machiavelli's prince ('learn how not to be virtuous') shows self-interest is mere amoral Realpolitik; Schopenhauer's malice and Schadenfreude ('injure all people as far as you can') are still self-interested pleasure; and only Kant's 'diabolical will' - doing evil because it is evil, Paradise Lost's 'Evil, be thou my good' - truly captures the Devil, though Kant deemed it impossible for humans. Hence nobody actually likes the Devil; people like the intelligence, charm, and underdog status of the characters who play him in The Devil's Advocate and Angel Heart.

60.title: The Devil and Philosophy
60.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether the Devil could actually get you by testing theories of the afterlife against Hamlet's ghost, Freddy Krueger, the possessions of The Exorcist and Evil Dead, Paranormal Activity, Dante's Inferno, Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, and Doom. Substance dualism cannot explain how a non-physical soul moves so much as a finger; the view that you are your body founders on recycled grave matter and the primacy of the brain; and if you are a program running on your brain, the Devil could torture infinite copies of you in Hell - even re-running you there from Heaven - unless duplication means neither copy is really you.

61.title: The Devil and Philosophy
61.relation: John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.

62.title: The Devil and Philosophy
62.relation: Robert Arp treats Voltaire's 'If God did not exist, then it would be necessary to invent Him' as a conditional claim and argues it is false: Kant's categorical imperative (universalize the action, as with lying and the collapsing practice of borrowing) and Mill's utilitarian cost-benefit calculus secure social order with no god and no Devil required. He then concedes that since most people are driven by guilt and fear rather than reason, inventing the Devil as an archetype of evil to be avoided at all costs may after all be a useful fiction.

65.title: The Devil and Philosophy
65.relation: Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.

67.title: The Devil and Philosophy
67.relation: Clint Jones argues LaVey's Satanic Bible rests on a misreading of Epicurus: genuine Epicurean hedonism is not limitless indulgence but the ordered life of the Tetrapharmakon - don't fear gods or death, the good is easy to get, pain is endurable - together with the threefold division of desires, which reserves constant gratification for natural and necessary things like water, bread, and friendship. By licensing gluttony and every whim so long as no one else is hurt, LaVeyan Satanism fails as the pleasure-as-virtue philosophy it claims to revive, leaving its followers with base, unfulfilling pleasures that are, well, Hellish.

69.title: The Devil and Philosophy
69.relation: Magus Peter Gilmore, High Priest of the Church of Satan, reads pop culture's turn to villains - Loki outshining Thor, Ledger's Joker, Hellboy, Man of Steel's killing Superman - as the mainstream finally arriving at the Satanist party, since LaVeyans always used Satan as a symbol of self-deification ('I-theist') and carnal pride. He answers Pitkänen that Satanism needs no 'higher knowledge' and cannot include theists, and he answers Jones by citing the Satanic Bible chapter 'INDULGENCE... NOT COMPULSION': LaVey taught self-controlled indulgence and rational self-interest, not reckless abandon, and Epicurean moderation is no basis for dismissing him.

70.title: The Devil and Philosophy
70.relation: Olli Pitkanen replies to Magus Peter Gilmore's critique: against the Church of Satan's claim to own 'Satanism', he argues definitions are never stable (materialism means Democritus', Newton's, quantum or Marx's) and that had LaVey's church never formed in the 1960s, some other - probably more religious - Satanism would have defined the term differently, so no group has final authority over the label.

72.title: The Devil and Philosophy
72.relation: Clint Jones answers Magus Gilmore by conceding he judged only The Satanic Bible but arguing that is the right target: even if LaVey later refined his views, he never retracted the book's Epicurean pretensions, and naming his system Epicurean is itself an appeal to an intellectual forebear. Since LaVey 'plundered' his sources - cherry-picking 'pretty gemstones rather than weightier keystones' - the foundation of Satanism remains shaky, and a Garden of Eden stripped of its Judeo-Christian trappings, Jones adds, was already a remarkably Epicurean life.

73.title: The Devil and Philosophy
73.relation: Magus Peter Gilmore closes the exchange: LaVeyan Satanism honestly embraces the selfishness most people already live by (sharing Ayn Rand's enshrined self-interest), and Epicurus's own letters to Menoeceus - on not fearing death, choosing the most pleasant over the longest life, pragmatic justice, and the need for natural science - show deep congruence with LaVey. Against Pitkänen on Eastern religions, whose reincarnation and karmic debt he reads as denigration of carnal existence, and against Jones's shaky-foundation charge (Christianity itself was a Hebraic/Hellenic mash-up), he concludes Satanists are proud 'Hell-raisers' celebrating the only life there is.

75.title: The Devil and Philosophy
75.relation: Robert Arp compiles the 'Devil made me do it' record: Flip Wilson's catchphrase, actual possession pleas from Christian v. State to the Demon Murder Trial of Arne Cheyenne Johnson, the M'Naghten Rule born of Daniel M'Naghten's botched assassination, the Son of Sam's possessed dog Harvey, exorcism lore from Roland Doe (The Exorcist) to Anneliese Michel (The Exorcism of Emily Rose), and the bizarre Mayo v. Satan lawsuit. The law's answer throughout is that only a defect of reason - never the Devil - robs defendants of free will, and the possession cases read better as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and negligence than as demons.

9.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
9.relation: Jason Holt's introduction argues there is a genuine paradox in Leonard Cohen: his songs count both as high-art poetry and as popular folk/pop music, challenging the assumed absolute divide between high and popular art. Holt considers whether film auteur theory - the way Hitchcock elevates genre thriller - resolves the paradox by making Cohen a transcendent auteur, or whether the songs remain gloriously popular without any supra-popular transubstantiation. He rejects mentor Louis Dudek's charge that taking up the guitar betrayed Cohen's poetry, insisting the literary lyrics and pleasing melody are perfect complements.

10.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md

11.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.

12.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.

13.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Wieland Schwanebeck surveys the many masculinities in Cohen's songs - spies, soldiers, cowboys, rabbis, captains - and argues they mostly appear broken, mocked, or failing (the losing partisan, the captain whose ship leaks or crew deserts), which puts the 'real man' ideal in doubt. He shows how Cohen's Jewishness plays against stereotypes of the bookish, unathletic Jewish man, usually embraced and then inverted with Socratic irony, as in 'Is This What You Wanted' and 'Lover Lover Lover.' Following Judith Butler's Gender Trouble, he reads Cohen's stage persona - the tailored suit, kneeling, clowning, and erotic ambiguity - as a repeated performance demonstrating that masculinity is 'an imitation without an origin.'

14.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Gary Shapiro treats The Future as a 'lyrical phenomenology' of time that stages multiple temporalities rather than one theory of time. 'The Future' evokes an apocalypse where the katechon - the Biblical restraining force holding back the end - no longer works, while 'Waiting for the Miracle' anatomizes passive deferral in a way Shapiro finds sharper than the Stoic critique of waiting by Seneca and Marcus Aurelius and Nietzsche's 'problem of those who wait,' opposing wasted chronos to the seized kairos of 'First We Take Manhattan.' 'Anthem's' crack that lets the light in gets a Gnostic reading, 'Democracy' is glossed through Derrida's 'democracy to come' as messianic, always-arriving futurity, and 'Closing Time' and 'Always' add honky-tonk eschatology and the vow of eternal love.

15.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md

16.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Jason Holt defends the serious question of whether Cohen is a good singer against both anti-fans and fandom, arguing that judgments of taste purport to objectivity and cannot be settled by polls or Juno Awards. Borrowing David Hume's standard of taste - ideal critics with strong sense, delicate sentiment, practice, comparison, and freedom from prejudice - he judges Cohen in his 'weight class' as a singer-songwriter and vocal stylist, ranks him between Paul Simon and Bob Dylan, and offers the 'great singer-songwriter argument' that excellence in both crafts implies being at least a good singer. Much dismissal, he argues, is really style prejudice or a category mistake, and he ends by confessing that Cohen's voice saved him from teenage suicide, biasing him in the best possible way.

17.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
17.relation: Adam Auch asks why the 'born with the gift of a golden voice' line of 'Tower of Song' is a joke in Cohen's mouth, a lament in Marianne Faithfull's, and a boast in Tom Jones's. Using indexicals, performer persona, and Paul Grice's conversational maxims, he argues interpretation depends on who sings and how: audiences fill the lyric's 'I' with the persona they associate with the performer, and Cohen's bald-faced flouting of the maxim of sincerity forces the ironic reading. The signature 'L. Cohen' in 'Famous Blue Raincoat' ties that song so tightly to Cohen's persona that cover artists must either inhabit the role (Tori Amos) or rewrite the lyrics (Jennifer Warnes), while post-boom 'Hallelujah' covers by Rufus Wainwright and Alexandra Burke perform it as a straight hymn, losing the tension between earthly and heavenly that Cohen and Jeff Buckley preserve.

18.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Edward Winters answers his sister's question - why listen to such depressing music - through Lorca's duende, the 'black sounds' of deep song that, as Nick Cave says, every true love song must contain. He argues duende resists definition yet is recognizable in Cohen, and connects it to Nietzsche's Dionysian art of participation (war dances, anthems, 'Dance Me to the End of Love') as against Kant's disinterested aesthetic distance, so music can re-enchant a disenchanted world. Via Kant's account of artistic genius and Cohen's testimony that Lorca and six flamenco chords gave him his voice, Winters concludes Cohen's dark, honest beauty has duende - which is why it lifts and tears at the heart rather than depressing.

20.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
20.relation: Christopher Lauer argues Cohen's lyrics seduce through Socratic irony as Kierkegaard analyzes it in The Concept of Irony: ostentatious self-concealment that makes hearers aware of the gap between words and intentions, building 'personality' and promising intimacy. Songs like 'Closing Time,' 'Everybody Knows,' and 'Democracy' oscillate between cynical third-person verdicts and sudden second-person address, offering a hidden sincerity only to withdraw it - an erotic improvement on Plato's Socrates that dissolves its own ironic distance. 'Hallelujah' and 'Anthem' make the program explicit, treating brokenness as the space in which love develops, while 'Tower of Song' shows the bleak side: irony collapsing into pure cynicism, the singer speaking sweetly from the Tower long after all promises of genuine intimacy have been disavowed.

21.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.

22.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Simon Riches argues that Cohen fuses the erotic with the spiritual - worshipping female beauty as religious experience in 'Light as the Breeze' and 'Night Comes On' - and that this produces conflicted, self-deceiving relationships in songs like 'Famous Blue Raincoat' and 'Chelsea Hotel #2.' Against the classical theory of concepts embodied in Socrates' demand for essences, he deploys Wittgenstein's language games and family resemblance, Wittgensteinian views of religious belief, and Davidson's divided mind to deny that love has a rationally coherent essence. Following Richard Rorty, Cohen emerges as an ironist who rejects any 'final vocabulary' of love, and this very contingency and irony ground his authenticity as a singer of romantic love.

23.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
23.relation: Babette Babich traces the shifting 'you' of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne' through Hegelian thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Empedocles's cycle of Love and Strife, reading the songs' ambiguity (David, Samson, the bound champion) as Cohen's sovereign having-it-both-ways. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity frames the human condition of being what one is not, while Nietzsche - on broken promises, on women and distance, on the Antichrist - supplies both the critique of Cohen's courtly projections onto the feminine Other and the model of singularizing solitude. 'Who by Fire' is read against the Rosh Hashanah prayer Unetanneh Tokef as a song of fate, judgment, and atonement whose closing 'who shall I say is calling?' is quasi-Augustinian and Heideggerian: death singularizes each 'who' at the moment of its claim.

25.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
25.relation: Steven Burns rejects both the Obscenity Reading and a merely Poetical Reading of Beautiful Losers in favor of a Political Reading: the four losers - Saint Catherine Tekakwitha, the constipated Anglophone Historian, the French sensualist F., and the Aboriginal wife Edith - represent Canada's founding peoples on the eve of the 1967 centennial. Defending his view that richer works admit a single 'best reading' (after Anthony Savile's aesthetics of best explanation), he reads F.'s Quebec separatism, the statue bombing, and the novel's orgasm-imagery as allegory of a nation inhibited and failing, in dialogue with George Grant's Lament for a Nation. The epilogue's blonde in the Oldsmobile who says 'I am Isis' signals Cohen's dream of a transformed, liberated Canada - Catherine updated - rather than Grant's lament.

26.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Paweł Dobrosielski and Marcin Napiórkowski read Flowers for Hitler as Cohen's answer to Adorno's dictum that to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric - Cohen writes poetry that self-consciously knows it comes after the end of poetry. Using Freud's distinction between the vocabulary and grammar of dreams, they show the collection is assembled from a small repertoire of recurring images (ovens, ashes, telephones, radios, green grass, Nazi names) whose awkward normality expresses repression: life goes on as if nothing had happened. Arendt's banality of evil, born of the Eichmann trial, is directly alluded to in 'All There Is to Know about Adolf Eichmann,' and the book ends by universalizing Holocaust memory - the poet waking with a number on his forearm, feeling like victim and perpetrator alike - until the grass itself is grown on ashes and every flower is a flower for Hitler.

27.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
27.relation: Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.

29.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
29.relation: Christopher Ketcham narrates a night listening to Dear Heather during a café blackout, in which darkness becomes Eugene Minkowski's 'lived space' - more personal than light, with auditory space as its own dark space - and Cohen's voice leads him down into a shared funk of loss and depression. Through Heidegger he diagnoses his own shrunken, past-bound, thrown existence and reinterprets being-toward-death not as a downward spiral but as being toward his own remaining possibilities, and through Freud's death drive he names the 'unobtrusive death wish' he had let dwell unchallenged in him. The essay closes with a Heideggerian resolve toward resoluteness and future possibility, glimpsing a street-worn 'Suzanne' in the dark as hope rather than absence.

30.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
30.relation: Rachel Haliburton asks what metaphysics underwrites Suzanne's world, where a mind can touch a perfect body. The materialist world inherited from Descartes reduces thoughts, meanings, and purposes to purposeless physical processes in which minds never touch bodies; Aristotle's teleological world, refurbished by Thomas Nagel's Mind and Cosmos, builds purposes into nature and treats subjective experience - what the tea and oranges are like for you - as real in its own right. She argues Suzanne's world, and our own ordinary mall-food-court world, is teleological: consciousness is 'biased towards the marvelous,' and we touch one another's bodies with our minds all the time.

31.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
