Because Raylan feels regret, the Aristotelian mark of the unselfrestrained person who knows his condition, he is curable and lacks self-restraint by habit rather than nature (Nicky Augustine's limo verdict: 'it's not who you are'). The chapter reads Raylan's signature move - forcing men to draw first so their deaths count as justified - as a perversion of justice by an akratic who is not wicked, and the series arc as his slow acquisition of self-restraint.

32.title: Justified and Philosophy
32.relation: The chapter assembles real contested self-defense cases beside Raylan's shooting of Tommy Bucks - the OK Corral and Wyatt Earp's far-from-clean vendetta ride, Curtis Reeves killing a texting moviegoer over thrown popcorn, George Zimmerman and Trayvon Martin, Ossian Sweet's mobbed house, Bernie Goetz's subway shooting, Gary Plauche executing his son's abuser on camera, and the Texas father who beat his daughter's rapist to death. Its philosophical machinery is Aquinas's principle of double effect from the Summa Theologica (self-defense may have two effects, saving one's life and slaying the aggressor, only the first intended), set against St. Augustine's condemnation of private self-defense as inordinate self-love. Florida's stand-your-ground law - where the dead man cannot tell his side - supplies the legal gray zone the show's title exploits.

9.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
9.relation: The editor's introduction ('hello.') recounts his own path from an Apple IIe through a PC interlude back to the iPod and iPhone, and frames Jobs's arc: a bold, brash entrepreneur of modest means who revolutionized computers, music, phones, and movies, yet was petulant, insensitive, and cruel, a 'barefoot billionaire hippy capitalist' shaped by Sixties counterculture and Eastern spirituality who set out to 'make a ding in the universe.' It presents the book as neither demonization nor hagiography but thoughtful, mostly philosophical examinations of Jobs's life, work, and cultural impact from many points of view.

10.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md

11.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.

12.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Biondi argues the 'counter-cultural capitalist' is no paradox: Jobs succeeded not as a Gordon Gekko-style greedy capitalist but through the creative individualism of the cognitive counter-culture—the garage techno-geeks—who pursued their own vision rather than the bottom line. She traces the greedy-capitalist stereotype to Glaucon's Ring-of-Gyges challenge in Plato's Republic (people act justly only from fear of punishment), Hobbes's restless desire for power after power, and Marx and Engels's picture of alienated wage slavery under capitalism, with Rawls as the toleration-only-if-redistributed alternative. Jobs's hippie exterior (drugs, fruitarianism, Zen) masked an entrepreneur who, in Rand's 'creative mind' mold, put a ding in the universe through products like the iPad instead of philanthropy.

13.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.

14.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Munkittrick argues that because personhood cannot be defined (trait lists like 'long-term planning' are circular) and behavior cannot prove an inner mind—as Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment shows—people have always identified persons intuitively, and Pixar trained Millennials to do exactly that. He reads the Pixar canon in three stages: Toy Story's self-aware Buzz as nascent non-human personhood, the Human-as-Partner films (Ratatouille's Remy and Linguini, WALL-E and EVE, Monsters, Inc.'s Sully and Boo, Up's Carl and Dug) as mutual recognition of persons across species lines, and The Incredibles as showing that even enhanced 'super-humans' face otherization—so a generation primed by these films will accept AI, animals, and uplifted beings as bearers of rights.

15.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md

16.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.

17.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
17.relation: Salvino casts Jobs as a billionaire egoist-visionary in the lineage of Adam Smith's insight that an entrepreneur's self-interest, not good intentions, best satisfies people's wants, Emerson's self-reliance, and Rand's virtues of independence and integrity—comparing Jobs to Howard Roark while noting his intuition was 'un-Randianly' unreasoned. Through Schumpeterian creative destruction (the automobile killing the horse-and-carriage; Wozniak's Apple I that HP rejected) and Deming's quality-first management, he explains Jobs's 'faster horse' contempt for market research, then rebuts the three standard ethical complaints—Foxconn labor conditions, his harsh verbal lashings, and his refusal to join the Giving Pledge—arguing Jobs did more good making the iPad than philanthropy ever could.

18.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Krause and Parker take on the charge that Jobs 'didn't invent anything'—Wozniak was the engineer, Xerox PARC had the GUI, MP3 players and smartphones already existed—by deploying Ayn Rand's objective theory of value, which rejects both intrinsic value in things and subjective value as whim. On Rand's distinction between 'philosophically objective' value (the best possible by the most rational mind, e.g. technically superior PCs) and 'socially objective' value (the sum of individual judgments in trade, her lipstick-versus-microscope example), Jobs's genius was converting the first into the second—making ease-of-use valuable to the early majority with the iMac, iPod, and iPhone—so inventing is neither necessary nor sufficient for entrepreneurship, and Jobs deserves the wealth and admiration his market success brought.

19.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
19.relation: Thomas asks whether the Apple II, Macintosh, and iPod were great products regardless of sales or great because they sold, and answers that market success is real evidence of value: each sale is a buyer's revealed preference in a voluntary trade, a stronger test than critics or focus groups, which is why Jobs's flops (NeXT, the G4 Cube) were overdesigned, overpriced failures of utility rather than quality. Against Hume's quoted doctrine that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions (hunger strikers and Jobs's own vegan fanaticism defeat any basic-desire theory), he follows Rand and Philippa Foot in grounding value in objective human needs and capacities, so products designed for those needs—like the iPhone the Apple team built for themselves—could be expected to succeed.

21.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.

22.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.

23.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
23.relation: White argues Apple's 'Think Different' commercial packages together two distinct character traits: genuine independence, in Rand's sense of judging from the facts of reality (thirteen-year-old Jobs confronting his pastor with the problem of evil via the Biafran children—'Does God know about this?'—rejecting dogma at Stanford, killing the iPod's screen, bending Corning to make gorilla glass on schedule), and pseudo-independence that asserts the primacy of consciousness over reality (refusing to bathe because his diet 'prevented' odor, treating cancer with fruit juice, NeXT's impossible eighteen-month promise). Using Binswanger's 'fallacy of false integration' (the surgeon-and-murderer 'cutter' example), he charges the ad with merging the traits into one folder, so Jobs should instead be praised without qualification for his independence and blamed without qualification for his pseudo-independence.

24.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
24.relation: Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.

25.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
25.relation: Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.

26.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy.md

27.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
27.relation: Pardi argues Jobs lived philosophically as an existentialist: the 'Steve Jobs Roll Your Own Calculator Construction Set' anecdote shows design by touch and intuition rather than master plans, every detail of a product mattered because it belongs to a life narrative of 'making a ding in the universe,' and he avoided both Kierkegaard's despair (the gap between actual and possible self) and Sartrean bad faith—quoted from Being and Nothingness—by never lying to himself about his products, calling faulty work 'shit' and redoing it. Against him stands Bill Gates the pragmatist, whose utilitarian Windows-for-every-desk business and 'rationality only goes so far' humility embody William James's pragmatic method, while Jobs's Zune taunt ('we made the iPod for ourselves') shows the existentialist refusing to compromise authenticity for market share.

28.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
28.relation: Cohen retells the DOJ ebook case—Amazon's $9.99 Kindle pricing, Eddy Cue's agency-model deals with the five publishers, the most-favored-nation clause, Jobs's warning email to James Murdoch, and Judge Cote's conspiracy ruling—to ask whether Jobs and other businessmen live and work to serve consumers or themselves. He argues antitrust law encodes the altruist-utilitarian demand that producers sacrifice their own goals to consumer welfare, and defends the Randian alternative ('your life belongs to you') on which Jobs, Cue, and the publishers were entitled to pursue their own happiness through their work, so readers inspired by Jobs's 'find what you love' Stanford challenge should reject the ethics behind antitrust.

29.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
29.relation: In an imagined Walter Cronkite-moderated afterlife debate, Jobs opens with 'most technology is shit,' holding up the iPod as art-through-simplicity—design as the soul of the thing, thought down to its essence—while Heidegger answers from 'The Question Concerning Technology': the iPod's four Aristotelian causes (material, form, purpose, maker) work together as co-responsible bringing-forth, a revealing whose essence is enframing, which conceals the human when technology is treated as mere standing-reserve and cheapest utility. The dialogue converges on Jobs's washer-and-dryer anecdote and the Mercedes line: technology that reveals rather than conceals our being—useful and beautiful—keeps it serving humanity instead of mastering it, and Heidegger's Nazi past is flagged for the reader to judge separately.

30.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
30.relation: Knepp asks why Jobs's 'simplicity is the ultimate sophistication' produced the friendly, MoMA-collected Macintosh (the face-like design, the inviting handle, the signed internals) but collapsed into the $6,500 NeXT Cube, answering with Žižek's reading of Hegel in Less than Nothing: the original idea is already self-contradictory, the failure of NeXT (the over-engineered perfect cube, the $100,000 Rand logo trying too hard to be friendly) is its symptom, and the iMac is the second attempt that only the failed first choice makes possible. He grounds this in Kant's Critique of Pure Reason—the antinomies and the phenomenon/noumenon distinction that Hegel radicalized into a world driven by oppositions—finding the dialectic everywhere in Jobs: two sets of parents, orchards and Silicon Valley, 'Apple' as both high-tech and organic, and a childish lowercase signature made with grand cursive flair.

7.title: Dracula and Philosophy
7.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Dracula's century-long grip on popular culture says more about us than about the Count, asking why we willingly seek out an evening of nightmares in Stoker's novel and its movie spin-offs when, as Van Helsing's failures show, Dracula just cannot be killed. It frames the volume's guiding questions: is Dracula truly evil, is his taste for human blood really worse than our meat-eating, and what does our fascination with this outdated, oddly accented aristocrat expose hidden in our own subconscious?

9.title: Dracula and Philosophy
9.relation: Mahon argues that vampiric immortality is a curse not because it brings decrepitude (against Swift's Struldbruggs model, since Dracula and his brides keep eternal youth) but because intelligent vampires know endless boredom awaits: following Bernard Williams and Shelly Kagan, boredom replaces death as the inevitable evil, giving vampires a Heideggerian 'being-toward-undeath' and 'being-toward-endless-pain'. Dracula's risky move from castle, brides, and slaves in Transylvania to London is read as the boredom escape it is, and since vampires still resist destruction, Mahon weighs the tedium curse against the alternative curse of compelled psychopathic bloodlust, concluding that staking Dracula is involuntary euthanasia - a mercy killing.

10.title: Dracula and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Pramik maps Kierkegaard's three stages from Either/Or and Stages on Life's Way onto the novel: Dracula lives the aesthetic stage of pleasure and possessive power (imprisoning Harker in the castle, refusing to let the brides feed on him), Harker the anxious ethical stage of moral rules and guilt, and Van Helsing the religious stage of faith 'by virtue of the absurd' - trusting God to do the impossible through crucifixes, garlic, and the beheading of Lucy. Against Seward's doubting questions about these absurd tactics, she argues that Van Helsing's renewed, tested faith proves itself and makes him the book's real hero, since neither pleasure nor ethics alone defeats Dracula or gives life meaning.

11.title: Dracula and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Willis and Strunk read the scene where Dracula forces Mina to drink blood from his bare chest through Plotinus's Enneads: the mutual blood exchange is a dark unicity, a perverted oneness joining life and death, through which the soulless, blood-dependent Count tries to steal Mina's agency, Intellect, and her link to the world soul because he cannot be self-sufficient or create his own meaning. Their interconnected minds are also his undoing - Mina's hypnotic bond tracks Dracula to his coffin, and his destruction at Van Helsing's hands frees her - so the chapter concludes that this perversion of Plotinian oneness exposes our fear that the veil between the living and the dead is dangerously thin.

12.title: Dracula and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Jordan asks what makes Dracula obey his rules (no entry without an invitation, native soil, garlic, the crucifix) when he obeys no morality: self-imposed Kantian moral rules and a vampire-cabal enforcing Hohfeldian duties both fail because the Count's self-interest is too strong, so the rules must be natural law set by God or nature. He then uses Wesley Hohfeld's jural relations (duty, claim, liberty, power, immunity, liability, disability) to analyze Dracula's rule over his brides, servants, and victims - Lucy's lost consent shifting power and letting the Count through her door - concluding that only this legal-relations analysis plus natural law explains both Dracula's restraints and his apparent violations of physics like defying gravity and commanding the weather.

13.title: Dracula and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Arp starts from Dracula's inability to love or find satisfaction and his awareness of it, then deploys Sidgwick's hedonistic paradox: pursuing pleasure for its own sake yields pain whether or not the pleasure is found, through mistaking pain for pleasure (Lestat on the dead twins), boredom, or emptiness. Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures explains how vampires can enjoy the bodily pleasure of blood yet lament lacking joy and love, while substance versus property dualism (Plato as the substance dualist) frames whether the Count's soul survives when his body crumbles to dust. Aristotle's Book X pleasures of completed states and the 'virtuous vampires' from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain show the only escape from the dilemma: pursue activities for their own sake and higher mental pleasures rather than bodily pleasure alone.

14.title: Dracula and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Dracula and Philosophy.md

15.title: Dracula and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Littmann turns vampirism into a thought experiment against meat-eating, using Jonathan's delight in the Hotel Royale chicken as the double standard: every justification for the Count preying on humans - might makes right, his superior intelligence and cunning, an arbitrary threshold of cleverness, or the human soul and its afterlife - would equally license beings superior to us (supernaturally strong, centuries-cunning Dracula himself) to prey on humans. Following Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', he argues the real wrong of vampirism is the net suffering it creates, and this utilitarian standard equally condemns factory farming, pushing us toward humanely raised meat or vegetarianism.

16.title: Dracula and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.

17.title: Dracula and Philosophy
17.relation: Bowman argues through Arendt that Dracula is not inherently evil but thoughtless: like Eichmann he cannot think from another's standpoint, treats people as cogs and means (Harker as captive, humans as prey), uses violence as a constructive tool, and protects himself with rhetorical safeguards like 'Enter freely' so he need never face his own cruelty. Measured against the Crew of Light's thoughtfulness - Harker's memos and recipes for Mina, Mina's care for Lucy, the suitors' gentlemanly bonds - the Count's evil is banal, lazy, 'Evil Lite'; but because Dracula stands outside humanity and knows humans only as livestock, Bowman concludes that Eichmann is banal yet truly evil, while Dracula, though careless, can never be evil.

18.title: Dracula and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.

19.title: Dracula and Philosophy
19.relation: Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.

21.title: Dracula and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
21.relation: McKinney argues Van Helsing should have studied Dracula's brain instead of staking him, because the Count is a philosophy-of-mind thought experiment: a mind that persists unchanged across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes mind-brain identity theory and fits functionalism (the mind as one song playable in many formats), while his telepathic bond with Mina and shapeshifting probe Cartesian dualism's mind-body interaction problem. Nagel's bats show that only Dracula could tell us what it is like to echo-locate or wolf-sense; yet since nothing like his unconstrained mind exists in our world, the novel finally maps what minds are not - evidence against the immaterial mind.

22.title: Dracula and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Dracula and Philosophy.md
22.relation: McCrossin uses Locke's memory theory of personal identity - consciousness extending to past and future actions, with 'all the right and justice of reward and punishment' founded in it - to ask whether Dracula is a monster but still a person, illustrated by an imagined Quincey-Seward body swap where only the mind that remembers the deed deserves blame. Mina, midway between human and vampire and fearing for her own future personhood, supplies the empathy and pity ('that poor soul') that turn the crew's campaign into one of mercy - they weep and grant the Count a peaceful death - adding a sentimental middle ground that Locke's claim that morality is demonstrable like mathematics cannot account for.

23.title: Dracula and Philosophy
23.relation: Wolfe asks what makes Stoker's mustachioed Count, Lugosi's, Dell Comics' science-hero Dracula, The Electric Company's malt-drinker, Blade's Drake, and Hotel Transylvania's overprotective dad all 'Dracula'. Plato's theory of Forms promises a shared ideal essence, but comparing particulars (origins from Vlad Tepes to Judas Iscariot, blood-drinking vs vanilla malts) finds no common thread, his 'Allegory of Dracula's Dungeon' recasts the cave to suggest Dracula may be only a shadow of some other Form like 'the undead', and the Republic's condemnation of art as imitation of imitation implies a fictional character may have no Form at all. Wolfe's own answer: the ideal Dracula is an outsider, an aristocrat, and a feeder on others, with everything else up for grabs.

24.title: Dracula and Philosophy
24.relation: Richard Greene uses Dracula's transformations (man, bat, wolf, mist, and human-to-vampire) plus Vlad the Impaler's ordinary aging to pose the puzzle of persistence: the claims of consistency, change, and persistence cannot all be true together. He raises the justice objection to mereological essentialism (if any change made Vlad a new person, imprisoning him would punish someone else) and then tests endurantism (wholly present with time-indexed properties), perdurantism (temporal parts), and exdurantism (temporal counterparts) against the Count. He concludes endurantism best captures the intuition that one and the same guy was first human and later vampire.

25.title: Dracula and Philosophy
25.relation: Versteeg and Barkman use Dracula's shapeshifting to stage Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': even if the Count becomes a bat, whatever he recalls afterward is filtered back through his human-ness, so no non-bat can access bat-ness from a human point of view. A scene of Van Helsing and bat-Dracula both finding a girl's corpse distinguishes objective from subjective experience. Because physicalism predicts all of reality should be objectively accessible, the impenetrability of subjective experience pressures physicalism and leaves room for the immaterial soul Van Helsing's religion wants.

26.title: Dracula and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Dracula and Philosophy.md

27.title: Dracula and Philosophy
27.relation: Karavitis applies Walter Benjamin's 'Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' to his own deflated re-reading of Dracula: mass reproduction stripped the novel of its ritual aura, and film (stage Lugosi versus screen Lugosi) made art analyzable, political, and economically driven. He reads Stoker's epistolary form and Mina's surviving transcription - the originals destroyed - as heralding a postmodern world where every viewpoint is equally valid, so each reader's gaze (feminist, Marxist, Blacula, Count Chocula) remakes the Count. A closing dialectic moves from passive contemplation (thesis) through critical reading (antithesis) to readers becoming authors themselves (synthesis).

28.title: Dracula and Philosophy
28.relation: De Waal reads Dracula through Judith Butler's gender performativity: the Count terrifies because he 'does' gender wrong - a captor who cooks and mothers Jonathan like an 'angel in the house,' feeds Mina from his breast, and turns Lucy from Victorian maiden into wanton vamp. Harker as a 'dude in distress,' Van Helsing's hysteria, and the Dracula-Mina scene that 'opens new orifices' become parodies exposing gender as an incessant citation of copies. The hunters' 'sterilizing' of Dracula's boxes of earth is read against the eugenics movement and society's police function against gender-nonconforming people.

29.title: Dracula and Philosophy
29.relation: Tim Jones uses Jung's Shadow to argue Dracula is the British Empire's Shadow Self: everything the Count does in Britain - draining resources, reshaping native identities - mirrors what Britain does abroad, minus the benevolent veneer, while Ego-projection explains why Harker's crew must annihilate him rather than admit what he reflects. The chapter adds that colonial stereotypes became self-fulfilling, with colonized peoples made to live the imposed identities, and reads the era's reverse-invasion fiction (mummies, The War of the Worlds) as a collective staking of the Shadow. It closes by recommending Jungian ownership of the Shadow instead of projection.

30.title: Dracula and Philosophy
30.relation: Pötzsch reads Dracula through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the Count fascinates because he lives out the aggression and sexual freedom civilization forces us to renounce, embodying the innate hostility in Freud's 'man is the wolf to man.' Freud's account - group power replacing individual might, 'love thy neighbor' as an impossible demand, the super-ego as an inner Van Helsing breeding guilt over forbidden impulses, with the id and ego mediating - is mapped onto Jonathan's 'wicked, burning desire' for the vampire women. The upshot: we resent culture because we traded happiness for security, yet living like Dracula would get our throats cut.

31.title: Dracula and Philosophy
31.relation: Callis reads the 1931 Lugosi film through Jung: Dracula is Mina's Shadow archetype and animus, embodying her repressed fear of sexuality and of the married life she claims to want, while the vampire's presence in every culture places him in the collective unconscious. Mina's arc - the Call to Adventure, crossing the threshold into Dracula's embrace, and 'resurrection' after his staking - becomes a Shero's Journey of confronting the shadow, with Dracula also playing the Shapeshifter archetype. The chapter ends doubting the happy ending, asking whether Mina defeated her shadow or merely surrendered her dreams of freedom.

33.title: Dracula and Philosophy
33.relation: Karavitis fabricates a recovered 'Dracula's Journal' in which the Count retells Stoker's plot as rational self-interest: he owes no one anything, Lucy 'came to me of her own free will,' Van Helsing's crew are a 'craven collective' spouting 'from each according to his ability,' and only objective reality - not their subjective feelings - counts. He claims a fundamental right to pursue his own happiness, casting himself as the thinking individual crushed by proletarian herd morality. An editor's framing email makes the point explicit: Rand-style egoism could justify even Dracula, a 'manual for vampires' set against Marx's collectivism.

34.title: Dracula and Philosophy
34.relation: In imaginary letters, Meursault of Camus's The Stranger describes his meaning-free life, his trial that condemned his refusal to perform feelings, and his death-row move from indifference to acceptance of the absurd, then inducts Dracula into Camus's gallery of absurd heroes beside Don Juan, Don Quixote, and Sisyphus - those who reject suicide, reject help from higher powers, and accept life's absurdity. Dracula accepts the first two traits but categorically rejects despairing acceptance, claiming love and conquest instead. An appendix lets Sisyphus himself grumble that Camus finding happiness in boulder-pushing is the real absurdity.

35.title: Dracula and Philosophy
35.relation: Ketcham's invented chronicle sends Dracula and a village rabbi to 1194 Cairo to interrogate Maimonides: can resurrection - one of the thirteen principles of faith - apply to a soulless undead being, and is his blood-drinking a divinely imposed penance? Maimonides answers from the Guide for the Perplexed and the Letter on Resurrection, offering that intelligence is the essence of the soul yet judging the Count a likely trickster, while Dracula presses that no scientific evidence of dust becoming flesh exists. The diarist closes with the heretical worry that Maimonidean resurrection - no food, drink, or sex - might itself be a kind of undeath.

36.title: Dracula and Philosophy
36.relation: Sexton's mock FBI COMPIC file stages a Cold War reading of Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein: screenwriters Lees and Rinaldo remake Dracula as Marx's Das Kapital vampire - capital as dead labour sucking living labour - so blood-draining becomes profit-draining and 'This man belongs to me!' the capitalist's claim on his workers. A fictional Ayn Rand review for HUAC decodes the film as collectivist propaganda that slanders the businessman McDougal and dreams of a creature with 'no will of his own,' touching Marxian alienation along the way. A final note links screenwriter Robert Lees's blacklisting by Sterling Hayden and his real-life decapitation to Stoker's vampire-killing instructions.

7.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
7.file: ch07 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
7.relation: Using 'Flowers for Charlie', where a placebo pill convinces two scientists and even the Waitress that Charlie has become a genius, the chapter asks what actually makes something philosophy. Sounding smart is not philosophy: big words, the Sokal-style hoax paper submitted to a leading journal, and the 'Guru Effect' of credulous admirers all fail, yet Charlie's pronouncements turn out true by sheer luck - which is exactly Edmund Gettier's problem of epistemic luck illustrated with the broken-clock example. Since we can never verify our premises or our reasoning, the chapter sides with Aristotle's response to Plato's theory of forms that we can never determine what a thing is, only what it is not, and concludes the show is philosophical precisely because the Gang is the exact antithesis of reality, truth, and right action.

8.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
8.file: ch08 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md

9.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
9.relation: Greg Littmann systematically compares the Gang's values - wealth, attention, bad-assery ('Project Badass'), sexual conquest, relentless competition, revenge, pride in cheating, and callousness toward even friends and family - with the values Homer's Iliad and Odyssey celebrate, showing Achilles and Odysseus behave like the Gang: sacking cities, taking women as war trophies like Briseis, boasting of deception (the Trojan Horse), and rigging the funeral games. The real difference is scope: the heroes honor bonds of loyalty to comrades, family, and their own communities where the Gang is loyal to no one, and moderns extend concern further still. Yet our morals fail the same way when people are far enough removed - we tolerate homelessness, prison rape, sweatshop goods, and national glory-seeking - so the chapter pleads for the universal moral principles Greek moral philosophy first sought against Homeric values.

10.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Jason Iuliano reads the Gang's 'no restrictions' motto as egoistic hedonism in the tradition of Aristippus of Cyrene: pleasure alone is intrinsically good, and specifically present, bodily, personal pleasure - exactly how Mac defends his fifty-pound weight gain and the pair's decision to smoke crack. The doctrine is shown in action through the Gang's treatment of Rickety Cricket, used as a mere instrument while his life is ruined without a flicker of guilt, and through get-rich-quick schemes from the impulse-bought boat to running for comptroller purely for the bribe. Robert Nozick's Experience Machine then shows why hedonism fails - we want to actually do things, be a certain kind of person, and touch reality, not float as an 'indeterminate blob' - and Mill's paradox of hedonism explains the Gang's misery: pursuing pleasure directly is precisely what drives it away.

11.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Christopher Ketcham's mock lost episode 'Charlie Gets Beatified' - in which Frank fakes a water-into-wine miracle with red food dye so the Gang can monetize Charlie's canonization - frames a genuine exercise in medieval modal metaphysics. Aristotle's definition of contingency, on which opposites can occur only at different times, is set against Duns Scotus's view that something can be otherwise at the very moment it acts, so that God's immutable foreknowledge coexists with a will 'endowed with something of his own freedom'. The chapter spells out necessity, contingency, and impossibility in possible-worlds terms (a gang needs at least two members in every world; Frank is impossible in Season One) and reads 'Gun Fever Too: Still Hot' as empirical confirmation of Scotus and Olivi: the Gang holds opposite positions within a single episode, proving real contingency and free will.

12.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md

13.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Charlene Elsby asks what makes the McPoyles cross the line from offensive (like the Gang) into irredeemably creepy, working through their bathrobes, unibrows, incest, and constant milk drinking. Her answer runs through violated social convention: the creepy person is not merely making non-standard choices but seems unaware conventions exist at all, and Liam's 'It's society that has the problem' raises moral relativism only for the chapter to insist the creep reaction tracks something actually wrong, not just different. Adding the legacy of physiognomy (we judge character from appearance, and more harshly when the trait is controllable) and an inductive inference (everything the McPoyles do is creepy, so even the milk must be), creepiness emerges as an art of detection rather than a science: whether someone is creepy differs from whether they seem creepy.

14.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Daniel Leonard takes CharDee MacDennis, the Gang's three-level drinking game, as an unconscious confession read through Freud's structural model. The 'Mind' level - grudge trivia like 'Denis is asshole. Why Charlie hate?' and drawing-guessing 'based solely on feel' - runs on the id and the pleasure principle; the 'Body' level of darts, kennels, and the no-cursing rule is restraint, properly the ego's job of deferring gratification (which only Dennis's manipulative D.E.N.N.I.S. System grotesquely exercises); and the 'Spirit' level of Emotional Battery and Public Humiliation externalizes the superego's guilt and ego-ideal, with Frank as the all-seeing punishing father. The Gang's psychology is backwards - their 'Mind' level tests exactly what is not conscious - and their over-strong superegos surface in rationalization and the Black Card's coin flip, while smashing the losers' idealized game pieces enacts a wishful symbolic patricide.

15.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Charlotte Knowles tests each Gang member against Heidegger's Being and Time: getting lost in the averageness of what 'they' do (das Man) is inauthenticity, but authenticity is not freakish uniqueness - Charlie's milk-steak, magnets, and bird-law delusions are unconventional without being authentic - rather a transformed relation to everyday roles in which one endorses the life one leads. Frank partly passes, having chosen squalor and owning it ('I'm going to get really weird with it'), yet unknowingly lives out Rambo as a cultural script; Dee consciously performs the Sex and the City script; Dennis is ruled by beauty norms (make-up, girdle, chemical peel); and Mac, despite the tough talk, is Frank's 'follower' hiding his relationship with Carmen. The upshot is that authenticity and inauthenticity are matters of degree, never either/or, and are not moral verdicts - Dennis could be an authentic rapist - so the Gang's norm-defiance does not make them authentic, bitches.

16.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md

17.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
17.relation: Kyle Alkema and Adam Barkman ask what would make the Gang happy and answer with Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness is long-run flourishing built on virtuous habits, with the golden mean (courage between cowardice and recklessness) as the rule for choice. The Gang instead lives a 'Reverse Virtue Ethic' - trying extremes first by crude trial and error, like sniffing gasoline to check that it is gasoline - along three roads: quick money (welfare crack scams, robbing their own parents' house), lust (the D.E.N.N.I.S. System's seduce-and-abandon script, where Dennis cheerfully accepts the charge of sociopathy), and validation ('You're not gay, you're just really, really vain'). Their residual Catholicism supplies consciences and limits - Mac's talk of God smiting them, confession, fears of Hell - but no reasoned morality, leaving them trapped in 'one day at a time' gratification as reverse role models.

18.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Adam Henschke argues that Frank Reynolds, of all people, is a role model - not a virtuous man overall, but virtuous in one structural sense. Using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, each Gang member's project is diagnosed as the vice of excessive self-delusion: Charlie's Waitress obsession he cannot see through even at her musical rejection, Dee's acting stardom she will not work for and that ends in suicide-adjacent despair, Mac's muscle-bound self-image despite 'diabitis', and Dennis's Golden God delusion culminating in 'the implication' and his car stash of 'fetish shit'. Rickety Cricket embodies the opposite vice, total loss of the capacity to imagine oneself otherwise (via Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy), and Frank charts the Aristotelian mean between the two - he rejected his delusive country-club life, knows exactly what he chose with Roxy, and his plans succeed where the Gang's fail - making 'What would Frank do?' a genuine exercise of practical wisdom.

19.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
19.relation: Roger Hunt answers 'what do philosophers do?' through Dennis's seduction methodology. Frank embodies empiricism, leaving the comfort of principle for the messiness of the world as Hume did when he found no impression of causation, space, or time; Mac embodies rationalism, reasoning with total confidence from a principle he cannot doubt, as Descartes did from the cogito; and the dialectic of Socrates and Plato, questioning beliefs in dialogue to see what survives scrutiny, describes philosophy as it is actually practiced. Boethius's Consolation - the imprisoned author consoled by dialogues with Lady Philosophy - supplies the frame of philosophy as an encounter with a woman one pursues, and each D.E.N.N.I.S. step maps onto the craft: Demonstrating value to the problem, Engaging physically in its awkward grind, Nurturing dependence through thesis panic, Neglect and Inspiring hope on the road to the defense, then Separating entirely - 'be a sociopath about it.'

20.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md

21.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Tim Aylsworth uses Dennis's boat speech - women will not refuse him 'because of the implication' that things might go wrong for them out on the open ocean - to build the necessary and sufficient conditions of sexual consent. Working through Gang cases (Dee and the high-schooler, Lil' Kev the apparently intellectually disabled boyfriend, the Waitress's MDMA black-out asking 'Did you rape me last night?', Dennis's milky negotiation with Margaret McPoyle while held hostage), the chapter argues that a 'yes' counts as consent only when given by fully-informed, competent moral agents in a context where they can freely express their genuine preferences. The upshot vindicates Mac's 'sounds like these women don't want to have sex with you': a fear-induced yes is no consent, as with the prisoner and the boss's secretary, because the woman's genuine preference is not to face that choice at all.

22.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Ethan Chambers asks whether we should pardon the Gang, arguing with Hume that their vices have a 'causal story' as rigid as physical law: Charlie's glue-sniffing, racism, and inability to connect trace to a Christmas Day childhood of squalor and Uncle Jack's abuse; Mac was bullied as 'Ronnie the Rat' for trying to be good and never once saw virtue pay in Philadelphia; Dennis, shaped by Frank's cruel parenting, claims and shows he cannot feel feelings, so Humean sympathy - the key moral sense - is simply beyond his reach; and Frank's 'donkey brains' asylum childhood or outright insanity directly undermines his responsibility. Knowing these psychological causes, sympathy (Hume's word for empathy) replaces blame: we blame the builders, not the house, and the chapter closes by urging compassionate rehabilitation over the show's never-ending circle of punishment and revenge.

23.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
23.relation: Skyler King uses the Gang's inheritance war over their dead mother's possessions as a metaphor for greed versus need, pressing our duties to those in extreme suffering. Peter Singer's utilitarian argument - prevent bad without sacrificing anything of comparable significance, absolute poverty is bad, therefore we ought to give - makes charity a requirement rather than a nicety, condemning Dennis's luxury purchases and crowning Bruce Mathis, the one character who consistently donates, as the utilitarian exemplar. Nel Noddings's feminist ethics of care counters that we owe help only to those within reach whose good we can see 'completed in the other' - so Mac and Dennis wronged Charlie by refusing him shelter in the recession, but owe nothing to children overseas - and the chapter weighs Dee-style objections that this licenses caring only when inconvenienced, closing with the question 'is it always sunny in your Philadelphia?'

24.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md

25.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Fenner Tanswell uses 'Reynolds vs. Reynolds: The Cereal Defense' - the Gang's in-bar trial over Frank's blind driving versus Dennis's cereal-at-the-wheel - as a catalogue of crooked thinking. We get valid forms distinguished from soundness (modus ponens with 'if poop is funny, then Frank pooped in the bed'; Charlie's modus tollens from Frank's no-donkey-brains certificate), then the fallacies: the argument from ignorance by which Dennis's lacking a certificate proves him donkey-brained, Dee's ad hominem against Mac, Dennis's appeal to authority, and Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' poster, which equivocates between mere skeptical doubt (even Descartes's) and reasonable doubt by straw-manning science as claiming infallibility. True to form, the Gang convicts Dee 'for comedy rather than on any logical basis.'

26.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Russ Hamer takes Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' defense - Aristotle, Galileo, and Newton each proved his predecessor 'a bitch' - and his claim that believing in evolution takes as much faith as belief in God, and answers with philosophy of science. Popper's falsificationism explains why Mac's 'I won't change my mind... regardless of the facts' is the essence of the non-scientific: only theories risking precise, falsifiable predictions (Einstein's light deflection) count as science, unlike vague astrology or Charlie's cherry-picked evidence that the Waitress will love him. Kuhn's distinction of normal and revolutionary science explains why past failures never discredited science - falsifications within a paradigm are tuning, and the Gang's group-configuration trials in 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' are normal science at its best - so revisability is science's strength, not a reason to fear looking like a science bitch.

27.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
27.relation: Martyn Jones stages a fictional Nietzsche telling Mac, Dennis, and Charlie the plot of 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' as a parable of metaphysics gone wrong. Mac and Dennis's scheming is Apollonian - imposing logical order and 'paradigms' on a recalcitrant world - while Charlie is Dionysian, the designated wildcard whose uncontainable energy (sabotaging the van and ripping out the brakes) dooms every plan that tries to harness him, since Apollonian schemes fatally imagine they can contain Dionysian force. Reason is a gloss, not a truth-tracker: like every theology and philosophy it is an expression of will, a survival tool serving selfish ends, so the delusional gas scheme needs no truth to serve its purpose. Charlie alone is praised as a proto-Übermensch - innocent, creative, founding his own values without resentment - and the tale closes musing that even an eternal recurrence of their botched schemes might be willed all over again.

28.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Robert Arp's gallery matches each Gang vice - dishonesty, egoism, selfishness, greed, pettiness, ignorance, laziness - to real-life scumbags from Nixon, Stephen Glass, and Janet Cooke to Charles Ponzi, Bernie Madoff, Crassus, the Empress Dowager Cixi, Imelda Marcos, and the Darwin Awards, and it opens with the chapter's philosophical spine: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from Book II of Plato's Republic, which predicts that even an upstanding person with the power to act unseen would seduce, steal, and murder - exactly the question the Gang's mostly unpunished antics keep staging. Against the ethical egoist's argument that because everyone is self-interested everyone should be (Vanderbilt's 'the public be damned'), the chapter deploys the is-ought point - children are naturally selfish without therefore deserving to be - alongside mothers, Mother Teresa, and 9/11 first responders, concluding that egoism is at most an admixture in every action, with Lord of the Flies as the reductio of universal egoism.

9.relation: The volume's introduction, 'Learning from the Insiders.' It introduces Orange Is the New Black (Piper Kerman's book and the Netflix series about Piper's time in Litchfield) and previews each contributor's topic: other minds, manipulation, the Prisoner's Dilemma, religion, existentialism, race, Crazy Eyes as Don Quixote, prisoners' moral obligations, Nietzsche on a trans woman, Aristotle on friendship, Bentham's panopticon, and Foucault on punishment. 11.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Hoyt argues the show's core lesson is dropping the little lies we tell ourselves: Bennett calls his crush on Daya 'love' to excuse framing Mendez, Pornstache is a man performing a blustering guard (Sartrean bad faith), and Larry and Polly's 'love just happened' dodges responsibility for betrayal. Piper's arc (the Colt 45 scene in '40 Oz. of Furlough') shows the payoff of authenticity, while Healy's Safe Place is a fantasy that cannot will a change of worldview. Using Wittgenstein's aspect-seeing from Philosophical Investigations, he shows how characters and viewers miss ethically significant meanings, like Taystee's shower 'compliment' as intimidation and Piper's convenient blindness to Soso's humanity when selling her for a blanket.

12.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.

13.file: ch13 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md

14.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
14.relation: DiEdoardo, a trans criminal-defense lawyer, reads Sophia Burset through Nietzsche: her 'why of life' (bringing her body into line with her gender identity) lets her endure the 'how' of misgendering by Figueroa, Red, and her wife Crystal, plus a sentencing disparity she compares to Piper's lighter drug deal. Burset's rational appeals ('Lesbian Request Denied,' her WAC run) fail, confirming Nietzsche's disdain for dialectics, but in 'A Whole Other Hole' she stops asking and acts, teaching the inmates vulval anatomy until Taystee's 'she's right' marks her acceptance. She is the 'creator' who breaks the tables of values, migrating from freak to woman with unique knowledge.

15.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Carveth examines African-American portrayal on the show through Piper, Taystee, and Sophia: Piper's whiteness wins Healy's favoritism and makes her complicit in keeping the inmates powerless ('we understand each other, don't we?'), while Taystee's parole violation shows Litchfield as the only place she fits. Using Lippmann's account of media stereotypes, he credits the show with multidimensional characters of color but faults it for a 'white voice': Black women's incarceration is framed as bad choices and culture of poverty, and only Piper's SHU suffering is shown while Black and Latina women cycle through it. The series critiques the prison system yet stops short of showing the structural forces that leave its inmates no options.

16.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md

17.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
17.relation: Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.

18.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.

19.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md

20.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Stephenson and Waller start from disliking bland, marketable Piper and use Foucault's Discipline and Punish to argue that Litchfield is a microcosm of State power: arbitrary unwritten rules, counts, strip searches, and constant surveillance train prisoners into docile, compliant participants in capitalism, with specialist wardens, psychologists, and lawyers molding the abnormal into the normal. Prisoners specialize too (Red's kitchen, Nicky's ear, Vee's drugs) to survive, and specialization hides the surveillance. The show itself embodies the mechanism, making viewers aware they too live under the Panopticon, though deviants like Crazy Eyes and her standing pee keep open the possibility of refusing State values.

21.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.

22.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md

23.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
23.relation: Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.

24.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.

25.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md

26.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Archibald casts Crazy Eyes as the show's Don Quixote, read through Descartes's Meditations: like Descartes ridding himself of conditioned false beliefs, Suzanne slaps her head to 'reset' and question everything, and like Quixote she blames an inner evil enchanter when her noble illusions collapse. Her rationalist imagination (chivalry, poetry, Piper as her Dulcinea) produces false beliefs that hurt, above all her devoted service to the manipulative Vee, yet the same faculty creates the beauty, coping, and nobility that make an ugly prison survivable, so truth may not be all that matters.

27.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
27.relation: Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.

28.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md

29.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.

30.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
30.relation: Elsby and Luzecky use Nicomachean Ethics VIII to sort Litchfield's bonds: Red's kitchen empire runs on friendships of utility that dissolve when her pipeline closes, race pre-assigns everyone's default friends, and Vee, who sleeps with RJ before having him killed, is incapable of friendship in any sense. The chapter locates genuine Aristotelian friendship only in Red's concern that Nicky stay off heroin (wishing her good for her own sake) and reads Red's sparing of Vee, held by a plastic bag, as respect without care, the recognition of a kindred quality that distinguishes Red from her evil counterpart.

31.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
31.relation: Greene reconstructs the Prisoner's Dilemma with Pennsatucky and Vee in separate interrogation rooms, then maps a variant onto 'Thirsty Bird': whatever Alex does, Piper is better off testifying against Kubra, yet mutual silence was the group-rational outcome the two pact on the van ride. Alex defects anyway, leaving Piper with perjury and no leniency, and Greene argues Piper should have done the 'rational' thing, since Balik's revenge is only a threat while extra time in Litchfield is a certain harm and Alex has always been willing to screw her. The episode shows why honor among the self-interested fails without trust.

32.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
32.file: ch32 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
32.relation: The editors' appendix, 'Sugar and Spice and Some Things Not So Nice!,' argues that part of the show's success is our cultural obsession with women-in-prison stories, from the film Caged to tabloid celebrity mugshots. It then catalogues famous imprisoned women from history and today: Marie Antoinette and Eleanor of Aquitaine under house arrest, Elizabeth Bathory and Joan of Arc in castle towers, the Salem witches, Patty Hearst, Billie Holiday and Martha Stewart at Alderson, Pussy Riot in Russian penal colonies, Aileen Wuornos, and the Tower of London's Anne Boleyn and Anne Askew. The survey supplies the real history behind the women-in-prison genre that Litchfield reworks, with no single philosopher or theory applied.

7.title: Once More into the Time Vortex
7.file: ch07 - Once More into the Time Vortex.md
7.relation: The editors' introduction: it surveys what changed since the first Doctor Who and Philosophy volume (the War Doctor, the Trenzalore death and survival, the Impossible Girl, Dalek divine hatred, the Master becoming 'the Mistress') and previews the volume's questions—whether Clara is possible, whether the Doctor may lie, whether he could have avoided Trenzalore, and whether the Ninth Doctor's 'coward, any day' pacifism gave way to the Twelfth's less-pacifistic cowboy streak. It also introduces the fandom insiders (podcasters, convention runners, a Time Lord Rock musician) who serve as 'Time Lord Presiding' over each Serial, framing the book around the show's emphasis on personal identity and time paradoxes.

8.title: Serial 1 The Real Never-Ending Story
8.file: ch08 - Serial 1 The Real Never-Ending Story.md

9.title: Magnetic North
9.relation: Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.

10.title: 1. A Good Man Goes to War
10.file: ch10 - 1. A Good Man Goes to War.md
10.relation: Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.

11.title: 2. How Time Lords Invented TV
11.file: ch11 - 2. How Time Lords Invented TV.md
11.relation: Dray reads Doctor Who as a metaphor for television itself: the Doctor and his box emerge from a junkyard just after FCC chairman Newton Minow called TV a 'vast wasteland,' and the show turns the medium's supposed weaknesses—shaky effects, departing actors, budget limits—into its fiction, most famously converting William Hartnell's failing health into regeneration. Following 'An Unearthly Child' through the cancellation-era New Adventures novels, the flawed 1996 TV movie, and the Davies and Moffat eras (including Amy literally believing the erased Doctor back into existence in 'The Big Bang'), he argues television's iterative, audience-entangled, endlessly rewritable nature is the show's real subject. The TARDIS, 'bigger on the inside,' is television itself, and 'The Day of the Doctor' celebrates a medium that can remake the old anew—self-interrogating its own dangers in stories like 'The Idiot's Lantern' and 'Bad Wolf.'

12.title: 3. The Mystical Alchemy of “Midnight”
12.file: ch12 - 3. The Mystical Alchemy of “Midnight”.md
12.relation: Sas uses literary alchemy's three-stage magnum opus to read 'Midnight' as the nigredo—the black stage of dissolution that begins the Tenth Doctor's arc of purification, death, and rebirth ending in his regeneration in 'The End of Time.' She shows Russell T Davies loading the episode with nigredo imagery: the deadly Xtonic sunlight that calcinates bodies to ash, the planet of endless 'midnight' and witching-hour folklore, the Salem-style mob panic modeled on The Crucible as the mimicking Sky drives the passengers to demand a sacrificial victim, and the Doctor stripped of TARDIS, companion Donna, authority, and finally his voice. The Doctor's humbling—he solves nothing and is saved only by the Hostess's self-sacrifice—purges the ego that later swells into 'Time Lord Victorious,' while his reunion with the fiery Donna foreshadows the alchemical fusion of the DoctorDonna and eventual rebirth.

13.title: 4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl
13.file: ch13 - 4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl.md
13.relation: Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.

14.title: 5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion
14.file: ch14 - 5. Every Lonely Monster Needs a Companion.md
14.relation: Gadsden asks why a near-omnipotent Time Lord needs companions at all and tests four hypotheses against his solo meltdowns—executing Solomon in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship,' nearly murdering Jex in 'A Town Called Mercy,' and declaring himself 'Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars.' He rejects the Lord Acton power-corrupts hypothesis via Glaucon's ring story in Plato's Republic, since powerless companions offer no threat of reprisal or dishonor, and qualifies J.J. Sylvia's care-ethics 'empathetic link' because the Doctor cares for non-human species like the Star Whale too. He favors two answers: Hume's fact/value gap as a millennium-long moral myopia ('I can't see it anymore,' the deleted 'Flesh and Stone' confession), and Aristotle's point in the Nicomachean Ethics that only virtuous friends—moral peers who mirror us—can expose the Doctor's blind spots, like his 'God Complex.'

15.title: Serial 2 Mind-Bending Impossibility-Shattering Jammie Dodgers
15.file: ch15 - Serial 2 Mind-Bending Impossibility-Shattering Jammie Dodgers.md

16.title: You’re Fantastic!
16.file: ch16 - You’re Fantastic!.md
16.relation: Viguié's Serial 2 preface argues the show's ultimate philosophy is 'you're fantastic': the Doctor takes people yearning for something more—Rose the shop girl becoming Bad Wolf, Rory becoming the Last Centurion, Donna the temp becoming in a way the Doctor herself—and actualizes potential they never believed they had. He applies the lesson to his own life, describing how the show's belief in untapped human potential pushed him from a soul-sucking job to creating his Doctor Geek's Laboratory STEM-outreach audio show and Science Fair, urging readers to answer the Doctor's call and live up to what the Fourth Doctor called our 'inventive, invincible, indomitable' species' promise.

17.title: 6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds
17.file: ch17 - 6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds.md
17.relation: Sutton argues the causal loops of 'Blink' and 'The Angels Take Manhattan' need not destroy libertarian free will: the Doctor's claim that a known future is 'written in stone' conflates ordinary foreknowledge, which leaves agents free to make the knower wrong, with infallible knowledge that only exists because the act occurs. Adapting Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to free choices, he shows how branching timelines let the Doctor read Melody Malone, decline to break River's wrist, and still close the loop—some parallel Doctor does what the book records—while Aristotle's future contingents in De Interpretatione secure the indeterminacy of what 'will' happen. Answering the objection that branch-splitting is really fatalism, he appeals to the subjective viewpoint (what matters is 'my me'), explains how Kathy and Billy's messages in 'Blink' reach Sally on at least one branch, and solves why the Doctor is always so lucky: we follow the one branch where he survives.

18.title: 7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change
18.file: ch18 - 7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change.md
18.relation: Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'

19.title: 8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore
19.file: ch19 - 8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore.md
19.relation: Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.

20.title: 9. How the Doctor Knows
20.relation: Smithka argues the Doctor is a reliabilist about knowledge rather than a Cartesian strong foundationalist: using 'Amy's Choice,' 'The Beast Below' (the glass of water, the engine room, Amy's inference that the Star Whale came willingly), 'Silence in the Library' (the chicken-leg experiment implicating the Vashta Nerada), and Davros's Dalek trials in 'Genesis of the Daleks,' she shows him trusting perception in the right causal chain and reasoning inductively and abductively—Peirce's inference to the best explanation—instead of demanding Cartesian certainty.
