7.title: Red Rising and Philosophy
7.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.

8.title: I. Conundrums for the Quality Control Board
8.file: ch08 - I. Conundrums for the Quality Control Board.md

9.title: 1. When Evolution Strikes Back
9.relation: Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.

10.title: 2. Not So Human After All
10.file: ch10 - 2. Not So Human After All.md
10.relation: Brendan Shea takes the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species (Homo flameus versus Homo sapiens) seriously and tests it first against Aristotle's essentialism—species fixed by necessary properties, complete with the doctrine of natural slaves—and then against three modern species concepts (Mayr's interbreeding criterion, the phylogenetic common-ancestry view, and the ecological-niche view), showing each gives the Jackal ambiguous or inconvenient verdicts, from sterile Pinks to horizontal gene transfer. He concludes with Peter Singer that moral equality never depended on equal intelligence or strength: Reds have interests just as Golds do, so enslaving them would be wrong even if Adrius were right about the biology. The deeper lesson is that the Jackal reasoned backwards from his commitment to Gold rule, finding whatever differences his prejudice needed—a warning against 'discovering' biological support for pre-existing biases.

11.title: 3. Hero or Villain
11.file: ch11 - 3. Hero or Villain.md
11.relation: Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.

12.title: 4. Raising Darrow
12.file: ch12 - 4. Raising Darrow.md
12.relation: Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.

13.title: 5. The One, the Only, Darrow
13.file: ch13 - 5. The One, the Only, Darrow.md
13.relation: Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.

14.title: II. Searching for Eo’s Dream
14.file: ch14 - II. Searching for Eo’s Dream.md

15.title: 6. Driven by Love to Go to War
15.file: ch15 - 6. Driven by Love to Go to War.md
15.relation: John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.

16.title: 7. Being for Red
16.file: ch16 - 7. Being for Red.md
16.relation: Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.

17.title: 8. Living for More
17.relation: Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.

18.title: III. To Live or Not to Live in the Society
18.file: ch18 - III. To Live or Not to Live in the Society.md

19.title: 9. Pierce’s Republic
19.relation: Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.

20.title: 10. Virtue Rising
20.relation: Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.

21.title: 11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies
21.file: ch21 - 11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies.md
21.relation: Devon Brickhouse-Bryson asks whether the Society, plainly dystopian with respect to justice, might nonetheless be utopian with respect to beauty. Treating a society as an abstract object—a system of persons ordered into a community, not reducible to its members or its gravBoots and razors—and beauty as harmoniousness, the ordering of parts into a unified whole in the tradition of Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hutcheson, he shows the Color system straightforwardly instantiates that definition, each caste an organ of one well-functioning clock. But the harmony holds only if the castes are genuinely teleologically distinct; if that is mere Gold propaganda, the Society is not beautiful but a cacophony. Either way the chapter's real lesson stands against Plato: identifying justice with each part fulfilling its role conflates beauty with justice, and the Society shows how radically the two can come apart—possibly beautiful and radically unjust at once.

22.title: 12. The Law of Red Rising
22.file: ch22 - 12. The Law of Red Rising.md
22.relation: Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.

23.title: IV. The Rising and Beyond
23.file: ch23 - IV. The Rising and Beyond.md

24.title: 13. Mustang’s Future Generations
24.relation: Courtland Lewis asks what Mustang owes future generations when rebuilding the Society, first showing that standard moral theories stall: nonexistent people lack rationality, cannot contract, cannot be treated virtuously, and utilitarian forecasting fails since we cannot know whether the Jackal's nuking of Luna might have led, in the deep future, to prosperity. Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons then strikes: any policy choice creates a different future generation, total utility drives the Repugnant Conclusion (a maximally populous world of barely-worth-living lives, uncomfortably like the Society's Reds), and average utility yields the mere addition paradox (Mustang's Society is both no worse off and worse off when Andromeda's low-pleasure civilization is added). The chapter's solution is Rawls: the original position behind the veil of ignorance—where the Sovereign would not know she is a Gold—yields justice as fairness and maximin reasoning for the just savings problem, choosing to save more than is consumed; against Tim Mulgan's objection that this loops back to the Repugnant Conclusion, Lewis answers that real carrying capacities make the repugnant world impossible.

25.title: 14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors
25.file: ch25 - 14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors.md
25.relation: Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.

26.title: 15. Death Begets Death
26.file: ch26 - 15. Death Begets Death.md
26.relation: The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'

27.title: 16. Can We All Get Along
27.file: ch27 - 16. Can We All Get Along.md
27.relation: Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.

8.title: Invitation to Initiation
8.relation: A short introduction that opens with the 'Hardhome' scene where Stannis tells Sam Tarly to 'keep reading' after learning from an old manuscript that dragonglass kills White Walkers, arguing that knowledge is itself a weapon in Westeros. Chaillan promises that the volume's philosophers ('Maester Kant on the King's Road,' 'Lord Machiavelli' in the Red Keep, Kierkegaard on Stannis) will initiate fans into the show's philosophical depth, from whether it is immoral to watch its violence to whether the Red Wedding can be justified.

10.title: I. Life Is Not a Song
10.file: ch10 - I. Life Is Not a Song.md

11.title: 1. Arya Stark as a Rough Hero
11.file: ch11 - 1. Arya Stark as a Rough Hero.md
11.relation: Dadlez asks whether Game of Thrones is morally defective for making audiences root for Arya Stark, a child murderer whose victims run from the insurance seller in Braavos to Walder Frey and his sons baked into a pie. Working through Hume's 'rough heroes' worry from 'Of the Standard of Taste' against Anne Eaton's 'robust immoralism' and the halo effect, she argues Martin's text never endorses Arya's killings but shows their cost to her - her suppression of doubt before the soup-shop assassination, her nightmare repetition of the names on her kill list, her reclaiming of 'Arya Stark of Winterfell' - so our investment is empathetic concern rather than corrupting approval, and the story is not ethically flawed.

12.title: 2. Ned Stark One Man in Ten Thousand
12.file: ch12 - 2. Ned Stark One Man in Ten Thousand.md
12.relation: Kirby reads Ned Stark's arc through Aristotle's Poetics: his excessive honor is a hamartia ('too much of a good thing'), his acceptance of Robert's summons and refusal of Renly's help and Littlefinger's plan are the peripeteia, and the fan mourning after 'Baelor' is catharsis binding viewers into a community. With Martha Nussbaum's work on Greek tragedy he then argues the series' deepest lesson is tragic conflict - Agamemnon sacrificing Iphigenia mirrored by Stannis and Shireen, and Maester Aemon's 'love is the death of duty' warning to Jon - where no hierarchy of values dissolves the moral residue, so we must suffer into learning instead of trusting philosophical prioritization.

13.title: 3. There’s Only One God and His Name Is Death
13.file: ch13 - 3. There’s Only One God and His Name Is Death.md
13.relation: McKeever observes that central characters rarely die suddenly and unexpectedly in art even though such deaths define our emotional lives, and argues this is a 'representational limit of art,' like Hollywood ugliness and costume-drama archaic speech. Using Plato's theory of art as a copy of a copy (a picture of Tyrion's chipped goblet imitating the Form of the goblet) and Aristotle's catharsis, he then argues Martin overcomes the limit through epic scale: with so many viewpoint characters, Ned can die at the end of season one and Joffrey mid-season-four because attention simply shifts, so making a work epic is the general cure for what art cannot represent.

14.title: 4. Tyrion’s Humor
14.file: ch14 - 4. Tyrion’s Humor.md
14.relation: Hietalahti reads Tyrion's wit - slapping Joffrey, his mock confession at the Eyrie, the dwarf-jester show at the Purple Wedding - through the classic theories of humor: Kant and Kierkegaard's incongruity, the Platonic-Hobbesian superiority laugh, and Freud's hidden hostility. Against those who see only a jester, he argues Tyrion's humor is social criticism grounded in what Erich Fromm calls affirmation of life: unlike the Joker, who laughs because nothing matters, Tyrion mocks hollow ritual, sham trials, and gods who want enemies burned because everyone matters, and having lost everything in A Dance with Dragons he still refuses the poisonous 'sweet death,' holding that life itself is worth living.

15.title: II. There Are No Men Like Me, Only Me
15.file: ch15 - II. There Are No Men Like Me, Only Me.md

16.title: 5. Guilty of Being a Dwarf
16.file: ch16 - 5. Guilty of Being a Dwarf.md
16.relation: Engels runs Tyrion's arc through Sartre's existentialism: his facticity as a dwarf makes everyone from Catelyn to Tywin presume his guilt, while 'Never forget what you are, wear it like armor' states the Sartrean authenticity of owning facticity while freely choosing one's essence. Catelyn's dagger accusation, the comic confession at the Eyrie, the wildfire ship at Blackwater, and the trial outburst ('I am guilty of a far more monstrous crime: the crime of being a dwarf') show him choosing rather than being defined; the murders of Shae and Tywin dramatize the slide into bad faith - embracing the 'monster' essence others assigned - before his choice to join Daenerys resumes the burden of self-creation.

17.title: 6. Jaime the Savior
17.relation: The Coxes defend Jaime's kingslaying with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Book III on voluntary, involuntary, and 'mixed' actions: like a storm-besieged crew jettisoning cargo, or the Blackfish's 'a knife to his throat is not a valid order,' Jaime faced a duress - kill Tywin on Aerys's order or let King's Landing burn - so his regicide was a mixed action that is praiseworthy as the least harmful option rather than blameworthy. They add Locke's right of revolution, where a ruler who makes his will rather than law the rule puts himself in a state of war with his people, to argue the Mad King's 'Burn them all' tyranny justified the killing, making the reviled Kingslayer the savior of the city.

18.title: 7. Jon Snow, a Misshapen Christ Figure
18.file: ch18 - 7. Jon Snow, a Misshapen Christ Figure.md
18.relation: Rosa argues Westeros is a moral wasteland stripped of exemplars - heroes die, and vice spreads by imitation, as with Joffrey, Ramsay, and the Mountain - so Jon Snow functions as the series' Christ figure: the humble hidden king revealed in Bran's vision, the reformer uniting wildlings and Watch against death, killed by his brothers in 'Mother's Mercy' and risen in 'Home.' Using Aristotle's virtue ethics - Bran's archery lesson as the image of eudaimonia, hamartia as missing the mark, character formed by watching and imitating exemplars like Ned at the deserter's execution - the chapter claims the world is redeemable only through 'minority moral reform' embodied in a complete life, as with Jesus, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.

19.title: 8. Brienne and the Struggle for Recognition
19.file: ch19 - 8. Brienne and the Struggle for Recognition.md
19.relation: Giladi reads Brienne as a challenge to the Westerosi recognition order: winning the melee at Renly's camp and requesting the Kingsguard, she embodies knightly virtue in a society that deems it naturally male, and the crowd's bewildered, muted applause is a recognition injustice that withholds the social conditions of her self-confidence and authenticity. He analyzes Jaime's mockery in 'The Prince of Winterfell' - sexualizing her as 'boring as you are ugly' where he would never treat Barristan Selmy so - as stripping Brienne of her status as a conversational peer and equal rational enquirer, while the attempted gang-rape by Locke's men in 'Walk of Punishment' shows the violent backlash her struggle for recognition provokes.

21.title: 9. Varys’s Riddle—Where Does Power Come From
21.file: ch21 - 9. Varys’s Riddle—Where Does Power Come From.md
21.relation: Iuliano uses Varys's riddle - king, priest, and rich man each bidding the same sellsword to kill the others - and 'power resides where men believe it resides' to stage a contest between John Austin's command theory of law (sovereign orders backed by force) and H.L.A. Hart's The Concept of Law, where authority rests on social acceptance. Cersei's 'power is power' scene with Littlefinger shows obedience that is mere coercion - Hart's gunman, being obliged rather than obligated - making the Lannisters gunmen writ large; the Hound's walkout on Joffrey exposes the illusion collapsing, and Plato's cave explains why Westerosi smallfolk prefer the comforting shadow to the truth that would free them.

22.title: 10. How to Be Free
22.file: ch22 - 10. How to Be Free.md
22.relation: O'Connell and Sirvent argue Seneca's Stoic freedom - release from fear of death and from every attachment - illuminates the two most enslaved groups in the story. The Unsullied's training strips them of possessions, names, lust, and fear, with Grey Worm's shame at fearing death for Missandei's sake showing exactly what attachment does to this freedom, while the Faceless Men's 'valar morghulis' mantra works like Seneca's recommended contemplation of death, letting Arya drink blindly from the cup at the House of Black and White. The chapter concludes that a fearlessness built by slaves and assassins really is a kind of freedom beyond their servitude, though Seneca would recoil at the brutal methods that produce it.

23.title: 11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due
23.file: ch23 - 11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due.md
23.relation: Ewing argues money is the real determinant of the Iron Throne: Lannister gold made Cersei queen, Tyrell grain and taxation bought Margaery's crown, Baelish's financing decided the Battle of the Bastards, and the Iron Bank disciplines kings. Reading Westeros as a late-feudal economy through Marx - smallfolk whose work and taxes support lords who 'reap where they never sowed,' a hierarchy held by coercion and fear as the High Sparrow tells Olenna ('You are the few, we are the many'), and money dissolving feudal bonds into a 'money aristocracy' - he predicts the throne will go not to dragons or White Walkers but to the capitalist-financier figure of Petyr Baelish.

24.title: 12. Margaery for Queen!
24.relation: Jones asks whether Margaery - who grooms Tommen, admits she was 'good at seeming good,' and may count as an abuser despite Westeros's norms - could still have been the best queen in the Seven Kingdoms. Against the prosecution's portrait of a cold egoist, he argues her charity to Flea Bottom's children shows a queen is good by what she does rather than why she did it, so selfish ambition welded to shrewdness can genuinely serve the common good. Comparing her with Ramsay (cruelty that provokes revolt) and Ned (benevolence without calculation that gets him killed), the chapter draws an implicitly Machiavellian conclusion - the people's best bet is hunger for power joined to the cunning to keep them onside - while doubting that cultural relativism can fully excuse her treatment of Tommen.

25.title: 13. Bran, Hodor, and Disability in Westeros
25.file: ch25 - 13. Bran, Hodor, and Disability in Westeros.md
25.relation: Pierce uses Westeros's many disabled characters - Bran's paralysis, Jaime's lost hand, Hodor, Aemon's blindness, Varys and Theon's castration - to test the medical and social models of disability and the 'mere difference' view, asking whether disability is merely unaccommodated impairment or intrinsically worse for the one who has it. With the left-handedness analogy and the distinction between local and global harm, he then pits Aristotle's natural teleology (legs are for walking and eyes for seeing, so their loss is a real local bad) against Lucretius's Epicurean anti-teleology (no purposes in nature, so no intrinsic lack), concluding that even if disabilities are locally bad, Bran, Hodor, and Varys can be globally flourishing and heroic.

26.title: IV. The Things I Do for Love
26.file: ch26 - IV. The Things I Do for Love.md

27.title: 14. The Gods Hate Incest
27.relation: Barkman defends the near-universal Westerosi condemnation of incest. Against Freud's Oedipal account - which Jaime and Cersei's childhood romance seems to fit - he deploys Edward Westermarck's aversion hypothesis, primate evidence, and the Taiwanese simpua-marriage studies to argue that co-raised siblings should feel natural sexual aversion, so the twins are either instinctually malformed or unconvincingly written, while cases like Black Walder and Littlefinger with Sansa fit the effect fine. He then grounds the taboo in Natural Law - deduced from 'do no harm,' care of the weak, and natural family roles, plus the harms of inbreeding and endogamy - and concludes that children of incest like Joffrey are abominations by choice, not by birth.

28.title: 15. Joffrey on the Couch
28.relation: Wills asks why audiences so relish hating Joffrey and answers with Freud's Totem and Taboo: the incest taboo was instituted precisely because the desire persists in the unconscious, and Joffrey - the product of 'accumulative incest' with cousin-grandparents and sibling parents - embodies the broken taboo. Reading the furious fan reactions (his death 'wasn't horrible enough,' the meticulous lists of his worst acts) as projection and successful repression, the chapter argues that vilifying Joffrey channels our own repressed taboo-breaking urges, while Westeros's distanced past setting lets us dissociate from the savagery exactly as Freud's staging of primitive peoples did.

29.title: 16. Hope for Bastards and Sand Snakes
29.file: ch29 - 16. Hope for Bastards and Sand Snakes.md
29.relation: Desveaux argues the hidden organizing concept of Game of Thrones is filiation - the legal system that transmits family belonging, name, status, and destiny. Sigils and house colors (the blond Lannister children as visible evidence of incest), Ned's law-enforcing beheading of the deserter, and the nature-names of bastards - Snow in the North, Sand in Dorne - all display its force: Jon's authenticity and open-mindedness come from standing outside it, Ramsay's legitimization after the Red Wedding and the Sand Snakes' Dornish independence mark its exceptions, while whores and smallfolk beyond all filiation have no protection at all, a contrast the chapter uses to measure how far modern law has removed these penalties.

30.title: 17. Sex, Consent, and Rape in Westeros
30.file: ch30 - 17. Sex, Consent, and Rape in Westeros.md
30.relation: Underwood distinguishes the legal consent of fifteenth-century-style Westeros - under the conjugal-debt doctrine neither Drogo nor Ramsay legally raped their wives, while every Cersei-Jaime union was treasonous regardless of desire - from the moral standard of consent developed from Alan Wertheimer's work. Applying his fraud and disregard cases, she argues Sansa's marriage obtained through Littlefinger's deception and Daenerys's coerced early nights with Drogo are immoral though legal, and proposes 'reciprocal subjectivity' as the criterion: Ramsay treats Sansa purely as an object, but the scene at Joffrey's body shows Jaime raping Cersei while still loving her as a subject, proving mutual recognition is necessary yet not sufficient for morally permissible sex.

31.title: V. I Swear before the Old Gods and the New
31.file: ch31 - V. I Swear before the Old Gods and the New.md

32.title: 18. Gods and Beetles
32.relation: Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies. Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'

33.title: 19. Prophetic Foreknowledge in Game of Thrones
33.file: ch33 - 19. Prophetic Foreknowledge in Game of Thrones.md
33.relation: Rennick argues that true prophecy threatens no one's freedom: a true prophecy merely reports the future the way a true history book reports the past - Jojen sees Jon among the wildlings because Jon chose as he chose, not the reverse - while fallible, misread prophecies (Melisandre mistaking Alys Karstark for Arya, the Stallion prophecy dying with Rhaego) constrain even less. Self-fulfilling prophecies like Azor Ahai actually demonstrate agency, since Stannis and Melisandre's belief in the prophecy brings the events about, and even infallible foreknowledge of a choice - 'you will watch season seven' - leaves open the alternate Westeros where you did otherwise, the standard reply to the God's-foreknowledge problem applied to green dreams and flames.

34.title: 20. Cersei, Sansa, and the Problem of Evil
34.file: ch34 - 20. Cersei, Sansa, and the Problem of Evil.md
34.relation: McCrossin reads Cersei and Sansa's post-imprisonment rises in season six as opposite answers to the problem of evil, framed by Susan Neiman's claim that Enlightenment thought split between making evil intelligible and refusing to. Cersei, taught by Tywin that 'the gods have no mercy - that's why they're gods,' becomes Sade's cruel god of Juliette, doing whatever feels good as the gods do; Sansa, hardened by Ramsay and Littlefinger's betrayal into 'no one can protect anyone,' embodies the Kantian response that virtue and happiness come apart, so one governs only what can be controlled - character, family, justice - as she engineers the Battle of the Bastards and has Ramsay eaten by his dogs without mercy or vengeance.

35.title: 21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero
35.file: ch35 - 21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero.md
35.relation: Devlin asks whether Stannis, who burns Shireen to save his army, is Kierkegaard's knight of faith or merely a tragic hero. Stannis's duty-obsessed deontology - knighting Davos while cutting off his fingertips, striking 'beloved brother' from a letter as a lie - is Kantian, and the Shireen dilemma looks like Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical; yet because Stannis always calculates and justifies ('Faith? In a real war, the side with the greater number wins nine times out of ten'), he never makes the leap on the strength of the absurd, and Davos ends up following Kant's own verdict on Abraham: 'If he commands you to burn children, your lord is evil.' He is therefore a tragic hero in the line of Agamemnon and Jephthah, rationally comprehensible and fittingly undone by Brienne's 'do your duty.'

36.title: 22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy
36.file: ch36 - 22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy.md
36.relation: Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.

38.title: 23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles
38.file: ch38 - 23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles.md
38.relation: Baldwin asks whether Westerosi characters can know anything inductive in a world without lawlike nature: seasons of unpredictable length, wargs in animal minds, Faceless Men changing faces, and resurrections by Thoros, Melisandre, and Qyburn. After laying out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge (those who saw the pyre are justified in believing Dany is the mother of dragons; those relying on rumor are not), he runs Hume's problem of induction - we never perceive causal connection, so no jar of wildfire must explode - against Reid's common-sense reply that reason and induction stand or fall together, concluding that Westeros gives its people special reasons for skepticism while we, lacking evidence of magical irregularity, are rational to trust everyday inductive belief.

39.title: 24. Samwell Tarly’s Renaissance
39.relation: Alves reads Westeros as a technologically stagnant society where knowledge is hoarded by monopolies - the Maesters' Citadel chain links and the Alchemists' wildfire secret - and asks what Samwell Tarly's library discoveries at Castle Black plus his battlefield experience with dragonglass against the White Walkers add up to. Arguing that empiricism - observation and experiment against the dubious authority of old texts, the mix that birthed modern science out of alchemy and astrology (with Mircea Eliade and even Newton as border cases) - is exactly what Sam practices, the chapter suggests he is igniting a Westerosi renaissance of lost Valyrian-age knowledge, while the Doom of Valyria warns, like Prometheus and Babel, against knowing too much.

40.title: 25. Should Catelyn Have Trusted Brienne
40.file: ch40 - 25. Should Catelyn Have Trusted Brienne.md
40.relation: McNabb and Andrews ask whether Catelyn was warranted in trusting Brienne as her sworn sword after Brienne failed to save Renly, and test two theories of warrant. On accessibilist coherentism, Catelyn's accessible evidence - Brienne's prowess, her devastation at Renly's death, 'Renly's death was no fault of yours' - fits her web of beliefs like a new strand in a spider's web; on Plantinga-style proper functionalism, illustrated by the accident-created Labman replica and the Lord of Light randomizing a design plan, Catelyn's naturally formed belief that Brienne is trustworthy is warranted if her faculties are properly functioning, truth-aimed, and well designed - which Brienne's record through rescuing Sansa vindicates.

41.title: VII. You Think I Would Trade My Honor
41.file: ch41 - VII. You Think I Would Trade My Honor.md

42.title: 26. Horrifying Violence, Gratuitous Sex, and the Truth
42.file: ch42 - 26. Horrifying Violence, Gratuitous Sex, and the Truth.md
42.relation: Silverman concedes Game of Thrones can be watched viciously - sadistically relishing Theon's flaying or using it as soft pornography - but denies the show is inherently immoral. From Plato's Republic he takes the test of whether a narrative serves or obscures reality (Socrates was executed partly on the slander of Aristophanes' Clouds) and argues the show is honest where epics lie: war is ugly and kills innocents, measured against the Augustinian just-war criteria that even the Brotherhood Without Banners decays past; humans really are as sexually preoccupied as Plato's appetitive soul, Freud's id, or Augustine's original sin; and honor without practical wisdom - Ned versus Tyrion on Aristotle's ideal - is a recipe for ruin.

43.title: 27. Was the Red Wedding Massacre a Good Thing
43.file: ch43 - 27. Was the Red Wedding Massacre a Good Thing.md
43.relation: Van der Deijl takes Tywin's line to Tyrion - 'explain to me why it is more noble to kill ten thousand men in battle than a dozen at dinner' - as a serious consequentialist challenge about the Red Wedding. Working through utilitarianism, prioritarianism, and dirty-hands cases like Hiroshima and shooting down a hijacked plane, he concedes the massacre could have been justified had breaking Guest Right and killing 3,500 brought peace at minimal cost; but the consequences fail - Joffrey and Roose Bolton keep power, the institution of guest right erodes, and Tywin's real motive was family power rather than the greater good - so the massacre fails even the consequentialist test, and Tywin is a power-hungry conspirator, not Machiavelli's prince.

44.title: 28. Severed Heads, Dirty Hands
44.relation: Ivanković and Božac argue that ruling Westeros necessarily means dirtying one's hands, staging the paradox through Varys's counsel to Ned and Jaime's 'finest act.' Hobbes supplies the baseline that anything preserving peace beats the war of all against all, Walzer permits dirty hands only to avert communal death (Daenerys swindling the Astapor slavers), and Kant's absolute refusal to lie - mirrored in Ned's honor - costs Ned his head and the realm a war. The chapter also indicts the reverse: Aemon's refusal of the throne and other too-clean refusals of responsibility are moral failures, Jon's killing of Qhorin Halfhand shows dirty hands are not just for kings, and rulers must resist the downward spiral while keeping, as Dany does, a gentle heart for the true goal.

45.title: 29. The Best of Friends
45.relation: Geyer sorts Game of Thrones friendships by Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics. Robert and Ned's bond, formed in Jon Arryn's fosterage and shared war, is friendship of pleasure, which frays over Rhaegar's 'dragonspawn'; Tyrion and Bronn is friendship of utility, dissolving exactly as Aristotle predicts when Lollys's marriage pays better than a trial by combat in 'Mockingbird'; and Jon and Sam, each valuing the other's character for its own sake at the Wall, approach the only true friendship - the virtue friendship - supporting the claim that eudaimonia needs such relationships alongside external goods.

46.title: 30. Trying to Do Good with Arya, Tyrion, and the Hound
46.file: ch46 - 30. Trying to Do Good with Arya, Tyrion, and the Hound.md
46.relation: Thomas sets Aristotle's practical wisdom against Bentham's utility calculus and Kant's consequence-proof rules, then watches all three struggle in season six. Arya's merciful refusal to poison Lady Crane backfires when the Waif kills her more painfully anyway; Tyrion's compromise with the Masters - phasing out slavery gradually, 'I trust their self-interest' - nearly loses Meereen when they attack by sea; and the resurrected Hound, after Brother Ray's massacre, concludes that 'lots of horrible shit in this world gets done for something larger than ourselves,' so being good in Westeros, as everywhere, means choosing without being able to know the consequences in advance.

47.title: 31. Paying the Iron Price
47.relation: Hansberger reads Theon's return to the Iron Islands as an Aristotelian failure of virtue: excess lust toward Yara on the road, the 'small soul' of gold-bought jewelry where Balon demands iron-price honor, and the rashness rather than courage of trying to hold Winterfell with twenty men. But Balon's virtues are the vices of a piratical society that rewards reaving and rape, and through Charles Taylor's ethics of authenticity the chapter argues Theon's deeper failure is not knowing who he is - Stark or Greyjoy - so Ramsay's breaking of him into Reek completes a collapse of self that began at home; authenticity, it concludes, depends on virtue and social relations, which is why Theon can only begin to recover by choosing to serve Yara.

50.title: Lineages and Histories of the Great Maesters
50.file: ch50 - Lineages and Histories of the Great Maesters.md

10.title: It Was a Dark and Philosophical Night
10.file: ch10 - It Was a Dark and Philosophical Night.md
10.relation: The editors' playful introduction stages the Peanuts gang together with Socrates, Plato, Descartes, Hume, Nietzsche, Wittgenstein, and Sartre at a Paris sidewalk cafe on the eve of Snoopy's dogfight with the Red Baron. It previews the seventeen essays' territory - the meaning of Christmas, kite-eating trees, the Great Pumpkin, baseball, critical thinking, induction, existence, happiness, virtue, friendship, ethics, and aesthetics - with the wink that to the kids it all sounds like 'Mwaa mwaa mwaa.'

11.title: I. Happiness Is a Warm Existence
11.file: ch11 - I. Happiness Is a Warm Existence.md

12.title: 1. Charlie’s Eternal Quest for the Little Red-Haired Girl
12.file: ch12 - 1. Charlie’s Eternal Quest for the Little Red-Haired Girl.md
12.relation: The chapter reads Charlie Brown's lifelong, unconsummated longing for the never-seen Little Red-Haired Girl as a quest narrative without closure: like Beckett's Vladimir and Estragon he cannot act, and like Camus's Sisyphus he is an absurd hero whose dignity lies in persisting (the 2,120 lunch hours, the losing team, the pulled football) without reward. Using Lacan's account of desire - the wish for the Other's recognition, suspended between the demand for need and the demand for love - it argues Schulz keeps her invisible (except one 1998 silhouette) precisely so Charlie's desire stays in permanent suspension, like a Hitchcock MacGuffin. The closing section attacks The Peanuts Movie (2015) for betraying this existential vision: by showing the girl, rewarding Charlie with a kiss, and swapping Sisyphean defiance for 'believe in yourself' truisms, it delivers Sisyphus from his rock and so kills what made him admirable.

13.title: 2. 3eanuts and the Existential Schulz
13.file: ch13 - 2. 3eanuts and the Existential Schulz.md
13.relation: The chapter introduces existentialism and reads Peanuts through it: Charlie Brown's defeats expose the 'groundlessness' of value, and the 3eanuts web project (deleting each strip's final gag panel) restores the despair that punchlines normally defuse. It explains Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' and the ideal of authenticity versus passively inhabiting roles, Heidegger's care and Dasein (even in despair there is an inner place where it happens), and Camus's absurd and Sisyphus revolting against a fate he cannot change. Lucy's hillside sermon ('WELL, LIVE IN IT, THEN!') and the final image of Charlie running at the football figure his revolt: he keeps kicking because in that moment a world without boxes exists in him.

14.title: 3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy
14.file: ch14 - 3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy.md
14.relation: The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.

15.title: II. Good Ol’ Metaphysics
15.file: ch15 - II. Good Ol’ Metaphysics.md

16.title: 4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown
16.file: ch16 - 4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown.md
16.relation: Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.

17.title: 5. Rhapsody on a Theme by Schroeder
17.file: ch17 - 5. Rhapsody on a Theme by Schroeder.md
17.relation: The chapter argues Schroeder's monomaniacal devotion to his toy piano and Beethoven is a Nietzschean way of life: he refuses the herd's path and the self-denying 'priestly' values of ordinary childhood, and treats music as the highest creative force, as The Birth of Tragedy claims. Nietzsche's demon of eternal recurrence becomes a test Schroeder passes - he lives for this life and could will its exact repetition - while Schopenhauer backs the claim that music discloses the world's inner nature as language cannot, and the Christmas-dance scene shows the communal fusion Nietzsche heard in song and dance. Strips about Lucy on the piano, his 'grown accustomed to that face' shock when she moves away, and the Beethoven's-birthday holiday cast Lucy as his unsuspecting muse; but as a would-be Ubermensch he must go beyond playing Beethoven and create his own compositions.

18.title: 6. Anti-Psychiatric Help 5¢—The Doctor is IN
18.file: ch18 - 6. Anti-Psychiatric Help 5¢—The Doctor is IN.md
18.relation: The chapter takes Lucy's five-cent psychiatry booth as a parody that vindicates the anti-psychiatry movement's three core criticisms: an abusive doctor-patient power relation (her insults, the threat of the stool, the football gag), ineffective or harmful treatment ('Snap out of it! Five cents, please'), and the impossibility of objective mental diagnosis (Thomas Szasz, the DSM's tangled history, Big Pharma's over-prescription). Foucault's History of Madness grounds the point that madness and psychiatric expertise are historically shifting social categories rather than neutral science. Lucy's accidental mindfulness-style advice and Charlie's 'existential depression' (Yalom's death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness) point toward alternatives, and the closing thought is that Charlie's willingness to voice his sadness destigmatizes getting help.

19.title: III. How Good Is Grief
19.file: ch19 - III. How Good Is Grief.md

20.title: 7. Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of a Warm Blanket
20.file: ch20 - 7. Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of a Warm Blanket.md
20.relation: The chapter explains Linus's blanket via Winnicott's transitional objects, then argues the gang's wider habits - Great Pumpkin taboos, baseball fetishes and rituals - are 'magical thinking' that manufactures an illusion of control over an uncertain world. A middle section tours the mind-body problem (Hippocrates, Descartes's dualism and pineal gland, Huxley's epiphenomenalism, Searle's emergent consciousness) to ask who is really doing the reading. The fallacies section dissects Linus's unfalsifiable Pumpkin doctrine (post hoc after the taboo-breaking 'if') and Charlie's confirmation bias, before reframing his 'pantophobia' as Kierkegaardian angst and Sartrean nausea: with adults reduced to 'Mwaa mwaa mwaa,' the kids are condemned to be free.

21.title: 8. For Hume the Ball Tolls!
21.file: ch21 - 8. For Hume the Ball Tolls!.md
21.relation: The chapter argues Charlie Brown's repeated falls for Lucy's football gag are failures of induction: given the history of the gag since 1951 (first with Violet, then Lucy's fake reasons each fall - a handshake, a contract, a hundred million dollars), he should draw the meta-level conclusion that she will always pull the ball away. It then tries Hume's problem of induction as his defense, but since that would cost him all knowledge of the external world (that Snoopy is a beagle, that Lucy is mean) and end in skepticism, Charlie - a student of his world, not a doubter of it - cannot take it. The verdict: he is not a blockhead but determined and committed, willing to lose every fall because kicking that ball would be worth it, as in the 1979 hospital strip where he finally gets his kick and still ends up on his back.

22.title: 9. I Hate Reasons!
22.file: ch22 - 9. I Hate Reasons!.md
22.relation: The chapter uses Lucy's worst lectures - birds don't fly south, the wearing-down of the Earth, the telephone-pole tree, piano-career statistics she admits she made up - to catalog adult critical-thinking failures: motivated reasoning, fallacious appeals to authority, suppressed evidence, post hoc, and appeal to superstition, with the kindergarten cast letting us laugh at our own practices without defensiveness. It then argues, with Kant and W.K. Clifford, that we owe each other more than not lying: we owe others assertions backed by evidence, since Lucy's fabricated numbers could crush Schroeder's dream of a musical career just as vaccine misinformation costs society herd immunity. Lucy's vice is a want of intellectual honesty and humility - she wants to know things, but wants to know them now.

23.title: 10. Does Snoopy Dream of Electric Sheep
23.file: ch23 - 10. Does Snoopy Dream of Electric Sheep.md
23.relation: Reading Snoopy through animal studies, the chapter sets Descartes's 'nature's machines' doctrine - animals as mindless, soulless property without rights - against Charlie Brown's attempts to keep his dog in his place, and shows how Snoopy's endless slippage between plain dog (stealing hats, begging at dinner, dragging Linus by the blanket) and near-human (reading publisher letters, typing novels, serving as Charlie's attorney) collapses the human/animal boundary. The kids' anxiety about his agency, and Snoopy's own gloomy 'I'm less than human,' show the hierarchy being internalized - yet a dog thinking about his inferiority already blurs it. When Snoopy hands Charlie his collar, the chapter reads it as a refusal of property status and proof that being human is a performance of gestures rather than an essence.

25.title: 11. The Sincerity of St. Linus
25.file: ch25 - 11. The Sincerity of St. Linus.md
25.relation: The chapter argues Linus confuses sincere faith with indubitable certainty: on the Thomistic model (faith as chosen propositional belief held with knowledge-like certainty, between opinion and knowledge), his fateful slip into 'if the Great Pumpkin comes' wrecks his faith, turning doubt into hypocrisy. Against this it deploys doxastic involuntarism - we cannot simply choose to believe, as his failed attempts to psych himself up ('I believed with every fiber of my being') show - and philosophers like Daniel Howard-Snyder who allow faith without belief: what Linus does, staying in the patch and risking hypothermia and ridicule while doubting, is faith as action in the face of doubt. Hence the closing paradox: where there is certainty there is no room for faith, and Linus's patch only became sincere once doubt crept in.

26.title: 12. Aaugh! Why Is Being Moral So Hard
26.file: ch26 - 12. Aaugh! Why Is Being Moral So Hard.md
26.relation: The chapter claims Schulz's humor is built on moral failure and illustrates the three main moral theories with specific strips: utilitarianism via Bentham's 'sovereign masters' of pain and pleasure and Charlie's 'to make others happy' (with Lucy noting nobody is making her happy), Kantian deontology via Sally's crayon lie and Snoopy's 'I haven't bitten anyone on the leg recently' as fulfilling a negative duty, and Aristotle's virtue ethics via the failed steal of home (foolhardy rather than courageous), the unmailed Valentine (cowardly), the golden mean, and Joe Shlabotnik as a hopeless role model. Charlie gritting his teeth shows mistaking a virtue's external markers for the virtue itself. It concludes we fit none of the theories well, yet Peanuts keeps a spirit of hope - happiness is a warm puppy, and Charlie's grit is genuine even if he cannot see it.

27.title: 13. Linus’s Wager
27.relation: The chapter stages a three-way debate over whether Linus may believe in the Great Pumpkin without evidence. Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner whose wishful thinking sinks his ship) condemns Linus's sincerity-based wager; Pascal's Wager endorses it (forgoing one night of trick-or-treating costs nothing if the Pumpkin is fake and wins toys if he is real) but assumes a doxastic voluntarism we lack, since no one can make themselves believe for even a million-dollar reward. William James's 'The Will to Believe' gets the final word: if Linus's option is live, forced, and momentous with no decisive evidence either way, his leap of faith - like loving without guarantees - is morally justified whenever life would be greatly impoverished without it.

28.title: 14. Is Lucy a Kantian or Just Mean and Nasty
28.file: ch28 - 14. Is Lucy a Kantian or Just Mean and Nasty.md
28.relation: The chapter tries to acquit Lucy of meanness by reading her as a Kantian: her maxim for throwing Schroeder's piano into the Kite-Eating Tree fails universalization as a contradiction in conception, her blanket confiscations and 'settling for average' lectures enforce Kant's duty of self-improvement, and her brutal truth-telling honors the absolute ban on lying (a Mill-and-Bentham contrast highlights that Kant locates moral worth in intentions, not comfort or consequences). The football gag then undermines the defense: by withholding what Charlie needs to know - that she will pull the ball - she treats him as a mere means, and since what matters is her real intentions rather than her stated ones, the Kantian verdict is left to the reader.

30.title: 15. We’re on Your Side, Charlie Brown
30.file: ch30 - 15. We’re on Your Side, Charlie Brown.md
30.relation: The chapter asks why Charlie Brown never abandons the friends who torment him and answers with friendship philosophy: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship fit the gang (pleasure-based childhood play - baseball, trick-or-treating, Christmas plays - as the nursery for later perfect friendships of good will), while Marilyn Friedman's 'moral growth' and 'moral empiricism' explain how even Lucy's blunt 'snap out of it' gives Charlie perspectives from 'reliable moral witnesses.' Annette Baier's account of trust as accepted vulnerability redeems his 'gullibility': better to risk the pulled football than live in an atmosphere of suspicion. The 'Our Manager' uniform of Charlie Brown's All-Stars and the decorated tiny Christmas tree show that on the things that matter his friends can always be trusted to take his side - and Charlie is always first to forgive.

31.title: 16. European Intellectuals Follow Charlie Brown!
31.file: ch31 - 16. European Intellectuals Follow Charlie Brown!.md
31.relation: The chapter traces how European intellectuals legitimized Peanuts: Eco read the strip as mass culture whose repeated patterns expose a microcosm of the human condition (children warped by industrial civilization, Lucy as contemporary values incarnate), while Bassano di Tufillo finds 'sociable individualism' and, via Bateson and aboriginal spirituality, an ecological vision granting animals, trees, and school buildings equal dignity. It then applies Heidegger's distinction between calculative and reflective thinking to management: Lucy's rigid direction of the Christmas play ('You've got to have respect for your director!') is calculative leadership that treats people as resources, while Charlie Brown's refusal of the All-Stars sponsor - which would have expelled girls and Snoopy - models the authentic, reflective organization that values dignity and diversity over results.

32.title: 17. Linus’s Blanket
32.relation: The chapter reads Linus's blanket through Winnicott's transitional objects: an intermediate area of experience where inner and outer reality stay separate yet related, a defense against anxiety that in healthy development diffuses into art, religion, and philosophy. Linus, stuck with his blanket, turns it into philosophy and prophecy - reciting Luke's nativity under the spotlight, inventing the Great Pumpkin as a private religion - while in You're in Love, Charlie Brown the blanket-less Charlie Brown has no buffer between inner longing and outer world, dissolving into 'nothing' over his peanut-butter sandwiches until the Little Red-Haired Girl's unsigned-name letter becomes a surrogate blanket. The moral for adults: no one person can be the community's lone conscience, for we are all transitional beings, still on the way.

33.title: 18. No End to Philosophy
33.relation: Four vignettes pin philosophical problems to Peanuts' marginal characters: Camus's absurd - caring beings condemned to an uncaring universe - is answered by Sally's School Building, which grows a heart and drops bricks on her enemies; the 95472 kids motivate a tour of personal identity (same soul, same body, memory) through the Ship of Theseus; Pigpen's dirt raises Sartre's bad faith (facticity, transcendence, being-for-others) - we prize his authenticity over cleanliness - and Aristotle's golden mean, which moderates cleanliness while crediting his curiosity as a virtue; and finally the ontology of fictional characters asks whether the Kite-Eating Tree and Red Baron really exist inside the fiction and whether The Peanuts Movie's changed Charlie Brown counts as canon.

8.title: It’s About F $&ing Time
8.relation: Editor Nicolas Michaud's introduction argues Deadpool brings an 'obscene number of philosophical questions'—about mortality, morality, the multiverse, killing, and what separates hero, villain, and asshole—and that only waiting for a movie delayed this book. It proposes that philosophers should be more like Deadpool: honest enough to admit no one knows the answers, willing to look into the abyss, laugh, and jump in anyway, and ready to tell unwelcome truths even if it makes them villains. The tone-setting piece closes with bawdy fourth-wall-style gags about the book being 'better than sex' and unlicensed by Deadpool.

10.title: 1. Breaking Sixteen Walls
10.file: ch10 - 1. Breaking Sixteen Walls.md
10.relation: Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.

11.title: 2. Deadpool the Dark Angel
11.file: ch11 - 2. Deadpool the Dark Angel.md
11.relation: Christopher Ketcham playfully argues that Deadpool's fourth-wall escapes show he exists partly in dimensions we cannot experience, read through string theory's ten curled dimensions and Maimonides's ten realms of angels—beings of form without matter—in the Mishneh Torah. Since only God and angels traverse those hidden dimensions, Deadpool must be an angel, likely a dark one, whose shuttling between realms explains his vacillation between mercenary violence and saving souls. Ezekiel's chariot vision, the vengeful Hebrew Bible God, and massless dark matter are recruited as supporting evidence for this deadpan-earnest science-and-scripture argument.

12.title: 3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!
12.file: ch12 - 3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!.md
12.relation: Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.

13.title: 4. How Much Deadpool Is Too Much Deadpool
13.file: ch13 - 4. How Much Deadpool Is Too Much Deadpool.md
13.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool is entertaining because of, not despite, his excesses: his gratuitous violence and rapid-fire wisecracks breach the disciplined hero ideal, measured against Zeno of Citium's stoic dichotomy of control (accept the torture you cannot change, master your response) and Aristotle's golden mean between deficient and excessive force, which Wade flouts when he savors punishing Ajax instead of finishing quickly. Bakhtin's carnival excess explains the grotesque, orifice-obsessed humor that mocks 'normal' decency, and Derrida's 'internal drifting' (via Poe's Purloined Letter) frames Deadpool's first appearance being FedExed back to sender and his threshold position, where gags spill across comic, game, and film frames—making vigilante justice 'a supplement to the supplement' of law and exposing how each medium works.

15.title: 5. The Anti-Hero’s Journey
15.file: ch15 - 5. The Anti-Hero’s Journey.md
15.relation: Andy Vink applies Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, in the Power of Myth version where heroism is a transformation of consciousness from selfishness to self-sacrifice, to the Duggan-Posehn arc 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly'. Deadpool starts self-centered—demanding pillowcases of money for killing zombie Presidents—is transformed by revelations (Dr. Butler holding his daughter Eleanor hostage, the North Korean mutate experiments echoing his own Weapon X trauma), and ends risking himself to free Butler's sister and the captive mutates and their families. The verdict: Deadpool genuinely becomes a hero by Campbell's test, which is also why, in Campbell's scheme, the hero never gets the girl.

16.title: 6. The Accidental Hero
16.file: ch16 - 6. The Accidental Hero.md
16.relation: Darian Shump judges Deadpool by Buddhist lights, applying karma as intentional action and skillful means—the permissibility of compassionate killing, after Rupert Gethin—to his Marvel NOW! career: protecting Agent Preston, saving a child and Nightcrawler Kim mid-battle, and the Niagara Bride assisted suicide whose fee he donates to a home for kids with cancer. A hypothetical Hydra spy with a bomb on a S.H.I.E.L.D. helicarrier shows how killing one murderer-to-be can be the compassionate act that saves everyone. He concludes Deadpool is an 'accidental hero'—a mercenary first whose good intentions make him a karmic hero—while Zenpool's failed pacifism in AXIS shows that renouncing violence betrays what makes Deadpool Deadpool.

17.title: 7. Why Deadpool Isn’t a Hero (Yet )
17.file: ch17 - 7. Why Deadpool Isn’t a Hero (Yet ).md
17.relation: Matthew Brake maps Deadpool onto Kierkegaard's three spheres (aesthetic, ethical, religious) and argues Wade is stuck in the boundary zone of humor between the ethical and the religious: his comedy sees the contradictions between everyday life and the heroic ideal but revokes suffering in jest, instead of embracing it as essential the way the religious hero does. Spider-Man is the contrast case—wisecracking as the incognito of inner suffering over Uncle Ben and Norman Osborn—while Deadpool's healing factor and knowledge of his own fictionality let him laugh off decapitation ('RESPAWN. LOL') and regress from every heroic step. The chapter ends with Wade's plan to earn heroism in Spider-Man/Deadpool #1 undercut by his taking a contract on Peter Parker.

18.title: 8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be
18.file: ch18 - 8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be.md
18.relation: Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.

20.title: 9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool
20.file: ch20 - 9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool.md
20.relation: Ben Fulman runs Deadpool's decapitations, the T-Ray personality split, and Evil Deadpool—his discarded body parts regenerating together in a dumpster—through the theories of personal identity: Locke's memory continuity, Reid's branching-memory 'Deadpool paradox', Chisholm's essential parts, the Ship of Theseus traced from Heraclitus to Plutarch, and later positions by Sider, Wiggins, Noonan, Grice, and Perry on overlapping memory chains and their circularity. Finding each account strained by Deadpool's cases, the chapter proposes that Deadpool stores his memories in the readers via the fourth wall. His identity over time is thus jointly sustained by the audience—a 'non-personal identity' that ends only when every reader has forgotten him.

21.title: 10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse
21.file: ch21 - 10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse.md
21.relation: Heidi Samuelson argues Deadpool is Camus's absurd hero improved: his origin and his survival of impossible dismemberments embody the absurd as 'disproportion between intention and reality', and facing Camus's one real philosophical problem—suicide—he tries to die via the Hulk to join mistress Death yet must live on, rejecting both actual and 'philosophical' suicide (dogma). His mercenary sense of purpose, jokes in the face of oblivion, and compassion for Blind Al, Weasel, deaf Hawkeye, and Evan exemplify Camus's revolt, freedom, and passion. Sisyphus is the model: like him, Deadpool owns his rock—the healing factor and the killing—and is happy, laughing where Sisyphus is silent.

22.title: 11. Immortality Is Misery
22.file: ch22 - 11. Immortality Is Misery.md
22.relation: In dialogue with Deadpool himself, John Altmann tests whether immortality is a blessing: Bentham's utilitarianism would prize a healing factor that lets Wade dive into a gamma meltdown to save the Southern Hemisphere for free, and Nietzsche would hail him as an Übermensch for refusing the Mithras Directive's Messiah and preserving humanity's freedom to create its own values rather than adopt herd morality. Bernard Williams gets the last word: since personalities become fixed—Wade stays a mercenary across every run, Zenpool notwithstanding—an endless life curdles into boredom and misery, so immortality is punishment rather than power unless one could radically change who one is.

23.title: 12. Only Deadpool Is Sane
23.relation: Chad William Timm argues Deadpool is not really insane but was made 'insane' by power: via Foucault's genealogy of madness, experts like Dr. Brighton (a robotic shell for Psycho Man) at Ravenscroft and Dr. Whitby at Crossmore, along with the courts that institutionalize him after the Hulk trial, run a knowledge/power nexus that labels, sorts, and disciplines him until he internalizes the madman identity ('I think I might actually be crazy'). Nineteenth-century psychiatry's invented link between crime and madness secured the experts' authority, and disciplinary power plus technologies of the self made Deadpool discipline himself. Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe's 'I can see through the bull##$%' and his fourth-wall awareness become resistance to these regimes of truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates's examined life on the reader: be careful whom you tell.

24.title: 13. Weapon X Machina
24.relation: Cole Bowman argues Deadpool is the Marvel Universe's deus ex machina: phenomenologically alienated from a body he treats as a prop (cutting off his own hand to escape Colossus's manacle and flipping the silver behemoth the bird), he can step outside the causal chain the way Leibniz's Primary Truths says any genuinely free agent in a created order must. Sartre supplies the engine—radical freedom against determinism, with She-Hulk's shallow fourth-wall gags (killing the already-dead Porcupine) as bad faith by contrast and Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe as the extreme exercise of freedom against his creators and fans. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy account of the deus ex machina replacing metaphysical consolation frames this new kind of inside-the-story god, who complicates plots rather than conveniently fixing them.

26.title: 14. I’m an X-Man!
26.file: ch26 - 14. I’m an X-Man!.md
26.relation: Daniel Alloy argues Deadpool keeps insisting 'I'm an X-Man!' because being a hero is not a private choice but a social standing: with Aristotle's beast-or-god line about those who cannot live in society and Hegel's account of mutual recognition in the Phenomenology of Spirit, he contends Wade needs heroes he recognizes to recognize him as one in return. The Thunderbolts ('the selfish Avengers') and X-Force recruited him as a merc and so could not grant that recognition, and Cable offers approval from superiority rather than recognition between equals—a friendship of utility where Wade wants one of virtue. Only Captain America's Avengers card treats him as an equal, and even that recognition must be completed by the whole hero community before Wade can accept himself as the hero he already is.

27.title: 15. Good Citizen Deadpool
27.relation: Using Aristotle's Politics, the chapter splits the good man from the good citizen and argues that the Marvel Universe's 'city' needs mercenaries to keep its balance between heroes and villains, as in Deadpool vs Thanos where the In-Betweener steps in when Death is imprisoned and the balance tips toward Chaos. Deadpool's contract killing - hitting Hydra and AIM targets heroes won't touch - fulfills his role in that city, so he can be a good citizen without being a good man, a standard of all-around virtue that Colossus, the 'boy scout' produced by CGI, better fits. The thought experiment of an assassin for 'Deadpooltopia' shows how a dreadful man can still be a good citizen by serving his city's own idea of the good.

28.title: 16. The Beautiful Face Behind the Mask
28.file: ch28 - 16. The Beautiful Face Behind the Mask.md
28.relation: Reading Deadpool through Levinas's Totality and Infinity, the chapter treats his mask and nonstop jokes as the closed totality of an isolated 'I,' and his face-to-face encounters - Siryn touching his scarred head, Vanessa and Mercedes seeing and accepting his face, the dead-shark dialogue, the North Korean clones who share his DNA - as the epiphany of the other that grounds ethics. Levinas's account of murder as denying the other's face explains why Theresa (Siryn) stops Wade from executing Dr. Killebrew, the Weapon X torturer whose eyes showed he regarded Wade as meat. The chapter concludes that Deadpool's face is beautiful as the expression of his inner self, and that living for others rather than for his own (impossible) death is the ethical path he keeps glimpsing.

29.title: 17. Wade Wilson Fights Like a Girl
29.file: ch29 - 17. Wade Wilson Fights Like a Girl.md
29.relation: Staged as a Socratic dialogue in a professor's office, the chapter tests Peter Coogan's definition of the superhero (mission, powers, identity) against the Deadpool movie and finds Wade qualifies while mocking the genre. It then argues the film subverts the superhero genre's sexist conventions: Vanessa refuses the damsel role by grabbing the bar mercenary's crotch and later skewering Francis herself, Angel Dust knocks Colossus out, and Negasonic Teenage Warhead is 'a damsel to the rescue.' Applying Laura Mulvey's male gaze, it shows the camera lingering on Deadpool's body and adopting Vanessa's viewpoint in the Calendar Girl scene, with the Women in Refrigerators trope, Gwen Stacy's death, and the Hawkeye Initiative as evidence of what the movie overturns.
