5.title: Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The
5.file: ch05 - Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The.md

6.title: Introduction Earth’s Mightiest Philosophers
6.relation: Editor Mark D. White introduces the volume: the Avengers fascinate because they are equal parts superhero epic and soap opera, and the contributors' questions mirror that mix. He previews the book's guiding questions—whether Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor embody three different moral philosophies, whether the Kree-Skrull War bears on the ethics of war, why the team keeps admitting reformed criminals like Hawkeye, Quicksilver, and the Scarlet Witch, whether Kang can kill his past self, whether we secretly admire Norman Osborn's Dark Avengers, and whether the android Vision can truly love the Scarlet Witch. It frames the collection but applies no philosophical framework itself.

7.title: Part One What Would an Avenger Do
7.file: ch07 - Part One What Would an Avenger Do.md

8.title: Ethicists Assemble!
8.relation: White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.

9.title: Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers
9.file: ch09 - Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers.md
9.relation: Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.

10.title: Let there be an Ending!
10.file: ch10 - Let there be an Ending!.md
10.relation: Southworth and Tallman ask why fans blame Hank Pym for Ultron's killings while never crediting Magneto for fathering two heroes, and answer with Aristotle's account of character formed by habitual imitation, renewed as 'moral exemplarism': praise and blame track exemplarship, not biology. Scott Lang earned credit because he actively taught Cassie right and wrong, making her the hero Stature; T'Chaka and stepmother Ramonda shaped T'Challa, while Heinrich Zemo's Nazi upbringing warped Helmut into the new Baron Zemo. The Avengers themselves—Cap's patient mentoring of Hawkeye, Stark hiring ex-con Scott Lang—function as moral exemplars for reformed villains, so the mentoring 'parents', not the siring ones, deserve the credit or blame.

11.title: Part Two Who is an Avenger
11.file: ch11 - Part Two Who is an Avenger.md

12.title: Are you the Next Goliath
12.file: ch12 - Are you the Next Goliath.md
12.relation: Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.

13.title: Maybe Jen’s Reading this Chapter Right Now
13.file: ch13 - Maybe Jen’s Reading this Chapter Right Now.md
13.relation: Cook analyzes John Byrne's and Dan Slott's She-Hulk runs as metacomics: Jen breaks the fourth wall to threaten readers into buying her book, deduces how long she was unconscious from comic-book time, steps across the gutter between panels to travel, and even attacks her own creator. Weezie's line 'We're inked and colored! Printed!' raises the problem that once published, the characters' actions are fixed, while her backstory (staying in print to stop aging) exploits comic conventions. The chapter ends by asking whether the Official Handbook's conflicting retcons make Jen's meta-awareness a delusion or a superpower, and what that uncertainty means for truth in metafiction and our understanding of comics storytelling itself.

14.title: Hoist by his Own Petard
14.file: ch14 - Hoist by his Own Petard.md
14.relation: Powell reads Norman Osborn's Dark Reign as a living lesson from Plato's Gorgias and Alcibiades: Osborn's media-staged killing of the Skrull Queen and his hollow rebranding of S.H.I.E.L.D. into H.A.M.M.E.R. are the sophistic 'knack' of persuasion substituting for the genuine craft of statecraft, just as Polus's ideal Sophist imagines power without self-control. Like Alcibiades, Osborn lacks the Socratic self-knowledge that comes only through critical self-reflection with honest friends, and instead surrounds himself with flatterers and villains while his own Goblin persona—mirrored in the Sentry's Void—grows stronger. Loki's goading of the unsanctioned Siege of Asgard completes the cautionary tale: the sophist who created fake institutions is destroyed by them, hoist by his own petard.

15.title: Part Three Should the Avengers Do More Than Avenge
15.file: ch15 - Part Three Should the Avengers Do More Than Avenge.md

16.title: Avengers, Forgive!
16.file: ch16 - Avengers, Forgive!.md
16.relation: Malloy builds an account of forgiveness around the Avengers' habit of recruiting ex-villains: Arendt's 'predicament of irreversibility' explains why we cannot undo Wonder Man's revenge scheme against Stark, so resentment must be overcome; Derrida's claim that only the unforgivable is truly forgivable frames the House of M question, whether Quicksilver's manipulation of Wanda's reality-warping is a crime beyond forgiveness. Forgiveness means relinquishing resentment without excusing responsibility or condoning the wrong, so Iron Man has the 'moral power' to forgive Hawkeye, while the team's charter-based standing lets the Avengers forgive Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch on the community's behalf. The chapter closes by separating avenging (justice) from revenge, and punishment (retribution that repays debts) from forgiveness, which is why expelled members like Iron Man and Hank Pym could be readmitted.

17.title: Neither Gods nor Beasts But Political Animals
17.file: ch17 - Neither Gods nor Beasts But Political Animals.md
17.relation: Spanakos denies the official line that the Avengers assemble from necessity—Thor beats Loki alone—arguing instead through Aristotle that the team is a polis: heroes join for safety but stay for the good life, since outside the polis one is either a god or a beast. Ms. Marvel's miserable solo run (unrecognized by Stilt-Man, a 'Where Are They Now?' has-been) ends only when she returns to lead the Mighty Avengers among friends who share her arete; the self-loathing Jessica Jones finds eudaimonia through philia with Carol, Luke Cage, and the team that delivers her baby; even the arrogant Hank Pym regains excellence by defending Tony and leading a new team. Even gods like Thor and near-beasts like the Hulk, the chapter concludes, need the Avengers to flourish.

18.title: Avengers Rehabilitate!
18.file: ch18 - Avengers Rehabilitate!.md
18.relation: Terjesen asks whether Cap's Kooky Quartet-style rehabilitation really works, pitting Aristotle's fixed-character virtue ethics against John Doris's situationist 'local traits' (backed by Milgram's experiments): Hawkeye succeeded because his regional traits—hotheadedness and a need for approval—were redirected to heroism, not erased, as when he cheats the Grandmaster to save the universe. Aristotle's continence-versus-virtue and vice-versus-incontinence distinctions explain why Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch keep backsliding, why Moonstone's true viciousness defeats rehabilitation while Songbird and MACH-1 reform. Against deterrence and retributivist theories of punishment, rehabilitation is defensible when applied early and to the unhardened—the Avengers Academy children and Young Avenger Patriot—so the Avengers can rehabilitate as well as avenge.

19.title: Part Four Do the Avengers Ever Go Too Far
19.file: ch19 - Part Four Do the Avengers Ever Go Too Far.md

20.title: And the war Rages on
20.file: ch20 - And the war Rages on.md
20.relation: Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.

21.title: “This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”
21.file: ch21 - “This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”.md
21.relation: Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.

22.title: Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of
22.file: ch22 - Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of.md
22.relation: Bogaerts asks why every proactive superhero comes to grief: Nick Fury's unauthorized Secret War in Latveria, Tony Stark's exile of the Hulk and registration crusade, and the Illuminati's blunder all backfire (World War Hulk, the Skrull invasion), and Aquinas's doctrine of double effect—elaborated by Foot and Anscombe—cannot absolve them, since the foreseen harms were massive and disproportionate to the intended goods. Comics theory supplies the deeper cause: Reynolds's status quo defense and Jewett and Lawrence's American monomyth (via Campbell's hero's journey) make the superhero genre intrinsically reactive, guarding a paradise rather than remaking it, so heroes who 'move up into governance'—Thor as Lord of Earth, the Squadron Supreme's utopia—slide into supervillainy. Foot's act/omission distinction and the priority of negative over positive duties explain the trap, and why even Steve Rogers, as the new top cop, retreats to being Captain America again.

23.title: Part Five What Kind of World do the Avengers Live In
23.file: ch23 - Part Five What Kind of World do the Avengers Live In.md

24.title: Time to End
24.relation: Jones uses Kang to walk through the physics and metaphysics of time travel: Einstein's twin paradox (Quicksilver aging one year while Wanda's clock runs twenty), Gödel's spinning universe and van Stockum's cylinder yielding closed timelike curves, Thorne's wormhole time machine, and Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture against energy-stealing paradox loops. Applied to the comics, Prime Kang's purge of his flawed selves, Immortus's Forever Crystal, and Iron Lad's murder of his future self all confirm the fixed-timeline view: attempts to change the past only prune variants or create transient branches that snap back, so Kang can never un-become Kang. The Avengers end up as the Marvel Universe's Chronology Protection Agency, enforcing the rule that even where time travel exists, the past cannot be rewritten.

25.title: Equal Opportunity—for Deities
25.relation: Barkman argues the Marvel Universe's 'One-Above-All'—depicted as Stan Lee and Jack Kirby—is the eternal Judeo-Christian Creator, and arranges its beings in a graded hierarchy: the Living Tribunal as God's judge, cosmic beings like Eternity and Galactus, elders, sky fathers Odin and Zeus, down to mortals, with only God eternal and everything else, gods included, able to die yet enduring by His decree. Ontological rank guarantees nothing morally—Mephisto, the Goddess, and Hera are powerful and wicked, and even Hercules can be beaten by the Wrecking Crew. A free-will theodicy answers where evil came from: 'no other gods before me' never denied other gods' existence but commands loving the Good above all, which mortal Avengers like Thor, loving justice perfected by sacrificial love, manage as well as any deity.

26.title: Love American Style
26.file: ch26 - Love American Style.md
26.relation: Klayman asks whether the android Vision can love the human Scarlet Witch, working through C.S. Lewis's four loves to show affection, friendship, Eros, and charity are all open to human-android pairs, with their marriage best read as Eros—preoccupation with one irreplaceable self rather than sexual desire. Peter Singer's attack on speciesism is extended into 'organicism', the prejudice that dismisses synthetic beings: the Vision suffers, has interests, and laments that 'we artificial life-forms are still the least accepted', so denying androids love is arbitrary bias. Peirce's pragmatic maxim settles the question by practical effects—the Vision's care, kindness, attentiveness, and intimacy with Wanda just are loving—whether the lover is flesh or machine.

27.title: The Way of the Archer
27.file: ch27 - The Way of the Archer.md
27.relation: White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.

28.title: Appendix Why are there Four Volumes of Avengers
28.file: ch28 - Appendix Why are there Four Volumes of Avengers.md
28.relation: A fan-guide appendix, not a philosophical essay: it untangles the Avengers' publication history to show which comics the book's chapters draw on—the original 1963–1996 volume, the thirteen-issue Heroes Reborn relaunch ('never cited in this book—for a reason'), the 1998 volume ending in Avengers Disassembled, then New Avengers, Young Avengers, the Civil War split, Mighty Avengers, Osborn's Dark Avengers, and the Heroic Age's fourth volume alongside Secret Avengers and Avengers Academy. It makes no philosophical argument; its point is navigational, mapping the canon that the essays' examples come from.

30.title: Index From Jarvis’s Secret Files
30.file: ch30 - Index From Jarvis’s Secret Files.md

3.title: The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series
3.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

9.title: PART ONE - DOES THE DARK KNIGHT ALWAYS DO RIGHT
9.file: ch09 - PART ONE - DOES THE DARK KNIGHT ALWAYS DO RIGHT.md

10.title: So, Case Closed-Right
10.file: ch10 - So, Case Closed-Right.md
10.relation: Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.

11.title: Sometimes Heroes Fail
11.file: ch11 - Sometimes Heroes Fail.md
11.relation: James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'

12.title: Lacking Balance
12.file: ch12 - Lacking Balance.md
12.relation: Stephen Kershnar argues that Batman's hatred of criminals is not a vice but a virtue, since hating what is evil is the morally appropriate attitude toward wrongdoers like the Joker or Batman: Year One's brutal Detective Flass. Against Aristotle's person-focused Virtuous-Persons Theory he defends a 'Virtuous-Thoughts-and-Actions Theory,' illustrated by Gordon's retaliatory beating of Flass and Batman elbow-smashing a pimp in Year One. The chapter closes on the golden mean of balanced love and hate: Batman's virtuous hatred leaves his life isolated and unflourishing, showing that virtue does not guarantee eudaimonia.

13.title: PART TWO - LAW, JUSTICE, AND THE SOCIAL ORDER WHERE DOES BATMAN FIT IN
13.file: ch13 - PART TWO - LAW, JUSTICE, AND THE SOCIAL ORDER WHERE DOES BATMAN FIT IN.md

14.title: The Thin Veil
14.file: ch14 - The Thin Veil.md
14.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads the No Man's Land storyline, in which earthquake-isolated Gotham is carved into gang territories by Two-Face, Penguin, and the Joker, alongside Hurricane Katrina's flooding of New Orleans as twin real-and-fictional tests of Hobbes's state of nature and the social contract. He contrasts Jim Gordon's lawful, Machiavellian-seeming rebuilding of trust with Officer William Petit's slide into execution-style 'despotic' power, and highlights the pacifist witness of Father Christian and Dr. Leslie Thompkins against Hobbes's demand that churches defer to the sovereign. Batman's turn as a benevolent gang lord working to hand the city back to Gordon shows, for Patterson, that Batman's real enemy is anarchy itself.

15.title: Theorizing Government
15.file: ch15 - Theorizing Government.md
15.relation: Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive. Working from Max Weber's definition of the state as monopoly on legitimate violence, Hobbes's Leviathan, and Nietzsche's state as 'new idol,' he reads Year One's corrupt Commissioner Loeb, Year Two's self-appointed Reaper, Anarky's failed anarchist dystopia, Two-Face's broken faith in the law, and The Dark Knight Returns' state-loyal Superman and Commissioner Yindel. The Batman-Gordon partnership emerges as a precarious unofficial order in which Gordon tolerates the one exception to the state's monopoly on violence.

16.title: Who Has the Last Laugh
16.file: ch16 - Who Has the Last Laugh.md
16.relation: Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.

17.title: PART THREE - ORIGINS AND ETHICS BECOMING THE CAPED CRUSADER
17.file: ch17 - PART THREE - ORIGINS AND ETHICS BECOMING THE CAPED CRUSADER.md

18.title: Batman Forever
18.file: ch18 - Batman Forever.md
18.relation: Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.

19.title: But This Ruins Everything!
19.relation: Mahesh Ananth and Ben Dixon pit young Bruce Wayne against Peter Singer: given seven billion dollars, Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' principle, illustrated by the drowning child, seems to require giving nearly everything to famine relief rather than dressing up as a bat. Against appeals to honoring his parents' memory and to supererogation, the authors deploy Singer's strong and moderate versions of giving and utilitarian indifference to distance, concluding that a true utilitarian would forbid becoming Batman. The irony they highlight is that the older Batman himself reasons utilitarianly when he abandons Jason Todd to intercept the Joker's poisoned convoy in A Death in the Family.

20.title: Batman Is a Moral Exemplar
20.file: ch20 - Batman Is a Moral Exemplar.md
20.relation: Ryan Indy Rhodes and David Kyle Johnson defend Batman as a genuine moral exemplar whose justice, beneficence, generosity, and courage (from reprinting No Man's Land land deeds to sacrificing his reputation in Batman Begins) are worth emulating even though no one can copy his feats. They rebut the unrealistic objection, the language objection that 'Batman is virtuous' lacks a truthmaker (likening it to 'dragons breathe fire'), and the exaggeration objection by noting that exemplars like Buddha, Jesus, and Socrates reach us through embellished, partly fictional depictions anyway. Fiction even helps, since we can read Batman's thought balloons, and his growth into an 'icon' supplies the stable true character that emulation requires.

21.title: PART FOUR - WHO IS THE BATMAN (IS THAT A TRICK QUESTION )
21.file: ch21 - PART FOUR - WHO IS THE BATMAN (IS THAT A TRICK QUESTION ).md

22.title: Can You Face the Bat
22.file: ch22 - Can You Face the Bat.md
22.relation: Sarah Donovan and Nicholas Richardson use Nietzsche and Foucault to present Batman as a self-constructed identity: across Batman: Year One, Arkham Asylum, and The Dark Knight Returns, Bruce consciously builds the persona ('Yes, Father, I shall become a bat') rather than revealing a deeper true self. Foucault's constructed categories of normal and abnormal surface in Arkham Asylum's 'super-sane' Joker and the Alice in Wonderland parallels that put Batman's own sanity in question alongside Amadeus Arkham's madness. Nietzsche's will to power and eternal recurrence, via the shepherd biting the snake in Zarathustra, explain why Bruce can face the bat that others flee, becoming heroic where Arkham and Dr. Cavendish go insane.

23.title: All Joking Aside, This Is a Modal Muddle
23.file: ch23 - All Joking Aside, This Is a Modal Muddle.md
23.relation: Sam Cowling and Chris Ragg ask whether Batman could have been the Joker, using the Indiscernibility of Identicals and the Necessity of Identity over possible worlds to argue that if 'Batman' is a name of a merely possible individual, he could not have been identical to the Joker. The 'Robin argument' (many people have been Robin) pushes back that 'Batman' might be a disguised description, and the authors then treat Batman and the Joker as abstract fictional characters whose modal properties are stipulated by their authors. On that view the Elseworlds tale Batman: Two-Faces, where the two are literally one Jekyll-and-Hyde person, shows Batman could have been the Joker after all.

24.title: Keeping It in the Family
24.file: ch24 - Keeping It in the Family.md
24.relation: Jason Southworth deploys counterexamples, from Golden Age Batman shooting the vampire Monk with silver bullets, through Jean-Paul Valley and Dick Grayson serving as Batman during Knightfall and Prodigal, to the Frankenstein twist of Castle of the Bat and the criminal Batman of Earth-A, to show that nothing (not being Bruce Wayne, not never killing, not murdered parents) is necessary or sufficient for being Batman. Turning to Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations, he applies family resemblance and the game examples: 'Batman' works like 'game,' identified through overlapping similarities rather than a fixed definition. Retconned Robins and disappearing Batarangs show language works without fixed meanings, which he warns undermines using Batman as a determinate moral exemplar.

25.title: What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum
25.file: ch25 - What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum.md
25.relation: Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.

26.title: PART FIVE - BEING THE BAT INSIGHTS FROM EXISTENTIALISM AND TAOISM
26.file: ch26 - PART FIVE - BEING THE BAT INSIGHTS FROM EXISTENTIALISM AND TAOISM.md

27.title: Paradox and Peace
27.relation: Christopher Drohan reads Batman and Alfred through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Batman, like Abraham, believes 'by virtue of the absurd,' resigning himself to an infinite, never-realizable justice as a knight of infinite resignation, while Alfred embodies the higher knight of faith whose justice is concrete love expressed in mending the suit, making sandwiches, and guarding the manor. Heidegger's thrownness and Sartre's condemned freedom frame both men's absurd existential condition, including Batman sparing Joe Chill and even allying with him against the Reaper. The chapter's verdict is that Alfred's faithful devotion to one person is the superior ethic, and that peace begins with him.

28.title: Conclusions, Capes, and Cowls
28.relation: Jason Howard asks how Batman keeps from becoming what he fights, answering with Heidegger's authentic conscience against Rousseau's innate moral-sense view. Bruce's guilt over his parents' death is reinterpreted in a Heideggerian 'moment of vision': the bat through the window summons Dasein out of the they-self, so becoming Batman is not vengeance but the call of an authentic conscience that owns guilt, fallenness, and death. Batman's return from alcoholic retirement in The Dark Knight Returns shows conscience as 'the loyalty of existence to its own Self,' a freedom-toward-death that makes him instructive rather than merely heroic.

29.title: Determinism and the Dark Knight
29.file: ch29 - Determinism and the Dark Knight.md
29.relation: David Hart uses Heidegger to dissolve the question of whether Batman is determined by childhood trauma or freely chooses his mission. Heidegger's being-in-the-world and thrown-project, illustrated by Alfred the butler for whom the clock is essentially something to dust, replace the subject-object picture that grounds both free-will and determinism talk. Read this way, the bat crashing through the window in Batman: Year One is Bruce's Angst-laden confrontation with death as 'the possibility of my own impossibility,' through which he freely takes up the project of being Batman when nothing forced him to.

30.title: PART SIX - FRIEND, FATHER, . . . RIVAL THE MANY ROLES OF THE BAT
30.file: ch30 - PART SIX - FRIEND, FATHER, . . . RIVAL THE MANY ROLES OF THE BAT.md

31.title: To Be Continued . .
31.relation: Galen Foresman arms Bat-fans with value theory: most evaluative comparisons of Batman and Superman beg the question, since Super-fans load pros-and-cons lists with superpowers and Bat-fans with intelligence without independently justifying why those traits count. He then argues that bravery is essential to superhero greatness, because the brave person knowingly confronts danger, so the powerless, bulletable Batman is systematically braver than the nearly invulnerable Superman. The conclusion inverts the fans' debate: the very superpowers Super-fans celebrate are what disqualify Superman from being the better hero.

32.title: BSFs Best Superfriends Forever
32.relation: Daniel Malloy argues Batman and Superman are friends who disagree about friendship itself: Superman practices Aristotle's highest philia between good men who are 'another self' and true equals, symbolized by the kryptonite ring he trusts Batman to use on him should he go rogue, while Batman's friendship is Nietzschean, loving in his friend the overman 'as your cause' in the one equal he respects as a rival. Stories like Tower of Babel, Bruce Wayne: Fugitive, and the Brother Eye satellite show Batman manipulates everyone except this one peer, and that he never fights Superman fairly because he does not need to. Their fundamental, unresolvable differences, Malloy concludes, are exactly what strengthen the World's Finest friendship.

33.title: Leaving the Shadow of the Bat
33.file: ch33 - Leaving the Shadow of the Bat.md
33.relation: Carsten Fogh Nielsen stages Aristotle against Kant on moral education: Aristotle says we become just by doing just acts and imitating exemplary people, as Robin imitates Batman, while Kant objects that every example must first be appraised by principles of morality and that imitation breeds heteronomy rather than autonomy. The Gordon-Yindel disagreement over Batman in The Dark Knight Returns shows people can genuinely clash about who counts as morally exemplary in the first place. Dick Grayson resolves the tension by using the courage, skills, and integrity Batman instilled in him to stand up to Batman and become Nightwing, proving emulation can be the route to, not the enemy of, Kantian autonomy.

34.title: NOTES
34.relation: The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.

3.title: Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch
3.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

5.title: Foreword
5.relation: Show writer David Weddle recounts how Ronald Moore pushed the 'Act of Contrition' script beyond Star Trek-style expository dialogue into interleaved flashback snippets dramatizing Starbuck's guilt over passing Zak Adama's flight test. He argues this stream-of-consciousness technique, letting memories, dreams and hallucinations flow out of characters' inner emotional lives (as later in 'Scar' and 'Maelstrom'), is what made the series groundbreaking, echoing Faulkner's 'the past isn't over. It isn't even past.' The foreword frames the book's philosophical interest as rooted in the show's narrative form itself.

6.title: “I Dare You to Watch This Show!”
6.file: ch06 - “I Dare You to Watch This Show!”.md
6.relation: The introduction argues, via Edward James Olmos's campus talks, that Battlestar Galactica is 'truth' television that dares viewers to think about war, insurgency, torture, abortion, genocide, race and identity. It traces the franchise from Glen Larson's 1978 original through Galactica 1980 to the Moore/Eick re-imagining, insisting the show is 'a cultural discussion' rather than a cultural artifact. Borrowing Orson Scott Card's claim that real science fiction works like true religious literature, it frames the contributors' essays as probing who we are, our place in the universe, and how we find or make meaning, and explains the book's conventions for naming the Sixes, Eights, Sharons and its own anonymous 'Final Five' chapters.

8.title: MODEL ONE - Some Are Programmed to Think They Are Human
8.file: ch08 - MODEL ONE - Some Are Programmed to Think They Are Human.md

9.title: Retelling Our Stories
9.relation: Milsky applies the narrative theory of personal identity drawn from Paul Ricoeur and Alasdair MacIntyre (we are the story we emplot about ourselves) to the two Sharons: Boomer's discovery that she is a sleeper Cylon is a 'factual disruption' of her self-story (she shoots Adama because her human narrative cannot cohere), while Athena's love for Helo is a 'disruption of belief' that rewrites her values about humans. He extends the analysis to humans: Starbuck's repressed childhood abuse, Roslin's Pythian-prophecy conversion, and Helo's love for a Cylon, plus Six expelling Athena and Tyrol refusing to acknowledge Boomer, show identity is also socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy. The chapter concludes disruptions are not identity-altering: like the Final Five in 'Crossroads, Part 2' (Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh, I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet'), integration and retelling preserve the continuity of self.

10.title: Frak-tured Finality
10.file: ch10 - Frak-tured Finality.md
10.relation: Booth argues the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across media, so viewers must actively construct the story (which is why Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' only makes sense if you watched them), and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performative roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's wet-floor amnesia in 'Water,' and Hera's human-Cylon hybridity as postmodern identity-in-process. Against Baltar, who waits for D'Anna to assign him an identity, Tigh actively constructs his ('that's the man I want to be'), and the chapter ends suggesting viewers too become human-machine hybrids by constructing themselves from the show's fragments.

11.title: The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities
11.file: ch11 - The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities.md
11.relation: Cuddy argues the gamer's bond with the avatar is an extension of the ego: Freud's id/ego/superego model explains why playing a Cylon Raider or flying the 'Bastille Day' mission lets gamers reconcile unconscious desires with the superego's demands in ways reality forbids. But when we lose we disconnect from the avatar and blame the game or 'cheating' opponents, which Sartre diagnoses as bad faith, a denial of freedom, contrasted with Adama's 'a man takes responsibility for his actions' in '33' and Baltar's vacillation over the vice-presidency. Through facticity (the unforgiving no-save 2003 game) and existence preceding essence, the chapter concludes that videogames offer unparalleled opportunities to practice Sartrean responsibility and achieve Freudian reconciliation through the right avatar.

12.title: Becoming One
12.file: ch12 - Becoming One.md
12.relation: The chapter reads Baltar's head-Six and Caprica Six's head-Baltar through the gothic Double and Doppelganger tradition and Dissociative Identity Disorder: Number Six is Baltar's repressed guilt over betraying humanity ('I'm your subconscious frakking with your mind'), letting him escape responsibility for signing execution orders in 'Precipice,' while Gina Six serves as a tangible Double. Plato's Symposium myth of the split self frames Baltar and Six as two halves of one whole, since he cannot function without some version of Six present, physical or hallucinated. The resolution is Aristotle's golden mean from Book Two of the Nicomachean Ethics: like integration therapy for DID, virtue is a balance between extremes rather than eliminating one side, so Baltar and Six's child Hera may embody the balanced union of human and Cylon.

13.title: No Reason to Get Excited
13.file: ch13 - No Reason to Get Excited.md
13.relation: The chapter turns the Final Five reveal (Tigh, Tyrol, Anders, Foster) and Boomer's sleeper activation into a skeptical problem about self-knowledge: Descartes's dreaming doubt (Roslin's Opera House dream) and the cogito show we can know that we exist but not what we are, and Baltar's rigged 'bright green' Cylon test destroys testimonial assurance. G.E. Moore's common-sense realism fails to engage the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism and Dretske's relevant-alternatives theory cannot help because in a world of sleeper Cylons the possibility 'I might be one' is always relevant. The answer is Hume's: like Tigh declaring 'I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet' and Anders repeating 'I am Samuel T. Anders' before his first combat mission, we banish skeptical paralysis by carrying on with life, dining and playing backgammon.

14.title: MODEL TWO - They Look Like Us Now
14.file: ch14 - MODEL TWO - They Look Like Us Now.md

15.title: This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again
15.file: ch15 - This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again.md
15.relation: Rennes reads the miniseries' opening kiss of death through Verges's 'colonial family romance' (built on Freud's family romance): humans created Cylon 'children' to serve them while fixing categories of racial difference (toaster, skin job, 'it') to keep them in their place. Using Homi Bhabha's ambivalence and mimicry ('almost the same, but not quite') and the history of miscegenation panic and blood taxonomies, she traces how human-Cylon intimacy (Gina's rape aboard Pegasus, Helo and Athena, Starbuck at the breeding Farm) makes difference collapse into sameness. Hera, the mixed-blood child whose fetal blood cures Roslin's cancer, is Bhabha's 'resemblance and menace': acknowledging her would force humans to admit they created Cylon slaves, so Roslin socially reconstructs Hera's difference and the romance ends happily never after.

16.title: Who They Are or Who They Want to Be
16.file: ch16 - Who They Are or Who They Want to Be.md
16.relation: Harwood-Smith argues, against Descartes's pre-given 'I think therefore I am,' that Judith Butler's performativity explains the Cylons: Six is female because she performs femininity, no copy performs identically, and Cylon society fractures into hybrid identities with an 'embarrassed etc.' Sexual contact with humans is the catalyst that makes performance constitute reality, producing Athena's defection, Caprica Six's celebrity status, and D'Anna's religious fervor, while Cylons who never slept with humans stay apart. The same dynamic destabilizes humans who sleep with Cylons: Baltar's 'I must be a Cylon because I slept with one,' Tyrol's fear, and Helo's 'toaster lover' stigma, with Tigh's chosen stability ('that's the man I want to be') as the counterexample of performing who you want to be.

17.title: The Secret Plot of ‘Baby Boomers’
17.file: ch17 - The Secret Plot of ‘Baby Boomers’.md
17.relation: Chess argues Battlestar Galactica is 'a narrative about queer reproduction': via Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto and Butler's account of heteronormativity, the Cylons are 'technoqueer,' embodying how fears of technology overlap with fears of non-heterosexual reproduction. Their download-based 'photocopying' reproduction and their obsessive pursuit of legitimate biological babies (the Farm's breeding facility, Athena's 'unnatural' pregnancy that Roslin calls a 'thing') express the anxiety that new reproductive technologies make heterosexuality obsolete, which the chapter pairs scene-for-scene with The L Word's Bette and Tina. Helo's 'I'm in love with a woman I know isn't a woman' and the Pegasus crew's 'you cannot rape a machine' debate show homophobia folding into technophobia, with Hera as the illegitimate queer child both societies fear.

18.title: Stable Bodies
18.file: ch18 - Stable Bodies.md
18.relation: Heinricy argues the one clear human-Cylon difference is the body, analyzed through Mary Douglas's account of bodies as culturally invented boundaries: Cylons are feared as 'contamination' of the fleet (Boomer's body, segregated like Jim Crow bodies), and Gina Six's torture and rape mark her body as out-of-place other even as her human-looking blood and wounds undermine the boundary. She contrasts messy, changing human bodies (Apollo's weight fluctuation, aging, scars as records of experience) with stable, disposable Cylon bodies that never mark learning, arguing human change yields potential and hope while Cylon bodily stability may cost mental stability (Tigh killing Ellen, Boomer attacking Hera). Cyborg theory then collapses the boundary (we are all cyborgs via vaccines and prosthetics, Cylons merely more integrated, the Hybrid a warning of over-integration), leaving Hera and Nicky as the 'ultimate contamination' that blends the two.

19.title: Into the Future
19.relation: Hanley dismantles the four alleged human-Cylon differences: humans are also 'made' (by God), contain non-organic parts, come as identical twins, and expect to survive death, so religious believers already believe they are Cylons. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), models Cylon resurrection as scanning-death-transmission-replication, and shows van Inwagen's replica-swap account of bodily resurrection faces the same worries about blank bodies and which body returns. Following Locke's consciousness criterion, that a soul independent of body and memory explains none of our identity judgments, he rejects karma-based reincarnation without memory, proposes a fission-style plot-fix for Athena's impossible memories of Tyrol, and ends with Cylons settling ancient Earth: 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'

20.title: MODEL THREE - We Became What We Beheld
20.file: ch20 - MODEL THREE - We Became What We Beheld.md

21.title: Hedging Our Bets
21.file: ch21 - Hedging Our Bets.md
21.relation: Kind asks whether the Fleet's treatment of Cylons (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine,' Cally's killing of Boomer charged as mere discharging of a firearm) presupposes that Cylons lack the moral status Mary Anne Warren defines against the stone-versus-child contrast. Against species membership as a criterion she deploys Singer's anti-speciesism (sentience grounds equal consideration: Gina's torture, the Raider Scar) and Regan's subject-of-a-life, and against the 'no souls' argument she cites Descartes's animal automata and Turing's reply that an omnipotent God could give machines souls, as Leoben himself suggests to Adama. Since no criterion rules Cylons out with certainty, the chapter closes with a Pascal's Wager structure: under uncertainty, treat plausible moral-status-holders as having it, because denying it costs us our moral compass, answering Adama's 'why are we worth saving?'.

22.title: Learning from Our Mistakes
22.file: ch22 - Learning from Our Mistakes.md
22.relation: Tamplin uses Baltar's landslide win on the New Caprica issue and Roslin's attempted election theft to argue democracy's guarantee of bad decisions is its saving feature: Plato and Aristotle ranked democracy among bad regimes because the many rule for private advantage rather than the common good, and Baltar's campaign of 'hope rather than truth' exploits exactly that weakness. A thought experiment about an oracle computer that always selects the best option shows that following it would abolish self-determination, the freedom to 'live as one wants' that democracy values above results. Only by choosing and frakking up (settling New Caprica, suffering the occupation, Apollo's shame speech at Baltar's trial) can citizens confront their role, learn from mistakes, and move toward Aristotle's polity aiming at virtue, making self-determination the mediating value between freedom and virtue.

23.title: History Will Judge
23.relation: Livingston reads Razor through George Lakoff's nation-as-family metaphor: Cain's Pegasus is the Strict Father family (the world is dangerous, Belzen shot for disobedience, Gina tortured for intelligence, Kendra's humiliating 'birth slap'), while Adama's Galactica is the Nurturant Parent (empathy, questioning authority, 'it's not enough to survive; one has to be worthy of surviving'). She traces how military kill-conditioning, desensitization plus objectifying 'toaster' and 'it' language, turns Kendra into 'a razor' and a PTSD case, while Apollo and Kendra hybridize the two family models on Pegasus. Adama's closing 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain's context matters more than villainizing, and that humanity's worthiness depends on the balance struck between our idealized parents.

24.title: It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life
24.file: ch24 - It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life.md
24.relation: Shipman argues the series first builds viewer sympathy for Cylons as rebel slaves (their monotheism and their New Caprica role as US-style occupiers make them 'more like the viewers than the humans'), then undercuts it: the Numbers rebuilt Cylon society as oppressors, breeding the voices out of Centurions, dismissing the Hybrids as mad, and breeding the sentient Raiders (Starbuck's discovery in 'Scar') into functional animals. The opening narration's claim that Cylons 'evolved' is disingenuous, since the model hierarchy was deliberately engineered, 'not evolution, but eugenics,' with Marx's 'from each according to his ability' division of labor as thin cover for literal class construction. The former slaves became slave-owners, fulfilling 'all of this has happened before': heroes of one story become villains of the next, inviting the muted models to rebel against the Numbers in turn.

25.title: Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back
25.relation: Gray asks whether the Cylons deserve moral status, testing them against Kant's formula of humanity as an end in itself: the resistance's suicide bombings on New Caprica and Adama's plan to weaponize virus-infected Cylons against the resurrection ship in 'A Measure of Salvation' use beings as mere means, while Athena's defection and D'Anna's dissent (and her line's boxing) display the rational autonomy Kant requires of persons. Singer's sentience principle (Gina's catatonia after torture, Leoben's suffering under interrogation) and Mary Anne Warren's multi-criterial personhood (Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded') independently support Cylon personhood. The chapter concludes that the show's double standards, accepting Athena while drawing guns on Caprica Six, mirror our own confusion as cloning and artificial intelligence advance.

26.title: MODEL FOUR - Battlestar Iraqtica
26.file: ch26 - MODEL FOUR - Battlestar Iraqtica.md

27.title: Fire Without Burn
27.relation: Pinedo argues the re-imagined series restages 'blowback,' the CIA-coined term for retaliation against covert intervention that public discourse avoids, in science-fiction guise: Adama's 'you cannot play God, then wash your hands of the things you've created' speech, and the episode 'Hero,' where Adama confesses his black-ops crossing of the Armistice Line ('I started it') before Roslin reframes his guilt into 'a thousand things' the Colonials did over forty years. The chapter shows how the sci-fi 'smokescreen' (Moore and Eick's own word) lets the show do what news coverage cannot: sympathetically depict suicide bombing on New Caprica and torture by the 'good guys' (Starbuck's waterboarding of Leoben, Cain's ordered rape of Gina), dismantling the Manichean myth of American innocence after 9/11 while avoiding the network wrath that naming blowback would bring.

28.title: The Future
28.relation: Dinello argues the New Caprica occupation arc deliberately dramatizes Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth applied to Iraq: Cylon colonization (Cavil as Cheney-Rumsfeld bringing 'the love of god,' Baltar as puppet leader, Colonial One as Green Zone, hooded detainees) enacts Fanon's colonial violence and psychological colonization of the mind, seen in Leoben's manipulation of Starbuck and Jammer's recruitment into the New Caprica Police. The insurgency enacts Fanon's violence-as-cleansing-force: Tigh's 'blood for blood,' Duck's suicide bombing of the NCP graduation, and Tyrol's Mario Savio-inspired 'throw your body on the gears' speech, which the chapter links to Marx's seizure of the means of production and Marcuse on technology's repressiveness, while Sartre's preface licenses anticolonial violence against liberal moralizing. It concludes that occupation breeds the terrorists it fights, insurgents win by not losing, and the show is subversive because it makes viewers sympathize with 'our real-world enemies.'

29.title: Living with Our Choices
29.relation: Peters reads 'The Resistance' webisodes through Sartre's occupied-France dilemma from Existentialism Is a Humanism (resist, collaborate, or do nothing, modeled on his student's choice between joining the Free French and caring for his mother): Tyrol joins the resistance for his family's future, Jammer joins the New Caprica Police to save lives and pays with execution by his former friends in 'Collaborators,' and Duck's choice to do nothing ends with wife Nora's death in the Temple massacre and his revenge suicide bombing. Since 'man is nothing other than what he makes of himself,' the chapter argues morality lies in the freedom to choose and in living with the consequences: Duck's refusal to accept his choice, not the choice itself, is the failure, and the Final Five revelation cannot retroactively alter choices made in good faith by Tigh, Tyrol, Anders and Foster. Which side holds the ethical high ground may simply be whichever side won and gets to write history.

30.title: Walking the Tightrope
30.relation: Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.

31.title: Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t
31.file: ch31 - Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t.md
31.relation: McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.

32.title: Misunderestimated
32.relation: Muir argues the 1978 original was serious political allegory rather than Moore's 'popcorn': Adar's armistice with the Cylons stands in for Carter-era detente and the SALT treaties, and the sneak attack dramatizes hard-right fears of unilateral disarmament. Adama's 'preparedness' and Sire Uri's disarmament proposal map onto the 'Peace through Strength' doctrine that carried Reagan to power, and 'Experiment in Terra' repeats the lesson as Apollo tells Terra's politicians the opposite of war is slavery, not peace. The chapter notes Soviet Izvestia read it the same way, and that the original thereby fulfilled Moore's own criterion of relevant science fiction from the opposite end of the political spectrum, including Apollo's wartime argument that dissent weakens Colonial resolve.

33.title: MODEL FIVE - Finding Purpose in the Void
33.file: ch33 - MODEL FIVE - Finding Purpose in the Void.md

34.title: Speed and Destination
34.relation: Martinon reads '33' as a phenomenology of temporality under exile: with sunrise, history, and open future gone, the fleet's existence becomes eschatological 'bare life' (following Agamben), sandwiched between the death of the Colonies and death at Cylon hands every thirty-three minutes. The FTL jump figures Derrida's messianic 'to-come' - an undecidable advent that may be salvation or destruction - while the Vipers' obsession with speed narrows life to the next possibility, in a Heideggerian shift from cultural to ontological questioning of death. The episode stays undecidable between Number Six's fatalism ('God is watching out for you, Gaius') and Baltar's contingency, with a birth aboard the fleet - Roslin's smile - as the one open future.

35.title: Finding Our Way
35.relation: Milburn uses Dewey's account of habit, impulse, and inquiry to explain how the humans navigate: Adama's blocked plans (the decommissioning) are reoriented into a new 'end-in-view' (Earth), and the fleet continuously reformulates its route from scriptures, star charts, pulsars, and the Tomb of Athena constellations as interchangeable signs. The Cylons by contrast cannot revise - Boomer's peace initiative gets her model boxed, and even Cavil's admissions of error lead back to the same path - because they locate their plan in God rather than in constructed, revisable inquiry, needing Baltar even to interpret the signs to Earth. On Deweyan grounds the chapter concludes the humans are never lost while the Cylons are.

36.title: Free to Be You and Me
36.file: ch36 - Free to Be You and Me.md
36.relation: Barker reconciles Cylon programming with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's 'intelligible character': Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama and her betrayal of the Cylons to save Tyrol both flow from one innate, conflicted character, just as Baltar's cowardly 'conversion' to the Cylon god expresses his opportunism. Tigh's decision to keep serving after learning he is a Cylon ('My name is Saul Tigh; I am an officer in the colonial fleet') shows character unchanged by revelation. Starbuck's 'special destiny' in 'Maelstrom' is reread not as fate but as her own character - mother-induced self-doubt at war with pilot confidence - which she finally accepts in the vortex; freedom is not freedom from programming but the necessity of manifesting who one already is.

37.title: Taking in the View from the Paranoid Position
37.file: ch37 - Taking in the View from the Paranoid Position.md
37.relation: Christian reads the fleet through Freud's death instinct and Melanie Klein's paranoid position: Starbuck's self-destruction, Tigh and Ellen's sadomasochism, and Baltar's relationship with Six fuse Eros and Thanatos, and 'Maelstrom' returns Starbuck to the abusive mother whose rejection of her love taught her that love itself is poisonous. Humans project all aggression and badness onto the Cylons they created - 'toaster' talk, Cain's torture of Gina - to keep a split between good self and evil other. The price is permanent vigilance in the watchtower: since anyone might be a Cylon (the Chief's fear, Baltar's test), the crew can never be sure the projected badness is not their own, which is why the machines must keep 'coming back.'

38.title: Embracing Death
38.relation: Vessey asks whether the humanoid Cylons' resurrection makes meaningful life impossible. Humans can aim at a 'successful death' - Socrates drinking the hemlock, the Greek warrior accepting his moira - in which dying completes a life understood as a whole oriented to something larger; a Cylon's death is a mere reset (download), and the exceptions available, dying out of range of a resurrection ship or D'Anna's boxing, occur only through failure or shame and so cannot contribute to meaning. Plato's Symposium link of children to immortality is inverted, since Cylons can only have mortal human-Cylon babies; what separates the Cylons from Sisyphus is not purpose but the option to opt out, which mortality forces on humans and resurrection denies the Cylons.

39.title: MODEL SIX - Near the End of Our Journey
39.file: ch39 - MODEL SIX - Near the End of Our Journey.md

40.title: To the Third Power . .
40.relation: Wolfe argues the original series is 'deeply Mormon' in ontology though not in epistemology: Kobol anagrams Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve and 'sealing' marriages mirror LDS structure, and the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were; as we are now, you may become' restates Lorenzo Snow's deification couplet, while Count Iblis, like the Mormon Satan, can only rule those who freely yield - agency is supreme. Because none of this is required to follow the show, later licensees could rebuild the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics incoherently (free will violated when inconvenient), Richard Hatch's novels with a new pure-blood-of-Kobol cosmology, and Ronald Moore with a circular 'all this has happened before' replacing eternal progression.

41.title: So Say We All
41.relation: Berger deploys Bakhtin's dialogism to answer the 'GINO' charge: the re-imagined series is not a betrayal of Larson's show but a heteroglossic utterance in an ongoing conversation that already included the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greco-Roman myth, and later fanfic and blogs, with each version sourcing its sources' sources. The 2003 series is read as polyphonic about belief: skeptic Adama, devout Number Six, the messianic convert Baltar, and Dawkins/Hitchens-style atheist critiques of fundamentalism are all given equal voice. The show's value lies in inviting debate across the whole continuum of belief rather than preaching a position.

42.title: The Cosmic Divide
42.relation: The chapter locates the real fan schism in worldview: the original series is Manichaean moral absolutism - Count Iblis and the Ships of Light wage a cosmic Light/Darkness war in which Evil is one force (Iblis sharing the Imperious Leader's voice) and humanity is the battleground - while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean relativism ('man is the measure'), where right depends entirely on context. Evidence: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of fuel reserves to find Starbuck; Leoben is airlocked after Starbuck's interrogation while Thorne is killed for torturing Athena; producer Eick even defends Caprica Six's killing of the baby as possibly a mercy. The two shows thus embody absolutist nostalgia for moral clarity versus post-9/11 moral ambiguity.

43.title: With or Without Starbuck
43.relation: Kirkland argues BSG imagines gender-free institutions (unisex heads and quarters, Starbuck never having to justify fighting) while installing a default masculinity under Adama, so that feminine-coded women die: Ellen the femme fatale is poisoned, pilots Kat and Kendra earn redemption only through death, and Cain's female command is written as militarist nightmare aligned with Gina's sexual abuse. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze and reverses rescue narratives, and 'The Farm' plus her captivity with Leoben on New Caprica literalize feminist critiques of patriarchal medicine and compulsory heterosexuality. Yet she is masculinized, pathologized via her abusive mother, brought to submit to Leoben as spiritual guide, and killed in 'Maelstrom' - containing the transgressive heroine within the show's patriarchy.

44.title: Human, Machine, or Something In-between
44.file: ch44 - Human, Machine, or Something In-between.md
44.relation: Rolufs maps Genesis' Eve onto Boomer (who shoots Adama without understanding her act, as Eve could not know betrayal before eating the fruit) and onto Caprica Six (whose fall required Baltar's Adam-like blame-shifting), and the Zohar's Lilith - seductress, child-killer, seeker of equality - onto Six's red dresses and neck-snapping and Sharon's sexual dominance of Helo. Both Cylon women are compromised figures who love the humans they betrayed, and their ambiguity between human and machine mirrors the ambiguity between woman and demon in the myths. Through them the chapter argues pop culture redeems Eve and Lilith from misogynistic readings: Six's killing of the baby becomes possibly merciful, and the first women get the chance at redemption the myths denied them.

45.title: 32 - Dreamers in the Night [ ]
45.relation: This fan-fiction interlude dramatizes the fandom debate aboard Galactica: Roslin voices the Frankfurt School view (a 'Scorpion School' of Adorno and Benjamin - mass culture as mindless absorption, reproduction destroying the artwork's aura), while aide Billy cites Henry Jenkins and Textual Poachers to defend fanzines as participatory culture repairing corporate ownership of myth, and a fan meeting wins the President over as community-building. Baltar and inner Number Six extend the argument: Six demands 'the singular truth of the show' against fan rewriting, and Baltar answers that the Cylons are themselves a fanfiction of the human brain - twelve unoriginal faces. Starbuck is revealed as the anonymous fanfic writer.

46.title: Case in Point
46.relation: The chapter introduces Wayne Booth's 'coduction' - ethical criticism of fiction validated by comparing one's reasoned judgments with other qualified readers in ongoing, open-minded conversation - and argues Battlestar is a highly ethical show not because its characters behave well but because it invites coduction: the abortion-under-extinction, torture, and New Caprica suicide-bombing plots (Baltar cornering Roslin, who cannot justify the bombings) open discussion instead of preaching, the mark of art rather than propaganda. Rules for genuine coduction follow - treat Iraq as one applicability among several occupations, stay informed, remain open to changing your mind - with Ron Moore's blog exchange on the absence of gay characters as the model case, and the book itself offered as one contribution to the continuing conversation.
