9.title: Foreword
9.relation: James S. A. Corey (Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck) frame both philosophy and science fiction as 'acts of critical imagination': philosophy advances into questions before data and measurement exist, and science fiction imagines what we do not yet know until it stops being speculative. They describe The Expanse as a collaborative project built from the science fiction they read growing up (Bester, Niven, Clarke, Cherryh) and from real history, its boundaries clear only at a distance. The foreword presents this volume as the conversation they inherited carrying forward, with The Expanse as touchstone, hoping it leaves readers 'a little more awed, a little wiser.'

10.title: Introduction
10.file: ch10 - Introduction.md
10.relation: Editor Jeffery L. Nicholas declares Leviathan Wakes 'that book' and the TV series 'that show' of philosophical science fiction, and explains that his own aphantasia makes the series especially precious to him (watching the Rocinante on screen, Naomi's torture to save lives). He frames the volume's guiding questions over the first five seasons with hints from Babylon's Ashes: whether Amos or Avasarala is more evil and Naomi or Holden good, the costs of interstellar migration through the Ring Gates, and whether humanity even has a choice about expansion. Like Joe Miller holding Julie's necklace, the contributors offer their love of the show through interrogation of Miller, Holden, Amos, Bobbie, Naomi, and Avasarala herself.

11.title: First Orbit FROM EARTH TO THE STARS
11.file: ch11 - First Orbit FROM EARTH TO THE STARS.md

12.title: Howl at the Moon If You Want To
12.file: ch12 - Howl at the Moon If You Want To.md
12.relation: Michael J. O'Neill argues that infinite space is The Expanse's most constant on-screen character, conveyed through chiaroscuro cinematography that deliberately echoes the seventeenth century (the Don Quixote references, 'Dulcinea', the Rocinante's name), when humanity first confronted infinite space. He reads Pascal's terror at man as 'a middle point between all and nothing' into Avasarala's losing debate with Nancy Gao over the Ring gold rush and into Miller's agoraphobic quest for Julie, then contrasts this with Kant's mathematically and dynamically sublime: spacewalks, the Behemoth dwarfed at the Gate, the Arboghast disassembled over Venus, and Inaros' asteroid attack as the weaponization of the infinite. Against Pascal's insignificance, Kant's sublime reveals our freedom — Holden's 'crazy notion about free will' while descending to the Ring station, Drummer's 'nothing in the void is foreign to us', and Amos' 'we're still here' — so the awe the show's visuals provoke is an intuition that we are greater than all nature's power.

13.title: What Really Matters
13.file: ch13 - What Really Matters.md
13.relation: Margarida Hermida deploys Parfit's comparison of peace, a war killing 99 percent of humanity, and one killing everyone to argue extinction is categorically worse than mass death, and makes the stakes concrete through The Expanse's threats: the protomolecule, all-out Earth-Mars-Belt war, and the Free Navy's asteroid attack that kills billions. She rejects Miller's 'stars are better off without us' pessimism by arguing human existence is a good when suffering is fought (Belter disease and Ceres trafficking are contingent injustices, not necessities), values humanity as the only species with civilization and as the universe 'starting to understand itself', and distinguishes the desirable biological colonization of lifeless worlds from the protomolecule makers' morally objectionable disregard for native life like Ilus'. Against Phil Torres' worry that human speciation means endless war, she points to the mixed Rocinante crew and Naomi's line that the real divide is 'people who want more violence and the ones who want less', concluding with Parfit's On What Matters that what matters most is avoiding the end of human history and of rational beings.

14.title: Actual Threats to Our Existence
14.file: ch14 - Actual Threats to Our Existence.md
14.relation: Leonard Kahn takes the season-four debate between Avasarala and Nancy Gao over Ring colonization and asks who should have won. Using Parfit's extinction asymmetry, Bostrom's 'astronomical waste', and Toby Ord's definition of existential risk, he calculates that the 1,300 Ring gates could make accessible between 10^34 and 10^71 future lives (versus the Epstein-drive Nauvoo's century-long crawl to Tau Ceti), yet because using the rings risks the annihilation that befell the protomolecule's creators, the loss of humanity's long-term potential outweighs Gao's 'unimaginable opportunities' — so Avasarala's caution should have won. He ends skeptically: like Socrates arguing against the execution of the Arginusae generals, philosophical Cassandras rarely prevail, Gao was probably right that ring colonization was politically inevitable, and we face the same dilemma with nuclear war, engineered pandemics, and runaway AI.

15.title: Conclusion Whatever I Goddamn Like
15.file: ch15 - Conclusion Whatever I Goddamn Like.md
15.relation: S. W. Sondheimer argues that Avasarala's election loss to Nancy Gao is explained not by competence but by millennia of gender expectations. She excavates the lineage: Aristotle's form/matter hierarchy ('matter yearns for form as the female for the male', women as incomplete 'deformed males' with 'fewer teeth') used to bar women from politics, Hume's portrait of women as near-livestock incapable of the sublime, and Romantic-era bodily confinement — mapping each onto Avasarala's staff recasting her as a 'nurturing, caring family matriarch', her forced public apology for the failed Inaros boarding raid that a male commander like Errinwright would never have had to make, and Arjun seizing control of the narrative of their son Charanpal's death. Closing the loop with the 2016 US election (Clinton versus Trump), the chapter argues that even in 2350 voters punish the 'nasty woman' and reward the comfortable mold Gao fits, and demands we 'dig this garbage philosophy out of our shared consciousness and set it on fire.'

16.title: Second Orbit IS IT THE PROTOMOLECULE, OR JUST HUMAN NATURE
16.file: ch16 - Second Orbit IS IT THE PROTOMOLECULE, OR JUST HUMAN NATURE.md

17.title: Should Mao Be Pardoned
17.relation: R. S. Leiby stages the trial of Jules-Pierre Mao alongside Hannah Arendt's report on Adolf Eichmann to ask whether someone can commit great evil without being evil. Mao, like Eichmann, would plead 'not guilty in the sense of the indictment': he mourns Julie at her tree, momentarily defends the children on Io ('We're torturing children'), yet lacks the imagination to think from the standpoint of his victims on Eros, the Canterbury, and Ganymede — unlike the genuine fanatics Dresden and Cortázar, whom appeals to morality cannot touch. The 'anyone would do it' defense is tested through Milgram's obedience experiments and Miller's killing of Dresden ('I killed him because he was making sense'), showing how seductive moral tradeoffs are; following the Eichmann court's rule that responsibility increases with distance from the fatal instrument, the chapter concludes that Mao — a free, autonomous agent with even less excuse than Eichmann — should not be pardoned.

18.title: Amos Is No Superman
18.file: ch18 - Amos Is No Superman.md
18.relation: Pankaj Singh reads Amos through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Amos' division of people into 'bad ones, ones you follow, and ones you need to protect', his outsourcing of moral judgment to Naomi and Holden ('Naomi wouldn't like it'), his fearlessness, and his violent spontaneity make him 'evil' by slave morality yet good by master morality. Unlike Prax, who has to be stopped from shooting Strickland out of ressentiment, Amos kills without revenge ('I am that guy'), and his fistfights with Miller and Alex discharge hostility immediately so it never poisons — the strong natures Nietzsche praises that 'form, mold, recuperate and forget.' His 'crew comes first' and 'better to go down swinging' express the will to power as discharge of strength rather than mere self-preservation, but because he never sublimates or overcomes his drives, the chapter concludes Amos is no Übermensch — 'but then again, who is?'

19.title: The Upsides of Amos
19.relation: Diana Sofronieva asks whether Amos is evil and answers no — in some ways he is better than most. Drawing on psychopathy research (Blair's moral/conventional distinction), Glover's 'moral resources', and Damasio's somatic markers to explain both his emotional absence (cauterized by a Baltimore childhood where children were sold for sex) and his difficulty making choices ('I've been trying to make choices of my own lately, and I can't seem to make the right ones'), she distinguishes him from bloodthirsty killers like Murtry and from Cortázar, who surgically chose the emotionless life Amos wants to escape. Against Arendt's banality of evil, Amos is no thoughtless 'joiner': he holds an uncompromising inner code (family first, bullying punished), deliberately selects good people — Naomi, Anna, Holden — as his moral compass after verifying their reasons, and his honesty, loyalty, trust in competence, and selflessness make him paradoxically less capable of evil than nearly anyone else on the Roci.

20.title: What Promotes Moral Behavior
20.relation: Matthew D. Atkinson and Darin DeWitt use the Canterbury's ignored mayday in 'Dulcinea' — Captain McDowell's 'let the good God Darwin sort it out' versus Ade Nygaard's appeal to law, karma, and obligation — to ask what binds people when no central authority enforces rules. Through Michael Walzer's just war theory they read the Earth-Mars war: moral language is not 'cheap talk' (even Errinwright must dress aggression as peace and manipulates Reverend Volovodov's words), aggression and imminence govern when to fight, and five 'how to fight' principles — noncombatant immunity on Eros and Ganymede, POW rights for the Martian marines on the Kittur Chennamma, leaders' rather than soldiers' responsibility (Fred Johnson's defection after Anderson Station), proportionality in Errinwright's 'a base for a base' Deimos strike, and the rejection of ends-justify-means utilitarianism — discipline even Holden and Amos as they reflect on free will and culpability. The chapter concludes The Expanse is optimistic: human decency survives even in the anarchic Belt because characters keep reflecting on what their obligations to one another are.

21.title: A Crossroads in Human History
21.file: ch21 - A Crossroads in Human History.md
21.relation: Trip McCrossin reads season five's asteroid strikes on Earth as a 9/11 allegory (Delgado's 'at least now they know it's an attack') and applies Michael Walzer's five conditions to define Marco Inaros' terrorism: deliberate harm to randomly selected innocents, meant to terrify a cohort into political change, as in Marco's 'crossroads in human history' broadcast. This yields the terrorist's dilemma — justice toward victims versus compassion toward beneficiaries — while Avasarala's opening gravity-torture scene and her 'dirty hands' assign the opponent blame for failing to relieve the oppression that makes terrorism seem a last resort. Lydia's 'churn' ('float to the top or sink to the bottom') and her lesson that one can 'lead a good life without being a good person' explain how Amos and Clarissa redeem each other on the road to Baltimore, whereas Marco, like Arendt's Eichmann, cannot think from anyone else's standpoint ('everything we ever dreamed of'); the chapter ends with Avasarala's proposed Inners-Belters union as her own redemption — 'this is how we win.'

22.title: Third Orbit REMEMBER THE CANT!
22.file: ch22 - Third Orbit REMEMBER THE CANT!.md

23.title: A More Human Future
23.relation: Sid Simpson argues, through Frantz Fanon, that Marco Inaros' asteroid attacks must be judged as anti-colonial violence rather than simple monstrosity. Using Black Skin, White Masks' ontological division (Belters as 'skinnies', 'possessions, animals', the dehumanization that made Eros an acceptable testing ground and Anderson Station a 'message'), reinforced by Columbus and las Casas on Spanish colonization, he shows why the Inners' 'peace' is merely the status quo of ongoing extraction — Fanon's 'hypnotherapy' — that no treaty or Ring can fix. Fanon's Wretched of the Earth then recasts anti-colonial violence as a 'cleansing force' that shatters the colonial ontology and lets the colonized create a 'new, better, more human form' of humanity, so that Marco's personal narcissism and possible insincerity do not settle the political question: for the Belt, violence may be not only the last option but the most just one, against Avasarala's champagne-toast universalism that never takes Belter grievances seriously.

24.title: Against Love of Nation
24.relation: Applies George Orwell's distinction between patriotism (defensive devotion open to critique) and nationalism (obsessive, unstable, indifferent to reality) to Belt politics, reading Drummer as the patriot — she works for the Earther Fred Johnson, turns her guns on Belter radicals in 'Pyre', and refuses to whitewash Marco's massacres ('We're scavengers') — and Marco Inaros as the nationalist, whose asteroid genocide, treatment of Naomi as a welwala, and brainwashing of Filip ('All I did, I did for all Belters') display obsession, loyalty-transfer, and indifference to reality. The chapter's twist is that by Season 5 the patriots lose, because nationalists can always outbid defenders who play only defense, so neither Drummer nor Marco has the right attitude; Avasarala's finale call to 'turn every Belter, Martian, and Earther into this [the Rocinante crew]' makes cosmopolitanism — shared humanity over national loyalty — the show's real answer.

25.title: “I Want to Conquer the World”
25.file: ch25 - “I Want to Conquer the World”.md
25.relation: Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.

26.title: Tilting at Windmills
26.file: ch26 - Tilting at Windmills.md
26.relation: Reads Protogen through Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment: like Odysseus tied to the mast while his sailors take the wax, Dresden's team had empathy surgically removed ('we modified our science team to remove ethical restraints'), Mao weeps at Julie's protomolecule corpse yet calls her death 'lucky', and Strickland experiments on Katoa and Mei Meng — self-made monsters serving the Baconian dream of conquering nature (New Atlantis, witch-trial language of 'penetrating her holes and corners'). Via Maria Mies and Carolyn Merchant's ecofeminism, it traces this domination of nature to pastoralist castration and the control of women's reproduction, culminating in Marco's theft of Filip and 'She left us. She left us both' — Naomi cast as nature to be mastered. Against them, Holden's childhood on the family farm, a cooperative 'let grow and make grow' world, is why Avasarala cannot play him and why he withholds broadcasts at Ilus: he is a knight who wants everyone to grow and speak for themselves, not to conquer.

27.title: Fourth Orbit THEY STILL DREAM
27.file: ch27 - Fourth Orbit THEY STILL DREAM.md

28.title: “Doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing”
28.file: ch28 - “Doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing”.md
28.relation: Reads The Expanse as a portrait of a survived-but-unlearned Anthropocene: Bobbie's mourning encounter with Earth's dead, walled ocean in 'Cascade', Prax Meng's cascade of cascading failures killing Ganymede's artificial ecosystem and manufacturing Belter climate refugees overnight, and the slum outside the UN gates where children drink sewer water. Drawing on Brian Henning's 'Technozoic' critique, Katie McShane, Keekok Lee's intrinsic value of inanimate nature, and Henry Shue and Kyle Whyte on climate justice and colonialism, it argues humanity simply exported its anthropocentric, colonial worldview to Mars terraforming, Ilus, and the Ring worlds instead of changing it — Belters standing in for the Global South — so the Roci's creed that 'doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing' becomes a demand for environmental justice and a non-anthropocentric ethics.

29.title: “What happens to us now ”
29.relation: Tests the moral limits of science against Dresden's defense of Eros ('hardly a rounding error', 'we become our own gods'): Descartes' evil demon explains why Holden can never verify the protomolecule-ghost Miller — or even the Roci's bulkhead — is real; Baconian induction and mastery of nature explain why Protogen feeds biomass to the protomolecule ('we can only learn by letting it learn'), though Bacon himself demanded knowledge be shared for universal good; Peirce's pragmatism explains how the Donnager infers stealth ships from their effects and why protomolecule victims count as no longer human; and Dewey's inseparability of means and ends indicts Fred Johnson's readiness to negotiate with Dresden. It culminates in Miller shooting Dresden — 'I killed him because he was making sense' — as the straightest critique of utilitarian calculation, concluding that when empathy is excised (Cortázar's stimulation) or ignored, even science aimed at saving humanity produces Eros, Project Caliban, and the Earth-Mars war.

30.title: It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It
30.file: ch30 - It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It.md
30.relation: Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.

31.title: Fifth Orbit TILTING AT WINDMILLS
31.file: ch31 - Fifth Orbit TILTING AT WINDMILLS.md

32.title: The Burden of the End of the World
32.file: ch32 - The Burden of the End of the World.md
32.relation: Reads Naomi's escape from collapsing Ganymede — sedating Amos to leave the freighter, then stepping out before a crowd of more than a hundred stranded Belters to propose saving only the youngest — as Arendt's 'doing' politics, action justified by the seeing-and-being-seen of shared speech rather than by the strategic 'making' calculus Melissa and Amos use to justify abandoning the crowd. Naomi must alternate between the two — Champa's measured violence organizes the crowd — without letting making become the ethical metric, because, as she says, 'every shitty thing we do makes the next one that much easier.' Marco embodies politics reduced to pure making (abandoning six million on Ceres), Holden stays trapped in righteous strategizing that never defeats the protomolecule's uncertainty, and the chapter closes on Arendt's story of Plato's philosopher-king: trying to eliminate uncertainty by preemptive rule only multiplies risk, so resilience comes from doing politics together.

33.title: Knuckles and the Augustín Gamarra
33.file: ch33 - Knuckles and the Augustín Gamarra.md
33.relation: Deploys Crenshaw's intersectionality to explain why Naomi — the only Belter and only woman aboard the Rocinante — reads as a serial traitor: giving the protomolecule to Fred Johnson out of loyalty to the Belt, leaving Filip to escape Inaros's control of her through motherhood, and siding with Miller after the Dresden shooting ('as a Belter, Miller wasn't wrong'). It scales the analysis up to Belters as a collectively intersectional group — race, class, refugee status, and colonial occupation at once, as with the Weeping Somnambulist fired on carrying 55 refugees and the Ilus colonists framed through the European conquest of the Americas — then walks through Naomi's past with Marco (the Augustín Gamarra bombing that killed 516 people, her suicide attempt, 'the right to walk away') to show that resisting intersecting oppressions forces impossible, betrayal-laden choices, with her chosen family on the Roci as a model of solidarity that crosses identity lines.

34.title: Risky Tradeoffs
34.relation: Maps conflicts between incommensurable kinds of value across the series: moral versus epistemic value in Dresden's 'we become our own gods' defense of Eros and Strickland's knowingly continued torture of children on Io; moral versus aesthetic value in Cortázar calling protomolecule-infected Julie 'beautiful' and Anna Volovodov ignoring Nemeroff's suicidal pleas on the Thomas Prince because she craves the sublime Ring; and epistemic versus prudential value in Iturbi and Janus losing the Arboghast and Okoye calling Holden's nightmares 'an acceptable tradeoff'. The chapter argues that because we can rarely be certain which value should govern, every such tradeoff is itself a moral risk — even a correct choice leaves a residue of sacrificed value, and Dresden's and Cortázar's certainty is reckless because unjustified — before weighing dilemma, permissibility, and ranking models and settling on pluralism, with Holden 'pushing buttons as we find them'.

35.title: Sixth Orbit RIDING THE ROCI
35.file: ch35 - Sixth Orbit RIDING THE ROCI.md

36.title: The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat
36.file: ch36 - The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat.md
36.relation: Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.

37.title: One and Multitudes
37.relation: Reads Naomi through Latina feminist phenomenology — Ortega's 'multiplicitous subjectivity', Lugones's 'world-traveling', Anzaldúa's borderlands — as one subject inhabiting several incompatible social worlds at once: Belter and Roci crewmate, Marco's former partner and Holden's lover, who experiences Miller's killing of Dresden simultaneously as her captain does and 'as a Belter, Miller wasn't wrong.' Du Bois's double consciousness names her two-ness when the Inaros faction pulls her back into a world she can still slip into 'as if she'd never stopped', and Ashford's list of her identities ('radical, betrayed, hid with the Inners, big hero') shows the borderlands Belters occupy between Inner and Outer worlds. The chapter argues this unsettlement is not a defect but a critical vantage: one stream of experience can carry multiple, conflicting meanings simultaneously, and all of it — no part more than another — is who Naomi is.

38.title: On the Other Side of the Ring A Difficult Consequence
38.file: ch38 - On the Other Side of the Ring A Difficult Consequence.md
38.relation: Uses Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk, we would not understand him' and his shift from the Tractatus picture-book model to the Investigations' language-game model to explain why Inners and Belters, though they share a language, still cannot understand each other: 'Rocinante' and 'MCRN Tachi' name the same ship but mean differently, Earth plays the post-scarcity-superpower game around Basic assistance while Mars plays the driven-upstart game and the Belt the liberation game, and Holden's family's casual 'skinnies' slur shows even love cannot supply missing context. The chapter runs through Okoye's lab 'scalpel' joke and the use–mention distinction to make the model precise, then draws the dark consequence: understanding fails at every scale, from Avasarala versus Dawes to Bobbie versus the Laconians to humanity versus the Ring Builders and Unknown Aggressors ('Some of them are even playing the language game of genocide'), leaving Star Trek-style optimism naive and only the small, personal understandings — Naomi, Amos, Bobby — attainable.

7.title: Flesh Is Weak, but Questions Endure
7.file: ch07 - Flesh Is Weak, but Questions Endure.md
7.relation: The editors' introduction recounts how Fallout overcame early adaptation jitters (Bethesda's Peter Hines warned in 2015 that more could go wrong than right in a screen version) because the games' blank overworld maps and faction-defining choices, from the original water-chip quest to New Vegas's player-decided ending, invite wondering about everyone else's story in the wastes. It argues that this world-building raises genuinely philosophical questions - why we are drawn to fictional atrocities, whether wasteland life is too bad to bring children into, whether ghouls and synths are persons, and what makes anything right or wrong - and presents the book's essays as attempts to raise, clarify, and answer them.

8.title: Part 1 LIVING AND DYING IN THE WASTELAND
8.file: ch08 - Part 1 LIVING AND DYING IN THE WASTELAND.md

9.title: Notes
9.relation: Mackenzie Graham uses Fallout 3's Project Purity - James's sacrificial death and the Lone Wanderer's choice among feeding the purifier with their own life, poisoning the water for the Enclave, or destroying it - to ask whether death and posthumous events can be bad for the one who dies. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, the chapter defends deprivationism with the Megaton quest (the Lone Wanderer's desire to save the town is thwarted even if the rearmed bomb destroys it unbeknownst to them) and weighs Feinberg and Pitcher's ante-mortem person against the problem of the subject, using the Great War's redefinition of October 22, 2077 to block backward causation. The 'Blood Ties' quest with the Family's cannibals then raises posthumous wrongs: since no existing subject is harmed or wronged, the chapter ends by asking whether cannibalism is an impersonal wrong against personhood itself, on the model of respecting nature.

10.title: Notes
10.file: ch10 - Notes.md
10.relation: Eric Silverman asks whether the Amazon series' Lucy and Maximus should have children, framing the wasteland through Hobbes's state of nature where life is 'nasty, brutish, and short' and even vaults are limiting experiments. He lays out Benatar's Harm Argument (pain outweighs pleasure, so procreation is procreational Russian roulette) and Shiffrin's Consent Argument (no one consents to being born, as Sartre's 'I did not ask to be born' concedes), then rebuts them: Socrates, the Stoics, and Aristotle make virtue and meaning rather than pleasure the goal of life, so a harsh wasteland full of people needing help suits a virtuous, sacrificial life like the hero's exile at the end of the original Fallout. Parental proxy consent legitimizes procreation as it does children's medical decisions, and Kant's universalization test defeats the demand for pre-natal consent, since universalizing it would eliminate the very rational beings whose consent it protects - so Lucy's 'Okey dokey!' optimism wins.

11.title: Notes
11.file: ch11 - Notes.md
11.relation: David Lawrence opens with Fallout 4's 'Blind Betrayal', where Elder Maxson orders the player to execute Paladin Danse once his synth origin is revealed, and argues that moral status is a matter of capacities - sense of self, notion of past and future, values, life-plans, moral agency - drawing on Charles Taylor's concept of a person and narrative identity, not on biological substrate. Nick Valentine's hunt for Eddie Winter in 'Long Time Coming' and Curie's chosen embodiment in 'Emergent Behavior' show machines weaving reconstructed pasts into new life-plans, while ghouls like Hancock and Raul ('Old School Ghoul') and super mutants like Fawkes (who refuses to enter the lethal radiation chamber: 'I would not rob you of that') and the community-builder Marcus prove branded monsters can be more human than human. The factions embody warring philosophies of moral status: the Institute's property-slavery of its creations, the Brotherhood's 'wisdom of repugnance' (Leon Kass), and the Railroad's capacity-based abolitionism, with DiMA's Far Harbor question - how do you know you are not a synth? - turning the issue on the player.

12.title: Notes
12.file: ch12 - Notes.md
12.relation: Trevor Hedberg asks whether 'Kill Everything' playthroughs of New Vegas are wrong, from the Goodsprings opening (where the player may massacre both Powder Gangers and settlers) to installing a mod that makes Freeside's unkillable children killable. He rejects the empirical aggression argument (the evidence is mixed and effects tiny, and alcohol or contact sports set a precedent) and the Kantian disrespect argument, since Fallout's NPCs - stuck on terrain, repeating dialogue - lack the rational agency the Humanity Formulation protects. The best case against virtual slaughter is Aristotle's virtue ethics: courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice, eudaimonia as activity in accord with virtue, so the morality of playing turns on motives - exploring narratives or seeking combat challenge can be innocent, but killing for the pleasure of settlers' horrified flight corrodes character.

13.title: Part 2 SYNTHS, CYBORGS, AND THE SELF
13.file: ch13 - Part 2 SYNTHS, CYBORGS, AND THE SELF.md

14.title: Notes
14.file: ch14 - Notes.md
14.relation: The Funkes apply Clark and Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis to the Pip-Boy, arguing it meets all three criteria for cognitive extension - availability (worn at all times), reliability (trusted rad and health monitoring), and active cognitive engagement (V.A.T.S. offloads targeting calculations) - so it is part of the Sole Survivor's and Courier's minds, as in 'The Glowing Sea' and the search for Virgil's cure. Donna Haraway's cyborg frames this human-machine hybridity alongside cyberdogs and Kellogg, but Fallout inverts her liberationist vision: the Pip-Boy is a survival lifeline forced by the wasteland, not an emancipatory choice, making the cyborg a dystopian necessity. Comparing the Pip-Boy with cochlear implants, prosthetics, and brain-computer interfaces, and the Old World Blues Think Tank with a dehumanizing bio-tech extreme, the chapter uses Alison Kafer's feminist crip critique to insist real augmentation carries pain, stigma, and unequal access the game's frictionless fiction erases, closing on a cautious transhumanist note.

15.title: Notes
15.file: ch15 - Notes.md
15.relation: Walter Barta presents transhumanism as a real philosophy (via Bostrom's history of the movement and 'Why I Want to Be a Posthuman When I Grow Up') that Fallout both practices and indicts: ghouls, FEV super mutants and the Children of the Cathedral, stimpak-Mentat-Jet self-medication, Brotherhood power armor, Mr. House, the Master, Robobrains, John Henry Eden, and Liberty Prime all embody enhancement or post-humanity, and the level-up loop makes every player a transhumanist. Bostrom's transhumanist value of 'the opportunity to explore' maps onto leaving Vault 13 for the open world, but the Red Queen race becomes the game's adaptive-leveling treadmill, and C.S. Lewis's Abolition of Man plus Fukuyama's 'Factor-X' warn that optimization can delete what made enhancement worth wanting - as when the Overseer exiles the too-powerful Vault 13 hero and the Enclave President rationalizes genocidal bioweapons ('No price is too high for the survival of the human race'). Existential risk (Toby Ord's Precipice, Bostrom's vulnerable world hypothesis) supplies the final warning: the G.E.C.K.'s energy is also a destruction kit, and the cycle of war repeats until post-humanity or extinction.

16.title: Notes
16.file: ch16 - Notes.md
16.relation: Albert Spencer reads Fallout 4's synth crisis as a philosophy-of-mind allegory - Brotherhood dualism, Institute reductive physicalism, Railroad functionalism - which he grounds in the classical pragmatists: Peirce's sign-interpreting mind, James's stream of consciousness, and Dewey's interactive consciousness make personhood a matter of social participation rather than essence. Quests dramatize the stakes: 'Human Error' has Covenant's interrogation of Amelia Stockton enact Du Bois's double consciousness (self-understanding against a devaluing gaze, as with the tragic Phyllis Daily), the Sole Survivor of 'The Battle of Bunker Hill' and Far Harbor becomes Anzaldua's Nepantlera straddling the human/synth binary, and the Railroad's memory-wipe 'resets' reproduce the domination they fight by ignoring Crenshaw's intersectionality (the Feral Historian's case that the Railroad kills the selves it saves). Acadia, where DiMA murdered and replaced Captain Avery to preserve peace, becomes Jane Addams's test case of democracy as associated living - an imperfect, lying community that nonetheless offers the only future of shared synth-human personhood.

17.title: Notes
17.relation: Matthew Watts sorts Fallout's artificial beings into cyborgs, synths, and pure robots and tests each against a theory of the self: Locke's memory theory explains the Robobrain socialites of Vault 118 and Nick Valentine's implanted prewar past, Parfit's psychological continuity (identity as a matter of degree) makes the Old World Blues Think Tank a caricature of a self stretched too thin, and Putnam's machine-table functionalism with multiple realizability (the Red Menace holotape running on any hardware) undermines Covenant's SAFE test by making function, not substrate, the mark of a mind. DiMA's excision of his own guilty memory in Far Harbor shows identity as Evan Thompson's enactive process rather than stored recall, since pruning memories can maintain or improve the self-in-progress. For moral standing below full personhood, Nussbaum's capabilities approach fits Curie's flourishing (research, companionship, watching a sunset in a synth body) and Singer's sentience criterion fits Victor the Securitron's avoidance of harm, exposing 'substrate prejudice' as a robot analog of speciesism - down to ED-E's triumphant arrival on the West Coast.

18.title: Part 3 OVERSEER, OVERSEEN FALLOUT AND POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY
18.file: ch18 - Part 3 OVERSEER, OVERSEEN FALLOUT AND POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY.md

19.title: Notes
19.relation: John Irish reads the Amazon series' Vault 33 as Locke's Two Treatises staged and then betrayed: Overseer elections (Betty Pearson against Reg McPhee and Woody Thomas), town-council deliberation over captured Vault 32 raiders, and Lucy's 1950s-styled domesticity all mimic natural equality, consent of the governed, majority rule, and the preservation of property. Norm's discovery that every election is rigged in favor of cryo-preserved technocrats from Vault 31, that Lucy's marriage 'application' is engineered population control, and that Vault-Tec executives - including Lucy's mother Barb - voted to launch the Great War itself shows Locke's forms of consent, law, and rights preserved as empty ceremony. The chapter's argument is that Enlightenment liberalism stripped of transparency becomes authoritarian experiment management: consent becomes choreography in a commonwealth that is really a lab, right down to composting the raiders' bodies.

20.title: Notes
20.relation: Curry and Lang test 'War never changes' through Hobbes and Xunzi: the wasteland - where the Ghoul asks who ever elected the 'President' in 'The Trap' and Cooper Howard decays outside all political order - is Hobbes's state of nature of restless power-seeking, while Xunzi's claim that bad human nature needs ritual (li) and righteousness (yi) explains a world with no moral education, where Elder Cleric Quintus pairs noble talk with 'power is taken, not given'. Fallout's Great War then fails every just-war test: China's invasion of Alaska stretches just cause, the corporatist US lacks right authority, propaganda undid last resort, mutually assured destruction explodes proportionality, and Vault-Tec shelters plus battlefield mini-nukes breach discrimination and proportionality in bello - with Operation Anchorage's propaganda simulation illustrating the revisionist point that fighting cleanly cannot redeem an unjust war. China's 'righteous army' (yi bing) tradition - Sunzi's strategic restraint, Mohist defensive war, Mengzi's true king, Xunzi's punitive righteous war - leaves no trace beyond Captain Zao, so the war's constancy marks the failure of every philosophical attempt to bind war to justice.

21.title: Notes
21.file: ch21 - Notes.md
21.relation: Sergio Uruena argues the Brotherhood of Steel converts preservation into monopoly: Scribe Yearling buys prewar books as sacred relics, squads seize a settlement's water-purification rigs, and Knight Titus dies on a mission to recover 'a fucking toaster' - read through Langdon Winner's 'Do Artifacts Have Politics?' and Feenberg's contrast between authoritarian and democratic rationalizations of technology. Fricker's epistemic injustice does the central work: 'Blind Betrayal' makes Danse's testimony inadmissible once his synth identity is known (testimonial injustice), while hoarding diagnostic terminals, schematics, and archives strips wastelanders of the interpretive devices through which they understand their world (hermeneutical injustice, extended via Ihde's hermeneutic mediation of technology). Jasanoff's co-production explains how this gatekeeping builds social order itself - Maximus is trained into obedience alongside repair, with access tiered even inside the Brotherhood - against the Followers of the Apocalypse's open archives, closing the parallel between locked bunkers and Silicon Valley's gated source code.

22.title: Notes
22.file: ch22 - Notes.md
22.relation: Dal Barco maps Lucy's arc in the Amazon series onto Plato's cave stage by stage: Vault 33's fake sky, curated history lessons, and Vault-Tec-managed information are the shadow-puppet show, her first step into the sun after Hank's abduction by Moldaver is the freed prisoner's blinding ascent, the hidden hospital vault tempts her (and Maximus, who wants to stay) like the return to the cave, and the truth - her father helped orchestrate the nuclear war, her mother is now a ghoul - plays the role the sun and the Good play in the Republic. Plato's claim that only the educated philosopher who has seen beyond the cave should govern (Republic 496a, 519a-d) explains why Lucy, unlike the frightened Norm or the tempted Maximus, goes back out into the wastes: she is becoming the philosopher-ruler whose hard-won knowledge enables Moldaver to restore power to the surface and begin a civilization no longer built on shadows. The chapter answers its own question - yes, it was worth leaving the vault for the truth.

23.title: Notes
23.relation: Andrea Conque argues the adult-free ('Mungo-free') children of Little Lamplight are genuinely political: they socialize each other into distrust of grownups (mandatory exile at 16 to Big Town), elect mayors by secret popular vote - MacCready's punch against Princess was a coup made legitimate by subsequent election - and fill every office from doctor Lucy to teacher Joseph to Knock Knock, whose Vault Boy jokes 'keep the peace' against social isolation. Sherif's Robber's Cave experiment supplies the comparison: unlike the Eagles and Rattlers, Lamplighters avoid in-group conflict because the radiation-absorbing cave fungus and shared survival give them permanent superordinate goals, while Biwwy's high-damage 'wazer wifle' shows they deter oppression by being, not just posturing as, tough. Against MacCready's claim of 'pure anarchy', the chapter concludes Little Lamplight is the Capital Wasteland's most successful government - freer and better ordered than Megaton, Andale, Paradise Falls, or even the Republic of Dave.

25.title: Notes
25.relation: The chapter asks whether Fallout's chems should be banned and answers no on Millian grounds: chem addiction harms only the user (and is trivially curable at any wasteland doctor, unlike Cait's Psycho addiction in Fallout 4, which shows what real addiction actually costs), so the New California Republic's firing squads for chem dealers and Caesar's Legion's crucifixion of the smuggler Anders violate the Harm Principle. Combat chem use is self-protection, drugging a Charisma check harms no one because NPCs act on their own programmed preferences, and paternalism fares no better in a wasteland where a failed speech check can get you killed. The analysis then extends to real-world performance-enhancing drugs: permissible for soldiers fighting a just war, but coercive in sports, where PED users force clean athletes to choose between their own health risks.

26.title: Notes
26.file: ch26 - Notes.md
26.relation: When Lucy shouts the Golden Rule at the Ghoul after he dunks her in a poison river to bait a gulper, the chapter takes her appeal seriously and grades the rival 'rules' of the wasteland (the Iron, Arsenic, Neon, and Bronze Rules) before arguing the Golden Rule needs St. Francis's 'in a similar situation' clause. Kant's criminal-versus-judge objection disqualifies the unqualified Platinum Rule of treating others as they want, Nietzsche's charge that mutual restraint denies life is parried, and Rawlsian imagining of ourselves in divergent positions explains why family partiality like Lucy's search for Hank is consistent with the rule. The chapter closes with Lucy's saving of the Ghoul retold as the Good Samaritan parable, extending the rule even to enemies.

27.title: Notes
27.relation: The chapter maps four schools of ethics onto Fallout 4's Commonwealth: Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Preston Garvey's settlement defense as the mean between recklessness and cowardice and temperance as moderate chem use; Kant's Categorical Imperative is tested on stealing ammo in Concord and on the Battle of Bunker Hill choice to warn the Railroad, where loyal silence to Father fails universalization and treats synths merely as means. Aquinas's natural law ethics, keyed to the telos of power armor, workbenches, and Pip-Boys, condemns the Institute's creation of synths by analogy to the IVF debate while still demanding dignity for synths who already exist. Finally, Bentham's utilitarianism is the one framework under which Father's Institute — adaptive labor force, scientific progress, stability and order — can sincerely believe itself morally justified.

28.title: Notes
28.relation: Tracing Fallout's own censorship history — the GURPS licensing cancellation threat, the invisibility of child NPCs in the European release, the moral panic after Columbine — the chapter asks whether it is wrong to simulate evil, framing the issue with Morgan Luck's gamer's dilemma. Plato's cave and the Forms ground the 'media impacts morals' worry: games are shadows of shadows whose simulated vice accumulates 'a large evil in our souls', which is also why Lucy's Vault upbringing leaves her underprepared for the wasteland's emotions. Against this, Aristotle's catharsis and Schulzke's claim that Fallout trains phronesis support depicting wrongdoing as practice for moral judgment, so the chapter concludes the right wrongs to depict are whichever maximize the simulation of choice, with Braun's player-controlled Tranquility Lane simulation as the dystopian counter-model.

29.title: Notes
29.relation: Weighing Vault-Tec's secret experiments — Vault 11's yearly human sacrifice, Vault 13's 200-year lockdown, the cryogenic freezing of the Sole Survivor — the chapter asks whether the ends could ever justify the vaults. On Kant's Universal Law and Humanity Formulations the answer is flatly no: dwellers were deceived into becoming mere means to data, whatever the hypothetical space-colonization motive that designer Tim Cain favors. Act and rule utilitarianism in Bentham's tradition give a more equivocal verdict — exposed deception would doom any future cooperation, yet safeguarding humanity might in extraordinary circumstances tip the calculus — and the chapter situates the games in real research-ethics history from the eugenics era to the Tuskegee study and the Belmont Report.

30.title: Part 5 A BEAUTIFUL DISASTER THE AESTHETICS OF FALLOUT
30.file: ch30 - Part 5 A BEAUTIFUL DISASTER THE AESTHETICS OF FALLOUT.md

31.title: Notes
31.relation: The chapter asks why Fallout's genre fusion — RPG plus first-person shooter plus post-apocalyptic Western plus black comedy — coheres rather than collapses, and answers with Kendall Walton's 'Categories of Art': works carry standard, variable, and contra-standard properties relative to each category they belong to, so every added category raises the number of expectations a designer must meet. C. Thi Nguyen's account of games as prescribing striving play explains why obstacle-free software would not even count as a game, while a hypothetical forced Moby-Dick book-report quest illustrates a contra-standard property that 'does violence' to the category. Fallout's S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system implicitly promises 'play how you want', so weak melee builds or underused speech skills are aesthetic risk — the designer's gamble that players will recognize every fused genre at once.

32.title: Notes
32.relation: The chapter argues modding is the deepest freedom Bethesda-era Fallout offers: Sartre and Beauvoir's absolute freedom and facticity explain why vanilla players merely pick among given priorities while modders inject new meaning into the game, constrained but not determined by the Creation Engine. Spinoza's causal determinism becomes a model of 'immanent freedom' — just as Spinoza's agent is free by understanding their place in Nature's web of causes, the modder is free by grasping how they fit into the load orders, plugin files, and tools of the Creation Kit. Simone Weil's ideal of self-directed labor culminates the argument: Fallout: London's five-year, unpaid total conversion (the Atta-Boy, Churchill the bulldog, the punk-anarchist Pistols) embodies the convergence of thought and action that Moira Brown's line about putting broken glass back together captures.

33.title: Notes
33.relation: The chapter argues Fallout 4's grip comes not from graphical fidelity but from first-person moral agency: deciding the fate of Gen 3 synths who do not know they are synths — supporting their escape, hunting them, or installing them as unwitting spies — forces the player through emotionally real moral deliberation. It connects this to Turing's worry about proving to another that you think ('it could've been me in their shoes') and to Nagel's bat, proposing that imagining what it is like to be a synth is a stepping stone toward ever stranger perspectives. Playing thus becomes the joy of actually doing philosophy — reawakening imagination, reshuffling our space of possibilities, and returning us to our own problems refreshed rather than merely escaped.

34.title: Notes
34.relation: Against the complaint that Fallout 3 is just Morrowind or Oblivion with a post-apocalyptic coat of paint, the chapter tests three aesthetic theories. Aristotle's didactic mimesis explains the tragic 'war never changes' framing and its moral lessons about resource wars and the AI president John Henry Eden, while Francis Hutcheson's 'uniformity amidst variety' locates Fallout's fun in the orderly S.P.E.C.I.A.L. rules and the 'crunch' of complex gear and crafting. Clive Bell's formalism finally secures the difference: Vault Boy's atomic-age cartoon style, the Pip-Boy's green monochrome, and the western motifs are formal properties no Elder Scrolls game shares, making Fallout 3 a formally distinct artwork to be appreciated for its own sake.

35.title: Notes
35.relation: The chapter rereads Fallout 3's original Project Purity ending — the forced walk into the lethal radiation chamber while radiation-immune followers Fawkes, Sergeant RL-3, and Charon each refuse — as the game's worst case of narrative paradox: the pre-authored story compels an action the player-authored character narrative cannot accommodate. On the narrative-identity view (mounted against Galen Strawson's denial of narrativity), the Karma system and companions like Fawkes matter through the story the player tells, so an evil, greed-driven Lone Wanderer dying nobly is a 'bad death' that unravels the motivation for the entire playthrough. Dying well requires death to fit the story, and Sarah Lyons's substitutable sacrifice — or a last-page redemption epiphany — is what restores narrative coherence.

37.title: Notes
37.relation: Opening from the author's own grief — she nearly stopped playing Fallout 4 because its murdered spouse and kidnapped son echoed the loss of her real infant son — the chapter applies the ethics of care of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto to Fallout's wasteland. Care relationships structure the games: the Fallout 3 father whose flight from Vault 101 propels the plot, Dogmeat's loyal responsiveness as relational reciprocity, and the Fallout 4 son Shaun, where caring for your child collides with caring for a Commonwealth his Institute endangers. Settlement-building, faction choice (Lyons's Brotherhood handing out clean water versus the Railroad's liberation of synths), and even the Black Widow perk path that saves Megaton all become care-laden moral acts — care as protest against the wasteland's ethos of bare survival.

38.title: Notes
38.relation: The chapter asks why audiences relish stories of civilization's end and answers with psychology: the wasteland is Hobbes's 'nasty, brutish, and short' (raiders abducting Hank, Vault-Tec's experiments on dwellers), yet Ernest Becker's death-denial and Maslow's hierarchy of needs explain the appeal — fiction lets us confront mortality safely while watching characters meet needs for security, control, and meaning. The show's scenes carry the argument: the Vault 33 Council suppressing Lucy's search party trades freedom for safety, Maximus letting Titus bleed out reclaims control of his destiny, and Lucy's gift of life-sustaining vials to the unconscious Ghoul models hope and retained humanity. Apocalypse originally means 'an uncovering', so these narratives reveal what viewers value and let them rehearse their own endings.

39.title: Notes
39.relation: Why is living in Fallout's hell — ghouls pouring through the ceiling, radroach dinners, Kellogg, Pickman, Vault-Tec — fun? The chapter tests the two classic solutions to the puzzle of dark art: Aristotle's katharsis works for Oedipus but stumbles because playing is actively enjoyable rather than unpleasant purgation, and RPGs blur feeling pity for a character with fear for oneself; Hume's 'Of Tragedy' account, on which artistic skill transforms negative emotions into pleasure by mixing them with beauty, fails because the wasteland is deliberately ugly, not beautiful, and Hume never explains how the transformation works. Neither the ancient nor the modern answer quite succeeds, so the 2,500-year-old puzzle is left open, like the best unfinished quests.

2.title: You Better Not Read This, Pal: An Introduction to Family Guy and Philosophy
2.file: ch02 - You Better Not Read This, Pal An Introduction to Family Guy and Philosophy.md
2.relation: Wisnewski's mock-hostile introduction argues that Family Guy is 'both really deep and really stupid': the show's vulgarity (Stewie's matricidal schemes, Quagmire's perversions, jokes about religion and disability) occasions genuine insight into the human condition. Its central claim is that the show's offense is exactly what we need, because being forced to laugh at what we hold sacred demands that we account for ourselves and admit our commitments may not be necessary. The introduction thereby defends the very project of doing philosophy on a cartoon, including 'the aesthetics of the fart joke.'

3.title: Part I: Those Good Ole' Fashion Values on which we used to rely
3.file: ch03 - Part I Those Good Ole' Fashion Values on which we used to rely.md

4.title: Killing the Griffins: A Murderous Exposition of Postmodernism
4.file: ch04 - Killing the Griffins A Murderous Exposition of Postmodernism.md
4.relation: Wisnewski stages a mock murder of the Griffin family to argue that Family Guy 'oozes the postmodern.' Baudrillard's Disneyland analysis explains why the Griffins are dangerously real: they know they are cartoons (the 'we've been cancelled' scene listing failed Fox shows), so their family is no less real than ours, which is likewise modeled on TV images. Lyotard's 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' is embodied in the show's joke-about-everything: the Petoria episode mocking the UN and dictators (Milosevic, Hussein, Khadafi) who party over Seinfeld. The chapter's twist is that Foucault's power/knowledge rescues postmodernism from cynicism: labeling Quagmire a 'pervert' situates him in power relations, but like Socrates, Jesus, Buddha, and Gandhi, deviants may just act uniquely, so we can be cynics about grand stories yet still fight locally (against the FCC, for tolerance).

5.title: Family Guy and God: Should Believers Take Offense?
5.file: ch05 - Family Guy and God Should Believers Take Offense.md
5.relation: VanArragon, a believer and fan, compares Family Guy's religious mockery (Peter asking at communion whether Christ was 'wasted 24 hours a day', God hitting on women in a bar, the pope left dangling from a statue, the fake Passion of the Christ II trailer) with The Simpsons' gentler treatment (dream-God, Barney's innocent blunders), finding Family Guy deliberately offensive without tact or sympathy. He tests two defenses: Kant's requirement to treat people as ends rather than means (mocking believers for laughs uses them as mere means) and Aristotle's virtue of moderation in laughter (the show pushes toward the extreme of nothing-is-sacred, unlike Gary Larson's Far Side). Conceding the show raises real questions (transubstantiation, God's gender, Stewie finding God 'deliciously evil' in the Old Testament), he concludes the offense is not justified by any benefit, yet the portrayals are so absurd that believer-fans do not actually laugh at God and need not take offense.

6.title: Quagmire: Virtue and Perversity
6.relation: Miller uses Aristotle to assess whether Quagmire's sex obsession is a vice. Eudaimonia, not the fleeting pleasure of 'giggity-giggity', is the telos of action, and Quagmire aims at pleasure, so he is not flourishing; Aristotle's dissipated person, pained by absent pleasures, 'must have been thinking of Quagmire.' The Cleveland-Loretta-Quagmire affair episode ('The Cleveland-Loretta Quagmire') supplies paradigm cases of the Golden Mean: Cleveland first shows a deficiency of anger (apologizing to his cheating wife) then an excess (near-homicide), while Quagmire's boxing match shows courage between rashness and cowardice. On temperance, Quagmire is a slave to his sex drive (roofies, the diary 'Jackpot'), yet the chapter ends by defending him: he cares for Joan, distracts the social worker to rescue Stewie, and is honest about his passions, making him 'the most virtuous pervert he can be.'

7.title: Francis Griffin and the Church of the Holy Fonz: Religious Exclusivism and Real Religion
7.file: ch07 - Francis Griffin and the Church of the Holy Fonz Religious Exclusivism and Real Religion.md
7.relation: Johnson argues that Francis Griffin's Catholic exclusivism (condemning Lois the Protestant to purgatory, calling Meg a harlot, founding Peter's Church of the Holy Fonz an 'abomination') is unjustified and immoral. Using Plantinga on exclusivism and a Quagmire-style inductive argument ('SHiTE' — Scripture, Historical tradition, religious Experience — leads rival religions to incompatible truths, so it is an unreliable witness like Quagmire's false alibis), he holds that no one's religious beliefs are adequately justified. Weighing Clifford's ethics of belief (the unseaworthy ship) against James's will to believe, he concludes one may hold beliefs without evidence but may not harm others or forcibly evangelize on their basis. The heap/sorites puzzle shows no criterion marks Fonzieism as an 'unreal' religion — Peter's founding experience parallels Joseph Smith's — so the moral is religious acceptance: disagree freely, but keep your SHiTE to yourself.

8.title: Part II: Lucky there's a family guy! (And what a family!)
8.file: ch08 - Part II Lucky there's a family guy! (And what a family!).md

9.title: Let Us Now Praise Clueless Men: Peter Griffin and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - Let Us Now Praise Clueless Men Peter Griffin and Philosophy.md
9.relation: Samet analyzes Peter's cluelessness through the 'I Need a Jew' song from 'When You Wish Upon a Weinstein', where Peter eagerly embraces stereotypes and anti-Semitic cliches with no reflection — making him the antiphilosopher, a paradigm of Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Borrowing Berenson on Giotto, he argues Family Guy, like great painting, gives us a 'realer than real' window on the unreflective, stimulus-response layer of our own cognition (the toddler clinging at day care, the Onion kitten 'thinking of nothing but murder'). Hobbes's theory of laughter as 'sudden glory' at deformity in another explains why Peter's fictional cluelessness is funny while real deformity evokes sympathy: comedy lets us glory that 'there but for reflection go I.' Finally, philosophy's Nagelian 'view from nowhere' totality is inherently unfunny because humor lives in the sheer particularity of experience.

10.title: Lois: Portrait of a Mother (Or, Nevermind Death, Motherhood is a Bitch)
10.file: ch10 - Lois Portrait of a Mother (Or, Nevermind Death, Motherhood is a Bitch).md
10.relation: Empey frames mothering (following Sara Ruddick's 'Maternal Thinking') as a disciplined response to a child's demands of preservation, growth, and social acceptability — even for a matricidal psychopath like Stewie. Lois cultivates the virtues of prudence (safeguarding the Rainy Day Fund against Peter's volcano insurance), tolerance, and peacefulness (enduring Stewie's lamp blows and Peter's laziness; her two Christmas and 'Lethal Weapons' violent eruptions are cured by appeals to her motherhood). The chapter then turns political: drawing on Okin, Williams, and Hays, it shows mothers' vulnerability by marriage, the incompatibility of the 'ideal worker' and 'intensive mother' models, and Peter's devaluing of Lois's theater directing. Peter's basement bar, where Lois sings nightly while minding the kids, models the institutional coordination (family plus economy) mothers need — until Peter's jealousy wrecks it.

11.title: Mmmyez: Stewie and the Seven Deadly Sins
11.file: ch11 - Mmmyez Stewie and the Seven Deadly Sins.md
11.relation: Kaye argues Stewie is funny because he portrays a truth we repress: Augustine's doctrine of original sin (defended as the only answer to why God lets the innocent suffer, and grounded in the pear-tree and jealous-infant episodes of the Confessions) — no one is innocent, not even babies. Systematically cataloging Stewie through Aquinas's Seven Deadly Sins, she shows lust (the Rupert-the-gay-teddy-bear projection, 'wee-wee stricken with rigor mortis', inverting Freud's Oedipal complex since Stewie hates his mother and barely tolerates his father), gluttony (hoarding Lois's breast milk, an orgy of fig newtons), sloth as Aquinas's 'oppressive sorrow' and malicious indignation ('Why don't you burn in hell?'), avarice, anger as revenge (bombs and graham crackers), envy (locking Jeremy in the car trunk), and pride, the Queen of Vices — Stewie's god complex ('Omnipotence. Gotta get me some of that'). Stewie's lone possibly-decent moment (warning Brian not to mock upside-down Jake Tucker's face) is left as the one loose thread.

12.title: The Other Children: The Importance of Meg and Chris
12.file: ch12 - The Other Children The Importance of Meg and Chris.md
12.relation: Dohnimm argues Meg and Chris matter because they lack essence: unlike predictable one-gag characters (pervert Quagmire, homicidal Stewie), their traits are accidental — Meg stays Meg after her 'Don't Make Me Over' makeover, Chris stays Chris despite flashes of artistic talent. On Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, character (hexis) explains action, but Meg and Chris are inexplicable (Chris hitting on his mother, claiming 'My dad is smarter than your dad' when they share one). The Isen and Levin dime-in-the-phone-booth helping experiment grounds the situationist alternative: tiny situational factors, not character, predict helping — Quagmire is predictable, but Chris (speaking hip-hop, covering himself in honey for ants) is not. Finally, Sartre's bad faith reframes them: appealing to fixed character is fleeing our radical freedom, so the 'anti-characters' Meg and Chris are the show's most realistic and philosophically honest figures.

13.title: He Thinks He's People: How Brian Made Personhood for the Dogs
13.file: ch13 - He Thinks He's People How Brian Made Personhood for the Dogs.md
13.relation: Argues that Brian the dog is a person because personhood, on a Kantian reading, requires a rational nature rather than species membership: Peter making Brian beg in 'Brian: Portrait of a Dog,' the councilman's 'Why are we listening to a dog?', and Chris's 'You don't have a soul!' in 'North by North Quahog' all wrongly treat humanity (or a soul) as the criterion, while Descartes' mechanical account of animal bodies is invoked to show the soul cannot be empirically tested. The chapter then applies the humanity-formulation of the categorical imperative both ways: Stewie framing the maid in 'Road to Rhode Island' shows treating persons as mere means, while Brian's Christmas-sweater lie to Lois shows how Kantian duty is stricter than the Golden Rule. Finally it grades Brian's own conduct as family conscience and drunk (his lapses like framing Jake Tucker, his condescension to Peter, his disrespected self in 'The Thin White Line'), concluding Brian owes the same duties he is owed.

14.title: Part III: You expected more lyrics, but you're getting logic, comedy, and the logic of comedy
14.file: ch14 - Part III You expected more lyrics, but you're getting logic, comedy, and the logic of comedy.md

15.title: The Logic of Expectation: Family Guy and the Non Sequitur
15.file: ch15 - The Logic of Expectation Family Guy and the Non Sequitur.md
15.relation: Argues that Family Guy's non sequiturs only seem random because they reverse specific expectations, so the show has a 'logic of expectation' even where it flouts inference: the Supreme Court fraternity hazing in 'Let's Go to the Hop,' Stewie's aristocratic-baby role reversal, Death hiding beer on his breath in 'Wasted Talent,' the Kool-Aid Man's sheepish exit in 'Death Has a Shadow,' and cutaways that run on shared pop-culture associations like Peter's 'no whammy' chant. The chapter deploys Kierkegaard's claim that wherever there is contradiction the comical is present, Schopenhauer's analysis of the ludicrous, Wittgenstein's joke-book remark, and Russell's ideal of disambiguating ambiguous sentences (Peter's 'I can also vomit' reply to Lois). It closes metaphysically: against Spinoza's necessity and Hume's 'one damn thing after another,' Quahog is not William James's 'mere withness' world because the gags depend on an orderly baseline, which Peter himself demonstrates by wearing a cardboard TV frame in 'I Never Met the Dead Man'.

16.title: What Are You Laughing At (And Why)? Exploring the Humor of Family Guy
16.file: ch16 - What Are You Laughing At (And Why) Exploring the Humor of Family Guy.md
16.relation: Runs Hobbes's superiority theory, Freud's relief theory, and Kant's incongruity theory against Family Guy jokes (Peter failing 'What color is a fire truck?' in 'Petarded,' the 1956 workplace sensitivity film in 'I Am Peter, Hear Me Roar,' the fire-truck hunting gazelles) to argue no single theory covers everything. Against Ken Tucker's charge of cheap mean humor, it uses Aristotle's idea that laughter's proper function is enforcing social norms to claim parodies of mean-spirited humor laugh AT the mean-spirited speaker, not his target, and then applies Russell's solution to the problem of other minds to the writers' intentions in 'When You Wish Upon a Weinstein': Peter's established idiocy (volcano-insurance gambler's fallacy) and Cleveland's corrective lines are the context clues that the song mocks anti-Semites rather than Jews.

17.title: Thinkin' is Freakin' Sweet: Family Guy and Fallacies
17.file: ch17 - Thinkin' is Freakin' Sweet Family Guy and Fallacies.md
17.relation: A logic primer built from Family Guy clips: it teaches premises and conclusions by reconstructing Peter's Y2K bomb-shelter argument in 'DaBoom,' contrasts deduction with induction via Brian's fart-powered descent in 'Wasted Talent' and the show's 'remember the last time?' flashbacks, and then diagnoses named fallacies. Stewie's vow to destroy all vegetables after one bad broccoli exemplifies hasty generalization, Peter's smear campaign against Lois's candidacy in 'Running Mates' is ad hominem, Francis Griffin's hellfire pronouncements in 'Holy Crap' are appeal to inappropriate authority, and Peter's 'if Liza is wrong, then I don't want to know what right is' shows blind deference to celebrity.

18.title: The Simpsons Already Did It! This Show Is A Freakin' Rip-Off!
18.file: ch18 - The Simpsons Already Did It! This Show Is A Freakin' Rip-Off!.md
18.relation: Takes up South Park's 'Simpsons did it!' charge and argues Family Guy is not a rip-off but a postmodern artwork: it tests representation, expression, and form theories of art (Hamlet, Guernica, sonnet form) and finds the show fails all three, since a martini-sipping college-educated dog and non-narrative cutaways fit none. Following Danto, Lyotard, and Baudrillard, it claims the show deliberately raises 'what is art?' while dissolving original and copy into hyperreality: Peter worships the Fonz and builds him a church in 'The Father, the Son, and the Holy Fonz,' lives inside television with a cardboard frame in 'I Never Met the Dead Man,' and 'Da Boom' turns out to be Pam Ewing's dream, so the obvious borrowing from The Simpsons is the point, like Warhol's Brillo Boxes or Duchamp's L.H.O.O.Q.

20.title: Is Brian More of a Person than Peter? (scan merges: Of Wills, Wantons, and Wives)
20.file: ch20 - Is Brian More of a Person than Peter (scan merges Of Wills, Wantons, and Wives).md
20.relation: Uses Frankfurt's distinction between first-order desires, second-order desires, and the wanton to argue Brian is more of a person than Peter: Brian's therapy-driven realization in 'Brian in Love' that he does not want to want Lois is a genuine second-order desire, while Peter's TV fixation in 'I Never Met the Dead Man' (wearing a cardboard TV frame, swapping TV for family without reflection) leaves him a wanton, and Cleveland and even Quagmire scrape into personhood. The chapter then turns to weakness of will from Aristotle's akrasia onward, bringing in Searle's claim in Rationality in Action that choice happens in uncaused 'gaps' between desire and action, so acting against one's better judgment can evidence rather than defeat rationality, with R. Jay Wallace's willpower-based volitionism rounding out the action theory.

21.title: The Ego is a Housewife Named Lois
21.file: ch21 - The Ego is a Housewife Named Lois.md
21.relation: Maps Freud's structural model of the mind onto the Griffin household: Stewie is the id (the broccoli-destroying weather machine in 'I Never Met the Dead Man,' the mind-control device foiled by Bill Cosby in 'Brian Does Hollywood'), Brian is the super-ego (talking kleptomaniac Lois into surrendering in 'Breaking Out Is Hard to Do'), and Lois is the ego that reality-tests and restrains both, with the id-ego miscommunication mirrored in Lois never understanding Stewie's speech. The Oedipus complex does the interpretive heavy lifting: Stewie's 'damn you, vile woman' obsession is misdirected maternal longing, Brian's 'Brian in Love' confession of love for his figurative mother resolves the complex and founds his moral boundaries, and Peter's Church of the Holy Fonz reads as failed father-identification, religion as substitute for the father.

22.title: The Lives and Times of Stewie Griffin
22.file: ch22 - The Lives and Times of Stewie Griffin.md
22.relation: Uses Stewie Griffin: The Untold Story (Stewie's ride with Stu to 2035, then his RPG-wedding killing of Vanessa at Lois's request) to argue that changing the past is impossible: David Lewis's definition of time travel as a discrepancy between personal and external time yields the grandfather paradox if Stewie guns for Carter Pewterschmidt, and Nicholas Smith's second-time-around fallacy shows Stewie cannot prevent his own pool accident because the event he revisits would no longer be the event. The Deutsch-Lockwood quantum-multiverse rescue is examined and rejected, since hopping to a universe-B past is travel across timelines rather than genuine time travel, and the alternative would smuggle in fatalism about the traveler's causal laws.

23.title: Kierkegaard and the Norm (MacDonald) of Death
23.file: ch23 - Kierkegaard and the Norm (MacDonald) of Death.md
23.relation: Reads Family Guy's personified Death (Norm MacDonald) through Kierkegaard's 'At a Graveside': the sprained ankle in 'Death is a Bitch' mocks the mistake of thinking death's arrival can be postponed, Death's boozing and cocoa complaints violate death's indefinability and the appropriate fear of it, and the clipboard-carrying harvester of 'Death Lives' treats death as the general human condition rather than my death, exactly Kierkegaard's criticism of Epicurus. But drawing on the Postscript's account of the comic as a painless contradiction that shows what not to do, the chapter concludes Death is a Kierkegaardian parody: its very absurdity (the high-five that kills a fan in 'I Take Thee Quagmire') exposes and corrects our superficial norms about death, unlike earnest personifications such as Meet Joe Black.

24.file: ch24 - Appendix Everything you ever needed to know about Meg Griffin.md
