8.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
8.relation: Benjamin Chandler argues that Final Fantasy VII realizes Roland Barthes's ideal of the writerly text: its nine playable characters carry bundles of preset signifiers (Cloud's spiky hair, Aeris's Cetra fate) that players multiply through customization, so each player produces the game's narrative for themselves. He shows how identification with Cloud makes the Sector 7 plate drop feel like the player's own moral burden, how Cloud's identity crisis and Aeris's death force players to reinterpret the whole text, and how Crisis Core (playing the doomed Zack), the passive film Advent Children (the least writerly text), and Dirge of Cerberus (Vincent) add further entry points into the FFVII universe.

9.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
9.relation: Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.

10.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Alex Nuttall applies Hume's essay on the standard of taste to video games as art: beauty is not in objects (Sin's FFX rendering is just digital information) but in trained sentiment, yet quality differences are real, as the gap between Final Fantasy VII and the broken Superman 64 shows. Using the Malboro's Bad Breath as a metaphor for the confused, blinded, charmed state of novice judges, he lays out Hume's remedies of practice, repeated viewing, comparison, and reason against bias, and defends Hume against the circularity charge that good judges and masterpieces like FFVII define each other.

11.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md

12.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Jay Foster runs a conceptual analysis of Marlene's opening description of the Lifestream in Advent Children, showing it can be read literally (a holist-organicist living planet, AVALANCHE's view) or metaphorically (a reductionist-mechanist aggregate of energies, Shinra's and Hojo's view). Comparing Dr. Cid's Gaia in The Spirits Within with James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis's Gaia hypothesis, understood as a homeostatic cybernetic system rather than a living spirit, he argues that General Hein's skepticism toward Cid's vitalist holism is warranted, that mechanism and reductionism have the stronger empirical record, and that Dr. Cid's Gaia belongs entirely in the world of Final Fantasy.

13.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Jason Blahuta reads The Spirits Within as staging the debate between General Hein's anthropocentric, domination-of-nature outlook (traced to the Genesis tradition and thinkers like Bacon and Descartes) and Aki's Gaia-hypothesis and ecofeminist view of nature as a self-regulating whole. Hein's repeated firings of the Zeus Cannon, which injure rather than kill the Phantoms and doom New York, dramatize what happens when we meddle with a self-regulating Gaia, while the chapter's survey of intrinsic-value versus enlightened-self-interest accounts of nature's worth ends with Lovelock's bleak verdict that humanity has become a tumor inside Gaia and must choose to be a benign or a malignant one.

14.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Robert Arp and Sarah Fisk test three moral theories against objectification in Final Fantasy: Kant's ban on using rational beings as mere means (Kuja's manipulation of Queen Brahne, the Geostigma children of Advent Children), Mill's greatest-happiness principle (Yuna's and Aeris's self-sacrifice), and Aristotle's character-based virtue ethics (Hojo and Sephiroth as vicious, Aeris as virtuous). They argue Kantianism generates a stalemate between 'moral sanctity' and 'moral autonomy' camps over cases like Guardian Force summoning in FFVIII, and utilitarianism a stalemate over mandatory self-sacrifice, leaving virtue ethics, Aristotelian or Nietzschean, as the view that escapes both, ending with the question 'Aeris or a Cloud?'

15.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md

16.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Greg Littmann asks what sort of life is worth living by holding Final Fantasy protagonists and FFXI Online players up to three standards. Hobbes's egoism and defense of absolute monarchy condemn the altruistic, authority-defying heroes (AVALANCHE, the rebels of FFII and FFVI) while partly approving the gil-grubbing, rule-breaking FFXI player; Mill's utilitarianism praises the world-saving heroes but condemns grinding down beastmen and rates most gaming a lower pleasure; Aristotle's function argument and golden mean find heroes like Yuna immoderately self-sacrificial yet credit ordinary FFXI adventurers with genuinely virtuous moderation, helping others while keeping their own interests in view.

17.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
17.relation: Nicolas Michaud asks whether the prophesied Four Warriors of Light of Final Fantasy I deserve thanks if the Sage Lukahn's foreknowledge meant they could not do otherwise, framing their plight with the problem of divine foreknowledge and Aquinas's answer that God stands outside time. He then deploys Frankfurt's preemption cases, Garland ready to mind-control you either way, to show moral responsibility can survive without alternative possibilities, but concludes the Warriors may still be unworthy of praise because they know they are predestined, a worry that spreads to us through Phineas Gage-style biological determinism: if our characters are hardwired, neither we nor Garland deserve praise or blame.

18.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md

19.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
19.relation: Jonah Mitropoulos reads Final Fantasy VII through Shinto: the Lifestream is a kami-filled world of spiritual energy pervading nature, and Jenova's corrupting influence works like tsumi, pollution contracted without intent that requires water purification, as when Aerith's Lifestream cures Geostigma in Advent Children and Lucrecia retreats to a waterfall. He reads Jenova as an allegory of Western, Christian, capitalist influence on Japan, citing Aizawa Seishisai's fear of ideological invasion, Wutai's postwar-style disarmament, and the disease metaphors both sides use. The chapter closes with Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology: Shinra treats the planet as a standing resource, and only a syncretic way of the kami reconciles technology and nature.

20.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
20.relation: Michel Beaulieu reads the series through Marx's materialist conception of history: the 'Proletariat Patrons' Movement' sign in FFIX's Alexandria, the job system as a class system, and Shinra dropping the Sector 7 plate on its own laboring class all instantiate class struggle, while Vaan's life in Rabanastre shows social existence determining consciousness. But he argues the heroes are not Marxist revolutionaries, since Cecil ends up King of Baron and the Light Warriors leave feudal structures intact, and the Moogles, the series' true proletarian serfs, never revolt, because no Final Fantasy world has yet matured to the stage where the Marxian transformation becomes possible.

21.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md
21.relation: David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.

22.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy.md

23.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
23.relation: Christopher Wood reads Cloud's arc as an existentialist quest: Heidegger's thrownness in Cloud's tumble off the Midgar train and his initial 'It's not my problem' denial of being-in-the-world; Nietzsche's death of God in Mako-powered Midgar's nihilism, with AVALANCHE as a call for revaluation of values and Sephiroth as a false aspirant god; and Sartre's bad faith in Cloud 'playing at being a SOLDIER,' a persona borrowed wholesale from Zack along with his sword and mercenary dream. Through the Lifestream reunion with Tifa, Cloud faces his fabricated past, admits 'I never was in SOLDIER,' and turns to authenticity by resolving to live without pretending, which Wood presents as the player's own existential task.

24.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
24.relation: Kevin Fitzpatrick uses Vivi Orunitia and the self-aware Black Mages of Final Fantasy IX, who call death 'stopping,' to ask whether the fear of death is justified, answering that death harms only insofar as it frustrates a person's values, such as Vivi's morality, his thirst for knowledge, and his care for others' happiness. He brings in Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us because the dead feel no pain, casts Necron, who wants to return all life to a painless 'zero world' because fear of death has corrupted it, as a darker Epicurean, and weighs the deprivation objection, death cheats us of future goods like Chocobo Hot and Cold, against the puzzle of when death's harm could even occur.

25.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
25.relation: Andrew Russo and Jason Southworth use the recurring Cid in every Final Fantasy game and the apparently identical Cloud Strife of FFVII and FF Tactics to test theories of reference: direct reference theory trivializes informative identity claims like 'Squall is Leon,' and Russell's descriptivism, names as abbreviations for definite descriptions, handles Cid but stumbles on Cloud, whose FF Tactics birthday makes him an Aquarius rather than a Leo, and on a Spira where Schmidt, not Braska, actually defeated Sin. Kripke's causal-historical theory, with its dubbing ceremonies and name-transference chains illustrated by Yuna tracking the Tidus lookalike in X-2, answers the modal challenge but faces the qua problem of 'Balamb Garden has moved,' leading the authors to call for a reflective equilibrium between the two theories.

6.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
6.file: ch06 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
6.relation: Foreword by Elio M. Garcia and Linda Antonsson (founders of Westeros.org). They argue that Martin's epic succeeds because its real subject is 'the human heart in conflict with itself': unlike Tolkien-style epics with a Dark Lord and morally obvious heroes, A Game of Thrones gives characters in shades of gray - Ned wrestling with honor and honesty, Jon with vows versus love, Tyrion craving his father's approval - and presents this volume's essays as illumination of that moral complexity, from Littmann's Hobbes-as-maester to Jacoby on warg consciousness.

7.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
7.file: ch07 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

8.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
8.file: ch08 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

9.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
9.relation: Henry Jacoby's introduction frames the volume around mortality: winter is coming, all men must die (valar morghulis), yet through honor, duty, and philosophy 'first we'll live' meaningful lives. Playing on Arya's mantra 'fear cuts deeper than swords,' he claims logic cuts deeper still - swords defend bodies, but logic defends our ideas, beliefs, and values - leaning on Socrates' claim that no evil can befall a good person, since the virtuous soul stands in harmony against desire and influence. He previews the essays: Hobbes as a maester, the dark side of chivalry, Robb's questionable war, Arya and Zen, and Ned's need of Machiavelli.

10.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

11.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Greg Littmann asks who should rule Westeros and answers with Hobbes's Leviathan: people act only from self-interest ('we are all Lord Littlefinger under the skin') and fight for gain, safety, and glory - the mountain clans, Robert's preemptive strike on Daenerys, Drogo's wars for pride - so without a sovereign life is a war of all against all, and only an absolute ruler makes oath-keeping self-interested. Mapping Hobbes's own civil war (the Stuarts onto the Targaryens), he argues that even Varys is right to serve 'the realm' and peace by betraying Ned, and that loyalty rightly transfers from Aerys to Robert to Joffrey because protection, not lineage or justice, is the point of the sovereign. He then criticizes Hobbes: Ned and Jon show people really do die for principle, and Mad King Aerys's overcentralized power left rebellion as the only remedy - the War of the Five Kings shows civil war's horror must be weighed against appeals to honor.

12.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.

13.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Marcus Schulzke reads the War of the Five Kings through The Prince: who wins the Iron Throne is decided by virtu - skill adapted to shifting circumstances - against fortuna, and morality is no guide, since actions are good or bad only as they gain or hold power. The failures illustrate the lessons: Viserys's arrogance binds him to the wrong allies, Robert's emotions make him capricious, Joffrey makes himself hated instead of feared, Ned's uncompromising honesty and trust in Littlefinger destroy him, and Robb's dependency on Walder Frey's auxiliary forces proves fatal. The true Machiavellians are the mask-wearers - Littlefinger, Arya, Jon as lion-and-fox - and above all Tyrion, who wins the Blackwater by planning, and Daenerys, who builds her own army from freed slaves and so makes her own luck.

14.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Richard H. Corrigan tests Robb Stark's war against Joffrey with just war theory, criteria for resorting to war (legitimate authority, just cause, right intention, last resort, probability of success, proportionality) and for conduct (discrimination, treatment of prisoners, no reprisals). Robb is a legitimate authority acclaimed King in the North, offers rejected peace terms, and fights cleanly - Jaime is humanely held at Riverrun while Sansa is beaten by Joffrey, and Gregor Clegane's murders, rapes, and the Dothraki sack of the Lhazareen mark the other side's atrocities. Yet Corrigan concludes Robb fails right intention: his dominant motive is vengeance for his father, not the free North he professes, so although we root for him, his war cannot strictly be called just.

15.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

16.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Eric Silverman argues Game of Thrones explodes the storybook link between virtue and worldly happiness: Ned, 'one man in ten thousand,' is betrayed and executed, so Plato's claim that the just person is happy must mean psychic order rather than material flourishing - reason ruling spirit and appetite - as with Bran, who flourishes as a greenseer though he will never walk again. Cersei is Plato's tyrant, her soul ruled by insatiable appetite and paranoia, so no external goods can ever satisfy her, while Aristotle's correction - virtue necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia, which also needs health, friends, and good fortune - explains why both Ned (virtue without external goods) and Cersei (goods without virtue) end up unhappy. Finally he inverts Pascal's Wager: since playing the game of thrones risks total loss (torture, humiliation, death) for limited gain, and even winning hollows you out - Robert confesses he was 'never so alive as when I was winning this throne or so dead as now that I've won it' - only a fool would play.

17.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
17.relation: David Hahn contends Ned died because of his honor, not for it. Hobbes explains why: words bind no one without fear of enforcement - Cersei ripping up Robert's will ('Is this meant to be your shield, Lord Stark?') exposes Ned's belief that allegiance alone secures the King's Justice - and the Iron Throne itself is a Leviathan, forged by Aegon's dragons ending the state of nature, whose force rather than justice holds the peace. Machiavelli supplies the indictment of Ned's idealism: 'we who presume to rule must do vile things for the good of the realm,' so Ned's refusal to assassinate Daenerys, his merciful warning to Cersei, and backing the rightful but war-prone Stannis over Renly cost him his head and plunged the realm into civil war; the security of the state demanded exiling or killing the Lannisters and crowning Renly.

18.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Albert Anglberger and Alexander Hieke contrast Ned, the virtue ethicist's genuinely good man, with Cersei, a 'minimally extended' egoistic consequentialist whose only morally relevant subjects are herself and her children. Aristotle's apparatus does the work: phronesis lets Ned rank his daughters' lives above honesty when he confesses falsely ('the lies we tell for love'), his 'you're too fat for your armor' quip shows the golden mean among competing virtues, and Cersei's unbalanced maternal love is excess, hence not a virtue. They then unsettle moral judgment itself: utilitarianism would license the Slaver's Bay slaveholders, virtue ethics lacks action rules and cross-cultural agreement (charity is no Dothraki virtue), and Martin's POV narration gives direct access to Ned's inner life but only Varys's and Littlefinger's unreliable reports about Cersei - so our verdicts on her, like real-life judgments of others, rest on shaky evidence.

19.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
19.relation: Matthew Tedesco reads Bran's coma and Drogo's living death as biomedical ethics: Jaime's 'good clean death' for Bran raises active versus passive euthanasia, and with James Rachels he argues the AMA's killing/letting-die distinction merely licenses more suffering, while Brock recasts withdrawal of treatment as intentional killing anyway. The Bran case frames end-of-life decisions for children - the Johns Hopkins and Baby John Pearson cases - and whether parents may weigh a handicap's burden on the family, a question made vivid by Bran riding Hodor. Dany's smothering of Drogo, by contrast, does not strike readers as murder because personhood rather than biological humanity carries moral standing: on Tooley's self-consciousness, Warren's five criteria, or Marquis's future-like-ours, Drogo is human but no longer a person - which leads straight to Peter Singer's claim that killing a disabled infant who is not a person may not be wrong at all, leaving us to ask whether our recoil is reason or taboo.

20.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

21.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.

22.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Edward Cox asks whether physicalism - everything is physical, and everything depends on the arrangement of physical stuff - is true in Westeros. The causal argument shows Jaime's love could move Bran's body only if it is itself a brain state, and the maesters' science (boiling wine against infection, Baratheon black hair as heredity, the Eyrie's winch) reveals a world running on our physics. But magic strains the picture: reanimated Othor and Jafer Flowers must physically change to walk, and Daenerys's walk into Drogo's pyre requires her resolve to disrupt combustion itself - so Cox concludes magic is either violation of physical law or a nonphysical force, and that in our world immaterial souls would be exactly as improbable as magic.

23.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
23.relation: Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.

24.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Jaime Lannister's question to Catelyn Stark - 'If the gods are real and they are just, then why is the world so full of injustice?' - launches a tour of the logical and evidential problems of evil across the religions of Westeros. Augustine's privation theory and free will defense are tested against the Faith of the Seven (with Catelyn answering 'Because of men like you'), Hume's dilemma of impotence or malevolence is applied to the old gods that Arya scolds at Harrenhal for failing to save Ned, and Leibniz's best-possible-world reply is weighed against natural evils like the storm that sank the Windproud. The chapter concludes that only the evidential problem sticks: the sheer quantity of suffering in Westeros is evidence against just gods, though nothing counts against the uncaring gods Brienne describes.

25.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

26.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Joffrey on the Iron Throne, immune from punishment for beheading Ned, is read as Glaucon's ring of Gyges made flesh: the chapter asks what reason he has to be moral when he can get away with everything, noting he lacks even Gyges's advantage of secrecy and is hated like the Mad King. Hobbes's social contract is considered and rejected as a motive for Joffrey - King's Landing is no Hobbesian community like the Night's Watch, and Joffrey does better free-riding on everyone else's morality. The Platonic answer carries the chapter: like Ned Stark, who refused the throne, lived honorably in Winterfell, and regretted trading his honor at Baelor, the just person with an ordered soul has the only genuine happiness, which Joffrey's desire-satisfying cruelty forfeits.

27.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
27.relation: Tyrion - born a reviled dwarf who killed his mother, yet heir to Lannister wealth, wits, and Jaime's knightly example - frames Nagel's paradox of moral luck: his compassion toward Jon Snow and Sansa is constitutive luck, and his carefully run wildfire defense of King's Landing shows resultant luck, since the same prudent act deserves praise in one outcome and blame had it burned the city. Kant's good will, applied to Tyrion's protection of Shae as treating her as an end and never merely as a means against Cersei, is offered as a rescue but only neutralizes resultant luck, leaving constitutive and circumstantial luck untouched. The chapter ends with Nagel's shrinking 'extensionless point' of genuine agency, concluding we cannot keep both moral responsibility and the principle that we are blamed only for what we control.

28.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Through Daenerys's horror at her Dothraki wedding - public sex, lethal duels, and later the gang-rape of captives that Drogo calls 'the way of war' - the chapter distinguishes descriptive cultural relativism from normative moral relativism. The diversity of ethical codes in Westeros (crannogmen, wildlings, Craster) plus Cersei and Jaime's incest and the Targaryen brother-sister marriages show moral codes genuinely vary, and the audience's harsher judgment of Tyrion's whoring than of his siblings' incest illustrates our own culturally conditioned gut reactions. But the chapter concludes relativism must be rejected: no culture's say-so makes rape acceptable, while eating horse meat is fine and sibling incest depends on circumstances.

29.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Sansa's journey from tourney-romance believer to 'they are no true knights' anchors a feminist argument that chivalry is unjust as a code, not merely corrupted by bad knights like Ser Gregor and Ser Meryn Trant, who beats Sansa at Joffrey's command. The pedestal, as Gloria Steinem says, is a prison: chivalry makes knights eternal guardians and ladies permanent childlike wards, a move the chapter explains through Spivak's account of saviors who turn the people they help into dependents and through Beauvoir's point that the custom of ladyhood manufactures the very 'fact' of female fragility it claims to protect. Arya's needlework, Brienne's unbeaten sword, Loras crowning Sansa while loving Renly, and Varys's riddle on power show the knight/lady roles are neither natural nor exhaustive, so 'there are no true knights' because chivalry itself blocks human flourishing.

30.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md

31.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
31.relation: The chapter asks whether Daenerys's fatalism - she feels truly free only once she believes fate is in control - can coexist with freedom in a Westeros where class and gender fix everyone's essence. Aristotle's sea-battle argument from bivalence and Cicero's Idle Argument (Dany will rule whether or not she leaves Meereen) are dismantled as having no practical consequences for deliberation, while Sartre's anguish and bad faith explain Cersei's 'necessity' excuse for arresting Ned and Sansa's refusal to own her lie about Joffrey and Mycah. Heidegger's authenticity then resolves the paradox: like Ned choosing between family and honor and Jon choosing his Night's Watch vows over kinship, freedom is not escape from one's past but owning it - Heraclitus's 'character is destiny,' becoming who you are.

32.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
32.file: ch32 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
32.relation: Arya's arc from Needle to answering 'No one' is read as Aristotelian virtue ethics fused with East Asian philosophy: virtues are habits acquired only through practice, so the Water Dance's endless drills and martial-arts blocks that must become automatic mirror the honest person who tells the truth without deliberating. Syrio's lessons - 'looking is not seeing,' the story of the ordinary tomcat the other bravos mistook for a fabulous beast, being fully present with your trouble - teach Zen seeing and mindfulness, while 'be like water' and the steel that must be part of your arm embody Laozi's effortless wu wei. The Faceless Men's initiation, from discarding her possessions to the literal removal of Arya's face, becomes the Zen slaying of the ego, making her a 'Zen-Ninja-Aristotelian' on the path to eudaimonia.

33.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
33.file: ch33 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
33.relation: The chapter models court intrigue as game theory: games of incomplete information over Joffrey's legitimacy, the predictability of honorable opponents like Barristan Selmy, and Catelyn's reverse induction from the seemingly 'irrational' attack on Bran to deduce that Jaime threw him. Tyrion is the star player, converting one-shot death sentences into repeated games - recruiting Bronn as his champion at the Eyrie, buying off the mountain clans with Lannister arms - and showing how 'A Lannister always pays his debts' works as strategic reputation. Against Plato's view of love as the madness that ruins rational play (Maester Aemon's 'love is the bane of honor'), the chapter uses Nietzsche's 'drop of reason in madness' to argue that lovers' merged interests expand rationality itself, culminating in a Golden Rule upgraded to 'understand others as they understand themselves.'

34.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
34.file: ch34 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
34.relation: Applying Foucault's History of Madness, the chapter argues that sanity in Westeros is an act of naming by the powerful: Joffrey literally remakes the drunken Ser Dontos into a court fool, and 'Mad King' Aerys's brutality gets labeled madness while comparable violence by Jaime (throwing Bran from the window) and Robert (ordering Daenerys's assassination) counts as sane necessity. The power/knowledge nexus and the psychiatric fusion of crime with insanity explain how Robert's personal hatred of Rhaegar hides behind a medicalized diagnosis of Targaryen madness. The chapter then tracks Foucault's shift from sovereign to disciplinary power and technologies of the self: Dontos internalizes and performs his fool identity, Dany wonders 'perhaps I am mad' at Drogo's pyre, and Catelyn's freeing of Jaime is written off by Robb's bannermen as 'a mother's madness.'

9.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
9.file: ch09 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
9.relation: The book's introduction argues that the trilogy is at root the truth 'about violence against women, and the men who enable it' in a distinctly Swedish, Stockholm-centered story. It casts Lisbeth Salander as a latter-day Socratic gadfly: like Socrates in Athens, she is an annoying pest who forces the city's sophists to face their hypocrisies, and like him she is tried and pre-condemned in the court of public opinion. Against the old ideal of eternal capital-T Truth (Keats's 'truth is beauty'), it sets Salander the anti-beautiful Pippi Longstocking heir for whom truth 'can be a moody bitch,' and previews the volume's questions about whether journalists and hackers are the new philosophers who will suffer the hemlock backlash.

10.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md

11.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Using Erving Goffman's Stigma and Asylums, the chapter reads Salander's psychiatric record as a textbook spoiled identity: her silence, refusal of medication, and tattoos are recorded at St. Stefan's as symptoms, and the same behaviors that pass unnoticed in 'normals' (Giannini's earrings, Teleborian's own youth) are recoded as pathology in the Hornet's Nest courtroom. It shows labels slipping from 'mentally ill' to violent, promiscuous 'lesbian Satanist,' allies divided into Goffman's 'wise' (Palmgren, Armansky) and those before whom she must pass (Blomkvist, Mimmi Wu), and real Ontario Mental Health Act hearings that generalize single incidents into dangerousness. The chapter's conclusion is that the trilogy's point is not that Lisbeth was wrongly labeled but that no one—including the 'rightly labeled'—should be reduced to a label, since sane/insane is a shifting continuum we all occupy.

12.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
12.relation: The chapter uses Foucault to explain how Salander could leave school without a certificate yet master Fermat-class mathematics: schools 'cut' students into fabricated 'human kinds'—the problem-solving child and the at-risk child (Popkewitz's alchemy)—and under No Child Left Behind that sorting licenses surveillance and discipline of everything an at-risk student does. Lisbeth's case shows the machinery: her correct answer marked wrong from the textbook key, her Rubik's-cube brilliance ignored, her 381 days strapped to a bed under Teleborian's silhouette-like gaze recasting Bentham's Panopticon, and her subsequent guardianship extending the watch over her money and behavior. Because power 'produces reality,' the at-risk label becomes self-fulfilling, and Lisbeth's refusal to be disciplined—her silence, tattoos, and asocial style—only supplies fresh evidence for the label.

13.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Reading Salander as genderqueer rather than simply a woman, the chapter argues her feminism lies in swift retaliation against those who abuse women and in economic and sexual independence from men, while her refusal of every identity label ('I don't know what I am') aligns her with queer theory's anti-identity politics. Judith Butler's performativity grounds the reading: Salander's body modifications and wardrobe 'undo' conventional gendering, and her drag-like aliases—the big-busted heiress Monica Sholes and the quiet Irene Nesser—succeed at fraud and flight only through absolute adherence to heteronormative femininity, proving gender is continuously constructed. Foucault's History of Sexuality frames her pathologization, institutionalization, and regulated sexuality as the medicalization of the sexually peculiar, a disciplinary script she reverses by hacking, surveilling, and exposing the authorities who pathologized her, tattooing i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist onto Bjurman.

14.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy

15.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Why do Berger, Cecilia, Harriet, Salander, and Figuerola all bed the unprepossessing Blomkvist? Testing Kant's claim that sexual desire makes 'the loved person an Object of appetite... a lemon which has been sucked dry,' the chapter argues his appeal is that he treats women as ends in themselves—he works beside them as equals, is 'not going to compete with you' with Figuerola, and never manipulates or controls—so his sex is the least objectifying in a Sweden full of men who hate women. Against Kant and Baumrim, Irving Singer's reply that desire can respond to the whole person explains why his no-strings honesty attracts powerful women, though his refusal to define, own, or 'cherish' any lover—walking in on Erika just as Salander arrives with the Elvis cabin ad—still leaves Salander heartbroken and Figuerola in sadness.

16.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
16.relation: A cultural history of the coffeehouse frames Larsson's caffeine-soaked cast: the 'penny universities' where Addison brought philosophy out of closets to coffee-house tables, Diderot and Marx plotting at the Café de la Régence, Trotsky at the Café Central, and the Viennese 'meridians of loneliness' that fit Salander's i am an alien T-shirt, Blomkvist hearing his sentence at Kafé Anna, and Niederman's need to sit among people he despises. Ritzer's McDonaldization and 'Starbuckization' explain the characters' Billy's Pan Pizza and chain-café habits as rationalization's homogenizing disenchantment, against which Henrik Vanger's slowly sipped Norrland coffee stands for an older ethics of conversation and community. The chapter closes with the counter-image Larsson's addicts never reach: the Zen tea ceremony of Suzuki and Kakuzo, tranquility emanating from inner consciousness and 'the cup of humanity.'

17.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
17.relation: The chapter reconstructs the real Swedish journalist behind Kalle Blomkvist: the 1950s reporter as the welfare state's mouthpiece alongside heroic police, the 1970s radical investigative journalist epitomized by Jan Guillou—whose exposure of the secret IB organization earned him a prison sentence and a revenge vindication, the direct template for Blomkvist—and the 1990s–2000s slide into 'sensation, scandal, and spectacle' around crime. It shows journalism decoupling from crime statistics—about a hundred killings a year in a country of 9.4 million, falling, yet alarmist coverage fueling tougher sentencing and the Nazi-rooted Sweden Democrats' entry into parliament—so the watchdog ideal of the muckraker who draws aside the veil on 'men who hate women and democracy' becomes a question: where have you gone, Kalle Blomkvist?

18.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md

19.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
19.relation: Philosopher Sven Ove Hansson's memoir shows the trilogy's realism came from Larsson's decades of unpaid extremism-watching: patiently archiving Nazi and racist networks, exposing the Sweden Democrats as Per Engdahl's 1979 repackaging of fascism in anti-immigrant dress (the same strategy as Britain's National Front), and forcing Skeptics' scrutiny onto the publisher of David Irving's Holocaust-denying Göring biography. It presents Larsson's anti-pseudoscience skepticism—astrology, faith healing, pyramidology, racist biology—his rejection of the postmodern idea that knowledge is mere social construction ('The Holocaust was not a social construction'), and his philosophically interesting argument that astrology's deterministic worldview is a stifling, self-fulfilling spiritual posture. The honor-killing analysis pairing Fadime Sahindal with Melissa Nordell demonstrates his method of using philosophical case-comparison to expose moral prejudice in taken-for-granted categories—habits of mind that resurface in the novels' hidden power structures and rationalist heroine.

20.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Asking whether the Millennium Trilogy is popular fiction or literature, the chapter proposes Wittgenstein's family resemblances instead of an essence: Larsson's books are devoured like genre series, yet they tackle the 'moral seriousness'—violence against women, corruption, journalistic ethics—that Sartre called committed literature, so the whodunit becomes the exposé. Nussbaum's account of reading as moral perception, not mere grasp of facts, is applied to Lisbeth's 'Bitch' verdict on Harriet Vanger—should we see a culpable sister or a victim?—and the paradox of fiction explains why we feel real pity and fear for characters we know are invented, down to the detective plot's 'consolatory fiction' that truth can be found. The verdict: socially conscious popular fiction whose high/low distinction (Arnold versus Meisel's level field) matters less than the words-as-force-for-justice theme summed up in 'an insufferable do-gooder who thought he could change everything with a book.'

21.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Why do we prefer the narrative where Bjurman handcuffs and rapes Salander to a boring one where Zalachenko is a good father? Rejecting Plato's Republic censorship of disturbing art—which would leave us nothing but nice stories—the chapter applies Aristotle's Poetics: Salander is an imperfect, exaggerated tragic hero whose flaws (defiant independence that keeps her from reporting Bjurman) arouse pity and terror, and reading the trilogy produces catharsis understood, with Nussbaum, as clarification rather than purgation. Thus the rape scenes illuminate how guardianship and power enable men who hate women (Bjurman's 'She had to understand who was in charge,' Martin Vanger's 'godlike feeling'), the heavy-metal concert models safe purgation of anger, and Salander's axing of Zalachenko joins Clytaemnestra's 'man-killing ax' tradition while her tattooed revenge on Bjurman, per Aristotle, yields moral satisfaction rather than tragedy.

22.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Applying Laura Mulvey's visual pleasure to the printed page, the chapter argues that Larsson's protest against woman-hating is compromised by styling Salander—four-eleven, ninety pounds, 'childlike breasts'—as a sexual spectacle whose rapes (Bjurman's coerced oral sex, the anal rape, the trial's play-by-play of implements) are the trilogy's most explicit scenes while consensual sex stays off-screen, making the books 'torture porn' for the voyeuristic reader. The films shift the gaze further: the revenge on Bjurman runs longer than the rapes, Salander actively watches Martin Vanger burn, and her bisexuality with Mimmi Wu is reduced to one silent morning, changes that make the violence against men more acceptable than against women. The chapter ends ambivalent: Laurie Penny and Gail Dines charge that 'Misogynist violence is appalling; now here's some more,' yet the distributor's RAINN partnership and a rape survivor's testimony that Salander was the first active, aggressive survivor she had ever seen show the books also work as Larsson intended.

23.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md

24.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
24.relation: The chapter reads Salander's hacking beside Julian Assange's WikiLeaks: both are hard to classify as criminal or activist, and both live by the hacker ethic Stephen Levy codified—unlimited access, all information free, mistrust authority, judgment by skill—which later versions soften with privacy and social responsibility, matching 'Salander's Principles' (a bastard is always a bastard) and Assange's 'capable, generous men do not create victims; they nurture victims.' Through David Brin's Transparent Society it asks who watches the watchers—the police-camera city of the state or the citizen-accessible city—and argues for WikiLeaks-style reciprocal transparency that keeps the 'mighty' (governments, the Vanger Corporation, Wennerström) exposed while protecting whistleblower anonymity. Blomkvist's choices—suppressing the Vanger murders, encouraging Salander to steal Wennerström's files, planting disinformation—mark him as the journalist half of Larsson's new information-age hero pair.

25.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Against Blomkvist's 'I don't believe in collective guilt,' the chapter argues the Section is not a few bad apples: with Rousseau, institutions outgrow the people's will and preserve themselves (the guardianship agency cannot welcome its own obsolescence; the Fälldin directive lets Säpo stand inside and outside the law at once), and with Arendt, institutions protect only those they already recognize, so the excluded Salander cannot be heard by Teleborian, Prosecutor Ekström, or the court that doubts Giannini. Through bell hooks's definition of patriarchy it shows the police, psychiatry, and Säpo prize rationality, stability, and power in a masculine code under which Salander's responsiveness to her mother's abuse and her retaliation read as insanity—her very self-sufficiency (pepper spray, Taser, forward planning) proving she needs no 'guardianship.' Rancière's policing-versus-politics distinction supplies the conclusion: perpetual political contestation of who institutions exclude, not Prime Minister-initiated cleanup, is the only answer to a hidden Section in every institution.

26.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Defending gossip against Sissela Bok's verdict ('trivializing' and 'reprehensible'), the chapter reads the trilogy as showing that loose talk is knowledge: Blomkvist's libel conviction, Bjurman's appointment through Björck, Gullberg's suspiciously empty reputation, and the Section's detection via the missing panic-talk at Millennium all run on trust and 'trust capital,' while Salander's hacking is electronic gossip—Solove's diary made public—in the old tradition of rumor as resistance from colonial India to pre-revolutionary Parisian libelles. Kant supplies the warning that Salander's principle turns people into 'mere means': her schadenfreude is 'moral' (Portmann) when it denatures powerful abusers like Wennerström but mere revenge against the condescending realtor, and the Malleus Maleficarum lineage shows the powerful gossiping best, their 'lesbian Satanist' smear a modern witch hunt. The trilogy closes on reciprocity—he knew her secrets just as she knew all of his—making mutual confession, not one-way scrutiny, the ground of trust.

27.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md

28.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Using the Nicomachean Ethics and the Rhetoric, the chapter vindicates the pleasure readers take in Salander's Taser-and-tattoo revenge on Bjurman: Aristotle distinguishes revenge, done for the satisfaction of the one wronged, from punishment, and requires that the wrongdoer know who avenges and why—which is why Lisbeth waits until Bjurman wakes before inking i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist across his torso. Proper anger on the right grounds is a virtue (hatred alone is corrosive), Larsson is cast as the rhetorician who must keep our trust to 'put the judge into a certain frame of mind,' and the revenge emerges as the deliberated, rational means toward the end Aristotle calls eudaimonia: independence from a bogus guardianship and a life worth living, since under 'proportionate reciprocity' those who cannot requite evil with evil are slaves.

29.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.

30.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy.md
30.relation: Taking J. L. Austin's distinction between justifying conduct (showing it was the right thing to do) and excusing it (accepting wrongdoing but denying full blame), the chapter audits the trilogy's deceptions: Blomkvist's lottery trick on the pedophile Björck, his intention to double-cross him, the fake-collapse 'double game' at Millennium, and the disinformation fed to the Section's bugs are justified, since they deceive only dangerous criminals engaged in murderous conspiracies. Salander is shakier—her hacking of the innocent Blomkvist and the tax-tip revenge on the realtor expose the flaw in 'a bastard is always a bastard' (she cannot know guilt in advance), though her lies to Bjurman, Forbes, and Zalachenko earn excuse or justification. The verdict falls hardest on the cover-up of Martin Vanger's murders—trading truth for Harriet's protection and crisis-center funding, it might have warned other women, so Blomkvist's 'unforgivable' stands—and on her final lies under oath to honest police, excusable only if she still cannot trust the state.
