8.title: Welcome Everything Is Great!
8.relation: The editors' introduction argues that The Good Place is unique among TV comedies in taking real moral philosophy seriously instead of playing the professor for a fool: Chidi Anagonye is a deontology-focused ethics professor whose 'mini ethics lessons' ground the plot, and philosophy becomes the vocabulary Eleanor and the others use to make sense of themselves. It recounts the show's premise (Eleanor waking in Michael's Neighborhood 12358W with Janet the 'vessel of all knowledge'), explains why a philosophy-professor character is rare on television, and sets out the volume's title conventions and spoiler warning.

10.title: I The Demons in the Details
10.file: ch10 - I The Demons in the Details.md

11.title: 1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic
11.file: ch11 - 1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic.md
11.relation: Reads the show's automatic, unquestionable point system as Hannah Arendt's bureaucracy — 'rule by Nobody' in which no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority over the system ('He's not God, he's a bureaucrat'). It argues via Arendt's power/violence distinction that bureaucracies deprive everyone subject to them of the power to act, leaving only resistance or violence, which is why Michael's Season Two plea before Gen ('the very method we use to deem them good or bad is fundamentally flawed') and his Season Three interference amount to revolt. Chidi's 'Most Improved Player' defense of Eleanor and Michael's case that souls can grow after death show the system cannot accommodate rehabilitation, only retribution.

12.title: 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny
12.file: ch12 - 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny.md
12.relation: Asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny and answers with incongruity theory (circus music under Michael's dejection; a comedy set in Hell) plus Bergson's view of comedy as social correction that deflates those who deserve it — Tahani's name-dropping, Michael failing 802 reboots. It centers on 'The Trolley Problem': Michael teleporting Chidi's ethics lesson into real runaway trolleys ('not real, but the pain is') is both incongruous humor and genuine torture, and invoking Bernard Williams shows the real wrongdoer is Michael, who rigged the situation, not Chidi who must choose. Eternal torture, it concludes, only works as endless low-grade everyday crappiness, which is comic in twenty-two-minute doses — and Eleanor's twice-given forgiveness of Michael, after seeing the centuries of torture in Janet's VR device, is the show's real moral marvel.

13.title: 3. Sympathy for the Devils
13.file: ch13 - 3. Sympathy for the Devils.md
13.relation: Argues, against Michael, that the Soul Squad still belongs in the Bad Place: drawing on William James's conditions for actions having moral worth (foreseeable consequences, no do-overs) and his meliorism about an unfinished, responsive universe, it shows the points system is contextualist (the tricycle fix worth +4.79 or +0.04; the two Dougs' rose gifts), but the afterlife simulation is a context where nothing the humans do is consequential or permanent, so their moral growth earns no points. Worse, their growth adds net unhappiness — Michael's suffering, the demon cast's misery, Judge Gen's distress — so becoming better ironically confirms they belong in the Bad Place. Only Michael, whose retirement is a real, irreversible consequence and whose sacrifices add genuine good, deserves the Good Place.

14.title: 4. Can We Do Enough Good
14.file: ch14 - 4. Can We Do Enough Good.md
14.relation: Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?

15.title: 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon
15.file: ch15 - 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon.md
15.relation: Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.

16.title: II Somewhere Else
16.file: ch16 - II Somewhere Else.md

17.title: 6. A Better Bad Place
17.relation: Asks whether Judge Gen could ever justly consign Team Cockroach to eternal torment. It reconstructs the Anselmian infinite-desert defense (God as 'than which none greater can be conceived', every sin against an infinite being meriting infinite punishment) and shows it fails on the show since no such God appears and neither Gen nor Michael is infinitely great; the continuing-sin model fails because the Bad Place's physical tortures (eyeball corkscrews, bees with teeth) preclude sinning, and Gen's own tests (Jason's Madden game, Tahani's hallway, Chidi's two hats) show vice persisting without added desert. Punishment as retribution also fails on utilitarian grounds (Jason's hypothetical spray-paint-can sentence adds only pain), so the chapter proposes a non-retributive 'Bad Place 3.0' where people face the natural consequences of their vices, comparing it to C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce.

18.title: 7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife
18.file: ch18 - 7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife.md
18.relation: Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.

19.title: 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning
19.file: ch19 - 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning.md
19.relation: Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.

21.title: 9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place
21.file: ch21 - 9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place.md
21.relation: Asks whether a show about ethics may lie to its audience for a whole season: the Season One twist breaks the viewer's implicit contract even though the show keeps its internal 'truth in fiction'. Through 'The Eternal Shriek' it stages the debate — Chidi's Kantian ban on lying (the red cowboy boots saga with Henry, ending in a confession that defeats Henry) against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means plot to 'kill' Janet — and reads the show's cascade of confessions as its answer that truth-telling absolves. Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' lets Chidi lie his way through Hell, leaving viewers to decide whether the twist's ethical education justifies the deception.

22.title: 10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis
22.file: ch22 - 10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis.md
22.relation: Casts Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis in an allegorical love story: Chidi's Kantian universalizability about lying and his utilitarian lesson (confess, because the neighborhood's welfare outweighs you) only move Eleanor when she sees Theory enacted — Michael's willingness to absorb eternal torture in her place convinces her the theory 'has legs'. Praxis repays the debt when Eleanor's moral particularism pushes Chidi to lie to demons and play his part in the Bad Place party, and Michael's conversion from torturer to someone who sacrifices his portal pin for Eleanor ('Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent') completes the union. The moral: theory is born in the world, but only practice lets it thrive there.

23.title: 11. Those Agonizing Choices
23.relation: Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.

25.title: 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here
25.file: ch25 - 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here.md
25.relation: Asks what makes the person sitting in Michael's office numerically identical to the person who died on Earth. The same-body theory fails because bodies stay behind (buried or cremated) with no spatiotemporal continuity; the same-mind theory of psychological continuity fails on the 802 memory-wiping reboots and the duplication case of two psychologically-continuous Eleanors; the same-soul theory cannot say what makes two souls the same soul. The chapter concludes that 'Janet(s)' — essences reconstituting themselves in Janet's void — quietly commits the show to Aristotelian and Aquinan hylomorphism, while leaving open how anyone (even Janet) could tell that two persons share an essence.

26.title: 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts
26.file: ch26 - 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts.md
26.relation: Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.

27.title: 14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors
27.file: ch27 - 14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors.md
27.relation: Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.

28.title: 15. Chidi’s Indecision
28.relation: Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.

30.title: 16. Is Hell Other People
30.relation: Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.

31.title: 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
31.file: ch31 - 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place.md
31.relation: Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.

32.title: VI The Leap to Faith
32.file: ch32 - VI The Leap to Faith.md

33.title: 18. Heaven Is Other People
33.relation: Treats the show as a theological sitcom whose afterlife (Gen's algorithmic judgment, cubicles, the Jeremy Bearimy timeline) critiques a pop-Christian eschatology of disembodied Heaven and eternal conscious torment while missing the bodily resurrection of Nicene and N.T. Wright's account. Levinas supplies the positive frame: ethics precedes ontology, the face of the Other demands responsibility before any impersonal verdict — which is why Gen's points system 'wouldn't cut it' and why the show's two-shots, Eleanor's spontaneous good acts, and Chidi's 802 yeses to teaching her matter. Bonhoeffer's religionless Christianity completes the reading of Eleanor's repentance, Donna's and Tahani's confessions, and Michael's self-sacrificing Christ figure: salvation comes through intersubjective, grace-infused transformation, so 'Heaven is other people'.

34.title: 19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right
34.file: ch34 - 19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right.md
34.relation: Argues Hinduism 'gets more than five percent right' via the Bhagavad Gita: the show's point system mirrors karma, Eleanor's failed point-chasing and quiet departure for the Bad Place enact nishkama karma (desire-less action), and the 802 reboots are rebirths without memory. The characters form a ladder of unfoldment — Jason's unknowing wrong action below Eleanor's knowing one, Tahani's corruptly motivated good deeds, Chidi's knowledge without decision, Michael swerving from his demonic dharma, and Janet highest: desireless, rebooting like cyclical rebirth, her void echoing boundless Brahman. Chidi's logic-bound indecision versus Eleanor's knowledge-producing logic completes the Gita reading.

36.title: 20. Moral Health Warning
36.relation: A health warning from Jonathan Dancy himself: the show's premise that Chidi's lessons in Kant, Scanlon, and the Trolley Problem can make Eleanor better is false, because becoming good requires a change in motivation and intellectual study shapes motivation at most indirectly — and might attach to the wrong as easily as the right, since moral philosophy studies both. Worse, studying ethics looks like self-indulgence, time spent on Kant that could have gone to doing actual good. Against the Kantian thought that only acting from a sense of duty earns moral credit, Dancy argues that sympathetic love — Doug Wynegar bringing his grandmother roses simply for her sake — is enough, which undermines both Kant and Chidi's entire teaching project.

37.title: 21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good
37.file: ch37 - 21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good.md
37.relation: Argues that no one can improve without first admitting they are bad: the rigid Good Place/Bad Place binary is ethical dualism whose cracks show in Mindy St. Claire's Medium Place and Jason, a naive moral neutral who fits neither side. Socrates' Apology supplies the method — wisdom is knowing what you do not know, so self-aware fault-finding precedes growth — while Aristotle's account of virtue as learned by practice, like an instrument, grounds the claim that goodness can be acquired even in the afterlife, though unlearning old habits is harder. Eleanor's trash storm, Tahani's failed party, and Chidi's theory-practice gap mark each character's admissions of error, and the worst offenders, Eleanor and Michael, improve most because they confess unprompted.

38.title: 22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience
38.relation: Brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings are evolved, body-based shortcuts built from a lifetime of social interaction that prune options in real-time moral choice, so Chidi's classroom mastery paired with real-world collapse mirrors Damasio's ventromedial patients — except Chidi has the alarms and refuses to trust them, insisting ethics is pure calculation. Mark Johnson's moral imagination (his own draft-number dilemma) and Scanlon's contractualism (morality is other people) reinforce that we are not disembodied reasoners. Combining Dewey's 'morals is education' with Damasio's claim that somatic learning never stops, the chapter explains how Eleanor and friends keep growing morally even after death — bodies, social bonds and all.

39.title: 23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness
39.file: ch39 - 23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness.md
39.relation: Begins with Schur's traffic-light story — the fourth car sneaking through the left-turn arrow as 'negative twenty points' — to argue the show is, before it is about ethics, an attack on selfish inauthenticity: Tahani's name-dropping charity, Eleanor's lunch-table declaration of friendlessness, Chidi's moral filibustering, and Jason's Acidcat gig each pursue a self at others' expense. Using Charles Guignon's On Being Authentic and Kant's language of means and ends, it traces the movement from authenticity that uses others to an authenticity that lives for others — Chidi's 802 unconditional yeses, Michael's shift from torturer to self-sacrificer to paralyzed would-be hero, and Eleanor giving up Chidi in 'Pandemonium' as the endpoint. Being true to yourself, the show teaches, is only ethical when it helps others be their truest selves.

7.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
7.relation: The editors' introduction explains why Green Lantern merits a philosophy volume: an intergalactic corps of different species that must cooperate, rings limited only by willpower and imagination, and a cast (Hal, Kyle, John, Guy, Sinestro, Mogo, Soranik Natu) dense with philosophical questions. It frames the book's guiding problems: what limits justice places on the ring, whether a Green Lantern can do literally anything, and how the color-coded emotional spectrum should affect judgment and decision-making.

9.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
9.relation: Southworth uses the War of Light to ask what role emotion should play in moral reasoning: Sinestro rules Korugar through fear, the Star Sapphires kidnap Sinestro Corps prisoners to convert them to love, Atrocitus's rage was forged by the Manhunters' massacre, Larfleeze hoards, and the Blue Lanterns merely hope that hope matters. On Aristotle's account every corps errs by excess: Atrocitus's rage makes him miss chances to kill Sinestro, Fatality's love benches John Stewart from saving his friends, and even the Green Lanterns' will-only ideal fails, since total fearlessness is itself vicious and Plato's picture has reason directing emotion like a general directing soldiers. He ends by defending Mill's utilitarianism: the Guardians' real failure was not detachment but pretending to be detached, and reading them as flawed 'benevolent, disinterested spectators' vindicates the Corps while explaining their moral growth after Scar and the Blackest Night.

10.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
10.relation: White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.

11.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns. The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.

12.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md

13.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Terjesen asks how Sinestro and Universo ever passed recruitment and answers that the Guardians' two-prong test of honesty and fearlessness reflects moral pluralism: universal rules kept deliberately thin so that different moral codes can coexist, which is why the vicious 'good bad man' Jack T. Chance keeps his ring on Hellhole. But honor, honesty, and justice are thick ethical concepts in Bernard Williams's sense, requiring cultural context to apply, so Laira's execution of a surrendered Amon Sur and the Guardians' own cover-ups (the Corpse, Kentor Omoto) cannot be settled by appealing to thin 'justice,' and the Alpha Lanterns' internal-affairs role cannot fix it. Moral particularism leaves the Corps with unresolvable disagreements about who the bad apples are.

14.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Dryden reads Hal and Sinestro through Hegel's account of the tragic hero: each acts from a one-sided individual moral compass (Hal rebuilding Coast City in Emerald Twilight and trying to reboot the universe in Zero Hour; Sinestro dictating order to Korugar), collides with communal ethical life, and is destroyed, yet stays aesthetically admirable for the magnificence of the commitment. Fichte's planned police state of ID cards, registered addresses, and total surveillance is exactly the order Sinestro would have liked, the scheme Hegel mocked as tyranny. Kyle escapes the tragic pattern because fear and self-doubt keep him responsive to his groups' shared values, making him 'corps conscience' rather than 'the greatest.'

15.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Michaud argues Hal is a murderer who should not be forgiven for Emerald Twilight even though the Parallax retcon blames a fear entity. Using Frankfurt's cases (a parasite that would force you to rob a bank you were already choosing to rob), he shows that lacking alternatives does not excuse, then applies Fischer and Ravizza: Hal's rampage issued from his own reasons-responsive mechanism ('it was still my hand that did it'), so he had guidance control. Since Hal's willpower later let him resist Parallax to reignite the sun in Final Night, Michaud concludes he likely had regulative control too, and that absolving him insults the very will that made him the greatest Lantern.

16.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Darowski traces Hal's shifting motivations across fifty years: the Showcase #22 origin where honesty and fearlessness make heroism a simple vow, the selfish Parallax era after Coast City's destruction, the Spectre's atonement, and the guilt-driven Lantern of Rebirth. Plato's claim that knowing the good suffices for doing good would mean Hal never really chose heroism, but the chapter rejects it, since morality alone failed to stop Hal's turn to Parallax. Set against the darker post-Watchmen industry, it asks whether guilt-driven atonement is a nobler motive than simple duty and what standards we should hold heroes to.

18.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Terjesen reads the O'Neil-Adams pairing as moral rationalism (Hal) versus moral sentimentalism (Ollie): Hal jails the boy assaulting slumlord Jubal Slade because 'He was breaking the law' and defends a racist senator's speech on free-speech principle, while Ollie works from the gut. Hume's 'Reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions' explains both Ollie's effectiveness and Hal's collapse into Parallax, since no argument from Kilowog could restrain a grief only a stronger passion could. But sentiment needs an impartial filter: Smith's impartial spectator condemns Ollie's near-murder of Black Canary's attacker and his abandonment of the heroin-addicted Speedy, while Hal's cooler principle keeps the Native American land dispute from Ollie's violent plan. The conclusion is that morality is sentiment-based but reason must police it, so each hero needs the other.

19.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
19.relation: Patterson maps the Comics Code censorship debate onto Plato's Republic Book X, where imitative art is thrice removed from the Forms (the god's table, the carpenter's table, the painter's picture) and feeds the passionate soul, versus Aristotle's Poetics, where imitation is natural and tragedy's pity and fear yield catharsis. The O'Neil-Adams run embodies Aristotle: the slum story where a black tenant asks why Green Lantern helps 'orange skins' and 'purple skins' but never 'black skins,' the Ulysses Star land dispute, and Speedy's heroin addiction broke Code taboos so readers would learn from engagement rather than distance. Within the comic, Hal plays the establishment Platonist who would change an unjust law rather than disobey it and Green Arrow the Aristotelian activist, so their friendship dramatizes the ancient quarrel over whether art corrupts or teaches.

20.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
20.relation: Dryden asks whether the Lanterns' relationships are weaknesses or strengths. Epictetus's dichotomy of control would have recruits greet the Sinestro Corps' display of their families' eyeballs with Stoic indifference, and Kant brands fear for loved ones heteronomous; yet Donna Parker refuses the ring for her children, Amnee and Matoo Pree surrender their rings rather than stop loving, and Kilowog dines with energy constructs of his dead family, showing attachments partly constitute who people are. Feminist relational autonomy resolves the tension: Kyle escapes Parallax only by grasping Hal's hand ('we don't have to do it alone'), and Soranik Natu cannot excise Sinestro's crest or parentage any more than Donchin's Huntington's-disease daughter can sever family ties, so autonomy competency means negotiating unchosen relationships rather than escaping them.

21.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md

22.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Tallman and Southworth set the Hippocratic Oath against the Green Lantern oath in Soranik Natu, a Korugarian surgeon who must either stop healing mid-battle or disobey the Book of Oa. They survey the options, with Wonder Woman discarding vows for consequences, Isamot Kol letting the Corps trump his vow to Qalyra, Dr. Mid-Nite always putting patients first, and Dick Grayson going by context, then argue through Hursthouse that Natu, who treats both oaths as absolute, is in an irresolvable dilemma of her own making, more like the double-betrothed man than Williams's tragic Jim and the twenty Indians. Their verdict is that she should turn in the ring, a cautionary tale for real military medics whose oaths also collide.

23.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
23.relation: White distinguishes retributivism from deterrence and rehabilitation through the Corps' execution vote on Sinestro and Fatality's lex talionis pursuit of John Stewart over Xanshi ('You have four billion eyes to account for'). Kant grounds retribution in dignity, so punishment must treat the criminal as an end, never merely as a means to deterrence, and is owed to him for his crime ('You did this to yourself,' Hal tells Sinestro), while Hegel adds that punishment annuls the crime and embodies the criminal's own right. Feinberg's expressive theory explains the Korugarian crowd that felt 'cheated of Korugar's redemption' when the execution stalled, and the chapter closes by separating justice from vengeance: Ollie's arrow through Prometheus and Laira's 'It was justice!' killing of a surrendered Amon Sur were personal revenge, which only impartial state agents may convert into justice.

24.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
24.relation: Novy uses Terry Berg's gay-bashing coma in 'Brother's Keeper' to argue hate crimes are a kind of terrorism: justice, in Iris Marion Young's enabling sense, requires social conditions in which citizens can develop and exercise their capacities, and an attack that makes every gay teenager police holding hands in public harms the whole group, so Mill's greatest-happiness principle and Feinberg's expressivism justify enhanced penalties. The chapter then turns on Kyle, who tortures Daniel Hirsh on Rikers Island and nearly beats his two accomplices to death, asking whether extraordinary crimes justify extraordinary procedures in a post-9/11 world. Kyle's horror afterward, begging Flash to undo the last twenty-four hours and losing his will to protect, and Batman's pointed 'But that is me, isn't it?' mark the line between punishing brutality and becoming it.

25.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
25.relation: Barkman retells Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, a shepherd's invisibility ring used to seduce the queen and murder the king, as Lord Acton's claim that absolute power corrupts, and answers with Plato: injustice disorders the tripartite soul, so the unjust sacrifice the happiness that matters most. The Guardians of the Universe are Plato's guardians writ cosmic, wise enough to rule themselves; Yalan Gur fell only when the yellow weakness was removed from his ring, Sinestro never had the wisdom ('You have never understood us'), and Hal's lapses, resigning for Carol Ferris and the Emerald Twilight rampage, are ignorance of the proper value of things rather than evil, since 'Hal's not evil... He believes he's acting for the right reasons.' The power ring is a modern Ring of Gyges, and Plato's test explains both who passes it and who fails.

26.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Green Lantern and Philosophy.md

27.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
27.relation: Finkelman uses the Corps' strangest members, Mogo the sentient planet, Leezle Pon the smallpox virus, the billion-puffball Collective, and Dkrtzy RRR the mathematical equation, to run the philosophy-of-biology debate over what counts as an individual. Plato's 'carving nature at its joints' frames the question; Heraclitean flux and Parmenidean changelessness picture monism's extremes; Aristotle's substance and soul deny Mogo is a living individual since its ecosystems (the Resal) do not serve it as organs serve a body; Darwin's natural selection makes organisms the real units, with Sinestro's attacks a kind of artificial selection that adapted the Corps. Gene reductionism (George C. Williams and Dawkins) versus Gould's contextual pluralism then decides how to count one billion puffballs as one Lantern.

28.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
28.relation: Jaissle reads the Book of Oa as Peirce's communal mind made physical: Kyle's ring translates the sounds of sector 3599 only because language 1,456 is already cataloged by the community, and even the Guardians cannot translate Hal's cursing until some Lantern has heard it. Because the individual apart from his fellows 'is only a negation,' the Guardians' deletion of the Blackest Night prophecy from the Book shows the fallibility of even immortal individual minds, while the Corps' shared experience across the War of Light vindicated the Cosmic Revelations. The green light beats the emotion-driven corps because willpower uniquely balances individual agency with communal knowledge.

29.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
29.relation: Kind uses John Stewart's Justice League arc, thrown into the future by Chronos, meeting his son Warhawk, and hiding it from Hawkgirl while dating Vixen, to stage fatalism: Pike and Taylor's arguments that a foreknown future, whether God's or a time traveler's, cannot be otherwise. Time travel itself forces a choice between presentism and eternalism, since Warhawk must 'exist now, already, in the future' for GL and Batman to visit him, and Smart's tenseless four-dimensionalism, with GL a series of timeslices and 'now' as subjective as 'here,' dissolves the fatalist worry by banishing tensed facts. The chapter lands on GL's battlefield advice to his son: 'Plant your feet,' owning a fate you cannot escape.

31.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
31.relation: Malloy explains Hal's endless giant hands and boxing gloves as an inherent limit of imagination rather than lazy writing: only the self-contradictory (square circles, married bachelors) cannot be imagined at all, and on Hume's empiricism imagination merely recombines copies of impressions, ideas, by the associations of contiguity, resemblance, and cause and effect, so Hal reproduces his most deeply impressed, most ordinary experiences. James's 'living options' bound what is worth imagining, and Kyle's JLA speed-to-sound machine shows invention's two stages: the experience-limited Lantern supplies the idea while the semisentient ring handles execution. The upshot is advice to go out and make new impressions.

32.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
32.relation: Nielsen asks whether a Green Lantern with unlimited willpower would be a god and answers no through Leibniz: God is the absolutely perfect being, where perfection excludes contradiction so that knowledge and power admit of perfection but 'the greatest of all numbers' does not, and such a being creates the best of all possible worlds. Hume's trilemma (impotent, malevolent, or whence evil?) is met with the theodicy that finite minds, like Lanterns baffled by Guardian decrees, cannot compare our world to the discarded possibilities, each perhaps as bad as Qward. Since omnipotence requires omniscience and omnibenevolence, not even Parallax, the Anti-Monitor, or Kyle as Ion counts as omnipotent: admirable and powerful, but not gods.

33.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
33.relation: Jones tests Clarke's law, that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, against the mythos's two green power sources: the Guardians' scientific Central Power Battery and the Starheart, the wild magic they quarantined, which later made Alan Scott's body pure green flame. Mauss's distinctions (magic private and rule-bound, religion communal and belief-powered, science open and collaborative) show the Guardians operate like sorcerers rather than scientists, secretive and incurious, while Kyle's Rebirth speech on the emotional electromagnetic spectrum explains why only willpower, the balancing center of the spectrum, can keep order where rage, fear, or love cannot.

3.title: The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series
3.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

7.title: Foreword
7.relation: Tom Morris recounts how the 2004 volume Harry Potter and Philosophy: If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts showed that academics were finding real wisdom in Rowling's series, and how he went from skeptic to reading all seven books six times and writing his own book on their insights into courage, love, and death. He presents this new collection, written after the series ended, as a 'Philosophical De-coder Ring' that reveals the deepest story behind the novels.

9.title: Introduction
9.relation: The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.

10.file: ch10 - PART ONE - THE HORCRUX OF THE MATTER DESTINY, IDENTITY, AND THE SOUL.md

15.relation: This section of the soul chapter lays out the Cartesian view: the immaterial soul explains only language and higher-level cognition, while material causes suffice for sensation, which consigns nonhuman animals to soullessness. It applies the view to Rowling's borderline creatures, such as owls that understand human speech and Crookshanks's suspicious intelligence, before introducing materialism as the fourth conception of the soul.

16.title: Unknown
16.file: ch16 - Unknown.md

17.title: Ghosts and “Going On”
17.relation: The section argues that everyday talk of soul mates, soulful art, and baring one's soul is metaphorical talk about our deepest emotions, love, and conscience, not commitment to an immaterial substance, and that even materialists can keep the vocabulary rather than translate Hoagy Carmichael into talk of C-fibers firing. It then forecasts the chapter's conclusion about Rowling: her Potter-world soul mixes this sentimental view with metaphysics borrowed from the Cartesian and sentience views.

18.title: The Dementor’s Kiss
18.file: ch18 - The Dementor’s Kiss.md
18.relation: The section argues that materialism is false in the Potter universe by cataloguing the ways souls outlive bodies: Hermione's claim that a sword through Ron would leave his soul untouched, the voices beyond the Ministry's veil, Nearly Headless Nick's ghostly imprint of a wizard who refused to 'go on,' Voldemort's wraith-like survival, and the 'neither ghost nor truly flesh' shades summoned from Voldemort's wand and by the Resurrection Stone. It sets up dementors and Horcruxes as the next tests of what souls are.

19.title: Horcruxes
19.relation: Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.

20.title: A Plausible View
20.relation: Reconstructing Slughorn's lesson to young Riddle, the section argues that because Voldemort's brain, senses, and magical powers survive his soul being ripped into seven, the Cartesian and sentience views are excluded and Rowling must hold the sentimental view: the soul is our capacity to love and our moral conscience. Voldemort's snake-faced transformation and his followers' fear-based loyalty, where even Bellatrix worships his power rather than being charmed, dramatize his lost humanity, and only remorse, which Harry begs him to 'try for' before the rebounding curse kills him, could have repaired the damage.

21.title: NOTES
21.file: ch21 - NOTES.md
21.relation: The concluding section of the soul essay asks whether Rowling's combined theory is likely true and answers probably not: there is no evidence of immaterial causes of brain events, the centuries-old mind-body interaction problem looms, and it is especially implausible that a separate substance handles only our deepest emotions and moral traits, with the added wrinkle that souls in the story display different physical powers depending on which spell conjures them. Yet it concedes that implausible metaphysics is no flaw in fiction that makes vivid what we care about and 'makes for a terrific story.'

22.title: Unknown
22.file: ch22 - Unknown.md

23.title: Mind-Body Distinctions
23.relation: Opening Eric Saidel's chapter, the section takes Sirius's tail-chasing as Padfoot in Order of the Phoenix as its puzzle: is Sirius a man sometimes in a dog's body, a dog sometimes in a man's body, or a third 'someone' who persists through the change? It widens the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations, framing it as a question about identity and the mind-body relation.

24.title: Whose Reasons
24.relation: The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.

25.title: A Step in the Right Direction
25.file: ch25 - A Step in the Right Direction.md
25.relation: Recasting the puzzle as a question of whose reasons cause Padfoot's actions, the section shows that strategy fails too: Harry as Runcorn and Ron as Cattermole act on Harry's and Ron's own reasons, never on those of the men whose bodies they wear, and dogs chase tails because it feels good, not for reasons at all. So reasons cannot explain either Padfoot's tail-chasing or werewolf Lupin's attacks, which come from his blood while his reasons would restrain him.

26.title: A Unified Self
26.file: ch26 - A Unified Self.md
26.relation: The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.

27.title: NOTES
27.relation: The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.
