Harry and his friends pass repeated tests of courage, loyalty, intelligence, and resourcefulness and emerge humble but battle-tested heroes like Frodo's fellowship, with Ron's temporary abandonment in Deathly Hallows the instructive exception.

95.title: Positioning Our Prejudgments
95.relation: Garver opens 'The Magic of Personal Transformation' by contrasting the Dudley who treats Harry 'like a dog that had rolled in something smelly' with the Deathly Hallows Dudley who leaves a cup of tea outside Harry's room, defies his parents, and shakes Harry's hand so that Harry sees a 'different personality.' He treats this as an epistemological puzzle about how the two boys came to know themselves and each other better, setting up the essay's account of knowing as a process of personal transformation in which encountering ourselves and others makes us better knowers.

96.title: The Ignorance of Ickle Dudleykins
96.file: ch96 - The Ignorance of Ickle Dudleykins.md
96.relation: The chapter presents Gadamer's claim that we can only interpret the world by coming to it with 'prejudgments,' the borrowed toolbox of questions, biases, and expectations without which anything we try to understand stays 'like a container sealed shut.' Whether prejudgments help or hinder depends on holding them loosely enough to let the situation reshape them, setting down the hammer and finding the screwdriver when the world resists.

97.title: Betrayed by Biases
97.relation: Applying Gadamer to Dudley, the chapter shows how Petunia and Vernon's doting ('no finer boy anywhere,' 'big-boned' rather than dieting, 'wouldn't hurt a fly') armor Dudley's prejudgments against every challenge. His close encounter with the dementors, forcing him to relive his worst moments, strips those rationalizations away so he finally sees himself as 'spoiled, pampered, bullying,' a radical readjustment that lets him recognize Harry's courage and feel gratitude and even affection.

98.title: Dangerous Dreams
98.relation: The chapter generalizes the pattern across the series: Harry's anti-Snape prejudice, misplaced trust in the fake Mad-Eye Moody and the Half-Blood Prince's potions book, Dumbledore's 'for the greater good' dreams with Grindelwald, Merope Gaunt's love-potion fantasy of Tom Riddle, the locket Horcrux magnifying the trio's suspicions until Ron storms off, and the Malfoys' underestimation of Voldemort all show prejudgments misreading reality until the pain of banging into it forces a rethink. Truth matters, Garver concludes, because false beliefs are an unreliable map for navigating the world.

99.title: The Cost of Overconfidence
99.relation: The chapter details Harry's overconfidence about his dream-connection to Voldemort's mind: cocky that he uniquely understands Voldemort, he dismisses Dumbledore's warning that the link runs both ways, neglects his Occlumency lessons out of distrust for Snape and irritation with Hermione, and never sees why the training matters. Snape's taunt, 'Maybe they make you feel special, important,' suggests Harry's prejudgment that his visions are a privileged window is also a temptation feeding his sense of mission.

100.title: Memories Help Make Meaning
100.relation: The chapter traces the fatal cost of Harry's unchecked prejudgments: trusting his O.W.L. dream-vision of Sirius being tortured, twisting Dumbledore's Occlumency warnings into confirmation that his dreams are real, and accepting Kreacher's cackling, self-interested testimony at Grimmauld Place without telling his friends the source, Harry launches the Department of Mysteries 'rescue' that gets Sirius killed. Garver softens the verdict, a fifteen-year-old with noble intentions, but the lesson stands: we see what we want to see through blinders we do not know we wear.

101.title: Moving Past Misdirection
101.relation: The chapter joins Augustine's Confessions analysis of time, where only in human experience does memory of the past meet anticipation of the future in the present, to Gadamer's view of prejudgments as tradition, memory 'passed down' that shapes how we approach the present. The Pensieve symbolizes this double, personal and social memory: Dumbledore's third-person viewing spots patterns, and the extracted memories of Riddle's orphanage sadism and the reconstructed testimonies of Hokey and Morfin Gaunt give Harry the knowledge of Voldemort's history, character, and vulnerabilities he needs to defeat him.

102.title: NOTES
102.relation: The essay's conclusion shows reality correcting every character's prejudgments: Dumbledore's wizard-supremacy dreams die with his sister, Merope's with the end of the love potion, Ron's with distance from the Horcrux, the Malfoys' when Voldemort threatens Draco, and Harry matures from naive boy to cocky teen to discerning young man. Garver draws the thesis that epistemology is inseparable from ethics, bravery and loyalty require true belief about danger and about Dumbledore's real faults, and Rowling's narrative misdirection makes readers undergo the same correction, so that following Harry's transformation we become better people, with even Dudley's change giving hope to the most resistant reader.

104.title: Tell Me One Last Thing
104.file: ch104 - Tell Me One Last Thing.md

106.title: Going Mental
106.relation: Opens the Just in Your Head? essay by taking Dumbledore's reply to Harry (of course it is happening inside your head, but why should that mean it is not real?) as a live metaphysical and epistemological question about appearance versus reality, noting that even A. J. Ayer dismissed his own near-death experience as hallucination. It retells Plato's cave allegory and reads Harry and Dumbledore's descent into the creepy cave in Half-Blood Prince, plus Harry's worry that the King's Cross dialogue was just a shadow on the wall, as a modern image of prisoners mistaking appearances for reality.

107.title: Rowling as an Inkling
107.relation: Argues Dumbledore's remark dissolves a false dilemma: the Hermione-as-idea versus Emma Watson contrast shows that existing in the head need not mean unreal. It then surveys thinkers who agree that mind and reality overlap: Plato's forms (the many broomsticks as imperfect copies of the ideal broomstick), Descartes on knowing essences by reason, Kant's mind-constructed objects, Berkeley's esse est percipi, Mill's phenomenalism, and Yogacara Buddhism's consciousness-fabricated emptiness, concluding that what is in the head can be genuinely real.

108.title: Harry’s Near-Death Experience
108.relation: Develops the essay's boldest suggestion: reading Rowling through C. S. Lewis and the Inklings, whose associate Barfield convinced Lewis that if thought were a purely subjective event, logical and moral claims to truth would collapse, the germ of Lewis's argument from reason later refined by Plantinga and contested by Anscombe. On this view our logic participates in a cosmic Logos, which Christians identify with Christ, a point the chapter ties to Rowling's remark that it was no coincidence Harry's fateful dialogue happened at King's Cross, so what occurs in the head can genuinely put us in touch with reality.

109.title: NOTES
109.relation: Surveys near-death-experience research from Moody's Life after Life to Susan Blackmore's debunking explanations (oxygen starvation, cultural variation) and argues the skeptical conclusion does not follow: a child's vision of her living dog Sparky on the other side could still be a genuine divinely created revelation happening wholly inside her head. It reads Harry's King's Cross way-station the same way, since wizards can channel themselves through portraits, ghosts, and Legilimency, and closes with Emerson's Over-Soul claim that moments of faith deserve to be ascribed more reality than ordinary experience.

111.title: “A Swirling, Silvery Mass”
111.relation: Opens Amy Kind's essay by presenting the Pensieve as a device for offloading memories like data from a hard drive, easing obsession and revealing patterns, and asks what that does to the boundaries of mind, memory, and self. If thoughts can be extracted from the head, tampered with, stored elsewhere, and shared, as with the Pensieve and Tom Riddle's diary, then memory-based accounts of what makes a person persist over time come under pressure, and it is no longer obvious whose mind a thought belongs to.

112.title: The Hallows of the Mind
112.file: ch112 - The Hallows of the Mind.md
112.relation: Uses Rowling's light-made-liquid description of the Pensieve's silvery contents to stage the materialism versus dualism debate: Hobbes-style materialists can treat ghosts like Nearly Headless Nick and the strands of thought clinging to wands or leaking from dying wizards as matter, while Cartesian dualists find support in Harry's fear at King's Cross that he might exist only as disembodied thought. Snape's remark that the mind is a complex and many-layered thing frames how little is settled about the mind-brain relation.

113.title: Confundus!
113.relation: Challenges the assumption that the mind stops at the skull by deploying Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis: just as a prosthetic leg, Moody's magic eye, or Harry's holly-and-phoenix-feather wand can count as part of the body, Otto's notebook shows external storage functioning as memory itself rather than a mere aid. Tom Riddle's diary, where a memory acts and thinks for itself because a soul fragment lived in it, and Snape's memories being his whether in his head, a phial, or the Pensieve make physical location incidental to mental ownership.

114.title: Mischief Managed
114.relation: Defends the Otto case against the obvious objection that notebook entries are not conscious beliefs: most beliefs, like Ron's that Ireland beat Bulgaria at the Quidditch World Cup, are nonoccurrent anyway, and Rita Skeeter pausing to recall where Bathilda Bagshot lives works exactly like Otto consulting his notebook. Constant integration is what separates genuine mind-extension from mere aids, which is why Harry's borrowed Half-Blood Prince textbook, Neville's password list, and even Hermione's well-thumbed Hogwarts, A History stay outside the mind.

115.title: Lumos!
115.relation: Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.

116.title: NOTES
116.relation: Resolves the threat by sorting memories into know-how, factual, and first-person experiential kinds: identity rides on experiential memories, but Pensieve replays are third-person, as Rowling confirmed about Dumbledore's memory of Bellatrix Lestrange's trial. So sharing a Pensieve memory endangers who you are no more than sharing an experience or using a Time-Turner, and whether your thoughts sit in a mind, a Pensieve, or a notebook, they remain your own.

118.title: The Good
118.relation: Opens Gregory Bassham's audit of Hogwarts: from a kid's point of view the school is paradise, all magic and no math, but he asks what the great philosophers of education, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and Dewey, would make of teaching and learning there. The chapter will weigh Susan Engel's claim that Hogwarts is a model school against problems documented by contemporary educational research.

120.title: Unknown
120.relation: Concedes Hogwarts succeeds at its one job, teaching magic, and explains how: effective lessons like Lupin teaching Harry to conjure a Patronus and Harry training Dumbledore's Army proceed apprenticeship-style through demonstration, practice, individualized coaching, and mastery. This hands-on learning by doing, not Professor Binns's droning lectures or Umbridge's theory-only textbook assignments, is why students actually acquire magical skill.

122.title: Unknown
122.relation: Applies Dewey's demand that education be part of life rather than preparation for some remote future, together with Whitehead's critique of inert, undigested knowledge: Hogwarts students see the practical payoff of Apparition, Transfiguration, and Defense Against the Dark Arts, which makes them eager learners, while Hagrid's Blast-Ended Skrewts and Trelawney's bogus crystal-ball gazing are the inert exceptions that prove the rule.

124.title: Unknown
124.relation: Catalogues the school's hazards, giant spiders and hostile centaurs in the Forbidden Forest, grindylows and a giant squid, the Whomping Willow, potions gone awry, injury-prone Quidditch and the Triwizard Tournament, and children carrying lethal wands, to argue that if Hogwarts really existed its danger would be indefensible. Magical medicine fixes much, but as Dumbledore says, no magic can reawaken the dead.

125.title: Unknown
125.relation: Grades the faculty from the competent and caring (Dumbledore, McGonagall, Flitwick, Sprout, Lupin) through the flawed (Hagrid, the disguised Crouch, the bullying Snape) to the downright crummy (Binns, Trelawney, Lockhart, Umbridge), then locates the deeper cause: the wizarding world has no teacher education or certification, so anyone from Hagrid to a homicidal impostor can take a classroom, making poor instruction structural rather than accidental.

126.title: The Ugly
126.relation: Argues the ugliest defect is curricular: Hogwarts teaches only vocational magic, giving students the tools of power without the wisdom to use them, and so fails Adler's three aims of secondary schooling and the aims every major philosopher of education defended, Plato's wisdom and just society, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Locke's virtue and wisdom, Rousseau's natural education, Kantian character, and Deweyan growth. Even allowing that Dumbledore's office is a school of virtue outside class, most students never get his mentorship, leaving wizards ill-equipped for problems like anti-Muggle bigotry.

127.title: Like Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans, a Mix
127.file: ch127 - Like Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans, a Mix.md
127.relation: Names pureblood supremacism, Voldemort's Nazi-like movement whose victory would mean totalitarianism, thought control, secret police, mock trials, and racial cleansing, as the greatest problem wizards face, and faults Hogwarts education for ignoring it: no antiracist teaching despite rampant slurs, silence about the oppressed house-elves of Hogwarts, A History, and Slytherin left as a hothouse breeding Death Eaters and fifth columnists. Against Prinzi's gradualist defense of Dumbledore as a persuasive libertarian, the chapter presses the fair question of why he did not do more.

130.title: PART FIVE - BEYOND THE VEIL DEATH, HOPE, AND MEANING
130.file: ch130 - PART FIVE - BEYOND THE VEIL DEATH, HOPE, AND MEANING.md

131.title: Remorse and Death
131.relation: Opens Charles Taliaferro's essay by reading Fawkes's burning and rebirth as a clue to a philosophical model of moral repair: the wrongdoer must confess, feel sincere remorse, repudiate the pleasure or gain of the wrongdoing, and form new intentions, a kind of death to the old self like Christian baptism, after which the repaired relationship is reborn and the friend is seen in a new light. It then sets up Voldemort as the perversion of this pattern, spreading death by clinging to life while Harry and Dumbledore move to deeper life by accepting death.

132.title: The Inversion of Voldemort
132.relation: Sharpens the remorse-versus-regret contrast through Voldemort's cold regret after having Nagini kill Snape, and shows true remorse at work in Dumbledore's confession about the Resurrection Stone ring, his arranged death at Snape's hand, and his tearful self-disclosure to Harry at King's Cross. Harry too must die to be regenerated: letting Voldemort strike him destroys the Horcrux inside so that his soul becomes whole and completely his own, while lesser purgings, like his furious outburst at Ron and Hermione, and his love for Ginny complete the pattern of dying to the old self.

133.title: The Integrity Objection
133.relation: Completes the inversion: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes Voldemort's soul, and only excruciating remorse could put it back together, something he will never attempt, while his evil literally disembodies him until he lives parasitically on the blood and limbs of others. Against this, Hermione's gloss on the Potters' gravestone, the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, means the soul survives whatever happens to the body, grounding the contrast between Voldemort's pathetic, unmourned end and the honored deaths of Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, and Colin Creevey.

134.title: The Fantasy Objection
134.relation: Takes up the integrity objection advanced by the Freudian psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renunciation cannot change the fact that it was you who did the wrong, so posing as an altogether new person invites self-deception, as with the reformed alcoholic who still calls himself an alcoholic. Taliaferro grants the regeneration model can be abused but argues renewal requires something very close to dying to the past, using Snape, unable to confess his love for Lily, still nursing resentment, honored only when Harry names his son Severus, as the tragedy of reform without full renunciation.

135.title: Fawkes’s Secret
135.relation: Answers the fantasy objection, that ethics drawn from a world of spells and talking portraits is escapist make-believe, by noting that Rowling's moral insight does not depend on the magic: loyalty, friendship, romantic love, fairness, opposition to enslavement, free the house-elves, and the roles of remorse, forgiveness, and reform are values of our own Muggle world. In the name of realism, the objector merely fails to engage the imagination.

136.title: NOTES
136.relation: Closes the essay by asking why Fawkes never cured Dumbledore's ring-curse or blocked Snape's killing curse, and answers that the phoenix may have left Hogwarts only because his work was done: rupture, betrayal, and vice are healed by a death and rebirth in which one rises from the flames of remorseful confession a new person, with radically new desires, ready to rejoin relationships and community.

139.title: The Approaching Battle
139.relation: Frames death as philosophy's ultimate question and contrasts the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is simply the end of us with Heidegger's authenticity: boldly facing that death may come at any moment keeps us from living half-asleep, a view Plato anticipated by teaching that true philosophers make dying their profession. Harry, confronted with death from infancy, lives authentically, while Voldemort's flight from death marks him as the inauthentic case the essay traces through the Deathly Hallows death march.

140.title: King’s Cross Station
140.relation: Reads Harry's walk into the Forbidden Forest, knowing he must die so the fragment of Voldemort's soul dies with him, his senses sharpening and gratitude welling for everything he never fully valued, as Heideggerian coming to terms with mortality rather than morbid brooding. Colin Creevey, the underage wizard who sneaks back to fight and falls, is offered as a second example of authentic living that recognizes limitations and seizes opportunities regardless of belief in an afterlife.

141.title: Reap a Destiny
141.relation: Interprets the King's Cross scene through Heidegger's counsel to choose an exemplar from the past and dialogue with them: Dumbledore, freshly repentant for his youthful hunger for glory, plays exactly that role in a way-station likened to purgatory, while the flayed child-like creature under the chair is Voldemort's soul beyond help. The chapter closes by linking his fear-driven quest for deathlessness to Tolkien's One Ring, in which Sauron poured his own life-force, both fantasy dark lords undone by the desire for deathlessness.

142.title: NOTES
142.relation: Uses William James's marginal motto, sow a thought and reap a destiny, together with Aristotle's account of how repeated acts shape the soul, to argue that Voldemort's maimed afterlife-state is the cumulative result of freely chosen evil he can no longer muster remorse to undo. Setting Heidegger's atheism against Rowling's depicted afterlife, and adding Locke's character-and-memory identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the soul's immortality must concern us, it concludes that if Rowling is right, every choice here is infinitely consequential.

144.title: Fulfillment for Muggles and Wizards
144.file: ch144 - Fulfillment for Muggles and Wizards.md

145.title: Voldemort and the Sophists
145.relation: Opens the comparison of Harry's willingness to die in Deathly Hallows with Socrates' death for his convictions, placing both inside ethics, the inquiry into how we ought to live and what kind of people we ought to be. It presents the challenge of why be moral at all and introduces Plato's Republic answer, endorsed by Socrates, that being moral is necessary and sufficient for true happiness, noting that Socrates, like Harry against Voldemort, had enemies of his own.

146.title: The Common Good versus the Greater Good
146.file: ch146 - The Common Good versus the Greater Good.md
146.relation: Casts the Harry-Voldemort conflict as Socrates versus the Sophists: Thrasymachus's Republic claim that the unjust always come out ahead describes Voldemort's exploitation of his followers' trust exactly. The flayed child under the chair at King's Cross enacts Plato's afterlife justice, and the Republic's tripartite soul and cardinal virtues explain why Harry's reason-ruled courage, wisdom, and justice make the moral life the rational choice, as rational as choosing bodily health over chronic illness.

147.title: Two Keys to the Good Life
147.file: ch147 - Two Keys to the Good Life.md
147.relation: Contrasts the greater good, young Dumbledore and Grindelwald's For the Greater Good scheme to subjugate Muggles, under which the rights, dignity, and integrity of individuals are up for grabs whenever the majority benefits, with the common good, where sacrifice serves all, as in the civil rights movement's appeal to the good of the whole American community. Harry's choice to return from King's Cross and finish Voldemort defeats the greater-good revolution and realizes the common good of Muggles and wizards alike.

148.title: The End of the Story
148.file: ch148 - The End of the Story.md
148.relation: Completes the parallel: Socrates died refusing to abandon the examined life, and his martyrdom, like Dumbledore's staged death that protected Snape's spying, served the common good, since there can be no common good without individual goodness. The chapter closes with two Muggle lessons, live devoted to something larger than yourself as Lily Potter, Dumbledore, Harry, King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates did, and find mentors, as Harry found Dumbledore and as readers can find in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics or Confucius.

3.title: The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series
3.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

7.title: NOTES
7.relation: The editor's introduction argues that Heroes is more reflective than average television, opening from Mohinder's 'Genesis' voice-over about life's mysteries and claiming that we are all philosophers seeking answers to the same fundamental questions. It frames narrative (from Aesop's fables to the Bible) as a powerful vehicle for moral lessons and previews the book's questions: is the Company good or evil, does Hiro really have a destiny, could mind reading be a power we already have, is time travel possible, what does Peter owe Nathan, and is it okay to lie to hide one's powers? It closes with John McCain's SNL joke defending Heroes against its competition.

9.title: NOTES
9.relation: Sharp argues that superpowered individuals break the equality assumption on which social contract theory rests: since Claire cannot be killed, D.L. can walk out of any jail, and Matt can sway juries, Hobbes's fear-of-death rationale for the contract seems not to apply to them. He then answers that the heroes remain effectively equal (Claire can still be killed by a wood splinter, Adam by decapitation) and shares Locke's and Rawls's reasons for contract, yet shows Rawls's difference principle would force the powered to serve society while the liberty principle forbids it, and that Sylar could not even be morally condemned under a pure Hobbesian reading. Cases like Claude's invisible petty theft (Glaucon's Ring of Gyges made real), the 'Five Years Gone' registered-superhumans future, and Linderman's plot to reunite society through the New York explosion lead to the conclusion that superpowers really would break society.

10.title: NOTES
10.file: ch10 - NOTES.md
10.relation: Miles asks whether extraordinary power generates extraordinary obligations, testing Spider-Man's 'with great power comes great responsibility' against Claude the invisible thief and the heroes' reluctance. He uses Singer's principle of minimal obligation (Micah diverting the train from the infant; Claire's negligible risk in burning-building rescues; Hiro teleporting across distance) and Kant's perfect/imperfect obligation distinction (Niki choosing between saving Monica and mothering Micah; Noah Bennet lying to protect Claire) before deploying Fishkin's three 'explosion' objections: too many endangered people, too many capable heroes, and too many repeated rescues dilute obligation. He concludes the heroes went beyond the call of duty in saving New York, so saving the world could legitimately be their paid job, like lifeguards or soldiers.

11.title: NOTES
11.file: ch11 - NOTES.md
11.relation: Robichaud evaluates the morally gray Company: its goal of mastering the evolutionary forces behind powers is tested against eugenics worries, the 'playing God' objection that natural processes have intrinsic value, and Sandel's Case against Perfection (that mastery breeds inflated responsibility, eroded community, and rigidity), each of which he finds inconclusive or outweighed by lives saved from people like Ted Sprague. He then turns to blame for the bag-and-tag program, applying Dennis Thompson's criterion to hold the founders plus hands-on agents like Bennet and the Haitian responsible while excusing accountants like Malsky. Finally he sets conditions for when an insider such as Bennet or Mohinder may blow the whistle, ruling out Bennet's murderous take-down-from-within scheme.

12.title: NOTES
12.file: ch12 - NOTES.md
12.relation: Southworth defends Tim Kring against comic fans' plagiarism charges (Heroes versus X-Men's Rogue and Wolverine, Rising Stars' identical plot), arguing plagiarism requires intending to pass off known others' ideas as one's own, which Kring's ignorance of the genre (he asked 'Who's Magneto?') rules out, even accidentally. But he then convicts Kring of failing his epistemic responsibility, applying Montmarquet's virtues: Kring lacked epistemic responsibility (not reading the Rising Stars Lindelof gave him), impartiality (deliberately refusing to learn the genre), and sobriety (pressing on despite Loeb's warning that everything he pitched had been done). Parallel cases from the show include Mohinder's early dismissal of his father's research and Niki's obligation to learn about Jessica.

13.title: PART TWO - SUPERMEN, SAMURAI, AND INVISIBLE MEN
13.file: ch13 - PART TWO - SUPERMEN, SAMURAI, AND INVISIBLE MEN.md

14.title: NOTES
14.file: ch14 - NOTES.md
14.relation: Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.

15.title: NOTES
15.file: ch15 - NOTES.md
15.relation: Baldwin argues the popular view of Bushido as a moral code (Nitobe, Star Wars, Kurosawa, Campbell's Jungian hero archetype) is historically wrong: by the Hagakure, Bushido is a death-ready 'mode of action' so morally neutral that even villains like Takezo Kensei or Sylar can practice it. He traces Hiro's evolution from comic-book and video-game hero-worship, through the Yaeko betrayal that turned Kensei into Adam Monroe, toward the fearless Future Hiro ideal of 'no-mind' readiness for death (echoing D.T. Suzuki's Zen reading). Because the Meiji reforms abolished the samurai class, Hiro can never literally be a samurai, only follow Bushido analogically, which lets him remain both superhero and samurai.

16.title: NOTES
16.file: ch16 - NOTES.md
16.relation: Adams uses Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask whether superpowered people have reason to be moral, answering through the tripartite soul: Claire declining credit for the fire rescue shows well-governed thumos, her calculated revenge on Brody shows logistics ruling spirit, while Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is textbook epithumetikon and intemperance that makes his life spin 'super' out of control. Cases like Micah's ATM thefts and Hiro's Vegas cheating (punished by a desert beating) illustrate that vice harms the agent's own soul, since justice is the soul's health. Claire's hospital apology to Brody is read through the Pagan Golden Rule and Sophocles' Ajax: enemies can become friends, so virtue, not mere conformity, is 'only natural' for heroes and ordinary people alike.

17.title: PART THREE - METAPHYSICS, REGULAR PHYSICS, AND HEROIC TIME TRAVEL
17.file: ch17 - PART THREE - METAPHYSICS, REGULAR PHYSICS, AND HEROIC TIME TRAVEL.md

18.title: NOTES
18.file: ch18 - NOTES.md
18.relation: Johnson asks whether Isaac's paintings and Hiro's visions make the future fated, running Aristotle's sea-battle argument: if propositions about the future are already true (by bivalence and the correspondence theory of a 'written timeline'), then Sylar's exploding New York is inevitable and no one is free. He extends the problem to infallible foreknowledge via Future Hiro as a stand-in for God, considers and rejects Boethius's timeless-knowledge solution, and uses open theism plus a probability calculation about Ando's waffles order to show probabilistic foreknowledge is useless. He concludes most of Isaac's 'prophecies' are really self-fulfilling, as when Noah's efforts to dodge the eighth painting cause his shooting, and that the Heroes universe leaves room to deny fate.

19.title: NOTES
19.relation: Luck argues backward time travel is nearly useless for a hero: after the grandfather paradox (Hiro hearing of Kaito's murder only because Kaito died), he shows Lewis's linear time travel makes Hiro necessarily fail to save Kaito, Charlie, or Isaac, yet cannot explain Hiro meeting Ando two days after a five-week absence or New York being spared. Branching time travel, where each trip into the past spawns an alternate universe, fits Volume 1 coherently by building a Heroes multiverse of Hiro-1 through Hiro-4 and explaining Future Hiro's subway appearance as a 'brute fact' copied into branching universes. The price of coherence is that Hiro only ever saves other universes' New Yorks, never his own.

20.title: NOTES
20.relation: Faraci asks why Hiro may prevent the nuclear future ('save the cheerleader') but comes to agree it would be wrong to save Kaito from the past ('we cannot play God'). Using thought experiments (a variant where Hiro learns of his father's death in the future) he isolates the past/future asymmetry as the candidate morally relevant factor, then tests justifications: Aquinas's natural law fails because observing the past would be equally 'unnatural,' and a duty to keep the timeline intact would also forbid changing the future, which is just as 'settled' to a time traveler. Since every theory of where Hiro's 'present' lies fails or collapses into subjectivity, he concludes there is no good reason to treat altering the past differently from altering the future, while demonstrating how normative ethics evaluates moral intuitions.

21.title: NOTES
21.file: ch21 - NOTES.md
21.relation: Tests the science behind the powers: Claire's and Adam Monroe's rapid healing is deemed barely possible (retained telomeres, error-free cell replication) but far too fast to be realistic, while Nathan's flight survives neither rocket-propellant nor magnetic-levitation explanations, leaving undirected manipulation of gravity as the only option. Hiro's teleportation and time travel are analyzed with Minkowski diagrams, worldlines, and light cones — his rescue of Claire from Sylar and Elle in 'The Eclipse: Part II' puts his broken worldline outside every light cone — and wormholes, quantum entanglement, and quantum tunneling are each rejected as workable mechanisms. The chapter then shows Darwinian evolution cannot produce Dr. Suresh's 'evolutionary jump': even Adam Monroe fathering children across the globe for four hundred years could not spread and diversify a power gene that fast, concluding that only design (God, aliens, or destiny) could explain the show's powers.

22.title: NOTES
22.file: ch22 - NOTES.md
22.relation: Asks how to tell genuine science from pseudoscience using Chandra Suresh's rejected Activating Evolution theory, Sheldrake's morphic fields, alchemy, and Behe's intelligent design. Kuhn's picture of normal science, anomalies, and revolutions explains why Suresh would need a full-blown crisis in evolutionary theory — such as people actually flying — before the community accepts him, and why time rather than mockery settles a theory's fate. Ockham's razor condemns the unnecessary organizing principles in both Sheldrake's and Suresh's theories, and intelligent design is exposed as bad method because, like creationism, it was devised to protect a prior commitment from disconfirming fossil and cosmological evidence.

23.title: PART FOUR - THE MINDS OF HEROES
23.file: ch23 - PART FOUR - THE MINDS OF HEROES.md

24.title: NOTE
24.relation: Asks whether amnesia preserves numerical identity: is the Peter who wakes in the shipping crate still Volume-1 Peter, are Niki and Jessica one person, and is the Sylar whom Matt rewrites with Nathan's memories now Nathan? The chapter builds Locke's memory criterion, breaks it with Reid's transitivity objection run through Mohinder's timeline in 'Five Years Gone,' repairs it with Grice's and Perry's memory-ancestor chains, then destroys the repair with Arthur Petrelli's wipe of Hiro (Forgetful Hiro vs. Stabby Hiro), Bernard Williams's torture thought experiment, Parfit's psychological spectrum, and the graphic novel's branching self-copier Evan. It concludes that no memory criterion can define personal identity, yet memory still matters practically: Claire must act as if she persists over time to keep her promise to Zach and to bother finishing the manatee assignment.

25.title: NOTES
25.relation: Distinguishes Matt Parkman's supernatural telepathy from the 'mundane mind reading' everyone performs, then argues even Matt's power cannot solve the problem of other minds: the suicidal woman's thoughts he hears in the bar ('One Giant Leap') could be part of a Maury-Parkman-style illusion, and a brain-to-brain link could never rule out that others are Chalmers-style philosophical zombies. After grounding the skepticism in Descartes' cogito and method of doubt, it defends our everyday attribution of minds by analogy (Audrey Hanson reading Claire's insincerity) on pragmatic grounds, and maps Matt's progression from hearing thoughts to nightmare manipulation and compulsion onto the four adaptive functions philosophers assign to mind reading: interpretation, prediction, coordination, and influence. It closes by showing why neuroimaging-based technological mind reading remains a pipe dream, since brain recordings are quantitative syntax without semantics.

26.title: NOTES
26.file: ch26 - NOTES.md
26.relation: Takes Claude's label of Peter as an 'empath' seriously and tests three accounts of empathy against his power: Hume's emotional resonance (rejected because Peter keeps powers after the donor leaves), Scheler's absorption into another's identity, and Hume's conversion of ideas into vivid impressions, settling on the mirror-neuron thought that Peter literally replicates other people's brain structures — which explains why he copies Isaac's painting skill and even Sylar's anger in 'Kindred.' It then asks whether empathy makes you moral and answers no — Elle enjoys Peter's pain and Mohinder feels his experimental subjects' terror — arguing instead that empathy needs a filter: Hume's general point of view and Adam Smith's impartial spectator, illustrated by Hiro's imagined Kensei ideal and by Nathan serving as Peter's emotional filter until his death leaves Peter without one.

27.title: PART FIVE - VILLAINS, FAMILY, AND LYING
27.file: ch27 - PART FIVE - VILLAINS, FAMILY, AND LYING.md

28.title: NOTES
28.relation: Reads the show's eclipse icon against Plato's sun of the good — goodness has become hard to discern — and tests four theories of evil on the characters: Socrates' claim that no one errs knowingly is half-confirmed since villains like Angela and Nathan always take themselves to be doing right; Aristotle's akrasia and vice as an excess or deficiency of disposition fit Sylar's blood-scrawled 'Forgive me' apartment and his uncontrolled hunger; and Nietzsche's Übermensch and pre-Christian master morality raise the uncomfortable question of why Sylar preying on inferiors is not heroic like Achilles. The chapter's endorsed answer is Gilligan's ethics of care: the heroes are good because they care — Matt for Molly and Daphne, Bennet for Claire — while evil is the absence of care, though Bennet's authoritarian, family-only care shows that care itself must be both widened and restrained.

29.title: NOTES
29.relation: Explains the seemingly incomprehensible things Heroes characters do for family by sorting their motives into three theories of family obligation: universal justice (framed by Socrates confronting Euthyphro for prosecuting his own father), care ethics' partiality to loved ones, and Confucian role-based duty with its asymmetrical parent–child, husband–wife, and sibling obligations. Noah Bennet turns out to be Confucian in practice ('I'm your father, Claire Bear') despite his universalist Company rhetoric, Hiro defies Kaito's Confucianism for the greater good while Kaito still teaches him the sword because that is a father's role, Niki and Janice act from care while D.L. and Micah act from roles, Mohinder's duty is Confucian sonship to his dead father, and the Haitian kills his own brother Baron precisely because stopping him is his brotherly role.

30.title: NOTES
30.relation: First defines lying — distinguishing it from mere error (Angela believing Peter dead), from the Haitian's non-verbal memory-wipe deception, and from Hiro's silent staging of Ando's fake death — then tests moral theories against the show's liars. Kant's categorical imperative bans all lying but is abandoned when Sylar demands a friend's hiding place; utilitarianism vindicates Victoria Pratt's lie about the virus vial yet also licenses Linderman's .07% explosion and Plato's noble lie of the earthborn metals, which the chapter rejects. Machiavelli's advice that princes may lie to keep power is played out by 'President Sylar' in 'Five Years Gone,' and the chapter finally endorses Sissela Bok's presumption against lying — a public-reasoning procedure modeled by Bob Bishop and Mohinder before Monica's virus injection.

6.title: introd.xhtml
6.relation: The editors' introduction frames The Hobbit as Plato's Allegory of the Cave retold 'there and back again': like the freed prisoner, Bilbo leaves his comfortable hole, has his eyes opened by a frightening journey, and returns 'queer' to neighbors who cannot accept that life offers more than order and routine. It lists the book's guiding questions - whether adventures are worth missing dinner, whether food and song outrank gold, whether powerful technology can be trusted or must be destroyed, and the duties of friends - as the essays' shared agenda.

8.title: a2.xhtml
8.relation: Bassham reads The Hobbit as a story of moral growth: the comfort-loving Bilbo who trembles like jelly at the dwarves' plans grows into the hobbit who volunteers to carry the Ring to Mordor. Growth in wisdom comes from Socratic self-examination (learning how little one knows) and from broadened experience of the wide world; growth in virtue comes either from sudden conversion (Thorin's Scrooge-like deathbed repentance) or, as Aristotle taught, from slow habituation - Bilbo's repeated courageous and generous acts (sparing Gollum, returning the elf-keys, giving up the Arkenstone) build lasting character. Seneca's view that hardship strengthens supplies the framework for why Bilbo's trials on the road ennobled rather than broke him.

10.title: a3.xhtml
10.file: ch10 - a3.xhtml.md
10.relation: Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.

11.title: a3.xhtml
11.file: ch11 - a3.xhtml.md

12.title: a4.xhtml
12.file: ch12 - a4.xhtml.md
12.relation: Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.

13.title: a4.xhtml
13.file: ch13 - a4.xhtml.md

14.title: a5.xhtml
14.file: ch14 - a5.xhtml.md
14.relation: Knepp maps Appiah's cosmopolitanism onto Bilbo's journey from provincial hobbit - the Shire-folk who find even across-Brandywine hobbits odd - to citizen of the world who wants the good of dwarves, elves and men. Shared adventure, not argument, teaches tolerance: Bilbo and the dwarves never convert each other but learn to live together through meals, bickering and shared survival, exactly Appiah's 'conversation' that helps people get used to one another. The elf-made swords and the mithril coat show 'cultural contamination' as a good; Gimli and Legolas illustrate fallibilism and pluralism; Smaug and the orcs are anti-cosmopolites who impose their single way by force.

15.title: a5.xhtml
15.file: ch15 - a5.xhtml.md

16.title: a6_parte-2.xhtml
16.file: ch16 - a6_parte-2.xhtml.md

17.title: a7.xhtml
17.relation: The chapter sets the bloody classical ideal of glory (Homer's kleos, Beowulf, Alexander modeling himself on Achilles) - which Augustine already condemned as libido dominandi - against Plato's alternative of a life aimed at the good, the true and the beautiful. Thorin's last charge at the Battle of Five Armies fits the heroic tradition, but Tolkien's real point is that Bilbo, the 'grocer' who feels the dwarves' treasure-lust yet walks away from it, and who ends by inviting the dwarves to four-o'clock tea instead of a victory feast, shows glory subordinated to domestic beauty and humility. Socrates' question in the Apology - why care so little for wisdom and the soul's improvement while chasing wealth, honor and reputation - is exactly the temptation Bilbo resists, and the Symposium's move from battle to a drinking-party of love-of-beauty mirrors Tolkien's placement of heroism in hobbits rather than warriors.

18.title: a7.xhtml
18.file: ch18 - a7.xhtml.md

19.title: a8.xhtml
19.relation: Garcia argues Tolkien writes with a virtue-ethical moral theory: Middle-earth peoples are characterized by moral traits (noble eagles, cruel orcs), intentions matter (Bilbo is not to blame for the discomforting barrel escape because he meant rescue, and he turns back through the mountain tunnels because loyalty and courage demand it), and the book's drama is the tension between Aristotle's 'great-souled' proper pride and Aquinas' Christian humility. Thorin's pride (self-styled 'King under the Mountain', refusing Bard's just claim), Smaug's vanity that Bilbo flatters to find the bare patch, and the dragon-sickness illustrate pride as vice, while Bilbo's growth - believing after the spiders that 'there was more in him' yet accepting Gandalf's 'you are only quite a little fellow in a wide world' with a laugh - exemplifies correct self-assessment between vanity and undue humility.

21.title: a9.xhtml
21.file: ch21 - a9.xhtml.md
21.relation: The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.

22.title: a9.xhtml
22.file: ch22 - a9.xhtml.md

23.title: a10.xhtml
23.relation: Johnson tests the Battle of Five Armies against just war theory as developed from Augustine through Aquinas: the men under Bard satisfy legitimate authority, just cause and last resort (they bargained, even using the Arkenstone as leverage and trying economic pressure), the Elvenking explicitly waits rather than start 'this war for gold', while the dwarves fail the criteria because greed and pride are not just causes and a thirteenth-share was a cheap price for peace. The war that actually happens - the three armies uniting against Bolg's orc-host - is justified self- and other-defense, whereas the orcs' motives (revenge, plunder, conquest) are unjust. Against apparent pacifist evidence (Tom Bombadil, Frodo at the Shire 'scouring', Gandalf's 'pity' for Gollum), Johnson reads Tolkien's letters as endorsing war as sometimes necessary and sometimes 'in the right', though Tolkien rejects the theory's reasonable-chance-of-success condition given the hopeless stands at Helm's Deep and the Morannon.

25.title: a11.xhtml
25.relation: Tallon reads The Hobbit as an exercise in aesthetics: Tolkien half-accepts the Kant-era 'art for art's sake' settlement - dwarves once made 'things of beauty for pure delight', elves sing 'lovely nonsense' without shame, Gandalf blows smoke-rings and fireworks - while rejecting both Victorian moralism and Wilde's amoralism. Instead aesthetic sensitivity is a moral thermometer grounded in Augustine's ordo amoris: orcs 'make no beautiful things, but many clever ones', dragons cannot tell good work from bad nor mend a loose scale (which is how Bard's arrow finds Smaug's bare patch), and Aule creates dwarves out of love so others might enjoy the beauty of Ea while Saruman's 'mind of metal and wheels' breeds Uruk-hai for domination. Beauty also acts morally: the dwarves' song awakens Bilbo's 'love of beautiful things made by hands' and, as Scarry and Murdoch hold, that awakening of desire beyond oneself is what prepares us for justice.

26.title: a11.xhtml
26.file: ch26 - a11.xhtml.md

27.title: a12.xhtml
27.relation: O'Hara argues that play is what makes hobbits - and us - fully human: Bilbo's childhood games of throwing stones, riddles and smoke-rings turn out to be training for the quest (his stone-throwing fells the spiders, his riddle-practice buys time with Gollum), and even Gollum's riddle-game makes him momentarily 'less a monster and more a person'. Following Schiller's and Huizinga's Homo ludens thesis that play completes humanity, he distinguishes play from idleness (Aquinas held recreation continues in heaven; Peirce called play 'vigorous exercise'), places leisure among the goods of Aristotle's 'we play in order to be serious', and contrasts Gandalf's beauty-directed fireworks with the orcs' merely useful explosions and work-chants. But play has limits: Kant warns against treating persons as toys, and Bilbo's lesson is 'Never laugh at live dragons!'

30.title: a14.xhtml
30.relation: Stewart argues Middle-earth magic is rule-bound engineering rather than Hume's miracle as 'a violation of the laws of nature': spells fail, the Ring hides neither shadow nor wet footprints, and magic comes in strengths like gravity, so fear of Gandalf is fear of superior knowledge of nature's laws, not of lawlessness. The deeper point is Tolkien's linkage of magic with technology as the impatient will to make one's will effective quickly - Sauron is 'Lord of magic and machines', the Ring is the supreme technological artifact, Saruman's forged men and blast-fires embody domination - while elvish 'Art' is sub-creation and Beorn's communion with animals models harmony with nature. Like Thoreau pricing possessions in 'how much life' they cost, the chapter ends with Tolkien's warning that 'if a thing can be done, it should be done' is the great false assumption of our age.

32.title: a15.xhtml
32.relation: Kind uses our genuine reactions to Bilbo - pity when he sits forlorn at the Lonely Mountain, anxiety at the riddle-game, outrage at Thorin's rebuke - to stage the paradox of fiction: how can emotions be rational toward someone we know never existed? She walks through the failed solutions: Radford's verdict that fiction-emotions are irrational like fearing a mountain lion after the sighting is debunked; Walton's 'quasi-emotions' of make-believe, which cannot explain why we cannot switch our fear of the wargs off at will; and thought theory's mental images, since what we fear is Smaug, not our mental image of Smaug. Her preferred route, following Richard Moran, relaxes the belief requirement itself - as Hume noted passions resist rational assessment and as Nussbaum argues fiction cultivates moral character, many emotions (grief for the dead Tolkien, fear of future floods) need no existence beliefs.

34.title: a16.xhtml
34.relation: Grimwood turns the riddle contest in the dark into a lesson in hermeneutics: Bilbo interprets like Hirsch's intentionalist, asking what Gollum means (and suspecting he means to eat him), while Gollum answers each of Bilbo's riddles by fusing the words with his own forgotten past - sun on daisies, eggs at his grandmother's hole - exactly Gadamer's claim that understanding is a dialogue of horizons shaped by 'prejudices'. Bilbo's final 'What have I got in my pocket?' breaks the game because it severs the good will that makes interpretation a genuine exchange, leaving Gollum no horizon to fuse with, so he simply constructs his own 'truth' that the hobbit stole his precious. The chapter generalizes: Gandalf's dismantling of 'Good morning' shows interpretation is everywhere, and there is no view from nowhere outside our horizons.

37.title: a18.xhtml
37.relation: Jensen dissects Bilbo's run of luck - the fish that leaps to his feet mid-riddle, the drunken elf-guards, above all his hand falling on the Ring in the dark - using Aristotle's account of luck as the rare, uncontrolled coincidence of ordinary causes (an orc leaving the back door ajar plus a hobbit's six-meals-a-day girth). He then deploys Nagel's kinds of moral luck: Bilbo's constitutive luck (born a Baggins with Took blood, Rawls' 'natural lottery'), circumstantial luck, and resultant luck (finding the Ring, which he could not control but which dooms Sauron). Against Kant's good will that is 'like a jewel' beyond luck and Plato's 'no harm can befall a good man', the chapter argues that Thorin's dragon-sickness, the orcs' unlucky birth, and Bilbo's outcome-dependent standing show that praise and blame do - and should - reach beyond the agent's control.

39.title: a19.xhtml
39.relation: Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.

41.title: a20.xhtml
41.relation: Watson uses the company's decisions under uncertainty - whether to approach the troll-fire that nearly gets them eaten, the elf-lights in Mirkwood, Bilbo's descent of Smaug's tunnel - to teach decision theory: expected utility (assigning probabilities and values shows they should have stayed put rather than follow the troll-light), conditional probability (the Mirkwood lights are treated as dependent events, dodging the gambler's fallacy), and simplifying the outcome set. He then judges Bilbo by Aristotle's doctrine that courage is the mean between the vice of cowardice and the vice of rashness, felt with respect to the appropriate passion, fear: Bilbo fears as he should (kettle-whistles and jelly-trembles), avoids unforced risks, yet risks death for his companions' lives - so he has acted courageously and is developing, not yet fully possessing, the virtue, which Aristotle says requires long practice.

43.title: a21.xhtml
43.relation: Kraus argues The Hobbit is two different books depending on the reader's experience: read cold it is a fairy-tale of adventure, but reread after The Lord of the Rings - knowing what the Ring did to Bilbo and what 'precious' means - it becomes a song of innocence and experience like Blake's Songs and Wordsworth's 'emotion recollected in tranquillity', where Elrond's opening description points to the deep Silmarillion history a first-time reader cannot yet feel. Emerson's 'transparent eye-ball' from Nature - the self stripped bare and made original in the woods - becomes Bilbo's first use of the Ring, where invisibility lets him see Gollum's miserable humanity and choose pity; but the image darkens into Sauron's Lidless Eye, the totalizing knowledge that defines and devours selves. 'There and back again' thus echoes nostos turned nostalgia: Bilbo never truly gets back, having traded the child's innocence Thorin praises on his deathbed for an experience he cannot undo.

5.title: Introduction Contemplating a House of Cards
5.file: ch05 - Introduction Contemplating a House of Cards.md
5.relation: The introduction reads Frank Underwood's opening mercy-killing of the injured dog and his unpunished rise from scorned congressman to president ('Democracy is so overrated') as a picture of politics where people do not reap what they sow. It argues the show channels real American anxieties — economic stagnation, the unfulfilled postracial promise, corporate money, inequality — so the titular house of cards may actually tumble. It frames the book's project as the contemplative life: withdrawing from politics to think before returning to action, invoking Plato's and Aristotle's claim that wonder is the beginning of philosophy and that wonder begets courage.

6.title: PART I SOCRATES, PLATO, AND FRANK
6.file: ch06 - PART I SOCRATES, PLATO, AND FRANK.md

7.title: Notes
7.relation: Argues House of Cards is a modern version of the Sophistical challenge in Books 1-2 of Plato's Republic: Thrasymachus' claim that justice is the advantage of the stronger and the unjust life is preferable. It maps Frank's proprietary 'my people' attitude and his shepherd-and-flock use of Russo, Stamper, Sharp, Meechum and his Gaffney constituents onto Thrasymachus' reversal of Socrates' shepherd analogy, and reads the Secretary of State snub, Blythe's naivety and Dunbar's descent into dirty tricks as proofs that the just are dupes. Frank's Sentinel ring and 'craft' make him Glaucon's perfectly unjust man of the Ring of Gyges story — unjust while seeming just — while the framed Lucas Goodwin plays the perfectly just man punished for a reputation for injustice. The chapter ends by arguing Frank falls short of the ideal tyrant (his conscience, his church visits asking 'what Justice is') and is coming to live the Book 9 tyrant's friendless 'worst sort of life' as Claire and the others abandon him.

8.title: Notes
8.relation: Argues that Underwood's fourth-wall asides are the show's device for dramatizing the Platonic being-versus-seeming distinction: his public performances (reassuring Blythe over the leaked education bill, the confessional letter typed on the Underwood typewriter to destroy Walker, goading the President into appointing a special prosecutor) are contradicted point by point by what he tells the camera. The chapter reads Frank as a Ring of Gyges success story — the show so far teaches it is better to be the bad guy who seems good — while Socrates' examined life from the Apology and Crito shows Frank never asks why he wants power, and his cockiness is the opposite of Socratic ignorance. It closes with the Gorgias' contrast of Sophistic rhetoric (producing belief, not knowledge) and Machiavelli's advice to feign, casting Frank as the manipulator of opinion Socrates called a tyrant's politics.

9.title: PART II IMAGINING POSSIBILITIES AMERICAN IDEALS IN HOUSE OF CARDS
9.file: ch09 - PART II IMAGINING POSSIBILITIES AMERICAN IDEALS IN HOUSE OF CARDS.md

10.title: Notes
10.file: ch10 - Notes.md
10.relation: Argues that Rawls' ideal theory rests on a 'strict compliance' assumption — citizens and politicians who pursue justice rather than self-interest — which makes his ideal society look like The West Wing, while House of Cards depicts the real one: teachers' unions fighting performance standards, Senator Haas blocking the omnibus bill for electoral fear, Jackie Sharp trading favors, and SanCorp's Remy Danton buying votes against Russo's watershed bill. The chapter traces the competing 'every man a knave' tradition — Smith's invisible hand converting the butcher's self-love into our dinner, Hume's maxim for constitution-designers, Madison's 'ambition counteract ambition', and Buchanan's public choice revival — and uses the theory of the second best to argue we must design institutions (publicly financed elections, balanced-budget and inflation amendments, a generality constraint) that assume Underwoods run for Congress.

11.title: Notes
11.file: ch11 - Notes.md
11.relation: Argues the Underwoods act out historian James Truslow Adams' warning that the American dream, severed from the question of values, degenerates into a means-first pursuit of power — 'burning the barn to find our penny in the hay'. Using Nietzsche's ressentiment and above all Max Scheler's account of its systematic repression of emotion, the chapter reads Claire's repressed longings for motherhood (the 'What will we leave behind?' scene), integrity and love erupting as spite against those who embody what she sacrificed: firing and persecuting the pregnant Gillian Cole, destroying Adam Galloway, and abandoning Megan Hennessey. Michael Corrigan's suicide in his Russian cell — an integrity she cannot drag down to her level — finally shatters her ressentiment, and the chapter ends with her walking out of the White House as the escape Adams' question demands.

12.title: PART III CHARACTERIZING FRANK ÜBERMENSCH OR THE PRINCE
12.file: ch12 - PART III CHARACTERIZING FRANK ÜBERMENSCH OR THE PRINCE.md

13.title: Notes
13.file: ch13 - Notes.md
13.relation: Argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure whose power play is staged through the show's postmodern techniques: the wave and the asides as metafiction that destroys our suspension of disbelief, self-referentiality in the mirror monologue ('Hunt or be hunted'), and a flattening of affect that lets us watch Zoe's murder at the train station with numbed indifference. Zarathustra's fearless overman is set against the risk-averse last man and the lambs-and-birds-of-prey passage against Christian slave morality, mapping onto Frank's breaking of Russo at the shipyard, the martyr's-sword maneuver on Blythe, and his spitting on the crucifix before taking 'God's ear'. The chapter reads Frank's ascent as will to power in both the political and personal Nietzschean sense, while warning that by Season 3 his hunger has cost him Jackie, Remy and Claire.

14.title: Notes
14.file: ch14 - Notes.md
14.relation: Argues against the title claim of the previous chapter: Frank is a Nietzschean master type — he defines good as good-for-him, embraces pain as strength, and keeps no allegiances once Walker and Vasquez break their promise — while Peter Russo is the paradigmatic reactive slave who cannot command himself and blames others, exactly Nietzsche's 'he who cannot command himself is commanded'. But the overman requires self-overcoming, the sublimation of drives into creation, and amor fati, and Frank only dominates others for vengeful ends: his whole scheme grows from ressentiment over the Secretary of State snub, he affirms other wills merely as investments, and in Season 3 he becomes a slave to his own position. The chapter uses the Cesare Borgia misreading (better a Borgia than a Parsifal as raw material, but Borgia was no overman), Napoleon's corruption, and Goethe's creative wholeness to conclude that Frank remains 'all-too-human' — destruction without creation.

15.title: Notes
15.file: ch15 - Notes.md
15.relation: Argues Frank's rise is a genuinely successful illustration of The Prince: Machiavelli's advice to be prepared not to be virtuous shows in his lying (feigning loyalty to Walker while engineering his impeachment, promising Russo the governorship), his strategic murders of Russo and Zoe, his audacity in making his own luck ('turn over the table'), and his cultivation of a pious family-man image while privately spitting on the crucifix. The chapter also lets Machiavelli criticize Frank — revenge on Tusk (better to pamper or crush), Claire's fruitless generosity at CWI, alliances with the stronger, and being feared to the point of being hated, which costs him Sharp, Remy and Claire. Finally it tests The Prince against modern democracy — party discipline, sex-scandal politics, Obama's donated Nobel money, birther smears — concluding that since Machiavellians will always adapt to whatever system exists, citizens must reward results and stop judging by image.

16.title: Notes
16.file: ch16 - Notes.md
16.relation: Runs through everything Frank does for a single project — the education reform bill: leaking Blythe's draft, gutting collective bargaining after promising Spinella ('I revised the parameters of my promise'), the Rasmussen speakership coup he then 'exposes', the shipyard-for-base trade, and the staged brick incident and strike-breaking — to show he endorses being 'other than good'. It then argues Machiavelli would not be impressed: Frank fails to keep up the appearance of integrity (Blythe, Feng and Vasquez all stop trusting him), inspires hatred rather than fear alone, and seeks power purely for its own sake where Machiavelli wanted it for the state's stability and liberty — the BBC's Francis Urquhart, who read The Prince and serves England, is the better Machiavellian. The chapter closes by weighing ironic and exposé readings of The Prince (Benner's critique, Rousseau's view that Machiavelli was unmasking princes, Dietz's sabotaging-gift reading) and concludes Frank fails even on the technique, not just the morality.

17.title: Notes
17.relation: Uses Sartre's play Dirty Hands and Walzer's 'Political Action: The Problem of Dirty Hands' to ask whether Frank's willingness to do the 'necessary thing' — from the opening mercy-killing of the dog to the Season 3 drone strike — could ever count in favor of an Underwood presidency, with utilitarians (nothing wrong with dirty hands) and absolutists like the bishop ('Love God, and love each other. Period.') dissolving the problem from opposite sides. Walzer's later 'supreme emergency' standard and threshold deontology frame the Jordan Valley staring contest with Petrov and the resulting deal as the one case where Frank's capability might genuinely matter, while Heather Dunbar's reluctance (her refusal of Stamper's offer of Claire's diary, then her reversal) tests the ideal of a leader both capable of and averse to dirtying her hands. The verdict: Frank's only advantage over Dunbar is his capacity for dirty hands, and even that fails because he lacks the scruples to keep them clean when it is not necessary.

18.title: PART IV CLASSICAL LIBERALISM AND DEMOCRACY
18.file: ch18 - PART IV CLASSICAL LIBERALISM AND DEMOCRACY.md

19.title: Notes
19.relation: Casts Frank as the 'Foole' of Leviathan chapter 15 — the man who grants that covenants exist but thinks injustice can 'stand with reason' — and documents his befriend-then-betray pattern: Russo groomed for governor then gassed in his car, Zoe fed stories then pushed under a train, Walker befriended, helped and maneuvered into resigning, all to reap the contract's benefits while breaking it for 'the getting of a kingdom'. The chapter then defends Hobbes' reply via Kavka: the Foole's vainglory makes him overestimate his ability to deceive, and a detailed audit of Frank's two murders (fingerprints, witnesses, electronic traces, forensic evidence, alibis, high-stakes deception 'tells') shows them contingency-riddled and irrational. Even Frank's success is no defense — his presidency rests on others' errors and luck (Skorsy, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and above all Claire all remain loose ends), so he exemplifies the vainglorious Foole acting against the reason of his preservation rather than a rational violator of the social contract.

20.title: Notes
20.relation: Argues Frank is 'Hobbesian to the core': for him democracy is just the state of nature with elections, which is why it produces mediocre, fearful presidents like Walker (a Xanax-taking incumbent undone by a mere legislator) while a real sovereign like Frank — or the autocrat Petrov, with whom Frank shares cigars precisely because no common power enforces rules between them — gets things done. The chapter reads Frank's appetites (ribs at Freddy's, power over money against Remy and Tusk, contempt for sleep and death) through Hobbes' pleasure-and-pain psychology and his account of conflict arising when equals want the same thing, which finally drives Claire from the White House. Frank's church scenes ('I pray to myself, for myself') illustrate Hobbes' subordination of religion to civil power, the Kate Baldwin 'he is the tyrant' charge illustrates that a tyrant is only a king disliked, and the closing appeal is to Madison's Federalist 51: only the ambition of others can contain this one.

21.title: Notes
21.file: ch21 - Notes.md
21.relation: Argues the Underwoods' success is not far-fetched fiction but the structural outcome four critics of democracy predict. Plato's Republic supplies the spine: the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decays through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, whose love of freedom invites the tyrant — Peter Russo with his random desires is the democratic soul, Frank the tyrannical soul ruled by one illicit appetite, doomed to the fear and friendlessness Book 9 describes (which Season 3 delivers). Hobbes and Hegel then explain why monarchy may beat popular rule (the monarch's private interest aligns with the public's; the monarch lets a people will as one), and Marx reframes the whole show economically — SanCorp, Tusk and Feng as capitalists, the laid-off shipyard workers as proletariat, and AmWorks as self-interested politicians flirting with expropriation. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government gives the democratic reply — elections force responsiveness, participation educates citizens — so the burden falls on viewers to keep elections fair, the press free, and checks on unscrupulous politicians effective.

22.title: Notes
22.file: ch22 - Notes.md
22.relation: Byron and Wood use Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' to read House of Cards: Raymond Tusk secretly dictates President Walker's policies, SanCorp buys influence over Frank through Claire's water-filters favor, and Frank's rise to the vice presidency is engineered by capitalists to protect their market interests. Even Frank's seemingly pro-worker America Works plan serves capital, since gutting Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid to subsidize $45,000 hiring costs boosts business profit, and the Dunbar-Walmart dispute shows the state arbitrating between conflicting capitalists rather than aiding workers. The chapter concludes that worker victories like a Dunbar minimum-wage win would only be the bourgeoisie losing a battle while winning the class war, confirming Frank's line that 'democracy is so overrated.'

23.title: Notes
23.relation: Sirvent and Diorio apply Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) to the show's web of watching: Frank manipulates Zoe through leaked stories, Doug keeps Rachel permanently locatable by phone, and Claire must demand the bug be removed from Michael Corrigan's Russian cell, showing watched subjects paralyzed by fear. Against Bauman and Lyon's 'liquid surveillance,' the chapter argues democracy is an anti-institutional force requiring free dissent and a press at arm's length from power, and that surveillance collapses the Greek public/private distinction so citizens fear punishment for questioning rulers. Frank's 'Nobody can hear you. Nobody cares about you' to Zoe captures how the surveillance state turns criticism into danger, leaving a society that is no longer a democracy.

24.title: PART V INTRAPERSONAL RELATIONSHIPS, SEXUALITY, AND RACE IN HOUSE OF CARDS

25.title: Notes
25.relation: Southworth and Tallman defend the Underwood marriage by way of Richard Wasserstrom's three grounds for condemning adultery (promise breaking, deception, pain): Frank and Claire's openly negotiated nonmonogamy - Frank disclosing the Zoe affair over breakfast, the Meechum threesome, Claire's nights with Adam Galloway - breaks no promise and involves minimal deception, so it is morally permissible. They reject Vincent Punzo's dualist claim that sex must merge souls, arguing that view rests on unverifiable theology and sets people up for guilt. The marriage's real strength is its egalitarian mutuality - Claire's sabotage of the watershed bill works as tit-for-tat strategy that restores the partnership - and agreed nonmonogamy suits Frank's bisexuality better than monogamy, which would force him to give up part of what it means to be Frank.

Rousseau's account of civilization degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into vanity (amour-propre) explains why Washington's corporate ethos leaves no friends, only 'loose ends' to be eliminated, from Zoe pushed onto the platform to Doug hunting Rachel. 29.title: Notes
29.relation: Cooper reads Frank's one prayer - kneeling to pray 'to myself, for myself' - as a self-love he calls autoeroticism, built on metaphysical atheism, ruthless pragmatism, and happiness as power. Peter's drunken enslavement and Zoe's freely chosen deal with Frank illustrate the ambiguity of a freedom that is still causally situated, and Frank's Season 3 miscalculations with Jackie, Remy, and Claire show egoism's inability to weigh others' self-interest. 32.title: Notes
32.relation: Kajtar asks why viewers root for a double-murdering politician, framing the show through Tamar Gendler's puzzle of imaginative resistance: we would refuse to imagine Zoe's murder narrated as 'brave and noble,' yet House of Cards dissolves that resistance. Using Jenefer Robinson's claim that emotional engagement is necessary for understanding, the chapter shows how the Greenville first-pitch embarrassment, the Fort Sumter swim confession, and above all Frank's fourth-wall asides (telling us the real Gaffney eulogy, admitting 'I despise children') grant voyeuristic intimacy that humanizes him bite by bite - 'that's how you devour a whale.' By the time Frank frames Lucas Goodwin and Corrigan dies, we have adopted the morally deviant perspective, and the chapter warns this is exactly how politicians and artists seduce audiences into values we would otherwise reject.

33.title: Notes
33.relation: Kaufmann tests Donald Davidson's reductionism (intentions as belief-desire pairs) against Michael Bratman's planning theory through Frank's scheming: Frank can simultaneously desire revenge on Walker and desire to stay near power, but he cannot intend both, so intention's distinctive consistency, partiality, and control explain why he swallows the snub, delivers the education bill, and adjusts when Claire derails Peter's water bill. Tusk's maxim 'Decisions made on emotions aren't decisions at all' and Frank's patience in destroying Tusk across time illustrate Bratman's point that intentions coordinate temporally extended, cross-temporal agency that mere beliefs and desires cannot. The chapter closes on the Iowa victory speech intercut with Claire closing her bedroom door - the first sign her plans have diverged from Frank's.

34.title: Notes
34.relation: Dressen and Taliaferro treat Frank's asides as a 'magical mystery tour' of concealment and disclosure, reading truth in Heidegger's fashion as disclosure rather than correspondence: the opening strangling of the dying dog, the Gaffney eulogy where Frank publicly mourns the father he privately calls 'quiet, timid, almost invisible,' and the tombstone urination ('It makes me seem more human') all play presence against absence to alienate Frank from responsibility. A close reading of five maxims - treading water, being a rock, loathing sleep, loving Claire 'more than sharks love blood,' and 'seem more human' - argues Frank consistently styles himself as barely human, the presidency rather than the person. Iris Murdoch's warning that art makes goodness seem dull and relaxes our moral guard explains why viewers find this fascinating rather than condemning.

36.title: Notes

Even Frank's marriage fails the test of true friendship, since Aristotle holds that only good people can mirror each other's character, and badness corrupts the self-knowledge friendship provides. Because Aristotle deems friendship 'most indispensable for life' and eudaimonia requires virtuous activity joined to good fortune, the chapter ends hoping Frank can still choose the good for its own sake - a hope Claire's walkout after Iowa badly dents.

Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, from McCarthyism and the Joe Welch moment to mass incarceration, explains the verdict that neither individual is worse alone: 'they are far worse together,' and the union, not the person, has no decency.

Frank's proprietary 'my people' politics replays the shepherd-sheep exchange: Russo, Stamper, Sharp and the Gaffney constituents are a flock groomed, fleeced, and slaughtered (the naval base closure), just as Thrasymachus says shepherds fatten sheep for their masters.
