8.relation: Davies defends Lost's convoluted plotting using Aristotle's Poetics, arguing the show works as a tragicomic epic that keeps closure and relevance even with Juliet's pre-crash storyline, genre mixing (Hurley's golf course beside Sayid's captivity), and shifting characters like Ben. He then uses the 'We have to go back' flash-forward to lay out McTaggart's two conceptions of time, eternalism versus presentism, and argues the flash-forward pushes viewers toward fatalism about Jack's already-fixed meeting with Kate near LAX. Finally he contends the past cannot be changed - Hurley in 2007 cannot undo his 1977 stay in the Dharma Initiative, since contradictions would entail everything - so viewers enjoy the time-travel plot by 'shielding' its mutually contradictory time lines.

9.title: None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It
9.file: ch09 - None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It.md
9.relation: Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.

10.title: NOTES
10.file: ch10 - NOTES.md
10.relation: Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.

11.title: NOTES
11.file: ch11 - NOTES.md
11.relation: Barnbaum treats the season 6 flash-sideways as counterfactual conditionals and evaluates them with David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics: in the closest possible world where James Ford's parents were still conned but he never became a grifter, Sawyer plausibly becomes a cop, whereas a world in which Jack fathers a child with Juliet demands too many extra changes to count as close to ours. She pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance - applied to dividing the crash survivors' water, where Jack's life-saving skill could justify unequal shares - as another famous hypothetical thought experiment whose conclusion rests on what people would agree to in the Original Position.

12.title: PART TWO - O IS FOR ORIGIN
12.file: ch12 - PART TWO - O IS FOR ORIGIN.md

13.title: NOTES
13.file: ch13 - NOTES.md
13.relation: Taliaferro and Kastrul ask what the reader would do in the castaways' place, using Aristotle's view that character is a disposition to act under other conditions to assess Mr. Eko, Ben, Michael, Charlie, and Sawyer: people are not merely what they do but what they would do. Plato's Ring of Gyges, quoted at length, tests whether characters like Sun behave honestly only when watched. Against the idea that the island could reverse all values, they argue morality cannot be completely relative to context - invoking Chesterton's 'Thou shalt not steal' on the remotest star - and place Lost in the island-narrative tradition of the Odyssey and Robinson Crusoe as a story of the journey of the soul.

14.title: NOTES
14.file: ch14 - NOTES.md
14.relation: Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.

15.title: NOTES
15.file: ch15 - NOTES.md
15.relation: Barris argues Lost fascinates because it dramatizes the basic structures of life itself: the castaways are Heideggerian thrown into an island none of them chose, brought there by Desmond's lapse at the Swan and by interlocking backstories such as Sawyer's bar conversation with Jack's father. Against the existentialist claim (Sartre, Camus) that life is simply absurd, he uses Wittgenstein's On Certainty - doubting everything presupposes certainties - to argue life is a riddle of partial sense, which is why the show's connections between Hurley and Libby or Jack and Desmond always hint at meaning without resolving it. The finale answers only the question of life after death, leaving life after birth as open as our own.

16.title: It Worked
16.file: ch16 - It Worked.md
16.relation: Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.

17.title: PART THREE - U IS FOR UNITY
17.file: ch17 - PART THREE - U IS FOR UNITY.md

18.title: NOTES
18.file: ch18 - NOTES.md
18.relation: Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.

19.title: NOTES
19.relation: Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.

20.title: “Lost”
20.relation: Karen Gaffney argues that Lost exposes ideology as a pair of glasses you do not know you are wearing, using Louis Althusser's interpellation and his distinction between repressive state apparatuses (Sawyer's outdoor cage) and ideological ones (the fake heart-rate monitor that makes Sawyer police himself inside a figurative jail). She reads the Swan button ritual, Claire 'drinking Locke's Kool-Aid,' and Desmond's 'stuck in a bloody snow globe' speech as images of being trapped inside a socially constructed worldview, and notes the viewer is interpellated too by the fake-off-island openings of seasons 2 and 3. The chapter then tracks how the show builds and dismantles the ideology of otherness - Rousseau's 'run, hide, or die,' Ana Lucia calling the Others animals, the theatrical glue and fake beard, 'Others 101' Latin lessons - until the survivor/Other border dissolves when Jack and Hurley become Jacob's successors.

21.title: PART FOUR - N IS FOR NECESSITY
21.file: ch21 - PART FOUR - N IS FOR NECESSITY.md

22.title: If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where
22.file: ch22 - If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where.md
22.relation: George Wrisley uses Lost as a testing ground against ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism: the disagreement over Sayid shooting young Ben (monster or innocent child?) motivates relativism, but the Argument from Disagreement fails for the same reason Locke and Mr. Eko's button dispute does not change what will actually happen if it goes unpushed. Simple subjectivism makes every judge infallible (the Man in Black could declare his murders right) and dissolves genuine disagreement between Jacob and his brother over killing their 'mother,' while cultural relativism makes the Dharma Initiative's torture of Sayid 'right' and would have ruled Martin Luther King Jr. wrong. He concludes that Lost's ambiguous cases - Michael's murder of Ana Lucia and Libby, Ben killing Jacob, Jack extorting Ben on the operating table - invite viewers to seek objective grounds Socratically, questioning their own moral judgments with further 'why's.

23.title: NOTES
23.relation: Michael Austin asks what adult children owe their fathers through Jack and Christian Shephard (the drunken-surgery cover-up, 'You don't have what it takes') and Locke and Anthony Cooper (the kidney con, the defenestration). He weighs Jane English's view that parental sacrifice creates friendship rather than debt - so Locke owed Cooper nothing, and true friends like Hurley and the crib-building Locke never keep accounts - against Sidgwick's three possible sources of filial obligation (relationship quality, biological tie, gratitude for services) and David Mellow's debt-of-gratitude argument. Austin concludes that the mutual needs of parents and children - Miles reaching for Pierre Chang in 1974, Jack and Christian's reconciliation in the church - best explain what they owe each other.

24.title: NOTES
24.relation: Becky Vartabedian applies W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethic of prima facie duties to Michael: at the dock his actual duty of beneficence toward the kidnapped Walt overrides fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, but does not erase his responsibility for Ana Lucia's and Libby's murders. Because Ross requires amends rather than giving a blank check, the chapter asks whether Michael's spying as 'Kevin Johnson' aboard the Kahana - culminating in giving Jin time to escape the bomb - repairs his wrongs, or whether Walt's rejection and Michael's exile from the closing church scene show he failed to make things right on the terms of those he wronged.

25.title: Real World Island
25.relation: Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue Lost redeems characters who stop objectifying others and instead freely 'objectify' themselves for the greater good. Kant's ban on treating persons as mere means condemns Ben's lifelong manipulation and Ben's use of Sayid as an assassin, yet autonomy justifies chosen self-sacrifice like Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission, Claire volunteering as bait for Ethan, and Jack becoming the new Jacob. Mill's utilitarianism makes Kate's shooting of the Man in Black a fair trade saving her friends, while Aristotle's virtues - respect against objectification, courage in Jack's death at the cliff, the engrained honesty of reformed con man Jim LaFleur, Kate's character-building motherhood of Aaron - complete the three-theory survey.

26.title: PART FIVE - D IS FOR DESTINY
26.file: ch26 - PART FIVE - D IS FOR DESTINY.md

27.title: NOTES
27.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost through C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory - the Lamp Post station and flight 316 (the Prince Caspian dedication page) wink at the source - with the island, like Narnia, a world of crisis and second chances entered by plane crash instead of wardrobe. Flashbacks of past failures (Kate the fugitive, Sayid the torturer, Charlie's addiction, Locke's kidney con) set up struggles for faith that he illuminates with H. Richard Niebuhr on faith as a center of value and revelation as communal, and with Levinas's claim that we become ourselves only through responsibility to the Other in community. The Jack-versus-Locke man-of-science/man-of-faith debate, Charlie's moth-cocoon trial, and Jacob and the Man in Black's black-and-white stone game map onto Aslan versus the White Witch, ending in redemption through the new community and Jack's sacrificial death.

28.title: NOTES
28.relation: Daniel Gallagher uses Aquinas to read Lost as a drama about mistaking finite goods for the ultimate good: Jack's hope in curing, Kate's in deceiving, Jin's in his father-in-law's employment, Locke's in Anthony Cooper, and the Virgin Mary statues full of heroin all instantiate Aquinas's approaching-Peter analogy, where we know only confusedly that someone (the perfect good) is coming toward us. Desmond's and Charlie's paralysis before the good is the sin of acedia, Rose's faith that the island itself healed her cancer is presumption, and her certainty that Bernard is alive illustrates Aquinas's claim - framed through Plato's episteme versus doxa - that faith sits midway between knowledge and opinion. The chapter closes on the harmony of faith and reason, from the Five Ways' first efficient cause to Eko's dying 'I ask for no forgiveness,' grounded in Augustine's restless heart that finds no peace until it rests in God.

29.title: NOTE
29.relation: Shai Biderman and William Devlin argue the character John Locke begins as an empiricist in the mold of his philosophical namesake - his boar hunting, tracking, and trebuchet-building against the hatch all follow the scientific method befitting a tabula rasa mind furnished by experience - but the miracle of his healed legs poses a 'why' that empirical explanation of 'how' cannot answer. He therefore converts to the Taoism of the Tao Te Ching: the moth-cocoon lesson to Charlie, 'I stopped looking' for Sun's ring, reading dreams and signs from the island, and finally his self-sacrifice to stop the time flashes all enact following the Way. The chapter reads the black-and-white backgammon stones, Locke's one-black-one-white eyes in Claire's dream, and Jacob versus the Man in Black as yin-yang complementarity, with empiricism and Taoism finally interdependent like the dots in each half.

30.title: Keep the Needle on the Record
30.file: ch30 - Keep the Needle on the Record.md
30.relation: Donavan Muir argues Lost's narrative world, unlike Jane Eyre's, requires its own metaphysics, and that this metaphysics is an order of balanced binary oppositions: Jacob and the Man in Black as twins diverged at birth, the cave scale's light and dark stones that Locke knocks out of balance in 'The Substitute,' science/faith, with characters like Jack converting from one pole into its opposite. The proper model is the yin-yang in motion - the Tao as a balanced ontological flow in which interdependent opposites wax and wane - so that treating the poles as independent is the delusion that threatens the island's order. The finale, where both Jacob and the Man in Black cease to exist and the castaways are freed, enacts the Mahayana Buddhist Middle Way: enlightenment as letting go of rigid oppositions that interdependence double-negates.

31.title: APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers
31.file: ch31 - APPENDIX - Who are Locke, Hume, and Rousseau The Losties’ Guide to Philosophers.md
31.relation: Scott Parker's appendix profiles the philosophers behind Lost's namesake characters: John Locke for the survivor (blank-slate empiricism, belief tempered by tolerance, The Reasonableness of Christianity), David Hume for Desmond (causation as habitual inference, with the button press as the image of induction, plus bundle-theory skepticism about the self), and Jean-Jacques Rousseau for Danielle ('man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' private property as the root of inequality). It adds Jeremy Bentham (the alias on Locke's coffin), Kierkegaard via the Fear and Trembling Hurley finds under the Temple (Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical and the leap of faith), Dogen on zazen, Edward Said for Sayid (Orientalism and the audience's own projected savagery onto the Others), and short lives of Kate Cooper Austin, Carlyle, Rutherford, Hugo Grotius, Bakunin, Ram Dass, Edmund Burke, Hawking, Minkowski, Faraday, C. S. Lewis, and Lennon.

3.title: The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series
3.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

7.title: Introduction
7.relation: The editors introduce the volume by framing Mad Men as a show that immerses viewers in the morally ambiguous world of 1960 Madison Avenue, where we find ourselves rooting for Don Draper to sell cigarettes, hide affairs, and conceal his stolen identity while cringing at the office's treatment of women. They argue the series teaches uncomfortable truths about the early 1960s (drinking, smoking, systemic sexism, racism, homophobia) while dramatizing how people experienced era-defining events as they happened, and so helps us understand both past and present. The chapters that follow, they say, are written by fans for fans who want to think further about the role of women, the morality of advertising, and how to lead a meaningful life.

8.title: PART ONE - “PEOPLE MAY SEE THINGS DIFFERENTLY, BUT THEY DON’T REALLY WANT TO”
8.file: ch08 - PART ONE - “PEOPLE MAY SEE THINGS DIFFERENTLY, BUT THEY DON’T REALLY WANT TO”.md

9.title: “It’s Like Watching a Dog Play the Piano”
9.file: ch09 - “It’s Like Watching a Dog Play the Piano”.md
9.relation: Schurtz argues the Mad Men characters are not stupid but epistemically bounded by what their era counts as a reason: Don dismisses Dr. Guttman's 'death wish' research (and the proto-Marlboro-Man danger angle) because a research psychologist's testimony does not register as expertise for him, and the senior partners ignore Pete's correctly pro-Kennedy insight because a junior account executive's word is not a justifier. Working through knowledge as justified true belief (Betty is justified but wrong to believe her husband is Don Draper), the chapter moves from epistemic individualism to social epistemology (testimony, expert disagreement) and finally standpoint epistemology, illustrated by the Belle Jolie secretaries whose 'moron' insight Peggy vindicates with the winning pitch. The upshot: sexism, closeted gay life (Salvatore in 'The Hobo Code'), and Betty's dry-cleaning-bag ignorance persist because 1960 society does not distribute justifying testimony to women, the young, or the marginalized.

10.title: “All That Is Solid Melts into Air”
10.file: ch10 - “All That Is Solid Melts into Air”.md
10.relation: Dunn reads Mad Men through Plato's Republic: the passions are the 'mad masters' Cephalus describes, embodied in Pete Campbell's au pair indiscretion and remorse, and because passions cannot tell staged appearance from reality, the mimetic perfection of Don's 'You're a whore' scene with Betty grips viewers exactly as Plato feared televised drama would, watering the parts of the soul that should be ruled. He extends the point to advertising: Don's 'I make pictures where people appear to be in love' and 'love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' work because mimesis bypasses reason and attaches feeling to images, while Aristotle's account of imitation shows drama can also train virtue by making us delight in what we should. Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air' frames the title sequence, where Don's office dissolves past advertising images revealed as empty simulacra, until the final shot restores the convincing façade of his confidence.

11.title: Bringing Corporations and Government Together
11.file: ch11 - Bringing Corporations and Government Together.md
11.relation: Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.

12.title: PART TWO - “THERE IS NO BIG LIE, THERE IS NO SYSTEM, THE UNIVERSE IS
12.file: ch12 - PART TWO - “THERE IS NO BIG LIE, THERE IS NO SYSTEM, THE UNIVERSE IS.md

13.title: “Have Done” with the Past
13.file: ch13 - “Have Done” with the Past.md
13.relation: Fritz applies Nietzsche's On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life and the Genealogy to the dialectic of remembering and forgetting: Pete cannot 'have done' with anything, so Ken Cosgrove's Atlantic Monthly story and Peggy's promotion become 'vermin' that eat into him, his reactive rancor and entitlement driving him to make Trudy broker his bad talking-bear story. Peggy is the opposite extreme of active forgetting, from not registering her own pregnancy to telling Pete flatly 'I had your baby and I gave it away. I wanted other things,' after Don's hospital advice that 'This never happened. It'll shock you how much this never happened.' Don knows forgetting is the strength of strong natures (the $5,000 offer to Adam, 'my life only goes in one direction, forward'), yet the Carousel's home-movie slides and other external triggers keep forcing the past back on him, so only Peggy fully inhabits the Nietzschean ideal.

14.title: Existential Values
14.file: ch14 - Existential Values.md
14.relation: Belliotti tests Roger Sterling against three existential standards. Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage fits him 'crisply': his quips about the chase, drinking 'because it's what men do,' and the penny-jar view of marriage reveal flight from commitment and terror of boredom, and even his twenty-year marriage to Mona lacked Kierkegaard's passionate inwardness, making it objectively true but existentially inauthentic. Measured by Nietzsche he falls between the last man who wants an agency 'where everybody has a summer house' and the will-to-power grand transcender he never becomes, oscillating between frustration and boredom; measured by Heidegger he settles for chatter, clings to fixity, and reflects on mortality only briefly after his heart attacks. The verdict: significantly inauthentic, capped by the blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' serenade that makes Don whisper 'Can we go?'

15.title: The Universe Is Not Indifferent
15.file: ch15 - The Universe Is Not Indifferent.md
15.relation: White takes Bert Cooper's shelf display of Atlas Shrugged seriously and argues, against Cooper's claim that Don is 'completely self-interested,' that Don is the conventional image of the egoist rather than a Randian one: he is a second-hander whose stolen identity makes his life a lie, so Betty is married to a man who does not exist and only Anna Draper, who sees Dick Whitman, gives him psychological visibility. Objectivism's primacy of existence explains why every lie collides with facts (the train recognition, Adam's newspaper photo, the misplaced dog-tag parcel) and why Don's 'ruthlessness' and the 'indifferent universe' he complains of are products of his own vices, since what is, is. The chapter walks through Rand's virtues (rationality, independence, honesty, productiveness, pride, self-esteem grounded in objective self-appraisal, not the 'whore-child' label) to show Don sought spiritual gain through deceit and so placed his self-esteem against reality.

16.title: Television and Existential Awakening
16.file: ch16 - Television and Existential Awakening.md
16.relation: Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.

17.title: PART THREE - “AND YOU KNOW WHAT HAPPINESS IS ” MAD MEN AND ETHICS
17.file: ch17 - PART THREE - “AND YOU KNOW WHAT HAPPINESS IS ” MAD MEN AND ETHICS.md

18.title: The Question of Ethical Advertising
18.file: ch18 - The Question of Ethical Advertising.md
18.relation: Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect. Kant's humanity formula and the lying-promise example show that manipulation wrongs the consumer as a rational agent, and Don's defense that advertising sells 'happiness' fails because Kant allows making others' happiness an end but never at the cost of truth, whether the consumer is a stranger or a wife. The chapter sets this against the era's brainwashing anxieties (Hunter's Brainwashing in Red China, Packard's The Hidden Persuaders, Precon subliminal projection) and concludes that honest advertising must survive disclosure of its methods, noting that real sponsors like Canada Dry and BMW responded to the show with stripped-down 'transparent' ads that let viewers be 'in on it.'

19.title: Each of Us Would See Ourselves
19.file: ch19 - Each of Us Would See Ourselves.md
19.relation: The Teschners cast Don as a Nietzschean creator of value in technological culture: his nihilism ('There is no big lie. There is no system. The universe is indifferent') and 'What you call love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' embody anti-foundationalism, while the beatnik Roy plays the resentful slave mentality whose passion lives only off what it despises. Don's creative process (sleep on it, 'forget it, and an idea will jump in your face') mirrors the camel-lion-child metamorphoses of Zarathustra, and the collapse of the principium individuationis explains his fluid identities from Dick Whitman to the 'Adam and Eve' fantasy with Rachel. Heidegger's techné frames the Kodak Carousel as genuine art, a revealing that transfigures 'a hell of a gadget' into 'a place where we know we are loved,' at the tragic price of a man outside community, and the falling figure of the credits is one 'we would each see ourselves' in.

20.title: “The Wrong Direction”
20.relation: Barkman builds a definition of lying (communicating what one believes false while hiding that fact, with intent to hurt or disrespect, which distinguishes mere deception and parts ways with Aquinas's blanket ban) and applies it to five advertising worries, from bags of chips designed to invite false inference to the Belle Jolie 'promise' no one actually believes and the Israeli Tourism ad that omits danger. Persuasion is legitimate because rational souls are equals to be treated as ends (Aristotle's justice), but manipulation (ads aimed at preschoolers that use children to pressure parents) and fear-preying coercion (Clearasil on insecure teenagers, nylons to unmarried women like Rachel Menken) treat people as means, while government must regulate factually (FDA 'smoking kills' labels) without overriding adult choice. Responsibility is then distributed across producer, agency, media, public, and state, and Don was indeed 'looking in the wrong direction' in this sense: being able to talk anyone into anything does not mean he should.

21.title: Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel
21.file: ch21 - Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel.md
21.relation: Terjesen asks whether Don is a good man, testing his mixed record (egalitarian instincts, loyalty to Mohawk Airlines, protecting Horace Jr., against habitual adultery and the stolen identity) through Aristotle's habituation, Plato's Protagoras unity-of-virtues theses, Hume's sensible knave, and John Doris's situationist attack on global character traits. The unity theses imply Don's vices undermine his virtues (affairs make him unavailable when Betty crashes; evasions about his past block honesty), and Doris's dime-in-the-payphone literature suggests even Don's reliability may be circumstance-bound, as with Pete's weddings-and-vacations-only philandering. Against full situationism, Don's consistent rules (never forcing women, valuing women he genuinely finds interesting) point to 'regional' traits, yet Roger's verdict stands: 'You're no good with relationships because you don't value them,' since Don runs family on a business code, from Adam's bribe to 'that's what people do' consolation for Pete.

22.title: Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle
22.file: ch22 - Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle.md
22.relation: Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.

23.title: PART FOUR - “NO ONE ELSE IS SAYING THE RIGHT THING ABOUT THIS” MAD MEN AND
23.file: ch23 - PART FOUR - “NO ONE ELSE IS SAYING THE RIGHT THING ABOUT THIS” MAD MEN AND.md

24.title: “To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”
24.file: ch24 - “To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”.md
24.relation: Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'

25.title: Don’t Go Mad
25.relation: Barkman applies a qualified Aristotelian standard of justice, that women possessing rational souls must be treated as equals, to Peggy, Betty, and Joan as second-wave feminism dawns. Peggy is the 'mad woman' in the best sense: she demands a desk, equal pay ('You have everything and so much of it'), and Don's apology while never resorting to blackmail like Pete, whereas Betty is repressed at home by a husband who shows her off ('I want to show you off, Betts') and Joan suppresses herself, measuring worth by appearance and enduring Greg's violation until the vase incident. The sexual objectification Peggy faces from her first day (Ken's elevator leers, Joan's paper-bag advice, the panty-hunt in 'Nixon vs. Kennedy') is the chapter's core injustice, and the warning is that women who cannot stand up to it may simply go mad.

26.title: What’s on the Horizon
26.file: ch26 - What’s on the Horizon.md
26.relation: Carveth traces race across three seasons: Carla and Hollis are seen but not heard in season one, Paul's Mississippi Freedom Ride with Sheila plays out in season two, and season three brings Roger's blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' and Pete's Admiral 'Negro market' pitch, which the client kills with 'monkey see, monkey do' and Cooper with 'no interest in becoming a colored television company.' The chapter argues the show practices differential racialization, black characters existing to support white ones without backstories (Carla silenced with 'This is not a conversation I am going to have with you,' Sheila reduced to proof Paul is interesting), while anti-Semitism gets more multidimensional treatment through Rachel Menken's 'we thrive at doing business with people who hate us.' Hollis mourning Marilyn Monroe yet silent on Medgar Evers illustrates race as a social construction and his silence as hiding in plain sight, and the chapter faults Mad Men for softening Northern racism while hoping season four moves forward.

27.title: “I’m Enjoying the Story So Far, but I Have a Feeling It’s Not Going to End Well”
27.file: ch27 - “I’m Enjoying the Story So Far, but I Have a Feeling It’s Not Going to End Well”.md
27.relation: South uses 'New Amsterdam' to examine how social convention, not personal authority, constrains agency: Bert Cooper's 'New York City is a marvelous machine' and 'There are other rules... His mother is Dorothy Dyckman Campbell' reveal that Pete's value lies in a name he doesn't understand, just as Don's authority dissolves before forces neither he nor Pete consented to. Reading through Plato's Republic city-soul analogy and Adeimantus's warning that changes in music insinuate themselves 'little by little' into character and laws, the chapter shows Pete missing the worth of his old-family name, the Bethlehem Steel man missing that steel cannot be advertised like flour, and Don, despite seizing a fresh identity, quietly conforming to the suburban corporate script he claims never to have envisioned. The Kennedy-assassination pitch to Peggy ('The way that they saw themselves is gone') and Conrad Hilton's 'It's business' close on Plato's caution: the city's gears keep turning, and 'people don't change' may be the show's last word.
