28.file: ch28 - Appendix It’s Not a List of Titles and Air Dates; It’s An Episode Guide.md

1.title: Heroes of the Day: Acknowledgments
1.file: ch01 - Heroes of the Day Acknowledgments.md

4.title: Whisper Things Into My Brain: Metallica, Emotion, and Morality
4.file: ch04 - Whisper Things Into My Brain Metallica, Emotion, and Morality.md
4.relation: Robert Fudge weighs whether Metallica's emotionally violent music corrupts or improves moral character. Against Plato's banishment of passion-stirring art (anger in 'Enter Sandman', indignation in '. . . And Justice for All'), he uses Aristotle's catharsis and the golden mean of healthy anger: 'One' purges pity and fear, and Hetfield's 'St. Anger' purged the rage behind his alcoholism. He then extends Adam Smith's empathy-based account - imaginative placement in the landmine victim's or addict's position - to argue the songs refine moral judgment, even making us question Kant's absolute duty against suicide by confronting the case where the body is a 'holding cell'.

5.title: This Search Goes On: Christian, Warrior, Buddhist
5.file: ch05 - This Search Goes On Christian, Warrior, Buddhist.md
5.relation: William Irwin traces Hetfield's journey through three sets of virtues: rejecting the Christian virtues of his Christian Science upbringing ('The God That Failed' as Nietzschean slave morality and Marx's opium of the masses), adopting the warrior virtues of Kill 'Em All (life as Hobbesian war, Nietzsche's will to power and 'no remorse'), and finally embracing Buddhist virtues on St. Anger. The warrior code fails without stoicism and collapses into addiction and despair, while the four noble truths - suffering caused by craving ('Frantic', 'Sweet Amber') - fit Hetfield's recovery and growing compassion.

6.title: Alcoholica: When Sweet Amber Becomes the Master of Puppets
6.file: ch06 - Alcoholica When Sweet Amber Becomes the Master of Puppets.md
6.relation: Bart Engelen reads 'Master of Puppets' and Hetfield's alcoholism as a case study in akrasia: the Socratic paradox from Plato's Protagoras, Plato's divided soul from the Republic, and Aristotle's weak-willed agent who knows the good but cannot act on it all describe the addict's 'struggle within'. Using Frankfurt's distinction between first- and second-order desires, he argues Hetfield became an 'unwilling addict' - and genuinely irrational - only when he stopped endorsing his desire to drink, and that recovery works through pre-commitment strategies like rehab, avoiding drinking cues, and relying on others.

7.title: Through the Mist and the Madness: Metallica's Message of Nonconformity, Individuality, and Truth
7.file: ch07 - Through the Mist and the Madness Metallica's Message of Nonconformity, Individuality, and Truth.md
7.relation: Thomas Nys argues Metallica's early message of nonconformity and individuality ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath') converges with Mill's On Liberty: conformity withers human capacities and breeds a stagnant society. Mill's higher pleasures and Nozick's experience machine show why real happiness requires autonomy and earned achievement rather than passive pleasure - the point of 'Escape''s 'Life's for my own to live my own way'. He reads 'Leper Messiah' and 'Eye of the Beholder' as Metallica's versions of Mill's defense of free inquiry and truth against mindless conformity and censorship.

9.title: The Metal Militia and the Existentialist Club
9.file: ch09 - The Metal Militia and the Existentialist Club.md
9.relation: Jeremy Wisnewski claims Metallica is an existentialist band: Kill 'Em All answers Camus' absurd by creating meaning through chosen, expressive projects ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath'), Ride the Lightning's catalogue of deaths ('Fight Fire with Fire' to 'Fade to Black') individualizes us in the Heideggerian confrontation with our own death, and Master of Puppets dramatizes Sartrean bad faith - the 'Sanitarium' label, the soldier as 'Disposable Hero', the addict's lost freedom. He concludes that accusing Metallica of selling out with the Black Album is itself bad faith, since authenticity has no fixed content.

10.title: The Struggle Within: Hetfield, Kierkegaard, and the Pursuit of Authenticity
10.file: ch10 - The Struggle Within Hetfield, Kierkegaard, and the Pursuit of Authenticity.md
10.relation: Philip Lindholm reads Metallica through Kierkegaard's demand for subjectivity: the soldier in 'One' crying 'Oh please God help me' exemplifies becoming a single individual before God against the untruth of the crowd, and 'The Struggle Within' stages Either/Or's passionate choice that decides the self. He then shows Hetfield himself living the inauthentic masked life Kierkegaard condemns - 'I was James Hetfield of Metallica' - until rehab forced the honest self-disclosure ('The God That Failed' and 'Until It Sleeps' mourning his parents) that marks a move toward authentic individuality.

11.title: Metallica, Nietzsche, and Marx: The Immorality of Morality
11.file: ch11 - Metallica, Nietzsche, and Marx The Immorality of Morality.md
11.relation: Peter Fosl argues Metallica's moral critique of religion in 'Leper Messiah' and 'The God That Failed' continues Nietzsche's genealogy of Christian slave morality born of ressentiment and Marx's 'opium of the people': religion gathers a docile herd, denies this world, and exercises power through sin and forgiveness. He diagnoses the band as often stuck in Nietzsche's incomplete nihilism - 'To Live is to Die' longs nostalgically for the Kingdom of Salvation - while 'Escape' and the sheer creative power of the music show a genuine Nietzschean transvaluation and overcoming of Christianity.

12.title: Metallica's Existential Freedom: From We to I and Back Again
12.file: ch12 - Metallica's Existential Freedom From We to I and Back Again.md
12.relation: Rachael Sotos reads Metallica's career as an existentialist quest for authentic freedom: the Arendtian shared 'we' of the early speed-metal community (Kill 'Em All), the Heideggerian 'I' attuned to death that breaks from das Man (Ride the Lightning's 'Fade to Black'), and the Kierkegaardian leap out of the over-technical system of . . . And Justice for All - compared to Kierkegaard's critique of Hegel - into the embodied groove of the Black Album. Sartre's bad faith explains the rock-star traps, and Some Kind of Monster shows the 'we' must be tended: therapy and a democratic band restore Arendtian public freedom.

13.title: Living and Dying, Laughing and Crying
13.file: ch13 - Living and Dying, Laughing and Crying.md

14.title: To Live is to Die: Metallica and the Meaning of Life
14.file: ch14 - To Live is to Die Metallica and the Meaning of Life.md
14.relation: Scott Calef argues Metallica holds there is no meaning of life: the universe is 'much too big to see' ('Through the Never'), Socratic and Schopenhauerian arguments show pleasure, wealth and fame bring only 'King Nothing', and religion is a dishonest Freudian wish-illusion ('The God That Failed') that alienates us from this world. Precisely because life has no objective meaning, Sartre's existence-precedes-essence applies: like Hetfield in his rehab 'confession' and the hunter of 'Of Wolf and Man', we must honestly create meaning by living in the now, with death making life precious rather than pointless.

15.title: Madness in the Mirror of Reason: Metallica and Foucault on Insanity and Confinement
15.file: ch15 - Madness in the Mirror of Reason Metallica and Foucault on Insanity and Confinement.md
15.relation: Brian Cameron reads 'Welcome Home (Sanitarium)' and 'Frayed Ends of Sanity' through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: the sanitarium is a total institution whose surveillance and power-knowledge produce docile bodies, confining madness as a threat to the rule of reason just as the seventeenth-century Hopital General confined the idle. Madness is not a mere disease but a socially defined deviance - and a form of rebellion against conformist society - whose violent 'cure' ('violent use brings violent plans') exacts an existential cost on the rebel, as 'The Unforgiven''s bitter old man shows.

16.title: Ride the Lightning: Why Not Execute Killers?
16.file: ch16 - Ride the Lightning Why Not Execute Killers.md
16.relation: Thom Brooks uses 'Ride the Lightning' - the condemned man in the electric chair pleading 'Who made you God to say / I'll take your life from you!' - to examine capital punishment. He presents Kantian retributivism (execution as the only proportional punishment for murder) and then argues against it: the condemned 'dies twice', living for years under a ritualized death sentence that Glover calls cruel, deterrence fails (the brutalization effect), and public justice must not become private vengeance - so even the guilty prisoner in the song is right that we have no right to kill him.

17.title: Living and Dying as One: Suffering and the Ethics of Euthanasia
17.file: ch17 - Living and Dying as One Suffering and the Ethics of Euthanasia.md
17.relation: Jason Eberl uses Joe Bonham of 'One' and Johnny Got His Gun to analyze suffering as loss of recognition (Hegel), loss of social contact (Aristotle's political animal), and loss of Kantian autonomy and dignity - 'a piece of meat that keeps on living'. He then works through the euthanasia debate: active versus passive euthanasia, Aquinas' doctrine of double effect for palliative care, Locke's psychological criterion of personal identity behind the higher-brain death standard applied to Terri Schiavo and PVS patients, concluding that the nurse's cutting of Joe's breathing tube would be active euthanasia because of the intention behind it.

18.title: Fade to Black: Absurdity, Suicide, and the Downward Spiral
18.file: ch18 - Fade to Black Absurdity, Suicide, and the Downward Spiral.md
18.relation: Justin Donhauser and Kimberly Blessing read 'Fade to Black' as a meditation on suicide. Against the Schopenhauerian pessimism that life is a downward spiral 'to the musty stench of corpses' - where suicide paradoxically affirms the Will-to-life - they set Camus' absurd: the narrator who loses the will to live surrenders, while Camus' absurd hero lives in revolt, freedom, and passion. Since Schopenhauer and Camus both reject suicide as escape, and Hetfield insists 'writing is therapy', the song's effect is Aristotelian catharsis - purging despair - rather than an endorsement of suicide.

20.title: Believer, Deceiver: Metallica, Perception, and Reality
20.file: ch20 - Believer, Deceiver Metallica, Perception, and Reality.md
20.relation: Robert Arp uses Hetfield's lyrics about lies, deception and misperception ('Bad Seed', 'The House Jack Built''s 'Is that the moon or just the light that lights this dead end street?') to stage the perception-reality problem: perceiver, perceptions, and external objects, as in Plato's cave allegory. He contrasts metaphysical/epistemological realism with idealism and antirealism, deploys the movie-theater picture of solipsism drawn from Hume's bundle of perceptions and Berkeley's denial of the external world, and argues Hetfield's own practice as a songwriter proves he is a realist - while distinguishing healthy philosophical skepticism from the lyric's irrational mistrust.

21.title: Trapped in Myself: "One" and the Mind-Body Problem
21.file: ch21 - Trapped in Myself One and the Mind-Body Problem.md
21.relation: Joanna Corwin reads 'One' - Joe Bonham, a mind fully conscious in a destroyed body, 'Trapped in myself / Body my holding cell' - as the mind-body problem. She walks through Descartes: methodological doubt and the dream argument mirrored in Joe's 'Can't tell if this is true or dream', the cogito as Joe's 'thinking thinking thinking', substance dualism, and the evil-deceiver worry. But Metallica's song also answers Descartes: a disembodied thinking-substance lives a 'life in hell', and Joe's tapping of S-O-S in Morse code shows a mind needs a body to communicate and complete itself.

22.title: Is It Still Metallica? On the Identity of Rock Bands Over Time
22.file: ch22 - Is It Still Metallica On the Identity of Rock Bands Over Time.md
22.relation: Manuel Bremer and Daniel Cohnitz ask whether the band on Kill 'Em All is identical with the band on St. Anger. Lars' drum kit, rebuilt part by part plus the reassembled original, is a Ship of Theseus case yielding their 'Nothing Else Matters Principle'; Locke's distinction between same substance, man, and person - illustrated by a brain swap between Kirk Hammett and an envious rival - shows identity must be 'suited to the idea'; and Searle and Gilbert on collective intention show a band is a social group, not a collection of people. Their revised musical-style-plus-line-up-continuity theory faces fission problems (Megadeth) and the eliminativist option Quine's 'no entity without identity' invites.

24.title: Metallica Drops a Load: What Do Bands and Fans Owe Each Other?
24.file: ch24 - Metallica Drops a Load What Do Bands and Fans Owe Each Other.md
24.relation: Mark White asks whether Metallica wronged its longtime fans by changing style on Load, using Kant's duty ethics. No duty to keep their thrash style survives the categorical imperative - a world where every band changes style is horrible but not contradictory - and Kantian duties to the band members' families, employees, and to their own talents and authenticity actually support the change. Symmetrically, fans' loyalty is only an imperfect duty with wiggle room: it is owed in return for the band's loyalty to its metal values, and lapses when the motivation is mere commercial sell-out.

25.title: The Unsocial Sociability of Humans and Metal Gods
25.file: ch25 - The Unsocial Sociability of Humans and Metal Gods.md
25.relation: Niall Scott applies Kant's 'unsocial sociability' - the human oscillation between solitude and society - to Metallica: the ego-clashes of Some Kind of Monster and the Hetfield-Mustaine rivalry ('Better Than You') instantiate Kant's vices of culture, yet produce the music as the reconciliation of the struggle. Using 'The Struggle Within' and 'Hero of the Day', he runs the categorical imperative on refusing help (the maxim cannot be universalized) to ground Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence, and answers Schiller's 'duty with hatred' objection - the 'My Friend of Misery' syndrome - by noting Kant allows feelings to support duty.

26.title: Boys Interrupted: The Drama of Male Bonding in Some Kind of Monster
26.file: ch26 - Boys Interrupted The Drama of Male Bonding in Some Kind of Monster.md
26.relation: Judith Grant reads Some Kind of Monster through Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's concept of homosociality: the Hetfield-Ulrich bond is the libidinal engine of the band, with Mustaine and Newsted as sibling rivals for James' attention, wives and children as intrusions that break the male-only bonding, and Lars' French-kissing of Kirk policing the homosocial/homosexual line within heteronormativity. The film's arc - James' exit to rehab, Lars' tirade against his control, and the firing of the feminized therapist Phil - is the interruption and rekindling of a homosocial bond that can no longer run on youthful rebellion now that the band has become 'The Man'.

27.title: Justice for All? Metallica's Argument Against Napster and Internet File Sharing
27.file: ch27 - Justice for All Metallica's Argument Against Napster and Internet File Sharing.md
27.relation: Robert Delfino evaluates the Napster lawsuit philosophically: Aristotle's law of non-contradiction exposes Lars Ulrich's inconsistent statements about money and his tolerance of 1980s home taping despite admitting to it, weakening the band's case. But the core argument is consistent and Lockean - Lars' Senate testimony that 'just like a carpenter who crafts a table gets to decide whether to keep it, sell it, or give it away' invokes Locke's labor theory of property, which Delfino defends against Tom Palmer's objection that copyright restricts bodily liberty, distinguishing it from the Constitution's utilitarian rationale for copyright.

28.title: Who's Who in the Metal Militia
28.file: ch28 - Who's Who in the Metal Militia.md

10.title: The Office and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Office and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Argues that the standard trio of moral failure - malice (Creed ogling Pam, Andy sabotaging Dwight with the toll-receipt trick), weakness of will (Jan returning to Michael, Meredith relapsing with alcohol), and ignorance (Pam trading away Jim's teapot in 'Christmas Party') - misses a fourth category: moral blindness, embodied by Michael Scott, who can recite moral rules but cannot see when they apply (his Martin Luther King name tag on Diversity Day, defending Phyllis from Todd Packer with a harassing kiss, the fake-firing prank on Pam). Against Plato's view that all wrongdoing is ignorance, the chapter claims knowledge of rules neither helps nor harms decency; what matters is moral perception - seeing what a situation requires - shown by Jim getting Dwight to the hospital and rescuing the Dundies, Pam protecting the Dwight-Angela secret, and Toby patiently answering Dwight's anatomy questions.

11.title: The Office and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Office and Philosophy.md
11.relation: Weighs the morality of Jim and Pam's workplace flirting (while Pam is engaged to Roy) using three ethical frameworks: act utilitarianism has them tot up their own happiness against effects on co-workers' morale and Dunder-Mifflin's bottom line; rule utilitarianism models HR's blanket anti-dating policies and asks whether Jim and Pam could justify an exception without destroying the rule (the Hawaiian shirt day analogy); deontology searches for duties against office romance (favoritism in evaluation, distraction from duties) and finds none once harassment is set aside, concluding that in the absence of a deontological prohibition, Jim and Pam may keep flirting until 5 p.m.

12.title: The Office and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Office and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Asks whether Michael can (not will) ever learn empathy, distinguishing cognitive empathy - explained via Russell's argument-by-analogy account of other minds, which Michael manages only with people like himself, hence his sales success in 'The Client' - from affective empathy, which he lacks (Kevin's possible skin cancer is 'terrible news for both of us'; he cannot read Phyllis's oven mitt in Yankee Swap). Traces his cluelessness to egocentrism, and following Hume and Smith's sentimentalist account of morals - decentring the ego toward the impartial spectator via emotional contagion - argues his only hope is a real friendship (Jim's) that could drag him outside himself, since sycophantic Dwight and one-sided Todd Packer never will.

13.title: The Office and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Office and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.

14.title: The Office and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Office and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of wit as a character virtue lying in a mean to map the UK office: David Brent is the buffoon of excess, the 'slave of his sense of humor' who cannot not joke (the 'crack of Dawn' line, the cruel Post-It Notes firing prank on Dawn), Gareth Keenan the boor of deficiency whose literalism leaves him unable to make or take a joke, and Tim Canterbury the ready wit whose responsive irony ('Does anybody have the right time?') hits the mean. Because humor, like morality, is uncodifiable - there is no Having a Sense of Humor for Dummies - the trio illustrates that virtue is qualitative appropriateness guided by practical wisdom, not moderation or rule-following.

15.title: The Office and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Office and Philosophy.md

16.title: The Office and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Office and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Gives a crash course in epistemology (knowledge vs hypothesis, mistake, and opinion; empirical and rational evidence) to solve the puzzle of how Pam can simultaneously know and not know that she loves Jim: the evidence is public (Jim is 'onto' her, the teapot gift, Angela's 'Pam Pong' tally, her inspection of Jim's bedroom in 'Email Surveillance'), yet she tells the camera she and Jim are 'just friends' and angrily rejects the evidence (being picked up in 'The Fight', the 'first date' remark in 'The Client'). The chapter models self-deception as two kinds of knowledge plus an unjustified belief - she rationalizes the lie with genuine reasons (security with Roy, fear of losing control) until second-order knowledge of her own lying erupts as anger and despair, concluding the show is great because it is honest about the lies viewers tell themselves.

17.title: The Office and Philosophy
17.relation: Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.

18.title: The Office and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Office and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Pits authenticity - understood both as self-discovery and as existentialist self-creation after Sartre and Heidegger, requiring self-knowledge and meaningful relationships - against happiness as subjective well-being, in a case study of Michael Scott. Michael's closest 'friendships' are relationships of convenience (Dwight's betrayal in 'The Coup', the fear-induced Packer bond, self-destructive Jan), his 'Packer norms' of locker-room humor are unshakeable, and Shelley Taylor-style positive illusions (his self-image as progressive on Diversity Day, 'The World's Best Boss' mug) keep his moods afloat while truth-tellers like Jan and the Chili's bar patrons knock them down. The conclusion challenges Socrates' dictum: since Michael is psychologically incapable of achieving authenticity, perhaps for some people the examined life is simply not available, and trying for it only produces misery.

19.title: The Office and Philosophy
19.relation: Against Hobbes's view that laughter expresses superiority and Bergson's that comedy humiliates the socially disruptive into conformity, argues that viewers of The Office feel humiliation 'by proxy': Michael Scott is immune to humiliation because his narcissism blocks the minimal condition for feeling it - recognizing he could do wrong (Prison Mike, his MLK name tag while stereotyping Kelly, reneging on the pledge to Oscar's nephew, Carol's rejection at Diwali). We blush, look away, and feel his shame in his place, which transforms neither Michael nor us but reaffirms our own decency, compassion, and grip on values like self-awareness - and the chapter answers the worry that this merely endorses 'Hollywood' values by noting the standards Michael violates (moral sight, honesty with oneself) cross value systems.

21.title: The Office and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Office and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Answers The New Yorker's claim that the American Office 'doesn't care about class' by reading it through Marx: capital's growth logic and surplus value explain the degraded office labor the show depicts (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock type of situation' truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors, Roy's 'unloading trucks without meaning', Ryan's rejected assembly line), while the salaried masses' class position survives precisely as unnamable and denied - Michael's botched condo purchase, his fury at Ryan's business-school ambition, and Prison Martin's observation that office and prison are both 'doing the same thing every day'. Drawing on Kracauer, the chapter argues the show's comedy walks between distraction and awakening, and ends with Walter Benjamin's 'authentic humanity' located in the gap between professional and private life: Michael's failures make him an unwitting critique of the system that produced him.

22.title: The Office and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Office and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Applies Sartre's Being and Nothingness to the mockumentary: Pam's bad faith consists in pretending she has no choice between Jim and Roy (her garbled 'I'm not into Jim' conversation with Karen in 'Ben Franklin'), while the camera's Look - Sartre's keyhole peeper caught in the hallway - turns her into an object not of her making when she is caught watching Jim and Karen in 'The Merger', and her shame finally lets her own her feelings. David Brent's pride (posing with his Inside Paper magazine cover) tries to control the Other's look and fails, since the freely respected gaze he craves cannot be extracted; and the ever-possible camera functions as Foucault's panopticon (Bentham's prison design), visible and unverifiable, silencing Jan on speakerphone in 'Cocktails' and forcing Dwight and Angela's 'Don't linger. Break left' choreography, which makes the viewer a complicit co-worker.

23.title: The Office and Philosophy
23.relation: Uses Baudrillard's three orders of simulacra to read the UK office: Neil Godwin embodies the first order where the boss's signs reflect real virtue (Aristotle's practical wisdom), Gareth's health-and-safety training of Donna - which degenerates into interrogation about her sex life - is the second order where virtuous signs mask desire, and David Brent is the third-order hyperreal, his management-speak ('team individuality', 'mutual likewise reciprocated', the 'rape' role-play outburst) signs with no referent masking that he is not a boss at all. The chapter's sting is that laughing at Brent we tacitly endorse the 'real' managerial system that produces Neil and redundancies, while Gareth - who models himself on Brent and pushes his codes to suicidal extremes ('will there ever be a boy born who can swim faster than a shark?') - instantiates Baudrillard's fatal strategy, a system carrying the seeds of its own destruction.

25.title: The Office and Philosophy
25.relation: Kraft uses Dunder Mifflin to test whether stockholder profit or stakeholder welfare should drive business decisions, introducing stakeholder theory via Ansoff and the Mitchell salience model. Michael's exclusive patronage of national chains (Chili's, Starbucks, USA Today) versus the staff's loyalty to local spots like Poor Richard's becomes a Millian case: by Mill's point that most good action benefits particular individuals, shopping locally spreads happiness through the Scranton community while Michael's habits export money and decision-making elsewhere. Dwight oscillates between stockholder logic (the cheapest health plan, poaching Jim's client in 'Diversity Day') and stakeholder-minded customer service, while 'Halloween,' 'Health Care,' and 'Branch Closing' show profit trumping people; Michael's successful sale to Christian at Chili's in 'The Client' balances both, and his 'Show me that farm' speech insists workers like Stanley and Phyllis are not replaceable cogs.

26.title: The Office and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Office and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Johnson works through the standard objections to affirmative action using Scranton material: Ryan's paralysis before the all-Black management team in 'Traveling Salesmen' shows a single-race workforce is not intrinsically bad, while Michael's Chris Rock routine and his do-it-yourself slur exercise in 'Diversity Day' show that Dunder Mifflin meeting every quota does nothing about racism. A hypothetical about Dwight's grandfather refusing to hire Stanley's grandfather at the beet farm frames the compensation objection, answered by the 'cycle of poverty' account of the present effects of past discrimination. Finally, a fictitious hiring of guard Hank Tate over a better-qualified white candidate - justified, following Nagel, by the consequences of calming branch unrest - sets up the conclusion that education, not racially preferential hiring, would break minority poverty without discrimination, so affirmative action is ultimately unjustified.

27.title: The Office and Philosophy
27.relation: Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.

28.title: The Office and Philosophy
28.relation: Dromm asks what makes Michael's behavior wrong even where the law cannot touch it: as an 'equal-opportunity harasser' of Pam, Ryan, and Oscar, Michael seems to escape Title VII's discrimination requirement. He tests Edmund Wall's 'wrongful communication' definition against the filthy emails, 'that's what she said,' and Michael's solution to the Kevin-Angela dispute in 'Conflict Resolution,' finds it too broad and too dependent on the victim's objection, then turns to MacKinnon's sex-discrimination account and Crosthwaite and Priest's oppression account to explain the distinctive harm to women (pressuring Pam to be a cheerleader in 'Basketball,' calling the party-planning committee his 'bitches'). He concludes that both views are needed, and that in the end harassment wrongs workers by undermining their legitimate expectation of being judged only on job-relevant merit, leaving Dwight's extra effort done for nothing.

29.title: The Office and Philosophy
29.relation: Johnson asks what Dunder Mifflin morally owes after the obscene watermark scandal in 'Product Recall': stockholder theory says only refund and apologize insofar as that protects the bottom line, while stakeholder theory demands real amends to Barbara Allen and the Dunmore High prom attendees even at a profit cost. He then argues corporate responsibility cannot attach to a mindless company, and builds a criterion of blameworthiness - failing to do what it is one's job to do when that failure causally contributes to the incident - which convicts Creed (skipping his weekly mill quality checks all year), Michael (never verifying the inspections happened, despite his 'escape goat' apology video), and Jan (retaining an incompetent manager), all of whom should have been fired.

31.title: The Office and Philosophy
31.relation: Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.

32.title: The Office and Philosophy
32.relation: Nys uses Brent's quiz grievance about Mr. Spock (half-Vulcan, half-human) and his Crufts pedigree-dog analogy, Gareth's 'look at the ears' classification test, the dwarf/midget/elf/pixie interrogation of Alex, and Tim and Dawn's 'lethal blow' prank to introduce the problem of natural kinds. Realist answers come from Kripke (water is H2O whatever we call it), Aristotle's matter-and-form essences, and the DNA evidence separating Bornean clouded leopards from mainland cousins, while Wittgenstein's language games and Quine's point that our innate similarity senses mislead support the constructivist that we lay classification on an unstructured world. The verdict: nature supplies real differences but never carves itself into kinds, and the line-drawing remains up to us.

33.title: The Office and Philosophy
33.relation: Luck defends Gareth's announcement that he 'knows no one is present' when Tim hides behind his wall of files: since Tim's presence is a fifty-fifty gamble, the Rule of Acceptance (believe only what is more likely than not) plus the Conjunction Principle commit Gareth to believing Tim both present and absent, so announcing is the only act consistent with both beliefs. A Brent-style redundancy lottery - rationally believing of each of thirty employees that they will not be fired while knowing someone must be - shows the same tolerable inconsistency, and the chapter concludes, following Graham Priest, that Gareth is an unwitting practitioner of paraconsistent logic.

34.title: The Office and Philosophy
34.relation: Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.

35.title: The Office and Philosophy
35.relation: Lonergan and Wisnewski read 'Grief Counseling' and 'Safety Training' as a case study in death-denial: Michael cannot parse the euphemism 'we lost Ed Truck,' Kelly must teach him to be sad, and Creed's report of the decapitation forces the Heideggerian realization that death is his own not-to-be-outstripped possibility, not just a fact of life. The office deflects with movie plots and euphemism (Jim's 'seriously hurt' about the rooftop stunt), Pam's eulogy for Toby's bird shows how mourning ritual copes with mortality, and Michael's longing to be remembered - hospital wings named after him, saving his own life - exemplifies Kierkegaard's 'world-historical' life as an ego defense, with living subjectively the recommended but unexplained alternative. Becker's thesis that all culture is a fabricated protest against death frames the whole chapter.

36.title: The Office and Philosophy
36.relation: Written as a fake email thread among University of Scranton faculty, the appendix has junior professor Joe Kraus propose reading the town through Baudrillard's simulacrum - the 'Scranton Welcomes You' sign from the credits becoming real for him only as a TV image - while senior colleagues tutor him through the history of representation theory. Stephen deploys Plato's Ion (Socrates' magnet-and-iron chain of imitation, with Ion's Brent-like obliviousness) and Aristotle on mimesis, pity, fear, and catharsis to explain the show's tragicomic discomfort, while Maria adds the Antiochene, Alexandrian, and Augustinian fourfold senses of scripture applied to Scranton; Michael Friedman contributes a Chekhovian reading of Pam's bird eulogy as subtext about Michael's fear of dying alone. The thread itself mirrors an Office plotline as the senior faculty quietly decide to cut the untenured Joe out of the project.

37.title: The Office and Philosophy
37.relation: This appendix compiles Dwight's talking-head 'facts' episode by episode through season four - his beet farm and volunteer sheriff's deputy credentials, the Assistant (to the) Regional Manager obsession, Schrute Bucks, the resorbed twin, shunning, bear lore, and recorder performances - followed by entries from his blog. It advances no philosophical argument and engages no philosopher; its role in the volume is to supply, in Dwight's own deadpan and self-contradictory idiom, the raw character material that the book's chapters on identity, classification, and workplace ethics draw on.

7.title: Cold Open The Introduction
7.relation: The editors introduce the volume by arguing that SNL, like philosophy, trains viewers to regard the world with a critical, questioning eye: four and a half decades of parody and satire wired generations of fans to think philosophically before they could articulate why. Land Shark, Spartan Cheerleaders, and Trump-era Update bits are cited as the shared generational memory the book will now analyze.

8.title: Part I THE OPENING MONOLOGUE
8.file: ch08 - Part I THE OPENING MONOLOGUE.md

9.title: When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer
9.file: ch09 - When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer.md
9.relation: Tallman asks why SNL may mock presidents (Chase's pratfalling Ford, Carvey's Bush) and Clintons but not unchosen groups, framing the question with the aesthetics debate among radical autonomism (Bell), radical moralism (traced to Plato and Tolstoy), and moderate moralism. Sketches from Samurai Futaba to Farley's Lunchlady Land show jokes can punch up, punch down, or elevate a low-status group. The Schmitts Gay beer sketch, she argues, ridicules not gay men but beer-ad conventions: swapping the usual female sex objects for men in speedos exposes the objectification and heteronormativity viewers had stopped noticing, so the butt is the advertising industry.

10.title: Responsibility
10.file: ch10 - Responsibility.md
10.relation: Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.

11.title: Robust Social Critique
11.file: ch11 - Robust Social Critique.md
11.relation: McGowan asks how SNL gets away with offensive material, from Larry David's concentration-camp monologue to the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' and 'Nude Beach.' He argues censorship fails because offense is historically relative and slippery-slope prone, and that on Mill's On Liberty the harm principle never licenses suppressing speech SNL viewers can freely avoid, a point he sharpens with Feinberg's Volenti maxim and the offense principle. He closes by defending offensive comedy as robust social critique: Mill's fallibilist case that free speech drives human progress, with Baldwin's Trump and Tina Fey's Charlottesville bit as comedians speaking truth to power.

12.title: And Now, Deep Thoughts…
12.file: ch12 - And Now, Deep Thoughts….md
12.relation: Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.

13.title: Part II SOME POLITICAL SKETCHES
13.file: ch13 - Part II SOME POLITICAL SKETCHES.md

14.title: Live from Omaha
14.file: ch14 - Live from Omaha.md
14.relation: Irwin argues that SNL's caricatures (Fey's Palin, Baldwin's Trump, Aristophanes' Socrates in the Clouds) misrepresent their targets and that learning politics from comedy traps viewers in ideological bubbles, since satire flatters rather than informs. He introduces the Ideological Turing Test, adapted from Turing's test: state your opponent's view so accurately and sympathetically that a neutral observer cannot tell it is not yours, and grounds the duty to learn the other side from its own partisans in Mill's On Liberty. The 2016 'Bubble' sketch passes the test, he says, but SNL's liberal bias (gentle Sanders, untouchable Obama) rarely challenges its audience, and a conservative 'Live from Omaha' alternative would just rebuild the bubble on the other side.

15.title: “We Always Have Something To Do”
15.file: ch15 - “We Always Have Something To Do”.md
15.relation: Engels uses Foucault's Archaeology of Knowledge, authorities of delimination, and power/knowledge to show that SNL now produces rather than merely reports political truth, as when the Fey-Palin sketch shifted media blame for the Couric interview from the McCain campaign onto Palin herself. The 2016 sketches (McKinnon's Clinton as the inevitable winner, David's Sanders as a fringe idealist, Baldwin's Trump as a self-sabotaging loser) are read as discursive framings that confirmed and shaped mainstream narratives. Like Foucault's doctors defining madness, comedy writers now set the boundaries of political truth, which spotlighted sexist double standards but proved dangerous when SNL's detached writers misread working-class voters; following Foucault's 'everything is dangerous,' she concludes we always have something to do.

16.title: Where in the Hell is Chris Rock
16.file: ch16 - Where in the Hell is Chris Rock.md
16.relation: Wisnewski reads SNL's race comedy as applied philosophy of race: the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' sketch shows Mr. Wilson's counter-slurs as an assertion of personhood against Mills's racial contract, Eddie Murphy's Mr. Robinson's Neighborhood and 'White Like Me' expose implicit bias and white privilege, and 'The Day Beyonce Turned Black' illustrates Du Bois's double consciousness. Appiah's racialism explains why Leslie Jones playing Trump strikes audiences as outrageous while white women play men routinely, and Appiah's biological anti-realism about race undercuts that reaction. 'Black Jeopardy' with Tom Hanks's MAGA-hatted Doug finds common ground across race that the 'Lives that Matter' ending sharply limits, Fanon's violence route is raised and set aside, and Crenshaw's intersectionality frames why cast diversity is more than skin-deep.

17.title: And in the End
17.relation: Irwin and addictions specialist Lombardo ask where comic inspiration comes from, using Socrates' discovery that poets do not know the meaning of their own work, Hume's account of creativity as recombining materials of experience, and Nietzsche's point that inspiration is really continuous production sifted by judgment, to explain why Belushi and Farley treated cocaine and alcohol as muses. They contrast Belushi's fatal 'I use drugs' hubris, which no one around him challenged, with Farley's genuine twelve-step recovery, three sober years, and relapses. Stuart Smalley's affirmations, which bullshit himself into feeling 'good enough,' spoof recovery culture's cliches while Farley's story shows what actual recovery demands, ending with the advice to look elsewhere for the muse.

18.title: Part III SOME SKETCHES FEATURING YOUR FAVORITE RECURRING CHARACTERS
18.file: ch18 - Part III SOME SKETCHES FEATURING YOUR FAVORITE RECURRING CHARACTERS.md

19.title: All Human Experience is an Impression
19.file: ch19 - All Human Experience is an Impression.md
19.relation: Ruetenik argues the best SNL impressions are not 'spot on': Carvey's Bush ('Not gonna do it. Wouldn't be prudent') and the Tom Brokaw pre-tapes sketch created new experiences rather than faithful copies, while Darrell Hammond's exact impressions made him a 'tribute band' without Carvey's artistry. Dewey's Art as Experience and James's selective attention, in which every perceiver is an impressionist ignoring the blooming buzzing confusion, ground the claim that all experience is creative re-presentation rather than tribute to reality. He then turns the point political: SNL casting Amy Poehler over a spot-on Black impressionist as Michael Jackson tells us something about the audience's own selective, and possibly racist, experience.

20.title: Fighting the Real Enemy
20.relation: Johnson asks why Sinead O'Connor tearing the Pope's photo ended her career while SNL's own religion sketches drew little fire: 'DJesus Uncrossed' targets Tarantino's gratuitous violence rather than Jesus, the Tebow sketch ridicules prayers for football wins that Nietzsche said cheapen God into a servant of chance, and 'God's a Boob Man' satirizes the God's Not Dead films' strawmanning of atheists. Louis C.K.'s God monologue, he argues, raises the burden of proof and the problem of natural evil, best answered by Carlin's joke of a God subject to physical laws. The Church Lady embodies Warmke and Tosi's moral grandstanding, whereas O'Connor's protest does not, and the chapter ends on Plato's Republic: better to be a virtuous person scorned as a villain, like O'Connor, than a celebrated villain, though her tragic life strains Plato's promise that virtue pays.

21.title: “We’re Not Worthy”
21.file: ch21 - “We’re Not Worthy”.md
21.relation: Holt reads Wayne's World as applied philosophy of play: Wayne and Garth's basement show is intrinsically motivated leisure in Huizinga's sense, free, rule-bound, absorbing, and outside ordinary life, and Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness' supplies the play ethic against the work ethic. Against Wittgenstein's claim that games cannot be defined, Suits's definition of games as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles is applied to 'A-sphincter-says-what?', the '...not!' game, and one-on-one hockey with Gretzky. The dark side of play closes the chapter: Wayne and Garth exclude and mock outsiders, and the leisure of their magic circle rests on unacknowledged labor like Wayne's mom's laundry.

22.title: It’s Good to Be a Fan if …
22.file: ch22 - It’s Good to Be a Fan if ….md
22.relation: Barrett uses Bill Swerski's Super Fans to map a spectrum of fandom from casual to moderate to Super Fan, then applies Aristotle's doctrine of the mean to the virtues and vices of fandom: knowing trivia is a virtue (the Trekkies sketch), admiring athletic excellence is noble, but excess becomes licentious obsession, Shatner's 'Get a life!', heart attacks at Ditka's, and spending Thanksgiving with da Bears instead of family. Deficiency appears in bandwagon fans who lack commitment and loyalty, and the Red Sox fans' hospitalized heartbreak shows misplaced priorities in grief. Moderate fandom, loyal to people first and teams second, is the virtuous mean.

23.title: Part IV AND NOW FOR OUR MUSICAL GUEST
23.file: ch23 - Part IV AND NOW FOR OUR MUSICAL GUEST.md

24.title: Andy Kaufman Lip‐synchs
24.relation: Gracyk argues that SNL's liveness lies in real-time broadcast rather than co-presence, rejecting the performance-studies claim that televised audiences see only simulations: a performance is whatever the performer frames for audience attention (Sparshott's isolating act of attention, Thom's for-an-audience condition, Davies's framing), and mediated viewing counts. On that basis Eminem's contested 'Mosh' and 'Bezerk' appearances either were not performances or were badly framed ones, since he failed to signal that his prerecorded vocal was meant as intentional doubling. Andy Kaufman's Mighty Mouse lip-synch on the 1975 premiere, by contrast, openly framed its own fakery as 'Foreign Man,' a Warholian act that made lip-synching itself the philosophical subject and so a great live performance about what performance is.

26.title: We’re Here to Pump ‐clap‐ You Up! The Goal of SNL and “Weekend Update”
26.file: ch26 - We’re Here to Pump ‐clap‐ You Up! The Goal of SNL and “Weekend Update”.md
26.relation: Fried recasts Norm Macdonald's firing from Weekend Update as a philosophical dispute about the goal of comedy: NBC executive Don Ohlmeyer wanted wall-to-wall laughter and applause, guaranteed by recurring characters and celebrity walk-ons, while Macdonald hated applause as a cheap voluntary 'we agree' and aimed only at involuntary laughter he could not pander his way to. Eastman's play theory of laughter as an instinctive, uncontrollable response supports Norm, while Freud's relief theory, humor as release of pent-up tension, fits Ohlmeyer's comfort comedy. Fried concludes that if SNL is merely a comedy platform Norm was right, but as a shared cultural ritual that also comforts after tragedy, SNL may legitimately aim at more than involuntary laughter.

27.title: A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics
27.file: ch27 - A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics.md
27.relation: Sudnick and Garrett stage the Dewey-Lippmann debate through Weekend Update's citizen journalists: Drunk Uncle and Girl at Party exemplify Lippmann's propagandized pseudo-environments and echo chambers, while Stefon parodies the expert gatekeeper his technocratic 'machinery of knowledge' would install. Dewey's The Public and its Problems answers that democracy needs public education, a free and publicly funded press, and wide participation, with Point/Counterpoint and Cathy Ann's plea to log off and meet face-to-face as comic images of deliberative citizenship. The chapter ends with Dewey's hope that artists, from Opera Man to Sandler's Chanukah Song, are the real purveyors of news in a democracy consummated by artful communication.

28.title: That’s the News. Good Night and Have a Pleasant Tomorrow
28.file: ch28 - That’s the News. Good Night and Have a Pleasant Tomorrow.md
28.relation: Erion reads Weekend Update as comic media theory built on Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death and McLuhan's 'medium is the message': television's entertainment bias shapes what its content can be, and SNL's fake newscast has demonstrated the 'Now...this' incoherence of TV news from the 1975 premiere's disaster teasers, Blaine Hotel slashings report, and Goggles-and-Pip feel-good story onward. Later sketches parodying Morning Joe, Dateline's Pervert Hunters, and CNN's animated reenactments keep the same critique alive for cable and social media. Because Postman himself proposed parody along the lines of SNL as television's only self-critique, the chapter closes asking whether comedy can expose TV from inside TV or is inevitably co-opted by it, leaving education as the last hope.

29.title: Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View
29.file: ch29 - Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View.md
29.relation: Southworth and Tallman use David Spade's 'falling star' joke about Eddie Murphy, and Murphy's twenty-year SNL boycott, to test three theories of familial obligation against the show's self-described 'family.' The role-based Just Because View, identified with Confucian filial piety, condemns Spade's disrespect toward an SNL elder but also forbids Murphy's divorce from the family; the contractarian Reciprocity View says Spade owes Dennis Miller but not Murphy, unless Murphy's saving the early show counts; and Jane English's No Special Obligations View, on which family should work like friendship, love rather than debt, clears Spade entirely. Sketches from the Vogelchecks' kissing family to Dysfunctional Family Feud supply the counterexamples.

30.title: Part VI THE ABSURD STUFF THAT HAPPENS NEAR THE END
30.file: ch30 - Part VI THE ABSURD STUFF THAT HAPPENS NEAR THE END.md

31.title: Live From New York
31.relation: Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.

32.title: Getting the Joke
32.relation: Gray reads Jack Handey's Deep Thoughts and Fuzzy Memories as packaged existentialism: Sartre's existence precedes essence grounds Handey's responsibility for self-made meaning ('if you're robbing a bank and your pants fall down... life is funny'), Camus's absurd and Sisyphus's happy perseverance match 'sometimes I think the world has gone completely mad. And then I think, Aw, who cares?', and Beauvoir's ruts of inferiority warn against the ease of 'just sitting there' wanting money. Heidegger's authenticity and mortality appear in the parachute-swimming gag, dying laughing rather than in dread. The chapter also explains why the deadpan delivery over serene stream imagery makes morbidity funny, and worries that Handey's 'truth is... unreal' anticipated post-truth politics.

33.title: Where Do We Go from Here – Buh‐Bye!
33.file: ch33 - Where Do We Go from Here – Buh‐Bye!.md
33.relation: Southworth asks whether SNL's dumb characters, the Ladies Man, Celebrity Jeopardy's Burt Reynolds, Ferrell's Bush, can be too stupid for moral responsibility. Aristotle's capacity for decision grounds moral agency; the Merit View, sharpened by Williams's constitutive moral luck and the Control Principle, blames Ferrell's deliberately nasty Connery but not the hapless Reynolds; and Mill's consequentialist view of praise and blame as nudges for 'progressive beings' explains Stuart Smalley's affirmations and Gilly's scoldings. Strawson's reactive attitudes finally resolve the puzzle: pitiable Bush is no proper target of blame, which is why we love him, though making him so lovable may have helped the real Bush escape accountability.

7.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
7.relation: The editor's Introduction explains why Spider-Man merits a philosophy book: Peter Parker is a self-reflective underdog with a strong moral compass he sometimes fails to follow, so his stories raise lived ethical questions rather than abstract metaphysics. Citing Plato's definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and a way of life, Sanford frames the whole volume around Socrates' question 'how are you going to live your life?' and lists the questions Peter's life poses: the good life, the obligations attached to talents, friendship, identity over time, the ethics of enhancement, and whether life has meaning.

9.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
9.relation: Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.

10.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
10.relation: Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.

11.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
11.relation: White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.

12.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md

13.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.

14.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Keeping asks what grounds the claim that great power brings great responsibility and answers through Good Samaritan ethics. Building on MacIntyre's account of human interdependence in family and community, and Mill's point that failing to aid can itself cause harm, he argues that Bad Samaritanism is a blameworthy harm-causing omission, so Spider-Man's rescues of strangers are obligatory negative duties rather than supererogatory favors. His vigilantism is excused because only he can stop supervillains, 'can implies ought' explains why his duties exceed ordinary people's, and his life-risking feats against the Sinister Six and Firelord still go beyond even what his enlarged duty demands.

15.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
15.relation: Tallon uses the problem of moral luck (Williams and Nagel) to ask how blameworthy Peter really is for Uncle Ben's death: the Peter who let the thief go and the counterfactual Peter whose thief was caught at the elevator act identically, yet outcome luck makes the first feel like a murderer, clashing with Kant's Control Principle that only the good will has moral worth. Drawing on Williams's 'agent regret' and Susan Wolf's 'nameless virtue' of taking responsibility for consequences, the chapter separates culpability — Peter is guilty only of letting a thief go, with the intervening agency of the criminal breaking the causal chain — from responsibility for damage. Aunt May's own misguided confession that she caused Ben's death by arguing with him (Amazing Spider-Man #479) shows how virtuous people confuse involvement in a causal chain with guilt.

16.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md

17.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
17.relation: Terjesen uses spider-sense to tour early-modern philosophy of perception: against direct realism, Locke's indirect realism and its primary/secondary quality distinction suggest 'dangerousness' is a perceiver-relative secondary quality — bombs threaten Spider-Man but not the Hulk, and Mysterio manufactures danger-experiences — while Berkeley's idealism and Hume's phenomenalism radicalize the resulting skepticism about ever verifying sense data. The decisive clue is that spider-sense fails when Aunt May conks Peter with a vase (Amazing Spider-Man #114) and when his mentor Miles Warren becomes the Jackal: Peter does not fear those he loves. This supports Hume's sentimentalist account of moral judgment, on which vice is found not in the act but in the disapproving sentiment, moderated by Reid's common-sense reply that perception always already contains judgment — so spider-sense is a moralized judgment about what to avoid, not a Geiger counter.

18.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.

19.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
19.relation: Spencer gives a phenomenological account of bodily transformation in the films: with Merleau-Ponty, Peter's new body changes his world — walls become surfaces to climb — and grants motor knowledge that needs no calculation, while Norman Osborn's deliberately seized powers feed pride and Doc Ock's grief shows how transformation can sweep a weak will into vice. Virtue, on Aquinas's definition as the perfection of a power, develops only through choices and habits worked out across a whole life, so ethics is deeper than rule-following. With Levinas, the call to goodness is experienced bodily: sympathy with others' suffering draws Peter out of himself — he rushes into a burning building even when powerless in Spider-Man 2 — and the Green Goblin lives a self-contradiction by feigning deafness to it, while eros for Mary Jane both distracts from and ennobles the quest.

21.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Novy asks whether it would be right to deliberately make a Spider-Man. Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge from Plato's Republic — that unchecked superpower breeds 'great corruptibility' — is made flesh in Doc Ock, Green Goblin, Lizard, and Morbius, while Bostrom's transhumanism supplies the movement the chapter defends. Against Fukuyama's bio-conservative worries about playing God, destroying equality, and violating a human essence, the chapter notes that Aunt May's bifocals and insulin already make her a cyborg, that Marvel grants personhood by behavior rather than biology (Kree, Skrulls, the Vision), and that the thought experiment of giving Mary Jane a painless 'super smile' shows we are at least sometimes obliged to enhance.

22.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Southworth and Timm use the Clone Saga to teach real cloning science: molecular, therapeutic, and reproductive cloning, Dolly's 1-in-277 success rate, the impossibility of clone caskets and inherited memories — while crediting the 1970s writers for correctly making mitochondrial DNA the blood test that distinguishes Peter from Ben Reilly. They then evaluate the characters' reactions: Leon Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance,' which holds that a clone's genotype 'has already lived' and despotically fixes its life's expectations, explains Kane's genocidal self-loathing and Peter's rage and despair when told he is the clone, while Gregory Pence's rebuttal — that such repugnance rests on false expectations, as with twins or children of interracial couples — vindicates MJ's and Ben's insistence that a clone's moral worth lies in what it does, not where its genes came from.

24.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
24.relation: Taliaferro and Little ask whether Spider-Man can champion justice and love Mary Jane at the same time, framed by Mandela's tension between obligations to family and to community. Through paired scenarios — rescuing an endangered coworker at possible mortal cost versus a lover's plea to become a surgeon rather than join a deadly crime-fighting unit — they conclude that justice trumps romance in unforeseen emergencies, while romance can rightly govern the choice of a vocation. For Spider-Man the two fuse rather than conflict, since MJ loves him partly for his commitment to justice, though Gwen Stacy's death on the bridge — where his webbing snapped her neck — shows a hero can lose both at once.

25.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
25.relation: Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.

26.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - Spider-Man and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.

28.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
28.relation: Malloy asks why Spider-Man jokes while fighting for his life. After surveying the superiority theory (Plato, Hobbes's 'sudden glory'), Kant's incongruity theory, and Freud's relief theory, he adapts F. H. Buckley's moral-superiority account: Spidey's quips at the Vulture's boasting, Doc Ock's mercilessness, Kingpin's girth, and J. Jonah Jameson's sourness are moral corrections meant to goad their butts toward the virtues they lack. Aristotle's buffoon/wit distinction saves Spidey from vulgarity — he can be serious after Gwen Stacy's death — and his teasing of allies like the Thing and Captain America teaches social virtues, though the jokes rarely reform anyone.

29.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
29.relation: White examines the fan fury over 'One More Day,' in which Peter and MJ trade their marriage to Mephisto to save Aunt May's life. Virtue ethics evaluates people by stable character traits, but situationist psychology (the pay-phone coin experiments, Doris's Lack of Character) argues behavior tracks trivial situational details, not traits — while fictional characters like Captain America and Peter Parker are written with simpler, firmer traits, so making a deal with the devil reads as glaringly out of character and betrays the audience's trust. Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.

30.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
30.relation: Sanford argues, through the arc of the Raimi trilogy, that Peter becomes good by becoming the narrator of his own life. On Aristotle's Poetics — a story has a beginning, middle, and end, and art imitates life — and MacIntyre's claim that man is a 'story-telling animal' whose life is 'the unity of a narrative quest,' Peter's involuntary obligations (orphanhood, Uncle Ben's death, the spider bite, love for MJ) ground the voluntary ones, and his quest is to use his great powers responsibly. Tracking Aristotle's categories, Peter moves from incontinence (vengeance on Flint Marko, the jazz-club strut in Spider-Man 3) through continence to genuine virtue, and his practice of telling his own story — 'it's the choices that make us who we are' — models how we must get our own stories straight to flourish.
