13.relation: Catherine Robb and Roos Slegers reconstruct a philosophy of reputation from the reputation album: with Sperber, Baumard, and Origgi, reputation is a shared group consensus ('they say I did something bad') that is fake, warped, and outside one's control, yet Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments explains why it still wounds - we deeply want not only to be loved but to be lovely, seen for who we really are (the invisible dance through the streets in 'Delicate'). The chapter's original contribution is Swift's 'tilted stage,' performed literally on the reputation tour: gendered double standards ('The Man,' 'mad woman') mean a woman's reputation is more fake, more imposed, and more punishing than a man's.

14.title: It's Me, Hi! I'm the Problem It's Me: Taylor Swift and Self-Blame
14.file: ch14 - It's Me, Hi! I'm the Problem It's Me Taylor Swift and Self-Blame.md
14.relation: Agnès Baehni asks whether the self-blame saturating 'Anti-Hero,' 'Afterglow,' 'High Infidelity,' and 'Dear John' models a justified or an excessive tendency, especially for Swift's young female audience. Against Dana Nelkin's risk-based explanation of the blame asymmetry, she argues the relevant notion is suffering plus self-knowledge: we may blame ourselves more than others only because we usually know our own aggravating and excusing conditions better ('maybe it's me / And my blind optimism to blame'), and since self-blame is always overt while other-blame can stay private, the proportionality norm sometimes forbids blaming ourselves at all.

15.title: Part III: The Girl in the Dress Wrote You a Song
15.file: ch15 - Part III The Girl in the Dress Wrote You a Song.md

16.title: Begin Again (Taylor's Version): On Taylor Swift's Repetition and Difference
16.file: ch16 - Begin Again (Taylor's Version) On Taylor Swift's Repetition and Difference.md
16.relation: King-Ho Leung casts Swift as a philosopher of repetition, using Kierkegaard's distinction between backward-looking recollection and forward-moving repetition to show that 'Back to December' is not reliving the past but rewriting it ('turn around and change my own mind ... make it alright'), and that tiny lyric changes ('I bet' becoming 'I hope' in 'I Almost Do') make repetition produce the difference. With Deleuze's Difference and Repetition, the chapter argues the 'Taylor's Versions' rerecordings are not inferior copies of lost originals but repetitions that generate newness - like 'Love Story' giving Romeo and Juliet a happy ending - so that rerecording becomes an act of self-reinvention and reclaimed ownership rather than mere restoration.

17.title: Is Taylor Swift's Music Timeless? A Metaphysical Proof
17.file: ch17 - Is Taylor Swift's Music Timeless A Metaphysical Proof.md
17.relation: Patrick Dawson offers a tongue-in-cheek 'metaphysical proof' that Swift's music is timeless in three senses. Her time-words (midnight, August, 'Back to December,' 'Christmas Tree Farm') name moods rather than objective locations, echoing Kant's view that time is a projection of the mind rather than an external structure; her lyric-world is fated and changeless ('Karma,' 'Mastermind,' 'the 1'), aligning her with determinist and necessitarian views of a closed future; and songs like 'All Too Well' ('Time won't fly, it's like I'm paralyzed by it') reject the passage of time McTaggart declared unreal, letting Swift jump freely between moments in a 'dynamic timelessness.'

18.title: I Remember It All Too Well: Memory, Nostalgia, and the Archival Art of Taylor Swift
18.file: ch18 - I Remember It All Too Well Memory, Nostalgia, and the Archival Art of Taylor Swift.md
18.relation: Reads Swift's songwriting as 'archival art' through Derrida's Archive Fever and Ricoeur's archival trace: songs like 'marjorie' (with her grandmother's actual backing vocals), 'august', and 'All Too Well (10 Minute Version)' preserve traces of what is gone while re-creating, not merely capturing, memory. With Foucault's power/knowledge it argues that controlling the archive means controlling the stories told about oneself, citing 'Dear John (Taylor's Version)' and the Speak Now rerecording as acts of reclaiming power through speech. Stuart Hall's 'living archive' frames the rerecordings as memory continually remade, and Derrida/Halbwachs ground the claim that her music is a public site of collective memory where fans archive their own lives, as in 'mirrorball' and the Eras Tour.

19.title: Taylor's Version: Rerecording, Narrative, and Self-Interpretation
19.file: ch19 - Taylor's Version Rerecording, Narrative, and Self-Interpretation.md
19.relation: Argues that the rerecording project succeeded because Swift masters narrative identity: using Ricoeur's tension between sameness and otherness (taxonomy lacks Ricoeur), it shows how the mountain of old Taylors in the 'Look What You Made Me Do' video and the near-identical rerecordings keep past selves in one coherent story. Charles Taylor's self-interpreting animals explains why hearing her songs is self-interpretation for fans, while Cavarero's 'narratable self' and the vault tracks show her story is never complete. Deliberate changes like the rewritten 'Better Than Revenge (Taylor's Version)' and the lost shaky breath in 'Last Kiss (Taylor's Version)' illustrate Velleman's point that narrative is felt, and that retelling can mark moral growth without erasing the past.

20.title: Part IV: With My Calamitous Love and Insurmountable Grief
20.file: ch20 - Part IV With My Calamitous Love and Insurmountable Grief.md

21.title: Taylor Swift on the Values and Vulnerability of Love
21.file: ch21 - Taylor Swift on the Values and Vulnerability of Love.md
21.relation: Uses 'hoax' to ask why we cling to love even when it harms us, answering with three values of love drawn from Swift's catalogue: Frankfurt's selfless devotion in 'I'm Only Me When I'm With You' and 'illicit affairs' ('For you, I would ruin myself'), Velleman and Iris Murdoch's loving attention that sees value in a lover's gap-toothed smile in 'Ours', and Vida Yao's escape from alienation in 'Sweet Nothing' and 'Dress'. Benjamin Bagley's 'mutual improvisation' explains why losing a lover means losing a secret language and color palette in 'illicit affairs' and 'Question...?', and why 'cardigan' needs Dessner while 'mirrorball' needs Antonoff. The chapter concludes that what makes love valuable also makes us vulnerable to the lover who 'knew the password', which is why 'hoax' is haunting yet hopeful.

22.title: Every Scrap of You Would Be Taken from Me: Taylor Swift on Grief
22.file: ch22 - Every Scrap of You Would Be Taken from Me Taylor Swift on Grief.md
22.relation: Applies Michael Cholbi's philosophy of grief to 'marjorie', 'Bigger Than the Whole Sky', and 'epiphany': grieving transforms rather than ends our relationship with the dead, rebuilding a practical identity rocked by loss, and yields self-knowledge about who mattered to us. It reads 'marjorie' as a successful post-grief song, treats 'Bigger Than the Whole Sky' (widely heard as about miscarriage) via Bortolotti on the value of delusions and confabulatory 'mythmaking' in early grief, and weighs the risk that false beliefs undermine grief's self-knowledge. 'epiphany' models collective grief, linking WWII and COVID-19, and the chapter extends Cholbi's framework to a shared 'collective practical identity' shattered by pandemic loss.

23.title: What a Shame She Went Mad: Anger, Affective Injustice, and Taylor Swift
23.file: ch23 - What a Shame She Went Mad Anger, Affective Injustice, and Taylor Swift.md
23.relation: Argues that 'mad woman' dramatizes 'affective injustice' (Whitney and Srinivasan): a woman's righteous anger is misread as Madness with a capital M, so her emotions get the wrong reception, snowballing into toxicity as she 'gets more crazy' each time she is called crazy. Srinivasan's version supplies the double bind of swallowing anger or being dismissed, while Macalester Bell grounds the claim that she 'should be mad' and Dotson's silencing explains why 'no one likes a mad woman'. Against treating affective injustice as a mere symptom of sexism, the chapter uses Marilyn Frye's structural account of sex-marking to argue the Mad woman stereotype is constitutive of sexism itself, with Swift reclaiming the slur like disability activists reclaiming 'crip'.

24.title: I'm Fine with My Spite: The Philosophy of Female Anger in the Work of Taylor Swift
24.file: ch24 - I'm Fine with My Spite The Philosophy of Female Anger in the Work of Taylor Swift.md
24.relation: Builds a philosophy of female anger from Aristotle's definition of anger (response to perceived injustice, desire for payback, pleasure in pain), applied to the 2016 Grammy call-out of Kanye and 'Vigilante Shit', and Agnes Callard's problem of eternal anger, which Swift answers in 'I Forgot That You Existed' by moving on without forgiving. Mill's Subjection of Women frames why femininity is constructed as incompatible with anger, and the chapter inventories Swift's 'Glitter Gel Pen Anger' ('Karma', 'Bejeweled') as walking away that renders the wrongdoer beneath contempt. Audre Lorde's 'Uses of Anger' closes the chapter: anger has conative and epistemic value against racist and sexist oppression, which also measures Swift's own limits around race.

25.file: ch25 - Part V I Should've Known - Taylor Swift's Philosophy of Knowledge.md

26.title: Summer Love or Just a Summer Thing? Feminist Standpoint Epistemology
26.file: ch26 - Summer Love or Just a Summer Thing Feminist Standpoint Epistemology.md
26.relation: Uses the folklore love triangle ('betty', 'cardigan', 'august') to argue for feminist standpoint epistemology against Ernest Nagel's 'view from nowhere': only by inhabiting each character's emotionally charged standpoint, above all Augustine's in 'august', do we escape the biased 'other woman' script and reach a fuller objectivity. Susan Stebbing and Michael Brady support the claim that emotion aids rather than corrupts knowledge, and the 'mad woman' lyric shows how women's emotion-laden beliefs get dismissed as hysteria. The chapter answers the 'barriers to knowledge' objection by arguing empathy expands, but never escapes, the limits of one's social location, so 'when you are young they assume you know nothing' is a bias to be unlearned.

27.title: The Trouble with Knowing You Were Trouble
27.file: ch27 - The Trouble with Knowing You Were Trouble.md
27.relation: Tests three readings of 'I knew you were trouble when you walked in': a stereotyping first-impression claim that fails as knowledge (via the racist-barista thought experiment and Finnis's 'achievement-word' point), a self-knowledge claim that risks Srinivasan's 'faux-feminism' in 'Blank Space' and 'The Man', and finally a justified claim of socially trained 'women's intuition' based on body language. Using Tommie Shelby's account of when beliefs are oppressive, it distinguishes Swift's inference from racist profiling, and Miranda Fricker's epistemic injustice explains how 'mad woman' and 'Nothing New' show women's testimony discounted. The upshot: knowledge is context-specific, and dismissing what marginalized people 'know when you walk in' gaslights their experience.

28.file: ch28 - I Knew Everything When I Was Young Examining the Wisdom of Youth.md

James's apology shows wisdom in action (Kekes) and Socratic intellectual humility, while 'tolerate it', 'Dear John', and All Too Well's dinner-party scene illustrate Spear on gaslighting via presumed epistemic superiority of older men.

29.file: ch29 - How Do We Know What Taylor Swift Is Feeling.md
29.relation: Asks how Swifties can know what Taylor feels, starting from Descartes' methodic doubt and answering with Edith Stein's phenomenology of empathy (taxonomy lacks Stein): we perceive others' emotions in blushing faces and stormy glares as in 'Would've, Could've, Should've', 'Afterglow', and 'You're Losing Me'. Against Lipps's inner-imitation account, Stein distinguishes empathy from sympathy and oneness, read through 'Long Live (Taylor's Version)' and the Speak Now Tour. R.K. Elliott's expression theory extends this to 'artistic empathy' for songs like 'Ronan' and 'Clean', while conceding limits: since 'betty' is written from a seventeen-year-old boy's perspective, fans know Taylor's expressed feelings, not her biography.

32.file: ch32 - Stained Glass Windows in My Mind Modality in the Imagery of Taylor Swift.md

7.title: A Taste of Athens
7.relation: The editors' introduction argues that the show's sugary surface hides systematic appearance/reality gaps: Nate the bumbling kit man is a tactical genius, Rebecca hires Ted to destroy the club, Jamie's arrogance masks a yearning for connection, and Ted's cheerfulness conceals trauma. 3.title: The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series
3.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

6.title: Introduction
6.relation: The editors' introduction frames the Terminator saga as philosophy's natural territory by telling how philosophers persisted through catastrophe: Leibniz's 'best of all possible worlds' collapsed after the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Hegel finished the Phenomenology of Spirit while Napoleon shelled Jena, and Adorno rebuilt cultural philosophy after Auschwitz. It compares that persistence to the human resistance against Skynet, and says the saga is founded on a paradox of human nature - we create our own worst nightmares. Quoting Bertrand Russell that most people would rather die than think, it urges readers to switch their CPU from read-only to learning mode and confront Judgment Day's paradoxes and the moral status of the machines.

7.title: PART ONE - LIFE AFTER HUMANITY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
7.file: ch07 - PART ONE - LIFE AFTER HUMANITY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE.md

8.title: NOTES
8.relation: Littmann asks whether personhood could survive humanity's extinction in 2029: if Terminators genuinely think and feel, a Skynet victory would not be the end of people. He argues the T-101, T-1000 and T-X pass substantial Turing Tests (fooling muggers, cops, Sarah on the phone as her 'mother'), then concedes Searle's Chinese Room - recast as a tiny Austrian inside the endoskeleton reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding - shows thinking behavior cannot prove thought. But he claims the films' red-tinted Terminator's-eye-view shots show what it is like to be a Terminator, giving proof of consciousness, and concludes the machines are probably persons: there is an 'I' in 'I'll be back.'

9.title: NOTES
9.relation: Dunn reads Descartes' bete-machine doctrine (animals as soulless automata explicable by 'billiard ball' mechanics) against the Terminator universe, since Descartes' two tests for true men - genuine language and versatile reason - are in fact passed by the machines: the T-101 deploys 'Hasta la vista, baby' hours after learning not to sound like a dork and marshals skills far beyond a clock. Sarah Connor instead locates the soul in the heart, and via Spinoza's conatus - the instinctual valuation of one's own existence that Terminators lack ('no emotion about it one way or another') - she judges even linguistically brilliant machines soulless and irrational, as Mary Midgley says of computers that do not know what matters. Kyle's line about 'dreaming about dogs' closes the chapter: by the Sarah Connor criterion dogs are ensouled sentinels, the very thing Descartes denied.

10.title: NOTES
10.file: ch10 - NOTES.md
10.relation: Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.

11.title: NOTES
11.file: ch11 - NOTES.md
11.relation: Butler argues the films' humans-versus-machines picture rests on a false dichotomy: we are ourselves 'meat machines,' and functionalism makes minds computational processes realizable in silicon as much as neurons - illustrated by a Henrietta thought experiment (adapted from William Lycan) in which a friend gradually replaced with T-101 parts remains the same conscious person, and refusing this is 'human chauvinism.' Following Dawkins's extended phenotype and Andy Clark's natural-born cyborgs, he claims our tools are components of our minds, so Skynet and even the Terminator films themselves (making Cameron a cyborg of his cameras and editing suites) are extensions of human nature rather than alien 'Others.' Judgment Day, if it came, would be human suicide rather than genocide, so the real question is what values we build into our technology - 'no fate but what we make for ourselves.'

12.title: PART TWO - WOMEN AND REVOLUTIONARIES
12.file: ch12 - PART TWO - WOMEN AND REVOLUTIONARIES.md

13.title: NOTES
13.file: ch13 - NOTES.md
13.relation: Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.

14.title: NOTES
14.file: ch14 - NOTES.md
14.relation: Culver explains Sarah Connor's harshness through Girard's Violence and the Sacred: like any warrior she is 'stained' by contact with violence and needs purification rites before reentering society, but her society refuses to recognize her as a warrior, so her cleansing becomes psychiatric wards, nine aliases, and fugitive life - measured against the true machine Cameron, whose 'inefficient' coldness throws Sarah's residual humanity into relief. She then applies Baudrillard's hyperreal: the Connors must prove a future nobody else sees while destroying every trace of the Terminators (lowering the T-101 into the steel), a simulation where a T-1000 wears a 'To Protect and Serve' uniform and law and order themselves may be simulated. The upshot is that Sarah's failures at conventional motherhood are those of a warrior-mother raising John inside a war only she experiences, staining him too (he kills Sarkasian) to give him a future.

15.title: NOTES
15.file: ch15 - NOTES.md
15.relation: Ewing reads Cameron as a Marxist: Cyberdyne's profit-driven reverse-engineering of the recovered Terminator arm, Dyson's alienated labor ('Don't ask'), and U.S. militarism absorbing Cyber Research Systems develop Skynet as capitalism's 'final contradiction,' in which the drive for destructive, labor-replacing technology converges with the profit motive to threaten humanity. Sarah and John are useful to the resistance only when they exit wage labor - waitress to warrior, ATM hacking instead of work - dramatizing Marx's claim that liberation requires transcending class positions. Yet technology itself is neutral and reclaimable: the reprogrammed T-101 learning 'I know now why you cry' shows even killing machines can be humanized for liberation, and the saga ends where Marx does - not interpreting the world but changing it.

16.file: ch16 - PART THREE - CHANGING WHAT’S ALREADY HAPPENED.md

17.title: NOTES
17.relation: Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.

18.title: NOTES
18.file: ch18 - NOTES.md
18.relation: Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.

19.title: NOTES
19.relation: Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.

20.title: NOTES
20.relation: Jason Blahuta reads the saga through Hegel's Philosophy of History: Sarah and John Connor are World Historical Individuals — mere 'tools' of Geist — whose attempts to rewrite history, Sarah's hit on Miles Dyson in T2 and John's second try through General Brewster in T3, can only postpone Judgment Day, never redirect it, as the T-101's line 'Judgment Day is inevitable' concedes. The cunning of reason explains why removing Dyson or Brewster is futile: historical forces merely recruit replacements, so the script gets acted out by other actors. Because the dialectic's thesis-antithesis pattern (even the young John versus his mother) yields syntheses that carry both sides forward, the chapter concludes neither species can stop the other's rise, and only full-scale battle in the moving present decides which becomes Geist's end.

21.title: PART FOUR - THE ETHICS OF TERMINATION
21.file: ch21 - PART FOUR - THE ETHICS OF TERMINATION.md

22.title: NOTES
22.file: ch22 - NOTES.md
22.relation: Wayne Yuen asks whether Sarah was wrong not to kill Miles Dyson, weighing Kant's categorical imperative against utilitarian interest-maximization: killing one innocent to save three billion looks decisive until the interests of self-aware Skynet and the empathetic, self-sacrificing T-101 are counted on the machine side of the ledger. The chapter argues personhood turns on intelligence, self-awareness, empathy, and moral reasoning rather than DNA, so Skynet — which struck only after humans tried to pull the plug — has as strong a self-defense claim as we do. Mill's sophisticated utilitarianism then rescues common sense: rights protect the security that satisfies our deepest interests, and since Sarah's foreknowledge is unreliable (Reese's 'We'd won' changes the calculus), she should do what typically maximizes interests — spare Dyson and certainly not kill John. The tempting detour — that Judgment Day might itself be the morally preferable event, maximizing machine interests — is shown to collapse once overlooked facts like Reese's line are restored.

23.title: NOTES
23.relation: Phillip Seng runs the human-Skynet war through the three parts of just-war theory and finds the moral ground shakier than it looks: T2's briefing reveals Skynet launched its strike only after humans tried to pull the plug, so the machines claim the same self-defense 'just cause' humans do, while Skynet flunks last resort (it decides 'in a microsecond' with no negotiation), legitimate authority, proportionality (killing everyone to avoid being switched off), and discrimination. He then shows Sarah becoming a Terminator herself when she locks her laser sight on the innocent Miles Dyson, violating the same just-conduct rules she judges the machines by, and stopping only at his crying family. The chapter closes by doubting the war could ever have a just resolution, since the films point toward genocide rather than a peace treaty with Skynet.

24.title: NOTES
24.relation: Daniel Malloy asks whether the T-101's self-destruction in the steel mill was suicide, and whether it was justified, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is philosophy's only serious problem and the ambiguous case of Socrates' hemlock. Using Heidegger, he argues the learning-mode Terminator qualifies as Da-sein whose death is being-toward-death — the end of possibility — so the T2 machine dies authentically while the T3 machine's 'We'll meet again' is inauthentic self-deception. Kant condemns the act because the Terminator uses itself merely as a means, and Kant cannot even conceive of its genuine conflict of duties (preserve its life vs. prevent Skynet), while Bentham-style utilitarianism initially endorses the sacrifice but is refuted by hindsight: Skynet rises anyway, and consequentialism gives no credit for noble motives. The chapter ends by concluding that dying for a cause is illogical, since the dead surrender all control over the meaning of their actions.

25.title: NOTES
25.relation: Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.

26.title: NOTES
26.file: ch26 - NOTES.md
26.relation: Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.

27.title: PART FIVE - BEYOND THE NEURAL NET
27.file: ch27 - PART FIVE - BEYOND THE NEURAL NET.md

28.title: NOTES
28.relation: Jacob Berger and Kyle Ferguson use John's diction lessons ('no problemo,' 'hasta la vista, baby') to ask how Skynet could design machines that use natural language. They argue the Terminator operates on the Shannon-Weaver Code Model — decode the signal, retrieve the information — which is exactly why it fails on lexical, syntactic, and referential ambiguity ('Step on it!') and underdetermination ('Keep it under 65'), and why it drops John when he yells 'Let go of me.' Humans instead follow Grice's Inferential Model, inferring a speaker's meaning from context and psychology, so only a machine tuned to human minds rather than mere lexicon and syntax could be less of a dork.

29.title: NOTES
29.relation: Richard Brown uses the title 'The Terminator' itself to run the debate over definite descriptions: Russell's theory of descriptions makes 'The Terminator can't be bargained with' false (there are many T-101s, and no real-life Terminator at all), while Strawson insists Kyle's utterance genuinely refers to the machine at the door. Donnellan's referential/attributive distinction is staged through Lieutenant Traxler's 'The phone book killer has no pity' — true of whoever fits the description, or of the very Terminator Sarah has in mind — and Kripke's arguments from 'Russell English,' anaphora, and indirect quotation are weighed against Devitt's pronoun-of-laziness and reference-borrowing replies. The chapter sides with Grice's modified Ockham's razor: descriptions are not semantically ambiguous, so the title is literally false but apt, since Cameron referentially means the T-101.

30.title: NOTES
30.relation: Antti Kuusela argues from Wittgenstein that behavior is the touchstone — indeed constitutive — of mental life, so the question is whether Terminators behave like beings with minds. Searle's Chinese room and Ned Block's blockhead explain the read-only T-101's head-up-display of canned responses as symbol-shuffling without understanding, and the T-1000's 'I know this hurts' seems empty from a machine that cannot feel pain. The pivot is the learning-mode switch John and Sarah flip: the T-101 acquires slang, keeps promises, and acts for reasons Skynet cannot predict, passing the Lovelace test, and the Wittgensteinian dismissal of Chalmers's philosophical zombie removes the last reason to deny it a mental life — making the steel-mill sacrifice the destruction of a rights-bearing someone rather than something.

3.title: The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series
3.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md

7.title: Introduction
7.relation: The editors frame the book with Jason Stackhouse's 'lick your mind' line and the claim that Bon Temps is a banquet of philosophical morsels: Reverend Newlin's charge that vampires are 'unnatural' opens the question of whether they are inherently evil, and vampires coming out of the coffin test whether humans and super-powered predators can share a political community as equals. It name-checks the book's guiding parallels — the gay-rights analogy of 'God hates fangs', the scapegoating around Maryann the maenad — and ends by inviting the reader across the threshold to 'think bad things', valuing the questioning itself over conclusive answers.

8.title: PART ONE - “I USED TO HATE VAMPIRES, UNTIL I GOT TO KNOW ONE” VAMPIRE-HUMAN ETHICS
8.file: ch08 - PART ONE - “I USED TO HATE VAMPIRES, UNTIL I GOT TO KNOW ONE” VAMPIRE-HUMAN ETHICS.md

9.title: NOTES
9.relation: Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.

10.title: NOTES
10.file: ch10 - NOTES.md
10.relation: Culver reads vampire 'mainstreaming' through play theory: using Huizinga's Homo Ludens (and Caillois), she argues Bill 'plays human' — ordering wine his first night at Merlotte's — within bounded spaces (the threshold requiring invitation), fixed rules ('she's mine', courtesy between vampires), and goals, and that play changes both species by building bonds across the boundary. Nest vampires like Malcolm and Diane who refuse to 'dress up and play human', and humans like the Fellowship of the Sun, are Huizinga's spoilsports who shatter the play-world, while Eric's incognito surveillance of Sookie in other sheriffs' territories is cheating rather than spoilsporting.

11.title: NOTES
11.file: ch11 - NOTES.md
11.relation: Blayde and Dunn use True Blood to expose speciesism from both directions: the philosophical tradition (Aristotle's rational animals, Aquinas's divine image, Kant's dignity versus price, Descartes's denials of animal pain) justified human exploitation of nonhumans, and the show's vampires invert the ladder by treating humans as 'pets and cattle' — the magister's 'humans exist to serve us' and his verdict that Bill 'murdered a higher life form' for a pet mirror how we talk about animals. Amy's torture of Eddie Gauthier is read against factory farming, and the chapter closes with Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's sentience criterion as Sookie's 'civic duty' grounds for extending moral consideration beyond our species.

12.title: PART TWO - “LIFE-CHALLENGED INDIVIDUALS” THE POLITICS OF BEING DEAD
12.file: ch12 - PART TWO - “LIFE-CHALLENGED INDIVIDUALS” THE POLITICS OF BEING DEAD.md

13.title: NOTES
13.file: ch13 - NOTES.md
13.relation: Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.

14.title: NOTES
14.file: ch14 - NOTES.md
14.relation: Curtis argues liberal society should be wary of integrating True Blood's vampires: their feudal system of kings, sheriffs, and the magister, enforced through maker bonds and punishment, violates even Kukathas's maximally tolerant liberalism because members cannot freely exit and humans are mistreated with impunity. Adapting Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to the question 'What is it like to be a vampire?', he contends that glamouring, blood bonds, and an eroticized hunger different in kind from ours leave humans unable to verify vampire trustworthiness — echoing Aristotle's claim that one who cannot live in the polis is a beast or a god — so mainstreaming demands the AVL first expose and reform vampire institutions.

15.title: NOTES
15.file: ch15 - NOTES.md
15.relation: McClelland traces the vampire's drift from demonic scapegoat — Marx's figure for capital draining the proletariat — to sympathetic protagonist, then reads TruBlood itself as a political device: the synthetic substitute is a trap that lures the ancient enemy out of opposition and into consumption-based communion, creating the 'ideal consumer' who is eternal, much as globalization absorbs adversaries into the marketplace. Godric's exhaustion with undead power struggles and the maenad Maryann's induced hedonism show, respectively, the hollowness of quasi-immortal consumer life and the human community's own susceptibility to buying bliss at the price of its principles.

16.title: PART THREE - “THEIR VERY BLOOD IS SEDUCTIVE” EROS, SEXUALITY, AND GENDER
16.file: ch16 - PART THREE - “THEIR VERY BLOOD IS SEDUCTIVE” EROS, SEXUALITY, AND GENDER.md

17.title: NOTES
17.relation: Brace and Arp systematically map the coffin-to-closet analogy: 'God hates fangs' echoes Fred Phelps, Eddie's leap from closeted family man to vampire lover parallels coming out, and vampire media normalization (Fang magazine, teen soaps) mirrors Ellen and Dawson's Creek. They distinguish orientation from action, rebut the natural-law argument that nonprocreative sex is unnatural (it would condemn infertile and contracepting heterosexuals too), and fix the moral line at consent — Bill asking before fang and penis penetrate is healthy, while Lorena's forced turning of Bill and the Rattrays' draining of him, 'objectified and crucified' for his blood, are violations; on that basis they argue vampires deserve equal rights under the VRA.

18.title: NOTES
18.file: ch18 - NOTES.md
18.relation: Craton and Jonell read Sookie as an emblem of contemporary feminist ambivalence: her 'I am woman, hear me roar' independence coexists with sexual caution, and the show stages feminism's sex wars — Lafayette's sex work and webcam pornography versus Maryann, whose 'pro-sex' liberation collapses into self-annihilating worship of Dionysus and whose death suggests unregulated sexuality is dangerous. Tara's plotline shows how race and class layer onto gender (her 'baby-daddy' scene, Maryann as failed white savior), exposing the limits of a united feminist front, while the 'kept woman' quarrel with Bill and Sookie's barmaid-versus-telepathic-detective career choice leave more questions about female empowerment than answers.

19.title: NOTES
19.relation: Hirschbein presents True Blood as a Freudian fable: vampires live the unrepressed id's Eros and Thanatos that civilization forces the rest of us to renounce, which is why they defeat all three sources of suffering (mortal bodies, nature, hostile neighbors) and why the show's convulsive sex and violence thrill us. Glamouring reproduces the posthypnotic suggestion that proved the unconscious to Freud, Sookie's mind-reading confirms his dark discoveries about our sexualized aggression, vampire myths work as projection screens for desires we disown, and Marcuse's complaint about 'genital tyranny' and sublimation frames Sookie's love as a near-realization of Freud's St. Francis ideal.

20.title: PART FOUR - “I AM ACTUALLY OLDER THAN YOUR JESUS” NATURAL, SUPERNATURAL, AND DIVINE
20.file: ch20 - PART FOUR - “I AM ACTUALLY OLDER THAN YOUR JESUS” NATURAL, SUPERNATURAL, AND DIVINE.md

21.title: NOTES
21.file: ch21 - NOTES.md
21.relation: Corn and Dunn read Maryann's takeover of Bon Temps through René Girard's scapegoat theory: mimetic desire breeds the resentments Sookie hears all day, the crowd's 'wild energy' dissolves the Apollonian individual into Dionysian self-forgetfulness (Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy, Plato's assembly that echoes blame until judgment drowns), and the town and the Fellowship of the Sun alike restore solidarity by uniting against vampires — or against Sam on the sacrificial oak. Godric's self-delivery to the Newlins is a failed Christlike sacrifice, so the chapter ends with Sookie's 'God doesn't punish, God forgives' as Girard's alternative to founding community on sacrificial violence.

22.title: NOTES
22.file: ch22 - NOTES.md
22.relation: The Terjesens dissect what 'unnatural' could mean for vampires: on modern evolutionary biology they are simply effective predators, so no unfairness or odd predation style (sleeping with one's food) makes them unnatural. Aristotle's four causes and Aquinas's God-ordered extrinsic finality would let 'unnatural' mean 'against the plan', but purposes cannot be observed — the source of bad medieval science — and Descartes's banishment of final causes from physics shows why; Godric's 'our existence is insanity' therefore commits the is–ought fallacy, and what remains to judge is not vampire nature but vampire choice, as Bill's mainstreaming and Godric's final 'I told a lie' about survival versus right and wrong show.

23.title: NOTES
23.relation: Barkman answers 'God hates fangs' with Aquinas: evil is no-thing, so God creates nothing inherently evil — fangs, sex, and free will are good gifts whose misuse explains fallen angels, witches (via the Malleus Maleficarum and Allatius's demon-animated vampires), and human sinners like Rene and the Rattrays. Since True Blood's vampires stand unmoved before crosses, hold church meetings, and can choose as Bill does, they are not soulless minions of the devil but created beings who, like humans, go wrong only by misusing free will — which is why Harris's inclusive Episcopalianism lets Gran say there is a purpose for everything God makes, even a vampire.

24.title: PART FIVE - “OUR EXISTENCE IS INSANITY” THE METAPHYSICS OF SUPERNATURAL BEINGS
24.file: ch24 - PART FIVE - “OUR EXISTENCE IS INSANITY” THE METAPHYSICS OF SUPERNATURAL BEINGS.md

25.title: NOTES
25.relation: Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.

26.title: NOTES
26.file: ch26 - NOTES.md
26.relation: Curry asks whether even Sookie's telepathy can breach the privacy of mind: a third-person account of shifter Sam hearing a dog-whistle leaves out the quale — the homage to Nagel's bat — and Locke's inverted spectrum (Jason and Tara both say 'green' while living different experiences) shows qualia are incommunicable. Reading the astrology-believing Maxine's mind traps Sookie in a dilemma: if she fully becomes Maxine she is no longer the Sookie who knows, and if she keeps her skeptical psychology she never experiences what it is like to believe — so, drawing on Dennett's coffee example for one's own past qualia, even the show's most powerful mind reader can never know what it is like to experience things as you.

27.title: NOTES
27.relation: Grubb tests theories of personal identity on the supes: the bodily theory fails because Bill's and Jessica's bodies died and refunctioned at transformation, Locke's memory theory stumbles on amnesiac Eric (who stays Eric despite remembering nothing), and psychological continuity fails because vampirism inflated Bill's aggression and collie-Sam's mind when Andy draws a gun is anyone's guess. She closes with Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism — lives as long stories of temporal parts — which lets the rambunctious vampire Jessica count as the same person as the demure human girl because both are episodes in one continuing story.

28.title: PART SIX - “TALKING ABOUT YOUR FEELINGS IS A MANLY THING TO DO” SUPERNATURAL LIFE LESSONS FROM SEASON THREE
28.file: ch28 - PART SIX - “TALKING ABOUT YOUR FEELINGS IS A MANLY THING TO DO” SUPERNATURAL LIFE LESSONS FROM SEASON THREE.md

29.title: NOTES
29.relation: Craton reads Sookie's arc through disability theory: her telepathy, treated by Bon Temps as a disability that barred her from college and respect, is reframed once vampires and Weres prize it — and finally her faerie 'light' — into an ability she controls for money, crime-solving, and saving a child. The chapter parallels the eugenics-era fears Sookie and Alcide share about passing on difference, and the freak-show histories of Joseph Merrick, Saartjie Baartman, and Julia Pastrana illuminate how vampires like Eric and Sophie-Anne value Sookie's blood as a possession to be consumed rather than a person to be respected, until she rescinds Bill's invitation and defends her light.

30.title: NOTES
30.relation: Grubb stages Arlene's decision to abort the baby fathered by serial killer Rene as a case study in Bentham's act utilitarianism: her prayer that ending the pregnancy will keep 'Rene's sickness' from Coby, Lisa, and Terry weighs pleasure and pain — the two sovereign masters — for the greatest number, from family to all of Bon Temps. The chapter shows why the calculus fails her: consequences cannot be known in advance (a crystal ball or Lafayette's visions would be needed), it is indeterminate whose happiness counts, and her premise that evil is biologically inheritable sits badly with the free-will account of sin, making the dilemma genuinely undecidable from inside the show.

31.title: NOTES
31.relation: The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.
