2.title: THE PHILOSOPHY OF POPULAR CULTURE
2.file: ch02 - THE PHILOSOPHY OF POPULAR CULTURE.md

5.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
5.file: ch05 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md

8.title: Introduction
8.relation: Editor Jerold Abrams argues Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent 'cinematic existentialism' in which a free subject stands against a cold, uncaring world, synthesized with strands of Stoicism and pragmatism. He surveys the volume's essays as variations on this theme: Camus' absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzschean flux in Full Metal Jacket, Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity in Paths of Glory, and Nietzsche's overman as the Star Child in 2001. The essay ties specific films (the ape's femur, HAL, Humbert, the Overlook) to the claim that each Kubrick subject must invent its own meaning in a meaningless universe.

9.title: Part One The Subject at War
9.file: ch09 - Part One The Subject at War.md

10.title: Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke
10.file: ch10 - Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke.md
10.relation: Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.

11.title: Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard
11.file: ch11 - Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard.md
11.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.

12.title: Existential Ethics Where the Paths of Glory Lead Jason Holt
12.file: ch12 - Existential Ethics Where the Paths of Glory Lead Jason Holt.md
12.relation: Holt uses Paths of Glory to illustrate existential ethics, framing the doomed 701st Regiment as 'thrown' beings-toward-death who retain full freedom in how they meet their fate. He resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' (denying objective values while commanding authenticity) by treating authenticity as a formal, second-order virtue like integrity: Colonel Dax is sincere and consistent, General Mireau an inauthentic hypocrite acting in bad faith. Addressing weakness of will (Roget's cowardice) and the condemned Paris 'dying well' before the firing squad, Holt argues that courage—an Aristotelian character virtue—is the smuggled-in content that grounds any formalist existential ethics.

13.title: Part Two The Subject in Love
13.file: ch13 - Part Two The Subject in Love.md

14.title: Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman
14.file: ch14 - Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman.md
14.relation: Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.

15.title: Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker
15.file: ch15 - Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker.md
15.relation: Decker reads Killer's Kiss (and later 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body ('I am my body'), recovering the somatic that Socrates and Plato's Phaedo denigrated. In Killer's Kiss the boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight where bodies become weapons, spatial camera work, and the theme of contingency foreground embodiment; 2001 makes viewers feel their own bodies in space, and A Clockwork Orange's Ludovico 'cure' rewires the body-mind. Drawing on pragmatists Shusterman and Sullivan and on Foucault's biopower, he argues the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut turn Merleau-Ponty's projective intentionality into domination rather than communication.

16.title: The Logic of Lolita Kubrick, Nabokov, and Poe Jerold J. Abrams
16.file: ch16 - The Logic of Lolita Kubrick, Nabokov, and Poe Jerold J. Abrams.md
16.relation: Abrams argues Kubrick's and Nabokov's Lolita is a philosophical detective story descended from Poe's Dupin tales, and that Humbert fails as a detective because he lacks the right logic. Using Peirce's abduction (and Eco's overcoded/undercoded/creative types), he shows Humbert excels at 'overcoded' guesses—spotting a nymphet at a glance—but cannot make the 'undercoded' abductions needed to see that Quilty is shadowing him, because he is all chess-like calculation and no playful 'musement' or acumen. Humbert (the resolvent) and Quilty (the creative) split Poe's 'bi-part' double-Dupin; Quilty the changeling-Minotaur controls the labyrinth and dies behind Lolita's portrait as a self without a unified identity.

17.title: Part Three The Subject and the Meaning of Life
17.file: ch17 - Part Three The Subject and the Meaning of Life.md

18.title: Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler
18.file: ch18 - Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler.md
18.relation: Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).

19.title: The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders
19.file: ch19 - The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders.md
19.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.

20.title: Part Four The Subject in History
20.file: ch20 - Part Four The Subject in History.md

21.title: Spartacus and the Second Part of the Soul Gordon Braden
21.file: ch21 - Spartacus and the Second Part of the Soul Gordon Braden.md
21.relation: Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's rivalries onto to thymoeides, the soul's 'second' spirited part governed by philotimia (love of honor): Crassus's obsessive hamilla with Gracchus, and his skewed contest with Spartacus over Varinia and Antoninus. Reading Draba's trident-throw and Crassus's closing 'now I fear him' as the spirited part's competitiveness overrunning reason, Braden shows the gladiatorial paired combat mirroring republican politics on its way to the Principate.

22.title: The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska
22.file: ch22 - The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska.md
22.relation: Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.

23.title: The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer
23.file: ch23 - The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer.md
23.relation: Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.

24.title: Part Five The Subject of the Future
24.file: ch24 - Part Five The Subject of the Future.md

25.title: Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw
25.file: ch25 - Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw.md
25.relation: Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.

26.title: “Please Make Me a Real Boy” The Prayer of the Artificially Intelligent Jason T. Eberl
26.file: ch26 - “Please Make Me a Real Boy” The Prayer of the Artificially Intelligent Jason T. Eberl.md
26.relation: Eberl argues that HAL 9000 in 2001 and David in A.I. present sufficient evidence of personhood, testing them against the Turing test, behaviorism, and Boethius's definition of a person as an individual substance of a rational nature. He uses Hegel's master-slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their self-conscious creations, reading Bowman's disconnection of HAL and the Flesh Fair's destruction of Mechas as humans failing to recognize persons. Invoking Aristotle's telos and virtue, he claims the Flesh Fair's real moral crime is precluding Mechas from pursuing their own flourishing, while David's Pinocchio-like leap of faith marks him as person-like.

27.title: Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams
27.file: ch27 - Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams.md
27.relation: Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.

5.title: Introduction
5.relation: Kowalski's Introduction argues that philosophy is an activity, not a possession—asking universally important questions, exposing contradictions, and defending answers with arguments—and asks whether a filmmaker can engage in that process through fictional narrative, using Joss Whedon's corpus (Buffy, Angel, Firefly, Dollhouse, The Avengers) as the test case. It contends that showing Whedon philosophizes would confirm the film-as-philosophy thesis and force its expansion to television. The chapter then prospectuses the book: authenticity via Heidegger, Sartre, Socrates, and Rawls; Platonic and Aristotelian accounts of the good life; Lockean-Kantian rights and Aristotelian virtue without God; Hick's religious non-realism via Shepherd Book; free will via d'Holbach and Kane; and the Mulhall debate—under the canon rule that only texts with Whedon's script approval count.

6.title: Seeking Authenticity
6.relation: The chapter argues that Whedon's heroes—Angel resisting the demon within in Pylea, Spike earning back his soul, Simon Tam abandoning his medical career for River, Echo asserting control over her Dollhouse imprints, and Buzz Lightyear redefining himself—live authentically by owning their values against depersonalizing forces, while Captain Hammer and Serenity's Operative are the true 'monsters' who surrender their identities to social roles and blind institutional loyalty. It then asks whether Whedon is a thoroughgoing Sartrean existentialist and answers no: the 'Paradiso Paradigm' (Mal returning the medicine in 'The Train Job') and Willow's 'Choices' speech show objective moral value independent of autonomous choice, making Whedon more Socratic than Sartrean. Rawls supplies the synthesis: heterogeneous life plans (Xander, Oz, Lorne) pursued within objective social conditions—basic rights, liberties, and opportunities—that make authentic self-formation possible for everyone.

7.title: On Being Horrible (and an Angel)
7.file: ch07 - On Being Horrible (and an Angel).md
7.relation: The chapter runs Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge from the Republic against the Whedonverse: invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and 'Gone' (where even Buffy takes a self-serving 'vacation from herself'), the invincibility ring in 'In the Dark' that Angel destroys rather than uses, and the Buffy-Faith body switch in 'Who Are You?' as the unjust person with a virtuous reputation versus the just person misunderstood. Plato's tripartite-soul answer is only partly confirmed—Faith spirals into torment after killing the deputy mayor, but Saffron cons without any inner turmoil—so the chapter turns to Aristotle: the good life needs external goods, above all friendship and community. This explains why Whedon's wrongdoers (Woody in Toy Story, Jayne in 'Ariel,' Gunn, Stark, Buffy in 'Revelations') must atone before their communities, why Mal's 'you only need a few [good people]' rebukes Saffron, and why both Dr. Horrible and Captain Hammer are tragic—each lives alone and friendless, having squandered Penny.

8.title: The Right and the Good without God
8.file: ch08 - The Right and the Good without God.md
8.relation: The chapter builds the case that Whedon's fiction grounds ethics without God: Foy's Lockean social-contract reading of the Firefly crew and Kant's person-as-end analysis explain why Mal insists Saffron is 'not to be bought' in 'Our Mrs. Reynolds' and why Loki's possession of Hawkeye and Jasmine's enthrallment of her worshippers are the Whedonverse's paradigm wrongs. Spike's arc—from selfish ally, through the 'Triangle' troll fight and 'Intervention' torture, to the 'Chosen' sacrifice—is read through Aristotelian habituation into virtue, while Angel's Darla-arc firing of Team Angel and the Better Days temple-money and Inara plots show where respecting rights and being a good person can come apart. Finally the Euthyphro dilemma, plus replies to Pojman and Craig (self-sacrifice is not 'stupid'), argue that Angel's 'Epiphany' ethic—doing what matters with no glorious end or divine reward—shows morality is neither arbitrary nor motivationally crippled without God.

9.title: Portrayals of Religion
9.relation: Starting from Whedon's self-description as 'a very hard-line, angry atheist' fascinated by devotion, the chapter argues that Hick's religious non-realism best unifies the Whedonverse's treatment of religion. Religion is 'demonized' when it serves domination or self-interest (Ken's Family Home in 'Anne,' the Patron's witch-burning in 'Safe'), but Shepherd Book—read through The Shepherd's Tale's soup-bowl epiphany—embodies a faith that needs no literal truth: 'You don't fix faith, River. It fixes you,' the mudders' Jaynestown statue, and 'I don't care what you believe, just believe it' all function as symbols that transform lives. The same lens dissolves the controversy over 'Amends': the snowfall that saves Angel may be miracle or freak cold front, and—like Book's epiphany—what matters is the redemption the ambiguity occasions, not its metaphysical source.

10.title: The Peculiarities of Free Will
10.file: ch10 - The Peculiarities of Free Will.md
10.relation: The chapter surveys how Whedon's fiction both dramatizes free choice—Angel answering Whistler's 'you could go either way' challenge, Cordelia reclaiming her visions in 'Birthday,' choices even the Powers That Be cannot predict—and suggests determinism, via the reverse-chronology of The Shepherd's Tale, the self-fulfilling prophecies Flamson identifies, and Topher's 'Everybody's programmed' speech in Dollhouse. It rejects Richardson and Rabb's Shestovian freedom (it implausibly denies that tragic choices between two evils, like Buffy killing re-ensouled Angel in 'Becoming, Part II,' are free) and Flamson's compatibilism (Jasmine's followers do what they want yet plainly lack choice, as Gunn's 'then we'll kick it over and start a new game' speech shows). Robert Kane's libertarianism—undetermined self-forming choices in moments of torn conflict—fits best, illuminating Book's soup-bowl pause, Billy/Dr. Horrible's street-corner hesitation with Penny, and Connor's choice between Darla and faux-Cordelia in 'Inside Out,' though the chapter concedes Whedon may sometimes sacrifice consistency for drama.

11.title: Mulhall and His Detractors
11.file: ch11 - Mulhall and His Detractors.md
11.relation: The chapter stages the film-as-philosophy debate: Mulhall's 'bold thesis' that films like the Alien series are 'philosophical exercises—philosophy in action,' Baggini's objection that they offer symbolic representations without reasons, and Mulhall's rejoinders that rationally reorienting a shared conceptual space (Socrates' polis-as-parent analogy in the Crito) and dramatizing visions of what ultimately matters are rational without formal argument. It then answers Murray Smith (film thought experiments like All of Me subordinate the epistemic to the artistic) and Paisley Livingston (philosophizing must occur via non-paraphrasable cinematic devices alone) by arguing that Whedon's portrayal of Angel's worldview—helping the helpless for its own sake with no glorious end—raises exactly the ultimate-ends questions Mill said admit of no proof, with Angel as a confirming instance of Mulhall. The Buffy episode 'Hush' closes the case: its dialogue-free middle, from Buffy and Riley's kiss to Willow and Tara's joined-hands spell, conveys a Zen-like lesson about the limits of propositional knowledge that resists linguistic mediation, answering Livingston's talking-head dilemma.

12.title: The Russell-Wartenberg Debate
12.file: ch12 - The Russell-Wartenberg Debate.md
12.relation: The chapter sets the book's standard for 'philosophy in action' by staging Bruce Russell's skepticism against Thomas Wartenberg's defense of the film-as-philosophy thesis: Russell holds that narrative films can at most raise questions or furnish counterexamples, so The Matrix merely inspires the viewer's own argument for external-world skepticism, while Wartenberg replies that The Matrix screens Descartes's evil-deceiver hypothesis so effectively that viewers are themselves deceived into skeptical doubt, accomplishing for audiences what Socrates did to his interlocutors. Wartenberg's reading of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind — where Dr. Mierzwiak's memory-erasure technology presents utilitarianism (via Mary's dialogue) and then a counterexample to it — is tested, and the author proposes the film targets hedonism more directly, working as a reverse variant of Nozick's experience machine that defends autonomy over happiness. Kant's obscure Transcendental Deduction is invoked to show that even canonical philosophical texts are ambiguous, blunting the explicitness objection. The chapter concludes that negative projects — modus tollens counterexamples cinematically conveyed — are where film most plausibly philosophizes, preparing the ground for reading the Whedonverse.

13.title: Exploring The Cabin in the Woods
13.file: ch13 - Exploring The Cabin in the Woods.md
13.relation: The chapter reads The Cabin in the Woods as Whedon and Goddard doing philosophy: the facility's ritual sacrifice of the five campers is given an explicit utilitarian defense (quoting Mill's greatest-happiness principle) through the Director's plea that Dana kill Marty to avert the apocalypse, which the film ultimately counters through the friends' care-based obligations. Drawing on Nel Noddings's ethics of care and Aristotle's claim that the severity of our duties varies with the closeness of relationships — and on Whedonverse parallels like Buffy refusing to sacrifice Dawn in 'The Gift' — it recasts the ending as an implicit counterargument to classic utilitarianism: Dana does nothing impermissible by refusing to murder her friend, so utilitarianism is false, while Dana's genuine dilemma is deliberately left unresolved in Socratic aporia. It then extends the ethics of care into a theory of the horror genre, reading Whedon's 'inoculation against real fear' as an Aristotelian catharsis that requires relatable characters who care for one another, and takes the film's monitors, two-way mirrors, and voyeurism scenes (Hadley's callousness, the control-room ogling of Jules) as a metalevel invitation to audit our own desensitization to pointless screen suffering.

14.title: Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity
14.file: ch14 - Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity.md
14.relation: The chapter uses the Wes–Holtz dispute over whether Angel owes punishment for Angelus's murders (Holtz's body-continuity view, glossed via Hobbes) to test theories of personal identity across the Whedonverse. It argues the shows present a Platonic separate soul as the metaphysical locus of identity — Fred ceasing to exist when Illyria consumes her soul, the shaman's soul-jar in 'Awakening,' the Judge finding Angelus 'clean' — while Angel's felt guilt, Darla's and Spike's resurrections, Buffy's and Faith's body switch, and Dollhouse's wiped Actives press the Lockean memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity successor. The Angel/Angelus case — eidetically shared memories but radically disconnected intentions, desires, and ethical sensibilities, developed over some 200 episodes — is offered as a richer cinematic counterexample than Locke's Day-Man/Night-Man or Parfit's fission triplet, forcing Neo-Lockeans to choose between memory chains and other psychological connections, and supporting Amy Kind's point that identity alone is not what matters for moral responsibility. Whedon's own verdict follows Parfit in discarding numerical identity but turns toward an ethics of care: what matters is staying properly psychologically connected to those one loves, so one 'finds out who you are' by being countable-on in ethically significant action.

15.title: Conclusion
15.file: ch15 - Conclusion.md
15.relation: The conclusion synthesizes the book's case that Whedon philosophizes, building a Shaw-style hierarchy from illustrating theories (Connor as Robert Kane's libertarian agent, 'stirred up' between Darla's and faux-Cordelia's competing visions) through ethical and metaphysical complexity ('Man on the Street,' Angel/Angelus) to epistemic endorsement of a Whedonian worldview. It reads Angel's epiphany — 'if there's no bigger meaning, then the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing in the world' — as a negative project against the thesis that ethics without God is incoherent, since Whedon's God-ambiguous fiction shows noble self-sacrifice (Buffy for Dawn, Cordy for Angel, Simon for River) that remains worthwhile regardless of cosmic justice. Following Mulhall's use of Socrates as an exemplar of ethically significant living, it casts Angel the Champion as a comparable exemplar grounded in authenticity, care-based relationships, and the transformation of moral character. It closes by extending the film-as-philosophy debate to television, deploying Carroll's gaze/glance distinction to argue nothing in principle keeps quality TV — from The Twilight Zone and Star Trek to Buffy and Angel — from being philosophy in action.

8.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
8.file: ch08 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
8.relation: Sanders reads Casino as a dramatization of ethical egoism, using the parasitic bond between Nicky Santoro and Ace Rothstein to ask whether an egoist who treats a friend as a mere instrument can have real friendship. He distinguishes 'maximizing' egoism (Nicky's ruinous take-everything drive, ending in his beating death) from a 'satisficing' egoism that restricts its own dispositions, arguing against Blum, Wilcox and an Aristotelian objection that only the maximizing version is truly incompatible with friendship. Aristotle's account of virtue and friendship supplies the standard the film's egoists fall short of.

9.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
9.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
9.relation: Skoble uses Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle to probe when vigilantism is justified, invoking Locke's claim that in civil society individuals delegate private vengeance to the state for objectivity. He argues Travis's rescue of the trapped child prostitute Iris is legitimate (the police won't help, she can't help herself) while his plan to assassinate Senator Palantine is madness, drawing the key line between correctly identifying a deserving target and mere perceived evil (contrasting Travis with Death Wish's Kersey, Batman, and Klan lynch mobs). He closes with Socrates' 'unexamined life' as the remedy: contemplating justice so we can confront real badness rather than turn away.

10.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
10.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
10.relation: Kowalski likens Goodfellas' Henry Hill to Plato's Gyges: both act immorally with near-total impunity, posing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic of why one should be just when one can escape all consequences. He applies Plato's tripartite soul (appetitive, spirited, rational) to Henry (runaway appetite/cocaine), Tommy (overstretched spirit, killing Billy Batts and Spider out of wounded pride) and cool, untroubled Paulie, treating them as the disharmonious 'unbalanced self.' Against the objection that these gangsters seem happy, he deploys Plato's health/happiness analogy and the feeling-happy vs being-happy distinction to argue they suffer 'cancer of the soul' and cannot be truly happy.

11.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
11.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
11.relation: Conard uses Mean Streets' guilt-ridden Charlie to survey conceptions of unhappiness against three definitions of happiness: beatitude (Aquinas), pleasure (Mill's hedonism), and flourishing (Aristotle's eudaimonia). He reads Charlie as damned in his own Catholic eyes, then invokes Nietzsche's Genealogy that religion manufactures guilt from internalized instinct, Plato's disordered soul and akrasia to explain Charlie's conflicting desires, and Schopenhauer's and Freud's pessimism that suffering is our natural state. He argues Charlie reaches dysdaimonia by acquiring vices and pursuing an ignoble (gangster) life, closing with Plato's Symposium and Sartre's facticity/transcendence to cast unhappiness as an ontological lack at the heart of human desire.

12.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
12.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md

13.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
13.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
13.relation: Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.

14.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
14.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
14.relation: Knight opens by denying that fiction films (Scorsese's included) actually 'do' philosophy, arguing they raise philosophical themes rather than construct arguments or thought experiments, then reads The Age of Innocence for its themes. Her thesis is that Scorsese renders the 'social semiotics' of 1870s New York high society—flowers, cutlery, seating, hand-kissing, the yellow-versus-red roses—as a code that constrains individual desire, with the outsider Countess Olenska as the catalyst who exposes its rigidity. Newland Archer is trapped between belonging and fleeing, and society (via May and the van der Luydens) quietly conspires to ship Ellen back to Europe and preserve the status quo, the camera and omniscient narrator judging the judges.

15.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
15.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
15.relation: McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.

16.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
16.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
16.relation: Richard Greene analyzes The King of Comedy's Rupert Pupkin, who kidnaps talk-show host Jerry Landers to force his way onto TV and emerges a celebrity, calling this the 'Pupkin gambit' (harming others and oneself to secure an overwhelming personal payoff). Distinguishing internalist accounts of rationality (Plato's well-ordered soul, Kant's universalizable maxims) from an externalist one, Greene argues the gambit is irrational for a sane agent like the financier Michael Milken but rational for Pupkin via a Pascal's-wager structure: because Pupkin is delusional, even imagined success satisfies his desire, so the wager has huge upside and no real downside for him. He also invokes ethical egoism to show unethical acts can still be assessed for self-interested rationality.

17.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
17.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md

18.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
18.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
18.relation: Karen D. Hoffman reads The Last Temptation of Christ and Bringing Out the Dead through Sartre's distinction between the for-itself (transcendence) and the in-itself (immanence), arguing both reluctant saviors are tempted into bad faith. Scorsese's Jesus, tempted on the cross to abandon his mission and live as an ordinary husband and father, passively drifts toward a life of pure immanence that denies his human transcendence, until (following Kazantzakis's 'sprouting of wings' image via Judas) he reclaims his choice to be crucified. Frank Pierce inversely faces a false transcendence—the temptation to think of himself as God, or to escape via drugs, violence, or suicide—and resists it, allowing the vegetative Mr. Burke to die. Hoffman frames avoiding either exaggeration as the path to authentic Sartrean humanity and grace.

19.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
19.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
19.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that The Aviator, unusually for Hollywood, is a libertarian celebration of the entrepreneur, turning billionaire Howard Hughes into a Scorsese underdog battling the establishment. Drawing on Adam Smith and the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, Cantor reads Hughes's willingness to risk his own money on Hell's Angels and TWA, his visionary anticipation of talkies and jets, and his Senate-hearing fight against the Pan Am/Senator Brewster monopoly as a dramatization of the true risk-taking entrepreneur versus the mere manager. The 'socialist dinner party' with the aristocratic Hepburns and Hughes's defeat of government-backed monopoly illustrate Smith's suspicion of merchants seeking privilege and his invisible-hand claim that self-interested competition, not those who 'trade for the publick good,' best serves the public.

20.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
20.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
20.relation: Richard Gilmore reads After Hours as a nocturnal katabasis in which office worker Paul Hackett is repeatedly offered, and repeatedly fails at, authentic encounter with the SoHo women and their artworks (Kiki's papier-mache man, the plaster-of-paris bagel). Using Levinas's totality-versus-infinity and the ethics of conversation, Kant's two worlds of interest and disinterested aesthetic judgment, and Dewey's Art as Experience, Gilmore argues that art and sex alike (per Picasso and Nagel's 'double reciprocal incarnation') demand abandoning one's 'logic of the same' to perceive the other. Foucault's disciplinary kronos-time versus kairos, and Zizek's anamorphic spot, frame Paul's entrapment in solipsism until, encased as a literal artwork and reborn at the office gates, he finally offers himself to June.

21.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
21.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
21.relation: Judith Barad explains the puzzling elements of Kundun—the compassion for enemies, the child taken from his parents, the swept-away sand mandala, the sky burial—through Tibetan Buddhist ethics, arguing it closely parallels Greek and Roman Stoicism. She reads the young Dalai Lama's growth into compassion and nonviolence toward Mao and the Chinese alongside Epictetus's teaching that only our own judgments, not others' acts, can harm us, and that we must restrain desire and attachment. The Four Noble Truths reframe the film: because all things (including the self) are impermanent and interconnected, the destruction of the mandala and the feeding of the father's corpse to vultures enact detachment, and true liberation via the Eightfold Path is self-won inner peace that China cannot seize.

22.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
22.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
22.relation: R. Barton Palmer situates Scorsese as a 'saint of cinema' whose Emersonian transcendentalism—the 'influx of light and power' breaking through the material everyday—pervades even his commercial films, focusing on Bringing Out the Dead against Casino and Taxi Driver. He traces the Bressonian 'decisive moment' and Schrader's Calvinist-Jansenist reading of predestination and grace (Ace Rothstein's inexplicable survival in Casino, the elect/damned divide of Taxi Driver and Hardcore), where Travis Bickle remains 'God's lonely man' beyond redemption. Palmer argues Scorsese departs from Schrader's bleak limited atonement: Frank Pierce earns communal grace through willed effort, releasing Mary's father, asking forgiveness, and ending in a Pieta embrace that affirms redemption is attainable within the material world.

4.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann

5.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
5.file: ch05 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
5.relation: Sanders's introductory survey frames Mann's cinema as suffused with existentialist themes—alienation, freedom, authenticity, and existential choice—citing Sartre's 'condemned to be free' as the key to protagonists like Thief's Frank and Heat's Neil McCauley, who choose personal truth over surrender. It maps the volume's essays: Nietzschean will to power in the crime films, Levinas's ethics of the Other in Thief and Collateral, and Lockean/Rousseauian visions of nature in The Last of the Mohicans. Mann's outsiders repeatedly face the fateful, doom-laden choices (McCauley abandoning Eady to kill Waingro) that define existential man.

6.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
6.file: ch06 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
6.relation: Arnett reads Mann's 'modern crime films' through Nietzsche and Marc Augé's 'nonplace,' arguing Mann is a director-architect who exerts a will to power over institutional space (Atlanta's High Museum becomes Lecktor's prison in Manhunter; Neil's glass beach house in Heat). Mann's heroes are Nietzsche's 'godless' who refuse the herd, becoming Dionysian figures who redefine space—Neil and Vincent as Dionysian/Apollonian artists whose LAX showdown is a 'frenzy' of convergence. The endless recurrence of place-versus-nonplace, and Vincent killing Neil only to be trapped in supermodernity himself, dramatizes Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Dionysian pessimism.

7.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
7.file: ch07 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
7.relation: Palmer casts the protagonists of The Jericho Mile and Thief as 'outsiders' in Colin Wilson's sense—men 'awakened to chaos'—read through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus. Rain Murphy, running endless meaningless laps and hurling away the timer, is Mann's Sisyphus: his fate belongs to him, the struggle itself filling his heart. Thief's Frank, who 'gets to where nothin' means nothin',' shreds his dream-collage and destroys everything rather than be owned by Leo, enacting the absurd hero's scorn for a Hobbesian 'war of all against all' where law lacks connection to justice.

8.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
8.file: ch08 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
8.relation: Sanders argues Mann's action serves existentialist ideas: identity, freedom, authenticity, and death. In Thief, Frank's insistence on 'the yield of my labor' and his self-immolating exit dramatize the individualist maximizer whose choice of principle—echoing Sartre's young man and Kierkegaard's 'purity of heart is to will one thing'—cannot be given from outside. The Miami Vice episode 'Heart of Darkness' is read as a morality play on authenticity: undercover agent Artie Lawson's flight into the fantasy persona is a bad-faith masquerade that ends in suicide, mirroring Crockett's own anxiety about his Sonny Burnett alter ego.

9.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
9.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
9.relation: Skoble examines evil in Manhunter through the film's Nietzsche epigraph—'whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster'—as profiler Will Graham must 'become' Lecktor and Dollarhyde to catch them, risking his own psyche. Lecktor's claim that killing feels good because doing 'what God does' makes one godlike frames the killers' evil as a will to power. Skoble invokes the Socratic dictum that to know the good is to do the good, asking whether Dollarhyde's murderous 'becoming the Red Dragon' is a large-scale delusion, and warns that truly seeing the killer's fantasy risks adopting it.

10.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
10.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
10.relation: Sterritt reads Manhunter's Hannibal Lecktor as a perverse image of Nietzsche's Übermensch: hedonistic, ascetic, and expressing an overwhelming will to power, exercising superhuman self-control (his pulse never exceeding eighty-five while mutilating a nurse). Using Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming' and the body without organs, he contrasts the genuinely self-transforming Lecktor (a 'schizovivisectionist') with Dollarhyde, whose bogus becoming—trapped in Blake's 'mind-forg'd manacles' and the Red Dragon—makes him a pathetic tooth fairy rather than an overman, aligning both killers with Kierkegaard's demonic individual who stands above the universal.

11.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
11.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
11.relation: Ritzer argues Mann's aesthetics of horror in The Keep and Manhunter is an aestheticization of horror—the frightening transformed into the beautiful through mise-en-scène, color, and montage. Against Hegel's Lectures on Fine Art, which bans the purely negative and horrific from aesthetics, Ritzer marshals Schiller, De Quincey, and Auden to split the ethical from the aesthetic: Dollarhyde stages corpses as artworks and Graham reads crime scenes as an art critic. The Keep pushes further into Barthes's 'obtuse meaning' and Deleuze and Guattari's 'planes of immanence,' its stylized images referring to nothing but themselves—horror filmed solely for horror's sake.

12.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
12.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
12.relation: Rybin links Mann's style-versus-substance debate to the existential self-definition of his characters, focusing on Public Enemies. Dillinger, who tells Billie 'the only thing that's important is where somebody's going,' is not yet an icon but is 'becoming Dillinger' as the film unfolds. In the penultimate scene, watching Clark Gable in Manhattan Melodrama—'die the way you lived, all of a sudden'—Dillinger achieves authentic self-definition by claiming the gangster myth as his own identity, a Warshovian 'experience of art'; Mann's editing collapses the space between Dillinger and the screen just before Dillinger is gunned down, the cost of authentic selfhood.

13.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
13.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
13.relation: Pomerance argues Public Enemies inverts the gangster genre's convention of the 'ecstatic' criminal viewed from law's judgmental exterior: Mann's handheld camera penetrates Dillinger's private, breathing, interior world (contrasting the mechanized, plan-driven Purvis), likening the film to Fantastic Voyage's journey inside a body. Drawing repeatedly on Walter Benjamin's Arcades Project—the flâneur who is 'utterly undiscoverable,' the bourgeois transformation of nature into interior—he reads the FBI's cataloging of Dillinger as modernity reducing an integrated person to a collectible 'public enemy,' culminating in the head shot that is both execution and publicity image.

14.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
14.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
14.relation: Paulus and Adriaensens argue that Mann's 'stylized realism' is best understood not as neobaroque spectacle but as mannerism: a self-conscious, image-conscious cinema in tension between classicism and anti-classicism. Reading Mann's green-screen shooting on Heat, the hyperreal night look of Collateral and the ultra-sharp digital of Public Enemies through Deleuze's letter to Daney on cinematic mannerism, they cast Mann as a Coppola-like 'bridge-builder' who offers a pedagogy of the image and gains Nietzsche's 'powers of the false.' Baudrillard's account of Apocalypse Now as excess of means and simulation frames the immersive spectacle Mann resists in favor of realism.

15.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
15.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
15.relation: LaRocca reads The Insider as a study of contracts, conscience and courage. He argues that when Jeffrey Wigand stops calculating consequences ('Fuck it. Let's go to court.') he becomes a Kantian: his testimony has moral worth because it is done from duty and the categorical imperative, not from the utilitarian hedonic calculus of Bentham and Mill that Bergman, Wallace and Scruggs press on him. Wigand's whistleblowing is then framed through Aristotle's account of courage as a mean between recklessness and cowardice, with Wigand as the 'citizen soldier' who acts from conscience while Mike Wallace exemplifies the coward who exceeds in fear.

16.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
16.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
16.relation: Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.

17.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
17.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
17.relation: Skrodzka reads Thief and Collateral as exercises in deontology grounded in Levinas's ethics of responsibility to the Other. Frank's violent courtship of Jessie and his final destruction of his possessions, and Max's crashing of the cab after Vincent's interpellation, are staged as the self's annihilating opening to the face of the Other (glimpsed in the rearview mirror as Max's doppelganger). Using Bauman's account of liquid-modern disconnection and a leftist critique of late capitalism, she argues Mann grounds Levinasian ethics in physical labor, and defines Vincent's evil as that which is 'knowing but unknowable,' deaf to the Other's call.

18.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
18.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
18.relation: Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.

19.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
19.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
19.relation: Corne unpacks Vincent Hanna's tirade in Heat against his wife's ex-husband's 'dead-tech, postmodernistic, bullshit house.' He reads the smashing of the television and the headless sculpture through Bataille's Against Architecture (buildings as latent prisons of authority) and Jameson's diagnosis of postmodern depthlessness and the silence of affect. Using Hegel, Hugo and Ruskin on architecture's obligation to tell the truth, and especially Frankfurt's On Bullshit, Corne argues the house is 'bullshit' because it is indifferent to truth; Vincent's workaholism becomes a Frankfurtian discipline, and the film reflexively treats truth, authenticity and space as a problem.

20.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
20.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann.md
20.relation: Rodriguez-Ruiz treats Ali and The Insider as dramatizing the methodology of philosophy, especially conceptual analysis and the politics of defining social concepts. Ali's challenges to 'patriotism,' 'freedom' and his slave name, and the manipulation of 'confidential,' 'addictive' and 'tortious interference' in The Insider, show how much rides on contested definitions. Against cultural relativism, he deploys James Rachels's Elements of Moral Philosophy (there are moral facts; some rules are needed for any society to exist) and discusses conceptual analysis (Jackson, Goldman) and Schiappa's 'how ought we use X,' leaving both heroes committed to independent thinking over consensus.

6.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
6.relation: Conard's editor's introduction defines film noir and neo-noir, cataloguing noir themes (moral ambivalence, alienation, pessimism, disorientation) across films like Blue Velvet, Angel Heart, L.A. Confidential, and The Usual Suspects, and previews the volume's thirteen essays. It argues neo-noir better embodies the noir outlook because its makers work self-consciously and can let criminals succeed. It closes by invoking Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living to justify philosophical reflection on these films.

8.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
8.relation: Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.

9.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
9.relation: Barad uses Blade Runner to test what distinguishes humans from machines. Against Turing's claim that indistinguishable input-output makes a computer a mind, she deploys Sartre's dictum that in humans existence precedes essence while manufactured replicants (like a designed android) have essence first, so they can blame their maker. She reads the Voigt-Kampff empathy test through Sartrean forlornness and despair, and argues Roy Batty achieves authentic humanity when he kills Tyrell and freely chooses to save Deckard, becoming a life-giver rather than his programmed combat model.

10.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
10.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
10.relation: Smith reads Memento as a test of Locke's memory theory of personal identity. He explains Locke's view that consciousness of past actions (not soul or body) constitutes the self, rehearses Reid's transitivity objection and the circularity objection, and uses Parfit's account of memory and fusion to defend a survival-not-identity reading. He distinguishes 'Leonard 1' (anterograde amnesiac who returns each cycle) from 'Leonard 2b', a person fused from his own memories and those projected onto Sammy Jankis, arguing we too are 'fused' survivors who reinterpret hazy pasts, complicating responsibility and concern for our futures.

11.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
11.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
11.relation: Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.

12.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
12.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md

13.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
13.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
13.relation: Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.

14.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
14.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
14.relation: Skoble argues that A Simple Plan dramatizes Plato's Republic almost exactly: justice as psychological harmony among the parts of the soul, and injustice as self-destructive disharmony. When Hank, Jacob, and Lou keep found money, they enact Thrasymachus's and the Ring of Gyges challenge (would you be unjust if you'd never be caught?). Hank miscalculates his own self-interest, mistaking wealth for happiness; the deception, distrust, and murders that follow (including Hank killing Jacob) show that even the criminal who evades capture is ruined by his corrupted character, exactly as Plato predicts.

15.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
15.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
15.relation: D'Aries and Hirsch read Paul Thomas Anderson's Hard Eight as a neo-noir moral inversion: the aging criminal Sydney seeks atonement not through religious penance but through selfless love, rescuing John and Clementine while removing the loathsome Jimmy (who knows Sydney killed John's father). They contrast him with Melville's Bob le flambeur and Besson's The Professional, where convention demands the criminal be punished. Sydney escapes formal justice but is sentenced to a 'prison without bars' of self-loathing (the bloodstained cuff), and the authors warn that such sympathy-for-the-devil inversions verge on nihilistic moral relativism.

16.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
16.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
16.relation: Conard argues that Tarantino's postmodernism makes redemption impossible in Reservoir Dogs (and Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill). Using Danto on the 'end of art', Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives', and Rorty's contingent 'vocabularies', he shows the films embrace relativism about knowledge (rearranged chronology, unreliable perspectives) and about values. Mr. Orange plays Judas and Christ; the opening tipping argument exposes moral conventions as arbitrary, so becoming a 'real person' rather than a gangster is merely being a dork rather than cool. With no metanarrative to ground it, one way of life cannot be morally superior, so redemption fails.

18.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
18.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
18.relation: Gilmore reads Chinatown as neo-noir that is itself a kind of philosophy, engaging the hermeneutics of suspicion (Nietzsche, Freud, Marx) and existentialist alienation. Curly eating the venetian blinds signals a desire to recover a less painful blindness; Jake Gittes's 'conceptual scotomas' (Dennett) and hubris make him miss counternarratives, paralleling Oedipus as detective. Using Freud on the uncanny and doppelgangers (Jake doubled with Hollis Mulwray and Noah Cross) and Aristotle's Poetics on catharsis and the sublime, Gilmore argues 'Chinatown' names the abyss where every narrative is undone, and that facing this dark sublimity is the way of wisdom.

19.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
19.relation: Hibbs argues that nihilism, a working assumption in neo-noir, turns the noir protagonist's quests pointless, absurd, and thus comic, and that the Coen brothers exemplify this comic response. Using Nietzsche on nihilism, the 'last man', the 'pathos of distance', and aristocratic self-creation, he reads films like The Silence of the Lambs and Cape Fear as celebrating the 'super-antihero'. The Big Lebowski comically levels nihilism (Walter: the German nihilists are 'cowards'; nihilism cannot be lived), while Fargo and Raising Arizona affirm family and fertility, a 'banality of goodness' answering Arendt's banality of evil, letting nature's comedy perpetuate itself.

20.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
20.relation: Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.

21.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
21.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
21.relation: Schuler and Murray read Chinatown through Marx and Plato as a critique of capitalism's compulsions. Drawing on Marx and Engels on capital's Promethean transformation of nature and Hegel on art embodying abstractions, they argue neo-noir's centrifugal Los Angeles makes water, not diamonds, the object of desire, with wealth taking the abstract form of value. Plato's Republic warns that the boundless love of money (linked to Gyges, invisibility, and tyranny) destroys justice as reasonable self-limitation; Noah Cross's incest mirrors the 'rape of the Owens Valley', and Jake's defeat ('Forget it, Jake, it's Chinatown') marks the exhaustion of the postwar golden age.

22.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
22.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir.md
22.relation: Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.
