7.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
7.file: ch07 - An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film.md
7.relation: Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.

8.title: Part 1 Enigmas of Identity and Agency
8.file: ch08 - Part 1 Enigmas of Identity and Agency.md

9.title: What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City
9.file: ch09 - What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City.md
9.relation: Knight and McKnight read Blade Runner and Dark City as noir-influenced cyberpunk that asks what it is to be human. They argue that Deckard's replicant status (the origami unicorn, the shared family photo) and Murdoch's serially reprogrammed memory show memory to be unreliable, invoking Locke's prince-and-cobbler thought experiment and the problem of new brains in one body. Their conclusion is that it is emotion and relationship, not memory, that ground agency and personhood: Roy's empathy in dying and Deckard's love for Rachael, Murdoch's love for Emma/Anna, are what mark the characters as human.

10.title: Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall
10.file: ch10 - Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall.md
10.relation: Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.

11.title: Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers
11.file: ch11 - Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers.md
11.relation: Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.

12.title: The Existential Frankenstein
12.file: ch12 - The Existential Frankenstein.md
12.relation: McMahon gives an existential reading of Whale's Frankenstein and Shelley's novel through Heidegger's being-toward-death and Ernest Becker's denial of death. Victor Frankenstein exemplifies Becker's 'defiant Promethianism,' the offensive denial that seeks to conquer death, and the monster personifies death itself. She argues his obsession erodes his humanity, estranges him from others, and generates moral dilemmas, illustrating Heidegger's claim that only authentic acceptance of mortality restores individuality and genuine community, so that mastering death would make us monsters.

13.title: Part 2 Extraterrestrial Visitation, Time Travel, and Artificial Intelligence
13.file: ch13 - Part 2 Extraterrestrial Visitation, Time Travel, and Artificial Intelligence.md

14.title: Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still
14.file: ch14 - Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still.md
14.relation: Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.

15.title: Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys
15.file: ch15 - Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys.md
15.relation: Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.

16.title: 2001 A Philosophical Odyssey
16.file: ch16 - 2001 A Philosophical Odyssey.md
16.relation: Stoehr interprets Kubrick's 2001 as inducing a feeling of disembodied presence through unrooted camerawork (contrasted with Ford's The Searchers), matching its theme of technology severing us from the natural world and our bodies. Drawing on Heidegger's Dasein and Hubert Dreyfus's On the Internet, he argues there are no context-free Archimedean standpoints and stages the Plato-versus-Nietzsche debate over the body: Plato's Phaedo prizes the soul's escape from the body, while Nietzsche's Zarathustra affirms embodied, situated existence. HAL's seeming humanity underscores that machines lacking bodies cannot fully replicate human intelligence.

17.title: Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction
17.file: ch17 - Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction.md
17.relation: Holt uses the Terminator's first-person infrared POV shots (evoking Nagel's 'what is it like' question about an alien artificial consciousness) to frame the paradox of fiction: how we feel fear toward things we know do not exist. He offers a contextual divide-and-conquer solution, arguing higher emotions like pity and admiration for Sarah and Reese are largely make-believe, while lower emotions like Terminator-fear are genuine and need no existential belief (thought and mere possibility suffice). He adds that such fear is more rational for a naturalist who admits artificial intelligence is possible than for a dualist, and speculates the Terminator functions as an archetype embodying tech-noir dread.

18.title: Part 3 Brave Newer World Science Fiction Futurism
18.file: ch18 - Part 3 Brave Newer World Science Fiction Futurism.md

19.title: The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis
19.file: ch19 - The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis.md
19.relation: Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.

20.title: Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984
20.file: ch20 - Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984.md
20.relation: Palmer compares the two film versions of Orwell's 1984 to argue that dystopian fiction projects present fears and desires onto an imagined future, engaging critically with the Enlightenment idea of progress (via Burnham's managerial thesis). Anderson's 1956 film 'talks to the future,' fusing science fiction and film noir to voice Cold War dread of a possible historical trajectory, while Radford's 1984 version, in the postmodern 'heritage film' mode Jameson and Higson describe, museumizes the novel: with history seemingly ended it becomes an honored, reverentially displayed relic that talks only to a dead past rather than warning of a coming one.

21.title: Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville
21.file: ch21 - Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville.md
21.relation: Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.

22.title: The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito
22.file: ch22 - The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito.md
22.relation: Conard argues that The Matrix alludes to Plato's cave (the pod-bound humans mistaking the program for reality, Neo's painful ascent) and to Descartes' dream argument and evil-genius doubt (the singular consciousness generating the Matrix), but betrays their spirit by rejecting transcendence and the a priori. Because the film is 'Christianity without God'—Neo can only remake the shadow-world of the Matrix, not touch ultimate reality—it grounds knowledge in a subjective gut feeling ('being the One is just like being in love') rather than Descartes' intellectual intuition of God or Plato's rational grasp of the Forms, leaving no answer to whether life outside the Matrix is itself another illusion.

5.title: Sherlock Holmes as Epistemologist
5.relation: Baggett reconstructs Holmes's detective practice as an expansive epistemology built on observation, background knowledge, and abductive inference-to-the-best-explanation, using cases like 'The Blue Carbuncle' hat and the 'eliminate the impossible' maxim. He argues Holmes's boldness in drawing inferences is intellectual courage rather than hubris, invoking William James on the risk of losing truth by excessive caution. He then tests Holmes against feminist epistemologists who fault his cult of cold objectivity and mistrust of women (the Mary Morstan and Irene Adler episodes), concluding Holmes is partly vindicated by his imagination, intuition, and passion but still too fragmented between reason and emotion.

6.title: Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton
6.file: ch06 - Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton.md
6.relation: Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.

7.title: A Case of Insincerity What does it Mean to Deceive Someone
7.file: ch07 - A Case of Insincerity What does it Mean to Deceive Someone.md
7.relation: Kinghorn builds a definition of deception by successively refining it against Holmes cases: honest error ('A Scandal in Bohemia'), double-bluffing ('The Empty House' wax bust), deceiving about a different proposition (the Windibank/'Hosmer Angel' interview), and non-deceptive manipulation (the drug-induced 'Creeping Man'). Invoking Wittgenstein on language as a public practice learned by trusting others' sincerity, he argues deception requires the target's mistaken reliance on someone's assumed sincerity. The surprising upshot: because Holmes and Moriarty mutually presume insincerity in their game, Holmes never truly deceives Moriarty.

8.title: Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox
8.relation: Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.

9.title: Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies
9.file: ch09 - Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies.md
9.relation: Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.

10.title: Eliminating the Impossible Sherlock Holmes and the Supernatural
10.file: ch10 - Eliminating the Impossible Sherlock Holmes and the Supernatural.md
10.relation: Blanchette uses the Guy Ritchie film's Lord Blackwood 'resurrection' and 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' to ask whether a supernatural explanation is ever admissible. Drawing on Draper's definition of nature vs. the supernatural, Plantinga's natural-vs-logical necessity distinction, and Hume on miracles, he argues miracles are naturally impossible but not logically impossible unless nature is proven a closed system. He defends a truth-aimed methodology (pursue natural causes until the best explanation of failure is that none exists), showing Holmes rightly debunks both cases while thought experiments reveal conditions under which a supernatural verdict would become the rational inference.

11.title: Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes
11.file: ch11 - Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes.md
11.relation: Terjesen asks whether Conan Doyle acted immorally in killing Holmes in 'The Final Problem,' framing it through property theory. He runs Locke's labor theory (illustrated via 'The Blue Carbuncle' gem), Proudhon and Marx's critiques, and both consequentialist and Kantian (respect-for-persons) justifications of intellectual property. He argues Conan Doyle's ownership of the iconic Holmes weakened as Paget, Gillette, Rathbone, and Dr. Joseph Bell co-authored the figure, so property rights alone can't justify the killing—but Conan Doyle's authorial dignity plus the narrative fitness of 'The Final Problem' and 'His Last Bow' make the send-off defensible.

12.title: Sherlock Holmes Artist of Reason
12.file: ch12 - Sherlock Holmes Artist of Reason.md
12.relation: McInerny argues Holmes is not a bloodless reasoning machine but an 'artist of reason' who fuses intellect with imagination ('the scientific use of imagination'). He lays out Holmes's four-stage method—fact-gathering interview and investigation, deep-thought hypothesis framing, denouement, and post-factum briefing—and notes his use of reasoning backward, reductio ad absurdum, and hypotheses over guesses. Finally he casts Holmes as a metaphysician who assumes a purposive, intelligible cosmos ('What is the meaning of it, Watson?'), a teleological order akin to Aristotle's Final End that grounds the local intelligibility Holmes exploits.

13.title: Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization
13.file: ch13 - Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization.md
13.relation: Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.

14.title: Passionate Objectivity in Sherlock Holmes
14.file: ch14 - Passionate Objectivity in Sherlock Holmes.md
14.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall pose the ethical clash between impartial detachment and partial loyalty, situating Holmes between Simon Keller (loyalty as a threat to being a 'good believer,' echoed by Holmes's 'Sign of Four' rejection of emotion) and Bernard Williams and Susan Wolf (who defend priority for loved ones—Williams's 'one thought too many'). Using Watson's shooting in 'The Three Garridebs,' Holmes's weaning off drugs, and 'perverted love' in the Sussex Vampire and Thor Bridge cases, they argue loyalty rightly understood as seeking the friend's good aids clear reasoning, and that Holmes exhibits a 'passionate objectivity' in which some acquaintance with passion is essential to being genuinely objective.

15.title: The Industrious Sherlock Holmes
15.file: ch15 - The Industrious Sherlock Holmes.md
15.relation: Bassham diagnoses Holmes as a workaholic against clinical criteria (obsessive work, few relationships, perfectionism, health neglect through fasting and cocaine), then traces the rise of the Protestant work ethic (Calvin, Weber, Carlyle) and its modern decline. Drawing on Thoreau's Walden critique of 'lives of quiet desperation,' Pieper on leisure, and the 'affluenza' literature, he distinguishes pathological from benign workaholism by warning signs and by motivation. He concludes Holmes is a pathological workaholic in his symptoms but redeemed by his noble, non-materialistic motive of fighting crime and achieving justice.

16.title: The Dog that did not Bark Learning how to Read “The Book of Life”
16.file: ch16 - The Dog that did not Bark Learning how to Read “The Book of Life”.md
16.relation: Biondi uses the silent dog of 'Silver Blaze' to teach reasoning from absence, arguing Holmes's 'imagination' is a cultivable art—Peircean abduction combining observation, background knowledge, and the virtues of independence, courage, patience, and impartiality. She traces how Holmes finds Silver Blaze at Mapleton and unmasks Straker as the horse's would-be nobbler by consulting 'the book of life.' Framed by Emerson's 'study nature' and 'know thyself' (and Aristotle on what holds 'for the most part'), she uses the Irene Adler and 'Norbury'/Yellow Face failures to show how prejudice and overconfidence blind even Holmes to alternative hypotheses.

17.title: Aristotle on Detective Fiction
17.relation: Sayers's 1935 essay reads Aristotle's Poetics as the finest guide to writing detective fiction, mapping tragedy onto the mystery: primacy of plot over character, unity of action, appropriate length, catharsis, and the parts of Peripety, Discovery, and Suffering with the criminal's hamartia. Its centerpiece is 'paralogismos'—the art of framing lies rightly by stating true consequents (B) so the reader infers a false antecedent (A) himself, illustrated by the Jones/Smith gramophone bluff, Knox's Viaduct Murder double bluff, and the 'Watsonity' fallacy behind Roger Ackroyd. She invokes 'The Hound of the Baskervilles,' 'The Speckled Band,' and 'The Copper Beeches' as Aristotelian exemplars.

18.title: The Grim Reaper on Baker Street
18.file: ch18 - The Grim Reaper on Baker Street.md
18.relation: Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.

21.title: Index
21.file: ch21 - Index.md

22.title: List
22.file: ch22 - List.md

8.title: I. Justice, Value, and the Nature of Evil
8.file: ch08 - I. Justice, Value, and the Nature of Evil.md

9.title: The Symbolism of Blood in Clockers
9.file: ch09 - The Symbolism of Blood in Clockers.md
9.relation: McFarland reads Lee's Clockers through Paul Ricoeur's account of defilement and Greek tragedy, arguing the film treats spilt blood as an 'unspeakable' evil that resists narrative and legal containment. He compares the ulcer-ridden, cleanliness-obsessed dealer Strike to Philoctetes and Oedipus, tracing how bloodstain passes through family lines (Rodney, Errol, Tyrone, Victor) and how detective Rocco's law fails to purge the contagion. The final train-into-the-desert shot leaves Strike, like an exiled tragic figure, neither cleansed nor at home.

10.title: The Prostitution Trap of Elite Sport in He Got Game
10.file: ch10 - The Prostitution Trap of Elite Sport in He Got Game.md
10.relation: Holt and Pitter argue that Lee's He Got Game exposes a 'prostitution trap' in which elite athletes, like literal prostitutes, become commodified bodies alienated from themselves. They read the parallel plots of star recruit Jesus Shuttlesworth, his father Jake pressured to broker a signing, and the prostitute Dakota as three versions of the same trap, invoking MacIntyre's internal-versus-external goods and Deci/Ryan's intrinsic-versus-extrinsic rewards to show how coercive money threatens Jesus's love of the game. Jesus escapes by exercising autonomy, negotiating on his own terms and skipping the press conference to reach an 'authentic realism.'

11.title: Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour
11.file: ch11 - Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour.md
11.relation: Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.

12.title: We Can’t Get Off the Bus A Commentary on Spike Lee and Moral Motivation
12.file: ch12 - We Can’t Get Off the Bus A Commentary on Spike Lee and Moral Motivation.md
12.relation: Beckles-Raymond reads Lee's Get on the Bus to defend a communitarian 'encumbered self' against the liberal 'unencumbered self,' arguing the Million Man March riders' racial identity is inseparable from their moral motivation. Drawing on Charles Taylor's strong evaluations and critiquing Tommie Shelby's thin-blackness solidarity, she shows each rider (George, Evan Sr., Jay, Jeremiah, Jamal, Xavier, Gary, Kyle, Randall) attends because being a good man is bound to being black, while the ejection of the self-hating Wendell marks the limits of thin identity. The film argues raced persons 'cannot get off the bus.'

13.title: Monsters and Moralism in Summer of Sam
13.file: ch13 - Monsters and Moralism in Summer of Sam.md
13.relation: Palmer argues Lee's Summer of Sam is less ethnography than moralism about the diffuse 'evil energy' that spreads through an Italian American Bronx enclave during the 1977 Son of Sam killings. Against Dan Flory's reading of the film as a veiled lynching parable, he contends Lee dismantles any clean line between the psychopath Berkowitz and his supposed innocent victims: the vigilantes become victimizers, punk outsider Richie doubles the killer through his violent stage act, and Vinny destroys himself through compulsive infidelity. Evil is shown as symptomatic of a whole social order in decline rather than located in one monster.

14.title: II. Race, Sexuality, and Community
14.file: ch14 - II. Race, Sexuality, and Community.md

15.title: (Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing
15.file: ch15 - (Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing.md
15.relation: Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.

16.title: Coworking in the Kingdom of Culture Identity and Community in the Films of Spike Lee
16.file: ch16 - Coworking in the Kingdom of Culture Identity and Community in the Films of Spike Lee.md
16.relation: Peterson uses W.E.B. Du Bois's 'Of Our Spiritual Strivings' and its 'co-worker in the kingdom of culture' to read Lee's New York films as studies of hyphenated identity and the making of American community. He traces how the Italian Americans of Do the Right Thing and Jungle Fever secure a fragile 'whiteness' only in negation of blackness (Sal, Pino, Frankie's egg-cream lament), how Summer of Sam's enclave turns on the difference embodied by punk Richie, and how 25th Hour's post-9/11 New York is disaggregated in Monty's mirror monologue. Lee's vision is a heteroglot city with 'many gates to the Kingdom of Culture.'

17.title: Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6
17.file: ch17 - Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6.md
17.relation: Hoffman assesses whether Lee's She's Gotta Have It and Girl 6 offer liberated female sexuality, drawing on second- and third-wave feminism and bell hooks. She argues Nola Darling only appears empowered before the rape scene and her submission ('Yours') reveal her as an underdeveloped object of the male gaze, whereas Girl 6, as a phone-sex worker consciously performing gender for callers, better exposes gender as socially constructed in a Butler-like sense. Even so, Girl 6's real feminist force lies not in its heroine but in its exposure of oppressive industries, especially the opening Tarantino audition where only the director's gaze counts.

18.title: The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing
18.file: ch18 - The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing.md
18.relation: Silberstein reads Do the Right Thing as staging the ideological dialectic between Martin Luther King Jr.'s absolute nonviolence and Malcolm X's defense of retaliatory self-defense, both grounded in a theologically informed natural-law view of rights (King's Christian imago dei, X's Islamic tradition). He argues King mixes a deontological ethic (violence is always wrong) with a Gandhian consequentialist claim that violence begets violence, while X frames a race war as a just holy war. The film's Radio Raheem (LOVE/HATE knuckles), Buggin' Out's boycott of Sal's Wall of Fame, the Racial Slur Montage, and Mookie throwing the trash can dramatize whether ends justify means; the closing Sal-Mookie money exchange reframes racism as symptom of a deeper capitalist greed both King and X came to critique.

19.title: Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever
19.file: ch19 - Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever.md
19.relation: Sundstrom uses Jungle Fever to dismantle the taboo (white and black versions) against interracial intimacy, treating Flipper and Angie's affair and the War Council's objections as a debate about black solidarity, loyalty, and self-hatred. He answers the War Council by invoking Mill's On Liberty and the tyranny of public opinion to defend sexual autonomy, and argues that demanding partners for political solidarity reduces them to props (objectification). He reads the psychoanalytic charge that interracial love is 'fevered' racial pathology as derived from Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks but ultimately baseless, and criticizes Lee for a puritanical ending that hides Orin and Paulie while exposing Flipper and Drew, failing to show interracial love as ordinary.

20.title: Bamboozled Philosophy through Blackface
20.relation: Flory argues Bamboozled deliberately makes its own audience laugh at Mantan's blackface coon routines to force self-reflection on how minstrel stereotypes still shape perceptions of African Americans. He reads Pierre Delacroix's shifting defenses of the show (free speech, art, 'get over slavery,' a simple-minded 'who is to judge' moral relativism) through Charles Mills's Racial Contract and 'epistemology of ignorance,' and his self-loathing through Fanon's struggle with racialization. Flory frames Lee as an Aristotelian gadfly: like Socrates, Lee arouses appropriately proportioned righteous anger (the Golden Mean) at injustice and goads viewers to philosophize, punishing Delacroix, Manray, and the Maumaus in a Manichaean moral structure to drive home minstrelsy's dehumanizing harm.

21.title: III. Time, the Subject, and Transcendence
21.file: ch21 - III. Time, the Subject, and Transcendence.md

22.title: Transcendence and Sublimity in Spike Lee’s Signature Shot
22.file: ch22 - Transcendence and Sublimity in Spike Lee’s Signature Shot.md
22.relation: Abrams analyzes Lee's 'signature shot'—a character silently gliding forward toward the viewer—as a phenomenological device that ejects the immersed viewer back into self-aware spectatorship, drawing on Heidegger's account of anticipation and being futural in Being and Time and Danto's claim that a self-conscious camera makes the film about being viewed. He tracks the shot in Malcolm X (levitating before his assassination), 25th Hour (Mary floating on Ecstasy), and Inside Man (Frazier's superhuman, robotic rush after the staged execution). He then argues the shot is aesthetically sublime in Longinus's and Kant's sense: it renders characters superhuman and elevated off the ground, an objective image of subjective transcendence that signs Lee as both filmmaker and philosopher.

23.title: Economies of Time in Clockers
23.file: ch23 - Economies of Time in Clockers.md
23.relation: Gilmore reads Clockers through DuBois's double-consciousness, arguing the film's dualities—the clockers' street dealing mirroring capitalist 'logic of maximum performance,' kronos versus kairos time, Hyde's commodity versus gift economies, systemic versus personal racism—make white and black viewers alike feel the anguish of Strike and Victor. The Gran Fury as predatory law, the slave-block-style police shakedown watched by Strike's mother, and Rocco seeing only his own reflection in Victor's eye illustrate Heideggerian thrownness and self-love-as-racism. Invoking Peirce's 'evolutionary love' (Radio Raheem's Right Hand/Left Hand speech), Rorty's renarrativization of who counts as 'white,' and Dewey's 'art is more moral than moralities,' Gilmore casts Lee as a pragmatist renarrativizing hate into love.

24.title: Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X
24.file: ch24 - Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X.md
24.relation: LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.

7.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
7.file: ch07 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
7.relation: Abrams's editorial introduction argues that Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent cinematic existentialism in which the isolated self stands against a cold, uncaring world. It threads the individual Kubrick films through named philosophers - Camus's absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzsche's flux and Overman in Full Metal Jacket and 2001, Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death in Paths of Glory, Kant's marriage-morality in Eyes Wide Shut - and notes Kubrick blends this existentialism with Stoicism (The Killing) and pragmatism. It frames each contributor's essay as reading one film through that lens.

8.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
8.file: ch08 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md

9.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
9.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
9.relation: Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.

10.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
10.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
10.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.

11.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
11.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
11.relation: Holt reads Paths of Glory as an illustration of existential ethics. The doomed men of the 701st are 'thrown' (Heidegger) into a suicidal attack on the Ant Hill, and the film contrasts the authentic Colonel Dax - sincere, consistent, refusing Mireau's command out of integrity - with the inauthentic, bad-faith General Mireau. Holt resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' by treating 'be authentic' as a formal meta-value, and argues that authenticity ultimately rests on the Aristotelian virtue of courage, shown when Paris 'dies well' before the firing squad despite an earlier failure of nerve.

12.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
12.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md

13.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
13.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
13.relation: Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.

14.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
14.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
14.relation: Decker reads Killer's Kiss (with 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and Eyes Wide Shut) to recover the philosophy of the body against the Socratic-Platonic-Cartesian denigration of the somatic. Using Merleau-Ponty's existential phenomenology ('I am my body') and pragmatists like Shusterman and Sullivan, he shows Kubrick's obsessive use of space, contingency, and the visceral - Davy's boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight, the weightless bodies of 2001, the Ludovico brainwashing of Alex, and the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut - to argue that subjectivity is corporeal and that anonymity of bodies can fund Foucauldian domination rather than liberation.

15.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
15.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
15.relation: Abrams reads Kubrick's Lolita as a parody of Poe's Dupin detective story, arguing that Humbert Humbert's method is not deduction but Peirce's logic of abduction (guessing). Humbert is the 'resolvent' half of Poe's double-Dupin - all calculation and chess - and excels only at overcoded abductions (spotting a nymphet) while failing the creative, undercoded abductions needed to see that Clare Quilty, the 'creative' double, is manipulating him. Abrams maps the film onto Poe's game-analysis (chess vs. cards) and the myth of the labyrinth, with Quilty as the ever-changing Minotaur whom Nabokov and Kubrick use for authorial 'involution.'

16.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
16.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md

17.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
17.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
17.relation: Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.

18.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
18.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
18.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a member of the 'cult of the cool' whose reticence and final resigned 'What's the difference?' surrender embody apatheia and acceptance of fate/logos. He tests Spencer Selby's claim that Clay and the sharpshooter Nikki must fail because their motives are immoral, arguing instead via an Aristotelian principle (virtues are stable dispositions) that their sudden lapses—the flimsy suitcase, Nikki's racial slur that loses him the lucky horseshoe—are Kubrick stacking the deck rather than genuine character. He closes by weighing Clay's life against models of a meaningful life (exuberance/romanticism vs. rationalism/self-fulfillment), faulting Clay for never subjecting his chosen ends to self-critical reason.

19.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
19.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md

20.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
20.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
20.relation: Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's gladiatorial paria and the Crassus–Gracchus rivalry onto to thymoeides, the spirited/competitive middle part of the soul that Plutarch renders as philotimia (love of honor) driving the alpha males of classical history. The central thesis is that Crassus (Laurence Olivier) is ruled by this competitive second part: his skewed hamilla with Spartacus plays out not just on the battlefield but through the erotic triangle over Varinia and Antoninus ('he steals my boy, I steal his girl'), so the Republic falls to a coup driven by the restless, honor-seeking part of the soul.

21.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
21.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
21.relation: Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Thomas Nagel's essay 'The Absurd' (built on Camus's Sisyphus), distinguishing conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) from philosophical absurdity (the collision of the engaged participant perspective with the detached external one). He argues Kubrick's three signature devices—the painterly aesthetic that renders eighteenth-century rituals AS rituals, the slow reverse zoom that literally moves from close-up participant view to overwhelming long-shot external view, and the ironic omniscient narrator—make viewers see Barry's conventional absurdity and then confront their own inescapable philosophical absurdity. He notes Kubrick laments this predicament pessimistically where Nagel counsels irony.

22.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
22.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
22.relation: Palmer reads The Shining through Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity as a 'perpetual present' that has lost its past and can only cannibalize it as pastiche and nostalgia film. He argues Kubrick's film enacts an 'anti-nostalgia' that invokes the nostalgic impulse—Jack Torrance's wish to escape an empty present into the Overlook's endless 1921 party—only to destroy him with it, refusing the genre's happy-ending wish-fulfillment. Drawing on Baudrillard's image of art 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness' merely 'playing with the pieces,' he casts Jack, endlessly typing 'All work and no play,' as the failed postmodern artist trapped between times, reduced to pointless Nietzschean ressentiment, with the film's Nietzschean death-of-God flux underlying its refusal of stable meaning.

23.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
23.file: ch23 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md

24.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
24.file: ch24 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
24.relation: Shaw asks whether Kubrick's worldview is nihilistic by tracking the free-will-versus-determinism question across his films, arguing (against Vincent Canby) that A Clockwork Orange celebrates rather than condemns Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice: the state's Ludovico conditioning, which makes him retch at sex and violence, is more monstrous than Alex because it destroys the free will that grounds human meaning. Invoking Kevin Stoehr's distinction between Nietzsche's passive and active nihilism, Shaw claims Kubrick highlights the negative to point beyond it. He surveys the oeuvre—Dax, Bowman, Barry, Wendy, Joker, Bill Harford as choosing agents—and reads Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's Being and Nothingness on the contradiction of wanting the beloved's freely-given yet secure love.

25.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
25.file: ch25 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
25.relation: Eberl compares HAL in 2001 and David in A.I. to ask whether an artificially created being can be a person meriting respect and rights. He runs both through criteria of personhood—self-consciousness, rationality, social activity, autonomy—and Turing's imitation game/behaviorism, concluding their responses give sufficient evidence of personhood even if the soul question is open. He uses Hegel's master–slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their creations (Bowman disconnecting HAL; the Flesh Fair destroying Mechas), warning against a moral crime of 'biological supremacy,' and invokes Aristotle's telos/virtue to argue Flesh Fairs wrongly preclude Mechas from fulfilling their function, while David's Pinocchio 'leap of faith' and cry 'I'm special, I'm David!' mark his approach to personhood.

26.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
26.file: ch26 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick.md
26.relation: Abrams argues that 2001 films the whole evolutionary arc of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, from ape-men through humanity to the Star Child as the overman/posthuman. He maps the moon monolith's discovery onto the death of God (science debunking the creation myth, guarded by a Platonic 'noble lie' cover-up), the astronauts Bowman/Poole/Floyd onto the Enlightenment 'higher men,' and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus his and Poole's fatal spacewalks onto the last man and the falling tightrope walker whom Zarathustra carries. He then extends the vision toward Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's 'mind children,' while criticizing Kubrick for replacing Nietzsche's godless self-overcoming with alien 'replacement gods' that thin out the death-of-God insight.

8.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
8.file: ch08 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
8.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.

9.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
9.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md

10.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
10.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
10.relation: Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.

11.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
11.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
11.relation: Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.

12.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
12.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
12.relation: Pomerance combines philosophy of sex and philosophy of language to argue that sex, lies, and videotape is less about sex than about speaking sex and being watched speaking it. He analyzes Cynthia's videotaped confession about her first encounter, showing how her circumlocutions ('smooth like a test tube,' 'Ladies first') tease and withhold, and how Graham as silent 'priest of carnality' becomes an absent audience. Videotape 'amplifies' situated speech to a diffuse mass audience, so Cynthia's sexuality becomes a 'television personality,' pornographic in form and effacing her individuality in the manner of Benjamin's mechanical reproduction. The face and presence-in-time make every filmed performance both erotic and a kind of illuminating lie.

13.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
13.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md

14.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
14.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
14.relation: Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.

15.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
15.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
15.relation: King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.

16.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
16.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
16.relation: de Waard argues that The Good German embodies Soderbergh's 'neo-meta' philosophy of history as polyphonic mediation, staged by Levi's line about a camera that turns the image upside-down to set it right. Shooting with 1940s-era equipment and pastiching Casablanca, The Third Man, Chinatown, and Schindler's List, the film presents not history's progression but 'history as time,' a simultaneity of broken mirrors. Reworking Benjamin's angel-of-history thesis, de Waard claims images of the present threaten to reappear ad infinitum, and contrasts Soderbergh's cold, morally relativist tale of American war-criminal whitewashing (Lena's confession that she betrayed twelve Jews) with Spielberg's emotionally manipulative Holocaust spectacle, invoking Eco on Casablanca as 'movies' itself.

17.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
17.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
17.relation: Baker uses Noel Carroll's aesthetic claim that film art requires 'sufficient' creative control ('no control, no style, no art') to defend Soderbergh's authorship across four remakes. The Underneath swaps noir shadow for suburban banality and green/blue color symbolism to externalize Michael's alienation; Traffic adapts a BBC series to indict NAFTA-era globalization and the treatment-starved drug war; Ocean's Eleven rewrites the Rat Pack ending so the thieves keep $150 million, an allegory of American wealth consolidation embodied by casino owner Benedict; Solaris strips science fiction to introspective desire. Baker further argues Soderbergh harnesses star images (Roberts, Douglas, Clooney) yet pushes them past type, synthesizing Hollywood's utopianism (per Dyer) with art-cinema social critique.

18.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
18.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md

19.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
19.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
19.relation: Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.

20.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
20.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
20.relation: Nelson argues that critics forget Soderbergh directed Erin Brockovich because they file his career under the art/commerce binary, and he uses Nietzsche's attack on the 'faith in antithetical values' and Derrida's deconstruction to expose such binaries (art/entertainment, independent/mainstream, activity/passivity) as gendered, hierarchical, and unstable. He then shows the film's real signature is a 'self-centered narration' totally focalized through Julia Roberts's Erin, so that a tension between the movie's altruistic content and its Erin-fixated form never resolves. The chapter treats the binary as a rhetorically useful but collapsing tool rather than a real opposition.

21.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
21.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
21.relation: Morton reads Schizopolis as Soderbergh's philosophical autobiography of identity, quoting Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding on memory as the ground of personal continuity to interpret Fletcher Munson's 'transmigration' into the doppelganger Dr. Korchek. Because Fletcher carries his own memory and nature into Korchek, he cannot escape his failed marriage (Korchek is sleeping with Fletcher's wife), confirming Lockean continuity: he 'cannot escape his own nature.' Morton ties the film's decayed language games and Elmo Oxygen's gibberish to a view that language masks action, and reads Fletcher's fate-frozen ending as identity surrendered to outside forces.

22.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
22.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md

23.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
23.file: ch23 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
23.relation: Sanders reads Soderbergh's HBO series K Street as a paranoid meditation on appearance and reality set in a Washington lobbying firm, where James Carville and Mary Matalin play fictionalized versions of themselves and the reclusive owner Richard Bergstrom manipulates everyone from afar while endlessly rewatching Mildred Pierce. Through three unresolved mysteries and a 'house of mirrors' structure, the show dramatizes the characters' skepticism about their capacity to know reality and Bergstrom's moral solipsism. Sanders argues Soderbergh's run-and-gun docudrama form itself enacts the epistemic uncertainty, leaving the text radically underdetermined about whether Bergstrom is a con man, a pawn, or a phantom-chasing paranoid.

24.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
24.file: ch24 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
24.relation: Sterritt 'schizoanalyzes' The Informant! by arguing that its lying protagonist Mark Whitacre, an ADM executive turned FBI informant, is a nut psychoanalysis cannot crack because he has no unconscious depth: his self is Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomatic, depthless flow of desire with 'nothing behind it' (echoing Warhol). He reads Mark's compulsive fabrication as deterritorialization against the corporation-as-psychopath, links the film to the Socratic unexamined life and to William James's open, flux-embracing empiricism (via Cassavetes), and interprets the climactic collision of Mark's voiceover and dialogue as the film itself intervening as the ultimate informant.

25.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
25.file: ch25 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
25.relation: Tait gives a Fredric Jameson-derived Marxist reading of Ocean's Eleven, treating Danny Ocean's heist crew as a utopian 'figure of collectivity' whose diverse, cross-class, pan-American membership recalls the WWII combat film and rallies against Terry Benedict as the polysemous 'monster' (Jameson's shark in Jaws) standing for globalized capital displacing nostalgic American Las Vegas. He argues the victimless heist allegorizes a competing value system in which love, solidarity, and friendship trump money, restaging class conflict from Asphalt Jungle, Rififi, and Big Deal on Madonna Street. The film's utopian happy ending imagines redistributing wealth and 'beating the house' within the very system of late capital it critiques.

26.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
26.file: ch26 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
26.relation: Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.

27.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
27.file: ch27 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md

28.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
28.file: ch28 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
28.relation: McFarland reads Soderbergh's Solaris as a meditation on recollection, recognition, and repetition, grounding it in Platonic recollection (the Phaedo, the cave, and the Symposium's love as desire) and Augustine's Confessions, where memory strains toward an elusive beloved-as-God, the 'cruel miracle' of present absence. When Solaris materializes Rheya, Chris Kelvin first jettisons the 'bad copy' but then, tempted by Snow, embraces Deleuze's endless degraded repetition of copies to erase his guilt over her suicide. Against this, Gibarian voices a Kierkegaardian call (Repetition, Either/Or) that there are 'only choices'; McFarland faults Chris, like Odysseus choosing Kalypso's island, for choosing the deathless eternal present over the human world of forward-moving choice.

29.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
29.file: ch29 - The Philosophy of Popular Culture.md
29.relation: Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.

5.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
5.file: ch05 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
5.relation: The editor's introduction frames the whole collection around three topics in Burton's corpus—identity, authority, and aesthetics—and previews each essay. On identity it contrasts an essentialist "core self" with an empirical, experience-built self, using Big Fish and Batman Returns as test cases; on authority it surveys Mars Attacks!, Sleepy Hollow, and Batman; on aesthetics it points to Sweeney Todd, death, and color. It functions as a roadmap that argues Burton's films merit philosophical reading rather than advancing one philosopher's thesis.

6.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
6.file: ch06 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md

7.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
7.file: ch07 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
7.relation: Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.

8.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
8.file: ch08 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
8.relation: Ryan Weldon reads Selina Kyle's transformation into Catwoman in Batman Returns through Sartre's existentialism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Pre-death Selina is Sartre's inauthentic 'waiter,' performing a servile secretary role in bad faith, and Beauvoir's objectified Other, defined by Max Shreck and the men who dismiss her. Her murder and feline resurrection free repressed drives, and her refusal of Batman's fairy-tale rescue—'I couldn't live with myself'—plus her choice to kill Shreck are cast as an assertion of facticity and transcendence, an authentic (if unfinished) self-creation that rejects the roles available to women rather than reaching a stable ending.

9.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
9.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
9.relation: Daniel Sullivan argues that Burton and Poe channel childhood 'ontological insecurity' (R. D. Laing) into horror fantasy, using Burton's short Vincent as case study. Seven-year-old Vincent Malloy, imagining himself as Vincent Price, escapes 'necessity's despair' into fantastic possibility but slides into what Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death calls defiant then demonic despair, clinging to a self-as-victim identity until he collapses. Sullivan reads fantasy as both consolation and danger—the flight into possibility further isolates the insecure child—and extends the possibility/necessity dialectic and Otto Rank's life/creation dialectic to Nightmare Before Christmas, Edward Scissorhands, and Big Fish.

10.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
10.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
10.relation: Mark Walling argues that the appeal of Burton-Depp characters lies in a recovered model of childhood consciousness. Against Freud's and Piaget's view that children perceive less and are locked in the here-and-now, Walling uses Alison Gopnik's cognitive science ('babies are more conscious than we are') and Rousseau's romantic ideal of the naturally good, untutored child to read Edward Scissorhands and Ed Wood. Edward is a naturally gifted, innocent artist destroyed by a corrupt suburban 'society'; Ed Wood, megaphone in hand, is 'an eight-year-old who wants to be a movie director,' whose inattentional, make-believe joy in filmmaking—not the finished product—embodies the wide, wondering child mind Burton celebrates.

11.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
11.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md

12.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
12.file: ch12 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
12.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.

13.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
13.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
13.relation: Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.

14.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
14.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
14.relation: Kevin S. Decker offers a 'philosophical hermeneutics' of Burton's Batman and Batman Returns, arguing that a long-lived cultural artifact like the Batman discloses a society's self-understanding. Using Heidegger's Dasein and 'working-out of possibilities,' Nietzsche's 'only interpretations,' and Gadamer's hermeneutic circle and fusion of horizons, Decker reads the shift from ABC's camp Adam West Batman to Burton's dark version as tracking cultural change (Vietnam, Watergate, 1980s decadence). He casts the Joker, Penguin, and Catwoman—and Batman himself—as Burton's recurring 'expressive outsider,' relating them to Nietzsche's Übermensch and Gotham's gullible crowds to Heidegger's das Man, and compares Burton's Expressionist Gotham to Max Beckmann's post-WWI Hell lithographs, positioning Burton as a prophet of modern decadence.

15.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
15.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
15.relation: Baltzer-Jaray uses Kant's phenomena/noumena split, Plato's Forms, and Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to ask whether Jack Skellington can know the essence of Christmas and whether Vincent Malloy can know what it is to BE Vincent Price. She argues Jack's lab-experiments on presents and snowflakes ('Jack's Obsession') can only yield phenomena, never the noumenal essence, so Kant would permit belief but not knowledge; Vincent, watching only Price's horror roles, grasps a mere phenomenal fragment. Via Nagel she concludes neither can occupy another's subjective viewpoint, so the lesson of both films is to celebrate otherness through communication rather than trying to be someone else.

16.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
16.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md

17.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
17.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
17.relation: Jenkins reads Burton's 'Sweeney Todd' (2007) through Edmund Burke's theory of the sublime and the device of synesthesia. She argues Burton relocates Burke's sublime from nature to the man-made, consuming city, staging beauty (Johanna, the flower-market flashbacks, saturated color) in losing tension with the 'dark and gloomy' urban sublime (desaturated Fleet Street, 'Epiphany'). Drawing on German Expressionist visual style (Caligari, Nosferatu) and the raindrop-to-blood credit sequence, she shows how sight, sound and represented taste (Mrs. Lovett's cannibal pies, the jugular-spray 'shooting star' during 'Johanna') mix the senses to force the queasy Burkean confrontation of terror and delight, ending in Burke's nihilistic darkness rather than redemption.

18.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
18.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
18.relation: Knight and McKnight apply Tzvetan Todorov's categories of 'the fantastic,' 'the uncanny,' and 'the marvelous' to the eight Burton films starring Johnny Depp, arguing that Burton treats the fantastic not as a genre but as a transgeneric film MODE that sustains the viewer's hesitation between natural and supernatural explanation. Using Wayne Booth's notion of the authorial 'second self,' they cast Depp as Burton's persona/surrogate who realizes and sustains that uncertainty (Edward, Ed Wood, Ichabod Crane, Willy Wonka, Sweeney, the Hatter). They classify 'Ed Wood' and 'Edward Scissorhands' as resolving into the uncanny (rationally explicable) and 'Sleepy Hollow,' 'Corpse Bride,' 'Alice in Wonderland,' and 'Dark Shadows' as passing into the marvelous, where new laws of nature must be accepted.

19.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
19.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
19.relation: McMahon argues Burton's death-saturated corpus functions as modern memento mori that fosters Heideggerian authenticity by arousing the uncanny and honest awareness of being-toward-death. She supplements Freud's account of the unheimliche (which she says wrongly substitutes castration anxiety for the primal fear of death) with Heidegger's link of angst, uncanniness, and finitude in 'Being and Time,' plus Terror Management Theory. Reading 'The Nightmare Before Christmas,' 'Corpse Bride,' and 'Dark Shadows,' she shows Jack, Bonejangles's Dance of Death, Emily, and vampire Barnabas use animation, comedy, and romance to make death palatable, and contrasts these films with Nozick's escapist experience machine—Burton supplements reality rather than replacing it.

20.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
20.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
20.relation: LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.

21.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
21.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
21.relation: Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.
