3.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of TV Noir
3.file: ch03 - An Introduction to the Philosophy of TV Noir.md
3.relation: Sanders's introduction argues that TV noir is an autonomous art form in which film noir's themes are aufgehoben (Hegel's term: preserved and transcended, not negated), and that noir television dramatizes philosophical questions about alienation, relativism, freedom, and meaning. He surveys the volume's arguments: Fitzgibbons on Naked City's conflation of the normal with the moral, Skoble's counterexample of moral clarity in The Fugitive (Richard Kimble), Lee's morally ambiguous John Drake in Secret Agent, and his own readings of Miami Vice's 'sunshine noir' and Crockett's merger with his undercover persona Sonny Burnett. He frames Part 2 through Sartre and Camus, contrasting their call for engagement and defiance with classic noir's passive doomed protagonists (D.O.A.'s Frank Bigelow, The Prisoner's Number 6), and applies Camus's man of revolt to Jack Bauer in 24. He also raises standing objections: Nagel's ironic alternative to Camus's scorn, the incoherence of 'nothing matters' applied to Tony Soprano, and the Foucault/Lyotard-style postmodern critique of institutional power he finds in Crime Story.

4.title: Part 1: Realism, Relativism, and Moral Ambiguity
4.file: ch04 - Part 1 Realism, Relativism, and Moral Ambiguity.md

5.title: Dragnet, Film Noir, and Postwar Realism
5.file: ch05 - Dragnet, Film Noir, and Postwar Realism.md
5.relation: Palmer argues that Dragnet's famous realism was forged from the noir semidocumentary (The House on 92nd Street, He Walked by Night, with its diabolical killer Roy Martin hunted through the LA sewers) and from the era's taste for Italian neorealism (Open City, The Bicycle Thief, The Men), but that Jack Webb deliberately inverted the noir formula. Where the semidocumentaries split their focus between dedicated police and charismatic monsters, Webb eliminated expressionist stylization and hard-boiled wisecracks to center 'a quiet, dedicated policeman... one little cog in a great enforcement machine.' The chapter details Dragnet's imitative realism as a fidelity to real things: actual case files, LAPD technical advisors, plaster casts of police-station doorknobs, Friday's date-and-time narration, the 'The story you are about to see is true' preamble, and mug-shot endings with sentences read aloud. This yields not noir's fascination with the perverse but a social realism that rhetorically affirms law, institutions, and inevitable conviction, complicating the standard story of 1950s television's aesthetic decline.

6.title: Naked City: The Relativist Turn in TV Noir
6.file: ch06 - Naked City The Relativist Turn in TV Noir.md
6.relation: Fitzgibbons argues that when The Naked City became the hour-long Naked City in 1960, TV noir underwent a 'relativist turn': episodes like 'Ooftus Goofus,' 'To Walk Like a Lion' (Arnold Platt's sympathetic embezzlement), and 'Memory of a Red Trolley Car' (Professor Johns, who refuses to save his own life) conflate the normal with the moral and leave viewers wondering whether conventionally wrong choices 'might not have been right in some way.' He traces this message to Ruth Benedict's cultural relativism, reconstructs her difference argument (from varying moral codes, as with Protagoras's 'man is the measure') and her conceptual argument (morality as socially approved habits), and shows both are invalid, the latter resting on the false assumption that 'morality' has one real definition. He then presses three objections to cultural relativism, including that its anti-ethnocentrism claim is a disguised absolute moral claim, making the position inconsistent, and that determining cultural membership collapses it into individual relativism, which licenses absurd conclusions like a moral right to rob and kill on Tuesdays.

7.title: John Drake in Greeneland: Noir Themes in Secret Agent
7.file: ch07 - John Drake in Greeneland Noir Themes in Secret Agent.md
7.relation: Lee argues that Secret Agent belongs to the Graham Greene noir tradition of The Ministry of Fear and The Third Man, not Bond escapism: Drake never kills, carries no gun, and refuses romantic entanglement, because McGoohan prized realism and ethical seriousness. Readings of Greene's Stephen Neale (who killed his wife out of pity) and Harry Lime's Ferris-wheel nihilism establish a world 'void of meaning, haphazard, and morally indifferent,' which Drake's episodes then dramatize: in 'It's Up to the Lady' his superior Hobbs (named, Lee contends, for Thomas Hobbes, whose Leviathan and war of all against all the essay explicates) betrays Drake's promised word and has the defector Charles arrested; in 'That's Two of Us Sorry' Drake unwittingly plays the villain, ruining an innocent Scottish village; in 'Judgement Day' he cannot say what justice for the Nazi scientist Garriga requires. Lee concludes that Drake, like Neale and Martins, acts in Sartrean bad faith by continuing to serve morally bankrupt masters, and that Greene's only exits are a Kierkegaardian leap of faith Drake never makes, or fantasized retirement and death.

8.title: Action and Integrity in The Fugitive
8.file: ch08 - Action and Integrity in The Fugitive.md
8.relation: Skoble challenges the standard view of noir as morally ambiguous, arguing each episode of The Fugitive is a self-contained morality play in which Richard Kimble makes tough decisions by clearly defined standards of right and wrong. He tests ethical frameworks against the episodes: Kant's categorical imperative cannot capture Kimble, who lies in every episode to survive, whereas Aristotle's virtue ethics explains his trained emotional responses, as when he tells the migrant workers in 'Ill Wind' 'For a doctor, every life is worth saving' while saving Lieutenant Gerard from a pitchfork, and again in 'Corner of Hell' from moonshiners. Kimble's integrity, understood as fidelity in action to principles reached through reflection, reconciles his lawbreaking with his morality and, via Plato's account in the Republic of the just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself,' constitutes the psychological wholeness that sustains his four-year quest. The essay closes with the finale, where Kimble clears his name, Gerard kills the one-armed man, and Kimble finally walks in sunlight.

9.title: Part 2: Existentialism, Nihilism, and the Meaning of Life
9.file: ch09 - Part 2 Existentialism, Nihilism, and the Meaning of Life.md

10.title: Noir et Blanc in Color: Existentialism and Miami Vice
10.file: ch10 - Noir et Blanc in Color Existentialism and Miami Vice.md
10.relation: Sanders reads Miami Vice as existentialist 'sunshine noir,' where color and pastel locations carry noir alienation, and Crockett and Tubbs live rootless lives with shambles of romances and a culturally impoverished compass (Bolt, Buddy Holly, Buffett, Beckett, Betts). The episode 'No Exit' (Bruce Willis as arms dealer Tony Amato, whose wife Rita shoots him at the courthouse steps) is analyzed through Sartre's being-in-itself/being-for-itself conflict and 'hell is other people,' from which Danto says 'there is no exit.' 'Heart of Darkness' presents Ed O'Neill's undercover FBI agent Arthur Lawson, who prefers his Artie Rollins persona and hangs himself after debriefing, as a failure of authenticity and flight into bad faith that Crockett recognizes as his own peril as Sonny Burnett. Crockett's amnesia arc ('Mirror Image' through 'Redemption in Blood' and 'Bad Timing'), where he believes he is Burnett working for the Manolo organization, is resolved through Sartrean existential recognition and a freely chosen dangerous mission that restores his identity, since the Kierkegaardian leap of faith is unavailable in the show's secular world; Sanders also attacks Sartre's sanction of revolutionary violence in his preface to Fanon and Beauvoir's defense of Sade.

11.title: 24 and the Existential Man of Revolt
11.file: ch11 - 24 and the Existential Man of Revolt.md
11.relation: McMahon argues that 24 is genuine TV noir (crime focus, cynical tone, split screens, the femmes fatale Nina Myers and Sherry Palmer, Jack's heroin addiction as his internal demon) and that Jack Bauer is Camus's man of revolt. She lays out Camus's account of the absurd as the confrontation between our appetite for clarity and the world's unreasonable silence, rejects actual and 'philosophical suicide' as evasions, and maps Jack onto the man of revolt's defining traits: lucidity (his refusal to trust appearances, as when only he suspects President Logan of corruption and murder) and courage (risking nerve-gas exposure at CTU and entering the gas-plant fire). The terrorist threats Jack fights symbolize the absurd because their success, from Palmer's assassination to citywide nerve gas, would annihilate order and meaning themselves; as Camus's 'conqueror,' Jack employs violence reluctantly, without appetite for it, to establish non-violence, accepting a crushing fate without resignation.

12.title: Carnivale Knowledge: Give Me That Old-time Noir Religion
12.file: ch12 - Carnivale Knowledge Give Me That Old-time Noir Religion.md
12.relation: Eric Bronson argues that Carnivale invents a 'religious noir' tradition in which Brother Justin's crisis of faith in the Dust Bowl 1930s replays the Christian existentialism of Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky. Sitting in the ruins of his burnt church, Justin recites Genesis 22 (the sacrifice of Isaac) and demands God explain why his orphans died, directly invoking Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: faith is impossible and absurd, and the crushing struggle itself makes life worth living. Ivan Karamazov's 'returning the ticket' over the suffering of children parallels Justin's fury at a silent God, while the carnies' Babylon storyline (Samson sparing the confessed killer under the carnival code, then secretly shooting him) and the inescapable dead souls echo Sartre's 'condemned to life' and the noir hero's inability to escape fate.

13.title: The Sopranos, Film Noir, and Nihilism
13.file: ch13 - The Sopranos, Film Noir, and Nihilism.md
13.relation: Kevin Stoehr reads The Sopranos as TV noir built on Nietzsche's passive, life-negating nihilism: Tony Soprano's 'What do we got?' laments the collapse of mob and family values, Uncle Junior's 'Each of us is alone in the fuckin' universe' voices noir alienation, and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' is the series' nihilistic creed. A.J.'s confirmation-eve rebellion reading Nietzsche and Camus's The Stranger ('Death just shows the ultimate absurdity of life') dramatizes the death of God inherited by the next generation. The chapter's dark irony is that therapy, meant to give Tony narrative unity and self-knowledge, becomes an instrument of self-deception: he substitutes psychology for ethics, rationalizes adultery and murder as signs of psychic power, and fails at Nietzschean self-overcoming despite the ducks and Pie-O-My that briefly symbolize transcendence.

14.title: Part 3: Crime Scene Investigation and the Logic of Detection
14.file: ch14 - Part 3 Crime Scene Investigation and the Logic of Detection.md

15.title: CSI and the Art of Forensic Detection
15.file: ch15 - CSI and the Art of Forensic Detection.md
15.relation: Knight and McKnight analyze CSI as 'procedural noir': Las Vegas instantiates the corrupt-city trope, and the show's methodological core is reading scientific evidence as a system of signs, generating and testing hypotheses through hypothetical flash reconstructions (Grissom's wrong incest-guess in 'Blood Drops', competing crash theories in 'Anonymous'). Three case studies carry the philosophy: Philip Gerard's defense attack on the team's competence makes forensic investigation an ethical matter of integrity and reliable process rather than mere evidence collection; the Paul Millander trilogy uses the trope of the double (Paul/Pauline, Judge Mason, the forged Grissom identity) to explore identity and self-knowledge; and Lady Heather's dominance-submission 'stop' convention reframes the femme fatale around reason, passion, and Grissom's desire to be known.

16.title: Detection and the Logic of Abduction in The X-Files
16.file: ch16 - Detection and the Logic of Abduction in The X-Files.md
16.relation: Abrams and Cooke map Mulder and Scully onto Holmes and Watson and onto the Clifford-James debate: Scully embodies Clifford's ethics of belief (suspend judgment without hard evidence), while Mulder's 'I Want to Believe' poster enacts James's will to believe, which lets him see what the paradigm excludes. The chapter formalizes both agents' actual method as Peirce's logic of abduction, using Eco's overcoded/undercoded/creative triad to analyze Scully's Fowley clothing inference and the mushroom episodes of 'Field Trip', and extends Peircean semiotics with Mulder's 'absence sign' (the missing nine minutes, missing acid burns, bodies taken without a trace). Kuhn's normal science versus revolution explains why Scully stays inside the FBI's paradigm while Mulder's passion makes him the revolutionary who, with Scully as error-corrector, fuses into a single 'whole person' detective facing the limits of reason.

17.title: Part 4: Autonomy, Selfhood, and Interpretation
17.file: ch17 - Part 4 Autonomy, Selfhood, and Interpretation.md

18.title: Kingdom of Darkness: Autonomy and Conspiracy in The X-Files and Millennium
18.file: ch18 - Kingdom of Darkness Autonomy and Conspiracy in The X-Files and Millennium.md
18.relation: Michael Valdez Moses reads The X-Files and Millennium as post-Cold War noir that depicts America as Foucault's carceral archipelago: nearly every character works for the state, Tocquevillian voluntary association has withered ('they don't go bowling at all'), and the FBI's landscape of prisons, clinics, and bases makes free space scarce. Against Hobbes's Leviathan, the chapter mobilizes Locke and Paine's classical liberalism (government as necessary evil securing pre-existing natural rights) to show that Carter's heroes are 'antipolitical' resisters: Frank Black's visions and the Grill Flame remote viewers make him a panoptical spy for the state, while Mulder's warrantless searches blur sovereign and criminal justice into one corrupt system, as in the Millennium episode 'The Judge'. The neo-noir conspiracy seeks not profit but absolute sovereignty, and the series end with Mulder, Scully, and Black as fugitives fleeing the state with their families, resisting Nietzsche's 'coldest of all cold monsters'.

19.title: The Prisoner and Self-Imprisonment
19.relation: Biderman and Devlin use The Prisoner to test three dimensions of selfhood: Number 6's 'I am not a number!' defends the material self against the Village's conformity (Rover, uniforms, human chess pieces), his reflective self echoes Descartes's certain thinking thing, Kant's rational self-legislation, and Sartrean authenticity ('existence precedes essence'), while the finale's trial of the rebels addresses the relational self. The revelation that Number 6 is Number 1 is then read through Foucault: hierarchical observation, normalization, and examination make the Village Bentham's panopticon internalized, so the prisoner monitors himself and the ideal of a freely self-created identity collapses into social conditioning, as Nietzsche's herd come home. The chapter leaves the noir ambiguity intact: either Number 6 is the authentic individual vindicated by the Village council, or the self is a fiction and his odyssey hopeless.

20.title: Twin Peaks, Noir, and Open Interpretation
20.file: ch20 - Twin Peaks, Noir, and Open Interpretation.md
20.relation: Jason Holt catalogs Twin Peaks' noir elements (the Laura Palmer quest narrative, Cooper's voiceover Dictaphone, femmes fatales, low-key lighting, the existential mood leavened by absurd humor in the manner of Camus) but argues the series is merely noirish, not noir, because it refuses noir's hard-boiled naturalistic metaphysics. The decisive case is BOB: the post-Leland dialogue between Cooper, Truman, and Albert stages the choice between reducing BOB to Leland's psychopathology and reifying him as a real malevolent spirit from the Black Lodge, and the show deliberately leaves the fictional ontology of BOB undecidable, in Todorov's 'fantastic' between the natural and supernatural. This interpretive openness (compared to The Prisoner's Number 1 revelation and the psychological indeterminacy of Sam Spade's motives in The Maltese Falcon) is defended as aesthetically desirable via Holt's 'omissive' aesthetic, the art of leaving important things out.

6.title: Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War
6.file: ch06 - Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War.md
6.relation: LaRocca argues that a war film can never be war itself but only a mediated, post-facto fabrication, and reads the camera and the gun as twinned instruments ('point and shoot' becoming digital 'point and click' in Skyfall). He mobilizes Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' to describe war video games and CGI spectacle (Avatar, Call of Duty) as hyperreal simulacra, and Freud's 'Why War?' letter and death instinct to explain the compulsive proliferation of war representation. Foucault ('peace is a coded war'), Heraclitus ('war is father of all'), and Isaiah Berlin's plurality of incompatible values frame war's ineffability and perpetuity, while Cavell's ontology of film grounds the viewer's 'mechanically assured' helplessness before on-screen dying bodies.

7.title: Part 1. The Aesthetics of War On-Screen
7.file: ch07 - Part 1. The Aesthetics of War On-Screen.md

8.title: War and Representation
8.relation: Jameson contends that war poses the 'nominalist dilemma'—the gap between abstract totality and sensory immediacy—making it ultimately unrepresentable, and enumerates eight recurring narrative situations (existential, collective, leaders, technology, landscape, atrocity, homeland attack, occupation). Using Burke's dramatistic pentad he argues the war narrative drifts from 'act/agent' toward 'scene,' where the anthropomorphic dissolves; Sartre's 'groups-in-fusion' and Deleuze's nomadic war machine model the collective buddy-squad, whose division of labor he compares to the heist film. Reading Grimmelshausen's Simplicissimus and Döblin's Wallenstein against Kluge's Stalingrad and Halberstadt collages, he shows war (from the Thirty Years' War to WWII aerial bombing) generating a rhizomatic, nonnarrative flow that defeats stable narrative convention.

9.title: War Pictures Digital Surveillance from Foreign Theater to Homeland Security Front
9.file: ch09 - War Pictures Digital Surveillance from Foreign Theater to Homeland Security Front.md
9.relation: Stewart argues that War on Terror films (Redacted, Battle for Haditha, The Situation, In the Valley of Elah, Waltz with Bashir) depict 'a soldiery without a genre' because digital surveillance has fused sighting and triggering, so combat is nowhere and everywhere and the classic movement-image spectacle collapses. Drawing on Deleuze's movement-image/time-image distinction, he recasts the soldier as spectator (SSS' rather than SAS'), watching under the panoptic drone eye rather than acting, and shows sci-fi 'temportation' thrillers (Déjà Vu, Source Code, Eagle Eye) travestying the time-image into computerized wish-fulfillment. The Hurt Locker succeeds precisely by reverting to a man-vs-machine 'duel,' while Waltz with Bashir alone achieves genuine political reframing by breaking from animation into archival massacre footage.

10.title: Lenses into War Digital Vérité in Iraq War Films
10.file: ch10 - Lenses into War Digital Vérité in Iraq War Films.md
10.relation: Peebles defends the 'digital vérité' of Iraq War films (Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, The Battle for Haditha, Redacted, Standard Operating Procedure) against Garrett Stewart's charge that grainy embedded footage elides critique, arguing instead that the multiplying lenses close the distance between soldier and viewer to build empathy. She invokes Baudrillard's 'the Gulf War did not take place' to show how CNN's video-game-like distance erased the common soldier, which the up-close soldier-shot cell-phone image corrects. Reading Hank Deerfield's reconstruction of his son's fatal Humvee incident in Elah and Errol Morris's reframing of the Abu Ghraib photos in Standard Operating Procedure, she argues each frame is 'both an aperture and a restriction,' and that these tragedies are inherently antiwar.

11.title: Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film
11.file: ch11 - Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film.md
11.relation: Gooch argues that the post-2005 surveillance film cycle moves 'beyond panopticism': Foucault's disciplinary gaze gives way to Deleuze's 'societies of control,' and the surveiling gaze becomes direct domination and a form of biopolitical labor (Hardt and Negri) rather than an impersonal structure. He reads the prestige dramas (Redacted, Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs) as exposing the soldier's proletarianization and self-surveillance, and the thrillers/blockbusters (Déjà Vu, The Kingdom, Body of Lies, The Bourne Ultimatum, Eagle Eye, Burn after Reading) as staging a Marxist antagonism between living labor (the watching hero) and the fixed capital of surveillance technology. Using Deleuze's 'degraded time-image,' Kant's needed separation of subject and law, and Benjamin/Agamben's state of exception, he shows Eagle Eye inverting law and subject to justify preemptive war and turn biopolitical labor into the labor of subjection.

12.title: Seeing Soldiers, Seeing Persons Wittgenstein, Film Theory, and Charlie Chaplin’s Shoulder Arms
12.file: ch12 - Seeing Soldiers, Seeing Persons Wittgenstein, Film Theory, and Charlie Chaplin’s Shoulder Arms.md
12.relation: Hilsabeck argues that Wittgenstein's notion of aspect perception ("seeing as") is not a phenomenology of illusion, as film theorists like Allen and Turvey take it, but an ethical matter of articulating experience within forms of life and language games. He reads Chaplin's Shoulder Arms through this lens: Doughboy's tree-disguise gag and his repurposing of war objects (Limburger cheese as grenade, gramophone horn as snorkel) demonstrate imaginative, ethical vision, while the German soldier who cannot see the tree-as-man exhibits "aspect blindness." The film makes viewers' willingness to "see anew" a test of attunement and mutual acknowledgment, casting the environment of WWI trench warfare and mechanized shock as what stifles this imaginative seeing.

13.title: Part 2. War as Condition of Self-Formation and Self-Dissolution
13.file: ch13 - Part 2. War as Condition of Self-Formation and Self-Dissolution.md

14.title: Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity
14.file: ch14 - Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity.md
14.relation: Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.

15.title: The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty
15.file: ch15 - The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty.md
15.relation: Burgoyne argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty places the violated body at the center of its rendering of the War on Terror, using somatic intensity and affective experience against Steven Shaviro's reading of the film as pure, affect-draining proceduralism. He traces Maya's arc from witness to coercive agent through the torture of Ammar, the Goya-like montage of interrogation videos, and the suicide-bomb killing of her friend Jessica, mapping the film onto Sarah Cole's poles of disenchanted violence (the raw, exposed flesh of the interrogations) and enchanted violence (the technologically choreographed, almost magical SEAL raid on Abbottabad, likened to Baudrillardian simulated combat). The closing unzipping of bin Laden's body bag deflates any triumph into embodied ambiguity.

16.title: “All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March
16.file: ch16 - “All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March.md
16.relation: Rhu reads Ross McElwee's Sherman's March—ostensibly a documentary about Sherman's Civil War campaign but really about a heartbroken filmmaker's search for love amid Cold War nuclear dread—through Walker Percy's The Last Gentleman and Stanley Cavell's The World Viewed. He shows how the film enacts Cavell's ontology of film (viewing the world "from behind the self," movies as reliefs from private fantasy) and the dialogue between perfectionism and skepticism Cavell draws from Emerson's "Experience" and Nietzsche and Kierkegaard. McElwee's deliberately unpolished, self-conscious "personal documentary"—stumbling on the riverbank, leaving in his own second thoughts—turns the war film into a meditation on consciousness, mediation, and being "all in war with Time."

17.title: The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki
17.file: ch17 - The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki.md
17.relation: Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.

18.title: Part 3. The Ethical Tribulations of War
18.file: ch18 - Part 3. The Ethical Tribulations of War.md

19.title: The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films
19.file: ch19 - The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films.md
19.relation: Pötzsch uses cognitive film theory (Murray Smith's alignment and allegiance, paradigm scenarios and schemata) to argue that Beaufort, Waltz with Bashir, and Lebanon, though hailed as antiwar films, covertly reinforce a militarist "scopic regime" through the "ubiquitously absent enemy." Formal devices—the tank scope's tunnel vision in Lebanon, shot/reverse-shot and voice-over confined to Israeli soldiers, the animated flashbacks of Waltz with Bashir—align and ally viewers exclusively with Israeli troops framed as helpless victims, while the Palestinian other stays faceless, voiceless, and objectified (the staggering Lebanese woman, the trauma displaced onto dead dogs and horses). Drawing on Judith Butler's frames of war and "ungrievable" lives, he reads this as Kimmerling's latent cognitive militarism that denies the enemy's competing subjectivity and forecloses nonviolent alternatives.

20.title: General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War
20.file: ch20 - General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War.md
20.relation: Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.

21.title: The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty
21.file: ch21 - The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty.md
21.relation: Evans argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty fails morally and epistemically because its immersive 'boots-on-the-ground' realism traps the viewer inside Maya's single point of view, so we can never see the CIA torture program's lunacy the way an outside witness would. Drawing on Wittgenstein's Tractatus claim that the subject is a limit of the world (the eye that cannot see itself), she shows how the film effaces its own privileged viewpoint to pass off a partial view as impartial reality. Against this she sets a Platonic point that genuine reality is glimpsed only through fiction that ironically juxtaposes contrasting viewpoints, citing scenes like the SEALs' banter and Maya's final weeping where the film briefly becomes true art. The 'depiction is not endorsement' defense collapses because the narrative logic still credits torture with finding bin Laden.

22.title: Part 4. War, Nature, and the Absolute
22.file: ch22 - Part 4. War, Nature, and the Absolute.md

23.title: Vernacular Metaphysics On Terrence Malick’s The Thin Red Line
23.file: ch23 - Vernacular Metaphysics On Terrence Malick’s The Thin Red Line.md
23.relation: Pippin reads Malick's The Thin Red Line as deliberately invoking then refusing Hollywood war-movie conventions (group solidarity, trackable characters, heroic assault) so the viewer is left 'lost' and forced toward a metaphysical rather than political or sentimental reckoning with death. Through unattributed poetic voice-overs—Train's Manichean questions, Witt's search for the calm 'immortality' he saw in his dying mother, Welsh's cynicism, Bell's romantic idealism—and lingering non-plot shots of nature bathed in sunlight, the film pursues a 'vernacular metaphysics': ordinary soldiers straining ordinary speech to ask what it is to live under certain death. Pippin aligns this disclosive, prediscursive truth of the image with the Hegel-to-Heidegger-Merleau-Ponty tradition of art as truth-bearer, while Witt's Emersonian 'one big soul' and his self-sacrifice ('all things shining') stage the film's unresolved question of whether nature and death can be seen as good.

24.title: War and Its Fictional Recovery On-Screen Narrative Management of Death in The Big Red One and The Thin Red Lin
24.file: ch24 - War and Its Fictional Recovery On-Screen Narrative Management of Death in The Big Red One and The Thin Red Lin.md
24.relation: Bronfen takes Freud's 'Thoughts for the Times on War and Death' (life 'recovers its full content' when war forces us to believe in death) and his theory of the death drive and the uncanny double as a template for how war films manage mortality through fiction. In Fuller's The Big Red One, the nameless Sergeant's guilt-driven distinction between killing and murder, his Nazi double Schroeder, and the compulsively repeated stabbing scene at the crucifix let the hero convert contingent slaughter into a restitutive story where survival is 'the only glory,' echoing Freud's Eros–Thanatos struggle. In Malick's The Thin Red Line, Private Witt splits not into warlike and peacetime selves but into bodily and spiritual presence, embracing death as transcendence into 'shining light' that doubles the light of cinema itself. Both films strike a pact with the viewer, who dies with the heroes yet safely survives them.

25.title: “Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films
25.file: ch25 - “Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films.md
25.relation: LaRocca argues against Thomas Weiskel that the 'humanistic sublime' is not an oxymoron, using Herzog's war films (Lessons of Darkness, Little Dieter Needs to Fly, Rescue Dawn) to show a sublime that returns us to the human at the limit of existence rather than transcending it. Building on Kant's link between the sublime and human dignity—and Kant's claim that sublimity lies in our ideas, not in nature—he reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' (fabrication that exceeds the 'accountant's truth') as the vehicle: staged monologues, borrowed music, and recontextualized documentary footage disclose an inner reality. Herzog's Heideggerian gloss on aletheia as un-concealment aligns cinema itself with truth, and Dengler's bear ('the only friend I had was death') exemplifies war as the space of radical mortality where the humanistic sublime dawns for the safe spectator, contrasted with Malick's more Darwinian, nature-indifferent vision.

26.title: Acknowledgments
26.file: ch26 - Acknowledgments.md

27.title: Appendix. The Multifarious Forms of War Films A Taxonomy of Subgenres
27.file: ch27 - Appendix. The Multifarious Forms of War Films A Taxonomy of Subgenres.md

5.title: Introduction Philosophy and the Western
5.file: ch05 - Introduction Philosophy and the Western.md
5.relation: McMahon and Csaki's introduction argues that the western and philosophy are joined through the mimetic theory of art (the western as a mirror of frontier history) and through shared interest in identity, community, and morality. It frames the volume's four parts and previews each essay, noting that canonical western tropes trace back to Plato and Aristotle and that films like High Noon, Shane, and The Searchers dramatize abstract philosophical theories. It treats the western as an unexplored 'frontier' for philosophic analysis rather than defending one thesis of its own.

6.title: Part 1 The Cowboy Way The Essence of the Western Hero
6.file: ch06 - Part 1 The Cowboy Way The Essence of the Western Hero.md

7.title: “Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns
7.file: ch07 - “Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns.md
7.relation: Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.

8.title: Civilization and Its Discontents The Self-Sufficient Western Hero
8.file: ch08 - Civilization and Its Discontents The Self-Sufficient Western Hero.md
8.relation: Den Uyl builds a composite philosophic picture of self-sufficiency from Aristotle's autarkeia (reason-guided virtuous activity, requiring external goods and civilization) and Spinoza's freedom as acting from one's own nature guided by adequate ideas, then tests it on John Ford's heroes. In The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, Tom Doniphon is 'procedurally' self-sufficient in the precivilized West while Ransom Stoddard embodies civilized reason, and neither can inhabit the other's world. He argues the western's deepest value is Emersonian self-reliance—fidelity to one's own unique nature (the 'cactus rose')—which civilization threatens even as it enables Aristotelian flourishing.

9.title: Mommas, Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Pragmatists
9.file: ch09 - Mommas, Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Pragmatists.md
9.relation: Csaki argues that John Wayne became the ultimate cinematic cowboy because his characters embody classical American pragmatism. Using William James's squirrel-and-tree parable and Dewey's account of 'inquiry' transforming an indeterminate situation, he reads Rooster Cogburn's split-second raft decision and Wil Anderson's hiring of schoolboys in The Cowboys as pragmatic problem-solving from experience. He treats the 'code of the West' not as fixed absolutes but as rules applied pragmatically (Rooster shooting men in the back, the cowboys letting Long Hair be dragged to death), where truth is what can be assimilated, verified, and made to 'work.'

10.title: Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma
10.file: ch10 - Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma.md
10.relation: Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.

11.title: Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad
11.file: ch11 - Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad.md
11.relation: Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).

12.title: Part 2 The Code of the West The Cowboy and Society
12.file: ch12 - Part 2 The Code of the West The Cowboy and Society.md

13.title: “Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature
13.file: ch13 - “Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature.md
13.relation: Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.

14.title: Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West
14.file: ch14 - Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West.md
14.relation: Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.

15.title: From Dollars to Iron The Currency of Clint Eastwood's Westerns
15.file: ch15 - From Dollars to Iron The Currency of Clint Eastwood's Westerns.md
15.relation: McNaron traces Clint Eastwood's evolving western hero from the amoral 'Man with No Name' to The Outlaw Josey Wales, using Will Wright's plot typology plus Nietzsche, Aristotle, and Kierkegaard. He reads the Eastwood antihero's 'manly nihilism' and prizing of strength and style through Nietzsche's master/slave morality and perspectivism, his virtues (self-control, phronesis) through Aristotle, and his elevation of the aesthetic over the ethical/religious against Kierkegaard's stages. The film's central claim—that only words with 'iron' behind them (Josey and Ten Bears's pact) can found genuine community, unlike government's 'double tongues'—grounds a transcendental argument about the conditions for authentic community and justified vengeance.

16.title: The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon
16.file: ch16 - The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon.md
16.relation: Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.

18.title: The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident
18.file: ch18 - The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident.md
18.relation: Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.

19.title: “Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch
19.file: ch19 - “Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch.md
19.relation: Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.

20.title: No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)
20.file: ch20 - No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern).md
20.relation: William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'

21.title: The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller
21.file: ch21 - The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller.md
21.relation: Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.

22.title: Part 4 On the Fringe The Encounter with the Other
22.file: ch22 - Part 4 On the Fringe The Encounter with the Other.md

23.title: Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western
23.file: ch23 - Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western.md
23.relation: Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.

24.title: Regeneration through Stories and Song The View from the Other Side of the West in Smoke Signals
24.file: ch24 - Regeneration through Stories and Song The View from the Other Side of the West in Smoke Signals.md
24.relation: Richard Gilmore reads Smoke Signals—the first feature written, directed, and coproduced by Native Americans—against Slotkin's myth of regeneration through violence, arguing it offers regeneration through stories and song instead. Drawing on Wilshire's claim that pragmatism is 'aboriginal,' he links Emerson and Thoreau's transcendentalism and Peirce's 'law of mind' to Deloria's American Indian metaphysics and Hyde's gift economy: Arlene's fry-bread story and Thomas's storytelling repair broken relationships, and Victor's final act of forgiving his father (and withholding that Arnold caused the fatal fire) is read as the film's central gift, completing relationships that violence had severed.

25.title: Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films
25.file: ch25 - Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films.md
25.relation: Gary Heba and Robin Murphy map women's identities in westerns onto Hegel's three-stage dialectic (aufheben as maintain/negate/transform), grafting on Bakhtin's monoglossic/heteroglossic discourse and Mulvey's and de Beauvoir's feminist film theory. Settler women (Marian in Shane, the mothers of The Searchers) are monoglossic—silenced, family-bound bearers of meaning; town women (Mrs. French in Appaloosa, Lily in How the West Was Won) are heteroglossic, sexualized spectacles marked by costume; and post-1970s figures like Ellen in The Quick and the Dead and Sara in Two Mules for Sister Sara become 'x-glossic,' transformational identities that subvert the male-gaze code and exceed the settler/town binary.

26.title: Beating a Live Horse The Elevation and Degradation of Horses in Westerns
26.file: ch26 - Beating a Live Horse The Elevation and Degradation of Horses in Westerns.md
26.relation: Jennifer L. McMahon gives an existential account of Americans' ambivalence toward horses in westerns: because horses mirror human anxiety, herd-boundness, and the flight instinct that Sartre and Heidegger locate at the core of being, we transfer our self-loathing onto them and, driven by Nietzsche's will to power and Hegel's lord-and-bondsman struggle for recognition, we break them to prove our own mastery. Reading breaking scenes in All the Pretty Horses and The Horse Whisperer via Foucault's Discipline and Punish (the round pen as panopticon producing 'docile bodies'), she contrasts films like Hidalgo and The Electric Horseman that model Hegelian reciprocity, urging us to 'let go, turn in, and hook on' rather than dominate.

7.title: Introduction
7.relation: Kowalski's editorial introduction previews all three sections of the volume, framing the collection around the idea that philosophy is something one 'does' and that Spielberg's films (from Jaws to A.I., Schindler's List, Amistad, Munich, and Minority Report) raise questions in ethics, aesthetics, mind, and political philosophy. It names each contributor's thesis rather than arguing an original one, and closes by posing the meta-question of whether popular film can itself 'do' philosophy.

8.title: Part I Philosophy, the Filmmaker, and the Human Condition
8.file: ch08 - Part I Philosophy, the Filmmaker, and the Human Condition.md

9.title: The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence
9.file: ch09 - The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence.md
9.relation: Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'

10.title: The Recovery of Childhood and the Search for the Absent Father
10.file: ch10 - The Recovery of Childhood and the Search for the Absent Father.md
10.relation: Le Gall and Taliaferro read E.T., Hook, and the Indiana Jones trilogy through a Socratic-Platonic ideal in which the true 'adventure' ends not in glory (kleos) but in homecoming, beauty, and restored parent-child love. Indiana abandons the grail to grab his father's hand and hears 'Indiana' instead of 'Junior'; Elliott becomes a father to E.T. while E.T. teaches him loss; Peter Banning must recover his Pan-childhood to save his kids. They tie this to the Republic's Myth of Er, the Symposium's ladder of love, and xenia (hospitality) as the setting for wisdom.

11.title: Levinasian Ethics of Alterity The Face of the Other in Spielberg’s Cinematic Language
11.file: ch11 - Levinasian Ethics of Alterity The Face of the Other in Spielberg’s Cinematic Language.md
11.relation: Wright argues that Spielberg's cinematic language (shot scale, montage editing, mise-en-scene) enacts Levinas's ethics of alterity, in which meeting the unknowable 'face' of the Other demands responsibility and sacrifice, wisdom through love rather than knowledge. He contrasts the distancing long shots that render the Jaws shark and The Thing as mere threats with the intimate close-ups that 'reveal the face' in Close Encounters and E.T., then shows Schindler's List turning the same technique onto the human Other, using the red coat as the face that pulls Schindler from detachment into responsibility.

12.title: The Paradox of Fictional Belief and Its Moral Implications in Jaws
12.file: ch12 - The Paradox of Fictional Belief and Its Moral Implications in Jaws.md
12.relation: Trogan and Kowalski use Jaws to pose the paradox of fiction: we feel real fear and pity for Chrissie, the Kintners, and Quint though we know they are not real. They rehearse Radford's charge that such emotions are incoherent (since based on false belief) and answer it with a cognitivist 'unasserted thought' account and Kendall Walton's theory of make-believe, arguing we self-consciously enter the film as an adult game. Drawing on Nussbaum, they claim appropriate emotional response to Jaws cultivates empathy and 'seeing,' honing ethical sensitivity rather than turning adults into children.

13.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence and the Tragic Sense of Life
13.file: ch13 - A.I. Artificial Intelligence and the Tragic Sense of Life.md
13.relation: Dunn interprets A.I. as a meditation on the 'tragic sense of life': treating David as a person, he argues the film dramatizes three doomed human desires (love, uniqueness, immortality) and tests two failed escapes from mortality, science (Professor Hobby, the Flesh Fair, David's suicide leap) and religious faith (the fraudulent Blue Fairy at drowned Coney Island). Defending the maligned finale, he reads the simulated Blue Fairy and the one-day resurrection of Monica as raising whether a perfect simulation of love can be 'real enough,' with David achieving a sober humanistic acceptance of impermanence.

14.title: Part II Values, Virtue, and Justice
14.file: ch14 - Part II Values, Virtue, and Justice.md

15.title: What Is Wrong with Cloning a Dinosaur Jurassic Park and Nature as a Source of Moral Authority
15.file: ch15 - What Is Wrong with Cloning a Dinosaur Jurassic Park and Nature as a Source of Moral Authority.md
15.relation: Spence uses the Hammond-Malcolm debate in Jurassic Park to ask whether nature can ground moral authority. He distinguishes prudential risk arguments (Grant, Sattler) from Malcolm's distinctly moral charge that cloning dinosaurs is 'anti-nature,' then deploys Hume's is/ought problem and Hume's essay 'On Suicide' to argue there is no principled natural/unnatural line and no valid inference from natural facts to moral oughts. Examining natural-law theory (Aquinas, Cicero, 'perverted faculty' arguments), he concludes tampering with nature may be unwise but is not inherently immoral.

16.title: Is Oskar Schindler a Good Man
16.file: ch16 - Is Oskar Schindler a Good Man.md
16.relation: Ebertz treats Schindler's List as a thought experiment on what makes a person good, judging Oskar Schindler against Kantian and virtue-ethical standards. On Kant he fails: many acts (lying, bribery, infidelity) violate the categorical imperative, and even his rescues spring from growing partial attachment to 'his Jews' rather than rational duty or a good will. On Aristotelian virtue ethics he only selectively exercises virtues, so is not fully 'good' either; Ebertz resolves the tension with a Principle of Moral Exemplarity, holding Schindler up as a flawed but genuine moral example whose care promotes human flourishing.

17.title: A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple
17.file: ch17 - A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple.md
17.relation: Clewis defines a 'Spielbergian ethics of the family,' a care-based virtue ethics holding that we owe unique obligations to family and close friends grounded in personal identity, and contrasts it with utilitarian and Kantian approaches. In Saving Private Ryan the squad-as-family and the Ryan brotherhood explain why Miller says Ryan must 'earn this' and why living an ordinary good life suffices; in The Color Purple sisterhood (Nettie/Celie), fatherhood, and motherhood ground obligations of care, forgiveness, and reconciliation. He evaluates the view's feasibility while warning it neglects wider social influences and the is/ought gap.

18.title: Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad
18.file: ch18 - Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad.md
18.relation: Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.

19.title: Terrorism, Counterterrorism, and “The Story of What Happens Next” in Munich
19.file: ch19 - Terrorism, Counterterrorism, and “The Story of What Happens Next” in Munich.md
19.relation: Foy reads Munich's Operation Wrath of God as Spielberg's argument for retribution over vengeance in state counterterrorism. Yvonne's Marcuse/Hegel relativism and the agents' 'think of yourself as a soldier' language-games are dismissed as Avner's psychological breakdown shows morality is objective. Foy deploys Nozick's five procedural differences between retribution and revenge and Kant's view of retribution as impersonal and rational, echoes Socrates in the Crito (retaliation harms one's own soul) via Avner's decay, and cites Aristotle's 'war for the sake of peace' and jus in bello discrimination/proportionality in the Hamshari and Jeanette assassinations.

20.title: Part III Realism, Mind, and Metaphysics
20.file: ch20 - Part III Realism, Mind, and Metaphysics.md

21.title: Spielberg and Cinematic Realism
21.file: ch21 - Spielberg and Cinematic Realism.md
21.relation: Dromm proposes three criteria for cinematic realism—disguised representation, fidelity to the real world, and emotional response—drawing on Saving Private Ryan's desaturated handheld Normandy footage, Schindler's List's black and white, Jurassic Park's dinosaurs, and Minority Report's plausible future tech. He answers Bertolt Brecht's Marxist objection that empathy dulls the audience's critical, world-changing capacity (Brecht echoing Marx's Theses on Feuerbach) by arguing, via Amistad's 'who they are' and Saving Private Ryan, that empathetic understanding of others' feelings is itself the strongest motive for humane action.

22.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry
22.file: ch22 - A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry.md
22.relation: White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.

23.title: Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime
23.file: ch23 - Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime.md
23.relation: Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.

24.title: Appendix Discussing Five Spielberg Films
24.file: ch24 - Appendix Discussing Five Spielberg Films.md
24.relation: This appendix is not an argumentative essay but a teaching aid: it gives roughly 1,000-1,500-word plot summaries of Schindler's List, Amistad, A.I., Minority Report, and Munich, each followed by discussion questions. The questions gesture at the volume's philosophical themes—moral objectivism vs relativism about the Holocaust, Locke-style natural rights and unjust law in Amistad, whether an android can love in A.I., the justice of infallible Precrime, and the ethics of counterterrorist vengeance in Munich—but the appendix itself advances no thesis and applies no single philosopher, instead prompting readers to consult the companion essays.

26.title: Index
26.file: ch26 - Index.md

6.title: Introduction
6.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Herzog, despite branding himself an anti-intellectual who dismisses critics with 'Go for it, losers!' and lives 'with as little reflection as possible,' has a genuine philosophy of filmmaking centered on 'ecstatic truth' against the 'accountant's truth.' It reads his persona of 'false Herzogs' and doppelgangers as itself a rhetorical construction, and invokes Wittgenstein's 'Don't think, but look!' to frame Herzog's demand that viewers approach films like Grizzly Man and Fitzcarraldo with open eyes rather than academic categories. It surveys each contributor's essay as a way of restoring the 'effability' of Herzog's work.

7.title: “I Am What My Films Are”
7.file: ch07 - “I Am What My Films Are”.md
7.relation: David LaRocca listens to Herzog's essayistic, self-mythologizing pronouncements in autobiographical documentaries like 'I Am My Films' and 'Werner Herzog: Filmemacher,' arguing that Herzog practices a 'vigorous essayism' that yields 'ecstatic truth' from fabrication (as in the story of walking to Paris to save Lotte Eisner, or seeing God who turned out to be a power-station worker). Drawing on Deleuze's remark on the defenseless walker and a Nietzschean stress on what is 'healthiest,' LaRocca connects Herzog's virtue of filmmaking-on-foot and his Rogue Film School anti-pedagogy to a 'humanistic sublime' that returns us to human limits and mortality rather than transcending them.

8.title: Herzog’s Sublime and Ecstatic Truth
8.file: ch08 - Herzog’s Sublime and Ecstatic Truth.md
8.relation: Patricia Castello Branco argues that Herzog's sublime is Burkean and physiological rather than Kantian and transcendental: in Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo, and Grizzly Man the protagonists' encounter with overwhelming nature defeats reason and works through the body (Kinski's distorted performance, Treadwell's death) rather than confirming reason's supremacy as in Kant's Critique of Judgment. She maps Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' onto Nietzsche's Dionysian from The Birth of Tragedy, where the principium individuationis dissolves and the hero merges with nature's creating-and-destroying flux, and glosses ecstatic truth via Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment reached through fabrication and stylization.

9.title: The Conquest of Uselessness as a Practice of Film and Thought
9.file: ch09 - The Conquest of Uselessness as a Practice of Film and Thought.md
9.relation: Daniele Dottorini reads Herzog's filmmaking as a 'conquest of the useless' through the figures of the Tightrope Walker (Philippe Petit), the Traveler, and the Pilgrim, whose bodily effort and risk over the abyss subtract film from any utilitarian logic. He aligns them with the tightrope walker of the prologue to Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, poised between animal and Overman, and uses Deleuze and Guattari's 'conceptual personae' from What Is Philosophy? to argue that Herzog becomes his own characters. The carrying of the ship over the mountain in Fitzcarraldo and Steiner's ecstatic ski-flight exemplify ecstatic truth (aletheia) as an unveiling that transfigures the world into music.

10.title: Filmmaking and Philosophizing against the Grain of Theory Herzog and Wittgenstein
10.file: ch10 - Filmmaking and Philosophizing against the Grain of Theory Herzog and Wittgenstein.md
10.relation: Mihai Ometita pairs Herzog's anti-intellectualism with Wittgenstein's later philosophy, arguing that the obstinacy of Herzog's protagonists (Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo) and the dogmatism of Wittgenstein's interlocutors are two faces of an unbounded attachment to a single theory. Herzog's dictum 'An ape is an ape' echoes Wittgenstein's motto that everything is what it is, warning against forced metaphor (the smoking monkey in Echoes from a Somber Empire). Citing the Big Typescript and On Certainty, Ometita reads philosophy's difficulty as one of the will, and treats Aguirre's 'delirium' and Fitzcarraldo's 'dream' as quasi-nonsense that resists hasty diagnoses of madness; he invokes Descartes's window and Merleau-Ponty on film being perceived, not thought.

11.title: Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man
11.file: ch11 - Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man.md
11.relation: Marc Furstenau reads Grizzly Man as Herzog's philosophy of nature, arguing that Herzog's vision of nature as chaos, hostility, and murder mirrors Schopenhauer's terrifying Will and the fact/value split, and that Herzog blames Timothy Treadwell's sentimental faith in natural harmony for his and Amie Huguenard's deaths while secretly sharing Treadwell's amor fati. Using Iris Murdoch's Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals and Mary Midgley's Beast and Man, Furstenau contends that both Herzog and Schopenhauer succumb to an 'outrageous simplicity' that denies animal agency; against them he argues, via Midgley, that culture is natural and interspecies sympathy is real, reading Treadwell's extreme close-up of the bear (where Herzog sees 'only the overwhelming indifference of nature') as evidence of imaginative continuity between human and animal.

12.title: Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death
12.file: ch12 - Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death.md
12.relation: M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.

13.title: Fake News and Ecstatic Truths
13.file: ch13 - Fake News and Ecstatic Truths.md
13.relation: Kyle Novak uses Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph in Lessons of Darkness to distinguish 'ecstatic truth' from Trump-era 'alternative facts,' arguing that unlike Kellyanne Conway's deception, Herzog openly reveals his inventions to deepen an artistic experience. Rejecting Russell's correspondence theory of truth, Novak turns to Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place to show how media create norms and a hyperreality independent of facts, then to Nietzsche's 'On Truth and Lies' (truth as agreed-upon metaphor) and Deleuze's affirmation of life as a non-relativist standard, concluding that Lessons of Darkness is 'sparse on facts but full of truths' that penetrate deeper than CNN footage.

14.title: The Great Ecstasy of Werner Herzog Truth, Heidegger, Apocalypse
14.file: ch14 - The Great Ecstasy of Werner Herzog Truth, Heidegger, Apocalypse.md
14.relation: Ian Alexander Moore reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' through Heidegger's account of truth as aletheia (unconcealment) and 'The Origin of the Work of Art,' arguing that Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph and Wagner Prelude in Lessons of Darkness and Lo and Behold elevate viewers into a sublime, ecstatic state that discloses a truth beyond the 'accountant's' factual. He connects the slow-motion ski-jumps of The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner to Heidegger's ecstatic standing-outside-oneself, and treats Lessons of Darkness's burning Kuwaiti oil fields as an apocalyptic un-covering. He also warns that planetary information technology (echoing Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology) threatens the very oblivion of ecstatic truth.

15.title: The Film Artist as Discoverer of the Marvels of Everyday Life a Kracauerian Reading of Werner Herzog
15.file: ch15 - The Film Artist as Discoverer of the Marvels of Everyday Life a Kracauerian Reading of Werner Herzog.md
15.relation: Christopher Turner reads Herzog through Siegfried Kracauer's Theory of Film, arguing that Herzog, like Kracauer's 'film artist as explorer,' redeems physical reality by transfiguring the boring, habitual everyday into marvels. Herzog's warning about the extinction-level 'lack of adequate imagery' is aligned with Kracauer's redemption of the familiar, and films like Land of Silence and Darkness (deaf-blind Fini Straubinger) and Even Dwarfs Started Small reveal 'the unfamiliar in the familiar.' Turner invokes Benjamin (via Miriam Hansen) on the modern decline of Erfahrung into isolated Erlebnis to frame Herzog's discovery of a deeper, mysterious physical reality obscured by scientific abstraction.

16.title: Werner Herzog and the Documentary as a Revelatory Practice
16.file: ch16 - Werner Herzog and the Documentary as a Revelatory Practice.md
16.relation: Antony Fredriksson argues that Herzog's documentaries are not veridical fact-representations but a 'revelatory practice,' aligning Herzog's ecstatic-versus-accountant's-truth distinction with phenomenology (Merleau-Ponty, Husserl, Waldenfels). Using Merleau-Ponty's reading of Fabrice at Waterloo, he claims lived experience is contingent and pre-narrative, and that films like La Soufriere (a catastrophe that never happens), White Diamond (swifts behind the waterfall), and Echoes from a Somber Empire (the nicotine-addicted monkey) reveal the alien, attention-grabbing world beyond habitual seeing — a 'pathos' that reads the viewer rather than neutrally recording facts.

17.title: On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society
17.file: ch17 - On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society.md
17.relation: Stefanie Baumann reads Herzog's attack on the 'accountant's truth' of the Minnesota Declaration alongside Horkheimer and Adorno's critical theory, arguing that the cult of facts reifies perception, creates norms, and serves the 'administered world' via the culture industry. She contends Herzog's films (Lessons of Darkness, Fata Morgana, Aguirre, The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser) resist this not by escaping society but by dialectically mediating singular, uncategorizable outsiders through the historically developed social order — Kaspar Hauser's 'obstinate otherness' exposing the social violence of enforced assimilation, a subversive constellation rather than an explicit political message.

18.title: Herzog’s Philosophy of Masculinism
18.file: ch18 - Herzog’s Philosophy of Masculinism.md
18.relation: Will Lehman argues that beneath Herzog's rejection of any guiding philosophy lies a 'masculinism' that exalts traditionally manly traits (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as the heroic. Drawing on gender theory (Dozier on beards and the performance of gender), he shows Herzog fetishizing 'manly men,' reading illiteracy and calloused hands as authentic manhood (Jared Talbert in Into the Abyss), and coding even his female subject Juliane Koepcke (Wings of Hope) in masculine terms. Lehman reads Herzog's reenactment 'therapy' with Dengler and Dorrington as an assertion of dominance, while noting Herzog avoids overt misogyny or homophobia.

19.title: Herzog’s Post-Tragic Aesthetic
19.relation: Anthony Eagan and Simon Thornton apply Kierkegaard's theory of tragedy (from the aesthete 'A' in Either/Or, plus the demonic in The Sickness unto Death) to argue that Timothy Treadwell (Grizzly Man) and Aguirre (Aguirre, the Wrath of God) are not tragic but comic figures. Both cross Herzog's 'invisible borderline' by asserting pure subjectivity over fate, romanticizing nature while ignoring the ambiguous collision of freedom and necessity that constitutes genuine tragedy. Treadwell freely engineers his own preventable death (so it cannot be tragic pain), and Aguirre, drifting in circles as self-proclaimed wrath of God, personifies the demonic refusal to repent — a 'post-tragic' comedy that aches.

20.title: Werner Herzog on Circles, Chickens and Impotency
20.file: ch20 - Werner Herzog on Circles, Chickens and Impotency.md
20.relation: Tyler Tritten argues that Even Dwarfs Started Small and Stroszek are not principally political but share an essence: the impotency of the powerless dramatized through cyclical, repetitive motion (circling trucks, ski lifts, and above all chickens). He defends Herzog's 'apoliticism' — citing Herzog's preference for the medieval melior pars over numerical voting (echoing Rousseau's general will versus the popular vote, and Socrates against the many) — as locating the human condition beneath contingent social conditions. The handless, cannibalistic, circumambulating chicken becomes the emblem of a self-consuming nature and a humanity too proportionate to the beast, provoking a pure, aching laughter as the only revolt.
