10.title: 1 Primal and Spontaneous Neil Young’s Aesthetics of Authenticity
10.file: ch10 - 1 Primal and Spontaneous Neil Young’s Aesthetics of Authenticity.md
10.relation: Forest argues that Neil Young's habit of keeping early, flawed takes with Crazy Horse ("audio verite") embodies an aesthetic of authenticity as primal spontaneity. He reads Young through Emerson's self-reliance and trust in first impressions, Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian split (Harvest vs. Tonight's the Night, Young's onstage abandon on "Like a Hurricane"), Benjamin's loss of aura in mechanical reproduction, and Collingwood's art/craft distinction, contending that the "garage band" imperfections of jams like "Down by the River" let fans identify with the band's expressive, un-repeatable moment.

11.title: 2 Neil Young and Creativity
11.file: ch11 - 2 Neil Young and Creativity.md
11.relation: Berger surveys Young's repeated claim that he does not intentionally compose but "receives" songs, comparing himself to a radio station or microphone and echoing Schubert's "I remember it." He illuminates this with C.S. Peirce's categories of firstness (feeling), secondness (reaction) and thirdness (thought/signs), arguing that Young's refusal to "judge" lyrics like "Tell Me Why" or "Cowgirl in the Sand" protects the originary feeling, and that songs communicate feeling through Peircean icons and metaphors rather than deliberate rational design.

12.title: 3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification
12.file: ch12 - 3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification.md
12.relation: Mitchell examines Young's Geffen-era lawsuit (sued in 1983 for "uncharacteristic" music like Trans and Everybody's Rockin') and the competing rebel/misunderstood-artist/lost-in-the-video-era narratives around it. Using Heilbroner on capitalism's commodification of rebellious art and Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and pre-corporation of dissent (Cobain as spectacle), he argues that Young himself actively authored the "rocker-turned-folkie" and anti-commercial persona, so that even his gestures of resistance to the music business were absorbed as marketable integrity.

13.title: 4 Extended Mind and the Music of Trans
13.file: ch13 - 4 Extended Mind and the Music of Trans.md
13.relation: Umbaugh reads Young's synthesizer/Vocoder album Trans, written amid efforts to communicate with his quadriplegic son Ben ("Transformer Man"), alongside Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis and its Parity Principle. He uses examples (Otto's notebook, bartenders' glassware, navigation, Dennett on the elderly) to argue cognition couples with external scaffolding, and parallels the "unnatural" reception of Trans (like the homophobic anti-disco backlash) with resistance to extended cognition, concluding both Trans and the extended mind are authentic once the "natural/artificial" boundary is questioned.

14.title: 5 Neil Young Lover of Sun, Moon and Cars
14.file: ch14 - 5 Neil Young Lover of Sun, Moon and Cars.md
14.relation: Anderson traces Young's environmentalism from the hippie-romantic nature worship of "After the Gold Rush" and Greendale toward a pragmatic "middle way" that reconciles his love of nature with his love of cars and recording technology (the Lincvolt project, Storytone). Drawing on Thoreau, Muir and Leopold's land ethic while rejecting the fixed prescriptions of Singer and Regan, he presents Young as an experimentalist "meliorist" who owns his own complicity in CO2 abuse and urges informed, practical, self-aware action rather than utopian or deontological solutions.

15.title: 6 Neil Young and American Indians Politics, Lyrics, and Authenticity
15.file: ch15 - 6 Neil Young and American Indians Politics, Lyrics, and Authenticity.md
15.relation: Hester critiques Young's treatment of American Indians, arguing "Cortez the Killer" idealizes the Aztecs into Montaigne-style "noble savages," makes their sacrifices seem voluntary, and ultimately centers Young's own lost-love lament rather than the conquest's real victims. He shows "Pocahontas" objectifies and commodifies a Native woman (the "thousand pelts" line, Young's cavalier interview remarks) as cultural appropriation and "playing Indian," yet notes Young's genuine activism (Honor the Treaties) leaves fans wanting to credit his good intentions.

16.title: 7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young
16.file: ch16 - 7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young.md
16.relation: Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).

17.title: 8 Images of Women in the Music and Life of Neil Young
17.file: ch17 - 8 Images of Women in the Music and Life of Neil Young.md
17.relation: McKenna uses Sarah Lucia Hoagland's feminist analysis of "heterosexualism" to argue that Young's songs ("Cinnamon Girl," "A Man Needs a Maid," "Unknown Legend," and the femicide of "Down by the River") portray women as objects to be desired, possessed, used and harmed, positioning them as helpmates (like Rousseau's Sophie, against which Wollstonecraft argued). She extends this to Young's own "backgrounding" of the women in his life (Pegi, Carrie Snodgress) in Waging Heavy Peace, comparing him to William James's reliance on his wife Alice.

18.title: 9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life
18.file: ch18 - 9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life.md
18.relation: Watson and Riches reinterpret "A Man Needs a Maid" not as simple misogyny but as Young's ambivalent inner conflict between craving companionship and fearing the pain of intimacy. They read his pursuit of the "simple life" ("Heart of Gold," avoidance of reading) through Epicurean simplicity, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Bowlby/Freudian avoidant attachment and cognitive dissonance, and Sartre's "bad faith" as self-deception, set against Thoreau's chosen solitude and Aristotle's claim that the non-social being is "beast or god."

19.title: 10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care
19.file: ch19 - 10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care.md
19.relation: Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.

21.title: Contributors
21.file: ch21 - Contributors.md

3.title: 01_LaRocca_Chapter_000.html
3.relation: LaRocca's introduction frames the whole volume through Plato's ancient 'quarrel between philosophy and poetry' and his critique of mimesis (Republic Book X), arguing that documentary film is just another kind of poetic imitation whose truth-claims deserve philosophical scrutiny. Drawing on Cavell's 'film was as if made for philosophy,' Kiarostami's 'cinema is nothing but fakery,' Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and Flaherty's 'sometimes you have to lie to tell the truth,' he shows how documentary blurs fiction/nonfiction and courts fabrication. He reads the digital turn (Manovich, Rodowick) as pushing cinema toward Baudrillard's hyperreal simulacra, images that no longer index reality but simulate it.

4.title: 02_LaRocca_Chapter_001.html
4.relation: Cavell argues that photography's power expresses the mind's fall into skepticism about the external world, reading film as 'a moving image of skepticism' since we see things present to us that are not actually before us. Interpreting Capra's Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, he treats Gary Cooper's Deeds defending his 'fidgetiness' as thinking as a popular-cinema reenactment of Descartes's cogito: after Emerson, who says we can no longer say 'I think, I am' for ourselves, the proof of existence shifts from the mind's self-certainty to the live body's visible restlessness caught by the camera. He links the fidgeting body to Heidegger's das Man and Nietzsche's last man, and invokes Wittgenstein and Emerson on our being 'away' from the world.

5.title: 03_LaRocca_Chapter_002.html
5.relation: Carroll offers a critical reconstruction of Andre Bazin's film theory, separating Bazin's lasting achievement as a historian of film style from his dubious metaphysical commitments. He shows how Bazin championed 'spatial realism'—deep-focus, long-take sequence shots as in Renoir's Rules of the Game and Welles's Citizen Kane—against Soviet and Hollywood montage, on the grounds that unedited homogeneous space imparts authenticity, grants the spectator freedom to discover meaning, and preserves the ambiguity of reality. Carroll treats Bazin's claim that recording realism is cinema's essential destiny as an anti-realist target to be demythologized, defending the study of film-realist style while rejecting the essentialist evolutionary scheme underneath it.

6.title: 04_LaRocca_Chapter_003.html
6.relation: Currie defines documentary via the distinction between a trace (a causal, intention-independent record like a photograph, footprint, or death mask) and testimony (an intention-mediated representation like a painting or written history), placing simulations between them. A film is an ideal documentary when its images' 'trace content' coheres with its narrative, whereas Casablanca or All the President's Men has a separate 'narrative content' representing fictional characters. He grades real cases—Night Mail's faked mail-sorting, Roger and Me's rearranged chronology, Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will—by degree of coherence, and argues trace content is nonconceptual while narrative content is conceptual, so most docudramas are really fictions.

7.title: 05_LaRocca_Chapter_004.html
7.relation: Plantinga attacks subjectivist theories that locate the fiction/nonfiction distinction solely 'in the mind of the audience,' using the fable of a naive student, Michael, who takes such theories literally and cites Star Wars and E.T. as sources in a history paper on space travel. Against Branigan and Eitzen ('When is a documentary?'), he argues you cannot legitimately comprehend a fiction film nonfictionally because that confuses a document with a documentary. He proposes a three-part account: the distinction resides in cultural convention, in the film's designed features, and in the viewer's reception, hinging on the filmmaker's 'assertive stance' versus 'fictive stance'—like the difference between a screwdriver and a hammer.

8.title: 06_LaRocca_Chapter_005.html
8.relation: Sobchack offers a semiotic phenomenology of how real death is represented in documentary, arguing that death itself always exceeds and confounds indexical representation—we never see death, only dying and the corpse. Using Aries on the modern taboo-ing of natural death, Barthes on the traumatic photograph, and the Zapruder assassination footage whose frame-by-frame scrutiny yields only mystification, she shows why violent, abrupt mortification of the lived body is the most effective cinematic sign of death. Drawing on Heidegger's Being-toward-death and its deferral, Beauvoir's 'no such thing as a natural death,' and Merleau-Ponty's lived body, she classifies documentary's ethical 'gazes' at death (accidental, helpless, endangered, interventional, humane, professional) as inscriptions of the filmmaker's moral stance in an embodied ethical space.

9.title: 07_LaRocca_Chapter_006.html
9.relation: Tom Gunning argues that pre-WWI 'actuality' film is a distinct form from Griersonian 'documentary,' governed by what he calls the 'view' aesthetic: films (phantom rides, travelogs, 'process films' like D'ou Viennent les Faux Cheveux or A Day in the Life of an English Coal Miner) that mime the act of looking and display rather than embedding images in an argument. He locates the shift to documentary in WWI propaganda films such as Londen in Oorlogstijd, where images become evidence within a discursive claim. The essay is film historiography rather than an application of a named philosopher, so no taxonomy slug fits its core argument.

10.title: 08_LaRocca_Chapter_007.html
10.file: ch10 - 08_LaRocca_Chapter_007.html.md
10.relation: Scott MacDonald contrasts Disney's True-Life Adventures (The Vanishing Prairie, The Living Desert), which anthropomorphize animals into 1950s middle-class nuclear families and naturalize Manifest Destiny, with Jean Painleve's science films (The Seahorse, Acera, The Vampire), which choose organisms precisely because their sexual and reproductive lives defy conventional human morality. Using Nichols's claim that nature film lacks documentary's 'voice,' MacDonald argues nature films always carry ideology, and that Microcosmos and the anti-anthropocentric attention to insects show the genre's untapped philosophical value against the humanities/sciences split dramatized in Su Friedrich's The Head of a Pin.

11.title: 09_LaRocca_Chapter_008.html
11.file: ch11 - 09_LaRocca_Chapter_008.html.md
11.relation: William Rothman reads Jean Rouch's ten-minute single-take The Drums of Yore: Tourou and Bitti (and the later Dogon films Funeral at Bongo and Ambara Dama) to argue that Rouch's 'cine-trance' and 'one take/one sequence' method fuse anthropology, philosophy and poetry, so that the camera's mere presence provokes the Songhay dancer's possession by the god Kure. Leaning wholly on Stanley Cavell's ontology of film (the world on film as 'skin of the world,' the photograph's object as its subject), Rothman claims filming itself possesses Rouch, revealing the invisible in the visible. Its governing philosopher, Cavell, is absent from the taxonomy.

12.title: 10_LaRocca_Chapter_009.html
12.file: ch12 - 10_LaRocca_Chapter_009.html.md
12.relation: William Day argues that Herzog's Cave of Forgotten Dreams, filming the 32,000-year-old Chauvet Cave paintings in 3D, works not by preserving a past but by transfiguring the present, placing the viewer in a 'mythological relation to time.' He reads three literary precursors to this cinematic 'doubleness'—Emerson's 'History' and 'The American Scholar' (the past made 'now'), Thoreau's spectator-self in Walden's 'Solitude,' and Weil's 'renunciation of time'—as antecedents to Cavell's ontology of film. The Fred Astaire shadow-dance from Swing Time, spliced into the cave footage, becomes Day's emblem of what becomes of things on film: the shadows dance on after Astaire stops.

13.title: 11_LaRocca_Chapter_010.html
13.file: ch13 - 11_LaRocca_Chapter_010.html.md
13.relation: Pederson and Zimmermann analyze Vincent Grenier's 'avant-doc' videos (Color Study: Slaterville New York, Watercolor: Fall Creek, Les Chaises, Armoire) as interventions in the philosophy of documentary landscape. They read his flattened tableau shots and digitally manipulated color fields against the Hudson River School and Ansel Adams's transcendentalist (Emersonian/Thoreauvian) American sublime, invoking Timothy Murray's Heideggerian poiesis of habitats and Baudrillard's simulation/simulacra to argue Grenier replaces representation of nature with simulation—e.g., the pigeon reacting to its mirror image in Armoire—dissolving the divide between the natural and the technological.

14.title: 12_LaRocca_Chapter_011.html
14.file: ch14 - 12_LaRocca_Chapter_011.html.md
14.relation: Ariella Azoulay reflects on her film Civil Alliances—Palestine 1947–48, built from Haganah-archive documents of over a hundred civil agreements between Jews and Arabs (such as the Deir Yassin/Givat Shaul good-neighbor pact) that historians erased to sustain a narrative of enduring national conflict. Filming twenty-five Arabs and Jews reciting these promises around a reconstructed 1947 map, she argues that 'sovereign citizenship' is a colonial historiographic tool and that these archival promises are not about the past but a renewable civil future. The argument is political and archival rather than an application of a taxonomy philosopher.

15.title: 13_LaRocca_Chapter_012.html
15.file: ch15 - 13_LaRocca_Chapter_012.html.md
15.relation: Diana Allan traces a single 1948 photograph of the Palestinian fisherman Said Otruk—the basis of her video portrait Still Life—to examine the tension between the evidentiary and the affective in documentary photographs. Drawing on Dewey's Art as Experience distinction between 'perception' that is fresh and alive and 'recognition' arrested for another purpose, plus Bazin, Barthes's punctum, Berger and Cavell, she argues that when seeing is subordinated to political/national purpose the image's resolution is reduced, and that her own misremembering of the photo mirrors Said's, revealing memory's mediated, refracted temporality.

16.title: 14_LaRocca_Chapter_013.html
16.file: ch16 - 14_LaRocca_Chapter_013.html.md
16.relation: Mieke Bal frames her documentaries Mille et un jours and the installation Nothing is Missing around the ethical tension between 'modesty' and 'intimacy' in filming trauma. She reads Descartes's Passions of the Soul against the vulgate dualist cogito—arguing the isolating 'I think, I am' enacts his own abandonment trauma—and sets it beside Spinoza's socially constituted subject, while using Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' (reversed via the empowering close-up of a mother's face) and Deleuze's affection-image and rhizome. The multiplied, dispersed 'voice' of the Tunisian wedding film and Elena's silences become tools of a 'migratory aesthetics.'

17.title: 15_LaRocca_Chapter_014.html
17.relation: Bernadette Wegenstein examines her own cinema-verite practice in The Good Breast (and See You Soon Again), arguing that verite 'provokes' rather than merely produces truth through the filmmaker's participatory presence. She grounds this in Italian neorealism via Bazin (the real 'aimed at,' not re-presented) and Deleuze's Cinema II 'time-image'—a Bergsonian cinema 'of the seer' attuned to lived duration. Through her breast-cancer patient-characters (Doris, Carol, Debra, Shelia) and the surgeon Dr. Schnaper's trip to Saint Agatha's Catania, she shows how editing calls forth an 'alternate reality' and an existential (Kracauerian) realism.

18.title: 16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html
18.file: ch18 - 16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html.md
18.relation: Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.

19.title: 17_LaRocca_Chapter_016.html
19.relation: Elan Gamaker analyzes Ken Loach's Cathy Come Home and Ken Russell's London Moods and Shelagh Delaney's Salford as British social-realist 'documentary style,' arguing that agency (in the Marxist sense of free choice against structure) is progressively eroded from funder to filmmaker to subject to viewer. He shows how Grierson's neo-Hegelian faith in state institutions turned documentary into 'good propaganda' that alienates the underclass it claims to serve, so the form reproduces cultural hegemony and false consciousness. Loach's stylization and Russell's ambiguity strip the depicted subjects of voice, though Gamaker holds that a later viewer's shifting interpretation can partly restore agency.

20.title: 18_LaRocca_Chapter_017.html
20.relation: Selmin Kara reads Victor Erice's Dream of Light (The Quince Tree Sun), about the painter Antonio Lopez trying to capture a quince tree in shifting autumn light, as a case for a 'new materialist' ontology of documentary against Bill Nichols-style representationalism. Drawing on Deleuze via De Landa's actual/virtual continuum, Spinoza's and Bergson's vital-matter lineage, and Bennett's 'vibrant matter,' she argues the film's dream sequence of the operator-less camera, dimmer and rotting fruit foregrounds the mediation rather than the mastery of light. She proposes updating Grierson's 'creative treatment of actuality' to 'the creative treatment of actuality and virtuality,' treating filmic and profilmic matter as intra-acting agents.

21.title: 19_LaRocca_Chapter_018.html
21.file: ch21 - 19_LaRocca_Chapter_018.html.md
21.relation: Rick Altman dismantles four and a half 'fallacies' that let film theory ignore sound: the historical fallacy (sound as a late add-on), the ontological fallacy (image alone is cinema), the reproductive fallacy (recording reproduces rather than represents sound), the nominalist fallacy, and the half-fallacy of indexicality. In the nominalist section he explicitly frames the dispute over whether the 'same' sound heard from different seats shares a real identity as the medieval realism-versus-nominalism debate, casting Plato and Augustine as the realists and William of Ockham as the nominalist, and warning that ultra-nominalism about sound jeopardizes shared understanding. He uses Peirce's index/icon/symbol distinction to argue electronics has desacralized cinema's indexicality.

22.title: 20_LaRocca_Chapter_019.html
22.file: ch22 - 20_LaRocca_Chapter_019.html.md
22.relation: Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg's DOGMA 95 manifesto and its 'Vow of Chastity' declare a rescue action against the 'individual film,' the auteur concept (dismissed as bourgeois romanticism) and the cinema of illusion and cosmetic trickery. The ten vows bind the director to location shooting, diegetic sound, handheld camera, no optical work, no superficial action or genre, the here-and-now, and no directorial credit, swearing off personal taste in order to 'force the truth out of' characters and settings. As a primary-source polemic it advances an anti-illusionist, anti-individualist ethic of documentary-adjacent truth-telling rather than applying any named philosopher.

23.title: 21_LaRocca_Chapter_020.html
23.relation: Werner Herzog's Minnesota Declaration is a thirteen-point primary-source polemic attacking Cinema Verite as 'the truth of accountants' that confounds fact with truth and merely photographs the 'ancient ruins of facts.' Herzog insists on a deeper 'poetic, ecstatic truth' that is mysterious and reachable only through fabrication, imagination and stylization, illustrated by his own Lessons of Darkness. The aphorisms about indifferent nature, the merciless ocean and 'you can't legislate stupidity' assert that documentary illumination lies beyond mere factual accuracy, but the piece names no philosopher and applies no taxonomy concept directly.

24.title: 22_LaRocca_Chapter_021.html
24.relation: V. F. Perkins performs a close reading of the final four-minute shot of Frederick Wiseman's High School, where principal Dr. Haller reads a soldier's letter from Vietnam ('I am only a body doing a job') and claims it proves the school's success. Against the critical consensus (Kael, Bordwell and Thompson) that fixes only on the 'body doing a job' line, Perkins recovers two overlooked features: the gendered, maternal significance of the female reader, and Wiseman's stealthy editorial dropping of the sound a half-second before the image fades, leaving the principal's triumphant smile 'hollowed out.' He argues film grades its effects so that meaning can register below conscious notice, and warns that pause-and-rewind analysis steals the filmmaker's control over time, so close reading must stay answerable to a true experience of the movie.

25.title: 23_LaRocca_Chapter_022.html
25.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Gabriela Cowperthwaite's Blackfish through Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, arguing the film's interviews with orca neuroscientists (Marino et al.) function as Nagel's proposed 'objective phenomenology,' conveying orca consciousness through objective indicators rather than mere anthropomorphic projection. She dissects the film's rhetoric around Tilikum and Dawn Brancheau, showing how the title, delayed naming, SeaWorld ad juxtapositions and emotional testimony first vilify then humanize the whale to argue captivity is morally unacceptable. Invoking Peggy Zeglin Brand's 'lenses,' Iris Murdoch's 'unselfing' and Marc Bekoff's inclusive ethic, she concludes the film approximates truth about orca minds even as it, like SeaWorld, is 'structured to sell.'

26.title: 24_LaRocca_Chapter_023.html
26.file: ch26 - 24_LaRocca_Chapter_023.html.md
26.relation: Keith Dromm argues against the 'assertoric view' of documentary (Carroll's presumptive assertion, Currie's photographic traces, Plantinga's asserted veridical representation), contending that documentary films aim less to make assertions than to promote understanding. Drawing on Elgin, Zagzebski and Kvanvig on understanding as a holistic, skill-like cognitive success, and on Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations account of how understanding is taught through examples, practice and 'perspicuous representation,' he shows how Resnais's Night and Fog, Ken Burns, Errol Morris and Frederick Wiseman convey an understanding of their subject through creative technique. He treats reenactments as scientific-model-like idealizations that serve understanding even when they depart from literal truth.

27.title: 25_LaRocca_Chapter_024.html
27.relation: K. L. Evans argues that Adam McKay's The Big Short is fiction that nonetheless borrows documentary's assertive stance to make true claims about the 2008 subprime crisis and to insist ordinary viewers are smart enough to 'read the signs.' Using Aristotle on fiction (concerned with meaning not fact), Auerbach and the Heraclitean maxim that 'a man's character is his fate,' she distinguishes real people from 'characters' (living images) like the film's Michael Burry and Billy Beane, arguing that casting Brad Pitt signals the fictive stance. She invokes Deleuze's question about the 'mode of existence' of whoever pronounces a proposition to explain how the unreliable narrator Vennett can still narrate reliably, and how the film embeds indigestible factual 'markers' to refute the idea that the crisis was too complex to understand.

28.title: 26_LaRocca_Chapter_025.html
28.relation: Bill Nichols writes an open letter to Errol Morris explaining his bodily 'revulsion' at Standard Operating Procedure, Morris's film on the Abu Ghraib torture photographs. Nichols gives three reasons: the painfully limited, remorseless perspective of the MP guards elevated to mythic screen scale; the morally impossible reenactment tracking shots that put the viewer in the torturers' point of view (compared to Schindler's List); and the total absence of the Iraqi detainees' voices. He faults Morris for decontextualizing and fetishizing the images and forfeiting a moral center, contrasting the film with Rithy Panh's S-21, and casts the missing ethical encounter in terms of Buber's I-Thou relation of mutual honesty while wishing he had Fanon's capacity to treat the perpetrators' suffering.

29.title: 27_LaRocca_Chapter_026.html
29.relation: Michael Fried reads Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno's Zidane: A Twenty-First Century Portrait, seventeen synchronized cameras trained on Zinedine Zidane through one Real Madrid match, as a portrait that lays bare a new relation between absorption and being-beheld. Set within Fried's own absorption/theatricality tradition, the film shows Zidane wholly absorbed yet acutely conscious of eighty thousand spectators ('you are never alone'), which Fried reads via Heidegger's notion that even this 'bare' absorbed consciousness discloses a shared world (underscored by the halftime global news montage). He then stages the film as evidence in the McDowell-Dreyfus dispute over whether perception is conceptual, arguing that Zidane's 'expert coping' looks 'permeated by mindedness' (McDowell) rather than the non-conceptual absorbed coping Dreyfus, following Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology, describes.

30.title: 28_LaRocca_Chapter_027.html
30.relation: Hagberg argues that Grant Gee's documentary Patience (After Sebald) achieves a truthful portrait of W. G. Sebald not by static correspondence but by enacting his shifting, connection-making sensibility, as displayed in The Rings of Saturn. He deploys Wittgenstein's remarks on aspect-perception and 'seeing-as' (the duck-rabbit, the 'lighting up of an aspect') to show that perception is always already inflected by imagination, memory and language-games, dismantling the empiricist picture of Locke, Hume and Berkeley in which brute sensation precedes reflection. Borges's 'The Garden of Forking Paths' and 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius' supply the model of a Heraclitean flux of forking, mind-dependent connections, and the film's darkroom-like fading images and layered soundtrack are read as mimetically faithful to how a human sensibility perceives and remembers.

31.title: 29_LaRocca_Chapter_028.html
31.relation: Warren draws on Chantal Akerman's own remark that she makes no distinction between documentary and fiction ('they are all just films') to argue that every Akerman work fuses observation and transfiguration, extension and 'intension.' Reading Je tu il elle, Jeanne Dielman, News from Home and From the Other Side, he shows how documentation of the mundane (Delphine Seyrig molding meatloaf, the Mexico border fence as a blank projection screen) is always already a fashioning, so the real becomes itself only through being made into film. He links the strange, surreal wonder Akerman's border and night-train images provoke to Heidegger's pre-Socratic question of Being ('How is it that we are?') and to a phenomenological attentiveness to the everyday, following Rancière and Cavell on film's double nature.

32.title: 30_LaRocca_Chapter_029.html
32.relation: Linda Williams analyzes Michelle Citron's What You Take for Granted, a feminist film that inhabits the gray zone between documentary and fiction by having actors impersonate real women workers (a truck driver, a doctor, a welder) entering male-dominated trades. She argues the film exposes the price women pay to be admitted to a male world of work structured by an absent, idealized-and-vilified paternal authority, mirroring the absent-mother structure of Citron's earlier Daughter Rite. By blending polished pseudo-documentary interviews with an improvised cinema-verite fiction of Anna and Dianna's friendship, the film interrogates the process of representation itself and shows how documentary 'truth' about women's typical experience is itself a fictional shaping.

33.title: 31_LaRocca_Chapter_030.html
33.relation: Hoffman reads Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell and Joshua Oppenheimer's The Act of Killing through Kierkegaard's account of indirect communication and 'deceiving into the truth.' Like the Socratic maieutic teacher who removes his authority and lets pupils reach their own conclusions, both directors withhold voice-of-God assertion and instead present multiple, conflicting, sometimes ethically monstrous storytellers, indulging their delusions to expose them. Polley stages fake Super-8 home movies and rival accounts of her mother and paternity so that truth becomes subjective appropriation rather than objective fact; Oppenheimer lets Indonesian genocide perpetrators reenact their killings as Hollywood fantasies until Anwar Congo is 'deceived' into his own broken self-awareness, indicting the regime that still celebrates him.

34.title: 32_LaRocca_Chapter_031.html
34.relation: LaRocca argues that Casey Affleck's I'm Still Here, in which Joaquin Phoenix faked a drug-addled retirement and hip-hop career, is best understood as a 'hoax-verite' whose collapse of the boundary between real and represented turns it into a Baudrillardian simulacrum and hyperreal artifact, a documentary of images 'without an original referent.' Against Noel Carroll's account of documentary as a film of presumptive assertion and Plantinga's assertive stance, LaRocca shows how Affleck exploited audience faith (staged home movies, the David Letterman 'beat down') so that the film's metaphysical, epistemic and ethical status transformed once the fraud was confirmed. He invokes Hegel's remarks on abstract individuality and compares the case to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' Roth's and Kaufman's metafiction, to argue the deception paradoxically discloses deeper truths about what documentary is.

3.title: Introduction
3.relation: The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre from Doodlebug through Interstellar, arguing that like Socrates's gadfly his films sting viewers out of complacency rather than delivering settled answers. It traces a running theme of self-destruction and self-identity: Buber's I-Thou thesis illuminates Following's Cobb and The Young Man (with a Hegelian master-slave twist), Leonard Shelby in Memento must invent a telos to keep his existence meaningful, Descartes's dream argument stands behind Inception's spinning top, and the Joker voices Hobbes on what 'a little anarchy' does to society. It closes by reading Interstellar as the culmination of these themes, with Cooper's partial love for Murph set against Dr. Mann and Prof. Brand, who are willing to squash their humanity to save the species.

4.title: Deceit, Desire, and Mimetic Doubling in the Films of Christopher Nolan
4.file: ch04 - Deceit, Desire, and Mimetic Doubling in the Films of Christopher Nolan.md
4.relation: Dunn reads Doodlebug's infinite regress of doppelgangers, Following's Cobb manufacturing a double of The Young Man, and The Prestige's Borden-Angier feud as cinematic illustrations of Girard's mimetic theory: we learn what to desire by imitating models, and as model and imitator converge on the same objects they become rivals and doubles. He shows Cobb in Following deliberately certifying The Blonde's desirability to entrap The Young Man (double mediation breeding Cobb's own jealousy), and Fischer's 'desire to be his own man' in Inception being incepted through the mediator of his father. In The Prestige, prestige itself becomes the contested object, a zero-sum metaphysical prize generated by the rivalry that demands escalating sacrifice. Drawing on Augustine's restlessness, Plato's Eros as longing for the Good, and Rousseau's amour-propre, he argues that desire born of ontological lack curdles into rivalry and scapegoating, with Memento's Leonard as the man who deliberately farms fresh scapegoats-in-waiting to keep his actions meaningful.

5.title: “So You Can Be My ‘John G.’”
5.file: ch05 - “So You Can Be My ‘John G.’”.md
5.relation: Eberl asks whether Leonard Shelby is morally culpable for killing Teddy, since the Leonard who tattoos the false clue and the Leonard who pulls the trigger are sundered by anterograde amnesia. Locke's forensic, memory-based concept of personhood suggests the shooting Leonard is not the same person as the one who set the trap, while Aquinas's analysis of concomitant, consequent, and antecedent ignorance makes Leonard culpable for deliberately willing his own ignorance yet not for the amnesiac moment of the killing itself. Hume's causal criterion of psychological continuity explains why Leonard can still rationally set a goal for his future self by making Teddy his 'John G.' The chapter closes on Aristotle: Leonard's ease in framing an innocent man betrays a corrupted moral character built on habit, and by turning himself into a 'living instrument'—Aristotle's definition of a slave—he has traded his dignity for the telos of an endless revenge quest.

6.title: White Nights of the Soul
6.file: ch06 - White Nights of the Soul.md
6.relation: Garcia reads Insomnia as the story of a cop who has lost himself and must choose between two doppelgangers: Walter Finch, the murderer who offers amoral 'partnership' and moral anti-realism ('that ultimate taboo? It doesn't exist outside our minds'), and rookie Ellie Burr, who embodies Dormer's better past as a conscientious policeman. Against Finch's 'moral math' and Dormer's own 'the end justifies the means' rationalizations, the chapter argues that the moral value of actions lies in intentions, motives, and character—Aquinas on what makes a killing an accident, Kant on being worthy of happiness rather than securing it. Dormer's sleeplessness becomes evidence of a conscience still alive, and his struggle figures what Kierkegaard calls purity of heart, willing one thing, with Socrates's refusal to escape in the Crito as the model of integrity. In dying to protect Ellie from losing her way, Dormer regains himself through commitment to another person, the Levinasian point that personhood is fulfilled only in and through other persons.

7.title: Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar
7.file: ch07 - Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar.md
7.relation: The chapter stages Interstellar's conflict between Cooper's partial love for his own family and Professor Brand's species-level duty as a question about the intrinsic value of humanity. Using Aristotle's account of friends and children as 'other selves' and of happiness as the one end sought for its own sake, it argues that the species survives only as a byproduct of particular, partial loves, so Plan B's bank of 5,000 faceless embryos could not preserve 'us' in any meaningful sense. Kant's unconditional dignity of rational persons supplies Brand's premise that our existence enriches the universe, but the chapter turns Kant against him: Brand's monstrous lie to the Endurance crew treats persons as mere means to an end they do not share, trampling the very dignity it claims to save. It closes by asking what value colonizing Edmunds's planet would destroy—ecosystems, microbial life, and possibly other rational persons whose dignity we would be obliged to respect—should humanity refuse to 'go gentle into that good night.'

8.title: “They Turned to a Man They Didn’t Fully Understand”
8.file: ch08 - “They Turned to a Man They Didn’t Fully Understand”.md
8.relation: Foy and Dale argue that the Dark Knight trilogy endorses a conservative critique of liberal democracy: Batman taps every citizen's phone, tortures criminals, and kidnaps Lau from Hong Kong because Gotham's institutions cannot cope with a permanent state of crisis. Hume's conservatism—authority resting on habit and order rather than abstract rights and consent—explains Batman's defense of the existing order against Ra's al Ghul's razing of Gotham, while Schmitt's sovereign who declares the 'state of exception' frames Batman as the extra-legal protector who suspends rights during crisis (with Rachel's Caesar warning marking the danger). Against Locke's natural rights and Rawls's inviolability of the person, the Joker and Bane dramatize Strauss's twin fears that liberalism degenerates into nihilistic value-chaos or coercive revolutionary equality, and Burke's natural aristocracy of 'virtual representation' justifies relying on an unchosen elite hero. The trilogy's central puzzle is Batman's illiberal means—taking the blame for Dent's death to preserve the White Knight myth—dirtying his hands so that Gotham's official powers stay clean.

9.title: The Vale of Top Hats
9.file: ch09 - The Vale of Top Hats.md
9.relation: Decker reads The Prestige's duplication as duplicity: the vale of top hats and the tank-preserved drowned doubles frame an argument that modern stage magic, and Nolan's filmmaking itself, run on the audience's willing self-deception—Robert-Houdin's 'clever man' who pays to be fooled and Nietzsche's artist 'accustomed to lying' meeting man's 'invincible inclination to allow himself to be deceived.' Weber's rationalization and the 'iron cage' supply the chapter's central allegory: Tesla's machine, unlike stage illusion, actually works, embodying a modernity of instrumental cost-benefit calculation in which progress demands ever-costlier sacrifice, making Borden the 'specialist without spirit' and Angier the 'sensualist without heart.' Benjamin's work of art in the age of mechanical reproduction dissolves the question of which Angier is the authentic original, since reproducibility abolishes authenticity and leaves Angier trading the intrinsic value of personhood for transcendence at the price of drowning himself nightly. Benjamin's dictum that every document of culture is also a document of barbarism ties the magicians' art, and Western technological progress from Edison's feuds to the coming World War, to its hidden human cost.

10.title: Plato, Habermas, and the Demonic Cobb
10.file: ch10 - Plato, Habermas, and the Demonic Cobb.md
10.relation: Murphy treats Following as a provocation keyed to the copy of Plato's Republic glimpsed in The Blonde's apartment: Cobb, who slips unseen into houses and lives and reads people's 'boxes,' is the shepherd with the Ring of Gyges, able to act unjustly without ever facing detection. Against Glaucon's challenge the chapter weighs Socrates's answer that injustice enslaves and disorders the soul—but notes that Nolan shows Cobb victorious, a 'demonic' figure with all of Socrates's abilities and none of his love of justice, who drags Bill and The Blonde into a cave of illusion rather than out of one. Habermas supplies the modern retort: our rationality and sanity depend on the communicative action, truth, and fairness of a shared lifeworld, commitments a sociopathic loner like Cobb cannot renounce without taking refuge in mental illness, though the film never shows Cobb paying that price. Man of Steel's Clark Kent clutching the Republic while letting himself be bullied, and Jonathan Kent's fatal secrecy, become the counterimage of someone who consistently wills justice at personal cost, the closest Nolan comes to showing why justice is worth choosing.

11.title: “Are You Watching Closely ”
11.file: ch11 - “Are You Watching Closely ”.md
11.relation: Knight and McKnight analyze how Nolan's early films withhold narrative transparency: Doodlebug's regress of killers, Following's framing device that ends with Cobb vanishing into a crowd, Memento's reverse chronology, and The Prestige's twin frames of top hats and drowned doubles all force viewers to build and revise hypotheses about what happened, when, and who is responsible. Because actions cannot be morally evaluated until we know who performed them and why, the chapter ties narrative comprehension to moral judgment—Leonard's confabulated revenge and inability to recognize his own self-deception, Dormer's ambiguous redemption, and Ellie's unresolved choice over the bullet. The Prestige's doubles raise the identity question the authors gloss with Parfit's teletransporter—perhaps it does not matter which Angier survives—while Cutter's helping Borden kill Caldlow enacts Francis Bacon's 'wild justice' that the law cannot provide. The chapter closes on Nolan as auteur, whose self-conscious framing devices and play of masks make 'Are you watching closely?' at once the film's theme and its admonition to the viewer.

12.title: Remembering, Reminding, and Forgetting with Leonard Shelby
12.file: ch12 - Remembering, Reminding, and Forgetting with Leonard Shelby.md
12.relation: Dennis Knepp reads Leonard Shelby's Polaroids, notes, and tattoos through Charles Sanders Peirce's triadic semiotics, showing how each memento works at once as icon, index, and symbol (Firstness, Secondness, Thirdness), as when the Discount Inn photo resembles the motel, is causally produced by the camera pointed at it, and needs Leonard to interpret its written words. He then argues Memento is less a detective story than a fable of self-deception: the printed word's permanence lends Leonard's tattooed list of 'THE FACTS' an illusion of absolute authority, down to the fatal mis-tattoo of Teddy's license plate (SG137IU copied as SG1371U). The chapter ends by reading Plato's Phaedrus tale of Theuth and Thamus - writing as a potion for reminding, not remembering, that breeds only the appearance of wisdom - as an ancient diagnosis of how Leonard's external signs deceive him.

13.title: False Tattoos and Failed Totems
13.file: ch13 - False Tattoos and Failed Totems.md
13.relation: Karen Hoffman reads Memento and Inception through Kierkegaard's Concluding Unscientific Postscript: Leonard's tattoos and Cobb's totems both fail to supply the objective certainty their owners expect, forcing each to confront subjective truth, 'an objective uncertainty held fast through appropriation with the most passionate inwardness.' She argues Leonard fails Kierkegaard's test twice over - he treats his facts-based system as objective knowledge, and his real commitment is to playing detective rather than catching a killer (Teddy: 'You don't want the truth. You make up your own truth'), culminating in the knowingly false tattoo that arranges Teddy's murder. Cobb, by contrast, faces his memories of Mal, accepts objective uncertainty, takes Saito's 'leap of faith,' and in the final scene walks away from the spinning top, choosing the world that reunites him with his children - an idea that sticks because of how he lives it, not because it is objectively true.

14.title: Inception and Perception
14.file: ch14 - Inception and Perception.md
14.relation: Jamie Carlin Watson uses Inception's dream thieves to stage the dream argument for skepticism - from Socrates' puzzle to Theaetetus and Descartes's Meditations, with Sextus Empiricus's diversity-of-perception argument - and contends that totems cannot debunk it, since even Arthur's loaded die and Cobb's top cannot rule out being in your own dream, where your subconscious knows how the totem behaves. Against both believing as normal and Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment, the chapter turns to William James's will to believe (live versus dead hypotheses) and to intellectual virtues drawn from Zagzebski and Kornblith: beliefs can be valuable for reasons other than truth. The upshot is that Cobb, Arthur, and the twelve shared-dream sleepers in Yusuf's basement can believe well even if they cannot believe truly - which is why Cobb's walking away from the spinning top at the end can be read as believing carefully rather than certainly.

15.title: Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats
15.file: ch15 - Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats.md
15.relation: William Lindenmuth reads Inception's ambiguous ending through Robert Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Cobb's choice of his real children over the dream-Mal ('you're just a shade of my real wife') shows we want our dreams to be reality, not reality to be a dream. He deploys Nozick's three reasons against plugging in - we want to do things, not merely seem to; we want to be a certain kind of person ('It's not who I am underneath, but what I do that defines me'); and a man-made reality confines and limits us - while invoking Bernard Williams's tedium of immortality for Cobb's fifty dream-years with Mal and Wittgenstein's talking lion for the alienation those years create. On this reading the wobbling top matters, because choosing limbo would be 'a kind of suicide,' the difference between the film ending as tragedy or not.

16.title: “You Don’t Know Who You Are”
16.file: ch16 - “You Don’t Know Who You Are”.md
16.relation: Peter Fosl argues that Nolan's protagonists are divided selves - public and private - whose self-creation runs through narratives and material signs (Memento's tattoos and Polaroids, Inception's safes, the Batcave, the Prestige twins' offstage swaps) that others can always reinterpret, steal, or manipulate. Following J.L. Austin on performative acts, he reads Following's Bill as losing authorship of his own story to Cobb's counter-narrative and Bruce Wayne as only ever performing roles written in advance, even at the Dark Knight ending's Florentine café. Augustine's memoria and Locke's memory-continuity ground the discussion of Leonard's broken self-knowledge ('You don't know who you are'), while Nietzsche on forgetting, Gadamer on the past's effective history, and Sartre on the dead as prey for the living frame how Leonard's forgotten past selves manipulate him into murdering Teddy and how Interstellar's Cooper reaches back through the Tesseract to alter his own past.

17.title: “Memory Man”
17.relation: David LaRocca reads Memento through Andy Clark and David Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis: Leonard's tattoos, Polaroids, and notecards just are his memory, doing exactly what Otto's notebook does in their original example - so that writing 'Don't believe his lies' on a Polaroid is literally modifying his mind and carries the moral significance of interfering with his person. Drawing on Liao and Sandberg's ethics of memory modification and Noël Carroll's account of the film's reverse-ordered narrative, the chapter argues Leonard remains a culpable moral agent in his lucid moments: he knowingly 'incepts' a false command into his own extended mind to preserve the avenging-husband narrative that constitutes his identity, becoming a serial killer. It closes on our epistemic and moral duty of cognitive fidelity - to build truthful narrative identities rather than lie to ourselves into murder.

18.title: Engaging Otherness through Following
18.file: ch18 - Engaging Otherness through Following.md
18.relation: Louis-Paul Willis reads Following as the prototype of Nolan's 'mind-tricking spectatorship,' where fragmented, multi-strand editing and staged details (the box of secrets, the hammer conversation, the near-identical glove shots) reveal to viewers that the film itself has taken their desire into account all along. Using Jacques Lacan's distinction between the look and the gaze, and the objet a as object-cause of desire, he argues that Bill's voyeuristic quest for the Other's hidden kernel - Cobb's 'everyone has a box' scene - is doomed because the voyeur becomes the viewed: the subject of the look becomes the object of the gaze, just as Bill the follower turns out to be the one followed and framed for murder. Bill's failure is thus the cinematic spectator's failure - there is no passive vantage point exempt from the Other's gaze.

19.title: We Are the Change That We Seek
19.file: ch19 - We Are the Change That We Seek.md
19.relation: Todd McGowan argues Interstellar enacts Hegel's critique of substance: the NASA scientists' 'they' who supposedly placed the wormhole is a Kantian thing-in-itself - the unknown deified by ignorance - until the Tesseract reveals that Cooper himself, and future humanity, are both Murph's 'ghost' and the 'they' ('We brought ourselves'). Against Spinoza's single substance and Leibniz's windowless monads, the film teaches that substance is subject, freeing Cooper and Murph to act and to change the past through retroactive causality, which the chapter connects to Sartre on the past's fixedness and Walter Benjamin's critique of historicist causality. Professor Brand's Plan A lie and Dr. Mann's self-exculpating murder show the ethical catastrophe of claiming a substantial, subject-transcending standpoint, while Murph - who treats her 'ghost' as just another subject rather than a supernatural substance - is the film's true hero.

5.title: We’ve Been Abducted by the Doctor, and We Love It!
5.file: ch05 - We’ve Been Abducted by the Doctor, and We Love It!.md

6.title: EPISODE 1 - I’m the Doctor. Who
6.file: ch06 - EPISODE 1 - I’m the Doctor. Who.md

7.title: A Dead End
7.relation: Patrick Stokes uses the Doctor's regeneration and the multi-Doctor stories ("The Five Doctors," "The Caves of Androzani") to test theories of personal identity. He runs Locke's memory criterion against Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's Branch-Line teleportation case (a Gallifrey-to-Skaro replica), Nozick's Closest Continuer schema applied to the Valeyard, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity, showing each fails to explain regeneration. He gestures that identity may lie in a subjective self-appropriation, the Doctor taking ownership of his incarnations.

8.title: Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer
8.file: ch08 - Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer.md
8.relation: Greg Littmann uses regeneration and dozens of Doctor Who transformations (doubles like the Abbot of Amboise, disembodied brains, transmats, Eldrad's body-hopping, Cassandra's possession) as hypotheticals to test criteria for personal identity. He shows bodily identity, spatiotemporal continuity of the body, the memory criterion (undercut by Donna and John Smith cases), and psychological/personality similarity each face counterexamples, deliberately leaving the question open so readers judge for themselves.

9.title: What’s Persistence Without Identity
9.relation: Richard Hanley asks what counts as personal survival for a Time Lord, distinguishing body, mind, and soul theories. Using the Tenth Doctor's "every single cell" regeneration, the severed hand grown into a Doctor in "Journey's End," John Smith's Chameleon-Arch amnesia, and Jackson Lake's infostamp fugue, he argues bodily and soul continuity fail and defends a neo-Lockean mental-continuity criterion refined by Nozick's closest-continuer schema, concluding with Parfit that persistence may not be what matters in survival.

10.title: I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think
10.file: ch10 - I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think.md
10.relation: David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.

11.title: EPISODE 2 - Wibbly-Wobbly, Timey-Wimey . . . Stuff
11.file: ch11 - EPISODE 2 - Wibbly-Wobbly, Timey-Wimey . . . Stuff.md

12.title: We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel
12.file: ch12 - We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel.md
12.relation: Peter Worley finishes the Doctor's "wibbly-wobbly" speech from "Blink" by distinguishing empirical from logical possibility (via a fictional chat with Leonardo about a round-square) and asking whether time travel is coherent. Using "The Edge of Destruction," "The Aztecs," "The Visitation," and "Turn Left," he deploys David Lewis's external-versus-personal time distinction and Lewis's rule that a time traveler's acts must be the very events that made history, then treats the Doctor and Lewis as "actualists" about possible worlds to dissolve grandfather-style paradoxes and time loops.

13.title: The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!
13.file: ch13 - The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!.md
13.relation: Philip Goff asks whether Daleks could travel back and stop the pyramids being built, arguing the answer turns on one's theory of time. He shows presentism forbids travel to a non-existent past and eternalism permits travel but forbids changing a static block, then defends the growing-block theory (past and present real, future not) as a middle way that lets time travelers genuinely alter history. He works out how a new pyramid-less history advances at the same rate as the present, never overwriting it, and distinguishes concrete from abstract past existence to keep historical records true.

14.title: Prognosis
14.file: ch14 - Prognosis.md
14.relation: William Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's "Blink" philosophy of time using David Lewis's four-dimensionalism. He shows how Lewis's external/personal-time distinction explains the Doctor meeting his own regenerations and reversed causation (a black eye before the punch), and how "Blink" hinges on a closed causal chain (the DVD Easter-egg transcript that authors itself). He rehearses the Grandfather/Bilking paradox and Lewis's "can" equivocation solution, then places the Doctor alongside Horwich and Ismael, arguing the Doctor goes furthest by holding closed causal chains actually exist.

15.title: This Is the Age of Steel
15.file: ch15 - This Is the Age of Steel.md
15.relation: Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.

16.title: They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too
16.file: ch16 - They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too.md
16.relation: Bonnie Green and Chris Willmott use the Daleks' human-factor experiments ("The Evil of the Daleks," "Dalek," "Daleks in Manhattan") to lay out the philosophy-of-biology "species problem": are species natural kinds, individuals, or sets? They trace essentialism from an Aristotelian God-given essence through Darwin's overthrow of it to modern genetic essentialism (the humanizing Dalek DNA), then use the Dalek/Thal split to survey biological species concepts and monism versus pluralism. They close with personhood and Peter Singer's speciesism, asking whether human-Dalek Sec would deserve rights.

17.title: Doomed to Be Perceived
17.relation: Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.

18.title: Aww, . . . Poor Monster. Should We Feel Sorry for the Carrionites
18.file: ch18 - Aww, . . . Poor Monster. Should We Feel Sorry for the Carrionites.md
18.relation: Simon Hewitt uses the Carrionites, who wield words instead of numbers, to ask whether science can be done without mathematics, a question in the philosophy of mathematics about mathematical Platonism (numbers existing outside space and time). He lays out the Quinean indispensability argument, then reviews Hartry Field's number-free Newtonian gravity and Mark Balaguer's attempt on Quantum Mechanics as "Carrionite physics," noting both fall short. He closes arguing that even if numbers were dispensable for science, our knowledge of mathematical truths still suggests numbers exist.

19.title: EPISODE 3 - It’s a Different Morality. Get Used to It, or Go Home!
19.file: ch19 - EPISODE 3 - It’s a Different Morality. Get Used to It, or Go Home!.md

20.title: “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler
20.file: ch20 - “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler.md
20.relation: Kevin S. Decker argues the Doctor's morality is an "ethics of ambiguity" poised between Romanticism and existentialism, not any formula. Rejecting positivism, deontology, and utilitarianism as fits for the Doctor, he reads the Doctor's freedom, wandering, and rejection of Time Lord values through Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith (the student torn between mother and Free French) and Beauvoir's "adventurer" who confers value by choosing. The Romantic search for the infinite in small things and the Prometheus myth frame the Doctor as a liberating, self-defining moral exemplar.

21.title: A Better Way of Living Your Life
21.file: ch21 - A Better Way of Living Your Life.md
21.relation: Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.

22.title: Toward Caring
22.file: ch22 - Toward Caring.md
22.relation: J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.

23.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
23.file: ch23 - Allons-y into the Starry Heavens.md
23.relation: Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.

24.title: The Dalek Within
24.relation: Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.

25.title: Why the Doctor Is So Special
25.file: ch25 - Why the Doctor Is So Special.md
25.relation: Sarah Honeychurch and Niall Barr argue Daleks and Cybermen will never beat humanity because they are speciesist, judging worth solely by logic and resemblance. Using Peter Singer's animal-liberation account of speciesism (and Ryder's coinage), they claim the capacity to feel pain and empathy grounds moral consideration, and that Martha Nussbaum's and Aristotle's view of emotions as trainable judgments makes feeling essential to good moral reasoning. The humanized Daleks (the "Dalek" who absorbs Rose's DNA, Dalek Sec) show emotion's transformative power, and the Doctor's empathy, unlike other Time Lords, is why he succeeds.

26.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
26.file: ch26 - Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign.md
26.relation: Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.

28.title: Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity
28.file: ch28 - Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity.md
28.relation: Michael Hand uses the Doctor's regeneration to argue that life after death is logically possible. Because the First-through-Tenth Doctors are the same person despite total personality change (a dandy becoming a clown), identity is distinct from personality, so a god perfecting flawed Joe for heaven need not make him someone else. He then tests the replica theory against 'Journey's End' (the metacrisis Doctor) and 'Human Nature' (John Smith), concluding we favor bodily continuity, and endorses van Inwagen's 'divine cryonicist' solution to the unavailability-of-atoms problem, echoing the Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' praise of frozen humanity in 'The Ark in Space'.

29.title: Love and Doctors
29.relation: Paul Dawson asks whether the Doctor dies when he regenerates by separating body, organism, and person. Using Kripke's rigid vs non-rigid designators he weighs whether 'the Doctor' names one individual or a role (the numbered Doctors, 'my replacements'), then applies Locke's memory criterion and Reid's transitivity objection, adopting Parfit's psychological-connectedness chain (via Sarah Jane's overlapping memories). He concludes the organism survives regeneration necessarily while the person survives only if psychological continuity holds, and argues the 'Journey's End' metacrisis Doctor Two is genuinely the person Rose loved through branching/fission.

30.title: I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You
30.file: ch30 - I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You.md
30.relation: Ruth Deller reads the Doctor as a savior/redeemer figure onto whom fans project ideals, invoking Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideal self onto Christ, then pivots to Nietzsche. Rather than a flawless Messiah, the Doctor is a flawed being who must overcome himself, and his 'ordinary' companions (Donna, Harriet Jones, the Hostess in 'Midnight', Rose in 'Turn Left') exemplify Nietzsche's Ubermensch by rising above their weaknesses. She argues the Doctor and humans have a symbiotic relationship: the universe needs a savior, but that savior must be challenged, so both overcome themselves together.

31.title: Life A Celebration
31.relation: Adam Riggio uses Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche to cast the Simm Master as a nihilist who, having seen the valueless dying universe at Utopia, wills nothingness and universal destruction out of ressentiment. The Doctor is Nietzsche's Overman who overcomes the reactive forces of revenge: in 'Dalek' he recognizes his own vengefulness and turns from it, and in 'Last of the Time Lords' he defeats the Master not with Martha's fake gun but by saying 'I forgive you,' affirming finite life with a 'beneficent Yes-saying' rather than surrendering to enmity.

32.title: Escape to Doctor Who
32.relation: Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.

33.title: The Master The Slave of the Time-Lord Cunning of Reason
33.file: ch33 - The Master The Slave of the Time-Lord Cunning of Reason.md
33.relation: Paula Smithka reads the Master through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and 'world-historical individual.' The Master craves recognition but seeks it from lessers (humans, the Toclafane, the human race turned into himself in 'The End of Time'), which Hegel shows is empty because genuine recognition must come from an equal, so the lord is really the dependent consciousness. The Master ironically already has an equal's recognition from the Doctor but cannot see it. As a world-historical individual driven by passion, he is the pawn ('cunning of Reason') the Time Lords use to escape the time lock, gaining freedom only when he turns on Rassilon.

34.title: I Am the Bad Wolf
34.file: ch34 - I Am the Bad Wolf.md
34.relation: Roman Altshuler answers Davros's charge that the Doctor is a 'destroyer of worlds' using Aristotelian virtue ethics. He argues the Doctor's chief virtue is not compassion but Heideggerian 'authentic concern': offering aggressors (the Nestene, Sontarans, the Master) a genuine choice so they become responsible for escalating, illustrated by the fly-swatter thought experiment. Companions, being 'another self' (Aristotle on friendship), make their acts partly the Doctor's own, yet their human 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' lets compassion override the impartial concern that requires respecting choice, which is why the Doctor runs from what his companions do in his name.

35.title: EPISODE 5 - Brilliant! Fantastic! Molto Bene!
35.file: ch35 - EPISODE 5 - Brilliant! Fantastic! Molto Bene!.md

36.title: One More Thing, Don’t Blink!
36.file: ch36 - One More Thing, Don’t Blink!.md
36.relation: Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.

37.title: A Beautiful Destiny
37.relation: Clive Cazeaux asks whether the Daleks can be beautiful, canvassing theories of beauty to resolve the puzzle of a monster being beautiful. He distinguishes Kant's higher natural beauty (and his suspicion of 'dependent,' purpose-designed beauty like the Dalek casing) from Hegel's view that beauty in art, perceiving thought in matter, is higher, and finds Plato most helpful: to call the Daleks beautiful is Platonic love, being drawn to engage with them as a wholly-other form of life whose design succeeds. He surveys Alexander of Hales, Rosenkranz's aesthetic inferno, and formalism (the Krutikov design parallel) without a final verdict, showing the dispute turns on metaphysics.

38.title: The Odd Thought of Doctor Who
38.file: ch38 - The Odd Thought of Doctor Who.md
38.relation: Gregory Kalyniuk maps Leibniz's monadology onto Doctor Who. The Doctor's identity across regenerations is a thinking monad whose individual concept holds necessary predicates while appurtenant body-monads are replaced; the Time Lords play Leibniz's God overseeing pre-established harmony and permitting evil in the best world (refusing to stop the Daleks in 'Genesis'). The dimensionally transcendental TARDIS illustrates the identity of indiscernibles, the Matrix is a Leibnizian mill of confused perceptions (with the Master as Descartes's evil demon), and the incompossible Valeyard of 'Trial of a Time Lord' is read via Leibniz's Theodicy pyramid and Borges's forking paths.

39.title: EPISODE 6 - Lots of Planets Have a North!
39.file: ch39 - EPISODE 6 - Lots of Planets Have a North!.md

40.title: Bunker Mentality or Love
40.relation: Robin Bunce recovers how Terry Nation's original 1963 'The Daleks' encodes evil, reading the script in its Cold War, post-Cuban-Missile-Crisis context. He argues Nation dehumanizes the Daleks not by making them less rational but MORE rational: they embody the unfeeling reason of the neutron bomb that destroyed Skaro, having lost individuality, laughter, and the capacity to feel. Drawing on Richard Rorty's claim that our humanity lies in feeling for one another rather than in reason (and on Wells's Morlocks), he concludes the Daleks are the dreaded post-nuclear human future, and Ian teaches the Thals that love and empathy, not abstract moralizing, resist evil.

41.title: The Doctor, Defender of British Dreams
41.file: ch41 - The Doctor, Defender of British Dreams.md
41.relation: Deborah Pless argues the Doctor functions as a national hero embodying the Britain that post-imperial Britain wished to be. Situating the show in the crises of decolonization, the 1948-1962 open-immigration act, and disputes over citizenship, she reads the Doctor (especially Tom Baker's 'romantic wanderer') as proudly British yet anti-imperial, a diplomat who never stays to rule, using John Fiske's structuralist reading of him as mediating god and man and as a Christ-like figure. Romana models the ideal modern British woman, and via propaganda-effect claims she contends Doctor Who helped re-imagine Britain in the Doctor's hopeful image.

42.title: The Doctor Dances
42.relation: Alexander Bertland uses Vico, Cassirer, and Horkheimer and Adorno to argue Doctor Who refuses to simply side with science over myth. Vico shows myth as world-constructing ritual that binds community and carries moral wisdom ('Snakedance's' Snakedance defeats the Mara; 'Meglos' shows myth's danger), while Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment argues science is itself a limiting, mythical framework: the Doctor's insistence that 'fixed points' in time cannot be changed ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Waters of Mars') reflects his own self-constructed scientific paradigm, not real necessity. The Doctor lives well by humbly balancing myth and science.

43.title: Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation
43.file: ch43 - Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation.md
43.relation: Courtland Lewis's closing essay argues Doctor Who and philosophy are complementary enterprises devoted to teaching rather than mere persuasion. Using Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching and rhetoric, he casts the Master as the master rhetorician who produces unreliable beliefs (even via hypnosis), while the Doctor is a Socratic teacher committed to truth who gives people information and lets them decide. He contends the show, begun as educational, challenges viewers to reflect on their own reasoning, on how they treat others (Daleks, Cybermen, strangers), and to revise beliefs in light of evidence, so that watching it is living philosophically engaged.

9.title: 1. Human, All Too Human
9.relation: Holdier reads Supernatural's finale through Nietzsche, arguing that Chuck's exposure as a cruel author-God and his defeat by the Winchesters dramatizes the 'death of God' as the freedom to invent one's own meaning. Dean and Sam's stubborn refusal to 'stay down' on the lakeshore against Chuck embodies amor fati—saying yes to circumstance—while Jack, birthed and taught by ordinary humans, becomes the Ubermensch who replaces God, showing humanity as a bridge to something greater than itself.

10.title: 2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan
10.file: ch10 - 2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan.md
10.relation: Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.

11.title: 3. Why Do I Have to Be Some Kind of Hero
11.file: ch11 - 3. Why Do I Have to Be Some Kind of Hero.md
11.relation: Zanin reads the Winchesters' sense of moral responsibility through Dostoevsky's The Karamazov Brothers, mapping Dean onto the sensualist/atheist Dmitri-Ivan and Sam onto the faithful Alyosha. Via Father Zossima's dictum that we are 'responsible to all for all,' she argues Sam and Dean's brotherhood is Christian self-sacrificial 'love in action'—shown in Dean choosing Sam over a normal life in 'Bad Boys' and the djinn world—which grounds why they keep saving strangers even after rejecting God's plan.

12.title: 4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest
12.file: ch12 - 4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest.md
12.relation: Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.

13.title: Part II “Every soul here is a monster. This is where they come to prey upon each other for all eternity.”
13.file: ch13 - Part II “Every soul here is a monster. This is where they come to prey upon each other for all eternity.”.md

14.title: 5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality
14.file: ch14 - 5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality.md
14.relation: Hellwig uses Dean's choice of Hell over Doc Benton's organ-replacement immortality in 'Time Is on My Side' to examine medical immortality. He pairs Dean's worry—that maiming and replacing your body makes you unrecognizably human—with Bernard Williams's Makropulos argument that immortality ends in categorical-desire-exhausting boredom, adding a third condition to Williams: a recognizably human life requires being able to self-identify with one's own body, illustrated by real disfigurement cases and Aubrey de Grey's biogerontology.

15.title: 6. How the Hell Are We Supposed to Kill an Idea
15.file: ch15 - 6. How the Hell Are We Supposed to Kill an Idea.md
15.relation: Simsek reads the 'Hell House' tulpa—a monster made real by mass belief on the HellHoundsLair website—as a philosophical challenge about the power of ideas and how one 'kills' an idea, which the brothers can only attempt by seeding a counter-belief. She invokes Socrates' call in the Republic to censor the arts that shape moral character, and the Streisand Effect, to argue that internet-amplified ideas (memes, conspiracy theories, gender and racial norms) take on autonomous, hard-to-kill life much as fandom overrides creators' intent.

16.title: 7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters
16.file: ch16 - 7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters.md
