Turning to fashion in clothing, he draws on Simmel's analysis of fashion as simultaneously imitation and differentiation, and on Adorno's account of autonomous art, to argue fashion can never be autonomous art because it is inescapably functional and commodified, yet still counts as an art with classic and ephemeral, high and popular forms.

17.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
17.relation: Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.

18.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
18.file: ch18 - FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
18.relation: Brunstein surveys emerging wearable technology — solar-charging jackets, the M-Dress cell-phone dress, invisibility cloaks, the Hug Shirt, Diana Eng's Heartbeat Hoodie — framed by superhero costumes (Wonder Woman's lasso, Iron Man's exoskeleton) and Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto.' She argues that as garments start to *do* things and integrate aesthetically, the grotesque cyborg becomes the glamorous 'supermodel' cyborg, and that this reshapes how we construct the self. Her central philosophical lens is Clark and Chalmers's 'extended mind' / active externalism (with the Tetris example): if clothing becomes a functional extension of cognition, our garments' capabilities become part of a reconstructed self.

20.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
20.relation: Yim argues that clothing is a primary vehicle for autonomy, authenticity, and moral solidarity. Drawing on Mill's *On Liberty* and 'experiments in living,' he treats a teenager testing modest-vs-expressive dress against her mother, and 'Fashion Freaks' patterns for wheelchair users, as cases where wardrobe choice actualizes self-determination. He then reads dress as an emblem of communal solidarity and critique — the 1968 Smith/Carlos Olympic salute, the Israeli Kibbutz and Amish plain dress (with Rumspringa as a test of authenticity), gang colors, hippie androgyny, vegan 'cruelty-free' clothing, gay Levi's 501s, and Lubna Hussein's trouser trial in Sudan — concluding 'we are what we wear.'

21.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
21.file: ch21 - FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
21.relation: Brennan argues that fashion sits at the boundary of public and private and is central to the 'sexual citizen' and the politics of recognition for gay, lesbian, and bisexual people. Using Hanson on philosophy's gendered fear of fashion and Phelan/Weeks/Walker on visibility as a political strategy, she shows that queer identities (femme, boi, hanky codes) are communicative and require a community that reads them — offering a 'private hanky' argument echoing Wittgenstein's private-language point. She draws on her own experience (labrys earring, later bisexual invisibility) and on Butler-style gender performativity to argue visibility empowers recognition but marginalizes those, like femmes, who cannot be read.

22.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
22.file: ch22 - FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
22.relation: Ashwell and Langton ask whether fashion is a 'badge of slavery' (Wollstonecraft), opening with Socrates in the *Phaedo* disdaining adornment and Rousseau's girl who becomes 'her own doll,' and using Kant's humanity formula and Nussbaum's seven-feature account of objectification. Focusing on denial of autonomy in ordinary followers, they distinguish the 'Servile Fashionista' (obeys experts) from the 'Sensible Fashionista' (follows what looks good), then argue that via Johnston's 'authority of affect' even the sensible one is under an *epistemic* bondage: fashion's extrinsic social pull is misperceived as the garment's intrinsic goodness, a projective illusion (like the Müller-Lyer) that on a Kantian view undermines agency and masks misogynist or racist norms such as straightened hair or the 'lotus feet' of stilettos.

23.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
23.relation: Collins analyzes paradigmatic Barbie play — dressing the doll and identifying with her as an idealized future self, from the 1959 TV ad to BarbieGirls.com — arguing it trains girls to define identity through fashionable bodily self-presentation for a male gaze (Brumberg's 'body project'). Using Sandra Bartky's feminist reworking of Foucault's *Discipline and Punish*, she treats beauty norms as a discipline producing 'docile bodies' whose self-surveillance internalizes a 'panoptical male connoisseur' (Bentham's Panopticon), offering cycles of pleasure and pain that bind women without any single sovereign to blame. Rather than banning Barbie (the failed 'Happy to be Me' doll), she proposes subversive play — Plump and Proud Barbie, Mursi lip-plate Barbie — as Heyes-style 'practices of freedom.'

25.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
25.relation: Pierlott examines sweatshops in the garment industry through the lens of ancient Cynicism (Antisthenes, the Stoics' Zeno of Citium and his thieving slave), using the Cynic critique of fashion-driven consumption to strip legitimacy from the demand that feeds sweatshops. He rebuts the 'inevitability argument' (comparing it to excusing the Holocaust as inevitable) and the free-choice defense using Aristotle's category of 'mixed' action — sweated workers' consent is coerced by desperate alternatives — and argues, via Adam Smith on the undervaluing of labor, that giant retailers like Wal-Mart distort natural labor prices. He stresses that sweatshops overwhelmingly exploit young women, tying objectification of women as fashion consumers to their oppression as producers.

26.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
26.file: ch26 - FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
26.relation: Cassidy, through an interior monologue of a shopper eyeing Indonesian-made sandals, weighs individual responsibility for consumerism. She contrasts Singer's drowning-child duty to relieve suffering with Pogge's 'you break it, you buy it' claim that the Global North caused Southern poverty, then uses Scheffler's 'restricted' common-sense responsibility and Cannon's butterfly-effect virtues (replacing the American Dream's acquisitiveness with interconnectedness). Adapting Claudia Card, she distinguishes three senses of responsibility — credit (backward-looking blame), management (of one's lifestyle), and care-taking — and, invoking Noddings's ethics of care, argues that since globalization's impact is uncertain we should shift from assigning blame to caring *about* distant workers, buying less out of boredom-driven habit.

27.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
27.relation: La Caze rehabilitates fashion against Kant's own dismissal of it (in the *Anthropology*) as vanity and imitation, arguing that Kant's aesthetics actually supply the tools to value it. She applies his account of the disinterested judgment of taste, free vs. adherent beauty, and 'genius' (originality that provides an exemplary model — Chanel's freer dressing, Dior's New Look, punk DIY, the Sartorialist's street style) to both the making and the wearing of clothes. Drawing on Kant's claim that the beautiful is a symbol of the morally good and the 'virtues of social intercourse,' and on Iris Marion Young's pleasures of touch, bonding, and fantasy, she argues fashion can be a proto-moral, cosmopolitan force, countering Plato's, Beauvoir's, and Svendsen's denigration.

8.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
8.relation: In this foreword, historian Stephen Nissenbaum frames the book's central puzzle by asking the reader to picture Santa Claus kneeling in the Bethlehem manger and feeling why the image jars. He argues Christmas began as a fourth-century compromise: the Church Fathers fixed Jesus' birthday on December 25 to co-opt Saturnalia and the solstice and to refute Docetism (the claim Christ only 'seemed' to have a body) by giving him a human birthday. He traces how the resulting tension between piety and revelry led the Puritans to ban Christmas and how the secular, commercial Santa of Moore's 1823 poem came to dominate the American holiday, leaving the manger and the sleigh perpetually unreconciled.

9.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
9.relation: Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.

10.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
10.file: ch10 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md

11.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
11.file: ch11 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
11.relation: Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.

12.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
12.file: ch12 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
12.relation: Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.

13.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
13.file: ch13 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
13.relation: Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.

14.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
14.file: ch14 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md

15.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
15.file: ch15 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
15.relation: Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.

16.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
16.file: ch16 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
16.relation: Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.

17.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
17.relation: Mark Mercer argues that a now largely secular Christmas can help build a liberal, rather than communitarian, multicultural society. He distinguishes liberal multiculturalism, which prizes each individual's flourishing and rests on respect, equality and decency, from communitarian multiculturalism, which treats cultural groups as basic units and breeds identity politics and envy. He detaches Christmas from its Christian origins – trees, lights and Santa now embodying good will and generosity rather than doctrine – and against those who would ban public displays or say only 'Season's Greetings', contends that a shared secular Christmas is one of the few common holidays that can bind citizens of a diverse society together.

18.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
18.file: ch18 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
18.relation: Haire and Nelson read the film A Christmas Story as evidence that consumerism has replaced religion as America's faith: the Parker family shows no religious markers, and Ralphie's single-minded quest for the Red Ryder BB gun mirrors the identity-defining, transformative role religion once played. Using Aristotle's virtue ethics, they name consumerism a Christmas vice opposed to candidate Christmas virtues of being religious, traditional and family-centered. When the BB gun nearly blinds Ralphie and the hounds ruin the turkey, the consumerist ideal fails; the family's makeshift Chinese-restaurant dinner shows the family-centered virtue overcoming the vice, so 'all was right with the world'.

20.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
20.relation: Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.

21.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
21.file: ch21 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
21.relation: Hancuff and O'Connor read the song 'Santa Claus Is Coming to Town' and films like The Polar Express and Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town through Foucault's Discipline and Punish. Santa's all-seeing list-checking is a version of Bentham's Panopticon: children, watched but never seeing the watcher, internalize permanent visibility and discipline themselves. Invoking Foucault's Power/Knowledge and discursive practices, they argue the surveillance does not actually make children 'good for goodness' sake' – punishment is rarely delivered – but instead disciplines them into wish-lists and consumption, training them to be good consumers in late-capitalist culture, with Santa doubling as a corporate pitchman (Coke, Budweiser).

22.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
22.file: ch22 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
22.relation: Will Williams recounts the legend that St. Nicholas of Myra, the historical basis of Santa Claus, attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and punched the heretic Arius, who taught that the Son was created and not fully God ('there was a time when the Son was not'). Setting the fight to a parody of 'The Night Before Christmas', Williams explains via Athanasius why the divinity of Christ mattered – only if Jesus is truly God can his death secure salvation. He contrasts this fiercely theological bishop with the de-Christianized modern Santa, using the syncretism of 'Here Comes Santa Claus' to argue Nicholas would deplore what consumerist Christmas has become.

23.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
23.relation: Brophy prosecutes Santa for 'elfploitation,' treating the North Pole workshop like an overseas sweatshop (with Willy Wonka's Oompa-Loompahs and Rowling's house-elfs as parallels) and dismantling a Nozickian entitlement-theory defense: the elfs' 'consent' is coerced by their bleak alternatives, so absolute property rights fail just as Locke's desert water-hole owner must grant access. He diagnoses the elfs' apparent contentment as Marxian false consciousness, invokes Kant's humanity formula to condemn using rational elfs as mere means, and rejects the utilitarian 'greatest happiness' justification via Le Guin's Omelas and Rawls's veil of ignorance. He concludes with a call to boycott Christmas until Santa's labor practices become transparent.

25.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
25.relation: Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.

26.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
26.file: ch26 - Christmas Philosophy for Everyone.md
26.relation: Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.

27.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
27.relation: Hales uses Nietzsche's verdict that truth matters less than a myth's usefulness (The Gay Science, The Anti-Christ) to argue Santa Claus is a truer exemplar of Christmas than Jesus. He traces Nietzsche's account of God's degeneration from a proud tribal mascot like Yahweh into a trivialized 'domestic servant,' and the 'death of God' as belief becoming useless. Documenting Christmas's commercial, pagan origins (Sol Invictus, Saturnalia, Mithras on December 25), he casts Santa as a practical, this-worldly demigod propped up by movies and NORAD — a giver who, unlike the credit-demanding Christian God, wants no thanks, embodying anonymous selfless generosity and thus the god Nietzsche awaited.

28.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
28.relation: Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.

30.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
30.relation: Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.

31.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
31.relation: Mason, a developmental psychologist writing as a Pagan, narrates her decades-long religious journey through James Fowler's Stages of Faith model, using each stage to reinterpret Christmas. She recounts childhood confusion over carols and chimney-invading strangers, fundamentalist-Christian zeal (stage 3 group belonging, then stage-4 doubt as she 'crusaded' against pagan Christmas trees), Unitarian Universalist questioning, and finally Wiccan/Pagan practice centered on Hecate and the winter-solstice Wheel of the Year (rediscovering Christmas's pagan roots in holly, mistletoe, and Yule). Reaching Fowler's stage 5 'Conjunctive Faith,' she concludes Christmas is neither hers nor anyone's to own but a self-perpetuating commercial 'Hallmark' phenomenon she can now greet with equanimity.

32.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
32.relation: Holt argues that Seinfeld's Festivus, invented by Frank Costanza as an anti-consumerist 'holiday for the rest of us,' is grounded in American pragmatism: truth is 'whatever works,' malleable and tested by results. Because commercialized Christmas fails to deliver the altruism it demands, it 'does not work' and by pragmatist standards ceases to be true, so Costanza pragmatically forges a holiday that fits his needs. Holt reads Festivus's elements pragmatically — the maintenance-free aluminum pole as a bare functional symbol, the airing of grievances as a needed cathartic release from everyday restraint, the wrestling as self-perpetuating ritual — and warns that as Festivus merchandise spreads it will lose its practicality and, being no longer pragmatic, be discarded; he closes with a mock 'airing of grievances' against philosophers including Plato and Bertrand Russell.

33.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
33.relation: Scheopner argues that the secular Santa Claus can serve as a cross-cultural, cross-religious point of connection, using a barefoot, shaka-waving Santa at Honolulu Hale in ethnically and religiously plural Hawaii as her central example. She contends Santa sidesteps the Establishment Clause conflicts that dog nativity displays — reviewing Lynch v. Donnelly and County of Allegheny v. ACLU, where crèches on public property were scrutinized while 'diluted' or tree-accompanied displays passed — and notes that early Puritan and Hawaiian missionaries actually banned Christmas. Because Santa is a universal yet customizable figure (signing Santas, ethnic Santas, a hypothetical Cowboy or Steeler Santa), he can represent a whole civic community's shared identity without marking citizens as religiously different.

34.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
34.relation: In a comic first-person afterword, Santa Claus reviews the book, recounting how he was 'guilt-tripped' into an annual gift-giving role that outlived even his death, distinguishing himself from pretenders like Odin, Thor, and the demonic Krampus. He endorses Steven Hales's claim that he outdoes Jesus at Christmas and accepts charges of consumerism and even elf 'labor exploitation' (with a jab at Marx over variable costs), but objects to the one assumption every contributor shares — that he does not exist — pleading for a little blind faith and threatening to put every doubting philosopher-contributor on the Naughty List.

9.title: CYCLING
9.relation: O'Brien's editorial introduction frames gardening as engaging core philosophical questions and previews the volume. It argues that gardening promotes a good life not through hedonistic pleasure but through virtuous traits like patience and a Stoic-tinged tranquility that ancient philosophers from Epicurus to Hume prized, and it invokes Kant to cast the gardener as a visual artist. It also sketches gardens as cosmic symbols (Pythagorean ratios at Versailles) and closes on Plato's Phaedrus image of educating the soul as tending plants.

10.title: CYCLING
10.file: ch10 - CYCLING.md

11.title: GARDENING
11.file: ch11 - GARDENING.md
11.relation: Isis Brook argues that gardening objectively improves both the land (through composting, nurturing plants, and Warwick Fox's 'responsive cohesion' with wider contexts) and the gardener's moral character. Taking a virtue-ethics approach and drawing on David Cooper, she holds that gardening practices incidentally cultivate patience, humility, recognition of reality, care for others, and open-heartedness. She uses concrete cases—Sackville-West's white garden at Sissinghurst, her own failed Cerinthe and thriving ferns—to show how collaborating with nature nurtures these flourishing-related virtues.

12.title: GARDENING
12.file: ch12 - GARDENING.md
12.relation: Meghan Ray reads classical agrarian texts to show that Greeks and Romans invested cultivating the soil with civic, moral, and religious meaning. Through Hesiod's Works and Days and Xenophon's Oeconomicus (with its Gardener/King Cyrus), and the Roman Scriptores Rei Rusticae (Cato, Varro, Columella) plus Virgil's Georgics, she argues farming was portrayed as the only honorable, pious profession that builds character—diligence, endurance, justice—and sustains the state. The chapter connects horticulture to a virtue-centered vision of the good and righteous life.

13.title: GARDENING
13.file: ch13 - GARDENING.md
13.relation: Matthew Hall challenges the exclusion of plants from gardening ethics, tracing it to the Garden of Eden where plants are denied life and given only instrumental value for humans. Against this he sets kincentric alternatives—the Achuar mothering manioc, the Raramuri treating plants as kin, and the living apple trees of the Hesperides—and Albert Schweitzer's reverence-for-life ethic. He proposes gardeners offer plants three 'gifts': acknowledging their autonomy, giving them care, and giving weeds space, extending moral consideration to plant life itself.

14.title: GARDENING
14.file: ch14 - GARDENING.md
14.relation: Helene Gammack surveys the seventeenth-century self-sufficient English estate as a fusion of pleasure and productivity, using Schellinks's account of Bridge Place, Celia Fiennes's journals, and figures like John Evelyn and Sir William Temple (whose Upon the Gardens of Epicurus links fruit to health and tranquility). She traces dovecotes, fishponds, deer parks, orchards, and glasshouse exotics, and connects the modern 'grow your own' revival—driven by sustainability, food miles, and provenance—to that older harmony of beauty and use in cultivating food.

15.title: CYCLING
15.file: ch15 - CYCLING.md

16.title: GARDENING
16.file: ch16 - GARDENING.md
16.relation: Jo Day uses archaeological and textual evidence to argue that the earliest elite gardens of Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Minoan Crete carried symbolic roles beyond pleasure. Assyrian kings like Sennacherib and Ashurnasirpal II displayed captured exotic plants as 'botanical imperialism' and tokens of power over nature and conquered lands, while Egyptian temple and tomb gardens (Hatshepsut's incense trees, plants tied to deities) served ritual and mythic functions. The chapter shows the ancient garden as a stage for status, military prowess, and religious performance.

17.title: GARDENING
17.relation: Michael Moss examines how the British grew Brussels sprouts and other 'English' vegetables across the Empire to recreate home and 'put down roots,' reading gardens as tropes of Britishness and imperial identity. He draws on David Cooper's claim—rooted in Heidegger's and Merleau-Ponty's notions of dynamic, embodied engagement—that 'certain garden practices necessarily induce virtues,' which colonial writers invoked to justify gardening's moral and civilizing purpose. He exposes the irony that most 'British' vegetables were themselves appropriated introductions, mirroring Kew's plant-hunting empire.

18.title: GARDENING
18.file: ch18 - GARDENING.md
18.relation: Laura Auricchio shows how General Lafayette made his estate at La Grange an embodiment of liberal, transatlantic political ideals. Inspired by Washington as a Cincinnatus figure and by Arthur Young's agrarian reform, Lafayette imported American plants and English husbandry, keeping meticulous farm records and staging tours that framed the land around liberty (Fox's planted ivy, self-sufficiency, beneficent stewardship). The chapter argues his cultivation of crops and identity presented the garden as 'American ground' expressing natural rights and republican virtue.

19.title: GARDENING
19.relation: Elizabeth Scott argues that the wartime allotment gardens of East London's Poplar were engines of working-class political development. Through allotment associations, laboring men learned letter-writing, accounting, public speaking, and democratic self-governance, negotiating with borough councils and the Port of London Authority and building solidarity that fed movements like the Poplar Rates Rebellion. She reads the 10-rod plot as restoring self-sufficiency and citizenship to a disenfranchised class, making gardening a grassroots site of cooperation, socialist activism, and political enfranchisement.

21.title: GARDENING
21.file: ch21 - GARDENING.md
21.relation: MacDonald reads the garden at Dumbarton Oaks as a 'technology of enchantment,' arguing against the nature/culture dualism that frames gardening as either a 'battle' with or a 'fusion' of nature. Drawing on Jane Bennett's account of enchantment (wonder mixed with the uncanny) and actor-network theory, he treats the garden as a shifting assemblage of humans and non-humans—Charles Simonds's hybrid 'Growth' sculpture, leaking water pipes, the inscribed Arbor Terrace wall speaking with Dante's and Mildred Bliss's voices—whose surprising 'crossings, complexity, and circuits' produce magic. Descartes appears as the philosopher who prized wonder as the most fundamental passion, and the disenchantment-of-the-world narrative (Weber) is set against gardening as re-enchantment.

22.title: GARDENING
22.file: ch22 - GARDENING.md
22.relation: Barwell and Powell challenge Kant's classification of landscape gardening as a subcategory of painting ('for the eye only') by arguing that gardens, unlike static paintings or sculpture, essentially present the passing of time visually. Because gardens are made of living organisms that grow, flower, senesce and decay at different rates—an oak, a drift of crocuses, a managed lawn—they generate visual rhythms analogous to musical rhythm, with diurnal and seasonal cycles supplying a 'rhythmus firmus' (pulse and meter) that nature, not the designer, provides. Using Susanne Langer's claim that 'music makes the passage of time audible,' they conclude gardens make time visible and so deserve status as a distinctive art form.

23.title: GARDENING
23.relation: Shapiro argues that Frederick Law Olmsted's Central Park is a major artwork realizing a 'pragmatic picturesque,' and reads the English picturesque garden as a 'diagram' (in Foucault's and Deleuze's sense) of the glance—the roving, liberated look—explicitly contrasted with Bentham's Panopticon, the diagram of the objectifying gaze. Using Derrida's paradox of the frame, he shows the picturesque hides its boundary (the ha-ha) while Olmsted inverts the diagram, making the frame explicit and admitting the city so citizens meet in democratic 'gregarious' recognition—a Platonic argument (aesthetic education in the Republic) turned pragmatic in the climate of Peirce, James and Dewey. Christo and Jeanne-Claude's 'The Gates' distills the park's diagram as a gift of time.

25.title: GARDENING
25.relation: Neuman decodes the Bosquet de la Colonnade at Versailles as a symbolic Temple of Apollo that glorifies Louis XIV as overseer of cosmic harmony. He argues Hardouin-Mansart fused the circular peripteral temple with Hadrian's Maritime Theatre, and used simple ratios (1:2 bays) drawn from the Pythagorean-Platonic system of universal proportion—the harmony of the spheres tied to Apollo's seven-stringed lyre and seven planets—to align architecture, the seven planets, and monarchical order. The spandrel pairing of lyre and panpipe evokes the Apollo–Marsyas/Pan contests, read as the reason-versus-passion, Apollonian-versus-Dionysian dichotomy; the whole garden is also linked to Descartes's geometrization of boundless axial space.

26.title: GARDENING
26.file: ch26 - GARDENING.md
26.relation: Mara Miller argues gardens do not merely sit inside time but actively structure six kinds of time (scientific, objective/shared, kairos, subjective, temporality, historical), opening with Augustine's puzzle that he knows what time is until asked to explain it. She contrasts Greek chronos with kairos (the right moment to plant after the last frost), shows how Versailles propagated a shared time (eternal, historic, recurring) and eighteenth-century English landscape gardens taught the long-range vision capitalism needed, and describes cyclical 'eternal recurrence' (Eliade). Watching a dry Zen garden or fireflies, the visitor becomes the constant who notices—reworking Descartes's cogito as 'I notice, therefore I am'—while Japanese stepping-stones enforce a Buddhist mindfulness of impermanence in the present moment.

27.title: GARDENING
27.relation: O'Brien reads Voltaire's closing injunction in Candide, 'we must cultivate our garden,' through David Hume to argue that gardening is therapy—a retreat from metaphysics and religion into the tranquility of common life. Hume rejects belief in miracles and religious 'enthusiasm' not by logic but by recalling everyday reasoning (a melon seed, not a miracle, explains melons in the greenhouse), and the gardener is the sophisticated artisan-reasoner attuned to nature's regularities. Gardening inculcates Humean virtues (industry, patience, balancing action, pleasure and indolence) and Haybron's attunement/engagement/endorsement, yielding Epicurean ataraxia; the Sisyphean gardener (Camus) fighting slugs, and Wittgenstein taking up gardening as a cure, illustrate the point.

29.title: GARDENING
29.relation: Evans presents Texcotzingo, the hilltop garden-retreat of the fifteenth-century Texcocan king Nezahualcoyotl, as the achievement of an Aztec philosopher-king who was landscape designer, hydraulic engineer and statesman. She argues the botanical garden as a genre—a 'green encyclopedia' cataloguing a realm's flora—was pioneered by Aztec kings, and that within an animist cosmos where mountains and water pulse with sacred spirit, Nezahualcoyotl's aqueduct, pools and terraced gardens made the hill a living embodiment of the altepetl (the 'water-hill' city-state). The garden thus symbolically enacts his political domain, dynastic history (three pools for three ancestral capitals) and cosmic order, even as she cautions his reputation as poet and monotheist was inflated by later Spanish and Christian chroniclers.

30.title: GARDENING
30.relation: Campbell explains why Epicurus set his school in a walled garden on the edge of Athens ('Live unnoticed'), contrasting it with the Stoics' public Stoa: the Garden was a self-sufficient community of friends pursuing ataraxia through natural, necessary pleasures and philosophy as therapy for the soul. Drawing on Lucretius's account of prehistory in On the Nature of Things, he shows the Epicureans saw cities as a decadent fall—driven by the fear of death and the gods—from a near-paradise of proto-Epicurean friendship pacts, and read the garden and the locus amoenus of pastoral picnics as a recovered golden age. Diogenes of Oinoanda's inscription imagines a future in which all become gardening philosophers and city walls become redundant.

31.title: GARDENING
31.relation: Cotton reads the grower image in Plato's Phaedrus—the wise gardener who sows seed in proper soil for a slow harvest rather than the frivolous 'gardens of Adonis'—as Plato's model of philosophical education as natural growth. The educator plants logoi (discourse) in a 'proper soul,' where it must be cultivated by the learner's own reflection and eventually reproduces itself in others, against Thrasymachus's vessel model of pouring knowledge in. She connects this to the Republic's cave, the Apology's gadfly, and the Symposium/Theaetetus images of pregnancy and midwifery, then argues Plato's own aporetic, contradiction-laden dialogues and the corpus as a whole act as the wise grower, teaching readers to become 'gardeners of their own souls.'

13.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
13.file: ch13 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
13.relation: In this memoir (book Chapter 1, 'A Cannabis Odyssey'), Harvard psychiatrist Lester Grinspoon recounts how his 1967 review of the anti-marijuana literature convinced him he had been 'brainwashed' by a fear-based 'cannabis catechism,' coining 'cannabinophobia' and likening it to the 'madness of crowds.' He argues from personal use — hearing Sgt. Pepper for the first time, quitting psychoanalysis after 'stoned' self-critiques — that beyond recreation and medicine there is a third category, 'enhancement.' The piece is autobiographical drug-policy advocacy rather than the application of a specific named philosopher.

14.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
14.file: ch14 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
14.relation: Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.

15.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
15.file: ch15 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
15.relation: Hathaway and Sharpley analyze the cannabis experience of medical-'compassion club' users through Csikszentmihalyi's concept of 'flow.' They ground flow in William James's 'stream of consciousness' and in Taoism, reading Tao as 'a patterned flow of the universe' and wu wei as the effortless equilibrium users describe ('it just centers me,' 'I take an inventory on my soul'). Against Western monophasic medicine, they defend users' 'anecdotal' testimony as legitimate knowledge of a body–mind–spirit balance that cannabis restores.

16.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
16.file: ch16 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md

17.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
17.relation: Montagne's 'Buzz, High, and Stoned' argues that the cannabis experience is largely constituted by the metaphors users apply to it. Tracing hashish descriptions from Gautier, Baudelaire, Bayard Taylor, Ludlow and jazzman Mezz Mezzrow to modern song lyrics and Robert Crumb's 'Stoned Agin!' cartoon, he maps 'buzz,' 'high' and 'stoned' onto dose-dependent levels documented by Moreau (1845) and Charles Tart, and shows the words carry more meaning than pharmacology, shaping set, setting and behavior. The Greek 'pharmakon' (remedy/poison/charm) frames the analysis of meaning-making in drug language.

18.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
18.file: ch18 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
18.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.

19.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
19.relation: Clack's 'Cannabis and the Human Condition' reads intoxication through Freud's Civilization and its Discontents, where drugs are the 'crudest but most effective' palliative against a life 'too hard for us,' tied to the pleasure principle and the Nirvana/death-instinct drive to discharge stimulus. He supplements Freud with Schopenhauer's pessimism — life oscillating between suffering and boredom — to add 'stimulus hunger' Freud ignored, arguing cannabis both dampens and stokes the 'fire in the brain' depending on THC potency (high vs. stoned). He concludes that, like religion, art and love, cannabis augments a bleak existence, so 'all cannabis use is medicinal.'

21.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
21.file: ch21 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
21.relation: Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.

22.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
22.file: ch22 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
22.relation: Holt and Kaufman's 'Marijuana and Creativity' surveys creativity research (Guilford's divergent thinking — fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) and US drug law (Anslinger, 'Reefer Madness,' Schedule I) to test the popular belief, held via figures like Cheech and Chong, Bob Marley and Willie Nelson, that cannabis boosts creativity. Controlled THC-vs-placebo biscuit studies show no benefit — placebo groups who merely believed they were high scored higher, while actual THC reduced fluency and flexibility. They explain the persistent belief through placebo/expectancy effects, spurious correlation, and salience bias, concluding any drug–creativity link is 'manufactured in the drug user's mind.'

23.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
23.relation: Jacquette argues that cannabis opens a 'creative inner space' of loosened associations but is skeptical it yields genuine, lasting insight, using Ginsberg's claim to have newly 'apprehended the structure' of jazz and classical music and the conjecture that Shakespeare's Sonnet 76 'invention in a noted weed' hints he wrote high. He treats the aesthetic case as a phenomenology problem: separating cannabis's real contribution to appreciation from mere buzz-glow. He then defends a right to get high by invoking the Declaration's 'pursuit of happiness' and a Mill-style principle that private, non-harming pleasure should not be criminalized.

25.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
25.relation: Thorsby reads 'getting high' as a rupture of ordinary, unreflective consciousness and asks why cannabis use grows fastest in the affluent capitalist West. He pairs Plato's allegory of the cave—ordinary consciousness as prisoners mistaking shadows for reality—with Marx's account of alienation and commodity fetishism, in which workers are estranged from the products of their labor and see value as inhering in things rather than in human labor. Drawing on Fromm's 'having vs. being,' he argues that cannabis offers a momentary escape from and critique of this alienated consciousness, though it cannot cure it.

26.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
26.file: ch26 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
26.relation: Tahko surveys the empirical evidence on cannabis from the standpoint of the individual and of society, concluding that its health harms (respiratory illness, mild cognitive impairment, possible dependence, weak links to psychosis) pale beside those of alcohol and tobacco. He argues the gravest costs—legal risk, social isolation, contaminated black-market supply—are consequences of prohibition itself, not the drug. Endorsing public-health experts, he recommends abandoning elimination-based policy for a harm-reduction approach modeled on the Dutch coffee-shop system and Portuguese decriminalization.

27.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
27.relation: Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.

29.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
29.relation: Musselman, Frohardt, and Lynch defend adult cannabis use through Mill's Harm Principle, using the hypothetical 'Patrick the pot smoker'—a professional who grows and smokes moderately on Friday nights—to argue that competent adults' self-regarding conduct is their own affair and does not violate the 'distinct and assignable obligations' Mill owes to family. They marshal health data (no lung-cancer link, negligible secondhand exposure, neuroprotective effects) to rebut the harm-to-others claim, and invoke Mill's higher intellectual pleasures plus the Michael-Phelps case to argue prohibition wastes resources better spent on the greater harms of alcohol and tobacco.

30.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
30.relation: Earleywine dissects the moral versus practical arguments over prohibition, attacking legal moralism—the drug-czar claim (Bennett, Wilson) that use is wrong simply because it is immoral—as circular, and noting that the law does not criminalize every immoral act (broken contracts, lying). He shows purported moral arguments collapse into utilitarian harm estimates that the data undercut, since use rates are essentially orthogonal to policy across Amsterdam, Australia, Portugal, and US states. He then weighs anti-prohibition rights arguments (religion, privacy in Ravin, property via Szasz, self-determination) and closes on proportionality: owning a harmless plant merits no punishment.

31.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
31.relation: Schick asks whether humans need to alter consciousness (Weil, Maslow's hierarchy, Siegel's animal examples of reindeer, elephants, and rats seeking intoxicants) and concludes we have no such need, though we can flourish from it. He applies Sen and Nussbaum's capabilities approach, arguing cannabis enhances Nussbaum's second (bodily health, via endocannabinoids and medical uses) and fourth (senses, imagination, thought, via enriched music perception and possible creativity) capabilities. Citing Aristotle's and the Buddha's golden mean against abuse, and evidence of no lasting brain harm, he judges paternalistic prohibition an unjustified deprivation of the capabilities needed for a good life.

32.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
32.relation: Funke examines how the 'gateway' argument is supposed to work by treating it as a claim about weakness of will, split into two mechanisms. Motivational externalism—illustrated by Milgram's obedience experiments and Doris's situationism—holds that the illicit-market situation, not the drug, pushes users toward hard drugs, which implies legalization, not prohibition. Motivational internalism, using Michael Smith's contest between normative and motivational reasons and second-order desires, locates the risk in cannabis's creative 'analysis paralysis' and idealizing imagination; Funke argues that this imaginative value, like religion, is worth its risk and that neuropharmacology (THC's distinct cannabinoid mechanism) undercuts the internalist gateway claim.

8.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
8.relation: Hans Florine's foreword frames climbing as a way of posing philosophical questions rather than settling them, echoing the book's 'it's the journey' ethos, and previews debates the volume takes up: the sanity/morality of free soloing, hold chipping, and how routes are graded. Florine describes himself as an Ayn Rand Objectivist who also carries Buddhist concern and treats logic as a reliable tool, and calls the 100-percent focus of climbing 'physical meditation.' No taxonomy philosopher (Rand) is actually deployed in argument; the piece is a personal, agenda-setting foreword rather than a sustained application of a philosophical position.

10.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
10.file: ch10 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
10.relation: Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.

11.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
11.file: ch11 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md

12.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
12.file: ch12 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
12.relation: Kevin Krein argues that the freedom climbers report feeling is not freedom of movement, political freedom, or free will—on those measures a roped climber pinned on a ledge is less free—but the Stoic freedom of aligning one's will with what nature allows. Using Chrysippus' tethered-dog image and the Stoic identification of human logos with cosmic reason, he claims the climber who understands and accepts the mountain's conditions and wills only what it permits becomes free, which is why experienced climbers feel freest when their options are fewest. He adds Epictetus' dichotomy of control: the mountain (storms, avalanches, one's own failing body) is largely outside our power, so limiting desire to what we control—composure, choices, effort—is how a climber stays free in any conditions.

13.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
13.file: ch13 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
13.relation: Prompted by the avalanche death of his climbing partner Charlie on the Super Couloir, Paul Charlton uses Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism to ask whether the risks of climbing can be ethically justified, insisting that blindly accepting risk is indefensible but deliberate, reasoned risk can be right. He weighs climbing's costs (frivolity, self-focus, danger to self and to grieving family) against its intrinsic value (joy, friendship, aesthetic experience) and instrumental value (cultivating human excellence, psychological growth, reprioritized lives), invoking Mill's higher/lower pleasures to argue quality of happiness matters, not just quantity. His conclusion is that climbing can be justified only when it produces more overall good than any alternative use of that time, leaving each climber to run the calculation for their own case.

14.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
14.file: ch14 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
14.relation: Joe Fitschen distinguishes justifying climbing (weak, self-revealing answers) from explaining why humans climb, and offers an evolutionary, naturalistic explanation: the ability and pleasure of climbing are inherited arboreal dispositions that were not selected out and can still have utility, so Mallory's 'because it's there' names a real, gene-rooted urge. He deploys Wittgenstein's analysis of 'game' and family resemblances to block the fallacy of universality—the fact that some people lack the urge to climb says nothing against its evolutionary roots—and warns against teleological thinking about traits. He also treats climbing's pleasures (physical, aesthetic, emotional) and its style-based ethics (bolting disputes, ego vs. the pleasure of the experience) as expressions of an evolved, social human nature.

15.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
15.file: ch15 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
15.relation: Heidi Howkins Lockwood examines the 'asymmetry thesis'—that a climber's gratuitous risk is less acceptable than an astronaut's necessary risk—and argues its two standard defenses fail: the Rule of Rescue is neither necessary (free soloists need no rescue yet are condemned) nor sufficient (Hornbein and Unsoeld's risky Everest traverse was praised because it succeeded), and the argument from compassion collapses into circularity. She then shows the intuition is really driven by external background assumptions, especially gender inequality: the media vilified climber-mother Alison Hargreaves while lauding astronaut-mother Christa McAuliffe, because ambition-for-profit violates the 'traditionally female' role of service. She concedes a limited, defensible version tied to the assumption that seeking risk as a mere end (rather than an ineliminable means) is irresponsible.

16.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
16.file: ch16 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md

17.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
17.relation: Brian Treanor argues from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that climbing is a crucible for cultivating virtues (arete) that contribute to flourishing (eudaimonia), stressing that virtue is acquired by habituation and lies in a mean 'relative to us'—so casting off on the Bachar-Yerian is courage for a 5.11 leader but rashness for a 5.9 climber. He shows how climbing's self-imposed 'rules' (Tejada-Flores' games) forge courage (feeling the right balance of fear and confidence, as in John Sherman's Fisher Towers epic and Steve House's judicious retreats on K7), humility (honestly measuring oneself against pioneers who used inferior gear, per Chouinard and Messner's 'murder of the impossible'), and reverence for nature (Thoreau, Muir, Brower). His thesis is that in a coddled, technological world climbing is uncommonly well suited to building these excellences of character.

18.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
18.file: ch18 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
18.relation: Pam Sailors distinguishes two kinds of high-altitude climber: the goal-oriented 'summiteer,' who pursues the summit at all costs for self-affirmation and may neglect others, and the process-oriented 'mountaineer,' who seeks relationship with the mountain, attains self-transcendence, and feels moral responsibility for comrades. Drawing on J. S. Russell and Jonathan Simon, and on cases like the 2006 abandonment of David Sharp versus Dan Mazur giving up his summit to save Lincoln Hall, she argues both types find value in dangerous sport but that the mountaineer—exhibiting courage, compassion, and care—is the morally better person. She backs this with Reinhold Messner, Ed Viesturs, and Sherpa judgment that mountains are not conquered but simply allow, or do not allow, us to climb them.

19.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
19.relation: Philip Ebert and Simon Robertson defend the self-sufficiency thesis (S): other things being equal, the more self-sufficiently a mountaineering objective is achieved, the better the achievement. Ranking Hermann Buhl's solo, free, alpine-style first ascent of Nanga Parbat above a hypothetical roped-team version and far above a guided, oxygen-and-porter Everest ascent, they argue self-sufficiency (alpine over siege, solo over team, free over aid) is good because it is more committing and adventurous and is partly constitutive of mountaineering itself. They handle objections about foolhardiness (Lafaille on Makalu), incomparable routes (Lhotse South Face), teamwork, and blind climber Erik Weihenmayer via an 'other things being equal' clause, and conclude self-sufficiency acts as a catalyst raising the subjective difficulty and thus the value of every other mountaineering good.

20.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
20.relation: Ben Levey uses the fast-food (sport) versus haute-cuisine (trad) analogy and then Hegel's Phenomenology to argue that trad climbing offers a more authentic experience than sport climbing. Applying the master–slave dialectic, he casts the trad climber (like his mentor Martin risking a groundfall on 'Resurrection' placing natural protection) as the slave: through genuine fear, the setting aside of desire, and work that leaves the rock in its independent, unaltered state, the climber comes to identify with the world rather than dominate it. Sport climbing, where bolts subordinate the rock's natural features to the climber's chosen safe line, corresponds to the master who never overcomes the world's independence, yielding only the limited satisfaction of having played the game ethically.

21.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
21.file: ch21 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
21.relation: Eric Swan argues that climbing embodies the principles and spirit of Zen, the experience of 'ordinary mind' finding the extraordinary in the ordinary and living fully in the present. Tracing Zen from the Buddha's Flower Sermon and Bodhidharma through Suzuki's 'Beginner's Mind' and Huineng's finger-and-moon, he maps Zen's four training paths—physical work, zazen (sitting meditation), koans, and interviews with masters—onto climbing: routes are like koans solved by insight and action rather than logic, 'being in the zone' is meditative absorption, and breath-regulation at the crux is zazen in motion. He holds up free soloist Derek Hersey, grinning hundreds of feet up Eldorado Canyon, and Chris Sharma, who writes of flowing 'like water' on the rock, as modern Zen masters who dissolve the separation between self, climb, and world.

23.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
23.relation: Scott reads three landmark climbs as expressions of the tension between individual freedom and community standards. He casts John Bachar's bold, ground-up, run-out Bachar-Yerian and its self-mastery ethic as a partial embodiment of Nietzsche's Übermensch and will to power, and Alan Watts' rule-breaking sport route To Bolt or Not to Be as an exercise of Mill's On Liberty defense of originality and diversity that benefits the whole community. Against both thinkers' negative view of community, he uses Charles Taylor's 'horizon of significance' to argue that Sonnie Trotter's The Path gains its meaning only through dialogue with the climbing community and its traditions.

24.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
24.relation: Ramsey applies the methods of practical/applied ethics to the taboo of hold manufacturing ('chipping'), using Peter Singer's drowning-child argument as his model of following an argument to its uncomfortable conclusion. He builds a syllogism: since climbers accept modifying rock (removing loose rock, vegetation) to make routes climbable, and hold manufacturing is another such modification, manufacturing is sometimes acceptable. He dismantles four common objections (safety, environment, harming future climbers, slippery slope) to argue the near-universal condemnation of chipping is an unjustified bias inconsistent with climbers' actual practices, like the chiseled Jardine Traverse on The Nose.

25.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
25.relation: Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.

26.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
26.file: ch26 - Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone.md
26.relation: Murray argues that the ecologically conscious climber's doubt that her single climb matters is a version of the free-rider problem, which he claims is just the sorites paradox (the paradox of the heap, illustrated with trail cairns built one stone fewer each time) applied to social life. Because 'environmental degradation' is a vaguely specified term with no precise tipping point, he draws on Timothy Williamson's account of vagueness and Richard Tuck's history of free-riding to argue climbers should act 'as if' a threshold exists and see themselves as sufficient (not necessary) causes of preservation, justifying self-restraint and quota systems.

27.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
27.relation: Halbert uses a Hawaiian route-setter friend upset that his 'secret' crag went public to argue climbing culture is a gift economy that defies Locke's labor theory of property and the self-interest of Locke and Adam Smith. Route setters spend money and labor establishing climbs, then give them freely to a commons, exemplifying Kropotkin's social-anarchist mutual aid over Social Darwinist competition. Citing the Red River Gorge Coalition and Muir Valley, she recasts Hardin's tragedy of the commons as Carol Rose's 'comedy of the commons,' where more participants enhance rather than diminish the shared value.

29.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
29.relation: Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.

30.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
30.relation: Graziano rejects the 'orthodox view' that a climbing grade like Serenity Crack's 5.10d is subjective (beauty in the eye of the beholder) and argues for realism about grades. Using Locke's primary/secondary quality distinction and his dispositional account of hardness, he defends 'relationalism': a grade is a real disposition of the rock to challenge a standard climber in standard conditions, just as hardness is a real disposition. He supports this with Pinched Rib changing from 5.7 to 5.10b when a hold broke, and argues the orthodox view confuses what a grade IS with how we determine it, rejecting even the 'weakly objective' money analogy.

31.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
31.relation: Karlsen argues that climbing routes are genuine aesthetic objects and that judging a route beautiful is a real aesthetic judgment, not mere pleasure. Against Kant's demand that beauty require detachment (which would confine climbing to the 'merely agreeable') and against Aristotle's exclusion of the bodily senses, he distinguishes a 'line' (seen from the ground, like The Nose) from a 'route' (actually climbed) and contends that proprioception, the felt sense of bodily movement, yields information about the route itself, not just the body. Invoking the phenomenological 'transparency of experience' (Moore's diaphanousness), he concludes proprioception is an aesthetic sense that lets widely-agreed classics emerge.

7.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
7.file: ch07 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
7.relation: This foreword by Rocky Rakovic, editor of Inked magazine, argues that tattoos were a 'harbinger of Twitter' – both are technologies of everyman self-expression born of a 'me generation' told it could be anything. It traces how reality-TV shows like Miami Ink and LA Ink, and figures such as Kat Von D, moved tattooing from the sailor-and-scofflaw margins into mainstream fashion, citing the Pew figure that forty percent of Americans aged 26–40 are tattooed. The connection to philosophy is thematic rather than argued: ink as individualist fashion that lets people 'scream their identity on their skin.'

8.file: ch08 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
8.relation: Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.

11.relation: Charles Taliaferro and Mark Odden survey the history and nature of tattooing – from the 3200 BCE Iceman's fifty-seven tattoos and Aetius' Constantinople recipe, through Leviticus' prohibition, Polynesian and Japanese irezumi, to Nazi concentration-camp numbering – to argue tattoos carry competing cultural (public) and individual (private) meanings. They advance a 'double skin' theory: a tattoo is both visible image and buried marking, juxtaposing interiority and exteriority. Their closing Lincoln puzzle ('calling a tail a leg doesn't make it a leg') stresses the body's stubborn reality and the 'inescapable seriousness' of permanently relabeling one's skin.

12.file: ch12 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
12.relation: Juniper Ellis shows tattoos resist any single interpretive scheme by running through cases: Loos and Lacassagne's criminological 'I tattoo, therefore I will commit murder'; the biblical Mark of Cain and St. Paul's stigmata as signs of protection and salvation; Lacan's claim that the tattoo is the first signifier that marks off the human subject; and Pacific tatau (Te Pehi Kupe's moko-as-signature, Queequeg's unreadable Moby-Dick tattoo) that incorporates a person into a collective. She reads Kant's Critique of Judgment dismissal of Maori tattooing and invokes Levinas' 'the face speaks' to argue a tattooed face is eloquent speech, crossing lines between individual and collective, saint and criminal.

14.relation: Nicolas Michaud asks whether tattoos are art by testing three theories against them: art world (institutional) theory, under which tattoos are not yet art because the artworld has not admitted them; formalism (Clive Bell's 'significant form'), under which a well-composed tattoo qualifies but its human canvas is irrelevant; and Tolstoyan expressionism, under which an emotionally infectious tattoo (his example of a broken-chain tattoo over an abuse survivor's bruise) counts. He concludes tattoos are best understood as performance art – like Duchamp mustaching the Mona Lisa, the living, mortal, changing human canvas adds context and meaning, making tattoos reflect on art and our own death.

15.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
15.file: ch15 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
15.relation: Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.

17.relation: Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues contemporary female tattoos have lost their one-dimensional identifying function and instead create a new 'tattoo space.' He dismantles the paradoxical 'savage/civilized' and 'nature/purity' schemes (drawing on Baudrillard on the smooth, made-up female body-screen that reflects male desire) and Loos' 'ornament and crime' verdict on women's tattoos. He proposes that female tattoos have 'become graffiti' – a Bergsonian spatial 'center of action' and 'skinscape' that disperses meaning horizontally rather than branding an identity, recuperating the female body as a political body against commercialized post-political bodies.

18.file: ch18 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
18.relation: Nancy Kang argues tattoos can function within a liberatory feminist ideology, accentuating rather than diminishing femininity by exposing the differential treatment of tattooed women. She surveys radical, Marxist, liberal and corporeal feminism (invoking Aristotle's dismissal of women, Mill's Subjection of Women, and Gramsci's hegemony), then reads pop-culture cases – Crash's tattooed Latino worker, Black Swan's Lily, the Perry 'pricks as needles' sexualization, carnival 'Tattooed Ladies' like Irene Woodward marked 'by the father's hand,' and the McGee/Bullock/Kat Von D scandal – to show corporeal feminism treats tattooing as a risky, self-owning revolutionary act.

20.relation: Kyle Fruh and Emily Thomas use tattoos to attack two questions of personal identity. Against Locke's dominant psychological (memory) account and for the unpopular somatic (bodily) account defended by Judith Thomson and Eric Olson, they argue the depth of people's attachment to their tattoos – individuating them or marking group membership – shows we identify with our bodies. On the 'Who am I?' question they argue tattoos have an 'anchoring effect' in narrative identity: permanent, irremovable ink (contrasted with new laser-removable ink, and with dehumanizing forced Auschwitz numbers) fixes a commitment 'come what may,' echoing Quine's phrase, so that 'when you get a tattoo, you tattoo you.'

21.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
21.file: ch21 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
21.relation: Rachel Falkenstern argues that although tattoos seem permanent, the embodied self is changing and finite, so tattoos are 'illusions of permanence.' Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology she dissolves the mind/body and self/tattoo boundary (we are our bodies, the world shapes us and we shape it); using the German aesthetic tradition from Kant to Hegel she reads a tattoo as a sensuous 'appearance of freedom' and links the Romantic notion of Bildung (self-formation) to choosing ink. She adds Foucault's aesthetic self-transformation and Shusterman's somaesthetics/Deweyan pragmatism to cast tattooing as reciprocal self-expression and self-creation that offers a glimpse of infinity within finitude.

22.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
22.file: ch22 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
22.relation: Clancy Smith argues that a tattoo's ink is permanent but the memory it evokes is not, because the past no longer exists and recollection is always present and in flux (citing Heraclitus' river and William James on never-identical brain states). Using Augustine's 'present of things past' and Proust's Swann's Way, plus Dewey's immediate empiricism and Merleau-Ponty's critique of memory-as-projection, he contends that gazing at a tattoo (his 'Not Fade Away' epitaph tattoo, his friend Kalju's crossed-rifles, American History X's swastika) constructs a present meaning that tells us who we are now rather than recovering the past intact.

24.relation: Felipe Carvalho frames a friend 'Toby's' worry – tattoos are forever, so should one be impulsive or cautious? – as a problem about bodily freedom versus irreversible change. He rejects the hedonist position (seize the day, regret is just part of freedom) as too simple and the Millian position (drawing on Mill's On Liberty argument that one cannot freely alienate one's freedom, as in selling oneself into slavery) as too precautionary, noting his friend's happy irreversible ear surgery. He proposes a 'middle path' learned from the tattoo community: a complex interplay of motif, the tattooist-as-artist, and the body-as-canvas that lets permanence guide more principled choices – so no 'I Love Becky' tattoos.

25.file: ch25 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
25.relation: Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.

27.relation: Lee argues that tattooing is a performative 'practice of writing' whose meaning always exceeds its origin, comparing Holocaust survivor Tova Friedman's Auschwitz number 'A27633' with the Suicide Girl Jaylin's chosen feminist ink. Drawing on Judith Butler's account of the body as a site of inscription and counter-inscription, and Walter Benjamin's 'Critique of Violence' distinguishing law-making from law-preserving force, she claims Friedman's tattoo resists the Nazi law itself while Jaylin's only satirizes heteropatriarchy. She then invokes Baudrillard's 'ecstasy of communication' and the obscene to show tattooing can desubjectify by dissolving the embodied self into pornographic information.

28.relation: Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.

30.relation: Baker dismisses common objections to tattoos (shallow individuality, permanence, ugliness) as aesthetic rather than moral, then uses Greco-Roman virtue ethics—quoting Seneca's Moral Epistles on the soul, the balanced psyche, and matching one's norms to one's motivations—to isolate her real target: the 'tough tattoo.' She argues that a badass or tough-guy tattoo appropriates an outlaw subculture's imagery and, per Seneca's warning that approving a little violence approves it all, cultivates a vicious rather than virtuous psyche. Recalling friends who bragged about beatings, she invokes Socratic self-examination ('know thyself') to test whether looking tough is an accurate or worthy self-representation.

31.file: ch31 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
31.relation: Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant and clinical bioethicist, separates personal ethics, professional ethics, and bioethics, then evaluates tattooing through Beauchamp and Childress's principles—especially autonomy (intention, understanding, freedom from outside influence) weighed against risk versus benefit. He concludes tattooing is bioethically fine because safer pigments and market forces reduced its disease risks and because autonomy makes 'to ink or not' the patient's own call, echoing a Millian liberty that one's choice not harming others is 'none of your beeswax.' He ends by defending the memorial tattoo as therapeutic 'memory remodeling' that gluing a positive event in place with pain can make good for you.
