32.file: ch32 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
32.relation: Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.

34.relation: Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.

35.file: ch35 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
35.relation: Lynch, a tattooed Buddhist philosophy professor, tests his largely Buddhist body art (an Om-mani-padme-hum armband, Bodhidharma, the Buddha's face, the eight-spoked Wheel and lotus, a double-vajra) against the Buddha's Three Marks of Existence. He argues a 'permanent' tattoo need not contradict impermanence any more than Gruzalski's washed-away sandcastle if approached mindfully, that custom ink need not reify a self given the chariot analogy of no-self (which he links to Hume's bundle view), and that the pain of tattooing directly instantiates dukkha and can become an object of meditation and compassion. Mindful tattooing, he concludes, can itself be authentic Buddhist practice.

36.relation: Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.

19.file: ch19 - College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits.md
19.relation: This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.

20.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
20.file: ch20 - College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits.md
20.relation: This span closes the walk-of-shame semiotics and then applies ancient ethics to college relationships. Puka defends long-distance college relationships through Aristotle's account of philia—arguing (provocatively, per Aristotle) that love is an activity, so being apart 'murders' love unless couples make Skype, sexting, and texting into the relationship's real medium rather than a substitute. Stephens brings Epicurus and Lucretius to 'friends with benefits': since sexual passion is a natural-but-unnecessary desire that breeds anxiety and love is a wound to the mind, while friendship is necessary for ataraxia, he concludes students should skip the sex and keep the friend—'friends are the real benefits,' echoing Tina Turner's 'What's Love Got to Do with It?' Levine/Mongeau and Smith/Morrison supply communication-research data on how FWB relationships form, are negotiated (usually not), and often end when one partner 'catches feelings.'

21.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
21.file: ch21 - College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits.md
21.relation: This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.

22.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
22.file: ch22 - College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits.md
22.relation: The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.

11.relation: Winters reads the Zodiac Killer's taunting letters through Sartre's account of 'the look' from Being and Nothingness. He argues Zodiac's letters function like a snapped twig or a lit window: they make Northern Californians experience themselves as seen objects, hunted 'slaves' and pawns in Zodiac's game rather than free subjects. A phenomenological (first-person) analysis of the fear Zodiac induces, and of how his letters restrict the choices available within our facticity, is offered as superior to psychological or analytic accounts for explaining our fascination with the macabre.

12.title: SERIAL KILLERS
12.file: ch12 - SERIAL KILLERS.md
12.relation: Schmid examines Moors Murderer Ian Brady's book The Gates of Janus, arguing that Brady built a genuine philosophy of serial murder from Sade and Nietzsche rather than merely name-dropping them. He corrects popular caricatures of the ubermensch and will to power, then shows Brady grounds his self-account in moral relativism and reframes serial killing as fundamentally about 'power and the will to power.' Brady's admiration for Carl Panzram and his likeness to the self-justifying, punishment-transcending Sadean hero illustrate how Nietzschean and Sadean ideas actually shape a killer's self-understanding.

13.title: SERIAL KILLERS
13.file: ch13 - SERIAL KILLERS.md
13.relation: Alfano uses the trial of 'Sunset Strip Killer' Doug Clark to argue that situational forces and attribution biases may have swayed his jury regardless of the actual evidence. Drawing on Milgram's obedience study, Zimbardo's prison simulation, Knobe's intentionality vignettes, and Haidt's disgust experiments, he shows how gender bias, pretrial media, and revulsion at Clark's necrophilia could distort judgments of guilt. He closes with Nozick's truth-tracking account of knowledge to press whether a juror who would have convicted anyway can be said to know Clark is guilty.

15.title: SERIAL KILLERS
15.file: ch15 - SERIAL KILLERS.md
15.relation: Howard surveys serial killers from Liu Pengli and Locusta through Gilles de Rais, Bathory, Bichel, Panzram, and modern killers she interviewed (Bobby Joe Long, Shawcross, Milat, Birnie) to illustrate 'practical moral skepticism': the thesis that one can know right from wrong yet feel no motivation to be good. She distinguishes this from epistemic moral skepticism and argues that many killers, often privileged or unconstrained, understood moral codes but were driven instead by power, sadism, fatigue, or anger, showing that a failure of moral motivation is ancient rather than modern.

16.title: SERIAL KILLERS
16.file: ch16 - SERIAL KILLERS.md
16.relation: Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.

17.title: SERIAL KILLERS
17.relation: Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.

19.title: SERIAL KILLERS
19.relation: Dietrich and Hall explain why fictional serial killers (Hannibal, the Joker, Dexter, Grendel) allure us. Curiosity drives us to seek explanations for the mysterious, but the deeper pull comes from 'co-activation' of fear and pleasure inside a 'protective frame' (the screen or page) that strips away empathy for victims. They argue humans are rule-following creatures who must assert selfhood through rule-breaking to secure freedom, so the serial killer becomes an alluring avatar of ultimate freedom — the idea of the killer, safely framed, lets us test how thin the veneer of morality really is, as the Joker taunts.

20.title: SERIAL KILLERS
20.relation: Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.

22.title: SERIAL KILLERS
22.file: ch22 - SERIAL KILLERS.md
22.relation: The Schechters contrast John Wayne Gacy with Jane Toppan and other female killers (Lydia Sherman, Carol Bundy) to ask what female serial murder reveals about human nature and the nativism/empiricism (nature/nurture) debate. They argue women tend to kill through poisoning and 'lethal nurturing' of intimates rather than phallic-aggressive stranger-murder, so female killers form a 'natural kind' that both violates and grotesquely exaggerates stereotypes of femininity. They conclude that serial killers, male and female, are also a single kind whose ruthlessness and egotism are a monstrous but recognizably human — and partly innate — reflection of our common nature.

23.title: SERIAL KILLERS
23.relation: Keegan analyzes Buffalo Bill's line from Silence of the Lambs ('It puts the lotion in the basket') to ask why it repulses us. He argues clinical labels like antisocial personality disorder smuggle in unexamined norms and focus only on behaviors, missing the deep-seated traits behind them, so psychopathy should be distinguished from ASPD. Using Habermas's communicative rationality — grounded in perspective-taking and reciprocity and, via de Waal, in our evolved primate sociality — he contends that psychopaths like Buffalo Bill, Ramirez, and Kemper have lost the communicative capacity underlying empathy, and our revulsion is our own communicative rationality registering that violation.

24.title: SERIAL KILLERS
24.relation: Terjesen critiques the 'lack of empathy' explanation of serial killing by disentangling empathy into understanding, vicarious feeling, and connection, and showing each either is possessed by killers or leads to circular reasoning (citing Deigh's 'mature empathy' and autism as a counterexample). Real killers like Dahmer, Rader, and 'Angels of Death' such as Cullen and Harvey act from sexual desire, rage, or even excessive empathy, so empathy shapes how they kill (intimate vs. distancing methods, echoing Greene's trolley/footbridge study) rather than whether they kill. He favors Kennett's lack-of-impulse-control and poor risk-assessment account instead.

26.title: SERIAL KILLERS
26.file: ch26 - SERIAL KILLERS.md
26.relation: Deal compares fictional Dexter Morgan with real killer John Wayne Gacy to explore whether serial killers are morally responsible, working through moral agency, free will, determinism, and Dennett's compatibilism (from Freedom Evolves). He argues moral responsibility requires intentional choice and the capacity to know right from wrong, which the delusional self-narratives of Dexter (the 'Dark Passenger') and the denying Gacy call into question. Drawing on experimental philosophy (Knobe and Nichols) and cognitive 'frames,' he shows our verdicts hinge on emotion: the 'abused child' frame makes Dexter sympathetic while the 'murderous psychopath' frame condemns Gacy, so how a killer's story is framed drives our attribution of responsibility.

27.title: SERIAL KILLERS
27.relation: Zirngibl asks why we rename killers with nicknames like 'White Wolf' (a literal predatory wolf) and 'Black Widow' (poisoner Lydia Trueblood), using the philosophy of language. She applies the Fregean/Russellian descriptivist theory of names and the notions of reference, denotation, and a 'second baptism' to show how a nickname distills a person into a short, pejorative set of descriptors that displaces their full identity. Through the substitution and Black's interactionist theories of metaphor, plus Nietzschean anthropomorphism and zoomorphism, she argues serial-killer animal metaphors do reciprocal violence to both the maligned animal and the human, humanizing beasts and dehumanizing killers to assert mastery over them.

28.title: SERIAL KILLERS
28.relation: Waller interviews two retired California officers (Amarillas and Kos), framing their front-line experience through Aristotle's 'natural philosophy' of theorizing from observation. The conversation raises the killing-versus-letting-die distinction over a neglect case, uses a harm principle to weigh whether rape can be worse than murder, and sets early-twentieth-century verificationism against later philosophy of mind in debating whether serial-killer 'types' (thrill-seeker, mission, power/comfort killers) are meaningful if only behaviors are observable. Kos recounts her own multiple-murderer grandfather, and both officers close by warning how media fiction distorts the public's grasp of real, charming, camouflaged killers.

30.title: SERIAL KILLERS
30.relation: Gray gives a psychological account of Ted Bundy and Dennis Rader (BTK), stressing that serial killers are ordinary-seeming — Arendt's banality of evil — and are psychopaths, not psychotics: rational, remorseless, genetically shaped, unable to learn conditioned fear, and guided by scripted fantasies of domination. He reads their pursuit of control as Nietzsche's will to power, citing Bundy's manipulation of preacher James Dobson and Rader's cold courtroom allocution. But he argues the psychopath is a failed, unnatural predator, not Nietzsche's ubermensch: lacking vision and moral self-discipline, he only masters deceit in service of petty, narrow fantasies.

31.title: SERIAL KILLERS
31.relation: Piven mounts an 'epistemology of murder,' invoking Hume and Nietzsche to argue that most of what we 'know' about serial killers and terrorists is projected fantasy and prejudice, amplified by fear (Terror Management Theory). Rereading Lord of the Flies and the Milgram studies, he claims violence follows from shame, humiliation, and abuse (Athens's 'violentization') rather than innate evil, and uses Freud's fort-da game and repetition compulsion to argue killers displace their own woundedness and 'soul murder' onto surrogate victims. He controversially links serial killers, who sexualize death and merge with victims, to terrorists who sanctify displaced sexual rage as God's will — a 'serial killer in sheik's clothing.'

8.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
8.relation: John Friend's foreword surveys yoga's three classical philosophical systems and connects them to how modern Hatha yoga is practiced: Classical (Patanjali) yoga as separating purusha (spirit) from prakriti (matter) to reach kaivalya; Vedanta as neutralizing maya to realize the unity of atman with the supreme; and non-dual Tantra, from which Hatha yoga derives, treating body and mind as frequencies of one divine Shiva-Shakti energy. It argues yoga's enduring claim is that the essential self is free, and that direct lived experience of that freedom outranks merely intellectual knowledge of the texts.

9.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
9.relation: Editor Liz Stillwaggon Swan uses her rejection of Descartes' mind–body dualism to reinterpret yoga's promise of 'union.' Drawing on Spinoza's view that mind and matter are two aspects of a single reality, she argues 'mind' is just a placeholder for embodied abilities, so a yogi who denies a separate spirit cannot literally 'unite' mind and body — they are already one. She reframes yogic union (via Megan Burke's essay) as uniting self with nature, and defends practicing yoga for physical and psychological benefit without any spiritual claim, likening secularized yoga to secular Christmas.

10.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
10.file: ch10 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md

11.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
11.file: ch11 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md

12.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
12.file: ch12 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
12.relation: Jennifer Munyer's 'How Yoga Won the West' narrates yoga's evolution — from the Pashupati seal and the Pre-Vedic age through the Vedas, Upanishads, Patanjali's Yoga Sutras and Raja yoga, to Krishnamacharya's traveling 'circuses,' Vivekananda, and Indra Devi. Her governing argument is that yoga's outer form constantly changes to fit each culture while its essence (union with the divine) stays the same, a claim she illustrates with the idea that a person changes appearance over a lifetime yet remains the same self — a lay expression of impermanence of form beneath continuity.

13.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
13.file: ch13 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
13.relation: Kieran McManus's travel memoir 'Will I Find My Guru in India?' recounts his search from Kathmandu to Rishikesh and the Agama Yoga School, where teacher Kushru's lectures on karma, breath, and diet finally make asana click for him. His reported insight — that every thought and act moves him toward or away from his sacred potential, and that the yogi transcends suffering by treating each experience as neutral and as an opportunity, remaining present — applies a karmic and present-moment ethic to his own practice rather than expounding doctrine abstractly.

14.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
14.file: ch14 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
14.relation: David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.

15.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
15.file: ch15 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
15.relation: Purcell and Shaffer's 'Men, Sports, and Yoga' asks why, though yoga began as a male discipline, ~80% of US practitioners are women, using the stories of three men (Mark, Carl, Jake) taught privately to avoid the competitive self-consciousness of group classes. Its philosophical thread is the ego (ahamkara, 'the I-maker'): rather than obliterating the ego, the men learn to keep it in check and channel competitiveness inward against their own limits, so 'unifying mind and body' turns out to be a competitive sport that works by managing one's own drives and self-image.

16.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
16.file: ch16 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
16.relation: Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'

18.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
18.file: ch18 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
18.relation: Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.

19.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
19.relation: J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.

20.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
20.relation: Luna Dolezal's 'Yoga for Women?' argues that Western yoga, once a male ascetic path, has been absorbed by consumer capitalism into a female beauty practice organized around 'body capital.' Reading Yoga Journal covers, Lululemon's 'Say No to Camel Toe' ad, and Toesox's nude campaigns, she shows the fashion/beauty industries cultivate shame to sell the yoga body, objectifying women. She counters that Hatha yoga should be a laboratory for compassionate self-acceptance beyond comparison and competition — 'yoga for every body' — rather than another instrument of the market's normalized ideal.

21.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
21.file: ch21 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
21.relation: Nicole Dunas's 'The Feeling of Beauty' recounts founding the Real Beauty Yoga Project after a teacher-training 'modeling day' where consultants photographed only the five thinnest students, enacting division rather than yogic union. Framing the beauty question against Kant's claim that beauty is objective, and drawing on David Abram's participatory perception and Susan Bordo on airbrushed bodies, she argues that objectifying beauty into an image to be gazed at (the male gaze, the isolated cosmetic-surgery gaze) severs us from it, whereas Hatha yoga's tantric, present-moment embodiment lets beauty be lived rather than consumed.

22.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
22.file: ch22 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
22.relation: Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.

24.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
24.relation: Eric Swan, a school counselor and yogi, argues yoga should be part of primary and secondary curricula because it fosters self-control, attention, body awareness, self-efficacy and — via 'namaste,' which his friend's daughter Harlow glosses as 'the light in me sees the light in you' — respect and compassion for self and others. Treating yoga as experiential education that develops the 'whole child' and 'soft skills,' he maps it onto counseling practice (individual, group, building levels) and cites data on academic gains, making an essentially Deweyan case for learning through embodied experience.

25.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
25.relation: Leigh Duffy pairs the yogic balance of sthira (strength/steadiness) and sukha (ease/openness) in asana with Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, prompted by her own stress-induced seizure while teaching the Nichomachean Ethics. She argues both frameworks make virtue/right balance 'relative to us' — the correct warrior I or the courageous or good-tempered act depends on the individual and moment — and both require self-knowledge and practical reason. Cultivating the mean of sthira and sukha on the mat becomes her model for finding balance among work, relationships, and self-care off it.

26.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
26.file: ch26 - YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
26.relation: Abby Thompson, a somatic psychologist, sets Raja yoga metaphysics (five koshas, a blissful true self distinct from the ego, nadis and chakras as energy flow) beside clinical psychology's brain-chemistry, DSM model, arguing the two paradigms are complementary. Using warrior II and camel pose plus the neuroscience maxim 'neurons that fire together wire together,' she shows how yoga trains self-regulation, distinguishes constructive discomfort from injurious pain, and can serve as complementary therapy — with instructors bearing therapist-like responsibility for the emotional vulnerability and transference that arise on the mat.

27.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
27.relation: Jim Berti's first-person memoir 'The Path to Happiness Begins with a Journey Inside' — riffing on Yoda as a stand-in for yoga — recounts how accidental stretching and belly-breathing pulled him out of anxiety, depression, and antidepressant numbness. He frames accumulated fear as garbage that rots the body–mind unless confronted, and describes a 'five-second' breathing rule that slows reactive thinking so he can take accountability for his responses. His account of finding sustained meaning and present-focused calm through practice reads as an experiential, self-taught search for meaning rather than doctrine.

29.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
29.relation: Iyengar-tradition teacher Jeff Logan argues that yoga philosophy — mythology such as the warrior Virabhadra behind virabhadrasana and Hanuman behind hanumanasana — must be taught alongside asana, or practice becomes 'mere acrobatics.' Using the parking-lot and door-cutting anecdotes to show yamas like non-harm and selflessness ignored, and citing a childhood-diet study, he contends teachers should not preach the eight limbs but embed subliminal precepts in physical cues ('extend your legs straight and true'), so students come to live rather than merely know yoga's virtue ethics.

30.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
30.relation: Julinna Oxley argues that yoga ethics is best understood as an Aristotelian virtue ethic rather than a rule-set: the yamas and niyamas name character traits to cultivate, not commands (citing Iyengar that 'violence is a state of mind, not a diet'). Laying out virtue ethics' elements — habituation, the mean, practical reason, community — she derives two paramount 'yogic virtues,' mindfulness and self-discipline/self-improvement, that are relative to each practitioner and community, so no single diet or lifestyle (e.g., vegetarianism, teetotaling) is universally required for the virtuous yogi off the mat.

31.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
31.relation: Megan Burke reads yoga's asanas through Vandana Shiva's 'Earth democracy,' arguing that poses named for other creatures (frog, camel, tree, sun salutation) shift the yogi's perspective and dissolve the sense of separation from nature that underwrites environmental destruction. 'Becoming-frog' yields non-human knowledge and, via the Vedic vasudhaiva kutumbakam (the Earth family) that both Shiva and Iyengar invoke, an ethic of care extending off the mat — casting yoga as a political, green practice that heals an anthropocentric, dominating relationship with the environment.

32.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
32.relation: Ethics professor Paul MacNeill argues ethics is intrinsic to yoga and knowable only through practice, not by mining texts — a Western reason-first bias that trivializes it. He shows the yamas and niyamas are counter-measures aimed at samadhi (paralleling how Aristotle's virtues aim at eudaimonia, though yoga subordinates reason), and that Vedanta's transcendent and Kashmir Shaivism's immanent metaphysics both function as instruments toward expanded awareness. From that dissolution of the separate self, he claims, compassion flows naturally, so Hatha yoga's asana and pranayama dissolve the ingrained bodily/mental habits that block ethical, equilibrium-born action.

33.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
33.relation: Heather Salazar interleaves philosophical arguments with yoga exercises to awaken a 'hidden ethical self.' Using Korsgaard's notion of practical identity, she has readers meditate on their roles and conflicts, then argues in Kantian fashion that recognizing the shared reasons behind everyone's pursuits obliges us to value others as we value ourselves; extending Korsgaard, that we must value the life and happiness we prize wherever they appear, in animals and plants; and via Buddhist interdependence (the world in a cup of tea) that caring for others and the environment just is a way of caring for ourselves.

8.title: BLUES
8.relation: In this foreword, Alligator Records founder Bruce Iglauer argues that the blues is 'magic' rooted in the specific 300-year African-American experience of slavery, sharecropping, and Jim Crow, yet reaches a worldwide audience. He dissects the 'tension and release' at the music's core — delayed vocals, notes bent up to pitch, Muddy Waters' slide, Albert King's guitar — as the mechanism of its emotional effect, and contrasts the communal call-and-response of black juke joints with the more passive reception of white festival audiences. The piece is a practitioner's testimony rather than a sustained philosophical argument, so no taxonomy philosopher's doctrine is genuinely applied.

9.title: BLUES
9.relation: The editors' introduction argues blues and philosophy are close kin in confronting the struggling soul. It reads Lightnin' Hopkins's 'Lonesome Dog' through Plato's tripartite soul from Republic IX — the howling 'dog' is the appetitive part — but claims the blues achieves a 'blues harmony' rather than Plato's reason-ruled harmony. It casts Socrates, calm before execution in the Phaedo, as having a 'bluesy sensibility' that rises above worry through philosophizing, invokes Bentham's claim that the capacity to suffer is what matters morally to gloss the blues as knowledge of suffering, and likens the blues' triumphant affirmation to Nietzsche's positivity.

10.title: BLUES
10.file: ch10 - BLUES.md

11.title: BLUES
11.file: ch11 - BLUES.md

12.title: BLUES
12.file: ch12 - BLUES.md
12.relation: Joel Rudinow stages a three-way internal dialogue ('Me,' 'Myself,' and 'I') debating whether the commercialized, white-inflected blues — the House of Blues chain, the Blues Brothers, Cyndi Lauper's Memphis Blues, Clapton's Cream 'Crossroads' — is still really the blues. 'I' introduces Heraclitus's doctrine that everything flows and you cannot step twice into the same river, using the Heraclitean flux of culture to argue the blues is a living, ever-changing tradition whose 'canon' cannot be pinned to a fixed time, place, or racial purity, dissolving the survive/thrive/arrive question into one about how a canon forms and evolves.

13.title: BLUES
13.file: ch13 - BLUES.md
13.relation: Ken Ueno recounts a B. B. King lecture where King played the 'right' notes, then 'turned it on' with identical notes made electric by personality, to argue that the blues locates a song's identity in the performer's aura rather than a written score. He appropriates Walter Benjamin's 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' but inverts it: where Benjamin held that mechanical reproduction withers the aura, Ueno claims recordings actually preserve and transmit the aura of blues performers (bent notes, B. B.'s voice) that classical notation cannot capture, making recordings a more democratic notation for an aural tradition.

14.title: BLUES
14.file: ch14 - BLUES.md
14.relation: Wade Fox and Richard Greene argue that no set of necessary and sufficient conditions — twelve-bar structure, AAB lyrics, mournful content — defines the blues, since paradigm cases violate each (Charley Patton's one-chord songs, cheerful jug band tunes, instrumentals). Invoking the 'Socratic fallacy,' they deny that failure to define a term means failure to grasp it, then apply Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations notion of family resemblance so that blues songs share overlapping features without a common essence. They extend this to argue contemporary blues (Stevie Ray Vaughan, Robert Cray, Jonny Lang) are 'twelve-bar zombies' — resembling the blues but lacking the lived authenticity that gives it a soul.

15.title: BLUES
15.file: ch15 - BLUES.md
15.relation: Philip Jenkins distinguishes the blues as musical form from the blues as cultural expression, defending a version of Amiri Baraka's expressivist claim that white musicians (imagining Barry Manilow) cannot authentically play the blues. Against the formalism of Rudinow and James O. Young, he theorizes that one's expressive 'options' are internalized from one's social group, so authentic blues requires the lived, embodied experience of African-American oppression that a cultural outsider lacks. He roots the disagreement in a 'too-loose' definition of culture that ignores how involuntary, systematic oppression makes African-American culture more experientially cohesive than voluntary subcultures.

16.title: BLUES
16.file: ch16 - BLUES.md

17.title: BLUES
17.relation: A trauma-psychology team (Steinberg, Pynoos, Abramovitz) argues that the blues functions like psychotherapy for trauma, loss, and adversity rooted in slavery, sharecropping, and disasters such as the 1927 Mississippi flood (Charley Patton, Bessie Smith). They map blues techniques onto clinical findings: the repeated AAB line mirrors the traumatized need to retell; verbal labeling of emotion dampens amygdala activity; delayed notes and tension-release (Muddy Waters, Sonny Boy Williamson II) recreate and discharge distress. They cite Hegel's Aesthetics on music's capacity to absorb the listener into inner life, and Robert Stoller on aesthetic excitement, to explain how the blues transforms raw trauma into bearable, shareable art.

18.title: BLUES
18.file: ch18 - BLUES.md
18.relation: David C. Drake argues that the blues' distinctive achievement is presenting 'sadness as beauty,' which lets performers and listeners find their own sorrow beautiful and thus therapeutic. He surveys theories of beauty — Plato's proportion/harmony/unity and Aristotle's order/symmetry (a beautiful life needs some sorrow), Kant's claim that beauty is a subjective-yet-universal judgment requiring reflection, Lyotard's sublime that 'pleases only by causing pain,' and Schopenhauer's view that aesthetic contemplation temporarily frees us from the striving Will — and links beauty to truth and goodness (Keats, Nietzsche's 'whoever despises himself respects himself as one who despises') to explain why blues sorrow feels good.

19.title: BLUES
19.relation: Ben and Owen Flanagan ask why people seek out 'anguished art,' comparing the blues to Aristotelian tragedy. They argue the blues protagonist, unlike the doomed tragic hero, survives — and his downfall comes from ordinary personal choices (wanderlust, whiskey, the wrong woman) rather than fated conflicts of duty, making imaginative identification easier for a plebeian audience. Aristotle's catharsis of pity and fear is broadened by Freud's account of sublimation and release of repressed sexual and aggressive drives; Robert Johnson's 'Love in Vain' and Muddy Waters' 'Five Long Years' are read as Sisyphean (Camus) images of loving and losing, so the blues offers beauty, release, and shared humanity by being more 'real' than happy pop.

20.title: BLUES
20.relation: Roopen Majithia asks why a music born of African-American suffering became universally beloved and answers with Aristotle's account of musical catharsis in the Politics. Drawing on the Nicomachean Ethics link between habituated action, emotion, and disposition (as courage is built by acting courageously), he argues music images real emotions and thereby purges excess feeling. Modern electric urban blues (T-Bone Walker's 'Stormy Monday,' Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf), with its danceable, sexually charged rhythm, recreates the emotional landscape of repetitive urban work and, aided by dancing, effects a broad catharsis — which also explains why non-black communal performers can play it and why intimate bars beat arenas.

21.title: BLUES
21.file: ch21 - BLUES.md

22.title: BLUES
22.file: ch22 - BLUES.md
22.relation: Brian Domino frames a choice between the reasoned Stoic life and the emotional life through the Rolling Stones and the blues. He presents Epictetus's Stoicism — apatheia, the dichotomy of control, and the Enchiridion's 'it was given back' — applied to blues themes of floods, death, and cheating women ('When the Levee Breaks,' Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues'), arguing emotions stem from false beliefs and akrasia. Against this he sets 'Jumping Jack Flash,' 'Monkey Man,' and '(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction' as celebrations of raw emotional existence, invoking Plato's tension of reason and passion and Nietzsche's image of the 'music-making Socrates' to leave the choice deliberately unresolved.

23.title: BLUES
23.relation: Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.

24.title: BLUES
24.relation: Robert and Benjamin Stolorow argue the blues is musical therapy that lets us face universally traumatizing dimensions of existence. Drawing on Robert Stolorow's Trauma and Human Existence, they hold that emotional pain becomes traumatic only when it finds no 'relational home,' and that trauma shatters the 'absolutisms of everyday life,' exposing the existential vulnerability of finite, mortal beings — an explicitly Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity of owning rather than evading vulnerability. Blues lyrics (Louisiana Red's 'Too Poor to Die,' Willie Dixon's 'One More Mile to Go') voice tragic-ironic mortality, while pitch-bending and major/minor ambiguity viscerally hold the pain in a shared, therapeutic conversation.

25.title: BLUES
25.relation: Joseph Lynch uses Son House's 'Preachin' the Blues' — a fallen preacher who preaches the blues, not the gospel — to explore the tension between blues sensuality and religion, arguing the expression of suffering is itself liberation from it. He reads Marx's 'religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature' as making the blues a heart of a heartless world that voices and eases alienated labor; the Buddha's Four Noble Truths and impermanence as embracing suffering to be freed from craving; and Kierkegaard's passionate leap of faith, born of doubt and despair and contrasted with Hume, as the model for how blues 'preachers' like Son House and Robert Johnson embrace the absurd contradiction of embodied spirituality.

26.title: BLUES
26.file: ch26 - BLUES.md
26.relation: Kimberly Connor reads the blues as story, song, and prayer — a secularized descendant of the spirituals and an African-American philosophical guide to making meaning from suffering, exemplified by the Robert Johnson crossroads myth. Using Albert Murray's idea of 'worrying the line' (breaking a phrase to emphasize or subvert) as both technique and survival philosophy, she casts the bluesman as an 'Omni-American' whose art dissolves black/white division, invoking Du Bois's double consciousness and Cornel West's claim that the blues chronicles catastrophe 'with grace and dignity.' She argues Martin Luther King, Jr.'s nonviolent resistance and Brother Will Hairston's 'Alabama Bus' show the blues functioning as prayer and an agent of social change.

28.title: BLUES
28.relation: Meghan Winsby answers George Carlin's gibe that white people have nothing to be blue about by arguing that women — black or white — legitimately sing the blues because they share an experience of oppression. She applies Iris Marion Young's 'five faces of oppression' (exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, violence) to women's silencing, sexual objectification, and gender exploitation, showing that early blueswomen (Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, Memphis Minnie) and later ones (Bonnie Raitt) asserted sexuality and independence against a patriarchal order. She then weighs, without fully endorsing, the moral cultural-appropriation and audience-appropriation objections (via James O. Young) to white men playing the blues.

29.title: BLUES
29.relation: Douglas and Nathaniel Langston argue that even white folks 'get' the blues, citing B. B. King and Howlin' Wolf treating the white Jimmie Rogers as a bluesman and looking to hard-life experience rather than color. They distinguish the experiential 'get' from two comprehension senses — understanding the lyrics and understanding the music — detailing twelve-bar form, slide, pitch-bending, and finger-picking to show any skilled musician can 'get' the music. To test whether black experience is required to grasp the lyrics they engage MacIntyre's thesis of incommensurable conceptual schemes (Aristotle vs. Augustine) and Davidson's reply, concluding that the common human hurt Howlin' Wolf sings about is accessible to anyone regardless of race.

30.title: BLUES
30.relation: Michael Neumann attacks the 'white rip-off' account of rock and roll as a species of 'distributive history' that redistributes reputation from white to black artists but relies on racial stereotypes. He marshals musical history — the banjo's black origin, Jimmie Rogers's blues, Chuck Berry and Howlin' Wolf borrowing from country, color-blind commercial exploitation by black label owner Don Robey — to argue black and white music were always intertwined, so cultural (as opposed to commercial) theft was impossible. He contends the account slanders black music by reducing it to 'jungle sex and violence,' ignoring doo-wop, sophisticated pianists, and the aesthetic range black audiences actually preferred. The argument is historical and aesthetic, applying no taxonomy philosopher's doctrine.

31.title: BLUES
31.relation: Ron Bombardi argues there are two incompatible histories of the blues, tracing the split to Plato's and Aristotle's opposed views of difference. Using Ian Hacking's 'making up people,' he says the 'orthodox' tale treats the blues as the product of a distinct kind of people (Platonic kinds generating individuals), while the 'unorthodox' tale — the hybrid, cosmopolitan music of the Mississippi Sheiks — fits Aristotle's nominalism, where only individuals exist and forms are things 'in name only.' Invoking the Socratic 'know thyself,' he concludes the blues has no essence and that the 'pay your dues' authenticity maxim reduces persons to social kinds and perpetuates the very oppression the blues protests; the blues, he says, is finally 'ours.'

7.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
7.relation: In this foreword Joshua Wolf Shenk recounts an intoxicating blind date with 'Rachael' to argue that dating exposes the core existential dilemma of social creatures: we crave ecstasy (ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself') yet can only connect by holding on to a discrete identity. He blames the modern isolation of the self on Descartes' claim that the self inhabits its own subjective realm and Hobbes' picture of natural man as solitary, and cites Camus that once you choose to live, the real question is how to relate to others. His unresolved paradox—needing the mantra 'I was complete before I met you' while knowing it is false—frames love as the tension between self-sufficiency and merger.

9.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
9.relation: Editors Kristie Miller and Marlene Clark introduce the volume by opening with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics claim that the human drive to couple is even stronger than the drive to live as a political being and that fulfillment rests in loving relationships. They frame dating as a rule-governed 'game' with aims and strategies and preview each contributor's essay—Jenkins on flirting, Langan on conservative men, Samp and Cohen against unconditional love, the elevator metaphor, cyberdating, evolutionary seduction, and Colyvan's game-theoretic mate search—tying age-old ethical questions about treating partners well to new work in evolutionary psychology, decision theory, and the ethics of online romance.

11.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
11.file: ch11 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
11.relation: Carrie Jenkins does analytic conceptual analysis of flirting, rejecting the Oxford English Dictionary's claim that flirting requires having no serious intentions. She distinguishes 'flirting' from merely 'behaving flirtatiously' (Joe who over-holds eye contact, the tourist touching her earlobe in Italy are flirtatious without flirting) and argues flirting requires an intention to act in ways disposed to raise flirter-flirtee romance to salience, done in a 'knowing yet playful' way. Borrowing Kripke's 'killer yellow' to imagine 'killer-flirts' who die on contact, and citing chatbot studies, she concludes one can flirt with an imagined or non-human target only if one believes it can respond significantly.

12.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
12.file: ch12 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
12.relation: Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'

13.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
13.file: ch13 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
13.relation: Jennifer Samp and Andrew Cohen argue against the Notebook-style romantic ideal of unconditional love, casting dating as a 'calculated exchange' explained by social-exchange and interdependence theory (comparison level and comparison level of alternatives). Adopting Aristotle's distinction between friendships of utility/pleasure and 'complete friendships' in which one values the friend as 'another self' and as an end in itself, they hold the best romances are complete friendships—yet insist even these must be conditioned. Their key thought experiment: a genuinely boundless love would survive discovering one's partner is a child-molesting murderer; since it should not, 'true love knows bounds' and remains part of a good life only because it can be defeated by such reasons.

14.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
14.file: ch14 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
14.relation: John Rowan and Patricia Hallen build an extended elevator metaphor for dating (Ann and Bob riding floors, pushing buttons to raise or lower intimacy, gravity pulling toward breakup) to capture Heraclitus's insight that a relationship is a reality in constant change, while invoking Plato to insist the conceptual reality of a relationship is as real as physical objects. They define dating as gauging the possibility of eventual commitment, cite Hume's canoe image for implicit communication of shared destination, and ground their strategies—be yourself, go slowly, communicate, befriend—in Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating honesty, courage, and loyalty as habits lying in the golden mean between deficiency and excess (e.g., the Look Who's Talking date who overshares is 'excessively honest').
