16.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
16.file: ch16 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
16.relation: Mary Beth Yount asks whether being 'crazy in love' really resembles mental illness, noting lovesickness was a diagnosis for nearly two millennia and that love's mood swings mimic bipolar or schizophrenic symptoms. She organizes the analysis around the four Greek loves—eros (with Plato's ladder from physical beauty to the Forms, i.e., 'Platonic love'), philia (Aristotle's Nicomachean friendship of good character), storge (familial affection), and agape (C.S. Lewis's unconditional charity)—arguing a full romance blends all four. She then surveys Fisher, Aron, and Brown's fMRI work showing romantic love as a dopamine-driven mammalian mate-choice drive stronger than the sex drive, and the 'protest'/'resignation' stages of rejection, to reassure daters their craziness is normal biology, not disorder.

17.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
17.relation: Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.

18.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
18.file: ch18 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
18.relation: Anne Barnhill uses John Cusack's boom-box serenade in Say Anything, his poolside pleading in The Sure Thing, and Andy Bernard's 'Take a Chance on Me' serenade in The Office to defend 'prospective boundary violation'—violating a boundary that would not exist in a closer relationship in order to create that relationship. She rejects the Kantian reading of Korsgaard and Hill that treating people as ends forbids all non-rational manipulation, arguing instead that such charming pushiness is 'faking it till you make it,' which works via Aristotle's habituation whereby feelings catch up with actions. She then sets four rules (no harm, not too much closer too fast, genuinely wanting the relationship, and that the other would plausibly want it) to separate appropriate from wrong boundary violations.

19.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
19.relation: Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.

21.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
21.file: ch21 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
21.relation: Joshua Heter mounts a virtue-theoretic case against being set up on blind dates, using Aristotle's notion of telos and the distinction between fleeting 'hot-fudge happiness' and eudaimonia, the flourishing of a well-lived life (illustrated by long-married Bill and Fran). He argues a 'guy's' function is achieved by exercising his whole nature, and dramatizes this with Zoo-bear versus Wild-bear: the zoo-fed bear has its hunger and safety met but cannot flourish because it never hunts or roams, just as matchmaking meets the romantic need while letting a man's 'social muscles' atrophy. Invoking Aristotle's philia (and Nussbaum on Aristotelian virtue), he concedes friends mean well but recommends they merely introduce people and let things progress naturally rather than force an 'unnatural' match.

22.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
22.file: ch22 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
22.relation: Hamilton reads the pick-up-artist 'Game' (Mystery, Style, negs, peacocking, the Alpha frame) against Aristotle's great-souled magnanimous man, arguing that the jerk and the PUA succeed because they inadvertently mimic the Megalopsuche's self-containment and indifference to others' approval. He contends the ethical route is to genuinely acquire that character through habituation ('we become brave by acting bravely') rather than fake it, so the nice guy's supplication fails while true magnanimity requires the full virtues. He then uses Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, and the highest disinterested philia) to argue that erotic relationships can rise to real friendship only where partners are equals, citing When Harry Met Sally on whether men and women can be friends.

23.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
23.relation: Terjesen defines a 'real date' as a shared intention to try out romantic possibility, using Abelard's claim that intention (not behavior) determines the nature of an act to show that identical activities are or aren't dates depending on mutual intent. He then invokes Russell's argument-from-analogy account of knowing other minds to explain how daters 'mind-read' each other's intentions, and notes this yields only probable conclusions, generating an infinite regress ('I know that you know...') that only 'the Talk' resolves. He cites Hume's problem of induction as the deeper reason analogical inference can never be certain, and uses the Friends 'Mayor of the Friend Zone' gag and Ross and Rachel to argue the Friend Zone is a step toward, not a trap against, committed relationships.

24.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
24.relation: Brown and Tien build a 'Kantian Gate' from Kant's Formula of Universal Law: you should date only if you wouldn't mind your dates acting on your own dating maxim, which bars the manipulative, deceptive, or coercive dater while permitting many ends. For those who pass the gate, they recommend pursuing Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' and the Zhuangzi's cultivated spontaneity, describing a two-part self-cultivation (purging debilitating social programming via 'forgetting' and xinzhai, then training to act in accord with the Dao) so one can 'be in the moment' and get truly lucky on a first date. They apply the seven elements of flow directly to dating conversation, eye contact, and feedback.

26.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
26.file: ch26 - DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE.md
26.relation: Brinkman uses the Second Life case of Ric and Janet (whose avatars Dutch and Tenaj dated and 'married' virtually before the couple left their spouses) to ask ontological questions about whether virtual dating and virtual cheating are real. Drawing on Huizinga's Homo Ludens, he argues dating is itself pervaded by the 'play-spirit' (the magic circle, the dating script, secrecy, rapture) and that virtual worlds and dating both breed 'spoilsports': he maps virtual-world 'griefers' and pick-up-artist 'wizards' and 'script kiddies' (via Strauss's The Game) onto Huizinga's cheater/spoilsport distinction, concluding that PUAs who treat targets as game pieces commit a moral transgression against ludus even when they don't lie, and that Ric really was cheating.

27.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
27.relation: Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.

29.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
29.relation: Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).

30.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
30.relation: Colyvan applies mathematics and game theory to mating: the 'secretary problem' yields the optimal strategy of dating and rejecting the first n/e (~37%) of candidates then taking the next best, and Rousseau's stag hunt models monogamy as cooperation (hunt stag = stay faithful) tempted by defection (hunt hare = an affair), with the prisoner's dilemma showing why individual rationality can undermine the Pareto-optimal cooperative outcome. He argues that iterated games and tit-for-tat strategies, plus the 'shadow of the future' and public commitments like weddings, make faithfulness explicable purely by narrow self-interest, quoting Hume on reciprocal service, and suggests love and ethics themselves may be useful fictions layered over the game.

31.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
31.relation: Clark uses Barry Schwartz's Paradox of Choice and the characters of Sex and the City to argue that too much dating choice turns people into unhappy 'maximizers' who seek the absolute best, rather than 'satisficers' content with the merely excellent. She traces how Charlotte, Miranda, Carrie, Big, and Samantha each attain their maximized 'ideal' mate (Trey, Robert Leeds, Petrovsky/Big, Richard Wright) and find it hollow, only becoming happy when they 'settle' for a reciprocal partner (Harry, Steve, John, Smith) after the post-9/11 shift in the series' mood. She frames maximizing as clinically narcissistic (choosing a mate as a mirror of oneself) and invokes Plato to warn that trying to make the ideal real yields only disappointment.

7.title: Introduction
7.relation: Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.

8.title: Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds
8.file: ch08 - Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds.md
8.relation: Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.

9.title: Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection
9.file: ch09 - Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection.md
9.relation: Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.

10.title: The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects
10.file: ch10 - The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects.md
10.relation: Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'

11.title: Hobbes, Human Nature, and the Culture of American Violence in Truman Capote's In Cold Blood
11.file: ch11 - Hobbes, Human Nature, and the Culture of American Violence in Truman Capote's In Cold Blood.md
11.relation: Thomas Fahy reads Capote's In Cold Blood as horror (the Clutter killers Hickock and Smith as 'realistic monsters' whose human shape terrifies because anyone could be like them) and maps it onto Hobbes's Leviathan. Hickock and Smith act in a Hobbesian state of nature, driven by appetite, power, and moral relativism without remorse. Herb Clutter functions as a Hobbesian sovereign whose Eden-like farm and community collapse into decay, mistrust, and 'war of all against all' after his murder. Fahy also casts Capote himself as a sovereign who, via Foucault's panopticon, imposes a fictionalized cathartic ending, though the book's Hobbesian message is that we all have the potential to kill.

12.title: Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World
12.file: ch12 - Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World.md
12.relation: Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.

13.title: The Vampire with a Soul Angel and the Quest for Identity
13.file: ch13 - The Vampire with a Soul Angel and the Quest for Identity.md
13.relation: Amy Kind uses Joss Whedon's Angel/Angelus to test theories of personal identity and moral responsibility. Body-swap episodes support the Lockean/Parfitian psychological (memory) theory over Olson's biological theory, and shared memories make Angel psychologically continuous with, hence identical to, Angelus. But Kind invokes Parfit's distinction between continuity and connectedness (with real cases like Katherine Power and Sara Jane Olson) to argue identity is not what matters: the ensouled Angel's radical break in psychological connectedness means he should not be held morally responsible for Angelus's atrocities. She closes with Mill that it is better to be Angel burdened by a soul than Angelus unburdened.

14.title: Ideological Formations of the Nuclear Family in The Hills Have Eyes
14.file: ch14 - Ideological Formations of the Nuclear Family in The Hills Have Eyes.md
14.relation: Lorena Russell reads both versions of The Hills Have Eyes through Althusser's Repressive vs. Ideological State Apparatuses (building on Gramsci's hegemony) and Foucault's account of power as multivalent with resistance internal to it, defending nuanced ideological criticism against Carroll's caricature. The films pit the 'normal' Carter family against the mutant/feral family produced by U.S. nuclear testing, using Clover's 'urbanoia' and class/Indian-exploitation guilt, Freudian repression, and the mannequin ghost town to expose 'family values' as constructed ideology. The Carters' descent into the mutants' own violence (Doug and Brenda 'butching up') destabilizes the bourgeois family rather than reaffirming it.

15.title: Zombies of the World, Unite Class Struggle and Alienation in Land of the Dead
15.file: ch15 - Zombies of the World, Unite Class Struggle and Alienation in Land of the Dead.md
15.relation: John Lutz reads Romero's Land of the Dead as a sustained Marxist allegory: the walled Pittsburgh with Kaufman's luxury Fiddler's Green tower over the exploited poor stands for America and global capitalist imperialism. The zombies embody Marx's alienated, dehumanized workers and the exploited underdeveloped South, while cannibalism/consumption figures commodities as 'dead labor.' The Fiddler's Green ad and Cholo's doomed aspiration illustrate Althusserian ideology (false consciousness). Big Daddy leading the zombies to arm themselves and cross the river dramatizes the growth of revolutionary class consciousness, and the destruction of Kaufman and the Green stages a socialist revolution in which the exploited are the ruling class's 'grave-diggers.'

16.title: The Fall of the House of Ulmer Europe vs. America in the Gothic Vision of The Black Cat
16.file: ch16 - The Fall of the House of Ulmer Europe vs. America in the Gothic Vision of The Black Cat.md
16.relation: Cantor reads Edgar Ulmer's The Black Cat (1934) as a European emigre's Gothic allegory of Europe vs. America, with Karloff's architect Poelzig and Lugosi's psychiatrist Werdegast as mirror-image 'living dead' fixated on the horrors of World War I. He connects Poelzig's modernist house-over-Fort-Marmaros to a Freudian map of ego and id and to the war-driven rise of psychoanalysis, and reads the naive, unconscious American honeymooners against the cultured but nihilistic Europeans. He explicitly links the film's high-culture/pop-culture opposition to Heidegger's vision of Europe squeezed between a leveling America and Russia and to the Frankfurt School critique of American mass entertainment.

17.title: From Domestic Nightmares to the Nightmare of History Uncanny Eruptions of Violence in King's and Kubrick's Ver
17.file: ch17 - From Domestic Nightmares to the Nightmare of History Uncanny Eruptions of Violence in King's and Kubrick's Ver.md
17.relation: Lutz argues that King's novel and Kubrick's film of The Shining both stage Freud's uncanny as the return of a repressed, corporeal past: the woman in Room 217 and Grady's ghosts, the father-mirroring of Jack, his abusive father, and Delbert Grady, and Danny's Tony double. He reads King as an 'inverted family romance' where the good replacement father is the Black cook Hallorann, then shows Kubrick widening domestic abuse into a Marxian nightmare of history: the Overlook built on an Indian burial ground, the Calumet cans, and Jack's craving to join the hotel's ghostly 'management' expose the racist, patriarchal, class violence founding American institutions. Jack's 'All work and no play' manuscript figures his entrapment in ideology and repetition.

18.title: “Hot with Rapture and Cold with Fear” Grotesque, Sublime, and Postmodern Transformations in Patrick Süskind's
18.file: ch18 - “Hot with Rapture and Cold with Fear” Grotesque, Sublime, and Postmodern Transformations in Patrick Süskind's.md
18.relation: Cokal reads Suskind's Perfume and Tykwer's film through the intertwined categories of the grotesque and the sublime. The odorless murderer Grenouille is a Bakhtinian grotesque body who nonetheless has Kantian sublime experiences of the plum girl's and Laure's scents, and Cokal uses Kant's and Lyotard's accounts of the sublime (the soul 'immobilized, as good as dead') to explain the awe that Grenouille both feels and, via his 'angel's scent,' induces in the orgy at his execution. Grenouille's uncanny encounter with his own lack of smell in the cave is read through Freud's uncanny, and his final cannibalistic dismemberment collapses the sublime back into the grotesque.

19.title: Shock Value A Deleuzean Encounter with James Purdy's Narrow Rooms
19.file: ch19 - Shock Value A Deleuzean Encounter with James Purdy's Narrow Rooms.md
19.relation: Gross stages a Deleuze-and-Guattari 'encounter' with Purdy's Narrow Rooms, refusing Freudian or Marxist 'interpretosis' in favor of asking what the novel does. He reads Roy Sturtevant the 'renderer' as a multiplicity and traces the characters' becomings-animal (Sid's 'becoming-shark' in the locker-room sex act, becoming-horse, becoming-insect) and the crucifixion of Roy on the barn door as horror that dissolves the boundaries between master and slave, lover and torturer. Invoking Deleuze's debt to Spinoza, Nietzsche, and the Stoics, Gross argues that the joyful amor fati of art embraces horror as an expansion of life rather than something to be vanquished.

20.title: Making Monsters The Philosophy of Reproduction in Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Universal Films Frankens
20.file: ch20 - Making Monsters The Philosophy of Reproduction in Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Universal Films Frankens.md
20.relation: Hall reads Shelley's Frankenstein and the 1931 film and its 1935 Bride sequel through Luce Irigaray's Speculum, arguing that Victor's and Walton's quests for a whole, self-sufficient identity enact a patriarchal desire to reproduce sameness and deny the 'maternal waters,' with women reduced to mirrors that will not reflect. She uses Lacan's mirror stage and the camera's power over sight to explain how identity is fixed by being seen, and Derrida's 'Structure, Sign and Play' to recast identity as a perpetually rewritten, misshapen text. The Bride's refusing scream and the exploding phallic tower mark female desire as a negating power that disrupts patriarchal reproduction.

21.title: Kitsch and Camp and Things That Go Bump in the Night; or, Sontag and Adorno at the (Horror) Movies
21.file: ch21 - Kitsch and Camp and Things That Go Bump in the Night; or, Sontag and Adorno at the (Horror) Movies.md
21.relation: Johnston uses his childhood TV horror host Sir Graves Ghastly to distinguish kitsch from camp in the horror genre. Drawing on Greenberg's 'Avant-garde and Kitsch' and Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, he argues that the Universal Horror sequels, Jaws, and most slasher films are kitsch: nonchallenging, formulaic variations that pacify consumers, while autonomous works like Carpenter's They Live or Craven's Scream interrogate the genre. Via Sontag's 'Notes on Camp' and Isherwood's making-fun-of versus making-fun-out-of, he sorts They Live, Scream, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Scary Movie into deliberate camp, naive camp, and mere kitsch.

22.title: Contributors
22.file: ch22 - Contributors.md

6.title: Introduction
6.relation: Rowlands introduces the 'sci-phi' project: science fiction confronts us with the alien 'other' as a mirror in which we understand ourselves, so lowbrow sci-fi films like The Matrix, Total Recall and Starship Troopers make abstract philosophy concrete. He argues philosophy is doing rather than knowing, invoking Fishburne's 'know the path vs walk the path' line and Nietzsche's dictum that one repays a teacher poorly by remaining a pupil. He mentions his own earlier 'fyborg' thesis that human cognition is embedded in the wider informational environment, prefiguring the extended mind.

7.title: 1. Frankenstein
7.relation: Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.

8.title: 2. The Matrix
8.relation: Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.

9.title: 3. Terminator I & II
9.relation: Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.

10.title: 4. Total Recall & The Sixth Day
10.file: ch10 - 4. Total Recall & The Sixth Day.md
10.relation: Rowlands treats Total Recall as a defence of the memory (psychological-continuity) theory of personal identity: erasing Quaid's memories and restoring Hauser's is an essential change that ends Quaid, so he fights for his existence. He works through and rejects the soul theory (dualism's problems) and body/brain theories via head-transplant and neuron-replacement thought experiments, distinguishing Aristotle's essential/accidental change and Heraclitus's river. The Sixth Day's cloning raises Parfit's fission/duplication problem: a double success cannot be a failure, driving him to abandon identity for a Heraclitean 'river of selves' bound by survival, not identity.

11.title: 5. Minority Report
11.file: ch11 - 5. Minority Report.md
11.relation: Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.

12.title: 6. Hollow Man
12.file: ch12 - 6. Hollow Man.md
12.relation: Rowlands reads Hollow Man as a retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges, posing 'why be moral?' once the invisible Kevin Bacon can act without sanction. He rejects the religious answer and Hobbesian social-contract theory (both reduce morality to prudence/fear of punishment and leave those outside the contract unprotected), and Hume's fellow-feeling as mere causal explanation not justification. He examines Kant's Categorical Imperative reducing immorality to inconsistency but argues it cannot answer 'why should I be moral,' concluding the choice is arational self-definition, closing with Nietzsche's 'become what you are' and the deed at the bottom of morality.

13.title: 7. Independence Day & Aliens
13.file: ch13 - 7. Independence Day & Aliens.md
13.relation: Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.

14.title: 8. Star Wars
14.file: ch14 - 8. Star Wars.md
14.relation: Rowlands reads Star Wars as Manichaean (light vs dark side of the Force) and contrasts it with Plato, for whom evil is merely absence of good and the form of the good is most real, an idea Augustine (via Plotinus) folded into Christianity. Siding with Lucas that Darth Vader's evil is palpably real, he then uses Nietzsche's 'Dionysus against the Crucified': the Christian strategy represses drives (Freudian repression), the 'hippy' strategy merely expresses them, but greatness requires sublimation into higher forms. Vader taps his dark side but fails to sublimate, so he is a flawed unbalanced megalomaniac (like Nietzsche's Borgia/Napoleon), not a true Ubermensch living life as art.

15.title: 9. Blade Runner
15.file: ch15 - 9. Blade Runner.md
15.relation: Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.

10.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
10.file: ch10 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
10.relation: The editors' introduction argues that The Lord of the Rings, though written by a philologist rather than a philosopher, dramatizes perennial questions Tolkien cared about as a Catholic: whether power always corrupts, whether death can be a gift, and the tension of fate versus free will. It frames the volume's method by invoking Socrates, who drew on art, sport, and music his listeners already knew to provoke examination of their lives, presenting Tolkien's fiction as the same kind of popular-culture doorway into the great questions.

11.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

12.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
12.file: ch12 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
12.relation: Eric Katz reads the One Ring as a variation on Plato's Ring of Gyges from the Republic: both grant impunity, and both pose the question of whether anyone would stay moral if able to act without consequence. Where Plato only argues that unchecked power corrupts the soul, Tolkien shows it through Gollum's ruin, Boromir's fall, and Frodo's final failure at the Cracks of Doom, while Galadriel, Bombadil, and Sam refuse the Ring by knowing who they are. Katz concludes Tolkien answers Plato's 'why be moral?' with 'to be yourself.'

13.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
13.file: ch13 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
13.relation: Theodore Schick treats the Rings of Power as an allegory-free meditation on externalized 'potency,' applying it to emerging genetics, nanotechnology, and robotics. He contrasts the Council of Elrond's choice to destroy the Ring with Boromir's wish to wield it, and with Bill Joy's call to relinquish dangerous research versus Drexler's promise that nanotech could end poverty and disease. Schick argues our situation differs from Middle-earth because the knowledge cannot be un-forged, so grassroots social taming, not destruction of a single artifact, is the realistic response to knowledge-enabled mass destruction.

14.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
14.file: ch14 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
14.relation: Alison Milbank reads the One Ring as a fetish in both Freud's sexual sense (an object severed from the whole, twice literally cut from a finger, warding off the castrating maternal power figured in Shelob) and Marx's economic sense (a commodity that estranges makers from things and reduces persons to hoarders like Smaug). Against fetishism she sets Tolkien's gift-economy, embodied by Bombadil tossing the Ring in the air and by Sam's elvish rope, and Heidegger's older sense of the 'thing' as a gathering, so the novel teaches us to receive the world back as gift rather than possession.

15.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
15.file: ch15 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

16.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
16.file: ch16 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
16.relation: Gregory Bassham mines the happy communities of the Shire, Rivendell, and Lothlorien for six keys to happiness: delight in simple things (linked to Epicurus's natural pleasures and Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles, close friendship (grounded in Aristotle's claim that friendship is the greatest external good), good character, cherishing beauty and creativity, and recovering wonder. He argues Tolkien's hobbits and elves illustrate what modern happiness research confirms, so Tolkien functions as a philosophical guide to a more joy-filled life.

17.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
17.file: ch17 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
17.relation: Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum, two hobbits of shared nature and culture who both pursue happiness but reach opposite ends. Gollum's happiness is possession of the Precious, a thing, sought in isolation and won by murdering Deagol, which destroys him; Sam's happiness is fellowship in the Shire with Frodo and Rosie, and his love for Frodo lets him surrender the Ring where Gollum cannot. Drawing on Aristotle's tie between happiness, one's nature, and friendship, Gracia concludes that for ordinary beings happiness is achievable only in a social context whose key is love expressed as loyalty and sharing.

18.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
18.file: ch18 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
18.relation: Eric Bronson reads the elves of Rivendell and especially Lothlorien through the 'merrier' existentialists, arguing that lasting joy requires facing the abyss and still affirming life, and knowing, as Nietzsche urged, what to remember and what to forget. Galadriel sings in dark times yet is burdened by remembering too much, unable to let go of her cursed past, so her regret shows the danger Jaspers and Arendt also diagnosed of losing oneself. When she refuses Frodo's Ring and chooses to 'diminish and remain Galadriel,' she embodies the existentialist's affirmation and trust in one's own inner light.

19.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
19.file: ch19 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

20.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
20.file: ch20 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
20.relation: Douglas Blount casts Sauron as a candidate for Nietzsche's Ubermensch, embodying the unabashed will to power in a world where God is dead, life is meaningless, and taste rather than reason or morality guides the self-created life. Tolkien answers this not by argument but by a rival portrait whose beauty lies in community, humility, love, and self-sacrifice: Gandalf dying on the bridge, Frodo's mercy to Gollum, and Sam refusing the Ring's vision of 'Samwise the Strong.' Blount argues that on Nietzsche's own criterion of taste, Tolkien's picture of abnegation is the more compelling vision of a life lived well.

21.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
21.file: ch21 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
21.relation: Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'

22.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
22.file: ch22 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
22.relation: Aeon Skoble uses the characters to argue for Aristotelian virtue ethics over Kantian duty and utilitarian consequence, since right action flows from developed character and practical reason rather than rule-following. He reads Sam's loyalty and Aragorn's temperance as genuine virtue, Boromir as flawed-but-decent (undone by resentment and pride), and Smeagol's swift murder of Deagol as proof the Ring's corrupting power depends partly on prior character. Skoble contends Kant's rules would make Sam's loyalty no better than a Ringwraith's, and utilitarianism's demand for foreknowledge suits only Galadriel, so virtue ethics best fits Tolkien's flawed, developing heroes.

23.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
23.file: ch23 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

24.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
24.file: ch24 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
24.relation: Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.

25.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
25.file: ch25 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
25.relation: Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, the mood that 'all that is solid melts into air' and that the past no longer matters, voiced by Marx, Freud, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead.' Tolkien's heroes survive because they remember lore and tradition (Gandalf watching the Shire, Sam's book-learning at Cirith Ungol), while Saruman and Denethor embody modern despair: they misuse the palantir, lose faith in tradition, and can only try to destroy the present. Against Berman's claim that there is no escape from modernism, Kraus reads Middle-earth as a fantasy where clinging to tradition still yields real, tangible power and certainty.

26.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
26.file: ch26 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
26.relation: Andrew Light resists reading the peoples of Middle-earth as simple stand-ins for parts of nature, noting that the ents, not the elves, truly speak for the forest, so nature is animated to stand and speak for itself. His central idea is 'green time': through Tom Bombadil and the ents, Tolkien represents a naturally scaled, ecosystemic, near-indifferent temporal perspective, seen when Bombadil is unconcerned with the Ring and the ents ignore the riders of Rohan. Light argues this indifference should not make us indifferent to nature but should teach humility and long-term responsibility for problems like global warming, imagining what it is to care for things as a process beyond our own lifespan.

27.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
27.file: ch27 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md

28.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
28.file: ch28 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
28.relation: Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.

29.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
29.file: ch29 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
29.relation: Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.

30.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
30.file: ch30 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
30.relation: J. Lenore Wright reads the Quest through the Western journey-narrative, both outward (Plato's climb out of the cave, Augustine's conversion) and inward (Descartes's methodological doubt turning toward the cogito). Frodo's leaving the Shire and freely accepting the Ring dramatizes the outward journey and the limits of freedom, while the wounding-and-healing of Sam, Merry, and Pippin marks an existential journey toward the Nietzschean charge to 'become who you are.' Wright contrasts the Yea-saying hobbits, transformed into resilient masters, with Nay-sayers Smeagol and Saruman locked in inauthentic self-pity, and argues Tolkien's ordinary pilgrims show that binding oneself to the good makes ordinary life extraordinary.

31.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
31.file: ch31 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy.md
31.relation: John Davenport argues The Lord of the Rings is religious not as Christian allegory but as an epic fairy tale in Tolkien's sense from 'On Fairy-stories,' delivering 'eucatastrophe,' the sudden joyous turn that, like Kierkegaard's faith in a salvation beyond our own power, hints at eschatological hope. Using Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as Tolkien's model for Frodo (both accept an impossible burden, both fail and bear a scar of mortality), he identifies the destruction of the Ring via Gollum, Eowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth as eucatastrophic 'turns.' Davenport concludes the veiled religious message is that evil cannot stand forever, yet deliverance requires our sacrifice and faith beyond rational hope that 'day shall come again.'

8.title: Who is Who
8.relation: The introduction argues that Doctor Who and philosophy share a common origin in wonder (quoting Plato's Socrates and Aristotle) and traces the show's shifting worldview across the eleven Doctors. It claims early Who embodied Enlightenment 'positivism' (the pro-science Hartnell/Pertwee eras) but that the post-1996 and post-2005 series turned toward Romanticism and Sartrean/de Beauvoirian existentialism, framing the surviving Doctor's post-Time War 'angst,' homelessness and burden of freedom through existentialist themes.

9.title: Who is Who
9.relation: This chapter reads the Doctor as poised between positivism and phenomenology. It uses Hume's Fork and the Vienna Circle's verificationism (via 'The Daemons' and 'Tomb of the Cybermen') to cast the pro-science Doctor as an empiricist, then argues he is equally a Husserlian phenomenologist attentive to the 'life-world' and a Heideggerian Dasein whose time-travelling homelessness and the show's sense of the uncanny (unheimlich) embody being-in-the-world, thrownness and the flight from the worldhood of the world.

10.title: Who is Who
10.file: ch10 - Who is Who.md
10.relation: Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.

11.title: Who is Who
11.file: ch11 - Who is Who.md
11.relation: Focused on the 'Monstrous Other' and the 'base under siege' story, the chapter uses Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition and Sartre's 'the look' to read Cybermen, the Flood ('Waters of Mars') and the Silurians as Others through which humans define themselves, with Levinas on the face and history. Its final section frames the Doctor and the Master as Gothic doubles of love and strife, using Spinoza's monism, principle of sufficient reason and conatus to argue the power-hungry Master paradoxically fits Spinoza's system better than the order-imposing 'Dark Doctor.'

12.title: Who is Who
12.file: ch12 - Who is Who.md
12.relation: This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.

13.title: Who is Who
13.file: ch13 - Who is Who.md
13.relation: On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'

14.title: Who is Who
14.file: ch14 - Who is Who.md
14.relation: This political chapter reads Gallifreyan bureaucracy ('The Deadly Assassin') and 1970s socialist-tinged serials, using Marx's alienation and critique of capital to interpret 'The Pirate Planet' and 'The Robots of Death,' and Aristotle's 'political animal' plus Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of democracy against Benjamin Barber's participatory democracy. It analyzes the pathologies of democratic consent through 'Vengeance on Varos' (Plato's ideal state inverted) and 'The Beast Below' (Arendt on totalitarianism, self-inflicted ignorance), with Isaiah Berlin's negative liberty in the vocabulary of materiality.

15.title: Who is Who
15.file: ch15 - Who is Who.md
15.relation: The time-travel chapter grounds Doctor Who's paradoxes in Parmenides and Zeno on the impossibility of change and Aristotle on the logical necessity of past and future statements ('You can't rewrite history!' in 'The Aztecs'), then deploys determinism, David Lewis on the paradoxes of time travel, and the consistency/autonomy principles ('Father's Day,' the Reapers). It uses Leibniz's possible worlds and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to read 'Inferno' and 'Turn Left,' arguing quantum indeterminacy and entanglement make the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' theory of fixed points and flux coherent.

16.title: Who is Who

5.title: index
5.relation: This composite chapter opens with the volume's Introduction and then runs several essays. Jeff McLaughlin's 'What If?' reads DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths and Marvel's What If? series as literal illustrations of Leibniz's possible-worlds metaphysics: the multiverse of Earth-1, Earth-2 and the 3,000 doomed universes dramatizes counterfactuals and Leibniz's Theodicy argument (via the principle of sufficient reason) that God actualizes only the best of infinitely many possible worlds, with Descartes invoked on why a perfect God permits imperfection. Amy Kiste Nyberg's essay analyzes the 1954 Senate hearings on EC horror comics (Gaines's 'The Orphan') as an applied-ethics clash between publishers' free expression and protecting children, explicitly deploying Mill's On Liberty and harm principle to argue why the child-audience framing defeats the anti-censorship case. Stanford Carpenter's piece treats the Black Captain America (Truth: Red, White, and Black) as an epistemology-of-authorship problem.

6.title: index
6.relation: This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.

7.title: index
7.relation: This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.

6.title: NOTES
6.relation: William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.

7.title: I - PHILOSOPHY AND POPULAR CULTURE
7.file: ch07 - I - PHILOSOPHY AND POPULAR CULTURE.md

8.title: NOTES
8.relation: Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.

9.title: NOTES
9.relation: Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).

10.title: NOTES
10.file: ch10 - NOTES.md
10.relation: Theodore Gracyk analyzes artistic allusion in mass art, arguing (against Carrier and partly with Carroll) that accessibility does not preclude esoteric interpretive richness. His signature case is that The Matrix's red/blue pill scene overtly alludes to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland yet covertly alludes to Lewis Carroll's Sylvie and Bruno lockets, foreshadowing Neo as a Christ figure who must 'love all.' Drawing on Paul Grice's conversational implicature and Austin's illocutionary/perlocutionary speech-act theory, he argues allusion (Alien/Star Wars, Randy Newman's 'I Love L.A.', the Deliverance banjo in The Simpsons) is intentional and normatively constrains which associations transfer from source to alluding text.

11.title: NOTES
11.file: ch11 - NOTES.md
11.relation: Noel Carroll examines how popular fictions bind audiences emotionally through their relation to characters, starting from Plato's claim in the Republic that the popular arts pander to the emotions (pity and fear). He rejects both 'identification' (we rarely share characters' states—we fear for lovers who feel bliss, feel joy when the villain is foiled) and the fashionable 'simulation' theory as comprehensive accounts, arguing instead that sympathy—a pro-attitude directed at morally endorsable protagonists like Maximus in Gladiator—is the real 'tie that binds,' supplemented by involuntary 'mirror reflexes' (mimicking a screaming face in horror films, tapping to Riverdance).

12.title: NOTES
12.file: ch12 - NOTES.md
12.relation: Ted Cohen denies there is any sound argument from 'X is better than Y' to 'it is better to like X,' using Bach vs. Elvis vs. Milton Babbitt on complexity to show the criterion collapses. He reframes art around 'communities of appreciation'—citing Augustine's claim that a people is defined by what it loves in common—and reports (via a blues club in Memphis and the Marriage of Figaro) that what all appreciators of a work share is 'nothing' but their love of it, a Goodman-style nominalism. He challenges Kant's insistence that genuine aesthetic judgments claim universality, arguing real appreciative communities are less-than-universal overlapping circles.

13.title: NOTES
13.file: ch13 - NOTES.md
13.relation: Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.

15.title: NOTES
15.file: ch15 - NOTES.md
15.relation: Cantor argues that TV shows like The Simpsons and The X-Files can be genuine art despite multiple authorship, contingency, and commercial pressure, using the Lone Gunmen's audience-driven revival and Scully's pregnancy-forced abduction plot as evidence of a 'feedback' rather than 'perfect plan' model of creation. He rejects the Romantic/New Critical ideal of the solitary genius producing organic form and reframes popular culture through Hayek's spontaneous order, drawing directly on Adam Smith's self-regulating markets (the invisible hand) and Darwinian selection. Aristotle's Poetics supplies the target organic-form doctrine—that every part serves the whole—which Cantor says wrongly theorizes contingency out of art.

16.title: NOTES
16.file: ch16 - NOTES.md
16.relation: Gracia examines six Dracula films (Murnau, Browning, Morrisey, Herzog, Badham, Coppola) and asks how they relate to Stoker's novel, tracing the count's evolution from Murnau's rat-like horror to Coppola's tragic romantic knight who dies for love. He rejects the topical, essentialist, and family-resemblance accounts of the films' relation to the book and proposes instead that they are 'relational interpretations'—works in their own right whose primary aim is to link Stoker's story to an outside agenda (sex, humor, sympathy, heroism) rather than to explicate the novel. The argument is a piece of interpretation theory, distinguishing work-oriented from relational interpretation to explain why popular adaptations legitimately diverge from their source.

17.title: NOTES
17.relation: Matthews argues that certain children's books are 'subversive' in a Socratic sense: they problematize concepts adults assume they command, challenging adult epistemic authority the way Socrates exposed the pretended knowledge of Athens' elite. Morris the Moose raises Aristotelian questions of natural kinds and essence-versus-accident; Leese Webster probes the concept of art; The Shrinking of Treehorn destabilizes 'normal' child development; Frog and Toad's 'The Garden' dramatizes the post hoc, ergo propter hoc fallacy about causation. In the Ozma of Oz Tik-Tok discussion, nine-year-old Paul reconstructs an argument that only brains think, which Matthews aligns with Searle's claim in The Mystery of Consciousness that consciousness is caused by specific neurobiological processes; he explicitly distinguishes his subversive stories from those promoting Pyrrhonian skepticism or Protagorean relativism.

18.title: NOTES
18.file: ch18 - NOTES.md
18.relation: South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.

19.title: NOTES
19.relation: Baur reads Don McLean's 'American Pie' as an enactment of how a culture can criticize itself from within, decoding its Buddy Holly, Dylan, Rolling Stones (Altamont), and Manson/Beatles allusions while insisting the song's meaning lies in simultaneous multiple meanings, not one-to-one correspondence. He argues McLean rejects any 'foundationalist' Archimedean point for critique—paralleling the standard objection that Descartes' cogito illicitly borrows the concept of finite substance from the tradition it claims to doubt—so the 'girl who sang the blues' shows that seeking a purer external origin only deepens disenchantment. Baur concludes with an Aristotelian point that cultural self-critique follows the model of the prudential sciences (phronesis) rather than techne: one reforms a tradition only by participating in it and exposing its internal contradictions.

20.title: NOTES
20.relation: Hare treats mass photography—from the daguerreotype through digital cameras, Abu Ghraib snapshots, and diagnostic imaging—as making everyone a practicing epistemologist caught between two folk tenets: the photo as mirror of reality and as manipulation of reality. Defending photography as a genuine causal 'mode of seeing' (a prosthetic like telescopes), he proposes 'flexible realism,' adjusting Dewey's warranted assertibility and virtue-epistemology standards to context, and invokes William James's defense of beneficial 'overbeliefs' when National Geographic images strengthen confidence in one's own culture. Reading the Fallujah lead-pipe photo debate between editors Sullivan and Kushner, he uses Quine's recalcitrant-experience and web-of-belief holism—extended by Morton White's 'holistic pragmatism'—to show moral, epistemic, sensory, and emotional claims are tested together, and frames photography's democratization via Walter Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and loss of aura.

7.title: How to Use this Book in a Philosophy Course
7.file: ch07 - How to Use this Book in a Philosophy Course.md

9.title: The Talking Cure for Our Culture
9.file: ch09 - The Talking Cure for Our Culture.md
9.relation: William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.

10.title: The Defense Rests
10.file: ch10 - The Defense Rests.md
10.relation: Robert Arp uses South Park's cartoon Johnnie Cochran and his 'Chewbacca Defense' from 'Chef Aid' to teach basic logic: premises, conclusions, deductive versus inductive arguments, and validity/soundness versus strength/cogency. The Chewbacca Defense exemplifies the red-herring fallacy, and other episodes illustrate hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. The chapter's subject is informal logic and fallacy theory rather than a single named philosopher or taxonomy concept.

11.title: How to do Philosophy
11.file: ch11 - How to do Philosophy.md
11.relation: David Kyle Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack individual and cultural relativism, arguing (via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany) that truth is not relative to persons or cultures. He deploys Locke's critique of 'enthusiasm' to show gut thinking is circular, and invokes Socratic admission of ignorance against the claim of a 'right to your opinion.' The upshot is a method: defend beliefs with argument, be agnostic when evidence is lacking.

12.title: Introduction
12.file: ch12 - Introduction.md

13.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
13.file: ch13 - Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress.md
13.relation: Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.

14.title: Skepticism Outside the Matrix
14.file: ch14 - Skepticism Outside the Matrix.md
14.relation: Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.

15.title: “You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”
15.file: ch15 - “You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”.md
15.relation: Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.

16.title: Introduction
16.file: ch16 - Introduction.md

17.title: The Role of Matter Biology or Function
17.file: ch17 - The Role of Matter Biology or Function.md
17.relation: Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind, arguing the 'brain-stimulation' premise favors materialism over Descartes's dualism (which alone easily explains Neo's mind-body separation at the Train Station but lacks empirical support and an interaction mechanism). He explains reductive versus eliminative materialism (Churchland's denial of folk-psychological 'beliefs' via Tastee Wheat) and then Searle's biological emergentism (the beer-can thirst machine) against functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain; Agent Smith's seamless transfer into Bane). He concludes the films are best read functionally, making sentient machines genuine minds.

18.title: Be Slow to Judge
18.file: ch18 - Be Slow to Judge.md
18.relation: Jason Southworth uses Wolverine's repeated memory erasures to test Locke's memory (and connected-memory) criterion of personal identity, arguing that on Locke's view a new 'person' inhabits Wolverine's body each time his memories are wiped, until House of M restores them all. He then deploys Jamie Madrox, whose duplicates share and re-merge memories yet act as distinct agents, as a real-comics version of Parfit's fission case, pushing Parfit's conclusion that identity requires physical (brain) continuity. Because Wolverine's healing factor constantly rebuilds his brain, the moral is to 'be slow to judge' whether a character is the same person who acted before.

19.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
19.file: ch19 - Time Travel and Fixed Time.md
19.relation: Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.

20.title: “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”
20.file: ch20 - “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”.md
20.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether the Terminators are 'people,' testing three criteria: passing as human, thinking, and feeling. The T-101, T-1000, and T-X repeatedly pass Turing Tests, giving behavioral evidence of thought, but Littmann recasts Searle's Chinese Room as the 'Austrian Terminator' to argue behavior never proves genuine understanding. He then argues personhood requires conscious experience (what it is like to be a Terminator), and takes the films' red- and blue-tinted first-person 'Terminator's-eye view' shots as evidence the machines really are conscious, so humanity's extinction need not end personhood.

21.title: Introduction
21.file: ch21 - Introduction.md

22.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
22.file: ch22 - Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy.md
22.relation: David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.

23.title: To Know … and Believe
23.relation: Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.

24.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
24.file: ch24 - “You Have to Believe in Something”.md
24.relation: Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.

26.title: But Isn’t It Only Natural
26.file: ch26 - But Isn’t It Only Natural.md
26.relation: Don Adams uses Heroes' superpowered characters (who could commit perfect crimes like Gyges with his invisibility ring) to argue Plato's case that virtue is its own reward. He maps Plato's tripartite soul onto the characters: Claire's thumos (spirit/honor) tempered by logistikos (reason) yields courage and wisdom, while Sylar's ruling appetite (his hunger for powers) is intemperance and injustice that makes his life spin out of control. Reading justice as psychic health, and glossing the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies, but enemies may become friends), Adams argues it is 'only natural' for even the powerful to be virtuous rather than exploit others.

27.title: Lessons Learned
27.relation: Sean McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, 'the slave of his sense of humor,' who jests inappropriately; Gareth is the boorish literalist who cannot take or get a joke; Tim is the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to the situation, exercising practical wisdom (phronesis). McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.

28.title: So, Case Closed – Right
28.relation: Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.

29.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
29.relation: J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.

31.title: Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia
31.relation: Fosl argues that Metallica's lyrics echo Nietzsche's and Marx's moral critiques of Christianity: songs like "Leper Messiah" and "The God that Failed" cast religion as slave-morality ressentiment, mind-control, and Marx's "opium of the people." He then asks whether the band achieves a Nietzschean transvaluation or lapses into the very nihilism Nietzsche said Christianity breeds — reading "To Live is to Die" and "One" as nostalgic death-wish, but "Escape" and "The Four Horsemen" as genuine defiant self-overcoming after the death of God.

32.title: “They Have a Plan”
32.relation: Sharp maps Battlestar Galactica's Cylon uprising onto Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the enslaved Cylons, like Nietzsche's early Christians under Rome, invent a slave morality that inverts their masters' values, condemning human pride and greed while exalting a single loving God, souls, and equality. He shows Leoben preaching the soul to Starbuck and the Cylons' consensus-based commune as the powerless revaluing weakness into virtue, converting their polytheistic, master-moral human creators much as Christianity converted Rome.

33.title: The Viewer and the Look
33.file: ch33 - The Viewer and the Look.md
33.relation: Meyer and Schneider read The Office through Sartre's "the Look" and bad faith: the mockumentary camera catches characters as objects, as when Pam is caught gazing at Jim and freezes in shame, or pretends she has no choice about Roy (bad faith). David Brent's prideful posing tries to control the Other's look and fails. They add Foucault's panopticon — Dwight, Angela, and Jan police themselves because the camera might be watching — making the viewer complicit in exposing the employees' existential crises.

34.title: Determinism and the Dark Knight
34.file: ch34 - Determinism and the Dark Knight.md
34.relation: Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman beyond the free-will/determinism binary. Dasein is a "thrown-project" always being-toward-death; Alfred's world of trays and clocks illustrates the interpretive horizon of a chosen life.
