Fleabag's addressing the camera and finally shutting it out is read as breaking the gaze of the Other; the Priest choosing priesthood over love exemplifies denial of transcendence. Through Beauvoir's Second Sex, woman-as-Other, and ethics of ambiguity, they show Waller-Bridge's transgressive, sexually frank women reclaim self-definition, arguing viewers 'could do better to be' the kind of free, choosing women her protagonists are.

81.title: 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain
81.file: ch81 - 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain.md
81.relation: Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

82.title: 77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime
82.file: ch82 - 77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime.md
82.relation: Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.

83.title: 78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed
83.file: ch83 - 78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed.md
83.relation: Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.

84.title: 79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine
84.file: ch84 - 79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine.md
84.relation: Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

85.title: 80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay
85.file: ch85 - 80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay.md
85.relation: Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.

86.title: 81. Papers, Please as Philosophy Playing with the Relations between Politics and Morality
86.file: ch86 - 81. Papers, Please as Philosophy Playing with the Relations between Politics and Morality.md
86.relation: Sievers argues that Papers, Please immerses the player as an immigration inspector in the totalitarian Arstotzka, where mechanically stamping 'approved'/'refused' and detaining Kolechians for bribes enacts Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, 'just following orders' functionary exemplified by Eichmann, who cannot think from another's standpoint. The paycheck-versus-family pressure and X-ray humiliation scenes show how fear and bureaucracy erase moral responsibility. Drawing on Butler's 'Can one lead a good life in a bad life?' and Foucault's biopower, she reads the visa candidates as 'precarious,' non-grievable lives whose worth the state allocates, and the game's Ezic resistance endings as showing how constrained moral resistance is under such a regime.

87.title: 82. Planescape Torment as Philosophy Regret Can Change the Nature of a Man
87.file: ch87 - 82. Planescape Torment as Philosophy Regret Can Change the Nature of a Man.md
87.relation: Gubka argues that Planescape: Torment answers Ravel's riddle 'What can change the nature of a man?' with 'regret,' read through Aristotle's claim that virtues are developed by habitually practicing virtuous action. The Nameless One's regret over betraying Deionarra and over the innocents killed to sustain his immortality motivates redemptive acts—apologizing to Deionarra, surrendering his immortality—shifting his alignment toward Good. The chapter rebuts Hobbes's Psychological Egoism (TNO's genuinely altruistic self-sacrifice) and Spinoza's warning that regret only doubles misery, arguing instead that apt regret is a golden-mean virtue between remorselessness and self-condemnation whose very painfulness makes it motivating.

88.title: 83. Disco Elysium as Philosophy Solipsism, Existentialism, and Simulacra
88.file: ch88 - 83. Disco Elysium as Philosophy Solipsism, Existentialism, and Simulacra.md
88.relation: Khamis reads Disco Elysium's 'Pale'—a property-less substance said to be decaying human thought that consumes reality—through three idealisms. The phasmid's warning that the world might vanish if humans stop thinking it evokes Berkeley's subjective idealism (esse est percipi) but without God as guarantor, leaving Harry in existential dread. The Pale as human-produced 'second nature' laid over 'first nature' evokes Kant's and Schelling's transcendental idealism, while the Pale as decaying signs without signification—like the vacuous dockworker 'sheriffs'—matches Baudrillard's hyperreality and simulacra, where information proliferates as meaning collapses, paralleling the amnesiac Harry's own loss and remaking of self.

89.title: 84. The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild as Philosophy Teaching the Player to Be Comfortable Being Alone
89.file: ch89 - 84. The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild as Philosophy Teaching the Player to Be Comfortable Being Alone.md
89.relation: Lay argues that Breath of the Wild teaches, chiefly through design rather than plot, that solitude is good for the player. He tests eternal return (the recurring Ganon-Zelda-Link cycle across the series), Sartrean absolute freedom and Kierkegaardian anxiety of choice (BotW's Korok-dung 'reward' and refusal to attach external meaning push players to make their own meaning), and Kierkegaard's inward 'repetition.' He lands on Mill's and Schopenhauer's defense of solitude-in-nature as self-actualizing rather than isolating, and reads sequence-breaking exploits as Marx-style spontaneous creative activity, concluding the game frames solitude as a path to eudaimonia and human flourishing.

90.title: 85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality
90.file: ch90 - 85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality.md
90.relation: Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.

91.title: 86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom
91.file: ch91 - 86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom.md
91.relation: Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'

93.title: 87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”
93.file: ch93 - 87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”.md
93.relation: Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.

94.title: 88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will
94.file: ch94 - 88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will.md
94.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.

95.title: 89. The Joker as Philosopher Killing Jokes
95.file: ch95 - 89. The Joker as Philosopher Killing Jokes.md
95.relation: Brake reads Moore and Bolland's The Killing Joke as staging Camus's absurd: the Joker tortures Commissioner Gordon to prove the world is random and unjust ('one bad day') and that reason, tied to continuous memory, should be abandoned for a fragmented 'multiple choice' self. Drawing on Nietzsche's wave-like unstable self (via Morrison's 'super-sane' Joker) and Foucault on how madness haunts modern reason, the chapter argues Batman and Gordon also flirt with madness, while questioning whether the Joker, seeking revenge, has really embraced the absurd or is more rational than he admits.

96.title: 90. From Hell as Philosophy Ripping Through Structural Violence
96.file: ch96 - 90. From Hell as Philosophy Ripping Through Structural Violence.md
96.relation: James and Mona Rocha argue that Moore and Campbell's From Hell links physical and structural violence under patriarchy: William Gull's Ripper murders of Whitechapel sex workers, and his premonition of the dull modern office ('the twentieth century, I have delivered it'), show how sensationalized physical violence pushes routine structural violence into the invisible background where it corrupts men morally (Gull and Abberline both lose their humanity). Using Galtung's structural violence and Crenshaw's intersectionality of poverty and gender, plus the male gaze in Gull's ghostly viewing of female workers, the chapter connects Victorian misogyny to present-day workplace sexual harassment.

97.title: 91. Deadpool’s Killogy as Philosophy The Metaphysics of a Homicidal Journey Through Possible Worlds
97.file: ch97 - 91. Deadpool’s Killogy as Philosophy The Metaphysics of a Homicidal Journey Through Possible Worlds.md
97.relation: Manninen argues that Cullen Bunn's Deadpool 'Killogy' is best read through David Lewis's genuine modal realism and counterpart theory: when Deadpool enters the Nexus of All Realities and finds piles of distinct Spider-Man corpses, he discovers other worlds are concrete and their inhabitants are counterparts, not identical selves, refuting Plantinga's actualist transworld identity. Framing Deadpool as an anti-Sisyphean 'hero' who tries to end the Absurd (the Continuity) by killing everyone rather than affirming it as Camus's Sisyphus does, the chapter supplements Lewis with Thomasson's artifact theory of fiction to handle the literary characters of the Ideaverse.

98.title: 92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy
98.file: ch98 - 92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy.md
98.relation: Nisley argues that Moore and Lloyd's V for Vendetta justifies V's violent rebellion against the Norsefire regime through Locke: the fascist state seized power without consent, tortured and experimented on citizens (V at Larkhill), and violated natural rights, thereby placing itself in a state of war so the people may overthrow it. Using Aristotle on deviant constitutions and the beast-like tyrant (Adam Susan) who lacks practical wisdom, and contrasting Locke's tolerable state of nature with Hobbes's brutal one, the chapter concludes the citizens should rebuild a rights-protecting social contract rather than V's leaderless anarchy, and maps the argument onto real-world 2020 events (BLM riots vs. the Whitmer kidnapping plot).

99.title: 93. Asterios Polyp as Philosophy Master of Two Worlds
99.file: ch99 - 93. Asterios Polyp as Philosophy Master of Two Worlds.md
99.relation: Richards reads Mazzucchelli's Asterios Polyp as a visual meditation on universals versus particulars and the abstract versus concrete, using its CMYK color coding and character styles (Asterios as cool geometric solids, Hana as warm crosshatching) to stage Plato's two worlds. Asterios, a 'paper architect' living in perfect uninstantiated abstraction, undergoes an inverted Hero's Journey (Campbell's monomyth) down into the concrete world—building an actual treehouse, telling the Ise shrine story—to become 'master of two worlds,' reconciling Form and matter, universal and particular, and accepting impermanence just as an asteroid closes on Earth.

100.title: 94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission
100.file: ch100 - 94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission.md
100.relation: Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.

101.title: 95. The Walking Dead as Philosophy Rick Grimes and Community Building in an Apocalypse
101.file: ch101 - 95. The Walking Dead as Philosophy Rick Grimes and Community Building in an Apocalypse.md
101.relation: Jones argues that Kirkman's The Walking Dead uses Rick Grimes's community-building to probe utopia and dystopia, reading the prison, Alexandria, Woodbury, the Saviors, and the Commonwealth through Aristotle's six constitutional forms—with the polity (rule by many for the common good enabling eudaimonia) as the standard for a good society and tyranny/oligarchy/corrupt forms marking dystopias like Negan's compound and the class-tyrannical Commonwealth. Invoking More's and Mill's coinages of utopia and dystopia, the chapter asks why Rick's final society, despite his moral evolution, ends up rebuilding the hierarchical pre-apocalyptic order rather than the more egalitarian, flourishing alliance he had forged.

7.title: Welcome Aboard the TARDIS—It’s Bigger on the Inside
7.file: ch07 - Welcome Aboard the TARDIS—It’s Bigger on the Inside.md
7.relation: The author argues that Doctor Who functions as a 'great educator' that shapes viewers' reality and their conception of the good life, framing our birth into the world as being 'thrown' into a new environment we must assimilate. He applies Hegel's historical dialectic to the Doctor-versus-Daleks conflict, treating the Doctor (wisdom, liberty, compassion) and the Daleks (obedience, hatred, conquest) as opposing theses whose ongoing struggle synthesizes the wider universe's fear of the Daleks. Drawing on Carroll and Danesi, he claims pop culture like Doctor Who validates experience and creates collective structures of meaning, and that our chosen first Doctor becomes the interpretive framework through which we judge every later one.

9.title: 1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor
9.file: ch09 - 1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor.md
9.relation: The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

10.title: 2. The Dangers of Being the Doctor
10.file: ch10 - 2. The Dangers of Being the Doctor.md
10.relation: The chapter weighs the Doctor's ethic of interference against the Time Lords' non-interference, using determinism and the 'butterfly effect' (Martha in 'The Shakespeare Code') to concede when disengaged observation is prudent, while insisting that non-interference fails to protect human dignity. Drawing on Terrence Des Pres's account of dignity as 'inward resistance,' and real-world dissidents Adam Michnik and Václav Havel's 'power of the powerless,' it reads 'Rosa,' 'The Woman Who Fell to Earth,' and the people of Le Chambon as models of dignified, communal resistance to wrongdoing. Citing Iris Young, it argues everyone bears moral responsibility to engage rather than remain a detached, complicit 'objective observer.'

11.title: II Everyday Life as the Doctor
11.file: ch11 - II Everyday Life as the Doctor.md

12.title: 3. What Is Who
12.file: ch12 - 3. What Is Who.md
12.relation: The chapter runs the Doctor's regenerations and the 'Timeless Child' reveal through competing theories of personal identity: Plato's soul/Forms, Locke's memory continuity, and bodily continuity, all of which the Doctor's body-swaps and forgotten lifetimes defeat (the Twelfth Doctor's 'you are a broom' speech recasts the Ship of Theseus). It endorses an existentialist answer—personal identity is chosen and constantly 'becoming,' as the Thirteenth Doctor declares 'I know exactly who I am. I'm the Doctor'—and uses Sartre against Freud to explain how the Doctor and the Whovian fandom reconcile internal and external selves in a community of acceptance. It closes arguing that only an 'objective' immortality (memories preserved in the Matrix) survives death, not a subjective self.

13.title: 4. The Good of the Doctor
13.file: ch13 - 4. The Good of the Doctor.md
13.relation: The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

14.title: 5. Monsters and Evil in Doctor Who
14.file: ch14 - 5. Monsters and Evil in Doctor Who.md
14.relation: The chapter defines a 'moral monster' as one who delights in evil acts, arguing (via Jonathan Glover and Laurence Thomas) that Hitler-style evil is all-too-human, not alien. Using Hume's claim that action springs from passion, it contends the emotionless Cybermen are a mere force of nature (bad but not evil), whereas the Daleks, driven by hatred, tribalism, and a closed belief system, are genuinely evil monsters; the manipulating Master mirrors our everyday lying. It then examines retributive justice through Solomon's execution in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship' and 'A Town Called Mercy,' rejecting purely backward- or forward-looking punishment (citing Rawls on utilitarianism's injustice) in favor of the Doctor's needs-based, 'reprobative' punishment, mercy, and self-forgiveness over the Time War.

15.title: III Beyond Everything
15.file: ch15 - III Beyond Everything.md

16.title: 6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife
16.file: ch16 - 6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife.md
16.relation: The chapter asks whether Doctor Who is a religion, testing it against Hopfe's and Ninian Smart's criteria and concluding it is best understood as a Humanist-and-religious 'philosophy'—sacred and 'holy' (Otto) but lacking a genuine transcendent 'unseen.' On loss, it uses Kierkegaard's 'aesthetic life' and 'rotation method' to explain why we fear endings and regenerations, urging viewers to root life in lasting meaning rather than fleeting pleasure. On death, it deploys Socrates in the Apology and Phaedo and Aristotle on courage (Jabe, Harriet Jones, Donna sacrificing themselves) to argue death is nothing to fear, and reads the Matrix and Nethersphere as the show's two Socratic afterlife options.

17.title: 7. Knowledge, Space, and Time
17.relation: The chapter uses the TARDIS to defend a 'block universe' theory of spacetime over Presentism (since the Doctor visits past and future), then turns to epistemology, distinguishing belief from knowledge and 'belief in' the Doctor from 'belief that' he exists. It re-stages Gettier's justified-true-belief counterexample as picking the Doctor's next companion by a blue jean jacket, surveys Descartes's Cogito foundationalism, Hume's induction, and Reid's direct perception, and endorses Alston's reliabilist two-level foundationalism plus Klein's infinitism. It argues the Doctor's benefit-of-the-doubt toward non-rational creatures fits a reliabilist 'lower level' of knowledge and an imaginative, engaged, virtuous (Zagzebski) search for truth.

18.title: Epilogue
18.file: ch18 - Epilogue.md
18.relation: The closing essay exhorts readers to 'approach life as the Doctor'—engaged, compassionate, and critically thinking—insisting each person is important and that fandom passion, even when fractious, expresses the Doctor's engaged life (invoking Voltaire on free expression). Using 'Father's Day' and 'The Day of the Doctor,' it argues we cannot change the past but must seize the present, and ties 'truth' and 'trust' to a shared root to claim a meaningful life requires trusting oneself and others rather than merely proving oneself right. It affirms that wisdom is lived truth, that being wrong is how we mature, and that courage is doing what must be done while afraid.

21.title: Index
21.file: ch21 - Index.md

unexamined-life.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
unexamined-life.title: Monologue
unexamined-life.relation: Editor William Irwin's introduction explains why Seinfeld is philosophical: 'Seinfeld' sounds like German for 'field of being,' echoing Heidegger's Sein und Zeit, and he tells students to picture the four at Monk's coffee shop when Heidegger describes the 'idle chatter' of the inauthentic mode of being, while George's 'what is the opposite of what I would normally do?' shows the courage of changing one's way of seeing. He frames the whole book with Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living - the Seinfeld characters examine their lives constantly, though Socrates would approve of neither their lives nor their examinations - and with Nietzsche's 'A Book for None and All' subtitle, then lays out the volume's four-act structure.

unexamined-life.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
unexamined-life.title: The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld
unexamined-life.relation: William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.

unexamined-life.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
unexamined-life.title: Unknown
unexamined-life.relation: Irwin compares the film's kitchen-table Oracle with the Pythia at Delphi: both utter cryptic prophecies that seekers misread, from Croesus's doomed war to Morpheus's certainty that Neo is the One, and both make self-knowledge the real key to interpretation. He reads the 'Temet Nosce' sign and the cookie scene through the Delphic maxims 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess', arguing Neo fulfills the prophecy only when he comes to know and believe in himself, and closes by linking Socrates' gadfly mission and 'the unexamined life is not worth living' to Fight Club, Boys Don't Cry, and Memento.

unexamined-life.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
unexamined-life.title: Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy
unexamined-life.relation: Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.

unexamined-life.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
unexamined-life.title: Last Pitch
unexamined-life.relation: Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.

unexamined-life.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
unexamined-life.title: Hope
unexamined-life.relation: Jill Gordon reads Another Woman as a film about self-knowledge structured by Socrates' self-seeing eye from Plato's Alcibiades I: just as an eye sees itself only in another eye, the emotionally walled-off philosophy professor Marion Post finally sees her own repression by overhearing the 'other woman' Hope's therapy through a vent. Each of her relationships, with husband Ken, brother Paul, renounced lover Larry, stepdaughter Laura, and friend Claire, mirrors back truths ('she stands above people and evaluates them') that her self-deception refuses until her dream stages her own analysis and the final session describes her own life exactly. Counting the irrecoverable cost of her chances (Larry, the aborted child), the chapter closes with Rilke's 'Archaic Torso of Apollo', 'You must change your life', as the command Marion finally obeys, yielding a hard-won and still hopeful transformation.

unexamined-life.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
unexamined-life.title: Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power
unexamined-life.relation: This section contrasts Voldemort and Dumbledore as two figures tempted by power. Tom Riddle's egocentrism - frightening and controlling other children at the orphanage, treating his 'friends' as mere followers, killing Lily, and splintering his soul for Horcruxes - violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means and fits Plato's category of the least trustworthy rulers. Dumbledore, though tempted in youth by Grindelwald's 'for the greater good' schemes and later by Marvolo Gaunt's ring, is venerable for Socratic self-knowledge: knowing 'I was not to be trusted with power,' he repeatedly refused the Ministry and so promoted justice by teaching.

unexamined-life.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
unexamined-life.title: Unknown
unexamined-life.relation: The section urges a Socratic habit of self-examination, with Dumbledore as its model: knowing his besetting weakness was the love of power, he repeatedly refused the post of Minister of Magic, and after his infatuation with Grindelwald made him 'lose his moral compass completely' he distrusted his own judgment in matters of the heart. The Pensieve, which lets Dumbledore siphon off excess memories and review them from a third-person perspective to 'spot patterns and links,' is presented as a literal device for living the examined life.

unexamined-life.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
unexamined-life.title: The End of the Story
unexamined-life.relation: Argues Socrates and Dumbledore both die for virtue and the common good: Socrates refuses exile because the examined life matters more than wealth or reputation, his martyrdom an exemplar that could benefit Athens, and Dumbledore's arranged death protects Snape's spying for the anti-Voldemort cause. Two Muggle lessons follow - live devoted to something larger than yourself (Lily's sacrifice, with King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates as real-world parallels) and find mentors, as Dumbledore's humility, honesty, and praise in the Order of the Phoenix prophecy conversation enable Harry to fulfill his destiny, with dead mentors like Aristotle, Confucius, and Jesus still able to teach us through their books.

unexamined-life.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
unexamined-life.title: Foreword
unexamined-life.relation: Cornel West argues that Plato's dialogues invented philosophy as a Socratic genre of cross-examination and bold frank speech (parrhesia) about ordinary life, and that hip-hop music - like the spirituals, blues, and jazz - enacts that same parrhesia against conventional morality and entrenched power. He claims reading hip hop philosophically demands metaphilosophical subtlety, showing how paideia, phronesis, and parrhesia operate in the work of cultural producers under free-market fundamentalism and authoritarianism. Because the racial dimension of hip hop is inescapable, he says philosophers must break their discipline's silence on race and music (neglected figures like Du Bois and Alain Locke alongside Aristotle, Kant, and Rorty), closing with Cicero's Socrates who turned philosophy from the heavens to earth and William James's pragmatism that took it from the academy to the streets.

unexamined-life.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
unexamined-life.title: From Rhyme to Reason This Shit Ain’t Easy
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction argues that hip hop and philosophy are both street-born examinations of life in pursuit of wisdom: Socrates's elenchus is likened to MC lyrical battles and call-and-response (his interrogations compared to Rakim's technique, his execution for corrupting the youth to the fate of a controversial rapper), while Plato's philosopher-king parallels Kurtis Blow and Run-D.M.C. claiming thrones. After a Bronx hip-hop history sketch (Kool Herc, BDP's "The Bridge is Over"), they frame the volume around hip hop's suppressed fifth element of knowledge and preview its pairings: Aquinas and Rakim on God, Plato and Lauryn Hill on love, Sartre and Lil' Kim's gaze, Kant and Ice Cube on punishment, Hegel and Nas, Hobbes and Dead Prez, Mill and Chappelle on epithets. Record companies don't own hip hop and universities don't own philosophy, they conclude - both belong to whoever understands, loves, and respects them.

unexamined-life.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
unexamined-life.title: And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism
unexamined-life.relation: Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.

unexamined-life.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
unexamined-life.title: The Talking Cure for Our Culture
unexamined-life.relation: Young argues South Park is perceived as dangerous for the very reasons Socrates was executed — corrupting the youth and impiety — and that like Socrates it is really a gadfly promoting the examined life. Cartman is read through Arendt's Eichmann: evil as thoughtlessness, the inability to think from another's standpoint or ask if one can live with oneself, while Kyle and Stan's dialogues (such as deliberating Stan's grandfather's euthanasia request in 'Death') model the perspective-taking Arendt calls thinking. A final Freudian section explains the show's vulgarity as essential: jokes work like dreams, releasing repressed drives so the culture can talk through what it forbids.

unexamined-life.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
unexamined-life.title: House and the Life of Reason
unexamined-life.relation: Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.

unexamined-life.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
unexamined-life.title: Resignation and Exploration—I’ll Climb the Hill in My Own Way
unexamined-life.relation: Steven Gimbel asks how to live with the 'pink' malaise of Waters's lyrics and tests five options: capitulation (Marx's four alienations via 'In the Flesh?', 'Have a Cigar', and 'Dogs'), medication ('Comfortably Numb' and the Prozac-ad mother as one of the 'neuro-chemically well-adjusted sheep'), re-creation of childhood (Nietzsche's child playing 'between the fences of past and future' against memory's 'it was' in 'Remember a Day'), and emancipation through LSD or romanticized madness ('See Emily Play', 'Brain Damage'), with Syd Barrett's vacant eyes as the fatal counterexample. What survives is Camus's Sisyphus — fully conscious of his futility yet 'superior to his fate', imagined happy — joined to 'Fearless''s 'I'll climb that hill in my own way' and the mutual care of 'Pigs on the Wing', closing on Socrates' unexamined life: the answer lies in the searching itself, so living pink means living.

unexamined-life.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
unexamined-life.title: Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'

unexamined-life.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
unexamined-life.title: Must I Repeat Myself
unexamined-life.relation: Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.

unexamined-life.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
unexamined-life.title: How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning
unexamined-life.relation: Adam Glover reads 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' through Kristeva's intertextuality: since every text and self is a 'mosaic of quotations' pirated from pre-existing sources, Buffett's confession that he was born 'two hundred years too late' makes him an ironic pirate who can no longer believe or plunder unselfconsciously, unlike the oblivious common-sense pirate. Invoking Barthes's death of the author, he argues the pirate's life is a hard freedom to improvise multiple meanings (the ever-changing 'head uptown' variations in the song) with full responsibility for one's choices. The chapter ends weighing Camus's worry that meaninglessness makes life not worth living against the Nietzsche of The Birth of Tragedy, who answers that the meaning of life is life itself, and it sides with Buffett against Socrates's 'unexamined life' while admitting it cannot settle the question.

unexamined-life.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
unexamined-life.title: Under-Confidence in Reason Once It’s Easier Said, then It’s Done
unexamined-life.relation: Roben Torosyan turns Colbert into a negative textbook for critical thinking: the character embodies the exact opposite of the American Philosophical Association's seven critical-thinking dispositions (inquisitive, open-minded, truthseeking, systematic, analytical, judicious, confident in reason), from refusing to imagine Lisa Randall's extra dimensions, to 'the market doesn't lie' about the Bible, to placing himself above Maimonides, Socrates, and Aquinas in the stem-cell Formidable Opponent. Each section names the fallacies his shtick commits - appeal to popularity, appeal to ignorance, composition, circular reasoning, wishful thinking, appeal to consequences - using real WØRD bits like the Iraq 'no casualties' monologue and the cake-metaphor exchange about the war. The WØRD's self-undermining bullet points are read as Derridean deconstruction (différance): every assertion shot through with what differs from and defers it. Watching Colbert fail at the examined life Socrates recommended, the viewer learns to catch such abuses in pundits and in themselves.

unexamined-life.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
unexamined-life.title: Philosophy in the Age of Truthiness
unexamined-life.relation: David Detmer explains how the twentieth century's scientific persuasion techniques plus electronic media, American anti-elitism ('science is elitist... Gravity Without Representation'), the conflation of a legal right to an opinion with its being right, and journalism's bankrupt objectivity doctrine produced the age of truthiness that Colbert satirizes (Britannica and the Panama Canal, Limbaugh, O'Reilly, and Coulter as the 'gasbags'). He then rebuts the book's implicit challenge that philosophers' appeals to intuition are themselves truthiness: self-evident truths like 'cruelty is wrong' or Euclid's axioms are needed to stop the infinite regress of justification, and they differ in kind from gut-feelings about historical or political claims whose denial is easily conceived. The Report's nightly ridicule of truthiness therefore serves Socrates' dictum that the unexamined life is not worth living, showing philosophy's value to a public that lets pundits decide by gut.

unexamined-life.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
unexamined-life.title: The Onion, Sarcasm, and the Good of Mankind
unexamined-life.relation: Noah Levin recounts how the Onion article 'Area Man Committed To Being Spicy Food Guy' made him recognize his own obnoxious boasting about hot food and quietly change, presenting satire as continuing philosophy's self-help tradition back to Socrates' 'know thyself.' He distinguishes parody, satire, and sarcasm, then formalizes Onion jokes — the RIAA suing radio stations for giving away free music, and 'That Teen-Abstinence Rally Totally Rocked!' — as implicit reductio ad absurdum arguments whose absurd conclusions force rejection of a hidden premise. The sarcastic route beats a direct lecture, he argues, because the target must complete the three-step argument himself: identify the mocked trait, admit having it, and decide whether to change.

unexamined-life.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
unexamined-life.title: Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation
unexamined-life.relation: Argues Doctor Who is philosophy's ally by way of Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching, which produces justified true belief, and rhetoric, which wins by persuasion: the Master is the master rhetorician whose hypnotic manipulation manufactures unreliable beliefs, while the Doctor is the Socratic teacher who gives information and lets companions decide. Socrates's descriptions of philosophy (the good life, sense of wonder, love of real knowledge) are matched to the show's career as an educational program that teaches viewers to reflect on how they reason, how they treat 'others' like Daleks and Silurians, and to revise their views, that is, to live the examined life.

unexamined-life.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
unexamined-life.title: Know Thyself
unexamined-life.relation: George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.

unexamined-life.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
unexamined-life.title: UNSC Briefing
unexamined-life.relation: Fred Van Lente's introduction argues that Master Chief is deliberately an empty shell—faceless, ageless, mostly silent—so the player's identity grafted onto him brings both to life at once in Halo: Combat Evolved's opening cryo-wakeup tutorial. He frames the book with Thoreau's Walden claim that philosophy is living simplicity, mapping it onto the Chief's ascetic soldier existence, and on Socrates: a game worth playing is worth examining, since the unexamined game is not worth playing. He closes with Aristotle's potentiality and actuality: the game actualizes the Chief as a kicker of alien ass, and the book actualizes the series' social and philosophical potential.

unexamined-life.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
unexamined-life.title: So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh
unexamined-life.relation: Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.

unexamined-life.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
unexamined-life.title: Group Will
unexamined-life.relation: Testerman turns inception against itself: Cobb and Saito believe they freely plan the Fischer job, but conscious will is a feeling, not a cause. From William James's effortful attention and Dewey's willpower she moves to Penfield's stimulated patients and Libet's readiness-potential experiments showing the brain prepares action before we feel we will it, so Fischer, Cobb and Saito are all equally 'incepted' by subconscious forces - 'freedom is ignorance of the causes of actions', as she glosses Spinoza, with Hume's point that causality is only inferred. Advertising, the foot-in-the-door effect and subliminal primes already do inception's work more cheaply, and the team's 'group will' flows from Saito's own unexamined drive for power, so against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly suitable for living.

unexamined-life.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
unexamined-life.title: Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself
unexamined-life.relation: Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?

unexamined-life.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
unexamined-life.title: Chapter 32 - “The Exit Door Leads In”
unexamined-life.relation: Eric Beck reads 'The Exit Door Leads In' as a modernized Platonic dialogue: like Oedipus before the Sphinx, the average salesman Bob Bibleman wins mandatory university admission by answering a computerized waiter's riddle, staging the Delphic 'Know Thyself' against Plato's Gorgias ideal of self-mastery, while Plato's Socrates in Charmides disclaims healthy self-knowledge. When Bibleman's terminal spills classified engine schematics, he decides not on universal principle but on what he thinks the authorities want; his honest answer that he would have handed them over anyway gets him expelled for failing a test he could not read, a double bind showing self-knowledge is contingent and situational. Dick thus revises knowing oneself as negotiation of the state's expectations rather than discovery of an essence, though the ending - Bibleman paying the computer after deciding not to - leaves open that he may one day rebel and need re-education.

unexamined-life.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
unexamined-life.title: Chapter 33 - “The Gun”
unexamined-life.relation: Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.

unexamined-life.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
unexamined-life.title: Out of the Cave
unexamined-life.relation: Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'

unexamined-life.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
unexamined-life.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Vannatta explains why Seinfeld reruns now fall flat through Klosterman's neologism 'unironically': since about 1991 irony has become the invisible background of American comedy, a pervasive detachment that David Foster Wallace named and that Jedediah Purdy's For Common Things attacks as the gap between phenomenon and essence. Against Purdy's ironist (Seinfeld's Jerry, mastered by irony, believing in nothing but his own interests), the chapter sets Kierkegaard's Socrates, whose 'infinite absolute negativity' and confessing ignorance serve a truth he cannot define, and asks whether Klosterman, probing the gap between Bono's rehearsed car-ride persona and his inner self, is master of irony or mastered by it. The answer places Chuck midway between the two jailed ironists, Socrates and the Seinfeld finale: like Socrates he knows his own ignorance and serves the undefined idea of self-understanding, but only through pop-culture resemblance (KISS where Jerry used Superman), unable to master irony any more than he can bite his own teeth.

unexamined-life.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
unexamined-life.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Jeopardy! champion Ken Jennings argues that the silly answer-in-the-form-of-a-question conceit is the engine of the show's appeal, because it turns every topic, even Belgium, into a fractal of surprising factual connections rather than a dull definition. He defends the old-school internalization of facts in a Google age - champions are congenitally curious 'sponges' whose stored knowledge makes them better citizens and thinkers - and speculates that what we call the Self is largely the accumulation of facts in one's head. His philosophy of the show in a nutshell: do not just answer in the form of a question, live your life in the form of a question.

unexamined-life.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
unexamined-life.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Daniel Wanless reads Jeopardy! through the Meno: contestants can formulate the right question only because the answer is already given, just as Socrates answers Meno's paradox by claiming that all inquiry is recollection of truths the immortal soul already holds - latent knowledge that explains how Ken Jennings buzzes in before he consciously knows the response. A priori logical ability (the slave boy's doubled square, the law of non-contradiction applied to which of three cities is southernmost) guides the search for answers, while Final Jeopardy!'s blind wagering embodies Kierkegaard's 'life is only understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.' Socrates would bet it all, Wanless concludes, because the unexamined life is not worth living: his whole life was preparation for the ultimate Final Jeopardy!, lived in the form of a question.

unexamined-life.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
unexamined-life.title: The Wire and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Prof Joe's introduction casts The Wire, like Socrates, as a gadfly that refuses to let any viewer rest comfortably: tough-on-crime conservatives, Hamsterdam-friendly libertarians, hopeful liberals watching Royce and Carcetti, techno-optimists watching Freamon's wire, and capitalists watching the docks and the Baltimore Sun all get their beliefs challenged with no easy answers. It retells Socrates's refusal to escape Athens as valuing the quality of life over its quantity, and sets that against the Puritan work-ethic myth that blames the corner boys and fiends for their own fate while Aristotle's flourishing is rebranded as the American pursuit of happiness. The essay closes by previewing the book's six 'Cases' (the Game, tactics, Omar, boundaries, tragedy, sentencing) around Socrates's own question: how ought we to live?

unexamined-life.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
unexamined-life.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.

unexamined-life.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
unexamined-life.title: The Devil and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Roger Hunt reads Bill Hicks's stand-up as a Socratic comedy exposing Satan's three-point plan: suppress knowledge, breed ignorance, and profit from hypocrisy - from the Waffle House 'readah' scene to Bush-era Gulf War spin ('we looked at the receipts'), JFK-assassination distraction via American Gladiators, and pop stars and marketers who 'suck Satan's cock' (Rick Astley, corporate rock, advertising). Where the Genesis serpent offered knowledge, Hicks's Devil is the force that suppresses it, and Hicks paid a Socratic price - an early death for 'corrupting' his audience - for pointing this out.

unexamined-life.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
unexamined-life.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.

unexamined-life.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
unexamined-life.title: Girls and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Girls is philosophical because it is stark, raw, and accurate about what is common to human existence: identity, friendship, expectations, and ultimately the meaning of life. It claims Hannah, for all her horribleness (the funeral pitch to her dying editor's widow, doing coke to write truthfully about drugs), follows Socrates's call to know thyself in a millennial register. It then surveys the volume's approaches - existentialism, business ethics, the seven deadly sins, Daoism and Confucianism, Freud, Kristeva - as ways of knowing Hannah, Marnie, Jessa, Shosh, Ray, and Adam, and thereby ourselves.

unexamined-life.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
unexamined-life.title: Girls and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Blessing and Wezowiczi test theories of life's meaning on the two narcissists of Girls: Hannah, whose purpose-driven pursuit of being a writer (manufacturing experiences, ignoring her father's medical procedure) shows that goal achievement alone collapses into Taylor's and Camus's Sisyphus problem, and Jessa, whose 'life addict' desire-satisfaction illustrates the Nietzschean live-in-the-moment view the authors find reckless and irresponsible. Using Wielenberg's excrement-eater and the subjectivist/objectivist debate, they land on Susan Wolf's 'loving objects that are worthy of love,' then argue via Socrates's examined life and Sartre's bad faith that neither Hannah's phony narrative nor Jessa's protective persona counts as authentic, examined living.

unexamined-life.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
unexamined-life.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Comparing Finn with Gilgamesh, Achilles, Cuchulainn and Beowulf, the chapter shows how deeply he belongs to the archaic heroic code: a warrior who loves combat, seeks glory in tough-guy contests, fights dirty like Odysseus, and is fiercely loyal to Jake, his friends and his community. Against this tradition, Finn's unprecedented willingness to help any stranger who cries for help and his refusal to kill the 'unaligned' ant mark the post-heroic morality that began when Socrates told Athenians to care for their souls rather than status and Plato designed a city serving the common good - the author explicitly frames this through Nietzsche's complaint that Greek philosophy derailed the healthy, competitive heroic values. The chapter sides with Finn and the self-sacrificing Lemonjohn over Achilles, concluding that the secret of the Enchiridion is doing whatever the common good requires, warrior or not.

unexamined-life.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
unexamined-life.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.

unexamined-life.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
unexamined-life.title: Choose!
unexamined-life.relation: The editor's introduction argues that Roth's series does not just contain philosophy but actually does it, proposing hypotheses about virtue, social order, evil, and forgiveness and testing them for consistency. It casts Tris as a Socratic figure who retraces the Allegory of the Cave: she starts 'chained' inside the cave of Chicago's faction system, climbs out to discover the faction life is a lie, and is tortured and eventually killed for the truth she tries to bring back, just as the cave-dwellers would kill the returning prisoner. The introduction closes by insisting the series is really about choice - that wisdom, unlike knowledge, must be lived, that self-reflection and even self-doubt are the hallmark of the wise, and that when life offers no options, like Tris and the factionless, you have to create your own.

unexamined-life.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
unexamined-life.title: Hello, Dr. Lecter
unexamined-life.relation: Westfall's introduction sorts Lecter's incarnations into four presentations: the psychopath (Brian Cox's 'Lecktor' in Manhunter, modeled on Harris's real-life Mexican prison doctor 'Dr. Salazar'), the anti-hero avenging Mischa in Hannibal Rising, the vampire (Hopkins's Silence of the Lambs Lecter as a Dracula figure who feeds from a sense of innate superiority), and the devil (Mikkelsen's fallen angel, Romula's 'Shaitan', wielder of the church-collapse argument that God enjoys killing). What unites them is a Nietzschean self-conception - Lecter as an Übermensch to whom ordinary law and morality do not apply - and a Socratic function: like Socrates in the Phaedrus, he goads Will, Clarice, and the audience into examining what we already are, posing questions he never resolves because each of us must take the 'rare gift' for ourselves.

unexamined-life.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
unexamined-life.title: 1. Breaking Sixteen Walls
unexamined-life.relation: Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.

unexamined-life.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
unexamined-life.title: 12. Only Deadpool Is Sane
unexamined-life.relation: Chad William Timm argues Deadpool is not really insane but was made 'insane' by power: via Foucault's genealogy of madness, experts like Dr. Brighton (a robotic shell for Psycho Man) at Ravenscroft and Dr. Whitby at Crossmore, along with the courts that institutionalize him after the Hulk trial, run a knowledge/power nexus that labels, sorts, and disciplines him until he internalizes the madman identity ('I think I might actually be crazy'). Nineteenth-century psychiatry's invented link between crime and madness secured the experts' authority, and disciplinary power plus technologies of the self made Deadpool discipline himself. Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe's 'I can see through the bull##$%' and his fourth-wall awareness become resistance to these regimes of truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates's examined life on the reader: be careful whom you tell.

unexamined-life.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
unexamined-life.title: 15. Happy in Oceania
unexamined-life.relation: Ćirić and Ćurko ask what philosophy could have done for Winston, imagining a counterfactual Oceania where he reads Walpole's line that the world is 'a comedy to those that think, a tragedy to those that feel' and learns from Julia that another worldview is possible. They present philosophy as therapy: Kant's notion of worldview (Weltanschauung), Epicurean ataraxia, the Buddhist four noble truths, Frankl's logotherapy, and Stoic premeditation of the worst as resources for reworking the beliefs that made Winston live in fear. The Party's true target, they argue, is critical thinking — from Dewey's ideal of education as learning to think to Frankfurt's On Bullshit — and Kant's Enlightenment motto 'have the courage to use your own understanding' is the weapon that could still defeat Ingsoc.

unexamined-life.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
unexamined-life.title: 2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!
unexamined-life.relation: Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.

unexamined-life.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
unexamined-life.title: 17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen
unexamined-life.relation: Uses Schopenhauer's World as Will to explain why the citizens of Twin Peaks keep living lives they despise: all willing arises from deficiency and suffering, so Shelly cannot leave Leo, Ben cannot face his children, and Ed is consumed oscillating between Norma and Nadine, while the blind will — not reflection — determines who we become. Since only pain is known directly and its absence slides into boredom and banality (Ed's restless drama-making), the town's double lives — Jacoby's coconut tapes hiding Laura's confession, Bobby's dealing, Ben's brothel — are the will's concealed kernels. Laura's wrapped corpse then functions as the reveal: death shows each character's truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates' unexamined life against itself, asking what happens when self-examination only uncovers what we wished hidden, as Cooper's daily-present advice offers the lone consolation.

unexamined-life.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
unexamined-life.title: Dare to Enter the Zone
unexamined-life.relation: The editors introduce the volume with Nietzsche's line about finding only 'apes of our ideal': TZ episodes dangle wishes (rejuvenated husbands, fallout shelters, Henry Bemis's time to read) that fate twists into cosmic jokes, so we laugh at what we fail to be. They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnation of Socrates, the gadfly of Athens, whose episodes work as thought experiments exposing expert promises as tricks, and set 'The Hunt' against this cynicism — the faithful dog Rip smells the Devil's gate so the old man reaches Heaven. The tension between our ideals and human frailty, they argue, is what made the show philosophical television.

unexamined-life.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
unexamined-life.title: 3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis
unexamined-life.relation: Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma: Henry Bemis's wish to own his time, away from the bank president's productivity, his wife's social demands, and the 'unrelenting clock,' is granted by a nuclear blast that turns solitude into a monotonous prison driving him to attempted suicide, until the library restores meaning, identity, and freedom. The shattered glasses then reveal his 'short-sightedness': his literal vision always depended on other people and on a piece of technology, so the possibility of meaning itself was socially and technologically manufactured. The episode's brilliance, he argues, is refusing to choose between accepting the social world's limits on our freedom and withdrawing from it — it only shows that misanthropic withdrawal is self-destruction.

unexamined-life.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
unexamined-life.title: 12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep
unexamined-life.relation: Jones argues the Twilight Zone is not elsewhere: episodes like 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'The Eye of the Beholder' never leave a recognizable America or an ordinary hospital, so the Zone is not a place on any map. Serling's border-crossing narrations plus the impossible catalysts (gremlins, aliens, Talky Tina) create a 'double distancing' — a metaphorical shelter that lets viewers handle mundane truths about selfishness, shakiness, and mortality as if they were strange. 'The Shelter' is the decisive exception: the one episode with no supernatural or futuristic catalyst, aired during the Berlin Crisis when Kennedy urged families to build fallout shelters, it collapses the shelter and forces viewers to see that the Zone is the room they are sitting in.

unexamined-life.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
unexamined-life.title: Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing
unexamined-life.relation: The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.

unexamined-life.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
unexamined-life.title: 7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.

unexamined-life.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
unexamined-life.title: 20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.

unexamined-life.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
unexamined-life.title: 19. If Everyone’s Special, … Is Anyone Special
unexamined-life.relation: Grace Wehniainen defends 'you are special' against the Fox & Friends 'evil man' charge by separating intrinsic from extrinsic value: on Rogers's 1 Corinthians 12 and Genesis 1:27 reading, worth is God-given and unearned, like the family dog whose napping life has intrinsic value (with Tom Regan's agreement) regardless of tricks. Specialness as 'belonging specifically to a particular person' needs no trophies, only Socratic self-examination before the mirror, Aristotle's true versus vulgar self-love from the Nicomachean Ethics, and Albert Ellis's self-acceptance over performance-based self-esteem.

unexamined-life.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
unexamined-life.title: 30. Socratic Superheroism
unexamined-life.relation: Stages a dialogue between Socrates and Nebula to build a four-part scorecard of 'Socratic Heroism' — question all assumptions, intellectual humility (Socrates before the Delphic oracle: 'I am very conscious that I am not wise at all'), improve society without ever doing injustice, and courage unto death (the gadfly of the Apology) — then scores Thanos 0 for 4: 'I am incapable of error' and 'reality can be whatever I want' are the very opposites of humility and of objective, heavenly truth. It nominates Doctor Strange as the MCU's Socratic hero, whose humbling at Kamar-Taj, willingness to hand over the Time Stone against the obvious choice, and trust in the one winning future among 14,000,605 pass the tests.

unexamined-life.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
unexamined-life.title: 3. Paul’s Lick It Up Philosophy
