unexamined-life.relation: Courtland Lewis reads Paul Stanley's autobiographies (Face the Music, Backstage Pass) and songs as a worked-out life philosophy. Stanley's turn from chasing approval to confronting his inner pain exemplifies Socrates' unexamined-life dictum; 'Reason to Live' is glossed through Camus's Sisyphus — ground your reason to live in something indestructible, your own self-chosen meaning — while Plato's Ion explains Stanley's mix of learned craft and divine-inspired performance. Aristotle's flourishing through moderation appears in the advice not to overplay 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' and Lewis adds Locke and Rousseau on how laws, boundaries, and education create rather than restrict freedom, closing with Stanley's 'questioning ourselves is not a weakness' as Socratic wisdom.

unexamined-life.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
unexamined-life.title: “Consider Your Verdict!”
unexamined-life.relation: Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.

unexamined-life.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
unexamined-life.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Tests Socrates' claim (via Plato's Apology and the Myth of the Cave) that the self-examined life is the happiest against the Bluths: Michael, the one who escapes the cave in the pilot (learning at the boat party that his father is a criminal and he was never getting partnership), turns out chronically miserable, while self-deceivers Gob, Lindsay, and Tobias are mostly content. The chapter concludes that Bertrand Russell's Conquest of Happiness fits better: reflection makes sinners (George Michael's self-loathing over Maeby), narcissists (Michael's need to be seen as good), and megalomaniacs (Kitty) unhappy, so the unexamined life is not a huge mistake, though moderate examination still pays.

unexamined-life.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
unexamined-life.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Uses Sartre's cafe waiter, directly mirrored when Gob play-acts a waiter in 'S.O.B.s', to define bad faith as denying one's freedom by disappearing into roles: illusionist, Bluth Company president in George Sr.'s suit, 'any man' winning back Marta, Ward Cleaver father to Steve Holt (!). Distinguishing bad faith from impossible self-deception (beings-for-themselves have no pre-given essence), the chapter argues that even sincerity ('be yourself, Gob') is bad faith, and provocatively concludes Gob is happier and kinder to others in bad faith, reversing Socrates' 'know thyself'.

unexamined-life.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
unexamined-life.title: Let's Go Fly a Kite!
unexamined-life.relation: Argues Mary Poppins is really the redemption story of George Banks, who leads what Socrates called the unexamined life: his six-minute paternal schedule, shredded nursery advertisement, and blindness to the bird woman show a man who has 'forgotten who he is' and lost the child's wonder. G. K. Chesterton supplies the diagnosis and cure — fairyland as the 'sunny country of common sense,' imagination that 'makes settled things strange,' and astonishment that there is something rather than nothing (with Leibniz's question and a Russell quote) — so that Banks is saved when the bank run strips his ambition. The mended kite, built by the whole family, closes the argument that one can keep the heart of a child while keeping the mind of an adult.

unexamined-life.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
unexamined-life.title: The Sorcerer Socratic
unexamined-life.relation: Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.

unexamined-life.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
unexamined-life.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'

unexamined-life.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
unexamined-life.title: Let Us Now Praise Clueless Men: Peter Griffin and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Samet analyzes Peter's cluelessness through the 'I Need a Jew' song from 'When You Wish Upon a Weinstein', where Peter eagerly embraces stereotypes and anti-Semitic cliches with no reflection — making him the antiphilosopher, a paradigm of Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Borrowing Berenson on Giotto, he argues Family Guy, like great painting, gives us a 'realer than real' window on the unreflective, stimulus-response layer of our own cognition (the toddler clinging at day care, the Onion kitten 'thinking of nothing but murder'). Hobbes's theory of laughter as 'sudden glory' at deformity in another explains why Peter's fictional cluelessness is funny while real deformity evokes sympathy: comedy lets us glory that 'there but for reflection go I.' Finally, philosophy's Nagelian 'view from nowhere' totality is inherently unfunny because humor lives in the sheer particularity of experience.

unexamined-life.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
unexamined-life.title: Choices
unexamined-life.relation: Opening 'Choices vs. Abilities: Dumbledore on Self-Understanding' with Socrates' 'know thyself,' Bassham frames the books as Harry's progress from appearance to reality: the boy under the stairs who thinks himself ordinary gradually learns who he is. The pivot is the end of Chamber of Secrets, where Harry, alarmed that he shares Parseltongue and Slytherin potential with Voldemort, receives Dumbledore's dictum 'It is our choices, Harry, that show us what we truly are, far more than our abilities,' which Bassham sets out to test.

unexamined-life.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
unexamined-life.title: Unknown
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter uses Gilderoy Lockhart as the failure case of self-knowledge by introspection: convinced he is a great Defense teacher and duelist, he cannot manage a cage of Cornish pixies, is floored by Snape's Expelliarmus, and removes all the bones from Harry's arm, because his rose-colored 'cognitive blinders' mean he looks but does not see. Bassham then previews four remedies for self-knowledge, each illustrated in the books: cultivate habitual self-examination, stay alert to irrational tendencies, get help from friends, and challenge yourself.

unexamined-life.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
unexamined-life.title: Unknown
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter urges the Socratic examined life as a standing habit rather than a crisis response, since, as Thomas Pangle observes, most of us reflect seriously only when in trouble. Dumbledore is the model: knowing his besetting weakness was love of power, he refused the Ministry repeatedly, and after losing his 'moral compass completely' over Grindelwald he chose a celibate scholarly life, using the Pensieve's third-person view of his own memories, which makes it 'easier to spot patterns and links,' as an instrument of self-examination.

unexamined-life.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
unexamined-life.title: The End of the Story
unexamined-life.relation: Completes the parallel: Socrates died refusing to abandon the examined life, and his martyrdom, like Dumbledore's staged death that protected Snape's spying, served the common good, since there can be no common good without individual goodness. The chapter closes with two Muggle lessons, live devoted to something larger than yourself as Lily Potter, Dumbledore, Harry, King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates did, and find mentors, as Harry found Dumbledore and as readers can find in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics or Confucius.

unexamined-life.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
unexamined-life.title: a7.xhtml
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter sets the bloody classical ideal of glory (Homer's kleos, Beowulf, Alexander modeling himself on Achilles) - which Augustine already condemned as libido dominandi - against Plato's alternative of a life aimed at the good, the true and the beautiful. Thorin's last charge at the Battle of Five Armies fits the heroic tradition, but Tolkien's real point is that Bilbo, the 'grocer' who feels the dwarves' treasure-lust yet walks away from it, and who ends by inviting the dwarves to four-o'clock tea instead of a victory feast, shows glory subordinated to domestic beauty and humility. Socrates' question in the Apology - why care so little for wisdom and the soul's improvement while chasing wealth, honor and reputation - is exactly the temptation Bilbo resists, and the Symposium's move from battle to a drinking-party of love-of-beauty mirrors Tolkien's placement of heroism in hobbits rather than warriors.

unexamined-life.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
unexamined-life.title: Notes
unexamined-life.relation: Argues that Underwood's fourth-wall asides are the show's device for dramatizing the Platonic being-versus-seeming distinction: his public performances (reassuring Blythe over the leaked education bill, the confessional letter typed on the Underwood typewriter to destroy Walker, goading the President into appointing a special prosecutor) are contradicted point by point by what he tells the camera. The chapter reads Frank as a Ring of Gyges success story — the show so far teaches it is better to be the bad guy who seems good — while Socrates' examined life from the Apology and Crito shows Frank never asks why he wants power, and his cockiness is the opposite of Socratic ignorance. It closes with the Gorgias' contrast of Sophistic rhetoric (producing belief, not knowledge) and Machiavelli's advice to feign, casting Frank as the manipulator of opinion Socrates called a tyrant's politics.

unexamined-life.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
unexamined-life.title: Notes
unexamined-life.relation: Gray argues Frank's fourth-wall asides dramatize Plato's being-versus-seeming distinction: the camera confidences reveal the true motive behind the public performance, as in the Blythe education-bill martyrdom gambit, the deliberately failed persuasion of Walker over the special prosecutor, and the seduction letter typed on the Underwood typewriter. The chapter reads Frank as winning the Ring of Gyges bet — enjoying adultery, corruption, and murder while seeming good — exactly the outcome the Republic sets out to refute. Against this it sets Socrates' examined life and Apology profession of ignorance: Frank pursues power without asking to what end, and his mastery of rhetoric over knowledge makes him the Sophist of the Gorgias rather than Plato's true politician, with Machiavelli's dissembling prince as his model.

unexamined-life.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
unexamined-life.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction frames the trilogy as Katniss's quest to peel away Panem's layers of lies, likening her self-examination and self-control to the Delphic 'Know Thyself' and 'Nothing in Excess' and calling her skeptical spirit the engine of her wisdom. It poses the book's driving questions: why we enjoy watching others suffer, whether ordinary morality survives the arena, and how easily our own reality-TV-shaped world could slide into Panem's, noting that Collins modeled the Games on the Roman Colosseum. It presents dystopian exaggeration (children slaughtered for entertainment, tyrants, starving workers) as a cautionary mirror of trends already present in our society, and casts the contributors' chapters as a therapeutic game of 'Real or Not Real' played with the reader.

unexamined-life.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
unexamined-life.title: Group Will
unexamined-life.relation: Testerman argues the film's heist is ironic because nobody in it acts from conscious will: citing Libet's readiness-potential experiments and Penfield's stimulation cases, she claims the feeling of willing is a post-hoc 'epistemic illusion,' so Fischer's inception merely dramatizes what happens all the time — Cobb's 'all experience is inception' becomes a thesis about ordinary agency, with Spinoza's dictum that freedom is ignorance of the causes of our actions as its motto. She reads the plot through this lens: Saito's unexamined hunger for power silently drives the team's 'group will,' Cobb's 'positive emotion trumps negative emotion' tactic exploits the limbic system, and cheaper tricks (Arthur's elephant, foot-in-the-door, subliminal advertising) would have worked as well. Against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly livable, since introspection can never reach the subconscious causes of behavior.

unexamined-life.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
unexamined-life.title: 13 Pride and Prudence in the Pursuit of Knowledge Indiana Jones, René Belloq, and Irina Spalko
unexamined-life.relation: Argues that the desire to know is natural and good (Aristotle's Metaphysics, Socrates via Plato's Meno) only when bounded by moral limits, using Gilbert Meilaender's warning that curiosity becomes a vice when driven by pride or the lust for power. René Belloq opens the Ark seeking a personal audience with God and is incinerated; Irina Spalko demands 'tell me everything you know' from the interdimensional beings at Akator and her eyes burn out; prudent Indy tells Marion 'Don't look, no matter what happens' and leaves before the beings' 'big gift' of knowledge. The chapter concludes that pride must give way to prudence when unlocking the secrets of the universe.

unexamined-life.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
unexamined-life.title: The Office and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Pits authenticity - understood both as self-discovery and as existentialist self-creation after Sartre and Heidegger, requiring self-knowledge and meaningful relationships - against happiness as subjective well-being, in a case study of Michael Scott. Michael's closest 'friendships' are relationships of convenience (Dwight's betrayal in 'The Coup', the fear-induced Packer bond, self-destructive Jan), his 'Packer norms' of locker-room humor are unshakeable, and Shelley Taylor-style positive illusions (his self-image as progressive on Diversity Day, 'The World's Best Boss' mug) keep his moods afloat while truth-tellers like Jan and the Chili's bar patrons knock them down. The conclusion challenges Socrates' dictum: since Michael is psychologically incapable of achieving authenticity, perhaps for some people the examined life is simply not available, and trying for it only produces misery.

unexamined-life.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
unexamined-life.title: Cold Open The Introduction
unexamined-life.relation: The editors introduce the volume by arguing that SNL, like philosophy, trains viewers to regard the world with a critical, questioning eye: four and a half decades of parody and satire wired generations of fans to think philosophically before they could articulate why. Land Shark, Spartan Cheerleaders, and Trump-era Update bits are cited as the shared generational memory the book will now analyze.

unexamined-life.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
unexamined-life.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: The editor's Introduction explains why Spider-Man merits a philosophy book: Peter Parker is a self-reflective underdog with a strong moral compass he sometimes fails to follow, so his stories raise lived ethical questions rather than abstract metaphysics. Citing Plato's definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and a way of life, Sanford frames the whole volume around Socrates' question 'how are you going to live your life?' and lists the questions Peter's life poses: the good life, the obligations attached to talents, friendship, identity over time, the ethics of enhancement, and whether life has meaning.

unexamined-life.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
unexamined-life.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
unexamined-life.relation: Young argues that South Park is perceived as dangerous for exactly the reasons Socrates was tried and executed in Plato's Apology: both 'corrupt the youth' by mocking religion, questioning authority, and exposing that the supposed teachers (Mr. Garrison's flip-flopping creationism, Mrs. Broflovski's moral panics, the 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip) do not know what they think they know. He diagnoses Cartman as an Eichmann figure whose banal, thoughtless evil—feeding Scott Tenorman his parents, torturing Muslims with farts—consists in the inability to think from another's standpoint, while Kyle and Stan's friendship embodies Arendt's dialogic thinking and Aristotle's mean between ideological extremes, as when they see both the merit and the smugness of hybrid drivers in 'Smug Alert'. Freud's theory that jokes break through repression explains why the show's vulgarity is essential rather than gratuitous: it verbalizes what culture silences so that it can be thought through, making South Park a Socratic gadfly rather than a corrupter.

unexamined-life.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
unexamined-life.title: Notes
unexamined-life.relation: Jason Eberl uses the amusement park of 'Shore Leave', Omicron Ceti III's spore paradise in 'This Side of Paradise', Landru's hedonistic 'red hour', and the Borg's relentless efficiency to argue that edifying play and leisure are necessary for intellectual, moral, and spiritual flourishing. Following Josef Pieper's Leisure, with Nozick's experience machine (applied to 'The Thaw' and Barclay's holodiction), Aristotle's 'we work in order to be at leisure', and Aquinas on wonder, he contrasts mere utility (bonum utile) with the common good a drone-only Collective can never have. He concludes that thoughtfully watching Star Trek is itself worthwhile leisure: science-fiction thought experiments that serve Socrates's examined life.

unexamined-life.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
unexamined-life.title: Front matter
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction (bundled with the series page, copyright page, contents, and contributor bios) sets up the book's premise: Swift's lyrics, speeches, and interviews - from her NYU commencement 'life hacks' to the Easter eggs of Midnights - pose philosophical questions about heartbreak, forgiveness, time, love, memory, feminism, and knowledge. Framed by the series' Socratic motto that the unexamined life (and the unexamined cartoon) is not worth living/watching, it declares Swift honorary Chair of the 'Tortured Philosophers Department,' claiming a philosopher can be a bejeweled young woman with a guitar as much as a professor behind ivy-covered walls.

unexamined-life.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
unexamined-life.title: Introduction Welcome to the Psychosphere
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction asks why viewers willingly linger in True Detective's bleak Louisiana bayou and season two's Vinci, suggesting we may recognize something of ourselves in those worlds. It argues detectives and philosophers share the pursuit of truth, framing Rust Cohle and Marty Hart (and Velcoro and Bezzerides) as morally compromised lawmen who open the door to philosophy, invoking Socrates' 'unexamined life is not worth living.' It previews the book's coverage of pessimism, good and evil, tragedy, personal identity, and time via Socrates, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Lacan, and Zizek.

unexamined-life.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
unexamined-life.title: Notes
unexamined-life.relation: Compares the noir detective's relation to Vinci with Socrates' gadfly role in Athens from the Apology, arguing both operate at the city's center and its margins as instruments of collective self-examination. Via Deleuze's 'Philosophy of Crime Novels' it contrasts the classic detective as an agent of truth (Poe, Christie) with the hard-boiled detective as an agent of action who stirs the system — Ani's undercover infiltration of the businessmen's party — forcing what Deleuze calls the 'power of falsehood' to reveal and conceal. Plato's Republic city–soul analogy then frames Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh as disordered souls mirroring Vinci's corrupt class structure, whose cases restore equilibrium without achieving Platonic justice.

unexamined-life.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
unexamined-life.title: Introduction Warm-Up
unexamined-life.relation: Andy Wible's introduction argues that if Plato and Aristotle were alive they would be avid golfers, because both golf and philosophy seduce great minds with problems that look easy yet prove endlessly difficult. It frames golf as 'a Sudoku that cannot be solved' and pairs it with the eternal questions (right and wrong, who am I, beauty, God, meaning) to preview the volume's chapters. Golf becomes a vehicle for the examined life, enlivening philosophy through the lived experience of the game.

unexamined-life.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
unexamined-life.title: 2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!
unexamined-life.relation: De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.

unexamined-life.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
unexamined-life.title: 17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen
unexamined-life.relation: Winters uses Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea to argue that the townsfolk (Shelly, Leo, Ben, Josie, Ed, and Laura) do not freely choose the lives they despise but are driven by the blind will, and so live double lives whose secrets a single death exposes. Laura, unlike the others who mismanage their passions, was denied the chance to develop her own values, so she pursued danger, drugs, and prostitution to see herself through her own eyes; death, he argues, reveals true character (the townsfolk's rush to bury her, their guilt), turning Socrates' unexamined-life dictum uneasy—sometimes what examination reveals is a monster we would rather not see.

unexamined-life.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
unexamined-life.title: Seeking Authenticity
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter argues that Whedon's heroes—Angel resisting the demon within in Pylea, Spike earning back his soul, Simon Tam abandoning his medical career for River, Echo asserting control over her Dollhouse imprints, and Buzz Lightyear redefining himself—live authentically by owning their values against depersonalizing forces, while Captain Hammer and Serenity's Operative are the true 'monsters' who surrender their identities to social roles and blind institutional loyalty. It then asks whether Whedon is a thoroughgoing Sartrean existentialist and answers no: the 'Paradiso Paradigm' (Mal returning the medicine in 'The Train Job') and Willow's 'Choices' speech show objective moral value independent of autonomous choice, making Whedon more Socratic than Sartrean. Rawls supplies the synthesis: heterogeneous life plans (Xander, Oz, Lorne) pursued within objective social conditions—basic rights, liberties, and opportunities—that make authentic self-formation possible for everyone.

unexamined-life.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
unexamined-life.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
unexamined-life.relation: Conard's editor's introduction defines film noir and neo-noir, cataloguing noir themes (moral ambivalence, alienation, pessimism, disorientation) across films like Blue Velvet, Angel Heart, L.A. Confidential, and The Usual Suspects, and previews the volume's thirteen essays. It argues neo-noir better embodies the noir outlook because its makers work self-consciously and can let criminals succeed. It closes by invoking Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living to justify philosophical reflection on these films.

unexamined-life.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
unexamined-life.title: Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization
unexamined-life.relation: Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.

unexamined-life.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
unexamined-life.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
unexamined-life.relation: Sterritt 'schizoanalyzes' The Informant! by arguing that its lying protagonist Mark Whitacre, an ADM executive turned FBI informant, is a nut psychoanalysis cannot crack because he has no unconscious depth: his self is Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomatic, depthless flow of desire with 'nothing behind it' (echoing Warhol). He reads Mark's compulsive fabrication as deterritorialization against the corporation-as-psychopath, links the film to the Socratic unexamined life and to William James's open, flux-embracing empiricism (via Cassavetes), and interprets the climactic collision of Mark's voiceover and dialogue as the film itself intervening as the ultimate informant.

unexamined-life.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
unexamined-life.title: Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity
unexamined-life.relation: Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.

unexamined-life.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
unexamined-life.title: Werner Herzog on Circles, Chickens and Impotency
unexamined-life.relation: Tyler Tritten argues that Even Dwarfs Started Small and Stroszek are not principally political but share an essence: the impotency of the powerless dramatized through cyclical, repetitive motion (circling trucks, ski lifts, and above all chickens). He defends Herzog's 'apoliticism' — citing Herzog's preference for the medieval melior pars over numerical voting (echoing Rousseau's general will versus the popular vote, and Socrates against the many) — as locating the human condition beneath contingent social conditions. The handless, cannibalistic, circumambulating chicken becomes the emblem of a self-consuming nature and a humanity too proportionate to the beast, provoking a pure, aching laughter as the only revolt.

unexamined-life.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
unexamined-life.title: Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation
unexamined-life.relation: Courtland Lewis's closing essay argues Doctor Who and philosophy are complementary enterprises devoted to teaching rather than mere persuasion. Using Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching and rhetoric, he casts the Master as the master rhetorician who produces unreliable beliefs (even via hypnosis), while the Doctor is a Socratic teacher committed to truth who gives people information and lets them decide. He contends the show, begun as educational, challenges viewers to reflect on their own reasoning, on how they treat others (Daleks, Cybermen, strangers), and to revise beliefs in light of evidence, so that watching it is living philosophically engaged.

unexamined-life.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
unexamined-life.title: 13. Chuckrates v. The Saulphists
unexamined-life.relation: Staged as a mock disciplinary-board trial, the chapter casts Chuck McGill as Socrates and Jimmy as a Sophist to replay Plato's dialectic-versus-rhetoric quarrel. Chuck prosecutes Jimmy as a mere rhetorician who 'makes the weaker argument defeat the stronger,' quoting the Gorgias, Apology, and Republic, while Jimmy counters that Socrates was himself a self-righteous show-off and that the legal system runs on Sophistic persuasion (juries, opening statements) as much as on truth. The Board's verdict finds Chuck blind to his own rhetoric and Jimmy a quintessential but empathetic Sophist, using the McGill brothers to argue that law fuses dialectic and rhetoric just as ancient Athens did.

unexamined-life.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
unexamined-life.title: The Last Supper Game
unexamined-life.relation: This editor's introduction frames Bourdain as a modern philosopher by playing a variation on his 'Last Meal' game and choosing Bourdain as the ideal dinner companion. It argues that Bourdain's professed humility about how little he knows ('realizing how small I am, and unwise') echoes Socratic ignorance and the love of wisdom, and previews the volume's questions about happiness, authenticity, taste, and freedom.

unexamined-life.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
unexamined-life.title: The Talking Cure for Our Culture
unexamined-life.relation: Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.

unexamined-life.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
unexamined-life.title: House and the Life of Reason
unexamined-life.relation: Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.

unexamined-life.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
unexamined-life.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Greg Littmann defends political mockery as an ancient tradition (Aristophanes, Juvenal, Twain) but warns, using J.S. Mill's On Liberty, that if viewers let The Daily Show's jokes substitute for reasoned judgment the effect is like censorship, silencing ideas that must be heard to be understood. He cites Mill's arguments against silencing discussion and Plato's Meno on shackling true opinion with reasons, arguing that Stewart's virtue over Limbaugh is that he bills himself as comedy ('the show that leads into me is puppets making crank phone calls') and never presents mockery as a replacement for informed citizenship.

unexamined-life.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
unexamined-life.title: Dare to Enter the Zone
unexamined-life.relation: Hooke and Rivera's editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone dramatizes the Nietzschean disappointment of the epigraph from Twilight of the Idols—that we seek great human beings and find only 'the apes of their ideal.' They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnated Socrates, a gadfly whose episodes ('Time Enough at Last,' 'The Hunt,' the eternal-youth trade-in) stage the gap between our ideals of love, justice, and truth and the treacherous, self-deluding creatures we actually are, so that viewers laugh at absurd twist endings because we are the species most deserving to be laughed at.

unexamined-life.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
unexamined-life.title: Oh, the Places You’ll Go! The Examined, Happy Life
unexamined-life.relation: Benjamin Rider reads Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living. He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.

unexamined-life.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
unexamined-life.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: Dougherty argues Austen's ideal marriage mirrors Aristotle's complete friendship, where the friend is loved for who they are and becomes a 'second self.' She sorts Austen's relationships into Aristotle's three kinds: utility (Emma and Mrs. Elton, Charlotte and Mr. Collins), pleasure (Lydia and Wickham, the fading Emma-Harriet bond), and complete friendship grounded in mutual good character (Jane and Bingley, Elizabeth and Darcy, Emma and Knightley). Central is the 'second self' as mirror: Darcy's letter and Knightley's rebukes let Elizabeth and Emma see themselves ('Till this moment I never knew myself'), so marriage-as-friendship improves self-knowledge and virtue and must not be left to chance as Charlotte urges.

unexamined-life.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
unexamined-life.title: Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)
unexamined-life.relation: Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.

unexamined-life.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
unexamined-life.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
unexamined-life.relation: Owen argues that parenting is a political act and that fathers, especially privileged white heterosexual ones, should raise anti-oppressive children. Prompted by the question 'Daddy, why is her face brown?', he uses the social construction of racialized difference and the mutually constitutive culture–individual relation (the Zulu maxim 'a person is a person through other persons') to reject color-blindness. He prescribes knowledge, practice, and character steps, invokes Socrates' 'unexamined life' for relentless self-reflection, and answers the worry about raising 'alienated' children via Sartre's bad faith – authentic existence means accepting responsibility for reproducing or resisting injustice.

unexamined-life.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
unexamined-life.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
unexamined-life.relation: Austin offers practical wisdom for fathers of daughters, grounding fatherly obligations in daughters' fundamental interests and focusing on self-knowledge, moral development, and the common good. Invoking the Delphic 'know thyself,' Charles Taylor's 'strong evaluations,' and Aristotle's view that virtue grows through practice, he explains how to cultivate humility (including 'existential humility' before nature), courage (including self-sacrifice), and wisdom (curiosity, versatility, critical thinking) – e.g., analyzing advertising assumptions and limiting screen time – so a daughter can flourish and contribute to the common good.

unexamined-life.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
unexamined-life.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
unexamined-life.relation: Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.

unexamined-life.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
unexamined-life.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
unexamined-life.relation: Phillips argues that there is something-it-is-like to be a knowledgeable coffee drinker, using Nagel's bat and Jackson's Mary thought experiments — but where the bat is 'fundamentally alien,' coffee expertise is learnable, and via David Lewis's ability hypothesis the reader can apply book-knowledge of acidity, body, finish, and flavor to abilities they already have. He then invokes Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (Homer's enduring appeal, the Don Quixote wine-tasters) to claim aesthetic and moral judgments spring from the same refinable sentiments, so that examining your cup free of prejudice is, echoing Socrates' 'unexamined life,' something we almost owe ourselves: the unexamined cup is not worth drinking.

unexamined-life.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
unexamined-life.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
unexamined-life.relation: Parker defends the coffeehouse as an accessible venue for real philosophy through Christopher Phillips's Socrates Café movement (and Marc Sautet's cafés-philos), arguing that Socratizing — sustained questioning that offers objections and alternatives, not mere talk — makes everyone a potential 'Socrates.' Answering the charge that amateur café philosophy is mere sophistry, he turns to Plato's Sophist to note the sophist is the one who takes payment and has an agenda, so it is salaried professors, not unpaid Phillips, who resemble sophists. Framing thoughtlessness (via Nietzsche's 'oblivion' and David Foster Wallace's cruise-ship essay) as philosophy's true adversary, he endorses a softened Socratic/Nozickian maxim that the unexamined life is simply not lived as fully.

unexamined-life.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
unexamined-life.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
unexamined-life.relation: Editor Nathan Kowalsky's introduction opens with his boyhood memory of his father shooting a whitetail buck and his own tears, using it to argue that hunting confronts us with life and death 'right there in front of your face.' He insists hunting and philosophy are not an oxymoron (mocking the Elmer Fudd stereotype against Socrates 'downtown'), casts hunting itself as a paradox worth philosophizing about, and previews all the volume's chapters, framing philosophy as 'thinking hard' about an activity that makes humans and wildness literally touch through death.

unexamined-life.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
unexamined-life.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
unexamined-life.relation: Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.

unexamined-life.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
unexamined-life.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
unexamined-life.relation: Baker dismisses common objections to tattoos (shallow individuality, permanence, ugliness) as aesthetic rather than moral, then uses Greco-Roman virtue ethics—quoting Seneca's Moral Epistles on the soul, the balanced psyche, and matching one's norms to one's motivations—to isolate her real target: the 'tough tattoo.' She argues that a badass or tough-guy tattoo appropriates an outlaw subculture's imagery and, per Seneca's warning that approving a little violence approves it all, cultivates a vicious rather than virtuous psyche. Recalling friends who bragged about beatings, she invokes Socratic self-examination ('know thyself') to test whether looking tough is an accurate or worthy self-representation.

unexamined-life.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
unexamined-life.title: BLUES
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction argues blues and philosophy are close kin in confronting the struggling soul. It reads Lightnin' Hopkins's 'Lonesome Dog' through Plato's tripartite soul from Republic IX — the howling 'dog' is the appetitive part — but claims the blues achieves a 'blues harmony' rather than Plato's reason-ruled harmony. It casts Socrates, calm before execution in the Phaedo, as having a 'bluesy sensibility' that rises above worry through philosophizing, invokes Bentham's claim that the capacity to suffer is what matters morally to gloss the blues as knowledge of suffering, and likens the blues' triumphant affirmation to Nietzsche's positivity.

unexamined-life.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
unexamined-life.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
unexamined-life.relation: The editors' introduction argues that The Lord of the Rings, though written by a philologist rather than a philosopher, dramatizes perennial questions Tolkien cared about as a Catholic: whether power always corrupts, whether death can be a gift, and the tension of fate versus free will. It frames the volume's method by invoking Socrates, who drew on art, sport, and music his listeners already knew to provoke examination of their lives, presenting Tolkien's fiction as the same kind of popular-culture doorway into the great questions.

unexamined-life.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
unexamined-life.title: Who is Who
unexamined-life.relation: The introduction argues that Doctor Who and philosophy share a common origin in wonder (quoting Plato's Socrates and Aristotle) and traces the show's shifting worldview across the eleven Doctors. It claims early Who embodied Enlightenment 'positivism' (the pro-science Hartnell/Pertwee eras) but that the post-1996 and post-2005 series turned toward Romanticism and Sartrean/de Beauvoirian existentialism, framing the surviving Doctor's post-Time War 'angst,' homelessness and burden of freedom through existentialist themes.

unexamined-life.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
unexamined-life.title: The Talking Cure for Our Culture
unexamined-life.relation: William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.

unexamined-life.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
unexamined-life.title: House Sitting
unexamined-life.relation: Ruff and Barris argue that House's rude, rule-breaking rhetoric works like a Zen koan: by insisting "everybody lies" and unsettling everyone's (and his own) habitual sense-making, he opens space for the true problem to reveal itself. Through cases like "DNR," "Mob Rules," and "House vs. God," they show his refusal of justification is a way of acting ethically, establishing naked intimacy, reaching truth, and healing — all one nondual "happening." House is inside the rhetoric, performed by it, ending each case in Zen-like equanimity amid personal chaos.

unexamined-life.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
unexamined-life.title: House and the Life of Reason
unexamined-life.relation: Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.

unexamined-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
unexamined-life.title: 23. The X-Files as Philosophy Navigating the “Truth Out There”
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter argues that Darin Morgan's X-Files episodes philosophize by critiquing the show's own 'the truth is out there' mantra from within. Through the conflicting hypnosis testimonies and identical camera blocking in 'Jose Chung's From Outer Space,' Morgan cinematically stages Nietzsche's perspectivism and the claim that 'truth is as subjective as reality'; through Clyde Bruckman and the doomed Ansel of 'Quagmire,' he mounts an anti-Socratic case that relentlessly pursuing truth (as Mulder does) is not worth the ruin it brings. Kowalski then rebuts Morgan using Descartes's cogito and inference-to-the-best-explanation to defend objective truth against radical skepticism, arguing subjectivism about truth is self-refuting.

unexamined-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
unexamined-life.title: 74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates
unexamined-life.relation: Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

unexamined-life.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
unexamined-life.title: 1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor
unexamined-life.relation: The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

das-man.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
das-man.title: Monologue
das-man.relation: Editor William Irwin's introduction explains why Seinfeld is philosophical: 'Seinfeld' sounds like German for 'field of being,' echoing Heidegger's Sein und Zeit, and he tells students to picture the four at Monk's coffee shop when Heidegger describes the 'idle chatter' of the inauthentic mode of being, while George's 'what is the opposite of what I would normally do?' shows the courage of changing one's way of seeing. He frames the whole book with Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living - the Seinfeld characters examine their lives constantly, though Socrates would approve of neither their lives nor their examinations - and with Nietzsche's 'A Book for None and All' subtitle, then lays out the volume's four-act structure.

das-man.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
das-man.title: Inauthenticity and Fascism
das-man.relation: David Detmer treats Zelig, the mock-documentary 'chameleon man' who turns black, Chinese, fat, or a Nazi depending on his company, as a stark dramatization of personal identity and the existentialist critique of inauthenticity. After rejecting the memory, bodily-continuity, and immaterial-soul criteria of identity, the chapter takes the existentialist line, quoting Heidegger on Dasein's selfhood, that a self is its choices, projects, and commitments, so Zelig's chameleonism is self-estrangement motivated by fear and the craving to be liked. Politically, the chapter draws Allen's lesson that genocides happen not because millions go mad but because millions passively conform, made literal by Zelig appearing at a Hitler rally, and supports it with Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience studies.

das-man.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
das-man.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
das-man.relation: Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.

das-man.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
das-man.title: U2 and Philosophy
das-man.relation: Delancey asks why anyone should take moral and political cues from a rock band and answers via Heidegger: in a mediascape where a few corporations orchestrate what everyone hears, the mass tune is das Man ('Numb'), and adopting it is inauthenticity - so U2, who believe what they sing for their own reasons ('Mothers of the Disappeared' against the official line on Latin America), may be among the most authentic voices available. Plato's tripartite soul and Aristotle's golden mean supply the thesis that reason needs rightly trained passion: the righteous anger of 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Silver and Gold' and the resolve of 'Walk On' are practical wisdom in song, the emotions democracy requires. Against Plato's philosopher-king and his noble lies, Delancey argues utopia can only be fostered, not enforced - so in a democracy, if you want to change the world, you may have to sing to people.

das-man.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
das-man.title: U2 and Philosophy
das-man.relation: Benfell reads U2's apocalyptic songs through Heidegger rather than through eschatological doctrine: 'The Playboy Mansion' depicts fallenness in the 'they', a consumerist paradise with 'no time for sorrow' that lets us flee our own death, while the angel's fall in Wenders' films evoked by 'Stay' and the day-to-day constraints of 'Some Days Are Better than Others' illustrate thrownness, and 'Gone' existential guilt as an unpayable debt. A verse-by-verse reading of 'Until the End of the World' - the Judas-at-the-last-supper reading as one register - shows the speaker moving from 'passing time' and playing roles in the 'they' to anxious guiltiness and the call of conscience, reaching for the one whose resolute waiting models anticipatory resoluteness. The 'end of the world', he concludes, is the end of the speaker's own world: U2's apocalyptic imagery calls listeners to authentic, finite existence, not to prediction of last things.

das-man.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
das-man.title: Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners
das-man.relation: Adam Barrows reads Stoker's Dracula through Being and Time: the staking of Lucy is the liberation of a true humanity trapped in a deathless shell, and Dracula's endless, mirror-less, selfless existence is Heideggerian inauthenticity - the 'they' that tranquilizes the dying, Renfield's seduction repeating the neighbors' comforting, the refusal of being-toward-death - so vampire-hunting becomes a philosophical task of enforcing authentic, death-claiming being. The chapter then turns the critique on Heidegger himself: his Nazi membership and fundamental ontology's contempt for the everyday leave a gap for racial purity thinking, making Van Helsing's 'butcher work' look like the ritual expulsion of the inauthentic from ontological purity, and asking whether, in adaptation after adaptation, we are Dracula's willing executioners.

das-man.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
das-man.title: Epilogue
das-man.relation: Auxier's epilogue teaches readers to build playful 'ontologies' from the book's list of Springsteen's proper names — imagining Elvis's .44 Magnum ('Betsy') traveling from a Vegas evidence room into 'Johnny 99' and '57 Channels,' and asking 'Would Bruce ride a Honda?' He borrows Heidegger's idea that the answer already lives in the question, and uses das Man — the inauthentic 'they-self' that chooses by appearances — to contrast Harley riders who confront an existential decision with Honda's self-conserving middle-class pragmatism. The Harley as 'suicide machine' (like Captain America in Easy Rider, like Jesus's passion) embodies freedom and authenticity; Foucault's Borgesian Chinese encyclopedia reminds us that orders of things are conventional, so the ontology itself is one imaginative path among many.

das-man.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
das-man.title: If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . .
das-man.relation: Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."

das-man.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
das-man.title: The Fruitcake as Performative Exemplar
das-man.relation: John Kaag pairs Buffett's 'Fruitcakes' with Judith Butler's constructivism: institutions 'girl' infants through interpellation (the sonogram naming), the heterosexual imperative abjects gay, lesbian, and transgender 'nobodies,' and these excluded fruitcakes are the cosmic baker's half-baked people. The movie-theater stanza ('a twelve pound Nestle Crunch for twenty-five dollars') becomes Heidegger's das Man, others thinking and choosing for us, while Buffett's 'mea culpa' refrain and 'Religion's in the hands of some crazy-ass people' attack the guilt constitutive of Christian subjecthood, with Dewey's broad, doctrine-free religious experience offered as common ground. Buffett concerts themselves are read as performative exemplars — drag-show-like borderland communities where four generations act out the 'little bit of fruitcake' in everyone as a quiet political protest against enforced normalcy.

das-man.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
das-man.title: One Last Anguished Existential Scream
das-man.relation: Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.

das-man.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
das-man.title: Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners
das-man.relation: Adam Barrows reads Stoker's Dracula through Being and Time: Stoker's staking of Lucy is framed as liberating the 'true' human from the 'false' Undead, and Mina urges pity on the trapped soul, exactly the structure of Heidegger's claim that only facing one's own death alone makes life a bounded, authentic whole. Dracula emerges as the inauthentic 'they' incarnate, with no reflection in mirrors, no fixed likeness in portraits, and a seduction of tranquilizing delay that mirrors how das Man lulls the dying away from their death, so vampire hunting becomes a philosophical task of forcing authenticity on the deathless. The chapter then reverses the charge: given Heidegger's Nazism, Van Helsing's gleeful 'butcher work' and the hunters' expulsion of 'inauthentic' beings from ontological purity implicate audiences as Dracula's 'willing executioners' in a ritual with chilling fascist overtones.

das-man.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
das-man.title: 13 - What Are Friends For
das-man.relation: Bloor reads Facebook anxiety through Heidegger's diagnosis of technological nihilism — an efficiency-driven 'being-in-the-world' with no shared arbiter of what matters — borrowing Dreyfus's HAL 9000 example from 2001: A Space Odyssey to show humans enhancing themselves like any other raw material. He argues Facebook's speed lures users into unreflective sharing and standardized behavior where the quirky authentic 'I' dissolves into Heidegger's 'one,' and recruits Aristotle's view that only a few deep friendships morally form us to warn that hundreds of contacts fragment that benefit. Adorno on leisure as mere recuperation between bouts of work frames the therapist who keeps Facebook strictly professional, and the chapter concludes the fault lies in ourselves, not the tools — suggesting a week offline as a test.

das-man.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
das-man.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
das-man.relation: Vannatta starts from Klosterman's confession that his first dates run on three and a half dates' worth of contrived material, and asks how self-knowledge is possible at all if, as Errol Morris tells Klosterman, we have no privileged access to our own minds. After a tour through Descartes's cogito, Kant's unity of apperception, Freud's unconscious, and Foucault's discourse-constructed subject, the chapter argues with Foucault's Ramist logic of similarity that Klosterman's thought really works by resemblance, mapping his exes onto members of KISS and hearing a dead friend in every Replacements song. Heidegger supplies the resolution: thrown into the crowd's world, we recover ourselves only through its inauthentic pop culture, and Klosterman's 'living is dying, little by little' and obsessive rock-death writing enact being-toward-death as the condition of authenticity.

das-man.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
das-man.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
das-man.relation: The chapter diagnoses the show's identity crises through Heidegger's Being and Time: Marshall's Goliath National Bank drudgery is anxiety over thrownness - the rent, the bills, the situation he never chose - while Lily's prom-night bolt to San Francisco is anxiety over freedom and possibility, and both fail anticipatory resoluteness, the commitment to be yourself while shouldering what you did not choose. das Man ('everybody's doing it') explains the gang's absorbed everydayness. Kierkegaard supplies the problem of time (life understood backwards but lived forwards) and Fear and Trembling's contrast between Abraham's leap of faith into the absurd and the 'demonic': Barney courts legendary moments yet manipulates uncertainty so he never becomes anyone new - the identity crisis that never ends.

das-man.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
das-man.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
das-man.relation: Charlotte Knowles tests each Gang member against Heidegger's Being and Time: getting lost in the averageness of what 'they' do (das Man) is inauthenticity, but authenticity is not freakish uniqueness - Charlie's milk-steak, magnets, and bird-law delusions are unconventional without being authentic - rather a transformed relation to everyday roles in which one endorses the life one leads. Frank partly passes, having chosen squalor and owning it ('I'm going to get really weird with it'), yet unknowingly lives out Rambo as a cultural script; Dee consciously performs the Sex and the City script; Dennis is ruled by beauty norms (make-up, girdle, chemical peel); and Mac, despite the tough talk, is Frank's 'follower' hiding his relationship with Carmen. The upshot is that authenticity and inauthenticity are matters of degree, never either/or, and are not moral verdicts - Dennis could be an authentic rapist - so the Gang's norm-defiance does not make them authentic, bitches.

das-man.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
das-man.title: 14. David Bowie’s Sadness
das-man.relation: Ketcham argues Bowie's sadness is ours: via Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus he casts consumer capitalism as a machine producing schizophrenic fad-following (the stuck high-school footballer, the Benetton self), of which Bowie's serial personas are both symptom and escape - 'always crashing in the same car' yet never repeating. Minkowski's lived time and the Buddha's anatman ground the dance as pure becoming without a dancer, while Heidegger's das Man and being-toward-death explain why authentic self-creation - which, unlike Sellers or Williams, Bowie survived - exacts the price Freud's beyond-the-pleasure-principle names as compulsive repetition, turned by Bowie into a life wish.

das-man.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
das-man.title: 7. A Life Along the Watchtower
das-man.relation: Reads 'All Along the Watchtower' as a dialogue between the Joker's Sartrean being-and-nothingness ('none of them along the line know what any of it is worth') and the Thief's Heideggerian reply — being-toward-death, anticipatory resoluteness, care, and the fallen 'they.' It argues Hendrix lived this struggle: the mirror-smashing of 'A Room Full of Mirrors,' the unborn speaker of 'Belly Button Window' who will throw himself into the world rather than be thrown, and the 'Electric Church Music' built to cut through 'they'-thinking and return listeners to child-like authenticity. Gramsci's point that oppressor and oppressed alike internalize the oppressor's message names the hegemony Hendrix's third way — neither victim nor revolutionary — simply denies.

das-man.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
das-man.title: 6. The Unique Horror of the Upside Down
das-man.relation: Pamerleau argues the Upside Down's distinctive horror is not its monsters, which offer familiar Jaws-style jump scares and supervillain plots, but the place itself: reading Will through Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world, our selves are constituted by the web of socially inherited meanings (the 'they') attached to familiar places and things. Waking in a dead replica of home, where the same houses, school, and Castle Byers no longer function or answer back, forces Will to spell 'R-I-G-H-T H-E-R-E' through the lights, an uncanny juxtaposition of the familiar and the alien that the chapter compares to an open-casket funeral and contrasts with Alien's wholly unknown ship.

das-man.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
das-man.title: 5. Another Day in the Neighborhood
das-man.relation: Sydney Ball and Eric Mohr interleave a college student's Tuesday with her six-year-old self watching the show: Plato's Republic (439c) on the rational part overruling the appetitive frames procrastination and lost youthful energy, Kant's autonomy frames doing what you should without being told, and Heidegger's 'They' frames her supermarket jealousy, dissolved by complimenting a stranger's shoes just as Henrietta Pussycat overcame jealousy of Grandpere's fancy granddaughter Collette (episodes 1176-1180). The lesson, learned from Mister Rogers's words about stopping, is authenticity: 'I like you just the way you are.'

das-man.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
das-man.title: Conclusions, Capes, and Cowls
das-man.relation: Jason Howard asks how Batman keeps from becoming what he fights, answering with Heidegger's authentic conscience against Rousseau's innate moral-sense view. Bruce's guilt over his parents' death is reinterpreted in a Heideggerian 'moment of vision': the bat through the window summons Dasein out of the they-self, so becoming Batman is not vengeance but the call of an authentic conscience that owns guilt, fallenness, and death. Batman's return from alcoholic retirement in The Dark Knight Returns shows conscience as 'the loyalty of existence to its own Self,' a freedom-toward-death that makes him instructive rather than merely heroic.

das-man.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
das-man.title: Notes
das-man.relation: Miller reads Emmet's arc from 'Tell me what to do, and I'll do it!' conformity toward Vitruvius' 'embrace what is special about you' as a Heideggerian journey from das Man — the anonymous 'one does not do that' of the they-self, named in her notes — toward authenticity. LEGO play exemplifies the ready-to-hand engaged dealing with equipment that is more primordial than detached present-at-hand analysis, moods like boredom disclose the exhaustion of Lord Business's 'calculative thinking', the technological enframing that treats everything as standing-reserve, and art (Heidegger's Van Gogh shoes, a #KeepBuilding ad) reveals hidden cultural truths. Heidegger's 'Only if we are capable of dwelling, only then can we build' grounds her claim that LEGO's 'new toy everyday' recyclability sustains the meditative, sustainable building the book's ethos demands — even while admitting the movie is itself a masterful advertisement.

das-man.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
das-man.title: Metallica's Existential Freedom: From We to I and Back Again
das-man.relation: Rachael Sotos reads Metallica's career as an existentialist quest for authentic freedom: the Arendtian shared 'we' of the early speed-metal community (Kill 'Em All), the Heideggerian 'I' attuned to death that breaks from das Man (Ride the Lightning's 'Fade to Black'), and the Kierkegaardian leap out of the over-technical system of . . . And Justice for All - compared to Kierkegaard's critique of Hegel - into the embodied groove of the Black Album. Sartre's bad faith explains the rock-star traps, and Some Kind of Monster shows the 'we' must be tended: therapy and a democratic band restore Arendtian public freedom.

das-man.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
das-man.title: Nothing Is Ever Black or White
das-man.relation: Miechels maps Witcher 3 onto Heidegger's Being and Time: with no character creator, the player is thrown into Geralt's fixed identity, the 'Butcher of Blaviken' with cat eyes whom villagers spit at, in a war-torn Velen he did not choose. Projection appears in the Triss-or-Yennefer romance (where refusing to choose is still a choice) and in the Bloody Baron, whose guilt shows that his war trauma and alcoholism never excused his choices: 'nothing is ever black and white' does not absolve him. Falling into das Man shows up in Gwent rounds, map question marks, and above all online walkthroughs of the 'optimal choice' for Willis's burned forge, which let players evade the responsibility of deciding for themselves.

das-man.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
das-man.title: Seeking Authenticity
das-man.relation: The chapter argues that Whedon's heroes—Angel resisting the demon within in Pylea, Spike earning back his soul, Simon Tam abandoning his medical career for River, Echo asserting control over her Dollhouse imprints, and Buzz Lightyear redefining himself—live authentically by owning their values against depersonalizing forces, while Captain Hammer and Serenity's Operative are the true 'monsters' who surrender their identities to social roles and blind institutional loyalty. It then asks whether Whedon is a thoroughgoing Sartrean existentialist and answers no: the 'Paradiso Paradigm' (Mal returning the medicine in 'The Train Job') and Willow's 'Choices' speech show objective moral value independent of autonomous choice, making Whedon more Socratic than Sartrean. Rawls supplies the synthesis: heterogeneous life plans (Xander, Oz, Lorne) pursued within objective social conditions—basic rights, liberties, and opportunities—that make authentic self-formation possible for everyone.

das-man.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
das-man.title: The Existential Frankenstein
das-man.relation: McMahon gives an existential reading of Whale's Frankenstein and Shelley's novel through Heidegger's being-toward-death and Ernest Becker's denial of death. Victor Frankenstein exemplifies Becker's 'defiant Promethianism,' the offensive denial that seeks to conquer death, and the monster personifies death itself. She argues his obsession erodes his humanity, estranges him from others, and generates moral dilemmas, illustrating Heidegger's claim that only authentic acceptance of mortality restores individuality and genuine community, so that mastering death would make us monsters.

das-man.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
das-man.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
das-man.relation: Kevin S. Decker offers a 'philosophical hermeneutics' of Burton's Batman and Batman Returns, arguing that a long-lived cultural artifact like the Batman discloses a society's self-understanding. Using Heidegger's Dasein and 'working-out of possibilities,' Nietzsche's 'only interpretations,' and Gadamer's hermeneutic circle and fusion of horizons, Decker reads the shift from ABC's camp Adam West Batman to Burton's dark version as tracking cultural change (Vietnam, Watergate, 1980s decadence). He casts the Joker, Penguin, and Catwoman—and Batman himself—as Burton's recurring 'expressive outsider,' relating them to Nietzsche's Übermensch and Gotham's gullible crowds to Heidegger's das Man, and compares Burton's Expressionist Gotham to Max Beckmann's post-WWI Hell lithographs, positioning Burton as a prophet of modern decadence.

das-man.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
das-man.title: Who is Who
das-man.relation: This chapter reads the Doctor as poised between positivism and phenomenology. It uses Hume's Fork and the Vienna Circle's verificationism (via 'The Daemons' and 'Tomb of the Cybermen') to cast the pro-science Doctor as an empiricist, then argues he is equally a Husserlian phenomenologist attentive to the 'life-world' and a Heideggerian Dasein whose time-travelling homelessness and the show's sense of the uncanny (unheimlich) embody being-in-the-world, thrownness and the flight from the worldhood of the world.

das-man.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
das-man.title: 73. Hasan Minhaj as Philosopher Navigating the Struggles of Identity
das-man.relation: Singh reads Minhaj's comedy of identity through existentialism, arguing his call for 'authenticity' over the first generation's 'assimilation' (the 'American dream tax' and 'biryani' arguments about choosing one's life) enacts Sartre's existence-precedes-essence and rejection of bad faith. He frames Minhaj's Indian-American-Muslim conflict via Heidegger's thrownness and facticity and the move from the they-self (das Man) to authentic self, contrasting it with Sartre's facticity as a limit on freedom. Minhaj's 'global citizen' anti-nationalism, his 'love is bigger than fear,' and 'may the best argument win' are presented as prescriptions for navigating national, ethnic, religious and personal identity while flagging fallacies like hasty generalization behind Islamophobia.

plato-cave.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
plato-cave.title: The Fates of Socrates and Seinfeld
plato-cave.relation: William Irwin compares Jerry and Socrates: the 'Jerry problem' of whether the fictional Jerry is the real Jerry (complicated by Seinlanguage) mirrors the Socratic problem of separating Socrates from Plato's dialogues. Jerry, like Socrates the gadfly, provokes his circle with questions that hunt for essences - the black-and-white cookie, 'is soup a meal?' - and shares Socrates' irony (the 'War: What Is It Good For?' gag in 'The Marine Biologist' works exactly like Socratic shamming ignorance). But where Socrates died serenely per the Apology and Phaedo, Jerry is self-absorbed and ends the series convicted under the Good Samaritan law, doing his stand-up 'gadfly' routine for prison inmates - an examined life, but not an exemplary one.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
