plato-cave.relation: Irwin reads Neo's unplugging as Plato's cave allegory restaged: the pod farms are the cave, the cables feeding the illusion are the chains, and Morpheus (named for the god of dreams) plays the liberator who drags the prisoner painfully into the light of 'the desert of the real'. He frames the 'prison for your mind' theme through figures who kept their minds free under captivity, notes that 'education' etymologically means 'leading out' as the prisoner is led out of the cave, and contrasts Neo, who would endure anything rather than return to illusion, with Cypher, who goes back to the shadows.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: Irwin argues the cave story's real point is Plato's Theory of Forms: life inside the Matrix, like ordinary sensory life, is a realm of copies - sunsets, just acts, really good noodles - imitating Beauty, Justice and Goodness themselves. He reads 'there is no spoon' and Morpheus's 'no one can be told what the Matrix is' as Plato's claim that the Forms are grasped by intellect rather than senses, and explains Neo's amnesia and the film's deja vu through Plato's doctrine of recollection (anamnesis), with the soul beholding the Forms between incarnations.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: Korsmeyer traces how the film deploys each sense: vision is both the channel of illusion and, as from Plato's cave onward, the metaphor for understanding ('Why do my eyes hurt?' 'You've never used them'); hearing serves surveillance and bodily invasion, from the centipede-like bug to the screaming 'WAKE UP!' and whispers that nearly touch; and smell marks corporeality, from Trinity's affectionate sniffing of the sleeping Neo to Agent Smith's disgust at human 'stink', which drives him to break protocol and remove his earpiece.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: The Metaphysics of The Matrix
plato-cave.relation: Gracia and Sanford open with Neo and Trinity in the club and the question that drives the film, 'What is the Matrix?', mapping Neo's path out of the pod onto Plato's cave ascent while stressing the twist: what Neo finds is not the shining realm of Forms but a war-scarred desert, preferred only because it is true, and like Plato's escaped prisoner he returns to free the others. They state their three questions - what are appearance and reality, what separates them, and what properties belong to each - as the paradigmatically metaphysical questions the film poses.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: The authors distinguish the two worlds twice over: by source, since everything in the Matrix issues from the AI machines' program while the real world's ultimate causes lie elsewhere; and by ontological status, since the unreal world depends entirely for its existence on real machines, electrical signals, and minds. They add that recognizing the difference requires a teacher - Morpheus playing to Neo's 'splinter in your mind', just as Plato's cave needs a first freed prisoner - though they file how we come to know this under epistemology rather than metaphysics.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: The chapter reads the pod farms as Plato's cave from Republic VII: prisoners chained from birth who mistake projected images for reality and 'do not know that they are prisoners', insisting on the truth of their world. Morpheus, named for the god of dreams, is the liberator-expert who can rouse sleepers in the right sequence, and Neo's sense of not being sure he is awake parallels the prisoner's primeval recollections. With Plato, it argues that happiness is objective like health - one can say 'I am happy' and be wrong, as the battery-humans are - so true happiness and freedom depend on knowledge of what is real.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: The chapter sets Neo and Cypher as the two poles of authenticity: Neo's unplugging is agony, like the prisoner dragged from Plato's cave - atrophied limbs, eyes that hurt because 'never used them before', and the cognitive shock of the 'desert of the real' - while Cypher, freed young and worn down by years of fear and gag-inducing goop, sells out the crew for a steak he knows does not exist: 'ignorance is bliss'. McMahon asks us to sympathize with Cypher, since in his place, facing perpetual annihilation, 'we too might opt for the illusion'.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: The chapter argues that the film's philosophical allusions—students comparing the pod-bound humans to Plato's cave prisoners and Neo's bewilderment to Descartes's First Meditation dream hypothesis—are designed to generate suspense, anxiety, and horror rather than philosophical reflection. Because genre texts are centrifugal, pointing viewers to outside connections, and their pacing never lingers on themes, The Matrix can use philosophy only to trigger audience interest and never to argue for answers. Its conclusion is that the film is unquestionably real genre but only virtual philosophy.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: Unknown
plato-cave.relation: Developing thesis one, the chapter shows Morpheus's question—'How would you know the difference between the dream world and the real world?'—restates Plato's cave dwellers mistaking shadows for things and Descartes's First Meditation progression from unreliable senses to dreaming to the malicious demon that makes every belief false. What is genuinely new is that computer simulation and brain science have made the once-outlandish demon scenario thinkable, so the film has made philosophy teachers' job easier: global skepticism no longer seems ridiculous, and maybe you are lying in a tub of goo right now.

plato-cave.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-cave.title: The Matrix Or, The Two Sides of Perversion
plato-cave.relation: Žižek opens with the 'ideal spectator' beside him exclaiming 'so there is no reality!' and notes the film works as a Rorschach test in which Lacanians, Frankfurt School partisans, and New Agers all recognize themselves. He reframes Plato's cave: when the prisoners escape The Matrix's version of the cave, what they find outside is not the sunlit realm of the Good but the desolate 'desert of the real', and he asks whether the choice between reading the film as Capital colonizing subjectivity or as the virtual symbolic order as such is itself a false alternative.

plato-cave.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
plato-cave.title: Conquering the Inner Demon
plato-cave.relation: James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.

plato-cave.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
plato-cave.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Lenore Wright reads Sam and Frodo's Quest through the two journey motifs of Western philosophy: the journey out (Plato's cave, structuring Augustine's Confessions and Descartes' escape from the senses' deceptions) and the journey inward (the cogito, self-transformation, with Nussbaum's claim that literature gives philosophy a body). Frodo's steps out of the Shire-cave - selling Bag End, 'I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way' - create the Fellowship and its freedoms, while Boromir attains self-knowledge only at death's door and Gandalf, Aragorn, and Sam are remade by the road. Against classical heroes like Theseus and Odysseus, Sam and Frodo are modern pilgrims - Nietzschean Yea-sayers becoming who they are, with Heideggerian 'potentiality-for-Being' - whereas Sméagol and Saruman live inauthentically, defined by their pasts.

plato-cave.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
plato-cave.title: Last Pitch
plato-cave.relation: Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.

plato-cave.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
plato-cave.title: What Is Real
plato-cave.relation: Presents the two lines Rowling said she waited seventeen years to write: dying Harry, in the King's Cross limbo, asks Dumbledore whether their conversation is real or only 'inside my head', and Dumbledore answers that of course it is in his head but that does not make it unreal. The section frames this as the philosophical question of separating appearance from reality, cites A. J. Ayer's dismissal of his own near-death experience as hallucination, and introduces Plato's cave as the classic image of mistaking shadows for reality.

plato-cave.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
plato-cave.title: The Jedi Model
plato-cave.relation: Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.

plato-cave.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
plato-cave.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Wendy Hamblet asks whether Narnia feeds children a dangerous militaristic moral imaginary: Homeric warrior heroes, swarthy Calormene villains, voiceless animals excluded from moral concern, and battles that decide truth, in a lineage running from Plato's censorship of nursery stories through Descartes's modernity to Heidegger's seduction by Hitler's myths. On closer reading she finds Lewis undermining militarism: morally mixed characters, condemnation of aggression, despotism, and 'reasons of state,' and room only for just war and righteous self-defense. The finale is read through Plato's cave, as the Last Battle's worlds-within-worlds expose our political 'truths' as shadow-images that unscrupulous leaders manipulate when the god is absent.

plato-cave.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
plato-cave.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Takes Digory's dying remark 'It's all in Plato' as the key to the Chronicles. It compares the Professor's guided questioning of Peter and Susan about Lucy's wardrobe testimony to the Socratic method, though noting he supplies evidential maxims rather than eliciting a virtue-definition as Socrates does with Cephalus on justice. It maps Underland in The Silver Chair onto the Allegory of the Cave (Rilian bound in his silver chair like the chained prisoners, the Green Witch's enchantment that denies any world beyond), observing that the Witch 'plays Aristotle' by ridiculing Aslan as an invented perfect Form, while Puddleglum's 'stand by the play-world' speech echoes Socrates's reply to Glaucon that the ideal pattern is none the worse for being unrealizable. Finally it reads the 'real Narnia' of The Last Battle ('world within world, Narnia within Narnia') as Christian Platonism, with the nested heavens even raising Plato's Third Man problem.

plato-cave.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
plato-cave.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.

plato-cave.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
plato-cave.title: U2 and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.

plato-cave.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
plato-cave.title: Plato’s Cave Again
plato-cave.relation: Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.

plato-cave.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
plato-cave.title: Curtain Down
plato-cave.relation: Silberstein reads Rear Window as a self-reflexive film about film-watching: the shades rise like a curtain, the courtyard apartments play like frames on a filmstrip, and wheelchair-bound Jeff with his binoculars is the movie spectator - the courtyard is Plato's cave and we are the chained prisoners watching shadows (copies of copies of the forms). The chapter stages the Plato-versus-Aristotle debate over imitative art from Republic Book X and the Poetics, then argues the film vindicates both: Jeff's voyeurism breeds detachment and misjudgment (he misreads Lisa, Miss Torso, the composer and the newlyweds), yet the same watching awakens - the song 'Lisa' saves Miss Lonelyhearts from suicide, Thorwald is brought to justice, and Jeff and the audience leave the theater wiser about fantasy, boredom and their own lives.

plato-cave.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
plato-cave.title: Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone
plato-cave.relation: Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.

plato-cave.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
plato-cave.title: Thinking Inside the Pod
plato-cave.relation: Condella reads the opening of Saturday Night Fever -- Tony Manero strutting to 'Stayin' Alive' while delivering a can of paint -- as the iPod condition in miniature: music that alters rather than captures reality, now dial-up-able for workouts ('Eye of the Tiger'), bus rides, and grocery runs. Through Heidegger he argues the iPod is calculative thinking incarnate, annihilating the time, silence, and solitude meditative thinking requires (the shower as last refuge), and deepening technological homelessness by flattening every place into whatever soundtrack we choose -- the Rhine dammed into a 'gigantic gasoline station,' the iPod pushing us 'pretty far down' in Plato's Cave, its very possibility prepared by Descartes's thinking thing. Yet his wife's yoga instructor chanting on a Bronx bus shows the iPod can also open meditative space, so what Heidegger demands is not Luddism but Gelassenheit, a free relationship to technology.

plato-cave.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
plato-cave.title: Youth and the Image
plato-cave.relation: Hickey argues the iPod is the 'iCon of a generation' because it is a Baudrillardian simulacrum of youth: like the Gulf War consumed as CNN fireworks or reality TV's fabricated 'real,' Apple's silhouette ads sell faceless dancers whose entire identity is the white device -- a 'symbolic cyborgism' read through Donna Haraway. The vernacular of iPodding, podcasting, and downloading forms what he calls, with Wittgenstein, a language game woven into the actions of the 'now' that authorizes this youthful, tech-savvy identity as natural, while the ads' imagery works like Platonic shadows in the caves of our desire. Still, citing Giddens's structure-agency negotiation and DeCerteau's consumer tactic of re-appropriating everyday images, he insists we are not brainwashed: we can switch off, refuse, or remake the images that 'tell us who we are.'

plato-cave.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
plato-cave.title: Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH
plato-cave.relation: The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'

plato-cave.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
plato-cave.title: Must I Repeat Myself
plato-cave.relation: Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.

plato-cave.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
plato-cave.title: Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We
plato-cave.relation: Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.

plato-cave.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
plato-cave.relation: Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.

plato-cave.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
plato-cave.title: You Can Discover More about a Person in an Hour of Play than in a Year of
plato-cave.relation: Tim Christopher weighs pseudonymity — multiple persistent in-game identities — against responsibility for what those identities do, opening with his accidental first 'honorable kill' and the real-world extremes of a stabbing over loud WoW and a murder over a borrowed virtual sword. Using the Tae Kwon Do mat as a model of the sacred gamespace, he argues that WoW's persistent world and anonymity invite misbehavior, yet since no one is kind in WoW out of fear of punishment, any kindness there may be kindness for its own sake — an honest character may be a better person than an honest player. Plato's Allegory of the Cave is his master image: players see only shadows (avatars) of the real people behind them and must remember the world outside the cave.

plato-cave.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
plato-cave.title: Cyborg Goddess
plato-cave.relation: Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.

plato-cave.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
plato-cave.title: He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes
plato-cave.relation: Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.

plato-cave.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
plato-cave.title: Guardian Training
plato-cave.relation: Roger Travis argues Plato would welcome Halo as guardian training: mimesis is really 'playing epic pretend,' and Halo, like the Homeric epics that were Athens' textbooks, trains players in a way of life. Plato's Republic Book 10 critique—the painted bed as copy of a copy of the Form of Bed—warns that playing Master Chief could let appetite rule, yet the Laws' admission that the ideal city's politeia is itself a mimesis turns the tables: the Republic is its own training simulation of philosophic pretend. Re-imagining the cave as prisoners tied to couches playing Super Mario Bros, he argues Halo's dutiful NPCs and waking-to-duty player (literal cryo-wakeups in Combat Evolved and Halo 3) make it philosophy in Plato's own sense, with Aristotle's catharsis leavening the verdict.

plato-cave.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
plato-cave.title: Happy Ending
plato-cave.relation: Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.

plato-cave.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
plato-cave.title: The Power of Choice
plato-cave.relation: Rennett tests Cobb's choice to leave Limbo against Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine: we want to actually do things (raise his real children, not loving projections), to be a certain kind of person (Yusuf's dream-den addicts are 'indeterminate blobs'), and to touch something deeper than a man-made world. He then recruits Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's sincerity - she perceives Limbo and remembers it, so for her it is real - and argues that shared dreams differ from private dreams and the experience machine because they leave waking traces, like Mal's bullet in Arthur's leg. The chapter ends by making reality a matter of choice: like the cave prisoners of Plato's allegory, each character believes a world, and Cobb's ignoring of the top is his choice to live in the world with his children.

plato-cave.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
plato-cave.title: The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’
plato-cave.relation: The authors read the film in descending layers: reality as an ideology of touch and unreliable sensory experience, framed by Descartes's wax thought experiment and dream argument, with the kick explained through Hume's account of belief as custom and the totems as broken game pieces marking broken people (Mal's choice of the dream echoing prisoners returning to Plato's cave). The heist is then read as an existentialist drama where Cobb's 'downwards is the only way forwards' rejects the passive waiting of Beckett's Waiting for Godot and the pharmacy dreamers, with Jaspers's analysis of solitude making Limbo a hell of lonely regret that only an encounter with another can end. The chapter then argues the film is reflexively about movies (the crew mirrors a film crew, the Penrose stairs expose cinema's flat illusions, crosscutting manufactures time) before ending on Descartes's unresolved doubt about whether the final reality deserves our trust.

plato-cave.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
plato-cave.title: Chapter 14 - Trauma of the Real
plato-cave.relation: Introduces Paul Livingston's part with Dick's confession that reading Plato in college convinced him the empirical world was not truly real, then retells the cave of Republic Book VII in detail: prisoners bound since birth watching shadows of puppets cast by a fire. The cave becomes the frame for Dick's fiction — the 'reality' our percept-systems report is a show of images, and the philosophical quest is the prisoner's turn toward the archetypal reality behind the scenes.

plato-cave.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
plato-cave.title: Breakthrough to the Real
plato-cave.relation: Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?

plato-cave.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
plato-cave.title: Procession of Dummies
plato-cave.relation: Uses Dick's 1972 one-sentence definition ('Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away') and his claim that absolute reality reveals itself only when our space-time categories collapse, arguing the definition fits Lacan's Real better than Plato's picture of looking away from the cave wall. Through Žižek's readings, Ragle Gumm's objects being literally replaced by their symbolic labels and Deckard's replicant recognition as a 'total loss of the hero's symbolic identity' show the traumatic Real first appearing precisely where symbolically constituted reality fails.

plato-cave.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
plato-cave.title: Out of the Cave
plato-cave.relation: Traces the light-versus-darkness metaphor tradition from Plato's cave and Socrates' unexamined life through medieval 'illumination' and the Enlightenment to St. Paul's glass darkly, then lets Nietzsche ('shadow is as needful as light') and Derrida's deconstruction of presence/absence oppositions overturn it. The Stones do the same work in song: 'Just as every cop is a criminal, and all the sinners saints' in 'Sympathy for the Devil,' with 'Here Comes the Sun' overturned by 'Paint It Black' and 'Let It Be' by 'Let It Bleed.'

plato-cave.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
plato-cave.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.

plato-cave.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
plato-cave.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.

plato-cave.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
plato-cave.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Rick Mayock stops a fictional Jeopardy! clock to apply Plato's divided line: most contestants, like the cave prisoners rewarded for predicting shadow sequences, trade in doxa - conjecture (eikasia) and belief (pistis) - while the Meno's slave boy shows how Socratic questioning ties true opinions down into knowledge. Winning requires only dianoia, hypothetical reasoning from hypotheses and definitions, never noesis, the dialectic that ascends to the eternal Forms; the Phaedo's example of perfect 'equality' shows why the 'Aha!' of recognition is re-cognition by an immortal soul already acquainted with the Forms. Watson, lacking such a soul, can clear a buzz threshold but never have an Aha! moment - it is Daedalus's statue, lifelike but sure to run away from the truth unless tied down.

plato-cave.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
plato-cave.title: Futurama and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Reitter reads the sewer mutants - banished underground, surviving on what the surface flushes, as in 'The Mutants Are Revolting' where Leela is deported without trial the moment Fry reveals she is not an alien - as philosophy's Other, illuminated by Plato's cave (surface dwellers fear and demonize what they have never seen) and Beauvoir's The Second Sex (Leela passes as an acceptable alien until exposed as a mutant). Mrs. Astor's United Mutant Scholarship Fund film, with its 'noble sewer mutants... uh, people, I guess,' is read alongside Said's Orientalism and racist charity imagery as a third face of Othering. The chapter then adds folklore theory: the mutants are a folk group with their own urban legends (alligators in the sewer, and the 'sub-urban legend' of sub-mutants), ballads like 'The Legend of El Chupanibre,' and freegan-style recycling ethics - a counterculture whose difference the dominant universe-view casts as monstrosity.

plato-cave.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
plato-cave.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.

plato-cave.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
plato-cave.title: Dracula and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Wolfe asks what makes Stoker's mustachioed Count, Lugosi's, Dell Comics' science-hero Dracula, The Electric Company's malt-drinker, Blade's Drake, and Hotel Transylvania's overprotective dad all 'Dracula'. Plato's theory of Forms promises a shared ideal essence, but comparing particulars (origins from Vlad Tepes to Judas Iscariot, blood-drinking vs vanilla malts) finds no common thread, his 'Allegory of Dracula's Dungeon' recasts the cave to suggest Dracula may be only a shadow of some other Form like 'the undead', and the Republic's condemnation of art as imitation of imitation implies a fictional character may have no Form at all. Wolfe's own answer: the ideal Dracula is an outsider, an aristocrat, and a feeder on others, with everything else up for grabs.

plato-cave.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
plato-cave.title: Choose!
plato-cave.relation: The editor's introduction argues that Roth's series does not just contain philosophy but actually does it, proposing hypotheses about virtue, social order, evil, and forgiveness and testing them for consistency. It casts Tris as a Socratic figure who retraces the Allegory of the Cave: she starts 'chained' inside the cave of Chicago's faction system, climbs out to discover the faction life is a lie, and is tortured and eventually killed for the truth she tries to bring back, just as the cave-dwellers would kill the returning prisoner. The introduction closes by insisting the series is really about choice - that wisdom, unlike knowledge, must be lived, that self-reflection and even self-doubt are the hallmark of the wise, and that when life offers no options, like Tris and the factionless, you have to create your own.

plato-cave.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
plato-cave.title: 2. Peculiar!
plato-cave.relation: Ketcham reads the faction system as the Bureau's behavioral-correction experiment after a eugenics disaster, and compares the Bureau to the Tuskegee syphilis study: subjects who never gave informed consent, were denied treatment, and were treated as expendable because 'the experiment must continue at all costs.' He maps W.E.B. Du Bois's 'twoness' - double consciousness - onto Tris, who thrives in Dauntless yet belongs to no faction, and onto Tobias, whose identity collapses when he learns he tests as merely Dauntless. Closing with Gramsci, he argues Chicagoans have bought into the oppressor's story about genes and factions, so they need an organic intellectual to lead them out of the cave, and proposes Freire's praxis as the unfinished sequel.

plato-cave.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
plato-cave.title: 14. You Have to Be Good before You Can Be Smart
plato-cave.relation: The Bocks argue that the Erudite pairing of ignorance with knowledge is morally loaded: with Linda Zagzebski's and James Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, high-end knowledge requires intellectual virtues like the courage to test your beliefs publicly, so you really do have to be good before you can be smart. The Erudite manifesto's curriculum omits the humanities that open the mind, and its IQ-only leadership test fails Plato's requirement that philosopher kings love wisdom itself and, like the freed cave-prisoner, return to benefit society - which is why Jeanine, driven by lust for power and concealment of the truth beyond the fence, is 'a poor example of a philosopher king.' Both the Erudite and the Bureau reason as consequentialists ('Knowledge is power... power to do good') to justify slaughtering Abnegation and experimenting on unconsenting Chicagoans, when the pursuit of knowledge must be constrained by informed consent and human dignity.

plato-cave.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
plato-cave.title: 19. The Playful Thought Experiments of Louis C.K
plato-cave.relation: Argues Louis's bits function as playful philosophical thought experiments in Ernst Mach's and Tamar Gendler's sense: the white-people time machine, sitting 'in a chair in the sky,' and the 'Indians' naming skit are make-believe scenarios that reconfigure our frames and draw out truths we already knew, just as Plato's cave and Nathan's parable to King David do. Pairing the cognitive 'Aha!' with the mirthful 'Ha-ha' (via Hurley, Dennett, and Adams's Inside Jokes) makes his humor an error-detection reward loop that takes audiences to upsetting territory and makes them glad they went.

plato-cave.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
plato-cave.title: 22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes
plato-cave.relation: Mapping both heroes onto Plato's cave, the chapter argues each must first see past shadows: Bruce abandons revenge on Joe Chill to change Gotham's whole idea of justice, its citizens climb out of apathy when the Dark Knight ferries refuse the Joker's detonators, and Clark needs Jonathan Kent ('It's not to score touchdowns') and Jor-El to learn what his powers are for. Socrates' Apology supplies the mask's rationale - the just man must lead a private life to survive, so secret identities protect loved ones from Luthor's kryptonite stabbing and FBI kidnapping - and Plato's warning that the returned cave-escapee would be killed explains why the heroes must lead by hope rather than force. The oracle story's lesson that wisdom is knowing that you know nothing grounds the close: anyone can be a hero, as Batman tells Gordon about the coat around a boy's shoulders.

plato-cave.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
plato-cave.title: 9. Pierce’s Republic
plato-cave.relation: Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.

plato-cave.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
plato-cave.title: 9. Varys’s Riddle—Where Does Power Come From
plato-cave.relation: Iuliano uses Varys's riddle - king, priest, and rich man each bidding the same sellsword to kill the others - and 'power resides where men believe it resides' to stage a contest between John Austin's command theory of law (sovereign orders backed by force) and H.L.A. Hart's The Concept of Law, where authority rests on social acceptance. Cersei's 'power is power' scene with Littlefinger shows obedience that is mere coercion - Hart's gunman, being obliged rather than obligated - making the Lannisters gunmen writ large; the Hound's walkout on Joffrey exposes the illusion collapsing, and Plato's cave explains why Westerosi smallfolk prefer the comforting shadow to the truth that would free them.

plato-cave.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
plato-cave.title: 1. Juliana in Plato’s Cave
plato-cave.relation: Dennis Weiss argues the Amazon series is really about television and screened images: Juliana screening the Grasshopper newsreel in her basement replays Plato's Cave, except that the projected images, not the 'real' world of Nazi America, are what offer her 'a way out.' Following her from transfixed belief to doubt (calling the final film 'a nightmare' and choosing to trust Joe over the reel), and reading the show's media surfaces (Nazi commercials, 'Edelweiss,' the Riefenstahl comparison, Tagomi's cross-world vision), the chapter uses media thinkers like McLuhan, Meyrowitz, and Don Ihde to describe learning to see with 'compound vision' in a placeless, image-saturated culture.

plato-cave.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
plato-cave.title: 10. Hendrix Out of the Cave
plato-cave.relation: Scores 'Are You Experienced?' and 'Purple Haze' against the Allegory of the Cave: the backwards guitar and reversed cymbals are the painful, clumsy ascent from shadows toward the Form of the Good, with Hendrix as the initiator who must first drag the prisoner violently and then gently — 'come on across to me... we'll hold hands.' 'Purple Haze' becomes the midway delirium between cave and sun ('don't know if I'm coming up or down,' 'scuse me while I kiss the sky'), and the chapter concludes that the psychedelia is philosophical — consciousness opened by liberation from received opinion, not by LSD — warning the freed prisoner not to remain a pale copy of Plato or Hendrix.

plato-cave.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
plato-cave.title: 17. The Cry of Love
plato-cave.relation: Reads Hendrix as a romantic idealist on a Platonic-Neoplatonic arc: 'Room Full of Mirrors' shatters the cave wall and its projections toward The One, whose presence is pursued through eros with the veiled Beloved of Plotinus — the semi-divine feminine of 'Little Wing,' 'One Rainy Wish,' and 'Angel.' Hegel's Zeitgeist and world-spirit then frame the planned First Rays of the New Rising Sun as music meant to carry humanity's collective evolution, with Hendrix as Hegel's 'spiritual workman' and self-described messenger ('I am only a messenger and you are a Sheep in the process of evolution').

plato-cave.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
plato-cave.title: 3. Gestational Totalitarianism
plato-cave.relation: Kolb reads Gilead through Arendt's The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism: when reproduction becomes the means of production, women's labor is targeted, forcing fertile women into Animal laborans status as 'national resources' while denying them the creative freedom of Homo faber. She traces the polis/oikos split from Aristotle through Puritan capitalism to show Gilead overcorrecting into Aunt Lydia's 'freedom from'—totalitarian control of birth legitimized by the Rachel and Bilhah story and a Pauline creation story. The chapter ends with the transitional generation's forgetting (Offred's cave-delusion with Nick evoking Plato's Allegory of the Cave, the Holocaust documentarian 'thinking about how not to think') and Ofglen's bomb, arguing that thoughtfulness and literacy, not violence, are the only hopes against totalitarianism.

plato-cave.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
plato-cave.title: 18. Smoke and Mirrors in Gilead
plato-cave.relation: St. Martin structures Gilead with Plato's Republic: Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger' is the Sons of Jacob's operating principle (the Wall, the cattle prods, 'removing the damaged ones' from the ambassador's reception), and Glaucon's claim that it is best to do injustice without paying the penalty describes Commanders, while Handmaids suffer injustice with no revenge. She maps Socrates's division of labor onto Gilead's color-coded castes (Handmaids, Marthas, Aunts, Wives), then uses Glaucon's mocking 'city of sows' to show Gilead betraying even that model, since the regime exists to keep men powerful rather than babies alive—baby Charlotte recovers only when reunited with Janine. Serena's awakening after Eden's execution is an emergence from the cave, and the chapter closes that justice must be chosen for its own sake, with biases checked.

plato-cave.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
plato-cave.title: 3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis
plato-cave.relation: The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.

plato-cave.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
plato-cave.title: On Philosophers and Drag Queens
plato-cave.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Drag Race is an unexplored philosophical playground because it builds on marginalized black and Latinx queer herstory and because RuPaul, whose creed of love and self-improvement makes her a philosopher in her own right, has made the show her magnum opus. It invokes Plato's cave to explain why philosophers crave the 'untucked' version of everything RuPaul shows on stage. Its central move is a virtue-ethics reading of the show's judging: Ru's demand that a queen first be fierce, and through fierceness achieve charisma, uniqueness, nerve and talent, mirrors Aristotle's question of what makes a good person, with fierceness playing the role phronesis plays in securing the other virtues. Comparing queens like Silky Nutmeg Ganache, Jinkx Monsoon, Yara Sofia and Sharon Needles, it poses 'what makes a good drag queen?' as a live philosophical problem.

plato-cave.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
plato-cave.title: The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the
plato-cave.relation: Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.

plato-cave.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
plato-cave.title: Perceptions Are Fine, but Dull Reality Is Still Better
plato-cave.relation: Distinguishes perceiver, perceptions, and perceived external objects to ask whether Alice, or anyone, can get beyond her perceptions to a mind-independent world, entering through Robert Arp's own painkiller hallucination of stones that were really Jell-O. The chapter sets epistemological idealism and metaphysical antirealism (the movie-theater-in-the-mind picture, traced to Plato's cave and Berkeley's suggestion that we are trapped inside perceptual reality) against the epistemological and metaphysical realism it finds in Alice and Carroll: fossilized ferns, dodo birds, and the Pythagorean theorem are discovered rather than invented, and at story's end everything rightly changes 'to dull reality'.

plato-cave.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
plato-cave.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Tests Socrates' claim (via Plato's Apology and the Myth of the Cave) that the self-examined life is the happiest against the Bluths: Michael, the one who escapes the cave in the pilot (learning at the boat party that his father is a criminal and he was never getting partnership), turns out chronically miserable, while self-deceivers Gob, Lindsay, and Tobias are mostly content. The chapter concludes that Bertrand Russell's Conquest of Happiness fits better: reflection makes sinners (George Michael's self-loathing over Maeby), narcissists (Michael's need to be seen as good), and megalomaniacs (Kitty) unhappy, so the unexamined life is not a huge mistake, though moderate examination still pays.

plato-cave.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
plato-cave.title: Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers
plato-cave.relation: Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.

plato-cave.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
plato-cave.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
plato-cave.relation: Drawing on fieldwork and surveys at the 2011 Tampa Lebowski Fest, Dufort and Lemire-Cadieux use Kierkegaard's Concept of Irony and indirect communication — contrasted with Plato's condemnation of mimesis in the cave and Aristotle's rehabiliation of it — to explain why Achievers who dress as rugs, memorize lines, and re-watch the film dozens of times find no objective message to decode. Kierkegaardian irony leaves each receiver to dig out a subjective existential truth through self-reflection and repetition, so that fans repeating the Dude's message become part of the irony itself: being an 'Achiever' achieves nothing objective and something deeply personal ('don't pee on other people's rugs').

plato-cave.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
plato-cave.title: Pretending to Talk about It
plato-cave.relation: Travis claims everyone misses the point of both Plato's cave and BioShock, and reads the post-assassination self-destruct sequence as the game's cave moment: though you may roam Ryan's office shooting walls ('active inaction', like the escaped prisoner contemplating the form of the Good), the sequence will not resolve until you insert the item, exposing 'a man chooses, a slave obeys' as hollow. The harvest-versus-save equivalence (Tenenbaum's gifts cancel the ADAM loss) is likewise a stroke of genius, not a flaw, because it shows in-game 'ethical choices' are as meaningless as the prisoners' shadow-naming contests. Since both cave and game run on mimesis, playing pretend, the way forward is to 'pretend to talk about it': performing philosophy through play as Plato's dialogues stage Socrates.

plato-cave.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
plato-cave.title: 25 Fear of a Black Museum Black Existentialism
plato-cave.relation: Charles Peterson reads the museum scene through Black existentialism and Africana phenomenology: colonial museums freeze African existence in an 'archaic amber' of aesthetic purity, and Killmonger's reclaiming of the mask and questioning of the curator perform a truth-telling that breaks the museum's performance of dominance. Du Bois's double-consciousness explains Killmonger's inseparable Wakandan-and-American two-ness (extended to Nakia and the War Dogs), while Paget Henry's contrast of the DuBoisian subject who oscillates between two 'We's' with Hegel's recognition-seeking subject explains why T'Chaka chooses Wakanda and abandons N'Jobu, and Plato's cave frames Killmonger as dragging Wakanda's comfortable council toward truths 'some truths are too much to bear.' The chapter concludes that Killmonger fails because wearing the mask he embraced negrification rather than shedding it, whereas T'Challa matures from a Hegelian into a DuBoisian subject by opening Wakanda to the world.

plato-cave.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
plato-cave.title: Happily Ever After
plato-cave.relation: The chapter maps the Beast's enchanted castle onto Plato's cave: the spellbound household, dimming in the decaying West Wing, are prisoners whose human capacities are suppressed, and Belle is the missing cause that breaks the chains Plato never explains. Using Diotima's teaching from the Symposium that beauty compels love, it reads the Beast's curse as externalizing his indifference to beauty, so that the staircase dance, his freeing of Belle, and Belle's 'I love you' trace Diotima's ladder from outward to inward beauty — the light that releases the prisoner.

plato-cave.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
plato-cave.title: Notes
plato-cave.relation: Dal Barco maps Lucy's arc in the Amazon series onto Plato's cave stage by stage: Vault 33's fake sky, curated history lessons, and Vault-Tec-managed information are the shadow-puppet show, her first step into the sun after Hank's abduction by Moldaver is the freed prisoner's blinding ascent, the hidden hospital vault tempts her (and Maximus, who wants to stay) like the return to the cave, and the truth - her father helped orchestrate the nuclear war, her mother is now a ghoul - plays the role the sun and the Good play in the Republic. Plato's claim that only the educated philosopher who has seen beyond the cave should govern (Republic 496a, 519a-d) explains why Lucy, unlike the frightened Norm or the tempted Maximus, goes back out into the wastes: she is becoming the philosopher-ruler whose hard-won knowledge enables Moldaver to restore power to the surface and begin a civilization no longer built on shadows. The chapter answers its own question - yes, it was worth leaving the vault for the truth.

plato-cave.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
plato-cave.title: Notes
plato-cave.relation: Tracing Fallout's own censorship history — the GURPS licensing cancellation threat, the invisibility of child NPCs in the European release, the moral panic after Columbine — the chapter asks whether it is wrong to simulate evil, framing the issue with Morgan Luck's gamer's dilemma. Plato's cave and the Forms ground the 'media impacts morals' worry: games are shadows of shadows whose simulated vice accumulates 'a large evil in our souls', which is also why Lucy's Vault upbringing leaves her underprepared for the wasteland's emotions. Against this, Aristotle's catharsis and Schulzke's claim that Fallout trains phronesis support depicting wrongdoing as practice for moral judgment, so the chapter concludes the right wrongs to depict are whichever maximize the simulation of choice, with Braun's player-controlled Tranquility Lane simulation as the dystopian counter-model.

plato-cave.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
plato-cave.title: Going Mental
plato-cave.relation: Opens the Just in Your Head? essay by taking Dumbledore's reply to Harry (of course it is happening inside your head, but why should that mean it is not real?) as a live metaphysical and epistemological question about appearance versus reality, noting that even A. J. Ayer dismissed his own near-death experience as hallucination. It retells Plato's cave allegory and reads Harry and Dumbledore's descent into the creepy cave in Half-Blood Prince, plus Harry's worry that the King's Cross dialogue was just a shadow on the wall, as a modern image of prisoners mistaking appearances for reality.

plato-cave.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
plato-cave.title: introd.xhtml
plato-cave.relation: The editors' introduction frames The Hobbit as Plato's Allegory of the Cave retold 'there and back again': like the freed prisoner, Bilbo leaves his comfortable hole, has his eyes opened by a frightening journey, and returns 'queer' to neighbors who cannot accept that life offers more than order and routine. It lists the book's guiding questions - whether adventures are worth missing dinner, whether food and song outrank gold, whether powerful technology can be trusted or must be destroyed, and the duties of friends - as the essays' shared agenda.

plato-cave.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
plato-cave.title: Happy Ending
plato-cave.relation: Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.

plato-cave.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
plato-cave.title: The Power of Choice
plato-cave.relation: Rennett stages Ariadne's 'who would want to be stuck in a dream for ten years?' against Nozick's experience machine: Nozick's three reasons for staying unplugged (doing rather than merely experiencing, being a determinate person, contact with a reality deeper than human construction) map onto Cobb's reasons for leaving Limbo — he wants to actually raise his children, be a good father, and love children who can love him back rather than projections. Against Nozick, the chapter enlists Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's choice: a perceived world is real, and Inception's shared dreams pass Berkeley's intersubjective test in ways private dreams cannot (Cobb apologizes to Arthur for being shot; dream acts carry waking consequences). It concludes that reality becomes what we choose to believe — Cobb's final refusal to watch the top, like the cave prisoners rejecting release, is the power of choice.

plato-cave.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
plato-cave.title: The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’
plato-cave.relation: Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.

plato-cave.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
plato-cave.title: 12 The Shadow Realities of Indiana Jones
plato-cave.relation: Matthew Crippen and Matthew Dixon read the franchise's caves through Plato's allegory: in Crusade, stand-ins for God (the Cross of Coronado, the Grail, with the decoy chalices as shadows of a representation) appear underground, while Indy's self-realizations with his father occur at sunlit cave mouths, inching from shadow toward the Good. They fuse this with newer, active accounts of truth — James's 'truth happens to an idea' realized in the leap from the lion's head, Dewey on poetry as revelation, and Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment — while Nietzsche's critique shows Platonic fictions can still be life-enhancing. The father and son 'shadow' one another (with Oedipal overtones through Elsa) until Henry Sr. relinquishes the Grail to save 'Indiana,' his path out of the cave.

plato-cave.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
plato-cave.title: Over Four Thousand Words to Say No
plato-cave.relation: Spanakos asks whether Stark's assembling, disassembling, and reassembling of the Avengers and his unseen-hand management of Civil War make him the Republic's philosopher guardian, and answers no. Tony fits the surface profile — the gold-souled ruler of Socrates' noble lie, the elite training, indifference to money, the technê of an MIT engineer who envisions the future — but he lacks epistêmê: he never climbs from the cave's shadows to grasp the forms of justice and the good, and his appetites (womanizing in The Ultimates, 'Demon in a Bottle') show a soul where passion is not ruled by reason. His puppet mastery is reactive problem-solving guided by each situation, not philosophy, and reading him as a philosopher king is our failure to read The Republic meditatively, as Ortega y Gasset urged.

plato-cave.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
plato-cave.title: Believer, Deceiver: Metallica, Perception, and Reality
plato-cave.relation: Robert Arp uses Hetfield's lyrics about lies, deception and misperception ('Bad Seed', 'The House Jack Built''s 'Is that the moon or just the light that lights this dead end street?') to stage the perception-reality problem: perceiver, perceptions, and external objects, as in Plato's cave allegory. He contrasts metaphysical/epistemological realism with idealism and antirealism, deploys the movie-theater picture of solipsism drawn from Hume's bundle of perceptions and Berkeley's denial of the external world, and argues Hetfield's own practice as a songwriter proves he is a realist - while distinguishing healthy philosophical skepticism from the lyric's irrational mistrust.

plato-cave.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
plato-cave.title: Live From New York
plato-cave.relation: Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.

plato-cave.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
plato-cave.title: Notes
plato-cave.relation: Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.

plato-cave.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
plato-cave.title: 22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes
plato-cave.relation: Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.

plato-cave.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
plato-cave.title: Notes
plato-cave.relation: Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.

plato-cave.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
plato-cave.title: Hoop Dreams, Blacktop Realities
plato-cave.relation: Bernard Jackson Jr. argues that basketball is an institution where black manhood is socially constructed (leaning on Naomi Zack's feminist point that gender identity is imposed by social designation), and that love among black players is essential to that construction while toughness is equivocal - the 'soft' label stuck to the gentlemanly David Robinson even as the Pistons walked off without congratulating the Bulls. Reading the documentary Hoop Dreams, he shows Arthur Agee and William Gates being used as commodities by recruiters, Coach Pingatore, and family expectations, invoking Marx on exploitation and 'use value' (Spike Lee's Nike-camp speech) and Kant's demand that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means. He likens William Gates's return to Chicago's Cabrini-Green as a minister to Plato's enlightened prisoner going back down into the cave.

plato-cave.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
plato-cave.title: The Philosophy and Non-Philosophy of Potato Salad
plato-cave.relation: Scribner uses Ginsberg's 'Howl for Carl Solomon'—and Solomon's throwing potato salad at a Dada lecture—to ask whether the Beats' performative acts count as philosophy at all. He argues philosophy is constituted by self-contestation, its relation to a 'non-philosophy' of madness and raw experience, reading Solomon's silence and Ginsberg's poetic mediation through Foucault's 'Madness and Civilization' and Derrida's rebuttal in 'Cogito and the History of Madness.' Ginsberg-to-Solomon is made analogous to philosophy-to-the-Beats: a betraying translator who nonetheless must give the mute event voice, grounded in Plato's failure to banish the poets from the Republic.

plato-cave.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
plato-cave.title: Raising Arizona as an American Comedy
plato-cave.relation: Gilmore reads Raising Arizona as a classical comedy (bad-beginning-to-good-ending) about the American 'optative mood' of self-creation, using Hi McDunnough's outlaw-to-family arc and his name-as-height-metaphor to figure Emerson's aspirational American self. He deploys Plato's two kinds of cave-laughter to distinguish the film's 'tender,' welcoming comedy (Hi and Ed, Gale and Evelle) from mocking ridicule, and frames Hi's need to abandon outlaw identity via Heidegger's Augenblick and Badiou's 'event' sparked in Ed's mug-shot flash. Nietzsche on dreams-as-origin-of-metaphysics grounds the film's dream/reality tension, and Hi's over-identification with the outlaw universal is glossed as Sartrean bad faith.

plato-cave.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
plato-cave.title: From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs
plato-cave.relation: Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.

plato-cave.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
plato-cave.title: 7. The Art of Playing Along with Dancing Little People
