Punk heroes serve as Aristotelian exemplars - Ian MacKaye (self-reliance, straight edge, Dischord Records), Jeff Ott (near-obscene value coherence, rejecting 'ought implies can' while defending Green Day from sellout pieties), Billie Joe Armstrong (humility, giving his guitar to a fan) - and Protest the Hero exemplifies the doctrine of the mean, where courage is calculation of the right action relative to circumstances, not moderation. Punk's pendulum between pious self-deprivation and soulless self-compromise is the space between vices, and its ethic is learned by doing: 'Try. Try. Try.'

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 6. The Morality of Mike’s Manifesto
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: The Gibsons analyze Mike Ehrmantraut's code—'if you make a deal with somebody, you keep your word'—through virtue ethics and Stoicism. Aristotle's function argument and Golden Mean partly vindicate Mike's counsel toward temperance and restraint (not carrying a gun, sparing the Salamanca driver), yet Aristotle's claim that 'bad people are full of regrets' marks him as a flawed 'wicked' man given his inner turmoil over breaking his son. They read his calm as Stoic (Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on controlling the mind, Spartan simplicity), and weigh Kant's intent-based defense of his killing the dirty cops Hoffman and Fensky against Mill's social-rule view of sanctionable wrongs.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 12. A Cave of His Own Making
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Golden reinterprets Plato's Allegory of the Cave to argue Chuck enslaves himself in a 'cave of his own making'—his hypochondriacal electromagnetic hypersensitivity—to keep Jimmy accountable and to exact vengeance for Jimmy's unpunished childhood thefts. Using Aristotle's De Anima psychology and the function argument, he places Chuck's imagination (phantasia) below reason: Chuck retains the rationality to serve clients like Mesa Verde and to detect Jimmy's document fraud, but sinks below the Golden Mean into the vices of meanness (short of kindness) and cowardice (short of courage) toward his brother. He adds Kierkegaard's Repetition: Chuck is stuck in backward-looking 'recollection' of vengeance and cannot make the forward, committed 'repetition' of simply being Jimmy's brother.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 6. Authenticity in a World of Bullshido
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Falcioni uses Aristotle's doctrine of the mean and Gillian Russell's 'epistemic viciousness in the martial arts' to read Bourdain's obsession with Brazilian jiu-jitsu as a struggle to cultivate the virtues of humility, courage, and authenticity against the vices of 'bullshido' (fraudulent martial arts). He connects Bourdain's craving for BJJ's brutal, ego-slaying honesty to a Heideggerian authenticity, while noting Bourdain's return to old vices near the end.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a character virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, slave to his need to be thought funny; Gareth Keenan the literalist boor who cannot take or get a joke; and Tim Canterbury the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to circumstance. McAleer argues wit shows Aristotle's morality is broader than duty or outcome, aiming at eudaimonia, and that humor's uncodifiability, like Wittgenstein's remarks, mirrors how virtue requires practical wisdom rather than rules.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: What Would You Do If Your Mother Asked You A Brief Introduction to Ethics
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Jacob Held and Eric Wilson introduce ethics by first dispatching cultural and normative relativism (the Butter Battle Book's Yooks and Zooks, the Once-ler's 'we're each allowed our own opinion') as a cowardly refusal to judge, then present three theories through Seuss characters. Horton is the paragon of Kantian dignity ('a person's a person, no matter how small') and the categorical imperative, tested against lying in The Cat in the Hat. Thidwick the Big-Hearted Moose dramatizes Mill's utilitarianism and its sacrifice of the individual to the greatest happiness, while Thidwick, courage, and Life's 'Great Balancing Act' illustrate Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, virtue as habituated character, and eudaimonia.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence. Manninen then presses Aristotle: his strict 'only good men' criterion and his debt-bound, property-like view of the parent-child bond fail the flawed-but-loyal Andy/Red and the abusive fathers in The Body, showing human friendship is more complex than his taxonomy allows.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Dougherty argues Austen's ideal marriage mirrors Aristotle's complete friendship, where the friend is loved for who they are and becomes a 'second self.' She sorts Austen's relationships into Aristotle's three kinds: utility (Emma and Mrs. Elton, Charlotte and Mr. Collins), pleasure (Lydia and Wickham, the fading Emma-Harriet bond), and complete friendship grounded in mutual good character (Jane and Bingley, Elizabeth and Darcy, Emma and Knightley). Central is the 'second self' as mirror: Darcy's letter and Knightley's rebukes let Elizabeth and Emma see themselves ('Till this moment I never knew myself'), so marriage-as-friendship improves self-knowledge and virtue and must not be left to chance as Charlotte urges.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Potzsch reads Emma as an Aristotelian study of eudaimonia, arguing Emma's self-deception and the flattery of those around her block her from true happiness, which for Aristotle is activity of the soul in accordance with reason and virtue. She diagnoses Emma's cruelty to Miss Bates at Box Hill as Aristotelian akrasia (moral weakness): Emma knows better but is overpowered by the desire to shine, showing virtue has not yet become her second nature. She contrasts Emma and Mrs. Elton's pursuit of honor (which Aristotle deems superficial, illustrated via Plato's Euthyphro) with Knightley's genuine virtue, and closes on Aristotle's ranking of the contemplative over the political life.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Chapter 5 Twain’s Last Laugh
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Kristina Gehrman argues that reading Huck as a moral hero who overcomes racism is Twain's ironic trap. Using Arne Naess's idea of identification, Aristotle on habituation of character, and Iris Murdoch's 'just and loving attention,' she gives a developmentally attuned reading of Huck as a traumatized, morally immature, still-racist child whose regard for Jim never generalizes ('I knowed he was white inside'). Twain lures his white readers into identifying with Huck's supposed triumph, then exposes their own stunted moral growth about race; Jim is the only mature adult yet is barred from identification by the novel's racist caricature. The novel's greatness is Socratic and gadfly-like rather than triumphant.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Nease lays out a game plan for raising ethical children, using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics – eudaimonia as a flourishing life, virtue as the mean between extremes, and the master-skills of practical wisdom and self-control – as the core, mocking 'character counts' posters as no substitute for early habit-formation. He folds in Kant's motive of duty, Nietzsche's will-to-power (glossed via Janet Jackson's Control) as the drive to master oneself, and argues empathy (Theodor Lipps' inner imitation), self-awareness, concentration (Husserl's foreground/background), and a respect for justice must be cultivated to 'stack the deck' toward a good adult.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Austin offers practical wisdom for fathers of daughters, grounding fatherly obligations in daughters' fundamental interests and focusing on self-knowledge, moral development, and the common good. Invoking the Delphic 'know thyself,' Charles Taylor's 'strong evaluations,' and Aristotle's view that virtue grows through practice, he explains how to cultivate humility (including 'existential humility' before nature), courage (including self-sacrifice), and wisdom (curiosity, versatility, critical thinking) – e.g., analyzing advertising assumptions and limiting screen time – so a daughter can flourish and contribute to the common good.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Jesse Steinberg and Michael Stuckart distinguish instrumental from intrinsic value (using Frankena's list) across sailing's gear, knowledge, and aesthetics, then argue via Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that sailing is a route to eudaimonia through the cultivation of virtue. They show sailing exemplifies courage as the golden mean between cowardice and foolhardiness (deciding whether to go out in twenty-knot winds, judging teen solo circumnavigators), being hard-working (the mean between laziness and workaholism), and cleverness (jury-rigging, navigation). They contend sailing demands a broader, deeper range of virtues than golf, bowling, or power-boating, making it an especially rich — though not the only — path to a flourishing, happy life.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Russell argues that being 'cool' is an aesthetic virtue distinct from being fashionable: the fashionable but anxious tryhard 'Allegra' fails to be cool precisely because her studied effort to win social approval is visible, whereas figures like James Dean or Marlene Dietrich seem effortlessly cool. Drawing an analogy to happiness and to moral virtues like compassion, he treats cool as a *self-effacing* goal — achieved only by caring about aesthetic matters for their own sake rather than for status, the way a genuinely virtuous person is moved directly by others' welfare rather than by a desire to be seen as good. He uses a Simpsons exchange (Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa on what makes someone cool) to show that not-caring alone is insufficient.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Haire and Nelson read the film A Christmas Story as evidence that consumerism has replaced religion as America's faith: the Parker family shows no religious markers, and Ralphie's single-minded quest for the Red Ryder BB gun mirrors the identity-defining, transformative role religion once played. Using Aristotle's virtue ethics, they name consumerism a Christmas vice opposed to candidate Christmas virtues of being religious, traditional and family-centered. When the BB gun nearly blinds Ralphie and the hounds ruin the turkey, the consumerist ideal fails; the family's makeshift Chinese-restaurant dinner shows the family-centered virtue overcoming the vice, so 'all was right with the world'.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Brian Treanor argues from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that climbing is a crucible for cultivating virtues (arete) that contribute to flourishing (eudaimonia), stressing that virtue is acquired by habituation and lies in a mean 'relative to us'—so casting off on the Bachar-Yerian is courage for a 5.11 leader but rashness for a 5.9 climber. He shows how climbing's self-imposed 'rules' (Tejada-Flores' games) forge courage (feeling the right balance of fear and confidence, as in John Sherman's Fisher Towers epic and Steve House's judicious retreats on K7), humility (honestly measuring oneself against pioneers who used inferior gear, per Chouinard and Messner's 'murder of the impossible'), and reverence for nature (Thoreau, Muir, Brower). His thesis is that in a coddled, technological world climbing is uncommonly well suited to building these excellences of character.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Leigh Duffy pairs the yogic balance of sthira (strength/steadiness) and sukha (ease/openness) in asana with Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, prompted by her own stress-induced seizure while teaching the Nichomachean Ethics. She argues both frameworks make virtue/right balance 'relative to us' — the correct warrior I or the courageous or good-tempered act depends on the individual and moment — and both require self-knowledge and practical reason. Cultivating the mean of sthira and sukha on the mat becomes her model for finding balance among work, relationships, and self-care off it.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: BLUES
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Roopen Majithia asks why a music born of African-American suffering became universally beloved and answers with Aristotle's account of musical catharsis in the Politics. Drawing on the Nicomachean Ethics link between habituated action, emotion, and disposition (as courage is built by acting courageously), he argues music images real emotions and thereby purges excess feeling. Modern electric urban blues (T-Bone Walker's 'Stormy Monday,' Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf), with its danceable, sexually charged rhythm, recreates the emotional landscape of repetitive urban work and, aided by dancing, effects a broad catharsis — which also explains why non-black communal performers can play it and why intimate bars beat arenas.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Anne Barnhill uses John Cusack's boom-box serenade in Say Anything, his poolside pleading in The Sure Thing, and Andy Bernard's 'Take a Chance on Me' serenade in The Office to defend 'prospective boundary violation'—violating a boundary that would not exist in a closer relationship in order to create that relationship. She rejects the Kantian reading of Korsgaard and Hill that treating people as ends forbids all non-rational manipulation, arguing instead that such charming pushiness is 'faking it till you make it,' which works via Aristotle's habituation whereby feelings catch up with actions. She then sets four rules (no harm, not too much closer too fast, genuinely wanting the relationship, and that the other would plausibly want it) to separate appropriate from wrong boundary violations.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Hamilton reads the pick-up-artist 'Game' (Mystery, Style, negs, peacocking, the Alpha frame) against Aristotle's great-souled magnanimous man, arguing that the jerk and the PUA succeed because they inadvertently mimic the Megalopsuche's self-containment and indifference to others' approval. He contends the ethical route is to genuinely acquire that character through habituation ('we become brave by acting bravely') rather than fake it, so the nice guy's supplication fails while true magnanimity requires the full virtues. He then uses Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, and the highest disinterested philia) to argue that erotic relationships can rise to real friendship only where partners are equals, citing When Harry Met Sally on whether men and women can be friends.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Sean McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, 'the slave of his sense of humor,' who jests inappropriately; Gareth is the boorish literalist who cannot take or get a joke; Tim is the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to the situation, exercising practical wisdom (phronesis). McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 1. The Good Place as Philosophy Moral Adventures in the Afterlife
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Engels argues that NBC's The Good Place, though premised on a merit-based afterlife, actually argues morality should not be grounded in afterlife reward. When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 13. Arrested Development as Philosophy Family First What We Owe Our Parents
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Phillips uses the dysfunctional Bluths to ask what, if anything, adult children owe their parents. Against Sidgwick's reluctance and various grounds for filial obligation, he argues negatively through the family: George Sr. and Lucille never meet the motivation and above-duty conditions for a debt of gratitude; adopted Lindsay's absentee mothering of Maeby shows biology alone grounds nothing; and Michael's dutiful-son and overbearing-father roles show the social role of 'parent' is not enough (Hardimon's 'reflectively acceptable' roles). Positively, deploying Aristotle's three friendships (utility, pleasure, virtue), he argues that only a voluntary friendship of virtue grounds special obligations — illustrated when a rock-bottom, 'useless' Gob and George Sr. finally bond as near-equals, the show's closest thing to genuine friendship.

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'

aristotle-virtue-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-virtue-ethics.title: 37. Groundhog Day as Philosophy Phil Connors Says “No” to Eternal Return
aristotle-virtue-ethics.relation: Blessing argues that Groundhog Day, despite frequent comparisons to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, actually rejects both. Phil Connors does not say the Nietzschean 'yes' to reliving the same day (his attitude is odium fati, not amor fati), nor does he find Camusian happiness by embracing absurdity; instead he keeps changing, striving toward a better tomorrow. She reads his transformation from misanthropic hedonist on a hedonic treadmill into a kind, generous, self-actualized man as a vindication of Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness comes from habitually doing the right thing (saving the falling boy, learning piano, serving others), pursuing objective and intrinsic goods rather than mere meaning-subjectivism, so redemption is not 'looking at things differently' but becoming a better person.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: 4 - Marge’s Moral Motivation
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Gerald Erion and Joseph Zeccardi present Marge as an everyday Aristotelian whose bravery (The Springfield Connection, escaping the Movementarian commune), temperance, and generosity each hit the mean between Springfield's vicious extremes, and whose eudaimonia is achieved through the good of her family. They contrast her reason-driven conscience with Ned Flanders's divine command theory—consulting Reverend Lovejoy over whether to play capture-the-flag on the sabbath—and side with Marge, invoking Plato's Euthyphro to argue that morality cannot simply be a function of God's commands. Marge emerges as a 'Christian-flavored Aristotelian' who cultivates virtue by habituation and models it for Lisa and Bart.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Happiness and Cypher’s Choice Is Ignorance Bliss
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Opening Griswold's essay (with Locke's line on happiness disturbed by new uneasiness as epigraph), the chapter asks why happiness - the question of existential urgency that Aristotle treated as the ultimate end of our activities - has received so little philosophical treatment (no Platonic dialogue is devoted to it) while non-philosophers assume there is an answer to be found. It presents The Matrix as a rare clever movie that genuinely presses the question of what happiness is, whether the film's answer is tenable, and how we would construct a better one of our own, with Cypher's choice as the test case.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Unknown
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: The chapter proposes three theses: happiness is centrally tranquillity (ataraxia), whose enemy is anxiety - the 'splinter in your mind' that things are out of kilter; the rival Aristotelian view treats happiness as activity (energeia) of soul in accordance with excellence (arete), an objectivism that explains how a contented 'human battery' or happy slave is mistaken about being happy; and neither view suffices alone, since a passionless apatheia is barren and dry. Lived happiness is instead equipoise - settledness in one's basic stance that is compatible with turbulent passions and commitments, more like Neo's active decision-making and discovery than a lazy virtual tryst with the woman in red.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Buffyverse’s Moral Compass
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Greg Forster argues the Buffyverse's moral structure is neither Christian nor Nietzschean vampire fiction but Platonic eudaimonism: the just person is always happier than the unjust. Faith is the test case — her pleasure-seeking turn to evil with Mayor Wilkins, her body-swap theft of Buffy's life in 'Who Are You?', her self-disgust ('You're nothing! Disgusting, murderous bitch!'), and her begging Angel to kill her in 'Five by Five' enact Plato's Republic examples of the Ring of Gyges and the unjust person mistakenly honored while the just one is punished. Buffy's invisible crime spree in 'Gone' and her 'the work that I have to do' sacrifice in 'The Gift' display the same eudaimonist pattern, with the caveat that the Buffyverse follows a Rousseau-like moral psychology in which compassion, not reason, does the moral work.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Gregory Bassham distills six keys to happiness from Tolkien's hobbits and elves: delight in simple pleasures (Epicurus on natural pleasures, Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles (Sam's star above Mordor, with Marcus Aurelius and Augustine on courage and hope), friendship (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics read against Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo go alone), good character, beauty and creativity (Lothlórien versus Mordor, 'flow'), and wonder (Tom Bombadil, Frodo's 'recovery' of fresh vision at Cerin Amroth). He argues Tolkien thereby becomes a philosophical guide, pointing from the Shire and Rivendell to a richer, more joy-filled life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Argues ancient ethics explains why Tony, who has 'the world by the balls', still feels like a loser. Plato's Republic diagnoses him as a 'civil war' of unintegrated motivations (loving father and murderer at once, as in 'College'), a condition power over others only worsens; Aristotle teaches that happiness is activity with self-sufficient, integrated desires rather than a list of possessions, and Epicurus's 'sober reasoning' is the therapy Tony never gets. The Hawthorne quotation Tony reads in 'College' and his Gary Cooper ideal from 'The Happy Wanderer' frame the point: Cooper in High Noon is unmesswithable because he does not need vengeance, whereas Tony's compulsive revenge shows the world has the grip on him.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Why Not to Buy the Porsche
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Skoble uses Manhattan's confrontation scene — Isaac telling Yale 'you're too easy on yourself... you'd rather buy the Porsche' over the hominid skeleton — to build an account of integrity as fidelity to correct moral principles, requiring an integrated character in which reason and desire agree. He distinguishes integrity from mere consistency (the 'consistent Nazi') and from stubbornness, and models it on Plato's just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself'. Aristotle's account of habituation defends Isaac's slippery slope: Yale's repeated lies for expediency are forming the kind of character who would inform on friends, so integrity is an objective yardstick of a well-lived life, as Isaac's amends to Tracy at the end confirms.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Ugly
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Argues Hogwarts' purely vocational curriculum gives students the tools of power without the wisdom to use them: measured against Adler's three aims of schooling, it surveys the classic accounts of education's purpose - Plato's wisdom and well-ordered society, Aristotle's eudaimonia as excellent activity, Locke's 'virtue and wisdom', Rousseau's natural child-centered education, Kant's character formation, Dewey's growth - and concludes Hogwarts fails to form lifelong learners equipped for wizarding society's problems, including, as Hermione says, wizards' sense of superiority to other creatures.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The End of the Story
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Argues Socrates and Dumbledore both die for virtue and the common good: Socrates refuses exile because the examined life matters more than wealth or reputation, his martyrdom an exemplar that could benefit Athens, and Dumbledore's arranged death protects Snape's spying for the anti-Voldemort cause. Two Muggle lessons follow - live devoted to something larger than yourself (Lily's sacrifice, with King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates as real-world parallels) and find mentors, as Dumbledore's humility, honesty, and praise in the Order of the Phoenix prophecy conversation enable Harry to fulfill his destiny, with dead mentors like Aristotle, Confucius, and Jesus still able to teach us through their books.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Need to Belong
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Working out Birthright's answer, Waid argues that even the solar-powered Kal-El shares the human need to belong, so he can connect with humanity not by hiding his alien side but by embracing it. Echoing a Marianne Williamson passage about our fear of being 'powerful beyond measure', Waid has Superman wear the S-shield - the banner of his Kryptonian 'tribe' - and use his powers openly, because only by living authentically in service of others does he truly belong. He links this to Aristotle's discovery that happiness is rooted in living with excellence, which Superman 'in his own way' found too.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Great Paradox
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Waid closes by drawing out the paradox that Superman's shining selflessness is achieved through acting in his own self-interest: in saving others he exercises his distinctive powers and fulfills his authentic destiny, which fulfills him, while embracing his own nature and history puts him in the one activity that most helps others. There is no blanket choice between self and community, he argues - properly fulfilling one's own nature redounds to everyone's benefit - and Superman thereby becomes a mirror for examining the balance of selflessness and self-interest in the reader's own life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Elusiveness of a Complete Friendship
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Argues that Batman himself is chiefly responsible for the elusiveness of complete friendship: the promise to his murdered parents consumes the personal investment such friendship needs, so everyone — Gordon, Dent, the Robins, Batgirl, Alfred — must fit into the mission, as his Hush confession to Catwoman ('I am not very good at this. Having friends.') shows. Aristotle's remark that the good man is a friend to himself lets the chapter cast Bruce and Batman as 'one soul in two personae,' the only virtue friendship left to him. It closes as a cautionary tale: a life of mission can cost the balance — and the friendship — that a good and happy life requires.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Devin Brown uses Eustace, who dodges work on Dragon Island until he wakes as a dragon and discovers he would rather be hungry among human friends than comfortable alone, to contrast Epicurean hedonism and Tom Sawyer's work-avoidance with Mill's higher pleasures and the 'Sherlock Holmes philosophy of work.' Weighing Aristotle's contemplative life against Lewis's love of quests, he reads Father Christmas's tailored gifts and 'everyone must do what he can do best' as an Acorn Philosophy of Vocation with a Marxian 'from each according to his ability' echo, condemns wrong livelihoods like Governor Gumpas's slave trade, and closes on leisure and Aristotle's golden mean, which Lewis turns into 'golden extremes.'

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: “Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics: the survivors' mall orgy curdles into boredom ('What have we done to ourselves?'), illustrating pleonexia, the graspingness for more than one's share of the goods of fortune that Aristotle roots in an unlimited desire for mere living - which may even explain why Romero's dead return, grasping from beyond the grave for more un-death. Aristotle's dismissal of the life of enjoyment as fit for cattle, his account of eudaimonia as the life in which our rational capacities flourish, and his defense of acquisition bounded by the good life explain why unlimited consumption zombifies the living, and why Peter and Fran must finally leave the mall empty-handed.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Bullshit Around the Globe
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Building on Peter Goldie's account of how life-narratives shape emotion, and Martha Nussbaum's view of emotions as judgments of value and importance (which the chapter identifies with the Greek Stoic view), it explains where bullshit gets its power over us. Because an episode's place in a narrative determines what we feel — Oedipus could be delighted to have married Jocasta but not his mother — bullshit works by 'educating' our emotions, telling us what should make us proud, patriotic, angry or frightened, and what belongs in a eudaimonistic life. It closes by warning that bullshit appeals to the base and non-rational part of us and so degrades us, before turning to examples from international politics.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: House and the Life of Reason
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Why Be Moral
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Sanders uses Bruno Anthony's 'criss-cross' murder-swap proposal to Guy Haines in Strangers on a Train to pose the classic question 'Why be moral?' to the charming amoralist. He tests three answers: Kant's categorical imperative fails because Bruno's egoist maxim ('remove obstacles to your happiness') can apparently be universalized; Hobbesian contractarian 'morality pays' fails because Bruno free-rides on others' restraint; and the Rachels/Nelson/Thomas psychological-health answer assumes rather than proves that Bruno should care about comparable suffering. A thought experiment comparing the moral life with the Bruno-state from an impartial standpoint leads to Aristotle's eudaimonia: morality is constitutive of human flourishing, so Bruno enjoys only a counterfeit happiness.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Tough and Tender, The Dead Keep Truckin’
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Gary Ciocco traces a line from Emerson and James through Kerouac, Ginsberg, and Neal Cassady to the Grateful Dead: Emerson's nonconformist 'infinitude of man' and James's 'live options' and religious appetite for being 'more fully alive' become, in the Beats, the project of living life itself as art ('the only people for me are the mad ones'). He argues the Beats splintered because each chased an atomistic, individual epiphany — Kerouac swinging wholesale from tender- to tough-minded temperament — while the Dead turned the same Jamesian hunger into a shared communal religious experience, a 'kindler, gentler' scene that better achieves Aristotle's eudaimonia. Cassady, muse of On the Road and driver of the Pranksters' bus, literally connects the two movements, but the Dead's unity-in-diversity made them the evolution, not the echo, of the Beats.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: A Happy Ending
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Bickham asks why Dorothy is so eager to leave heroic, Technicolor Oz for the gray, childless, Gulch-dominated farm, and whether, like Hamlet's delay, her rash choice can be evaluated as hers rather than her author's. Aristotle's account of the good life as the exercise of our highest capacities, requiring friends and material goods, makes Oz look like the better home for the competent twelve- or thirteen-year-old he takes Dorothy to be, against the hedonisms of Aristippus, Epicurus, and Bentham and Plato's body-denying dualism. But caring about Dorothy first needs defending from the paradox of fiction, which he works through Currie's simulation theory and Walton's make-believe emotions before dissolving the puzzle: storytelling suspends the reign of logic, so wishing Dorothy well is natural. Finally Heidegger's being-toward-death shows 'happily ever after' is impossible anywhere, and he throws the problem to the reader: write a happy ending for Dorothy in Kansas.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Lott takes up Augustine's puzzle about why we enjoy watching sufferings we would flee, and answers for Radiohead with Aristotle's theory of tragedy: songs like 'Karma Police', 'Exit Music', and 'Fake Plastic Trees' sketch fragmentary characters in breakdown whose undeserved yet partly self-inflicted sufferings — 'Just'''s 'you do it to yourself' is hamartia — evoke pity and fear and then catharsis. Singing along makes identification uniquely intense in pop ('for a minute there, I lost myself' blurs the listener into the character), while music's 'natural sweetness' and its dynamics of build, climax, and release carry the purgation, from the terror of 'Climbing Up the Walls' to the slow ache of 'Videotape'. Because tragedy, unlike history, deals in universals, songs like 'The Bends' and 'High and Dry' open onto reflection on happiness, vulnerability, and the culture that fosters isolation, ending in the thin but real community of listeners who recognize their shared fragility.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Transformers and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Plauche grounds Optimus Prime's line 'Freedom is the right of all sentient beings' in 'Aristotelian liberalism': since Energon, like our food, is scarce and requires labor and creativity, any volitional artificial life needs a moral code whose standard is flourishing (following Foot's natural goodness), cultivating intellectual and moral virtues from prudence, independence, and honesty to benevolence and courage. Ricardo and Mises's law of association - illustrated by Ratchet and a human mechanic both profiting from specialization despite Ratchet's absolute superiority - plus the ruinous cost of war give even superior aliens reason to respect our rights to life, liberty, and property rather than enslave or exterminate us, as Megatron would.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Aftermath of Tragedy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Argues that Grave of the Fireflies works as a critique of anime's child-hero convention: Seita acts exactly like a plucky anime protagonist when he defies his not-actually-evil aunt, strikes out on his own with Setsuko, ignores the farmer's advice to apologize and return, and demands a quick fix from the doctor — but these 'heroic' choices kill them both, because he lacks the developed capacity to reason. Against the medieval 'child as little adult' picture that most anime (Dragon Ball, Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!) romanticizes, the chapter deploys Aristotle's view of children as unfinished beings who cannot yet reason or achieve happiness, concluding the film is a cautionary tale about the years of nurture and guidance real children need.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Equivalent Exchange
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Reads alchemy's law of equivalent exchange as a parable of capitalism: Locke's labor-mixing argument explains how hours of a life become property and why money is 'distilled life'; Aristotle's attack on limitless wealth-getting (the Midas problem) and Aquinas's capital vices explain how pursuing money for its own sake brings the homunculi — Greed, Pride, and the Sloth the Elric brothers' forbidden act produced — into the world. Marx's 1844 Manuscripts supply the punchline that money performs 'human alchemy' on people, buying their time, esteem, and bodies the way red stones are made from sacrificed humans, so the chapter concludes that capital, like the Philosopher's Stone, profits only by consuming lives and that markets must be held to a promise of fairness and care beyond mere exchange.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: “Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead's survivors, who loot the mall, gorge, grow bored, and degenerate into glitzy despair beside the zombies clawing to get back in, through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. Peter's 'They're us' is glossed by pleonexia, the grasping disposition to want more, which Aristotle roots in being serious about mere living rather than living well, and the quartet's hedonistic 'sweet life' is the life of enjoyment Aristotle dismisses as fit for cattle because it atrophies the rational capacities that make us human. Romero is no Puritan scold: material goods remain instrumentally useful and the mall a sanctuary, but like Aristotle he shows a life of unlimited acquisition is a kind of living death, which is why Peter and Fran must leave empty-handed.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Final Whistle
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The End of the Story
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Reads the Gom Jabbar test as Herbert's definition of humanity: Paul endures Mohiam's pain box because a human stays in the trap to turn it on the trapper and protect the species, while an animal only chews off its own leg. The Butlerian Jihad's ban on 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' is applied to our own iPod-and-PDA dependence, with Mentat Thufir Hawat showing that losing the machine-crutch 'forced human minds to develop,' in line with Aristotle's phronesis and the politics of the common good (and Plato's contemplation as the core of happiness). The chapter closes by turning the human/animal test on the modern West—Baron Harkonnen-like consumers whose water-hungry beef habit makes us the trap of our own environmental collapse.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Why Is It the Best Day Ever
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Flanders reads Killing Yourself to Live as asking whether dying can be good for the person who dies: Jeff Buckley's 'Hallelujah' and Kurt Cobain's myth became deeper and more successful only after the fact, as if death were a career move. He answers with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where the fortunes of descendants can affect the happiness of the dead: our life-stories outlive their authors, so fans' posthumous devotion can really benefit Buckley, though no posthumous fame can add virtue that was never lived (Michael Jackson's rehabilitation cannot touch how he actually lived). Klosterman's road trip ultimately undercuts the question: the earnest Great White concert mourners remember what truly was there, while Cobain's fans retroactively invent meaning to gain 'credibility by mourning retrospectively', so worshipping the rock dead manufactures an inauthentic afterlife, and Klosterman must kill the unserious fan in himself to live.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Fitzpatrick asks whether Klosterman's low-culture project (tribute bands, Toby Keith, the McNuggets diet) is mere titillation or genuinely valuable. Bentham's pushpin-versus-poetry hedonism matches Klosterman's rejection of 'guilty pleasures,' while Aristotle's eudaimonia — and Plato's forms, on which a tribute band is a copy of a copy of a copy — condemns a life of amusement. Mill resolves the question twice over: higher and lower pleasures justify ranking Klosterman's contemplative criticism above mere sensation, and On Liberty's free market of ideas shows that even false or partial low-culture claims (about Garth Brooks, Spurlock's Super Size Me) keep high culture's truths from decaying into unexamined dogma.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Littmann answers the charge that D&D is a waste of time with Aristotle: pleasure is good as an end in itself, humanity's function is thinking, so even munchkin power-gaming and 4E combat roles are worthwhile intellectual activity under the function argument. He then treats D&D as participatory art—improvisational storytelling offering catharsis (smacking goblins to purge aggression) and the Poetics' license to explore what could be, like the dwarf chieftain grieving a disintegrated son or deciding what a friend owes the thief in the scorpion nest. A good DM, on this Aristotelian view, makes plots unfold with internal probability and characters act from consistent personality, yet 'just playing my character' never excuses ruining another player's fun, since artistic value never suspends the virtues governing how we treat people.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Classicist and Jeopardy! champion Daniel Melia reads the show as a mirror of American exceptionalism, contrasting it with European hits like Big Brother: Jeopardy! is pure individual contest rewarding a faith in classless meritocracy, its Daily Doubles and come-from-behind Final Jeopardy! wagers enact the American belief in redemption and self-reinvention, and its buzzer timing and Before-and-After clues test frontier virtues of physical reflex and improvisation. He argues that its middlebrow categories (Magritte, Sibelius, Paul Revere) preserve shared American cultural capital, and that the show's free-flowing, low-context, information-sharing format answers the question 'What does it mean to be an American, Alex?' and indexes what Americans count as living the good life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Five-time champion Matt Kohlstedt argues that winning Jeopardy! reflects gamesmanship and a love of learning rather than education itself, and warns against the 'Jeopardy!-ization' of schooling: high-stakes testing makes teachers assembly-line trainers and students regurgitators, and produces the on-air 'Jeopardy! effect' of choking under pressure that made him flub the number of articles in the Constitution. Drawing on his late grandfather's book on teacher education and Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs and peak experiences, he defends a philosophy of education aimed at self-actualized teachers who, like Alex Trebek's mid-round contestant interviews, treat students as whole human beings rather than test statistics.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Wire and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Prof Joe's introduction casts The Wire, like Socrates, as a gadfly that refuses to let any viewer rest comfortably: tough-on-crime conservatives, Hamsterdam-friendly libertarians, hopeful liberals watching Royce and Carcetti, techno-optimists watching Freamon's wire, and capitalists watching the docks and the Baltimore Sun all get their beliefs challenged with no easy answers. It retells Socrates's refusal to escape Athens as valuing the quality of life over its quantity, and sets that against the Puritan work-ethic myth that blames the corner boys and fiends for their own fate while Aristotle's flourishing is rebranded as the American pursuit of happiness. The essay closes by previewing the book's six 'Cases' (the Game, tactics, Omar, boundaries, tragedy, sentencing) around Socrates's own question: how ought we to live?

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Wire and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Trerise argues Omar is virtuous in Aristotle's full sense: honest on the stand ('I robs drug dealers... I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), courageous, consistent, and generous, with even his vengefulness a mean between extremes given a world where no one else will check Avon or Marlo - unlike Marlo he never guns on citizens and even pays Prop Joe for clock repairs. Virtue theory's attention to context separates his killings of Stinkum, Savino, and Stringer from Marlo's power-consolidating murders and shows him achieving whatever eudaimonia his world allows, though his obsession after Stringer's setup, which got Tosha killed, marks his one real excess. The catch is exemplification - Omar is disturbed that children play at being Omar, and Michael becomes the new him - yet the chapter concludes that some vigilantism is a social necessity on the streets and that Omar's swapped body tag names the injustice done to the street's truly virtuous.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Psych and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jennifer Swanson asks whether Alicia can 'have it all', starting from Aristotle: Peter fails the moral virtues (faithfulness, honesty, courage), Jackie's intrusive moments undermine her kindness since Aristotle's unity of the virtues ties them together, and Eli Gold's perfect frankness leaves no room for perfect tact. Following Michael Slote's partial values and impossibility of perfection, she argues career and family are paired values in which gaining one loses the other, as Alicia discovers being pulled between Molly the nanny, Cary's 'she'll have something to fall back on', Diane's partner-track warning, and dumping Will after Grace's twelve butt-dials in 'Parenting Made Easy'. Since perfection is impossible in principle, the answer is balance across all the values of a good life, not Caitlin's retreat into 'I just want to be a mom'.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: John Fitzpatrick asks whether voters should care that Alicia stands beside Peter, from the Season One resignation press conference to the finale's withheld hand. After a rapid tour of right-action theories grounded in the show - Eli Gold's egoism, Peter's 'pitted' evidence tip as consequentialism, Alicia keeping Jonas Stern's dementia secret as deontology, the Florrick-Childs no-children pact as social contract - he turns to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia as a life weaving pleasure, friendship, and practical activity, in which mentors like Will and Diane let us contemplate virtue in others and improve our own character. His conclusion: Alicia's endorsement matters not because she is a good wife but because she is a good person whose judgment reveals Peter's character.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: The chapter argues HIMYM offers two complementary feminist icons: Robin embodies personal autonomy and independence - fighting from 'but, um' early-morning shifts to lead anchor, and grieving infertility as stolen autonomy rather than lost motherhood - while Lily, and even more Marshall, exemplify Carol Gilligan's feminist care ethics with its emphasis on emotion over impartiality, cooperation over competition, and partiality toward loved ones. Aristotle's golden mean supplies the test Robin passes by balancing career and love instead of pushing one to an extreme. The twist that a male character best exemplifies care ethics, with Lily bridging the two moral outlooks, is offered as the show's progressive complexity about gender.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Framed as a sports broadcast with Aristotle as commentator, the chapter tests an evolutionary ethics ('BEES': the good is the naturally desirable, so the Pleistocene Stinson strategy of spreading genes grounds Barney's womanizing) against its classic critics. Hume's is-ought gap and Moore's open question argument are deployed against deriving Barney's right to pursue tail from human nature, while William Casebeer's evolutionary ethics replies that 'good' can be defined by present reproductive success - under which lying and eternal bachelorhood fail, since commitment is what reproduces genomes in urban New York ('BIRDS'). The chapter concludes that evolutionary ethics can support the Bro Code only by contestable redefinition, and the lying objection stands.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: The chapter argues Finn is not yet a true hero but is on a quest to become one: against rule systems like Mill's greatest-happiness utilitarianism and Kantian respect for persons, virtue ethics asks not 'what should I do' but 'who should I be', and Aristotle's point that children lack fully developed practical reason explains why Finn's good intentions misfire - removing Donny exposes the house people to Why-wolves, and Penny's trick humiliates him in the City of Thieves. Martha Nussbaum's ideal of every person as free and of equal dignity grounds heroism in the common good, and her work on literature and popular culture explains how watching Finn's exaggerated choices trains our own moral judgment. Citing Franco and Zimbardo's psychology of real heroes - empathy, risk tolerance, persistence - and closing with Seneca's 'how nobly you live', it concludes that since Aristotelian virtue is a habit, anyone can start by admitting they suck at heroism and practicing, as Jake's advice puts it.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Thomas asks whether the Apple II, Macintosh, and iPod were great products regardless of sales or great because they sold, and answers that market success is real evidence of value: each sale is a buyer's revealed preference in a voluntary trade, a stronger test than critics or focus groups, which is why Jobs's flops (NeXT, the G4 Cube) were overdesigned, overpriced failures of utility rather than quality. Against Hume's quoted doctrine that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions (hunger strikers and Jobs's own vegan fanaticism defeat any basic-desire theory), he follows Rand and Philippa Foot in grounding value in objective human needs and capacities, so products designed for those needs—like the iPhone the Apple team built for themselves—could be expected to succeed.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Dracula and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Kyle Alkema and Adam Barkman ask what would make the Gang happy and answer with Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness is long-run flourishing built on virtuous habits, with the golden mean (courage between cowardice and recklessness) as the rule for choice. The Gang instead lives a 'Reverse Virtue Ethic' - trying extremes first by crude trial and error, like sniffing gasoline to check that it is gasoline - along three roads: quick money (welfare crack scams, robbing their own parents' house), lust (the D.E.N.N.I.S. System's seduce-and-abandon script, where Dennis cheerfully accepts the charge of sociopathy), and validation ('You're not gay, you're just really, really vain'). Their residual Catholicism supplies consciences and limits - Mac's talk of God smiting them, confession, fears of Hell - but no reasoned morality, leaving them trapped in 'one day at a time' gratification as reverse role models.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
