He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: It’s Not Personal . . . It’s Just Bizzyneuss Business Ethics, the Company, and Its Stakeholders
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Pierlott frames the shareholder-versus-stakeholder debate (Friedman versus Freeman) using Aristotle's function argument to ask what makes a 'good' company, then judges business relationships by Kant's humanity formula. McBean's manipulation of the Sneetches and the digital-TV cases show consumers used merely as means; McGurk's cavalier overworking of Sneelock in If I Ran the Circus and Maitland's sweatshop defense are answered with Marx's account of labor exploitation and Aristotle's voluntary-versus-mixed actions; the Once-ler's Lorax devastation shows firms externalizing environmental costs when profit is maximized at any value unprotected by law.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Introduction
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence. Manninen then presses Aristotle: his strict 'only good men' criterion and his debt-bound, property-like view of the parent-child bond fail the flawed-but-loyal Andy/Red and the abusive fathers in The Body, showing human friendship is more complex than his taxonomy allows.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Marinucci's editorial introduction surveys the volume, framing Austen's six novels as a body of work with philosophical value across love/marriage, morality/virtue, wealth/class, concepts, and zombie mashups. It previews each contributor's thesis: Bufacchi reading Anne Elliot and the Bennets through Fricker's epistemic injustice, Dougherty aligning Austen's ideal marriage with Aristotelian complete friendship, Lindenmuth pairing Austen with Nietzsche on marital happiness, and Bane's Marxist reading of the 1940 Pride and Prejudice film. It argues Austen is an 'accidental philosopher' whose insight into social relations, especially women's vulnerability, carries philosophical weight.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Lindenmuth pairs Austen with Nietzsche on what makes a happy marriage, reading Pride and Prejudice's clashes over Lizzy's refusals of Mr. Collins and Darcy, and Lady Catherine's and Sir Thomas Bertram's aristocratic insistence that superiors should choose for inferiors. He uses Nietzsche's 'philosophizing with a hammer' to cast Austen as smashing the dead traditions of entailment and arranged marriage, and Nietzsche's aphorisms (a good marriage rests on a talent for friendship and good conversation; sensuality makes love grow too fast) to judge the couples, concluding Austen holds an Aristotelian, objective view of happiness as a reward for getting life right rather than mere desire-satisfaction.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Potzsch reads Emma as an Aristotelian study of eudaimonia, arguing Emma's self-deception and the flattery of those around her block her from true happiness, which for Aristotle is activity of the soul in accordance with reason and virtue. She diagnoses Emma's cruelty to Miss Bates at Box Hill as Aristotelian akrasia (moral weakness): Emma knows better but is overpowered by the desire to shine, showing virtue has not yet become her second nature. She contrasts Emma and Mrs. Elton's pursuit of honor (which Aristotle deems superficial, illustrated via Plato's Euthyphro) with Knightley's genuine virtue, and closes on Aristotle's ranking of the contemplative over the political life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 268 - Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Chapter 2
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Verene interprets Plutarch's Dinner of the Seven Wise Men, in which Thales, Solon, Bias and the others gather at Corinth under Periander and turn a plain dinner into a symposium on good government, household economics, and the soul. He reads their exchanges through Aristotle: Thales' claim that a ruler's happiness is to die naturally in old age is glossed by Aristotle's eudaimonia (no one is called happy until life is complete), the assigned-seating companions exemplify Aristotle's friendship of utility, and the pivot from politics to home management mirrors Aristotle linking Politics to Economics. Solon's Stoic argument that dependence on food enslaves the soul, and Thales' correction of the Ethiopian king's riddle-answers (virtue not God as most helpful), show the Seven speaking as philosophers rather than gourmets, with Epicurus invoked on death being nothing to the living.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: MOTHERHOOD
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Nin Kirkham applies neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to define the 'virtues of motherhood' as character dispositions that let a mother flourish (achieve eudaimonia) qua mother. She elaborates three virtues – endurance (commitment, selflessness, and long-view 'vision,' likened to endurance running), liberality (knowing when to let a child go), and moral exemplarity – each analyzed as an Aristotelian mean between vices of excess and deficit, and argues good mothering is learned by example and does not license judging other mothers against one's own ideal.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Crista Lebens narrates a C-Scow sail on an inland lake — preparing the boat, casting off, coming about, capsizing, returning to the pier — as a journey toward Aristotelian eudaimonia (human flourishing). She argues sailing demands phronesis (practical wisdom) as body-knowledge, that coming about requires the Greek 'middle path' between being 'in irons' and capsizing, and that competence 'cannot be faked' so sailing forces one to live 'in truth' (via Werth's and Kierkegaard's account of the crowd 'in untruth'). Using Borgmann's device/thing distinction, she casts the sailboat as a 'thing' that calls forth skilled engagement, unlike the powerboat as a 'device' of consumption, and links truth to the beauty of a well-trimmed sail.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jesse Steinberg and Michael Stuckart distinguish instrumental from intrinsic value (using Frankena's list) across sailing's gear, knowledge, and aesthetics, then argue via Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that sailing is a route to eudaimonia through the cultivation of virtue. They show sailing exemplifies courage as the golden mean between cowardice and foolhardiness (deciding whether to go out in twenty-knot winds, judging teen solo circumnavigators), being hard-working (the mean between laziness and workaholism), and cleverness (jury-rigging, navigation). They contend sailing demands a broader, deeper range of virtues than golf, bowling, or power-boating, making it an especially rich — though not the only — path to a flourishing, happy life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Sadler argues black coffee, unlike ceremonial tea, is the realist emblem of our anxious, isolated postmodern condition, and that the chain coffeehouse is a 'non-place' of public anonymity that only simulates the sociality we crave. Against Aristotle's confident view of humans as social animals whose eudaimonia presupposes a settled social order, she sets Nietzsche's alienated individual free to create values — then argues Nietzsche errs: using the trivial cappuccino-vs-latte choice, she shows (via Wittgenstein's private-language argument and Korsgaard) that even solitary choices need reasons intelligible to others, so individual choice cannot be self-justifying and our search for meaningful, non-arbitrary lives is irreducibly social.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Keleher applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to coffee, arguing that eudaimonia (flourishing, not mere pleasant feeling) is rational activity in accordance with virtue, that the human ergon is reason, and that money, pleasure, and honor are only instrumental to it. She illustrates the golden mean and phronêsis with coffee choices—the temperate drinker like Katherine or Samantha calibrates cups to her own tolerance and circumstances rather than a fixed number—and distinguishes the truly virtuous drinker from the merely continent one who still craves the forbidden 750-calorie frappuccino. She coins the minor virtue of 'javavity,' the habit of drinking good coffee the right way for the right reasons with the right feeling, and suggests that were Aristotle alive, coffee would join his 'external goods,' the proper equipment for doing noble acts.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Opening with his intimate encounter with a wolf, Vitali argues that 'fair chase' cannot mean fairness to the animal — since a right to fair chase would imply a more basic right not to be hunted, conceding the anti-hunting case. Instead, invoking Aristotelian human flourishing and Leopold's land ethic, he relocates fair chase to the hunter: hunting is moral only if it serves the biotic community through conservation and lets the hunter enter the predator-prey life-death continuum. He illustrates self-handicapping through master hunter Milo Burcham stalking a distant muley with a recurve bow.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Haire and Nelson read the film A Christmas Story as evidence that consumerism has replaced religion as America's faith: the Parker family shows no religious markers, and Ralphie's single-minded quest for the Red Ryder BB gun mirrors the identity-defining, transformative role religion once played. Using Aristotle's virtue ethics, they name consumerism a Christmas vice opposed to candidate Christmas virtues of being religious, traditional and family-centered. When the BB gun nearly blinds Ralphie and the hounds ruin the turkey, the consumerist ideal fails; the family's makeshift Chinese-restaurant dinner shows the family-centered virtue overcoming the vice, so 'all was right with the world'.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: CYCLING
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: O'Brien's editorial introduction frames gardening as engaging core philosophical questions and previews the volume. It argues that gardening promotes a good life not through hedonistic pleasure but through virtuous traits like patience and a Stoic-tinged tranquility that ancient philosophers from Epicurus to Hume prized, and it invokes Kant to cast the gardener as a visual artist. It also sketches gardens as cosmic symbols (Pythagorean ratios at Versailles) and closes on Plato's Phaedrus image of educating the soul as tending plants.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: GARDENING
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Isis Brook argues that gardening objectively improves both the land (through composting, nurturing plants, and Warwick Fox's 'responsive cohesion' with wider contexts) and the gardener's moral character. Taking a virtue-ethics approach and drawing on David Cooper, she holds that gardening practices incidentally cultivate patience, humility, recognition of reality, care for others, and open-heartedness. She uses concrete cases—Sackville-West's white garden at Sissinghurst, her own failed Cerinthe and thriving ferns—to show how collaborating with nature nurtures these flourishing-related virtues.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Schick asks whether humans need to alter consciousness (Weil, Maslow's hierarchy, Siegel's animal examples of reindeer, elephants, and rats seeking intoxicants) and concludes we have no such need, though we can flourish from it. He applies Sen and Nussbaum's capabilities approach, arguing cannabis enhances Nussbaum's second (bodily health, via endocannabinoids and medical uses) and fourth (senses, imagination, thought, via enriched music perception and possible creativity) capabilities. Citing Aristotle's and the Buddha's golden mean against abuse, and evidence of no lasting brain harm, he judges paternalistic prohibition an unjustified deprivation of the capabilities needed for a good life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Brian Treanor argues from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that climbing is a crucible for cultivating virtues (arete) that contribute to flourishing (eudaimonia), stressing that virtue is acquired by habituation and lies in a mean 'relative to us'—so casting off on the Bachar-Yerian is courage for a 5.11 leader but rashness for a 5.9 climber. He shows how climbing's self-imposed 'rules' (Tejada-Flores' games) forge courage (feeling the right balance of fear and confidence, as in John Sherman's Fisher Towers epic and Steve House's judicious retreats on K7), humility (honestly measuring oneself against pioneers who used inferior gear, per Chouinard and Messner's 'murder of the impossible'), and reverence for nature (Thoreau, Muir, Brower). His thesis is that in a coddled, technological world climbing is uncommonly well suited to building these excellences of character.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Ethics professor Paul MacNeill argues ethics is intrinsic to yoga and knowable only through practice, not by mining texts — a Western reason-first bias that trivializes it. He shows the yamas and niyamas are counter-measures aimed at samadhi (paralleling how Aristotle's virtues aim at eudaimonia, though yoga subordinates reason), and that Vedanta's transcendent and Kashmir Shaivism's immanent metaphysics both function as instruments toward expanded awareness. From that dissolution of the separate self, he claims, compassion flows naturally, so Hatha yoga's asana and pranayama dissolve the ingrained bodily/mental habits that block ethical, equilibrium-born action.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: BLUES
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Roopen Majithia asks why a music born of African-American suffering became universally beloved and answers with Aristotle's account of musical catharsis in the Politics. Drawing on the Nicomachean Ethics link between habituated action, emotion, and disposition (as courage is built by acting courageously), he argues music images real emotions and thereby purges excess feeling. Modern electric urban blues (T-Bone Walker's 'Stormy Monday,' Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf), with its danceable, sexually charged rhythm, recreates the emotional landscape of repetitive urban work and, aided by dancing, effects a broad catharsis — which also explains why non-black communal performers can play it and why intimate bars beat arenas.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Joshua Heter mounts a virtue-theoretic case against being set up on blind dates, using Aristotle's notion of telos and the distinction between fleeting 'hot-fudge happiness' and eudaimonia, the flourishing of a well-lived life (illustrated by long-married Bill and Fran). He argues a 'guy's' function is achieved by exercising his whole nature, and dramatizes this with Zoo-bear versus Wild-bear: the zoo-fed bear has its hunger and safety met but cannot flourish because it never hunts or roams, just as matchmaking meets the romantic need while letting a man's 'social muscles' atrophy. Invoking Aristotle's philia (and Nussbaum on Aristotelian virtue), he concedes friends mean well but recommends they merely introduce people and let things progress naturally rather than force an 'unnatural' match.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Gregory Bassham mines the happy communities of the Shire, Rivendell, and Lothlorien for six keys to happiness: delight in simple things (linked to Epicurus's natural pleasures and Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles, close friendship (grounded in Aristotle's claim that friendship is the greatest external good), good character, cherishing beauty and creativity, and recovering wonder. He argues Tolkien's hobbits and elves illustrate what modern happiness research confirms, so Tolkien functions as a philosophical guide to a more joy-filled life.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum, two hobbits of shared nature and culture who both pursue happiness but reach opposite ends. Gollum's happiness is possession of the Precious, a thing, sought in isolation and won by murdering Deagol, which destroys him; Sam's happiness is fellowship in the Shire with Frodo and Rosie, and his love for Frodo lets him surrender the Ring where Gollum cannot. Drawing on Aristotle's tie between happiness, one's nature, and friendship, Gracia concludes that for ordinary beings happiness is achievable only in a social context whose key is love expressed as loyalty and sharing.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Sean McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, 'the slave of his sense of humor,' who jests inappropriately; Gareth is the boorish literalist who cannot take or get a joke; Tim is the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to the situation, exercising practical wisdom (phronesis). McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: House and the Life of Reason
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: 25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: 84. The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild as Philosophy Teaching the Player to Be Comfortable Being Alone
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Lay argues that Breath of the Wild teaches, chiefly through design rather than plot, that solitude is good for the player. He tests eternal return (the recurring Ganon-Zelda-Link cycle across the series), Sartrean absolute freedom and Kierkegaardian anxiety of choice (BotW's Korok-dung 'reward' and refusal to attach external meaning push players to make their own meaning), and Kierkegaard's inward 'repetition.' He lands on Mill's and Schopenhauer's defense of solitude-in-nature as self-actualizing rather than isolating, and reads sequence-breaking exploits as Marx-style spontaneous creative activity, concluding the game frames solitude as a path to eudaimonia and human flourishing.

aristotle-eudaimonia.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-eudaimonia.title: 95. The Walking Dead as Philosophy Rick Grimes and Community Building in an Apocalypse
aristotle-eudaimonia.relation: Jones argues that Kirkman's The Walking Dead uses Rick Grimes's community-building to probe utopia and dystopia, reading the prison, Alexandria, Woodbury, the Saviors, and the Commonwealth through Aristotle's six constitutional forms—with the polity (rule by many for the common good enabling eudaimonia) as the standard for a good society and tyranny/oligarchy/corrupt forms marking dystopias like Negan's compound and the class-tyrannical Commonwealth. Invoking More's and Mill's coinages of utopia and dystopia, the chapter asks why Rick's final society, despite his moral evolution, ends up rebuilding the hierarchical pre-apocalyptic order rather than the more egalitarian, flourishing alliance he had forged.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
aristotle-golden-mean.title: George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Elaine, Kramer, and Newman Not Wise
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Aeon Skoble argues Seinfeld explicates Aristotelian virtue ethics against utilitarian and Kantian rivals: Jerry's 'I don't want to be an orgy guy' and George's fear of becoming 'one of those guys' ask what sort of person to be, not which rule to follow. George's 'do the opposite' in 'The Opposite' is an update of the Delphic oracle - only he who recognizes his own idiocy (Socratic ignorance) can act well, with Jerry deducing the logic and serving as his phronemos, alongside Superman. Elaine's rule-worship and Jujyfruits utilitarianism backfire, Kramer lacks the social dialectic virtue needs, and the ironic appeals to Newman as arbiter expose the paradox that choosing a role model wisely already requires the wisdom one lacks.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 4 - Marge’s Moral Motivation
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Gerald Erion and Joseph Zeccardi present Marge as an everyday Aristotelian whose bravery (The Springfield Connection, escaping the Movementarian commune), temperance, and generosity each hit the mean between Springfield's vicious extremes, and whose eudaimonia is achieved through the good of her family. They contrast her reason-driven conscience with Ned Flanders's divine command theory—consulting Reverend Lovejoy over whether to play capture-the-flag on the sabbath—and side with Marge, invoking Plato's Euthyphro to argue that morality cannot simply be a function of God's commands. Marge emerges as a 'Christian-flavored Aristotelian' who cultivates virtue by habituation and models it for Lisa and Bart.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Aeon Skoble uses Tolkien's characters to defend Aristotelian virtue ethics against Kantian and utilitarian rivals. Sam's loyalty is a virtue because critically directed at a worthy friend while Wormtongue's loyalty to Saruman is not; Sméagol's instant murder of Déagol reveals prior vice that let the Ring corrupt him quickly, whereas Bilbo resists it for sixty years; Aragorn's temperance and teachableness contrast Boromir's resentment and pride. Working through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (courage between cowardice and rashness), practical wisdom, and the phronemos as role model, he argues that rule-following cannot capture moral perception (do we owe truth to Black Riders?) and that utilitarianism absurdly requires Galadriel's foresight.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Jedi Model
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Daredevil’s Faith as a Source of Strength
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Testing whether Daredevil's fearlessness is really the vice of rashness, Morris invokes Aristotle's doctrine that every virtue is a mean between two vices, with courage between cowardice and foolhardiness - but since fear is not the only brake on recklessness, prudence can do that work instead, as when Matt calmly backs down from Iron Man's federal authority in Born Again. He concludes that the religious values Matt absorbed - love of neighbor, respect for truth, concern for justice - supply exactly the guidance prudence needs, making faith a distinct form of spiritual strength.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Devin Brown uses Eustace, who dodges work on Dragon Island until he wakes as a dragon and discovers he would rather be hungry among human friends than comfortable alone, to contrast Epicurean hedonism and Tom Sawyer's work-avoidance with Mill's higher pleasures and the 'Sherlock Holmes philosophy of work.' Weighing Aristotle's contemplative life against Lewis's love of quests, he reads Father Christmas's tailored gifts and 'everyone must do what he can do best' as an Acorn Philosophy of Vocation with a Marxian 'from each according to his ability' echo, condemns wrong livelihoods like Governor Gumpas's slave trade, and closes on leisure and Aristotle's golden mean, which Lewis turns into 'golden extremes.'

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
aristotle-golden-mean.title: U2 and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Delancey asks why anyone should take moral and political cues from a rock band and answers via Heidegger: in a mediascape where a few corporations orchestrate what everyone hears, the mass tune is das Man ('Numb'), and adopting it is inauthenticity - so U2, who believe what they sing for their own reasons ('Mothers of the Disappeared' against the official line on Latin America), may be among the most authentic voices available. Plato's tripartite soul and Aristotle's golden mean supply the thesis that reason needs rightly trained passion: the righteous anger of 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Silver and Gold' and the resolve of 'Walk On' are practical wisdom in song, the emotions democracy requires. Against Plato's philosopher-king and his noble lies, Delancey argues utopia can only be fostered, not enforced - so in a democracy, if you want to change the world, you may have to sing to people.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
aristotle-golden-mean.title: James Bond and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Arp and Decker examine Bond's objectification of women - using a dancing girl as a human shield in the Goldfinger pre-credits sequence, M ordering Bond to 'pump her for information' - through three moral theories. Kant's humanity formula condemns treating women as sexual tools, but Kantian autonomy generates a stalemate since consensual, reciprocal liaisons like Bond and Anya Amasova's might qualify as permissible; Millian utilitarianism condemns the male gaze by its long-term social costs yet stalls against pro-sex feminist counterarguments. They settle on Aristotelian virtue ethics - the mean between extremes, with respect as the key virtue against the power-centered virtue of Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Nietzsche - to argue objectification is vicious, and they trace Bond's moral progress from skipping the young Bibi in For Your Eyes Only to the reciprocal relationships with Kara Milovy, Pam Bouvier, Wai Lin, and Jinx.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Virtues of Superhumans
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
aristotle-golden-mean.title: “Unchained” The Inspired Anger of a Religious Man
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Dan Haggerty uses Aristotle's account of anger as a virtuous mean—felt at the right people, time, and degree—to show that songs like 'San Quentin,' 'The Man in Black,' and 'Oney' express justified anger at real injustices done to prisoners and workingmen, contra pop psychology's blanket rejection of anger. He then coins 'inspired anger' (drawing on Plato's Ion: the artist possessed and blown away by emotion): a painful, hopeless desire for a justice or restoration that can never be, exemplified by Cash's 'Hurt' video and its regret over irrecoverable time—mourning rather than self-pity or depression. The chapter closes with 'Unchained' as a prayer showing how a Christian like Cash can live with this futile desire rather than argue it away.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Becoming One
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: The chapter reads Baltar's Head-Six (and Caprica Six's Head-Baltar) through the gothic Double and Doppelgänger tradition, re-imagined via dissociative identity disorder: Baltar splits off his guilt over the genocide into a female doppelgänger who lets him evade responsibility, as in 'Precipice' where he finds the execution order signed without any memory of signing it. It then links this doubling to Plato's Symposium myth of lovers as split halves seeking their other half, since Baltar cannot function without some version of Six. Its resolution is Aristotle's golden mean: virtue is not choosing one self over another but balancing extremes, for individuals and for humanity and its Double, the Cylons — with Hera as the embodied balance.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
aristotle-golden-mean.title: “All Good Things Must Come to an End”
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Horn argues the three Triforce pieces are morally neutral: by Kant's Groundwork, only the good will that acts from duty (Link never rescues Zelda for a reward) is good without qualification, so courage, wisdom, and power can each serve evil, and the Triforce would have corrupted Zelda or Link too if fortune had dealt it otherwise. Plato's Ring of Gyges and the Glaucon-Socrates debate explain Ganondorf: he chose to lust for power, and his wealth, status, and fear-based honor are hollow because justice is good for its own sake and his soul is out of balance (which is why the Triforce split at his touch in Ocarina of Time). Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then defines proper use: Link's courage between cowardice and rashness (getting the map, compass, and weapon before the boss), Zelda's internalized prudence, and Ganondorf's power in insatiable excess.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: McCall and Auxier use Aristotle's virtue ethics to unpack the Wizard's claim to be 'a good man but a bad wizard' and to argue that no external token—the diploma, heart watch, or medal—can confer virtue, which is cultivated only through practice and experience. Each companion lacks something specific: the Scarecrow the intellectual virtues and phronesis, the Tin Man the feelings and stable states of character that regulate emotion, the Lion the sophrosyne that balances thinking and feeling into courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice. Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, virtue) frame the companions' bond with Dorothy, and MacIntyre's account of virtues internal to practices explains why the Wizard's public recognition still matters. Dorothy herself begins as the child Aristotle says cannot yet be virtuous—fleeing Miss Gulch in Kansas—but by defending Toto against the Lion and leading the quest she grows into a responsible moral agent, which is what her delayed homecoming requires.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Close the Door, Put Out the Lights
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
aristotle-golden-mean.title: You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Redemption and Hope for the Future
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Peters applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of courage — the mean between confidence and fear, shown only in facing an honorable death in war for a noble motive — to Colin MacLeod's two-thousand-year hunt for Marcus Octavius, the Immortal Roman who killed his wife Moya, in Highlander: The Search for Vengeance. Because MacLeod fights from pain and rage, 'like wild beasts,' and secretly seeks death as refuge from grief ('to seek death as a refuge from poverty, or love... is not the act of a brave man'), Aristotle would judge him a coward despite his fearlessness — Amergan the spirit guide diagnoses him the same way. Redemption comes only when Dahlia and the villagers threatened by Marcus's new Rome give him a noble cause and hopefulness: he becomes their general, fights with discipline instead of rage, and turns Marcus's own quickening to destroying the virus, illustrating the chapter's closing thought that for an Immortal dying is easy and living courageously is hard.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Forgiveness and the Fenway Faithful
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Rory Kraft uses Aristotle's virtue ethics to explain why Red Sox Nation forgave Tim Wakefield (whose mistake Aaron Boone turned into the 2003 ALCS-ending homer) and Ted Williams, but scapegoated Bill Buckner for 'the error' and eventually cast off Manny Ramirez. Because Aristotle judges a complete life, one swallow does not make a summer, Buckner's .991 fielding percentage and 2,715 hits should contextualize his lapse, yet some acts are bad without degrees like Aristotle's adultery, theft and murder, and a World Series-deciding error crossed that line. Kraft distinguishes Aristotle's categories, Wakefield's mistake (ignorance of Boone's changed plan) versus Buckner's misadventure (contrary to reasonable expectation) versus Manny's voluntary injustices, concluding that learning when to forgive players who are family taught the Nation what forgiveness itself means, sealed by Buckner's 2008 standing ovation.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Tie Goes to the Runner
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: St. Martin runs the Fenway 'pink hat' controversy through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the virtuous fan is the mean between the deficient bandwagoner who waves at NESN cameras mid-pitch and the excessive diehard who memorizes Dice-K's ERA to belittle others. Terry Francona's courage in sending Dave Roberts in the 2004 ALCS (versus a reckless Ortiz steal attempt) illustrates virtue as the mean between cowardice and foolhardiness, and Aristotle's contrast between the love of honor and the love of contemplation shows both pink hatters and stats-obsessed diehards err by making fandom about themselves. She concludes that accepting fans in any color hat is the truly virtuous mean.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Manny
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Santaniello reads five nonconformist Red Sox through ethical theory. Ruth's sale to New York becomes a Kantian case: he tore up his signed three-year contract and demanded a trade while expecting others to keep promises, violating the categorical imperative on promise-keeping. Ted Williams's lifelong war with the 'Knights of the Keyboard' exemplifies existentialist authenticity ('It just wouldn't have been me' tipping his cap), Spaceman Bill Lee embodies Sartre's condemned freedom and existence precedes essence, Jim Rice's Hall of Fame delay is Aristotle's failure to hit the mean between silent deficiency on Boston's racism and excess toward reporters, and Manny's 'Gas is up and so am I' money grab shows Aristotle's point that wealth is an incomplete end pursued for the sake of something else.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Extra Time
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Kent argues soccer is Aristotle's favorite sport because everything in both is organized around the goal: the four causes explain shinguards (plastic, curved shape, Mitre's workers, protection) and the game itself, with the final cause—scoring—defining a thing's identity and goodness, so two differently made balls are both soccerballs if kicked toward a net. Soccer best fulfills sport's three purposes (physical and moral discipline, theatrical imitation with catharsis, recreation): its ninety minutes of uninterrupted continuity force hundreds of renewed acts of self-mastery in Aristotle's sense of courage and the right amount, its single referee with limited powers embodies Aristotle's preferred limited monarchy, and Argentina's sportsmanlike throw-in returning the ball after Cameroon kicks it out for an injured player exemplifies equity—making a rightful exception to the letter of the law. Own goals, where a defender's error harms his own side, supply the hamartia of Aristotelian tragedy, giving fans a healthy catharsis of pity and fear.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Jousting for Virtue
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Farrell argues that the medieval code of chivalry is a living case study for Aristotle's virtue ethics: Lancelot, 'mekest in hall and sternest to his foe', embodies the paradox C.S. Lewis names as meek and fierce 'to the nth', which Farrell reads as Aristotle's courage, the golden mean between cowardice and rashness, exercised 'to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive'. The joust, meanwhile, was a proving ground where knightly virtues became second nature through habituated practice, since as Aristotle says 'it is no easy task to be good'. Western martial arts, he concludes, are 'moral kung fu': a fencing match with one's own standards of virtue.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Boxing, a School for Virtues
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Marino answers colleagues who call college boxing 'teaching violence' with an Aristotelian defense: courage is the mean between fearlessness and excessive fear, and the ring is one of the few workshops where fear is actually practiced. He cites Wacquant's boxing gym as 'a school of morality' in Durkheim's sense, Rotella's 'education at the fights', and boxers like Maja Cavlovic and George Foreman on how training takes over when fear hits, to argue boxing forges emotional self-command. His challenge to his own students: 'How can you be consistently honest or just if you don't have the mettle to take a hit?'

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
aristotle-golden-mean.title: In All Fucking Seriousness
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Arp asks why well-placed 'fucks' in Onion headlines like 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' are funny, and answers with the golden mean traced to Aristotle and Confucius, who both prized self-control and being a good role model to children: swearing is virtuous when it hits the mean between the vice of too much (gangsta rap's every-other-word profanity, the cemetery gardener's rant, Glengarry Glen Ross) and the vice of too little. He sorts Onion stories into vice tables—'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer' illustrates the vice of cowardice, with courage as the hitting-the-mark mean—and concludes that a well-placed fuck is both funny and virtuous precisely because so many people treat the word as taboo.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Alone into the Desert
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Audits Duniverse lives by Socrates's standard—the condition of the soul over wealth and power, with justice, courage, temperance, and wisdom—finding Baron Harkonnen utterly wanting, 'Leto the Just' compromised by forgery and concubinage, Paul unjust in his myth-making holy war (though Plato's Republic would smile on ruling myths), and the Fremen admirable in temperance and courage but fatally sure of themselves where Socrates prized knowing that you do not know. Aristotle's function argument and golden mean follow: Paul's first worm-ride is courage between rashness and cowardice, but Paul's and Leto II's extreme, humanity-saving selflessness has no excess to moderate and so breaks the doctrine of the mean. The author concludes Socrates is too harsh and Aristotle closer, yet even he fails: sometimes the best life requires extreme virtue and even injustice, as with the two Atreides emperors.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Why Is It the Best Day Ever
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Wire and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Trerise argues Omar is virtuous in Aristotle's full sense: honest on the stand ('I robs drug dealers... I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), courageous, consistent, and generous, with even his vengefulness a mean between extremes given a world where no one else will check Avon or Marlo - unlike Marlo he never guns on citizens and even pays Prop Joe for clock repairs. Virtue theory's attention to context separates his killings of Stinkum, Savino, and Stringer from Marlo's power-consolidating murders and shows him achieving whatever eudaimonia his world allows, though his obsession after Stringer's setup, which got Tosha killed, marks his one real excess. The catch is exemplification - Omar is disturbed that children play at being Omar, and Michael becomes the new him - yet the chapter concludes that some vigilantism is a social necessity on the streets and that Omar's swapped body tag names the injustice done to the street's truly virtuous.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Psych and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
aristotle-golden-mean.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: The chapter argues HIMYM offers two complementary feminist icons: Robin embodies personal autonomy and independence - fighting from 'but, um' early-morning shifts to lead anchor, and grieving infertility as stolen autonomy rather than lost motherhood - while Lily, and even more Marshall, exemplify Carol Gilligan's feminist care ethics with its emphasis on emotion over impartiality, cooperation over competition, and partiality toward loved ones. Aristotle's golden mean supplies the test Robin passes by balancing career and love instead of pushing one to an extreme. The twist that a male character best exemplifies care ethics, with Lily bridging the two moral outlooks, is offered as the show's progressive complexity about gender.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
aristotle-golden-mean.title: The Devil and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Jennifer Baker asks whether the Devil does ethics any good and answers no. Against the tempter hypothesis she sets the traditional virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, where bad behavior traces to habituated vice rather than demons, and the cure is consciously cultivating virtues by hitting the mean between excess and deficiency - Johnny's practiced honesty, the Evangelical cousin's marital vows. She faults the Devil as a one-size-fits-all explanation of evil, a glamour machine (via Postrel and the Romantic Satan of Blake, Byron, and Milton), and a scare tactic the Epicureans warned corrupts character, closing with Plato's divided-soul counsel to aim at long-term goods and a dismissal of Luther's spite-drinking stratagem.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: The chapter assembles real-life versions of Finn's Enchiridion, starting with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the Golden Mean locates each virtue between two vices, so true courage is knowing when to fight and when to run - cowardice and 'stupidteous' recklessness as deficiency and excess - a balance Finn's all-out bravery lacks. Epictetus's Stoic Handbook (which inspired the emperor Marcus Aurelius) teaches that happiness depends only on one's own reactions and that events are good or bad by how we take them, making it a manual even the chronically disappointed Ice King could use, while Christine de Pizan's book of chivalry prepares heroes for defeat and Erasmus's Handbook of the Christian Knight with Praise of Folly makes Finn and Jake's 'foolish' mercy look righteous. Finally Kant's Groundwork supplies duty for duty's sake: by the categorical imperative, Finn was entitled to steal the ogre's dollar only if, as an ogre who had swallowed Jake, he would accept the same theft from a hero.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
aristotle-golden-mean.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
aristotle-golden-mean.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Kyle Alkema and Adam Barkman ask what would make the Gang happy and answer with Aristotle's virtue ethics: happiness is long-run flourishing built on virtuous habits, with the golden mean (courage between cowardice and recklessness) as the rule for choice. The Gang instead lives a 'Reverse Virtue Ethic' - trying extremes first by crude trial and error, like sniffing gasoline to check that it is gasoline - along three roads: quick money (welfare crack scams, robbing their own parents' house), lust (the D.E.N.N.I.S. System's seduce-and-abandon script, where Dennis cheerfully accepts the charge of sociopathy), and validation ('You're not gay, you're just really, really vain'). Their residual Catholicism supplies consciences and limits - Mac's talk of God smiting them, confession, fears of Hell - but no reasoned morality, leaving them trapped in 'one day at a time' gratification as reverse role models.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
aristotle-golden-mean.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Adam Henschke argues that Frank Reynolds, of all people, is a role model - not a virtuous man overall, but virtuous in one structural sense. Using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, each Gang member's project is diagnosed as the vice of excessive self-delusion: Charlie's Waitress obsession he cannot see through even at her musical rejection, Dee's acting stardom she will not work for and that ends in suicide-adjacent despair, Mac's muscle-bound self-image despite 'diabitis', and Dennis's Golden God delusion culminating in 'the implication' and his car stash of 'fetish shit'. Rickety Cricket embodies the opposite vice, total loss of the capacity to imagine oneself otherwise (via Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy), and Frank charts the Aristotelian mean between the two - he rejected his delusive country-club life, knows exactly what he chose with Roxy, and his plans succeed where the Gang's fail - making 'What would Frank do?' a genuine exercise of practical wisdom.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 13. Dauntless Courage
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: The Bocks test whether the Dauntless are brave or merely reckless using Plato's Laches and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics. Socrates refutes Eric's definition of courage as never surrendering - the Scythian cavalry fights while fleeing, and endurance without wisdom is foolhardiness - while Aristotle locates courage as the mean between rashness and cowardice, acquired by habituation ('we become brave by doing brave acts'), which redeems much Dauntless training: Tris jumps onto the roof a second time without hesitation because practice has shaped her. Fearlessness is neither necessary nor sufficient - Four ignores his four fears rather than lacking them, and only madmen feel none - so the brave person fears the right things, at the right time, for noble ends: Eric is ruthless rather than courageous, while Tris's mother's sacrifice and Tris's taking Caleb's place at the death-serum lab show courage aimed at the good of others, with Four's grieving perseverance showing it can even serve self-preservation out of love.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 12. Should I Really Stop That Rhyming
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Yuen uses the rhyming scene to analyze annoyance - rhyme hijacks Vizzini's attention, the Goldman/Morgenstern interruptions betray invested expectations, and fans' endless quotation is annoying through sheer repetition - concluding that annoyance is irreducibly relative and contextual. Aristotle's virtue theory supplies the moral frame: friendliness and wittiness, golden means between obsequiousness and surliness, buffoonery and boorishness, make being annoying a character flaw that damages the communal eudaimonia Aristotle takes the good life to require. Since these virtues may be supererogatory ideals rather than obligations, Yuen borrows Kant's imperfect duty to develop one's talents to explain why Inigo had to become a master swordsman - failing to hone the skill his one great goal demands would be a failure of self-respect.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 3. When to Hate and When to Be Irate
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Daniel Alloy opens with Aristotle's demand that one be angry 'as and when and for as long as one ought' and builds a theory distinguishing anger (a response to a specific offense, seeking proportional payback) from hatred (a response to a thing's very existence, seeking its destruction). He tests the theory on Louis's bits - hating deer as a class and fantasizing about giving them AIDS, the six-year-old 'Jizzanthapuss,' the Pig Newtons fight with a three-year-old, the Cinnabon clerk, the 'Awesome Possum' hipster, and the justified driver who yells 'suck a sack of dicks.' He argues justified hatred is impossible, since it would require a pure-malevolence being that could not be an autonomous person, so hatred is always wrong while properly proportioned anger remains a necessary part of the moral life. Kant supplies the self-respect dimension ('one who makes himself a worm cannot complain if people step on him'): failing to get angry at real wrongs done to you or your children signals a character deficiency, not virtue.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 9. Masks, Hearts, and Superheroes
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Dupree and Fuš build an independent definition of the "true superhero" from identity statements (Batman = Bruce Wayne, Clark Kent = Superman): only an essentially human character who forges near-superhuman excellence through cultivated virtue can count, and Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the standard. Batman qualifies - his refusal to kill the Joker shows the struggle for the golden mean between foolhardiness and cowardice, and Gotham Knights #31 shows how far he plans to avoid killing - whereas powers merely given, Superman's Kryptonian biology or the Green Lantern ring (their update of Gyges's Ring), bestow no virtue, as Kyle Rayner's and Guy Gardner's early careers show. Since Clark Kent is "in his heart" the alien Superman while Bruce Wayne is merely Batman's mask, Batman is a true superhero and Superman is not.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 11. Can a Leopard Change Its Shorts
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Alloy asks whether Rincewind - the wizard who runs from Twoflower, the Dungeon Dimensions, and the Agatean Empire alike - is really a coward. Aristotle's doctrine of the mean frames cowardice as the deficiency of fear-regulation between foolhardy Cohen the Barbarian and true courage, with character traits describing, explaining, and predicting Rincewind's flight. But the situationist challenge - Harman's reading of the cookie, hurry, and obedience experiments - denies that character traits exist, and the replies available to the virtue ethicist (Miller's continence/incontinence distinction, Alfano's 'dodge') leave almost nobody with virtues or vices, so the chapter concludes Rincewind cannot be a coward: cowardice, like the leopard's shorts, was never there to begin with.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 15. Death Begets Death
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 2. Ned Stark One Man in Ten Thousand
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Kirby reads Ned Stark's arc through Aristotle's Poetics: his excessive honor is a hamartia ('too much of a good thing'), his acceptance of Robert's summons and refusal of Renly's help and Littlefinger's plan are the peripeteia, and the fan mourning after 'Baelor' is catharsis binding viewers into a community. With Martha Nussbaum's work on Greek tragedy he then argues the series' deepest lesson is tragic conflict - Agamemnon sacrificing Iphigenia mirrored by Stannis and Shireen, and Maester Aemon's 'love is the death of duty' warning to Jon - where no hierarchy of values dissolves the moral residue, so we must suffer into learning instead of trusting philosophical prioritization.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 31. Paying the Iron Price
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Hansberger reads Theon's return to the Iron Islands as an Aristotelian failure of virtue: excess lust toward Yara on the road, the 'small soul' of gold-bought jewelry where Balon demands iron-price honor, and the rashness rather than courage of trying to hold Winterfell with twenty men.
