McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.

aristotle-golden-mean.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
aristotle-golden-mean.title: 82. Planescape Torment as Philosophy Regret Can Change the Nature of a Man
aristotle-golden-mean.relation: Gubka argues that Planescape: Torment answers Ravel's riddle 'What can change the nature of a man?' with 'regret,' read through Aristotle's claim that virtues are developed by habitually practicing virtuous action. The Nameless One's regret over betraying Deionarra and over the innocents killed to sustain his immortality motivates redemptive acts—apologizing to Deionarra, surrendering his immortality—shifting his alignment toward Good. The chapter rebuts Hobbes's Psychological Egoism (TNO's genuinely altruistic self-sacrifice) and Spinoza's warning that regret only doubles misery, arguing instead that apt regret is a golden-mean virtue between remorselessness and self-condemnation whose very painfulness makes it motivating.

moral-psychology.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
moral-psychology.title: George and Virtue—Like Oil and Water
moral-psychology.relation: Daniel Barwick runs George through Aristotle's function argument and finds him wanting: a paradigm of 'the many' who thinks happiness is fortune and momentary victories over others (free parking, perfect airport pickups) rather than activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. His 'do the opposite' epiphany in 'The Opposite' embraces the more extreme vice rather than steering toward the rationally chosen mean, and his self-hatred, laziness, and pleasure-seeking fail all three of Aristotle's tips for hitting the mean. Since George will never practice virtuous action until it becomes habit, Barwick concludes George is doomed to his miserable existence - which is, conveniently for us, why he is funny.

moral-psychology.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
moral-psychology.title: [Cue Bass]
moral-psychology.relation: Jason Holt asks whether it is rational for George to 'do the opposite' and answers no. Distinguishing minimal, medial, and maximal rationality, he argues the Costanza Maneuver is neither reliable (its .800 batting average in 'The Opposite' is dumb luck - insulting Steinbrenner into a job and cowing movie thugs should not work) nor feasible: George's akrasia and impulse problems betray him, and the opposite of an action is usually indeterminate (Jerry: 'chicken salad is not the opposite of tuna... salmon swim against the current'). Since George knows all this, betting on the Maneuver is irrational - its success is precisely the joke, 'not as good, works better.'

moral-psychology.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
moral-psychology.title: Conclusion
moral-psychology.relation: Robert Epperson defends the show against the 'no hugging, no learning' charge by arguing Seinfeld is about the pursuit of the moral life: the four constantly consult each other on right conduct (gift-giving, break-up timing, obligations to friends and parents), distinguishing the moral life from mere integrity. He grades each character - Kramer is Plato's man of right opinion without knowledge whose one maxim is 'listen to your little man,' George means rightly but is the man of wrong opinion, Elaine is undone by indecisiveness, Jerry is the moral axis whose flaw is vanity - and argues with Aristotle that it is precisely their imperfect characters that make their concern with acting rightly possible.

moral-psychology.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
moral-psychology.title: 1 - Homer and Aristotle
moral-psychology.relation: Raja Halwani evaluates Homer against Aristotle's four character types (virtuous, continent, incontinent, vicious), arguing Homer is not virtuous and is genuinely vicious in the domain of food and drink (eating Frank Grimes's marked sandwich, the 64 slices of American cheese), while shuttling between continence and incontinence elsewhere. He catalogues Homer's lack of practical wisdom (phronesis) through gaffes like inferring the Bear Patrol works because there are no bears, and his lack of genuine friendship since he has only drinking buddies. Homer is judged neither malicious nor wholly vicious, so we pity him for his Springfield upbringing and the Simpson gene, and the chapter closes by crediting his 'in-your-face humanity'—his unregulated 'love of life'—as an admirable but dangerous ethical trait that does not make him an admirable person.

moral-psychology.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
moral-psychology.title: 12 - Springfield Hypocrisy
moral-psychology.relation: Jason Holt argues that hypocrisy is a formal vice - an inconsistency between the values one espouses (tacitly or explicitly) and one's deliberate actions - and that philosophers wrongly build deception into its essence. Springfield supplies the counterexample: Chief Wiggum takes bribes, uses drugs, and abandons his post in plain view ('Lookin' good, boys!' after pocketing the counterfeit jeans), so his hypocrisy is pointless and non-deceptive, showing the vice survives without clever pretense like Moliere's Tartuffe. Mayor Quimby's double-talk on the 'chick vote', Mr. Burns's fake environmentalist PR in 'The Old Man and the Lisa', and Reverend Lovejoy's lukewarm ministry illustrate the classic deceptive pattern, while Apu's false 'American' front in 'Much Apu About Nothing' and Lisa's cool-kid pose in 'Summer of 4 ft. 2' show hypocrisy can be excusable or sympathetic when coerced.

moral-psychology.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
moral-psychology.title: Making the Pain Go “Poof”
moral-psychology.relation: James B. South argues Willow's Season Six turn — magic addiction, torturing Warren with a 'bored now,' attempting to end the world in 'Grave' — is tragic precisely because it is unintelligible: against Aristotle's account of tragedy, where pity requires seeing an intelligible mistake, Willow's destruction flows from Freudian depths (via Plato's 'lawless' desires and Jonathan Lear's 'enigmatic signifiers') that cannot be explained, only pointed to. The chapter traces the available evidence — her sidekick insecurity ('I'm not your sidekick!' in 'Fear, Itself'), her 'spurty knowledge' slip, making pain go 'poof' in 'Something Blue' — while insisting these unconscious swerves never add up to a reason for the final break. Xander's yellow-crayon memory in 'Grave' works not as explanation but as a second kind of break that opens space for Willow to regroup.

moral-psychology.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
moral-psychology.title: 24b
moral-psychology.relation: A paired philosophy-of-education debate on whether baseball players were better role models then or now. Edward Sullivan answers 'then' from lived memory: Ted Williams's Korean War service and his 1966 Hall of Fame induction speech demanding Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson be enshrined, and Jackie Robinson enduring Jim Crow spring training under Branch Rickey's pact of 'guts enough not to fight back.' Graham Harman answers 'now,' turning Socrates's Apology complaint that his most dangerous accusers are those safely dead into a diagnosis of nostalgia: the past buried Ty Cobb's and Cap Anson's racism, the Black Sox, and Hal Chase, while today's game is more racially open, physically dedicated, and union-protected.

moral-psychology.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
moral-psychology.title: Love and Self-Discovery
moral-psychology.relation: Mary Nichols argues The Curse of the Jade Scorpion answers The Maltese Falcon: where Sam Spade's cynicism leaves society no reason to trust its lone hero, C.W. Briggs, unknowingly stealing for the magician Polgar while hypnotized, is saved by love, friendship, and the office community of North Coast Casualty. The jade scorpion's trance, meant to cover crime, uncovers truth, as C.W. and Betty Ann admit under hypnosis the love and fear their waking selves hide, so that 'crystal clear' memory and self-knowledge, rather than Spade's rejection of dreams, free them from both the curse and crime. Against the noir world and Lester's 'comedy is tragedy plus time', the chapter holds that everyone has 'a little bit of larceny' in them and that experiences of love, friendship, and community are what form the character that keeps it in check.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: A Plausible View
moral-psychology.relation: Reconstructs Slughorn's lesson to young Tom Riddle, that murder rips the soul and the torn piece can be hidden in a Horcrux, an act 'against nature', and argues that because Voldemort's intellect and magical powers remain intact while his capacity to charm gives way to rule by fear and his body becomes snake-like, Rowling's soul must be the sentimental one: our humanity, love, and moral conscience. On this view the soul is damaged by supreme evil and can be repaired only through remorse, which is exactly what Harry urges on Voldemort ('be a man... try for some remorse') before the final killing curse rebounds.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: Snape’s Choice
moral-psychology.relation: Defines love, with Aristotle, Aquinas, and M. Scott Peck, as willing the good of the other for the other's own sake, and reads Snape's double-agent life as love expressed in action despite real hatred: he protects Harry's enemies at constant risk while disliking most of them. His Occlumency, the skill to lie to Voldemort's face, reveals both strength and weakness, for rather than renouncing love as Voldemort did he only conceals it, and his dying gift of memories to Harry, revealing that Harry is a Horcrux, must be freely offered because his thoughts can never be taken.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: NOTES
moral-psychology.relation: Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: Abilities
moral-psychology.relation: Bassham tests each sense of choice against the novels: internal-choices are uninformative (Dudley resolving to give up sweets), act-choices mislead since character is settled habit - Hermione's occasional rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army doesn't make her a rebel - and overt acts cannot reveal motives, as Snape's apparent Death Eater loyalty conceals devotion to Dumbledore and Lily. Motive-choices like Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny are most revealing, but self-deception (Vernon Dursley's rationalizations) and wizarding complications - Harry's vision of attacking Arthur Weasley, Voldemort's implanted false memory in Morfin Gaunt, the Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and a Priori Incantatem thought experiment - show that in Rowling's world choices may be unknowable even to their maker.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: Beyond Choices Toward a Deeper Self-Understanding
moral-psychology.relation: Bassham concedes that most abilities reveal little: trivial, widely shared, involuntary, innate, or unrecognized capacities (Harry's Parseltongue before Sorcerer's Stone) say nothing about character, and even impressive gifts are morally neutral - the resourcefulness, determination, and disregard for rules Dumbledore lists are shared by Harry and Voldemort and differ only in how they are used. But abilities won through hard work and ethical capacities like empathy, prudence, and resilience do disclose character, so Dumbledore is right that choices are generally more revealing, provided we are also honest about what our abilities say about us.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: Unknown
moral-psychology.relation: This section catalogues the novels' full range of irrational thinking - Percy Weasley's rule fetish, Malfoy's racism and classism, Ron's jealousy, Fudge's closed-mindedness, Luna Lovegood's credulity - before concentrating on wizards' ethical blindness toward house-elf slavery. Because elves like Winky have been conditioned to regard freedom as shameful, most wizards see nothing wrong; Hermione insists that internalized oppression doesn't justify servitude, and Harry's moral growth is marked by digging Dobby's grave with his own hands and writing 'Here lies Dobby, a Free Elf.'

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: The Inversion of Voldemort
moral-psychology.relation: Distinguishes remorse from mere regret through Voldemort's cold 'I regret it' after ordering Nagini to kill Snape: remorse requires owning one's act, and at the final duel Harry addresses him as 'Tom Riddle' and demands he 'try for some remorse' - the death-to-self Riddle cannot perform. Dumbledore's remorse over the cursed Resurrection Stone ring and his arranged death, and Harry's voluntary death that destroys the Horcrux within him and restores his whole soul, exemplify dying to the past self for renewal, while Harry's renunciation of his temper toward Ron and Hermione and his love for Ginny mark his continuous moral regeneration.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: The Integrity Objection
moral-psychology.relation: Draws Voldemort's inversion in full: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes his soul (Hermione notes only excruciating remorse could reunite it, a pain that could destroy him), his attempt on baby Harry leaves him disembodied vapor parasitic on others' blood and limbs, in stark contrast to the feasting, affection, and romance of Harry's circle. The Godric's Hollow inscription 'the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death' and Hermione's claim that the soul survives whatever happens to the body ground the contrast between Voldemort's unmourned, mundane death and the honored, grieved dead - Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, Colin Creevey.

moral-psychology.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
moral-psychology.title: NOTES
moral-psychology.relation: Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.

moral-psychology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
moral-psychology.title: Fear and the Superhero Stories
moral-psychology.relation: The authors argue superhero stories speak to our fears twice: first by dramatizing external dangers (mad scientists, terrorists, alien menaces), and second by confronting the subtler fear of what using violence will do to our own souls, since habit and a 'rising threshold' of expectations can make once-unthinkable force come to seem necessary. Superheroes like Batman, Spider-Man, Daredevil, and Superman model the answer: they exercise force within strict limits and draw lines they will not cross, fighting evil without becoming evil, and so show that courage, determination, and character can prevail against adversity.

moral-psychology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
moral-psychology.title: From Olympus to Galactus
moral-psychology.relation: Taliaferro and Lindahl-Urben open with the Greek lesson of Icarus, destroyed by his intoxicated pursuit of glory, and map it onto the Marvel Universe, where a scientific accident made the Fantastic Four 'use their power to help mankind' while their great foes embody a maniacal pursuit of more. The section sets up the two contrasts to come: Dr. Doom, Reed Richards' megalomaniacal classmate, and Galactus, the planet-devourer 'almost beyond good and evil', with the Silver Surfer as his scout.

moral-psychology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
moral-psychology.title: The Perfect Storm
moral-psychology.relation: Storm's journey from being worshipped as a weather goddess in Kenya to joining Xavier's school fits Campbell's heroic cycle, and her bond with the demonic-looking, rosary-carrying Nightcrawler shows strangeness as a bridge to growth - the duality transcended into singularity when she tells him 'I have faith in you'. Housel then grades Storm at Kohlberg's post-conventional level of justice ethics, yet shows her shifting into Gilligan's care ethics when she dashes off to save eight mutant children from a government lab, mastering both 'masculine' justice and 'feminine' care - hence the 'perfect hero'.

moral-psychology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
moral-psychology.title: The Shape-Shifting Mystique
moral-psychology.relation: Mystique, Nightcrawler's abandoned mother, embodies unstable duality - female and male, serpent symbolism, a name rooted in the mystery priesthood - but Housel argues she can never complete the hero cycle because she is a sociopath who abandons her newborn, comas Xavier, impersonates a senator, and joins terrorist attacks. She perverts Kohlberg's rule-governed justice into wicked principles - 'her deeds are rule-governed, but the rules are clearly her own' - and her blanket hatred of humanity ironically betrays the fear and insecurity of a repressed humanity beneath: Storm's perfect anti-hero.

moral-psychology.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
moral-psychology.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'

moral-psychology.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
moral-psychology.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Bill Davis argues that Narnia works as a classical moral-education environment: against Experiment House's science-worship, Narnia supplies the three ingredients Aristotle and Aquinas require, namely instruction, virtuous exemplars to imitate (Reepicheep's courage, Puddleglum's temperance), and habituation through repeated right action, which together transform Peter's indecision, Edmund's treachery, Lucy's envy, and Jill's timidity. What finally lasts beyond Narnia, he contends, is a transforming encounter with Aslan: Eustace's dragon skin torn off by the Lion, Jill's drink at the stream where 'there is no other stream,' and Digory's tearful confession. He closes by arguing today's self-esteem-based character education cannot replicate this, since it pursues virtue from love of self rather than love of the good.

moral-psychology.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
moral-psychology.title: The Mystery Solved
moral-psychology.relation: Avery Kolers uses "Only a Pawn in Their Game" and its companion "Who Killed Davey Moore?" to argue that Dylan treats Byron de la Beckwith as a pawn: a poor white duped by divide-and-rule tactics, the psychological wage of whiteness, shame, and lynch-mob indoctrination into fearing a Hobbesian war of all against all. Against Aristotle's account of acting in ignorance, the chapter asks whether Beckwith's ignorance of his real enemies was culpable, concluding his bad moral luck (in Bernard Williams's sense) was manufactured by white supremacy and so reflects back on all white people. Dylan's refusal to name or voice Beckwith adopts Strawson-style objective attitudes, making blaming itself a political act aimed at the system rather than the shooter.

moral-psychology.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
moral-psychology.title: Poker and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Bassham and Marchese catalogue seven critical-thinking traps that cost even good players money: self-serving bias (Rochester Ricky donating $10,000 to Brunson's Texas road gamblers), short-term thinking (aimed at Aristippus' live-for-today hedonism), the availability heuristic (Brunson's red eights on a four-flush board), the fundamental attribution error (crediting wins to skill and losses to luck), loss aversion (which breeds tight-passive 'rocks'), superstitious thinking (Alexander ripping the pockets off his shirt for luck), and the gambler's fallacy (Ken Warren's bogus 'rush' theory of streaky cards). The moral is psychological self-knowledge: great players must know their own cognitive frailties, because — as Clint Eastwood says — a man's got to know his limitations.

moral-psychology.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
moral-psychology.title: U2 and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Werther answers Tollefsen with Aristotle's Politics: musical images of character effect real 'change[s] of soul', so a three-premise argument concludes that repeated exposure to U2's images of fine character and good action can habituate delight in virtue - King's courage in 'Pride (In the Name of Love)' (whatever the botched time of day, and as proved when Adam Clayton stepped between Bono and an FBI-confirmed death threat), the indignation and shame at global poverty in 'Crumbs from Your Table', and the compassion of 'Miracle Drug' for the locked-in writer Christopher Nolan. 'Exit' purges the band's demons and 'Until the End of the World' offers purification through holy fear, matching the medical and religious readings of Aristotelian catharsis. C.S. Lewis's Abolition of Man closes the case: without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless, so a culture raised on U2's feelings may be better prepared to act well than one raised on syllogisms alone.

moral-psychology.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
moral-psychology.title: Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans
moral-psychology.relation: John Draeger asks which Undead can be held accountable for bloodthirsty behavior: Romero's zombies are amoral, like a poisonous plant or Cleckley's empathy-free psychopath Milt, while Dracula meticulously plans his move to London and so passes the cognitive test. Stoker's narcissistic Count stays amoral, but Coppola's Dracula (who warns Mina of her curse), Rice's guilt-torn Louis, and the self-deceiving, cruelty-enjoying Lestat show empathy, self-control, and moral reflection, making them immoral and responsible - which entitles vampires to due process rather than Van Helsing's vigilantism, to punishment aimed at rehabilitation, and to equal rights including civic participation and marriage, since the same standard would govern space aliens, robots, and humans.

moral-psychology.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
moral-psychology.title: James Bond and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: South reads the famous opening of Thunderball - life as 'a heap of six to four against' - as Fleming's challenge to Western philosophy's promise of a harmonious fit between reason, personal good, and social good. Bond's shame at his hangover and bad bridge (analyzed through Bernard Williams's account of shame as grounding identity) drives him to the Shrublands spa and a new healthy, patient self, but SPECTRE's atomic blackmail and an assassination attempt push him back to scrambled eggs, bacon, and bourbon: 'life's too short.' With Adorno's bleak view that modern societies are implicated in evil (SPECTRE's bureaucratically worded ransom memo, gas chambers built by the same ingenuity as medicine) and Williams's thick ethical concepts, South argues Fleming's Bond shows there is no universal pattern making life meaningful; the spy's work lies outside conventional morality, and the odds of a happy, philosophically vindicated life are six to four against.

moral-psychology.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time
moral-psychology.title: Chapter 6 - Performing Bullshit and the Post-Sincere Condition
moral-psychology.relation: Concluding an essay on personality disorders, this chapter argues that pathological personalities (the antisocial, borderline, dependent, paranoiac) are especially good bullshitters and that their bullshit and distorted perceptions are what wreck their social relationships, since good relationships thrive on truth as much as on truthfulness. Against Frankfurt's claim that bullshit is the greater enemy of truth because indulging it erodes attention to reality, the author counters that the bullshitter does track truth at some level; bullshit's distinctive danger is that, unlike lying, it can be unconscious, so the sting of conscience never checks the habit.

moral-psychology.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
moral-psychology.title: An Amoral Universe
moral-psychology.relation: James Spence rejects the DVD's profile of the Dogs as amoral psychopaths, arguing instead that Reservoir Dogs is filled with morality of just the kind Hume describes: natural sympathies plus artificial virtues constructed to manage conflicts among self-interested people. The tipping debate shows Mr. Pink reasoning with desert and fairness; Mr. Blonde's excuse that the clerks 'touched the alarm', White's 'Just cops' dehumanization, and the professional code restricting violence all display exactly the moral identity-management human psychology predicts. The film thus indirectly supports a third view on which morality grows from human nature and social interaction—criminals cannot actually think outside it.

moral-psychology.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
moral-psychology.title: Le temps de me laver les mains, or Bathroom Loyalties
moral-psychology.relation: Randall Auxier reads Pulp Fiction's scrambled sequence through Bergson's distinction between clock time and lived, experienced time and through Aristotle's Poetics: Tarantino toys with the three unities to make viewers attend to every character, and only when the film is re-sequenced does it become 'Vinnie's Very Bad Day'. Vincent's fatal flaw is Aristotle's incontinence—weakness of will—signaled by the running bathroom gag and his unwashed hands, while Jules and Butch pass the same moral test of loyalty, whether delivering the briefcase or saving Marsellus from Zed. The moral: be loyal, don't be weak-willed, and wash your hands thoroughly, since in Tarantino nothing lacks perceptible difference.

moral-psychology.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
moral-psychology.title: And Beware of the Beast in Me
moral-psychology.relation: Barnes takes Cash's infidelity despite the pledged fidelity of "I Walk the Line" and refuses the easy diagnoses of hypocrisy or lying: "Guess Things Happen that Way" voices a good will overcome by weakness, a frail human nature anyone shares. He supports this with the situationist experiments, the dime in the pay-phone slot, the Princeton seminarians in a hurry, Milgram's obedient schoolteachers, and the Stanford prison simulation that turned a pacifist student into an abusive guard, showing situation outweighs character. From Cash's songs he draws two moral lessons: charity toward wrongdoers, since the man in "I Never Picked Cotton" or the drunkard of "Kneeling Drunkard's Plea" might be us under the same circumstances, and prudence about compromising situations, as when Billy Joe's fatal pride in "Don't Take Your Guns to Town" proves his mother right.

moral-psychology.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
moral-psychology.title: The Doors Are Never Locked
moral-psychology.relation: Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.

moral-psychology.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
moral-psychology.title: History Will Judge
moral-psychology.relation: Livingston reads the Razor movie through George Lakoff's Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models: Cain's Pegasus assumes a dangerous world and enforces obedience (shooting Belzen for refusing orders, the torture of Gina), while Adama's Galactica assumes empathy and open questioning (asking Boomer 'Why do you hate us so much?', sparing Starbuck). Kendra Shaw is the 'child' conditioned by desensitization and objectifying language into a killing razor and a PTSD victim, whose recovery under Apollo shows the two family models being blended — boldness with communication. Adama's verdict that 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain requires seeing the family culture that produced her.

moral-psychology.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
moral-psychology.title: This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)
moral-psychology.relation: Milsky argues that Radiohead practice what environmental virtue ethics preaches, organizing the chapter around Aristotle's akrasia (Nicomachean Ethics VII): Sting, who champions rainforests while advertising Jaguar and topping the 'dirtiest band' carbon table, acts against his own better judgment, whereas Radiohead — confronted with an audit showing their 2003 and 2006 tours emitted roughly 11,368 tons of CO2, mostly from fans driving — changed their actual practice (venues near public transit, car-pool lots, sea freight instead of air, LED lighting and auxilary power units). He reads the King Canute imagery of The Eraser and lines from 'The Clock' and 'And It Rained All Night' as environmental narrative in the tradition of Thoreau's Walden and Leopold's Sand County Almanac, obligating listeners to act or risk akrasia themselves, and presents the band's Friends of the Earth 'Big Ask' commitment as linking environmental virtue to human flourishing. 'Idioteque'''s 'this is really happening' becomes the wake-up call to the akratic fan driving to Lollapalooza with a bottled water.

moral-psychology.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
moral-psychology.title: Transformers and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: A fictional five-session counseling narrative in which a burned-out Optimus Prime - running out of gas, embarrassed by 'WASH ME' written in his own dirt - secretly sees therapist Dr. Sara Sawyer. Through the empty-chair technique he speaks to the dead Jazz, admitting the survivor guilt of a leader who was fighting Megatron when Jazz fell, and confesses the night he nearly smashed a human teenager's car mistaken for a Decepticon; the Miracle Question helps him imagine peace. The dialogue dramatizes an internal transformation: the machine learns to name grief, anger, and sadness, admit mistakes to his team, and take R and R - in the authors' phrase, becoming more human.

moral-psychology.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
moral-psychology.relation: Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.

moral-psychology.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
moral-psychology.title: You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him
moral-psychology.relation: Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.

moral-psychology.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
moral-psychology.title: The Emotion-Reason Dilemma, Part II
moral-psychology.relation: Pribram places Monk and Dr. House in the tradition of the brilliantly rational but emotionally plagued detective (Dragnet's emotionless Joe Friday vs Cracker's Fitz), arguing both shows treat excessive emotion as the price of genius: Monk's OCD is tied to his pattern-spotting ('You're a freak of nature'), and when medication cures the OCD in 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' his detective genius vanishes. She applies Foucault's Birth of the Clinic to House's subtracting of the patient, but shows both series critique that modernist rationality through Eve in 'One Day, One Room', who forces House to face the rationally inexplicable. Using feminist scholarship (Jaggar, Alberti, Battersby), she argues the opposition of male reason to female emotion is a historically specific construction, and offers the best friends Stottlemeyer and Wilson as integrated alternatives who pay for their balance with ordinariness: polarization equals greatness, integration signals the mundane.

moral-psychology.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
moral-psychology.title: Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans
moral-psychology.relation: John Draeger argues Romero's catatonic zombies, like plants, lack the cognition and empathy to be blamed, while vampires split: Stoker's narcissistic Dracula resembles Cleckley's amoral psychopath Milt, but Coppola's remorseful Dracula, Anne Rice's guilt-tormented Louis, and the self-deceiving Lestat ('the trick is not to think about it') all grasp consequences, feel others' pain, and can exercise self-control, so they are immoral rather than amoral and accountable for their killings. Accountability brings rights: Van Helsing's summary staking is vigilantism that denies Dracula a fair trial, rehabilitable vampires like Louis might earn civic participation, and a nonviolent, honest vampire suitor cannot be rejected merely for being Undead. The principle generalizes to aliens and robots: whatever can reflect morally must be held responsible and treated with equal dignity.

moral-psychology.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
moral-psychology.title: Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies
moral-psychology.relation: Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.

moral-psychology.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
moral-psychology.title: You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It
moral-psychology.relation: Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.

moral-psychology.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
moral-psychology.title: Vigilante Hero
moral-psychology.relation: Epright and Worth argue that rule-following - the Ten Commandments, the Golden Rule, Kant's categorical imperative (whose consistent Kantian never lies even to Nazis), or the Bentham-Mill principle of utility (whose consistent utilitarian must torture if stakes are high) - never made anyone moral, and Dexter's Code is the case in point: it gives the appearance of morality while licensing murder, and its source (Harry, 'God', the texts) cannot vindicate it. Drawing on Jonah Lehrer's neuroscience that moral judgment is emotional first with reason as post-hoc lawyer, they argue the emotionless Dexter is the madman who has lost everything except his reason, and Kohlberg's moral-development stages find him stuck at the pre-conventional level, below a fifth-grader - punishment-avoidance and you-scratch-my-back reasoning, never universal principles or respect for persons. Real Dexter-inspired killers (Mark Twitchell, Andrew Conley) clinch the verdict: he is neither vigilante hero nor moral agent, just a selfish addict whose rule-governed kills justify nothing.

moral-psychology.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
moral-psychology.title: De-Deontologizing Dexter
moral-psychology.relation: Sultan Ahmed argues Dexter is not really a Kantian deontologist: the urge to kill came first (the teenage animal killings, and his brother Rudy/Brian, who developed the same dark desire without Harry and rationalized it differently), and Harry's Code is a post-hoc rationalization built on top of that desire. Drawing on psychological research (Joshua Greene, Jonathan Haidt) that deontological judgment tends to be emotional rationalization rather than moral reasoning, he reads Dexter's killings as serving emotional needs - the need to control the helplessness of the shipping-container trauma and the Ernest Becker-style need to belong, seen in his bonding with Miguel, Rita, and the kids. Even Dexter's refusals to kill Ellen Wolf or the bound Tony Tucci are framed as feelings and standards, not a sense of moral duty.

moral-psychology.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
moral-psychology.title: Becoming a Real Boy
moral-psychology.relation: Phillip Deen places Dexter on the scale of character types from Book VII of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics - temperate, morally strong (Angel Batista), morally weak (Deb), self-indulgent (Masuka), and the beast - rejecting the Socratic view that vice is mere ignorance, and argues Dexter is neither self-indulgent nor simply beastly but a 'morally strong beast.' The decisive test is Kant's tribunal of conscience and the morality-versus-prudence question: Dexter gathers proof before killing, feels remorse for Jonathan Farrow, and tells Trinity 'No, but I want to be' morally superior - yet his delight at Doakes's death exposes mere prudence. Deen closes with Brian's Heideggerian offer of authenticity ('you could be yourself around me') refused: Dexter hopes that by pretending the feelings are there he may one day 'turn into a real boy.'

moral-psychology.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
moral-psychology.title: What You Really Wanted Was Inside You All Along
moral-psychology.relation: Robert Kincaid maps Freud's structural model of the psyche onto Conch Street: Patrick under his rock is the pleasure-principle Id, guilt-administering Squidward the Super-Ego, and mediating SpongeBob the Ego, so 'Mermaid Man and Barnacle Boy IV' becomes the Ego minimizing, rationalizing and literally shrinking its own conscience and desires to dodge guilt over the belt. Episodes missing one member ('Squidville', 'SB-129', 'Big Pink Loser') dramatize egolessness and what each part contributes, and the chapter closes by asking whether Freudian psychic causation — the mind 'outnumbering itself' in 'Squilliam Returns' — undermines moral responsibility for what SpongeBob does.

moral-psychology.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
moral-psychology.title: Secret Revealed . . . I Wonder
moral-psychology.relation: Robert Vuckovich reads 'The Secret Box' through Plato's Theaetetus — wonder as the birth of philosophy, with Patrick playing Socratic midwife to SpongeBob's desire to know — and Hobbes's diagnosis of curiosity as 'a lust of the mind' that obsesses and torments until satisfied. SpongeBob's masked break-in turns epistemic desire into what Cicero condemns as 'knavery that wears the mask of wisdom', nearly destroying the friendship, while the Charmides ideal of self-knowledge as temperance is exactly what he lacks. The episode ends like a Platonic dialogue in aporia: SpongeBob peeks but does not search, learns nothing, and Patrick still guards the secret.

moral-psychology.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
moral-psychology.title: The Game’s Afoot
moral-psychology.relation: Littmann poses Holmes's cocaine habit as philosophy's classic akrasia puzzle: Socrates denies weakness of will, treating it as mis-measured pleasure in which nearer pleasures loom larger — the King of Bohemia risking scandal for Irene Adler's company, Sir George Burnwell's gambling, Holmes's immediate relief of boredom — while Aristotle objects in the Nicomachean Ethics that reason really is clouded by passion, the way 'Black Peter' Carey's murderous violence is clouded by rum, so the cure is habituated practice rather than a science of measuring pleasures. Aristotle's account fits our sense that Holmes, 'the most perfect reasoning and observing machine,' knowingly chooses the lesser good. The verdict is that this is the one case Holmes failed to solve: it was Watson, not Holmes's own reason and will, who 'weaned him from that drug mania.'

moral-psychology.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
moral-psychology.title: Cobol’s Backyard
moral-psychology.relation: Malloy argues the real protagonists of Inception are corporations: Cobol Engineering, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow move Cobb, Saito and Fischer like chess pieces, making the film a case study in corporate moral personhood. He builds personhood from the capacity to contract and hold rights (Saito buying the airline as Proclus's representative), to bear responsibility for what is done in its name, and to decide through corporate procedures, and he rebuts the objections that corporations lack moral emotions and virtues or vices by distinguishing personhood from personality - psychopaths are still moral persons. He ends with Fischer-Morrow's dilemma between Friedman's shareholder-primacy view and the duties of a member of a moral community, concluding that a monopoly on half the world's energy supply would wrong that community.

moral-psychology.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
moral-psychology.title: Does This Matter
moral-psychology.relation: Garvin asks whether anything done in a dream can be right or wrong, arguing that the dream-share changes the stakes: lies told inside Fischer's shared dream deceive a real dreamer, so ordinary moral rules carry over even when violence targets 'just projections'. The hard case is that projections are indistinguishable from fellow dreamers - his Turing-test argument that either you cannot know whom you are shooting, or a projection as convincing, independent and communicative as a person deserves the same moral standing. For ordinary unshared dreams he parts ways with Augustine on dream-lust: the sleeping self that neither knows nor controls what it does is not responsible for it, though the partial control of lucid dreaming would reopen dream actions to moral judgment.

moral-psychology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
moral-psychology.title: Only Remembered as the Blonde Shot in the Head
moral-psychology.relation: Asks whether Total Recall's Lori and Harry — liars, adulterers, willing killers — are immoral people, noting the utilitarian excuse of serving a greater good fails because the Martian government they serve is itself profit-driven and rules by 'the one-way dialogue of the truncheon and rifle.' Following Godfrey, it concludes that an employer who bases jobs on violating individuals' rights will damage the moral frameworks of the employees, whatever their prior calibration.

moral-psychology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
moral-psychology.title: Self-Deception
moral-psychology.relation: Explains Cohaagen's plan — 'Hauser volunteered to become Doug Quaid. It was the only way to fool the psychics' — through Nietzsche's observation that great deceivers are overcome by belief in themselves in the very act of deception, and that one lie obligates twenty more. Against the Impostor replicant and the misled Arctor, the chapter sets the philosophical puzzle that intentional self-deception seems impossible, locating most cases, like Earth's poor clinging to the Whale's Mouth advertisements, in motivated, non-conscious belief maintenance.

moral-psychology.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
moral-psychology.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Audits Walt's killings through Season Four - Emilio by phosphine gas in the RV, the captive Krazy-8, Jane left choking in 'Phoenix', the dealers he rams with the Aztec to save Jesse, ordering Jesse to shoot Gale, and the wheelchair bomb that kills Gus and Tyrus - grading each with Aristotle's criteria of capacity, motive, consequences, justification, and proximate cause. It argues self-defense excuses Emilio but dissolves for the imprisoned Krazy-8, that Walt actively created the danger he then refused to relieve when he let Jane die, and that special-relationship duties to Jesse plus a utilitarian ledger justify running down the dealers. Compatibilism is invoked to show guilt survives determinism, while the remote Wayfarer 515 crash is pinned mainly on Donald Margolis's own choices rather than on Walt.

moral-psychology.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
moral-psychology.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Explains why we believe a chemistry teacher could become a drug lord by reading Walt through Shakespeare's Macbeth with Aristotle's Poetics: drama must make a particular psychology feel universal, so interiority - here Walt's wounded masculinity (the veggie bacon, Hank's 'that's why they hire men', post-murder aggression toward Skyler) - supplies the hamartia of insecure pride. The chapter tracks Aristotle's reversals (crime restores manliness while breeding shame, driving ever more viciousness), casts Jesse as Walt's Lady Macbeth and Walt as his own Macduff, and reads the staged psychiatry lie as Walt deceiving himself about resenting his family. It predicts that if the show is Aristotelian tragedy, Walt's final reversal will come from a recognition, with cancer as the evil he embraces 'in' him and catharsis our pity and fear.

moral-psychology.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
moral-psychology.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Stages the standard three-way ethics debate on Walt: deontology's universalizability (Kant) absurdly forbids killing Krazy-8 even to save Walt's family, utilitarianism (Mill) licenses both cooking meth and murdering dealers - a outright contradiction - while Aristotle's virtue ethics judges character rather than acts and convicts Walt of vice: he endangers his family, misses Holly's birth, habituates himself into Heisenberg, and defrauds his school. Because acts and consequences alone cannot see character, virtue ethics is offered as the needed complement. The closing move widens the lens to America itself, arguing the capitalist success ethos and our appetite for anti-heroes like Tony Soprano and Dexter reveal a society that praises viciousness - 'we are what we repeatedly do.'

moral-psychology.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
moral-psychology.title: Psych and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Mahon and Ceballos read the pilot through the big-lie principle credited to Hitler and Goebbels: the truth - hyper-observation plus a photographic memory - is too mundane to be believed, so only the biggest possible lie, 'I am a psychic,' saves Shawn from jail, exploiting the reverse psychology by which hearers assume no liar would say something so implausible. The lie's durability is then explained with Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion: like horoscopes and psychoanalysis, Shawn's psychic claim is unfalsifiable, so the ex-con's finger-counting 'tests' in 'Woman Seeking Dead Husband' can confirm it but never refute it - a virtue for a liar, and precisely what makes a claim unscientific. Finally the chapter shifts blame to the victims: like Madoff investors who 'kind of saw it coming,' the SBPD is self-deceived, complicit in a lie it half knows is a lie because the gift horse keeps closing cases.

moral-psychology.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
moral-psychology.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: James Edwin Mahon sorts the show's plots by the gap between deed and motive: Patti Nyholm helps save Marjorie Garnett's liver in 'In Sickness' purely to leverage her firm, Lockhart Gardner sues Chumhum in 'Great Firewall' for the mercenary reason Alicia laments, and the Demorys bribe a juror in 'Fixed' out of altruism. Working through Mill's exchange with Llewellyn Davies and Kant's shopkeeper, he argues motives can be good or bad but never right or wrong, and that no good motive makes a wrong action right - Kant denied even a philanthropic right to lie. Hence Alicia's persuading Shen Yuan to lie about his torture, however compassionate, was wrong.

moral-psychology.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
moral-psychology.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Skyler King and Robert Arp catalogue the excuses cheating men offer - 'my wife let herself go', 'so much eye candy', 'a moment of weakness' - and add evolutionary psychology's parental investment theory to explain why Peter Florrick-types stray while women like Alicia cheat less. The centerpiece is Glaucon's Ring of Gyges story from Book II of Plato's Republic: politicians such as Peter, Bill Clinton, and Eliot Spitzer wear the invisibility ring of power and come to think moral rules no longer bind them. The chapter closes with prudential and moral reasons against infidelity - scorned spouses, broken promises, wounded children - capped by Eli Gold fielding questions about a Brazil-shaped birthmark in 'Anatomy of a Joke'.

moral-psychology.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
moral-psychology.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Roger Hunt treats Louis Canning, Peter Florrick, and Colin Sweeney as psychiatric cases read through Freud's later drive theory, in which a life drive (Eros) and a death drive (Thanatos) fuse in varying proportions. Sweeney is the purest death-driven type, deriving low-grade sadistic pleasure while feigning personhood to escape punishment; Peter's paranoia assembles a protective barrier of handlers (Eli, Jackie, Alicia, the DNC); Canning may convert self-attack into the very tardive dyskinesia symptoms he weaponizes before juries. The chapter's claim is that the show's evil is not absolute lawlessness but pathology seen from the other characters' perspective, and that the death drive accounts for much of the wickedness on screen.

moral-psychology.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
moral-psychology.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Kokotz casts Victor as a pioneer of human 'enhancement' whose eight-foot daemon - stronger, faster, smarter, kinder, and vegetarian - actually achieved his goal of perfecting the human body, yet whose hideous appearance locked him out of society and love, twisting success into catastrophe: the 'Midas problem' of getting exactly what you wished for. Victor's deeper error was trusting Mill's On Liberty test that what people actually desire is thereby desirable; desires come from the human mind rather than nature, so a desired enhancement can make things worse, as the daemon's revenge on William, Henry, and Elizabeth proves. The lesson is institutional as well as conceptual: science must not proceed behind closed doors but under shared ethical oversight, since a Frankensteinian breakthrough carries too much responsibility for any single scientist to bear.

moral-psychology.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
moral-psychology.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.

moral-psychology.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
moral-psychology.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.

moral-psychology.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
moral-psychology.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: William Rodriguez argues Branagh's 1994 Mary Shelley's Frankenstein deliberately overturns what Plato's account of art as mimesis that forms character, and Colin McGinn's aesthetic theory of virtue (G-beings versus E-beings), lead us to expect - that beauty of soul shows in beauty of body - since the handsome Victor is the moral degenerate while De Niro's hideous creature is a moral virtuoso whose first words are 'friend' and 'father.' The beautiful Frankenstein family harbors ugliness: Oedipal scenes between Victor and his mother Caroline, the wedding that makes Elizabeth 'brother, sister no more; husband and wife,' and Victor's relish in abandoning his creation. The creature's questions - 'Do I have a soul?', 'Who am I?' - and his secret harvest for the peasant family credit moral worth to the ugly, so the monster fascinates us because the monster is us: evil may be attractive and lurking inside rather than deformed and outside.

moral-psychology.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
moral-psychology.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. could only get a compassionate child to commit xenocide by presenting war as a game, a framing that neutralizes moral agency just as Milgram's shock experiments and the fake game show The Game of Death did. Using Sunzi's 'know your enemy' to frame the empathy paradox, Walzer's problem of dirty hands for Graff's lesser-evil choices, and Foot's trolley problem alongside drone 'Nintendo warfare' to show how distance makes killing easier, he concludes Ender was likely a willing pawn who let himself be deceived because he endorsed the war's survivalist goal.

moral-psychology.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
moral-psychology.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Brendan Shea starts from Wittgenstein's claim that 'game' resists definition and classifies Ender's battleroom fights, buggers-and-astronauts, and the open-ended Giant's Drink, then applies Bernard Suits' definition of games as voluntary attempts to overcome unnecessary obstacles (prelusory goals, constitutive rules, lusory means and attitude). He argues games build Ender's skills and empathy but that Battle School's 'winning is the only thing' ethos endangers moral character - the same rule-breaking that wins the war keeps players from ever questioning whether the buggers needed defeating at all.

moral-psychology.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
moral-psychology.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive' against Aquinas' Doctrine of Double Effect and Frankfurt's second-order intentions, arguing Ender's killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail double-effect proportionality because he intends excessive, fear-inducing harm to deter future attackers. He allows that Ender bears only partial responsibility for the xenocide since he could not know the 'simulation' was real, but concludes that, contrary to the Speakers for the Dead doctrine, Ender is not the blameless moral exemplar Card makes of him.

moral-psychology.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
moral-psychology.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Danielle Wylie uses Aristotle's conditions for voluntary action - control and knowledge - to argue Ender's planetary strike is one of his 'mixed cases' made under coercion and factual ignorance, so praise and blame attach elsewhere: Graff and Rackham, who foresaw the attack and could easily have stopped it, meet both conditions through culpable omission. Borrowing Rachels' Smith-and-Jones drowning case to show moral responsibility can exist without causal responsibility, she ends with Ender's non-blameworthy 'taking responsibility' as Speaker for the Dead.

moral-psychology.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
moral-psychology.title: The Devil and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Jim Berti opens with a dream-fable in which the Devil tempts him with a bank-robbing 'quick fix' for his house-buying cash crunch, then reads the Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil' as the Devil's resume of history's atrocities - Anastasia, the Blitzkrieg, the Kennedys - where he supplies the lighter fluid but never strikes the match. The chapter argues we give God too much credit and the Devil too much blame while omitting ourselves: the Devil is the 'drug dealer of sin,' peddling the seven deadly sins as shortcuts like Rocky IV's steroids, and only effortful virtue refuses them. As the song says, 'it was you and me.'

moral-psychology.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
moral-psychology.title: Girls and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: McCrossin asks whether Adam's Season Two finale run across Brooklyn to break down the door of a dangerously unraveling Hannah ('I was always here') is heroic, set against Hannah's 'You don't need to be like a hero' chair-and-mattress scene and Adam's 'I don't want to help... I was doing it because I love you' quarrel. He argues an act is heroic - being an 'Extraordinary Samaritan' like Wesley Autrey, the Subway Samaritan, unlike the trained Sullenberger - only when done on purpose to help, not from obligation, training, or love's compulsion, testing the point with Batman's motives. Since Adam insists no one ever does anything from a want to help, his rescue's heroic status is left genuinely open.

moral-psychology.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
moral-psychology.title: Girls and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Mahon and Walker rebrand the seven deadly sins for Girls: Self-Absorption as Augustine's 'love of one's own excellence' (Hannah pitching her e-book at her editor's funeral, calling her grandmother 'the old Flo Job... sluttin' around'), Entitlement for Hannah's 'voice of my generation' demands and Marnie's rage at Charlie's success, and Sleeping Around as the John Paul II point about reducing a person to an object of gratification - Adam's fantasy sex with Hannah and his degradation of Natalia. Envy (Hannah on Tally's tragedy), gluttony in drug-fueled relapses (Aquinas's five ways), flakiness as Kant's indolent free-rider who needs others but never helps (Jessa missing her own abortion), and Senecan irritability (Jessa spitting at the Bushwick party, Ray's hatreds, Shoshanna's 'whiny nothings' outburst) complete the survey - redeemed by the girls' stubborn friendship.

moral-psychology.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
moral-psychology.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Karavitis argues Finn's 'Finn-losophy' is a metaphysics that prefers magic over Princess Bubblegum's science, and that this choice shapes his ethics: magic is the 'easy way out' requiring no understanding (Jake's stretching, the Glasses of Nerdicon), while science demands observation, experiment, and falsifiable ideas—'reality is the ultimate spell-checker.' Because magic promises instant gratification, Finn rushes into danger ('Wizard,' 'Donny,' the Goblin Kingdom) behind an inflexible hero code, and his altruism misfires, as the never-ending prize-winning battles of the 'Mystery Train' episode illustrate. The chapter concludes that your view of how the world works—magical or scientific—determines whether you can grow ethically at all.

moral-psychology.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
moral-psychology.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: McCrossin asks why Finn and Jake forgive Marceline although she tries to kill Jake, evicts them twice, drains Princess Bubblegum, and never shows remorse. Jake's change of heart ('my fear was based on ignorance') comes from witnessing her father Hunson Abadeer's cruelty and her abandoned childhood, so her bad acts flow from causes outside her control rather than pure choice. The chapter presses the remaining problem: we normally forgive the penitent offender, not the unrepentant one, and Marceline—unlike the moping vampires of Twilight, Underworld, and True Blood—never regrets, leaving readers to decide whether understanding without remorse can ground trust and friendship.

moral-psychology.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
moral-psychology.title: Justified and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: The chapter diagnoses Raylan with Aristotle's akrasia (lack of self-restraint): Art's 'lost cause' lecture, Arlo's boast that he has never shot anyone, and Boyd's 'you wake up in the morning pretending that you are not the bad guy' all charge him with acting on passion against his own calculations - sleeping with witness Ava, resuming adultery with Winona when her ring comes off. Because Raylan feels regret, the Aristotelian mark of the unselfrestrained person who knows his condition, he is curable and lacks self-restraint by habit rather than nature (Nicky Augustine's limo verdict: 'it's not who you are'). The chapter reads Raylan's signature move - forcing men to draw first so their deaths count as justified - as a perversion of justice by an akratic who is not wicked, and the series arc as his slow acquisition of self-restraint.

moral-psychology.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
moral-psychology.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.

moral-psychology.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
moral-psychology.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Ethan Chambers asks whether we should pardon the Gang, arguing with Hume that their vices have a 'causal story' as rigid as physical law: Charlie's glue-sniffing, racism, and inability to connect trace to a Christmas Day childhood of squalor and Uncle Jack's abuse; Mac was bullied as 'Ronnie the Rat' for trying to be good and never once saw virtue pay in Philadelphia; Dennis, shaped by Frank's cruel parenting, claims and shows he cannot feel feelings, so Humean sympathy - the key moral sense - is simply beyond his reach; and Frank's 'donkey brains' asylum childhood or outright insanity directly undermines his responsibility. Knowing these psychological causes, sympathy (Hume's word for empathy) replaces blame: we blame the builders, not the house, and the chapter closes by urging compassionate rehabilitation over the show's never-ending circle of punishment and revenge.

moral-psychology.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
moral-psychology.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.

moral-psychology.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
moral-psychology.title: Magnetic North
moral-psychology.relation: Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.

moral-psychology.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
moral-psychology.title: 20. The Doctor Lies
moral-psychology.relation: McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.

moral-psychology.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
moral-psychology.title: 23. Failing and Forgiving in the Name of the Doctor
moral-psychology.relation: Hoffman reads the Doctor's banishment of the War Doctor ('Doctor no more,' his actions 'not done in the name of the Doctor') as a failure of self-forgiveness driven by what Jeffrie Murphy calls the moral hatred of self and Robin Dillon the 'self-as-feared,' rather than mere guilt over the genocide of Gallifrey. Drawing on the self-forgiveness literature (Blustein, Griswold, Westlund), he argues that 'The Day of the Doctor' shows forgiveness neither excuses nor extinguishes blame: the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors forgive their past self by recognizing he shared their Doctorly motives and was forced into an impossible choice. Clara's outsider faith ('be a doctor') supplies the third-party affirmation that dissolves the identity-destroying dilemma and frees the Doctor to find the third option that saves Gallifrey.

moral-psychology.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
moral-psychology.title: 12. The Courage of Selflessness
moral-psychology.relation: Pless argues that courage and selflessness are not the opposed traits of Dauntless and Abnegation but one and the same virtue: any properly selfless act requires moral courage, any truly courageous act requires sacrifice so that others may prosper, and both depend on an outside party in need and on overriding the instinct of self-preservation. Because a rewarded sacrifice becomes social capital - the lunch-giving and bullet-catching examples - neither virtue can be institutionalized: Abnegation's legalistic rules and Marcus's publicly displayed selflessness destroy selflessness by removing choice, and Eric's fear-eradicating initiation produces glory and cruelty instead of courage, since fear connotes responsibility. Natalie and Andrew Prior's shared, gender-subverting sacrifices, and Tris stepping in to take Al's knives, show the single virtue of selfless courage chosen in the moment, culminating in a death that is an extension of her character rather than a surprise.

moral-psychology.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
moral-psychology.title: 5. The Morality of Manners
moral-psychology.relation: Dougherty argues that at Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating moral character and respect. Matthew's shift from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation for a grown man' to valuing Molesley's role shows decorum tracking his growing respect; Branson's tweed suit at white-tie dinners and 'uniforms of oppression' display disrespect even where his politics are sound; Sir Richard's parting boorishness betrays a lack of moral character; and the Dowager Countess's polished barbs prove manners can serve as a mask for self-interest rather than virtue. The framework combines Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' Aristotle's person of extraordinary virtue whose goodness must appear in particular ways, and Sarah Buss's idea that good manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect.

moral-psychology.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
moral-psychology.title: 7. Psychopaths, Outlaws, and Us
moral-psychology.relation: McClelland argues Lecter is neither psychopath nor sociopath, marshaling his empathic childhood (softening a bread crust for Mischa, polishing an eggplant because she loved purple, sensing Lady Murasaki's fatigue), his genuinely compassionate psychiatric work with Margot Verger, and his chess-master planning as evidence that both cognitive and emotional empathy operate normally - unlike Grutas, 'here's your real psychopath'. Reading Lecter's preternatural calm, mutism, and suppressed memories as PTSD and resilience after Mischa's death, and his fundamental project as the pursuit of autonomy (with Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework explaining his contempt for declining institutions like the FBI), he reclassifies Lecter as an outlaw - one placed beyond the law's protection yet living inside civil society - who kills instrumentally the way evolutionary psychology says humans do, concluding that 'there is an outlaw in all of us'.

moral-psychology.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
moral-psychology.title: 8. Consuming Homicidal Art
moral-psychology.relation: McAteer uses Bullough's aesthetic distance to test whether the psychopath Hannibal can have genuine aesthetic experience, arguing against Maibom and Harold that egocentric pleasure in an artwork is compatible with aesthetic distancing - so a Lecter who loves Bach and Italian architecture (unlike Cleckley's unmoved psychopath and the Tooth Fairy's graceless 'performances') could really exist. But since psychopaths can value nothing as an end in itself - they treat persons and artworks merely as means - homicidal art like the Muralist's corpse cathedral and Hannibal's gourmet cannibalism is the logical extreme of Wildean aestheticism, proving Wittgenstein's 'Aesthetics and ethics are one' false; yet in homicidal art Hannibal's moral deficit becomes an aesthetic deficit too, because anyone who can see beauty in human bodies as mere material is over-distanced - the bodies, like any sculpture's material, matter.
