Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.

moral-psychology.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
moral-psychology.title: Notes
moral-psychology.relation: Tim Challans treats Kirk, Picard, Archer, and Janeway as case studies in moral psychology, with the captain as Plato's charioteer balancing the horses of Spock's logic and McCoy's feeling. He reads Picard's 'there are four lights' coercion in 'Chain of Command' and his Locutus guilt in 'Family' through Rawls's shame/guilt distinction and Nancy Sherman's 'moral injury', while Kirk's 'I need my pain' refusal of Sybok and Archer's Xindi-era regrets show commanders owning guilt, regret, and remorse. Drawing on Nussbaum's 'upheavals of thought' and Hume's passions, he argues that a rare, well-integrated moral psychology—pride tempered by humility, as Q's lesson in 'Tapestry' demonstrates—is what qualifies the one-in-a-million starship captain.

moral-psychology.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
moral-psychology.title: Notes
moral-psychology.relation: Malloy argues loyalty's moral value is exaggerated, asking what loyalty is via Royce's cause-loyalty, Fletcher's historical self, and Keller's thin motive theory, applied to Leia torn between Alderaan and the Alliance and to Luke's emotional flight from Dagobah. The Sith embody a paradox: under the Rule of Two a loyal Sith must betray, so Vader's final turn on Palpatine was loyalty to Luke and thus betrayal of the Sith itself, while stormtrooper-style loyalty shows devotion is only as good as its object. Betrayal wrongs because it irreversibly alters a relationship - which is why Lando's Bespin gamble was right - and loyalty's real value is the commitment, dedication, and selflessness behind it.

moral-psychology.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
moral-psychology.title: Do Not Ask Him to Be Rational
moral-psychology.relation: The Rochas argue the Jedi Council's conduct across the Temple-bombing arc — letting Tarkin take jurisdiction, then expelling Ahsoka and handing her over for trial on flimsy evidence in 'The Wrong Jedi' — exposes a Jedi ethics corrupted by deference to hierarchy. Ahsoka's decision to walk away enacts Kantian moral autonomy (self-legislation) against the Council's heteronomy, while Anakin, despite sharing her doubts, seeks another master in Palpatine and falls into heteronomy instead. Using Baier's account of trust and Iris Marion Young on social roles, they contend the Jedi's repudiation of feeling was the real failure: emotions like Ahsoka's fear rightly guided her to distrust the Council and even to trust Ventress.

moral-psychology.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
moral-psychology.title: “So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”
moral-psychology.relation: Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.

moral-psychology.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
moral-psychology.title: 24. The Fifty-Third Card
moral-psychology.relation: Written in the Joker's voice, it plays the fifty-third card no other contributor considered: maybe both 'heroes' are the villains—Superman's public saves are attention-seeking ego when he could help unseen, and Batman selfishly pours billions into Bat-toys instead of donating it to save millions of dying children. Its deeper target is our hypocrisy: the Dark Knight ferry scene is unbelievable because in reality we would climb over each other to push the button, since we are only as moral as our circumstances allow while buying sweatshop chocolate and bacon and calling ourselves good. The genuine 'super-man' would drop the pretense of morality altogether, live by his own lights before dancing with the devil, and laugh as the world burns.

moral-psychology.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
moral-psychology.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Nathan Stout uses P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility through 'reactive attitudes' to ask when Sam and Dean are justified in killing what they hunt. Monsters sort into three groups: low-functioning animal killers like the wendigo and 'Heart''s werewolf Madison, intelligent but conscienceless 'antisocial' monsters like demons and leviathans, and 'moral monsters' like the cow-blood-drinking vampires of 'Bloodlust' and the kitsune Amy from 'The Girl Next Door,' who can understand and be motivated by moral reasons. Because Group 3 monsters are members of the moral community, Dean's 'if it's supernatural, we kill it' bigotry and his secret killing of Amy make the supposedly good hunters morally suspect, since killing a fellow member of the moral community ought to weigh on them.

moral-psychology.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
moral-psychology.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: You Should Find Another Guiding Light: Is Taylor Swift Admirable?
moral-psychology.relation: Kate Schmidt asks whether Swift is admirable, starting from 'Dear Reader,' where Swift herself warns fans not to take her as a guiding light. After showing that admiring the songs without the artist fails (Swift says her songwriting and her life are 'one in the same') and that her character resists assessment (the Matty Healy controversy, private-jet use, silence on political issues), the chapter borrows Alfred Archer and Benjamin Matheson's account of admiration for ideals: what fans should admire and imitate is the ideal protagonist of resilience and joy-after-heartbreak in songs like 'Shake It Off,' 'Bejeweled,' and 'long story short,' not Swift's whole person.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: Can I Forgive You for Breaking My Heart?
moral-psychology.relation: Sophia and Glen Pettigrove attack the near-universal philosophical assumption that forgiveness presupposes wrongdoing by examining heartbreak without fault: incompatible dreams in 'Midnight Rain,' fading love in 'right where you left me,' and unrequited love in 'Teardrops on My Guitar.' Because even innocent heartbreaking inflicts undeserved harms - obsessive pain, damaged self-esteem, distrust, a rewritten past ('happiness') - and runs the same emotional and relational course as being wronged, they propose revising the definition of forgiveness to cover letting go of hard feelings toward blameless heartbreakers, with Swift's songs as the first-person evidence.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: How to Forgive an Innocent: Taylor, Kanye, and the Ethics of Forgiveness
moral-psychology.relation: Sarah Köglsperger asks whether Swift's song 'Innocent,' performed at the 2010 VMAs for Kanye West after he hijacked her 2009 acceptance speech, is genuine forgiveness or a condescending 'slam disguised as forgiveness.' Using P.F. Strawson's reactive attitudes and objective attitude to rule out the readings that Kanye is a blameless child or that Taylor merely became indifferent (as in 'I Forgot That You Existed'), she defends the song as Jean Hampton-style 'change of heart' forgiveness that separates the wrongdoer from the wrong ('who you are is not what you did'), legitimate even without certain repentance because of our shared human fallibility.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: This Is Why We Can't Have Nice Things: Goodwill as a Finite Resource
moral-psychology.relation: Georgie Mills develops a philosophical account of goodwill - trust extended with the expectation of honest reciprocity - through 'This Is Why We Can't Have Nice Things': Swift forgave Kanye after 2009, extended goodwill again during their 2016 'Famous' phone call, and had that goodwill destroyed by the secretly recorded, edited clip Kim Kardashian released, sparking #TaylorSwiftIsOverParty. The song's 'shaking my head and locking the gates' shows goodwill is finite and fragile, and following P.F. Strawson (against Kant's 'good will,' which is explicitly set aside) refusing a second forgiveness is not pettiness but taking Kim and Kanye seriously as members of the moral community.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: Taylor Swift's Philosophy of Reputation
moral-psychology.relation: Catherine Robb and Roos Slegers reconstruct a philosophy of reputation from the reputation album: with Sperber, Baumard, and Origgi, reputation is a shared group consensus ('they say I did something bad') that is fake, warped, and outside one's control, yet Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments explains why it still wounds - we deeply want not only to be loved but to be lovely, seen for who we really are (the invisible dance through the streets in 'Delicate'). The chapter's original contribution is Swift's 'tilted stage,' performed literally on the reputation tour: gendered double standards ('The Man,' 'mad woman') mean a woman's reputation is more fake, more imposed, and more punishing than a man's.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: It's Me, Hi! I'm the Problem It's Me: Taylor Swift and Self-Blame
moral-psychology.relation: Agnès Baehni asks whether the self-blame saturating 'Anti-Hero,' 'Afterglow,' 'High Infidelity,' and 'Dear John' models a justified or an excessive tendency, especially for Swift's young female audience. Against Dana Nelkin's risk-based explanation of the blame asymmetry, she argues the relevant notion is suffering plus self-knowledge: we may blame ourselves more than others only because we usually know our own aggravating and excusing conditions better ('maybe it's me / And my blind optimism to blame'), and since self-blame is always overt while other-blame can stay private, the proportionality norm sometimes forbids blaming ourselves at all.

moral-psychology.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
moral-psychology.title: I'm Fine with My Spite: The Philosophy of Female Anger in the Work of Taylor Swift
moral-psychology.relation: Builds a philosophy of female anger from Aristotle's definition of anger (response to perceived injustice, desire for payback, pleasure in pain), applied to the 2016 Grammy call-out of Kanye and 'Vigilante Shit', and Agnes Callard's problem of eternal anger, which Swift answers in 'I Forgot That You Existed' by moving on without forgiving. Mill's Subjection of Women frames why femininity is constructed as incompatible with anger, and the chapter inventories Swift's 'Glitter Gel Pen Anger' ('Karma', 'Bejeweled') as walking away that renders the wrongdoer beneath contempt. Audre Lorde's 'Uses of Anger' closes the chapter: anger has conative and epistemic value against racist and sexist oppression, which also measures Swift's own limits around race.

moral-psychology.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
moral-psychology.title: Notes
moral-psychology.relation: Mills asks why Nate is more hurt than relieved when Roy declines to headbutt him over kissing Keeley, while Jamie had to fight for forgiveness. Using Strawson's reactive attitudes - anger is how we take someone seriously as a member of the moral community - plus Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness and Radzik's transactional account of amends, she argues Roy's instant absolution dismisses Nate as a pitiable non-agent rather than a culpable moral equal. The chapter contrasts this with earned, transactional forgiveness across Season 3 (Nate apologizing to Will and Ted, Beard's own story of betrayal and forgiveness), showing the headbutt as the recognition Nate needed.

moral-psychology.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
moral-psychology.title: Notes
moral-psychology.relation: Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.

moral-psychology.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
moral-psychology.title: Notes
moral-psychology.relation: Confronts a puzzle in Rust's naturalism: he dismisses the occult, yet talks freely of monsters and evil, concepts often thought irredeemably supernatural. The chapter distinguishes natural from supernatural senses of 'monster' (Aristotle's explicable hybrids versus Carroll's order-violating beings) to argue Errol Childress is a monster consistent with naturalism, then defends a 'modest proposal' — the evil person just is the morally worst sort of person, whose vices are extreme in both intensity and object. Betty's line that Childress is 'worse than anybody' and his extreme cruelty and callousness fit this account, teaching that recognizing creatures like us can be evil, not positing inhuman monsters, is the first step to combating evil.

moral-psychology.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
moral-psychology.title: “Haven’t Thought of You Lately at All”
moral-psychology.relation: George Dunn uses Dr. Kinny's mock-prison experiment at Hearst — where 'cool guy' Rafe torments Horshack, even gentle Wallace turns taunting guard, and Mercer perhaps first bonded with his future victim Moe — as a rerun of Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, arguing that bad situations and corrupting power, not just bad apples, produce Neptune's villains. Against pure situationism he sets Hannah Arendt's diagnosis that great evil usually requires not wicked hearts but an 'inability to think': Woody Goodman's rehearsed excuses about neglected boys and Mercer's 'I'm just taking what you would have happily given' show wrongdoers rationalizing rather than reflecting. The chapter ends by suggesting the town's gulf between 09-ers and everyone else may be the situational 'apple barrel' breeding the arrogance, entitlement, resentment, and envy behind Neptune's crime wave.

moral-psychology.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
moral-psychology.title: “Do You Not Instinctively Fear Me ”
moral-psychology.relation: George Dunn weighs Veronica's creed that 'someone's always supposed to pay' — Carrie Bishop destroying Mr. Rooks for her friend, Logan getting himself jailed to beat Mercer, Veronica forfeiting the Kane Scholarship to watch Aaron Echolls convicted — against the case against vengeance running from Socrates' 'one must never do wrong in return' through Seneca's claim that the angry are insane and Plato's subordination of thumos to reason, with the ultimatum game showing people pay to punish even at their own expense. Nietzsche's creditor-debtor account explains the payoff: punishing the offender restores the status and self-esteem that humiliation stole, turning passive grief into an active grievance like Madison's crushed-and-cubed Mercedes. Yet Machiavelli's 'much safer to be feared than loved' finally vindicates a measure of payback, since Veronica's threats are how a disgraced outsider demands the respect fickle Neptune withholds from Meg.

moral-psychology.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
moral-psychology.title: Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character
moral-psychology.relation: Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.

moral-psychology.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
moral-psychology.title: Seventh Hole Cheating and Gamesmanship among Amateur and Professional Golfers
moral-psychology.relation: Lumpkin argues that amateur golfers routinely cheat while professionals do not, and dissects four rationalizations amateurs use: appeal to ignorance, appeal to popularity, appeal to tradition (Callahan's 'cheating culture'), and the belief that 'no one will ever know' — a golf-course version of Plato's Ring of Gyges where invisibility dissolves restraint. Drawing on Kohlberg's stages of moral development, she claims professionals reason at higher levels because officials, peers, and disqualification (e.g., J. P. Hayes) enforce the sport's social contract, whereas amateurs face no punishment. She concludes casual golfers would do better not to keep score than to keep a 'mythical' one, earning the right to score only once they follow the rules.

moral-psychology.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
moral-psychology.title: Excuses, Excuses Inside the Mind of a Complainer
moral-psychology.relation: Kevin Kinghorn, drawing on interviews with coach Brad Gilbert, dissects why tennis players and their parents complain and make excuses. He catalogs cognitive biases and the vividness effect (why a bad call, like McEnroe's 'You cannot be serious!' outburst, sticks and feels like persecution) as forms of irrationality, and notes Stoicism (which he attributes to Zeno) as a philosophy that would suppress the complaining temperament. His central mechanism is Freudian self-deception: citing Freud's hypnotized-umbrella subject who invents a reason for his own behavior, he argues tennis parents pretend their child is destined for greatness and then genuinely come to believe the lie, so excuse-making becomes a self-destructive sign a player will never be a champion. He also reads Andrea Jaeger's ambivalence about winning as evidence of mixed, partly unconscious motivations.

moral-psychology.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
moral-psychology.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
moral-psychology.relation: Couch reads two Eastwood gestures — Josey Wales's spitting and the Man with No Name's smiling — as expressions of self-reliance that generate a 'motivational polarity,' simultaneously repelling and attracting others. Drawing on Miller and Mason on contempt and disgust as moral attitudes, and on evolutionary coalitional psychology, he argues Wales's 'contemptuous disgust' (spitting on dead bounty hunters, at the Comancheros) marks moral boundaries and forms surrogate-family coalitions, while the Man with No Name's deceptive non-Duchenne smile in the Dollars trilogy conceals lethal intent yet occasionally shows genuine compassion (freeing Tuco). The self-reliant individual, adhering to his own moral compass, inevitably divides others into allies and foes.

moral-psychology.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
moral-psychology.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
moral-psychology.relation: Karen Hoffman traces the gun across Eastwood's career as an evolving argument about violence: Dirty Harry's .44 Magnum ends violence without cost to the shooter, High Plains Drifter and Pale Rider treat the gun as righteous retribution and a proof of masculine honor, but Unforgiven shows William Munny killing men who may not deserve it and dwelling on how killing brutalizes the shooter. In Gran Torino Walt Kowalski finally gives up the gun entirely, walking unarmed into Spider's gang and being gunned down in a Christlike pose so that Thao is spared both victimhood and the guilt of killing. The chapter argues Eastwood shifts from celebrating the gun as physical protection to warning of the psychological damage violence inflicts on its user.

moral-psychology.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
moral-psychology.title: “And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo
moral-psychology.relation: Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.

moral-psychology.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
moral-psychology.title: Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds
moral-psychology.relation: Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.

moral-psychology.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
moral-psychology.title: Psychological Determinism in the Films of David Cronenberg
moral-psychology.relation: Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.

moral-psychology.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
moral-psychology.title: 15. The Evil in These Woods
moral-psychology.relation: Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.

moral-psychology.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
moral-psychology.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
moral-psychology.relation: Skoble examines evil in Manhunter through the film's Nietzsche epigraph—'whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster'—as profiler Will Graham must 'become' Lecktor and Dollarhyde to catch them, risking his own psyche. Lecktor's claim that killing feels good because doing 'what God does' makes one godlike frames the killers' evil as a will to power. Skoble invokes the Socratic dictum that to know the good is to do the good, asking whether Dollarhyde's murderous 'becoming the Red Dragon' is a large-scale delusion, and warns that truly seeing the killer's fantasy risks adopting it.

moral-psychology.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
moral-psychology.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
moral-psychology.relation: Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.

moral-psychology.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
moral-psychology.title: Passionate Objectivity in Sherlock Holmes
moral-psychology.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall pose the ethical clash between impartial detachment and partial loyalty, situating Holmes between Simon Keller (loyalty as a threat to being a 'good believer,' echoed by Holmes's 'Sign of Four' rejection of emotion) and Bernard Williams and Susan Wolf (who defend priority for loved ones—Williams's 'one thought too many'). Using Watson's shooting in 'The Three Garridebs,' Holmes's weaning off drugs, and 'perverted love' in the Sussex Vampire and Thor Bridge cases, they argue loyalty rightly understood as seeking the friend's good aids clear reasoning, and that Holmes exhibits a 'passionate objectivity' in which some acquaintance with passion is essential to being genuinely objective.

moral-psychology.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
moral-psychology.title: The Industrious Sherlock Holmes
moral-psychology.relation: Bassham diagnoses Holmes as a workaholic against clinical criteria (obsessive work, few relationships, perfectionism, health neglect through fasting and cocaine), then traces the rise of the Protestant work ethic (Calvin, Weber, Carlyle) and its modern decline. Drawing on Thoreau's Walden critique of 'lives of quiet desperation,' Pieper on leisure, and the 'affluenza' literature, he distinguishes pathological from benign workaholism by warning signs and by motivation. He concludes Holmes is a pathological workaholic in his symptoms but redeemed by his noble, non-materialistic motive of fighting crime and achieving justice.

moral-psychology.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
moral-psychology.title: White Nights of the Soul
moral-psychology.relation: Garcia reads Insomnia as the story of a cop who has lost himself and must choose between two doppelgangers: Walter Finch, the murderer who offers amoral 'partnership' and moral anti-realism ('that ultimate taboo? It doesn't exist outside our minds'), and rookie Ellie Burr, who embodies Dormer's better past as a conscientious policeman. Against Finch's 'moral math' and Dormer's own 'the end justifies the means' rationalizations, the chapter argues that the moral value of actions lies in intentions, motives, and character—Aquinas on what makes a killing an accident, Kant on being worthy of happiness rather than securing it. Dormer's sleeplessness becomes evidence of a conscience still alive, and his struggle figures what Kierkegaard calls purity of heart, willing one thing, with Socrates's refusal to escape in the Crito as the model of integrity. In dying to protect Ellie from losing her way, Dormer regains himself through commitment to another person, the Levinasian point that personhood is fulfilled only in and through other persons.

moral-psychology.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Bunker Mentality or Love
moral-psychology.relation: Robin Bunce recovers how Terry Nation's original 1963 'The Daleks' encodes evil, reading the script in its Cold War, post-Cuban-Missile-Crisis context. He argues Nation dehumanizes the Daleks not by making them less rational but MORE rational: they embody the unfeeling reason of the neutron bomb that destroyed Skaro, having lost individuality, laughter, and the capacity to feel. Drawing on Richard Rorty's claim that our humanity lies in feeling for one another rather than in reason (and on Wells's Morlocks), he concludes the Daleks are the dreaded post-nuclear human future, and Ian teaches the Thals that love and empathy, not abstract moralizing, resist evil.

moral-psychology.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
moral-psychology.title: 3. Why Do I Have to Be Some Kind of Hero
moral-psychology.relation: Zanin reads the Winchesters' sense of moral responsibility through Dostoevsky's The Karamazov Brothers, mapping Dean onto the sensualist/atheist Dmitri-Ivan and Sam onto the faithful Alyosha. Via Father Zossima's dictum that we are 'responsible to all for all,' she argues Sam and Dean's brotherhood is Christian self-sacrificial 'love in action'—shown in Dean choosing Sam over a normal life in 'Bad Boys' and the djinn world—which grounds why they keep saving strangers even after rejecting God's plan.

moral-psychology.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
moral-psychology.title: 8. Which Brother Is the Good One
moral-psychology.relation: Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.

moral-psychology.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
moral-psychology.title: 11. Why Sacrifice Yourself
moral-psychology.relation: Browning interrogates the nobility of the Winchesters' repeated self-sacrifice, asking whether their deals (Dean's soul for Sam, John's soul for Dean) are selfless or selfish—driven by codependency, fear of being alone, and ego. He weighs utilitarian justification (sacrificing one who saves the world) against the trickster's 'Mystery Spot' lesson that 'nothing good comes' of it, and invokes Kant's notion of a true gift expecting nothing in return, alongside Milbank on life-as-gift, to question whether self-sacrifice is the 'ultimate ethical agent' when death isn't final.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 1. Scamming for Fun
moral-psychology.relation: Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 2. Don’t Go to Lawyers for Moral Guidance
moral-psychology.relation: Ralston reads Jimmy McGill's slide into Saul Goodman as a study in moral decline, using Dewey's (and Bourdieu's) theory of habit to explain why a person capable of right action repeatedly chooses the wrong path—the pressures of criminal clients, Chuck's contempt, and HHM's rejection wear down his will as an ingrained disposition. He contrasts Kant's categorical imperative with mere 'imperatives of prudence' (rules of thumb for achieving any end), arguing Jimmy consistently follows the latter, as when he unhinges Chuck at the disbarment hearing to win. Invoking Hart's separability of law and morality and Singer on the ethicist's training, he concludes lawyers like Saul make poor moral guides.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 11. The Self-Deception Road
moral-psychology.relation: Doll analyzes self-deception across the series using Gregg Ten Elshof's four mechanisms—attention management, procrastination, perspective shifting, and rationalization. Chuck's electromagnetic hypersensitivity is a real psychological condition about which he deceives himself as to its physical cause, reinforced by everyone accommodating him; his refusal to see Jimmy as anything but 'Slippin' Jimmy' is rationalized as protecting others while sabotaging his brother. Jimmy, via perspective-shifting through Chuck's eyes, comes to believe he can only be Slippin' Jimmy, then rationalizes the Saul persona. Drawing on Joseph Butler and Adam Smith, Doll argues self-deception blinds moral judgment and is ultimately Saul's undoing, leaving him alone in hiding.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 14. Salvaging Sunk Costs
moral-psychology.relation: Using Jimmy's wish to quit law despite years of study, and Kim's objection, the chapter examines whether the 'sunk cost fallacy' is always a fallacy. It grants that unrecoverable past investments are irrelevant to a narrow cost-benefit goal, but argues via Nozick's opera-ticket case and Thomas Kelly that reflecting on sunk costs can be rational for habit formation, regret avoidance, and signaling resolve to opponents (illustrated by Mesa Verde's land, Jimmy and Kim's office lease, and Jimmy re-scamming Irene). It concludes that a complex career choice legitimately weighs a wider range of psychological, social, and moral costs than the relentless gambler's simple case.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 18. Dissenting Opinions
moral-psychology.relation: Framing Kim and Jimmy's clashes as a problem in the epistemology of peer disagreement, the chapter asks whether learning an epistemic peer disagrees should make you suspend judgment (the conciliatory view) or stay steadfast, using a tip-calculation dispute and their office-versus-practice compromise. It argues moral disagreements differ because we rarely count someone who disagrees on one moral question as a genuine peer, and rejects 'no fact of the matter' relativism for implying slavery could be permissible. It then reads Kim's arc, including 'Wouldn't I?', as her moral beliefs genuinely shifting toward Jimmy's, complicated by self-interested and self-deceiving reasons for holding beliefs.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 21. Finding the Good in Nacho
moral-psychology.relation: The chapter uses Kant to argue that Nacho Varga, though a genuinely bad drug dealer, can perform morally worthy acts in isolated moments. Because Kant locates morality in the rational will and intention rather than accomplishment, it treats Nacho's attempts on the Salamancas and his desire to leave the game as evidence of active moral reasoning, while conceding his motives are muddied by self-interest and love for his father (the shopkeeper example warns against acts done for loved ones). Its clean case is the phone call in 'Something Unforgivable,' where Nacho risks everything to plead for Lalo's near-innocent staff, doing the right thing purely because it is right.

moral-psychology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-psychology.title: 22. Breaking Bad Promises
moral-psychology.relation: The first half of this chapter lays out the moral paradox of 'bad' promises through Better Call Saul: Jimmy's payment to the Lindholm twins for the staged accident, the Kettlemans' bribe for silence, Nacho and Mike's hit contract on Tuco, Gus and Mike's criminal alliance, and Jimmy and Ira's Hummel heist. It stresses Mike's code ('if you make a deal, you keep your word') and his refund to Nacho when the hit fails, then builds a taxonomy of illicit promises as legal or illegal crossed with moral or immoral, setting up the question of whether we may break promises that are wrongful.

moral-psychology.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
moral-psychology.title: NOTES
moral-psychology.relation: Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'

moral-psychology.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
moral-psychology.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Griffioen dissects Colbert's 'truthiness' as two forms of motivated epistemic irrationality—preferring what one wishes true (wishful thinking) and intuiting truth from the gut over facts (self-deception). Using a running example of Samantha Bee believing in Jason Jones's fidelity against the evidence, she rejects Freud-style divided-mind accounts (with their static and dynamic paradoxes) in favor of self-deception as an attention-directing process, and skewers Colbert's circular 'truthinessiness' (proving truthiness with more truthiness). She argues gut feelings only justify belief when they implicitly track relevant facts, proposing a fallacy of 'argumentum ad ventrem.'

moral-psychology.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
moral-psychology.title: 18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing
moral-psychology.relation: Vuckovich analyzes 'Still Valley,' where Confederate Sergeant Paradine can win the Civil War using a witchcraft handbook that freezes Union troops but only by renouncing God. He reads Paradine's temptation through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges myth in Plato's Republic (the committed unjust man who outdoes enemies without scruple) and Aristotle's friendships of shared pleasure (Paradine and the witchman Teague bonded by hatred of the enemy). Paradine burns the handbook rather than damn the Confederacy, preserving a core principle of fairness even at the cost of an easy victory—winning isn't everything.

moral-psychology.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
moral-psychology.title: The Grinch’s Change of Heart Whodunit
moral-psychology.relation: Cunningham asks whether the Grinch's sudden metanoia is a matter of head or heart, staging a debate between Kant and Hume. A Kantian reading treats the change as reason reasserting the moral law after the Grinch's inclinations (envy, resentment) hijacked it, so he realizes stealing Christmas disrespects the Whos as ends in themselves. A Humean reading, favored by the author given that the Grinch's 'small heart grew three sizes,' treats it as a new sentiment of sympathy rather than a rational apprehension, invoking Hume's claim that reason is the slave of the passions.

moral-psychology.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Potzsch reads Emma as an Aristotelian study of eudaimonia, arguing Emma's self-deception and the flattery of those around her block her from true happiness, which for Aristotle is activity of the soul in accordance with reason and virtue. She diagnoses Emma's cruelty to Miss Bates at Box Hill as Aristotelian akrasia (moral weakness): Emma knows better but is overpowered by the desire to shine, showing virtue has not yet become her second nature. She contrasts Emma and Mrs. Elton's pursuit of honor (which Aristotle deems superficial, illustrated via Plato's Euthyphro) with Knightley's genuine virtue, and closes on Aristotle's ranking of the contemplative over the political life.

moral-psychology.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Cantwell reads Emma through 'perfectionism' and parody, arguing that Cassandra and later readers turned Jane Austen into a 'picture of perfection' while Emma herself is a flawed paragon. Drawing on Andrew Miller's Burdens of Perfection, she treats moral improvement as socially constructed and responsive to exemplars, set against Highbury's upward mobility (the Westons, Coles, Martins destabilizing class lines). Emma's attempt to remake Harriet Smith in her own image is a parody of the gentlewoman (Bakhtin on parody) that exposes Emma's own vanity; the crisis of imagining Harriet marrying Knightley forces the self-knowledge that lets Emma finally pursue genuine, socially situated perfection.

moral-psychology.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
moral-psychology.relation: Olson and Taliaferro examine the ethics of secrets in Austen, refining Sissela Bok's definition so that a secret conceals what convention would normally make public. They argue secrets in Austen are usually corrosive (Wickham and Lydia's elopement endangering the Bennets, Brandon's silence about Willoughby harming Marianne, Lucy Steele's engagement binding Elinor) yet can be virtuous, as when Darcy secretly funds Lydia's marriage to avoid self-aggrandizement. They propose an 'ideal observer' standpoint (an all-knowing, impartial, affective narrator) for judging when a secret is honorable, and argue the Emma-Miss Bates incident is not a failure to keep a secret but a genuine vice of contempt Austen condemns.

moral-psychology.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Introduction
moral-psychology.relation: Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.

moral-psychology.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Chapter 1 The Conscience of Huckleberry Finn
moral-psychology.relation: Jonathan Bennett reads the chapter 16 raft episode as a clash between 'bad morality' and sympathy: Huck's conscience (slave-owning principles telling him to return Jim to Miss Watson) supplies all the reasons, while his sympathy for Jim is a bare, reasonless feeling that wins by weakness of will, so Huck does right while believing he does wrong. He contrasts Huck with Himmler, whose bad morality overrode his surviving sympathy, and Jonathan Edwards, whose Calvinist approval of eternal damnation left no sympathy to conflict. The lesson is that principles should be kept open to revision under pressure from sympathy, since one cannot declare one's own morality bad but should stay open to correction.

moral-psychology.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Chapter 2 Huckleberry Finn and Moral Motivation
moral-psychology.relation: Alan Goldman argues against Bennett and against Arpaly and Schroeder that Huck is not weak-willed or irrational: his sympathy for Jim is an intentional emotion containing implicit judgments and awareness of the genuine moral reasons to help Jim, so Huck acts on his strongest reasons and is courageous rather than akratic. Because Huck is rational yet not motivated by his explicit (corrupt) moral judgments, and his real motivation comes only through emotional attachment, Goldman concludes against Kant that moral motivation is not rationally required. He uses Huck's failure to extend concern to other slaves, and analogies to meat-eaters and arbitrary aesthetic taste, to show moral inconsistency is not practical irrationality.

moral-psychology.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Chapter 3 Sympathy, Principles, and Conscience
moral-psychology.relation: Robert Fudge uses Adam Smith to reinterpret Huck's conscience and praiseworthiness. Against Bennett (conscience as accepted principles) and Arpaly-Schroeder (inverse akrasia via a whole-self theory), Fudge argues, following Smith, that conscience is the sentiment-based judgment of the 'man within the breast,' the impartial spectator, and that propriety rests on sympathetic 'feeling with' others rather than abstract principle. Huck's sympathy for Jim in the chapter 16 raft scene is a reason-bearing emotion, so he is not acting akratically or against his true conscience; instead he is growing morally, molding his conscience toward the loyalty and friendship that already constitute his core self.

moral-psychology.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Chapter 4 Huckleberry Finn’s Struggle between Sympathy and Moral Principle Reconsidered
moral-psychology.relation: Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.

moral-psychology.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: Chapter 14 Moral Value and Moral Psychology in Twain’s “Carnival of Crime”
moral-psychology.relation: Boardman treats Twain's 'The Facts Concerning the Recent Carnival of Crime in Connecticut'—in which a narrator kills his personified conscience (a shabby dwarf) and gleefully commits a spree of crimes—as staging an 'exasperating metaphysical question' about the value and psychology of morality. On a Nietzschean reading the narrator becomes an Overman revaluing values, seeing conscience as the internalized lie of slave morality; on a Humean reading conscience is moral feeling (not reason), so once it is destroyed the narrator can still reason about right yet has no motive to act morally, illustrating the oak-tree and willful-murder arguments that vice lies in sentiment, not relations or facts. Boardman concludes both interpretations fit yet neither settles whether Twain endorses or lampoons the result—our horror at the crimes is what makes the story funny.

moral-psychology.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
moral-psychology.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
moral-psychology.relation: Florell and Wilson, psychologists, survey parenting through the nature–nurture debate, casting Locke's tabula rasa against Rousseau's noble-savage view of children, alongside Piaget and Kohlberg on moral development and Walter Mischel's marshmallow experiment on impulse control. They map the four parenting styles (authoritarian, permissive, uninvolved, authoritative) on responsiveness and control, argue authoritative parenting is optimal, and advise fathers to adjust discipline to each child's innate temperament rather than enforce rigid gender roles.

moral-psychology.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
moral-psychology.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
moral-psychology.relation: Gary Jobson, writing from a long racing career with no philosophical vocabulary, offers practical wisdom on generating the inner strength and courage to win: focus on the task at hand rather than the outcome, visualize the race, stay calm under adversity, and 'have fun.' Through stories of Buddy Melges, Ted Turner's Fastnet, and Dennis Conner's America's Cup comeback, plus his own collegiate turnaround under coach Graham Hall, he argues resolve (not luck) drives comebacks, and he treats leadership, mentorship, patience, and consistency as cultivated traits of character — an implicit account of the virtues a competitive sailor must build.

moral-psychology.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
moral-psychology.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
moral-psychology.relation: Geist, a conservation biologist, argues from physiology (elastin-digesting enzymes, B12 need), athletics (one-legged balancing for stalking, precision throwing), and the herbivore-like pattern of human speciation that humans evolved as hunters — a 'carnivorous herbivore.' He contends morality itself was born from hunting: because tools-as-weapons (clubs, spears) let an aggressor kill without retaliation, escaping natural selection's check, early humans had to invent social taboos distinguishing right from wrong. He contrasts Neanderthal 'rodeo' close-quarters spearing with Cro-Magnon distance throwing, linking spear-tracking to endurance running, language, and art — concluding that questioning hunting's morality questions our humanity.

moral-psychology.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
moral-psychology.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
moral-psychology.relation: Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.

moral-psychology.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
moral-psychology.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
moral-psychology.relation: Funke examines how the 'gateway' argument is supposed to work by treating it as a claim about weakness of will, split into two mechanisms. Motivational externalism—illustrated by Milgram's obedience experiments and Doris's situationism—holds that the illicit-market situation, not the drug, pushes users toward hard drugs, which implies legalization, not prohibition. Motivational internalism, using Michael Smith's contest between normative and motivational reasons and second-order desires, locates the risk in cannabis's creative 'analysis paralysis' and idealizing imagination; Funke argues that this imaginative value, like religion, is worth its risk and that neuropharmacology (THC's distinct cannabinoid mechanism) undercuts the internalist gateway claim.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: Alfano uses the trial of 'Sunset Strip Killer' Doug Clark to argue that situational forces and attribution biases may have swayed his jury regardless of the actual evidence. Drawing on Milgram's obedience study, Zimbardo's prison simulation, Knobe's intentionality vignettes, and Haidt's disgust experiments, he shows how gender bias, pretrial media, and revulsion at Clark's necrophilia could distort judgments of guilt. He closes with Nozick's truth-tracking account of knowledge to press whether a juror who would have convicted anyway can be said to know Clark is guilty.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: Howard surveys serial killers from Liu Pengli and Locusta through Gilles de Rais, Bathory, Bichel, Panzram, and modern killers she interviewed (Bobby Joe Long, Shawcross, Milat, Birnie) to illustrate 'practical moral skepticism': the thesis that one can know right from wrong yet feel no motivation to be good. She distinguishes this from epistemic moral skepticism and argues that many killers, often privileged or unconstrained, understood moral codes but were driven instead by power, sadism, fatigue, or anger, showing that a failure of moral motivation is ancient rather than modern.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: Dietrich and Hall explain why fictional serial killers (Hannibal, the Joker, Dexter, Grendel) allure us. Curiosity drives us to seek explanations for the mysterious, but the deeper pull comes from 'co-activation' of fear and pleasure inside a 'protective frame' (the screen or page) that strips away empathy for victims. They argue humans are rule-following creatures who must assert selfhood through rule-breaking to secure freedom, so the serial killer becomes an alluring avatar of ultimate freedom — the idea of the killer, safely framed, lets us test how thin the veneer of morality really is, as the Joker taunts.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: The Schechters contrast John Wayne Gacy with Jane Toppan and other female killers (Lydia Sherman, Carol Bundy) to ask what female serial murder reveals about human nature and the nativism/empiricism (nature/nurture) debate. They argue women tend to kill through poisoning and 'lethal nurturing' of intimates rather than phallic-aggressive stranger-murder, so female killers form a 'natural kind' that both violates and grotesquely exaggerates stereotypes of femininity. They conclude that serial killers, male and female, are also a single kind whose ruthlessness and egotism are a monstrous but recognizably human — and partly innate — reflection of our common nature.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: Keegan analyzes Buffalo Bill's line from Silence of the Lambs ('It puts the lotion in the basket') to ask why it repulses us. He argues clinical labels like antisocial personality disorder smuggle in unexamined norms and focus only on behaviors, missing the deep-seated traits behind them, so psychopathy should be distinguished from ASPD. Using Habermas's communicative rationality — grounded in perspective-taking and reciprocity and, via de Waal, in our evolved primate sociality — he contends that psychopaths like Buffalo Bill, Ramirez, and Kemper have lost the communicative capacity underlying empathy, and our revulsion is our own communicative rationality registering that violation.

moral-psychology.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
moral-psychology.title: SERIAL KILLERS
moral-psychology.relation: Terjesen critiques the 'lack of empathy' explanation of serial killing by disentangling empathy into understanding, vicarious feeling, and connection, and showing each either is possessed by killers or leads to circular reasoning (citing Deigh's 'mature empathy' and autism as a counterexample). Real killers like Dahmer, Rader, and 'Angels of Death' such as Cullen and Harvey act from sexual desire, rage, or even excessive empathy, so empathy shapes how they kill (intimate vs. distancing methods, echoing Greene's trolley/footbridge study) rather than whether they kill. He favors Kennett's lack-of-impulse-control and poor risk-assessment account instead.

moral-psychology.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
moral-psychology.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
moral-psychology.relation: Iyengar-tradition teacher Jeff Logan argues that yoga philosophy — mythology such as the warrior Virabhadra behind virabhadrasana and Hanuman behind hanumanasana — must be taught alongside asana, or practice becomes 'mere acrobatics.' Using the parking-lot and door-cutting anecdotes to show yamas like non-harm and selflessness ignored, and citing a childhood-diet study, he contends teachers should not preach the eight limbs but embed subliminal precepts in physical cues ('extend your legs straight and true'), so students come to live rather than merely know yoga's virtue ethics.

moral-psychology.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
moral-psychology.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
moral-psychology.relation: Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.

moral-psychology.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
moral-psychology.title: Introduction
moral-psychology.relation: Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.

moral-psychology.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: 36. The Godfather as Philosophy Honor, Power, Family, and Evil
moral-psychology.relation: Belliotti reads The Godfather as a study of the irresolvable conflict between a nineteenth-century Sicilian value system, l'ordine della famiglia, grounded in honor and the accumulation of power within a fixed family order, and a twentieth-century American ethic of individualism and commercial success, arguing the Sicilian vision must wither in the US for lack of its sustaining conditions. He offers a four-part philosophical analysis of honor (a binding code, group affiliation, internalization, and disproportionate redress) that explains Don Vito's contempt for the assimilationist undertaker Bonasera and his willingness to risk everything (the severed horse head sent to Woltz) on a matter of principle, insisting through Michael that 'it's all personal.' He supplements this with a taxonomy of power-over as oppression, paternalism, and empowerment, and argues Don Vito's evils are morally sanitized so viewers cheer his revenge.

moral-psychology.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
moral-psychology.title: 80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay
moral-psychology.relation: Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.

moral-psychology.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
moral-psychology.title: 5. Monsters and Evil in Doctor Who
moral-psychology.relation: The chapter defines a 'moral monster' as one who delights in evil acts, arguing (via Jonathan Glover and Laurence Thomas) that Hitler-style evil is all-too-human, not alien. Using Hume's claim that action springs from passion, it contends the emotionless Cybermen are a mere force of nature (bad but not evil), whereas the Daleks, driven by hatred, tribalism, and a closed belief system, are genuinely evil monsters; the manipulating Master mirrors our everyday lying. It then examines retributive justice through Solomon's execution in 'Dinosaurs on a Spaceship' and 'A Town Called Mercy,' rejecting purely backward- or forward-looking punishment (citing Rawls on utilitarianism's injustice) in favor of the Doctor's needs-based, 'reprobative' punishment, mercy, and self-forgiveness over the Time War.

care-ethics.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
care-ethics.title: Elaine’s Moral Character
care-ethics.relation: Sarah Worth asks whether Elaine is a feminist icon or 'just one of the boys.' Elaine passes every liberal-feminist benchmark - a Tufts education, the only steady career (Pendant Publishing, then the J. Peterman catalogue), financial and emotional independence - but fails the ethic of care: her dating ethics run on pettiness (dumping men for not offering pie, for dirty bathrooms, over Puddy's high-fiving), the 'spongeworthy' episode commodifies her own relationships, she shows no maternal instinct toward the ugly baby, and she secretly resents George's engagement. The conclusion: being one of the boys does not a feminist make, though Elaine still models an independence the women of Friends and Frasier lack.

care-ethics.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
care-ethics.title: “The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self
care-ethics.relation: Jessica Prata Miller reads Buffy through Carol Gilligan's care perspective: Buffy's self is relational (the Scooby Gang, 'Dawn is a part of me' in 'The Gift'), her moral reasoning contextual rather than rule-bound (caging Oz instead of killing the werewolf, rejecting Riley's Initiative 'demons bad' abstraction), and her emotions a moral resource ('My emotions give me power'). She also weighs the criticisms — Buffy's secret harboring of Angel exposed in 'Revelations,' and Faith's utilitarian 'plus column' defense of hiding a killing, which Buffy rejects ('I am' the one who cries over the bystander). Comparing the three Slayers, Miller argues only Buffy attains moral autonomy: Kendra's unquestioning obedience and Faith's hyper-individualistic action-hero isolation both fail, while Buffy's 'I like to think of it as graduation' break from the Watchers' Council shows autonomy achieved within, not against, relationships.

care-ethics.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
care-ethics.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
care-ethics.relation: Answers the title with 'fugheddaboutit' - Carmela is no feminist - but argues she reasons as a Gilligan-style care ethicist. Her moral voice evolves from Church-based justice arguments against Angie's divorce ('Commendatori'), through the justice-tradition confrontation with Dr. Krakower's refusal of 'blood money' ('Second Opinion'), to mature care ethics that balances self with others when she throws Tony out after the Svetlana revelation ('Whitecaps'). Using Noddings on reciprocity and 'total engrossment', the chapter reads the marriage's failure as failed caring, and the Furio romance and the Georgetown ricotta-pie intimidation as care reasoning that defies the submissive female stereotype feminists fear care ethics valorizes.

care-ethics.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
care-ethics.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
care-ethics.relation: Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.

care-ethics.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
care-ethics.title: The Perfect Storm
care-ethics.relation: Storm's journey from being worshipped as a weather goddess in Kenya to joining Xavier's school fits Campbell's heroic cycle, and her bond with the demonic-looking, rosary-carrying Nightcrawler shows strangeness as a bridge to growth - the duality transcended into singularity when she tells him 'I have faith in you'. Housel then grades Storm at Kohlberg's post-conventional level of justice ethics, yet shows her shifting into Gilligan's care ethics when she dashes off to save eight mutant children from a government lab, mastering both 'masculine' justice and 'feminine' care - hence the 'perfect hero'.

care-ethics.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
care-ethics.title: Phoenix Rising Jean Grey
care-ethics.relation: Jean Grey, the self-doubting original X-Man of the Cyclops-Wolverine love triangle, evolves across the films - the phoenix necklace, growing powers, growing confidence - through all three Kohlberg levels to her self-sacrifice that saves the X-Men at the end of X2. Housel rejects reading that act as utilitarian calculation or as the unbalanced self-sacrifice some feminist readings of care ethics would fault: Jean acts not out of duty but out of love and care, beyond the call of duty - what philosophers call supererogation - becoming a female Christ figure whose phoenix image foreshadows resurrection and Campbell's return as 'Master of the Two Worlds'.

care-ethics.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
care-ethics.title: Yes, but What About the Killer Rabbit
care-ethics.relation: Argues the Pythons invert Arthurian legend's traditional patriarchal function, using Holy Grail — made amid 1970s women's liberation and legal abortion — to expose the absurdity of patriarchy rather than endorse it. The Black Knight's 'None shall pass' embodies an abstract, relationship-blind masculine ethics that the chapter sets against care ethics, while the witch-weighing scene shows Arthur and Bedevere's male bonding eclipsing the mob's victim. Castle Anthrax's 'perilous bed' and the Prince Herbert rescue — Launcelot's heterosexual-matrix heroics collapsing when the damsel in the tower is a prince who enjoys musicals — turn courtly love and gender roles into farce, making the film as much a document of 1970s gender politics as a medieval satire.

care-ethics.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
care-ethics.title: Poker and Philosophy
care-ethics.relation: Housel surveys a century of poker on screen — from the Tombstone Birdcage Theater's 'bird in a gilded cage' through Maverick, The Gambler, Rounders, and ESPN's Tilt with its brothel-break 'Matador' — to show women cast as eye-candy, damsels, or flukes (Joanne Woodward winning a high-stakes game without knowing how to play). Against the myth stands Annie Duke, who beat her brother Howard on the way to the 2004 Tournament of Champions title. The argument: poker rewards reading and projecting emotion, so women socialized into emotional intelligence hold an edge over macho men who suppress it — a retooled Stoicism fusing Epictetus's 'make the best use of what is in your power' with Gilligan's care ethics, backed by Nietzsche's trust in the senses and Sun Tzu's 'pretend inferiority and encourage his arrogance.'

care-ethics.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
care-ethics.title: U2 and Philosophy
care-ethics.relation: The authors apply Gilligan's and Noddings' ethics of care to U2: 'Bad' shows the speaker as Noddings' 'one-caring', and 'Sometimes You Can't Make It on Your Own' - Bono caring for his dying father through anger and resentment - exemplifies care's insistence on the particular relationship over universal rules, refusing abstraction even of the usual songwriting metaphors. 'Peace on Earth' names the Omagh bomb's dead (Sean, Julia, Gareth, Ann, Breda) and 'Van Diemen's Land' refuses both IRA and British sides, showing care ethics rejecting the utilitarian accounting and the Kantian universalizability arguments that could rationalize such violence. They conclude U2 are philosophical rather than political feminists: Gilligan's 'different voice' is not a woman's voice, and the band's connected knowing - debt relief sung as connection in 'Beautiful Day' - makes maternal thinking 'loud, rhythmic, catchy, even cool'.

care-ethics.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
care-ethics.title: You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”
care-ethics.relation: Renee Kyle sets House's detached "doctor knows best" medicine against Cameron's practice to argue for Carol Gilligan's feminist ethic of care: Cameron builds trust, refuses to deceive or bully (defending Ezra's control over his body in "Informed Consent"), and sees patients as embedded in relationships, arranging for parents to hold their newborn in "Maternity," where House sees only abstract puzzles. The chapter also presses the standard feminist worry that valorizing care can backfire: Cameron's unresolved grief stops her from telling terminal patients the truth, and by "Que Sera Sera" she secretly injects a patient who wants to leave the hospital, so that caring too much turns her into House.

care-ethics.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
care-ethics.title: Plato’s Cave Again
care-ethics.relation: Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.

care-ethics.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
care-ethics.title: Turning the Tables
care-ethics.relation: Wartenberg argues that North by Northwest pits two defective ethical stances against each other: the Professor's 'zealous patriotism,' exposed as callous in the USIA scene where he lets the innocent Thornhill be killed as the Kaplan decoy and spends Eve in the line of danger ('War is hell, Mr. Thornhill, even when it's a cold one'), and Thornhill's 'ethical particularism,' akin to the feminist ethics of care, exposed as headstrong when love-driven rashness leaves both lovers dangling on Mount Rushmore and only the Professor's intervention saves them. Yet the ending's match cut from Rushmore to the train berth reveals Hitchcock's real McGuffin: the Professor fails less as a moralist than as a bad director whose staged deceptions misfire, and the film's true philosophical claim is self-reflexive, that only film has the power to reconcile patriotism and romantic love, an optimistic world existing only in the artifice of the camera.

care-ethics.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
care-ethics.title: You May Wonder How Come I Love You Care and Ethics
care-ethics.relation: Gimbel asks what the E Street Band's marathon multiple encores mean, starting from social contract theory: Hobbes's state of nature ('no home, no job, no peace, no rest') and Locke's contract explain the ticket as a financial IOU — so a drunk, short Hendrix show wrongs you financially but not morally — while the contractual view of moral duty (the 'Hungry Heart' narrator who abandoned his wife and kids in Baltimore) cannot explain why a missing encore feels like personal betrayal. The gift theory fails too, since encores are expected, and expected things are not gifts. Care ethics (Ruddick, Noddings) fits instead: devoted fans make the band part of their identity, Springsteen sings 'to you about you,' and the No Nukes 90-minute set became permanent because he would not give his people less — while 'Pink Cadillac' shows the limit case, since you cannot love someone for her Cadillac.

care-ethics.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
care-ethics.title: History Will Judge
care-ethics.relation: Livingston reads the Razor movie through George Lakoff's Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models: Cain's Pegasus assumes a dangerous world and enforces obedience (shooting Belzen for refusing orders, the torture of Gina), while Adama's Galactica assumes empathy and open questioning (asking Boomer 'Why do you hate us so much?', sparing Starbuck). Kendra Shaw is the 'child' conditioned by desensitization and objectifying language into a killing razor and a PTSD victim, whose recovery under Apollo shows the two family models being blended — boldness with communication. Adama's verdict that 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain requires seeing the family culture that produced her.

care-ethics.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
care-ethics.title: 12 - Care Ethics, Friendship, and facebook
