They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.

feminism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
feminism.title: 67. Hari Kondabolu as Philosopher Enacting a Philosophy of Liberation
feminism.relation: Heppard frames Kondabolu—who resists the 'political comic' label—as enacting Enrique Dussel's 'philosophy of liberation' and Marcuse's aesthetics of liberation: comedy as 'barbarian philosophy' spoken from the periphery. Kondabolu's Swiftian 'eat the rich' health-care proposal, his 'White Chocolate Joke,' 'Feminist Dick Joke,' Columbus/Joe DiMaggio bit, and Bobby Jindal takedown rupture the audience's identification with white supremacy, patriarchy, and liberal hypocrisy (negative freedom) while his absurd alternatives exercise the 'radical imagination' (positive freedom). Heppard concludes that although comedians are not revolutionaries, the revolution must be funny.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
kierkegaard-stages.title: Conclusion
kierkegaard-stages.relation: William Irwin argues Kramer is Kierkegaard's aesthete par excellence: his endless abandoned schemes (make-your-own-pizza, beach-smelling cologne, Kramerica Industries), his aliases (H.E. Pennypacker, Dr. Van Nostrand), and his 'Kavorka' revolving door of women enact Either/Or's 'crop rotation' method and the Diary of the Seducer, all flight from the despair hinted at in 'The Switch' ('All this time I'm trying not to be me'). His brief office job in 'The Bizarro Jerry' - 'structure... TCB, taking care of business' - is a flirtation with Judge William's ethical stage of commitment, and Irwin closes with a thought experiment: could Kramer ever make the leap of faith to the religious stage, performing his own teleological suspension of the ethical like Abraham?

kierkegaard-stages.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
kierkegaard-stages.title: U2 and Philosophy
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
kierkegaard-stages.title: James Bond and Philosophy
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Butterfield takes Bond's answer to Elektra in The World Is Not Enough - he survives by 'tak[ing] pleasure in great beauty' - and asks whether hedonism can answer the problem of suffering and death. She reads Bond through Heidegger's being-towards-death (quoting Live and Let Die's 'You start to die the moment you are born'), then diagnoses him as Kierkegaard's aesthetic 'seducer', an immature escapist who dreads boredom and flees commitment, before rehabilitating him with Nietzsche and Camus: Bond flushing the cyanide pill down the toilet in From Russia with Love and Mathis's advice in Casino Royale to make evil 'personal' show Bond creating his own values beyond good and evil, surviving the absurd through style and personal vendetta. Bond emerges as an existentialist role model for courage and creativity, though we should not copy his hedonism or lawlessness.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
kierkegaard-stages.title: Stop That Persistent Clicking
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Paul Brown argues that Warcraft II begins by saving the player from boredom and ends by offering something like eternal happiness. Kierkegaard's 'rotation of crops' from Either/Or explains why Medivh and the Orcs grow bored into war and how console play relieves the living room's intellectual dead zone, with Heidegger supplying the definition of boredom; Nietzsche's will to power accounts both for the player's overt domination of peasants and sheep ('Stop that persistent clicking') and for the sublimated, ascetic self-overcoming of mastering the game, which Maslow redescribes as growth-needs and peak experiences. Kierkegaard's third, religious existence stage — subjective faith giving 'eternal happiness' — is playfully applied to becoming 'contemporary' with the game itself.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
kierkegaard-stages.title: Girls and Philosophy
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Keszeg first maps Sex and the City's four women onto classic fashion theories - Barthes's fashion system for Carrie, Carlyle's clothing morality for Samantha, Spencer's evolutionary equity for Charlotte, Veblen and Simmel's status signaling for Miranda - then argues Girls' four break these inherited codes. Marnie's perfectly status-calibrated outfits fall into 'complete freefall' with her life; Jessa wears bohemian otherness (Yves Saint-Laurent, 'Down with the Ritz - long live the street'); Shoshanna embodies the Kierkegaardian aesthetic stage of shifting, consequence-free equivocation ('I think it's time to unchoose some of those choices'); and Hannah's one-piece pyjamas, worn outside, invent a 'sophomoric dress' that negates the fashion system entirely - the generational attitude (via Mannheim) the show both celebrates and satirizes.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
kierkegaard-stages.title: Dracula and Philosophy
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Pramik maps Kierkegaard's three stages from Either/Or and Stages on Life's Way onto the novel: Dracula lives the aesthetic stage of pleasure and possessive power (imprisoning Harker in the castle, refusing to let the brides feed on him), Harker the anxious ethical stage of moral rules and guilt, and Van Helsing the religious stage of faith 'by virtue of the absurd' - trusting God to do the impossible through crucifixes, garlic, and the beheading of Lucy. Against Seward's doubting questions about these absurd tactics, she argues that Van Helsing's renewed, tested faith proves itself and makes him the book's real hero, since neither pleasure nor ethics alone defeats Dracula or gives life meaning.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
kierkegaard-stages.title: 10. On “Crying Like a Bitch”
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Roberto Sirvent and Joel Avery read Louie through Kierkegaard's claim that wherever there is contradiction the comical is present: Louie is a walking contradiction - the devoted dad who does masturbation bits - and the show stages incongruities like the homeless man showering behind a subway violinist and the decapitation in an episode called 'Bummer/Blueberries.' Kierkegaard's aesthetic sphere maps both of Louie's failures in 'Something Is Wrong' and 'Moving': the instant-gratification aesthete (the impulse motorcycle, the unaffordable townhouse fantasy) and the overthinking aesthete who cannot break up with his girlfriend or park his car, while his girlfriend shows what it is to actually choose and act. Eddie, who spits abstract truths but does nothing with them, 'plays Hegel to Louie's Kierkegaard,' embodying the gap between abstract philosophizing and lived existence that Kierkegaard attacked in Hegelianism. The closing distinction between irony (spotting the contradiction) and comedy (living with its permanent implications) is what Louis's Conan confession - crying like a bitch and finding happiness rushing in to meet the sadness - gets right.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
kierkegaard-stages.title: 9. When Jumpin’ Jack Flash Met Ziggy Stardust
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Auxier reads the 1973 Jagger-Bowie intimacy and rivalry ethically: Keith Richards's portrait of Mick's envy frames Kierkegaard's Either/Or warning against the aesthetic life and the Kantian morality-duty wedding Bowie fled, against Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity, which demands that one own one's freely chosen hollowing-out without appeal to any authority. Beauvoir's bad faith and authenticity then explain the outcome - Bowie beat Jagger by killing Ziggy, firing the Spiders, and finally making his very death a persona ('authentically Bowie'), while Jagger, forever only the Stones' singer, can respond only in bad faith, because 'hell is other people': each glimpsed the faker in the other.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
kierkegaard-stages.title: 7. Why Deadpool Isn’t a Hero (Yet )
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Matthew Brake maps Deadpool onto Kierkegaard's three spheres (aesthetic, ethical, religious) and argues Wade is stuck in the boundary zone of humor between the ethical and the religious: his comedy sees the contradictions between everyday life and the heroic ideal but revokes suffering in jest, instead of embracing it as essential the way the religious hero does. Spider-Man is the contrast case—wisecracking as the incognito of inner suffering over Uncle Ben and Norman Osborn—while Deadpool's healing factor and knowledge of his own fictionality let him laugh off decapitation ('RESPAWN. LOL') and regress from every heroic step. The chapter ends with Wade's plan to earn heroism in Spider-Man/Deadpool #1 undercut by his taking a contract on Peter Parker.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
kierkegaard-stages.title: 8. Believing the Impossible in a World of Compromise
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Brake maps Kierkegaard's spheres onto the rivals: Tony inhabits the ethical sphere of universal reason and compromise (Ross's 'that's how the world works', the tragic hero choosing lesser evils), while Steve lives the religious sphere of faith in the impossible - 'my faith's in people'. Through Fear and Trembling's Abraham, the comic Civil War (Tony manipulating Spider-Man, Steve's Japanese-internment warning), and Hickman's incursions where Steve alone tells the calculating Illuminati to believe, he argues a hero is judged by how he begins in faith, not by results. Steve's trust that the world can be saved 'by the absurd' is vindicated when Secret Wars restores the multiverse, and his simple 'I believe you' rescues Tony in Avengers Disassembled.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
kierkegaard-stages.title: 4. Scoundrels, the Lot of Us
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
kierkegaard-stages.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Karavitis sorts TZ episodes into three types — nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'Walking Distance,' 'The Incredible World of Horace Ford'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), and second chances ('Mr. Bevis,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil') — to argue that the past is unalterable and that only moving forward, knowing yourself well enough to use it, earns a do-over. Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-fulfilling Hell and Jesse Cardiff's eternity in the pool hall embody the aesthetic stage's repetitive despair, while Douglas Winter's renunciation of his Devil's contract in 'Printer's Devil' shows the transition to the ethical stage of taking responsibility for one's actions.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
kierkegaard-stages.title: 18. K’s Most Excellent Kierkegaardian Pilgrimage
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Ben Franz runs K and Luv through Kierkegaard's Either/Or and Fear and Trembling. Luv is the Knight of Faith, an Abraham whose total devotion to her god Wallace involves the teleological suspension of the ethical — killing the Rachael copy, torturing Joshi — and who dies, film-noir fashion, for failing her creator's command. K is the Knight of Infinite Resignation, repeatedly raised to believe he is special and repeatedly deflated — the wooden horse date, the nursemaid's denial, Joi's death — until he resigns himself to faking Deckard's death and reuniting father and daughter; in the noir inversion, the villain has perfect faith and the hero never attains it.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
kierkegaard-stages.title: 19. Thanos Is No Abraham
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Uses Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling to compare Thanos's killing of Gamora on Mount Vormir with Abraham's binding of Isaac, laying out the aesthetic, ethical, and religious stages. It argues Thanos initially looks 'religious' — his sacrifice expresses a particular, personal encounter with the absolute balance of all things, neither an aesthetic whim nor an ethical calculation — but that his Endgame slip ('what I'm about to do to your stubborn, annoying little planet… I'm gonna enjoy it. Very, very much') exposes him as a mere aesthete dressing bloodlust in metaphysics. Hence Thanos is no Abraham, and the truly religious type remains a frightening but unrealized possibility.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
kierkegaard-stages.title: Rafiki Holds the Mirror Up to Nature
kierkegaard-stages.relation: The chapter reads The Lion King as a Disney retelling of Hamlet: Scar's murder of Mufasa parallels Claudius, and Simba's guilt-ridden exile acts out Hamlet's 'to be or not to be.' Timon and Pumbaa's 'hakuna matata' is Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage of pleasure without commitment, which Simba must leave for the ethical stage when Nala, Rafiki ('Whooo are you?'), and Mufasa's ghost demand he 'remember who you are.' Sartre's 'optimistic toughness' and Nietzsche's 'Become who you are' frame Simba's defiant 'I am' before the assembled Pride Lands as existential self-creation.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
kierkegaard-stages.title: Existential Values
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Belliotti tests Roger Sterling against three existential standards. Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage fits him 'crisply': his quips about the chase, drinking 'because it's what men do,' and the penny-jar view of marriage reveal flight from commitment and terror of boredom, and even his twenty-year marriage to Mona lacked Kierkegaard's passionate inwardness, making it objectively true but existentially inauthentic. Measured by Nietzsche he falls between the last man who wants an agency 'where everybody has a summer house' and the will-to-power grand transcender he never becomes, oscillating between frustration and boredom; measured by Heidegger he settles for chatter, clings to fixity, and reflects on mortality only briefly after his heart attacks. The verdict: significantly inauthentic, capped by the blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' serenade that makes Don whisper 'Can we go?'

kierkegaard-stages.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
kierkegaard-stages.title: Notes
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
kierkegaard-stages.title: Purpose or Futility
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Tiernan reads Din Djarin as an Abraham figure from Fear and Trembling: like Kierkegaard's knight of faith, he teleologically suspends the ethical when he surrenders Grogu to the Jedi despite paternal attachment, just as Abraham consented to sacrifice Isaac. The chapter maps his journey onto Kierkegaard's three stages - the aesthetic temptation of settling down with Omera on Sorgan, the ethical duty of the Resol'nare and the Way, and the religious leap of faith in which purpose is regained by being given up. To become a true Mandalorian he must paradoxically abandon the creed that defines him, twice removing the helmet he swore never to remove - for the Morak facial scan and to bid Grogu farewell.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
kierkegaard-stages.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Karavitis sorts episodes into three types to show that the past is dead and only moving forward counts: nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'A Stop at Willoughby,' 'Walking Distance'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past,' where every attempt to fix history fails), and granted second chances ('A Nice Place to Visit,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil'). Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-factory and Jesse Cardiff's poolhall limbo depict the aesthetic stage's despair, while Douglas Winter taking responsibility for his pact shows the ethical stage. Second chances succeed only for those who, in Kierkegaard's words, live life forwards.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
kierkegaard-stages.title: P A R T F O U R
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Four Part Four essays beyond ethics. Aaron Meskin asks whether Watchmen is literature at all, testing definitions from Beardsley, Eagleton, Lamarque/Olsen and Hirsch in the Socratic 'what is X?' way, and concludes the question is indeterminate because comics are a hybrid art form — though the book's literary allusions (Shelley's 'Ozymandias,' Blake's 'Tyger,' Burroughs) deserve literary appreciation regardless. Sarah Donovan and Nick Richardson read the two Silk Spectres through three feminisms: Sally and Laurie as liberal feminists (Wollstonecraft, Mill) who fight crime, their hypersexual costumes as Irigaray-style subversive mimicry of gender stereotypes that risks reinforcing them (the Silhouette's expulsion exposing the heterosexual norm), the Comedian's attempted rape exposing 'she asked for it' attitudes, and Laurie as Beauvoir's woman in bad faith, living out her mother's fantasies until she finally names and dresses herself. Robert Arp uses Hooded Justice and Captain Metropolis's closeted relationship to dismantle 'homosexuality is unnatural' arguments — the ideal-function view would condemn the infertile too, and Hume's is-ought point undermines the procreation argument — before defending gay marriage against slippery-slope and parenting objections. Taneli Kukkonen maps Kierkegaard's stages onto the Comedian's mocking irony (hiding even his paternity of Laurie and his Kennedy confession as jokes) and Rorschach's deeper humor of the ethical stage, a knight of resignation whose 'never compromise, not even in the face of Armageddon' expects nothing back from the world.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
kierkegaard-stages.title: Philosophies of Comedy in O Brother, Where Art Thou
kierkegaard-stages.relation: McFarland explains the comedy of O Brother through Bergson's 'mechanical encrusted on the living' (the chain-gang pratfall where McGill forgets he is shackled, the toon-like plasticity of the escapees) and Kierkegaard's account of the comic as unresolved contradiction, like men bustling on a sinking ship. He argues the Klan-rally set piece refuses Jamesonian 'pastiche' by grounding its Wizard-of-Oz and Odyssey allusions in real historical guilt, forcing the postmodern aesthete-viewer, as in Kierkegaard's Either/Or, from the aesthetic to the ethical stage. The subverted ending—Penny rejecting the non-bona-fide ring—enacts Kierkegaard's view that marriage is comic because it 'binds' time and acknowledges contradiction rather than resolving it.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
kierkegaard-stages.title: From Dollars to Iron The Currency of Clint Eastwood's Westerns
kierkegaard-stages.relation: McNaron traces Clint Eastwood's evolving western hero from the amoral 'Man with No Name' to The Outlaw Josey Wales, using Will Wright's plot typology plus Nietzsche, Aristotle, and Kierkegaard. He reads the Eastwood antihero's 'manly nihilism' and prizing of strength and style through Nietzsche's master/slave morality and perspectivism, his virtues (self-control, phronesis) through Aristotle, and his elevation of the aesthetic over the ethical/religious against Kierkegaard's stages. The film's central claim—that only words with 'iron' behind them (Josey and Ten Bears's pact) can found genuine community, unlike government's 'double tongues'—grounds a transcendental argument about the conditions for authentic community and justified vengeance.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
kierkegaard-stages.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
kierkegaard-stages.relation: Karavitis groups twist-ending episodes into nostalgia, time-travel, and second-chance types and reads them through Kierkegaard's Either/Or distinction between the aesthetic and ethical modes of life. Living aesthetically—chasing present gratification—leads to despair, as in 'A Nice Place to Visit' (Rocky's boring 'heaven' is Hell) and 'A Game of Pool' (Jesse wins only an eternity in Limbo). Living ethically—taking responsibility and moving forward—earns a real second chance, as when 'Printer's Devil' editor Winter reclaims his soul; life must be understood backward but lived forward.

kierkegaard-stages.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
kierkegaard-stages.title: 6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife
kierkegaard-stages.relation: The chapter asks whether Doctor Who is a religion, testing it against Hopfe's and Ninian Smart's criteria and concluding it is best understood as a Humanist-and-religious 'philosophy'—sacred and 'holy' (Otto) but lacking a genuine transcendent 'unseen.' On loss, it uses Kierkegaard's 'aesthetic life' and 'rotation method' to explain why we fear endings and regenerations, urging viewers to root life in lasting meaning rather than fleeting pleasure. On death, it deploys Socrates in the Apology and Phaedo and Aristotle on courage (Jabe, Harriet Jones, Donna sacrificing themselves) to argue death is nothing to fear, and reads the Matrix and Nethersphere as the show's two Socratic afterlife options.

leap-of-faith.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
leap-of-faith.title: Conclusion
leap-of-faith.relation: William Irwin argues Kramer is Kierkegaard's aesthete par excellence: his endless abandoned schemes (make-your-own-pizza, beach-smelling cologne, Kramerica Industries), his aliases (H.E. Pennypacker, Dr. Van Nostrand), and his 'Kavorka' revolving door of women enact Either/Or's 'crop rotation' method and the Diary of the Seducer, all flight from the despair hinted at in 'The Switch' ('All this time I'm trying not to be me'). His brief office job in 'The Bizarro Jerry' - 'structure... TCB, taking care of business' - is a flirtation with Judge William's ethical stage of commitment, and Irwin closes with a thought experiment: could Kramer ever make the leap of faith to the religious stage, performing his own teleological suspension of the ethical like Abraham?

leap-of-faith.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
leap-of-faith.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: John Davenport argues that The Lord of the Rings is neither mere adventure nor Christian allegory but an epic fairy tale whose 'eucatastrophe' - Tolkien's term for the sudden joyous turn, a miraculous reprieve - carries religious hope even though the book contains no churches or prayers. Drawing on Tolkien's 'On Fairy-stories', he makes Sir Gawain and the Green Knight the model for Frodo: Gawain accepts the girdle and is scarred yet reprieved, just as Frodo claims the Ring, loses a finger as Beren lost a hand, and is saved only because the mercy shown Gollum lets the Ring fall into the fire. Gandalf's return, Éowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth extend the pattern; with Kierkegaard the deliverance is grace 'by virtue of the absurd', an echo of the eschaton answering Boethius's question whether our struggles have final significance.

leap-of-faith.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
leap-of-faith.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.

leap-of-faith.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
leap-of-faith.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: Irwin takes Pilate's Quid est veritas as a guided tour of theories of truth applied to the film: Gibson's sympathetic Pilate embodies relativism, met with Nietzsche's 'truth is a woman' perspectivism and Baudrillard's postmodern laughter and rejected; Caiaphas and the bad thief demanding Jesus come down from the cross put the correspondence theory to work ('the proof is out there'), though beliefs hang on other beliefs ad infinitum; Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction models the coherence theory, exposed as necessary but not sufficient by Swinburne's case for versus Wells's case against the divinity of Jesus; and Pilate's Barabbas gambit parodies James's pragmatic theory, where working is not enough if there is no corresponding reality. He then retrieves Heidegger's reading of aletheia as uncovering, helped by the Quid est veritas anagram ('Est qui vir adest': it is the man before you) and Gadamer on truth seizing us like beauty, so that Jesus's 'I am the truth' and Claudia's dream-guided warnings point to truth as disclosure. Since disclosure alone cannot decide between inconsistent revealed claims, Irwin ends by leaving the viewer with a leap of faith and a first instinct as final answer.

leap-of-faith.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
leap-of-faith.title: The Ends of Despair From “Things Have Changed” to “Love and Theft”
leap-of-faith.relation: Rick Furtak traces an existential arc through Dylan's later albums, reading Blood on the Tracks ("Tangled Up in Blue," "You're a Big Girl Now") as Camus's absurd divorce between a mind that cares and a world that has gone silent, and Heideggerian care as what the narrator loses in "Simple Twist of Fate." "Brownsville Girl" and "Most of the Time" embody Kierkegaard's knight of infinite resignation - hope abandoned but the precious past never forgotten - while "Not Dark Yet" and "Things Have Changed" mark the nadir of despair. On Love and Theft ("Mississippi," "Sugar Baby") the singer turns toward an absurd, Kierkegaardian faith that keeps caring and even loves without demanding that life make sense.

leap-of-faith.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
leap-of-faith.title: Poker and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: The editor's introduction stages poker and philosophy as twin crafts of risk: 'philosopher' was once slang for a card cheat, Socrates and Wild Bill Hickok both died for keeping villainous company, and the Buddha's six years to enlightenment are measured against the Birdcage Theater's eight-year poker game. It recruits Nietzsche's 'live dangerously' and Kierkegaard's leap of faith to defend the all-in as the only meaningful way to live, then traces probability from Cardano's Book on Games of Chance to Pascal's wager that believing in God is the smarter bet — the ancestor of today's pot-odds reasoning. Chris Ferguson's PhD, Annie Duke's psycholinguistics, and Jesse May's 'the trick to poker is mastering the luck — that's philosophy' set up the book's Texas Hold'em focus.

leap-of-faith.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
leap-of-faith.title: Poker and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.

leap-of-faith.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
leap-of-faith.title: U2 and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: Wrathall reads 'Vertigo' through Heidegger's vertigo-before-a-question and Kierkegaard's account of despair as the dizziness of a self whose sensual and spiritual sides are both essential. He uses rock's own testimony - Rammstein's 'Engel' and 'Sehnsucht', Nine Inch Nails' 'Down in It' - to confirm the existentialist thesis that neither flesh nor spirit can be renounced, with Pascal's God-shaped void as the diagnosis. He then argues that 'Beautiful Day', 'When I Look at the World', 'Grace' and 'Mysterious Ways' sketch an existential Christianity in which faith is not propositional confidence but a world-disclosing skill acquired like any know-how, and in which concrete erotic love ('if you want to kiss the sky, better learn how to kneel', the girl with crimson nails who 'has Jesus round her neck') discloses God on earth.

leap-of-faith.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
leap-of-faith.title: Reason to Believe When There’s None
leap-of-faith.relation: Couch takes a night drive through Springsteen's road songs guided by Karl Jaspers's 'ultimate situations' — death ('Wreck on the Highway,' the bottomless gorge under the cruise-controlled life), suffering (the never-ending badlands, shared in Tom Joad's ghost), struggle (violent like 'Johnny 99,' loving as the search for 'one clear moment of love and truth'), and guilt ('Everybody's got a secret, Sonny'; 'you learn to sleep at night with the price you pay'). Jaspers's Existenz-philosophy — built on Kierkegaard's inward self and Nietzsche's diagnosis of the herd, against Kant's optimism about knowledge — explains the songs' endless border-crossings as attempts to evade limits that cannot be evaded, and the fear that turns 'your God filled soul' to 'devils and dust.' The answer to how there's a 'Reason to Believe' is Jaspers's leap of philosophic (not religious) faith toward the unknowable Transcendent, chosen in complete freedom.

leap-of-faith.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
leap-of-faith.title: “Something to Believe In”
leap-of-faith.relation: Reads Worf's crisis over the clone 'second coming' of Kahless in 'Rightful Heir' as a live, forced, and momentous option in William James's sense, where 'faith creates its own verification.' Peirce's methods of fixing belief — tenacity, authority, and science — explain why Worf cannot accept Koroth's pious fraud once Gowron's DNA test exposes the clone, while Data's own 'leap of faith' in believing he is more than a machine supplies the Jamesian model of believing without evidence. Worf's compromise — telling the Klingon people the truth but installing Kahless-the-clone as spiritual emperor because 'the words are more important than the man' — is offered as pragmatist truth: what works while staying answerable to hard facts.

leap-of-faith.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
leap-of-faith.title: The Lesson
leap-of-faith.relation: Karolina Lewestam and Orla Richardson argue that the Red Sox fan is a moral hero in Kierkegaard's sense: like Abraham in Fear and Trembling, the fan fully accepts that loss is inevitable (the Curse, Aaron Boone, Buckner's grounder) yet refuses the rational course of infinite resignation and keeps believing 'this could be the year.' Where liberal individualism licenses walking away from any loyalty and the modern reflex is to sue luck out of existence, the fan lives at the mercy of fate and thereby enacts Kierkegaard's movement beyond resignation into true faith, the absurd belief against all evidence that Isaac will be spared. Fenway thus becomes the best university for learning to live fully under uncertainty, with Ortiz's 'keep the faith' speech and Schilling's bloody sock as its lessons in perseverance and courage.

leap-of-faith.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
leap-of-faith.title: Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox
leap-of-faith.relation: Lee casts pre-2004 fandom as a Kierkegaardian leap of faith ('We Believe') and the Curse of the Bambino as Schopenhauer's irrational deterministic will, with the 1918–2004 cycle of spring hope and October collapse as Camus's Sisyphus. But he argues fans are really existentialists: blaming losses on fate or the Curse is Sartrean bad faith that evades responsibility, since fans did hold Bill Buckner (1986 error) and Grady Little (leaving a spent Pedro in during 2003 ALCS Game 7) individually accountable. The 2004 and 2007 champions remain 'our' Red Sox because we freely choose to care about the team's journey, not because it has a fixed essence; a coda borrows Russell's point about ambiguous reference for the word 'Yankee,' and Andy Wasif's appendix runs Yankees-as-evil through relativism, objectivism and subjectivism.

leap-of-faith.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
leap-of-faith.title: Does the Totem Tumble
leap-of-faith.relation: Auxier brings Bergson's memory theory, the past gnawing into the present, all dreaming as remembering, and Whitehead's process philosophy to Nolan's 'pathologies of temporal experience', defending the film's supposedly selective physics: with each deeper level the same five minutes disperses across a larger dream space, diluting the carry-over of effects while time expands geometrically, because 'space is frozen time'. He then re-reads the ending through the narrative gaps the audience was lured across: the top was Mal's totem, which Cobb spin as an act of mourning after handling it and betraying her, and Cobb's real totem is his gun, which Saito uses to shoot them both out of Limbo. The top's tumbling in the finale matters only as a sign that Cobb, the coward who once needed total control over Mal, has finally learned the leap of faith of trusting another person.

leap-of-faith.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
leap-of-faith.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: The chapter diagnoses the show's identity crises through Heidegger's Being and Time: Marshall's Goliath National Bank drudgery is anxiety over thrownness - the rent, the bills, the situation he never chose - while Lily's prom-night bolt to San Francisco is anxiety over freedom and possibility, and both fail anticipatory resoluteness, the commitment to be yourself while shouldering what you did not choose. das Man ('everybody's doing it') explains the gang's absorbed everydayness. Kierkegaard supplies the problem of time (life understood backwards but lived forwards) and Fear and Trembling's contrast between Abraham's leap of faith into the absurd and the 'demonic': Barney courts legendary moments yet manipulates uncertainty so he never becomes anyone new - the identity crisis that never ends.

leap-of-faith.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
leap-of-faith.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.

leap-of-faith.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
leap-of-faith.title: Girls and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: Van Loon explains the q-tip scene ('On All Fours') as Kierkegaardian anxiety made flesh: freed by her parents and facing the e-book deadline, Hannah confronts the infinity of possibilities and, like Sartre's vertigo over the cliff, shoves the q-tip into her ear - embracing all possibilities at once and relapsing into bad faith by becoming a victim of fate. Each girl handles freedom differently: Shoshanna remains in an innocence prior to freedom, Jessa jokes her way out of seriousness, Marnie denies her anxiety. Against these, the Season Two FaceTime call to Adam models Kierkegaard's leap of faith and the 'knight of faith' - surrendering, making oneself vulnerable, and accepting that anxiety will return.

leap-of-faith.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
leap-of-faith.title: Justified and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: The chapter reads preacher Billy St. Cyr's snake-handling through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: like Abraham, Billy performs the absurd double movement - fully resigning himself to dying by rattlesnake while believing he will be spared - which is why Boyd Crowder, who abandoned faith for Hegel's objective rational certainty, can neither buy him out nor understand him. Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical explains why Billy and Abraham may set obedience to God above self-preservation and social morality, while Boyd's showdown in 'Truth and Consequences', where he hands Billy an un-milked rattlesnake, exposes that Billy's certainty has curdled into the hubris de Silentio warns against, so Billy is no Abraham. De Silentio's three marks - love, humility, no desire to instruct others - separate genuine faith from cult leaders and violent extremists.

leap-of-faith.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
leap-of-faith.title: Dracula and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: Pramik maps Kierkegaard's three stages from Either/Or and Stages on Life's Way onto the novel: Dracula lives the aesthetic stage of pleasure and possessive power (imprisoning Harker in the castle, refusing to let the brides feed on him), Harker the anxious ethical stage of moral rules and guilt, and Van Helsing the religious stage of faith 'by virtue of the absurd' - trusting God to do the impossible through crucifixes, garlic, and the beheading of Lucy. Against Seward's doubting questions about these absurd tactics, she argues that Van Helsing's renewed, tested faith proves itself and makes him the book's real hero, since neither pleasure nor ethics alone defeats Dracula or gives life meaning.

leap-of-faith.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
leap-of-faith.title: 21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero
leap-of-faith.relation: Devlin asks whether Stannis, who burns Shireen to save his army, is Kierkegaard's knight of faith or merely a tragic hero. Stannis's duty-obsessed deontology - knighting Davos while cutting off his fingertips, striking 'beloved brother' from a letter as a lie - is Kantian, and the Shireen dilemma looks like Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical; yet because Stannis always calculates and justifies ('Faith? In a real war, the side with the greater number wins nine times out of ten'), he never makes the leap on the strength of the absurd, and Davos ends up following Kant's own verdict on Abraham: 'If he commands you to burn children, your lord is evil.' He is therefore a tragic hero in the line of Agamemnon and Jephthah, rationally comprehensible and fittingly undone by Brienne's 'do your duty.'

leap-of-faith.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
leap-of-faith.title: 13. Linus’s Wager
leap-of-faith.relation: The chapter stages a three-way debate over whether Linus may believe in the Great Pumpkin without evidence. Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner whose wishful thinking sinks his ship) condemns Linus's sincerity-based wager; Pascal's Wager endorses it (forgoing one night of trick-or-treating costs nothing if the Pumpkin is fake and wins toys if he is real) but assumes a doxastic voluntarism we lack, since no one can make themselves believe for even a million-dollar reward. William James's 'The Will to Believe' gets the final word: if Linus's option is live, forced, and momentous with no decisive evidence either way, his leap of faith - like loving without guarantees - is morally justified whenever life would be greatly impoverished without it.

leap-of-faith.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
leap-of-faith.title: 7. Why Deadpool Isn’t a Hero (Yet )
leap-of-faith.relation: Matthew Brake maps Deadpool onto Kierkegaard's three spheres (aesthetic, ethical, religious) and argues Wade is stuck in the boundary zone of humor between the ethical and the religious: his comedy sees the contradictions between everyday life and the heroic ideal but revokes suffering in jest, instead of embracing it as essential the way the religious hero does. Spider-Man is the contrast case—wisecracking as the incognito of inner suffering over Uncle Ben and Norman Osborn—while Deadpool's healing factor and knowledge of his own fictionality let him laugh off decapitation ('RESPAWN. LOL') and regress from every heroic step. The chapter ends with Wade's plan to earn heroism in Spider-Man/Deadpool #1 undercut by his taking a contract on Peter Parker.

leap-of-faith.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
leap-of-faith.title: 8. Believing the Impossible in a World of Compromise
leap-of-faith.relation: Brake maps Kierkegaard's spheres onto the rivals: Tony inhabits the ethical sphere of universal reason and compromise (Ross's 'that's how the world works', the tragic hero choosing lesser evils), while Steve lives the religious sphere of faith in the impossible - 'my faith's in people'. Through Fear and Trembling's Abraham, the comic Civil War (Tony manipulating Spider-Man, Steve's Japanese-internment warning), and Hickman's incursions where Steve alone tells the calculating Illuminati to believe, he argues a hero is judged by how he begins in faith, not by results. Steve's trust that the world can be saved 'by the absurd' is vindicated when Secret Wars restores the multiverse, and his simple 'I believe you' rescues Tony in Avengers Disassembled.

leap-of-faith.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
leap-of-faith.title: 2. Dystopia from a Woman’s Point of View
leap-of-faith.relation: Robison-Greene reads The Handmaid's Tale as Atwood's answer to Nineteen Eighty-Four—a dystopia 'from the female point of view'—comparing how both regimes suppress critical thought by banning women's reading, rewriting texts (the Marx slogan 'from each according to her ability' passed off as St. Paul), and manufacturing perpetual war. She deploys Nietzsche's 'monumental' abuse of history, Kierkegaard's leap of faith (Offred's three contradictory versions of Luke's fate), and doublethink to show that believing contradictions becomes both the regime's tool and the victim's survival strategy. The woman's lens adds that reducing women to reproductive function (Marthas, Aunts, Jezebels) thrives where thinking is suppressed, that Beauvoir's point about women's complicity in their oppression is embodied by the Aunts, and that Offred and Nick's affair, like Winston and Julia's, is the act of freedom the Party can never quite own.

leap-of-faith.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
leap-of-faith.title: 12. Why Blood Sacrifice
leap-of-faith.relation: Philip Wilson defines sacrifice as gift-giving with payback ('I give x in order to get y') and reads Thanos's murder of Gamora through Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, while Black Widow's willing leap from the same cliff parallels Christ's atoning self-sacrifice. The core is Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Abraham's binding of Isaac as the 'teleological suspension of the ethical,' where obeying God suspends universal morality, sharpened by Kant's argument that Abraham should have told the supposed divine voice he could never be certain it came from God. Wilson argues the films restore rather than suspend ethics, Gamora was murdered rather than sacrificed, Natasha died willingly with no collateral harm, and Tony's final 'I am Iron Man' self-sacrifice completes the tragic arc, leaving readers with Kierkegaard's sleepless questions about a moral order that demands blood.

leap-of-faith.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
leap-of-faith.title: 19. Thanos Is No Abraham
leap-of-faith.relation: Uses Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling to compare Thanos's killing of Gamora on Mount Vormir with Abraham's binding of Isaac, laying out the aesthetic, ethical, and religious stages. It argues Thanos initially looks 'religious' — his sacrifice expresses a particular, personal encounter with the absolute balance of all things, neither an aesthetic whim nor an ethical calculation — but that his Endgame slip ('what I'm about to do to your stubborn, annoying little planet… I'm gonna enjoy it. Very, very much') exposes him as a mere aesthete dressing bloodlust in metaphysics. Hence Thanos is no Abraham, and the truly religious type remains a frightening but unrealized possibility.

leap-of-faith.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
leap-of-faith.title: Paradox and Peace
leap-of-faith.relation: Christopher Drohan reads Batman and Alfred through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Batman, like Abraham, believes 'by virtue of the absurd,' resigning himself to an infinite, never-realizable justice as a knight of infinite resignation, while Alfred embodies the higher knight of faith whose justice is concrete love expressed in mending the suit, making sandwiches, and guarding the manor. Heidegger's thrownness and Sartre's condemned freedom frame both men's absurd existential condition, including Batman sparing Joe Chill and even allying with him against the Reaper. The chapter's verdict is that Alfred's faithful devotion to one person is the superior ethic, and that peace begins with him.

leap-of-faith.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
leap-of-faith.title: Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually
leap-of-faith.relation: The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'

leap-of-faith.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
leap-of-faith.title: Does the Totem Tumble
leap-of-faith.relation: Randall Auxier claims to settle whether the totem tumbles: it does, but it does not matter, because the top was Mal's totem rather than Cobb's — Cobb spins it as mourning for the wife whose trust he destroyed by handling her totem, while Cobb's real totem is the gun, which Saito must use (shooting them both in Limbo) once Cobb finally takes the leap of faith and entrusts his life to another person. Building on Bergson's memory theory — the past 'gnaws into the future,' all dreaming is remembering, and shared dreaming is possible because embodied species-memory can be tapped with the right chemist — the chapter recasts Cobb's rule against building from memory as the need to introduce gaps between dream and world, and his inability to keep architecting as personal memory increasingly overrunning perception with age. Through Whitehead's process philosophy — narrative as algebraic order, space as 'frozen time,' generic contrasts like 'and then I ate it' — he also defends the film's 'selective physics': at each level the same five minutes disperses across a larger dreamspace, diluting the gravitational carryover while geometrically expanding dream time.

leap-of-faith.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
leap-of-faith.title: Introduction “Indiana Jones—I Always Knew Some Day You’d Come Walking Back through My Door. I Never Doubted Th
leap-of-faith.relation: Dean Kowalski's introduction uses the iconic theme music and Ford's underplaying of heroism to argue that Indy is expressive of the human condition: he loses fights, doesn't always choose wisely, and persists for decades despite unrequited love, estrangement from his father, and repeated failures. It poses the questions the volume pursues through the films — whether Indy should take a leap of faith about the supernatural events he witnesses, why artifacts belong in a museum, and what his 'fact, not truth' lecture (and the real Dr. Tyree 'right down the hall') means.

leap-of-faith.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
leap-of-faith.title: 6 The Absurd Hero Indiana Jones, God, and Sisyphus
leap-of-faith.relation: Justin Fetterman takes the Big Bang Theory objection seriously — Indy is superfluous in Raiders and loses nearly every artifact he chases — diagnosing him first with Kierkegaard's despair of possibility from The Sickness Unto Death, where each failure only convinces him success lies just ahead. But Indy refuses Kierkegaard's leap of faith even after witnessing Shiva's Sankara Stones and the Ark, since multiple gods' demonstrations cancel any single revelation, and Kierkegaard demands faith without comprehension. The chapter then re-reads him through Camus: like Sisyphus he repeats near-identical quests (Raiders and Crusade both have him lead the Nazis to a Judeo-Christian relic that destroys them), and his value lies in 'the most living' and the struggle itself, making him an absurd hero rather than a failed believer.

leap-of-faith.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
leap-of-faith.title: 15 Indiana Jones and the Leap of Faith
leap-of-faith.relation: Uses Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling to argue that Indy's step off the lion's head in Last Crusade is not a genuine leap of faith: Abraham's leap rests on absurd trust in God and the 'teleological suspension of the ethical,' whereas Indy acts to save his father and risks arming the Nazis — making him at most a tragic hero choosing between competing ethical duties. The chapter then sorts the film's believers into Kierkegaard's two knights, classifying Kazim of the Brotherhood as a Knight of Infinite Resignation, the Grail Knight as a near-miss Knight of Faith (he guards rather than lives in the ordinary world), and Henry and Marcus as devout but neither. Kierkegaard would complain that modern faith is 'dirt cheap' compared with Abraham's arduous biblical faith, and Indy's relief at not falling confirms he is no Knight of Faith.

leap-of-faith.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
leap-of-faith.title: It Worked
leap-of-faith.relation: Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.

leap-of-faith.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
leap-of-faith.title: NOTES
leap-of-faith.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost through C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory - the Lamp Post station and flight 316 (the Prince Caspian dedication page) wink at the source - with the island, like Narnia, a world of crisis and second chances entered by plane crash instead of wardrobe. Flashbacks of past failures (Kate the fugitive, Sayid the torturer, Charlie's addiction, Locke's kidney con) set up struggles for faith that he illuminates with H. Richard Niebuhr on faith as a center of value and revelation as communal, and with Levinas's claim that we become ourselves only through responsibility to the Other in community. The Jack-versus-Locke man-of-science/man-of-faith debate, Charlie's moth-cocoon trial, and Jacob and the Man in Black's black-and-white stone game map onto Aslan versus the White Witch, ending in redemption through the new community and Jack's sacrificial death.

leap-of-faith.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
leap-of-faith.title: Notes
leap-of-faith.relation: Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.

leap-of-faith.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
leap-of-faith.title: Purpose or Futility
leap-of-faith.relation: Tiernan reads Din Djarin as an Abraham figure from Fear and Trembling: like Kierkegaard's knight of faith, he teleologically suspends the ethical when he surrenders Grogu to the Jedi despite paternal attachment, just as Abraham consented to sacrifice Isaac. The chapter maps his journey onto Kierkegaard's three stages - the aesthetic temptation of settling down with Omera on Sorgan, the ethical duty of the Resol'nare and the Way, and the religious leap of faith in which purpose is regained by being given up. To become a true Mandalorian he must paradoxically abandon the creed that defines him, twice removing the helmet he swore never to remove - for the Morak facial scan and to bid Grogu farewell.

leap-of-faith.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
leap-of-faith.title: Two Ways of Enduring the Flames The Existential Dialectics of Love in Kierkegaard and Bukowski
leap-of-faith.relation: Andreas Seland argues that Kierkegaard and Bukowski offer opposed responses to a Romantic 'paradox of love': the beloved is a dialectical object, part inner imago (Shelley's veiled maid in 'Alastor,' Stendhal's crystallization, Lacan/Zizek) and part uncontrollable external person, and this gap breeds despair. Kierkegaard's Knight of Faith in Fear and Trembling resolves it by infinite resignation and the absurd leap, internalizing the gap and severing the tie to the real to love the princess only interiorly. Bukowski's Chinaski in Women does the opposite, deliberately choosing unstable 'Lydia-object' women who embody the gap, seeking the insecurity itself as a line of flight beyond bourgeois love and even beyond himself.

leap-of-faith.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
leap-of-faith.title: Inconclusive Unscientific Postscript Late Remarks on Kierkegaard and Kaufman
leap-of-faith.relation: LaRocca pairs Kaufman with Kierkegaard on anxiety as the constitutive human condition—not worry but 'the dizziness of freedom,' the awareness of radical possibility. He argues both use pseudonymity and 'indirect communication' to distance author from work so the audience confronts its own individuality: Kierkegaard's Haufniensis/Climacus, Kaufman's Caden Cotard and the character 'Charlie Kaufman' in Adaptation. The chapter analyzes acting as inhabitation vs. impersonation (Being John Malkovich vs. The Talented Mr. Ripley), the diegesis/mimesis layering (Plato and Aristotle) of Kaufman's doubles and replicas, and repetition/recursion as the Kierkegaardian leap that love, like faith, demands—so 'the end is built into the beginning.'

leap-of-faith.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
leap-of-faith.title: Carnivale Knowledge: Give Me That Old-time Noir Religion
leap-of-faith.relation: Eric Bronson argues that Carnivale invents a 'religious noir' tradition in which Brother Justin's crisis of faith in the Dust Bowl 1930s replays the Christian existentialism of Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky. Sitting in the ruins of his burnt church, Justin recites Genesis 22 (the sacrifice of Isaac) and demands God explain why his orphans died, directly invoking Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: faith is impossible and absurd, and the crushing struggle itself makes life worth living. Ivan Karamazov's 'returning the ticket' over the suffering of children parallels Justin's fury at a silent God, while the carnies' Babylon storyline (Samson sparing the confessed killer under the carnival code, then secretly shooting him) and the inescapable dead souls echo Sartre's 'condemned to life' and the noir hero's inability to escape fate.

leap-of-faith.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
leap-of-faith.title: False Tattoos and Failed Totems
leap-of-faith.relation: Karen Hoffman reads Memento and Inception through Kierkegaard's Concluding Unscientific Postscript: Leonard's tattoos and Cobb's totems both fail to supply the objective certainty their owners expect, forcing each to confront subjective truth, 'an objective uncertainty held fast through appropriation with the most passionate inwardness.' She argues Leonard fails Kierkegaard's test twice over - he treats his facts-based system as objective knowledge, and his real commitment is to playing detective rather than catching a killer (Teddy: 'You don't want the truth. You make up your own truth'), culminating in the knowingly false tattoo that arranges Teddy's murder. Cobb, by contrast, faces his memories of Mal, accepts objective uncertainty, takes Saito's 'leap of faith,' and in the final scene walks away from the spinning top, choosing the world that reunites him with his children - an idea that sticks because of how he lives it, not because it is objectively true.

leap-of-faith.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
leap-of-faith.title: 11. An Interstellar Leap of Faith
leap-of-faith.relation: Barta and Lee read Seldon's Plan as a providence narrative and stage a three-way debate over it. Hegel's dialectical, Spirit-driven history (thesis-antithesis-synthesis, even yielding 'psycho-history' as a synthesis) is mirrored in the Foundation's succession of ruling crises and its Encyclopedia Galactica as absolute knowledge. Kierkegaard's leap of faith describes how Foundationists obey a plan they cannot see and whose Vault confirms only in hindsight, an ignorance the Plan actually requires (an observer effect). Marx's materialist dialectic appears in Hober Mallow's 'historic forces' and the priesthood of the Galactic Spirit as ideological control, but the authors argue the Foundationists' sincere faith in Seldon nests all critiques back inside a Hegelian providence.

leap-of-faith.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
leap-of-faith.title: It Worked
leap-of-faith.relation: Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.

leap-of-faith.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
leap-of-faith.title: BLUES
leap-of-faith.relation: Joseph Lynch uses Son House's 'Preachin' the Blues' — a fallen preacher who preaches the blues, not the gospel — to explore the tension between blues sensuality and religion, arguing the expression of suffering is itself liberation from it. He reads Marx's 'religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature' as making the blues a heart of a heartless world that voices and eases alienated labor; the Buddha's Four Noble Truths and impermanence as embracing suffering to be freed from craving; and Kierkegaard's passionate leap of faith, born of doubt and despair and contrasted with Hume, as the model for how blues 'preachers' like Son House and Robert Johnson embrace the absurd contradiction of embodied spirituality.

leap-of-faith.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
leap-of-faith.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
leap-of-faith.relation: John Davenport argues The Lord of the Rings is religious not as Christian allegory but as an epic fairy tale in Tolkien's sense from 'On Fairy-stories,' delivering 'eucatastrophe,' the sudden joyous turn that, like Kierkegaard's faith in a salvation beyond our own power, hints at eschatological hope. Using Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as Tolkien's model for Frodo (both accept an impossible burden, both fail and bear a scar of mortality), he identifies the destruction of the Ring via Gollum, Eowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth as eucatastrophic 'turns.' Davenport concludes the veiled religious message is that evil cannot stand forever, yet deliverance requires our sacrifice and faith beyond rational hope that 'day shall come again.'

leap-of-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
leap-of-faith.title: 31. Inception as Philosophy Choose Your Dreams or Seek Reality
leap-of-faith.relation: Johnson uses Nolan's Inception—Cobb's dream-heists, the ambiguous spinning top, and the case that the whole film may be a dream—to test the moral Todd McGowan draws from it: that since we can't be sure what is real, we should abandon the quest for reality and choose the dream (his object of desire, his children) as Cobb does at the end. He evaluates six defenses of that moral, rejecting Descartes' skeptical dream/evil-demon problem (answered by abduction and by Plato's cave and Nozick's experience machine showing true belief is valuable), Baudrillard's denial of reality, Locke/Kant on the unknowable noumenal world, and Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Pascal's Wager, before softening it with Hume's return from skepticism to backgammon: entertain the doubt, then walk away when your children walk in.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
kierkegaard-despair.title: Conclusion
kierkegaard-despair.relation: William Irwin argues Kramer is Kierkegaard's aesthete par excellence: his endless abandoned schemes (make-your-own-pizza, beach-smelling cologne, Kramerica Industries), his aliases (H.E. Pennypacker, Dr. Van Nostrand), and his 'Kavorka' revolving door of women enact Either/Or's 'crop rotation' method and the Diary of the Seducer, all flight from the despair hinted at in 'The Switch' ('All this time I'm trying not to be me'). His brief office job in 'The Bizarro Jerry' - 'structure... TCB, taking care of business' - is a flirtation with Judge William's ethical stage of commitment, and Irwin closes with a thought experiment: could Kramer ever make the leap of faith to the religious stage, performing his own teleological suspension of the ethical like Abraham?

kierkegaard-despair.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
kierkegaard-despair.title: The Ends of Despair From “Things Have Changed” to “Love and Theft”
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Rick Furtak traces an existential arc through Dylan's later albums, reading Blood on the Tracks ("Tangled Up in Blue," "You're a Big Girl Now") as Camus's absurd divorce between a mind that cares and a world that has gone silent, and Heideggerian care as what the narrator loses in "Simple Twist of Fate." "Brownsville Girl" and "Most of the Time" embody Kierkegaard's knight of infinite resignation - hope abandoned but the precious past never forgotten - while "Not Dark Yet" and "Things Have Changed" mark the nadir of despair. On Love and Theft ("Mississippi," "Sugar Baby") the singer turns toward an absurd, Kierkegaardian faith that keeps caring and even loves without demanding that life make sense.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
kierkegaard-despair.title: U2 and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Wrathall's introduction argues U2 is philosophically interesting because its enormous popularity holds up a mirror to what 'we' care about (by Nietzsche's test of how a culture stands toward life) and because the band publicly wrestles with the contradictions of the technological-global economy: unprecedented freedom of choice paired with loss of rooted identity, and distant suffering ('Crumbs from Your Table') that we feel both powerless to fix and responsible for. Its showcase reading treats 'Miracle Drug' as a musical theodicy: Bono's plea 'God, I need your help tonight' is answered by the Edge's guitar and by the Matthew 25:35 refrain, so science and medicine count as works of Christian charity. The piece then frames the volume's essays: Plato's ascent of love in the early songs, Kierkegaardian despair after Achtung Baby, Bono's search for authentic identity, the simulacra of 'Even Better than the Real Thing', being-toward-death in the apocalyptic songs, and the Plato-versus-Aristotle quarrel over music's emotional power.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
kierkegaard-despair.title: U2 and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
kierkegaard-despair.title: U2 and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Wrathall reads 'Vertigo' through Heidegger's vertigo-before-a-question and Kierkegaard's account of despair as the dizziness of a self whose sensual and spiritual sides are both essential. He uses rock's own testimony - Rammstein's 'Engel' and 'Sehnsucht', Nine Inch Nails' 'Down in It' - to confirm the existentialist thesis that neither flesh nor spirit can be renounced, with Pascal's God-shaped void as the diagnosis. He then argues that 'Beautiful Day', 'When I Look at the World', 'Grace' and 'Mysterious Ways' sketch an existential Christianity in which faith is not propositional confidence but a world-disclosing skill acquired like any know-how, and in which concrete erotic love ('if you want to kiss the sky, better learn how to kneel', the girl with crimson nails who 'has Jesus round her neck') discloses God on earth.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
kierkegaard-despair.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Brittingham reads Klosterman's celebrity interviews through Kierkegaard's The Sickness unto Death, taking the self as a synthesis of the immediate and the symbolic, finite and infinite. Britney Spears, who claims never to have thought about the sexual iconography behind her curtain, embodies the despair of ignorance in not knowing one has a self; Bono, embarrassed by his messianic 1980s posturing and wishing to shed that iconic self while remaining 'self-conscious about being self-conscious', embodies despair at not willing to be oneself; Metallica's Some Kind of Monster breakdown, with rehab, a hired therapist, and Kirk Hammett dreading having to take out the trash, embodies defiant despair, the 'king without a country' who would be absolute master of himself. Jeff Tweedy's uncool acceptance of both his suburban dad-life and his silly symbolic persona, plus Kierkegaard's remedy of resting transparently in the power that established us, mark the only way to be 'for real' rather than full of shit.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
kierkegaard-despair.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
kierkegaard-despair.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Pardi argues Jobs lived philosophically as an existentialist: the 'Steve Jobs Roll Your Own Calculator Construction Set' anecdote shows design by touch and intuition rather than master plans, every detail of a product mattered because it belongs to a life narrative of 'making a ding in the universe,' and he avoided both Kierkegaard's despair (the gap between actual and possible self) and Sartrean bad faith—quoted from Being and Nothingness—by never lying to himself about his products, calling faulty work 'shit' and redoing it. Against him stands Bill Gates the pragmatist, whose utilitarian Windows-for-every-desk business and 'rationality only goes so far' humility embody William James's pragmatic method, while Jobs's Zune taunt ('we made the iPod for ourselves') shows the existentialist refusing to compromise authenticity for market share.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
kierkegaard-despair.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Karavitis sorts TZ episodes into three types — nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'Walking Distance,' 'The Incredible World of Horace Ford'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), and second chances ('Mr. Bevis,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil') — to argue that the past is unalterable and that only moving forward, knowing yourself well enough to use it, earns a do-over. Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-fulfilling Hell and Jesse Cardiff's eternity in the pool hall embody the aesthetic stage's repetitive despair, while Douglas Winter's renunciation of his Devil's contract in 'Printer's Devil' shows the transition to the ethical stage of taking responsibility for one's actions.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
kierkegaard-despair.title: 5. Horror Appeals to Our Dual Nature
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Allaire and Gehring argue horror works on Kierkegaard's dual nature, the tug-of-war between finitude and infinitude that produces despair: the show's corporeal terrors (the Demogorgon's kills, Barb's decomposing body with a slug in its mouth, Will's tentacle) trigger the fear of mutilation and extinction, while the intelligent Shadow Monster shatters our sense of being unique, echoing Ernest Becker's claim that we build cultural 'armor' against mortality. Using Carroll's paradox of horror and Stephen King's three levels (revulsion, horror, terror), they contend we enjoy confronting these fears safely from the couch, with the Shadow Monster looming over the Snow Ball as an emblem of real horrors, from AIDS to 9/11, still to come.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
kierkegaard-despair.title: Paradox and Peace
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Christopher Drohan reads Batman and Alfred through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Batman, like Abraham, believes 'by virtue of the absurd,' resigning himself to an infinite, never-realizable justice as a knight of infinite resignation, while Alfred embodies the higher knight of faith whose justice is concrete love expressed in mending the suit, making sandwiches, and guarding the manor. Heidegger's thrownness and Sartre's condemned freedom frame both men's absurd existential condition, including Batman sparing Joe Chill and even allying with him against the Reaper. The chapter's verdict is that Alfred's faithful devotion to one person is the superior ethic, and that peace begins with him.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
kierkegaard-despair.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Brown and Fosl read the twin Lebowskis as America's post-1960s despair: the Big Lebowski is Kierkegaard's failed Caesar who despairs because he cannot rid himself of the self that did not become Caesar (a fake achiever living on an allowance), while the Dude is the failed leftist whose revolutions collapsed. Against nihilism Walter pulverizes with Nietzschean will, Kierkegaard prescribes the leap of faith, and Camus revolt — but the Dude offers a distinctly American answer, abiding repetition: rolling balls frame after frame like Camus's happy Sisyphus, repeating phrases and roles (Butlerian performativity) so that re-creating himself is his victory over meaninglessness, with No Country for Old Men as the dark twin where nihilism may be winning.

kierkegaard-despair.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
kierkegaard-despair.title: 6 The Absurd Hero Indiana Jones, God, and Sisyphus
kierkegaard-despair.relation: Justin Fetterman takes the Big Bang Theory objection seriously — Indy is superfluous in Raiders and loses nearly every artifact he chases — diagnosing him first with Kierkegaard's despair of possibility from The Sickness Unto Death, where each failure only convinces him success lies just ahead. But Indy refuses Kierkegaard's leap of faith even after witnessing Shiva's Sankara Stones and the Ark, since multiple gods' demonstrations cancel any single revelation, and Kierkegaard demands faith without comprehension.
