the-look.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
the-look.title: 7 - Why I Am Not a Friend
the-look.relation: Thalos argues she is not a 'friend' on Facebook because bonding requires credible, fixed self-presentation, and a profile 'can lie like a rug' since everything on it is elective and revisable at whim. Through Sartre's phenomenology of the gaze - being displaced from Subject to object-for-another when caught in another's look - she explains why face-to-face interaction alone builds the mutual bonds and social intelligence we rely on. With Beauvoir she shows how the gaze also carries power, marking woman as the Other, and warns that Facebook's plastic faces offer choice without traction, inhibiting both true bonding and resistance to subjugating looks.

the-look.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
the-look.title: Bad or Bad Faith
the-look.relation: Rebecca Steiner Goldner reads the show through Sartre's Being and Nothingness: Dexter's watching is the Look that crystallizes his victims into a fixed essence - Matt Chambers can never again reinvent himself in a new town - and the kill room stages the demanded shame and confession ('Look at what you did!'), echoing Sartre's caught peeping-Tom. She then argues Dexter's belief that he was born a killer, that his Dark Passenger leaves him no choice, is itself bad faith: existence precedes essence, and by Sartre's account even the reformed thief remains responsible for his past, as with Jeremy Downs and Dr. Meridian. We viewers root for Dexter because we see the freedom he denies - and love him because he never makes the authentic choice to abandon his murderous project.

the-look.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
the-look.title: The Scanner-Self
the-look.relation: The chapter identifies Kant's deeper, non-experiencing self, the pure organizer of data behind ordinary experience, as 'a Kantian scanner', then maps the police scanners planted in Arctor's house onto Sartre's analysis of the gaze: another's look downgrades you from observing-subject to observed object, and God's all-penetrating stare would strip you of subjectivity and freedom entirely. Arctor's relentless surveillance culminates in Bruce, the identity-less pure watcher, the scanner-self incarnate, with a closing joke that Facebook profiles are how 'we see ourselves through a profile darkly.'

the-look.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
the-look.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Round argues the real horror of The Walking Dead is humanity itself, read through existentialism: walkers cannot choose, so the humans who attack, torture, and steal from each other are the true 'zombie Other.' She traces Rick's self-made, revisable moral code — from law-enforcer to 'You kill? You die' to killing Dexter — as authentic situation-based morality, paralleled with Kierkegaard's Abraham and with Abraham Ford's confession 'I did what I wanted to do' set against Eugene's bad-faith 'I did what I had to do.' Suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol embody existential angst before an absurd world, the Governor's Woodbury is an Adorno-style inauthentic hierarchy that manipulates its people, and Rick's 'WE ARE THE WALKING DEAD!' speech uses facticity to insist the group admit what they have already become.

the-look.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
the-look.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Reads Larry as a textbook existentialist: his agonizing over trivia ('Doctor?... Pharmacist?') instantiates Heideggerian anxiety and Sartrean anguish, because every choice, even yanking his 5 wood out of a casket in 'The 5 Wood,' proclaims an image of how everyone ought to live. Since existence precedes essence there is no fixed human nature for Larry to appeal to; he must author his values alone, which the chapter says also makes him an optimist ('I'm not an inventor, but I'm an improver'). Larry dispels others' bad faith when he tells Susie she obviously can share the brownie recipe in 'The Benadryl Brownie,' and his baldness crusade, firing the toupee-wearing chef Phil Dunlap in 'The Grand Opening,' is a demand for authenticity about one's facticity. The 'Larry David Stare' is analyzed through Sartre's Look: the squinter tries to inspect another consciousness empirically and necessarily fails, since the other's freedom can never be objectified.

the-look.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
the-look.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'

the-look.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
the-look.title: The Devil and Philosophy
the-look.relation: James McLachlan splits the Satans of history into 'the Rebel' of Romanticism (Blake, Shelley's turn to Prometheus, the sexy vampires of film) and 'the Asshole' who wants to be God. Using Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the desire to be a complete being, he reads Dracula, Scarface's Tony Montana, and Bond villains as figures who cannot endure the otherness of real persons. With Bohme and especially Schelling's two wills - self-assertion and love of others - he argues evil is a positive, perverted order of pure egoism, and that not even Satan can achieve the total asshole-ness he wants, because selfhood exists only in relation to others.

the-look.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
the-look.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.

the-look.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
the-look.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.

the-look.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
the-look.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.

the-look.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
the-look.title: 11. Louis C.K.’s No-Bullshit Philosophy
the-look.relation: Marie Snyder uses Sartre's existentialism to unpack Louis's Conan monologue about the 'forever empty': with God gone we are condemned to be free, thrown into a world with no ready-made purpose and alone with our choices - which explains both the cellphone distraction economy and the Live in Portland bit that 'even if you're with someone, you're alone.' Authenticity means ruthlessly honest self-awareness and owning every choice with no excuses - Sartre's waiter example, the claim that there is no cowardly temperament, and Louis's refusal to let 'a flaw in the human male' excuse the tits bit or porn masturbation. Since in choosing for ourselves we choose for all humanity, Snyder pairs Sartre's universalized responsibility with Louis's 'act in a way that, if everybody acted that way, things would work out,' and reads intimate others, as in the Sartre-Beauvoir open relationship, as mirrors that reflect us back to ourselves against the connectionless 'we're just cummers' porn culture. Bad faith - self-deception, distraction, blame - is the fallenness Louis keeps diagnosing in his audiences and confessing in himself.

the-look.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
the-look.title: 7. Being for Red
the-look.relation: Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.

the-look.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
the-look.title: 4. Faces from Another Dimension
the-look.relation: Hooke frames the volume through Levinas's claim that the face presents itself from a dimension of transcendence, with Kierkegaard's Abraham, Sartre's existential look, and Beauvoir's faces of the elderly and the second sex in the background, plus Lingis on trust. He shows how TZ masks its deadliest figures with trusted faces — Robert Redford as Death in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's avuncular Pip revealing 'This is the other place!' in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' the witch of 'Jess-Belle,' the gentle Kanamits whose book turns out to be a cookbook — so that proof of trust is nearly impossible and the show has us laughing with the Devil. The Turing test is applied to Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' (clearly in love 'regardless of the organs or hardware beneath'), the slot machine of 'The Fever,' and the aged couple of 'The Trade-Ins,' whose faces silently recognize a lost shared life.

the-look.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
the-look.title: 8. Tom Petty Didn’t Really Need to Know
the-look.relation: Zelinski and Fallis chart Petty's epistemic arc. His early songs ("I Need to Know," "Fooled Again," "Shadow of a Doubt") crave certainty about lovers' fidelity, a Desmond-free obsession closest to Descartes' quest for certainty beyond doubt, except Petty's problem is other minds, not the external world, and his trust that eyes directly reveal feeling sides with Moore's common-sense perception; Sartre's "hell is other people" names why another free person's future love can never be certain. From Full Moon Fever onward ("Into the Great Wide Open," "Time to Move On," "Learning to Fly") Petty instead embodies Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment and the Buddha's "don't know mind" and Daoist farmer's "we'll see," finding tranquility in uncertainty, craving nothing, flying with eyes open.

the-look.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
the-look.title: 9. Another Wig Underneath
the-look.relation: Cooper argues that the 'vulnerability' Drag Race demands is really a marketable persona, not truth. Working through Butler's Gender Trouble (built on Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes a woman'), she concedes drag reveals gender's imitative structure, but shows it also confirms identity: Latrice Royale's padded 'Natural Woman' lip sync reads as authentic, and trans queens like Peppermint and Gia Gunn use drag to articulate womanhood, with Husserl's intersubjectivity invoked to insist that constructed gender is no less real for not being empirical. Willam's edit-spliced 'I'm not acting' breakdown and Shannel's deliberate wig-doff show honesty becoming inconsequential next to spectacle, while Untucked's Interior Illusions Lounge is framed as Sartre's No Exit hell of unending observation. Against RuPaul's 'born naked' self-help nihilism ('identity is a joke'), she ends warning that the show no longer lets Katya take off the chicken suit.

the-look.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
the-look.title: 16. Is Hell Other People
the-look.relation: Berk compares the show to Sartre's No Exit, where Garcin, Inez, and Estelle are locked in a drawing room as each other's torturers, and notes that Michael's experiment 'in the spirit of Sartre' fails because the four humans befriend and improve each other instead. She then corrects the standard reading: Sartre himself insisted 'Hell is other people' is conditional on twisted, bad-faith relationships of over-dependence on others' judgment, as with Tahani's craving for her parents' approval, and the footnote in Being and Nothingness about a 'radical conversion' to authenticity leaves room for healthy relations. Read this way, the show's message that flawed people can find salvation through each other is compatible with, not a refutation of, Sartre.

the-look.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
the-look.title: The Grain Can Lead Us to Know Too Much
the-look.relation: The chapter argues that the Grain in The Entire History of You ruins Liam and Ffion's marriage not because the truth is bad but because total transparency destroys trust (via Luhmann), feeds a paranoid cycle where any deleted footage looks like guilt, and strips Fi of authority over her own life story. Goffman, Plessner, and Simmel ground the claim that social masks, tact, and privacy are preconditions of selfhood, while Sartre's 'look' explains Fi's shame when Liam forces her to replay her infidelity and Rousseau explains how dependence on others' gaze makes us unfree. Framed by Foucault's reading of Oedipus as a victim of his own knowledge, it concludes that Liam should have let the past lie — and ends with Byung-Chul Han's transparency society as our own already-arrived trajectory.

the-look.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
the-look.title: A Black Mirror of Our Anxieties
the-look.relation: Nosedive's star ratings are read as a digital panopticon — Bentham's prison design generalized by Foucault's Discipline and Punish — with China's Zhima Credit and Social Credit Systems showing the 'future is already here.' Rousseau's general will and Plato's ship-of-state frame the tyranny-of-the-majority worry (Chester destroyed by an office mob, Lacie jailed for a wedding toast, post-truth tribalism), which Mill's harm principle rebuts: Lacie's rant harms no one and should not be punished. Sartre's 'look' and No Exit explain Lacie's staged cookie photo ('Heaven!') and her final liberating exchange of insults with her cellmate, while Goffman's masks ground the epistemological worry that digital profiles are performances we nonetheless trust, and Bourdieu's symbolic capital names what the scores actually measure.

the-look.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
the-look.title: A Hope for the Future
the-look.relation: Reads The Little Mermaid as a step forward from the man-requiring damsels of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty: Ariel reverses the rescue by saving Eric, and Aristotle's 'all men by nature desire to know' is stretched to cover her curiosity about the human world. But Ursula's bargain trading Ariel's voice for legs dramatizes the long history of silenced women (Eve, Pandora, Cassandra, the scold's bridle), and the film's sexy, silent Ariel is exactly what Mulvey's male gaze, built on Sartre's 'the look,' criticizes. Applying Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman,' the chapter argues Ariel shows biology is not destiny yet still regresses into needing a man, concluding she is a flawed but real advance toward better heroines.

the-look.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
the-look.title: 16. Is Hell Other People
the-look.relation: Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.

the-look.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
the-look.title: Notes
the-look.relation: Chelstrom uses the progression from guided DUPLO builds to free design to argue that autonomy develops in degrees and is relational rather than purely individualist. Kant's self-thinking agent — for whom precepts and formulas are the 'ball and chain' of immaturity — explains Emmet's dependence on Octan's instruction booklets and Lord Business's profit from deference, and Korsgaard's definition frames the individualist autonomy the Master Builders embody. Yet their lone-wolf autonomy fails, and Sartre's look plus Beauvoir's account of woman forced to assume herself as Other explain Wyldstyle/Lucy's deference to others' expectations; Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy recasts 'Everything is Awesome' as peers supporting each other's self-development, with Emmet's friendship letting Lucy accept herself.

the-look.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
the-look.title: The Office and Philosophy
the-look.relation: Applies Sartre's Being and Nothingness to the mockumentary: Pam's bad faith consists in pretending she has no choice between Jim and Roy (her garbled 'I'm not into Jim' conversation with Karen in 'Ben Franklin'), while the camera's Look - Sartre's keyhole peeper caught in the hallway - turns her into an object not of her making when she is caught watching Jim and Karen in 'The Merger', and her shame finally lets her own her feelings. David Brent's pride (posing with his Inside Paper magazine cover) tries to control the Other's look and fails, since the freely respected gaze he craves cannot be extracted; and the ever-possible camera functions as Foucault's panopticon (Bentham's prison design), visible and unverifiable, silencing Jan on speakerphone in 'Cocktails' and forcing Dwight and Angela's 'Don't linger. Break left' choreography, which makes the viewer a complicit co-worker.

the-look.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
the-look.title: Responsibility
the-look.relation: Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.

the-look.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
the-look.title: 4. Faces from Another Dimension
the-look.relation: Hooke uses Levinas's account of the face (and Lingis on trust) to read the Zone's faces: the bandaged woman and pig-faced surgeons of 'The Eye of the Beholder' unseat our standards of the normal, while trusted faces are weaponized by Robert Redford's Grim Reaper in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's Satan in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the gentle Kanamit of 'To Serve Man.' Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' and John and Marie Holt's wordless recognition in 'The Trade-Ins' show trust and love exceeding proof or evidence. Sartre's existential look, with Kierkegaard's Abraham and Beauvoir's second sex, frames how a face puts our freedom and trust in question.

the-look.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
the-look.title: Acknowledgment
the-look.relation: William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.

the-look.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
the-look.title: I'm Part Elf, I'm Part Human
the-look.relation: Perez reads racism in Netflix's Witcher through Ibram X. Kendi's power-based account of racism, tracing the humans-versus-elves conflict through colorism (pointy ears and elven blood), 'drop rules' of racial purity that stigmatize Yennefer's quarter-elven lineage, and mutual dehumanization from Stregobor's 'mongrels' slur to Francesca's vow that the next genocide will be the humans'. He tests Kant's humanity formula against Nilfgaard's 'haven' for elves and the Battle of Aretuza, finding both sides guilty of using persons as mere means, then uses Suzy Killmister's three-strand dignity to explain why Calanthe's hidden heritage destroys her while Jaskier's Sandpiper smuggling and Cahir kneeling before Ciri restore dignity. Sartre's Other frames Yennefer's fluctuating identity between human and elf, and Dara laying down his hatred plus Ciri renouncing her power and taking the name Falka model Kendi's claim that being racist or antiracist is chosen moment by moment.

the-look.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
the-look.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
the-look.relation: Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.

the-look.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
the-look.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
the-look.relation: McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.

the-look.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
the-look.title: Noir et Blanc in Color: Existentialism and Miami Vice
the-look.relation: Sanders reads Miami Vice as existentialist 'sunshine noir,' where color and pastel locations carry noir alienation, and Crockett and Tubbs live rootless lives with shambles of romances and a culturally impoverished compass (Bolt, Buddy Holly, Buffett, Beckett, Betts). The episode 'No Exit' (Bruce Willis as arms dealer Tony Amato, whose wife Rita shoots him at the courthouse steps) is analyzed through Sartre's being-in-itself/being-for-itself conflict and 'hell is other people,' from which Danto says 'there is no exit.' 'Heart of Darkness' presents Ed O'Neill's undercover FBI agent Arthur Lawson, who prefers his Artie Rollins persona and hangs himself after debriefing, as a failure of authenticity and flight into bad faith that Crockett recognizes as his own peril as Sonny Burnett. Crockett's amnesia arc ('Mirror Image' through 'Redemption in Blood' and 'Bad Timing'), where he believes he is Burnett working for the Manolo organization, is resolved through Sartrean existential recognition and a freely chosen dangerous mission that restores his identity, since the Kierkegaardian leap of faith is unavailable in the show's secular world; Sanders also attacks Sartre's sanction of revolutionary violence in his preface to Fanon and Beauvoir's defense of Sade.

the-look.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
the-look.title: 4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest
the-look.relation: Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.

the-look.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
the-look.title: 20. Punks Pissing People Off
the-look.relation: Juneko Robinson mixes memoir of circa-1980 anti-punk violence (routine beatings, the murder of Brian Deneke) with Sartrean existentialism to explain why punks 'pissed people off': punk's confrontational appearance exposed the contingency and hypocrisy of mainstream values, forcing others to take responsibility for them. Using Sartre's keyhole-peeper example from Being and Nothingness and No Exit's 'hell is other people', she argues that harassers lived in bad faith, dependent on how others see them, while punks were the witnesses who objectified the mainstream rather than the deviants being watched. Howard Becker's moral entrepreneurs explain the 'de-punking' panics and psychiatric commitments of kids who merely dressed weird, and Marmysz's 'nihilistic incongruity' shows punk converting society's hypocrisy into self-legislated virtue.

the-look.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
the-look.title: 8. Self-Hatred as Identity
the-look.relation: Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.

the-look.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
the-look.title: The Viewer and the Look
the-look.relation: Meyer and Schneider use The Office's mockumentary camera to dramatize Sartre's 'the Look' and bad faith. Pam pretends she cannot choose between Roy and Jim (bad faith as being-in-itself), and is shamed when the camera catches her watching Jim and Karen; David Brent's prideful self-promotion tries and fails to control the Other's gaze. They tie the ever-present camera to the Foucault/Bentham panopticon: Jan, Dwight, and Angela police themselves because they might be watched, making the viewer complicit in the workers' existential crises.

the-look.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
the-look.title: It Worked
the-look.relation: Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.

the-look.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
the-look.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
the-look.relation: Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.

the-look.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
the-look.title: SERIAL KILLERS
the-look.relation: Winters reads the Zodiac Killer's taunting letters through Sartre's account of 'the look' from Being and Nothingness. He argues Zodiac's letters function like a snapped twig or a lit window: they make Northern Californians experience themselves as seen objects, hunted 'slaves' and pawns in Zodiac's game rather than free subjects. A phenomenological (first-person) analysis of the fear Zodiac induces, and of how his letters restrict the choices available within our facticity, is offered as superior to psychological or analytic accounts for explaining our fascination with the macabre.

the-look.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
the-look.title: Who is Who
the-look.relation: Focused on the 'Monstrous Other' and the 'base under siege' story, the chapter uses Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition and Sartre's 'the look' to read Cybermen, the Flood ('Waters of Mars') and the Silurians as Others through which humans define themselves, with Levinas on the face and history. Its final section frames the Doctor and the Master as Gothic doubles of love and strife, using Spinoza's monism, principle of sufficient reason and conatus to argue the power-hungry Master paradoxically fits Spinoza's system better than the order-imposing 'Dark Doctor.'

the-look.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
the-look.title: The Viewer and the Look
the-look.relation: Meyer and Schneider read The Office through Sartre's "the Look" and bad faith: the mockumentary camera catches characters as objects, as when Pam is caught gazing at Jim and freezes in shame, or pretends she has no choice about Roy (bad faith). David Brent's prideful posing tries to control the Other's look and fails. They add Foucault's panopticon — Dwight, Angela, and Jan police themselves because the camera might be watching — making the viewer complicit in exposing the employees' existential crises.

the-look.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
the-look.title: 46. The Shawshank Redemption as Philosophy Freedom and Panopticism
the-look.relation: Hooke reads The Shawshank Redemption through two lenses. From Sartre he takes 'hell is other people' and the objectifying look from No Exit and Being and Nothingness — Shawshank's warden and 'sisters' embody a worldly hell of 'never' and 'always' — but argues Andy and Red's friendship, Andy's Mozart broadcast, and the hopeful ending invert Sartre, making freedom the shared warmth of friendship rather than the devouring gaze. From Foucault's Discipline and Punish he reads the prison's shift from spectacle to disciplinary surveillance and solitary confinement as panopticism, extending Foucault's insight that prisons, schools, and hospitals mirror one another (illustrated by his COVID-era campus). He closes with Nietzschean genealogy and redemption through laughter, joy, and giving.

existentialism.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
existentialism.title: No Exit and The Vault Sartre and Seinfeld on the Inescapability of Others
existentialism.relation: Jennifer McMahon defends the heretical reading of Sartre as a relational theorist of the self: in Being and Nothingness consciousness is a nothingness, not an essential ego, and only the Other - 'the Other accomplishes... to see ourselves as we are' - lets us grasp ourselves as objects. Seinfeld illustrates this better than Sartre's own suspicion of others: Jerry's identity exists only through his entanglement with George, Kramer, and Elaine (change them and you get a 'bizarro-Jerry'), and the finale's prison cell ('The Vault') replays No Exit's locked room with the trial's parade of wounded minor characters - except that Seinfeld's chattering foursome shows friendship as a positive, not hellish, dependency.

existentialism.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
existentialism.title: 12 - Springfield Hypocrisy
existentialism.relation: Jason Holt argues that hypocrisy is a formal vice - an inconsistency between the values one espouses (tacitly or explicitly) and one's deliberate actions - and that philosophers wrongly build deception into its essence. Springfield supplies the counterexample: Chief Wiggum takes bribes, uses drugs, and abandons his post in plain view ('Lookin' good, boys!' after pocketing the counterfeit jeans), so his hypocrisy is pointless and non-deceptive, showing the vice survives without clever pretense like Moliere's Tartuffe. Mayor Quimby's double-talk on the 'chick vote', Mr. Burns's fake environmentalist PR in 'The Old Man and the Lisa', and Reverend Lovejoy's lukewarm ministry illustrate the classic deceptive pattern, while Apu's false 'American' front in 'Much Apu About Nothing' and Lisa's cool-kid pose in 'Summer of 4 ft. 2' show hypocrisy can be excusable or sympathetic when coerced.

existentialism.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
existentialism.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Eric Bronson places Tolkien among the 'sometimes merry' existentialists: Nietzsche's artist who says Yes amid catastrophe and needs 'the power to forget', Jaspers on machines estranging us from our past, and Arendt on Eichmann's obedient inhumanity and the few who create joy in dark times. The elves' songs in Rivendell and Lórien are joy born of sorrow and dispossession - Galadriel suffers because she remembers too much, trying to 'embalm time', while Arwen forgoes immortality for Aragorn. Her refusal of the Ring ('I will diminish, and go into the West, and remain Galadriel') embodies the existentialist affirmation: trust your own light, know what to remember and what to forget.

existentialism.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
existentialism.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.

existentialism.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
existentialism.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Argues the show's underlying moral vision is Nietzschean passive nihilism filtered through film noir. Tony, unlike the active nihilist who converts value-collapse into self-overcoming, sinks into resentment and life-negation: he wants to rip the throat of the 'happy wanderer', therapy never redeems him, and he quits it with 'I'm a fat fucking crook from New Jersey' in 'Calling All Cars'. The chapter traces the noir lineage (Tony watching White Heat, the Godfather references, Bogart imagery at Satriale's) and reads A.J.'s 'D-Girl' existentialism (Camus's The Stranger, 'There is no God') and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' as the family inheritance of meaninglessness and death-dread.

existentialism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
existentialism.title: Rethinking the Superhero Concept
existentialism.relation: Skoble widens the question to the concept itself: could anyone be trusted as watchman over the world, or is the savior mindset inherently dangerous for a human being to adopt? He reads the embedded Tale of the Black Freighter as the law of unintended consequences - the castaway's vigilante justice destroys the very people he meant to avenge - warning that any hero's limited perspective and fallible beliefs can doom rogue efforts. Moore's move, he argues, is the classic existentialist one of throwing responsibility for meaning and justice back onto ordinary people: if we did our part, no Ozymandias would ever conclude that drastic salvation was needed.

existentialism.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
existentialism.title: Poker and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.

existentialism.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
existentialism.title: Previews and Opening Credits
existentialism.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Hitchcock is a profound artist whose classic films are organized around ideas, citing Chabrol and Rohmer's claim that each film rests on a 'formal postulate,' so that philosophical issues arise directly from his cinematic motifs. It previews four features of Hitchcock's vision the volume will explore: an anti-utopian outlook on a fallen world perpetually at risk of chaos, an existentialist affirmation of self-definition through choice and commitment, a construal of spectatorship as flight from commitment and authenticity, and an anticipation of later thinking on the social roles of women. It closes with acknowledgments to the contributors, series editor Bill Irwin, and Open Court.

existentialism.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
existentialism.title: Reason to Believe When There’s None
existentialism.relation: Couch takes a night drive through Springsteen's road songs guided by Karl Jaspers's 'ultimate situations' — death ('Wreck on the Highway,' the bottomless gorge under the cruise-controlled life), suffering (the never-ending badlands, shared in Tom Joad's ghost), struggle (violent like 'Johnny 99,' loving as the search for 'one clear moment of love and truth'), and guilt ('Everybody's got a secret, Sonny'; 'you learn to sleep at night with the price you pay'). Jaspers's Existenz-philosophy — built on Kierkegaard's inward self and Nietzsche's diagnosis of the herd, against Kant's optimism about knowledge — explains the songs' endless border-crossings as attempts to evade limits that cannot be evaded, and the fear that turns 'your God filled soul' to 'devils and dust.' The answer to how there's a 'Reason to Believe' is Jaspers's leap of philosophic (not religious) faith toward the unknowable Transcendent, chosen in complete freedom.

existentialism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
existentialism.title: Living with Our Choices
existentialism.relation: Peters applies Sartre's occupied-France analysis from Existentialism Is a Humanism to 'The Resistance' webisodes: on New Caprica one can resist (Tyrol, Tigh), collaborate (Jammer joining the NCP), or do nothing (Duck staying home with Nora), each path a Sartrean project whose morality lies in choosing freely and living with the consequences. Jammer's execution for treason in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing after Nora's death dramatize the stakes — for Sartre, Duck's immorality lies in refusing to own the choice he made at the crossroads, and the Final Four revelation changes nothing since they chose as they believed themselves human. The chapter leaves open the Sartrean worry that wartime morality may simply be written by the winners.

existentialism.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
existentialism.title: Home Again
existentialism.relation: Flamm and Rea read the Oz story as an existential fable of the appearance-reality distinction in human development: children delight in admitted unrealities while adults live by ideals, and Dorothy's growth is learning to trade the one for the other, dramatized in the China Princess scene where Dorothy must abandon her plan to keep the animated figure frozen on Aunt Em's mantel. The Wizard embodies the American humbug in the P.T. Barnum mold, forcing green spectacles on the Emerald City's citizens so the city only appears green, science as technical illusion without deeper ideals, while the silver shoes reveal that the imaginative escape Dorothy sought was hers all along. Her homecoming is therefore bittersweet and existential: she can never return to the Kansas she left, 'but she can return to herself,' carrying the crayon box of self-chosen ideals with which to color her own reality.

existentialism.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
existentialism.title: Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again
existentialism.relation: Surber proposes Kristeva's 'abject aesthetics' as the new pair of shades that makes Radiohead legible: 'Creep' expresses abjection (the creep excluded even from recognition by the beautiful people), the android of 'Paranoid Android' is a borderline phenomenon neither human nor machine, and the bodily imagery of 'Bones', 'My Iron Lung', and the corpse in 'Knives Out' enacts the eruption of the pre-linguistic, formless abject, as do Donwood's dissolving Kid A letters. He contrasts the Beatles' aesthetics of psychedelic transcendence and Pink Floyd's existentialist aesthetics of alienation — built on Sartre's 'Hell is other people' gaze and the being-for-itself/being-in-itself split — with Radiohead's fluid, boundary-less world where meanings never come into focus and no existential revolt is possible because the embodied self is part of the world. Against the charge of nihilism, he reads Hail to the Thief and In Rainbows ('How come I end up where I started?') as postmodern reconstruction: if boundaries and meanings are fluid, they can also be remade.

existentialism.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
existentialism.title: Double Dutch
existentialism.relation: Krnac explains Holland's five missed penalties against Italy at Euro 2000 — Frank de Boer twice, Kluivert, Stam, Bosvelt — through Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety rather than Cruyff's 'chance' or Vergouw's 'poor preparation'. The self, a synthesis of body, mind and spirit (and of the temporal and eternal), must stake itself on a future-oriented choice, but freedom as 'the possibility to be able' makes every free choice an embrace of the unknown, breeding the anxiety that is 'the dizziness of freedom' — visible in de Boer's slide from a five-out-of-ten miss to a lifeless zero that telegraphed his shot to Toldo. Panenka's 1976 chip shows free action chosen without guarantee, while choosing not to choose is itself an evasion of freedom, in penalties as in life.

existentialism.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
existentialism.title: Living the Absurd Life
existentialism.relation: Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.

existentialism.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
existentialism.title: Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.

existentialism.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
existentialism.title: “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler
existentialism.relation: Decker argues the Doctor's morality resists formula — his motives are private, his timey-wimey perspective complicates consequentialist calculation, and the 'Genesis of the Daleks' child hypothetical breaks rule theories like Kant's and Mill's — so he reads it as an 'ethics of ambiguity' fusing Romanticism (Shelley's imagination, the infinite glimpsed in cups of tea and small beautiful events, Romantic-Gothic divided consciousness) with Sartrean existentialism. Via Sartre's WWII student, bad faith, and Beauvoir's 'adventurer' contrasted with the sub-man and the serious man, he casts the Doctor as a Gallifreyan Prometheus whose gifts of freedom are both dreadful and delightful.

existentialism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
existentialism.title: A Variety of Free Will Worth Having
existentialism.relation: Takes Dick's self-description as a 'fictionalizing philosopher' and reads 'Adjustment Team' — Ed Fletcher stumbling into a world of grey dust animated by an external hidden force — as determinism as we concretely live it: working toward goals we never chose in jobs that are not our own. Thompson's toothpaste line in The Adjustment Bureau becomes the image of consumption-only freedom, while Norris choosing love and politics over the Bureau's plan dramatizes freedom as accepting responsibility for one's own values.

existentialism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
existentialism.title: Terrible Freedom
existentialism.relation: Quotes Dick's A Scanner Darkly author's note — drug misuse 'is a decision,' and the druggie life-style is 'no different from your life-style... only faster' — to argue that dropping out of the plan continues the Sixties' questioning of war, segregation, and monogamy. Dick's refusal of bourgeois moralizing exposes it as part of the social-determinist control system, but a morally neutral natural cause-and-effect is what actually destroyed the druggies, so being free requires taking control, not merely rejecting control.

existentialism.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
existentialism.title: In Her Glass was a Bleeding Man
existentialism.relation: This section sets the Stones' marriages beside Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir's fifty-year open 'pact', contrasting Charlie Watts's monogamy with Jagger's wandering. Sartre and Beauvoir refused religious or social templates and defined their own rules: 'contingent' love affairs permitted, provided each told the other everything. Even this pact of honesty had casualties — lies told to their other lovers, abortions, stolen partners — so the existentialist point is that self-authored relationships trade the guilt of broken monogamy for another kind of tension.

existentialism.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
existentialism.title: Get What You Need
existentialism.relation: The chapter closes by matching each man's relationship style to what he 'needs': Watts keeps the beat (literally knocking Jagger out for phoning 'Where's my drummer?'), Jagger gets serial seduction, Richards trades the Anita Pallenberg cauldron for Patti Hansen's steadying presence, while Sartre died in 1980 surrounded by quarreling lovers instead of family. Every arrangement, from an Okie widow's 'plate of shit you can deal with' to the Sartre-Beauvoir pact, involves trade-offs, and the existentialist lesson is that we remain responsible for whichever romantic path we choose. Heraclitus's dictum that life is tension, and Sartre's nausea at our own choices, frame both monogamy and the pact as equally legitimate gambits.

existentialism.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
existentialism.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Pits act utilitarianism against existentialism to ask whether moral rules change at life's end: briefly cooking meth can maximize happiness (family provision against limited street harm), while a long career cannot, and utilitarians are trapped by the limits of their own foresight. Walt is read as the existentialist converting mortality into meaning - money, power, and masculinity in a godless world - while Skyler mostly calculates like a utilitarian (white lies to Marie, Ted's accounting), Hank mixes both codes, and Marie's kleptomania marks her an egoist until she defends Walt's right to choose his own death at the intervention. A marathon-runner metaphor lands the thesis: to be a utilitarian in life's early miles is itself an existential decision, and the last mile is when we 'wake up' like Walt.

existentialism.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
existentialism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Kempner reads The Walking Dead through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old value-system gone, survivors who cling to pre-made essence die — Hershel keeps his zombified son locked in the barn awaiting restoration, and Shane tries to steal Rick's old cop-and-husband identity rather than live his own existence. Rick's waking in the hospital is a rebirth: he first exists in the new world, then creates a way of being human, and his relapses into the sheriff uniform nearly get him killed. Carl shooting Shane to save his father completes the family's existential freedom (children are no longer 'innocent'), walkers — without will or choice — are the ultimate inauthentic beings, and the volume's tagline, 'forced to finally start living,' makes the zombie world a sternly optimistic humanist story.

existentialism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
existentialism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.

existentialism.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
existentialism.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.

existentialism.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
existentialism.title: 25. Meeting Up with Your Self
existentialism.relation: Sylvia and Stevens use Doctor Who's crossover episodes to complicate the Self-Other distinction: existentially (via Yalom and Maslow), the Doctor's name-promise - 'never cruel or cowardly... never give up, never give in' - supplies meaning, while Ten and Eleven must stop treating the War Doctor as Other. Deleuze's account of learning through the shock of encountering the Other structures the reading of 'The Girl Who Waited,' where young Amy and her thirty-six-years-older self form an assemblage in which the older Amy relearns her love for Rory and chooses annihilation for his sake. Locke's memory theory of personal identity frames the puzzle that a version of you with different memories may be an Other, which the authors extend to confronting our recorded past selves on social media and learning empathy from the shock.

existentialism.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
existentialism.title: 12. Confronting the “Forever Empty”
existentialism.relation: Argues that Louis's 2013 Conan 'forever empty' confession—welcoming the sadness of listening to Bruce Springsteen alone in his car instead of texting—is an exemplary case of existentialist authenticity: Heideggerian anxiety discloses the nothingness beneath our projects, and Sartre's radical freedom, facticity, and bad faith explain why texting while driving and other distractions are escapes from self-creation. It then contrasts Eddie in Louie's 'Eddie' episode, whose suicide plan is a bad-faith loss of care and passion, with the 'Late Show' trilogy, where Janet exposes Louie's bad faith over the Letterman audition and he ends by shouting 'I did it!' at the Ed Sullivan Theater after Tardigan's scam.

existentialism.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
existentialism.title: 8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir
existentialism.relation: Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.

existentialism.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
existentialism.title: 13. Reason and Catharsis
existentialism.relation: Argues that Twin Peaks frees viewers from the "tyranny of rationality" by refusing to make sense: Plato's sensible-versus-intelligible finger example explains our habit of abstracting concepts to resolve contradiction (the pale horse in the living room, Diane's texts, Dougie-as-tulpa), but Lynch keeps adding facts — the frog-moth crawling into the girl in Part 8 — that no framework absorbs. Drawing on Nietzsche's Twilight of the Idols claim that Socrates made rationality a treatment for weakness, and on the existentialist pairing of despair and freedom in a meaningless universe, the chapter says viewers can either demand the irrational fit their rationality like inauthentic existentialists or let go. Trela's alternative reading of Aristotle's catharsis — emotions purged of their connection to reality and felt for once in themselves — explains why we can savor the show's absurdity without despair, precisely because that world is not ours.

existentialism.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!
existentialism.title: 8. Sexistentialism
existentialism.relation: Reads Schumer through Camus's absurd: Trainwreck's gender-reversed commitment-phobe and the sketch where friends kill themselves rather than accept a compliment expose the futility of finding meaning in patriarchal gender scripts. Browning argues that advocating change against so systemic a sexism is a Sisyphean task, and that the film's romantic-comedy ending is 'existential' because Amy freely chooses commitment and owns the absurdity rather than escaping it. The chapter ends by asking whether Schumer's jokes are a battle cry whose very pointlessness might be the point.

existentialism.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
existentialism.title: 10. On Being and Meeseeks
existentialism.relation: The chapter asks what kind of being Mr. Meeseeks is and answers with Sartre: despite being 'created to serve a singular purpose', Meeseeks exhibit subjectivity, from the self-assertion of 'I'm Mr. Meeseeks!' to transcendence in envisioning Jerry's fixed golf swing and the anguish, forlornness, and despair of 'Meeseeks and Destroy' ('Your failures are your own, old man!'), so they must be beings-for-itself whose existence precedes essence, freely choosing accomplishment as their meaning. Along the way it glosses Sartre's facticity with Morty's hopeless crush on Jessica, essence-precedes-existence with the butter-passing robot, and bad faith with Jerry's assumed mediocrity and Beth's shrinking of herself into horse surgeon, wife, and mother until Mr. Meeseeks reminds her she is still an individual.

existentialism.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
existentialism.title: 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
existentialism.relation: Hubbard-Mattix frames the show's central paradox, each person is responsible for her choices yet those choices are formed by her relationships, as a collision between the existentialism of Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and the feminist idea of relational autonomy. Each character embodies a failure mode: Eleanor's futile rejection of social dependence, Chidi's evasion of accountability in bad faith, Tahani's destruction by living for others' approval, and Jason's unexamined loyalty to Pillboi, Donkey Doug, and the Jaguars. Their failures before Judge Gen teach the audience to choose relationships that enable growth while still owning one's choices.

existentialism.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
existentialism.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Baird contrasts Camus's absurdity — the divorce between man and world demanding 'lucid indifference' and an absurd art that refuses counterfeit meaning — with Sartre's, where the world's meanings are contingent human projections and freedom entails absolute responsibility (Being and Nothingness sits by the Dude's bed). He argues the film is Sartrean rather than Camusian: the Dude weaves random events (the peed-on rug, the ransom) into the interpretation 'Bunny kidnapped herself', holding it provisionally as one story among possible ones, while Walter never takes responsibility for his Corvette-swinging choices. The viewers, knowing all interpretations are groundless, watch the absurd from the front row.

existentialism.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
existentialism.title: Rafiki Holds the Mirror Up to Nature
existentialism.relation: The chapter reads The Lion King as a Disney retelling of Hamlet: Scar's murder of Mufasa parallels Claudius, and Simba's guilt-ridden exile acts out Hamlet's 'to be or not to be.' Timon and Pumbaa's 'hakuna matata' is Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage of pleasure without commitment, which Simba must leave for the ethical stage when Nala, Rafiki ('Whooo are you?'), and Mufasa's ghost demand he 'remember who you are.' Sartre's 'optimistic toughness' and Nietzsche's 'Become who you are' frame Simba's defiant 'I am' before the assembled Pride Lands as existential self-creation.

existentialism.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
existentialism.title: 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
existentialism.relation: Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.

existentialism.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
existentialism.title: The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’
existentialism.relation: Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.

existentialism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
existentialism.title: 7 Indiana Jones and Existential Self-Affirmation
existentialism.relation: Daniel Tilsley reads The Last Crusade as an excavation of identity: the fedora Fedora bestows after young Indy's defeat, the twenty-six-year quest for the Cross of Coronado ('All my life'), and the chosen name 'Indiana' (taken from the family dog) are acts of Nietzschean self-affirmation — amor fati and the willingness to will the Eternal Recurrence of one's life. The villains fail because they seek external artifacts to patch deficient lives, whereas the Grail Knight, like Camus's Sisyphus, authentically affirms his endless task of guarding the cup. The arc completes when Henry Sr. finally calls his son 'Indiana' while hanging from the abyss, recognizing the man he chose to become, and Crystal Skull repeats the pattern with Mutt and the fedora's eventual inheritance.

existentialism.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
existentialism.title: Franken-Stark
existentialism.relation: Curtis argues Iron Man dramatizes the problem of progress: Schopenhauer's insatiable will explains why every technological fix — the chest plate, the armor, the artificial nervous system — spawns new suffering and dependency, and his pessimism, with Kierkegaard's freedom within insecurity, Nietzsche's flawed Übermensch going out 'in a blaze of glory,' and Sartre's 'cautiously optimistic' existentialism, recasts Iron Man as a tragic antihero rather than a perfected Superman or Batman. Stark's wounded heart, alcoholism as self-medication ('the demon is not in the bottle but in the addict'), and doomed romances with Bethany Cabe and Rumiko Fujikawa make him the flawed hero who has simply learned to live with imperfection. Like Mary Shelley's monster, his extensions have become him — we are all 'Franken-Starks' facing the consequences of our own inventions.

existentialism.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
existentialism.title: The Struggle Within: Hetfield, Kierkegaard, and the Pursuit of Authenticity
existentialism.relation: Philip Lindholm reads Metallica through Kierkegaard's demand for subjectivity: the soldier in 'One' crying 'Oh please God help me' exemplifies becoming a single individual before God against the untruth of the crowd, and 'The Struggle Within' stages Either/Or's passionate choice that decides the self. He then shows Hetfield himself living the inauthentic masked life Kierkegaard condemns - 'I was James Hetfield of Metallica' - until rehab forced the honest self-disclosure ('The God That Failed' and 'Until It Sleeps' mourning his parents) that marks a move toward authentic individuality.

existentialism.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
existentialism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
existentialism.relation: Kempner reads the comic through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old world gone, survivors like Rick, Michonne, and Dale must create their own values, while characters who cling to pre-apocalypse essences (Hershel keeping his zombified son in the barn, Shane waiting for the government) bring death on themselves. Rick's hospital awakening is treated as an existential rebirth in which his cop uniform is an 'essence precedes existence' trap, and Carl shooting Shane (and later Ben in 'Fear the Hunters') shows children making free choices outside conventional morality. The chapter concludes the series is 'sternly optimistic' because total freedom, not zombification, is what defines the humans: 'in a world ruled by the dead, we are forced to finally start living.'

existentialism.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
existentialism.title: IV - X-ISTENTIAL X-MEN JEWS, SUPERMEN, AND THE LITERATURE OF STRUGGLE
existentialism.relation: Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature rooted in the Jewish experience of their creators. Stan Lee and Jack Kirby's mutants, and Claremont's reinvention of Magneto as a Holocaust survivor, reverse Superman's assimilationist fantasy: being a minority makes the X-Men entitled to equal treatment, and human fear of difference is the norm rather than a Lex Luthor-style pathology. Sartre's bad faith explains the anti-Semite's chosen hatred (and why Xavier refuses to simply mind-control humans into tolerance), while Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem makes moral judgment everyone's burden. Against Camus' opening question of suicide and Mr. Incredible's wish that the world 'stay saved,' the chapter argues the X-Men's endless Sisyphean cycle of deaths, resurrections, and reboots is not futile: one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

existentialism.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
existentialism.title: VII - X-WOMEN AND X-ISTENCE
existentialism.relation: Housel gives an existential history of the X-Women. Jean Grey embodies the paradox of 'existence precedes essence,' a fictional character whose meaning is assigned by creators and fans yet who perpetually re-creates herself through the Phoenix, while Rachel Summers 'makes her own existence at every single moment' in Ortega's sense across timelines. The Scarlet Witch's reality-warping is Baudrillard's 'line of fracture' where an expanding system cracks, and her denial of the past is Sartrean bad faith; Storm shows angstless responsibility, Mystique the 'cynical consciousness' of self-deception, Rogue Camus' absurdity in a life without touch, and Kitty Pryde Ortega's 'substantial emigrant on a pilgrimage of being.'

existentialism.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
existentialism.title: Introduction
existentialism.relation: Elkholy's editorial introduction defines 'Beat' (the New York/West Coast writers) versus 'beat' (a lifestyle of weariness and disaffiliation), tracing the term through Kerouac, Ginsberg's 'Howl,' and Snyder. She frames the Beats' turning-inward and self-marginalization philosophically, noting that Brustein's charge that beats pursue aimless 'kicks' echoes Kierkegaard's critique of the Romantics as engaged in purposeless, rootless striving that evades responsibility. Against this she sets Holmes's reading of beat detachment as a search for meaning and belief, and casts the Beats' global travels as anticipating an emerging cosmopolitanism.

existentialism.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
existentialism.title: John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism
existentialism.relation: Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.

existentialism.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
existentialism.title: “There’s No More Watching” Artifice and Meaning in Synecdoche, New York and Adaptation
existentialism.relation: Hill argues that Adaptation and Synecdoche, New York both dramatize artists (the character Charlie Kaufman and Caden Cotard) struggling to portray 'real life' through artifice, and that Kaufman achieves authenticity not through neorealist naturalism but through surrealism and fantasy. He distinguishes the existentialist sense of authenticity—living self-awarely and choosing outside a community's rules (via Macquarrie)—from cinematic realism, tracing Kaufman's fusion of inner and outer life to Fellini's 8½. The chapter reads Synecdoche as an unflinching, near-horror examination of what it costs to make honest art, concluding its buried message is that creation is meaningless unless shared.

existentialism.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
existentialism.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
existentialism.relation: Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.

existentialism.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
existentialism.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
existentialism.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.

existentialism.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
existentialism.title: Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There
existentialism.relation: Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.

existentialism.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
existentialism.title: 13. Reason and Catharsis
existentialism.relation: Elsby and Luzecky argue that we compulsively rationalize Twin Peaks (tulpas, pale-horse omens, Diane-as-tulpa) the way we abstract concepts to tame the contradictory sensible world (Plato's long-and-short finger), but Lynch—especially in Part 8—deliberately thwarts this, exposing what Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols calls the post-Socratic tyranny of rationality. They offer an alternative reading of Aristotelian catharsis (via Trela): because the fictional world is not ours, we can experience its irrationality and absurdity, emotions purged of their tie to reality, as freedom rather than the existential despair the absurd would cause in our own world.
