commodity-fetishism.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
commodity-fetishism.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Alison Milbank argues we are all in thrall to the Ring because it mirrors our own fetishism: she reads the film's lingering close-ups, Smaug-like hoarding, and Gollum's baby-talking self-division through Freud's theory of the fetish and Marx's commodity fetishism, with Sauron as the emptied idolater who poured his power into the thing. Against this she sets Middle-earth's gift economy - Bilbo's party, Galadriel's gifts, Sam's elven rope - glossed by Heidegger's 'Thinging gathers': Sam praises the rope by restoring it to its elven makers and its use. Tom Bombadil, who treats the Ring as 'a very pretty ring' and nothing more, and Frodo's final sacrifice model the unfetishized life; the chapter closes with Sam's homecoming, where chairs are only chairs and the family circle replaces the Ring.

commodity-fetishism.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
commodity-fetishism.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Bar On examines the Atkins website's country-by-country packaging and asks what kind of commodity the diet is, answering with Marx's Capital: use-value versus exchange-value, money's erasure of qualitative difference (an Atkins cookbook priced like a tub of supplements), and capitalists who produce use-values only as 'material depositories of exchange-value.' Advertising succeeds not by manipulation but because alienated people — labor sold, selves split to fit the job market — already live in exchange relations, and Atkins mediates even the dieter's relation to herself through purchased bars, supplements, and books. Her conclusion: a weight-loss diet only the relatively privileged can afford, in a world where the poor eat carbohydrates because they are cheap, is itself a symptom of the alienation Marx diagnosed.

commodity-fetishism.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
commodity-fetishism.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.

commodity-fetishism.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
commodity-fetishism.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Ferriss explains biker leather through the two forms of fetishism: Freud's fetish object, by which the black jacket augments masculine potency against castration anxiety (while women riders negotiate pink leather, rhinestones, and the dominatrix option, as Dot Robinson of the Motor Maids did with her lipstick holder), and Marx's commodity fetishism, in which Capital's dancing wooden table becomes the H-D-branded jacket whose exchange value carries Americana and rebellion to dentists, Vogue spreads, Harley Ken dolls, and the Phoenix Art Museum. From Brando's promotional still and Girl on a Motorcycle's 'black bull' to Kenneth Anger's gay Nazi bikers in Scorpio Rising, leather's erotic charge is fashion, a language of gender that changes, and it is now fading as motorcycles themselves become mere accessories in deodorant ads.

commodity-fetishism.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
commodity-fetishism.title: Progress Is a Myth that Truly Makes Life Worthwhile
commodity-fetishism.relation: Garnar contrasts the material practice of collecting CDs -- shelving some 1,500-2,000 discs by genre, the Rachels' Egon Schiele packaging, and Humean associations binding particular discs to memories like buying blue hair dye the day he got New Order's Lowlife -- with the iPod-era 'iPhenomenon' of buying songs piecemeal from iTunes. Using William James's question 'How is the practice real?' he rejects the real/virtual split, and reads the freedom of iMedia as a corollary of Marx and Engels's 'single, unconscionable freedom -- Free Trade': the solipsistic consumer never confronts the artist the way the album as artifact (Coltrane's My Favorite Things ending, he realizes, had to end with 'But Not for Me') forces him to. The body supposedly made unnecessary by 'iLiving' remains, with Foucault, a site of discipline -- eating disorders, outsourced assembly labor, e-waste -- so he keeps his iPod but defends a plurality of media and calls progress a myth.

commodity-fetishism.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
commodity-fetishism.title: Modding Mavens and the Limits of Reification
commodity-fetishism.relation: Schaeffer starts from the felt aliveness of the click wheel -- 'it whirs and clicks, demanding my attention' -- and argues we personify iPods precisely because mass production hides their makers, applying Marx's account of alienation and reification ('the personification of things and the reification of persons') to the Foxconn 'iPod City' exposé of fifteen-hour shifts and hundred-worker dorm rooms paid fifty dollars a month. Extending the analysis through Lukacs, he reads Apple's fluctuating stock price as 'phantom objectivity' and the iPod bubbles of his Brooklyn coffee shop and his classroom -- couples passing 'like ships in the night' -- as a reified world that appears as the only possible world. Against the thesis's bleakness, modders -- a bicycle-dynamo charger, a fist-sized remote with five large switches built for visually impaired users -- re-inscribe humanity into the commodity, marking the limits of reification.

commodity-fetishism.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
commodity-fetishism.title: I’m Gonna Crawl
commodity-fetishism.relation: Richard Wilson and Emma Rees apply Freud's theory of fetishism—the boy's disavowal of castration displaced onto a substitute object—to Zeppelin's lyrics and imagery. 'Trampled Underfoot' continues Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues' car-as-lover convention, 'Custard Pie' and 'Black Dog' turn women into consumable food (Freud's cannibalistic pregenital sexual organization), and 'The Lemon Song' and 'Whole Lotta Love' avert the castrating vagina, with the Seattle red snapper episode read through the vagina dentata myth. The band's misogyny ('Soul of a woman was created below' in 'Dazed and Confused', echoing Lear), the voyeuristic die-cut windows of the Physical Graffiti cover, and Plant's cock-rock persona in The Song Remains the Same all illustrate how fetishistic substitution neutralizes the threatening female body and explains the band's compulsive doomed-relationship songs; the authors briefly borrow Marx's language of commodification for the woman-car-drugs as status objects.

commodity-fetishism.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
commodity-fetishism.title: So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh
commodity-fetishism.relation: Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.

commodity-fetishism.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
commodity-fetishism.title: The Wire and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.

commodity-fetishism.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
commodity-fetishism.title: Futurama and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Buchanan reads 'A Big Piece of Garbage' as political ecology: the trash ball Old New York blasted into space in 2000 returns to threaten New New York, showing that even a society that has 'mastered recycling' cannot escape a capitalist economy whose commodities are designed to end as waste. On the trash ball, Fry's nostalgia ('junk isn't garbage... a glorious monument to the twentieth century') debates Leela's 'this stuff was garbage when it was new,' and Fry's rescue plan - building a second trash ball to knock the first into the Sun - merely recreates the disaster, celebrated as 'the twentieth-century spirit' of willful ignorance. Drawing on Bryant and Bailey's political ecology and Rodgers's waste stream, the chapter argues trash unmasks the exploitation of nature crystallized in commodities, so green technology and recycling alone cannot avert ecological crisis.

commodity-fetishism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
commodity-fetishism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Fitzpatrick runs Marx's account of alienated labor from the 1844 Manuscripts through the novel: Victor's creature is the product of estranged labor, 'an alien object exercising power over him,' which he cannot name, comes to loathe, and which finally destroys him - the devaluation of the creator tracking the increasing value of the thing made, while workers become commodities producing commodities. The De Laceys' eviction in Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Ingolstadt cholera riots stage class struggle at feudalism's end, and Victor's failure to self-actualize (to 'hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon... criticize after dinner') shows how capitalism turns science into 'a tool of our own destruction.' The chapter closes with 'Frankenstorm' climate change as the alienated externality par excellence - capitalists selling us the rope with which we hang ourselves.

commodity-fetishism.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
commodity-fetishism.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.

commodity-fetishism.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
commodity-fetishism.title: 14. The Value of a Handmaid
commodity-fetishism.relation: Pérez assesses a Handmaid's value through Kant—Gilead gives women a price, not a dignity, so the Gilead–Mexico trade deal is human trafficking dressed as diplomacy—and through Marx's use value and exchange value, with fertility the commodity and Jezebels carrying both market and affective price. He adds Bourdieu's forms of capital to show Offred's social and resistant cultural capital against Janine's collapse, then weighs cultural relativism (via Renteln and Herodotus) before rejecting it for Gilead: its values were improvised and forced rather than naturally evolved, so the culture itself earns no pass. The Handmaids' refusal to stone Janine shows their collective worth: 'They should've never given us uniforms if they didn't want us to be an army.'

commodity-fetishism.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
commodity-fetishism.title: “Medicine’s Not a Science!”
commodity-fetishism.relation: Decker explains the paradox of Dr. Leo Spaceman, incompetent ('Science is whatever we want it to be'), paternalistic, yet beloved by Tracy and Jack, through social theory: Parsons's pattern variables and professional ethics codes that Leo flouts, Marx's commodity fetishism, which makes patients desire medicalized enhancements the way direct-to-consumer pharma ads teach them to want Cialis and Viagra. Habermas's colonization of the lifeworld by systems organizations names the deeper diagnosis: managed-care bureaucracy and the market have reorganized medicine's social meanings, so 'medicine's not a science' because health itself has become a fashionable commodity. The chapter adds that 30 Rock works as satire because it shows the lifeworld pushing back against the system.

commodity-fetishism.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
commodity-fetishism.title: The End of History
commodity-fetishism.relation: Diagnoses the Alien universe through Marx's Grundrisse: workers like Parker and Fifield ('I'm here to make money') live only to have and consume, wage labor is avoided like the plague (Pvt. Frost's 'I hate this job'), money replaces the faith people should place in each other, and employees become disposable commodities (Vickers to Shaw: 'that makes you an employee'). Only the conscience-free android Ash fits the Corporation's ideal 'pure capitalist,' and because the saga's future stays capitalist, it vindicates Fukuyama's end-of-history thesis over Marx's prediction of collapse.

commodity-fetishism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
commodity-fetishism.title: Resistance
commodity-fetishism.relation: Reading Fifteen Million Merits through Marx, the chapter treats Bing's world of endless pedaling, Wraith Babes, and Hot Shot as a commodity society in which people themselves carry use and exchange values — Oliver the 'lemon,' Glee deemed 'quite worthless,' Abi's unsellable papier-mache penguin discarded as detritus. Marx's commodity fetish explains the universalized pricing in merits, and Lukacs-style reification shows things commanding people (Cuppliance compelling compliance). Adorno's culture industry explains why all the shows share one form and why Bing's glass-shard rebellion is absorbed as just another commodity, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man supplies the hope that reason, love (Bing's love for Abi as something 'real'), and switching off the media can still seed resistance.

commodity-fetishism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
commodity-fetishism.title: “He’s done tech detox weekends here and there, but ten days ”
commodity-fetishism.relation: Reading Smithereens as today's reality rather than a dystopia, the chapter explains the crash that killed Chris's fiancée through Herbert Simon's attention economy: platforms like Smithereen are free because they harvest and sell attention, and Billy Bauer admits the app was deliberately tuned 'like a crack pipe' with dopamine targets. Using Marx's analysis of capitalist surplus, the chapter argues (with Zuboff's 'behavioral surplus' and Crary's 24/7 capitalism) that users are wageless laborers generating value for free, and that compulsive checking is Gerald Moore's 'dopamining' - brain plasticity exploited by a hostile attention environment - rather than free choice. It rejects individual tech-detox consumerism as a false solution and closes with Simondon: knowing our machines is the beginning of the political reflection needed to dissolve the alienating 'fetishism of the tool.'

commodity-fetishism.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
commodity-fetishism.title: 20 The Value of Vibranium
commodity-fetishism.relation: Edwardo Pérez asks what makes vibranium 'the most valuable metal known to man' through Marx's distinction between use value and exchange value: Klaue prizes exchange value (money, power, a black-market arm), while Wakandans structure their whole society around use value and never trade the metal. The museum scene raises cultural property - does vibranium belong to Wakanda, as the cultural nationalist holds, or to humanity, as the cultural internationalist holds? - and T'Challa's shift on sharing it is analyzed through Kant's categorical imperative versus Bentham's utilitarian calculus, with his saving of Agent Ross and sparing of M'Baku vindicated by their consequences. Vibranium's greatest value, the chapter concludes, is atonement: redeeming T'Chaka's crime and uniting humanity as 'one single tribe.'

commodity-fetishism.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
commodity-fetishism.title: NOTES
commodity-fetishism.relation: McClelland traces the vampire's drift from demonic scapegoat — Marx's figure for capital draining the proletariat — to sympathetic protagonist, then reads TruBlood itself as a political device: the synthetic substitute is a trap that lures the ancient enemy out of opposition and into consumption-based communion, creating the 'ideal consumer' who is eternal, much as globalization absorbs adversaries into the marketplace. Godric's exhaustion with undead power struggles and the maenad Maryann's induced hedonism show, respectively, the hollowness of quasi-immortal consumer life and the human community's own susceptibility to buying bliss at the price of its principles.

commodity-fetishism.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
commodity-fetishism.title: Hoop Dreams, Blacktop Realities
commodity-fetishism.relation: Bernard Jackson Jr. argues that basketball is an institution where black manhood is socially constructed (leaning on Naomi Zack's feminist point that gender identity is imposed by social designation), and that love among black players is essential to that construction while toughness is equivocal - the 'soft' label stuck to the gentlemanly David Robinson even as the Pistons walked off without congratulating the Bulls. Reading the documentary Hoop Dreams, he shows Arthur Agee and William Gates being used as commodities by recruiters, Coach Pingatore, and family expectations, invoking Marx on exploitation and 'use value' (Spike Lee's Nike-camp speech) and Kant's demand that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means. He likens William Gates's return to Chicago's Cabrini-Green as a minister to Plato's enlightened prisoner going back down into the cave.

commodity-fetishism.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Sharpe analyzes the Olympics as an aestheticized 'spectacle' (Debord, after Marx's commodity analysis) whose real product is the shareable 'Olympic moment.' Reading Kant's Critique of Judgment through Terry Eagleton, he argues the games trade on the sensus communis Kant finds in the judgment 'this is beautiful', an intimated universal harmony among humans that mirrors the ancient Olympic ekecheiria (truce). He links Beijing 2008's simulated fireworks and lip-synced girl to Baudrillard's simulacra, and uses Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay, Riefenstahl's Olympia and Hegel's account of Greek sculpture to show how the Nazis' 1936 Games weaponized this aesthetic power, warning the spectacle serves both good and evil.

commodity-fetishism.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
commodity-fetishism.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
commodity-fetishism.relation: Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.

commodity-fetishism.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
commodity-fetishism.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
commodity-fetishism.relation: Schuler and Murray read Chinatown through Marx and Plato as a critique of capitalism's compulsions. Drawing on Marx and Engels on capital's Promethean transformation of nature and Hegel on art embodying abstractions, they argue neo-noir's centrifugal Los Angeles makes water, not diamonds, the object of desire, with wealth taking the abstract form of value. Plato's Republic warns that the boundless love of money (linked to Gyges, invisibility, and tyranny) destroys justice as reasonable self-limitation; Noah Cross's incest mirrors the 'rape of the Owens Valley', and Jake's defeat ('Forget it, Jake, it's Chinatown') marks the exhaustion of the postwar golden age.

commodity-fetishism.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
commodity-fetishism.title: The Prostitution Trap of Elite Sport in He Got Game
commodity-fetishism.relation: Holt and Pitter argue that Lee's He Got Game exposes a 'prostitution trap' in which elite athletes, like literal prostitutes, become commodified bodies alienated from themselves. They read the parallel plots of star recruit Jesus Shuttlesworth, his father Jake pressured to broker a signing, and the prostitute Dakota as three versions of the same trap, invoking MacIntyre's internal-versus-external goods and Deci/Ryan's intrinsic-versus-extrinsic rewards to show how coercive money threatens Jesus's love of the game. Jesus escapes by exercising autonomy, negotiating on his own terms and skipping the press conference to reach an 'authentic realism.'

commodity-fetishism.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
commodity-fetishism.title: Economies of Time in Clockers
commodity-fetishism.relation: Gilmore reads Clockers through DuBois's double-consciousness, arguing the film's dualities—the clockers' street dealing mirroring capitalist 'logic of maximum performance,' kronos versus kairos time, Hyde's commodity versus gift economies, systemic versus personal racism—make white and black viewers alike feel the anguish of Strike and Victor. The Gran Fury as predatory law, the slave-block-style police shakedown watched by Strike's mother, and Rocco seeing only his own reflection in Victor's eye illustrate Heideggerian thrownness and self-love-as-racism. Invoking Peirce's 'evolutionary love' (Radio Raheem's Right Hand/Left Hand speech), Rorty's renarrativization of who counts as 'white,' and Dewey's 'art is more moral than moralities,' Gilmore casts Lee as a pragmatist renarrativizing hate into love.

commodity-fetishism.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
commodity-fetishism.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
commodity-fetishism.relation: Tait gives a Fredric Jameson-derived Marxist reading of Ocean's Eleven, treating Danny Ocean's heist crew as a utopian 'figure of collectivity' whose diverse, cross-class, pan-American membership recalls the WWII combat film and rallies against Terry Benedict as the polysemous 'monster' (Jameson's shark in Jaws) standing for globalized capital displacing nostalgic American Las Vegas. He argues the victimless heist allegorizes a competing value system in which love, solidarity, and friendship trump money, restaging class conflict from Asphalt Jungle, Rififi, and Big Deal on Madonna Street. The film's utopian happy ending imagines redistributing wealth and 'beating the house' within the very system of late capital it critiques.

commodity-fetishism.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
commodity-fetishism.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
commodity-fetishism.relation: Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.

commodity-fetishism.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.title: 3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification
commodity-fetishism.relation: Mitchell examines Young's Geffen-era lawsuit (sued in 1983 for "uncharacteristic" music like Trans and Everybody's Rockin') and the competing rebel/misunderstood-artist/lost-in-the-video-era narratives around it. Using Heilbroner on capitalism's commodification of rebellious art and Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and pre-corporation of dissent (Cobain as spectacle), he argues that Young himself actively authored the "rocker-turned-folkie" and anti-commercial persona, so that even his gestures of resistance to the music business were absorbed as marketable integrity.

commodity-fetishism.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
commodity-fetishism.title: 19. Punk Consciousness and Class Consciousness
commodity-fetishism.relation: Tiffany Montoya reads punk lyrics and the DIY scene through Marx, Gramsci, and Lukacs, finding an emerging class consciousness in three stages: nihilistic discontent ('TV Party', 'Lost in the Supermarket'), systemic awareness of exploitation (Bad Religion's 'Suffer'), and full revolutionary consciousness with proletarian agency ('Class War', the Suicide Machines' 'Strike'). She shows how musical devices - Oi!-style gang vocals, work-song rhythms, the industrial drumming of Flogging Molly's 'The Power's Out' - create affective unity like military cadence, while mutual aid (Kropotkin) and do-it-yourself production make the scene a 'proletarian culture'. The chapter closes on Gramsci's warning that the capitalist state appropriates subversive culture (corporate festival sponsors, Hot Topic punk), asking whether punk will keep its vanguard or become 'rock for sustainable capitalism'.

commodity-fetishism.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
commodity-fetishism.title: 4. How Anthony Bourdain United the Local and the Universal
commodity-fetishism.relation: Barta and Miranda contrast Kant's 'universally communicable' taste with Bourdieu's view that taste is a social construct shaped by field, habitus, and cultural capital that reinforces class distinctions. Using Bourdain's episodes (Portuguese bacalao, New York hot dogs, the French Laundry), they argue he synthesizes both: acknowledging taste's locality while democratizing it as a cosmopolitan 'citizen of the world' in the tradition of Diogenes and Kant's perpetual peace.

commodity-fetishism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
commodity-fetishism.title: Gertrude McFuzz Should’ve Read Marx, or Sneetches of the World Unite
commodity-fetishism.relation: Jacob Held uses the Once-ler, Pontoffel Pock, the Sneetches, and Gertrude McFuzz to explain Marx's theory of alienation. The Once-ler is the capitalist owning the means of Thneed production; Pontoffel Pock's dull pickle-works job shows labor severed from the worker's essence as a free, conscious producer (an idea Held traces to Hegel on self-expression through work). The Sneetches buying stars from Sylvester McMonkey McBean and Gertrude popping pill-berries dramatize how alienated people chase belonging through consumption, which Held elaborates via Fromm's 'having vs being' and Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, concluding the fault lies not in the characters but in a society that denies self-realization through labor.

commodity-fetishism.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
commodity-fetishism.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
commodity-fetishism.relation: Wear traces the espresso aesthetic from the idealized, egalitarian Italian caffè—which he reads as an 'aestheticized Marxist' image of identical shots for businessman and street sweeper—to its dilution under neoliberal consumer choice, epitomized by the endless-customization L.A. Story 'half-caf twist of lemon' scene. He invokes Kant's Critique of Judgement and the sublime to argue that flavor and taste-judgment are neglected aesthetic faculties, and enlists the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse) and Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain how the market absorbs the espresso's beauty. He concludes that a single humble shot, as a memorial to the vast exploited labor chain behind it, is a truer aesthetic object than a branded frappuccino.

commodity-fetishism.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
commodity-fetishism.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
commodity-fetishism.relation: Hamilton defends a dual account of design — solving functional problems *and* improving look or feel through style — against both the reduction of design to fashion/styling and the modernist reduction of it to pure engineering, using the London Design Museum dispute (Dyson vs. Rawsthorn), the Citroën 2CV, Dyson cyclonic cleaners, and Pye's notion of 'useless work' (directly functionless work like a jewelled sword handle). Turning to fashion in clothing, he draws on Simmel's analysis of fashion as simultaneously imitation and differentiation, and on Adorno's account of autonomous art, to argue fashion can never be autonomous art because it is inescapably functional and commodified, yet still counts as an art with classic and ephemeral, high and popular forms.

commodity-fetishism.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
commodity-fetishism.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
commodity-fetishism.relation: Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.

commodity-fetishism.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
commodity-fetishism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
commodity-fetishism.relation: Thorsby reads 'getting high' as a rupture of ordinary, unreflective consciousness and asks why cannabis use grows fastest in the affluent capitalist West. He pairs Plato's allegory of the cave—ordinary consciousness as prisoners mistaking shadows for reality—with Marx's account of alienation and commodity fetishism, in which workers are estranged from the products of their labor and see value as inhering in things rather than in human labor. Drawing on Fromm's 'having vs. being,' he argues that cannabis offers a momentary escape from and critique of this alienated consciousness, though it cannot cure it.

commodity-fetishism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
commodity-fetishism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
commodity-fetishism.relation: Luna Dolezal's 'Yoga for Women?' argues that Western yoga, once a male ascetic path, has been absorbed by consumer capitalism into a female beauty practice organized around 'body capital.' Reading Yoga Journal covers, Lululemon's 'Say No to Camel Toe' ad, and Toesox's nude campaigns, she shows the fashion/beauty industries cultivate shame to sell the yoga body, objectifying women. She counters that Hatha yoga should be a laboratory for compassionate self-acceptance beyond comparison and competition — 'yoga for every body' — rather than another instrument of the market's normalized ideal.

commodity-fetishism.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
commodity-fetishism.title: Zombies of the World, Unite Class Struggle and Alienation in Land of the Dead
commodity-fetishism.relation: John Lutz reads Romero's Land of the Dead as a sustained Marxist allegory: the walled Pittsburgh with Kaufman's luxury Fiddler's Green tower over the exploited poor stands for America and global capitalist imperialism. The zombies embody Marx's alienated, dehumanized workers and the exploited underdeveloped South, while cannibalism/consumption figures commodities as 'dead labor.' The Fiddler's Green ad and Cholo's doomed aspiration illustrate Althusserian ideology (false consciousness). Big Daddy leading the zombies to arm themselves and cross the river dramatizes the growth of revolutionary class consciousness, and the destruction of Kaufman and the Green stages a socialist revolution in which the exploited are the ruling class's 'grave-diggers.'

commodity-fetishism.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
commodity-fetishism.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.relation: Alison Milbank reads the One Ring as a fetish in both Freud's sexual sense (an object severed from the whole, twice literally cut from a finger, warding off the castrating maternal power figured in Shelob) and Marx's economic sense (a commodity that estranges makers from things and reduces persons to hoarders like Smaug). Against fetishism she sets Tolkien's gift-economy, embodied by Bombadil tossing the Ring in the air and by Sam's elvish rope, and Heidegger's older sense of the 'thing' as a gathering, so the novel teaches us to receive the world back as gift rather than possession.

commodity-fetishism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
commodity-fetishism.title: Downsizing Dreams
commodity-fetishism.relation: Bray argues the American Office does depict class — precisely as a "salaried mass" whose identity rests on denying class difference. Using Marx's account of surplus value and alienated, deskilled labor (Stanley's "run-out-the-clock" situation, Pam's deadened art), he shows the office as a site of exploitation Michael Scott cannot properly manage. Michael's condo, the ex-convict comparing prison to Dunder-Mifflin, and Ryan's ambitions expose the gap between self-image and reality; via Walter Benjamin, Bray locates "authentic humanity" in that very tension.

commodity-fetishism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
commodity-fetishism.title: 72. Ricky Gervais as Philosopher The Comedy of Alienation
commodity-fetishism.relation: Gardner argues that Gervais's series are not merely 'cringe comedy' but a 'comedy of alienation' dramatizing Marx's four aspects of estrangement under capitalism. The Office illustrates alienation from the product of labor (Wernham Hogg workers reduced to sales figures, Tim's crushed inner life); Extras shows alienation from the activity of labor (background artists treated as props, Maggie humiliated by Clive Owen); The Office/Extras/After Life show alienation from species-being and from others (Brent's 'anyone of them will do'); and Derek depicts a character who transcends alienation. She reads The Invention of Lying through Marx's 'religion is the opium of the people,' showing belief in an afterlife pacifies workers without changing an exploitative, commodifying society.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
philosophy-of-humor.title: What’s so Funny about That
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Jorge Gracia proposes that we laugh at the significance of the insignificant and cry at the insignificance of the significant, then reads 'The Outing' nearly scene by scene: the eavesdropped 'just because you two are homosexuals' joke, the washed pear, the whiny voice on tape, Kramer's 'I thought we were going to take a steam,' and the refrain 'not that there's anything wrong with that.' The episode is funny because it lays bare society's stereotype of the gay man (thin, single, neat) and its duplicity - everyone disavows bigotry in exactly the breath with which they panic at being thought gay - turning an insignificant coffee-shop prank into a mirror of well-intentioned bigotry.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
philosophy-of-humor.title: 8 - The Simpsons, Hyper-Irony, and the Meaning of Life
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Carl Matheson argues The Simpsons is defined by quotationalism—rapid-fire pop-culture allusions like the Ayn Rand School, The Great Escape score, and The Birds tableau in 'A Streetcar Named Marge'—and hyper-ironism, positions put forward only to be undercut. He links both to a pervasive crisis of authority in art, science, and philosophy: Danto's 'end of art', Kuhn and Feyerabend against scientific progress, and Rorty's Derrida recasting philosophy as conversation. Reading the Frank Grimes funeral and 'Scenes from the Class Struggle in Springfield' as refusing any stable moral ground, he concludes the heart-warming family endings exist mainly to let viewers tolerate the next round of cruelty, papering over a paradox of comedy.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
philosophy-of-humor.title: You Better Not Read This, Pal: An Introduction to Family Guy and Philosophy
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Wisnewski's mock-hostile introduction argues that Family Guy is 'both really deep and really stupid': the show's vulgarity (Stewie's matricidal schemes, Quagmire's perversions, jokes about religion and disability) occasions genuine insight into the human condition. Its central claim is that the show's offense is exactly what we need, because being forced to laugh at what we hold sacred demands that we account for ourselves and admit our commitments may not be necessary. The introduction thereby defends the very project of doing philosophy on a cartoon, including 'the aesthetics of the fart joke.'

philosophy-of-humor.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
philosophy-of-humor.title: Let Us Now Praise Clueless Men: Peter Griffin and Philosophy
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Samet analyzes Peter's cluelessness through the 'I Need a Jew' song from 'When You Wish Upon a Weinstein', where Peter eagerly embraces stereotypes and anti-Semitic cliches with no reflection — making him the antiphilosopher, a paradigm of Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Borrowing Berenson on Giotto, he argues Family Guy, like great painting, gives us a 'realer than real' window on the unreflective, stimulus-response layer of our own cognition (the toddler clinging at day care, the Onion kitten 'thinking of nothing but murder'). Hobbes's theory of laughter as 'sudden glory' at deformity in another explains why Peter's fictional cluelessness is funny while real deformity evokes sympathy: comedy lets us glory that 'there but for reflection go I.' Finally, philosophy's Nagelian 'view from nowhere' totality is inherently unfunny because humor lives in the sheer particularity of experience.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
philosophy-of-humor.title: The Logic of Expectation: Family Guy and the Non Sequitur
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Argues that Family Guy's non sequiturs only seem random because they reverse specific expectations, so the show has a 'logic of expectation' even where it flouts inference: the Supreme Court fraternity hazing in 'Let's Go to the Hop,' Stewie's aristocratic-baby role reversal, Death hiding beer on his breath in 'Wasted Talent,' the Kool-Aid Man's sheepish exit in 'Death Has a Shadow,' and cutaways that run on shared pop-culture associations like Peter's 'no whammy' chant. The chapter deploys Kierkegaard's claim that wherever there is contradiction the comical is present, Schopenhauer's analysis of the ludicrous, Wittgenstein's joke-book remark, and Russell's ideal of disambiguating ambiguous sentences (Peter's 'I can also vomit' reply to Lois). It closes metaphysically: against Spinoza's necessity and Hume's 'one damn thing after another,' Quahog is not William James's 'mere withness' world because the gags depend on an orderly baseline, which Peter himself demonstrates by wearing a cardboard TV frame in 'I Never Met the Dead Man'.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
philosophy-of-humor.title: What Are You Laughing At (And Why)? Exploring the Humor of Family Guy
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Runs Hobbes's superiority theory, Freud's relief theory, and Kant's incongruity theory against Family Guy jokes (Peter failing 'What color is a fire truck?' in 'Petarded,' the 1956 workplace sensitivity film in 'I Am Peter, Hear Me Roar,' the fire-truck hunting gazelles) to argue no single theory covers everything. Against Ken Tucker's charge of cheap mean humor, it uses Aristotle's idea that laughter's proper function is enforcing social norms to claim parodies of mean-spirited humor laugh AT the mean-spirited speaker, not his target, and then applies Russell's solution to the problem of other minds to the writers' intentions in 'When You Wish Upon a Weinstein': Peter's established idiocy (volcano-insurance gambler's fallacy) and Cleveland's corrective lines are the context clues that the song mocks anti-Semites rather than Jews.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
philosophy-of-humor.title: Kierkegaard and the Norm (MacDonald) of Death
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Reads Family Guy's personified Death (Norm MacDonald) through Kierkegaard's 'At a Graveside': the sprained ankle in 'Death is a Bitch' mocks the mistake of thinking death's arrival can be postponed, Death's boozing and cocoa complaints violate death's indefinability and the appropriate fear of it, and the clipboard-carrying harvester of 'Death Lives' treats death as the general human condition rather than my death, exactly Kierkegaard's criticism of Epicurus. But drawing on the Postscript's account of the comic as a painless contradiction that shows what not to do, the chapter concludes Death is a Kierkegaardian parody: its very absurdity (the high-five that kills a fan in 'I Take Thee Quagmire') exposes and corrects our superficial norms about death, unlike earnest personifications such as Meet Joe Black.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
philosophy-of-humor.title: 40. Deadpool as Philosophy Using Humor to Rebel Against the System
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Brake argues that Deadpool advances an implicit thesis about humor as a threefold vehicle of liberation, testing it against Horkheimer and Adorno's Frankfurt School charge that the culture industry produces interchangeable, aesthetically impoverished pop-culture 'trash' (the formulaic MCU) that pacifies workers, and Marcuse's warning that revolutionary material gets absorbed as just another commodity. Following Kathryn Tanner's rejoinder that consumers can creatively repurpose pop culture, he shows Wade Wilson's self-mocking, fourth-wall-breaking humor achieving personal liberation from tragedy (invoking Freud on humor as the ego's assertion of invulnerability), liberation from the oppressive Mutant Factory by exposing Ajax/Francis's vulnerability and asserting his own autonomy, and a partial liberation from superhero genre tropes, while conceding humor's reactionary tendency to reinforce the status quo since Deadpool ultimately reproduces the genre and hands Disney its money.

philosophy-of-humor.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
philosophy-of-humor.title: 62. Hannah Gadsby as Philosopher Is Comedy Really Such a Good Thing
philosophy-of-humor.relation: The chapter treats Hannah Gadsby's Nanette as philosophical comedy, weighing her four reasons for quitting: self-deprecation is humiliation for the marginalized, jokes' setup-punchline structure cannot heal trauma, comic relief lets audiences off the hook, and anger only spreads hatred. It distinguishes self-lacerating from ethical, existential, and ironic self-deprecation, and contrasts Critchley's Freudian neo-Stoic humor (super-ego viewing the ego as trivial, akin to Epictetus and cognitive therapy) with the Willetts' feminist 'collective catharsis.' Against Gadsby's claim that anger cannot be constructive, it sets Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness alongside Lorde and Srinivasan to argue anger can recover agency and register injustice, and defends Nanette as genuine comedy and 'stand-up catharsis.'

philosophy-of-humor.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
philosophy-of-humor.title: 70. Jerry Seinfeld as Philosopher The Assimilated Sage of New Chelm
philosophy-of-humor.relation: Stern and Gimbel argue that Seinfeld's observational comedy is 'neo-Talmudic': like the rabbis who interpret the fixed text of the Torah, Seinfeld takes an accepted 'given' (shared phenomenological experience, e.g. the milk bit) and generates surprising wisdom by viewing it from an oblique angle. They read Seinfeld's outsider vantage through Du Bois's double consciousness (the assimilated Ashkenazi Jew who sees through two lenses at once) and invoke Derrida's differance as reintegrating Jewish pluralist epistemology into Western thought, with Nietzsche's slave-revolt as an analogy for how Jewish philosophy was made invisible. The sitcom Seinfeld, by contrast, is cast as the modern 'Chelm' joke cycle, parodying that same neo-Talmudic reasoning by pushing local logic (Elaine's Jujyfruits, Schindler's List) into absurdity.

virtue-ethics.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
virtue-ethics.title: Conclusion
virtue-ethics.relation: Robert Epperson defends the show against the 'no hugging, no learning' charge by arguing Seinfeld is about the pursuit of the moral life: the four constantly consult each other on right conduct (gift-giving, break-up timing, obligations to friends and parents), distinguishing the moral life from mere integrity. He grades each character - Kramer is Plato's man of right opinion without knowledge whose one maxim is 'listen to your little man,' George means rightly but is the man of wrong opinion, Elaine is undone by indecisiveness, Jerry is the moral axis whose flaw is vanity - and argues with Aristotle that it is precisely their imperfect characters that make their concern with acting rightly possible.

virtue-ethics.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
virtue-ethics.title: Buffy As a Watcher (of Sorts)
virtue-ethics.relation: Jason Kawal tests virtue ethics's 'act as the virtuous person would act' (Hursthouse's criterion) against Xander's 'What would Buffy do?': Buffy qualifies as a moral exemplar with heroic actions (nightly patrols, the 'Gift' plunge) and saintly sacrifices (the 'Doublemeat Palace' McJob for Dawn), but imitation fails — Xander lacks her abilities, tastes, relationships, and pure bravery, and stripping those away one by one turns Buffy into a copy of Xander. Worse, much of what Buffy does is supererogatory (Giles: 'She's a hero... She's not like us' in 'The Gift,' before killing Ben himself), so ordinary people are not morally required to do what she would do. His fix: ask what a fully informed, unimpaired virtuous observer — an 'angelic Buffy looking over our shoulders,' never drugged into 'Beer Bad' cave-Buffy — would deem right for us, given our own abilities and commitments.

virtue-ethics.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
virtue-ethics.title: Abilities
virtue-ethics.relation: Bassham tests each sense of choice against the novels: internal-choices are uninformative (Dudley resolving to give up sweets), act-choices mislead since character is settled habit - Hermione's occasional rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army doesn't make her a rebel - and overt acts cannot reveal motives, as Snape's apparent Death Eater loyalty conceals devotion to Dumbledore and Lily. Motive-choices like Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny are most revealing, but self-deception (Vernon Dursley's rationalizations) and wizarding complications - Harry's vision of attacking Arthur Weasley, Voldemort's implanted false memory in Morfin Gaunt, the Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and a Priori Incantatem thought experiment - show that in Rowling's world choices may be unknowable even to their maker.

virtue-ethics.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
virtue-ethics.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.

virtue-ethics.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
virtue-ethics.title: Defining a Hero and a Superhero
virtue-ethics.relation: Loeb and Morris take on the argument that 'superhero' is an oxymoron - the more super (and invulnerable) a being, the less it risks, so the less heroic it can be, which would disqualify Superman except under Kryptonite. They rebut it by insisting heroism is a moral category: a hero is a person of noble character whose worthy achievements are guided by the good, so a superhero is a person of noble character with superhuman powers or superhumanly developed abilities, which gets Batman and Green Arrow into the fray. They extend heroism to everyday firefighters, nurses, and stay-at-home mothers, and use J. Jonah Jameson's resentment of Spider-Man to show how the hero's sacrifice stands as a standing rebuke to spectators' inertia.

virtue-ethics.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
virtue-ethics.title: How to Be a Hero
virtue-ethics.relation: Using Superman for All Seasons, the authors argue that Clark's heroic choice required real sacrifice - leaving his family, Smallville, and Lana Lang to serve more people - and that sacrifice and the self-discipline behind it are underappreciated virtues, down payments on great goods attainable no other way, as with Peter Parker and Matt Murdock too. The hero, they say, is a normative concept with a claim on us, and since Plato held that the good is inherently attractive and draws us toward it, well-told superhero stories have genuine moral force, keeping self-discipline, self-sacrifice, and aspiration alive while entertaining us.

virtue-ethics.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
virtue-ethics.title: The Example of the Superhero
virtue-ethics.relation: Quoting Seneca's advice to 'choose for yourself a moral hero' as an ethical pattern and to 'live as if he were watching you', the chapter argues that superheroes can function for us exactly as the Stoic recommended: Superman inspires us, Batman keeps us going when the going is tough, Spider-Man teaches that conscience outranks the crowd's voices, and Daredevil shows that limitations need not hold us back. It closes practically: ask 'What would Superman do?' and go do your version of it.

virtue-ethics.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
virtue-ethics.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.

virtue-ethics.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
virtue-ethics.title: A Call to Unchanging Truths
virtue-ethics.relation: Francis Beckwith argues the 1979-81 Christian albums are no aberration: Dylan's whole career presupposes moral realism, an objective moral law built into the universe - "Dignity never been photographed" names an irreducible moral property, and the judgments in "With God on Our Side" and "Blowin' in the Wind" only make sense if right and wrong are unchanging across eras. The six-month sentence William Zanzinger receives in "The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll" is condemned on retributive, lex talionis grounds rather than any utilitarian calculus of consequences, and "Forever Young" and "What Good Am I?" urge virtue practiced for its own sake. The chapter thus reads Dylan's conversion as the surfacing of commitments - against relativism, for virtue and unchanging truths - always latent in songs like "The Times They Are A-Changin'."

virtue-ethics.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
virtue-ethics.title: It’s Not That Simple
virtue-ethics.relation: Donal O'Mathuna uses 24 to run the torture debate: the ticking bomb scenario (Syed Ali's nuclear bomb, Miles pressing to torture Audrey) dramatizes the utilitarian case for forward-looking interrogational torture, while Jack slicing off the Russian consul's finger and Morris's broken guilt show torture as a deontological violation that destroys character on both sides and usually fails to extract truth. Against the show's sanitized, banal presentation (Agent Burke as the "kindly torturer"), he sets Abu Ghraib, the systematic training of torturers, and the metastatic spread of torture programs once permitted. Fiction can open the ethical question, he concludes, but must not be mistaken for the reality of torture.

virtue-ethics.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
virtue-ethics.title: Lessons Learned
virtue-ethics.relation: Curry argues that The Wiz, the all-Black 1978 remake, dramatizes the acquisition of a distinctively Black 'racial virtue'—a habitual excellence defined in quasi-Aristotelian terms and grounded in W.E.B. Du Bois's picture of races as 'vast families' bound by common history and a divinely rooted race feeling (with Alexander Crummell and William H. Ferris as supporting race theorists). Dorothy, a Harlem kindergarten teacher who has never been south of 125th Street, lacks knowledge of self, and each companion personifies a virtue she must claim: the newspaper-stuffed Scarecrow, whose crows' 'crow commandments' and song 'You Can't Win' embody internalized racist miseducation; the Tin Man's capacity for feeling; and Fleetwood Coupe de Ville's courage outside the New York Public Library, glossed through Ferris's call for 'lion-like men.' Evillene's sweatshop creed that 'suffering is food for the soul' personifies the redemptive-suffering myth and failed-integrationism the chapter rejects, while Glinda's 'believe in yourself' and 'A Brand New Day' make honest admittance of racial reality the precondition of 'co-authoring' the world.

virtue-ethics.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
virtue-ethics.title: Transformers and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Neil maps Optimus Prime onto Joseph Campbell's hero's journey: the naive dock worker Orion Pax is deceived and nearly killed by Megatron, rebuilt by the ancient Primus as the first Autobot, and raised to leadership through the four stages of separation, trials, supernatural aid, and return. Evolutionary 'group-fitness' psychology explains why children wept at his 1986 death, and his cooperative coaching-style leadership is cataloged episode by episode - honoring the duel he lost to Megatron's cheating in 'Heavy Metal War,' refusing to condemn Mirage without evidence, exposing the evil clone by insisting on rescuing Spike, and turning Omega Supreme from revenge to save San Francisco before his sacrificial passing of the Matrix.

virtue-ethics.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
virtue-ethics.title: Why More Beautiful Means Morally Better
virtue-ethics.relation: Durà-Vilà distinguishes narrow on-pitch morality (condemning dives, feigned fouls, and simulation, which no cultural permissiveness justifies) from a broader ethics of how one conducts a fulfilling life, and argues football should be appreciated two-dimensionally—result and aesthetic pleasure together—as shown by Barcelona and Real Madrid fans who grow angry at ugly play even in victory. His positive thesis is that playing beautifully is morally better: the aesthetic tradition of the Brazilian and Dutch schools, Michels and Cruyff's total football flowing into Guardiola's Barcelona, Wenger's Arsenal, and the Spain of Xavi and Iniesta promotes life-enhancing values of creativity, skill, and vision, while results-only football invites the tricks of technically limited players and managers. He concedes a dull team could be narrowly moral and a beautiful team could still dive, but maintains that beauty makes unethical play less sensible and more perverse, and that aesthetic football carries values worth exporting beyond the pitch.

virtue-ethics.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
virtue-ethics.title: Ridicule Is a Survival Strategy
virtue-ethics.relation: Kaye argues that the highest form of ridicule, which The Onion has mastered, targets not stupidity but cheating—specifically 'asscheating,' believing what you want to be true. She reads 'I Believe In Evolution, Except For The Whole Triassic Period' as skewering people who understand Darwin perfectly but exempt humans from evolution because admitting we are just another animal means admitting we die like everything else, the move behind Aquinas-style teleological add-ons that only invite a regress of gods supplying 'extras.' Articles on breast implants, the 'New Nietzschean Diet,' and Tour de France doping all show asscheats artificially inflating their evolutionary fitness; since natural selection stamps every organism with the purpose of survival and reproduction, asscheating is a vice, and ridiculing the asscheats who pollute the gene pool is itself a survival strategy.

virtue-ethics.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
virtue-ethics.title: Cobol’s Backyard
virtue-ethics.relation: Malloy argues the real protagonists of Inception are corporations: Cobol Engineering, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow move Cobb, Saito and Fischer like chess pieces, making the film a case study in corporate moral personhood. He builds personhood from the capacity to contract and hold rights (Saito buying the airline as Proclus's representative), to bear responsibility for what is done in its name, and to decide through corporate procedures, and he rebuts the objections that corporations lack moral emotions and virtues or vices by distinguishing personhood from personality - psychopaths are still moral persons. He ends with Fischer-Morrow's dilemma between Friedman's shareholder-primacy view and the duties of a member of a moral community, concluding that a monopoly on half the world's energy supply would wrong that community.

virtue-ethics.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
virtue-ethics.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Barkman takes Andrea's mermaid-necklace question ('I don't think those rules apply any more') as a test of natural law: self-evident principles — general beneficence (Glenn's 'shit creek' rescue, Morgan's warning that it 'takes away a piece of your soul'), special beneficence toward family (Lori's 'Don't be so trusting,' Morales's 'best for my family'), and piety (Guillermo staying with the abandoned elders) — still bind after the state's collapse, while 'do not steal' is merely derived, so the unowned necklace is fair game and Rick could take some but not most of Andrea's food. Aristotle's practical wisdom resolves the cannibal hunters' collision between preserving their lives and not killing innocents — starving is the morally preferable choice — since virtue weighs principles 'all things considered.' Against Carol's 'we can make new rules' relativism the natural law outlives governments, and Father Gabriel errs by calling walkers 'abominations,' conflating bad (dysfunctional) with evil (willful) — whereas the Governor, who knowingly ignores the moral law, reduces himself to walker level.

virtue-ethics.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
virtue-ethics.title: The Wire and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Bzdak uses Wee-Bey's 'you askin' too much' - and his ultimate yes to letting Bunny take Namond out of the Game - to pose the Puzzle of Impartiality: morality seems to require equal consideration (Plato's Socrates rejecting justice as helping friends and harming enemies; the impartialism built into Bentham's, Mill's, and Singer's utilitarianism), yet the show's most admirable moment is a father's partiality, and its worst parents, De'Londa and Raylene, fail exactly by not being partial to their own children. He tests a Greater Good Principle against cops protecting cops, Kima choosing honesty over loyalty to McNulty and Freamon, and Bunk's disgusted speech to Omar about the code that splits the community into victims who matter and victims who don't. The principle handles Carver reporting Colicchio but not the burning-building cases, and the show's verdict is that both too much and too little partiality destroy lives, with no single criterion deciding.

virtue-ethics.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
virtue-ethics.title: The Wire and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: McAleer ranks three Season-long deceptions - Sobotka's smuggling least wrong, McNulty's fake serial killer worse, Templeton's fabricated Sun stories worst - and argues that only the agents' motives and character explain the degrees of wrongness, against Mill's claim that motive has nothing to do with an action's morality and Kant's distinction between acting in accordance with and from duty. Aristotle's virtue ethics and his difference between practical wisdom and mere cleverness vindicate these verdicts: Sobotka lies to save a dying union, McNulty's cleverness is corrupted by his need to be the smartest boy in the room while Lester's additions lack all wisdom, and Templeton lies from naked careerism with no redemption arc. The chapter closes with the 'Haynes Principle' - 'you need a lot of context to seriously examine anything' - as the case for a messier, character-based moral philosophy.

virtue-ethics.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
virtue-ethics.title: The Devil and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Jennifer Baker asks whether the Devil does ethics any good and answers no. Against the tempter hypothesis she sets the traditional virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, where bad behavior traces to habituated vice rather than demons, and the cure is consciously cultivating virtues by hitting the mean between excess and deficiency - Johnny's practiced honesty, the Evangelical cousin's marital vows. She faults the Devil as a one-size-fits-all explanation of evil, a glamour machine (via Postrel and the Romantic Satan of Blake, Byron, and Milton), and a scare tactic the Epicureans warned corrupts character, closing with Plato's divided-soul counsel to aim at long-term goods and a dismissal of Luther's spite-drinking stratagem.

virtue-ethics.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
virtue-ethics.title: Homeland and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Robert Arp uses Saul's interrogation of Afsal Hamid (sleep-deprivation via cold, strobe lights, heavy metal) and the good cop/bad cop dynamics of Brody's 'Q&A' interrogation to examine deception in interrogations, including the nine-step Reid technique and its role in false confessions documented by the Innocence Project. He then tests the routine practice of lying to sources against three frameworks: Kant's absolute duty not to lie, Mill-inspired rule utilitarianism, which permits lies when telling truth regularly harms but lets interrogation exceptions serve the greater good, and Aristotle's virtue theory, on which habitual lying makes the agent vicious. Saul's lie about Hamid's family shows why the utilitarian exception dominates in the war on terror.

virtue-ethics.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
virtue-ethics.title: Girls and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Sirvent and Avery take Shoshanna's Listen, Ladies! advice book to ask whether rules can govern romance, contrasting Kantian rule-duty ethics (Ray's dating rules that are 'not commandments') with Bentham-Mill utilitarian calculation (Jessa's 'depends on the virgin'). Kierkegaard and Nietzsche - extended through Žižek's Lacanian 'Big Other' of God, Duty, or Utility - show such impersonal systems let us dodge responsibility: Jessa plays Kierkegaard's aesthete escaping boredom, while Hannah's 'just to be an asshole' boss seduction and the Marnie-Elijah hookup express ressentiment and self-hatred. Their positive proposal is Aristotelian virtue ethics - becoming a certain kind of person - completed by Butler's Undoing Gender: to be ethical you must risk being 'undone by each other,' as Adam demands of Hannah ('You don't wanna know me').

virtue-ethics.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
virtue-ethics.title: Girls and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Mahon and Walker rebrand the seven deadly sins for Girls: Self-Absorption as Augustine's 'love of one's own excellence' (Hannah pitching her e-book at her editor's funeral, calling her grandmother 'the old Flo Job... sluttin' around'), Entitlement for Hannah's 'voice of my generation' demands and Marnie's rage at Charlie's success, and Sleeping Around as the John Paul II point about reducing a person to an object of gratification - Adam's fantasy sex with Hannah and his degradation of Natalia. Envy (Hannah on Tally's tragedy), gluttony in drug-fueled relapses (Aquinas's five ways), flakiness as Kant's indolent free-rider who needs others but never helps (Jessa missing her own abortion), and Senecan irritability (Jessa spitting at the Bushwick party, Ray's hatreds, Shoshanna's 'whiny nothings' outburst) complete the survey - redeemed by the girls' stubborn friendship.

virtue-ethics.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
virtue-ethics.title: Girls and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: LaRocca asks what the liberal arts (Dunham's Oberlin, the girls' rural-college degrees) are for, reading Girls through the Greek notion of paideia: Plato's discussions of whether virtue can be taught (Protagoras), rhetoric as a mere 'knack' versus care of the soul (Gorgias), and education as becoming human (Republic), joined to Isocrates's 'development of judgment' as the father of liberal education. Against contemporary self-expression-and-selfie culture, he holds that the self is constituted outer-directed - Hannah's mentorship of her traumatized cousin Rebecca being the show's clinic in empathy - and he uses the agon (Honig, Mouffe) to recast the Beach House blowup as contest over whether the others are 'worthy' opponents. Dunham-as-doppelganger (like Plato's Socrates, like Kaufman in Adaptation) makes the show itself a work of paideia and a criticism of modern academic humanism, with Aristotle's Poetics invoked for drama's basis in conflict.

virtue-ethics.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
virtue-ethics.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Reading Finn's first season as a three-stage hero's journey - winning the Enchiridion on Mount Cragdor, being tested in 'Business Time', 'City of Thieves', 'Ocean of Fear' and 'Henchman', then doubly confirmed when Billy recognizes him - the chapter extracts a working handbook of heroism from his stumbles. Its lessons: heroism needs reason as much as courage (thinking through the gnome 'illusions', knocking himself unconscious to beat the Fear Feaster), plain luck plays a real and uneven part in saving Jake from the ogre, retribution should be temporary (the ogre's returned dollar), and heroes must check their sources (Penny's con). The deepest tension is that justice and compassion, instinct and reason, violence and non-violence must be perpetually balanced - Billy's nonviolent way becomes its own injustice when Finn medicates villagers without consent - so a real hero is simply someone who never stops trying to hold the balance.

virtue-ethics.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
virtue-ethics.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Hicks starts from young Jobs the 'little terror' expelled from third grade and asks whether he failed the school system or the system failed him, answering that America's entrepreneurs are produced by culture outside school—garage workshops, Heathkits, dirt-bike ramps, and parents who back initiative—rather than rows, rote learning, and standardized tests. He catalogues the entrepreneurial character traits Jobs displayed (informed creative judgment, ambition and integrity like the carpenter's hidden plywood, initiative calling Bill Hewlett at home, courage, perseverance through the Lisa, NeXT, and Pixar losses, win-win trade, leadership) and proposes risk-exercise curricula, Montessori methods, and programs like NFTE so schooling can deliberately cultivate the virtues of a flourishing entrepreneurial life.

virtue-ethics.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
virtue-ethics.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Meyer reads Jobs through 'individualistic perfectionism'—the Aristotelian tradition (via Rasmussen and Den Uyl, and Veatch) on which flourishing is objective to human nature yet agent-relative, an endless striving unique to each person's talents rather than Kant's by-the-book categorical imperative applied impersonally to all. Jobs embodied this: the 'bicycle of the mind' faith that reason and tools extend human efficiency, practical wisdom weighing goods like friendship, health, and art through Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, experimental self-discovery (Zen, calligraphy, fruitarian diets), and the exile-to-NeXT-to-Pixar-to-iMac arc of constant re-evaluation—so the right question is not whether Jobs 'was' a moral perfectionist but whether each of us keeps striving in our own key.

virtue-ethics.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
virtue-ethics.title: Magnetic North
virtue-ethics.relation: Siler answers the Twelfth Doctor's question 'Am I a good man?' from 'Into the Dalek' by arguing that goodness is the Doctor's 'magnetic north'—the stable moral orientation his regenerations bend back toward, the force that drove him from Gallifrey's corrupt Time Lords. He concedes a dark side, from the would-be caveman killing of 'An Unearthly Child' to the 'Time Lord Victorious' arrogance of 'The Waters of Mars,' but insists character must be judged over a whole life, including the Doctor's effect on companions like Jo Grant, Leela, Ace, and Rose, whom he teaches 'a better way of livin' your life.' Clara's closing verdict—that he tries to be good and 'that's probably the point'—caps the claim that a settled direction of character, not perfection, makes him a good man.

virtue-ethics.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
virtue-ethics.title: 1. A Good Man Goes to War
virtue-ethics.relation: Pless argues the Doctor's shift from the Ninth's self-avowed 'coward, any day' to the Eleventh's gun-toting action hero tracks real-world politics and markets rather than internal story logic: after the 7/7 London bombings and amid the War on Terror, and as the show's global export grew, a war-weary British ideal gave way to the decisive 'Oncoming Storm.' She traces the arc through the Tenth's gleeful xenocide of the Racnoss in 'The Runaway Bride,' the eternal punishment of the Family of Blood, the Eleventh brainwashing humanity to exterminate the Silence in 'Day of the Moon,' and the assault of 'A Good Man Goes to War,' before 'The Day of the Doctor' retcons the Time War so the Doctor never destroyed the Time Lords, validating the action-hero persona. Her conclusion: in a crisis culture demanding proactive heroes, cowardice—once the Doctor's honest self-assessment—was rebranded as vice.

virtue-ethics.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
virtue-ethics.title: 5. Overcoming Evil with Love
virtue-ethics.relation: Bogosian argues the film locates evil not in human nature itself, as Jeanine claims when she calls human nature 'the enemy,' but in cultivable vices - Al's jealousy and fear of failure leading to attempted murder and suicide, Eric's and Jeanine's lust for power - and that only altruistic, self-sacrificial love can counteract them. With Aristotle's point that friendship is essential to developing virtue and to the good life, he shows the faction system fails on its own terms: a single virtue in isolation corrupts (Candor's truth without kindness), and a system that removes real moral and political freedom destroys the flourishing it promises. Tris's parents' sacrifices and the Tris-Four relationship - honest training advice, protection of her Divergence, and the gun-to-her-own-forehead scene where love breaks the simulation's grip - model the love that overcomes the corrupt system.

virtue-ethics.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
virtue-ethics.title: 12. The Courage of Selflessness
virtue-ethics.relation: Pless argues that courage and selflessness are not the opposed traits of Dauntless and Abnegation but one and the same virtue: any properly selfless act requires moral courage, any truly courageous act requires sacrifice so that others may prosper, and both depend on an outside party in need and on overriding the instinct of self-preservation. Because a rewarded sacrifice becomes social capital - the lunch-giving and bullet-catching examples - neither virtue can be institutionalized: Abnegation's legalistic rules and Marcus's publicly displayed selflessness destroy selflessness by removing choice, and Eric's fear-eradicating initiation produces glory and cruelty instead of courage, since fear connotes responsibility. Natalie and Andrew Prior's shared, gender-subverting sacrifices, and Tris stepping in to take Al's knives, show the single virtue of selfless courage chosen in the moment, culminating in a death that is an extension of her character rather than a surprise.

virtue-ethics.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
virtue-ethics.title: 14. You Have to Be Good before You Can Be Smart
virtue-ethics.relation: The Bocks argue that the Erudite pairing of ignorance with knowledge is morally loaded: with Linda Zagzebski's and James Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, high-end knowledge requires intellectual virtues like the courage to test your beliefs publicly, so you really do have to be good before you can be smart. The Erudite manifesto's curriculum omits the humanities that open the mind, and its IQ-only leadership test fails Plato's requirement that philosopher kings love wisdom itself and, like the freed cave-prisoner, return to benefit society - which is why Jeanine, driven by lust for power and concealment of the truth beyond the fence, is 'a poor example of a philosopher king.' Both the Erudite and the Bureau reason as consequentialists ('Knowledge is power... power to do good') to justify slaughtering Abnegation and experimenting on unconsenting Chicagoans, when the pursuit of knowledge must be constrained by informed consent and human dignity.

virtue-ethics.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
virtue-ethics.title: 15. Tell the Truth at All Costs
virtue-ethics.relation: Bowman argues Candor is the most philosophically important faction because its absolute honesty is Kant's ethics: truthfulness as a perfect duty grounded in free will, making even politeness 'deception in pretty packaging,' and forbidding a lie even when the Erudite come to Merciless Mart hunting Tris - which mirrors Kant's reply to Benjamin Constant that one must not lie even to the murderer at the door. Against this he sets Aristotle's virtue ethics, where truth bows to wisdom, justice, and fortitude when the choice is handing hidden Jews to the SS, and Bentham's utilitarianism, which Amity enacts when it lies at the gates to keep the peace and save lives.
