The Candor Manifesto's 'web of individual-to-individual relationships' and Kant's kingdom of ends explain why universal honesty alone could make truth safe - and why Christina, the Candor, is the one left standing when the city's deception finally destroys it.

virtue-ethics.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
virtue-ethics.title: 19. Why Divergent are Actually Convergent
virtue-ethics.relation: Schenkewitz argues Chicago's downfall is built into its ideal: each faction drills a single virtue through total lifestyle discipline - Abnegation's mirror rules and gray houses, Candor's black and white dress - until 'you become what you do,' but a solitary virtue inverts into its own vice once it is cut off from the others: Erudite's knowledge becomes a lust for power, Dauntless bravery cruelty, Candor honesty callousness, Amity peace passivity, Abnegation selflessness stifling. The Divergent, who naturally hold all the virtues together in one unified character, are therefore the city's apex rather than its disease: Tris never stops being Abnegation while being Dauntless, and her worth lies in negotiating among virtues and making real choices from real alternatives, unlike the faction archetypes. Justice, the chapter concludes, requires the convergence of all the virtues within each person - the Divergent are actually convergent.

virtue-ethics.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
virtue-ethics.title: 3. What’s So Bad about Eating People
virtue-ethics.relation: McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.

virtue-ethics.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
virtue-ethics.title: 4. A Cape and a Code
virtue-ethics.relation: Farrell traces the heroes' knightly nicknames (Dark Knight, Caped Crusader, Man of Steel) to medieval chivalry as C.S. Lewis defines it in "The Necessity of Chivalry": the knight's double demand to be both stern and meek, each "to the nth degree," with knightly character a work of art achieved rather than a gift of nature. Both heroes show the split (playboy Bruce versus Spartan Batman in Batman Begins, meek Clark versus bold Superman), and both go to extremes - Batman's interrogation-room brutality in The Dark Knight, Superman turning back time for Lois in Superman: The Movie - but Lewis's hardest test is the mighty man who restrains himself. Superman's lifelong self-restraint, contrasted with uninhibited red-kryptonite Clark in Smallville's "Red," makes him the truer modern knight.

virtue-ethics.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
virtue-ethics.title: 3. Hero or Villain
virtue-ethics.relation: Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.

virtue-ethics.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
virtue-ethics.title: 4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown
virtue-ethics.relation: Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.

virtue-ethics.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
virtue-ethics.title: 1. Breaking Sixteen Walls
virtue-ethics.relation: Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.

virtue-ethics.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
virtue-ethics.title: 19. Deadpool Can’t Know Fear
virtue-ethics.relation: Borrowing Socrates' definition of courage as remaining steadfast in the face of danger and choosing death above dishonor, the chapter argues that Deadpool's healing factor removes his risk of death, so he cannot experience the fear of helpless annihilation, cannot display courage, and is not an anti-hero but 'post-heroic.' Worse, mapping Luttwak's post-heroic warfare of drones and ballistic missiles onto his invulnerability, the chapter shows how fighting Deadpool drags opponents like the ULTIMATUM contract army and Crossbones into a trap where they can never test his courage and are stripped of their role as defenders, becoming mere targets. It closes that having a little fear and the chance to overcome it might be better than being unable to die.

virtue-ethics.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
virtue-ethics.title: 14. The Gods of Marvel
virtue-ethics.relation: Gerald Browning argues that Marvel's heroes reprise ancient mythic archetypes: Tony Stark is Hephaestus, the smith-god who forges wonders in darkness (mirrored in the cave scene where Stark builds the arc reactor and later the Thorbuster armor), while Steve Rogers is a Heracles-like demigod who stays rooted in humanity yet battles Death itself (Thanos as Captain America's Thanatos). He frames the Civil War split as the old brains-versus-brawn, realist-versus-idealist divide, with Cap seeing registration as a repeat of Hitler registering the Jews and Stark seeing cold logic in it. Judged as characters stripped of their powers, the round goes to Captain America because selflessness is a virtue Stark's ego cannot match.

virtue-ethics.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
virtue-ethics.title: 15. Clueless Rebels
virtue-ethics.relation: Luft reads Petty's apology for flying the Confederate flag as the awakening of justice, the Platonic cardinal virtue and Aristotle's common-good virtue, and asks what is worth defending. Socrates refusing escape in the Crito, Jesus, Njal's saga and Harry Potter exemplify self-sacrificial refusal to defend oneself for a higher ideal, the model Petty aspires to in "I Won't Back Down." Through Royce, Fletcher and Keller on loyalty, the Confederate "clueless rebels" are diagnosed with misplaced loyalty: regional pride is ethical only when we hold something as ours because it is right, never as right because it is ours.

virtue-ethics.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
virtue-ethics.title: 14. Friends Don’t Lie
virtue-ethics.relation: Bowman tests Hawkins friendships against Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics: Dustin and Lucas's shared-comics pleasure collapses into rivalry over Max, Nancy and Jonathan's utility ends once Will and Barb are found, and Barb's fatal poolside loyalty to Nancy, though one-directional, is a friendship of virtue. Nietzsche's ideal of friends who strengthen us through conflict recasts those very fights (Lucas confronting Eleven's power misuse) as the best friendship, care ethics (Gilligan and Noddings) makes the mutual one-caring Party the real answer to who teaches Eleven friendship, and Derrida's Politics of Friendship grounds democracy and society itself in such everyday reciprocity, which is why Eleven's 'friends don't lie' compass pulls her back from Kali's violence to close the gate.

virtue-ethics.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
virtue-ethics.title: 20. What Would Mister Rogers Say
virtue-ethics.relation: Jennifer Shaw Fischer and Bob Fischer apply Rogers's ideal of 'making goodness attractive' to the 2018 family-separation crisis: knowing his own son's abrupt, unexplained surgical separation caused lifelong trauma, and that his King Friday bomb-scare arc rejects trigger-happy generals for 'Generals of peace,' they argue any policy requiring border agents to lie that children are 'going to a shower' is too ugly to balance our values rightly. Rogers's unpushy vegetarianism ('I don't want to eat anything that has a mother') shows the difference between having a reason and being virtuous: making goodness lovely rather than argumentative.

virtue-ethics.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
virtue-ethics.title: 3. Confronting Grief in the Post-Snap World
virtue-ethics.relation: Benjamin Carpenter applies Judith Butler's idea of grievability from Precarious Life and Frames of War to Endgame: lives matter insofar as they can be mourned, and Thanos renders his billions of victims ungrievable by scale, turning deaths into statistics beside white stone monuments Scott finds his own name on. Most Avengers turn away (Tony retreats, Thor kills Thanos and sinks into depression, Clint goes on a murderous rampage), but Natasha stays at her post, keeping agency and hope alive, which is what lets Scott find her and the team reassemble. Her willing self-sacrifice on Vormir makes her the moral opposite of Thanos, 'the ultimate egoist' who wraps genocide in the language of balance and kills only others, and the chapter asks why Tony's funeral gets a long communal mourning while Natasha is mostly forgotten.

virtue-ethics.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
virtue-ethics.title: Ethicists Assemble!
virtue-ethics.relation: White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.

virtue-ethics.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
virtue-ethics.title: Sometimes Heroes Fail
virtue-ethics.relation: James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'

virtue-ethics.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
virtue-ethics.title: Batman Is a Moral Exemplar
virtue-ethics.relation: Ryan Indy Rhodes and David Kyle Johnson defend Batman as a genuine moral exemplar whose justice, beneficence, generosity, and courage (from reprinting No Man's Land land deeds to sacrificing his reputation in Batman Begins) are worth emulating even though no one can copy his feats. They rebut the unrealistic objection, the language objection that 'Batman is virtuous' lacks a truthmaker (likening it to 'dragons breathe fire'), and the exaggeration objection by noting that exemplars like Buddha, Jesus, and Socrates reach us through embellished, partly fictional depictions anyway. Fiction even helps, since we can read Batman's thought balloons, and his growth into an 'icon' supplies the stable true character that emulation requires.

virtue-ethics.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
virtue-ethics.title: To Be Continued . .
virtue-ethics.relation: Galen Foresman arms Bat-fans with value theory: most evaluative comparisons of Batman and Superman beg the question, since Super-fans load pros-and-cons lists with superpowers and Bat-fans with intelligence without independently justifying why those traits count. He then argues that bravery is essential to superhero greatness, because the brave person knowingly confronts danger, so the powerless, bulletable Batman is systematically braver than the nearly invulnerable Superman. The conclusion inverts the fans' debate: the very superpowers Super-fans celebrate are what disqualify Superman from being the better hero.

virtue-ethics.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Michaud asks whether the Dude's sloth is a vice and answers no: from Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness' he argues that overwork chiefly serves the rich — exactly how the Big Lebowski exploits the Dude as unpaid courier while sneering 'The bums will always lose' — and from Aristotle's and Cicero's moderatio he argues the Dude practices a mean between frantic work and paralysis, working hard when it matters (the drop, the rug). The fable of the ant and the grasshopper, retold, shows both die anyway, while the Dude 'works at being unemployed' and enjoys the time he has — sloth, ironically, does a kind of work.

virtue-ethics.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
virtue-ethics.title: Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror
virtue-ethics.relation: Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.

virtue-ethics.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
virtue-ethics.title: “King of space, right here!”
virtue-ethics.relation: The chapter asks whether Robert Daly wrongs the USS Callister NPCs even if they are 'merely' sentient code: his theft of co-workers' DNA violates a fundamental right to privacy, and Kant's focus on the will shows his in-game intentions aim at real people — he logs in solely to strangle James's NPC and make him confess to being pathetic, wanting to harm the actual James. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the second indictment: because hyperrealistic VR blurs game and life, Daly's daily practice of cruelty habituates vice and makes cruelty part of who he is, unlike clearly fictional violence such as Mortal Kombat. Merleau-Ponty's intentionality links avatar actions to the self, so the chapter ends by asking what our own intentions in games like The Sims or Grand Theft Auto reveal about our character.

virtue-ethics.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
virtue-ethics.title: Learning from Mia’s Mistakes
virtue-ethics.relation: The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.

virtue-ethics.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
virtue-ethics.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Merli argues from alignment role-play against Aristotelian virtue ethics: a morally decent player convincingly runs a vicious treacherous thief who frames others for murder, and a 'moral mediocrity' runs a genuinely good paladin, so the ability to judge what the virtuous agent would do is one thing and being virtuous another. This undermines the McDowell/Hursthouse/Jacobson line that only the virtuous, with habituated emotional responses, can 'see what to do' — the role-playing skill works off-line, without feeling the character's fear or sharing its motives, so right-action judgment does not require trained emotion. He adds that if the virtue ethicist retorts that non-virtuous players never really get it right, the contrast between guessing dice in a fist (verifiable success) and claiming to read auras (unverifiable) shows the retort makes virtue look fraudulent, and that role-playing, unlike reading Austen, demands active deliberation from another's point of view, exposing abilities literary examples miss.

virtue-ethics.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
virtue-ethics.title: Lois: Portrait of a Mother (Or, Nevermind Death, Motherhood is a Bitch)
virtue-ethics.relation: Empey frames mothering (following Sara Ruddick's 'Maternal Thinking') as a disciplined response to a child's demands of preservation, growth, and social acceptability — even for a matricidal psychopath like Stewie. Lois cultivates the virtues of prudence (safeguarding the Rainy Day Fund against Peter's volcano insurance), tolerance, and peacefulness (enduring Stewie's lamp blows and Peter's laziness; her two Christmas and 'Lethal Weapons' violent eruptions are cured by appeals to her motherhood). The chapter then turns political: drawing on Okin, Williams, and Hays, it shows mothers' vulnerability by marriage, the incompatibility of the 'ideal worker' and 'intensive mother' models, and Peter's devaluing of Lois's theater directing. Peter's basement bar, where Lois sings nightly while minding the kids, models the institutional coordination (family plus economy) mothers need — until Peter's jealousy wrecks it.

virtue-ethics.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
virtue-ethics.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Henry Jacoby's introduction frames the volume around mortality: winter is coming, all men must die (valar morghulis), yet through honor, duty, and philosophy 'first we'll live' meaningful lives. Playing on Arya's mantra 'fear cuts deeper than swords,' he claims logic cuts deeper still - swords defend bodies, but logic defends our ideas, beliefs, and values - leaning on Socrates' claim that no evil can befall a good person, since the virtuous soul stands in harmony against desire and influence. He previews the essays: Hobbes as a maester, the dark side of chivalry, Robb's questionable war, Arya and Zen, and Ned's need of Machiavelli.

virtue-ethics.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
virtue-ethics.title: Voldemort and Dumbledore Two Tempted by Power
virtue-ethics.relation: The chapter grades would-be Ministers of Magic on Plato's ruler criteria: Dolores Umbridge fails utterly, her 'I must not tell lies' blood-quill detentions and multiplying Educational Decrees exposing a lust for power that grows with her authority and a total lack of courage, wisdom, justice, and self-control. Cornelius Fudge's insecurity breeds dictatorial damage control, trashing Harry in the press and rigging his hearing over the dementor attack on Dudley, so that craving power, he loses it; both are Platonic object lessons in how not to rule.

virtue-ethics.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
virtue-ethics.title: Beyond Choices Toward a Deeper Self-Understanding
virtue-ethics.relation: The chapter concedes Dumbledore's claim with qualifications: trivial, universal, unconscious, innate, or unrecognized abilities (Harry's Parseltongue before Sorcerer's Stone) reveal nothing, and the qualities Slytherin prized in Harry, resourcefulness, determination, and a certain disregard for rules, are morally neutral, since Voldemort's resourcefulness serves domination and immortality while Harry's saves his friends and fights tyranny. Yet abilities won only through hard work and self-sacrifice, and ethical capacities like empathy, prudence, and resilience do disclose character, so honest self-reflection about abilities matters too.

virtue-ethics.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
virtue-ethics.title: The Ultimate Measure of a Person
virtue-ethics.relation: Quoting Lucretius, that in danger and peril 'the mask is torn off, the reality remains,' the chapter argues that ordinary behavior is stereotypical and only situations of challenge and adversity reveal what kind of person someone truly is. Harry and his friends pass repeated tests of courage, loyalty, intelligence, and resourcefulness and emerge humble but battle-tested heroes like Frodo's fellowship, with Ron's temporary abandonment in Deathly Hallows the instructive exception.

virtue-ethics.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
virtue-ethics.title: NOTES
virtue-ethics.relation: The essay's conclusion shows reality correcting every character's prejudgments: Dumbledore's wizard-supremacy dreams die with his sister, Merope's with the end of the love potion, Ron's with distance from the Horcrux, the Malfoys' when Voldemort threatens Draco, and Harry matures from naive boy to cocky teen to discerning young man. Garver draws the thesis that epistemology is inseparable from ethics, bravery and loyalty require true belief about danger and about Dumbledore's real faults, and Rowling's narrative misdirection makes readers undergo the same correction, so that following Harry's transformation we become better people, with even Dudley's change giving hope to the most resistant reader.

virtue-ethics.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
virtue-ethics.title: Relax, Tony—You’re Safe!
virtue-ethics.relation: Nielsen uses the unity-of-virtue thesis (UVT) to ask how morally flawed Tony can be a virtuous Iron Man. Plato's Meno and Laches — Nicias' 'thoughtful courage' versus mere rashness — explain why apparently brave villains like Doctor Doom, Iron Monger, and the Mandarin are actually fearless rather than courageous, while Aristotle's distinction between natural virtue and full virtue plus prudence explains how Tony can be courageous yet intemperate with alcohol and women. Susan Wolf's argument that practical knowledge is essentially unified justifies UVT while making perfect virtue an unreachable ideal, so flawed, striving Stark — unlike Doom — is about as virtuous as a human being gets.

virtue-ethics.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
virtue-ethics.title: Here Lies an Avenger
virtue-ethics.relation: The Pattersons read 'The Mask in the Iron Man' as moral education: Tony's repeated 'I have a good life' litany maps onto Aristotle's eudaimonia — friends like Rhodey, Pepper, and Happy, wealth, health, sobriety, and life itself as goods chosen for the sake of happiness — while Niebuhr's community of value makes the Avengers the community of trust and loyalty that grounds those ideals. Tony fails as teacher when the sentient armor kills Whiplash, cannot grieve with him, and fails Aristotle's friendship test of willing good for the friend for his own sake, its identity dangerously conflated with Tony's. The reversal comes when Tony lives the virtue of self-sacrifice — dying 'because I'm an Avenger' — and the armor, finally grasping nobility, rips out its own mechanical heart to save him, earning the grave marker 'Here lies Iron Man, Avenger.'

virtue-ethics.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
virtue-ethics.title: Notes
virtue-ethics.relation: Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.

virtue-ethics.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
virtue-ethics.title: The Universe Is Not Indifferent
virtue-ethics.relation: White takes Bert Cooper's shelf display of Atlas Shrugged seriously and argues, against Cooper's claim that Don is 'completely self-interested,' that Don is the conventional image of the egoist rather than a Randian one: he is a second-hander whose stolen identity makes his life a lie, so Betty is married to a man who does not exist and only Anna Draper, who sees Dick Whitman, gives him psychological visibility. Objectivism's primacy of existence explains why every lie collides with facts (the train recognition, Adam's newspaper photo, the misplaced dog-tag parcel) and why Don's 'ruthlessness' and the 'indifferent universe' he complains of are products of his own vices, since what is, is. The chapter walks through Rand's virtues (rationality, independence, honesty, productiveness, pride, self-esteem grounded in objective self-appraisal, not the 'whore-child' label) to show Don sought spiritual gain through deceit and so placed his self-esteem against reality.

virtue-ethics.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
virtue-ethics.title: Nonetheless, Don Can Be a Real Heel
virtue-ethics.relation: Terjesen asks whether Don is a good man, testing his mixed record (egalitarian instincts, loyalty to Mohawk Airlines, protecting Horace Jr., against habitual adultery and the stolen identity) through Aristotle's habituation, Plato's Protagoras unity-of-virtues theses, Hume's sensible knave, and John Doris's situationist attack on global character traits. The unity theses imply Don's vices undermine his virtues (affairs make him unavailable when Betty crashes; evasions about his past block honesty), and Doris's dime-in-the-payphone literature suggests even Don's reliability may be circumstance-bound, as with Pete's weddings-and-vacations-only philandering. Against full situationism, Don's consistent rules (never forcing women, valuing women he genuinely finds interesting) point to 'regional' traits, yet Roger's verdict stands: 'You're no good with relationships because you don't value them,' since Don runs family on a business code, from Adam's bribe to 'that's what people do' consolation for Pete.

virtue-ethics.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
virtue-ethics.title: Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle
virtue-ethics.relation: Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.

virtue-ethics.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
virtue-ethics.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: White examines the fan fury over 'One More Day,' in which Peter and MJ trade their marriage to Mephisto to save Aunt May's life. Virtue ethics evaluates people by stable character traits, but situationist psychology (the pay-phone coin experiments, Doris's Lack of Character) argues behavior tracks trivial situational details, not traits — while fictional characters like Captain America and Peter Parker are written with simpler, firmer traits, so making a deal with the devil reads as glaringly out of character and betrays the audience's trust. Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.

virtue-ethics.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
virtue-ethics.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'

virtue-ethics.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
virtue-ethics.title: 4. A Cape and a Code
virtue-ethics.relation: Farrell traces the heroes to medieval knighthood and evaluates them by C.S. Lewis's 'The Necessity of Chivalry': both live the double demand of fierceness and meekness (Batman brutalizing the Joker in The Dark Knight yet gifting a boy his surveillance gear; Superman turning back time for Lois yet rescuing a girl's cat), and both must achieve knightly character 'by art, not nature'. The decisive difference is restraint: Superman's Pa Kent lessons and the Smallville 'Red' red-kryptonite episode show the mighty man choosing self-control, making Kal-El the truer chivalric knight, where Lewis's examples (Achilles, triumphant generals) show power without meekness is no heroism.

virtue-ethics.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
virtue-ethics.title: 5. How Heroes Argue
virtue-ethics.relation: LaBauve opens with an imagined Justice League showdown over a Joker hostage where Batman sways the crowd with pathos (fear of failing the innocent) and Superman wins them back through ethos — years of trusted character — to stage the chapter's claim from Aristotle's On Rhetoric. Superman alone balances all three appeals: Batman's pathos is all too human (Nolan's tormented Bruce) and his logos is master-detective method, but pure pathos risks Hitler-style demagoguery and pure logos is inhuman, while Superman's surpassing ethos — reinforced by the Kill Bill Vol. 2 monologue that Clark Kent is the costume — makes him the virtuous exemplar who 'must win'.

virtue-ethics.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
virtue-ethics.title: You Should Find Another Guiding Light: Is Taylor Swift Admirable?
virtue-ethics.relation: Kate Schmidt asks whether Swift is admirable, starting from 'Dear Reader,' where Swift herself warns fans not to take her as a guiding light. After showing that admiring the songs without the artist fails (Swift says her songwriting and her life are 'one in the same') and that her character resists assessment (the Matty Healy controversy, private-jet use, silence on political issues), the chapter borrows Alfred Archer and Benjamin Matheson's account of admiration for ideals: what fans should admire and imitate is the ideal protagonist of resilience and joy-after-heartbreak in songs like 'Shake It Off,' 'Bejeweled,' and 'long story short,' not Swift's whole person.

virtue-ethics.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
virtue-ethics.title: Notes
virtue-ethics.relation: Loftin argues the Diamond Dogs enact Aristotle's complete friendship: Jamie and Rebecca fail at friendship because they misconceive the good as self-gratification, and following Philippa Foot's natural-kind account of human good (plus Cicero on goodwill and C. S. Lewis's Four Loves) he shows friendship is an intrinsic good of human beings as such. Ted's vulnerability before Beard, Nate, and Higgins invites them into virtuous activity, Higgins's defection from Rebecca's sabotage scheme displays friendship against a relationship fueled by hurt, and Nate's status-hunger explains why he mistakes Ted's laughter and Rupert's patronage for friendship.

virtue-ethics.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
virtue-ethics.title: Notes
virtue-ethics.relation: Austin weighs Lombardi's 'winning is the only thing' (embodied in Beard's protest when Ted refuses to bench Roy against Man City) against the sportsmanship tradition and Robert Simon's view of sport as a mutual quest for excellence through challenge. He argues the 'New Lasso Way' vindicates both: Ted's locker-room speech after relegation, his note to Jamie ('Way to make the extra pass') after Jamie's assist beats Richmond, Pep's cameo, and the retitling of Trent's book to The Richmond Way show that people matter more than winning while winning still matters, with Ted's humility ('It's not about me') as the ground of the balance.

virtue-ethics.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
virtue-ethics.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Barkman distinguishes the self-evident natural law (general beneficence, special preference for family, piety to parents as Confucius taught, duties to the weak) from derivative rules like 'do not steal' and from positive law, concluding that Andrea's mermaid necklace looting question in 'Guts' is really about whether natural law still binds when the state has collapsed. He argues it does: Andrea's necklace is unowned and free to take, Rick taking surplus food from Andrea would be justified by equal claims to survival, and Carol's 'we can make new rules' polygamy proposal fails because the natural law is prior to any government. The cannibal hunters of Issues #61-66 show what happens without virtue and Aristotle's practical wisdom for weighing conflicting principles, and walkers are bad but not evil, while a Governor-like human who ignores the natural law 'reduces himself to the level of a walker.'

virtue-ethics.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
virtue-ethics.title: Notes
virtue-ethics.relation: White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.

virtue-ethics.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
virtue-ethics.title: The Wizard versus the General
virtue-ethics.relation: Walls argues Bob Knight ('the General') is a greater coach than John Wooden ('the Wizard') on two criteria. First, drawing on Aristotle's remark that a good general makes the most of the troops at his disposal and Mortimer Adler's proportional standard of achievement, he says Knight won three titles with far less NBA talent while Wooden always had all-stars like Alcindor and Walton. Second, on integrity (Sophocles' 'fail with honor' over 'win by cheating'), he contrasts Knight's clean, high-graduation-rate program against widely alleged NCAA violations by UCLA booster Sam Gilbert, concluding Knight's temper flaws damage his legacy less than cheating damages Wooden's.

virtue-ethics.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
virtue-ethics.title: Fourth Hole “Quiet…Please!” Reflections on Golf and Civility
virtue-ethics.relation: McNaron argues that golf promotes civility both empirically and normatively through its rules (self-scoring, self-called penalties) and its etiquette (silence during a swing, care for the course). Using an Aristotelian virtue-ethics frame plus Kekes's 'conduct according to custom' and Calhoun's expressivist account of civility as communicating respect, he treats civility as a mean acquired by habituation and opposes it to skloka, the petty hostility of win-at-all-costs sport. He defends golf's quiet against charges of classism, reads Tiger Woods's outburst at a shutter-clicking photographer as justified anger at an etiquette breach, and names the Ryder Cup's jingoism, boorish spectators, and intrusive media as threats to golf's civil, contemplative character.

virtue-ethics.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
virtue-ethics.title: Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character
virtue-ethics.relation: Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.

virtue-ethics.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
virtue-ethics.title: Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf
virtue-ethics.relation: McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.

virtue-ethics.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Michael Austin argues that a truly Olympic greatness requires moral, not merely athletic, excellence, reading Aristotle's magnanimity (megalopsychia, 'greatness of soul') as the crowning virtue that unifies all others. He tests this against three Olympians: bobsledder Eugenio Monti, who lent a rival team a part and lost gold; sprinter Wilma Rudolph, who forced her homecoming parade to be integrated; and runner Emil Zatopek, who gave away his gold medal and defied the Soviet invasion of Prague. Using Robert Adams's idea of 'modules of virtue,' he explains why some champions show self-control in sport but not in life, whereas the magnanimous person holds every virtue across every domain.

virtue-ethics.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.

virtue-ethics.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
virtue-ethics.title: Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis
virtue-ethics.relation: Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.

virtue-ethics.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
virtue-ethics.title: Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play
virtue-ethics.relation: Opening with Gunther Parche's stabbing of Monica Seles to injure Steffi Graf's rival, the chapter argues that a win-at-all-costs mentality misunderstands sport's value. Using Suits's account of games (lusory goals, means, rules, attitude) and rejecting bare formalism for Simon's broad internalism, it grounds tennis's intrinsic worth in the difficulty of achievement, the level of the opponent, and MacIntyre's notion of a practice with internal goods. It reframes fair play as 'respect for the game,' classifies fans as partisan, purist, or ideally moderate partisan, and concludes that by eliminating Seles, Parche damaged not just her but Graf's legacy and tennis itself because he loved the game too little.

virtue-ethics.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
virtue-ethics.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
virtue-ethics.relation: Roberts argues that across Lee's 'Father Knows Best' trilogy (Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman) the clash between traditional Confucian values and Western modernity is best resolved by the virtue ethics of Confucius and Aristotle rather than by deontology or utilitarianism. Master Chu literally refusing to be pushed, the Gaos accepting Winston's homosexual relationship, and Chef Chu adapting to his daughters all require Aristotle's golden mean and habituated virtue, which accommodate special relationships and situations. Kant's categorical imperative (rejecting paternalism as treating persons as means) and Mill's harm principle are shown to be too rule-bound to reconcile tradition with modern individualism.

virtue-ethics.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
virtue-ethics.title: “And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo
virtue-ethics.relation: Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.

virtue-ethics.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
virtue-ethics.title: 15. The Evil in These Woods
virtue-ethics.relation: Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.

virtue-ethics.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
virtue-ethics.title: Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir
virtue-ethics.relation: Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.

virtue-ethics.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
virtue-ethics.title: The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders
virtue-ethics.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.

virtue-ethics.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
virtue-ethics.title: Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton
virtue-ethics.relation: Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.

virtue-ethics.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
virtue-ethics.title: Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies
virtue-ethics.relation: Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.

virtue-ethics.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
virtue-ethics.title: Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization
virtue-ethics.relation: Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.

virtue-ethics.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
virtue-ethics.title: The Dog that did not Bark Learning how to Read “The Book of Life”
virtue-ethics.relation: Biondi uses the silent dog of 'Silver Blaze' to teach reasoning from absence, arguing Holmes's 'imagination' is a cultivable art—Peircean abduction combining observation, background knowledge, and the virtues of independence, courage, patience, and impartiality. She traces how Holmes finds Silver Blaze at Mapleton and unmasks Straker as the horse's would-be nobbler by consulting 'the book of life.' Framed by Emerson's 'study nature' and 'know thyself' (and Aristotle on what holds 'for the most part'), she uses the Irene Adler and 'Norbury'/Yellow Face failures to show how prejudice and overconfidence blind even Holmes to alternative hypotheses.

virtue-ethics.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
virtue-ethics.title: Aristotle on Detective Fiction
virtue-ethics.relation: Sayers's 1935 essay reads Aristotle's Poetics as the finest guide to writing detective fiction, mapping tragedy onto the mystery: primacy of plot over character, unity of action, appropriate length, catharsis, and the parts of Peripety, Discovery, and Suffering with the criminal's hamartia. Its centerpiece is 'paralogismos'—the art of framing lies rightly by stating true consequents (B) so the reader infers a false antecedent (A) himself, illustrated by the Jones/Smith gramophone bluff, Knox's Viaduct Murder double bluff, and the 'Watsonity' fallacy behind Roger Ackroyd. She invokes 'The Hound of the Baskervilles,' 'The Speckled Band,' and 'The Copper Beeches' as Aristotelian exemplars.

virtue-ethics.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
virtue-ethics.title: No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)
virtue-ethics.relation: William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'

virtue-ethics.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
virtue-ethics.title: A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple
virtue-ethics.relation: Clewis defines a 'Spielbergian ethics of the family,' a care-based virtue ethics holding that we owe unique obligations to family and close friends grounded in personal identity, and contrasts it with utilitarian and Kantian approaches. In Saving Private Ryan the squad-as-family and the Ryan brotherhood explain why Miller says Ryan must 'earn this' and why living an ordinary good life suffices; in The Color Purple sisterhood (Nettie/Celie), fatherhood, and motherhood ground obligations of care, forgiveness, and reconciliation. He evaluates the view's feasibility while warning it neglects wider social influences and the is/ought gap.

virtue-ethics.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: Why the Doctor Is So Special
virtue-ethics.relation: Sarah Honeychurch and Niall Barr argue Daleks and Cybermen will never beat humanity because they are speciesist, judging worth solely by logic and resemblance. Using Peter Singer's animal-liberation account of speciesism (and Ryder's coinage), they claim the capacity to feel pain and empathy grounds moral consideration, and that Martha Nussbaum's and Aristotle's view of emotions as trainable judgments makes feeling essential to good moral reasoning. The humanized Daleks (the "Dalek" who absorbs Rose's DNA, Dalek Sec) show emotion's transformative power, and the Doctor's empathy, unlike other Time Lords, is why he succeeds.

virtue-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
virtue-ethics.title: 3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty
virtue-ethics.relation: Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.

virtue-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
virtue-ethics.title: 19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy
virtue-ethics.relation: The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.

virtue-ethics.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
virtue-ethics.title: 12. Bourdain’s Taste for Freedom
virtue-ethics.relation: Porot and Simon argue Bourdain's goodness is best captured by virtue ethics rather than deontology or consequentialism, and read his life through Isaiah Berlin's positive/negative liberty (via MacCallum and Carter). They contend Bourdain's indulgence of his 'lower self' through addiction and excess was paradoxically the path by which his 'higher self' of empathy and compassion grew — echoing Hesse's Siddhartha, the Buddhist Middle Way, and Aristotle's mean — recasting his suicide in mystical rather than cynical terms.

virtue-ethics.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
virtue-ethics.title: NOTES
virtue-ethics.relation: Charles Taliaferro and Dan Kastrul argue, following Aristotle's dispositional account of character, that who the castaways are is a matter of what they would do under different conditions, illustrated by Mr. Eko's circumstance-driven violence and Ben Linus's shifting good-guy/bad-guy conduct. They deploy Plato's Myth of Gyges (the ring of invisibility) to test whether characters like Sun would act justly only when watched, and, against a completely reversed morality ('an island where skinning babies is good'), they argue via Chesterton that some overriding values are non-relative, so the show never fully reverses good and evil even amid its mysteries.

virtue-ethics.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
virtue-ethics.title: Real World Island
virtue-ethics.relation: Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.

virtue-ethics.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: Stephen King and the Art of Horror
virtue-ethics.relation: Littmann stages a mock trial of King's horror using classical aesthetics: Plato prosecutes, condemning fiction as lies that misrepresent gods, afterlife, and paternal authority (Carrie's mother, Jack Torrance, the Loser's Club disobeying elders) and corrupt morals through spectacle. Aristotle counters that Poetics-style poetry is 'more philosophical than history' and that tragedy's catharsis purges pity and fear, which King echoes in Danse Macabre's claim that horror lances real terrors via Danny Torrance, Paul Sheldon, and Louis Creed. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' explains why we enjoy fictional suffering (Pennywise, Annie Wilkes) we would hate in life; Littmann finally revises Hume, arguing horror's pleasure is the spur to imagination rather than mere appreciation of artistic skill.

virtue-ethics.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: From Desperation to Haven
virtue-ethics.relation: Held reads The Tommyknockers, Desperation, and The Regulators through Arthur Schopenhauer's pessimism, arguing King's worlds are 'always already sunk in evil' and that the will to live swings life between pain and boredom even before the supernatural arrives. He identifies egoism as the root of King's cruelty (Hilly banishing David Brown to Altair-4, Bobbi turning her dog into a battery) and offers Schopenhauer's compassion-based virtue ethic, 'injure no one; help everyone,' as the answer, supported by MacIntyre on the degradation of happiness and set against Nietzsche's 'last man' and nihilism. Gard's rescue of David Brown ('the kid matters or nothing matters') and Johnny Marinville's self-sacrifice in Desperation exemplify the heroic, compassionate life that defies the dark.

virtue-ethics.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: LaRocca unpacks MacIntyre's After Virtue claim that Austen is 'the last great representative of the classical tradition of the virtues.' He traces MacIntyre's argument that Austen synthesizes Homeric social roles, Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis), and Christian humility, making constancy her master virtue (analogous to phronesis) and distinguishing genuine amiability from mere agreeableness (Knightley on Frank Churchill: 'amiable only in French'). He contrasts Austen's internal, teleological virtue with Franklin's utilitarian ledger, cites Ryle's 'gradal' Aristotelian reading of Austen's character vocabulary and C.S. Lewis on her Christian 'undeception,' and reads Fanny Price's charmless constancy as exemplary of virtue over charm.

virtue-ethics.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.relation: Cantwell reads Emma through 'perfectionism' and parody, arguing that Cassandra and later readers turned Jane Austen into a 'picture of perfection' while Emma herself is a flawed paragon. Drawing on Andrew Miller's Burdens of Perfection, she treats moral improvement as socially constructed and responsive to exemplars, set against Highbury's upward mobility (the Westons, Coles, Martins destabilizing class lines). Emma's attempt to remake Harriet Smith in her own image is a parody of the gentlewoman (Bakhtin on parody) that exposes Emma's own vanity; the crisis of imagining Harriet marrying Knightley forces the self-knowledge that lets Emma finally pursue genuine, socially situated perfection.

virtue-ethics.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
virtue-ethics.title: Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life
virtue-ethics.relation: Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.

virtue-ethics.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
virtue-ethics.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
virtue-ethics.relation: Komasinski explains Confucius's advice to fathers through three ideas: ritual (li, glossed as 'cultural grammar' – engagement rings, saying 'I love you'), excellence/virtue as excelling at relating to others (ren, 'co-humanity'), and wisdom. Using the Analects' 'Upright Gong' passage (fathers and sons cover for each other) beside Plato's Euthyphro, he shows Confucius prizes the father-son bond over law, and reads the parable of the prodigal son and Tu Wei-ming's 'personality ideal' to argue fathers should lead by virtuous example rather than punishment.

virtue-ethics.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: MOTHERHOOD
virtue-ethics.relation: Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.

virtue-ethics.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: MOTHERHOOD
virtue-ethics.relation: Jen Baker interrogates why unmedicated 'natural' childbirth is treated as morally superior, dissecting five senses of 'natural' and rejecting each, including a social-Darwinist appeal to evolution she deems dangerous. She engages Montaigne (via Cicero) on philosophizing as learning to die and cites Dylan Thomas and Neil Young on facing pain soberly, then turns to the Stoics' claim that pain 'is nothing to us' – arguing from a neo-Aristotelian/Stoic virtue ethics that pain has no moral value and that keeping one's wits with an epidural can preserve moral agency, so natural birth is an 'optional and amoral' thrill, not a virtue; she frames it with Bill Cosby's and Carol Burnett's labor jokes.

virtue-ethics.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: MOTHERHOOD
virtue-ethics.relation: Nin Kirkham applies neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to define the 'virtues of motherhood' as character dispositions that let a mother flourish (achieve eudaimonia) qua mother. She elaborates three virtues – endurance (commitment, selflessness, and long-view 'vision,' likened to endurance running), liberality (knowing when to let a child go), and moral exemplarity – each analyzed as an Aristotelian mean between vices of excess and deficit, and argues good mothering is learned by example and does not license judging other mothers against one's own ideal.

virtue-ethics.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
virtue-ethics.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.

virtue-ethics.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
virtue-ethics.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Opening with his intimate encounter with a wolf, Vitali argues that 'fair chase' cannot mean fairness to the animal — since a right to fair chase would imply a more basic right not to be hunted, conceding the anti-hunting case. Instead, invoking Aristotelian human flourishing and Leopold's land ethic, he relocates fair chase to the hunter: hunting is moral only if it serves the biotic community through conservation and lets the hunter enter the predator-prey life-death continuum. He illustrates self-handicapping through master hunter Milo Burcham stalking a distant muley with a recurve bow.

virtue-ethics.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
virtue-ethics.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Marvin, a social anthropologist, argues that for 'nature hunters' (Kellert's typology) a taxidermy trophy is not a dead animal but a living souvenir — un recuerdo — that enshrines the memory of a fair-chase hunt. Using Susan Stewart on the souvenir's part/whole incompleteness and Appadurai on value as 'difficulty of acquisition,' he shows how the lethal shot, the pose-reversed photograph, and the taxidermist's craft convert a wild animal into a personal memento that only lives through the hunter's narrative. How the animal was killed (ethically, authentically) matters more than that it was killed; the trophy is the hunter's self-awarded token of ethical excellence.

virtue-ethics.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
virtue-ethics.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Brophy warns of a coming 'pornographic singularity' when veridical, immersive, interactive, unbounded virtual reality (extrapolated from Second Life, Rapelay, and Sony's brain-stimulation patent) makes hypersex and hyper-romance supplant real intimacy. He uses Baudrillard's hyperreal/simulacra to explain how airbrushed models and 'pornbots' render real women 'just bad porn', invokes Nozick's experience machine as literally realized, and argues that utilitarianism and Kant's humanity formula fail to condemn using pornbots, so only Aristotelian virtue theory locates the wrong—the user malfunctions and cannot flourish as escalating deviance (furries, age-play, rape games) conditions vice. His bleak prophecy is that unbounded virtual desire will corrode families and community.

virtue-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
virtue-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
virtue-ethics.relation: Russell argues that being 'cool' is an aesthetic virtue distinct from being fashionable: the fashionable but anxious tryhard 'Allegra' fails to be cool precisely because her studied effort to win social approval is visible, whereas figures like James Dean or Marlene Dietrich seem effortlessly cool. Drawing an analogy to happiness and to moral virtues like compassion, he treats cool as a *self-effacing* goal — achieved only by caring about aesthetic matters for their own sake rather than for status, the way a genuinely virtuous person is moved directly by others' welfare rather than by a desire to be seen as good. He uses a Simpsons exchange (Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa on what makes someone cool) to show that not-caring alone is insufficient.

virtue-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
virtue-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
virtue-ethics.relation: La Caze rehabilitates fashion against Kant's own dismissal of it (in the *Anthropology*) as vanity and imitation, arguing that Kant's aesthetics actually supply the tools to value it. She applies his account of the disinterested judgment of taste, free vs. adherent beauty, and 'genius' (originality that provides an exemplary model — Chanel's freer dressing, Dior's New Look, punk DIY, the Sartorialist's street style) to both the making and the wearing of clothes. Drawing on Kant's claim that the beautiful is a symbol of the morally good and the 'virtues of social intercourse,' and on Iris Marion Young's pleasures of touch, bonding, and fantasy, she argues fashion can be a proto-moral, cosmopolitan force, countering Plato's, Beauvoir's, and Svendsen's denigration.

virtue-ethics.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
virtue-ethics.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Haire and Nelson read the film A Christmas Story as evidence that consumerism has replaced religion as America's faith: the Parker family shows no religious markers, and Ralphie's single-minded quest for the Red Ryder BB gun mirrors the identity-defining, transformative role religion once played. Using Aristotle's virtue ethics, they name consumerism a Christmas vice opposed to candidate Christmas virtues of being religious, traditional and family-centered. When the BB gun nearly blinds Ralphie and the hounds ruin the turkey, the consumerist ideal fails; the family's makeshift Chinese-restaurant dinner shows the family-centered virtue overcoming the vice, so 'all was right with the world'.

virtue-ethics.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
virtue-ethics.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.

virtue-ethics.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
virtue-ethics.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
virtue-ethics.relation: Scott reads Dickens's A Christmas Carol through virtue theory, treating Scrooge's transformation as a lesson in the virtues of generosity and gratitude that constitute eudaimonia (human flourishing). Drawing on Niebuhr, he explains Scrooge's greed as an anxious, insecurity-driven quest for security through wealth that fails because flourishing depends on relationships, not money (the poor-but-happy Cratchits). He invokes MacIntyre's 'just generosity' and Aristotelian habituation to show virtues are cultivated through practice, and uses Charles Taylor's weak/strong evaluations to warn that Christmas consumerism threatens 'keeping Christmas' by reducing moral worth to preferences and purchases.

virtue-ethics.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: CYCLING
virtue-ethics.relation: O'Brien's editorial introduction frames gardening as engaging core philosophical questions and previews the volume. It argues that gardening promotes a good life not through hedonistic pleasure but through virtuous traits like patience and a Stoic-tinged tranquility that ancient philosophers from Epicurus to Hume prized, and it invokes Kant to cast the gardener as a visual artist. It also sketches gardens as cosmic symbols (Pythagorean ratios at Versailles) and closes on Plato's Phaedrus image of educating the soul as tending plants.

virtue-ethics.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: GARDENING
virtue-ethics.relation: Isis Brook argues that gardening objectively improves both the land (through composting, nurturing plants, and Warwick Fox's 'responsive cohesion' with wider contexts) and the gardener's moral character. Taking a virtue-ethics approach and drawing on David Cooper, she holds that gardening practices incidentally cultivate patience, humility, recognition of reality, care for others, and open-heartedness. She uses concrete cases—Sackville-West's white garden at Sissinghurst, her own failed Cerinthe and thriving ferns—to show how collaborating with nature nurtures these flourishing-related virtues.

virtue-ethics.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: GARDENING
virtue-ethics.relation: Meghan Ray reads classical agrarian texts to show that Greeks and Romans invested cultivating the soil with civic, moral, and religious meaning. Through Hesiod's Works and Days and Xenophon's Oeconomicus (with its Gardener/King Cyrus), and the Roman Scriptores Rei Rusticae (Cato, Varro, Columella) plus Virgil's Georgics, she argues farming was portrayed as the only honorable, pious profession that builds character—diligence, endurance, justice—and sustains the state. The chapter connects horticulture to a virtue-centered vision of the good and righteous life.

virtue-ethics.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
virtue-ethics.title: GARDENING
virtue-ethics.relation: Michael Moss examines how the British grew Brussels sprouts and other 'English' vegetables across the Empire to recreate home and 'put down roots,' reading gardens as tropes of Britishness and imperial identity. He draws on David Cooper's claim—rooted in Heidegger's and Merleau-Ponty's notions of dynamic, embodied engagement—that 'certain garden practices necessarily induce virtues,' which colonial writers invoked to justify gardening's moral and civilizing purpose.
