aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Reitsma defends keeping the 'second-rate' Olympic men's football tournament against Bob Harig's 'Simply the best' litmus test, which would de-roster any event that is not the pinnacle of its sport. He likens Harig's proposed 'Olympic calculus' (scoring sports on tradition, parity, marketability) to Bentham and Mill's utilitarian maximization of a single value, and rejects both as oversimplifying an irreducibly plural decision. He argues the IOC instead rightly practices casuistry, case-by-case judgment that requires Aristotelian practical wisdom, and that dropping men's football (an under-23, FIFA-hampered tournament) would sacrifice the Olympics' global breadth for a false ideal of excellence.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Knight and McKnight use Northrop Frye's master genres to chart Eastwood's move from romance (the superior hero who defends a community, as Jed Cooper in Hang 'Em High, the Stranger in High Plains Drifter, Harry Callahan in Dirty Harry) toward tragedy with Mystic River, where Jimmy Markum kills the innocent Dave as his daughter's murderer and, like Oedipus, recognizes his error too late. They read the law-versus-justice tension through Aristotle's point in the Nichomachean Ethics that the lawful and the just are not coterminous, and cite McClelland glossing Walt Kowalski's self-sacrifice in Gran Torino as a supreme instance of Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis) that solves multiple problems at once.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: I Am the Bad Wolf
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Roman Altshuler answers Davros's charge that the Doctor is a 'destroyer of worlds' using Aristotelian virtue ethics. He argues the Doctor's chief virtue is not compassion but Heideggerian 'authentic concern': offering aggressors (the Nestene, Sontarans, the Master) a genuine choice so they become responsible for escalating, illustrated by the fly-swatter thought experiment. Companions, being 'another self' (Aristotle on friendship), make their acts partly the Doctor's own, yet their human 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' lets compassion override the impartial concern that requires respecting choice, which is why the Doctor runs from what his companions do in his name.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: 30. Good Guys Don’t Wear White
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Lindsey Schwartz argues punk is virtue ethics in action: a DIY version of Aristotle's account of becoming virtuous through practice, habituation, and practical wisdom, where no one ever simply IS good and the point is perpetual becoming. Punk heroes serve as Aristotelian exemplars - Ian MacKaye (self-reliance, straight edge, Dischord Records), Jeff Ott (near-obscene value coherence, rejecting 'ought implies can' while defending Green Day from sellout pieties), Billie Joe Armstrong (humility, giving his guitar to a fan) - and Protest the Hero exemplifies the doctrine of the mean, where courage is calculation of the right action relative to circumstances, not moderation. Punk's pendulum between pious self-deprivation and soulless self-compromise is the space between vices, and its ethic is learned by doing: 'Try. Try. Try.'

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a character virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, slave to his need to be thought funny; Gareth Keenan the literalist boor who cannot take or get a joke; and Tim Canterbury the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to circumstance. McAleer argues wit shows Aristotle's morality is broader than duty or outcome, aiming at eudaimonia, and that humor's uncodifiability, like Wittgenstein's remarks, mirrors how virtue requires practical wisdom rather than rules.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: LaRocca unpacks MacIntyre's After Virtue claim that Austen is 'the last great representative of the classical tradition of the virtues.' He traces MacIntyre's argument that Austen synthesizes Homeric social roles, Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis), and Christian humility, making constancy her master virtue (analogous to phronesis) and distinguishing genuine amiability from mere agreeableness (Knightley on Frank Churchill: 'amiable only in French'). He contrasts Austen's internal, teleological virtue with Franklin's utilitarian ledger, cites Ryle's 'gradal' Aristotelian reading of Austen's character vocabulary and C.S. Lewis on her Christian 'undeception,' and reads Fanny Price's charmless constancy as exemplary of virtue over charm.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Nease lays out a game plan for raising ethical children, using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics – eudaimonia as a flourishing life, virtue as the mean between extremes, and the master-skills of practical wisdom and self-control – as the core, mocking 'character counts' posters as no substitute for early habit-formation. He folds in Kant's motive of duty, Nietzsche's will-to-power (glossed via Janet Jackson's Control) as the drive to master oneself, and argues empathy (Theodor Lipps' inner imitation), self-awareness, concentration (Husserl's foreground/background), and a respect for justice must be cultivated to 'stack the deck' toward a good adult.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Crista Lebens narrates a C-Scow sail on an inland lake — preparing the boat, casting off, coming about, capsizing, returning to the pier — as a journey toward Aristotelian eudaimonia (human flourishing). She argues sailing demands phronesis (practical wisdom) as body-knowledge, that coming about requires the Greek 'middle path' between being 'in irons' and capsizing, and that competence 'cannot be faked' so sailing forces one to live 'in truth' (via Werth's and Kierkegaard's account of the crowd 'in untruth'). Using Borgmann's device/thing distinction, she casts the sailboat as a 'thing' that calls forth skilled engagement, unlike the powerboat as a 'device' of consumption, and links truth to the beauty of a well-trimmed sail.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Keleher applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to coffee, arguing that eudaimonia (flourishing, not mere pleasant feeling) is rational activity in accordance with virtue, that the human ergon is reason, and that money, pleasure, and honor are only instrumental to it. She illustrates the golden mean and phronêsis with coffee choices—the temperate drinker like Katherine or Samantha calibrates cups to her own tolerance and circumstances rather than a fixed number—and distinguishes the truly virtuous drinker from the merely continent one who still craves the forbidden 750-calorie frappuccino. She coins the minor virtue of 'javavity,' the habit of drinking good coffee the right way for the right reasons with the right feeling, and suggests that were Aristotle alive, coffee would join his 'external goods,' the proper equipment for doing noble acts.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Leigh Duffy pairs the yogic balance of sthira (strength/steadiness) and sukha (ease/openness) in asana with Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, prompted by her own stress-induced seizure while teaching the Nichomachean Ethics. She argues both frameworks make virtue/right balance 'relative to us' — the correct warrior I or the courageous or good-tempered act depends on the individual and moment — and both require self-knowledge and practical reason. Cultivating the mean of sthira and sukha on the mat becomes her model for finding balance among work, relationships, and self-care off it.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Julinna Oxley argues that yoga ethics is best understood as an Aristotelian virtue ethic rather than a rule-set: the yamas and niyamas name character traits to cultivate, not commands (citing Iyengar that 'violence is a state of mind, not a diet'). Laying out virtue ethics' elements — habituation, the mean, practical reason, community — she derives two paramount 'yogic virtues,' mindfulness and self-discipline/self-improvement, that are relative to each practitioner and community, so no single diet or lifestyle (e.g., vegetarianism, teetotaling) is universally required for the virtuous yogi off the mat.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Aeon Skoble uses the characters to argue for Aristotelian virtue ethics over Kantian duty and utilitarian consequence, since right action flows from developed character and practical reason rather than rule-following. He reads Sam's loyalty and Aragorn's temperance as genuine virtue, Boromir as flawed-but-decent (undone by resentment and pride), and Smeagol's swift murder of Deagol as proof the Ring's corrupting power depends partly on prior character. Skoble contends Kant's rules would make Sam's loyalty no better than a Ringwraith's, and utilitarianism's demand for foreknowledge suits only Galadriel, so virtue ethics best fits Tolkien's flawed, developing heroes.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: NOTES
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Baur reads Don McLean's 'American Pie' as an enactment of how a culture can criticize itself from within, decoding its Buddy Holly, Dylan, Rolling Stones (Altamont), and Manson/Beatles allusions while insisting the song's meaning lies in simultaneous multiple meanings, not one-to-one correspondence. He argues McLean rejects any 'foundationalist' Archimedean point for critique—paralleling the standard objection that Descartes' cogito illicitly borrows the concept of finite substance from the tradition it claims to doubt—so the 'girl who sang the blues' shows that seeking a purer external origin only deepens disenchantment. Baur concludes with an Aristotelian point that cultural self-critique follows the model of the prudential sciences (phronesis) rather than techne: one reforms a tradition only by participating in it and exposing its internal contradictions.

aristotle-practical-wisdom.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
aristotle-practical-wisdom.title: Lessons Learned
aristotle-practical-wisdom.relation: Sean McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, 'the slave of his sense of humor,' who jests inappropriately; Gareth is the boorish literalist who cannot take or get a joke; Tim is the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to the situation, exercising practical wisdom (phronesis). McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.

punishment-theory.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing
punishment-theory.title: Crime and Character
punishment-theory.relation: Theodore Schick uses the Latham Good Samaritan law to argue that doing nothing can be something: against Jackie Chiles' bystander defense he sets the French bad-Samaritan statute, Thomson's Henry Fonda cases (distinguishing supererogatory aid from the duty of the 'minimally decent Samaritan'), and Rachels' Smith/Jones pair - Jones lets the child drown and is exactly as culpable as killer Smith - to show a duty of easy rescue exists, so the gang's failure to dial 911 on Jerry's cell phone deserved punishment. But in the 'Crime and Character' section he argues the trial itself was rigged: character evidence was inadmissible, and the four are not bad people, just people who failed their duty once.

punishment-theory.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
punishment-theory.title: Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben
punishment-theory.relation: Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.

punishment-theory.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
punishment-theory.title: 19b
punishment-theory.relation: A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.

punishment-theory.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
punishment-theory.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.

punishment-theory.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
punishment-theory.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Frames the problem of pain with Hume's Dialogues (Demea and Philo) and reconstructs Lewis's answer as played out on Aslan: pain is God's megaphone that rouses Edmund on the Witch's frozen sledge and strips Eustace's dragon skin in the transforming embrace. Suffering also reveals hidden strengths, as when Aslan's pursuit goads Shasta into unexpected courage, modeled on Augustine's reading of the binding of Isaac as teaching Abraham, not God, what Abraham could endure. Aravis's claw wounds are treated as retributive punishment, tear for tear, exactly proportioned to the drugged slave's whipping, which the chapter defends via Lewis's retributivist theory against purely deterrent punishment. Because divine goodness aims at making creatures good rather than merely happy, Aslan can be both good and terrible, 'not a tame lion', since free will cannot be coerced into perfection.

punishment-theory.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
punishment-theory.title: Prison Ghetto
punishment-theory.relation: Kelly takes gangsta rap's payback attitude (50 Cent, Nas, Dr. Dre, OutKast) as the starting point for the philosophy of punishment: rappers doubt retribution because police, courts, and prisons lack legitimate authority over them - Public Enemy's "Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos" rejects the government's letter. Weighing Kantian and Nozickian retributivism against Bentham's consequentialist rationales, she argues desert, proportionality, and authority all fail in a racist system - racial profiling, the crack-versus-powder sentencing disparity, Wacquant's prison-ghetto thesis, Goodie Mob's "Cell Therapy", Dead Prez's "Behind Enemy Lines", KRS-One's officer-overseer analogy - leaving incapacitation as racialized social control rather than justice.

punishment-theory.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
punishment-theory.title: A Call to Unchanging Truths
punishment-theory.relation: Francis Beckwith argues the 1979-81 Christian albums are no aberration: Dylan's whole career presupposes moral realism, an objective moral law built into the universe - "Dignity never been photographed" names an irreducible moral property, and the judgments in "With God on Our Side" and "Blowin' in the Wind" only make sense if right and wrong are unchanging across eras. The six-month sentence William Zanzinger receives in "The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll" is condemned on retributive, lex talionis grounds rather than any utilitarian calculus of consequences, and "Forever Young" and "What Good Am I?" urge virtue practiced for its own sake. The chapter thus reads Dylan's conversion as the surfacing of commitments - against relativism, for virtue and unchanging truths - always latent in songs like "The Times They Are A-Changin'."

punishment-theory.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
punishment-theory.title: Just Desserts
punishment-theory.relation: Asks how the exploding-glutton Mr. Creosote sequence in 'The Autumn Years' of The Meaning of Life can provoke laughter rather than horror, given that Creosote shares the monster's marks of physiological impossibility and disgusting category-violation (like Frankenstein's monster or the Alien). The answer: horror requires disgust plus fear, and Creosote, like the slapstick clown, is marked as neither able to harm nor be harmed, so the audience's fear-condition for horror is never met. A second layer of the laughter is vindictive: the maitre d''s wafer-thin mint is retributive justice, a morality-play punishment for gluttony in the lineage of Spenser's Gluttony and Dante's Inferno, so black comedy trades on our sense that the victim deserves what he gets.

punishment-theory.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
punishment-theory.title: Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans
punishment-theory.relation: John Draeger asks which Undead can be held accountable for bloodthirsty behavior: Romero's zombies are amoral, like a poisonous plant or Cleckley's empathy-free psychopath Milt, while Dracula meticulously plans his move to London and so passes the cognitive test. Stoker's narcissistic Count stays amoral, but Coppola's Dracula (who warns Mina of her curse), Rice's guilt-torn Louis, and the self-deceiving, cruelty-enjoying Lestat show empathy, self-control, and moral reflection, making them immoral and responsible - which entitles vampires to due process rather than Van Helsing's vigilantism, to punishment aimed at rehabilitation, and to equal rights including civic participation and marriage, since the same standard would govern space aliens, robots, and humans.

punishment-theory.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
punishment-theory.title: James Bond and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Held argues that our pleasure in Bond's kill-then-quip routine - 'Shocking' after electrocuting a henchman in Goldfinger, tossing Killifer to the sharks that ate Felix with 'You earned it, you keep it' - reveals tacit retributive and deterrent theories of punishment that place villains outside the moral community. Using the distinction between mere humiliation (deflating Dr. No's pretense: 'Minnows pretending they're whales') and Humiliation that denies common humanity, he shows Bond dehumanizes disfigured, 'othered' villains, even as the novels present them as disenfranchised figures - Dr. No rejecting his father's name, Mr. Big demanding recognition as the first great black criminal - whose rage is a warped demand for Hegelian mutual recognition. He proposes instead Jean Hampton's moral education theory, which treats criminals as moral agents capable of reform, concluding with Jaws's redemption in Moonraker as proof that no one is beyond it.

punishment-theory.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
punishment-theory.title: So, Case Closed – Right
punishment-theory.relation: White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.

punishment-theory.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
punishment-theory.title: Gaining Trust from the Past
punishment-theory.relation: Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors' beach as a "framed" state of nature: the stolen water is a tragedy of the commons, Sawyer's "finders keepers" defense of Shannon's inhalers stages Hobbes's war of all against all against Locke's natural rights, and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward civil society, a claim to punish on another's behalf. He argues no theory of human nature (Rousseau's "Innocence" versus a "Trust No. 1" attitude) is needed to understand the castaways: cooperation grows through iterated prisoner's-dilemma tit-for-tat strategies, which also recasts the real difference between Hobbesian and Lockean states of nature.

punishment-theory.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
punishment-theory.title: Are We Going Too Far
punishment-theory.relation: David Kyle Johnson distinguishes revenge (personal, emotional, unlimited) from retribution and argues that 'Tarantino's view'—mercy should be common practice yet revenge can be justified—is consistent: Jules buys Pumpkin and Honey Bunny's lives but never waives a right of vengeance, since they never wronged him. He tests the view against Bushido, showing Beatrix's revolt against her lord Bill violates the samurai code, and against karma, which makes revenge unnecessary. After finding that Hobbes, Locke, Nietzsche and Socrates all leave revenge's justification open, he defends it—citing Budd's 'that woman deserves her revenge'—so long as the punishment fits the crime and spares innocents, as when Beatrix refuses to make herself even by killing Vernita's daughter Nikki.

punishment-theory.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
punishment-theory.title: Mr. Rawls and the Decision Procedure
punishment-theory.relation: Joseph Ulatowski uses Mr. Blonde's torture of Marvin to test theories of punishment. He argues Blonde is not a mere psychopath but a retributivist within his social code—punishing clerks who 'touched the alarm' and cops who violated Mill's harm principle—while distinguishing acting on a principle from merely acting in accordance with one, since Blonde acts from sadistic urges. After reviewing Kant's lex talionis and the utilitarian theory's flaws, he asks whether Hart and Sterba's Rawlsian 'retributivism as fairness', whose principles are chosen behind a veil of ignorance, could justify Blonde's actions, concluding Blonde could not by his own lights have done otherwise than punish.

punishment-theory.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
punishment-theory.title: John Henry, the Steam-Engine, and Folsom Prisoners
punishment-theory.relation: Mulnix pairs Cash with John Stuart Mill on the priority of quality of life over mere life: Mill's 1868 Parliament speech defends capital punishment as more humane than the "living tomb" of life imprisonment, and Cash agrees in the Folsom liner notes (the prisoner envying the cockroach that can leave) and in "The Mercy Seat," where the electric chair becomes both mercy and the throne of God. Mill's higher and lower pleasures, competent judges, and On Liberty's individuality illuminate Cash's gallery of fools, the "Folsom Prison Blues" narrator who shot a man just to watch him die, the mother-defying Billy Joe of "Don't Take Your Guns to Town," characters whose unreflective rebellion squanders rational freedom. John Henry, by contrast, exercised his higher faculties against the steam-engine and so died happy, proving the chapter's Millian thesis that freedom matters as a means to self-directed, deliberated happiness.

punishment-theory.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
punishment-theory.title: The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly
punishment-theory.relation: Johnson and Schmitz argue that Cash, through songs like 'San Quentin,' 'Jacob Green,' and his cover of 'The Mercy Seat,' championed reforming prisons from a retributive to a rehabilitative model and abolishing capital punishment (songs like 'Joe Bean' and 'Long Black Veil' center executed innocents). They defend Cash with Mill: Socrates shows vengeful retributive sentiment is immoral, Mill's harm principle says government may coerce only to prevent harm, so punishment should be justified only by future deterrence and rehabilitation. Since the death penalty's deterrent effect is empirically weak (California, Missouri-vs-Iowa murder rates) and wrongful convictions are common, Mill today would join Cash in calling for abolition.

punishment-theory.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
punishment-theory.title: Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans
punishment-theory.relation: John Draeger argues Romero's catatonic zombies, like plants, lack the cognition and empathy to be blamed, while vampires split: Stoker's narcissistic Dracula resembles Cleckley's amoral psychopath Milt, but Coppola's remorseful Dracula, Anne Rice's guilt-tormented Louis, and the self-deceiving Lestat ('the trick is not to think about it') all grasp consequences, feel others' pain, and can exercise self-control, so they are immoral rather than amoral and accountable for their killings. Accountability brings rights: Van Helsing's summary staking is vigilantism that denies Dracula a fair trial, rehabilitable vampires like Louis might earn civic participation, and a nonviolent, honest vampire suitor cannot be rejected merely for being Undead. The principle generalizes to aliens and robots: whatever can reflect morally must be held responsible and treated with equal dignity.

punishment-theory.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
punishment-theory.title: You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It
punishment-theory.relation: Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.

punishment-theory.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
punishment-theory.title: The Final Thrust to the Abdomen
punishment-theory.relation: Eric Holmes argues that what we enjoy in Dexter is not killing but punishing, and reads the show through Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (with Hobbes and Locke on the right to punish): since the eighteenth century punishment has moved from public torture to the abstract, painless deprivation of liberty, and Dexter is a deliberate throwback to the older Sovereign. Every detail of the ritual is analyzed as torture designed to make the victim recognize he deserves it - displaying photos or the corpses of their victims (Mike Donovan), forced nudity and harsh light, and letting the punishment fit the crime (Trinity's own claw hammer, telling Miguel he killed Oscar). Dexter is 'the Sovereign we've been waiting for,' an unemotional agent of deserved pain that modern incarceration no longer provides.

punishment-theory.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
punishment-theory.title: An Eye for an Eye
punishment-theory.relation: Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.

punishment-theory.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
punishment-theory.title: Pre-Crime and Pre-Punishment
punishment-theory.relation: Frames 'Minority Report' with Nietzsche's charge that men were considered 'free' only so they could be judged and punished, and with Anselm's De Concordia, where God, outside time, foreknows our choices without determining them. Pre-Crime can punish Anderton and the pre-criminals now only because their not-yet-made choices are treated as absolutely free, and the 1954 context — HUAC, Hoover's anonymous accusations, the Communist Control Act — shows people punished for the present guilt of a future crime.

punishment-theory.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
punishment-theory.title: 01. Don’t We Arrest Innocent People
punishment-theory.relation: Writing as a Precrime PR manual, the section answers the charge that arresting people who have broken no law punishes the innocent: pre-criminals genuinely lack mens rea, so punitive blame would be inappropriate, but their detention is justified as prophylactic quarantine, like isolating an infant with a dangerous contagious disease, under a non-punitive containing attitude. It cites Dick's own 'Minority Report' language of 'neutralizing' Anderton and 'the prophylactic pre-detection of criminals,' plus the film's Hall of Containment, as evidence the system is preventive rather than punitive.

punishment-theory.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
punishment-theory.title: 02. But Is It Really Inappropriate to Punish Pre-criminals
punishment-theory.relation: The section defends punitive attitudes toward pre-criminals through a 'pre-punishment' thought experiment: if Walter Wrath credibly announces tomorrow's wrongful harm and will escape all future blame, punishing him now is better than never blaming him at all. Precrime cases are analogous, it argues, because being stopped by others is no credit to the offender and not the right kind of fact to exculpate him; the person who would have done it 'remains on the hook.'

punishment-theory.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
punishment-theory.title: 04. What about Leaks
punishment-theory.relation: The section weighs leaking predictions to pre-criminals so they can reroute (the I-future), and rejects it for three reasons: the precogs' predictions are accurate only for people who never learn of them, standing by to catch a forewarned killer is costly, and would-be murderers have no right to know, since unlike a citizen facing contaminated water they could have avoided their path by not choosing it. It closes the guide's case that Precrime arrests people who deserve arrest, with appropriate attitudes and compelling evidence, without violating rights.

punishment-theory.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
punishment-theory.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Najwa Al-Tabaa reads Sandman: Season of Mists through Derrida's paradox that only the unforgivable can truly be forgiven: Morpheus's freeing of Nada works as forgiveness precisely because condemning his lover to Hell was unforgivable, while Lucifer, who was never wronged by the damned, can give them only a devalued semblance of pardon, and they cling to punishment they feel they deserve. She then brings in Foucault's Discipline and Punish and Bentham's Panopticon to read the angels' rebuilt Hell of redemption as the modern rehabilitative prison, where watched souls are expected to reform themselves. The experiment fails, she argues, because redemption is imposed without hearing the prisoners, violating Derrida's condition that forgiveness needs a shared language, so the inmates prefer Lucifer's honest eternity of despair to a salvation they never asked for, a lesson about real prisons that seek rehabilitation through punishment.

punishment-theory.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
punishment-theory.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Yuen distinguishes heroic survival cannibalism, as in the Andes crash of Alive, from the 'Fear the Hunters' cannibals: both utilitarianism and Kantianism permit eating those who already died out of necessity, since the dead lose no utility and corpses lack the rationality that grounds Kantian dignity. But Chris's band killed children to eat them and kept the living Dale as a food store, which fails both theories and cannot be excused by 'we don't do this because we want to,' since alternatives existed — joining other survivors, eating walkers ('zombitarianism'), or starving, because survival is never a moral obligation. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended as Kantian retributive punishment: if Chris universalized his maxim that people may be hunted for food, then, as Rick suggests while biting Chris's neck, 'if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris.'

punishment-theory.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
punishment-theory.title: The Wire and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.

punishment-theory.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
punishment-theory.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Littmann argues that stripped of religious scruple, Shelley's own supreme virtue - kindness, embodied in Victor's family, Elizabeth, Clerval, and the cottagers - actually supports creating artificial life: the monster is benevolent until mistreated, and superior corpse-people would be a race of geniuses rather than a threat we may preemptively suppress. The monster himself invents utilitarianism ('relative as they were, as I applied them, to pleasure and pain alone'), De Lacey nearly lives it by promising the stranger rehabilitation over punishment, but Victor's case against building a mate is exposed as speciesism - he tallies unborn humans' futures while ignoring the joys of unborn cadaver folk, though utilitarians were the first to speak for animal rights. Since intelligent otherness is humanity's only chance at non-human friendship and the risks of Prometheus's fire paid off, the chapter rewrites the modern Prometheus as a blessing and ends with a re-imagined creation scene where the monster says 'I love you' to a Victor who finally names him Nigel.

punishment-theory.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
punishment-theory.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Galliott treats Frankenstein as the template for blaming lethal autonomous robots: Victor alone created his creature, but today's 'frankennovation' - Ronald Arkin's 'ethical governor' algorithms, DARPA funding, degree programs in robot warfare, and the South African robotic cannon that killed nine spectators - distributes responsibility across engineers, educators (Victor's father and Professors Krempe and Waldman, who never properly warned him about Agrippa's 'sad trash'), universities, and the military-industrial complex. Yet Shelley's articulate, Paradise Lost-quoting monster is a rational, intentional killer who can be held morally responsible and even punished, as Rob Sparrow demands of machines. Because responsibility does not dilute with numbers - two murderers do not get half a life sentence each - the chapter concludes that everyone in the chain, and all of us who do nothing to stop it, shares the blame for monstrous creations.

punishment-theory.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
punishment-theory.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.' Since deterministic causation and randomness exhaust the options, we are 'machines made of meat' wearing ice crowns inside our skulls, so deserved suffering makes no sense. The chapter concludes that just-deserts retribution (Princess Cookie's life sentence, America's prisons) should give way to deterrence, protection, and rehabilitation—freeing the Simon Petrikovs underneath.

punishment-theory.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
punishment-theory.title: Justified and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Cast as a pub dialogue between philosopher Christian Cotton and therapist Anthony Palazzo over Ava Crowder's killing of her abusive husband Bowman at supper, the chapter asks when extra-legal violence is morally justified. It explains her entrapment through systems theory - homeostasis, learned helplessness, self-esteem destruction, false hope - and takes up Kant's debt metaphor for punishment, on which wrongdoers owe a penalty and retribution restores balance, to ask who may collect when the legal system treats domestic violence as a 'family matter'. They conclude Bowman did not strictly deserve death, but Ava's 'I did what I had to do' is best understood as acting from anger in pursuit of justice and self-reclamation rather than on anger for vengeance.

punishment-theory.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
punishment-theory.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.

punishment-theory.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
punishment-theory.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.

punishment-theory.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
punishment-theory.title: 7. Give Peace a Chance
punishment-theory.relation: Lewis argues the Dauntless Manifesto's claim that 'justice is more important than peace' rests on a mistake: following Nicholas Wolterstorff's account of shalom, real peace just is justice - each person receiving what Ulpian called their due and enjoying their rights - so the two cannot come apart. He shows each faction works with a different, deficient conception of peace (Amity's drug-induced calm, Erudite's negotiated order, Abnegation's self-erasure), then uses Aristotle's three types of justice to dismantle Jeanine's best defense, that her slaughter of Abnegation and the Divergents is retributive justice: the accused are innocent and her 'peace' is coercion, propaganda, and fear. The chapter ends with concrete reforms - welcome the factionless as a sixth service faction, let factions teach each other their virtues - so that Roth's Chicago could actually achieve the ethical community of peace-through-justice.

punishment-theory.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
punishment-theory.title: 6. Punishing Negan
punishment-theory.relation: Yuen asks why Rick imprisons Negan after the Saviors' war instead of executing the man who beats people to death with 'Lucille' and runs a mafia-like protection racket. He surveys retributivism (fair play and eye-for-an-eye equality) and deterrence, including Glenn's lawless Challenger driving, then defends Rick's refusal to kill via 'we're better than him,' the weakness of execution as a deterrent for Negan's followers, and the brutalization effect that would poison the character of the fledgling civilization. But he argues Negan's basement isolation - no exercise, no decency, his victim as judge and warden - fails Rick's own civilizing vision, and proposes restorative justice with apology, forgiveness, and mediated reparations as the punishment a civilization that claims human life is precious ought to build.

punishment-theory.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
punishment-theory.title: 9. Why Revenge Is So Sweet
punishment-theory.relation: Haas asks why we cheer Inigo's vendetta against Rugen when moral philosophy condemns vengeance as emotionally driven injustice. Distinguishing impartial, proportional punishment from personal revenge, he then uses the honor-culture literature (Nisbett and Cohen, Tamler Sommers) to argue that in lawless Florin - where the 'justice system' is run by the villain who ordered the murder - Inigo's personal retribution is a justified duty of honor, since no institutional avenue exists. The deeper pull of revenge stories, he concludes, is that victims have a special moral standing to punish - which is why Rugen dying by anyone's hand but Inigo's would be unsatisfying - while a variant story (Westley as the killer) would call instead for atonement and forgiveness, showing that revenge is made admirable by how stories are told.

punishment-theory.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
punishment-theory.title: 10. Making the Punishment Fit the Crime
punishment-theory.relation: Heter defends Inigo's killing of Rugen as pure retribution - not deterrence or prevention, since Rugen 'deserves' to die for a murder long past. Locke's state of nature grounds the right to punish in victims, who merely transfer it to the state for prudential reasons, so in tyrannical Florin, where no reasonable expectation of justice exists, Montoya is within his rights to execute punishment himself. Kant's retributivism (the island whose inhabitants become accomplices if they spare convicted murderers, from the Metaphysics of Morals) supports the claim that murderers deserve death, and against the objection that proportionality need not mean identity of kind (following M.A. Moore, using Fezzik's hypothetical house-burning), the chapter argues death is the only punishment weighty enough to fit murder.

punishment-theory.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
punishment-theory.title: 15. Death Begets Death
punishment-theory.relation: The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'

punishment-theory.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
punishment-theory.title: 16. Can We All Get Along
punishment-theory.relation: Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.

punishment-theory.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
punishment-theory.title: 1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession
punishment-theory.relation: Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.

punishment-theory.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
punishment-theory.title: 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon
punishment-theory.relation: Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.

punishment-theory.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
punishment-theory.title: 6. A Better Bad Place
punishment-theory.relation: Grosz asks whether Judge Gen could justly condemn Team Cockroach to eternal torment, testing the classic 'sins against an infinite being deserve infinite punishment' defense built on Anselm's God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived, and finding that no such being exists on the show. He rejects the continuing-sin model of Hell because the Bad Place's physical torture precludes both further sinning and moral reform, and argues purely retributive eternal punishment fails the utilitarian test. His proposal, a non-torturous 'Bad Place 3.0' modeled on C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce where people face the natural consequences of their vice until they reform, could be justified as what is best for the person.

punishment-theory.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
punishment-theory.title: Avengers, Forgive!
punishment-theory.relation: Malloy builds an account of forgiveness around the Avengers' habit of recruiting ex-villains: Arendt's 'predicament of irreversibility' explains why we cannot undo Wonder Man's revenge scheme against Stark, so resentment must be overcome; Derrida's claim that only the unforgivable is truly forgivable frames the House of M question, whether Quicksilver's manipulation of Wanda's reality-warping is a crime beyond forgiveness. Forgiveness means relinquishing resentment without excusing responsibility or condoning the wrong, so Iron Man has the 'moral power' to forgive Hawkeye, while the team's charter-based standing lets the Avengers forgive Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch on the community's behalf. The chapter closes by separating avenging (justice) from revenge, and punishment (retribution that repays debts) from forgiveness, which is why expelled members like Iron Man and Hank Pym could be readmitted.

punishment-theory.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
punishment-theory.title: Avengers Rehabilitate!
punishment-theory.relation: Terjesen asks whether Cap's Kooky Quartet-style rehabilitation really works, pitting Aristotle's fixed-character virtue ethics against John Doris's situationist 'local traits' (backed by Milgram's experiments): Hawkeye succeeded because his regional traits—hotheadedness and a need for approval—were redirected to heroism, not erased, as when he cheats the Grandmaster to save the universe. Aristotle's continence-versus-virtue and vice-versus-incontinence distinctions explain why Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch keep backsliding, why Moonstone's true viciousness defeats rehabilitation while Songbird and MACH-1 reform. Against deterrence and retributivist theories of punishment, rehabilitation is defensible when applied early and to the unhardened—the Avengers Academy children and Young Avenger Patriot—so the Avengers can rehabilitate as well as avenge.

punishment-theory.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
punishment-theory.title: “Don’t forget, she’s a dangerous individual”
punishment-theory.relation: The chapter tests the White Bear Justice Park's daily torture of Victoria Skillane against every major theory of punishment: Kant and Hegel's retributivism makes her deserve punishment (her crime could not be universalized and annulled justice) but cannot justify a punishment disproportionate to the crime. Locke's memory criterion suggests Punished Victoria is not the person who did the crime, though Parfit's psychological continuity and Thomson's bodily continuity restore the identity. Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism partially vindicates the park as deterrence and incapacitation, but cannot explain the laughing crowds — which Machiavelli's civic spectacle and Nietzsche's genealogy of punishment (Schadenfreude as moralized creditor-debtor pleasure) explain: the crowd is gleefully reenacting Victoria's own crime and calling it justice.

punishment-theory.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
punishment-theory.title: A White Christmas with Dark Reflections
punishment-theory.relation: The chapter follows White Christmas's three escalating uses of the Z-eye digital block — Beth blocking Joe (whose information deprivation leads to two deaths), court-ordered blocks extending to children, and Matthew's society-wide red-blur sex-offender block — as a conflict between privacy and access to information. Utilitarian and Kantian frameworks (autonomy, persons as ends) leave the trade-offs genuinely unsettled, while Nozick's minimal state shows the automatic, loophole-free blocking regime is an indefensibly paternalistic state violating proportionality. Arendt's account of meaningfulness through speech grounds the conclusion that erasing someone's face and voice violates their humanity, and the chapter's final move is defamiliarization: if digital blocks are wrong, we should re-examine the social-media blocking, restraining orders, prisons, and sex-offender registries they mirror.

punishment-theory.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
punishment-theory.title: Do We Attain Justice by Punishment
punishment-theory.relation: Kenny's blackmail arc in Shut Up and Dance — the twist that reclassifies the sympathetic protagonist as a child-pornography offender — anchors an argument that the hackers' vigilantism cannot attain justice: their punishments are unannounced, disproportionate, aimed at merely moral wrongs (infidelity, racist emails), and exempt from the presumption of innocence and nulla poena sine lege that states replaced vendetta with. A distinction between natural-law and legal-positivist conceptions of justice shows why punishment belongs to the state alone. Against retribution ('a mere prison sentence is too good for Kenny'), Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism — deterrence, incapacitation, and above all rehabilitation, capped by the harm principle — shows punishment should be no more than deterrence requires, making the hackers sadists rather than agents of justice.

punishment-theory.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
punishment-theory.title: 2 Transforming Wakanda Justice (or Not ) in Black Panther
punishment-theory.relation: Bein and Lewis imagine Killmonger surviving his duel to face Wakandan justice, and sort what justice would demand into retributive justice (Kant: punishment only what the offender deserves, never using him merely as a means to public safety, though they note Kant's own racist views), reparatory justice (Locke's natural rights and what Wakanda owes N'Jadaka for T'Chaka killing N'Jobu and abandoning him in Oakland), and the restorative-to-transformative justice of Changamire's gatherings in Coates's 'A Nation Under Our Feet,' modeled on South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. They argue a restorative Wakanda would seat Killmonger with his victims and even the king at the table to repair harm rather than imprison him, and sketch a prison-abolitionist Wakanda meeting Thanos with 'Wakandan justice is more civilized.'

punishment-theory.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
punishment-theory.title: 3 Sins of the Fathers Historical Injustice and Its Repair in lack Panther
punishment-theory.relation: Almassi contrasts Rawlsian ideal theory (the veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) with Charles Mills's critique that idealization marginalizes actual historic oppression, arguing the film's characters seek Aristotle's corrective justice in a world already steeped in wrongdoing: the 1991 deaths of W'Kabi's parents at Klaue's hands and of N'Jobu at T'Chaka's. He works through the Museum of Great Britain axe scene as restitution, W'Kabi's 'you kill him where he stands' and Killmonger's 'I'mma make sure we're even' as retribution (tested against Walen's proportionality principles, with vengeance untethered from legitimate punishment), and Nakia's and T'Challa's outreach centers as Margaret Urban Walker-style relational repair, reading T'Chaka's concealment of N'Jobu's death as actively constructed ignorance in service of isolationism.

punishment-theory.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
punishment-theory.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Using the Nicomachean Ethics and the Rhetoric, the chapter vindicates the pleasure readers take in Salander's Taser-and-tattoo revenge on Bjurman: Aristotle distinguishes revenge, done for the satisfaction of the one wronged, from punishment, and requires that the wrongdoer know who avenges and why—which is why Lisbeth waits until Bjurman wakes before inking i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist across his torso. Proper anger on the right grounds is a virtue (hatred alone is corrosive), Larsson is cast as the rhetorician who must keep our trust to 'put the judge into a certain frame of mind,' and the revenge emerges as the deliberated, rational means toward the end Aristotle calls eudaimonia: independence from a bogus guardianship and a life worth living, since under 'proportionate reciprocity' those who cannot requite evil with evil are slaves.

punishment-theory.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
punishment-theory.title: 1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic
punishment-theory.relation: Reads the show's automatic, unquestionable point system as Hannah Arendt's bureaucracy — 'rule by Nobody' in which no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority over the system ('He's not God, he's a bureaucrat'). It argues via Arendt's power/violence distinction that bureaucracies deprive everyone subject to them of the power to act, leaving only resistance or violence, which is why Michael's Season Two plea before Gen ('the very method we use to deem them good or bad is fundamentally flawed') and his Season Three interference amount to revolt. Chidi's 'Most Improved Player' defense of Eleanor and Michael's case that souls can grow after death show the system cannot accommodate rehabilitation, only retribution.

punishment-theory.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
punishment-theory.title: 6. A Better Bad Place
punishment-theory.relation: Asks whether Judge Gen could ever justly consign Team Cockroach to eternal torment. It reconstructs the Anselmian infinite-desert defense (God as 'than which none greater can be conceived', every sin against an infinite being meriting infinite punishment) and shows it fails on the show since no such God appears and neither Gen nor Michael is infinitely great; the continuing-sin model fails because the Bad Place's physical tortures (eyeball corkscrews, bees with teeth) preclude sinning, and Gen's own tests (Jason's Madden game, Tahani's hallway, Chidi's two hats) show vice persisting without added desert. Punishment as retribution also fails on utilitarian grounds (Jason's hypothetical spray-paint-can sentence adds only pain), so the chapter proposes a non-retributive 'Bad Place 3.0' where people face the natural consequences of their vices, comparing it to C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce.

punishment-theory.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
punishment-theory.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: White distinguishes retributivism from deterrence and rehabilitation through the Corps' execution vote on Sinestro and Fatality's lex talionis pursuit of John Stewart over Xanshi ('You have four billion eyes to account for'). Kant grounds retribution in dignity, so punishment must treat the criminal as an end, never merely as a means to deterrence, and is owed to him for his crime ('You did this to yourself,' Hal tells Sinestro), while Hegel adds that punishment annuls the crime and embodies the criminal's own right. Feinberg's expressive theory explains the Korugarian crowd that felt 'cheated of Korugar's redemption' when the execution stalled, and the chapter closes by separating justice from vengeance: Ollie's arrow through Prometheus and Laira's 'It was justice!' killing of a surrendered Amon Sur were personal revenge, which only impartial state agents may convert into justice.

punishment-theory.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
punishment-theory.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Novy uses Terry Berg's gay-bashing coma in 'Brother's Keeper' to argue hate crimes are a kind of terrorism: justice, in Iris Marion Young's enabling sense, requires social conditions in which citizens can develop and exercise their capacities, and an attack that makes every gay teenager police holding hands in public harms the whole group, so Mill's greatest-happiness principle and Feinberg's expressivism justify enhanced penalties. The chapter then turns on Kyle, who tortures Daniel Hirsh on Rikers Island and nearly beats his two accomplices to death, asking whether extraordinary crimes justify extraordinary procedures in a post-9/11 world. Kyle's horror afterward, begging Flash to undo the last twenty-four hours and losing his will to protect, and Batman's pointed 'But that is me, isn't it?' mark the line between punishing brutality and becoming it.

punishment-theory.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
punishment-theory.title: The Guilt Never Goes Away
punishment-theory.relation: Robichaud asks whether Iron Man can atone for Tony Stark's wrongs, using the Iron Monger's reprogrammed-suit example to distinguish causal from moral responsibility and to argue that omissions can be causes. Tony's negligence in running Stark Industries is blameworthy because his playboy ignorance was itself negligent (as with the Mandarin's willful ignorance), and via T. M. Scanlon's account of blame the families harmed by the illegal weapons sales are the ones most warranted in blaming him. Since 'I'm sorry' is not enough for wrongs this serious and Tony never submits to punishment, the chapter concludes that even his crusade as Iron Man to 'right the wrongs' — crushing Raza's group and collecting rogue weapons — may not yet warrant forgiveness.

punishment-theory.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
punishment-theory.title: Notes
punishment-theory.relation: Writing as a mechanic, Gordon argues Max embodies Plato's Republic: like the ship-of-state navigator, only someone who knows justice may rule, and the Myth of the Charioteer — reason holding the reins over spirit and appetite — explains why the Nightrider's unchecked spirit crashes while the cool-headed, deliberative Max endures. On punishment, Plato's rejection of retaliation (the unjust should be made just, not harmed) interrogates Max's execution of Johnny the Boy, while Polemarchus's 'render to each his due' frames the just-deserts debate. Mill's harm principle then justifies Max's force against the gangs once the state and its courts have vanished, leaving Max an administrator of street justice.

punishment-theory.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
punishment-theory.title: NOTES
punishment-theory.relation: Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.

punishment-theory.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
punishment-theory.title: Ride the Lightning: Why Not Execute Killers?
punishment-theory.relation: Thom Brooks uses 'Ride the Lightning' - the condemned man in the electric chair pleading 'Who made you God to say / I'll take your life from you!' - to examine capital punishment. He presents Kantian retributivism (execution as the only proportional punishment for murder) and then argues against it: the condemned 'dies twice', living for years under a ritualized death sentence that Glover calls cruel, deterrence fails (the brutalization effect), and public justice must not become private vengeance - so even the guilty prisoner in the song is right that we have no right to kill him.

punishment-theory.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
punishment-theory.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.

punishment-theory.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
punishment-theory.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.

punishment-theory.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
punishment-theory.title: Notes
punishment-theory.relation: Uses Hans Kelsen's legal positivism — law as amoral coercive order sustained by sanction, validated by authority rather than morality — to interpret season two's competing normative systems, from Vinci's city hall to the cartel's execution of the informant Irina. Against this background it separates revenge from Hegelian retributivism, reading Velcoro's shift from killing his wife's rapist to persuading Lenny Osterman to seek exposure instead, and Frank's communicative, confessing execution of the traitor Blake, as conflicted exercises of justice. The finale's bloodshed is read through Hegel's theory of tragedy as a collision of spheres of justice, each justified in its own eyes, whose transgression may precipitate change in Vinci.

punishment-theory.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
punishment-theory.title: “Do You Not Instinctively Fear Me ”
punishment-theory.relation: George Dunn weighs Veronica's creed that 'someone's always supposed to pay' — Carrie Bishop destroying Mr. Rooks for her friend, Logan getting himself jailed to beat Mercer, Veronica forfeiting the Kane Scholarship to watch Aaron Echolls convicted — against the case against vengeance running from Socrates' 'one must never do wrong in return' through Seneca's claim that the angry are insane and Plato's subordination of thumos to reason, with the ultimatum game showing people pay to punish even at their own expense. Nietzsche's creditor-debtor account explains the payoff: punishing the offender restores the status and self-esteem that humiliation stole, turning passive grief into an active grievance like Madison's crushed-and-cubed Mercedes. Yet Machiavelli's 'much safer to be feared than loved' finally vindicates a measure of payback, since Veronica's threats are how a disgraced outsider demands the respect fickle Neptune withholds from Meg.

punishment-theory.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
punishment-theory.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
punishment-theory.relation: Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.

punishment-theory.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
punishment-theory.title: H O N O R
punishment-theory.relation: This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.

punishment-theory.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
punishment-theory.title: Notes
punishment-theory.relation: This multi-author epilogue collects short 'cutting-room-floor' reflections on poignant WoT quotes. Cooke reads Ingtar's confession as the existential fear of historical oblivion (historia as both history and story) driving a patriot into Darkfriendship. DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.

punishment-theory.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
punishment-theory.title: Notes
punishment-theory.relation: Chavez, Gavaler, and Goldberg trace Marston's 'Love Leader' kink - bracelets of submission, Venus girdles, Paradise Island bondage games, Earth One's collaring of Steve Trevor - to nineteenth-century maternalist feminism, then map the care ethics of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto onto both the comic and real-world BDSM. Reform (later Transformation) Island embodies a care-based alternative to punishment: rather than retribution, von Gunther and Irene are transformed by loving authority into people who save their captors, and Wonder Woman rescues the drowning villain Eviless because 'Aphrodite's Law commands us to save lives always - enemies or not.' The BDSM community's 4Cs (consent, communication, caring, caution) turn out to be Tronto's four elements of care, so the good dominant just is the good care-giver.

punishment-theory.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
punishment-theory.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
punishment-theory.relation: Flynn contends certain Westerns depict a 'law that stands behind the law' — a moral/natural law transcending and grounding the weak civil order — using High Noon, where Hadleyville proves unworthy of Kane's rectitude. High Plains Drifter evolves this into divine, supernatural retribution: the nameless Stranger, a pale-horse agent of apocalyptic justice, precisely punishes Lago for abetting the marshal Duncan's murder (whipping the whippers, renaming the town Hell).
