Jackson's Zen Buddhism, especially zazen meditation and selfless 'triangle offense' play, teaches players to empty the ego and stay in the present, transforming Jordan from point-maker to play-maker; and Jackson's gift of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics to Shaquille O'Neal, who then dubbed himself 'the Big Aristotle,' illustrates Aristotle's doctrine that excellence (his improved free-throw shooting, his generosity) is a habit built by repetition.

zen.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
zen.title: Tenth Hole Life Lessons
zen.relation: Tom Regan narrates his return to golf, playing hallowed Pebble Beach and then a humble nine-hole course at Pismo Beach, dogged throughout by a perfectionist inner 'doppelganger' who demands he hit his best shot every time and berates him when he fails. The lesson comes from Jason, an ex-convict at Pismo, who tells him it doesn't matter how good you are 'as long as you're there when you play' and to 'just let it go' rather than think about golfing. Regan then plays nine holes without a word from his doppelganger, dramatizing an effortless, present, ego-quieting acceptance close to wu wei and Zen letting-go rather than any doctrine he names.

zen.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
zen.title: Eleventh Hole Philosophy in the Kingdom Golf, Mysticism, and Philosophy
zen.relation: Mark Huston diagnoses why golf, more than baseball, gets mystical treatment in pop culture, using Michael Murphy's novel 'Golf in the Kingdom' (Shivas Irons, 'true gravity') and the film 'The Legend of Bagger Vance' (Junuh's 'authentic swing'). He plays William James's four marks of mysticism against Bertrand Russell's skeptical criteria, ties golf's appeal to individuality, contemplative time, nature (citing Emerson's 'transparent eye-ball') and Sartrean existential freedom, arguing that a golfer's freedom over whether to follow the rules mirrors Sartre's claim that in play man sets his own rules and must take responsibility. He reads Shivas Irons and Bagger Vance as Zen roshi figures using paradoxical, koan-like teaching to bring the student to a self-transforming 'authentic swing.'

zen.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
zen.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
zen.relation: Hole reads The Ice Storm's prophetic opening as a meditation on 'what is impending', weaving existentialism with Zen Buddhism and Daoism. He uses the Four Noble Truths and the Zen story of the monk 'still carrying the woman' to show the families suffer through attachment to rigid self-images, and Jung's synchronicity and the Daoist dao/wu-wei to read the ice storm's formation and Mikey's chance electrocution as an interdependent flow the characters resist. Centrally he applies Heidegger's being-toward-death—death as ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped—arguing that fleeing one's death is fleeing one's authentic being, alongside Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Nietzsche's living dangerously; he closes by applying the argument to his own mortality.

zen.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
zen.title: Being-at-Home Gary Snyder and the Poetics of Place
zen.relation: Hayes reads Gary Snyder's poetry and prose on 'being-at-home' through Heidegger's claim that 'poetically man dwells' and his earth/world distinction, arguing Snyder's bioregionalism (renaming California the 'Shasta Bioregion,' America 'Turtle Island') roots identity in place while embracing Zen impermanence learned from Dōgen. Snyder's shamanic 'tawny grammar,' his pragmatic environmental program in 'Four Changes,' and his Transcendentalist lineage (Thoreau, Emerson) turn wildness into 'the state of complete awareness,' letting a place 'set free into its own presencing' and grounding a poetics of dwelling that is at once local, geological, and impermanent.

zen.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
zen.title: Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground
zen.relation: Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.

zen.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
zen.title: Mulhall and His Detractors
zen.relation: The chapter stages the film-as-philosophy debate: Mulhall's 'bold thesis' that films like the Alien series are 'philosophical exercises—philosophy in action,' Baggini's objection that they offer symbolic representations without reasons, and Mulhall's rejoinders that rationally reorienting a shared conceptual space (Socrates' polis-as-parent analogy in the Crito) and dramatizing visions of what ultimately matters are rational without formal argument. It then answers Murray Smith (film thought experiments like All of Me subordinate the epistemic to the artistic) and Paisley Livingston (philosophizing must occur via non-paraphrasable cinematic devices alone) by arguing that Whedon's portrayal of Angel's worldview—helping the helpless for its own sake with no glorious end—raises exactly the ultimate-ends questions Mill said admit of no proof, with Angel as a confirming instance of Mulhall. The Buffy episode 'Hush' closes the case: its dialogue-free middle, from Buffy and Riley's kiss to Willow and Tara's joined-hands spell, conveys a Zen-like lesson about the limits of propositional knowledge that resists linguistic mediation, answering Livingston's talking-head dilemma.

zen.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
zen.title: Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West
zen.relation: Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.

zen.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
zen.title: “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons
zen.relation: James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.

zen.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
zen.title: House Sitting
zen.relation: Ruff and Barris cast Dr. House's rude, rule-breaking rhetoric as a form of Zen practice, working like a koan that unsettles everyone's (and House's own) habitual sense so genuine sense can emerge. In cases like 'DNR,' 'Mob Rules,' and 'House vs. God,' his 'everybody lies' provocations strip away presuppositions until the true problem reveals itself, making his irresponsibility a way of acting ethically, establishing naked intimacy, finding truth, and healing. Invoking Suzuki and 'beginner's mind,' they argue House is nondualistically inside the rhetoric, at peace once the insight arrives.

zen.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
zen.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
zen.relation: James Whitehill treats sailing his Cape Cod catboat, named Garuda, as a Zen practice modeled on Zen archery (kyudo) and tea ceremony. He organizes it into 'outer work' (technique and ritualized performance) and 'inner work' (cultivating ki energy through breathing and belly-awareness, then 'self-forgetting'), quoting Dogen's dictum that studying the self is forgetting the self, and forgetting the self is being authenticated by all things. The goal is a boat-and-sailor unity in which the sailor 'sails without sailing' — reaching, through mundane repetitive discipline rather than a sought-after peak experience, a nirvana-like state where wind, wave, and self merge.

zen.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
zen.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
zen.relation: Eric Swan argues that climbing embodies the principles and spirit of Zen, the experience of 'ordinary mind' finding the extraordinary in the ordinary and living fully in the present. Tracing Zen from the Buddha's Flower Sermon and Bodhidharma through Suzuki's 'Beginner's Mind' and Huineng's finger-and-moon, he maps Zen's four training paths—physical work, zazen (sitting meditation), koans, and interviews with masters—onto climbing: routes are like koans solved by insight and action rather than logic, 'being in the zone' is meditative absorption, and breath-regulation at the crux is zazen in motion. He holds up free soloist Derek Hersey, grinning hundreds of feet up Eldorado Canyon, and Chris Sharma, who writes of flowing 'like water' on the rock, as modern Zen masters who dissolve the separation between self, climb, and world.

zen.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
zen.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
zen.relation: Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.

zen.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
zen.title: House Sitting
zen.relation: Ruff and Barris argue that House's rude, rule-breaking rhetoric works like a Zen koan: by insisting "everybody lies" and unsettling everyone's (and his own) habitual sense-making, he opens space for the true problem to reveal itself. Through cases like "DNR," "Mob Rules," and "House vs. God," they show his refusal of justification is a way of acting ethically, establishing naked intimacy, reaching truth, and healing — all one nondual "happening." House is inside the rhetoric, performed by it, ending each case in Zen-like equanimity amid personal chaos.

plato-euthyphro.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
plato-euthyphro.title: 4 - Marge’s Moral Motivation
plato-euthyphro.relation: Gerald Erion and Joseph Zeccardi present Marge as an everyday Aristotelian whose bravery (The Springfield Connection, escaping the Movementarian commune), temperance, and generosity each hit the mean between Springfield's vicious extremes, and whose eudaimonia is achieved through the good of her family. They contrast her reason-driven conscience with Ned Flanders's divine command theory—consulting Reverend Lovejoy over whether to play capture-the-flag on the sabbath—and side with Marge, invoking Plato's Euthyphro to argue that morality cannot simply be a function of God's commands. Marge emerges as a 'Christian-flavored Aristotelian' who cultivates virtue by habituation and models it for Lisa and Bart.

plato-euthyphro.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
plato-euthyphro.title: Unknown
plato-euthyphro.relation: Irwin parallels Neo's mission with Socrates' divine commission from the Oracle at Delphi to 'wake up' Athens: both are driven by a single question ('What is the Matrix?' versus 'What is the good life?'), both are charged by the authorities, and both sting a complacent public. He explains the Socratic method through the Euthyphro exchange on holiness, where a follow-up question ('Is the holy holy because the gods approve it, or do they approve it because it is holy?') exposes Euthyphro's ignorance, and introduces Socrates' mantra 'I know nothing' as the humility that launches his quest just as Neo's lack of self-knowledge launches his.

plato-euthyphro.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
plato-euthyphro.title: The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet
plato-euthyphro.relation: The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.

plato-euthyphro.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
plato-euthyphro.title: Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)
plato-euthyphro.relation: Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.

plato-euthyphro.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
plato-euthyphro.title: House and the Life of Reason
plato-euthyphro.relation: Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.

plato-euthyphro.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
plato-euthyphro.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.relation: Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.

plato-euthyphro.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
plato-euthyphro.title: Homeland and Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.relation: Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.

plato-euthyphro.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
plato-euthyphro.title: 25. Deadpool Kills God
plato-euthyphro.relation: The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'

plato-euthyphro.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
plato-euthyphro.title: 24. Aftermath
plato-euthyphro.relation: Faller argues Civil War is Marvel's meditation on the aftermath of 9/11 - the Raft as Guantanamo, Zemo's interrogation as the waterboarding debate - and on America's red-blue polarization, with Steve Rogers embodying the virtue of the Good and Tony Stark the virtue of Truth as the two values democracy constantly pits against each other. Turning to Athens, he reads Plato's Euthyphro - are the gods good because goodness is a standard above them, or because their power decrees whatever they do good? - as the exact dilemma splitting Democrats, who define truth by the good it does, from Republicans, who define good by conformity to law and constitutional process, the same democratic dynamic that voted to execute Socrates and, in the comics, leaves Captain America assassinated by a sniper on his way to trial. Transcending the dualism is modeled by Spider-Man's identity disclosure and Black Panther's renunciation of vengeance over Zemo.

plato-euthyphro.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
plato-euthyphro.title: 4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk
plato-euthyphro.relation: Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.

plato-euthyphro.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
plato-euthyphro.title: 16 Sacred Objects and Cosmic Justice in Indiana Jones
plato-euthyphro.relation: Argues that the Indyverse is a moral universe: whoever profanes a sacred object for selfish ends is punished regardless of personal religion — Belloq and the Nazis are consumed for opening the Ark, Mola Ram plunges from the rope bridge when the Sankara Stones burn his hand, Donovan ages to dust for choosing the ornate false grail, and Elsa falls carrying the true Grail past the Great Seal. Durkheim's sacred/profane distinction and Tillich's account of religious symbols explain why respectful handling (Indy's 'don't look,' returning the stone to Mayapore's altar) succeeds where theft fails. The closing Euthyphro move concludes that the three traditions' objects enforce one universal ethic: respect is a moral truth binding independently of any divine command, like 2+2=4.

plato-euthyphro.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.relation: Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.

plato-euthyphro.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
plato-euthyphro.title: The Right and the Good without God
plato-euthyphro.relation: The chapter builds the case that Whedon's fiction grounds ethics without God: Foy's Lockean social-contract reading of the Firefly crew and Kant's person-as-end analysis explain why Mal insists Saffron is 'not to be bought' in 'Our Mrs. Reynolds' and why Loki's possession of Hawkeye and Jasmine's enthrallment of her worshippers are the Whedonverse's paradigm wrongs. Spike's arc—from selfish ally, through the 'Triangle' troll fight and 'Intervention' torture, to the 'Chosen' sacrifice—is read through Aristotelian habituation into virtue, while Angel's Darla-arc firing of Team Angel and the Better Days temple-money and Inara plots show where respecting rights and being a good person can come apart. Finally the Euthyphro dilemma, plus replies to Pojman and Craig (self-sacrifice is not 'stupid'), argue that Angel's 'Epiphany' ethic—doing what matters with no glorious end or divine reward—shows morality is neither arbitrary nor motivationally crippled without God.

plato-euthyphro.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
plato-euthyphro.title: 7. Anthony Bourdain’s Extremely Objectionable Stories
plato-euthyphro.relation: Holmes examines Bourdain's horror graphic novel Hungry Ghosts as cautionary folklore in the tradition of Aesop and EC Comics. He stages a debate between Aristotle, who in the Rhetoric endorses fables as accessible moral tools, and Plato, who in the Republic wants to censor frightening tales for children — yet Holmes shows Plato himself (Euthyphro, Laws) praised fear as 'modesty,' and notes Bourdain used cautionary tales (Ronald McDonald 'has cooties') to steer his own daughter from fast food.

plato-euthyphro.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
plato-euthyphro.title: Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation
plato-euthyphro.relation: Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.

plato-euthyphro.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
plato-euthyphro.title: House and the Life of Reason
plato-euthyphro.relation: Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.

plato-euthyphro.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.title: 4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism
plato-euthyphro.relation: Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.

plato-euthyphro.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.title: 19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion
plato-euthyphro.relation: The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.

plato-euthyphro.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.title: 61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists
plato-euthyphro.relation: The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

plato-euthyphro.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
plato-euthyphro.title: 74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates
plato-euthyphro.relation: Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

master-slave-morality.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
master-slave-morality.title: 5 - Thus Spake Bart On Nietzsche and the Virtues of Being Bad
master-slave-morality.relation: Mark Conard asks whether Bart could be a Nietzschean ideal, tracing Nietzsche's path from Schopenhauer's will/representation split in The Birth of Tragedy—where art redeems us from the horror of existence, with Lisa cast as the Socratic theoretical optimist whose reason never fixes Springfield's absurdity—to the later view that there is no 'being behind the doing', a condition cartoons embody perfectly since Bart is nothing but the sum of his misdeeds. He explains master and slave morality, with Nelson's bullying as master morality and the slaves' ressentiment inventing 'evil', before concluding Bart fails as Übermensch: he defines himself only reactively against authority, as Lisa diagnoses in the Brad Goodman episode, and collapses when the repressive milieu disappears. Bart thus exemplifies the post-Nietzschean danger of nihilism, though the show itself may perform the artistic 'discharge of the nausea of absurdity' Nietzsche praised in Greek comedy.

master-slave-morality.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
master-slave-morality.title: Persuasion As Drama
master-slave-morality.relation: Karl Schudt contends that Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality cannot be refuted by reason (Nietzsche denies reason itself), so drama must persuade where dialectic cannot: a believable story of a Nietzschean life acts as an empathic experiment. Faith is constructed as the Nietzschean ideal — strong, healthy, ruthless ('Find a couple of studs, use them, and discard them'), dismissive of reflection ('You think too much') — serving Mayor Wilkins, whom Schudt reads as a genuine Übermensch sacrificing mankind's mass for his ascension. Watching her world collapse (the accidental killing in 'Bad Girls', her mirror scene in 'Who Are You?', the torture of Wesley and confession on Angel) gives viewers an Aristotelian pity-and-fear warning that the unjust life ends badly, completing her 'leap from Nietzsche to Socrates.'

master-slave-morality.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
master-slave-morality.title: Why Are the X-Men Good
master-slave-morality.relation: Systematically rejects candidate explanations of the X-Men's goodness: not self-interested calculation (the world's hostility undercuts it, blunting Magneto's argument), not innate constitution (Magneto chose otherwise, and the Cyclops–Wolverine–Jean Grey triangle shows ordinary desires), not fear of punishment, and not Nietzschean pity or herd resentment — the X-Men are the strong and healthy ones. The chapter's positive account: love of the good is learned through relationships with those who are good to us, from Xavier's loving school that gradually transforms Wolverine and Magneto's Nazi-scarred past to Peter Parker's formative upbringing by Uncle Ben and Aunt May.

master-slave-morality.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
master-slave-morality.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.

master-slave-morality.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
master-slave-morality.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Reads Eustace, Uncle Andrew, Experiment House, and Miraz's censored Narnia as Lewis's portraits of modern secularism, which treats the world as mere resource and dismisses the transcendent regardless of evidence. It argues that denying intrinsic value collapses into a Nietzschean master morality of power, visible in Uncle Andrew's use of the children as guinea pigs and the Lone Islands' slave trade, and exposes the secular 'conditioner's' self-exemption as a violation of the Principle of Relevant Difference. Against the Green Witch's debunking of Puddleglum's sun and Aslan as copies of a lamp and a cat, it deploys the Platonic-Cartesian copy/original model of ideas to argue transcendent ideas (eternity, perfection, necessary being) cannot be derived from lower material causes, suggesting instead that the material world is the 'shadowland' copy of a divine original.

master-slave-morality.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
master-slave-morality.title: James Bond and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Matheson examines the 'master animal' imagery saturating Fleming's novels - Donovan Grant's reptilian physique in From Russia with Love, Blofeld's animal magnetism, villains feeding victims to sharks and crocodiles - as an exercise in Social Darwinism where, as Mr. Big puts it, wolves live by wolf's laws and sheep call them criminals. Using Nietzsche's Übermensch, the blond beast of the Genealogy, and Zarathustra's self-overcoming, she distinguishes Apollonian eaters like M (who curb appetite) from doomed Dionysian gluttons like Giuseppe Petacchi, arguing that Fleming makes dining and will power the test of who counts as an Overman. Bond differs from his megalomaniac foes only in keeping his own will to power and stomach under control, and the chapter closes by warning that Hollywood's romanticizing of the master animal keeps us valuing a brutally primitive masculinity Fleming himself mocked as a 'cardboard booby'.

master-slave-morality.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
master-slave-morality.title: James Bond and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Landa argues that Bond's apparent defense of democracy against Übermensch villains is itself profoundly Nietzschean: Bond's exquisite, disciplined hedonism (the Minton-china breakfast, disgust at Mr. Du Pont's 'eating like a pig'), his obsessive competitiveness at baccarat and golf, and his contempt for mass democracy mark him as an aristocratic bourgeois hero in Nietzsche's mold. The gambling scenes enact a Calvinist logic of predestination in which losing at Casino Royale devastates Bond because his very worth depends on winning, and the 'human muck' he defends at Blades turns out to be the exclusive elite. Dr. No, Mr. Big, Drax, and Blofeld are cast as evil, explicit Nietzscheans while Bond serves a good, unspoken Western Nietzscheanism - so the Cold War showdown with Blofeld, who invokes Nietzsche by name, is elitism fighting counterfeit elitism, making Bond 'a secret agent in the service of Nietzscheanism'.

master-slave-morality.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
master-slave-morality.title: Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia
master-slave-morality.relation: Peter Fosl reads Metallica's lyrics ("Leper Messiah," "The God That Failed," "One," "To Live Is to Die," "Escape") as extending Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: religion as slave morality born of ressentiment and as opium deadening the oppressed, illustrated by the landmine veteran of "One" pleading with a silent God and Hetfield's abandoned-childhood grief. He argues the band often falls into the "incomplete nihilism" Nietzsche predicted, lamenting God's failure and longing nostalgically for the Christian meaning it can no longer believe in rather than transvaluating values. Yet the defiance of "The Four Horsemen" and "Escape" and the band's creative power show it also working toward an overcoming of Christian nihilism, confirmed for Fosl by Hetfield's post-rehab health.

master-slave-morality.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
master-slave-morality.title: “They Have a Plan”
master-slave-morality.relation: Robert Sharp reads the Cylon uprising in Battlestar Galactica as Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality: enslaved by humans, the Cylons react with resentment and overturn their masters' values, just as early Christians did under Rome. The humans keep a master morality (Colonial polytheism, warrior elites, call signs like Apollo and Athena), while Cylon monotheism, doctrines of the soul (Leoben's sermons to Starbuck, Gina's suicidal faith), equality, and consensus government reproduce slave morality's move from bodily weakness to spiritual superiority. The New Caprica occupation debate among the Cavils, Six, and Boomer, and D'Anna's boxing, show the former slaves seeking not just destruction but conversion of their masters to a religion that makes Cylons equal.

master-slave-morality.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
master-slave-morality.title: The Doors Are Never Locked
master-slave-morality.relation: Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.

master-slave-morality.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
master-slave-morality.title: Meaning The Final Frontier
master-slave-morality.relation: Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.

master-slave-morality.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
master-slave-morality.title: Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil
master-slave-morality.relation: Drzaic and Rauch argue Link is 'good by default' because ludus play (rule-bound, goal-directed, winning the designed story) locks the player into the designers' morality, while paidia play, player-invented goals like the Ocarina of Time flying glitch or the Fierce Deity rampage in Majora's Mask, escapes the story's moral frame entirely. They then map this onto Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil: protagonist Link embodies slave morality (reactive, fear-avoiding, pity, patience, restoring the old Hyrule Ganon disturbed), while the elite paidia player is value-creating like the master, honoring power and secrecy (Huizinga) rather than the protagonist's virtue. The chapter concludes that in videogames the good/evil opposition is welded to ludus, and Zelda fans' naughtiness shows play can go beyond good and evil.

master-slave-morality.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
master-slave-morality.title: Transformers and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Barkman takes the 1986 movie poster's 'Beyond Good. Beyond Evil.' as a Nietzsche allusion and argues the cartoon refutes it: Skyfire's 'It is wrong,' Orion Pax's repudiation of admired power in 'War Dawn,' and Optimus's humble 'Thrones are for Decepticons' make Megatron a would-be superman and villain while Optimus is a Platonic guardian of a universal moral law binding even Unicron and the Quintessons. A reductio against cultural relativism (the Decepticon invasion of Earth, First Aid's failed pacifism in 'The Ultimate Weapon') plus C.S. Lewis-style archetypes explain why Optimus - a Christ-type who died saving the world - endures while GoBots do not.

master-slave-morality.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
master-slave-morality.title: What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything)
master-slave-morality.relation: In full truthiness voice, Michaud explains Colbert's failed 2008 presidential run — the South Carolina Democratic Executive Council's 13-3 vote keeping him off the ballot — as exactly what Nietzsche predicted: the resentful weak, the 'sheep,' hold the super-man down by redefining meekness as strength. He walks through will-to-power as self-overcoming, the lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable from the Genealogy, and Christianity as slave morality, then 'corrects' Nietzsche by relocating slave morality in the liberal media rather than God, ending with Colbert as the man of the future who 'affirms life without resentment.'

master-slave-morality.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
master-slave-morality.title: The Will to Nothingness, or What Happens when the Red Sox Win
master-slave-morality.relation: Nolen Gertz runs the Sox-Yankees rivalry through Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals: the Steinbrenner Yankees are masters whose 'good' simply means strong and winning, while Sox fans are slaves whose 'Yankees suck!' is ressentiment's imaginary revenge, intensified into the most spiritual and poisonous hatred by eighty-six years of impotence. The priestly slaves defeated the masters by cleverness rather than force, mirrored when Epstein's sabermetric 'religion' of prospects and projections terrified the Yankees into converting, building a farm system and embracing the slavish virtues they had scorned. The final twist is Nietzsche's will to nothingness: once the masters fell in 2004 the fans' suffering lost its meaning, breeding bandwagon guilt, pink-hat resentment and nihilistic exhaustion, so freedom requires a transvaluation that lets fans simply enjoy watching baseball.

master-slave-morality.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
master-slave-morality.title: Does Life Imitate Soccer
master-slave-morality.relation: Minister condemns 'negative soccer'—Sunderland at 28% possession and zero shots at Old Trafford, Stoke's goalless stalemate at Anfield, Bolton's two shots at the Emirates—through Nietzsche's genealogy of morality: teams that recognize superior opponents redefine the game's goal in slave-like resentment, replacing the pursuit of excellence, creativity, courage, and honor with a safety-first legalism of not losing, just as individual diving (Ronaldo's 'superman' dive, Drogba's histrionics) betrays the strong character, while Di Canio catching the ball for the injured keeper and Arshavin protesting his own penalty display honor. Marx then explains why the tactic is structural rather than a personal failing: Premier League revenue gaps, Champions League money, Abramovich's Chelsea billions, and the $55 million cost of relegation economically compel small clubs into what Minister reads as Marxian alienation—players unable to express themselves or flourish because economic forces dictate their play. He ends asking whether life imitates soccer: whether our own financial pressures likewise price excellence, honor, and self-expression out of ordinary lives.

master-slave-morality.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
master-slave-morality.title: Life A Celebration
master-slave-morality.relation: Reads John Simm's Master as Nietzsche's most advanced nihilist: having seen the universe die at Utopia, he judges life valueless and converts ressentiment into a joyful will to nothingness, dancing to the Scissor Sisters over his victims. The Ninth Doctor's arc in 'Dalek' mirrors this danger ('What are you changing into?') until he refuses to destroy the last Dalek, beginning his yes-saying to finite life. Following Deleuze's reading, the Doctor defeats the Master not with Martha's gun but with forgiveness ('I forgive you') and her storytelling network, embodying the Übermensch who carries his affirmation into the abyss of the end of the universe.

master-slave-morality.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
master-slave-morality.title: That Naive Cube! How Long Must I Suffer This
master-slave-morality.relation: Nicholas Michaud inverts the show's morality through Nietzsche: Plankton's tenacity, ambition and self-overcoming make him a super-organism driven by the will to power (traced to Schopenhauer's will to live), while Bikini Bottom's lionizing of SpongeBob's mediocrity is slave morality that judges by intentions to keep the strong down. Quoting the lambs and birds of prey from On the Genealogy of Morals and the 'incurably mediocre' passage from Beyond Good and Evil, he argues Plankton is the unsung hero who treats SpongeBob as an equal, Krabs a mere exploiter — and SpongeBob, who makes mediocrity contagious, the true villain.

master-slave-morality.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
master-slave-morality.title: Flowers
master-slave-morality.relation: Reads the Flowers album's blooms as dark—'Ruby Tuesday' can't be chained to a life where nothing's gained, and the heliotrope becomes Derrida's figure for philosophy forever turning toward its conceptual sun of truth, knowledge, or the good. That heliotropic bias, the metaphysics of presence, is illustrated by Augustine's treatment of evil as mere privation of good, which Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality overturns by deriving good and evil from the same source, 'beyond good and evil.'

master-slave-morality.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
master-slave-morality.title: Mother’s Little Helpers
master-slave-morality.relation: Introduces the Cambridge scholar Jane Ellen Harrison, whose books trace Greek religion from a swampy matriarchy to the Olympian age, with Dionysus as the holy child of the Mother — flayed and divided among the faithful — the very pattern Christianity retold in the Jesus story. Auxier credits Jagger's "keen intellect" and wide sense of history, then endorses Nietzsche's complaint that Christianity is "a puny, slave morality" that renders humanity effeminate: "That's exactly what I like about Christianity," since over-weaning masculinity needs opposing.

master-slave-morality.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
master-slave-morality.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Framed by Dick's wait in a Klosterman signing line, the chapter asks how a critic acquires rock-star power. Plato's Ion supplies the magnet chain of inspiration (muse, poet, rhapsode, spectator), which puts Klosterman near the spectator end — he 'only got to second base' with the muse Thalia until Downtown Owl. Nietzsche's master and slave moralities then explain the critic's ascent: Klosterman is the cunning slave-priest who seizes power from warrior-artists through wit and articulate opinion, exactly as priestly values overthrew warrior values. Dick half-endorses the diagnosis, admits he prefers the slave's world of safety, and concludes that power — even the power to sell books and pay rent — is how we stay alive.

master-slave-morality.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
master-slave-morality.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Rard tests whether objective morality survives the apocalypse by running four theories against Season Two: Plato's Forms explain universal truths about walkers ('walkers survive so long as their brains are relatively undamaged') but cannot handle white lies or changed circumstances, and Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Rick's rush from the shot Carl as rashness and Shane's supply run as courage, yet virtues prove relative and luck-dependent in a collapsed world. Natural law founders on clashing intuitions — Merle's racism and Hershel's barn of walkers each claim self-evidence. The chapter's center is Nietzschean: Hershel's barn is slave morality that pities the 'sick,' Maggie breaks from it, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and opening of the barn enact a will-to-power master morality without joy, while Rick alone moves toward amor fati — embracing the world as it is, refusing guilt over Lori's affair, and insisting the baby be born into the Walk Age.

master-slave-morality.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
master-slave-morality.title: The Wire and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Clifton measures Omar against four Nietzschean criteria for the overman: as a free spirit he is 'in the wind, so to speak,' detached from home, money, and eventually even lovers like Brandon and Butchie; as a non-dogmatist about truth he uses it as a tool, lying under oath at Bird's trial yet sparing Brother Mouzone when the lie no longer holds; and as a noble of the Genealogy he is an active hunter who embraces the will to power, telling Wee-Bey 'you come at the king, you best not miss.' But Omar fails the fourth test, value-creation: his code keeps the good/evil scale intact rather than overturning it, so in the Three Metamorphoses he remains the lion who slays 'Thou Shalt' but never becomes the value-creating child. The verdict, in Nietzsche's own phrase, is that Omar is noble but 'human, all too human.'

master-slave-morality.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
master-slave-morality.title: Psych and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Ruiz casts Lassiter as Nietzsche's slave - his worth defined reactively against Shawn, his advice that 'all romance ends in despair or death' reproducing the Judeo-Christian slave revolt in morality that turned weakness into virtue - and Shawn as the master, a self-propelled wheel who bakes a pineapple cake in an Easy Bake oven for nineteen hours whether or not anyone is watching. Shawn's generosity (helping the wrongly accused, the ghost-struck, and the deluded, once even crediting a cat with solving murders in '9 Lives') is read as the noble overflow of superabundant power rather than pity, and his hostage-saving risk-taking as will to power understood as self-mastery. Even the central lie gets a dialectical reading - like art, pretending to be psychic reveals the truth hidden behind appearances - though the chapter concedes Shawn's slavish moments, from daddy issues to his obsession with one-upping Declan in 'Shawn 2.0.'

master-slave-morality.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
master-slave-morality.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.

master-slave-morality.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
master-slave-morality.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Comparing Finn with Gilgamesh, Achilles, Cuchulainn and Beowulf, the chapter shows how deeply he belongs to the archaic heroic code: a warrior who loves combat, seeks glory in tough-guy contests, fights dirty like Odysseus, and is fiercely loyal to Jake, his friends and his community. Against this tradition, Finn's unprecedented willingness to help any stranger who cries for help and his refusal to kill the 'unaligned' ant mark the post-heroic morality that began when Socrates told Athenians to care for their souls rather than status and Plato designed a city serving the common good - the author explicitly frames this through Nietzsche's complaint that Greek philosophy derailed the healthy, competitive heroic values. The chapter sides with Finn and the self-sacrificing Lemonjohn over Achilles, concluding that the secret of the Enchiridion is doing whatever the common good requires, warrior or not.

master-slave-morality.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
master-slave-morality.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.

master-slave-morality.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
master-slave-morality.title: Dracula and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.

master-slave-morality.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
master-slave-morality.title: 4. Nietzsche’s Faction Test
master-slave-morality.relation: Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.

master-slave-morality.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
master-slave-morality.title: 7. How Batman Cowed a God
master-slave-morality.relation: Reider reads the two heroes through Nietzsche's genealogy of morals: Superman's humility, guilt, empathy, and farmer-parent values (he is Clark Kent at heart, keeping the alter ego to unload the burden of his power) are textbook slave morality, making him the unwitting pawn of the weak rather than Nietzsche's Übermensch, while Batman's pride, wrath, and vow of vengeance - he refuses to kill the Joker or Robin's attacker not from respect for life but from aristocratic pride - revive the pagan "good" of Achilles dragging Hector's body. From this he builds a deliberately provocative strategic claim: because slave morality leaves Superman secretly craving to be bested and made ordinary again, the merely human Batman can stare down and "cow" the god in their showdowns, winning the psychological war Wonder Woman's and Lois's preferences supposedly confirm.

master-slave-morality.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
master-slave-morality.title: 15. The C-Word
master-slave-morality.relation: Works through the ethics of cloning and genetic selection, starting with the objection that such technologies are "unnatural": that reasoning commits the naturalistic fallacy, since following Hume you can't get an ought from an is, and human ingenuity (roads, eyeglasses, IVF) is itself part of nature. Using Nietzsche's Genealogy account of master morality — good as the noble traits of intelligence, beauty, and strength — the chapter asks whether parents would then be obliged to engineer better children, while warning where trait-selection slides: Nazi eugenics, racist trait-lists (both Leda and Castor are white and conventionally attractive), and "abilism" against the deaf. It concludes that cloning itself is not evil: Projects Leda and Castor are immoral not because they clone but because they treat clones as mere means to an end, in Kant's sense, and trample their autonomy.

master-slave-morality.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
master-slave-morality.title: 18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool
master-slave-morality.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.

master-slave-morality.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
master-slave-morality.title: 11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them
master-slave-morality.relation: Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.

master-slave-morality.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
master-slave-morality.title: 4. He’s a Hero in a Bottle, Baby
master-slave-morality.relation: Insooks deploys Nietzsche to argue Iron Man is the better hero: Cap's prized humility and relatability are sheep morality, the resentful herd value that drags the excellent down to average (as when society savored the Olympic swimmer's fall), while Tony honestly owns his superiority and keeps self-overcoming, building ever-better suits rather than resting on a serum gifted in a bottle. On this view Cap's manufactured modesty insults people who genuinely struggle, and the true super hero inspires from the mountaintop - build yourself a suit and get up here - instead of pretending to be just like us.

master-slave-morality.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
master-slave-morality.title: 8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need
master-slave-morality.relation: Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.

master-slave-morality.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
master-slave-morality.title: 26. Thanos’s Mistake
master-slave-morality.relation: Argues Thanos embodies Nietzschean master morality — his will as its own justification, 'the hardest choices require the strongest wills,' echoing the Melian dialogue's 'the strong do what they will, the weak suffer what they must,' with Doctor Strange answering in kind ('you'll find our will equal to yours') — while the Avengers speak from slave morality, judging by intentions and branding genocide evil. Thanos's real error, though, is a categorical one: imposing a technical quantity fix (a one-time 50 percent cull) on a social relationship problem, since Hardin's carrying-capacity logic and the St. Matthew Island reindeer show populations must self-limit like apex predators, making his correction a mere stopgap that confuses quantity with relationship.

master-slave-morality.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
master-slave-morality.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Reads Bluth contradiction through Kant's categorical imperative: Lindsay's lie about her shopgirl job, Gob's jealousy bred by comparative parenting, and George Michael's conformist drift show both the imperative's force and the danger of its empty formalism, while the 'Afternoon Delight' double entendres test whether good intentions suffice for Kantian worth. Nietzsche then answers that morality itself is the contradiction: virtue manufactured from ressentiment ('weakness is being lied into something meritorious'), the will to power turned inward as nihilism, with self-overcoming and value creation as the exit; Mary Douglas's joke theory closes the chapter by explaining why all this contradiction is comic and why the joke is on Gob.

master-slave-morality.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
master-slave-morality.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.

master-slave-morality.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
master-slave-morality.title: “Exit Game”
master-slave-morality.relation: Reading 'Striking Vipers' through its closed- and open-door imagery, the chapter asks whether Danny and Karl's virtual sex as Lance and Roxette is adultery, testing the question with Plato's Ring of Gyges (what people do when no one can see them), Locke's memory theory (if Danny remembers Roxette's sex acts, is Roxette Danny?), and behaviorist replies that only physical penetration counts. Nietzsche supplies the chapter's frame: his master/slave morality and his view of life as self-created representational art explain how the characters' hidden, mind-only moral inversion creates real existential meaning in virtual sex. The episode's fusion of bodily and mental pleasure is said to break down Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction - 'lower' physical virtual pleasures yield a 'higher' sense of wholeness - and Schopenhauer's insatiable striving plus Husserl's meaning-conferring perception underwrite the conclusion that virtual love can be real, with Danny and Theo's once-a-year open marriage endorsed as an act-consequentialist balance between monotonous fidelity and escapist fantasy.

master-slave-morality.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
master-slave-morality.title: A Shared Higher Thirst
master-slave-morality.relation: Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.

master-slave-morality.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
master-slave-morality.title: 17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence
master-slave-morality.relation: Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.

master-slave-morality.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
master-slave-morality.title: Amos Is No Superman
master-slave-morality.relation: Pankaj Singh reads Amos through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Amos' division of people into 'bad ones, ones you follow, and ones you need to protect', his outsourcing of moral judgment to Naomi and Holden ('Naomi wouldn't like it'), his fearlessness, and his violent spontaneity make him 'evil' by slave morality yet good by master morality. Unlike Prax, who has to be stopped from shooting Strickland out of ressentiment, Amos kills without revenge ('I am that guy'), and his fistfights with Miller and Alex discharge hostility immediately so it never poisons — the strong natures Nietzsche praises that 'form, mold, recuperate and forget.' His 'crew comes first' and 'better to go down swinging' express the will to power as discharge of strength rather than mere self-preservation, but because he never sublimates or overcomes his drives, the chapter concludes Amos is no Übermensch — 'but then again, who is?'

master-slave-morality.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
master-slave-morality.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.

master-slave-morality.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
master-slave-morality.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
master-slave-morality.relation: David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.

master-slave-morality.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
master-slave-morality.title: Notes
master-slave-morality.relation: Argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure whose power play is staged through the show's postmodern techniques: the wave and the asides as metafiction that destroys our suspension of disbelief, self-referentiality in the mirror monologue ('Hunt or be hunted'), and a flattening of affect that lets us watch Zoe's murder at the train station with numbed indifference. Zarathustra's fearless overman is set against the risk-averse last man and the lambs-and-birds-of-prey passage against Christian slave morality, mapping onto Frank's breaking of Russo at the shipyard, the martyr's-sword maneuver on Blythe, and his spitting on the crucifix before taking 'God's ear'. The chapter reads Frank's ascent as will to power in both the political and personal Nietzschean sense, while warning that by Season 3 his hunger has cost him Jackie, Remy and Claire.

master-slave-morality.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
master-slave-morality.title: Notes
master-slave-morality.relation: Argues against the title claim of the previous chapter: Frank is a Nietzschean master type — he defines good as good-for-him, embraces pain as strength, and keeps no allegiances once Walker and Vasquez break their promise — while Peter Russo is the paradigmatic reactive slave who cannot command himself and blames others, exactly Nietzsche's 'he who cannot command himself is commanded'. But the overman requires self-overcoming, the sublimation of drives into creation, and amor fati, and Frank only dominates others for vengeful ends: his whole scheme grows from ressentiment over the Secretary of State snub, he affirms other wills merely as investments, and in Season 3 he becomes a slave to his own position. The chapter uses the Cesare Borgia misreading (better a Borgia than a Parsifal as raw material, but Borgia was no overman), Napoleon's corruption, and Goethe's creative wholeness to conclude that Frank remains 'all-too-human' — destruction without creation.

master-slave-morality.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
master-slave-morality.title: Notes
master-slave-morality.relation: Palm and Stikkers read the Underwoods through James Truslow Adams's American dream as a question of values gone rotten: lacking ends, they pursue power for its own sake while repressed longings (Frank's Sentinel camaraderie, song, and friendship; Claire's motherhood — 'What will we leave behind?') erupt as the ressentiment Nietzsche introduced and Max Scheler systematized, hating those who embody the sacrificed values. Claire's hatred thus targets Gillian Cole's pregnancy and integrity (fired, then threatened with letting her child 'wither and die') and Adam Galloway's freedom and love — Scheler's pedestal-smashing pattern — after the slave-morality-like repression of her normal human affects. The ressentiment finally shatters when Michael Corrigan refuses to betray himself and hangs himself in Petrov's cell: Claire tells the cameras the truth and walks out on Frank at the end of Season 3, free of the resentment.

master-slave-morality.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
master-slave-morality.title: Notes
master-slave-morality.relation: Aarons argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure delivered through postmodern technique: the metafictional wave in 'Chapter 1,' self-referential mirror monologues ('Did you think I've forgotten you?'), and the flattening of affect in Zoe's death at the train station. Zarathustra's fearless overman, contrasted with the comfort-loving last man, maps onto Frank's 'hunt or be hunted' creed and his 'money is the McMansion in Sarasota... power is the old stone building' will-to-power, played out on Russo, Zoe, and Walker. The Genealogy's birds of prey and lambs frame Russo's Christian hypocrisy, and The Antichrist's equation of good with heightened power explains the church scene where Frank spits on the crucifix and leaves with the statue's ear — 'I've got God's ear now.'

master-slave-morality.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
master-slave-morality.title: Notes
master-slave-morality.relation: Meyer mounts the counter-case: Frank exemplifies Nietzsche's master type (good as good-for-him, 'no longer are we bound by allegiances') and Russo the slave type ('he who cannot command himself is commanded'), but the overman is a synthesis of neither. He corrects the Leopold-and-Loeb 'above the law' reading and the Cesare Borgia identification: the genuine overman sublimates strong drives into creation — Goethe's self-discipline, Beethoven's new norms — and affirms other wills in themselves rather than as instruments, which Frank never does with Zoe, Peter, or Claire. Frank's revenge-driven scheming is slave-like psychological warfare, ruling others is the 'pettiest' form of power, and by Season 3 he is the slave of his own presidency — destructive without creating, and lacking even amor fati.

master-slave-morality.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
master-slave-morality.title: 8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse
