ubermensch.relation: Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.

ubermensch.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
ubermensch.title: Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle
ubermensch.relation: Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.

ubermensch.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
ubermensch.title: Transformers and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Barkman takes the 1986 movie poster's 'Beyond Good. Beyond Evil.' as a Nietzsche allusion and argues the cartoon refutes it: Skyfire's 'It is wrong,' Orion Pax's repudiation of admired power in 'War Dawn,' and Optimus's humble 'Thrones are for Decepticons' make Megatron a would-be superman and villain while Optimus is a Platonic guardian of a universal moral law binding even Unicron and the Quintessons. A reductio against cultural relativism (the Decepticon invasion of Earth, First Aid's failed pacifism in 'The Ultimate Weapon') plus C.S. Lewis-style archetypes explain why Optimus - a Christ-type who died saving the world - endures while GoBots do not.

ubermensch.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
ubermensch.title: What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything)
ubermensch.relation: In full truthiness voice, Michaud explains Colbert's failed 2008 presidential run — the South Carolina Democratic Executive Council's 13-3 vote keeping him off the ballot — as exactly what Nietzsche predicted: the resentful weak, the 'sheep,' hold the super-man down by redefining meekness as strength. He walks through will-to-power as self-overcoming, the lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable from the Genealogy, and Christianity as slave morality, then 'corrects' Nietzsche by relocating slave morality in the liberal media rather than God, ending with Colbert as the man of the future who 'affirms life without resentment.'

ubermensch.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
ubermensch.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.

ubermensch.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
ubermensch.title: Death Knight as Overman
ubermensch.relation: Luke Cuddy asks whether playing WoW can answer nihilism, using Schopenhauer's bleak remark on our sudden existence and Nietzsche's death of God to set up the problem — King Bangalash dies and WoW goes on, just as humans die and the universe continues. Entering Huizinga's Magic Circle gives Azeroth its meanings, but the player must then dissolve the circle, recognize that the game itself is meaningless, and keep playing anyway — creating the toon as a work of art in the Dionysian spirit. A maxed Death Knight still is not Nietzsche's Overman, because the player affirms only her in-game existence; the fifth step is carrying that self-creation back into real life.

ubermensch.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
ubermensch.title: Mr. Monk’s Greatness
ubermensch.relation: Lewis argues Monk is Nietzsche's Übermensch. Sketching Sartre's existence-precedes-essence through the contrast between the designed wipe and self-defining humans, the chapter claims Monk creates his own essence through choices — keeping the coffee table askew in memory of Trudy, 'dirtying' his house in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend,' drinking stream water in 'Mr. Monk Gets Cabin Fever' — and lives by self-prescribed values (hourly flossing, bagged tissues, relentless truth-seeking) that separate him from the herd of the Court of Public Opinion. The comparison with Stottlemeyer — Nietzsche's lookalike with the mustache, 'the quintessential man' of the herd — inverts the expected hierarchy: 'He was a yardstick for me, of both detection and character' ('Mr. Monk Goes to Mexico') shows the badge-carrying everyman is the inferior one. Monk therefore challenges the macho sci-fi stereotype of the superman: the Übermensch can be gentle and kind, fight for truth and a cleaner world, and still have room to improve ('What does not kill me makes me stronger').

ubermensch.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
ubermensch.title: A New Lease of Life for the Undead
ubermensch.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the twenty-first-century zombie and vampire boom (Twilight, True Blood, Zombieland, Fido, Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, zombie walks, Humans Versus Zombies) and asks why the Undead fascinate us when bears would not. Its answer contrasts the vampire, who embodies a Nietzschean super-humanity beyond good and evil still charged with unheeded guilt, with the zombie, a sub-Nietzschean, Spinozan force of decomposition where matter interacts with matter beyond all morality. Zombies thus work as hyperdead memento mori: imagining zombiehood lets us imagine our own annihilation as entry into a condition of liberated power, while the obviously unreal monster helps us shut out the real terrors it reflects.

ubermensch.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
ubermensch.title: Oh to Be a Gooner
ubermensch.relation: Kilpatrick reads Nietzsche's madman's question 'what sacred games shall we have to invent?' as answered by the stadium: after the death of God, soccer has replaced religion as the shared narrative where modern communities make and worship heroes. Using The Birth of Tragedy, he reads a goal as an Apollonian–Dionysian fusion—the scorer's individuated ecstasy merging with the collective joy of teammates and fans—and, on Nietzsche's claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, argues the game is defensible only when played creatively and artistically rather than by negative, win-at-all-costs tactics. Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism (the state as 'the new idol', the 'good European', Zarathustra's 'children's land') means club over country, and Wenger's Arsenal—with its dietary and training laboratory at London Colney cultivating an Overman, its Invincibles season, and its young, passport-blind signings—emerges as the club Nietzsche would support through its very will-to-power.

ubermensch.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
ubermensch.title: I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You
ubermensch.relation: Reads the Doctor as a Christ-figure and savior (the 'Voyage of the Damned' ascension that drew Christian Voice protests, Martha's year of gospel-telling in 'The Last of the Time Lords'), applying Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideals onto God. But the show under Russell T Davies also distrusts godlike power: Davros's 'you made this' accusation, the Racnoss massacre, and Joan Redfern's question in 'The Family of Blood' show the lonely god's devastation. Against this, companions like Donna embody Nietzsche's Übermensch ('There's no such thing as an ordinary human'), so the chapter concludes the Doctor and ordinary humans need each other, mutually overcoming their weaknesses.

ubermensch.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
ubermensch.title: Life A Celebration
ubermensch.relation: Reads John Simm's Master as Nietzsche's most advanced nihilist: having seen the universe die at Utopia, he judges life valueless and converts ressentiment into a joyful will to nothingness, dancing to the Scissor Sisters over his victims. The Ninth Doctor's arc in 'Dalek' mirrors this danger ('What are you changing into?') until he refuses to destroy the last Dalek, beginning his yes-saying to finite life. Following Deleuze's reading, the Doctor defeats the Master not with Martha's gun but with forgiveness ('I forgive you') and her storytelling network, embodying the Übermensch who carries his affirmation into the abyss of the end of the universe.

ubermensch.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
ubermensch.title: The Prophet
ubermensch.relation: Presents Muad'Dib as Nietzsche's Zarathustra in the Dune universe: the sardonic self-mockery that keeps a great man from believing his own myth, the valuation of life-enhancing 'truths' over correspondence-truth (behind all logic stand 'value judgments,' as Beyond Good and Evil has it), and monumental, mythologized history against Mentat-accurate history that kills religion. Paul's Fremen, first hard and vital, go 'water-fat' under the paradise his jihad built, becoming Nietzsche's 'Ultimate Man'—the last man who has left the places where living was hard and demands 'a little poison now and then'—so Muad'Dib must become the Preacher to destroy the rigid code he created, as Zarathustra came to undo Zoroaster's morality; both prophets preach self-overcoming toward the Superman.

ubermensch.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
ubermensch.title: Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps
ubermensch.relation: Argues that Herbert is a genuine philosopher extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra into the twentieth century, via three narrative parallels: the Preacher entering Arrakeen mirrors Zarathustra's first down-going into the town with its tightrope walker and mocking buffoon; Paul's empire of water-fat Fremen and Alia's orthodoxy realizes the 'Ultimate Man' whom the crowd begs for instead of the Superman; and prescience reworks eternal recurrence's gateway 'Moment,' where every timeline ends in Krazilec. Reading Paul's sixty-five-billion-death jihad through Arendt's banality of evil and Herbert's 'superheroes are disastrous' thesis, the chapter concludes Paul is the failed tightrope walker and Leto II the goad—'not lightning, but lightning rod'—pushing humanity beyond man toward the Superman, with Spannungsbogen naming the tension of the drawn bow between animal and Overman.

ubermensch.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
ubermensch.title: That Naive Cube! How Long Must I Suffer This
ubermensch.relation: Nicholas Michaud inverts the show's morality through Nietzsche: Plankton's tenacity, ambition and self-overcoming make him a super-organism driven by the will to power (traced to Schopenhauer's will to live), while Bikini Bottom's lionizing of SpongeBob's mediocrity is slave morality that judges by intentions to keep the strong down. Quoting the lambs and birds of prey from On the Genealogy of Morals and the 'incurably mediocre' passage from Beyond Good and Evil, he argues Plankton is the unsung hero who treats SpongeBob as an equal, Krabs a mere exploiter — and SpongeBob, who makes mediocrity contagious, the true villain.

ubermensch.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
ubermensch.title: His Work Is Its Own Reward
ubermensch.relation: Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.

ubermensch.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
ubermensch.title: The Good
ubermensch.relation: Makes the case for eugenics' good side through Jason's uncontroversially desirable traits, invoking Nietzsche's call to 'give birth to a dancing star' and create superhuman successors as a moral philosophy of human improvement. It then probes the limits — beauty is relative (Japan's yaeba), and screening would have lost Van Gogh and Stephen Hawking — before weighing Dick's own compassion for small lives (the electric toad, the avenged cat of 'The Alien Mind,' the potter Mary Anne Dominic) against the blunt statistical claim that healthier, more capable lives go better.

ubermensch.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
ubermensch.title: Chapter 25 - Untimely Speculations
ubermensch.relation: Heath Massey's introduction to Chapter 25 opens with Nietzsche's Gay Science passage on intellects that might experience time backward, then stages the demon of eternal recurrence: every pain and joy returning in the same sequence in a world without aim, which either crushes you or becomes 'the highest formula of affirmation', amor fati. Eternal recurrence is a test of the will separating 'man' from 'overman', since one could not celebrate it while believing the world needs a divine purpose. The chapter then maps Dick's imaginative variations of temporality onto two Nietzschean tendencies - disruptions of time-sense that render characters powerless, and extraordinary temporalities that liberate them beyond finite human time, culminating in Dick's theory of supertemporality.

ubermensch.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
ubermensch.title: Preparatory Human Beings
ubermensch.relation: The counter-tendency gathers Dick's empowering temporalities. 'The Golden Man' presents Cris Johnson, a golden-haired mutant with virtually no frontal cortex, who survives a random-firing gun by 'pre-thinking' a panorama of possible futures - Homo superior as superhuman beast, by instinct rather than intelligence. In Now Wait for Last Year, General Molinari uses the drug JJ-180 to trip sideways into parallel presents and recruit healthy duplicates of himself, virtually overcoming mortality with 'a dynasty consisting of himself'. And in The Man in the High Castle, Abendsen's The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, Frank Frink's handwrought jewelry and Tagomi's meditative slip all point toward an alternate present - ours - where the Allies won, making art and the I Ching oracles of resistance to totalitarian domination.

ubermensch.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
ubermensch.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.

ubermensch.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
ubermensch.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: A close scene-reading of the pilot argues Nietzsche's will to power explains Walt's transformation: he is repeatedly 'out willed' by Chad's chair-scrape, Bogdan's register demands, and Hank's birthday-party toasts, until the cancer diagnosis powers his 'Fuck you... and your eyebrows!' reversal at the car wash. Walt's decision to cook, declared to Jesse as 'I am awake', is presented as the Ubermensch's creation of his own morality - family provision over society's 'drugs are bad' - and the phosphine-gas killing of Emilio as his ultimate exertion of will. The chapter concludes Nietzsche would have been a fan of the show.

ubermensch.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
ubermensch.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Scores Walt and Mad Men's Don Draper against Nietzsche's Overman and Last Man: Roger Sterling (and the early, passive Jesse) are Last Men, while Walt moves from weak negation of the status quo to genuine self-affirmation - 'going under' in the 'Crawl Space' crawl hole and emerging in 'Face Off' having poisoned Brock and out-created Gus, which the chapter takes as proof that in a capitalist world two creators cannot coexist. Killing Gus is framed as accepting the eternal recurrence of joy and sorrow, willing even his own bad acts. Don, by contrast, negates far more than he creates, and the chapter ends by asking why viewers empathize with the one failed Overman and find the other inspiring.

ubermensch.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
ubermensch.title: The Wire and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Clifton measures Omar against four Nietzschean criteria for the overman: as a free spirit he is 'in the wind, so to speak,' detached from home, money, and eventually even lovers like Brandon and Butchie; as a non-dogmatist about truth he uses it as a tool, lying under oath at Bird's trial yet sparing Brother Mouzone when the lie no longer holds; and as a noble of the Genealogy he is an active hunter who embraces the will to power, telling Wee-Bey 'you come at the king, you best not miss.' But Omar fails the fourth test, value-creation: his code keeps the good/evil scale intact rather than overturning it, so in the Three Metamorphoses he remains the lion who slays 'Thou Shalt' but never becomes the value-creating child. The verdict, in Nietzsche's own phrase, is that Omar is noble but 'human, all too human.'

ubermensch.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
ubermensch.title: Psych and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Malloy maps Nietzsche's three metamorphoses onto Shawn's life: the camel who carried Henry's burdensome training and the expectation he become a cop, the lion who slew the dragon 'Thou shalt' by stealing a car at eighteen and ending Henry's dream, and the child who creates his own values of fun, laughter, and silliness - defended as genuinely Nietzschean since the Overman must overcome the 'spirit of gravity.' Gus and Lassiter figure as last men, the herd animals Shawn manipulates and pities (Lassie's literal crap list a study in ressentiment), while only Pierre Despereaux and Mr. Yin count as true rivals because only fellow Overmen, forging values beyond good and evil, can genuinely challenge Shawn. The chapter closes on the Overman's dilemma - loneliness, backsliding into the herd, or trying to make Overmen of others - which explains why Shawn treats his friends and enemies the way he does.

ubermensch.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
ubermensch.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.

ubermensch.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
ubermensch.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'

ubermensch.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
ubermensch.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Jeffery Nicholas argues Card tries to write Ender as Nietzsche's self-sufficient superman - Graff's isolation program, the will to power, and Rackham's 'humanity does not ask us to be happy' - but the novel actually vindicates Aristotle's claim in the Politics that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Ender's difference from the beast-like Peter and the hive-minded buggers, his longing for Valentine, Alai, and Petra, and his despair in isolation show that friendship, not domination, is what makes him human.

ubermensch.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
ubermensch.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Jeff Ewing reads the park as Nietzsche's will-to-power in action: Hammond's 'creation is an act of sheer will', resurrecting extinct species because science enables it, is the drive to remake the world godlike in one's own image, and Malcolm's 'so preoccupied with whether or not they could' marks exactly the external mastery Hammond achieved. But the Nietzschean great man also needs internal mastery - control over himself before control over nature - and Hammond failed it: one man (Nedry) held the whole security grid, frog-DNA surprises were foreseeable, raptor intelligence was underestimated, and the storm was ignored. For Nietzsche, lying to yourself about your strength is not arrogance but weakness, so Hammond's disaster was not a moral crime but a failure of self-mastery - a lesson Ewing extends to modern cloning, drones, and weapons pursued without honest reckoning.

ubermensch.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
ubermensch.title: The Devil and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.

ubermensch.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
ubermensch.title: Dracula and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.

ubermensch.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
ubermensch.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Martyn Jones stages a fictional Nietzsche telling Mac, Dennis, and Charlie the plot of 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' as a parable of metaphysics gone wrong. Mac and Dennis's scheming is Apollonian - imposing logical order and 'paradigms' on a recalcitrant world - while Charlie is Dionysian, the designated wildcard whose uncontainable energy (sabotaging the van and ripping out the brakes) dooms every plan that tries to harness him, since Apollonian schemes fatally imagine they can contain Dionysian force. Reason is a gloss, not a truth-tracker: like every theology and philosophy it is an expression of will, a survival tool serving selfish ends, so the delusional gas scheme needs no truth to serve its purpose. Charlie alone is praised as a proto-Übermensch - innocent, creative, founding his own values without resentment - and the tale closes musing that even an eternal recurrence of their botched schemes might be willed all over again.

ubermensch.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
ubermensch.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: DiEdoardo, a trans criminal-defense lawyer, reads Sophia Burset through Nietzsche: her 'why of life' (bringing her body into line with her gender identity) lets her endure the 'how' of misgendering by Figueroa, Red, and her wife Crystal, plus a sentencing disparity she compares to Piper's lighter drug deal. Burset's rational appeals ('Lesbian Request Denied,' her WAC run) fail, confirming Nietzsche's disdain for dialectics, but in 'A Whole Other Hole' she stops asking and acts, teaching the inmates vulval anatomy until Taystee's 'she's right' marks her acceptance. She is the 'creator' who breaks the tables of values, migrating from freak to woman with unique knowledge.

ubermensch.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
ubermensch.title: 4. Nietzsche’s Faction Test
ubermensch.relation: Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.

ubermensch.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
ubermensch.title: Hello, Dr. Lecter
ubermensch.relation: Westfall's introduction sorts Lecter's incarnations into four presentations: the psychopath (Brian Cox's 'Lecktor' in Manhunter, modeled on Harris's real-life Mexican prison doctor 'Dr. Salazar'), the anti-hero avenging Mischa in Hannibal Rising, the vampire (Hopkins's Silence of the Lambs Lecter as a Dracula figure who feeds from a sense of innate superiority), and the devil (Mikkelsen's fallen angel, Romula's 'Shaitan', wielder of the church-collapse argument that God enjoys killing). What unites them is a Nietzschean self-conception - Lecter as an Übermensch to whom ordinary law and morality do not apply - and a Socratic function: like Socrates in the Phaedrus, he goads Will, Clarice, and the audience into examining what we already are, posing questions he never resolves because each of us must take the 'rare gift' for ourselves.

ubermensch.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
ubermensch.title: 10. The Light from Friendship
ubermensch.relation: Pavelich sets Aristotle's account of friendship - recognized and reciprocated goodwill between equals, perfected in the friendship of the good who 'share our souls', a standard met only by Jack and Bella Crawford - against Nietzsche's friendship as striving between overmen, who honor 'one's best enemy' in the friend and grow through conflict. He reads Hannibal's treatment of Will (hiding the encephalitis, framing him, serving the Nietzschean trout) as Nietzschean friend-making - Lies that are supposed to spur Will's growth, consistent with an Übermensch who tells Will 'Killing must feel good to God' and says 'I don't hide from God' - while Will's masquerade of friendship is betrayal in both senses, since Will seeks an Aristotelian soulmate and finds a killer he must stop. Because each betrays the other, neither Aristotelian nor Nietzschean friendship survives, though the moments before the Mizumono bloodbath - Hannibal inviting Will to just walk away - glimpse a real friendship already made impossible.

ubermensch.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
ubermensch.title: 16. Empathy for the Devil
ubermensch.relation: Shaw explains our identification with Lecter through mirror neurons triggered by Demme's extreme close-ups, Lecter's impeccable aesthetic and culinary taste, his evil-genius plotting, and his choice of 'free range rude' victims — but the deepest ground is Nietzsche's will to power, quoting The Gay Science and The Antichrist on the feeling of power as what makes action valuable. Lecter is read as Nietzsche's Overman in complete control of himself, his environment, and his inferiors, and the TV series confirms the theory because, with the black humor and romance stripped away, Mikkelsen's Lecter out-plots Will, Jack and Alana alike and walks triumphant from the Season 2 finale, having played everyone 'like his beloved Theremin'.

ubermensch.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
ubermensch.title: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
ubermensch.relation: Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.

ubermensch.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
ubermensch.title: 7. How Batman Cowed a God
ubermensch.relation: Reider reads the two heroes through Nietzsche's genealogy of morals: Superman's humility, guilt, empathy, and farmer-parent values (he is Clark Kent at heart, keeping the alter ego to unload the burden of his power) are textbook slave morality, making him the unwitting pawn of the weak rather than Nietzsche's Übermensch, while Batman's pride, wrath, and vow of vengeance - he refuses to kill the Joker or Robin's attacker not from respect for life but from aristocratic pride - revive the pagan "good" of Achilles dragging Hector's body. From this he builds a deliberately provocative strategic claim: because slave morality leaves Superman secretly craving to be bested and made ordinary again, the merely human Batman can stare down and "cow" the god in their showdowns, winning the psychological war Wonder Woman's and Lois's preferences supposedly confirm.

ubermensch.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
ubermensch.title: 21. Batman Is Superman
ubermensch.relation: The chapter argues that Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, is Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian emotion and Apollonian reason - vengeance against justice in Batman Begins - and who relives his traumas as Nietzschean eternal recurrence, from the bat-filled well to the prison leap of The Dark Knight Rises. The Joker is his dark double, whose will to power and ferry-boat experiment nearly extinguish Gotham's hope, but Batman absorbs the chaos and sacrifices his heroic name, whereas Superman in Injustice, losing Lois, falls into a vengeful Dionysian abyss he cannot master. Only a mortal who extends his limits without succumbing to the herd's 'gravity of madness' can be Nietzsche's superman, so the mortal, conflicted, imitable Batman is the true superman.

ubermensch.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
ubermensch.title: 7. David Bowie, Political Philosopher
ubermensch.relation: Hill reconstructs Bowie's political odyssey as a working-out of what freedom and oppression are: 'Cygnet Committee' repudiates revolution powered by resentment (echoing Nietzsche on socialism's despotic annihilation of the individual), 'Big Brother' and Diamond Dogs diagnose the crowd's flight from freedom into leadership, and the Nietzschean self-as-artwork - 'give style to one's character,' the 'mortal with potential of a superman' - curdles into the Thin White Duke's 'rock stars are fascists' collapse of celebrity into totalitarian leadership. The Berlin Trilogy then turns the critique inward: 'Heroes'' ironic lovers unmask romantic anti-totalitarianism (either side of the Antifaschistischer Schutzwall), 'Neuköln' discovers immigrants' mere survival, and Lodger's 'Fantastic Voyage' lands on structural, Marxist questions of how 'we' are to become free.

ubermensch.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
ubermensch.title: 12. David Bowie’s Sincerity
ubermensch.relation: Cooper distinguishes sincerity - communicating a self to an audience - from authenticity, and uses Critchley's reading of Bowie's visible seams ('maybe we're lying,' 'saying no but meaning yes') to argue that openly displayed artifice can carry real feeling, even as 'Conversation Piece' and the suffocating mask of 'The Mask' dramatize language's failure to transmit a self. Descartes's cogito secures self-certainty but not communication - Bowie stays 'a thinker, not a talker' - and against the Nietzschean 'Supermen' whose self-creation shades into self-alienation, Bowie moves past cold postmodern irony to a new sincerity that admits its own insincerity ('It's not the side-effects of the cocaine... I'm thinking that it must be love!').

ubermensch.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
ubermensch.title: 5. Rhapsody on a Theme by Schroeder
ubermensch.relation: The chapter argues Schroeder's monomaniacal devotion to his toy piano and Beethoven is a Nietzschean way of life: he refuses the herd's path and the self-denying 'priestly' values of ordinary childhood, and treats music as the highest creative force, as The Birth of Tragedy claims. Nietzsche's demon of eternal recurrence becomes a test Schroeder passes - he lives for this life and could will its exact repetition - while Schopenhauer backs the claim that music discloses the world's inner nature as language cannot, and the Christmas-dance scene shows the communal fusion Nietzsche heard in song and dance. Strips about Lucy on the piano, his 'grown accustomed to that face' shock when she moves away, and the Beethoven's-birthday holiday cast Lucy as his unsuspecting muse; but as a would-be Ubermensch he must go beyond playing Beethoven and create his own compositions.

ubermensch.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
ubermensch.title: 11. Immortality Is Misery
ubermensch.relation: In dialogue with Deadpool himself, John Altmann tests whether immortality is a blessing: Bentham's utilitarianism would prize a healing factor that lets Wade dive into a gamma meltdown to save the Southern Hemisphere for free, and Nietzsche would hail him as an Übermensch for refusing the Mithras Directive's Messiah and preserving humanity's freedom to create its own values rather than adopt herd morality. Bernard Williams gets the last word: since personalities become fixed—Wade stays a mercenary across every run, Zenpool notwithstanding—an endless life curdles into boredom and misery, so immortality is punishment rather than power unless one could radically change who one is.

ubermensch.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
ubermensch.title: 18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool
ubermensch.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.

ubermensch.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
ubermensch.title: 11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them
ubermensch.relation: Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.

ubermensch.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
ubermensch.title: 4. He’s a Hero in a Bottle, Baby
ubermensch.relation: Insooks deploys Nietzsche to argue Iron Man is the better hero: Cap's prized humility and relatability are sheep morality, the resentful herd value that drags the excellent down to average (as when society savored the Olympic swimmer's fall), while Tony honestly owns his superiority and keeps self-overcoming, building ever-better suits rather than resting on a serum gifted in a bottle. On this view Cap's manufactured modesty insults people who genuinely struggle, and the true super hero inspires from the mountaintop - build yourself a suit and get up here - instead of pretending to be just like us.

ubermensch.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
ubermensch.title: 8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need
ubermensch.relation: Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.

ubermensch.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
ubermensch.title: 5. RuPaul versus Zarathustra
ubermensch.relation: The van der Wielen sisters read RuPaul against Nietzsche's Zarathustra: both are outcasts who descend from solitude bearing a spiritual teaching in a marketplace that mocks them, and both announce that inherited values are ungrounded — Zarathustra through the death of God and the call to become the over-man, Ru through 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' and the cosmic life force that makes every identity a costume. But where Zarathustra refuses followers and shuns the people's values, Ru's creed polices female stereotypes (long hair, breasts, heels) and pulls the cart of consumerist values — money, fame, individualism — so that she comes to resemble the priests and wise men Zarathustra condemns. Her openly admitted fakeness and opportunism (the Wigstock 'gender fuck' abandoned for the glamazon brand) leave the chapter asking who flies higher: the tragic free spirit or the pragmatic, honestly dishonest superstar.

ubermensch.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
ubermensch.title: 8. Philosophy and the Personae
ubermensch.relation: Randall Auxier builds a characterology of the four personae using Aristotle's methods (endoxa and aporia) and the band's wealth hierarchy as his map. The Demon is Nietzsche — an uninhibited cosmopolitan beyond good and evil who philosophizes with a hammer and whispers eternal recurrence; the Starchild is Epicurus — Paul's microtia and bullied childhood formed the detached soul that Plato's Republic ties to being a philosopher, yielding ataraxia, aponia, therapy, and disciplined long-term pleasures; the Catman has Kundera's lightness of being around 'Beth'; and the Spaceman's otherworldly detachment explains both his guitar genius and the Nazi-regalia incident. The chapter's thesis: KISS succeeded because Gene and Paul's detached, centered self-knowledge let them give fans exactly what they secretly wanted.

ubermensch.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
ubermensch.title: Introduction
ubermensch.relation: Book introduction: recounts how the 1979 cast were the first casualties of the Chestburster scene (real butcher-shop organs, Veronica Cartwright fainting), then previews the volume's payload - personhood questions about Ash, Bishop, David and the Ripley clone; Marx on why Weyland-Yutani sacrifices crews for profit; Plato's Republic on children in warfare via Newt; Lovecraftian cosmic horror; feminist readings of Ripley as care ethicist and mother; and continental takes - Xenomorphs as Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Camus on Ripley-8's refusal to commit suicide, and Sartre on a Xenomorph's right to resist us.

ubermensch.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
ubermensch.title: “You are…a beautiful, beautiful, butterfly”
ubermensch.relation: Argues the Xenomorph realizes Nietzsche's Ubermensch: it is what Ash describes - unclouded by 'conscience, remorse, or delusions of morality' - and perfects its predatory function down to its acidic blood, while paycheck-fixated crewmen like Brett and Parker are Nietzsche's complacent 'last men,' the type Zarathustra's townspeople clamor for. The alien's egg-Facehugger-Chestburster-adult metamorphosis maps onto the camel, lion, and child of the three metamorphoses of the spirit, and the chapter closes by wondering whether the creature's monstrosity might have made Nietzsche himself reconsider the vital perfection he preached.

ubermensch.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
ubermensch.title: BSFs Best Superfriends Forever
ubermensch.relation: Daniel Malloy argues Batman and Superman are friends who disagree about friendship itself: Superman practices Aristotle's highest philia between good men who are 'another self' and true equals, symbolized by the kryptonite ring he trusts Batman to use on him should he go rogue, while Batman's friendship is Nietzschean, loving in his friend the overman 'as your cause' in the one equal he respects as a rival. Stories like Tower of Babel, Bruce Wayne: Fugitive, and the Brother Eye satellite show Batman manipulates everyone except this one peer, and that he never fights Superman fairly because he does not need to. Their fundamental, unresolvable differences, Malloy concludes, are exactly what strengthen the World's Finest friendship.

ubermensch.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
ubermensch.title: A Shared Higher Thirst
ubermensch.relation: Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.

ubermensch.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
ubermensch.title: The Prophet
ubermensch.relation: Reads Paul-Muad'Dib as a Nietzschean prophet: his sardonic greatness mirrors Zarathustra the laughing prophet, the Fremen's implanted legends illustrate Nietzsche's point that value matters more than truth (logic being only one perspective on the world), and the Untimely Meditations account of monumental myth explains why Muad'Dib must become the Preacher to destroy his own petrified religion. It likens the water-fat new Fremen of Children of Dune to Nietzsche's soft, risk-averse last men, and presents both Zarathustra and Muad'Dib as all-too-human founders who create a religion, recognize it as 'the most fateful of errors', and turn against it, with self-discipline rather than divine intervention as the true virtue.

ubermensch.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
ubermensch.title: Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps
ubermensch.relation: Claims Herbert is a philosopher whose Dune saga is a novelistic thought experiment extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra in the light of twentieth-century horrors: the Preacher's entry into Arrakeen parallels Zarathustra's first discourse on the Ubermensch at the tightrope, Paul is the failed tightrope-walker while Leto II is both devil-buffoon and goad toward the Superman, and the empire of Dune Messiah is enumerated trait by trait as Nietzsche's realm of the Ultimate Man. Eternal recurrence is paralleled with prescience as both the trap of destiny and the gateway 'Moment' that frees humanity from apparent necessity, and Arendt's banality of evil frames Paul's sixty-five billion jihad deaths as an ordinary, human result rather than demonic villainy.

ubermensch.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
ubermensch.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Jeffery Nicholas contrasts the superman Card seems to write — Graff's isolated Ender conditioned to impose his will like Nietzsche's overman, for whom happiness is only the feeling of overcoming resistance — with Aristotle's claim that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Peter is Aristotle's 'tribeless, lawless, hearthless' beast, the speechless buggers lack a common good until the queen communicates with Ender, and Ender's despair lifts only through friendship with Valentine, Alai, and Petra, proving the novel a meditation on 'without friends no one would choose to live.'

ubermensch.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
ubermensch.title: Amos Is No Superman
ubermensch.relation: Pankaj Singh reads Amos through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Amos' division of people into 'bad ones, ones you follow, and ones you need to protect', his outsourcing of moral judgment to Naomi and Holden ('Naomi wouldn't like it'), his fearlessness, and his violent spontaneity make him 'evil' by slave morality yet good by master morality. Unlike Prax, who has to be stopped from shooting Strickland out of ressentiment, Amos kills without revenge ('I am that guy'), and his fistfights with Miller and Alex discharge hostility immediately so it never poisons — the strong natures Nietzsche praises that 'form, mold, recuperate and forget.' His 'crew comes first' and 'better to go down swinging' express the will to power as discharge of strength rather than mere self-preservation, but because he never sublimates or overcomes his drives, the chapter concludes Amos is no Übermensch — 'but then again, who is?'

ubermensch.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
ubermensch.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
ubermensch.relation: Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.

ubermensch.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
ubermensch.title: NOTES
ubermensch.relation: Reads the show's eclipse icon against Plato's sun of the good — goodness has become hard to discern — and tests four theories of evil on the characters: Socrates' claim that no one errs knowingly is half-confirmed since villains like Angela and Nathan always take themselves to be doing right; Aristotle's akrasia and vice as an excess or deficiency of disposition fit Sylar's blood-scrawled 'Forgive me' apartment and his uncontrolled hunger; and Nietzsche's Übermensch and pre-Christian master morality raise the uncomfortable question of why Sylar preying on inferiors is not heroic like Achilles. The chapter's endorsed answer is Gilligan's ethics of care: the heroes are good because they care — Matt for Molly and Daphne, Bennet for Claire — while evil is the absence of care, though Bennet's authoritarian, family-only care shows that care itself must be both widened and restrained.

ubermensch.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure whose power play is staged through the show's postmodern techniques: the wave and the asides as metafiction that destroys our suspension of disbelief, self-referentiality in the mirror monologue ('Hunt or be hunted'), and a flattening of affect that lets us watch Zoe's murder at the train station with numbed indifference. Zarathustra's fearless overman is set against the risk-averse last man and the lambs-and-birds-of-prey passage against Christian slave morality, mapping onto Frank's breaking of Russo at the shipyard, the martyr's-sword maneuver on Blythe, and his spitting on the crucifix before taking 'God's ear'. The chapter reads Frank's ascent as will to power in both the political and personal Nietzschean sense, while warning that by Season 3 his hunger has cost him Jackie, Remy and Claire.

ubermensch.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Argues against the title claim of the previous chapter: Frank is a Nietzschean master type — he defines good as good-for-him, embraces pain as strength, and keeps no allegiances once Walker and Vasquez break their promise — while Peter Russo is the paradigmatic reactive slave who cannot command himself and blames others, exactly Nietzsche's 'he who cannot command himself is commanded'. But the overman requires self-overcoming, the sublimation of drives into creation, and amor fati, and Frank only dominates others for vengeful ends: his whole scheme grows from ressentiment over the Secretary of State snub, he affirms other wills merely as investments, and in Season 3 he becomes a slave to his own position. The chapter uses the Cesare Borgia misreading (better a Borgia than a Parsifal as raw material, but Borgia was no overman), Napoleon's corruption, and Goethe's creative wholeness to conclude that Frank remains 'all-too-human' — destruction without creation.

ubermensch.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Aarons argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure delivered through postmodern technique: the metafictional wave in 'Chapter 1,' self-referential mirror monologues ('Did you think I've forgotten you?'), and the flattening of affect in Zoe's death at the train station. Zarathustra's fearless overman, contrasted with the comfort-loving last man, maps onto Frank's 'hunt or be hunted' creed and his 'money is the McMansion in Sarasota... power is the old stone building' will-to-power, played out on Russo, Zoe, and Walker. The Genealogy's birds of prey and lambs frame Russo's Christian hypocrisy, and The Antichrist's equation of good with heightened power explains the church scene where Frank spits on the crucifix and leaves with the statue's ear — 'I've got God's ear now.'

ubermensch.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Meyer mounts the counter-case: Frank exemplifies Nietzsche's master type (good as good-for-him, 'no longer are we bound by allegiances') and Russo the slave type ('he who cannot command himself is commanded'), but the overman is a synthesis of neither. He corrects the Leopold-and-Loeb 'above the law' reading and the Cesare Borgia identification: the genuine overman sublimates strong drives into creation — Goethe's self-discipline, Beethoven's new norms — and affirms other wills in themselves rather than as instruments, which Frank never does with Zoe, Peter, or Claire. Frank's revenge-driven scheming is slave-like psychological warfare, ruling others is the 'pettiest' form of power, and by Season 3 he is the slave of his own presidency — destructive without creating, and lacking even amor fati.

ubermensch.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
ubermensch.title: 8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse
ubermensch.relation: Duncan Gale reads Raiders through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the Nazis' contempt for those they exploit ('They hire only strong backs and they pay pennies') enacts master morality, while their ressentiment-driven project is itself a fatal misreading — both of the Ark and of Nietzsche, whom Walter Kaufmann shows was distorted by his anti-Semitic sister rather than responsible for it. Indy emerges as an overman candidate whose improvised self-legislation ('I'm making this up as I go,' casually shooting the scimitar-wielding warrior) creates life-affirming values, unlike Belloq, who has no code at all. The finale inverts the death of God: the Nazis die because they disturb a divine power they cannot harness, while America's de facto agnosticism — warehousing the Ark with 'top men' — proves the survivable response to nihilism.

ubermensch.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
ubermensch.title: Franken-Stark
ubermensch.relation: Curtis argues Iron Man dramatizes the problem of progress: Schopenhauer's insatiable will explains why every technological fix — the chest plate, the armor, the artificial nervous system — spawns new suffering and dependency, and his pessimism, with Kierkegaard's freedom within insecurity, Nietzsche's flawed Übermensch going out 'in a blaze of glory,' and Sartre's 'cautiously optimistic' existentialism, recasts Iron Man as a tragic antihero rather than a perfected Superman or Batman. Stark's wounded heart, alcoholism as self-medication ('the demon is not in the bottle but in the addict'), and doomed romances with Bethany Cabe and Rumiko Fujikawa make him the flawed hero who has simply learned to live with imperfection. Like Mary Shelley's monster, his extensions have become him — we are all 'Franken-Starks' facing the consequences of our own inventions.

ubermensch.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.

ubermensch.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
ubermensch.title: Each of Us Would See Ourselves
ubermensch.relation: The Teschners cast Don as a Nietzschean creator of value in technological culture: his nihilism ('There is no big lie. There is no system. The universe is indifferent') and 'What you call love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' embody anti-foundationalism, while the beatnik Roy plays the resentful slave mentality whose passion lives only off what it despises. Don's creative process (sleep on it, 'forget it, and an idea will jump in your face') mirrors the camel-lion-child metamorphoses of Zarathustra, and the collapse of the principium individuationis explains his fluid identities from Dick Whitman to the 'Adam and Eve' fantasy with Rachel. Heidegger's techné frames the Kodak Carousel as genuine art, a revealing that transfigures 'a hell of a gadget' into 'a place where we know we are loved,' at the tragic price of a man outside community, and the falling figure of the credits is one 'we would each see ourselves' in.

ubermensch.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Victor Grech presents Klingons as a cultural pastiche—Mongol horde stereotypes, Japanese Bushido, Viking Valhalla, Shakespeare 'restored to the original Klingon'—whose 1500-year honor code and embrace of honorable death (Klag's dishonored father, Jadzia's rebuke of Kang) make them Nietzschean Ubermenschen who slew their own gods, echoing Nietzsche's 'God is dead'. The Kahless clone of 'Rightful Heir' ('perhaps the words are more important than the man') shows a messianism surviving deicide. He then reads Worf through Roland Barthes's 'Occidentalism' and one-way acculturation—Picard praising Worf's 'humanity' after 'Reunion'—while Azetbur's 'human rights' is racist jab in The Undiscovered Country and Trekkers' Klingon cosplay raise cultural relativism and appropriation.

ubermensch.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Argues Q embodies Nietzsche's revaluation of values: contemptuous of herd-like safety, Q subjects Picard and the crew to trials ("Encounter at Farpoint", "Hide and Q", "All Good Things"'s "the trial never ends") meant to force growth beyond conventional morality, seek out other "supermen", and embrace risk - Q's "bloody nose" defense after eighteen crewmen die at the Borg in "Q Who?". The Borg figure as everything Nietzschean individualism despises, a mindless collectivism that robs drones of the passion the strong need to individuate, and Q's offer to join Picard as guide pictures a friendship between Nietzsche's self-mastered few. The lesson of "Tapestry" is amor fati: Picard must embrace the Nausicaan knife fight that nearly killed him, since undoing it makes a safe, unnoticed man - though the authors finally refuse Nietzsche's harsher dictum that the weak should perish, siding with healing over Q's education-by-death.

ubermensch.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
ubermensch.title: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
ubermensch.relation: Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.

ubermensch.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
ubermensch.title: 7. How Batman Cowed a God
ubermensch.relation: Reider reads Batman as Nietzsche's aristocratic 'good' man — pagan wrath and vengeance without shame, his no-kill rule in Under the Red Hood mere pride, like Achilles dragging Hector's body — and Superman as the unwitting pawn of slave morality, his Kent-farm humility, guilt, and protect-the-weak ethos the very values the resentful revolt installed. The provocation: a god whose morality favors the weak may secretly wish to be overcome, so the imagined confrontation where Batman growls 'follow the plan or I'll take you out myself' lets Superman feel happily, honestly human again — which is also why Wonder Woman pursues Batman and Clark pines for the domineering Lois.

ubermensch.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
ubermensch.title: 21. Batman Is Superman
ubermensch.relation: Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.

ubermensch.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
ubermensch.title: H O N O R
ubermensch.relation: This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.

ubermensch.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
ubermensch.title: Notes
ubermensch.relation: Michels reads the Amazon series' first two seasons as a Nietzschean tale organized around eternal recurrence, treating the turning Wheel as Nietzsche's 'existential imperative' and greatest weight: the ferryman who dies vainly saving his son fails the test, while Loial urges the heroes to make themselves unforgettable. He maps Nietzsche's monumental, antiquarian, and critical uses of history onto Moiraine's lesson about the song of Manetheren, contrasts the Ubermensch with the 'last man,' and reads Moiraine's will to power against the ascetic, life-denying Way of the Leaf of the Tuatha'an. Lanfear and Ishamael embody nihilism and resentment, while amor fati names the life-affirming embrace of fate Nietzsche prized.

ubermensch.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
ubermensch.title: Friendship, Rivalry, and Excellence
ubermensch.relation: The chapter uses Aristotle's three friendships (pleasure, usefulness, virtue) to ask how tennis rivals competing for one prize can be friends, illustrating pleasure with Borg and Gerulaitis, usefulness with the tense but genuine Ashe-McEnroe Davis Cup bond, and virtue with the Evert-Navratilova rivalry that grew into deep mutual care despite a competitive women's tour. It adds C. S. Lewis's view that friends stand side by side absorbed in a shared thing, then reads Jimmy Connors as a Nietzschean Ubermensch whose master-morality drive to dominate makes him, paradoxically, the best 'star friend' by pushing rivals to their limits. It closes unresolved on whether the tension between friendship and rivalry can ever be eliminated.

ubermensch.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
ubermensch.title: Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams
ubermensch.relation: Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.

ubermensch.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
ubermensch.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
ubermensch.relation: Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.

ubermensch.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
ubermensch.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
ubermensch.relation: Sterritt reads Manhunter's Hannibal Lecktor as a perverse image of Nietzsche's Übermensch: hedonistic, ascetic, and expressing an overwhelming will to power, exercising superhuman self-control (his pulse never exceeding eighty-five while mutilating a nurse). Using Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming' and the body without organs, he contrasts the genuinely self-transforming Lecktor (a 'schizovivisectionist') with Dollarhyde, whose bogus becoming—trapped in Blake's 'mind-forg'd manacles' and the Red Dragon—makes him a pathetic tooth fairy rather than an overman, aligning both killers with Kierkegaard's demonic individual who stands above the universal.

ubermensch.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
ubermensch.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
ubermensch.relation: Abrams argues that 2001 films the whole evolutionary arc of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, from ape-men through humanity to the Star Child as the overman/posthuman. He maps the moon monolith's discovery onto the death of God (science debunking the creation myth, guarded by a Platonic 'noble lie' cover-up), the astronauts Bowman/Poole/Floyd onto the Enlightenment 'higher men,' and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus his and Poole's fatal spacewalks onto the last man and the falling tightrope walker whom Zarathustra carries. He then extends the vision toward Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's 'mind children,' while criticizing Kubrick for replacing Nietzsche's godless self-overcoming with alien 'replacement gods' that thin out the death-of-God insight.

ubermensch.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
ubermensch.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
ubermensch.relation: Kevin S. Decker offers a 'philosophical hermeneutics' of Burton's Batman and Batman Returns, arguing that a long-lived cultural artifact like the Batman discloses a society's self-understanding. Using Heidegger's Dasein and 'working-out of possibilities,' Nietzsche's 'only interpretations,' and Gadamer's hermeneutic circle and fusion of horizons, Decker reads the shift from ABC's camp Adam West Batman to Burton's dark version as tracking cultural change (Vietnam, Watergate, 1980s decadence). He casts the Joker, Penguin, and Catwoman—and Batman himself—as Burton's recurring 'expressive outsider,' relating them to Nietzsche's Übermensch and Gotham's gullible crowds to Heidegger's das Man, and compares Burton's Expressionist Gotham to Max Beckmann's post-WWI Hell lithographs, positioning Burton as a prophet of modern decadence.

ubermensch.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
ubermensch.title: The Conquest of Uselessness as a Practice of Film and Thought
ubermensch.relation: Daniele Dottorini reads Herzog's filmmaking as a 'conquest of the useless' through the figures of the Tightrope Walker (Philippe Petit), the Traveler, and the Pilgrim, whose bodily effort and risk over the abyss subtract film from any utilitarian logic. He aligns them with the tightrope walker of the prologue to Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, poised between animal and Overman, and uses Deleuze and Guattari's 'conceptual personae' from What Is Philosophy? to argue that Herzog becomes his own characters. The carrying of the ship over the mountain in Fitzcarraldo and Steiner's ecstatic ski-flight exemplify ecstatic truth (aletheia) as an unveiling that transfigures the world into music.

ubermensch.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
ubermensch.title: I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You
ubermensch.relation: Ruth Deller reads the Doctor as a savior/redeemer figure onto whom fans project ideals, invoking Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideal self onto Christ, then pivots to Nietzsche. Rather than a flawless Messiah, the Doctor is a flawed being who must overcome himself, and his 'ordinary' companions (Donna, Harriet Jones, the Hostess in 'Midnight', Rose in 'Turn Left') exemplify Nietzsche's Ubermensch by rising above their weaknesses. She argues the Doctor and humans have a symbiotic relationship: the universe needs a savior, but that savior must be challenged, so both overcome themselves together.

ubermensch.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
ubermensch.title: Life A Celebration
ubermensch.relation: Adam Riggio uses Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche to cast the Simm Master as a nihilist who, having seen the valueless dying universe at Utopia, wills nothingness and universal destruction out of ressentiment. The Doctor is Nietzsche's Overman who overcomes the reactive forces of revenge: in 'Dalek' he recognizes his own vengefulness and turns from it, and in 'Last of the Time Lords' he defeats the Master not with Martha's fake gun but by saying 'I forgive you,' affirming finite life with a 'beneficent Yes-saying' rather than surrendering to enmity.

ubermensch.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
ubermensch.title: 1. Human, All Too Human
ubermensch.relation: Holdier reads Supernatural's finale through Nietzsche, arguing that Chuck's exposure as a cruel author-God and his defeat by the Winchesters dramatizes the 'death of God' as the freedom to invent one's own meaning. Dean and Sam's stubborn refusal to 'stay down' on the lakeshore against Chuck embodies amor fati—saying yes to circumstance—while Jack, birthed and taught by ordinary humans, becomes the Ubermensch who replaces God, showing humanity as a bridge to something greater than itself.

ubermensch.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
ubermensch.title: Introduction
ubermensch.relation: Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.

ubermensch.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
ubermensch.title: 1. How to De-Nazify Nietzsche’s Philosophical Anthropology
ubermensch.relation: Golomb argues the Nazi reading of the will to power as military conquest confuses Nietzsche's Macht (sublimated spiritual power) with Kraft (brute force) and Gewalt (violence), showing through Human, All Too Human and Daybreak that self-overcoming and creative sublimation, not domination, define the Übermensch. He builds a typology of 'positive' versus 'negative' power in which the anti-Semite figures as the vengeful, ressentiment-driven 'slave,' and insists Nietzsche's morality is not naturalistic—power must be transfigured by self-education—so his anthropology stands beyond the eugenic and racial distinctions central to Nazi ideology, even in the misused 'blond beast' passage.

ubermensch.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
ubermensch.title: 3. Experiences with Nietzsche
ubermensch.relation: Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.

ubermensch.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
ubermensch.title: 4. Nietzsche and “Hitler”
ubermensch.relation: Nehamas puts 'Hitler' in scare-quotes to pose an abstract problem—does Nietzsche's ideal of nobility permit the evil hero?—rooting it in the Greek notion of aretê and Plato's Republic.
