The chapter's twist is that Foucault's power/knowledge rescues postmodernism from cynicism: labeling Quagmire a 'pervert' situates him in power relations, but like Socrates, Jesus, Buddha, and Gandhi, deviants may just act uniquely, so we can be cynics about grand stories yet still fight locally (against the FCC, for tolerance).

grand-narratives.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
grand-narratives.title: 11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True
grand-narratives.relation: Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.

grand-narratives.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
grand-narratives.title: The Witcher as Postmodern Fairy Tale
grand-narratives.relation: Vega and Barta argue The Witcher is a 'postmodern fairytale' in Lyotard's sense of incredulity toward metanarratives: the saga uses the forms of fairytales while doubting them. Jaskier's ballads (and Geralt's 'a story is a largely false account, of largely trivial events, fed to us by historians who are largely idiots') expose how lore constructs and misrepresents its subjects; 'The Lesser Evil,' the cursed-moon skepticism about Stregobor's story, and the 'grain of truth' in 'true love breaks a spell' make Geralt and the reader distrust destiny and fable morals - Ciri demands a moral from Geralt's fable and gets only 'Survive.' Adaptation across books, the Netflix show, and choice-driven games (Triss versus Yennefer, the branching Ciri endings, the ambiguous close of The Lady of the Lake) demolishes any single canonical, authoritative telling of the story.

grand-narratives.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
grand-narratives.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
grand-narratives.relation: Milan Hosta traces a dialectical line from the individual athlete through nationalism and internationalism to the transnational Olympic movement, arguing individualism 'turns into itself again' since the whole order is reproduced by individuals like Paavo Nurmi ('I run for myself, not for Finland'). He reads Coubertin's 'sincere internationalism' as a moral epistemology of knowing others (glossed via Morgan and a Hegelian account of tolerance as recognizing but not truly accepting difference) against the hollow cosmopolitanism of tourism and 'popular ethnography.' Drawing on postmodern pluralism and the end of grand narratives, plus Hardt and Negri's Empire, he frames the IOC as a peace-preaching yet blood-bathed transnational power sustained by record-seeking individuals.

grand-narratives.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
grand-narratives.title: Deceit, Desire, and Dark Comedy Postmodern Dead Ends in Blood Simple
grand-narratives.relation: Woolfolk argues that Blood Simple is 'resolutely postmodern': it recycles noir motifs as Jamesonian pastiche but, unlike classic noir (Double Indemnity, Detour), offers no modernist critique of capitalist civilization and no saving metanarrative, leaving only a profane comic present. He reads the three men who go 'simple'—Ray, Marty, Visser—through Girard's triangular desire, driven by unchecked, mutually imitated passions with no external mediating authority, while Visser's sidewalk individualism supplies a minimal social philosophy. Crucially the film's world is ruled by chance, not fate (the pistol's three bullets, Abby's lucky single shot), so Abby's clueless 'health' and survival affirm postmodern contingency rather than any critique of late modernity.

grand-narratives.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
grand-narratives.title: The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy
grand-narratives.relation: Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.

grand-narratives.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
grand-narratives.title: The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer
grand-narratives.relation: Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.

grand-narratives.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
grand-narratives.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
grand-narratives.relation: Conard argues that Tarantino's postmodernism makes redemption impossible in Reservoir Dogs (and Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill). Using Danto on the 'end of art', Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives', and Rorty's contingent 'vocabularies', he shows the films embrace relativism about knowledge (rearranged chronology, unreliable perspectives) and about values. Mr. Orange plays Judas and Christ; the opening tipping argument exposes moral conventions as arbitrary, so becoming a 'real person' rather than a gangster is merely being a dork rather than cool. With no metanarrative to ground it, one way of life cannot be morally superior, so redemption fails.

grand-narratives.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
grand-narratives.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
grand-narratives.relation: Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.

grand-narratives.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
grand-narratives.title: Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984
grand-narratives.relation: Palmer compares the two film versions of Orwell's 1984 to argue that dystopian fiction projects present fears and desires onto an imagined future, engaging critically with the Enlightenment idea of progress (via Burnham's managerial thesis). Anderson's 1956 film 'talks to the future,' fusing science fiction and film noir to voice Cold War dread of a possible historical trajectory, while Radford's 1984 version, in the postmodern 'heritage film' mode Jameson and Higson describe, museumizes the novel: with history seemingly ended it becomes an honored, reverentially displayed relic that talks only to a dead past rather than warning of a coming one.

grand-narratives.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
grand-narratives.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
grand-narratives.relation: Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.

grand-narratives.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
grand-narratives.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
grand-narratives.relation: de Waard argues that The Good German embodies Soderbergh's 'neo-meta' philosophy of history as polyphonic mediation, staged by Levi's line about a camera that turns the image upside-down to set it right. Shooting with 1940s-era equipment and pastiching Casablanca, The Third Man, Chinatown, and Schindler's List, the film presents not history's progression but 'history as time,' a simultaneity of broken mirrors. Reworking Benjamin's angel-of-history thesis, de Waard claims images of the present threaten to reappear ad infinitum, and contrasts Soderbergh's cold, morally relativist tale of American war-criminal whitewashing (Lena's confession that she betrayed twelve Jews) with Spielberg's emotionally manipulative Holocaust spectacle, invoking Eco on Casablanca as 'movies' itself.

grand-narratives.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
grand-narratives.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
grand-narratives.relation: Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.

grand-narratives.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
grand-narratives.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
grand-narratives.relation: Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.

grand-narratives.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
grand-narratives.title: Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!
grand-narratives.relation: J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate. Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.

grand-narratives.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
grand-narratives.title: On Beyond Modernity, or Conrad and a Postmodern Alphabet
grand-narratives.relation: Jacob Held explains postmodernism as Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives' using On Beyond Zebra! Conrad's twenty-six-letter alphabet is the metanarrative that fixes what can be said and known, while the narrator's invented letters (Yuzz, Snee, Floob) show language expanding to present the unpresentable. Held casts Kant's three Critiques, phenomena/noumena, and his defining of the mind's 'alphabet' as the exemplary modern grand narrative Lyotard rejects, then turns to Foucault's Nietzschean genealogy, using You're Only Old Once! for the medicalization of life and (via a Beauvoir quotation) the claim that gender is a constructed mechanism of control that can be transgressed.

grand-narratives.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
grand-narratives.title: Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection
grand-narratives.relation: Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.

grand-narratives.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
grand-narratives.title: Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World
grand-narratives.relation: Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.

grand-narratives.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
grand-narratives.title: Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!
grand-narratives.relation: Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.

categorical-imperative.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
categorical-imperative.title: 10 - The Moral World of the Simpson Family A Kantian Perspective
categorical-imperative.relation: James Lawler reads the Simpson family through Kant's conflict of duty and desire: Homer rationalizes 'duty' to please Moe in 'Dumbell Indemnity' yet achieves moral heroism renouncing General Sherman for his marriage, while Bart's limit-case ('Even I know stealing from the collection basket is wrong') shows morality from the negative side. Marge's honesty as a realtor in 'Realty Bites' dramatizes Kantian duty to self and the highest good in which happiness should flow from duty, and Lisa embodies inner-determined morality—testing maxims for universalizability when she becomes a vegetarian—though she learns tolerance from Apu. Lisa's isolation and her doleful saxophone ('Moaning Lisa') express the sacrifice morality demands of a sensitive child, giving the comedy its undertone of tragedy.

categorical-imperative.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
categorical-imperative.title: 14 - Hey-diddily-ho, Neighboreenos Ned Flanders and Neighborly Love
categorical-imperative.relation: David Vessey asks how 'love your neighbor as yourself' can coexist with tolerance when you believe your unbaptized neighbor faces eternal suffering, using 'Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily' where Ned baptizes the Simpson children in his care but never proselytizes beyond his household. He constructs the argument that love of neighbor, like love of self, would seem to require trying to baptize everyone, then dissolves it: proper self-love means perfecting one's nobler aspects by acting on principle rather than desire, so loving others can require respecting principled choices that risk even their lives. Kant's account of autonomy - rationally legislating one's own maxims, per the categorical imperative - supplies the missing condition, showing Ned is justified in not interfering with autonomous adults, a point capped by the irony that the only person he actually baptizes is pleasure-driven Homer.

categorical-imperative.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
categorical-imperative.title: Following the Moral Law
categorical-imperative.relation: Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.

categorical-imperative.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
categorical-imperative.title: Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater
categorical-imperative.relation: Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.

categorical-imperative.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
categorical-imperative.title: Five Questions about Good Sportsmanship
categorical-imperative.relation: Mark Hamilton asks whether there is lying in baseball (riffing on Jimmy Dugan's 'There's no crying in baseball') and sorts plays of deception by their target. Kant's absolute duty of truthfulness proves too broad for the hidden ball trick, Omar Vizquel's decoys, and faking a tag to fool Manny Ramirez: Aquinas's taxonomy of officious, jocose, and mischievous lies (with Bonhoeffer's situational truth-telling) shows these are jocose falsehoods in an agreed artificial contest, not immoral lies. But deception aimed at umpires is mischievous and immoral, as when Barry Bonds sells a trapped ball as a catch or runners cut bases in the illegal double squeeze; his five questions conclude that tricking opponents is strategy while tricking the officials destroys character and sport.

categorical-imperative.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
categorical-imperative.title: 22b
categorical-imperative.relation: A paired legal-philosophy debate on whether steroids should be banned. Michael McGrath argues yes from Kant: PED use cannot be universalized and 'the ends do not justify the means,' so the Ken Caminiti, Mark McGwire, and José Canseco confessions stain America's pastime, whose stars are role models and whose users risk devastating health effects — down to wrestler Davey Boy Smith's fatal steroid-related heart attack. Simon Eassom replies no by reframing drugs as Performance Enhancing Technologies: rules merely define the game, enhancers (unlike bat-cannons or netted catcher's gloves) do not de-skill baseball, and banning them because we dislike them is a matter of taste — of aesthetics, not ethics.

categorical-imperative.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
categorical-imperative.title: I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!
categorical-imperative.relation: Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.

categorical-imperative.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
categorical-imperative.title: Reasons to Be Moral
categorical-imperative.relation: Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.

categorical-imperative.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
categorical-imperative.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.

categorical-imperative.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
categorical-imperative.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Cox and Bender subject Atkins to Kant's universal-law formula — could every one of the billion overweight people on earth adopt it? — in a 'factive' thought experiment: a 25 percent rise in animal-protein output, nearly 250 million additional feed-grain acres, overgrazed ranges, and possibly a tenth of the world's remaining forests cleared for pasture. Calling Atkins reductionism's child (a metabolic switch judged on bathroom scales), they use Marx's 'metabolic rift' — soil nutrients shipped to cities, feedlots severing crops from livestock — and the Cartesian body-as-machine (via Federici) to place low-carb's atomized foods (bungalow subs, soy 'mashed potatoes,' pork rinds) as capitalism's latest rupture in the food system. Their verdict: only plant-leaning regimens could survive universalization, and the deeper fix is Wendell Berry's — eating understood as an agricultural act.

categorical-imperative.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
categorical-imperative.title: Poker and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Huss tests four models of bluffing on one K-9 all-in: it is not lying, because everyone at the table expects deception, so the victim is never Frankfurt's 'twice deceived' (and Kant's argument that lying fails where everyone lies applies); it is not bullshit, because Frankfurt's bullshitter ignores the facts a poker player cannot afford to ignore; it is not pure acceptance in Jonathan Cohen's sense, since bluffing adds deception to acting-as-if; and it is not full self-deception, since nobody can make themselves believe that 2+2=5 or that 4-7 offsuit is pocket aces. Good bluffing is an art blending all four: deceiving about hand and beliefs, prying attention away from your cards, acting as if, and trying — and necessarily failing — to fool yourself.

categorical-imperative.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
categorical-imperative.title: James Bond and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Tedesco dissects what the double-0 'license to kill' could actually mean, ruling out self-defense and mere on-the-job killing and concluding that Bond is a state-sanctioned assassin who earned his status through two assassinations in Casino Royale. He tests that status against Kant's categorical imperative - persons as ends in themselves, though Kant also defended capital punishment as respecting the murderer's choice - and against consequentialism, which vindicates Bond's elimination of Kananga but stumbles on the surgeon's organ-harvesting dilemma. Because ordinary morality mixes duty-based and consequence-based intuitions, the chapter leaves Bond's moral status genuinely open and links it to live policy debates on assassination and torture after 9/11, including Britain's Intelligence Services Act that leaves room for a real-life double-0 agent.

categorical-imperative.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
categorical-imperative.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
categorical-imperative.relation: Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.

categorical-imperative.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
categorical-imperative.title: Plato’s Cave Again
categorical-imperative.relation: Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.

categorical-imperative.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
categorical-imperative.title: Why Be Moral
categorical-imperative.relation: Sanders uses Bruno Anthony's 'criss-cross' murder-swap proposal to Guy Haines in Strangers on a Train to pose the classic question 'Why be moral?' to the charming amoralist. He tests three answers: Kant's categorical imperative fails because Bruno's egoist maxim ('remove obstacles to your happiness') can apparently be universalized; Hobbesian contractarian 'morality pays' fails because Bruno free-rides on others' restraint; and the Rachels/Nelson/Thomas psychological-health answer assumes rather than proves that Bruno should care about comparable suffering. A thought experiment comparing the moral life with the Bruno-state from an impartial standpoint leads to Aristotle's eudaimonia: morality is constitutive of human flourishing, so Bruno enjoys only a counterfeit happiness.

categorical-imperative.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
categorical-imperative.title: Encore
categorical-imperative.relation: Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.

categorical-imperative.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
categorical-imperative.title: The Virtues of Superhumans
categorical-imperative.relation: Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.

categorical-imperative.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
categorical-imperative.title: If I Were a Carpenter
categorical-imperative.relation: Butler asks what makes an activity work, testing the market definition against Socrates' refusal of fees, Aristotle's Politics, Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, Eva Kittay's care work, and the split between extrinsic and intrinsic value. He reads Cash's catalog through it: "One Piece at a Time" (the Detroit line worker stealing a Cadillac he builds but cannot afford), "Get Rhythm" (the shoeshine boy singing through menial labor), "I Never Picked Cotton" (escaping work into an empty identity), "Let Him Roll" and "Southern Accents," and the San Quentin monologue after "Wreck of the Ol' 97" where Cash refuses to be told what to play before inmates. The chapter closes by lining up Kant's categorical imperative, Jesus' Golden Rule, and Rawls's veil of ignorance: nobody would choose a society of company-store wage slavery without knowing they were not the worker, and Cash, knowing he stood on the stage rather than in the cellblock, used his freedom to side with prisoners and carpenters anyway.

categorical-imperative.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
categorical-imperative.title: From Cash to Kant—and Back Again
categorical-imperative.relation: Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.

categorical-imperative.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
categorical-imperative.title: Democratization of Media—Philosophy for All!
categorical-imperative.relation: Parker recounts training for the Seoul Marathon on a treadmill with philosophy podcasts (Philosophy Talk, Philosophy Bites, LibriVox) to argue the iPod works as a 'next-generation book' that can democratize philosophy -- yet, like the book, it cannot supply the two-way dialogue that Socrates practiced in the agora and that Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, and Epicurus's Garden were built to sustain. He distinguishes studying philosophy -- compiling, say, Kant's claim that one cannot act except in ways one could will all others to act -- from doing it, and argues that credentials and canon cannot displace each person's inescapable role as 'the arbiters of our own thoughts.' The Nazis' misconstrual of Nietzsche is his example of interpretation without critical guardianship, and he concludes that the academy's stronghold on teaching philosophy is loosening even if wikis and virtual forums never fully replace professional expertise.

categorical-imperative.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
categorical-imperative.title: “Make It So”
categorical-imperative.relation: Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.

categorical-imperative.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
categorical-imperative.title: “I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”
categorical-imperative.relation: Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.

categorical-imperative.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
categorical-imperative.title: There’s No Place Like Home
categorical-imperative.relation: Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.

categorical-imperative.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
categorical-imperative.title: Transformers and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Michaud reads the Autobot-Decepticon war as a contest of ethical systems: Optimus's fair fighting, his refusal to ignore human casualties, and Bumblebee's friendship with the inferior Spike instantiate Kant's categorical imperative and the treatment of rational beings as ends in themselves. The Decepticons run through the egoist tradition - Hobbes's psychological egoism from Leviathan, Starscream's self-defeating normative egoism, and Megatron as Ayn Rand's rational egoist taunting 'You still fight for the weak; that is why you lose' - leaving the reader to choose between Kant's world of peaceful obligation and Rand's world of power where, like Starscream, you die alone.

categorical-imperative.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
categorical-imperative.title: Explaining Moral Doubt
categorical-imperative.relation: Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.

categorical-imperative.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
categorical-imperative.title: Close the Door, Put Out the Lights
categorical-imperative.relation: Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.

categorical-imperative.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
categorical-imperative.title: Achievement Unlocked Ethical Considerations
categorical-imperative.relation: Monica Evans opens with the 2006 'Serenity Now' funeral raid — a PvP guild massacring an in-game funeral for a real player — to argue that in-game ethics depend on each player's perception of the gameworld: mourners treat Azeroth as an extension of real life, raiders as a competitive game, and both are right. Plato's Ring of Gyges fails as an analogy because WoW hands everyone invisibility, yet morality still operates as a social construction through reputation, guilds, and the ostracism of ninja-looters. She finds the Borean Tundra 'torture quest' ethically hollow since the prisoner respawns and nothing persists, applies Mill's utilitarianism to good-samaritan players and universally loathed ninja-looters, and uses Kant's Categorical Imperative both to explain why players don't desert dungeon parties and why fair PvP killing of friends is permissible.

categorical-imperative.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
categorical-imperative.title: Embrace the Shadow!—There Is No Moral Dilemma
categorical-imperative.relation: Phil Serchuk asks whether ninja looters — say, a raid leader Master-Looting the Warglaive of Azzinoth — act immorally, and answers no. After reviewing act and rule utilitarianism through Medivh's opening of the Dark Portal and the theft of Napoleon's sarcophagus, and Kant's Categorical Imperative through Kil'jaeden's deception of Ner'zhul, he argues that virtual items cannot be owned at all and that there is no moral agent in WoW for either theory to condemn: neither the player (who kills thousands of PCs in battlegrounds without blame) nor the avatar (which makes no decisions) can be held liable. Ninjaing is therefore as morally benign as a natural disaster.

categorical-imperative.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
categorical-imperative.title: Manny
categorical-imperative.relation: Santaniello reads five nonconformist Red Sox through ethical theory. Ruth's sale to New York becomes a Kantian case: he tore up his signed three-year contract and demanded a trade while expecting others to keep promises, violating the categorical imperative on promise-keeping. Ted Williams's lifelong war with the 'Knights of the Keyboard' exemplifies existentialist authenticity ('It just wouldn't have been me' tipping his cap), Spaceman Bill Lee embodies Sartre's condemned freedom and existence precedes essence, Jim Rice's Hall of Fame delay is Aristotle's failure to hit the mean between silent deficiency on Boston's racism and excess toward reporters, and Manny's 'Gas is up and so am I' money grab shows Aristotle's point that wealth is an incomplete end pursued for the sake of something else.

categorical-imperative.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
categorical-imperative.title: Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies
categorical-imperative.relation: Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.

categorical-imperative.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
categorical-imperative.title: Back at the Bins, or Loving Your Enemy Like Your Neighbor
categorical-imperative.relation: Kohn begins with her own response to a serial bin-tipper: practicing iaido sword draws in full view of the neighbours to intimidate an imagined Other. Contrasting iaido's virtual opponent (a mere tool for the self) with aikido's real partners, she deploys Levinas's face of the Other, responsibility without waiting for reciprocity and philosophy as 'the Wisdom of Love', alongside Arendt's shared responsibility for the world's conflicts, to argue that care for even one's attacker comes first, with Kant's categorical imperative as the generalizable counterpart to Levinas's ethics. Her confession: she treated the imagined culprit as an object of hate, when meeting 'the Face' would have demanded an apology and maybe a hug.

categorical-imperative.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
categorical-imperative.title: Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal
categorical-imperative.relation: Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.

categorical-imperative.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
categorical-imperative.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
categorical-imperative.relation: Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.

categorical-imperative.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
categorical-imperative.title: The (Single) Garden Path
categorical-imperative.relation: Compares Herbert's three eugenics programs: the Bene Gesserit's centuries-long Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (explicitly modeled on the communal breeding of the guardians in Plato's Republic, undone when Jessica bears Paul a generation early and he escapes their control), Leto II's Golden Path breeding for Siona's invisibility to prescience, and the Tleilaxu axolotl-tank immortality that collapses when their Face Dancers out-mimic them. Each program is weighed ethically—Leto as the 'ultimate consequentialist' whose species-saving tyranny invokes Mill's utilitarianism and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means, the Sisterhood as shifting toward Kantian duties against using persons as mere means. Herbert's lesson: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics,' whether aimed at a single person, a single result, or a single agenda.

categorical-imperative.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
categorical-imperative.title: I’ve Got No Strings . .
categorical-imperative.relation: Richard Greene asks whether it was practically rational for Dexter to trust Lumen rather than kill her, to help her revenge-kill the Fowler ring, and to train her as a killer. The good outcomes do not help - Masuka's strip-club windfall shows luck is not rationality, and Socrates' Apology argument that corrupters risk harm from those they corrupt, together with Dexter's prior disaster in training Miguel, means the consequences were not foreseeably good. Kantian tests fail too - no one could will a universal law of killing, and killing violates the victim's autonomy and humanity as an end in itself - as do decision theory and instrumentality theories, so no account of practical rationality vindicates Dexter's choices, suggesting instead that the emotionless 'wooden boy' is beginning to become a real one.

categorical-imperative.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
categorical-imperative.title: Vigilante Hero
categorical-imperative.relation: Epright and Worth argue that rule-following - the Ten Commandments, the Golden Rule, Kant's categorical imperative (whose consistent Kantian never lies even to Nazis), or the Bentham-Mill principle of utility (whose consistent utilitarian must torture if stakes are high) - never made anyone moral, and Dexter's Code is the case in point: it gives the appearance of morality while licensing murder, and its source (Harry, 'God', the texts) cannot vindicate it. Drawing on Jonah Lehrer's neuroscience that moral judgment is emotional first with reason as post-hoc lawyer, they argue the emotionless Dexter is the madman who has lost everything except his reason, and Kohlberg's moral-development stages find him stuck at the pre-conventional level, below a fifth-grader - punishment-avoidance and you-scratch-my-back reasoning, never universal principles or respect for persons. Real Dexter-inspired killers (Mark Twitchell, Andrew Conley) clinch the verdict: he is neither vigilante hero nor moral agent, just a selfish addict whose rule-governed kills justify nothing.

categorical-imperative.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
categorical-imperative.title: You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You
categorical-imperative.relation: Waller and McAlear first rebut the amoral reading: Dexter does feel (he sobs over Rita, loves Deb, misses Harry) and does control his urges through the Code, so morality applies to him, and the Dark Passenger is merely everyone's socially unacceptable desires - the very thing that gives rise to moral codes. They then test the three theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics mostly fails because murder admits no mean and Harry's Code teaches killer's skills rather than virtues (though its 'don't kill innocents' dispositions are genuine virtues); utilitarianism fails even in rule-utilitarian form - via the organ-harvesting doctor and Harry's own utilitarian guilt over Laura Moser's death - because Dexter kills because the Code requires it, not because it maximizes happiness. What fits is dark deontology: like Kant's argument that murderers consent to their own execution out of respect for their rationality, Dexter kills only killers, acts from duty rather than enjoyment, and treats 'don't get caught' as a condition for the possibility of his true imperative.

categorical-imperative.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
categorical-imperative.title: Invisibility or Honesty
categorical-imperative.relation: Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.

categorical-imperative.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
categorical-imperative.title: Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem
categorical-imperative.relation: Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.

categorical-imperative.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
categorical-imperative.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Solves the 'riddle' of Gus by showing his empire runs on corporate instrumental rationality: the careful, emotion-disciplined Los Pollos CEO launders meth through legitimate business, treats chemists as replaceable parts (the Gale plan), and exacts revenge on the cartel in 'Salud' by drinking his own poisoned tequila. The chapter defines this as the critical theorists' amoral means-end reason - Kant's hypothetical imperative without the categorical - making Gus a sociopath who violates the injunction to treat persons as ends, and reads his cartel war through Machiavelli and Hobbes's power-first picture of the state. Gus's Two-Face-like corpse reveals the split between the rage-driven avenger of Max and the respectable mask, foreshadowing what Walt becomes.

categorical-imperative.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
categorical-imperative.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Stages the standard three-way ethics debate on Walt: deontology's universalizability (Kant) absurdly forbids killing Krazy-8 even to save Walt's family, utilitarianism (Mill) licenses both cooking meth and murdering dealers - a outright contradiction - while Aristotle's virtue ethics judges character rather than acts and convicts Walt of vice: he endangers his family, misses Holly's birth, habituates himself into Heisenberg, and defrauds his school. Because acts and consequences alone cannot see character, virtue ethics is offered as the needed complement. The closing move widens the lens to America itself, arguing the capitalist success ethos and our appetite for anti-heroes like Tony Soprano and Dexter reveal a society that praises viciousness - 'we are what we repeatedly do.'

categorical-imperative.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
categorical-imperative.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Yuen distinguishes heroic survival cannibalism, as in the Andes crash of Alive, from the 'Fear the Hunters' cannibals: both utilitarianism and Kantianism permit eating those who already died out of necessity, since the dead lose no utility and corpses lack the rationality that grounds Kantian dignity. But Chris's band killed children to eat them and kept the living Dale as a food store, which fails both theories and cannot be excused by 'we don't do this because we want to,' since alternatives existed — joining other survivors, eating walkers ('zombitarianism'), or starving, because survival is never a moral obligation. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended as Kantian retributive punishment: if Chris universalized his maxim that people may be hunted for food, then, as Rick suggests while biting Chris's neck, 'if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris.'

categorical-imperative.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
categorical-imperative.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Cogburn protests Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments and rebuilds the system philosophically: Lawful means willing universalizable law in Kant's categorical-imperative sense (the liar and murderer treating themselves as exceptions), Good means willing the greatest happiness in Mill's utilitarian sense, yielding a nine-box grid of moral psychologies. He populates it with fantasy archetypes—Haomane Firstborn as pathological Lawful Neutral, Karsa Orlong as Chaotic Neutral, Abercrombie's torturer Glotka as Neutral Neutral in Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil' mold, hierarchic vampires and cynical politicians as Lawful Evil, Conan's raiders as Chaotic Evil. On this scheme Chaotic Good is genuinely empty, Drizzt and Robin Hood types are really Lawful or Neutral Good, and a Neutral Good versus Lawful Good dispute over killing one innocent to save thousands shows how gameplay can stage classic ethics thought experiments.

categorical-imperative.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
categorical-imperative.title: The Wire and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Fallis tests Kant's claim that a universal 'lie whenever it is to your advantage' would necessarily destroy itself, and David Lewis's stricter thesis that communication requires mostly truth-tellers, against a West Baltimore where Avon, Omar, the cops, the lawyers, and Templeton all lie constantly. Parfit's rejoinder - that as long as some people sometimes tell the truth, deception stays possible - explains how Bubbles's lies keep working, while the heroin market shows Kant's mechanism at full scale: Stringer cutting product and rebranding 'pandemic' until 'every dope fiend in the city knows that Avon been putting out piss, calling it shit' and Westside dope collapses. Since Gant's and Greggs's costly truths still anchor the practice, the chapter concludes The Wire cannot quite refute Kant: it is not possible for nobody to walk the straight and narrow track.

categorical-imperative.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
categorical-imperative.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: John Wilkins treats Caesar, who spares the neighbor he has beaten, as a Kantian exemplar whose reason lets him adopt the Categorical Imperative, contrasting him with the rational egoism of the film's human keepers and executives. He argues the film trades on the outdated Great Chain of Being, which Darwinian tree thinking dissolves: with no higher or lower species, only branching homologies, human nature must be continuous with ape nature, and talk of innate species essences must allow for statistical variation and dispositions rather than determination. Caesar's morality also needs more than reason, namely the primate dispositions of deference and empathy scaffolded by his human family, though Buck's instant moral conversion after enhancement shows the film is ambivalent about whether scaffolding alone explains it.

categorical-imperative.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
categorical-imperative.title: Psych and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Stephenson tests Shawn's ruse against the major theories of justified deceit and finds it wanting: Plato's Myth of the Metals excuses paternalistic noble lies for social harmony that Shawn's self-aggrandizing motives cannot claim, utilitarianism collapses on the long-term costs of exposure (Gus, Juliet, Henry, and the SBPD condemned by association; clients betrayed; trust in law enforcement eroded), Kant's universalizability test sinks maxims like 'lie whenever a career opportunity is at stake,' and Popper's open society condemns just the deceit on which the psychic brand runs. Even the mutual-deceit analogy to poker and Sissela Bok's reasonable-person publicity test fail, since no public forum of reasonable people would bless duping paying private clients. The escape is extra-moral: Shawn's mischievous hokum is the socially necessary boundary-pusher, whose lesson against unreflective occult belief lands best when delivered with a laugh.

categorical-imperative.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
categorical-imperative.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.

categorical-imperative.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
categorical-imperative.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Lisa McNulty asks what could oblige us to believe someone: Peter's lying fails Kant's Categorical Imperative (a world of universal liars makes lying impossible), while friendship explains Alicia's readiness to believe client Kenny Chatham even before the evidence does. The 'Death Zone' libel trial over an Everest death shows that one's position of power fixes whom one owes presumptive belief - a reader should side with Cardiff, a judge must presume Lambrose innocent - and Pascal's Wager supplies the method of 'behaving like a believer': withholding rumors, withholding conviction, and Alicia publicly playing the wife and sleeping with Peter in a bid to believe in her marriage again. She concludes Peter forfeited any right to be believed, so Alicia has no moral obligation to behave like a good wife.

categorical-imperative.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
categorical-imperative.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Fallis sorts Atlantic City's lies to show which are wrong and why. Kant's and Augustine's absolute bans go too far and Grotius's life-saving exception does not apply - most of these lies get people killed - yet even altruistic lies (Margaret for Madame Jeunet and the ledger), lies told to those who want to be deceived, lies to liars, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that no one believes (Jimmy's flat movie alibi, Rothstein's 'skilled player' whopper) remain wrong: they take informed choice out of the victim's hands, violating the Kantian autonomy that grounds the wrong of lying, and they corrode the trust on which even criminals' co-operation depends.

categorical-imperative.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
categorical-imperative.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.

categorical-imperative.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
categorical-imperative.title: The Devil and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Danny Smith applies Kant's three grades of evil from Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone to The Dark Knight. Batman's saving Harvey over Rachel out of love is normal evil (pathological inclination trumping duty, his 'never kill' rule hardened into moral self-satisfaction), Two-Face's coin is radical evil (outsourcing his freedom and responsibility to chance), and the Joker - burning his own money, making his scarred face the true mask, wanting only chaos - is diabolical evil done for its own sake. Smith then presses Kant's embarrassing problem that evil pursued purely on principle, with no pathological motive, is indistinguishable from the highest good, and half-sympathetically re-reads the Joker as the honest rebel in a corrupt Gotham.

categorical-imperative.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
categorical-imperative.title: The Devil and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.

categorical-imperative.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
categorical-imperative.title: The Devil and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.

categorical-imperative.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
categorical-imperative.title: The Devil and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Robert Arp treats Voltaire's 'If God did not exist, then it would be necessary to invent Him' as a conditional claim and argues it is false: Kant's categorical imperative (universalize the action, as with lying and the collapsing practice of borrowing) and Mill's utilitarian cost-benefit calculus secure social order with no god and no Devil required. He then concedes that since most people are driven by guilt and fear rather than reason, inventing the Devil as an archetype of evil to be avoided at all costs may after all be a useful fiction.

categorical-imperative.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
categorical-imperative.title: Homeland and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Edwin Jacob contrasts the utilitarian calculus behind Walden's drone strike - Estes's eighty percent estimate, 'potential collateral damage falls within current matrix parameters', eighty-three children killed - with Kant's three formulations of the categorical imperative applied to that decision. On the universal-law formula Walden cannot will a world of strikes on one's own soil, on the humanity formula the schoolchildren are used merely as means, and the kingdom-of-ends formula condemns treating foreign lives as quantities in a matrix. The chapter adds that drones, like Brody's suicide vest, are asymmetric terror at a distance, and that blowback (Shahzad's Times Square attempt) shows the strategy fails even consequentialist test.

categorical-imperative.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
categorical-imperative.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Montoya tests Simon's choice to sacrifice his sanity by wearing the crown to save child Marceline against three ethical theories. Aquinas's doctrine of double effect clears him because the intended good (saving her life) outweighs the merely foreseen side effect (her tears, his possible future evils); Kant's categorical imperative rules out universalizing 'let children die to save myself,' since a world of universal using destroys the rule itself; and a fountain case where Finn must choose between world-saving plans and a drowning candy child separates act from rule utilitarianism, with rule utilitarianism preserving the duty to rescue. All three converge on the verdict that Simon, not Finn, is Ooo's greatest hero.

categorical-imperative.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
categorical-imperative.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter assembles real-life versions of Finn's Enchiridion, starting with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the Golden Mean locates each virtue between two vices, so true courage is knowing when to fight and when to run - cowardice and 'stupidteous' recklessness as deficiency and excess - a balance Finn's all-out bravery lacks. Epictetus's Stoic Handbook (which inspired the emperor Marcus Aurelius) teaches that happiness depends only on one's own reactions and that events are good or bad by how we take them, making it a manual even the chronically disappointed Ice King could use, while Christine de Pizan's book of chivalry prepares heroes for defeat and Erasmus's Handbook of the Christian Knight with Praise of Folly makes Finn and Jake's 'foolish' mercy look righteous. Finally Kant's Groundwork supplies duty for duty's sake: by the categorical imperative, Finn was entitled to steal the ogre's dollar only if, as an ogre who had swallowed Jake, he would accept the same theft from a hero.

categorical-imperative.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
categorical-imperative.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.

categorical-imperative.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
categorical-imperative.title: Dracula and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.

categorical-imperative.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
categorical-imperative.title: 15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception
categorical-imperative.relation: Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible. Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.

categorical-imperative.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
categorical-imperative.title: 20. The Doctor Lies
categorical-imperative.relation: McCain distinguishes lying (directly asserting what you believe false to make another believe it) from mere deception - the Sixth Doctor feeding Jamie false information for Sontaran Stike to overhear in 'The Two Doctors' deceives without lying - then asks whether the Doctor can lie to himself, answering that incarnations can lie to later selves (the Eleventh's suspicious 'I have absolutely no idea' about the children on Gallifrey in 'The Day of the Doctor') but a current self cannot. The stakes are moral: against Kant's and Augustine's absolute prohibition of lying, Plato's Republic and Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics defend noble lies, and Robert C. Solomon's view of self-deception as coping with the unbearable suggests that if the Doctor did engineer himself to forget the Time War genocide - as Ten and Wilf did to Donna in 'Journey's End' - it might be a good man's forgivable way of going on.

categorical-imperative.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
categorical-imperative.title: 24. Who’s Duty to Whom
categorical-imperative.relation: Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'

categorical-imperative.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
categorical-imperative.title: 15. Tell the Truth at All Costs
categorical-imperative.relation: Bowman argues Candor is the most philosophically important faction because its absolute honesty is Kant's ethics: truthfulness as a perfect duty grounded in free will, making even politeness 'deception in pretty packaging,' and forbidding a lie even when the Erudite come to Merciless Mart hunting Tris - which mirrors Kant's reply to Benjamin Constant that one must not lie even to the murderer at the door.
