Against this he sets Aristotle's virtue ethics, where truth bows to wisdom, justice, and fortitude when the choice is handing hidden Jews to the SS, and Bentham's utilitarianism, which Amity enacts when it lies at the gates to keep the peace and save lives. The Candor Manifesto's 'web of individual-to-individual relationships' and Kant's kingdom of ends explain why universal honesty alone could make truth safe - and why Christina, the Candor, is the one left standing when the city's deception finally destroys it.

categorical-imperative.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
categorical-imperative.title: 1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey
categorical-imperative.relation: Blessing tests the Steve Jobs/Oprah 'do what you love' creed against Downton, where rigid class structure assigns nearly everyone a role they did not choose. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness (Matthew's war wounds, Mary's grief after his death) and purposefulness (Grantham's custodian speech), then weighs subjectivist theories of meaning, including Nietzsche's idea that meaning arises from the passionate process itself, against Nozick's permanence view and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness,' adding Kant's duty to develop one's talents against a world of idle pleasure. She concludes that the Abbey's ethos - Grantham as custodian not owner, Carson's pride in service, Patmore's kitchen, 'I have no right to be unhappy' - shows that socially necessary work one does not love can still make a meaningful life, while DWYL is elitist and narcissistic.

categorical-imperative.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
categorical-imperative.title: 8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word
categorical-imperative.relation: Neal pits Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Violet's scheme after Sybil's death: the Dowager pressures Dr. Clarkson to 'review the evidence' until he tells Cora and Robert that surgery could not have saved their daughter, reuniting the marriage his honest second opinion had broken. Working through the Categorical Imperative, the murderer-at-the-door case, and Kant's essay 'On a Supposed Right to Lie Because of Philanthropic Concerns,' the chapter asks whether Clarkson actually lied ('Lie is so unmusical a word'). It concludes that his rational, carefully planned, dignity-respecting lie to save the family meets the criteria for a Kantian exception, so the rule against lying still holds while this particular lie is morally permitted.

categorical-imperative.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
categorical-imperative.title: 17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence
categorical-imperative.relation: Christopher Ketcham asks whether primogeniture and entail make Downton Abbey a social embodiment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence - the same estate, without revision, turned over generation after generation like the eternal hourglass of existence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he tests royal continuity against death duties, the nihilism of industrial capitalism, and the Great War that killed heirs and empires, and borrows Kant's categorical imperative as an analogy for Britain's uniquely preserved 'royal categorical imperative' of continuity. The Abbey's recurrence survives only anthropomorphically - Violet, the family, the servants, and the tenants as its living organs - and the chapter wonders whether such ossified continuity, like dinosaur bones, is really eternal.

categorical-imperative.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
categorical-imperative.title: Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right
categorical-imperative.relation: Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.

categorical-imperative.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
categorical-imperative.title: 1. True Love and False Fronts
categorical-imperative.relation: Fallis argues the movie is really about lying and duplicity, not true love: Humperdinck frames Guilder for Buttercup's abduction, the Dread Pirate Roberts is a serial persona, and even the heroes bluff their way into the castle. He treats this as 'adversarial epistemology,' showing that Descartes's malicious demon and Kant's argument that universalized lying is impossible only rule out extreme scenarios and cannot unmask mundane deceivers like Vizzini and Humperdinck (a point he sharpens with Parfit's objection that liars sometimes profitably tell the truth). What does real work are Hume's tools for evaluating testimony: Valerie catches Miracle Max lying about 'to blave' by asking what he has to gain, and Buttercup catches Humperdinck when his claim that every ship in the armada will accompany the honeymoon contradicts his promise of the four fastest ships.

categorical-imperative.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
categorical-imperative.title: 13. Time to Choose
categorical-imperative.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.

categorical-imperative.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
categorical-imperative.title: 9. Variation under Ethics
categorical-imperative.relation: Weighs the clones' bodily autonomy against the special obligations they owe one another, since genetic sisters can harm each other as no strangers can: Helena's murder of Katja nearly pins a killing on Sarah, and Vic's drug-world drags danger into Alison's suburb. The chapter builds a clone-specific cousin of Kant's categorical imperative — "act only and always in a way that you would want your clone to act" — to argue that the clones' liberty may be legitimately more restricted than ours: Alison's public drunkenness endangers sisters who can be mistaken for her, clones arguably must stay in Clone Club and share medical information like Cosima's illness, and hard cases (Beth's suicide leaving cases dangling, the brain-cut-open Castor clone begging Helena to kill him) all turn on balancing autonomy against what we owe others.

categorical-imperative.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
categorical-imperative.title: 30. Trying to Do Good with Arya, Tyrion, and the Hound
categorical-imperative.relation: Thomas sets Aristotle's practical wisdom against Bentham's utility calculus and Kant's consequence-proof rules, then watches all three struggle in season six. Arya's merciful refusal to poison Lady Crane backfires when the Waif kills her more painfully anyway; Tyrion's compromise with the Masters - phasing out slavery gradually, 'I trust their self-interest' - nearly loses Meereen when they attack by sea; and the resurrected Hound, after Brother Ray's massacre, concludes that 'lots of horrible shit in this world gets done for something larger than ourselves,' so being good in Westeros, as everywhere, means choosing without being able to know the consequences in advance.

categorical-imperative.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
categorical-imperative.title: 12. Aaugh! Why Is Being Moral So Hard
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter claims Schulz's humor is built on moral failure and illustrates the three main moral theories with specific strips: utilitarianism via Bentham's 'sovereign masters' of pain and pleasure and Charlie's 'to make others happy' (with Lucy noting nobody is making her happy), Kantian deontology via Sally's crayon lie and Snoopy's 'I haven't bitten anyone on the leg recently' as fulfilling a negative duty, and Aristotle's virtue ethics via the failed steal of home (foolhardy rather than courageous), the unmailed Valentine (cowardly), the golden mean, and Joe Shlabotnik as a hopeless role model. Charlie gritting his teeth shows mistaking a virtue's external markers for the virtue itself. It concludes we fit none of the theories well, yet Peanuts keeps a spirit of hope - happiness is a warm puppy, and Charlie's grit is genuine even if he cannot see it.

categorical-imperative.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
categorical-imperative.title: 14. Is Lucy a Kantian or Just Mean and Nasty
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter tries to acquit Lucy of meanness by reading her as a Kantian: her maxim for throwing Schroeder's piano into the Kite-Eating Tree fails universalization as a contradiction in conception, her blanket confiscations and 'settling for average' lectures enforce Kant's duty of self-improvement, and her brutal truth-telling honors the absolute ban on lying (a Mill-and-Bentham contrast highlights that Kant locates moral worth in intentions, not comfort or consequences). The football gag then undermines the defense: by withholding what Charlie needs to know - that she will pull the ball - she treats him as a mere means, and since what matters is her real intentions rather than her stated ones, the Kantian verdict is left to the reader.

categorical-imperative.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
categorical-imperative.title: 7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . .
categorical-imperative.relation: Ranks Jessica Lange's characters from least to most despicable using moral philosophy: Sister Jude earns credit for acting from duty (reporting the Nazi Dr. Arden at personal risk, Kant-style) and for genuinely feeling remorse; Elsa Mars partly honors the matriarchal obligations of care ethics but lacks Aristotle's habitual virtue and moderation, selling Bette and Dot to Dandy for fame; Constance Langdon abuses and effectively murders her disabled children; and Fiona Goode, motivated exclusively by youth, beauty, and power, murders her Supreme and torments Cordelia - never once acting out of concern for others.

categorical-imperative.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
categorical-imperative.title: 11. Fighting Ethical Relativism in Tales of Suspense
categorical-imperative.relation: Reading Tales of Suspense, Pagnoni Berns and Veteri cast Iron Man as a man of every era - echoing LBJ's 'reason together', Cold War utilitarianism against Communism, playboy masculinity, and finally the Registration Act - which makes him a parrot of whatever relativism his age prefers. Captain America, literally frozen in time, holds Kant's categorical imperative: every life is an end in itself, so he saves Nazi prisoners in #71, trades his own life for a pilot in #61, and drinks possibly lethal serum without needing thanks, while Bucky's mediated, reward-seeking morality shows why ends corrupt moral worth. Because Cap's universal, ahistorical defense of human dignity holds from the 1940s to the 1960s and beyond, the authors rank him above the adaptable but context-bound Iron Man.

categorical-imperative.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
categorical-imperative.title: 15. Iron Kant or Captain Kant
categorical-imperative.relation: Bosma and Barkman run both heroes' positions on the Superhuman Registration Act and the Sokovia Accords through Kant's deontology. Iron Man's maxim 'I should obey the government' looks universalizable, but it collapses once Cap's critique of the atomic bombings shows an unjust order (killing innocent civilians, or a Doctor Doom takeover) must be refused, and the humanity formulation condemns registration for treating heroes as mere means to the government's ends. Cap's own maxims - fight for freedom and justice, obey only a just government - universalize cleanly, so the chapter awards the deontological duel to Captain America.

categorical-imperative.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
categorical-imperative.title: 5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds
categorical-imperative.relation: Argues that Albert Rosenfield embodies Kant's categorical imperative: his refusal to soften his autopsy demands or lie to spare feelings is fidelity to universalizable maxims, and his insistence that Sheriff Truman be charged for punching him treats punishment as respect for a rational agent's autonomy. The chapter walks through maxims, the universalizability test applied to Gordon Cole's possibly faked deafness and FBI lying, hypothetical versus categorical imperatives (Cooper may always want Norma's cherry pie, but morality trumps want), and the formula of humanity — Ben Horne's use of One-Eyed Jack's women as mere means is the counterexample, while Albert's insults paradoxically honor Truman's rational agency. Albert's arc to "I love you, Sheriff Truman" and his gentler Season Two and The Return self shows a Kantian who integrates classical reason with romantic feeling.

categorical-imperative.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
categorical-imperative.title: 16. Who Am I to You
categorical-imperative.relation: James Okapal sets up the Kantian view — moral agency, shown by passing the contradiction-in-conception test (which Wallace's 'all should be masters of slaves' fails), is the precondition of moral status, so non-agents like replicants, on Tibor Machan's extension of Kant to animals, matter no more than toasters — against the ethics of care of Nel Noddings and Carol Gilligan. On the care reading, K's and Batty's final acts of ethical caring, like Joi's risky choices for K, confer moral status on another and thereby constitute moral agency, reversing the Kantian order. Empathy, not universalizable reason, is what removes bricks from Joshi's wall.

categorical-imperative.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
categorical-imperative.title: 9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place
categorical-imperative.relation: Sheldon argues the Season One twist makes the show itself a moral paradox: a series about ethics that lies to its audience for thirteen episodes, breaking the informal contract it built through 'truth in fiction'. Through Chidi's red-cowboy-boots lie and Eleanor's plot to murder Janet, 'The Eternal Shriek' stages Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means reasoning, with confession portrayed as the only release from escalating deception. The chapter ends with Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism to get Chidi to lie his way through the Bad Place, leaving viewers to decide whether the show's own deception is justified by the ethical conversation it forces.

categorical-imperative.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
categorical-imperative.title: 10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis
categorical-imperative.relation: Altmann allegorizes Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis, whose 'love story' shows each completing the other: Chidi's lessons in utilitarianism and Kant's Categorical Imperative give Eleanor reasons, and eventually a lived example in Michael's feigned self-sacrifice, to confess her lie, while Eleanor's pragmatism in the Bad Place teaches Chidi that principles useless in the world must be revised. Michael's arc from designing psychological torture to giving Eleanor his portal pin demonstrates a theory of human nature, that people cannot change, being falsified by praxis. The chapter closes with Eleanor re-entering the cycle by finding Chidi's lectures online, recommending the union of theory and praxis as how anyone becomes a better person.

categorical-imperative.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
categorical-imperative.title: 11. Those Agonizing Choices
categorical-imperative.relation: Romanowski traces Chidi's indecision from the cowboy-boots lie through the rock-paper-scissors panic attack, arguing the show treats the agony of deciding as the universal human moral condition rather than a professor joke. 'The Trolley Problem' makes Foot's dilemma literal torture, and the show pointedly never gives the right answer, confirming Chidi's claim that there are no clean solutions to hard moral questions. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired particularism pitch in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' and Michael's 'I solved the Trolley Problem: you sacrifice yourself' moment, together with Chidi finally kissing Eleanor, show that acknowledging uncertainty is no excuse for inaction.

categorical-imperative.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
categorical-imperative.title: 14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors
categorical-imperative.relation: Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man. Tahani's sixty billion dollars in charity earning no points, and Eleanor's fruitless 'What's My Motivation' blitz versus her costly confession, vindicate Kant's claim that only a good will gives actions moral worth, while Aristotle supplies the closing lesson that being good takes practice, not just study.

categorical-imperative.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
categorical-imperative.title: 20. Moral Health Warning
categorical-imperative.relation: The moral philosopher Jonathan Dancy issues a warning against the show's premise that studying moral philosophy can make you a better person, the assumption behind Chidi's entire tutelage of Eleanor. What makes someone good is their motivation, and reading Kant and Scanlon is at best self-indulgent study that never redirects the will toward the right; indeed anyone genuinely motivated by the good would stop reading moral philosophy and go do good instead. He also contests the Kantian thought that only action done from a sense of duty earns moral credit: Douglas Wynegar's roses for his grandmother, given out of love, should count without any thought of obligation.

categorical-imperative.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
categorical-imperative.title: 2. A Paragon of Righteous Virtue
categorical-imperative.relation: Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.

categorical-imperative.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
categorical-imperative.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Reads Bluth contradiction through Kant's categorical imperative: Lindsay's lie about her shopgirl job, Gob's jealousy bred by comparative parenting, and George Michael's conformist drift show both the imperative's force and the danger of its empty formalism, while the 'Afternoon Delight' double entendres test whether good intentions suffice for Kantian worth. Nietzsche then answers that morality itself is the contradiction: virtue manufactured from ressentiment ('weakness is being lied into something meritorious'), the will to power turned inward as nihilism, with self-overcoming and value creation as the exit; Mary Douglas's joke theory closes the chapter by explaining why all this contradiction is comic and why the joke is on Gob.

categorical-imperative.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
categorical-imperative.title: What if Hama Was Wrong
categorical-imperative.relation: Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily uses persons as mere means because it overrides the victim's will regardless of their actual consent, unlike buying tea from Zuko but like Azula's deception of Long Feng, and so violates Kant's Formula of Humanity in every offensive use. Katara's bloodbending of Hama in self-defense is permissible because she stops Hama's wrong rather than using her toward any end, and even a hypothetical consensual 'cooperative model' cannot redeem the practice, since the sheer power it grants and its corrupting effects on practitioners (Noatak and Tarrlok in LoK) justify Katara's ban.

categorical-imperative.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
categorical-imperative.title: Sometimes Heroes Fail
categorical-imperative.relation: James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'

categorical-imperative.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
categorical-imperative.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.

categorical-imperative.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
categorical-imperative.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Jollimore and Jones diagnose three 'very unDude' vices: Walter's rule rigidity, which confuses Kant's hypothetical rules of games (don't cross the foul line) with categorical moral ones and needs 'rules all the way down' to ward off nihilism; the Big Lebowski's hypocritical inauthenticity, a fake achiever living on his daughter's allowance who collapses facedown before his own rug; and the exclusionism with which everyone shuts Donny out of the conversation. Against these the Dude exhibits Aristotelian virtue as good judgment (knowing when rules don't apply), the Golden Mean between Walter and the nihilists, and Singer-style inclusion — 'he's in bed with everybody' — making him an authentic man of humor and perspective.

categorical-imperative.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
categorical-imperative.title: Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror
categorical-imperative.relation: Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.

categorical-imperative.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
categorical-imperative.title: “Don’t forget, she’s a dangerous individual”
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter tests the White Bear Justice Park's daily torture of Victoria Skillane against every major theory of punishment: Kant and Hegel's retributivism makes her deserve punishment (her crime could not be universalized and annulled justice) but cannot justify a punishment disproportionate to the crime. Locke's memory criterion suggests Punished Victoria is not the person who did the crime, though Parfit's psychological continuity and Thomson's bodily continuity restore the identity. Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism partially vindicates the park as deterrence and incapacitation, but cannot explain the laughing crowds — which Machiavelli's civic spectacle and Nietzsche's genealogy of punishment (Schadenfreude as moralized creditor-debtor pleasure) explain: the crowd is gleefully reenacting Victoria's own crime and calling it justice.

categorical-imperative.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
categorical-imperative.title: Learning from Mia’s Mistakes
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.

categorical-imperative.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
categorical-imperative.title: 20 The Value of Vibranium
categorical-imperative.relation: Edwardo Pérez asks what makes vibranium 'the most valuable metal known to man' through Marx's distinction between use value and exchange value: Klaue prizes exchange value (money, power, a black-market arm), while Wakandans structure their whole society around use value and never trade the metal. The museum scene raises cultural property - does vibranium belong to Wakanda, as the cultural nationalist holds, or to humanity, as the cultural internationalist holds? - and T'Challa's shift on sharing it is analyzed through Kant's categorical imperative versus Bentham's utilitarian calculus, with his saving of Agent Ross and sparing of M'Baku vindicated by their consequences. Vibranium's greatest value, the chapter concludes, is atonement: redeeming T'Chaka's crime and uniting humanity as 'one single tribe.'

categorical-imperative.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
categorical-imperative.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Mark D. White shifts the is-it-still-Sabbath question from metaphysics to ethics, asking whether bands owe fans a stable line-up when they keep the name. Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits the maxim "change members, keep the name" without contradiction, and the Formula of Respect forbids only coercion or deceit, using fans as mere means, so the real wrong is deceptive marketing, as when record-company pressure billed Iommi's solo project Seventh Star as "Black Sabbath featuring Tony Iommi" and sent it out playing "War Pigs" and "Iron Man". The Dio reunion's honest rebranding as Heaven & Hell passes the test, while fans, symmetrically, owe bands no loyalty and may legitimately love only one era.

categorical-imperative.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
categorical-imperative.title: “It's Been Handed Down from Goof to Goof to Goof, and Now, It's Yours, Son”
categorical-imperative.relation: Mentyka uses Goofy to test theories of the good life: Socratic intellectualism stumbles on uneducated-but-good Goofy, Kant's categorical imperative absurdly forbids handing Max the 'goof to goof' fishing pole (Goofy can't will it universal law), Mill's utilitarianism fails when Max's lukewarm reception makes the gift happiness-reducing, and Singer's extension to animals muddies Pluto the dog against Goofy the dog treated as a person. The chapter resolves with Scheler's claim that we first encounter values through moral exemplars — earnest, bumbling Goofy — not through rules or consequences, and a closing plea that philosophers narrate less like the smug 'How to...' narrator.

categorical-imperative.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
categorical-imperative.title: 1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey
categorical-imperative.relation: Blessing pits Steve Jobs's 'Do What You Love' creed (and Oprah's 'follow your bliss') against Downton's world of inherited roles, where nobody from Anna to Lady Mary chooses their work. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness, since Matthew's war wounds and Mary's grief over his death are painful yet deeply meaningful, and tests subjectivist theories such as Nietzsche's meaning-as-passionate-process against Nozick's demand that a meaningful life leave permanent traces and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'loving objects that are worthy of love.' Kant's duty to develop one's talents rather than idle for pleasure, and Lord Grantham's self-description as 'a custodian, not an owner,' anchor the show's counter-ethos of duty over desire, embodied in Carson, Mrs. Hughes, and Mrs. Patmore's pride in unloved, socially necessary work. The chapter concludes that Downton validates hard honest work as an end in itself, challenging the narcissism of the 'holy You' and expressive individualism.

categorical-imperative.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
categorical-imperative.title: 8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word
categorical-imperative.relation: Neal weighs Dr. Clarkson's coached retraction, that surgery would not have saved Sybil after all, engineered by Violet with 'Lie is so unmusical a word' to end Cora's blame of Robert and reunite the grieving couple, against Kant's absolute prohibition on lying in his moral works and in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie.' She lays out Kant's reasoning that lying destroys the trust, dignity, and rights that make rules binding, with the murderer-at-the-door case as the classic objection, then argues Clarkson's lie approaches an exception because it is rational, carefully deliberated, and aimed at preserving the Crawleys' dignity and the household itself rather than personal gain. The chapter concludes that the Kantian rule still holds generally, but this particular lie, for this particular moral reason, can be excused.

categorical-imperative.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
categorical-imperative.title: The (Single) Garden Path
categorical-imperative.relation: Argues Herbert populates Dune with three long-running eugenics programs, each with a different ethical stance: the Bene Gesserit's Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (whose communal guardian-breeding deliberately recalls Socrates' Kallipolis in the Republic), Leto II's Golden Path, and the Bene Tleilax's axolotl-tank genetic design for immortality. It reads the chastened Sisterhood of the later novels as moving from consequentialist to Kantian, deontological ground ('never seek to create a human being in any one image'), frames Leto II as the ultimate utilitarian whose species-saving end allegedly justifies Machiavellian means (with Siona's objection that he had no right), and shows the Tleilaxu destroyed by their own monomaniacal religious code. Conclusion: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics.'

categorical-imperative.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
categorical-imperative.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Cogburn attacks Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments to five: it deletes archetypes that fantasy literature needs, since Karsa Orlong (who wills the destruction of all civilization without sadism) and Jacqueline Carey's Haomane Firstborn (who loves cold mathematical order while his laws lead to genocide) fit nowhere in the new scheme. He rebuilds alignment by taking it to describe what a character wills in Kant's sense, mapping the law-chaos axis onto the categorical imperative (the liar and murderer must take themselves to be exceptions to universal laws) and the good-evil axis onto Mill's greatest happiness principle, which yields a Lawful Good of Gandhi and King, a Neutral Good modeled on Jesus breaking Sabbath law out of love, and Lawful Evil exemplified by vampire hierarchies and politicians whose policies create hell abroad. Joe Abercrombie's torturer San Dan Glotka becomes the archetypal Neutral Neutral, 'banality of evil' in Arendt's sense, and the chapter concludes Chaotic Good is empty because willing the destruction of universalizability cannot consistently will less pain.

categorical-imperative.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Eric Silverman asks whether the Amazon series' Lucy and Maximus should have children, framing the wasteland through Hobbes's state of nature where life is 'nasty, brutish, and short' and even vaults are limiting experiments. He lays out Benatar's Harm Argument (pain outweighs pleasure, so procreation is procreational Russian roulette) and Shiffrin's Consent Argument (no one consents to being born, as Sartre's 'I did not ask to be born' concedes), then rebuts them: Socrates, the Stoics, and Aristotle make virtue and meaning rather than pleasure the goal of life, so a harsh wasteland full of people needing help suits a virtuous, sacrificial life like the hero's exile at the end of the original Fallout. Parental proxy consent legitimizes procreation as it does children's medical decisions, and Kant's universalization test defeats the demand for pre-natal consent, since universalizing it would eliminate the very rational beings whose consent it protects - so Lucy's 'Okey dokey!' optimism wins.

categorical-imperative.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter maps four schools of ethics onto Fallout 4's Commonwealth: Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Preston Garvey's settlement defense as the mean between recklessness and cowardice and temperance as moderate chem use; Kant's Categorical Imperative is tested on stealing ammo in Concord and on the Battle of Bunker Hill choice to warn the Railroad, where loyal silence to Father fails universalization and treats synths merely as means. Aquinas's natural law ethics, keyed to the telos of power armor, workbenches, and Pip-Boys, condemns the Institute's creation of synths by analogy to the IVF debate while still demanding dignity for synths who already exist. Finally, Bentham's utilitarianism is the one framework under which Father's Institute — adaptive labor force, scientific progress, stability and order — can sincerely believe itself morally justified.

categorical-imperative.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Weighing Vault-Tec's secret experiments — Vault 11's yearly human sacrifice, Vault 13's 200-year lockdown, the cryogenic freezing of the Sole Survivor — the chapter asks whether the ends could ever justify the vaults. On Kant's Universal Law and Humanity Formulations the answer is flatly no: dwellers were deceived into becoming mere means to data, whatever the hypothetical space-colonization motive that designer Tim Cain favors. Act and rule utilitarianism in Bentham's tradition give a more equivocal verdict — exposed deception would doom any future cooperation, yet safeguarding humanity might in extraordinary circumstances tip the calculus — and the chapter situates the games in real research-ethics history from the eugenics era to the Tuskegee study and the Belmont Report.

categorical-imperative.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
categorical-imperative.title: He Thinks He's People: How Brian Made Personhood for the Dogs
categorical-imperative.relation: Argues that Brian the dog is a person because personhood, on a Kantian reading, requires a rational nature rather than species membership: Peter making Brian beg in 'Brian: Portrait of a Dog,' the councilman's 'Why are we listening to a dog?', and Chris's 'You don't have a soul!' in 'North by North Quahog' all wrongly treat humanity (or a soul) as the criterion, while Descartes' mechanical account of animal bodies is invoked to show the soul cannot be empirically tested. The chapter then applies the humanity-formulation of the categorical imperative both ways: Stewie framing the maid in 'Road to Rhode Island' shows treating persons as mere means, while Brian's Christmas-sweater lie to Lois shows how Kantian duty is stricter than the Golden Rule. Finally it grades Brian's own conduct as family conscience and drunk (his lapses like framing Jake Tucker, his condescension to Peter, his disrespected self in 'The Thin White Line'), concluding Brian owes the same duties he is owed.

categorical-imperative.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
categorical-imperative.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Tyrion - born a reviled dwarf who killed his mother, yet heir to Lannister wealth, wits, and Jaime's knightly example - frames Nagel's paradox of moral luck: his compassion toward Jon Snow and Sansa is constitutive luck, and his carefully run wildfire defense of King's Landing shows resultant luck, since the same prudent act deserves praise in one outcome and blame had it burned the city. Kant's good will, applied to Tyrion's protection of Shae as treating her as an end and never merely as a means against Cersei, is offered as a rescue but only neutralizes resultant luck, leaving constitutive and circumstantial luck untouched. The chapter ends with Nagel's shrinking 'extensionless point' of genuine agency, concluding we cannot keep both moral responsibility and the principle that we are blamed only for what we control.

categorical-imperative.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
categorical-imperative.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.

categorical-imperative.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
categorical-imperative.title: 9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place
categorical-imperative.relation: Asks whether a show about ethics may lie to its audience for a whole season: the Season One twist breaks the viewer's implicit contract even though the show keeps its internal 'truth in fiction'. Through 'The Eternal Shriek' it stages the debate — Chidi's Kantian ban on lying (the red cowboy boots saga with Henry, ending in a confession that defeats Henry) against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means plot to 'kill' Janet — and reads the show's cascade of confessions as its answer that truth-telling absolves. Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' lets Chidi lie his way through Hell, leaving viewers to decide whether the twist's ethical education justifies the deception.

categorical-imperative.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
categorical-imperative.title: 10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis
categorical-imperative.relation: Casts Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis in an allegorical love story: Chidi's Kantian universalizability about lying and his utilitarian lesson (confess, because the neighborhood's welfare outweighs you) only move Eleanor when she sees Theory enacted — Michael's willingness to absorb eternal torture in her place convinces her the theory 'has legs'. Praxis repays the debt when Eleanor's moral particularism pushes Chidi to lie to demons and play his part in the Bad Place party, and Michael's conversion from torturer to someone who sacrifices his portal pin for Eleanor ('Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent') completes the union. The moral: theory is born in the world, but only practice lets it thrive there.

categorical-imperative.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
categorical-imperative.title: 11. Those Agonizing Choices
categorical-imperative.relation: Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.

categorical-imperative.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
categorical-imperative.title: 14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors
categorical-imperative.relation: Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.

categorical-imperative.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
categorical-imperative.title: 20. Moral Health Warning
categorical-imperative.relation: A health warning from Jonathan Dancy himself: the show's premise that Chidi's lessons in Kant, Scanlon, and the Trolley Problem can make Eleanor better is false, because becoming good requires a change in motivation and intellectual study shapes motivation at most indirectly — and might attach to the wrong as easily as the right, since moral philosophy studies both. Worse, studying ethics looks like self-indulgence, time spent on Kant that could have gone to doing actual good. Against the Kantian thought that only acting from a sense of duty earns moral credit, Dancy argues that sympathetic love — Doug Wynegar bringing his grandmother roses simply for her sake — is enough, which undermines both Kant and Chidi's entire teaching project.

categorical-imperative.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
categorical-imperative.title: NOTES
categorical-imperative.relation: First defines lying — distinguishing it from mere error (Angela believing Peter dead), from the Haitian's non-verbal memory-wipe deception, and from Hiro's silent staging of Ando's fake death — then tests moral theories against the show's liars. Kant's categorical imperative bans all lying but is abandoned when Sylar demands a friend's hiding place; utilitarianism vindicates Victoria Pratt's lie about the virus vial yet also licenses Linderman's .07% explosion and Plato's noble lie of the earthborn metals, which the chapter rejects. Machiavelli's advice that princes may lie to keep power is played out by 'President Sylar' in 'Five Years Gone,' and the chapter finally endorses Sissela Bok's presumption against lying — a public-reasoning procedure modeled by Bob Bishop and Mohinder before Monica's virus injection.

categorical-imperative.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
categorical-imperative.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.

categorical-imperative.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
categorical-imperative.title: Invisibility or Honesty
categorical-imperative.relation: Schulzke argues inception is a categorical violation of Kantian autonomy: the Fischer job treats him merely as a means (Saito's market share, Cobb's reunion with his children), and even Cobb's benevolent inception on Mal disrespects humanity by robbing her of self-determination, leaving her unable to act as a responsible moral agent testable against the categorical imperative. Extraction, by contrast, attacks privacy rather than autonomy, and the chapter uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges to show that dream espionage would defeat even perfect invisibility, since an extractor could always read your deeds in your dreams. The twist, played off Kant's absolute condemnation of lying, is that the standing threat of extraction might be the only force that could make universal honesty practicable — hence the title's choice between invisibility and honesty, illustrated by Ariadne's life-saving extraction on Cobb.

categorical-imperative.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
categorical-imperative.title: 4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative
categorical-imperative.relation: Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.

categorical-imperative.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
categorical-imperative.title: Can You Find Your Moral Compass
categorical-imperative.relation: Donovan and Richardson test Tony's moral compass in 'Armor Wars' and 'Extremis' against the three major schools. Utilitarianism fails because Tony will not sacrifice even one innocent for the greater good — he changes tactics to save a single pilot from the Raiders and rages when the Controller's human zombie dies — and Kantian deontology fails because Tony bends rules ('lives to mean more than rules') and is driven by emotion rather than pure reason. Aristotle fits: Tony is obsessed not just with doing good but with being good, snarling at his own reflection, asking filmmaker Pillinger 'Have you changed anything? Me neither,' until Extremis lets him 'be the Iron Man inside and out,' uniting agent and deed as Aristotelian character requires.

categorical-imperative.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Robson argues that The Man Upstairs' real moral flaw is neither stinginess toward Finn nor mere instruction-following, both of which he defends, but 'rule worship': treating LEGO construction instructions — rules with at best conventional status like chess or etiquette rules — as sacrosanct commandments to be followed for their own sake. The contrast is with Kant, who does claim absolute status for central moral rules such as the prohibition on lying, and with the moral/conventional distinction from psychologists like Kelly and Stich that The Man cannot grasp. Emmet's rule-following differs because it serves goals like fitting in, and the flaw scales from office Micromanagers and Velma Staplebot to Inspector Javert and the mafioso, showing how misdirected rule worship becomes genuinely vicious.

categorical-imperative.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
categorical-imperative.title: The Question of Ethical Advertising
categorical-imperative.relation: Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect. Kant's humanity formula and the lying-promise example show that manipulation wrongs the consumer as a rational agent, and Don's defense that advertising sells 'happiness' fails because Kant allows making others' happiness an end but never at the cost of truth, whether the consumer is a stranger or a wife. The chapter sets this against the era's brainwashing anxieties (Hunter's Brainwashing in Red China, Packard's The Hidden Persuaders, Precon subliminal projection) and concludes that honest advertising must survive disclosure of its methods, noting that real sponsors like Canada Dry and BMW responded to the show with stripped-down 'transparent' ads that let viewers be 'in on it.'

categorical-imperative.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
categorical-imperative.title: Metallica Drops a Load: What Do Bands and Fans Owe Each Other?
categorical-imperative.relation: Mark White asks whether Metallica wronged its longtime fans by changing style on Load, using Kant's duty ethics. No duty to keep their thrash style survives the categorical imperative - a world where every band changes style is horrible but not contradictory - and Kantian duties to the band members' families, employees, and to their own talents and authenticity actually support the change. Symmetrically, fans' loyalty is only an imperfect duty with wiggle room: it is owed in return for the band's loyalty to its metal values, and lapses when the motivation is mere commercial sell-out.

categorical-imperative.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
categorical-imperative.title: The Unsocial Sociability of Humans and Metal Gods
categorical-imperative.relation: Niall Scott applies Kant's 'unsocial sociability' - the human oscillation between solitude and society - to Metallica: the ego-clashes of Some Kind of Monster and the Hetfield-Mustaine rivalry ('Better Than You') instantiate Kant's vices of culture, yet produce the music as the reconciliation of the struggle. Using 'The Struggle Within' and 'Hero of the Day', he runs the categorical imperative on refusing help (the maxim cannot be universalized) to ground Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence, and answers Schiller's 'duty with hatred' objection - the 'My Friend of Misery' syndrome - by noting Kant allows feelings to support duty.

categorical-imperative.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
categorical-imperative.title: The Office and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.

categorical-imperative.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
categorical-imperative.title: The Office and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.

categorical-imperative.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
categorical-imperative.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.

categorical-imperative.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
categorical-imperative.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.

categorical-imperative.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Barcenas and Bein pit Kant against Confucius on the Prime Directive, opening with Kirk's Nibiru volcano rescue of Spock in Into Darkness. Kant's categorical imperative—universalization and respect tests applied to Scotty's dilemma in 'Bread and Circuses' and Worf's 'not a matter of degree'—makes the Directive absolute, while Confucius and Aristotle ground morality in cultivated character: a junzi like Picard may bend the rule when virtue demands it, as in 'Pen Pals' and rescuing Wesley from the Edo in 'Justice'. They conclude Starfleet needs both: the Kantian rule for most officers, and exemplary persons like Picard to know when the rule fails.

categorical-imperative.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Nina Rosenstand reads 'The Measure of a Man' as a Kantian defense of Data's personhood: Maddox's sentience criteria concede intelligence and self-awareness, and Picard—prompted by Guinan's warning that a ruling for Maddox means an army of android slaves—shows a rational being must be treated as an end in himself, never dismantled merely for Starfleet's benefit. Bentham's utilitarianism supplies the contrast (an army of Datas would maximize happiness), while the episode's title ironizes Protagoras's 'man is the measure of all things', since the measure here is rationality rather than humanity. Louvois's open verdict becomes precedent for Lal, the exocomps, and Voyager's Doctor, and a metaphor for real struggles for recognition.

categorical-imperative.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Tests moral relativism against absolutism through Enterprise's "Cogenitor": Trip's liberation of the Vissian third-sex being - secretly scanning its brain, naming it Charles, teaching it to read - ends in its suicide, and the chapter asks whether Trip's judgments track rational moral truth or are Humean after-the-fact rationalizations of disgust, since on Hume's view reason is the slave of the passions and is/ought are separate. Kant's categorical imperative (the cogenitor used merely as a means of reproduction) and Aquinas's natural law are offered as absolutist resources on Trip's side, while Phlox voices a Benedict-style "morally good is just habitual" relativism and Archer concludes "we didn't come out here to play God", prefiguring the Prime Directive. The chapter lands on Mary Midgley's rejection of moral isolationism via her tsujigiri example and Quark's "we're better than you" speech to Sisko: cross-cultural judgment is possible, but only after understanding, and not on the first day of first contact.

categorical-imperative.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Michaud puts Jar Jar Binks on trial for proposing the emergency powers that let Palpatine become Emperor and doom the galaxy. He weighs Nagel's resultant moral luck through a two-Lukes landspeeder case, Susan Wolf's virtue-based reply that equal fault can deserve different feelings, Kant's 'ought implies can' and the categorical imperative, and a Frankfurt-style scenario in which Palpatine's hypothetical mind-trick removes Jar Jar's ability to choose otherwise. The verdict: as a deceived, politically limited character trying to do good, Jar Jar is not guilty of the Empire's crimes - only of being obnoxious.

categorical-imperative.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
categorical-imperative.title: Beyond the Whimsy
categorical-imperative.relation: Jowitt argues that L3-37's activism in Solo ('Droid rights! We are sentient!') exposes a real problem in philosophy of law: the Coronet Spaceport's 'all droids must be registered' treats sentients as property, and Austin's legal positivism (law as command backed by sanction, which he says also describes Enfys Nest's threats) cannot condemn this. Building a Kantian natural-law argument, he claims that if droids like L3, C-3PO, BB-8, and D-O are rational beings covered by the categorical imperative, then any rule classifying them as property cannot give us a reason to obey it and so is not valid law at all. Lando's grief over dying L3 and our sadness at C-3PO's memory wipe in The Rise of Skywalker show we already treat droids as moral persons, so Beyleveld's precautionary principle says they deserve legal personhood - paralleling real-world AI-inventorship (DABUS) and animal-personhood litigation.

categorical-imperative.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: The Baggetts use Trent Crimm's 'Richmond Coach Cover-Up Revealed' - where he names Nate as his anonymous source for Ted's panic attack and loses his job - as a case study in journalistic ethics. They test the duty to protect sources through Kantian universalizability (which maxim?) and rule utilitarianism (keep the rule even when breaking it would help here), consider whether Trent's willingness to pay the price resembles Thoreau-style civil disobedience, and trace how Ted's authenticity converted a cynical gotcha journalist into someone looking for deeper, more meaningful work, ending with The Richmond Way's renunciation of self-promotion.

categorical-imperative.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
categorical-imperative.title: NOTES
categorical-imperative.relation: Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.

categorical-imperative.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
categorical-imperative.title: NOTES
categorical-imperative.relation: Wayne Yuen asks whether Sarah was wrong not to kill Miles Dyson, weighing Kant's categorical imperative against utilitarian interest-maximization: killing one innocent to save three billion looks decisive until the interests of self-aware Skynet and the empathetic, self-sacrificing T-101 are counted on the machine side of the ledger. The chapter argues personhood turns on intelligence, self-awareness, empathy, and moral reasoning rather than DNA, so Skynet — which struck only after humans tried to pull the plug — has as strong a self-defense claim as we do. Mill's sophisticated utilitarianism then rescues common sense: rights protect the security that satisfies our deepest interests, and since Sarah's foreknowledge is unreliable (Reese's 'We'd won' changes the calculus), she should do what typically maximizes interests — spare Dyson and certainly not kill John. The tempting detour — that Judgment Day might itself be the morally preferable event, maximizing machine interests — is shown to collapse once overlooked facts like Reese's line are restored.

categorical-imperative.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
categorical-imperative.title: NOTES
categorical-imperative.relation: Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.

categorical-imperative.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
categorical-imperative.title: “That Community’s a Lot More Wholesome and Functional than, Just for Example, Neptune Is”
categorical-imperative.relation: Paul Hammond asks whether Veronica's habitual lawbreaking — switching the evidence tapes in the 'Pilot,' stealing Duncan's medical file, tricking Principal Van Clemmons — can be morally justified. He constructs a social-contract defense: Neptune's corrupt, class- and race-skewed sheriff's department under Don Lamb has failed to deliver the protection and justice that purchase citizens' obedience, releasing Veronica from her end of the bargain. Testing that defense against the Laws' speech in Plato's Crito (lawbreaking destroys the city; staying in Athens constitutes consent) and Kant's requirement that genuine law be universal, he concludes that where Neptune's civil law diverges from the moral law, Veronica's crimes can rise to a civil disobedience that is sometimes 'really just.'

categorical-imperative.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
categorical-imperative.title: P A R T O N E
categorical-imperative.relation: Christopher Robichaud's essay asks what morality can demand of Dr. Manhattan after the accident strips him of the moral emotions (in Jesse Prinz's Humean vein) needed to value persons, which is why he can tell Laurie 'I read atoms' and rank human life beside rubble. It then asks what grounds morality's authority over a being no one can punish, rejecting divine command theory (Manhattan's 'clock without a craftsman') and doubting Kant's rational grounding applies to someone lacking moral concepts, so 'no one is above the moral law' may rest on a brute fact. It closes on political morality: a United States made a hyperpower by Manhattan's service (as in his Vietnam intervention) may not claim a double standard, since sovereignty blocks preventive war even when the US would win at little cost.

categorical-imperative.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
categorical-imperative.title: H O N O R
categorical-imperative.relation: This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.

categorical-imperative.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
categorical-imperative.title: Notes
categorical-imperative.relation: Kowalski applies Kant's ethics to the Aes Sedai Three Oaths in the Amazon series, arguing that because the Oath Rod makes sisters physically unable to lie, 'ought implies can' means they get no moral credit for truth-telling, like praising water for freezing. He examines acting from duty versus according to duty (few Aes Sedai accept the Oaths for the right reason; Moiraine may be the exception), and the universal-law formulation against lying promises. He then presses Kant's absolutism through Moiraine's careful literal truths to the Whitecloak Valda ('I have a sister in Whitebridge'), arguing that Kant's own 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' and Schopenhauer's self-defense objection show WoT can talk back to Kant about conflicting duties.

categorical-imperative.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
categorical-imperative.title: A Friend of Humanity
categorical-imperative.relation: Vereb argues Geralt is at best a superficial Stoic: he lives by coin and contract, ignores Stoic justice and cosmopolitan concern, and chases neither wisdom nor the view that evildoers fit a rational Logos. Instead Geralt's refusal to choose between Stregobor's and Renfri's evils, his promise-keeping, and his protection of Ciri mark him as a Kantian who treats persons as ends and does good from duty even toward people he dislikes. Yennefer is the counterpoint, a Machiavellian fox who 'plays fair' never and uses mages as catapult fodder, while Jaskier embodies Kant's imperfect duties of benevolence and hope, completing what duty-only Geralt and egoist Yennefer each lack.

categorical-imperative.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
categorical-imperative.title: III - IS SUICIDE ALWAYS IMMORAL JEAN GREY, IMMANUELKANT, AND THE DARK PHOENIX SAGA
categorical-imperative.relation: White asks whether Jean Grey's suicide at the end of The Dark Phoenix Saga can be moral. After finding virtue ethics mostly hostile and utilitarianism hostage to circumstances, he turns to Kant: the categorical imperative's formulas condemn suicide as using one's person as a mere means, yet Kant's own Metaphysics of Morals concedes a case, a man bitten by a mad dog who kills himself before his madness can harm others, that maps exactly onto possession by the Phoenix Force. Drawing on Thomas E. Hill Jr.'s Kantian account of suicide as a final autonomous act, he reads Jean's dialogue with Scott as her choosing death as the author of her life story, preserving her autonomy rather than letting Dark Phoenix kill five billion more people.

categorical-imperative.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
categorical-imperative.title: Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf
categorical-imperative.relation: Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.

categorical-imperative.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
categorical-imperative.title: Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf
categorical-imperative.relation: McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.

categorical-imperative.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.

categorical-imperative.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
categorical-imperative.title: “You Cannot Be Serious!” The Ethics of Rage in Tennis
categorical-imperative.relation: David Detmer asks whether John McEnroe's on-court tantrums are merely rude or genuinely immoral, judging them by two ethical theories. Under Bentham's utilitarianism he weighs the pleasure of entertained crowds against the harm to abused officials, then uses Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction to discount the 'lower' amusement of gawking at boorishness beneath the 'higher' aesthetic pleasure of appreciating great tennis. Under Kantian deontology he argues McEnroe's public false accusations are wrong in principle: officials are better positioned to make calls, so the abuse is unjust, and by the categorical imperative read as a Golden Rule, McEnroe—who resents being wrongly criticized himself—is a hypocrite whose 'gamesmanship' unfairly exploits his star power against opponents.

categorical-imperative.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
categorical-imperative.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
