categorical-imperative.relation: Roberts argues that across Lee's 'Father Knows Best' trilogy (Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman) the clash between traditional Confucian values and Western modernity is best resolved by the virtue ethics of Confucius and Aristotle rather than by deontology or utilitarianism. Master Chu literally refusing to be pushed, the Gaos accepting Winston's homosexual relationship, and Chef Chu adapting to his daughters all require Aristotle's golden mean and habituated virtue, which accommodate special relationships and situations. Kant's categorical imperative (rejecting paternalism as treating persons as means) and Mill's harm principle are shown to be too rule-bound to reconcile tradition with modern individualism.

categorical-imperative.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
categorical-imperative.title: “Takin’ ’er Easy for All Us Sinners” Laziness as a Virtue in The Big Lebowski
categorical-imperative.relation: Douglass and Walls read the Dude's 'principled laziness' as a coherent ethos and test it against the film's rival worldviews: the villains' hollow nihilism (which they distinguish from Nietzsche's will to power and death-of-God), Bunny's Aristippan hedonism versus Epicurus, the Big Lebowski's Nietzschean master-morality egoism, and Walter Sobchak's rules-worship read through Kant's categorical imperative and Locke's social contract. They argue dude-ism works as a personal path to contentment but, lacking any objective standard, cannot condemn true evil like Bunny's threatened murder, exposing its purposeless-universe premise as its real flaw.

categorical-imperative.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
categorical-imperative.title: No Country for Old Men as Moral Philosophy
categorical-imperative.relation: McFarland reads the film as moral philosophy: Sheriff Bell faces a post-Kantian predicament, able to reconstruct how crimes happen but unable to 'measure' why, and dooms himself by tying duty to an outcome (his promise to make Llewelyn safe) rather than to Kant's unconditional imperative, so failure yields Bernard Williams-style shame. Llewelyn is cast against Kierkegaard's Abraham/Brutus distinction as a tragic hero who cannot suspend the ethical, while Chigurh functions as an ironic anti-philosopher who alternately grounds killing in self-interest ('what good is a rule if it got you here?') and in a perverse Kantian promise-keeping, until Carla Jean restores moral responsibility by refusing his coin toss.

categorical-imperative.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
categorical-imperative.title: 5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds
categorical-imperative.relation: The Phillipses argue that abrasive forensic agent Albert Rosenfield is a model Kantian: his refusal to lie to spare Truman's feelings follows the formula of universal law, and his insistence that Truman be punished for the assault treats Truman as an autonomous end. They run Gordon Cole's manipulative lying through the universalizability test (it fails, unlike wanting pie), distinguish hypothetical from categorical imperatives via Cooper's rebuff of Audrey, and read Albert's 'I love you, Sheriff Truman' and Gandhi/King nonviolence as respect for persons as ends in themselves—duty done for the right reason.

categorical-imperative.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
categorical-imperative.title: Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir
categorical-imperative.relation: Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.

categorical-imperative.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
categorical-imperative.title: Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman
categorical-imperative.relation: Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.

categorical-imperative.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
categorical-imperative.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
categorical-imperative.relation: LaRocca reads The Insider as a study of contracts, conscience and courage. He argues that when Jeffrey Wigand stops calculating consequences ('Fuck it. Let's go to court.') he becomes a Kantian: his testimony has moral worth because it is done from duty and the categorical imperative, not from the utilitarian hedonic calculus of Bentham and Mill that Bergman, Wallace and Scruggs press on him. Wigand's whistleblowing is then framed through Aristotle's account of courage as a mean between recklessness and cowardice, with Wigand as the 'citizen soldier' who acts from conscience while Mike Wallace exemplifies the coward who exceeds in fear.

categorical-imperative.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
categorical-imperative.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
categorical-imperative.relation: Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.

categorical-imperative.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
categorical-imperative.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
categorical-imperative.relation: Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.

categorical-imperative.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
categorical-imperative.title: Action and Integrity in The Fugitive
categorical-imperative.relation: Skoble challenges the standard view of noir as morally ambiguous, arguing each episode of The Fugitive is a self-contained morality play in which Richard Kimble makes tough decisions by clearly defined standards of right and wrong. He tests ethical frameworks against the episodes: Kant's categorical imperative cannot capture Kimble, who lies in every episode to survive, whereas Aristotle's virtue ethics explains his trained emotional responses, as when he tells the migrant workers in 'Ill Wind' 'For a doctor, every life is worth saving' while saving Lieutenant Gerard from a pitchfork, and again in 'Corner of Hell' from moonshiners. Kimble's integrity, understood as fidelity in action to principles reached through reflection, reconciles his lawbreaking with his morality and, via Plato's account in the Republic of the just person who 'harmonizes the three parts of himself,' constitutes the psychological wholeness that sustains his four-year quest. The essay closes with the finale, where Kimble clears his name, Gerard kills the one-armed man, and Kimble finally walks in sunlight.

categorical-imperative.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
categorical-imperative.title: The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon
categorical-imperative.relation: Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.

categorical-imperative.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
categorical-imperative.title: The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident
categorical-imperative.relation: Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.

categorical-imperative.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
categorical-imperative.title: Is Oskar Schindler a Good Man
categorical-imperative.relation: Ebertz treats Schindler's List as a thought experiment on what makes a person good, judging Oskar Schindler against Kantian and virtue-ethical standards. On Kant he fails: many acts (lying, bribery, infidelity) violate the categorical imperative, and even his rescues spring from growing partial attachment to 'his Jews' rather than rational duty or a good will. On Aristotelian virtue ethics he only selectively exercises virtues, so is not fully 'good' either; Ebertz resolves the tension with a Principle of Moral Exemplarity, holding Schindler up as a flawed but genuine moral example whose care promotes human flourishing.

categorical-imperative.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
categorical-imperative.relation: Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.

categorical-imperative.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
categorical-imperative.title: 2. Don’t Go to Lawyers for Moral Guidance
categorical-imperative.relation: Ralston reads Jimmy McGill's slide into Saul Goodman as a study in moral decline, using Dewey's (and Bourdieu's) theory of habit to explain why a person capable of right action repeatedly chooses the wrong path—the pressures of criminal clients, Chuck's contempt, and HHM's rejection wear down his will as an ingrained disposition. He contrasts Kant's categorical imperative with mere 'imperatives of prudence' (rules of thumb for achieving any end), arguing Jimmy consistently follows the latter, as when he unhinges Chuck at the disbarment hearing to win. Invoking Hart's separability of law and morality and Singer on the ethicist's training, he concludes lawyers like Saul make poor moral guides.

categorical-imperative.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
categorical-imperative.title: 3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty
categorical-imperative.relation: Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.

categorical-imperative.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
categorical-imperative.title: 20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.

categorical-imperative.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
categorical-imperative.title: 13. In Defense of Demerzel
categorical-imperative.relation: Nurkic asks whether Demerzel, the loyal robot of the Apple TV+ Foundation, violates Asimov's Laws of Robotics when she poisons Zephyr Halima and kills Cleon XIV (Brother Dawn). He argues she is governed not by the ordinary First/Second Laws but by a reprogrammed priority—Daneel's 'Zeroth Law' (protect humanity) narrowed to 'Cleon I's vision'—and then contends the Laws are incoherent when applied to real cases (Buridan's-donkey paralysis, the surgeon dilemma, ambiguity of 'human' and 'harm'). He closes by testing the Laws against Kant's categorical imperative (the lying/murderer-at-the-door case) and Bentham-style utilitarianism to show robot ethics cannot be reduced to fixed programmed codes.

categorical-imperative.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
categorical-imperative.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
categorical-imperative.relation: Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.

categorical-imperative.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
categorical-imperative.title: What Would You Do If Your Mother Asked You A Brief Introduction to Ethics
categorical-imperative.relation: Jacob Held and Eric Wilson introduce ethics by first dispatching cultural and normative relativism (the Butter Battle Book's Yooks and Zooks, the Once-ler's 'we're each allowed our own opinion') as a cowardly refusal to judge, then present three theories through Seuss characters. Horton is the paragon of Kantian dignity ('a person's a person, no matter how small') and the categorical imperative, tested against lying in The Cat in the Hat. Thidwick the Big-Hearted Moose dramatizes Mill's utilitarianism and its sacrifice of the individual to the greatest happiness, while Thidwick, courage, and Life's 'Great Balancing Act' illustrate Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, virtue as habituated character, and eudaimonia.

categorical-imperative.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
categorical-imperative.title: Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons
categorical-imperative.relation: Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.

categorical-imperative.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
categorical-imperative.title: The Grinch’s Change of Heart Whodunit
categorical-imperative.relation: Cunningham asks whether the Grinch's sudden metanoia is a matter of head or heart, staging a debate between Kant and Hume. A Kantian reading treats the change as reason reasserting the moral law after the Grinch's inclinations (envy, resentment) hijacked it, so he realizes stealing Christmas disrespects the Whos as ends in themselves. A Humean reading, favored by the author given that the Grinch's 'small heart grew three sizes,' treats it as a new sentiment of sympathy rather than a rational apprehension, invoking Hume's claim that reason is the slave of the passions.

categorical-imperative.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
categorical-imperative.title: MOTHERHOOD
categorical-imperative.relation: Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').

categorical-imperative.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
categorical-imperative.title: SERIAL KILLERS
categorical-imperative.relation: Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.

categorical-imperative.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
categorical-imperative.title: SERIAL KILLERS
categorical-imperative.relation: Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.

categorical-imperative.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
categorical-imperative.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
categorical-imperative.relation: Brown and Tien build a 'Kantian Gate' from Kant's Formula of Universal Law: you should date only if you wouldn't mind your dates acting on your own dating maxim, which bars the manipulative, deceptive, or coercive dater while permitting many ends. For those who pass the gate, they recommend pursuing Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' and the Zhuangzi's cultivated spontaneity, describing a two-part self-cultivation (purging debilitating social programming via 'forgetting' and xinzhai, then training to act in accord with the Dao) so one can 'be in the moment' and get truly lucky on a first date. They apply the seven elements of flow directly to dating conversation, eye contact, and feedback.

categorical-imperative.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
categorical-imperative.title: 6. Hollow Man
categorical-imperative.relation: Rowlands reads Hollow Man as a retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges, posing 'why be moral?' once the invisible Kevin Bacon can act without sanction. He rejects the religious answer and Hobbesian social-contract theory (both reduce morality to prudence/fear of punishment and leave those outside the contract unprotected), and Hume's fellow-feeling as mere causal explanation not justification. He examines Kant's Categorical Imperative reducing immorality to inconsistency but argues it cannot answer 'why should I be moral,' concluding the choice is arational self-definition, closing with Nietzsche's 'become what you are' and the deed at the bottom of morality.

categorical-imperative.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
categorical-imperative.title: NOTES
categorical-imperative.relation: South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.

categorical-imperative.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
categorical-imperative.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
categorical-imperative.relation: J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 1. The Good Place as Philosophy Moral Adventures in the Afterlife
categorical-imperative.relation: Engels argues that NBC's The Good Place, though premised on a merit-based afterlife, actually argues morality should not be grounded in afterlife reward. When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey
categorical-imperative.relation: Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)
categorical-imperative.relation: Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 59. Don’t Look Up as Philosophy Comets, Climate Change, and Why the Snacks Are Not Free
categorical-imperative.relation: The chapter argues Don't Look Up is less a film than a moral imperative: its comet is an allegory for climate change, and Randall Mindy's on-air breakdown presents Singer-style simple premises (the end of human life is bad; prevent bad things you can) that compel action. It uses Plato's knowledge-as-the-Good and 'blameworthy ignorance' to condemn the willfully ignorant (Kate's parents, the Orlean Bros) who act as if they know, and Kant's categorical imperative to condemn General Themes's 'free snacks' lie and to cast the moral as the rational. It defends the comet/climate analogy against critics and insists individual action is insufficient while collective government action is required.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain
categorical-imperative.relation: Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay
categorical-imperative.relation: Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”
categorical-imperative.relation: Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.

categorical-imperative.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
categorical-imperative.title: 94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission
categorical-imperative.relation: Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.

kant-autonomy.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
kant-autonomy.title: 10 - The Moral World of the Simpson Family A Kantian Perspective
kant-autonomy.relation: James Lawler reads the Simpson family through Kant's conflict of duty and desire: Homer rationalizes 'duty' to please Moe in 'Dumbell Indemnity' yet achieves moral heroism renouncing General Sherman for his marriage, while Bart's limit-case ('Even I know stealing from the collection basket is wrong') shows morality from the negative side. Marge's honesty as a realtor in 'Realty Bites' dramatizes Kantian duty to self and the highest good in which happiness should flow from duty, and Lisa embodies inner-determined morality—testing maxims for universalizability when she becomes a vegetarian—though she learns tolerance from Apu. Lisa's isolation and her doleful saxophone ('Moaning Lisa') express the sacrifice morality demands of a sensitive child, giving the comedy its undertone of tragedy.

kant-autonomy.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
kant-autonomy.title: 14 - Hey-diddily-ho, Neighboreenos Ned Flanders and Neighborly Love
kant-autonomy.relation: David Vessey asks how 'love your neighbor as yourself' can coexist with tolerance when you believe your unbaptized neighbor faces eternal suffering, using 'Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily' where Ned baptizes the Simpson children in his care but never proselytizes beyond his household. He constructs the argument that love of neighbor, like love of self, would seem to require trying to baptize everyone, then dissolves it: proper self-love means perfecting one's nobler aspects by acting on principle rather than desire, so loving others can require respecting principled choices that risk even their lives. Kant's account of autonomy - rationally legislating one's own maxims, per the categorical imperative - supplies the missing condition, showing Ned is justified in not interfering with autonomous adults, a point capped by the irony that the only person he actually baptizes is pleasure-driven Homer.

kant-autonomy.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-autonomy.title: Unknown
kant-autonomy.relation: Schick distinguishes negative freedom, the absence of coercion - which Cypher would gain by plugging back into the Matrix - from positive freedom, the power to act on one's own choices, which the Matrix would still deny him. He then brings in Kant's claim that only a good will, the ability to make rational choices, is good without qualification: on the Kantian view Cypher's comfortable Matrix life fails as a life, since what matters is not the experiences had but the choices made.

kant-autonomy.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-autonomy.title: Unknown
kant-autonomy.relation: The chapter contrasts two theories of liberation: the Platonic one, where an exceptional external liberator - a philosopher-king, or the traditional God-man savior the film's characters initially expect - leads humanity out of illusion, and Kant's Enlightenment alternative that 'the slaves can only be truly free if they free themselves', with Jesus recast as the model of our own inner potential rather than a miracle-working savior. The film's arc, it argues, moves from Choi's 'my own personal Jesus Christ' (a caricature of liberation) to a finale that overturns all expectations of an external savior.

kant-autonomy.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-autonomy.title: Unknown
kant-autonomy.relation: The chapter argues that egotism - each individual's spontaneous belief that he is 'the One', the center of the universe for which everything was made - is the fundamental moral error, and that morality demands recognizing our oneness with all intelligent beings. The red pill symbolizes the basic choice between two matrices: the world of separate egos, bodies colliding in space and time under deterministic causality, and the world of human unity and freedom seen from the standpoint of moral consciousness - and the initial choice must then survive a crisis in which its realizability is doubted.

kant-autonomy.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-autonomy.title: Unknown
kant-autonomy.relation: This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.

kant-autonomy.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-autonomy.title: Unknown
kant-autonomy.relation: The chapter reinterprets Kant's second postulate: God is not the external distributor of justice whose theological counterpart is our sense of powerlessness before the all-powerful machines, but the power of united humanity - 'one for all and all for one', the third, still-unfinished Matrix of Zion. The spoon-bending boy supplies the illustration: we cannot bend the spoon so long as we believe reality is a separate material substance, but recognizing its unity with us, 'it is only yourself' that bends - and Neo's real lesson is not that he is a special being but that he is One with all existence.

kant-autonomy.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-autonomy.title: Unknown
kant-autonomy.relation: Locating the Matrix's power in the fear of death - Neo frozen on the ledge, then discovering in the jump program that he must 'let it all go... fear, doubt, and disbelief' - the chapter reads 'the body cannot live without the mind' as meaning that even outside the Matrix the body depends on the mind's beliefs. The Oracle's either/or prophecy embodies the postulates: Neo's Fate is fulfilled through free choice (his life for Morpheus's) and through faith in our own Potential, so the God or savior we postulate is finally revealed as an extension of ourselves as we transcend separateness, not a separate miracle-worker.

kant-autonomy.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
kant-autonomy.title: Conquering the Inner Demon
kant-autonomy.relation: James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.

kant-autonomy.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
kant-autonomy.title: Following the Moral Law
kant-autonomy.relation: Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.

kant-autonomy.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
kant-autonomy.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').

kant-autonomy.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
kant-autonomy.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.

kant-autonomy.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
kant-autonomy.title: Both Sides of Dylan and Politics
kant-autonomy.relation: Jordy Rocheleau reads Dylan's protest era ("The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll," "Hurricane," "Chimes of Freedom") as Enlightenment social criticism in Kant's and Mill's sense: reason can expose injustice and secure autonomy against majority tyranny. The post-protest Dylan ("My Back Pages," "Desolation Row," "It's Alright, Ma") turns postmodern - Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives, Derrida's ever-deferred meanings, and Foucault's power/knowledge, where ideals of freedom become instruments of domination. Yet Dylan keeps crying for justice ("Political World," "Dignity"), so the chapter concludes postmodern skepticism can only serve as a cautionary check within, not a replacement of, Enlightenment politics - the thief's line in "All Along the Watchtower" as commitment amid confusion.

kant-autonomy.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
kant-autonomy.title: Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life
kant-autonomy.relation: Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.

kant-autonomy.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
kant-autonomy.title: Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back
kant-autonomy.relation: Gray asks whether Cylons deserve moral consideration, starting from Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means: the New Caprica suicide bombings and Adama's plan to weaponize a Cylon virus treat captives merely as means, while Helo's sabotage of 'A Measure of Salvation' acknowledges their intrinsic value. D'Anna's dissent before being boxed and Athena's defection for Helo show the rational autonomy Kant's personhood requires; if that is dismissed as programming, Singer's sentience criterion (Leoben tortured, Gina catatonic) and Warren's multi-criterial personhood — including Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded' — still open personhood to Cylons. The chapter ends on the humans' double standard (Athena accepted, guns drawn on Caprica Six) as a mirror for our own treatment of uncertain others.

kant-autonomy.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
kant-autonomy.title: “Make It So”
kant-autonomy.relation: Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.

kant-autonomy.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
kant-autonomy.title: The Authentic Red Sox Fan, or The Importance of Turning off NESN and Finding
kant-autonomy.relation: Corey McCall asks what makes a 'true' Red Sox fan, contrasting the beer-soaked bleacher loudmouth with one-hundred-year-old honorary batboy Arthur Giddon, and treats the nostalgia and resentment around the 2004 bandwagon as the Enlightenment problem of authenticity in miniature. Through Kant's 'Sapere aude' and the ideal of autonomy, he argues the authentic fan is the critical fan who uses reason about the team (questioning Francona's moves, judging whole careers) instead of losing herself in uncritical devotion, reading Jason Varitek's 2004 muzzle of A-Rod as the moment the team's identity crystallized for fans who wanted to be like him. With the Curse gone, fans are freed from fated suffering but inherit Kant's burden of autonomously choosing how fandom will define them, since circumstances no longer decide.

kant-autonomy.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
kant-autonomy.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
kant-autonomy.relation: Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.

kant-autonomy.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
kant-autonomy.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
kant-autonomy.relation: Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.

kant-autonomy.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
kant-autonomy.title: Invisibility or Honesty
kant-autonomy.relation: Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.

kant-autonomy.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
kant-autonomy.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: A palliative-care bioethicist dissects the 'Gray Matter' family meeting, arguing Skyler's ambush coerces Walt's autonomy through an implied threat of emotional isolation, while Walt Jr.'s honest 'I'm pissed off!' and Marie's defense of his choice are non-coercive. The chapter frames the issue with Kant's ideal of choice free from emotion and circumstance and Mill's insistence that even self-destructive decisions are beyond legitimate coercion, and indicts doctors too for 'selling' futile treatment rather than admit mortality. The verdict: Walt accepted chemotherapy through 'autonomous beneficence' - a freely made sacrifice for his son - so Skyler's manipulation was unethical even though the decision it produced was genuinely his own.

kant-autonomy.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
kant-autonomy.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Takes apart Walt and Jesse's 'legalize it' excuse: Kantian autonomy would license adult drug choices, but knowingly self-harming meth use is a performative contradiction no rational adult can will, and Mill's utilitarianism condemns cooking because harms to all users must be weighed against one family's benefit. It reads the 'Cancer Man' revenge on Ken's BMW and the Tuco deal as proof that the meth world's criminality spreads like a cancer into Walt's ordinary life, and 'Gray Matter' as Greek tragedy - pride refusing Elliot's money when a way out existed. Against On Liberty's libertarian pull, it finally argues addicts forfeit full rational autonomy and so may be 'caged' by paternalistic law.

kant-autonomy.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
kant-autonomy.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case that walkers deserve respect as 'residual humans': Rick dwelling on organ-donor Wayne Dunlap before harvesting his corpse for camouflage shows that bodies carry the dead's chosen ends, so using Wayne is honoring, not using, him. Because walkers are corpses bound by the presumptive wishes of the deceased, and retain residual subjectivity (Jenny returning again and again to her family's door), survivors wrong them by treating them as mere objects - Merle's sport killing of walkers on the rooftop is the moral low, Rick's swift, risk-accepting headshots of Hannah and Deputy Leon the respectful execution. Jim's informed choice to be left by the road to turn, over Shane's and Rick's objections, shows the autonomy of the infected that no one else may override.

kant-autonomy.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
kant-autonomy.title: Psych and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: C. Scott Sevier argues Henry deliberately recreated Shawn as Aristotle's 'another self' - Lassiter's 'which one?' joke in the kidnapping episode makes the identity explicit - and reads this through Plato's Symposium: via Diotima's ladder of love and the doctrine of forms, Henry achieves immortality by reproducing beauty in his son's educated soul, not just his body. The chapter then frames Shawn's fierce independence against his constant recourse to Henry's voice as the collision between medieval deference to authority and the modern ideal of autonomy in Descartes and Kant, showing that both thinkers quietly borrowed from Augustine (the causal adequacy principle, the good will), so Shawn's 'autonomy' is itself the product of his father's training - an internalized authority indistinguishable from his own.

kant-autonomy.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
kant-autonomy.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Tim Jones argues the films show why Kant's Enlightenment ideal - the courage to use your own understanding without others' guidance, embodied in Hammond's isolated, independently funded genius - has become dangerous now that one man's project can shape the world future people must live in. He tracks Hammond's arc from dismissing Malcolm's review to conceding 'I was wrong', but shows in the sequels that one convert to caution cannot contain a technology: Ludlow ships a T. rex to San Diego and paragliding entrepreneurs land on Isla Sorna anyway, so the damage to future people is done before anyone repents. Against this he proposes Rupert Read's 'Guardians of the Future', a super jury that would veto laws and technologies threatening future people's basic needs - meaning Hammond should have been stopped before he started.

kant-autonomy.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
kant-autonomy.title: The Devil and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Danny Smith applies Kant's three grades of evil from Religion within the Limits of Reason Alone to The Dark Knight. Batman's saving Harvey over Rachel out of love is normal evil (pathological inclination trumping duty, his 'never kill' rule hardened into moral self-satisfaction), Two-Face's coin is radical evil (outsourcing his freedom and responsibility to chance), and the Joker - burning his own money, making his scarred face the true mask, wanting only chaos - is diabolical evil done for its own sake. Smith then presses Kant's embarrassing problem that evil pursued purely on principle, with no pathological motive, is indistinguishable from the highest good, and half-sympathetically re-reads the Joker as the honest rebel in a corrupt Gotham.

kant-autonomy.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
kant-autonomy.title: Girls and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.

kant-autonomy.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
kant-autonomy.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.

kant-autonomy.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
kant-autonomy.title: 5. Office Hours Are for Patients
kant-autonomy.relation: Alloy argues that the psychiatric code of ethics - confidentiality with Franklyn ('It would be unethical to approach a patient'), the formal boundaries Lecter scrupulously observes once Will becomes an official patient, and even the oath-violating concealment of Will's encephalitis with Dr. Sutcliffe - is the closest Hannibal can come to friendship, because professional rules artificially manufacture the trust that friends enjoy organically. Working through informed consent, placebo deception, paternalism, and psychiatry's extraordinary power to declare patients incompetent to exercise autonomy at all, he shows the Will-Hannibal relationship cycling through four stages between professional ethics and friendship - 'Office hours are for patients. My kitchen is always open to friends' - while never achieving either, since every display of trust is a manipulation and the power asymmetry never disappears.

kant-autonomy.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
kant-autonomy.title: 7. Psychopaths, Outlaws, and Us
kant-autonomy.relation: McClelland argues Lecter is neither psychopath nor sociopath, marshaling his empathic childhood (softening a bread crust for Mischa, polishing an eggplant because she loved purple, sensing Lady Murasaki's fatigue), his genuinely compassionate psychiatric work with Margot Verger, and his chess-master planning as evidence that both cognitive and emotional empathy operate normally - unlike Grutas, 'here's your real psychopath'. Reading Lecter's preternatural calm, mutism, and suppressed memories as PTSD and resilience after Mischa's death, and his fundamental project as the pursuit of autonomy (with Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework explaining his contempt for declining institutions like the FBI), he reclassifies Lecter as an outlaw - one placed beyond the law's protection yet living inside civil society - who kills instrumentally the way evolutionary psychology says humans do, concluding that 'there is an outlaw in all of us'.

kant-autonomy.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
kant-autonomy.title: 2. Golem Morality in the Modern World
kant-autonomy.relation: Skene weighs Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' - opened with a River Ankh drowning-child variant - against the golem morality of Going Postal and Feet of Clay. Mr. Pump's charge that Moist von Lipwig's frauds 'hastened the deaths' of 2.338 people grounds a golem standard of actuarial murder that Skene applies to the 2008 banking crisis and Mao's Great Leap Forward. With Kant, the chapter holds that free choice is the foundation of moral responsibility and respect for others' wills, but unlike Singer's unlimited demands, golem morality asks us to own the foreseeable consequences of our choices without sacrificing everything.

kant-autonomy.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
kant-autonomy.title: 5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds
kant-autonomy.relation: Argues that Albert Rosenfield embodies Kant's categorical imperative: his refusal to soften his autopsy demands or lie to spare feelings is fidelity to universalizable maxims, and his insistence that Sheriff Truman be charged for punching him treats punishment as respect for a rational agent's autonomy. The chapter walks through maxims, the universalizability test applied to Gordon Cole's possibly faked deafness and FBI lying, hypothetical versus categorical imperatives (Cooper may always want Norma's cherry pie, but morality trumps want), and the formula of humanity — Ben Horne's use of One-Eyed Jack's women as mere means is the counterexample, while Albert's insults paradoxically honor Truman's rational agency. Albert's arc to "I love you, Sheriff Truman" and his gentler Season Two and The Return self shows a Kantian who integrates classical reason with romantic feeling.

kant-autonomy.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
kant-autonomy.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
kant-autonomy.relation: Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.

kant-autonomy.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
kant-autonomy.title: 16. Who Am I to You
kant-autonomy.relation: James Okapal sets up the Kantian view — moral agency, shown by passing the contradiction-in-conception test (which Wallace's 'all should be masters of slaves' fails), is the precondition of moral status, so non-agents like replicants, on Tibor Machan's extension of Kant to animals, matter no more than toasters — against the ethics of care of Nel Noddings and Carol Gilligan. On the care reading, K's and Batty's final acts of ethical caring, like Joi's risky choices for K, confer moral status on another and thereby constitute moral agency, reversing the Kantian order. Empathy, not universalizable reason, is what removes bricks from Joshi's wall.

kant-autonomy.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
kant-autonomy.title: 5. Another Day in the Neighborhood
kant-autonomy.relation: Sydney Ball and Eric Mohr interleave a college student's Tuesday with her six-year-old self watching the show: Plato's Republic (439c) on the rational part overruling the appetitive frames procrastination and lost youthful energy, Kant's autonomy frames doing what you should without being told, and Heidegger's 'They' frames her supermarket jealousy, dissolved by complimenting a stranger's shoes just as Henrietta Pussycat overcame jealousy of Grandpere's fancy granddaughter Collette (episodes 1176-1180). The lesson, learned from Mister Rogers's words about stopping, is authenticity: 'I like you just the way you are.'

kant-autonomy.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
kant-autonomy.title: “It’s a robot! A goddamn droid!”
kant-autonomy.relation: Tests three grounds of moral status against the franchise: species membership (Singer's charge of speciesism - would the human-DNA Newborn count?), Kantian autonomy (which makes Bishop matter but excludes babies and animals, and is itself doubtful once his behavioral inhibitors fix his choices), and Bentham's sentience ('can they suffer?' - Bishop's 'I hurt. Do me a favor. Disconnect me'). Settling on interests and preferences, the chapter argues synthetics with desires - even Ash's admiration for the 'perfect organism' - can be moral patients, so Weyland-Yutani's treatment of them as tools and slaves is wrong.

kant-autonomy.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
kant-autonomy.title: Leaving the Shadow of the Bat
kant-autonomy.relation: Carsten Fogh Nielsen stages Aristotle against Kant on moral education: Aristotle says we become just by doing just acts and imitating exemplary people, as Robin imitates Batman, while Kant objects that every example must first be appraised by principles of morality and that imitation breeds heteronomy rather than autonomy. The Gordon-Yindel disagreement over Batman in The Dark Knight Returns shows people can genuinely clash about who counts as morally exemplary in the first place. Dick Grayson resolves the tension by using the courage, skills, and integrity Batman instilled in him to stand up to Batman and become Nightwing, proving emulation can be the route to, not the enemy of, Kantian autonomy.

kant-autonomy.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
kant-autonomy.title: Power Behind the Cloak
kant-autonomy.relation: The chapter asks whether Wong's hereditary service to the Sorcerer Supreme is culpable servility, framing the charge with Kant's line that 'one who makes himself a worm cannot complain' and Thomas E. Hill's Kantian account of servility as failing to claim one's dignity as a person. It answers with Hegel's master-slave dialectic: Strange, free to haunt the astral plane, becomes dependent on Wong for everything worldly, while Wong, by working on the world rather than merely commanding it, develops the self-consciousness Hegel says work produces—he serves the shared mission rather than the master—so the relationship is a partnership in which servitude grounds rather than forfeits Wong's self-respect.

kant-autonomy.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
kant-autonomy.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.

kant-autonomy.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
kant-autonomy.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.

kant-autonomy.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
kant-autonomy.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Dryden asks whether the Lanterns' relationships are weaknesses or strengths. Epictetus's dichotomy of control would have recruits greet the Sinestro Corps' display of their families' eyeballs with Stoic indifference, and Kant brands fear for loved ones heteronomous; yet Donna Parker refuses the ring for her children, Amnee and Matoo Pree surrender their rings rather than stop loving, and Kilowog dines with energy constructs of his dead family, showing attachments partly constitute who people are. Feminist relational autonomy resolves the tension: Kyle escapes Parallax only by grasping Hal's hand ('we don't have to do it alone'), and Soranik Natu cannot excise Sinestro's crest or parentage any more than Donchin's Huntington's-disease daughter can sever family ties, so autonomy competency means negotiating unchosen relationships rather than escaping them.

kant-autonomy.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
kant-autonomy.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge. Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.

kant-autonomy.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
kant-autonomy.title: Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head
kant-autonomy.relation: The book's introduction frames Inception as the newest chapter in the dream-skepticism tradition: Plato's question about how we explain our perceptions of reality and Descartes's point that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, with the twist that Descartes never doubted our thoughts are our own while the film contests exactly that. It previews the volume's rival readings — the single-dream theory of the airline flight, Brophy's claim that the shared dreams are server-based electronic worlds like Second Life, and neuroscience suggesting we act on thoughts before we are aware of them. It also stakes out the ethics: inception as a violation of autonomy akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing, and the diagnosis that Inception is fundamentally a tale from the business world of corporations.

kant-autonomy.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
kant-autonomy.title: Invisibility or Honesty
kant-autonomy.relation: Schulzke argues inception is a categorical violation of Kantian autonomy: the Fischer job treats him merely as a means (Saito's market share, Cobb's reunion with his children), and even Cobb's benevolent inception on Mal disrespects humanity by robbing her of self-determination, leaving her unable to act as a responsible moral agent testable against the categorical imperative. Extraction, by contrast, attacks privacy rather than autonomy, and the chapter uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges to show that dream espionage would defeat even perfect invisibility, since an extractor could always read your deeds in your dreams. The twist, played off Kant's absolute condemnation of lying, is that the standing threat of extraction might be the only force that could make universal honesty practicable — hence the title's choice between invisibility and honesty, illustrated by Ariadne's life-saving extraction on Cobb.

kant-autonomy.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
kant-autonomy.title: Notes
kant-autonomy.relation: Chelstrom uses the progression from guided DUPLO builds to free design to argue that autonomy develops in degrees and is relational rather than purely individualist. Kant's self-thinking agent — for whom precepts and formulas are the 'ball and chain' of immaturity — explains Emmet's dependence on Octan's instruction booklets and Lord Business's profit from deference, and Korsgaard's definition frames the individualist autonomy the Master Builders embody. Yet their lone-wolf autonomy fails, and Sartre's look plus Beauvoir's account of woman forced to assume herself as Other explain Wyldstyle/Lucy's deference to others' expectations; Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy recasts 'Everything is Awesome' as peers supporting each other's self-development, with Emmet's friendship letting Lucy accept herself.

kant-autonomy.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
kant-autonomy.title: The Office and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.

kant-autonomy.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
kant-autonomy.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
kant-autonomy.relation: Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.

kant-autonomy.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
kant-autonomy.title: Notes
kant-autonomy.relation: Barbara Stock uses the Borg to analyze autonomy: Picard's 'they took everything I was' names the Collective's destruction of self-governance, while Hugh's choice to return to the crash site in 'I, Borg' displays the Kantian core of autonomy—acting on universalizable principle against inclination. She defends relational autonomy through Janeway's pleading with Kes in 'The Gift' and the Ferengi woman's internalized oppression, then combines it with Clark's extended cognition to ask whether the Borg Queen's 'I am the Collective' might make the Collective itself an autonomous agent. Finally she judges Janeway's forcible de-assimilation of Seven defensible only while Seven is non-autonomous, and her promise never to let Seven return ethically suspect.

kant-autonomy.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
kant-autonomy.title: Notes
kant-autonomy.relation: Uses the Zillo Beast arc, battle droids, mynocks, and Han shooting Greedo to test theories of moral status: Schweitzer-style reverence for life would forbid a Jedi from eating anything, genetic views breed Palpatine-style human chauvinism, Singer's sentience view makes droid suffering and Luke dropping the rancor's door morally troubling, and Kantian autonomy excludes cognitively impaired beings too harshly.
