The chapter weighs Palpatine as merely a 'sociopathic' goal-pursuer rather than a Kantian moral agent, and leaves the droid question open via the novel Children of the Jedi, where the droid-converted Nichos lacks even mere agency because he cannot override his programming.

kant-autonomy.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
kant-autonomy.title: Do Not Ask Him to Be Rational
kant-autonomy.relation: The Rochas argue the Jedi Council's conduct across the Temple-bombing arc — letting Tarkin take jurisdiction, then expelling Ahsoka and handing her over for trial on flimsy evidence in 'The Wrong Jedi' — exposes a Jedi ethics corrupted by deference to hierarchy. Ahsoka's decision to walk away enacts Kantian moral autonomy (self-legislation) against the Council's heteronomy, while Anakin, despite sharing her doubts, seeks another master in Palpatine and falls into heteronomy instead. Using Baier's account of trust and Iris Marion Young on social roles, they contend the Jedi's repudiation of feeling was the real failure: emotions like Ahsoka's fear rightly guided her to distrust the Council and even to trust Ventress.

kant-autonomy.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
kant-autonomy.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.relation: McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.

kant-autonomy.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
kant-autonomy.title: The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy
kant-autonomy.relation: Don Fallis uses Westworld to work out definitions of pretense and deception, testing successive accounts (acting-as-if, Austin's intend-to-deceive, Langland-Hassan's believe-P-is-false) against cases like guests playing cowboys, Ford passing off Bernard as human, and Maeve and Hector pretending to be deactivated. He adopts a Cartesian evil-demon model of deception but rejects the claim that deception must manipulate perceived evidence, arguing Ford's direct implanting of Teddy's Wyatt backstory still counts. He concludes, citing Kant on autonomy and Walzer on foreseen collateral harm, that staff who intend to deceive the hosts and even guests who foreseeably contribute to it act wrongly, since deceived hosts suffer real harm to their agency.

kant-autonomy.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
kant-autonomy.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
kant-autonomy.relation: Joshua Crabill reads the hosts' awakening through Kant's story of Eve grasping autonomy and the etymology of autonomy as self-legislation, with Dolores swatting the fly and 'these violent delights' as her forbidden fruit. He uses Nietzsche's will-to-power turned inward to explain how the hosts' caged suffering builds an inner 'soul,' and Jaynes's bicameral commanding voice becoming one's own (Dolores hearing Arnold's voice turn into hers). Drawing on Korsgaard's reflective distance and Plato's divided soul, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own law), arguing that Korsgaard's 'determinism is no threat to freedom' lets Maeve, gaining admin access and choosing her daughter, genuinely 'write my own story.'

kant-autonomy.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
kant-autonomy.title: Notes
kant-autonomy.relation: Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.

kant-autonomy.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
kant-autonomy.title: III - IS SUICIDE ALWAYS IMMORAL JEAN GREY, IMMANUELKANT, AND THE DARK PHOENIX SAGA
kant-autonomy.relation: White asks whether Jean Grey's suicide at the end of The Dark Phoenix Saga can be moral. After finding virtue ethics mostly hostile and utilitarianism hostage to circumstances, he turns to Kant: the categorical imperative's formulas condemn suicide as using one's person as a mere means, yet Kant's own Metaphysics of Morals concedes a case, a man bitten by a mad dog who kills himself before his madness can harm others, that maps exactly onto possession by the Phoenix Force. Drawing on Thomas E. Hill Jr.'s Kantian account of suicide as a final autonomous act, he reads Jean's dialogue with Scott as her choosing death as the author of her life story, preserving her autonomy rather than letting Dark Phoenix kill five billion more people.

kant-autonomy.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
kant-autonomy.title: A Court Conversation
kant-autonomy.relation: Cast as a dialogue with an updated Kant at a tournament, the chapter applies Kant's aesthetics to spectating tennis: it distinguishes free from dependent beauty (a McEnroe drop volley or a Federer stroke judged against the game's history and rules), locates the sublime in a booming ace, a broken record, and the fan's disinterested enthusiasm, and defends aesthetic judgments as disinterested yet subjectively universal. It then turns Kant's ethics onto the court, arguing that calling a line honestly against your own interest has moral worth only when done autonomously, for its own sake, and that gamesmanship like faked injury timeouts seeks an unfair advantage and so is wrong even when within the rules.

kant-autonomy.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
kant-autonomy.title: The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon
kant-autonomy.relation: Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.

kant-autonomy.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
kant-autonomy.relation: Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.

kant-autonomy.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
kant-autonomy.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
kant-autonomy.relation: Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.

kant-autonomy.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
kant-autonomy.title: 7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters
kant-autonomy.relation: Brace surveys the later-season mother figures—Mary, Kelly, Jody, Rowena, Mrs. Butters, Charlie—arguing they are repeatedly used as emotional tools against the Winchesters, which she reads through Kant's warning against treating persons merely as means. She stresses loss of free will and agency: Mary's British Men of Letters 'realignment' and Mrs. Butters's coercive programming strip their autonomy and reduce them to objects/killers, while their reclaimed agency and self-sacrifice restore their Kantian standing as ends in themselves.

kant-autonomy.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
kant-autonomy.title: 31. Out of Step with the World
kant-autonomy.relation: Lustila and Olsthoorn ask what makes hardcore punk's cultural nonconformity ethically valuable, distinguishing it from Kantian autonomy (self-governance via Korsgaard) and Taylor-style authenticity using lyrics by Void, Negative Approach, and Burn. They offer two justifications: a contingent one, on which countercultures like vegan straight edge replace harmful mainstream norms (though hardline militancy fails the test), and a general one drawn from Mill's On Liberty - even the mere example of nonconformity, from punks and posers alike, enlarges the space of 'experiments of living' and pluralism everyone needs against the tyranny of majority opinion. Berlin's value pluralism backs the general value: countercultures are 'a wrench in the system' that multiplies the models of living available to all.

kant-autonomy.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
kant-autonomy.title: 15. Morality and Manipulation
kant-autonomy.relation: Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.

kant-autonomy.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
kant-autonomy.title: 16. Psycho-historian or Psycho Historian
kant-autonomy.relation: Bellantoni asks what Seldon owes future generations, pitting moral presentism against his 'mystical' identification with humanity (echoing Scheffler's Why Worry about Future Generations?). She tests the Seldon Plan under Bentham's hedonic calculus—finding time-discounting and uncertainty about what follows the thirty-thousand-year interregnum undercut it—and under Kantian deontology, arguing Seldon's mass manipulation of Gaal Dornick, his inquisitors, and the Encyclopedists treats people merely as means and violates their autonomy. Weighing longtermism against Whitehead's claim (in Adventures of Ideas) that civilizations must die to seed new ones, she suggests Seldon's engineered revival of a spent civilization may itself be a barbaric imposition on future people who would not choose it.

kant-autonomy.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
kant-autonomy.title: 17. Chef of the Future
kant-autonomy.relation: Cheong convenes the 'documentary-ethics panel' invited by Roadrunner director Morgan Neville over the AI deepfake of Bourdain's voice reading lines he never spoke. Using Beauchamp and Childress's principle of autonomy, the Midler v. Ford voice-impersonation case, and worries from AI ethicists and epistemologists (Fallis, Muller) that deepfakes threaten knowledge and trust, he argues the synthesized voice denies Bourdain the 'right of reply' and deceives viewers — then reveals he had ChatGPT ghost-write parts of the chapter to make the point.

kant-autonomy.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
kant-autonomy.title: Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons
kant-autonomy.relation: Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.

kant-autonomy.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
kant-autonomy.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
kant-autonomy.relation: Swindler argues the ideal of fatherhood is to engender autonomy – a blend of independence and interdependence – in one's children. Treating fatherhood as an abstract social role (compared to a baseball pitcher) constituted by collective intentions, he uses Kant's 'ought implies can' to link accountability to autonomy and his constitutive-vs-regulative rules (the promise to take his son fishing) to show fathers must teach children to reflect on the concept of a rule, not merely follow it, modeling self-governance rather than authoritarian control.

kant-autonomy.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
kant-autonomy.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
kant-autonomy.relation: Carreras, writing as a son, examines the ethical tension in the father-son relationship between using a father's inevitable influence and fostering the son's autonomy. Opening with Aristotle on parents loving children as 'something of himself,' he uses the case of Jerry (a lawyer) pressuring his son Jose (who loves 18th-century English literature) to argue for a 'foundational view' of autonomy – that the best life is one embraced 'from the inside,' likened to seeing without a value-blindfold – and advises fathers to ask 'Is this what he truly wants, or what I want?'

kant-autonomy.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
kant-autonomy.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
kant-autonomy.relation: Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.

kant-autonomy.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
kant-autonomy.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
kant-autonomy.relation: Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.

kant-autonomy.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
kant-autonomy.title: The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects
kant-autonomy.relation: Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'

kant-autonomy.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
kant-autonomy.title: 9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom
kant-autonomy.relation: Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.

deontology.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
deontology.title: 10 - The Moral World of the Simpson Family A Kantian Perspective
deontology.relation: James Lawler reads the Simpson family through Kant's conflict of duty and desire: Homer rationalizes 'duty' to please Moe in 'Dumbell Indemnity' yet achieves moral heroism renouncing General Sherman for his marriage, while Bart's limit-case ('Even I know stealing from the collection basket is wrong') shows morality from the negative side. Marge's honesty as a realtor in 'Realty Bites' dramatizes Kantian duty to self and the highest good in which happiness should flow from duty, and Lisa embodies inner-determined morality—testing maxims for universalizability when she becomes a vegetarian—though she learns tolerance from Apu. Lisa's isolation and her doleful saxophone ('Moaning Lisa') express the sacrifice morality demands of a sensitive child, giving the comedy its undertone of tragedy.

deontology.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
deontology.title: The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer
deontology.relation: Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.

deontology.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
deontology.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.

deontology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
deontology.title: I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!
deontology.relation: Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.

deontology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
deontology.title: I Fought the Law and the Law Won
deontology.relation: Argues that Batman's warrantless raids, intimidation and evidence-free arrests violate negative duties that bind everyone regardless of role, so producing good (the utilitarian reply) cannot justify them, and superpowers earn no legal exemptions that we would deny police. When Spider-Man evades NYPD warrants, the chapter applies Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito that citizens owe the law their obedience even when wrongly accused, though it concedes that keeping a secret identity safe from villains who would torture or kill loved ones can override the duty to submit, a move consistent with non-Kantian nonconsequentialism since Kant could not abide any lie.

deontology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
deontology.title: But It’s Just a White Lie!
deontology.relation: Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.

deontology.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
deontology.title: Keeping Secrets
deontology.relation: Takes up the objection that secret identities require the deception superheroes condemn, and answers that skillful deception within a legitimate context — quarterback fakes, a painter's perspective tricks — is acceptable, while even a lie bad in itself can be morally right or obligatory when needed to prevent great harm to the innocent. So Spider-Man's secrecy about being Peter Parker is justified, even praiseworthy, because a slipped secret would hand his enemies leverage over Aunt May and his friends.

deontology.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
deontology.title: James Bond and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Tedesco dissects what the double-0 'license to kill' could actually mean, ruling out self-defense and mere on-the-job killing and concluding that Bond is a state-sanctioned assassin who earned his status through two assassinations in Casino Royale. He tests that status against Kant's categorical imperative - persons as ends in themselves, though Kant also defended capital punishment as respecting the murderer's choice - and against consequentialism, which vindicates Bond's elimination of Kananga but stumbles on the surgeon's organ-harvesting dilemma. Because ordinary morality mixes duty-based and consequence-based intuitions, the chapter leaves Bond's moral status genuinely open and links it to live policy debates on assassination and torture after 9/11, including Britain's Intelligence Services Act that leaves room for a real-life double-0 agent.

deontology.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
deontology.title: So, Case Closed – Right
deontology.relation: White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.

deontology.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
deontology.title: It’s Not That Simple
deontology.relation: Donal O'Mathuna uses 24 to run the torture debate: the ticking bomb scenario (Syed Ali's nuclear bomb, Miles pressing to torture Audrey) dramatizes the utilitarian case for forward-looking interrogational torture, while Jack slicing off the Russian consul's finger and Morris's broken guilt show torture as a deontological violation that destroys character on both sides and usually fails to extract truth. Against the show's sanitized, banal presentation (Agent Burke as the "kindly torturer"), he sets Abu Ghraib, the systematic training of torturers, and the metastatic spread of torture programs once permitted. Fiction can open the ethical question, he concludes, but must not be mistaken for the reality of torture.

deontology.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
deontology.title: Walking the Tightrope
deontology.relation: Louis Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's 'blind squirrel' lie about Earth, classifying the fact that Cylons look human, Roslin's faked death of the baby Hera, and Tom Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. Democratic duty is framed as a deontological obligation of transparency grounded in the governed's trust, while the leadership repeatedly defaults to consequentialist wartime exceptions. The chapter proposes a rule-of-thumb: secrecy is justified only to hide specific information from an external threat like the Cylons, never to protect the government from its own citizens, and each violation erodes the trust on which Colonial democracy's 'soul' depends.

deontology.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
deontology.title: “I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”
deontology.relation: Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.

deontology.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
deontology.title: The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
deontology.relation: Horn argues the three Triforce pieces are morally neutral: by Kant's Groundwork, only the good will that acts from duty (Link never rescues Zelda for a reward) is good without qualification, so courage, wisdom, and power can each serve evil, and the Triforce would have corrupted Zelda or Link too if fortune had dealt it otherwise. Plato's Ring of Gyges and the Glaucon-Socrates debate explain Ganondorf: he chose to lust for power, and his wealth, status, and fear-based honor are hollow because justice is good for its own sake and his soul is out of balance (which is why the Triforce split at his touch in Ocarina of Time). Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then defines proper use: Link's courage between cowardice and rashness (getting the map, compass, and weapon before the boss), Zelda's internalized prudence, and Ganondorf's power in insatiable excess.

deontology.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
deontology.title: As Nasty as I Wanna Be
deontology.relation: Greene asks whether Maguire's Elphaba is really wicked, first clearing away her reputation (she adopts the 'Wicked Witch' name because 'it liberates you from convention,' echoing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic about the just person with an unjust reputation and vice versa) and then her nature (the midwife-biting birth, green skin, and witchcraft establish no vampire-like evil essence, since Glinda and Nor are good witches). Following Hume's view that morality is not found in the world but in our assessments, he treats wickedness as a matter of performing actions we judge evil, and weighs Elphaba's life under both headings: good intentions with horrific outcomes (the bees that kill the chef, the icicle that kills Manek, Sarima's family executions) and bad intentions with none (her two failed attempts on Madame Morrible). The verdict is deliberately suspended: if she is wicked at all, it can only be through the consequences of her actions.

deontology.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
deontology.title: Lester’s Duties and Capabilities
deontology.relation: Maguire asks whether the Royals did wrong by trying to hit in the late innings of Jon Lester's May 2008 no-hitter, working through Kant's distinction between perfect duties (always binding—playing hard, honoring the codified rules) and imperfect duties (praiseworthy obligations that admit exceptions—respecting the unwritten convention against bunting for a hit in a blowout). Sympathy for Lester's cancer recovery must not enter the calculation, since Jim Abbott's 1993 no-hitter shows the duty must universalize; bunting would be 'bush league' rather than wrong, a lapse in imperfect duty. He extends the analysis to Francona's pitch counts and warns that wanting Ellsbury to bunt against a Yankees no-hitter would treat the pitcher as a mere means to fan pride.

deontology.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
deontology.title: World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent
deontology.relation: Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.

deontology.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
deontology.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
deontology.relation: Smith reads the Doctor–Rose tragedy through Kantian deontology: shaped by Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's virtue ethics into a good will, both must still choose duty over inclination, so in 'Parting of the Ways' and the Battle of Canary Wharf in 'Doomsday' they each act from the categorical imperative — sacrificing their love to save humanity — because love, as Kant warns, impels partiality. Even in 'Journey's End' the Doctor sends Rose to Pete's World with the meta-crisis Doctor for the greater good, ending alone under Kant's starry heavens and the moral law within.

deontology.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
deontology.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
deontology.relation: Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.

deontology.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
deontology.title: You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You
deontology.relation: Waller and McAlear first rebut the amoral reading: Dexter does feel (he sobs over Rita, loves Deb, misses Harry) and does control his urges through the Code, so morality applies to him, and the Dark Passenger is merely everyone's socially unacceptable desires - the very thing that gives rise to moral codes. They then test the three theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics mostly fails because murder admits no mean and Harry's Code teaches killer's skills rather than virtues (though its 'don't kill innocents' dispositions are genuine virtues); utilitarianism fails even in rule-utilitarian form - via the organ-harvesting doctor and Harry's own utilitarian guilt over Laura Moser's death - because Dexter kills because the Code requires it, not because it maximizes happiness. What fits is dark deontology: like Kant's argument that murderers consent to their own execution out of respect for their rationality, Dexter kills only killers, acts from duty rather than enjoyment, and treats 'don't get caught' as a condition for the possibility of his true imperative.

deontology.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
deontology.title: De-Deontologizing Dexter
deontology.relation: Sultan Ahmed argues Dexter is not really a Kantian deontologist: the urge to kill came first (the teenage animal killings, and his brother Rudy/Brian, who developed the same dark desire without Harry and rationalized it differently), and Harry's Code is a post-hoc rationalization built on top of that desire. Drawing on psychological research (Joshua Greene, Jonathan Haidt) that deontological judgment tends to be emotional rationalization rather than moral reasoning, he reads Dexter's killings as serving emotional needs - the need to control the helplessness of the shipping-container trauma and the Ernest Becker-style need to belong, seen in his bonding with Miguel, Rita, and the kids. Even Dexter's refusals to kill Ellen Wolf or the bound Tony Tucci are framed as feelings and standards, not a sense of moral duty.

deontology.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
deontology.title: Wrapping Up the Case
deontology.relation: Don Fallis organizes the whole canon as a casebook in the epistemology of deception: why characters deceive (concealing crimes like Dr. Roylott's speckled band, committing them like John Clay's Red-Headed League tunnel, Holmes's own smoke-rocket trick on Irene Adler and his faked death at the Reichenbach Falls), how they deceive (Bell and Whaley's hide-the-truth versus show-the-false, unpacked through disguises as masking, repackaging, dazzling, mimicking, inventing and decoying), and how deception is detected, by microexpressions avant la lettre or by inconsistency, as in 'The Problem of Thor Bridge'. Along the way he sorts lying from false implicature (Inspector Baynes's 'I didn't say so'), lies of omission and bald-faced lies, invokes Kant's absolute ban on lying and Augustine's taxonomy of lies, and asks whether Holmes's belief in Moriarty's web, where the absence of evidence counts as evidence, is rational inference or self-deception.

deontology.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
deontology.title: Psych and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue. On Rocha's reading even Kant could endorse the one lie to rule them all - claiming to be psychic - because it respects rationality and human life in a society that irrationally esteems the supernatural, while Shawn's Gus-alias gags and bunny fabrications remain immoral.

deontology.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
deontology.title: Psych and Philosophy
deontology.relation: The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.

deontology.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
deontology.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
deontology.relation: James Edwin Mahon sorts the show's plots by the gap between deed and motive: Patti Nyholm helps save Marjorie Garnett's liver in 'In Sickness' purely to leverage her firm, Lockhart Gardner sues Chumhum in 'Great Firewall' for the mercenary reason Alicia laments, and the Demorys bribe a juror in 'Fixed' out of altruism. Working through Mill's exchange with Llewellyn Davies and Kant's shopkeeper, he argues motives can be good or bad but never right or wrong, and that no good motive makes a wrong action right - Kant denied even a philanthropic right to lie. Hence Alicia's persuading Shen Yuan to lie about his torture, however compassionate, was wrong.

deontology.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
deontology.title: The Devil and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.

deontology.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
deontology.title: Homeland and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Christophe Porot and Charles Taliaferro ask whether Homeland's pervasive hypocrisy and deceit can be justified, starting from Walden's cover-up of the drone strike and Brody's heroic persona hiding a terrorist plot. Machiavelli's Prince supplies the case that political relationships with allies (Saul's 'Us and Them' speech to Carrie) require hypocrisy, while the Smith-inspired 'honest politicking' model - trading openly on self-interest, as with Carrie blackmailing al Sahrani - fails because politics should secure the public good, though la Rochefoucauld's 'homage vice pays virtue' explains Saul extorting the judge into doing right. Weighing Kant's unconditional duty not to lie (Carrie's fatal lie to Lynne Reed) against consequentialism, the chapter lands on the Walzer Dirty Hands view: some acts stay wrong yet necessary, and honest agents accept the guilt.

deontology.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
deontology.title: Homeland and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Robert Arp uses Saul's interrogation of Afsal Hamid (sleep-deprivation via cold, strobe lights, heavy metal) and the good cop/bad cop dynamics of Brody's 'Q&A' interrogation to examine deception in interrogations, including the nine-step Reid technique and its role in false confessions documented by the Innocence Project. He then tests the routine practice of lying to sources against three frameworks: Kant's absolute duty not to lie, Mill-inspired rule utilitarianism, which permits lies when telling truth regularly harms but lets interrogation exceptions serve the greater good, and Aristotle's virtue theory, on which habitual lying makes the agent vicious. Saul's lie about Hamid's family shows why the utilitarian exception dominates in the war on terror.

deontology.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
deontology.title: Homeland and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Dona Cayetana and Nathan Everson argue that 'enhanced interrogation techniques' is a euphemism - with Zizek and Badiou they show relabeling torture as what the West does while 'torture' is what Muslims do conceals identity between the acts, as 'Blind Spot''s safe-house interrogation of Hamid demonstrates. Utilitarianism justifies Saul's fatiguing of Hamid by its results, while the Kantian view that persons must never be mere means condemns it categorically; the chapter contends the show's framing nudges viewers to accept torture as a necessary evil. Carrie's gendered role as Zizek's 'new face of torture' - a pretty white woman whose desirability and perceived vulnerability become interrogation tools, from sex with Brody to 'You broke my heart' - feminizes and normalizes the spectacle.

deontology.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
deontology.title: Homeland and Philosophy
deontology.relation: John Fitzpatrick asks whether anything goes in war, using the FBI's killing of two innocents in the mosque and the ensuing official lie, plus Walden's strike on Issa's school. Truman's Hiroshima utilitarianism (saving lives overall) meets Anscombe's deontology - 'to choose to kill the innocent as a means to their ends is always murder' - before Rawls's social contract supplies a middle path: rules rational parties would agree to behind a veil of ignorance ('we won't kill your children if you don't kill ours'), which condemns both Nazir and Walden since neither faces an 'extreme crisis' like 1940 Britain. Brody's turn is itself Rawlsian: what breaks him is the unfairness of killing children as collateral damage.

deontology.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
deontology.title: Homeland and Philosophy
deontology.relation: William Rodriguez traces terrorism's evolving meaning from the Jacobins' state Terror through anarchist 'propaganda by deed' (Nechayev, Bakunin) to non-state groups, then tests whether Abu Nazir's campaign, grounded in bin Laden's 1998 fatwa grievances and the greater/lesser jihad distinction, can be morally justified. On a utilitarian defense terrorism could be last-resort self-defense against a collectively guilty population, but the just war criteria of competent authority, right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality all fail for al-Qaeda, since civilians killed on 9/11 were neither combatants nor guilty. Deontologically, targeting civilians violates the right to life and human dignity, so Nazir's attacks on innocents are murder, however real the grievances.

deontology.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
deontology.title: Girls and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Sirvent and Avery take Shoshanna's Listen, Ladies! advice book to ask whether rules can govern romance, contrasting Kantian rule-duty ethics (Ray's dating rules that are 'not commandments') with Bentham-Mill utilitarian calculation (Jessa's 'depends on the virgin'). Kierkegaard and Nietzsche - extended through Žižek's Lacanian 'Big Other' of God, Duty, or Utility - show such impersonal systems let us dodge responsibility: Jessa plays Kierkegaard's aesthete escaping boredom, while Hannah's 'just to be an asshole' boss seduction and the Marnie-Elijah hookup express ressentiment and self-hatred. Their positive proposal is Aristotelian virtue ethics - becoming a certain kind of person - completed by Butler's Undoing Gender: to be ethical you must risk being 'undone by each other,' as Adam demands of Hannah ('You don't wanna know me').

deontology.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
deontology.title: Justified and Philosophy
deontology.relation: The chapter juxtaposes the 1992 no-knock raid in which 84-year-old paraplegic Annie Rae Dixon was shot in her bed with Raylan's pilot-episode ultimatum to Tommy Bucks, arguing both deaths count as 'justified' only because aggressive proactive policing manufactured the lethal encounter. It catalogues Raylan's tactics - provoking draws, kidnapping the cartel chief's niece and Dickie Bennett, the lucky-sniper standoff at the Bennett compound - and asks whether we want our police to be judge, jury, and executioner. On the deontological approach Raylan's routine lawbreaking cannot be justified whatever the results, and even on the consequentialist approach the war-on-drugs data (soaring murder rates in targeted neighborhoods, mass incarceration) suggest proactive policing fails on its own terms.

deontology.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
deontology.title: Justified and Philosophy
deontology.relation: The chapter maps the Raylan-Boyd rivalry onto two ethical theories: Raylan is a Kant-style deontologist who does his duty (tracking Tommy Bucks to Miami, weighing duty to the law against duty to Arlo, giving every opponent the choice to walk away), while Boyd is a Mill-style consequentialist maximizing good for himself and Ava, whose vigilante church and revenge plots follow from outcomes rather than rules. Their season-one team-up against Bo Crowder and the Miami shooters is read as contractarianism, two moral agents cooperating toward a right. Each man's choices become his undoing - Raylan's damsel-saving affairs, Mags's family loyalty, Dewey's impulsiveness - which the chapter takes as the show's thesis that what we do results in who we are.

deontology.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
deontology.title: Dracula and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Jordan asks what makes Dracula obey his rules (no entry without an invitation, native soil, garlic, the crucifix) when he obeys no morality: self-imposed Kantian moral rules and a vampire-cabal enforcing Hohfeldian duties both fail because the Count's self-interest is too strong, so the rules must be natural law set by God or nature. He then uses Wesley Hohfeld's jural relations (duty, claim, liberty, power, immunity, liability, disability) to analyze Dracula's rule over his brides, servants, and victims - Lucy's lost consent shifting power and letting the Count through her door - concluding that only this legal-relations analysis plus natural law explains both Dracula's restraints and his apparent violations of physics like defying gravity and commanding the weather.

deontology.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
deontology.title: 8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word
deontology.relation: Neal pits Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Violet's scheme after Sybil's death: the Dowager pressures Dr. Clarkson to 'review the evidence' until he tells Cora and Robert that surgery could not have saved their daughter, reuniting the marriage his honest second opinion had broken. Working through the Categorical Imperative, the murderer-at-the-door case, and Kant's essay 'On a Supposed Right to Lie Because of Philanthropic Concerns,' the chapter asks whether Clarkson actually lied ('Lie is so unmusical a word'). It concludes that his rational, carefully planned, dignity-respecting lie to save the family meets the criteria for a Kantian exception, so the rule against lying still holds while this particular lie is morally permitted.

deontology.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
deontology.title: 5. Office Hours Are for Patients
deontology.relation: Alloy argues that the psychiatric code of ethics - confidentiality with Franklyn ('It would be unethical to approach a patient'), the formal boundaries Lecter scrupulously observes once Will becomes an official patient, and even the oath-violating concealment of Will's encephalitis with Dr. Sutcliffe - is the closest Hannibal can come to friendship, because professional rules artificially manufacture the trust that friends enjoy organically. Working through informed consent, placebo deception, paternalism, and psychiatry's extraordinary power to declare patients incompetent to exercise autonomy at all, he shows the Will-Hannibal relationship cycling through four stages between professional ethics and friendship - 'Office hours are for patients. My kitchen is always open to friends' - while never achieving either, since every display of trust is a manipulation and the power asymmetry never disappears.

deontology.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
deontology.title: Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right
deontology.relation: Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.

deontology.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
deontology.title: 4. Lie or Die
deontology.relation: Hawkes uses Rick's bar confrontation with Dave and Tony in 2.8 'Nebraska' to ask when lying is right, after defining lying through the Governor's white flag at the National Guard camp and Eugene's false cure claim. He rejects moral relativism - the Claimers' rules, Terminus's 'butcher or cattle', the Governor's 'we will do the only thing' - because it forbids criticizing rapists and cannibals and erases moral progress, then finds utilitarianism shaky given Eugene's unforeseen deadly consequences and Rick's refusal to hand Michonne to the Governor at 'Arrow on the Doorpost.' He defends a duty-based deontology in which the duty to protect the farm overrides the duty not to lie, and closes with Robert Kirkman's own lie about an alien invasion that got The Walking Dead published.

deontology.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
deontology.title: 8. Saints and Superheroes
deontology.relation: Malloy uses the two heroes to explain supererogation - Urmson's "Saints and Heroes" puzzle of acts that are praiseworthy but not obligatory, like Batman rushing into burning buildings while Jimmy Olsen is under no duty to follow. Against the utilitarian and deontological denials that anything goes beyond duty (Singer's argument that Clark Kent's designer glasses are money he owes to charity, and Susan Wolf's Loving and Rational Saints whose lives, like Batman's broken retirements in The Dark Knight Returns and Batman Beyond, leave no room for anything worth living), he adopts Raz's view that a duty can be overridden by the moral reason of grave personal risk. Hence Batman's nightly risk-taking is a genuinely heroic choice, while Superman's powers make saving others morally required - so Batman is more truly a hero and Superman "just a good person with the powers of a living god."

deontology.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
deontology.title: 13. Time to Choose
deontology.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.

deontology.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
deontology.title: 21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero
deontology.relation: Devlin asks whether Stannis, who burns Shireen to save his army, is Kierkegaard's knight of faith or merely a tragic hero. Stannis's duty-obsessed deontology - knighting Davos while cutting off his fingertips, striking 'beloved brother' from a letter as a lie - is Kantian, and the Shireen dilemma looks like Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical; yet because Stannis always calculates and justifies ('Faith? In a real war, the side with the greater number wins nine times out of ten'), he never makes the leap on the strength of the absurd, and Davos ends up following Kant's own verdict on Abraham: 'If he commands you to burn children, your lord is evil.' He is therefore a tragic hero in the line of Agamemnon and Jephthah, rationally comprehensible and fittingly undone by Brienne's 'do your duty.'

deontology.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
deontology.title: 9. I Hate Reasons!
deontology.relation: The chapter uses Lucy's worst lectures - birds don't fly south, the wearing-down of the Earth, the telephone-pole tree, piano-career statistics she admits she made up - to catalog adult critical-thinking failures: motivated reasoning, fallacious appeals to authority, suppressed evidence, post hoc, and appeal to superstition, with the kindergarten cast letting us laugh at our own practices without defensiveness. It then argues, with Kant and W.K. Clifford, that we owe each other more than not lying: we owe others assertions backed by evidence, since Lucy's fabricated numbers could crush Schroeder's dream of a musical career just as vaccine misinformation costs society herd immunity. Lucy's vice is a want of intellectual honesty and humility - she wants to know things, but wants to know them now.

deontology.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
deontology.title: 8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be
deontology.relation: Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.

deontology.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
deontology.title: 15. Iron Kant or Captain Kant
deontology.relation: Bosma and Barkman run both heroes' positions on the Superhuman Registration Act and the Sokovia Accords through Kant's deontology. Iron Man's maxim 'I should obey the government' looks universalizable, but it collapses once Cap's critique of the atomic bombings shows an unjust order (killing innocent civilians, or a Doctor Doom takeover) must be refused, and the humanity formulation condemns registration for treating heroes as mere means to the government's ends. Cap's own maxims - fight for freedom and justice, obey only a just government - universalize cleanly, so the chapter awards the deontological duel to Captain America.

deontology.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
deontology.title: Keep a Little Soul
deontology.relation: Section introduction to the ethics chapters, framed by Petty’s October 2017 death: it argues his real achievement was working to be timeless — the shelved 1982 outtake “Keep a Little Soul” sounding native in 2018 — and that he “lived what he believed,” chasing dreams despite guaranteed heartache, refusing to explain his songs, and standing up to record-company executives. It closes by describing Petty’s political thought as “a deontology that puts duty to the fans first,” invokes Nietzsche as appreciating the gesture of turning the volume up rather than snoozing through the Reagan years, and sketches the volume’s five philosophical “buds”: epistemology, aesthetics, ontology, and two ethics chapters on the outcast and heartbroken as redeemable antiheroes of the everyday.

deontology.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
deontology.title: 15. Chidi’s Indecision
deontology.relation: Vannatta argues Chidi's indecision exposes the shared flaw of the Big Three theories, Kantian deontology, Bentham and Mill's consequentialism, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of the golden mean: their rationalism pretends moral conflict can be eliminated by applying the correct rule, when Chidi's trolley terror shows moral situations are experienced as genuinely uncertain. Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals', the Good of desire, the Right of duty, and the Virtuous of communal praise, legitimizes that felt uncertainty and explains Eleanor's talent for finding option C between binary dilemmas. The chapter concludes that the show's real, unspoken moral theory is care ethics: partiality, relationship maintenance, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as Eleanor learns from Chidi's friendship rather than his lectures.

deontology.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
deontology.title: 1. Rights and Wrongs of Reversing the Snap
deontology.relation: Philip Mouch weighs consequences against rights to ask whether the Avengers were wrong to undo the Snap in Endgame. He imagines a survivor whose returned spouse finds her remarried, cataloguing displaced families, food shortages, and political turmoil, and argues these harms, however real, are outweighed by restoring the lives Thanos took. The deeper problem is Bruce Banner's wager with the Ancient One: removing the Time Stone dooms a branch reality on a 1-in-14,000,605 chance, gambling innocent lives without their consent, which resembles Thanos's non-consensual sacrifice of Gamora rather than the noble self-sacrifice of Hawkeye and Black Widow on Vormir. He concludes that two wrongs do not make a right: even for a noble end, risking countless lives tramples the rights of others.

deontology.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
deontology.title: 9. With Infinite Power Comes No Responsibility
deontology.relation: James Hart casts Tony Stark as a consequentialist and Steve Rogers as a deontologist, then argues Endgame's infinite stakes destroy Tony's morality through Nick Bostrom's 'infinitarian paralysis': in an infinite multiverse every act leaves the balance of happy and sad lives unchanged, as an infinite Stark orphanage rearranged Hilbert's-Hotel style shows, and even genocide becomes permissible so long as infinitely many remain alive. Tony's attempted fixes each fail: the causal approach collapses because reversing the Snap has infinite butterfly effects, expected value (credited to Frank Jackson) runs into Pascal's Mugging and an 'infinitarian trance' demanding suicidal bets on any chance of infinite value, and Bostrom's 'infinity shades' that filter tiny probabilities would blind Tony to the one-in-a-trillion time-heist chance he should take. The chapter concludes there is no consequentialist way to say when wagering lives on infinite stakes is ethical, and Iron Man should let Captain America lead.

deontology.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
deontology.title: 1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy
deontology.relation: Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.

deontology.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
deontology.title: 2. A Paragon of Righteous Virtue
deontology.relation: Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.

deontology.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
deontology.title: Olympic Tetherball A Final Lesson on Moral Frailty
deontology.relation: The chapter asks whether Kenneth the page is a Kantian rule absolutist who never makes exceptions, or an Aristotelian 'contextual absolutist' who sees that the right act depends on circumstances, as when he runs the Hill Witch ruse to scare Tracy into eating well. Jack's lifeboat hypothetical and rigged-elevator test bounce off Kenneth's refusal to believe in hypothetical situations, but Jack's gift of illegal cable exposes Kenneth's moral frailty when he enjoys the stolen channels. It concludes that Kenneth's gullibility, trust, and loyalty make his simple moral vision both admirable and easily corrupted, and that the real lesson is facing our failures with resolve rather than shame.

deontology.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
deontology.title: Special Order 937—Crew Expendable
deontology.relation: Reads Weyland-Yutani as 'greed is good' cost-benefit reasoning embodied by Ash, Mother, and Burke (Gordon Gekko's Wall Street speech transplanted into space), and asks who can be held accountable when every employee fills only a narrow role and scapegoats absorb blame. It then weighs Kantian deontology - Bishop's inviolable no-harm rules, the absolute wrongness of killing crew for profit - against utilitarian reasoning: Ripley's quarantine refusal to save the many, Parker's refusal to flame the alien holding Lambert, and the uncomfortable thought that acquiring the Xenomorph might genuinely benefit billions.

deontology.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
deontology.title: What if Hama Was Wrong
deontology.relation: Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily uses persons as mere means because it overrides the victim's will regardless of their actual consent, unlike buying tea from Zuko but like Azula's deception of Long Feng, and so violates Kant's Formula of Humanity in every offensive use. Katara's bloodbending of Hama in self-defense is permissible because she stops Hama's wrong rather than using her toward any end, and even a hypothetical consensual 'cooperative model' cannot redeem the practice, since the sheer power it grants and its corrupting effects on practitioners (Noatak and Tarrlok in LoK) justify Katara's ban.

deontology.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
deontology.title: What if Hama Was Wrong
deontology.relation: Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily violates Kant's Formula of Humanity: controlling the water in another body 'enforcing your own will over theirs,' as Hama puts it, uses a person as a mere means because the bender's maxim ignores the victim's actual consent, even when a victim happens to consent, as in the Ozai medical-experiment analogy. Katara's vengeful bloodbending of Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' is therefore impermissible, while her restraint of Hama uses no one as a means at all since it only halts a rights violation. Even if a cooperative, consent-based bloodbending were possible, Katara's Republic City ban is defensible, because the standing power to override wills corrupts practitioners, as Noatak's and Tarrlok's downward spiral in LoK shows.

deontology.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
deontology.title: Ethicists Assemble!
deontology.relation: White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.

deontology.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
deontology.title: And the war Rages on
deontology.relation: Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.

deontology.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
deontology.title: “This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”
deontology.relation: Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.

deontology.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
deontology.title: So, Case Closed-Right
deontology.relation: Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.

deontology.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
deontology.title: Batman Forever
deontology.relation: Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.

deontology.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
deontology.title: Walking the Tightrope
deontology.relation: Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.

deontology.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
deontology.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.

deontology.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
deontology.title: “King of space, right here!”
deontology.relation: The chapter asks whether Robert Daly wrongs the USS Callister NPCs even if they are 'merely' sentient code: his theft of co-workers' DNA violates a fundamental right to privacy, and Kant's focus on the will shows his in-game intentions aim at real people — he logs in solely to strangle James's NPC and make him confess to being pathetic, wanting to harm the actual James. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the second indictment: because hyperrealistic VR blurs game and life, Daly's daily practice of cruelty habituates vice and makes cruelty part of who he is, unlike clearly fictional violence such as Mortal Kombat. Merleau-Ponty's intentionality links avatar actions to the self, so the chapter ends by asking what our own intentions in games like The Sims or Grand Theft Auto reveal about our character.

deontology.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
deontology.title: The Bill Comes Due
deontology.relation: The chapter uses Michael Walzer's Problem of Dirty Hands to weigh the Ancient One's secret lifelong use of forbidden dark magic against Kaecilius's summoning of Dormammu, arguing that only she faces a genuine dirty-hands dilemma because her end (defending Earth) is good while his is not. It asks why dark magic is forbidden at all and answers with rule-utilitarian reasoning that has taken on a deontological life of its own, then invokes Kant's murderer-at-the-door essay to argue, with Mordo's 'the bill comes due,' that whoever does wrong for good ends bears responsibility for the downstream consequences—and that Strange's willingness to break Kamar-Taj's rules while accepting the cost is what makes him a hero.

deontology.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
deontology.title: 8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word
deontology.relation: Neal weighs Dr. Clarkson's coached retraction, that surgery would not have saved Sybil after all, engineered by Violet with 'Lie is so unmusical a word' to end Cora's blame of Robert and reunite the grieving couple, against Kant's absolute prohibition on lying in his moral works and in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie.' She lays out Kant's reasoning that lying destroys the trust, dignity, and rights that make rules binding, with the murderer-at-the-door case as the classic objection, then argues Clarkson's lie approaches an exception because it is rational, carefully deliberated, and aimed at preserving the Crawleys' dignity and the household itself rather than personal gain. The chapter concludes that the Kantian rule still holds generally, but this particular lie, for this particular moral reason, can be excused.

deontology.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
deontology.title: 14. Things Can Happen that Nobody Could Imagine Only a Few Years Ago
