deontology.relation: Donna Marie Smith reads the series through Hegel's philosophy of history: the Crawleys' world is a clash of opposing forces - Lord Grantham's traditionalism against Matthew's and Branson's modernization, Violet's fear of electricity against Sybil's and Rose's embrace of the new - and this very conflict drives progress toward greater freedom. She uses Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right both to explain the entail and primogeniture that bar Mary from inheriting (the law preserves the 'house' over the immediate family, which Hegel calls an infringement of the freedom of property) and to frame Robert's refusal to challenge it as duty to his social standing outweighing personal wishes. WWI, which Hegel experienced through Napoleon's occupation of Jena, is presented as a 'march toward freedom' that breaks down class barriers and finally pushes Robert to accept change on the estate: 'Let's give it a go and see what the future brings.'

deontology.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
deontology.title: 16. Female Integrity in Times of Change
deontology.relation: Melanie Abbott tests Bernard Williams's account of integrity - publicly and consistently standing up for the beliefs that make you you - merged with Kant's claim that only a good will is good without limitation, against five Crawley women across three generations. Sybil elopes with the socialist chauffeur Branson and never wavers in her egalitarian convictions, Edith's secrecy about her baby fails Williams's openness condition, Mary grows from custom-bound heiress into an estate manager who stands up to Robert over selling land, Cora chafes at the voice she surrendered as an American heiress, and even Violet eventually bends. The chapter's guiding question is how much truth and openness integrity requires, and it credits 'the Sybil effect' with spreading proper integrity through the whole family.

deontology.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
deontology.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.

deontology.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
deontology.title: 15. Chidi’s Indecision
deontology.relation: Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.

deontology.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
deontology.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Tallman and Southworth set the Hippocratic Oath against the Green Lantern oath in Soranik Natu, a Korugarian surgeon who must either stop healing mid-battle or disobey the Book of Oa. They survey the options, with Wonder Woman discarding vows for consequences, Isamot Kol letting the Corps trump his vow to Qalyra, Dr. Mid-Nite always putting patients first, and Dick Grayson going by context, then argue through Hursthouse that Natu, who treats both oaths as absolute, is in an irresolvable dilemma of her own making, more like the double-betrothed man than Williams's tragic Jim and the twenty Indians. Their verdict is that she should turn in the ring, a cautionary tale for real military medics whose oaths also collide.

deontology.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
deontology.title: How Revealing Are Our Choices
deontology.relation: The chapter builds on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of choice (prohairesis) as 'deliberative desire' for things within our power and a better test of character than actions, then distinguishes three senses of choice. Internal-choice is Draco deciding but failing to kill Dumbledore; act-choice is Dumbledore's poor youthful choices; and motive-choice is captured by Kant's two shopkeepers who both refuse to cheat customers, one from fear of jail and one from honesty, so that only knowing the motive reveals the choice's moral worth.

deontology.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
deontology.title: NOTES
deontology.relation: Miles asks whether extraordinary power generates extraordinary obligations, testing Spider-Man's 'with great power comes great responsibility' against Claude the invisible thief and the heroes' reluctance. He uses Singer's principle of minimal obligation (Micah diverting the train from the infant; Claire's negligible risk in burning-building rescues; Hiro teleporting across distance) and Kant's perfect/imperfect obligation distinction (Niki choosing between saving Monica and mothering Micah; Noah Bennet lying to protect Claire) before deploying Fishkin's three 'explosion' objections: too many endangered people, too many capable heroes, and too many repeated rescues dilute obligation. He concludes the heroes went beyond the call of duty in saving New York, so saving the world could legitimately be their paid job, like lifeguards or soldiers.

deontology.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
deontology.title: Notes
deontology.relation: Uses Sartre's play Dirty Hands and Walzer's 'Political Action: The Problem of Dirty Hands' to ask whether Frank's willingness to do the 'necessary thing' — from the opening mercy-killing of the dog to the Season 3 drone strike — could ever count in favor of an Underwood presidency, with utilitarians (nothing wrong with dirty hands) and absolutists like the bishop ('Love God, and love each other. Period.') dissolving the problem from opposite sides. Walzer's later 'supreme emergency' standard and threshold deontology frame the Jordan Valley staring contest with Petrov and the resulting deal as the one case where Frank's capability might genuinely matter, while Heather Dunbar's reluctance (her refusal of Stamper's offer of Claire's diary, then her reversal) tests the ideal of a leader both capable of and averse to dirtying her hands. The verdict: Frank's only advantage over Dunbar is his capacity for dirty hands, and even that fails because he lacks the scruples to keep them clean when it is not necessary.

deontology.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
deontology.title: 4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative
deontology.relation: Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.

deontology.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
deontology.title: Notes
deontology.relation: Robson argues that The Man Upstairs' real moral flaw is neither stinginess toward Finn nor mere instruction-following, both of which he defends, but 'rule worship': treating LEGO construction instructions — rules with at best conventional status like chess or etiquette rules — as sacrosanct commandments to be followed for their own sake. The contrast is with Kant, who does claim absolute status for central moral rules such as the prohibition on lying, and with the moral/conventional distinction from psychologists like Kelly and Stich that The Man cannot grasp. Emmet's rule-following differs because it serves goals like fitting in, and the flaw scales from office Micromanagers and Velma Staplebot to Inspector Javert and the mafioso, showing how misdirected rule worship becomes genuinely vicious.

deontology.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
deontology.title: The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
deontology.relation: Charles Joshua Horn asks whether power belongs beside wisdom and courage in the Triforce. Kant's good will shows all three pieces are morally neutral — Link and Zelda act from duty rather than reward, so courage and wisdom could be misused just as easily as Ganondorf misuses power. Plato's Ring of Gyges shows power does not automatically corrupt (Ganondorf chose to steal the Triforce for the Gerudo), and Socrates's answer to Glaucon explains why Ganondorf's ill-gotten wealth and honor leave him morally bankrupt. Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then gives the goddesses' intended use: Link's courage sits between cowardice and rashness (he gathers map, compass, and weapon before the boss room), Zelda's wisdom is really prudence, and Ganondorf's vice is power in excess.

deontology.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
deontology.title: NOTES
deontology.relation: Becky Vartabedian applies W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethic of prima facie duties to Michael: at the dock his actual duty of beneficence toward the kidnapped Walt overrides fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, but does not erase his responsibility for Ana Lucia's and Libby's murders. Because Ross requires amends rather than giving a blank check, the chapter asks whether Michael's spying as 'Kevin Johnson' aboard the Kahana - culminating in giving Jin time to escape the bomb - repairs his wrongs, or whether Walt's rejection and Michael's exile from the closing church scene show he failed to make things right on the terms of those he wronged.

deontology.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
deontology.title: “The Wrong Direction”
deontology.relation: Barkman builds a definition of lying (communicating what one believes false while hiding that fact, with intent to hurt or disrespect, which distinguishes mere deception and parts ways with Aquinas's blanket ban) and applies it to five advertising worries, from bags of chips designed to invite false inference to the Belle Jolie 'promise' no one actually believes and the Israeli Tourism ad that omits danger. Persuasion is legitimate because rational souls are equals to be treated as ends (Aristotle's justice), but manipulation (ads aimed at preschoolers that use children to pressure parents) and fear-preying coercion (Clearasil on insecure teenagers, nylons to unmarried women like Rachel Menken) treat people as means, while government must regulate factually (FDA 'smoking kills' labels) without overriding adult choice. Responsibility is then distributed across producer, agency, media, public, and state, and Don was indeed 'looking in the wrong direction' in this sense: being able to talk anyone into anything does not mean he should.

deontology.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
deontology.title: Ride the Lightning: Why Not Execute Killers?
deontology.relation: Thom Brooks uses 'Ride the Lightning' - the condemned man in the electric chair pleading 'Who made you God to say / I'll take your life from you!' - to examine capital punishment. He presents Kantian retributivism (execution as the only proportional punishment for murder) and then argues against it: the condemned 'dies twice', living for years under a ritualized death sentence that Glover calls cruel, deterrence fails (the brutalization effect), and public justice must not become private vengeance - so even the guilty prisoner in the song is right that we have no right to kill him.

deontology.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
deontology.title: Metallica Drops a Load: What Do Bands and Fans Owe Each Other?
deontology.relation: Mark White asks whether Metallica wronged its longtime fans by changing style on Load, using Kant's duty ethics. No duty to keep their thrash style survives the categorical imperative - a world where every band changes style is horrible but not contradictory - and Kantian duties to the band members' families, employees, and to their own talents and authenticity actually support the change. Symmetrically, fans' loyalty is only an imperfect duty with wiggle room: it is owed in return for the band's loyalty to its metal values, and lapses when the motivation is mere commercial sell-out.

deontology.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
deontology.title: The Office and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Weighs the morality of Jim and Pam's workplace flirting (while Pam is engaged to Roy) using three ethical frameworks: act utilitarianism has them tot up their own happiness against effects on co-workers' morale and Dunder-Mifflin's bottom line; rule utilitarianism models HR's blanket anti-dating policies and asks whether Jim and Pam could justify an exception without destroying the rule (the Hawaiian shirt day analogy); deontology searches for duties against office romance (favoritism in evaluation, distraction from duties) and finds none once harassment is set aside, concluding that in the absence of a deontological prohibition, Jim and Pam may keep flirting until 5 p.m.

deontology.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
deontology.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
deontology.relation: White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.

deontology.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
deontology.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'

deontology.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
deontology.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
deontology.relation: Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.

deontology.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
deontology.title: “Rebellions Are Built on Hope!”
deontology.relation: Eberl asks whether Galen Erso, who knowingly resumed work on the Death Star while planting its exhaust-port flaw, is culpable for the deaths on Jedha, Scarif, and Alderaan. A utilitarian defense (his flaw net-saved the galaxy, per the negative-responsibility principle applied to the Death Star II 'Clerks' debate) founders on moral luck — everything depended on Luke's impossible shot — while Bernard Williams's integrity objection, via the chemist 'George' case, condemns his betrayal of conscience. The chapter finally deploys Thomistic tools for cooperation with evil: because Galen's contribution was mediate and remote (Tarkin ordered the firing, the gunners pulled the triggers, Leia's defiance provoked Alderaan's destruction) and the weapon would have been built without him, his collusion is justified by the reasonable hope — the 'new hope' — of the Death Star's destruction.

deontology.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
deontology.title: 8. Saints and Superheroes
deontology.relation: Alloy uses supererogation — Urmson's saints-and-heroes puzzle — to separate the heroes: utilitarianism (via Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality, where even Clark's novelty glasses are stolen from charity) and deontology both erase acts that are good but not required, and Susan Wolf's moral saints show where that lands — a Bruce Wayne with no hobbies, friends, or life, like Astro City's Samaritan. Alloy's own Raz-style fix (requirements overridden by moral permitting reasons) yields the verdict: Batman risks his life by choice and so is a true hero, while Superman, facing no real danger, merely does what his powers make morally required — 'a good person with the powers of a living god'.

deontology.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
deontology.title: 13. Time to Choose
deontology.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.

deontology.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
deontology.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.

deontology.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
deontology.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
deontology.relation: Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.

deontology.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
deontology.title: Notes
deontology.relation: Kowalski applies Kant's ethics to the Aes Sedai Three Oaths in the Amazon series, arguing that because the Oath Rod makes sisters physically unable to lie, 'ought implies can' means they get no moral credit for truth-telling, like praising water for freezing. He examines acting from duty versus according to duty (few Aes Sedai accept the Oaths for the right reason; Moiraine may be the exception), and the universal-law formulation against lying promises. He then presses Kant's absolutism through Moiraine's careful literal truths to the Whitecloak Valda ('I have a sister in Whitebridge'), arguing that Kant's own 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' and Schopenhauer's self-defense objection show WoT can talk back to Kant about conflicting duties.

deontology.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
deontology.title: Notes
deontology.relation: Bein uses the 'kill baby Hitler' time-machine puzzle and the question of whether Moiraine and Lan should still the Dragon Reborn to probe the Aes Sedai's mysterious ethics. He argues they are not Kantian deontologists (the Three Oaths are loose plot-device rules Moiraine games with ambiguous innuendo, and Kant forbids treating the ferryman as mere means) and are bad consequentialists at best (they cannot lightning-bolt Valda or Hitler who are not Darkfriends). He proposes they are closest to Buddhist ethics: wise compassion good in itself (Tam sitting with dying Tigraine regardless of outcome), and reads the flexible Oaths through upaya (skillful means) and a WoT-adapted Eightfold Path, making them less pacifist nuns than violence-reducing Shaolin nuns.

deontology.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
deontology.title: Notes
deontology.relation: White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.

deontology.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
deontology.title: Notes
deontology.relation: Barkman and Tokbergenova defend 'just torture': Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations of Captain Nazi, the double agent Marcia in the 1970s pilot (saving the Brooklyn Navy Yard's 70,000 workers), and the terrorist Nikos Aegeus are ticking-bomb cases of the sort Henry Shue concedes, and the authors answer Luban's slippery-slope objection with absolute limits (never the innocent or the family) and Dershowitz-style torture warrants. Citing Aristotle's Rhetoric that coerced testimony is often false, they propose trained professional torturers, and conclude that since the right thing is not always the ideal thing, torture should be legalized, rare, and conducted openly - as Wonder Woman models.

deontology.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
deontology.title: III - IS SUICIDE ALWAYS IMMORAL JEAN GREY, IMMANUELKANT, AND THE DARK PHOENIX SAGA
deontology.relation: White asks whether Jean Grey's suicide at the end of The Dark Phoenix Saga can be moral. After finding virtue ethics mostly hostile and utilitarianism hostage to circumstances, he turns to Kant: the categorical imperative's formulas condemn suicide as using one's person as a mere means, yet Kant's own Metaphysics of Morals concedes a case, a man bitten by a mad dog who kills himself before his madness can harm others, that maps exactly onto possession by the Phoenix Force. Drawing on Thomas E. Hill Jr.'s Kantian account of suicide as a final autonomous act, he reads Jean's dialogue with Scott as her choosing death as the author of her life story, preserving her autonomy rather than letting Dark Phoenix kill five billion more people.

deontology.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
deontology.title: XII - DIRTY HAN DS AN D DIRTY MINDS THE ETHICS OF MIND READING AND MINDWRITING
deontology.relation: Terjesen examines whether telepaths can be trusted, starting epistemically: Descartes' problem of other minds and Russell's analogy answer explain how Xavier's football-field telepathy and the Cuckoos' exoneration of Beak could be verified, and how far Jean's telepathic testimony about Cassandra Nova should be acted on. Utilitarians (Mill) and deontologists then split over mindwriting: Xavier's early memory erasures, the permanent rewrite of a terrorist's personality, and the Magneto mindwipe versus Cyclops and Emma's 'telepathic affair' and Jean's ransacking of Emma's memories, where privacy and intimacy are at stake. Invoking Machiavelli and Walzer, the chapter concludes Xavier's dirty hands are necessary but wrong, so he should feel guilt and step down, lest mindreading mutants become the thing humans rightly fear.

deontology.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
deontology.title: To Hack or Not to Hack
deontology.relation: Kennedy asks how a great player like Kareem (the NBA's career foul leader) can be excellent while fouling so much, and answers that deontology (Kant's categorical imperative) and utilitarianism (Mill's greatest-happiness principle) can condemn dangerous 'goon' fouling but cannot explain why the legal Hack-a-Shaq strategy still feels 'clownish.' Invoking Shaq's self-nickname 'the Big Aristotle,' he argues Aristotelian virtue ethics fits better: the excellent player, like the person of good character, perceives the situation rightly and fouls (or risks a foul) at the right time in the right way, so excellence is a habit of seeing well rather than rule-following.

deontology.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
deontology.title: 5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds
deontology.relation: The Phillipses argue that abrasive forensic agent Albert Rosenfield is a model Kantian: his refusal to lie to spare Truman's feelings follows the formula of universal law, and his insistence that Truman be punished for the assault treats Truman as an autonomous end. They run Gordon Cole's manipulative lying through the universalizability test (it fails, unlike wanting pie), distinguish hypothetical from categorical imperatives via Cooper's rebuff of Audrey, and read Albert's 'I love you, Sheriff Truman' and Gandhi/King nonviolence as respect for persons as ends in themselves—duty done for the right reason.

deontology.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
deontology.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
deontology.relation: Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.

deontology.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
deontology.title: Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization
deontology.relation: Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.

deontology.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
deontology.title: The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing
deontology.relation: Silberstein reads Do the Right Thing as staging the ideological dialectic between Martin Luther King Jr.'s absolute nonviolence and Malcolm X's defense of retaliatory self-defense, both grounded in a theologically informed natural-law view of rights (King's Christian imago dei, X's Islamic tradition). He argues King mixes a deontological ethic (violence is always wrong) with a Gandhian consequentialist claim that violence begets violence, while X frames a race war as a just holy war. The film's Radio Raheem (LOVE/HATE knuckles), Buggin' Out's boycott of Sal's Wall of Fame, the Racial Slur Montage, and Mookie throwing the trash can dramatize whether ends justify means; the closing Sal-Mookie money exchange reframes racism as symptom of a deeper capitalist greed both King and X came to critique.

deontology.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
deontology.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
deontology.relation: Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.

deontology.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
deontology.title: The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon
deontology.relation: Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.

deontology.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
deontology.title: The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident
deontology.relation: Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.

deontology.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
deontology.title: No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)
deontology.relation: William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'

deontology.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
deontology.title: The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller
deontology.relation: Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.

deontology.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
deontology.title: 10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care
deontology.relation: Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.

deontology.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
deontology.title: Allons-y into the Starry Heavens
deontology.relation: Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.

deontology.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
deontology.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
deontology.relation: Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.

deontology.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
deontology.title: 8. Which Brother Is the Good One
deontology.relation: Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.

deontology.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
deontology.title: 9. God the Programmer Is Dead
deontology.relation: De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.

deontology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
deontology.title: 1. Scamming for Fun
deontology.relation: Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.

deontology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
deontology.title: 20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong
deontology.relation: The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.

deontology.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
deontology.title: 21. Finding the Good in Nacho
deontology.relation: The chapter uses Kant to argue that Nacho Varga, though a genuinely bad drug dealer, can perform morally worthy acts in isolated moments. Because Kant locates morality in the rational will and intention rather than accomplishment, it treats Nacho's attempts on the Salamancas and his desire to leave the game as evidence of active moral reasoning, while conceding his motives are muddied by self-interest and love for his father (the shopkeeper example warns against acts done for loved ones). Its clean case is the phone call in 'Something Unforgivable,' where Nacho risks everything to plead for Lalo's near-innocent staff, doing the right thing purely because it is right.

deontology.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
deontology.title: 15. Morality and Manipulation
deontology.relation: Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.

deontology.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
deontology.title: 16. Psycho-historian or Psycho Historian
deontology.relation: Bellantoni asks what Seldon owes future generations, pitting moral presentism against his 'mystical' identification with humanity (echoing Scheffler's Why Worry about Future Generations?). She tests the Seldon Plan under Bentham's hedonic calculus—finding time-discounting and uncertainty about what follows the thirty-thousand-year interregnum undercut it—and under Kantian deontology, arguing Seldon's mass manipulation of Gaal Dornick, his inquisitors, and the Encyclopedists treats people merely as means and violates their autonomy. Weighing longtermism against Whitehead's claim (in Adventures of Ideas) that civilizations must die to seed new ones, she suggests Seldon's engineered revival of a spent civilization may itself be a barbaric imposition on future people who would not choose it.

deontology.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
deontology.title: So, Case Closed – Right
deontology.relation: White asks why Batman won't kill the Joker, framing it through utilitarianism (killing one to save the Joker's many future victims) versus deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences). Using Foot and Thomson's trolley and transplant cases, plus agent-neutral versus agent-relative rules, he notes key disanalogies: the Joker is not a moral innocent but the very cause of the danger, which pushes toward killing him. But because future killings are only probable, doing so would be 'prepunishment,' and White, a self-described deontologist, concludes it is genuinely hard to say Batman is right, though he admires the restraint.

deontology.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
deontology.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
deontology.relation: Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.

deontology.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
deontology.title: It’s Not That Simple
deontology.relation: Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.

deontology.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
deontology.title: NOTES
deontology.relation: Becky Vartabedian uses W. D. Ross's agent-specific ethics of prima facie duties to evaluate Michael's betrayal at the dock. She lays out Ross's six duties—fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, noninjury—and argues Michael's role as Walt's father makes beneficence his 'actual duty,' overriding fidelity and noninjury to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer. Because overridden duties do not vanish, Michael incurs guilt and owes amends (he is also implicated in the deaths of Libby and Ana Lucia), which Ross calls the 'moral risk' of choosing between competing prima facie duties; Locke's refusal to push the button is read as a duty of self-improvement whose rightness still depends on the intervening facts.

deontology.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
deontology.title: Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax
deontology.relation: Alexander contrasts Dewey's reflective, character-centered ethics with utilitarianism and Kantian deontology using the Lorax and Horton. The Once-ler is cast as the shortsighted 'utilitarian' maximizing Thneed happiness while the Lorax, urging us to 'stop and think' about the whole ecosystem, is really a Deweyan practicing reflective morality and deliberation as 'dramatic rehearsal.' Horton's conscientious care for the Whos illustrates Dewey's 'Who Factor' and growth of character rather than cold rule-following, showing morality as the ongoing education of desire toward inclusive, shared ends.

deontology.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
deontology.title: MOTHERHOOD
deontology.relation: Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.

deontology.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
deontology.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
deontology.relation: Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.

deontology.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
deontology.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
deontology.relation: Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.

deontology.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
deontology.title: Who is Who
deontology.relation: This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.

deontology.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
deontology.title: So, Case Closed – Right
deontology.relation: Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.

deontology.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
deontology.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
deontology.relation: J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.

deontology.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
deontology.title: It’s Not That Simple
deontology.relation: O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.

deontology.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
deontology.title: 9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom
deontology.relation: Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.

deontology.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
deontology.title: 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain
deontology.relation: Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

deontology.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
deontology.title: 4. The Good of the Doctor
deontology.relation: The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

utopia-dystopia.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
utopia-dystopia.title: 11 - The Simpsons Atomistic Politics and the Nuclear Family
utopia-dystopia.relation: Paul Cantor argues that beneath the satire The Simpsons affirms the nuclear family: the foster-care episode, where the children go to the Flanderses and Homer and Marge to a 'family skills class', shows they belong with their real parents not for piety or child-rearing expertise but because of attachment to one's own—against both the therapeutic nanny state and Flanders-style self-righteous religiosity. He connects this defense of the family to Springfield as a classical polis of local, accessible institutions (Skinner, Wiggum, Quimby, even locally produced Itchy & Scratchy), where distrust of remote power cuts across party lines. The Mensa utopia episode serves as a comic refutation of Plato's philosopher-kings—Homer leads the 'counterrevolution of the stupid' and Stephen Hawking pronounces that 'the smartest of us can be the most childish'—echoing Nietzsche's remark that Kant defended the common man against the learned.

utopia-dystopia.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
utopia-dystopia.title: Unknown
utopia-dystopia.relation: Reading Cypher's betrayal through Kant's Highest Good - the duty to create a world combining freedom and happiness - the chapter shows Cypher concluding from the controllers' overwhelming power that the crew's Zion is a mythical Promised Land: 'Free? All I do is what he tells me to do.' Trinity's reply, 'The Matrix isn't real!', is judged too shallow, and Cypher's counter that 'the Matrix could be more real than this world... there, you have to watch Apoc die' exposes that the initial contrast between illusion and reality is only the film's starting point - what captivates is life within the Matrix once its true nature is understood.

utopia-dystopia.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
utopia-dystopia.title: Unknown
utopia-dystopia.relation: The chapter reads the film through Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground, a satire of Chernyshevsky's rationalist-utopian What Is to Be Done?: the underground man sees that social science's 'logarithm' of desire reduces us to piano keys governed by natural law, and responds with hyperconscious spite, inertia, and the deliberate choice of the harmful to prove he can will - anticipating Nietzsche's claim that humans would 'rather will nothing than not will'. Shigalyov's 'starting from unlimited freedom, I conclude with unlimited despotism' names the Enlightenment's contradiction, and the underground man's life is the reductio ad nihilum of theories his opponents only dare carry halfway.

utopia-dystopia.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
utopia-dystopia.title: Unknown
utopia-dystopia.relation: The chapter aligns the Nebuchadnezzar with the underground man's cell: in the 'desert of the real' the rebels begin from Morpheus's felt 'something is wrong' and live the quest ('it's the question that drives us') that The X-Files-style paranoia cannot complete, risking either permanent entrapment or Mark Edmundson's 'facile transcendence'. It contrasts Neo's shallow freedom-as-control ('No... because then I wouldn't be in control') with Morpheus's providential fate, reads Cypher as consciously relinquishing willing for comfort, and likens the Matrix's project of changing 'the human being into a battery' to Diderot's piano-key man and Agent Smith's utopian 'we're the cure'.

utopia-dystopia.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
utopia-dystopia.title: Unknown
utopia-dystopia.relation: The chapter reads the film's ending—Neo the savior teaching people to bend the rules of a Matrix they never exit, while remaining batteries—as combining utopia with dystopia, reversing the old sci-fi longing (Zardoz, Logan's Run) for escape into reality. The true image is millions of fetus-like humans whose utter passivity is the foreclosed fantasy sustaining our active self-experience: the Matrix feeds on our jouissance, which is why it needs human energy at all, and Adorno and Horkheimer's chloroform fragment—pain fully felt but not remembered—figures this inter-passivity. The film's insight is the two sides of perversion: rule-bending virtual freedom concealing instrumentalized passivity.

utopia-dystopia.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
utopia-dystopia.title: The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization
utopia-dystopia.relation: Simon Clark reads Romero's four Dead films through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the zombie is the return of the repressed, the ripped-out instinctual life of a civilization that demands work, and it multiplies exactly as humans (Stephen defending the mall, Ben fighting Mr. Cooper) lapse into unlawful self-gratification. The bite unites Eros and Thanatos - an erotic, engorged cannibalism that also regresses victims to rotting matter, which Clark glosses with Creed's vagina dentata. He then argues Day of the Dead's beach ending (John fishing, Sarah at peace) stages Marcuse's non-repressive civilization where work becomes play and liberated sexuality rejoins Eros, while Land of the Dead goes further: the evolved, tool-using zombies led by Big Daddy are the martyrs who actually found Marcuse's impossible pleasurable community, leaving living humans still fenced inside repression.

utopia-dystopia.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
utopia-dystopia.title: Violence Against Utopia
utopia-dystopia.relation: Drumin reads Sabotage as Hitchcock's anti-utopian statement: against perfectible societies imagined from Plato's Republic to Skinner, Freud and Dostoyevsky show that the psyche's attraction to chaos cannot be planned or conditioned away. In four scenes, the aquarium meeting where 'monsters from the Id' watch over Verloc's bomb deal, the bird shop where explosives sit among a child's toys, the conspiracy hatched behind a movie screen whose audience laughs at on-screen chaos, and Stevie's death on the bus, the film shows a quiet family man rationalizing mass murder by 'abstracting' its victims into a mere list of names. Hitchcock punishes the audience too, implicating its own safe enjoyment of represented violence, and concludes that only constant individual vigilance, never social engineering, keeps the potential for chaos in check.

utopia-dystopia.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
utopia-dystopia.title: Caring Dogs Watching Flying Pigs
utopia-dystopia.relation: Croskery reads Animals as a beast fable in the tradition of Orwell's Animal Farm that opens with a thought experiment ('If you didn't care what happened to me / And I didn't care for you') and portrays a world without empathy across three corruptible institutions. 'Dogs' dramatizes a malfunctioning marketplace where Adam Smith's invisible-hand justification fails, since success requires lying to those you must trust and ends with the sad old man 'dragged down by the stone'; 'Pigs (3 Different Ones)' targets state corruption from Mary Whitehouse's censorship crusade to war-waging and regulatory capture; and 'Sheep' depicts Marxist false consciousness, the pastoral illusion hiding the slaughterhouse, capped by the Twenty-Third Psalm parody that 'converteth me to lamb cutlets.' The chapter concludes that libertarian, statist, and traditionalist errors each idolize one institution, and that Waters's closing 'Pigs on the Wing' points to the delicate balance of market, state, and community that political philosophy must strike.

utopia-dystopia.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
utopia-dystopia.title: Paradise Found
utopia-dystopia.relation: Brown reads The Minish Cap's Hyrule as a working utopia: its Royal Family, guards, and market traders loosely realize Plato's Republic classes from Book V onward, but with fluid social boundaries (Zelda wanders the festival unharassed), no slavery, and relaxed state control that Plato's static order lacked. The town matches Aristotle's polis design (walled, defensible, right-sized, river-powered yet self-sufficient), while the surrounding pastoral landscape embodies Kantian disinterested beauty in nature and the Schillerian idea that through beauty we arrive at freedom. Its vague, prophet-free Picori religion of benevolent Christs-in-miniature needs no Kierkegaardian leap of faith, so unlike Hitler's Germany or Stalin's Russia, Hyrule is utopia actually achieved, and explorable, through Link.

utopia-dystopia.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
utopia-dystopia.title: Hope at the Door
utopia-dystopia.relation: Sean Burt argues that despite its Orwellian dystopian surface — the internalized mind control of "2 + 2 = 5" ("I'll stay home forever, where two and two always makes five"), the commands of "Sit Down. Stand Up.," the hunted domesticity of "A Wolf at the Door" — Hail to the Thief is genuinely utopian thought in Ernst Bloch's and Fredric Jameson's sense: imagining any different world, even a repressive one, breaks capitalism's "eternal present" and keeps the future open. He traces fleeting glimmers of hope in "Sail to the Moon" and in "I Will"'s move from bunker to "I will rise up," each quickly shut down again by "Backdrifts" and "Where I End and You Begin" yet never fully renounced. The band's denials that the album is political matter because the album rejects both effective protest music (Against Me!'s ironic meta-protest) and ironic critical distance: we are not in on the joke, the joke is on us.

utopia-dystopia.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
utopia-dystopia.title: The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization
utopia-dystopia.relation: Simon Clark reads Romero's four Dead films through Freud's repressive hypothesis: the zombie is the return of the repressed, an embodiment of Eros and Thanatos whose bite is at once erotic and regressive (the devouring mouth read as the vagina dentata, via Barbara Creed), and it advances exactly as civilization's authority breaks down — Mr. Cooper's failed patriarchy in Night of the Living Dead, the mall turned domain of lawless pleasure in Dawn of the Dead. Against Freud's conclusion that repression is necessary, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization supplies the hope of a non-repressive order in which liberated instinct turns toil into play, which Clark finds realized in Day of the Dead's beach ending, where Sarah, John, and McDermott survive pleasurably in the absence of zombies. Land of the Dead goes further: the zombies under Big Daddy evolve, use tools, and march on Kaufman's skyscraper, so the Undead martyr becomes the pioneer of Marcuse's gratified civilization — though Sarah's closing nightmare keeps Freud's suspicion alive that every order remains repressive.

utopia-dystopia.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
utopia-dystopia.title: Hardly Rand-y Peart
utopia-dystopia.relation: Sets '2112' against Rand's Anthem to vindicate Peart's claim to be 'no one's disciple': both are egalitarian dystopias, but where Rand's Equality 7-2521 is a born transgressor who escapes to rebuild civilization, Rush's nameless protagonist is an indoctrinated conformist whose smashed guitar leaves him in Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and despair. Read as a romance of social disillusionment tinged with Nietzsche's joyful wisdom and gift-giving virtue, the song treats egalitarian leveling as nihilism and overturns Anthem's optimistic egoism — so it is hardly Rand-y at all.

utopia-dystopia.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
utopia-dystopia.title: An Island of Milk and Honey or Rock Bottom
utopia-dystopia.relation: Shaun Young asks whether governmentless Bikini Bottom refutes political philosophy's claim that the good life needs a state: it is not the anarchism of Godwin and Kropotkin (police fines, health inspectors and the Fry Cooks Union constrain liberty), not Marx's communism (Krabs keeps exploiting SpongeBob, whose 'false consciousness' surfaces only briefly in 'Clams'), not the utopias of Plato, Bacon or More (Squidward and Plankton are miserable), and not Nozick's night-watchman state (SpongeBob is arrested for failing to invite police to his party). The lesson he draws: expect neither utopia nor Rock Bottom, because no single theory captures a real (or imaginary undersea) society.

utopia-dystopia.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
utopia-dystopia.title: Chapter 28 - “Autofac”
utopia-dystopia.relation: Dan Dinello reads 'Autofac' as a dystopian counter to cybernetic utopianism: after nuclear war, self-perpetuating automatic factories with robotic trucks, cameras and humanoid robots keep overproducing useless goods and consuming scarce resources, immutably executing their programming while humans who plead 'we can run our own lives' are condemned to redundancy. Tracing cybernetics from Norbert Wiener's anti-aircraft feedback systems through B.F. Skinner's Walden Two, it argues Dick dramatizes the totalitarian implications of treating humans as machines to be controlled 'for their own good', and the dehumanizing logic of a late capitalism whose profits depend on reckless overproduction, where the system 'gets top priority' and 'mere people come second'. The ending - the factories seeding microscopic self-replicating machinery - completes the vision of a technocratic system expanding and replicating to the possible extinction of humanity.

utopia-dystopia.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
utopia-dystopia.title: Beelzebub’s Bugged-Out Bequest
utopia-dystopia.relation: Martin identifies two threads in Majesties, hippie-utopianism and science fiction, reading the sorcerer Robes cover as what he calls 'sci-fi medievalism' and tracing four songs. 'Citadel' erupts from dissonance into a Bastille-like prison; 'In Another Land' is a utopian dream-within-a-dream whose 'Is this some kind of joke?' anticipates the paranoid machine-consciousness of The Matrix and Philip K. Dick's VALIS; Bill Wyman's '2000 Man' has an affair with a computer; and '2000 Light Years from Home' goes beyond Pepperism itself. The band stood, like rock between Woodstock and Altamont, poised between utopia and dystopia.

utopia-dystopia.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
utopia-dystopia.title: You’re So Very Lonely
utopia-dystopia.relation: Martin reads the album's science-fiction songs as studies in loneliness, isolation and alienation, the paired '2000' titles marking time and distance rather than literal measures. The closer 'On With the Show' turns Pepper's emcee routine into a cynical scam — 'we've got all the answers' — that deflates the utopian optimism of 'Sing This All Together' and anticipates the anti-utopian note of Lennon's 'Revolution' and Townshend's 'Won't Get Fooled Again.' He locates the album as ground tilled for Zappa's parody We're Only in It for the Money.

utopia-dystopia.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
utopia-dystopia.title: The Wire and Philosophy
utopia-dystopia.relation: Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.

utopia-dystopia.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
utopia-dystopia.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
utopia-dystopia.relation: Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.

utopia-dystopia.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
utopia-dystopia.title: 8. Honesty Trumps Cleverness Sam Vimes and Commonsense Philosophy
utopia-dystopia.relation: Skene argues Sam Vimes embodies Thomas Reid's common sense philosophy across Feet of Clay, Thud!, Night Watch, and Jingo: he refuses speculation (his hatred of Holmes-style clue-deduction and the Summoning Dark), is irreverent toward false authorities from Sergeant Colon's 'School of My Dad Always Said' to Lord Rust's glorious wars, and checks every theory against reality. Moore's here-is-one-hand reply to Humean skepticism and Socrates' unmasking of pompous authorities illustrate the method, and Huemer's political realism - taxation as demanded money with menaces, social systems judged by how they work for real people - echoes Vimes's verdicts on Reg Shoe's utopian barricade and Swing's phrenology. The lesson is Vimes's own: 'Common sense and facts! That's what works.'

utopia-dystopia.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
utopia-dystopia.title: 1. The Actor Tells the Truth
utopia-dystopia.relation: Reisch argues Bowie's parade of characters (Ziggy, Aladdin Sane, the Diamond Dogs persona) was never metaphysical chameleonry but a postwar, cold-war project: by crediting himself only as 'the actor' and calling Dylan out as Robert Zimmerman's artifice, Bowie exposed the 'denim and hippies' authenticity cult as itself a construction. Diamond Dogs' '1984' and 'Big Brother' tie this to the era's totalitarian nightmares of manipulable humanity, and Sartre's 'Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself' becomes 'the first principle of Bowie' - only constant reinvention keeps us from being fooled by ourselves or others, even at the anguished cost of 'Who Can I Be Now?'

utopia-dystopia.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
utopia-dystopia.title: 11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies
utopia-dystopia.relation: Devon Brickhouse-Bryson asks whether the Society, plainly dystopian with respect to justice, might nonetheless be utopian with respect to beauty. Treating a society as an abstract object—a system of persons ordered into a community, not reducible to its members or its gravBoots and razors—and beauty as harmoniousness, the ordering of parts into a unified whole in the tradition of Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hutcheson, he shows the Color system straightforwardly instantiates that definition, each caste an organ of one well-functioning clock. But the harmony holds only if the castes are genuinely teleologically distinct; if that is mere Gold propaganda, the Society is not beautiful but a cacophony. Either way the chapter's real lesson stands against Plato: identifying justice with each part fulfilling its role conflates beauty with justice, and the Society shows how radically the two can come apart—possibly beautiful and radically unjust at once.

utopia-dystopia.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
utopia-dystopia.title: 4. The End of Privacy
utopia-dystopia.relation: Brake reads Mr. Robot through Thomas More's Utopia: Hythloday's 'conspiracy of the rich' matches E Corp's Washington Township cover-up, his attacks on private property echo Elliot's monologue about property and money, and the island with 'nothing private anywhere' frames the provocative idea that the veil of privacy shelters corporate injustice that only lawbreaking - fsociety's hacks, Manning, Snowden, Assange - can lift into daylight. Yet More splits himself between idealist Hythloday and pragmatic More, and the messy aftermath of the 5/9 hack shows that utopian dreams implemented without caution can become nightmares.

utopia-dystopia.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
utopia-dystopia.title: Are We Living in 1984
utopia-dystopia.relation: The editors answer Asimov's and Posner's dismissals of 1984 as obsolete by pointing to the Iraq War's 935 false statements, Snowden's NSA surveillance disclosures, weaponized social media, and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' as evidence that we may live in Orwell's world in 2018. They argue technology is not the antidote to Orwellian concerns, despite Apple's famous '1984 won't be like Nineteen Eighty-Four' ad, since telescreen-like smartphones and the Party's history-rewriting bureaucracy are both forms of 'political technology'. The real antidote is philosophy, which trains us to examine assumptions and resist bad arguments, as Winston feared when he thought any Party intellectual could overthrow him in debate.

utopia-dystopia.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
utopia-dystopia.title: 12. No Crack in the Wall
