meaning-of-life.relation: Editor David Baggett frames the collection with his own lifelong love of tennis (watching the 1980 Borg-McEnroe Wimbledon final, idolizing Borg and Gerulaitis) and argues tennis is an ideal springboard for philosophy, glossing 'philosophy' as the etymological 'love of wisdom.' He invokes Plato's idea that instances of beauty in this world make the heart ache for beauty's truest source, applying it to the sublime excellence of great play. He positions the whole book as using tennis to reach questions that matter, including the meaning of life, citing David Foster Wallace's quip that the title Tennis and the Meaning of Life is 'redundant.'

meaning-of-life.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
meaning-of-life.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
meaning-of-life.relation: Douglas McFarland argues that Hereafter is philosophical in Nehamas's sense of an 'art of living': its three characters (Marie, George, the boy Marcus) must fashion meaning in the face of absence and abandonment rather than settle the existence of an afterlife. He aligns their struggles with Augustine's grief over his mother's death in the Confessions, Montaigne's 'I portray not being but becoming' and his revision of Socrates' Phaedo claim that philosophy is practice for death, and Sartre's view that God's absence grounds the freedom to make meaning through work. George's turn from listening to the dead to genuinely seeing the living Marcus, and his letter to Marie, mark authentic self-fashioning in the here and now.

meaning-of-life.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
meaning-of-life.title: Introduction
meaning-of-life.relation: Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.

meaning-of-life.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
meaning-of-life.title: Film Noir and the Meaning of Life
meaning-of-life.relation: Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.

meaning-of-life.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
meaning-of-life.title: Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler
meaning-of-life.relation: Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).

meaning-of-life.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
meaning-of-life.title: The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders
meaning-of-life.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.

meaning-of-life.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
meaning-of-life.title: The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska
meaning-of-life.relation: Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.

meaning-of-life.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
meaning-of-life.title: Conclusion
meaning-of-life.relation: The conclusion synthesizes the book's case that Whedon philosophizes, building a Shaw-style hierarchy from illustrating theories (Connor as Robert Kane's libertarian agent, 'stirred up' between Darla's and faux-Cordelia's competing visions) through ethical and metaphysical complexity ('Man on the Street,' Angel/Angelus) to epistemic endorsement of a Whedonian worldview. It reads Angel's epiphany — 'if there's no bigger meaning, then the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing in the world' — as a negative project against the thesis that ethics without God is incoherent, since Whedon's God-ambiguous fiction shows noble self-sacrifice (Buffy for Dawn, Cordy for Angel, Simon for River) that remains worthwhile regardless of cosmic justice. Following Mulhall's use of Socrates as an exemplar of ethically significant living, it casts Angel the Champion as a comparable exemplar grounded in authenticity, care-based relationships, and the transformation of moral character. It closes by extending the film-as-philosophy debate to television, deploying Carroll's gaze/glance distinction to argue nothing in principle keeps quality TV — from The Twilight Zone and Star Trek to Buffy and Angel — from being philosophy in action.

meaning-of-life.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
meaning-of-life.title: Sherlock Holmes Artist of Reason
meaning-of-life.relation: McInerny argues Holmes is not a bloodless reasoning machine but an 'artist of reason' who fuses intellect with imagination ('the scientific use of imagination'). He lays out Holmes's four-stage method—fact-gathering interview and investigation, deep-thought hypothesis framing, denouement, and post-factum briefing—and notes his use of reasoning backward, reductio ad absurdum, and hypotheses over guesses. Finally he casts Holmes as a metaphysician who assumes a purposive, intelligible cosmos ('What is the meaning of it, Watson?'), a teleological order akin to Aristotle's Final End that grounds the local intelligibility Holmes exploits.

meaning-of-life.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
meaning-of-life.title: The Grim Reaper on Baker Street
meaning-of-life.relation: Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.

meaning-of-life.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
meaning-of-life.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
meaning-of-life.relation: Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.

meaning-of-life.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
meaning-of-life.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
meaning-of-life.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a member of the 'cult of the cool' whose reticence and final resigned 'What's the difference?' surrender embody apatheia and acceptance of fate/logos. He tests Spencer Selby's claim that Clay and the sharpshooter Nikki must fail because their motives are immoral, arguing instead via an Aristotelian principle (virtues are stable dispositions) that their sudden lapses—the flimsy suitcase, Nikki's racial slur that loses him the lucky horseshoe—are Kubrick stacking the deck rather than genuine character. He closes by weighing Clay's life against models of a meaningful life (exuberance/romanticism vs. rationalism/self-fulfillment), faulting Clay for never subjecting his chosen ends to self-critical reason.

meaning-of-life.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
meaning-of-life.title: Vernacular Metaphysics On Terrence Malick’s The Thin Red Line
meaning-of-life.relation: Pippin reads Malick's The Thin Red Line as deliberately invoking then refusing Hollywood war-movie conventions (group solidarity, trackable characters, heroic assault) so the viewer is left 'lost' and forced toward a metaphysical rather than political or sentimental reckoning with death. Through unattributed poetic voice-overs—Train's Manichean questions, Witt's search for the calm 'immortality' he saw in his dying mother, Welsh's cynicism, Bell's romantic idealism—and lingering non-plot shots of nature bathed in sunlight, the film pursues a 'vernacular metaphysics': ordinary soldiers straining ordinary speech to ask what it is to live under certain death. Pippin aligns this disclosive, prediscursive truth of the image with the Hegel-to-Heidegger-Merleau-Ponty tradition of art as truth-bearer, while Witt's Emersonian 'one big soul' and his self-sacrifice ('all things shining') stage the film's unresolved question of whether nature and death can be seen as good.

meaning-of-life.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
meaning-of-life.title: “Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films
meaning-of-life.relation: LaRocca argues against Thomas Weiskel that the 'humanistic sublime' is not an oxymoron, using Herzog's war films (Lessons of Darkness, Little Dieter Needs to Fly, Rescue Dawn) to show a sublime that returns us to the human at the limit of existence rather than transcending it. Building on Kant's link between the sublime and human dignity—and Kant's claim that sublimity lies in our ideas, not in nature—he reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' (fabrication that exceeds the 'accountant's truth') as the vehicle: staged monologues, borrowed music, and recontextualized documentary footage disclose an inner reality. Herzog's Heideggerian gloss on aletheia as un-concealment aligns cinema itself with truth, and Dengler's bear ('the only friend I had was death') exemplifies war as the space of radical mortality where the humanistic sublime dawns for the safe spectator, contrasted with Malick's more Darwinian, nature-indifferent vision.

meaning-of-life.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
meaning-of-life.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence and the Tragic Sense of Life
meaning-of-life.relation: Dunn interprets A.I. as a meditation on the 'tragic sense of life': treating David as a person, he argues the film dramatizes three doomed human desires (love, uniqueness, immortality) and tests two failed escapes from mortality, science (Professor Hobby, the Flesh Fair, David's suicide leap) and religious faith (the fraudulent Blue Fairy at drowned Coney Island). Defending the maligned finale, he reads the simulated Blue Fairy and the one-day resurrection of Monica as raising whether a perfect simulation of love can be 'real enough,' with David achieving a sober humanistic acceptance of impermanence.

meaning-of-life.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
meaning-of-life.title: 5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality
meaning-of-life.relation: Hellwig uses Dean's choice of Hell over Doc Benton's organ-replacement immortality in 'Time Is on My Side' to examine medical immortality. He pairs Dean's worry—that maiming and replacing your body makes you unrecognizably human—with Bernard Williams's Makropulos argument that immortality ends in categorical-desire-exhausting boredom, adding a third condition to Williams: a recognizably human life requires being able to self-identify with one's own body, illustrated by real disfigurement cases and Aubrey de Grey's biogerontology.

meaning-of-life.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
meaning-of-life.title: 11. Why Sacrifice Yourself
meaning-of-life.relation: Browning interrogates the nobility of the Winchesters' repeated self-sacrifice, asking whether their deals (Dean's soul for Sam, John's soul for Dean) are selfless or selfish—driven by codependency, fear of being alone, and ego. He weighs utilitarian justification (sacrificing one who saves the world) against the trickster's 'Mystery Spot' lesson that 'nothing good comes' of it, and invokes Kant's notion of a true gift expecting nothing in return, alongside Milbank on life-as-gift, to question whether self-sacrifice is the 'ultimate ethical agent' when death isn't final.

meaning-of-life.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
meaning-of-life.title: 12. Finally Free
meaning-of-life.relation: McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.

meaning-of-life.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
meaning-of-life.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
meaning-of-life.relation: Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar, Six, Adama and Roslin to debate God's existence and meaning. Against Baltar's scientific naturalism they present Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, first cause, and the argument from design applied to the universe's ordered laws) and dismiss Pascal's Wager as insincere, like Baltar's. They then raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will defense and Hick's soul-making theodicy against Hume's faulty-architect analogy. Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.

meaning-of-life.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
meaning-of-life.title: Reap a Destiny
meaning-of-life.relation: Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Harry Potter's Deathly Hallows through the question of death and afterlife. Harry's willing death-march models Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. At King's Cross the maimed Voldemort-soul embodies William James's 'sow a character, reap a destiny': having refused remorse, he has become evil beyond repair, whereas the repentant Dumbledore has grown. Against Heidegger's atheism, Rowling's Christian resurrection imagery, backed by Locke on memory-identity, Kant, and Pascal, makes our character-forming choices infinitely consequential.

meaning-of-life.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
meaning-of-life.title: House and the Life of Reason
meaning-of-life.relation: Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.

meaning-of-life.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
meaning-of-life.title: Part Five D Is for Destiny
meaning-of-life.relation: This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.

meaning-of-life.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
meaning-of-life.title: NOTES
meaning-of-life.relation: Jeremy Barris argues that Lost dramatizes the structure of life itself, using Heidegger's claim that the inquirer's own being is the clue to all questions and his notion of 'thrownness' to read the castaways' accidental arrival as a mirror of our own bewildering birth into circumstances we did not make. He reframes the show's central puzzle as 'the question of life after birth,' contends against Sartre and Camus that life is neither fully sensible nor fully absurd but a half-understood riddle, and invokes Wittgenstein's On Certainty to show that total doubt is impossible because understanding senselessness presupposes understanding something.

meaning-of-life.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
meaning-of-life.title: NOTES
meaning-of-life.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost alongside C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory, arguing both use a fantasy world of second chances to stage redemption in community. He aligns the castaways' violent arrival on the island with the Pevensie children's magical passage into Narnia and Edmund's betrayal-and-forgiveness arc, using the island's life-and-death setting to force existential commitment. Emmanuel Levinas's ethics of responsibility to the face of the Other and H. Richard Niebuhr's relational theology are invoked to argue that healing and faith come not individually but in communion with others.

meaning-of-life.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
meaning-of-life.title: NOTES
meaning-of-life.relation: Daniel B. Gallagher uses Thomas Aquinas on the knowledge of God to read the characters' searches for meaning on Lost. Aquinas's 'approaching Peter' image—recognizing a human without yet knowing it is Peter—models how everyone confusedly knows God as the object of happiness while mistaking finite goods (Jack's curing, Kate's deception, Jin's job, Charlie's brother) for the ultimate good, paralleled with the castaways staring at the unidentifiable Smoke Monster. Gallagher then applies Aquinas's sin of acedia (spiritual sloth that deems the good unattainable) to Desmond's fear over Penny and Charlie's despair before Rose tells him faith is never impossible, tying the desire for happiness to Augustine's restless heart.

meaning-of-life.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
meaning-of-life.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
meaning-of-life.relation: Karavitis groups twist-ending episodes into nostalgia, time-travel, and second-chance types and reads them through Kierkegaard's Either/Or distinction between the aesthetic and ethical modes of life. Living aesthetically—chasing present gratification—leads to despair, as in 'A Nice Place to Visit' (Rocky's boring 'heaven' is Hell) and 'A Game of Pool' (Jesse wins only an eternity in Limbo). Living ethically—taking responsibility and moving forward—earns a real second chance, as when 'Printer's Devil' editor Winter reclaims his soul; life must be understood backward but lived forward.

meaning-of-life.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: Introduction
meaning-of-life.relation: Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.

meaning-of-life.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: “Sometimes Dead Is Better”
meaning-of-life.relation: Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.

meaning-of-life.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
meaning-of-life.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
meaning-of-life.relation: Barnwell argues that fatherhood can constitute the ultimate meaning of a man's life, answering the paradox that a meaningful life 'all about the kids' seems not to be about the father by noting fatherly acts are still the father's own freely chosen activities. He confronts Camus's Myth of Sisyphus – the worry that childrearing is endless pointless rock-pushing across generations – by insisting children, unlike rocks, have intrinsic value, and invokes the Sartrean existentialist idea that choosing an activity confers value on it (illustrated by his buying oatmeal for 'Sally').

meaning-of-life.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
meaning-of-life.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
meaning-of-life.relation: Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.

meaning-of-life.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
meaning-of-life.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
meaning-of-life.relation: In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.

meaning-of-life.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
meaning-of-life.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
meaning-of-life.relation: Jack Stillwaggon recounts his 1965 voyage as a seventeen-year-old crewing the replica HMS Bounty from New York to Florida — fires aboard, thirty-five-foot seas, seasickness, a crewman nearly left to die — and asks why modern people abandon comfort to court danger and discomfort. His answer is that we face the sea to prove something to ourselves about our worth and abilities: like the paratrooper who stays under fire or the soldier earning his 'red badge of courage,' the survived ordeal becomes a cherished high point that adds meaning to an otherwise 'silly' comfortable existence, leaving him more at peace and expecting more of himself thereafter.

meaning-of-life.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
meaning-of-life.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
meaning-of-life.relation: Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.

meaning-of-life.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
meaning-of-life.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
meaning-of-life.relation: Nicholas Hayes describes the Chicago-to-Mackinac race, cataloguing its boats (passenger trains, Model Ts, booster rockets, retreads), its nights (darkest, stormy, breathless, velvet, brightest), and its sailor-types (tweener, superhero, teammate, yogi, minister, salt) to build toward a claim about an 'awareness shift.' He argues that far from land and its electric lights, sailors slip into a place where the emotional self meets 'the most real and primitive world' and confronts a new relationship with time, culminating on the 'day of hope' in the realization that one controls nothing but oneself and owns nothing but one's time — 'Everything is now' — a transcendence he loosely likens to skepticism and enlightenment themes.

meaning-of-life.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
meaning-of-life.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
meaning-of-life.relation: Hilaire Belloc's essay 'The Channel,' serving as the volume's literary epilogue, argues that the 'glamour in the mind' and 'freshness of beginnings' our ancestors knew can be recovered by using the body simply and hardly — best of all by sailing a small boat under twenty-five feet across the Channel. Narrating his own first crossing from the Goodwins to Calais, drifting on the ebb and waiting for the flood, he presents sailing as the 'old drama by which the soul of a healthy man is kept alive,' teaching terror, salvation, exultation, and repose as lived realities rather than mere words. He closes by withholding the tale of the stormy return, imploring readers not to hear of it but to sail it themselves.

meaning-of-life.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
meaning-of-life.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
meaning-of-life.relation: Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.

meaning-of-life.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
meaning-of-life.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
meaning-of-life.relation: Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.

meaning-of-life.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
meaning-of-life.title: Introduction
meaning-of-life.relation: Rowlands introduces the 'sci-phi' project: science fiction confronts us with the alien 'other' as a mirror in which we understand ourselves, so lowbrow sci-fi films like The Matrix, Total Recall and Starship Troopers make abstract philosophy concrete. He argues philosophy is doing rather than knowing, invoking Fishburne's 'know the path vs walk the path' line and Nietzsche's dictum that one repays a teacher poorly by remaining a pupil. He mentions his own earlier 'fyborg' thesis that human cognition is embedded in the wider informational environment, prefiguring the extended mind.

meaning-of-life.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
meaning-of-life.title: 1. Frankenstein
meaning-of-life.relation: Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.

meaning-of-life.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
meaning-of-life.title: 9. Blade Runner
meaning-of-life.relation: Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.

meaning-of-life.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
meaning-of-life.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
meaning-of-life.relation: John Davenport argues The Lord of the Rings is religious not as Christian allegory but as an epic fairy tale in Tolkien's sense from 'On Fairy-stories,' delivering 'eucatastrophe,' the sudden joyous turn that, like Kierkegaard's faith in a salvation beyond our own power, hints at eschatological hope. Using Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as Tolkien's model for Frodo (both accept an impossible burden, both fail and bear a scar of mortality), he identifies the destruction of the Ring via Gollum, Eowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth as eucatastrophic 'turns.' Davenport concludes the veiled religious message is that evil cannot stand forever, yet deliverance requires our sacrifice and faith beyond rational hope that 'day shall come again.'

meaning-of-life.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
meaning-of-life.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
meaning-of-life.relation: Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.

meaning-of-life.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
meaning-of-life.title: Reap a Destiny
meaning-of-life.relation: The Walls brothers read Harry Potter's confrontation with death through Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death: Harry's calm march to the Forbidden Forest and Colin Creevey's sacrifice exemplify accepting mortality, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. The King's Cross scene lets Dumbledore be Harry's Heideggerian hero from the past; via William James's "sow a thought … reap a destiny," Aristotle, Locke on memory-identity, and Kant on the afterlife, they argue our choices forge a character — and Voldemort's refusal of remorse seals his ruin.

meaning-of-life.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
meaning-of-life.title: House and the Life of Reason
meaning-of-life.relation: Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism
meaning-of-life.relation: Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human
meaning-of-life.relation: Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 51. Magnolia As Philosophy Meaning and Coincidence
meaning-of-life.relation: Engelen interprets Paul Thomas Anderson's Magnolia as a meditation on sense-making and Camus's notion of the absurd: the film's raining frogs and the interlocking coincidences (Sydney Barringer's death, the narrator's insistence that 'this cannot be one of those things') stage our compulsion to find meaning colliding with a universe that yields none. He reads characters' struggles with trauma and regret through Epictetus's Stoic dichotomy of control and Jung's synchronicity, and the 'Wise Up' sing-along as a call to accept what cannot be changed. The chapter endorses Camus's third response to the absurd—neither denial nor suicide but defiant acceptance—linking it to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Nagel's take on life's meaning.

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality
meaning-of-life.relation: Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 60. Little Women as Philosophy Death or Marriage and the Meaning of Life
meaning-of-life.relation: The chapter tests Susan Wolf's 'fitting fulfillment' theory (meaning as subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) against Greta Gerwig's Little Women, arguing the March sisters and most historical women are ill-fitted to it. Jo is forced to make her writing 'mercenary and commercial' and marries; Amy abandons painting and marries Laurie because 'marriage is an economic proposition'; Marmee, Hannah, and Mrs. Hummel live from duty and self-sacrifice without joy. Invoking Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but becomes a woman' and Imposter Syndrome, it concludes fulfillment is indicative but not necessary for meaning, urging a purely objective theory that can value women's lives 'appropriately appreciated at least in principle.'

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 66. Marc Maron as Philosopher Comedy, Therapy, and Identification
meaning-of-life.relation: Kapica argues Maron's 'WTF' philosophy—both indignation and liberation—turns Kenneth Burke's rhetorical theory of identification and 'consubstantiality' into comedic catharsis, treating stand-up as therapy. He reads Maron's opening move from 'What is the meaning of life?' to 'How am I being used?' through Richard Taylor and Camus's Sisyphus: in 2009, a broke and failing Maron is Sisyphus, and WTF is his license to invent meaning. Via his cold-sore and sobriety bits and his WTF podcast interviews (Seinfeld, Gallagher), Maron makes his audience a surrogate therapist, using performed vulnerability to bind them into an 'acting-together' that Kapica claims genuinely saved Maron's life.

meaning-of-life.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
meaning-of-life.title: 77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime
meaning-of-life.relation: Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.

meaning-of-life.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
meaning-of-life.title: 6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife
meaning-of-life.relation: The chapter asks whether Doctor Who is a religion, testing it against Hopfe's and Ninian Smart's criteria and concluding it is best understood as a Humanist-and-religious 'philosophy'—sacred and 'holy' (Otto) but lacking a genuine transcendent 'unseen.' On loss, it uses Kierkegaard's 'aesthetic life' and 'rotation method' to explain why we fear endings and regenerations, urging viewers to root life in lasting meaning rather than fleeting pleasure. On death, it deploys Socrates in the Apology and Phaedo and Aristotle on courage (Jabe, Harriet Jones, Donna sacrificing themselves) to argue death is nothing to fear, and reads the Matrix and Nethersphere as the show's two Socratic afterlife options.

meaning-of-life.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
meaning-of-life.title: Epilogue
meaning-of-life.relation: The closing essay exhorts readers to 'approach life as the Doctor'—engaged, compassionate, and critically thinking—insisting each person is important and that fandom passion, even when fractious, expresses the Doctor's engaged life (invoking Voltaire on free expression). Using 'Father's Day' and 'The Day of the Doctor,' it argues we cannot change the past but must seize the present, and ties 'truth' and 'trust' to a shared root to claim a meaningful life requires trusting oneself and others rather than merely proving oneself right. It affirms that wisdom is lived truth, that being wrong is how we mature, and that courage is doing what must be done while afraid.

golden-rule.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
golden-rule.title: 14 - Hey-diddily-ho, Neighboreenos Ned Flanders and Neighborly Love
golden-rule.relation: David Vessey asks how 'love your neighbor as yourself' can coexist with tolerance when you believe your unbaptized neighbor faces eternal suffering, using 'Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily' where Ned baptizes the Simpson children in his care but never proselytizes beyond his household. He constructs the argument that love of neighbor, like love of self, would seem to require trying to baptize everyone, then dissolves it: proper self-love means perfecting one's nobler aspects by acting on principle rather than desire, so loving others can require respecting principled choices that risk even their lives. Kant's account of autonomy - rationally legislating one's own maxims, per the categorical imperative - supplies the missing condition, showing Ned is justified in not interfering with autonomous adults, a point capped by the irony that the only person he actually baptizes is pleasure-driven Homer.

golden-rule.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
golden-rule.title: Cold Clammy Consistency
golden-rule.relation: Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents - rational by Aristotle's standard of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgments about evildoers tasting better) and free despite their blood-craving, since craving is a strong preference, not the compulsion of the heroin addict or the castaway drinking seawater. Since animal blood is a viable alternative (Louis's rats, Angel and Spike's butcher's blood), the justifications for drinking human blood - taste, reaching full potential, spiritual peace - all fail against the principle that a world with less unnecessary suffering is better. Then the consistency argument turns on us: factory-farmed meat inflicts unnecessary suffering for the sake of taste while vegetarianism is fully viable, so condemning vampires while eating chicken is inconsistent - we as human beings are vampiric.

golden-rule.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
golden-rule.title: But Isn’t It Only Natural
golden-rule.relation: Adams answers Plato's ring-of-Gyges challenge with Heroes: even when invisible, wrongdoing corrupts the wrongdoer, because justice is to the soul what health is to the body. Claire's refusal to claim credit for the fire rescue shows thumos (spirit) responsive to logistikos (reason), Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is epithumetikon (appetite) ruling the soul, and Hiro's Vegas cheating shows how injustice makes life spin out of control; Claire's apology to Brody illustrates the Pagan Golden Rule — help your friends, harm your enemies — tempered by Plato's caution that enemies may become friends.

golden-rule.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
golden-rule.title: The Finder of Lost Children
golden-rule.relation: Timothy Dean Roth reads Kill Bill as a modern Divine Comedy: Tarantino punishes by contrapasso like Dante—O-Ren dies by Japanese steel, Budd by snake, Elle by blindness, Bill by a broken heart—and both treat vengeance as a form of truth-telling and an act of love. Hattori Hanzo's warning that revenge 'is a forest' echoes Aristotle on how hard it is to set the limits of anger, while the stories-within-stories of orphaned Nikki and O-Ren enact the cycle of violence vengeance perpetuates. Against this, Aquinas's doctrine of double effect shows every one of the Bride's killings is defensive self-preservation, and the film ends where Jules's arc ends: in mercy, mutual forgiveness and a whispered 'thank you' of grace.

golden-rule.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
golden-rule.title: If I Were a Carpenter
golden-rule.relation: Butler asks what makes an activity work, testing the market definition against Socrates' refusal of fees, Aristotle's Politics, Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, Eva Kittay's care work, and the split between extrinsic and intrinsic value. He reads Cash's catalog through it: "One Piece at a Time" (the Detroit line worker stealing a Cadillac he builds but cannot afford), "Get Rhythm" (the shoeshine boy singing through menial labor), "I Never Picked Cotton" (escaping work into an empty identity), "Let Him Roll" and "Southern Accents," and the San Quentin monologue after "Wreck of the Ol' 97" where Cash refuses to be told what to play before inmates. The chapter closes by lining up Kant's categorical imperative, Jesus' Golden Rule, and Rawls's veil of ignorance: nobody would choose a society of company-store wage slavery without knowing they were not the worker, and Cash, knowing he stood on the stage rather than in the cellblock, used his freedom to side with prisoners and carpenters anyway.

golden-rule.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
golden-rule.title: From Cash to Kant—and Back Again
golden-rule.relation: Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.

golden-rule.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
golden-rule.title: Wonder Why We Ever Go Home
golden-rule.relation: Duke Richey maps Buffett's West — 'Ringling, Ringling,' the Rancho Deluxe soundtrack, Tully Mars — onto Josiah Royce's philosophy of community: only people who root in a place, face its history ('wise provincialism'), and sacrifice selfish desires for the whole can build Beloved Communities, a lesson enacted when cattle rustlers Jack and Cecil accept community sanction and find belonging working the Rancho Deluxe. Wallace Stegner's coral-reef metaphor from Angle of Repose supplies the image of communities built up millimeter by millimeter yet still vulnerable to pollution and over-fishing, with Royce's environmental regret (covering 'the wounds' of the landscape with gardens) anticipating the chapter's sustainability ethic. 'Wonder Why We Ever Go Home' thus asks what we really seek when we seek grace through community: not the nomadic Pickup Truck Death of every-man-for-himself, but cooperation that makes a society to match the scenery.

golden-rule.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
golden-rule.title: Cold Clammy Consistency
golden-rule.relation: Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents because they meet Aristotle's test of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgment that 'evildoers... taste better') and retain free will, since their blood-lust is a craving not a compulsion and Louis's rat diet in Interview with the Vampire, like Angel's in Buffy, proves an alternative exists. TASTE, full potential, and spiritual peace all fail to justify human blood, because killing a person brings more unnecessary suffering than killing a rat, the same suffering-based principle that condemns factory farming. The 'cold clammy consistency' punchline: since humans need not eat meat, condemning vampire blood-drinkers while dining on chicken, pork, and beef is hypocrisy, because we are vampiric too and only our choice of which life to ingest separates the monstrous from the virtuous.

golden-rule.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
golden-rule.title: Fifty Ways to Love Your Other
golden-rule.relation: The section reads Levinas's demand to experience the Other's suffering in the Other's place as Dick's empathy made literal: the shifting points of view that blur heroes and villains, Felix Buckman's tears, Molinari developing his people's symptoms, and the empathy boxes bonding users to Mercer's endless stoning, a fraud whose falsity is beside the point because the concern is the real thing. Villains are precisely those who refuse the transfer, and the ordinary one-way gift, buying a stranger a drink with no return, enacts the Golden Rule: even if the universe isn't real, Melina is right, kiss each other anyway.

golden-rule.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
golden-rule.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
golden-rule.relation: Allaire argues walkers have no moral value and can be killed without remorse: a Bentham-style act-utilitarian tally favors killing any walker, and, following Kant, genetic humanity is neither necessary nor sufficient for membership in the moral community. Applying Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, he shows walkers lack pain response (Hannah's severed half still dragging itself at Rick), language, planning (Glenn's gun-bag mission versus aimless shuffling), and self-reflection, so as beings incapable of duty they can have no rights. Morgan's inability to shoot his walker-wife and Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' illustrate Kant's 'duality of the human situation' — we irrationally project personhood onto former people — and our hesitation is precisely the walkers' greatest advantage.

golden-rule.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
golden-rule.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
golden-rule.relation: Svolba and Flanders read Curb as an extended investigation of civility—the rules of what people 'just don't do,' from using the doctor's phone to touring Susie's new house to singing 'Happy Birthday' at Ben Stiller's party. Larry plays Socratic gadfly: refusing the tour harms no one and treats no one unfairly, and Susie's only justification ('it's just not done') is circular, so his incivility can seem admirable, even like minor civil disobedience. Against this, the chapter argues (crediting Cheshire Calhoun) that rules of civility are conventional vehicles for communicating respect for others' feelings and interests—what matters to Susie ought to matter to Larry—and, more consequentially, that a social world full of Larry Davids would be unbearable. Larry's own Golden-Rule litmus test, by which he never talks in movie theaters because he would hate it himself, misses this point, since civility is precisely about what others happen to want and like.

golden-rule.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
golden-rule.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
golden-rule.relation: Argues against the obvious reading that Larry is a rule-breaker: properly analyzed, he is a dedicated rule-follower, since a good rule-follower need only accept the legitimacy of some rules and consistently follow the ones he accepts. Bekka Williams works through cases like Rachel's ski-lift jump versus Jewish law in 'The Ski Lift,' the moving 10:30 pm phone cutoff in 'The Wire,' and Larry's rejection of his mother's tattoo-driven reburial in 'The Special Section' to distinguish breaking a rule you accept from rejecting a rule's legitimacy altogether. Kant supplies the point that duty is only visible when it frustrates self-interest (Larry absorbing the cost of his own waiting-room rule in 'The Interior Decorator,' refusing to fire the Tourette's chef), while J.J.C. Smart's attack on 'rule-worship' explains why Larry rejects purposeless rules like the drive-thru walking ban and the one-year wedding-gift cutoff. The underlying justification is the Golden Rule: the water bottle in 'The Doll,' the caviar allotment, and even the stolen memorial flowers in 'The Ida Funkhouser Roadside Memorial' are defended as fairness and reciprocity, leaving the jacket money in 'The Korean Bookie' as the single admitted counterexample.

golden-rule.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
golden-rule.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
golden-rule.relation: The chapter presents Barney as a Humean moral philosopher: reason is the slave of the passions, and norms like the Bro Code are invented conventions that evolve, Adam Smith's invisible-hand style, rather than being designed, revealed, or deduced. The Platinum Rule ('never, ever love thy neighbor') is grounded in Humean reciprocity: the eight-stage arc of attraction to fallout in Barney's Wendy the Waitress disaster, the Gerards' brunch tyranny, and Robin's romance with co-worker Curt shows the retaliation costs that make the norm a rational solution to coordination failures. Against the Golden Rule's painterly elegance, the anatomist's cautious observation of behavior explains why a norm banning neighborly love emerges even in a society of non-saints.

golden-rule.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
golden-rule.title: Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful
golden-rule.relation: Muntersbjorn argues that freedom comes in kinds and degrees and that selves are social fictions sustained by others, building on Annette Baier's claims that we are 'second persons' whose self-consciousness and freedom grow out of childhood interaction and mutual cross-examination. She reads the hosts' selective ignoring ('that doesn't look like anything to me') as Baier's dangerous art of self-deception, and contrasts Descartes' solitary introspection (hats and coats that may cover automata) and Russell's analogy-based answer to the problem of other minds with the hosts' deliberately scripted interpersonal checks that keep them from questioning their reality. Plato's Meno statues of Daedalus (opinion 'fastened up' into knowledge) frame hosts as property whose freedom is a matter of degree, and the chapter closes that if artificial beings are ever to become persons they must be treated as second persons first - the Golden Rule applied to the park.

golden-rule.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
golden-rule.title: Notes
golden-rule.relation: When Lucy shouts the Golden Rule at the Ghoul after he dunks her in a poison river to bait a gulper, the chapter takes her appeal seriously and grades the rival 'rules' of the wasteland (the Iron, Arsenic, Neon, and Bronze Rules) before arguing the Golden Rule needs St. Francis's 'in a similar situation' clause. Kant's criminal-versus-judge objection disqualifies the unqualified Platinum Rule of treating others as they want, Nietzsche's charge that mutual restraint denies life is parried, and Rawlsian imagining of ourselves in divergent positions explains why family partiality like Lucy's search for Hank is consistent with the rule. The chapter closes with Lucy's saving of the Ghoul retold as the Good Samaritan parable, extending the rule even to enemies.

golden-rule.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
golden-rule.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
golden-rule.relation: The chapter models court intrigue as game theory: games of incomplete information over Joffrey's legitimacy, the predictability of honorable opponents like Barristan Selmy, and Catelyn's reverse induction from the seemingly 'irrational' attack on Bran to deduce that Jaime threw him. Tyrion is the star player, converting one-shot death sentences into repeated games - recruiting Bronn as his champion at the Eyrie, buying off the mountain clans with Lannister arms - and showing how 'A Lannister always pays his debts' works as strategic reputation. Against Plato's view of love as the madness that ruins rational play (Maester Aemon's 'love is the bane of honor'), the chapter uses Nietzsche's 'drop of reason in madness' to argue that lovers' merged interests expand rationality itself, culminating in a Golden Rule upgraded to 'understand others as they understand themselves.'

golden-rule.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
golden-rule.title: Notes
golden-rule.relation: Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.

golden-rule.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
golden-rule.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
golden-rule.relation: Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.

golden-rule.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
golden-rule.title: Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful
golden-rule.relation: Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.

golden-rule.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
golden-rule.title: “You Cannot Be Serious!” The Ethics of Rage in Tennis
golden-rule.relation: David Detmer asks whether John McEnroe's on-court tantrums are merely rude or genuinely immoral, judging them by two ethical theories. Under Bentham's utilitarianism he weighs the pleasure of entertained crowds against the harm to abused officials, then uses Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction to discount the 'lower' amusement of gawking at boorishness beneath the 'higher' aesthetic pleasure of appreciating great tennis. Under Kantian deontology he argues McEnroe's public false accusations are wrong in principle: officials are better positioned to make calls, so the abuse is unjust, and by the categorical imperative read as a Golden Rule, McEnroe—who resents being wrongly criticized himself—is a hypocrite whose 'gamesmanship' unfairly exploits his star power against opponents.

golden-rule.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
golden-rule.title: 21. Jesus the Punk Rocker
golden-rule.relation: Josh Cangelosi argues that Jesus as portrayed in the Gospels - homeless outcast, associate of prostitutes, denounced as a blasphemer, flipping tables - was effectively a punk, so Christianity and punk are compatible despite their mutual rejection. Comparing Leftover Crack's 'Atheist Anthem' with Matthew 23's woes against the Pharisees, he shows both Jesus and punks curse smug religious insiders while inviting outcasts, and reads Jesus's ethic as the Golden Rule or 'practice what you preach', which demands living authentically by your own standards and judging not. The analysis extends to Pussy Riot, the drag-pastor Craig Duke, and 'punks' who exclude queer people, concluding that Christians and punks alike must recover their blasphemous, outcast hardcore heritage.

golden-rule.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
golden-rule.title: 7. Independence Day & Aliens
golden-rule.relation: Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.

golden-rule.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
golden-rule.title: But Isn’t It Only Natural
golden-rule.relation: Don Adams uses Heroes' superpowered characters (who could commit perfect crimes like Gyges with his invisibility ring) to argue Plato's case that virtue is its own reward. He maps Plato's tripartite soul onto the characters: Claire's thumos (spirit/honor) tempered by logistikos (reason) yields courage and wisdom, while Sylar's ruling appetite (his hunger for powers) is intemperance and injustice that makes his life spin out of control. Reading justice as psychic health, and glossing the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies, but enemies may become friends), Adams argues it is 'only natural' for even the powerful to be virtuous rather than exploit others.

kant-respect.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
kant-respect.title: 14 - Hey-diddily-ho, Neighboreenos Ned Flanders and Neighborly Love
kant-respect.relation: David Vessey asks how 'love your neighbor as yourself' can coexist with tolerance when you believe your unbaptized neighbor faces eternal suffering, using 'Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily' where Ned baptizes the Simpson children in his care but never proselytizes beyond his household. He constructs the argument that love of neighbor, like love of self, would seem to require trying to baptize everyone, then dissolves it: proper self-love means perfecting one's nobler aspects by acting on principle rather than desire, so loving others can require respecting principled choices that risk even their lives. Kant's account of autonomy - rationally legislating one's own maxims, per the categorical imperative - supplies the missing condition, showing Ned is justified in not interfering with autonomous adults, a point capped by the irony that the only person he actually baptizes is pleasure-driven Homer.

kant-respect.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
kant-respect.title: But It’s Just a White Lie!
kant-respect.relation: Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.

kant-respect.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
kant-respect.title: James Bond and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Held argues that our pleasure in Bond's kill-then-quip routine - 'Shocking' after electrocuting a henchman in Goldfinger, tossing Killifer to the sharks that ate Felix with 'You earned it, you keep it' - reveals tacit retributive and deterrent theories of punishment that place villains outside the moral community. Using the distinction between mere humiliation (deflating Dr. No's pretense: 'Minnows pretending they're whales') and Humiliation that denies common humanity, he shows Bond dehumanizes disfigured, 'othered' villains, even as the novels present them as disenfranchised figures - Dr. No rejecting his father's name, Mr. Big demanding recognition as the first great black criminal - whose rage is a warped demand for Hegelian mutual recognition. He proposes instead Jean Hampton's moral education theory, which treats criminals as moral agents capable of reform, concluding with Jaws's redemption in Moonraker as proof that no one is beyond it.

kant-respect.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
kant-respect.title: Transformers and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Watson and Arp ask whether Ironhide and Chromia's embrace means Autobots can love, rejecting programmed loving behavior, implanted souls, and wired-in human brains as insufficient for genuine personhood, then sort Transformer relationships into Western conceptions of love. Empedoclean cosmic Love and Strife map onto Primus versus Unicron; Platonic philia ascends to the Form of Beauty, with Transformer souls originating in and returning to the All Spark; Aristotle's three friendships separate Optimus and Sparkplug's virtue-friendship from Megatron and Starscream's mere utility; and Stoic-Kantian equal love explains Autobots saving Decepticons who immediately try to kill them, alongside Christian agape in Autobot family bonds.

kant-respect.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
kant-respect.title: The Valuable Self
kant-respect.relation: The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.

kant-respect.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
kant-respect.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife is still a person, which decides whether shooting her is murder. On the dominant Western view - Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellect, Kantian dignity against Singer's speciesism challenge - walkers lack intelligence and so are not persons, so Morgan should shoot. They then argue walkers are metaphysically impossible beings, square-circles: dead tissue that somehow sees, smells, and runs down prey without functioning organs, energy intake, or the reanimated neocortex that movement and sensation require. Zombies fascinate because they are projections of our fears - dead yet moving, an afterlife of horror - a Hamlet-like caught-between-being-and-nonbeing.

kant-respect.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
kant-respect.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues the creature is a person on every serious criterion: it satisfies Kant's rationality test and Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-concept) in both Shelley's novel and I, Frankenstein, and it possesses all ten of Nussbaum's capabilities for flourishing. The twist is that judging the monster a blameworthy murderer already concedes the personhood we deny him, while our exclusion of him is bare Othering and speciesism of the kind Tom Regan attacks in animal ethics. Michaud ends by reversing the question: after humanity's record of crushing minorities, which the creature learns from Volney's Ruins of Empires and weeps over with Safie, what argument could Victor give Adam for sparing us?

kant-respect.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
kant-respect.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.

kant-respect.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
kant-respect.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Karavitis maps the three films onto the history of animal ethics: Jurassic Park treats dinosaurs as property on Aristotle's ground that only rational humans matter; The Lost World adds Kant's indirect duties, where the sporting rules of Tembo's hunt express duties owed to other humans rather than to the T. rex; and Jurassic Park III moves to Tom Regan, whose 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value fits raptors that remember, plan, and finally choose to spare the humans. The cow and goat fed live to the raptors test how far each view protects animals we treat as mere means.

kant-respect.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
kant-respect.title: The Devil and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.

kant-respect.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
kant-respect.title: Homeland and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Christian Cotton asks whether Carrie's clandestine surveillance of the Brody home, though illegal, is morally wrong, distinguishing legality from morality. Locke's state of nature grounds natural rights to life, liberty, property - and by extension privacy - that government exists to protect and that no national-security goal automatically overrides; Mill's utilitarianism would justify violating one family's privacy to prevent an attack, but Mill's own harm principle and 'tyranny of the majority' caution blocks it when Carrie has only a hunch. Kant's respect for persons as ends in themselves condemns Saul's blackmail of Judge Turner as using a man merely as means, so the Right constrains pursuit of the Good.

kant-respect.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
kant-respect.title: 15. The Way of the Doctor Is Deception
kant-respect.relation: Dodge takes Rule #1 - the Doctor lies - through the major theories of lying: Bernard Williams's definition (asserting what you believe false with intent to deceive), Aristotle's claim that all lies are base, Kant's categorical imperative and respect for persons (even the Vinvocci's shimmer disguises in 'The End of Time' abuse trust), and Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus, which condemns the faked death at Lake Silencio ('The Impossible Astronaut') for the grief it caused Amy and Rory yet rewards the greater happiness it made possible.
