Against the absolutists he sets Plato's Noble Lie from the Republic - the elite falsehood that keeps society functioning - as what the Doctor emulates by deceiving the universe into thinking him dead ('The Wedding of River Song'), and Nietzsche's point in Human, All Too Human that lying is ethically neutral when the pretense is sustainable, as when the Doctor hides the ganger-Amy switch from Rory ('The Almost People'). The upshot: the Doctor's lies are wrong in themselves but routinely justified by the good they do, which is why sometimes the hero lies.

kant-respect.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
kant-respect.title: 18. The Virtues of Choosing Your Faction
kant-respect.relation: Pascoe contrasts Aristotle's and Kant's theories of virtue through the Choosing Ceremony. On Aristotle's account virtues are taught (intellectual) and then habituated into character (moral), tied to one's function, so Susan flourishes because aptitude, upbringing, and choice align while the transfer Al withers - but Tris, Divergent with multiple aptitudes, needs Kant instead: natural virtues are mere 'gifts of nature' that become good only through good will, and her perfect duties to herself and imperfect duties regarding family and faction can justify choosing Dauntless over staying in Abnegation. Kant wins the day: because a corrupted community like Eric's Dauntless redefines bravery into obedience, Tris must think for herself - 'maybe I am wired like the Divergent' - choosing her virtues out of duty and self-respect rather than inheriting them.

kant-respect.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
kant-respect.title: 3. When to Hate and When to Be Irate
kant-respect.relation: Daniel Alloy opens with Aristotle's demand that one be angry 'as and when and for as long as one ought' and builds a theory distinguishing anger (a response to a specific offense, seeking proportional payback) from hatred (a response to a thing's very existence, seeking its destruction). He tests the theory on Louis's bits - hating deer as a class and fantasizing about giving them AIDS, the six-year-old 'Jizzanthapuss,' the Pig Newtons fight with a three-year-old, the Cinnabon clerk, the 'Awesome Possum' hipster, and the justified driver who yells 'suck a sack of dicks.' He argues justified hatred is impossible, since it would require a pure-malevolence being that could not be an autonomous person, so hatred is always wrong while properly proportioned anger remains a necessary part of the moral life. Kant supplies the self-respect dimension ('one who makes himself a worm cannot complain if people step on him'): failing to get angry at real wrongs done to you or your children signals a character deficiency, not virtue.

kant-respect.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
kant-respect.title: 10. Trust Systems or People
kant-respect.relation: Malloy locates the heroes' core disagreement in trust: Cap trusts people, recruiting reformed villains (Hawkeye, Scarlet Witch, Quicksilver, Deadpool) and inspiring the 'kooky quartet', while Tony trusts systems, running the Initiative with pay and the threat of Prison 42. Using Adorno and Horkheimer's critique of instrumental reason, he shows Tony losing sight of what and why he acts - the Armor Wars killing Titanium Man, Civil War destroying the safety it sought - and treating people as means rather than ends in themselves. Via Darwall's two respects (grounded in Kant), Cap's recognition respect for autonomous persons beats Tony's appraisal respect for qualities (he respects even Doom's intellect), so only Cap's trust preserves freedom - and wins.

kant-respect.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
kant-respect.title: 14. Of Course It Sucks—It’s Work
kant-respect.relation: Wible stages three theories of work against Dilbert strips: the Greek view of Plato and Aristotle that labor is freedom-sapping and leisure is the civilized ideal, Marx's capitalist critique in which workers become objects and machines (Wally gives off no human vibe, and robots are coming for the engineers), and Desjardins's human-fulfillment model built on Schumacher's creativity, challenge, development, honesty, and beauty, with Wells Fargo's fake accounts showing how jobs that force lying corrupt character. He endorses instead a Kantian middle ground anchored in Norman Bowie's moral minimum: never treating workers as mere means, so the CEO making intern Asok drink industrial sludge on stage is a violation of respect for persons, not just bad management. Sisyphus supplies the image of pointless labor, though even he might be redeemed if he loved the rock.

kant-respect.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
kant-respect.title: 13. Gilead vs. the Self
kant-respect.relation: Holberg argues that on Kantian grounds Gilead is morally incoherent—Handmaids are treated as mere means, vessels without agency—and that it sustains itself by attacking self-respect through two temporal modes: the quick onset of fear (Aristotle's account in the Rhetoric applied to the machine-gun arrests of women at their jobs) and the slow grind of shame (empty time that turns women into 'objects not in use' and manufactures a veneer of consent: 'nothing is going on here that I haven't signed up for'). Agency needs recognition from others—love as the most basic acknowledgment, or invoking Moira ('Moira would never stand for this shit')—so June's 'I tell, therefore you are' and the reader's duty to affirm her judgment carry the feminist-Kantian point: dependency on others does not negate the self, it is what constitutes it.

kant-respect.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
kant-respect.title: 14. Jerryboree!
kant-respect.relation: Arguing that even the interchangeable Jerrys of Jerryboree deserve better, the chapter uses Stephen Darwall's distinction between recognition and appraisal respect: Jerry lacks both, while Rick has appraisal self-respect (he loves his genius) but squanders recognition self-respect by portal-hopping away from every consequence. Jerry's spinelessness is then Sartrean bad faith, from celebrating being 'assigned a function' in 'The Wedding Squanchers' to needing the parasite Sleepy Gary to vouch for his very existence in 'Total Rickall' and lying to Keara in 'The ABCs of Beth'. The chapter closes with Thomas Hill's Kantian case that servility disrespects the moral law in oneself, quoting Kant's worm maxim against Jerry's failed him-or-me ultimatum in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption'.

kant-respect.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
kant-respect.title: Power Behind the Cloak
kant-respect.relation: The chapter asks whether Wong's hereditary service to the Sorcerer Supreme is culpable servility, framing the charge with Kant's line that 'one who makes himself a worm cannot complain' and Thomas E. Hill's Kantian account of servility as failing to claim one's dignity as a person. It answers with Hegel's master-slave dialectic: Strange, free to haunt the astral plane, becomes dependent on Wong for everything worldly, while Wong, by working on the world rather than merely commanding it, develops the self-consciousness Hegel says work produces—he serves the shared mission rather than the master—so the relationship is a partnership in which servitude grounds rather than forfeits Wong's self-respect.

kant-respect.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
kant-respect.title: 5. The Morality of Manners
kant-respect.relation: Dougherty argues that in Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating and cultivating moral character, above all respect for persons, though they can also mask its absence. Matthew's growth from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation' to honoring Molesley's dignity, and Branson's journey from tweed defiance ('uniforms of oppression') to worrying that a tuxedo is insufficient for the Dowager's dinner, show manners tracking their growing respect for the Crawleys as particular individuals. The chapter anchors this in Aristotle's person of visible virtue, Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' and Sarah Buss's claim that manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect, while Sir Richard's boorishness and the Dowager Countess's weaponized courtesy show manners failing or serving self-interest. Mrs. Crawley's etiquette-breaking kindness, praised even by Violet, complicates the picture by showing care can be morally outrun by propriety.

kant-respect.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
kant-respect.title: a12.xhtml
kant-respect.relation: O'Hara argues that play is what makes hobbits - and us - fully human: Bilbo's childhood games of throwing stones, riddles and smoke-rings turn out to be training for the quest (his stone-throwing fells the spiders, his riddle-practice buys time with Gollum), and even Gollum's riddle-game makes him momentarily 'less a monster and more a person'. Following Schiller's and Huizinga's Homo ludens thesis that play completes humanity, he distinguishes play from idleness (Aquinas held recreation continues in heaven; Peirce called play 'vigorous exercise'), places leisure among the goods of Aristotle's 'we play in order to be serious', and contrasts Gandalf's beauty-directed fireworks with the orcs' merely useful explosions and work-chants. But play has limits: Kant warns against treating persons as toys, and Bilbo's lesson is 'Never laugh at live dragons!'

kant-respect.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
kant-respect.title: Notes
kant-respect.relation: Koepsell argues the franchise stages the bioconservatism-versus-transhumanism debate: the villains are machine-altered (Immortan Joe's breathing gear, the People Eater's prosthetic nose, Master Blaster's contraption) while the saved live green and unmodified, so George Miller's films side with Leon Kass's bioconservatism against Nick Bostrom's transhumanist embrace of enhancement. Dignity — derived from Kant and contested between Kass and Bostrom — is the hinge, and the recurring green places (the family farm, the Sunshine Coast, the Crack in the Earth, the Green Place) mark the dignity of nature the Wasteland destroyed. The bioconservative lesson holds even though Max and Furiosa, patched with prosthetics, must partially embrace their posthuman condition to survive.

kant-respect.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
kant-respect.title: The Question of Ethical Advertising
kant-respect.relation: Novakovic and Whitney use the Heineken incident, where Betty discovers she was the target demographic for her husband's campaign ('Must be so funny, being in on it'), to test advertising against Kantian honesty and respect. Kant's humanity formula and the lying-promise example show that manipulation wrongs the consumer as a rational agent, and Don's defense that advertising sells 'happiness' fails because Kant allows making others' happiness an end but never at the cost of truth, whether the consumer is a stranger or a wife. The chapter sets this against the era's brainwashing anxieties (Hunter's Brainwashing in Red China, Packard's The Hidden Persuaders, Precon subliminal projection) and concludes that honest advertising must survive disclosure of its methods, noting that real sponsors like Canada Dry and BMW responded to the show with stripped-down 'transparent' ads that let viewers be 'in on it.'

kant-respect.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
kant-respect.title: NOTES
kant-respect.relation: Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.

kant-respect.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
kant-respect.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife Jenny is a person, weighing Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellectual soul, and Kantian dignity against Peter Singer's speciesism challenge to the person/animal moral line. They then argue walkers are 'impossible beings' like square-circles: Jenner's brain-stem-only reanimation cannot explain Hannah the bicycle girl crawling without organs, walkers smelling Rick in the rain, or cafeteria walkers moving for weeks without energy. On either the soul view or materialism walkers are not persons, so Morgan should shoot, and zombies fascinate because they are metaphysical projections of our fears, caught between being and nonbeing.

kant-respect.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
kant-respect.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
kant-respect.relation: McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.

kant-respect.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
kant-respect.title: Friendship in the Wild
kant-respect.relation: Vardar argues that the Witcher 3 ending players most prefer, Ciri becoming a witcher, is reached precisely when the player curbs curiosity and limits love with respect, as Kant requires of ideal friendship in the Metaphysics of Morals. She reads the snowball-fight encouragement, letting Ciri face the Lodge sorceresses alone, cheering the destruction of Avallac'h's lab, and refusing the visit to Emperor Emhyr as choices that balance Kantian love and respect, while the alternative choices wound Ciri's pride or undermine her autonomy. George Herbert Mead's 'taking the role of the other' explains how playing both Geralt and Ciri in turn lets the player develop the perspectives needed for this moral friendship, a lesson the game carries into real-life friendships.

kant-respect.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
kant-respect.title: Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf
kant-respect.relation: Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.

kant-respect.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
kant-respect.title: Fourth Hole “Quiet…Please!” Reflections on Golf and Civility
kant-respect.relation: McNaron argues that golf promotes civility both empirically and normatively through its rules (self-scoring, self-called penalties) and its etiquette (silence during a swing, care for the course). Using an Aristotelian virtue-ethics frame plus Kekes's 'conduct according to custom' and Calhoun's expressivist account of civility as communicating respect, he treats civility as a mean acquired by habituation and opposes it to skloka, the petty hostility of win-at-all-costs sport. He defends golf's quiet against charges of classism, reads Tiger Woods's outburst at a shutter-clicking photographer as justified anger at an etiquette breach, and names the Ryder Cup's jingoism, boorish spectators, and intrusive media as threats to golf's civil, contemplative character.

kant-respect.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
kant-respect.title: General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War
kant-respect.relation: Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.

kant-respect.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
kant-respect.title: Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons
kant-respect.relation: Kowalski reads Horton Hatches the Egg and Horton Hears a Who! through Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative. Mayzie's lying promise to Horton fails the universal-law test just like Kant's lying-loan and tax-shirking (Jo-Jo) cases, while Horton's insistence that 'a person's a person, no matter how small' embodies the ends-in-themselves formula treating the Whos as ends with dignity, not things. The essay argues Horton's fidelity is heroic rather than strictly required, revising Kant's moral absolutism (the inquiring-murderer case) so that when duties conflict one should act to disrespect persons least.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
paradox-of-fiction.title: 15 - The Function of Fiction The Heuristic Value of Homer
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Jennifer McMahon extends Martha Nussbaum's claim in Love's Knowledge that certain moral truths can only be fittingly stated in narrative form, arguing fiction educates through identification plus 'frustrated identification' - it draws us in safely while blocking habitual responses, forcing reflection. The Simpsons' caricatured ordinariness lets viewers admit Homer's irascibility or Marge's forbearance are caricatures of themselves, its comedy displaces anxieties and disables resistances (we laugh at Homer's idiocy because we see ourselves), its animation reminds us nothing is real, and its mass reach amplifies the effect - e.g. episodes on gambling ('$pringfield'), animal rights ('Lisa the Vegetarian'), and women in military academies ('The Secret War of Lisa Simpson'). She concludes popular cartoons like this one, not just canonical literature, have genuine heuristic value against elitist assumptions.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
paradox-of-fiction.title: Unknown
paradox-of-fiction.relation: The chapter states the paradox of fiction formally - we respond emotively only to what we believe real, we do not believe fiction is real, yet we respond - and rejects both Coleridge's 'willing suspension of disbelief' and simple empathy as explanations. Using The Matrix's special effects and IMAX-scale immersion, it argues our engagement tracks how the story is told rather than belief in its reality, and with Kendall Walton's make-believe suggests that entering a fiction is cognitively akin to Neo entering the Matrix, which would make the real/unreal belief condition irrelevant.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
paradox-of-fiction.title: Evaluating Zelda
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, or care when Tetra's identity is revealed, though we know none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never suspend disbelief enough to call the police), Carroll's thought theory (fear is too fast and too vivid for mere thoughts), and Walton's pretend theory (involuntary pretending and the uniform way all players see the sail break it). Instead he argues for a multi-level mind, modeled on Plato's divided soul in the Republic and Fodor's mental modules: local unconscious appraisals react to the fire as if real, while a global appraisal of reality-status keeps us in our chairs.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
paradox-of-fiction.title: A Happy Ending
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Bickham asks why Dorothy is so eager to leave heroic, Technicolor Oz for the gray, childless, Gulch-dominated farm, and whether, like Hamlet's delay, her rash choice can be evaluated as hers rather than her author's. Aristotle's account of the good life as the exercise of our highest capacities, requiring friends and material goods, makes Oz look like the better home for the competent twelve- or thirteen-year-old he takes Dorothy to be, against the hedonisms of Aristippus, Epicurus, and Bentham and Plato's body-denying dualism. But caring about Dorothy first needs defending from the paradox of fiction, which he works through Currie's simulation theory and Walton's make-believe emotions before dissolving the puzzle: storytelling suspends the reign of logic, so wishing Dorothy well is natural. Finally Heidegger's being-toward-death shows 'happily ever after' is impossible anywhere, and he throws the problem to the reader: write a happy ending for Dorothy in Kansas.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
paradox-of-fiction.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Carl Ehrett and Sarah Worth ask whether D&D is really a game (imagining Bill and Ted challenging Death to a campaign) and model the search for a definition of 'game' on Socrates dismantling Euthyphro's attempted definitions of piety, only for Wittgenstein's family resemblance to dissolve the project. On that view D&D still counts as a game despite lacking winning and losing, because its rule-governedness survives 'rule 0' license to bend rules whenever bending them crafts a better story. To explain why players who know the world is not real are nonetheless engrossed, they present Radford's paradox of fiction and adopt Walton's make-believe theory: the miniature on the table is a prop prescribing the imagining of an owlbear, so genuine quasi-emotions respond to truths in the fiction, making D&D an unusually gripping interactive story.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
paradox-of-fiction.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
paradox-of-fiction.relation: The chapter poses the 'Barney Paradox': viewers identify and empathize with a character who is utterly awful (selling a woman, the Scuba Diver con that dupes all his friends), even though we would shun him in real life. Nanay tests and finds insufficient several explanations - Barney is just immature, we only feel schadenfreude at his slap-bet punishments, or his emotions are simply contagious - since none explains why Barney's badness increases our engagement. Using Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table example and Adam Smith's idea of imagining ourselves in another's situation, he argues identification targets the character's situation, which is not itself evil. The appeal is vicarious badness: fiction lets us be 'virtual tourists' in immorality we would never choose for real.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
paradox-of-fiction.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Michael Muniz argues the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park are real 'in the most important ways' - not cloned in a lab, but real whenever the film runs: they terrify, they occupy our dreams (his T. rex-at-the-window opening), and they re-actualize deep time on screen. He weighs whether the franchise is genuinely horror - preying on fear for a negative response - or something stranger, a tension between fear and excitement in which extinction itself is the source of the scare.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
paradox-of-fiction.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Muniz uses the 'Ocean of Fear' material to stage the paradox of fiction—we know Finn, Jake, and the Lich are drawings, yet we genuinely fear for the child hero in danger—and works through its three sentences: we respond emotionally only to what we believe real, we disbelieve fiction, yet we respond to fiction constantly. Distinguishing passive startle from active dwelling, he tests escape routes: fear at Marceline's abandonment may really be fear for our own children, the robot attack in 'Business Men' may become 'real' to a viewer, and some philosophers call our responses mere 'fictional emotions.' Finding no sentence safely deniable, he concludes that our emotional responses to Adventure Time are, strictly speaking, irrational—but no less honest for it.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
paradox-of-fiction.title: 14. Diane, I Am Now Upside Down
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Tackles the paradox of fiction — how we can love Cooper, hate James, and mourn the child Richard runs over while knowing none of them exist — running through Radford's failed explanations (forgetting, suspension of disbelief, association with real people). Its solution is Amie Thomasson's view that fictional characters are abstract artifacts: like the United States or its laws, Cooper really exists as a human creation with causal powers, so grieving him is rational, not confused. Parasocial interaction and wishful identification (Rubin and McHugh, Ramasubramanian and Kornfield) then explain why viewers befriend and emulate him — the one-sided Diane tapes and the coffee ritual function as intimacy-building shared experience, letting us cycle between friend, avatar, and outside observer.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
paradox-of-fiction.title: “When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Lean treats Bernard's discovery in 'Trompe L'Oeil' that his son Charlie never existed as a richly detailed thought experiment about intentionality: his memories of Charlie seem to refer to nothing, so his grief looks like 'grieving about nothing.' After setting up Brentano's aboutness and Frege's sense/reference distinction (Dolores learns that 'William' and 'the Man in Black' are one referent known under two senses), he tests two consolations: a fiction theory drawing on Lamarque, on which Bernard's implanted memories are a story rather than a lie and his emotions are rationally grounded because thoughts need only be entertained, not believed, to move us; and an 'inheritance theory' on which a causal theory of reference might make Bernard's copied memories genuinely about Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that whichever theory Bernard adopts, his suffering is what makes him 'real,' echoing the Man in Black's line that suffering is when you are most real.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
paradox-of-fiction.title: 15 Wakandan Resources The Epistemological Reality of Black Panther’s Fiction
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Ruby Komic treats Black Panther as an 'epistemic resource' in Gaile Pohlhaus's sense: because of its majority-Black creative team the film supplies audiences with narrative tools that answer to real Black experience, against Anthony Mackie's charge that the film's Black-only hiring is itself racist. The chapter reads the film's plural representations - the T'Challa/Killmonger ideological tension, Nakia's 'No, I save my country' defiance of Okoye's institutional loyalty, Okoye throwing away her wig, Black viewers rooting for the 'villain' - as the kind of nuanced material that remedies decades of stereotypical representation. Following Miranda Fricker, it concludes that the historic scarcity of such resources is an epistemic injustice against Black knowers, and that Black Panther is a partial act of epistemic justice.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
paradox-of-fiction.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Ehrett and Worth ask whether D&D is really a game and why we invest so much in it. Against the Socratic model (the Euthyphro dialogue's search for a common thread defining piety, here applied to 'game'), they deploy Wittgenstein's family-resemblance account from the Philosophical Investigations, concluding D&D lacks clear winning and losing but is rule-governed, with the twist that rule-breaking is legitimate exactly when it serves the game's primary purpose of group storytelling. They then take up the paradox of fiction: since players know the world is not real, Radford's puzzle arises, and Kendall Walton's make-believe theory of props and fictional truths supplies their answer, making D&D an especially gripping fiction because players are participants rather than observers.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
paradox-of-fiction.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Asking whether the Millennium Trilogy is popular fiction or literature, the chapter proposes Wittgenstein's family resemblances instead of an essence: Larsson's books are devoured like genre series, yet they tackle the 'moral seriousness'—violence against women, corruption, journalistic ethics—that Sartre called committed literature, so the whodunit becomes the exposé. Nussbaum's account of reading as moral perception, not mere grasp of facts, is applied to Lisbeth's 'Bitch' verdict on Harriet Vanger—should we see a culpable sister or a victim?—and the paradox of fiction explains why we feel real pity and fear for characters we know are invented, down to the detective plot's 'consolatory fiction' that truth can be found. The verdict: socially conscious popular fiction whose high/low distinction (Arnold versus Meisel's level field) matters less than the words-as-force-for-justice theme summed up in 'an insufferable do-gooder who thought he could change everything with a book.'

paradox-of-fiction.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
paradox-of-fiction.title: a15.xhtml
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Kind uses our genuine reactions to Bilbo - pity when he sits forlorn at the Lonely Mountain, anxiety at the riddle-game, outrage at Thorin's rebuke - to stage the paradox of fiction: how can emotions be rational toward someone we know never existed? She walks through the failed solutions: Radford's verdict that fiction-emotions are irrational like fearing a mountain lion after the sighting is debunked; Walton's 'quasi-emotions' of make-believe, which cannot explain why we cannot switch our fear of the wargs off at will; and thought theory's mental images, since what we fear is Smaug, not our mental image of Smaug. Her preferred route, following Richard Moran, relaxes the belief requirement itself - as Hume noted passions resist rational assessment and as Nussbaum argues fiction cultivates moral character, many emotions (grief for the dead Tolkien, fear of future floods) need no existence beliefs.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
paradox-of-fiction.title: Evaluating Zelda
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Jonathan Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, and feel touched when Aryll gives him her telescope, given that none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never call the police when Aryll is kidnapped), Carroll's thought theory (on-screen monsters act too fast for conscious thought), and Walton's pretend theory (we cannot voluntarily stop seeing the sail as a sail). Instead he proposes a multi-level mind — drawing on Plato's Republic (the thirsty non-drinker and Leontius and the corpses) plus Fodor's modules and Grodal's local/global appraisals — on which lower-level processes react to Hyrule as real while the global appraisal knows it is only a game.

paradox-of-fiction.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
paradox-of-fiction.title: Notes
paradox-of-fiction.relation: Takes the carbon-freezing scene - Leia's 'I love you,' Han's 'I know,' Chewie's howls - to pose the paradox of fiction: we feel genuine, involuntary fear and pity for characters we know do not exist. It tests and rejects the illusion theory (we do not flee Vader's 501st Legion), the thought theory (we pity Han himself, not our mental representation of him), and Walton's pretend theory (viewers' emotions, unlike a child's Darth Maul lightsaber play, are not voluntary), landing on Radford's conclusion that our tears over the binary sunset and Obi-Wan's death are real emotions but not rational ones.

film-as-philosophy.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
film-as-philosophy.title: 15 - The Function of Fiction The Heuristic Value of Homer
film-as-philosophy.relation: Jennifer McMahon extends Martha Nussbaum's claim in Love's Knowledge that certain moral truths can only be fittingly stated in narrative form, arguing fiction educates through identification plus 'frustrated identification' - it draws us in safely while blocking habitual responses, forcing reflection. The Simpsons' caricatured ordinariness lets viewers admit Homer's irascibility or Marge's forbearance are caricatures of themselves, its comedy displaces anxieties and disables resistances (we laugh at Homer's idiocy because we see ourselves), its animation reminds us nothing is real, and its mass reach amplifies the effect - e.g. episodes on gambling ('$pringfield'), animal rights ('Lisa the Vegetarian'), and women in military academies ('The Secret War of Lisa Simpson'). She concludes popular cartoons like this one, not just canonical literature, have genuine heuristic value against elitist assumptions.

film-as-philosophy.title: Introduction
film-as-philosophy.relation: Kowalski's Introduction argues that philosophy is an activity, not a possession—asking universally important questions, exposing contradictions, and defending answers with arguments—and asks whether a filmmaker can engage in that process through fictional narrative, using Joss Whedon's corpus (Buffy, Angel, Firefly, Dollhouse, The Avengers) as the test case. It contends that showing Whedon philosophizes would confirm the film-as-philosophy thesis and force its expansion to television. The chapter then prospectuses the book: authenticity via Heidegger, Sartre, Socrates, and Rawls; Platonic and Aristotelian accounts of the good life; Lockean-Kantian rights and Aristotelian virtue without God; Hick's religious non-realism via Shepherd Book; free will via d'Holbach and Kane; and the Mulhall debate—under the canon rule that only texts with Whedon's script approval count.

film-as-philosophy.title: Mulhall and His Detractors
film-as-philosophy.relation: The chapter stages the film-as-philosophy debate: Mulhall's 'bold thesis' that films like the Alien series are 'philosophical exercises—philosophy in action,' Baggini's objection that they offer symbolic representations without reasons, and Mulhall's rejoinders that rationally reorienting a shared conceptual space (Socrates' polis-as-parent analogy in the Crito) and dramatizing visions of what ultimately matters are rational without formal argument. It then answers Murray Smith (film thought experiments like All of Me subordinate the epistemic to the artistic) and Paisley Livingston (philosophizing must occur via non-paraphrasable cinematic devices alone) by arguing that Whedon's portrayal of Angel's worldview—helping the helpless for its own sake with no glorious end—raises exactly the ultimate-ends questions Mill said admit of no proof, with Angel as a confirming instance of Mulhall. The Buffy episode 'Hush' closes the case: its dialogue-free middle, from Buffy and Riley's kiss to Willow and Tara's joined-hands spell, conveys a Zen-like lesson about the limits of propositional knowledge that resists linguistic mediation, answering Livingston's talking-head dilemma.

film-as-philosophy.title: The Russell-Wartenberg Debate
film-as-philosophy.relation: The chapter sets the book's standard for 'philosophy in action' by staging Bruce Russell's skepticism against Thomas Wartenberg's defense of the film-as-philosophy thesis: Russell holds that narrative films can at most raise questions or furnish counterexamples, so The Matrix merely inspires the viewer's own argument for external-world skepticism, while Wartenberg replies that The Matrix screens Descartes's evil-deceiver hypothesis so effectively that viewers are themselves deceived into skeptical doubt, accomplishing for audiences what Socrates did to his interlocutors. Wartenberg's reading of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind — where Dr. Mierzwiak's memory-erasure technology presents utilitarianism (via Mary's dialogue) and then a counterexample to it — is tested, and the author proposes the film targets hedonism more directly, working as a reverse variant of Nozick's experience machine that defends autonomy over happiness. Kant's obscure Transcendental Deduction is invoked to show that even canonical philosophical texts are ambiguous, blunting the explicitness objection. The chapter concludes that negative projects — modus tollens counterexamples cinematically conveyed — are where film most plausibly philosophizes, preparing the ground for reading the Whedonverse.

film-as-philosophy.title: Conclusion
film-as-philosophy.relation: The conclusion synthesizes the book's case that Whedon philosophizes, building a Shaw-style hierarchy from illustrating theories (Connor as Robert Kane's libertarian agent, 'stirred up' between Darla's and faux-Cordelia's competing visions) through ethical and metaphysical complexity ('Man on the Street,' Angel/Angelus) to epistemic endorsement of a Whedonian worldview. It reads Angel's epiphany — 'if there's no bigger meaning, then the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing in the world' — as a negative project against the thesis that ethics without God is incoherent, since Whedon's God-ambiguous fiction shows noble self-sacrifice (Buffy for Dawn, Cordy for Angel, Simon for River) that remains worthwhile regardless of cosmic justice. Following Mulhall's use of Socrates as an exemplar of ethically significant living, it casts Angel the Champion as a comparable exemplar grounded in authenticity, care-based relationships, and the transformation of moral character. It closes by extending the film-as-philosophy debate to television, deploying Carroll's gaze/glance distinction to argue nothing in principle keeps quality TV — from The Twilight Zone and Star Trek to Buffy and Angel — from being philosophy in action.

film-as-philosophy.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of TV Noir
film-as-philosophy.relation: Sanders's introduction argues that TV noir is an autonomous art form in which film noir's themes are aufgehoben (Hegel's term: preserved and transcended, not negated), and that noir television dramatizes philosophical questions about alienation, relativism, freedom, and meaning. He surveys the volume's arguments: Fitzgibbons on Naked City's conflation of the normal with the moral, Skoble's counterexample of moral clarity in The Fugitive (Richard Kimble), Lee's morally ambiguous John Drake in Secret Agent, and his own readings of Miami Vice's 'sunshine noir' and Crockett's merger with his undercover persona Sonny Burnett. He frames Part 2 through Sartre and Camus, contrasting their call for engagement and defiance with classic noir's passive doomed protagonists (D.O.A.'s Frank Bigelow, The Prisoner's Number 6), and applies Camus's man of revolt to Jack Bauer in 24. He also raises standing objections: Nagel's ironic alternative to Camus's scorn, the incoherence of 'nothing matters' applied to Tony Soprano, and the Foucault/Lyotard-style postmodern critique of institutional power he finds in Crime Story.

film-as-philosophy.title: “Are You Watching Closely ”
film-as-philosophy.relation: Knight and McKnight analyze how Nolan's early films withhold narrative transparency: Doodlebug's regress of killers, Following's framing device that ends with Cobb vanishing into a crowd, Memento's reverse chronology, and The Prestige's twin frames of top hats and drowned doubles all force viewers to build and revise hypotheses about what happened, when, and who is responsible. Because actions cannot be morally evaluated until we know who performed them and why, the chapter ties narrative comprehension to moral judgment—Leonard's confabulated revenge and inability to recognize his own self-deception, Dormer's ambiguous redemption, and Ellie's unresolved choice over the bullet. The Prestige's doubles raise the identity question the authors gloss with Parfit's teletransporter—perhaps it does not matter which Angier survives—while Cutter's helping Borden kill Caldlow enacts Francis Bacon's 'wild justice' that the law cannot provide. The chapter closes on Nolan as auteur, whose self-conscious framing devices and play of masks make 'Are you watching closely?' at once the film's theme and its admonition to the viewer.

class-struggle.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer
class-struggle.title: 16 - A (Karl, not Groucho) Marxist in Springfield
class-struggle.relation: James Wallace tests The Simpsons' 'subversive' reputation with Marxist ideology critique, granting that Kantian incongruity jokes - Homer offering aliens his family ('Treehouse of Horror VII') or the Richie Rich/Casper exchange in 'Three Men and a Comic Book' - can momentarily distance viewers from ideology. But he argues the show subverts its own subversion: 'Scenes from the Class Struggle in Springfield' ends with the Simpsons restored to the Krusty Burger 'dump' and Lisa silenced from complaining by a pony, workers (the union trading its dental plan for a beer keg in 'Last Exit to Springfield') are lampooned as hard as Mr. Burns, and Homer's capitalist one-liner in 'Crepes of Wrath' carries no more weight than his lazy-worker lines. Without a vision of a better world, the satire collapses into the joke, and the show ends up reflecting and conserving bourgeois capitalist ideology - laughter as opiate.

class-struggle.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
class-struggle.title: The Matrix , Marx, and the Coppertop’s Life
class-struggle.relation: Danahay and Rieder read the film as dramatizing Marx's account of the exploited worker, from UPS drivers with tracking devices to keystroke-counted data clerks, continuing the workplace surveillance Marx attacked. The pivotal scene is Morpheus's loading-program lesson: 'You've been living in a dream world' followed by 'Welcome to the desert of the real' and the definition of the Matrix as control that turns a human being into the Duracell battery he holds up—the 'coppertop' Switch earlier called Neo.

class-struggle.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
class-struggle.title: Unknown
class-struggle.relation: The chapter reads the pod power plant—naked humans stacked like workers in corporate cubicles—through the Communist Manifesto's enslaved factory masses and 'Wage-Labor and Capital's' claim that labor power is a commodity sold by the clock like sugar. Against readings of alienation as private feeling, it uses Morpheus's 'The Matrix is a system' speech to show Marx's point that alienation is produced by the system of social relations: workers see their own labor as a commodity and cannot recognize their connection to the capital they generate.

class-struggle.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
class-struggle.title: The Superhero As Liberal Reformer
class-struggle.relation: Jeffrey Pasley traces the show's radical surface — capitalism equated with vampirism (Anya's greed, Glory the über-consumer, the Master's blood factory in 'The Wish'), Big Bads tearing down dimensional barriers exactly as Marx's Communist Manifesto describes the bourgeoisie dissolving feudal ties into free trade, Buffy refusing to commodify slaying into wage labor, and Giles's Magic Box selling mystified junk at inflated margins — but concludes the heroes are not revolutionaries. In the comic-book lineage of Superman and Spider-Man, Buffy and Angel are liberal reformers bound by a superhero code against killing, so Giles must murder the innocent Ben precisely to preserve Buffy's heroic mercy; Angel's 'champions' speech in 'Deep Down' states the incrementalist creed.

class-struggle.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
class-struggle.title: Hip Hop and “This Makin’ Dollars Shit”
class-struggle.relation: Pittman argues the rap battle - UTFO's "Roxanne, Roxanne" answered by Roxanne Shanté's "Roxanne's Revenge", Run-D.M.C.'s "Sucker MC's", Jay-Z's "Takeover" versus Nas's "Ether" - is hip hop's enactment of Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition, where self-consciousness proves itself only through an all-or-nothing contest ending in domination rather than destruction. Gangsta rap (N.W.A's "Gangsta Gangsta", Ice Cube's fantasy raid on the suburbs) radicalizes the battle into a collective demand that America recognize black urban conditions, and the chapter turns to Du Bois's race-centered and Marx's class-centered revisions of Hegel's history to read "this makin' dollars shit" - Wu-Tang's "C.R.E.A.M.", Talib Kweli on capitalism and crack, Mos Def's "The Rape Over" - as the dialectic's capture of the cipher by corporate beef.

class-struggle.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
class-struggle.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.

class-struggle.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
class-struggle.title: Downsizing Dreams
class-struggle.relation: Michael Bray argues the American Office portrays the "salaried masses," a class that exists in denying class: Jim, Pam, and Michael's rationalized, meaningless paper work realizes Marx's account of surplus value and degraded labor (the "run-out-the-clock" truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors), while their self-image survives by distinguishing itself from warehouse and prison labor. Episodes like Michael's condo purchase and Pam's "dreams are just dreams" show characters secretly longing for downsizing to force a different life. Against the New Yorker's claim that the show ignores class, Bray reads its comedy as standing on the edge of naming its economic conditions, with Michael's failure to inhabit management-speak making him, via Walter Benjamin, a last glimpse of "authentic humanity."

class-struggle.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
class-struggle.title: Quittin’ Time
class-struggle.relation: Michels surveys Marx (alienation, false consciousness, the Communist Manifesto's reduction of family to economics), Weber's Protestant work ethic, and Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, then reads Springsteen's whole career against them, from 'Factory' (the working life that 'takes his hearing' and leaves 'someone's gonna get hurt tonight') through 'Hungry Heart,' 'Mansion on the Hill,' and The Ghost of Tom Joad ('Youngstown,' 'Sinaloa Cowboys,' 'Straight Time'). The verdict: Springsteen is a man of the left but no Marxist — his characters struggle with their own restlessness and with each other rather than with class oppressors, the wealthy suffer their own bourgeois malaise, and work, however brutal, is no cause for revolution. Nor does he share Arendt's ideal: his realm of freedom is unapologetically middle-class — cruising in a cool car, hanging with friends, getting with your favorite girl, and always the radio.

class-struggle.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
class-struggle.title: It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life
class-struggle.relation: Shipman argues that the re-imagined Cylons, having rebelled as slaves, recreated oppression inside their own society: the human-form Numbers rule over mute Centurions (voices literally bred out, like banning slave literacy), animalized Raiders, and dismissed 'insane' Hybrids, whose sentience ('Scar' shows strategy and self-preservation) the Numbers willfully deny. The division of labor echoes Marx's 'from each according to his ability,' but assignments are engineered by their makers, and the model-making program is eugenics rather than evolution — the series' own word 'evolved' is, he says, disingenuous. Hence the Numbers lose the moral superiority their victimhood earned, and the scriptural 'all of this has happened before' implies the subaltern models may rebel next.

class-struggle.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
class-struggle.title: 22 - The Proles and Cons of facebook
class-struggle.relation: Morgan and Clulow stage a second-person narrative in which the reader joins a friend's 'Against Corporate Polluters' Cause and receives a manifesto opening with the Communist Manifesto's 'history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles,' updating the proletariat into the internet-era 'iProles' via a mock discussion board voiced by Chomsky, Engels, Luxemburg, and Liebknecht. Facebook's global reach builds real coalitions — the group links up with Iranian environmentalists — but distraction, fragmented duplicate groups, one-click commitment (the 200,000-member 'Obama Grow an Afro' group dwarfing a 57-member Kyoto group), and Facebook's corporate power to silence users (Kieron Bimpson's 'Justice for Francesca' group deleted as spam) blunt its activist promise. Only disciplined uses like Obama's campaign and Carrotmob convert the network into offline change — and elites can play on the same platform.

class-struggle.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
class-struggle.title: The Wire and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Curry refuses to celebrate The Wire, arguing that Simon's class-based realism ('more about class than race') misrepresents Black urban life, and he contrasts it with Black film from New Jack City to Menace II Society where these issues were already explored. Reading scenes like Rawls's 'project nigger' murders no one cares about, Bunk shrugging at Stringer's unsolved killing, and McNulty telling Brianna that nobody will look into D'Angelo's death, he argues the show registers an indifference specific to Black life, not to the poor as such. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois's account of colonialism and the slave trade as the genesis of modern capital ('capital noir') and rejecting the intersectional race-class-gender frame as a 'discursive distraction', he demands a racial realism in Derrick Bell's sense: racism is permanent, the underclass is really an racialized undercaste, and the War on Drugs continues Jim Crow by other means.

class-struggle.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
class-struggle.title: The Wire and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.

class-struggle.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
class-struggle.title: Psych and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.

class-struggle.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
class-struggle.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Fitzpatrick runs Marx's account of alienated labor from the 1844 Manuscripts through the novel: Victor's creature is the product of estranged labor, 'an alien object exercising power over him,' which he cannot name, comes to loathe, and which finally destroys him - the devaluation of the creator tracking the increasing value of the thing made, while workers become commodities producing commodities. The De Laceys' eviction in Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Ingolstadt cholera riots stage class struggle at feudalism's end, and Victor's failure to self-actualize (to 'hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon... criticize after dinner') shows how capitalism turns science into 'a tool of our own destruction.' The chapter closes with 'Frankenstorm' climate change as the alienated externality par excellence - capitalists selling us the rope with which we hang ourselves.

class-struggle.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
class-struggle.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.

class-struggle.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
class-struggle.title: Justified and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: The chapter argues coal made Boyd Crowder possible: company scrip, Bloody Harlan's union-busting terror, black lung (Boyd's would-be assassin takes the bridge job because mining ruined his lungs), and Black Pike's mountaintop removal leave Harlan no viable work outside the mines, so crime is the rational alternative. It reads this through Hegel's 'rabble' from the Philosophy of Right - civil society is never wealthy enough to prevent an excess of poverty, and the rabble loses the honor of self-support - plus Marcuse's affluent-society critique of an existence that 'violently defends its own servitude'. Boyd's outlawry, which sets its own code above mere criminality, is a rebellion against being pushed into the rabble, and Hegel's remedy of emigration explains why leaving Harlan is the only escape, though the coal train hauls coal out while the people stay.

class-struggle.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
class-struggle.title: Dracula and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Karavitis fabricates a recovered 'Dracula's Journal' in which the Count retells Stoker's plot as rational self-interest: he owes no one anything, Lucy 'came to me of her own free will,' Van Helsing's crew are a 'craven collective' spouting 'from each according to his ability,' and only objective reality - not their subjective feelings - counts. He claims a fundamental right to pursue his own happiness, casting himself as the thinking individual crushed by proletarian herd morality. An editor's framing email makes the point explicit: Rand-style egoism could justify even Dracula, a 'manual for vampires' set against Marx's collectivism.

class-struggle.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
class-struggle.title: Dracula and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Sexton's mock FBI COMPIC file stages a Cold War reading of Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein: screenwriters Lees and Rinaldo remake Dracula as Marx's Das Kapital vampire - capital as dead labour sucking living labour - so blood-draining becomes profit-draining and 'This man belongs to me!' the capitalist's claim on his workers. A fictional Ayn Rand review for HUAC decodes the film as collectivist propaganda that slanders the businessman McDougal and dreams of a creature with 'no will of his own,' touching Marxian alienation along the way. A final note links screenwriter Robert Lees's blacklisting by Sterling Hayden and his real-life decapitation to Stoker's vampire-killing instructions.

class-struggle.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
class-struggle.title: 9. Class Warfare in Chicago
class-struggle.relation: Canode reads the trilogy as a study in class warfare: the factionless are the invisible lower class kept poor as a warning, the factions the middle class distracted by initiation rankings and faction pride, and the Bureau the self-righteous upper class that created and manipulates the whole system. Marx's analysis structures the argument - the ruling class's specter now haunts the powerless, and 'from each according to his ability' shades into coerced harmony - while the American Dream rhetoric of Carter, Reagan, and Obama plays the aptitude test's role: an ideology of merit that converts structural limits into personal failure. The Bureau's genetic sorting of GP scientists above GD support staff mirrors how meritocracy blames the poor for their poverty, so Tris's verdict - the factions 'gave us the illusion of choice without actually giving us a choice' - indicts the US class system too.

class-struggle.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
class-struggle.title: 2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic
class-struggle.relation: Walderczak stages the Branson-Robert-Matthew triangle as socialism, aristocratic conservatism, and capitalism colliding over the estate's duty to its people. He tracks how Tom's Marx-flavored socialism - really closer to Owen's and Fourier's utopian cooperatism - evaporates once he marries Sybil and co-manages the land, the chauffeur 'Branson' becoming family-member 'Tom,' a case of David Harvey's capitalist pacification. Meanwhile Robert's noblesse oblige - secretly paying a tenant's overdue rent from private funds, ranting 'profits, profits, profits,' treating ownership as custodianship of the tenants - leaves the author asking who the real socialist is, and answering that Robert's conservatism has far more in common with socialist ideals than Tom's self-confessed politics ever did.

class-struggle.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
class-struggle.title: 4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful
class-struggle.relation: Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership against acceptance or rejection of the existing social order. Those who accept their place stagnate - Violet ('We don't work,' 'What is a weekend?'), Robert the mismanaging custodian, the perpetually jobless Molesley - while those who reject it flourish: Isobel's drive to be 'useful,' Sybil's nursing ('I feel useful for the first time in my life'), Gwen's hidden typewriter, Alfred's Ritz training. He surveys Rousseau on work's role in inequality, Smith on the division of labor, and Marx on labor and ideology on the negative side, and Aristotle, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper on leisure and personal projects on the positive side, ending with the prediction that automation will soon give everyone the Crawley daughters' problem of what to do with a life without work.

class-struggle.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
class-struggle.title: 12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys
class-struggle.relation: Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.

class-struggle.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
class-struggle.title: Red Rising and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.

class-struggle.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
class-struggle.title: 1. When Evolution Strikes Back
class-struggle.relation: Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.

class-struggle.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
class-struggle.title: 11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due
class-struggle.relation: Ewing argues money is the real determinant of the Iron Throne: Lannister gold made Cersei queen, Tyrell grain and taxation bought Margaery's crown, Baelish's financing decided the Battle of the Bastards, and the Iron Bank disciplines kings. Reading Westeros as a late-feudal economy through Marx - smallfolk whose work and taxes support lords who 'reap where they never sowed,' a hierarchy held by coercion and fear as the High Sparrow tells Olenna ('You are the few, we are the many'), and money dissolving feudal bonds into a 'money aristocracy' - he predicts the throne will go not to dragons or White Walkers but to the capitalist-financier figure of Petyr Baelish.

class-struggle.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
class-struggle.title: 23. A Chimichanga for the Mercenary Soul
class-struggle.relation: Through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks the chapter casts Deadpool as the 'Eternal Proletariat': the military superstructure (Weapon X) recruited him precisely because he was broke and class-positioned, and as a mercenary he has no capital, no upward mobility, and no exit from wage-killing. His hunger beyond money - the Bullseye payday that ends in him shooting himself, the dead shark's verdict 'what you are . . . is alone' - drives him toward the X-Men, read as a subaltern coalition of the marginalized like Gramsci's socialist parties. But as a non-mutant 'mutate' who cannot meet the hegemonic standard of heroism (the Hit-Monkey arc with Spider-Man, his bitter plea to Wolverine that 'at least they wanted you'), his only Gramscian options are coalition building or reshaping the X-Men's culture from inside.

class-struggle.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
class-struggle.title: 10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution
class-struggle.relation: Writing as a guilt-ridden fsociety member haunted by James Plouffe's on-air suicide, Altmann tests the 5/9 revolution against three theorists: Burke's conservatism condemns all revolution as destruction of social tradition (and fsociety's blackout chaos and Susan Jacobs's death seem to prove him right), while Marx's class struggle between E Corp's bourgeoisie and the indebted proletariat makes revolution the only exit from history's cycle. Kai Nielsen's condition - revolution is justified only when no other recourse exists - settles it: Angela's failed attempt to reform E Corp from within shows non-revolutionary change is impossible, so the author keeps fighting 'with a keyboard whose clacking is endless.'

class-struggle.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
class-struggle.title: 1 Introduction
class-struggle.relation: Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.

class-struggle.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
class-struggle.title: 2 Power and Politics
class-struggle.relation: The chapter traces politics from the classical ethics-fused view (Aristotle's Politics, where politics exists for the sake of the good life yet also supplies one of the first justifications of patriarchy and the public/private split) to the Machiavelli-Hobbes break where politics becomes simply the possession and exercise of power, adopting Bertrand Russell's claim that power is the fundamental concept of social science. It then builds the book's central instrument, a Weber-derived analysis of nine power bases (money, knowledge/technology/information, religion, morality, authority, charisma, size/solidarity, violence, status), contrasting the Marxian reading - money as ultimately determinative, the ruling ideas of each age as the ideas of the ruling class, religion as the opium of the people, the state as a committee for managing bourgeois affairs - with the liberal-Weberian reading in which no single base is decisive. It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.

class-struggle.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
class-struggle.title: 7 The Bourgeoisie and the Blacks
class-struggle.relation: The chapter sets business - the US bourgeoisie whose privileged position Charles Beard read into the Constitution and which survived the Jacksonian and New Deal challenges by breaking labor through Taft-Hartley, right-to-work laws and the PATCO lockout, its solidarity secured while worker solidarity was undercut by what Marx called the Achilles heel of racism - against blacks as the paradigmatic powerless, shut out of every power base since slavery, which the chapter treats with Baptist and Marx's 1846 letter as a totalitarian system of super-exploited, tortured labor that built American capitalism, its neo-slavery progeny (Blackmon) pauperizing the black community under Dred Scott's 'subordinate and inferior class of beings'. It then narrates black counter-power base by base: the abolitionist interracial coalition wielding charisma (Douglass, Nat Turner, John Brown), information, morality and religion; the NAACP era and King's fusion of charisma, church religion, Myrdal's An American Dilemma and televised nonviolent provocation against Bull Connor's violence, contested by Malcolm X, SNCC and the Black Panthers; and a post-civil-rights scorecard showing a wealth base 94.2 percent white, persistent education and media gaps, constrained black officials from mayors to the symbolic Obama presidency, and a captive but potentially leveraged black vote in a 'Sisyphean' struggle.

class-struggle.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
class-struggle.title: 8 Conclusion
class-struggle.relation: The conclusion restates the book's method - centering political philosophy in a consciously normative, empirical study of power - around its two contrasts: the family as a natural, subordination-requiring institution in liberalism versus a property-rooted, historically determined one in Marxism, and the state as a freely agreed contract of all (Locke, hence no food stamps) versus what actually happened, a charter 'ordained and established by a small group of wealthy white men, meeting in secret' to protect their wealth, so that the state which created gender and racial inequality must now play an equally decisive role in undoing it. Reviewing the nine bases since the 1960s, it finds women have closed the knowledge gap and nearly completed Engels's liberation program except universal child-care and non-exploitative housework, against conservative marriage-movement scholars like the Lockean Yenor, while blacks still face a tripling wealth gap that only social democratic capitalism on the Danish model plus comprehensive reparations can close - the latter argued on the moral base of power, Congress's 2009 apology, and Bernard Boxill's Lockean inheritance argument for a decades-long 'Reparations Superfund' as the civil rights issue of the 21st century.

class-struggle.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
class-struggle.title: 3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over
class-struggle.relation: Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.

class-struggle.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
class-struggle.title: 11. Forever the Wild One
class-struggle.relation: Anders grounds Petty's artistic freedom in Kant's Critique of Judgment: genius, the innate talent for original art freed from patron control, describes Petty's refusal to let commercial success measure his work. Singer's practical ethics supplies the frame for the $8.98 fight over Hard Promises, where Petty weighed outcomes for all affected, especially teenage fans, and threatened to withhold the masters or rename the album "Eight Ninety-Eight." Marx's worker-owner analysis maps the Shelter-to-MCA contract saga, in which Petty was sold like a piece of meat, countersued, hid the master tapes nightly, and filed for bankruptcy like a worker confronting the owners who pocket the value of the records he produced.

class-struggle.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
class-struggle.title: 28. Replicants of California, Unite!
class-struggle.relation: Christopher Innes gives 2049 a Marxist class analysis: the replicants are an enslaved working class, the Wallace Corporation the ruling class owning the means of production, and the LAPD a state apparatus with 'relative autonomy' that really upholds the system — K is a slave who kills his own kind without seeing his class position. Applying the materialist (not idealist) dialectic and the Eighteenth Brumaire's lesson about conflicting ruling-class interests, he reads Wallace, Atari, and even Ana as factions with divergent interests. Freysa's 'we are our own masters' and 'we are building our own army' mark the replicants as class conscious, aware of their Marxian 'species being', with nothing to lose but their chains.

class-struggle.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
class-struggle.title: 22. Won’t You Be My Comrade
class-struggle.relation: Christopher Innes runs Marx's critique of Hegel's idealism against Mister Rogers: the show treats problems (divorce, war, the Clemmons pool scene) ideally, as symbolic gestures rather than material change, much as Hegel's storybook individuals miss money's role. Measured against Capital's alienated worker, 'an appendage to the machine,' contrasted with the suitcase worker who 'knows her work,' and the Communist Manifesto's 'bourgeois socialist' who demands reform not liberation, Rogers emerges as a progressive bourgeois socialist whose make-believe may console children for, or subtly resist, their future exploitation.

class-struggle.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
class-struggle.title: Alien Nation
class-struggle.relation: Reads Alien as a film about alienation in Marx's fourfold sense from the 1844 Manuscripts: the crew is estranged from the product of its labor (the retrieved Xenomorph turns on them), from the labor process (Brett and Parker's bonus dispute, Dallas shilling for the Company that deems him disposable), from species-being (infantile dependence on Mother, whose Special Order 937 merely formalizes an expendability they already live), and from one another (they never unite against the Company or suspect Ash). In Aliens the Colonial Marines repeat the failure, while the coordinated alien 'nation' under its queen - possible victims of Engineer colonization - makes the humans look like the inferior species.

class-struggle.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
class-struggle.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
class-struggle.relation: Applies Marx's fourfold alienation (from product, from labor, from species-being, from others) to Bluth capitalism: George Michael dips and sells bananas he cannot keep, Lupe cleans Lucille's home under duress, and classes divide the family from the people it exploits. George Sr.'s Boyfights tapes and Caged Wisdom show the capitalist commodifying his children and himself, Gob's figurehead presidency turns employees into resources, Lindsay is 'having without being', and Engels's property-based account of the nuclear family explains Tobias's repressed sexuality; the cure offered is democratic socialism, since within-system fixes only get more absurd.

class-struggle.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
class-struggle.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
