socratic-method.relation: Johnson argues that the Santa Claus lie is immoral and should be abandoned, giving three reasons: it is deceptive lying (Kant's absolute prohibition is too strong, but the lie lacks life-saving justification and functions as a Platonic 'noble lie' no more noble than a cult leader's); Santa robs parents of credit and warps children's moral development and trust, illustrated by anguished 'finding out' stories and Virginia O'Hanlon's letter; and it damages credulity, invoking Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief' against belief on insufficient evidence while James's 'Will to Believe' cannot rescue Santa since evidence against him is overwhelming. He recommends revealing the truth early, even via a Socratic-Method questioning game.

socratic-method.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
socratic-method.title: GARDENING
socratic-method.relation: Cotton reads the grower image in Plato's Phaedrus—the wise gardener who sows seed in proper soil for a slow harvest rather than the frivolous 'gardens of Adonis'—as Plato's model of philosophical education as natural growth. The educator plants logoi (discourse) in a 'proper soul,' where it must be cultivated by the learner's own reflection and eventually reproduces itself in others, against Thrasymachus's vessel model of pouring knowledge in. She connects this to the Republic's cave, the Apology's gadfly, and the Symposium/Theaetetus images of pregnancy and midwifery, then argues Plato's own aporetic, contradiction-laden dialogues and the corpus as a whole act as the wise grower, teaching readers to become 'gardeners of their own souls.'

socratic-method.book: 284 - College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits
socratic-method.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
socratic-method.relation: This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.

socratic-method.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
socratic-method.title: NOTES
socratic-method.relation: Matthews argues that certain children's books are 'subversive' in a Socratic sense: they problematize concepts adults assume they command, challenging adult epistemic authority the way Socrates exposed the pretended knowledge of Athens' elite. Morris the Moose raises Aristotelian questions of natural kinds and essence-versus-accident; Leese Webster probes the concept of art; The Shrinking of Treehorn destabilizes 'normal' child development; Frog and Toad's 'The Garden' dramatizes the post hoc, ergo propter hoc fallacy about causation. In the Ozma of Oz Tik-Tok discussion, nine-year-old Paul reconstructs an argument that only brains think, which Matthews aligns with Searle's claim in The Mystery of Consciousness that consciousness is caused by specific neurobiological processes; he explicitly distinguishes his subversive stories from those promoting Pyrrhonian skepticism or Protagorean relativism.

socratic-method.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
socratic-method.title: The Talking Cure for Our Culture
socratic-method.relation: William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.

socratic-method.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
socratic-method.title: 69. Larry David as Philosopher Interrogating Convention
socratic-method.relation: Carroll treats Curb Your Enthusiasm as a Kantian/Marxian 'critique'—an inquiry into the conditions of possibility—of everyday norms of civility, built on incongruity humor and Mary Douglas's theory of jokes as 'anti-rites.' Through episodes like the handicapped-stutterer, the new-house tour Larry refuses, the phone-call cutoff time, Ben Stiller's no-gifts party, and the buried five-wood, David shows that manners are non-necessary and arbitrary yet held in place only by intense (uncurbed) emotional 'enthusiasm,' epitomized by Susie Greene's operatic rage. Carroll answers the analytic skeptic by casting David's method as Socratic/maieutic (like Plato's Meno): the argument is completed in the reflective viewer's mind.

socratic-method.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
socratic-method.title: 78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed
socratic-method.relation: Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.

socratic-method.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
socratic-method.title: 1. Engaging Life Like the Doctor
socratic-method.relation: The chapter casts the Doctor as a 'flâneur' who teaches an engaged, critical-thinking way of life, illustrated through episodes like 'Blink,' 'Heaven Sent,' and 'Kerblam!' where the Doctor (and viewer) solve mysteries through trial and error. It uses Hume and William James to argue the mind actively constructs reality into a narrative, and pairs the Doctor with Socrates as a truth-seeking 'midwife' teacher who withholds answers so companions can learn by living rather than being told. The Doctor's rejection of Time Lord non-interference models the Socratic examined life of engaging the world to know oneself and others.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Skepticism, Morality, and The Matrix
skepticism.relation: Erion and Smith place Thomas Anderson's ordinary beliefs alongside the reader's: both are radically mistaken, since the everyday world is 'a vast, deliberate deception' produced by computers that grow and harvest humans as an energy source. Quoting Morpheus's 'prison for your mind' speech and Cypher's 'ignorance is bliss' deal with Agent Smith, they announce a two-part project: to examine, in the spirit of Descartes, the hypothesis that we ourselves live in a matrix and show that it rests on a fundamental error, and then to assess the morality of Cypher's choice to return.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: The authors reconstruct Descartes's First Meditation as the philosophical engine of the film: the senses sometimes deceive, dreams are indistinguishable from waking experience - reinforced by Morpheus's 'what if you were unable to wake from that dream?' speech - and finally a 'malicious demon of the utmost power and cunning' could falsify even mathematics and the belief in an external world. They conclude that anyone who has watched The Matrix has fresh reason to wonder whether our lives too are deceptions implanted by intelligent computer systems.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: The authors carry the skeptical scenario into the twentieth century: Peter Unger's evil scientist uses computer-driven electrodes to fabricate our belief in rocks and chairs, and Hilary Putnam's brain-in-a-vat story from Reason, Truth, and History deceives us about everything we seem to perceive, with the computer supplying feedback for our attempted actions. Noting how closely this matches the pod-bound humans of The Matrix, they pose Putnam's question - 'How do you know you aren't in this predicament?' - as a sword of Damocles hanging over everyday knowledge.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: The authors answer the skeptic on two fronts. Descartes's demand for absolute certainty, they argue, is appropriate only in special philosophical contexts, while everyday and scientific contexts license the ordinary knowledge we all clearly possess - that we are not dreaming, that The Matrix is just a film. They add that the certainty principle is self-defeating, since skeptics who are not certain that knowledge requires certainty cannot know that it does, and deploy Bernard Williams's point that distinguishing dreams from waking life presupposes we really are awake sometimes.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: In a brief coda the authors restate their double conclusion: skeptical doubts about the external world are groundless outside the special context of the philosophical seminar, and Cypher's retreat into illusion is a drastic mistake. Reason, they argue, compels us not only to admit the world exists but to face it and build meaningful lives within it - the serious business of adult living.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: The Matrix Possibility
skepticism.relation: Nixon names and motivates his essay's central thesis, 'the Matrix Possibility': it is possible that you or I are, right now, floating in a pod of pink goo while a computer generates everything we take to be real. He sets the agenda for the three sections that follow - what the possibility does to our knowledge, how Neo could ever come to know he was in the Matrix, and whether the possibility is even coherent - warning that the conclusions will be counter-intuitive.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: Nixon weighs two reactions to the possibility that most of our beliefs are false: the Cartesian demand that nothing possibly false counts as knowledge, and the ordinary-language reply that outside the seminar we happily claim to know the time from a watch that might be wrong. He proposes reconciling them through two senses of knowledge - a 'super knowledge' immune to every possibility of error, which the Matrix Possibility does destroy, and ordinary knowledge requiring only probability, which it leaves intact.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: Nixon asks whether Neo's harrowing post-pill experiences justify believing Morpheus's story, given that knowledge is justified true belief and testimony alone would be foolish to believe. He argues the belief is self-defeating: if Neo discards twenty-five years of experience as machine-fed lies, he loses the interpretive rules of thumb (people don't lie, heads don't pop off, objects exist unobserved) needed to justify any new experience, so by epistemological holism he cannot be justified in concluding he was ever in the Matrix - even though the audience, with the bigger picture, knows he is right.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: Nixon tests whether the Matrix story is even conceptually coherent by asking whether we can make sense of someone whose beliefs are almost all false. Through the Cletus dialogue ('Bears are scary... Are they animals? News to me') he argues that belief attribution requires concept possession, and concept possession requires a background of true beliefs, so total falsehood is unintelligible - a meaning-holist point he credits to Quine, Davidson and Sellars - though he concedes the machines could still make most of our beliefs false, so the Matrix Possibility survives.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: Korsmeyer reads the film through classic problems of perception: Descartes's dreaming argument (Neo's sweaty awakenings), the evil deceiver updated as the evil computer, and the pod scene as her 'scariest philosophical problem', the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, with Berkeley's esse est percipi as the Matrix's governing premise. She also notes the film's structural constraint - like all dreaming plots from Calderon to The X-Files its viewpoint must stand outside the Matrix - and uses Mouse's Tasty Wheat puzzle to show how reference to a never-experienced world breaks down.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.

skepticism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
skepticism.title: Unknown
skepticism.relation: Developing thesis one, the chapter shows Morpheus's question—'How would you know the difference between the dream world and the real world?'—restates Plato's cave dwellers mistaking shadows for things and Descartes's First Meditation progression from unreliable senses to dreaming to the malicious demon that makes every belief false. What is genuinely new is that computer simulation and brain science have made the once-outlandish demon scenario thinkable, so the film has made philosophy teachers' job easier: global skepticism no longer seems ridiculous, and maybe you are lying in a tub of goo right now.

skepticism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
skepticism.title: Smelly Knowledge
skepticism.relation: Andrew Aberdein sorts the Buffyverse's science-supernatural encounters into three grades — reduction to present science, reduction to a future science, and the irreducibly supernatural — illustrated by Sunnydale's rationalizers and Giles's inner skeptic in 'Tabula Rasa,' the Initiative's DNA testing of Oz in 'New Moon Rising,' and the show's characteristic 'creepy mix of magic and science' (Jenny Calendar's 'the divine exists in cyberspace'). He reads 'Normal Again' through Descartes's deceiving-demon skepticism, links Spike's chip and Walsh's Adam to the Phineas Gage case (emotion is needed for rational decision), and maps the grades onto the ancients-versus-moderns quarrel and Feyerabend's methodological anarchism. Giles's 'smelly knowledge' speech about books versus computers anticipates a pluralist, socially sensitive epistemology that enriches rather than rejects science.

skepticism.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
skepticism.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.

skepticism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
skepticism.title: “May The Force Be with You”
skepticism.relation: Jones uses the Force's telekinesis (Luke's lightsaber flying to his hand, Yoda raising the X-wing) to probe the metaphysics of causation. Hume shows we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect - only constant conjunction and habit - so Jedi mind-power is no more mysterious than gravity or magnetism; Leibniz's Monadology argues one substance cannot transfer properties to another, so 'how' any cause works is unintelligible; and Hume's problem of induction (will Tatooine's twin suns rise tomorrow? will Vader's officers always choke?) shows law-governed expectations cannot be non-circularly justified. Concurring with Russell that 'cause' is a relic, the chapter concludes the Force qualifies as a kind of cause precisely because our causal concept is too vague to exclude it - and plugs science fiction as a laboratory for sharpening concepts.

skepticism.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
skepticism.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Thomas Senor turns the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (lying, mad, or telling the truth) into a general account of when to believe incredible testimony: weigh the testifier's reliability against how well the claim fits your background beliefs. He shows why Lucy's siblings should have believed her second report of Aslan in Prince Caspian, since by then talking animals and a resurrected Lion no longer clashed with what they knew, and then applies the framework to 'Julia's' report of hearing God, arguing that believing, disbelieving, or withholding rationally depends on the hearer's own background commitments. A footnote explains why Hume on miracles does not fit Lucy's case, since she claims no violation of natural law.

skepticism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
skepticism.title: The Blessings of Tranquility
skepticism.relation: Michael Chiariello takes Dylan's "the truth is true whether you wanna believe it or not" as a correspondence theory of truth, then rejects both the gospel-era absolutism of "Precious Angel" and the relativism (from Protagoras' man-the-measure to modern subjectivism) that would make Dylan's changes of course harmless. The alternative he defends is Pyrrhonian skepticism in Sextus Empiricus's sense: truth is objective but never fully assured, so suspending judgment yields tranquility. Dylan's career - from the ambiguous "Blowin' in the Wind" through "Watching the River Flow" and "Things Have Changed" to the two versions of "Every Grain of Sand" ("the reality of man" vs "a perfect finished plan") - embodies this balanced, non-dogmatic search the way of God designed it.

skepticism.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
skepticism.title: The Epilogue A Question of Belief
skepticism.relation: Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'

skepticism.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time
skepticism.title: The Problem with Bullshitting
skepticism.relation: Against the bullshitter the chapter recruits Peirce: genuine inquiry is defined not by method or results but by the attitude of truly wanting true answers, so homicide detectives, philologists, and car mechanics all count as scientists in this sense. Bullshitting is a free-rider riding the bus of real inquiry - even the bullshitter wants his doctor not to bullshit - and the chapter formulates an epistemic imperative: proceed on the hope that there is a true answer and act from the desire to find it, with fallibilism, not skepticism, the viable stance (the passenger who can occupy any vacant seat cannot occupy them all).

skepticism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
skepticism.title: Introduction
skepticism.relation: Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.

skepticism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
skepticism.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
skepticism.relation: Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.

skepticism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
skepticism.title: Skepticism Outside the Matrix
skepticism.relation: Lawrence uses The Matrix to walk through Descartes' method of doubt: the dream argument, the evil demon reborn as a machine-run simulation, and invented worse cases ('Neo's Worst Nightmare,' a Matrix-within-the-Matrix that deceives even Morpheus' awakened rebels). The cogito is the only certainty that survives and Descartes' proof of God falls short, so certainty about the external world is unavailable; the chapter then borrows Russell's red-chair analysis of color, texture, and solidity to argue that even outside any Matrix, naive realism is false and we know only appearances.

skepticism.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
skepticism.title: Vertigo and Epistemological Vertigo
skepticism.relation: Flory reads Vertigo as an epistemological parable: Scottie's 'hardheaded Scot' method, collecting facts and deducing from universal principles, fails three times (the step-stool 'cure' for his acrophobia, explaining away Madeleine's 'possession' with the horse statue, forcing Judy up the bell tower for confirmation), delivering an implicit critique of Vienna Circle positivism in the manner of Carnap and Ayer. Against Scottie, the chapter mobilizes Kuhn's theory-laden facts, Aristotle's point that human conduct resists codification by exceptionless laws, and Hume's 'slave of the passions,' with Descartes's automata and Chalmers's philosophical zombies framing the problem of other minds. Midge, who knows people emotionally as well as factually, models the alternative: philosophers who fear 'epistemological vertigo' should give up epistemological training wheels and accept that minds, especially emotions, escape law-like rules.

skepticism.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
skepticism.title: Marnie An Enigma to Herself
skepticism.relation: Yanal sets Descartes's two claims about mind - certainty about one's own thoughts (via the method of doubt and the deceiving-evil-genius possibility) and skepticism about other minds (hats and coats that may cover automata) - against Wittgenstein's counters, then reads Shadow of a Doubt and Marnie as Hitchcock's counterexamples. In Shadow of a Doubt the two Charlies, twins in blood and in the film's doubling motifs, are 'transparent' to each other - Young Charlie alone knows her uncle is the Merry Widow Murderer - refuting other-minds skepticism; in Marnie, repressed memory of killing her mother's sailor client leaves Marnie ignorant of her own mind until Mark's amateur therapy recovers it, refuting Cartesian self-certainty. Both films thus side with Wittgenstein: one person can know another's mind, and one can be an enigma to oneself.

skepticism.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
skepticism.title: Wondering and Dreaming. The Words Have Different Meanings
skepticism.relation: Scott Calef argues that the causal theory of perception — the inflatable pig over Battersea reaches you only as an internal representation — breeds Cartesian skepticism: the dreaming argument, asylum inmates who don't know they're mad ('the lunatic is in my head'), the evil demon, and the modern brain-in-a-vat version behind The Matrix. Locke's unknowable substratum behind the Dark Side jacket's qualities and Berkeley's idealism deepen the veil of perception, with 'Julia Dream', Waters's 'If I go insane, please don't stick your wires in my brain', and Syd's 'Jugband Blues' self-diagnosis as Floyd illustrations. Against skepticism he deploys mutual corroboration ('It takes two to know'), J.L. Austin's point that waking experience is qualitatively unlike dreams ('A Pillow of Winds': 'the dream is gone'), and Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box private language argument (rebranded as Lucifer Sam's cat) — a purely private language is impossible, so skepticism expressed in language defeats itself, leaving the Barrett-era enigma to keep philosophy's original wonder alive.

skepticism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
skepticism.title: No Reason to Get Excited
skepticism.relation: After 'Crossroads, Part 2' revealed Anders, Foster, Tigh, and Tyrol as Cylons, the chapter argues we can know that we exist (Descartes' cogito) without knowing what we are, since even Boomer's Cylon-detection result — Baltar's lie about the green light — could itself be a dream, returning us to Descartes' whirlpool. Moore's common-sense realism fails against the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism / relevant alternatives (Dretske) lets Starbuck dismiss dreaming-hypotheses about a Viper but cannot dismiss the possibility that you are a sleeper Cylon in a world where anyone might be one. Following Hume, who escaped skeptical paralysis by dining and playing backgammon, Tigh's 'report to your stations' shows the only live option: carry on being the person you want to be.

skepticism.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
skepticism.title: Transformers and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Steiff reads the 2007 movie as a sustained lesson in perceptual error: Sam's Porsche disappointment at the dealership, the parents' 'earthquake' misperception, and the Camaro that no one at Bobby B's lot suspects show that we see what context, expectation, and conditioning (the kitten experiments) lead us to see. She distinguishes illusion - misperceiving an object really present, as Sam misperceives Bumblebee as just a car - from hallucination, and weighs direct realism against representative realism's 'veil of perception' using film tricks from Melies's jammed camera to the Lumiere brothers' panic-inducing train, leaving Sam's knowledge resting on fallible but indispensable sense experience.

skepticism.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
skepticism.title: It-Getting The Truth about Truthiness
skepticism.relation: Ethan Mills runs a 'Better Know a Skeptic' four-parter applied to the show: Pyrrhonian skepticism (Sextus Empiricus's suspension of judgment and living by appearances, played out in the Jon-says-worst-versus-Stephen-says-greatest Bush debate), Modern skepticism (Montaigne's fideist custom-worship and Hume's dream argument for why knowledge of couches, Doritos, and presidents is impossible), and Indian skepticism (Nagarjuna's circle that means of knowledge cannot be established without things known, illustrated with Stephen Sr. and Stephen Jr. as both father and son, plus Jayarasi's destruction of epistemology). He adds 'political skepticism' - the American sense that political knowledge is impossible - which breeds wikiality, an internet relativism ('reality we just agreed on') that the WØRD's own bullet points ('Wikipedia can tell a lie') undermine. Truthiness, he concludes, is Stephen's false cure for political skepticism: commitment without facts, a 'truthiness of the appearances'; but Sextus shows skeptics can still act on appearances without dogmatism, so we can vote and argue on the best evidence, as in Sagan's science-as-democracy, without certainty.

skepticism.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
skepticism.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Michaud wonders whether the Magisterium's censorship of Dust research could be epistemically justified, building the answer from Descartes's dreaming and deceiving-demon doubts (imagine waking to find your dæmon was only a dream), Moore's common-sense 'I know I have two hands' reply, and Dretske's relevant alternatives, arriving at Lewis's 'Elusive Knowledge': inquiry itself ratchets up the standards for knowledge until certainty dissolves, which is exactly what happens to Lyra, and to readers, once they start asking questions about Dust and other worlds. On this view the Magisterium had a Lewisian motive to suppress inquiry, since unquestioning belief preserves the certainty on which its power and promise of salvation rest. But because philosophical questions like 'Is God good?' can never meet the raised standards anyway, the chapter concludes that a little doubt is preferable to the dogmatism and bigotry certainty breeds.

skepticism.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
skepticism.title: Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid
skepticism.relation: Cuddy stages the generational-decline debate between Mark Bauerlein's The Dumbest Generation and Stephen Johnson's Everything Bad Is Good for You, showing that Onion stories can be marshaled for both sides: Aristophanes complaining that today's audiences 'just don't get me' vindicates the perennial declinist, while 'US Students Lead World in Detention' wryly supports Johnson's sleeper curve. Comparing Bauerlein to Aristophanes and the 'Our Dumb World' entry on Aristotle and Plato's schools closing, he concludes every era teems with idiots, so The Onion could have existed in any century. Because induction from earlier generations' failed predictions cannot settle whether Millennials really are dumber, he suspends judgment and toasts The Onion as the smartest perspective around.

skepticism.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
skepticism.title: Point-Counterpoint Funny versus Really, Really Funny
skepticism.relation: Andrew Terjesen starts from real cases of Onion satire taken literally — a Michigan sheriff warning about al-Qaida telemarketing, the Beijing Evening News plagiarizing 'Congress Threatens To Leave D.C.', Deborah Norville reporting that 58 percent of American exercise is televised — and explains them through the Problem of Other Minds. Descartes' hats-and-cloaks worry and Russell's analogy solution show how we infer that a straight-faced writer is 'just kidding,' but the analogy fails when cultural context, prejudice (Fred Phelps citing the gay-recruitment story, Christians forwarding the Harry Potter Satanism piece), or wishful thinking breaks the comparison with our own joking behavior. The upshot is that humor is engineered misunderstanding — the Onion works by analogy to real news, and could never warn readers off without destroying the joke.

skepticism.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
skepticism.title: Doomed to Be Perceived
skepticism.relation: Smithka tests Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived' against two monsters: the Vashta Nerada, whose existence is inferred from indirect evidence (counting shadows, the 'ghosting' of Miss Evangelista) much like Neptune was inferred from Uranus's orbit, and the Weeping Angels, which act only when unperceived and so falsify Berkeley's principle. Working through Locke on substance, Hume's skepticism about unperceivable causes like God, Paley's watchmaker design argument, and scientific realism (Sellars, Churchland) versus van Fraassen's empirically adequate anti-realism, she concludes the Doctor is a realist about unobservables — for whom the Angels are real but 'doomed to be perceived'.

skepticism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
skepticism.title: Know Thyself
skepticism.relation: George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.

skepticism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
skepticism.title: More than a Feeling
skepticism.relation: Rachel Robison-Greene asks whether Dexter's rule to 'be sure' actually gives him knowledge of his victims' guilt. Distinguishing Cartesian certainty - skeptical hypotheses about deceiving senses, dreams and evil demons, echoing The Matrix - from mere felt certainty, she tests the belief-truth-justification analysis of knowledge traced to Plato against the show: LaGuerta's witness theory fails on belief, Deb's conviction that Neil Perry is the Ice Truck Killer fails on truth, and Astor's accusation of Dexter fails on justification. Neither strong internalism (Dexter straps down Jamie Jaworski without knowing how the murder was done), weak internalism, coherence theory (his false but coherent case against Jonathan Farrow), nor reliabilism (his spidey-sense is explicitly not sufficient by his own admission) captures his practice, so his 'certainty' is just a feeling - and the people on his table may include ones he does not know to be guilty.

skepticism.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
skepticism.title: Do I Even Care if I’m Dreaming
skepticism.relation: Kate Elson Anderson reads 'Sleepy Time' — SpongeBob's tour of his neighbors' dream clouds, from Gary's library to Patrick's quarter-fed kiddie ride to Krabs's Moby Dollar — through Descartes's First Meditation dream argument that no sure mark distinguishes waking from dreaming. Norman Malcolm's claim that one cannot even ask 'Am I dreaming?' while asleep is contradicted by SpongeBob's lucid wandering, and Patrick's mundane dream (he would not even conjure another quarter) proves Descartes's point that dreams can be indistinguishable from reality. SpongeBob's final move — asking the question but never waiting for an answer — leaves Descartes baffled by a truth-seeker immune to skepticism.

skepticism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
skepticism.title: Happy Ending
skepticism.relation: Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.

skepticism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
skepticism.title: Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End
skepticism.relation: Andersen contends Inception goes one deeper than Descartes: where the dream argument threatened only the external world, inception threatens the autonomy of thought itself, since the 'core conception' that defines identity - Fischer's reading of his father's dying word 'disappointed' - can be implanted. Tracing Nolan's obsession with thought-manipulation through his earlier films (the manipulator Cobb of Following, Leonard's self-deception in Memento, the Joker's schemes), he shows inception as co-opting subjectivity. Against the Cartesian answer of doubting everything, the fates of Mal and Cobb in Limbo - where doubt, once planted, grows devastatingly, and where a totem cannot guard against self-deception - teach that the way back to reality is the leap of trust in others: only by opening himself to Ariadne, Miles and his children can Cobb turn away from the top and go home.

skepticism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
skepticism.title: Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word
skepticism.relation: Kapper reads Inception as epistemology rather than metaphysics - not what is real but how we could know - running from Plato's Theaetetus (the first dream-recognition question) through Descartes's deceptive demon and Freud's royal road to the unconscious, to Wittgenstein's point that 'I may be dreaming' is senseless because the remark itself would be dreamed, and Heraclitus's line that only the waking share a common world. The Ariadne thread is the clue: as in the Theseus myth, dream architecture gives the labyrinth a shareable narrative place, but only a hint, never a way to wake. He then goes east - Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflecting jewels, Schopenhauer's universe dreamed by a single dreamer, William James's many consciousnesses - to ask how many times we must die before waking, ending with Buddhism: 'Buddha means awakened one', and Cobb's turning from the top enacts Nirvana, where the real-versus-dream question stops pertaining.

skepticism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
skepticism.title: An Old Man, Filled with Regret . .
skepticism.relation: Brophy argues Cobb's shared dreams are best modeled on MMORPG virtual worlds like Second Life and World of Warcraft: Ariadne is a world-building architect in the mold of Second Life's Escher Relativity House, dreamers are avatars, and the film's looping architectures mirror the toroidal grids of game worlds. Reading the film as an addict's 'long con', he claims the real inception was planting in Cobb's own head the idea that his game-world is real: Mal is a 'gamer's widow' whose in-game suicide deleted her character, and Cobb is the avatar of an unseen addicted player who has forgotten the game. Borges's map that covers the empire, Baudrillard's claim that the simulacrum becomes the preferred reality, Bostrom's simulation argument, and Homer's lotus-eaters all support the warning that we already prefer simulated worlds, so the last shot means the real Cobb will one day wake as an old man filled with regret.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick
skepticism.relation: Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale
skepticism.relation: Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: Skepticism for Fun and Profit
skepticism.relation: Mills uses the Blade Runner cuts to stage skepticism: the theatrical happy ending hides the question, the Director's Cut unicorn hints Scott wants Deckard to be a replicant, but Dick's novel has Luba Luft tell Deckard 'You must be an android' and presses him on whether his Voigt-Kampff memories are false, leaving the question unresolved for the reader and for Deckard himself. Since any evidence (empathy, the test's own accuracy) can itself be doubted, the novel is more radically skeptical than the films, because it makes both hypotheses compatible with all the evidence. He then shows Ubik pushing this to the limit, where characters cannot tell what year it is, whether their money is real, or even whether they are alive or dead.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: What’s So Bad about Skepticism
skepticism.relation: Mills argues that for the ancient skeptics skepticism was the cure, not the disease: Sextus Empiricus prescribes setting equally strong arguments against each other until judgment is suspended and tranquility follows. He reads Nagarjuna and Jayarashi as more radical, using contradictions to uproot the very impulse to hold philosophical views at all, weaning themselves from attachment even to Buddhist views. Applied to Dick, both approaches would have us stop agonizing over whether Deckard is an android or the Ubik characters are dead: the best way to stop worrying is to stop wanting the answers.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: Selfless
skepticism.relation: The chapter concedes that no rule, psyche, body, soul, or combined, accommodates all of Dick's transformations, and refuses to blame Dick for incoherence: his stories force our own conflicting intuitions about wubs, Quaids and downloaded minds into the open. Pessimist, optimist and skeptic each get a verdict, the skeptic's being the chapter's cliffhanger: if we are none of these things, maybe there are no enduring persons at all.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: How Do You Know You’re Not an Android
skepticism.relation: The chapter weaponizes the cogito for Deckard's predicament: the fact that 'the lights are on' for you seems to prove you are human, but Descartes' leap from thinking to an immaterial soul is unjustified, since introspection cannot show whether your thoughts run on a soul, a bundle of neurons, or a silicon chip. Hume's 'I never can catch myself at any time without a perception' supplies the precedent, and the conclusion is that no amount of inner experience rules out being an android, so you will have to go take the V-K test after all.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: The Art of Knowing Arctor
skepticism.relation: The chapter takes Fred's surveillance of Arctor as a literal solution to the eye-cannot-see-itself problem: split in two, Bob finally observes himself from a detached, evaluative outside, hoping the scanner sees 'clearly' where he sees 'only murk'. Real self-scanning follows, since an fMRI revealing synthetic parts behind your eye sockets would settle the android question and neural correlates might someday sort enduring love from lust, before Alva Noe's Out of Our Heads objection that mental states must be sought in whole organisms interacting with their environments, which would give Arctor's whole-habitat self-scanning the edge over the constrained brain scan.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: How Are Things in Glocca Morra—or Anywhere Else, for That Matter
skepticism.relation: Opens Gerard Casey's part by asking whether David Norris is really free or governed by an external agency, then argues from perception itself: the stick that looks bent in the fish tank and the rainbow that exists only for an observer positioned between sunlight and raindrops show that ordinary experience is already a construct of sensory limits, expectations, and language. This prepares the radical question of whether everything in our experience is in some way an illusion.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: Chapter 15 - Lies, Incorporated
skepticism.relation: Opens Don Fallis's part with an inventory of Dickian deception: Quaid's implanted memories, replicants deceived into believing they are human in Blade Runner and Impostor, the framed Anderton, Ragle Gumm's manufactured town, and the Bureau's constant adjustments. Unlike Descartes' malicious demon or The Matrix, these are not skeptical hypotheticals but the kinds of deception that corporations, parties, and governments actually perpetrate — with us often complicit in our own deception.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: Who Deceives Us
skepticism.relation: Defines the conspiracy through Cohaagen's team — Lori, Harry, Benny, and the turncoat Hauser — with the Adjustment Bureau as 'the quintessential conspiracy' claiming good consequences for humanity. Popper's argument that belief in efficient grand conspiracies is irrational (his 'cock-up theory of society') is tested against the Bureau's own bungled coffee spill that lets David meet Elise, while Keeley's Hume-style critique and the specter of unbridled skepticism about spouses, friends, and memories frame what it would cost to believe in such conspiracies.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: Chapter 20 - If the Universe Isn’t Real, How Should We Treat Other People
skepticism.relation: Andrew M. Butler's introduction opens with the ambiguous endings of Total Recall, Minority Report, and Blade Runner (the fade to white, the too-neat reunion, the improbable sunset) to pose skeptical doubt about whether any of Dick's realities are real, surveying Eye in the Sky, Flow My Tears, Time Out of Joint, and Next. Against the thought that if nothing is real nothing matters, it sets Eric Sweetscent returning to his failing wife, and introduces Dick's aim to fuse Hebrew monotheism with Heidegger's philosophy of thrownness, noting that Levinas made the attempt first and that for Dick the authentic human is the one who cares for others.

skepticism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
skepticism.title: To Be or Not To Be—Is That the Question
skepticism.relation: The section introduces Levinas (Heidegger's student, Nazi internment camp survivor, Talmudic scholar) for whom ethics outranks ontology ('To be or not to be? Is that the question?'), and illustrates his strange distinction between existents and existing through Dick's existing-without-existents: the hallucinated town of The Cosmic Puppets, the aura of fake American relics in The Man in the High Castle, Freck's nonexistent aphids. Working through phenomenology, the idios kosmos / koinos kosmos split of A Maze of Death and Eye in the Sky, and the eerie 'There is' of the void, it reworks Descartes's cogito into Levinas's question ('I think, therefore what should I do?') because out there is the Other.

skepticism.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
skepticism.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.

skepticism.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
skepticism.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Tom McBride reads the film through Wittgenstein's On Certainty: Dr. Zaius's certainties (flight is impossible, humans come from the forests) are hinge or riverbed propositions that cannot be doubted within the ape form of life, so Taylor's true story sounds not false but insane, like claiming to have slept on the moon. Speaking and able to prompt empirical investigation, Taylor fractures a foundational principle where G.E. Moore, facing a 'wild tribe' playing a different language game, could only confess that things 'stand fast' with him; and Zaius's explicit origin myth, a parallel to Plato's Myth of the Metals, is flimsy precisely because rulers who must insist on rules are not potent and are reduced to destroying the cave evidence. The genre's appeal is Margaret Atwood's 'controlled hallucination': crazy doors that swing on safe hinges, rivers that still have stable beds.

skepticism.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
skepticism.title: Psych and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: McCraw turns the question 'should we trust Shawn?' into the philosophy of testimony: Lassiter's policy of never believing without independent evidence embodies Hume's demand that testimony be backed by evidence of the speaker's reliability, while Buzz McNab's instant faith embodies Reid's innate principles of veracity and credulity, and both extremes fail the department - Lassiter solves too late, McNab chases every early false lead. Juliet's developing, flexible trust - suspicious at first, convinced by results, never naive - models the circumstantial middle path that no hard-and-fast Humean or Reidian rule can capture. The verdict: treat Shawn's testimony as both psychic and psychotic, trusting the track record in some cases and discounting the wilder 'visions' in others, because when to trust is unavoidably vague and case-by-case.

skepticism.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
skepticism.title: Psych and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.

skepticism.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
skepticism.title: Psych and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.

skepticism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
skepticism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: John Karavitis (with tongue-in-cheek co-author 'Lucifer') treats The Ninth Gate as an epistemology case study, sorting the characters' beliefs about the Devil - true-believer Balkan, skeptic book-dealer Corso, the occult-tourist Order of the Silver Serpent - and testing them against Plato's Theaetetus definitions of knowledge as perception, true belief, and justified true belief. Balkan's justification is only an internally coherent web of book-learned beliefs, while Corso's external evidence (engravings signed 'LCF,' his journey's experiences) is weighed by the general reliability of his sources. Descartes' dreaming and the deceiving demon then leave the viewer skeptical that the Devil ever appeared at all.

skepticism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
skepticism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: The Bocks use the courtroom frame of The Exorcism of Emily Rose to ask whether anyone could be justified in believing in demon possession, since the same seizures, polyglot voices, and levitations read differently under naturalism and supernaturalism. Kuhn's paradigms explain why neither worldview abandons ship at anomalies, and they weigh Wiebe's 'finite spirits as theoretical entities,' Hume's miracles argument (with Levine's Red Sea thought experiment as rebuttal), and the Cartesian ghost-in-the-machine premise that possession would require. Testing even a Men in Black alien hypothesis against the religiously specific phenomena, they conclude that a witnessed case like Emily's could rationally justify belief in possession.

skepticism.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
skepticism.title: Homeland and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Don Fallis frames Homeland as a world of real epistemic warfare - unlike Descartes' hypothetical malicious demon, terrorists and the CIA actively engineer false appearances (Brody the war hero, Carrie the support-group veteran, Saul's memory-card trick). He analyzes lying versus true-but-misleading statements, uses Russell's barber paradox to define double agents without contradiction, and shows how Carrie, Dana, and Lauder each detect an inconsistency (Yorkshire Gold tea, the locked bedroom, Walker's three missed shots). Following Hume on testimony and Peirce's abduction - inference to the best explanation - Dana concludes her father is a terrorist, and Coady's defense of conspiracy theories vindicates Lauder's Brody-Walker hypothesis.

skepticism.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
skepticism.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Michaud plays the 'David Hume' Card Wars deck against Princess Bubblegum's confidence in science: following Hume's problem of induction, every scientific law rests on observation and is only probabilistic—we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect, whether in magnetism, Jake's hunger-induced jerkiness, or the first law of thermodynamics. Humans are pattern-makers who project causal order onto the world (seeing Gunter in clouds, blaming one bubblegum incident), while quantum physics reveals genuine randomness that Einstein hated. Ooo's residents, who watch Tree Trunks explode and simply move on, may grasp reality better than we do, because they never smuggle in stable, lawlike expectations that the show—and the universe—keep violating.

skepticism.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
skepticism.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.

skepticism.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
skepticism.title: Justified and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.

skepticism.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
skepticism.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Using 'Flowers for Charlie', where a placebo pill convinces two scientists and even the Waitress that Charlie has become a genius, the chapter asks what actually makes something philosophy. Sounding smart is not philosophy: big words, the Sokal-style hoax paper submitted to a leading journal, and the 'Guru Effect' of credulous admirers all fail, yet Charlie's pronouncements turn out true by sheer luck - which is exactly Edmund Gettier's problem of epistemic luck illustrated with the broken-clock example. Since we can never verify our premises or our reasoning, the chapter sides with Aristotle's response to Plato's theory of forms that we can never determine what a thing is, only what it is not, and concludes the show is philosophical precisely because the Gang is the exact antithesis of reality, truth, and right action.

skepticism.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
skepticism.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Fenner Tanswell uses 'Reynolds vs. Reynolds: The Cereal Defense' - the Gang's in-bar trial over Frank's blind driving versus Dennis's cereal-at-the-wheel - as a catalogue of crooked thinking. We get valid forms distinguished from soundness (modus ponens with 'if poop is funny, then Frank pooped in the bed'; Charlie's modus tollens from Frank's no-donkey-brains certificate), then the fallacies: the argument from ignorance by which Dennis's lacking a certificate proves him donkey-brained, Dee's ad hominem against Mac, Dennis's appeal to authority, and Mac's 'Science Is a Liar Sometimes' poster, which equivocates between mere skeptical doubt (even Descartes's) and reasonable doubt by straw-manning science as claiming infallibility. True to form, the Gang convicts Dee 'for comedy rather than on any logical basis.'

skepticism.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
skepticism.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Archibald casts Crazy Eyes as the show's Don Quixote, read through Descartes's Meditations: like Descartes ridding himself of conditioned false beliefs, Suzanne slaps her head to 'reset' and question everything, and like Quixote she blames an inner evil enchanter when her noble illusions collapse. Her rationalist imagination (chivalry, poetry, Piper as her Dulcinea) produces false beliefs that hurt, above all her devoted service to the manipulative Vee, yet the same faculty creates the beauty, coping, and nobility that make an ugly prison survivable, so truth may not be all that matters.

skepticism.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
skepticism.title: 11. What Mary Didn’t Know
skepticism.relation: Demeter reconstructs five rival explanations of Mary's hesitation to accept Matthew - emotional uncertainty, greed, fear of social exclusion over Pamuk, bad conscience, and conflicting family pressures - and argues none can be singled out as true. Via Frayn's Copenhagen, Dennett's 'Real Patterns,' and Henry James's The Golden Bowl as read by Robert Pippin, he defends the indeterminacy of psychological interpretation: motives are accessed only through behavior filtered through the interpreter's own psychological apparatus, and on the stronger view there are no motivation-facts prior to interpretation at all. What Mary did not know about her own hesitation may therefore not be knowable in principle, by her or by us.

skepticism.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
skepticism.title: 17. What if Our Reality Is One Big Hallucination
skepticism.relation: Arp starts from Rick's hallucinations of Lori - the disconnected phone in "Hounded," the touch and kiss in "Home" - and Michonne's confessed visions, showing how Rick distinguishes them through coherence with causal law and through third-person verification (Michonne watching him stroke empty air; Morgan's isolation in "Clear" showing why social checks matter). He then widens this into the theory of knowledge: the perceiver-perception-perceived triangle, epistemological and metaphysical realism versus idealism and antirealism, Berkeley's picture of the mind as a movie theater we cannot exit, and the Walking Dead twist on the falling tree in the forest, concluding that even if reality were one big hallucination we would still live - and refuse to walk off cliffs - as realists.

skepticism.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
skepticism.title: 18. Gruesome Walkers
skepticism.relation: Yuen turns the walkers into a lesson on Hume's problem of induction: the pre-apocalyptic belief that the dead do not rise was justified by all past experience until Rick wakes to a world where they do, and Rick's distrust of Alexandria repeats the same inductive move from Woodbury, Terminus, and Grady - useful, Hume says, since custom compels us, but never knowledge. Russell's chicken illustrates the fatal surprise, and Goodman's grue (the pun of the title) shows the outbreak could be a future-swinging regularity like the seventeen-year cicadas, undermining even Jenner's experimental science. Popper's falsificationism is offered as the rescue - Shane's reanimation falsifies the "walkers make walkers" theory, leaving the "everyone is infected" theory corroborated but never known.

skepticism.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
skepticism.title: 15. It Would Take a Miracle!
skepticism.relation: Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.

skepticism.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
skepticism.title: 8. Honesty Trumps Cleverness Sam Vimes and Commonsense Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Skene argues Sam Vimes embodies Thomas Reid's common sense philosophy across Feet of Clay, Thud!, Night Watch, and Jingo: he refuses speculation (his hatred of Holmes-style clue-deduction and the Summoning Dark), is irreverent toward false authorities from Sergeant Colon's 'School of My Dad Always Said' to Lord Rust's glorious wars, and checks every theory against reality. Moore's here-is-one-hand reply to Humean skepticism and Socrates' unmasking of pompous authorities illustrate the method, and Huemer's political realism - taxation as demanded money with menaces, social systems judged by how they work for real people - echoes Vimes's verdicts on Reg Shoe's utopian barricade and Swing's phrenology. The lesson is Vimes's own: 'Common sense and facts! That's what works.'

skepticism.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
skepticism.title: 16. Getting at the Truth
skepticism.relation: The chapter sets out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge with Discworld examples—Archchancellor Ridcully as a fallible authority, the physics of thaum particles as coherentist justification—before constructing a Discworld Gettier case in which a young wizard sees a fake level-seven wizard killed and truly but accidentally reports that 'a level seven wizard was killed.' It then tests the standard repairs, applying Nozick's truth-tracking function and Goldman's causation function to a case where a man blames the notorious Reacher Gilt for a theft actually committed by the dwarf he bumped into, and argues that neither truth-tracking nor specificity makes the problem go away. The upshot is that Discworlders, used to expecting to be wrong, may let go of false 'knowledge' more easily than our confidently wrong Roundworld.

skepticism.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
skepticism.title: 23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles
skepticism.relation: Baldwin asks whether Westerosi characters can know anything inductive in a world without lawlike nature: seasons of unpredictable length, wargs in animal minds, Faceless Men changing faces, and resurrections by Thoros, Melisandre, and Qyburn. After laying out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge (those who saw the pyre are justified in believing Dany is the mother of dragons; those relying on rumor are not), he runs Hume's problem of induction - we never perceive causal connection, so no jar of wildfire must explode - against Reid's common-sense reply that reason and induction stand or fall together, concluding that Westeros gives its people special reasons for skepticism while we, lacking evidence of magical irregularity, are rational to trust everyday inductive belief.

skepticism.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
skepticism.title: 8. For Hume the Ball Tolls!
skepticism.relation: The chapter argues Charlie Brown's repeated falls for Lucy's football gag are failures of induction: given the history of the gag since 1951 (first with Violet, then Lucy's fake reasons each fall - a handshake, a contract, a hundred million dollars), he should draw the meta-level conclusion that she will always pull the ball away. It then tries Hume's problem of induction as his defense, but since that would cost him all knowledge of the external world (that Snoopy is a beagle, that Lucy is mean) and end in skepticism, Charlie - a student of his world, not a doubter of it - cannot take it. The verdict: he is not a blockhead but determined and committed, willing to lose every fall because kicking that ball would be worth it, as in the 1979 hospital strip where he finally gets his kick and still ends up on his back.

skepticism.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
skepticism.title: Real, This Book
skepticism.relation: The volume's introduction is written in Elliot's paranoid voice, doubting whether the book, the reader, or reality itself exist. It lays out the questions the essays will tackle: fsociety's hack of the Evil Corporation, whether it was political ideology or revenge for the corporation killing Elliot's and Darlene's father, whether either motive (or hacking in general) can be justified, and what order could survive after the financial system falls.

skepticism.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
skepticism.title: 9. What Elliot Doesn’t Know Won’t Hurt You (Or Will It )
skepticism.relation: Greene argues Elliot is in the worst possible position for a knower: Descartes's skeptical scenarios of madness, dreams, and the evil demon apply to everyone, but hit Elliot harder through morphine and ecstasy hallucinations, lucid dreams indistinguishable from waking (as Whiterose suggests), and a dissociative disorder so severe he spends months in prison believing he lives at his mother's house - with Mr. Robot even hiding facts from him, blocking the Socratic 'know thyself.' Yet by the Meno's knowledge problem he may be no worse off: he still catches the pedophile ring and brings down E Corp, so the hero of the show succeeds without knowledge.

skepticism.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
skepticism.title: 17. Our Lying Eyes
skepticism.relation: Wood asks how Elliot - and we, who see only what he sees - can know anything, and contrasts two empiricisms: Locke's white-paper mind furnished by ideas copied from mind-independent objects, which explains Mr. Robot as perceptual error, and Berkeley's idealism, on which only ideas and their divine cause exist, which makes Elliot's unshared hallucination of Mr. Robot dangerously hard to distinguish from reality. Consistency of perception is the only test left, and it fails Elliot until the pier video proves no one pushed him - and fails us again when his cozy Season Two routine turns out to be prison.

skepticism.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
skepticism.title: 18. How to Deal with Reality when We’re not Built To
skepticism.relation: The Zawadzkis and Cisowski argue Dick's deliberate confusion enacts what psychology and radical skepticism say about cognition: our 'cognitive miser' brains build simplified models, and the films shatter them, producing Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance — Frank's chain of external justifications for his rebellion, Joe and John facing excuses they cannot so easily make, Tagomi's overload after killing the two Nazi agents. Following Karl Jaspers, such limit situations can force a leap into a new mode of thinking (Tagomi's transport to a world where the killings never happened), with radical skepticism — Bertrand Russell's five-minute hypothesis — and the I Ching as vehicles for dealing with a reality we are not built to handle.

skepticism.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
skepticism.title: 2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . .
skepticism.relation: Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.

skepticism.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
skepticism.title: 17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris
skepticism.relation: Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being. The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.

skepticism.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
skepticism.title: 8. What Are You Hearing
skepticism.relation: Wissner reads TZ's musical scores through Plato's account of music as manufactured, mimetic signs and Aristotle's doctrine of ethos — that melodies represent character and emotion and can change minds without words. She shows how in 'Perchance to Dream' and 'A Stop at Willoughby' reverberation, Theremin-like electronics, and recurring five-note motifs mark dream states against the acoustic French horn of waking reality, how shared cues in 'Twenty-Two' and 'Shadow Play' trap Liz and Adam in circular nightmares that may also be premonitions, and how the piano ostinato of 'The Midnight Sun' reveals Norma's heat-death dream — music answering whether we, or the characters, can ever be sure we are awake rather than dreaming or imagining.

skepticism.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
skepticism.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
skepticism.relation: Nisley applies Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence — built from resemblance, constancy, 'force and vivacity,' and testimony — to 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' where Colonel Harrington, then Clegg Forbes, then Major Gart each cease to exist as memory and corroboration (bartender, girlfriend, general, headlines) collapse layer by layer. 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's speakeasy reunion with his dead wife Laura shows the imagination feigning the uninterrupted existence of a person whose constancy and vivacity no longer match his memories, so the senses and memory are exposed as no foundation for rational belief in continued existence.

skepticism.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
skepticism.title: 3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis
skepticism.relation: The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.

skepticism.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
skepticism.title: 9. The Fallacy of the Many Heads
