skepticism.relation: The chapter uses Headism in 'Get Schwifty' as a case study in illusory correlation: Principal Vagina walks out to pray just as the Cromulons approve of Rick and Morty's song, so the town builds a false cause-and-effect religion from coincidence, compounding false positives until Beth and Jerry are nearly sacrificed to the Giant Heads. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's System 1/System 2 model and Peter Wason's confirmation-bias studies, it argues the characters reason rationally on the information available but never check whether their information is sufficient, the same lazy thinking that sustains religious faith, ghost photos, and the Loch Ness Monster. The cure is effortful skepticism, stopping to ask whether we might be wrong, lest we end up shooting Mr. Poopybutthole.

skepticism.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
skepticism.title: 11. Are You Imagining That Poopybutthole
skepticism.relation: Reading 'Total Rickall' as an evil-genius scenario, the chapter treats the memory parasites (Uncle Steve, Sleepy Gary, Reverse Giraffe) as Descartes's deceiving demon lodged in the Smiths' reconstructive memories, with Rick's written headcount an empirical defense that methodical doubt undermines. Morty's formula that parasites implant only good memories is shown to be merely inductive rather than certain like the cogito, so Beth's shooting of Mr. Poopybutthole becomes the test case: applying Aquinas's three kinds of ignorance, the chapter argues she remains morally responsible despite genuine remorse because she neglected the chance to reconsider Morty's probabilistic rule. The upshot is Descartes's advice to restrain the will beyond what the intellect certifies: shoot for the arm, not the head.

skepticism.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
skepticism.title: 6. The Facts Don’t Speak for Themselves
skepticism.relation: Muyskens asks why Burger and Tragg's evidence keeps pointing at innocent people, answering with Hume's distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact and the problem of induction: inferences from past experience are never guaranteed. In 'The Case of the Shapely Shadow' the prosecution's seven pieces of testimony against Janice Wainwright are reasonable but false, and only Mason, because he believes his client, presses to the water-records discovery that exposes Cole Troy; 'The Case of the Runaway Corpse' then shows Burger and Tragg settling on Myrna Davenport on flimsy, self-contradictory evidence and simply failing to investigate, while Mason withholds judgment, checks her account against documents and witnesses, and digs until justified true belief is achieved.

skepticism.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
skepticism.title: 7. Beyond a Reasonable Doubt
skepticism.relation: Jordan argues Mason's real superpower is logic rather than client selection or legal brilliance: since conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a unanimous jury, and since by the problem of induction (traced from Sextus Empiricus's regression arguments through Hume) no accumulation of probabilities yields deductive certainty, the prosecution can never conclusively prove guilt while Mason need only exploit that structural gap, as in The Case of the Howling Dog's cab-driver and document evidence and the TV movie Perry Mason Returns where Della is the accused. He illustrates with modus ponens examples about Della and Hamilton Burger, contrasting sound deductive arguments with merely strong inductive ones like predicting Mason's next win.

skepticism.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
skepticism.title: 15. The Rashomon Effect in KISS’s Autobiographies
skepticism.relation: Michael Forest and Matthew Mitchell read the four original members' autobiographies as a Rashomon effect, focused on the conflicting accounts of recording Destroyer and of who really wrote 'Beth.' Bernard Lonergan's 'scotosis' — the intellectual blind spot that censors evidence against our preferred view — explains how each memoirist constructs memories protecting his self-image, while Sartre's bad faith from Being and Nothingness (distinguished from lying via the woman-on-a-date example) explains how they may have deceived themselves rather than lied. Comparing Gene's, Ace's, Peter's, Paul's, and Lydia Criss's five accounts, the chapter concludes that no one is a reliable narrator and no one a sheer fabricator — and that fans reading the memoirs must guard against their own blind spots and bad faith.

skepticism.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
skepticism.title: Perceptions Are Fine, but Dull Reality Is Still Better
skepticism.relation: Distinguishes perceiver, perceptions, and perceived external objects to ask whether Alice, or anyone, can get beyond her perceptions to a mind-independent world, entering through Robert Arp's own painkiller hallucination of stones that were really Jell-O. The chapter sets epistemological idealism and metaphysical antirealism (the movie-theater-in-the-mind picture, traced to Plato's cave and Berkeley's suggestion that we are trapped inside perceptual reality) against the epistemological and metaphysical realism it finds in Alice and Carroll: fossilized ferns, dodo birds, and the Pythagorean theorem are discovered rather than invented, and at story's end everything rightly changes 'to dull reality'.

skepticism.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
skepticism.title: The Real Is Fake and the Fake Is Real
skepticism.relation: Takes Morpheus's red-pill speech at face value to ask whether Alice is a drug story, then argues the deeper point: the distinction between normal and distorted experience is exaggerated or specious because all perception is conditioned by expectation, mood, and chemistry, whether on caffeine or psilocybin. Scott F. Parker reads the Red King's dream alongside Plato's Theaetetus dream argument and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream to show we can never prove we are awake, then weighs William James's nitrous-oxide revelations and Aldous Huxley's mescaline 'Mind at Large' as reasons altered states might sometimes show reality more truly, concluding that the real is fake, the fake is real, and Wonderland's syndrome is now a recognized medical condition.

skepticism.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
skepticism.title: No Reason to Get Excited
skepticism.relation: The chapter turns the Final Five reveal (Tigh, Tyrol, Anders, Foster) and Boomer's sleeper activation into a skeptical problem about self-knowledge: Descartes's dreaming doubt (Roslin's Opera House dream) and the cogito show we can know that we exist but not what we are, and Baltar's rigged 'bright green' Cylon test destroys testimonial assurance. G.E. Moore's common-sense realism fails to engage the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism and Dretske's relevant-alternatives theory cannot help because in a world of sleeper Cylons the possibility 'I might be one' is always relevant. The answer is Hume's: like Tigh declaring 'I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet' and Anders repeating 'I am Samuel T. Anders' before his first combat mission, we banish skeptical paralysis by carrying on with life, dining and playing backgammon.

skepticism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
skepticism.title: Heaven is a Place on Earth
skepticism.relation: The chapter argues Black Mirror's perception tech works because the brain constructs experience top-down (predictive coding), so implants like Playtest's mushroom, Arkangel's filter, and Men Against Fire's MASS can inject perceptions and suppress error signals - and Cooper's total VR illusion defeats every one of Descartes's strategies (memory continuity, cross-checking the senses, reason) for telling dream from reality, killing him seconds after implantation. Nozick's experience machine illuminates Danny's preference for Striking Vipers X over his marriage and Arkangel's lesson that filtering Sara's childhood perceptions left her unable to read danger or emotion. Foucault's panopticon (via Bentham) frames White Christmas's cookie interrogation modeled on real police deception (Frazier v. Cupp), the MASS implant's manufacture of 'roach' targets for killing, and Nosedive's self-imposed social ratings as modern perceptual discipline - with only trusted others (Catarina, Susan, Kelly) punching through the manipulation.

skepticism.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
skepticism.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
skepticism.relation: Kevin McCain turns Ozzy's "Am I Going Insane?" into a lived version of Descartes' skeptical scenarios, the madman who cannot trust his senses, the dream argument, the deceiving demon, and asks whether Ozzy can know anything at all. Using inference to the best explanation, he argues the commonsense external-world view beats skeptical scenarios because it predicts experiences (drop the book on your toe) and raises fewer unanswerable questions, so Ozzy keeps knowledge in the no-answer and "no" cases, but if he has reason to think he is insane and everyone tells him "yes", his reasons are defeated and he cannot even know their answers, leaving him, like the rest of us, one testimonial crisis from the void.

skepticism.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
skepticism.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.

skepticism.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
skepticism.title: Happily Ever After
skepticism.relation: Runs Descartes' dreaming argument and evil-genius doubt on Aurora, for whom the scenario is literal: Maleficent is an actually existing deceiver who could have enchanted her whole life in a dungeon. G. E. Moore's common-sense proof — 'here is a hand,' dubbed the Pinocchio test after the real boy — and the Moorean shift answer the skeptic, illustrated by Maleficent deploying Zeno's paradox to stop Prince Phillip's sword, where Phillip rightly clings to the more certain premise that motion is possible. Nozick's experience machine explains why Aurora should care: we want to actually be good and live real lives rather than merely experience them, so authentic 'happily ever after' requires knowing our experiences are backed by reality.

skepticism.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
skepticism.title: Out of the Orb
skepticism.relation: Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.

skepticism.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
skepticism.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.

skepticism.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
skepticism.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Philosopher Sven Ove Hansson's memoir shows the trilogy's realism came from Larsson's decades of unpaid extremism-watching: patiently archiving Nazi and racist networks, exposing the Sweden Democrats as Per Engdahl's 1979 repackaging of fascism in anti-immigrant dress (the same strategy as Britain's National Front), and forcing Skeptics' scrutiny onto the publisher of David Irving's Holocaust-denying Göring biography. It presents Larsson's anti-pseudoscience skepticism—astrology, faith healing, pyramidology, racist biology—his rejection of the postmodern idea that knowledge is mere social construction ('The Holocaust was not a social construction'), and his philosophically interesting argument that astrology's deterministic worldview is a stifling, self-fulfilling spiritual posture. The honor-killing analysis pairing Fadime Sahindal with Melissa Nordell demonstrates his method of using philosophical case-comparison to expose moral prejudice in taken-for-granted categories—habits of mind that resurface in the novels' hidden power structures and rationalist heroine.

skepticism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
skepticism.title: NOTES
skepticism.relation: Surveys near-death-experience research from Moody's Life after Life to Susan Blackmore's debunking explanations (oxygen starvation, cultural variation) and argues the skeptical conclusion does not follow: a child's vision of her living dog Sparky on the other side could still be a genuine divinely created revelation happening wholly inside her head. It reads Harry's King's Cross way-station the same way, since wizards can channel themselves through portraits, ghosts, and Legilimency, and closes with Emerson's Over-Soul claim that moments of faith deserve to be ascribed more reality than ordinary experience.

skepticism.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
skepticism.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
skepticism.relation: The editors' introduction frames the trilogy as Katniss's quest to peel away Panem's layers of lies, likening her self-examination and self-control to the Delphic 'Know Thyself' and 'Nothing in Excess' and calling her skeptical spirit the engine of her wisdom. It poses the book's driving questions: why we enjoy watching others suffer, whether ordinary morality survives the arena, and how easily our own reality-TV-shaped world could slide into Panem's, noting that Collins modeled the Games on the Roman Colosseum. It presents dystopian exaggeration (children slaughtered for entertainment, tyrants, starving workers) as a cautionary mirror of trends already present in our society, and casts the contributors' chapters as a therapeutic game of 'Real or Not Real' played with the reader.

skepticism.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
skepticism.title: Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head
skepticism.relation: The book's introduction frames Inception as the newest chapter in the dream-skepticism tradition: Plato's question about how we explain our perceptions of reality and Descartes's point that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, with the twist that Descartes never doubted our thoughts are our own while the film contests exactly that. It previews the volume's rival readings — the single-dream theory of the airline flight, Brophy's claim that the shared dreams are server-based electronic worlds like Second Life, and neuroscience suggesting we act on thoughts before we are aware of them. It also stakes out the ethics: inception as a violation of autonomy akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing, and the diagnosis that Inception is fundamentally a tale from the business world of corporations.

skepticism.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
skepticism.title: Happy Ending
skepticism.relation: Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.

skepticism.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
skepticism.title: Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End
skepticism.relation: Andersen argues Inception goes one step deeper than Descartes's dream argument: where Descartes doubted the world but kept ownership of his thoughts, the film imagines an identity-defining conviction — Fischer's sense of his father's judgment — being implanted so it never occurs to the victim to question it, which is to co-opt subjectivity itself. He reads Nolan's whole oeuvre (Following, Memento, The Prestige, Batman Begins) as variations on manipulation by misdirection, and diagnoses Cobb's inception on Mal in Limbo as the infection of her mind with Cartesian doubt, a philosophy impossible to live by. Since a totem guards against others' dreams but not self-deception, the film's answer is not universal doubt but trust: only by opening himself to Ariadne and choosing intimacy can Cobb go home and spin the top without looking.

skepticism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
skepticism.title: 10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree
skepticism.relation: Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.

skepticism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
skepticism.title: 11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True
skepticism.relation: Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.

skepticism.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
skepticism.title: NOTES
skepticism.relation: Barris argues Lost fascinates because it dramatizes the basic structures of life itself: the castaways are Heideggerian thrown into an island none of them chose, brought there by Desmond's lapse at the Swan and by interlocking backstories such as Sawyer's bar conversation with Jack's father. Against the existentialist claim (Sartre, Camus) that life is simply absurd, he uses Wittgenstein's On Certainty - doubting everything presupposes certainties - to argue life is a riddle of partial sense, which is why the show's connections between Hurley and Libby or Jack and Desmond always hint at meaning without resolving it. The finale answers only the question of life after death, leaving life after birth as open as our own.

skepticism.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
skepticism.title: Believer, Deceiver: Metallica, Perception, and Reality
skepticism.relation: Robert Arp uses Hetfield's lyrics about lies, deception and misperception ('Bad Seed', 'The House Jack Built''s 'Is that the moon or just the light that lights this dead end street?') to stage the perception-reality problem: perceiver, perceptions, and external objects, as in Plato's cave allegory. He contrasts metaphysical/epistemological realism with idealism and antirealism, deploys the movie-theater picture of solipsism drawn from Hume's bundle of perceptions and Berkeley's denial of the external world, and argues Hetfield's own practice as a songwriter proves he is a realist - while distinguishing healthy philosophical skepticism from the lyric's irrational mistrust.

skepticism.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
skepticism.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
skepticism.relation: The editors' introduction argues that South Park is one of TV's most important series because it lampoons the fanatical extremists of every social, ethical, economic, and religious position, modeling the fallibilist skepticism critical thinkers need (quoting Parker's line that the people screaming on both sides are the same and it is OK to laugh from the middle). It offers Peirce's account of thinking through incomplete signs and Derrida's 'play of differences' as case studies of this healthy skepticism, defends laughing at fanatics because their reasoning withers in sunlight, and previews the volume: Murtagh's 'sledgehammer' defense of blasphemous humor, Jacoby's Clifford-style case that belief without evidence is wrong, Dueck on rationally defensible faith, Gray on the 'Douche or Turd' election, and Held on gay marriage.

skepticism.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
skepticism.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
skepticism.relation: Jacoby defends W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief—it is wrong to believe on insufficient evidence and the burden of proof falls on the claimant—through Stan's exposures of TV psychic John Edward ('The Biggest Douche in the Universe'), the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the faith-based story of Joseph Smith in 'All About Mormons'. The centerpiece is a South Park-illustrated demolition of Pascal's Wager: Kyle's hemorrhoid-driven despair in 'Cartmanland' shows a perfectly good God would not eternally reward evil Cartman or torture honest nonbelievers, and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' shows the wagerer cannot even know which religion pays out. Stan's closing speech to Edward's frightened audience carries the moral: comforting lies weaken the mind and slow the progress of finding the real, amazing answers.

skepticism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
skepticism.title: Notes
skepticism.relation: Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.

skepticism.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
skepticism.title: Notes
skepticism.relation: Asks whether Han Solo's 'hokey religions' dismissal of the Force is unreasonable given his evidence, answering no: Hume's argument against miracles explains why testimony of lightsaber tricks and mind tricks should not overturn Han's experience of consistent natural law, while Hume's problem of induction and custom/habit explain why both Han's 'luck' verdict and Obi-Wan's 'no such thing as luck' are habit-based generalizations. Peirce's fallibilism (backed by Putnam's 'fallibilism does not entail skepticism') lets Han and Obi-Wan each claim knowledge without certainty, echoing Obi-Wan's line that many truths depend greatly on our own point of view.

skepticism.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
skepticism.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
skepticism.relation: Nisley reads 'And When the Sky Was Opened' through Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence: Colonel Forbes's conviction that Harrington exists rests on memory's force and vivacity, and when testimony collapses (newspaper headlines, the bartender, his girlfriend, the general) the three spacemen are erased one by one, 'no longer part of the memory of man.' 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's belief that the woman in the speakeasy is his dead Laura is the imagination's feigned continuity, a resemblance across interrupted perceptions rather than a rational foundation. Memory alone, the chapter concludes, never grounds our beliefs that things or persons persist unperceived.

skepticism.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
skepticism.title: Introduction
skepticism.relation: George Dunn's introduction pitches Veronica herself as a philosopher of the noir: her Neptune is a world where 'the innocent suffer, the guilty go free,' nothing is what it seems (a shy geek turns out to be a psychopathic rapist, a beloved baseball-owning politician a child molester), and her rendering of Pope's Essay on Man as 'Life's a bitch until you die' is answered by her practical code 'get tough and get even.' It argues that the show's marriage of truth-seeking detective work to pervasive deception makes it natural ground for philosophical investigation of Neptune's racial and class divisions, the morality of law breaking, the nature of evil, injustices suffered by women at Neptune High and Hearst College, friendship, and good reasoning, all timed to the Kickstarter-funded movie revival that inspired the volume.

skepticism.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
skepticism.title: When Life Gives You Chlamydia
skepticism.relation: Andrew Zimmerman Jones explains Veronica's casework as inductive reasoning: Occam's razor dispatches Meryl's 'space laser' speculation and identifies Gia's stalker via the simplest explanation (the stalker drove off in the pick-up), while Keith's refusal to accept Abel Koontz's confession shows the razor's limits — Sheriff Lamb's laziness being Sidney Brenner's 'Occam's broom,' whisking inconvenient facts like Lilly's body temperature under the rug. Distinguishing Aristotle's particulars-to-universal induction from deduction, the chapter teaches the probability fallacy through the Mercer evidence (clippers, cologne, and GHB make it likely the rapist owns them, not that their owner is the rapist — the same confusion fueling suspicion of PCH-ers) and catalogues the fallacies — false dilemma, false cause, ad hominem, appeal to emotion — that Veronica's jealousy-driven reasoning commits in the Sully case. The chlamydia diagnosis revealing Cassidy raped her is the final lesson: new evidence overturns even well-confirmed conclusions, so certainty is a sucker's bet.

skepticism.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
skepticism.title: Kickstarting Inductive Inference
skepticism.relation: Daniel Wilkenfeld analyzes Veronica's 'magic trick' in the 'One Angry Veronica' juryroom and her season-long bus-crash solution as Peter Lipton's inference to the best explanation: the hypothesis 'Beaver is a killer' wins by consilience (explaining the explosion, the dead rat, Curly Moran, even her chlamydia), simplicity, and completeness. But the criteria face Hume's problem of induction — why think the future will resemble the past, when yesterday's popular girl is today's pariah? — and Descartes's evil demon undermines even what Veronica 'sees,' since Curly Moran could fake a bus crash, leaving no non-circular justification for inferential habits none of us can live without. Following Nelson Goodman, Wilkenfeld concludes the demand for justification is misplaced: what matters is that Veronica reasons consistently, in the juryroom as at the cliff.

skepticism.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
skepticism.title: The Hot Hand in Basketball
skepticism.relation: Steven Hales rebuts the Gilovich-Vallone-Tversky studies (and Stephen Jay Gould) claiming that hot hands in basketball are statistical illusions. He dismantles their three skeptical arguments - 'success doesn't breed success' (76ers data), the demand for statistically improbable streaks (Joe DiMaggio's 56-game hitting streak), and the chance argument about run frequencies - showing each rests on an arbitrary, unprincipled cutoff for how 'hot' a streak must be, in the classic skeptical pattern of setting knowledge standards impossibly high. He then defends a commonsense definition on which a hot hand just is any run of above-average shooting: Wilt Chamberlain's thirty-five straight makes made him genuinely hot even if no one could feel the streak ending, and fans' and players' widespread judgments are vindicated rather than error-theorized away.

skepticism.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
skepticism.title: The Basket That Never Was
skepticism.relation: Thomas Flint's thought experiment - a conference-championship buzzer-beater waved off because the clock expired, with inconclusive video - asks whether South Shore 'really' scored. He rejects the 'Goofy View' that game facts are referee-independent, since it would entail that only he and his camcorder-owning boss know who won any game ever (imperiling even Michael Jordan's 1982 title and Pistol Pete's scoring record) and would poison a coach's duty to teach rule-following when officials miss traveling. He also rejects the 'Tyranny of the Zebras' that makes officials infallible like the pope, since NCAA replay rules presuppose fallibility, and settles on officials as contest judges who award points: without the verdict no points exist, yet a blown call remains a genuine mistake in failing to apply the rules properly.

skepticism.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
skepticism.title: Inside the Helmet What Do Football Players Know
skepticism.relation: Geivett uses football to illustrate epistemology, distinguishing factual (propositional) from competence (skill) knowledge through what running backs and quarterbacks must know and enact under split-second pressure, including 'football physics' vectors on a rollout pass. He treats the athlete's need to be mindful of knowledge amid stadium noise as a lesson in reliable belief, then critiques classroom skeptics who deploy Descartes's evil-demon and the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, arguing mere logical possibility is no evidence for skepticism.

skepticism.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
skepticism.title: Why Roger Federer Is the Best Or Is It McEnroe
skepticism.relation: David Baggett asks who is the all-time best male tennis player and treats it as a genuine problem in metaphysics ('what is the case?') and epistemology ('how do we know it?'), surveying candidates from Tilden to Federer against ten criteria. He argues the sentence 'Federer is the all-time best' is vague, running the tennis-ball-losing-an-atom sorites through three theories of vagueness—fuzzy logic, supervaluationism, and Timothy Williamson's epistemicism, which he favors: there is a fact of the matter (God knows it) but our closeness-to-the-margin ignorance keeps us from knowing it. He uses Anselm's ontological argument and Guanilo's perfect-island reply to distinguish the all-time best from the best-possible player, and invokes Sartre's existentialist rejection of mere potentiality ('could've/should've') to insist he is asking who actually was best, not who might have been.

skepticism.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
skepticism.title: Living a Part Synecdoche, New York, Metaphor, and the Problem of Skepticism
skepticism.relation: Deming argues that Caden Cotard's attempt to build a full-scale replica of New York inside a warehouse enacts a skepticism toward the givenness of life—the belief that reality can be denied and remade as art. Drawing on Cavell's claim that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' and Heidegger on world, earth, and dwelling, he shows the play traps Caden rather than freeing him: to represent the world is to be flung outside it. He invokes Wittgenstein's image of language as an ancient city one can never step outside of, and Baudrillard's simulacra (Caden even considers titling the play 'Simulacrum'), to explain why the literal doubling fails to yield the 'true self' Caden seeks.

skepticism.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
skepticism.title: Synecdoche, in Part
skepticism.relation: Smith reads every Kaufman film as a farce about the self-defeating quest to 'become who you are,' with Synecdoche, New York as its culmination: Caden's MacArthur-funded attempt to represent all of life in a warehouse collapses into infinite regress because a representation of everything must contain itself. He frames Kaufman's films as Montaignean/Emersonian essays—fragmentary self-portraits—and argues the film's limits are death and language, since language always puts us at one remove from the life we already are. The transcendence it evokes is naturalistic, akin to Nietzsche's amor fati and Emerson's 'we are born to a whole': wholeness is not achieved but already possessed, and the hidden knowledge of it turns tragedy into farce.

skepticism.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
skepticism.title: eXistenZial Angst
skepticism.relation: Duncan Pritchard reads eXistenZ as staging radical skepticism with existential force: unlike the standard brain-in-a-vat scenario, the game 'creeps up' on Ted and Allegra so they feel the transition from reality to doubt, producing angst. Invoking Wittgenstein's On Certainty (doubt radicalized is madness), he argues sanity requires belief but not true belief, so the pair achieve a new doxastic equilibrium. He also reads the spinal 'bioport' pod as a case of Clark and Chalmers's extended cognition, where technology becomes part of and subverts the agents' cognitive processes.

skepticism.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
skepticism.title: 1. Dream Investigations of Tree House Operations
skepticism.relation: The Rochas argue that Agent Cooper's grab-bag of methods—rock-throwing named for suspects, dream clues, Tibetan intuition, plus Albert's forensics and Truman's teamwork—exposes the fallacy of scientism, the over-application of scientific method to what it cannot settle. They stress that Cooper's dream-derived 'deductive technique' is not really deductive but intuitive guesswork, and that real crime-solving (like the PCAST critique of forensic matching) is a messy blend of induction, instinct, and luck rather than the certainty shows like CSI pretend to. The chapter is really about the limits of scientific certainty in knowledge of the world.

skepticism.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
skepticism.title: 4. Special Epistemic Agent Dale Cooper
skepticism.relation: Written as Cooper's dictations to Diane, Rard uses the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge and the internalism/externalism debate to ask whether Cooper is justified in trusting dreams and visions in a world with supernatural forces. Through the Invitation to Love Ouija-board example she shows how a reliable but unrecognized source yields externally justified belief (reliabilism); Cooper then earns internal justification the way one tests a hypothesis—treating the giant's predictions ('man in a smiling bag', 'the owls are not what they seem', 'without chemicals he points') as testable predictions that come true, making him a 'special epistemic agent.'

skepticism.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
skepticism.title: 8. I Sure Feel Uncomfortable Being in This Situation with You
skepticism.relation: Rosenbaum argues that Twin Peaks deliberately engineers audience discomfort to make its point about the limits of human understanding and the blurred lines between categories we prefer distinct. He analyzes its straddling of melodrama and cringe comedy, its ambiguously diegetic Badalamenti score (a Brecht-like estrangement effect that ruptures our absorption), and its 'behavioral uncanny valley' plus bathos—Cooper casually chewing gum mid-murder-talk—arguing the real horror is epistemic uncertainty about who and what the townspeople really are.

skepticism.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
skepticism.title: Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler
skepticism.relation: Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).

skepticism.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
skepticism.title: The Russell-Wartenberg Debate
skepticism.relation: The chapter sets the book's standard for 'philosophy in action' by staging Bruce Russell's skepticism against Thomas Wartenberg's defense of the film-as-philosophy thesis: Russell holds that narrative films can at most raise questions or furnish counterexamples, so The Matrix merely inspires the viewer's own argument for external-world skepticism, while Wartenberg replies that The Matrix screens Descartes's evil-deceiver hypothesis so effectively that viewers are themselves deceived into skeptical doubt, accomplishing for audiences what Socrates did to his interlocutors. Wartenberg's reading of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind — where Dr. Mierzwiak's memory-erasure technology presents utilitarianism (via Mary's dialogue) and then a counterexample to it — is tested, and the author proposes the film targets hedonism more directly, working as a reverse variant of Nozick's experience machine that defends autonomy over happiness. Kant's obscure Transcendental Deduction is invoked to show that even canonical philosophical texts are ambiguous, blunting the explicitness objection. The chapter concludes that negative projects — modus tollens counterexamples cinematically conveyed — are where film most plausibly philosophizes, preparing the ground for reading the Whedonverse.

skepticism.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
skepticism.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
skepticism.relation: Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.

skepticism.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
skepticism.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
skepticism.relation: Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.

skepticism.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
skepticism.title: Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers
skepticism.relation: Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.

skepticism.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
skepticism.title: Sherlock Holmes as Epistemologist
skepticism.relation: Baggett reconstructs Holmes's detective practice as an expansive epistemology built on observation, background knowledge, and abductive inference-to-the-best-explanation, using cases like 'The Blue Carbuncle' hat and the 'eliminate the impossible' maxim. He argues Holmes's boldness in drawing inferences is intellectual courage rather than hubris, invoking William James on the risk of losing truth by excessive caution. He then tests Holmes against feminist epistemologists who fault his cult of cold objectivity and mistrust of women (the Mary Morstan and Irene Adler episodes), concluding Holmes is partly vindicated by his imagination, intuition, and passion but still too fragmented between reason and emotion.

skepticism.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
skepticism.title: (Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing
skepticism.relation: Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.

skepticism.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
skepticism.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
skepticism.relation: Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.

skepticism.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
skepticism.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
skepticism.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.

skepticism.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
skepticism.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
skepticism.relation: Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.

skepticism.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
skepticism.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
skepticism.relation: Sanders reads Soderbergh's HBO series K Street as a paranoid meditation on appearance and reality set in a Washington lobbying firm, where James Carville and Mary Matalin play fictionalized versions of themselves and the reclusive owner Richard Bergstrom manipulates everyone from afar while endlessly rewatching Mildred Pierce. Through three unresolved mysteries and a 'house of mirrors' structure, the show dramatizes the characters' skepticism about their capacity to know reality and Bergstrom's moral solipsism. Sanders argues Soderbergh's run-and-gun docudrama form itself enacts the epistemic uncertainty, leaving the text radically underdetermined about whether Bergstrom is a con man, a pawn, or a phantom-chasing paranoid.

skepticism.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
skepticism.title: “All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March
skepticism.relation: Rhu reads Ross McElwee's Sherman's March—ostensibly a documentary about Sherman's Civil War campaign but really about a heartbroken filmmaker's search for love amid Cold War nuclear dread—through Walker Percy's The Last Gentleman and Stanley Cavell's The World Viewed. He shows how the film enacts Cavell's ontology of film (viewing the world "from behind the self," movies as reliefs from private fantasy) and the dialogue between perfectionism and skepticism Cavell draws from Emerson's "Experience" and Nietzsche and Kierkegaard. McElwee's deliberately unpolished, self-conscious "personal documentary"—stumbling on the riverbank, leaving in his own second thoughts—turns the war film into a meditation on consciousness, mediation, and being "all in war with Time."

skepticism.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
skepticism.title: 02_LaRocca_Chapter_001.html
skepticism.relation: Cavell argues that photography's power expresses the mind's fall into skepticism about the external world, reading film as 'a moving image of skepticism' since we see things present to us that are not actually before us. Interpreting Capra's Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, he treats Gary Cooper's Deeds defending his 'fidgetiness' as thinking as a popular-cinema reenactment of Descartes's cogito: after Emerson, who says we can no longer say 'I think, I am' for ourselves, the proof of existence shifts from the mind's self-certainty to the live body's visible restlessness caught by the camera. He links the fidgeting body to Heidegger's das Man and Nietzsche's last man, and invokes Wittgenstein and Emerson on our being 'away' from the world.

skepticism.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
skepticism.title: Introduction
skepticism.relation: The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre from Doodlebug through Interstellar, arguing that like Socrates's gadfly his films sting viewers out of complacency rather than delivering settled answers. It traces a running theme of self-destruction and self-identity: Buber's I-Thou thesis illuminates Following's Cobb and The Young Man (with a Hegelian master-slave twist), Leonard Shelby in Memento must invent a telos to keep his existence meaningful, Descartes's dream argument stands behind Inception's spinning top, and the Joker voices Hobbes on what 'a little anarchy' does to society. It closes by reading Interstellar as the culmination of these themes, with Cooper's partial love for Murph set against Dr. Mann and Prof. Brand, who are willing to squash their humanity to save the species.

skepticism.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
skepticism.title: Inception and Perception
skepticism.relation: Jamie Carlin Watson uses Inception's dream thieves to stage the dream argument for skepticism - from Socrates' puzzle to Theaetetus and Descartes's Meditations, with Sextus Empiricus's diversity-of-perception argument - and contends that totems cannot debunk it, since even Arthur's loaded die and Cobb's top cannot rule out being in your own dream, where your subconscious knows how the totem behaves. Against both believing as normal and Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment, the chapter turns to William James's will to believe (live versus dead hypotheses) and to intellectual virtues drawn from Zagzebski and Kornblith: beliefs can be valuable for reasons other than truth. The upshot is that Cobb, Arthur, and the twelve shared-dream sleepers in Yusuf's basement can believe well even if they cannot believe truly - which is why Cobb's walking away from the spinning top at the end can be read as believing carefully rather than certainly.

skepticism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
skepticism.title: Doomed to Be Perceived
skepticism.relation: Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.

skepticism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
skepticism.title: How to do Philosophy
skepticism.relation: Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.

skepticism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
skepticism.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
skepticism.relation: Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'

skepticism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
skepticism.title: Skepticism Outside the Matrix
skepticism.relation: Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.

skepticism.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
skepticism.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
skepticism.relation: Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.

skepticism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
skepticism.title: Neither Here, nor There, nor Anywhere
skepticism.relation: Randall Auxier reads Green Eggs and Ham as a primer in Peircean pragmatism. The contrarian 'C' illustrates how thinking only begins when a problem interrupts action, and Peirce's distinction between 'genuine doubt' and settled belief-as-habit explains why C clings to 'I do not like them' without ever trying them. Auxier runs C's stubbornness through Peirce's four methods of fixing belief (Authority, A Priori, Tenacity, Science), arguing C relies on tenacity, and likens Sam-I-Am to Saint Monica pestering Augustine into genuine doubt, so that even after C eats the eggs he only knows they settled belief in one context.

skepticism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
skepticism.title: McElligot’s Pool Epistemology (with Fish!)
skepticism.relation: Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'

skepticism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
skepticism.title: Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution
skepticism.relation: Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.

skepticism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
skepticism.title: Chapter 11 Socratic Irony in Twain’s Skeptical Religious Jeremiads
skepticism.relation: Jacquette demands a precise definition of Twain's much-invoked irony, adopting Vlastos's/Quintilian's formula that irony says the contrary of what is meant while letting the real meaning be recovered. He classifies Twain's irony as local vs. global and comic vs. sober (tragic/historical): 'Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc' is globally ironic (falsely presented as de Conte's eyewitness manuscript), while the relic-mocking passages of 'The Innocents Abroad' (St. Luke's Madonna, kegs of true-cross nails, three skulls of John the Baptist) are local comic irony. Jacquette concludes Twain's irony is distinctively Socratic: like Socrates interpreting the Delphic oracle, Twain makes a moral and epistemic virtue of ridiculing experts who claim to know what no one can know about God, sin, and the afterlife.

skepticism.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
skepticism.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
skepticism.relation: Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.

skepticism.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
skepticism.title: GARDENING
skepticism.relation: O'Brien reads Voltaire's closing injunction in Candide, 'we must cultivate our garden,' through David Hume to argue that gardening is therapy—a retreat from metaphysics and religion into the tranquility of common life. Hume rejects belief in miracles and religious 'enthusiasm' not by logic but by recalling everyday reasoning (a melon seed, not a miracle, explains melons in the greenhouse), and the gardener is the sophisticated artisan-reasoner attuned to nature's regularities. Gardening inculcates Humean virtues (industry, patience, balancing action, pleasure and indolence) and Haybron's attunement/engagement/endorsement, yielding Epicurean ataraxia; the Sisyphean gardener (Camus) fighting slugs, and Wittgenstein taking up gardening as a cure, illustrate the point.

skepticism.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
skepticism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
skepticism.relation: Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.

skepticism.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
skepticism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
skepticism.relation: Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.

skepticism.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
skepticism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
skepticism.relation: Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.

skepticism.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
skepticism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
skepticism.relation: Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.

skepticism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
skepticism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
skepticism.relation: David Robles's 'The Seeker' argues that declining trust in Western absolutist religion drives people toward yoga as an experiential, self-directed spirituality. His central move is that Patanjali's Yoga Sutras rank direct perception above testimony and scripture — mirroring the scientific method — so yoga functions as a 'spiritual science' harmonious with empiricism, whereas established religion rests on second-hand revelation. He distinguishes 'spiritual' (personal, inspiration-based) from 'religious' (culturally binding dogma) and casts the American 'seeker' as building a better, results-oriented, pragmatic spirituality.

skepticism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
skepticism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
skepticism.relation: Steve Jacobson's 'Standing on Your Head' asks whether an educated Westerner can reasonably believe 'yoga theory' (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas) given that science has superseded ancient theories. He raises a 'standard objection' from the superior predictive power of science (invoking Hume's problem of induction), rejects weak replies, but argues via the epistemology of testimony that people with weak scientific grounds and strong critical testimony can rationally accept yoga theory. He concludes that even if no part of it is credible, abandoning it would leave yoga intact — 'yoga with fewer illusions.'

skepticism.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
skepticism.title: BLUES
skepticism.relation: Jesse Steinberg argues that doubt — a pervasive blues theme (B. B. King's 'nobody loves me but my momma,' Otis Spann's 'another mule kickin' in my stall,' Buddy Guy's 'I Smell a Rat') — supports Descartes's external-world skepticism, since knowledge would require ruling out the dreaming hypothesis. Against the 'I don't care' hedonistic reply he deploys Nozick's experience machine to show we value authentic reality over mere pleasant appearance, and he rejects contextualism as a solution. Endorsing Socrates' examined life, he settles for strong justification rather than certainty, reading Charley Patton's 'can't tell my future, can't tell my past' as the blues' honest coping with irreducible doubt.

skepticism.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
skepticism.title: Horror and the Idea of Everyday Life On Skeptical Threats in Psycho and The Birds
skepticism.relation: Philip J. Nickel argues horror has an epistemological value structurally parallel to philosophical skepticism: it maliciously rips away the tacit 'cognitive trust' backing our everyday actions. In The Birds, the diner 'symposium' where Mrs. Bundy's confident science that birds cannot coordinate an attack is refuted moments later dramatizes a paranoid scenario we cannot rationally rule out. In Psycho, Marion Crane's isolation and misplaced trust in the seemingly normal Norman Bates enacts the skeptical premise that the ordinary person you rely on could murder you. Like Hume returning to backgammon, viewers can only resume everyday life, which Nickel says horror exposes as a necessary but insecure construction.

skepticism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
skepticism.title: 2. The Matrix
skepticism.relation: Rowlands reads The Matrix as a vivid staging of Cartesian skepticism: Neo's pod-world is Descartes's dream and evil-demon conjectures (AI plays the demon) plus the modern brain-in-a-vat, showing we cannot be certain the external world exists. He uses the 'there is no air/muscles' and 'twin buildings' variant of Putnam's Twin Earth to argue we cannot even be certain which thoughts we think. The Hume-Nietzsche bundle critique undermines even the cogito, and the spoon-bending boy ('there is no spoon') illustrates Berkeley's idealism as the endpoint of skepticism about the physical world.

skepticism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
skepticism.title: Skepticism Outside the Matrix
skepticism.relation: Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.

skepticism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
skepticism.title: 23. The X-Files as Philosophy Navigating the “Truth Out There”
skepticism.relation: The chapter argues that Darin Morgan's X-Files episodes philosophize by critiquing the show's own 'the truth is out there' mantra from within. Through the conflicting hypnosis testimonies and identical camera blocking in 'Jose Chung's From Outer Space,' Morgan cinematically stages Nietzsche's perspectivism and the claim that 'truth is as subjective as reality'; through Clyde Bruckman and the doomed Ansel of 'Quagmire,' he mounts an anti-Socratic case that relentlessly pursuing truth (as Mulder does) is not worth the ruin it brings. Kowalski then rebuts Morgan using Descartes's cogito and inference-to-the-best-explanation to defend objective truth against radical skepticism, arguing subjectivism about truth is self-refuting.

skepticism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
skepticism.title: 49. A Serious Man as Philosophy The Elusiveness of Moral Knowledge
skepticism.relation: Biderman reads the Coens' A Serious Man through Beauvoir's figure of the 'serious man' (from The Ethics of Ambiguity), the man who craves a single absolute value and blinds himself to moral complexity: physics professor Larry Gopnik, beset by divorce, a bribing student Clive, and Sy Ableman's death, seeks moral knowledge that would let him be such a man. The chapter argues Larry's quest fails across cognitivist, noncognitivist, and pluralist accounts of moral knowledge, showing moral knowledge to be elusive if not impossible. The film's Kafkaesque fables (the Dibbuk, the Goy's Teeth, Rabbi Nachtner's 'L'olam ha-ba', Schrodinger's cat, and the Binding of Isaac in Caravaggio's painting) all stage the absurd collapse of interpretation, echoing the Book of Job, which Maimonides read as a parable rather than history.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
brain-in-a-vat.title: Unknown
brain-in-a-vat.relation: The authors carry the skeptical scenario into the twentieth century: Peter Unger's evil scientist uses computer-driven electrodes to fabricate our belief in rocks and chairs, and Hilary Putnam's brain-in-a-vat story from Reason, Truth, and History deceives us about everything we seem to perceive, with the computer supplying feedback for our attempted actions. Noting how closely this matches the pod-bound humans of The Matrix, they pose Putnam's question - 'How do you know you aren't in this predicament?' - as a sword of Damocles hanging over everyday knowledge.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
brain-in-a-vat.title: Unknown
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Korsmeyer reads the film through classic problems of perception: Descartes's dreaming argument (Neo's sweaty awakenings), the evil deceiver updated as the evil computer, and the pod scene as her 'scariest philosophical problem', the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, with Berkeley's esse est percipi as the Matrix's governing premise. She also notes the film's structural constraint - like all dreaming plots from Calderon to The X-Files its viewpoint must stand outside the Matrix - and uses Mouse's Tasty Wheat puzzle to show how reference to a never-experienced world breaks down.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
brain-in-a-vat.title: Does Rush Offer a Way Out
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Uses Rush's 1980s lyrics about facades and trust — 'Limelight''s strangers, 'Show Don't Tell''s refusal to take things on faith, 'War Paint''s lying mirror, and the synthesizer as an instrument that can fake any other sound — to stage skepticism about other minds, running from Descartes's cogito through solipsism and behaviorism. Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box and private-language argument dissolve the inner/outer confusion as a grammatical one, and 'Turn the Page' supplies the way out of the fly-bottle: nothing survives a vacuum, and with other people all we can do is be reminded.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
brain-in-a-vat.title: The Evil Genius that Turns Moriarty into a Brain in a Vat
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Samardzija reads Star Trek's holodeck Moriarty as Descartes updated: Data plays Holmes on the holodeck while Dr. Pulaski's Nietzschean jibe (from 'The Illogical Necessary' in Human, All Too Human) denies that computation can be human, and the holographic Moriarty proves his sentience not by deduction but by feelingCrowded intuitions first and then invoking Descartes' cogito ergo sum to Picard. In 'Ship in a Bottle' he nests a simulation of the Enterprise inside the Holmes holodeck to trick the crew into believing he has escaped — an evil-genius, brain-in-a-vat scenario that ends with Picard admitting our own reality 'might be nothing more than an elaborate simulation.' The paradox is that only the unemotional android Data can detect the deception, so rationality bars him from humanity while Moriarty stays eternally deceived into thinking he has become human — and Doyle's own 'hereditary tendencies' account of Moriarty's evil, the chapter notes, is a Victorian biological determinism the hologram rebels against.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
brain-in-a-vat.title: Happy Ending
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
brain-in-a-vat.title: 9. How the Doctor Knows
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Smithka argues the Doctor is a reliabilist about knowledge rather than a Cartesian strong foundationalist: using 'Amy's Choice,' 'The Beast Below' (the glass of water, the engine room, Amy's inference that the Star Whale came willingly), 'Silence in the Library' (the chicken-leg experiment implicating the Vashta Nerada), and Davros's Dalek trials in 'Genesis of the Daleks,' she shows him trusting perception in the right causal chain and reasoning inductively and abductively—Peirce's inference to the best explanation—instead of demanding Cartesian certainty. Against Descartes's dream and evil-genius skepticism, updated as Putnam-style brain-in-a-vat scenarios via the Dream Crabs of 'Last Christmas' and the Dream Lord's two-worlds game, she deploys Goldman's three criteria for perceptual knowledge: justification is packed into reliable belief-forming processes, and doubt is warranted only in known abnormal contexts like funhouses or Dream Lord games.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
brain-in-a-vat.title: 11. What the Soufflé Girl Could Teach Descartes
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Becker-Lindenthal uses 'Amy's Choice' to revise Descartes's dream skepticism: the Dream Lord is not an external evil demon but the Doctor's own repressed alter ego fed by psychic pollen, so the self-delusion Descartes dismissed becomes the real deceiver, read through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams (Rory's death as the Doctor's wish, Amy's choice as Thanatos). She then reads Oswin in 'Asylum of the Daleks' as a brain-in-a-vat variant (Putnam's Reason, Truth and History) with a crucial difference—Oswin hacks the Dalek program and follows her own agenda—so her self-deceptive soufflé-baking fantasy is a self-formation that preserves her 'I' inside Dalek hardware, complicating Ryle's rejection of the ghost in the machine. Finally, the Doctor judges Oswin by a Turing test plus Putnam's test of reference (the impossible milk and eggs), but her self-deception is vindicated when it lets her save the Doctor and the universe.

brain-in-a-vat.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
brain-in-a-vat.title: Happy Ending
brain-in-a-vat.relation: Wenmackers uses the spinning-top ending — Cobb reuniting with his children while the top wobbles off-screen — to run a guided tour of skeptical philosophy through the film's dream mechanics (totems, kicks, Limbo, exponential dream-time). She diagrams and compares Zhuangzi's butterfly, Plato's Cave and theory of Forms, Socratic know-that-you-know-nothing, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine, arguing that Inception does to its viewers what Plato's Cave was meant to do: make us doubt our own level of reality, so that Nolan himself performs inception on the audience. Her resolution is subjectivist — from inside, every level feels equally real, so like Cobb you should turn away from the top and make the best of wherever you are, which even rescues the happy ending since dream-time runs faster than real time.
