The monster's acquisition of language at the De Lacey cottage - grasping 'fire, milk, and bread' but not 'good,' 'dearest,' and 'unhappy' - becomes the test case between Descartes's private inner theater (with its evil demon) and Gilbert Ryle's reply, glossing Locke on ideas of reflection, that we learn emotion words by responding directly to behavior rather than by cracking a hidden code. On Ryle's reading the monster's deformity is horror precisely because it is put to Cartesian use, a body that seems to shield its inner life, so the creature only truly comes alive when it behaves like a human being.

ghost-in-the-machine.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
ghost-in-the-machine.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues that when you go extinct you do not come back, dismantling our three hopes: the soul, cloning, and an essential self. Cloning a T. rex yields a new individual 'Rex' with her own perspective, not the original; the soul cannot both be beyond science's reach and record memories and move bodies; and he deploys Gilbert Ryle's view that 'soul' is a language mistake - a mind is just what a functioning brain does, the way 'Jurassic Park' is just buildings, dinosaurs, staff, and money working together, ceasing when the functioning stops. A Hammond stripped by Alzheimer's and atom-replacement of every memory, trait, and particle still gets called John Hammond, so there is no essence over time: we already die constantly and never notice, which is why a second extinction holds no fresh terror.

ghost-in-the-machine.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
ghost-in-the-machine.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: The chapter asks whether Marceline has lost Simon Petrikov forever now that he is the Ice King, and tests every criterion of personal identity - body, memories, beliefs, personality, soul - finding each one either something that changes over time without ending a person (Finn survives losing his arm, Jake his fear of vampires) or something shared that then explains nothing. Borrowing Ryle's deflation of the soul as just the way the brain works - like Lemongrab renaming and remaking the Candy Kingdom, killing it without touching a single building - the author concludes Simon and the Ice King are two different people sharing one piece of machinery, like two operating systems on one computer. The dark payoff: bringing Simon back permanently would delete the Ice King, and by the same reasoning our own past selves are equally gone, a 'thousand deaths' a day that the chapter offers as Marceline's consolation, with Death's line 'you're gonna be the Ice King' as the haunting exception.

ghost-in-the-machine.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
ghost-in-the-machine.title: 20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: A comic sprint through Western thought anchored in the Science of Discworld books, the chapter runs from Aristotle—whose geocentric four-element physics, it notes, fits Discworld better than Roundworld, and whose condemnations of usury it digresses over—through Descartes's cogito and mind-body dualism, Ryle's 'ghost in the machine,' behaviorism, identity theory, eliminative materialism, and functionalism's brain-as-computer picture, to show how philosophy of mind advances by each theory picking on its predecessor. Newton's occult-seeming gravity, later overturned by Einstein, illustrates the chapter's real thesis drawn from Pratchett's 'Lies-to-Wizards': neither science nor philosophy erects a timeless edifice of facts, since 'every so often, you have to unlearn what you thought you already knew,' while Diogenes and the Cynics supply the model of philosophy done in the common tongue that Pratchett shares.

ghost-in-the-machine.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
ghost-in-the-machine.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.

ghost-in-the-machine.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
ghost-in-the-machine.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.

ghost-in-the-machine.title: Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.

ghost-in-the-machine.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
ghost-in-the-machine.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
ghost-in-the-machine.relation: J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.

hard-problem.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
hard-problem.title: The Machine-Made Ghost Or, The Philosophy of Mind, Matrix Style
hard-problem.relation: Holt announces his menu: after setting aside the standard ports of entry - Descartes's malicious demon, the brain-in-a-vat remade as body-in-a-vat, and the truth-versus-happiness question - he takes up the philosophy of mind his title advertises, the 'machine-made ghost' playing on the 'ghost in the machine' picture of the mind as a spirit inhabiting the body. He previews two entrees - arguing that artificial minds are possible and that mental states are brain states - and for dessert a solution to the hard problem of consciousness.

hard-problem.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
hard-problem.title: Unknown
hard-problem.relation: Holt takes Mouse's Tasty Wheat question - how do the machines know what it tasted like? - as the problem of other minds raised for machines, and defends mind-brain identity against multiple realizability with the artificial-pain analogy: like artificial hearts and prostheses, silicon 'pain' is a synthetic twin, not pain itself, so a single neural type may still realize it. He then sketches a speculative solution to the hard problem: consciousness is a 'had perspective' the brain creates - meaning-laden awareness of oneself and the world - which makes mind-brain identity intelligible and keeps the Matrix premise coherent.

hard-problem.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
hard-problem.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep
hard-problem.relation: Larry Hauser reads Blade Runner's replicants alongside the philosophical-zombie thought experiment: like Rachel, who passes as human until a Voigt-Kampff test, zombies are outwardly perfect replicas with 'nobody home' inside. He traces the problem from Descartes's beast-automata and hats-and-coats worry about other minds, through Turing's universal machines and Kripke's necessary identifications (water is H2O), to the way zombie scenarios devour behaviorism, functionalism, and mind-brain identity theory, using Searle's silicon-chip replacement to imagine consciousness shrinking while behavior continues. His own 'familiar' and 'super-smart' zombies (a beloved with no qualia, NEXUS-9 geniuses) argue thought without felt experience is conceivable, before he concludes the phenomenal-zombie conception may self-destruct because a first-person point of view requires the very qualia it strips away.

hard-problem.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
hard-problem.title: A Single, Perfect Sphere
hard-problem.relation: Reads Rush's 'Hemispheres' as a correction to Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: Apollo's gifts of reason leave the people joyless, Dionysus's release into passion leaves them starving in winter, and Cygnus is made god of Balance because human nature thinks and feels at once. Against Descartes's two substances and the 'Robots Plus' picture, the author argues feeling is not supernatural icing on a machine but how survival-minded organisms stay in phenomenal contact with the world, so physicalism needs deepening rather than a nonphysical mind.

hard-problem.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
hard-problem.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
hard-problem.relation: Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.

hard-problem.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
hard-problem.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
hard-problem.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.

hard-problem.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
hard-problem.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
hard-problem.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether 'you' survive a walker bite, testing bodily identity, behaviorism, and functionalism as theories of personal survival against Jenner's verdict that after death 'everything you ever were... gone'. His centerpiece adapts Daniel Dennett: survivors yoke walkers to plows and tanks, dangle meat to move them between positions labeled 1 and 0, and gradually build a rope-and-corpse computer functionally identical to a human brain - which behaviorism and functionalism must call conscious, yet which we can conceive as utterly dark inside. The lesson is that we cannot know whether any system, walker, animal, or AI, is conscious, so treatment of non-human systems may need to err on the side of caution.

hard-problem.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
hard-problem.title: Violent Ends
hard-problem.relation: Richards asks what it is like to be a host, combining three lenses: Searle's biological naturalism (thinking machines must be built from materials with the right causal powers, and the hosts' synthetic flesh may qualify), Nagel's bat (even if hosts are conscious, their perfectly relived memories, curated pain, and blind spots like 'it doesn't look like anything to me' may make their experience as inconceivable to us as echolocation), and Chalmers's philosophical zombies (hosts behave exactly like us, yet beings identical to them with no inner light are conceivable). He reads Ford's contradictory testimony — praising Bernard's guilt as 'a thing of beauty' while denying consciousness exists — as a shift to a deflationary view with no threshold for being alive, and argues the show's choice to film human and host experience in the same style keeps the question deliberately open while fostering empathy.

hard-problem.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
hard-problem.title: 31. Does the Hulk Have a Soul
hard-problem.relation: Weighs whether the Hulk has a soul by running philosophy of mind's three positions: substance dualism (qualia and the hard problem, Plantinga's modal argument via Leibniz's Law — Peter Parker really is Spider-Man — but an unresolved mind–body interaction problem), physicalism (causal closure and conservation of energy, rebutted through objective truths and Einstein's dynamic spacetime), and idealism (Berkeley's master argument plus the holographic principle and quantum observation). It concludes idealism best explains Banner: Hulk and Banner share one mind/soul whose information is projected as two different 3D bodies, with the Ancient One's 'source code that shapes reality' speech in Doctor Strange as idealism's on-screen statement.

hard-problem.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
hard-problem.title: The Last Bit
hard-problem.relation: Cook asks whether Rapture's Plasmids and ghosts refute physicalism and answers no: Plasmid powers are genetically engineered via ADAM and thus describable in physical vocabulary, while contractor Bill McDonagh's audio diary explains the ghosts of Rapture as leaked memories passed through gene-swapping, so all their facts supervene on physical facts in Chalmers's sense. The classic anti-physicalist pressures, Chalmers's zombie argument and the Nagel-style gap between objective physical description and subjective qualia ('the smell of poo'), do not apply because Rapture's phenomena carry no extra subjective residue. Invoking Clarke's third law that advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, he concludes Andrew Ryan did not choose the impossible.

hard-problem.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
hard-problem.title: “Do you even know where you are ”
hard-problem.relation: Marcus Arvan argues from show evidence (William stepping onto a moving train, pyrotechnic effects, instant crowds, graphically rearranging the park) that all of Westworld, lab included, is a videogame, and defends his 'Peer-to-Peer Simulation Hypothesis' as an explanation of quantum mechanics and relativity, citing Bostrom and Chalmers. Adopting functionalism/structuralism, he claims that anything doing what a human does is a person, so hosts like Dolores and Maeve are no less real or human than us, inverting Descartes' cogito and invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature. He warns that dehumanizing hosts, or dismissing Siri and Watson as unconscious, repeats the logic used to justify slavery and the Holocaust: to be simulated is to be real.

hard-problem.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
hard-problem.title: Violent Ends
hard-problem.relation: Bradley Richards asks what it is like to be a host, using Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' to argue that whether we can conceive host experience depends on how similar it is to ours, and Searle's biological view to ask whether hosts are made of the right stuff. He catalogs how host perception, emotion, and especially memory differ from human (Maeve's perfect reliving of memories versus our hazy constructive recall, 'is this now?'), and weighs Chalmers's philosophical zombies against the hosts. He notes the show depicts host and human experience in the identical cinematic style to preserve ambiguity, and links memory, self-consciousness, and freedom via Dolores's maze, suggesting hosts may be phenomenally conscious before becoming self-aware.

hard-problem.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
hard-problem.title: Does the Piano Play Itself
hard-problem.relation: Michael Versteeg and Adam Barkman use the player piano to introduce Ford's eliminative materialism, aligning his 'consciousness does not exist' speech with Churchland and Dennett against the common-sense view of a self distinct from the body. They present Descartes' res cogitans/res extensa dualism and the pineal-gland 'magical transaction' as the target, then Churchland's claim that Folk-Psychology's beliefs and desires will be eliminated by neuroscience, and Dennett's Multiple Drafts model rejecting the Cartesian Theater and the manifest self. They note Ford's self-contradiction in speaking of a 'who' who makes choices while denying selves exist, concluding that if eliminativism holds, humans are complex machines like the piano and the hosts, everything being 'what it isn't.'

hard-problem.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
hard-problem.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
hard-problem.relation: Richard McClelland analyzes Eastwood's deployment of silence in Hereafter, cataloguing four types (from long soundless episodes during Marie's near-death experience to musical rests) and grounding them in neuroscience showing the auditory cortex represents silence as an object and spontaneously fills silence with self-generated signals. He argues Eastwood intuits how silence modulates attention and memory, limiting salient characters (Marie, George, the twins) so viewers attend to and remember key emotional beats. The chapter proposes 'neurocinematics' and a 'practical realism' whereby Eastwood's laconic, minimalist style and silences latch onto real, cross-cultural features of human cognition rather than merely subjective response.

hard-problem.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
hard-problem.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
hard-problem.relation: Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.

hard-problem.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
hard-problem.title: Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction
hard-problem.relation: Holt uses the Terminator's first-person infrared POV shots (evoking Nagel's 'what is it like' question about an alien artificial consciousness) to frame the paradox of fiction: how we feel fear toward things we know do not exist. He offers a contextual divide-and-conquer solution, arguing higher emotions like pity and admiration for Sarah and Reese are largely make-believe, while lower emotions like Terminator-fear are genuine and need no existential belief (thought and mere possibility suffice). He adds that such fear is more rational for a naturalist who admits artificial intelligence is possible than for a dualist, and speculates the Terminator functions as an archetype embodying tech-noir dread.

hard-problem.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
hard-problem.title: 18. Foundation and Consciousness
hard-problem.relation: Lang and Haun use Foundation to explore consciousness, noting Asimov's robots (Daneel, Andrew Martin) are simply granted minds and that a system giving all the right signs could still be a Chalmers-style philosophical zombie. Their central case is Golan Trevize merging with the starship Far Star, which they read through Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis and the Otto-and-Inga notebook example, arguing Trevize goes beyond Otto because he gains qualitatively new experiences (feeling magnetic fields, 360-degree sight). They then test extension against Integrated Information Theory and split-brain evidence, and read the planetary group mind Gaia as panpsychism (invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature, Leibniz's monads, and Fechner's world-mind) that faces the Combination Problem, partly eased by telepathic links that relax the privacy of minds.

hard-problem.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
hard-problem.title: The Role of Matter Biology or Function
hard-problem.relation: Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind. Neo's apparent mind-body separation fits Descartes's dualism, but Lawrence argues dualism fails on the interaction problem and lack of evidence, so the Matrix scenario supports materialism. He explains reductive (identity) and eliminative materialism (via Churchland and the Tastee Wheat question), then frames the biology-versus-function debate: Searle's emergent-property view (the beer-can thirst model) holds brain biochemistry is essential to consciousness, while functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain) holds any system with the right input-output relations has mental states, and Lawrence argues functionalism underlies the very idea of sentient machines like Agent Smith.

hard-problem.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
hard-problem.title: The Role of Matter Biology or Function
hard-problem.relation: Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind, arguing the 'brain-stimulation' premise favors materialism over Descartes's dualism (which alone easily explains Neo's mind-body separation at the Train Station but lacks empirical support and an interaction mechanism). He explains reductive versus eliminative materialism (Churchland's denial of folk-psychological 'beliefs' via Tastee Wheat) and then Searle's biological emergentism (the beer-can thirst machine) against functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain; Agent Smith's seamless transfer into Bane). He concludes the films are best read functionally, making sentient machines genuine minds.

hard-problem.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
hard-problem.title: 45. A.I. Artificial Intelligence as Philosophy Machine Consciousness and Intelligence
hard-problem.relation: Gamez uses Spielberg/Kubrick's A.I. to separate three things the film conflates: intelligence, consciousness, and emotion. He argues intelligence is a functional property (David could pass a Turing test but a skilled interrogator would spot him), whereas consciousness is a physical property that cannot be inferred from David's human-like behavior — only a mathematical theory mapping physical to conscious states could tell whether David really experiences the love, fear, and pain that drive our empathy in the Flesh Fair. He insists the ethics of destroying mechas should hinge on their consciousness, not their intelligence, and connects David's engineered, irreversible imprinting-love to Lorenz's ethology and Damasio/James theories of emotion, and his eerie early behavior to Mori's uncanny valley.

cartesian-dualism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
cartesian-dualism.title: Unknown
cartesian-dualism.relation: Holt runs a crash course in the mind-body problem: Descartes's thinking, unextended mind - the 'ghost in the machine' he also hears in the Police album - fails to explain how essentially different substances interact; behaviorism mistakes the evidence for mental states (dispositions to say 'Ouch!') for what the evidence is evidence of; so he defends materialism, the view that mental states are brain states, against the objections that it makes mind causally inert (epiphenomenal) and that pain is multiply realizable, teasing that the Matrix machines could in principle feel silicon pain.

cartesian-dualism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
cartesian-dualism.title: Unknown
cartesian-dualism.relation: The chapter contrasts the films' opening codes—digital green bits versus amorphous cellular pink—and invokes the feminist critique that western philosophy, from Plato's transcendent Forms through Augustine and Aquinas to Descartes's identity as mind not body, is a male quest for escape from the flesh that The Matrix repeats with its sleek leather-clad stars. It then reads both Keanu's Neo and Jude Law's Ted as 'pretty', graceful, penetrated male heroes paired with stronger women, setting up the analysis of scenes of male penetration.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: Unknown
cartesian-dualism.relation: Explains Descartes' narrowing of the soul to higher cognition: sensation can be accounted for materially, but language and complex belief require an immaterial soul, so nonhuman animals are soulless. It shows how magical creatures complicate this in Rowling's world, since owls seem to understand speech and Crookshanks seems abnormally intelligent, and notes that the first three views all treat the soul as an immaterial substance able to survive death, motivating the materialist alternative.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: Horcruxes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Uses Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, whose victims like Barty Crouch Jr. go on existing as empty shells without memory or self, to eliminate the leading views of the soul: the soul cannot be the source of life, of sentience, or even of Cartesian higher thought, since the soulless victim may still sense and think dimly. The chapter compares the Kiss's aftermath to severe dementia or to Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of whether the person rather than just the body survives.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: NOTES
cartesian-dualism.relation: Steps outside the fiction to ask whether Rowling's hybrid soul theory is actually plausible, answering probably not: neuroscience shows no brain events lacking physical cause, mind-body interaction remains the classic obstacle for any dualism, and it is doubly implausible that an immaterial substance would be responsible only for our deepest emotions and conscience. The differing physical powers of ghosts, Resurrection Stone shades, and Horcrux-souls make the metaphysics even harder, though the chapter concedes that a fictional soul picture that vividly dramatizes what we care about needs no truth to make a terrific story.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: Whose Reasons
cartesian-dualism.relation: Tests the Cartesian division of the transformed Padfoot into mind plus body across four possible combinations and rejects them all: Sirius's human body cannot plausibly slip 'into non-being' during transformation (against McGonagall's quip), yet a Sirius-mind cannot explain tail-chasing and a dog-mind cannot explain Padfoot standing on his hind legs to embrace Harry at King's Cross. Mind-body dualism thus fails as an account of what the transformed person is.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: A Unified Self
cartesian-dualism.relation: Proposes that some of Padfoot's behavior is explained by his dog's body rather than Sirius's mind, imagined through a counterfactual in which Sirius became a bear instead and would never have chased his tail. But the strategy generates absurd costs: if tail-chasing feels good, it is unclear whether the feeling belongs to Sirius's mind or to the dog's body, forcing the strange conclusion that a person's body might have reasons of its own that clash with the person's will.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: NOTES
cartesian-dualism.relation: Concludes that transformed persons are unified mind-body wholes rather than pilot-and-ship pairings, enlisting Descartes himself, who insisted he is 'not only lodged in my body, like a pilot in his ship' but compounded with it into a single whole. The evidence is textual: Polyjuiced Harry naturally 'thunders' with Runcorn's powerful frame while acting for Harry's reasons, Luna recognizes Harry through Barny Weasley's facial expression, and Crouch-as-Moody makes sense as an indivisible embodiment, so Padfoot is neither man nor dog but a third kind of being, a man-dog.

cartesian-dualism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
cartesian-dualism.title: The Hallows of the Mind
cartesian-dualism.relation: Sets Hobbes-style materialism (everything, ghosts included, must be matter; Rowling's thoughts that cling to wands like hairs and leak from dying wizards support it) against Cartesian dualism, on which the immaterial mind could exist without the body - the possibility Harry entertains in King's Cross before concluding he still has a body. It reads Rowling's 'light made liquid' description of the Pensieve's silver contents as an image of the pull between the two views of the mind.

cartesian-dualism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
cartesian-dualism.title: The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet
cartesian-dualism.relation: The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.

cartesian-dualism.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
cartesian-dualism.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.

cartesian-dualism.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
cartesian-dualism.title: Dead People
cartesian-dualism.relation: William Larkin uses Romero's films - Karen Cooper devouring her father in Night of the Living Dead, Roger begging Peter to shoot him in Dawn, Riley's 'Those people are all dead' in Land - to argue that persons are res corporealis, bodily continuers, rather than Descartes's res cogitans. Our terror of becoming a zombie ourselves and our grief at recognized neighbors in the horde reveal that deep down we think persons survive as corpses, so bodily continuity suffices for identity while psychological continuity is unnecessary. The Locke-style body-switching intuition (prince and cobbler) that supports the psychological approach is dismissed as theoretically biased data compared to what good zombie fiction draws out of us.

cartesian-dualism.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
cartesian-dualism.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep
cartesian-dualism.relation: Larry Hauser stages the philosophy-of-mind zombie debate through Blade Runner's Replicants: Descartes's animal automata and his hats-and-coats worry about other minds, Turing's universal machines grounding functionalism, Kripke's necessity of scientific identifications (water is necessarily H2O), and Searle's silicon-chip replacement scenario show how zombies 'eat' behaviorist, functionalist, and identity-theoretic accounts of mind. He then deploys his own 'good zombies' - the beloved who might be a zombie, super-smart NEXUS 9s, venerable zombie thinkers - to block the dualist retreat on the cognitive side of the mind. The essay closes by doubting, with Chalmers's phenomenal zombies in view, that such zombies are coherently conceivable after all, and asks whether Deckard has been 'retiring' persons like Rachel all along.

cartesian-dualism.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
cartesian-dualism.title: Good Guy Vampires
cartesian-dualism.relation: Robert Arp models the vampire's ontology with substance versus property dualism - Rice's vampires whose souls outlast the stake versus Blade's vampires who perish with their bodies - and uses Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures from Utilitarianism to explain how vampires can both feel nothing bodily and suffer mentally (the opening quotation's regret at missing the wind in one's hair). Their real plight is the hedonistic paradox: pleasure pursued for its own sake yields pain, mistaken pleasures (Lestat on the dead twins, Blade's rave), or the boredom of an immortality that has 'seen it all.' The good guy vampires from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain escape by pursuing higher pleasures and activities for their own sake, vindicating Mill's closing advice that only those whose minds are fixed on something other than their own happiness find it.

cartesian-dualism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
cartesian-dualism.title: The Role of Matter Biology or Function
cartesian-dualism.relation: Lawrence asks which theory of mind best fits the Matrix trilogy. Cartesian dualism (with its pineal-gland plug standing in for Neo's headjack) would explain Neo's jackless mind in the Train Station but lacks evidence and faces the interaction problem, so the chapter defends a fully materialist reading — Neo's sentinel-destroying signal and burnt-eye sight reconstrued as Matrix hardware in his skull. It then contrasts reductive and eliminative materialism, Searle's beer-can biological naturalism, and functionalism via Lewis's Martian pain, concluding that the films' sentient machines — Agent Smith's seamless copy into Bane's body — presuppose functionalism.

cartesian-dualism.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
cartesian-dualism.title: Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up
cartesian-dualism.relation: Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.

cartesian-dualism.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
cartesian-dualism.title: Thinking in Rainbows
cartesian-dualism.relation: Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.

cartesian-dualism.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
cartesian-dualism.title: Transformers and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Using the hidden sides of Transformers - a robot inside a Camaro, a tank inside a robot - the authors stage the philosophy of perception: Descartes's innate geometrical rules and Berkeley's bodily cross-referencing both fail to explain how Sam Witwicky can know the steelyard robot is his Camaro, while Merleau-Ponty's embodied account of focus, background, and 'indeterminate vision' explains it through the perceiver's lived body. They extend this to the 'Autobot Spike' mind-transfer episode and to CGI: virtual Transformers on screen feel hollow because light-created images have no hidden surfaces for our bodies to investigate and grasp.

cartesian-dualism.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
cartesian-dualism.title: Transformers and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Pike asks what the All Spark's zap would have to do to give brought-to-life vending machines and steering wheels genuine minds, testing logical behaviorism's dispositions and Turing's conversation test against Searle's Chinese Room ('syntax is insufficient for semantics'), and weighing Descartes's God-given soul against physicalist alternatives: functionalism, Searle's biological naturalism, and reductive physicalism. Since we can never access another mind from the inside, he concludes that by abductive inference to the best explanation - Optimus Prime's mourning, planning, and moral decision-making being too complex for mere programming - we have as much reason to credit a Transformer with a mind as any human around us.

cartesian-dualism.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
cartesian-dualism.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Harris and Baer use the Boatman scene ('Pan is me... we'd die') to test criteria of personal identity against the trilogy: Lyra and Will's inference to a thinking third part, the ghost, reenacts Descartes's dualist reasoning about mind-body distinctness, Iorek's lack of a ghost exemplifies the same-body criterion, and Pantalaimon's instant shape-shifting favors the psychological criterion, spelled out through Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory thought experiment and Parfit's psychological connectedness and continuity. They ask whether Lee Scoresby's dissolution into conscious atoms that reunite with Hester's counts as genuine survival, best accommodated by Locke's consciousness criterion or a panpsychist matter criterion, with Chalmers cited as the contemporary defender of conscious matter. The chapter closes with individuation, whether Lyra and Pan are one person or two, applied to a Primal Fear-style multiple-personality murder trial, the hypothetical of Pan killing someone while Lyra is innocent, and living wills in persistent vegetative states.

cartesian-dualism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
cartesian-dualism.title: The Transforming Body
cartesian-dualism.relation: McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.

cartesian-dualism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
cartesian-dualism.title: Is Everybody Disembodied (or, Have We Always Been Posthuman Beings )
cartesian-dualism.relation: Stevens uses the film's closing voice-over 'I am Tetsuo' in Otomo's Akira to run the classic identity-and-mind problems: Heraclitus's river and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus ask whether the grotesquely transformed, Akira-absorbed Tetsuo is still the same person, while Descartes's cogito — riffed as 'cogito ergo Tetsuo' — Turing's Test, and Searle's Chinese Room test whether a voice that seems to think proves a thinker behind it (syntax is not yet shown sufficient for semantics, though Edwin Hutchins's distributed cognition reads the Room from the inside out). Weighing embodiment (Pinker's brain-makes-mind, Dennett's self as a 'center of narrative gravity') against disembodiment (Akira levelling Neo-Tokyo from nothing but cryogenically stored remains; Tetsuo's matter teleportation), he concludes through the problem of representation — every utterance is re-presented, as in Augustine's guilty tears over Dido — that we always treat semblances of thinkers as thinkers, so we may have always been decentered, re-presented, posthuman beings no different from Tetsuo and Akira.

cartesian-dualism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
cartesian-dualism.title: Who Wants to Be Human Anyway
cartesian-dualism.relation: Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.

cartesian-dualism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
cartesian-dualism.title: Cyborg Goddess
cartesian-dualism.relation: Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.

cartesian-dualism.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
cartesian-dualism.title: Dead People
cartesian-dualism.relation: William Larkin pits Descartes's res cogitans (the person as psychological continuum, reinforced by Locke's prince-and-cobbler body-switch) against a res corporealis view in which bodily continuity suffices for identity, using Romero's Dead films as intuition pumps. The terror of Roger's 'I don't want to be walking around like that' and Rain's request in Resident Evil only makes sense if we think it would be us rising as zombies, and the tragedy of Karen Cooper devouring her father or Johnny menaging Barbara only lands if the same person persists. Against the 'just dead flesh' scientists and the mall-memory reading of Dawn, he argues zombie psychology is merely residual instinct, so our fear and pity reveal we really believe persons survive as corpses, hence as bodies, not as minds.

cartesian-dualism.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
cartesian-dualism.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep
cartesian-dualism.relation: Larry Hauser reads Blade Runner's replicants alongside the philosophical-zombie thought experiment: like Rachel, who passes as human until a Voigt-Kampff test, zombies are outwardly perfect replicas with 'nobody home' inside. He traces the problem from Descartes's beast-automata and hats-and-coats worry about other minds, through Turing's universal machines and Kripke's necessary identifications (water is H2O), to the way zombie scenarios devour behaviorism, functionalism, and mind-brain identity theory, using Searle's silicon-chip replacement to imagine consciousness shrinking while behavior continues. His own 'familiar' and 'super-smart' zombies (a beloved with no qualia, NEXUS-9 geniuses) argue thought without felt experience is conceivable, before he concludes the phenomenal-zombie conception may self-destruct because a first-person point of view requires the very qualia it strips away.

cartesian-dualism.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
cartesian-dualism.title: Good Guy Vampires
cartesian-dualism.relation: Robert Arp models the vampire's unlife with substance and property dualism (a cursed soul persisting after the staked body in Rice and Stoker versus perishing with it in Blade), then uses Mill's distinction between lower bodily feelings and higher mental pleasures from Utilitarianism to explain how vampires can lament, in higher-pain, their inability to enjoy wind in their hair or wine. The hedonistic paradox dooms Lestat-style pleasure-seekers: seeking pleasure for its own sake yields either the pain of frustration (Louis's dead-twins trick) or boredom across immortal lifetimes ('it's somewhat boring, living forever'), while Aristotle's completed-state pleasures suggest the way out. Good guy vampires from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain escape the paradox by pursuing higher pleasures and activities for their own sake, confirming Mill's closing counsel that only those fixed on objects other than their own pleasure find happiness.

cartesian-dualism.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
cartesian-dualism.title: The Moving Shadow of Truth
cartesian-dualism.relation: Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.

cartesian-dualism.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
cartesian-dualism.title: I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think
cartesian-dualism.relation: Johnson argues that the Platonic-Cartesian soul is refuted by neuroscience (Phineas Gage, Penfield's stimulation studies), and that Locke's memory criterion fails on Reid-style transitivity cases like DoctorDonna and on Bernard-Williams-inspired worry about the amnesiac John Smith, who would still dread the Family of Blood's torture. Parfit's causal-continuity criterion then wrongly makes the meta-crisis Doctor of 'Journey's End' identical with the Tenth, so Johnson defends a four-dimensionalist 'time worm' view on which the Doctors are stages of one person — before a final sorites-style argument (heaps, spin-offs like Torchwood) suggests that 'persons' may not exist at all.

cartesian-dualism.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
cartesian-dualism.title: A Single, Perfect Sphere
cartesian-dualism.relation: Reads Rush's 'Hemispheres' as a correction to Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: Apollo's gifts of reason leave the people joyless, Dionysus's release into passion leaves them starving in winter, and Cygnus is made god of Balance because human nature thinks and feels at once. Against Descartes's two substances and the 'Robots Plus' picture, the author argues feeling is not supernatural icing on a machine but how survival-minded organisms stay in phenomenal contact with the world, so physicalism needs deepening rather than a nonphysical mind.

cartesian-dualism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
cartesian-dualism.title: The User Illusion
cartesian-dualism.relation: The chapter interleaves a doctor's line-card quiz of Fred with Bogen and Wigan's claims that each cerebrum is 'a distinct and perfect whole as an organ of thought' and that our cherished 'inner conviction of Oneness' is mere opinion. Descartes supplies the target: a partless mind known directly and with certainty, external things known only indirectly through possibly misleading ideas, and Dick, we are told, flips this picture so the inside is messy and the outside clear.

cartesian-dualism.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
cartesian-dualism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Editor Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that zombies are worth doing philosophy over: an apocalyptic world without government, law enforcement, or private property raises live questions about how survivors should treat one another, whether life becomes 'nasty, brutish, and short', and whether it is wrong to kill a walker. He frames walkers philosophically through Descartes's mindless human-looking automatons and David Chalmers's P-zombies, creatures functionally like us with no inner life. Morgan keeping photo albums instead of supplies in 'Days Gone Bye' shows that what we leave behind after the apocalypse is how we lived - our philosophy.

cartesian-dualism.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
cartesian-dualism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.

cartesian-dualism.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
cartesian-dualism.title: Futurama and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Williams uses Hermes's slide from chest-harpoon to extendo-arm to Cylon eye to full robot body in 'The Six Million Dollar Mon' - until Zoidberg's 'Monster Mash' surgery restores his brain to Li'l Hermes - to ask what makes a person themselves under voluntary enhancement. The 'Ship of Planet Express' and the seven-year cell-replacement fact recast the Ship of Theseus, exposing our terror of upgrades as inconsistent with our constant physical change, while the therapeutic-versus-enhancement line (medical steroids vs doping, Aimee Mullins's blades) explains why Hermes's chosen upgrades disturb us. Cartesian interactionist dualism predicts Mecha-Hermes stays the same person, yet his personality shifts with his parts, so the chapter turns to physicalism and lands on functionalism: Hermes persists through each swap until the Roberto brain-chip replaces the brain that houses his memories and motivations.

cartesian-dualism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
cartesian-dualism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Spyros Petrounakos reads Frankenstein as a Cartesian narrative whose external events run parallel to the inner worlds of Victor and the creature, from Victor's solitary conception of 'bestowing animation upon lifeless matter' to his imprisonment in a truth nobody would believe when Justine's life is at stake. The monster's acquisition of language at the De Lacey cottage - grasping 'fire, milk, and bread' but not 'good,' 'dearest,' and 'unhappy' - becomes the test case between Descartes's private inner theater (with its evil demon) and Gilbert Ryle's reply, glossing Locke on ideas of reflection, that we learn emotion words by responding directly to behavior rather than by cracking a hidden code. On Ryle's reading the monster's deformity is horror precisely because it is put to Cartesian use, a body that seems to shield its inner life, so the creature only truly comes alive when it behaves like a human being.

cartesian-dualism.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
cartesian-dualism.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.

cartesian-dualism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
cartesian-dualism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: The Bocks use the courtroom frame of The Exorcism of Emily Rose to ask whether anyone could be justified in believing in demon possession, since the same seizures, polyglot voices, and levitations read differently under naturalism and supernaturalism. Kuhn's paradigms explain why neither worldview abandons ship at anomalies, and they weigh Wiebe's 'finite spirits as theoretical entities,' Hume's miracles argument (with Levine's Red Sea thought experiment as rebuttal), and the Cartesian ghost-in-the-machine premise that possession would require. Testing even a Men in Black alien hypothesis against the religiously specific phenomena, they conclude that a witnessed case like Emily's could rationally justify belief in possession.

cartesian-dualism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
cartesian-dualism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether the Devil could actually get you by testing theories of the afterlife against Hamlet's ghost, Freddy Krueger, the possessions of The Exorcist and Evil Dead, Paranormal Activity, Dante's Inferno, Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, and Doom. Substance dualism cannot explain how a non-physical soul moves so much as a finger; the view that you are your body founders on recycled grave matter and the primacy of the brain; and if you are a program running on your brain, the Devil could torture infinite copies of you in Hell - even re-running you there from Heaven - unless duplication means neither copy is really you.

cartesian-dualism.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
cartesian-dualism.title: Dracula and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Arp starts from Dracula's inability to love or find satisfaction and his awareness of it, then deploys Sidgwick's hedonistic paradox: pursuing pleasure for its own sake yields pain whether or not the pleasure is found, through mistaking pain for pleasure (Lestat on the dead twins), boredom, or emptiness. Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures explains how vampires can enjoy the bodily pleasure of blood yet lament lacking joy and love, while substance versus property dualism (Plato as the substance dualist) frames whether the Count's soul survives when his body crumbles to dust. Aristotle's Book X pleasures of completed states and the 'virtuous vampires' from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain show the only escape from the dilemma: pursue activities for their own sake and higher mental pleasures rather than bodily pleasure alone.

cartesian-dualism.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
cartesian-dualism.title: Dracula and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: McKinney argues Van Helsing should have studied Dracula's brain instead of staking him, because the Count is a philosophy-of-mind thought experiment: a mind that persists unchanged across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes mind-brain identity theory and fits functionalism (the mind as one song playable in many formats), while his telepathic bond with Mina and shapeshifting probe Cartesian dualism's mind-body interaction problem. Nagel's bats show that only Dracula could tell us what it is like to echo-locate or wolf-sense; yet since nothing like his unconstrained mind exists in our world, the novel finally maps what minds are not - evidence against the immaterial mind.

cartesian-dualism.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
cartesian-dualism.title: 11. What the Soufflé Girl Could Teach Descartes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Becker-Lindenthal uses 'Amy's Choice' to revise Descartes's dream skepticism: the Dream Lord is not an external evil demon but the Doctor's own repressed alter ego fed by psychic pollen, so the self-delusion Descartes dismissed becomes the real deceiver, read through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams (Rory's death as the Doctor's wish, Amy's choice as Thanatos). She then reads Oswin in 'Asylum of the Daleks' as a brain-in-a-vat variant (Putnam's Reason, Truth and History) with a crucial difference—Oswin hacks the Dalek program and follows her own agenda—so her self-deceptive soufflé-baking fantasy is a self-formation that preserves her 'I' inside Dalek hardware, complicating Ryle's rejection of the ghost in the machine. Finally, the Doctor judges Oswin by a Turing test plus Putnam's test of reference (the impossible milk and eggs), but her self-deception is vindicated when it lets her save the Doctor and the universe.

cartesian-dualism.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
cartesian-dualism.title: 20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork
cartesian-dualism.relation: A comic sprint through Western thought anchored in the Science of Discworld books, the chapter runs from Aristotle—whose geocentric four-element physics, it notes, fits Discworld better than Roundworld, and whose condemnations of usury it digresses over—through Descartes's cogito and mind-body dualism, Ryle's 'ghost in the machine,' behaviorism, identity theory, eliminative materialism, and functionalism's brain-as-computer picture, to show how philosophy of mind advances by each theory picking on its predecessor. Newton's occult-seeming gravity, later overturned by Einstein, illustrates the chapter's real thesis drawn from Pratchett's 'Lies-to-Wizards': neither science nor philosophy erects a timeless edifice of facts, since 'every so often, you have to unlearn what you thought you already knew,' while Diogenes and the Cynics supply the model of philosophy done in the common tongue that Pratchett shares.

cartesian-dualism.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
cartesian-dualism.title: 7. Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of a Warm Blanket
cartesian-dualism.relation: The chapter explains Linus's blanket via Winnicott's transitional objects, then argues the gang's wider habits - Great Pumpkin taboos, baseball fetishes and rituals - are 'magical thinking' that manufactures an illusion of control over an uncertain world. A middle section tours the mind-body problem (Hippocrates, Descartes's dualism and pineal gland, Huxley's epiphenomenalism, Searle's emergent consciousness) to ask who is really doing the reading. The fallacies section dissects Linus's unfalsifiable Pumpkin doctrine (post hoc after the taboo-breaking 'if') and Charlie's confirmation bias, before reframing his 'pantophobia' as Kierkegaardian angst and Sartrean nausea: with adults reduced to 'Mwaa mwaa mwaa,' the kids are condemned to be free.

cartesian-dualism.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
cartesian-dualism.title: 10. Does Snoopy Dream of Electric Sheep
cartesian-dualism.relation: Reading Snoopy through animal studies, the chapter sets Descartes's 'nature's machines' doctrine - animals as mindless, soulless property without rights - against Charlie Brown's attempts to keep his dog in his place, and shows how Snoopy's endless slippage between plain dog (stealing hats, begging at dinner, dragging Linus by the blanket) and near-human (reading publisher letters, typing novels, serving as Charlie's attorney) collapses the human/animal boundary. The kids' anxiety about his agency, and Snoopy's own gloomy 'I'm less than human,' show the hierarchy being internalized - yet a dog thinking about his inferiority already blurs it. When Snoopy hands Charlie his collar, the chapter reads it as a refusal of property status and proof that being human is a performance of gestures rather than an essence.

cartesian-dualism.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
cartesian-dualism.title: 3. Saving Hitler’s Life
cartesian-dualism.relation: The chapter claims the show takes dualism — the same physical world with different 'histories' as its mind — and multiplies it into many overlapping versions of each person: Juliana and Frank swap awe and fear between the first and ninth episodes' screenings, and the newsreel in which Joe executes Frank shifts how they see the real Joe. Its centerpiece is the finale, where viewers find themselves rooting for the Nazis Smith and Wegener to keep Hitler alive and prevent a worse war, forcing the audience to confront its own shifting allegiances and how easily fascism could take root in America.

cartesian-dualism.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
cartesian-dualism.title: 1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession
cartesian-dualism.relation: Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.

cartesian-dualism.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
cartesian-dualism.title: 19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie
cartesian-dualism.relation: Presents Twin Peaks as pataphysics — Alfred Jarry's "science of imaginary solutions" that studies exceptions rather than rules, superimposed on metaphysics as metaphysics is on physics. Its metaphysical scaffolding combines Descartes' two-realm dualism (Leland possessed by BOB; Cooper split across our world, the Lodge, and Dougie's life) with Gustav Fechner's dual-aspect, animistic universe — the "day view" and "night view," souls of plants seen in his garden — embodied in the Log Lady and her clairvoyant log. Cooper's Tibetan rock-throwing, tree-sniffing, blinking-light clues, and dream-code are pataphysical solutions: knowledge from absurd connections with worlds superimposed on ours, making the show, in the authors' formula, "metaphysics with humor."

cartesian-dualism.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!
cartesian-dualism.title: 4. To Be or Not to Be Perfect
cartesian-dualism.relation: Asks whether chasing externally imposed perfection is worthwhile and reads Schumer's comedy as an invitation to drop society's 'suggested' standards, from the impossible pre-sex grooming ritual of 'Sex Prep' to the pole-dancing hypocrisy of 'Judging Strippers'. Flieswasser tests three models of human perfection: the Platonic and Cartesian privileging of mind over body, monotheistic modesty, and Aristotle's telos as an individual purpose. She then lands on the Japanese aesthetics of wabi-sabi and kintsugi, where broken pieces are rejoined into something more beautiful, as the truest picture of Schumer's self-acceptance.

cartesian-dualism.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
cartesian-dualism.title: 2. Where Is the Twilight Zone
cartesian-dualism.relation: Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of Breton's surrealism, starting from Descartes: the cogito and the mind–body problem made reason the measure of the 'clear and distinct,' and surrealism seeks to unbind the imagination from exactly that rational leash. He reads 'A World of His Own' as surrealist automatic writing, 'The Mirror' as Dalí's paranoiac-critical method, and Freud's psychoanalysis as both allied with and (following Adorno's diagnosis of the movement's death) too restrictive for surrealism's project. Episodes like 'Shadow Play' (a man who dreams the world), 'The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' and 'A Stop at Willoughby' provoke the uncanny — the strangely familiar — in viewers, which is where the Zone is located.

cartesian-dualism.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
cartesian-dualism.title: Does the Piano Play Itself
cartesian-dualism.relation: Versteeg and Barkman use the player piano — keys that depress themselves with no ghost at the keyboard — to frame Robert Ford's 'we can't define consciousness because consciousness does not exist' as eliminative materialism, the view shared by Paul Churchland and Daniel Dennett that the common-sense self with its beliefs, desires, and central first-person perspective is a fiction. They set this against Descartes's dualism of res cogitans and res extensa, noting the failed pineal-gland 'magical transaction' and Dennett's replacement of the Cartesian Theater with multiple drafts of consciousness and the manifest-versus-scientific image. The chapter closes on Ford's inconsistency — denying consciousness yet sacrificing his life so the hosts can become self-aware — and asks whether, if the piano plays itself, humans are just complex machines too.

cartesian-dualism.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
cartesian-dualism.title: 2. Is Joi a Person
cartesian-dualism.relation: Chris Lay argues Joi is a person. He raises Searle's objection that programs only simulate understanding and need the right biological 'stuff', then answers it: Joi apparently violates her 'everything you want her to be' programming, so her affection for K is authentic either way. Testing Joi against Locke's personhood criteria — rationality, sentience, and self-consciousness grounded in memory and in her self-sacrifice before Luv — he adds a Cartesian reading in which her transfers between console and emanator make her a disembodied soul, closer to Descartes's essence of the human than embodied replicants are. If a digital person like Joi would also fail the baseline, the wall separating kind would need a full societal reset.

cartesian-dualism.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
cartesian-dualism.title: 31. Does the Hulk Have a Soul
cartesian-dualism.relation: Weighs whether the Hulk has a soul by running philosophy of mind's three positions: substance dualism (qualia and the hard problem, Plantinga's modal argument via Leibniz's Law — Peter Parker really is Spider-Man — but an unresolved mind–body interaction problem), physicalism (causal closure and conservation of energy, rebutted through objective truths and Einstein's dynamic spacetime), and idealism (Berkeley's master argument plus the holographic principle and quantum observation). It concludes idealism best explains Banner: Hulk and Banner share one mind/soul whose information is projected as two different 3D bodies, with the Ancient One's 'source code that shapes reality' speech in Doctor Strange as idealism's on-screen statement.

cartesian-dualism.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
cartesian-dualism.title: “There is nothing in the desert, and no man needs nothing”
cartesian-dualism.relation: Argues David in Prometheus qualifies as a Lockean person - intelligence, rule-following rationality, self-reflection via an active power of thought (his self-modeling on Lawrence of Arabia, his judged desire to be free of Weyland's programming), and mental pleasure and pain - while Ash fails the test, reacting only passively to company orders like Locke's unfree tennis ball. Against Weyland's and Shaw's Cartesian soul-based denial ('you're a robot'), this leaves open that beings humans create could share our moral status, making David's ostracism arbitrary and cruel.

cartesian-dualism.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
cartesian-dualism.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Sorts the Oscar/George Sr. twin confusion into the metaphysical, persistence, and evidential problems of personal identity, testing Aristotle's essential properties (why two actresses play one Marta, what makes each Richter brother distinct) and Descartes's immaterial soul (undermined by surrogate Larry, who stays Larry while Buster remotely operates him). Locke's memory criterion then explains why Oscar is not guilty of George's crimes and why Gob disowns what his forget-me-nows erased, before Thomas Reid's transitivity objection, staged through a lifetime of Gob's roofies, shows Locke committed to old Gob both being and not being young Gob.

cartesian-dualism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
cartesian-dualism.title: Reflections on Technophobia
cartesian-dualism.relation: The chapter asks whether the technophobia of 'Metalhead' - robo-dogs hunting Bella and her friends across a wasteland - is justified, testing Daniel Dinello's list of fears (identity, values, emotion, freedom, life). Descartes's and Aquinas's human-uniqueness over the mechanical fails because the robo-dogs, like DeepMind, learn and problem-solve, while the episode's Rousseau-style romanticism (only the non-technological cliff, tree, sunlight and stream aid Bella) and the teddy-bear mission show technology amplifying compassion rather than threatening it. The real dangers are robots as Latourian 'black boxes': Asimov's Three Laws cannot be operationalized, and if we cannot know how robo-dogs decide, our frameworks for blame and punishment break down (who answers for a killing - robot, programmer, or, on Marx's analysis of capitalist technology as an instrument of oppression, the economic system behind it?). The chapter concludes that since we already share the world with robots, learning to live responsibly alongside them must replace simple fear.

cartesian-dualism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
cartesian-dualism.title: Ethical Issues
cartesian-dualism.relation: Focusing on White Christmas's cookies and Ashley Too's synaptic snapshot, the chapter argues behavior can never settle whether an artificial system is conscious: the Turing test fails against Geminoid-robot-style cases where recorded signals produce human-like behavior, and philosophical-zombie possibilities plus the point that computations and information patterns are subjective interpretations (not objective physical properties) mean only discovering the physical neural correlates of consciousness could tell us whether a cookie feels pain. It then separates copying from transferring: with souls and substance dualism rejected, Black Museum's 'transfers' are really copies, and San Junipero's upload would house a copy whose future experiences are as alien to Yorkie as a plaster cast of her feet. Ethically, if cookies are conscious, then Matt's breaking of Cookie-Greta, Daly's captives, and Clayton's keychain are torture of persons, and it is the very uncertainty about cookie consciousness that lets characters rationalize the abuse - which is why the in-world legislation granting cookies human rights matters.

cartesian-dualism.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
cartesian-dualism.title: 13 The Ancestral Plane Metaphysical Mystery or Meaningful Metaphor
cartesian-dualism.relation: Kowalski treats the Heart-Shaped Herb's Ancestral Plane visits as a test case for Cartesian substance dualism: if T'Challa truly embraces T'Chaka's soul, the film commits to bodies and souls as distinct substances, with the film's own analogy — Shuri remotely driving T'Challa's car from her lab — standing in for soul-body interactionism. But Princess Elisabeth's interaction problem (how a non-physical soul could be embraced, seen, or chemically affected) makes dualism implausible, so he argues the second and third visits work better as metaphor: Killmonger's audience with N'Jobu and T'Challa's 'You were wrong! All of you!' confrontation with his ancestors dramatize taking stock of how one's father shaped who one is, with T'Challa's sunlit third visit symbolizing his choice not to be bound by that past.

cartesian-dualism.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
cartesian-dualism.title: 14 The Afterlife of Erik Killmonger in African Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Paul Dottin argues that Black Panther lore inherited the racist 'Hamitic Hypothesis' (crediting Egypt rather than sub-Saharan Africa for Wakanda's civilization) and that Ta-Nehisi Coates and Ryan Coogler begin a Wiredu-style conceptual decolonization of it. Taking Killmonger's dying wish to be buried with the ancestors who jumped from slave ships literally, the chapter asks which African metaphysics could make his postmortem survival of substance, subjectivity, and setting rationally intelligible. It rejects Cartesian substance dualism (illustrated by T'Challa defeating the demon Mephisto only after trapping his spirit in a body) in favor of Wiredu's Akan quasi-physicalism and Adeofe's Yoruba theory of destiny (ipin) and inner head (ori-inu), then ranks Killmonger's afterlife options from limbo through the Ancestral Plane to deification as the ocean deity Olokun.

cartesian-dualism.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
cartesian-dualism.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Ken Pepper uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to explain how Tony Iommi's homemade plastic fingertips work: like the blind man's cane, they are incorporated into his body schema so that he perceives the fretboard through them, refuting the Cartesian "objective body" picture on which playing would be inner plans causing finger movements.
