On creative freedom, the chapter stages Merleau-Ponty against Sartre's radical freedom, Iommi did choose to relearn guitar after hearing two-fingered Django Reinhardt, and his restricted two-finger chords, lighter strings, and drop tunings birthed heavy metal, but Sartre is wrong that attitude alone transcends disability, since some possibilities (playing at all without the tips) were simply not live. Only Iommi, taking up the possibilities his body-in-his-situation afforded, could have invented metal.

cartesian-dualism.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
cartesian-dualism.title: Inside the Lived Body
cartesian-dualism.relation: Pits Merleau-Ponty's embodied self against Descartes' representationalism and mind-over-matter dualism to read Inside Out: Riley's five personified emotions look like homunculi inviting an infinite regress, but the film actually shows a holistic body-subject whose emotions arise in situations and with others. Joy's campaign to keep Riley 'okay' dramatizes the futility of constant happiness and the necessity of Sadness, while Riley's hockey stick becoming an extension of her body illustrates Merleau-Ponty's claim that skillful coping lives in the body rather than in Sadness's 'mind manuals.' The chapter ends on childhood's lived present and the film's power to hold loss before us instead of pushing past it.

cartesian-dualism.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
cartesian-dualism.title: Out of the Orb
cartesian-dualism.relation: Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.

cartesian-dualism.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
cartesian-dualism.title: “Strange Magic,” Electric Light Orchestra, 1975
cartesian-dualism.relation: Kowalski reads the film's astral-form scenes as a dramatization of Cartesian substance dualism against Strange's opening physicalism ('There is no such thing as spirit! We are made of matter and nothing more'): the Ancient One pushing his astral body out refutes physicalism, his soul reads books while his body sleeps, and he fights Kaecilius's acolyte as a visible astral form in Christine Palmer's ER. The chapter then confronts the classic interaction problem — Descartes' pineal gland and 'animal spirits,' Elisabeth of Bohemia's and Garrett Thomson's objections — asking how an immaterial astral form can turn pages or knock over vending machines, joking that it would take 'a very strange form of interactionism.' The Ancient One's account of magic as energy drawn from other dimensions of the multiverse is offered as the film's own dualist reply, with a closing plea for the epistemic humility Strange had to learn.

cartesian-dualism.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
cartesian-dualism.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: Unknown
cartesian-dualism.relation: This section of the soul chapter lays out the Cartesian view: the immaterial soul explains only language and higher-level cognition, while material causes suffice for sensation, which consigns nonhuman animals to soullessness. It applies the view to Rowling's borderline creatures, such as owls that understand human speech and Crookshanks's suspicious intelligence, before introducing materialism as the fourth conception of the soul.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: Horcruxes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: A Plausible View
cartesian-dualism.relation: Reconstructing Slughorn's lesson to young Riddle, the section argues that because Voldemort's brain, senses, and magical powers survive his soul being ripped into seven, the Cartesian and sentience views are excluded and Rowling must hold the sentimental view: the soul is our capacity to love and our moral conscience. Voldemort's snake-faced transformation and his followers' fear-based loyalty, where even Bellatrix worships his power rather than being charmed, dramatize his lost humanity, and only remorse, which Harry begs him to 'try for' before the rebounding curse kills him, could have repaired the damage.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: NOTES
cartesian-dualism.relation: The concluding section of the soul essay asks whether Rowling's combined theory is likely true and answers probably not: there is no evidence of immaterial causes of brain events, the centuries-old mind-body interaction problem looms, and it is especially implausible that a separate substance handles only our deepest emotions and moral traits, with the added wrinkle that souls in the story display different physical powers depending on which spell conjures them. Yet it concedes that implausible metaphysics is no flaw in fiction that makes vivid what we care about and 'makes for a terrific story.'

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: Whose Reasons
cartesian-dualism.relation: The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: A Unified Self
cartesian-dualism.relation: The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: NOTES
cartesian-dualism.relation: The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.

cartesian-dualism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
cartesian-dualism.title: The Hallows of the Mind
cartesian-dualism.relation: Uses Rowling's light-made-liquid description of the Pensieve's silvery contents to stage the materialism versus dualism debate: Hobbes-style materialists can treat ghosts like Nearly Headless Nick and the strands of thought clinging to wands or leaking from dying wizards as matter, while Cartesian dualists find support in Harry's fear at King's Cross that he might exist only as disembodied thought. Snape's remark that the mind is a complex and many-layered thing frames how little is settled about the mind-brain relation.

cartesian-dualism.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
cartesian-dualism.title: Putting One’s Mind into a Body
cartesian-dualism.relation: Seng reads the 2008 film's crash-and-stabilizer flying lessons as philosophy of mind: at first the armor seems to confirm Descartes' dualism, with Stark the thinking substance piloting a mechanical body and Jarvis playing the pineal gland. But Stark smashing into the ceiling while learning to fly shows the embodied mind of Dewey and Merleau-Ponty — habits, spatial existence, and the imported home preferences that make the suit feel like his own skin, so that the repulsors whir closed when he stands down before the village gunmen. Dewey's view of intelligence as acting on estimates of a situation then explains Stark's growth from selfish playboy to sharable goods (beating the merely self-interested Stane), and Jarvis counts as Stark's mind made manifest in the suit.

cartesian-dualism.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
cartesian-dualism.title: Trapped in Myself: "One" and the Mind-Body Problem
cartesian-dualism.relation: Joanna Corwin reads 'One' - Joe Bonham, a mind fully conscious in a destroyed body, 'Trapped in myself / Body my holding cell' - as the mind-body problem. She walks through Descartes: methodological doubt and the dream argument mirrored in Joe's 'Can't tell if this is true or dream', the cogito as Joe's 'thinking thinking thinking', substance dualism, and the evil-deceiver worry. But Metallica's song also answers Descartes: a disembodied thinking-substance lives a 'life in hell', and Joe's tapping of S-O-S in Morse code shows a mind needs a body to communicate and complete itself.

cartesian-dualism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
cartesian-dualism.title: Notes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Dan Dinello reads the Borg as the nightmare double of Data: where Data embodies Asimov's Laws of Robotics and Federation humanism, the Borg realize Jacques Ellul's and Langdon Winner's thesis that technology is an autonomous, totalitarian force assimilating its makers rather than a neutral tool. He traces the Collective's shared mind and quest for 'perfection' to transhumanism (Max More, James Hughes), whose philosophical roots lie in Descartes's mechanical body and mind-as-information—the very premise of Ira Graves's consciousness upload in 'The Schizoid Man'. Picard's tear as Locutus and Hugh's acquired individuality in 'I, Borg' show that creativity and liberal humanist values, not technology, defeat the ultimate techno-totalitarian dystopia.

cartesian-dualism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
cartesian-dualism.title: Notes
cartesian-dualism.relation: William Jaworski argues, opening with Breaking Bad's Skinny Pete and Badger, that you should never enter a transporter: after showing the MEM converter violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, he asks whether the reassembled pattern is you or a replica. He tests three escape routes—Vulcan katra substance dualism (The Wrath of Khan, The Search for Spock) in the tradition of Plato and Descartes; constitutionalism, on which you survive total replacement by robotic parts as Picard nearly does under Borg assimilation; and Parfit's survival-without-identity answer to Riker's fission in 'Second Chances'. Each fails or costs too much: dualism wrecks moral intuitions about killing, constitutionalism faces the two-Riker indeterminacy, and mere 'survival' cannot sustain the particularity of love.

cartesian-dualism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
cartesian-dualism.title: Notes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.

cartesian-dualism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
cartesian-dualism.title: Notes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Argues through Alfred North Whitehead's philosophy of organism - reality as momentary actual occasions with mental and physical poles, nested societies, and canalization - that Star Trek's advanced beings are not, and could not be, purely incorporeal. Mindless feeders like the dikironium cloud creature and the Drella show bodilessness is not sufficient for advancement, while parasitic Zetars and Ronin show it can be a liability; the Douwd, the Companion, and Amanda Rogers's Q parents voluntarily tether to bodies for love and new experience. The Q's stagnation and civil war ("Death Wish", "The Q and the Grey") illustrate Whitehead's balance of survival against creative advance: what looks like "freedom from physical form" is really "freedom of physical form", since a purely mental entity would be an unsustainable organism.

cartesian-dualism.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
cartesian-dualism.title: Notes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Uses a vintage Blue Snaggletooth action figure to illustrate Dennett's three stances - physical (AFA wear-grading of dented boots), design (why the Sears-exclusive mispack is valuable), and intentional (predicting whether Han would shoot first at a pedant correcting his parsec gaffe) - arguing that play trains a third-person science of mind that Descartes' first-person introspection and dualism could never verify. Dennett's account of religion as a misapplied intentional stance then explains begging the Falcon to 'hold together' and Zeus's lightning as projected intention, with the twist that children playing with figures know they are pretending while the superstitious mind does not.

cartesian-dualism.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
cartesian-dualism.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.

cartesian-dualism.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
cartesian-dualism.title: NOTES
cartesian-dualism.relation: Dunn reads Descartes' bete-machine doctrine (animals as soulless automata explicable by 'billiard ball' mechanics) against the Terminator universe, since Descartes' two tests for true men - genuine language and versatile reason - are in fact passed by the machines: the T-101 deploys 'Hasta la vista, baby' hours after learning not to sound like a dork and marshals skills far beyond a clock. Sarah Connor instead locates the soul in the heart, and via Spinoza's conatus - the instinctual valuation of one's own existence that Terminators lack ('no emotion about it one way or another') - she judges even linguistically brilliant machines soulless and irrational, as Mary Midgley says of computers that do not know what matters. Kyle's line about 'dreaming about dogs' closes the chapter: by the Sarah Connor criterion dogs are ensouled sentinels, the very thing Descartes denied.

cartesian-dualism.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
cartesian-dualism.title: NOTES
cartesian-dualism.relation: Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.

cartesian-dualism.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
cartesian-dualism.title: 2. Where Is the Twilight Zone
cartesian-dualism.relation: Scalambrino reads the Zone as a televised expression of surrealist philosophy: Breton's sought 'point of the mind' where life and death, real and imagined cease to be contradictions, realized in episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing) and 'The Mirror' (Dali's paranoiac-critical method). Descartes's cogito and the mind-body dualism supply the rational 'leash' that surrealism unbinds, questioned by 'Shadow Play,' where a man insists the world is his dream. Following Adorno's verdict that psychoanalytic interpretation killed official surrealism, he argues the show endures by provoking the uncanny ('The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' 'A Stop at Willoughby') without being pinned to Freudian readings.

cartesian-dualism.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
cartesian-dualism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.

cartesian-dualism.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
cartesian-dualism.title: Does the Piano Play Itself
cartesian-dualism.relation: Michael Versteeg and Adam Barkman use the player piano to introduce Ford's eliminative materialism, aligning his 'consciousness does not exist' speech with Churchland and Dennett against the common-sense view of a self distinct from the body. They present Descartes' res cogitans/res extensa dualism and the pineal-gland 'magical transaction' as the target, then Churchland's claim that Folk-Psychology's beliefs and desires will be eliminated by neuroscience, and Dennett's Multiple Drafts model rejecting the Cartesian Theater and the manifest self. They note Ford's self-contradiction in speaking of a 'who' who makes choices while denying selves exist, concluding that if eliminativism holds, humans are complex machines like the piano and the hosts, everything being 'what it isn't.'

cartesian-dualism.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
cartesian-dualism.title: Notes
cartesian-dualism.relation: Swanstrom and Fletcher analyze the saidin/saidar gender distinction through Aristotelian gender essentialism (men hot/active dominating saidin, women cool/passive surrendering to saidar) and hylomorphism. Using Balthamel's soul placed in a woman's body (Halima/Aran'gar) who still channels saidin, plus Avicenna's floating man and Descartes' dualism elevating soul to essence, they argue the soul, not the body, determines which half of the Power one touches, while Aquinas's soul-body union (needed by Birgitte and shown by the soulless Gray Men) preserves 'balance.' They then use hylomorphism to let showrunner Rafe Judkins strip gender essentialism yet keep saidin/saidar via 'Jain Doe': an ungendered soul leaning one way, correlated to sex only by biological population balance.

cartesian-dualism.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
cartesian-dualism.title: XVII - HIGH-TECH MYTHOLOGY IN X-MEN
cartesian-dualism.relation: Teschner reads X-Men as high-tech mythology: the superhero images are Freud's dream work, disguising unconscious wishes about technological power that the conscious ego cannot face, with Wolverine's adamantium and constant pain symbolizing human alienation under the machine. The psionic mind, telepathy and telekinesis that move matter directly, breaks the Cartesian dualism of mind and body, marking the upper limit of technological control. On the latent level, Xavier's psionic blocks and School represent repression of the unconscious while Magneto's plastic prison, mutant machine, and Liberty Island plan represent acceptance of a humanity redefined by its union with the machine.

cartesian-dualism.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
cartesian-dualism.title: Joanne Kyger “Descartes and the Splendor Of” Bridging Dualisms through Collaboration and Experimentation
cartesian-dualism.relation: Falk analyzes Joanne Kyger's 1968 experimental video 'Descartes' and its script 'Descartes and the Splendor Of,' a condensed rewrite of the 'Discourse on Method' that subverts Descartes's mind-body dualism and privileging of reason. Kyger deflates the cogito with slang ('to doubt is a drag'), substitutes Buddhist, Taoist (Zhuangzi's butterfly dream), and Confucian terms, and—voicing and performing Descartes as a woman doing housework and as 'Mother God'—feminizes the most masculine of professions. Reading this through Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' and gender performativity, Falk shows the parody destabilizes the mind/body, male/female hierarchy Cartesian dualism underwrites.

cartesian-dualism.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
cartesian-dualism.title: Introduction
cartesian-dualism.relation: LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.

cartesian-dualism.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
cartesian-dualism.title: On Being John Malkovich and Not Being Yourself
cartesian-dualism.relation: Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.

cartesian-dualism.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
cartesian-dualism.title: Heidegger and the Problem of Interpretation in Barton Fink
cartesian-dualism.relation: Conard uses Barton Fink as a springboard into Heidegger's theory of interpretation, contrasting it with Cartesian dualism. Barton, the 'life of the mind' artist whose skull-like hotel room symbolizes his isolation, is a Cartesian subject cut off from the practical, meaning-giving contexts (Heidegger's workshop, the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand typewriter) in which equipment is understood and interpreted. Conard argues the film's uninterpretable elements—the box, the wall photo, the mosquitoes—resist meaning precisely because Barton is severed from the web of relations that would let anything show up as meaningful, illustrating Dasein's temporal, potentiality-driven being.

cartesian-dualism.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
cartesian-dualism.title: Introduction
cartesian-dualism.relation: Simon Riches's introduction frames the whole volume around Cronenberg's obsession with the Cartesian mind-body split, quoting the director that horror comes from being unable to reconcile a sharp mind with a dying body. It surveys the three parts of the book, showing how films like The Fly stage bodily transformation and personal identity, eXistenZ stages skepticism about the external world, and A History of Violence stages the nature of the self, arguing Cronenberg wears his philosophical interests 'on his sleeve.'

cartesian-dualism.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
cartesian-dualism.title: The Fly and the Human Ironies of Disgust
cartesian-dualism.relation: Colin McGinn reads Cronenberg's The Fly as a meditation on human disgust and self-disgust: Seth Brundle's metamorphosis into Brundlefly does not cross an ontological boundary but dramatizes that the human being was already a loathsome organic monster, a 'god who shits.' McGinn ties this to a Cartesian mind-body duality (a fine mind trapped in a decaying insect shell mirrors our own embodiment) and, via Nussbaum, to how projected self-disgust stigmatizes despised groups; the cinematic image itself is an 'antidisgust medium' that lets us feel only quasi-disgust.

cartesian-dualism.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
cartesian-dualism.title: 19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie
cartesian-dualism.relation: Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'

cartesian-dualism.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
cartesian-dualism.title: Brave new worlds cyborg futures and female subjectivity
cartesian-dualism.relation: Examining 'reproductive technohorror' from Shelley's Frankenstein through Splice, The Unborn and The Machine, the chapter argues these films code science as masculine domination of feminised nature (via Bordo's Cartesian masculinisation and Merchant's Bacon) and eliminate the female body altogether so man can create life without woman. It contrasts this with Haraway's post-gender cyborg and Braidotti's Deleuzean metal-morphoses, using becoming-woman and the rhizome to imagine reproductive difference as productive rather than as the erasable 'female problem'.

cartesian-dualism.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
cartesian-dualism.title: Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity
cartesian-dualism.relation: Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.

cartesian-dualism.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
cartesian-dualism.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry
cartesian-dualism.relation: White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.

cartesian-dualism.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
cartesian-dualism.title: 14_LaRocca_Chapter_013.html
cartesian-dualism.relation: Mieke Bal frames her documentaries Mille et un jours and the installation Nothing is Missing around the ethical tension between 'modesty' and 'intimacy' in filming trauma. She reads Descartes's Passions of the Soul against the vulgate dualist cogito—arguing the isolating 'I think, I am' enacts his own abandonment trauma—and sets it beside Spinoza's socially constituted subject, while using Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' (reversed via the empowering close-up of a mother's face) and Deleuze's affection-image and rhizome. The multiplied, dispersed 'voice' of the Tunisian wedding film and Elena's silences become tools of a 'migratory aesthetics.'

cartesian-dualism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.title: I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think
cartesian-dualism.relation: David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.

cartesian-dualism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
cartesian-dualism.title: 16. Better Call Saul Because Chuck’s Condition Is Real
cartesian-dualism.relation: The chapter treats Chuck McGill's electromagnetic hypersensitivity as a case study in the metaphysics and phenomenology of medicine, asking whether an unmeasurable condition is 'real.' It contrasts a realist demand for a biomarker with an anti-realist, phenomenological stance that privileges Chuck's first-person lived experience, and blames Cartesian mind-body dualism for medicine's split between neurology and psychiatry that leaves Chuck uncared for. Reading his blackouts, space blanket, and nocebo-driven coma as psychosomatic, it argues that stigmatizing 'crazy' media portrayals of Chuck worsened his isolation and that a whole-person, first-person-narrative approach was needed.

cartesian-dualism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
cartesian-dualism.title: The Role of Matter Biology or Function
cartesian-dualism.relation: Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind. Neo's apparent mind-body separation fits Descartes's dualism, but Lawrence argues dualism fails on the interaction problem and lack of evidence, so the Matrix scenario supports materialism. He explains reductive (identity) and eliminative materialism (via Churchland and the Tastee Wheat question), then frames the biology-versus-function debate: Searle's emergent-property view (the beer-can thirst model) holds brain biochemistry is essential to consciousness, while functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain) holds any system with the right input-output relations has mental states, and Lawrence argues functionalism underlies the very idea of sentient machines like Agent Smith.

cartesian-dualism.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
cartesian-dualism.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
cartesian-dualism.relation: Steve Matthews uses windsurfing to analyze Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' — the loss of self-awareness in skilled action between boredom and anxiety — and argues its intensity comes from 'integration,' where footstraps and harness bind sailor to kit so the equipment becomes 'an extension of oneself.' Invoking Descartes' own admission that mind and body form a unity (not merely pilot in a vessel), he applies Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis: the windsurfer's kit and body form a coupled cognitive system, so 'I' extends to include the gear. He distinguishes true flow from mere goal-satisfaction (rejecting the ocean-cruiser's landfall as flow) and, via Velleman, locates flow's value in intrinsically motivated action that is its own end.

cartesian-dualism.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
cartesian-dualism.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
cartesian-dualism.relation: Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.

cartesian-dualism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
cartesian-dualism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
cartesian-dualism.relation: Editor Liz Stillwaggon Swan uses her rejection of Descartes' mind–body dualism to reinterpret yoga's promise of 'union.' Drawing on Spinoza's view that mind and matter are two aspects of a single reality, she argues 'mind' is just a placeholder for embodied abilities, so a yogi who denies a separate spirit cannot literally 'unite' mind and body — they are already one. She reframes yogic union (via Megan Burke's essay) as uniting self with nature, and defends practicing yoga for physical and psychological benefit without any spiritual claim, likening secularized yoga to secular Christmas.

cartesian-dualism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
cartesian-dualism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
cartesian-dualism.relation: Ken Burak describes teaching yoga in his philosophy class — a 'three wheels' exercise moving from the true self behind our masks to the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman ('Thou Art That') — to give students embodied access to the universal/particular problem. He reads Western philosophy from Plato's Phaedo (Socrates seeking death as liberation of soul from body) through Descartes' doubt as a 2500-year practice of pratyahara (sense-withdrawal), one limb mistaken for the whole journey, and asks what asana and this long retreat could each bring the other.

cartesian-dualism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
cartesian-dualism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
cartesian-dualism.relation: J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.

cartesian-dualism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
cartesian-dualism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
cartesian-dualism.relation: Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.

cartesian-dualism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
cartesian-dualism.title: 3. Terminator I & II
cartesian-dualism.relation: Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.

cartesian-dualism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
cartesian-dualism.title: 5. Minority Report
cartesian-dualism.relation: Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.

cartesian-dualism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
cartesian-dualism.title: The Role of Matter Biology or Function
cartesian-dualism.relation: Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind, arguing the 'brain-stimulation' premise favors materialism over Descartes's dualism (which alone easily explains Neo's mind-body separation at the Train Station but lacks empirical support and an interaction mechanism). He explains reductive versus eliminative materialism (Churchland's denial of folk-psychological 'beliefs' via Tastee Wheat) and then Searle's biological emergentism (the beer-can thirst machine) against functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain; Agent Smith's seamless transfer into Bane). He concludes the films are best read functionally, making sentient machines genuine minds.

cartesian-dualism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.title: 41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human
cartesian-dualism.relation: Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.

cartesian-dualism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
cartesian-dualism.title: 55. Avatar as Philosophy The Metaphysics of Switching Bodies
cartesian-dualism.relation: Tepley asks whether Jake Sully's final body-switch with his avatar in Cameron's Avatar is metaphysically possible without brain transplant or souls. Using Locke's definition of a person and the transitivity of numerical identity, he shows animalism forbids body-switching, substance dualism (Descartes/Plato) is unavailable in the film's materialist world, and merely copying a brain pattern creates a duplicate, not the same person. His positive solution uses the constitution view (Aristotelian in origin) plus Clark's extended-mind idea to argue Jake literally extends into his avatar, then—via an analogy with split-brain corpus-callosum cases discussed by Nagel, Parfit, and van Inwagen—shrinks back so long as no second stream of consciousness forms, a model he extends to secular survival of death by mind-uploading.

what-is-it-like.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
what-is-it-like.title: Unknown
what-is-it-like.relation: Holt takes Mouse's Tasty Wheat question - how do the machines know what it tasted like? - as the problem of other minds raised for machines, and defends mind-brain identity against multiple realizability with the artificial-pain analogy: like artificial hearts and prostheses, silicon 'pain' is a synthetic twin, not pain itself, so a single neural type may still realize it. He then sketches a speculative solution to the hard problem: consciousness is a 'had perspective' the brain creates - meaning-laden awareness of oneself and the world - which makes mind-brain identity intelligible and keeps the Matrix premise coherent.

what-is-it-like.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
what-is-it-like.title: “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”
what-is-it-like.relation: Littmann asks whether Skynet's machines are people, testing three criteria on the Terminator films. The T-101 and T-1000 pass demanding Turing Tests by passing as humans; Searle's Chinese room — recast as a little Austrian inside the T-101 reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding — shows behavior alone cannot prove thought; and feelings are equally unproven by behavior, since the T-101 can smile on command. But the films' first-person 'Terminator's-eye-view' sequences, Littmann argues, display what it is like to be a Terminator and thus prove machine consciousness, so humanity's extinction might not be the end of persons.

what-is-it-like.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
what-is-it-like.title: Pink Floyd From Pompeii to Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: George Reisch's introduction reads the 1971 Live at Pompeii film, with the band playing to no audience inside a circular stone amphitheatre, as an ironic anticipation of The Wall, tracing how Waters's fury at stadium crowds (culminating in the 1977 Montreal spitting incident that spawned the wall concept) had not yet arrived. It frames the band's post-Barrett move from psychedelic whimsy to minimal formalism as philosophical stripping-away: Barrett wrote like an Aristotle fascinated by odd particulars ('Lucifer Sam,' 'The Gnome'), whose puzzlement at his impenetrable cat prefigures Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, while Waters pursued Plato's monolithic 'forms' of time, money, and madness. On this reading Dark Side's closing 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon' indicts Being itself, making life essentially and permanently tragic, a circular trap signaled by The Wall's interlocking 'we came in?' and 'Isn't this where...'

what-is-it-like.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
what-is-it-like.title: Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up
what-is-it-like.relation: Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.

what-is-it-like.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
what-is-it-like.title: Chapter 04 - Ewe, Robot
what-is-it-like.relation: Seegert opens with the V-K tortoise scene: Leon knows what a turtle is but cannot feel what it would be like to be one, making empathy the litmus of humanity, even though empathy just is imaginative simulation, so the test ironically demands that humans simulate better than the simulations do. He notes the double irony that replicants show empathy for each other (Roy mourning Pris) while Deckard shoots Zhora in the back without wincing, and that the test's real function is keeping androids enslaveable in an arms race of verisimilitude; the deeper anxiety the chapter sets up is not whether androids can pass for human but whether I might not be human myself.

what-is-it-like.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
what-is-it-like.title: Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub
what-is-it-like.relation: Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.

what-is-it-like.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
what-is-it-like.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.

what-is-it-like.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
what-is-it-like.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.

what-is-it-like.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
what-is-it-like.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Dave Beisecker amplifies Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why would anyone enjoy watching, let alone compete for, AMC's 'stagger-on role' as a repulsive walker? Curiosity fails as an answer, since by Nagel's bat argument no amount of staggering around a set tells us what it is like to be a zombie - and since zombification destroys memory, desire, and self-concern, we would not survive it as persons in any interesting sense anyway. His solution is that zombies are the endearing losers and clowns of the undead world: playing one is a way to celebrate our inner awkward nerd and laugh at universal human ineptitude, which is exactly why Kirkman's shambling walkers, unlike fast zombies or glamorous vampires, invite impersonation.

what-is-it-like.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
what-is-it-like.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Silcox and Cox present D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind': the Tomb of Horrors' plane-shifting doorway forces Parfit's teletransporter question of whether the character who emerges is you, a copy, or an annihilation, extended to Tieflings and Warforged; Eberron's sentient Warforged raise Nagel's bat problem of whether a human player can know what it is like to be a machine, answered with the conclusion that players really explore human pretense, like Greek actors in masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood strain against orcs who meet them yet attack on sight, and against the players who killed the lawful-good Flumph without parley. The deep difference is perspective: philosophy imagines sub specie aeternitatis while D&D demands immersion sub specie temporis, which nonetheless cultivates the open-minded intellectual virtues philosophers prize.

what-is-it-like.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
what-is-it-like.title: Futurama and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Von Gunten asks whether Bender, Calculon, and the robot mafia have moral worth, arguing first that they are sentient: behavioral similarity plus functional equivalence (pain as electric signals in neurons or circuits) defeat both behavior-only objections (the Sphex wasp's preprogrammed loop, knife-avoiding toy robots) and composition-based prejudice - Fry's 'I'm all squishy and flabby' defense at the Hal Institute - which would be 'biologism' analogous to racism. He then distinguishes moral patiency (Nibbler can be harmed but only behaviorally reinforced) from moral agency (deliberation and accountability), concluding that Bender's flexible life - Iron Cook, wrestling, folk music with Beck's head, jacking-on addiction - shows robots transcend their programming as humans transcend evolutionary presets. Limiting moral status to biology or species would be speciesism, so the thirty-first century's robots deserve the full protections and responsibilities humans have.

what-is-it-like.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
what-is-it-like.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.

what-is-it-like.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
what-is-it-like.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Christopher Ketcham writes a mock chronicle in which velociraptors escape to inhabited Nava, deliberately avoid humans, and over decades learn to share a hunting language with a Congo tribe, asking whether we would ever grant such beings equal intelligence and rights. He reads raptor pack behavior and cooperation through Dawkins's selfish gene, and uses Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to argue we can never peer into raptor consciousness, just as we brand human races inferior without looking. Citing Plessy v. Ferguson's whiteness-as-property and Mill's point that mistreating animals belongs in the same category as racial discrimination, he ends with a senate-hearing parody and the Neanderthal precedent: a human 'superiority gene' means coexistence with smart raptors would likely end as it did for them.

what-is-it-like.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
what-is-it-like.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Rachel Haliburton asks what metaphysics underwrites Suzanne's world, where a mind can touch a perfect body. The materialist world inherited from Descartes reduces thoughts, meanings, and purposes to purposeless physical processes in which minds never touch bodies; Aristotle's teleological world, refurbished by Thomas Nagel's Mind and Cosmos, builds purposes into nature and treats subjective experience - what the tea and oranges are like for you - as real in its own right. She argues Suzanne's world, and our own ordinary mall-food-court world, is teleological: consciousness is 'biased towards the marvelous,' and we touch one another's bodies with our minds all the time.

what-is-it-like.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
what-is-it-like.title: Dracula and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: McKinney argues Van Helsing should have studied Dracula's brain instead of staking him, because the Count is a philosophy-of-mind thought experiment: a mind that persists unchanged across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes mind-brain identity theory and fits functionalism (the mind as one song playable in many formats), while his telepathic bond with Mina and shapeshifting probe Cartesian dualism's mind-body interaction problem. Nagel's bats show that only Dracula could tell us what it is like to echo-locate or wolf-sense; yet since nothing like his unconstrained mind exists in our world, the novel finally maps what minds are not - evidence against the immaterial mind.

what-is-it-like.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
what-is-it-like.title: Dracula and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Versteeg and Barkman use Dracula's shapeshifting to stage Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': even if the Count becomes a bat, whatever he recalls afterward is filtered back through his human-ness, so no non-bat can access bat-ness from a human point of view. A scene of Van Helsing and bat-Dracula both finding a girl's corpse distinguishes objective from subjective experience. Because physicalism predicts all of reality should be objectively accessible, the impenetrability of subjective experience pressures physicalism and leaves room for the immaterial soul Van Helsing's religion wants.

what-is-it-like.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
what-is-it-like.title: 11. Of Bats and Supermen
what-is-it-like.relation: Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the proper goal of transhumanism - Batman's training and gadgets are only a stage toward transcending the human condition - and that the eugenics and Social Darwinism objection fails because Superman directs his superior fitness at saving the less fit. Through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's churning stomach over a deadline, Alfred retracing his steps and posture to recall a thought, the "Subway Superman" Wesley Autrey's instinctive track rescue) he shows that radically different bodies mean radically different minds and moral perception. That turns Nagel's "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" into "what is it like to be Superman?" - a problem of other minds for our transhuman future, with Watchmen's Doctor Manhattan as the warning of a transcendent being who simply stops caring about humans.

what-is-it-like.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
what-is-it-like.title: 19. The Alchemy of Flat Worlds
what-is-it-like.relation: Staged as Professor Moby Dickens Melville's 'Philosophy of Worlds' course uniting Discworld wizards with the geometric Flatlanders of Abbott's novella, the chapter contrasts a storytelling, narrative-causality philosophy of Discworld with Flatland's mathematical, hierarchy-obsessed rationalism, and extends the contrast to physics (wizards favor loop quantum gravity, Flatlanders string theory) and theology (Hex's self-designed universe and words of power versus Flatland's circle-priests who rule women declared 'deficient in Reason'). When a Flatlander woman, Ms. Transversal, protests that calling the new softer approach 'feminine' repeats Abbott's sexism, the class closes with the narrator's suggestion, from a chalk-nub's-eye view, that everything we know may reflect the direction from which we see rather than the truth itself.

what-is-it-like.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
what-is-it-like.title: 21. Welcome to My World
what-is-it-like.relation: Built on Jakob von Uexküll's Umwelt—the 'island of the senses' that enfolds each creature, illustrated by a moth that smells only a mate's pheromone and hears only the bat's echolocation—the chapter argues that every Discworld being likewise inhabits a sliced-down life world rather than the world as a whole. The ambiguous puzuma running near light speed, dream-spinning dromes that starve victims inside stolen Umwelten, the two-dimensional Shadowing Lemma, Gaspode's pathogen-warring skin, the hermit elephant's hut, and the re-annual plant that flowers a year before its seeds each show a life world carved out by what an organism can sense and use, whether its world runs on science or magic—prompting the suggestion that the Umwelt is more fundamental than either.

what-is-it-like.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
what-is-it-like.title: 8. The Babe with the Power
what-is-it-like.relation: Michaud uses Bowie's Jareth and Labyrinth to make Berkeley's case that only minds and ideas exist: the taste of Sarah's tainted fruit, colors no culture without a word for 'blue' can see, dreams and optical illusions, and hallucinations all show the perceived world is a brain-made prediction, so the Goblin King's magic realm is 'more possible than we realize.' Because each of us builds a private world - Sarah and Jareth can never compare experiences ('I wonder what your basis for comparison is') - Bowie's death is literally the collapse of the world as he created it, 'as the world falls down,' though music may still reach across the void.

what-is-it-like.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
what-is-it-like.title: Violent Ends
what-is-it-like.relation: Richards asks what it is like to be a host, combining three lenses: Searle's biological naturalism (thinking machines must be built from materials with the right causal powers, and the hosts' synthetic flesh may qualify), Nagel's bat (even if hosts are conscious, their perfectly relived memories, curated pain, and blind spots like 'it doesn't look like anything to me' may make their experience as inconceivable to us as echolocation), and Chalmers's philosophical zombies (hosts behave exactly like us, yet beings identical to them with no inner light are conceivable). He reads Ford's contradictory testimony — praising Bernard's guilt as 'a thing of beauty' while denying consciousness exists — as a shift to a deflationary view with no threshold for being alive, and argues the show's choice to film human and host experience in the same style keeps the question deliberately open while fostering empathy.

what-is-it-like.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
what-is-it-like.title: What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum
what-is-it-like.relation: Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.

what-is-it-like.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
what-is-it-like.title: Is a Man Not Entitled to the Sweat of His Brow
what-is-it-like.relation: Schevelier uses the Andrew Ryan assassination to teach phenomenology: the moment the controller stops responding, the 'mineness' of the experience collapses and the story stops being yours, revealing that Jack's (and the player's) freedom depended on a thin self-narrative the mind 'desperately struggles to create', per Lutece's epigraph. Nagel's bat shows why no brain scan captures what it is like to play, while Husserl, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty supply the toolkit; Heidegger's hammer, which shows itself in use or in breakdown, explains both immersive scenes like the Kashmir restaurant and what breaks them (bugs, wrong display, a talking protagonist). Following Merleau-Ponty's claim that art records subjective experience, the chapter treats Levine's team as artistic phenomenologists whose design question 'What is this experience we are trying to make?' turned Columbia and Elizabeth into phenomenological analyses to be read.

what-is-it-like.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
what-is-it-like.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Silcox and Cox read D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind'. The Tomb of Horrors' four overlapping plane-shifted buildings restate Parfit's teletransporter puzzle — did the character who stepped through get annihilated, or is an exact copy walking around elsewhere, and does the answer differ for a Warforged or Tiefling? — while the Eberron setting's magically sentient Warforged run into Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': players cannot access Warforged experience and are really exploring what it is like for a human to suspend disbelief, like Greek actors donning masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood collapse on contact with orcs who pass them yet eat you, and with the Flumph — lawful good, rational, but killed on sight by the authors' own party — showing personhood cannot be the only criterion for how to treat strangers; the closing twist is that philosophy contemplates scenarios sub specie aeternitatis while D&D forces immersion sub specie temporis, a habit of entertaining the impossible that is itself a philosophical virtue.

what-is-it-like.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
what-is-it-like.title: Notes
what-is-it-like.relation: The chapter argues Fallout 4's grip comes not from graphical fidelity but from first-person moral agency: deciding the fate of Gen 3 synths who do not know they are synths — supporting their escape, hunting them, or installing them as unwitting spies — forces the player through emotionally real moral deliberation. It connects this to Turing's worry about proving to another that you think ('it could've been me in their shoes') and to Nagel's bat, proposing that imagining what it is like to be a synth is a stepping stone toward ever stranger perspectives. Playing thus becomes the joy of actually doing philosophy — reawakening imagination, reshuffling our space of possibilities, and returning us to our own problems refreshed rather than merely escaped.

what-is-it-like.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
what-is-it-like.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.

what-is-it-like.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
what-is-it-like.title: 11. Of Bats and Supermen
what-is-it-like.relation: Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the right goal for a transhumanist future: through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's deadline nausea, Alfred recovering a thought by redoing his posture, real-life 'Subway Superman' Wesley Autrey's gut-level rescue) he shows bodies shape thought and morality, so a super-body means a super-mind. Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' becomes 'what is it like to be Superman' — a problem of superhero minds, with Doctor Manhattan's indifference as the cautionary case — while Superman's rescues of the less fit show transcendence need not slide into eugenics or Social Darwinism.

what-is-it-like.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
what-is-it-like.title: NOTES
what-is-it-like.relation: Littmann asks whether personhood could survive humanity's extinction in 2029: if Terminators genuinely think and feel, a Skynet victory would not be the end of people. He argues the T-101, T-1000 and T-X pass substantial Turing Tests (fooling muggers, cops, Sarah on the phone as her 'mother'), then concedes Searle's Chinese Room - recast as a tiny Austrian inside the endoskeleton reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding - shows thinking behavior cannot prove thought. But he claims the films' red-tinted Terminator's-eye-view shots show what it is like to be a Terminator, giving proof of consciousness, and concludes the machines are probably persons: there is an 'I' in 'I'll be back.'

what-is-it-like.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
what-is-it-like.title: NOTES
what-is-it-like.relation: Curtis argues liberal society should be wary of integrating True Blood's vampires: their feudal system of kings, sheriffs, and the magister, enforced through maker bonds and punishment, violates even Kukathas's maximally tolerant liberalism because members cannot freely exit and humans are mistreated with impunity. Adapting Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to the question 'What is it like to be a vampire?', he contends that glamouring, blood bonds, and an eroticized hunger different in kind from ours leave humans unable to verify vampire trustworthiness — echoing Aristotle's claim that one who cannot live in the polis is a beast or a god — so mainstreaming demands the AVL first expose and reform vampire institutions.

what-is-it-like.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
what-is-it-like.title: NOTES
what-is-it-like.relation: Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.

what-is-it-like.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
what-is-it-like.title: NOTES
what-is-it-like.relation: Curry asks whether even Sookie's telepathy can breach the privacy of mind: a third-person account of shifter Sam hearing a dog-whistle leaves out the quale — the homage to Nagel's bat — and Locke's inverted spectrum (Jason and Tara both say 'green' while living different experiences) shows qualia are incommunicable. Reading the astrology-believing Maxine's mind traps Sookie in a dilemma: if she fully becomes Maxine she is no longer the Sookie who knows, and if she keeps her skeptical psychology she never experiences what it is like to believe — so, drawing on Dennett's coffee example for one's own past qualia, even the show's most powerful mind reader can never know what it is like to experience things as you.

what-is-it-like.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
what-is-it-like.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.

what-is-it-like.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
what-is-it-like.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether you survive a walker bite, rejecting the body view via Dr. Jenner's 'Everything you ever were or ever will be—gone' because a mindless corpse is not you. He tests philosophical behaviorism and functionalism against walker behavior—Jenny turning her old doorknob, walkers distinguishing humans by smell—then adapts Dennett's thought experiment into a walker-and-rope computer functionally identical to a human brain. Since we can conceive that groaning machine lacking inner experience, behavior and function cannot settle which systems are conscious, leaving the bitten dying in ignorance of whether they face annihilation or reanimation.

what-is-it-like.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
what-is-it-like.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
what-is-it-like.relation: Dave Beisecker takes AMC's 'stagger-on role' zombie contest as an amplified version of Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why relish playing a repulsive walker when zombification is the fate no rational creature would wish even on its remains? He rejects the curiosity solution through Nagel's bat—no staggering around a set could reveal what it is like to be a zombie, and we wouldn't survive zombification anyway except as our remains—and notes we fantasize about being survivors, not monsters. His answer is affection and release: walkers are the geeks and clowns of the undead pantheon, and playing one lets us comically own our inner loser, which is why Kirkman's symbol-free zombies invite identification where Nazi zombies would not.

what-is-it-like.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
what-is-it-like.title: Violent Ends
what-is-it-like.relation: Bradley Richards asks what it is like to be a host, using Nagel's 'what is it like to be a bat?' to argue that whether we can conceive host experience depends on how similar it is to ours, and Searle's biological view to ask whether hosts are made of the right stuff. He catalogs how host perception, emotion, and especially memory differ from human (Maeve's perfect reliving of memories versus our hazy constructive recall, 'is this now?'), and weighs Chalmers's philosophical zombies against the hosts. He notes the show depicts host and human experience in the identical cinematic style to preserve ambiguity, and links memory, self-consciousness, and freedom via Dolores's maze, suggesting hosts may be phenomenally conscious before becoming self-aware.

what-is-it-like.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
what-is-it-like.title: XV - MUTANT PHENOMENOLOGY
what-is-it-like.relation: Wisnewski applies phenomenology to mutant embodiment: if consciousness is 'I can' and the body is our point of view on the world, then Kitty Pryde's walls, Nightcrawler's teleportation, Angel's flight, Madrox's duplicate spaces, and Rogue's untouchability describe genuinely different worlds, not merely different powers. Apocalypse's millennia of near-immortality and the X-Verse's reversible deaths unsettle Heidegger's being-toward-death and Becker's death-denial that organizes human culture. Concluding with Nagel's bat, he argues we cannot know what it is like to be a mutant, only what our own being-in-the-world would become if our bodily limitations changed.

what-is-it-like.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
what-is-it-like.title: The Instructive Impossibility of Being John Malkovich
what-is-it-like.relation: Hagberg treats Being John Malkovich as a refutation of the dualist fantasy that one could achieve transparent knowledge of another mind by occupying it. Through the film's four levels—Schwartz as spectator inside Malkovich, Lotte's transgender re-embodiment, Schwartz's puppeteering, and Malkovich falling into his own portal to the 'Malkovich, Malkovich' hell—he shows, via Jamesian relational sensation and Wittgenstein's private-language argument, that it is always still Schwartz who senses, so no one ever becomes Malkovich. The self-enclosed Malkovich world, where everyone can only say 'Malkovich,' dramatizes that selfhood is relationally emergent (Royce, Mead) and that experience is inviolably one's own (Margalit on remembered emotion).

what-is-it-like.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
what-is-it-like.title: “Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg
what-is-it-like.relation: Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D.
