Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.

what-is-it-like.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
what-is-it-like.title: Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction
what-is-it-like.relation: Holt uses the Terminator's first-person infrared POV shots (evoking Nagel's 'what is it like' question about an alien artificial consciousness) to frame the paradox of fiction: how we feel fear toward things we know do not exist. He offers a contextual divide-and-conquer solution, arguing higher emotions like pity and admiration for Sarah and Reese are largely make-believe, while lower emotions like Terminator-fear are genuine and need no existential belief (thought and mere possibility suffice). He adds that such fear is more rational for a naturalist who admits artificial intelligence is possible than for a dualist, and speculates the Terminator functions as an archetype embodying tech-noir dread.

what-is-it-like.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
what-is-it-like.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
what-is-it-like.relation: Baltzer-Jaray uses Kant's phenomena/noumena split, Plato's Forms, and Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to ask whether Jack Skellington can know the essence of Christmas and whether Vincent Malloy can know what it is to BE Vincent Price. She argues Jack's lab-experiments on presents and snowflakes ('Jack's Obsession') can only yield phenomena, never the noumenal essence, so Kant would permit belief but not knowledge; Vincent, watching only Price's horror roles, grasps a mere phenomenal fragment. Via Nagel she concludes neither can occupy another's subjective viewpoint, so the lesson of both films is to celebrate otherness through communication rather than trying to be someone else.

what-is-it-like.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
what-is-it-like.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence Artistic Indulgence or Advanced Inquiry
what-is-it-like.relation: White argues A.I. dramatizes the mind-body problem through the mecha child David, proposing a 'Strengthened Turing Test' (STT) in which the audience knows he is a machine yet must judge whether he truly loves Monica. He runs Searle's Chinese Room (David as mere rule-follower with no qualia) against Nagel's 'what is it like' and Chalmers's zombie argument and property-dualist multiple realizability, which would let a sufficiently complex David be genuinely conscious. White contends the imprinting device—David's built-in need for one other being—is what lets him pass the STT, sidestepping Cartesian dualism's interaction problem.

what-is-it-like.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
what-is-it-like.title: 23_LaRocca_Chapter_022.html
what-is-it-like.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Gabriela Cowperthwaite's Blackfish through Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, arguing the film's interviews with orca neuroscientists (Marino et al.) function as Nagel's proposed 'objective phenomenology,' conveying orca consciousness through objective indicators rather than mere anthropomorphic projection. She dissects the film's rhetoric around Tilikum and Dawn Brancheau, showing how the title, delayed naming, SeaWorld ad juxtapositions and emotional testimony first vilify then humanize the whale to argue captivity is morally unacceptable. Invoking Peggy Zeglin Brand's 'lenses,' Iris Murdoch's 'unselfing' and Marc Bekoff's inclusive ethic, she concludes the film approximates truth about orca minds even as it, like SeaWorld, is 'structured to sell.'

what-is-it-like.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
what-is-it-like.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
what-is-it-like.relation: Phillips argues that there is something-it-is-like to be a knowledgeable coffee drinker, using Nagel's bat and Jackson's Mary thought experiments — but where the bat is 'fundamentally alien,' coffee expertise is learnable, and via David Lewis's ability hypothesis the reader can apply book-knowledge of acidity, body, finish, and flavor to abilities they already have. He then invokes Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (Homer's enduring appeal, the Don Quixote wine-tasters) to claim aesthetic and moral judgments spring from the same refinable sentiments, so that examining your cup free of prejudice is, echoing Socrates' 'unexamined life,' something we almost owe ourselves: the unexamined cup is not worth drinking.

what-is-it-like.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
what-is-it-like.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
what-is-it-like.relation: Zangwill argues that 'fashionable' is a relational, sociological property (like 'famous'), yet things also directly *appear* fashionable or 'cool' to us in first-person perceptual experience as if coolness were a simple, non-relational quality (illustrated by seeing 1965 Mick Jagger as 'groovy'). He claims these two aspects — the third-person sociological concept and the first-person phenomenological one — cannot be united, so the concept of fashion is 'schizoid.' Invoking Nagel on consciousness and Bernard Williams's charge of alienation in Kantian and utilitarian ethics, he concludes fashion involves a projective illusion and is a genuine source of alienation.

what-is-it-like.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
what-is-it-like.title: “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”
what-is-it-like.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether the Terminators are 'people,' testing three criteria: passing as human, thinking, and feeling. The T-101, T-1000, and T-X repeatedly pass Turing Tests, giving behavioral evidence of thought, but Littmann recasts Searle's Chinese Room as the 'Austrian Terminator' to argue behavior never proves genuine understanding. He then argues personhood requires conscious experience (what it is like to be a Terminator), and takes the films' red- and blue-tinted first-person 'Terminator's-eye view' shots as evidence the machines really are conscious, so humanity's extinction need not end personhood.

what-is-it-like.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
what-is-it-like.title: 85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality
what-is-it-like.relation: Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.

knowledge-argument.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
knowledge-argument.title: Unknown
knowledge-argument.relation: Barwick argues reductive materialism fails twice. First, via the Mary story (told here from Michael Tye's retelling): a scientist raised in a black-and-white room who knows all the physical facts about color still learns something new when she sees her first rose - what it is like - which no physical theory addresses. Second, the identity claim is meaningless: 'mental state = brain state' cannot be true because the experiential report and the scientific explanation have different subject matters, against Churchland's plea that we merely lack the needed concepts - so the metaphysics underwriting The Matrix is false.

knowledge-argument.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
knowledge-argument.title: Lonesome Day
knowledge-argument.relation: Calef asks how fictional story-songs can teach: lyrics yield neither know-how nor know-that, since Plato's Theaetetus shows true belief is not knowledge (the 'Meeting Across the River' narrator's plan works only by luck). The answer is a third kind — knowing what something is like: 'The River' lets a comfortable listener inhabit Mary's husband's slide into a dry marriage, and 'Nebraska' lets us feel Starkweather's numb void, 'what it's like to have no soul.' Aristotle's Poetics (we delight in imitation because learning pleases; poetry is more philosophic than history because it speaks in universals) explains why sad songs satisfy us, and Sartre's universal human condition grounds the empathy that makes The Rising render 9/11 ('You're Missing,' 'Empty Sky') thinkable at a personal scale.

knowledge-argument.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
knowledge-argument.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
knowledge-argument.relation: Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.

knowledge-argument.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
knowledge-argument.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
knowledge-argument.relation: Hess asks whether the monster has a soul and makes him the test case between physicalism (Kim, Churchland, van Inwagen) and dualism: recasting Frank Jackson's Mary as a color-blind monster who learns every physical fact about color vision, receives new eyes on Walton's ship, and then learns the 'what it is like' of seeing red for the first time, he argues there are nonphysical mental facts, so physicalism is false. He then runs Plantinga's argument that we are not our bodies or brains through a machine that replaces the monster's parts and hemispheres one by one while he stays conscious, and adds near-death out-of-body evidence like Maria's window-ledge shoe to suggest we can exist disembodied. The upshot is symmetric: whatever we conclude about the monster's soul we must conclude about our own - so be careful about assuming who does and does not have a soul, even monsters.

knowledge-argument.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
knowledge-argument.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
knowledge-argument.relation: Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.

knowledge-argument.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
knowledge-argument.title: 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts
knowledge-argument.relation: Schiltz tests Janet's claim to know 'literally everything' against the philosophical definition of omniscience as believing all true propositions, finding she lacks knowledge of Michael's demonhood, of the future, and of current events on Earth. Divine-omniscience puzzles drawn from Averroes and Aquinas, and Boethius's solution that God sees all things in an eternal present, frame why Janet's ignorance of the future is what protects the characters' free will and moral responsibility. Frank Jackson's Mary thought experiment illuminates Judge Gen's failure to know what human life is like, and Janet's gradual acquisition of empathy across her reboots shows why her imperfect knowledge is a feature rather than a glitch.

knowledge-argument.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
knowledge-argument.title: What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum
knowledge-argument.relation: Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.

knowledge-argument.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
knowledge-argument.title: 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts
knowledge-argument.relation: Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.

knowledge-argument.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
knowledge-argument.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
knowledge-argument.relation: Phillips argues that there is something-it-is-like to be a knowledgeable coffee drinker, using Nagel's bat and Jackson's Mary thought experiments — but where the bat is 'fundamentally alien,' coffee expertise is learnable, and via David Lewis's ability hypothesis the reader can apply book-knowledge of acidity, body, finish, and flavor to abilities they already have. He then invokes Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (Homer's enduring appeal, the Don Quixote wine-tasters) to claim aesthetic and moral judgments spring from the same refinable sentiments, so that examining your cup free of prejudice is, echoing Socrates' 'unexamined life,' something we almost owe ourselves: the unexamined cup is not worth drinking.

knowledge-argument.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
knowledge-argument.title: 43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)
knowledge-argument.relation: Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.

eliminative-materialism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
eliminative-materialism.title: Unknown
eliminative-materialism.relation: Barwick considers whether the film's authors might instead be eliminative materialists - there are no mental states, only physical ones and our talk of them - and rejects the doctrine through the 'ownership' of experience: my pleasure in a glass of vintage port is had only by me, a feature Searle admits is difficult to accommodate scientifically and Dennett's 'user illusion' cannot explain, since a seeming requires a someone it seems to. Decisively, eliminativism would make the Matrix pointless - with no experiences there is nothing to deceive - so the film instead needs the intentionality of consciousness.

eliminative-materialism.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
eliminative-materialism.title: Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up
eliminative-materialism.relation: Tests three theories of mind against Spock's katra transfer in The Wrath of Khan and The Search for Spock and his mind melds with Kirk, the Horta, and Rock people. Descartes's divisibility argument backs the dualism the katra assumes, but the argument from parsimony (Ockham's razor), the problem of mental causation, and the conservation of energy weigh against it; Churchland's eliminative materialism plays by science's rules but runs into Nagel's 'what it is like' objection, dramatized by Geordi failing to describe anger to Data without circularity. The author lands, cautiously, on Searle-style emergentism — mind as an emergent, irreducible feature of neural complexity, as when Nomad and V'Ger exceed their programming — while conceding Kim's charge that it may be dualism in disguise.

eliminative-materialism.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
eliminative-materialism.title: 20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork
eliminative-materialism.relation: A comic sprint through Western thought anchored in the Science of Discworld books, the chapter runs from Aristotle—whose geocentric four-element physics, it notes, fits Discworld better than Roundworld, and whose condemnations of usury it digresses over—through Descartes's cogito and mind-body dualism, Ryle's 'ghost in the machine,' behaviorism, identity theory, eliminative materialism, and functionalism's brain-as-computer picture, to show how philosophy of mind advances by each theory picking on its predecessor. Newton's occult-seeming gravity, later overturned by Einstein, illustrates the chapter's real thesis drawn from Pratchett's 'Lies-to-Wizards': neither science nor philosophy erects a timeless edifice of facts, since 'every so often, you have to unlearn what you thought you already knew,' while Diogenes and the Cynics supply the model of philosophy done in the common tongue that Pratchett shares.

eliminative-materialism.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
eliminative-materialism.title: Does the Piano Play Itself
eliminative-materialism.relation: Versteeg and Barkman use the player piano — keys that depress themselves with no ghost at the keyboard — to frame Robert Ford's 'we can't define consciousness because consciousness does not exist' as eliminative materialism, the view shared by Paul Churchland and Daniel Dennett that the common-sense self with its beliefs, desires, and central first-person perspective is a fiction. They set this against Descartes's dualism of res cogitans and res extensa, noting the failed pineal-gland 'magical transaction' and Dennett's replacement of the Cartesian Theater with multiple drafts of consciousness and the manifest-versus-scientific image. The chapter closes on Ford's inconsistency — denying consciousness yet sacrificing his life so the hosts can become self-aware — and asks whether, if the piano plays itself, humans are just complex machines too.

intentionality.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
intentionality.title: Unknown
intentionality.relation: Barwick completes his 'neo-materialism' by killing the subject: after Hume finds no self on introspection - perceptions but no perceiver - and Sartre defines consciousness as pure intentionality, a transparency through which we fall to its object, Wittgenstein's 'no such thing as the subject that thinks' leaves features like the lovable Tasty Wheat and the fearsome Agents on the side of objects. Consciousness emerges as not a thing but the revelation of things - immaterial yet no substance - forcing us to put the mind into the world rather than the world into the mind.

intentionality.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
intentionality.title: “Unchained” The Inspired Anger of a Religious Man
intentionality.relation: Dan Haggerty uses Aristotle's account of anger as a virtuous mean—felt at the right people, time, and degree—to show that songs like 'San Quentin,' 'The Man in Black,' and 'Oney' express justified anger at real injustices done to prisoners and workingmen, contra pop psychology's blanket rejection of anger. He then coins 'inspired anger' (drawing on Plato's Ion: the artist possessed and blown away by emotion): a painful, hopeless desire for a justice or restoration that can never be, exemplified by Cash's 'Hurt' video and its regret over irrecoverable time—mourning rather than self-pity or depression. The chapter closes with 'Unchained' as a prayer showing how a Christian like Cash can live with this futile desire rather than argue it away.

intentionality.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
intentionality.title: Driftin’ Off to a Foreign Land
intentionality.relation: Dick explains how 'Straight Time' makes us see Charlie's cycle of drudgery through Sartre's The Imaginary: the title is a Sartrean sign that welds prison time, rendering-factory time and straight-and-narrow time into one image of endless oppression, and Bruce's first-person characterization works like Dana Carvey impersonating Jimmy Stewart — consciousness overlooks discrepancies until we recognize 'our' Charlie. Against the escape fantasy of 'Thunder Road,' Camus's Sisyphus frames Charlie as swapping rocks (prison, factory, his uncle's car-theft heist) while the hill remains and 'there is no top of the hill.' Springsteen's answer to the absurd is to climb alongside his characters in empathetic brotherly love.

intentionality.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
intentionality.title: Tell Me No Lies, Make Me a Happy Man
intentionality.relation: Luke Dick gives a phenomenological analysis of what it is to be moved by 'Black Dog', introducing affectivity through a fantasy in which a stranger insulting Zeppelin instantly provokes anger. Sartre's account of emotions as unreflective, 'magical' transformations directed at intentional objects explains how fast the insulted fan's world changes, while Heidegger's claim that we are never moodless grounds the idea of a distinct 'Zeppelin mood' that the band's sound articulates better than language could. Schopenhauer's misogynist essay 'On Women' is set beside the song's predatory canine sexuality, and the chapter ends by asking which of the three 'males'—Schopenhauer, Plant's character, or the author with his carefully chosen six-song mix CD—a father could endorse as a son-in-law.

intentionality.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
intentionality.title: The Essence of Perception Holmes’s Intention and Objects Intended
intentionality.relation: Kilroy romanticizes not the drugs but the woodshed: Holmes's cocaine sessions, violin, and clattered study cultivate a Husserlian field of consciousness in which reality is the intercourse of subject and object, so a clue (the Trichinopoly cigar ash, 'Rache' as German for revenge) only appears to a detective whose knowledge, observation, and deduction are unified — Gregson and Lestrade misread the same room in A Study in Scarlet because they theorize before the evidence. Heidegger's distinction between merely present (Vorhandenheit) and usefully present (Zuhandenheit) objects explains what counts as a clue — the lipstick-stained wineglass, not the tablecloth — and Husserl's 'things seen are always more than what we really and actually see' explains the frozen-coaster chair. Watson's see-it-to-believe-it empiricism, drained by the Afghan war, is precisely why he has no 'special powers': he never furnishes his brain-attic with the furniture that lets objects speak.

intentionality.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
intentionality.title: Guilt Can be a Real Bitch
intentionality.relation: Howard treats Inception as a lesson in Husserlian phenomenology: perceiving, remembering and dreaming are distinct intentional states, each with its own mode of givenness, standards of evidence and horizon of expectations, and the film's dream architecture dramatizes what happens when those modes are artificially crossed. Cobb's prohibition on building dreams from memories shows the disorientation caused by severing a memory's intrinsic temporal signature from the dream image, while the totems work because dreamed physics violates the continuity and intersubjective verifiability of the shared life-world. The chapter ends with guilt as the Ariadne's thread of the plot: dreams and memories hold only 'shades' of other people, so Cobb's guilt over Mal is what drags him back to the waking life-world where real others exist in their own right.

intentionality.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
intentionality.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
intentionality.relation: Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.

intentionality.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
intentionality.title: “When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”
intentionality.relation: Lean treats Bernard's discovery in 'Trompe L'Oeil' that his son Charlie never existed as a richly detailed thought experiment about intentionality: his memories of Charlie seem to refer to nothing, so his grief looks like 'grieving about nothing.' After setting up Brentano's aboutness and Frege's sense/reference distinction (Dolores learns that 'William' and 'the Man in Black' are one referent known under two senses), he tests two consolations: a fiction theory drawing on Lamarque, on which Bernard's implanted memories are a story rather than a lie and his emotions are rationally grounded because thoughts need only be entertained, not believed, to move us; and an 'inheritance theory' on which a causal theory of reference might make Bernard's copied memories genuinely about Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that whichever theory Bernard adopts, his suffering is what makes him 'real,' echoing the Man in Black's line that suffering is when you are most real.

intentionality.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
intentionality.title: “King of space, right here!”
intentionality.relation: The chapter asks whether Robert Daly wrongs the USS Callister NPCs even if they are 'merely' sentient code: his theft of co-workers' DNA violates a fundamental right to privacy, and Kant's focus on the will shows his in-game intentions aim at real people — he logs in solely to strangle James's NPC and make him confess to being pathetic, wanting to harm the actual James. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the second indictment: because hyperrealistic VR blurs game and life, Daly's daily practice of cruelty habituates vice and makes cruelty part of who he is, unlike clearly fictional violence such as Mortal Kombat. Merleau-Ponty's intentionality links avatar actions to the self, so the chapter ends by asking what our own intentions in games like The Sims or Grand Theft Auto reveal about our character.

intentionality.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
intentionality.title: Guilt Can be a Real Bitch
intentionality.relation: Jason Howard argues Inception is phenomenological philosophy in Husserl's sense: the film dramatizes how dreaming, remembering, and perceiving are distinct intentional states with different 'modes of givenness' and horizons — time dilates, dreams begin mid-scene with no past, and memories carry a temporal signature that collapses when Cobb rebuilds them into dreamscapes, which is why he warns Ariadne never to build dreams from memory. Totems work because waking perception alone is governed by laws of nature and by the shared life-world (Lebenswelt): Saito's carpet with the wrong fabric, Cobb's backwards watch, and the Penrose steps that could never close real space all betray the dream. The chapter extends this to embodiment — Yusuf's dreamers register rain and balance from their bodies, and Saito's comatose body still atrophies — and closes with intersubjectivity: Cobb's guilt is 'always there reminding me of the truth' because reality is inseparable from the community of others, and the 'shades' of people in dreams and memories can never capture the real Mal or his children.

intentionality.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
intentionality.title: Notes
intentionality.relation: Applies Husserl's phenomenology - noesis (the act of meaning-giving), noema (the meaning arrived at), and the life-world - to Voyager's Doctor and Seven of Nine as they build selves from conscious experience. Reads "Latent Image" (the Doctor's deleted memories of choosing Harry Kim's life over another ensign's) and "Infinite Regress" (Seven's channeling of assimilated personalities) as parallel guilt experiences whose noemata teach each that past choices remain part of identity without governing it. Their forced isolation in "One", the Doctor's unrequited love in "Someone to Watch over Me", and "Body and Soul", where the Doctor savors food and sensation through Seven's body, generate a shared noema: social interaction and embodied experience are what make a life-world, even for photons and drones.

intentionality.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
intentionality.title: “When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”
intentionality.relation: Lean treats Bernard's grief over the fabricated son Charlie as a thought experiment about intentionality, using Brentano's 'aboutness' and Frege's sense/reference (illustrated by Dolores knowing 'William' and 'the Man in Black' as one referent) to ask whether Bernard's memories refer to nothing. He offers Lamarque's fiction theory (emotion needs only entertained, not believed, thoughts, so Charlie could be a fiction rather than a lie) and an 'inheritance theory' using a causal theory of reference to ask whether Bernard's memories actually refer to Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that grieving makes Bernard 'most real' whatever the metaphysics.

intentionality.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
intentionality.relation: Douglas McLaughlin and Cesar Torres argue that Coubertin's vague Olympism is best clarified by the phenomenological concept of intersubjectivity developed by Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, and Levinas. Treating competitive sport (via Suits's lusory attitude and the 'testing family' notion of a mutual quest for excellence) as inherently social, they use intersubjectivity to dissolve the apparent contradiction between the motto's excellence and the creed's participation, since one's victory is meaningful only through worthy opponents one is answerable to. Invoking Levinas's ethics of the face, they ground Olympic values of mutual respect, fairness, and peace in the reciprocity athletes owe one another 'running shoulder to shoulder.'

intentionality.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
intentionality.title: Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World
intentionality.relation: Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.

hume-bundle.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
hume-bundle.title: Unknown
hume-bundle.relation: Barwick completes his 'neo-materialism' by killing the subject: after Hume finds no self on introspection - perceptions but no perceiver - and Sartre defines consciousness as pure intentionality, a transparency through which we fall to its object, Wittgenstein's 'no such thing as the subject that thinks' leaves features like the lovable Tasty Wheat and the fearsome Agents on the side of objects. Consciousness emerges as not a thing but the revelation of things - immaterial yet no substance - forcing us to put the mind into the world rather than the world into the mind.

hume-bundle.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
hume-bundle.title: “Nobody’s Bob Dylan”
hume-bundle.relation: Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.

hume-bundle.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
hume-bundle.title: Zombies and Us
hume-bundle.relation: Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.

hume-bundle.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
hume-bundle.title: I Ain’t Gonna Tell You One Thing that You Really Ought to Know . . . Ooh!
hume-bundle.relation: Scott Calef reads the black 'Object' on the Presence cover—which Storm Thorgerson calls not a presence but a hole—to argue that absence permeates Zep's album art (the cut-out wheel of III, the die-cut windows of Physical Graffiti, the spindle holes of Coda) and that holes are a genuine metaphysical puzzle: immaterial yet extended, seemingly causal, and hard to see on a causal theory of perception. Descartes's immaterial soul is compared to holes (both non-physical, though holes suspiciously have size and location), Plato's Forms explain how the Object and we ourselves partake of both Being and Non-Being, and Hume's failure to find a self in introspection makes the self 'a hole'. Kierkegaard and Heidegger connect nothingness to the anxiety of death—fitting an album made after Plant's near-fatal crash—Socrates's two alternatives about death frame the end, and Wittgenstein's 'not a something but not a nothing either' caps the Object's dual nature.

hume-bundle.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
hume-bundle.title: Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk
hume-bundle.relation: Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.

hume-bundle.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
hume-bundle.title: Zombies and Us
hume-bundle.relation: Hamish Thompson asks what could justify killing zombies, canvassing self-defense, total-brain-death criteria, and release from obligations to a radically altered person, using Shaun of the Dead's mother-killing, Bub's trained shooting in Day of the Dead, White Zombie's piano-playing heroine, and the pod-people substitutions of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He deploys Hume's bundle theory of the self as a fiction of succeeding perceptions and Parfit's graded psychological continuity (with Locke's prince/cobbler case) to argue identity comes in degrees, so zombie termination is never as clean as the genre pretends. The chapter ends by turning the lens around: Shaun's checkout-line beepers and Ed's sofa-and-video-game existence suggest ordinary lives differ from zombiehood only by intermittent acts of imaginative self-direction.

hume-bundle.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
hume-bundle.title: Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.

hume-bundle.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
hume-bundle.title: In a Mirror, Darkly
hume-bundle.relation: The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'

hume-bundle.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
hume-bundle.title: You Don’t Always Get Along
hume-bundle.relation: The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.

hume-bundle.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
hume-bundle.title: How Do You Know You’re Not an Android
hume-bundle.relation: The chapter weaponizes the cogito for Deckard's predicament: the fact that 'the lights are on' for you seems to prove you are human, but Descartes' leap from thinking to an immaterial soul is unjustified, since introspection cannot show whether your thoughts run on a soul, a bundle of neurons, or a silicon chip. Hume's 'I never can catch myself at any time without a perception' supplies the precedent, and the conclusion is that no amount of inner experience rules out being an android, so you will have to go take the V-K test after all.

hume-bundle.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
hume-bundle.title: Psych and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.

hume-bundle.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
hume-bundle.title: Homeland and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Frank Scalambrino probes Carrie's 'personality paradox' through the 'You can't change your soul!' / 'Yes you can' exchange. Aristotle's Metaphysics offers one pole: only generation and corruption are substantial change, so Carrie persists essentially as human however her mania, job, and loves shift. Hume's rejoinder - sameness of kind is not given in sense experience but added by interpretation - opens the question of whether Carrie's identity is determined by intrinsic factors (love, soul, truth) or extrinsic ones (the CIA's rules, religious affiliation), with Saul representing extrinsic determination and Carrie privileging the intrinsic, while Brody's conversion shows a soul can change and re-order which factors govern a self.

hume-bundle.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
hume-bundle.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.

hume-bundle.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
hume-bundle.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.

hume-bundle.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
hume-bundle.title: 12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld
hume-bundle.relation: Pierce uses Moist von Lipwig's rehabilitation (Albert Spangler becomes Postmaster General), Cosmo Lavish's doomed project of literally becoming Vetinari, the Auditor Myria LeJean, Angua's transformations, the Librarian's orangutan body, Miss Level's two bodies, and duplicated Rincewind teleportation cases to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory theory, patched by Leibniz into psychological continuity, collapses into circularity under false-memory cases like a wizard implanting Teatime's murders in Rincewind's mind, while bodily and brain-continuity views founder on Igor part-swaps, splitting hemispheres, and identical-twin-style fission. Leibniz's own soul view and Reid's treatment of identity as a primitive, unanalyzable fact get their due, and Hume's skepticism about any continuing self marks the chapter's conclusion that every available view exacts a price.

hume-bundle.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
hume-bundle.title: 23. I’d Rather Stay an Orangutan Because That’s Why Discworld Exists
hume-bundle.relation: In a self-fictionalizing chapter, editor Nicolas Michaud is summoned by Vetinari to prove Discworld is real, and the answer arrives in the Unseen University library: the Librarian stays an orangutan because language distances us from experience—humans never simply experience a banana, only 'holding a banana,' so for us the words create the reality. Along the way the chapter takes issue with Hume's bundle-of-perceptions view of the self, since word-using humans are never just a collection of present perceptions, and contrasts the Librarian's immediate, unmediated experience of each singular thing with our word-reduced world. It concludes that because we always experience the world as stories, narratives, and terms, 'narratives are all we have,' making the Disc no less real than the Roundworld we talk and think about.

hume-bundle.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
hume-bundle.title: 3. The Flux of It All
hume-bundle.relation: Ammon asks whether anything persists beneath Bowie's serial personas, staging Parmenides's denial of change (with Zeno's paradoxes) and Descartes's melting wax against the Heraclitean flux of 'ch-ch-ch-changes.' Rejecting soul-substance views, he takes the empiricist line - Hume's introspection finds only particular perceptions, never a self - warns via the intentional fallacy (Manson's 'Helter Skelter,' Bloom's hawk) against letting Bowie's own pronouncements fix his songs' meanings, and tests 'meaning is use' on Bowie's calling rock stars fascists. Recurring undercurrents (dancing, apocalypse, distrust of authority) survive, but the conclusion is that Bowie's essence just is flux, 'the river we can't step into twice.'

hume-bundle.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
hume-bundle.title: 7. Being for Red
hume-bundle.relation: Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.

hume-bundle.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
hume-bundle.title: 2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!
hume-bundle.relation: Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.

hume-bundle.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
hume-bundle.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
hume-bundle.relation: Nisley applies Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence — built from resemblance, constancy, 'force and vivacity,' and testimony — to 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' where Colonel Harrington, then Clegg Forbes, then Major Gart each cease to exist as memory and corroboration (bartender, girlfriend, general, headlines) collapse layer by layer. 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's speakeasy reunion with his dead wife Laura shows the imagination feigning the uninterrupted existence of a person whose constancy and vivacity no longer match his memories, so the senses and memory are exposed as no foundation for rational belief in continued existence.

hume-bundle.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
hume-bundle.title: 4. Can We Do Enough Good
hume-bundle.relation: Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.

hume-bundle.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
hume-bundle.title: Liz Lemon and High School The More Things Change, the More They Don’t
hume-bundle.relation: Shores uses Jack's cookie jar collection and his fiftieth-birthday home movies in 'Apollo, Apollo', plus Liz's catastrophic high-school reunion in 'Reunion', to examine personal identity over time. Hume's bundle theory denies any self beyond a flux of perceptions, Whitehead offers three senses of a person over time, and Augustine locates past, present, and future in the mind as memory, sight, and expectation, which explains why Jack cannot recover his tenth-birthday joy by buying the Apollo Lunar Module toy yet feels 'like a kid' after laughing until he vomits. Ryle's 'elusiveness of I' and Rousseau on happiness as a fleeting state frame the conclusion that we continually reinterpret the past from the present, so the self is a stretched-out temporal continuity.

hume-bundle.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
hume-bundle.title: A Dilemma
hume-bundle.relation: The chapter asks 'Is your cookie you?', running theories of personal identity through Black Mirror's copies: the soul theory surfaces when Clayton signs away his 'digital self'; Locke's memory theory implies Cookie-Greta is Greta - a reductio, since one person cannot be wholly in two places at once (the same problem for Ashley Too and the thousand Hang the DJ simulations) - and the perdurantist patch recasts Greta and her cookie as time-slices of one four-dimensional person. Physical theories (Olson's animalism, Unger's brain-essentialism) rule out survival by upload, so Yorkie dies when her body dies even though digital Yorkie continues in San Junipero; Parfit's no-self bundle view and the teletransporter case then dissolve the fear, since there is no ego to lose and ordinary survival is 'about as bad' as being destroyed and replaced by a replica. The upshot: the punishment and immortality plots (Joe's million-year Christmas loop, San Junipero) require cookies to be both conscious and psychologically connected in the right way, and the episodes' horror depends on leaving that genuinely uncertain.

hume-bundle.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
hume-bundle.title: 4. Can We Do Enough Good
hume-bundle.relation: Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?

hume-bundle.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
hume-bundle.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.

hume-bundle.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
hume-bundle.title: The Office and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.

hume-bundle.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
hume-bundle.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
hume-bundle.relation: Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.

hume-bundle.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
hume-bundle.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
hume-bundle.relation: Nisley reads 'And When the Sky Was Opened' through Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence: Colonel Forbes's conviction that Harrington exists rests on memory's force and vivacity, and when testimony collapses (newspaper headlines, the bartender, his girlfriend, the general) the three spacemen are erased one by one, 'no longer part of the memory of man.' 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's belief that the woman in the speakeasy is his dead Laura is the imagination's feigned continuity, a resemblance across interrupted perceptions rather than a rational foundation. Memory alone, the chapter concludes, never grounds our beliefs that things or persons persist unperceived.

hume-bundle.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
hume-bundle.title: P A R T T H R E E
hume-bundle.relation: James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.

hume-bundle.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
hume-bundle.title: 2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!
hume-bundle.relation: De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.

hume-bundle.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
hume-bundle.title: Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall
hume-bundle.relation: Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.

hume-bundle.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
hume-bundle.title: Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X
hume-bundle.relation: LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.

hume-bundle.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
hume-bundle.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
hume-bundle.relation: Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.

hume-bundle.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
hume-bundle.title: 7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young
hume-bundle.relation: Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).

hume-bundle.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
hume-bundle.title: “So You Can Be My ‘John G.’”
hume-bundle.relation: Eberl asks whether Leonard Shelby is morally culpable for killing Teddy, since the Leonard who tattoos the false clue and the Leonard who pulls the trigger are sundered by anterograde amnesia. Locke's forensic, memory-based concept of personhood suggests the shooting Leonard is not the same person as the one who set the trap, while Aquinas's analysis of concomitant, consequent, and antecedent ignorance makes Leonard culpable for deliberately willing his own ignorance yet not for the amnesiac moment of the killing itself. Hume's causal criterion of psychological continuity explains why Leonard can still rationally set a goal for his future self by making Teddy his 'John G.' The chapter closes on Aristotle: Leonard's ease in framing an innocent man betrays a corrupted moral character built on habit, and by turning himself into a 'living instrument'—Aristotle's definition of a slave—he has traded his dignity for the telos of an endless revenge quest.

hume-bundle.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
hume-bundle.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
hume-bundle.relation: Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.

hume-bundle.book: 284 - College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits
hume-bundle.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
hume-bundle.relation: This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.

hume-bundle.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
hume-bundle.title: Who is Who
hume-bundle.relation: On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'

hume-bundle.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
hume-bundle.title: 26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion
hume-bundle.relation: The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
fate-vs-free-will.title: Fate, Freedom, and Foreknowledge
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Schick opens with the Morpheus-Neo exchange on Fate ('I don't like the idea that I'm not in control of my life') and Cypher's 'You call this free?', arguing that whatever freedom the enslaved enjoy outside the Matrix may be equally illusory: if the Oracle's prophecies are true, the future is fixed, and then no one, not even Neo, is in control of his life. He poses the subversive question of whether Cypher's return to happy slavery was really a betrayal, and sets out to examine the natures of fate and freedom.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
fate-vs-free-will.title: Unknown
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Schick parallels the film's Oracle with Delphi - tripod beside the oven's fumes, 'Know Thyself' inscribed at both shrines, the cigarette a wink at the priestesses' smoke - and recalls Alexander the Great's forced prophecy and Oedipus as emblems of belief in fate. He then introduces Richard Taylor's corrected fatalism, 'whatever happens is unavoidable' rather than events fated no matter what anyone does, and grants that given the Oracle's accuracy, fatalism is an eminently reasonable view to hold about the world of The Matrix.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
fate-vs-free-will.title: Unknown
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Schick presses the Oracle's foreknowledge into the classic theological dilemma: if she knows Neo will knock over the vase - as she correctly foresaw that and the fates of Morpheus, Trinity, and Neo himself - then it must happen, and no one is free; the price of omniscience is freedom. He walks through Boethius's formulation of the incompatibility, Calvin's predestination of lives fixed like film frames, and the Aquinas-style rejoinder that omnipotence and omniscience extend only to the logically possible, leaving the Oracle's own noodle-baker - would you still have broken it if I hadn't said anything? - and the worry that even predictability by psychological law would doom free will.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
fate-vs-free-will.title: Unknown
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The chapter argues that the Oracle's predictions come true not because the future is fixed but because they are self-fulfilling: her remark about the vase is what brings about its breaking ('would you still have broken it if I hadn't said anything?'), and Morpheus's 'she told you exactly what you needed to hear' shows she shapes rather than reads the future. On this reading the Oracle needs no real foreknowledge, only believers who trust that she knows the path. Only so can Neo be in control of his life in a world where 'anything, within the bounds of reason, is possible.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
fate-vs-free-will.title: Unknown
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Locating the Matrix's power in the fear of death - Neo frozen on the ledge, then discovering in the jump program that he must 'let it all go... fear, doubt, and disbelief' - the chapter reads 'the body cannot live without the mind' as meaning that even outside the Matrix the body depends on the mind's beliefs. The Oracle's either/or prophecy embodies the postulates: Neo's Fate is fulfilled through free choice (his life for Morpheus's) and through faith in our own Potential, so the God or savior we postulate is finally revealed as an extension of ourselves as we transcend separateness, not a separate miracle-worker.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
fate-vs-free-will.title: Unknown
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The chapter presents the subway confrontation as the film's turning point: defying the crew's iron rule that one runs from Agents, and Cypher's 'realistic' sneering, Neo freely accepts death to save Morpheus, overcoming the fundamental fear that grounds the Matrix's power in both worlds. The Oracle's 'next life' prophecy is then fulfilled to the letter when Trinity - 'I'm not afraid anymore... you can't be dead. Because I love you' - refuses to believe in death, and Neo returns in his next life as the One.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Thomas Hibbs reads the Quest's ending as providential: the Ring is destroyed against Frodo's own will at the Cracks of Doom, through Gollum, exactly as Gandalf hinted when he said Bilbo was 'meant' to find the Ring, 'and not by its maker'. Providence first appears as chance - Bilbo's arrival, Aragorn's landing at the Pelennor, Gandalf 'sent back' until his task is done - and is discerned only in hindsight as the epic's dramatic unity. Against the worry that providence cancels freedom, he uses Kant on duty and dignity (Frodo's 'I will take the Ring', Sam's 'I must see it through', set against Denethor ruling his 'own end'), while noting Tolkien rejects Kant's autonomy/heteronomy split, and with Augustine he treats evil as parasitic, able only to mar itself ('Oft evil will shall evil mar').

fate-vs-free-will.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
fate-vs-free-will.title: Fallible Prophecies
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Credits Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed and builds a sevenfold taxonomy of how a Seer might access the future, from fallible sensory prediction like Trelawney's and Muggle weather reports, through glimpses of likely or possible futures as Dumbledore describes, to infallible access to a deterministic or actual future. The section then asks which kind Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
fate-vs-free-will.title: Self-Fulfilling Prophecies
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Reads Dumbledore's gloss on the prophecy, 'you are free to choose your way, quite free to turn your back on the prophecy', as treating even real prophecies as non-compelling, and argues the two true prophecies cannot be mere likelihoods because they are involuntary trances with a magical source. Trelawney's card-reading episodes in Half-Blood Prince, accurate while she is oblivious to Harry behind the statue and to the lightning-struck tower, hint at inconsistent unconscious access to the future.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
fate-vs-free-will.title: Destiny
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Examines Dumbledore's suggestion that the first prophecy was self-fulfilling: it did not originally mean Harry rather than Neville, but Voldemort's choice of the half-blood he saw himself in marked Harry as his equal, and Snape's ejection from the interview left Voldemort ignorant of the risk that attacking Harry would transfer power to him. Invoking Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus prophecy, the section argues a genuine prophecy reveals rather than causes the future, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish Trelawney's real predictions, since the prophecy never made Voldemort do anything.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
fate-vs-free-will.title: A Rodent’s Destiny
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Takes Rowling's 2007 remark that there is 'no such thing as destiny' and maps the logical space it could occupy: compatibilist freedom within a predetermined course, libertarian freedom with a fixed future of true statements about what will happen, or an open future where claims about free choices are neither true nor false until made. The section asks whether Dumbledore means prophecies do not compel anyone or that their content is merely one of several possible futures.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
fate-vs-free-will.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Argues Trelawney's second prophecy, that the servant will break free and rejoin the Dark Lord that very night, was far too improbable to be a merely likely prediction given how easily Wormtail's escape could have failed. Likewise the chain running from the first prophecy through Wormtail becoming Secret-Keeper to Lily's protective sacrifice shows the 'real' prophecies need a stronger connection to the actual future than probability.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
