fate-vs-free-will.relation: Defends a fixed-time theory from the Prisoner of Azkaban time-travel episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and Buckbeak and Sirius are saved without anything changing, while acknowledging Hermione's warnings about wizards killing their past selves complicate the picture, and adds special relativity's absence of an absolute present as further support. The section then argues that the sheer improbability of the luck fulfilling the prophecies, the Myrtle's-bathroom Polyjuice chain, Felix Felicis, the capture that delivers Griphook, and Harry's arrival at the Shrieking Shack, makes better sense with something like divine providence guiding events than with pure chance.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
fate-vs-free-will.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
fate-vs-free-will.title: “This One a Long Time Have I Watched”
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Eberl argues that Anakin and Luke are radically free despite the Chosen One prophecy and Obi-Wan's 'you cannot escape your destiny.' Borrowing Augustine and Aquinas on God's eternity, he holds that foreknowledge (like the Jedi prophecy fulfilled when Vader destroys the Emperor) does not compel events - Anakin's choice makes the prophecy true, not vice versa - and applies Aristotle's tomorrow's-sea-battle to future-contingents like Obi-Wan's self-surrender on the Death Star. Using Locke's locked-room example and Augustine's account of 'inordinate desire,' he concludes that Anakin's fall stems from his own disordered will to control fate ('learn to stop people from dying'), while Han Solo embodies libertarian alternative possibilities ('No mystical energy field controls my destiny').

fate-vs-free-will.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Starts from Narnia's time discrepancies (hours in the wardrobe, reigns of years that cost seconds in England, 1303 Narnian years in one) and shows Einstein's relativity makes different time frames plausible before admitting science cannot explain Aslan's 'I call all times soon'. It interprets that claim through Boethius's doctrine of God's timelessness, the eternal present embracing all moments as a simultaneous whole, and defends its compatibility with creaturely free choice: not even Aslan can override the Dwarfs' self-imprisoned perception or force Uncle Andrew to hear him. The chapter closes on the end of Narnian time in The Last Battle, Father Time making an end, and Aslan's timeless country as the fuller reality the temporal world shadowed.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
fate-vs-free-will.title: Look Up, Look Up
fate-vs-free-will.relation: James Spiegel reads Dylan's God-haunted songwriting through philosophy of religion, sorting strong Augustinian-Aquinian providence ("Every Grain of Sand," "When He Returns") from the weak, risk-taking God of "Highway 61 Revisited" and "Joey." Dylan's moral judgmentalism combined with theological determinism makes him a compatibilist in Augustine's mold, while "Disease of Conceit" and "Pressing On" ("it run in my vein") press the compatibilist puzzle that Plantinga's libertarian power of contrary choice is meant to solve. Original sin becomes the "disease of conceit," and Socrates' Phaedo plus Kant's three postulates - God, freedom, immortality - ground Dylan's hope that "death is not the end," closing with Love and Theft's "Look up, look up."

fate-vs-free-will.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
fate-vs-free-will.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Feldman tests Harley's 'Great American Freedom Machine' slogan against each conception of freedom: metaphysical freedom (universal causation, divine foreknowledge, fate) cannot depend on your vehicle; legal freedom actually shrinks for riders through helmet mandates and extra licensing; and circumstantial freedom is gained equally by any vehicle, a wheelchair being the true freedom machine. Borrowing Socrates' comparison method from the Philebus, he argues the alleged 'feeling of freedom' is really a feeling of happiness or exhilaration combined with the false belief that one is freer than a Camry driver. What really binds him to his 1986 FXRT is fun, the thrill of leaning to the edge, and the sensory and historical pleasures of the air-cooled V-twin line back to the Silent Grey Fellow, which have nothing to do with freedom.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
fate-vs-free-will.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Pierce asks what kind of prophecies Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are, starting from Aristotle's problem of future contingents and Alexander of Aphrodisias on self-fulfilling prophecy: Dumbledore's point that Voldemort's choice marked Harry shows the prophecy did not cause its own fulfillment. The Prisoner of Azkaban time travel — later Harry had always cast that Patronus — plus special relativity support a fixed future on which Rowling's denial of destiny amounts only to libertarian openness, and the chapter concludes that the wildly improbable luck fulfilling the prophecies (Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, the Sword of Gryffindor) makes best sense if some providential being is quietly guiding events.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
fate-vs-free-will.title: Free to Be You and Me
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Bryan Barker reconciles Cylon programming and human 'destiny' with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's intelligible character: Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama under activation, Baltar's cowardly conversion to the Cylon God, Tigh's decision to stay at his post upon learning he is a Cylon, and Starbuck's flight into the storm in 'Maelstrom' all express innate, unchanging character rather than external compulsion. Even destiny, as in Leoben's prophecies to Starbuck, works like determinism unless reframed as character. On this view we are free because everything we do manifests who we immutably are, whether that character is programmed or born.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
fate-vs-free-will.title: Tomorrow Is Yesterday
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Uses the Bajoran Prophets, who experience no linear time ('What is this... time?'), to frame a tour of time's metaphysics: Newton's absolute container versus Leibniz's relationism (the incoherence of a 'temporal vacuum'), Augustine's mind-dependent time (illustrated by 'The Inner Light' and O'Brien's implanted prison years in 'Hard Time'), and McTaggart's argument that neither the A-series nor the B-series can account for change, illustrated by Tasha Yar's death in 'Skin of Evil' and Kirk's Liar-paradox victories over Nomad and Norman. The chapter defends the A-series via tense, then weighs presentism — which would make 'Tomorrow Is Yesterday' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' impossible — against eternalism, whose fatalism Data embraces when his severed head turns up in 'Time's Arrow' ('It has occurred. It will occur.'), and which finally makes sense of prophets who see the future in 'Destiny.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
fate-vs-free-will.title: “Livin’ and Dyin’ in Three-Quarter Time”
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Randall Auxier uses Buffett's catalog to think about fortune and fate, reading Buffett's bold career moves (walking out on Nashville for the beach, later annexing it via 'It's Five o'Clock Somewhere') through Machiavelli's advice to marry Fortuna and master her tricks with virtù. Against Aristotle's demanding answer that only aretē, moral excellence, defends happiness against bad luck, he takes Vico's middle path: natural causes, moral causes, and the occasions of fortune are gathered under providence, so Buffett's seaplane crash ('God, Buddha, St. Christopher, my guardian angel... luck, and the United States Navy water-survival training') shows any fate can be turned to good ends for others. Sorting Buffett's songs into places, times, meetings, sentiments, and thoughts — the key sentiment being the wistful — the chapter lands on contentment as gratitude: being 'livin' and dyin' in three-quarter time.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Robison measures Pullman's Authority against the three attributes that make the Christian God worthy of worship and finds it fails all three: the suffering of intercision victims like Tony Makarios and the Authority's delegation to the malevolent Metatron defeat omnibenevolence, because unlike with the real God we know no free-will theodicy applies, since the Authority simply does not care; his ignorance of Lyra's destiny (which witches and the Consistorial Court learn long before he does) defeats omniscience; and his demented weeping in the crystal litter before dissolving in open air defeats omnipotence. Since the Authority never created the universe and lied about being its creator, he is not God at all, so Pullman's plot never refutes the God of the philosophers. What the books do establish, she argues, is a powerful attack on organized religion: the Magisterium's suppression of Dust research and harming of children mirror real religious institutions' punishment of Galileo, resistance to evolution, and persecution of dissenters.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
fate-vs-free-will.title: A New Path
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Marcus Giamatti narrates his upbringing as an 'Old School' fan under 'Dame Mutability,' his father's personification of the certainty that the Red Sox would always break New England's heart through Bucky Dent, Mookie Wilson, Calvin Schiraldi and Aaron Boone. He argues that being born a Sox fan is an inescapable duty and lifelong quest whose real payoff is not a pennant but the character, faith and perseverance built by enduring, so that when he lay curled up ready to quit during Game Four of the 2004 ALCS, Millar's walk, Roberts's steal and Mueller's single vindicated the whole method. He ends by vowing to pass this philosophy of survival to his unborn daughter Ophelia in Southern California, applying the one-pitch-at-a-time discipline to acting, music and life.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
fate-vs-free-will.title: Red Sox Future
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
fate-vs-free-will.title: Intending the Way Out
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Stages the paradox of foreknowledge through Paul's prescient dream of meeting Chani and his futile struggle against the foreseen jihad: since knowledge (on Plato's justified-true-belief account) is factive, a known future seems unalterable. It tests the classic escapes—Boethius's God in ever-present eternity and Aquinas's seeing all time 'under the aspect of eternity,' Laplace's demon, Richard Taylor's fatalism—and finds the Atreides oracles are no gods, only probabilistic predictors whose visions fix the possibilities they see. The way out is Anscombe's Intention: like God knowing creation because He authored it, Paul and Leto know their futures practically, as agents whose intentions help decide which possibilities become actual, so freedom survives as terrific responsibility.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
fate-vs-free-will.title: In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . .
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Continues the earlier defense of oracular freedom ('Curse of the Golden Path'): because an oracle's gaze from a present moment fixes the very set of future possibilities, Paul and Leto are free precisely where they are blind—above all in their 'vision-battle' in the Tanzerouft, which no oracle can foresee, and which Paul's single whispered 'Don't' concedes to his son's Golden Path. Leto's breeding of Siona, invisible to prescience, is read as his deliberate self-blinding—'the price of freedom is an invigilance of eternity'—and the whole affair vindicates heroism as steering probabilities rather than escaping fate. Paul emerges as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense, whose hamartia is his all-too-human refusal to become a monster to save the future.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Pre-Crime and Pre-Punishment
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Frames 'Minority Report' with Nietzsche's charge that men were considered 'free' only so they could be judged and punished, and with Anselm's De Concordia, where God, outside time, foreknows our choices without determining them. Pre-Crime can punish Anderton and the pre-criminals now only because their not-yet-made choices are treated as absolutely free, and the 1954 context — HUAC, Hoover's anonymous accusations, the Communist Control Act — shows people punished for the present guilt of a future crime.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: 04. What about Leaks
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section weighs leaking predictions to pre-criminals so they can reroute (the I-future), and rejects it for three reasons: the precogs' predictions are accurate only for people who never learn of them, standing by to catch a forewarned killer is costly, and would-be murderers have no right to know, since unlike a citizen facing contaminated water they could have avoided their path by not choosing it. It closes the guide's case that Precrime arrests people who deserve arrest, with appropriate attitudes and compelling evidence, without violating rights.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Chapter 21 - Knowing Tomorrow While Choosing Today
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sara Worley's introduction frames Minority Report and 'Adjustment Team' as versions of the classic free will problem: if precogs foresee my crime before I commit it, or the Adjustment Team knows what I will do, my action seems already settled, like a sunflower's turn toward the sun. Influence alone does not cancel freedom, since we can do otherwise where plants cannot, but foreknowledge threatens exactly that, the same quandary long posed by an omniscient God who already knows every action we will perform.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Freedom and Prediction
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section distinguishes two models of foreknowledge: prediction, as when you confidently predict that sci-fi-loving Jill will skip the John Wayne retrospective, and Molina's 'middle knowledge' of how each person will respond to various circumstances. It then argues prediction can be certain only if character and circumstances guarantee the outcome, the way facts and laws fix where Mars will appear, which would leave no alternatives to choose; so on the predictive model, infallible foreknowledge and the ability to do otherwise cannot coexist.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Outside of Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: This section presents the Boethian-Anselmian alternative: God is outside time, so nothing is past, present, or future for him; all events are eternally laid out for him simply to 'look' at, rather than learn about past events from fossils or future ones from predictions. On this model God has no foreknowledge strictly speaking, and his seeing Jill buy her ticket no more constrains her choice than my watching someone choose would make them unfree.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Prediction, or Sight
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section tests both models against the stories and finds 'sight' incoherent: the precogs foresee murders that never happen, the Adjustment Bureau tracks two incompatible previsions per circumstance, and a precog genuinely seeing the actual future would generate an oscillating loop in which her own report makes the prevision false. Prediction fits instead: the adjusters tweak Mr. Douglas's cautious character in 'Adjustment Team,' and Anderton's three discrepant predictions in 'The Minority Report' track how leaked information changes his circumstances and motivation to kill Kaplan.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Perfect or Probabilistic
fate-vs-free-will.relation: This section argues predictive foresight is compatible with freedom only if probabilistic, yet Precrime treats its predictions as certain, arresting people for what they will rather than might do. Lisa's doubts in 'The Minority Report' turn out to concern incomplete information rather than free will, while The Adjustment Bureau dramatizes freedom differently: the adjusters work by making the preferred path easiest, but David and Elise's three-year persistence shows that those who 'fight' for their free will get it, leaving open how predictable we really are.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: I Can Predict What You (Don’t) Do Next Summer
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Using Bergson's imprevisible and 'The Possible and the Real', this section argues that the story's Precrime works by prediction-as-elimination: investigators discard the precogs' babblings that do not fit the world, 'closing the gate' on the impossible to leave only a statistically possible future. Bergson's gate metaphor shows prediction never yields the real future, only the negatively 'not impossible', yet Precrime arrests people for an abstract possible event they have never actually lived. It ends by asking whether Anderton, accused of a future murder in advance, would still commit it, since ever-changing memory and knowledge make a possible future never identical to the actual one.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Summarizing the Future
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Applying Bergson's Time and Free Will claim that recalling the past shortens it into a 'thing', the section uses the curriculum-vitae metaphor: like a CV or Facebook page, we imagine the future as a summary compiled from the past. In 'Paycheck', Jennings's sack becomes a plan only when he reflects - the wire at the police station, the token on the bus - until past, present and future fuse and he feels 'a strange elation' at fulfilling his past self's design, raising again whether awareness of the future changes what we do. The film diverges by having Jennings sabotage the atomic-bomb future he foresees, echoing Minority Report's contest between an inevitable future and present action.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
fate-vs-free-will.title: Chapter 26 - The Day Roosevelt Was Assassinated
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Peter Simons opens Chapter 26 with the real 1933 Zangara shooting that missed President-elect Roosevelt by inches and killed mayor Anton Cermak, then asks the counterfactual question: what if Zangara had hit, as happens in the divergence launching The Man in the High Castle, the 1962 Hugo winner? Dick's epigraph about chance, accident and 'one great figure... strategically placed' frames whether anyone can alter fate. The section positions the novel within Dick's alternate-reality work (Minority Report's possible futures, 'The Golden Man', The Divine Invasion) as the one book that fully immerses the reader in a single alternate history.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
fate-vs-free-will.title: Chapter 1 - The Glimmer Twins
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Randall E. Auxier opens his chapter on the Jagger-Richards collaboration by musing that certain pairs seem 'ordained by the gods' to stay entangled for life, calling Mick and Keith 'destiny's children' who grew up a Stone's throw apart in Dartford. He admits he cannot quite believe in destiny yet claims to have seen cosmic entanglement first hand, and he poses the counterfactual of the two boys taking different buses on the day their collaboration began — a world with no Rolling Stones. The section frames the chapter's question of whether their life-long creative entanglement was inevitable or, as he punningly insists, evitable.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
fate-vs-free-will.title: Just as Every Cop Is a Criminal, and All the Sinners Saints
fate-vs-free-will.relation: This section lays out Augustine's journey from the Manichean two-gods heresy, through reading Plato, to the view of evil as an 'absence' rather than a force. Its core is the dilemma of Confessions 7.3: if God is wholly good, who sowed the 'seed of bitterness' — the wicked will — into us, and who made the devil? Augustine's answer runs through original sin (the pride of Adam and Eve, demons as fallen angels) and an awkward compromise on which humans are free yet constrained by predestination, so that evil becomes necessary — and confession itself a good.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
fate-vs-free-will.title: Please Allow Me to Introduce Myself
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section tells how Bulgakov's novel, begun in 1928, stifled by Stalin, and published in English only in 1967, reached Jagger through Faithfull in 1968. It summarizes the opening: Satan disguised as Professor Woland interrupts two Moscow atheists, savages the literary elite's vanity and secularism, and argues in explicitly Augustinian, predestinarian terms that man cannot even vouch for his own tomorrow — in a Russia so Godless it takes the Devil himself to restore belief, since everyone, Devil included, is part of the divine plan.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
fate-vs-free-will.title: And I Was ’Round when Jesus Christ Had His Moment of Doubt and Pain
fate-vs-free-will.relation: This section follows the novel-within-the-novel — the Master's gospel of Yeshua Ha-Nozri before a reluctant Pilate, with Matthew the Levite embellishing the miracles — and its frame: Margarita's masked ball of the risen dead, Berlioz's talking severed head, and God's final order to Woland granting the lovers peace and forgiving even Pilate. Bulgakov thus agrees with Augustine that evil exists yet all of us carry good that can unite with the Divine by turning from the material world; his Satan, operating 'like an employee of a large organization' inside God's constraints, is why we naturally have sympathy for this Devil.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
fate-vs-free-will.title: But What’s Puzzling You Is the Nature of My Game
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section situates the song after the 1967 Redlands Bust and amid 1968's collapses — Paris riots, Vietnam, Bobby Kennedy's assassination, which forced the lyric change from 'Who killed Kennedy?' to 'Who killed the Kennedys?' the night before a recording session. Against both Augustine and Bulgakov, it argues Jagger's Devil is far more human and unpredestined: by demanding we 'guess my name', the song fingers us as Satan, tracing the world's malice to our own impulses rather than any divinely scripted plan.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
fate-vs-free-will.title: I Tell You One Time, You’re to Blame
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The closing section follows the song's aftermath through Godard's session film — Brian Jones inaudible in his booth as a Dylanesque draft turns into a 'rocking samba' — to Jones's death, the Altamont killing (shown by Gimme Shelter to have happened during 'Under My Thumb', not 'Sympathy'), and the end of Mick and Marianne. Its verdict: Augustine's narrow, predestined free will leaves humanity out of the picture, while Jagger's human Devil puts responsibility back on us — a world without the Stones would be less enlightened about evil, and their song 'demands more of us, perhaps, than Augustine's Confessions'.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
fate-vs-free-will.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sienkiewicz takes Klosterman's hyperthetical of a crystal ball showing an unchangeable future in which you are blissfully obsessed with CFL football as a secular version of the traditional Jewish and Christian problem of divine foreknowledge versus human freedom. He offers the 'movie' solution: as when watching the chest-wax scene in The 40-Year-Old Virgin, a vantage point outside the event's time (God's, or yours before the fixed future) can behold it without having scripted it, so foreknowledge and free will remain logically compatible. Since we already live toward the one absolutely certain future, our own deaths, the portal should change nothing about how you act, though you still should not watch a league that plays with only three downs.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
fate-vs-free-will.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Vannatta reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture — the Left Behind novels, Victory TV's Steven, Kurt Warner's Super Bowl, Jesus Camp — as living Puritan Calvinism: original sin (Klosterman's cruel third-graders), justification by faith alone, unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest'), and predestination that leaves uncertain whether our actions matter in the divine equation. The chapter's pivot is truth versus peace: Puritan-born-again certainty sacrifices peace for antecedent truth, from the 1675 Massachusetts settlements to Robertson and Falwell on 9/11. Against this Vannatta sets the pragmatist alternative — truth as the outcome of communal inquiry in service of peaceful living — recasting God as the web of relationships and dissolving his own childhood camp's contradiction between 'I'm Third' and its cult of competition.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
fate-vs-free-will.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sirvent and Baker take Van Alden's 'strong providential theology' - 'his fate rests in God's hands' at the burned Agent Clarkson's bedside - as a live version of the problem of evil, traced through Augustine and Aquinas to Calvin's all-determining divine omnipotence. The Arminian free-will escape leaves God like a parent watching a child run into traffic, and the 'mysterious ways' reply makes God's moral vocabulary so alien that a God who burns his beloved is 'one-sided' and unworshipable - the same theology that lets Van Alden shift blame for Lucy's pregnancy onto a 'charge from God' before drowning Sebso as 'the judgment of the wicked.' They close with Nucky's God, an inner impetus toward good that asks rather than coerces, and with process theology's persuading God, while Gyp Rosetti's Easter rant at the crucifix shows what believing in the omnipotent alternative costs.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Devil and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Devil and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Ray Bossert reads Tolkien's Silmarillion through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy: elves, being artists, understand Melkor not as tempter but as bad artist, from his rebellious solo in the Music of the Ainur to his botched sub-creations - orcs bred from kidnapped elves - and his covetous collecting of the silmarils. Boethius supplies the machinery: evil seeks a good by unnatural means and only approximates it, wickedness debases its practitioner into a beast, God's foreknowledge embraces free choices without causing them, and Providence is a spinning disc at whose center alone one is steady - so Melkor's rebellion leaves him less free, dragged around the rim. Tolkien's contrast between art (for beauty) and magic (for control) explains why the Devil can only mimic creation, never make anything real.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
fate-vs-free-will.title: Homeland and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Trip McCrossin reads Carrie's 'I missed something once before... everyone's not me' as the modern, secular problem of evil: as Susan Neiman argues, unreasonable suffering threatens reason itself, and the Rousseau-Voltaire split defines the responses. Carrie takes Rousseau's side - 'All is good leaving the hands of the author of things' degenerates in human hands, so evil is intelligible and redemption possible, the chance at redemption she offers Brody and even Nazir - against Voltaire's Candide-style tending of the garden. The finale deepens this with Boethius's Consolation: Carrie's 'I believe one of the reasons I was put on this Earth was for our paths to cross' fuses fate with providence, and she accepts Brody's execution as a redemptive end 'more so if he dies'.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
fate-vs-free-will.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Miller argues from Jake's croak dream, the Cosmic Owl, and the Dungeon Train's future crystal that Ooo's future is real, visible, and changeable—hence a case of soft determinism: the dream of Jake dying in space is what caused Finn to accompany him and avert it, so the only being who could have intended the change, the Owl, is the sole certain free agent in Ooo. Every alternate Finn is missing his right arm—Shoko the thief, Farmworld Finn, pillow-world Finn, the Dungeon Train elder—hinting at an epic destiny, yet Finn altered the train future once he saw where it led Jake. The chapter closes on the open question of whether choosing one's fate differs from having it thrust on one, since every choice is caused by the past no one can change.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
fate-vs-free-will.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Christopher Ketcham's mock lost episode 'Charlie Gets Beatified' - in which Frank fakes a water-into-wine miracle with red food dye so the Gang can monetize Charlie's canonization - frames a genuine exercise in medieval modal metaphysics. Aristotle's definition of contingency, on which opposites can occur only at different times, is set against Duns Scotus's view that something can be otherwise at the very moment it acts, so that God's immutable foreknowledge coexists with a will 'endowed with something of his own freedom'. The chapter spells out necessity, contingency, and impossibility in possible-worlds terms (a gang needs at least two members in every world; Frank is impossible in Season One) and reads 'Gun Fever Too: Still Hot' as empirical confirmation of Scotus and Olivi: the Gang holds opposite positions within a single episode, proving real contingency and free will.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
fate-vs-free-will.title: 7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
fate-vs-free-will.title: 8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
fate-vs-free-will.title: 18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
fate-vs-free-will.title: 19. Prophetic Foreknowledge in Game of Thrones
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Rennick argues that true prophecy threatens no one's freedom: a true prophecy merely reports the future the way a true history book reports the past - Jojen sees Jon among the wildlings because Jon chose as he chose, not the reverse - while fallible, misread prophecies (Melisandre mistaking Alys Karstark for Arya, the Stallion prophecy dying with Rhaego) constrain even less. Self-fulfilling prophecies like Azor Ahai actually demonstrate agency, since Stannis and Melisandre's belief in the prophecy brings the events about, and even infallible foreknowledge of a choice - 'you will watch season seven' - leaves open the alternate Westeros where you did otherwise, the standard reply to the God's-foreknowledge problem applied to green dreams and flames.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
fate-vs-free-will.title: 21. A Naughty Little Puppet, but Still a Puppet
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Deadpool's Killogy realization that the 'progenitors' puppeteer him becomes a tour of fatalism's three classic puppet masters: Aristotle's sea-battle argument from On Interpretation that truths about the future are already fixed, Augustine's problem of an all-knowing God whose foreknowledge (like Cullen Bunn's scripts) seems to cancel free choice, and the causal closure of the laws of nature, reinforced by Benjamin Libet's brain-activity experiments. Because cutting the strings of logic, God, or physics is impossible - 'you can hack away forever and never find the beginning . . . or the end' - the chapter concludes that the audience is no freer than Wade. The surviving Deadpool copes by embracing the absurdity of a scripted existence.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
fate-vs-free-will.title: 25. Deadpool Kills God
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
fate-vs-free-will.title: 8. Is It Free Will If You Pay for It
fate-vs-free-will.relation: John Karavitis contrasts the novel, where Frank, Juliana, and Tagomi treat the I Ching oracle as alive, infallible, and inescapable even though its hexagrams are cast at random, with the TV series, where Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' asserts that choice shapes reality. After reviewing Laplace's demon, quantum uncertainty, and Libet's experiments, it concludes that the show's world, unlike the novel's fatalism, teaches us to act as the authors of our own futures, with John Smith's self-made rise the starkest exercise of free will.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
fate-vs-free-will.title: 1. Lost in Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Rard applies David Lewis's definition of time travel — a discrepancy between the journey's duration and externally elapsed time — to argue that the suspended-animation gold thieves of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' never time-traveled, while Flight Lieutenant Decker in 'Last Flight' does, creating a consistent causal loop in which his 1959 knowledge that he saved Mackaye is what sends him back to 1917 to save him. She then reads 'No Time Like the Past' as enacting the impossibility of changing the past: Paul Driscoll's attempt to shoot Hitler is thwarted by a maid and SS officers exactly as Lewis's 'bananas peel' account predicts, and his retreat to 1881 Homeville makes him the unwitting cause of the very schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent — his foreknowledge, not fate, was always the cause.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
fate-vs-free-will.title: 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Schiltz tests Janet's claim to know 'literally everything' against the philosophical definition of omniscience as believing all true propositions, finding she lacks knowledge of Michael's demonhood, of the future, and of current events on Earth. Divine-omniscience puzzles drawn from Averroes and Aquinas, and Boethius's solution that God sees all things in an eternal present, frame why Janet's ignorance of the future is what protects the characters' free will and moral responsibility. Frank Jackson's Mary thought experiment illuminates Judge Gen's failure to know what human life is like, and Janet's gradual acquisition of empathy across her reboots shows why her imperfect knowledge is a feature rather than a glitch.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
fate-vs-free-will.title: 8. Time Travel and the Problem of Evil
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Ray Bossert reads Endgame through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, arguing that Doctor Strange and Tony Stark, who permit the Snap and five years of suffering for the sake of the one winning outcome, run 'uncannily parallel' to Thanos, who decided for Gamora that her unwilling death served the greater good. Strange's viewing of 14,000,605 futures illustrates Boethius's distinction between an infinite being riding along the timeline and an eternal one seeing all moments at once, and the refusal to tell Stark his role mirrors why God's foreknowledge sees our choices without compelling them. Boethius's providence weaving free choices into justice, the Avengers' passion-driven failures on Titan (Star-Lord and Thor avenging lost lovers), justice as the wicked's own punishment (Thanos dying wretched twice in one film), and Umberto Eco's 'Myth of Superman' all frame a universe where suffering is allowed because it is woven into a pattern that ends in justice.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
fate-vs-free-will.title: 21. I Plucked My Soul Out of Its Secret Place
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Traces the Soul Stone across comics and film — Thanos courting Death, the Vormir 'a soul for a soul' trade of Gamora, and Natasha's parallel sacrifice for Clint in Endgame — reading it through sacrifice and resurrection motifs from the Binding of Isaac and asking why the film's Thanos must complete the offering Abraham was spared. It contrasts Thanos, who styles himself a god but is a 'false god,' an idol beside the sentient being that existed before all realities and became the six Infinity Gems, with Adam Warlock, who dwells in the Soul World and 'knows his soul' (the chapter's title borrows Claude McKay's poem), while Thanos is driven by destiny — 'I ignored my destiny once. I cannot do that again.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
fate-vs-free-will.title: 24. The Left Hand of Thanos
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Reads the Endgame 'I am' exchange through Martin Luther's two hands of God: Thanos's left-handed gauntlet enacts God's 'alien work' of law, judgment and destruction (his 'inevitability,' seen in all 14,000,605 of Strange's futures), while Tony's right-handed snap enacts the 'proper work' of grace, where freedom means relying on a promise — Strange's gift of the Time Stone, the Ancient One resting reality on Banner's promise. It applies the law/grace contrast to Thor's reconciliation with Frigga ('you're going to be the man you're meant to be'), Tony's with Howard, and Steve's gift of the shield to Sam, arguing the heroes' failures at who they were 'supposed to be' are the law's condemnation, while the promise delivers a freedom that turns Thanos's inevitability into impossibility.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
fate-vs-free-will.title: To the Third Power . .
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Wolfe argues the original series is 'deeply Mormon' in ontology though not in epistemology: Kobol anagrams Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve and 'sealing' marriages mirror LDS structure, and the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were; as we are now, you may become' restates Lorenzo Snow's deification couplet, while Count Iblis, like the Mormon Satan, can only rule those who freely yield - agency is supreme. Because none of this is required to follow the show, later licensees could rebuild the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics incoherently (free will violated when inconvenient), Richard Hatch's novels with a new pure-blood-of-Kobol cosmology, and Ronald Moore with a circular 'all this has happened before' replacing eternal progression.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
fate-vs-free-will.title: Final Thoughts
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Squires and McBain argue the ending wrongly necessitates that Booker's baptism must produce Comstock in every possible world, cashing out the necessity in possible-world terms and quoting William James on determinism's closed future. Against this 'God of necessity' they defend a traditional omniscient, omnipresent (panentheist) God whose foreknowledge does not determine choices, citing the justice requirement for free will and the biblical case of Hezekiah's prayer adding twenty years as proof the future stays open. Read this way, Booker never had to become a racist zealot, and the game's shockingly limited ending unfairly reinforces the stereotype that deep religious devotion necessarily leads to extremism.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
fate-vs-free-will.title: Changing Fate or Being Changed by Fate
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Colombo and Jones read Brave through Aristotle's virtue ethics and Heraclitus's 'character is fate': the dispute between Merida and Elinor over 'what is a queen' is whether royalty is a mere position or a character requiring cultivated excellence and habituated 'second nature,' which Elinor's poise displays and Merida's hot temper lacks. Merida's witch's bargain to 'change my fate' only scrambles fortune (turning Elinor into a bear) until she follows the riddle 'mend the bond torn by pride,' replacing pride with empathy — and only then, at the Mor'du confrontation where fate, fortune, and character converge, can it be said her fate was changed rather than she by it.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
fate-vs-free-will.title: Intending the Way Out
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Works through the paradox of foreknowledge: because Paul's Caladan dream of first meeting Chani is knowledge in Plato's justified-true-belief sense, the foreseen future is factive, so his struggle against the jihad he visions (even hoping to die on Feyd-Rautha's blade rather than become a martyr) is futile. It tests the classical escape routes, Boethius's God who views all times as an ever-present eternity and Aquinas's God seeing the whole road 'under the aspect of eternity', and Laplace's Demon's causal determinism, but finds the Atreides oracles unlike God since they are creatures in time who see many possible futures rather than one. The resolution comes through Anscombe's Intention: practical knowledge lets Paul and Leto, whose present choices shift the balance of probability among foreseen timelines, intend their way out as creative authors of events.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
fate-vs-free-will.title: In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . .
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sequel to 'Intending the Way Out': since oracles fix the set of possible futures they see, the single meeting of two Atreides oracles in the Tanzerouft, the vision-battle where Paul's whispered 'Don't' cedes the Golden Path to Leto, shows they are free precisely where each is blind to the other. It reads Paul as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense whose defining flaw is his humanity, and argues that by breeding Siona's prescience-invisibility 'Leto frees himself by blinding himself', so freedom rests on a mixture of knowledge and ignorance, with ordinary intentional actors, not God, as the proper analogue of the oracles.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
fate-vs-free-will.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Nicolas Michaud asks whether the prophesied Four Warriors of Light of Final Fantasy I deserve thanks if the Sage Lukahn's foreknowledge meant they could not do otherwise, framing their plight with the problem of divine foreknowledge and Aquinas's answer that God stands outside time. He then deploys Frankfurt's preemption cases, Garland ready to mind-control you either way, to show moral responsibility can survive without alternative possibilities, but concludes the Warriors may still be unworthy of praise because they know they are predestined, a worry that spreads to us through Phineas Gage-style biological determinism: if our characters are hardwired, neither we nor Garland deserve praise or blame.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
fate-vs-free-will.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The chapter asks whether Daenerys's fatalism - she feels truly free only once she believes fate is in control - can coexist with freedom in a Westeros where class and gender fix everyone's essence. Aristotle's sea-battle argument from bivalence and Cicero's Idle Argument (Dany will rule whether or not she leaves Meereen) are dismantled as having no practical consequences for deliberation, while Sartre's anguish and bad faith explain Cersei's 'necessity' excuse for arresting Ned and Sansa's refusal to own her lie about Joffrey and Mycah. Heidegger's authenticity then resolves the paradox: like Ned choosing between family and honor and Jon choosing his Night's Watch vows over kinship, freedom is not escape from one's past but owning it - Heraclitus's 'character is destiny,' becoming who you are.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
fate-vs-free-will.title: 13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
fate-vs-free-will.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Kind uses John Stewart's Justice League arc, thrown into the future by Chronos, meeting his son Warhawk, and hiding it from Hawkgirl while dating Vixen, to stage fatalism: Pike and Taylor's arguments that a foreknown future, whether God's or a time traveler's, cannot be otherwise. Time travel itself forces a choice between presentism and eternalism, since Warhawk must 'exist now, already, in the future' for GL and Batman to visit him, and Smart's tenseless four-dimensionalism, with GL a series of timeslices and 'now' as subjective as 'here,' dissolves the fatalist worry by banishing tensed facts. The chapter lands on GL's battlefield advice to his son: 'Plant your feet,' owning a fate you cannot escape.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: Varieties of Prophecy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section sets up Jeremy Pierce's chapter by contrasting Trelawney the 'old fraud,' whose tea leaves, tarot, and crystal balls yield elastic generalities and false death forecasts, with the two predictions Dumbledore calls her only 'real predictions,' which McGonagall and the centaur Firenze also treat as different in kind. It asks what distinguishes genuine prophecy from fortune-telling in a world where magic might connect tea leaves or dreams to actual future events.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: Fallible Prophecies
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Crediting Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed, the section distinguishes fallible from infallible prophecies and builds a seven-fold menu of how a Seer could access the future, from fallible sense-based guessing like Muggle weather reports and Trelawney's usual act, through probabilities over possible futures, to infallible access to a deterministic outcome or to the actual fixed future. The question becomes which of these Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: Self-Fulfilling Prophecies
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section argues that Dumbledore treats even the real prophecy as fallible, telling Harry he is 'quite free to turn your back on the prophecy,' which suggests likelihood rather than guarantee. Yet the involuntary trance source, Trelawney's spade readings that fit the hidden Harry she cannot see, and the lightning-struck tower card point to occasional access to possible or fixed futures beyond mere category-1 guessing.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: Destiny
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Testing whether Trelawney's first prophecy was self-fulfilling, the section deploys Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus story, where a prediction that causes its own fulfillment would be the prophet's deed rather than a revelation of what was going to happen. It concludes the prophecy did not make Voldemort attack: he chose Harry as the half-blood he saw himself in, acting on incomplete information from Snape's interrupted eavesdropping, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish real predictions from Trelawney's usual fare.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: A Rodent’s Destiny
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section argues the second real prophecy, about the servant rejoining the Dark Lord that night, cannot be merely 'likely but fallible': Wormtail's escape depended on a chain of improbable contingencies such as Lupin forgetting his Wolfsbane potion and the last-minute switch of Secret-Keeper. The first prophecy likewise required Voldemort to mark Harry through events, from Snape's plea to Lily's sacrifice, that flow from the prophecy itself, so genuine prophecy needs a stronger tie to the actual future than probability.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Johnson asks whether Isaac's paintings and Hiro's visions make the future fated, running Aristotle's sea-battle argument: if propositions about the future are already true (by bivalence and the correspondence theory of a 'written timeline'), then Sylar's exploding New York is inevitable and no one is free. He extends the problem to infallible foreknowledge via Future Hiro as a stand-in for God, considers and rejects Boethius's timeless-knowledge solution, and uses open theism plus a probability calculation about Ando's waffles order to show probabilistic foreknowledge is useless. He concludes most of Isaac's 'prophecies' are really self-fulfilling, as when Noah's efforts to dodge the eighth painting cause his shooting, and that the Heroes universe leaves room to deny fate.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
fate-vs-free-will.title: a19.xhtml
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
fate-vs-free-will.title: Notes
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Eberl applies Augustine's theodicy to the Force: since evil is privation rather than a thing, the dark side is not a real half of the Force but its willful misuse by free beings, answering why a Force with a will permits Alderaan. Anakin's fall is Augustine's inordinate desire (cupiditas) for the temporal good of Padme's life against Yoda's counsel to let go, while Jacen Solo's willingness to kill for peace shows love destroyed rather than merely disordered, placing him beyond the redemption Anakin's rightly ordered love for his children still permits. Free will remains a divine gift whose misuse, not its giver, explains moral evil, and Anakin could still freely fulfill the Chosen One prophecy.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
fate-vs-free-will.title: “I Know All of This Because I Have Done Everything I Can to Get to the Truth”
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Daniel Wack reads Veronica Mars as film noir refashioned for teen television: the class-riven town without a middle class supplies the corrupt noir milieu, but the genre's gender roles are reversed, so Logan becomes the homme fatal whose drunken promise of an 'epic' love offers the redemption-through-romance the femme fatale always dangles and never delivers. Following Cavell and Pippin, he argues the characters are trapped by a fatalism they did not choose — inherited zip codes, Aaron Echolls's abuse, Jake Kane's affair with Lianne — and Logan's dream of a private, redeemed world fails because accepting it would cost Veronica the active, truth-generating detective self she built after her rape. Investigating Lilly's murder, her mother's disappearance, and her own assault, she learns the truth restores nothing, but that detective work gives her a new way to order and survive her world.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
fate-vs-free-will.title: H E N R I B E R G S O N
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
fate-vs-free-will.title: Notes
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Kowalski uses Min Farshaw's visions in the Amazon series to explore whether foreknowledge is compatible with free action, tracing the problem from Aristotle and Cicero through Augustine. He lays out the argument that if Min truly foreknows Tam raising Rand, it must come true and thus seems unfree, then surveys reconciliation projects: Boethius and Aquinas make God timeless so he does not literally foreknow, while Augustine (in the dialogue with Evodius) argues foreknowledge does not cause what is foreknown, so choices explain foreknowledge rather than vice versa. He notes Min is not timeless and her visions are fallible (Mat spears rather than stabs Rand), concluding WoT keeps its characters both free and fated for dramatic tension while offering only 'a semblance of choice.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
fate-vs-free-will.title: Destiny, Fate, and the Law
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Lee separates destiny (an outcome necessary given a person's purpose and character, per Robert Solomon) from fate, then tests three interpretations of free will against the Witcher 1 Glossary entries on Destiny and the Law of Surprise. Hard determinism fails because the Glossary says one can resist Destiny's path 'of one's own free will', and compatibilism (Frankfurt's willing agent) fails because the witcher demanding the Law's reward does not even know what he desires. The three invocations of the Law, Roegner's promising of Pavetta to Duny, Geralt's claims on Ciri via Duny and the merchant Yurga, all leave room for choices that need not have been made, so Lee concludes libertarian freedom in van Inwagen's sense best fits the Witcher world.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
fate-vs-free-will.title: Compatibilism and the Law
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Ralston takes the opposite tack from Lee, arguing the Law of Surprise is best explained by compatibilism: the betrothal banquet in 'Of Banquets, Bastards, and Burials' shows Duny and Pavetta's fated bond fixed in advance yet freely lived out, and Geralt's grudging acceptance of Ciri shows that resisting destiny only narrows his options while accepting it restores his freedom. Drawing on Sara Bizarro's polythetic free will, he casts Geralt as a 'self-winding mechanism' whose fated choices remain voluntary, reasons-responsive, and self-constrained, with Yennefer's abandonment and Ciri's reunion with Geralt as further cases of shared destiny pursued along free paths. The Oedipus myth supplies the ancient parallel: fight the prophecy and you fulfill it.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
fate-vs-free-will.title: No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'

fate-vs-free-will.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Peculiarities of Free Will
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The chapter surveys how Whedon's fiction both dramatizes free choice—Angel answering Whistler's 'you could go either way' challenge, Cordelia reclaiming her visions in 'Birthday,' choices even the Powers That Be cannot predict—and suggests determinism, via the reverse-chronology of The Shepherd's Tale, the self-fulfilling prophecies Flamson identifies, and Topher's 'Everybody's programmed' speech in Dollhouse. It rejects Richardson and Rabb's Shestovian freedom (it implausibly denies that tragic choices between two evils, like Buffy killing re-ensouled Angel in 'Becoming, Part II,' are free) and Flamson's compatibilism (Jasmine's followers do what they want yet plainly lack choice, as Gunn's 'then we'll kick it over and start a new game' speech shows). Robert Kane's libertarianism—undetermined self-forming choices in moments of torn conflict—fits best, illuminating Book's soup-bowl pause, Billy/Dr. Horrible's street-corner hesitation with Penny, and Connor's choice between Darla and faux-Cordelia in 'Inside Out,' though the chapter concedes Whedon may sometimes sacrifice consistency for drama.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
fate-vs-free-will.title: Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
fate-vs-free-will.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
fate-vs-free-will.title: Part Five D Is for Destiny
fate-vs-free-will.relation: This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
fate-vs-free-will.title: NOTES
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.title: Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.title: Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil
fate-vs-free-will.relation: James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
fate-vs-free-will.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
