fate-vs-free-will.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
fate-vs-free-will.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
fate-vs-free-will.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.title: 57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing
fate-vs-free-will.relation: The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.

fate-vs-free-will.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
fate-vs-free-will.title: 86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom
fate-vs-free-will.relation: Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Fate, Freedom, and Foreknowledge
free-will-determinism.relation: Schick opens with the Morpheus-Neo exchange on Fate ('I don't like the idea that I'm not in control of my life') and Cypher's 'You call this free?', arguing that whatever freedom the enslaved enjoy outside the Matrix may be equally illusory: if the Oracle's prophecies are true, the future is fixed, and then no one, not even Neo, is in control of his life. He poses the subversive question of whether Cypher's return to happy slavery was really a betrayal, and sets out to examine the natures of fate and freedom.

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Unknown
free-will-determinism.relation: Schick quotes Nozick's experience-machine passage at length and catalogs the parallels with the Matrix: floating in a tank, electrodes stimulating the brain, experiences indistinguishable from reality, the only difference being that Nozick's users unplug every two years. He rehearses Nozick's three reasons not to plug in - we want to do things rather than merely experience doing them, we want to be a certain sort of person rather than an 'indeterminate blob', and we want contact with a deeper reality - then turns the lesson on the Oracle's world: do the freed make real choices either, or are their choices pre-ordained?

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Unknown
free-will-determinism.relation: This section lays out causal determinism through Laplace's demon: an intelligence that knew every force and every position could compute the entire future, leaving no one free or responsible, so people in the Matrix would be no worse off than we are. It notes that both sides of the nature-nurture debate (including B.F. Skinner) agree behavior is caused by forces beyond our control, and turns to Epicurus, who posited random atomic 'swerves' to make room for free will. Modern quantum indeterminacy, it concludes, likewise expels determinism from physics and at least makes free will possible, though randomness alone cannot ground responsibility.

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Unknown
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter argues that the Oracle's predictions come true not because the future is fixed but because they are self-fulfilling: her remark about the vase is what brings about its breaking ('would you still have broken it if I hadn't said anything?'), and Morpheus's 'she told you exactly what you needed to hear' shows she shapes rather than reads the future. On this reading the Oracle needs no real foreknowledge, only believers who trust that she knows the path. Only so can Neo be in control of his life in a world where 'anything, within the bounds of reason, is possible.'

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Unknown
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter argues that egotism - each individual's spontaneous belief that he is 'the One', the center of the universe for which everything was made - is the fundamental moral error, and that morality demands recognizing our oneness with all intelligent beings. The red pill symbolizes the basic choice between two matrices: the world of separate egos, bodies colliding in space and time under deterministic causality, and the world of human unity and freedom seen from the standpoint of moral consciousness - and the initial choice must then survive a crisis in which its realizability is doubted.

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Unknown
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter reads the film through Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground, a satire of Chernyshevsky's rationalist-utopian What Is to Be Done?: the underground man sees that social science's 'logarithm' of desire reduces us to piano keys governed by natural law, and responds with hyperconscious spite, inertia, and the deliberate choice of the harmful to prove he can will - anticipating Nietzsche's claim that humans would 'rather will nothing than not will'. Shigalyov's 'starting from unlimited freedom, I conclude with unlimited despotism' names the Enlightenment's contradiction, and the underground man's life is the reductio ad nihilum of theories his opponents only dare carry halfway.

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Unknown
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter aligns the Nebuchadnezzar with the underground man's cell: in the 'desert of the real' the rebels begin from Morpheus's felt 'something is wrong' and live the quest ('it's the question that drives us') that The X-Files-style paranoia cannot complete, risking either permanent entrapment or Mark Edmundson's 'facile transcendence'. It contrasts Neo's shallow freedom-as-control ('No... because then I wouldn't be in control') with Morpheus's providential fate, reads Cypher as consciously relinquishing willing for comfort, and likens the Matrix's project of changing 'the human being into a battery' to Diderot's piano-key man and Agent Smith's utopian 'we're the cure'.

free-will-determinism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
free-will-determinism.title: Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.

free-will-determinism.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Uses the show to argue the problem of evil is evidential rather than logical, and tests each theodicy against Sopranos cases: evil as natural-law by-product (Junior's and Jackie's cancers), punishment for sin (Carmela's cancer scare, Ralph telling Father Phil his hospitalized son is God's payback in 'Whoever Did This'), God's higher morality (rejected as meaningless as 'a triangle with four sides'), long-run goods (Artie's restaurant fire), and character-building (rejected with Melfi's 'How many people have to die for your personal growth?'). The free-will defense also fails - God could have given us Meadow-like dispositions - and Tony's 'You're born to this shit' versus Melfi's insistence on genuine choice dramatizes the debate. The chapter ends with Tony as the Old Testament Yahweh writ small: a jealous, vengeful, tribal ruler whose appeal is no more mysterious than His.

free-will-determinism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
free-will-determinism.title: NOTES
free-will-determinism.relation: Defends a fixed-time theory from the Prisoner of Azkaban time-travel episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and Buckbeak and Sirius are saved without anything changing, while acknowledging Hermione's warnings about wizards killing their past selves complicate the picture, and adds special relativity's absence of an absolute present as further support. The section then argues that the sheer improbability of the luck fulfilling the prophecies, the Myrtle's-bathroom Polyjuice chain, Felix Felicis, the capture that delivers Griphook, and Harry's arrival at the Shrieking Shack, makes better sense with something like divine providence guiding events than with pure chance.

free-will-determinism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
free-will-determinism.title: Not His Mother’s Son
free-will-determinism.relation: Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.

free-will-determinism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
free-will-determinism.title: NOTES
free-will-determinism.relation: Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.

free-will-determinism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
free-will-determinism.title: NOTES
free-will-determinism.relation: Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.

free-will-determinism.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
free-will-determinism.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.

free-will-determinism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
free-will-determinism.title: “This One a Long Time Have I Watched”
free-will-determinism.relation: Eberl argues that Anakin and Luke are radically free despite the Chosen One prophecy and Obi-Wan's 'you cannot escape your destiny.' Borrowing Augustine and Aquinas on God's eternity, he holds that foreknowledge (like the Jedi prophecy fulfilled when Vader destroys the Emperor) does not compel events - Anakin's choice makes the prophecy true, not vice versa - and applies Aristotle's tomorrow's-sea-battle to future-contingents like Obi-Wan's self-surrender on the Death Star. Using Locke's locked-room example and Augustine's account of 'inordinate desire,' he concludes that Anakin's fall stems from his own disordered will to control fate ('learn to stop people from dying'), while Han Solo embodies libertarian alternative possibilities ('No mystical energy field controls my destiny').

free-will-determinism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
free-will-determinism.title: The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire
free-will-determinism.relation: Brown treats Luke's 'Is the Dark Side stronger?' as the problem of evil: distinguishing natural evils (the wampa, bigger fish) from moral evils (Tarkin destroying Alderaan), he surveys the Platonic craftsman working recalcitrant matter and the Manichean dualism of two gods - the Emperor as would-be 'evil incarnate' - before giving Augustine's answer. On Augustine's free-will defense, no creature is inherently evil; the origin of each moral evil is the creature's own pride and free choice, so Anakin, not the Emperor's seduction, is responsible for his turn ('I'm a Jedi. I know I'm better than this'). The chapter ends on whether evil can ever be finally defeated, arguing the Jedi prophecies of 'balance' fit a world where evil is a permanent possibility that heroism needs.

free-will-determinism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
free-will-determinism.title: The Vigilante Man of Faith Hero or Tragic Figure
free-will-determinism.relation: Morris answers his title question 'both': Daredevil refuses to kill even Doctor Octopus ('Then I'd be no better than you'), saves the cancer-stricken Bullseye, and tells Typhoid Mary 'You are who you are because of the choices you make', denying that accidents or heritage define a person. To Detective Manolis he gives a law-and-society argument against private killing - 'The moment one man takes another man's life in his own hands, he is rejecting the law... I'm not God - I'm not the law - and I'm not a murderer' - yet his repeated sparing of Bullseye makes him feel complicit in later murders, the tragic cost of his faith, which he nonetheless concludes is strength rather than weakness.

free-will-determinism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
free-will-determinism.title: Moral Autonomy
free-will-determinism.relation: Martin van Hees reads "Who Killed Davey Moore?" and "Ballad of Hollis Brown" as arguments that shared consent generates shared responsibility for tragedy even when fate makes the events inevitable - the referee, crowd, manager, and gambler all endorsed the fight, and we who tolerate poverty consent to the next Hollis Brown. He distinguishes a "limited optimistic view" (twisting fate by preventing particular tragedies) from the proclaimed inevitability of "The Times They Are A-Changin'" and the pessimism of "Blind Willie McTell," then defends compatibilism through Frankfurt's Jones/Black case: responsibility needs no alternative possibilities, only that one act from one's own will. Dylan's "moral autonomy" is taking a stance - singing the blues - inside a determined world.

free-will-determinism.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
free-will-determinism.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Feldman tests Harley's 'Great American Freedom Machine' slogan against each conception of freedom: metaphysical freedom (universal causation, divine foreknowledge, fate) cannot depend on your vehicle; legal freedom actually shrinks for riders through helmet mandates and extra licensing; and circumstantial freedom is gained equally by any vehicle, a wheelchair being the true freedom machine. Borrowing Socrates' comparison method from the Philebus, he argues the alleged 'feeling of freedom' is really a feeling of happiness or exhilaration combined with the false belief that one is freer than a Camry driver. What really binds him to his 1986 FXRT is fun, the thrill of leaning to the edge, and the sensory and historical pleasures of the air-cooled V-twin line back to the Silent Grey Fellow, which have nothing to do with freedom.

free-will-determinism.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
free-will-determinism.title: Poker and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.

free-will-determinism.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
free-will-determinism.title: Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood
free-will-determinism.relation: Rachel Robison asks why blood, of all substances, carries metaphysical powers in vampire lore - Elizabeth Bathory's youth-giving baths, Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, Sookie's bond with Bill in True Blood. Her explanation is historical: the ancient cardiocentric view (Aristotle, Empedocles, Chrysippus placing the rational center in the heart and making blood its product) plus Galenic humorism and bloodletting made blood the carrier of the self, so drinking someone's blood plausibly transmits bits of their personal identity, knowledge, and even domination over one's free will. She then tests the show's synthetic 'True Blood': either some essential property of blood (or of the act of drinking it) carries the power, or the legend is parasitic on our lingering habit of locating emotion and character in the heart ('hot blooded') - either way the myth stays credible because our metaphors of blood never died.

free-will-determinism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
free-will-determinism.title: Determinism and the Dark Knight
free-will-determinism.relation: David Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman's dedication without reducing it to trauma-determined compulsion: Alfred's butler's-world illustrates being-in-the-world and the thrown-project, and Bruce's confrontation with death, culminating in the bleeding alley scene of Miller's Batman: Year One, is Angst, the recognition of finitude that strips ordinary meanings away. Seen this way, "I shall become a bat" is an authentic, responsible choice of a whole life rather than a mechanical effect of childhood trauma. Hart concludes that Heidegger's analysis dissolves the free will versus determinism debate, since Batman neither blindly follows causes nor chooses from nowhere.

free-will-determinism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
free-will-determinism.title: Reap a Destiny
free-will-determinism.relation: Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Deathly Hallows philosophically: Harry's willing march into the Forbidden Forest is Heideggerian authenticity, confronting being-toward-death, while Voldemort's horcruxes and the maimed King's Cross stowaway are the inauthentic flight from mortality that ruins the soul. The afterlife scene raises the stakes of this life: by James's "sow a thought... reap a destiny," Aristotle's habituation, and Locke's memory-based identity, Voldemort's lifelong refusal of remorse fixes his character beyond repair, and Kant and Pascal supply reasons why belief in an afterlife transforms morality. Dumbledore's purgatory-like repentance, contrasted with Voldemort's fate, shows that our choices reap a destiny we must live with forever.

free-will-determinism.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
free-will-determinism.title: “Your Heavenly Father Feeds Them”
free-will-determinism.relation: Calef takes the Tides restaurant scene ('Who are you? What are you?') and Diogenes's plucked rooster versus Plato's 'featherless biped' as a springboard for testing every classic criterion of humanity against the film. Aristotle's rational soul fails because Mrs. Bundy's 'brain pans' reasoning is wrong and some humans cannot reason; Descartes's language test fails because the myna bird can learn to talk while horrified humans go mute; Rousseau's free will fails because the birds behave unpredictably and resist instinct while humans are trapped, caged, and herd-like; Aristotle's political animal and Hobbes's social contract fail because the town's hoods and lawbreakers contrast with birds that flock together across species. Even the appeal to God's favor turns dark, as the drunk quotes scripture while Revelation's birds gather for a supper of human flesh, leaving the film a mirror in which we must examine ourselves.

free-will-determinism.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
free-will-determinism.title: “Just Like Mary Shelley, Just Like Frankenstein”
free-will-determinism.relation: Chuck Ward uses 'Mama Tried' (the meek family's rebel son doing life without parole) and the mysterious birthmark in 'Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodleloo' to ask whether character is fixed from birth, setting the songs' fatalism against Aristotle's account of character as habituated choice and Plato's claim that traits tend to be inherited. He surveys behavioral genetics, twin studies, The Bell Curve, and the supposed 'criminality gene' before arguing that genetic determinism is a mistaken reductionism: like the groovy atmosphere of a Dead show, which shapes the very individuals who produce it, complex systems admit top-down causation, so genes never act alone. The chapter's payoff is that the songs' studied ambiguity — mama tried, yet 'that leaves no one but me to blame' — shows art expressing, rather than resolving, the tension between free will and determinism.

free-will-determinism.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
free-will-determinism.title: Christmas in Jamaica
free-will-determinism.relation: David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.

free-will-determinism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
free-will-determinism.title: Free to Be You and Me
free-will-determinism.relation: Bryan Barker reconciles Cylon programming and human 'destiny' with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's intelligible character: Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama under activation, Baltar's cowardly conversion to the Cylon God, Tigh's decision to stay at his post upon learning he is a Cylon, and Starbuck's flight into the storm in 'Maelstrom' all express innate, unchanging character rather than external compulsion. Even destiny, as in Leoben's prophecies to Starbuck, works like determinism unless reframed as character. On this view we are free because everything we do manifests who we immutably are, whether that character is programmed or born.

free-will-determinism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
free-will-determinism.title: To the Third Power . .
free-will-determinism.relation: Ivan Wolfe shows that Glen Larson's original series is 'ontologically Mormon': Kobol anagrammatizes Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve mirrors the LDS hierarchy, marriage is a 'sealing' for eternity, the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were' restates Lorenzo Snow's couplet on human deification, and Count Iblis can rule only those who freely submit, since agency is supreme in Mormon theology. Because none of this is epistemologically required viewing knowledge, later licensees could rewrite the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics became an incoherent muddle by abandoning the inviolability of free will, while Hatch's novels and Moore's re-imagining built new ontologies, Moore replacing progressive godhood with the circular 'all this has happened before.'

free-will-determinism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
free-will-determinism.title: Human, Machine, or Something In-between
free-will-determinism.relation: Heather Rolufs maps Boomer Sharon and Caprica Six onto Eve and Lilith: Boomer's unwitting shooting of Adama parallels Eve eating the fruit before she could understand disobedience, raising whether her free will was ever real, while Baltar repeats Adam's blame-shifting and Six gains the rebuttal Eve never had. The Lilith material from the Alphabet of Ben Sira and the Zohar explains Six's red-dressed seduction of Baltar and her ambivalent violence, snapping a baby's neck as a mercy before the attack yet later risking herself to return Hera. The chapter argues the show lets these demonized first women of myth be reread as neither machines nor demons but human.

free-will-determinism.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.title: A Link to the Present
free-will-determinism.relation: Compagno argues that the word 'I' in Zelda simultaneously names Link, the virtual body, and the player, the invisible will, and builds this into a 'Schopenhauerian Console': as Schopenhauer held, we have freedom of action but not freedom of will, since the decisions of the unknowable will never appear in consciousness (against Descartes' free mind and Dennett's Cartesian theater critique). Kant's transcendental subject, standing at the border of experience, becomes the player's perspective from which Hyrule exists, what Foucault would call an empirical-transcendental doublet. The payoff: Link's quest is fated and scripted, yet the player wills it in a perpetual present, enacting Schopenhauer's lesson that a determined life is still lived as one's own free act.

free-will-determinism.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.title: Rescuing Princess Zelda
free-will-determinism.relation: Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.

free-will-determinism.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
free-will-determinism.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Auxier tests Pullman's many-worlds premise, setting Asriel's coin-toss explanation and the Barnard-Stokes hypothesis against Book III's claim that unchosen possibilities are 'snuffed out like candles,' then measures the trilogy against David Lewis's causally independent possible worlds, which forbid the subtle knife's transworld travel and leave the chill Lyra feels at the thought of 'another Lyra' in Will's Oxford as an unresolved transworld-identity puzzle. Compiling fourteen kinds of conscious beings from humans and dæmons to specters and the Abyss itself, he argues Pullman's cosmology is panpsychist and aesthetic rather than moral or epistemic, ordered by what the alethiometer, the knife, and the spyglass can and cannot do, with the alethiometer submitting to the knife and love alone able to break it, as Will's love for his mother and for Lyra does twice. Peirce's agapicism, evolution by creative love alongside chance and mechanical necessity, supplies the closest philosophical analogue to Pullman's 'Matter loved Dust.'

free-will-determinism.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
free-will-determinism.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.

free-will-determinism.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
free-will-determinism.title: Singing of the Good Things
free-will-determinism.relation: Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.

free-will-determinism.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
free-will-determinism.title: True Selves Found or Made
free-will-determinism.relation: Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.

free-will-determinism.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
free-will-determinism.title: Which World Am I In
free-will-determinism.relation: Juan Ferret tells the story from inside the game: Admetus the Human Mage, chased through Alterac Valley by an Undead Rogue, works through Zeno's paradox of motion, the convergence of infinite series, and whether space and time are discrete, coached by a bodiless voice that turns out to be his player. The voice's revelations — 'You are my creation,' autorun, polymorph, Blink — force the free-will-versus-determinism question from the character's side, since every action is controlled from above. Reference frames, Heisenberg's uncertainty, EPR entanglement, and hidden nods to David Lewis ('Siwel Divad' on possible worlds) and many-worlds theory leave the mage wondering which world, server, or parallel universe he really inhabits.

free-will-determinism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
free-will-determinism.title: One Last Anguished Existential Scream
free-will-determinism.relation: Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.

free-will-determinism.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
free-will-determinism.title: Added Time
free-will-determinism.relation: McDermid takes Maradona's cheeky 'a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God' claim literally and asks what would make either 1986 goal against England—the obvious handball or the Goal of the Century—a miracle, using Aquinas's definition of miracles as intentional divine acts beyond the order commonly observed in nature. He explores how God could intervene without breaking natural law, analogizing God to a goalkeeper exempt from the handball rule or a spectator outside the game: in a deterministic world He could only arrange initial conditions (a domino setup requiring fine-tuning at the Big Bang), while in an indeterministic quantum world He could load the chancy micro-events along Maradona's mazy, sensitively balanced run. Hume's empiricist argument against miracles then shows we could never be justified in believing either goal miraculous, since the mundane explanation—Maradona's cheek and skill, lapses of concentration, a missed handball call—always has the whole of past experience on its side.

free-will-determinism.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
free-will-determinism.title: Choosing the Scapegoat
free-will-determinism.relation: Northcott dissects England's penalty shoot-out misery to ask whether 'bad luck' is objective or a scapegoat: what counts as luck depends on the reasonable standard of preparation, so what was bad luck twenty years ago (no practice) is negligence today, and under Laplace's demon's determinism no sixty-percent chances would exist at all. He rehabilitates objective luck relative to shared standards of reasonableness, concluding that shoot-outs genuinely are more of a lottery than open play — though not a total one. On blame, he uses the deviation-from-default account of causation and Mill's problem of causal selection to argue that singling out a referee over missed open goals or injuries has no objective justification; moral feelings and prejudice pick our scapegoats.

free-will-determinism.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
free-will-determinism.title: Intending the Way Out
free-will-determinism.relation: Stages the paradox of foreknowledge through Paul's prescient dream of meeting Chani and his futile struggle against the foreseen jihad: since knowledge (on Plato's justified-true-belief account) is factive, a known future seems unalterable. It tests the classic escapes—Boethius's God in ever-present eternity and Aquinas's seeing all time 'under the aspect of eternity,' Laplace's demon, Richard Taylor's fatalism—and finds the Atreides oracles are no gods, only probabilistic predictors whose visions fix the possibilities they see. The way out is Anscombe's Intention: like God knowing creation because He authored it, Paul and Leto know their futures practically, as agents whose intentions help decide which possibilities become actual, so freedom survives as terrific responsibility.

free-will-determinism.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
free-will-determinism.title: In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . .
free-will-determinism.relation: Continues the earlier defense of oracular freedom ('Curse of the Golden Path'): because an oracle's gaze from a present moment fixes the very set of future possibilities, Paul and Leto are free precisely where they are blind—above all in their 'vision-battle' in the Tanzerouft, which no oracle can foresee, and which Paul's single whispered 'Don't' concedes to his son's Golden Path. Leto's breeding of Siona, invisible to prescience, is read as his deliberate self-blinding—'the price of freedom is an invigilance of eternity'—and the whole affair vindicates heroism as steering probabilities rather than escaping fate. Paul emerges as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense, whose hamartia is his all-too-human refusal to become a monster to save the future.

free-will-determinism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
free-will-determinism.title: You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It
free-will-determinism.relation: Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.

free-will-determinism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
free-will-determinism.title: Almost Caught!
free-will-determinism.relation: Nicolas Michaud deploys Harry Frankfurt's attack on the principle that blame requires alternative possibilities: through a 'Dex kills Deb' case with a counterfactual intervener and a locked-steering-wheel driver, he shows one can be blameworthy despite having no choice, provided one acts because one wants to. Applied to Dexter, the question is which level of compulsion he has - and since he never truly restrains himself, never turns himself in, and his Season 2 relapse reads as empowerment rather than addiction, he seems to want to want to kill, so Frankfurt's verdict is guilt despite inevitability. The chapter closes with a fictional Princeton encounter where Dexter faces a dilemma - either his victims are blameless compulsives, making him a killer of innocents who violates Harry's Code, or wanting to kill makes them and him blameworthy - and Dexter's choice to kill Frankfurt himself proves he acts freely and is guilty.

free-will-determinism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
free-will-determinism.title: A Second Look at Dexter’s Motives
free-will-determinism.relation: David Ramsay Steele first calculates that Dexter is a public benefactor - each killed predator saves several net lives a year - and then explains the deeper appeal through Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and Adam Smith's invisible hand: like good law, Harry's Code channels an amoral appetite (the thrill of killing) into socially beneficial results without reforming the appetite itself, refuting Christianity's fixation on pure motives. Dexter thus does totally the right thing for totally the wrong reason. Finally Steele doubts Dexter's own story: the spontaneously unlocked door of the Castillos' shed shows real empathy, and it was Harry's deliberate instruction (Nurse Mary), not fate, that made him a killer - 'addiction is always a choice.'

free-will-determinism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
free-will-determinism.title: Dexter, Hero of Our Time
free-will-determinism.relation: David Ramsay Steele compares Dexter with the rational vigilante heroes of earlier popular fiction - Edgar Wallace's Four Just Men, E.W. Hornung's Raffles, Bulldog Drummond, the Saint - who killed bad guys for justice and were read without moral panic, and asks why the Parents Television Council now singles Dexter out. His answer: Dexter is ideologically 'safe' because the modern 'ideology of childhood trauma' works like the folk-tale love potion, presenting the hero as a puppet of irresistible compulsion rather than a responsible agent, so no one can accuse the show of endorsing calculated vigilantism. The chapter is thus a free-will-and-excuse argument: determinism-as-excuse has become the price of admission for unofficial justice on screen.

free-will-determinism.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
free-will-determinism.title: Videogame Apocalypses and Secularism
free-will-determinism.relation: Rachel Wagner, Tyler DeHaven, and Chris Hendrickson argue Halo satisfies the Society of Biblical Literature definition of apocalypse: revelatory narrative, otherworldly mediators (Cortana, 343 Guilty Spark), predetermined eschatology, with Master Chief as a Davidic messiah whose name John-117 echoes the Gospel of John. The Covenant's Tower-of-Babel hubris versus human secularism, and the Flood read through the Book of Enoch's Watchers, turn the story into a critique of rampant consumption and blind religion. Where traditional apocalypses are quietist—God the programmer's deterministic script, salvation not depending on human action—Halo's procedural rhetoric hands agency to the player as messiah, and the chapter closes asking whether videogame apocalypse offers only temporary, magic-circle comfort for secular angst in a morally relativist age.

free-will-determinism.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
free-will-determinism.title: What You Really Wanted Was Inside You All Along
free-will-determinism.relation: Robert Kincaid maps Freud's structural model of the psyche onto Conch Street: Patrick under his rock is the pleasure-principle Id, guilt-administering Squidward the Super-Ego, and mediating SpongeBob the Ego, so 'Mermaid Man and Barnacle Boy IV' becomes the Ego minimizing, rationalizing and literally shrinking its own conscience and desires to dodge guilt over the belt. Episodes missing one member ('Squidville', 'SB-129', 'Big Pink Loser') dramatize egolessness and what each part contributes, and the chapter closes by asking whether Freudian psychic causation — the mind 'outnumbering itself' in 'Squilliam Returns' — undermines moral responsibility for what SpongeBob does.

free-will-determinism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
free-will-determinism.title: Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head
free-will-determinism.relation: The book's introduction frames Inception around two threats to the self: the old Cartesian doubt that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, and a newer neuroscience-based worry that even our thoughts are not our own because we act on them before we become aware of them. It surveys the volume's guiding questions - whether inception, unlike the implants of Blade Runner and Dark City, is a wrong akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing; whether Second Life-style virtual worlds mean walking away from reality; and whether even 'true inspiration' can be faked. It also previews the book's boldest readings, such as the theory that the whole film is Cobb's single dream on the flight and the claim that the dreams run on a server, making Mal into 'Mal-ware'.

free-will-determinism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
free-will-determinism.title: Group Will
free-will-determinism.relation: Testerman turns inception against itself: Cobb and Saito believe they freely plan the Fischer job, but conscious will is a feeling, not a cause. From William James's effortful attention and Dewey's willpower she moves to Penfield's stimulated patients and Libet's readiness-potential experiments showing the brain prepares action before we feel we will it, so Fischer, Cobb and Saito are all equally 'incepted' by subconscious forces - 'freedom is ignorance of the causes of actions', as she glosses Spinoza, with Hume's point that causality is only inferred. Advertising, the foot-in-the-door effect and subliminal primes already do inception's work more cheaply, and the team's 'group will' flows from Saito's own unexamined drive for power, so against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly suitable for living.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick
free-will-determinism.relation: Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale
free-will-determinism.relation: Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Free Will at the Box Office
free-will-determinism.relation: Mills contrasts Dick's 'The Minority Report', where Anderton knowingly kills Kaplan exactly as the final Precog prediction foretold and accepts exile contentedly, with Spielberg's film in which Agatha insists 'You still have a choice' and Crow is spared. He pairs 'Adjustment Team', where Ed Fletcher grovels and accepts the adjustments as for the greater good, with The Adjustment Bureau, where Damon's love teaches the Chairman a lesson and wins the couple their freedom. In both cases the story doubts free will while the movie insists the hero's choice secures human dignity, which Mills attributes to the Dickian worldview being box-office poison rather than to mere economics.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Determinism’s Bounty on Free Will
free-will-determinism.relation: Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: A Variety of Free Will Worth Having
free-will-determinism.relation: Takes Dick's self-description as a 'fictionalizing philosopher' and reads 'Adjustment Team' — Ed Fletcher stumbling into a world of grey dust animated by an external hidden force — as determinism as we concretely live it: working toward goals we never chose in jobs that are not our own. Thompson's toothpaste line in The Adjustment Bureau becomes the image of consumption-only freedom, while Norris choosing love and politics over the Bureau's plan dramatizes freedom as accepting responsibility for one's own values.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Terrible Freedom
free-will-determinism.relation: Quotes Dick's A Scanner Darkly author's note — drug misuse 'is a decision,' and the druggie life-style is 'no different from your life-style... only faster' — to argue that dropping out of the plan continues the Sixties' questioning of war, segregation, and monogamy. Dick's refusal of bourgeois moralizing exposes it as part of the social-determinist control system, but a morally neutral natural cause-and-effect is what actually destroyed the druggies, so being free requires taking control, not merely rejecting control.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Pre-Crime and Pre-Punishment
free-will-determinism.relation: Frames 'Minority Report' with Nietzsche's charge that men were considered 'free' only so they could be judged and punished, and with Anselm's De Concordia, where God, outside time, foreknows our choices without determining them. Pre-Crime can punish Anderton and the pre-criminals now only because their not-yet-made choices are treated as absolutely free, and the 1954 context — HUAC, Hoover's anonymous accusations, the Communist Control Act — shows people punished for the present guilt of a future crime.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Freedom and Madness
free-will-determinism.relation: Updates the McCarthyite stakes of pre-guilt with Michelle Bachmann's 'anti-American' probing and the Guantánamo detainees who are 'too dangerous to transfer but not feasible for prosecution.' Dick's own post-2-3-74 spiral — after the pink light he was writing in his Exegesis about telepathic crab-clawed invaders from Sirius — becomes the case study for the book's closing practical problem: how to free yourself from received social, political, and religious determination without careering into drugs, isolation, or madness.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Chapter 21 - Knowing Tomorrow While Choosing Today
free-will-determinism.relation: Sara Worley's introduction frames Minority Report and 'Adjustment Team' as versions of the classic free will problem: if precogs foresee my crime before I commit it, or the Adjustment Team knows what I will do, my action seems already settled, like a sunflower's turn toward the sun. Influence alone does not cancel freedom, since we can do otherwise where plants cannot, but foreknowledge threatens exactly that, the same quandary long posed by an omniscient God who already knows every action we will perform.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Freedom and Prediction
free-will-determinism.relation: The section distinguishes two models of foreknowledge: prediction, as when you confidently predict that sci-fi-loving Jill will skip the John Wayne retrospective, and Molina's 'middle knowledge' of how each person will respond to various circumstances. It then argues prediction can be certain only if character and circumstances guarantee the outcome, the way facts and laws fix where Mars will appear, which would leave no alternatives to choose; so on the predictive model, infallible foreknowledge and the ability to do otherwise cannot coexist.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Prediction, or Sight
free-will-determinism.relation: The section tests both models against the stories and finds 'sight' incoherent: the precogs foresee murders that never happen, the Adjustment Bureau tracks two incompatible previsions per circumstance, and a precog genuinely seeing the actual future would generate an oscillating loop in which her own report makes the prevision false. Prediction fits instead: the adjusters tweak Mr. Douglas's cautious character in 'Adjustment Team,' and Anderton's three discrepant predictions in 'The Minority Report' track how leaked information changes his circumstances and motivation to kill Kaplan.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Perfect or Probabilistic
free-will-determinism.relation: This section argues predictive foresight is compatible with freedom only if probabilistic, yet Precrime treats its predictions as certain, arresting people for what they will rather than might do. Lisa's doubts in 'The Minority Report' turn out to concern incomplete information rather than free will, while The Adjustment Bureau dramatizes freedom differently: the adjusters work by making the preferred path easiest, but David and Elise's three-year persistence shows that those who 'fight' for their free will get it, leaving open how predictable we really are.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Owning Your Actions, Owning Your Past
free-will-determinism.relation: This section reconstructs the traditional view of free agency from Aristotle: an action is freely mine when it 'has its origin in the agent himself,' so owning an action means tracing its causal chain back to one's own decision. It explains Aristotle's picture of natures as internal sources of motion and decision as the distinctively human motion, then asks whether Quaid, following the suitcase, video, and clues Hauser pre-arranged, is picking up the chain of his own prior decision, and so becoming himself again.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Inpsychation and Chains of Will
free-will-determinism.relation: The section develops freedom as extending the will through tools and other people, via Nietzsche's 'inpsychation' and Emerson's conversion of fate into force: Cohaagen shuts off the air through Lori and Harry as Hitler invaded Poland through his soldiers. Locke's memory theory returns demoted to a useful tool rather than an identity-maker, and Nietzsche's Genealogy II.1 on the unbroken 'long chain of will' explains Hauser's masterpiece, planning around his own memory wipe so that Quaid, following the planted clues, re-inpsychates Hauser's decisions.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Quaid’s Problem—Mucky Origins
free-will-determinism.relation: This section complicates everything: two taped Hausers contradict each other, rebel hero or Cohaagen's 'bosom buddy,' so Quaid cannot settle who he is by tracing his origins. It then generalizes: in the scientific worldview of universal causation, from gravity to DNA inherited through chimps and sea squirts from the primeval muck, no one originates anything, a conclusion quoted at length from Baron d'Holbach's System of Nature, yet first-person deliberation still leaves Quaid feeling the weight of choice.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Freedom Without Origins
free-will-determinism.relation: The section rejects randomness as a foundation for freedom, quantum indeterminacy being Epicurus's swerve again, since actions tracing to random particle events are no more mine than law-determined ones, then turns to the ethical problem: if Hauser volunteered and Cohaagen's story is true, freedom-as-origination would require Quaid to become Hauser again, Mercedes included. Quaid's verdict ('The guy's a fucking asshole') shows freedom is also changing course to do what is right; as Lowe says in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' what defines us is 'not a memory but a desire,' and in breaking with his past Quaid decisively becomes free.

free-will-determinism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
free-will-determinism.title: Determinism
free-will-determinism.relation: Citing Dick's 1976 'soap-bubble' reality interview, this section observes that Lewis's many worlds, each complete in all detail at all times, are deterministic in Laplace's sense - history on rails. Three considerations tell against determinism in our world: our experience of free choice, which grounds praise and blame; quantum indeterminacy, where a nucleus splits when it splits; and objective chance and coincidence - Zangara's near-miss, two wheat grains touching in a granary, Churchill's silence at the crucial meeting tipping the premiership from Halifax, who would likely have negotiated with Hitler. Simons grants that hinge events deviate history by mere inches, but rejects Dick's hint, and Lewis's theory, that all the possible worlds are equally real: only our world is real.

free-will-determinism.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
free-will-determinism.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Sienkiewicz takes Klosterman's hyperthetical of a crystal ball showing an unchangeable future in which you are blissfully obsessed with CFL football as a secular version of the traditional Jewish and Christian problem of divine foreknowledge versus human freedom. He offers the 'movie' solution: as when watching the chest-wax scene in The 40-Year-Old Virgin, a vantage point outside the event's time (God's, or yours before the fixed future) can behold it without having scripted it, so foreknowledge and free will remain logically compatible. Since we already live toward the one absolutely certain future, our own deaths, the portal should change nothing about how you act, though you still should not watch a league that plays with only three downs.

free-will-determinism.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
free-will-determinism.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.

free-will-determinism.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
free-will-determinism.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Audits Walt's killings through Season Four - Emilio by phosphine gas in the RV, the captive Krazy-8, Jane left choking in 'Phoenix', the dealers he rams with the Aztec to save Jesse, ordering Jesse to shoot Gale, and the wheelchair bomb that kills Gus and Tyrus - grading each with Aristotle's criteria of capacity, motive, consequences, justification, and proximate cause. It argues self-defense excuses Emilio but dissolves for the imprisoned Krazy-8, that Walt actively created the danger he then refused to relieve when he let Jane die, and that special-relationship duties to Jesse plus a utilitarian ledger justify running down the dealers. Compatibilism is invoked to show guilt survives determinism, while the remote Wayfarer 515 crash is pinned mainly on Donald Margolis's own choices rather than on Walt.

free-will-determinism.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
free-will-determinism.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Sets Walt's 'There's nothing but chemistry here' materialism - the missing 0.111958 percent of the human body that Gretchen calls the soul - against Augustine's Confessions, arguing both men want redemption without giving up their sins: 'give me chastity, but not yet.' It maps Augustine's problem of evil (evil as corruption of the will toward self-destruction) onto Walt's pros-and-cons list over killing Krazy-8 and his 'no-rough-stuff-type deal' fantasy after Tuco. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle then turns chemistry's laws into tendencies, opening room for free choice inside a materialist world - so Walt's remission in 'Over' saves the body, while only changed choices, which he keeps deferring, could save the man.

free-will-determinism.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
free-will-determinism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.

free-will-determinism.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
free-will-determinism.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Ralph Shain argues forward and backward time travel are categorically different: relativistic time dilation is conceptually harmless (in Boulle's novel Merou could not return to Soror for a thousand years), but Escape from the Planet of the Apes' backward jump is conceptually impossible because it treats the open future as fixed like the past - Hasslein's plan to kill baby Milo is the Grandfather Paradox, checked against presentist, possibilist, and eternalist ontologies of time. The real philosophical engine is Aristotle's sea-battle argument from the law of excluded middle: since Cornelius's story of the takeover is past for the apes and future for 1973 humans, the film's causal loop (Milo saved at the circus) enacts the fatalist conclusion that the ape takeover will necessarily occur. Hasslein's freeway image of time defeats itself - switching lanes means landing in the past of a different, parallel universe, so the apes' jump would be travel between worlds, not times.

free-will-determinism.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
free-will-determinism.title: Futurama and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Von Gunten asks whether Bender, Calculon, and the robot mafia have moral worth, arguing first that they are sentient: behavioral similarity plus functional equivalence (pain as electric signals in neurons or circuits) defeat both behavior-only objections (the Sphex wasp's preprogrammed loop, knife-avoiding toy robots) and composition-based prejudice - Fry's 'I'm all squishy and flabby' defense at the Hal Institute - which would be 'biologism' analogous to racism. He then distinguishes moral patiency (Nibbler can be harmed but only behaviorally reinforced) from moral agency (deliberation and accountability), concluding that Bender's flexible life - Iron Cook, wrestling, folk music with Beck's head, jacking-on addiction - shows robots transcend their programming as humans transcend evolutionary presets. Limiting moral status to biology or species would be speciesism, so the thirty-first century's robots deserve the full protections and responsibilities humans have.

free-will-determinism.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
free-will-determinism.title: Futurama and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Pless asks whether Bender is responsible for his misdeeds given that MomCorp designed him to be an alcoholic kleptomaniac (revealed through Bender Vision in 'Mother's Day') and Planet Express regularly orders him into morally dirty work. Against Asimov's utilitarian Three Laws - embodied by the servile, selfless Robot 1-X of 'Obsoletely Fabulous' - Futurama's 'robot subjectivism' makes every robot a self-interested agent, and Bender's autonomy is proven by his refusal of Mom's 'kill all humans' order and by his fear of punishment in Robot Hell ('Hell Is Other Robots'), which also shows the show's universe is not morally relativist. Because Bender can rewrite his own code - his unprogrammed friendship with Fry, the adoption scam that turns heartfelt in 'The Cyber House Rules' - he sits on the same sliding scale of moral agency as humans, so if Bender can break his programming, we have no excuse for not exercising our own free will.

free-will-determinism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
free-will-determinism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.

free-will-determinism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
free-will-determinism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.

free-will-determinism.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
free-will-determinism.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Jeremy Proulx reads Ender through F.W.J. Schelling's account of evil as a real, positive force rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: Ender's kicks to Stilson and Bonzo, his killing of the Giant in the mind game, and his 'I destroy them' confession all display the 'contraction into the self' Schelling thinks haunts every moral agent. He argues Graff deliberately isolates Ender to force this dark ground to the surface, and that Valentine's 'welcome to the human race' and the hive-queen's forgiveness teach Ender that evil, though never excusable, can be understood and atoned for - his fate also shows freedom tainted by a necessity we neither choose nor control.

free-will-determinism.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
free-will-determinism.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: David Morgan unpacks the chaos theory behind Malcolm's 'I hate being right all the time', starting from Newtonian causal determinism and Laplace's demon, according to which the future is fixed and calculable - then showing that non-linear systems like weather and the park show sensitive dependence (Lorenz's butterfly effect), so even a fully determined universe is unpredictable in practice because we can never know initial conditions exactly. He raises the philosophy-of-science question of whether chaos is a property of nature or only of our computer models, and reads 'life finds a way' as Malcolm extending the same contingency to Darwinian evolution: rewind the tape and you get different species. He ends by noting Malcolm's own paradox - a chaos theorist certain of one specific doom - and settles on chaos theory predicting unpredictability: ignore tiny factors and do not be surprised when they bite you.

free-will-determinism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
free-will-determinism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.

free-will-determinism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
free-will-determinism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Aaron Rabinowitz argues that modern Devil stories - Milton's 'Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven', Neil Gaiman's Sandman where Lucifer quits Hell like a two-weeks notice, and Mike Carey's Lucifer building a second creation whose only commandment forbids worship - reveal a Devil whose real motive is free will and autonomy in a predetermined cosmos. Rereading the serpent in Eden, the wager over Job, and the temptation of Jesus through that lens makes Lucifer look reasonable, even commendable, and since we all feel pushed around by obligations, survival needs, and neuroscience, our sympathy for the Devil is inevitable.

free-will-determinism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
free-will-determinism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Robert Arp compiles the 'Devil made me do it' record: Flip Wilson's catchphrase, actual possession pleas from Christian v. State to the Demon Murder Trial of Arne Cheyenne Johnson, the M'Naghten Rule born of Daniel M'Naghten's botched assassination, the Son of Sam's possessed dog Harvey, exorcism lore from Roland Doe (The Exorcist) to Anneliese Michel (The Exorcism of Emily Rose), and the bizarre Mayo v. Satan lawsuit. The law's answer throughout is that only a defect of reason - never the Devil - robs defendants of free will, and the possession cases read better as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and negligence than as demons.

free-will-determinism.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
free-will-determinism.title: Homeland and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Dan Burkett defends Brody against blame for flipping the suicide-vest switch in 'Marine One' by arguing he was not free. On the desire-satisfaction view Brody freely avenge Issa, but via Locke's locked-room thought experiment (Carrie contentedly 'freely' staying in a house she cannot leave) the chapter motivates the libertarian requirement that one could have done otherwise, which Nazir's years of torture and brainwashing may have removed. The malfunctioning vest then raises moral luck - Brody is no better a person because the bomb failed - and since Dana's plea restricts his options just as coercively, the best defense grants Brody freedom throughout, making the switch blameworthy and his free choice to come home genuinely redemptive.

free-will-determinism.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
free-will-determinism.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.'
