free-will-determinism.relation: Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.

free-will-determinism.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
free-will-determinism.title: Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw
free-will-determinism.relation: Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.

free-will-determinism.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
free-will-determinism.title: The Peculiarities of Free Will
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter surveys how Whedon's fiction both dramatizes free choice—Angel answering Whistler's 'you could go either way' challenge, Cordelia reclaiming her visions in 'Birthday,' choices even the Powers That Be cannot predict—and suggests determinism, via the reverse-chronology of The Shepherd's Tale, the self-fulfilling prophecies Flamson identifies, and Topher's 'Everybody's programmed' speech in Dollhouse. It rejects Richardson and Rabb's Shestovian freedom (it implausibly denies that tragic choices between two evils, like Buffy killing re-ensouled Angel in 'Becoming, Part II,' are free) and Flamson's compatibilism (Jasmine's followers do what they want yet plainly lack choice, as Gunn's 'then we'll kick it over and start a new game' speech shows). Robert Kane's libertarianism—undetermined self-forming choices in moments of torn conflict—fits best, illuminating Book's soup-bowl pause, Billy/Dr. Horrible's street-corner hesitation with Penny, and Connor's choice between Darla and faux-Cordelia in 'Inside Out,' though the chapter concedes Whedon may sometimes sacrifice consistency for drama.

free-will-determinism.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
free-will-determinism.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
free-will-determinism.relation: R. Barton Palmer situates Scorsese as a 'saint of cinema' whose Emersonian transcendentalism—the 'influx of light and power' breaking through the material everyday—pervades even his commercial films, focusing on Bringing Out the Dead against Casino and Taxi Driver. He traces the Bressonian 'decisive moment' and Schrader's Calvinist-Jansenist reading of predestination and grace (Ace Rothstein's inexplicable survival in Casino, the elect/damned divide of Taxi Driver and Hardcore), where Travis Bickle remains 'God's lonely man' beyond redemption. Palmer argues Scorsese departs from Schrader's bleak limited atonement: Frank Pierce earns communal grace through willed effort, releasing Mary's father, asking forgiveness, and ending in a Pieta embrace that affirms redemption is attainable within the material world.

free-will-determinism.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
free-will-determinism.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
free-will-determinism.relation: Shaw asks whether Kubrick's worldview is nihilistic by tracking the free-will-versus-determinism question across his films, arguing (against Vincent Canby) that A Clockwork Orange celebrates rather than condemns Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice: the state's Ludovico conditioning, which makes him retch at sex and violence, is more monstrous than Alex because it destroys the free will that grounds human meaning. Invoking Kevin Stoehr's distinction between Nietzsche's passive and active nihilism, Shaw claims Kubrick highlights the negative to point beyond it. He surveys the oeuvre—Dax, Bowman, Barry, Wendy, Joker, Bill Harford as choosing agents—and reads Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's Being and Nothingness on the contradiction of wanting the beloved's freely-given yet secure love.

free-will-determinism.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
free-will-determinism.title: Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime
free-will-determinism.relation: Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.

free-will-determinism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: Prognosis
free-will-determinism.relation: William Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's "Blink" philosophy of time using David Lewis's four-dimensionalism. He shows how Lewis's external/personal-time distinction explains the Doctor meeting his own regenerations and reversed causation (a black eye before the punch), and how "Blink" hinges on a closed causal chain (the DVD Easter-egg transcript that authors itself). He rehearses the Grandfather/Bilking paradox and Lewis's "can" equivocation solution, then places the Doctor alongside Horwich and Ismael, arguing the Doctor goes furthest by holding closed causal chains actually exist.

free-will-determinism.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
free-will-determinism.title: 2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan
free-will-determinism.relation: Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.

free-will-determinism.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
free-will-determinism.title: 12. Finally Free
free-will-determinism.relation: McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.

free-will-determinism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
free-will-determinism.title: 9. The Prequel versus Free Will
free-will-determinism.relation: Frim argues that Better Call Saul, precisely because it is a prequel, illustrates Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason—every event, including Walt's meth empire or Jimmy's burner-phone hustle, has a causal 'because' stretching infinitely back—and thus a deterministic universe. He dismantles the appeal to Heisenberg/quantum indeterminacy (randomness is not free choice) and refutes three myths: that determinism is boring (the causal 'Story One' is far more gripping than the free-will 'Story Two'), amoral (murder is wrong for its effects; we can keep 'suffering' and drop 'guilt'), and mindless (Nacho's ordered mind versus Tuco's drug-addled one shows minds function well or badly). He enlists Socrates' 'no one goes willingly toward the bad' to recast wrongdoing as disordered reasoning.

free-will-determinism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
free-will-determinism.title: 19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.

free-will-determinism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
free-will-determinism.title: In the Wrong Hands, It’s a Weapon—in the Right Hands, Deliverance
free-will-determinism.relation: The editors' introduction frames Foundation's central conceit, psychohistory, as a vehicle for the question of determinism: if the chain of events from the founding of Rome to the reader's own hands was fixed by preceding causes, only a predictor's lack of information stands between us and perfect foresight. It uses Gibbon's Decline and Fall (Asimov's model) to raise whether the fall of empires must happen as it does, and previews the volume's further questions about obligations to future generations, science versus religion, and the ethics of deception and robot programming.

free-will-determinism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
free-will-determinism.title: 4. Demons, Game Shows, and Baguettes
free-will-determinism.relation: Wenmackers traces psychohistory's scientific lineage from Newtonian determinism through Laplace's demon, arguing Foundation stays within nineteenth-century limits by predicting only probabilities. She uses Newcomb's Paradox to capture the unease of living under a predicted Seldon Plan, Poincare's chaos and the three-body problem to show determinism need not mean predictability, and Poincare's baguette-fraud tale plus Quetelet's social physics and statistical mechanics to explain psychohistory's core assumption that mobs of billions behave lawfully even when individuals do not. She suggests Seldon's science was in some sense historically inevitable.

free-will-determinism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
free-will-determinism.title: 21. A Foundation-al Lesson on Free Will and Determinism
free-will-determinism.relation: Simpson argues Asimov balances determinism and free will through probabilistic psychohistory and reads the Mule—an unpredictable mutant—as an Epicurean 'swerve' meant to break the plan's apparent determinism, though he shows randomness no more secures freedom than determinism (the free-will dilemma). Turning to compatibilism, he uses Han Pritcher's mental 'Conversion' by the Mule to defeat classical hypothetical analyses and Gary Watson's valuational account, since Pritcher still does what he 'wants.' He builds on Frankfurt's rejection of alternative possibilities and Susan Wolf's requirement of responsiveness to the True and the Good, contrasting the manipulated Lord Stettin with Second-Foundationer Lady Callia, to give an account of free agency that would have let Asimov grant his characters agency in a deterministic universe without needing the Mule.

free-will-determinism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
free-will-determinism.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
free-will-determinism.relation: Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.

free-will-determinism.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
free-will-determinism.title: NOTES
free-will-determinism.relation: Richard Davies uses Aristotle's Poetics (the principles of closure, relevance, and the unities of place and time) to defend Lost's tangled narrative as an epic rather than a broken tragedy, arguing that flashbacks, flash-forwards like Jack's 'We have to go back,' and multi-season arcs such as Juliet's remain within Aristotelian bounds. He then imports McTaggart's contrast between eternalism and presentism to explain why a flash-forward is philosophically unsettling, and argues that changing the past (as season 5's time travel invites) generates a logical contradiction from which anything follows, so viewers must 'shield' Hurley's 1977 experiences to keep enjoying the plot.

free-will-determinism.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
free-will-determinism.title: NOTES
free-will-determinism.relation: Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'

free-will-determinism.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
free-will-determinism.title: 1. Lost in Time
free-will-determinism.relation: Rard uses David Lewis's definition of time travel—a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the gap between departure and arrival—to show that 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' suspended-animation heist is NOT time travel, while 'Last Flight' (Terry returning to save Mackaye) is, complete with a self-consistent causal loop. She then applies Lewis's argument that mundane events always thwart attempts to change the past to 'No Time Like the Past,' where Paul Driscoll is repeatedly distracted from killing Hitler and even accidentally causes the schoolhouse fire he meant to prevent, illustrating that the past is unalterable but interactable.

free-will-determinism.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone
free-will-determinism.relation: Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.

free-will-determinism.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Dromm and Salter analyze Persuasion by distinguishing persuasion (rational, argument-based belief change), influence (nonrational, resting on a person's charisma or status, as Lady Russell has over the Elliots), and 'overpersuasion.' Against Captain Wentworth's view that persuadability is a vice and firmness of mind a virtue (his hazelnut analogy, Louisa Musgrove's fatal fall from the Cobb), they adapt Mill's On Liberty: just as free discussion lets a society exchange error for truth and gain confidence in true beliefs, a persuadable person is happier and epistemically better off. They add that Anne broke the engagement from a sense of duty, not fickleness, and it is her own persuasion that finally reunites her with Wentworth.

free-will-determinism.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
free-will-determinism.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
free-will-determinism.relation: Ilundáin-Agurruza, Gagliardini Graça, and Jáuregui-Olaiz chart sailing's aesthetic facets — sublime, tempestuous, graceful, existential. They deploy Kant's analysis of the sublime as the balance between the imagination's failure before the ocean's immensity/power and the pleasure of meeting it through skill and reason (Ilundáin sailing in thirty-knot gusts on the point of balance between fear and joy). Dewey's notion of 'an experience' anchors sailing's transformative, self-revealing potential, terrifying storms included (Jáuregui's Snowgoose ordeal mistaking a bordello's red light for a harbor). Closing with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, they argue freedom is 'relative' and earned: we cannot change the wind but adjust the sails, gaining restrained autonomy by cultivating skill within constraint.

free-will-determinism.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
free-will-determinism.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
free-will-determinism.relation: Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.

free-will-determinism.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.relation: Felipe Carvalho frames a friend 'Toby's' worry – tattoos are forever, so should one be impulsive or cautious? – as a problem about bodily freedom versus irreversible change. He rejects the hedonist position (seize the day, regret is just part of freedom) as too simple and the Millian position (drawing on Mill's On Liberty argument that one cannot freely alienate one's freedom, as in selling oneself into slavery) as too precautionary, noting his friend's happy irreversible ear surgery. He proposes a 'middle path' learned from the tattoo community: a complex interplay of motif, the tattooist-as-artist, and the body-as-canvas that lets permanence guide more principled choices – so no 'I Love Becky' tattoos.

free-will-determinism.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.relation: Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.

free-will-determinism.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
free-will-determinism.relation: Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.

free-will-determinism.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
free-will-determinism.title: SERIAL KILLERS
free-will-determinism.relation: Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.

free-will-determinism.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
free-will-determinism.title: SERIAL KILLERS
free-will-determinism.relation: Deal compares fictional Dexter Morgan with real killer John Wayne Gacy to explore whether serial killers are morally responsible, working through moral agency, free will, determinism, and Dennett's compatibilism (from Freedom Evolves). He argues moral responsibility requires intentional choice and the capacity to know right from wrong, which the delusional self-narratives of Dexter (the 'Dark Passenger') and the denying Gacy call into question. Drawing on experimental philosophy (Knobe and Nichols) and cognitive 'frames,' he shows our verdicts hinge on emotion: the 'abused child' frame makes Dexter sympathetic while the 'murderous psychopath' frame condemns Gacy, so how a killer's story is framed drives our attribution of responsibility.

free-will-determinism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
free-will-determinism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
free-will-determinism.relation: J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.

free-will-determinism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
free-will-determinism.title: 3. Terminator I & II
free-will-determinism.relation: Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.

free-will-determinism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
free-will-determinism.title: 5. Minority Report
free-will-determinism.relation: Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.

free-will-determinism.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
free-will-determinism.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'

free-will-determinism.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
free-will-determinism.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
free-will-determinism.relation: Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.

free-will-determinism.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
free-will-determinism.title: Who is Who
free-will-determinism.relation: The time-travel chapter grounds Doctor Who's paradoxes in Parmenides and Zeno on the impossibility of change and Aristotle on the logical necessity of past and future statements ('You can't rewrite history!' in 'The Aztecs'), then deploys determinism, David Lewis on the paradoxes of time travel, and the consistency/autonomy principles ('Father's Day,' the Reapers). It uses Leibniz's possible worlds and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to read 'Inferno' and 'Turn Left,' arguing quantum indeterminacy and entanglement make the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' theory of fixed points and flux coherent.

free-will-determinism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
free-will-determinism.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
free-will-determinism.relation: Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.

free-will-determinism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
free-will-determinism.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
free-will-determinism.relation: David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.

free-will-determinism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
free-will-determinism.title: Determinism and the Dark Knight
free-will-determinism.relation: Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman beyond the free-will/determinism binary. Dasein is a "thrown-project" always being-toward-death; Alfred's world of trays and clocks illustrates the interpretive horizon of a chosen life. Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce Wayne with Angst and his own finitude, and — as in Miller's Year One, where a bat crashes through the window and he decides "I shall become a bat" — he authentically chooses his crime-fighting mission rather than being mechanically driven by trauma or vengeance.

free-will-determinism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: 7. Doctor Who as Philosophy Four-Dimensionalism and Time Travel
free-will-determinism.relation: Decker asks what the universe must be like if Doctor Who's time travel were real, using David Lewis's distinction between personal and external time and the TARDIS as a Wellsian (not Thornian) time machine traversing a 'hypertime' vortex. After surveying the arrows of time and paradoxes like the bootstrap paradox ('Day of the Daleks') and the grandfather paradox (imagined via Tegan's grandfather), and rejecting Deutsch-Lockwood's Many-Worlds and growing-block solutions, he argues the Whoniverse fits 'Four-Dimensional Realism'/eternalism, quoting the Twelfth Doctor that time's passage is an illusion of 'still pictures.' He then confronts 4DR's threat to free will and moral responsibility, finding compatibilism and 'fixed points' inadequate given eternalism's succession-not-production of events.

free-will-determinism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: 11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy
free-will-determinism.relation: Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.

free-will-determinism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: 48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality
free-will-determinism.relation: Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.

free-will-determinism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: 57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.

free-will-determinism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: 86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom
free-will-determinism.relation: Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'

free-will-determinism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
free-will-determinism.title: 88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will
free-will-determinism.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.

free-will-determinism.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
free-will-determinism.title: 2. The Dangers of Being the Doctor
free-will-determinism.relation: The chapter weighs the Doctor's ethic of interference against the Time Lords' non-interference, using determinism and the 'butterfly effect' (Martha in 'The Shakespeare Code') to concede when disengaged observation is prudent, while insisting that non-interference fails to protect human dignity. Drawing on Terrence Des Pres's account of dignity as 'inward resistance,' and real-world dissidents Adam Michnik and Václav Havel's 'power of the powerless,' it reads 'Rosa,' 'The Woman Who Fell to Earth,' and the people of Le Chambon as models of dignified, communal resistance to wrongdoing. Citing Iris Young, it argues everyone bears moral responsibility to engage rather than remain a detached, complicit 'objective observer.'

atomism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
atomism.title: Unknown
atomism.relation: This section lays out causal determinism through Laplace's demon: an intelligence that knew every force and every position could compute the entire future, leaving no one free or responsible, so people in the Matrix would be no worse off than we are. It notes that both sides of the nature-nurture debate (including B.F. Skinner) agree behavior is caused by forces beyond our control, and turns to Epicurus, who posited random atomic 'swerves' to make room for free will. Modern quantum indeterminacy, it concludes, likewise expels determinism from physics and at least makes free will possible, though randomness alone cannot ground responsibility.

atomism.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
atomism.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
atomism.relation: In an imaginary salon hosted by the baker 'la Brioche,' the goddess Eris drops a golden apple inscribed 'Atkins,' and three philosophers fight over the credit. Rousseau claims Atkins's war on refined flour and 'invented fake food' as his own back-to-nature, state-of-nature legacy; Confucius counters that Americans are 'grazers' without li, that culture is nature's flower, and that only ritual propriety can counteract the advertising that fills the void; Democritus claims the scientific core — 'hyperinsulism,' 'benign dietary ketosis' — as atomism's heir, deriding Rousseau's general will as democratic truth-concocting and Plato's otherworldly philosopher-king. The debate ranges over free will versus scientific prediction-and-control and ends unresolved over a refusal of brioche.

atomism.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
atomism.title: Too Big a Byte to Chew
atomism.relation: Kylie Prymus uses a slain Orc to stage the metaphysics of Azeroth: whether the 'dead' Orc is anything more than electrons obeying code (Democritus's atomism), and why explaining Ironforge's empty Tuesday mornings forces us to 'go meta' just as Aristotle's Metaphysics went beyond his Physics. The problem of other minds gets a WoW twist: without nameplates we would sort NPC from PC by the argument from analogy, the same imperfect tool we use offline for pain, coma patients, and animal minds. David Lewis's plurality of worlds becomes concrete through servers — 'the gates could be open' is true for the Uther player because on Medivh they opened on January 23rd — and she concludes that the real world is no better defined than Azeroth.

atomism.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
atomism.title: Hope
atomism.relation: Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.

atomism.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
atomism.title: Architecture and the Dream Machine
atomism.relation: Botz-Bornstein argues Inception presents dreams neither as separate worlds nor as Freudian symbols but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense: it synchronizes kicks, safe codes and the Piaf countdown like a computer coordinating contradictory layers of time. He links inception to Dawkins's meme theory, with the planted idea growing 'like a cancer' in Mal, and to the projections of Solaris, showing how the film unusually combines cognitive and psychoanalytic models in one vertical dream structure. Democritus's atomism frames Epstein's 'grains of reality' and the film's atomized media-images of the real world, while Benjamin and Baudrillard let him read Cobb's Limbo dystopia, Mombasa and Dubai's empty skyscrapers as an allegory of a globalized world of hackable neoliberal dream machines.

atomism.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
atomism.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
atomism.relation: Levi Bryant argues the D&D universe models a 'flat ontology' of active substances whose powers (affects) actualize differently under local conditions, asking Democritus-style individuation questions about whether a band of ogres at a tavern is one entity or many. Characters and their gear form alliances that generate genuinely new beings, so the blind man with his cane, or Moorcock's Elric fed by the soul-drinking sword Stormbringer, is a different entity than without it, and he borrows Clark and Chalmers' extended mind hypothesis to deny that thinking happens only inside the head. The dice then supply chance that generates necessity: the Dungeon Master's throws conjure traps, wraiths and saving throws that form 'regimes of attraction' to which every player and monster must respond.

atomism.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
atomism.title: 6. You’re Gonna Die
atomism.relation: Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.

atomism.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
atomism.title: 18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld
atomism.relation: Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.

atomism.title: Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya
atomism.relation: Exposes Kanada's Vaisheshika pluralistic realism: seven categories (substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and absence) and nine eternal substances, with earth, water, fire, and air atoms combining to form all composite objects - the red of a red rose illustrating quality, inherence, universality, and particularity. It then presents Gotama's Nyaya contribution: a formal five-membered inferential method (thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion - 'there is fire on the hill because there is smoke') grounded in perception and invariable rules rather than Vedic testimony, plus criteria (doubt, purpose, possibility of certainty) for when enquiry is legitimate. Nyaya uses this method to 'prove' a plurality of eternal selves from the plurality of consciousnesses and their qualities, and the chapter notes the standing modern comparison of the method with Aristotle's syllogism. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

atomism.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
atomism.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
atomism.relation: Levi Bryant uses the D&D universe to expound a 'flat ontology' of active substances: every entity, from enchanted swords to white dragons, has a virtual proper being (powers or 'affects') that actualizes variable 'local manifestations' depending on circumstances like lighting or armor. Adopting Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis, he argues a blind man with a cane, a smartphone owner, or Elric wielding Stormbringer is a literally different mind or entity, and that alliances (Raistlin's Staff of Magius, a warrior's plate armor) generate genuinely new powers rather than mere tool-use. Against Democritus's atomism, he holds aggregates can be individuals, and the game's dice embody his claim that chance produces necessity: throws generate 'regimes of attraction' no DM or player controls. D&D thus mirrors our own world of hidden powers, aleatory encounters and collectives of humans and nonhumans.

atomism.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
atomism.title: Architecture and the Dream Machine
atomism.relation: Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues that Inception presents dreams neither as divine messages nor as stylized fantasy but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense — a 'robot brain' whose synchronized kicks, Piaf countdown, and phone-number safes 'think' the different layers of time instead of reproducing a reality, with slow motion as cognition rather than dream-sign (against Bazin). He reads inception as Dawkins's meme theory given a psychoanalytic vertical dimension: the idea is implanted deep in the subconscious (Fischer's relation to his father), can grow autonomously 'like a cancer' as Mal's did, and subconscious projections converge 'like white blood cells' as in Solaris. The chapter then traces how the computer era — hypertext, Second Life, media-absorbed realities like Baudrillard's 9/11 — reshaped cinematic dreams and architecture, so that Ariadne's 'pure creation,' Cobb's Limbo dystopia, and Dubai's empty speculative towers all become the 'gilded dreamworlds' of an ephemeralized, hacker-ready built world — the dream machine as allegory of the globalized world, with atomized grains of reality echoing Democritus via Epstein and Benjamin's account of cinema bursting the prison of the everyday.

atomism.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
atomism.title: Notes
atomism.relation: Shores opens with Sophie's World comparing LEGO bricks to Democritus' indivisible, endlessly recombinable atoms, and argues LEGO is a system of play and an 'object to think with' that models how ideas and worldviews are assembled, disassembled, and rebuilt. He contrasts Plato's Republic-era suspicion that children's play must be regulated with the Socratic playfulness that treats philosophy itself as serious play, and enlists Locke and Rousseau on play-based learning and Freud on the child at play as a creative writer rearranging its world. Lord Business' Kragle shows play taken too seriously becoming inert, while Caillois' ludus/paidia distinction frames the difference between themed narrative sets, free building, and the goal-directed rigidity of the LEGO video games.

buddhist-non-self.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
buddhist-non-self.title: Unknown
buddhist-non-self.relation: Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.

buddhist-non-self.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
buddhist-non-self.title: Unknown
buddhist-non-self.relation: The chapter reads 'the One' through the concentration-camp survivor who, by sheer presence, retained others' dignity and will to live—a place in the social link filled by transference rather than real qualities—and opposes this to the film's One, who merely learns the virtualized reality's rules can be suspended, a paranoid notion that reduces the resistance of the Real to weak will. The spoon-bending child's 'there is no spoon' should have pushed the film to the Buddhist proposition that I myself do not exist, while Agent Smith's speech that humans 'define their reality through suffering and misery' makes him the analyst-figure whose lesson is that reality is that which resists.

buddhist-non-self.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
buddhist-non-self.title: “Nobody’s Bob Dylan”
buddhist-non-self.relation: Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.

buddhist-non-self.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
buddhist-non-self.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
buddhist-non-self.relation: Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.

buddhist-non-self.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
buddhist-non-self.title: Mind the Mindfulness
buddhist-non-self.relation: Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).

buddhist-non-self.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
buddhist-non-self.title: “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons
buddhist-non-self.relation: James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.

buddhist-non-self.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
buddhist-non-self.title: Analyzing Emptiness
buddhist-non-self.relation: Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.

buddhist-non-self.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
buddhist-non-self.title: “Logic Without Need Is Sterile”
buddhist-non-self.relation: Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.

buddhist-non-self.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
buddhist-non-self.title: Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy
buddhist-non-self.relation: Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.

buddhist-non-self.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
buddhist-non-self.title: 2 - An Interview with Bodhidharma
buddhist-non-self.relation: Priest stages a spoof radio interview with Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Temple to argue that the monks' fighting exercises are really meditation: a fist passing an inch from your nose focuses the mind, and repeatedly practicing violent techniques makes practitioners less violent. Bodhidharma explains that a liter of goat's milk, a marauding thug, and even the reporter's self are only conceptual labels over 'thusness' (tathata), that attachment and the desire to strike cause suffering to the striker, and that the Buddha's compassion permits self-defense without aggression. The punchline is the reporter's unanswered last question: 'They're not really about fighting, are they?'

buddhist-non-self.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
buddhist-non-self.title: And the Winner Is
buddhist-non-self.relation: Lynch pits Plato against the Shaolin monks on the nature of the self that martial training is supposed to master. Plato's Republic makes the athlete-warrior Guardian a harmonious, rationally ruled tripartite soul whose bravery is 'remembering what ought and ought not to be feared', trained so reason governs aggression; Buddhism instead dissolves the self into five impermanent aggregates (illustrated by the chariot analogy) and reads mushin as a direct taste of no-self. He awards the practical decision to the Buddhist fighting monks, since no-self explains martial spontaneity and naturally arising compassion, while admitting Plato's substantive rational soul is not strictly refuted.

buddhist-non-self.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
buddhist-non-self.title: Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame
buddhist-non-self.relation: Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.

buddhist-non-self.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
buddhist-non-self.title: Chapter 07 - Scan Thyself
buddhist-non-self.relation: Butler frames Dick as the latest in philosophy's self-knowledge line: the Delphic 'know thyself' that Socrates made essential to the good life at the cost of his own, the Buddha who sought himself and found only an illusion at the root of suffering, Descartes whose entire philosophy rests on confidence in knowledge of himself as an immaterial being, and Dick's own 8,000-page Exegesis. The chapter's hook is the stakes of self-ignorance (what if you turned out to be something horrible?) and its Dickian version: how do you know you are not an android?

buddhist-non-self.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
buddhist-non-self.title: The Devil and Philosophy
buddhist-non-self.relation: John Thompson argues Mara, who unleashes armies and seductive daughters on the Buddha-to-be under the bodhi tree, is not 'the Buddhist Satan': he has not fallen, wages no cosmic war against a supreme God, and merely personifies trsna (grasping) as overlord of samsara. He finds textbook glosses like Huston Smith's misleading, and praises Bertolucci's Little Buddha, where Mara rises from a pool as Siddhartha's mirror twin - 'Oh Lord of my own Ego, you are pure illusion. You do not exist' - a portrayal he reads through Karen Armstrong's Jungian shadow self and Campbell's Freudian eros-and-thanatos frame, concluding that we are Mara/Satan.

buddhist-non-self.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
buddhist-non-self.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
buddhist-non-self.relation: Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.

buddhist-non-self.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
buddhist-non-self.title: 3. Tris Finds Enlightenment
buddhist-non-self.relation: Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.

buddhist-non-self.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
buddhist-non-self.title: 23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep
buddhist-non-self.relation: Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.

buddhist-non-self.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
buddhist-non-self.title: 6. One Clone from Another
buddhist-non-self.relation: Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.

buddhist-non-self.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
buddhist-non-self.title: 17. Dialog with the Buddha
buddhist-non-self.relation: A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.

buddhist-non-self.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
buddhist-non-self.title: 6. Bowie the Buddhist
buddhist-non-self.relation: Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'

buddhist-non-self.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
buddhist-non-self.title: 14. David Bowie’s Sadness
buddhist-non-self.relation: Ketcham argues Bowie's sadness is ours: via Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus he casts consumer capitalism as a machine producing schizophrenic fad-following (the stuck high-school footballer, the Benetton self), of which Bowie's serial personas are both symptom and escape - 'always crashing in the same car' yet never repeating. Minkowski's lived time and the Buddha's anatman ground the dance as pure becoming without a dancer, while Heidegger's das Man and being-toward-death explain why authentic self-creation - which, unlike Sellers or Williams, Bowie survived - exacts the price Freud's beyond-the-pleasure-principle names as compulsive repetition, turned by Bowie into a life wish.

buddhist-non-self.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
buddhist-non-self.title: 22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy
buddhist-non-self.relation: Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.

buddhist-non-self.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking
buddhist-non-self.title: The Buddha’s Middle Way
buddhist-non-self.relation: Reconstructs the Buddha's teaching as a Middle Way on three levels: socially between householder ritualism and renouncer asceticism, in monastic life between indulgence and austerities, and metaphysically between every permutation of existence and non-existence. It details the Enlightenment's three insights, the Four Noble Truths (dukkha better rendered 'unsatisfactoriness' grounded in the impermanence of all conditioned things), and dependent origination as the 'regularity of things'. Against the standard reading of anatta as 'there is no self', it argues the Buddha denied only independent existence and shifted inquiry from ontology to the workings of the cognitive apparatus (the five khandhas), citing his refusal to answer the Unanswered Questions. It also gives the Buddha's specific critiques of brahmin claims to authority, the purposelessness of ritual, and reliance on tradition over one's own experience. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

buddhist-non-self.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking
buddhist-non-self.title: Developments in Buddhist thought
buddhist-non-self.relation: Traces Buddhist scholasticism from the eighteen early schools (Lokottaravadins, Sammatiyas, Sautrantikas, Sarvastivadins, with Theravada the survivor) through the Abhidharma projects - Sarvastivada dharmas existing in all three time modes with an essence (svabhava), Theravada's categorization of some 28 physical and 52 mental dharmas - and their critique of Nyaya-Vaisheshika partless atoms. It then presents the Mahayana response: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras' teaching that all dharmas are empty of own-being, and Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka demonstration that nothing with own-being can arise from itself, from another, from both, or spontaneously, together with his two truths (conventional and ultimate) and the 'emptiness of emptiness' - emptiness affirms, rather than denies, the dependently originated world, since without it no change or knowledge would be possible. It closes with Vasubandhu's Yogacara 'Mind-Only' analysis of transformations of consciousness, karmic 'seeds' in a storehouse consciousness, and the constructed, dependent, and perfected aspects of experience, which denies that perception establishes the external existence of its objects. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

buddhist-non-self.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
buddhist-non-self.title: 12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton
buddhist-non-self.relation: Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.

buddhist-non-self.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
buddhist-non-self.title: 8. Ode to Joi
buddhist-non-self.relation: Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.

buddhist-non-self.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
buddhist-non-self.title: 14. After the Blackout
buddhist-non-self.relation: Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.

buddhist-non-self.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
buddhist-non-self.title: 4. Can We Do Enough Good
buddhist-non-self.relation: Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.

buddhist-non-self.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
buddhist-non-self.title: Fearlessness and Power
buddhist-non-self.relation: Rebuts Ozai's taunt 'you are still weak' with a Buddhist reading of energybending: Aang wins not by domination but because his unbendable spirit is total vulnerability, a true heart that has abandoned the five hindrances (sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt — each traced through the chakras, the Serpent's Pass, and 'Nightmares and Daydreams') and a true mind freed from the fundamental delusion of a separate self that 'The Swamp' and 'The Guru' dissolve. The spirit-merging with Ozai is read through Indra's net, and Aang's merciful halt mirrors Indra's Jataka victory where compassion for eagle hatchlings — not force — defeats the demons. Fearlessness, on Sylvia Boorstein's Zen story, is the natural corollary of compassion, so Aang's weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely his power.

buddhist-non-self.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
buddhist-non-self.title: Fearlessness and Power
