buddhist-karma.relation: The chapter argues the film is by no means a Christian movie: Neo is a violent, far-from-sinless mere human savior; the fundamental human problem is ignorance and illusion (Gnostic and Eastern) rather than sin and alienation from God; the rebels' belief that Neo is the reincarnation of the earlier liberator mirrors the Dalai Lama search the Wachowskis cite, though reincarnation is rejected by all major Christian sects; and 'there is no spoon' asserts the illusoriness of empirical reality that Christianity denies. The film's malleable, cyclical time and the Wachowskis' answer that faith is 'in oneself' complete a syncretistic tapestry the essay goes on to examine as religious pluralism.

buddhist-karma.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
buddhist-karma.title: Unknown
buddhist-karma.relation: The chapter argues the third postulate must be a this-worldly immortality: since no single lifetime suffices to realize the Highest Good, Kant himself (in Universal Natural History) imagined the soul reborn over and over as it climbs the ladder of human perfection, and Mahayana Buddhism's bodhisattva - who chooses to remain on the wheel of rebirth to enlighten all beings - matches the monkish boy 'Potential' and the Oracle's hints. The One accordingly appears in three incarnations: the earlier liberator who freed the first rebels, Neo's second life, and the third life glimpsed at the film's end.

buddhist-karma.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
buddhist-karma.title: In It for the Long Run
buddhist-karma.relation: Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.

buddhist-karma.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
buddhist-karma.title: Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures
buddhist-karma.relation: Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.

buddhist-karma.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
buddhist-karma.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
buddhist-karma.relation: Observes that only Talking Animals enter Aslan's country when Narnia ends in The Last Battle, then critically examines Lewis's case against wider animal salvation: derivative immortality through human love (Sarah Smith's train of beasts in The Great Divorce), compensation of animal pain in an afterlife, Lewis's follow-Descartes claim that most animals are sentient but not conscious enough to feel pain or have a surviving 'self'. The chapter argues each point fails: the physiological evidence shows animals suffer, resurrection or God-given souls remain possible (Strawberry's transformation into a winged Talking horse), and a compensatory hereafter is still the most promising answer to why a loving God permits the fawn's miserable death. Aquinas's rational-creature hierarchy frames the Talking/Dumb divide, and the Hindu-Buddhist rebirth theodicy is considered and rejected as unbiblical.

buddhist-karma.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
buddhist-karma.title: “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons
buddhist-karma.relation: James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's sleepless FTL jumps in "33" and Roslin's dwindling survivor counts enact the four noble truths, Leoben's interrogation scenes teach that suffering comes from ignorant attachment, and Dogen's no-self and impermanence frame the show's interdependent characters. Cylon resurrection, D'Anna's serial deaths, and the prophecy that "all of this has happened before" model karma and samsara, while Nishida's kenotic God of Absolute Nothingness makes sense of Six and Leoben's God of love. Because Cylons feel pain, fear death away from a resurrection ship, and act volitionally, McRae concludes they are persons in the Buddhist sense, owed the compassion of the Eightfold Path.

buddhist-karma.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
buddhist-karma.title: Are We Going Too Far
buddhist-karma.relation: David Kyle Johnson distinguishes revenge (personal, emotional, unlimited) from retribution and argues that 'Tarantino's view'—mercy should be common practice yet revenge can be justified—is consistent: Jules buys Pumpkin and Honey Bunny's lives but never waives a right of vengeance, since they never wronged him. He tests the view against Bushido, showing Beatrix's revolt against her lord Bill violates the samurai code, and against karma, which makes revenge unnecessary. After finding that Hobbes, Locke, Nietzsche and Socrates all leave revenge's justification open, he defends it—citing Budd's 'that woman deserves her revenge'—so long as the punishment fits the crime and spares innocents, as when Beatrix refuses to make herself even by killing Vernita's daughter Nikki.

buddhist-karma.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
buddhist-karma.title: Sudden Enlightenment
buddhist-karma.relation: Luke Cuddy and Michael Bruce ask whether Beatrix Kiddo could reach enlightenment, reading Kill Bill's nonlinear plotting as a Buddhist interconnected web of causes: Pai Mei's Five Point Palm technique causes both the coffin escape and Bill's death, and Budd's degraded trailer life is karma catching up. Beatrix grasps the structure of suffering and its cause—she locates it in Bill and the squad and eliminates them—but mistakes that for ending suffering itself, and her declared lack of 'mercy, compassion, and forgiveness' blocks the compassion enlightenment requires, while Bill's 'natural born killer' story contradicts impermanence and no-self. The chapter closes on her bathroom-floor ecstasy as a candidate case of Zen sudden enlightenment, left to the reader to judge by how she would one day treat a vengeful Nikki.

buddhist-karma.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
buddhist-karma.title: Into the Future
buddhist-karma.relation: Hanley dismantles the four claimed human/Cylon differences: artificial reproduction is in principle possible for us; prosthetics already blur what we are made of; model copies differ like identical twins (Boomer is not Athena); and resurrection has human analogues — he proposes an SDTR (scanning, death, transmission, replication) model and uses van Inwagen's replica-switch account of bodily resurrection while rejecting soul-based reincarnation on Lockean grounds, since consciousness rather than soul is the criterion of identity. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction, not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), and reads Athena's memories of Tyrol as evidence she is a replicated Boomer. The upshot: being a Cylon is nothing to fear — 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'

buddhist-karma.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
buddhist-karma.title: What Monkey Should Have Known
buddhist-karma.relation: Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.

buddhist-karma.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
buddhist-karma.title: 23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep
buddhist-karma.relation: Staged as a Fight Club parody in which a Buddhist psychiatrist, Dr. Quinzel, evaluates a costumed narrator sent to Arkham, the chapter argues neither hero is close to awakening: Batman's crime-fighting is craving that perpetuates dukkha, his secret identities a twice-constructed self that the Buddha's no-self teaching dissolves, and his violence fails the test that 'hostility is never appeased by hostility.' Superman fares no better - his super-intellect imposes illusory order on impermanence, his flight and X-ray vision are distractions beside the Buddha-eye and tapas, and as one of the titans of the six realms he is further from Buddhahood than a human - while the doctor defines justice as karma rather than retaliation and finds Batman one step from American Psycho's Bateman. Only conquering Mara, one's own inner deceiver, is 'the only superpower worth having,' and the closing reveal that the doctor has a plan of her own for 'Mr. Kent' caps the diagnosis.

buddhist-karma.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
buddhist-karma.title: 17. Dialog with the Buddha
buddhist-karma.relation: A Platonic-style fictional dialogue in which a newly enlightened "Canadian Buddha" walks out of the northern Ontario bush to the Prolethean farm and debates Tomas, Henry, and Bonnie over whether clones are abominations. Using karma, rebirth, the gandhabba that carries consciousness-flux to a new embryo, the no-soul doctrine, and the eightfold path, the Buddha argues clones are ordinary beings of the karmic flux — like the split bacterium, nothing unnatural — but that cloning multiplies clinging: hosts crave immortality through copies, each clone inherits the host's whole accumulated karma, and Henry's dream of training an army of Helena-clones would only deepen the unsatisfactoriness the Buddha's mustard-seed lesson says clinging to the dead always brings. Only ending the cycle through enlightenment releases anyone; the clone, like the lost child, is not the one you lost.

buddhist-karma.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
buddhist-karma.title: 6. The Accidental Hero
buddhist-karma.relation: Darian Shump judges Deadpool by Buddhist lights, applying karma as intentional action and skillful means—the permissibility of compassionate killing, after Rupert Gethin—to his Marvel NOW! career: protecting Agent Preston, saving a child and Nightcrawler Kim mid-battle, and the Niagara Bride assisted suicide whose fee he donates to a home for kids with cancer. A hypothetical Hydra spy with a bomb on a S.H.I.E.L.D. helicarrier shows how killing one murderer-to-be can be the compassionate act that saves everyone. He concludes Deadpool is an 'accidental hero'—a mercenary first whose good intentions make him a karmic hero—while Zenpool's failed pacifism in AXIS shows that renouncing violence betrays what makes Deadpool Deadpool.

buddhist-karma.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking
buddhist-karma.title: Richness and diversity in Indian thought
buddhist-karma.relation: Argues that in India philosophy and religion were never separated as the post-Kantian West separates them: philosophizing is a soteriological quest in which understanding the nature of reality directly affects one's destiny, more comparable to Socrates' quest for wisdom than to modern academic philosophy. It introduces the framework of darshanas ('views' of reality taught by seers), the claim that disciplined mental exercises can yield yogic perception of metaphysical truth, and karma-rebirth as the shared Indian worldview, contrasting ritual-correctness karma with the Buddha's radically intention-based version and discussing verbal testimony as an everyday but religiously unchecked means of knowledge. It closes by delimiting the book's scope (the six classical darshanas plus Buddhism; Jainism, Carvaka, and Shaivism omitted) and warning against the Western habit of romanticizing Indian thought as mystical rather than recognizing its strong rational-debate tradition. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

buddhist-karma.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking
buddhist-karma.title: Sacrifice, cosmic speculation, oneness
buddhist-karma.relation: Presents the two coexisting branches of the Brahmanical tradition around 500 BCE: the Vedic sacrificial religion, in which precisely performed ritual actions (physical and verbal karma) maintained cosmic order (dharma) and underwrote brahmin social authority, and the Upanishadic internalization of the sacrifice. The Upanishads shift the focus to the person, teaching that experiential insight into the identity of one's essential self (atman) and the cosmos (Brahman) - 'tat tvam asi' - brings moksha from rebirth, illustrated with the Rig Veda 10.129 creation hymn and passages from the Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka Upanishads. It carefully distinguishes monism (one existent thing) from monotheism, sets the Upanishadic oneness against the pluralistic realism of the ritualists, and shows how this internal tension became the fault line along which later Indian philosophical debate would run. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

buddhist-karma.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking
buddhist-karma.title: The Buddha’s Middle Way
buddhist-karma.relation: Reconstructs the Buddha's teaching as a Middle Way on three levels: socially between householder ritualism and renouncer asceticism, in monastic life between indulgence and austerities, and metaphysically between every permutation of existence and non-existence. It details the Enlightenment's three insights, the Four Noble Truths (dukkha better rendered 'unsatisfactoriness' grounded in the impermanence of all conditioned things), and dependent origination as the 'regularity of things'. Against the standard reading of anatta as 'there is no self', it argues the Buddha denied only independent existence and shifted inquiry from ontology to the workings of the cognitive apparatus (the five khandhas), citing his refusal to answer the Unanswered Questions. It also gives the Buddha's specific critiques of brahmin claims to authority, the purposelessness of ritual, and reliance on tradition over one's own experience. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

buddhist-karma.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking
buddhist-karma.title: Developments in Buddhist thought
buddhist-karma.relation: Traces Buddhist scholasticism from the eighteen early schools (Lokottaravadins, Sammatiyas, Sautrantikas, Sarvastivadins, with Theravada the survivor) through the Abhidharma projects - Sarvastivada dharmas existing in all three time modes with an essence (svabhava), Theravada's categorization of some 28 physical and 52 mental dharmas - and their critique of Nyaya-Vaisheshika partless atoms. It then presents the Mahayana response: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras' teaching that all dharmas are empty of own-being, and Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka demonstration that nothing with own-being can arise from itself, from another, from both, or spontaneously, together with his two truths (conventional and ultimate) and the 'emptiness of emptiness' - emptiness affirms, rather than denies, the dependently originated world, since without it no change or knowledge would be possible. It closes with Vasubandhu's Yogacara 'Mind-Only' analysis of transformations of consciousness, karmic 'seeds' in a storehouse consciousness, and the constructed, dependent, and perfected aspects of experience, which denies that perception establishes the external existence of its objects. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

buddhist-karma.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
buddhist-karma.title: 11. 999 Fingers
buddhist-karma.relation: Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.

buddhist-karma.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
buddhist-karma.title: 8. Ode to Joi
buddhist-karma.relation: Steve Bein first tests Joi against Mary Anne Warren's five functionalist personhood criteria — consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness — and finds she passes, which makes Luv's stomping of the emanator a murder. The Buddha's no-self doctrine then denies that anyone, Joi included, is an enduring person: we are bundles of fleeting psychophysical processes, 'like tears in rain', which threatens to let Luv plead that the Luv who killed Joi no longer exists. Nagarjuna's two truths resolve the courtroom problem: ultimately there are no persons, but conventionally 'Luv killed Joi' is perfectly true, and the karma ripples through the whole network.

buddhist-karma.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
buddhist-karma.title: 19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right
buddhist-karma.relation: Kaur and Gupta argue Hinduism got far more than five percent right, mapping the show's points onto karmic theory and the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of action: right action, inaction, and wrong action. Eleanor's fruitless point-grubbing and selfless departure exemplify nishkama karma, desire-less action, while the 802 reboots and Janet's memory-wiped revivals mirror the birth-death-rebirth cycle on the way to self-realization. Ranking the cast on the Gita's ladder of unfoldment, desire-driven Eleanor and Jason below Tahani and knowledgeable Chidi, with Michael straying from his dharma and detached, duty-bound Janet nearest to Brahman, they show the series dramatizes the Gita's teaching that motivation, not the deed itself, determines an act's worth.

buddhist-karma.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
buddhist-karma.title: The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the
buddhist-karma.relation: Barkman reads the 30 Rock cast as prisoners who prefer delusion, using Plato's allegory of the cave and the Upanishadic scheme of samsara, karma, maya, and moksha, in which Atman is realized as one with Brahman, as twin diagnoses. Drew's 'bubble' of good looks, Liz's false memory of being a harmless nerd in 'Reunion' and her belief she can have it all, Jack's pride about his terrible sketch ideas, Kenneth's unexamined dogma ('I can't handle the truth!'), Jenna's age-hiding, and Tracy's white myths about diabetes and Colorado all illustrate ignorance of reality that costs happiness. The Hindu-Platonic lesson is that knowledge of reality, not Dr. Spaceman's 'science is whatever we want it to be', is the route to happiness, because ignorance is not bliss.

buddhist-karma.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
buddhist-karma.title: Happily, Ever After
buddhist-karma.relation: The chapter asks whether Nish's revenge in 'Black Museum' - poisoning Rolo and downloading his digital self into her father Clayton's eternal-electrocution exhibit - is morally justified. Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness condemns payback as sadism plus 'magical thinking' and prescribes transition-anger, then unconditional forgiveness, then best of all unconditional love (the prodigal son); Christian agape commands loving enemies and leaving wrath to God; and the Buddhist analysis of dukkha, karma and non-self shows Nish's hateful revenge generates worse karma than Rolo's greed and deepens the very suffering it means to end. The verdict: revenge, however emotionally satisfying, is never justified - even the tourists zapping Clayton and Nish zapping Rolo fall into the same trap.

buddhist-karma.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
buddhist-karma.title: 23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep
buddhist-karma.relation: A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.

buddhist-karma.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
buddhist-karma.title: “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons
buddhist-karma.relation: James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.

buddhist-karma.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
buddhist-karma.title: Rāma of Gilead
buddhist-karma.relation: Matthew Butkus reads Roland Deschain of The Dark Tower as a parallel to Rama of the Ramayana and Arjuna of the Bhagavad Gita, mapping his cyclical existence onto the Hindu concepts of karma (his coupling with the demon spawning Mordred, letting Jake fall), dharma (the gunslinger's duty to protect the Beams as an avatar restoring cosmic order), samskara (character shaped by all past lives) and samsara (the death-rebirth cycle the Horn of Eld may or may not break). Like Krishna instructing the reluctant Arjuna, the text tells Roland he must 'stand and be true' regardless of misgivings; Butkus concludes the moral for readers is not violence but fulfilling one's own svadharma—to stand and be true in one's own station.

buddhist-karma.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
buddhist-karma.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
buddhist-karma.relation: Geisz reads his daily morning coffee ritual through Buddhist metaphysics: the pre-caffeine grogginess and its transient relief illustrate saṃsāra and duḥkha, the First Noble Truth, driven by self-centered craving (the Second). The transience of the perfect-temperature cup shows impermanence (anitya), and the question of whether a 'self' pre- or post-coffee exists is answered by anatman — he offers three hypotheses (full self dormant, half coffee-cyborg, self created ex Coffea) then dissolves them into no-self plus dependent arising, where the cup and drinker are empty nodes in a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions. Each intentional sip lays down karma that binds tomorrow's 'me' further into the cycle.

buddhist-karma.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
buddhist-karma.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
buddhist-karma.relation: Deal and Waller use Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual-metaphor theory to explain how we grasp Santa's God-like moral omniscience through human metaphors. Santa 'sees from above' (North Pole, flight), judges with 'cool' reason yet remains jolly, and – echoing Plato's Phaedrus charioteer and Descartes' solitary reasoner – masters his appetites and decides free of bias. His gift-giving runs on a 'moral accounting' metaphor where good deeds are commodities exchanged for presents and 'moral authority is parental authority'; they read A Christmas Story's BB-gun lesson through this frame and finally liken Santa's impartial, dispassionate sorting of naughty and nice to the impersonal law of karma.

buddhist-karma.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
buddhist-karma.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
buddhist-karma.relation: Kieran McManus's travel memoir 'Will I Find My Guru in India?' recounts his search from Kathmandu to Rishikesh and the Agama Yoga School, where teacher Kushru's lectures on karma, breath, and diet finally make asana click for him. His reported insight — that every thought and act moves him toward or away from his sacred potential, and that the yogi transcends suffering by treating each experience as neutral and as an opportunity, remaining present — applies a karmic and present-moment ethic to his own practice rather than expounding doctrine abstractly.

buddhist-karma.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
buddhist-karma.title: “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons
buddhist-karma.relation: McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism, using Dogen and the Four Noble Truths. The fleet's relentless suffering (the "33" jumps, the Olympic Carrier), impermanence (Roslin's dwindling headcount), and no-self frame duhkha; Leoben functions as a roshi whose koan-like preaching makes Starbuck and Adama question their false ideals, and the Cylon death-and-resurrection cycle parallels karma and rebirth. Because Cylons feel and are cognitively aware of pain and can accrue karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori, so human and Cylon liberation are intertwined.

faith-vs-reason.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
faith-vs-reason.title: Unknown
faith-vs-reason.relation: Taking the film's cafeteria religion seriously as 'Neo-pluralism', the chapter distinguishes four varieties of religious pluralism and finds each wanting: extreme pluralism dies by simple logic since of 100,000 religions many contradict one another; fundamental-teachings pluralism fails because the great religions differ on genuinely fundamental doctrines (Islam's personal God versus Theravada's non-theism versus the Trinity); cafeteria pluralism produces incoherent transplantings (reincarnation fits Hinduism but not Buddhism or Christianity) and lacks any rational justification short of wishful thinking; and Hick's Kantian transcendental pluralism posits an unintelligible, wholly unknowable Real while demanding the doublethink - highlighted by Alvin Plantinga - of continuing to hold beliefs one recognizes as literally false.

faith-vs-reason.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
faith-vs-reason.title: Unknown
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter rebuts three pluralist objections to religious exclusivism: the 'equal fruits' argument confuses hard exclusivism with the common soft (inclusivist) form that freely admits salvation and authentic experience outside one tradition; the arrogance charge rests on a principle that would condemn every political and moral conviction held in the face of reasonable disagreement, and is self-refuting - Plantinga's 'philosophical tar baby'; and the arbitrariness charge begs the question, since pluralists assume rather than argue that no religion could have better evidence, which is precisely the point at issue between exclusivism and pluralism.

faith-vs-reason.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
faith-vs-reason.title: Unknown
faith-vs-reason.relation: This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.

faith-vs-reason.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
faith-vs-reason.title: Who Should Be Committed
faith-vs-reason.relation: Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.

faith-vs-reason.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
faith-vs-reason.title: From Knowledge to Faith
faith-vs-reason.relation: Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.

faith-vs-reason.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
faith-vs-reason.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.

faith-vs-reason.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
faith-vs-reason.title: The Man and His Faith
faith-vs-reason.relation: Morris argues Daredevil is the rare mainstream hero with a religious interior life: raised nominally Catholic in Hell's Kitchen, his absent mother a nun who calls him 'a servant of God', he prays, thinks in religious categories, and complains to God like King David in the Psalms ('Why do the wicked prosper?'). Distinguishing mere outward religiosity from authentic faith, he proposes his 'Double Power Principle' - whatever has power for ill has equal power for good, religion included - and asks whether faith is blind like Matt Murdock or perceptive like his radar sense: a source of strength or of weakness for a costumed vigilante.

faith-vs-reason.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
faith-vs-reason.title: Faith and Fear
faith-vs-reason.relation: Against Quentin Beck's claim that 'a man without fear is a man without faith', Morris argues the fear-based account of religion (Freud's) mistakes superstition for faith: authentic faith is a commitment of the heart rather than intellectual certitude, so the truly fearless are likely people of strong faith, as the martyrs show. He then distinguishes paralyzing self-referential 'fear of' from motivating 'fear that' (better called concern), concluding Daredevil genuinely is the Man Without Fear precisely because his deep-down faithfulness sustains him - he lives 'by faith and not by sight'.

faith-vs-reason.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
faith-vs-reason.title: Gloom, Doom, and Morality
faith-vs-reason.relation: Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.

faith-vs-reason.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
faith-vs-reason.title: A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics
faith-vs-reason.relation: Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.

faith-vs-reason.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
faith-vs-reason.title: Hope and the Human Challenge
faith-vs-reason.relation: Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.

faith-vs-reason.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
faith-vs-reason.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.

faith-vs-reason.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
faith-vs-reason.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Debunks the 'Anscombe legend' that Lewis abandoned rational apologetics for children's stories after his 1948 Socratic Club defeat by Elizabeth Anscombe over the argument that naturalism is self-refuting. It shows Lewis revised and expanded the argument in the 1960 Miracles, incorporating Anscombe's reasons/causes distinction, and kept writing apologetic essays, while the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (liar, lunatic, or truthful) mirrors the Trilemma of Mere Christianity and shows Narnia using logic, not fleeing it. It rejects A.N. Wilson's identification of the Green Witch with Anscombe and argues the Chronicles teach that prudence and faith are compatible virtues: Edmund's rationalizing, Trumpkin's honest skepticism, and Puzzle's blind trust in Shift all show that fideistic faith is a vice, not what Lewis asks of children.

faith-vs-reason.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
faith-vs-reason.title: Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)
faith-vs-reason.relation: Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.

faith-vs-reason.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
faith-vs-reason.title: U2 and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.

faith-vs-reason.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
faith-vs-reason.title: U2 and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Cleveland sorts the knowing and feeling of U2's lyrics ('Vertigo', 'Beautiful Day', 'Staring at the Sun', 'Daddy's Gonna Pay for Your Crash Car') into Russell's varieties of knowledge - propositional, acquaintance, know-how - and argues that the feeling U2 champions against thought is knowledge by acquaintance: direct, concept-free awareness that, in religious cases, just is Jamesian mystical revelation as against revelation as a set of propositional truths, which is why Bono tells his father he 'hears something back from the silence' rather than holding doctrines. James supplies both the view that feeling is the deeper source of religion and the pragmatist answer to the problem of origins - 'by their fruits ye shall know them', so religious feeling is vindicated by moral transformation. Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis explains why such feeling, not inert moral knowledge, moves Bono's social justice work: 'God is love, and as much as I respond... in acting in that love, that's my religion'.

faith-vs-reason.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
faith-vs-reason.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
faith-vs-reason.relation: Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.

faith-vs-reason.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
faith-vs-reason.title: Introduction
faith-vs-reason.relation: Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.

faith-vs-reason.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
faith-vs-reason.title: To Know … and Believe
faith-vs-reason.relation: Gallagher reads Lost's Rose through Aquinas: faith is 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion,' sharing the certainty of episteme and the imperfection of doxa, so Rose's 'I just know' about Bernard's survival and her island cure confuses what she believes with what she knows. Aquinas' five ways ground natural knowledge that God exists, and the castaways' failures are diagnosed as sins against faith — Charlie's despair is acedia while Rose's certainty is the presumption (praesumptio) of elevating faith to demonstrated knowledge; the lesson is that faith perfects reason without replacing it.

faith-vs-reason.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
faith-vs-reason.title: Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t
faith-vs-reason.relation: Bryan McHenry asks whether manipulating religious belief for political ends is ever moral, using Adama's motivational lie about Earth, Roslin's Pythia-driven 'dying leader' campaign (compared with George W. Bush's faith-based politics), and the Cylons' evangelical monotheism aimed at scaring Baltar into conversion. Machiavelli's Prince licenses rulers who use a religion they do not share, and the chapter judges Adama's hope-based use of the Earth myth and Roslin's uniting religiosity as essentially moral while the Cylons wield faith as a coercive weapon. Madison's Enlightenment demand that religion be directed by reason and conviction rather than force supplies the standard the fear-based Cylon conversion of Baltar fails.

faith-vs-reason.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
faith-vs-reason.title: So Say We All
faith-vs-reason.relation: Richard Berger reads the 're-imagined' series through Bakhtin's dialogism: Moore's show is not a GINO remake but a polyphonic dialogue with the 1978 series and its own sources, including the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greek myth and fan fiction. That polyphony appears on screen as a spectrum of belief, from Baltar's militant atheism argued over with Number Six's fundamentalism, a staging of the Dawkins-Hitchens debate in which the two extremes prove close enough for conversion, to Roslin's prophetic politics. The chapter argues the reboot is 'more Battlestar Galactica' because it makes the original's latent religious debates explicit.

faith-vs-reason.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
faith-vs-reason.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Yuen reads the silver guillotine of intercision against infant circumcision: both cut unconsenting children as acts of faith, Mrs. Coulter's belief that severing dæmons prevents original sin mirroring the Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 17. Deploying W.K. Clifford's shipowner ('It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence') and Hume's claim that belief is an involuntary feeling no will can command, he argues that the real moral fault lies in acting on uninvestigated beliefs in ways that harm others, while Mrs. Coulter's non-consensual experiments on kidnapped children are wrong independently of what she believes. He concludes that if cutting Pantalaimon from Lyra is wrong, circumcision is wrong for the same reasons though less severely, at worst as irresponsible as exposing a child to chicken pox.

faith-vs-reason.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
faith-vs-reason.title: Do You Believe It
faith-vs-reason.relation: Patrick Tiernan argues that Fenway fandom is a genuine religion: William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity) map onto memories of Buckner's error and Dave Roberts's steal, and Peter Berger's 'signals of transcendence' structure the rituals of Truck Day, the hopes of spring training, the damnation of Bucky Dent and Johnny Damon, and the humor of 'Cowboy Up.' He roots the Curse of the Bambino in New England's Puritan-Calvinist legacy of persecution and original sin (Frazee's sale of Ruth), then deploys Hume's account of superstition from 'Of Superstition and Enthusiasm' to deflate the exorcism rituals fans actually performed, from a Sox hat on Everest to dredging for Ruth's piano, as post hoc fallacies. Even so, the rituals reveal the human need for religious practice, and Maslow's peak experience renders the 2004 comeback a brush with the sacred, so the Faithful believe because they have to.

faith-vs-reason.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
faith-vs-reason.title: Breaking the Eighth Commandment
faith-vs-reason.relation: Joel Cade maps baseball's traditionalist-versus-sabermetric war onto the faith-and-reason debate: Joe Morgan's refusal to even read Moneyball repeats Tertullian's fideism, Ted Williams's Science of Hitting exemplifies Augustine's 'faith seeking understanding,' and Wade Boggs's game-day chicken ritual completes his rational hitting exactly as Aquinas says faith completes reason. Theo Epstein's 2004 front office fused the models under the motto 'understanding justifies faith,' using statistics to discover when supposedly obsolete traditional weapons like the stolen base actually work, which is why the seemingly anti-Moneyball Dave Roberts trade paid off in The Steal against Mariano Rivera in Game Four of the ALCS. The chapter closes with the joke that Augustine, who stole pears, would bless stealing second: reconciling faith and reason is how the Sox reversed the Curse, and maybe how faith- and reason-guided people might reconcile.

faith-vs-reason.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
faith-vs-reason.title: Get Serious
faith-vs-reason.relation: David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.

faith-vs-reason.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
faith-vs-reason.title: Hope
faith-vs-reason.relation: Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.

faith-vs-reason.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
faith-vs-reason.title: Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love
faith-vs-reason.relation: Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.

faith-vs-reason.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
faith-vs-reason.title: Humanism Needs Its Evangelists, Too
faith-vs-reason.relation: Treats Snakes & Arrows ('Far Cry,' 'Armor and Sword,' 'Faithless') as secular humanism stung by resurgent fundamentalism, and reads Peart's revolutionary trilogy — 'Beneath, Between and Behind,' 'Bastille Day,' 'A Farewell to Kings' — as Enlightenment humanism already anxious about its own decline. The core argument is rhetorical: Rush deliberately clothes humanist content in sacred and mystical language ('Something for Nothing''s Lord's Prayer motif, 'Jacob's Ladder''s storm read through Spinoza's God-as-nature and the experience of the sublime) because humanism needs evangelists who inspire wonder rather than mere argument.

faith-vs-reason.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
faith-vs-reason.title: Videogame Apocalypses and Secularism
faith-vs-reason.relation: Rachel Wagner, Tyler DeHaven, and Chris Hendrickson argue Halo satisfies the Society of Biblical Literature definition of apocalypse: revelatory narrative, otherworldly mediators (Cortana, 343 Guilty Spark), predetermined eschatology, with Master Chief as a Davidic messiah whose name John-117 echoes the Gospel of John. The Covenant's Tower-of-Babel hubris versus human secularism, and the Flood read through the Book of Enoch's Watchers, turn the story into a critique of rampant consumption and blind religion. Where traditional apocalypses are quietist—God the programmer's deterministic script, salvation not depending on human action—Halo's procedural rhetoric hands agency to the player as messiah, and the chapter closes asking whether videogame apocalypse offers only temporary, magic-circle comfort for secular angst in a morally relativist age.

faith-vs-reason.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
faith-vs-reason.title: Risks of Faith
faith-vs-reason.relation: Ringer argues inception is philosophically impossible because dream consciousness lacks genuine apperception, the filling-in of an external world that structures waking experience, so Cobb's team must instead manufacture 'because of' motives, like the planted 528-491 safe combination, that let Fischer mistake his own dream for waking life. Working with the phenomenology of everyday consciousness, perception versus apperception and the coffee-cup example, he reads the totem as a sacred, untouchable object through which private revelation of reality is mediated. Tillich's distinction between faith as ultimate concern and mere evidential belief then diagnoses Mal: by locking the totem in the safe and choosing the dream world as her reality she commits idolatry, a misplaced faith whose price is her suicide.

faith-vs-reason.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
faith-vs-reason.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Vannatta reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture — the Left Behind novels, Victory TV's Steven, Kurt Warner's Super Bowl, Jesus Camp — as living Puritan Calvinism: original sin (Klosterman's cruel third-graders), justification by faith alone, unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest'), and predestination that leaves uncertain whether our actions matter in the divine equation. The chapter's pivot is truth versus peace: Puritan-born-again certainty sacrifices peace for antecedent truth, from the 1675 Massachusetts settlements to Robertson and Falwell on 9/11. Against this Vannatta sets the pragmatist alternative — truth as the outcome of communal inquiry in service of peaceful living — recasting God as the web of relationships and dissolving his own childhood camp's contradiction between 'I'm Third' and its cult of competition.

faith-vs-reason.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
faith-vs-reason.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.

faith-vs-reason.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
faith-vs-reason.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Takes the show's title as a literal ethical command and asks which senses of enthusiasm should be curbed, tracing the concept's history: Plato's muse-inspired poet in the Ion and Apology, the early Christian Enthusiasts, Wesley and Shaftesbury's attempts to separate good from bad enthusiasm, and the Enlightenment ridicule of Locke and Hume, for whom enthusiasm meant fanaticism, a pretended insight into the supernatural that Larry is right to mock. Kant gets the most sustained treatment: enthusiasts of friendship, religion, or patriotism inflame a good principle beyond its proper degree, which explains Larry's failure as a friend, while 'aesthetic enthusiasm,' the sublime 'idea of good with affect' before the morally good, is valuable, and Larry's single moment of it comes when the Arizona preacher's sermon on moral goodness sends him flying back to Los Angeles to donate his kidney to Richard Lewis. The verdict: curb fanatic and inauthentic enthusiasm (Ted Danson's everything-is-heaven), keep ordinary resoluteness and aesthetic enthusiasm, and accept that a society needs a few Larrys, the Socratic fools who yell for society.

faith-vs-reason.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
faith-vs-reason.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.

faith-vs-reason.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
faith-vs-reason.title: The Devil and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Michael Versteeg and Adam Barkman explain C.S. Lewis's Screwtape doctrine that the Devil conquers minds not by argument but by unreason, since human reason fights on God's side. They unpack Screwtape's tactics as textbook fallacies: jargon like 'religious phase' working as a red herring, dismissing Christianity out of boredom as a non sequitur, the 'Historical Point of View' as the chronological snobbery that cuts generations off from the past, and the endless loop of pride about one's humility as an infinite regress that paralyzes thought. Because reason is, for Lewis, the road toward Heaven, the Devil's highway to Hell is built entirely of bad logic.

faith-vs-reason.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
faith-vs-reason.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Timothy P. Jackson argues Cohen is the closest thing today to a Biblical prophet - a 'strong poet' in Harold Bloom's sense, wearing a coat of many colors drawn from Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Taoism, and Sufism, sustained by an 'epistemic humility' that lives between dogmatism and doubt. Cohen leads Christian texts back to their Hebraic origins, critiques every arrogant nationalism including Israel (Book of Mercy, psalm 27), and gave his Tel Aviv concert profits to Israeli-Palestinian reconciliation. Jackson reads Cohen's equanimity at his business manager's embezzlement trial as forgiveness overcoming resentment, weighs his hesed/agape-style unconditional love against his failures in erotic love, and ends with Cohen's reticence about personal immortality - a prophet for the living.

faith-vs-reason.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
faith-vs-reason.title: Homeland and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.

faith-vs-reason.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
faith-vs-reason.title: Justified and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter asks whether Boyd's survival of Raylan's bullet in the premiere was a genuine sign from God: the atheist invokes Ockham's Razor and the promise of a naturalistic explanation, while the theist replies that a world-creating God would act through the laws of nature, making such explanations neutral rather than negative evidence. It then applies William James's pragmatist standard from his study of mystical experience - judge the sign by the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians' love, joy, peace, self-control) it bears - to Boyd's prison ministry, his urging Raylan to forgive Arlo, and his meth-lab crusade. Despite Boyd's eventual apostasy after Bo murders his congregation, the author concludes he passes James's test, since faith is a maintained journey that can be lost, and the born-again Boyd still struggles - like Jacob becoming Israel - rather than scheming coldly.

faith-vs-reason.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
faith-vs-reason.title: Justified and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter reads preacher Billy St. Cyr's snake-handling through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: like Abraham, Billy performs the absurd double movement - fully resigning himself to dying by rattlesnake while believing he will be spared - which is why Boyd Crowder, who abandoned faith for Hegel's objective rational certainty, can neither buy him out nor understand him. Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical explains why Billy and Abraham may set obedience to God above self-preservation and social morality, while Boyd's showdown in 'Truth and Consequences', where he hands Billy an un-milked rattlesnake, exposes that Billy's certainty has curdled into the hubris de Silentio warns against, so Billy is no Abraham. De Silentio's three marks - love, humility, no desire to instruct others - separate genuine faith from cult leaders and violent extremists.

faith-vs-reason.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
faith-vs-reason.title: Dracula and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Ketcham's invented chronicle sends Dracula and a village rabbi to 1194 Cairo to interrogate Maimonides: can resurrection - one of the thirteen principles of faith - apply to a soulless undead being, and is his blood-drinking a divinely imposed penance? Maimonides answers from the Guide for the Perplexed and the Letter on Resurrection, offering that intelligence is the essence of the soul yet judging the Count a likely trickster, while Dracula presses that no scientific evidence of dust becoming flesh exists. The diarist closes with the heretical worry that Maimonidean resurrection - no food, drink, or sex - might itself be a kind of undeath.

faith-vs-reason.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
faith-vs-reason.title: 21. God-Talk at the Abbey
faith-vs-reason.relation: Samuel Lumpenhouwer takes the Abbey's religious silences - Anna's 'we'll only fall out,' Alfred's baffled 'What?' at transubstantiation, and the Catholic baptism fight over baby Sybbie - and brings in Aquinas to make God-talk possible. Reason alone can know that God exists (the argument from design through final causes like the candle flame, carefully distinguished from Paley's watchmaker), revelation grasped by faith tells us God is personal, and human words reach God only analogically, as when Matthew calls God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave, or by way of negation. Against Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death, the chapter insists that mystery limits rather than excuses reason, ending with Aquinas's 'straw' and the Abbey's three attitudes: confident belief, searching doubt, and keep-it-private spirituality.

faith-vs-reason.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
faith-vs-reason.title: 1. Reading the Signs
faith-vs-reason.relation: Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'

faith-vs-reason.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
faith-vs-reason.title: 15. It Would Take a Miracle!
faith-vs-reason.relation: Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.

faith-vs-reason.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
faith-vs-reason.title: 14. Louis C.K.’s God
faith-vs-reason.relation: Argues Louis's God material is a negativistic, immanent critique of religion in Adorno's sense of 'damaged human life': the 'God' episode's crucifixion doctor who makes young Louie hammer a nail shows faith wrecking children with guilt until his mother's skeptical 'malarkey' speech and donuts rescue him. His SNL 'did you look in the downstairs bathroom?' bit becomes an evidentialist ethics of belief aimed at over-certain atheists, his 'shitty girlfriend' Abraham bit and body/food/shopping jokes illustrate Tillich's functionalist test of what we treat with ultimate concern (echoing David Foster Wallace's 'everybody worships'), and the chapter closes that comedy here works like Ignatian Catholic reflection, keeping faith and doubt together.

faith-vs-reason.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
faith-vs-reason.title: 15. God Started in 1983
faith-vs-reason.relation: Uses the SNL bit of a God who has been standing in a room since 1983 to argue Louis is an 'apathetic agnostic': he cannot know whether God exists, lambastes atheists who claim certainty, and thinks the question barely matters for our lives. The chapter weighs Pascal's Wager against Epicurus's four-part cure ('Don't fear god, don't worry about death'), faults Louis's 'downstairs bathroom' bit for putting the burden of proof on atheists, reads the 'Heaven' glory-hole sketch through Clifford's ethics of belief as a rejection of faith without evidence, and ends with Louie's mother's line that you have to be good to people whether or not God is watching.

faith-vs-reason.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
faith-vs-reason.title: 18. Gods and Beetles
faith-vs-reason.relation: Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies.
