Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'

faith-vs-reason.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
faith-vs-reason.title: 4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown
faith-vs-reason.relation: Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.

faith-vs-reason.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
faith-vs-reason.title: 11. The Sincerity of St. Linus
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter argues Linus confuses sincere faith with indubitable certainty: on the Thomistic model (faith as chosen propositional belief held with knowledge-like certainty, between opinion and knowledge), his fateful slip into 'if the Great Pumpkin comes' wrecks his faith, turning doubt into hypocrisy. Against this it deploys doxastic involuntarism - we cannot simply choose to believe, as his failed attempts to psych himself up ('I believed with every fiber of my being') show - and philosophers like Daniel Howard-Snyder who allow faith without belief: what Linus does, staying in the patch and risking hypothermia and ridicule while doubting, is faith as action in the face of doubt. Hence the closing paradox: where there is certainty there is no room for faith, and Linus's patch only became sincere once doubt crept in.

faith-vs-reason.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
faith-vs-reason.title: 2. Deadpool the Dark Angel
faith-vs-reason.relation: Christopher Ketcham playfully argues that Deadpool's fourth-wall escapes show he exists partly in dimensions we cannot experience, read through string theory's ten curled dimensions and Maimonides's ten realms of angels—beings of form without matter—in the Mishneh Torah. Since only God and angels traverse those hidden dimensions, Deadpool must be an angel, likely a dark one, whose shuttling between realms explains his vacillation between mercenary violence and saving souls. Ezekiel's chariot vision, the vengeful Hebrew Bible God, and massless dark matter are recruited as supporting evidence for this deadpan-earnest science-and-scripture argument.

faith-vs-reason.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
faith-vs-reason.title: 20. There’s Only One God, Ma’am
faith-vs-reason.relation: Holt takes Captain America's line 'There's only one God, ma'am' and asks how Christian monotheism survives in a universe where Thor, Odin and the One-above-all really exist, answering with henotheism - Moses's 'I am', Jacob's household idols, and the Living Tribunal as the merely representative 'biggest kid in the playground' of a supreme Creator whose 'only weapon is love'. He then deploys Hume's Natural History of Religion, where the ignorant multitude progress from polytheism to monotheism, to explain why Cap dismisses Asgardians as superstition Thor says is 'no stranger' than his Sunday churchgoing, while Hume's own trajectory - all religion as vulgar superstition - lands instead in the post-religious rationalism of Tony Stark's 'I prefer fact to fantasy' futurism, which the Goddess calls a soul imprisoned in the ice of rationalism.

faith-vs-reason.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
faith-vs-reason.title: 16. Gotta Have Faith
faith-vs-reason.relation: Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.

faith-vs-reason.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
faith-vs-reason.title: Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t
faith-vs-reason.relation: McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.

faith-vs-reason.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
faith-vs-reason.title: So Say We All
faith-vs-reason.relation: Berger deploys Bakhtin's dialogism to answer the 'GINO' charge: the re-imagined series is not a betrayal of Larson's show but a heteroglossic utterance in an ongoing conversation that already included the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greco-Roman myth, and later fanfic and blogs, with each version sourcing its sources' sources. The 2003 series is read as polyphonic about belief: skeptic Adama, devout Number Six, the messianic convert Baltar, and Dawkins/Hitchens-style atheist critiques of fundamentalism are all given equal voice. The show's value lies in inviting debate across the whole continuum of belief rather than preaching a position.

faith-vs-reason.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
faith-vs-reason.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Barkman and Kowalski mine the Cooper household for science-and-religion lessons: Mary's 'Third-World demon' diagnosis of Raj raises religious diversity (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), her 'But intelligently designed by a creator, right?' prompts an assessment of Behe's irreducible complexity against Darwinian counterexamples like the flagellum-turned-syringe and a warning against god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Her claim that 'all that science stuff comes from Jesus' occasions Plantinga's argument that Darwinian naturalism undermines trust in our cognitive faculties, plus origin-of-life and fine-tuning probability arguments, tempered by Kitcher's caution that such estimates rest on unknown background conditions. Van Inwagen on why Genesis need not teach literal science, and Locke's advice to proportion belief to evidence, frame the mutual education Mary and Sheldon owe each other.

faith-vs-reason.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
faith-vs-reason.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Sirvent and Baker use Daily Show segments (Wyatt Cenac reporting from a Vegas-style heaven, Lewis Black on Jesus as a primary requirement, Stewart on Pat Robertson praying down the Supreme Court) to skewer politicians who claim God's endorsement, from Michele Bachmann's guaranteed Iowa 'miracle' to Glenn Beck's apocalyptic readings. Locke's critique of religious 'enthusiasm' explains why taking private intuition for divine direction breeds arrogant conviction immune to counterevidence, while Gadamer's hermeneutics shows that Beck and Robertson practice objectivist misreading of texts written in a culture two thousand years distant. The chapter closes with the demand for humility about claiming the mind of God.

faith-vs-reason.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
faith-vs-reason.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.

faith-vs-reason.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
faith-vs-reason.title: Might God Be Hidden for Love's Sake
faith-vs-reason.relation: Uses Hidden Mickeys — like the ambiguous log-and-dump-truck at the Once Upon a Toy store — to attack the first premise of Schellenberg's argument from divine hiddenness: just as an arrangement of shapes can be a deliberate Hidden Mickey or a decorative accident, so God's traces in the world can be genuinely ambiguous, letting a non-resistant non-believer rationally fail to believe. Mother Teresa's decades of felt abandonment and C. S. Lewis's 'door slammed in the face' from A Grief Observed frame the experiential problem, and the authors concede the disanalogy that we independently know agents run Disney but not that God exists. As a partial response they offer Lewis's Screwtape suggestion that 'He cannot ravish, He can only woo': God hides precisely so that love can be freely given.

faith-vs-reason.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
faith-vs-reason.title: Knock and the Door Will Be Opened… Eventually
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter reads Strange pounding on Kamar-Taj's door as Kierkegaard's passionate collision with 'that which thought cannot think': the materialist surgeon hits the unknown as a frontier, takes offense at the Ancient One's talk of healing through belief, and can only proceed by surrendering intellectual control ('I control it by surrendering control?'). It applies Kierkegaard's two teachers from Philosophical Fragments: Pangborn is healed the Socratic way, recollecting a power already within him, while the Ancient One's astral knock-out and eviction of Strange acts like the god as teacher, forcing him to discover that he is untruth, until faith becomes 'controlling magic by surrendering to it.'

faith-vs-reason.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
faith-vs-reason.title: Magic and Deep Magic
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter argues that Strange's universe implicitly contains the Creator God of theism rather than just Marvel's gods: Aristotle's impersonal prime mover will not do because Strange needs a relatable source of an objective moral order, so Aquinas's all-good author of eternal, natural, and divine law supplies the framework. It reads three comics as evidence: Strange defeating Dracula by invoking the Tetragrammaton, the Sise-Neg saga where a sorcerer who attains godhood at the dawn of time learns to recreate the universe exactly as the first cause made it, and the World War Hulk story where summoning Zom shows the hubris of violating the moral order—closing with C.S. Lewis's 'deep magic' as cooperation with the created order versus dark magic's will to control it.

faith-vs-reason.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
faith-vs-reason.title: 21. God-Talk at the Abbey
faith-vs-reason.relation: Samuel Klumpenhouwer uses the Abbey's awkward silences about religion - Anna refusing to discuss it over dinner, Thomas showing off with 'transubstantiation' - to introduce Aquinas on how God can be known and talked about. Mary's wartime bedside prayer ('I'm not even sure that you're there') shows she wants not just proof of existence but a personal God, so the chapter distinguishes Aquinas's argument from design - carefully separated from Paley's divine-watchmaker version - from knowledge of God through revelation and faith. Aquinas's two indirect ways of speaking, analogy (Matthew calling God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave) and negation, explain why the 'God is good' sign over Charles Grigg's workhouse should trouble us, and why Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death overstates the mystery of God's otherness.

faith-vs-reason.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
faith-vs-reason.title: 10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree
faith-vs-reason.relation: Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.

faith-vs-reason.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
faith-vs-reason.title: 11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True
faith-vs-reason.relation: Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.

faith-vs-reason.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
faith-vs-reason.title: Paradise Found
faith-vs-reason.relation: Paul Brown maps The Minish Cap's Hyrule onto utopian theory: Plato's Republic classes reappear as royal family (guardians), castle guards (auxiliaries), and market traders (producers), but Hyrule improves on Plato with no slavery, fluid social boundaries (Princess Zelda wandering the festival unrecognized), and Mayor Hagen's local democracy. Aristotle's polis supplies the town's design — small enough for community, walled for defense, river-powered — while Kant's disinterested appreciation of the beautiful fits Miyamoto's 'miniature garden' of pastoral idyll. The spiritual dimension completes the utopia: the benevolent Picori/Minish are a God walking unseen among people, a fuzzy religion without prophet or persecution, so no leap of faith is even necessary.

faith-vs-reason.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
faith-vs-reason.title: NOTES
faith-vs-reason.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads Lost through C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia as myth rather than allegory - the Lamp Post station and flight 316 (the Prince Caspian dedication page) wink at the source - with the island, like Narnia, a world of crisis and second chances entered by plane crash instead of wardrobe. Flashbacks of past failures (Kate the fugitive, Sayid the torturer, Charlie's addiction, Locke's kidney con) set up struggles for faith that he illuminates with H. Richard Niebuhr on faith as a center of value and revelation as communal, and with Levinas's claim that we become ourselves only through responsibility to the Other in community. The Jack-versus-Locke man-of-science/man-of-faith debate, Charlie's moth-cocoon trial, and Jacob and the Man in Black's black-and-white stone game map onto Aslan versus the White Witch, ending in redemption through the new community and Jack's sacrificial death.

faith-vs-reason.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
faith-vs-reason.title: NOTES
faith-vs-reason.relation: Daniel Gallagher uses Aquinas to read Lost as a drama about mistaking finite goods for the ultimate good: Jack's hope in curing, Kate's in deceiving, Jin's in his father-in-law's employment, Locke's in Anthony Cooper, and the Virgin Mary statues full of heroin all instantiate Aquinas's approaching-Peter analogy, where we know only confusedly that someone (the perfect good) is coming toward us. Desmond's and Charlie's paralysis before the good is the sin of acedia, Rose's faith that the island itself healed her cancer is presumption, and her certainty that Bernard is alive illustrates Aquinas's claim - framed through Plato's episteme versus doxa - that faith sits midway between knowledge and opinion. The chapter closes on the harmony of faith and reason, from the Five Ways' first efficient cause to Eko's dying 'I ask for no forgiveness,' grounded in Augustine's restless heart that finds no peace until it rests in God.

faith-vs-reason.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
faith-vs-reason.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
faith-vs-reason.relation: Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.

faith-vs-reason.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
faith-vs-reason.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
faith-vs-reason.relation: Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.

faith-vs-reason.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
faith-vs-reason.title: Notes
faith-vs-reason.relation: Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.

faith-vs-reason.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
faith-vs-reason.title: Notes
faith-vs-reason.relation: Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.

faith-vs-reason.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
faith-vs-reason.title: The Last Jedi A New Hope
faith-vs-reason.relation: Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.

faith-vs-reason.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
faith-vs-reason.title: Notes
faith-vs-reason.relation: Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.

faith-vs-reason.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
faith-vs-reason.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.

faith-vs-reason.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
faith-vs-reason.title: Notes
faith-vs-reason.relation: Held asks what a god is and which gods deserve worship, using Rachels's definition (all-powerful, perfectly good, perfectly wise) to show no DC deity - dying Zeus, cruel Darkseid, creation-unmaking Parallax - qualifies, and that mere power generates fear, not the moral authority that could ground worship-worthiness or a parent-like right to command. Against the Christian campaigner Darrel Keyes, who calls Wonder Woman's cults idolatrous, he notes her gods visibly exist while his God is both unprovable and, per the Anselmian concept problem, indescribable without ceasing to be supreme. The chapter ends by relocating worship on earth: since we need orienting values whether or not gods exist, 'we could do worse than submit to the loving authority' of the justice, care, and integrity Diana embodies - pray to 'yourself, your own strength and character.'

faith-vs-reason.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
faith-vs-reason.title: Is the Gridiron Holy Ground
faith-vs-reason.relation: Hamilton analyzes the fusion of football, patriotism, and religion (Friday Night Lights' Odessa, Super Bowl rituals) as Rousseau's 'civil religion' from the Social Contract—socially unifying but content-empty and anti-intellectual, keeping faith bifurcated from real life. Drawing on Augustine's account of virtue as 'rightly ordered love' and vice as disordered love, he argues football has been wrongly elevated above higher goods. He rejects Higgs's incompatibility thesis for a Christian worldview approach—exemplified by Tony Dungy, Lovie Smith, and Joe Ehrman's 'men for others'—that makes the gridiron holy ground.

faith-vs-reason.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
faith-vs-reason.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
faith-vs-reason.relation: Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.

faith-vs-reason.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
faith-vs-reason.title: Portrayals of Religion
faith-vs-reason.relation: Starting from Whedon's self-description as 'a very hard-line, angry atheist' fascinated by devotion, the chapter argues that Hick's religious non-realism best unifies the Whedonverse's treatment of religion. Religion is 'demonized' when it serves domination or self-interest (Ken's Family Home in 'Anne,' the Patron's witch-burning in 'Safe'), but Shepherd Book—read through The Shepherd's Tale's soup-bowl epiphany—embodies a faith that needs no literal truth: 'You don't fix faith, River. It fixes you,' the mudders' Jaynestown statue, and 'I don't care what you believe, just believe it' all function as symbols that transform lives. The same lens dissolves the controversy over 'Amends': the snowfall that saves Angel may be miracle or freak cold front, and—like Book's epiphany—what matters is the redemption the ambiguity occasions, not its metaphysical source.

faith-vs-reason.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
faith-vs-reason.title: Carnivale Knowledge: Give Me That Old-time Noir Religion
faith-vs-reason.relation: Eric Bronson argues that Carnivale invents a 'religious noir' tradition in which Brother Justin's crisis of faith in the Dust Bowl 1930s replays the Christian existentialism of Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky. Sitting in the ruins of his burnt church, Justin recites Genesis 22 (the sacrifice of Isaac) and demands God explain why his orphans died, directly invoking Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: faith is impossible and absurd, and the crushing struggle itself makes life worth living. Ivan Karamazov's 'returning the ticket' over the suffering of children parallels Justin's fury at a silent God, while the carnies' Babylon storyline (Samson sparing the confessed killer under the carnival code, then secretly shooting him) and the inescapable dead souls echo Sartre's 'condemned to life' and the noir hero's inability to escape fate.

faith-vs-reason.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
faith-vs-reason.title: 15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)
faith-vs-reason.relation: Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.

faith-vs-reason.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
faith-vs-reason.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
faith-vs-reason.relation: Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'

faith-vs-reason.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
faith-vs-reason.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.

faith-vs-reason.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
faith-vs-reason.title: To Know … and Believe
faith-vs-reason.relation: Gallagher uses Lost's Rose Henderson, who says 'I just know,' to expound Aquinas on faith and reason. Aquinas places faith midway between Plato's knowledge (epistêmê) and opinion (doxa) and distinguishes its material object (God) from its formal object (first truth). Gallagher explains that all knowledge begins in the senses, so God's existence is known only by demonstration (the five ways), while faith's fuller content requires grace. Rose's sins bracket the argument: Charlie's despair is acedia, while Rose's insistence that she 'knows' the island cured her is presumption, mistaking faith for scientific knowledge.

faith-vs-reason.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
faith-vs-reason.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Sirvent and Baker use Stewart's mockery of politicians who claim a divine endorsement (Bachmann's certainty of a 'miracle,' Wyatt Cenac reporting from a Las Vegas-style heaven) to apply John Locke's critique of religious 'enthusiasm'—the arrogance of taking one's own intuitions for divine direction without weighing them against reason. They then deploy Gadamer's philosophical hermeneutics against the 'objectivism' of Glenn Beck and Pat Robertson, arguing that treating scripture as an unambiguous rulebook ignores how every reading is conditioned by culture and history.

faith-vs-reason.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
faith-vs-reason.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: LoPresti uses the 'This Week in God' segments (the God Machine, Ed Helms's Hindu-vs-Mayan 'faith-off,' Colbert's inclusivist White House roast) to lay out three responses to religious diversity—exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism—and defends John Cobb's Whiteheadian process-metaphysics pluralism. He insists the distinct concepts of religions be respected rather than collapsed, citing Buddhist impermanence and no-Self and the South Asian Atman/Brahman as unique and non-reducible, and closes by reading the show's turn to political framing of religion through Marx's claim that religion is a mechanism for controlling the masses.

faith-vs-reason.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
faith-vs-reason.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.relation: Johnson argues that Fox News's 'war on Christmas' is fabricated and that the real conflict is a centuries-long Christian war FOR Christmas—Constantine tacking Jesus's birth onto pagan late-December Saturnalia and solstice celebrations. Using Stewart's and Colbert's segments plus Kevin Bleyer-style history, he defends the separation of church and state (courthouse nativities and school Nativity plays as unconstitutional endorsements of Christianity), debunks David Barton's claims that Jefferson was a conservative Christian, and shows Jefferson the deist coining 'a wall of separation between church and state.'

faith-vs-reason.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.title: There Is No God in Desperation
faith-vs-reason.relation: Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.

faith-vs-reason.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.title: Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)
faith-vs-reason.relation: Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.

faith-vs-reason.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
faith-vs-reason.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
faith-vs-reason.relation: Morgan asks when it is wrong for fathers to impose their ideals on children, arguing that forcing activities (like violin practice) risks alienation because meaningful pursuits must be embraced 'from the inside.' Using Robert Noggle's Rawls-derived hierarchy of goods (basic, pre-primary, primary, secondary, specialized), he grants fathers may guide toward universal goods but rejects Noggle's claim that parents may impose a full religious worldview, favoring David Archard's weaker right to 'guide family life' while respecting the child's growing capacity to choose – permitting compelled practice of talents only in light of the child's emerging identity.

faith-vs-reason.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
faith-vs-reason.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Austin uses the everyday sense that 'we need the bean' to introduce a metaphysical debate about whether we need God to ground ethics, framed through the fair-trade coffee case. He contrasts Erik Wielenberg, who treats necessary ethical truths (e.g., that unfair trade is wrong, that suffering is intrinsically evil) as brute 'furniture of the universe' and follows Kant in holding that we ought to be moral simply because it is our duty, with J. P. Moreland, who argues such objective moral values, our knowledge of them, and the normative pull of obligation fit a theistic worldview better than naturalism. The chapter presents God as the 'Necessary Ground of Being' behind moral reality without settling the dispute.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: In this foreword, historian Stephen Nissenbaum frames the book's central puzzle by asking the reader to picture Santa Claus kneeling in the Bethlehem manger and feeling why the image jars. He argues Christmas began as a fourth-century compromise: the Church Fathers fixed Jesus' birthday on December 25 to co-opt Saturnalia and the solstice and to refute Docetism (the claim Christ only 'seemed' to have a body) by giving him a human birthday. He traces how the resulting tension between piety and revelry led the Puritans to ban Christmas and how the secular, commercial Santa of Moore's 1823 poem came to dominate the American holiday, leaving the manger and the sleigh perpetually unreconciled.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Will Williams recounts the legend that St. Nicholas of Myra, the historical basis of Santa Claus, attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and punched the heretic Arius, who taught that the Son was created and not fully God ('there was a time when the Son was not'). Setting the fight to a parody of 'The Night Before Christmas', Williams explains via Athanasius why the divinity of Christ mattered – only if Jesus is truly God can his death secure salvation. He contrasts this fiercely theological bishop with the de-Christianized modern Santa, using the syncretism of 'Here Comes Santa Claus' to argue Nicholas would deplore what consumerist Christmas has become.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.

faith-vs-reason.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
faith-vs-reason.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Mason, a developmental psychologist writing as a Pagan, narrates her decades-long religious journey through James Fowler's Stages of Faith model, using each stage to reinterpret Christmas. She recounts childhood confusion over carols and chimney-invading strangers, fundamentalist-Christian zeal (stage 3 group belonging, then stage-4 doubt as she 'crusaded' against pagan Christmas trees), Unitarian Universalist questioning, and finally Wiccan/Pagan practice centered on Hecate and the winter-solstice Wheel of the Year (rediscovering Christmas's pagan roots in holly, mistletoe, and Yule). Reaching Fowler's stage 5 'Conjunctive Faith,' she concludes Christmas is neither hers nor anyone's to own but a self-perpetuating commercial 'Hallmark' phenomenon she can now greet with equanimity.

faith-vs-reason.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
faith-vs-reason.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
faith-vs-reason.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.

faith-vs-reason.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
faith-vs-reason.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
faith-vs-reason.relation: Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.

faith-vs-reason.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
faith-vs-reason.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
faith-vs-reason.relation: Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.

faith-vs-reason.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
faith-vs-reason.title: To Know … and Believe
faith-vs-reason.relation: Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.

faith-vs-reason.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.title: 19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.

faith-vs-reason.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.title: 26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.

faith-vs-reason.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.title: 29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself
faith-vs-reason.relation: Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.

faith-vs-reason.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
faith-vs-reason.title: 61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists
faith-vs-reason.relation: The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

religious-pluralism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
religious-pluralism.title: Unknown
religious-pluralism.relation: Taking the film's cafeteria religion seriously as 'Neo-pluralism', the chapter distinguishes four varieties of religious pluralism and finds each wanting: extreme pluralism dies by simple logic since of 100,000 religions many contradict one another; fundamental-teachings pluralism fails because the great religions differ on genuinely fundamental doctrines (Islam's personal God versus Theravada's non-theism versus the Trinity); cafeteria pluralism produces incoherent transplantings (reincarnation fits Hinduism but not Buddhism or Christianity) and lacks any rational justification short of wishful thinking; and Hick's Kantian transcendental pluralism posits an unintelligible, wholly unknowable Real while demanding the doublethink - highlighted by Alvin Plantinga - of continuing to hold beliefs one recognizes as literally false.

religious-pluralism.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
religious-pluralism.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
religious-pluralism.relation: Argues that Lewis is an inclusivist about salvation, not a universalist or pluralist: Shift and the self-enclosed Dwarfs are lost, and Aslan explicitly denies being one with Tash, yet Emeth's service to Tash is counted by Aslan as service to him ('all find what they truly seek'). Shasta's providential guidance by a lion he has never heard of, and Jill being saved by drinking from the one stream before knowing whose stream it is, illustrate that the water saves, not knowledge about the water. The chapter supports inclusivism over exclusivism with Lewis's Mere Christianity passages, the 'ought implies can' justice argument against condemning those who never heard the gospel, and Rabadash's healing in Tash's own temple as Aslan working through pagan means.

religious-pluralism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
religious-pluralism.title: Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes
religious-pluralism.relation: Barkman argues that anime's Christian imagery — the legendary Santa on a cross, Earthian's gay angel lovers, Trinity Blood's bishonen pope and female cardinal, Evangelion's hostile Angels — encodes Japanese religious pluralism rather than orthodox Christianity. He lays out the pluralist position (following Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction and John Hick: Ultimate Reality is only equivocally describable, so doctrine matters less than spiritual mood), contrasts it with exclusivism and inclusivism, and charges pluralism with self-undermining intolerance, then traces Japan's historical demonization of Christianity from the 1637 Shimabara massacre (Ninja Resurrection, Samurai Champloo) to Eva's alien invaders, with Armageddon imagery fueled by the atomic bombs. Because Shinto-Buddhist-Daoist anti-realism dissolves fixed categories, anime dissolves good and evil (Chrno Crusade's I Ching balance) and gender itself, gravitating to the symbol-rich 'jungle' of Catholicism (C.S. Lewis's phrase) — and where Trinity Blood lets some vampires be righteous, Augustine's City of God marks the one nearly orthodox note.

religious-pluralism.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
religious-pluralism.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
religious-pluralism.relation: LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.

religious-pluralism.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
religious-pluralism.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
religious-pluralism.relation: Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.

second-order-desires.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
second-order-desires.title: Unknown
second-order-desires.relation: Through Cypher's steak deal the chapter separates contentment - the subjective tranquility of satisfied desire, as in the contented slave, the happy tyrant, or a dog - from happiness, which must be answerable to an objective arrangement of one's life. Four thought experiments (a painless Ataraxy drug, an impostor posing as Keanu Reeves, the heating-vent fantasist imagining he is Mr. Onassis, the drunk's morning-after mirror) and Othello show self-deluded 'happiness' is unstable, truncated, and not the real thing. Happiness therefore requires reflective second-order endorsement of one's desires - wanting the desires one has - as when Neo takes the hard path of saving Morpheus, and this links happiness to a conception of the life worth living.

second-order-desires.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
second-order-desires.title: Moral Autonomy
second-order-desires.relation: Martin van Hees reads "Who Killed Davey Moore?" and "Ballad of Hollis Brown" as arguments that shared consent generates shared responsibility for tragedy even when fate makes the events inevitable - the referee, crowd, manager, and gambler all endorsed the fight, and we who tolerate poverty consent to the next Hollis Brown. He distinguishes a "limited optimistic view" (twisting fate by preventing particular tragedies) from the proclaimed inevitability of "The Times They Are A-Changin'" and the pessimism of "Blind Willie McTell," then defends compatibilism through Frankfurt's Jones/Black case: responsibility needs no alternative possibilities, only that one act from one's own will. Dylan's "moral autonomy" is taking a stance - singing the blues - inside a determined world.

second-order-desires.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed
second-order-desires.title: True Selves Found or Made
second-order-desires.relation: Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.

second-order-desires.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
second-order-desires.title: One More Thing, Don’t Blink!
second-order-desires.relation: Uses Carroll's art-horror theory (monster = threat plus disgust) to ask why the Weeping Angels of 'Blink' terrify despite being beautiful, harmless-seeming statues. The answer: by dumping Kathy and Billy in the past they destroy identity itself, understood through Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity, since everything a person cares about is tied to a time and place. Since the Angels provoke no disgust, the chapter revises Carroll: horror is fear plus impotence, and forcing victims to survive by not blinking makes viewers feel their powerlessness over their own bodies.

second-order-desires.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
second-order-desires.title: Almost Caught!
second-order-desires.relation: Nicolas Michaud deploys Harry Frankfurt's attack on the principle that blame requires alternative possibilities: through a 'Dex kills Deb' case with a counterfactual intervener and a locked-steering-wheel driver, he shows one can be blameworthy despite having no choice, provided one acts because one wants to. Applied to Dexter, the question is which level of compulsion he has - and since he never truly restrains himself, never turns himself in, and his Season 2 relapse reads as empowerment rather than addiction, he seems to want to want to kill, so Frankfurt's verdict is guilt despite inevitability. The chapter closes with a fictional Princeton encounter where Dexter faces a dilemma - either his victims are blameless compulsives, making him a killer of innocents who violates Harry's Code, or wanting to kill makes them and him blameworthy - and Dexter's choice to kill Frankfurt himself proves he acts freely and is guilty.

second-order-desires.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
second-order-desires.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
second-order-desires.relation: Don Fallis proposes deception rather than language as the personhood test: following Dennett, a deceiver must be a second-order intentional system who can want someone else to have a false belief, as when General Thade lies to Senator Sandar about Ari's kidnapping, Zira and Cornelius feign muteness before the Presidential Commission, and Caesar fakes his own electrocution in Conquest. The roles' reversal makes this a test for the films' mute humans too, while Descartes's beast machines, Wittgenstein on dogs that cannot simulate pain, and Lloyd Morgan's canon voice the skeptical reading of fake alarm calls and Koko's 'Cat did it.' Against them Fallis invokes Occam's Razor over Hare, Call and Tomasello's food-competition experiments: apes track who sees what, but they fail the misinformed false-belief version, so real apes may not be 'sneaky enough to be people.'

second-order-desires.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
second-order-desires.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
second-order-desires.relation: Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.

second-order-desires.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
second-order-desires.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
second-order-desires.relation: Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive' against Aquinas' Doctrine of Double Effect and Frankfurt's second-order intentions, arguing Ender's killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail double-effect proportionality because he intends excessive, fear-inducing harm to deter future attackers. He allows that Ender bears only partial responsibility for the xenocide since he could not know the 'simulation' was real, but concludes that, contrary to the Speakers for the Dead doctrine, Ender is not the blameless moral exemplar Card makes of him.

second-order-desires.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
second-order-desires.title: 18. Thoughtcrime or Feelingcrime
second-order-desires.relation: Alba Montes Sánchez argues that the real crime in Oceania is not thoughtcrime but 'feelingcrime': Winston lands in the Ministry of Love only once he falls in love, because beliefs alone do not motivate action while emotions and loves do — the problem of akrasia that puzzled Aristotle, since Winston carries his proof of Party lies for eleven years without acting. Using Harry Frankfurt's account of love as an involuntary, non-utilitarian, rigidly focused, self-affirming concern that organizes a person's priorities, she explains why Julia is irreplaceable and why Room 101 must destroy Winston's deepest allegiance rather than just his opinions. Surveying theories of individuality from Locke's memory to recognition and narrative, she concludes that a stubborn residue of selfhood survives in what we love — which is why Ingsoc must make war on love itself.

second-order-desires.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
second-order-desires.title: “I Always Felt this Place was Missing a Real Villain. Hence, My Humble Contribution.”
second-order-desires.relation: Eberl asks whether living out Sizemore-style fantasies can reveal or only corrode character: applying Aristotle's account of virtues and vices as habituated dispositions, he argues William's three decades in the park habituated the vices that made him the Man in Black — the park reveals rather than suspends the self — while cruelty toward humanlike hosts hardens us toward people, as Aquinas and Kant warn about kindness to animals. Against Ford's claim that humans are wantons in tight loops, Maeve's editing of her own code after learning her escape was scripted makes her a Frankfurtian person who aligns first-order desires with second-order volitions, grounding her narrative identity and personhood. William too attains personhood by actualizing a second-order desire for a different life, with the hosts' free fight back evoking Nietzsche's will to power and Nozick's point that we want to actually do things, not merely experience them.

second-order-desires.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
second-order-desires.title: Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person
second-order-desires.relation: The Azevedos contrast Maeve's awakening with Dolores's: Maeve becomes conscious not by recognizing a guiding voice as her own but through a change of heart on the escape train, after learning even her rebellion was scripted. Deploying Frankfurt's compatibilism, they sort hosts into wantons with only first-order desires (Hector and Armistice obey Maeve's altered scripts without reflection) and persons capable of second-order desires, arguing Maeve's decision to return for her daughter expresses a desire she reflectively identifies with and so is free even if determined — contra Berlin's claim that no one really believes determinism because it would wreck our practices of praise and blame. Jaynes's bicameral mind supplies the model of unreflective command-following that Dolores transcends when the voice in her head becomes her own.

second-order-desires.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
second-order-desires.title: Who Has the Last Laugh
second-order-desires.relation: Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.

second-order-desires.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
second-order-desires.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
second-order-desires.relation: Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive, and not at all in the act' against Aquinas's Doctrine of Double Effect, finding that Ender's self-defense killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail the proportionality condition — he intended to 'win all the next fights' — so he bears moral responsibility despite his tears. After weighing Frankfurt's second-order intentions as a way to keep Ender a good person who did bad things, he concludes with Anscombe's 'double-think about double effect' that Ender is deceived about his own intentions and is no moral exemplar.

second-order-desires.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
second-order-desires.title: What Really Matters
second-order-desires.relation: Margarida Hermida deploys Parfit's comparison of peace, a war killing 99 percent of humanity, and one killing everyone to argue extinction is categorically worse than mass death, and makes the stakes concrete through The Expanse's threats: the protomolecule, all-out Earth-Mars-Belt war, and the Free Navy's asteroid attack that kills billions. She rejects Miller's 'stars are better off without us' pessimism by arguing human existence is a good when suffering is fought (Belter disease and Ceres trafficking are contingent injustices, not necessities), values humanity as the only species with civilization and as the universe 'starting to understand itself', and distinguishes the desirable biological colonization of lifeless worlds from the protomolecule makers' morally objectionable disregard for native life like Ilus'. Against Phil Torres' worry that human speciation means endless war, she points to the mixed Rocinante crew and Naomi's line that the real divide is 'people who want more violence and the ones who want less', concluding with Parfit's On What Matters that what matters most is avoiding the end of human history and of rational beings.

second-order-desires.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
second-order-desires.title: Is Brian More of a Person than Peter? (scan merges: Of Wills, Wantons, and Wives)
second-order-desires.relation: Uses Frankfurt's distinction between first-order desires, second-order desires, and the wanton to argue Brian is more of a person than Peter: Brian's therapy-driven realization in 'Brian in Love' that he does not want to want Lois is a genuine second-order desire, while Peter's TV fixation in 'I Never Met the Dead Man' (wearing a cardboard TV frame, swapping TV for family without reflection) leaves him a wanton, and Cleveland and even Quagmire scrape into personhood. The chapter then turns to weakness of will from Aristotle's akrasia onward, bringing in Searle's claim in Rationality in Action that choice happens in uncaused 'gaps' between desire and action, so acting against one's better judgment can evidence rather than defeat rationality, with R. Jay Wallace's willpower-based volitionism rounding out the action theory.

second-order-desires.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
second-order-desires.title: Amazing and Inspiring
second-order-desires.relation: White explains Tony's drinking as weakness of will: Davidson's denial that akrasia is possible (Black Widow skipping Fury's spying order for a visit to Stark would have to have revised her judgment) is set against Searle's 'gaps,' where a person freely chooses against her all-things-considered judgment and nothing fills the gap. Frankfurt's wanton and second-order desires sharpen the picture — Tony wants a drink but does not want to want it, unlike the unreflective heroin addict — and volitionists like Wallace and Holton (the will as a muscle that Stane's orchestrated disasters exhaust) explain both his lapses and his daily resistance. If Searle is right, Tony's struggle with the bottle is not a defect of rationality but proof of it: akrasia is a symptom of freedom, which is what makes Iron Man amazing and inspiring.

second-order-desires.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
second-order-desires.title: Notes
second-order-desires.relation: Kitchen asks who is to blame in a Wasteland where Nux's 'We're not to blame!' is the standing excuse. Blaster's death in Thunderdome illustrates the problem of many hands — no one, from Max to Ironbar, was sufficient and maybe no one necessary — while Nagel's resultant, circumstantial, and constitutive luck seem to excuse War Boys indoctrinated from puphood. Applying Frankfurt's freedom of action and freedom of the will together with Susan Wolf's Real Self view through three hypothetical War Boys (Maniac, Fanatic, Addict), he argues Nux becomes praiseworthy when Capable prompts him to reflect on and revise his desires, while Immortan Joe, Slit, and the other leaders are fully responsible.

second-order-desires.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
second-order-desires.title: Alcoholica: When Sweet Amber Becomes the Master of Puppets
second-order-desires.relation: Bart Engelen reads 'Master of Puppets' and Hetfield's alcoholism as a case study in akrasia: the Socratic paradox from Plato's Protagoras, Plato's divided soul from the Republic, and Aristotle's weak-willed agent who knows the good but cannot act on it all describe the addict's 'struggle within'. Using Frankfurt's distinction between first- and second-order desires, he argues Hetfield became an 'unwilling addict' - and genuinely irrational - only when he stopped endorsing his desire to drink, and that recovery works through pre-commitment strategies like rehab, avoiding drinking cues, and relying on others.

second-order-desires.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
second-order-desires.title: Notes
second-order-desires.relation: Michaud puts Jar Jar Binks on trial for proposing the emergency powers that let Palpatine become Emperor and doom the galaxy. He weighs Nagel's resultant moral luck through a two-Lukes landspeeder case, Susan Wolf's virtue-based reply that equal fault can deserve different feelings, Kant's 'ought implies can' and the categorical imperative, and a Frankfurt-style scenario in which Palpatine's hypothetical mind-trick removes Jar Jar's ability to choose otherwise. The verdict: as a deceived, politically limited character trying to do good, Jar Jar is not guilty of the Empire's crimes - only of being obnoxious.

second-order-desires.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
second-order-desires.title: “Good Soldiers Follow Orders”
second-order-desires.relation: Brace uses Aristotle on numerical versus specific sameness, Locke's memory theory, and above all Frankfurt's second-order desires to argue the Jango Fett clones are distinct persons despite shared DNA: Fives's and Echo's accumulated memories and choices individuate them, and the Bad Batch's personalized quarters display what Yoda means by 'very different, each one of you are.' Frankfurt's 'wanton' frames Wrecker's impulsive Hulking, while Order 66 distinguishes freedom of action from freedom of will — Rex resists the chip's compulsion but cannot act on his second-order volition, so he never loses personhood. Crosshair's reveal that his chip was long removed recasts his loyalty to the Empire as a freely chosen (if immoral) second-order volition, his right as a person.
