second-order-desires.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
second-order-desires.title: Notes
second-order-desires.relation: Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.

second-order-desires.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
second-order-desires.title: “I Always Felt this Place was Missing a Real Villain. Hence, My Humble Contribution.”
second-order-desires.relation: Jason Eberl argues Westworld cultivates real moral character: using Aristotle's account of virtue and vice as habituated dispositions, he shows William's thirty years of habitual killing make the Man in Black his genuine 'second nature,' not merely a vacation persona, citing Aquinas and Kant on how cruelty to animals (or human-like hosts) hardens moral character. Drawing on Frankfurt's second-order desires and narrative identity, he contends Maeve attains personhood by reprogramming her own first-order desires, while Ford views most humans as wantons trapped in first-order loops. He concludes the park can both corrupt (William) and potentially free hosts to flourish as self-authoring persons rather than devolve into wantons whose 'violent delights have violent ends.'

second-order-desires.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
second-order-desires.title: Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person
second-order-desires.relation: Marco and Ana Azevedo analyze Maeve's decision to leave the train as the moment she becomes free, contrasting determinism and the principle of alternate possibilities (via Isaiah Berlin's claim that determinism is incompatible with how we live) with Frankfurt's compatibilism. Using Frankfurt's wanton/person distinction and second-order desires, they argue Maeve becomes a person when she reflects on her competing desires (escape versus finding her daughter) and identifies with the latter, even though her escape was scripted. They tie this to Jaynes's bicameral mind, casting unreflective hosts like Hector and Armistice as wantons and bicameral beings who follow a commanding voice, while Maeve and Dolores achieve the reflective self-identification Frankfurt calls freedom.

second-order-desires.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
second-order-desires.title: One More Thing, Don’t Blink!
second-order-desires.relation: Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.

second-order-desires.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
second-order-desires.title: 21. A Foundation-al Lesson on Free Will and Determinism
second-order-desires.relation: Simpson argues Asimov balances determinism and free will through probabilistic psychohistory and reads the Mule—an unpredictable mutant—as an Epicurean 'swerve' meant to break the plan's apparent determinism, though he shows randomness no more secures freedom than determinism (the free-will dilemma). Turning to compatibilism, he uses Han Pritcher's mental 'Conversion' by the Mule to defeat classical hypothetical analyses and Gary Watson's valuational account, since Pritcher still does what he 'wants.' He builds on Frankfurt's rejection of alternative possibilities and Susan Wolf's requirement of responsiveness to the True and the Good, contrasting the manipulated Lord Stettin with Second-Foundationer Lady Callia, to give an account of free agency that would have let Asimov grant his characters agency in a deterministic universe without needing the Mule.

second-order-desires.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
second-order-desires.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
second-order-desires.relation: Funke examines how the 'gateway' argument is supposed to work by treating it as a claim about weakness of will, split into two mechanisms. Motivational externalism—illustrated by Milgram's obedience experiments and Doris's situationism—holds that the illicit-market situation, not the drug, pushes users toward hard drugs, which implies legalization, not prohibition. Motivational internalism, using Michael Smith's contest between normative and motivational reasons and second-order desires, locates the risk in cannabis's creative 'analysis paralysis' and idealizing imagination; Funke argues that this imaginative value, like religion, is worth its risk and that neuropharmacology (THC's distinct cannabinoid mechanism) undercuts the internalist gateway claim.

second-order-desires.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
second-order-desires.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
second-order-desires.relation: Purcell and Shaffer's 'Men, Sports, and Yoga' asks why, though yoga began as a male discipline, ~80% of US practitioners are women, using the stories of three men (Mark, Carl, Jake) taught privately to avoid the competitive self-consciousness of group classes. Its philosophical thread is the ego (ahamkara, 'the I-maker'): rather than obliterating the ego, the men learn to keep it in check and channel competitiveness inward against their own limits, so 'unifying mind and body' turns out to be a competitive sport that works by managing one's own drives and self-image.

second-order-desires.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
second-order-desires.title: 9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom
second-order-desires.relation: Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.

second-order-desires.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
second-order-desires.title: 80. Detroit Become Human as Philosophy Moral Reasoning Through Gameplay
second-order-desires.relation: Engels and Evans argue that Detroit: Become Human stages moral reasoning through the interactive stories of the androids Connor, Kara, and Markus, whose 'deviant' awakening they read through Frankfurt's distinction between wantons and persons with second-order desires and through Kant's requirement of the ability to do otherwise. Scenes like Markus scavenging a pump regulator from a dying android, the blood-on-hands visualization after his speech, and Kara protecting Alice force players to weigh Kantian, utilitarian, virtue, and Gilligan-style care frameworks. Through Alice's reveal as an android and the grieving-widower scene, the game makes an implicit anti-speciesist argument (via Singer) that beings who can suffer are morally considerable, and that agency and responsibility emerge through suffering and struggle.

stoicism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
stoicism.title: Unknown
stoicism.relation: The chapter proposes three theses: happiness is centrally tranquillity (ataraxia), whose enemy is anxiety - the 'splinter in your mind' that things are out of kilter; the rival Aristotelian view treats happiness as activity (energeia) of soul in accordance with excellence (arete), an objectivism that explains how a contented 'human battery' or happy slave is mistaken about being happy; and neither view suffices alone, since a passionless apatheia is barren and dry. Lived happiness is instead equipoise - settledness in one's basic stance that is compatible with turbulent passions and commitments, more like Neo's active decision-making and discovery than a lazy virtual tryst with the woman in red.

stoicism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
stoicism.title: Emotions and Aesthetic Response
stoicism.relation: Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.

stoicism.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
stoicism.title: Kierkegaard Lays It Down
stoicism.relation: Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.

stoicism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
stoicism.title: “Control, Control, You Must Learn Control”
stoicism.relation: Stephens reads Yoda as a Stoic sage: Luke's first impressions are blinded by appearance, but Yoda exhibits the Stoic virtues of patience, timeliness, focus on the present, apatheia (freedom from fear, anger, and hate), and ascetic discipline (askesis), living by the dichotomy of control. He reconstructs the contrasting 'logic of the Dark Side' - anger to hatred to aggression to the mastery of others - showing the Emperor as a tyrant who, unlike the self-mastering Stoic (Marcus Aurelius being the counterexample among rulers), seeks to control what is not up to him, so Vader's 'I must obey my master' is servitude to vice. The chapter also marks Stoic limits: the Emperor rightly rejects felt compassion but wrongly refuses beneficence and Stoic cosmopolitanism, and Stoic physicalism cannot accommodate Yoda's 'luminous beings' afterlife.

stoicism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
stoicism.title: A Doomed Pursuit of Power and Glory
stoicism.relation: Doom, declaring 'Power has ever been my God', steals the Silver Surfer's cosmic power, and the authors correct Lord Acton: power itself does not corrupt - only the flawed vessel it is poured into, while the uncorrupted are not destroyed by its loss ('Though bereft of my power - I do not crawl!'). The imprisoned Surfer's tranquil equanimity, they argue, is the voice of a Stoic philosopher, and Marvel shares with the best ancient philosophers a faith in a built-in cosmic justice whereby wrongly gotten power destroys its holder - fulfilled when Galactus strips Doom of what was never his.

stoicism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
stoicism.title: What Wisdom Requires
stoicism.relation: Explains what wisdom demands: subordinating the loud, here-and-now deliverances of the senses and emotions to reason and the larger picture — as in Plato's wise person contemplating the eternal Forms and the Republic's long course of training, the Bhagavad-Gita's detachment, and Stoic meditative practice. It argues experience is nonetheless central (a sixteen-year-old Captain Marvel could not have it), cites Stick's parting from Matt Murdock in Daredevil over uncontrolled emotion, and uses Casablanca to mark the cultural shift that makes us doubt the larger picture's claims.

stoicism.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
stoicism.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Over an evening at the Iron Post biker bar, Auxier maps four habitues onto the Hellenistic schools: Cowboy, the Vietnam chopper pilot whose bar is a Garden of modest pleasures, loyalty, and withdrawal from power games, is an Epicurean; the laconic Bear, who doubts that even possessing knowledge would make us better off and suspends judgment, is a Pyrrhonian (unlike the coffee-house Carneadean); Happy Jack, the 'true nature's child' of 'Born to Be Wild' who defies convention and keeps nothing six months, is Diogenes's Cynic; and Gary, the Vietnam-damaged recovering alcoholic, is a damaged Stoic who has not reached apatheia. He concludes that bikers are postmodern pagans whose philosophy is enacted rather than propounded, a Biker Platonism that refuses the Christian-Platonic divorce of body and spirit and lives by honor, freedom, and a pagan fatalism that accepts the consequences of one's choices.

stoicism.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
stoicism.title: “All Good Things Must Come to an End”
stoicism.relation: Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'

stoicism.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
stoicism.title: “Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”
stoicism.relation: Tschaepe reads Professor Marvel and the Wizard as skilled givers of 'folk explanations'—stories about desires, beliefs, and feelings that work where logical, scientific, or mechanistic explanations fail—because each explanation is fitted to the pragmatic considerations of its audience and problem. With the companions the Wizard works through a failed dualist argument (a brain is not a mind) for the Scarecrow, an abbreviated Stoic ataraxy pitch for the Tin Man, and Aristotle's discretion-is-valor point for the Lion, settling in each case on folk psychology plus a token (Th.D. diploma, heart-shaped clock, Legion of Courage medal) that supplies the recognition actually needed. Dorothy, whose desire for home is real rather than mistaken, gets no folk explanation from anybody: she must combine the heel-tapping instruction with her own articulated desire—'there's no place like home'—which the chapter treats as pragmatically, not logically, effective.

stoicism.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
stoicism.title: Too Much Tequila, Or Not Quite Enough
stoicism.relation: Doug Anderson reads Buffett as an 'American Stoic' — unlike his friend the Cynic Hunter S. Thompson, who dropped out and died, Buffett accepts his fated world of competitive capitalism and controls the one thing Stoics say we can: his own attitudes, 'changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes.' He leans on Seneca's advice to Serenus that wine and dreaming liberate the mind ('drink washes cares away') to interpret the dialectic of dreaming and drinking in 'Margaritaville,' 'Five o'Clock Somewhere,' and 'License to Chill' as Stoic self-renewal — the margarita even frees the singer to admit his own fault — with Emerson's intoxication-speaking poet as the American model. Excess is the failure mode: the expatriates of 'Banana Republics' who mistake the dream for an end state and Buffett's late-thirties hangover reckoning mark the Stoic middle path between deadening routine and 'too much tequila.'

stoicism.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
stoicism.title: It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie
stoicism.relation: Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.

stoicism.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
stoicism.title: Red Sox Fandom and Internal Harmony
stoicism.relation: John McHugh uses his urge to confront Grady Little, who left a spent Pedro Martinez in during Game Seven of the 2003 ALCS, to ask how fans should govern the primal emotions fandom generates. Stoic self-command fails because Epictetus's advice (avoid caring about games entirely, focus only on what you control) would extinguish fandom itself, so McHugh adapts Adam Smith's impartial spectator: the virtuous fan imagines being watched by a sympathetic but emotionally distant fellow fan, settling on a Chicago Cubs fan who gets Bartman the way a Sox fan gets Buckner and Grady. He concludes that we each harbor a team of role-specific inner consciences, and the practical task is harmonizing the Red Sox-fan identity with our other identities rather than suppressing it or being consumed by it.

stoicism.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
stoicism.title: Fighting Talk
stoicism.relation: The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.

stoicism.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
stoicism.title: An Enemy Lying in Ambush
stoicism.relation: Fuller reads his teenage collapse while holding shiko dachi at his Eighth Kyu grading as a weakness of will, and argues that karate is Stoic discipline embodied. He explains the dichotomy of control through Epictetus's barbecue etiquette and the Kill Bill II buried-alive scene (only the Bride's years of disciplined training, not magic, break the coffin), then lays out living according to nature, Zeno's apatheia, Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, and Seneca's nightly self-examination as the model of askesis. Kata becomes 'a defiant stand against irrational emotion-chasing', and since only virtue is up to us, the enemy 'lying in ambush' is always internal: ourselves.

stoicism.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
stoicism.title: Time Enough to Drink the Poison
stoicism.relation: Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.

stoicism.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
stoicism.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Curko and Greguric read Klosterman's glam-rock fandom as a problem of identity and masks: Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian split casts Chuck as a self-controlled Apollonian writing about Dionysian excess in Guns N' Roses, Motley Crue, and Whitesnake, while Descartes's remark that actors wear masks to hide their shame introduces the tribute band Paradise City, a 'real copy' whose members would have no personalities left if they fully succeeded. The authors extend the mask question to Facebook and online avatars, where media saturation makes us 'copies without the original' and identity stops being self-same. They end by crowning Klosterman a modern Socrates of 'Know thyself' and a Stoic exemplar: admire your heroes like Satriani but do not steal their identities, control what you can (never your reputation or your time of death), and keep daring the endless search for self-knowledge.

stoicism.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
stoicism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Ashley Barkman argues that feminism is unrealistic and inefficient in the apocalypse: citing sex-difference research such as Bandura's Bobo doll experiments, she claims masculine aggression and strength are what leadership requires when authority must be asserted physically, as when Rick pipes Merle and shoves Daryl, or Shane tackles Ed and Jim. The quarry laundry scenes stage the debate - Jacqui's protest at 'all the Hattie McDaniel work' versus Lori's 'this isn't about women's rights... doing what needs to be done' - and Barkman sides with Lori, treating the division of labor as survival logistics under a natural-law premise that it is moral to act according to nature. Andrea the sharpshooter and Michonne the swordswoman show women can excel as heroic exceptions without leading, and the chapter concludes leadership should stay with good men like Rick.

stoicism.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
stoicism.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Schwanebeck reads Nucky's fastidious grooming and Prohibition's purity crusade through the body politic metaphor: from Cicero and Seneca's De Clementia, where head and body of the state depend on each other, through Hobbes's bearded Leviathan frontispiece, to temperance propaganda that framed alcohol as poison entering the national bloodstream and wartime posters demanding 'a clean America.' The show exposes the purity ideal as illusion - the true purists are the Klan massacring Chalky's men and the hand-washing Van Alden shouting 'Let these waters wash you clean!' over Sebso's drowning body. Nucky rules less like Seneca's genuinely clement emperor than like Machiavelli's prince who merely appears virtuous, and the gangster genre's kingly tropes ('Et tu, Eli?') crown him head of Atlantic City's body politic.

stoicism.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
stoicism.title: Futurama and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Laderoute reads 'The Late Philip J. Fry' - the forward-only time machine overshooting past the year one billion and the last protons to a second Big Bang and an identical universe (ten feet lower, conveniently crushing its duplicates) - as a tour of cosmology from Aristotle's static, eternal, Earth-centered heavens through the Stoics' providential determinism and fiery ekpyrosis to Big Bang cosmology and heat death, which is why the Professor is so shocked. Nietzsche's Gay Science 341 supplies the existential payoff: faced with living identically forever, one can react with horror or delight, and eternal recurrence becomes a challenge to become the person you want to be. Fry, a billion years late for his Cavern on the Green dinner, reads Leela's message carved in stone, and in the repeated universe finally arrives on time - 'That was the old Fry... he's dead now' - amor fati enacted.

stoicism.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
stoicism.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Billard concedes the Stoic point that we control neither our passions nor nature ('life will always find a way', Sattler's 'you never had control'), as the bucardo cloning failure shows, but argues this proves the park rushed, not that de-extinction is impossible. Dangerousness is subjective, raptor intelligence is a logistics problem rather than a metaphysical objection, and since humans have already caused the sixth mass extinction we may have a duty to bring species back. Because revived animals would be 'neo-dinosaurs' built from fragmentary DNA, de-extinction is creation rather than resurrection, less like playing God than like the transhumanist enhancement humans already practice.

stoicism.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
stoicism.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.

stoicism.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
stoicism.title: Homeland and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: John Karavitis evaluates four suicide events: Afsal Hamid's suicide in CIA custody, Aileen Morgan's cutting her throat with a lens, Brody's aborted suicide bombing, and Carrie's ECT as a 'suicide' of her old self. Kant's absolute ban on suicide (it denies your humanity) clashes with Seneca's Stoic counsel that a life of miserable captivity need not be continued, and with Singer's utilitarian permission of euthanasia that reduces suffering - under both, Hamid's and Aileen's suicides are defensible while Brody's emotionally driven bombing is not. Dana's plea that her father is needed recasts Aristotle's point that suicide wrongs the community, and Sloterdijk's analysis of rage turned on oneself frames Carrie's amoral self-destruction.

stoicism.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
stoicism.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Re-examining 'The Enchiridion!' trial by trial - the gnome illusions, the ogre whose dollar Finn steals and then returns, the dark mage's brain world, the wallop given the Key-per in devil pajamas - the chapter argues Finn wins the hero's handbook without being righteous: he is brave, tender and ingenious, but gullible, hasty and violent, slaying whatever he is told is evil and running from the gnome test. Epictetus's Stoic Enchiridion supplies the standard the show's book lacks: only virtue matters, wealth, fame and comfort are indifferents, and a real handbook teaches how to lose, age and admit mistakes, not just how to win, which is exactly what Billy's quit-heroism shows Ooo's greatest hero never learned. Because bravery without good judgment could as easily serve a Nazi, a terrorist or the Lich, Finn's lack of practical wisdom means the 'most righteous hero' in Ooo is an impetuous boy - proof of how morally broken the Land of Ooo is.

stoicism.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
stoicism.title: 4. On Being a Dead Person Who Hasn’t Died Yet
stoicism.relation: Mark Ralkowski argues that Louis's 'dead people who haven't died yet' bit sounds like Marcus Aurelius, and that Dr. Bigelow's Season Four advice about back pain, the three-legged dog, and heartbreak works as the Stoic spiritual exercises Pierre Hadot described - above all the 'view from above' that re-describes things to strip them to their true value. Epictetus's dichotomy of control explains Bigelow's core advice: pain is not 'up to us' but our judgments about it are, so Louie should adjust his expectations to nature ('every second without back pain is a lucky second') instead of demanding a pain-free life. The apparently un-Stoic counsel to savor heartbreak ('misery is wasted on the miserable') is defended as genuinely Stoic: viewing his lost love from the perspective of a dead-person-who-hasn't-died-yet, Louie can accept sadness as precious and impermanent rather than being crushed by it. The chapter concedes Louis is no philosopher, but suggests his bits - contrasted with Seinfeld's 'polished' version on Talking Funny - can be read as newly discovered Meditations for comedy audiences.

stoicism.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
stoicism.title: 5. Just Want a Shitty Body
stoicism.relation: Bekka Williams argues that Louis's 'just want a shitty body' bit restates Epictetus's central Stoic teaching - want events to happen as they do happen, because only judgments, efforts, and desires are 'up to us' while bodies, reputations, and outcomes are not. She reads the Late Show arc (Tardigan's non-offer of the job, then Louie's triumphant 'Hey Letterman, I did it!' when Letterman stays) as Epictetus's cardplayer ideal: total effort on what is controllable, calm acceptance of what is not, alongside the bits about disgusting bodies, 'do the shit out of your job,' Jane and the mango pop, and Louis's self-trained habit of intercepting impulsive desires like the motorcycle urge. Like Epictetus, Louis is presented as a truth-teller who corrects mistaken impressions even when it is unpleasant, and the chapter uses him to rebut the charge that Stoicism means not caring.

stoicism.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
stoicism.title: 10. How to Be Free
stoicism.relation: O'Connell and Sirvent argue Seneca's Stoic freedom - release from fear of death and from every attachment - illuminates the two most enslaved groups in the story. The Unsullied's training strips them of possessions, names, lust, and fear, with Grey Worm's shame at fearing death for Missandei's sake showing exactly what attachment does to this freedom, while the Faceless Men's 'valar morghulis' mantra works like Seneca's recommended contemplation of death, letting Arya drink blindly from the cup at the House of Black and White. The chapter concludes that a fearlessness built by slaves and assassins really is a kind of freedom beyond their servitude, though Seneca would recoil at the brutal methods that produce it.

stoicism.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
stoicism.title: 3. Can Charlie Brown Be Happy
stoicism.relation: The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.

stoicism.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
stoicism.title: 10. Defying Fate
stoicism.relation: Benjamin Evans reads Frank as fate's plaything, Tagomi's hydrogen-bomb gambit as an attempt to steer an uncontrollable web of events, and Hitler's claim that destiny belongs only to 'some men' as political exploitation of fate-talk. Stoicism (Zeno through Marcus Aurelius) explains Ed's serenity-prayer acceptance and the sinister Nazi version in which the 'natural order' means wolves eating sheep, but the chapter's verdict follows Adorno's studies of astrology and the occult: believing in fate seeds authoritarian submission, so Juliana letting Joe sail to Mexico — trusting her own judgment over the prophetic film — is the show's Adornian heroism.

stoicism.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
stoicism.title: 15. Bias Is Rational!
stoicism.relation: Percival, whose Myth of the Closed Mind Adams cites, rebuts the Moist Robot Hypothesis that visual, emotional, repetitive anchors make us ninety-percent irrational. Against Kahneman's fast-and-dumb System 1 he sets Gigerenzer's ecological rationality (the gaze-angle heuristic that catches fly balls, the recognition heuristic that lets ignorant German students beat Americans on Detroit versus Milwaukee), then goes further with Popper's critical rationalism: babies as little scientists conjecturing and refuting, experience always theory-laden (the duck-rabbit), and Newton's boy on the seashore facing an infinite but navigable ocean of error elimination. The Stoic insight that all emotion is thoughtful and all thought emotional (the falling-tiles misperception that flips anger to relief) shows feelings track beliefs, so a free battle of the biases, not fact-free affirmation in the lineage of Le Bon and Pavlovian conditioning, is how rationality actually works.

stoicism.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
stoicism.title: 15. June the Stoic
stoicism.relation: Lequien asks how June might endure Gilead and answers with Epictetus: like the slave-philosopher, she can locate freedom in what is 'up to her'—detaching from her body during the Ceremony ('What he is fucking is the lower part of my body'), relinquishing property, and learning not to call husband or daughter her own. He tests alternatives—Camus's question of suicide (the shatterproof glass), utilitarianism (the coerced 'We are very happy'), Tronto's care ethics (Gilead smothers the sorority that could make care meaningful), and the Particicution as a licensed Two Minutes Hate—before concluding that 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum' functions as June's Stoic mantra: mastery of her own responses is the one victory the Sons of Jacob cannot take.

stoicism.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
stoicism.title: 20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style
stoicism.relation: The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.

stoicism.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
stoicism.title: 5. A Replicant’s Guide to Becoming Human
stoicism.relation: Justin Kitchen uses the Stoic 'cradle argument' — Chrysippus on self-preservation, echoed in Wallace's 'the first thought tends to fear, to preserve the clay' — to deny that replicant slavery is natural, noting Seneca's point that rage like Batty's derails reason. Mapping the Stoic process of oikeiosis through Hierocles's concentric circles onto the films, he traces four stages: the Nexus-6's fight for survival, Rachael identifying with Deckard in love, the Nexus-8s' revolutionary community under Freysa, and finally K, who disobeys Freysa's order and sacrifices himself for Deckard as a Stoic cosmopolitan, a fellow citizen of the world. Replicants can become human because they develop through the same expanding circles of concern.

stoicism.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
stoicism.title: 18. What Does It Mean if the Band Plays Forever
stoicism.relation: Robert Grant Price treats KISS's repeated farewell tours — the 2000 Farewell Tour followed by twelve more tours, then the End of the Road Tour — as false endings that keep reshaping the band's story, running two counterfactuals: folding in 1982 would have made a tragedy of celebrity, quitting after the 2001 Farewell Tour a comedy of graceful closure, while the actual open-ended career risks farce. He then asks whether an aging rock star can be wise, contrasting Stoic virtue — Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on self-control and humility, the cardinal virtues of Prudence, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance — with the hedonism and libertinism of rock's party ethos, from 'Uh! All Night' to Bernini's Ecstasy of St. Teresa. Knowing when to place an ending, he concludes, is ultimately the philosophical question of what one's life is for.

stoicism.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
stoicism.title: Sometimes We Can Let Go
stoicism.relation: Sets P.F. Strawson's blame-as-moral-anger picture against the Seneca/Buddhist case that anger is revenge-hungry poison, then reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. Katara may stay angry at Yon Rha after 'The Southern Raiders' yet forgo revenge because he is incorrigible and not worth it, while forgiving Zuko on Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' logic since his villainy no longer reflects his character. Iroh's 'I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way' and his tea with the mugger Tycho show blame being skipped entirely in favor of compassion, and Zuko's shift from hypocritical self-blame to self-compassion after confronting Ozai lets him take responsibility without self-destructive rage.

stoicism.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
stoicism.title: Sometimes We Can Let Go
stoicism.relation: Sets the intuition that angry blame is how we hold people responsible (Strawson; Katara's useful fury at Pakku's sexism, Iroh's 'whatever you do to that spirit, I will unleash on you tenfold') against the Senecan and Buddhist verdict that anger is greedy for revenge, and reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. In 'The Southern Raiders' Katara neither forgives Yon Rha nor kills him, showing that blame can be set down when expressing it is pointless, while she forgives Zuko in Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' sense because his past betrayal no longer speaks to his present character. Iroh's handling of the mugger in Ba Sing Se ('I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way') models responding to the suffering behind wrongdoing with compassion instead of blame, and Zuko's self-anger is diagnosed as hypocritical self-blame whose antidote is self-compassion: acknowledging how he himself was hurt is what finally lets him take ownership of his wrongs.

stoicism.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
stoicism.title: 6. Keeping It under Control
stoicism.relation: Mills reads Mr. Bates, the lame, twice-imprisoned, uncomplaining valet, as Downton's Epictetus, using him and the household to teach the Stoic dichotomy of control: only our judgments, desires, and actions are up to us, while jobs, reputations, and inheritances (Thomas's coveted valet post, Mary's scandal, Molesley's flower cup) are 'preferred indifferents' to be pursued without enslavement. Death figures as the great rejected indifferent, handled through Pamuk's demise and Mrs. Hughes's calm 'One day, I will die' upon finding a lump, as well as the grief of Isobel and Mary over Matthew. The closing section turns to Hierocles's concentric circles, with Sybil helping Gwen and Carson comforting Mary as drawing outsiders into the inner circle, a Stoic cosmopolitanism that Thomas, who sees the Crawleys as mere employers, fails entirely. The Dowager's 'I hope we're in control of something, if only ourselves' serves as the chapter's Stoic motto.

stoicism.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
stoicism.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: George Dunn tests Katniss's luck-saturated life against Kant's claim that the good will shines 'like a jewel' regardless of fortune, with Peeta's vow to 'die as myself' as the stronghold the Gamemakers cannot touch, and with Seneca's dictum that what Fortune has not given she cannot take away. He then runs Nagel's four kinds of moral luck through the trilogy: Haymitch's reaping-made alcoholism as constitutive luck, Rue's death sparing Katniss an impossible final choice as circumstantial luck, Peeta's rooftop words echoing unconsciously behind the flowers for Rue as causal luck, and the revolution's success as resultant luck without which Katniss would have been the destroyer of District 12 rather than its torchbearer. Framing the Gamemakers as Fortuna on her wheel, he ends with the berries: since Katniss can never untangle whether she held them out from love, defiance, or self-protection, even moral worth proves hostage to luck and to the opacity of our own motives.

stoicism.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
stoicism.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Abigail Myers runs Stoic doctrine against Katniss's biography: Zeno's thesis that only moral goodness is good (with Plutarch Heavensbee's renunciation of Capitol privilege as indifference to wealth and status), Seneca's 'On the Shortness of Life' against deferring living, Epictetus's dichotomy of control including the uncomfortable advice to kiss wife and child as mortals, and Marcus Aurelius's practical Meditations as the gentler 'Stoic for beginners' who would be president of Panem. Katniss comes out Stoic in her frugality, her mortality-shadowed appreciation of small joys, and her firm moral code, but decidedly un-Stoic in her fierce attachments to Rue, Peeta, and Prim. Yet her final choice of Peeta over Gale is itself Stoic, Myers argues: she forgives what Peeta's hijacking made him do since it was never in his control, refuses a noble friendship that would endorse Gale and Coin's slaughter of innocents, and chooses in accordance with nature and reason so as to survive as herself with her values intact.

stoicism.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
stoicism.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Barkman reads the trilogy's Roman texture — panem et circenses, gladiatorial Games, tyrants named Coriolanus and Caesar — through the Stoic Seneca, who lived under Nero just as Katniss lives under Snow. Seneca's distinction between the good (virtue alone), the merely preferable (wealth, fame, power), and the bad (vice) explains the Capitol: Snow and Coin traded virtue for preferables and so became vicious, while the citizens' binge-and-purge luxury mirrors the Roman decadence Seneca condemned. The Hunger Games are the gladiatorial 'pure murder' that corrupts emperors, crowds, and tributes alike, and the districts are slaves whose liberation — like Katniss declaring 'I'm done killing their slaves' — is Seneca's freedom from slavery to fear and vice. Katniss and Peeta's self-sacrificial love and refusal to be changed exemplify the Stoic virtue the Capitol cannot take away.

stoicism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
stoicism.title: 1 Acting Without Thinking The Sagacity of Indiana Jones
stoicism.relation: Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.

stoicism.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
stoicism.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
stoicism.relation: Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.

stoicism.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
stoicism.title: Notes
stoicism.relation: Hummel maps the Jedi Order onto Epictetus's Stoicism: philosophy as a way of life, virtue through wisdom, the dichotomy of control ('some things are up to us'), and treating outcomes like flying or other people's fates as preferred indifferents within the will of the Force. Anakin falls because he misconceives power as the ability to do amazing things - stopping people from dying - instead of mastery of his own judgments, and he refuses Stoic indifference toward Shmi and Padme. The chapter also indicts the Jedi's own un-Stoic lapses: mind tricks on Watto, entering the Clone Wars, and Mace Windu's attempt to execute a subdued Sidious.

stoicism.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
stoicism.title: Notes
stoicism.relation: Taliaferro and Beck trace a philosophy of love through Anakin: fatherless, he attaches compulsively to Shmi and then Padme, refusing the Stoic limits on control that Yoda and Epictetus teach, so that love curdles into the vow to 'stop people from dying.' Vader's fatherhood is the caricature of love - offering Luke power instead of care - until Luke's compassion and Vader's final self-sacrifice redeem it. The lesson: love must be tempered by humility about what Zeno and the Stoics placed outside our control, and broken family bonds can be partly repaired through costly self-sacrifice.

stoicism.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
stoicism.title: Wildest Dreams: Stoic Fate and Acceptance (Taylor's Version)
stoicism.relation: Argues Swift is a Stoic about fate: Epictetus's warning against handing your mind to anyone who attacks you explains 'I Forgot That You Existed' as reaching the Stoic ideal of indifference, and Cicero's physical, non-supernatural causation makes the 'Getaway Car' meeting fated by the couple's pasts rather than by stars. The determinism of 'Treacherous' ('I can't decide if it's a choice / Getting swept away') is balanced by the open future of 'Blank Space', while the responsibility objection to Stoic fate is met by Epictetus's 'it is not things that disturb men but their judgments', enacted in 'Shake It Off' and the cleansing acceptance of 'Clean' and 'Wildest Dreams'.

stoicism.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
stoicism.title: Notes
stoicism.relation: Quinn argues Rebecca is the show's Stoic: Marcus Aurelius's maxims about judgments, obstacles, and morning meetings with the ungrateful map onto her recovery from Rupert - accepting reality, forgiving as a choice within her control, the lion power pose, 'every disadvantage has its advantage' - with the dichotomy of control as her operating principle. Framed by Gen X self-reliance and second-wave feminism (Friedan's problem with no name, Beauvoir's woman as Other under Rupert), the chapter follows her from vengeful boss to mentor of Keeley and Nora, Bantr-era 'bossgirl' dater of Sam, and finally the Richmond family's matriarch.

stoicism.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
stoicism.title: Acknowledgment
stoicism.relation: William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.

stoicism.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
stoicism.title: H E N R I B E R G S O N
stoicism.relation: Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.

stoicism.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
stoicism.title: Hardwood Dojos
stoicism.relation: Bassham and Hamilton distill six success principles from coaches Smith, Pitino, Summitt, and Krzyzewski and show each echoes great philosophers, treating the court as a 'dojo' or place of enlightenment. Setting goals and pursuing excellence through habit map to Aristotle's eudaimonia and doctrine of habituation (Shaq the 'Big Aristotle' given the Nicomachean Ethics by Phil Jackson); the emphasis on outworking adversity and controlling only one's own effort maps to Stoics like Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius, as when Summitt and Dean Smith tell players to control what they can and accept the rest.

stoicism.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
stoicism.title: “They Don't Pay Nobody to Be Humble!” Football's Ego Problem
stoicism.relation: Holowchak diagnoses football's ego problem—Keyshawn Johnson's deactivation, Terrell Owens's self-promotion, Deion Sanders's showboating—as fed by sensationalism (via Dewey) and statistical obsession that pull players out of the team framework. He proposes 'Aretism,' a modern progressivist ethics built on Stoic oikeiosis (Chrysippus, Cicero, Seneca, Epictetus and Hierokles's concentric circles) balancing self- and other-concern, and on Kant's injunction to treat others as ends. The virtuous athlete competes fully while respecting opponents, sport, and the 'moral zone' of Stoic sagacity.

stoicism.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
stoicism.title: Heroes of the Coliseum
stoicism.relation: Reid draws an extended analogy between big-time college football players and Roman gladiators—both socially marginalized entertainers, controlled by coaches/editors and crowds, risking their bodies for others' entertainment. Through Roman Stoicism (Seneca, Epictetus, Cicero) she argues virtus does not depend on external wealth, status, or freedom but on accepting fate and excelling within one's role, so exploited athletes can still be genuine heroes of virtue. Following Marcus Aurelius's distaste for the games, she concludes those with power over players' unjust conditions are morally obliged to improve them.

stoicism.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
stoicism.title: Excuses, Excuses Inside the Mind of a Complainer
stoicism.relation: Kevin Kinghorn, drawing on interviews with coach Brad Gilbert, dissects why tennis players and their parents complain and make excuses. He catalogs cognitive biases and the vividness effect (why a bad call, like McEnroe's 'You cannot be serious!' outburst, sticks and feels like persecution) as forms of irrationality, and notes Stoicism (which he attributes to Zeno) as a philosophy that would suppress the complaining temperament. His central mechanism is Freudian self-deception: citing Freud's hypnotized-umbrella subject who invents a reason for his own behavior, he argues tennis parents pretend their child is destined for greatness and then genuinely come to believe the lie, so excuse-making becomes a self-destructive sign a player will never be a champion. He also reads Andrea Jaeger's ambivalence about winning as evidence of mixed, partly unconscious motivations.

stoicism.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
stoicism.title: Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis
stoicism.relation: Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.

stoicism.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
stoicism.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
stoicism.relation: Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.

stoicism.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
stoicism.title: The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders
stoicism.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.

stoicism.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
stoicism.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
stoicism.relation: Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.

stoicism.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
stoicism.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
stoicism.relation: Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a member of the 'cult of the cool' whose reticence and final resigned 'What's the difference?' surrender embody apatheia and acceptance of fate/logos. He tests Spencer Selby's claim that Clay and the sharpshooter Nikki must fail because their motives are immoral, arguing instead via an Aristotelian principle (virtues are stable dispositions) that their sudden lapses—the flimsy suitcase, Nikki's racial slur that loses him the lucky horseshoe—are Kubrick stacking the deck rather than genuine character. He closes by weighing Clay's life against models of a meaningful life (exuberance/romanticism vs. rationalism/self-fulfillment), faulting Clay for never subjecting his chosen ends to self-critical reason.

stoicism.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
stoicism.title: “Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns
stoicism.relation: Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.

stoicism.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
stoicism.title: 26. Be Like Johnny
stoicism.relation: George Dunn reads Johnny Ramone's transformation from Queens delinquent to disciplined band foreman through craftsmanship: the Ramones' identical uniforms, downstrokes-only rig, and synchronized stagecraft embody the tradesman's virtues, and the band's 'fun' is MacIntyre's good internal to the practice of rocking out, not external rewards like money or fame. Against punk's 'Year Zero' originality conceit, Girard's mimesis shows imitation is inescapable - even distinguishing yourself is negative imitation - so the Ramones' apprenticeship to rock-and-roll radio and the teenage band Yee Loi faithfully imitating Johnny (Mosrite replica, one-legged spin) illustrate how mastery of models produces genuine creativity and freedom, a Stoic self-sufficiency of the skilled worker. Illich's 'convivial' tools like iPhones and YouTube let DIY players build their own lane past the corporate gatekeepers.

stoicism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
stoicism.title: 6. The Morality of Mike’s Manifesto
stoicism.relation: The Gibsons analyze Mike Ehrmantraut's code—'if you make a deal with somebody, you keep your word'—through virtue ethics and Stoicism. Aristotle's function argument and Golden Mean partly vindicate Mike's counsel toward temperance and restraint (not carrying a gun, sparing the Salamanca driver), yet Aristotle's claim that 'bad people are full of regrets' marks him as a flawed 'wicked' man given his inner turmoil over breaking his son. They read his calm as Stoic (Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on controlling the mind, Spartan simplicity), and weigh Kant's intent-based defense of his killing the dirty cops Hoffman and Fensky against Mill's social-rule view of sanctionable wrongs.

stoicism.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
stoicism.title: 5. Friendship, Fun, Freedom, Food, and the Future
stoicism.relation: Le Gall and Taliaferro read Bourdain's Libya and Iran episodes of Parts Unknown through Pierre Hadot's 'philosophy as a way of life,' arguing that Gaddafi and Khomeini were failed Platonic philosopher-kings. They interpret ordinary Libyans and Iranians eating Uncle Kentucky chicken, playing pinball, or hosting feasts as popular 'spiritual exercises' — tatonnement — showing how the personal becomes political and how friendship, fun, freedom, and food nourish the Socratic care of the soul.

stoicism.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
stoicism.title: 11. The One Truly Serious Philosophical Problem
stoicism.relation: Doll surveys philosophical views on suicide to make sense of Bourdain's death, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is the one serious philosophical problem. She weighs Plato's Phaedo prohibition (we are the gods' possessions) against his allowance for extreme misfortune, Aristotle's view that suicide violates one's duty to self and community, and Seneca's Stoic position that a wise man 'lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can' — framing Bourdain's death as an autonomous choice.

stoicism.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
stoicism.title: MOTHERHOOD
stoicism.relation: Jen Baker interrogates why unmedicated 'natural' childbirth is treated as morally superior, dissecting five senses of 'natural' and rejecting each, including a social-Darwinist appeal to evolution she deems dangerous. She engages Montaigne (via Cicero) on philosophizing as learning to die and cites Dylan Thomas and Neil Young on facing pain soberly, then turns to the Stoics' claim that pain 'is nothing to us' – arguing from a neo-Aristotelian/Stoic virtue ethics that pain has no moral value and that keeping one's wits with an epidural can preserve moral agency, so natural birth is an 'optional and amoral' thrill, not a virtue; she frames it with Bill Cosby's and Carol Burnett's labor jokes.

stoicism.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
stoicism.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
stoicism.relation: Gregory and Tod Bassham argue Stoicism is the seaman's philosophy of agency, teaching a clear-eyed grasp of what we can control, influence, or not control at all. Using Epictetus's play metaphor and 'you will fetter my leg but not my will,' Seneca and Marcus Aurelius on fear, they map three techniques onto sailing: cheerful resignation (Gerry Spiess righting Yankee Girl, Shackleton's James Caird crew laughing amid the Southern Ocean), self-sufficiency (splicing lines, emotional independence on a cramped boat), and negative visualization / premeditatio malorum (practicing docking under sail, imagining lost rudders). Skip Allen scuttling Wildflower and Dinelli's endurance illustrate the trichotomy of control and freedom of mind.

stoicism.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
stoicism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
stoicism.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.

stoicism.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
stoicism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
stoicism.relation: Kevin Krein argues that the freedom climbers report feeling is not freedom of movement, political freedom, or free will—on those measures a roped climber pinned on a ledge is less free—but the Stoic freedom of aligning one's will with what nature allows. Using Chrysippus' tethered-dog image and the Stoic identification of human logos with cosmic reason, he claims the climber who understands and accepts the mountain's conditions and wills only what it permits becomes free, which is why experienced climbers feel freest when their options are fewest. He adds Epictetus' dichotomy of control: the mountain (storms, avalanches, one's own failing body) is largely outside our power, so limiting desire to what we control—composure, choices, effort—is how a climber stays free in any conditions.

stoicism.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
stoicism.title: BLUES
stoicism.relation: Brian Domino frames a choice between the reasoned Stoic life and the emotional life through the Rolling Stones and the blues. He presents Epictetus's Stoicism — apatheia, the dichotomy of control, and the Enchiridion's 'it was given back' — applied to blues themes of floods, death, and cheating women ('When the Levee Breaks,' Robert Johnson's 'Terraplane Blues'), arguing emotions stem from false beliefs and akrasia. Against this he sets 'Jumping Jack Flash,' 'Monkey Man,' and '(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction' as celebrations of raw emotional existence, invoking Plato's tension of reason and passion and Nietzsche's image of the 'music-making Socrates' to leave the choice deliberately unresolved.

stoicism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
stoicism.title: 3. Star Trek as Philosophy Spock as Stoic Sage
stoicism.relation: Pigliucci argues that Gene Roddenberry built an implicit argument for Stoicism into Star Trek's Spock, contra both the 'suppressed emotion / stiff upper lip' caricature and Farren's claim that Kirk is the truer Stoic. Reading Spock's talk of 'emotion' as the disruptive pathe and his 'logic' as the broad Stoic study of reason, he shows Spock embodying the dichotomy of control ('my legs, they're broken'), the four cardinal virtues, and Stoic cosmopolitanism aboard the Enterprise. Drawing on Brouwer's account of the sage, he tracks Spock's development from prokopton toward sagehood, cultivating eupatheiai like love and friendship (the Wrath of Khan sacrifice) and declaring 'logic is the beginning of wisdom, not the end.'

stoicism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
stoicism.title: 25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”
stoicism.relation: The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'

stoicism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
stoicism.title: 35. Star Wars as Philosophy A Genealogy of the Force
stoicism.relation: Eberl builds a genealogy of the Force across the Skywalker saga, using Augustine to reject the Manichaean light/dark dualism Yoda voices ('Luminous beings are we') in favor of evil as a privation of good and as 'inordinate desire' for temporal goods, which explains Anakin's fall through his refusal to let Padme die. He casts Palpatine as a Nietzschean who declares 'good is a point of view' and pursues will to power and the ubermensch, contrasting this with the Stoicism of Seneca and Yoda ('train yourself to let go of everything you fear to lose'). The sequel trilogy's disenchanted galaxy is read through Charles Taylor, and Rey and Ben's redemption shows evil defeated not by hatred but by rightly-ordered love ('Saving what we love').

stoicism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
stoicism.title: 62. Hannah Gadsby as Philosopher Is Comedy Really Such a Good Thing
stoicism.relation: The chapter treats Hannah Gadsby's Nanette as philosophical comedy, weighing her four reasons for quitting: self-deprecation is humiliation for the marginalized, jokes' setup-punchline structure cannot heal trauma, comic relief lets audiences off the hook, and anger only spreads hatred. It distinguishes self-lacerating from ethical, existential, and ironic self-deprecation, and contrasts Critchley's Freudian neo-Stoic humor (super-ego viewing the ego as trivial, akin to Epictetus and cognitive therapy) with the Willetts' feminist 'collective catharsis.' Against Gadsby's claim that anger cannot be constructive, it sets Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness alongside Lorde and Srinivasan to argue anger can recover agency and register injustice, and defends Nanette as genuine comedy and 'stand-up catharsis.'

transcendental-idealism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
transcendental-idealism.title: Unknown
transcendental-idealism.relation: The chapter introduces the Kantian reading of the pod-bank revelation: since Plato and the Buddha philosophers have called the everyday world mere appearance, but Kant gives the most sophisticated version, arguing that even the objective properties of physics rest on projections of human consciousness. Crucially, unlike Descartes's malicious demon, no external deceiver is responsible for the hoax: we project and reify the world of experience ourselves, and this self-imposed illusion is the 'matrix' of the socio-economic and political world in which we alienate our own freedom.

transcendental-idealism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
transcendental-idealism.title: Unknown
transcendental-idealism.relation: Reading Agent Smith's revelation that the first Matrix was a perfect world 'where none suffered' that 'no one would accept', the chapter argues that captive humanity itself vetoes its illusions: because human beings 'define their reality through suffering and misery', the machines had to rebuild the Matrix as the rat-race world of 1999, the 'peak of your civilization'. This is the film's version of Kant's self-imposed appearance - even under alien captors, sleeping humanity holds a veto over possible Matrices and instinctively gets what it wants.

transcendental-idealism.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
transcendental-idealism.title: Unknown
transcendental-idealism.relation: Through Copernicus the chapter explains Kant's Copernican revolution in philosophy: Aristotle's geocentrism was not stupidity but a faithful formulation of how the sky actually looks, and rejecting it means accepting that the perceived world is an illusion. Perception is inherently egocentric - the world each of us sees centers on our own body - and taking this body-centered appearance for reality is childish egocentrism in children and egotism in adults, which is the condition the Matrix universalizes.

transcendental-idealism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
transcendental-idealism.title: Conquering the Inner Demon
transcendental-idealism.relation: James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.

transcendental-idealism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
transcendental-idealism.title: Going Mental
transcendental-idealism.relation: Argues Harry's question rests on a false dilemma between 'in the head' and 'real', which Dumbledore's reply dissolves. It distinguishes merely-in-the-head items (Hermione as fictional character) from mind-independent ones (Emma Watson, King's Cross), then surveys philosophers who make the mental real: Plato's forms via broomsticks as imperfect copies of the ideal essence, Descartes's rationalism, Kant's mind-constituted objects, Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived', Mill's phenomenalism, and Yogacara Buddhism's consciousness-fabricated emptiness.

transcendental-idealism.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
transcendental-idealism.relation: Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.
