Through facticity (the unforgiving no-save 2003 game) and existence preceding essence, the chapter concludes that videogames offer unparalleled opportunities to practice Sartrean responsibility and achieve Freudian reconciliation through the right avatar.

bad-faith.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
bad-faith.title: Two Philosophies, Two Compasses to Navigate Life
bad-faith.relation: Against 'Hang the DJ,' where Frank and Amy's coaching system assigns partners and expiration dates inside a simulated dating park, the chapter argues a Stoic would refuse to sign up: delegating judgments to the coach violates Epictetus's dichotomy of control, and the endless date-cycle fails all four virtues, treating dates (like Amy's bored lovemaking) as means rather than inherently worthy persons. An existentialist reading via Sartre says nearly every system-arranged relationship is bad faith - couples act as if compatible against the expiry they were given, as Frank and Nicola do - and only Frank and Amy's open-ended, freely chosen relationship escapes it, so their 'fuck off' to the system is a leap of faith that 998 of 1000 simulated couples make, which is how the app computes its 99.8% match. The authors close with Camus's absurd, doubting that the real Frank and Amy, who cannot rebel against an app that tells them they belong together, will fare as well as their simulations.

bad-faith.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
bad-faith.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
bad-faith.relation: William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.

bad-faith.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
bad-faith.title: “I Am Moana!”
bad-faith.relation: Stages Moana's dilemma between her father's Aristotelian essentialism — everything on Motunui has a fixed function, so Moana's essence as chief precedes her birth — and Sartre's existence precedes essence, with Heihei the unchanging chicken as a being whose essence really does precede existence. Tui embodies bad faith and the crowd (his own aborted voyage left him enforcing 'no one goes beyond the reef'), while Tala and then Moana live authentically through anguish, forlornness, and despair, until 'I am Moana!' marks her self-defined identity. Nietzsche's 'become who you are' and 'what does not destroy me makes me stronger' frame her resilience, which lets her free Maui ('Hook. No hook. I'm Maui.') and unmask Te Ka as Te Fiti whose stolen heart 'does not define you.'

bad-faith.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
bad-faith.title: The Existential Redefinition of Doctor Strange
bad-faith.relation: DiGeorgio traces Strange's 'existential conversion' from scientific nihilism ('matter and nothing more') through Sartrean bad faith — playing the brilliant surgeon while not really believing life meaningless, refusing the Ancient One's widened keyhole — to authenticity. His hesitation to stay and fight after killing a zealot, and the Ancient One's 'it's not about you,' set up his choice to defend humanity as Sartre's universal decree, choosing for all humankind in anguish and freedom. The endless time loop imposed on Dormammu is read as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence demanding total commitment to one's choices, so that by the end Strange lives existence-precedes-essence: what he does, not his 'brilliant surgeon' essence, defines him.

bad-faith.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
bad-faith.title: The Other Children: The Importance of Meg and Chris
bad-faith.relation: Dohnimm argues Meg and Chris matter because they lack essence: unlike predictable one-gag characters (pervert Quagmire, homicidal Stewie), their traits are accidental — Meg stays Meg after her 'Don't Make Me Over' makeover, Chris stays Chris despite flashes of artistic talent. On Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, character (hexis) explains action, but Meg and Chris are inexplicable (Chris hitting on his mother, claiming 'My dad is smarter than your dad' when they share one). The Isen and Levin dime-in-the-phone-booth helping experiment grounds the situationist alternative: tiny situational factors, not character, predict helping — Quagmire is predictable, but Chris (speaking hip-hop, covering himself in honey for ants) is not. Finally, Sartre's bad faith reframes them: appealing to fixed character is fleeing our radical freedom, so the 'anti-characters' Meg and Chris are the show's most realistic and philosophically honest figures.

bad-faith.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
bad-faith.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
bad-faith.relation: Christopher Wood reads Cloud's arc as an existentialist quest: Heidegger's thrownness in Cloud's tumble off the Midgar train and his initial 'It's not my problem' denial of being-in-the-world; Nietzsche's death of God in Mako-powered Midgar's nihilism, with AVALANCHE as a call for revaluation of values and Sephiroth as a false aspirant god; and Sartre's bad faith in Cloud 'playing at being a SOLDIER,' a persona borrowed wholesale from Zack along with his sword and mercenary dream. Through the Lifestream reunion with Tifa, Cloud faces his fabricated past, admits 'I never was in SOLDIER,' and turns to authenticity by resolving to live without pretending, which Wood presents as the player's own existential task.

bad-faith.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
bad-faith.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
bad-faith.relation: The chapter asks whether Daenerys's fatalism - she feels truly free only once she believes fate is in control - can coexist with freedom in a Westeros where class and gender fix everyone's essence. Aristotle's sea-battle argument from bivalence and Cicero's Idle Argument (Dany will rule whether or not she leaves Meereen) are dismantled as having no practical consequences for deliberation, while Sartre's anguish and bad faith explain Cersei's 'necessity' excuse for arresting Ned and Sansa's refusal to own her lie about Joffrey and Mycah. Heidegger's authenticity then resolves the paradox: like Ned choosing between family and honor and Jon choosing his Night's Watch vows over kinship, freedom is not escape from one's past but owning it - Heraclitus's 'character is destiny,' becoming who you are.

bad-faith.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
bad-faith.title: 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon
bad-faith.relation: Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.

bad-faith.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
bad-faith.title: 16. Is Hell Other People
bad-faith.relation: Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.

bad-faith.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
bad-faith.title: 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
bad-faith.relation: Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.

bad-faith.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
bad-faith.title: It Worked
bad-faith.relation: Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.

bad-faith.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
bad-faith.title: Television and Existential Awakening
bad-faith.relation: Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.

bad-faith.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
bad-faith.title: The Metal Militia and the Existentialist Club
bad-faith.relation: Jeremy Wisnewski claims Metallica is an existentialist band: Kill 'Em All answers Camus' absurd by creating meaning through chosen, expressive projects ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath'), Ride the Lightning's catalogue of deaths ('Fight Fire with Fire' to 'Fade to Black') individualizes us in the Heideggerian confrontation with our own death, and Master of Puppets dramatizes Sartrean bad faith - the 'Sanitarium' label, the soldier as 'Disposable Hero', the addict's lost freedom. He concludes that accusing Metallica of selling out with the Black Album is itself bad faith, since authenticity has no fixed content.

bad-faith.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
bad-faith.title: Metallica's Existential Freedom: From We to I and Back Again
bad-faith.relation: Rachael Sotos reads Metallica's career as an existentialist quest for authentic freedom: the Arendtian shared 'we' of the early speed-metal community (Kill 'Em All), the Heideggerian 'I' attuned to death that breaks from das Man (Ride the Lightning's 'Fade to Black'), and the Kierkegaardian leap out of the over-technical system of . . . And Justice for All - compared to Kierkegaard's critique of Hegel - into the embodied groove of the Black Album. Sartre's bad faith explains the rock-star traps, and Some Kind of Monster shows the 'we' must be tended: therapy and a democratic band restore Arendtian public freedom.

bad-faith.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
bad-faith.title: The Office and Philosophy
bad-faith.relation: Applies Sartre's Being and Nothingness to the mockumentary: Pam's bad faith consists in pretending she has no choice between Jim and Roy (her garbled 'I'm not into Jim' conversation with Karen in 'Ben Franklin'), while the camera's Look - Sartre's keyhole peeper caught in the hallway - turns her into an object not of her making when she is caught watching Jim and Karen in 'The Merger', and her shame finally lets her own her feelings. David Brent's pride (posing with his Inside Paper magazine cover) tries to control the Other's look and fails, since the freely respected gaze he craves cannot be extracted; and the ever-possible camera functions as Foucault's panopticon (Bentham's prison design), visible and unverifiable, silencing Jan on speakerphone in 'Cocktails' and forcing Dwight and Angela's 'Don't linger. Break left' choreography, which makes the viewer a complicit co-worker.

bad-faith.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
bad-faith.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
bad-faith.relation: Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.

bad-faith.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
bad-faith.title: NOTES
bad-faith.relation: Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.

bad-faith.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
bad-faith.title: Notes
bad-faith.relation: Reads Cohle's arc as an existentialist passage toward authenticity, using Sartre's being-for-itself to explain why Hart's 'family man' identity is bad faith — a clinging to social roles that denies the freedom of a consciousness that is an activity, not a thing. Beauvoir's analysis of women as the passive, objectified Other illuminates why Rust, despite his nihilism, persistently protects vulnerable women and children such as Sophia, Dora Lange, and Marie Fontenot: threats to others' freedom threaten our own. Nietzsche's Silenus wisdom, the spirit of gravity on the tightrope, and the shepherd who bites the head off the snake frame Ledoux's and Childress' warped eternal return as the poison Cohle must overcome before he can will life eternally and declare 'the light is winning.'

bad-faith.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
bad-faith.title: 12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep
bad-faith.relation: Jones argues the Zone is not somewhere else: Serling's map-language of signposts, thresholds, and borders describes episodes that actually unfold in recognizable American places, from Nan Adams's real highway in 'The Hitch-Hiker' to an ordinary hospital in 'The Eye of the Beholder.' The show's impossible catalysts, gremlins, aliens, sentient dolls, perform a double distancing that lets viewers face mundane truths about selfishness, gullibility, and vulnerability while pretending those truths are fantastic. 'The Shelter' is the exception that breaks the shelter: with no supernatural or futuristic cause, only the very real 1961 fallout-shelter panic, it forces the audience to see that the Zone is their own living room and the monsters are us.

bad-faith.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
bad-faith.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
bad-faith.relation: Round argues modern zombie fiction's real horror is humanity, reading The Walking Dead existentially: Rick builds meaning through self-imposed missions, revises his morals ('You kill, you die' then killing Dexter anyway), and demands in his 'We ARE the walking dead' speech (Issue #24) that the group admit their new nature instead of hiding in bad faith behind old rules. Kierkegaard's Abraham illuminates Rick's suspension of universal ethics, while Sergeant Abraham Ford's confession 'No. I did what I wanted to do' models owning one's choices, and his angst after Eugene's lie shows the cost of projected meaning collapsing. Camus supplies persistence against the absurd (suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol exert the only control left), and Adorno's Marxist critique frames the Governor's Woodbury as an inauthentic hierarchy that denies its people authentic choice.

bad-faith.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
bad-faith.title: P A R T F O U R
bad-faith.relation: Four Part Four essays beyond ethics. Aaron Meskin asks whether Watchmen is literature at all, testing definitions from Beardsley, Eagleton, Lamarque/Olsen and Hirsch in the Socratic 'what is X?' way, and concludes the question is indeterminate because comics are a hybrid art form — though the book's literary allusions (Shelley's 'Ozymandias,' Blake's 'Tyger,' Burroughs) deserve literary appreciation regardless. Sarah Donovan and Nick Richardson read the two Silk Spectres through three feminisms: Sally and Laurie as liberal feminists (Wollstonecraft, Mill) who fight crime, their hypersexual costumes as Irigaray-style subversive mimicry of gender stereotypes that risks reinforcing them (the Silhouette's expulsion exposing the heterosexual norm), the Comedian's attempted rape exposing 'she asked for it' attitudes, and Laurie as Beauvoir's woman in bad faith, living out her mother's fantasies until she finally names and dresses herself. Robert Arp uses Hooded Justice and Captain Metropolis's closeted relationship to dismantle 'homosexuality is unnatural' arguments — the ideal-function view would condemn the infertile too, and Hume's is-ought point undermines the procreation argument — before defending gay marriage against slippery-slope and parenting objections. Taneli Kukkonen maps Kierkegaard's stages onto the Comedian's mocking irony (hiding even his paternity of Laurie and his Kennedy confession as jokes) and Rorschach's deeper humor of the ethical stage, a knight of resignation whose 'never compromise, not even in the face of Armageddon' expects nothing back from the world.

bad-faith.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
bad-faith.title: Conclusion An Infinity of Possibilities
bad-faith.relation: Kimberly Engels reads William's transformation into the Man in Black through Sartre's existential 'project': rather than discovering a pre-existing true self 'among the dead,' William's new situation in the park (loving and losing Dolores, killing the Confederados, Logan's betrayal) produces an existential rupture in which he chooses new ends, symbolized by trading the white hat for the black. She argues the Man in Black's claim to have 'found himself' is Sartrean bad faith, denying his freedom and facticity to evade responsibility for the harm he causes. Extending existentialism to androids, she reads Maeve's choice to leave the train and seek her daughter as her first freely formulated project, the start of her own 'infinity of possibilities.'

bad-faith.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
bad-faith.title: IV - X-ISTENTIAL X-MEN JEWS, SUPERMEN, AND THE LITERATURE OF STRUGGLE
bad-faith.relation: Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature rooted in the Jewish experience of their creators. Stan Lee and Jack Kirby's mutants, and Claremont's reinvention of Magneto as a Holocaust survivor, reverse Superman's assimilationist fantasy: being a minority makes the X-Men entitled to equal treatment, and human fear of difference is the norm rather than a Lex Luthor-style pathology. Sartre's bad faith explains the anti-Semite's chosen hatred (and why Xavier refuses to simply mind-control humans into tolerance), while Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem makes moral judgment everyone's burden. Against Camus' opening question of suicide and Mr. Incredible's wish that the world 'stay saved,' the chapter argues the X-Men's endless Sisyphean cycle of deaths, resurrections, and reboots is not futile: one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

bad-faith.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
bad-faith.title: VII - X-WOMEN AND X-ISTENCE
bad-faith.relation: Housel gives an existential history of the X-Women. Jean Grey embodies the paradox of 'existence precedes essence,' a fictional character whose meaning is assigned by creators and fans yet who perpetually re-creates herself through the Phoenix, while Rachel Summers 'makes her own existence at every single moment' in Ortega's sense across timelines. The Scarlet Witch's reality-warping is Baudrillard's 'line of fracture' where an expanding system cracks, and her denial of the past is Sartrean bad faith; Storm shows angstless responsibility, Mystique the 'cynical consciousness' of self-deception, Rogue Camus' absurdity in a life without touch, and Kitty Pryde Ortega's 'substantial emigrant on a pilgrimage of being.'

bad-faith.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
bad-faith.relation: Dale and Foy argue that across Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Hulk and Brokeback Mountain, Lee presents a pessimistic, Sartrean philosophy of identity in which authentic selves are irreconcilable with a hostile social world. They read Jen's caged gender rebellion and Jade Fox's rejection, Bruce's suppressed origins and rage-fueled transformation, and Ennis and Jack's concealed love as hidden identities that produce dislocation, deception and disorder. Invoking Kierkegaard and Heidegger's dasein on authenticity and Foucault's Discipline and Punish, they show society disciplining deviance so each hero is displaced or destroyed—Jack beaten to death like Matthew Shepard, the Hulk exiled to the Amazon.

bad-faith.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
bad-faith.relation: Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.

bad-faith.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
bad-faith.title: William Burroughs as Philosopher From Beat Morality to Third Worldism to Continental Theory
bad-faith.relation: Jones Irwin makes the case for 'Burroughs as philosopher,' tracing an 'impassioned moralism' and antihumanism (human as adjective, not noun) that separates him from other Beats and postmodernists. He links Burroughs's critique of alienation to Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and to Sartrean existentialism and bad faith ('there are no victims, just accomplices'), and reads the Beats' 'third force' Third Worldism via Freire, Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, and Paz. Close readings of Naked Lunch's 'Bradley the Buyer' and the sex-and-death delirium of 'AJ's Annual Party' connect Burroughs to Artaud's body without organs, Bataille's Sadean tradition, and Derrida's deconstruction of embodiment and 'distance touching.'

bad-faith.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
bad-faith.title: Human Nature and Freedom in Adaptation
bad-faith.relation: Ganssle uses Adaptation's four main characters to test Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence against Walker Percy's account of immanence and transcendence. Laroche, endlessly adaptable ('Done with fish'), embodies Sartrean radical freedom and pure immanence; Donald owns his love ('You are what you love, not what loves you') and lives without bad faith; Orlean and Charlie are paralyzed in bad faith, unable to choose. Ganssle contrasts Sartre's rejection of a fixed human nature (grounded in atheism, against Plato's and Augustine's Forms) with Percy's view that persons are unlike infinitely mutable orchids, arguing the film sides with Percy: the antiessentialist self is 'lost in the cosmos.'

bad-faith.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
bad-faith.title: Self-Creation, Identity, and Authenticity A Study of A History of Violence and Eastern Promises
bad-faith.relation: Daniel Moseley distinguishes metaphysical from practical problems of personal identity, arguing A History of Violence and Eastern Promises explore the practical: who Tom/Joey and Nikolai really are, as a matter of self-creation and self-discovery of a 'practical identity' (Korsgaard). Using Sartre's bad faith and Cavell on movie-star 'individualities,' plus Charles Taylor's critique of individualist authenticity, he argues even the wicked Semyon exemplifies authenticity, so authenticity is not a moral ideal, and Nikolai's decent double life may be worth being less authentic.

bad-faith.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
bad-faith.title: Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke
bad-faith.relation: Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.

bad-faith.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
bad-faith.title: Existential Ethics Where the Paths of Glory Lead Jason Holt
bad-faith.relation: Holt uses Paths of Glory to illustrate existential ethics, framing the doomed 701st Regiment as 'thrown' beings-toward-death who retain full freedom in how they meet their fate. He resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' (denying objective values while commanding authenticity) by treating authenticity as a formal, second-order virtue like integrity: Colonel Dax is sincere and consistent, General Mireau an inauthentic hypocrite acting in bad faith. Addressing weakness of will (Roget's cowardice) and the condemned Paris 'dying well' before the firing squad, Holt argues that courage—an Aristotelian character virtue—is the smuggled-in content that grounds any formalist existential ethics.

bad-faith.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
bad-faith.title: Seeking Authenticity
bad-faith.relation: The chapter argues that Whedon's heroes—Angel resisting the demon within in Pylea, Spike earning back his soul, Simon Tam abandoning his medical career for River, Echo asserting control over her Dollhouse imprints, and Buzz Lightyear redefining himself—live authentically by owning their values against depersonalizing forces, while Captain Hammer and Serenity's Operative are the true 'monsters' who surrender their identities to social roles and blind institutional loyalty. It then asks whether Whedon is a thoroughgoing Sartrean existentialist and answers no: the 'Paradiso Paradigm' (Mal returning the medicine in 'The Train Job') and Willow's 'Choices' speech show objective moral value independent of autonomous choice, making Whedon more Socratic than Sartrean. Rawls supplies the synthesis: heterogeneous life plans (Xander, Oz, Lorne) pursued within objective social conditions—basic rights, liberties, and opportunities—that make authentic self-formation possible for everyone.

bad-faith.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
bad-faith.relation: McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.

bad-faith.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
bad-faith.relation: Karen D. Hoffman reads The Last Temptation of Christ and Bringing Out the Dead through Sartre's distinction between the for-itself (transcendence) and the in-itself (immanence), arguing both reluctant saviors are tempted into bad faith. Scorsese's Jesus, tempted on the cross to abandon his mission and live as an ordinary husband and father, passively drifts toward a life of pure immanence that denies his human transcendence, until (following Kazantzakis's 'sprouting of wings' image via Judas) he reclaims his choice to be crucified. Frank Pierce inversely faces a false transcendence—the temptation to think of himself as God, or to escape via drugs, violence, or suicide—and resists it, allowing the vegetative Mr. Burke to die. Hoffman frames avoiding either exaggeration as the path to authentic Sartrean humanity and grace.

bad-faith.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
bad-faith.relation: Sanders argues Mann's action serves existentialist ideas: identity, freedom, authenticity, and death. In Thief, Frank's insistence on 'the yield of my labor' and his self-immolating exit dramatize the individualist maximizer whose choice of principle—echoing Sartre's young man and Kierkegaard's 'purity of heart is to will one thing'—cannot be given from outside. The Miami Vice episode 'Heart of Darkness' is read as a morality play on authenticity: undercover agent Artie Lawson's flight into the fantasy persona is a bad-faith masquerade that ends in suicide, mirroring Crockett's own anxiety about his Sonny Burnett alter ego.

bad-faith.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
bad-faith.title: Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall
bad-faith.relation: Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.

bad-faith.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
bad-faith.relation: Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.

bad-faith.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
bad-faith.relation: Holt reads Paths of Glory as an illustration of existential ethics. The doomed men of the 701st are 'thrown' (Heidegger) into a suicidal attack on the Ant Hill, and the film contrasts the authentic Colonel Dax - sincere, consistent, refusing Mireau's command out of integrity - with the inauthentic, bad-faith General Mireau. Holt resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' by treating 'be authentic' as a formal meta-value, and argues that authenticity ultimately rests on the Aristotelian virtue of courage, shown when Paris 'dies well' before the firing squad despite an earlier failure of nerve.

bad-faith.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
bad-faith.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
bad-faith.relation: Ryan Weldon reads Selina Kyle's transformation into Catwoman in Batman Returns through Sartre's existentialism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Pre-death Selina is Sartre's inauthentic 'waiter,' performing a servile secretary role in bad faith, and Beauvoir's objectified Other, defined by Max Shreck and the men who dismiss her. Her murder and feline resurrection free repressed drives, and her refusal of Batman's fairy-tale rescue—'I couldn't live with myself'—plus her choice to kill Shreck are cast as an assertion of facticity and transcendence, an authentic (if unfinished) self-creation that rejects the roles available to women rather than reaching a stable ending.

bad-faith.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
bad-faith.title: John Drake in Greeneland: Noir Themes in Secret Agent
bad-faith.relation: Lee argues that Secret Agent belongs to the Graham Greene noir tradition of The Ministry of Fear and The Third Man, not Bond escapism: Drake never kills, carries no gun, and refuses romantic entanglement, because McGoohan prized realism and ethical seriousness. Readings of Greene's Stephen Neale (who killed his wife out of pity) and Harry Lime's Ferris-wheel nihilism establish a world 'void of meaning, haphazard, and morally indifferent,' which Drake's episodes then dramatize: in 'It's Up to the Lady' his superior Hobbs (named, Lee contends, for Thomas Hobbes, whose Leviathan and war of all against all the essay explicates) betrays Drake's promised word and has the defector Charles arrested; in 'That's Two of Us Sorry' Drake unwittingly plays the villain, ruining an innocent Scottish village; in 'Judgement Day' he cannot say what justice for the Nazi scientist Garriga requires. Lee concludes that Drake, like Neale and Martins, acts in Sartrean bad faith by continuing to serve morally bankrupt masters, and that Greene's only exits are a Kierkegaardian leap of faith Drake never makes, or fantasized retirement and death.

bad-faith.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
bad-faith.title: Noir et Blanc in Color: Existentialism and Miami Vice
bad-faith.relation: Sanders reads Miami Vice as existentialist 'sunshine noir,' where color and pastel locations carry noir alienation, and Crockett and Tubbs live rootless lives with shambles of romances and a culturally impoverished compass (Bolt, Buddy Holly, Buffett, Beckett, Betts). The episode 'No Exit' (Bruce Willis as arms dealer Tony Amato, whose wife Rita shoots him at the courthouse steps) is analyzed through Sartre's being-in-itself/being-for-itself conflict and 'hell is other people,' from which Danto says 'there is no exit.' 'Heart of Darkness' presents Ed O'Neill's undercover FBI agent Arthur Lawson, who prefers his Artie Rollins persona and hangs himself after debriefing, as a failure of authenticity and flight into bad faith that Crockett recognizes as his own peril as Sonny Burnett. Crockett's amnesia arc ('Mirror Image' through 'Redemption in Blood' and 'Bad Timing'), where he believes he is Burnett working for the Manolo organization, is resolved through Sartrean existential recognition and a freely chosen dangerous mission that restores his identity, since the Kierkegaardian leap of faith is unavailable in the show's secular world; Sanders also attacks Sartre's sanction of revolutionary violence in his preface to Fanon and Beauvoir's defense of Sade.

bad-faith.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life
bad-faith.relation: Watson and Riches reinterpret "A Man Needs a Maid" not as simple misogyny but as Young's ambivalent inner conflict between craving companionship and fearing the pain of intimacy. They read his pursuit of the "simple life" ("Heart of Gold," avoidance of reading) through Epicurean simplicity, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Bowlby/Freudian avoidant attachment and cognitive dissonance, and Sartre's "bad faith" as self-deception, set against Thoreau's chosen solitude and Aristotle's claim that the non-social being is "beast or god."

bad-faith.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
bad-faith.title: “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler
bad-faith.relation: Kevin S. Decker argues the Doctor's morality is an "ethics of ambiguity" poised between Romanticism and existentialism, not any formula. Rejecting positivism, deontology, and utilitarianism as fits for the Doctor, he reads the Doctor's freedom, wandering, and rejection of Time Lord values through Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith (the student torn between mother and Free French) and Beauvoir's "adventurer" who confers value by choosing. The Romantic search for the infinite in small things and the Prometheus myth frame the Doctor as a liberating, self-defining moral exemplar.

bad-faith.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
bad-faith.title: 6. When Punks Grow Up
bad-faith.relation: Meagher asks whether punks can mature, arguing via Sartre and Beauvoir that punk revolts against the 'spirit of seriousness' - the bad faith of treating values as externally imposed by God, law, or convention - and against the weak nihilism that merely abandons valuing after serious values fail. Following Devon Johnson's Black nihilism distinction, mature punk is strong nihilism: destroying decadent (Euromodern, colonial) values in order to create new ones, building scenes, labels, and institutions for future generations, fighting for others' freedom and decolonization as Arendtian politics, and - with Nietzsche's dead God and Crass's 1978 declaration - being willing to proclaim even punk itself dead.

bad-faith.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
bad-faith.title: 20. Punks Pissing People Off
bad-faith.relation: Juneko Robinson mixes memoir of circa-1980 anti-punk violence (routine beatings, the murder of Brian Deneke) with Sartrean existentialism to explain why punks 'pissed people off': punk's confrontational appearance exposed the contingency and hypocrisy of mainstream values, forcing others to take responsibility for them. Using Sartre's keyhole-peeper example from Being and Nothingness and No Exit's 'hell is other people', she argues that harassers lived in bad faith, dependent on how others see them, while punks were the witnesses who objectified the mainstream rather than the deviants being watched. Howard Becker's moral entrepreneurs explain the 'de-punking' panics and psychiatric commitments of kids who merely dressed weird, and Marmysz's 'nihilistic incongruity' shows punk converting society's hypocrisy into self-legislated virtue.

bad-faith.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
bad-faith.title: 8. Self-Hatred as Identity
bad-faith.relation: Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.

bad-faith.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
bad-faith.title: 11. The Self-Deception Road
bad-faith.relation: Doll analyzes self-deception across the series using Gregg Ten Elshof's four mechanisms—attention management, procrastination, perspective shifting, and rationalization. Chuck's electromagnetic hypersensitivity is a real psychological condition about which he deceives himself as to its physical cause, reinforced by everyone accommodating him; his refusal to see Jimmy as anything but 'Slippin' Jimmy' is rationalized as protecting others while sabotaging his brother. Jimmy, via perspective-shifting through Chuck's eyes, comes to believe he can only be Slippin' Jimmy, then rationalizes the Saul persona. Drawing on Joseph Butler and Adam Smith, Doll argues self-deception blinds moral judgment and is ultimately Saul's undoing, leaving him alone in hiding.

bad-faith.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
bad-faith.title: 8. Why Do We Care Who Bourdain Really Was
bad-faith.relation: Finn asks why fans cared about Bourdain's 'authenticity,' arguing his persona of freedom from bourgeois convention embodied Sartre's rejection of 'bad faith' while his meticulous control made him, per Keefe, 'Apollo in drag as Dionysus.' Reading the Hanoi/Obama episode as proof that even the President wanted to be Bourdain, she suggests his freedom (Kierkegaard's 'dizziness') may have become a trap, and proposes 'integrity' rather than authenticity as the word for his consistency.

bad-faith.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
bad-faith.title: The Viewer and the Look
bad-faith.relation: Meyer and Schneider use The Office's mockumentary camera to dramatize Sartre's 'the Look' and bad faith. Pam pretends she cannot choose between Roy and Jim (bad faith as being-in-itself), and is shamed when the camera catches her watching Jim and Karen; David Brent's prideful self-promotion tries and fails to control the Other's gaze. They tie the ever-present camera to the Foucault/Bentham panopticon: Jan, Dwight, and Angela police themselves because they might be watched, making the viewer complicit in the workers' existential crises.

bad-faith.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
bad-faith.title: It Worked
bad-faith.relation: Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.

bad-faith.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
bad-faith.title: Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution
bad-faith.relation: Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.

bad-faith.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
bad-faith.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
bad-faith.relation: Collins-Cavanaugh asks what makes a 'real' father, framing it as authenticity. He pairs Sartre's existentialist authenticity – free choice, anxiety, and the bad faith of adopting others' ready-made plans, with 'real cookie' and Derek Jeter examples – against Charles Taylor's dialogical authenticity, in which choices are made within a 'horizon of meaning' set by others. He argues authentic fatherhood combines both: a father must freely own his choices (provider dad vs nurturer dad) while grounding them in his child's needs, concluding he'll go bake cookies with his son Connor.

bad-faith.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
bad-faith.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
bad-faith.relation: Owen argues that parenting is a political act and that fathers, especially privileged white heterosexual ones, should raise anti-oppressive children. Prompted by the question 'Daddy, why is her face brown?', he uses the social construction of racialized difference and the mutually constitutive culture–individual relation (the Zulu maxim 'a person is a person through other persons') to reject color-blindness. He prescribes knowledge, practice, and character steps, invokes Socrates' 'unexamined life' for relentless self-reflection, and answers the worry about raising 'alienated' children via Sartre's bad faith – authentic existence means accepting responsibility for reproducing or resisting injustice.

bad-faith.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
bad-faith.title: SERIAL KILLERS
bad-faith.relation: Winters reads the Zodiac Killer's taunting letters through Sartre's account of 'the look' from Being and Nothingness. He argues Zodiac's letters function like a snapped twig or a lit window: they make Northern Californians experience themselves as seen objects, hunted 'slaves' and pawns in Zodiac's game rather than free subjects. A phenomenological (first-person) analysis of the fear Zodiac induces, and of how his letters restrict the choices available within our facticity, is offered as superior to psychological or analytic accounts for explaining our fascination with the macabre.

bad-faith.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
bad-faith.title: SERIAL KILLERS
bad-faith.relation: Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.

bad-faith.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
bad-faith.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
bad-faith.relation: Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.

bad-faith.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
bad-faith.title: Who is Who
bad-faith.relation: This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.

bad-faith.book: 301 - Comics as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: index
bad-faith.relation: This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.

bad-faith.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
bad-faith.title: The Viewer and the Look
bad-faith.relation: Meyer and Schneider read The Office through Sartre's "the Look" and bad faith: the mockumentary camera catches characters as objects, as when Pam is caught gazing at Jim and freezes in shame, or pretends she has no choice about Roy (bad faith). David Brent's prideful posing tries to control the Other's look and fails. They add Foucault's panopticon — Dwight, Angela, and Jan police themselves because the camera might be watching — making the viewer complicit in exposing the employees' existential crises.

bad-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey
bad-faith.relation: Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.

bad-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 52. Fight Club as Philosophy I Am Jack’s Existential Struggle
bad-faith.relation: Oya reads Fincher's Fight Club in existentialist, nonethical terms as the story of the unnamed narrator 'Jack' and his struggle for an authentic, self-governed life. Consumerism (the 'Ikea nesting instinct'), the masculinity of underwear ads, religion, and finally Tyler Durden's hunter-gatherer creed are all rejected as externally imposed answers that deny authenticity; Fight Club and Project Mayhem merely swap one alienation for another. Jack's shooting himself to purge Tyler dramatizes self-affirmation. The chapter grounds this in Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity ('the genuine man will not agree to recognize any foreign absolute'), contrasts Nietzsche and Unamuno on self-affirmation, cites Hobbes on the brutish state of nature to condemn Tyler's utopia, and invokes Plato's cave to argue a comfortable but externally governed life is still not authentic.

bad-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 56. Pulp Fiction as Philosophy Bad Faith, Authenticity, and the Path of the Righteous Man
bad-faith.relation: The chapter argues that in Pulp Fiction the authentic characters get 'saved' and the inauthentic do not. Using Sartre's bad faith, it reads Vincent as fleeing into his facticity (his gangster role and social obligations) and Pumpkin as evading responsibility, while Butch acknowledges both his past (the father's watch) and his freedom. Heidegger's 'falling' and das Man explain Vincent's unmoved everyday mode after the miracle. Kierkegaard's three forms of despair from The Sickness unto Death rank the characters, with Jules alone transcending despair by accepting God's grace after 'divine intervention' stopped the bullets, making his Ezekiel monologue the film's key to a deeper authenticity.

bad-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 73. Hasan Minhaj as Philosopher Navigating the Struggles of Identity
bad-faith.relation: Singh reads Minhaj's comedy of identity through existentialism, arguing his call for 'authenticity' over the first generation's 'assimilation' (the 'American dream tax' and 'biryani' arguments about choosing one's life) enacts Sartre's existence-precedes-essence and rejection of bad faith. He frames Minhaj's Indian-American-Muslim conflict via Heidegger's thrownness and facticity and the move from the they-self (das Man) to authentic self, contrasting it with Sartre's facticity as a limit on freedom. Minhaj's 'global citizen' anti-nationalism, his 'love is bigger than fear,' and 'may the best argument win' are presented as prescriptions for navigating national, ethnic, religious and personal identity while flagging fallacies like hasty generalization behind Islamophobia.

bad-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates
bad-faith.relation: Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

bad-faith.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bad-faith.title: 75. Phoebe Waller-Bridge as Philosopher Conscious Women Making Choices
bad-faith.relation: Pande and Engels argue that Fleabag and Lulu (Crashing) embody Sartrean authenticity: they own their choices, balance facticity and transcendence, and stay outside bad faith, while the men (Anthony, the Priest) fall back on pregiven roles and let 'the Look' or their fundamental project decide for them. Fleabag's addressing the camera and finally shutting it out is read as breaking the gaze of the Other; the Priest choosing priesthood over love exemplifies denial of transcendence. Through Beauvoir's Second Sex, woman-as-Other, and ethics of ambiguity, they show Waller-Bridge's transgressive, sexually frank women reclaim self-definition, arguing viewers 'could do better to be' the kind of free, choosing women her protagonists are.

the-absurd.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
the-absurd.title: Popping a Bitter Pill Existential Authenticity in The Matrix and Nausea
the-absurd.relation: The chapter frames Neo's red/blue choice as the existential choice between authenticity - honest awareness of a condition without inherent purpose or design - and inauthenticity, named as Sartre's bad faith, Camus's intellectual suicide, and Heidegger's 'levelling down of all possibilities'. It notes the irony that although existentialists praise authenticity, their literary portraits make authentic characters anxious, alienated, and near-mad while the inauthentic remain tranquil - raising the possibility that ignorance is bliss and the blue pill is wiser - before promising an argument, via The Matrix and Sartre's Nausea, for the red pill.

the-absurd.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
the-absurd.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.

the-absurd.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
the-absurd.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Argues the show's underlying moral vision is Nietzschean passive nihilism filtered through film noir. Tony, unlike the active nihilist who converts value-collapse into self-overcoming, sinks into resentment and life-negation: he wants to rip the throat of the 'happy wanderer', therapy never redeems him, and he quits it with 'I'm a fat fucking crook from New Jersey' in 'Calling All Cars'. The chapter traces the noir lineage (Tony watching White Heat, the Godfather references, Bogart imagery at Satriale's) and reads A.J.'s 'D-Girl' existentialism (Camus's The Stranger, 'There is no God') and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' as the family inheritance of meaninglessness and death-dread.

the-absurd.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
the-absurd.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Wrathall defends the film's violence by contrasting Fra Angelico's serene Descent from the Cross with Corinth's Red Christ and Gibson's Gethsemane rebuke ('You could not watch even one hour with me'), arguing the gore resists rationalizing Christ's suffering into an economy of exchange, as Camus's Father Paneloux in The Plague insists true faith must not. Drawing on Pascal's instrumental reason, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty, he develops a 'world-disclosive' account of faith: the tall-table scene between Mary and the young carpenter Jesus shows that new practices train new perception, and film reaches the body directly in ways written description cannot. He closes by faulting Gibson for pessimism: Christ's world looks as God-forsaken and demon-haunted as Judas's, closer to Dostoevsky's ascetic Father Ferapont than to a world made new.

the-absurd.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
the-absurd.title: The Ends of Despair From “Things Have Changed” to “Love and Theft”
the-absurd.relation: Rick Furtak traces an existential arc through Dylan's later albums, reading Blood on the Tracks ("Tangled Up in Blue," "You're a Big Girl Now") as Camus's absurd divorce between a mind that cares and a world that has gone silent, and Heideggerian care as what the narrator loses in "Simple Twist of Fate." "Brownsville Girl" and "Most of the Time" embody Kierkegaard's knight of infinite resignation - hope abandoned but the precious past never forgotten - while "Not Dark Yet" and "Things Have Changed" mark the nadir of despair. On Love and Theft ("Mississippi," "Sugar Baby") the singer turns toward an absurd, Kierkegaardian faith that keeps caring and even loves without demanding that life make sense.

the-absurd.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle
the-absurd.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Pratt reads the outlaw biker's FTW (Fuck the World) posture as pop-culture nihilism: Nietzsche's 'danger of dangers' and Camus's answer of scorn to an absurd universe ('there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn') are embodied by Brando's Johnny in The Wild One, Sonny Barger's Hells Angels, and the wanton Born to Lose club of The Born Losers, whose smashing matches Pisarev's Russian nihilism. He then shows how Willie G. Davidson's 1977 Low Rider and events like Daytona's Bike Week sanitized and marketed the rebellion, reducing skulls and DILLIGAF patches to ubiquitous fashion worth $340 million a week. Freud supplies the psychology: the superego keeps the rest of us tame, so we voyeuristically buy a tasteful version of outlaw freedom, even though pure nihilism, denying all truth, refutes even itself.

the-absurd.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
the-absurd.title: And Where the @#$%^& is the Queen
the-absurd.relation: The editors' introduction recounts Monty Python's 1969 debut and argues the troupe's absurdism bears a deep connection to philosophy because the British Pythons absorbed the Oxford and Cambridge linguistic analysis of Russell, Wittgenstein, Moore, and Ryle while at university in the 1960s. It tours the volume's three parts, previewing each contributor's pairing: Schilbrack reading Life of Brian through Camus's absurd hero, Brighouse using the Argument Clinic for Rawls's analysis of social practices, Asma finding Buddhist mindfulness in The Meaning of Life, Huss pairing the Pythons with Hume on religion, and Spinelli reading sketches through Foucault on the social construction of madness. It concludes there is no single connection between Python and philosophy but many: sketches illuminate philosophy, philosophy illuminates sketches, and Python's empire says something about philosophy's cultural standing (with Wittgenstein's duck-rabbit figuring how the remaining chapters can be seen).

the-absurd.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
the-absurd.title: “Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism
the-absurd.relation: Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.

the-absurd.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
the-absurd.title: A Nietzschean Conclusion
the-absurd.relation: Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.

the-absurd.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
the-absurd.title: Poker and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.

the-absurd.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
the-absurd.title: A Political Philosophy of Vampires
the-absurd.relation: Phillip Cole takes Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof - the Arnold Paole exhumations - and argues Rousseau's real point was political: authorities manufacture imaginary monsters, as in the witch craze, to exploit fear and hold power over their own populations. Freud's account of the uncanny explains why the horror is not death itself but the returning dead (the watching eyes of Scratchy in Itchy and Scratchy, versus the serene corpses of Six Feet Under, whose absurdity the show meets with wry amusement), and Julia Kristeva's abjection explains the corpse as the ultimate boundary-breaker. The vampire then resurfaces as the demonized outsider - Stoker's Dracula coded as the unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's terrorist - exposing political borders as arbitrary fabrications. Buffy completes the collapse of the us/them binary: Angel and Spike join the slayer, and the most shocking killings (Faith's accidental human kill, Warren's stray bullet hitting Tara) are all too human, so the real subject of border policing is the community's own members.

the-absurd.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
the-absurd.title: James Bond and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Butterfield takes Bond's answer to Elektra in The World Is Not Enough - he survives by 'tak[ing] pleasure in great beauty' - and asks whether hedonism can answer the problem of suffering and death. She reads Bond through Heidegger's being-towards-death (quoting Live and Let Die's 'You start to die the moment you are born'), then diagnoses him as Kierkegaard's aesthetic 'seducer', an immature escapist who dreads boredom and flees commitment, before rehabilitating him with Nietzsche and Camus: Bond flushing the cyanide pill down the toilet in From Russia with Love and Mathis's advice in Casino Royale to make evil 'personal' show Bond creating his own values beyond good and evil, surviving the absurd through style and personal vendetta. Bond emerges as an existentialist role model for courage and creativity, though we should not copy his hedonism or lawlessness.

the-absurd.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
the-absurd.title: Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone
the-absurd.relation: Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.

the-absurd.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
the-absurd.title: Celebrating Transience
the-absurd.relation: Kaag reads 'Atlantic City' (Nebraska) as a parable of fatalism: after the Chicken Man bombing in Philadelphia and stuck with 'debts no honest man can pay,' the narrator takes the Coast City bus and finally agrees to 'do a little favor' for a criminal. Following the American philosopher John J. McDermott's philosophy of transience, the refrain 'Everything dies, baby, that's a fact / but maybe someday everything comes back' holds Heidegger's ownmost death together with tentative pragmatic hope. Suburban 'winners' who leave before dark are dead to experience, while the transient, like Camus's indifferent Stranger in 'Nebraska' ('I guess there's just a meanness in this world'), must celebrate meaning in the fleeting qualitative moments of the journey itself.

the-absurd.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
the-absurd.title: Driftin’ Off to a Foreign Land
the-absurd.relation: Dick explains how 'Straight Time' makes us see Charlie's cycle of drudgery through Sartre's The Imaginary: the title is a Sartrean sign that welds prison time, rendering-factory time and straight-and-narrow time into one image of endless oppression, and Bruce's first-person characterization works like Dana Carvey impersonating Jimmy Stewart — consciousness overlooks discrepancies until we recognize 'our' Charlie. Against the escape fantasy of 'Thunder Road,' Camus's Sisyphus frames Charlie as swapping rocks (prison, factory, his uncle's car-theft heist) while the hill remains and 'there is no top of the hill.' Springsteen's answer to the absurd is to climb alongside his characters in empathetic brotherly love.

the-absurd.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
the-absurd.title: How to Misunderstand Politics Completely
the-absurd.relation: Melançon argues Radiohead's real politics lie not in the overt content of Hail to the Thief but in a Camusian movement from absurdity to revolt: 'Exit Music'''s violent shift from Romeo's tender 'you' to the distorted 'we hope that you choke' enacts revolt against imposed rules and wisdom, while the android of 'Fitter Happier' ('a pig in a cage on antibiotics') and the wished-for alien of 'Subterranean Homesick Alien' dramatize absurd life under others' dictates. Following The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel — 'I revolt, therefore we are' — he shows how the songs' 'I' becomes a collective 'we' ('Karma Police', 'Lucky', 'Dollars and Cents') whose revolt, like Sisyphus's conscious walk back down the mountain, affirms life without ever justifying murder. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of expression then explains why the songs are political anyway: artists express a still-unspoken 'fever' (it took years before 'Nude' could be said), creating a public and a common world — politics as unveiling rather than governing, down to 'Electioneering'''s admission that the band too campaigns for our vote.

the-absurd.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
the-absurd.title: A Large Rock Saved My Life
the-absurd.relation: Lindsey Fiorelli reads OK Computer as Camus's absurd universe: "Subterranean Homesick Alien" and "Fitter Happier" portray a technological world drained of meaning, where to belong you must become a robotic "pig in a cage on antibiotics" and "Let Down" offers only the "emptiest of feelings." She stresses that Camus demands revolt, not escape — Sisyphus and Meursault embrace the absurd and thereby become happy — whereas Yorke's lyrics keep longing to flee (spaceships, growing wings, the resigned "No Surprises"). Yet the music itself embraces the technology the lyrics curse, and this, she concludes, is Radiohead's real Camusian move: like Camus writing novels about an alienating world, they carve Sisyphus's rock — modern technology, synthesizers and computers — into new and marvelous sounds, overcoming alienation by working within it.

the-absurd.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
the-absurd.title: How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning
the-absurd.relation: Adam Glover reads 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' through Kristeva's intertextuality: since every text and self is a 'mosaic of quotations' pirated from pre-existing sources, Buffett's confession that he was born 'two hundred years too late' makes him an ironic pirate who can no longer believe or plunder unselfconsciously, unlike the oblivious common-sense pirate. Invoking Barthes's death of the author, he argues the pirate's life is a hard freedom to improvise multiple meanings (the ever-changing 'head uptown' variations in the song) with full responsibility for one's choices. The chapter ends weighing Camus's worry that meaninglessness makes life not worth living against the Nietzsche of The Birth of Tragedy, who answers that the meaning of life is life itself, and it sides with Buffett against Socrates's 'unexamined life' while admitting it cannot settle the question.

the-absurd.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
the-absurd.relation: Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.

the-absurd.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
the-absurd.title: Mr. Monk Meets Alexander the Great
the-absurd.relation: Wittkower argues that Monk's daily, unwinnable war on dirt and disorder is Camus's happy Sisyphus made concrete: Monk vacuums ceilings, touches lampposts, and solves murders knowing the dirt and the murderers will always return ('There's never hope...
