Hope. I hate hope's guts' in 'Mr. Monk Can't See a Thing'), yet he still finds enough satisfaction to take up the wipe again. Reading Ecclesiastes' vanity alongside the uncaring wasp of the opening, the chapter claims Monk shows us how to live wisely without resignation in an absurd world that does not care. He is paired with Diogenes the Cynic, whose barrel, raw onions, and midday lantern mirror Monk's pot-pie-Tuesdays and his refusal to overlook what everyone else ignores; like Diogenes telling Alexander the Great 'get out of my sun,' Monk lives by his own ideals no matter how society judges him. The essay closes that, like Camus addressing the Dominican monks, we should refuse to 'be reasonable' about evil and disorder and keep struggling without hope, wipe in hand.

the-absurd.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
the-absurd.title: The Lesson
the-absurd.relation: Karolina Lewestam and Orla Richardson argue that the Red Sox fan is a moral hero in Kierkegaard's sense: like Abraham in Fear and Trembling, the fan fully accepts that loss is inevitable (the Curse, Aaron Boone, Buckner's grounder) yet refuses the rational course of infinite resignation and keeps believing 'this could be the year.' Where liberal individualism licenses walking away from any loyalty and the modern reflex is to sue luck out of existence, the fan lives at the mercy of fate and thereby enacts Kierkegaard's movement beyond resignation into true faith, the absurd belief against all evidence that Isaac will be spared. Fenway thus becomes the best university for learning to live fully under uncertainty, with Ortiz's 'keep the faith' speech and Schilling's bloody sock as its lessons in perseverance and courage.

the-absurd.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
the-absurd.title: A Political Philosophy of Vampires
the-absurd.relation: Phillip Cole starts from Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof, and argues the panics — like the witch craze Trevor-Roper ties to the Reformation's power struggles — reveal how political authorities constitute borders and power by cultivating fear of imaginary enemies. Freud's uncanny (fear not of death but of the returning dead) and Kristeva's abject (the corpse as the ultimate waste) explain why the Undead horrify and fascinate — Scratchy's ever-watching eyes in Itchy and Scratchy, the drowning corpse in Thérèse Raquin, Six Feet Under's serener dead and its wryly absurdist tone — while the vampire also plays the romantic monster of Coppola's Dracula and Interview with the Vampire. Politically the vampire is the demonized outsider — Stoker's unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's asylum seeker or terrorist — and Buffy blurs the boundary by making demons neighbors and Angel and Spike heroes, while the truly shocking killings (Faith's accidental shooting of a human ally, Warren's gunning down of Tara) are human, all too human. The chapter concludes that we should stop mistaking fear-made borders for moral ones and the constructed outsider for a mortal enemy.

the-absurd.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
the-absurd.title: Living the Absurd Life
the-absurd.relation: Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.

the-absurd.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
the-absurd.title: The Guy Is Not Alone. .
the-absurd.relation: Matt Laubenthal confesses he was the philosophy-class windbag and defends Darrin Floen of 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' as heir to Socrates' gadfly role, noting the Athenians also wanted their relentless questioner dead. He teaches Russell's Paradox through a Burger King 's.h.i.t. load' — the set of all sets that are not members of themselves — and reconstructs Darrin's Heraclitean rejoinder that if everything flows and nothing stands still, the static either/or of set membership dissolves the contradiction. Along the way he reads the Onion's Kafka International Airport story ('Are you who you say you are?' repeated for eighty minutes) as existentialist absurdity, and the Star Trek Voyager holographic Doctor as a puzzle about whether a self could be nothing more than mathematical code.

the-absurd.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
the-absurd.title: Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love
the-absurd.relation: Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.

the-absurd.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
the-absurd.title: The Stoic Warrior
the-absurd.relation: Jeff Sharpless imagines a Spartan mourning Kurt-051 and asking what his abduction, augmentation, and endless war mean, concluding his life is absurd in Camus's sense: bred as an instrument by the very humanity he is celebrated for saving. Camus's Sisyphus supplies one answer—meaning in the defiant moment of turning back down the hill, which recasts Master Chief's 'I need a weapon' as either hollow absurdity or quiet revolt. Epictetus supplies the alternative: distinguish what is up to us from what is not, withhold assent from impressions like 'we are all going to die,' and the Chief's silence becomes Stoic tranquility—though the chapter concedes Stoicism risks minimizing the injustice done to the Spartan children.

the-absurd.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
the-absurd.title: The Lung-less, All-Penetrating Masterful World-Silence
the-absurd.relation: The section reads Do Androids Dream through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': mood organs, empathy boxes, Buster Friendly and catalog-bought animals alienate humans from the world, each other and themselves until only the 'silence of the world' remains, which Isidore theorizes as the inevitable kipple-ization of the universe. Byron's 'Darkness' and Nietzsche's parable of the clever beasts frame Deckard's drive into the dead desert after his last retirement, where he confronts a universe of dead stones that perceive and remember nothing.

the-absurd.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
the-absurd.title: Chapter 23 - Lonely Wolves
the-absurd.relation: Travis Paterson's introduction reads A Scanner Darkly as Dick's most autobiographical novel and explains Arctor's disgust at the over-happy Brown Bear Lodge audience through Sartre's Nausea: Roquentin's discovery that existence is sheer contingency, that we are superfluous, vaguely alarmed beings who cannot define existence as necessity. Arctor never finds Roquentin's slender chance of acceptance, so the nausea curdles into addiction and the wolf parable, the magnificent lone wolf shot to protect the meager, over-fed animals, poses the chapter's question of why the sensitive outsider is the one sacrificed.

the-absurd.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
the-absurd.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Argues Heisenberg is not an alter ego but Walt finally escaping the Prufrock-like bad faith of his pre-cancer life: the pork-pie-hat persona acknowledges the absurd, owns his freedom and responsibility, and so achieves the authenticity Camus and Sartre demand. Walt becomes Camus's Sisyphus - rebelling against death, social norms, and Skyler, owning his rock with silent joy - citing the fulminated-mercury showdown with Tuco in 'Crazy Handful of Nothin'', running down Gus's dealers in 'Half Measures', and confessing to Skyler in 'No Mas'. The chapter closes that, like Sisyphus, we must imagine Walt happy.

the-absurd.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
the-absurd.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Rachel Robison-Greene reads the survivors through Camus: walkers are mere digger wasps, living tedious, meaningless loops without the consciousness that would make it agonizing, but the living - Morgan longing for the real Jenny back, Andrea losing Amy - face the absurd confrontation between human longing and an indifferent universe, just like Oran in Camus's The Plague. Of Camus's options, suicide (Jacqui and Dr. Jenner staying in the exploding CDC) and religion ('GOD FORGIVE US' on the farmhouse wall) are escapist, so she offers the absurd hero: Sisyphus with his rock, Rieux with his plague, matched by Rick hunting Atlanta for his family, Merle's self-preservation, and Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side. Against Nagel's ironic alternative, she argues we cheer Rick when he alone will shoot Sophia in Hershel's barn because his subjective commitments stay noble even with no objective meaning behind them.

the-absurd.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
the-absurd.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Round argues the real horror of The Walking Dead is humanity itself, read through existentialism: walkers cannot choose, so the humans who attack, torture, and steal from each other are the true 'zombie Other.' She traces Rick's self-made, revisable moral code — from law-enforcer to 'You kill? You die' to killing Dexter — as authentic situation-based morality, paralleled with Kierkegaard's Abraham and with Abraham Ford's confession 'I did what I wanted to do' set against Eugene's bad-faith 'I did what I had to do.' Suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol embody existential angst before an absurd world, the Governor's Woodbury is an Adorno-style inauthentic hierarchy that manipulates its people, and Rick's 'WE ARE THE WALKING DEAD!' speech uses facticity to insist the group admit what they have already become.

the-absurd.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
the-absurd.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Moosa uses the apocalypse as a moral laboratory: since 'murder' is by definition wrongful killing, Carl's shooting of Shane must be judged by his reasoning (saving his father), and Hobbes's state of nature — 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — fits Kirkman's world, yet the survivors import morality into it, as when parents mercy-kill their children just as one would turn up a dying child's morphine. Taking up Camus's claim that suicide is the one truly serious philosophical problem, he argues our world is nearly as bad as the zombie landscape, so consistency commits comfortable readers to the same duty of aid (helping sufferers rather than opting out) that justifies the survivors' fighting on. Finally he argues procreation is the worst thing survivors can do — nonexistent children cannot suffer, so Lori's pregnancy and Glenn and Maggie's crib plans are immoral, and adopting existing children as Andrea and Dale did is the consistent course, an obligation that transfers to our world right now.

the-absurd.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
the-absurd.title: The Wire and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Crosby takes Bunk's 'misdemeanor homicide' exchange about Marlo as the show's thesis that post-industrial capitalism makes human lives worth less, season by season devaluing beat cops, longshoremen, would-be reformers, the schoolkids of Season Four, and finally the journalists meant to sound the alarm. She deploys Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how institutions train docile participants and then require their regular sacrifice to keep operating, so that Simon's 'indifferent gods' of Greek tragedy are now postmodern institutions whose lightning bolts hit everyone in the 'hood. She ends with Camus's Sisyphus: Simon's call to commit to a righteous cause you probably will not win is the only response that offers human dignity, because 'this ain't Aruba... this America, man.'

the-absurd.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
the-absurd.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'

the-absurd.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
the-absurd.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.

the-absurd.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
the-absurd.title: Girls and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Archibald reads Jessa as Girls' quintessential existentialist: her unbothered abortion ('I'm offended by all the supposed to's'), her 'I am a junkie' honesty, and her refusal to blame her rough past (Sartrean facticity) enact existence precedes essence and Camus's embrace of the absurd. Kierkegaard's 'the crowd is untruth' and 'leveling' explain her contempt for rehab group conformity, while her panic marriage to Thomas-John after Katherine's motherly intervention is diagnosed as bad faith and angst. Her assisting the dying Beadie's suicide attempt - and calling 911 when Beadie recants - becomes the chapter's closing confrontation with Camus's one serious philosophical question, answered by living 'without appeal.'

the-absurd.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
the-absurd.title: Dracula and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: In imaginary letters, Meursault of Camus's The Stranger describes his meaning-free life, his trial that condemned his refusal to perform feelings, and his death-row move from indifference to acceptance of the absurd, then inducts Dracula into Camus's gallery of absurd heroes beside Don Juan, Don Quixote, and Sisyphus - those who reject suicide, reject help from higher powers, and accept life's absurdity. Dracula accepts the first two traits but categorically rejects despairing acceptance, claiming love and conquest instead. An appendix lets Sisyphus himself grumble that Camus finding happiness in boulder-pushing is the real absurdity.

the-absurd.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
the-absurd.title: 2. Maybe Jenner Was Right
the-absurd.relation: Cowan uses Jenner's suicide in the exploding CDC (1.6 'TS-19') to pose Camus's question 'Why should I not commit suicide?', and rejects Jenner's despair the Camusian way: Michonne in 4.9 'After' - slaying her own walker look-alike and then her two pet walkers - is his Sisyphus in revolt, unlike Gareth, whose revolt lacks the respect for human dignity that makes Sisyphus happy. He then objects that Camus never explains why human life has intrinsic dignity in a godless universe, noting that Sartrean authenticity could equally license the Governor's Woodbury experiments or Gareth's cannibalism, and turns to Hershel's providential hope as the religious alternative. Following Plantinga, he argues belief in God can be properly basic through a sensus divinitatis - Hershel seeing God's hand in 2.4 'Cherokee Rose' and the tornado-spared barn of 5.10 'Them' - so if God exists, Jenner was not right.

the-absurd.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
the-absurd.title: 6. The Absurdity of the Luggage
the-absurd.relation: Kempner reads the Luggage - the sapient, homicidal pearwood chest that pursues Rincewind from The Color of Magic through The Light Fantastic and Interesting Times - as the embodiment of Camus's absurd: the 'divorce' between our demand that the world make sense and a world that does not care. Rincewind, who dreams of a rational, scientifically ordered universe while the Disc sails on a turtle and the gods smash atheists' windows, is cast as Sisyphus, and the trolls who 'suffer from philosophy' and freeze solid show where the futile quest for order ends. When Rincewind finally says 'Come on' to the huddled Luggage and readers come to love what once terrified them, the chapter performs Camus's acceptance of the absurd as freedom.

the-absurd.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
the-absurd.title: 8. Laughing in the Face of the Absurd
the-absurd.relation: Argues that watching Beth die on the platform is Sarah's existential awakening — the absurd realization that "it is no longer true that everyone has their own face" — analyzed through Camus's absurd (the impossible and the contradictory), Sartre's nausea at inhuman humans, and Beauvoir's "subman" who never wakes from the mechanical life. Sarah must repeatedly witness "her own" death (Beth, Katja, Jennifer, the Helsinki clones), which robs death and life of settled meaning, yet she refuses nihilism: exercising the radical freedom Sartre says grounds all values, she fights Dyad on behalf of everyone's freedom, implicitly choosing it for all humanity. Like Camus's Sisyphus, whose rock is his thing, her struggle is her thing — and the Season Two clone dance party is her laughing in the face of the absurd.

the-absurd.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
the-absurd.title: 10. David Bowie and Death
the-absurd.relation: Potter and Cobb sort Bowie's death lyrics into seven interpretations - evil to be feared ('Space Oddity'/'Ashes to Ashes'), source of social unity ('Five Years,' 'Rock'n'Roll Suicide'), absurd defiance ('Heroes,' 'The Next Day'), revelation ('Quicksand,' 'We Are the Dead'), inevitable acceptance ('The Hearts Filthy Lesson'), transition between forms ('Lazarus'), and signifier of human singularity ('Blackstar' as the incommunicable uniqueness every death extinguishes) - all animated by Bertrand Russell's moral psychology of impulses, desires, and the 'principle of growth.' Ambivalence, they argue, is Bowie's honest response: no interpretation is privileged, and 'Blackstar' fuses celebrity's illusory immortality with the impulse to individuality, culminating in the artfully managed death itself.

the-absurd.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
the-absurd.title: 8. Living for More
the-absurd.relation: Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.

the-absurd.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
the-absurd.title: 1. Charlie’s Eternal Quest for the Little Red-Haired Girl
the-absurd.relation: The chapter reads Charlie Brown's lifelong, unconsummated longing for the never-seen Little Red-Haired Girl as a quest narrative without closure: like Beckett's Vladimir and Estragon he cannot act, and like Camus's Sisyphus he is an absurd hero whose dignity lies in persisting (the 2,120 lunch hours, the losing team, the pulled football) without reward. Using Lacan's account of desire - the wish for the Other's recognition, suspended between the demand for need and the demand for love - it argues Schulz keeps her invisible (except one 1998 silhouette) precisely so Charlie's desire stays in permanent suspension, like a Hitchcock MacGuffin. The closing section attacks The Peanuts Movie (2015) for betraying this existential vision: by showing the girl, rewarding Charlie with a kiss, and swapping Sisyphean defiance for 'believe in yourself' truisms, it delivers Sisyphus from his rock and so kills what made him admirable.

the-absurd.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
the-absurd.title: 2. 3eanuts and the Existential Schulz
the-absurd.relation: The chapter introduces existentialism and reads Peanuts through it: Charlie Brown's defeats expose the 'groundlessness' of value, and the 3eanuts web project (deleting each strip's final gag panel) restores the despair that punchlines normally defuse. It explains Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' and the ideal of authenticity versus passively inhabiting roles, Heidegger's care and Dasein (even in despair there is an inner place where it happens), and Camus's absurd and Sisyphus revolting against a fate he cannot change. Lucy's hillside sermon ('WELL, LIVE IN IT, THEN!') and the final image of Charlie running at the football figure his revolt: he keeps kicking because in that moment a world without boxes exists in him.

the-absurd.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
the-absurd.title: 18. No End to Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Four vignettes pin philosophical problems to Peanuts' marginal characters: Camus's absurd - caring beings condemned to an uncaring universe - is answered by Sally's School Building, which grows a heart and drops bricks on her enemies; the 95472 kids motivate a tour of personal identity (same soul, same body, memory) through the Ship of Theseus; Pigpen's dirt raises Sartre's bad faith (facticity, transcendence, being-for-others) - we prize his authenticity over cleanliness - and Aristotle's golden mean, which moderates cleanliness while crediting his curiosity as a virtue; and finally the ontology of fictional characters asks whether the Kite-Eating Tree and Red Baron really exist inside the fiction and whether The Peanuts Movie's changed Charlie Brown counts as canon.

the-absurd.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
the-absurd.title: 10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse
the-absurd.relation: Heidi Samuelson argues Deadpool is Camus's absurd hero improved: his origin and his survival of impossible dismemberments embody the absurd as 'disproportion between intention and reality', and facing Camus's one real philosophical problem—suicide—he tries to die via the Hulk to join mistress Death yet must live on, rejecting both actual and 'philosophical' suicide (dogma). His mercenary sense of purpose, jokes in the face of oblivion, and compassion for Blind Al, Weasel, deaf Hawkeye, and Evan exemplify Camus's revolt, freedom, and passion. Sisyphus is the model: like him, Deadpool owns his rock—the healing factor and the killing—and is happy, laughing where Sisyphus is silent.

the-absurd.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
the-absurd.title: 14. The Absurdity at the Heart of Horror
the-absurd.relation: Uses Camus's Myth of Sisyphus to argue that AHS's deepest horror is absurdity - the human quest for meaning in a meaningless universe: the Harmons' doomed attempts to protect each other in the Murder House mirror Sisyphus's futile push, Dr. Arden's experiments on aliens who mock him ('Arden you quack who would make a better duck?') show comprehension of the universe is beyond reach, the Countess's bored immortality and Ma Petite's casual murder stage the confrontation between human longing and a universe that cannot care, and the answer to 'why do bad things happen to good people?' is simply: 'because they do. There is no reason.'

the-absurd.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
the-absurd.title: 9. A Human Fighting the Gods
the-absurd.relation: Luzecky and Elsby argue gods cannot be heroes: Thor's strength, Hulk's rage and Tony's godlike intellect stand outside humanity, whereas Erskine's serum amplified Cap's nascent human goodness (as it exposed the Red Skull's badness), making him the best human rather than a superhuman. Reading Cap through Camus's absurd - the paradox of beings who strive for universality while stuck in particularity - they show him refusing both nihilistic reduction (Alexander Pierce's helicarriers in Winter Soldier) and Nietzsche's flight to 'other worlds' that hates this one. When Loki commands the crowd to kneel, the refusal Cap embodies is Sisyphus's defiant persistence, which is why he, and not the gods, is the Avengers' greatest hero.

the-absurd.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
the-absurd.title: 11. Dilbert’s Absurd World
the-absurd.relation: Christian contrasts Camus's absurdity, the futile collision between our demand for meaning and a silent world whose only exits are suicide, a leap of faith, or Sisyphean revolt (an active defiance he takes partly from Nietzsche's rejection of resignation), with Adams's office absurdities. In Dilbert the absurd is contained and epistemic rather than pervasive and metaphysical: the battery-dead LED request, Dadaist mission statements, Catbert's evil HR policies, Wally's self-congratulatory Wally Reports, and Alice's harpoon all trace to people being idiots about different things, and could be fixed by honest credit and realizable plans. Dilbert's Business Dorky acceptance therefore looks Camusian but is not: it is recognition minus revolt, bewildered amusement where revolt and reform remain genuinely available.

the-absurd.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
the-absurd.title: 13. Reason and Catharsis
the-absurd.relation: Argues that Twin Peaks frees viewers from the "tyranny of rationality" by refusing to make sense: Plato's sensible-versus-intelligible finger example explains our habit of abstracting concepts to resolve contradiction (the pale horse in the living room, Diane's texts, Dougie-as-tulpa), but Lynch keeps adding facts — the frog-moth crawling into the girl in Part 8 — that no framework absorbs. Drawing on Nietzsche's Twilight of the Idols claim that Socrates made rationality a treatment for weakness, and on the existentialist pairing of despair and freedom in a meaningless universe, the chapter says viewers can either demand the irrational fit their rationality like inauthentic existentialists or let go. Trela's alternative reading of Aristotle's catharsis — emotions purged of their connection to reality and felt for once in themselves — explains why we can savor the show's absurdity without despair, precisely because that world is not ours.

the-absurd.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!
the-absurd.title: 8. Sexistentialism
the-absurd.relation: Reads Schumer through Camus's absurd: Trainwreck's gender-reversed commitment-phobe and the sketch where friends kill themselves rather than accept a compliment expose the futility of finding meaning in patriarchal gender scripts. Browning argues that advocating change against so systemic a sexism is a Sisyphean task, and that the film's romantic-comedy ending is 'existential' because Amy freely chooses commitment and owns the absurdity rather than escaping it. The chapter ends by asking whether Schumer's jokes are a battle cry whose very pointlessness might be the point.

the-absurd.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
the-absurd.title: 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning
the-absurd.relation: Montoya reads Chidi's breakdown upon learning he has been tortured for three hundred years as Nietzsche's death of God, quoting the Parable of the Madman from 'Jeremy Bearimy' to show how the guaranteed meaning of Chidi's worldview collapses into nihilism. Michael's midlife-crisis makeover and partying embody Camus's embrace of the absurd, while Sartre's existence precedes essence, abandonment, and anguish explain why Eleanor's confession to Michael and her sacrifice in the Judge's test count as authentic choices. With the Judge's verdict stripping away any hope of reward, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake, which the chapter presents as the show's answer to nihilism.

the-absurd.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
the-absurd.title: 18. Iron Man’s Choice to Die
the-absurd.relation: Argues Tony's death in Endgame is best explained three ways: via Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives (Tony oscillates between the cabin family-life drive and the risk-seeking death drive that takes him aboard the donut ship in Infinity War and has him lay down to die with Nebula), via Camus's absurd (like Sisyphus, Tony creates subjective meaning by choosing — Pepper, Morgan, and finally the snap itself, 'Part of the journey is the end'), and via consequentialism (the snap as a desirable consequence, contrasting Infinity War's deontological 'We don't trade lives' with Endgame's 'whatever it takes'). It contends that because the time heist rewrites history, deaths in both films — Vision's, Natasha's, Tony's — risk becoming meaningless, so Tony dies on his terms to make his death meaningful.

the-absurd.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
the-absurd.title: 3. Paul’s Lick It Up Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Courtland Lewis reads Paul Stanley's autobiographies (Face the Music, Backstage Pass) and songs as a worked-out life philosophy. Stanley's turn from chasing approval to confronting his inner pain exemplifies Socrates' unexamined-life dictum; 'Reason to Live' is glossed through Camus's Sisyphus — ground your reason to live in something indestructible, your own self-chosen meaning — while Plato's Ion explains Stanley's mix of learned craft and divine-inspired performance. Aristotle's flourishing through moderation appears in the advice not to overplay 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' and Lewis adds Locke and Rousseau on how laws, boundaries, and education create rather than restrict freedom, closing with Stanley's 'questioning ourselves is not a weakness' as Socratic wisdom.

the-absurd.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
the-absurd.title: Introduction
the-absurd.relation: Book introduction: recounts how the 1979 cast were the first casualties of the Chestburster scene (real butcher-shop organs, Veronica Cartwright fainting), then previews the volume's payload - personhood questions about Ash, Bishop, David and the Ripley clone; Marx on why Weyland-Yutani sacrifices crews for profit; Plato's Republic on children in warfare via Newt; Lovecraftian cosmic horror; feminist readings of Ripley as care ethicist and mother; and continental takes - Xenomorphs as Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Camus on Ripley-8's refusal to commit suicide, and Sartre on a Xenomorph's right to resist us.

the-absurd.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
the-absurd.title: One Must Imagine Ripley Happy
the-absurd.relation: Reads Ripley-8 through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: discovering the room of failed clones confronts her with the absurd gap between her longing to be Ellen Ripley and the world's answer that she is lab-grown Number 8. Of Camus's three responses she refuses physical suicide (declining Call's knife - 'What makes you think I would let you do that?') and philosophical suicide (mocking the auton's programmed crossing herself in the chapel), instead living in revolt - 'I rebel--therefore we exist' - shared with Call, so that her serial extermination of Xenomorphs across four films becomes Sisyphean toil, and one must imagine Ripley happy.

the-absurd.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
the-absurd.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Baird contrasts Camus's absurdity — the divorce between man and world demanding 'lucid indifference' and an absurd art that refuses counterfeit meaning — with Sartre's, where the world's meanings are contingent human projections and freedom entails absolute responsibility (Being and Nothingness sits by the Dude's bed). He argues the film is Sartrean rather than Camusian: the Dude weaves random events (the peed-on rug, the ransom) into the interpretation 'Bunny kidnapped herself', holding it provisionally as one story among possible ones, while Walter never takes responsibility for his Corvette-swinging choices. The viewers, knowing all interpretations are groundless, watch the absurd from the front row.

the-absurd.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
the-absurd.title: Two Philosophies, Two Compasses to Navigate Life
the-absurd.relation: Against 'Hang the DJ,' where Frank and Amy's coaching system assigns partners and expiration dates inside a simulated dating park, the chapter argues a Stoic would refuse to sign up: delegating judgments to the coach violates Epictetus's dichotomy of control, and the endless date-cycle fails all four virtues, treating dates (like Amy's bored lovemaking) as means rather than inherently worthy persons. An existentialist reading via Sartre says nearly every system-arranged relationship is bad faith - couples act as if compatible against the expiry they were given, as Frank and Nicola do - and only Frank and Amy's open-ended, freely chosen relationship escapes it, so their 'fuck off' to the system is a leap of faith that 998 of 1000 simulated couples make, which is how the app computes its 99.8% match. The authors close with Camus's absurd, doubting that the real Frank and Amy, who cannot rebel against an app that tells them they belong together, will fare as well as their simulations.

the-absurd.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
the-absurd.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
the-absurd.relation: William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.

the-absurd.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
the-absurd.title: 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning
the-absurd.relation: Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.

the-absurd.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
the-absurd.title: 6 The Absurd Hero Indiana Jones, God, and Sisyphus
the-absurd.relation: Justin Fetterman takes the Big Bang Theory objection seriously — Indy is superfluous in Raiders and loses nearly every artifact he chases — diagnosing him first with Kierkegaard's despair of possibility from The Sickness Unto Death, where each failure only convinces him success lies just ahead. But Indy refuses Kierkegaard's leap of faith even after witnessing Shiva's Sankara Stones and the Ark, since multiple gods' demonstrations cancel any single revelation, and Kierkegaard demands faith without comprehension. The chapter then re-reads him through Camus: like Sisyphus he repeats near-identical quests (Raiders and Crusade both have him lead the Nazis to a Judeo-Christian relic that destroys them), and his value lies in 'the most living' and the struggle itself, making him an absurd hero rather than a failed believer.

the-absurd.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
the-absurd.title: Notes
the-absurd.relation: Kohoutek tests Max against two models of heroism: Joseph Campbell's 'hero with a thousand faces' and Camus's absurd hero from The Myth of Sisyphus. Max never completes the Campbellian cycle — no apotheosis, no decisive victory, no return and reintegration — because the refinery tribe and the Waiting Ones mythologize him from outside (as Messiah, as Captain Walker) while he himself returns each film to the same desert. Like Sisyphus, for whom 'the whole being is exerted toward accomplishing nothing,' Max helps people build pockets of civilization he is always shut out of, making his heroism absurd rather than archetypal.

the-absurd.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
the-absurd.title: NOTES
the-absurd.relation: Barris argues Lost fascinates because it dramatizes the basic structures of life itself: the castaways are Heideggerian thrown into an island none of them chose, brought there by Desmond's lapse at the Swan and by interlocking backstories such as Sawyer's bar conversation with Jack's father. Against the existentialist claim (Sartre, Camus) that life is simply absurd, he uses Wittgenstein's On Certainty - doubting everything presupposes certainties - to argue life is a riddle of partial sense, which is why the show's connections between Hurley and Libby or Jack and Desmond always hint at meaning without resolving it. The finale answers only the question of life after death, leaving life after birth as open as our own.

the-absurd.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
the-absurd.title: Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle
the-absurd.relation: Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.

the-absurd.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
the-absurd.title: The Metal Militia and the Existentialist Club
the-absurd.relation: Jeremy Wisnewski claims Metallica is an existentialist band: Kill 'Em All answers Camus' absurd by creating meaning through chosen, expressive projects ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath'), Ride the Lightning's catalogue of deaths ('Fight Fire with Fire' to 'Fade to Black') individualizes us in the Heideggerian confrontation with our own death, and Master of Puppets dramatizes Sartrean bad faith - the 'Sanitarium' label, the soldier as 'Disposable Hero', the addict's lost freedom. He concludes that accusing Metallica of selling out with the Black Album is itself bad faith, since authenticity has no fixed content.

the-absurd.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
the-absurd.title: Fade to Black: Absurdity, Suicide, and the Downward Spiral
the-absurd.relation: Justin Donhauser and Kimberly Blessing read 'Fade to Black' as a meditation on suicide. Against the Schopenhauerian pessimism that life is a downward spiral 'to the musty stench of corpses' - where suicide paradoxically affirms the Will-to-life - they set Camus' absurd: the narrator who loses the will to live surrenders, while Camus' absurd hero lives in revolt, freedom, and passion. Since Schopenhauer and Camus both reject suicide as escape, and Hetfield insists 'writing is therapy', the song's effect is Aristotelian catharsis - purging despair - rather than an endorsement of suicide.

the-absurd.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
the-absurd.title: Responsibility
the-absurd.relation: Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.

the-absurd.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
the-absurd.title: Getting the Joke
the-absurd.relation: Gray reads Jack Handey's Deep Thoughts and Fuzzy Memories as packaged existentialism: Sartre's existence precedes essence grounds Handey's responsibility for self-made meaning ('if you're robbing a bank and your pants fall down... life is funny'), Camus's absurd and Sisyphus's happy perseverance match 'sometimes I think the world has gone completely mad. And then I think, Aw, who cares?', and Beauvoir's ruts of inferiority warn against the ease of 'just sitting there' wanting money. Heidegger's authenticity and mortality appear in the parachute-swimming gag, dying laughing rather than in dread. The chapter also explains why the deadpan delivery over serene stream imagery makes morbidity funny, and worries that Handey's 'truth is... unreal' anticipated post-truth politics.

the-absurd.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
the-absurd.title: Notes
the-absurd.relation: Blessing diagnoses Ted's 'rom-communism' as the naive optimism Voltaire satirized in Candide: Pangloss's 'best of all possible worlds' is Leibniz's greater-goods theodicy and Principle of Sufficient Reason, and its fatalism ('it will all work out exactly as it's supposed to') collapses under Ted's panic attacks and 'belief can't score goals.' Against it she sets Camus's The Plague: Dr. Rieux's absurd heroism, refusal of hope as 'philosophical suicide,' and 'strange hope' grounded in collective decency, arguing Ted's real, sustainable creed is Camus-like faith in teamwork and human goodness rather than belief that everything works out.

the-absurd.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
the-absurd.title: NOTES
the-absurd.relation: Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.

the-absurd.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
the-absurd.title: Introduction
the-absurd.relation: George Dunn's introduction pitches Veronica herself as a philosopher of the noir: her Neptune is a world where 'the innocent suffer, the guilty go free,' nothing is what it seems (a shy geek turns out to be a psychopathic rapist, a beloved baseball-owning politician a child molester), and her rendering of Pope's Essay on Man as 'Life's a bitch until you die' is answered by her practical code 'get tough and get even.' It argues that the show's marriage of truth-seeking detective work to pervasive deception makes it natural ground for philosophical investigation of Neptune's racial and class divisions, the morality of law breaking, the nature of evil, injustices suffered by women at Neptune High and Hearst College, friendship, and good reasoning, all timed to the Kickstarter-funded movie revival that inspired the volume.

the-absurd.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
the-absurd.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Rachel Robison-Greene applies Camus's absurdity to the series: walkers, like digger wasps, live meaningless loops without the self-reflective consciousness that 'poisons' experience, while survivors like Morgan longing for Jenny and Andrea for fishing trips with her father embody the clash between human longing and an indifferent universe, exactly as in Camus's The Plague at Oran. Suicide (Jacqui and Jenner as the CDC explodes) and religious consolation are escapist responses—the latter 'philosophical suicide'—so the authentic path is the absurd hero: Rick searching Atlanta for his family, Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side, the Vatos group caring for abandoned elders. Weighing Nagel's objection that absurdity arises from our clashing subjective and objective perspectives, she concludes we cheer Rick shooting Sophia in the barn because subjective commitment stays noble even where objective meaning is nowhere to be found.

the-absurd.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
the-absurd.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
the-absurd.relation: Round argues modern zombie fiction's real horror is humanity, reading The Walking Dead existentially: Rick builds meaning through self-imposed missions, revises his morals ('You kill, you die' then killing Dexter anyway), and demands in his 'We ARE the walking dead' speech (Issue #24) that the group admit their new nature instead of hiding in bad faith behind old rules. Kierkegaard's Abraham illuminates Rick's suspension of universal ethics, while Sergeant Abraham Ford's confession 'No. I did what I wanted to do' models owning one's choices, and his angst after Eugene's lie shows the cost of projected meaning collapsing. Camus supplies persistence against the absurd (suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol exert the only control left), and Adorno's Marxist critique frames the Governor's Woodbury as an inauthentic hierarchy that denies its people authentic choice.

the-absurd.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
the-absurd.title: Notes
the-absurd.relation: Pike stages Rand al'Thor's final confrontation with the Dark One in A Memory of Light as a live version of anti-natalism, examining David Benatar's misanthropic, philanthropic, and inevitability-of-extinction arguments that coming into existence is always a serious harm and that the Forsaken embody. He argues Rand's answer to the Dark One's offer of oblivion mirrors a rebuttal to Benatar: because argument 'in the alternative' invites the charge of dogmatism (citing Hitchens that what is asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence), and because extinction guarantees we can never improve, Rand chooses persistence and the hope of doing better. He closes with Camus that value lies in the struggle itself, however absurd.

the-absurd.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
the-absurd.title: IV - X-ISTENTIAL X-MEN JEWS, SUPERMEN, AND THE LITERATURE OF STRUGGLE
the-absurd.relation: Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature rooted in the Jewish experience of their creators. Stan Lee and Jack Kirby's mutants, and Claremont's reinvention of Magneto as a Holocaust survivor, reverse Superman's assimilationist fantasy: being a minority makes the X-Men entitled to equal treatment, and human fear of difference is the norm rather than a Lex Luthor-style pathology. Sartre's bad faith explains the anti-Semite's chosen hatred (and why Xavier refuses to simply mind-control humans into tolerance), while Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem makes moral judgment everyone's burden. Against Camus' opening question of suicide and Mr. Incredible's wish that the world 'stay saved,' the chapter argues the X-Men's endless Sisyphean cycle of deaths, resurrections, and reboots is not futile: one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

the-absurd.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
the-absurd.relation: Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.

the-absurd.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
the-absurd.title: John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism
the-absurd.relation: Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.

the-absurd.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
the-absurd.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.

the-absurd.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
the-absurd.title: No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western
the-absurd.relation: Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'

the-absurd.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
the-absurd.title: “What Kind of Man Are You ” The Coen Brothers and Existentialist Role Playing
the-absurd.relation: Gaughran argues the Coens presuppose an absurd, valueless world (announced by Blood Simple's 'you're on your own' voice-over) in which characters must, per Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' invent a self by adopting a style. He surveys the hats of Miller's Crossing, Everett's Dapper Dan dandyism in O Brother read through Camus's The Rebel, and Ed Crane of The Man Who Wasn't There as a Meursault-like figure who forges an identity through violence. Against Camus, murder and suicide are illegitimate revolts, and Sisyphus—not the nihilistic killers—stands as the true absurd hero who never resolves the tension between mind and indifferent world.

the-absurd.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
the-absurd.title: Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There
the-absurd.relation: Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.

the-absurd.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
the-absurd.title: Thinking beyond the Failed Community Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn’t There
the-absurd.relation: Palmer reads Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn't There as a diptych re-composing James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity, whose core theme is a failed community where self-interest poisons human bonds. Blood Simple dramatizes the Cainian problem—Visser and the others destroyed by instrumentalization and fatal miscommunication—while The Man Who Wasn't There, framed by Camus's The Stranger and Sartre's Nausea, stages its utopian solution. Ed's Sartrean disgust at hair and physicality drives his dry-cleaning scheme; like Meursault he kills and is condemned for the wrong crime, but unlike Cain's solipsistic heroes he ends yearning for communion with Doris beyond the grave, imagining the restoration of the lost community.

the-absurd.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
the-absurd.title: 13. Reason and Catharsis
the-absurd.relation: Elsby and Luzecky argue that we compulsively rationalize Twin Peaks (tulpas, pale-horse omens, Diane-as-tulpa) the way we abstract concepts to tame the contradictory sensible world (Plato's long-and-short finger), but Lynch—especially in Part 8—deliberately thwarts this, exposing what Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols calls the post-Socratic tyranny of rationality. They offer an alternative reading of Aristotelian catharsis (via Trela): because the fictional world is not ours, we can experience its irrationality and absurdity, emotions purged of their tie to reality, as freedom rather than the existential despair the absurd would cause in our own world.

the-absurd.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
the-absurd.title: 19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie
the-absurd.relation: Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'

the-absurd.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
the-absurd.title: Introduction
the-absurd.relation: Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.

the-absurd.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
the-absurd.title: Film Noir and the Meaning of Life
the-absurd.relation: Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.

the-absurd.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
the-absurd.title: The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent
the-absurd.relation: Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.

the-absurd.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
the-absurd.title: Introduction
the-absurd.relation: Editor Jerold Abrams argues Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent 'cinematic existentialism' in which a free subject stands against a cold, uncaring world, synthesized with strands of Stoicism and pragmatism. He surveys the volume's essays as variations on this theme: Camus' absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzschean flux in Full Metal Jacket, Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity in Paths of Glory, and Nietzsche's overman as the Star Child in 2001. The essay ties specific films (the ape's femur, HAL, Humbert, the Overlook) to the claim that each Kubrick subject must invent its own meaning in a meaningless universe.

the-absurd.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
the-absurd.title: Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke
the-absurd.relation: Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.

the-absurd.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
the-absurd.title: Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler
the-absurd.relation: Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).

the-absurd.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
the-absurd.title: The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska
the-absurd.relation: Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.

the-absurd.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
the-absurd.relation: McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.

the-absurd.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
the-absurd.relation: Palmer casts the protagonists of The Jericho Mile and Thief as 'outsiders' in Colin Wilson's sense—men 'awakened to chaos'—read through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus. Rain Murphy, running endless meaningless laps and hurling away the timer, is Mann's Sisyphus: his fate belongs to him, the struggle itself filling his heart. Thief's Frank, who 'gets to where nothin' means nothin',' shreds his dream-collage and destroys everything rather than be owned by Leo, enacting the absurd hero's scorn for a Hobbesian 'war of all against all' where law lacks connection to justice.

the-absurd.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
the-absurd.relation: Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.

the-absurd.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
the-absurd.relation: Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.

the-absurd.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
the-absurd.relation: Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.

the-absurd.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
the-absurd.title: Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville
the-absurd.relation: Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.

the-absurd.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.relation: Abrams's editorial introduction argues that Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent cinematic existentialism in which the isolated self stands against a cold, uncaring world. It threads the individual Kubrick films through named philosophers - Camus's absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzsche's flux and Overman in Full Metal Jacket and 2001, Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death in Paths of Glory, Kant's marriage-morality in Eyes Wide Shut - and notes Kubrick blends this existentialism with Stoicism (The Killing) and pragmatism. It frames each contributor's essay as reading one film through that lens.

the-absurd.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.relation: Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.

the-absurd.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.relation: Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.

the-absurd.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
the-absurd.relation: Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Thomas Nagel's essay 'The Absurd' (built on Camus's Sisyphus), distinguishing conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) from philosophical absurdity (the collision of the engaged participant perspective with the detached external one). He argues Kubrick's three signature devices—the painterly aesthetic that renders eighteenth-century rituals AS rituals, the slow reverse zoom that literally moves from close-up participant view to overwhelming long-shot external view, and the ironic omniscient narrator—make viewers see Barry's conventional absurdity and then confront their own inescapable philosophical absurdity. He notes Kubrick laments this predicament pessimistically where Nagel counsels irony.

the-absurd.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
the-absurd.title: 24 and the Existential Man of Revolt
the-absurd.relation: McMahon argues that 24 is genuine TV noir (crime focus, cynical tone, split screens, the femmes fatale Nina Myers and Sherry Palmer, Jack's heroin addiction as his internal demon) and that Jack Bauer is Camus's man of revolt. She lays out Camus's account of the absurd as the confrontation between our appetite for clarity and the world's unreasonable silence, rejects actual and 'philosophical suicide' as evasions, and maps Jack onto the man of revolt's defining traits: lucidity (his refusal to trust appearances, as when only he suspects President Logan of corruption and murder) and courage (risking nerve-gas exposure at CTU and entering the gas-plant fire). The terrorist threats Jack fights symbolize the absurd because their success, from Palmer's assassination to citywide nerve gas, would annihilate order and meaning themselves; as Camus's 'conqueror,' Jack employs violence reluctantly, without appetite for it, to establish non-violence, accepting a crushing fate without resignation.

the-absurd.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
the-absurd.title: Twin Peaks, Noir, and Open Interpretation
the-absurd.relation: Jason Holt catalogs Twin Peaks' noir elements (the Laura Palmer quest narrative, Cooper's voiceover Dictaphone, femmes fatales, low-key lighting, the existential mood leavened by absurd humor in the manner of Camus) but argues the series is merely noirish, not noir, because it refuses noir's hard-boiled naturalistic metaphysics. The decisive case is BOB: the post-Leland dialogue between Cooper, Truman, and Albert stages the choice between reducing BOB to Leland's psychopathology and reifying him as a real malevolent spirit from the Black Lodge, and the show deliberately leaves the fictional ontology of BOB undecidable, in Todorov's 'fantastic' between the natural and supernatural. This interpretive openness (compared to The Prisoner's Number 1 revelation and the psychological indeterminacy of Sam Spade's motives in The Maltese Falcon) is defended as aesthetically desirable via Holt's 'omissive' aesthetic, the art of leaving important things out.

the-absurd.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
the-absurd.title: “Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch
the-absurd.relation: Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.

the-absurd.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
the-absurd.title: 3. The Nasty Bits
the-absurd.relation: Calef asks how Bourdain could find disgusting foods (cobra heart, blood soup, warthog anus) delicious, using Korsmeyer's taxonomy of disgust and the 'paradox of aversion.' He argues their appeal comes from Aristotelian learning-through-representation, Burke's and Bullough's sublime experienced at psychical distance, and Kristeva's 'abject' — foods that remind us of death and mortality let Bourdain transcend and disarm it by eating them appreciatively.

the-absurd.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
the-absurd.title: Dare to Enter the Zone
the-absurd.relation: Hooke and Rivera's editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone dramatizes the Nietzschean disappointment of the epigraph from Twilight of the Idols—that we seek great human beings and find only 'the apes of their ideal.' They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnated Socrates, a gadfly whose episodes ('Time Enough at Last,' 'The Hunt,' the eternal-youth trade-in) stage the gap between our ideals of love, justice, and truth and the treacherous, self-deluding creatures we actually are, so that viewers laugh at absurd twist endings because we are the species most deserving to be laughed at.

the-absurd.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
the-absurd.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
the-absurd.relation: Seitz gives an existential-phenomenological meditation on hunting's essence, leaning on Ortega y Gasset's Meditations on Hunting: 'one does not hunt in order to kill; on the contrary, one kills in order to have hunted.' Using his daughter Sabina's squirrel-versus-grouse reasoning and his own pronghorn stalks, he argues meat is the 'sign' but not the essence, and (via Heidegger) that hunting is 'a mode of revealing.' Contrasting Marx and Heidegger on technology with Ortega's claim that hunting 'cannot progress,' he frames the hunter as 'natural/prehistoric man' annihilating historical time — a vanishing figure in a climate-changed, thirsty future.

the-absurd.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
the-absurd.title: 1. Frankenstein
the-absurd.relation: Using the De Niro monster of Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Rowlands argues absurdity arises from a clash between the view of ourselves from the inside (a locus of meaning) and from the outside (sub specie aeternitatis, insignificant). The monster is assembled from second-hand parts and thrown into a hostile world he did not choose, just as we are stitched together by genes and environment we did not choose (Sartre/Heidegger thrownness). He develops Camus's Myth of Sisyphus, arguing the horror is futility not difficulty, to frame the problem of the meaning of life that underlies every deep philosophical problem.
