objectification.relation: Olson's first D&D Encounters session handed her a sexualized female miniature in a chainmail bikini and high-heeled boots, and the chapter audits the game as a feminist would: research on the 'token girl' and male-default storytelling, women like Dowsett pushed to play male characters to be taken seriously, and harassment ranging from 'date at least one of the party or bring food' to condescension toward women in the industry. Against this she argues the rules themselves are egalitarian — identical power pools for male and female characters, embodying Plato's Republic claim that women 'are by nature the same with respect to guarding the city', and even the evil deities are stereotyped symmetrically (scheming Lolth and Tiamat versus war-god patrons of power) — while the collaborative party structure (clerics healing strikers, shared goals) has exactly the care-ethical, anti-individualist flavor Friedman and Bolte attribute to women's moral perspectives. Sexism is thus a consequence of unreflective practices, marketing that ignores women, and industry culture rather than the game; all-female systems like Portal Worlds are a real response but, she worries, separatism risks deepening the divide.

objectification.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
objectification.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Robert Arp and Sarah Fisk test three moral theories against objectification in Final Fantasy: Kant's ban on using rational beings as mere means (Kuja's manipulation of Queen Brahne, the Geostigma children of Advent Children), Mill's greatest-happiness principle (Yuna's and Aeris's self-sacrifice), and Aristotle's character-based virtue ethics (Hojo and Sephiroth as vicious, Aeris as virtuous). They argue Kantianism generates a stalemate between 'moral sanctity' and 'moral autonomy' camps over cases like Guardian Force summoning in FFVIII, and utilitarianism a stalemate over mandatory self-sacrifice, leaving virtue ethics, Aristotelian or Nietzschean, as the view that escapes both, ending with the question 'Aeris or a Cloud?'

objectification.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
objectification.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Why do Berger, Cecilia, Harriet, Salander, and Figuerola all bed the unprepossessing Blomkvist? Testing Kant's claim that sexual desire makes 'the loved person an Object of appetite... a lemon which has been sucked dry,' the chapter argues his appeal is that he treats women as ends in themselves—he works beside them as equals, is 'not going to compete with you' with Figuerola, and never manipulates or controls—so his sex is the least objectifying in a Sweden full of men who hate women. Against Kant and Baumrim, Irving Singer's reply that desire can respond to the whole person explains why his no-strings honesty attracts powerful women, though his refusal to define, own, or 'cherish' any lover—walking in on Erika just as Salander arrives with the Elvis cabin ad—still leaves Salander heartbroken and Figuerola in sadness.

objectification.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
objectification.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Applying Laura Mulvey's visual pleasure to the printed page, the chapter argues that Larsson's protest against woman-hating is compromised by styling Salander—four-eleven, ninety pounds, 'childlike breasts'—as a sexual spectacle whose rapes (Bjurman's coerced oral sex, the anal rape, the trial's play-by-play of implements) are the trilogy's most explicit scenes while consensual sex stays off-screen, making the books 'torture porn' for the voyeuristic reader. The films shift the gaze further: the revenge on Bjurman runs longer than the rapes, Salander actively watches Martin Vanger burn, and her bisexuality with Mimmi Wu is reduced to one silent morning, changes that make the violence against men more acceptable than against women. The chapter ends ambivalent: Laurie Penny and Gail Dines charge that 'Misogynist violence is appalling; now here's some more,' yet the distributor's RAINN partnership and a rape survivor's testimony that Salander was the first active, aggressive survivor she had ever seen show the books also work as Larsson intended.

objectification.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: Rivera Berruz argues that Freddy Hayes's storyline - the BBQ joint whose franchise design keeps linoleum peeling so 'white folks feel like they slumming,' his son's parole violation destroying the deal, and Frank publicly dropping him when the bad press lands - commodifies black male life as consumable 'spice' for a predominantly white show. Using bell hooks's account of ethnicity as seasoning in commodity culture, Tommy Curry and Michelle Alexander on blackness coded as criminality, and Nancy Leong's racial capitalism, the chapter shows Freddy's value is entirely derivative of his usefulness to Underwood. It closes by adopting Derrick Bell's racial realism ('I live to harass white folks') as the proper stance: the critique cannot dismantle racial capitalism but can harass the representation so viewers stop assuming the stereotype is 'just the way things are.'

objectification.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
objectification.title: 5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide
objectification.relation: Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.

objectification.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
objectification.title: Zelda and Reality
objectification.relation: Joyce Havstad and Iris Jahng catalogue the women of Zelda — Zelda's many incarnations, Impa, the Twinrova sisters, the oracles Din and Nayru, Midna — finding the typologies of maiden, mother, and crone, then explain them with Beauvoir's The Second Sex: the myth of woman (Mother, Wife, Idea), femininity as made rather than born, and woman's enforced passivity against man's transcendence. Zelda is woman as Idea, traced to Platonic Forms: young, beautiful, virtuous, and radically passive (turned to stone in The Minish Cap, asleep through The Adventure of Link, imprisoned in nearly every game), an object that exists to motivate Link's heroism. Significantly, only the masculine-garbed Sheik and the pirate Tetra escape passivity, a shift the authors link to Miyamoto's design philosophy of 'reality over realism' and to changing conceptions of women.

objectification.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.

objectification.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: Quick applies Cary Wolfe's humaninized/animalized humans and Carol Adams's animalized women to the Citadel: Max is hunted, caged, and muzzled as an unnamed 'it', War Pups serve like littermates, and the milking mothers produce Adams's 'feminized protein' while the 'breeders' are groomed like show animals. Following Val Plumwood's ecofeminist critique of the masculinity that conquers mother nature — and Joe's branding of water as Aqua Cola — the chapter reads Furiosa's return to the Citadel as an ecofeminist revolution in which 'We are not things' restores women, men like Nux and Max, and nature itself from property to personhood.

objectification.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
objectification.title: Real World Island
objectification.relation: Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue Lost redeems characters who stop objectifying others and instead freely 'objectify' themselves for the greater good. Kant's ban on treating persons as mere means condemns Ben's lifelong manipulation and Ben's use of Sayid as an assassin, yet autonomy justifies chosen self-sacrifice like Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission, Claire volunteering as bait for Ethan, and Jack becoming the new Jacob. Mill's utilitarianism makes Kate's shooting of the Man in Black a fair trade saving her friends, while Aristotle's virtues - respect against objectification, courage in Jack's death at the cliff, the engrained honesty of reformed con man Jim LaFleur, Kate's character-building motherhood of Aaron - complete the three-theory survey.

objectification.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
objectification.title: Television and Existential Awakening
objectification.relation: Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.

objectification.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
objectification.title: Don’t Go Mad
objectification.relation: Barkman applies a qualified Aristotelian standard of justice, that women possessing rational souls must be treated as equals, to Peggy, Betty, and Joan as second-wave feminism dawns. Peggy is the 'mad woman' in the best sense: she demands a desk, equal pay ('You have everything and so much of it'), and Don's apology while never resorting to blackmail like Pete, whereas Betty is repressed at home by a husband who shows her off ('I want to show you off, Betts') and Joan suppresses herself, measuring worth by appearance and enduring Greg's violation until the vase incident. The sexual objectification Peggy faces from her first day (Ken's elevator leers, Joan's paper-bag advice, the panty-hunt in 'Nixon vs. Kennedy') is the chapter's core injustice, and the warning is that women who cannot stand up to it may simply go mad.

objectification.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
objectification.title: Boys Interrupted: The Drama of Male Bonding in Some Kind of Monster
objectification.relation: Judith Grant reads Some Kind of Monster through Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's concept of homosociality: the Hetfield-Ulrich bond is the libidinal engine of the band, with Mustaine and Newsted as sibling rivals for James' attention, wives and children as intrusions that break the male-only bonding, and Lars' French-kissing of Kirk policing the homosocial/homosexual line within heteronormativity. The film's arc - James' exit to rehab, Lars' tirade against his control, and the firing of the feminized therapist Phil - is the interruption and rekindling of a homosocial bond that can no longer run on youthful rebellion now that the band has become 'The Man'.

objectification.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
objectification.title: The Office and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.

objectification.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
objectification.title: The Office and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Dromm asks what makes Michael's behavior wrong even where the law cannot touch it: as an 'equal-opportunity harasser' of Pam, Ryan, and Oscar, Michael seems to escape Title VII's discrimination requirement. He tests Edmund Wall's 'wrongful communication' definition against the filthy emails, 'that's what she said,' and Michael's solution to the Kevin-Angela dispute in 'Conflict Resolution,' finds it too broad and too dependent on the victim's objection, then turns to MacKinnon's sex-discrimination account and Crosthwaite and Priest's oppression account to explain the distinctive harm to women (pressuring Pam to be a cheerleader in 'Basketball,' calling the party-planning committee his 'bitches'). He concludes that both views are needed, and that in the end harassment wrongs workers by undermining their legitimate expectation of being judged only on job-relevant merit, leaving Dwight's extra effort done for nothing.

objectification.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
objectification.title: When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer
objectification.relation: Tallman asks why SNL may mock presidents (Chase's pratfalling Ford, Carvey's Bush) and Clintons but not unchosen groups, framing the question with the aesthetics debate among radical autonomism (Bell), radical moralism (traced to Plato and Tolstoy), and moderate moralism. Sketches from Samurai Futaba to Farley's Lunchlady Land show jokes can punch up, punch down, or elevate a low-status group. The Schmitts Gay beer sketch, she argues, ridicules not gay men but beer-ad conventions: swapping the usual female sex objects for men in speedos exposes the objectification and heteronormativity viewers had stopped noticing, so the butt is the advertising industry.

objectification.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
objectification.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Applies Luce Irigaray's account of patriarchal society to Charming's women: Gemma and Tara are strong and resourceful, but their identity, power, and even survival run through men, as Clay's 'you are NOT a member of this club — you're just an old lady!' and Jax's 'She's just an old lady, not a member' make brutally literal. Irigaray's claim that patriarchal orders circulate women as commodities exchanged among men fits the 'sweet butt' Cherry being offered to Clay in 'Patch Over' and Gemma's 'Only men need to feel loved. Women need to feel wanted.' Tara's sacrificed surgical career and Jax's refusal to live off his wife ('I'm not gonna live off my wife. I can't.') illustrate woman as a being who exists for another, and the chapter ends asking what Gemma could say if she had a genuinely feminine voice of her own.

objectification.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: Argues that Leia and Padme really are strong feminist characters, using Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to defuse the two stock objections: Padme's motherhood is 'freely chosen' rather than an oppressive role, and Leia chained in Jabba's palace keeps command of her sexuality, turning the damsel-in-distress plot around by strangling Jabba with her own chain and later rescuing Han herself. The chapter's real complaint is structural: with only six speaking women in the original trilogy, almost all of them royalty, Leia and Padme are forced to represent all women (the 'affluent few' problem), while Shmi, Aunt Beru, Mon Mothma, and the handmaidens Sabe, Corde, and Dorme never get the screen time to show their strength.

objectification.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: Reads Leia's gold-bikini captivity in Jabba's palace as an image of contemporary culture's fear of fat: Jabba, the rancor, and the Sarlaac personify uncontrolled appetite and Sartre's 'slimy' being-in-itself, while Leia's thin, disciplined body epitomizes the anorexic ideal. Drawing on Susan Bordo and Foucault's docile bodies, the chapter argues the scene chains women to a tyrannical ideal of slimness so that Leia herself becomes the oppressor, and closes with Sartre's point that consciousness depends on its body, so we should suspend the fear of flesh and embrace embodied life as the Force does.

objectification.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
objectification.title: A New Hope Inclusive Representation in the Galaxy
objectification.relation: Lakka uses Beauvoir's The Second Sex (the Mother/Mistress dichotomy, woman tied to nature and denied transcendence) and Butler on the mother-daughter separation to argue that Revenge of the Sith reduces Padme from the active senator and warrior of the first two prequels to a pregnant figure confined to her apartment, whose death gets read as martyrdom or even 'mom-shaming.' She reads Anakin's jealousy, interrogations ('Obi-Wan's been here, has he not?'), and Force-choke on Mustafar — explicitly paralleled with Othello and Desdemona — as an abusive relationship, suggesting Padme's death may be a feminicide. The deleted Petition of the 2000 scenes, and successors like Rey, Ahsoka, Rose Tico, and Jyn Erso, point toward the inclusive representation the galaxy still needs.

objectification.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
objectification.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects. She reads Mary, Ellen, and Jo as warrior mothers whose duty and sacrifice, following Jean Bethke Elshtain, the brothers most respect, while Mill's utilitarianism explains the lovers (Jessica, Lisa, the djinn-dream Carmen) each brother sacrifices to the mission. The 'Jus in Bello' virgin-sacrifice debate exposes the tension, since Dean invokes Kantian respect yet ignores Nancy's free choice to die, and the killings of female monsters like Amy and Emma show objectification running in both directions.

objectification.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
objectification.title: NOTES
objectification.relation: Brace and Arp systematically map the coffin-to-closet analogy: 'God hates fangs' echoes Fred Phelps, Eddie's leap from closeted family man to vampire lover parallels coming out, and vampire media normalization (Fang magazine, teen soaps) mirrors Ellen and Dawson's Creek. They distinguish orientation from action, rebut the natural-law argument that nonprocreative sex is unnatural (it would condemn infertile and contracepting heterosexuals too), and fix the moral line at consent — Bill asking before fang and penis penetrate is healthy, while Lorena's forced turning of Bill and the Rattrays' draining of him, 'objectified and crucified' for his blood, are violations; on that basis they argue vampires deserve equal rights under the VRA.

objectification.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
objectification.title: NOTES
objectification.relation: Craton and Jonell read Sookie as an emblem of contemporary feminist ambivalence: her 'I am woman, hear me roar' independence coexists with sexual caution, and the show stages feminism's sex wars — Lafayette's sex work and webcam pornography versus Maryann, whose 'pro-sex' liberation collapses into self-annihilating worship of Dionysus and whose death suggests unregulated sexuality is dangerous. Tara's plotline shows how race and class layer onto gender (her 'baby-daddy' scene, Maryann as failed white savior), exposing the limits of a united feminist front, while the 'kept woman' quarrel with Bill and Sookie's barmaid-versus-telepathic-detective career choice leave more questions about female empowerment than answers.

objectification.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
objectification.title: NOTES
objectification.relation: Craton reads Sookie's arc through disability theory: her telepathy, treated by Bon Temps as a disability that barred her from college and respect, is reframed once vampires and Weres prize it — and finally her faerie 'light' — into an ability she controls for money, crime-solving, and saving a child. The chapter parallels the eugenics-era fears Sookie and Alcide share about passing on difference, and the freak-show histories of Joseph Merrick, Saartjie Baartman, and Julia Pastrana illuminate how vampires like Eric and Sophie-Anne value Sookie's blood as a possession to be consumed rather than a person to be respected, until she rescinds Bill's invitation and defends her light.

objectification.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
objectification.title: 9. Machines Who Care
objectification.relation: Weiss reads 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric' as fifty-year-old anticipations of today's debate over relational artifacts: Alexa, therapeutic robot seals, and care robots for the aged (via Turkle, the Sparrows' objection, and Coeckelbergh's embrace of robots that care). Alicia's tear wins Corry's trust only to end with her shot in the face, while the electric grandma saves Anne's life, yet both are assembly-line products answering loneliness that the same consumer society produces. The chapter asks whether buying care and companionship from robotic women, designed, boxed, and disposed of by men, is fable or nightmare.

objectification.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
objectification.title: Getting Tough and Getting Even
objectification.relation: Jordan Pascoe uses the 'Like a Virgin' purity test — Meg's fake 48 making her a 'slut' while a low score would make a guy a stud — to argue slut shaming strips girls of Kantian personhood, treating as things those autonomous beings who must be respected as ends in themselves. Kant's bleak view of sex as a desire for a body rather than a person explains why Tad's drugging and popsicle-video blackmail of Carmen reduce her to an object, and why objectification goes viral: once an object of one person's appetite, Kant warns, a person 'can be treated and used as such by everyone.' Catherine MacKinnon's power-based account then explains the double standard — men's pleasure in forcing the world to conform turns promiscuous men into studs and promiscuous women into sluts — so the fault lies with the slut sneezers, never Meg, Carmen, or Veronica, who must 'get tough, get even' to demand respect.

objectification.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
objectification.title: Back to the Rough Ground!
objectification.relation: Finnegan applies Wittgenstein's language games and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are captivated by an 'ideal' transcendent narrative, while marginalized hosts Dolores and Maeve gain traction precisely from their lostness. Dolores refuses the damsel role by grabbing a gun in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and Maeve seizes admin privileges to 'write my own fucking story,' each inventing new language games. Drawing on Mulvey's male gaze, Finnegan casts their objectified position as closer to women's experience, and reads them as using the master's tools to dismantle the master's house.

objectification.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
objectification.title: In Closing, The Naked Truth
objectification.relation: Meyer argues the hosts' nudity is rarely gratuitous, sorting it into three categories using theorists of the nude in art. Drawing on Kenneth Clark's naked/nude distinction, the posed, idealized, 'made' Dolores in 'The Original' is the nude as artform; using John Berger's Ways of Seeing, the brothel and El Lazo orgy scenes and the bathing Armistice are the nude as male sexual dominance and objectification. Finally, invoking Leo Steinberg's account of Christ's nudity as incarnation, Meyer reads the naked awakening of Maeve, Hector, and Armistice as signaling machines 'becoming human,' concluding humans' duplicity, not nakedness, is the true shame.

objectification.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
objectification.title: Ciri's Agency and Autonomy
objectification.relation: Vega and Barta read Ciri's Elder Blood power, which activates only through controlled female emotion, through Hélène Cixous's 'Laugh of the Medusa' and écriture féminine: her awakening scream at dying Calanthe's side and her cry of 'NO!' are forbidden female self-expression breaking patriarchal control. Renfri, silenced by Stregobor's narrative into villain and victim, and the bruxa Vereena, killed when her power exceeds her control, are the cautionary Medusas against which Ciri's mastery and the Lodge of Sorceresses' vote of 'sentimentality, gentleness, trust, and hope' to release her stand out. Calanthe's 'I bow to no law made by men who never bore a child' is pure écriture féminine undercut by her own complicity in auctioning Pavetta, and Ciri's final victory over Emhyr comes not through the sword but through tears, emotional expression defeating patriarchy's rationalizations.

objectification.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
objectification.title: I'm Part Elf, I'm Part Human
objectification.relation: Perez reads racism in Netflix's Witcher through Ibram X. Kendi's power-based account of racism, tracing the humans-versus-elves conflict through colorism (pointy ears and elven blood), 'drop rules' of racial purity that stigmatize Yennefer's quarter-elven lineage, and mutual dehumanization from Stregobor's 'mongrels' slur to Francesca's vow that the next genocide will be the humans'. He tests Kant's humanity formula against Nilfgaard's 'haven' for elves and the Battle of Aretuza, finding both sides guilty of using persons as mere means, then uses Suzy Killmister's three-strand dignity to explain why Calanthe's hidden heritage destroys her while Jaskier's Sandpiper smuggling and Cahir kneeling before Ciri restore dignity. Sartre's Other frames Yennefer's fluctuating identity between human and elf, and Dara laying down his hatred plus Ciri renouncing her power and taking the name Falka model Kendi's claim that being racist or antiracist is chosen moment by moment.

objectification.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: A mother-daughter pair tracks Wonder Woman's and Harley Quinn's costume histories (the 1990s Artemis-era near-thong Diana, the New 52 brothel-styled Harley) and argues with Aristotle that sexualized drawing strips both characters of phronesis, the practical wisdom a virtuous agent needs - the wisdom by which an outmatched Wonder Woman talks Strife into carrying her to safety and Harley exploits the Joker's vanity to beat him. The paradox: the more provocatively each is drawn, the less she can succeed as moral hero or anti-hero, since objectification replaces goal-directed cunning with one-dimensional sex display. The New 52's armor-clad, Hephaestus-consulting Wonder Woman shows phronesis restored.

objectification.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
objectification.title: Notes
objectification.relation: Brake applies Zizek's distinction between symptom and fetish to Grant Morrison's treatment of Wonder Woman: in Final Crisis, making her Darkseid's masked, bondage-suited thrall is a symptomal reading that forces the repressed kinky truth of Marston's origin to the surface, while the industry's chant that she is a 'feminist icon' works as a fetish - a fetishistic disavowal letting misogynist comics practice continue ('they know very well what they are doing, but still, they are doing it'). He extends the analysis to Earth One, where Hippolyta's clay-birth story is the primordial lie founding the Amazon community, Diana herself being the fetish that lets her mother sustain a separatist utopia while raising a weapon against Man's World.

objectification.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
objectification.title: She Got Game
objectification.relation: The Wallaces argue that both the detractors (Stacey Pressman's claim that women's basketball 'sucks') and the admirers (John Wooden's 'purest basketball' praise) judge the women's game by patriarchal standards drawn from the men's game. Using Sandra Bartky's feminist extension of Foucault, they show how the female body was disciplined under male surveillance - early rule changes split the court and banned stealing to protect 'femininity', while players deflected the 'Amazon' charge with beauty pageants, revealing uniforms, and the Playboy offer to Lisa Harrison. The modern WNBA of Lisa Leslie and Michelle Snow, who can dunk but choose team play, points to a new game that escapes the feminine/masculine dichotomy instead of measuring women against men.

objectification.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
objectification.title: Eighth Hole Playing Through Racism and Sexism in Golf
objectification.relation: Gray examines whether golf is a model of equality or a preserve of 'wealthy white men,' using George Carlin's polemic and the Tiger Woods 'Chosen One' narrative as foils. He documents 'social closure' and the 'Grass Ceiling' through Augusta National's history, the Shoal Creek and Martha Burk/NCWO controversies, and the PGA's former Caucasian-only clause, then turns to sexism via McGinnis, McQuillan, and Chapple's interviews and Connell's 'hegemonic masculinity,' showing how gendered 'red/women's tees' entrench a false dualism of male and female play. Citing McDonagh and Pappano's Playing with the Boys, he argues coercive sex-segregation rests on false assumptions and calls for transparency about club membership.

objectification.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
objectification.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Jonsson argues that modern sport enforces masculine norms and that the East German 'wonder girls' (Koch, Ender, Krabbe), along with Stella Walsh, Jarmila Kratochvilova and Caster Semenya, were 'gender radical' Amazons who challenged the link between masculinity and maleness by winning with 'masculine' bodies. Drawing on Judith Butler's claim that gender ideals are not static and women's sport can rearticulate them, he treats the doping-built Eastern Bloc athletes as progressive because they contradicted how female athletes are 'supposed' to look. He critiques Jane English's appeal to 'permanent biological differences' and laments that after 1989 commercialized sport (symbolized by Flo Jo's marketed femininity) hardened conservative gender norms again.

objectification.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
objectification.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
objectification.relation: Weaving argues from a liberal-feminist standpoint that the FIVB's mandatory bikini-bottom rule for women's Olympic beach volleyball sexualizes and objectifies the athletes, contradicting Coubertin's ideals of universal humanity. Using Paul Davis's distinction between acceptable sexuality and objectionable sexualization (deliberate focus on body parts, freezing postures, punning captions like 'Buns of Gold'), and citing Nussbaum, Baker and Bartky on when treating someone as a sexual object becomes wrong, she shows the rule detaches athletes' bodies from their athletic agency. She traces harms including physical risk, the APA-documented effects of sexualization, a 'trickle-down' to school volleyball short-shorts, and exclusion of Islamic women.

objectification.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
objectification.title: The “Kournikova Phenomenon”
objectification.relation: The chapter asks why Anna Kournikova was celebrated as a beauty despite a mediocre record while the far more successful Williams sisters were praised for athleticism, not looks. It uses Plato's Symposium (the ascent from a beautiful body to the Form of Beauty) to show beauty can be more than appearance, then deploys Nussbaum's analysis of objectification (contrasting Playboy's demeaning caption on tennis-player Nicollette Sheridan with Lady Chatterley) and MacKinnon's dominance view to critique the media's commodification of female players. Weaving in commodity racism and bell hooks on black hair, it argues Kournikova's fame reflects a whiteness-privileging color-caste standard of beauty rather than any real athletic or aesthetic superiority.

objectification.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
objectification.title: Laugh of the Revolutionary Diane di Prima, French Feminist Philosophy, and the Contemporary Cult of the Beat H
objectification.relation: Quinn reads Diane di Prima's serial poem 'Loba' and 'Memoirs of a Beatnik' through Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' and its call to 'écriture féminine'—women writing the body. She argues di Prima's she-wolf/Medusa figure, sex-positive candor, and refusal of narrative closure enact Cixous's boundless feminine writing, while Cixous's anti-Freudian, anti-Lacanian mockery of 'penis envy' and the 'big dick' illuminates di Prima's transgressive motherhood and bisexuality. Against the male Beats' dismissal of women writers (and Beauvoir's foremother status), the essay centralizes di Prima as a serious feminist philosopher-poet rather than a nostalgic icon.

objectification.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
objectification.title: 3. Laura Palmer—Madonna and Whore
objectification.relation: Jones argues that Laura Palmer is trapped in Freud's Madonna-whore complex—the male inability to see a woman as both virtuous and sexual—with BOB voicing the cultural signals that brand her 'dirty and sleazy' for her sexuality. He reads the Fireman/Giant, who births Laura as a golden antidote to BOB, as a patriarchal 'nice guy' whose idealizing Madonna role is as much a trap as the whore role BOB imposes. The chapter uses Laura's dual life to expose how patriarchy forces women to choose between two reductive poles, both maintained by male power.

objectification.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
objectification.title: 10. The Miss Twin Peaks Award Goes To . .
objectification.relation: Rard (as her 'doppelganger') distinguishes 'power-over' (getting others, mostly men, to do your bidding through beauty and manipulation) from the more stable 'power-to' (skills, resources, ability to act for oneself). She traces Josie Packard, who lives by manipulating Harry and Pete and is destroyed when surrounded by people immune to her charms, against Audrey Horne, who begins with the Norwegian stunt and the perfume-counter blackmail but transitions to running her father's business—acquiring real power—while Lana Milford's near-total charm and Nadine's adrenaline strength mark the extremes.

objectification.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
objectification.title: 11. The Mother of All Bombs
objectification.relation: Kolb argues Laura Palmer embodies the 'Angel in the House' ideal (Gilbert and Gubar) whose perfection is a beautiful dead girl, and reads The Return's linkage of the Trinity bomb to BOB/Judy through Arendt's On Violence—violence begets a more violent, hostile world that especially victimizes women. Using Gilligan's In a Different Voice, she shows how women's voices (Naido/Diane, the Log Lady, Laura's diary) are silenced by toxic masculinity (Mr. C, Richard, Chad), while the 'good men' embody an ethic of care; the manufactured post-war social order names its bombs after mothers and treats women as perfect-yet-fallen others.

objectification.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
objectification.title: Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6
objectification.relation: Hoffman assesses whether Lee's She's Gotta Have It and Girl 6 offer liberated female sexuality, drawing on second- and third-wave feminism and bell hooks. She argues Nola Darling only appears empowered before the rape scene and her submission ('Yours') reveal her as an underdeveloped object of the male gaze, whereas Girl 6, as a phone-sex worker consciously performing gender for callers, better exposes gender as socially constructed in a Butler-like sense. Even so, Girl 6's real feminist force lies not in its heroine but in its exposure of oppressive industries, especially the opening Tarantino audition where only the director's gaze counts.

objectification.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
objectification.title: Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever
objectification.relation: Sundstrom uses Jungle Fever to dismantle the taboo (white and black versions) against interracial intimacy, treating Flipper and Angie's affair and the War Council's objections as a debate about black solidarity, loyalty, and self-hatred. He answers the War Council by invoking Mill's On Liberty and the tyranny of public opinion to defend sexual autonomy, and argues that demanding partners for political solidarity reduces them to props (objectification). He reads the psychoanalytic charge that interracial love is 'fevered' racial pathology as derived from Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks but ultimately baseless, and criticizes Lee for a puritanical ending that hides Orin and Paulie while exposing Flipper and Drew, failing to show interracial love as ordinary.

objectification.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
objectification.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
objectification.relation: Pomerance combines philosophy of sex and philosophy of language to argue that sex, lies, and videotape is less about sex than about speaking sex and being watched speaking it. He analyzes Cynthia's videotaped confession about her first encounter, showing how her circumlocutions ('smooth like a test tube,' 'Ladies first') tease and withhold, and how Graham as silent 'priest of carnality' becomes an absent audience. Videotape 'amplifies' situated speech to a diffuse mass audience, so Cynthia's sexuality becomes a 'television personality,' pornographic in form and effacing her individuality in the manner of Benjamin's mechanical reproduction. The face and presence-in-time make every filmed performance both erotic and a kind of illuminating lie.

objectification.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
objectification.title: The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films
objectification.relation: Pötzsch uses cognitive film theory (Murray Smith's alignment and allegiance, paradigm scenarios and schemata) to argue that Beaufort, Waltz with Bashir, and Lebanon, though hailed as antiwar films, covertly reinforce a militarist "scopic regime" through the "ubiquitously absent enemy." Formal devices—the tank scope's tunnel vision in Lebanon, shot/reverse-shot and voice-over confined to Israeli soldiers, the animated flashbacks of Waltz with Bashir—align and ally viewers exclusively with Israeli troops framed as helpless victims, while the Palestinian other stays faceless, voiceless, and objectified (the staggering Lebanese woman, the trauma displaced onto dead dogs and horses). Drawing on Judith Butler's frames of war and "ungrievable" lives, he reads this as Kimmerling's latent cognitive militarism that denies the enemy's competing subjectivity and forecloses nonviolent alternatives.

objectification.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
objectification.title: Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad
objectification.relation: Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).

objectification.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
objectification.title: Herzog’s Philosophy of Masculinism
objectification.relation: Will Lehman argues that beneath Herzog's rejection of any guiding philosophy lies a 'masculinism' that exalts traditionally manly traits (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as the heroic. Drawing on gender theory (Dozier on beards and the performance of gender), he shows Herzog fetishizing 'manly men,' reading illiteracy and calloused hands as authentic manhood (Jared Talbert in Into the Abyss), and coding even his female subject Juliane Koepcke (Wings of Hope) in masculine terms. Lehman reads Herzog's reenactment 'therapy' with Dengler and Dorrington as an assertion of dominance, while noting Herzog avoids overt misogyny or homophobia.

objectification.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
objectification.title: 6 Neil Young and American Indians Politics, Lyrics, and Authenticity
objectification.relation: Hester critiques Young's treatment of American Indians, arguing "Cortez the Killer" idealizes the Aztecs into Montaigne-style "noble savages," makes their sacrifices seem voluntary, and ultimately centers Young's own lost-love lament rather than the conquest's real victims. He shows "Pocahontas" objectifies and commodifies a Native woman (the "thousand pelts" line, Young's cavalier interview remarks) as cultural appropriation and "playing Indian," yet notes Young's genuine activism (Honor the Treaties) leaves fans wanting to credit his good intentions.

objectification.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
objectification.title: 8 Images of Women in the Music and Life of Neil Young
objectification.relation: McKenna uses Sarah Lucia Hoagland's feminist analysis of "heterosexualism" to argue that Young's songs ("Cinnamon Girl," "A Man Needs a Maid," "Unknown Legend," and the femicide of "Down by the River") portray women as objects to be desired, possessed, used and harmed, positioning them as helpmates (like Rousseau's Sophie, against which Wollstonecraft argued). She extends this to Young's own "backgrounding" of the women in his life (Pegi, Carrie Snodgress) in Waging Heavy Peace, comparing him to William James's reliance on his wife Alice.

objectification.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
objectification.title: 30_LaRocca_Chapter_029.html
objectification.relation: Linda Williams analyzes Michelle Citron's What You Take for Granted, a feminist film that inhabits the gray zone between documentary and fiction by having actors impersonate real women workers (a truck driver, a doctor, a welder) entering male-dominated trades. She argues the film exposes the price women pay to be admitted to a male world of work structured by an absent, idealized-and-vilified paternal authority, mirroring the absent-mother structure of Citron's earlier Daughter Rite. By blending polished pseudo-documentary interviews with an improvised cinema-verite fiction of Anna and Dianna's friendship, the film interrogates the process of representation itself and shows how documentary 'truth' about women's typical experience is itself a fictional shaping.

objectification.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
objectification.title: 7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters
objectification.relation: Brace surveys the later-season mother figures—Mary, Kelly, Jody, Rowena, Mrs. Butters, Charlie—arguing they are repeatedly used as emotional tools against the Winchesters, which she reads through Kant's warning against treating persons merely as means. She stresses loss of free will and agency: Mary's British Men of Letters 'realignment' and Mrs. Butters's coercive programming strip their autonomy and reduce them to objects/killers, while their reclaimed agency and self-sacrifice restore their Kantian standing as ends in themselves.

objectification.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
objectification.title: 28. Riot Grrrl Punk as Feminist Creation
objectification.relation: Patrick Anderson presents Riot Grrrl (Bikini Kill and the Riot Grrrl Manifesto) as feminist aesthetic creation rather than merely feminist politics: bands attacked the sexism within punk itself with 'women to the front' tactics, women-only shows, and stopping sets to call out harassers. Explaining Mary Devereaux's three levels of the male gaze (production, narrative, spectator) and the muse/whore versus one-of-the-guys/girl-with-balls taxonomy, he shows how Kathleen Hanna performing with 'SLUT' scrawled across her midriff collapses the muse/whore dichotomy, while 'Rebel Girl's' woman-loving-woman solidarity replaces women-as-objects with women as subjects. Zines, Xerox machines, and indie labels extend the feminist-aesthetic tactics of Hilde Hein and Carolyn Korsmeyer (violating standards of taste, the body as artwork), though the chapter notes criticisms of Riot Grrrl's white, middle-class limits.

objectification.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
objectification.title: 14. Did Bourdain Go #MeToo Far
objectification.relation: Finn tests Catharine MacKinnon's 'Rape Redefined' — rape as sex compelled by inequality rather than lack of consent — against Bourdain's #MeToo allyship and his payment to Asia Argento's teenage accuser Jimmy Bennett. She argues MacKinnon's power-based standard could recognize Argento's act as assault, and reframes Bourdain's hush-money payment, via the Wendat/Huron compensation practices in Graeber and Wengrow, as a compassionate vengeance-staying reparation consistent with his empathy.

objectification.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
objectification.title: Real World Island
objectification.relation: Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.

objectification.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
objectification.title: From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere
objectification.relation: Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.

objectification.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
objectification.title: MOTHERHOOD
objectification.relation: Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.

objectification.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
objectification.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Lee reads Gustave Courbet's life-size painting The Quarry (La curée) alongside Daumier's caricatures of incompetent bourgeois Parisian 'hobby hunters' and contemporary works by John Byrd and Christopher Carroll to trace how the hunter became a swaggering, masculine, lower-class 'savage' figure mediating wildness and civilization. She shows how the aristocratic ritual of the curée (feeding the deer's parts to the hounds) inverts into bourgeois provisioning, and invokes Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' to gloss Byrd's Tricky Buck as defiance of urban squeamishness about the mammalian, gendered reality of hunting.

objectification.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
objectification.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Merskin takes an ecofeminist view (Karen Warren's linkage of the domination of women and nature) of women who hunt, testing Marti Kheel's 'happy/holistic/holy' hunter typology against online interviews with female hunters and finding their motivations mirror men's. She surveys how hunting became a male-coded rite of separation from the mother—drawing on Freud's 'instinctive urge'—and how hunting media (Traditional Bowhunter) juxtapose women, animals, weapons, and sexual conquest as objects of male predation. Invoking Artemis/Diana and Mary Zeiss Stange's 'woman the hunter,' she argues women who hunt expose aggression as a human, not merely male, trait.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Evolutionary psychologists Anne Gordon and Shane Kraus coin 'porngasm' and, via a survey of 264 undergraduates, argue that watching porn may make men bad lovers because porn caters to male short-term mating psychology and misrepresents female orgasm (which they estimate is 80–95% faked on screen). Men more than women infer that female porn stars genuinely enjoy the sex, and more viewing predicts stronger such belief. They explain the male bias through the correspondence bias (reading moans as real arousal despite the filming situation) and Haselton and Buss's error-management theory, whereby men systematically over-infer women's sexual interest.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Theodore Bach argues that consuming porn co-opts the mind-reading 'simulation heuristic' (the same process behind the Mr. Tees airport puzzle), so that a viewer like 'Max' watching Naughty Office simulates being the boss rather than objectively watching. This explains porn's popularity, the money shot (a prop that keeps the viewer inside the off-line simulation), and why heterosexual men watch penises — they simulate their own. Invoking Nozick's experience machine and extending MacKinnon's critique via simulation and motor-imagery research, Bach warns that simulating aggressive, degrading acts toward women may transfer those dispositions into the real world.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Fiona Woollard asks whether Zach's solo use of pornography (while partner Kelly is out) counts as cheating on their monogamous relationship. Drawing on her account of monogamy as restricting sexual intercourse to loving relationships, she argues that masturbation to porn is not sexual intercourse — there is no interaction with 'Jenna' — and that fantasizing about loveless sex is not the same as having it, so it need not undermine the significance of lovemaking; indeed masturbation aids healthy sexual self-exploration. She concedes, however, that porn which eroticizes the degradation of women (per Dworkin and MacKinnon, and Alice Walker's story 'Porn') can betray a loving relationship by revealing objectifying attitudes.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Mimi Marinucci asks 'what's wrong with porn?' and, rejecting both the Dworkin-MacKinnon censorship route and Strossen's pure free-speech reply, uses Audre Lorde's notion of the erotic as power and the personal test 'it feels right to me' as an entering wedge. She examines 'feminist porn,' resisting its easy equation with lesbian or couples porn, and contrasts it with 'fuck machine porn' (e.g., machines named Annihilator, Predator), which feels wrong to her not for size or domination but because mainstream porn fixates on decontextualized acts and the money shot. Citing Irigaray on women's diffuse, non-localized sexuality, she argues women want more richly contextualized representations than porn typically offers.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Rose takes a paradigm plotless YouPorn-style clip and tests the four standard charges against porn—obscenity, coercion/exploitation, harm to women, and harm to society—arguing each either collapses into cultural relativism or applies equally to any aesthetic object. He answers the feminist (MacKinnon/Dworkin-style) claim that porn subordinates women by noting that unjustified hierarchical power distorts the self-understanding of dominator and dominated alike (comparing it to 50 Cent's 'P.I.M.P.' and blaxploitation), so the wrong is not gender-specific. His conclusion is that porn should not be treated as different in kind from other art but judged aesthetically and morally by whether it distorts equitable social relationships, locating the real problem in capitalist cultural production rather than in porn as such.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: Parkhill challenges Jenefsky and Miller's second-wave feminist reading of Penthouse 'girl–girl' pictorials (that they present lesbians as sexually available to naturalize heterosexuality) by arguing that what some straight men enjoy is their own ABSENCE from the scene. He deploys Butler's 'Imitation and Gender Insubordination' to show mock-lesbian-wedding drag can subvert rather than confirm heterosexual 'originality', Foucault's repressive hypothesis and productive power to argue the lesbian is a product of, not outside, patriarchal norms, and Lacan-derived 'projective identification' and feminine jouissance to explain the male viewer's libidinal investment in his own ego-erasure. He concludes both the 'conqueror' and the self-shattering 'jouissance-chasing' pleasures coexist, and that girl–girl porn is ethically no different from ordinary hetero porn since the consumer still assumes a right of access to women's bodies.

objectification.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
objectification.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
objectification.relation: In this interview, dominatrix-director Mz. Berlin answers the classic moral objections to porn from inside the industry: she rebuts objectification by insisting she chooses to be 'a commodity' and that choice makes it permissible, rejects the rape-myth/harm claim by citing declining rape rates and comparing porn to violent TV, and grounds BDSM's legitimacy entirely on INFORMED CONSENT, contrasting her voluntary waterboarding with her real torture abroad. Endorsing a strongly Millian self-ownership view ('my body is my own commodity'), she extends consent to selling kidneys, assisted suicide, and even display of her corpse, while drawing hard limits at sex with children, animals, or the dead where genuine informed consent is impossible. She also frames femdom porn as subverting male hegemony and normalizing fluid gender roles.

objectification.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
objectification.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: The editors' introduction argues that fashion, despite philosophers' contempt for it, raises serious questions in aesthetics, ethics, identity, and political philosophy. It surveys the volume's contributors: fashionability as an expert-plus-masses property (Prinz/Farennikova), Zangwill's alienation thesis, Russell on 'cool' as aesthetic virtue, the objectification of women through Barbie play and sweatshops, and Singer's demand (via the drowning-child argument) that spare money go to poverty relief rather than trendy clothes. It uses concrete cases — Ugg boots, the National Airlines 'Fly me' campaign, Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute, foot binding — to show fashion carries the zeitgeist and can both liberate and enslave.

objectification.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
objectification.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.

objectification.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
objectification.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Ashwell and Langton ask whether fashion is a 'badge of slavery' (Wollstonecraft), opening with Socrates in the *Phaedo* disdaining adornment and Rousseau's girl who becomes 'her own doll,' and using Kant's humanity formula and Nussbaum's seven-feature account of objectification. Focusing on denial of autonomy in ordinary followers, they distinguish the 'Servile Fashionista' (obeys experts) from the 'Sensible Fashionista' (follows what looks good), then argue that via Johnston's 'authority of affect' even the sensible one is under an *epistemic* bondage: fashion's extrinsic social pull is misperceived as the garment's intrinsic goodness, a projective illusion (like the Müller-Lyer) that on a Kantian view undermines agency and masks misogynist or racist norms such as straightened hair or the 'lotus feet' of stilettos.

objectification.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
objectification.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Collins analyzes paradigmatic Barbie play — dressing the doll and identifying with her as an idealized future self, from the 1959 TV ad to BarbieGirls.com — arguing it trains girls to define identity through fashionable bodily self-presentation for a male gaze (Brumberg's 'body project'). Using Sandra Bartky's feminist reworking of Foucault's *Discipline and Punish*, she treats beauty norms as a discipline producing 'docile bodies' whose self-surveillance internalizes a 'panoptical male connoisseur' (Bentham's Panopticon), offering cycles of pleasure and pain that bind women without any single sovereign to blame. Rather than banning Barbie (the failed 'Happy to be Me' doll), she proposes subversive play — Plump and Proud Barbie, Mursi lip-plate Barbie — as Heyes-style 'practices of freedom.'

objectification.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
objectification.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Pierlott examines sweatshops in the garment industry through the lens of ancient Cynicism (Antisthenes, the Stoics' Zeno of Citium and his thieving slave), using the Cynic critique of fashion-driven consumption to strip legitimacy from the demand that feeds sweatshops. He rebuts the 'inevitability argument' (comparing it to excusing the Holocaust as inevitable) and the free-choice defense using Aristotle's category of 'mixed' action — sweated workers' consent is coerced by desperate alternatives — and argues, via Adam Smith on the undervaluing of labor, that giant retailers like Wal-Mart distort natural labor prices. He stresses that sweatshops overwhelmingly exploit young women, tying objectification of women as fashion consumers to their oppression as producers.

objectification.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
objectification.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
objectification.relation: Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.

objectification.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
objectification.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
objectification.relation: Nancy Kang argues tattoos can function within a liberatory feminist ideology, accentuating rather than diminishing femininity by exposing the differential treatment of tattooed women. She surveys radical, Marxist, liberal and corporeal feminism (invoking Aristotle's dismissal of women, Mill's Subjection of Women, and Gramsci's hegemony), then reads pop-culture cases – Crash's tattooed Latino worker, Black Swan's Lily, the Perry 'pricks as needles' sexualization, carnival 'Tattooed Ladies' like Irene Woodward marked 'by the father's hand,' and the McGee/Bullock/Kat Von D scandal – to show corporeal feminism treats tattooing as a risky, self-owning revolutionary act.

objectification.book: 284 - College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits
objectification.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
objectification.relation: This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.

objectification.book: 284 - College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits
objectification.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
objectification.relation: This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.

objectification.book: 284 - College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits
objectification.title: College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits
objectification.relation: The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.

objectification.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
objectification.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Luna Dolezal's 'Yoga for Women?' argues that Western yoga, once a male ascetic path, has been absorbed by consumer capitalism into a female beauty practice organized around 'body capital.' Reading Yoga Journal covers, Lululemon's 'Say No to Camel Toe' ad, and Toesox's nude campaigns, she shows the fashion/beauty industries cultivate shame to sell the yoga body, objectifying women. She counters that Hatha yoga should be a laboratory for compassionate self-acceptance beyond comparison and competition — 'yoga for every body' — rather than another instrument of the market's normalized ideal.

objectification.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
objectification.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Nicole Dunas's 'The Feeling of Beauty' recounts founding the Real Beauty Yoga Project after a teacher-training 'modeling day' where consultants photographed only the five thinnest students, enacting division rather than yogic union. Framing the beauty question against Kant's claim that beauty is objective, and drawing on David Abram's participatory perception and Susan Bordo on airbrushed bodies, she argues that objectifying beauty into an image to be gazed at (the male gaze, the isolated cosmetic-surgery gaze) severs us from it, whereas Hatha yoga's tantric, present-moment embodiment lets beauty be lived rather than consumed.

objectification.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
objectification.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.

objectification.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
objectification.title: BLUES
objectification.relation: Meghan Winsby answers George Carlin's gibe that white people have nothing to be blue about by arguing that women — black or white — legitimately sing the blues because they share an experience of oppression. She applies Iris Marion Young's 'five faces of oppression' (exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, violence) to women's silencing, sexual objectification, and gender exploitation, showing that early blueswomen (Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, Memphis Minnie) and later ones (Bonnie Raitt) asserted sexuality and independence against a patriarchal order. She then weighs, without fully endorsing, the moral cultural-appropriation and audience-appropriation objections (via James O. Young) to white men playing the blues.

objectification.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
objectification.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.

objectification.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
objectification.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
objectification.relation: Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.

objectification.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
objectification.title: 63. Amy Schumer as Philosopher Fuck the Feminine Mystique
objectification.relation: Elsby argues Amy Schumer's honest comedy revolts against a 'feminine mystique' broader than Friedan's housewife version, running back to Beauvoir's claim that woman is constructed as the 'Other' and to Aristotle's 'rational animal' definition that cast women as irrational and thus less than human. Through bits like 'Madame President,' 'Last Fuckable Day,' the 'New Twitter Button' sketch, and gross-out honesty about pregnancy and her own body in Growing and The Leather Special, Schumer refuses to let women's physical, sexual, and social experience stay mysterious. Elsby reads this as de-'othering' and re-humanizing women by forcing our concept of 'woman' to expand to include flawed, fully human hot-mess figures.

male-gaze.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
male-gaze.title: Unknown
male-gaze.relation: The chapter catalogues the film's penetration scenes—the Agents' scorpion bug forced through Neo's navel, its bloody extraction, the fetal pod farm and 'birth' down the flush tube, the acupuncture rebuilding, the neck-plug uploads, and finally the bullets he becomes immune to—arguing that Neo's arc ends in a perfect, closed body with no vulnerability and no relation to actual flesh. It attacks the gender stereotypes: Trinity is reduced to a decorative, nurturant sidekick who never hacks and exists as love interest, the Oracle is a cookie-baking 'Mammy' figure, and there are no female Agents—the machines are sexist too.

male-gaze.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
male-gaze.title: Poker and Philosophy
male-gaze.relation: Housel surveys a century of poker on screen — from the Tombstone Birdcage Theater's 'bird in a gilded cage' through Maverick, The Gambler, Rounders, and ESPN's Tilt with its brothel-break 'Matador' — to show women cast as eye-candy, damsels, or flukes (Joanne Woodward winning a high-stakes game without knowing how to play). Against the myth stands Annie Duke, who beat her brother Howard on the way to the 2004 Tournament of Champions title. The argument: poker rewards reading and projecting emotion, so women socialized into emotional intelligence hold an edge over macho men who suppress it — a retooled Stoicism fusing Epictetus's 'make the best use of what is in your power' with Gilligan's care ethics, backed by Nietzsche's trust in the senses and Sun Tzu's 'pretend inferiority and encourage his arrogance.'

male-gaze.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
male-gaze.title: James Bond and Philosophy
male-gaze.relation: Arp and Decker examine Bond's objectification of women - using a dancing girl as a human shield in the Goldfinger pre-credits sequence, M ordering Bond to 'pump her for information' - through three moral theories. Kant's humanity formula condemns treating women as sexual tools, but Kantian autonomy generates a stalemate since consensual, reciprocal liaisons like Bond and Anya Amasova's might qualify as permissible; Millian utilitarianism condemns the male gaze by its long-term social costs yet stalls against pro-sex feminist counterarguments. They settle on Aristotelian virtue ethics - the mean between extremes, with respect as the key virtue against the power-centered virtue of Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Nietzsche - to argue objectification is vicious, and they trace Bond's moral progress from skipping the young Bibi in For Your Eyes Only to the reciprocal relationships with Kara Milovy, Pam Bouvier, Wai Lin, and Jinx.

male-gaze.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
male-gaze.title: The Price of Existence
male-gaze.relation: Bonnie Mann reads Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" whose existence has meaning only in orbit around Edward, clumsy, self-sacrificing, carried and watched, living the myth of the eternal feminine in which the masculine gaze confers being on a girl otherwise taught the world is defined without reference to her. She locates the fantasy's pull in the contradictory messages of twenty-first-century girlhood (Pipher, Phillips, Bordo), where being attractive to boys remains the first avenue to existing at all. Yet she also finds a feminist subtext: the vampire transformation returns Bella to the "I can" body, faster and stronger than Edward and saving the day herself, though Meyer ultimately re-sells the old promise that a woman wins existence through self-annihilation for others.

male-gaze.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
male-gaze.title: With or Without Starbuck
male-gaze.relation: Ewan Kirkland argues BSG's gender-free surface, unisex bunks and a Starbuck who never has to defend her right to fly, masks a default masculinity under Adama's patriarchal regime: Ellen is killed off as the negative femme fatale, Kat and Cain die or turn monstrous, and 'The Farm' literalizes feminist fears of patriarchal medicine turning women into breeders. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze, never objectified, repeatedly rescuing men and reversing damsel-in-distress plots, yet her success is entirely masculinized, bought by becoming like a man.
