Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.

culture-industry.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
culture-industry.title: Go Slowly
culture-industry.relation: Wittkower frames In Rainbows' pay-what-you-want release with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry: music is expressive communication awkwardly trapped in commodity form — even 'Happy Birthday' has an owner until 2030 — and digital distribution is finally tearing that frame down. He then applies Rawls's justice as fairness to music distribution: the first principle now supports everyone's liberty to listen, rip, and share, because viable alternative models mean restricting listeners can no longer be justified as necessary to artists; and the difference principle, with the sadists-objection to utilitarian aggregation, shows that how benefits are distributed among persons matters, which he extends to racial wealth gaps and the affirmative-action dilemma. His conclusion is that we must 'go slowly': listeners' rights to their culture outweigh labels' legitimate profit expectations, the way emancipation outweighed plantation business models, and labels must adapt into service providers rather than gatekeepers.

culture-industry.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
culture-industry.title: Social Networking - How to Win Virtual Friends and Influence Virtual People
culture-industry.relation: Written as a breakup letter to Facebook, the chapter first reconstructs the Frankfurt School hope that new media could overcome old mass media's passivity — Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, Althusser's ideology as the form of media — and then tests the site against Ivan Illich's criteria for 'convivial tools.' Briggle finds Facebook fails on Illich's terms: its public walls and News Feed force self-censored persona management before a mixed audience, and its shapeless, undifferentiated flood of updates leaves the user disoriented like Nietzsche's madman after the death of God. Because the site's 'grain' channels users into 'reluctant, hapless exhibitionism' and even imposes the obligation to join, he logs off, concluding that tools reflect our image more than they remake it.

culture-industry.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
culture-industry.title: The Dalek Within
culture-industry.relation: Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.

culture-industry.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
culture-industry.title: Chapter 09 - Matt Damon Is a Vast Sinister Conspiracy
culture-industry.relation: Argues that 'Matt Damon' is an industrially manufactured person — a simulacrum sustained by executives, marketers, and gossip media that exploits instincts once used to judge trustworthy tribemates. Reading David Norris's tie-choosing specialists in The Adjustment Bureau, Tyrell's 'More human than human,' and the novels The Simulacra and Time Out of Joint, it claims Dick's paranoid fantasy is true: manufactured fake realities keep us docile, distracted, and consuming so we never notice we would rather be lying on a rock in the warm sun.

culture-industry.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
culture-industry.title: Chapter 33 - “The Gun”
culture-industry.relation: Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.

culture-industry.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
culture-industry.title: Mad Men
culture-industry.relation: Auxier argues rock periodically cleanses itself of commercial packaging, citing Hall and Oates versus Johnny Rotten and Culture Club versus Kurt Cobain as each era's corrective upheaval. The Madison Avenue 'Mad Men' sell kids sanitized three-minute morsels like Herman's Hermits, but the kids' own bottled energy finds ground anyway, and once they 'get their ya-yas out' the packaged pop stops working. The Stones enter as the real rhythm that arrives when something has to be put 'under the whip.'

culture-industry.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
culture-industry.title: Girls and Philosophy
culture-industry.relation: Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.

culture-industry.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
culture-industry.title: 16. European Intellectuals Follow Charlie Brown!
culture-industry.relation: The chapter traces how European intellectuals legitimized Peanuts: Eco read the strip as mass culture whose repeated patterns expose a microcosm of the human condition (children warped by industrial civilization, Lucy as contemporary values incarnate), while Bassano di Tufillo finds 'sociable individualism' and, via Bateson and aboriginal spirituality, an ecological vision granting animals, trees, and school buildings equal dignity. It then applies Heidegger's distinction between calculative and reflective thinking to management: Lucy's rigid direction of the Christmas play ('You've got to have respect for your director!') is calculative leadership that treats people as resources, while Charlie Brown's refusal of the All-Stars sponsor - which would have expelled girls and Snoopy - models the authentic, reflective organization that values dignity and diversity over results.

culture-industry.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
culture-industry.title: 18. Psycho-Politics in a Burnout Society
culture-industry.relation: Pagnoni Berns and Aguilar read the show through Byung-Chul Han's philosophy: in the transparency society everyone stacks their life online - Krista is transparent to Elliot because her password is Dylan and her birthday, while he stays opaque - and psycho-politics replaces Foucauldian punishment with seduction, a digital panopticon (Operation Berenstain, Minister Zhang) whose inmates voluntarily build it. Elliot's attention deficits, Tyrell's breakdown over Sharon Knowles's corpse, and Gideon's fatigue embody the burnout society's neuronal violence, and even fsociety reproduces the systemic coercion it fights, leaving 'real life' only outside the system.

culture-industry.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
culture-industry.title: 19. Please Tell Me You’re Seeing This Too
culture-industry.relation: Ehrnberger argues Mr. Robot hooks us like a Trojan horse: Todorov's 'ambiguity of the fantastic' - the irresolvable hesitation over whether Elliot's world is real or imagined - makes his unreliable narration endlessly rewatchable, which is how a mainstream network show smuggles in Adorno's critique of the very culture industry that airs it. Adorno explains the sedation Elliot decries ('we wanna be sedated') and why enlightenment reverts to mythology - meritocracy, consumerism, digital connection as modern myths we no longer recognize as myths - while Ehrenberg's 'illness of responsibility' explains why freed people retreat into the comfort of those myths rather than bear freedom's weight.

culture-industry.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
culture-industry.title: 19. Looking Like Number 12
culture-industry.relation: Busk argues 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' disturbs because it dramatizes Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry: standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects, and Marilyn's forced Transformation into Number 8 — complete with 'Instant Smile' — is the literal industrial production of a person with the capacity for critical resistance stripped out. 'The After Hours' extends the point, with mannequin Marsha as the culture-industry subject reduced to a plastic prop granted brief prearranged 'free time,' and he ends on Adorno's residual hope: the very existence of these failed protesters, like the theory itself, proves some subjectivity survives the system.

culture-industry.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
culture-industry.title: Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”
culture-industry.relation: The Forests ask whether Westworld is self-referential modernist art or 'meta-kitsch,' reading the park's dueling productions (Sizemore's clichéd narratives versus Ford's ambitions, with Cullen's corporate meddling mirroring HBO's pressure on Nolan and Joy) through Kant's relocation of aesthetic judgment to the subjective, Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch divide, Adorno's contrast of liberating autonomous art with standardized heteronomous commodity culture, and Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles. Guests mistaking Teddy for a fellow guest and actors' 'reverse-reveries' show that host/guest indiscernibility mirrors the show's own indiscernibility from formulaic prestige TV. Their conclusion: the series counts as art rather than entertainment only for 'autonomous viewers' alert to its self-referential critique, the viewer-side counterpart of Dolores's 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free.'

culture-industry.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
culture-industry.title: 1. Free Falling into Postmodernism
culture-industry.relation: Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.

culture-industry.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
culture-industry.title: 12. When Money Shouldn’t Be King
culture-industry.relation: Berkey reconstructs Petty's two industry battles, the bankruptcy gambit to void the contract sold along with Shelter Records and the month-long standoff against MCA's $9.98 superstar pricing, then reads The Last DJ as Petty's considered position on the business of music. He argues Petty rejected subjectivism about music's value: because listeners can be mistaken about the value of their own enjoyment, a formal argument shows executives like "Joe" who program only what profits act wrongly, even if consumers willingly pay. "Money Becomes King" completes the critique, showing how profit-focus degrades the fan's quasi-religious concert experience and corrodes Johnny's motivation to make valuable music at all.

culture-industry.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
culture-industry.title: 32 - Dreamers in the Night [ ]
culture-industry.relation: This fan-fiction interlude dramatizes the fandom debate aboard Galactica: Roslin voices the Frankfurt School view (a 'Scorpion School' of Adorno and Benjamin - mass culture as mindless absorption, reproduction destroying the artwork's aura), while aide Billy cites Henry Jenkins and Textual Poachers to defend fanzines as participatory culture repairing corporate ownership of myth, and a fan meeting wins the President over as community-building. Baltar and inner Number Six extend the argument: Six demands 'the singular truth of the show' against fan rewriting, and Baltar answers that the Cylons are themselves a fanfiction of the human brain - twelve unoriginal faces. Starbuck is revealed as the anonymous fanfic writer.

culture-industry.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
culture-industry.title: Resistance
culture-industry.relation: Reading Fifteen Million Merits through Marx, the chapter treats Bing's world of endless pedaling, Wraith Babes, and Hot Shot as a commodity society in which people themselves carry use and exchange values — Oliver the 'lemon,' Glee deemed 'quite worthless,' Abi's unsellable papier-mache penguin discarded as detritus. Marx's commodity fetish explains the universalized pricing in merits, and Lukacs-style reification shows things commanding people (Cuppliance compelling compliance). Adorno's culture industry explains why all the shows share one form and why Bing's glass-shard rebellion is absorbed as just another commodity, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man supplies the hope that reason, love (Bing's love for Abi as something 'real'), and switching off the media can still seed resistance.

culture-industry.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
culture-industry.title: The Real World
culture-industry.relation: Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.

culture-industry.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
culture-industry.title: Things Worth Believing
culture-industry.relation: Butterfield stages the Frankfurt School critique of her own Disney love: Marx's three alienations (from work, from others, from species-being) explain the Seven Dwarfs' 'dig dig dig' and the FastPass-scheduled vacation that converts leisure into consumption, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man diagnoses the parks' engineered euphoria and 'false needs' as a 'comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom' that blunts protest — with Adorno adding that consumers see through the advertising and buy anyway. Against the critic, she argues a Disney trip done right can challenge alienation by reviving play, family togetherness, and childlike belief in 'things worth believing.'

culture-industry.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
culture-industry.title: 19. Looking Like Number 12
culture-industry.relation: Busk explains why 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' is so disturbing despite having no monsters: through Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects whose critical capacities and powers of resistance atrophy until difference itself looks pathological, as with Marilyn's doctors diagnosing her refusal. 'The After Hours' extends the diagnosis, with mannequin Marsha as the subject reduced to an industrial prop granted brief furloughs of 'free time.' Yet the very existence of Marilyn's and Marsha's doomed protests, like Adorno and Horkheimer's own theory, shows some subjectivity survives the production line.

culture-industry.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
culture-industry.title: Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”
culture-industry.relation: Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.

culture-industry.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
culture-industry.title: The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers
culture-industry.relation: R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.

culture-industry.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
culture-industry.title: Film Noir and the Frankfurt School America as Wasteland in Edgar Ulmer's Detour
culture-industry.relation: Cantor argues that Ulmer's Detour deconstructs the American dream in a manner that closely parallels the Frankfurt school's culture critique. Al Roberts's westward journey toward success collapses into crime and doom, dramatizing Horkheimer and Adorno's claim in 'The Culture Industry' that Hollywood sells the masses an illusory lottery of hope (Haskell's horse 'Paradisical,' Sue's failed stardom) to reconcile them to capitalism. Cantor ties Roberts's disgust at jukebox music and his 'jazzing up' of Brahms directly to Adorno's polemics against mechanical reproduction and Benjamin's loss of the artwork's aura. He finally suggests both Ulmer and the émigré Marxists project a European elitist alienation onto an America they picture as an empty wasteland.

culture-industry.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
culture-industry.title: The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis
culture-industry.relation: Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.

culture-industry.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
culture-industry.title: Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville
culture-industry.relation: Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.

culture-industry.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
culture-industry.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
culture-industry.relation: Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.

culture-industry.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
culture-industry.title: On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society
culture-industry.relation: Stefanie Baumann reads Herzog's attack on the 'accountant's truth' of the Minnesota Declaration alongside Horkheimer and Adorno's critical theory, arguing that the cult of facts reifies perception, creates norms, and serves the 'administered world' via the culture industry. She contends Herzog's films (Lessons of Darkness, Fata Morgana, Aguirre, The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser) resist this not by escaping society but by dialectically mediating singular, uncategorizable outsiders through the historically developed social order — Kaspar Hauser's 'obstinate otherness' exposing the social violence of enforced assimilation, a subversive constellation rather than an explicit political message.

culture-industry.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
culture-industry.title: 3 Lawsuits, Master Narratives, and Artistic Commodification
culture-industry.relation: Mitchell examines Young's Geffen-era lawsuit (sued in 1983 for "uncharacteristic" music like Trans and Everybody's Rockin') and the competing rebel/misunderstood-artist/lost-in-the-video-era narratives around it. Using Heilbroner on capitalism's commodification of rebellious art and Mark Fisher's "capitalist realism" and pre-corporation of dissent (Cobain as spectacle), he argues that Young himself actively authored the "rocker-turned-folkie" and anti-commercial persona, so that even his gestures of resistance to the music business were absorbed as marketable integrity.

culture-industry.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
culture-industry.title: The Dalek Within
culture-industry.relation: Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.

culture-industry.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
culture-industry.title: The Doctor Dances
culture-industry.relation: Alexander Bertland uses Vico, Cassirer, and Horkheimer and Adorno to argue Doctor Who refuses to simply side with science over myth. Vico shows myth as world-constructing ritual that binds community and carries moral wisdom ('Snakedance's' Snakedance defeats the Mara; 'Meglos' shows myth's danger), while Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment argues science is itself a limiting, mythical framework: the Doctor's insistence that 'fixed points' in time cannot be changed ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Waters of Mars') reflects his own self-constructed scientific paradigm, not real necessity. The Doctor lives well by humbly balancing myth and science.

culture-industry.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
culture-industry.title: 3. Success and Failure of Punk
culture-industry.relation: Stock reads failure as fused into punk's circuitry from its origins: the 'WE KILLED ELVIS' billboard was a lie, since the Pistols, Clash, Ramones, and Damned covered their heroes and signed to majors. In a sequence of numbered theses built on Debord's Society of the Spectacle, Malcolm McLaren's Situationist merchandising, the Bill Grundy TV appearance as the moment punk became spectacle, and Adorno on the New Music, he argues punk's absorption into the spectacle of capital dooms it - Sid Vicious and Ian Curtis are 'authenticated' only by dying into pure spectacle - so to succeed as punk is to fail and to fail is to succeed.

culture-industry.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
culture-industry.title: 10. The Post-Punk Struggle for Authenticity
culture-industry.relation: Kohl traces post-punk's shift from outward models of authenticity - Sex Pistols shock tactics, Sid Vicious's swastika, Gang of Four's Rock Against Racism activism - to inward ones, arguing the culture industry co-opts both spectacle and virtue-signaling, turning dissent into image. Post-punk's pessimist intellectual influences (Schopenhauer, Dostoevsky, Camus's The Stranger behind The Fall's RAR disenchantment) and Nietzsche's Zarathustra - the herd, the last man, keeping chaos within to give birth to a dancing star in Magazine's 'Shot by Both Sides' - plus Kierkegaard's 'the crowd is untruth' and subjectivity-is-truth, are read into Joy Division's ambiguous lyrics as a defensible, ethically uncommitted inward authenticity.

culture-industry.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
culture-industry.title: 12. Early Punk and the Dionysian Lion-Child
culture-industry.relation: Rentmeester reads early punk through Nietzsche's three metamorphoses of the spirit: the Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' (the Thames boat arrest during the Silver Jubilee) is the lion destroying worn-out values, while the Stooges' 'I Wanna Be Your Dog' and Raw Power embody the child's sacred Yes, making punk a hybrid Dionysian lion-child. Punk is Dionysian rather than Apollonian - raw instinct over measured restraint, Iggy Pop's self-mutilation and the Gzowski interview - with 'camelistic' pop and soft rock critiqued via Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, and Sid Vicious's violence named as Freud's death drive.

culture-industry.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
culture-industry.title: 18. Wartime Propaganda as Punk Critique
culture-industry.relation: Karen Fournier reads Julien Temple's 1979 film short Punk Can Take It as a bricolage of the 1940 wartime propaganda film London Can Take It!, hijacking its searchlights, steel helmets, and BBC announcer John Snagge's narration to recast the story as class warfare: the wartime 'people's army' produced a generation of working-class punks betrayed by postwar promises. Scenes like mannequins attacking a window dresser, tuxedoed Oxford-Cambridge types invading the pit, and a punk mob toppling a Johnny Rotten statue dramatize the real enemy: a corporate consumer culture that annexes the subculture and reduces it to mass-produced 'punk' products. The chapter argues that punk film, like Jamie Reid's safety-pinned Union Jack, turns the dominant culture's own tokens against it.

culture-industry.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
culture-industry.title: 8. Between Cynicism and Faith
culture-industry.relation: Buhlert contrasts the Apple TV+ series' reverent treatment of religion (the sincere anti-science faith of Synnax, the elaborate Luminism whose 'walking the spiral' ritual seems to vindicate that clones lack souls) with Asimov's cynical originals, where religion is Marx's 'opium of the people'. She shows the fake religion of Scientism in 'The Mayors' and the hypocritical Askonian elders in 'The Traders' treat faith as an instrument of control, situates this within Golden Age SF (Leiber's Gather, Darkness!, de Camp's Lest Darkness Fall) and its techno-optimism, and speculates on why the showrunners omitted Scientism.

culture-industry.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
culture-industry.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
culture-industry.relation: Gerald Erion reads The Daily Show through Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, arguing that Stewart's opening headline mockery of hurricane 'reporters in canoes,' 'Senior Correspondents,' and graphics packages like 'Mess O'Potamia' targets not the day's events but television's own entertainment bias, which renders even serious news trivial. He treats Stewart's Crossfire plea to 'stop hurting America,' the Jim Cramer 'Brawl Street' interview, and the Rally to Restore Sanity's '24-hour politico pundit perpetual panic conflictinator' as Postman-style critiques that a medium built to amuse cannot carry rational public discourse.

culture-industry.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
culture-industry.title: 19. Looking Like Number 12
culture-industry.relation: Busk reads 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' through Horkheimer and Adorno's 'culture industry' and a philosophical account of subjectivity as active, critical agency. Marilyn's forced 'Transformation' into a standardized model (with banned books, 'Instant Smile,' and 'super soccer') dramatizes how commodified mass culture produces conformist, mannequin-like subjects who cannot resist—linking it to 'The After Hours,' where Marsha is literally a department-store mannequin. Yet Marilyn's and Marsha's very existence, like Adorno's theory, is a faint hopeful sign that critical subjectivity survives.

culture-industry.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
culture-industry.title: Gertrude McFuzz Should’ve Read Marx, or Sneetches of the World Unite
culture-industry.relation: Jacob Held uses the Once-ler, Pontoffel Pock, the Sneetches, and Gertrude McFuzz to explain Marx's theory of alienation. The Once-ler is the capitalist owning the means of Thneed production; Pontoffel Pock's dull pickle-works job shows labor severed from the worker's essence as a free, conscious producer (an idea Held traces to Hegel on self-expression through work). The Sneetches buying stars from Sylvester McMonkey McBean and Gertrude popping pill-berries dramatize how alienated people chase belonging through consumption, which Held elaborates via Fromm's 'having vs being' and Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, concluding the fault lies not in the characters but in a society that denies self-realization through labor.

culture-industry.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
culture-industry.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
culture-industry.relation: Wear traces the espresso aesthetic from the idealized, egalitarian Italian caffè—which he reads as an 'aestheticized Marxist' image of identical shots for businessman and street sweeper—to its dilution under neoliberal consumer choice, epitomized by the endless-customization L.A. Story 'half-caf twist of lemon' scene. He invokes Kant's Critique of Judgement and the sublime to argue that flavor and taste-judgment are neglected aesthetic faculties, and enlists the Frankfurt School (Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse) and Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain how the market absorbs the espresso's beauty. He concludes that a single humble shot, as a memorial to the vast exploited labor chain behind it, is a truer aesthetic object than a branded frappuccino.

culture-industry.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
culture-industry.title: The Fall of the House of Ulmer Europe vs. America in the Gothic Vision of The Black Cat
culture-industry.relation: Cantor reads Edgar Ulmer's The Black Cat (1934) as a European emigre's Gothic allegory of Europe vs. America, with Karloff's architect Poelzig and Lugosi's psychiatrist Werdegast as mirror-image 'living dead' fixated on the horrors of World War I. He connects Poelzig's modernist house-over-Fort-Marmaros to a Freudian map of ego and id and to the war-driven rise of psychoanalysis, and reads the naive, unconscious American honeymooners against the cultured but nihilistic Europeans. He explicitly links the film's high-culture/pop-culture opposition to Heidegger's vision of Europe squeezed between a leveling America and Russia and to the Frankfurt School critique of American mass entertainment.

culture-industry.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
culture-industry.title: Kitsch and Camp and Things That Go Bump in the Night; or, Sontag and Adorno at the (Horror) Movies
culture-industry.relation: Johnston uses his childhood TV horror host Sir Graves Ghastly to distinguish kitsch from camp in the horror genre. Drawing on Greenberg's 'Avant-garde and Kitsch' and Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, he argues that the Universal Horror sequels, Jaws, and most slasher films are kitsch: nonchallenging, formulaic variations that pacify consumers, while autonomous works like Carpenter's They Live or Craven's Scream interrogate the genre. Via Sontag's 'Notes on Camp' and Isherwood's making-fun-of versus making-fun-out-of, he sorts They Live, Scream, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Scary Movie into deliberate camp, naive camp, and mere kitsch.

culture-industry.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
culture-industry.title: NOTES
culture-industry.relation: William Irwin's introduction argues philosophy must engage popular culture rather than fear it as Plato feared Homer and the poets. He invokes Plato's allegory of the cave to make the case that the philosopher who has left the cave must return and 'learn to see the shadows again'—use The Simpsons, The Matrix and Seinfeld as the vernacular through which prisoners can be led out—and answers Adorno-style culture-industry worries that mass entertainment is mere opiate. He closes by echoing Aristotle's serious treatment of the popular art (tragedy) of his day as warrant for treating today's pop culture philosophically.

culture-industry.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
culture-industry.title: NOTES
culture-industry.relation: Irwin asks 'what is popular culture?', rejecting Noel Carroll's 'mass art' accessibility criterion (using the Sex Pistols, Slipknot and the Beatles as counterexamples of inaccessible-yet-popular art) and Walter Benjamin's aura/mechanical-reproduction account, settling on popular culture as 'artifacts and subjects of mass interest and appreciation.' He rebuts Adorno's and Zizek's culture-industry charge that pop culture (e.g. The Matrix, The X-Files) ideologically ensnares audiences, and again deploys Plato's cave and the returning prisoner—citing Socrates meeting interlocutors where they are—to justify using pop culture as a bridge to philosophy while warning against 'abuse' (studying pop culture as philosophy).

culture-industry.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
culture-industry.title: NOTES
culture-industry.relation: Richard Shusterman defends the entertainment value of popular art from a pragmatist ('meliorist') stance, tracing entertainment's genealogy through Plato, Aristotle, Montaigne, Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Adorno—whose 'culture industry' opposes pleasure to cognition. Using rap (KRS-One's 'Edutainment', Public Enemy, Ice-T) and T.S. Eliot's 'superior amusement,' he argues knowledge and enjoyment are compatible. He rejects Hannah Arendt's contrast of imperishable art vs. life-serving entertainment, and critiques G.E. Moore's Principia Ethica 'method of absolute isolation' for intrinsic value, replacing it with a Deweyan transactional account in which even intrinsic values are relational and temporal.

culture-industry.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
culture-industry.title: NOTES
culture-industry.relation: South reads Batman, Batgirl, and Catwoman comics through J. M. Bernstein's Adorno-derived account of the 'damaged life' lived under Weberian rationalization and the disenchantment of the world. The Joker's 'one bad day' in The Killing Joke embodies 'affective skepticism'—the split between rational universal norms and agent-specific motivation—while the debate between moral internalism and externalism (which he ties to Kant-style abstract justification) expresses the hurt of a disenchanted world where justifying and motivating reasons no longer converge. Barbara Gordon's 'because I can,' Bruce Wayne's vow, and Selina Kyle's turn toward 'basic human dignity' exemplify Bernstein's 'fugitive ethics,' fragile promises that restore authority outside juridico-legal channels and produce genuine happiness in damaged lives.

culture-industry.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
culture-industry.title: 21. Black Mirror as Philosophy A Dark Reflection of Human Nature
culture-industry.relation: The chapter asks whether Black Mirror condemns technology or human nature, and argues for the latter: the 'black mirror' reflects the viewer's character. It tests and rejects the reading of the show as depicting Bostrom-style existential risk or superintelligence (via 'Metalhead' and 'San Junipero') and rejects that Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind coupling (the 'grain' in 'The Entire History of You,' 'Arkangel,' 'Crocodile') destroys human identity. Drawing on Frankfurt School critique—Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry, Marcuse's one-dimensional man—and Plato's and Aristotle's natural-versus-artificial distinction, it concludes technology is an agency-less imitation that magnifies preexisting human vices, and closes with Benjamin's reproducibility thesis and Bandersnatch's interactivity to suggest the show can prompt viewers to confront their own darkness.

culture-industry.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
culture-industry.title: 40. Deadpool as Philosophy Using Humor to Rebel Against the System
culture-industry.relation: Brake argues that Deadpool advances an implicit thesis about humor as a threefold vehicle of liberation, testing it against Horkheimer and Adorno's Frankfurt School charge that the culture industry produces interchangeable, aesthetically impoverished pop-culture 'trash' (the formulaic MCU) that pacifies workers, and Marcuse's warning that revolutionary material gets absorbed as just another commodity. Following Kathryn Tanner's rejoinder that consumers can creatively repurpose pop culture, he shows Wade Wilson's self-mocking, fourth-wall-breaking humor achieving personal liberation from tragedy (invoking Freud on humor as the ego's assertion of invulnerability), liberation from the oppressive Mutant Factory by exposing Ajax/Francis's vulnerability and asserting his own autonomy, and a partial liberation from superhero genre tropes, while conceding humor's reactionary tendency to reinforce the status quo since Deadpool ultimately reproduces the genre and hands Disney its money.

culture-industry.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
culture-industry.title: 79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine
culture-industry.relation: Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

culture-industry.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
culture-industry.title: Welcome Aboard the TARDIS—It’s Bigger on the Inside
culture-industry.relation: The author argues that Doctor Who functions as a 'great educator' that shapes viewers' reality and their conception of the good life, framing our birth into the world as being 'thrown' into a new environment we must assimilate. He applies Hegel's historical dialectic to the Doctor-versus-Daleks conflict, treating the Doctor (wisdom, liberty, compassion) and the Daleks (obedience, hatred, conquest) as opposing theses whose ongoing struggle synthesizes the wider universe's fear of the Daleks. Drawing on Carroll and Danesi, he claims pop culture like Doctor Who validates experience and creates collective structures of meaning, and that our chosen first Doctor becomes the interpretive framework through which we judge every later one.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Unknown
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: The chapter contrasts Kant's Real (a noumenal domain perceived through the screen of categories) with Hegel's (the screen itself is the distortion, so subtracting it loses the Thing), and reads the Matrix as the screen that is also the Real distorting our perception. Lévi-Strauss's Winnebago village drawings—the same village drawn as concentric or split circles by different moieties—show two symbolic attempts to heal an unsymbolizable social antagonism, a structure the chapter extends to sexual difference (Lacan's homme/femme over two identical doors) and left/right politics, with the nation as the 'zero-institution', ideology at its purest, in which social antagonism is obliterated.

kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Harman argues the real heroes of Easy Rider are the two Harley-Davidsons: the exploding Captain America bike that drowns out its rider's corpse, the cocaine hidden in the gas tank like a prosthetic organ, and the obscured helmets and muffled dialogue reduce Fonda, Hopper, and Nicholson to 'stowaways and parasites' of their machines. He uses this reversal to attack Kant's Copernican Revolution, on which we could know only how Harleys appear to us and never the things in themselves, and to champion the Whitehead-Deleuze-Latour current in which genes, pickup trucks, bridges, and Harleys are autonomous actors no less than humans, against Plato's two-world heir of appearances and unknowable things. Billy and Captain America's 1960s transgression, he concludes, quietly ends in submission to the power, rhythm, and demands of their bikes.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: The Verdict
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Turner runs an ethical audit of iPod use through Levinas's face-to-face: sharing one iPod with his wife forces 'musical justice' negotiations (veto power over a Motörhead cut, gnashing through Bette Midler), his toddler son's listening requires vigilance, and illegal downloading fails Levinas's test that morality begins by ceding 'my place in the sun' to the Other — hence Radiohead's pay-what-you-want release as the Levinasian move, and iPod cafés where strangers DJ for each other while language preserves alterity. Heidegger supplies the counterweight: the shuffle's 'openness to mystery' versus calculative mastery that reduces The Who's Tommy to the 'Pinball Wizard' riff and silences all non-digital media, just as Kant's conditions of possible experience (space, time) would silence things outside them. Derrida's point that categories contain traces of what they exclude illuminates unclassifiable marginal works — bluegrass Pink Floyd, San Francisco Symphony plays Metallica — and the verdict closes with Hölderlin's 'where danger is, grows the saving power also', exiting Plato's cave by thinking the iPod's ethics at all.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Barkman argues that anime's Christian imagery — the legendary Santa on a cross, Earthian's gay angel lovers, Trinity Blood's bishonen pope and female cardinal, Evangelion's hostile Angels — encodes Japanese religious pluralism rather than orthodox Christianity. He lays out the pluralist position (following Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction and John Hick: Ultimate Reality is only equivocally describable, so doctrine matters less than spiritual mood), contrasts it with exclusivism and inclusivism, and charges pluralism with self-undermining intolerance, then traces Japan's historical demonization of Christianity from the 1637 Shimabara massacre (Ninja Resurrection, Samurai Champloo) to Eva's alien invaders, with Armageddon imagery fueled by the atomic bombs. Because Shinto-Buddhist-Daoist anti-realism dissolves fixed categories, anime dissolves good and evil (Chrno Crusade's I Ching balance) and gender itself, gravitating to the symbol-rich 'jungle' of Catholicism (C.S. Lewis's phrase) — and where Trinity Blood lets some vampires be righteous, Augustine's City of God marks the one nearly orthodox note.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Escape to Doctor Who
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Reads the Master as the personification of Schopenhauer's blind, pointless Will: the Doctor's line 'In many ways we have the same mind' is taken literally, so the Master is the dark noumenal side in everyone, seen in the hypnotized Farrel whose ambition the Master acts out and Colonel Trenchard whose patriotism becomes the Master's weapon in 'The Sea Devils'. Building from Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction, he explains the Will as the inaccessible force we glimpse through inner bodily awareness, evil because purposeless. Watching the Doctor's serial victories is then offered as a light, Schopenhauerian escape through art from the terror of the Will.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: The Outer Workings of the Mind
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: The chapter has Kant complete the flip of Descartes: we know the self only indirectly and external objects directly, because the mind is a car factory that shapes raw material into everyday experience, so you inspect only the finished products, reverse-engineer the assembly line from them, and the thing in itself stays forever outside knowledge. Rotoscoping becomes the visual correlate: reality is partly constructed by the mind but not totally, and the philosophical task is figuring out which parts of the scene are ours.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Vannatta's introduction frames the volume with a traffic-intersection metaphor: Klosterman's campaign against the phrase 'guilty pleasure' questions whether the one-way roads of high and low culture are real at all, and the contributors deliberately violate the traffic rules (Kierkegaard meets KISS, Baudrillard meets Britney Spears). It reads Klosterman's line that 'nothing is ever in and of itself' through Kant's noumena-phenomena distinction: like Kant's knowing subject, we never reach the in-itself but only perspectives refracted through rock bands, sports teams, and TV. The introduction presents the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City (identity effaced to imitate an equally constructed identity) and the rock-death road trip of Killing Yourself to Live as Klosterman's way of recovering authenticity, arguing that living with the possibility of one's own death is more authentic than fleeing it.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Cogburn and Hebert sort fantasy magic into formulaic natural magic (wizards as scientists exploiting a world's universal laws, in Kant's sense of nature—Salvatore's Cadderly, Snape's potions, Eberron's Artificer), sublimate natural magic (shamans, sorcerers, and warlocks surrendering to forces, as in African diaspora possession religions), and unnatural magic that violates a world's laws, whose horror Sartre's Nausea passage about flesh rebelling captures. Using Lovecraft's indescribable monsters and Noël Carroll's theory of art-horror as categorical impurity (with Mary Douglas on Leviticus-style purity codes), they argue Fourth Edition's algorithmic spell rules make casting feel like chemistry homework rather than the impossible, so unnatural magic cannot be modeled ludologically. Dungeon Masters must instead express the inexpressible through narrative techniques—character reaction, reader-relative impossibility, and limit impossibility—since D&D at its best is shared storytelling, not rule fetishism.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Franklin Allaire uses Cliff Clavin's defiant 'Who are three people who've never been in my kitchen?' on Cheers to stage the fight between modern and postmodern theories of knowledge. He rehearses Plato's Theaetetus account of knowledge as justified true belief, Descartes's cogito, and Kant's thing-in-itself as modernity's quest for objective truth via universal intersubjective agreement, then argues through Foucault and Deleuze that Trebek and the judges are gatekeepers whose power controls the narrative - his Civil War renaming example ('What is the War of Northern Aggression?') shows many knowledges competing for one answer. On this view, Cliff's insistence that different questions can fit the same answer exposes the non-objectivity of Jeopardy!'s 'objective' knowledge, making the barfly a postmodern champion.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Knepp asks why Jobs's 'simplicity is the ultimate sophistication' produced the friendly, MoMA-collected Macintosh (the face-like design, the inviting handle, the signed internals) but collapsed into the $6,500 NeXT Cube, answering with Žižek's reading of Hegel in Less than Nothing: the original idea is already self-contradictory, the failure of NeXT (the over-engineered perfect cube, the $100,000 Rand logo trying too hard to be friendly) is its symptom, and the iMac is the second attempt that only the failed first choice makes possible. He grounds this in Kant's Critique of Pure Reason—the antinomies and the phenomenon/noumenon distinction that Hegel radicalized into a world driven by oppositions—finding the dialectic everywhere in Jobs: two sets of parents, orchards and Silicon Valley, 'Apple' as both high-tech and organic, and a childish lowercase signature made with grand cursive flair.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: 2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . .
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.

kant-phenomena-noumena.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Baltzer-Jaray uses Kant's phenomena/noumena split, Plato's Forms, and Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to ask whether Jack Skellington can know the essence of Christmas and whether Vincent Malloy can know what it is to BE Vincent Price. She argues Jack's lab-experiments on presents and snowflakes ('Jack's Obsession') can only yield phenomena, never the noumenal essence, so Kant would permit belief but not knowledge; Vincent, watching only Price's horror roles, grasps a mere phenomenal fragment. Via Nagel she concludes neither can occupy another's subjective viewpoint, so the lesson of both films is to celebrate otherness through communication rather than trying to be someone else.

kant-phenomena-noumena.title: We Are the Change That We Seek
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Todd McGowan argues Interstellar enacts Hegel's critique of substance: the NASA scientists' 'they' who supposedly placed the wormhole is a Kantian thing-in-itself - the unknown deified by ignorance - until the Tesseract reveals that Cooper himself, and future humanity, are both Murph's 'ghost' and the 'they' ('We brought ourselves'). Against Spinoza's single substance and Leibniz's windowless monads, the film teaches that substance is subject, freeing Cooper and Murph to act and to change the past through retroactive causality, which the chapter connects to Sartre on the past's fixedness and Walter Benjamin's critique of historicist causality. Professor Brand's Plan A lie and Dr. Mann's self-exculpating murder show the ethical catastrophe of claiming a substantial, subject-transcending standpoint, while Murph - who treats her 'ghost' as just another subject rather than a supernatural substance - is the film's true hero.

kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Escape to Doctor Who
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: On Beyond Modernity, or Conrad and a Postmodern Alphabet
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Jacob Held explains postmodernism as Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives' using On Beyond Zebra! Conrad's twenty-six-letter alphabet is the metanarrative that fixes what can be said and known, while the narrator's invented letters (Yuzz, Snee, Floob) show language expanding to present the unpresentable. Held casts Kant's three Critiques, phenomena/noumena, and his defining of the mind's 'alphabet' as the exemplary modern grand narrative Lyotard rejects, then turns to Foucault's Nietzschean genealogy, using You're Only Old Once! for the medicalization of life and (via a Beauvoir quotation) the claim that gender is a constructed mechanism of control that can be transgressed.

kant-phenomena-noumena.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
kant-phenomena-noumena.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
kant-phenomena-noumena.relation: Kakko's 'Hallucinatory Terror' uses Fitz Hugh Ludlow's 1857 The Hasheesh Eater to ask 'How can these things be?' — the ontological status of hallucinations that neither exist nor fail to exist. He traces Ludlow's own reading from Locke's empiricism through Hume's skeptical worry that all perception may be hallucinatory with no verifiable external object, to Kant's Copernican turn: the phenomenal/noumenal distinction, synthetic a priori judgments, and space and time as pure forms of intuition. Kant's framework lets Kakko recast Ludlow's 'virtual change of worlds' as a literal, non-metaphorical restructuring of the intuitions conditioning experience.

hegemony.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real
hegemony.title: Unknown
hegemony.relation: The chapter contrasts Kant's Real (a noumenal domain perceived through the screen of categories) with Hegel's (the screen itself is the distortion, so subtracting it loses the Thing), and reads the Matrix as the screen that is also the Real distorting our perception. Lévi-Strauss's Winnebago village drawings—the same village drawn as concentric or split circles by different moieties—show two symbolic attempts to heal an unsymbolizable social antagonism, a structure the chapter extends to sexual difference (Lacan's homme/femme over two identical doors) and left/right politics, with the nation as the 'zero-institution', ideology at its purest, in which social antagonism is obliterated.

hegemony.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
hegemony.title: The Gift of Baseball
hegemony.relation: McDaniels reads the Negro Leagues through Nietzsche's account of resentment as revolt and Cornel West's tragic philosophy of resistance: excluded from the white majors after Cap Anson's 1887 stand against George Stovey, black players converted resentment into counter-narratives of excellence, with Satchel Paige, Josh Gibson, and Buck O'Neil showboating and clowning in the tradition of plantation dance, gallows humor, and the blues. The call-and-response sermon scene from The Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars & Motor Kings — Bingo Long on the mound answered by the crowd like a black church congregation — shows performance as ritual that sustains community, while bell hooks's 'absence of presence' frames remembering as resistance to hegemonic definitions of race. The chapter closes with the author's grandfather, for whom Robinson, Aaron, Mays, and Paige proved with every pitch 'We're American Too.'

hegemony.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
hegemony.title: After . . . Word!
hegemony.relation: Marcyliena Morgan's afterword traces hip-hop battling to the philosophical houses and crews of Saturday kung-fu cinema (Wu-Tang's obsession included), reading hip hop's South Bronx birth through Victor Turner's ritual threshold state and defining "flow" as conscious movement within chaos to create balance and collective identity. The mantra represent-recognize-come correct, shout outs as a system of indexicality, and hip hop's counterpublic sphere function, she argues, to expose hegemony and contest Foucault's technologies of power - answering Cornel West's "ignoble paradox of modernity" - so that hip hop battles through the theoretical houses of Foucault, Bakhtin, Butler, Gramsci, and Habermas, where "there is no such thing as a dead philosopher - just one that has not been resurrected yet."

hegemony.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
hegemony.title: Playlisting the iPod White Soul
hegemony.relation: Austin unboxes his new black iPod Classic to argue that its true constant -- the glowing white body, white click wheel, and above all the white earbuds -- makes it 'the quintessential contemporary White good': an industry standard whose supremacy mirrors the invisible default of whiteness described by Richard Dyer and whiteness studies, from white magic versus black to white lab coats and the 'flesh-colored band-aid.' Using Said's Orientalism -- the West strong, rational, and civilized against a binary-opposite Orient -- he reads iPod history as racial history: blackface minstrelsy, black vinyl and the sociable jukebox supplanted by white digital privatization, Black musical forms sanitized into the white 'mainstream,' and colored 'skins' as cosmetic diversity over the unchanged white core. bell hooks's challenge to white theorists to interrogate whiteness rather than only Blackness supplies the chapter's imperative to re-experience this most mundane object critically.

hegemony.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
hegemony.title: Unity in Diversity
hegemony.relation: Lombardo asks whether the podcast, born as an unsanctioned side effect users reinvented out of the iPod (as hip hop reinvented the turntable before corporate co-option made it the hegemonic form), can be a public-sphere institution. Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.

hegemony.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
hegemony.title: Coda
hegemony.relation: Bowman surveys the fifty-four recorded Rush tributes of 1996-2005, from the Barenaked Ladies quoting the 'Tom Sawyer' swagger riff in 'Grade 9' to DJ Z-Trip's trip-hop remix, Disarray's death-metal version, Deadsy's industrial take, and string-quartet translations, arguing that Rush's ambiguous genre coding is what lets this 'musicians' music' travel across mutually exclusive fan communities. He builds his own 'scholarly meta-remix' interleaving six versions of 'Tom Sawyer' in different keys and meters, and reads the 7/4 instrumental section's fate in each cover. Borrowing Robert Walser's claim that musical meanings are grounded in an ideological field where institutions enforce preferred meanings, he concludes that tribute artists find 'refractive, distorted, and disruptive' meanings in Rush, and that progressive rock served as 'substitute classical music' for working- and lower-middle-class fans.

hegemony.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
hegemony.title: Outro
hegemony.relation: Asks how Rush is Canadian: CanCon radio quotas, the band's hybrid of British prog and Anglo-American hard rock, and McLuhan's 'flexible' national character, before a detailed musical reading of 'The Trees' — its 6/8-to-4/4 shifts, countertenor outburst, and woodpecker solos — as an aural 'Royal Commission' that may satirize legislated equality like Canadian content regulations defending against US media dominance. Bakhtin's monologic worldview frames the Oaks, and the chapter closes with later Canadian signs from the inukshuk cover of Test for Echo to Trailer Park Boys.

hegemony.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
hegemony.title: Society’s a Bad Hit (If You’re Banging Up, Cranking, or Popping)
hegemony.relation: This section argues A Scanner Darkly's primary philosophical contribution is the recognition that the fate of Dick's drug circle was social violence against those who did not fit in: dominant California normalizes the apathetic, slothful 'straights' of the Brown Bear Lodge while phone-tapping peace advocates, ransacking writers' homes, and hunting or abandoning drug users whose pain gets attributed to addiction rather than rejection. The Thelma Kornford mosquito-hawk episode, the deposition about color TVs, animals, and My Lai, and Donna's final 'It is easy to win' all expose how winning requires never choosing your own values.

hegemony.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
hegemony.title: The Problem with Drugs
hegemony.relation: The closing section rebuts the communitarian defense of California's drug laws, noting there is more than one community and most people belong to several, then turns to Douglas Husak: moral rights exist to protect persons from majority interference, and the crusade against drugs is cultural hegemony. Cocaine, marijuana, and opiates were outlawed along racial lines (blacks, Mexicans, and Chinese respectively) while the ruling class's alcohol and tobacco remained 'autonomous choices,' suggesting the real problem with drugs is who uses them.

hegemony.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
hegemony.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
hegemony.relation: The chapter argues the Bro Code's real value lies not in getting laid but in structuring homosocial bonds, listing its best articles (loyalty, equality, generosity) alongside its most sexist ones (the Hot/Crazy Scale, Article 101). Karioris explains men's competitive relations through hegemonic masculinity - the school-bully dominance that forces all masculinities to compete and pushes women out - and invokes Foucault's 'Friendship as a Way of Life' for how bonds between men can escape taboo and emotional distance. Robin as wingwoman ('a better Ted than Ted') and the gang's gender transgressions show the Code can be amended toward equality, with Aristotle's friendship of mutual cooperation and benefit, 'quid pro bro', as the standard.

hegemony.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
hegemony.title: 2. Peculiar!
hegemony.relation: Ketcham reads the faction system as the Bureau's behavioral-correction experiment after a eugenics disaster, and compares the Bureau to the Tuskegee syphilis study: subjects who never gave informed consent, were denied treatment, and were treated as expendable because 'the experiment must continue at all costs.' He maps W.E.B. Du Bois's 'twoness' - double consciousness - onto Tris, who thrives in Dauntless yet belongs to no faction, and onto Tobias, whose identity collapses when he learns he tests as merely Dauntless. Closing with Gramsci, he argues Chicagoans have bought into the oppressor's story about genes and factions, so they need an organic intellectual to lead them out of the cave, and proposes Freire's praxis as the unfinished sequel.

hegemony.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
hegemony.title: 4. The Liberating Power of Nanny Ogg’s Bouncing Bosom
hegemony.relation: Froehlich reads Witches Abroad through Mikhail Bakhtin's theory of carnival and the grotesque from Rabelais and His World: Lily Weatherwax's palace ball is 'high culture' as tyrannical hierarchy, while the Genua street carnival, Nanny Ogg's bouncing bosom, and Baron Saturday's untamable swamp bring grotesque low-culture energy that crashes the ball and shatters Lily's frozen fairy-tale order. Against Bakhtin's pessimism that carnival merely lets the oppressed blow off steam, the chapter argues that Granny Weatherwax and Nanny break the cycle, giving Genua a real chance at self-determined, more fun lives.

hegemony.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
hegemony.title: 13. How to Be a Dwarf
hegemony.relation: Using Carrot (a human raised in a dwarf mine who is accepted as a dwarf), Cheery Littlebottom (an openly female dwarf), and Gladys the golem, the chapter argues that social identity is neither biology nor a one-time choice but an ongoing performance that must also be recognized by insiders and outsiders. It applies de Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' to Cheery's creation of a female dwarf gender against the deep-downers' equality that treats every dwarf as male, and reads the black ribboners versus the Magpyrs as assimilation versus doubling down on identity. Essentialist outsiders like Fred Colon and the Campaign for Equal Heights fail because they cling to stereotypes when individuals like Cheery or Carrot do not fit the mold, while Vetinari's indifference and Mrs. Cake's accommodations leave identity to those who must choose and perform it.

hegemony.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
hegemony.title: 12. The Law of Red Rising
hegemony.relation: Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.

hegemony.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
hegemony.title: 23. A Chimichanga for the Mercenary Soul
hegemony.relation: Through Gramsci's Prison Notebooks the chapter casts Deadpool as the 'Eternal Proletariat': the military superstructure (Weapon X) recruited him precisely because he was broke and class-positioned, and as a mercenary he has no capital, no upward mobility, and no exit from wage-killing. His hunger beyond money - the Bullseye payday that ends in him shooting himself, the dead shark's verdict 'what you are . . . is alone' - drives him toward the X-Men, read as a subaltern coalition of the marginalized like Gramsci's socialist parties. But as a non-mutant 'mutate' who cannot meet the hegemonic standard of heroism (the Hit-Monkey arc with Spider-Man, his bitter plea to Wolverine that 'at least they wanted you'), his only Gramscian options are coalition building or reshaping the X-Men's culture from inside.

hegemony.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
hegemony.title: 7. A Life Along the Watchtower
hegemony.relation: Reads 'All Along the Watchtower' as a dialogue between the Joker's Sartrean being-and-nothingness ('none of them along the line know what any of it is worth') and the Thief's Heideggerian reply — being-toward-death, anticipatory resoluteness, care, and the fallen 'they.' It argues Hendrix lived this struggle: the mirror-smashing of 'A Room Full of Mirrors,' the unborn speaker of 'Belly Button Window' who will throw himself into the world rather than be thrown, and the 'Electric Church Music' built to cut through 'they'-thinking and return listeners to child-like authenticity. Gramsci's point that oppressor and oppressed alike internalize the oppressor's message names the hegemony Hendrix's third way — neither victim nor revolutionary — simply denies.

hegemony.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
hegemony.title: 3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over
hegemony.relation: Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.

hegemony.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
hegemony.title: Hey Goofy! Somebody Just Slipped My Culture a Mickey…
hegemony.relation: Schuchardt argues Disney's real product is 'getting you in there' — colonizing the geography of the imagination: Pirates of the Caribbean is read as an allegory of corporate globalization, White Wilderness fabricated the lemming-suicide myth, and the parks' visual containment keeps visitors inside a world with 'more reality than nature' (Eco's hyperreality, in Baudrillard's territory). He claims Disney built this on Jung's archetypes via Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey under the mantra 'We Create the Mythology of the Future,' so that media consolidation (the Fox merger shrinking six conglomerates to five) narrows the Overton Window and Disney's manufactured mythology displaces Christianity as the reigning worldview.

hegemony.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
hegemony.title: 2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic
hegemony.relation: Walderezak tracks Tom Branson's trajectory from Marxist-quoting socialist chauffeur to estate manager, arguing that the show quietly makes Robert, not Tom, the 'real socialist.' Robert's aristocratic conservatism is read as noblesse oblige (funding the hospital, the Downton Fair, and secretly paying a tenant's arrears), while Matthew's capitalist drive for 'investment, increasing productivity, and reducing waste' is presented as the profit-first ownership system that Marx and Fourier actually criticized. Tom's socialism, closer to the utopian visions of Robert Owen and Charles Fourier than to Marx's class struggle, dissolves as he assimilates into the family ('I haven't abandoned all of my socialism, although sometimes it feels like it'), a capitulation the chapter explains through David Harvey's 'capitalist pacification,' whereby capitalism absorbs all facets of society. The chapter concludes that Robert's treatment of ownership as a duty owed to tenants approaches the cooperative ideals of Fourier and Owen more than Tom's abandoned radicalism ever did.

hegemony.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
hegemony.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
hegemony.relation: Timm uses Bourdieu's forms of capital (economic, social, cultural) and habitus to explain why Panem needed no brute force for seventy-five years: District 12's school teaches the Hunger Games as normal, doles out history as 'what we owe the Capitol,' keeps districts ignorant of each other, and trains Seam children for the mines, so education reproduces inequality instead of curing it. Katniss and Gale's hunting and trading skills are only 'resistant cultural capital' — worthless to Capitol taste but a habitus of lawbreaking that made rebellion thinkable for them alone. Katniss's public defiance exposes the 'wavy squares' in the force field of taken-for-granted power, and the chapter likens her fate to Socrates, condemned by Athens's holders of capital yet igniting a revolution in values.

hegemony.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
hegemony.title: 17_LaRocca_Chapter_016.html
