Shawn's generosity (helping the wrongly accused, the ghost-struck, and the deluded, once even crediting a cat with solving murders in '9 Lives') is read as the noble overflow of superabundant power rather than pity, and his hostage-saving risk-taking as will to power understood as self-mastery. Even the central lie gets a dialectical reading - like art, pretending to be psychic reveals the truth hidden behind appearances - though the chapter concedes Shawn's slavish moments, from daddy issues to his obsession with one-upping Declan in 'Shawn 2.0.'

will-to-power.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
will-to-power.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'

will-to-power.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
will-to-power.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Jeffery Nicholas argues Card tries to write Ender as Nietzsche's self-sufficient superman - Graff's isolation program, the will to power, and Rackham's 'humanity does not ask us to be happy' - but the novel actually vindicates Aristotle's claim in the Politics that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Ender's difference from the beast-like Peter and the hive-minded buggers, his longing for Valentine, Alai, and Petra, and his despair in isolation show that friendship, not domination, is what makes him human.

will-to-power.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
will-to-power.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Jeff Ewing reads the park as Nietzsche's will-to-power in action: Hammond's 'creation is an act of sheer will', resurrecting extinct species because science enables it, is the drive to remake the world godlike in one's own image, and Malcolm's 'so preoccupied with whether or not they could' marks exactly the external mastery Hammond achieved. But the Nietzschean great man also needs internal mastery - control over himself before control over nature - and Hammond failed it: one man (Nedry) held the whole security grid, frog-DNA surprises were foreseeable, raptor intelligence was underestimated, and the storm was ignored. For Nietzsche, lying to yourself about your strength is not arrogance but weakness, so Hammond's disaster was not a moral crime but a failure of self-mastery - a lesson Ewing extends to modern cloning, drones, and weapons pursued without honest reckoning.

will-to-power.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
will-to-power.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Noel measures Jobs against the four cardinal virtues from Plato's Republic and finds him wanting: imprudent (NeXT, the Lisa), unjust (taking the GUI from Xerox PARC, 'more fun to be a pirate'), intemperate (cruel outbursts like the 'dogshit for icing' cake), with only a brash, mind-changing courage. Drawing on Aristotle's golden mean from the Nicomachean Ethics, Nietzsche's master-slave morality and his Will to Power line about the man who 'determines values' for millennia, and Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, he argues entrepreneurs are a breed apart whose real virtues are independence of mind, vision, and audacity—and that Jobs, the anti-social creator who would not fit in, changed the world precisely because the cardinal virtues were 'prison walls' to him.

will-to-power.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
will-to-power.title: Dracula and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.

will-to-power.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
will-to-power.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Martyn Jones stages a fictional Nietzsche telling Mac, Dennis, and Charlie the plot of 'The Gang Solves the Gas Crisis' as a parable of metaphysics gone wrong. Mac and Dennis's scheming is Apollonian - imposing logical order and 'paradigms' on a recalcitrant world - while Charlie is Dionysian, the designated wildcard whose uncontainable energy (sabotaging the van and ripping out the brakes) dooms every plan that tries to harness him, since Apollonian schemes fatally imagine they can contain Dionysian force. Reason is a gloss, not a truth-tracker: like every theology and philosophy it is an expression of will, a survival tool serving selfish ends, so the delusional gas scheme needs no truth to serve its purpose. Charlie alone is praised as a proto-Übermensch - innocent, creative, founding his own values without resentment - and the tale closes musing that even an eternal recurrence of their botched schemes might be willed all over again.

will-to-power.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
will-to-power.title: 14. The Doctor’s Desire for Human Suffering
will-to-power.relation: Cooper reads 'Rise of the Cybermen' and 'The Age of Steel' as staging Nietzsche against Mill's pain-eradicating utilitarianism: John Lumic, who builds the Cybermen to abolish his sickness, exemplifies the life-denying herd—losing his creativity, craving 'unity and uniformity,' becoming 'a living brain with a heart of steel'—while the Doctor, answering that a life without pain would be 'you might as well kill me,' affirms suffering as the source of creativity, striving, and strength. She extends the Nietzschean reading to the Doctor's character: his guilt over the Time War double-genocide and his loneliness ('the only certainty left is that you'll end up alone') become the pain that makes him merciful, from offering Dalek Caan compassion after 'Evolution of the Daleks' to forgiving the Master in 'Last of the Time Lords,' so that mercy is, as the Genealogy of Morals says, 'the privilege of the most powerful man.'

will-to-power.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
will-to-power.title: 4. Nietzsche’s Faction Test
will-to-power.relation: Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.

will-to-power.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
will-to-power.title: 16. Empathy for the Devil
will-to-power.relation: Shaw explains our identification with Lecter through mirror neurons triggered by Demme's extreme close-ups, Lecter's impeccable aesthetic and culinary taste, his evil-genius plotting, and his choice of 'free range rude' victims — but the deepest ground is Nietzsche's will to power, quoting The Gay Science and The Antichrist on the feeling of power as what makes action valuable. Lecter is read as Nietzsche's Overman in complete control of himself, his environment, and his inferiors, and the TV series confirms the theory because, with the black humor and romance stripped away, Mikkelsen's Lecter out-plots Will, Jack and Alana alike and walks triumphant from the Season 2 finale, having played everyone 'like his beloved Theremin'.

will-to-power.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
will-to-power.title: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
will-to-power.relation: Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.

will-to-power.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
will-to-power.title: 21. Batman Is Superman
will-to-power.relation: The chapter argues that Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, is Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian emotion and Apollonian reason - vengeance against justice in Batman Begins - and who relives his traumas as Nietzschean eternal recurrence, from the bat-filled well to the prison leap of The Dark Knight Rises. The Joker is his dark double, whose will to power and ferry-boat experiment nearly extinguish Gotham's hope, but Batman absorbs the chaos and sacrifices his heroic name, whereas Superman in Injustice, losing Lois, falls into a vengeful Dionysian abyss he cannot master. Only a mortal who extends his limits without succumbing to the herd's 'gravity of madness' can be Nietzsche's superman, so the mortal, conflicted, imitable Batman is the true superman.

will-to-power.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
will-to-power.title: 22. The Irrelevance of Truth
will-to-power.relation: Jan Kyrre Berg Friis argues, with Nietzsche, that truth is a 'mobile army of metaphors', a relational event between people rather than an objective correspondence, and that the will to truth is subordinate to the will to power — the difference being that Trump-style 'alternative truth' is dishonest domination while Nietzsche's askesis is self-transformation. He layers in the Buddhist and Zen (Dogen) diagnosis of perception as conceptual distortion, Descartes' ego cogito as the fatal Western turn, and Heidegger's warning that calculative, technological thinking covers over our tacit lived background, producing exactly the one-dimensional minds a Ministry of Truth can feed. Rorty's advice to drop the truth-talk, Kant's insight that reality is sifted through the perceiver, and the cognitive-science of confirmation bias explain why facts no longer bite in the post-truth newsfeed.

will-to-power.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
will-to-power.title: “I Always Felt this Place was Missing a Real Villain. Hence, My Humble Contribution.”
will-to-power.relation: Eberl asks whether living out Sizemore-style fantasies can reveal or only corrode character: applying Aristotle's account of virtues and vices as habituated dispositions, he argues William's three decades in the park habituated the vices that made him the Man in Black — the park reveals rather than suspends the self — while cruelty toward humanlike hosts hardens us toward people, as Aquinas and Kant warn about kindness to animals. Against Ford's claim that humans are wantons in tight loops, Maeve's editing of her own code after learning her escape was scripted makes her a Frankfurtian person who aligns first-order desires with second-order volitions, grounding her narrative identity and personhood. William too attains personhood by actualizing a second-order desire for a different life, with the hosts' free fight back evoking Nietzsche's will to power and Nozick's point that we want to actually do things, not merely experience them.

will-to-power.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
will-to-power.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
will-to-power.relation: Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.

will-to-power.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
will-to-power.title: 2. Echoes of Past and Present
will-to-power.relation: Crippen and Dixon treat the album Echo, written during Petty's divorce, heroin use and severe depression, as organized by crisis and reversion: its lyrics and productions compulsively echo earlier eras of his life, from 1950s TV westerns and his abusive father in "About to Give Out" to the Jeff Lynne years and Wildflowers in "Accused of Love" and "Echo." They invoke Freud and Lacan's psychoanalytic account of trauma repetition, where the past is relived in hope of a different outcome and sublimated into art. The album's sparse, energy-conserving repetition is then read through Nietzsche's will-to-power cycle, in which merely holding on is symptomatic of illness, yet the closing "One More Day, One More Night" and the album's very creation exemplify Nietzschean health as strength to expand against obstacles, since we possess art lest we perish of the truth.

will-to-power.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
will-to-power.title: 4. Tom Petty and the Meaning of Life
will-to-power.relation: Innes reads Petty through The Birth of Tragedy: Petty fuses Dionysian frenzy (the Oakland Coliseum "Makin' Some Noise" crowd as communal creation) with Apollonian form, and his refusal of genres, synthesizers and the hit-factory gives life the creative meaning Nietzsche demands. Jeff Lynne and ELO are cast as the contemporary Wagner, Socratic and Apollonian producers of pleasant ditties like "Don't Bring Me Down" that lack access to tragedy. Petty's "Trailer" models Greek tragedy (impulse as hamartia foreclosing freedom), while his lawsuits against MCA and The Last DJ dramatize the tragic bind that free musical expression needs the very industry that restrains it.

will-to-power.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
will-to-power.title: 8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need
will-to-power.relation: Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.

will-to-power.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
will-to-power.title: 5. Greatness or Nothingness
will-to-power.relation: Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.

will-to-power.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
will-to-power.title: Dull Reality The Tragic View of Life
will-to-power.relation: A Nietzschean interpretation: Alice's unastonished pursuit of the White Rabbit exemplifies the 'will to ignorance' hidden within the will to truth, since every perspective is created by selecting and simplifying while we convince ourselves we have discovered rather than invented. Rick Mayock reads the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and the mushroom as lessons in perspectivism and in the self as a grammatical fiction (no doer behind the deed, no lightning behind the flash), the Queen's beheadings and ruleless croquet as a flux of competing wills to power, and the Hatter's madness as Dionysian against Alice's Apollonian calm, with Greek tragedy supplying the metaphysical comfort that makes 'dull reality' livable.

will-to-power.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
will-to-power.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Reads Bluth contradiction through Kant's categorical imperative: Lindsay's lie about her shopgirl job, Gob's jealousy bred by comparative parenting, and George Michael's conformist drift show both the imperative's force and the danger of its empty formalism, while the 'Afternoon Delight' double entendres test whether good intentions suffice for Kantian worth. Nietzsche then answers that morality itself is the contradiction: virtue manufactured from ressentiment ('weakness is being lied into something meritorious'), the will to power turned inward as nihilism, with self-overcoming and value creation as the exit; Mary Douglas's joke theory closes the chapter by explaining why all this contradiction is comic and why the joke is on Gob.

will-to-power.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
will-to-power.title: Can You Face the Bat
will-to-power.relation: Sarah Donovan and Nicholas Richardson use Nietzsche and Foucault to present Batman as a self-constructed identity: across Batman: Year One, Arkham Asylum, and The Dark Knight Returns, Bruce consciously builds the persona ('Yes, Father, I shall become a bat') rather than revealing a deeper true self. Foucault's constructed categories of normal and abnormal surface in Arkham Asylum's 'super-sane' Joker and the Alice in Wonderland parallels that put Batman's own sanity in question alongside Amadeus Arkham's madness. Nietzsche's will to power and eternal recurrence, via the shepherd biting the snake in Zarathustra, explain why Bruce can face the bat that others flee, becoming heroic where Arkham and Dr. Cavendish go insane.

will-to-power.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
will-to-power.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.

will-to-power.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
will-to-power.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.

will-to-power.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
will-to-power.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Decker asks whether the 'Stephen Colbert' persona is the ironist of the Romantics and Rorty: the precise inverse of Socrates, who was declared wisest by the Delphic oracle precisely because he knew he knew nothing. Through Schlegel's Romantic irony, Hegel's complaint that the ironist abdicates responsibility, Kierkegaard's reading of Socrates as standing ironically above every relationship, and Rorty's ironist with her radically doubtable 'final vocabulary', he reads Colbert's self-redescription, Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear, and Super PAC stunt as exposing the contingency of political selves. Yet truthiness at its worst is dangerous subjectivism, and the chapter ends with Colbert breaking persona before Congress ('I like talking about people who have no power') as the non-ironic face that keeps the irony honest.

will-to-power.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
will-to-power.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Jeffery Nicholas contrasts the superman Card seems to write — Graff's isolated Ender conditioned to impose his will like Nietzsche's overman, for whom happiness is only the feeling of overcoming resistance — with Aristotle's claim that man is a political animal who cannot flourish without friends. Peter is Aristotle's 'tribeless, lawless, hearthless' beast, the speechless buggers lack a common good until the queen communicates with Ender, and Ender's despair lifts only through friendship with Valentine, Alai, and Petra, proving the novel a meditation on 'without friends no one would choose to live.'

will-to-power.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
will-to-power.title: Amos Is No Superman
will-to-power.relation: Pankaj Singh reads Amos through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Amos' division of people into 'bad ones, ones you follow, and ones you need to protect', his outsourcing of moral judgment to Naomi and Holden ('Naomi wouldn't like it'), his fearlessness, and his violent spontaneity make him 'evil' by slave morality yet good by master morality. Unlike Prax, who has to be stopped from shooting Strickland out of ressentiment, Amos kills without revenge ('I am that guy'), and his fistfights with Miller and Alex discharge hostility immediately so it never poisons — the strong natures Nietzsche praises that 'form, mold, recuperate and forget.' His 'crew comes first' and 'better to go down swinging' express the will to power as discharge of strength rather than mere self-preservation, but because he never sublimates or overcomes his drives, the chapter concludes Amos is no Übermensch — 'but then again, who is?'

will-to-power.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Argues the Underwoods act out historian James Truslow Adams' warning that the American dream, severed from the question of values, degenerates into a means-first pursuit of power — 'burning the barn to find our penny in the hay'. Using Nietzsche's ressentiment and above all Max Scheler's account of its systematic repression of emotion, the chapter reads Claire's repressed longings for motherhood (the 'What will we leave behind?' scene), integrity and love erupting as spite against those who embody what she sacrificed: firing and persecuting the pregnant Gillian Cole, destroying Adam Galloway, and abandoning Megan Hennessey. Michael Corrigan's suicide in his Russian cell — an integrity she cannot drag down to her level — finally shatters her ressentiment, and the chapter ends with her walking out of the White House as the escape Adams' question demands.

will-to-power.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure whose power play is staged through the show's postmodern techniques: the wave and the asides as metafiction that destroys our suspension of disbelief, self-referentiality in the mirror monologue ('Hunt or be hunted'), and a flattening of affect that lets us watch Zoe's murder at the train station with numbed indifference. Zarathustra's fearless overman is set against the risk-averse last man and the lambs-and-birds-of-prey passage against Christian slave morality, mapping onto Frank's breaking of Russo at the shipyard, the martyr's-sword maneuver on Blythe, and his spitting on the crucifix before taking 'God's ear'. The chapter reads Frank's ascent as will to power in both the political and personal Nietzschean sense, while warning that by Season 3 his hunger has cost him Jackie, Remy and Claire.

will-to-power.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Palm and Stikkers read the Underwoods through James Truslow Adams's American dream as a question of values gone rotten: lacking ends, they pursue power for its own sake while repressed longings (Frank's Sentinel camaraderie, song, and friendship; Claire's motherhood — 'What will we leave behind?') erupt as the ressentiment Nietzsche introduced and Max Scheler systematized, hating those who embody the sacrificed values. Claire's hatred thus targets Gillian Cole's pregnancy and integrity (fired, then threatened with letting her child 'wither and die') and Adam Galloway's freedom and love — Scheler's pedestal-smashing pattern — after the slave-morality-like repression of her normal human affects. The ressentiment finally shatters when Michael Corrigan refuses to betray himself and hangs himself in Petrov's cell: Claire tells the cameras the truth and walks out on Frank at the end of Season 3, free of the resentment.

will-to-power.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Aarons argues Frank is a Nietzschean Übermensch figure delivered through postmodern technique: the metafictional wave in 'Chapter 1,' self-referential mirror monologues ('Did you think I've forgotten you?'), and the flattening of affect in Zoe's death at the train station. Zarathustra's fearless overman, contrasted with the comfort-loving last man, maps onto Frank's 'hunt or be hunted' creed and his 'money is the McMansion in Sarasota... power is the old stone building' will-to-power, played out on Russo, Zoe, and Walker. The Genealogy's birds of prey and lambs frame Russo's Christian hypocrisy, and The Antichrist's equation of good with heightened power explains the church scene where Frank spits on the crucifix and leaves with the statue's ear — 'I've got God's ear now.'

will-to-power.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Meyer mounts the counter-case: Frank exemplifies Nietzsche's master type (good as good-for-him, 'no longer are we bound by allegiances') and Russo the slave type ('he who cannot command himself is commanded'), but the overman is a synthesis of neither. He corrects the Leopold-and-Loeb 'above the law' reading and the Cesare Borgia identification: the genuine overman sublimates strong drives into creation — Goethe's self-discipline, Beethoven's new norms — and affirms other wills in themselves rather than as instruments, which Frank never does with Zoe, Peter, or Claire. Frank's revenge-driven scheming is slave-like psychological warfare, ruling others is the 'pettiest' form of power, and by Season 3 he is the slave of his own presidency — destructive without creating, and lacking even amor fati.

will-to-power.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
will-to-power.title: 8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse
will-to-power.relation: Duncan Gale reads Raiders through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the Nazis' contempt for those they exploit ('They hire only strong backs and they pay pennies') enacts master morality, while their ressentiment-driven project is itself a fatal misreading — both of the Ark and of Nietzsche, whom Walter Kaufmann shows was distorted by his anti-Semitic sister rather than responsible for it. Indy emerges as an overman candidate whose improvised self-legislation ('I'm making this up as I go,' casually shooting the scimitar-wielding warrior) creates life-affirming values, unlike Belloq, who has no code at all. The finale inverts the death of God: the Nazis die because they disturb a divine power they cannot harness, while America's de facto agnosticism — warehousing the Ark with 'top men' — proves the survivable response to nihilism.

will-to-power.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
will-to-power.title: Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil
will-to-power.relation: Kristina Drzaic and Peter Rauch split Zelda play into two modes: the designed ludus game, in which Link is morally good by default (he cannot lie, steal, or hurt innocents), and player-generated paidia play through glitches, like making Link fly in Ocarina of Time or unlocking the Fierce Deity a day early in Majora's Mask, which crash the game but lie outside the story's morality. Using Caillois and Frasca on ludus versus paidia, they map this onto Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil: Link exemplifies slave morality (pity, patience, humility, avoiding fear) while the paidia player is a value-creating master who honors power and secrecy in gaming culture. The conclusion is that good-and-evil in videogames is welded to ludus, and some players just want to be naughty.

will-to-power.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
will-to-power.title: Will You Say Yes
will-to-power.relation: Michael Bruce ('Zeldathustra') reads the original Legend of Zelda through Nietzsche's thought of eternal recurrence: with no game clock, the ability to save, and looped enemy patterns, every playthrough repeats the same structure, and the player faces the demon's question — do you will to play once more and innumerable times more? The Triforce's split between Wisdom and Power becomes Nietzsche's opposition of the will-to-truth and the will-to-power, with Link's dungeon-by-dungeon self-overcoming enacting amor fati. Against Plato's two-world doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly, the chapter insists the game (like life) gets its meaning from this world only — experimentation, repetition as training, and saying yes.

will-to-power.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
will-to-power.title: Existential Values
will-to-power.relation: Belliotti tests Roger Sterling against three existential standards. Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage fits him 'crisply': his quips about the chase, drinking 'because it's what men do,' and the penny-jar view of marriage reveal flight from commitment and terror of boredom, and even his twenty-year marriage to Mona lacked Kierkegaard's passionate inwardness, making it objectively true but existentially inauthentic. Measured by Nietzsche he falls between the last man who wants an agency 'where everybody has a summer house' and the will-to-power grand transcender he never becomes, oscillating between frustration and boredom; measured by Heidegger he settles for chatter, clings to fixity, and reflects on mortality only briefly after his heart attacks. The verdict: significantly inauthentic, capped by the blackface 'My Old Kentucky Home' serenade that makes Don whisper 'Can we go?'

will-to-power.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
will-to-power.title: This Search Goes On: Christian, Warrior, Buddhist
will-to-power.relation: William Irwin traces Hetfield's journey through three sets of virtues: rejecting the Christian virtues of his Christian Science upbringing ('The God That Failed' as Nietzschean slave morality and Marx's opium of the masses), adopting the warrior virtues of Kill 'Em All (life as Hobbesian war, Nietzsche's will to power and 'no remorse'), and finally embracing Buddhist virtues on St. Anger. The warrior code fails without stoicism and collapses into addiction and despair, while the four noble truths - suffering caused by craving ('Frantic', 'Sweet Amber') - fit Hetfield's recovery and growing compassion.

will-to-power.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Argues Q embodies Nietzsche's revaluation of values: contemptuous of herd-like safety, Q subjects Picard and the crew to trials ("Encounter at Farpoint", "Hide and Q", "All Good Things"'s "the trial never ends") meant to force growth beyond conventional morality, seek out other "supermen", and embrace risk - Q's "bloody nose" defense after eighteen crewmen die at the Borg in "Q Who?". The Borg figure as everything Nietzschean individualism despises, a mindless collectivism that robs drones of the passion the strong need to individuate, and Q's offer to join Picard as guide pictures a friendship between Nietzsche's self-mastered few. The lesson of "Tapestry" is amor fati: Picard must embrace the Nausicaan knife fight that nearly killed him, since undoing it makes a safe, unnoticed man - though the authors finally refuse Nietzsche's harsher dictum that the weak should perish, siding with healing over Q's education-by-death.

will-to-power.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: MacMullan argues Darth Plagueis is a paradox for Plato: wisdom as reason ruling spirit and appetite should be impossible for a Sith who feeds on passion, yet Plagueis stays patient, restrained, and rational for over a century. He reads Sidious's 'I will make it legal' and the Sith Code as Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' and notes Plagueis even shares Plato's noble lie and eugenic breeding programs. Finding that Plato's prediction of self-destruction fails for Plagueis, the chapter turns to Nietzsche: master morality, the will to power, and life beyond good and evil better explain a Sith who cherishes bodily life and seeks to conquer death where Yoda and Socrates calmly disdain 'crude matter.'

will-to-power.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
will-to-power.title: Abilities Some Considered to Be Non‐organic
will-to-power.relation: Shores stages the fandom debate over 'Jake Skywalker' - Star Wars Theory's charge that Rian Johnson betrayed the character versus the Auralnauts' defense - and resolves it with Deleuze's forces of becoming, drawn from Nietzsche's will to power: bodies are whirlwinds of competing forces defined by affecting and being affected, and Luke's defining trait is extreme self-variance, from whiny farm boy and X-wing quitter to Trench Run hero. On this reading The Last Jedi's broken Luke is not a betrayal but a supreme becoming-other: his powers of transformation overpower even the Force's pull on Ahch-To, and his lethal Force projection exemplifies Deleuze's noble combat-between-oneself (the ascending, light-side will to become) rather than the Emperor's self-destructive will-to-dominate, the scorpion that cannot change its character.

will-to-power.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
will-to-power.title: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
will-to-power.relation: Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.

will-to-power.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
will-to-power.title: Notes
will-to-power.relation: Traces Cohle's opening monologue directly to Schopenhauer — reality as a purposeless will whose satisfied desires breed only boredom, answered by ascetic denial of the will-to-live rather than suicide. It then explains Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as the true test of life-affirmation, via the Gay Science demon and Zarathustra's ordeal with the Small Man, and interprets will to power as finding meaning in overcoming resisting conditions, so that affirmation does not mean approving everything that happens. Hatab argues the show's horrified version of the flat circle is Schopenhauerian rather than Nietzschean, and that Cohle's 'light is winning' ending is ambiguous — if it rests on a supernatural reunion with Sophia, it would betray Nietzsche's this-worldly affirmation.

will-to-power.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
will-to-power.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Rard tests whether any morality survives the apocalypse with an objective basis: Plato's Forms fail to capture changing facts (Hannah the bicycle girl decaying from mom to walker) and white lies, and Aristotle's function-based virtue ethics proves too relative and luck-dependent for survivors like Rick (rashness at Carl's shooting) and Shane (courage fetching supplies, rage at the barn). Nietzsche then supplies the frame: Hershel's barn of pitied 'sick people' is Christian slave morality that guilts the strong, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and forcing open of the barn doors grope toward a master morality 'for the Walker Age' without ever achieving nobility. Rick alone approaches the higher type, refusing to judge Lori's affair, insisting the baby be born, and embracing the post-walker world as one he would choose again.

will-to-power.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
will-to-power.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
will-to-power.relation: Joshua Crabill reads the hosts' awakening through Kant's story of Eve grasping autonomy and the etymology of autonomy as self-legislation, with Dolores swatting the fly and 'these violent delights' as her forbidden fruit. He uses Nietzsche's will-to-power turned inward to explain how the hosts' caged suffering builds an inner 'soul,' and Jaynes's bicameral commanding voice becoming one's own (Dolores hearing Arnold's voice turn into hers). Drawing on Korsgaard's reflective distance and Plato's divided soul, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own law), arguing that Korsgaard's 'determinism is no threat to freedom' lets Maeve, gaining admin access and choosing her daughter, genuinely 'write my own story.'

will-to-power.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
will-to-power.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Scott Parker argues that distance runner Steve Prefontaine, who finished a medal-less fourth at Munich 1972, embodied the true essence of the Olympics better than any champion, an essence he identifies with Nietzsche's 'higher man' and Emerson's self-reliance rather than winning. He aligns Pre's front-running, effort, confidence, and will with Nietzschean self-overcoming and life-affirmation and Emersonian self-valuation, arguing value is what the valuer assigns himself through hard work. Reading Pre's exhausted stumble to the finish as a possible enactment of amor fati, love of fate, Parker holds that if Pre did his best he should love rather than merely accept his defeat.

will-to-power.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
will-to-power.title: Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman
will-to-power.relation: Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.

will-to-power.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
will-to-power.title: The Human Comedy Perpetuates Itself Nihilism and Comedy in Coen Neo-Noir
will-to-power.relation: Hibbs argues that neo-noir turns classic noir's grim fatalism comic by making nihilism a working assumption, and that Nietzsche supplies the diagnosis: the 'death of God,' the passive 'last man,' and the aristocratic 'pathos of distance' of will-to-power super-antiheroes (Hannibal Lecter, the villains of Cape Fear/Basic Instinct). He reads The Big Lebowski as the Coens' comic leveling of nihilism, with Walter insisting the Germans are 'nihilists' and 'cowards' and the Dude 'abiding,' showing that full nihilism cannot be lived. In Fargo and Raising Arizona, Marge's 'banality of virtue' (a comic counterpoint to Arendt's banality of evil) and the resilience of familial/procreative instinct reassert a comic order over the noir trap.

will-to-power.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
will-to-power.title: From Sherlock Holmes to the Hard-Boiled Detective in Film Noir
will-to-power.relation: Jerold Abrams argues that the noir detective inherits the Holmes/Dupin detective logic but inhabits a fundamentally different maze. Using Eco's three labyrinths, he maps the classical Greek maze (with faith as Ariadne's string) and the mannerist maze (with Cartesian/Kantian pure reason) onto the escapable world of classic detection, and the Deleuzian rhizomatic maze, born after Nietzsche dissolved reason into will to power, onto noir's inescapable world (The Third Man, Kiss Me Deadly, The Maltese Falcon's fake statue). He shows both detectives use Peircean abduction (the logic of guessing) rather than pure deduction, illustrating it with knife-wound examples and Calloway's trapdoor inference in The Third Man, while the noir femme fatale becomes the anti-Ariadne whose thread of clues leads only to the hangman's rope.

will-to-power.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
will-to-power.title: Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard
will-to-power.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.

will-to-power.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
will-to-power.title: Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw
will-to-power.relation: Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.

will-to-power.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
will-to-power.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
will-to-power.relation: Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.

will-to-power.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
will-to-power.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
will-to-power.relation: Arnett reads Mann's 'modern crime films' through Nietzsche and Marc Augé's 'nonplace,' arguing Mann is a director-architect who exerts a will to power over institutional space (Atlanta's High Museum becomes Lecktor's prison in Manhunter; Neil's glass beach house in Heat). Mann's heroes are Nietzsche's 'godless' who refuse the herd, becoming Dionysian figures who redefine space—Neil and Vincent as Dionysian/Apollonian artists whose LAX showdown is a 'frenzy' of convergence. The endless recurrence of place-versus-nonplace, and Vincent killing Neil only to be trapped in supermodernity himself, dramatizes Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Dionysian pessimism.

will-to-power.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
will-to-power.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
will-to-power.relation: Skoble examines evil in Manhunter through the film's Nietzsche epigraph—'whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster'—as profiler Will Graham must 'become' Lecktor and Dollarhyde to catch them, risking his own psyche. Lecktor's claim that killing feels good because doing 'what God does' makes one godlike frames the killers' evil as a will to power. Skoble invokes the Socratic dictum that to know the good is to do the good, asking whether Dollarhyde's murderous 'becoming the Red Dragon' is a large-scale delusion, and warns that truly seeing the killer's fantasy risks adopting it.

will-to-power.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
will-to-power.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
will-to-power.relation: Sterritt reads Manhunter's Hannibal Lecktor as a perverse image of Nietzsche's Übermensch: hedonistic, ascetic, and expressing an overwhelming will to power, exercising superhuman self-control (his pulse never exceeding eighty-five while mutilating a nurse). Using Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming' and the body without organs, he contrasts the genuinely self-transforming Lecktor (a 'schizovivisectionist') with Dollarhyde, whose bogus becoming—trapped in Blake's 'mind-forg'd manacles' and the Red Dragon—makes him a pathetic tooth fairy rather than an overman, aligning both killers with Kierkegaard's demonic individual who stands above the universal.

will-to-power.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
will-to-power.title: The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis
will-to-power.relation: Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.

will-to-power.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
will-to-power.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
will-to-power.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.

will-to-power.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
will-to-power.title: Beating a Live Horse The Elevation and Degradation of Horses in Westerns
will-to-power.relation: Jennifer L. McMahon gives an existential account of Americans' ambivalence toward horses in westerns: because horses mirror human anxiety, herd-boundness, and the flight instinct that Sartre and Heidegger locate at the core of being, we transfer our self-loathing onto them and, driven by Nietzsche's will to power and Hegel's lord-and-bondsman struggle for recognition, we break them to prove our own mastery. Reading breaking scenes in All the Pretty Horses and The Horse Whisperer via Foucault's Discipline and Punish (the round pen as panopticon producing 'docile bodies'), she contrasts films like Hidalgo and The Electric Horseman that model Hegelian reciprocity, urging us to 'let go, turn in, and hook on' rather than dominate.

will-to-power.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
will-to-power.title: Life A Celebration
will-to-power.relation: Adam Riggio uses Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche to cast the Simm Master as a nihilist who, having seen the valueless dying universe at Utopia, wills nothingness and universal destruction out of ressentiment. The Doctor is Nietzsche's Overman who overcomes the reactive forces of revenge: in 'Dalek' he recognizes his own vengefulness and turns from it, and in 'Last of the Time Lords' he defeats the Master not with Martha's fake gun but by saying 'I forgive you,' affirming finite life with a 'beneficent Yes-saying' rather than surrendering to enmity.

will-to-power.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
will-to-power.title: 2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan
will-to-power.relation: Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.

will-to-power.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
will-to-power.title: 12. Early Punk and the Dionysian Lion-Child
will-to-power.relation: Rentmeester reads early punk through Nietzsche's three metamorphoses of the spirit: the Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' (the Thames boat arrest during the Silver Jubilee) is the lion destroying worn-out values, while the Stooges' 'I Wanna Be Your Dog' and Raw Power embody the child's sacred Yes, making punk a hybrid Dionysian lion-child. Punk is Dionysian rather than Apollonian - raw instinct over measured restraint, Iggy Pop's self-mutilation and the Gzowski interview - with 'camelistic' pop and soft rock critiqued via Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, and Sid Vicious's violence named as Freud's death drive.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: Introduction
will-to-power.relation: Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 1. How to De-Nazify Nietzsche’s Philosophical Anthropology
will-to-power.relation: Golomb argues the Nazi reading of the will to power as military conquest confuses Nietzsche's Macht (sublimated spiritual power) with Kraft (brute force) and Gewalt (violence), showing through Human, All Too Human and Daybreak that self-overcoming and creative sublimation, not domination, define the Übermensch. He builds a typology of 'positive' versus 'negative' power in which the anti-Semite figures as the vengeful, ressentiment-driven 'slave,' and insists Nietzsche's morality is not naturalistic—power must be transfigured by self-education—so his anthropology stands beyond the eugenic and racial distinctions central to Nazi ideology, even in the misused 'blond beast' passage.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 2. Misinterpretation as the Author’s Responsibility (Nietzsche’s fascism, for instance)
will-to-power.relation: Berel Lang asks whether an author is responsible for being misinterpreted, defining a 'Fascist Minimum' (priority of the state over the individual, plus natural inequality asserted through war) and testing Nietzsche against it. He finds Nietzsche flatly rejects the first condition—his 'coldest of all cold monsters' attacks on the state and nationalism—and accepts the second only with heavy qualification. Lang locates Nietzsche's partial culpability in a 'Fallacy of Composition' by which readers like Bäumler transposed individual will to power onto the collective state, arguing that Nietzsche, foreseeing this abuse, chose not to 'build a fence' around his meaning and so bears responsibility 'up to a point.'

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 4. Nietzsche and “Hitler”
will-to-power.relation: Nehamas puts 'Hitler' in scare-quotes to pose an abstract problem—does Nietzsche's ideal of nobility permit the evil hero?—rooting it in the Greek notion of aretê and Plato's Republic. He argues Nietzsche's own doctrine that 'there is no doer behind the deed' (Genealogy I:13) collapses the split between noble soul and noble action, so that deeds confer status; using the case of the police torturing a random woman and the fortuitousness of the Jews' extermination, he contends that when what separates us from victims is mere accident we are their peers, and Nietzsche needs the very doer/deed distinction he attacks in order to reject morality absolutely, so his refusal to condemn the evil hero can be refuted on Nietzschean grounds.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 7. Between the Cross and the Swastika A Nietzschean Perspective
will-to-power.relation: Wistrich answers the charge that Nietzsche was a philosophical godfather of fascism by marshalling his biography and letters—the 'shoot all anti-Semites' twilight notes, the rupture with the anti-Semite Förster and with Wagner, the praise of Heine, Offenbach, and Spinoza. He distinguishes Nietzsche's demonization of Christianity and priestly Judaism as the 'slave revolt in morals' from his admiration for biblical and Diaspora Jews as Europe's toughest race and a possible catalyst of the Übermensch, arguing that the Nazi and Hitlerian echoes (via Table Talk and Rosenberg's forgeries) grossly distort a 'good European' who denounced nationalism, racism, and the state-cult, and would have been repelled by the swastika.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 8. Ecce Caesar Nietzsche’s Imperial Aspirations
will-to-power.relation: Conway argues Nietzsche was not fascism's father but its 'godfather': openly contemptuous of nationalism and anti-Semitism, yet sharing its primal impulses. He reconstructs Nietzsche's fantasy of reviving a Roman-style pan-European empire (the 'new ruling caste' of Beyond Good and Evil), reading his admiration for Pilate's 'noble scorn'—'one Jew more or less, what does it matter?'—as Nietzsche's own ventriloquized wish to assimilate and neutralize the Jews he both needed and feared as the arch-enemies of empire. The chapter ties this imperial will to power and revaluation of noble-versus-slave values to Nietzsche's ambivalent Judeophobia, showing his cosmopolitanism was shallower than he claimed.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 9. A Question of Responsibility Nietzsche with Hölderlin at War, 1914 –1946
will-to-power.relation: Corngold and Waite argue Nietzsche programmed a deliberately esoteric doctrine of 'order of rank' (Rangordnung) and will to power meant to work as a delayed actio in distans across centuries, taking responsibility ('Ich bin verantwortlich') even for what followed. They trace how the Nietzsche-Hölderlin nexus—Hölderlin's 'Thought' as father to Nietzsche's/Hitler's 'Deed'—was cultivated from George's circle through Heidegger's wartime lectures to Rosenberg's 1944 Weimar address, showing the Nazis staged a controlled 'debate' over Nietzsche while treating Hölderlin as untouchable, so the nexus itself functioned as Gramscian non-coercive hegemony.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 10. The Elisabeth Legend The Cleansing of Nietzsche and the Sullying of His Sister
will-to-power.relation: Holub dismantles the postwar 'Elisabeth legend' by which Schlechta, Kaufmann and Roos scapegoated Förster-Nietzsche to rehabilitate Nietzsche from his fascist reputation. Examining her actual forgeries and biographical writings, he shows they never made Nietzsche more nationalist or anti-Semitic—indeed she consistently and accurately recorded his opposition to anti-Semitism and was herself not a biological racist. He concludes the responsibility lies with Nietzsche himself: his praise of war, cruelty, hierarchy, slavery and European hegemony, and his rhetorical hyperbole, made his thought genuinely susceptible to Nazi appropriation.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 11. Nietzsche, Mussolini, and Italian Fascism
will-to-power.relation: Sznajder examines how Nietzsche entered Italian Fascism through two bridging figures. Gabriele D'Annunzio relocated Nietzsche from philosophy into literature, staged the 'Übermensch' and 'live dangerously' as an aesthetic politics at Fiume and in the Carta del Carnaro, aestheticizing mass politics in ways fascism inherited. Mussolini, reading Beyond Good and Evil and the Genealogy from his socialist years, seized on the will to power, transvaluation and anti-egalitarian elitism (Rome undone by 'the pale Jews') as a virile theory of revolution. The chapter stresses the paradox that official fascism never listed the individualist, anti-statist Nietzsche as a godfather even as his vocabulary pervaded it.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 12. Nietzsche and the Fascist Dimension The Case of Ernst Jünger
will-to-power.relation: Ohana locates fascism's 'nihilistic-totalitarian syndrome' in the Janus-faced combination of Nietzschean nihilism and the Overman's will to power, whereby ethics is replaced by aesthetics and the self-creating 'new man' shapes reality ex nihilo. He reads Ernst Jünger's Stahlgewittern, Der Arbeiter and 'Total Mobilization' as the aestheticization of war and technology into a work-state, and traces Heidegger's fascination with Jünger's 'will to will' back to Nietzsche and Hölderlin—arguing that, following Camus, one cannot ignore the directionless dynamism leading from Nietzschean perspectivism toward Rosenberg's marching-column politics.

will-to-power.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
will-to-power.title: 13. A Godfather Too Nazism as a Nietzschean “Experiment”
will-to-power.relation: Fischer contends that the 'historically effective' (not the 'real') Nietzsche could be read from opposite perspectives, and that Nazism is best understood as a post-Nietzschean 'experiment' licensed by the death of God and the collapse of accepted values ('wir machen einen Versuch mit der Wahrheit'). Invoking Nietzsche's own perspectivism from the Genealogy, and citing calls to 'push what is falling,' the coming 'fight for dominion of the earth' and the Cesare-Borgia-over-Parsifal remark, he argues Nietzsche was 'half a Nazi and half an anti-Nazi'—a genuine part-time godfather, against Kaufmann's overly 'gentle' de-Nazified reading.

will-to-power.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
will-to-power.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
will-to-power.relation: Scott reads three landmark climbs as expressions of the tension between individual freedom and community standards. He casts John Bachar's bold, ground-up, run-out Bachar-Yerian and its self-mastery ethic as a partial embodiment of Nietzsche's Übermensch and will to power, and Alan Watts' rule-breaking sport route To Bolt or Not to Be as an exercise of Mill's On Liberty defense of originality and diversity that benefits the whole community. Against both thinkers' negative view of community, he uses Charles Taylor's 'horizon of significance' to argue that Sonnie Trotter's The Path gains its meaning only through dialogue with the climbing community and its traditions.

will-to-power.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
will-to-power.title: SERIAL KILLERS
will-to-power.relation: Schmid examines Moors Murderer Ian Brady's book The Gates of Janus, arguing that Brady built a genuine philosophy of serial murder from Sade and Nietzsche rather than merely name-dropping them. He corrects popular caricatures of the ubermensch and will to power, then shows Brady grounds his self-account in moral relativism and reframes serial killing as fundamentally about 'power and the will to power.' Brady's admiration for Carl Panzram and his likeness to the self-justifying, punishment-transcending Sadean hero illustrate how Nietzschean and Sadean ideas actually shape a killer's self-understanding.

will-to-power.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
will-to-power.title: SERIAL KILLERS
will-to-power.relation: Gray gives a psychological account of Ted Bundy and Dennis Rader (BTK), stressing that serial killers are ordinary-seeming — Arendt's banality of evil — and are psychopaths, not psychotics: rational, remorseless, genetically shaped, unable to learn conditioned fear, and guided by scripted fantasies of domination. He reads their pursuit of control as Nietzsche's will to power, citing Bundy's manipulation of preacher James Dobson and Rader's cold courtroom allocution. But he argues the psychopath is a failed, unnatural predator, not Nietzsche's ubermensch: lacking vision and moral self-discipline, he only masters deceit in service of petty, narrow fantasies.

will-to-power.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
will-to-power.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
will-to-power.relation: Douglas Blount casts Sauron as a candidate for Nietzsche's Ubermensch, embodying the unabashed will to power in a world where God is dead, life is meaningless, and taste rather than reason or morality guides the self-created life. Tolkien answers this not by argument but by a rival portrait whose beauty lies in community, humility, love, and self-sacrifice: Gandalf dying on the bridge, Frodo's mercy to Gollum, and Sam refusing the Ring's vision of 'Samwise the Strong.' Blount argues that on Nietzsche's own criterion of taste, Tolkien's picture of abnegation is the more compelling vision of a life lived well.

will-to-power.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
will-to-power.title: 35. Star Wars as Philosophy A Genealogy of the Force
will-to-power.relation: Eberl builds a genealogy of the Force across the Skywalker saga, using Augustine to reject the Manichaean light/dark dualism Yoda voices ('Luminous beings are we') in favor of evil as a privation of good and as 'inordinate desire' for temporal goods, which explains Anakin's fall through his refusal to let Padme die. He casts Palpatine as a Nietzschean who declares 'good is a point of view' and pursues will to power and the ubermensch, contrasting this with the Stoicism of Seneca and Yoda ('train yourself to let go of everything you fear to lose'). The sequel trilogy's disenchanted galaxy is read through Charles Taylor, and Rey and Ben's redemption shows evil defeated not by hatred but by rightly-ordered love ('Saving what we love').

will-to-power.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
will-to-power.title: 87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”
will-to-power.relation: Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.

utilitarianism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
utilitarianism.title: “The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self
utilitarianism.relation: Jessica Prata Miller reads Buffy through Carol Gilligan's care perspective: Buffy's self is relational (the Scooby Gang, 'Dawn is a part of me' in 'The Gift'), her moral reasoning contextual rather than rule-bound (caging Oz instead of killing the werewolf, rejecting Riley's Initiative 'demons bad' abstraction), and her emotions a moral resource ('My emotions give me power'). She also weighs the criticisms — Buffy's secret harboring of Angel exposed in 'Revelations,' and Faith's utilitarian 'plus column' defense of hiding a killing, which Buffy rejects ('I am' the one who cries over the bystander). Comparing the three Slayers, Miller argues only Buffy attains moral autonomy: Kendra's unquestioning obedience and Faith's hyper-individualistic action-hero isolation both fail, while Buffy's 'I like to think of it as graduation' break from the Watchers' Council shows autonomy achieved within, not against, relationships.

utilitarianism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
utilitarianism.title: Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben
utilitarianism.relation: Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.

utilitarianism.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
utilitarianism.title: The Obligation to Play Baseball
utilitarianism.relation: Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.

utilitarianism.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
utilitarianism.title: 19b
utilitarianism.relation: A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.

utilitarianism.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
utilitarianism.title: The Dangers of Hedonism
utilitarianism.relation: Sander Lee reads A Midsummer Night's Sex Comedy as Allen's warning against hedonism, tracing that ethos to empiricist thought from Hobbes and Locke through Bentham's utilitarianism to American pragmatism, embodied in Leopold Sturgis, an Ayer-style positivist philosopher who denies everything unprovable yet dies of passion with Dulcy and is deified by Andrew's spirit ball as pagan 'pure essence'. Using Sartre's Nausea, the chapter shows Andrew and Ariel's attempt to recreate their lost 'perfect moment' by the brook failing on every count, proving such moments inauthentic fantasies that ignore freedom, responsibility, and the passage of time. Through Bazin's Nietzschean reading of Renoir (Apollonian order versus Dionysian impulse), it argues that unlike Isaac Davis in Manhattan, the film's characters end more committed to hedonism than they began, with no character left qualified to condemn it.

utilitarianism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
utilitarianism.title: The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness
utilitarianism.relation: This section argues that patriotism violates the principle of equal moral worth shared by utilitarians and Kantians alike: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' means the Minister of Magic's pain counts no more than a house-elf's, while Kant's formula forbids treating anyone (Muggle or wizard) merely as a means. It reads Death Eater pureblood ideology as ordinary racism and sexism, cites Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against 'slave labor,' and asks how preferring countrymen over foreigners differs from preferring people of one's race or gender, since neither is something a person controls.

utilitarianism.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
utilitarianism.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
utilitarianism.relation: Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.

utilitarianism.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
utilitarianism.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
utilitarianism.relation: Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.

utilitarianism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
utilitarianism.title: “You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”
utilitarianism.relation: Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.

utilitarianism.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
utilitarianism.title: “Trust Your Feelings”
utilitarianism.relation: Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.
