utilitarianism.title: NOTES
utilitarianism.relation: Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.

utilitarianism.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
utilitarianism.title: NOTES
utilitarianism.relation: Grubb stages Arlene's decision to abort the baby fathered by serial killer Rene as a case study in Bentham's act utilitarianism: her prayer that ending the pregnancy will keep 'Rene's sickness' from Coby, Lisa, and Terry weighs pleasure and pain — the two sovereign masters — for the greatest number, from family to all of Bon Temps. The chapter shows why the calculus fails her: consequences cannot be known in advance (a crystal ball or Lafayette's visions would be needed), it is indeterminate whose happiness counts, and her premise that evil is biologically inheritable sits badly with the free-will account of sin, making the dilemma genuinely undecidable from inside the show.

utilitarianism.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
utilitarianism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
utilitarianism.relation: Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.

utilitarianism.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
utilitarianism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
utilitarianism.relation: Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.

utilitarianism.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
utilitarianism.title: P A R T T W O
utilitarianism.relation: Three Part Two essays. Robert Loftis argues Moore and Gibbons use Ozymandias's squid attack to indict consequentialism — Veidt uses New York's dead as mere means to world peace, and Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' shows the utilitarian ledger dissolves into an infinite future — while Rorschach's 'never compromise' mantra is a counterfeit deontology rationalizing fascist thuggery, the comic's real target being anyone who sets himself up as guardian of society ('Who watches the watchmen?'). Mark White argues the potbellied second Nite Owl is the truest hero on Aristotelian terms: his courage in the tenement fire and the prison break hits the mean between Laurie's caution and Rorschach's recklessness, making him a flourishing moral exemplar whom John Doris's situationism fails to unseat. Alex Nuttall asks whether Rorschach was wrong to walk out and expose Veidt, using Kant's murderer-at-the-door case to show there is a duty not to lie but no duty to tell the truth (blame falls on Veidt), while act and rule utilitarianism both counsel silence.

utilitarianism.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
utilitarianism.title: Notes
utilitarianism.relation: Bein uses the 'kill baby Hitler' time-machine puzzle and the question of whether Moiraine and Lan should still the Dragon Reborn to probe the Aes Sedai's mysterious ethics. He argues they are not Kantian deontologists (the Three Oaths are loose plot-device rules Moiraine games with ambiguous innuendo, and Kant forbids treating the ferryman as mere means) and are bad consequentialists at best (they cannot lightning-bolt Valda or Hitler who are not Darkfriends). He proposes they are closest to Buddhist ethics: wise compassion good in itself (Tam sitting with dying Tigraine regardless of outcome), and reads the flexible Oaths through upaya (skillful means) and a WoT-adapted Eightfold Path, making them less pacifist nuns than violence-reducing Shaolin nuns.

utilitarianism.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
utilitarianism.title: Notes
utilitarianism.relation: DeVan uses Rand's marriage to Aviendha, Elayne, and Min (and Jordan's own two-girlfriend anecdote) to survey ethical frameworks on polyamory, arguing the answer depends on which lens one uses. Sorting love into the Greek types (ludus, eros, mania, pragma, storge, philia, agape), he runs romantic, sexual, and marital polyamory through emotivism (Ayer), ethical egoism (Ayn Rand, the Forsaken), cultural relativism and social contract (Hobbes, the Aiel), natural law and Kantian duty (the Mahabharata's Draupadi, Genesis), divine command and religion (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), and consequentialism/utilitarianism, rights, and Aristotelian/virtue ethics, invoking Cadsuane's cattle analogy and Brad Wilcox's data favoring monogamy.

utilitarianism.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
utilitarianism.title: Lesser of Two Evils
utilitarianism.relation: Horn reads the Blaviken conflict as a clash of two utilitarianisms: Stregobor locks up women born during the black sun on Benthamite grounds that maximizing humanity's happiness justifies evil, while Renfri's revenge on Stregobor follows Popper's negative utilitarianism of minimizing suffering, and Foot's runaway trolley shows both reasoning toward killing the one. Le Guin's Omelas, with its tortured child beneath a utopia, exposes where Stregobor's and Renfri's 'lesser evil' logic leads. Geralt rejects both because he deliberates as Raff Donelson's ethical pragmatist: he accepts the facts but tests options against the shared Witcher's Code values (kill only to save, never from fear), which is why he prefers not to choose at all.

utilitarianism.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
utilitarianism.title: Notes
utilitarianism.relation: White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.

utilitarianism.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
utilitarianism.title: Notes
utilitarianism.relation: Barkman and Tokbergenova defend 'just torture': Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations of Captain Nazi, the double agent Marcia in the 1970s pilot (saving the Brooklyn Navy Yard's 70,000 workers), and the terrorist Nikos Aegeus are ticking-bomb cases of the sort Henry Shue concedes, and the authors answer Luban's slippery-slope objection with absolute limits (never the innocent or the family) and Dershowitz-style torture warrants. Citing Aristotle's Rhetoric that coerced testimony is often false, they propose trained professional torturers, and conclude that since the right thing is not always the ideal thing, torture should be legalized, rare, and conducted openly - as Wonder Woman models.

utilitarianism.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
utilitarianism.title: VIII - MUTANT RIGHTS, TORTURE, AND X-PERIMENTATION
utilitarianism.relation: McWilliams asks whether mutants have 'human' rights, arguing that rights track reasoning ability, sentience, and autonomy rather than species membership: the Down syndrome comparison shows the X-gene itself justifies nothing, and her alien-landing thought experiment, echoing Singer on speciesism, shows peaceful aliens, and therefore mutants, belong in the class of 'everyone.' Because mutants can look human yet wield omega-level power, she grants they may owe greater duties not to harm, but Wolverine's nonconsensual adamantium grafting and The Last Stand's weaponizable 'cure' remain rights violations. The chapter ends on the cliffhanger of when, if ever, consequentialist benefits may override the rights not to be tortured or experimented on.

utilitarianism.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
utilitarianism.title: XII - DIRTY HAN DS AN D DIRTY MINDS THE ETHICS OF MIND READING AND MINDWRITING
utilitarianism.relation: Terjesen examines whether telepaths can be trusted, starting epistemically: Descartes' problem of other minds and Russell's analogy answer explain how Xavier's football-field telepathy and the Cuckoos' exoneration of Beak could be verified, and how far Jean's telepathic testimony about Cassandra Nova should be acted on. Utilitarians (Mill) and deontologists then split over mindwriting: Xavier's early memory erasures, the permanent rewrite of a terrorist's personality, and the Magneto mindwipe versus Cyclops and Emma's 'telepathic affair' and Jean's ransacking of Emma's memories, where privacy and intimacy are at stake. Invoking Machiavelli and Walzer, the chapter concludes Xavier's dirty hands are necessary but wrong, so he should feel guilt and step down, lest mindreading mutants become the thing humans rightly fear.

utilitarianism.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
utilitarianism.title: To Hack or Not to Hack
utilitarianism.relation: Kennedy asks how a great player like Kareem (the NBA's career foul leader) can be excellent while fouling so much, and answers that deontology (Kant's categorical imperative) and utilitarianism (Mill's greatest-happiness principle) can condemn dangerous 'goon' fouling but cannot explain why the legal Hack-a-Shaq strategy still feels 'clownish.' Invoking Shaq's self-nickname 'the Big Aristotle,' he argues Aristotelian virtue ethics fits better: the excellent player, like the person of good character, perceives the situation rightly and fouls (or risks a foul) at the right time in the right way, so excellence is a habit of seeing well rather than rule-following.

utilitarianism.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
utilitarianism.title: Does the Salary Cap Make the NFL a Fairer League
utilitarianism.relation: Collins-Cavanaugh presents the NFL salary cap as a model of utilitarian distributive justice via Mill's greatest happiness principle: owners and fans gain (guaranteed revenue and a fairer, more competitive league) while players lose relatively little. He then tests empirically—competitive-balance scores, playoff berths, championship distribution, and comparison to MLB and the NBA—and finds little evidence the cap actually increases fairness. Because the claimed fan happiness is not genuinely caused by the cap, the utilitarian justification collapses, leaving only the players' net loss against the owners' gain.

utilitarianism.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
utilitarianism.relation: Stephen Kershnar examines the three strongest arguments for the IOC's ban on performance-enhancing drugs, harm-to-self, harm-to-others, and unfairness, and argues each fails, using cases such as Ben Johnson's stripped 1988 gold and Marion Jones. Against harm-to-self he cites anti-paternalism and the far greater accepted risks of NFL play and boxing; against harm-to-others he shows PED pressure is no different from the pressure of rivals' superior training (a Prisoner's Dilemma leagues need not solve); against unfairness he tests four accounts of fairness, including a Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance model whose choosers might find banning steroids while allowing Lasik and high-tech gear arbitrary. He concludes the ban, if justified at all, rests only on contested utilitarian grounds like audience preference and protecting children.

utilitarianism.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
utilitarianism.relation: Reitsma defends keeping the 'second-rate' Olympic men's football tournament against Bob Harig's 'Simply the best' litmus test, which would de-roster any event that is not the pinnacle of its sport. He likens Harig's proposed 'Olympic calculus' (scoring sports on tradition, parity, marketability) to Bentham and Mill's utilitarian maximization of a single value, and rejects both as oversimplifying an irreducibly plural decision. He argues the IOC instead rightly practices casuistry, case-by-case judgment that requires Aristotelian practical wisdom, and that dropping men's football (an under-23, FIFA-hampered tournament) would sacrifice the Olympics' global breadth for a false ideal of excellence.

utilitarianism.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
utilitarianism.title: “You Cannot Be Serious!” The Ethics of Rage in Tennis
utilitarianism.relation: David Detmer asks whether John McEnroe's on-court tantrums are merely rude or genuinely immoral, judging them by two ethical theories. Under Bentham's utilitarianism he weighs the pleasure of entertained crowds against the harm to abused officials, then uses Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction to discount the 'lower' amusement of gawking at boorishness beneath the 'higher' aesthetic pleasure of appreciating great tennis. Under Kantian deontology he argues McEnroe's public false accusations are wrong in principle: officials are better positioned to make calls, so the abuse is unjust, and by the categorical imperative read as a Golden Rule, McEnroe—who resents being wrongly criticized himself—is a hypocrite whose 'gamesmanship' unfairly exploits his star power against opponents.

utilitarianism.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
utilitarianism.title: The Russell-Wartenberg Debate
utilitarianism.relation: The chapter sets the book's standard for 'philosophy in action' by staging Bruce Russell's skepticism against Thomas Wartenberg's defense of the film-as-philosophy thesis: Russell holds that narrative films can at most raise questions or furnish counterexamples, so The Matrix merely inspires the viewer's own argument for external-world skepticism, while Wartenberg replies that The Matrix screens Descartes's evil-deceiver hypothesis so effectively that viewers are themselves deceived into skeptical doubt, accomplishing for audiences what Socrates did to his interlocutors. Wartenberg's reading of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind — where Dr. Mierzwiak's memory-erasure technology presents utilitarianism (via Mary's dialogue) and then a counterexample to it — is tested, and the author proposes the film targets hedonism more directly, working as a reverse variant of Nozick's experience machine that defends autonomy over happiness. Kant's obscure Transcendental Deduction is invoked to show that even canonical philosophical texts are ambiguous, blunting the explicitness objection. The chapter concludes that negative projects — modus tollens counterexamples cinematically conveyed — are where film most plausibly philosophizes, preparing the ground for reading the Whedonverse.

utilitarianism.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
utilitarianism.title: Exploring The Cabin in the Woods
utilitarianism.relation: The chapter reads The Cabin in the Woods as Whedon and Goddard doing philosophy: the facility's ritual sacrifice of the five campers is given an explicit utilitarian defense (quoting Mill's greatest-happiness principle) through the Director's plea that Dana kill Marty to avert the apocalypse, which the film ultimately counters through the friends' care-based obligations. Drawing on Nel Noddings's ethics of care and Aristotle's claim that the severity of our duties varies with the closeness of relationships — and on Whedonverse parallels like Buffy refusing to sacrifice Dawn in 'The Gift' — it recasts the ending as an implicit counterargument to classic utilitarianism: Dana does nothing impermissible by refusing to murder her friend, so utilitarianism is false, while Dana's genuine dilemma is deliberately left unresolved in Socratic aporia. It then extends the ethics of care into a theory of the horror genre, reading Whedon's 'inoculation against real fear' as an Aristotelian catharsis that requires relatable characters who care for one another, and takes the film's monitors, two-way mirrors, and voyeurism scenes (Hadley's callousness, the control-room ogling of Jules) as a metalevel invitation to audit our own desensitization to pointless screen suffering.

utilitarianism.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
utilitarianism.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
utilitarianism.relation: LaRocca reads The Insider as a study of contracts, conscience and courage. He argues that when Jeffrey Wigand stops calculating consequences ('Fuck it. Let's go to court.') he becomes a Kantian: his testimony has moral worth because it is done from duty and the categorical imperative, not from the utilitarian hedonic calculus of Bentham and Mill that Bergman, Wallace and Scruggs press on him. Wigand's whistleblowing is then framed through Aristotle's account of courage as a mean between recklessness and cowardice, with Wigand as the 'citizen soldier' who acts from conscience while Mike Wallace exemplifies the coward who exceeds in fear.

utilitarianism.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
utilitarianism.title: The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence
utilitarianism.relation: Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'

utilitarianism.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
utilitarianism.title: Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad
utilitarianism.relation: Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.

utilitarianism.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care
utilitarianism.relation: Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.

utilitarianism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: This Is the Age of Steel
utilitarianism.relation: Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.

utilitarianism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: Toward Caring
utilitarianism.relation: J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.

utilitarianism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
utilitarianism.relation: Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.

utilitarianism.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
utilitarianism.title: 9. God the Programmer Is Dead
utilitarianism.relation: De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.

utilitarianism.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
utilitarianism.title: 11. Why Sacrifice Yourself
utilitarianism.relation: Browning interrogates the nobility of the Winchesters' repeated self-sacrifice, asking whether their deals (Dean's soul for Sam, John's soul for Dean) are selfless or selfish—driven by codependency, fear of being alone, and ego. He weighs utilitarian justification (sacrificing one who saves the world) against the trickster's 'Mystery Spot' lesson that 'nothing good comes' of it, and invokes Kant's notion of a true gift expecting nothing in return, alongside Milbank on life-as-gift, to question whether self-sacrifice is the 'ultimate ethical agent' when death isn't final.

utilitarianism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
utilitarianism.title: 3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty
utilitarianism.relation: Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.

utilitarianism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
utilitarianism.title: 13. In Defense of Demerzel
utilitarianism.relation: Nurkic asks whether Demerzel, the loyal robot of the Apple TV+ Foundation, violates Asimov's Laws of Robotics when she poisons Zephyr Halima and kills Cleon XIV (Brother Dawn). He argues she is governed not by the ordinary First/Second Laws but by a reprogrammed priority—Daneel's 'Zeroth Law' (protect humanity) narrowed to 'Cleon I's vision'—and then contends the Laws are incoherent when applied to real cases (Buridan's-donkey paralysis, the surgeon dilemma, ambiguity of 'human' and 'harm'). He closes by testing the Laws against Kant's categorical imperative (the lying/murderer-at-the-door case) and Bentham-style utilitarianism to show robot ethics cannot be reduced to fixed programmed codes.

utilitarianism.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
utilitarianism.title: 2. To Eat or Not to Eat
utilitarianism.relation: Barta and Miranda read Bourdain's 'good eating is all about risk' credo through Bentham's cost-benefit hedonic calculus, sorting risk/reward into Ascetic, Epicurean, Cyrenaic, and Utilitarian quadrants. They classify Bourdain's fugu-eating and drunk cliff-driving as failed calculations, his comfort-food returns as Epicurean, and his gluttonous adventures (French Laundry, Russian vodka) as Cyrenaic high-risk/high-reward living.

utilitarianism.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
utilitarianism.title: 16. Fine Dining with Children Starving
utilitarianism.relation: Barta and Miranda pose Bourdain's Haiti dilemma — feasting on camera while people starve — as Peter Singer's 'Shallow Pond' / drowning-child argument about affluence and obligation. They test justifications for luxury from Bentham's intensity-vs-extent calculus, Mill's higher/lower pleasures, and Sidgwick's dualism of practical reason, then use Singer's Expanding Circle to show how Bourdain extended moral consideration to the poor, the foreign, and (partially) non-human animals through his work.

utilitarianism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
utilitarianism.title: So, Case Closed – Right
utilitarianism.relation: White asks why Batman won't kill the Joker, framing it through utilitarianism (killing one to save the Joker's many future victims) versus deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences). Using Foot and Thomson's trolley and transplant cases, plus agent-neutral versus agent-relative rules, he notes key disanalogies: the Joker is not a moral innocent but the very cause of the danger, which pushes toward killing him. But because future killings are only probable, doing so would be 'prepunishment,' and White, a self-described deontologist, concludes it is genuinely hard to say Batman is right, though he admires the restraint.

utilitarianism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
utilitarianism.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
utilitarianism.relation: Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.

utilitarianism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
utilitarianism.title: It’s Not That Simple
utilitarianism.relation: Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.

utilitarianism.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
utilitarianism.title: Real World Island
utilitarianism.relation: Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.

utilitarianism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
utilitarianism.title: What Would You Do If Your Mother Asked You A Brief Introduction to Ethics
utilitarianism.relation: Jacob Held and Eric Wilson introduce ethics by first dispatching cultural and normative relativism (the Butter Battle Book's Yooks and Zooks, the Once-ler's 'we're each allowed our own opinion') as a cowardly refusal to judge, then present three theories through Seuss characters. Horton is the paragon of Kantian dignity ('a person's a person, no matter how small') and the categorical imperative, tested against lying in The Cat in the Hat. Thidwick the Big-Hearted Moose dramatizes Mill's utilitarianism and its sacrifice of the individual to the greatest happiness, while Thidwick, courage, and Life's 'Great Balancing Act' illustrate Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, virtue as habituated character, and eudaimonia.

utilitarianism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
utilitarianism.title: Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax
utilitarianism.relation: Alexander contrasts Dewey's reflective, character-centered ethics with utilitarianism and Kantian deontology using the Lorax and Horton. The Once-ler is cast as the shortsighted 'utilitarian' maximizing Thneed happiness while the Lorax, urging us to 'stop and think' about the whole ecosystem, is really a Deweyan practicing reflective morality and deliberation as 'dramatic rehearsal.' Horton's conscientious care for the Whos illustrates Dewey's 'Who Factor' and growth of character rather than cold rule-following, showing morality as the ongoing education of desire toward inclusive, shared ends.

utilitarianism.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: What’s Wrong with Roland
utilitarianism.relation: Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.

utilitarianism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: Chapter 8 The Noble Art of Lying
utilitarianism.relation: James Edwin Mahon reconstructs Twain's two essays on lying ('On the Decay of the Art of Lying' and 'My First Lie') into a philosophy of lying. Twain holds that everyone lies constantly, that lying need not be spoken or deceptive (the 'silent lie,' nondeceptive polite lies, acts as lies, and 'modified' lies/palters), and that the gravest lies are the 'silent National Lies' such as the collective silence that slavery was not unjust. Mahon shows Twain's ethics of lying is broadly utilitarian and Rossian: guided by nonmaleficence and beneficence, an injurious truth is no better than an injurious lie, and self-sacrificing lies that help others are virtuous, so lying should be practiced as a cultivated art.

utilitarianism.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
utilitarianism.title: MOTHERHOOD
utilitarianism.relation: Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').

utilitarianism.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
utilitarianism.title: MOTHERHOOD
utilitarianism.relation: Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.

utilitarianism.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
utilitarianism.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.

utilitarianism.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
utilitarianism.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Clark analyzes Disney's Bambi as anti-hunting art, showing how the animators used music and the Kantian sublime — keeping Man and Death offscreen, 'felt rather than seen' — to make viewers feel hunting is cosmic murder, while the cute cartoon animals stay merely 'seen.' He then critiques Matt Cartmill, who dissolves hunting by using science and utilitarianism to erase the Man/Nature split (making hunting indistinguishable from murder), faulting Cartmill for flattening life and rejecting the sublime. He resolves the tension via Richard Nelson's The Island Within and Koyukon hunting, which honors continuity and the sublime without a Man/Nature dichotomy.

utilitarianism.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
utilitarianism.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.

utilitarianism.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
utilitarianism.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Brophy prosecutes Santa for 'elfploitation,' treating the North Pole workshop like an overseas sweatshop (with Willy Wonka's Oompa-Loompahs and Rowling's house-elfs as parallels) and dismantling a Nozickian entitlement-theory defense: the elfs' 'consent' is coerced by their bleak alternatives, so absolute property rights fail just as Locke's desert water-hole owner must grant access. He diagnoses the elfs' apparent contentment as Marxian false consciousness, invokes Kant's humanity formula to condemn using rational elfs as mere means, and rejects the utilitarian 'greatest happiness' justification via Le Guin's Omelas and Rawls's veil of ignorance. He concludes with a call to boycott Christmas until Santa's labor practices become transparent.

utilitarianism.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
utilitarianism.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.

utilitarianism.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
utilitarianism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.

utilitarianism.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
utilitarianism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
utilitarianism.relation: Prompted by the avalanche death of his climbing partner Charlie on the Super Couloir, Paul Charlton uses Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism to ask whether the risks of climbing can be ethically justified, insisting that blindly accepting risk is indefensible but deliberate, reasoned risk can be right. He weighs climbing's costs (frivolity, self-focus, danger to self and to grieving family) against its intrinsic value (joy, friendship, aesthetic experience) and instrumental value (cultivating human excellence, psychological growth, reprioritized lives), invoking Mill's higher/lower pleasures to argue quality of happiness matters, not just quantity. His conclusion is that climbing can be justified only when it produces more overall good than any alternative use of that time, leaving each climber to run the calculation for their own case.

utilitarianism.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
utilitarianism.title: SERIAL KILLERS
utilitarianism.relation: Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.

utilitarianism.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
utilitarianism.title: SERIAL KILLERS
utilitarianism.relation: Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.

utilitarianism.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
utilitarianism.title: The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects
utilitarianism.relation: Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'

utilitarianism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
utilitarianism.title: 7. Independence Day & Aliens
utilitarianism.relation: Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.

utilitarianism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
utilitarianism.title: So, Case Closed – Right
utilitarianism.relation: Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.

utilitarianism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
utilitarianism.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
utilitarianism.relation: J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.

utilitarianism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
utilitarianism.title: It’s Not That Simple
utilitarianism.relation: O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey
utilitarianism.relation: Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 32. Okja as Philosophy Why Animals Matter
utilitarianism.relation: Jensen frames Okja around three views of the super-pig Okja's moral status: Mirando treats her as mere property, the Animal Liberation Front as a symbol to be sacrificed for the cause, and the girl Mija as a friend and person. He dismantles Mirando's 'human exceptionalism'—amoralism, Aquinas's natural-law teleology, the Kantian persons-only view, and Descartes' claim that animals are unfeeling automata—then develops the ALF's liberation through Singer's equal consideration of interests, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and speciesism as prejudice, weighing consequentialist (utilitarian) against deontological (rights, Regan) foundations. He closes with hierarchical moral status and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many,' arguing Mija's love for Okja shows that at some point relationship matters more than moral calculation.

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 47. Snowpiercer as Philosophy The Danger to Humanity
utilitarianism.relation: Marquez 'pierces the veils' of Snowpiercer to argue the greatest danger to humanity is humanity itself. He reads Wilford's authoritarian, precisely population-controlled train through Plato's noble lie / myth of the metals (Mason's 'know your place'), Hobbes's social contract against a cannibalistic state of nature, and Machiavellian ends-justify-means to weigh whether Gilliam's secret compromise with Wilford is morally acceptable. He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 50. The Cabin in the Woods as Philosophy Cinematic Reflections on Ethical Complexity, Human Nature, and Worthw
utilitarianism.relation: Kowalski argues Whedon and Goddard's The Cabin in the Woods stages a clash between classical utilitarianism and an ethics of care, and cinematically favors the latter. The Facility, sacrificing five campers to placate the Ancient Ones and save humanity, embodies Mill's greatest-happiness reasoning, but its callous celebration while Dana suffers on the dock undercuts that view. When the Director tells Dana she must kill her only remaining friend Marty to save the world, Dana's refusal is defended via Noddings's care ethics and Aristotle's claim that obligations track close personal relationships (special obligations), with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis and Plato's Leontius grounding the film's theory of worthwhile horror: 'people are more important than humanity.'

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain
utilitarianism.relation: Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”
utilitarianism.relation: Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.

utilitarianism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
utilitarianism.title: 94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission
utilitarianism.relation: Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.

utilitarianism.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
utilitarianism.title: 4. The Good of the Doctor
utilitarianism.relation: The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

philosophy-of-love.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
philosophy-of-love.title: The Noir Consequences of Sex Eros, Death, and the Possibility of Love
philosophy-of-love.relation: Thomas Hibbs reads BtVS as feminist noir: like classic noir it traps characters in labyrinths where the past bears down on the present (Buffy torn from heaven in 'After Life,' Angel's gypsy curse in 'Innocence,' the psych-ward ending of 'Normal Again'), and it rejects both Enlightenment optimism and the Nietzschean beyond-good-and-evil self-creation Hibbs finds in neo-noir like Body Heat and Thelma and Louise. Sex in Sunnydale always carries noir consequences — Angel losing his soul at the moment of 'true happiness,' Buffy's self-lacerating Spike affair ending in his attempted rape — so the show is skeptical of sexual liberation while recovering a classical eros as longing for wholeness. The Season Six finale locates the 'true essence of magic' in sacrificial love: Xander's yellow-crayon plea in 'Grave' reaches the 'spark of humanity' in Willow where all force fails.

philosophy-of-love.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
philosophy-of-love.title: Emotions and Aesthetic Response
philosophy-of-love.relation: Carolyn Korsmeyer uses BtVS to stage philosophy's ambivalence about emotion — dangerous passion versus intuitive sagacity — through three cases: anger as beast within and practical power (Xander's love spell in 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered,' Willow's wish-spells in 'Something Blue,' 'My emotions give me power' to Kendra), grief as the one emotion no magic can undo (Epictetus's jug-and-child counsel set against 'The Body' and Dawn trying to resurrect Joyce), and love's non-fungibility (Anya's vengeance-demon past leaves her without the wider affection that makes singular love credible, while Spike's messy human history makes his obsession believable). She draws on Plato's wild-beast appetites and spirited element of the Republic, Aristotle on anger and emotional disposition as character, Kant's reason-above-nature picture, and Martha Nussbaum on art's particular cases. Finally she turns to aesthetic response: the show's comedy ('She saved the world a lot') regulates audience emotion, keeping the serial's catharsis from tipping into manipulation.

philosophy-of-love.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
philosophy-of-love.title: Erotic Love and Friendship
philosophy-of-love.relation: Maps Aristotle's three levels of friendship onto Buffy's three boyfriends: Riley is a utility friendship chosen for the rational goal of a 'normal' boyfriend (echoed by Warren's robot April and the Buffybot, which prove programmed perfection cannot be loved), Spike is a pleasure friendship driven by passion and danger that Buffy ends in 'As You Were,' and Angel is a complete friendship where each values the other for his own sake despite the gypsy curse. This lets the authors solve Aristotle's love paradox (is erotic love chosen or does it choose us?) by adding Augustine's and William of Ockham's third power of the soul, the will: an arational faculty that values the other as an end in himself, neither rationally chosen nor irrationally caused.

philosophy-of-love.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
philosophy-of-love.title: Psychical Dynamics of Love and Lust
philosophy-of-love.relation: Levine and Schneider apply Freud's 1912 essay on the debasement in love — 'where they love they do not desire and where they desire they cannot love' — to argue that BtVS succeeds not through innovation or moral seriousness but through the conventional 'girl next door': Angel's forbidden-vampire sex is the show's best because forbiddenness heightens desire, Xander's pedestal-placing of Buffy forecloses satisfaction, and Drusilla and Cordelia are already 'debased' sexual objects. Along the way they polemicize against Buffy scholars for projecting their own fantasies onto a show that reinforces, rather than subverts, gender stereotypes and the forbiddenness of sex for young women.

philosophy-of-love.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
philosophy-of-love.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
philosophy-of-love.relation: Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum as two hobbits of the same nature and culture seeking the same happy life, so their success and failure are instructive for ordinary people like us. Gollum's happiness is solitary possession of the Ring - he murders Déagol for it and ends 'into the dust' - while Sam's is fellowship in the Shire with Rosie and Frodo, pursued through loyalty and giving (spending Galadriel's seed-box to restore the Shire). The pivotal episode is Gollum's trembling caress of Frodo's knee, 'the most tragic moment in the Tale', squandered when Sam's jealous rebuke drives him back to treachery. With Aristotle on friendship and self-love, the chapter concludes that happiness is achievable only in a social context and its key is love.

philosophy-of-love.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
philosophy-of-love.title: “Just What They Say It for I Never Knew”
philosophy-of-love.relation: South argues Allen's signature old recordings from the American songbook are a philosophical device grounded in Aristotle: the Rhetoric's view that emotions carry cognitive orientations that reshape judgment, and the Politics' claim that music forms character, explain why songs comment on the plots they score. He reads Hannah and Her Sisters through 'You Made Me Love You', 'Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered', and 'I'm in Love Again' — scoring Elliot's inconstancy, Mickey's 'You don't deserve Cole Porter' judgment of Holly, and her growth into someone whose new musical taste signals ethical maturity — and Everyone Says I Love You as a darker cycle where fantasy and finitude ('It's Later Than You Think') drive the compulsion to love again. The happy ending is precisely why Allen called the film a 'cop out': its music says love fades and is out of our control, while the plot pretends otherwise.

philosophy-of-love.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
philosophy-of-love.title: Humor and Philosophy
philosophy-of-love.relation: Ascione deploys Schopenhauer's theory of laughter — the sudden, paradoxical subsumption of an object under a heterogeneous concept — as the framework for showing how Annie Hall's gags do philosophical work. The subtitled balcony conversation exposes the self-monitoring deception of new romance, the street-interview 'love fades' scene smuggles in the unpopular thesis that lasting romantic love is mythical (culminating in the dead-shark line), the grammar-school reunion raises questions about what shapes adult character, and the 'dynamite ham' dinner, the pastrami-on-white-with-mayo, and the California scenes diagnose Alvy's own New York provincialism. Because humor suspends judgment and deflects resistance, Allen can deliver social and cultural analysis that audiences would reject if stated straight.

philosophy-of-love.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
philosophy-of-love.title: Love and Self-Discovery
philosophy-of-love.relation: Mary Nichols argues The Curse of the Jade Scorpion answers The Maltese Falcon: where Sam Spade's cynicism leaves society no reason to trust its lone hero, C.W. Briggs, unknowingly stealing for the magician Polgar while hypnotized, is saved by love, friendship, and the office community of North Coast Casualty. The jade scorpion's trance, meant to cover crime, uncovers truth, as C.W. and Betty Ann admit under hypnosis the love and fear their waking selves hide, so that 'crystal clear' memory and self-knowledge, rather than Spade's rejection of dreams, free them from both the curse and crime. Against the noir world and Lester's 'comedy is tragedy plus time', the chapter holds that everyone has 'a little bit of larceny' in them and that experiences of love, friendship, and community are what form the character that keeps it in check.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: Snape and the Many-Splendored Thing
philosophy-of-love.relation: Catherine Jack Deavel and David Paul Deavel open with the puzzle of Dumbledore's 'ironclad' certainty about Snape, maintained even after Snape kills him and attested by McGonagall's report that his repentance was 'absolutely genuine'. Their answer is Snape's unrequited love for Lily Potter, and they set the chapter's task: to examine, against the suspicion that redemptive love-talk is mere sentimentality, what philosophers have said about love's nature and its power to transform and to mislead judgment.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: The Abandoned Boys
philosophy-of-love.relation: Surveys the classical triad of eros, philia, and agape from Plato's Symposium onward and maps it onto the series: the Weasleys, Ron and Hermione, and Harry and Ginny exemplify romantic love, Dumbledore's remark that Voldemort never had a friend dramatizes the absence of philia, and Lily's self-giving love that repels Quirrell and Voldemort is agape. Because traditional accounts treat love as an act of the will rather than a feeling, Snape's persistent dislikes cannot disprove that his love for Lily has transformed him.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: Snape’s Choice
philosophy-of-love.relation: Defines love, with Aristotle, Aquinas, and M. Scott Peck, as willing the good of the other for the other's own sake, and reads Snape's double-agent life as love expressed in action despite real hatred: he protects Harry's enemies at constant risk while disliking most of them. His Occlumency, the skill to lie to Voldemort's face, reveals both strength and weakness, for rather than renouncing love as Voldemort did he only conceals it, and his dying gift of memories to Harry, revealing that Harry is a Horcrux, must be freely offered because his thoughts can never be taken.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: A Work in Progress
philosophy-of-love.relation: Reads Snape's love for Lily through Plato's Symposium: his childhood watching of Lily with 'undisguised greed', his failure to ask Voldemort to spare her husband and child, 'You disgust me', shows a love that desires Lily's good only as it relates to him, falling short of Aristotle's beloved as 'second self'. Diotima's 'possession of the good forever' and 'giving birth in beauty' describe how his love matures into genuine virtue, a deepening Pope Benedict XVI's picture of love as 'ecstasy', an exodus out of the closed self toward self-giving, completes.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: NOTES
philosophy-of-love.relation: Argues Snape's redemption is gradual virtue-building rather than instant transformation, since vice and virtue are habits built up over time and his resentments persist even as his actions serve the good. His doe Patronus, matching Lily's, manifests Aristotle's beloved as a second self, his remorse, an emotion he shares with Harry but Voldemort cannot feel, begins to knit his damaged soul whole, and Harry's forgiveness, naming his son Albus Severus for 'the bravest man I ever knew', completes the arc love began.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: Violently Pink Products
philosophy-of-love.relation: Gregory Bassham opens by contrasting Muggle spending on attractiveness with the wizarding world's far more reliable magical love potions, and poses the ethical problem of their nonconsensual use. The chapter's test cases are the two key episodes: Merope Gaunt's use of a love potion to ensnare Tom Riddle Sr., Voldemort's father, and her eventual choice to stop dosing him at great cost to herself and her unborn son.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: Little Hangleton
philosophy-of-love.relation: Catalogues what Half-Blood Prince establishes about love potions: Fred and George sell them legally at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Hermione identifies Amortentia by its mother-of-pearl sheen and personal smell, and Slughorn warns it 'doesn't really create love... It is impossible to manufacture or imitate love', producing only obsessive infatuation, as Ron's Romilda Vane episode demonstrates. The section ends by introducing Voldemort's mother as the person who actually used one.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: Real Love or Mere Infatuation
philosophy-of-love.relation: Retells Dumbledore's reconstruction of Merope Gaunt's ensnarement of Tom Riddle Sr.: Harry correctly narrows the cause of the squire's son's behavior to the Imperius Curse or a love potion, and Dumbledore concludes she dosed him, then chose to stop, wrongly hoping he had come to love her or would stay for the baby. The section closes on Dumbledore's insistence that this backstory 'has everything to do with the prophecy' about Harry and Voldemort.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: Not His Mother’s Son
philosophy-of-love.relation: Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: NOTES
philosophy-of-love.relation: Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.

philosophy-of-love.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
philosophy-of-love.title: The Triumph of Love
philosophy-of-love.relation: Tracks love's escalation across the series as a force that overwhelms evil without competing: Lily's skin-deep sacrificial love repels Quirrell in Sorcerer's Stone, Harry spares Pettigrew out of love for Lupin and Sirius, his love for Sirius expels Voldemort's possession at the Ministry, and Dumbledore names it 'a force that is at once more wonderful and more terrible than death'. In Deathly Hallows love extends to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby, and culminates in Harry's astonishing plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse', his redefinition of manhood in 'be a man', and victory through willing sacrifice and a single defensive spell rather than a duel, vindicating traditionally feminine values over hypermasculine domination.

philosophy-of-love.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
philosophy-of-love.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
philosophy-of-love.relation: Laura Garcia assembles Narnian heroes: Jill, Eustace, and Puddleglum untying Rilian at likely lethal cost, Eustace hacking at the Sea Serpent, unarmed Shasta charging the lion to save Aravis, and Digory refusing the Witch's offer of the apple that could heal his dying mother. She asks whether egoist theories can explain such deeds and argues they cannot: Hobbes's disguised self-interest, Butler's and Paley's reward schemes, Hume's sympathy, and MacIntyre's identity-based interests all fall short. Only love of others for their own sake, and (for Jill and Digory) trust in Aslan's proven goodness, explains both the heroic choices and our admiration of them as supererogatory acts beyond the call of duty.

philosophy-of-love.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
philosophy-of-love.title: The Mysteries of Love Revealed
philosophy-of-love.relation: Shelby stages Plato's Symposium as a cipher of raps on love to answer hip-hop "love haters" like Jay-Z ("I got ninety-nine problems but a bitch ain't one"): Pausanias's vulgar versus spiritual love, Aristophanes's myth of split halves read through Method Man and Mary J. Blige's "You're All I Need" and Biggie's "Me & My Bitch", and Socrates's ladder from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself, with Lauryn Hill's "Zion" as birth of beautiful offspring. He objects that Socrates makes the beloved a replaceable means to the good, and argues that Alcibiades's drunken confession supplies what is missing - love's possession, exclusivity, reciprocity, and drama (The Roots: "lies come in, that's where the drama begins") - concluding that love ain't just 'bout da booty but demands a vulnerability the love hater rightly fears.

philosophy-of-love.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
philosophy-of-love.title: Love Minus Zero, No Limit or Going, Going Gone
philosophy-of-love.relation: Doug Anderson reads Dylan's Planet Waves as a modern Symposium: each song stages a rung on Diotima's ladder, from the puppy love of "You Angel You" through the physical eros of "Tough Mama" and "Hazel," the agape of "Forever Young," and the complementary true love of "Wedding Song." Like Socrates refusing Alcibiades in "Going, Going Gone," Dylan abandons finite beloveds because his highest eros is the creative act itself - poets achieve the immortality Diotima demands by giving birth to immortal works rather than children. The chapter argues both Plato and Dylan finally define love as desire for truth and beauty that outlasts any particular relationship.

philosophy-of-love.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
philosophy-of-love.title: A Meditation on the Word
philosophy-of-love.relation: Randall Auxier and Eileen Townsend fictionalize the history of philosophy as vampire predation in letters, emails, and IMs (1983-2009) between the 800-year-old Etienne Lavec - a student of Siger de Brabant who drained Thomas Aquinas over the Summa's Treatise on Angels, which wrote vampires out of existence - and Paulie, a freshman turned at Memphis State. Lavec recounts tasting Pico, Spinoza, Hegel, and the willing Kierkegaard, sparing Nietzsche who 'stole some of my ideas about free death', and contrasts vampire self-knowledge (embracing desire) with the Socratic beginning in affirmed ignorance. The centerpiece is Foucault: Lavec summarizes his genealogies of how institutions create the sick, the mad, the prisoner, and the pervert, fails to drain him, and is then haunted for decades by posthumous publications, taunting 'nietzsche26' emails, and finally a catacombs trap - power/knowledge that refuses to die. Lavec's embedded 'Meditation on the Word' recasts the Logos of John's Gospel so that vampires are the uncreated darkness at the boundary of the divine Word, pure self-grounding desire 'beyond good and evil', while the closing Twilight-era chats satirize Stephenie Meyer's sparkling, abstinent Edward as Foucauldian 'sin by words'.

philosophy-of-love.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
philosophy-of-love.title: James Bond and Philosophy
philosophy-of-love.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall rebut Paul Johnson's 1958 charge that Doctor No combines 'the sadism of a schoolboy bully', adolescent sex longings, and suburban snobbery. They show Bond kills for justice rather than spite (his reluctant assignment against von Hammerstein in 'For Your Eyes Only'), that Colonel Sun repudiates de Sadean torture before dying, and that the disturbing 'semi-rape' passage of The Spy Who Loved Me reflects Vivienne Michel's voice, not Bond's conduct. They read Bond's eros as an ironic use of the medieval courtly-love and Mariology tradition in which sex redeems 'lost women' like Pussy Galore, defend his dress and manners through the ancient heroic tradition (Theseus's fatal neglect of the white sails, Leonidas combing his beard at Thermopylae), and conclude Bond is a chivalric, comic hero - a 'delightful impossibility' in Aristotle's Poetics' sense who embodies Socratic soldierly virtue and Platonic optimism.

philosophy-of-love.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
philosophy-of-love.title: To Nest or Not to Nest
philosophy-of-love.relation: Halwani and Jones read The Birds as Hitchcock's warning about romantic love: love compromises autonomy through joint decision-making, emotional dependence, and exposure to contingencies like jealousy, betrayal, sickness, and death. Plato's Symposium stages the alternatives, Socrates's ladder of love culminating in the eternal Form of Beauty versus Alcibiades's speech for the painful, contingent love of a unique person, and Nussbaum's reading underscores that these two visions of romantic love are mutually exclusive. In the film, bird attacks strike whenever Melanie, Mitch, Annie, or Lydia treat love as a game or possession, while the caged lovebirds, the only birds that never attack, show that only love sealed in a 'gilded cage' could be cost-free; lovers must instead face love's price wisely, maturely, and courageously.

philosophy-of-love.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
philosophy-of-love.title: Knots
philosophy-of-love.relation: Carroll argues that Vertigo rewards repeated viewing not because of its wildly improbable crime plot but because its double love story is a contribution to the philosophy of love: citing Aristotle's Poetics on drama as a 'concrete universal,' he treats Scottie and Judy as ideal character types, the projective fantasist and the enabler, whose sequential romances invite viewers to compare them and so discover love's inherent fault line, fantasy.
