problem-of-evil.title: Introduction
problem-of-evil.relation: Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.

problem-of-evil.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
problem-of-evil.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
problem-of-evil.relation: Johnson turns 'Cartmanland' into a survey of answers to the problem of evil: Kyle's hemorrhoid-versus-Cartman's-wealth argument is the logical problem of moral evil; the story of Job fails because Job's continued belief does not rebut the evidence; Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards' God-glorifying answer; and Stan's 'Cartman is totally miserable' restores Kyle's faith via second-order goods. The free will defense (via Augustine) handles moral evil but not natural evil, so the chapter closes with John Hick's soul-making theodicy — mirrored by South Park's Jesus saying life is about overcoming problems and growing — before conceding the evidential problem of evil still stands.

problem-of-evil.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
problem-of-evil.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
problem-of-evil.relation: Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'

problem-of-evil.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
problem-of-evil.title: A Proper Answer
problem-of-evil.relation: Tallon takes Psycho as a case study in the problem of evil: after Hume's Epicurean challenge, Marion's shower murder and Norman's shattered psyche exemplify Marilyn McCord Adams's 'horrendous evils,' whose grotesque disproportion between any crime and its fate threatens to destroy the positive meaning of a life. The free will defense (Plantinga, Augustine) fails because Marion's death is bad luck rather than punished choice, and Hick's soul-making theodicy fails because evil here shatters character rather than building it. Carroll's definition of monsters is revised so that monsters are beings of severe disorder and disproportion, which Norman, Dracula, and Hitler all display, and Swinburne's Principle of Honesty offers the closest answer: God allows horrors because systematically preventing them would deceive us about the truth that evil is the privation of proper order, inherently grotesque and disordered.

problem-of-evil.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
problem-of-evil.title: Encore
problem-of-evil.relation: Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.

problem-of-evil.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
problem-of-evil.title: Introduction
problem-of-evil.relation: The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.

problem-of-evil.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
problem-of-evil.title: Redemption
problem-of-evil.relation: Stephen Bilynskyj tests John Hick's soul-making theodicy—that God allows suffering because virtues like courage, temperance, and compassion need pain to form—against Cash's life and songs. Using Aristotle on habituation by pleasure and pain (Cash's first amphetamine euphoria and the ostrich-attack painkillers as missed occasions for temperance) and Aquinas on innate aptitude and divinely infused virtue, he argues virtue can form without suffering (by genes or miracle), so soul-making alone cannot justify evil, as Cash himself implies about his mother's grief after Jack's death. Cash instead locates redemption in Christ's suffering ('Redemption,' 'Why Me, Lord?'), while the intervention by his son John Carter shows pain still occasioning real growth in temperance.

problem-of-evil.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
problem-of-evil.title: “A Boy Named Sue” A Cashian Theodicy
problem-of-evil.relation: Jamie Carlin Watson reads Cash's Christian worldview as Augustinian: evil is not a positive substance but a privation or corruption of good (contra the monism Leibniz risks and the Manichean dualism Augustine rejected), so humans alone bear blame for moral evil through freely corrupting good things—'Cocaine Blues,' 'The Wall,' the Folsom prisoner who admits he 'had it coming,' and the divided self of 'The Beast in Me' echoing Romans 7. Natural evil, as in 'Guess Things Happen That Way' and the flood of 'Five Feet High and Rising' (Cash's mother's 'blessing' of rich river dirt), serves punishment or greater goods. 'A Boy Named Sue' dramatizes the residual tension: the father's get-tough-or-die theodicy convinces neither Sue nor us that the sheer amount of evil is justified.

problem-of-evil.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
problem-of-evil.title: Christmas in Jamaica
problem-of-evil.relation: David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.

problem-of-evil.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
problem-of-evil.title: Moments of Redemption
problem-of-evil.relation: Ventimiglia sets Augustine's three answers to the problem of evil (free will, the toddler-at-the-doctor 'greater good,' evil as privation) against Nebraska's title track, where mass murderer Charlie Starkweather's 'I guess there's just a meanness in this world' makes Augustine's metaphysical gymnastics look like sophistry. 'Atlantic City' and 'Johnny 99' show free will compromised by debts, job loss and winners-and-losers, and Springsteen neither glorifies nor explains evil away. What Bruce and Augustine share is the yearning for redemption: Plato's Symposium pictures Eros — poor, barefoot, homeless, a hunger for the beautiful — and Springsteen answers that hunger with temporary moments of deliverance ('meet me tonight in Atlantic City') rather than guaranteed salvation.

problem-of-evil.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
problem-of-evil.title: Death on Veridian III
problem-of-evil.relation: Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.

problem-of-evil.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
problem-of-evil.title: Rescuing Princess Zelda
problem-of-evil.relation: Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.

problem-of-evil.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
problem-of-evil.title: Roll Credits
problem-of-evil.relation: Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.

problem-of-evil.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
problem-of-evil.title: Thinking in Rainbows
problem-of-evil.relation: Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.

problem-of-evil.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
problem-of-evil.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Robison measures Pullman's Authority against the three attributes that make the Christian God worthy of worship and finds it fails all three: the suffering of intercision victims like Tony Makarios and the Authority's delegation to the malevolent Metatron defeat omnibenevolence, because unlike with the real God we know no free-will theodicy applies, since the Authority simply does not care; his ignorance of Lyra's destiny (which witches and the Consistorial Court learn long before he does) defeats omniscience; and his demented weeping in the crystal litter before dissolving in open air defeats omnipotence. Since the Authority never created the universe and lied about being its creator, he is not God at all, so Pullman's plot never refutes the God of the philosophers. What the books do establish, she argues, is a powerful attack on organized religion: the Magisterium's suppression of Dust research and harming of children mirror real religious institutions' punishment of Galileo, resistance to evolution, and persecution of dissenters.

problem-of-evil.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
problem-of-evil.title: Red Sox Future
problem-of-evil.relation: Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.

problem-of-evil.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
problem-of-evil.title: Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory
problem-of-evil.relation: Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.

problem-of-evil.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
problem-of-evil.title: Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article
problem-of-evil.relation: Littmann runs Hume's Dialogues argument from evil through Onion headlines: 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy' (Timmy Yu's resounding no), 'God Outdoes Terrorists Yet Again,' 'God Wastes Miracle On Running Catch In Outfield,' and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways As Motive In Killing Of 3,000 Papua New Guineans.' He dispatches the theodicies one by one: limiting God's power or goodness (as Mill's lesser deity would) abandons the God of the tradition; the free will defense fails because police rightly restrain gunmen and no human freedom explains hurricanes; soul-building is pointless for a being who could implant compassion innately or stage fake evils; the 'no best possible world' dodge would excuse the reporter who watches a man burn; and the mystery defense makes reason useless. He concludes no all-knowing, all-good, all-powerful God exists, while insisting readers think it through for themselves.

problem-of-evil.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
problem-of-evil.title: Voltaire Lives
problem-of-evil.relation: Douglas Ficek traces The Onion's God stories — 'Lord Under Investigation For Failure To Provide,' God refusing to heal paralyzed little Timmy Yu, and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways' — back through Voltaire's Candide to Leibniz's theodicy, the 'best of all possible worlds' doctrine that Dr. Pangloss keeps reciting through hanging, slavery, and syphilis until Candide concludes we must cultivate our garden. The chapter's sharpest claim is that theodicy works by victim-blaming: Jerry Falwell's 9/11 rant earned the headline-only 'Jerry Falwell: Is That Guy A Dick Or What?' because he excused God by blaming secular Americans, just as Pastor Ellsworth blames heathen tsunami victims. Following theologian Dorothee Soelle, Ficek names this 'theological sadism,' and offers the Bible-drop missionaries of 'Poverty-Stricken Africans Receive Desperately Needed Bibles' as a modern Pangloss who mistakes moral obliviousness for grace.

problem-of-evil.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
problem-of-evil.title: The Emergence of Good from Evil
problem-of-evil.relation: Uses David Lynch's film—Baron Harkonnen as evil personified, Paul's prophetic dreams as biblical revelation, 'the sleeper must awaken'—to stage the problem of evil: if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly good, why do Harkonnens and man-eating worms exist? It lays out the free will defense, J.L. Mackie's objection that God could have created beings who always freely choose good, and the moral/natural evil distinction (Feyd's poisoned blade versus the worm destroying the spice crawler), then extracts the film's own alternative theodicy: good is defined against evil, since the Fremen's dormant 'goodness' awakens only in the struggle Paul leads against their enslavers. The chapter ends with John Hick's soul-making thought that spiritual growth comes through response to challenges, while conceding the evidential problem of evil's sheer quantity.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: What Happens in Carthage Stays in Carthage
problem-of-evil.relation: The section likens Augustine's adolescence in Carthage — the Las Vegas of his day — to a rolling-stone youth of sex and sin, noting that Jagger was actually the more responsible teen, enrolling at the London School of Economics. Its key move: in the song's catalog of atrocities the Devil only watches ('I watched with glee') and never causes, so if Lucifer is not the guilty party, the evil must be human — exactly the question Augustine's Confessions was written to answer.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: (I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction . . . Or the Satisfaction that I Ought To
problem-of-evil.relation: Augustine's theory of evil is explained through a concert-photography analogy: a dark photo of a brightly lit stage contains no real darkness, just a camera lacking proper exposure, fixable with editing. Likewise, evil is not an entity or polar opposite of good but a privation — something missing the 'good-making' features it ought to have — so no Devil is needed to explain the darkness in the world or in us.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: Who’s to Blame
problem-of-evil.relation: The section turns to Augustine's pear theft, where 'it was the sin that sweetened' the act: evil is chosen for the thrill of the forbidden, not forced by any demonic power. It names this 'moral impotence' — knowing the right yet willingly choosing the wrong, as with a missed curfew — an instinct no era has cured. The background vocals' 'Who? Who?' and Jagger's 'I'll tell you one time, you're to blame' thus land the blame for history's catastrophes squarely on 'you and me'.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: Just as Every Cop Is a Criminal, and All the Sinners Saints
problem-of-evil.relation: This section lays out Augustine's journey from the Manichean two-gods heresy, through reading Plato, to the view of evil as an 'absence' rather than a force. Its core is the dilemma of Confessions 7.3: if God is wholly good, who sowed the 'seed of bitterness' — the wicked will — into us, and who made the devil? Augustine's answer runs through original sin (the pride of Adam and Eve, demons as fallen angels) and an awkward compromise on which humans are free yet constrained by predestination, so that evil becomes necessary — and confession itself a good.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: But What’s Puzzling You Is the Nature of My Game
problem-of-evil.relation: The section situates the song after the 1967 Redlands Bust and amid 1968's collapses — Paris riots, Vietnam, Bobby Kennedy's assassination, which forced the lyric change from 'Who killed Kennedy?' to 'Who killed the Kennedys?' the night before a recording session. Against both Augustine and Bulgakov, it argues Jagger's Devil is far more human and unpredestined: by demanding we 'guess my name', the song fingers us as Satan, tracing the world's malice to our own impulses rather than any divinely scripted plan.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: I Tell You One Time, You’re to Blame
problem-of-evil.relation: The closing section follows the song's aftermath through Godard's session film — Brian Jones inaudible in his booth as a Dylanesque draft turns into a 'rocking samba' — to Jones's death, the Altamont killing (shown by Gimme Shelter to have happened during 'Under My Thumb', not 'Sympathy'), and the end of Mick and Marianne. Its verdict: Augustine's narrow, predestined free will leaves humanity out of the picture, while Jagger's human Devil puts responsibility back on us — a world without the Stones would be less enlightened about evil, and their song 'demands more of us, perhaps, than Augustine's Confessions'.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: It’s Just that Demon Life Has Got Me in Its Sway
problem-of-evil.relation: Reads "Sympathy for the Devil" through Saint Augustine's Confessions rather than only through Bulgakov's Master and Margarita, which supposedly inspired the lyrics. Augustine's stolen pears and his confession that he loved evil "solely because it was evil" show him needing "the companionship of others sinning," which the chapter pairs with the song's "Who killed the Kennedys?... It was you and me" and with Lee Harvey Oswald's refusal to have acted alone. But the paths split: Jagger's Devil makes evil real and ours, while for Augustine evil has no positive existence at all.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: It’s Only Rock’n’Roll, But I Complicate It
problem-of-evil.relation: Casts Augustine as the first Christian rock artist — a rebellious, sex-obsessed convert who, like Plato, ranked the body below the soul — and explains his privation doctrine: "evil has no positive nature; but the loss of good has received the name 'evil.'" Evil is "a swerving of the will which is turned toward lower things," so free will is crucial: God permits evil because virtues like courage could not exist in a world without it. The chapter closes with the constellation of opposites (soul/body, pride/humility, temporal/eternal) Augustine says we must live through to approach philosophical truth.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: I Shouted Out, Who Killed Meredith Hunter
problem-of-evil.relation: Takes the refrain "what's puzzling you is the nature of my game" to mean the song presents the Devil as a real, personal force present at the crucifixion, the Russian Revolution, World War II and the Kennedy assassinations — not the mere lack of goodness Augustine allows. It cites Richards's 2002 remark, on the heels of 9/11, that confronting evil puts him "out of a job," and reads "Sweet Neo Con" as Jagger still indicting ideology. Against Augustine's weak-willed sinner, "every cop is a criminal" locates evil in human strength and resolve — with Godard's Eve Democracy answering "Yes" to "Is the Devil God in exile?"

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: Under Our Thumb
problem-of-evil.relation: Corrects the popular error that Meredith Hunter was killed while "Sympathy for the Devil" played: eyewitnesses and the Gimme Shelter footage show the murder happened during "Under My Thumb" at the Altamont free concert of December 6, 1969. It surveys the assigning of blame — Rolling Stone captioning Jagger's picture "Is Mick responsible for the killing?", Norma Coates blaming the era's burden on the counterculture — and concludes Jagger sides against Augustine's privation view: Hunter did not die "at the hands of a bunch of privations," since the evil the band saw was an in-your-face reality.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: A Wild Murder Couldn’t Drag Me Away
problem-of-evil.relation: Draws Augustine and Jagger together as brothers who fell far before finding restraint: Augustine's many conflicting wills must collapse into one good will by actually choosing, and his Manichean past taught him some truths must be performed or willed, like his "grant me chastity — just not yet." The chapter reads Gimme Shelter as likewise double — harrowing documentary or joyous concert footage, forced to choose — and argues the post-Altamont Stones had to make "Sympathy for the Devil" a performative force for understanding evil rather than a scapegoat, then stayed in the flesh, confronting good and evil through the blues.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: Chapter 21 - Lucifer Rising and Falling
problem-of-evil.relation: Opens Dan Dinello's chapter with Richards's 1971 "Everybody's Lucifer" and sets up its two rival accounts of evil: the Christian Satan enshrined by Augustine — Lucifer expelled for prideful disobedience, seducing God's weak-willed children into sin — and the moral authorities of the 1960s (press, police, clergy) who cast the Stones as "Satan's Jesters" luring youth astray. The Stones answered with a nineteenth-century Romantic Lucifer, the rebellious angel fighting moral repression, blaming the mob of hypocritical authorities for the world's horrors.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: From Satyrs to Martyrs
problem-of-evil.relation: Shows how Augustine forged the machinery of Christian evil — sex as sin, the invention of Original Sin, The City of God's mandate to compel heretics, and the goat-god Pan as Satan's visual model — then maps it onto the 1960s persecution of the Stones: press mockery, police drug busts, Bill Wyman hauled into court as a "shaggy monster." The persecution backfired, making the Stones martyrs and pushing Jagger toward the self-embraced "Lucifers of Rock" image of "Paint It, Black" and the Their Satanic Majesties Request cover.

problem-of-evil.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
problem-of-evil.title: The Devil Is My Name
problem-of-evil.relation: Reports Jagger's own genealogy of the song — "an old idea of Baudelaire's," Bulgakov's Master and Margarita (given to him by Marianne Faithfull), and his Lucifer Rising conversations with Kenneth Anger — and follows its studio metamorphosis from country dirge to voodoo samba under Godard's camera. The finished recording, whose working title was "The Devil is My Name," builds into a celebration of humanity's hatred and hypocrisy from the crucifixion through the Blitzkrieg to the Kennedys (pluralized when RFK was shot on June 5, 1968, during the sessions), putting humanity on trial by the devil rather than the other way around.

problem-of-evil.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
problem-of-evil.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Sets Walt's 'There's nothing but chemistry here' materialism - the missing 0.111958 percent of the human body that Gretchen calls the soul - against Augustine's Confessions, arguing both men want redemption without giving up their sins: 'give me chastity, but not yet.' It maps Augustine's problem of evil (evil as corruption of the will toward self-destruction) onto Walt's pros-and-cons list over killing Krazy-8 and his 'no-rough-stuff-type deal' fantasy after Tuco. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle then turns chemistry's laws into tendencies, opening room for free choice inside a materialist world - so Walt's remission in 'Over' saves the body, while only changed choices, which he keeps deferring, could save the man.

problem-of-evil.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
problem-of-evil.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Sirvent and Baker take Van Alden's 'strong providential theology' - 'his fate rests in God's hands' at the burned Agent Clarkson's bedside - as a live version of the problem of evil, traced through Augustine and Aquinas to Calvin's all-determining divine omnipotence. The Arminian free-will escape leaves God like a parent watching a child run into traffic, and the 'mysterious ways' reply makes God's moral vocabulary so alien that a God who burns his beloved is 'one-sided' and unworshipable - the same theology that lets Van Alden shift blame for Lucy's pregnancy onto a 'charge from God' before drowning Sebso as 'the judgment of the wicked.' They close with Nucky's God, an inner impetus toward good that asks rather than coerces, and with process theology's persuading God, while Gyp Rosetti's Easter rant at the crucifix shows what believing in the omnipotent alternative costs.

problem-of-evil.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
problem-of-evil.title: Futurama and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Oschman reads 'Godfellas' as an answer to the problem of evil: Bender, made god of the Shrimpkins, destroys them by meddling too much, and the God Entity explains 'if you do too much, people get dependent. And if you do nothing, they lose hope.' After testing the contrast response (pain makes Slurm sweet) and the Free Will Defense (which covers moral evils like the returning garbage ball of 'A Big Piece of Garbage' but not natural evils or the taste of anchovies), the chapter adopts John Hick's soul-making theodicy: God's epistemic distance - compared to Fry's obsession after tasting super Slurm - keeps creatures uncompelled so they can grow into free moral agents. Fry's slow evolution from delivery boy to 'slightly less lazy slob' is soul-making, and 'The Late Philip J. Fry' wryly confirms life's purpose is 'probably some hogwash about the human spirit.'

problem-of-evil.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
problem-of-evil.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.

problem-of-evil.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
problem-of-evil.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Jeremy Proulx reads Ender through F.W.J. Schelling's account of evil as a real, positive force rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: Ender's kicks to Stilson and Bonzo, his killing of the Giant in the mind game, and his 'I destroy them' confession all display the 'contraction into the self' Schelling thinks haunts every moral agent. He argues Graff deliberately isolates Ender to force this dark ground to the surface, and that Valentine's 'welcome to the human race' and the hive-queen's forgiveness teach Ender that evil, though never excusable, can be understood and atoned for - his fate also shows freedom tainted by a necessity we neither choose nor control.

problem-of-evil.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
problem-of-evil.title: The Devil and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Robert Arp's introduction opens with Halloween culture and his own seminarian past to ask whether belief in the Devil can survive scrutiny. He lays out a 'just deserts' argument - Hitler, Stalin, and Mao died unpunished while Job, Socrates, and Thomas More died unrewarded, so God, the Devil, Heaven, and Hell must exist to balance the scales - and then answers it with Freud's projection critique (religion as wishful thinking for comfort and moral control) and with the neuroscience tying the mind to a dying brain, which undermines the soul that Hell would punish. The chapter frames the whole book's project: testing devil-belief with arguments and evidence rather than taking it on authority.

problem-of-evil.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
problem-of-evil.title: The Devil and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: A.G. Holdier pits Augustine against Star Wars: South Park's pay-per-view Satan-Jesus boxing match and the Force's balanced light and dark sides picture God and the Devil as equals, but Augustine - drawing on his Manichaean past and Zoroastrianism's Ahura Mazda versus Angra Mainyu - shows this is really two-gods worship, not monotheism. For Augustine the Devil is a derivative creature, created good and freely fallen, and evil is not a positive force but a privation, an absence of God like cold or darkness, so Vader's corruption and redemption both hang on free choice. Mordred's rebellion against Arthur gives the right picture: the Dark Side can never win because it is only diminished goodness.

problem-of-evil.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
problem-of-evil.title: The Devil and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Ray Bossert reads Tolkien's Silmarillion through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy: elves, being artists, understand Melkor not as tempter but as bad artist, from his rebellious solo in the Music of the Ainur to his botched sub-creations - orcs bred from kidnapped elves - and his covetous collecting of the silmarils. Boethius supplies the machinery: evil seeks a good by unnatural means and only approximates it, wickedness debases its practitioner into a beast, God's foreknowledge embraces free choices without causing them, and Providence is a spinning disc at whose center alone one is steady - so Melkor's rebellion leaves him less free, dragged around the rim. Tolkien's contrast between art (for beauty) and magic (for control) explains why the Devil can only mimic creation, never make anything real.

problem-of-evil.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
problem-of-evil.title: The Devil and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Thomas Ward reconstructs C.S. Lewis's argument from The Problem of Pain that either demons exist or God doesn't. The free will defense, credited to Augustine, covers the evil humans freely do - freedom being required for love, as the rubber-ducky world shows - but John Perry's baby bat eaten by cockroaches and William Rowe's burned fawn are natural evils no human is responsible for. Given the not-crazy assumptions that God exists and is never morally responsible for evil, something non-human, personal, and wicked must bear that responsibility: hence demons, who like us misused their freedom, stretching the free will defense to cover every evil whatsoever.

problem-of-evil.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
problem-of-evil.title: The Devil and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.

problem-of-evil.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
problem-of-evil.title: Homeland and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.

problem-of-evil.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
problem-of-evil.title: Homeland and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin reads Carrie's 'I missed something once before... everyone's not me' as the modern, secular problem of evil: as Susan Neiman argues, unreasonable suffering threatens reason itself, and the Rousseau-Voltaire split defines the responses. Carrie takes Rousseau's side - 'All is good leaving the hands of the author of things' degenerates in human hands, so evil is intelligible and redemption possible, the chance at redemption she offers Brody and even Nazir - against Voltaire's Candide-style tending of the garden. The finale deepens this with Boethius's Consolation: Carrie's 'I believe one of the reasons I was put on this Earth was for our paths to cross' fuses fate with providence, and she accepts Brody's execution as a redemptive end 'more so if he dies'.

problem-of-evil.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
problem-of-evil.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Montoya asks whether Prismo, Adventure Time's wish-granting stand-in for God, produced the best possible world when he restored Ooo over Farmworld. After explaining Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil—that an all-good, all-knowing God permits some evil because every possible world contains some, and ours contains the least—the chapter compares Farmworld (no Lich, but Finn becomes the Ice King, Jake mutates into the Lich, Marceline dies ancient and insane) with Ooo, where the same characters flourish as heroes. Prismo, no omnibenevolent deity, remakes Ooo out of friendship with Jake, and Farmworld's horrors vindicate the Leibnizian point that wishing one evil out of existence can unleash far worse.

problem-of-evil.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
problem-of-evil.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: White argues Apple's 'Think Different' commercial packages together two distinct character traits: genuine independence, in Rand's sense of judging from the facts of reality (thirteen-year-old Jobs confronting his pastor with the problem of evil via the Biafran children—'Does God know about this?'—rejecting dogma at Stanford, killing the iPod's screen, bending Corning to make gorilla glass on schedule), and pseudo-independence that asserts the primacy of consciousness over reality (refusing to bathe because his diet 'prevented' odor, treating cancer with fruit juice, NeXT's impossible eighteen-month promise). Using Binswanger's 'fallacy of false integration' (the surgeon-and-murderer 'cutter' example), he charges the ad with merging the traits into one folder, so Jobs should instead be praised without qualification for his independence and blamed without qualification for his pseudo-independence.

problem-of-evil.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
problem-of-evil.title: 6. Tris’s Compassion and the Problem of Evil
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads Tris's whole arc as a struggle with the problem of evil, both the theological version from Job and the modern secular one Susan Neiman describes, in which unreasonable suffering threatens trust in human reason. He casts Tris as cut from Rousseau's mold - her insistence on making the evils of Jeanine, Marcus, and Evelyn intelligible - against Voltaire's Candide refusal to rationalize suffering, and treats the faction system as Rousseau's social-contract strategy for containing the inclination to evil while Tris herself plays a wartime Emile. The key is Tobias's lesson that selflessness and bravery are not that different: selflessness enables the courage that compassion motivates, from pressing her forehead to Jeanine's gun in the fear landscape to taking Caleb's place at the weapons lab, so that the trilogy ends with Tobias's 'we mend each other.'

problem-of-evil.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
problem-of-evil.title: 18. Wondering What It’s All For
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin reads Lord Grantham's 'we've dreamed a dream' as an echo of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 and follows the war story line - Matthew and William missing before Amiens, William's slow death, Mr. Lang's shell shock, Mrs. Patmore's nephew Archie shot for cowardice - to show how obscure war's causes and realities remain to those who have not lived them. The Dowager Countess's 'we don't always get our just deserts' as Matthew dies under his car, and the stretcher-bearer's 'it comes down to luck,' raise the problem of evil from the Book of Job: good and bad fortune fall without premonition or meaning. Against complacency about war's inevitability, the chapter argues that since class and traffic harms can be reduced, warfare's can be too - we should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret the wars a few dream up, and not allow them to come to be.

problem-of-evil.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
problem-of-evil.title: 4. Acts of God
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads Lecter's parable of the church collapses - 'It must feel good to God - He does it all the time, and are we not made in His image?' - as Lecter's solution to the problem of evil in both its theological (Job) and secular (Neiman) forms: a malevolent deity of the kind de Sade's Saint-Fond describes, doing God's work becomes Lecter's justification, and killing feels good because 'if one does what God does enough times, one will become as God is'. Following Neiman, he sets Rousseau's tradition (evil must be made intelligible - 'All is well leaving the hands of the author of things') against Voltaire's Candide refusal of theodicy, showing that Will and Starling live in Rousseau's camp except when facing Lecter himself, and that the Hannibal/Hannibal Rising revelation that Mischa's murder 'happened' to him radically revises his earlier claim that 'we don't invent our natures', with Starling's reason finally making 'a place for Mischa' in Lecter and Starling together.

problem-of-evil.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
problem-of-evil.title: 6. The Psychiatrist as Sociopathic God
problem-of-evil.relation: Hassert takes Lecter's 'First principles, Clarice' at its Aristotelian word - nature is revealed through capacities and action, as an acorn's telos is not pumpkins and a kitten will never be a Great Dane - to explain Lecter's psychiatry: he reads each patient's essence and potential, prescribing Mason Verger's face-peeling so appearance finally matches essence, and force-raising Will toward equality so that Aristotelian perfect friendship between the alike-in-virtue (which Franklyn's flattery can never reach) might become possible. Reading God through Augustine's account of evil as the destruction of a preexisting good and Mischa's murder, the chapter argues that Lecter emulates a capricious deity - 'Typhoid and swans - it all comes from the same place' - and, unlike Nietzsche, does not pronounce God dead but merely misconceptualized, while his friendships fail because he must corrupt the other into his own image rather than love an equal.

problem-of-evil.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
problem-of-evil.title: 10. Gods Are Overrated
problem-of-evil.relation: Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.

problem-of-evil.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
problem-of-evil.title: 20. What It Takes
problem-of-evil.relation: The chapter argues Batman is the more heroic superhero because his heroism is supererogatory and replicable: like Wesley Autrey the Subway Samaritan rather than the duty-bound Captain Sullenberger, he acts beyond obligation with human abilities we could imitate, while Superman's alien powers make his help barely optional and himself impossible to emulate. It frames Batman as Bruce's answer to the problem of evil in Susan Neiman's secular version - Rachel Dawes's challenge that good people must 'do something' about Falcone's Gotham - siding with the Rousseau line that reason must make evil intelligible against Voltaire's refusal. Batman earns his 'super' by marshaling reason as well as wealth, like the cell-phone sonar he submits to Lucius Fox's veto in The Dark Knight, and his parting 'anyone can be a hero' to Gordon shows heroes begetting heroes, which Superman's otherworldliness never manages.

problem-of-evil.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
problem-of-evil.title: 4. Raising Darrow
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.

problem-of-evil.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
problem-of-evil.title: 18. Gods and Beetles
problem-of-evil.relation: Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies. Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'

problem-of-evil.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
problem-of-evil.title: 20. Cersei, Sansa, and the Problem of Evil
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads Cersei and Sansa's post-imprisonment rises in season six as opposite answers to the problem of evil, framed by Susan Neiman's claim that Enlightenment thought split between making evil intelligible and refusing to. Cersei, taught by Tywin that 'the gods have no mercy - that's why they're gods,' becomes Sade's cruel god of Juliette, doing whatever feels good as the gods do; Sansa, hardened by Ramsay and Littlefinger's betrayal into 'no one can protect anyone,' embodies the Kantian response that virtue and happiness come apart, so one governs only what can be controlled - character, family, justice - as she engineers the Battle of the Bastards and has Ramsay eaten by his dogs without mercy or vengeance.

problem-of-evil.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
problem-of-evil.title: 25. Deadpool Kills God
problem-of-evil.relation: The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'

problem-of-evil.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
problem-of-evil.title: 26. Why We Love to Watch Deadpool . . . Play with Himself
problem-of-evil.relation: Using the Deadpool video game, the chapter argues Wade is a god who is all-powerful (rewriting the game world with his crayon-scrawled script and manufacturing fake credits), all-knowing (reading the player's mind through the fourth wall and literally entering Rogue's), and plainly not all-good (slapping an unconscious Wolverine, ogling dead Vertigo, ignoring Apocalypse three times for a billion dollars), so that dystheism - belief in a god with serious issues - dissolves the problem of evil. The free-will defense collapses because Deadpool wrote the script the villains obey, giving players only the illusion of choice. The voices in Wade's head are explicitly cast as Freud's structural model, with his Ego and SuperEgo talking while WadePrime, the Id, does most of the voice-work.

problem-of-evil.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
problem-of-evil.title: 11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them
problem-of-evil.relation: Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.

problem-of-evil.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
problem-of-evil.title: 2. Just Not the Hero Type (Not!)
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin builds a six-part definition of heroism (moral, altruistic, atypical, supererogatory, replicable safeguarding) and tests it on Wesley Autrey versus Captain Sullenberger and a Super Autrey thought experiment: Iron Man's engineering-based feats are refinements of abilities we share and so inspire imitation, while there can only ever be one Captain America, making Tony the more heroic. The Sokovia Accords debate then contrasts two humilities, with Stark's willingness to accept oversight more heroic than Rogers' safest-hands-are-our-own confidence. The chapter closes by explaining why we invent super heroes at all through Susan Neiman's account of the problem of evil after twentieth-century atrocities, from the Stamford explosion to Charlie Spencer's death in Lagos.

problem-of-evil.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
problem-of-evil.title: 15. The Evil in These Woods
problem-of-evil.relation: Tests three accounts of evil against the show. Augustine's privation theory — evil as nothingness, forged against Manichean dualism — fails to capture a Twin Peaks that is genuinely Manichean, with the Experiment vomiting BOB out of the Trinity blast and the Black and White Lodges in eternal conflict; Ricoeur's symbolism of defilement fits the filthy-haired BOB, the sooty Woodsmen, and the frog-moth contaminating the sleeping girl. The decisive framework is Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics triad of vice, incontinence, and bestiality: Ben Horne's and Laura's weakness of will, the town's ordinary vices, and BOB's appetite-only bestiality ("I don't need anything. I want") versus Windom Earle, whose intact but corrupted reason — the macabre chess game, murdering Catherine beside Cooper, hunting Cooper's soul — makes him, per Aristotle's claim that vice is worse than bestiality, the show's truly evil person and proof that evil is human and fightable.

problem-of-evil.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
problem-of-evil.title: 17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' (Lutze tried by his victims' ghosts at Dachau and sentenced to madness) and 'He's Alive' (neo-Nazi Vollmer groomed by Hitler's ghost) as Serling's twin responses to the Eichmann trial, situating them among the docufiction Operation Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman episode, and his abhorred Hogan's Heroes. Tracking Serling's maturation from the heartless, monstrous Lutze to the needy, speechmaking Vollmer — 'frustrated men, sick men, angry men' — he argues the later episode foreshadows Arendt's banality of evil, evil as the end product of a political process and a thoughtless inability to think from another's standpoint, all framed by Susan Neiman's problem of evil.

problem-of-evil.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
problem-of-evil.title: 8. From the Handmaid’s Tale to the Handmaids’ Tale
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads Offred's silent prayers ('I want to know what I did to deserve this') as channeling the Book of Job, using Susan Neiman's distinction between the theological and secular problem of evil: even if we stop demanding explanations from God, we must still make evil intelligible, as Janine's Testifying cruelly refuses to do. He sets Rousseau against Voltaire on whether morality requires making evil intelligible, finding June Rousseauian for piecing together Gilead's hidden prehistory at the Boston Globe and for acting from compassion, as with the bread-truck driver's secret Quran. The Salvaging refusal—Ofglen first, then Offred, then sixty-five stones dropped with 'I'm sorry, Aunt Lydia'—shows compassion becoming solidarity and solidarity becoming a general will, transforming The Handmaid's Tale into The Handmaids' Tale.

problem-of-evil.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
problem-of-evil.title: 2. Can Anything Good Come from the Upside Down
problem-of-evil.relation: Kuzma maps Augustine's two cities onto the two Hawkinses: not two places but two mixed moral orientations in one world, since Will is literally 'right here' in the same house flipped upside down. Augustine's privation view of evil (evil as absence of good, a nougat-less Three Musketeers) explains how Dart can come from the 'evil' Upside Down yet love Dustin and let the party pass, while Brenner, from the right side up, is ruled by libido dominandi like the Mind Flayer and Dr. Owens proves Hawkins Lab is not automatically bad; it is how you act, not where you are from.

problem-of-evil.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
problem-of-evil.title: I Know What’s Real
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin's afterword works out what Deckard can mean by 'I know what's real': given the green eyes in the Voight-Kampff playback versus the brown eyes in Wallace's staged memory, Deckard is claiming the overwhelming authority of his own lived experience — of Rachael's eye color, their love, her personhood — over any recording or replica. He folds this into the book's larger move from the problem of personhood to the problem of evil, why bad things happen to good people, and the secular task of justifying the ways of Wallace, Tyrell, and the other ersatz gods. With Mr. Cotton's 'raining fire' echoing the Book of Job, the afterword presents the volume as an invitation to save ourselves by saving one another.

problem-of-evil.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
problem-of-evil.title: 23. The Neighborhood Is Us
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin frames the show, via Susan Neiman, as Rousseau's answer to the problem of evil: bad things (including bad television) happen to good kids, but education can mitigate evil, which is why Rogers prefers Rousseau's demand to make evil intelligible to Voltaire's Candidean refusal and Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds. Rogers pursued only Emile's second prong, making us as we ought to be by loving children 'just the way they are,' and the post-9/11 PSAs before King Friday's empty castle merge Make-Believe into reality, the last 'modulation' of his thirty-four-year ministry.

problem-of-evil.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
problem-of-evil.title: 8. Time Travel and the Problem of Evil
problem-of-evil.relation: Ray Bossert reads Endgame through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, arguing that Doctor Strange and Tony Stark, who permit the Snap and five years of suffering for the sake of the one winning outcome, run 'uncannily parallel' to Thanos, who decided for Gamora that her unwilling death served the greater good. Strange's viewing of 14,000,605 futures illustrates Boethius's distinction between an infinite being riding along the timeline and an eternal one seeing all moments at once, and the refusal to tell Stark his role mirrors why God's foreknowledge sees our choices without compelling them. Boethius's providence weaving free choices into justice, the Avengers' passion-driven failures on Titan (Star-Lord and Thor avenging lost lovers), justice as the wicked's own punishment (Thanos dying wretched twice in one film), and Umberto Eco's 'Myth of Superman' all frame a universe where suffering is allowed because it is woven into a pattern that ends in justice.

problem-of-evil.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
problem-of-evil.title: 4. The Case of the Other Renegade Refugee
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads 'The Case of the Renegade Refugee' (aired December 9, 1961, days before Eichmann's verdict) alongside the film Operation Eichmann and Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem as three competing pop-culture portrayals of the Nazi criminal: monstrous, repentant, and banal. The episode's 'other' refugee, Arthur Hennings/Max Kleinerman, whose Father Paul-inspired 'religious peace' lets him recant on the stand and save Mason's client Harlan Merrill (himself a Battle of the Bulge 'deserter' living a lie created by concussion), supplies what Arendt found absent in Eichmann: empathy and genuine acceptance of guilt, complicating her banality-of-evil picture. The whole is set against the Holocaust as the century's starkest form of the problem of why the innocent suffer while the wicked thrive, and closed with Hogan's Heroes' provocative reuse of the same actors four years later.

problem-of-evil.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
problem-of-evil.title: Equal Opportunity—for Deities
problem-of-evil.relation: Barkman argues the Marvel Universe's 'One-Above-All'—depicted as Stan Lee and Jack Kirby—is the eternal Judeo-Christian Creator, and arranges its beings in a graded hierarchy: the Living Tribunal as God's judge, cosmic beings like Eternity and Galactus, elders, sky fathers Odin and Zeus, down to mortals, with only God eternal and everything else, gods included, able to die yet enduring by His decree. Ontological rank guarantees nothing morally—Mephisto, the Goddess, and Hera are powerful and wicked, and even Hercules can be beaten by the Wrecking Crew. A free-will theodicy answers where evil came from: 'no other gods before me' never denied other gods' existence but commands loving the Good above all, which mortal Avengers like Thor, loving justice perfected by sacrificial love, manage as well as any deity.

problem-of-evil.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
problem-of-evil.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.

problem-of-evil.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
problem-of-evil.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Liz Stillwaggon Swan surveys Sabbath's pictures of moral evil (nuclear annihilation in "Electric Funeral", heroin's "deadly pin" in "Hand of Doom", social oppression allegorized as the Satan of "Black Sabbath") and argues the band poses the problem of evil without solving it theologically. Against the view that invoking evil presupposes God, she aligns Sabbath with Augustine's rejection of Manichaean evil-as-a-force, reading evil as a privation traceable to free human choices, and with Bertrand Russell's "A Free Man's Worship": "Children of the Grave", "Into the Void", "Spiral Architect", and "Symptom of the Universe" urge that we defeat evil by imagining and building a better possible reality through love, vegan-pacifist Geezer Butler being the living proof behind the stage persona.

problem-of-evil.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
problem-of-evil.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.

problem-of-evil.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
problem-of-evil.title: The Dread Conclusion!
problem-of-evil.relation: The chapter asks whether Dormammu is truly evil and tests him against Augustine's three types of evil: metaphysical evil as privation fails because Dormammu is a positive being with a face and a voice, natural evil fails because he is a sentient agent with intentions, so he lands squarely in moral evil—freely intending to deprive intelligent beings of the good of existence. It entertains the Galactus-style alternative that Dormammu, like a lion taking a gazelle, is an amoral force consuming worlds for survival, but his rage in the time loop ('your world is mine, like all worlds') reveals a drive for domination rather than sustenance, while conceding we know him only through the Ancient One's possibly biased testimony.

problem-of-evil.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
problem-of-evil.title: 18. Wondering What It’s All For
problem-of-evil.relation: Trip McCrossin follows Lord Grantham's 'We've dreamed a dream' - an allusion to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 - through the warfare story line of seasons 2 and 3, from Matthew and William missing in action to Matthew's death under a truck. Mr. Lang's shell-shocked confrontations with the eager volunteer William and with Mrs. Patmore over her executed nephew Archie dramatize the gulf between those who know what war is like and those who can only imagine it, while the meaningless deaths of Matthew and the stretcher-bearer who is shot mid-sentence raise the Job-like problem of evil in the Dowager's words, 'we don't always get our just deserts.' The chapter argues against complacency about warfare's inevitability: because total war is dreamed up by the few, the rest of us should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret those dreams in advance, and refuse to let them come to be.

problem-of-evil.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
problem-of-evil.title: The Emergence of Good from Evil
problem-of-evil.relation: Reads David Lynch's Dune as staging the problem of evil on an interplanetary scale: Baron Harkonnen as Satan-like evil personified against the Fremen, Paul's prophetic dreams as biblical-style revelation, and 'the sleeper must awaken' as spiritual awakening. Against the free will defense it deploys J.L. Mackie's argument that an omnipotent God could have created beings who always freely choose good, and uses the sandworm destroying the spice crawler as natural evil the defense cannot easily cover. It then proposes the film's own implicit theodicy, that goodness is defined against and emerges from evil (the Fremen's goodness awakened by liberation from Harkonnen tyranny, Paul good against the background of the Baron), closes with John Hick's point that moral growth requires challenges, and concedes the evidential problem posed by the sheer quantity of evil.

problem-of-evil.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
problem-of-evil.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Jeremy Proulx reads Ender's refrain 'I didn't want to hurt him!' through Schelling's account of evil as a real 'contraction into the self' rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: the beatings of Stilson, the boy on the shuttle, Bonzo, and the Giant reveal a Peter-like monstrosity in Ender that he can neither understand nor control. Graff's engineered isolation forces Ender to confront this dark ground, and his moral development culminates in Valentine's 'Welcome to the human race' — the recognition that freedom is tainted by a necessity we do not choose, so Ender stays responsible for xenocide even though he was tricked.

problem-of-evil.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
problem-of-evil.title: Mmmyez: Stewie and the Seven Deadly Sins
problem-of-evil.relation: Kaye argues Stewie is funny because he portrays a truth we repress: Augustine's doctrine of original sin (defended as the only answer to why God lets the innocent suffer, and grounded in the pear-tree and jealous-infant episodes of the Confessions) — no one is innocent, not even babies. Systematically cataloging Stewie through Aquinas's Seven Deadly Sins, she shows lust (the Rupert-the-gay-teddy-bear projection, 'wee-wee stricken with rigor mortis', inverting Freud's Oedipal complex since Stewie hates his mother and barely tolerates his father), gluttony (hoarding Lois's breast milk, an orgy of fig newtons), sloth as Aquinas's 'oppressive sorrow' and malicious indignation ('Why don't you burn in hell?'), avarice, anger as revenge (bombs and graham crackers), envy (locking Jeremy in the car trunk), and pride, the Queen of Vices — Stewie's god complex ('Omnipotence. Gotta get me some of that'). Stewie's lone possibly-decent moment (warning Brian not to mock upside-down Jake Tucker's face) is left as the one loose thread.

problem-of-evil.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
problem-of-evil.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Jaime Lannister's question to Catelyn Stark - 'If the gods are real and they are just, then why is the world so full of injustice?' - launches a tour of the logical and evidential problems of evil across the religions of Westeros. Augustine's privation theory and free will defense are tested against the Faith of the Seven (with Catelyn answering 'Because of men like you'), Hume's dilemma of impotence or malevolence is applied to the old gods that Arya scolds at Harrenhal for failing to save Ned, and Leibniz's best-possible-world reply is weighed against natural evils like the storm that sank the Windproud. The chapter concludes that only the evidential problem sticks: the sheer quantity of suffering in Westeros is evidence against just gods, though nothing counts against the uncaring gods Brienne describes.

problem-of-evil.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
problem-of-evil.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Nielsen asks whether a Green Lantern with unlimited willpower would be a god and answers no through Leibniz: God is the absolutely perfect being, where perfection excludes contradiction so that knowledge and power admit of perfection but 'the greatest of all numbers' does not, and such a being creates the best of all possible worlds. Hume's trilemma (impotent, malevolent, or whence evil?) is met with the theodicy that finite minds, like Lanterns baffled by Guardian decrees, cannot compare our world to the discarded possibilities, each perhaps as bad as Qward. Since omnipotence requires omniscience and omnibenevolence, not even Parallax, the Anti-Monitor, or Kyle as Ion counts as omnipotent: admirable and powerful, but not gods.

problem-of-evil.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
problem-of-evil.title: Notes
problem-of-evil.relation: Treats Frank's soliloquies-strangling the dog's 'useless pain', the Peachoid eulogy that goads a grieving congregation toward hating God, urinating on his father's grave 'to seem more human'-as a Heideggerian tour of concealment and disclosure, where truth is disclosure rather than correspondence and Frank alienates himself from responsibility and even from being human. Quoting Iris Murdoch on how fiction makes goodness seem dull and invoking Roth's 'theodicy of protest', the chapter warns that Frank's shuffling of morality into maneuver relaxes our moral guard about blame, God, and evil.

problem-of-evil.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
problem-of-evil.title: Rescuing Princess Zelda
problem-of-evil.relation: Dwayne Collins runs the problem of evil against Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem sets the all-good, all-powerful Goddesses against the existence of Ganondorf, and Plantinga's free-will defense transposes neatly because the wish-granting Triforce must permit evil wishes or its power would be limited. The evidential problem and John Hick's soul-making theodicy get recast as a 'game-making theodicy': if Hyrule's evil were neither excessive nor randomly distributed, its people (like players of a too-easy game) would stop striving to overcome it. Hyrule's distinctive solution, unavailable on Earth, is Link — a divinely chosen hero who counteracts excessive evil and returns the world to a 'normal' amount of it.

problem-of-evil.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
problem-of-evil.title: Fighting the Real Enemy
problem-of-evil.relation: Johnson asks why Sinead O'Connor tearing the Pope's photo ended her career while SNL's own religion sketches drew little fire: 'DJesus Uncrossed' targets Tarantino's gratuitous violence rather than Jesus, the Tebow sketch ridicules prayers for football wins that Nietzsche said cheapen God into a servant of chance, and 'God's a Boob Man' satirizes the God's Not Dead films' strawmanning of atheists. Louis C.K.'s God monologue, he argues, raises the burden of proof and the problem of natural evil, best answered by Carlin's joke of a God subject to physical laws. The Church Lady embodies Warmke and Tosi's moral grandstanding, whereas O'Connor's protest does not, and the chapter ends on Plato's Republic: better to be a virtuous person scorned as a villain, like O'Connor, than a celebrated villain, though her tragic life strains Plato's promise that virtue pays.

problem-of-evil.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
problem-of-evil.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.

problem-of-evil.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
problem-of-evil.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
problem-of-evil.relation: Johnson formalizes Kyle's crisis in 'Cartmanland'—evil Cartman inherits a million dollars and buys the amusement park while good Kyle suffers hemorrhoids and loses faith—as a valid argument from the logical problem of evil, then evaluates the town's theodicies against the philosophical ones.
