The Job story Kyle's parents read him fails like skeptical theism (it proves too much and ends in moral agnosticism), Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards's God-glorifying account, Stan's restored faith via Cartman's perfect misery is a greater-goods response, Augustine's free will defense purchases goodness at the price of God's control of prayers and elections and cannot explain natural evils, and Hick's soul-making theodicy founders on fawns, tsunamis, and Kenny's deaths. Pascal's Wager and Plantinga's divine sense are dismissed in turn: evil does not disprove God, but proportioning belief to evidence makes non-belief the rational stance.

problem-of-evil.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
problem-of-evil.title: Notes
problem-of-evil.relation: Eberl applies Augustine's theodicy to the Force: since evil is privation rather than a thing, the dark side is not a real half of the Force but its willful misuse by free beings, answering why a Force with a will permits Alderaan. Anakin's fall is Augustine's inordinate desire (cupiditas) for the temporal good of Padme's life against Yoda's counsel to let go, while Jacen Solo's willingness to kill for peace shows love destroyed rather than merely disordered, placing him beyond the redemption Anakin's rightly ordered love for his children still permits. Free will remains a divine gift whose misuse, not its giver, explains moral evil, and Anakin could still freely fulfill the Chosen One prophecy.

problem-of-evil.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
problem-of-evil.title: Notes
problem-of-evil.relation: Asks how an all-encompassing, good Force can have a dark side: after framing the Force as panentheistic, it tests Augustine's privation theory (Alderaan's destruction as an absence of 'measure, order, and form') and a Daoist reading of Yoda's equanimity modeled on Zhuangzi drumming and singing after his wife's death, rejecting both because Vader's evil is active, disciplined, and full of the Force rather than a lack. The answer endorsed is Schelling's: the will needs a dark 'ground' - Yoda's 'anger, fear, aggression' - which is benign when ordered by the will of love and becomes evil when it separatisitically defies it, which is what 'bringing balance to the Force' means.

problem-of-evil.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
problem-of-evil.title: 10. Gods Are Overrated
problem-of-evil.relation: Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.

problem-of-evil.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
problem-of-evil.title: 20. What It Takes
problem-of-evil.relation: Argues Batman is more heroic than Superman because heroism requires supererogation and replicability: Wesley Autrey's subway rescue, done without obligation, outranks Sullenberger's 'just what we're trained for,' and unlike otherworldly Superman, Batman's human abilities let the rest of us imagine imitating him—heroism begets heroism, as Gordon's coat around young Bruce's shoulders helped make Batman. Batman is framed as the answer to the problem of evil in Susan Neiman's secular form: Rachel Dawes' challenge that good people do something, on the Rousseau side of the Enlightenment debate that morality must make evil intelligible (against Voltaire's refusal). Superman's overwhelming power makes relying on reason superfluous, so he becomes a symbol of what we can't be, while the Dark Knight models what we can.

problem-of-evil.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
problem-of-evil.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Haas uses Dean's stubborn refusal to believe in God, even after meeting Castiel, escaping Hell, and visiting Heaven, to run through the problem of evil. Casey's challenge in 'Sin City' states the logical problem; the free-will theodicy answers it but falters before Supernatural's designed horrors like the rugaru, a creature God built to suffer an irresistible hunger that ends with it eating its spouse. Dean's real objection is the evidential problem, that the amount and severity of apparently pointless evil makes the omni-God unlikely, and neither a 'natural order' defense (Dick Roman humanely farming humans for food) nor John Hick's soul-making theodicy explains suffering far beyond what character formation requires.

problem-of-evil.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
problem-of-evil.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.

problem-of-evil.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
problem-of-evil.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Evolutionary biologist Graves applies naturalist method to the Supernatural universe: assume natural explanations first, as the Catholic Church does before granting an exorcism, and only posit the supernatural where naturalism fails. He builds a naturalistic phylogeny in which souls behave like genetic codes (50,000 new souls when Balthazar unsinks the Titanic), and demons, ghosts, and most monsters derive from human souls, which explains why mundane salt, iron, fire, and burned bones work on them, while pagan gods killable by wooden stakes and dog's blood are 'more akin to monsters' than gods. The framework yields rules and predictions about the Colt, holy water, and the Croatoan virus, and even suggests God and Death may be natural beings obeying laws lesser beings do not share.

problem-of-evil.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
problem-of-evil.title: NOTES
problem-of-evil.relation: Barkman answers 'God hates fangs' with Aquinas: evil is no-thing, so God creates nothing inherently evil — fangs, sex, and free will are good gifts whose misuse explains fallen angels, witches (via the Malleus Maleficarum and Allatius's demon-animated vampires), and human sinners like Rene and the Rattrays. Since True Blood's vampires stand unmoved before crosses, hold church meetings, and can choose as Bill does, they are not soulless minions of the devil but created beings who, like humans, go wrong only by misusing free will — which is why Harris's inclusive Episcopalianism lets Gran say there is a purpose for everything God makes, even a vampire.

problem-of-evil.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
problem-of-evil.title: 17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited,' where SS Captain Lutze is tried by his Dachau victims and driven mad, and 'He's Alive,' where a phantom Hitler grooms the failed neo-Nazi Peter Vollmer, as Serling's two-part response to the Eichmann trial. Setting them against the film Operation Eichmann's monster-Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman, Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, and Serling's hatred of Hogan's Heroes' comic Klink, he traces a maturation: from the Nazi as heartless monster to Arendt's banality of evil, the thoughtless, frustrated everyman. Vollmer, the chapter argues, shows what Lutze's origins were, and remembering the Dachaus is the guard against becoming his like.

problem-of-evil.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
problem-of-evil.title: Notes
problem-of-evil.relation: Silver argues WoT gives a new spin on the free-will defense to the problem of evil: when Rand weaves a world without Shai'tan in A Memory of Light, Elayne appears as if turned, robbed of the ability to be an individual, showing that freedom's value lies in authentic individuality and that abolishing evil equals a world run entirely from the Dark One's single perspective. On fate, he reads ta'veren as freedom-affirming rather than controlling and defends Rand's Dragonmount epiphany via 'deep self' compatibilist views (Frankfurt, Watson) while calling it partly bad faith. On the Wheel's eternal recurrence he sets Nietzsche's amor fati against Adorno's charge that it is a failure of hope, arguing Rand's 'do better next time' is hope, not acceptance.

problem-of-evil.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
problem-of-evil.title: Notes
problem-of-evil.relation: Held reads Rand's final confrontation with the Dark One in A Memory of Light as a recapitulation of the free-will defense to the problem of evil, opening with Hume's statement of Epicurus's questions and Camus's refusal to love a world that tortures children. Drawing on Augustine (evil as privation, our limited perspective, the corruptible will) and Alvin Plantinga's claim that a world with significantly free creatures is more valuable, he argues Rand's competing visions teach that a world without Shai'tan removes choice: Elayne 'simpering,' Aviendha vapid, people reduced to complacent automatons who cannot choose to be good. He concludes with Camus that the struggle itself justifies existence and that heroism is impossible without the possibility of cowardice.

problem-of-evil.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
problem-of-evil.title: Notes
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin builds a six-part definition of heroism (systematic, moral, altruistic, radically atypical, supererogatory, replicable safeguarding) using Wesley Autrey's Harlem subway save against Captain Sullenberger's Hudson landing, and argues Wonder Woman is genuinely heroic because her mission is voluntary and supererogatory - she wins the contest to leave Paradise Island and can retire to it at will, unlike a compulsory Superman. He then uses the demoted, powerless Diana Prince era with I Ching to show her deeds stay in principle replicable, like Batman's rather than Superman's. The payoff: Wonder Woman works only as a 'super hero' who inspires imitation, which is how 'we' answer the problem of evil - why innocent people suffer destructive, ruthless evil.

problem-of-evil.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
problem-of-evil.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
problem-of-evil.relation: Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.

problem-of-evil.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
problem-of-evil.title: 15. The Evil in These Woods
problem-of-evil.relation: Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.

problem-of-evil.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
problem-of-evil.title: ‘Pro-life’ and Pro-Life
problem-of-evil.relation: The chapter argues that horror films about pregnancy (Rosemary's Baby, Demon Seed, The Reaping, Prophecy, Inside) pit a foetal 'subject' against the pregnant woman, eroding her selfhood by conflating her body with an invadable house or environment. Drawing on Young's, Battersby's and Tyler's phenomenologies of pregnant embodiment and Irigaray's 'woman as place', it shows how foetal-imaging technology and abortion politics (The Life Zone versus Carpenter's Pro-Life) reduce the woman to a vessel while the foetus is granted autonomous personhood.

problem-of-evil.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
problem-of-evil.title: Carnivale Knowledge: Give Me That Old-time Noir Religion
problem-of-evil.relation: Eric Bronson argues that Carnivale invents a 'religious noir' tradition in which Brother Justin's crisis of faith in the Dust Bowl 1930s replays the Christian existentialism of Kierkegaard and Dostoevsky. Sitting in the ruins of his burnt church, Justin recites Genesis 22 (the sacrifice of Isaac) and demands God explain why his orphans died, directly invoking Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: faith is impossible and absurd, and the crushing struggle itself makes life worth living. Ivan Karamazov's 'returning the ticket' over the suffering of children parallels Justin's fury at a silent God, while the carnies' Babylon storyline (Samson sparing the confessed killer under the carnival code, then secretly shooting him) and the inescapable dead souls echo Sartre's 'condemned to life' and the noir hero's inability to escape fate.

problem-of-evil.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: Escape to Doctor Who
problem-of-evil.relation: Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.

problem-of-evil.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
problem-of-evil.title: 12. Finally Free
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.

problem-of-evil.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
problem-of-evil.title: 13. Does God Have the Right to Destroy the Universe
problem-of-evil.relation: Foresman asks whether Chuck has a negative right to destroy the multiverse, rejecting the question-begging 'God can do whatever God wants' and the bare creation/ownership argument (using the scrambled-eggs example) as insufficient. Drawing on Locke's Two Treatises—property arises from mixing labor, but even in the state of nature one may not destroy a creature except for a 'nobler use,' and hoarding beyond use is illegitimate—he concludes Chuck is a Lockean tyrant destroying universes he could simply recreate, so Sam and Dean's rebellion is justified.

problem-of-evil.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
problem-of-evil.title: 15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)
problem-of-evil.relation: Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.

problem-of-evil.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
problem-of-evil.title: 21. Jesus the Punk Rocker
problem-of-evil.relation: Josh Cangelosi argues that Jesus as portrayed in the Gospels - homeless outcast, associate of prostitutes, denounced as a blasphemer, flipping tables - was effectively a punk, so Christianity and punk are compatible despite their mutual rejection. Comparing Leftover Crack's 'Atheist Anthem' with Matthew 23's woes against the Pharisees, he shows both Jesus and punks curse smug religious insiders while inviting outcasts, and reads Jesus's ethic as the Golden Rule or 'practice what you preach', which demands living authentically by your own standards and judging not. The analysis extends to Pussy Riot, the drag-pastor Craig Duke, and 'punks' who exclude queer people, concluding that Christians and punks alike must recover their blasphemous, outcast hardcore heritage.

problem-of-evil.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
problem-of-evil.title: 9. Foundation’s Optimism
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads the sequels Foundation's Edge and Foundation and Earth as an Optimistic response to the problem of evil, in the lineage of Leibniz, Rousseau, and Hegel's 'All is well', set against the WWII, Holocaust, Nuremberg, and Eichmann-trial backdrop of Asimov's writing and Arendt's banality of evil. Tracking Gendibal's mantra 'all will happen well', the Gaia/Galaxia choice via Trevize's 'talent for rightness', and Daneel Olivaw's Zeroth Law and plan to merge with Fallom's brain, he uses the Book of Job to frame whether the series' recurring reassurance is earned or merely reframed.

problem-of-evil.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
problem-of-evil.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
problem-of-evil.relation: Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.

problem-of-evil.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
problem-of-evil.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
problem-of-evil.relation: Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar, Six, Adama and Roslin to debate God's existence and meaning. Against Baltar's scientific naturalism they present Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, first cause, and the argument from design applied to the universe's ordered laws) and dismiss Pascal's Wager as insincere, like Baltar's. They then raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will defense and Hick's soul-making theodicy against Hume's faulty-architect analogy. Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.

problem-of-evil.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
problem-of-evil.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Pigliucci uses the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series and the Dover trial to argue that intelligent design is not science because it is unfalsifiable and invokes supernatural causation. He cites Popper's falsificationism (and Popper's recantation about Darwinism), contrasts Descartes's rationalism with Hume's empiricism to characterize science as a tentative blend of the two, flags Feyerabend's 'anything goes' as an irrational view of knowledge, invokes Aristotle's eudaimonia to argue meaning in life is a personal work in progress, and turns Dembski's theistic-evolution concession into a Pyrrhic victory via the problem of evil ('argument from bad design').

problem-of-evil.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
problem-of-evil.title: 17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone
problem-of-evil.relation: McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.

problem-of-evil.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: There Is No God in Desperation
problem-of-evil.relation: Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.

problem-of-evil.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: Introduction
problem-of-evil.relation: Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.

problem-of-evil.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)
problem-of-evil.relation: Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.

problem-of-evil.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil
problem-of-evil.relation: James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.

problem-of-evil.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution
problem-of-evil.relation: Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.

problem-of-evil.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
problem-of-evil.title: MOTHERHOOD
problem-of-evil.relation: George Dunn asks whether classical theism can call God 'Mother,' beginning with the Book of Job (taught in his Problem of Evil course) and the divine name Shadday's link to womb-love and 'blessings of breasts and womb.' He works through Anselm's 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' the attributes of impassibility and incorporeality, and Aquinas's doctrine of analogy, arguing Aquinas wrongly rejected maternal God-language because he swallowed Aristotle's biology of woman as 'defective and misbegotten'; drawing on Nel Noddings's caring 'receptivity' and Julian of Norwich, Dunn contends divine impassibility should yield to a maternal, receptive God, with a nod to Homer Simpson's burrito paradox.

problem-of-evil.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
problem-of-evil.title: Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection
problem-of-evil.relation: Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.

problem-of-evil.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
problem-of-evil.title: Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World
problem-of-evil.relation: Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.

problem-of-evil.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
problem-of-evil.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'

problem-of-evil.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
problem-of-evil.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
problem-of-evil.relation: Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.

problem-of-evil.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
problem-of-evil.title: Who is Who
problem-of-evil.relation: Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.

problem-of-evil.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
problem-of-evil.title: Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
problem-of-evil.relation: David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.

problem-of-evil.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
problem-of-evil.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
problem-of-evil.relation: Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.

problem-of-evil.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: 4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism
problem-of-evil.relation: Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.

problem-of-evil.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: 26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion
problem-of-evil.relation: The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.

problem-of-evil.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: 35. Star Wars as Philosophy A Genealogy of the Force
problem-of-evil.relation: Eberl builds a genealogy of the Force across the Skywalker saga, using Augustine to reject the Manichaean light/dark dualism Yoda voices ('Luminous beings are we') in favor of evil as a privation of good and as 'inordinate desire' for temporal goods, which explains Anakin's fall through his refusal to let Padme die. He casts Palpatine as a Nietzschean who declares 'good is a point of view' and pursues will to power and the ubermensch, contrasting this with the Stoicism of Seneca and Yoda ('train yourself to let go of everything you fear to lose'). The sequel trilogy's disenchanted galaxy is read through Charles Taylor, and Rey and Ben's redemption shows evil defeated not by hatred but by rightly-ordered love ('Saving what we love').

problem-of-evil.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: 61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists
problem-of-evil.relation: The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

problem-of-evil.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
problem-of-evil.title: 74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates
problem-of-evil.relation: Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

fascism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
fascism.title: Against Fascism
fascism.relation: Neal King argues the Buffyverse is proto-fascist: Buffy kills demons and vampires on sight within a race-like hierarchy, tempered only by an Augustinian split between natural and moral evil (soulless vampires cannot choose otherwise; soul-bearing humans like Faith, Willow, and Warren can repent), she derives authority from an ancient calling rather than democracy, and the graduation battle of 'Graduation Day, Part Two' stages citizenship forged in mass combat. He imagines a fascist Buffyverse of 'brownskirt' death squads and concludes only the show's secrecy prevents full fascism, finally recommending that the racism be dropped but the ritual sacrifice of evildoers kept — with Willow's flaying of Warren as the model.

fascism.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
fascism.title: Transformers and Philosophy
fascism.relation: Shook diagnoses Megatron through William James's expansive, possessive self turned pathological: a megalomaniac whose self encompasses everything and who must control it all ('My hunger for power!', 'Compassion is for fools!'). Reconstructing Megatron's pronouncements into a 'philosophy of Strength' - might makes right, perpetual war against the weak, 'Peace through tyranny' echoing Orwell - he identifies it as fascism on the model of Hitler and Mussolini's perpetual-war state, against which Optimus's cooperative 'till all are one' Community is not a rival regime but an ethical ideal that only we can put into practice.

fascism.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
fascism.title: 16. Punk Politics
fascism.relation: Prinz surveys punk's political paradox - anarchist punks from Crass and Rock Against Racism to straight edge versus the fascist flirtation of skinheads, the National Front, and Skrewdriver's 'White Power' - and tests four candidate unifiers (anti-authoritarianism, nihilism, individualism, and McLaren's politics of boredom), finding each one-sided. He proposes instead a politics of disaffection: alienation and negative affect toward the status quo that spans anarchist, Nazi, and apolitical punks alike, making punk a confrontational counterculture that says 'Fuck you' with a self-satisfied sneer, even if it never ended a war like the hippies claimed to.

fascism.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
fascism.title: Introduction
fascism.relation: Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.

fascism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
fascism.title: 30. The Boys as Philosophy Superheroes, Fascism, and the American Right
fascism.relation: Johnson treats The Boys as an argument from analogy that MAGA Trumpism is fascist, walking through how the show equates Homelander and Vought with the Nazi supe Stormfront and with Trump: the Big Lie, gaslighting, fearmongering, over-policing, conspiracy theories (QAnon as rebranded blood libel), cults of personality, projection, and loyal propaganda outlets. Drawing on Wittgenstein's notion of family resemblance, he argues 'fascism' has no necessary-and-sufficient definition but a cluster of shared traits, and compiling scholars' checklists shows MAGA belongs to the fascist family. Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism supplies the 'alternative universe' of nonfacts and the leader who is 'always right,' and he invokes the banality of evil and totalitarian fiction to gauge the analogy's strength.

consequentialism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
consequentialism.title: Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben
consequentialism.relation: Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.

consequentialism.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
consequentialism.title: The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer
consequentialism.relation: Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.

consequentialism.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
consequentialism.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Argues Tony is a good man and a bad man for the same reason: a moral code of partiality toward family, crew and Italian-Americans ('This family comes before everything else' in 'Fortunate Son', avenging Janice, caring for Livia 'because she's my mother'), whereas morality must ultimately be justified from the impartial point of view (Sidgwick's 'point of view of the universe'). Using the drowning case - save Meadow or two strangers - the chapter shows partiality can receive an impartial justification, then applies this to Dr. Melfi's decision to treat Tony, defensible only while harms to others (her patient's suicide when she is driven into hiding) do not outweigh the good of his treatment.

consequentialism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
consequentialism.title: Two Keys to the Good Life
consequentialism.relation: Uses young Dumbledore's confession about Grindelwald - 'it would all be for the greater good' while Muggles were forced into subservience - to distinguish the greater good, which sacrifices individuals' rights and dignity for a supposed collective benefit, from the common good, sacrifice for the good of all, as in the civil rights movement's claim that violating some Americans' rights harms the whole community. Harry's choice to return from King's Cross and finish Voldemort is a decision for the common good of wizards and Muggles alike.

consequentialism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
consequentialism.title: Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day
consequentialism.relation: Presses four objections to utilitarianism through superhero cases: a weakened Jean Grey dying to save Juggernaut's bus victims shows utilitarianism obliterates supererogation — she would be blameworthy whichever way she chose; Ares' demand that Wonder Woman kill an innocent girl to avert global biowar forces her against her character; Batman refusing to let an innocent-of-this-crime Joker die in The Joker: Devil's Advocate shows the theory sacrificing justice; and the Green Goblin accidentally doing great good by dragging a would-be mass shooter down Fifth Avenue shows consequences alone cannot make an intended wrong right.

consequentialism.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
consequentialism.title: James Bond and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Tedesco dissects what the double-0 'license to kill' could actually mean, ruling out self-defense and mere on-the-job killing and concluding that Bond is a state-sanctioned assassin who earned his status through two assassinations in Casino Royale. He tests that status against Kant's categorical imperative - persons as ends in themselves, though Kant also defended capital punishment as respecting the murderer's choice - and against consequentialism, which vindicates Bond's elimination of Kananga but stumbles on the surgeon's organ-harvesting dilemma. Because ordinary morality mixes duty-based and consequence-based intuitions, the chapter leaves Bond's moral status genuinely open and links it to live policy debates on assassination and torture after 9/11, including Britain's Intelligence Services Act that leaves room for a real-life double-0 agent.

consequentialism.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
consequentialism.title: James Bond and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Held argues that our pleasure in Bond's kill-then-quip routine - 'Shocking' after electrocuting a henchman in Goldfinger, tossing Killifer to the sharks that ate Felix with 'You earned it, you keep it' - reveals tacit retributive and deterrent theories of punishment that place villains outside the moral community. Using the distinction between mere humiliation (deflating Dr. No's pretense: 'Minnows pretending they're whales') and Humiliation that denies common humanity, he shows Bond dehumanizes disfigured, 'othered' villains, even as the novels present them as disenfranchised figures - Dr. No rejecting his father's name, Mr. Big demanding recognition as the first great black criminal - whose rage is a warped demand for Hegelian mutual recognition. He proposes instead Jean Hampton's moral education theory, which treats criminals as moral agents capable of reform, concluding with Jaws's redemption in Moonraker as proof that no one is beyond it.

consequentialism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
consequentialism.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
consequentialism.relation: Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.

consequentialism.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
consequentialism.title: Doing Things in Private
consequentialism.relation: Skoble asks exactly what Jeff does wrong in Rear Window and whether his illicit snooping can generate genuine duties. Against a purely consequentialist verdict ('it all worked out okay'), he argues that knowledge creates conditional obligations - given what he has seen of Thorwald, Jeff's intervention is obligatory rather than supererogatory, by 'ought implies can' - and he weighs autonomy-respecting limits on intervening in Miss Lonelyhearts' despair. He then analyzes privacy as a moral right grounded in reciprocal legitimate expectations, concluding that Jeff violated no such right since everything he watched was on public display, so the ends-justify-the-means charge mostly dissolves.

consequentialism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
consequentialism.title: Walking the Tightrope
consequentialism.relation: Louis Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's 'blind squirrel' lie about Earth, classifying the fact that Cylons look human, Roslin's faked death of the baby Hera, and Tom Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. Democratic duty is framed as a deontological obligation of transparency grounded in the governed's trust, while the leadership repeatedly defaults to consequentialist wartime exceptions. The chapter proposes a rule-of-thumb: secrecy is justified only to hide specific information from an external threat like the Cylons, never to protect the government from its own citizens, and each violation erodes the trust on which Colonial democracy's 'soul' depends.

consequentialism.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
consequentialism.title: As Nasty as I Wanna Be
consequentialism.relation: Greene asks whether Maguire's Elphaba is really wicked, first clearing away her reputation (she adopts the 'Wicked Witch' name because 'it liberates you from convention,' echoing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic about the just person with an unjust reputation and vice versa) and then her nature (the midwife-biting birth, green skin, and witchcraft establish no vampire-like evil essence, since Glinda and Nor are good witches). Following Hume's view that morality is not found in the world but in our assessments, he treats wickedness as a matter of performing actions we judge evil, and weighs Elphaba's life under both headings: good intentions with horrific outcomes (the bees that kill the chef, the icicle that kills Manek, Sarima's family executions) and bad intentions with none (her two failed attempts on Madame Morrible). The verdict is deliberately suspended: if she is wicked at all, it can only be through the consequences of her actions.

consequentialism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
consequentialism.title: The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back
consequentialism.relation: Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.

consequentialism.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
consequentialism.title: 11 - The Friendship that Makes No Demands
consequentialism.relation: Tedesco sets Facebook's demand-free friendship against the modern moral requirement of impartiality, running from Godwin's burning-archbishop case through Bentham's 'everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one' and Williams's 'one thought too many' objection. He canvasses the escapes - Mill's rarely-demanded public benefactor, Singer's global village where aid is a click away, Jackson's sector plan and Railton's sophisticated consequentialism - and finds each inadequate to friendship's partiality. Facebook friendship looks like a third way that reconciles the two, but it turns out only to be friendship where it supplements a real offline relationship, so the impartiality problem stands.

consequentialism.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
consequentialism.title: World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent
consequentialism.relation: Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.

consequentialism.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
consequentialism.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Fitzpatrick uses Klosterman's hyperthetical — kick a shackled Clydesdale to death in twenty minutes and every political prisoner on earth goes free — to stage the consequentialism-versus-non-consequentialism dispute. He argues the scenario's framing (a warm, cuddly horse) rigs it for the anti-consequentialist, but once you grant that Amnesty International's prisoners suffer worse than the horse — the tortured Syrian teenage protestor is his example — the question becomes whether one awful act to a horse is permissible to prevent worse suffering to many humans. His only remaining hesitation is practical: could you actually finish the job in twenty minutes?

consequentialism.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
consequentialism.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Runs Walt's choices through consequentialist machinery: his cost-benefit habit (the $737,000 target, 'non-sustainable business model'), the Krazy-8 pros-and-cons list, and whether manufacturing meth harms users or merely enables them. It argues act consequentialism fails on unforeseen consequences (Hank killing Tuco helps Heisenberg; the tow-truck driver aids a murder), defends rule consequentialism via Tuco - rational for him, disastrous as a universal rule - and weighs agent-centered views for Walt's family-first logic. It closes with Singer's drowning-child standard: Walt could have saved Jane and accepted Elliot's charity at little cost, and so could we by redirecting wasted money to OXFAM - so Walt breaks bad, and maybe we do too.

consequentialism.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
consequentialism.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Svolba and Flanders read Curb as an extended investigation of civility—the rules of what people 'just don't do,' from using the doctor's phone to touring Susie's new house to singing 'Happy Birthday' at Ben Stiller's party. Larry plays Socratic gadfly: refusing the tour harms no one and treats no one unfairly, and Susie's only justification ('it's just not done') is circular, so his incivility can seem admirable, even like minor civil disobedience. Against this, the chapter argues (crediting Cheshire Calhoun) that rules of civility are conventional vehicles for communicating respect for others' feelings and interests—what matters to Susie ought to matter to Larry—and, more consequentially, that a social world full of Larry Davids would be unbearable. Larry's own Golden-Rule litmus test, by which he never talks in movie theaters because he would hate it himself, misses this point, since civility is precisely about what others happen to want and like.

consequentialism.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
consequentialism.title: The Wire and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.

consequentialism.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
consequentialism.title: Psych and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Robert Arp's introduction argues Psych is perfect for philosophy because Henry's games train observation and inference exactly as philosophers hone them, while Shawn's ruse shows how clever people abuse those powers to deceive - quoting Machiavelli's line that one who deceives will always find those who allow themselves to be deceived. It sets up the book's recurring ethical question about lying: lies for the liar's profit (Shawn avoiding jail in the pilot), paternalistic lies for the hearer's own good (Henry telling seven-year-old Shawn he 'blacked out' about his mother's death), and lies to benefit many (promising a terrorist freedom to find his bomb). Since Shawn's lies solve cases and save lives, the introduction suggests they may not be so bad in the end, though it admits wishing he would just come clean as a talented honest detective.

consequentialism.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
consequentialism.title: Psych and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Michaud argues that Shawn's whole psychic career runs on fallacies of relevance - the red herring of claiming to be psychic to dodge arrest, plus ad hominem mockery that deflects Lassiter's fraud accusations - so the show's comedy turns on bad logic being used to lead people to true conclusions. Socrates supplies the opposing voice: like the Sophists who argued any side for money, Shawn reasons for convenience and amusement, and his deception is an inconsistency of the kind Socrates refused in Plato's Crito, where he would not bribe his way out of a death sentence. An invented Platonic-style dialogue has Socrates question Shawn until he concedes that lying breeds more lying and harm - 'her name is Truth!' - before Shawn escapes the elenchus by spotting lipstick on Socrates's collar. The chapter leaves the verdict open: Shawn saves lives and raises the world's happiness, but his trickery also trains Santa Barbara to reason badly and trust con artists.

consequentialism.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
consequentialism.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Rod Carveth maps Bentham's act-utilitarianism onto Lockhart Gardner's defense-side reasoning and Mill's rule-utilitarianism onto the prosecution's, then tests the pairing on the firm's recurring client Colin Sweeney. Sweeney's cases - the wrongful-death suit in 'Bad' where Alicia says 'Of course' he killed his wife, the manslaughter plea and merger opportunism in 'Hybristophilia', and the perjured testimony Alicia may still use in 'Long Way Home' - show the firm letting the end of client and firm gain justify the means. Sweeney walking free, restored to his company, and a father despite admitting the murder is the counter-intuitive consequence that makes Carveth question whether act-utilitarianism should ground our decisions at all.

consequentialism.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
consequentialism.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Seth Walker asks whether Nick Van Owen - the Earth First! documentarian who monkeywrenches InGen's camp and frees the caged dinosaurs in The Lost World - is a bastard or morally justified. He runs the consequentialist cost-benefit (the escaped T. rex slaughters a cargo ship crew and trashes San Diego; the sabotage costs the team their radio and rescue) against the ecodefense argument built on Arne Naess's deep ecology and biocentric equality, on which Isla Sorna is our 'home' and rescuing the injured baby T. rex Roland Tembo crippled is Self-defense. Singer's principle of equal consideration of suffering - a difference in ability never justifies a difference in consideration - bridges the gap for those who reject biocentrism, and Walker answers the consistency objection (must Nick accept InGen sabotaging him back?) before crediting Nick's defense of his larger home.

consequentialism.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
consequentialism.title: Homeland and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Dan Burkett defends Brody against blame for flipping the suicide-vest switch in 'Marine One' by arguing he was not free. On the desire-satisfaction view Brody freely avenge Issa, but via Locke's locked-room thought experiment (Carrie contentedly 'freely' staying in a house she cannot leave) the chapter motivates the libertarian requirement that one could have done otherwise, which Nazir's years of torture and brainwashing may have removed. The malfunctioning vest then raises moral luck - Brody is no better a person because the bomb failed - and since Dana's plea restricts his options just as coercively, the best defense grants Brody freedom throughout, making the switch blameworthy and his free choice to come home genuinely redemptive.

consequentialism.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
consequentialism.title: Homeland and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Christophe Porot and Charles Taliaferro ask whether Homeland's pervasive hypocrisy and deceit can be justified, starting from Walden's cover-up of the drone strike and Brody's heroic persona hiding a terrorist plot. Machiavelli's Prince supplies the case that political relationships with allies (Saul's 'Us and Them' speech to Carrie) require hypocrisy, while the Smith-inspired 'honest politicking' model - trading openly on self-interest, as with Carrie blackmailing al Sahrani - fails because politics should secure the public good, though la Rochefoucauld's 'homage vice pays virtue' explains Saul extorting the judge into doing right. Weighing Kant's unconditional duty not to lie (Carrie's fatal lie to Lynne Reed) against consequentialism, the chapter lands on the Walzer Dirty Hands view: some acts stay wrong yet necessary, and honest agents accept the guilt.

consequentialism.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
consequentialism.title: Justified and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: The chapter juxtaposes the 1992 no-knock raid in which 84-year-old paraplegic Annie Rae Dixon was shot in her bed with Raylan's pilot-episode ultimatum to Tommy Bucks, arguing both deaths count as 'justified' only because aggressive proactive policing manufactured the lethal encounter. It catalogues Raylan's tactics - provoking draws, kidnapping the cartel chief's niece and Dickie Bennett, the lucky-sniper standoff at the Bennett compound - and asks whether we want our police to be judge, jury, and executioner. On the deontological approach Raylan's routine lawbreaking cannot be justified whatever the results, and even on the consequentialist approach the war-on-drugs data (soaring murder rates in targeted neighborhoods, mass incarceration) suggest proactive policing fails on its own terms.

consequentialism.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
consequentialism.title: Justified and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: The chapter maps the Raylan-Boyd rivalry onto two ethical theories: Raylan is a Kant-style deontologist who does his duty (tracking Tommy Bucks to Miami, weighing duty to the law against duty to Arlo, giving every opponent the choice to walk away), while Boyd is a Mill-style consequentialist maximizing good for himself and Ava, whose vigilante church and revenge plots follow from outcomes rather than rules. Their season-one team-up against Bo Crowder and the Miami shooters is read as contractarianism, two moral agents cooperating toward a right. Each man's choices become his undoing - Raylan's damsel-saving affairs, Mags's family loyalty, Dewey's impulsiveness - which the chapter takes as the show's thesis that what we do results in who we are.

consequentialism.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
consequentialism.title: 14. You Have to Be Good before You Can Be Smart
consequentialism.relation: The Bocks argue that the Erudite pairing of ignorance with knowledge is morally loaded: with Linda Zagzebski's and James Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, high-end knowledge requires intellectual virtues like the courage to test your beliefs publicly, so you really do have to be good before you can be smart. The Erudite manifesto's curriculum omits the humanities that open the mind, and its IQ-only leadership test fails Plato's requirement that philosopher kings love wisdom itself and, like the freed cave-prisoner, return to benefit society - which is why Jeanine, driven by lust for power and concealment of the truth beyond the fence, is 'a poor example of a philosopher king.' Both the Erudite and the Bureau reason as consequentialists ('Knowledge is power... power to do good') to justify slaughtering Abnegation and experimenting on unconsenting Chicagoans, when the pursuit of knowledge must be constrained by informed consent and human dignity.

consequentialism.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
consequentialism.title: 3. What’s So Bad about Eating People
consequentialism.relation: McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.

consequentialism.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
consequentialism.title: Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right
consequentialism.relation: Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.

consequentialism.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
consequentialism.title: 5. Back from the Dead
consequentialism.relation: Devlin and Cooper trace Rick's moral arc as a struggle between Mill-style consequentialism - twisted by the apocalypse into a 'Greatest Survival Principle' of mere survival (Dawn Lerner's Grady, Enid's 'JSS') - and Aristotelian virtue ethics. Shane's murder of Otis, the Governor's rule over Woodbury and killing of Martinez and Pete, and Terminus's cannibalism all show survival-only reasoning dissolving humanity, a decline the show underlines with literal mirror reflections of Shane as a walker. Rick falls after killing Shane and nearly trades Michonne to the Governor, is brought back by Lori's judging vision and the sight of Carl going cold, and reclaims virtues as habits grown like Hershel's seeds - 'We get to come back' (4.8 'Too Far Gone') - though Seasons 4 and 5 leave him balancing a harder character, down to 'We didn't want to waste the bullets,' with the drive to survive.

consequentialism.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
consequentialism.title: 14. Who Watches the Justice League
consequentialism.relation: Judged by negative consequentialism - the view the chapter attributes to Hume and Popper, that ethics means minimizing future suffering - Superman is the more ethical hero because he plans failsafes against himself: the gold Kryptonite vault he enters after killing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', the de-powering device he entrusts to Batman in Injustice, even his own death as harm prevention. Batman's countermeasures against the League (Tower of Babel, Justice League: Doom) fall short because he builds no failsafe for himself, hiding behind 'My failsafe is the Justice League.' The chapter reads Superman's killing of Zod in Man of Steel and Bruce's compulsive detective work through Hume's claim that reason is the slave of the passions, concluding that Clark's willingness to enable his own defeat wins the ethical contest.

consequentialism.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
consequentialism.title: 3. Hero or Villain
consequentialism.relation: Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.

consequentialism.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
consequentialism.title: 12. Margaery for Queen!
consequentialism.relation: Jones asks whether Margaery - who grooms Tommen, admits she was 'good at seeming good,' and may count as an abuser despite Westeros's norms - could still have been the best queen in the Seven Kingdoms. Against the prosecution's portrait of a cold egoist, he argues her charity to Flea Bottom's children shows a queen is good by what she does rather than why she did it, so selfish ambition welded to shrewdness can genuinely serve the common good. Comparing her with Ramsay (cruelty that provokes revolt) and Ned (benevolence without calculation that gets him killed), the chapter draws an implicitly Machiavellian conclusion - the people's best bet is hunger for power joined to the cunning to keep them onside - while doubting that cultural relativism can fully excuse her treatment of Tommen.

consequentialism.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
consequentialism.title: 27. Was the Red Wedding Massacre a Good Thing
consequentialism.relation: Van der Deijl takes Tywin's line to Tyrion - 'explain to me why it is more noble to kill ten thousand men in battle than a dozen at dinner' - as a serious consequentialist challenge about the Red Wedding. Working through utilitarianism, prioritarianism, and dirty-hands cases like Hiroshima and shooting down a hijacked plane, he concedes the massacre could have been justified had breaking Guest Right and killing 3,500 brought peace at minimal cost; but the consequences fail - Joffrey and Roose Bolton keep power, the institution of guest right erodes, and Tywin's real motive was family power rather than the greater good - so the massacre fails even the consequentialist test, and Tywin is a power-hungry conspirator, not Machiavelli's prince.

consequentialism.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
consequentialism.title: 3. Sympathy for the Devils
consequentialism.relation: Bromhall contends the Soul Squad's moral growth cannot earn them Good Place points, because the contextualist point system rewards only the happiness an action actually adds to the universe, as the two Dougs' rose gifts show. Using William James's conditions for morally valuable action, foreseeable consequences and no do-overs, he argues the afterlife is the wrong context for human action since Michael can rewrite reality and wipe memories at will. Ironically the humans' growth only makes Michael and the demons miserable, while Michael's own high-stakes, irreversible self-sacrifice meets all of James's conditions and so alone deserves The Good Place.

consequentialism.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
consequentialism.title: 1. Rights and Wrongs of Reversing the Snap
consequentialism.relation: Philip Mouch weighs consequences against rights to ask whether the Avengers were wrong to undo the Snap in Endgame. He imagines a survivor whose returned spouse finds her remarried, cataloguing displaced families, food shortages, and political turmoil, and argues these harms, however real, are outweighed by restoring the lives Thanos took. The deeper problem is Bruce Banner's wager with the Ancient One: removing the Time Stone dooms a branch reality on a 1-in-14,000,605 chance, gambling innocent lives without their consent, which resembles Thanos's non-consensual sacrifice of Gamora rather than the noble self-sacrifice of Hawkeye and Black Widow on Vormir. He concludes that two wrongs do not make a right: even for a noble end, risking countless lives tramples the rights of others.

consequentialism.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
consequentialism.title: 9. With Infinite Power Comes No Responsibility
consequentialism.relation: James Hart casts Tony Stark as a consequentialist and Steve Rogers as a deontologist, then argues Endgame's infinite stakes destroy Tony's morality through Nick Bostrom's 'infinitarian paralysis': in an infinite multiverse every act leaves the balance of happy and sad lives unchanged, as an infinite Stark orphanage rearranged Hilbert's-Hotel style shows, and even genocide becomes permissible so long as infinitely many remain alive. Tony's attempted fixes each fail: the causal approach collapses because reversing the Snap has infinite butterfly effects, expected value (credited to Frank Jackson) runs into Pascal's Mugging and an 'infinitarian trance' demanding suicidal bets on any chance of infinite value, and Bostrom's 'infinity shades' that filter tiny probabilities would blind Tony to the one-in-a-trillion time-heist chance he should take. The chapter concludes there is no consequentialist way to say when wagering lives on infinite stakes is ethical, and Iron Man should let Captain America lead.

consequentialism.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
consequentialism.title: 18. Iron Man’s Choice to Die
