consequentialism.relation: Argues Tony's death in Endgame is best explained three ways: via Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives (Tony oscillates between the cabin family-life drive and the risk-seeking death drive that takes him aboard the donut ship in Infinity War and has him lay down to die with Nebula), via Camus's absurd (like Sisyphus, Tony creates subjective meaning by choosing — Pepper, Morgan, and finally the snap itself, 'Part of the journey is the end'), and via consequentialism (the snap as a desirable consequence, contrasting Infinity War's deontological 'We don't trade lives' with Endgame's 'whatever it takes'). It contends that because the time heist rewrites history, deaths in both films — Vision's, Natasha's, Tony's — risk becoming meaningless, so Tony dies on his terms to make his death meaningful.

consequentialism.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
consequentialism.title: 22. The Mad Titan and the Mother of Dragons
consequentialism.relation: Pairs Thanos with Game of Thrones' Daenerys as twin Machiavellian utopians acting on 'the ends justify the means' (quoting The Prince and the Discourses): Daenerys burns King's Landing to 'break the wheel,' Thanos snaps half of life away 'at random, dispassionate, fair to rich and poor alike' as 'a small price to pay for salvation.' It roots both villains in cruel childhoods and a nature-versus-nurture question (with historical analogies to Hitler and Stalin), and in messiah complexes built on improbable success — 'Dread it, run from it, destiny arrives all the same' — while noting the key inversion: Thanos refuses to rule and dies content watching the sunrise, whereas the breaker of chains claims a new throne.

consequentialism.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
consequentialism.title: 28. How Captain Rogers Became a Good Man
consequentialism.relation: Traces Steve Rogers's arc from Erskine's charge — 'Not a perfect soldier, but a good man' — through Aristotle's virtue ethics (virtues are learned, none innate, each a mean between vices like courage between cowardice and rashness) to argue that the perfect soldier's obedience is not itself a virtue, so saving Bucky in Winter Soldier, outlaw leadership in Civil War, and gracious command in Endgame move Cap from black-and-white moral absolutism into the grey area where real virtue lives. The payoff is worthiness: only after pain has refined him can he lift Mjölnir, and the chapter warns that a 'perfect soldier' Cap — Thanos's ideological twin — might have heard the Mad Titan out.

consequentialism.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
consequentialism.title: 1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy
consequentialism.relation: Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.

consequentialism.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
consequentialism.title: And the war Rages on
consequentialism.relation: Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.

consequentialism.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
consequentialism.title: “This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”
consequentialism.relation: Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.

consequentialism.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
consequentialism.title: Batman Forever
consequentialism.relation: Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.

consequentialism.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
consequentialism.title: Walking the Tightrope
consequentialism.relation: Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.

consequentialism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
consequentialism.title: Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror
consequentialism.relation: Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.

consequentialism.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
consequentialism.title: The Bill Comes Due
consequentialism.relation: The chapter uses Michael Walzer's Problem of Dirty Hands to weigh the Ancient One's secret lifelong use of forbidden dark magic against Kaecilius's summoning of Dormammu, arguing that only she faces a genuine dirty-hands dilemma because her end (defending Earth) is good while his is not. It asks why dark magic is forbidden at all and answers with rule-utilitarian reasoning that has taken on a deontological life of its own, then invokes Kant's murderer-at-the-door essay to argue, with Mordo's 'the bill comes due,' that whoever does wrong for good ends bears responsibility for the downstream consequences—and that Strange's willingness to break Kamar-Taj's rules while accepting the cost is what makes him a hero.

consequentialism.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
consequentialism.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Greg Littmann defends Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in Mill's own image, noting that Mill's father raised him in calculated isolation and brutal study as a tool to reform humanity just as Graff engineers Ender, so both acted rightly given the stakes even though Mill's harm principle and his regard for animal suffering also condemn the xenocide itself. Against Crime and Punishment and 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas,' he argues Ender's Game shows consequences can genuinely justify breaking any moral rule when human extinction is on the table.

consequentialism.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
consequentialism.title: What Promotes Moral Behavior
consequentialism.relation: Matthew D. Atkinson and Darin DeWitt use the Canterbury's ignored mayday in 'Dulcinea' — Captain McDowell's 'let the good God Darwin sort it out' versus Ade Nygaard's appeal to law, karma, and obligation — to ask what binds people when no central authority enforces rules. Through Michael Walzer's just war theory they read the Earth-Mars war: moral language is not 'cheap talk' (even Errinwright must dress aggression as peace and manipulates Reverend Volovodov's words), aggression and imminence govern when to fight, and five 'how to fight' principles — noncombatant immunity on Eros and Ganymede, POW rights for the Martian marines on the Kittur Chennamma, leaders' rather than soldiers' responsibility (Fred Johnson's defection after Anderson Station), proportionality in Errinwright's 'a base for a base' Deimos strike, and the rejection of ends-justify-means utilitarianism — discipline even Holden and Amos as they reflect on free will and culpability. The chapter concludes The Expanse is optimistic: human decency survives even in the anarchic Belt because characters keep reflecting on what their obligations to one another are.

consequentialism.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
consequentialism.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.

consequentialism.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
consequentialism.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Albert Anglberger and Alexander Hieke contrast Ned, the virtue ethicist's genuinely good man, with Cersei, a 'minimally extended' egoistic consequentialist whose only morally relevant subjects are herself and her children. Aristotle's apparatus does the work: phronesis lets Ned rank his daughters' lives above honesty when he confesses falsely ('the lies we tell for love'), his 'you're too fat for your armor' quip shows the golden mean among competing virtues, and Cersei's unbalanced maternal love is excess, hence not a virtue. They then unsettle moral judgment itself: utilitarianism would license the Slaver's Bay slaveholders, virtue ethics lacks action rules and cross-cultural agreement (charity is no Dothraki virtue), and Martin's POV narration gives direct access to Ned's inner life but only Varys's and Littlefinger's unreliable reports about Cersei - so our verdicts on her, like real-life judgments of others, rest on shaky evidence.

consequentialism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
consequentialism.title: 1 Acting Without Thinking The Sagacity of Indiana Jones
consequentialism.relation: Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.

consequentialism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
consequentialism.title: 2 Does It Always Belong in a Museum
consequentialism.relation: Edwardo Pérez reconstructs the reasoning behind Indy's unargued mantra 'It belongs in a museum' via Bentham's principle of utility: museums maximize happiness because scholars and the public can study and enjoy artifacts for generations, unlike private collectors like Panama Hat. The same calculus explains his rule-breaking — he leaves the Mayapore Sankara Stone with the villagers ('It'd be another rock collecting dust' in a museum) because a flourishing village outweighs his fortune and glory, and he concedes the government's Area 51 warehouse may have been the utility-maximizing choice for the Ark after what it did to Belloq and Toht. Indy's apparent inconsistencies thus dissolve into case-by-case consequence weighing.

consequentialism.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
consequentialism.title: 19 Meddling with (Almost) Incomprehensible Powers
consequentialism.relation: Argues that archaeology can never escape politics: Nazi relic plunder for the planned Führermuseum, French removals at Angkor Wat, the UNESCO 1970 convention, and Zahi Hawass's cultural nationalism versus James Cuno's 'encyclopedic museums' all determine what Indy — or any archaeologist — may legitimately do. Measured against Alison Wylie's stewardship principle, Indy emerges as a 'loot-and-scoot' adventurer whose 'it belongs in a museum' cosmopolitanism sits uneasily with national patrimony claims, and the chapter weighs backward-looking title-based versus forward-looking value-based approaches to the Golden Idol, the Sankara Stone he returns, and the Cross of Coronado. It closes by asking whether the living can wrong the dead and vanished cultures, and whether the government 'top men' warehousing the Ark were right after all.

consequentialism.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
consequentialism.title: So, That’s It No Solution
consequentialism.relation: Rieder argues Iron Man is the one 'realistic' superhero: nothing about him requires a different world, only incremental nanotech advances — precision engineering, miniaturized computing, and carbon nanotubes a hundred times stronger than steel — already pursued at MIT's Institute for Soldier Nanotechnologies. He then uses Iron Man as a nanoethics case study, pitting cost-benefit analysis (with David Schmidtz's proviso that it is necessary but not sufficient for right action) against the precautionary principle exemplified by Bill Joy's call for relinquishment, asking whether an Obadiah Stane selling 'Iron Armies' to the highest bidder is a risk we may not take even if it is improbable. He leans precautionary: we may be morally required to forgo the experiment because the world's population never consented to the risk.

consequentialism.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
consequentialism.title: The Office and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: Johnson works through the standard objections to affirmative action using Scranton material: Ryan's paralysis before the all-Black management team in 'Traveling Salesmen' shows a single-race workforce is not intrinsically bad, while Michael's Chris Rock routine and his do-it-yourself slur exercise in 'Diversity Day' show that Dunder Mifflin meeting every quota does nothing about racism. A hypothetical about Dwight's grandfather refusing to hire Stanley's grandfather at the beet farm frames the compensation objection, answered by the 'cycle of poverty' account of the present effects of past discrimination. Finally, a fictitious hiring of guard Hank Tate over a better-qualified white candidate - justified, following Nagel, by the consequences of calming branch unrest - sets up the conclusion that education, not racially preferential hiring, would break minority poverty without discrimination, so affirmative action is ultimately unjustified.

consequentialism.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
consequentialism.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
consequentialism.relation: White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.

consequentialism.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
consequentialism.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
consequentialism.relation: Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.

consequentialism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
consequentialism.title: Notes
consequentialism.relation: Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.

consequentialism.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
consequentialism.title: The Last Jedi A New Hope
consequentialism.relation: Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.

consequentialism.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
consequentialism.title: 13. Time to Choose
consequentialism.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.

consequentialism.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
consequentialism.title: 14. Who Watches the Justice League
consequentialism.relation: Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.

consequentialism.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
consequentialism.title: Notes
consequentialism.relation: White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.

consequentialism.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
consequentialism.title: Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person
consequentialism.relation: Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.

consequentialism.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
consequentialism.title: A True MVP
consequentialism.relation: Kershnar analyzes what makes a football player valuable, arguing a player's value is his net benefit to his own team measured against a baseline. He compares three models—no-substitute, average/reasonable-substitute, and actual-substitute—using cases like Joe Montana backed by Steve Young and Emmitt Smith behind an all-pro line, and defends the actual-substitute model as the correct measure of value even though it yields counterintuitive results. He connects the account to a broader question of measuring a person's contribution to any organization or to the world.

consequentialism.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
consequentialism.title: Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf
consequentialism.relation: McElreath tests three ethical theories against golf intuitions and argues virtue ethics wins. Consequentialism rightly judges a postal carrier's choice to work over golf but wrongly permits Judge Smails in Caddyshack to kick his ball when no bad consequences follow; Kantian ethics correctly condemns Smails's deceptive maxim as non-universalizable but mishandles the play-versus-work case. Virtue ethics, judging acts by what an ideally virtuous person would characteristically do, gets both right via the relevant virtues of justice and honesty, and he then applies benevolence, justice, and tolerance to argue golf should better treat women, minorities, disabled players (Casey Martin's cart), and homosexuals.

consequentialism.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
consequentialism.title: Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton
consequentialism.relation: Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.

consequentialism.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
consequentialism.title: Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes
consequentialism.relation: Terjesen asks whether Conan Doyle acted immorally in killing Holmes in 'The Final Problem,' framing it through property theory. He runs Locke's labor theory (illustrated via 'The Blue Carbuncle' gem), Proudhon and Marx's critiques, and both consequentialist and Kantian (respect-for-persons) justifications of intellectual property. He argues Conan Doyle's ownership of the iconic Holmes weakened as Paget, Gillette, Rathbone, and Dr. Joseph Bell co-authored the figure, so property rights alone can't justify the killing—but Conan Doyle's authorial dignity plus the narrative fitness of 'The Final Problem' and 'His Last Bow' make the send-off defensible.

consequentialism.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
consequentialism.title: Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization
consequentialism.relation: Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.

consequentialism.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
consequentialism.title: The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence
consequentialism.relation: Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'

consequentialism.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
consequentialism.title: White Nights of the Soul
consequentialism.relation: Garcia reads Insomnia as the story of a cop who has lost himself and must choose between two doppelgangers: Walter Finch, the murderer who offers amoral 'partnership' and moral anti-realism ('that ultimate taboo? It doesn't exist outside our minds'), and rookie Ellie Burr, who embodies Dormer's better past as a conscientious policeman. Against Finch's 'moral math' and Dormer's own 'the end justifies the means' rationalizations, the chapter argues that the moral value of actions lies in intentions, motives, and character—Aquinas on what makes a killing an accident, Kant on being worthy of happiness rather than securing it. Dormer's sleeplessness becomes evidence of a conscience still alive, and his struggle figures what Kierkegaard calls purity of heart, willing one thing, with Socrates's refusal to escape in the Crito as the model of integrity. In dying to protect Ellie from losing her way, Dormer regains himself through commitment to another person, the Levinasian point that personhood is fulfilled only in and through other persons.

consequentialism.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
consequentialism.title: 8. Which Brother Is the Good One
consequentialism.relation: Browning contrasts the brothers' ethics: Dean is a consequentialist who judges hunts by outcomes ('the ends justify the means,' killing werewolf Madison or faith-healer Roy for the greater good), while Sam is a deontologist who treats lying, stealing, and killing as wrong in themselves. Tracking episodes like 'Bloodlust,' 'Croatoan,' and 'Fresh Blood,' he argues the murder-versus-kill distinction and the blurring line between human and monster show Dean's darker consequentialism is better suited to the Hunter's war, though both are driven to do good.

consequentialism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
consequentialism.title: 3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty
consequentialism.relation: Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.

consequentialism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
consequentialism.title: 20. Why Is Breaking Skateboarders’ Legs Wrong
consequentialism.relation: The chapter uses three characters to test three single-value moral theories: Chuck as a Kantian deontologist whose rigid loyalty to the categorical imperative and the 'sacred' law destroys his bond with Jimmy; Jimmy as a Mill-style consequentialist whose ends-justify-means scams (Sandpiper, the squat-cobbler film) let him decide what counts as good outcomes and cost him integrity, invoking Bernard Williams; and Mike as a Scanlonian contractualist who honors even immoral agreements like the Tuco hit. Through cases like the 'murderer at the door,' it argues each theory alone leads people to do wrong, so a moral life must combine outcomes, rules, and contracts.

consequentialism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
consequentialism.title: 15. Morality and Manipulation
consequentialism.relation: Kahn frames the Foundation series around personal autonomy, using Mill's image of humans as a growing tree rather than a machine 'built after a model' to condemn both coercion and manipulation. He shows Hari Seldon as a paradoxical champion of autonomy who nonetheless deceives his own followers about the fraudulent Encyclopedia Galactica and secretly forecloses their freedom of action via the Seldon Plan and Second Foundation—echoing the Mule's mind-control of Han Pritcher. He reads Salvor Hardin's maxim ('never let your sense of morals prevent you from doing what is right') as consequentialism that maximizes galaxy-wide autonomy, contrasts it with the deontology exemplified by Gaia/Bliss (who refuse to manipulate Trevize) and critics like Toran Darell and Branno, and leaves the reader to judge as Bliss urges Pelorat to think for himself.

consequentialism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
consequentialism.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
consequentialism.relation: Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.

consequentialism.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
consequentialism.title: What’s Wrong with Roland
consequentialism.relation: Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.

consequentialism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
consequentialism.title: Chapter 4 Huckleberry Finn’s Struggle between Sympathy and Moral Principle Reconsidered
consequentialism.relation: Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.

consequentialism.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
consequentialism.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
consequentialism.relation: Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.

consequentialism.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
consequentialism.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
consequentialism.relation: Naar and Masala defend the 'Secret Underground Internet Seduction Community' by grounding it in Darwinian sexual selection (the peacock's tail, mate value, women prioritizing status and men prioritizing youth/beauty) and an Aristotelian ideal of happiness as excellence: they read the community's aim of becoming a well-rounded seducer as cultivating virtue and social/emotional 'mating intelligence' that yields eudaimonic fulfillment. Against the Kantian objection that seduction training uses women merely as means, they offer a consequentialist and 'deflationist' reply that deception and manipulation already pervade ordinary courtship (makeup, lying about age), so raising one's mate value is morally neutral, and they extend the point to women's active and passive seduction strategies (Cleopatra, groupies).

consequentialism.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
consequentialism.title: Who is Who
consequentialism.relation: Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.

consequentialism.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
consequentialism.title: Who is Who
consequentialism.relation: This chapter tests the Doctor's ethics against consequentialism and Kantian/Nagelian deontology, arguing both fail because his alien longevity and time-travelling relation to consequences resist algorithmic moral judgment ('School Reunion,' 'Attack of the Cybermen'). It proposes instead de Beauvoir's 'ethics of ambiguity' rooted in Romanticism and Sartrean radical freedom and bad faith (the student anecdote; Turlough refusing the Enlightenment diamond), casting the Doctor as a Promethean figure who liberates companions into risky self-perfection.

consequentialism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
consequentialism.title: “Who watches the watchmen ”
consequentialism.relation: J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.

consequentialism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
consequentialism.title: 9. The Handmaid’s Tale as Philosophy Autonomy and Reproductive Freedom
consequentialism.relation: Robison-Greene argues that Gilead's core wrong is denying women autonomy, reducing them from Kantian moral agents to moral patients — walking incubators. She uses Frankfurt's theory of personhood (second-order desires and volitions about what we care about) to show how Gilead dismantles a woman's will by restricting first-order options, language, and critical thinking, so Offred's Scrabble tiles and forbidden reading become acts of reclaimed autonomy. She situates the Sons of Jacob's 'feminine function' ideology in Plato's Republic classes, Aristotle's natural slaves and History of Animals, Aquinas's natural-law subordination of women, and Malebranche's brain-fiber claims, contrasting Beauvoir's complicity of women and framing forced reproduction as the deontology-versus-consequentialism clash over whether species survival could ever justify treating women as mere means.

consequentialism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
consequentialism.title: 50. The Cabin in the Woods as Philosophy Cinematic Reflections on Ethical Complexity, Human Nature, and Worthw
consequentialism.relation: Kowalski argues Whedon and Goddard's The Cabin in the Woods stages a clash between classical utilitarianism and an ethics of care, and cinematically favors the latter. The Facility, sacrificing five campers to placate the Ancient Ones and save humanity, embodies Mill's greatest-happiness reasoning, but its callous celebration while Dana suffers on the dock undercuts that view. When the Director tells Dana she must kill her only remaining friend Marty to save the world, Dana's refusal is defended via Noddings's care ethics and Aristotle's claim that obligations track close personal relationships (special obligations), with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis and Plato's Leontius grounding the film's theory of worthwhile horror: 'people are more important than humanity.'

consequentialism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
consequentialism.title: 53. Tarantino as Philosopher Vengeance – Unfettered, Uncensored, but Not Unjustified
consequentialism.relation: Johnson treats Tarantino's post-2000 filmography as an argument that vengeance is morally permissible when proportionate and directed at the genuinely guilty: Beatrix in Kill Bill, Shosanna in Inglourious Basterds, and Django all get celebrated revenge, while The Hateful Eight is used to distinguish vengeance from retribution and legal versus 'frontier' justice via Nozick's and Bacon's definitions. He rebuts common and historical objections—reading Plato's Gorgias as endorsing due punishment, arguing Spinoza's monism and Hobbes's and Locke's social-contract views do not forbid proportional revenge, and citing Nietzsche and Beauvoir's Eye for an Eye (her refusal to pardon the collaborator Brasillach) to conclude cost-free, proportional revenge can be justified though mercy remains praiseworthy.

consequentialism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
consequentialism.title: 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain
consequentialism.relation: Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

animal-rights.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale
animal-rights.title: The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer
animal-rights.relation: Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.

animal-rights.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
animal-rights.title: Hedging Our Bets
animal-rights.relation: Kind asks whether humanoid Cylons have moral status, using Warren's stone-versus-child contrast to show that the Fleet's blender-and-toaster attitude (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine') rests on the unargued assumption that Cylons are mere machines. Singer's anti-speciesism grounds status in sentience (Gina's suffering, even Scar the Raider), while Regan's subject-of-a-life criteria are met by rational, self-aware Cylons; Helo's 'no human could do the things they've done' argument fails because humans commit equal evils, as the legal limits on punishing criminals show. Since we cannot rule Cylon status out, she closes with Pascal's Wager: treat them as morally considerable, because the asymmetry of error costs us our moral compass.

animal-rights.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
animal-rights.title: Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub
animal-rights.relation: Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.

animal-rights.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
animal-rights.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.

animal-rights.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
animal-rights.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Norva Lo and Andrew Brennan set Richard Routley's 'last man' thought experiment beside Taylor's triggering of the doomsday bomb in Beneath the Planet of the Apes: both ask whether wiping out every living thing would be wrong once no humans remain to be harmed, which basic human chauvinism cannot condemn. The chapter argues the act is wrong from both sides: non-anthropocentrism counts the apes, mutants, and horses as intrinsically valuable beings, and even human-centered standards condemn it, since the talking apes and mutants are Locke's rational persons and Nova's people are biologically human, making Taylor's outburst 'you damned dirty ape' a form of speciesism. Taylor emerges not as simply mad or evil but as the Cold War logic of mutually assured destruction made flesh, a warning that excessive self-interest, personal or species-level, is itself the danger.

animal-rights.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
animal-rights.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues the creature is a person on every serious criterion: it satisfies Kant's rationality test and Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-concept) in both Shelley's novel and I, Frankenstein, and it possesses all ten of Nussbaum's capabilities for flourishing. The twist is that judging the monster a blameworthy murderer already concedes the personhood we deny him, while our exclusion of him is bare Othering and speciesism of the kind Tom Regan attacks in animal ethics. Michaud ends by reversing the question: after humanity's record of crushing minorities, which the creature learns from Volney's Ruins of Empires and weeps over with Safie, what argument could Victor give Adam for sparing us?

animal-rights.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
animal-rights.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Karavitis maps the three films onto the history of animal ethics: Jurassic Park treats dinosaurs as property on Aristotle's ground that only rational humans matter; The Lost World adds Kant's indirect duties, where the sporting rules of Tembo's hunt express duties owed to other humans rather than to the T. rex; and Jurassic Park III moves to Tom Regan, whose 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value fits raptors that remember, plan, and finally choose to spare the humans. The cow and goat fed live to the raptors test how far each view protects animals we treat as mere means.

animal-rights.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
animal-rights.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Lisa Kadonaga stages a choice between two sealed vials - clone the T. rex or the extinct thicktail chub - and weighs purposes for de-extinction: education and fundraising, Veblen-style prestige and conspicuous consumption, making amends for human-caused extinctions (the chub's wetlands were drained, the tyrannosaur died out before us), and Bentham-style utility of ecosystem function. She argues the chub wins on utility because it could resume a real niche while a top carnivore would wreck modern ecosystems, and questions whether Hammond-style engineering that makes recreated animals dependent on humans (the lysine contingency, terminator genes) violates the animals' right to exist as themselves. Her verdict is 'Pister's Bucket': defer resurrection until habitat and resources exist, and spend the effort saving the species we are killing right now.

animal-rights.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
animal-rights.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Kenn Fisher reads the franchise as the extinction of the Great Chain of Being: from Plato's humans mid-way between gods and beasts, through Genesis dominion and Descartes's non-conscious animals, to Malcolm's 'God creates man. Man destroys God. Man creates dinosaurs' - with computers (Hammond's control room, Wikipedia, Google) replacing God at the top. He then tracks animals' ascent from property: Francione on welfare versus personhood, Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', and Singer's equality-as-prescription, applied to Dieter Stark tasering a compy (punished by the compys) versus the unexamined electric fences that keep InGen's 'zoo animals' caged. He closes with Carol Adams's meat-masculinity link - Roland Tembo will hunt only a male T. rex, the dinosaurs are all female - and holds up vegetarian Lex as hope that the Chain bends into a Circle.

animal-rights.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
animal-rights.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Roger Hunt argues the films show that whoever assumes human superiority or ownership of created life gets eaten: Dieter Stark zaps a compy and is devoured by a swarm of them, Ludlow claims InGen's patent and becomes a hunting lesson for the baby T. rex. He stages the real debate over dinosaur moral status between the 'value of life' view (Harding and Sattler: experiment on them if enough sentient beings benefit) and Tom Regan's rights view - anything sentient has basic rights from unconditional individual value, and grading lives by usefulness is speciesism like racism or sexism. He then prefers Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach: a T. rex penned in San Diego cannot roam, hunt, or play, so it cannot flourish, and the point is not granting rights but recognizing we have no right to block other beings' flourishing for fun.

animal-rights.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
animal-rights.title: 3. I Want You to Survive
animal-rights.relation: Seth Walker asks what makes a life worth saving, testing the show's survival choices against instrumental value (usefulness to the group) and Tom Regan's subject-of-a-life criterion of inherent value. Shane's sacrifice of Otis for Carl, Lori's fatal pregnancy and Judith's birth, the Governor's obsession with Meghan, and the hunts for Sophia all show that neither usefulness nor Regan's equal, non gradated inherent value explains why children are selectively elevated - and perceived 'innocence' fails with the colder Carl and with Lizzie. He concludes with Bob Stookey's line in 4.10 'Inmates' ('Not everything has to mean something... but it can'): following Sartre's claim that man is nothing but what he makes of himself, the survivors are condemned to be free and must make their survival mean something, as Daryl and Carol's search for Sophia did.

animal-rights.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
animal-rights.title: 17. Sin, My Young Man, Is When You Treat People as Things
animal-rights.relation: Taking Granny Weatherwax's definition that sin 'is when you treat people as things' and Vetinari's that sin is not saying no to evil, the chapter reads Discworld through C. S. Lewis's argument that a universal Law of Human Nature—felt on the Disc by dwarfs, trolls, and even atheists—points to a divine lawgiver. The enchanted wolf in Witches Abroad, whose agony every witch intuits as wrong and who is granted a merciful death and human funeral, shows that shared moral intuition at work, and grounds the chapter's notes on Pratchett's own campaign for assisted dying. Finally, the Assassins' Guild, which only inhumes the rich who can afford bodyguards under its motto nil mortifi sine lucre, illustrates John Paul II's 'structures of sin': killing sanctified by contract and city law, treating people as things.

animal-rights.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
animal-rights.title: 10. Does Snoopy Dream of Electric Sheep
animal-rights.relation: Reading Snoopy through animal studies, the chapter sets Descartes's 'nature's machines' doctrine - animals as mindless, soulless property without rights - against Charlie Brown's attempts to keep his dog in his place, and shows how Snoopy's endless slippage between plain dog (stealing hats, begging at dinner, dragging Linus by the blanket) and near-human (reading publisher letters, typing novels, serving as Charlie's attorney) collapses the human/animal boundary. The kids' anxiety about his agency, and Snoopy's own gloomy 'I'm less than human,' show the hierarchy being internalized - yet a dog thinking about his inferiority already blurs it. When Snoopy hands Charlie his collar, the chapter reads it as a refusal of property status and proof that being human is a performance of gestures rather than an essence.

animal-rights.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
animal-rights.title: 15. Red Harvest in Roanoke
animal-rights.relation: Reads Roanoke through ecocriticism and ecofeminism: the culture-nature dualism collapses as the urban Millers' wooded retreat turns predatory (rain of teeth, pig-men); the Butcher's backstory - a colonial woman starved by men whose blood-sacrifice pact makes the land flourish - aligns women and Nature as co-exploited by patriarchy, with Shelby's 'irrational' warnings ignored and Lee's maternal fury a force of nature; the animalizing of victims (pig-headed roasting, the Polks' barn-raised children, Matt's tryst with the Witch of the Wood) dissolves the human/animal hierarchy; and the media crew's attempt to package wilderness for ratings ends with Nature striking back at Agnes in the woods.

animal-rights.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
animal-rights.title: 3. Save the Demogorgons!
animal-rights.relation: Puumala asks whether killing the Demogorgons is speciesist: Dart's pain response to light makes the demodogs sentient (Bentham's 'Can they suffer?'), giving them moral considerability, while the Mind Flayer may or may not be a moral agent and could even be a keystone species whose destruction collapses the Upside Down ecosystem. He tests whether demogorgons count as invasive species (they may be native to a causally connected mirror dimension), invokes Regan's lifeboat case to argue they must still lose out to humans in a conflict of interests, and ends with the uncomfortable thought that humans are themselves an invasive species turning Earth into an Upside Down, so Eleven closing the gate was compassionate conservation.

animal-rights.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
animal-rights.title: Hedging Our Bets
animal-rights.relation: Kind asks whether the Fleet's treatment of Cylons (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine,' Cally's killing of Boomer charged as mere discharging of a firearm) presupposes that Cylons lack the moral status Mary Anne Warren defines against the stone-versus-child contrast. Against species membership as a criterion she deploys Singer's anti-speciesism (sentience grounds equal consideration: Gina's torture, the Raider Scar) and Regan's subject-of-a-life, and against the 'no souls' argument she cites Descartes's animal automata and Turing's reply that an omnipotent God could give machines souls, as Leoben himself suggests to Adama. Since no criterion rules Cylons out with certainty, the chapter closes with a Pascal's Wager structure: under uncertainty, treat plausible moral-status-holders as having it, because denying it costs us our moral compass, answering Adama's 'why are we worth saving?'.

animal-rights.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
animal-rights.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
animal-rights.relation: Jason Eberl treats the muttations, jabberjays that mimic speech without understanding, tracker jackers, the wolf-mutts with Glimmer's eyes that torment Cato, and the lizard-mutts hissing Katniss's name, alongside real chimeras (geeps, the SCID-hu mouse, Balaban's quail-chick brain transplants, Weissman's human-neural mouse) to ask whether biotechnology could create a person. Working through Boethius's definition of a person as an 'individual substance of a rational nature' and Locke's 'thinking intelligent Being' that can consider itself the same over time, he argues that human DNA alone confers no personhood, while a chimera genuinely capable of self-conscious rational thought would be a person whose weaponized creation and lab captivity would violate its rights, which is why ethicists allow mouse chimeras but hesitate with primates. He notes that the Gamemakers' refusal to see tributes as persons is exactly the move that made slavery and Nazi dehumanization possible, and that Katniss's suspicion about whether the mutts remember their deaths is the right ethical question to keep open.

animal-rights.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
animal-rights.title: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
animal-rights.relation: Karavitis places thirteen robot and android episodes on a spectrum from the X109B14 computer of 'The Brain Center at Whipple's' to indistinguishable androids like Alicia, arguing that the moral duties we owe artificial creations depend on personhood. By Locke's memory-continuity account of identity, the mind-transferred couple of 'The Trade-Ins' remain persons, and so would androids created from scratch, which makes the routine destruction of Alicia, Grandma, and Jana murder. The animal-ethics tradition from Aristotle's property view through Kant's indirect duties to Singer and Regan's moral patients supplies the analogy, and the show's unstated definition of evil is treating persons as disposable objects.

animal-rights.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
animal-rights.title: Notes
animal-rights.relation: Griem uses Perrin's telepathic bond with wolves, especially Hopper, to examine human-animal relationships and the assumed divide between human rationality and animal instinct. She traces the wolf's ambiguous image across Roman, Norse, Native American, and Christian traditions (Fenrir versus Geri and Freki; the Big Bad Wolf), and uses Plato's charioteer of the soul and Elyas's advice to control fear to frame the rational/emotional contrast. Citing cognition studies (Betty the tool-making crow) that suggest continuity between human and animal minds, she reads Perrin's fear of losing his humanity, his axe-versus-hammer struggle, and Hopper as anthropomorphized guardian animal in Tel'aran'rhiod to argue we should recognize animal rationality and embrace the beast within.

animal-rights.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
animal-rights.title: 23_LaRocca_Chapter_022.html
animal-rights.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Gabriela Cowperthwaite's Blackfish through Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, arguing the film's interviews with orca neuroscientists (Marino et al.) function as Nagel's proposed 'objective phenomenology,' conveying orca consciousness through objective indicators rather than mere anthropomorphic projection. She dissects the film's rhetoric around Tilikum and Dawn Brancheau, showing how the title, delayed naming, SeaWorld ad juxtapositions and emotional testimony first vilify then humanize the whale to argue captivity is morally unacceptable. Invoking Peggy Zeglin Brand's 'lenses,' Iris Murdoch's 'unselfing' and Marc Bekoff's inclusive ethic, she concludes the film approximates truth about orca minds even as it, like SeaWorld, is 'structured to sell.'

animal-rights.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
animal-rights.title: Chapter 9 Twain’s Critique of Human Exceptionalism
animal-rights.relation: VanDette argues that Twain's late anti-vivisection writings anticipate posthumanist animal ethics by inverting the Darwinian species hierarchy. Through 'Letters from a Dog,' the essay 'Man's Place in the Animal World,' his 1899 London Anti-Vivisection Society letter, and the mother-dog narrator Aileen in 'A Dog's Tale,' Twain gives animals voice and subjectivity to attack human exceptionalism. His refusal to weigh vivisection's benefit against animal pain echoes Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', while his target is the Cartesian view of animals as insensible machines and the evolutionary logic used to justify experiments; Dr. Gray's cold killing of Aileen's puppy indicts a science that deadens compassion.

animal-rights.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
animal-rights.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
animal-rights.relation: Kretz systematically attacks the claim that hunting is environmental, using the Ducks Unlimited Canada case. She wields Hume's is-ought gap to deny that 'natural' hunting is thereby moral, cites evidence that hunters remove the fittest breeders and eliminate predators, and rejects Thoreau's hope that young hunters 'outgrow' killing as counterproductive (analogous to teaching theft to prevent it). Drawing on Brian Luke, she presses 'the paradox of ethical hunting': the sportsman's code (quick kills, retrieve the wounded) shows concern for the animal that, fully realized, entails not hunting at all.

animal-rights.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
animal-rights.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
animal-rights.relation: Parker asks whether 'photographic hunting' (the camera) is an ethically superior replacement for weaponized sport hunting (the gun), against Singer's and Regan's blanket condemnations of hunting. He concedes the camera captures most benefits—environmental knowledge, immersive learning, Leopold-style love of the land—but argues that only the kill roots the hunter in the ecosystem (citing Ortega and Paul Shepard), forcing confrontation with predation and death. He warns that treating photography as a wholesale replacement positions the human as detached 'spectator/master' over nature, the very hubris that drives environmental degradation.

animal-rights.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
animal-rights.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
animal-rights.relation: Carmine argues that in America hunting is a sacred rite of a secular 'religion' of individual natural rights granted by the Deist 'Nature's God,' where—revising Locke via Jefferson's 'pursuit of happiness'—one owns game only by actual capture, and early game law kept even private land open to the common hunter against English enclosure. He attacks Leopold's land ethic and Tom Regan's animal rights, and Garrett Hardin's 'Tragedy of the Commons,' as an 'eco-gentry' that demotes humans to mere biosphere/carbonate and threatens human rights, insisting (with Burkert's Homo Necans) that to kill and eat the rabbit is to reserve dignity for humans alone.

animal-rights.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
animal-rights.title: GARDENING
animal-rights.relation: Matthew Hall challenges the exclusion of plants from gardening ethics, tracing it to the Garden of Eden where plants are denied life and given only instrumental value for humans. Against this he sets kincentric alternatives—the Achuar mothering manioc, the Raramuri treating plants as kin, and the living apple trees of the Hesperides—and Albert Schweitzer's reverence-for-life ethic. He proposes gardeners offer plants three 'gifts': acknowledging their autonomy, giving them care, and giving weeds space, extending moral consideration to plant life itself.

plato-justice.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
plato-justice.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Eric Katz reads Tolkien's One Ring as a modern retelling of Plato's Ring of Gyges: Glaucon's challenge in Republic II that no one, given impunity, would remain just. He traces each character's moment of choice - Gollum already corrupted and split into 'Slinker and Stinker', Boromir trying to seize the Ring at Amon Hen and dying redeemed, Galadriel passing the test ('I will diminish, and go into the West'), Tom Bombadil untouched, Frodo finally claiming the Ring at the Cracks of Doom while Sam rejects the vision of 'Samwise the Strong'. Katz argues Tolkien improves on Plato by showing, through living characters, that unlimited power corrupts the soul, and that the answer to 'Why be moral?' is 'to be yourself': those who refuse the Ring are exactly those who know their own limits.

plato-justice.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
plato-justice.title: The End Is It All Darkness
plato-justice.relation: John Pappas reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Glaucon's ring of Gyges in Plato's Republic: Judah Rosenthal's wealth and prestige are his invisibility ring, and when his mistress Dolores threatens exposure he 'pushes the button', has his gangster brother Jack murder her, and gets away with it. Against Socrates' claim that injustice corrodes the harmonious soul and that virtue is its own reward, the film, unlike Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, lets the murderer and the 'yutz' Lester prosper while honest Clifford loses everything; Bergson's theory of the comic explains why Lester is invisible to himself, and Rousseau's reverie about what he would do with the ring marks Clifford as the one man who might use it decently. Aunt May's post-Holocaust atheism, 'might makes right' with nothing 'handed down in stone', supplies the argument from evil that releases Judah, leaving only the qualified hope that it is 'not all darkness'.

plato-justice.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
plato-justice.title: Voldemort and the Sophists
plato-justice.relation: Opens Michael Austin's chapter with the common question of Harry and Socrates - why die for one's convictions, i.e., why be moral at all? - and states Plato's Republic answer that being moral is necessary and sufficient for true happiness, positioning the Harry/Voldemort conflict as Socrates against his sophisticated enemies.

plato-justice.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
plato-justice.title: The Common Good versus the Greater Good
plato-justice.relation: Maps Voldemort onto the Sophists - Thrasymachus's claim that the unjust always come out ahead - through his pattern of exploiting followers' trust for power and pleasure, while Plato's two-pronged reply runs: cosmic justice in the afterlife (the flayed child beneath the bench as Voldemort's just fate, sealing it by refusing remorse) and the intrinsic goodness of justice via the tripartite soul with reason ruling spirit and appetite, the four cardinal virtues, and the health analogy. Harry, seeking Dumbledore's wisdom, showing courage in facing death, and devoted to justice for wizards and Muggles, embodies the moral life as the rational choice, while Voldemort's snakelike appearance externalizes his disordered, sick soul.

plato-justice.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
plato-justice.title: The Jedi Model
plato-justice.relation: Barad presents a handbook of Jedi virtue modeled on Plato's Republic: the Jedi are Plato's Guardians, trained through physical exercise and Socratic questioning to guard peace and justice. Aristotle's golden mean explains courage as the balance between Chewbacca's cowardly fear and Anakin's rash rush at Dooku, with Luke's decision to leave Dagobah counting as courage because it has just cause. Luke's Dagobah cave vision (Vader's mask opening to reveal his own face) is read as Plato's Cave allegory turned inward - self-knowledge of one's fear of becoming evil - while compassion and forgiveness, not forbidden attachment, complete the Jedi character. The chapter even defends Jedi mind tricks via Plato's noble lie (the myth of the metals) as manipulation of the weak-minded for the common good.

plato-justice.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
plato-justice.title: Forming Family Bonds
plato-justice.relation: Reads the Fantastic Four's origin through Plato and the 1960s space race: Reed's heedless rush to beat the Russians into space embodies Thrasymachus' Republic claim that the drive for power dominates human life, and Sue shames the reluctant Ben into flying the unshielded ship. Socrates' belief that virtue is its own reward frames the cosmic-ray price each pays — powers eerily matching their personalities — until Ben proposes the team mission statement: 'We've gotta use that power to help mankind, right?'

plato-justice.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
plato-justice.title: Plato and the Question of Why We Should Be Good
plato-justice.relation: Reconstructs Glaucon's challenge from the Republic: with a ring making injustice cost-free, no one would keep hands off others' possessions, and anyone who stayed just would be mocked as 'a great fool' behind our self-protective praise; Socrates must show that the truly just person 'stripped of the seeming' — enduring the lash, the rack, and the cross — lives better than the honored unjust one. The chapter then turns Plato's thought-experiment on comic-book worlds: why should someone with superpowers care about being good?

plato-justice.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
plato-justice.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.

plato-justice.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
plato-justice.title: But Isn’t It Only Natural
plato-justice.relation: Adams answers Plato's ring-of-Gyges challenge with Heroes: even when invisible, wrongdoing corrupts the wrongdoer, because justice is to the soul what health is to the body. Claire's refusal to claim credit for the fire rescue shows thumos (spirit) responsive to logistikos (reason), Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is epithumetikon (appetite) ruling the soul, and Hiro's Vegas cheating shows how injustice makes life spin out of control; Claire's apology to Brody illustrates the Pagan Golden Rule — help your friends, harm your enemies — tempered by Plato's caution that enemies may become friends.

plato-justice.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
plato-justice.title: Once I Was the Student, Now I Am the Master
plato-justice.relation: Johannes Bulhof reads 'Me and My Uncle' — the Dead's most-performed song, though hardly a fan favorite — as a parable against rational self-interest. The nephew learned everything from his uncle: how to cheat at cards, steal, and shoot first, so he rationally guns down the cowboys, takes the gold, and leaves his uncle's 'dead ass there by the side of the road' — the student out-mastering the teacher. Framing the song with Thrasymachus's Republic I claim that the unjust always profit (and his own students' admission they would cheat if they could get away with it), then with Hobbes's state of nature where equality, contested goods, and anticipatory striking make everyone enemies — even family — Bulhof argues the song's drunken lesson is that rational self-interest is communally irrational.

plato-justice.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
plato-justice.title: What Is Justice
plato-justice.relation: Johnny Huss extracts multiple theories of justice from 'Jacob Green'—desert (traced to Plato's Republic), equal treatment, conventionalism, and systemic injustice—and argues that desert collapses once responsibility is pushed back to factors beyond our control (Cash's God-given voice, the 'victim of the times').
