Rawls's veil of ignorance supplies the standard for judging institutions: since anyone could be Jacob Green, we could not accept principles that let anyone 'get done like Jacob Green got done.' The chapter extends this to social justice for Native Americans via 'The Ballad of Ira Hayes' and 'As Long as the Grass Shall Grow,' including the flooded Cornplanter Tract, and closes insisting justice requires action, not just principles.

plato-justice.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
plato-justice.title: Springsteen’s Martyrdom
plato-justice.relation: The Bells parallel Socrates' forcible 'abduction' to the house of the arms merchant Cephalus in Republic Book I with Springsteen's 1984 political abduction, when Reagan and Mondale both pretended he had endorsed them and George Will invited him to be laureate of 'joyous overconsumption.' They read the Republic's luxurious city — its Ring of Gyges parasites, censorship of poets, and wars born of appetite — as an elenchus run against the control (epoche) of the healthy working city of Book II, so readers who take the 'ideal' city at face value err exactly like fans who hear patriotism in 'Born in the U.S.A.' Songs like 'Youngstown,' 'The Angel' and 'Galveston Bay' likewise critique overconsumption, imperialism and the censorship of artists, and both artist-critics risk the martyrdom Socrates suffered for speaking truth to the powerful.

plato-justice.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
plato-justice.title: Paradise Found
plato-justice.relation: Brown reads The Minish Cap's Hyrule as a working utopia: its Royal Family, guards, and market traders loosely realize Plato's Republic classes from Book V onward, but with fluid social boundaries (Zelda wanders the festival unharassed), no slavery, and relaxed state control that Plato's static order lacked. The town matches Aristotle's polis design (walled, defensible, right-sized, river-powered yet self-sufficient), while the surrounding pastoral landscape embodies Kantian disinterested beauty in nature and the Schillerian idea that through beauty we arrive at freedom. Its vague, prophet-free Picori religion of benevolent Christs-in-miniature needs no Kierkegaardian leap of faith, so unlike Hitler's Germany or Stalin's Russia, Hyrule is utopia actually achieved, and explorable, through Link.

plato-justice.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
plato-justice.title: The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
plato-justice.relation: Horn argues the three Triforce pieces are morally neutral: by Kant's Groundwork, only the good will that acts from duty (Link never rescues Zelda for a reward) is good without qualification, so courage, wisdom, and power can each serve evil, and the Triforce would have corrupted Zelda or Link too if fortune had dealt it otherwise. Plato's Ring of Gyges and the Glaucon-Socrates debate explain Ganondorf: he chose to lust for power, and his wealth, status, and fear-based honor are hollow because justice is good for its own sake and his soul is out of balance (which is why the Triforce split at his touch in Ocarina of Time). Aristotle's doctrine of the mean then defines proper use: Link's courage between cowardice and rashness (getting the map, compass, and weapon before the boss), Zelda's internalized prudence, and Ganondorf's power in insatiable excess.

plato-justice.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
plato-justice.title: Dorothy and the Art of War
plato-justice.relation: The Bells read Baum's book against Bleeding Kansas and John Brown: 1900 readers, they argue, heard 'Kansas' as the slave-or-free question, making Dorothy the Great Emancipator who frees the Munchkins, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Winkies, and finally herself from the Witch's servitude. They pair her with Socrates, recasting the Republic's opening scene at Cephalus's slave-owning mansion (Thrasymachus's 'injustice on a sufficiently large scale' pays) as an abolitionist confrontation, and quoting the Phaedo's claim that philosophy is practicing for death to explain why vastly outnumbered reformers—Socrates, Brown at Harpers Ferry and Osawatomie, Dorothy facing the Witch's forty wolves, forty crows, bee swarms, and Winkie army—do not fear the odds. The shared moral: the love of wisdom, pursued in a community of inquirers, charms away the fear of death, which is why tyrants and slave-owners, whose own best part is enslaved, live in terror and cannot sleep at night.

plato-justice.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
plato-justice.title: I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion
plato-justice.relation: Smith dissects Stephen's free-market worship — the market as a God requiring faith, 'the market has spoken' on global warming, supply-side economics, and the plan to run universities as businesses with credit-card-swiper desks and tuition priced by marketability. Against this he deploys Socrates in the Republic: a practice is defined by its aim, so a physician aiming at his own wealth is not practicing medicine badly but moneymaking, and by the same argument a corporatized university whose primary aim is shareholder profit is no longer higher education — privatization alters its nature and so destroys it, while Smith's invisible hand is exposed as the South Park gnomes' missing Step Two and wikiality as supply-side epistemology where facts are supplied by majority vote instead of known.

plato-justice.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
plato-justice.title: How Beckenbauer and Zidane Practiced the Four Cardinal Virtues
plato-justice.relation: Coumoundouros explains soccer greatness through three Platonic ideas: the Form of the footballer, which Pelé (1,281 goals, three World Cups, the save by Banks his header 'infected' with greatness and the infamous miss against Uruguay) and Maradona (the Hand of God and the Goal of the Century past five English defenders) approximate as near-perfect imitations, with position-specific Forms like forward Form for Pelé and attacking-midfielder Form for Maradona. Excellence as performing a proper function well (Republic 353a) then accounts for modern players—Ronaldo's evolved winger role, Henry converted by Wenger into a striker, Marta averaging a goal per game proving women's soccer equals the men's. Finally the Republic's four cardinal virtues grounded in the tripartite soul apply off and on the pitch: Beckenbauer playing the 1970 'Game of the Century' with a fractured clavicle and marshaling the 1974 final shows courage, wisdom, and moderation in just balance, while Zidane's 2006 head-butt on Materazzi shows the spirited part overwhelming reason, and with it greatness itself.

plato-justice.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
plato-justice.title: A Palace Revolution
plato-justice.relation: The fantasy election brings in Plato's Republic: Richards's defense attorney Bill Carter functions as his Ring of Gyges, letting him vanish from legal consequences and raising Plato's question of whether we act justly only from fear of punishment. The tripartite soul is mapped onto Keef — appetites (drugs, sex, Jagger's 'Bitch'), spirit (the Glimmer Twins' rivalry), rationality (busting his head reaching for a library book) — and justice becomes the harmony under rationality's rule. In the ideal city of philosopher kings, auxiliaries, and workers, the sign at the gate reads 'NO POETS, NO ROCK'N'ROLLERS': Richards is exactly the corrupting poet Plato bars.

plato-justice.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
plato-justice.title: Compromise Solution
plato-justice.relation: This section pushes back on Plato: the author has never met anyone as harmonious as the just man and calls the philosopher king 'a fairytale'. Quoting Republic Book VIII's portrait of the democratic soul that 'lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour', he concedes the description fits his own life and polity — yet insists that a life without good sex, good food, and good conversation would be 'bereft of serious value', which sets up the book's compromise.

plato-justice.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
plato-justice.title: What Can a Poor Boy Do, but Sing in a Rock’n’Roll Band
plato-justice.relation: The finale concedes Plato's point that justice involves self-control — enough to make a voter pause at the sexual appetites of JFK and Bill Clinton — while refusing the ascetic cure and the President-Keith ticket. The author decides he could not live under Keef's rule but wants him permanently at the edge of town, playing a juke joint: a spirit worth tuning into as a reminder that control is 'ultimately an illusion', visited on midnight rides and returned from before morning comes.

plato-justice.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
plato-justice.title: The Wire and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Bzdak uses Wee-Bey's 'you askin' too much' - and his ultimate yes to letting Bunny take Namond out of the Game - to pose the Puzzle of Impartiality: morality seems to require equal consideration (Plato's Socrates rejecting justice as helping friends and harming enemies; the impartialism built into Bentham's, Mill's, and Singer's utilitarianism), yet the show's most admirable moment is a father's partiality, and its worst parents, De'Londa and Raylene, fail exactly by not being partial to their own children. He tests a Greater Good Principle against cops protecting cops, Kima choosing honesty over loyalty to McNulty and Freamon, and Bunk's disgusted speech to Omar about the code that splits the community into victims who matter and victims who don't. The principle handles Carver reporting Colicchio but not the burning-building cases, and the show's verdict is that both too much and too little partiality destroy lives, with no single criterion deciding.

plato-justice.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
plato-justice.title: The Wire and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Grinnell reads Rawls's dotted case lists, Marimow's rip-and-run, Burrell's 'dope on the table,' and Prez being told he teaches the test rather than math as Aristotle's function argument gone wrong: professionals who reduce their purpose to stats and pleasing bosses are 'doing well' instead of 'doing good,' which is just what Plato says badly governed cities reward with honor. The characters who grasp their real function - Daniels refusing cheap felony stats, Bunk refusing to turn cases black without the true murderer, Freamon hunting bodies in vacants despite Landsman's fury - defy the Game at career cost, while Colvin's Hamsterdam and McNulty's fake killer show the opposite failure of zealous judgment without humility or rule of law. The chapter ends on the paradox that trusting professional judgment risks messes, but defining professions by numbers eliminates excellence altogether.

plato-justice.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
plato-justice.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Greg Littmann maps Ape City onto Plato's Republic class by class: orangutan rulers who legislate, censor, and propagandize; gorilla warriors who enforce; chimpanzee producers who do all the work - including, pointedly, the science Plato made no provision for; and humans as the 'barbarians' Plato says may be enslaved or exterminated. The overlaps are detailed: the Sacred Scrolls' first article of faith functions as the noble lie's myth of the metals, orangutan funerals promise heaven to keep gorillas unafraid of death, and Zaius's erasing of Taylor's dust-writing and blowing up of the archaeological cave enact the rulers' duty to supervise stories. But the films also refute Plato: hereditary orangutans show that power corrupts philosopher kings, Dr. Honorius's 'reason' is dogma serving the faith, the gelding threat that finally breaks Taylor cracks the tripartite-soul analogy of justice, and democracy's rough virtue is that it lets us remove rulers 'without sticking anybody with iron spears.'

plato-justice.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
plato-justice.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: The Azevedos read Plato's Republic Book I as a manual for professionalism: Socrates argues the practitioner - doctor, ruler, lawyer - serves the patient, citizen, and client rather than himself, while Thrasymachus's cynicism that injustice pays and people only seem just is embodied by Eli Gold ('I lie for a living') and by stunt lawyers Nancy Crozier, Patti Nyholm, Louis Canning, and the secretive Jonas Stern. Alicia answers with Aristotle's virtue ethics: professionalism as a cluster virtue cultivated through habituated action, hitting the mean and doing the right thing at the right time for the right reasons. Saint Alicia shows how costly being good all the time is, yet the chapter sides with her striving for virtue over Thrasymachus's goldbrick glory.

plato-justice.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
plato-justice.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Mirko Garasic reads Victor as the Modern Prometheus of the myth Plato tells in the Protagoras: like the Titan punished for stealing fire, Victor's purely technical gift of life fails because, as Zeus tells Hermes, justice and reverence must be shared by all or cities cannot exist. The chapter's real subject is love - Prometheus suffers for loving the humans he made, and the creature asks for a female companion while Victor's hate-filled destruction of her unleashes the second wave of revenge. Tim Burton's Frankenweenie splits this love/hate dualism: young Victor's tear over Sparky makes the experiment work, the classmates' prize-greed and the xenophobic mayor produce the real monsters, and Mr. Rzykruski teaches that science severed from emotion is empty. Via Zygmunt Bauman's liquid modernity, Garasic concludes that our own detached, networked isolation is the danger: scientific progress alone never makes a better society, love and community do.

plato-justice.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
plato-justice.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Comparing Finn with Gilgamesh, Achilles, Cuchulainn and Beowulf, the chapter shows how deeply he belongs to the archaic heroic code: a warrior who loves combat, seeks glory in tough-guy contests, fights dirty like Odysseus, and is fiercely loyal to Jake, his friends and his community. Against this tradition, Finn's unprecedented willingness to help any stranger who cries for help and his refusal to kill the 'unaligned' ant mark the post-heroic morality that began when Socrates told Athenians to care for their souls rather than status and Plato designed a city serving the common good - the author explicitly frames this through Nietzsche's complaint that Greek philosophy derailed the healthy, competitive heroic values. The chapter sides with Finn and the self-sacrificing Lemonjohn over Achilles, concluding that the secret of the Enchiridion is doing whatever the common good requires, warrior or not.

plato-justice.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
plato-justice.title: Justified and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: The chapter argues Boyd Crowder personifies coolness - composure, wily cleverness, unconventionality, intelligence, likability - as shown in the 'Cottonmouth' payroll-robbery scene where he turns his flip phone into a room bug, overhears Kyle planning to blow him up in the mine, and lets the plotters kill themselves. Jon Cotton borrows Wittgenstein's family-resemblance model to define coolness as an indefinable cluster of traits (with Dewey Crowe as the agreed uncool case), and reaches back to Socrates' defining of ethical virtues and the Republic's just, well-ordered soul to argue that coolness is a genuine ethical virtue - the excellence of a properly functioning person - in a scientific, post-religious ethics.

plato-justice.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
plato-justice.title: 8. Plato’s Chicago
plato-justice.relation: Littmann systematically maps Roth's Chicago onto Plato's Republic: like Marcus, Plato rejects democracy after Athens executed Socrates; both dissolve the family ('faction before blood' versus children raised in common and bred by state schedule); Erudite's IQ-selected leadership mirrors the rigorously trained philosopher-rulers, Dauntless the warrior class whose purely physical training Plato warns turns 'savage and harsh,' Abnegation's poverty the guardians's communism of property, and the factionless the powerless producers - with Plato's noble lie about the metals matching the Erudite's propaganda and serums as instruments of control. The shared flaw, he argues, is concentrated power without external checks, which corrupted Abnegation, corrupts every Dauntless leadership change, and would corrupt Plato's guardians too. The lesson is not to hand power to the least vicious but for democratic voters to confront their own ignorance - or end like Roth's America, in apocalyptic war.

plato-justice.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
plato-justice.title: 23. Justice in Love
plato-justice.relation: Adam Barkman and Noah van Brenk read Downton through C. S. Lewis's four loves (storge, eros, philia, agape) and Plato's Republic definition of justice as each thing performing its role, arguing that agape satisfies justice and then transcends it by loving the naturally unlovable. Their examples are Anna and Bates's forged thirty-pound note for the jobless Molesley, Bates and Lord Grantham sparing Thomas prison after the Jimmy incident by introducing 'a little kindness into the equation,' and Lavinia refusing Matthew's justice-only dismissal of her after his paralyzing injury. False agape appears in Thomas's manipulation of the nanny and in Vera Bates's possessive 'love,' which ends in her suicide staged as Bates's crime.

plato-justice.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
plato-justice.title: 20. The Good and the Gracious
plato-justice.relation: Olson and Taliaferro read manners as the story's moral barometer: the genuine, effusive compliments exchanged by Westley and Inigo atop the Cliffs of Insanity, and Fezzik's sporting wrestling, express care and connection, while Humperdinck's and Rugen's courtly politeness is camouflage for torture, murder, and war. Against Machiavelli's instrumental use of courtesy in The Prince, they recruit Plato's sophrosyne as 'good form' inseparable from justice, wisdom, and courage, and Confucian li as etiquette that instructs and steadies us toward virtue, with Hobbes's 'small morals' marking the hollow version; they add that manners also police class, from Buttercup's 'Farm Boy' to reality TV and the financiers of the Great Recession who used the correct fork.

plato-justice.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
plato-justice.title: 7. Pratchett’s Republic
plato-justice.relation: Kempner maps Plato's Republic onto Ankh-Morpork: Vetinari is the Philosopher King, the Watch of Guards! Guards! are the Guardians who devote themselves to the good of the whole community, and Platonic justice as keeping everything in its right place is Vetinari's guild-licensing, topiary-tending rule - including the jail cell whose locks are all on the inside. Against Plato's banishment of poets, The Truth shows words serving the just city: William de Worde's pursuit of 'the big truth' exposes the frame-up of Vetinari and extends the circle of Guardians to the free press. The chapter concludes that Pratchett keeps Plato's ideal only by bending it to observable reality - Vetinari rules for the city rather than remaking its people.

plato-justice.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
plato-justice.title: 9. Pierce’s Republic
plato-justice.relation: Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.

plato-justice.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
plato-justice.title: 11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies
plato-justice.relation: Devon Brickhouse-Bryson asks whether the Society, plainly dystopian with respect to justice, might nonetheless be utopian with respect to beauty. Treating a society as an abstract object—a system of persons ordered into a community, not reducible to its members or its gravBoots and razors—and beauty as harmoniousness, the ordering of parts into a unified whole in the tradition of Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hutcheson, he shows the Color system straightforwardly instantiates that definition, each caste an organ of one well-functioning clock. But the harmony holds only if the castes are genuinely teleologically distinct; if that is mere Gold propaganda, the Society is not beautiful but a cacophony. Either way the chapter's real lesson stands against Plato: identifying justice with each part fulfilling its role conflates beauty with justice, and the Society shows how radically the two can come apart—possibly beautiful and radically unjust at once.

plato-justice.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!
plato-justice.title: 11. The Unruly Woman
plato-justice.relation: Sets Plato's Republic case against the poets, with its censored storytellers, heroes who bear misfortune quietly, and worry that comedy feeds the soul's appetitive part, against Schumer's program of celebrating flaws. Young Amy raiding her roommate's hidden Twinkies and lasagna illustrates the appetitive soul overruling reason, and memoir chapters like 'Secret Bad Habits' do exactly what Plato feared by licensing readers to enjoy what they would be ashamed to confess. Li argues that the unruly women of Schumer, Dunham, Broad City, and Kaling legitimately answer Plato's ancient quarrel by representing messy, complicated female experience rather than modeling virtue.

plato-justice.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
plato-justice.title: 18. Smoke and Mirrors in Gilead
plato-justice.relation: St. Martin structures Gilead with Plato's Republic: Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger' is the Sons of Jacob's operating principle (the Wall, the cattle prods, 'removing the damaged ones' from the ambassador's reception), and Glaucon's claim that it is best to do injustice without paying the penalty describes Commanders, while Handmaids suffer injustice with no revenge. She maps Socrates's division of labor onto Gilead's color-coded castes (Handmaids, Marthas, Aunts, Wives), then uses Glaucon's mocking 'city of sows' to show Gilead betraying even that model, since the regime exists to keep men powerful rather than babies alive—baby Charlotte recovers only when reunited with Janine. Serena's awakening after Eden's execution is an emergence from the cave, and the chapter closes that justice must be chosen for its own sake, with biases checked.

plato-justice.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
plato-justice.title: 15. Clueless Rebels
plato-justice.relation: Luft reads Petty's apology for flying the Confederate flag as the awakening of justice, the Platonic cardinal virtue and Aristotle's common-good virtue, and asks what is worth defending. Socrates refusing escape in the Crito, Jesus, Njal's saga and Harry Potter exemplify self-sacrificial refusal to defend oneself for a higher ideal, the model Petty aspires to in "I Won't Back Down." Through Royce, Fletcher and Keller on loyalty, the Confederate "clueless rebels" are diagnosed with misplaced loyalty: regional pride is ethical only when we hold something as ours because it is right, never as right because it is ours.

plato-justice.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
plato-justice.title: Should Your Child Watch Aliens
plato-justice.relation: Maps Aliens onto Plato's Republic: Hadley's Hope is an isolated city of fixed roles, Newt is an apprentice guardian taken along on campaign, and Ripley is her auxiliary supervisor who knows which military ventures are safe (making her look away from the cocooned colonists on the monitors). Exposure to violence has made Newt mentally tough and courageous in Plato's exact sense of retaining what reason dictates about what is and is not to be feared - she stays calm in the APC and leads Ripley and Hicks through the vents while Hudson panics - so the authors conclude parents should discuss violent media like Aliens with children rather than shield them.

plato-justice.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
plato-justice.title: Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers
plato-justice.relation: Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.

plato-justice.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
plato-justice.title: 23. Justice in Love
plato-justice.relation: Adam Barkman and Noah van Brenk apply C.S. Lewis's four loves to Downton, arguing that every love requires Platonic justice - each thing treated according to its role, as in the servants' 'My Lord' hierarchy and Bates's equal right to a fair trial - but that agape, sacrificial love, satisfies justice and then transcends it by loving the unlovable. Anna and Bates's forged thirty-pound note for the destitute Molesley, Bates sparing his hated enemy Thomas from prison, and Lavinia refusing Matthew's 'think of me as dead' dismissal are true agape, while Vera Bates's possessive blackmail and Thomas's scheme against the nanny merely ape it. The upshot is Lord Grantham's line to Alfred: do not abandon your beliefs, 'just introduce a little kindness into the equation' - justice tempered by mercy in both directions.

plato-justice.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
plato-justice.title: The (Single) Garden Path
plato-justice.relation: Argues Herbert populates Dune with three long-running eugenics programs, each with a different ethical stance: the Bene Gesserit's Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (whose communal guardian-breeding deliberately recalls Socrates' Kallipolis in the Republic), Leto II's Golden Path, and the Bene Tleilax's axolotl-tank genetic design for immortality. It reads the chastened Sisterhood of the later novels as moving from consequentialist to Kantian, deontological ground ('never seek to create a human being in any one image'), frames Leto II as the ultimate utilitarian whose species-saving end allegedly justifies Machiavellian means (with Siona's objection that he had no right), and shows the Tleilaxu destroyed by their own monomaniacal religious code. Conclusion: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics.'

plato-justice.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
plato-justice.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Cam Cobb pits Socratic critical inquiry and Plato's Republic-style vocational streaming (classes sorted by the 'myth of the metals,' sold through a noble lie) against the Battle School curriculum, which is almost purely vocational and lacks the music, poetry, and liberal paideia that harmonize the soul. Testing Socrates' dialogic method, Dewey's aptitude-tracking education, and Freire's problem-posing alternative against the battleroom, the Giant's Drink, and Graff's secretly rewritten game rules, Cobb concludes Ender's schooling mixes conflicting pedagogies and ends in the teacher domination Freire feared, crystallized in Ender's lament 'I've spent my life as someone's pawn.'

plato-justice.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
plato-justice.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Eric Silverman argues Game of Thrones explodes the storybook link between virtue and worldly happiness: Ned, 'one man in ten thousand,' is betrayed and executed, so Plato's claim that the just person is happy must mean psychic order rather than material flourishing - reason ruling spirit and appetite - as with Bran, who flourishes as a greenseer though he will never walk again. Cersei is Plato's tyrant, her soul ruled by insatiable appetite and paranoia, so no external goods can ever satisfy her, while Aristotle's correction - virtue necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia, which also needs health, friends, and good fortune - explains why both Ned (virtue without external goods) and Cersei (goods without virtue) end up unhappy. Finally he inverts Pascal's Wager: since playing the game of thrones risks total loss (torture, humiliation, death) for limited gain, and even winning hollows you out - Robert confesses he was 'never so alive as when I was winning this throne or so dead as now that I've won it' - only a fool would play.

plato-justice.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
plato-justice.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Joffrey on the Iron Throne, immune from punishment for beheading Ned, is read as Glaucon's ring of Gyges made flesh: the chapter asks what reason he has to be moral when he can get away with everything, noting he lacks even Gyges's advantage of secrecy and is hated like the Mad King. Hobbes's social contract is considered and rejected as a motive for Joffrey - King's Landing is no Hobbesian community like the Night's Watch, and Joffrey does better free-riding on everyone else's morality. The Platonic answer carries the chapter: like Ned Stark, who refused the throne, lived honorably in Winterfell, and regretted trading his honor at Baelor, the just person with an ordered soul has the only genuine happiness, which Joffrey's desire-satisfying cruelty forfeits.

plato-justice.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
plato-justice.title: Voldemort and the Sophists
plato-justice.relation: Opens the comparison of Harry's willingness to die in Deathly Hallows with Socrates' death for his convictions, placing both inside ethics, the inquiry into how we ought to live and what kind of people we ought to be. It presents the challenge of why be moral at all and introduces Plato's Republic answer, endorsed by Socrates, that being moral is necessary and sufficient for true happiness, noting that Socrates, like Harry against Voldemort, had enemies of his own.

plato-justice.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
plato-justice.title: The Common Good versus the Greater Good
plato-justice.relation: Casts the Harry-Voldemort conflict as Socrates versus the Sophists: Thrasymachus's Republic claim that the unjust always come out ahead describes Voldemort's exploitation of his followers' trust exactly. The flayed child under the chair at King's Cross enacts Plato's afterlife justice, and the Republic's tripartite soul and cardinal virtues explain why Harry's reason-ruled courage, wisdom, and justice make the moral life the rational choice, as rational as choosing bodily health over chronic illness.

plato-justice.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
plato-justice.title: NOTES
plato-justice.relation: Adams uses Plato's Ring of Gyges to ask whether superpowered people have reason to be moral, answering through the tripartite soul: Claire declining credit for the fire rescue shows well-governed thumos, her calculated revenge on Brody shows logistics ruling spirit, while Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is textbook epithumetikon and intemperance that makes his life spin 'super' out of control. Cases like Micah's ATM thefts and Hiro's Vegas cheating (punished by a desert beating) illustrate that vice harms the agent's own soul, since justice is the soul's health. Claire's hospital apology to Brody is read through the Pagan Golden Rule and Sophocles' Ajax: enemies can become friends, so virtue, not mere conformity, is 'only natural' for heroes and ordinary people alike.

plato-justice.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Argues House of Cards is a modern version of the Sophistical challenge in Books 1-2 of Plato's Republic: Thrasymachus' claim that justice is the advantage of the stronger and the unjust life is preferable. It maps Frank's proprietary 'my people' attitude and his shepherd-and-flock use of Russo, Stamper, Sharp, Meechum and his Gaffney constituents onto Thrasymachus' reversal of Socrates' shepherd analogy, and reads the Secretary of State snub, Blythe's naivety and Dunbar's descent into dirty tricks as proofs that the just are dupes. Frank's Sentinel ring and 'craft' make him Glaucon's perfectly unjust man of the Ring of Gyges story — unjust while seeming just — while the framed Lucas Goodwin plays the perfectly just man punished for a reputation for injustice. The chapter ends by arguing Frank falls short of the ideal tyrant (his conscience, his church visits asking 'what Justice is') and is coming to live the Book 9 tyrant's friendless 'worst sort of life' as Claire and the others abandon him.

plato-justice.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Ketchen and Yeo read the show's cynicism as Thrasymachus's challenge in Books 1-2 of the Republic — 'justice is the advantage of the stronger' — under which the just (Blythe, Lucas Goodwin) are dupes while the crafty win. Frank's proprietary 'my people' politics replays the shepherd-sheep exchange: Russo, Stamper, Sharp and the Gaffney constituents are a flock groomed, fleeced, and slaughtered (the naval base closure), just as Thrasymachus says shepherds fatten sheep for their masters. Frank's Sentinel ring makes him Glaucon's Ring of Gyges craftsman — perfectly unjust with a reputation for justice from the library dedication — while Lucas Goodwin is the just man made to seem unjust and destroyed. Yet against Petrov, Frank shows a conscience and tortured questions about justice in church, so the chapter ends with Republic Book 9: the tyrant, isolated and abandoned by Season 3's close, lives 'the worst sort of life.'

plato-justice.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
plato-justice.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Anne Torkelson reads Panem through the Republic and the Laws: because mousike imitates states of soul and slowly molds character, Socrates polices music and poetry in the just city and fears innovation in musical modes, and the Capitol's own outlawing of songs quietly confirms music's power. She shows 'The Meadow Song' replacing Katniss's grief with hope and inspiring the flowers for Rue, the forbidden 'Hanging Tree' planting the Socratic question of whether an unjust life is a fate worse than death (paralleling Socrates's own unjust execution, the hemlock, and the nightlock pact Katniss, Gale, and Peeta make), and Rue's four notes mutating from an orchard work-signal into a salute of defiance when the District 11 man whistles them on the Victory Tour, at the cost of his life. Music, which Katniss dismisses as 'somewhere between hair ribbons and rainbows,' turns out to be the force that shapes her character and carries the revolution.

plato-justice.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
plato-justice.title: Paradise Found
plato-justice.relation: Paul Brown maps The Minish Cap's Hyrule onto utopian theory: Plato's Republic classes reappear as royal family (guardians), castle guards (auxiliaries), and market traders (producers), but Hyrule improves on Plato with no slavery, fluid social boundaries (Princess Zelda wandering the festival unrecognized), and Mayor Hagen's local democracy. Aristotle's polis supplies the town's design — small enough for community, walled for defense, river-powered — while Kant's disinterested appreciation of the beautiful fits Miyamoto's 'miniature garden' of pastoral idyll. The spiritual dimension completes the utopia: the benevolent Picori/Minish are a God walking unseen among people, a fuzzy religion without prophet or persecution, so no leap of faith is even necessary.

plato-justice.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Writing as a mechanic, Gordon argues Max embodies Plato's Republic: like the ship-of-state navigator, only someone who knows justice may rule, and the Myth of the Charioteer — reason holding the reins over spirit and appetite — explains why the Nightrider's unchecked spirit crashes while the cool-headed, deliberative Max endures. On punishment, Plato's rejection of retaliation (the unjust should be made just, not harmed) interrogates Max's execution of Johnny the Boy, while Polemarchus's 'render to each his due' frames the just-deserts debate. Mill's harm principle then justifies Max's force against the gangs once the state and its courts have vanished, leaving Max an administrator of street justice.

plato-justice.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
plato-justice.title: “I’m Enjoying the Story So Far, but I Have a Feeling It’s Not Going to End Well”
plato-justice.relation: South uses 'New Amsterdam' to examine how social convention, not personal authority, constrains agency: Bert Cooper's 'New York City is a marvelous machine' and 'There are other rules... His mother is Dorothy Dyckman Campbell' reveal that Pete's value lies in a name he doesn't understand, just as Don's authority dissolves before forces neither he nor Pete consented to. Reading through Plato's Republic city-soul analogy and Adeimantus's warning that changes in music insinuate themselves 'little by little' into character and laws, the chapter shows Pete missing the worth of his old-family name, the Bethlehem Steel man missing that steel cannot be advertised like flour, and Don, despite seizing a fresh identity, quietly conforming to the suburban corporate script he claims never to have envisioned. The Kennedy-assassination pitch to Peggy ('The way that they saw themselves is gone') and Conrad Hilton's 'It's business' close on Plato's caution: the city's gears keep turning, and 'people don't change' may be the show's last word.

plato-justice.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
plato-justice.title: Fighting the Real Enemy
plato-justice.relation: Johnson asks why Sinead O'Connor tearing the Pope's photo ended her career while SNL's own religion sketches drew little fire: 'DJesus Uncrossed' targets Tarantino's gratuitous violence rather than Jesus, the Tebow sketch ridicules prayers for football wins that Nietzsche said cheapen God into a servant of chance, and 'God's a Boob Man' satirizes the God's Not Dead films' strawmanning of atheists. Louis C.K.'s God monologue, he argues, raises the burden of proof and the problem of natural evil, best answered by Carlin's joke of a God subject to physical laws. The Church Lady embodies Warmke and Tosi's moral grandstanding, whereas O'Connor's protest does not, and the chapter ends on Plato's Republic: better to be a virtuous person scorned as a villain, like O'Connor, than a celebrated villain, though her tragic life strains Plato's promise that virtue pays.

plato-justice.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
plato-justice.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Presents three ancient alternatives to SAMCRO's warrior ethic. Diogenes the Cynic, 'the earliest of all the fathers of anarchy,' matches J.T.'s Harley-commune ideal — reject greed, convention, and wage slavery like Tig punching the clock at Teller-Morrow — but the chapter argues pure anarchy regenerates hierarchy: with no authority, revenge becomes the only justice and 'a big guy like Clay' mugs 'a small guy like Chuckie.' Plato's Republic supplies the reformist pole — impartial justice for all citizens rather than loyalty circles, rulers picked from proven warriors for wisdom (Tara belongs healing, not scheming), family curbed where it breeds Gemma-style favoritism — yet proves too authoritarian, so Aristotle's function argument (reason as the human ergon), virtue, and the three kinds of friendship (SAMCRO's pleasure-friendships, Clay–Unser's usefulness) sketch a livable middle way with duties even to strangers.

plato-justice.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.

plato-justice.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Littmann shows Luke, Leia, and Han repeatedly put friends and family above the galaxy's freedom - Luke abandoning Dagobah for Bespin, the Jabba rescue, refusing to kill Vader - in the tradition of Homer's heroes, then submits them to Athenian scrutiny. Socrates's refusal to escape his Athens prison and his implicit just agreement with the city set civic duty over friendship; Plato would abolish the guardians' family and censor the Zeus-Kronos patricide myth yet approves of Luke sparing Vader; Aristotle prizes philia but holds citizens belong to the state. He concludes the philosophers mostly win: heroic loyalty is often moral failure, and good moral reasoning asks how many people an action affects, not just whom you love.

plato-justice.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Barkman and Alkema map Plato's Republic onto the fall of the Old Republic: the bickering Senate and Anakin's 'someone wise' exchange with Padme enact democracy's degeneration into tyranny, with Palpatine as Plato's werewolf-like protector-tyrant and Dooku's Sith name 'Tyranus' marking Thrasymachus's justice-as-strength as Sith doctrine. The Jedi approximate Plato's philosopher-guardians - courageous, temperate, reluctant to rule, surrendering their children to the Temple much like the Republic's breeding deceptions and noble lies. Justice as each part doing its own work applies to the tripartite soul as much as the state, and the chapter closes that democracy survives Endor but only if truth stays a beacon of the light side.

plato-justice.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
plato-justice.title: Notes
plato-justice.relation: Compares the noir detective's relation to Vinci with Socrates' gadfly role in Athens from the Apology, arguing both operate at the city's center and its margins as instruments of collective self-examination. Via Deleuze's 'Philosophy of Crime Novels' it contrasts the classic detective as an agent of truth (Poe, Christie) with the hard-boiled detective as an agent of action who stirs the system — Ani's undercover infiltration of the businessmen's party — forcing what Deleuze calls the 'power of falsehood' to reveal and conceal. Plato's Republic city–soul analogy then frames Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh as disordered souls mirroring Vinci's corrupt class structure, whose cases restore equilibrium without achieving Platonic justice.

plato-justice.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
plato-justice.title: Plato and Aristotle on the Role of Soul in Taking the Rock to the Hole
plato-justice.relation: Daniel Gallagher reads Patrick Sparks's 2005 Elite Eight free-throw clank and miracle buzzer-beater through Plato's tripartite soul: the rational part failed at the line but the spirited part carried the off-balance game-tying three, while the Republic's three classes map onto basketball's workers (Steve Nash's passes), warriors (Dennis Rodman's rebounding), and rulers (John Stockton's leadership). Aristotle's four character types structure learning a jump shot - vicious, weak, self-controlled, and finally virtuous, as reason and inclination harmonize through repetition ('we are what we repeatedly do') - and the golden mean governs shot selection between the ball hog and the compulsive passer, with Michael Jordan as the player whose habituated instincts find the mean. Against Kantian armchair ethics, the jump shot and Kareem's sky hook were discovered by trial and error: virtuous performers set the standard, and we become good shooters by watching and imitating them.

plato-justice.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
plato-justice.title: Ethics, Heart, and Violence in Miller’s Crossing
plato-justice.relation: Herling reads Miller's Crossing through Hume's moral psychology of passion versus reason, arguing the film's dominant 'ethics' (voiced by Johnny Caspar) is Hobbes's social contract plus Thrasymachus's advantage-of-the-stronger and Plato's 'do good to friends, harm to enemies'—a relativism of power that Tom Reagan navigates by cool calculation. 'Heart,' the capacity for sympathetic attachment Hume makes the real basis of morality, keeps breaking through: Tom spares the pleading Bernie ('Look in your heart') at Miller's Crossing, and his loyalty to Leo secretly drives his 'plays.' But Bernie's betrayal, the surreal sympathy-crushing violence (the beatings, Leo's tommy-gun ballet, Caspar shooting the faceless Dane), and Leo and Verna's reunion steel Tom into lonely noir stoicism—'What heart?'—when he finally executes Bernie without mercy.

plato-justice.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
plato-justice.title: Spartacus and the Second Part of the Soul Gordon Braden
plato-justice.relation: Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's rivalries onto to thymoeides, the soul's 'second' spirited part governed by philotimia (love of honor): Crassus's obsessive hamilla with Gracchus, and his skewed contest with Spartacus over Varinia and Antoninus. Reading Draba's trident-throw and Crassus's closing 'now I fear him' as the spirited part's competitiveness overrunning reason, Braden shows the gladiatorial paired combat mirroring republican politics on its way to the Principate.

plato-justice.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
plato-justice.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
plato-justice.relation: Kowalski likens Goodfellas' Henry Hill to Plato's Gyges: both act immorally with near-total impunity, posing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic of why one should be just when one can escape all consequences. He applies Plato's tripartite soul (appetitive, spirited, rational) to Henry (runaway appetite/cocaine), Tommy (overstretched spirit, killing Billy Batts and Spider out of wounded pride) and cool, untroubled Paulie, treating them as the disharmonious 'unbalanced self.' Against the objection that these gangsters seem happy, he deploys Plato's health/happiness analogy and the feeling-happy vs being-happy distinction to argue they suffer 'cancer of the soul' and cannot be truly happy.

plato-justice.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
plato-justice.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
plato-justice.relation: Skoble argues that A Simple Plan dramatizes Plato's Republic almost exactly: justice as psychological harmony among the parts of the soul, and injustice as self-destructive disharmony. When Hank, Jacob, and Lou keep found money, they enact Thrasymachus's and the Ring of Gyges challenge (would you be unjust if you'd never be caught?). Hank miscalculates his own self-interest, mistaking wealth for happiness; the deception, distrust, and murders that follow (including Hank killing Jacob) show that even the criminal who evades capture is ruined by his corrupted character, exactly as Plato predicts.

plato-justice.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
plato-justice.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
plato-justice.relation: Schuler and Murray read Chinatown through Marx and Plato as a critique of capitalism's compulsions. Drawing on Marx and Engels on capital's Promethean transformation of nature and Hegel on art embodying abstractions, they argue neo-noir's centrifugal Los Angeles makes water, not diamonds, the object of desire, with wealth taking the abstract form of value. Plato's Republic warns that the boundless love of money (linked to Gyges, invisibility, and tyranny) destroys justice as reasonable self-limitation; Noah Cross's incest mirrors the 'rape of the Owens Valley', and Jake's defeat ('Forget it, Jake, it's Chinatown') marks the exhaustion of the postwar golden age.

plato-justice.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
plato-justice.title: Plato, Habermas, and the Demonic Cobb
plato-justice.relation: Murphy treats Following as a provocation keyed to the copy of Plato's Republic glimpsed in The Blonde's apartment: Cobb, who slips unseen into houses and lives and reads people's 'boxes,' is the shepherd with the Ring of Gyges, able to act unjustly without ever facing detection. Against Glaucon's challenge the chapter weighs Socrates's answer that injustice enslaves and disorders the soul—but notes that Nolan shows Cobb victorious, a 'demonic' figure with all of Socrates's abilities and none of his love of justice, who drags Bill and The Blonde into a cave of illusion rather than out of one. Habermas supplies the modern retort: our rationality and sanity depend on the communicative action, truth, and fairness of a shared lifeworld, commitments a sociopathic loner like Cobb cannot renounce without taking refuge in mental illness, though the film never shows Cobb paying that price. Man of Steel's Clark Kent clutching the Republic while letting himself be bullied, and Jonathan Kent's fatal secrecy, become the counterimage of someone who consistently wills justice at personal cost, the closest Nolan comes to showing why justice is worth choosing.

plato-justice.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
plato-justice.title: 6. How the Hell Are We Supposed to Kill an Idea
plato-justice.relation: Simsek reads the 'Hell House' tulpa—a monster made real by mass belief on the HellHoundsLair website—as a philosophical challenge about the power of ideas and how one 'kills' an idea, which the brothers can only attempt by seeding a counter-belief. She invokes Socrates' call in the Republic to censor the arts that shape moral character, and the Streisand Effect, to argue that internet-amplified ideas (memes, conspiracy theories, gender and racial norms) take on autonomous, hard-to-kill life much as fandom overrides creators' intent.

plato-justice.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
plato-justice.title: 17. Is Morality for Suckers
plato-justice.relation: The chapter reads Jimmy through Plato's Republic, likening his resolve to stop letting conscience stop him to Glaucon's Ring of Gyges thesis that people act immorally whenever they can escape detection, as when Jimmy dodges 'bullets' in his Matrix-like winning speech. Using Plato's tripartite soul, it diagnoses Jimmy as ruled by his appetitive and spirited parts rather than reason, hence lacking self-control and unable to find morality pleasant in itself. It then tests and finds wanting Plato's arguments (contemplative pleasure, connectedness, the immortality of the rational part) that a healthy, reason-ruled soul is both moral and happiest, granting Jimmy's intense scamming pleasures their pull.

plato-justice.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
plato-justice.title: 2. Socrates’s City and Seldon’s Galaxy
plato-justice.relation: Goldberg maps Plato's Republic onto Asimov's Foundation Trilogy: Socrates's three-class city (Guardians, Auxiliaries, Producers ruling by knowledge of the Forms) parallels Seldon's galaxy (Second Foundationers, First Foundationers, and everyone else, ruling by the abstract mathematics of psychohistory), with the tyrannical Thrasymachus paralleling the Mule. He shows the Prime Radiant functions as Plato's Allegory of the Cave, and that both Guardians and Second Foundationers govern through 'noble lies' (the metals myth; the Encyclopedia sham and the Second Foundation's fake destruction), then questions whether those lies are truly noble given doubts about objective truth.

plato-justice.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
plato-justice.title: 17. Psychohistory’s Noble Lie
plato-justice.relation: Silcox explains why readers forgive Seldon's confessed lie that the Encyclopedia Galactica 'is a fraud, and always has been' by comparing it to Socrates's noble lie in Plato's Republic, which Popper and I.F. Stone condemn as antidemocratic. He contrasts the two—Socrates's lie preserves an existing kallipolis while Seldon's brings about a distant political goal that requires trusting psychohistory—and weighs them against modern transparency doctrines: Bentham's consequentialist case for publicity and Rawls's publicity condition grounding autonomy, plus Nguyen's worry that transparency distorts expert 'cognitive islands.' He concludes that a genuinely predictive science of history might rationally lead us to treat political transparency as negotiable, which is why Hari Seldon remains a noble hero despite 'engineering the narrative.'

plato-justice.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
plato-justice.title: But Isn’t It Only Natural
plato-justice.relation: Adams uses the superpowered characters of Heroes to teach Plato's Republic. The Ring of Gyges question, whether one with the power to escape consequences has reason to be just, is posed by Sylar, Daphne, and Hiro cheating in Vegas. Adams maps Plato's tripartite soul, thumos, logistikon, and epithumetikon, onto Claire's courage and wisdom and Sylar's ruinous intemperance, arguing justice is psychic health so vices grow worse the more power one has. He adds the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies) to read Claire's apology to Brody, concluding virtue is natural to a well-ordered human soul and is its own reward.

plato-justice.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
plato-justice.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
plato-justice.relation: Eric Katz reads the One Ring as a variation on Plato's Ring of Gyges from the Republic: both grant impunity, and both pose the question of whether anyone would stay moral if able to act without consequence. Where Plato only argues that unchecked power corrupts the soul, Tolkien shows it through Gollum's ruin, Boromir's fall, and Frodo's final failure at the Cracks of Doom, while Galadriel, Bombadil, and Sam refuse the Ring by knowing who they are. Katz concludes Tolkien answers Plato's 'why be moral?' with 'to be yourself.'

plato-justice.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
plato-justice.title: But Isn’t It Only Natural
plato-justice.relation: Don Adams uses Heroes' superpowered characters (who could commit perfect crimes like Gyges with his invisibility ring) to argue Plato's case that virtue is its own reward. He maps Plato's tripartite soul onto the characters: Claire's thumos (spirit/honor) tempered by logistikos (reason) yields courage and wisdom, while Sylar's ruling appetite (his hunger for powers) is intemperance and injustice that makes his life spin out of control. Reading justice as psychic health, and glossing the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies, but enemies may become friends), Adams argues it is 'only natural' for even the powerful to be virtuous rather than exploit others.

plato-justice.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
plato-justice.title: 16. House of Cards as Philosophy Democracy on Trial
plato-justice.relation: The chapter uses the Underwoods' extra-electoral rise to autocracy in House of Cards to test Plato's and Hobbes's antidemocratic arguments. Frank and Claire exploit the exact weaknesses Plato's Republic diagnoses—Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' the decay of oligarchy into freedom-loving democracy into tyranny, and Peter Russo as the disordered-soul 'democratic man' and 'drone.' It then invokes Hobbes's Leviathan, arguing the show's power-struggle resembles a state of nature and that Hobbes would welcome Claire's absolute rule as more predictable and less corrupt than democracy, before weighing modern defenses of democracy (Levitsky and Ziblatt, Locke, Mill, Rawls, Sen) against these critiques.

plato-justice.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
plato-justice.title: 53. Tarantino as Philosopher Vengeance – Unfettered, Uncensored, but Not Unjustified
plato-justice.relation: Johnson treats Tarantino's post-2000 filmography as an argument that vengeance is morally permissible when proportionate and directed at the genuinely guilty: Beatrix in Kill Bill, Shosanna in Inglourious Basterds, and Django all get celebrated revenge, while The Hateful Eight is used to distinguish vengeance from retribution and legal versus 'frontier' justice via Nozick's and Bacon's definitions. He rebuts common and historical objections—reading Plato's Gorgias as endorsing due punishment, arguing Spinoza's monism and Hobbes's and Locke's social-contract views do not forbid proportional revenge, and citing Nietzsche and Beauvoir's Eye for an Eye (her refusal to pardon the collaborator Brasillach) to conclude cost-free, proportional revenge can be justified though mercy remains praiseworthy.

applied-ethics.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
applied-ethics.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Theodore Schick takes Tolkien's remark that the Ring represents 'potency' externalized beyond its maker's control and applies it to emerging nanotechnology, genetics, and robotics. He sets Bill Joy's call for relinquishment against Eric Drexler's promise of universal assemblers, cell-repair machines, and soldier nanosuits, weighing the 'grey goo' risk against the Rings' own power to heal and preserve (Lothlórien, Bilbo 'well-preserved'). Against the Council of Elrond's solution of destroying the Ring, he argues our situation is disanalogous - Ring-making knowledge is now spread worldwide and there is no single device to destroy - so grass-roots social response, not bans, must tame the new technologies.

applied-ethics.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
applied-ethics.title: 22b
applied-ethics.relation: A paired legal-philosophy debate on whether steroids should be banned. Michael McGrath argues yes from Kant: PED use cannot be universalized and 'the ends do not justify the means,' so the Ken Caminiti, Mark McGwire, and José Canseco confessions stain America's pastime, whose stars are role models and whose users risk devastating health effects — down to wrestler Davey Boy Smith's fatal steroid-related heart attack. Simon Eassom replies no by reframing drugs as Performance Enhancing Technologies: rules merely define the game, enhancers (unlike bat-cannons or netted catcher's gloves) do not de-skill baseball, and banning them because we dislike them is a matter of taste — of aesthetics, not ethics.

applied-ethics.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
applied-ethics.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.

applied-ethics.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
applied-ethics.title: Send in the Clones!
applied-ethics.relation: Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.

applied-ethics.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
applied-ethics.title: It’s Not Our Lot in Life!
applied-ethics.relation: Arp argues that C-3PO and R2-D2 satisfy the standard functional criteria of personhood - rationality, mental states, language, social relationships, and moral agency - opening with a blind listener who took Threepio's frightened chatter for a man, a Turing-test-style judgment from behavior alone. He catalogues evidence: Threepio's odds-calculating and Wookiee-winning deduction, Artoo's deceptive manipulation of Luke, the droid torture victim's screams at Jabba's palace, and the Chewbacca-Threepio quasi-familial bond on Cloud City. Since droids meet the conditions, their restraining bolts, cantina bans, and forced servitude are slavery, and the Galactic Senate should grant them limited rights - perhaps cheering a droid rebellion against the organic empire - a question the chapter urges on us as robotics approaches Moravec's predictions.

applied-ethics.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
applied-ethics.title: Poker and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Barnhill and Solomon use Robert Varkonyi's staged five-minute 'agony' over pocket aces — pure theater that lured Ralph Perry into an all-in at the 2002 WSOP (and later busted Phil Hellmuth's A-K with Q-10 suited) — to ask when poker deception is morally acceptable and when it crosses the line: the towed-car lie, the fake-Marine claim, racist goading, and collusion are wrong. Their answer is an implicit-permission theory: by sitting down, players waive the right not to be deceived, but only where deception tests poker skills, so bluffs, disguised strength, and silently reading exposed cards are fine. The underlying order of the implicit rules — the game must test only poker skills — also explains everyday white lies and what you may tell a mugger.

applied-ethics.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
applied-ethics.title: Deserving to Be a Vampire
applied-ethics.relation: Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through Forever Knight's Nick draining his lover, Blade feeding on stored blood, and The Lost Boys' promise that Michael will 'never grow old'. He argues vampires are not evil by nature: if they cannot control their hunger they are pitied rather than blamed (though we remain Aristotle-responsible for choosing to become addicted), and consensual, non-lethal feeding is no worse than mortals eating animals, since the bite only becomes murder by choice. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, he uses Furley and Nussbaum's deprivation view - death vindictively empties our long-term projects like marriage or a career - so vampiric immortality genuinely preserves value, while the standard boredom objection fails because there are repeatable pleasures in a changing world. The thought experiment ends as moral psychology for mortals: since neither of us will become a vampire, live a life that would be worthy of eternity.

applied-ethics.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
applied-ethics.title: James Bond and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Tedesco dissects what the double-0 'license to kill' could actually mean, ruling out self-defense and mere on-the-job killing and concluding that Bond is a state-sanctioned assassin who earned his status through two assassinations in Casino Royale. He tests that status against Kant's categorical imperative - persons as ends in themselves, though Kant also defended capital punishment as respecting the murderer's choice - and against consequentialism, which vindicates Bond's elimination of Kananga but stumbles on the surgeon's organ-harvesting dilemma. Because ordinary morality mixes duty-based and consequence-based intuitions, the chapter leaves Bond's moral status genuinely open and links it to live policy debates on assassination and torture after 9/11, including Britain's Intelligence Services Act that leaves room for a real-life double-0 agent.

applied-ethics.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
applied-ethics.title: 13 - Don’t Talk to Me
applied-ethics.relation: Pitt argues the iPod is 'pernicious' not because technology is intrinsically bad — a device is judged by the uses it is put to and their consequences — but because its consequences are antisocial: silent subways, 'brainsnatched' beach-walkers, and the silenced graduate corridor where loud philosophical argument used to live. Comparing the gadget to Huxley's soma (each user programs his own blissful isolation, going so far as to avoid domestic conflict by plugging back in), he contends social skills — argument, eye contact, advocacy for ideas — are what drive both technological innovation (even Steve Jobs had a co-inventor) and functioning democracy. Hence the earbud habituation summarized as 'Don't talk to me, I'm listening to MY music!' is, he claims, one of the final nails in the coffin of the social skills a civil, democratic society needs.

applied-ethics.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
applied-ethics.title: “Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”
applied-ethics.relation: Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.

applied-ethics.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
applied-ethics.title: Transformers and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.

applied-ethics.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
applied-ethics.title: Transformers and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Hall predicts what real alien Transformers would be like: any starfaring civilization is at least Kardashev Type 1 and would send nanotechnological, shape-shifting robots rather than biological explorers, since minds upload into machine bodies and colonies go all-robot. He proposes a logarithmic 'Hall scale' of ethics, arguing that interstellar cooperation requires Level 10 morality whose expanding inclusiveness would give visitors enough concern for indigenous species to leave Earth as a nature preserve, since robots need only the matter and energy of Mercury and the outer planets, not our biosphere.

applied-ethics.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
applied-ethics.title: Transformers and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Arp defines personhood through five capacities (rationality, robust mental states, genuine language rather than information transmission, social relationships, and free autonomous action) and argues Transformers meet them all: Bumblebee's homing-signal syllogism, Frenzy's Air Force One hack, Megatron's curses when foiled, and Optimus's fatherly bond with Sam. A thought experiment of gradually replacing a man's brain, then body, with silicon shows that cognitive capacities, not carbon, make a person, so deceiving Decepticons are morally responsible persons who deserve blame and 'robot jail' rather than the scrapping reserved for mindless machines.

applied-ethics.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
applied-ethics.title: Transformers and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Koepsell accepts that Autobots are virtuous and Decepticons vicious, then asks whether ethical war-bots are even possible, using the military's autonomous-weapons program, Asimov's Three Laws, and a kitten-sensing washing machine to argue that designed-in 'ethics' is only the designer's morality, like A Clockwork Orange's conditioned Alex, because it involves no real choice. Searle's Chinese Room and Turing's test then cast doubt on whether any mind, even our own, makes genuinely free choices, so he concludes that the appearance of virtue - behavior that reliably works - is all we ever have for humans or Autobots alike, and we should build machines as well as Optimus Prime and Bumblebee.

applied-ethics.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
applied-ethics.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Yuen reads the silver guillotine of intercision against infant circumcision: both cut unconsenting children as acts of faith, Mrs. Coulter's belief that severing dæmons prevents original sin mirroring the Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 17. Deploying W.K. Clifford's shipowner ('It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence') and Hume's claim that belief is an involuntary feeling no will can command, he argues that the real moral fault lies in acting on uninvestigated beliefs in ways that harm others, while Mrs. Coulter's non-consensual experiments on kidnapped children are wrong independently of what she believes. He concludes that if cutting Pantalaimon from Lyra is wrong, circumcision is wrong for the same reasons though less severely, at worst as irresponsible as exposing a child to chicken pox.

applied-ethics.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
applied-ethics.title: Questioning the Question
applied-ethics.relation: Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.

applied-ethics.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
applied-ethics.title: 2 - It’s Like Talking to a Wall
applied-ethics.relation: Meikle analyzes Facebook as media convergence: status updates and wall posts blur one-to-one communication with the broadcast 'message addressed to nobody in particular', reaching an undifferentiated friend list that mixes intimates, colleagues, and people one dislikes. Cases like the MI6 chief's wife's holiday photos, Amanda Knox's 'Foxy Knoxy' nickname, the Dartmouth professor's Wikipedia lecture note, and the Dunblane survivors story show how private turns instantly public, from Bozeman's password demand to tabloid mining of profiles. He concludes that Facebook demands an ethics of online communication: who gets access to what we generate, and what may they do with it.

applied-ethics.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
applied-ethics.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
applied-ethics.relation: Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: Sure I Deceived You, but What about Me
applied-ethics.relation: Classifies Bob Arctor's undercover drug enforcement, Quail's covert action in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' and Quaid's HUMINT work as species of spying — one party manipulating or dominating another, as James McCargar's secret-war tradecraft describes. It asks how manipulation is actually done, answering that the manipulator finds weaknesses and links desired behaviors to them, and turns the moral question back on the deceivers themselves.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: Finding a Lever for Manipulation
applied-ethics.relation: Explains the spy tradecraft acronym MISE (Money, Ideology, Sex, Ego) and walks through 'Fred's' recruitment method in A Scanner Darkly — building trust through drug purchases under false pretenses until the mark must betray another confidant for Fred's benefit. The same template covers Lori, Harry, and Hauser in Total Recall, for whom Quaid 'becomes nothing more than a means': monitoring his return to Mars, or locating the rebel leadership.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: Like People, Like Organizations
applied-ethics.relation: Extends the moral-damage analysis one level up: organizations develop their own moral personas, and the LAPD's compartmentalization — where 'Fred' may be spying on fellow detectives and is required to lie to his supervisor 'Hank' — normalizes law-breaking in the name of law enforcement. It argues that society's oversight, the intelligence committees created after the Pike and Church hearings, is the 'bullet-proof vest' allowing risky utilitarian spying to continue without corroding everyone involved.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: Chapter 12 - Grow, My Dears, the Eugenicist Said
