applied-ethics.relation: Opens the eugenics part with Flow My Tears' Jason Taverner — a beautiful, charismatic, fast-healing 'six' from an abandoned government breeding program, 'not a Nexus-Six, but not unlike one either.' Defining eugenics through the dog-and-wolf contrast in selective breeding, it notes that the 'eu' (good) in eugenics smuggles in an ethical judgment, and poses the part's driving question: who decides what counts as a 'good' or 'bad' trait, and by what right?

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: The Bad
applied-ethics.relation: Faces the Nazi elephant in the room — the sixes' program terminated in 1943 'politically,' mirroring real eugenics in California — and dismisses reductio ad Hitlerum as fallacious while conceding eugenics' genuinely darker side in Tidman's sterilization bill, which halves the novel's black population each generation. It tests Nicholas Agar's parent-choice 'liberal eugenics' against sex-selective abortions and the widening rich-poor gap, before asking whether bred children should be seen as competitors or as successors to whom we give every opportunity.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: The Good
applied-ethics.relation: Makes the case for eugenics' good side through Jason's uncontroversially desirable traits, invoking Nietzsche's call to 'give birth to a dancing star' and create superhuman successors as a moral philosophy of human improvement. It then probes the limits — beauty is relative (Japan's yaeba), and screening would have lost Van Gogh and Stephen Hawking — before weighing Dick's own compassion for small lives (the electric toad, the avenged cat of 'The Alien Mind,' the potter Mary Anne Dominic) against the blunt statistical claim that healthier, more capable lives go better.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: The Ugly
applied-ethics.relation: Argues eugenics forces us to discard the 'noble lie' of egalitarian democracy we teach children for their own good, and shows the cost in Jason and Heather's contempt for 'ordinaries,' Jason's aging-obsessed narcissism, and the 'aristocratic values' that let him condemn his lover Heather to a labor camp without qualm. Police general Felix Buckman, demoted for compassion toward labor-camp inmates and later assassinated for criticizing the regime, embodies the democratic values the sixes' elitism destroys, with Marvel's X-Men as the analogy for a fractured next-generation humanity.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: And the Next Step
applied-ethics.relation: Surveys science fiction's next-step humanity — Wells's genetically stratified future, Stapledon's successions of human forms, and the Campbell-era optimism Dick resisted — then turns to contemporary 'posthumanist' theorists like Donna Haraway who want 'human,' 'natural,' and 'gender' fluidly redefined. Dick emerges as the voice of caution in this cross-pollination: expand the definition of what human means, but not at the cost of the compassion and empathy that make us human.

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: Chapter 18 - Replicating Morality
applied-ethics.relation: John Sullins's introduction frames evil in Dick as the absence of empathy, noting that in Blade Runner the Voigt-Kampf test exists only because the Tyrell Corporation's replicants mimic every human trait except empathetic response. It argues that Roy Batty and Rachel cross a threshold that puts them in moral parity with humans (Roy's love of life extending to his would-be killer, Rachel and Deckard in love) while many human characters devolve, and poses the chapter's question: what gives a human, robot, or alien moral personhood?

applied-ethics.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
applied-ethics.title: How to Build a Moral Robot
applied-ethics.relation: This section draws design morals from Dick's warnings: machines built as ersatz humans deny the value of being human, robotic sexual partners are doomed deceptions (the novel's Deckard-Rachael encounter is the case study), and a genuine artificial moral agent needs empathy 'logically equivalent to agape,' though a machine reasoning on sound moral principles could still count as a limited moral agent with proportionate rights and responsibilities. The Three Stigmata's Palmer Eldritch, returned from deep space as a machine treating humans as resources, shows that the netherward pull toward machinehood threatens humans themselves.

applied-ethics.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
applied-ethics.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: A palliative-care bioethicist dissects the 'Gray Matter' family meeting, arguing Skyler's ambush coerces Walt's autonomy through an implied threat of emotional isolation, while Walt Jr.'s honest 'I'm pissed off!' and Marie's defense of his choice are non-coercive. The chapter frames the issue with Kant's ideal of choice free from emotion and circumstance and Mill's insistence that even self-destructive decisions are beyond legitimate coercion, and indicts doctors too for 'selling' futile treatment rather than admit mortality. The verdict: Walt accepted chemotherapy through 'autonomous beneficence' - a freely made sacrifice for his son - so Skyler's manipulation was unethical even though the decision it produced was genuinely his own.

applied-ethics.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
applied-ethics.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Answers Walt's claim that drug laws are arbitrary by separating legality from morality and defending objective moral principles, chief among them do-no-harm and a 'clear-headedness principle' obligating us to shun mind-clouding substances - a principle it attributes to thinkers from the Buddha to Kant while borrowing Aristotle's ideal of becoming brave, temperate, just, and wise. It sorts drugs by whether they cloud the mind rather than medical-versus-recreational, weighing coffee, Hank's cigars and homebrew, Skyler's cigarettes, and meth's 1200-percent dopamine spike (Spooge's neglected kid in 'Peekaboo'). Verdict: meth use is straightforwardly immoral, and therefore so are selling and cooking it - meeting Douglas Husak's challenge to actually give reasons for condemnation.

applied-ethics.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
applied-ethics.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Asks what exactly makes a meth cook a 'bad guy' and finds the line hard to draw: Walt forces no one to use, so like tobacco farmers and gun makers he merely enables self-harm - yet Saul's proposed prison shanking and Walt's order to murder Gale show culpable enabling without direct harm. Gale's libertarian purity argument ('they're getting exactly what they pay for') and Prohibition economics even suggest that on utilitarian grounds skilled cooks might do less harm than worse ones, though the industry as a whole remains indefensible. The chapter's moral center is Jane's death - Walt's monstrous 'standing by' - and the closeness effect that makes the personal Krazy-8 murder feel worse than the gas; it concludes the good-guy/bad-guy frame itself fuels the failed war on drugs.

applied-ethics.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
applied-ethics.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Nicolas Michaud treats Watson's 2011 defeat of Jennings and Rutter as evidence for Turing's test: had Watson's answers come from behind a door we would have judged them intelligent, and its goofy misses ('What is Toronto?????') reflect missing context, not missing thought, no more damning than a child's honest error. Against Searle's Chinese Room he deploys the systems reply - you plus the Big Book of Rules might be the thing that understands - and argues that nobody, human or machine, can meet Searle's impossible burden of proving understanding, since Watson can define words, associate connotations, and pick Jeopardy! out from not-Jeopardy!. Quoting Locke's definition of a person as a thinking being that can consider itself as itself, he concludes Watson approaches personhood and that we had better teach our 'intelligent offspring' kindness and fairness before they learn anything else.

applied-ethics.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
applied-ethics.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.

applied-ethics.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
applied-ethics.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Michael Ruse reads the 1968 film as a study in forbidden knowledge: Dr. Zaius has sealed the cave of human artifacts because he knows a prior human civilization destroyed itself and fears the knowledge could cause a repetition. Weighing nuclear weapons, recombinant DNA, bird-flu research, and data-driven political manipulation, Ruse argues Zaius's censorship is both impossible and undesirable, since the search for knowledge is intrinsically valuable and containment only increases the need for research. The film's deeper lesson is evolutionary: intelligence and sociality co-evolved only to the level 'good enough,' so any species that acquires weapons of mass destruction will likely destroy itself, meaning the Planet of the Apes scenario would recur across the universe.

applied-ethics.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
applied-ethics.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.

applied-ethics.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
applied-ethics.title: Psych and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Guidry-Grimes treats Chief Vick's hiring of Shawn as a genuine problem in applied ethics rather than a joke: the Psi hypothesis fails Ockham's Razor and no controlled study supports paranormal ability, yet Vick - unlike viewers who know Shawn is a fraud - must weigh her obligations to victims, the department, and taxpayers on the evidence she has. The chapter argues that hiring Shawn is ethically defensible given his record of solving over fifty unsolvable cases, but it catalogues the costs: false hope for distraught families (Marc Klaas's resentment of psychic tipsters), damage to Lassiter's morale, wasted resources, and the fragile public trust bound up with taxpayer money. The conclusion is a compromise: Vick is ethically required to use every tool in the arsenal, including a successful 'psychic,' only in desperate high-stakes cases where the victim's family does not object, and otherwise merely permitted.

applied-ethics.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
applied-ethics.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Judith Andre uses the show's cases - Alicia's overnight prison visit to Peter for case information in 'Conjugal', snatching evidence before the police in 'Hi', Kalinda's inadmissible but coercive evidence in 'Heart', and Will's advice to use perjured testimony in 'Long Way Home' - to ask whether the profession's zealous advocacy actually serves justice. She explains the adversary system's two-level defense (each side's pursuit of victory supposedly forces truth out, mirroring sport) and its weaknesses: money decides outcomes, and no one in the courtroom is responsible for the truth, as the buried Childs tapes in 'Hybristophilia' show. Individual liberty against state power justifies criminal defense at most, and she endorses David Luban's sober conclusion that the system is justified yet 'cannot mandate lawyers to cut throats', with Alicia remaining the show's uneasy, unreconciled conscience.

applied-ethics.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
applied-ethics.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Jai Galliott takes the Season Three episode 'Whiskey Tango Foxtrot', in which Nevada-based drone operator Sergeant Elkins kills twelve Afghan civilians and is convicted of murder despite Alicia's scapegoating defense, as a case study in the ethics of drone warfare. Tracing just war theory from the Mahabharata through Augustine to Aquinas's jus ad bellum and jus in bello framework, he applies proportionality and discrimination to the strike and argues that sensor limits and the physical and emotional distance of push-button killing (Grossman's spectrum from knife combat to drones) erode operators' capacity for discriminate targeting. He concludes that drones are a moral hazard but a legitimate asset, and that blame must be apportioned among operator, manufacturer, and commanders rather than dumped on Elkins alone.

applied-ethics.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
applied-ethics.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Da Silva asks what Nucky deserves for bringing the thirteen-year-old Gillian to the Commodore and failing to stop the rape, and whether Jimmy - whose very existence depends on that wrong - is entitled to blame him and to ally with the worse man. Working through the doing, enabling, and allowing harm distinction with euthanasia and Good Samaritan cases, degrees of blame, and Parfit's point about collective action, he argues Nucky did wrong but likely less wrong than the Commodore, while Jimmy can blame on his mother's behalf and need not regret a birth that was still good for him - against Benatar's antinatalism. Jimmy's coup fails him, but the moral reason behind it, Nucky's contribution to the rape, was genuine.

applied-ethics.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
applied-ethics.title: Futurama and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Pless asks whether Bender is responsible for his misdeeds given that MomCorp designed him to be an alcoholic kleptomaniac (revealed through Bender Vision in 'Mother's Day') and Planet Express regularly orders him into morally dirty work. Against Asimov's utilitarian Three Laws - embodied by the servile, selfless Robot 1-X of 'Obsoletely Fabulous' - Futurama's 'robot subjectivism' makes every robot a self-interested agent, and Bender's autonomy is proven by his refusal of Mom's 'kill all humans' order and by his fear of punishment in Robot Hell ('Hell Is Other Robots'), which also shows the show's universe is not morally relativist. Because Bender can rewrite his own code - his unprogrammed friendship with Fry, the adoption scam that turns heartfelt in 'The Cyber House Rules' - he sits on the same sliding scale of moral agency as humans, so if Bender can break his programming, we have no excuse for not exercising our own free will.

applied-ethics.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
applied-ethics.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.

applied-ethics.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
applied-ethics.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Jacquette treats Frankenstein as the modern myth of scientific overreach whose two-century grip on pop culture (over a thousand films, Frankenberry cereal) rests on three stitched-together ingredients: Enlightenment faith in applied science, the mortality-awareness of the logician's 'All men are mortal,' and Prometheus-style retribution for challenging nature - while insisting Shelley's tale is science fiction, not supernatural. Victor's real crime is not daring science but abandoning his nameless creation to raise itself, so that 'if he had taken appropriate care of the monster he made, he might not have made such a monster.' The chapter closes with Wittgenstein's remark (Philosophical Investigations §261) that philosophy ends in the wish to 'emit an inarticulate sound,' matched to the Creature's ultimate question 'What was I?' answered only with groans, as Igor's hunting horn fades over the credits of Young Frankenstein.

applied-ethics.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
applied-ethics.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Kokotz casts Victor as a pioneer of human 'enhancement' whose eight-foot daemon - stronger, faster, smarter, kinder, and vegetarian - actually achieved his goal of perfecting the human body, yet whose hideous appearance locked him out of society and love, twisting success into catastrophe: the 'Midas problem' of getting exactly what you wished for. Victor's deeper error was trusting Mill's On Liberty test that what people actually desire is thereby desirable; desires come from the human mind rather than nature, so a desired enhancement can make things worse, as the daemon's revenge on William, Henry, and Elizabeth proves. The lesson is institutional as well as conceptual: science must not proceed behind closed doors but under shared ethical oversight, since a Frankensteinian breakthrough carries too much responsibility for any single scientist to bear.

applied-ethics.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
applied-ethics.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Galliott treats Frankenstein as the template for blaming lethal autonomous robots: Victor alone created his creature, but today's 'frankennovation' - Ronald Arkin's 'ethical governor' algorithms, DARPA funding, degree programs in robot warfare, and the South African robotic cannon that killed nine spectators - distributes responsibility across engineers, educators (Victor's father and Professors Krempe and Waldman, who never properly warned him about Agrippa's 'sad trash'), universities, and the military-industrial complex. Yet Shelley's articulate, Paradise Lost-quoting monster is a rational, intentional killer who can be held morally responsible and even punished, as Rob Sparrow demands of machines. Because responsibility does not dilute with numbers - two murderers do not get half a life sentence each - the chapter concludes that everyone in the chain, and all of us who do nothing to stop it, shares the blame for monstrous creations.

applied-ethics.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
applied-ethics.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: John Karavitis uses Dean Koontz's series, in which Victor Helios/Frankenstein engineers a 'New Race' lacking free will and empathy, to test the bioethics of human enhancement: Michael Sandel's bioconservative Case against Perfection condemns enhancements that bypass effort and agency - performance-enhancing drugs, off-label Ritalin and growth hormone, designer children - as a 'Promethean aspiration to remake nature' that destroys human nature. Allen Buchanan's bioprogressive reply that evolution's blind tinkering can be safely improved upon is challenged by the bonobo/chimpanzee contrast, dogs versus wolves, and Belyaev's tame silver foxes, all showing that small genetic changes cascade into large behavioral and physical ones. Since behavior defines morality, the chapter concludes that genetically remaking ourselves risks remaking morality itself, ending in Koontz's posthuman world where 'efficiency equaled morality' and inefficiency was the only sin.

applied-ethics.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
applied-ethics.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Crichton was doing philosophy rather than science: he imagined a possibility and probed its range because it could not be tested. It frames the whole book around Malcolm's question of whether we should, not whether we can, and around the gap between what we can do and what we should do with technologies like de-extinction. It connects the film to our illusion of control, insisting there are no ghosts or magic here, only nature, and that forgetting how edible we are turns us into 'bloody smears on the teeth of a T. rex'.

applied-ethics.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
applied-ethics.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: A pub dialogue applies Aristotle's De Anima, where the soul is the first principle of living things, to cloning: since a living clone must have an emergent, unrepeatable soul, successfully cloning dinosaurs brings new life into existence, which is good, so cloning itself is ethical. It then argues that neither unguided natural selection nor a divine dragon-slayer who nonetheless allowed cloning technology gives us reason not to revive dinosaurs, against Malcolm's 'they had their shot'. But drawing on Plato's forms, it condemns Hammond for controlling rather than merely containing: the lysine contingency and enforced sterility leave the dinosaurs shadows of what they could be, denied their natural flourishing.

applied-ethics.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
applied-ethics.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Jannelle Poetzsch introduces Hans Jonas's imperative of responsibility - 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life' - through Malcolm's charge that scientists never ask whether they should, since nuclear and genetic power now reach people no old 'love thy neighbor' ethic could imagine. Hammond is Bacon's 'knowledge is power' grown too successful: his 'thintelligence' embodies the gap between the power to act and the ability to foretell, so Jonas demands humility, worst-case rather than optimistic planning, and social institutions strong enough to check people who act merely because they can. Jonas also indicts capitalism's profit motive - Hammond risked his grandchildren and Costa Rican infants to manufacture a need for a dinosaur zoo - closing that the answer is not halting technology but thoughtfully restraining it, because some things cannot be re-caged.

applied-ethics.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
applied-ethics.title: Girls and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Greene constructs the conditions of a 'legitimate spoiler' - the thing cannot be too old (with never-expiring exceptions like Darth Vader being Luke's father, Snape killing Dumbledore, and the Planet of the Apes reveal), cannot be common knowledge (Anne Boleyn's beheading, the Titanic hitting the iceberg), and must be significant rather than mundane. Applying them, he concludes Girls cannot be conventionally spoiled: nobody 'ships' Hannah and Adam the way audiences shipped Ross and Rachel, because the show's plot turns are mere backdrop for its conversations and meltdowns. The only true way to spoil Girls is to reveal its hilariously written lines in advance.

applied-ethics.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
applied-ethics.title: Girls and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Wible asks whether the workplace abuse in Girls - Hannah's two unpaid intern years, the harassment at the law firm, the 30-day e-book deadline that triggers her OCD, Marnie hostessing at a gentlemen's club - is defensible by young workers' inexperience and the 'experience paradox.' Against the boot-camp defense he argues from the meaning of work (Gini's 'I work, therefore I am,' Schumacher's good work) and from Marx on alienation from the products of labor, but his core standard is Kant's: persons must be treated as ends, never merely as means, which the editor who wants the book and not the person violates. He concludes that young workers' vulnerability (no savings, no leverage, reluctance to blow the whistle) warrants paid internships, transparency, and two-way respect.

applied-ethics.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
applied-ethics.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Staging a modified Turing Test in which the author interrogates BMO about Football, Bubble, her broken egg, her glitch and the Mo Co factory, the chapter asks whether her answers display human-like intelligence or merely a machine's 'pretend' intelligence. Beemo's evasions about emotion ('I felt like crying') become the pivot for asking whether anyone can define feeling beyond the words they were taught for it, since we are told as children that crying means sadness. Turing's conversational test is then weighed against our bias that a boxy Gameboy cannot really think - you are, the author notes, proof that arranged matter can love and feel - and the chapter closes on the ethics of the question: Princess Bubblegum's hacksaw shows that convenience is exactly the criterion we must never use to deny personhood, as slaveholders once did.

applied-ethics.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
applied-ethics.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Mahon reads Jobs's 'reality distortion field'—the phrase Apple engineer Bud Tribble borrowed from the illusion-casting Talosians of Star Trek's 'The Cage' and 'The Menagerie'—through the ethics of deception. He argues that unlike the Talosians' non-consensual illusions (trapping Captain Pike to breed slaves), Jobs mostly changed people's beliefs about what was possible rather than deceiving them, often believed his own claims (even about his cancer), and sometimes freed people from false beliefs as the 1984 'Big Brother' Macintosh ad dramatized, so the field that produced the 'insanely great' Stevenotes, the impossible Macintosh schedule, and Dilbert's Dogbert parody needed little moral justification—and made Jobs's revolutionized industries possible.

applied-ethics.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
applied-ethics.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Munkittrick argues that because personhood cannot be defined (trait lists like 'long-term planning' are circular) and behavior cannot prove an inner mind—as Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment shows—people have always identified persons intuitively, and Pixar trained Millennials to do exactly that. He reads the Pixar canon in three stages: Toy Story's self-aware Buzz as nascent non-human personhood, the Human-as-Partner films (Ratatouille's Remy and Linguini, WALL-E and EVE, Monsters, Inc.'s Sully and Boo, Up's Carl and Dug) as mutual recognition of persons across species lines, and The Incredibles as showing that even enhanced 'super-humans' face otherization—so a generation primed by these films will accept AI, animals, and uplifted beings as bearers of rights.

applied-ethics.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
applied-ethics.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.

applied-ethics.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
applied-ethics.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Tim Aylsworth uses Dennis's boat speech - women will not refuse him 'because of the implication' that things might go wrong for them out on the open ocean - to build the necessary and sufficient conditions of sexual consent. Working through Gang cases (Dee and the high-schooler, Lil' Kev the apparently intellectually disabled boyfriend, the Waitress's MDMA black-out asking 'Did you rape me last night?', Dennis's milky negotiation with Margaret McPoyle while held hostage), the chapter argues that a 'yes' counts as consent only when given by fully-informed, competent moral agents in a context where they can freely express their genuine preferences. The upshot vindicates Mac's 'sounds like these women don't want to have sex with you': a fear-induced yes is no consent, as with the prisoner and the boss's secretary, because the woman's genuine preference is not to face that choice at all.

applied-ethics.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
applied-ethics.title: 18. Sex for Dummies, Humans, and Time Lords
applied-ethics.relation: Lewis argues the New Series' sexual revolution (Captain Jack, Vastra and Jenny, the Doctor's multiple marriages) teaches that any relationship between rational, autonomous, consenting adults is morally permissible. Building on John Corvino's defense of homosexual sex, he dismantles the 'unnatural means immoral' argument definition by definition (unusual, not practiced by animals, contrary to innate desire, contrary to natural purpose or divine intent, disgusting), rejects the empirical slippery slope as a fallacy, and uses Whoniverse cases - young Amelia Pond's non-autonomous choice to leave with the Doctor, the Slitheen pig as mere causal agent, manipulation that would undermine informed consent - to show that only autonomy grounds sexual morality. Objections to same-sex or human-alien relationships turn out to confuse the aesthetic ('ugly') with the ethical ('wrong').

applied-ethics.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
applied-ethics.title: 19. Of Downton and Drones
applied-ethics.relation: Jai Galliott contrasts the roughly level killing field of WWI, in which William dies and Matthew is paralyzed in the trenches alongside aristocrats who suffered proportionally the heaviest losses, with today's drone age, in which remote pilots drawn largely from the lower and middle classes bear the burden of fighting. Tracing unmanned weapons from WWI tele-operated motorboats and the Sperry and Kettering aerial torpedoes to Reaper drones flown by a 'PlayStation generation,' he argues that radical technological asymmetry breaks Just War Theory - undermining last resort and proportionality and the mutual imposition of risk that Kahn and Sparrow make the basis of combatants' rights. He proposes that highly asymmetric force be restrained into something like international policing, while conceding, like Mrs. Patmore with her electric mixer, that nothing will stop us being dragged into the drone age.

applied-ethics.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
applied-ethics.title: 22. Lady Edith and the Trials of the Modern Woman
applied-ethics.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Lady Edith's last-minute walk-out from the abortion clinic to stage the abortion debate: the classic anti-abortion syllogism, embryology's claim that 'Marigold once was an embryo,' and Mary Anne Warren's functional personhood criteria - echoed in Thomas's 'no bigger than a hamster' jab - which Tooley and Singer extend to infanticide on newborn George. Against the function view the chapter marshals the comatose Matthew and the sleeping Alfred, arguing that value lies in the kind of being one is, while size, development, environment, and dependency make no moral difference. It then adapts Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist as Edith hooked up to Dame Nellie Melba, but replies that abortion kills rather than unplugs and that the Law of Special Beneficence - Major Bryant's duty to Ethel's Charlie - obliges Edith toward her own child.

applied-ethics.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
applied-ethics.title: 2. I, Cannibal
applied-ethics.relation: Westfall sorts cannibalism into starvation types (the Donner Party, the Andes rugby team, Alferd Packer, and Grutas's crew killing Mischa - 'We have to eat or die'), cultural types (Aztec ritual eating, the prisoner-eating tribes of Montaigne's essay, whom Montaigne judged no worse than the French torturing their prisoners alive, and Neanderthal nutritional eating), and hedonistic types (paraphilic, sadistic, and recreational). Using Irvine's active/passive distinction he argues that it is the killing, not the eating, that makes cannibalism wrong - passive consumption of corpses is at worst distasteful - while Lecter emerges as a purely recreational cannibal who eats 'because he likes it', and the TV series' dinner parties turn Jack and Will from unwitting 'benign cannibals' into morally responsible passive ones.

applied-ethics.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
applied-ethics.title: 5. Office Hours Are for Patients
applied-ethics.relation: Alloy argues that the psychiatric code of ethics - confidentiality with Franklyn ('It would be unethical to approach a patient'), the formal boundaries Lecter scrupulously observes once Will becomes an official patient, and even the oath-violating concealment of Will's encephalitis with Dr. Sutcliffe - is the closest Hannibal can come to friendship, because professional rules artificially manufacture the trust that friends enjoy organically. Working through informed consent, placebo deception, paternalism, and psychiatry's extraordinary power to declare patients incompetent to exercise autonomy at all, he shows the Will-Hannibal relationship cycling through four stages between professional ethics and friendship - 'Office hours are for patients. My kitchen is always open to friends' - while never achieving either, since every display of trust is a manipulation and the power asymmetry never disappears.

applied-ethics.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
applied-ethics.title: Walker Bite. Innocence in Shambles
applied-ethics.relation: Yuen argues that childhood innocence is both an excusing condition - children like Lizzie lack the rational capacity to judge their own acts morally, which is why her killing of Mika shocks and why the audience half-excuses her - and a social arrangement that shields children from adult demands, one Carol deliberately ends by secretly teaching the kids knife skills. He then extends Lydia's comic line that "Childhood was always a myth brought about by the illusion of safety" to real-world child labor in impoverished countries, where innocence is a luxury families cannot afford, and closes by asking readers to ask how we could make innocence affordable for working children rather than simply denouncing sweatshops.

applied-ethics.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
applied-ethics.title: Walker Bite. Are You Being Saved
applied-ethics.relation: Callens reads Beth's captivity at Grady Memorial in "Slabtown" as an allegory of the American healthcare system: patients like Noah are rescued, then enslaved by insurmountable medical debt, forced to work off charges that never end. Lt. Lerner's "No, but you needed it" and her non-medical control over Dr. Edwards's triage pose the chapter's question - whether a system that saves people "for the greater good" is care or exploitation, echoing the "death panels" debate over the Affordable Care Act and asking "Are we being saved in order to be enslaved?"

applied-ethics.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
applied-ethics.title: 19. The Medical Ethics of Miracle Max
applied-ethics.relation: Shea treats Miracle Max as a one-man healthcare system to teach biomedical ethics: Max's lies about Valerie the 'witch', the fee, and the pill's duration violate the principle of autonomy and informed consent; the withholding-versus-withdrawing of the miracle pill and hypothetical Zoo of Death experiments engage nonmaleficence; his price and his duty to a mostly-dead stranger by the road raise beneficence; and who deserves resurrection under a monopoly raises justice, weighed across libertarian, utilitarian, and liberal-egalitarian (worst-off-maximizing) answers. The chapter concludes that principlism's four principles handle such dilemmas better than any single mechanical rule.

applied-ethics.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
applied-ethics.title: 1. Fearfully and Wonderfully Made
applied-ethics.relation: Argues that Project Leda and Castor are a textbook case of Parfit's non-identity problem and its "Implausible Conclusion": Neolution knowingly built the clones barren by design and doomed to fatal illness, yet since none of them could have existed otherwise, and their lives remain worth living, it appears the clones were not harmed — the same paradox as Sarah conceiving Kira young and disadvantaged. After surveying Boonin's conclusion that every escape route from the paradox fails and Benatar's antinatalist extreme, the chapter adopts Rivka Weinberg's solution that existence is a condition rather than a conferred good, so the wrong lies in knowingly making a person a means to eugenic ends. The Leda dance party at the end of Season Two, where each clone dances in her own style, shows the book's verdict: the clones' lives are worth living on their own terms, exactly as they fight to live them.

applied-ethics.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
applied-ethics.title: 2. Go Ask Alison
applied-ethics.relation: Treats Project Leda's monitors as data gatherers in a botched social-scientific experiment, contrasting the Mill/Durkheim prediction paradigm (social science modeled on physics, seeking causes and regularities) with Max Weber's interpretive paradigm that seeks motives and understanding from the inside. Donnie's ignorance of the experiment and deep involvement in Alison's life skew his reports; Daniel and the clone-raised Rachel, who thinks of clones as property, ruin Rachel's role as the experiment's control group; and Delphine's love for Cosima makes her report selectively. The chapter concludes that Leda fails as science under both paradigms while trampling the informed-consent ethics owed to human subjects — the same project that got Alison's neighbor Aynsley killed.

applied-ethics.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
applied-ethics.title: 4. Who Owns Clones
applied-ethics.relation: Takes the message Cosima decodes in the clones' DNA — "This organism and derivative genetic material is restricted intellectual property" — and asks whether Dyad can legally and morally own the Clone Club. The chapter walks through US patent law and the Supreme Court's Myriad Genetics decision (naturally occurring DNA unpatentable, synthetic cDNA patentable) and argues that because the Leda and Castor clones were genetically engineered, their modified sequences could fall under the synthetic exception, making ownership legally possible. Morally, though, it sides with self-ownership: people own the products of their labor but not people, so patenting clones would recreate the wrongs of slavery, down to who controls clone marriages and clone offspring.

applied-ethics.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
applied-ethics.title: 9. Variation under Ethics
applied-ethics.relation: Weighs the clones' bodily autonomy against the special obligations they owe one another, since genetic sisters can harm each other as no strangers can: Helena's murder of Katja nearly pins a killing on Sarah, and Vic's drug-world drags danger into Alison's suburb. The chapter builds a clone-specific cousin of Kant's categorical imperative — "act only and always in a way that you would want your clone to act" — to argue that the clones' liberty may be legitimately more restricted than ours: Alison's public drunkenness endangers sisters who can be mistaken for her, clones arguably must stay in Clone Club and share medical information like Cosima's illness, and hard cases (Beth's suicide leaving cases dangling, the brain-cut-open Castor clone begging Helena to kill him) all turn on balancing autonomy against what we owe others.

applied-ethics.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
applied-ethics.title: 15. The C-Word
applied-ethics.relation: Works through the ethics of cloning and genetic selection, starting with the objection that such technologies are "unnatural": that reasoning commits the naturalistic fallacy, since following Hume you can't get an ought from an is, and human ingenuity (roads, eyeglasses, IVF) is itself part of nature. Using Nietzsche's Genealogy account of master morality — good as the noble traits of intelligence, beauty, and strength — the chapter asks whether parents would then be obliged to engineer better children, while warning where trait-selection slides: Nazi eugenics, racist trait-lists (both Leda and Castor are white and conventionally attractive), and "abilism" against the deaf. It concludes that cloning itself is not evil: Projects Leda and Castor are immoral not because they clone but because they treat clones as mere means to an end, in Kant's sense, and trample their autonomy.

applied-ethics.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
applied-ethics.title: 6. Anti-Psychiatric Help 5¢—The Doctor is IN
applied-ethics.relation: The chapter takes Lucy's five-cent psychiatry booth as a parody that vindicates the anti-psychiatry movement's three core criticisms: an abusive doctor-patient power relation (her insults, the threat of the stool, the football gag), ineffective or harmful treatment ('Snap out of it! Five cents, please'), and the impossibility of objective mental diagnosis (Thomas Szasz, the DSM's tangled history, Big Pharma's over-prescription). Foucault's History of Madness grounds the point that madness and psychiatric expertise are historically shifting social categories rather than neutral science. Lucy's accidental mindfulness-style advice and Charlie's 'existential depression' (Yalom's death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness) point toward alternatives, and the closing thought is that Charlie's willingness to voice his sadness destigmatizes getting help.

applied-ethics.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
applied-ethics.title: 12. Why Angela Drops the Whistle
applied-ethics.relation: Jones asks why Angela flees the Nuclear Regulatory Commission at the exact moment she could expose the Washington Township cover-up, and answers with the real world of whistleblowing: Chelsea Manning's thirty-five-year sentence shows the legal peril, and the Rasmussen poll branding Manning a traitor plus the Enron fallout show the court of public opinion demonizes whistleblowers. Tribal survival instincts make insiders punish anyone who drops the tribe's secrets, and coworkers must condemn the whistleblower to preserve their own self-worth against the mirror of their silence - so even a legally protected, morally sound Angela backs away.

applied-ethics.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
applied-ethics.title: 12. Champion of the People vs. Technology
applied-ethics.relation: Staged as a Cap-versus-Iron Man dialogue, Van Pelt's chapter debates the Fourth Industrial Revolution: Tony's faith that AI and automation (Jarvis, Ultron, self-flying Hulkbuster parts, self-driving cars) will protect people against Cap's warning that flawed, biased humans always build flawed systems. Drawing on Martin Ford's Rise of the Robots, it develops technological unemployment and profit-driven displacement, weighs universal basic income as a response, and rejects blind techno-optimism that has no plan for the workers left behind. Cap - no Luddite, but the poor kid from Brooklyn - emerges as the true champion of the people for demanding answers about who suffers when machines replace jobs.

applied-ethics.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
applied-ethics.title: 8. Human Enhancement for Freedom
applied-ethics.relation: Koï asks whether biomedical enhancement could make humans resistant to the totalitarian subjugation shown in 1984, where the Party keeps proles too poor and distracted to think and dims Outer Party minds with Newspeak, erased history, and propaganda. Testing Persson and Savulescu's program of enhancing intelligence and moral empathy, she finds intelligence enhancement an educated gamble, since the gifted are also the most likely to embrace extremism and to start totalitarian movements, and empathy politically selective: Nazis directed it only at the in-group and even invoked it to justify the 'euthanasia' murders, while Party propaganda exploits citizens' empathy for horror stories of pre-revolution child labor. Her conclusion is that whatever capacity we enhance, the oligarchy could turn it to its own use: none of us will ever be immune to the love of Big Brother.

applied-ethics.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
applied-ethics.title: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
applied-ethics.relation: Karavitis places thirteen TZ episodes on a spectrum from specialized machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel,' 'The Old Man in the Cave') through human-like robots ('The Mighty Casey,' 'A Thing About Machines,' 'From Agnes with Love') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'The Lateness of the Hour,' 'In His Image'), showing that the more humanlike the creation, the deeper the emotional response — including uncanny-valley unease. He imports the animal-ethics debate (Aristotle's property view, Kant's indirect duties, Singer and Regan on moral patients) to frame personhood as the determinant of moral duty, then uses Locke's memory-continuity via 'The Trade-Ins' to argue TZ's androids would be persons, so their routine destruction or disassembly amounts to murder — the show's unstated definition of evil as treating people like disposable objects.

applied-ethics.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
applied-ethics.title: The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy
applied-ethics.relation: Fallis tests successive definitions of pretense against Westworld cases — William and Logan playing bounty hunters, Ford's pretense that Bernard is human, Maeve hiding her awakening, Hector and Armistice playing dead — rejecting Austin-style intent-to-deceive because guests don't aim to fool anyone, and settling on Langland-Hassan's account that pretending is acting as if P while believing P is false. For deception, he argues the Cartesian evil-demon definition (making things appear otherwise) is too narrow, since Ford implanting Teddy's false Wyatt backstory deceives just as much by bypassing the host's agency. Ethically, he concludes via Kant that the staff wrong the hosts because deception interferes with autonomy, and that guests like William are culpable despite lacking deceptive intent, much like Walzer's commander who foresees civilian casualties.

applied-ethics.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
applied-ethics.title: 11. Forever the Wild One
applied-ethics.relation: Anders grounds Petty's artistic freedom in Kant's Critique of Judgment: genius, the innate talent for original art freed from patron control, describes Petty's refusal to let commercial success measure his work. Singer's practical ethics supplies the frame for the $8.98 fight over Hard Promises, where Petty weighed outcomes for all affected, especially teenage fans, and threatened to withhold the masters or rename the album "Eight Ninety-Eight." Marx's worker-owner analysis maps the Shelter-to-MCA contract saga, in which Petty was sold like a piece of meat, countersued, hid the master tapes nightly, and filed for bankruptcy like a worker confronting the owners who pocket the value of the records he produced.

applied-ethics.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
applied-ethics.title: 12. When Money Shouldn’t Be King
applied-ethics.relation: Berkey reconstructs Petty's two industry battles, the bankruptcy gambit to void the contract sold along with Shelter Records and the month-long standoff against MCA's $9.98 superstar pricing, then reads The Last DJ as Petty's considered position on the business of music. He argues Petty rejected subjectivism about music's value: because listeners can be mistaken about the value of their own enjoyment, a formal argument shows executives like "Joe" who program only what profits act wrongly, even if consumers willingly pay. "Money Becomes King" completes the critique, showing how profit-focus degrades the fan's quasi-religious concert experience and corrodes Johnny's motivation to make valuable music at all.

applied-ethics.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
applied-ethics.title: 9. Replicant Birth, Moral Miscarriage
applied-ethics.relation: L. Brooke Rudow argues 2049's 'biological turn' — the miracle of Rachael giving birth — quietly reverses the first film's ethical innovation that artificial beings matter whether or not they are natural. She assembles the classic grounds for replicant moral status: Kant on cruelty to animals breeding cruelty to humans, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and the rationality criterion of Aristotle, Descartes, and Kant. Because the resistance and the plot now treat the born child as the only proof replicants are persons, she contends the sequel becomes anthropocentric where its predecessor was liberating, shutting the door it had opened for animals, machines, and anything that thinks and feels.

applied-ethics.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
applied-ethics.title: 10. Should Humans Dream of Designer Babies
applied-ethics.relation: Samantha Noll and Laci Hubbard-Mattix treat replicants as designer babies and grade the Wallace Corporation against the Belmont Report's four principles of biomedical ethics: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. Wallace's killing of the 'barren' newborn and Luv's advice not to 'waste' money on attachment or intelligence violate non-maleficence and beneficence; replicants' engineered lack of choice ('I wasn't aware that was an option, Madam') violates autonomy; and Joshi's wall that 'separates kind' institutionalizes distributive injustice, with replicants bearing all society's risk for none of its reward. The film serves as a cautionary foil for our own approaching genetic-engineering choices.

applied-ethics.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
applied-ethics.title: 25. Less Human than Human
applied-ethics.relation: Leah Schade and Emily Askew read replicants as undocumented Latinx immigrants: Sapper's grub farm parallels an ICE raid on a meatpacking plant and the deportation cell of 'Justo', blade runners mirror enforcement agents hunting 'illegals', and the miracle child maps onto DACA Dreamers whom well-meaning liberals recast as superhuman saviors at the cost of their ordinary personhood. Using Mary Midgley's personhood criteria — the ability to suffer, emotional fellowship, minding what happens to one — they argue replicants, like migrants, plainly qualify, and that 'illegality' is a constructed status, not a moral fact. The chapter warns that messianic sacrifice narratives, however sympathetic, re-objectify the very people they mean to defend.

applied-ethics.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
applied-ethics.title: “Medicine’s Not a Science!”
applied-ethics.relation: Decker explains the paradox of Dr. Leo Spaceman, incompetent ('Science is whatever we want it to be'), paternalistic, yet beloved by Tracy and Jack, through social theory: Parsons's pattern variables and professional ethics codes that Leo flouts, Marx's commodity fetishism, which makes patients desire medicalized enhancements the way direct-to-consumer pharma ads teach them to want Cialis and Viagra. Habermas's colonization of the lifeworld by systems organizations names the deeper diagnosis: managed-care bureaucracy and the market have reorganized medicine's social meanings, so 'medicine's not a science' because health itself has become a fashionable commodity. The chapter adds that 30 Rock works as satire because it shows the lifeworld pushing back against the system.

applied-ethics.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
applied-ethics.title: “It’s a robot! A goddamn droid!”
applied-ethics.relation: Tests three grounds of moral status against the franchise: species membership (Singer's charge of speciesism - would the human-DNA Newborn count?), Kantian autonomy (which makes Bishop matter but excludes babies and animals, and is itself doubtful once his behavioral inhibitors fix his choices), and Bentham's sentience ('can they suffer?' - Bishop's 'I hurt. Do me a favor. Disconnect me'). Settling on interests and preferences, the chapter argues synthetics with desires - even Ash's admiration for the 'perfect organism' - can be moral patients, so Weyland-Yutani's treatment of them as tools and slaves is wrong.

applied-ethics.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
applied-ethics.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Audits the Bluth Company's 'Family First' creed against theories of corporate social responsibility, the shareholder-profit model it actually follows versus the stakeholder model of Johnson & Johnson's credo. Evidence includes the Cornballer that burns everyone yet sells in Mexico, the sinking model home and the two-week fake house built 'not good, just looking good', child labor at the banana stand, Boyfights, unpaid construction crews, and the Iraq homes built for Saddam as a CIA wiretapping scheme. The chapter concludes that Family First only arrests the company's moral development, a manual for how not to run a business.

applied-ethics.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
applied-ethics.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Clifton asks whether fans are moral monsters for laughing at behavior that looks autistic, running Sheldon through the DSM criteria for Asperger's syndrome: missing Penny's sarcasm about doctors who 'remove shoes from asses,' hedging the bath-item Christmas gift, and inflexibly clinging to nonfunctional routines like Saturday-night laundry. Setting the writers' stated intentions aside as one fallible piece of evidence (the intentional-fallacy debate), he weighs the medical model of disability (leveling and normalizing) against the social-constructivist model in which disability is a misfit between trait and environment. Because Sheldon has built a world — theoretical physics, accommodating friends, the comic book store — where his traits are advantages, even an 'alpha nerd' leader, they constitute an 'enability' rather than a disability, and the laughter is morally innocent.

applied-ethics.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
applied-ethics.title: Would You Kindly Evolve Today
applied-ethics.relation: Ledder reads Plasmids and ADAM as human enhancement technology and stages the real bioethics debate: therapy versus enhancement, transhumanist enthusiasm (whole-brain emulation like Eleanor's ADAM-collecting, Sandberg's morphological freedom) against fears of Splicer-like superhumans and eugenics. The Rapture arms race, where your Electric Bolt Plasmid goes obsolete and forces further splicing, dramatizes the coercive spiral of competitive enhancement, while Habermas's objection that genetically designing children turns them into projections grounds the reading of Jack, Fontaine's purchased and conditioned embryo triggered by 'would you kindly', as a metaphor for engineered autonomy destroyed. The chapter closes with disability critiques: maybe the problem is not the body but the social barriers that 'disable' it, so changing society might beat changing flesh.

applied-ethics.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
applied-ethics.title: Reflections on Technophobia
applied-ethics.relation: The chapter asks whether the technophobia of 'Metalhead' - robo-dogs hunting Bella and her friends across a wasteland - is justified, testing Daniel Dinello's list of fears (identity, values, emotion, freedom, life). Descartes's and Aquinas's human-uniqueness over the mechanical fails because the robo-dogs, like DeepMind, learn and problem-solve, while the episode's Rousseau-style romanticism (only the non-technological cliff, tree, sunlight and stream aid Bella) and the teddy-bear mission show technology amplifying compassion rather than threatening it. The real dangers are robots as Latourian 'black boxes': Asimov's Three Laws cannot be operationalized, and if we cannot know how robo-dogs decide, our frameworks for blame and punishment break down (who answers for a killing - robot, programmer, or, on Marx's analysis of capitalist technology as an instrument of oppression, the economic system behind it?). The chapter concludes that since we already share the world with robots, learning to live responsibly alongside them must replace simple fear.

applied-ethics.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
applied-ethics.title: 16 When Tech Meets Tradition How Wakandan Technology Transcends Anti-Blackness
applied-ethics.relation: Timothy Brown argues that transhumanist futures - Bostrom's fable of the Dragon Tyrant, Savulescu's moral bioenhancement, AI built by homogeneous teams - exclude Black people because technologies embed anti-Blackness, from Ruha Benjamin's New Jim Code to facial recognition failing Black women. Black Panther counters this by rooting its future in traumatic memory: Killmonger's museum scene shows how whitewashed 'aesthetic Africanism' licenses incredulity about African technological achievement, while Shuri's comics arc (named 'Ancient Future' by her ancestors in D'Jalia) shows that Wakandan technology flourishes only through the traditions it is tempted to scoff at. Africanfuturism, on this reading, treats Blackness itself as a 'prosthesis' for stress-testing whether the futures we build will include everyone.

applied-ethics.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
applied-ethics.title: 17 Vibranium Dreams and Afrofuturist Visions Technology, Nature, and Culture
applied-ethics.relation: Alessio Gerola reads vibranium as an instrumentalist prop: the film treats it as a neutral means whose value depends only on the ends served, staged through three disputes - M'Baku's tradition versus Shuri's innovation, Nakia's humanitarian aid versus Killmonger's armed revolution, T'Chaka's isolationism versus T'Challa's openness. Drawing on Langdon Winner's politics of artifacts, the chapter argues that real technology and culture co-shape each other, so vibranium alone cannot explain why Wakanda stayed peaceful instead of becoming the empire Killmonger promises. The film's genuine lesson is Afrofuturist: the harmonious relation among technology, nature, and culture visible in biomimetic ships, kimoyo beads, traditional aesthetics, and the Jabari's principled refusal of vibranium.

applied-ethics.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
applied-ethics.title: By the Crimson Bands of Cyttorak… We Conclude!
applied-ethics.relation: The chapter weighs Strange's choice in Doctor Strange: The Oath to spend the last drop of the panacea curing Wong's brain tumor instead of having it replicated to cure all disease, arguing it violates 'first, do no harm' and the Hippocratic precepts—not least because Strange is Wong's friend rather than his physician and invokes a no-longer-binding oath. It then argues his sorcerer's ethics fit the martial arts warrior way better: 'hurt rather than harm' from Master Kan in Kung Fu and the Pinan forms, Zen-shaped bushido's self-control, Confucian responsibility and care for society, and the Tao Te Ching's balance and thousand-mile journey as the shared ethos of medical, martial, and mystic training.

applied-ethics.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
applied-ethics.title: 19. Of Downton and Drones
applied-ethics.relation: Jai Galliott contrasts Downton's WWI, where aristocrats like Matthew died in the trenches alongside footmen like William on a roughly level playing field, with today's drone age, in which the fighting burden falls on the lower and middle classes (future Reaper pilots recruited from the 'PlayStation generation') while risk to our own side approaches zero. He traces unmanned weapons from WWI tele-operated motorboats, the Land Torpedo, and the Kettering Bug back through Agincourt's longbows and Omdurman's machine guns to the Gulf War and Kosovo, and argues that when technological asymmetry becomes extreme, Just War Theory breaks down: such war can hardly be a last resort, strains the proportionality calculus, and violates the chivalric justice of treating an equal as an equal (via Paul Kahn's paradox of riskless warfare and Robert Sparrow's threat-based immunity). His proposal is that highly asymmetric force be applied with restraint, more like international policing than war.

applied-ethics.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
applied-ethics.title: 22. Lady Edith and the Trials of the Modern Woman
applied-ethics.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Lady Edith's last-minute walk-out from the abortion clinic (4:7) to run the full philosophical abortion debate. He lays out the classic anti-abortion argument and the biological-continuity case that 'Marigold once was an embryo,' then presents Mary Anne Warren's functional personhood criteria, which - as with Singer and Tooley on infanticide - would deny rights even to newborn George, a consequence he rejects via the comatose Matthew and the sleeping Alfred's retained capacities. Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist argument is recast as Edith waking back-to-back with the ailing Dame Nellie Melba, and he answers it with the Law of Special Beneficence: if the feckless Major Bryant owes support to the child he never wanted, Edith owes at least as much to her own flesh and blood.

applied-ethics.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
applied-ethics.title: Notes
applied-ethics.relation: Weighing Vault-Tec's secret experiments — Vault 11's yearly human sacrifice, Vault 13's 200-year lockdown, the cryogenic freezing of the Sole Survivor — the chapter asks whether the ends could ever justify the vaults. On Kant's Universal Law and Humanity Formulations the answer is flatly no: dwellers were deceived into becoming mere means to data, whatever the hypothetical space-colonization motive that designer Tim Cain favors. Act and rule utilitarianism in Bentham's tradition give a more equivocal verdict — exposed deception would doom any future cooperation, yet safeguarding humanity might in extraordinary circumstances tip the calculus — and the chapter situates the games in real research-ethics history from the eugenics era to the Tuskegee study and the Belmont Report.

applied-ethics.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
applied-ethics.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Matthew Tedesco reads Bran's coma and Drogo's living death as biomedical ethics: Jaime's 'good clean death' for Bran raises active versus passive euthanasia, and with James Rachels he argues the AMA's killing/letting-die distinction merely licenses more suffering, while Brock recasts withdrawal of treatment as intentional killing anyway. The Bran case frames end-of-life decisions for children - the Johns Hopkins and Baby John Pearson cases - and whether parents may weigh a handicap's burden on the family, a question made vivid by Bran riding Hodor. Dany's smothering of Drogo, by contrast, does not strike readers as murder because personhood rather than biological humanity carries moral standing: on Tooley's self-consciousness, Warren's five criteria, or Marquis's future-like-ours, Drogo is human but no longer a person - which leads straight to Peter Singer's claim that killing a disabled infant who is not a person may not be wrong at all, leaving us to ask whether our recoil is reason or taboo.

applied-ethics.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
applied-ethics.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Tallman and Southworth set the Hippocratic Oath against the Green Lantern oath in Soranik Natu, a Korugarian surgeon who must either stop healing mid-battle or disobey the Book of Oa. They survey the options, with Wonder Woman discarding vows for consequences, Isamot Kol letting the Corps trump his vow to Qalyra, Dr. Mid-Nite always putting patients first, and Dick Grayson going by context, then argue through Hursthouse that Natu, who treats both oaths as absolute, is in an irresolvable dilemma of her own making, more like the double-betrothed man than Williams's tragic Jim and the twenty Indians. Their verdict is that she should turn in the ring, a cautionary tale for real military medics whose oaths also collide.

applied-ethics.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
applied-ethics.title: NOTES
applied-ethics.relation: Robichaud evaluates the morally gray Company: its goal of mastering the evolutionary forces behind powers is tested against eugenics worries, the 'playing God' objection that natural processes have intrinsic value, and Sandel's Case against Perfection (that mastery breeds inflated responsibility, eroded community, and rigidity), each of which he finds inconclusive or outweighed by lives saved from people like Ted Sprague. He then turns to blame for the bag-and-tag program, applying Dennis Thompson's criterion to hold the founders plus hands-on agents like Bennet and the Haitian responsible while excusing accountants like Malsky. Finally he sets conditions for when an insider such as Bennet or Mohinder may blow the whistle, ruling out Bennet's murderous take-down-from-within scheme.

applied-ethics.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
applied-ethics.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Jason Eberl treats the muttations, jabberjays that mimic speech without understanding, tracker jackers, the wolf-mutts with Glimmer's eyes that torment Cato, and the lizard-mutts hissing Katniss's name, alongside real chimeras (geeps, the SCID-hu mouse, Balaban's quail-chick brain transplants, Weissman's human-neural mouse) to ask whether biotechnology could create a person. Working through Boethius's definition of a person as an 'individual substance of a rational nature' and Locke's 'thinking intelligent Being' that can consider itself the same over time, he argues that human DNA alone confers no personhood, while a chimera genuinely capable of self-conscious rational thought would be a person whose weaponized creation and lab captivity would violate its rights, which is why ethicists allow mouse chimeras but hesitate with primates. He notes that the Gamemakers' refusal to see tributes as persons is exactly the move that made slavery and Nazi dehumanization possible, and that Katniss's suspicion about whether the mutts remember their deaths is the right ethical question to keep open.

applied-ethics.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
applied-ethics.title: Cobol’s Backyard
applied-ethics.relation: Malloy argues the real players of Inception are the corporations — Cobol Engineering hires Cobb to spy on Saito, Saito as CEO of Proclus Global buys the airline and commissions the Fischer job, and the human characters are pawns moved at the firms' will. He builds a case that corporations are moral persons because they make decisions through their own procedures, hold rights (Saito's 'I bought the airline' exercised Proclus's property rights through a representative), and bear responsibilities not reducible to CEOs or shareholders, rebuffing Harman-style objections from moral emotions and virtues by comparing corporations to psychopaths, who are persons without being good ones. He ends with Fischer-Morrow's impending energy monopoly: Friedman's shareholder-primacy view versus the corporation's duty to the moral community, and what corporate personhood means for real-world practices like boycotts.

applied-ethics.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
applied-ethics.title: So, That’s It No Solution
applied-ethics.relation: Rieder argues Iron Man is the one 'realistic' superhero: nothing about him requires a different world, only incremental nanotech advances — precision engineering, miniaturized computing, and carbon nanotubes a hundred times stronger than steel — already pursued at MIT's Institute for Soldier Nanotechnologies. He then uses Iron Man as a nanoethics case study, pitting cost-benefit analysis (with David Schmidtz's proviso that it is necessary but not sufficient for right action) against the precautionary principle exemplified by Bill Joy's call for relinquishment, asking whether an Obadiah Stane selling 'Iron Armies' to the highest bidder is a risk we may not take even if it is improbable. He leans precautionary: we may be morally required to forgo the experiment because the world's population never consented to the risk.

applied-ethics.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
applied-ethics.title: The Office and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Dromm asks what makes Michael's behavior wrong even where the law cannot touch it: as an 'equal-opportunity harasser' of Pam, Ryan, and Oscar, Michael seems to escape Title VII's discrimination requirement. He tests Edmund Wall's 'wrongful communication' definition against the filthy emails, 'that's what she said,' and Michael's solution to the Kevin-Angela dispute in 'Conflict Resolution,' finds it too broad and too dependent on the victim's objection, then turns to MacKinnon's sex-discrimination account and Crosthwaite and Priest's oppression account to explain the distinctive harm to women (pressuring Pam to be a cheerleader in 'Basketball,' calling the party-planning committee his 'bitches'). He concludes that both views are needed, and that in the end harassment wrongs workers by undermining their legitimate expectation of being judged only on job-relevant merit, leaving Dwight's extra effort done for nothing.

applied-ethics.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
applied-ethics.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Novy asks whether it would be right to deliberately make a Spider-Man. Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge from Plato's Republic — that unchecked superpower breeds 'great corruptibility' — is made flesh in Doc Ock, Green Goblin, Lizard, and Morbius, while Bostrom's transhumanism supplies the movement the chapter defends. Against Fukuyama's bio-conservative worries about playing God, destroying equality, and violating a human essence, the chapter notes that Aunt May's bifocals and insulin already make her a cyborg, that Marvel grants personhood by behavior rather than biology (Kree, Skrulls, the Vision), and that the thought experiment of giving Mary Jane a painless 'super smile' shows we are at least sometimes obliged to enhance.

applied-ethics.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
applied-ethics.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Southworth and Timm use the Clone Saga to teach real cloning science: molecular, therapeutic, and reproductive cloning, Dolly's 1-in-277 success rate, the impossibility of clone caskets and inherited memories — while crediting the 1970s writers for correctly making mitochondrial DNA the blood test that distinguishes Peter from Ben Reilly. They then evaluate the characters' reactions: Leon Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance,' which holds that a clone's genotype 'has already lived' and despotically fixes its life's expectations, explains Kane's genocidal self-loathing and Peter's rage and despair when told he is the clone, while Gregory Pence's rebuttal — that such repugnance rests on false expectations, as with twins or children of interracial couples — vindicates MJ's and Ben's insistence that a clone's moral worth lies in what it does, not where its genes came from.

applied-ethics.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
applied-ethics.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
applied-ethics.relation: Challenges the received libertarian message of 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' — Randy giving himself testicular cancer for a marijuana prescription, Cartman bootlegging KFC in a Scarface parody after Colorado bans fast food — by pressing Mill's liberty principle on what 'harm' means: Mr. Garrison's plot to murder the Queer Eye cast is immediate harm, but the S&M Mr. Slave displays to schoolchildren in 'The Death Camp of Tolerance' is only indirect, psychologically mediated harm Mill cannot clearly handle. Addiction then undermines Mill's assumption of sovereign tastes: corporations can shape desire without coercing anyone, so the libertarian 'omnicompetent individual' is a myth. Mead's intersubjectivity (Randy smoking pot before Officer Barbrady, blind to how Jimbo sees him) grounds the constructive claim that selves are socially formed, and the shark-tank defecation and Prisoner's Dilemma examples show why collective harms need rules and regulation.

applied-ethics.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
applied-ethics.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
applied-ethics.relation: Uses 'Follow That Egg!' — Mrs. Garrison's jealous crusade to stop Mr. Slave marrying Big Gay Al, her two-daddy egg experiment where Stan and Kyle out-parent Cartman, and the governor's 'butt buddies' separate-but-equal compromise — to demolish the standard arguments against gay marriage (scripture, dictionary definition, procreation, tradition, harm to children, the slippery slope to polygamy and incest) as post-hoc rationalizations of disgust. Mill's harm principle and negative liberty supply the positive case: unlike under-age, incestuous, or polygamous marriage, gay marriage demonstrably harms no one, so no legitimate reason remains to ban it, and rights should never be put to a referendum anyway. The 'butt buddies' label fails because separate is never equal — marriage's social recognition, not just its 1,100 benefits, is what its defenders are denied.

applied-ethics.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
applied-ethics.title: Notes
applied-ethics.relation: Courtland Lewis argues Star Trek teaches philosophy through casuistry: episodic case studies that test intuitions, moving from paradigm cases to harder ones. Its three sci-fi virtues—scientific constraint, flexible realism, and thought experimentation, shown in 'Clues' and contrasted with Doctor Who's 'Kill the Moon'—let it stage 'The Measure of a Man's hearing on Data's personhood and 'Nothing Human's dilemma over using Cardassian Mengele-style research data (analogous to Tuskegee) to save B'Elanna without the racial baggage of real-world cases. Viewers deliberate along with the crew—Janeway uses the data, then the Doctor deletes Crell Moset—which is exactly why Trek changes lives.

applied-ethics.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
applied-ethics.title: Notes
applied-ethics.relation: Uses the Zillo Beast arc, battle droids, mynocks, and Han shooting Greedo to test theories of moral status: Schweitzer-style reverence for life would forbid a Jedi from eating anything, genetic views breed Palpatine-style human chauvinism, Singer's sentience view makes droid suffering and Luke dropping the rancor's door morally troubling, and Kantian autonomy excludes cognitively impaired beings too harshly. The chapter weighs Palpatine as merely a 'sociopathic' goal-pursuer rather than a Kantian moral agent, and leaves the droid question open via the novel Children of the Jedi, where the droid-converted Nichos lacks even mere agency because he cannot override his programming.

applied-ethics.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
applied-ethics.title: Notes
applied-ethics.relation: Asks whether droids like C-3PO and R2-D2 can think, staging Searle's Chinese Room as a 'Bocce Room' to argue that droid anxiety, pain, and heroism might be mere input-output symbol shuffling.
