It then rebuts Searle with the systems reply (the room as a whole, not the person inside, might understand) and a neuron-by-neuron mechanical brain-replacement thought experiment showing the biological/mechanical divide is arbitrary, concluding that restraining bolts, memory wipes, and the Mos Eisley cantina's 'we don't serve their kind here' prejudice lose their justification if droids might genuinely suffer.

applied-ethics.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
applied-ethics.title: Bringing Balance to the Force
applied-ethics.relation: Harter argues that Revenge of the Sith manipulates audiences into fearing the medical technology that saves Anakin on Mustafar, portraying his prosthetic transformation into Vader as horrifying when in real bioethical terms saving a burn victim with ventilators, feeding tubes, and prosthetics is something we applaud. He diagnoses Lucas's framing as the naturalistic fallacy (what is natural is good), grounded in Hume's is-ought gap, and flags the mirror-image 'technological fallacy' of assuming enhancement like General Grievous's cyborg body must be good. The chapter concludes that technology is value-neutral and its worth depends on the context of use — which is what it means for Anakin and Luke, both maimed and prosthetized, to 'bring balance to the Force.'

applied-ethics.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
applied-ethics.title: Beyond the Whimsy
applied-ethics.relation: Jowitt argues that L3-37's activism in Solo ('Droid rights! We are sentient!') exposes a real problem in philosophy of law: the Coronet Spaceport's 'all droids must be registered' treats sentients as property, and Austin's legal positivism (law as command backed by sanction, which he says also describes Enfys Nest's threats) cannot condemn this. Building a Kantian natural-law argument, he claims that if droids like L3, C-3PO, BB-8, and D-O are rational beings covered by the categorical imperative, then any rule classifying them as property cannot give us a reason to obey it and so is not valid law at all. Lando's grief over dying L3 and our sadness at C-3PO's memory wipe in The Rise of Skywalker show we already treat droids as moral persons, so Beyleveld's precautionary principle says they deserve legal personhood - paralleling real-world AI-inventorship (DABUS) and animal-personhood litigation.

applied-ethics.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
applied-ethics.title: NOTES
applied-ethics.relation: Grubb stages Arlene's decision to abort the baby fathered by serial killer Rene as a case study in Bentham's act utilitarianism: her prayer that ending the pregnancy will keep 'Rene's sickness' from Coby, Lisa, and Terry weighs pleasure and pain — the two sovereign masters — for the greatest number, from family to all of Bon Temps. The chapter shows why the calculus fails her: consequences cannot be known in advance (a crystal ball or Lafayette's visions would be needed), it is indeterminate whose happiness counts, and her premise that evil is biologically inheritable sits badly with the free-will account of sin, making the dilemma genuinely undecidable from inside the show.

applied-ethics.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
applied-ethics.title: 9. Machines Who Care
applied-ethics.relation: Weiss reads 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric' as fifty-year-old anticipations of today's debate over relational artifacts: Alexa, therapeutic robot seals, and care robots for the aged (via Turkle, the Sparrows' objection, and Coeckelbergh's embrace of robots that care). Alicia's tear wins Corry's trust only to end with her shot in the face, while the electric grandma saves Anne's life, yet both are assembly-line products answering loneliness that the same consumer society produces. The chapter asks whether buying care and companionship from robotic women, designed, boxed, and disposed of by men, is fable or nightmare.

applied-ethics.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
applied-ethics.title: “It Was a Mistake”
applied-ethics.relation: James and Mona Rocha reconstruct the night of Shelly Pomeroy's party — Logan supplying the GHB, Dick drugging Madison's drink that reached Veronica, Dick and Sean goading Cassidy — and apply a three-part test of moral responsibility (causal contribution, foreseeability, intention) to conclude Dick and Sean deserve the most blame, Logan substantial negligence, and Madison very little since she did not know the drink was drugged. Veronica's own choices, crashing an unwelcoming party and taking an unknown drink, were prudential mistakes that put only herself at risk, not the moral wrongs that generate blame, so Cassidy remains fully culpable without Veronica sharing any of it. Even Kant's duty to safeguard one's own rational agency, they concede, at most makes taking the drink wrong in itself and never grounds blaming the victim, who deserves sympathy.

applied-ethics.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
applied-ethics.title: Introduction
applied-ethics.relation: The editors' introduction frames Westworld as a show that forces viewers to take sides not just on plot allegiances but on the meaning of basic concepts like 'choice,' using Dolores's line about choosing to see beauty and Ford's 'you're only human, after all.' It argues the series destabilizes the very 'we' of what counts as human. It dedicates the volume to Susanne Foster, invoking Cora Diamond's 'difficulty of reality' and Aristotle's claim that wonder and astonishment prompt understanding of painful questions like the mass slaughter of animals and injustice to Native Americans.

applied-ethics.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
applied-ethics.title: The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy
applied-ethics.relation: Don Fallis uses Westworld to work out definitions of pretense and deception, testing successive accounts (acting-as-if, Austin's intend-to-deceive, Langland-Hassan's believe-P-is-false) against cases like guests playing cowboys, Ford passing off Bernard as human, and Maeve and Hector pretending to be deactivated. He adopts a Cartesian evil-demon model of deception but rejects the claim that deception must manipulate perceived evidence, arguing Ford's direct implanting of Teddy's Wyatt backstory still counts. He concludes, citing Kant on autonomy and Walzer on foreseen collateral harm, that staff who intend to deceive the hosts and even guests who foreseeably contribute to it act wrongly, since deceived hosts suffer real harm to their agency.

applied-ethics.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
applied-ethics.title: Allure of the West
applied-ethics.relation: Nicholas Moll reads the Westworld park as a tabletop-style sandbox and LARP role-play experience with Ford as Game Master mediating guests' mediated 'illusion of choice.' Drawing on MacIntyre's narrative unity of a life and Bernard Williams's critique about the constraints of coherence, he argues guests author competing self-narratives to reach greater self-knowledge, as William discovers his capacity for ruthlessness and becomes the Man in Black. He contends violence functions as the rule-mediated engine of this 'gameful,' educative experience, and that Ford's transformative insight is aimed less at the guests than at the hosts who are engaged in the park's production.

applied-ethics.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
applied-ethics.title: Notes
applied-ethics.relation: Gibson argues Rand's creation of the Asha'man and the Black Tower is a 'dirty hands' problem (Michael Walzer, tracing to Machiavelli): even in the just war against the Dark One, Rand does something morally objectionable by building men trained to be weapons and then, distrusting Mazrim Taim, abdicating oversight so Taim (a Forsaken) corrupts them. He reframes the Asha'man as lethal autonomous weapons, using the ICRC's Ingvild Bode on algorithmic bias in data, design, and use to argue Rand and Taim's biases were 'trained' into these walking weapons, and connects the speed and loss of control of autonomous war to WoT's theme of balance and the real-world ethics of emerging military AI.

applied-ethics.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
applied-ethics.title: V - MAD GENETICS THE SINISTER SIDE OF BIOLOGICAL MASTERY
applied-ethics.relation: Burnett traces Nathaniel Essex's transformation into Mister Sinister to explore the ethics of genetic mastery. Set in Darwin's 1859 London, where Essex, grieving a child, debates taking control of evolution with Darwin himself, the chapter uses Paley's natural theology and Tennyson's crisis of natural evil to frame Sinister's rejection of moral restraint, and Herbert Spencer's evolutionary ethics to argue that cooperation, not 'dog eat dog,' is what fitness actually favors. Sinister's breeding of the Summers bloodline and Bolivar Trask's Sentinels embody Galton's eugenics, and Sinister's careers as 'Dr. Windsor' and 'Dr. Milbury' behind Weapon X and the Black Womb project mirror real cases like the Tuskegee study, where researchers lost sight of the moral whole.

applied-ethics.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
applied-ethics.title: XIII - THE MUTANT CURE OR SOCIAL CHANGE DEBATING DISABILITY
applied-ethics.relation: Ilea uses The Last Stand's mutant cure to stage the debate over disability. Worthington's 'affliction... a disease' speech is the medical model; Storm's 'there's nothing to cure' is the social model, on which society, not the body, disables, as with Deaf culture and communities without eyeglasses. Rogue, who cannot touch anyone, and Jean, whose power she cannot control, show some mutations genuinely impair, so the chapter weighs beneficence, nonmaleficence, and utility across Angel's aborted cure, cochlear implants, prenatal Down syndrome screening, and the history of eugenics from Nazi euthanasia to American sterilization laws, concluding the cure can be both liberation and weapon.

applied-ethics.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
applied-ethics.title: Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person
applied-ethics.relation: Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.

applied-ethics.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
applied-ethics.title: What's so Bad about Performance-Enhancing Drugs
applied-ethics.relation: Ryan evaluates three arguments that using performance-enhancing drugs is wrong, drawing on cases like Barry Bonds, Lyle Alzado, and Ben Johnson. The Against-the-Rules argument shows only that PED use breaks current rules, not that it should be banned; the Unfairness argument overgeneralizes, since sport is full of tolerated unfairness (better coaching, nutrition, natural gifts); and the Harm-and-Pressure argument turns on empirical facts and a paternalism-versus-autonomy debate about whether adults may choose the risk. She concludes no argument yet establishes that PEDs ought to be banned as inherently wrong.

applied-ethics.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
applied-ethics.title: The True Nature of Cheating
applied-ethics.relation: Swain and Brand build a definition of cheating by successive counterexamples set in a fictional State-versus-Central championship. They move from breaking a formal rule for unfair advantage, to including informal conventions (the hypothetical pre-rule Bonds steroid case), to 'enhancing one's chances of winning' (a coach fielding ineligible players to level the field), and finally add a defeasibility clause so that convention-sanctioned tactics like running out the play clock are not cheating. Trash-talking within the rules is classed as gamesmanship, not cheating.

applied-ethics.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
applied-ethics.title: Upon Further Review Instant Replay Is an All-or-Nothing Affair
applied-ethics.relation: Smith argues that consistency in applying rules and their motivations forces instant replay to be all-or-nothing: either every play is reviewable or none is. He shows the two rationales—'get the calls right' and 'preserve the flow of the game'—each apply to all plays, then dismantles the reviewable/nonreviewable line by arguing neither the 'judgment call' distinction (goal-line and fumble calls are judgment-laden, field goals are not) nor the 'correctable call' distinction (every play is correctable, e.g. via replaying the down) can hold, using the Roethlisberger Super Bowl XL touchdown as a case.

applied-ethics.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
applied-ethics.title: Eighth Hole Playing Through Racism and Sexism in Golf
applied-ethics.relation: Gray examines whether golf is a model of equality or a preserve of 'wealthy white men,' using George Carlin's polemic and the Tiger Woods 'Chosen One' narrative as foils. He documents 'social closure' and the 'Grass Ceiling' through Augusta National's history, the Shoal Creek and Martha Burk/NCWO controversies, and the PGA's former Caucasian-only clause, then turns to sexism via McGinnis, McQuillan, and Chapple's interviews and Connell's 'hegemonic masculinity,' showing how gendered 'red/women's tees' entrench a false dualism of male and female play. Citing McDonagh and Pappano's Playing with the Boys, he argues coercive sex-segregation rests on false assumptions and calls for transparency about club membership.

applied-ethics.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Stephen Kershnar examines the three strongest arguments for the IOC's ban on performance-enhancing drugs, harm-to-self, harm-to-others, and unfairness, and argues each fails, using cases such as Ben Johnson's stripped 1988 gold and Marion Jones. Against harm-to-self he cites anti-paternalism and the far greater accepted risks of NFL play and boxing; against harm-to-others he shows PED pressure is no different from the pressure of rivals' superior training (a Prisoner's Dilemma leagues need not solve); against unfairness he tests four accounts of fairness, including a Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance model whose choosers might find banning steroids while allowing Lasik and high-tech gear arbitrary. He concludes the ban, if justified at all, rests only on contested utilitarian grounds like audience preference and protecting children.

applied-ethics.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall examine when a nation or athlete may justifiably boycott the Olympics, distinguishing 'material' from 'formal' contribution and weighing available alternatives and the stringency of values (e.g., Gandhi's boycott of British goods, apartheid boycotts, the Lysistrata sex strike). They argue attending is not itself endorsement of the host regime, so the heavy, often irrecoverable cost to individual athletes places a strong burden of proof on any boycott. Surveying the 1956, 1980 and 1984 boycotts (which changed little) and the 1936 Berlin Games (where Jesse Owens's participation did real good), they conclude only a credible threat of serious bodily harm clearly justifies boycotting.

applied-ethics.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
applied-ethics.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
applied-ethics.relation: Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.

applied-ethics.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
applied-ethics.title: High Off the Page Representing the Drug Experience in the Work of Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg
applied-ethics.relation: Erik Mortenson argues that Kerouac's and Ginsberg's drug writing works 'through the body' to transmit the altered temporality of intoxication to the reader, using Merleau-Ponty's account of original speech and the lived body as gesture, and Deleuze and Guattari's 'Body Without Organs' and speeds. Marijuana expands the present into Kerouac's long exfoliating sentences and empathetic 'digging' (Visions of Cody, On the Road), while Benzedrine contracts it into the accelerated confessional rush of The Subterraneans; Ginsberg's LSD poems ('Lysergic Acid,' 'Wales Visitation') hit the limit of representing timelessness. The chapter concludes the writing lets the nonuser get 'high off the page' without the dependency Deleuze and Guattari warn of.

applied-ethics.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
applied-ethics.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
applied-ethics.relation: Karen Hoffman traces the gun across Eastwood's career as an evolving argument about violence: Dirty Harry's .44 Magnum ends violence without cost to the shooter, High Plains Drifter and Pale Rider treat the gun as righteous retribution and a proof of masculine honor, but Unforgiven shows William Munny killing men who may not deserve it and dwelling on how killing brutalizes the shooter. In Gran Torino Walt Kowalski finally gives up the gun entirely, walking unarmed into Spider's gang and being gunned down in a Christlike pose so that Thao is spared both victimhood and the guilt of killing. The chapter argues Eastwood shifts from celebrating the gun as physical protection to warning of the psychological damage violence inflicts on its user.

applied-ethics.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
applied-ethics.title: The Fly and the Human Ironies of Disgust
applied-ethics.relation: Colin McGinn reads Cronenberg's The Fly as a meditation on human disgust and self-disgust: Seth Brundle's metamorphosis into Brundlefly does not cross an ontological boundary but dramatizes that the human being was already a loathsome organic monster, a 'god who shits.' McGinn ties this to a Cartesian mind-body duality (a fine mind trapped in a decaying insect shell mirrors our own embodiment) and, via Nussbaum, to how projected self-disgust stigmatizes despised groups; the cinematic image itself is an 'antidisgust medium' that lets us feel only quasi-disgust.

applied-ethics.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
applied-ethics.title: Tragedy and Terrible Beauty in A History of Violence and Eastern Promises
applied-ethics.relation: Cynthia Freeland argues A History of Violence and Eastern Promises qualify as Aristotelian tragedies, using the Poetics' 'recognition and reversal' as Tom Stall is exposed as Joey Cusack and Nikolai's undercover identity is revealed. Analyzing the stairway sex scene, the Philadelphia gunfight, and Nikolai's naked bathhouse fight, she deploys Korsmeyer's notion of 'terrible beauty' (beauty in the horrific, like the bloody newborn) and Carroll/Gaut on empathy and identification, concluding both heroes commit an Aristotelian hamartia through their acceptance of violence.

applied-ethics.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
applied-ethics.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
applied-ethics.relation: Rodriguez-Ruiz treats Ali and The Insider as dramatizing the methodology of philosophy, especially conceptual analysis and the politics of defining social concepts. Ali's challenges to 'patriotism,' 'freedom' and his slave name, and the manipulation of 'confidential,' 'addictive' and 'tortious interference' in The Insider, show how much rides on contested definitions. Against cultural relativism, he deploys James Rachels's Elements of Moral Philosophy (there are moral facts; some rules are needed for any society to exist) and discusses conceptual analysis (Jackson, Goldman) and Schiappa's 'how ought we use X,' leaving both heroes committed to independent thinking over consensus.

applied-ethics.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
applied-ethics.title: Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still
applied-ethics.relation: Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.

applied-ethics.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
applied-ethics.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
applied-ethics.relation: Baker uses Noel Carroll's aesthetic claim that film art requires 'sufficient' creative control ('no control, no style, no art') to defend Soderbergh's authorship across four remakes. The Underneath swaps noir shadow for suburban banality and green/blue color symbolism to externalize Michael's alienation; Traffic adapts a BBC series to indict NAFTA-era globalization and the treatment-starved drug war; Ocean's Eleven rewrites the Rat Pack ending so the thieves keep $150 million, an allegory of American wealth consolidation embodied by casino owner Benedict; Solaris strips science fiction to introspective desire. Baker further argues Soderbergh harnesses star images (Roberts, Douglas, Clooney) yet pushes them past type, synthesizing Hollywood's utopianism (per Dyer) with art-cinema social critique.

applied-ethics.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
applied-ethics.title: The Paradox of Fictional Belief and Its Moral Implications in Jaws
applied-ethics.relation: Trogan and Kowalski use Jaws to pose the paradox of fiction: we feel real fear and pity for Chrissie, the Kintners, and Quint though we know they are not real. They rehearse Radford's charge that such emotions are incoherent (since based on false belief) and answer it with a cognitivist 'unasserted thought' account and Kendall Walton's theory of make-believe, arguing we self-consciously enter the film as an adult game. Drawing on Nussbaum, they claim appropriate emotional response to Jaws cultivates empathy and 'seeing,' honing ethical sensitivity rather than turning adults into children.

applied-ethics.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
applied-ethics.title: “Memory Man”
applied-ethics.relation: David LaRocca reads Memento through Andy Clark and David Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis: Leonard's tattoos, Polaroids, and notecards just are his memory, doing exactly what Otto's notebook does in their original example - so that writing 'Don't believe his lies' on a Polaroid is literally modifying his mind and carries the moral significance of interfering with his person. Drawing on Liao and Sandberg's ethics of memory modification and Noël Carroll's account of the film's reverse-ordered narrative, the chapter argues Leonard remains a culpable moral agent in his lucid moments: he knowingly 'incepts' a false command into his own extended mind to preserve the avenging-husband narrative that constitutes his identity, becoming a serial killer. It closes on our epistemic and moral duty of cognitive fidelity - to build truthful narrative identities rather than lie to ourselves into murder.

applied-ethics.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
applied-ethics.relation: Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.

applied-ethics.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
applied-ethics.title: 6. How the Hell Are We Supposed to Kill an Idea
applied-ethics.relation: Simsek reads the 'Hell House' tulpa—a monster made real by mass belief on the HellHoundsLair website—as a philosophical challenge about the power of ideas and how one 'kills' an idea, which the brothers can only attempt by seeding a counter-belief. She invokes Socrates' call in the Republic to censor the arts that shape moral character, and the Streisand Effect, to argue that internet-amplified ideas (memes, conspiracy theories, gender and racial norms) take on autonomous, hard-to-kill life much as fandom overrides creators' intent.

applied-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
applied-ethics.title: 4. Better Call the DEA
applied-ethics.relation: White uses Better Call Saul's cartel world—the 'Bagman' shootout, Mike's account of Philadelphia police corruption, Tuco's meth-driven violence—to frame the ethics of the U.S. War on Drugs, tracing its racist origins and drawing a sustained analogy to alcohol Prohibition. She marshals Mill's harm principle from On Liberty to argue adults may choose their own risks absent harm to others, making criminalization inconsistent given legal alcohol. She then fairly lays out the pro-War case (Bennett on deterrence, the Robins Vietnam-heroin study, Mill's own bar on selling oneself into slavery applied to addiction) before favoring decriminalization on the Portugal model.

applied-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
applied-ethics.title: 22. Breaking Bad Promises
applied-ethics.relation: The first half of this chapter lays out the moral paradox of 'bad' promises through Better Call Saul: Jimmy's payment to the Lindholm twins for the staged accident, the Kettlemans' bribe for silence, Nacho and Mike's hit contract on Tuco, Gus and Mike's criminal alliance, and Jimmy and Ira's Hummel heist. It stresses Mike's code ('if you make a deal, you keep your word') and his refund to Nacho when the hit fails, then builds a taxonomy of illicit promises as legal or illegal crossed with moral or immoral, setting up the question of whether we may break promises that are wrongful.

applied-ethics.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
applied-ethics.title: 22. Breaking Bad Promises
applied-ethics.relation: The second half surveys and rejects existing solutions to bad promises: Seana Shiffrin's claim that an immoral promise is no promise and David Owens's 'transfer of authority' theory both fail Hume's objection that words alone change nothing and beg the question of who has authority, while Altham and Gilbert's 'not binding because wicked' is circular. Drawing on Saul/Jimmy's common-law training, the author distinguishes void (malum in se) from voidable (malum prohibitum) promises and proposes a harm-based framework keyed to the location of harm, arguing third-party harms void a promise while purely internal harms grant the harmed party a 'moral veto.'

applied-ethics.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
applied-ethics.title: 13. In Defense of Demerzel
applied-ethics.relation: Nurkic asks whether Demerzel, the loyal robot of the Apple TV+ Foundation, violates Asimov's Laws of Robotics when she poisons Zephyr Halima and kills Cleon XIV (Brother Dawn). He argues she is governed not by the ordinary First/Second Laws but by a reprogrammed priority—Daneel's 'Zeroth Law' (protect humanity) narrowed to 'Cleon I's vision'—and then contends the Laws are incoherent when applied to real cases (Buridan's-donkey paralysis, the surgeon dilemma, ambiguity of 'human' and 'harm'). He closes by testing the Laws against Kant's categorical imperative (the lying/murderer-at-the-door case) and Bentham-style utilitarianism to show robot ethics cannot be reduced to fixed programmed codes.

applied-ethics.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
applied-ethics.title: 17. Chef of the Future
applied-ethics.relation: Cheong convenes the 'documentary-ethics panel' invited by Roadrunner director Morgan Neville over the AI deepfake of Bourdain's voice reading lines he never spoke. Using Beauchamp and Childress's principle of autonomy, the Midler v. Ford voice-impersonation case, and worries from AI ethicists and epistemologists (Fallis, Muller) that deepfakes threaten knowledge and trust, he argues the synthesized voice denies Bourdain the 'right of reply' and deceives viewers — then reveals he had ChatGPT ghost-write parts of the chapter to make the point.

applied-ethics.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
applied-ethics.title: It’s Not That Simple
applied-ethics.relation: Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.

applied-ethics.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
applied-ethics.title: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
applied-ethics.relation: Karavitis arranges thirteen Twilight Zone android/machine episodes on a moral spectrum from simple machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'I Sing the Body Electric,' 'The Lateness of the Hour') to fully synthetic humans ('The Trade-Ins'). Using personhood, moral-agent/moral-patient distinctions, Aristotle's and Kant's views on animals, Singer and Regan on degrees not kinds, and Locke's memory theory of identity, he argues that if body-swapped Holts remain persons then scratch-built androids are persons too—so the destroyed androids were murdered, and evil is treating persons as disposable objects.

applied-ethics.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
applied-ethics.title: 9. Machines Who Care
applied-ethics.relation: Weiss examines 'robots that care' through 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric,' invoking Sherry Turkle's 'relational artifacts' and current debates (PARO, Alexa, Coeckelbergh, the Sparrows) about outsourcing companionship and care to machines. He notes Alicia becomes a relational artifact the moment she weeps, and that both she and the electric grandma are gendered, boxed, assembly-line products designed to fill human loneliness that a consumer culture itself produced. The essay asks whether we want a society where care and love are purchased off an assembly line—fable or nightmare.

applied-ethics.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
applied-ethics.title: 12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep
applied-ethics.relation: Jones argues the Twilight Zone is not really 'somewhere else': Serling's narration insists on a remote realm, but episodes like 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'Eye of the Beholder' take place in recognizable America. He claims the show performs a 'double distancing'—framing mundane, uncomfortable truths (we're selfish, easily manipulated, not special, mortal) as strange by locating them elsewhere and delivering them via impossible catalysts (gremlins, the Devil). 'The Shelter,' with no supernatural cause and a Cold War fallout-shelter premise Kennedy actually urged, breaks the pattern, forcing viewers to see that the Twilight Zone is the room they sit in.

applied-ethics.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
applied-ethics.title: It’s Not Personal . . . It’s Just Bizzyneuss Business Ethics, the Company, and Its Stakeholders
applied-ethics.relation: Pierlott frames the shareholder-versus-stakeholder debate (Friedman versus Freeman) using Aristotle's function argument to ask what makes a 'good' company, then judges business relationships by Kant's humanity formula. McBean's manipulation of the Sneetches and the digital-TV cases show consumers used merely as means; McGurk's cavalier overworking of Sneelock in If I Ran the Circus and Maitland's sweatshop defense are answered with Marx's account of labor exploitation and Aristotle's voluntary-versus-mixed actions; the Once-ler's Lorax devastation shows firms externalizing environmental costs when profit is maximized at any value unprotected by law.

applied-ethics.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
applied-ethics.title: Speaking for Business, Speaking for Trees Business and Environment in The Lorax
applied-ethics.relation: The Klaassens read The Lorax as a joint business-and-environmental-ethics text organized around three questions the Thneed provokes: do we consume too much (invoking Thoreau's 'simplify' and DesJardins on practical, ethical, and environmental over-consumption), must business grow (Daly's distinction between quantitative growth and qualitative development), and why the Once-ler ignores sustainability (the Brundtland definition and Daly's rules for natural capital). The Lorax's self-appointment as one who 'speaks for the trees' is tied to Christopher Stone's argument that natural objects should have legal standing through guardians, like corporations or incompetents.

applied-ethics.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: “Sometimes Dead Is Better”
applied-ethics.relation: Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.

applied-ethics.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Olson and Taliaferro examine the ethics of secrets in Austen, refining Sissela Bok's definition so that a secret conceals what convention would normally make public. They argue secrets in Austen are usually corrosive (Wickham and Lydia's elopement endangering the Bennets, Brandon's silence about Willoughby harming Marianne, Lucy Steele's engagement binding Elinor) yet can be virtuous, as when Darcy secretly funds Lydia's marriage to avoid self-aggrandizement. They propose an 'ideal observer' standpoint (an all-knowing, impartial, affective narrator) for judging when a secret is honorable, and argue the Emma-Miss Bates incident is not a failure to keep a secret but a genuine vice of contempt Austen condemns.

applied-ethics.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Riter analyzes Pride and Prejudice and Zombies as mashup literature, arguing the form requires readers to know the source while denying its prestige, so Austen must be both 'dead' and 'alive.' She uses Roland Barthes's 'The Death of the Author' to explain how the loss of Austen's authorial authority opens her text to reinterpretation and legally permits Grahame-Smith's rewriting. But she argues Grahame-Smith actually attacks a caricatured 'living Jane' of popular culture (the saintly, class-obsessed romance writer) rather than the historically complex Austen, noting his inconsistency in celebrating the class-conscious zombie-slayer Lady Catherine while mocking Mrs. Bennet for the same class focus.

applied-ethics.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: Chapter 8 The Noble Art of Lying
applied-ethics.relation: James Edwin Mahon reconstructs Twain's two essays on lying ('On the Decay of the Art of Lying' and 'My First Lie') into a philosophy of lying. Twain holds that everyone lies constantly, that lying need not be spoken or deceptive (the 'silent lie,' nondeceptive polite lies, acts as lies, and 'modified' lies/palters), and that the gravest lies are the 'silent National Lies' such as the collective silence that slavery was not unjust. Mahon shows Twain's ethics of lying is broadly utilitarian and Rossian: guided by nonmaleficence and beneficence, an injurious truth is no better than an injurious lie, and self-sacrificing lies that help others are virtuous, so lying should be practiced as a cultivated art.

applied-ethics.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
applied-ethics.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Baron, a new father, weighs whether to let his son Maxwell consume violent popular media (from Halloween to SpongeBob, Grand Theft Auto, and Schindler's List) by testing three hypotheses. He uses Plato's Republic warning against exposing the young to stories they can't interpret for the 'causal hypothesis'; Aristotle's Poetics on learning pleasure from painful images for the 'edification hypothesis'; and Aristotle's account of tragic catharsis (homeopathic vs allopathic purging) for the 'catharsis hypothesis,' concluding that context matters more than ratings and that fathers watching alongside their children are the decisive influence.

applied-ethics.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
applied-ethics.title: MOTHERHOOD
applied-ethics.relation: Chris Mulford, a nurse and lactation consultant, analyzes infant feeding as an ethical question of rights, duties, and responsibilities, drawing on a feminist ethic of care and the claim that women learn empathy through caregiving (linked to oxytocin's role in birth and nursing). She argues that the right at stake is the mother-child dyad's 'protection from interference' with breastfeeding, that no mother is saddled with a solitary duty to breastfeed, and that the duty toward breastfeeding falls on the whole community; she frames the mother's dependency on 'the kindness of strangers' via A Streetcar Named Desire and the innate 'breast crawl.'

applied-ethics.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
applied-ethics.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Parker interviews Stumptown's director of operations Matt Lounsbury, probing for a single underlying value that unifies the roaster's ethics and aesthetics. Lounsbury insists quality—'how good the coffee can be'—is the gravitational center that pulls ethical behavior (record-breaking direct-trade prices, building washing stations in Rwanda, full health care for baristas, the Meet the Producers program) into orbit, while Parker suspects a deeper commitment to community and justice. The exchange enacts the book's recurring ethics/aesthetics entanglement: whenever asked about one, Lounsbury 'slips into' the other, framing direct trade as a win-win-win business model rather than idealism.

applied-ethics.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
applied-ethics.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Bramucci and Mulholland use Kenyan smallholder farmers—Lucy Wanja, David Gachigi, Henry Maina, who earn $0.02–$0.10 per pound for coffee sold north for $12—to argue that fair-trade certification, while an improvement, secures only a 'minimum' wage and leaves growers trapped by mills, middlemen, and depressed global prices. They advance direct trade (Intelligentsia, Stumptown, and the author's own Safi Coffee, which makes farmers shareholders and pays up to twenty-fold more) as a more genuinely just alternative that invests in producers' long-term capacity. The ethical claim is that 'fair' as a sticker falls short of real equity, and that consumers' smug conscience is only earned by paying beyond the fair-trade minimum.

applied-ethics.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
applied-ethics.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Kirkwood argues that caffeine is uncontroversially a performance-enhancing drug—boosting memory, reaction time, endurance—and that by WADA's own three-part test (performance-enhancing, potentially harmful, against the spirit of sport) coffee should count as doping, yet never has. He dismantles the standard anti-doping arguments as applied to coffee: the cheating/unfairness charge is circular and dissolves when everyone may use it; the 'unnaturalness' argument commits a non sequitur (umbrellas are unnatural too, and chewed coffee beans seem natural); and the harm test fails because the positive threshold sits at a mere 20-ounce serving, far below caffeinism. His conclusion is that coffee escapes the 'doping' label not through moral reasoning but through public acceptance—the emotive word 'drug' is withheld from the substance everyone uses.

applied-ethics.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
applied-ethics.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Aleman, an ethnobotanist, asks 'Is coffee green?' and unpacks the many senses of 'green' (raw bean, naïve, money, and ecologically friendly) before weighing coffee's growth, organic and shade-grown methods, fair trade, globalization, and value chain. She judges coffee greenest at the source (shade-grown farms preserve migrating-bird habitat) but least green in the fossil-fueled journey from Global South farm to Global North cup, invoking Vandana Shiva's claim that 'drinking coffee is a political act' and Rigoberta Menchú on coffee and indigenous survival. She concludes the answer is partly subjective—withholding final judgment while resolving to keep drinking fair-trade, organic, shade-grown, single-source coffee—and warns of the cognitive dissonance, mirroring oil dependence, between judging coffee ungreen and drinking it anyway.

applied-ethics.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
applied-ethics.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Geist, a conservation biologist, argues from physiology (elastin-digesting enzymes, B12 need), athletics (one-legged balancing for stalking, precision throwing), and the herbivore-like pattern of human speciation that humans evolved as hunters — a 'carnivorous herbivore.' He contends morality itself was born from hunting: because tools-as-weapons (clubs, spears) let an aggressor kill without retaliation, escaping natural selection's check, early humans had to invent social taboos distinguishing right from wrong. He contrasts Neanderthal 'rodeo' close-quarters spearing with Cro-Magnon distance throwing, linking spear-tracking to endurance running, language, and art — concluding that questioning hunting's morality questions our humanity.

applied-ethics.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
applied-ethics.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Duerr surveys the worldwide 'Master/Mistress of Animals' figure (Artemis, the /Kaggen of the Bushmen, the Huaulu Lord of the Forest) as a mythic sanction against over-hunting, arguing that the near-universal guilt hunters feel over killing sentient, human-like game reflects a real moral dilemma. She invokes Singer's utilitarian claim that painlessly killing non-self-conscious animals whose deaths are compensated by replacement 'may not be wrong,' reading the mythic 'solutions' (denial, propitiation, taking only what you need, restoring bones so game is reborn) as a folk 'hunting code of ethics' that manages the wrong of ending a life without starting another.

applied-ethics.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
applied-ethics.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Darci Doll treats celebrity sex tapes (Pamela Anderson/Tommy Lee, Paris Hilton, Kim Kardashian, Colin Farrell) as a cautionary tale about privately recorded porn. She argues taping is defensible only with informed adult consent and agreed terms of distribution, then analyzes the appeal — celebrity obsession, voyeurism, and the fantasy of 'having sex with' a star — and the motives for release, including career boosts. Against these she sets the risks of theft, accident, and betrayal by a jilted ex, plus the 'sexting' problem among minors, concluding that because release is essentially irreversible, a sexually positive culture must protect trust rather than assume amateur tapes are safe from a market.

applied-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
applied-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: The editors' introduction argues that fashion, despite philosophers' contempt for it, raises serious questions in aesthetics, ethics, identity, and political philosophy. It surveys the volume's contributors: fashionability as an expert-plus-masses property (Prinz/Farennikova), Zangwill's alienation thesis, Russell on 'cool' as aesthetic virtue, the objectification of women through Barbie play and sweatshops, and Singer's demand (via the drowning-child argument) that spare money go to poverty relief rather than trendy clothes. It uses concrete cases — Ugg boots, the National Airlines 'Fly me' campaign, Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute, foot binding — to show fashion carries the zeitgeist and can both liberate and enslave.

applied-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
applied-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Farennikova and Prinz ask what makes something fashionable, arguing through thought experiments (Calvin Klein jeans, khakis, Robinson Crusoe's leather jacket, the accidental thrift-store punk, Gang Green, the mod couple) that four conditions must hold: many people wear the look, recognized experts endorse it, wearers intend to conform, and they regard it as having aesthetic value. They distinguish being fashionable from being merely popular or 'cool,' show fashionability is relative to group and to time, and note fashion must change to serve its signaling purpose — the Amish are 'intentionally unfashionable.'

applied-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
applied-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Pierlott examines sweatshops in the garment industry through the lens of ancient Cynicism (Antisthenes, the Stoics' Zeno of Citium and his thieving slave), using the Cynic critique of fashion-driven consumption to strip legitimacy from the demand that feeds sweatshops. He rebuts the 'inevitability argument' (comparing it to excusing the Holocaust as inevitable) and the free-choice defense using Aristotle's category of 'mixed' action — sweated workers' consent is coerced by desperate alternatives — and argues, via Adam Smith on the undervaluing of labor, that giant retailers like Wal-Mart distort natural labor prices. He stresses that sweatshops overwhelmingly exploit young women, tying objectification of women as fashion consumers to their oppression as producers.

applied-ethics.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
applied-ethics.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Cassidy, through an interior monologue of a shopper eyeing Indonesian-made sandals, weighs individual responsibility for consumerism. She contrasts Singer's drowning-child duty to relieve suffering with Pogge's 'you break it, you buy it' claim that the Global North caused Southern poverty, then uses Scheffler's 'restricted' common-sense responsibility and Cannon's butterfly-effect virtues (replacing the American Dream's acquisitiveness with interconnectedness). Adapting Claudia Card, she distinguishes three senses of responsibility — credit (backward-looking blame), management (of one's lifestyle), and care-taking — and, invoking Noddings's ethics of care, argues that since globalization's impact is uncertain we should shift from assigning blame to caring *about* distant workers, buying less out of boredom-driven habit.

applied-ethics.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
applied-ethics.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.

applied-ethics.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
applied-ethics.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Mark Mercer argues that a now largely secular Christmas can help build a liberal, rather than communitarian, multicultural society. He distinguishes liberal multiculturalism, which prizes each individual's flourishing and rests on respect, equality and decency, from communitarian multiculturalism, which treats cultural groups as basic units and breeds identity politics and envy. He detaches Christmas from its Christian origins – trees, lights and Santa now embodying good will and generosity rather than doctrine – and against those who would ban public displays or say only 'Season's Greetings', contends that a shared secular Christmas is one of the few common holidays that can bind citizens of a diverse society together.

applied-ethics.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: In this memoir (book Chapter 1, 'A Cannabis Odyssey'), Harvard psychiatrist Lester Grinspoon recounts how his 1967 review of the anti-marijuana literature convinced him he had been 'brainwashed' by a fear-based 'cannabis catechism,' coining 'cannabinophobia' and likening it to the 'madness of crowds.' He argues from personal use — hearing Sgt. Pepper for the first time, quitting psychoanalysis after 'stoned' self-critiques — that beyond recreation and medicine there is a third category, 'enhancement.' The piece is autobiographical drug-policy advocacy rather than the application of a specific named philosopher.

applied-ethics.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.

applied-ethics.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Holt and Kaufman's 'Marijuana and Creativity' surveys creativity research (Guilford's divergent thinking — fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) and US drug law (Anslinger, 'Reefer Madness,' Schedule I) to test the popular belief, held via figures like Cheech and Chong, Bob Marley and Willie Nelson, that cannabis boosts creativity. Controlled THC-vs-placebo biscuit studies show no benefit — placebo groups who merely believed they were high scored higher, while actual THC reduced fluency and flexibility. They explain the persistent belief through placebo/expectancy effects, spurious correlation, and salience bias, concluding any drug–creativity link is 'manufactured in the drug user's mind.'

applied-ethics.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Tahko surveys the empirical evidence on cannabis from the standpoint of the individual and of society, concluding that its health harms (respiratory illness, mild cognitive impairment, possible dependence, weak links to psychosis) pale beside those of alcohol and tobacco. He argues the gravest costs—legal risk, social isolation, contaminated black-market supply—are consequences of prohibition itself, not the drug. Endorsing public-health experts, he recommends abandoning elimination-based policy for a harm-reduction approach modeled on the Dutch coffee-shop system and Portuguese decriminalization.

applied-ethics.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Penrose subjects the 'soft drug / hard drug' distinction to conceptual analysis, arguing that—unlike genuinely graded soft-vs-hard eggs—it tracks no single real spectrum. He tests three candidate bases: phenomenological intensity of the high (incoherent, since 'comparable amounts' and interpersonal 'highness' can't be measured), addictiveness (fails, since the traditional distinction counts non-addictive LSD as 'hard'), and dangerousness (Nutt's Lancet study ranks cannabis as more dangerous than some 'hard' drugs, and the distinction trades on illicitly excluding legal alcohol and nicotine). He concludes drugs vary along many distinct property-lines, so the traditional binary is simply false.

applied-ethics.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Earleywine dissects the moral versus practical arguments over prohibition, attacking legal moralism—the drug-czar claim (Bennett, Wilson) that use is wrong simply because it is immoral—as circular, and noting that the law does not criminalize every immoral act (broken contracts, lying). He shows purported moral arguments collapse into utilitarian harm estimates that the data undercut, since use rates are essentially orthogonal to policy across Amsterdam, Australia, Portugal, and US states. He then weighs anti-prohibition rights arguments (religion, privacy in Ravin, property via Szasz, self-determination) and closes on proportionality: owning a harmless plant merits no punishment.

applied-ethics.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.

applied-ethics.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Heidi Howkins Lockwood examines the 'asymmetry thesis'—that a climber's gratuitous risk is less acceptable than an astronaut's necessary risk—and argues its two standard defenses fail: the Rule of Rescue is neither necessary (free soloists need no rescue yet are condemned) nor sufficient (Hornbein and Unsoeld's risky Everest traverse was praised because it succeeded), and the argument from compassion collapses into circularity. She then shows the intuition is really driven by external background assumptions, especially gender inequality: the media vilified climber-mother Alison Hargreaves while lauding astronaut-mother Christa McAuliffe, because ambition-for-profit violates the 'traditionally female' role of service. She concedes a limited, defensible version tied to the assumption that seeking risk as a mere end (rather than an ineliminable means) is irresponsible.

applied-ethics.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Pam Sailors distinguishes two kinds of high-altitude climber: the goal-oriented 'summiteer,' who pursues the summit at all costs for self-affirmation and may neglect others, and the process-oriented 'mountaineer,' who seeks relationship with the mountain, attains self-transcendence, and feels moral responsibility for comrades. Drawing on J. S. Russell and Jonathan Simon, and on cases like the 2006 abandonment of David Sharp versus Dan Mazur giving up his summit to save Lincoln Hall, she argues both types find value in dangerous sport but that the mountaineer—exhibiting courage, compassion, and care—is the morally better person. She backs this with Reinhold Messner, Ed Viesturs, and Sherpa judgment that mountains are not conquered but simply allow, or do not allow, us to climb them.

applied-ethics.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Philip Ebert and Simon Robertson defend the self-sufficiency thesis (S): other things being equal, the more self-sufficiently a mountaineering objective is achieved, the better the achievement. Ranking Hermann Buhl's solo, free, alpine-style first ascent of Nanga Parbat above a hypothetical roped-team version and far above a guided, oxygen-and-porter Everest ascent, they argue self-sufficiency (alpine over siege, solo over team, free over aid) is good because it is more committing and adventurous and is partly constitutive of mountaineering itself. They handle objections about foolhardiness (Lafaille on Makalu), incomparable routes (Lhotse South Face), teamwork, and blind climber Erik Weihenmayer via an 'other things being equal' clause, and conclude self-sufficiency acts as a catalyst raising the subjective difficulty and thus the value of every other mountaineering good.

applied-ethics.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
applied-ethics.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
applied-ethics.relation: Ramsey applies the methods of practical/applied ethics to the taboo of hold manufacturing ('chipping'), using Peter Singer's drowning-child argument as his model of following an argument to its uncomfortable conclusion. He builds a syllogism: since climbers accept modifying rock (removing loose rock, vegetation) to make routes climbable, and hold manufacturing is another such modification, manufacturing is sometimes acceptable. He dismantles four common objections (safety, environment, harming future climbers, slippery slope) to argue the near-universal condemnation of chipping is an unjustified bias inconsistent with climbers' actual practices, like the chiseled Jardine Traverse on The Nose.

applied-ethics.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
applied-ethics.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
applied-ethics.relation: Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant and clinical bioethicist, separates personal ethics, professional ethics, and bioethics, then evaluates tattooing through Beauchamp and Childress's principles—especially autonomy (intention, understanding, freedom from outside influence) weighed against risk versus benefit. He concludes tattooing is bioethically fine because safer pigments and market forces reduced its disease risks and because autonomy makes 'to ink or not' the patient's own call, echoing a Millian liberty that one's choice not harming others is 'none of your beeswax.' He ends by defending the memorial tattoo as therapeutic 'memory remodeling' that gluing a positive event in place with pain can make good for you.

applied-ethics.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
applied-ethics.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
applied-ethics.relation: Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.

applied-ethics.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
applied-ethics.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Abby Thompson, a somatic psychologist, sets Raja yoga metaphysics (five koshas, a blissful true self distinct from the ego, nadis and chakras as energy flow) beside clinical psychology's brain-chemistry, DSM model, arguing the two paradigms are complementary. Using warrior II and camel pose plus the neuroscience maxim 'neurons that fire together wire together,' she shows how yoga trains self-regulation, distinguishes constructive discomfort from injurious pain, and can serve as complementary therapy — with instructors bearing therapist-like responsibility for the emotional vulnerability and transference that arise on the mat.

applied-ethics.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
applied-ethics.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'

applied-ethics.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
applied-ethics.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.

applied-ethics.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
applied-ethics.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Anne Barnhill uses John Cusack's boom-box serenade in Say Anything, his poolside pleading in The Sure Thing, and Andy Bernard's 'Take a Chance on Me' serenade in The Office to defend 'prospective boundary violation'—violating a boundary that would not exist in a closer relationship in order to create that relationship. She rejects the Kantian reading of Korsgaard and Hill that treating people as ends forbids all non-rational manipulation, arguing instead that such charming pushiness is 'faking it till you make it,' which works via Aristotle's habituation whereby feelings catch up with actions. She then sets four rules (no harm, not too much closer too fast, genuinely wanting the relationship, and that the other would plausibly want it) to separate appropriate from wrong boundary violations.

applied-ethics.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
applied-ethics.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
applied-ethics.relation: Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.

applied-ethics.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
applied-ethics.title: Introduction
applied-ethics.relation: Thomas Fahy's editorial introduction frames the volume by comparing horror to his skydiving experience: both offer the thrill of confronting danger within a promise of safety. He organizes the collection's essays around morality, identity, cultural history, and aesthetics, previewing how each contributor yokes a pop-culture horror text to a philosopher (Nickel's skeptical reading of Psycho/The Birds, Morris on Kant and torture-horror, his own Hobbes reading of In Cold Blood, Lutz's Marx and Land of the Dead). He argues horror's 'play,' hybridity, and repetition let it raise questions about fear, suffering, justice, and the human capacity for violence.

applied-ethics.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
applied-ethics.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
applied-ethics.relation: Theodore Schick treats the Rings of Power as an allegory-free meditation on externalized 'potency,' applying it to emerging genetics, nanotechnology, and robotics. He contrasts the Council of Elrond's choice to destroy the Ring with Boromir's wish to wield it, and with Bill Joy's call to relinquish dangerous research versus Drexler's promise that nanotech could end poverty and disease. Schick argues our situation differs from Middle-earth because the knowledge cannot be un-forged, so grassroots social taming, not destruction of a single artifact, is the realistic response to knowledge-enabled mass destruction.

applied-ethics.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
applied-ethics.title: It’s Not That Simple
applied-ethics.relation: O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.

applied-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: 15. Grey’s Anatomy as Philosophy Ethical Ambiguity in Shades of Grey
applied-ethics.relation: The chapter argues that Meredith Grey embodies Simone de Beauvoir's existentialist ethics from The Ethics of Ambiguity, rejecting the childlike 'spirit of seriousness' that treats moral rules as absolute. Through episodes where Meredith stabilizes a bomb inside a patient's chest, coaches a death-row inmate to induce his own brain death, switches an Alzheimer's-trial placebo for Adele, and commits insurance fraud to treat an immigrant child, it shows her breaking institutional protocol to positively will the freedom of others while owning her choices. It contrasts her authentic embrace of moral ambiguity and risk against Shepherd's, Bailey's, and Webber's rule-bound seriousness or self-interest, framing medical dilemmas as an ambiguous moral realm where no single correct answer exists.

applied-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: 44. Gattaca as Philosophy Genoism and Justice
applied-ethics.relation: Grinnell argues Gattaca depicts a society built on 'intrinsic genoism' and diagnoses it with Rawls's justice as fairness. He adapts Appiah's distinction between racialism and intrinsic vs. extrinsic racism to genoism, showing that Valids like Josef, Anton, and Eugene treat In-valids like Vincent as inferior simply for being In-valid, discounting all counterevidence. Using Janet Radcliffe Richards's 'separate spheres' argument he shows the caste system is either superfluous or unjust, and via Kitcher's 'life theme' he argues nearly everyone — Vincent, Irene, Anton, Eugene — suffers a low quality of life from having their theme thrust upon them. He concludes that Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle would dismantle the separate spheres and give everyone a fair, autonomy-respecting shot at their chosen life.

applied-ethics.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
applied-ethics.title: 45. A.I. Artificial Intelligence as Philosophy Machine Consciousness and Intelligence
applied-ethics.relation: Gamez uses Spielberg/Kubrick's A.I. to separate three things the film conflates: intelligence, consciousness, and emotion. He argues intelligence is a functional property (David could pass a Turing test but a skilled interrogator would spot him), whereas consciousness is a physical property that cannot be inferred from David's human-like behavior — only a mathematical theory mapping physical to conscious states could tell whether David really experiences the love, fear, and pain that drive our empathy in the Flesh Fair. He insists the ethics of destroying mechas should hinge on their consciousness, not their intelligence, and connects David's engineered, irreversible imprinting-love to Lorenz's ethology and Damasio/James theories of emotion, and his eerie early behavior to Mori's uncanny valley.

existence-risk.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
existence-risk.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
existence-risk.relation: Theodore Schick takes Tolkien's remark that the Ring represents 'potency' externalized beyond its maker's control and applies it to emerging nanotechnology, genetics, and robotics. He sets Bill Joy's call for relinquishment against Eric Drexler's promise of universal assemblers, cell-repair machines, and soldier nanosuits, weighing the 'grey goo' risk against the Rings' own power to heal and preserve (Lothlórien, Bilbo 'well-preserved'). Against the Council of Elrond's solution of destroying the Ring, he argues our situation is disanalogous - Ring-making knowledge is now spread worldwide and there is no single device to destroy - so grass-roots social response, not bans, must tame the new technologies.

existence-risk.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
existence-risk.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
existence-risk.relation: Michael Ruse reads the 1968 film as a study in forbidden knowledge: Dr. Zaius has sealed the cave of human artifacts because he knows a prior human civilization destroyed itself and fears the knowledge could cause a repetition. Weighing nuclear weapons, recombinant DNA, bird-flu research, and data-driven political manipulation, Ruse argues Zaius's censorship is both impossible and undesirable, since the search for knowledge is intrinsically valuable and containment only increases the need for research. The film's deeper lesson is evolutionary: intelligence and sociality co-evolved only to the level 'good enough,' so any species that acquires weapons of mass destruction will likely destroy itself, meaning the Planet of the Apes scenario would recur across the universe.

existence-risk.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
existence-risk.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
existence-risk.relation: Michaud and Watkins blame Crichton and Malcolm for frightening us away from science, arguing that most life does not 'find a way' and that science is the shield keeping vulnerable humanity a step ahead of extinction by meteors, plagues, and predators. They take up Rousseau's anti-Enlightenment longing to return to nature and reject it, arguing that humility comes from science itself (a 13.72-billion-year-old Earth, Sagan's 'star stuff' making us the universe become conscious of itself), not from abandoning it. Hammond, not science, embodies the real arrogance: he was so certain he could not fail that he tested the park on his own grandchildren.

existence-risk.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
existence-risk.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
existence-risk.relation: Tim Jones argues the films show why Kant's Enlightenment ideal - the courage to use your own understanding without others' guidance, embodied in Hammond's isolated, independently funded genius - has become dangerous now that one man's project can shape the world future people must live in. He tracks Hammond's arc from dismissing Malcolm's review to conceding 'I was wrong', but shows in the sequels that one convert to caution cannot contain a technology: Ludlow ships a T. rex to San Diego and paragliding entrepreneurs land on Isla Sorna anyway, so the damage to future people is done before anyone repents. Against this he proposes Rupert Read's 'Guardians of the Future', a super jury that would veto laws and technologies threatening future people's basic needs - meaning Hammond should have been stopped before he started.

existence-risk.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
existence-risk.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
existence-risk.relation: Jannelle Poetzsch introduces Hans Jonas's imperative of responsibility - 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life' - through Malcolm's charge that scientists never ask whether they should, since nuclear and genetic power now reach people no old 'love thy neighbor' ethic could imagine. Hammond is Bacon's 'knowledge is power' grown too successful: his 'thintelligence' embodies the gap between the power to act and the ability to foretell, so Jonas demands humility, worst-case rather than optimistic planning, and social institutions strong enough to check people who act merely because they can. Jonas also indicts capitalism's profit motive - Hammond risked his grandchildren and Costa Rican infants to manufacture a need for a dinosaur zoo - closing that the answer is not halting technology but thoughtfully restraining it, because some things cannot be re-caged.

existence-risk.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
existence-risk.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
existence-risk.relation: Trip McCrossin takes Grant's 'they'll just have to evolve, too' as addressed to the audience and asks whether human behavior, not meteors, could cause our extinction, using Malcolm's toolkit: self-organizing life on fitness landscapes, the Red Queen arms race you must run to stay in place, and Gambler's Ruin - once things go bad they cluster and go to hell together. The deepest lens is the Tragedy of the Commons: like herders each adding a sheep to a shared pasture, we do what is best for ourselves without concern for the common good, and the films chart ever-failing 'fences' - the paddock, the coastline, the Navy, the Marines - until pteranodons simply fly off Isla Sorna. Since ours is self-destruction (we run as fast as we can, but really from ourselves), the real fence, he concludes, is daring ourselves to collective restraint.

existence-risk.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
existence-risk.title: 21. The Extended Fight
existence-risk.relation: Porot applies Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to the final Civil War fight: Iron Man extends his cognition technologically (Friday analyzing Cap's fight pattern mid-bout, JARVIS remembering to suggest calling Pepper), while Captain America extends his mind socially through trusted, autonomous teammates - 'Alright, Sam, what's the plan?' - and that social extension is precisely what wins when Bucky autonomously steps in.
