DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.

amor-fati.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
amor-fati.title: Shocks of Destiny
amor-fati.relation: Shores reads witchers and the Law of Surprise through Deleuze's figure of the sorcerer, the anomaly at the edge of the village who mutates through 'nuptials against nature' with unforeseeable outcomes - like the Trial of Grasses, which kills most initiates and leaves survivors infertile outcasts. He shows that the Law of Surprise, in Calanthe's words 'a game with chance, a game with destiny,' is exactly Deleuze's Nietzschean dicethrow: the throw affirms chance, the falling dice affirm necessity, an amor fati completed only through co-fated mutual affirmation ('the Sword of Destiny has two blades') among Geralt, Pavetta, and Ciri, with Chrysippus's co-fatedness supplying the logic. Pavetta's devastating cry at the betrothal banquet, scattering furniture and throne, figures the 'diabolical powers of the future' erupting into a contested present.

amor-fati.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy
amor-fati.title: The Olympics and Philosophy
amor-fati.relation: Scott Parker argues that distance runner Steve Prefontaine, who finished a medal-less fourth at Munich 1972, embodied the true essence of the Olympics better than any champion, an essence he identifies with Nietzsche's 'higher man' and Emerson's self-reliance rather than winning. He aligns Pre's front-running, effort, confidence, and will with Nietzschean self-overcoming and life-affirmation and Emersonian self-valuation, arguing value is what the valuer assigns himself through hard work. Reading Pre's exhausted stumble to the finish as a possible enactment of amor fati, love of fate, Parker holds that if Pre did his best he should love rather than merely accept his defeat.

amor-fati.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats
amor-fati.title: Wholly Communion Poetry, Philosophy, and Spontaneous Bop Cinema
amor-fati.relation: Sterritt reads Peter Whitehead's 1965 film 'Wholly Communion,' shot at London's International Poetry Incarnation, as 'spontaneous bop cinema' embodying Beat poetics through Bakhtin's dialogic/carnivalesque and the schizoanalysis of Deleuze and Guattari. Ginsberg's drunken recitation of 'The Change' becomes a 'body without organs' entering the 'chaosmos' on the plane of immanence; Jandl's sound poetry is pure Deleuzian sensation. Adrian Mitchell's anti-Vietnam 'To Whom It May Concern' is read through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati and Deleuze's 'difference in repetition,' its incantatory counter-words a materialist line of flight against the order-words of war.

amor-fati.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
amor-fati.title: Synecdoche, in Part
amor-fati.relation: Smith reads every Kaufman film as a farce about the self-defeating quest to 'become who you are,' with Synecdoche, New York as its culmination: Caden's MacArthur-funded attempt to represent all of life in a warehouse collapses into infinite regress because a representation of everything must contain itself. He frames Kaufman's films as Montaignean/Emersonian essays—fragmentary self-portraits—and argues the film's limits are death and language, since language always puts us at one remove from the life we already are. The transcendence it evokes is naturalistic, akin to Nietzsche's amor fati and Emerson's 'we are born to a whole': wholeness is not achieved but already possessed, and the hidden knowledge of it turns tragedy into farce.

amor-fati.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
amor-fati.title: Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman
amor-fati.relation: Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.

amor-fati.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
amor-fati.title: 9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends
amor-fati.relation: Potter and Cobb argue that Twin Peaks is a Romantic refusal of resolution: mysteries live by not being solved, so Lynch and Frost break the rules that stories need authors, protagonists who solve problems, and endings. They read Cooper's entrapment in a time loop through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati (quoting The Gay Science and The Will to Power), tie Wally Brando's Dharma speech and Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism to the theme, and argue the real 'story' is the endless meta-narrative co-created between the show and each viewer—Life itself as process without endpoint.

amor-fati.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
amor-fati.title: Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man
amor-fati.relation: Marc Furstenau reads Grizzly Man as Herzog's philosophy of nature, arguing that Herzog's vision of nature as chaos, hostility, and murder mirrors Schopenhauer's terrifying Will and the fact/value split, and that Herzog blames Timothy Treadwell's sentimental faith in natural harmony for his and Amie Huguenard's deaths while secretly sharing Treadwell's amor fati. Using Iris Murdoch's Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals and Mary Midgley's Beast and Man, Furstenau contends that both Herzog and Schopenhauer succumb to an 'outrageous simplicity' that denies animal agency; against them he argues, via Midgley, that culture is natural and interspecies sympathy is real, reading Treadwell's extreme close-up of the bear (where Herzog sees 'only the overwhelming indifference of nature') as evidence of imaginative continuity between human and animal.

amor-fati.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
amor-fati.title: Life A Celebration
amor-fati.relation: Adam Riggio uses Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche to cast the Simm Master as a nihilist who, having seen the valueless dying universe at Utopia, wills nothingness and universal destruction out of ressentiment. The Doctor is Nietzsche's Overman who overcomes the reactive forces of revenge: in 'Dalek' he recognizes his own vengefulness and turns from it, and in 'Last of the Time Lords' he defeats the Master not with Martha's fake gun but by saying 'I forgive you,' affirming finite life with a 'beneficent Yes-saying' rather than surrendering to enmity.

amor-fati.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
amor-fati.title: 1. Human, All Too Human
amor-fati.relation: Holdier reads Supernatural's finale through Nietzsche, arguing that Chuck's exposure as a cruel author-God and his defeat by the Winchesters dramatizes the 'death of God' as the freedom to invent one's own meaning. Dean and Sam's stubborn refusal to 'stay down' on the lakeshore against Chuck embodies amor fati—saying yes to circumstance—while Jack, birthed and taught by ordinary humans, becomes the Ubermensch who replaces God, showing humanity as a bridge to something greater than itself.

amor-fati.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
amor-fati.title: 12. Nietzsche and the Fascist Dimension The Case of Ernst Jünger
amor-fati.relation: Ohana locates fascism's 'nihilistic-totalitarian syndrome' in the Janus-faced combination of Nietzschean nihilism and the Overman's will to power, whereby ethics is replaced by aesthetics and the self-creating 'new man' shapes reality ex nihilo. He reads Ernst Jünger's Stahlgewittern, Der Arbeiter and 'Total Mobilization' as the aestheticization of war and technology into a work-state, and traces Heidegger's fascination with Jünger's 'will to will' back to Nietzsche and Hölderlin—arguing that, following Camus, one cannot ignore the directionless dynamism leading from Nietzschean perspectivism toward Rosenberg's marching-column politics.

amor-fati.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
amor-fati.title: My Troubles Are Going to Have Troubles with Me Schopenhauer, Pessimism, and Nietzsche
amor-fati.relation: Jacob Held pits Schopenhauer's pessimism against Nietzschean affirmation using I Had Trouble in Getting to Solla Sollew. He reads Schopenhauer's will-to-life and 'pendulum between pain and boredom' into Seuss's endlessly striving characters, and treats the mirage-towns Solla Sollew and Boola Boo Ball as proof there is no escape from suffering. The protagonist's final line, 'I've bought a big bat... now my troubles are going to have troubles with me,' becomes Nietzsche's yes-saying: instead of the ascetic renunciation Schopenhauer prescribes, Seuss's child-hero affirms life, redeeming its accidents the way Nietzsche's eternal-recurrence thought experiment and 'become a child' passage in Zarathustra demand.

amor-fati.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
amor-fati.title: “Gan Is Dead”
amor-fati.relation: Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.

amor-fati.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
amor-fati.title: Shock Value A Deleuzean Encounter with James Purdy's Narrow Rooms
amor-fati.relation: Gross stages a Deleuze-and-Guattari 'encounter' with Purdy's Narrow Rooms, refusing Freudian or Marxist 'interpretosis' in favor of asking what the novel does. He reads Roy Sturtevant the 'renderer' as a multiplicity and traces the characters' becomings-animal (Sid's 'becoming-shark' in the locker-room sex act, becoming-horse, becoming-insect) and the crucifixion of Roy on the barn door as horror that dissolves the boundaries between master and slave, lover and torturer. Invoking Deleuze's debt to Spinoza, Nietzsche, and the Stoics, Gross argues that the joyful amor fati of art embraces horror as an expansion of life rather than something to be vanquished.

amor-fati.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
amor-fati.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
amor-fati.relation: Eric Bronson reads the elves of Rivendell and especially Lothlorien through the 'merrier' existentialists, arguing that lasting joy requires facing the abyss and still affirming life, and knowing, as Nietzsche urged, what to remember and what to forget. Galadriel sings in dark times yet is burdened by remembering too much, unable to let go of her cursed past, so her regret shows the danger Jaspers and Arendt also diagnosed of losing oneself. When she refuses Frodo's Ring and chooses to 'diminish and remain Galadriel,' she embodies the existentialist's affirmation and trust in one's own inner light.

amor-fati.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
amor-fati.title: Epilogue
amor-fati.relation: The closing essay exhorts readers to 'approach life as the Doctor'—engaged, compassionate, and critically thinking—insisting each person is important and that fandom passion, even when fractious, expresses the Doctor's engaged life (invoking Voltaire on free expression). Using 'Father's Day' and 'The Day of the Doctor,' it argues we cannot change the past but must seize the present, and ties 'truth' and 'trust' to a shared root to claim a meaningful life requires trusting oneself and others rather than merely proving oneself right. It affirms that wisdom is lived truth, that being wrong is how we mature, and that courage is doing what must be done while afraid.

death-of-god.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
death-of-god.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.

death-of-god.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
death-of-god.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings in part as a protest against modernism - the post-WWI mood (Berman, Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', Nietzsche's 'God is dead') that tradition is obsolete and whatever can be done must be done. The heroes win by remembering: Gandalf alone thinks to watch the Shire, Sam's book-learning about elves and the password 'Elbereth' saves the day at Cirith Ungol, while Saruman and Denethor fall into modern despair through the palantír and Pippin's stone dropped in Moria brings Gandalf down. The Ring itself is modernism's false promise of remaking the world, and Tolkien answers it with a fantasy where ancient lore has tangible power - sealed by Pippin's maturing into one of Middle-earth's great librarians.

death-of-god.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_
death-of-god.title: And There Is No Escape
death-of-god.relation: Abrams reads Allen through Foucault's panopticon: modern society is unlimited voyeurism in which the medieval God whose 'eyes are on us always' has been replaced by the omniscient gaze of Film — Cliff's exposé documentary forcing Lester to watch his own life in Crimes and Misdemeanors, Tom Baxter stepping off the screen in The Purple Rose of Cairo, and the nested eavesdropping layers of Another Woman, which he counts to infinity via Noël Carroll's 'mass art'. Against Mary Nichols's virtue-ethics reading, he argues Allen's ethics is Nietzschean self-fashioning: Judah lives 'beyond good and evil' where Raskolnikov failed, Allan Felix sheds the Bogart alter ego and 'gives style' to his character in Play It Again, Sam, while Eve in Interiors stages Hegel's master–slave dialectic, the 'master' artist dependent for her identity on those she objectifies.

death-of-god.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
death-of-god.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.

death-of-god.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
death-of-god.title: Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)
death-of-god.relation: Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.

death-of-god.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
death-of-god.title: And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism
death-of-god.relation: Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.

death-of-god.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
death-of-god.title: Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life
death-of-god.relation: Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.

death-of-god.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
death-of-god.title: U2 and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Malpas takes The Joshua Tree as an album about place: its desert imagery and restless movement ('Where the Streets Have No Name', 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' as 'an anthem of doubt more than faith') carry the listener from Ireland to Reagan's America to Pinochet's Chile, while its political references - Ethiopian famine, El Salvador, Dublin high-rises - always work through concrete locations rather than abstract ideals. Using Heidegger on homelessness as the inability to dwell, and Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air', he argues that modernity has not erased our relatedness to place but covered it over. The album's desolation is therefore readable the other way: belonging is constituted through care, commitment and uncertain journeying in the places we already are ('Heartland').

death-of-god.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
death-of-god.title: James Bond and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Butterfield takes Bond's answer to Elektra in The World Is Not Enough - he survives by 'tak[ing] pleasure in great beauty' - and asks whether hedonism can answer the problem of suffering and death. She reads Bond through Heidegger's being-towards-death (quoting Live and Let Die's 'You start to die the moment you are born'), then diagnoses him as Kierkegaard's aesthetic 'seducer', an immature escapist who dreads boredom and flees commitment, before rehabilitating him with Nietzsche and Camus: Bond flushing the cyanide pill down the toilet in From Russia with Love and Mathis's advice in Casino Royale to make evil 'personal' show Bond creating his own values beyond good and evil, surviving the absurd through style and personal vendetta. Bond emerges as an existentialist role model for courage and creativity, though we should not copy his hedonism or lawlessness.

death-of-god.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
death-of-god.title: Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia
death-of-god.relation: Peter Fosl reads Metallica's lyrics ("Leper Messiah," "The God That Failed," "One," "To Live Is to Die," "Escape") as extending Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: religion as slave morality born of ressentiment and as opium deadening the oppressed, illustrated by the landmine veteran of "One" pleading with a silent God and Hetfield's abandoned-childhood grief. He argues the band often falls into the "incomplete nihilism" Nietzsche predicted, lamenting God's failure and longing nostalgically for the Christian meaning it can no longer believe in rather than transvaluating values. Yet the defiance of "The Four Horsemen" and "Escape" and the band's creative power show it also working toward an overcoming of Christian nihilism, confirmed for Fosl by Hetfield's post-rehab health.

death-of-god.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
death-of-god.title: Rupert’s Response and Responsibility
death-of-god.relation: Biderman and Jacobowitz read Rope through Nietzsche: Brandon and Philip strangle their classmate David as would-be Nietzschean supermen, acting on mentor Rupert Cadell's cocktail-party theory that murder can be an art for a superior few. The chapter explains the will to power, the Ubermensch, and the death of God, then argues Brandon is no superman: he kills from weakness and a bully's need for an audience, mistaking crass destruction for the refined self-creation Nietzsche demanded, just as the fascist appropriation of Nietzsche fails. Rupert's horrified final speech, renouncing 'superior or inferior beings' and insisting each of us is 'a separate human being,' raises whether a teacher can disavow responsibility when students act out his provocative ideas: ideas have consequences, and the only true test of a philosophy is whether we can live by it.

death-of-god.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
death-of-god.title: Kill Bill Volume 2 Mommy Kills Daddy
death-of-god.relation: Mark Conard reads the two Kill Bill volumes as Tarantino's Oedipal play and self-therapy: Volume 1 fuses the movie genres of his childhood with women in the lead roles while Bill lurks as the absent, godlike father, and the Bride's empowerment is traced from the Pussy Wagon through the Hanzo sword—a transformation from 'pussy to cock'. In Volume 2, Pai Mei teaches her that her strength lies in her own hands, freeing her from a masculine conception of power, while Bill is humanized—sandwiches, flute-playing, a heart that can break—so that killing him means killing the father's God-like hold, explicitly glossed through Nietzsche's death of God. The final duel's sheathed sword lets the woman, as woman, defeat the man, and the Oedipal act succeeds where Oedipus himself had to go blind.

death-of-god.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
death-of-god.title: Like Caine in Kung Fu
death-of-god.relation: Bence Nanay and Ian Schnee argue Pulp Fiction is genuinely Nietzschean, but not by celebrating violence: the film stages the crisis of meaning after God's death through two reactions to chance. Vincent is the passive nihilist—dogmatically insisting the six bullets mean nothing, inheriting gangster values unquestioned, modeling himself on Elvis—while Jules's 'moment of clarity' makes him a Nietzschean free spirit who creates perspective-relative meaning and breaks the cycle of violence by buying Ringo and Honey Bunny's lives. His plan to 'walk the earth, like Caine in Kung Fu' reworks Zarathustra's wandering, and the running toilets gag marks Vincent's blindness to the significance of events, which is why only one of them survives.

death-of-god.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
death-of-god.title: There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark
death-of-god.relation: Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.

death-of-god.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
death-of-god.title: Meaning The Final Frontier
death-of-god.relation: Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.

death-of-god.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
death-of-god.title: Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight
death-of-god.relation: Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.

death-of-god.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
death-of-god.title: Game Over
death-of-god.relation: Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.

death-of-god.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
death-of-god.title: Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle
death-of-god.relation: Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.

death-of-god.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
death-of-god.title: The Missionary
death-of-god.relation: Christopher Hoyt reads Buffett's escape from Catholicism as a case study in secular meaning-making after Nietzsche's death of God, taking the Mardi Gras ritual of Folly swatting Death out of town as Buffett's core spiritual attitude — interpreted the way Wittgenstein criticized Frazer, as an expression of our stance toward death rather than mere magic. Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' frames the post-1960s task of self-definition without God, while Marx's alienation explains what the persona of *Jimmy* refuses: the impersonal work and borrowed values that leave moderns living an alien narrative, like McGuane's character Skelton in Ninety-Two in the Shade. The twist is that *Jimmy*'s pop-culture vocabulary — Tully Mars built from Donovan's Reef and Slim Pickens, Bogart, the Brylcreem jingle — is itself authentic, and the 'semi-true story' of the myth tells deeper truths than a literal biography could, making Buffett something like a pop prophet for late modernity.

death-of-god.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
death-of-god.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.

death-of-god.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
death-of-god.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Fairweather casts the campaign against Pullman's books as Socrates's trial rerun (impiety plus corrupting the young) and asks whether legally protected speech can still be morally wrong, weighing Mill's On Liberty point that children lack the 'maturity of their faculties' against the charge that Pullman's 'killing God' rhetoric inflicts spiritual violence on young believers, by his own image of intercision. The answer comes through Nietzsche's Three Metamorphoses: Asriel, Will, and Lyra play the lion that slays the great 'thou shalt' of the Authority, but the lion's destruction is only the possibility of freedom, since full freedom is Nietzsche's child creating its own values rather than lapsing into nihilism or Sartrean bad faith. Pullman's Republic of Heaven, with its virtues of courage, compassion, love, kindness, and curiosity held in community, is a social ideal rather than a radically Nietzschean one, so the charge of corrupting young readers is deflated.

death-of-god.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
death-of-god.title: Death Knight as Overman
death-of-god.relation: Luke Cuddy asks whether playing WoW can answer nihilism, using Schopenhauer's bleak remark on our sudden existence and Nietzsche's death of God to set up the problem — King Bangalash dies and WoW goes on, just as humans die and the universe continues. Entering Huizinga's Magic Circle gives Azeroth its meanings, but the player must then dissolve the circle, recognize that the game itself is meaningless, and keep playing anyway — creating the toon as a work of art in the Dionysian spirit. A maxed Death Knight still is not Nietzsche's Overman, because the player affirms only her in-game existence; the fifth step is carrying that self-creation back into real life.

death-of-god.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
death-of-god.title: Oh to Be a Gooner
death-of-god.relation: Kilpatrick reads Nietzsche's madman's question 'what sacred games shall we have to invent?' as answered by the stadium: after the death of God, soccer has replaced religion as the shared narrative where modern communities make and worship heroes. Using The Birth of Tragedy, he reads a goal as an Apollonian–Dionysian fusion—the scorer's individuated ecstasy merging with the collective joy of teammates and fans—and, on Nietzsche's claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, argues the game is defensible only when played creatively and artistically rather than by negative, win-at-all-costs tactics. Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism (the state as 'the new idol', the 'good European', Zarathustra's 'children's land') means club over country, and Wenger's Arsenal—with its dietary and training laboratory at London Colney cultivating an Overman, its Invincibles season, and its young, passport-blind signings—emerges as the club Nietzsche would support through its very will-to-power.

death-of-god.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
death-of-god.title: Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.

death-of-god.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
death-of-god.title: Get Serious
death-of-god.relation: David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.

death-of-god.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
death-of-god.title: I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You
death-of-god.relation: Reads the Doctor as a Christ-figure and savior (the 'Voyage of the Damned' ascension that drew Christian Voice protests, Martha's year of gospel-telling in 'The Last of the Time Lords'), applying Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideals onto God. But the show under Russell T Davies also distrusts godlike power: Davros's 'you made this' accusation, the Racnoss massacre, and Joan Redfern's question in 'The Family of Blood' show the lonely god's devastation. Against this, companions like Donna embody Nietzsche's Übermensch ('There's no such thing as an ordinary human'), so the chapter concludes the Doctor and ordinary humans need each other, mutually overcoming their weaknesses.

death-of-god.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
death-of-god.title: The Ethics of Dexter’s Appeal
death-of-god.relation: James F. Pontuso reconstructs Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals - promise-keeping, the unpayable debt to ancestor-founders that becomes God, cruelty turned inward as bad conscience, and Christianity's divine self-ransom that only deepens guilt - to explain why Dexter, who feels no guilt, is not abnormal but a man before morality. Following Gibbon's picture of Roman soldiers whose civil religion justified slaughter without remorse, he imagines Dexter thriving in the legions ('Dexter SPQR') rather than hiding behind Harry's Code, and argues the show appeals because Aristotle's ethics concerned outward conduct and justice rather than inner conscience. In our levelled age we secretly crave what Nietzsche craved: the sight of 'something perfect... still capable of inspiring fear.'

death-of-god.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
death-of-god.title: His Work Is Its Own Reward
death-of-god.relation: Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.

death-of-god.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
death-of-god.title: The New Man or the Old
death-of-god.relation: Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'

death-of-god.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!
death-of-god.title: Neil Gaiman and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.

death-of-god.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
death-of-god.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Zanelotti takes up the charge that Larry is a self-hating Jew, from whistling Wagner to 'The End,' where learning he is a gentile turns him into a churchgoing enthusiast who sings 'Go Tell It on the Mountain' and gives Richard Lewis his kidney. Sartre's bad faith diagnoses both poles: Larry denying his facticity by imagining he can simply shed his Jewish past and re-adopt it at will, and critics who demand he live up to an 'authentic' Jewish essence; Marx's false consciousness, meanwhile, explains the self-hating baldy who buys into the haired agenda. Using Ronald de Sousa's rejection of the 'Just Joking Defense'—we are accountable for laughter because we let ourselves become people who cannot restrain it—the chapter argues the show sets a comic frame that mocks bad faith rather than Judaism. Its deeper target, via Nietzsche's death of God, is the overenthusiastic meaning we manufacture when faith is 'curbed,' which is why Larry ridicules only public displays of religion, not belief itself.

death-of-god.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
death-of-god.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.

death-of-god.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
death-of-god.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'

death-of-god.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
death-of-god.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Kenn Fisher reads the franchise as the extinction of the Great Chain of Being: from Plato's humans mid-way between gods and beasts, through Genesis dominion and Descartes's non-conscious animals, to Malcolm's 'God creates man. Man destroys God. Man creates dinosaurs' - with computers (Hammond's control room, Wikipedia, Google) replacing God at the top. He then tracks animals' ascent from property: Francione on welfare versus personhood, Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', and Singer's equality-as-prescription, applied to Dieter Stark tasering a compy (punished by the compys) versus the unexamined electric fences that keep InGen's 'zoo animals' caged. He closes with Carol Adams's meat-masculinity link - Roland Tembo will hunt only a male T. rex, the dinosaurs are all female - and holds up vegetarian Lex as hope that the Chain bends into a Circle.

death-of-god.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
death-of-god.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Namvol argues that 'Glob' is the post-apocalyptic corpse of the Christian God: combining Don Cupitt's claim that gods live only in worship and practice with Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' he traces how the Mushroom War destroyed the believers, churches, and rituals that kept God alive, leaving Ooo an empty exclamation. Pantheism fails as a rescue because evil is native to Ooo's nature (Gunter, the eternally self-existing Abadeer), so God cannot simply have become the land. Against Dostoevsky's 'without God all things are permitted,' the chapter sides with Žižek—that morality's shadow, guilt, outlives God—as when Finn's self-regulation kicks in after 'All the Little People' and 'Dungeon Train,' making Finn, not Glob, the true savior of a godless world.

death-of-god.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
death-of-god.title: Dracula and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.

death-of-god.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
death-of-god.title: 17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence
death-of-god.relation: Christopher Ketcham asks whether primogeniture and entail make Downton Abbey a social embodiment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence - the same estate, without revision, turned over generation after generation like the eternal hourglass of existence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he tests royal continuity against death duties, the nihilism of industrial capitalism, and the Great War that killed heirs and empires, and borrows Kant's categorical imperative as an analogy for Britain's uniquely preserved 'royal categorical imperative' of continuity. The Abbey's recurrence survives only anthropomorphically - Violet, the family, the servants, and the tenants as its living organs - and the chapter wonders whether such ossified continuity, like dinosaur bones, is really eternal.

death-of-god.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
death-of-god.title: 10. The Light from Friendship
death-of-god.relation: Pavelich sets Aristotle's account of friendship - recognized and reciprocated goodwill between equals, perfected in the friendship of the good who 'share our souls', a standard met only by Jack and Bella Crawford - against Nietzsche's friendship as striving between overmen, who honor 'one's best enemy' in the friend and grow through conflict. He reads Hannibal's treatment of Will (hiding the encephalitis, framing him, serving the Nietzschean trout) as Nietzschean friend-making - Lies that are supposed to spur Will's growth, consistent with an Übermensch who tells Will 'Killing must feel good to God' and says 'I don't hide from God' - while Will's masquerade of friendship is betrayal in both senses, since Will seeks an Aristotelian soulmate and finds a killer he must stop. Because each betrays the other, neither Aristotelian nor Nietzschean friendship survives, though the moments before the Mizumono bloodbath - Hannibal inviting Will to just walk away - glimpse a real friendship already made impossible.

death-of-god.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
death-of-god.title: 1. Reading the Signs
death-of-god.relation: Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'

death-of-god.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
death-of-god.title: 1. Everything’s Amazing and Nobody’s Happy
death-of-god.relation: Max Elder reads Louis through Nietzsche's Gay Science claim that all philosophy is unconscious memoir, arguing Louis's confession-like comedy reveals dark truths we would rather flee - the Conan 'everything's amazing and nobody's happy' bit, the 'I know the darkness' exchange with the Christian woman, and the Subway/Pamela scene where a homeless man bathes behind a subway violinist. Using Nietzsche's line that man alone laughs because he suffers so deeply, and The Birth of Tragedy's comic as the artistic discharge of the nausea of absurdity, the chapter argues Louis's laughter performs a gestalt switch that ties the ugly to the beautiful and so redeems it. It reads the religions-supply-meaning argument - God's mockery-laughter versus Nietzsche's holy laughter - as the reason redemption now happens in comedy clubs rather than churches, and closes with Louie's 'Country Drive' scolding of Jane ('you don't get to be bored') as Nietzschean embrace of the amazing fact of being alive.

death-of-god.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
death-of-god.title: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
death-of-god.relation: Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.

death-of-god.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
death-of-god.title: 5. How Heroes Argue
death-of-god.relation: LaBauve opens with a staged Justice League debate over rescuing the Joker's hostages, where Batman's emotional, vengeance-tinged appeal loses to Superman's trust-based plea, and reads it through Aristotle's On Rhetoric: Batman persuades almost entirely by pathos (the relatable brokenness of Nolan's trilogy) with detective's logos, while Superman balances pathos, logos, and above all ethos, since Aristotle calls the speaker's character the strongest appeal. Against Max Landis's claim that Superman is irrelevant, he pairs the Death of Superman with Nietzsche's "God is dead" parable and the Kill Bill monologue to argue that Superman is a mythology of virtue - alongside real moral heroes like Gandhi, King, and Jesus - showing humans the ideal they ought to become, so Superman not only wins but must win.

death-of-god.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
death-of-god.title: 6. The God We Need Now
death-of-god.relation: Ketcham stages the essay as a 1939 diary (a boyhood piece longing for a new god now that the biblical God has, he feels, abandoned the Depression-era world) followed by an old man's reread: America made Superman its messiah - born in a flash of light like the star of Bethlehem, canonized by DC's "publishing synod" much as the church redacted the New Testament - but he suspects the god will age as badly as the God of Abraham. Rereading after Korea, Vietnam, and Wall Street scandals, he argues we now need and worship a darker god modeled on Hades: the rich, hidden, vengeful billionaire Bruce Wayne, whose subterranean mansion, Cerberus-like Alfred, and tax-break tributes from citizens mirror the underworld god and Greek sacrifice. He ends imagining our grandchildren's next god as a cyber-god of AI, and declares Batman, not Superman, the god we need now.

death-of-god.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
death-of-god.title: 10. Gods Are Overrated
death-of-god.relation: Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.

death-of-god.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
death-of-god.title: 18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool
death-of-god.relation: The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.

death-of-god.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
death-of-god.title: 8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir
death-of-god.relation: Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.

death-of-god.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
death-of-god.title: 11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them
death-of-god.relation: Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.

death-of-god.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
death-of-god.title: 3. Mermen and Dismemberment
death-of-god.relation: Contends that Hendrix's discord is philosophy-as-discord: 'I Don't Live Today' (the Native American dead-in-life), the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' with its bombs and sirens against sporting-event sentimentality, 'Machine Gun,' and 'House Burning Down' lacerate listeners so they actually feel war's atrocities instead of parroting patriotic clichés. Against this the chapter sets the oceanic, womb-like escape fantasies of '1983 (A Merman I Should Turn to Be)' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' treating them through Schopenhauer as metaphysical consolation, Marx's opiate, and Nietzsche's 'hangman's metaphysics,' and concludes that Hendrix finally refuses such world-denying illusions — and Heideggerian inauthentic withdrawal — in favor of existential engagement with suffering here and now.

death-of-god.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
death-of-god.title: 11. 999 Fingers
death-of-god.relation: Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.

death-of-god.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
death-of-god.title: 19. Nineteen Eighty-Four’s Religion
death-of-god.relation: Crossley and Markou trace Orwell's ambivalence about religion — a lifelong atheist who loved the Church of England's liturgy — into the novel: Goldstein's book repeats the socialist critique of priests who 'softened by promises of compensation in an imaginary world beyond the grave' propped up hierarchy, yet the Party then occupies religion's vacant place itself, with O'Brien as 'priest of power', Goldstein as arch-heretic, and 'Thou art' replacing the old despotisms' 'Thou shalt not'. They argue Orwell thought a purer socialism needed the communal goods of religion, from the proles' fuzzy 'Christianness' to the radical Christian tradition of the Diggers and Levellers, and read Ingsoc as that utopian tradition betrayed. The novel's warning is therefore double: what fills the gap when religion dies, and how religion itself can be a blueprint for totalitarianism.

death-of-god.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
death-of-god.title: Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing
death-of-god.relation: The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.

death-of-god.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
death-of-god.title: 8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need
death-of-god.relation: Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.

death-of-god.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
death-of-god.title: 14. After the Blackout
death-of-god.relation: Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.

death-of-god.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
death-of-god.title: 5. RuPaul versus Zarathustra
death-of-god.relation: The van der Wielen sisters read RuPaul against Nietzsche's Zarathustra: both are outcasts who descend from solitude bearing a spiritual teaching in a marketplace that mocks them, and both announce that inherited values are ungrounded — Zarathustra through the death of God and the call to become the over-man, Ru through 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' and the cosmic life force that makes every identity a costume. But where Zarathustra refuses followers and shuns the people's values, Ru's creed polices female stereotypes (long hair, breasts, heels) and pulls the cart of consumerist values — money, fame, individualism — so that she comes to resemble the priests and wise men Zarathustra condemns. Her openly admitted fakeness and opportunism (the Wigstock 'gender fuck' abandoned for the glamazon brand) leave the chapter asking who flies higher: the tragic free spirit or the pragmatic, honestly dishonest superstar.

death-of-god.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
death-of-god.title: 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning
death-of-god.relation: Montoya reads Chidi's breakdown upon learning he has been tortured for three hundred years as Nietzsche's death of God, quoting the Parable of the Madman from 'Jeremy Bearimy' to show how the guaranteed meaning of Chidi's worldview collapses into nihilism. Michael's midlife-crisis makeover and partying embody Camus's embrace of the absurd, while Sartre's existence precedes essence, abandonment, and anguish explain why Eleanor's confession to Michael and her sacrifice in the Judge's test count as authentic choices. With the Judge's verdict stripping away any hope of reward, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake, which the chapter presents as the show's answer to nihilism.

death-of-god.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
death-of-god.title: 2. What Does Life Mean after the Snap
death-of-god.relation: This chapter reads four post-Snap Avengers as existentialist answers to how life keeps meaning after catastrophe. Tony Stark embodies Sartre's existence precedes essence, defining himself through free choice up to his final 'I am Iron Man' snap that erases Thanos and his army; the merged Professor Hulk lives Camus's Sisyphus, embracing the absurd and concluding 'all is well' after watching his own past rage; Captain America lives Levinas's ethics of the Other, from refusing to abandon brainwashed Bucky in Civil War to wielding Mjolnir to save Thor; and Ronin-era Hawkeye enacts Nietzschean nihilism until Black Widow's Vormir sacrifice, read through Zarathustra's burning in one's own flame, restores his meaning. The authors conclude Marvel's answer is affirmation: courage to affirm freedom, the Other, and life itself against Thanos as personification of genocide, climate change, and war.

death-of-god.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
death-of-god.title: “You are…a beautiful, beautiful, butterfly”
death-of-god.relation: Argues the Xenomorph realizes Nietzsche's Ubermensch: it is what Ash describes - unclouded by 'conscience, remorse, or delusions of morality' - and perfects its predatory function down to its acidic blood, while paycheck-fixated crewmen like Brett and Parker are Nietzsche's complacent 'last men,' the type Zarathustra's townspeople clamor for. The alien's egg-Facehugger-Chestburster-adult metamorphosis maps onto the camel, lion, and child of the three metamorphoses of the spirit, and the chapter closes by wondering whether the creature's monstrosity might have made Nietzsche himself reconsider the vital perfection he preached.

death-of-god.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
death-of-god.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
death-of-god.relation: William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.

death-of-god.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
death-of-god.title: A Shared Higher Thirst
death-of-god.relation: Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.

death-of-god.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
death-of-god.title: 17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence
death-of-god.relation: Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.

death-of-god.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
death-of-god.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.

death-of-god.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
death-of-god.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.

death-of-god.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
death-of-god.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Christopher Wood reads Cloud's arc as an existentialist quest: Heidegger's thrownness in Cloud's tumble off the Midgar train and his initial 'It's not my problem' denial of being-in-the-world; Nietzsche's death of God in Mako-powered Midgar's nihilism, with AVALANCHE as a call for revaluation of values and Sephiroth as a false aspirant god; and Sartre's bad faith in Cloud 'playing at being a SOLDIER,' a persona borrowed wholesale from Zack along with his sword and mercenary dream. Through the Lifestream reunion with Tifa, Cloud faces his fabricated past, admits 'I never was in SOLDIER,' and turns to authenticity by resolving to live without pretending, which Wood presents as the player's own existential task.

death-of-god.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
death-of-god.title: 8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning
death-of-god.relation: Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.

death-of-god.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_
death-of-god.title: 8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse
death-of-god.relation: Duncan Gale reads Raiders through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the Nazis' contempt for those they exploit ('They hire only strong backs and they pay pennies') enacts master morality, while their ressentiment-driven project is itself a fatal misreading — both of the Ark and of Nietzsche, whom Walter Kaufmann shows was distorted by his anti-Semitic sister rather than responsible for it. Indy emerges as an overman candidate whose improvised self-legislation ('I'm making this up as I go,' casually shooting the scimitar-wielding warrior) creates life-affirming values, unlike Belloq, who has no code at all. The finale inverts the death of God: the Nazis die because they disturb a divine power they cannot harness, while America's de facto agnosticism — warehousing the Ark with 'top men' — proves the survivable response to nihilism.

death-of-god.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
death-of-god.title: Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight
death-of-god.relation: Toni Fellela gives an existentialist reading of Zelda, confessing she leaves Ocarina of Time and Twilight Princess permanently paused before the final Ganon fight because the meaning lies in the process of becoming, not the ending. Sartre's existence precedes essence structures Link's growth from a swordless Kokiri boy collecting equipment into the hero; Nietzsche's death of God ('we must become gods') fits Link restoring meaning to a godless Hyrule, while Camus's Sisyphus dignifies the repetitive drudge work of slashing grass for rupees.
