Viktor Frankl's logotherapy anchors the chapter's payoff: even the most mundane tasks — in a camp or a laundromat or Hyrule Field — become bearable and meaningful when connected to a future goal, which is why the author can play for four hours straight.

death-of-god.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
death-of-god.title: This Search Goes On: Christian, Warrior, Buddhist
death-of-god.relation: William Irwin traces Hetfield's journey through three sets of virtues: rejecting the Christian virtues of his Christian Science upbringing ('The God That Failed' as Nietzschean slave morality and Marx's opium of the masses), adopting the warrior virtues of Kill 'Em All (life as Hobbesian war, Nietzsche's will to power and 'no remorse'), and finally embracing Buddhist virtues on St. Anger. The warrior code fails without stoicism and collapses into addiction and despair, while the four noble truths - suffering caused by craving ('Frantic', 'Sweet Amber') - fit Hetfield's recovery and growing compassion.

death-of-god.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
death-of-god.title: Metallica, Nietzsche, and Marx: The Immorality of Morality
death-of-god.relation: Peter Fosl argues Metallica's moral critique of religion in 'Leper Messiah' and 'The God That Failed' continues Nietzsche's genealogy of Christian slave morality born of ressentiment and Marx's 'opium of the people': religion gathers a docile herd, denies this world, and exercises power through sin and forgiveness. He diagnoses the band as often stuck in Nietzsche's incomplete nihilism - 'To Live is to Die' longs nostalgically for the Kingdom of Salvation - while 'Escape' and the sheer creative power of the music show a genuine Nietzschean transvaluation and overcoming of Christianity.

death-of-god.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
death-of-god.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.

death-of-god.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
death-of-god.title: Notes
death-of-god.relation: Victor Grech presents Klingons as a cultural pastiche—Mongol horde stereotypes, Japanese Bushido, Viking Valhalla, Shakespeare 'restored to the original Klingon'—whose 1500-year honor code and embrace of honorable death (Klag's dishonored father, Jadzia's rebuke of Kang) make them Nietzschean Ubermenschen who slew their own gods, echoing Nietzsche's 'God is dead'. The Kahless clone of 'Rightful Heir' ('perhaps the words are more important than the man') shows a messianism surviving deicide. He then reads Worf through Roland Barthes's 'Occidentalism' and one-way acculturation—Picard praising Worf's 'humanity' after 'Reunion'—while Azetbur's 'human rights' is racist jab in The Undiscovered Country and Trekkers' Klingon cosplay raise cultural relativism and appropriation.

death-of-god.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
death-of-god.title: Notes
death-of-god.relation: Argues that despite Roddenberry's strident atheism, Star Trek develops a "humanist theology": godlike beings - Gary Mitchell, Charlie X, Trelane, Q, and Apollo in "Who Mourns for Adonais?" - are demoted to powerful aliens whose demand for worship disqualifies them as gods, echoing the 1960s death-of-God theology in which god-figures are consistently disappointing and the God of traditional theism is symbolically dead. Divinity is relocated into a possible human future requiring compassion above power - Kirk's charge to the dying Mitchell that "a god needs compassion", and Picard's "perhaps there's a residue of humanity in Q after all". The chapter also weighs Trek's anti-posthuman bias ("Dr. Korby was never here", the Borg) against the consensual Decker-V'Ger union in The Motion Picture, and reads Star Trek V's "What does God need with a starship?" as the uneasy remainder of Shatner's religiosity inside Roddenberry's secular vision.

death-of-god.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
death-of-god.title: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
death-of-god.relation: Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.

death-of-god.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
death-of-god.title: 6. The God We Need Now
death-of-god.relation: Ketcham frames a fictional 1939 memoir asking which god a god-forsaken age gets: Depression-era America needed Superman as a messiah (Siegel and Shuster as gospel-writers, DC's clerics redrawing him all-good like the church editing the New Testament), but a jaded modern America, he argues, now worships the dark billionaire as a Hades figure — Wayne Manor's hidden underworld with Alfred as Cerberus, the rich sacrificed to like Greeks propitiating Zeus. Superman is dismissed as unattainable alien fiction while Bruce Wayne is the self-made god of the American dream, with the essay ending on the prospect of a cybergod for his grandchildren.

death-of-god.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
death-of-god.title: 10. Gods Are Overrated
death-of-god.relation: Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.

death-of-god.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
death-of-god.title: 21. Batman Is Superman
death-of-god.relation: Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.

death-of-god.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
death-of-god.title: H O N O R
death-of-god.relation: This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.

death-of-god.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
death-of-god.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
death-of-god.relation: Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.

death-of-god.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
death-of-god.title: The Human Comedy Perpetuates Itself Nihilism and Comedy in Coen Neo-Noir
death-of-god.relation: Hibbs argues that neo-noir turns classic noir's grim fatalism comic by making nihilism a working assumption, and that Nietzsche supplies the diagnosis: the 'death of God,' the passive 'last man,' and the aristocratic 'pathos of distance' of will-to-power super-antiheroes (Hannibal Lecter, the villains of Cape Fear/Basic Instinct). He reads The Big Lebowski as the Coens' comic leveling of nihilism, with Walter insisting the Germans are 'nihilists' and 'cowards' and the Dude 'abiding,' showing that full nihilism cannot be lived. In Fargo and Raising Arizona, Marge's 'banality of virtue' (a comic counterpoint to Arendt's banality of evil) and the resilience of familial/procreative instinct reassert a comic order over the noir trap.

death-of-god.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
death-of-god.title: “Takin’ ’er Easy for All Us Sinners” Laziness as a Virtue in The Big Lebowski
death-of-god.relation: Douglass and Walls read the Dude's 'principled laziness' as a coherent ethos and test it against the film's rival worldviews: the villains' hollow nihilism (which they distinguish from Nietzsche's will to power and death-of-God), Bunny's Aristippan hedonism versus Epicurus, the Big Lebowski's Nietzschean master-morality egoism, and Walter Sobchak's rules-worship read through Kant's categorical imperative and Locke's social contract. They argue dude-ism works as a personal path to contentment but, lacking any objective standard, cannot condemn true evil like Bunny's threatened murder, exposing its purposeless-universe premise as its real flaw.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: Foreword
death-of-god.relation: Robert Porfirio's foreword traces film noir's dark sensibility to a native strain in American culture rather than only to imported existentialism, running from Puritan gloom through Poe, Melville, and Hawthorne to the hard-boiled pulp of Hammett, Chandler, and Woolrich. He argues that William James's pragmatism sounded the death knell of the Emersonian/Thoreauvian transcendentalist faith in self-reliance and nature, leaving the way open for Darwinism, Freudianism, and Nietzschean pessimism to reduce the individual to a 'waif amidst forces.' He connects this to the Germanic emigres who brought expressionist style, suggesting they were drawn to an American darkness already present, and closes wondering what post-9/11 neo-noir will make of the same fear and paranoia.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: Introduction
death-of-god.relation: Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: Nietzsche and the Meaning and Definition of Noir
death-of-god.relation: Mark Conard uses The Postman Always Rings Twice and Goodis's Night Squad to survey the failed attempts to define noir (genre, style, cycle, mood) and contrasts two theories of definition: Socrates/Plato's search for the essential form versus Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, in which no stable 'being' exists behind becoming and language falsifies a world in motion, making essences and definitions fictions ('I am afraid we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar'). He proposes that noir is best understood as an American artistic response to Nietzsche's death of God, the loss of transcendent meaning and value that produces noir's pessimism, alienation, and moral disorientation, citing Sam Spade shrugging off his partner's murder and Ole Andersen passively awaiting his killers. Ironically, the same flux that makes noir what it is (the death of God) is what makes noir impossible to define.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir
death-of-god.relation: Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: From Sherlock Holmes to the Hard-Boiled Detective in Film Noir
death-of-god.relation: Jerold Abrams argues that the noir detective inherits the Holmes/Dupin detective logic but inhabits a fundamentally different maze. Using Eco's three labyrinths, he maps the classical Greek maze (with faith as Ariadne's string) and the mannerist maze (with Cartesian/Kantian pure reason) onto the escapable world of classic detection, and the Deleuzian rhizomatic maze, born after Nietzsche dissolved reason into will to power, onto noir's inescapable world (The Third Man, Kiss Me Deadly, The Maltese Falcon's fake statue). He shows both detectives use Peircean abduction (the logic of guessing) rather than pure deduction, illustrating it with knife-wound examples and Calloway's trapdoor inference in The Third Man, while the noir femme fatale becomes the anti-Ariadne whose thread of clues leads only to the hangman's rope.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent
death-of-god.relation: Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.

death-of-god.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
death-of-god.title: Symbolism, Meaning, and Nihilism in Quentin TaranTino's Pulp Fiction
death-of-god.relation: Conard reads Pulp Fiction as a study of American nihilism in Nietzsche's 'God is dead' sense: with no transcendent framework of value, Jules and Vincent orient their lives by transient pop-culture icons (Jack Rabbit Slim's, the Fonz) and by Marsellus Wallace's arbitrary power, so the mysterious briefcase has worth only because he wills it. He contrasts this void with Aristotelian ethics, where a thing's good lies in realizing its rational essence. Jules's transformation begins when he survives the misfired shots and reinterprets his Ezekiel 25:17 recitation as a call to be 'the Shepherd,' while Butch's choice of the samurai sword over the baseball bat signals a return to an objective warrior code beyond the empty pop icons.

death-of-god.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
death-of-god.title: Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard
death-of-god.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.

death-of-god.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
death-of-god.title: Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams
death-of-god.relation: Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.

death-of-god.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
death-of-god.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
death-of-god.relation: Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.

death-of-god.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
death-of-god.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
death-of-god.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.

death-of-god.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
death-of-god.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
death-of-god.relation: Palmer reads The Shining through Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity as a 'perpetual present' that has lost its past and can only cannibalize it as pastiche and nostalgia film. He argues Kubrick's film enacts an 'anti-nostalgia' that invokes the nostalgic impulse—Jack Torrance's wish to escape an empty present into the Overlook's endless 1921 party—only to destroy him with it, refusing the genre's happy-ending wish-fulfillment. Drawing on Baudrillard's image of art 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness' merely 'playing with the pieces,' he casts Jack, endlessly typing 'All work and no play,' as the failed postmodern artist trapped between times, reduced to pointless Nietzschean ressentiment, with the film's Nietzschean death-of-God flux underlying its refusal of stable meaning.

death-of-god.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
death-of-god.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
death-of-god.relation: Abrams argues that 2001 films the whole evolutionary arc of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, from ape-men through humanity to the Star Child as the overman/posthuman. He maps the moon monolith's discovery onto the death of God (science debunking the creation myth, guarded by a Platonic 'noble lie' cover-up), the astronauts Bowman/Poole/Floyd onto the Enlightenment 'higher men,' and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus his and Poole's fatal spacewalks onto the last man and the falling tightrope walker whom Zarathustra carries. He then extends the vision toward Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's 'mind children,' while criticizing Kubrick for replacing Nietzsche's godless self-overcoming with alien 'replacement gods' that thin out the death-of-God insight.

death-of-god.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
death-of-god.title: The Sopranos, Film Noir, and Nihilism
death-of-god.relation: Kevin Stoehr reads The Sopranos as TV noir built on Nietzsche's passive, life-negating nihilism: Tony Soprano's 'What do we got?' laments the collapse of mob and family values, Uncle Junior's 'Each of us is alone in the fuckin' universe' voices noir alienation, and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' is the series' nihilistic creed. A.J.'s confirmation-eve rebellion reading Nietzsche and Camus's The Stranger ('Death just shows the ultimate absurdity of life') dramatizes the death of God inherited by the next generation. The chapter's dark irony is that therapy, meant to give Tony narrative unity and self-knowledge, becomes an instrument of self-deception: he substitutes psychology for ethics, rationalizes adultery and murder as signs of psychic power, and fails at Nietzschean self-overcoming despite the ducks and Pie-O-My that briefly symbolize transcendence.

death-of-god.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
death-of-god.title: “Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch
death-of-god.relation: Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.

death-of-god.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
death-of-god.title: I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You
death-of-god.relation: Ruth Deller reads the Doctor as a savior/redeemer figure onto whom fans project ideals, invoking Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideal self onto Christ, then pivots to Nietzsche. Rather than a flawless Messiah, the Doctor is a flawed being who must overcome himself, and his 'ordinary' companions (Donna, Harriet Jones, the Hostess in 'Midnight', Rose in 'Turn Left') exemplify Nietzsche's Ubermensch by rising above their weaknesses. She argues the Doctor and humans have a symbiotic relationship: the universe needs a savior, but that savior must be challenged, so both overcome themselves together.

death-of-god.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
death-of-god.title: 1. Human, All Too Human
death-of-god.relation: Holdier reads Supernatural's finale through Nietzsche, arguing that Chuck's exposure as a cruel author-God and his defeat by the Winchesters dramatizes the 'death of God' as the freedom to invent one's own meaning. Dean and Sam's stubborn refusal to 'stay down' on the lakeshore against Chuck embodies amor fati—saying yes to circumstance—while Jack, birthed and taught by ordinary humans, becomes the Ubermensch who replaces God, showing humanity as a bridge to something greater than itself.

death-of-god.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
death-of-god.title: 9. God the Programmer Is Dead
death-of-god.relation: De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.

death-of-god.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
death-of-god.title: 6. When Punks Grow Up
death-of-god.relation: Meagher asks whether punks can mature, arguing via Sartre and Beauvoir that punk revolts against the 'spirit of seriousness' - the bad faith of treating values as externally imposed by God, law, or convention - and against the weak nihilism that merely abandons valuing after serious values fail. Following Devon Johnson's Black nihilism distinction, mature punk is strong nihilism: destroying decadent (Euromodern, colonial) values in order to create new ones, building scenes, labels, and institutions for future generations, fighting for others' freedom and decolonization as Arendtian politics, and - with Nietzsche's dead God and Crass's 1978 declaration - being willing to proclaim even punk itself dead.

death-of-god.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
death-of-god.title: Introduction
death-of-god.relation: Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.

death-of-god.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
death-of-god.title: 3. Experiences with Nietzsche
death-of-god.relation: Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.

death-of-god.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
death-of-god.title: 5. Nietzsche and the Jews
death-of-god.relation: Brinker surveys Duffy-Mittelman, Santaniello, and Yovel to argue that reading Nietzsche as simply pro-Jewish oversimplifies a genuine ambivalence toward the 'Jewish race' running through all periods of Jewish history. He shows that in The Antichrist Nietzsche separates ressentiment from decadence: Jesus is the 'most perfect decadent' incapable of hatred, while Paul and the priests embody ressentiment, and the Jews, being too strong to be decadent, cunningly poison their conquerors with a faith they do not share—an old anti-Semitic stereotype transplanted into new soil. Brinker concludes this ambivalence, plus Nietzsche's post-Zarathustra equation of equality, democracy, and socialism with slave-morality decadence, is exactly what let the Nazis manipulate him.

death-of-god.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
death-of-god.title: 6. Nietzsche contra Wagner on the Jews
death-of-god.relation: Yovel reads Nietzsche's break with Wagner as a self-overcoming that freed him to hand Wagner's redemptive role—catalyst of a new Dionysian Europe—to the modern secular Jews Wagner despised. He maps a structured ambivalence: fierce anti-anti-Semitism (grounded philosophically in Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism, racism, the state-cult, and ressentiment) coexisting with a fierce critique of ancient 'priestly' Judaism as the genealogical root of Christian slave morality. Contrasting Nietzsche with Wagner's Judaism in Music, he shows Wagner legitimized public hate-speech (dramatized in Siegfried's gratuitous loathing of Mime) while Nietzsche prized self-mastery, so the two men's later Nazi abuse—by Elisabeth and Winifred, the two 'women-priests'—rests on opposite relations to what each actually held.

death-of-god.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
death-of-god.title: 7. Between the Cross and the Swastika A Nietzschean Perspective
death-of-god.relation: Wistrich answers the charge that Nietzsche was a philosophical godfather of fascism by marshalling his biography and letters—the 'shoot all anti-Semites' twilight notes, the rupture with the anti-Semite Förster and with Wagner, the praise of Heine, Offenbach, and Spinoza. He distinguishes Nietzsche's demonization of Christianity and priestly Judaism as the 'slave revolt in morals' from his admiration for biblical and Diaspora Jews as Europe's toughest race and a possible catalyst of the Übermensch, arguing that the Nazi and Hitlerian echoes (via Table Talk and Rosenberg's forgeries) grossly distort a 'good European' who denounced nationalism, racism, and the state-cult, and would have been repelled by the swastika.

death-of-god.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
death-of-god.title: 14. Critique as Apologetics Nolte’s Interpretation of Nietzsche
death-of-god.relation: Stackelberg critiques Ernst Nolte's essentialist reading, in which Nietzsche's Ecce Homo 'party of life' and its call for the 'ruthless destruction of all that is degenerate' furnish the counter-concept of extermination mirroring Marx, dignifying fascism as an anti-Bolshevik European civil war. He shows Nolte must explain away Nietzsche's denunciations of anti-Semitism, nationalism, the Reich and Wagner, and counters that Nazism was itself a moralistic 'slave revolt'—the ascetic, purity-seeking mentality Nietzsche attacked—so that Nietzsche's real susceptibility to Nazi use lies in his shared anti-egalitarian enemies and his refusal of concrete social analysis, not in an exterminatory program.

death-of-god.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
death-of-god.title: Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia
death-of-god.relation: Peter Fosl reads Metallica lyrics through Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: 'Leper Messiah' and 'The God that Failed' cast religion as a slave morality born of ressentiment and as Marx's 'opium' that pacifies the exploited. He asks whether Metallica achieves Nietzsche's transvaluation of values or stays trapped in 'incomplete nihilism' - songs like 'One' and 'To Live is to Die' longing nostalgically for the God that failed - while 'Escape' and 'The Four Horsemen' point toward a life-affirming overcoming of Christianity.

death-of-god.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
death-of-god.title: “Gan Is Dead”
death-of-god.relation: Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.

death-of-god.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
death-of-god.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
death-of-god.relation: Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.

death-of-god.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
death-of-god.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
death-of-god.relation: Hales uses Nietzsche's verdict that truth matters less than a myth's usefulness (The Gay Science, The Anti-Christ) to argue Santa Claus is a truer exemplar of Christmas than Jesus. He traces Nietzsche's account of God's degeneration from a proud tribal mascot like Yahweh into a trivialized 'domestic servant,' and the 'death of God' as belief becoming useless. Documenting Christmas's commercial, pagan origins (Sol Invictus, Saturnalia, Mithras on December 25), he casts Santa as a practical, this-worldly demigod propped up by movies and NORAD — a giver who, unlike the credit-demanding Christian God, wants no thanks, embodying anonymous selfless generosity and thus the god Nietzsche awaited.

death-of-god.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
death-of-god.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Douglas Blount casts Sauron as a candidate for Nietzsche's Ubermensch, embodying the unabashed will to power in a world where God is dead, life is meaningless, and taste rather than reason or morality guides the self-created life. Tolkien answers this not by argument but by a rival portrait whose beauty lies in community, humility, love, and self-sacrifice: Gandalf dying on the bridge, Frodo's mercy to Gollum, and Sam refusing the Ring's vision of 'Samwise the Strong.' Blount argues that on Nietzsche's own criterion of taste, Tolkien's picture of abnegation is the more compelling vision of a life lived well.

death-of-god.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
death-of-god.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
death-of-god.relation: Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, the mood that 'all that is solid melts into air' and that the past no longer matters, voiced by Marx, Freud, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead.' Tolkien's heroes survive because they remember lore and tradition (Gandalf watching the Shire, Sam's book-learning at Cirith Ungol), while Saruman and Denethor embody modern despair: they misuse the palantir, lose faith in tradition, and can only try to destroy the present. Against Berman's claim that there is no escape from modernism, Kraus reads Middle-earth as a fantasy where clinging to tradition still yields real, tangible power and certainty.

death-of-god.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
death-of-god.title: Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia
death-of-god.relation: Fosl argues that Metallica's lyrics echo Nietzsche's and Marx's moral critiques of Christianity: songs like "Leper Messiah" and "The God that Failed" cast religion as slave-morality ressentiment, mind-control, and Marx's "opium of the people." He then asks whether the band achieves a Nietzschean transvaluation or lapses into the very nihilism Nietzsche said Christianity breeds — reading "To Live is to Die" and "One" as nostalgic death-wish, but "Escape" and "The Four Horsemen" as genuine defiant self-overcoming after the death of God.

death-of-god.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
death-of-god.title: 38. The Big Lebowski Nihilism, Masculinity, and Abiding Virtue
death-of-god.relation: Fosl argues that The Big Lebowski critiques traditional masculine ideals (soldier, tycoon, detective, patriarch) and offers in The Dude an alternative 'abiding' virtue rooted in Epicurean contented poverty and ataraxia (his simple pleasures, White Russians, and indifference to property), Aristotelian civic friendship or philia with Walter and Donny that holds a divided polity together, and a Wittgenstein/Aristotle-informed flexibility about applying rules that positions The Dude at a mean between Walter's rigid absolutism and the nihilists' deficiency. Most centrally the film confronts Nietzschean European nihilism ('God is dead'); The Dude answers it as a halfway Ubermensch through comedy, friendship, and Kierkegaardian and Camusian existential repetition (bowling as rolling the rock, Sisyphus made meaningful), abiding and reproducing his form of life against despair, death, and disillusionment.

epicurean-death.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
epicurean-death.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift. The Ringwraiths show that existence can be worse than death - undead kings whose frustrated nature is perpetual torment - while Socrates in the Apology, Lucretius, Sartre, and Camus supply reasons not to fear annihilation, and the elves' endless life raises Boethius's and Bernard Williams's problem of boring immortality (Camus's Sisyphus, Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged). He concludes that Arwen and Aragorn, uncommonly wise and loving, accept death as Ilúvatar's gift: she prefers a finite life of deep love, and they trust the old stories of a world 'remade' beyond the circles of Arda.

epicurean-death.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
epicurean-death.title: The Approaching Battle
epicurean-death.relation: Introduces the chapter's Heideggerian frame: authenticity comes from facing mortality rather than evading it, against the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is merely the end of experience and so happens to no one; death's imminence forces us to define ourselves and not live half-asleep. Harry, death-marked since infancy, lives authentically where Voldemort lives inauthentically, with Plato's dictum that true philosophers make dying their profession as ancient corroboration.

epicurean-death.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
epicurean-death.title: Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It
epicurean-death.relation: Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead and why we rank it worse than death, restricting himself to unfriendly vampires and zombies (setting aside soulful exceptions like Angel, Spike, Louis, and Ed from Shaun of the Dead). He tests Nagel's deprivation view (vampires gain infinite experiences, so nothing is deprived) and Williams's desire-frustration view (undeath replaces rather than frustrates desires: scotch for blood, pork roast for raw flesh), then Mill's better-Socrates-dissatisfied comparison and the thought that the Undead's evil nature makes undeath objectively bad. Each fails, so he concludes undeath is not objectively bad, only comparatively bad, and one might as well make the best of it.

epicurean-death.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
epicurean-death.title: Deserving to Be a Vampire
epicurean-death.relation: Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through Forever Knight's Nick draining his lover, Blade feeding on stored blood, and The Lost Boys' promise that Michael will 'never grow old'. He argues vampires are not evil by nature: if they cannot control their hunger they are pitied rather than blamed (though we remain Aristotle-responsible for choosing to become addicted), and consensual, non-lethal feeding is no worse than mortals eating animals, since the bite only becomes murder by choice. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, he uses Furley and Nussbaum's deprivation view - death vindictively empties our long-term projects like marriage or a career - so vampiric immortality genuinely preserves value, while the standard boredom objection fails because there are repeatable pleasures in a changing world. The thought experiment ends as moral psychology for mortals: since neither of us will become a vampire, live a life that would be worthy of eternity.

epicurean-death.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
epicurean-death.title: I’ll Get Up and Fly Away
epicurean-death.relation: Ian Duckles and Eric Rubenstein use the community's losses of Pigpen and Jerry Garcia to ask whether death is bad, running Epicurus's argument that being dead is no experience and hence no harm, the tedium-of-immortality argument that eternal life would eventually exhaust every fundamental desire, and Socrates's Phaedo claim that death frees the soul to philosophize — which disturbingly implies Pigpen's early 'burn out' was the better fate. Their resolution is Heidegger: authentically confronting death as the end of all possibilities strips socially imposed values (consumerist 'keeping up with the Joneses') and frees us to create our own projects, so mortality itself is something to be grateful for. On this reading the Deadhead counterculture — rejecting 1950s suburban scripts for free love, psychedelics, and life on tour — lived Heideggerian authenticity, and it is better to fade away (like Garcia) than to burn out (like Pigpen).

epicurean-death.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
epicurean-death.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Greene applies the philosophy of death to Pullman's worlds, starting from the Epicurean puzzle that death is bad only if experienced, so it cannot be bad, plus the asymmetry puzzle about prenatal non-existence, then testing the Deprivation View (Father Gomez's bullet would rob Lyra of Oxford, the alethiometer, and love) and the Desire-Frustration View (Iorek's frustrated desires) against a universe whose dead do persist as ghosts. The world of the dead, with its harpies, eternal boredom, and the pain of leaving Pan with the Boatman, seems to refute Epicurus by making death a miserable experience after all. But the twist reframes everything: the dead who stream through Will's knife-hole to dissolve into Dust are choosing death over the afterlife, and since for them the good things of life are already off the table, death is not bad at all, which is exactly why they choose it.

epicurean-death.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
epicurean-death.title: Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It
epicurean-death.relation: Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead, and why it seems worse than death, testing vampire and zombie cases against the standard accounts of death's badness. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' sets the experiential-blank frame, but Nagel's deprivation view fails because immortal vampires lose far fewer goods than they gain, and Williams's desire-frustration view fails because zombification replaces desires (scotch for blood) rather than frustrating cancelled ones. Mill's 'better Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied' comparison also falls short since it yields only comparative, not objective, badness; Greene concludes Undeath is dreaded because the Undead do evil things, but no argument shows it is objectively bad, so one might as well make the best of it.

epicurean-death.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
epicurean-death.title: Deserving to Be a Vampire
epicurean-death.relation: Ted Preston asks whether becoming a vampire would be morally good or desirable, working through The Lost Boys, Underworld, Blade, Forever Knight, and Interview with the Vampire. He argues vampirism is not intrinsically immoral: if vampires cannot restrain their feeding we pity rather than blame them, though with Aristotle we still hold people responsible for choosing to become the kind of being that cannot; and feeding need be no worse than mortal carnivory, since consensual feeding (Blade's stored blood, Karen Jenson's donation, Madeleine's offer to Louis) makes the bite more like dentistry with consent than assault. On desirability he weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the Furley-Nussbaum claim that death deprives a life of its long-term projects and relationships, concluding immortality's appeal is rational and that boredom is not inevitable in a changing world. The thought experiment ends in ethics: vampire or mortal, a life's worth depends on choices, so live a life worthy of eternity.

epicurean-death.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
epicurean-death.title: Futurama and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Salazar takes Professor Farnsworth's cry that the crew's age regression in 'Teenage Mutant Leela's Hurdles' will end in 'a fate worse than death: pre-life! Then death' as a test of whether death is bad. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' says death cannot be experienced, so the deprivation account of Nagel's 'Death' is needed to explain how death is bad for the one deprived of a valuable future - a dispute staged by Bender's suicide-booth despair in 'Space Pilot 3000' after learning his bending built the booths. The chapter then argues losing one's identity and values can be worse than death (Bender's and Fry's flight from career-chip assignments, the Professor's love of being 161, Leela's frustrated teen redo), closing with Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning and Leela's sacrifice of her regained youth: inner integrity, not erasing the past, makes life worth living.

epicurean-death.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
epicurean-death.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.

epicurean-death.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
epicurean-death.title: The Devil and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Clint Jones argues LaVey's Satanic Bible rests on a misreading of Epicurus: genuine Epicurean hedonism is not limitless indulgence but the ordered life of the Tetrapharmakon - don't fear gods or death, the good is easy to get, pain is endurable - together with the threefold division of desires, which reserves constant gratification for natural and necessary things like water, bread, and friendship. By licensing gluttony and every whim so long as no one else is hurt, LaVeyan Satanism fails as the pleasure-as-virtue philosophy it claims to revive, leaving its followers with base, unfulfilling pleasures that are, well, Hellish.

epicurean-death.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
epicurean-death.title: The Devil and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Magus Peter Gilmore closes the exchange: LaVeyan Satanism honestly embraces the selfishness most people already live by (sharing Ayn Rand's enshrined self-interest), and Epicurus's own letters to Menoeceus - on not fearing death, choosing the most pleasant over the longest life, pragmatic justice, and the need for natural science - show deep congruence with LaVey. Against Pitkänen on Eastern religions, whose reincarnation and karmic debt he reads as denigration of carnal existence, and against Jones's shaky-foundation charge (Christianity itself was a Hebraic/Hellenic mash-up), he concludes Satanists are proud 'Hell-raisers' celebrating the only life there is.

epicurean-death.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
epicurean-death.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.

epicurean-death.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
epicurean-death.title: 1. Reading the Signs
epicurean-death.relation: Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'

epicurean-death.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
epicurean-death.title: 15. My Zombie, My Self
epicurean-death.relation: Greene asks what Walking Dead-type walkers are and answers with the Platonic method of definition learned from Socrates: place them in the genus undead (died but not at rest, neither alive nor dead) and differentiate them by differentia - corporeal, mindless, lacking superhuman or magical powers, still decomposing. Aristotle's hierarchy of life functions (nutrition, locomotion, reason) explains why walkers are not alive despite ambulating, and the standards of death (putrefaction, heart-lung, whole-brain, higher-brain) all certify that walkers are dead yet active. The chapter closes on personal identity - whether you survive becoming a zombie, as Carol's face at the barn and Carl's "she'll turn" about Lori presuppose - and admits the author chooses the self-interested reading that he could become his own zombie, for the sake of the scare.

epicurean-death.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
epicurean-death.title: 6. You’re Gonna Die
epicurean-death.relation: Ethan Mills uses the Buddha and Epicurus to show that Louis meets death with laughter instead of fear. The Buddha's diagnosis of dukkha ('dissatisfactoriness') explains the Blu-Ray player and cellphone bits - consumer desire just restarts the craving cycle - and impermanence frames both the Amia heartbreak that Dr. Bigelow reframes as 'misery is wasted on the miserable' and Louie's 'life isn't that long... it's happy math' reflection, while rebirth would only make things worse since you would have to repeat junior high forever. Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us (where death is, you are not) grounds Louie's 'lots of things happen after you die, just none of them include you,' backed by atomism - at death our atoms scatter - and by gods who, like Louie's maybe-God with no heaven, guarantee no immortality. The USO duckling episode models the payoff: comedy defuses our deepest anxiety about annihilation the way it defuses the soldiers' tension in Afghanistan.

epicurean-death.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
epicurean-death.title: 21. After Death It Can Get Worse
epicurean-death.relation: Sam Director asks whether Amazon's unauthorized changes to Dick's novel posthumously harmed him, and against Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus claim that the dead no longer exist to be harmed, he defends harm as desire-frustration that need not be experienced (Childan's unknown counterfeit antiques, Juliana's deception by Joe) and can involve desires reaching past death (Baynes's Operation Dandelion warning dying with Tedeki). Since Dick delighted in the Blade Runner footage and wanted science fiction to thrive, the chapter concludes the TV adaptation fulfilled rather than thwarted his desires — he is no worse off, maybe better off.

epicurean-death.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
epicurean-death.title: 13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness
epicurean-death.relation: The chapter diagnoses Rick's 'Wubba Lubba dub-dub' ('I am in great pain, please help me') as chronic Epicurean suffering and prescribes the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure. Don't fear the gods: Epicurus's indifferent atomist gods versus Rick's atheism, his panic prayer in 'A Rickle in Time', and Toxic Rick's 'If god exists, it's me' as ego rather than argument. Don't fear death, since 'where death is, I am not', though infinite replacements make Rick and Morty fear each other's death rather than their own. The good is easy to get, so booze, Eyeholes, and Szechuan sauce must yield to water, friends, and family; and the terrible is easy to endure, as when Rick stops resenting Birdperson's wedding and finally turns himself in for his family.

epicurean-death.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
epicurean-death.title: 16. Death Becomes Her
epicurean-death.relation: Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.

epicurean-death.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
epicurean-death.title: Batman Forever
epicurean-death.relation: Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.

epicurean-death.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
epicurean-death.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: O'Loughlin reads Walter biting off a nihilist's ear and the Dude refusing to walk out on league play as concrete realizations of ancient friendship: Aristotle's eudaimonia requires friends as 'second selves' whose shared activity (bowling in the friends' company) structures the excellent life, while Epicurus's Garden ordered life around simple pleasures and ataraxia, with friendship supplying pleasant memory and a kind of immortality after death. Because we moderns claim friendship's value without practicing its costs, the Dude's priorities look comic yet pierce us — and Donny's death, the Ralph's coffee can, and 'let's go bowling' become Epicurean commemoration rather than irreverence.

epicurean-death.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
epicurean-death.title: The Value of Finitude
epicurean-death.relation: The chapter tests each motive for uploading to San Junipero and finds it wanting: Kantian cosmic justice fails because the resort neither rewards the good nor can punish the wicked; Tolstoy's cosmic-insignificance dread fails because a finite life can still be meaningful, and even Epicurus and Lucretius deflate the fear of death (while Nagel notes death's evil lies in foreclosed possibilities, and Williams's Makropulos case warns eternal life breeds boredom). Nozick's experience machine is the closest analogy, but the chapter argues San Junipero differs — residents know it is digital and share it with other conscious people — before Nussbaum's argument lands: without finitude there is no risk, so no courage, sacrifice, or deep love, which is why Kelly's forty-nine real years with Richard outweigh forever with Yorkie.

epicurean-death.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
epicurean-death.title: The Death of Death
epicurean-death.relation: Reading Black Mirror's deaths through Bandersnatch's train ending, Be Right Back's AshBot, and San Junipero, the chapter uses Heidegger's presence-at-hand (Stefan's absent mother and rabbit remain present as possibilities he can act on) and Derrida's différance (the meaning of life and death is endlessly deferred as technology scrambles the presence/absence binary - Martha's simulated Ash, Liam's Grain deletions, Chris's guilt-haunted fiancée). A central section frames the whole debate as transhumanism - Kurzweil's three bridges to the posthuman against Fukuyama's warning that self-directed evolution replaces God - before Camus resolves the question of meaning: Kelly and Yorkie, like Sisyphus, create meaning by choosing their fate in a VR heaven that objectively matters nothing. Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' close the chapter's question of whether to extend, hasten, or simply accept mortality.

epicurean-death.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
epicurean-death.title: I think we've all arrived at a very special place, eh Spiritually Ecumenically Grammatically —Captain Jack Spa
epicurean-death.relation: Miller uses Disney deaths to stage the philosophy of death: Plato's immortal soul and Phaedo's affinity argument illuminate Frollo's lust-driven plunge into hellfire, while Epicurus's atomism, his 'death is nothing to us' argument applied to Marlin's terror in Finding Nemo, and Lucretius's symmetry argument are tested against Coco, where Ernesto's forgotten 'final death' versus Hector's restored place on the ofrenda makes posthumous harm plausible. Aquinas's 'my soul is not me' grounds embodiment, Confucius makes Mulan's risking death for father, ancestors, and country a virtuous Confucian death, and Deloria's indigenous web of relations reads Mufasa's Circle of Life, Moana's grandmother, and Brother Bear's ancestral spirits.

epicurean-death.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
epicurean-death.title: Notes
epicurean-death.relation: Mackenzie Graham uses Fallout 3's Project Purity - James's sacrificial death and the Lone Wanderer's choice among feeding the purifier with their own life, poisoning the water for the Enclave, or destroying it - to ask whether death and posthumous events can be bad for the one who dies. Against Epicurus's claim that death is nothing to us, the chapter defends deprivationism with the Megaton quest (the Lone Wanderer's desire to save the town is thwarted even if the rearmed bomb destroys it unbeknownst to them) and weighs Feinberg and Pitcher's ante-mortem person against the problem of the subject, using the Great War's redefinition of October 22, 2077 to block backward causation. The 'Blood Ties' quest with the Family's cannibals then raises posthumous wrongs: since no existing subject is harmed or wronged, the chapter ends by asking whether cannibalism is an impersonal wrong against personhood itself, on the model of respecting nature.

epicurean-death.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
epicurean-death.title: Kierkegaard and the Norm (MacDonald) of Death
epicurean-death.relation: Reads Family Guy's personified Death (Norm MacDonald) through Kierkegaard's 'At a Graveside': the sprained ankle in 'Death is a Bitch' mocks the mistake of thinking death's arrival can be postponed, Death's boozing and cocoa complaints violate death's indefinability and the appropriate fear of it, and the clipboard-carrying harvester of 'Death Lives' treats death as the general human condition rather than my death, exactly Kierkegaard's criticism of Epicurus. But drawing on the Postscript's account of the comic as a painless contradiction that shows what not to do, the chapter concludes Death is a Kierkegaardian parody: its very absurdity (the high-five that kills a fan in 'I Take Thee Quagmire') exposes and corrects our superficial norms about death, unlike earnest personifications such as Meet Joe Black.

epicurean-death.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
epicurean-death.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Kevin Fitzpatrick uses Vivi Orunitia and the self-aware Black Mages of Final Fantasy IX, who call death 'stopping,' to ask whether the fear of death is justified, answering that death harms only insofar as it frustrates a person's values, such as Vivi's morality, his thirst for knowledge, and his care for others' happiness. He brings in Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us because the dead feel no pain, casts Necron, who wants to return all life to a painless 'zero world' because fear of death has corrupted it, as a darker Epicurean, and weighs the deprivation objection, death cheats us of future goods like Chocobo Hot and Cold, against the puzzle of when death's harm could even occur.

epicurean-death.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
epicurean-death.title: The Approaching Battle
epicurean-death.relation: Frames death as philosophy's ultimate question and contrasts the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is simply the end of us with Heidegger's authenticity: boldly facing that death may come at any moment keeps us from living half-asleep, a view Plato anticipated by teaching that true philosophers make dying their profession. Harry, confronted with death from infancy, lives authentically, while Voldemort's flight from death marks him as the inauthentic case the essay traces through the Deathly Hallows death march.

epicurean-death.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
epicurean-death.title: The Office and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.

epicurean-death.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
epicurean-death.title: NOTES
epicurean-death.relation: Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.

epicurean-death.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
epicurean-death.title: The Grim Reaper on Baker Street
epicurean-death.relation: Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.

epicurean-death.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
epicurean-death.title: Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death
epicurean-death.relation: M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.

epicurean-death.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
epicurean-death.title: 11. The One Truly Serious Philosophical Problem
epicurean-death.relation: Doll surveys philosophical views on suicide to make sense of Bourdain's death, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is the one serious philosophical problem. She weighs Plato's Phaedo prohibition (we are the gods' possessions) against his allowance for extreme misfortune, Aristotle's view that suicide violates one's duty to self and community, and Seneca's Stoic position that a wise man 'lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can' — framing Bourdain's death as an autonomous choice.

epicurean-death.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
epicurean-death.title: Chapter 12 The American Diogenes
epicurean-death.relation: Johnson argues Twain is best understood not as a religious skeptic but as an 'American Diogenes'—a Cynic of Christianity-as-practiced. As Diogenes 'defaced the coinage' to remove counterfeit customs, Twain uses 'sacred profanity' (honest, even profane speech that exposes phony piety, e.g. the swearing butcher, Satanic narrators in 'The Mysterious Stranger' and 'Letters from the Earth') to strike four counterfeit coins: superstition/special providence, hypocrisy, artificial 'Moral Sense'/conscience, and heavenly rewards. On death Twain matches Diogenes and Epicurus (annihilation is nothing to fear), and his self-description as 'Member at Large for the Human Race' mirrors Diogenes the cosmopolitan; Diogenes carries a lantern to find a real human, Twain a mirror to show we are worse than we think.

epicurean-death.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
epicurean-death.title: Chapter 13 An Epicurean Consideration of Superstitions in Mark Twain and in the Good Life
epicurean-death.relation: Baker reads Twain's ghost stories and superstition through Epicurean virtue ethics, which holds that false beliefs—above all the terror of death—breed empty desires that block eudaimonia. Citing Twain's Autobiography passage that 'annihilation has no terrors for me' as a near-verbatim Epicurean line, and using Lucretius and Nussbaum's 'Therapy of Desire,' she aligns Huck's disdain for a useless conscience and his rejection of wealth ('being rich ain't what it's cracked up to be') with the Epicurean pursuit of simple natural pleasures. She notes a tension: by making tall-tale-telling and Sunday-school-shirking so enjoyable, Twain the satirist spreads the very superstitions the Epicureans would eradicate, seeming to work at cross-purposes with them.

epicurean-death.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
epicurean-death.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
epicurean-death.relation: Kover argues that anti-hunting animal-liberation thought (Singer, Regan) objects to hunting not because it alienates us from nature but because it connects us too intimately to it—to the cycle of eating and being eaten and thus to our own mortality. Using Ernest Becker's 'denial of death' and Paul Rozin on disgust at our animality, he reads vegetarianism from Pythagoras's flesh-renouncing purification to modern ethical veganism as an ascetic refusal of edibility, and cites Val Plumwood's critique of humans placing themselves outside the food chain, concluding with Petersen and Shepard that the hunter's acceptance of death affirms life.

epicurean-death.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
epicurean-death.title: GARDENING
epicurean-death.relation: Campbell explains why Epicurus set his school in a walled garden on the edge of Athens ('Live unnoticed'), contrasting it with the Stoics' public Stoa: the Garden was a self-sufficient community of friends pursuing ataraxia through natural, necessary pleasures and philosophy as therapy for the soul. Drawing on Lucretius's account of prehistory in On the Nature of Things, he shows the Epicureans saw cities as a decadent fall—driven by the fear of death and the gods—from a near-paradise of proto-Epicurean friendship pacts, and read the garden and the locus amoenus of pastoral picnics as a recovered golden age. Diogenes of Oinoanda's inscription imagines a future in which all become gardening philosophers and city walls become redundant.

epicurean-death.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
epicurean-death.title: 9. Blade Runner
epicurean-death.relation: Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.

epicurean-death.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
epicurean-death.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
epicurean-death.relation: Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.

epicurean-death.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
epicurean-death.title: 54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality
epicurean-death.relation: Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.

sisyphus.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
sisyphus.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
sisyphus.relation: Bill Davis asks why Arwen would 'choose a mortal life' with Aragorn and why wise elves and men call death a gift.
