Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.

yin-yang.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
yin-yang.title: Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat
yin-yang.relation: White stages a mock interview with "Bat-Tzu" (revealed to be Alfred) to read Batman through Taoism. Lao-Tzu and Chuang-Tzu supply the ideal of balancing yin and yang: Bruce lets his hard, vengeful yang dominate and needs Robin's yin, while Dick keeps balance and Tim risks losing his. Bruce's intimidating shadow illustrates the usefulness of nothingness, and Chuang-Tzu's teaching on accepting death frames Jason Todd's fate. Alfred embodies the Taoist sage — wei-wu-wei, water-like flexibility, and effortless, unspoken guidance.

boethius-consolation.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All
boethius-consolation.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
boethius-consolation.relation: John Davenport argues that The Lord of the Rings is neither mere adventure nor Christian allegory but an epic fairy tale whose 'eucatastrophe' - Tolkien's term for the sudden joyous turn, a miraculous reprieve - carries religious hope even though the book contains no churches or prayers. Drawing on Tolkien's 'On Fairy-stories', he makes Sir Gawain and the Green Knight the model for Frodo: Gawain accepts the girdle and is scarred yet reprieved, just as Frodo claims the Ring, loses a finger as Beren lost a hand, and is saved only because the mercy shown Gollum lets the Ring fall into the fire. Gandalf's return, Éowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth extend the pattern; with Kierkegaard the deliverance is grace 'by virtue of the absurd', an echo of the eschaton answering Boethius's question whether our struggles have final significance.

boethius-consolation.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
boethius-consolation.title: The Wisdom of Captain Marvel
boethius-consolation.relation: Shows how natural it was in 1940 to list the wisdom of Solomon first among Captain Marvel's Shazam-granted powers, then examines Geoff Johns' JSA retelling as the modern 'but': Billy Batson's transformation is purely physical, so Solomon's wisdom becomes an external advising voice — a device the chapter compares to the personified Philosophy who visits Boethius in prison. The Stargirl romance dilemma reveals wisdom's advice to break up with Courtney as designed to preserve its own authority — fitting to an admirer of wisdom, yet reading to modern eyes as the self-interested calculation of a skeptical age.

boethius-consolation.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
boethius-consolation.title: “The Foggy Ruins of Time”
boethius-consolation.relation: Kevin Stoehr stages Plato's ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry over Dylan: from the Republic's banishment of the poets, through Boethius's Consolation where Lady Philosophy banishes the Muses yet the book stays a prose-poem satura, to Nietzsche, who attacks philosophy philosophically just as Dylan discounts thinking while waxing philosophical about it. Dylan's own remarks ("the song wrote itself," "trust my intuition") side with poetic intuition against analysis, and Holderlin's question "what are poets for in a destitute time" frames Dylan as the smirking antiquary of a nihilistic age who makes us feel the darkness philosophy can only point at. The chapter concludes that the ambiguity of songs like "Lay, Lady, Lay" resists universalization yet occasions the wonder in which philosophy begins - poetry as the bridge to philosophy.

boethius-consolation.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
boethius-consolation.title: Intending the Way Out
boethius-consolation.relation: Stages the paradox of foreknowledge through Paul's prescient dream of meeting Chani and his futile struggle against the foreseen jihad: since knowledge (on Plato's justified-true-belief account) is factive, a known future seems unalterable. It tests the classic escapes—Boethius's God in ever-present eternity and Aquinas's seeing all time 'under the aspect of eternity,' Laplace's demon, Richard Taylor's fatalism—and finds the Atreides oracles are no gods, only probabilistic predictors whose visions fix the possibilities they see. The way out is Anscombe's Intention: like God knowing creation because He authored it, Paul and Leto know their futures practically, as agents whose intentions help decide which possibilities become actual, so freedom survives as terrific responsibility.

boethius-consolation.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
boethius-consolation.title: The Devil and Philosophy
boethius-consolation.relation: Ray Bossert reads Tolkien's Silmarillion through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy: elves, being artists, understand Melkor not as tempter but as bad artist, from his rebellious solo in the Music of the Ainur to his botched sub-creations - orcs bred from kidnapped elves - and his covetous collecting of the silmarils. Boethius supplies the machinery: evil seeks a good by unnatural means and only approximates it, wickedness debases its practitioner into a beast, God's foreknowledge embraces free choices without causing them, and Providence is a spinning disc at whose center alone one is steady - so Melkor's rebellion leaves him less free, dragged around the rim. Tolkien's contrast between art (for beauty) and magic (for control) explains why the Devil can only mimic creation, never make anything real.

boethius-consolation.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
boethius-consolation.title: Homeland and Philosophy
boethius-consolation.relation: Trip McCrossin reads Carrie's 'I missed something once before... everyone's not me' as the modern, secular problem of evil: as Susan Neiman argues, unreasonable suffering threatens reason itself, and the Rousseau-Voltaire split defines the responses. Carrie takes Rousseau's side - 'All is good leaving the hands of the author of things' degenerates in human hands, so evil is intelligible and redemption possible, the chance at redemption she offers Brody and even Nazir - against Voltaire's Candide-style tending of the garden. The finale deepens this with Boethius's Consolation: Carrie's 'I believe one of the reasons I was put on this Earth was for our paths to cross' fuses fate with providence, and she accepts Brody's execution as a redemptive end 'more so if he dies'.

boethius-consolation.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
boethius-consolation.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
boethius-consolation.relation: Roger Hunt answers 'what do philosophers do?' through Dennis's seduction methodology. Frank embodies empiricism, leaving the comfort of principle for the messiness of the world as Hume did when he found no impression of causation, space, or time; Mac embodies rationalism, reasoning with total confidence from a principle he cannot doubt, as Descartes did from the cogito; and the dialectic of Socrates and Plato, questioning beliefs in dialogue to see what survives scrutiny, describes philosophy as it is actually practiced. Boethius's Consolation - the imprisoned author consoled by dialogues with Lady Philosophy - supplies the frame of philosophy as an encounter with a woman one pursues, and each D.E.N.N.I.S. step maps onto the craft: Demonstrating value to the problem, Engaging physically in its awkward grind, Nurturing dependence through thesis panic, Neglect and Inspiring hope on the road to the defense, then Separating entirely - 'be a sociopath about it.'

boethius-consolation.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
boethius-consolation.title: 8. Time Travel and the Problem of Evil
boethius-consolation.relation: Ray Bossert reads Endgame through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, arguing that Doctor Strange and Tony Stark, who permit the Snap and five years of suffering for the sake of the one winning outcome, run 'uncannily parallel' to Thanos, who decided for Gamora that her unwilling death served the greater good. Strange's viewing of 14,000,605 futures illustrates Boethius's distinction between an infinite being riding along the timeline and an eternal one seeing all moments at once, and the refusal to tell Stark his role mirrors why God's foreknowledge sees our choices without compelling them. Boethius's providence weaving free choices into justice, the Avengers' passion-driven failures on Titan (Star-Lord and Thor avenging lost lovers), justice as the wicked's own punishment (Thanos dying wretched twice in one film), and Umberto Eco's 'Myth of Superman' all frame a universe where suffering is allowed because it is woven into a pattern that ends in justice.

boethius-consolation.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
boethius-consolation.title: Intending the Way Out
boethius-consolation.relation: Works through the paradox of foreknowledge: because Paul's Caladan dream of first meeting Chani is knowledge in Plato's justified-true-belief sense, the foreseen future is factive, so his struggle against the jihad he visions (even hoping to die on Feyd-Rautha's blade rather than become a martyr) is futile. It tests the classical escape routes, Boethius's God who views all times as an ever-present eternity and Aquinas's God seeing the whole road 'under the aspect of eternity', and Laplace's Demon's causal determinism, but finds the Atreides oracles unlike God since they are creatures in time who see many possible futures rather than one. The resolution comes through Anscombe's Intention: practical knowledge lets Paul and Leto, whose present choices shift the balance of probability among foreseen timelines, intend their way out as creative authors of events.

boethius-consolation.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
boethius-consolation.title: a19.xhtml
boethius-consolation.relation: Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.

boethius-consolation.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
boethius-consolation.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
boethius-consolation.relation: Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.

boethius-consolation.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
boethius-consolation.title: 86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom
boethius-consolation.relation: Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'

the-uncanny.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
the-uncanny.title: Rounding Third and Heading Home
the-uncanny.relation: Joe Kraus uses Gaston Bachelard's Poetics of Space to read baseball's 'home': the batter begins at home yet must leave it, face the pitcher's threat, and return to make scoring meaningful, which is Bachelard's dialectic of shelter versus threat (with Joseph Campbell's monomyth alongside). Freud's uncanny (unheimlich, un-home-like) explains why home plate is both inviting and demoralizing. Bachelard's 'well-determined centers of revery' and Benedict Anderson's shared-news account of nationhood then explain ballparks as communal homes, from Wrigleyville to 'Cardinal Nation' in Quincy, Illinois, and why the Dodgers leaving Brooklyn felt like losing a home.

the-uncanny.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
the-uncanny.title: A Political Philosophy of Vampires
the-uncanny.relation: Phillip Cole takes Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof - the Arnold Paole exhumations - and argues Rousseau's real point was political: authorities manufacture imaginary monsters, as in the witch craze, to exploit fear and hold power over their own populations. Freud's account of the uncanny explains why the horror is not death itself but the returning dead (the watching eyes of Scratchy in Itchy and Scratchy, versus the serene corpses of Six Feet Under, whose absurdity the show meets with wry amusement), and Julia Kristeva's abjection explains the corpse as the ultimate boundary-breaker. The vampire then resurfaces as the demonized outsider - Stoker's Dracula coded as the unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's terrorist - exposing political borders as arbitrary fabrications. Buffy completes the collapse of the us/them binary: Angel and Spike join the slayer, and the most shocking killings (Faith's accidental human kill, Warren's stray bullet hitting Tara) are all too human, so the real subject of border policing is the community's own members.

the-uncanny.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
the-uncanny.title: Fast Zombies
the-uncanny.relation: K. Silem Mohammad explains the classic slow zombie via Spinoza's account of bodies defined by ratios of motion and rest, where death is no absolute state but a redisposition of parts, so voodoo zombies at industrial modernity's dawn figure alienated labor and Romero's ghouls an impersonal, relentless compulsion. Through Deleuze's reading of composition and decomposition, zombie feeding becomes an ethological process of absorbing other bodies' relations, and Spinoza's replacement of good/evil with good/bad (anticipating Nietzsche) dissolves the zombie's supposed evil into 'bad encounters' between bodies. The fast zombies of 28 Days Later and the Dawn remake then mark a shift from Freudian uncanny return to full-blown crisis: pure rage without hunger or grievance, bodies in faster motion, leaving us an impossible identification with the composition that will decompose us.

the-uncanny.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
the-uncanny.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
the-uncanny.relation: Cynthia Coe argues the novel's horror lies in the creature's liminality: he is neither human nor inhuman, and Victor's instant labeling of him as 'monster,' 'demon,' and 'fiend' shields Victor from his own responsibility, since the word 'monster' descends from a sign or omen we mistake for the evil itself. Freud's uncanny - the heimlich turning unheimlich, the repressed coming to light - explains why a being 'more horrid from its very resemblance' to us terrifies more than an obvious alien, a mechanism the chapter parallels with European anti-Semitism as hatred of an internal enemy. Shelley's moral point is that failures of empathy are moral failures: Victor holds the creature responsible as a free-willed demon while denying him personhood, and the tragedy grows from that contradictory projection until the neat categories of victim, monster, and evil collapse.

the-uncanny.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
the-uncanny.title: 2. Where Is the Twilight Zone
the-uncanny.relation: Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of Breton's surrealism, starting from Descartes: the cogito and the mind–body problem made reason the measure of the 'clear and distinct,' and surrealism seeks to unbind the imagination from exactly that rational leash. He reads 'A World of His Own' as surrealist automatic writing, 'The Mirror' as Dalí's paranoiac-critical method, and Freud's psychoanalysis as both allied with and (following Adorno's diagnosis of the movement's death) too restrictive for surrealism's project. Episodes like 'Shadow Play' (a man who dreams the world), 'The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' and 'A Stop at Willoughby' provoke the uncanny — the strangely familiar — in viewers, which is where the Zone is located.

greatest-happiness.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
greatest-happiness.title: The Obligation to Play Baseball
greatest-happiness.relation: Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.

greatest-happiness.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
greatest-happiness.title: Start Stitchin’ That Costume, Bub. Duty Calls
greatest-happiness.relation: Explains Mill-style utilitarianism — rightness fixed entirely by consequences for overall pleasure and pain, counting every sentient being (a cat may enjoy tuna but not Watchmen) — and applies it: Clark Kent must rescue the failing plane over the Daily Planet press conference, and you must give the jeans money to charity. Since adopting a role is obligated whenever it produces the most overall good, anyone with superpowers has a duty to become a superhero, so Peter Parker's misery in Spider-Man 2 is morally beside the point: utilitarianism says he must remain Spider-Man.

greatest-happiness.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
greatest-happiness.title: John Henry, the Steam-Engine, and Folsom Prisoners
greatest-happiness.relation: Mulnix pairs Cash with John Stuart Mill on the priority of quality of life over mere life: Mill's 1868 Parliament speech defends capital punishment as more humane than the "living tomb" of life imprisonment, and Cash agrees in the Folsom liner notes (the prisoner envying the cockroach that can leave) and in "The Mercy Seat," where the electric chair becomes both mercy and the throne of God. Mill's higher and lower pleasures, competent judges, and On Liberty's individuality illuminate Cash's gallery of fools, the "Folsom Prison Blues" narrator who shot a man just to watch him die, the mother-defying Billy Joe of "Don't Take Your Guns to Town," characters whose unreflective rebellion squanders rational freedom. John Henry, by contrast, exercised his higher faculties against the steam-engine and so died happy, proving the chapter's Millian thesis that freedom matters as a means to self-directed, deliberated happiness.

greatest-happiness.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
greatest-happiness.title: Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent
greatest-happiness.relation: Cooper and Taylor argue that Kano's judo principles, seiryokuzenyou (maximum efficiency) and jitakyouei (mutual welfare and benefit), echo Bentham's principle of utility: both men swept away archaic rules to reach one efficient ethical goal, and Kano accepted the comparison. They run the hedonic calculus over training bruises versus the joy of a clean throw, use Mill's secondary principles as rule-utilitarian guidelines (release the armbar at the tap rather than calculating each time), and answer the objection that utilitarianism demands too much with Kano's own ethos: like judo, it is about continual improvement, not impossible maximization.

greatest-happiness.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
greatest-happiness.title: This Is the Age of Steel
greatest-happiness.relation: Littmann asks what a genuinely logical creature would do and grades the Cybermen against three accounts of reason: Hobbes's self-preservation and social contract, which the survival-focused Cybermen of 'The Tenth Planet' roughly satisfy but their later wars of conquest betray; Mill's utilitarianism, whose greatest-happiness principle, higher pleasures, liberty, and individuality condemn emotion-stripping, forced 'upgrades', and uniformity; and Hume's claim that reason alone motivates nothing, under which perfectly logical but emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing at all. The upshot is that Cyberman 'logic' is incoherent — no theory of reason makes them rational.

greatest-happiness.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
greatest-happiness.title: The Good Life and The Dexter-like Life
greatest-happiness.relation: Abrol Fairweather uses Dexter as a controlled case study in the philosophy of emotion via Nozick's 'Spock Problem': like Spock, Dexter has beliefs, values and flawless practical reasoning but no emotional feelings, so Mill's Method of Difference lets us isolate what exactly emotions add. Distinguishing 'mere feelings' (beer on the boat, lust for Lila) from emotional feelings that run through our beliefs and values, he adopts Nozick's answer that emotions are value-perceptions - Dexter intellectually recognizes the value of Rita, Deb and his kids but cannot feel it, and that felt value is what his life lacks. Yet Dexter strikes back: he kills because he is too rational rather than too passionate, so whether the Dexter-like life beats the good life depends on whether emotions would help or hinder whatever matters most to us, a question the chapter briefly weighs in Millian terms of the balance of pleasure over pain his meta-killing produces.

greatest-happiness.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
greatest-happiness.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Pits act utilitarianism against existentialism to ask whether moral rules change at life's end: briefly cooking meth can maximize happiness (family provision against limited street harm), while a long career cannot, and utilitarians are trapped by the limits of their own foresight. Walt is read as the existentialist converting mortality into meaning - money, power, and masculinity in a godless world - while Skyler mostly calculates like a utilitarian (white lies to Marie, Ted's accounting), Hank mixes both codes, and Marie's kleptomania marks her an egoist until she defends Walt's right to choose his own death at the intervention. A marathon-runner metaphor lands the thesis: to be a utilitarian in life's early miles is itself an existential decision, and the last mile is when we 'wake up' like Walt.

greatest-happiness.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
greatest-happiness.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Cogburn protests Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments and rebuilds the system philosophically: Lawful means willing universalizable law in Kant's categorical-imperative sense (the liar and murderer treating themselves as exceptions), Good means willing the greatest happiness in Mill's utilitarian sense, yielding a nine-box grid of moral psychologies. He populates it with fantasy archetypes—Haomane Firstborn as pathological Lawful Neutral, Karsa Orlong as Chaotic Neutral, Abercrombie's torturer Glotka as Neutral Neutral in Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil' mold, hierarchic vampires and cynical politicians as Lawful Evil, Conan's raiders as Chaotic Evil. On this scheme Chaotic Good is genuinely empty, Drizzt and Robin Hood types are really Lawful or Neutral Good, and a Neutral Good versus Lawful Good dispute over killing one innocent to save thousands shows how gameplay can stage classic ethics thought experiments.

greatest-happiness.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
greatest-happiness.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Bateman replies to Cogburn that Law and Chaos descend not from Kant but from Michael Moorcock's Eternal Champion stories, where they are liberal and conservative political tendencies held in check by the Cosmic Balance, which restores Chaotic Good, Lawful Evil, and the Druid's true Neutral as viable positions. He rejects the 'sausage machine' universalization of maxims for Kant's humanity formula and Realm of Ends, and argues act utilitarianism makes a poor model of Good: an overpopulation scenario could mandate genocide, and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure the good. Alain Badiou's ethic of truths supplies the positive case for Chaotic Good—pursuing what you take to be good without submitting to a single moral law—while Buddhist and Jain renunciation dignifies Lawful Neutral.

greatest-happiness.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
greatest-happiness.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Greg Littmann reads Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in John Stuart Mill's mold, drawing a detailed parallel between Ender's engineered Battle School childhood and James Mill's grueling raising of his son to be utilitarianism's champion, down to both boys' breakdowns. He argues that although the xenocide was a tragic wrong by Mill's own lights (the hive-queens' happiness counted too), the harm principle permits overriding individual liberty when humanity's survival is at stake - which is why Card's novel, unlike Crime and Punishment or 'The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas,' shows consequentialism at its most troubling rather than its most absurd.

greatest-happiness.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
greatest-happiness.title: Dracula and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Arp starts from Dracula's inability to love or find satisfaction and his awareness of it, then deploys Sidgwick's hedonistic paradox: pursuing pleasure for its own sake yields pain whether or not the pleasure is found, through mistaking pain for pleasure (Lestat on the dead twins), boredom, or emptiness. Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures explains how vampires can enjoy the bodily pleasure of blood yet lament lacking joy and love, while substance versus property dualism (Plato as the substance dualist) frames whether the Count's soul survives when his body crumbles to dust. Aristotle's Book X pleasures of completed states and the 'virtuous vampires' from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain show the only escape from the dilemma: pursue activities for their own sake and higher mental pleasures rather than bodily pleasure alone.

greatest-happiness.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
greatest-happiness.title: Dracula and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.

greatest-happiness.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
greatest-happiness.title: 5. Back from the Dead
greatest-happiness.relation: Devlin and Cooper trace Rick's moral arc as a struggle between Mill-style consequentialism - twisted by the apocalypse into a 'Greatest Survival Principle' of mere survival (Dawn Lerner's Grady, Enid's 'JSS') - and Aristotelian virtue ethics. Shane's murder of Otis, the Governor's rule over Woodbury and killing of Martinez and Pete, and Terminus's cannibalism all show survival-only reasoning dissolving humanity, a decline the show underlines with literal mirror reflections of Shane as a walker. Rick falls after killing Shane and nearly trades Michonne to the Governor, is brought back by Lori's judging vision and the sight of Carl going cold, and reclaims virtues as habits grown like Hershel's seeds - 'We get to come back' (4.8 'Too Far Gone') - though Seasons 4 and 5 leave him balancing a harder character, down to 'We didn't want to waste the bullets,' with the drive to survive.

greatest-happiness.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
greatest-happiness.title: 10. Natasha, Gamora, and the Soul Stone
greatest-happiness.relation: T.J. McSherry frames the two Vormir deaths as 'a futuristic, utilitarian trolley problem,' using Mill's greatest-happiness principle to argue Natasha's martyrdom was the more utilitarian choice (only the Avengers mourn her, while Clint's children need a father), even as Thanos's tossing of Gamora shows the same sacrifice-of-few arithmetic the Avengers rely on. Because the amoral Soul Stone rewards good and evil deaths identically, the chapter turns to Plato's Symposium, casting Red Skull as a Diotiman spirit-mediator of love and ranking each relationship on Diotima's ladder: Thanos is 'stuck at level one' in his stunted love for Gamora, kept alive only as a useful sacrifice, while Clint and Natasha's non-romantic love reaches level four through shared history, empathy, and their fight over who gets to die for the other.

greatest-happiness.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
greatest-happiness.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Cogburn attacks Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments to five: it deletes archetypes that fantasy literature needs, since Karsa Orlong (who wills the destruction of all civilization without sadism) and Jacqueline Carey's Haomane Firstborn (who loves cold mathematical order while his laws lead to genocide) fit nowhere in the new scheme. He rebuilds alignment by taking it to describe what a character wills in Kant's sense, mapping the law-chaos axis onto the categorical imperative (the liar and murderer must take themselves to be exceptions to universal laws) and the good-evil axis onto Mill's greatest happiness principle, which yields a Lawful Good of Gandhi and King, a Neutral Good modeled on Jesus breaking Sabbath law out of love, and Lawful Evil exemplified by vampire hierarchies and politicians whose policies create hell abroad. Joe Abercrombie's torturer San Dan Glotka becomes the archetypal Neutral Neutral, 'banality of evil' in Arendt's sense, and the chapter concludes Chaotic Good is empty because willing the destruction of universalizability cannot consistently will less pain.

greatest-happiness.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
greatest-happiness.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Bateman replies to Cogburn by recovering the alignment system's actual literary source: Moorcock's Elric saga, where Law and Chaos are rival political ideologies (conservative and liberal tendencies) held in check by the Cosmic Balance, so a Chaotic person need only refuse law's authority, not will horror, and Chaotic Good remains possible. He rejects Cogburn's 'sausage machine' reading of Kant's first formula in favor of the humanity formula and the Realm of Ends, and rejects act utilitarianism as a model of the Good alignment, since an overpopulation scenario shows Mill's calculus mandating culling-genocide and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure goodness. Drawing on Badiou's ethic of truths, Buddhist and Jain renunciation, and the true-Neutral Druid as servant of the Cosmic Balance, he argues neutrality between Good and Evil need not be monstrous and mourns 4e's 'childishly simplistic' new system.

greatest-happiness.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
greatest-happiness.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Greg Littmann defends Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in Mill's own image, noting that Mill's father raised him in calculated isolation and brutal study as a tool to reform humanity just as Graff engineers Ender, so both acted rightly given the stakes even though Mill's harm principle and his regard for animal suffering also condemn the xenocide itself. Against Crime and Punishment and 'The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas,' he argues Ender's Game shows consequences can genuinely justify breaking any moral rule when human extinction is on the table.

greatest-happiness.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
greatest-happiness.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Southworth uses the War of Light to ask what role emotion should play in moral reasoning: Sinestro rules Korugar through fear, the Star Sapphires kidnap Sinestro Corps prisoners to convert them to love, Atrocitus's rage was forged by the Manhunters' massacre, Larfleeze hoards, and the Blue Lanterns merely hope that hope matters. On Aristotle's account every corps errs by excess: Atrocitus's rage makes him miss chances to kill Sinestro, Fatality's love benches John Stewart from saving his friends, and even the Green Lanterns' will-only ideal fails, since total fearlessness is itself vicious and Plato's picture has reason directing emotion like a general directing soldiers. He ends by defending Mill's utilitarianism: the Guardians' real failure was not detachment but pretending to be detached, and reading them as flawed 'benevolent, disinterested spectators' vindicates the Corps while explaining their moral growth after Scar and the Blackest Night.

greatest-happiness.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
greatest-happiness.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Novy uses Terry Berg's gay-bashing coma in 'Brother's Keeper' to argue hate crimes are a kind of terrorism: justice, in Iris Marion Young's enabling sense, requires social conditions in which citizens can develop and exercise their capacities, and an attack that makes every gay teenager police holding hands in public harms the whole group, so Mill's greatest-happiness principle and Feinberg's expressivism justify enhanced penalties. The chapter then turns on Kyle, who tortures Daniel Hirsh on Rikers Island and nearly beats his two accomplices to death, asking whether extraordinary crimes justify extraordinary procedures in a post-9/11 world. Kyle's horror afterward, begging Flash to undo the last twenty-four hours and losing his will to protect, and Batman's pointed 'But that is me, isn't it?' mark the line between punishing brutality and becoming it.

greatest-happiness.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
greatest-happiness.title: The Office and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.relation: Kraft uses Dunder Mifflin to test whether stockholder profit or stakeholder welfare should drive business decisions, introducing stakeholder theory via Ansoff and the Mitchell salience model. Michael's exclusive patronage of national chains (Chili's, Starbucks, USA Today) versus the staff's loyalty to local spots like Poor Richard's becomes a Millian case: by Mill's point that most good action benefits particular individuals, shopping locally spreads happiness through the Scranton community while Michael's habits export money and decision-making elsewhere. Dwight oscillates between stockholder logic (the cheapest health plan, poaching Jim's client in 'Diversity Day') and stakeholder-minded customer service, while 'Halloween,' 'Health Care,' and 'Branch Closing' show profit trumping people; Michael's successful sale to Christian at Chili's in 'The Client' balances both, and his 'Show me that farm' speech insists workers like Stanley and Phyllis are not replaceable cogs.

greatest-happiness.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
greatest-happiness.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
greatest-happiness.relation: Murtagh asks whether the Virgin Mary statue spraying menstrual blood on a cardinal and the pope in 'Bloody Mary' is morally wrong, and answers with a utilitarian weighing of blasphemous humor's consequences. On the negative side, offense to believers (with Cartman's sudden piety about Family Guy's Muhammad in 'Cartoon Wars Part I' articulating the utilitarian worry that millions watching intensifies the harm) and a possible desensitizing erosion of tolerance; on the positive side, pleasure and the show's power to provoke thought, as when Randy learns from Stan that his five sober days came from his own willpower, not 'divine ass blood'. Drawing on Mill's greatest happiness principle and On Liberty's defense of open discussion, he concludes blasphemous humor is morally justified when it is an important part of a presentation with significant social value, and wrong when used merely to piss people off or for profit.

greatest-happiness.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
greatest-happiness.title: Notes
greatest-happiness.relation: Greg Littmann tests utilitarianism against Star Trek's heroes, reading Spock's 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few' (The Wrath of Khan, Into Darkness) as Bentham's greatest-happiness principle, with Kirk's radiation-chamber death as its mirror image. He uses Mill's higher and lower pleasures to contrast the TNG crew's improbably refined holodeck tastes with Kirk's Argelius shore leave and Quark's 'Vulcan Love Slave', and Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis to defend emotion against Vulcan suppression. Against Janeway killing Tuvix, Sisko's conspiracy in 'In the Pale Moonlight', and Kirk letting Edith Keeler die, he notes Trek never shows the many actually harmed, but sides with the utilitarians: favoring friends and the few is arbitrary discrimination.

greatest-happiness.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
greatest-happiness.title: NOTES
greatest-happiness.relation: Grubb stages Arlene's decision to abort the baby fathered by serial killer Rene as a case study in Bentham's act utilitarianism: her prayer that ending the pregnancy will keep 'Rene's sickness' from Coby, Lisa, and Terry weighs pleasure and pain — the two sovereign masters — for the greatest number, from family to all of Bon Temps. The chapter shows why the calculus fails her: consequences cannot be known in advance (a crystal ball or Lafayette's visions would be needed), it is indeterminate whose happiness counts, and her premise that evil is biologically inheritable sits badly with the free-will account of sin, making the dilemma genuinely undecidable from inside the show.

greatest-happiness.book: 210 - Football and Philosophy - Going Deep
greatest-happiness.title: Does the Salary Cap Make the NFL a Fairer League
greatest-happiness.relation: Collins-Cavanaugh presents the NFL salary cap as a model of utilitarian distributive justice via Mill's greatest happiness principle: owners and fans gain (guaranteed revenue and a fairer, more competitive league) while players lose relatively little. He then tests empirically—competitive-balance scores, playoff berths, championship distribution, and comparison to MLB and the NBA—and finds little evidence the cap actually increases fairness. Because the claimed fan happiness is not genuinely caused by the cap, the utilitarian justification collapses, leaving only the players' net loss against the owners' gain.

greatest-happiness.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
greatest-happiness.title: What’s Wrong with Roland
greatest-happiness.relation: Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.

pascals-wager.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
pascals-wager.title: Who Should Be Committed
pascals-wager.relation: Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.

pascals-wager.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
pascals-wager.title: The Catholic in Spandex
pascals-wager.relation: Weighing whether Matt Murdock can be a 'good Catholic', Morris catalogs his commandment-keeping and lapses, then argues his real safety net is his mother Maggie's faith: her intercessory prayer over his broken body in Born Again is the force behind his rebirth, on a communitarian view where one person's faith covers another. When Matt's crisis of faith comes in Kevin Smith's Guardian Devil, Maggie's peasant-and-knight fable delivers a version of Pascal's Wager - bet on God, since atheism risks infinite loss for finite gain - and his heart is calmed; Pascal's 'greatness and wretchedness of man' also echoes in Daredevil's own prayer about humanity's 'disparity of magnificence to actions'.

pascals-wager.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
pascals-wager.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
pascals-wager.relation: Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.

pascals-wager.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
pascals-wager.title: Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)
pascals-wager.relation: Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.

pascals-wager.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
pascals-wager.title: Poker and Philosophy
pascals-wager.relation: The editor's introduction stages poker and philosophy as twin crafts of risk: 'philosopher' was once slang for a card cheat, Socrates and Wild Bill Hickok both died for keeping villainous company, and the Buddha's six years to enlightenment are measured against the Birdcage Theater's eight-year poker game. It recruits Nietzsche's 'live dangerously' and Kierkegaard's leap of faith to defend the all-in as the only meaningful way to live, then traces probability from Cardano's Book on Games of Chance to Pascal's wager that believing in God is the smarter bet — the ancestor of today's pot-odds reasoning. Chris Ferguson's PhD, Annie Duke's psycholinguistics, and Jesse May's 'the trick to poker is mastering the luck — that's philosophy' set up the book's Texas Hold'em focus.

pascals-wager.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time
pascals-wager.title: Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter
pascals-wager.relation: Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.

pascals-wager.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
pascals-wager.title: Introduction
pascals-wager.relation: Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.

pascals-wager.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
pascals-wager.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
pascals-wager.relation: Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.

pascals-wager.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
pascals-wager.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
pascals-wager.relation: Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'

pascals-wager.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
pascals-wager.title: Hedging Our Bets
pascals-wager.relation: Kind asks whether humanoid Cylons have moral status, using Warren's stone-versus-child contrast to show that the Fleet's blender-and-toaster attitude (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine') rests on the unargued assumption that Cylons are mere machines. Singer's anti-speciesism grounds status in sentience (Gina's suffering, even Scar the Raider), while Regan's subject-of-a-life criteria are met by rational, self-aware Cylons; Helo's 'no human could do the things they've done' argument fails because humans commit equal evils, as the legal limits on punishing criminals show. Since we cannot rule Cylon status out, she closes with Pascal's Wager: treat them as morally considerable, because the asymmetry of error costs us our moral compass.

pascals-wager.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
pascals-wager.title: Questioning the Question
pascals-wager.relation: Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.

pascals-wager.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
pascals-wager.title: The Good Wife and Philosophy
pascals-wager.relation: Lisa McNulty asks what could oblige us to believe someone: Peter's lying fails Kant's Categorical Imperative (a world of universal liars makes lying impossible), while friendship explains Alicia's readiness to believe client Kenny Chatham even before the evidence does. The 'Death Zone' libel trial over an Everest death shows that one's position of power fixes whom one owes presumptive belief - a reader should side with Cardiff, a judge must presume Lambrose innocent - and Pascal's Wager supplies the method of 'behaving like a believer': withholding rumors, withholding conviction, and Alicia publicly playing the wife and sleeping with Peter in a bid to believe in her marriage again. She concludes Peter forfeited any right to be believed, so Alicia has no moral obligation to behave like a good wife.

pascals-wager.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
pascals-wager.title: 15. God Started in 1983
pascals-wager.relation: Uses the SNL bit of a God who has been standing in a room since 1983 to argue Louis is an 'apathetic agnostic': he cannot know whether God exists, lambastes atheists who claim certainty, and thinks the question barely matters for our lives. The chapter weighs Pascal's Wager against Epicurus's four-part cure ('Don't fear god, don't worry about death'), faults Louis's 'downstairs bathroom' bit for putting the burden of proof on atheists, reads the 'Heaven' glory-hole sketch through Clifford's ethics of belief as a rejection of faith without evidence, and ends with Louie's mother's line that you have to be good to people whether or not God is watching.

pascals-wager.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
pascals-wager.title: 13. Linus’s Wager
pascals-wager.relation: The chapter stages a three-way debate over whether Linus may believe in the Great Pumpkin without evidence. Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner whose wishful thinking sinks his ship) condemns Linus's sincerity-based wager; Pascal's Wager endorses it (forgoing one night of trick-or-treating costs nothing if the Pumpkin is fake and wins toys if he is real) but assumes a doxastic voluntarism we lack, since no one can make themselves believe for even a million-dollar reward. William James's 'The Will to Believe' gets the final word: if Linus's option is live, forced, and momentous with no decisive evidence either way, his leap of faith - like loving without guarantees - is morally justified whenever life would be greatly impoverished without it.

pascals-wager.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
pascals-wager.title: 11. The Truth about Lying
pascals-wager.relation: Fallis reads the series through the philosophy of testimony: TZ relentlessly punishes both truth-tellers (Bob Wilson's gremlin warning and nine more episodes) and liars ('Hocus-Pocus and Frisby,' 'The Four of Us Are Dying'), while Kant's letter on reticence suggests the untried third option of keeping quiet. On the receiving side, Hume's rules for discounting witnesses and his argument that one should never believe miracle reports explain why the crew disbelieves the gremlin and why 'Printer's Devil's' Devil reasons like Hume, Descartes' malicious demon returns in the disguised devils of 'The Hunt' and 'The Howling Man,' and the chapter ends endorsing Pascal's Wager: 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' argues we should believe even crazy, lying testimony just in case it is true.

pascals-wager.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
pascals-wager.title: 9. With Infinite Power Comes No Responsibility
pascals-wager.relation: James Hart casts Tony Stark as a consequentialist and Steve Rogers as a deontologist, then argues Endgame's infinite stakes destroy Tony's morality through Nick Bostrom's 'infinitarian paralysis': in an infinite multiverse every act leaves the balance of happy and sad lives unchanged, as an infinite Stark orphanage rearranged Hilbert's-Hotel style shows, and even genocide becomes permissible so long as infinitely many remain alive. Tony's attempted fixes each fail: the causal approach collapses because reversing the Snap has infinite butterfly effects, expected value (credited to Frank Jackson) runs into Pascal's Mugging and an 'infinitarian trance' demanding suicidal bets on any chance of infinite value, and Bostrom's 'infinity shades' that filter tiny probabilities would blind Tony to the one-in-a-trillion time-heist chance he should take. The chapter concludes there is no consequentialist way to say when wagering lives on infinite stakes is ethical, and Iron Man should let Captain America lead.

pascals-wager.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
pascals-wager.title: 5. Greatness or Nothingness
pascals-wager.relation: Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.

pascals-wager.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
pascals-wager.title: Hedging Our Bets
pascals-wager.relation: Kind asks whether the Fleet's treatment of Cylons (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine,' Cally's killing of Boomer charged as mere discharging of a firearm) presupposes that Cylons lack the moral status Mary Anne Warren defines against the stone-versus-child contrast. Against species membership as a criterion she deploys Singer's anti-speciesism (sentience grounds equal consideration: Gina's torture, the Raider Scar) and Regan's subject-of-a-life, and against the 'no souls' argument she cites Descartes's animal automata and Turing's reply that an omnipotent God could give machines souls, as Leoben himself suggests to Adama. Since no criterion rules Cylons out with certainty, the chapter closes with a Pascal's Wager structure: under uncertainty, treat plausible moral-status-holders as having it, because denying it costs us our moral compass, answering Adama's 'why are we worth saving?'.

pascals-wager.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
pascals-wager.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
pascals-wager.relation: Malloy examines Walter's incorrigible leaps — Bunny kidnapped herself on no evidence, the toe is a fake ('I can get you a toe by three o'clock'), the Big Lebowski can walk — through Clifford's ethics of belief (the ship-owner who sinks his passengers) and James's 'Will to Believe' reply with its living, forced, and momentous genuine options, applied to Walter's 'dabbled' pacifism and his preference for Nazism's ethos over nihilism's nothing. Walter's conversion to Judaism for Cynthia raises whether practice can will belief, tested via Pascal's wager and James's objection, and the verdict borrows Bernard Williams: we cannot choose beliefs, but Walter's reckless policy of dismissing counterevidence makes him 'not just an asshole, he is also wrong'.

pascals-wager.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
pascals-wager.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
pascals-wager.relation: Eric Silverman argues Game of Thrones explodes the storybook link between virtue and worldly happiness: Ned, 'one man in ten thousand,' is betrayed and executed, so Plato's claim that the just person is happy must mean psychic order rather than material flourishing - reason ruling spirit and appetite - as with Bran, who flourishes as a greenseer though he will never walk again. Cersei is Plato's tyrant, her soul ruled by insatiable appetite and paranoia, so no external goods can ever satisfy her, while Aristotle's correction - virtue necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia, which also needs health, friends, and good fortune - explains why both Ned (virtue without external goods) and Cersei (goods without virtue) end up unhappy. Finally he inverts Pascal's Wager: since playing the game of thrones risks total loss (torture, humiliation, death) for limited gain, and even winning hollows you out - Robert confesses he was 'never so alive as when I was winning this throne or so dead as now that I've won it' - only a fool would play.

pascals-wager.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
pascals-wager.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
pascals-wager.relation: Jacoby defends W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief—it is wrong to believe on insufficient evidence and the burden of proof falls on the claimant—through Stan's exposures of TV psychic John Edward ('The Biggest Douche in the Universe'), the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the faith-based story of Joseph Smith in 'All About Mormons'. The centerpiece is a South Park-illustrated demolition of Pascal's Wager: Kyle's hemorrhoid-driven despair in 'Cartmanland' shows a perfectly good God would not eternally reward evil Cartman or torture honest nonbelievers, and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' shows the wagerer cannot even know which religion pays out. Stan's closing speech to Edward's frightened audience carries the moral: comforting lies weaken the mind and slow the progress of finding the real, amazing answers.

pascals-wager.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
pascals-wager.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
pascals-wager.relation: Johnson formalizes Kyle's crisis in 'Cartmanland'—evil Cartman inherits a million dollars and buys the amusement park while good Kyle suffers hemorrhoids and loses faith—as a valid argument from the logical problem of evil, then evaluates the town's theodicies against the philosophical ones. The Job story Kyle's parents read him fails like skeptical theism (it proves too much and ends in moral agnosticism), Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards's God-glorifying account, Stan's restored faith via Cartman's perfect misery is a greater-goods response, Augustine's free will defense purchases goodness at the price of God's control of prayers and elections and cannot explain natural evils, and Hick's soul-making theodicy founders on fawns, tsunamis, and Kenny's deaths. Pascal's Wager and Plantinga's divine sense are dismissed in turn: evil does not disprove God, but proportioning belief to evidence makes non-belief the rational stance.

pascals-wager.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
pascals-wager.title: 11. The Truth about Lying
pascals-wager.relation: Fallis treats the Zone as a seminar in the philosophy of testimony: truth-tellers like Bob Wilson warning of a gremlin get dismissed as insane ('The Whole Truth' forces truth-telling as a curse), while convincing liars like Arch Hammer come to bad ends, so Kant's letter recommending reticence, saying true things but not the whole truth, looks like the best policy. On the receiving end, Descartes's malicious demon returns as aliens and devils ('To Serve Man,' 'The Howling Man,' 'Printer's Devil'), and Hume's advice to reject miracle-like testimony fails because in the Zone crazy stuff is often true. The chapter ends by endorsing Pascal's wager through 'The Big Tall Wish' and Jeff Myrtlebank's threat: believe the incredible witness just in case.

pascals-wager.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
pascals-wager.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
pascals-wager.relation: Richard Greene analyzes The King of Comedy's Rupert Pupkin, who kidnaps talk-show host Jerry Landers to force his way onto TV and emerges a celebrity, calling this the 'Pupkin gambit' (harming others and oneself to secure an overwhelming personal payoff). Distinguishing internalist accounts of rationality (Plato's well-ordered soul, Kant's universalizable maxims) from an externalist one, Greene argues the gambit is irrational for a sane agent like the financier Michael Milken but rational for Pupkin via a Pascal's-wager structure: because Pupkin is delusional, even imagined success satisfies his desire, so the wager has huge upside and no real downside for him. He also invokes ethical egoism to show unethical acts can still be assessed for self-interested rationality.

pascals-wager.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
pascals-wager.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
pascals-wager.relation: Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'

pascals-wager.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
pascals-wager.title: 11. The Truth about Lying
pascals-wager.relation: Fallis treats the Twilight Zone as a workbook in the philosophy of testimony (the ethics and epistemology of communication). Truth-tellers get dismissed as insane ('Nightmare at 20,000 Feet') while liars come to bad ends even when believed ('The Four of Us Are Dying'); Kant's reticence offers a third option to truth-telling and lying. On receiving testimony, he uses Hume on evaluating witnesses and disbelieving reports of miracles, then argues the show endorses Pascal's Wager—believe crazy testimony just in case—citing 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' and 'Mr. Garrity and the Graves,' plus Descartes's deceiving demon for the show's alien and devil deceivers.

pascals-wager.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
pascals-wager.title: Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress
pascals-wager.relation: Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.

pascals-wager.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
pascals-wager.title: “You Have to Believe in Something”
pascals-wager.relation: Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.

pascals-wager.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
pascals-wager.title: 31. Inception as Philosophy Choose Your Dreams or Seek Reality
pascals-wager.relation: Johnson uses Nolan's Inception—Cobb's dream-heists, the ambiguous spinning top, and the case that the whole film may be a dream—to test the moral Todd McGowan draws from it: that since we can't be sure what is real, we should abandon the quest for reality and choose the dream (his object of desire, his children) as Cobb does at the end. He evaluates six defenses of that moral, rejecting Descartes' skeptical dream/evil-demon problem (answered by abduction and by Plato's cave and Nozick's experience machine showing true belief is valuable), Baudrillard's denial of reality, Locke/Kant on the unknowable noumenal world, and Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Pascal's Wager, before softening it with Hume's return from skepticism to backgammon: entertain the doubt, then walk away when your children walk in.

will-to-believe.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
will-to-believe.title: Who Should Be Committed
will-to-believe.relation: Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.

will-to-believe.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
will-to-believe.title: 21b
will-to-believe.relation: A paired metaphysics debate on whether superstition helps performance. Steven Streeter argues yes: baseball's mystery-rich outcomes breed ritual (Sparky Anderson refusing to step on foul lines, Wade Boggs's chicken, Nomar Garciaparra's glove taps), whose invisible forces — like black holes — can be inferred from their measurable effects on attention, preparation, and focus, with William James's belief-makes-reality as the capstone. Neil Feit counters no: on the counterfactual account of helping, a player cured of superstition would perform the same since his athletic ability is untouched, routines that aid concentration need involve no magical belief, and the burden of proof lies with the believer.

will-to-believe.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
will-to-believe.title: “A New Hope”
will-to-believe.relation: Long stages William Clifford's ethics of belief against William James's will to believe, with Luke Skywalker as James's exemplar. Clifford's shipowner story condemns faith as 'wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone,' which would convict Luke of immorality when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the Force; James replies that where a choice is intellectually undecidable and a genuine option - live, forced, and momentous, like Luke's turn to the Jedi life or Obi-Wan's response to Leia's hologram - pragmatic faith is justified and even salvific. Faith can create truths: Han flying into the asteroid field, Luke's unjustified belief that there is good in Vader bringing Anakin back, the author's faith in his students, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s dream - all illustrating 'a new hope.'

will-to-believe.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
will-to-believe.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
will-to-believe.relation: Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.

will-to-believe.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
will-to-believe.title: Poker and Philosophy
will-to-believe.relation: Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.

will-to-believe.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
will-to-believe.title: Introduction
will-to-believe.relation: Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.

will-to-believe.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
will-to-believe.title: “You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”
will-to-believe.relation: Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'

will-to-believe.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
will-to-believe.title: Tough and Tender, The Dead Keep Truckin’
will-to-believe.relation: Gary Ciocco traces a line from Emerson and James through Kerouac, Ginsberg, and Neal Cassady to the Grateful Dead: Emerson's nonconformist 'infinitude of man' and James's 'live options' and religious appetite for being 'more fully alive' become, in the Beats, the project of living life itself as art ('the only people for me are the mad ones'). He argues the Beats splintered because each chased an atomistic, individual epiphany — Kerouac swinging wholesale from tender- to tough-minded temperament — while the Dead turned the same Jamesian hunger into a shared communal religious experience, a 'kindler, gentler' scene that better achieves Aristotle's eudaimonia. Cassady, muse of On the Road and driver of the Pranksters' bus, literally connects the two movements, but the Dead's unity-in-diversity made them the evolution, not the echo, of the Beats.

will-to-believe.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
will-to-believe.title: Back from the Edge
will-to-believe.relation: McKenna and Pratt use McDermott's 'Promethean self' and meliorism to answer the riddle of Nebraska's closer 'Reason to Believe': among the dead dog, the deserted bride and the groom left at the altar, 'still at the end of every hard earned day people find some reason to believe.' They trace Springsteen's shift from escape songs ('Born to Run,' 'Thunder Road') to life at the edge ('Badlands,' 'Darkness on the Edge of Town,' and the two midnight drivers of 'State Trooper' and 'Open All Night'), arguing meaning is made by cutting and connecting relations at the margins. Belief without evidence of salvation is legitimate hope but illegitimate certainty; the reason to believe is Jamesian meliorism — making things 'not perfect, simply better.'

will-to-believe.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
will-to-believe.title: Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH
will-to-believe.relation: The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know.
