The chapter notes Soviet Izvestia read it the same way, and that the original thereby fulfilled Moore's own criterion of relevant science fiction from the opposite end of the political spectrum, including Apollo's wartime argument that dissent weakens Colonial resolve.

democracy-theory.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
democracy-theory.title: Bird or Cage
democracy-theory.relation: Elmore reads Columbia's founding through Carl Schmitt: Comstock's baptism Voxophone ('who is that man who lies submerged?') dramatizes how every legal order is founded from outside the law, and the city's identity is built on friend/enemy antagonisms, racial, class, and theocratic, against the 'Sodom below'. The Vox Populi's collapse into tyranny (Daisy Fitzroy threatening Fink's son) follows logically from an identity defined purely by opposition, while Columbia's dependence on Georgia's penal labor shows the friend group materially needs its enemy, making politics an endless war like the War on Terror. Schmitt's sovereign ('he who decides on the exception') and the tears' endless splitting of Booker and Elizabeth mirror the infinite regress of legitimate decision, leaving 'you can't lose if you don't play' as the bleak lesson, softened only by old Elizabeth's tear that lets Booker try again.

democracy-theory.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
democracy-theory.title: After the Waldo Moment
democracy-theory.relation: Littmann reads The Waldo Moment through Donald Trump — Waldo's 'knobber' and 'dickhead' taunts anticipate 'Little Marco' and 'Crooked Hillary' — to ask what is wrong with mockery and disrespect in democratic politics. Plato's Meno shows why true beliefs acquired by mockery rather than understanding are unstable and steerable toward any content, and ad hominem attacks substitute ridicule for engagement with arguments. Mill's On Liberty arguments against censorship and orthodoxy — we might be wrong, collision with error clarifies truth — show that refusing to engage opponents (as Waldo refuses Monroe) locks everyone in 'reality bubbles,' and the chapter concludes that letting anger and mockery replace reasoned engagement, as when Waldo's followers riot, sabotages democracy.

democracy-theory.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
democracy-theory.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: Erion reads The Daily Show's sharpest bits as jokes that only work if the audience already grasps Neil Postman's thesis in Amusing Ourselves to Death that television's entertainment bias renders news irrational, irrelevant and incoherent, from hurricane-reporter parodies and 'The Less You Know' to news-style graphics like 'Mess O' Potamia'. He treats Stewart's 2004 Crossfire confrontation ('stop hurting America', 'you're doing theater, when you should be doing debate'), the 2009 Jim Cramer CNBC 'Brawl Street' interview after the financial crisis, and the 2011 Chris Wallace exchange as explicit versions of the same critique that TV's real bias is toward sensationalism, conflict and laziness rather than partisanship. He closes with the Rally to Restore Sanity and/or Fear's 'conflictinator' speech, noting Stewart is ultimately more optimistic than Postman that television could clarify rather than obfuscate.

democracy-theory.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
democracy-theory.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: Sotos locates The Daily Show within an emergent 'Fifth Estate', a watchdog for the failing Fourth Estate press, and recruits Arendt's actor/spectator distinction to defend Stewart's refusal of activism: like judge, journalist or comedian, the spectator withdraws from action yet gives events their meaning and voice in public conversation. She traces an American fake-news lineage from James and Benjamin Franklin's colonial papers (Silence Dogood, Polly Baker, the Vindex Patriae hoax) through Twain to Stewart, contrasting honest satire with Glenn Beck and Rush Limbaugh's 'fake fake news' and the repeal of the Fairness Doctrine. Juvenalian indignatio ( Stewart's somber 'Fuck you' to CNBC in the Clusterf#@k to the Poor House) and Horatian playfulness (Colbert's Super PAC saga) supply the ethos, and she reads the Rally to Restore Sanity as Aristophanic Old Comedy, complete with agon, parabasis ('A Moment of Sincerity') and a reconciliatory ending that makes 'We the People' exist.

democracy-theory.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
democracy-theory.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: Vanderheiden treats America (The Book)'s textbook parody as serious democratic theory: its 'Democracy Inaction' diagnosis (a president chosen from a field of two, 99% incumbency, lobbyists as 'the white knights of democracy') tracks the thin versus thick democracy distinction and Benjamin Barber's deliberative democracy, with Putnam's social capital as the remedy for the satirized life cycle of national decline. The 'Dress the Supreme Court' gag, Senate color-by-numbers, and third-party graveyard expose representational exclusion, while the media chapter indicts conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role, invoking Mill's marketplace of ideas. The Earth (The Book) postscript notes that social contracts were historically written without the assent of the women and minorities they subjugated.

democracy-theory.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
democracy-theory.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: Sotos reads America (The Book)'s fake Jefferson foreword and Daily Show writer Kevin Bleyer's Me the People as anti-originalist satire aimed at Tea Party 'historical fundamentalism', Jill Lepore's 'anti-history' that literally cancels historical time and treats the Founders as infallible prophets. Jefferson's anti-originalist principle that 'the earth belongs to the living' and his call for a constitutional convention every generation anchor the book, dramatized in Bleyer's imaginary lunch with Justice Scalia (the originalist as Ahab) against Stephen Breyer's living constitutionalism. John Oliver's Morristown Tea Party interviews and the Beck-Hannity-O'Reilly nostalgia montage ('the best time in American history was when they were all six years old') show how altar-worship of the Framers abandons popular sovereignty.

democracy-theory.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
democracy-theory.title: “Look at This Stuff; Isn't It Neat ” disney and the Commodification of Political Values
democracy-theory.relation: Dale and Foy tour the parks' political philosophy: Cinderella's Castle looming over Liberty Square embodies the contradiction between princess hierarchy and Lockean self-government, since Locke's Second Treatise grounds rule in consent and majority will, forbids special rights for rulers, and justifies revolution — the very ideals the 'Declaration salad' celebrates under a monarchy's silhouette. The Epcot World Showcase, judged through Kymlicka, Benhabib, and Taylor's recognition-based multiculturalism, reduces eleven cultures to a consumable menu, so that per Barber's 'McWorld' Disney sells pre-packaged 'freedom' and 'multiculturalism' as spectator values that reinforce rather than transform.

democracy-theory.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
democracy-theory.title: Leto’s Not So Golden Path
democracy-theory.relation: Rejects Herbert's own explanation (hero-worship) for the repeated collapse of Duniverse empires, arguing instead that every ruler from Shaddam IV through Paul and Alia to Leto II governs purely through strategic action, authority enforced by coercion and sanctions, with no democratic legitimacy. Using Habermas's distinction between strategic and communicative action, it reads the Atreides council's evasion of the Landsraad constitution demand, Alia's cry that 'Atreides power must never be marginalized by the chaos of democracy', and Leto II's reliance on breeding programs and deterrence as failures to make the ruled into authors of the law, concluding that physical stability can only last when built on normative stability that democracy provides.

democracy-theory.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Andrea Conque argues the adult-free ('Mungo-free') children of Little Lamplight are genuinely political: they socialize each other into distrust of grownups (mandatory exile at 16 to Big Town), elect mayors by secret popular vote - MacCready's punch against Princess was a coup made legitimate by subsequent election - and fill every office from doctor Lucy to teacher Joseph to Knock Knock, whose Vault Boy jokes 'keep the peace' against social isolation. Sherif's Robber's Cave experiment supplies the comparison: unlike the Eagles and Rattlers, Lamplighters avoid in-group conflict because the radiation-absorbing cave fungus and shared survival give them permanent superordinate goals, while Biwwy's high-damage 'wazer wifle' shows they deter oppression by being, not just posturing as, tough. Against MacCready's claim of 'pure anarchy', the chapter concludes Little Lamplight is the Capital Wasteland's most successful government - freer and better ordered than Megaton, Andale, Paradise Falls, or even the Republic of Dave.

democracy-theory.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
democracy-theory.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: The chapter reconstructs the real Swedish journalist behind Kalle Blomkvist: the 1950s reporter as the welfare state's mouthpiece alongside heroic police, the 1970s radical investigative journalist epitomized by Jan Guillou—whose exposure of the secret IB organization earned him a prison sentence and a revenge vindication, the direct template for Blomkvist—and the 1990s–2000s slide into 'sensation, scandal, and spectacle' around crime. It shows journalism decoupling from crime statistics—about a hundred killings a year in a country of 9.4 million, falling, yet alarmist coverage fueling tougher sentencing and the Nazi-rooted Sweden Democrats' entry into parliament—so the watchdog ideal of the muckraker who draws aside the veil on 'men who hate women and democracy' becomes a question: where have you gone, Kalle Blomkvist?

democracy-theory.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
democracy-theory.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: The chapter reads Salander's hacking beside Julian Assange's WikiLeaks: both are hard to classify as criminal or activist, and both live by the hacker ethic Stephen Levy codified—unlimited access, all information free, mistrust authority, judgment by skill—which later versions soften with privacy and social responsibility, matching 'Salander's Principles' (a bastard is always a bastard) and Assange's 'capable, generous men do not create victims; they nurture victims.' Through David Brin's Transparent Society it asks who watches the watchers—the police-camera city of the state or the citizen-accessible city—and argues for WikiLeaks-style reciprocal transparency that keeps the 'mighty' (governments, the Vanger Corporation, Wennerström) exposed while protecting whistleblower anonymity. Blomkvist's choices—suppressing the Vanger murders, encouraging Salander to steal Wennerström's files, planting disinformation—mark him as the journalist half of Larsson's new information-age hero pair.

democracy-theory.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Argues Frank is 'Hobbesian to the core': for him democracy is just the state of nature with elections, which is why it produces mediocre, fearful presidents like Walker (a Xanax-taking incumbent undone by a mere legislator) while a real sovereign like Frank — or the autocrat Petrov, with whom Frank shares cigars precisely because no common power enforces rules between them — gets things done. The chapter reads Frank's appetites (ribs at Freddy's, power over money against Remy and Tusk, contempt for sleep and death) through Hobbes' pleasure-and-pain psychology and his account of conflict arising when equals want the same thing, which finally drives Claire from the White House. Frank's church scenes ('I pray to myself, for myself') illustrate Hobbes' subordination of religion to civil power, the Kate Baldwin 'he is the tyrant' charge illustrates that a tyrant is only a king disliked, and the closing appeal is to Madison's Federalist 51: only the ambition of others can contain this one.

democracy-theory.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Argues the Underwoods' success is not far-fetched fiction but the structural outcome four critics of democracy predict. Plato's Republic supplies the spine: the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decays through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, whose love of freedom invites the tyrant — Peter Russo with his random desires is the democratic soul, Frank the tyrannical soul ruled by one illicit appetite, doomed to the fear and friendlessness Book 9 describes (which Season 3 delivers). Hobbes and Hegel then explain why monarchy may beat popular rule (the monarch's private interest aligns with the public's; the monarch lets a people will as one), and Marx reframes the whole show economically — SanCorp, Tusk and Feng as capitalists, the laid-off shipyard workers as proletariat, and AmWorks as self-interested politicians flirting with expropriation. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government gives the democratic reply — elections force responsiveness, participation educates citizens — so the burden falls on viewers to keep elections fair, the press free, and checks on unscrupulous politicians effective.

democracy-theory.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Sirvent and Diorio apply Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) to the show's web of watching: Frank manipulates Zoe through leaked stories, Doug keeps Rachel permanently locatable by phone, and Claire must demand the bug be removed from Michael Corrigan's Russian cell, showing watched subjects paralyzed by fear. Against Bauman and Lyon's 'liquid surveillance,' the chapter argues democracy is an anti-institutional force requiring free dissent and a press at arm's length from power, and that surveillance collapses the Greek public/private distinction so citizens fear punishment for questioning rulers. Frank's 'Nobody can hear you. Nobody cares about you' to Zoe captures how the surveillance state turns criticism into danger, leaving a society that is no longer a democracy.

democracy-theory.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Auxier asks who is morally worse, judging Frank and Claire by past deeds (Frank's murders of Zoe and Peter), future consequences (a president with the nuclear button), and the subjunctive (what each would do), while tracing Claire's lineage from Lady Macbeth and Elizabeth Urquhart, who assassinates Francis in the British series. Plato's and Aristotle's warning that democracy degenerates into tyranny frames the answer: Frank symbolizes the House, Claire the Senate, both coveting executive power, and Meechum - 'utterly loyal, utterly deadly' - is the military they seduce in the menage a trois and will underestimate. Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, from McCarthyism and the Joe Welch moment to mass incarceration, explains the verdict that neither individual is worse alone: 'they are far worse together,' and the union, not the person, has no decency.

democracy-theory.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Michels reads Frank as 'Hobbesian to the core' and democracy as 'the state of nature with elections': Walker, Matthews, and Vasquez show that elections elevate mediocrities, while Frank's America Works and his FEMA/Stafford Act end-run around Congress display the energetic sovereign for whom 'a tyrant is only a king disliked.' Hobbes's pleasure-pain psychology of appetite and aversion explains the cast — Frank's ribs, PlayStation, and pure taste for power; Russo's indiscriminate addictions; Doug's serial ones — while Hobbes's competition for gain, fear, and glory structures the Tusk money-versus-power war whose casualties include Freddy. With Hobbes's subordination of religion to civil power, Frank's crucifix-spitting 'I pray to myself, for myself' caps the case that truth only obstructs sovereignty, leaving Madison's 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' as the lone check.

democracy-theory.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Shea argues the Underwoods' rise is structurally guaranteed rather than far-fetched, surveying democracy's critics: Plato's Republic Books 8-9 has the kallipolis of philosopher-guardians decay through timocracy and oligarchy into democracy, where a 'protector'-tyrant like Frank exploits the drones and the people's love of freedom (Russo as the prototypical democratic soul, Tusk as the oligarch-in-fact), while the tyrant ends fear-ridden and friendless — precisely Frank's Season 3. Hobbes and Hegel then reverse the verdict, arguing monarchy aligns the ruler's private interest with the public good and lets a people will as one instead of a formless mass — the insight Tom Yates has about voters identifying with the Underwoods as people — and Marx reframes it economically: SanCorp, Tusk, and Feng are the capitalist structure, and Frank's AmWorks, entitlement cuts, and nationalization threats show self-interested politicians siding with a growing proletariat. Against all four, Mill's Considerations on Representative Government supplies the democratic reply — responsiveness, better information, and citizen participation mean an Underwood cannot last if we keep fair elections, a free press, and real checks.

democracy-theory.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Uses Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) and Bauman's 'liquid surveillance' to read Frank's Washington as a surveillance society: Zoe's archived texts, Doug's inescapable tracking of Rachel, and the bugged cell where Claire visits Michael Corrigan all show how being watched destroys privacy and paralyzes dissent. It argues that democracy needs free spaces in which citizens can question power without later punishment, so the culture of fear Frank rules through-'you are a rock, you absorb nothing, you say nothing'-turns checks and balances into instruments of control even inside an elected government.

democracy-theory.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Asks who is morally worse by three standards-what each has done, is doing, and would do in the future subjunctive-and answers that Frank and Claire are far worse together, read symbolically as the US Constitution itself: Frank is the mercurial House, Claire the deliberate, more ambitious Senate, and Meechum the loyal military they seduce and underestimate at the republic's peril. Working from Plato's and Aristotle's claim that democracy declines into tyranny, Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, and the Welch-McCarthy 'have you no decency' moment, it asks whether a system that produced them is one 'we the people' deserve.

democracy-theory.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
democracy-theory.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
democracy-theory.relation: Argues that South Park performs Popper's defense of the open society by ridiculing 'enemies' on both flanks: Cartman as a Glenn Beck-style ranter in 'Dances with Smurfs' and a xenophobic border agent in 'The Last of the Meheecans', versus liberal fanatics like Rob Reiner in 'Butt Out', Rosie O'Donnell's recount antics in 'Trapper Keeper', and Tom Cruise's litigious Scientology in 'Trapped in the Closet'. The show does not silence extremists but lets them speak and then mocks them, which the authors read through Popper's paradox of tolerance: tolerance cannot be extended to those who suppress criticism, as the Church of Scientology's pressure campaigns showed. A closing section links this to Jefferson's Virginia Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom — 'truth is great and will prevail if left to herself' — making free, offensive argument and dissent the lifeblood of democracy.

democracy-theory.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
democracy-theory.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
democracy-theory.relation: Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.

democracy-theory.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
democracy-theory.title: Notes
democracy-theory.relation: Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.

democracy-theory.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
democracy-theory.title: “We Were Trained to Be Keepers of the Peace, not Soldiers”
democracy-theory.relation: Shakibnia reads The Clone Wars through Cornel West's three dogmas threatening democracy — free-market fundamentalism, aggressive militarism, escalating authoritarianism — and Chomsky's critique of inequality: Senator Halle Burtoni is a deliberate Halliburton/Cheney nod, and the banking-deregulation vote in 'Heroes on Both Sides' mirrors the US military-industrial complex. He argues the Separatist people's movement ('Corporations do not rule us!') was justified in seeking self-determination, while 'Sabotage' shows the Jedi losing legitimacy by becoming 'military weapons' — underpaid Temple worker Jackar Bowmani's squalid housing indicts the Republic's class divide. Ahsoka's departure and her maxim that 'it's every citizen's duty to challenge their leaders' model the accountability movement (like Black Lives Matter) that the Jedi failed to be.

democracy-theory.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
democracy-theory.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
democracy-theory.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.

democracy-theory.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
democracy-theory.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
democracy-theory.relation: Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.

democracy-theory.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
democracy-theory.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: Vanderheiden reads America (The Book) as a work of democratic theory dressed as textbook parody, arguing its satire is a 'rhetoric of challenge' enacting deliberative democracy. He contrasts 'thin' (merely electoral) with 'thick' participatory democracy using Putnam's social capital and Barber's strong democracy, and invokes J.S. Mill's 'marketplace of ideas' and On Liberty to indict media conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role. He reads the companion Earth (The Book) through social-contract theory (Hobbes-style), noting its jab that contractual authority historically required the assent of subjugated groups it never obtained.

democracy-theory.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News
democracy-theory.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
democracy-theory.relation: Sotos uses America (The Book)'s fake Jefferson foreword and Kevin Bleyer's Me the People to attack constitutional 'originalism' and Tea Party 'historical fundamentalism' (per Jill Lepore), arguing the Framers were revolutionaries who intended a living, amendable document. She champions Jefferson's view that 'the earth belongs to the living' and every generation should refound its constitution, contrasts Justice Breyer's living-constitutionalist 'active liberty' with Scalia's originalism ('the Constitution is dead'), invokes Plato's Laws as thinking in similarly living terms, and uses John Oliver's Tea Party interviews to expose 'anti-history' that cancels historical time.

democracy-theory.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
democracy-theory.title: Who is Who
democracy-theory.relation: This political chapter reads Gallifreyan bureaucracy ('The Deadly Assassin') and 1970s socialist-tinged serials, using Marx's alienation and critique of capital to interpret 'The Pirate Planet' and 'The Robots of Death,' and Aristotle's 'political animal' plus Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of democracy against Benjamin Barber's participatory democracy. It analyzes the pathologies of democratic consent through 'Vengeance on Varos' (Plato's ideal state inverted) and 'The Beast Below' (Arendt on totalitarianism, self-inflicted ignorance), with Isaiah Berlin's negative liberty in the vocabulary of materiality.

democracy-theory.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
democracy-theory.title: 6. Black Sails as Philosophy Pirates and Political Discourse
democracy-theory.relation: Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.

democracy-theory.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
democracy-theory.title: 16. House of Cards as Philosophy Democracy on Trial
democracy-theory.relation: The chapter uses the Underwoods' extra-electoral rise to autocracy in House of Cards to test Plato's and Hobbes's antidemocratic arguments. Frank and Claire exploit the exact weaknesses Plato's Republic diagnoses—Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' the decay of oligarchy into freedom-loving democracy into tyranny, and Peter Russo as the disordered-soul 'democratic man' and 'drone.' It then invokes Hobbes's Leviathan, arguing the show's power-struggle resembles a state of nature and that Hobbes would welcome Claire's absolute rule as more predictable and less corrupt than democracy, before weighing modern defenses of democracy (Levitsky and Ziblatt, Locke, Mill, Rawls, Sen) against these critiques.

democracy-theory.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
democracy-theory.title: 27. Squid Game as Philosophy The Myths of Democracy
democracy-theory.relation: The chapter argues that Squid Game exposes five 'myths' of democracy by showing how its trappings mask control by the wealthy few. Using Aristotle's Politics and Nicomachean Ethics it attacks the myth of free choice (the players' consent is coerced by debt) and the failure to cultivate virtue and transparency (Gi-hun deceives Il-nam in the marble game); it uses Sen and Nussbaum's capability approach to deny genuine empowerment; and it applies Plato's Phaedo two-worlds doctrine to argue the game instantiates no true form of truth, beauty, goodness, or justice. Il-nam's tie-breaking vote and Player 111's advantages illustrate that equality is only superficial, leaving a Hobbesian war of all against all inside a democratic shell.

invisible-hand.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
invisible-hand.title: Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy
invisible-hand.relation: Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.

invisible-hand.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
invisible-hand.title: 20b
invisible-hand.relation: A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.

invisible-hand.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
invisible-hand.title: Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life
invisible-hand.relation: Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.

invisible-hand.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
invisible-hand.title: Need that Cash to Feed that Jones
invisible-hand.relation: Steven Gimbel and Brendan Cushing-Daniels argue that the Dead's parking-lot economy — tie-dye shirts priced at ten, twelve, or fifteen dollars, veggie burritos, dueling bootlegs — realized Adam Smith's classical picture of capitalism, not the corporate capitalism Marx attacked. They trace Smith's Newtonian invisible hand and market equilibrium, his ethics of sympathy tempering self-interest, then the Social Darwinist twist given Smith under industrialization and Marx's four types of alienation under postwar white-collar work that pushed hippies to drop out. The punchline: deadhead sellers were not alienated — making shirts was creative self-expression — and buyer-seller sympathy ('it was simply uncool to screw over a fellow deadhead') made the lot a sustainable, kinder 'caring capitalism' that kept the scene alive.

invisible-hand.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
invisible-hand.title: Caring Dogs Watching Flying Pigs
invisible-hand.relation: Croskery reads Animals as a beast fable in the tradition of Orwell's Animal Farm that opens with a thought experiment ('If you didn't care what happened to me / And I didn't care for you') and portrays a world without empathy across three corruptible institutions. 'Dogs' dramatizes a malfunctioning marketplace where Adam Smith's invisible-hand justification fails, since success requires lying to those you must trust and ends with the sad old man 'dragged down by the stone'; 'Pigs (3 Different Ones)' targets state corruption from Mary Whitehouse's censorship crusade to war-waging and regulatory capture; and 'Sheep' depicts Marxist false consciousness, the pastoral illusion hiding the slaughterhouse, capped by the Twenty-Third Psalm parody that 'converteth me to lamb cutlets.' The chapter concludes that libertarian, statist, and traditionalist errors each idolize one institution, and that Waters's closing 'Pigs on the Wing' points to the delicate balance of market, state, and community that political philosophy must strike.

invisible-hand.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
invisible-hand.title: “There’s More to Life than Profit”
invisible-hand.relation: Held argues business ethics stalls because it begins from capitalism's presuppositions instead of asking what we fundamentally value, staging the impasse as Quark versus Rom and as Friedman's stockholder theory against Freeman's stakeholder theory ('The Dogs of War', Zek's reforms, 'Profit and Lace'). He recovers Aristotle's Politics distinction between economics serving the household's good and chrematistics — money-making as sheer accumulation, embodied in Quark's 'pure profit' embezzlement — and corrects the libertarian caricature of Adam Smith: the invisible hand works only within commutative justice and virtue, markets serving welfare rather than profit. Through Sen's capability approach and Quark's own defense of greed as promoting human development in 'Prophet Motive', the chapter concludes profit is only a means to freedom and well-being — 'there's more to life than profit' — and the Rules of Acquisition themselves must stand before the ethical judge.

invisible-hand.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
invisible-hand.title: I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion
invisible-hand.relation: Smith dissects Stephen's free-market worship — the market as a God requiring faith, 'the market has spoken' on global warming, supply-side economics, and the plan to run universities as businesses with credit-card-swiper desks and tuition priced by marketability. Against this he deploys Socrates in the Republic: a practice is defined by its aim, so a physician aiming at his own wealth is not practicing medicine badly but moneymaking, and by the same argument a corporatized university whose primary aim is shareholder profit is no longer higher education — privatization alters its nature and so destroys it, while Smith's invisible hand is exposed as the South Park gnomes' missing Step Two and wikiality as supply-side epistemology where facts are supplied by majority vote instead of known.

invisible-hand.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King
invisible-hand.title: Buffing Our Economic Knowledge with World of Warcraft
invisible-hand.relation: Eli Kosminsky argues that Blizzard, probably unintentionally, built a perfectly competitive market: the auction house satisfies the textbook conditions of innumerable sellers (everyone dumping Mithril bars), homogeneous goods (every piece of Spellweave identical), perfect communication (instantly visible prices, no opportunity cost), and no barriers to entry (switching from farming Crystallized Shadows to Crystallized Fire costs nothing). He then tests the theory against server data — prices on high-population servers are nearly twice as stable as on low-population ones, and lesser and greater planar essences trade at almost exactly the predicted 3:1 ratio. Adam Smith's invisible hand works in Azeroth, making WoW a laboratory for economics that no real market could match.

invisible-hand.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
invisible-hand.title: Don’t Be a Vegeta
invisible-hand.relation: Argues that shonen fighting anime stage a choice between Adam Smith's and Darwin's models of competition: Zoro hunting Mihawk in One Piece, Goku's technique-by-technique training, and Rock Lee's specialization show competition improving people within the limits of a human excellence, while Cell's absorbing evolutions, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's risky hollowification represent limitless 'leveling up' that changes what you are. The chapter concludes that the Darwinian win-at-all-costs model produces the perpetually dissatisfied Vegeta, and that framing competition around being a certain kind of person (a great swordsman, not just a winner) gives life a completable aim — while conceding that Darwinians rightly warn our picture of the 'normal human' has unjustly cast off jinchūriki like Naruto and Gaara and Devil Fruit users like Luffy.

invisible-hand.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
invisible-hand.title: A Second Look at Dexter’s Motives
invisible-hand.relation: David Ramsay Steele first calculates that Dexter is a public benefactor - each killed predator saves several net lives a year - and then explains the deeper appeal through Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and Adam Smith's invisible hand: like good law, Harry's Code channels an amoral appetite (the thrill of killing) into socially beneficial results without reforming the appetite itself, refuting Christianity's fixation on pure motives. Dexter thus does totally the right thing for totally the wrong reason. Finally Steele doubts Dexter's own story: the spontaneously unlocked door of the Castillos' shed shows real empathy, and it was Harry's deliberate instruction (Nurse Mary), not fate, that made him a killer - 'addiction is always a choice.'

invisible-hand.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
invisible-hand.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
invisible-hand.relation: The chapter presents Barney as a Humean moral philosopher: reason is the slave of the passions, and norms like the Bro Code are invented conventions that evolve, Adam Smith's invisible-hand style, rather than being designed, revealed, or deduced. The Platinum Rule ('never, ever love thy neighbor') is grounded in Humean reciprocity: the eight-stage arc of attraction to fallout in Barney's Wendy the Waitress disaster, the Gerards' brunch tyranny, and Robin's romance with co-worker Curt shows the retaliation costs that make the norm a rational solution to coordination failures. Against the Golden Rule's painterly elegance, the anatomist's cautious observation of behavior explains why a norm banning neighborly love emerges even in a society of non-saints.

invisible-hand.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
invisible-hand.title: Homeland and Philosophy
invisible-hand.relation: Christophe Porot and Charles Taliaferro ask whether Homeland's pervasive hypocrisy and deceit can be justified, starting from Walden's cover-up of the drone strike and Brody's heroic persona hiding a terrorist plot. Machiavelli's Prince supplies the case that political relationships with allies (Saul's 'Us and Them' speech to Carrie) require hypocrisy, while the Smith-inspired 'honest politicking' model - trading openly on self-interest, as with Carrie blackmailing al Sahrani - fails because politics should secure the public good, though la Rochefoucauld's 'homage vice pays virtue' explains Saul extorting the judge into doing right. Weighing Kant's unconditional duty not to lie (Carrie's fatal lie to Lynne Reed) against consequentialism, the chapter lands on the Walzer Dirty Hands view: some acts stay wrong yet necessary, and honest agents accept the guilt.

invisible-hand.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
invisible-hand.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
invisible-hand.relation: Salvino casts Jobs as a billionaire egoist-visionary in the lineage of Adam Smith's insight that an entrepreneur's self-interest, not good intentions, best satisfies people's wants, Emerson's self-reliance, and Rand's virtues of independence and integrity—comparing Jobs to Howard Roark while noting his intuition was 'un-Randianly' unreasoned. Through Schumpeterian creative destruction (the automobile killing the horse-and-carriage; Wozniak's Apple I that HP rejected) and Deming's quality-first management, he explains Jobs's 'faster horse' contempt for market research, then rebuts the three standard ethical complaints—Foxconn labor conditions, his harsh verbal lashings, and his refusal to join the Giving Pledge—arguing Jobs did more good making the iPad than philanthropy ever could.

invisible-hand.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
invisible-hand.title: 3. Will the Real American Hero Please Stand Up
invisible-hand.relation: Samuelson argues Tony Stark is the real American hero because he embodies the Locke-to-Smith lineage of American values - natural rights, property from mixing labor, free trade and the invisible hand, plus Smithian sympathy - carried forward into twenty-first-century neoliberalism, from Stark Industries to backing the Registration Act. Steve, by contrast, keeps abandoning the Captain America identity (Nomad after the Secret Empire, The Captain under Nuke's government, handing the shield to Bucky and Sam Wilson) whenever America betrays the dream, and admits his true fight is against bullies and for human rights everywhere. Hence Cap is a great hero but not strictly an American one, while Tony lives American values practically, warts and all.

invisible-hand.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
invisible-hand.title: This is Rumor Control. Here are the Facts!
invisible-hand.relation: Uses the Weyland corporations' treatment of crews - Special Order 937, Vickers's 'that makes you an employee,' Burke's Facehugger scheme, the debriefing that mourns a $42 million ship but never the crew - to pit stockholder theory (Friedman, Berle) against libertarian contract theory (Machan) and stakeholder theory (Freeman). The libertarian middle way fails because in deep space crews have neither Hirschman's exit nor voice, so only stakeholder theory explains why hiding workplace hazards and marking employees expendable wrongs them; the market's invisible hand behaves like Ash's very visible murdering hand.

invisible-hand.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
invisible-hand.title: 4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful
invisible-hand.relation: Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership versus acceptance or rejection of the social order: the Dowager's 'we don't work' stagnation, Isobel and the Crawley sisters' redemptive projects, Molesley's grateful endurance, and the escapes of Gwen, Alfred, and Branson. The Anna scene, in which she answers her attacker Mr. Green with trained servant courtesy moments after the assault, shows how work 'becomes' us, while the alphabetical ordering of the opening credits suggests that only fulfilling work, not class position, matters. Rousseau, Adam Smith, and Marx frame the negative view of work (agriculture breeding inequality, the pin factory's deadening division of labor, wage exploitation and ideology), against which the chapter endorses Aristotle's pleasures of play and leisure, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper, predicting that automation will soon force everyone to confront what leisure is for.

invisible-hand.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
invisible-hand.title: Notes
invisible-hand.relation: Argues that Rawls' ideal theory rests on a 'strict compliance' assumption — citizens and politicians who pursue justice rather than self-interest — which makes his ideal society look like The West Wing, while House of Cards depicts the real one: teachers' unions fighting performance standards, Senator Haas blocking the omnibus bill for electoral fear, Jackie Sharp trading favors, and SanCorp's Remy Danton buying votes against Russo's watershed bill. The chapter traces the competing 'every man a knave' tradition — Smith's invisible hand converting the butcher's self-love into our dinner, Hume's maxim for constitution-designers, Madison's 'ambition counteract ambition', and Buchanan's public choice revival — and uses the theory of the second best to argue we must design institutions (publicly financed elections, balanced-budget and inflation amendments, a generality constraint) that assume Underwoods run for Congress.

invisible-hand.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
invisible-hand.title: Notes
invisible-hand.relation: Kogelmann argues that political philosophers' ideal theory rests on Rawls's 'strict compliance' assumption — the West Wing picture where citizens and politicians pursue the public good — while House of Cards depicts the reality: Russo's zoning constituent, the teachers' union fighting performance standards, Senator Haas and Sharp's colleagues trading votes for self-interest. By the theory of the second best, ideals designed for selfless politicians misfire in a world with Frank and Remy Danton in it, so he recruits the older 'every man a knave' tradition — Adam Smith's self-love turned to public benefit, Hume's maxim, Madison's ambition-countering-ambition, Buchanan's 'politics without romance' — to redesign institutions against rent-seeking (SanCorp's purchase of votes on Russo's watershed bill) and politicians' short election-cycle horizons (Claire courting Senator Mendoza), via public financing and balanced-budget and inflation rules.

invisible-hand.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
invisible-hand.title: Tony Learns His Lesson
invisible-hand.relation: Terjesen tests Andrew Carnegie's 'Gospel of Wealth' — that self-made men like Tony are uniquely qualified to administer their surplus wealth and technology for the common good — against Tony's monopolization of the Iron Man armor in 'Armor Wars' (neutralizing even S.H.I.E.L.D.'s Mandroids, attacking the innocent Stingray by mistake) and his futurist manipulations during Civil War. Spencer's social Darwinism underwrites Carnegie's faith that the successful know best, while Adam Smith's skepticism about those who 'affected to trade for the public good' explains why Tony's centralized control ended in the Skrull invasion and Norman Osborn's rise. The lesson is Smithian magnanimity: Tony begins to listen when an employee corrects his volcano trench, keeping his expertise but conceding he does not always know best.

invisible-hand.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
invisible-hand.title: Notes
invisible-hand.relation: Thomas reads Bartertown's economy as embedded in social and political relations rather than a free market: the Underworld laborers versus Bartertown's elite stage Marx's class struggle, and the Aunty Entity–Master Blaster conflict runs through Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis of capital versus labor. He treats the franchise as a post-peak-oil world, applies the tragedy of the commons and lifeboat ethics to water rationing and the Citadel's hierarchy, and counterposes Gandhi's cooperation, Adam Smith's invisible hand, and open-source-style collaboration. The conclusion: the Wasteland shows the failure of self-interest-based capitalism and the need for cooperative alternatives like direct democracy.

invisible-hand.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
invisible-hand.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
invisible-hand.relation: Cantor frames South Park with Plato's Silenus image from the Symposium — Socrates' ridiculous, ass-and-cobbler talk hiding wisdom inside — to argue the show's obscenity wraps genuinely philosophical libertarianism, just as Aristophanes' Clouds gave Socrates fart jokes about thunder. Reading 'Gnomes' closely (the gnomes' Collect Underpants/?/Profit plan, Mr. Tweek's slick nostalgia advertising and sale of his son into slavery rhetoric, the boys' flip on Prop 10), the chapter applies Smith's invisible hand: business activity looks like sneaky theft to outsiders, but Harbucks wins by serving consumers, while Mr. Tweek's real sin is enlisting government power against a rival. 'Cripple Fight' (Big Gay Al defending the Boy Scouts' freedom of association) and 'Something Wall Mart This Way Comes' (the store's heart is a mirror reflecting consumer desire) extend the same lesson — freedom cuts both ways, and the market answers to shoppers, not regulators.

invisible-hand.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
invisible-hand.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
invisible-hand.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that The Aviator, unusually for Hollywood, is a libertarian celebration of the entrepreneur, turning billionaire Howard Hughes into a Scorsese underdog battling the establishment. Drawing on Adam Smith and the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, Cantor reads Hughes's willingness to risk his own money on Hell's Angels and TWA, his visionary anticipation of talkies and jets, and his Senate-hearing fight against the Pan Am/Senator Brewster monopoly as a dramatization of the true risk-taking entrepreneur versus the mere manager. The 'socialist dinner party' with the aristocratic Hepburns and Hughes's defeat of government-backed monopoly illustrate Smith's suspicion of merchants seeking privilege and his invisible-hand claim that self-interested competition, not those who 'trade for the publick good,' best serves the public.

invisible-hand.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
invisible-hand.title: 15. Punk Political Philosophy
invisible-hand.relation: Sulek finds punk's only consistent political feature to be contempt for authority, and models its 'apolitical politics without rulers' on self-organizing civil society: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Adam Ferguson's civil society - dismissed by Hegel and Marx but resurrected by Václav Havel and East European dissidents. Bob Geldof's Band Aid/Live Aid 'punk diplomacy' (a 'constituency of compassion' saying the unsayable to Ethiopian officials) and the improbable line from the Velvet Underground via Havel to the Plastic People of the Universe, Charter 77, and the Velvet Revolution show punk 'living in truth' against entropic ideology-as-ritual: destroying stagnant cultural regimes while owing them the building of alternatives.

invisible-hand.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
invisible-hand.title: Whose Egg Is It, Really Property Rights and Distributive Justice
invisible-hand.relation: Cribbs treats the Horton-versus-Mayzie custody fight over the egg as a property-rights puzzle, applying Locke's labor-mixing theory (Horton's season of incubation versus Mayzie's laying and abandonment, plus squatter's rights) and its provisos against waste and taking more than 'enough and as good,' illustrated by the Once-ler and Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Adam Smith's invisible hand and the Wubble-chap's skilled labor defend market inequality, while Sylvester McBean's Sneetch exploitation, Yertle, and Marx's alienated proletariat motivate Rawls's veil of ignorance and distributive justice as a corrective to unregulated property rights.

invisible-hand.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There
invisible-hand.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
invisible-hand.relation: Halbert uses a Hawaiian route-setter friend upset that his 'secret' crag went public to argue climbing culture is a gift economy that defies Locke's labor theory of property and the self-interest of Locke and Adam Smith. Route setters spend money and labor establishing climbs, then give them freely to a commons, exemplifying Kropotkin's social-anarchist mutual aid over Social Darwinist competition. Citing the Red River Gorge Coalition and Muir Valley, she recasts Hardin's tragedy of the commons as Carol Rose's 'comedy of the commons,' where more participants enhance rather than diminish the shared value.

invisible-hand.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture
invisible-hand.title: NOTES
invisible-hand.relation: Cantor argues that TV shows like The Simpsons and The X-Files can be genuine art despite multiple authorship, contingency, and commercial pressure, using the Lone Gunmen's audience-driven revival and Scully's pregnancy-forced abduction plot as evidence of a 'feedback' rather than 'perfect plan' model of creation. He rejects the Romantic/New Critical ideal of the solitary genius producing organic form and reframes popular culture through Hayek's spontaneous order, drawing directly on Adam Smith's self-regulating markets (the invisible hand) and Darwinian selection. Aristotle's Poetics supplies the target organic-form doctrine—that every part serves the whole—which Cantor says wrongly theorizes contingency out of art.

macintyre-tradition.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
macintyre-tradition.title: America’s Game
macintyre-tradition.relation: William Morgan answers Richard Rorty's charge that American pop culture breeds only militaristic chauvinism by pointing to baseball's moral self-story: played for love of the game (Whitman) rather than market value. Using MacIntyre's notion of a practice's internal goods, he argues baseball's excellences and fair play are shared, socially constructed goods that resist commodification; through Annette Baier's ethics of trust and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' (saving your wife because she is your wife), the home team extends familial trust into a public moral community. Hence the moral outrage of 'Say it ain't so, Joe' after the 1919 Black Sox scandal and 'Say It Ain't So Sammy' after Sosa's corked bat: fans demand that players justify themselves to the community whose common good the game embodies.

macintyre-tradition.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
macintyre-tradition.title: 20b
macintyre-tradition.relation: A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.

macintyre-tradition.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
macintyre-tradition.title: Goals for All Ages and All Occasions
macintyre-tradition.relation: Opening with Camus's line that crushing truths perish from being acknowledged (and his Sisyphus, invoked to show the intrinsically interested player always wins), the authors force football to face its ugly side—divers, Pepe kicking Casquero on the ground, Catania's mooning free-kick screen, referee Pérez Burrull's robbery of Osasuna, the Heysel disaster, Bilardo pinning opponents and drugging Branco, FIFA's resistance to technology—analyzing it all with MacIntyre's account of social practices: football's constitutive rules and internal goods generate standards of excellence that cheating betrays for extrinsic rewards. Their positive ideal is the Greek Kalon, the noble-and-beautiful they field for Plato and Aristotle, exemplified when De Rossi confesses his handball goal against Messina or opponents return the ball after an injury stoppage—the beau geste uniting aesthetic grace and moral honor, as in the 4–4 Arsenal–Liverpool classic where 'neither side deserved to lose'. The ugly, they conclude, is exactly what lets the beautiful shine, as Eto'o floats over Scholes's tackle to assist a Messi goal.

macintyre-tradition.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
macintyre-tradition.title: An Eye for an Eye
macintyre-tradition.relation: Mihaela Frunza and Anatolia Bessemer use MacIntyre's Whose Justice? Which Rationality? to frame Holmes's casual felonies, the disguised-clergyman trick on Irene Adler, freeing Captain Croker after staging a mock courtroom in 'The Abbey Grange', and compounding a felony with Isadora Klein in 'The Three Gables', as one tradition of justice among several with no neutral court of appeal. Against the police's letter-of-the-law tradition stand the criminals' own codes of retribution, above all Jefferson Hope in A Study in Scarlet letting 'the high God judge' between the poisoned and harmless pills, making Holmes and his prey mirror-image vigilantes who prefer restitution or chivalric acquittal to statutory punishment.

macintyre-tradition.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
macintyre-tradition.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
macintyre-tradition.relation: Mudde and Piercey argue Curb depicts Nietzschean nihilism made humdrum: in Larry's world 'the highest values devalue themselves,' so Ted Danson's 'anonymous' donation is leaked for glory, a terrorist warning becomes leverage in a tiff with Mindy Reiser, and strangers judge everyone constantly because no one is a moral authority. The Platonic and Aristotelian answers to what 'the good' is have no purchase here; moral language survives only as a hollow shell, which is MacIntyre's 'simulacra of morality,' and his own remedy—rebuilding communities that give moral rules a point—fails because on Curb community is hell ('I'd rather have the thieves than the neighbors'). Since ought no longer implies can, the show is tragic, though the Tourettic chef's opening night in 'The Grand Opening,' where Larry leads a communal torrent of obscenities in solidarity, offers a fragile glimpse of doing a little good.

macintyre-tradition.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
macintyre-tradition.title: 8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be
macintyre-tradition.relation: Corey Horn maps the Deadpool movie onto Joseph Campbell's monomyth—ordinary world, call to adventure (the cancer diagnosis), refusal of the recruiter's offer, acceptance, and the ordeal of hunting Ajax—then asks whether a mercenary chasing reward can be a hero at all. MacIntyre's chess example distinguishes instrumental from intrinsic rewards of a practice, and Kant splits motivation into duty versus self-interested motives; since Wade hunts Ajax to recover his face and Vanessa, both thinkers would deny his journey is moral. Still, MacIntyre's allowance for migrating from instrumental to intrinsic motivation leaves Deadpool a hero-in-progress, already promising Colossus he will consider joining the X-Men.

macintyre-tradition.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
macintyre-tradition.title: 7. How Captain America and Iron Man Embody America
macintyre-tradition.relation: Altmann contrasts Tony's individualist cosmopolitanism - privatizing world peace, building Ultron alone - with Steve's community-rooted patriotism, the team player from war bonds through the Howling Commandos to Winter Soldier. Using Scruton's definition of patriotism as standing or falling together, MacIntyre's claim that morality grows only within a particular community, and Nussbaum's suggestion to be a patriot first and grow into a cosmopolitan, he concludes Cap's thoughtful patriotism is morally preferable while Tony's globe-saving individualism keeps backfiring. The best American would combine Tony's concern for the whole Earth with Steve's love of neighbor, so no civil war is needed.

macintyre-tradition.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
macintyre-tradition.title: 14. After the Blackout
macintyre-tradition.relation: Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.

macintyre-tradition.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
macintyre-tradition.title: Too Big to Function
macintyre-tradition.relation: Terjesen argues Jack's combined title, Vice President of East Coast Television and Microwave Oven Programming, exhibits the corporate mentality: following Robert Jackall's Moral Mazes, credit flows up (Jack's Trivection oven) and blame flows down (Greenzo, the fireworks fiasco), so managers learn to avoid decisive action. Peter French's thesis that corporations are moral persons explains why GE runs fine with Don Geiss in a coma and Kathy Geiss playing with unicorns, so no one at the top needs to understand the businesses they oversee. MacIntyre's distinction between practices with internal goods and external rewards shows profit-thinking erasing comedy's internal good, turning TGS into 'pos-mens' and product integration, and Adam Smith's attack on distant, ignorant regulators is turned against conglomerate central management itself.

macintyre-tradition.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
macintyre-tradition.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
macintyre-tradition.relation: Interrogates Gob's catchphrase 'I've made a huge mistake': on Aristotle's account of hexis, the mean of truthfulness and proper pride, and justice as proportional distribution, Gob's prison-escape key stunt and 'Hermano' jealousy make him wicked rather than merely error-prone, since he lacks grasp of his own injustices. Hume's sentimentalist reply is that immorality is a nonrational moral sense refined only through experience, so mistakes could educate Gob, except he roofies away his one growth moment with Steve Holt (!). MacIntyre's practices (the Magician's Alliance versus non-practitioner Gob) and the narrative unity of character explain why a man who tells no coherent story of himself ends up with no wisdom.

macintyre-tradition.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
macintyre-tradition.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
macintyre-tradition.relation: Nicholas argues the film's supposed nihilists, Walter, and the Big Lebowski are all failed Nietzschean value-creators: Walter's arbitrary givings of value ('Donny was a good man... he was one of us') just enact nihilism, and the disabled achiever's money-and-plaques world mistakes symbols for value. He then uses Charles Taylor's three malaises of modernity — disenchantment, disengagement, atomism — to explain the Dude's world (even bowling stops mattering: 'Fuck the tournament'), and finds the way out in MacIntyre's notion of a practice: bowling's internal goods, standards of excellence, and community of giving and receiving tie the three friends to meanings outside themselves, resisting nihilism.

macintyre-tradition.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
macintyre-tradition.title: It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It
macintyre-tradition.relation: Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.

macintyre-tradition.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
macintyre-tradition.title: Notes
macintyre-tradition.relation: Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.

macintyre-tradition.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
macintyre-tradition.title: Reconciliation Doesn’t Come in a Bottle
macintyre-tradition.relation: Elia reads Don through Camus's Clamence in The Fall, an establishment success shadowed by guilt and self-medication, while insisting Don is no existential hero: unlike Sisyphus or Meursault, Dick Whitman never lucidly chose his freedom, he merely fled his past by stealing dog tags in Korea. Using MacIntyre's After Virtue opposition between Nietzschean value-creation and Aristotelian tradition-embeddedness, the chapter argues Don lacks integrity, the virtue that justifies breaks in one's narrative by deeper commitments, which is why peace appears only when past and present reconcile: phoning Anna as 'Dick Whitman,' the ocean immersion, and the confession to Betty ('I can explain' / 'You're a very, very gifted story-teller'). His justice is real but thin, a merit-based accounting that works at the office (promoting Peggy on talent) yet fails Betty, the children, and Adam, and reconciliation, the title insists, doesn't come in a bottle.

macintyre-tradition.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
macintyre-tradition.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
macintyre-tradition.relation: Sanford argues, through the arc of the Raimi trilogy, that Peter becomes good by becoming the narrator of his own life. On Aristotle's Poetics — a story has a beginning, middle, and end, and art imitates life — and MacIntyre's claim that man is a 'story-telling animal' whose life is 'the unity of a narrative quest,' Peter's involuntary obligations (orphanhood, Uncle Ben's death, the spider bite, love for MJ) ground the voluntary ones, and his quest is to use his great powers responsibly. Tracking Aristotle's categories, Peter moves from incontinence (vengeance on Flint Marko, the jazz-club strut in Spider-Man 3) through continence to genuine virtue, and his practice of telling his own story — 'it's the choices that make us who we are' — models how we must get our own stories straight to flourish.

macintyre-tradition.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
macintyre-tradition.title: Allure of the West
macintyre-tradition.relation: Nicholas Moll reads the Westworld park as a tabletop-style sandbox and LARP role-play experience with Ford as Game Master mediating guests' mediated 'illusion of choice.' Drawing on MacIntyre's narrative unity of a life and Bernard Williams's critique about the constraints of coherence, he argues guests author competing self-narratives to reach greater self-knowledge, as William discovers his capacity for ruthlessness and becomes the Man in Black. He contends violence functions as the rule-mediated engine of this 'gameful,' educative experience, and that Ford's transformative insight is aimed less at the guests than at the hosts who are engaged in the park's production.

macintyre-tradition.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
macintyre-tradition.title: Basketball Purists
macintyre-tradition.relation: Kretchmar defends a 'modified purist' view that team-oriented, fundamentals-based basketball is generally better than the individualist modernist game, offering three arguments. The functionalist argument borrows Searle's account of constitutive rules to say ten-person interactive complexity makes a richer, more durable 'test' (like chess vs. tic-tac-toe); the variety argument uses Mill's On Liberty to warn that market pressures homogenize basketball toward football; and the communitarian argument uses MacIntyre's notion of a 'practice' with internal goods to show ESPN Streetball's isolated one-on-one feats erode basketball as a cooperative practice.

macintyre-tradition.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
macintyre-tradition.title: Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis
macintyre-tradition.relation: Tommy Valentini argues that because winning lies outside a player's control (he could never beat Nadal by simply choosing to), success in tennis should be redefined around what is controllable. Using Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue, he treats tennis as a MacIntyrean practice and distinguishes external goods (trophies, prize money, ranking—zero-sum, tied to winning) from internal goods (full effort, positive attitude, sportsmanship) that require the virtues of justice, honesty, and courage and are available to winner and loser alike. Drawing on Aristotelian justice ('giving each their due') and Randolph Feezell on the opponent as competitor-and-friend, he holds up Arthur Ashe's Stoic response to AIDS in Days of Grace as the exemplar of carrying tennis's internal goods into life in the face of an uncontrollable outcome, death.

macintyre-tradition.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
macintyre-tradition.title: Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play
macintyre-tradition.relation: Opening with Gunther Parche's stabbing of Monica Seles to injure Steffi Graf's rival, the chapter argues that a win-at-all-costs mentality misunderstands sport's value. Using Suits's account of games (lusory goals, means, rules, attitude) and rejecting bare formalism for Simon's broad internalism, it grounds tennis's intrinsic worth in the difficulty of achievement, the level of the opponent, and MacIntyre's notion of a practice with internal goods. It reframes fair play as 'respect for the game,' classifies fans as partisan, purist, or ideally moderate partisan, and concludes that by eliminating Seles, Parche damaged not just her but Graf's legacy and tennis itself because he loved the game too little.

macintyre-tradition.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
macintyre-tradition.title: Charlie Kaufman, Screenwriter
macintyre-tradition.relation: Evans reads Adaptation as a creation story: the character Charlie Kaufman must make a script 'out of nothing' rather than transcribe Susan Orlean's Orchid Thief, so the film enacts Deleuze's idea of the writer as fabulator who confronts the audience with the text as invention. She sets Charlie's Genesis-like 'beginning without end' against Donald and Robert McKee's Aristotelian, plot-driven Story where the ending justifies the means (glossing MacIntyre's 'stories are lived before they are told'). Naming the character after himself, she argues, marks the distance between imaginative making (poesis) and Orlean's realist journalism (mimesis).

macintyre-tradition.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
macintyre-tradition.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
macintyre-tradition.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Eastwood, though no academic, does 'practical philosophy' through his films as a craftsman who inherits and then revises genres (revising the Western in Unforgiven, rethinking rugged individualism in Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino). Invoking MacIntyre's claim that we are only co-authors of interlocking narratives, it reads Eastwood's focus on decisive moral choices (Francesca's refusal to leave in Bridges of Madison County, Butch Haynes in A Perfect World) as a 'laboratory of moral psychology' echoing Aristotle's 'choice discriminates character.' It ties his concern with loss, justice, and Aristotelian friendship and flourishing (Grinnell on Million Dollar Baby) to a Socratic 'know thyself,' arguing his philosophizing is implicit and nonverbal rather than argued in words.

macintyre-tradition.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
macintyre-tradition.title: “A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo
macintyre-tradition.relation: Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.

macintyre-tradition.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
macintyre-tradition.title: Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour
macintyre-tradition.relation: Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.

macintyre-tradition.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
macintyre-tradition.title: One More Thing, Don’t Blink!
