power-knowledge.title: I Remember It All Too Well: Memory, Nostalgia, and the Archival Art of Taylor Swift
power-knowledge.relation: Reads Swift's songwriting as 'archival art' through Derrida's Archive Fever and Ricoeur's archival trace: songs like 'marjorie' (with her grandmother's actual backing vocals), 'august', and 'All Too Well (10 Minute Version)' preserve traces of what is gone while re-creating, not merely capturing, memory. With Foucault's power/knowledge it argues that controlling the archive means controlling the stories told about oneself, citing 'Dear John (Taylor's Version)' and the Speak Now rerecording as acts of reclaiming power through speech. Stuart Hall's 'living archive' frames the rerecordings as memory continually remade, and Derrida/Halbwachs ground the claim that her music is a public site of collective memory where fans archive their own lives, as in 'mirrorball' and the Eras Tour.

power-knowledge.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
power-knowledge.title: The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy
power-knowledge.relation: Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.

power-knowledge.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
power-knowledge.title: Monstrous motherhood
power-knowledge.relation: The chapter argues that horror films about mothers are not static representations but Foucauldian sites where 'discourses of motherhood' are produced, policed and contested; using Foucault's account of bodies disciplined through power/knowledge, it treats films as cultural artefacts that both enforce and challenge norms of 'essential' and 'ideal' motherhood. It reworks Sarah Arnold's Lacanian 'Good Mother/Bad Mother' schema (the mother who sacrifices herself so the child enters the Symbolic and submits to the Law of the Father) alongside popularised Freudian mother-blame (the 'refrigerator mother', 'tell me about your mother') to read Psycho's Norma(n), the phallic mothers of The Killing Kind and The Brood, and the doomed single mothers of The Ring, Silent Hill and Triangle. It coins the 'monstrous-maternal' to argue that motherhood is framed as always-already monstrous because no woman can meet the impossible, shifting criteria of ideal motherhood, illustrated through Grace's Vivian/Madeline generational clash and Serial Mom's Beverly Sutphin.

power-knowledge.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
power-knowledge.title: The ageing woman as (American) horror story
power-knowledge.relation: The chapter theorises the 'abject barren body' — the menstruating, menopausal and post-menopausal woman — connecting menarche as an upswell of feminine power (Carrie's telekinesis, Ginger Snaps, The Witch's Thomasin) to menopause's cultural construction as loss and 'living decay'. Drawing on Mary Douglas and Kristeva on pollution and abjection, and on Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' and bodies defined by capacities rather than fixed being, it argues that the female reproductive body is more often barren than fecund and that this state is another generative modality, not an absence. It reads the Western biomedical pathologisation of menopause (Wilson's Feminine Forever, HRT) as a Foucauldian disciplinary discourse, then tracks older women through Sunset Boulevard's Norma Desmond, the hagsploitation cycle (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?, Strait-Jacket, Hush Hush Sweet Charlotte), and The Taking of Deborah Logan, concluding that Jessica Lange's American Horror Story roles offer the fullest, sexually frank rebuttal to the abjection and invisibility of the ageing woman.

power-knowledge.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
power-knowledge.title: Kingdom of Darkness: Autonomy and Conspiracy in The X-Files and Millennium
power-knowledge.relation: Michael Valdez Moses reads The X-Files and Millennium as post-Cold War noir that depicts America as Foucault's carceral archipelago: nearly every character works for the state, Tocquevillian voluntary association has withered ('they don't go bowling at all'), and the FBI's landscape of prisons, clinics, and bases makes free space scarce. Against Hobbes's Leviathan, the chapter mobilizes Locke and Paine's classical liberalism (government as necessary evil securing pre-existing natural rights) to show that Carter's heroes are 'antipolitical' resisters: Frank Black's visions and the Grill Flame remote viewers make him a panoptical spy for the state, while Mulder's warrantless searches blur sovereign and criminal justice into one corrupt system, as in the Millennium episode 'The Judge'. The neo-noir conspiracy seeks not profit but absolute sovereignty, and the series end with Mulder, Scully, and Black as fugitives fleeing the state with their families, resisting Nietzsche's 'coldest of all cold monsters'.

power-knowledge.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
power-knowledge.title: Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!
power-knowledge.relation: J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate. Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.

power-knowledge.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
power-knowledge.title: On Beyond Modernity, or Conrad and a Postmodern Alphabet
power-knowledge.relation: Jacob Held explains postmodernism as Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives' using On Beyond Zebra! Conrad's twenty-six-letter alphabet is the metanarrative that fixes what can be said and known, while the narrator's invented letters (Yuzz, Snee, Floob) show language expanding to present the unpresentable. Held casts Kant's three Critiques, phenomena/noumena, and his defining of the mind's 'alphabet' as the exemplary modern grand narrative Lyotard rejects, then turns to Foucault's Nietzschean genealogy, using You're Only Old Once! for the medicalization of life and (via a Beauvoir quotation) the claim that gender is a constructed mechanism of control that can be transgressed.

power-knowledge.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
power-knowledge.title: Propaganda and Pedagogy for Apt Pupils
power-knowledge.relation: Potter and Cobb read Apt Pupil—the blackmail-driven 'teaching' relationship between the boy Todd Bowden and the fugitive Nazi Kurt Dussander—to argue that all effective teaching is propaganda: persuasion by nonrational means (ethos and pathos beyond logos). They analyze the shifting teacher-student dynamic through Foucault's Power/Knowledge, showing power as a fluid relational 'order' rather than a possession, with Russell's definition of power and Nietzsche's Genealogy on the pleasures of subordination explaining Dussander's relief in obeying. Citing Bernays and Chomsky, they contend Todd and Dussander's oppressive, sadism-soaked curriculum merely strips the artifice from ordinary schooling, which has always been a system of control—culminating in Todd's transformation into a killer.

power-knowledge.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
power-knowledge.title: The Shining ’s Overlook Hotel as Heterotopia
power-knowledge.relation: Elizabeth Hornbeck analyzes King's Overlook Hotel through Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' arguing the hotel is a heterotopia—a socially produced space of crisis and deviance that juxtaposes and inverts normal relations, accumulating time as a 'chronic heterotopia' stuffed with its own ghosts and murders (Mrs. Massey, the Gradys, the 1921 photo). Cut off in winter, it strips away the norms of 'home' so Jack Torrance's inherited monsters (alcoholism, his father's abuse) can turn him from protector into a family-killer. She contrasts the maze-like Overlook with the panopticon of Grand Hotel and Bentham's surveillance-prison from Discipline and Punish, noting that King, unlike Foucault, treats transgression as horrific: the conservative horror genre restores the status quo only when Jack dies and the hotel burns.

power-knowledge.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
power-knowledge.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
power-knowledge.relation: Parkhill challenges Jenefsky and Miller's second-wave feminist reading of Penthouse 'girl–girl' pictorials (that they present lesbians as sexually available to naturalize heterosexuality) by arguing that what some straight men enjoy is their own ABSENCE from the scene. He deploys Butler's 'Imitation and Gender Insubordination' to show mock-lesbian-wedding drag can subvert rather than confirm heterosexual 'originality', Foucault's repressive hypothesis and productive power to argue the lesbian is a product of, not outside, patriarchal norms, and Lacan-derived 'projective identification' and feminine jouissance to explain the male viewer's libidinal investment in his own ego-erasure. He concludes both the 'conqueror' and the self-shattering 'jouissance-chasing' pleasures coexist, and that girl–girl porn is ethically no different from ordinary hetero porn since the consumer still assumes a right of access to women's bodies.

power-knowledge.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink
power-knowledge.title: Porn Philosophy for Everyone
power-knowledge.relation: Through the narrative of 'Aisha', a feminist who is aroused by SM imagery she has been taught to disown, Khan attacks the censorship of SM pornography and its 'monkey see, monkey do' harm hypothesis (citing declining rape rates). She names three state-inflicted harms: physical violence (prison sentences in Guglielmi and R. v. Brown), phenomenological violence—using Husserl and Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology to argue courts dismiss submissives' lived reality as 'worthless'—and epistemic violence, using Foucault's power/knowledge to show how the Supreme Court of Canada in Little Sisters overrode expert and practitioner testimony about coded SM meaning. She argues SM consent and pleasure are real knowledge that censorship, aligned with MacKinnon/Dworkin anti-porn feminism, coercively erases.

power-knowledge.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
power-knowledge.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
power-knowledge.relation: Hancuff and O'Connor read the song 'Santa Claus Is Coming to Town' and films like The Polar Express and Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town through Foucault's Discipline and Punish. Santa's all-seeing list-checking is a version of Bentham's Panopticon: children, watched but never seeing the watcher, internalize permanent visibility and discipline themselves. Invoking Foucault's Power/Knowledge and discursive practices, they argue the surveillance does not actually make children 'good for goodness' sake' – punishment is rarely delivered – but instead disciplines them into wish-lists and consumption, training them to be good consumers in late-capitalist culture, with Santa doubling as a corporate pitchman (Coke, Budweiser).

power-knowledge.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
power-knowledge.title: Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!
power-knowledge.relation: Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.

woman-as-other.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
woman-as-other.title: Softball The Good Is the Enemy of the Best
woman-as-other.relation: Heaphy asks whether softball limits women's potential to be equals on the baseball diamond, using feminist philosophy to explain why women are steered to the 'soft' game. Judith Williamson's analysis of women in mass culture and Simone de Beauvoir's woman-as-invisible-Other explain why female players — the AAGPBL's skirts and charm school, Toni Stone and Mamie Johnson in the Negro Leagues, Ila Borders in the minors — are covered as women first and ballplayers second. Iris Marion Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl' supplies the phenomenology: women throw differently not from anatomy but from experiencing the body as a burden, a socially produced self-fulfilling prophecy. Softball, 'the good,' becomes the enemy of the best — women playing hardball — by letting society postpone hard questions about gender.

woman-as-other.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
woman-as-other.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: Argues that Narnia is 'unfriendly to the feminine' by reading Susan's exclusion from Aslan's country at the end of The Last Battle ('no longer a friend of Narnia', too interested in nylons and invitations) as the fate of the one heroine who stays stereotypically feminine. It shows that the admired girls (Lucy, Aravis, Jill) succeed only by approximating a masculine standard of adventure, applying Beauvoir's point that measuring women against a male norm implies something wrong with femaleness itself. It further traces how evil in Narnia wears a feminine face: the Green Witch seduces Prince Rilian into Underland, the White Witch tempts Edmund and Digory where the girls resist, and the Witch's Lilith/Jinn lineage ties women to the Fall via 'Daughters of Eve'.

woman-as-other.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
woman-as-other.title: Sick of Love
woman-as-other.relation: Krein and Levin read Dylan's portraits of fallen socialites in "Like a Rolling Stone," "Just Like a Woman," and "To Ramona" as critiques of bad faith - characters who hide from freedom and responsibility in consumerist status games, in Sartre's sense that existence precedes essence. But Beauvoir's Second Sex exposes the cost: the women Dylan praises ("Girl from the North Country," "One More Cup of Coffee") are praised precisely for staying in immanent, pastoral passivity, denied the transcendence that for Beauvoir constitutes full humanity. Borrowing Benjamin's and Buck-Morss's notion of modern "dreamworlds," they finally read Dylan's pastoral utopias as a counter-dreamworld spun after the collapse of the mass-utopian promise of consumer happiness.

woman-as-other.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
woman-as-other.title: The Price of Existence
woman-as-other.relation: Bonnie Mann reads Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" whose existence has meaning only in orbit around Edward, clumsy, self-sacrificing, carried and watched, living the myth of the eternal feminine in which the masculine gaze confers being on a girl otherwise taught the world is defined without reference to her. She locates the fantasy's pull in the contradictory messages of twenty-first-century girlhood (Pipher, Phillips, Bordo), where being attractive to boys remains the first avenue to existing at all. Yet she also finds a feminist subtext: the vampire transformation returns Bella to the "I can" body, faster and stronger than Edward and saving the day herself, though Meyer ultimately re-sells the old promise that a woman wins existence through self-annihilation for others.

woman-as-other.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
woman-as-other.title: Zelda and Reality
woman-as-other.relation: Havstad and Jahng inventory every Zelda across the series (royal, wise, resolved, foreseeing, yet passive, imprisoned, even turned to stone in The Minish Cap or asleep through all of Adventure of Link) and read the maiden typology through Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman as Idea, modeled on Plato's Forms, gives men a feminine ideal that real women are then judged against, and 'women are not born, but made' explains how femininity is a male-defined myth serving male interests. Zelda is the glorified yet objectified prize whose passivity lets Link's transcendence happen, and Aonuma's 'reality over realism' design philosophy explains why such stereotypes feel true to players. Sheik and Tetra, who act while disguised as (or turned into) something other than the princess, are the promising cracks in the ideal.

woman-as-other.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
woman-as-other.title: 7 - Why I Am Not a Friend
woman-as-other.relation: Thalos argues she is not a 'friend' on Facebook because bonding requires credible, fixed self-presentation, and a profile 'can lie like a rug' since everything on it is elective and revisable at whim. Through Sartre's phenomenology of the gaze - being displaced from Subject to object-for-another when caught in another's look - she explains why face-to-face interaction alone builds the mutual bonds and social intelligence we rely on. With Beauvoir she shows how the gaze also carries power, marking woman as the Other, and warns that Facebook's plastic faces offer choice without traction, inhibiting both true bonding and resistance to subjugating looks.

woman-as-other.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
woman-as-other.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: Robison-Greene applies Beauvoir to the show's women. Powerful men are the One and women (like Chalky's community under the Klan) are made the inessential Other, and Beauvoir's apparatus - bad faith, the 'appeal' free beings must make to one another, and the happiness that lets women be complicit in their own oppression - frames Lucy, Gillian, and Margaret. Lucy happily performs the role her men write for her, Gillian is so consumed by the fact of her rape that even her apparent freedom keeps her the object of male desire ('just the loneliest person on earth'), while Margaret - Temperance Leaguer, advocate for women's reproductive health, and finally the woman who shuts the door on Nucky's cash - comes closest to making the appeal and to freedom.

woman-as-other.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
woman-as-other.title: Futurama and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: Reitter reads the sewer mutants - banished underground, surviving on what the surface flushes, as in 'The Mutants Are Revolting' where Leela is deported without trial the moment Fry reveals she is not an alien - as philosophy's Other, illuminated by Plato's cave (surface dwellers fear and demonize what they have never seen) and Beauvoir's The Second Sex (Leela passes as an acceptable alien until exposed as a mutant). Mrs. Astor's United Mutant Scholarship Fund film, with its 'noble sewer mutants... uh, people, I guess,' is read alongside Said's Orientalism and racist charity imagery as a third face of Othering. The chapter then adds folklore theory: the mutants are a folk group with their own urban legends (alligators in the sewer, and the 'sub-urban legend' of sub-mutants), ballads like 'The Legend of El Chupanibre,' and freegan-style recycling ethics - a counterculture whose difference the dominant universe-view casts as monstrosity.

woman-as-other.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
woman-as-other.title: The Devil and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: Jones, Hansmann, and Stachura trace the trope of woman as the Devil's handmaiden - Eve and Lilith, succubae and Sirens, the sixteenth-century witch hunts, down to 'maneater' and 'Poison' rock songs and Blurred Lines - arguing it perpetuates patriarchal power. They apply Beauvoir's The Second Sex: woman constructed as the perpetual Other, defined as secondary to man with sexuality at the heart of her Othering, and extend the analysis with Gloria Anzaldua's Borderlands and mestiza consciousness, which rejects the gender binary the woman-as-Devil trope depends on.

woman-as-other.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
woman-as-other.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: Babette Babich traces the shifting 'you' of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne' through Hegelian thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Empedocles's cycle of Love and Strife, reading the songs' ambiguity (David, Samson, the bound champion) as Cohen's sovereign having-it-both-ways. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity frames the human condition of being what one is not, while Nietzsche - on broken promises, on women and distance, on the Antichrist - supplies both the critique of Cohen's courtly projections onto the feminine Other and the model of singularizing solitude. 'Who by Fire' is read against the Rosh Hashanah prayer Unetanneh Tokef as a song of fate, judgment, and atonement whose closing 'who shall I say is calling?' is quasi-Augustinian and Heideggerian: death singularizes each 'who' at the moment of its claim.

woman-as-other.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
woman-as-other.title: 21. Buttercup and the Eternal Feminine
woman-as-other.relation: Archibald reads Buttercup wholly through Beauvoir's The Second Sex: as the farm's natural leader she is not yet 'woman as Other', but Humperdinck's ultra-feminized public presentation, the arranged marriage, the old woman's 'Queen of Filth' nightmare, and the men dismissing her advice all enact the myth of the eternal feminine that punishes a woman for asserting herself. Her leap toward the shrieking eels becomes an emblem of autonomy that society punishes, the 'privilege' of compliance a curse that leaves her suicidal, and the closing image of the couple riding together as one sketches Beauvoir's ideal of a relationship founded on mutual liberty.

woman-as-other.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
woman-as-other.title: 14. Re Production
woman-as-other.relation: Framed as leaked Project memoranda, the chapter argues Projects Leda and Castor embody philosophy's male-rational/female-reproductive dichotomy: Aristotle's function argument defined the human good (eudaimonia) through rationality while relegating women to reproduction, and the clones' engineered diseases literalize the split — fatal illness of the reproductive organs in the Leda clones, of the brain in the Castor. Simone de Beauvoir's Second Sex supplies the critique: "woman" treated as synonymous with womb, the Other denied the rich self-definition granted men, visible in Leda's passive unmonitored clones versus Castor's self-aware, active brothers. Combining a redeemed Aristotle (practical wisdom shows virtuous potential is not set by biological sex) with Beauvoir's free, independent woman, the chapter concludes both reproductive and rational autonomy must be restored to the clones of both sexes.

woman-as-other.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
woman-as-other.title: 9. But Women Can Vote . .
woman-as-other.relation: Hansmann and Jones set Adams's gender posts against the four waves of feminism and the men's rights movement: his March 2011 Men's Rights post telling activists to get over it while lumping women with four-year-olds and the mentally handicapped, his Global Gender War matriarchy in which any country where women can vote counts as female-ruled, his framing of sex as a woman's currency for extracting male strategy (sacrifice a pawn to nail the queen), and his serial interrupting of women. They show the rhetoric eerily echoes anti-suffragists like Mrs. William Force Scott and Senator Sanford and the Goldilocks Dilemma, note the red-pill fantasy borrowed from The Matrix, and conclude that calling America a matriarchy defies scholarly consensus, with Beauvoir's The Second Sex marking why the vote never delivered the balance of power.

woman-as-other.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!
woman-as-other.title: 15. Are There Certain Things We Should Not Talk About
woman-as-other.relation: Reads Schumer's taboo-breaking through The Second Sex: man makes woman the mysterious Other, and silences around menstruation, aging, and wives' desire keep that mystery intact. 'Last Fuckable Day' dramatizes the expiry of the idolized 'real woman', 'Sex Prep' shows the metamorphosis into a sex-representation collapsing into hiding under the bed, and '12 Angry Men' stages a male jury defining a woman's value. Ehrnberger argues Schumer's demystifying candor, from publishing her teenage journals to calling herself a 'flawed fuckup', dissolves the Other's aura and restores power, exactly as Beauvoir predicted when women assert themselves as human beings.

woman-as-other.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
woman-as-other.title: 23. The Future Is Female … Robots!
woman-as-other.relation: Emily Cox-Palmer-White applies Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' to the mechanical women of both films: the girl as universal other, a vacuum or absence at the center of femininity, is exactly what lets Rachael, Pris, Luv, and Joi destabilize the patriarchal world that manufactured them. Wallace's drones undressing the barren replicant with their gaze before he slashes her womb gives the male gaze a literal, lethal form, while the Joi-Mariette sync scene stages the frightening interchangeability of women under that gaze. Deckard's 'Her eyes were green' — a lie, since Rachael's eyes were brown — refuses the premise that women are replaceable products.

woman-as-other.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
woman-as-other.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: White and Fisher run the show's women (and men) through feminist philosophy: the sex/gender distinction from Plato's Republic Book V and Mill's Subjection of Women through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Butler's antiessentialist performativity. Penny's hyper-femininity reads as Butlerian parody that satirizes the script, the Penny–Bernadette–Amy lineup exposes the custom that smarts and beauty must trade off, and Elizabeth Plimpton and Leslie Winkle ('come for the breasts, stay for the brains') break it — while the four guys fail every 'real man' stereotype beside Penny's muscle-bound exes like Zack. Gender emerges as an artificial label that limits everyone, and seeing that would be the show's ultimate change through parody.

woman-as-other.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
woman-as-other.title: “Smother Him in the Crib”—Booker
woman-as-other.relation: Origitano reads Elizabeth through Beauvoir and Frye: Columbia's propaganda infantilizes and objectifies her ('the Seed of the Prophet', 'Lamb', 'Specimen', always defined relative to a man), the tower literalizes Frye's birdcage of systematic oppression, and her confinement for an uncontrollable power mirrors women caged by a supposed natural inferiority. Booker's rescue only grants freedom, echoing Beauvoir's point that women have 'only received' what men are willing to give, so Elizabeth remains caged as his poker chip, her lock-picking skills formed by captivity and her tears dismissed as foreign. Her emancipation comes through action and collective solidarity, allying with Lady Comstock's ghost, taking control of Songbird, and finally drowning Booker/Comstock as equals, which enacts Beauvoir's claim that liberation must be won, not granted.

woman-as-other.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
woman-as-other.title: 12 Panther Mystique Wakandan Feminism Demystified
woman-as-other.relation: Wright and Pérez ask whether Wakanda's powerful women are feminists, arguing M'Baku's dismissal of Shuri as a child trades on Friedan's feminine mystique while Wakandan women escape Beauvoir's woman as the Other because their society, lacking any history of female oppression, never inscribed the second sex. Drawing on Lorde, Davis, Collins, and Walker's womanism, they read Shuri's rejection of romance, Okoye's throne-loyalty, and Nakia's stubbornness as self-definition and interdependency across difference, then use Butler's gender performativity to explain why Okoye squirms in a wig while Nakia breezes through Seoul: womanhood performed in womanist (community-centered) versus feminist (individual-transcendence) modes, with Wakanda modeling the collective call for solidarity the authors hope the future inherits.

woman-as-other.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
woman-as-other.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
woman-as-other.relation: Jessica Miller shows Katniss coded masculine, since Collins built her from Theseus and Spartacus and her breadwinning, hunting, and defiance fit masculine norms, while Prim embodies everything Beauvoir says civilization 'produces' as feminine, and Panem itself proves oddly gender-neutral: women work the mines, Finnick is the sex symbol sold by Snow, and Coin is as ruthless as any man. She then reads Katniss's romance performance through Judith Butler: the kisses, caresses, and televised wedding gowns do not express a preexisting femininity but constitute one, down to Butler's radical claim that sex itself is a cultural norm, which reframes even the Games' reaping of one boy and one girl as a gendered ritual rather than a presocial biological fact. Cinna's burning bridal gown that transforms Katniss into the mockingjay makes the political payoff explicit: gender performed strategically becomes the rebellion's power, and the hunter-and-baker partnership offers an alternative to the dominant romance script.

woman-as-other.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Chelstrom uses the progression from guided DUPLO builds to free design to argue that autonomy develops in degrees and is relational rather than purely individualist. Kant's self-thinking agent — for whom precepts and formulas are the 'ball and chain' of immaturity — explains Emmet's dependence on Octan's instruction booklets and Lord Business's profit from deference, and Korsgaard's definition frames the individualist autonomy the Master Builders embody. Yet their lone-wolf autonomy fails, and Sartre's look plus Beauvoir's account of woman forced to assume herself as Other explain Wyldstyle/Lucy's deference to others' expectations; Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy recasts 'Everything is Awesome' as peers supporting each other's self-development, with Emmet's friendship letting Lucy accept herself.

woman-as-other.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
woman-as-other.title: Zelda and Reality
woman-as-other.relation: Joyce Havstad and Iris Jahng catalogue the women of Zelda — Zelda's many incarnations, Impa, the Twinrova sisters, the oracles Din and Nayru, Midna — finding the typologies of maiden, mother, and crone, then explain them with Beauvoir's The Second Sex: the myth of woman (Mother, Wife, Idea), femininity as made rather than born, and woman's enforced passivity against man's transcendence. Zelda is woman as Idea, traced to Platonic Forms: young, beautiful, virtuous, and radically passive (turned to stone in The Minish Cap, asleep through The Adventure of Link, imprisoned in nearly every game), an object that exists to motivate Link's heroism. Significantly, only the masculine-garbed Sheik and the pirate Tetra escape passivity, a shift the authors link to Miyamoto's design philosophy of 'reality over realism' and to changing conceptions of women.

woman-as-other.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
woman-as-other.title: Television and Existential Awakening
woman-as-other.relation: Jaarsma argues Mad Men dramatizes an existential rather than Kantian-enlightenment model of advertising: Don's 'freedom from fear' pitch ('Whatever you are doing is okay. You are okay') sells escape from the anxiety of real choice, which is precisely Sartrean bad faith and what de Beauvoir calls the stagnant 'happiness' of women rewarded for being the other. Betty on her psychiatrist's couch, Peggy measured by Joan's paper-bag mirror and the Playtex bullet-bra silhouette, and the closeted Salvatore all internalize the dominant values Marcuse describes, finding meaning in conformity to the objectifying gaze ('bras are for men; women want to see themselves the way men see them'). Rachel Menken, who refuses to 'put on an apron' and calls out the contingency of gendered embodiment, models authenticity as choosing to choose, and the chapter closes with the hope that television itself can occasion the viewer's existential awakening.

woman-as-other.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Argues that Leia and Padme really are strong feminist characters, using Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to defuse the two stock objections: Padme's motherhood is 'freely chosen' rather than an oppressive role, and Leia chained in Jabba's palace keeps command of her sexuality, turning the damsel-in-distress plot around by strangling Jabba with her own chain and later rescuing Han herself. The chapter's real complaint is structural: with only six speaking women in the original trilogy, almost all of them royalty, Leia and Padme are forced to represent all women (the 'affluent few' problem), while Shmi, Aunt Beru, Mon Mothma, and the handmaidens Sabe, Corde, and Dorme never get the screen time to show their strength.

woman-as-other.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
woman-as-other.title: A New Hope Inclusive Representation in the Galaxy
woman-as-other.relation: Lakka uses Beauvoir's The Second Sex (the Mother/Mistress dichotomy, woman tied to nature and denied transcendence) and Butler on the mother-daughter separation to argue that Revenge of the Sith reduces Padme from the active senator and warrior of the first two prequels to a pregnant figure confined to her apartment, whose death gets read as martyrdom or even 'mom-shaming.' She reads Anakin's jealousy, interrogations ('Obi-Wan's been here, has he not?'), and Force-choke on Mustafar — explicitly paralleled with Othello and Desdemona — as an abusive relationship, suggesting Padme's death may be a feminicide. The deleted Petition of the 2000 scenes, and successors like Rey, Ahsoka, Rose Tico, and Jyn Erso, point toward the inclusive representation the galaxy still needs.

woman-as-other.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Quinn argues Rebecca is the show's Stoic: Marcus Aurelius's maxims about judgments, obstacles, and morning meetings with the ungrateful map onto her recovery from Rupert - accepting reality, forgiving as a choice within her control, the lion power pose, 'every disadvantage has its advantage' - with the dichotomy of control as her operating principle. Framed by Gen X self-reliance and second-wave feminism (Friedan's problem with no name, Beauvoir's woman as Other under Rupert), the chapter follows her from vengeful boss to mentor of Keeley and Nora, Bantr-era 'bossgirl' dater of Sam, and finally the Richmond family's matriarch.

woman-as-other.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Reads Cohle's arc as an existentialist passage toward authenticity, using Sartre's being-for-itself to explain why Hart's 'family man' identity is bad faith — a clinging to social roles that denies the freedom of a consciousness that is an activity, not a thing. Beauvoir's analysis of women as the passive, objectified Other illuminates why Rust, despite his nihilism, persistently protects vulnerable women and children such as Sophia, Dora Lange, and Marie Fontenot: threats to others' freedom threaten our own. Nietzsche's Silenus wisdom, the spirit of gravity on the tightrope, and the shepherd who bites the head off the snake frame Ledoux's and Childress' warped eternal return as the poison Cohle must overcome before he can will life eternally and declare 'the light is winning.'

woman-as-other.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
woman-as-other.title: Mea culpa
woman-as-other.relation: Correcting her own initial dismissal of the show as Nancy Drew redux, the author argues Neptune is structured by a white/Hispanic racial binary laid over the millionaire/work-for-millionaires class binary, enforced through Logan's 'spic and span' jab at Weevil, Mr. Daniels's 'pumping his gas' insult, and the 'coconut' label for Latinos who cross over. Borrowing Saussure's binary oppositions and de Beauvoir's account of how a dominant group constructs a stigmatized Other, she shows the 09-ers defining themselves against everyone else, with teacher Daniels quietly siding with wealth against both boys. Bourdieu's cultural capital then explains why Wallace (basketball, scholarship, colorblind friendships) can cross boundaries that leave Weevil working as a janitor, and she concludes the show keeps race admirably visible in a supposedly postracial era.

woman-as-other.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
woman-as-other.title: The Witcher and the Monstrous Feminine
woman-as-other.relation: Cameron reads Geralt's battles with the striga (Foltest's cursed daughter by his sister Adda) and the bruxa Vereena in 'A Grain of Truth' through French feminist theory: Cixous's claim that women are frozen 'between the Medusa and the abyss,' Irigaray's reading of Nietzsche's feminine hysteria, and Kristeva's abject maternal in Powers of Horror. Both stories are phallocentric - men deliberate while Adda never speaks and Vereena can only scream - and in both the female monster is sacrificed to restore the symbolic order, Nivellen's curse broken by Vereena's death at Geralt's silver sword. Geralt himself is abjected: bitten and bled by the striga in her own crypt, nursed wounded at the Temple of Melitele, he becomes permeable and monstrous in her place, paying the cost of policing the patriarchal boundary.

woman-as-other.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
woman-as-other.title: Note
woman-as-other.relation: Held's introduction frames Wonder Woman as an ambiguous figure - a sexy superhero, feminist icon, even a god - and borrows Simone de Beauvoir's term 'ambiguity' from The Second Sex to name women's bind: acquiesce to gender norms and lose yourself, or become yourself and lose your place. He runs through Diana's either/ors (Steve Trevor, Themyscira or Boston, mortal or god, American or cosmopolitan) and argues she creates an identity only by defining herself against each expectation. Because everyone is torn between what they are and what they want to become, he concludes we should embrace Wonder Woman's contradictions and stake our commitments while living in ambiguity.

woman-as-other.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Wright reads Wonder Woman's 75-year history through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,' arguing Diana's move from Paradise Island to Man's World - surrendering eternal life for Steve Trevor - enacts the hard-won transcendence of immanence that The Second Sex demands. She shows the comics alternating between empowerment (Marston's 'woman of tomorrow,' an unpatriotic George Washington scolding women war workers) and regression (Trevor persuading Wonder Woman to marry and type memos about women's place being the home, the 1990s hyper-sexualized art), evidence that woman remains the Other to man's Subject. Wonder Woman's durability, she says, lies in exactly this ambiguity, and like Beauvoir's woman of tomorrow she models forging identity through projects in the world.

woman-as-other.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Donovan uses the New 52 Azzarello run's gods as a catalogue of gender stereotypes - jealous Hera hunting Zola, woman-incinerating Apollo, hyper-masculine First Born, self-sacrificing Demeter - then tracks Hera's transformation after Apollo makes her mortal as a Beauvoirian passage from immanence (being Zeus's Other, defined by his desire) to transcendence (charting an independent identity, aiding baby Zeke). Foucault's Panopticon explains how gender norms are internalized without an enforcer, and Butler's drag example grounds the claim that Wonder Woman accepting the god of war mantle - leading a female Amazon army 'not as your princess but as the god of war' - is a subversive performance of gender.

woman-as-other.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
woman-as-other.title: Notes
woman-as-other.relation: Zanin surveys 75 years of Wonder Woman - Marston's bondage-inflected feminism (the Ordeal of a Thousand Links, bracelets that forfeit power to any man who chains them), Kanigher's romance-era drift, the 1968 Diana Prince fashion-bouticless era that opened just as feminists protested Miss America, and the Taco Whiz years - to ask whether 'wonder woman' has become an unattainable ideal that belittles women. Reading through Beauvoir's analyses of woman as Other, imposed femininity as immanence, and the body as situation, she argues the superwoman 'have it all' standard is a feminist faux pas, yet closes with Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity: rather than resent her perfection, women should accept the challenge on their own terms instead of acquiescing in mediocrity.

woman-as-other.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
woman-as-other.title: Gynaehorror as convention and challenge
woman-as-other.relation: This introductory chapter defines 'gynaehorror' as horror rooted in women's reproductive bodies (menstruation, virginity, pregnancy, motherhood, menopause), reading films like Inside, Vigil, Teeth, Alien, The Brood and Rosemary's Baby through it. It leverages Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome/becoming to reframe the monstrous female body not as a fixed molar 'being' but as a productive, boundary-breaching 'becoming', while positioning woman as the abject Other against which the male subject defines himself. It argues horror is simultaneously conservative (punishing women) and potentially radical.

woman-as-other.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
woman-as-other.title: ‘Pro-life’ and Pro-Life
woman-as-other.relation: The chapter argues that horror films about pregnancy (Rosemary's Baby, Demon Seed, The Reaping, Prophecy, Inside) pit a foetal 'subject' against the pregnant woman, eroding her selfhood by conflating her body with an invadable house or environment. Drawing on Young's, Battersby's and Tyler's phenomenologies of pregnant embodiment and Irigaray's 'woman as place', it shows how foetal-imaging technology and abortion politics (The Life Zone versus Carpenter's Pro-Life) reduce the woman to a vessel while the foetus is granted autonomous personhood.

woman-as-other.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
woman-as-other.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
woman-as-other.relation: Ryan Weldon reads Selina Kyle's transformation into Catwoman in Batman Returns through Sartre's existentialism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Pre-death Selina is Sartre's inauthentic 'waiter,' performing a servile secretary role in bad faith, and Beauvoir's objectified Other, defined by Max Shreck and the men who dismiss her. Her murder and feline resurrection free repressed drives, and her refusal of Batman's fairy-tale rescue—'I couldn't live with myself'—plus her choice to kill Shreck are cast as an assertion of facticity and transcendence, an authentic (if unfinished) self-creation that rejects the roles available to women rather than reaching a stable ending.

woman-as-other.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
woman-as-other.title: Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films
woman-as-other.relation: Gary Heba and Robin Murphy map women's identities in westerns onto Hegel's three-stage dialectic (aufheben as maintain/negate/transform), grafting on Bakhtin's monoglossic/heteroglossic discourse and Mulvey's and de Beauvoir's feminist film theory. Settler women (Marian in Shane, the mothers of The Searchers) are monoglossic—silenced, family-bound bearers of meaning; town women (Mrs. French in Appaloosa, Lily in How the West Was Won) are heteroglossic, sexualized spectacles marked by costume; and post-1970s figures like Ellen in The Quick and the Dead and Sara in Two Mules for Sister Sara become 'x-glossic,' transformational identities that subvert the male-gaze code and exceed the settler/town binary.

woman-as-other.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
woman-as-other.title: The Price of Existence
woman-as-other.relation: Bonnie Mann reads the Twilight saga through Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Bella embodies the 'relative being' who orbits Edward like a satellite, a self-sacrificing girl who loses Husserl's 'I can' body and exists only through the constant, faithful male gaze that confers meaning. Mann traces a buried feminist subtext - Bella's demand to 'be Superman too' and her transformation into a strong, agentive vampire - but argues Meyer ultimately reinstates the old promise that a woman gains existence through self-annihilation in a man, making the books' success cause for despair.

woman-as-other.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
woman-as-other.title: Female Subjectivity in Carrie
woman-as-other.relation: Kellye Byal reads Carrie White through Beauvoir's The Second Sex, treating Carrie's first menstruation, her mother Margaret's ascetic 'Mystic' piety, and Miss Collins/Sue Snell's push toward makeup and the prom as two imposed versions of 'feminine destiny.' Carrie is caught between rejecting femininity (becoming an outcast/monster) and assuming it (surrendering her subjectivity to immanence and the male gaze), so her telekinesis becomes an externalized act of authentic, radically free agency against both scripts. Byal argues her tragic death indicts a failed community of women who never posit themselves as Subjects, illustrating Beauvoir's claim that female subjectivity needs a solidarity of others in which to thrive.

woman-as-other.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
woman-as-other.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
woman-as-other.relation: Ashwell and Langton ask whether fashion is a 'badge of slavery' (Wollstonecraft), opening with Socrates in the *Phaedo* disdaining adornment and Rousseau's girl who becomes 'her own doll,' and using Kant's humanity formula and Nussbaum's seven-feature account of objectification. Focusing on denial of autonomy in ordinary followers, they distinguish the 'Servile Fashionista' (obeys experts) from the 'Sensible Fashionista' (follows what looks good), then argue that via Johnston's 'authority of affect' even the sensible one is under an *epistemic* bondage: fashion's extrinsic social pull is misperceived as the garment's intrinsic goodness, a projective illusion (like the Müller-Lyer) that on a Kantian view undermines agency and masks misogynist or racist norms such as straightened hair or the 'lotus feet' of stilettos.

woman-as-other.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
woman-as-other.title: The Price of Existence
woman-as-other.relation: Mann reads Stephenie Meyer's Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" who orbits Edward like a satellite, valued only through the constant masculine gaze, embodying the adolescent girl's renunciation of her "I can" body. Mann finds a buried feminist subtext — Bella's desire, Edward's restraint, and her vampire transformation into a fierce, powerful equal — but ultimately faults Meyer for reinstating the old promise that a woman gains subjecthood through self-annihilation in a sovereign man's eyes.

woman-as-other.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
woman-as-other.title: 63. Amy Schumer as Philosopher Fuck the Feminine Mystique
woman-as-other.relation: Elsby argues Amy Schumer's honest comedy revolts against a 'feminine mystique' broader than Friedan's housewife version, running back to Beauvoir's claim that woman is constructed as the 'Other' and to Aristotle's 'rational animal' definition that cast women as irrational and thus less than human. Through bits like 'Madame President,' 'Last Fuckable Day,' the 'New Twitter Button' sketch, and gross-out honesty about pregnancy and her own body in Growing and The Leather Special, Schumer refuses to let women's physical, sexual, and social experience stay mysterious. Elsby reads this as de-'othering' and re-humanizing women by forcing our concept of 'woman' to expand to include flawed, fully human hot-mess figures.

woman-as-other.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
woman-as-other.title: 75. Phoebe Waller-Bridge as Philosopher Conscious Women Making Choices
woman-as-other.relation: Pande and Engels argue that Fleabag and Lulu (Crashing) embody Sartrean authenticity: they own their choices, balance facticity and transcendence, and stay outside bad faith, while the men (Anthony, the Priest) fall back on pregiven roles and let 'the Look' or their fundamental project decide for them. Fleabag's addressing the camera and finally shutting it out is read as breaking the gaze of the Other; the Priest choosing priesthood over love exemplifies denial of transcendence. Through Beauvoir's Second Sex, woman-as-Other, and ethics of ambiguity, they show Waller-Bridge's transgressive, sexually frank women reclaim self-definition, arguing viewers 'could do better to be' the kind of free, choosing women her protagonists are.

embodiment.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box
embodiment.title: Softball The Good Is the Enemy of the Best
embodiment.relation: Heaphy asks whether softball limits women's potential to be equals on the baseball diamond, using feminist philosophy to explain why women are steered to the 'soft' game. Judith Williamson's analysis of women in mass culture and Simone de Beauvoir's woman-as-invisible-Other explain why female players — the AAGPBL's skirts and charm school, Toni Stone and Mamie Johnson in the Negro Leagues, Ila Borders in the minors — are covered as women first and ballplayers second. Iris Marion Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl' supplies the phenomenology: women throw differently not from anatomy but from experiencing the body as a burden, a socially produced self-fulfilling prophecy. Softball, 'the good,' becomes the enemy of the best — women playing hardball — by letting society postpone hard questions about gender.

embodiment.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
embodiment.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
embodiment.relation: Wrathall defends the film's violence by contrasting Fra Angelico's serene Descent from the Cross with Corinth's Red Christ and Gibson's Gethsemane rebuke ('You could not watch even one hour with me'), arguing the gore resists rationalizing Christ's suffering into an economy of exchange, as Camus's Father Paneloux in The Plague insists true faith must not. Drawing on Pascal's instrumental reason, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty, he develops a 'world-disclosive' account of faith: the tall-table scene between Mary and the young carpenter Jesus shows that new practices train new perception, and film reaches the body directly in ways written description cannot. He closes by faulting Gibson for pessimism: Christ's world looks as God-forsaken and demon-haunted as Judas's, closer to Dostoevsky's ascetic Father Ferapont than to a world made new.

embodiment.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
embodiment.title: The Atkins Diet and Philosophy
embodiment.relation: A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.

embodiment.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever
embodiment.title: James Bond and Philosophy
embodiment.relation: Gibson argues that Bond's meticulous sensory attention - the three-and-a-third-minute boiled egg, the Mouton Rothschild '53, 'shaken, not stirred' - makes him a phenomenologist in Maurice Merleau-Ponty's sense, a thinker whose fleshly style of perception is the very means of his spycraft and his access to the invisible world of plots and dangers. She reads the Casino Royale mirror scene as Merleau-Ponty's 'flesh' and the reversibility of vision, and casts Goldfinger (who shrinks from 'the touch') and Dr. No with his steel pincers as villains doomed by their flight from the carnal world Bond embraces. Against Descartes's mind-body split and Plato's distrust of appearance, Bond's gun is an organic extension of his body rather than a symbol, and his sensual immersion in the world is what lets him see what others cannot.

embodiment.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
embodiment.title: The Price of Existence
embodiment.relation: Bonnie Mann reads Twilight through Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex: Bella is the "relative being" whose existence has meaning only in orbit around Edward, clumsy, self-sacrificing, carried and watched, living the myth of the eternal feminine in which the masculine gaze confers being on a girl otherwise taught the world is defined without reference to her. She locates the fantasy's pull in the contradictory messages of twenty-first-century girlhood (Pipher, Phillips, Bordo), where being attractive to boys remains the first avenue to existing at all. Yet she also finds a feminist subtext: the vampire transformation returns Bella to the "I can" body, faster and stronger than Edward and saving the day herself, though Meyer ultimately re-sells the old promise that a woman wins existence through self-annihilation for others.

embodiment.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth
embodiment.title: “I Got this Guitar and I Learned How to Make It Talk”
embodiment.relation: The editors unpack Springsteen's 1988 speech inducting Bob Dylan: Elvis freed America's body from Cold War-era repression (duck-and-cover fear, Calvinist stiffness), Dylan freed the mind by bringing ambiguity ('Mr. Tambourine Man,' 'Maggie's Farm'), and Springsteen's own project was to free heart and soul — 'heartwork' in the early songs, 'soulwork' from Nebraska on. Their key philosophical move is embodied: you are not under the school desk because you are afraid, you are afraid because your body is under the desk, so intellectual freedom grows out of bodily freedom, and the guitar — flesh stretched over wood — literally talks for and with the audience. The revolution still fails, they concede, since hearts stay broken and the soul finds only hope in hard work, decency, family, and conversation.

embodiment.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
embodiment.title: Stable Bodies
embodiment.relation: Heinricy argues the human/Cylon line is drawn on the body: following Mary Douglas, bodies function as cultural boundaries, so Cylons figure as contamination to be hunted (Boomer in the fleet) and marked as other by violence (Gina's torture), though Athena's loyal service and Tigh's exposure show the fear is socially constructed rather than natural. Cylon insides are known only through technology (Caprica Six's glowing spine, Athena's blood interface in 'Flight of the Phoenix'), and their bodies' stability — no scars, aging, or change — is paid for in unstable minds (Tigh killing Ellen, Boomer strangling Hera), whereas messy human bodies carry potential, hope, and change, as Apollo's weight fluctuation shows. Since we are all already cyborgs (vaccines, pills, GMOs), the Numbers are a further human-machine integration, and Hera and Nicky's blending is the ultimate 'contamination' and a new hope.

embodiment.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
embodiment.title: Game versus Place
embodiment.relation: Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warp sacrifices environmental presence for goal-oriented play: the long, uneventful sails where waves, cloud patterns, and quiet soundscapes dominate are precisely when Hyrule feels like a place, and teleporting turns it into a disposable grid of destinations. Drawing on Castells' spaces of flows versus places, Schivelbusch's 'annihilation of space and time' by the railway (the player becomes a 'human parcel'), and de Certeau's opposition between the panoptic map view and the embodied everyday view, he contends the very existence of the warp option colors all distance traveled. Even panoramic pleasures like hang-gliding over Outset Island, he notes, must be balanced against pure map-grid travel.

embodiment.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
embodiment.title: Nightmares
embodiment.relation: Auxier asks why the flying monkeys and the shriveling feet of the Wicked Witch of the East give children lifelong nightmares, and answers with a phenomenology of three frightening sequences in escalating duration: the instant shriveling shot, the five-minute cyclone (paired with 'The Great Gig in the Sky' in the Dark Side of the Rainbow sync), and the monkey air-raid. Kierkegaard's Concept of Anxiety supplies the depth psychology: innocence is ignorance, and the child's dreaming spirit projects its own nothing outward, fastening fear onto figures like the monkeys (who are, he notes, played by the Munchkin actors themselves). Merleau-Ponty's lived body versus habit body explains the mechanics: cinema seizes the body's usual 'tour of inspection,' Fleming manipulates active and passive synthesis (the scoreless build-up to the window blow, the barely noticed arsenal of weapons in the Haunted Forest, the dimming lights), and children construct a rigid, inescapable habit body within a single viewing, so the nightmare is the monkey inside our own projected world.

embodiment.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
embodiment.title: Knives Out
embodiment.relation: Michael Thompson argues that the much-debated rhythm of "Pyramid Song" — 4/4 with syncopation, 3/3/4/3/3 groupings, or shifting signatures; Yorke says it is only "felt" — is philosophically pointed: by violating ordinary temporal expectations it forces an awareness of time itself, just as Chopin's nocturnes used time-signature changes to voice the nostalgia and melancholy of his Polish exile. Drawing on Gadamer's historically affected consciousness and the embodied, rhythmic daily life described by Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, he reads the lyrics' row-boat to heaven ("all my past and futures") as a synoptic flash in which one sees past, present, and future as one organic whole. Because Yorke's heaven echoes Talking Heads' "Heaven" as a place where nothing happens, the song's consolation is that nothing lies outside our temporal embedding — with past and future united "there was nothing to fear and nothing to doubt."

embodiment.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
embodiment.title: Transformers and Philosophy
embodiment.relation: Using the hidden sides of Transformers - a robot inside a Camaro, a tank inside a robot - the authors stage the philosophy of perception: Descartes's innate geometrical rules and Berkeley's bodily cross-referencing both fail to explain how Sam Witwicky can know the steelyard robot is his Camaro, while Merleau-Ponty's embodied account of focus, background, and 'indeterminate vision' explains it through the perceiver's lived body. They extend this to the 'Autobot Spike' mind-transfer episode and to CGI: virtual Transformers on screen feel hollow because light-created images have no hidden surfaces for our bodies to investigate and grasp.

embodiment.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
embodiment.relation: Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.

embodiment.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
embodiment.title: Wave Goodbye from the Catbus
embodiment.relation: Heinricy argues anime is the richest medium for posthuman theory because it shows bodies 'in a state of becoming' rather than as grotesque boundary violations: Miyazaki's Catbus and Totoro, Haku's dragon transformation and Chihiro's pig parents in Spirited Away, and the cursed pig-headed aviator of Porco Rosso all treat morphing bodies as possibility, not horror. She sorts anime posthumanism into two valences: a 'Ghost in the Machine' dream of consciousness leaving the body altogether (Motoko merging with the net in Ghost in the Shell), which she rebuts via N. Katherine Hayles's point that consciousness is embodied and would change with any new body, and hybrid configurations like mecha (Gundam, Robotech) where body and machine drive each other. Following Donna Haraway, she contends we are all already cyborgs — vaccines, engineered food, treated water — and credits Japan's nuclear history (via Susan Napier) and its shape-shifting folklore for why anime embraces rather than fears the transformed body.

embodiment.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
embodiment.title: The Transforming Body
embodiment.relation: McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.

embodiment.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
embodiment.title: The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again)
embodiment.relation: Winters celebrates the goalkeeper's fingertip save—Gordon Banks denying Pelé's header in 1970—as football's aesthetic summit, reading the keeper as the lonely, 'stark mad' outsider of existentialist fiction, a lineage he anchors in Camus, the goalkeeper of Algiers who said all he knew of morality he learnt from football. Kant supplies both the dove of the first Critique—needing the air's resistance, just as the tango's strict steps enable the dancer's personality—and the target of critique: against Kantian disinterested contemplation, he adopts Graham's Nietzschean, Dionysiac aesthetics of participation, so spectators proprioceptively feel the keeper twisting in mid-air, as Wittgenstein's question about the galloping horse picture suggests the movement enters our muscles and joints. Understanding a save or a back-heel means seeing it under a general type ('that' free kick, 'that' volley, from Beckham at Wembley back to Garrincha), and Bloch's ruminations in Handke's The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick show the keeper alone at the liminal limit where concession and prevention meet.

embodiment.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
embodiment.title: The Moving Shadow of Truth
embodiment.relation: Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.

embodiment.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
embodiment.title: Leap of Faith
embodiment.relation: Dionne argues Cobb's 'most resilient parasite' works only as an idea embedded in a coherent story - 'my father doesn't want me to be him' - and that since ideas define who we are, each person is less a host than a collection of well-planted narratives. Using Bergson on embodied, memory-and-desire-mediated perception (Cobb's fear of the bridge triggering Mal's projection) and Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil on perspectival appearance as the price of life, she claims dreams differ from reality in degree, not kind: we are beings-in-the-world who stabilize contingency through story-making and 'strive for positive logic'. Hence knowledge always demands the leap of faith that Saito and Mal demand of Cobb, the film becomes a meta-narrative with Fischer as its audience, and the wobbling top offers only an interpretation of a fact, never the fact itself.

embodiment.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
embodiment.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
embodiment.relation: Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.

embodiment.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
embodiment.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
embodiment.relation: Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.

embodiment.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
embodiment.title: 26. Time Lords Are Us
embodiment.relation: Elder argues the 'back to front' love story of the Doctor and River Song - her past is his future, as at Lake Silencio - refutes both the objective 'river' model of time and the subjective 'song' model on which the mind assembles moments like notes into a flow. Following Merleau-Ponty, he grounds the experience of flow in pre-reflective embodied perception: Clara's walk around the TARDIS and her 'it's smaller on the outside' show a finite body gripping a multifaceted world, so that 'time is the subject and the subject is time.' Because temporalities, unlike private consciousnesses, can intertwine in a shared present, the Doctor and River can build a relationship out of each other's pasts and futures - and in this sense we are all Time Lords.

embodiment.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
embodiment.title: 11. Of Bats and Supermen
embodiment.relation: Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the proper goal of transhumanism - Batman's training and gadgets are only a stage toward transcending the human condition - and that the eugenics and Social Darwinism objection fails because Superman directs his superior fitness at saving the less fit. Through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's churning stomach over a deadline, Alfred retracing his steps and posture to recall a thought, the "Subway Superman" Wesley Autrey's instinctive track rescue) he shows that radically different bodies mean radically different minds and moral perception. That turns Nagel's "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" into "what is it like to be Superman?" - a problem of other minds for our transhuman future, with Watchmen's Doctor Manhattan as the warning of a transcendent being who simply stops caring about humans.

embodiment.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
embodiment.title: 21. Welcome to My World
embodiment.relation: Built on Jakob von Uexküll's Umwelt—the 'island of the senses' that enfolds each creature, illustrated by a moth that smells only a mate's pheromone and hears only the bat's echolocation—the chapter argues that every Discworld being likewise inhabits a sliced-down life world rather than the world as a whole. The ambiguous puzuma running near light speed, dream-spinning dromes that starve victims inside stolen Umwelten, the two-dimensional Shadowing Lemma, Gaspode's pathogen-warring skin, the hermit elephant's hut, and the re-annual plant that flowers a year before its seeds each show a life world carved out by what an organism can sense and use, whether its world runs on science or magic—prompting the suggestion that the Umwelt is more fundamental than either.

embodiment.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
embodiment.title: 7. I Am and Am Not You
embodiment.relation: Reads the opening scene phenomenologically: when Sarah sees her face on Beth, her identity does not merely change genetically but unravels generatively, since her birth, ancestry, and place in world-history are all thrown into question. Using Husserl's lived-body (the absolute "here" of experience), his static/genetic/generative levels of analysis, the homeworld/alienworld distinction (Clone Club solidifies its identity against the Castor "brothers," until Helena cradles the dying Rudy), and Husserl's co-originality of I and world, the chapter presents identity as intersubjective, constituted by shared projects like Sarah's fight for Kira and the Clone Club's tribe-rituals. Kierkegaard's "life must be lived forwards but understood backwards" is broadened: to understand identity we must look before our own birth and beyond our death, into the lifeworld we inherit and pass on.

embodiment.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
embodiment.title: 5. Other People’s Body Parts
embodiment.relation: Explains Kyle Spencer's horror at the body Madison and Zoe assembled from other people's parts through the history of soul-body theories: Aristotle's De Anima account of the soul as the faculties of a living body (plus the Physiognomonics claim that small people have small minds - poor Ma Petite), Plato's Timaeus on body parts designed for philosophy and reincarnation into bodies fitted to one's vices, Avicenna's soul as a faculty-binding nexus that chooses its bodily vehicle like a vehicle serves its owner, and Merleau-Ponty's habitual body (the Axeman's axe as part of his body, phantom limbs), which best explains why walking around on someone else's legs 'has got to mess with you a little'.

embodiment.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
embodiment.title: 6. You Don’t Need to Be Human to Have a Human Hand
embodiment.relation: Sue Zemka contrasts the film's opening eye — reason and consciousness, in a tradition Arendt summarizes as thinking figured as seeing — with its closing image of Deckard's hand reaching toward Ana's through glass, the sense of touch leading out toward others. Schopenhauer explains K's wondering gaze at his own hands in the snow as the human predicament of being both will and representation, subject and object at once, while Condillac's and Maine de Biran's statue thought experiments ('I feel, therefore I am' against Descartes's cogito) are charged with imagining humanness in isolated figures. The film's answer is relational and political: humanness is made in relationships and resistance, from the Joi-Mariette hand-synced sex scene to the final father-daughter touch.

embodiment.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
embodiment.title: 15. The Phenomenology of Replicant Life and Death
embodiment.relation: Zachary Sheldon analyzes 2049's style of violence through Merleau-Ponty's account of film as perceived conduct that shows consciousness thrown into the world, plus the defamiliarizing power of camera choices. In the killings of Sapper and Joshi and the underwater K-Luv fight, the fatal blows are elided, glimpsed only in reaction shots, or distanced through high angles and blurred bodies, so the audience's embodied, empathetic response makes a replicant's death feel exactly as real as a human's. If we feel Sapper die as we would feel a man die, the film's stylistic answer goes, the divide between kinds was never really there; K dies on the stairs because he has truly lived.

embodiment.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
embodiment.title: 22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience
embodiment.relation: Zebrowski brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to bear on Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings built from a lifetime of social experience are essential decision-making shortcuts, not noise corrupting pure reason, as the tirelessly deliberating frontal-lobe patient shows. Chidi's failure is not brain damage but a refusal to trust his own somatic alarms while insisting ethics can be computed, exactly the mind-body split that Scanlon's contractualism, where morality is negotiated with other people, and Dewey's 'morals is education' both reject. Combined with Mark Johnson's moral imagination, this explains how the dead humans keep growing morally after death: bodies, relationships, and culture continue tuning their ethical instincts.

embodiment.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
embodiment.title: I’m an Alien. And That’s OK
embodiment.relation: Reads Ripley's arc through Alison Stone's maternal subjectivity: her mothering of Jonesy and Newt shows the maternal is relational as much as bodily (neither ever gestated in her), Mother (MU/TH/UR) and the Queen stage the 'malevolent mother' against her ('Get away from her, you BITCH!'), and Alien3's unwanted pregnancy forces a violent separation in which only death asserts her selfhood. In Resurrection, Ripley-8 relives Helene Deutsch's quasi-infantile emotional fusion with her hybrid child before killing it, illustrating why Stone demands nonviolent differentiation rather than a complete break from the maternal body - 'I'm a stranger here myself.'

embodiment.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
embodiment.title: Is a Man Not Entitled to the Sweat of His Brow
embodiment.relation: Schevelier uses the Andrew Ryan assassination to teach phenomenology: the moment the controller stops responding, the 'mineness' of the experience collapses and the story stops being yours, revealing that Jack's (and the player's) freedom depended on a thin self-narrative the mind 'desperately struggles to create', per Lutece's epigraph. Nagel's bat shows why no brain scan captures what it is like to play, while Husserl, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty supply the toolkit; Heidegger's hammer, which shows itself in use or in breakdown, explains both immersive scenes like the Kashmir restaurant and what breaks them (bugs, wrong display, a talking protagonist).
