Knowing these psychological causes, sympathy (Hume's word for empathy) replaces blame: we blame the builders, not the house, and the chapter closes by urging compassionate rehabilitation over the show's never-ending circle of punishment and revenge.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
hume-sentimentalism.title: 24. Who’s Duty to Whom
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'

hume-sentimentalism.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
hume-sentimentalism.title: 18. Believies are Not Motivaties
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Uses the 'believies' bit, the 'I think it's wrong to eat meat... I eat them all' confession, and 'of course, but maybe' to place Louis in the meta-ethics of moral motivation: he is a cognitivist and partial success theorist, but a Humean who treats beliefs as causally inert without desire and an externalist who denies a necessary link between moral judgment and motivation. That combination, the chapter argues, lets Louis sincerely judge and not be moved without incoherence—making the amoralist conceivable and avoiding 'the moral problem.'

hume-sentimentalism.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
hume-sentimentalism.title: 3. What Should a Queen Do
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Sznajder uses All Stars' winner-eliminates-you twist (Naomics Smalls cutting Manila, BenDeLaCrème quitting) to ask what a rational queen should do, grounding instrumental rationality in Hume's 'reason is the slave of the passions'. She runs the Ultimatum Game (Latrice rejecting a 99-to-1 split from Valentina), diminishing marginal utility (Trixie's twenty-dollar tip then and now), expected utility with the pink mystery box, and a Trixie–Shangela Prisoner's Dilemma in which rational utility-maximizers eliminate each other when cooperation would leave both better off. The clash between the normative theory and what queens and experimental subjects actually do leads her to the chapter's 'No Sure Thing Principle': Drag Race's plot twists always add an option game theory never modeled, as BenDeLaCrème saw.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
hume-sentimentalism.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Interrogates Gob's catchphrase 'I've made a huge mistake': on Aristotle's account of hexis, the mean of truthfulness and proper pride, and justice as proportional distribution, Gob's prison-escape key stunt and 'Hermano' jealousy make him wicked rather than merely error-prone, since he lacks grasp of his own injustices. Hume's sentimentalist reply is that immorality is a nonrational moral sense refined only through experience, so mistakes could educate Gob, except he roofies away his one growth moment with Steve Holt (!). MacIntyre's practices (the Magician's Alliance versus non-practitioner Gob) and the narrative unity of character explain why a man who tells no coherent story of himself ends up with no wisdom.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
hume-sentimentalism.title: Is Propaganda Permissible
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Manninen surveys Disney's WWII Donald Duck shorts (Donald's Decision, The New Spirit, Der Fuehrer's Face, Commando Duck) to argue propaganda is not only the enemy's tool and not always wrong. Hume's 'slave of the passions' explains why The Spirit of '43 works through the Thrifty-versus-Spendthrift slugfest rather than its implicit argument, and Mill's fallibility-corrigibility case for free expression gives even propaganda a seat in public discourse — though Mill's caveat against expression that instigates mischievous acts marks the real limit, which the contrast with the Axis's 'barefaced lies' (and the Yensid thought experiment) is meant to satisfy.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
hume-sentimentalism.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Andrew Zimmerman Jones treats Ender's conflicts as games analyzable by von Neumann's minimax theorem and the theory of zero-sum, imperfect-information games, arguing Ender wins by redefining the game itself ('the enemy's gate is down') while his empathy fails only with Graff, whose larger game Ender never suspects because he never treats the adults as the enemy. He unpacks Ender's claim that to understand an enemy is to love him through Socrates' words in Plato's Laches on courage, Hume's account of sympathy, and the Christian agape of 'love your enemies,' mapping a continuum from sympathy through empathy to love.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
hume-sentimentalism.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Terjesen reads the O'Neil-Adams pairing as moral rationalism (Hal) versus moral sentimentalism (Ollie): Hal jails the boy assaulting slumlord Jubal Slade because 'He was breaking the law' and defends a racist senator's speech on free-speech principle, while Ollie works from the gut. Hume's 'Reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions' explains both Ollie's effectiveness and Hal's collapse into Parallax, since no argument from Kilowog could restrain a grief only a stronger passion could. But sentiment needs an impartial filter: Smith's impartial spectator condemns Ollie's near-murder of Black Canary's attacker and his abandonment of the heroin-addicted Speedy, while Hal's cooler principle keeps the Native American land dispute from Ollie's violent plan. The conclusion is that morality is sentiment-based but reason must police it, so each hero needs the other.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
hume-sentimentalism.title: NOTES
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Takes Claude's label of Peter as an 'empath' seriously and tests three accounts of empathy against his power: Hume's emotional resonance (rejected because Peter keeps powers after the donor leaves), Scheler's absorption into another's identity, and Hume's conversion of ideas into vivid impressions, settling on the mirror-neuron thought that Peter literally replicates other people's brain structures — which explains why he copies Isaac's painting skill and even Sylar's anger in 'Kindred.' It then asks whether empathy makes you moral and answers no — Elle enjoys Peter's pain and Mohinder feels his experimental subjects' terror — arguing instead that empathy needs a filter: Hume's general point of view and Adam Smith's impartial spectator, illustrated by Hiro's imagined Kensei ideal and by Nathan serving as Peter's emotional filter until his death leaves Peter without one.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
hume-sentimentalism.title: The Office and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Asks whether Michael can (not will) ever learn empathy, distinguishing cognitive empathy - explained via Russell's argument-by-analogy account of other minds, which Michael manages only with people like himself, hence his sales success in 'The Client' - from affective empathy, which he lacks (Kevin's possible skin cancer is 'terrible news for both of us'; he cannot read Phyllis's oven mitt in Yankee Swap). Traces his cluelessness to egocentrism, and following Hume and Smith's sentimentalist account of morals - decentring the ego toward the impartial spectator via emotional contagion - argues his only hope is a real friendship (Jim's) that could drag him outside himself, since sycophantic Dwight and one-sided Todd Packer never will.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
hume-sentimentalism.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Terjesen uses spider-sense to tour early-modern philosophy of perception: against direct realism, Locke's indirect realism and its primary/secondary quality distinction suggest 'dangerousness' is a perceiver-relative secondary quality — bombs threaten Spider-Man but not the Hulk, and Mysterio manufactures danger-experiences — while Berkeley's idealism and Hume's phenomenalism radicalize the resulting skepticism about ever verifying sense data. The decisive clue is that spider-sense fails when Aunt May conks Peter with a vase (Amazing Spider-Man #114) and when his mentor Miles Warren becomes the Jackal: Peter does not fear those he loves. This supports Hume's sentimentalist account of moral judgment, on which vice is found not in the act but in the disapproving sentiment, moderated by Reid's common-sense reply that perception always already contains judgment — so spider-sense is a moralized judgment about what to avoid, not a Geiger counter.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
hume-sentimentalism.title: Notes
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Tests moral relativism against absolutism through Enterprise's "Cogenitor": Trip's liberation of the Vissian third-sex being - secretly scanning its brain, naming it Charles, teaching it to read - ends in its suicide, and the chapter asks whether Trip's judgments track rational moral truth or are Humean after-the-fact rationalizations of disgust, since on Hume's view reason is the slave of the passions and is/ought are separate. Kant's categorical imperative (the cogenitor used merely as a means of reproduction) and Aquinas's natural law are offered as absolutist resources on Trip's side, while Phlox voices a Benedict-style "morally good is just habitual" relativism and Archer concludes "we didn't come out here to play God", prefiguring the Prime Directive. The chapter lands on Mary Midgley's rejection of moral isolationism via her tsujigiri example and Quark's "we're better than you" speech to Sisko: cross-cultural judgment is possible, but only after understanding, and not on the first day of first contact.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
hume-sentimentalism.title: “This Is the Way”
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Holdier uses the imagined scene of stormtroopers roasting Grogu over a cookfire to test moral sentimentalism: our disgust at eating Baby Yoda either perceives moral truth, informs our motivations, or simply is our judgment, but popular sentiment cannot settle its aptness, since our culture happily eats sentient chickens - the same inconsistency fans felt when Grogu ate the Frog Lady's eggs in 'The Passenger'. Adam Smith's impartial spectator supplies the corrective standard: if a bias-free spectator would recoil at a Grogu barbecue, that feeling is appropriate, and by parity the same spectator should recoil at factory-farmed meat (via Singer's speciesism and Kasperbauer's infrahumanization). So Din Djarin's sentimental attachment to the Child, which overrides Guild code in 'The Sin', is vindicated as genuinely moral rather than merely subjective.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
hume-sentimentalism.title: 14. Who Watches the Justice League
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
hume-sentimentalism.title: NOTES
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
hume-sentimentalism.title: P A R T O N E
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Christopher Robichaud's essay asks what morality can demand of Dr. Manhattan after the accident strips him of the moral emotions (in Jesse Prinz's Humean vein) needed to value persons, which is why he can tell Laurie 'I read atoms' and rank human life beside rubble. It then asks what grounds morality's authority over a being no one can punish, rejecting divine command theory (Manhattan's 'clock without a craftsman') and doubting Kant's rational grounding applies to someone lacking moral concepts, so 'no one is above the moral law' may rest on a brute fact. It closes on political morality: a United States made a hyperpower by Manhattan's service (as in his Vietnam intervention) may not claim a double standard, since sovereignty blocks preventive war even when the US would win at little cost.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
hume-sentimentalism.title: Ethics, Heart, and Violence in Miller’s Crossing
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Herling reads Miller's Crossing through Hume's moral psychology of passion versus reason, arguing the film's dominant 'ethics' (voiced by Johnny Caspar) is Hobbes's social contract plus Thrasymachus's advantage-of-the-stronger and Plato's 'do good to friends, harm to enemies'—a relativism of power that Tom Reagan navigates by cool calculation. 'Heart,' the capacity for sympathetic attachment Hume makes the real basis of morality, keeps breaking through: Tom spares the pleading Bernie ('Look in your heart') at Miller's Crossing, and his loyalty to Leo secretly drives his 'plays.' But Bernie's betrayal, the surreal sympathy-crushing violence (the beatings, Leo's tommy-gun ballet, Caspar shooting the faceless Dane), and Leo and Verna's reunion steel Tom into lonely noir stoicism—'What heart?'—when he finally executes Bernie without mercy.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.title: This Is the Age of Steel
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
hume-sentimentalism.title: 1. Is Rationality an Illusion
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Litman and Zelcer argue that Foundation dramatizes Hume's thesis that reason is the slave of the passions: the robot Demerzel (Daneel Olivaw) and the mutant Mule accomplish history by directly amplifying emotions like Seldon's pride, after which their victims' reason confabulates rational justifications (motivated reasoning). They trace the emotion-versus-reason debate from Plato's tripartite charioteer soul through Aristotle's rational animal and Christian moral psychology to Hume's secularized version, and use the Wye rebellion and Pritcher's converted loyalty to show emotional manipulation works like an optical illusion, persisting even once the victim knows about it.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
hume-sentimentalism.title: The Grinch’s Change of Heart Whodunit
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Cunningham asks whether the Grinch's sudden metanoia is a matter of head or heart, staging a debate between Kant and Hume. A Kantian reading treats the change as reason reasserting the moral law after the Grinch's inclinations (envy, resentment) hijacked it, so he realizes stealing Christmas disrespects the Whos as ends in themselves. A Humean reading, favored by the author given that the Grinch's 'small heart grew three sizes,' treats it as a new sentiment of sympathy rather than a rational apprehension, invoking Hume's claim that reason is the slave of the passions.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.title: Chapter 2 Huckleberry Finn and Moral Motivation
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Alan Goldman argues against Bennett and against Arpaly and Schroeder that Huck is not weak-willed or irrational: his sympathy for Jim is an intentional emotion containing implicit judgments and awareness of the genuine moral reasons to help Jim, so Huck acts on his strongest reasons and is courageous rather than akratic. Because Huck is rational yet not motivated by his explicit (corrupt) moral judgments, and his real motivation comes only through emotional attachment, Goldman concludes against Kant that moral motivation is not rationally required. He uses Huck's failure to extend concern to other slaves, and analogies to meat-eaters and arbitrary aesthetic taste, to show moral inconsistency is not practical irrationality.

hume-sentimentalism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
hume-sentimentalism.title: Chapter 14 Moral Value and Moral Psychology in Twain’s “Carnival of Crime”
hume-sentimentalism.relation: Boardman treats Twain's 'The Facts Concerning the Recent Carnival of Crime in Connecticut'—in which a narrator kills his personified conscience (a shabby dwarf) and gleefully commits a spree of crimes—as staging an 'exasperating metaphysical question' about the value and psychology of morality. On a Nietzschean reading the narrator becomes an Overman revaluing values, seeing conscience as the internalized lie of slave morality; on a Humean reading conscience is moral feeling (not reason), so once it is destroyed the narrator can still reason about right yet has no motive to act morally, illustrating the oak-tree and willful-murder arguments that vice lies in sentiment, not relations or facts. Boardman concludes both interpretations fit yet neither settles whether Twain endorses or lampoons the result—our horror at the crimes is what makes the story funny.

moral-relativism.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am
moral-relativism.title: The Sopranos and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Argues Simple Subjectivism ('right for Tony') fails as a reading of the show because it cannot make sense of genuine moral disagreement - Carmela and Tony's adultery battle in 'Whitecaps', Agent Ciccerone versus Tony on extortion - nor ground outrage at the killings of Pussy and the sobbing Matt Bevilaqua. Humean ethical subjectivism, grounded in a common human nature and the sentiment of sympathy (with Berkeley's pin example to explain vice as perception-dependent), fares better: it lets us condemn Tony while explaining his warped sympathy - grieving Pie-O-My more than his human victims - as the product of a mob upbringing that Melfi's alexithymia diagnosis in 'House Arrest' targets.

moral-relativism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
moral-relativism.title: With Great Power Comes—What
moral-relativism.relation: Turns Uncle Ben's dictum into normative ethics: the question is not how super-powered people do live but how they ought to, whether they have a duty to take up the hero role, and what obligations follow from it. Two 'hobgoblins' — ethical nihilism and ethical relativism — are dismissed as contrary to our ordinary convictions (Mother Teresa's charity objectively good, Hitler's genocide absolutely bad), clearing the ground for utilitarianism.

moral-relativism.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
moral-relativism.title: Worldviews, Values, and Superheroes
moral-relativism.relation: Argues that in a naturalist universe of particles and force fields nothing grounds objective good and evil, so a defiant Superman who fights evil just because he wants to prizes sympathy while downplaying truth. Wonder Woman's challenge — "Truth and justice" — raises whether they are in league: Socrates and the classic tradition held truth, beauty and goodness are one, while Nietzsche, godfather of postmodernism, snarls that "Truth is ugly," leaving naturalism a dilemma between believing in ultimate justice or accepting that it is an illusion.

moral-relativism.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
moral-relativism.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.

moral-relativism.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
moral-relativism.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Janice Daurio sets Plato's Thrasymachus and Callicles and Nietzsche's immoralism against three Narnian immoralists: Uncle Andrew, who exempts 'profound students and great thinkers' from rules meant for little boys, servants, and women; Queen Jadis, whose Deplorable Word and 'What else were they there for but to do my will?' embody might-makes-right; and the Green Witch, who extends going beyond good and evil to going beyond truth itself. Following Lewis's moral realism (the Golden Rule and Natural Law as facts like gravity, with Hobbes's lesson that someone always turns up with more power), she shows the immoralists cannot live by their own creed, since Uncle Andrew resents being treated as Jadis's slave, and since Lewis ties real authority to service, as when humble Frank the Cabby is made king.

moral-relativism.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
moral-relativism.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Gayne Anacker defines moral imagination, the capacity to see one's values and life from fresh moral perspectives, and argues the Chronicles exercise it through three character types readers live through: flawed repenters (Edmund, Eustace, Bree, Aravis), the essentially good under trial (Lucy believing her Aslan sighting in Prince Caspian, Caspian's greed on Goldwater Island), and the fatally self-absorbed (Uncle Andrew, Shift), together with portrayals of worship and of true versus usurped nobility (Peter versus Miraz). Philosophically he contends the stories' effectiveness supports virtue ethics over action-centered modern theories, and that disagreement among ethical theorists is no ground for relativism: no one needs theoretical consensus to know Miraz is evil.

moral-relativism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
moral-relativism.title: So, What’s the Bottom Line
moral-relativism.relation: James Klagge, defining terms in Socratic fashion, distinguishes bootlegs like Great White Wonder from piracy and argues unreleased Dylan material (the New York Blood on the Tracks, "Blind Willie McTell," the 1966 Live concert) has genuine musical and historical value. He rejects the Sophist view that morality is just self-interest and the relativist "everybody's doing it" defense, then weighs the artist's Lockean property and privacy rights against fans' rights of access, noting legal-but-immoral and illegal-but-moral cases in the spirit of Martin Luther King's civil disobedience. His verdict: bootlegging is morally acceptable when royalties are fair, stolen tapes are not used, and mainly public performances circulate.

moral-relativism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
moral-relativism.title: The Blessings of Tranquility
moral-relativism.relation: Michael Chiariello takes Dylan's "the truth is true whether you wanna believe it or not" as a correspondence theory of truth, then rejects both the gospel-era absolutism of "Precious Angel" and the relativism (from Protagoras' man-the-measure to modern subjectivism) that would make Dylan's changes of course harmless. The alternative he defends is Pyrrhonian skepticism in Sextus Empiricus's sense: truth is objective but never fully assured, so suspending judgment yields tranquility. Dylan's career - from the ambiguous "Blowin' in the Wind" through "Watching the River Flow" and "Things Have Changed" to the two versions of "Every Grain of Sand" ("the reality of man" vs "a perfect finished plan") - embodies this balanced, non-dogmatic search the way of God designed it.

moral-relativism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
moral-relativism.title: A Call to Unchanging Truths
moral-relativism.relation: Francis Beckwith argues the 1979-81 Christian albums are no aberration: Dylan's whole career presupposes moral realism, an objective moral law built into the universe - "Dignity never been photographed" names an irreducible moral property, and the judgments in "With God on Our Side" and "Blowin' in the Wind" only make sense if right and wrong are unchanging across eras. The six-month sentence William Zanzinger receives in "The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll" is condemned on retributive, lex talionis grounds rather than any utilitarian calculus of consequences, and "Forever Young" and "What Good Am I?" urge virtue practiced for its own sake. The chapter thus reads Dylan's conversion as the surfacing of commitments - against relativism, for virtue and unchanging truths - always latent in songs like "The Times They Are A-Changin'."

moral-relativism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
moral-relativism.title: How to do Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Johnson argues through Colbert's satire that truth is neither individual ('My Truth') nor cultural ('wikiality' — a Wikipedia entry does not become true by consensus), since relativism is self-contradictory and implies slavery was not wrong before abolition. He deploys Locke's attack on 'enthusiasm' to show 'truthiness' is circular reasoning — sure because one is sure — and dismantles the 'right to my opinion' as a bid to shield beliefs from evidence, closing with Socrates' model: when evidence runs out, admit ignorance and keep doing philosophy.

moral-relativism.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
moral-relativism.title: So There’s No Accounting for Taste
moral-relativism.relation: Mary MacLeod stages her quarrel with her husband over the musical value of the Dead's Space jams as a problem in metaethics: she claims Space objectively lacks merit, Eric claims it has value, and the chapter asks whether either 'should' claim can be true. She lays out Value Realism (value as intrinsic, detectable properties), Subjectivism ('no accounting for taste'), Mackie's Humean error theory (we project feelings onto the world as we do with color), and the 'oughts by agreement' view that expert or social consensus makes things right the way traffic conventions make right-side driving correct. The Dahmer and torture cases show why subjectivism fails for ethics, and the chapter concludes that 'beauty by agreement' quietly collapses back into Realism — so Deadheads' fierce debates about Space are legitimate disagreements after all.

moral-relativism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
moral-relativism.title: The Cosmic Divide
moral-relativism.relation: The chapter casts the two series as opposed worldviews: the original is Manichaean moral absolutism, with 'War of the Gods' staging Count Iblis and the Ships of Light as cosmic Darkness and Light battling over humanity, while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean moral relativism where context decides right and wrong. Its clearest cases are comparative: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of the fleet's fuel reserves to rescue Starbuck, and Leoben is airlocked after interrogation while the tortured Athena and Gina are treated with mercy. The fan schism between the shows, it concludes, is really the centuries-old quarrel between absolutism and relativism.

moral-relativism.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
moral-relativism.title: Transformers and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Barkman takes the 1986 movie poster's 'Beyond Good. Beyond Evil.' as a Nietzsche allusion and argues the cartoon refutes it: Skyfire's 'It is wrong,' Orion Pax's repudiation of admired power in 'War Dawn,' and Optimus's humble 'Thrones are for Decepticons' make Megatron a would-be superman and villain while Optimus is a Platonic guardian of a universal moral law binding even Unicron and the Quintessons. A reductio against cultural relativism (the Decepticon invasion of Earth, First Aid's failed pacifism in 'The Ultimate Weapon') plus C.S. Lewis-style archetypes explain why Optimus - a Christ-type who died saving the world - endures while GoBots do not.

moral-relativism.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
moral-relativism.title: Where Do We Go from Here
moral-relativism.relation: David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.

moral-relativism.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
moral-relativism.relation: Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.

moral-relativism.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
moral-relativism.title: Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes
moral-relativism.relation: Barkman argues that anime's Christian imagery — the legendary Santa on a cross, Earthian's gay angel lovers, Trinity Blood's bishonen pope and female cardinal, Evangelion's hostile Angels — encodes Japanese religious pluralism rather than orthodox Christianity. He lays out the pluralist position (following Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction and John Hick: Ultimate Reality is only equivocally describable, so doctrine matters less than spiritual mood), contrasts it with exclusivism and inclusivism, and charges pluralism with self-undermining intolerance, then traces Japan's historical demonization of Christianity from the 1637 Shimabara massacre (Ninja Resurrection, Samurai Champloo) to Eva's alien invaders, with Armageddon imagery fueled by the atomic bombs. Because Shinto-Buddhist-Daoist anti-realism dissolves fixed categories, anime dissolves good and evil (Chrno Crusade's I Ching balance) and gender itself, gravitating to the symbol-rich 'jungle' of Catholicism (C.S. Lewis's phrase) — and where Trinity Blood lets some vampires be righteous, Augustine's City of God marks the one nearly orthodox note.

moral-relativism.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
moral-relativism.title: So Why Do I Support Aston Villa
moral-relativism.relation: Rose—made a Villan by misreading a 1978 Panini sticker as Aston Villa's claret and blue—asks whether supporting Aston Villa is rational and argues ethics is far more like fandom than philosophers admit. Reasons for supporting Villa (local team, the 1982 European Cup, the colors) explain but never justify his allegiance, and the impartial procedures ethics prizes—the utilitarian benevolent spectator and Rawls's original position behind the veil of ignorance, with its 'sort of Kantian' consent-based alternative—turn out too demanding and too abstract: they would force him to donate his match ticket to charity, forbid the Premiership manager favoring his academy son, and reduce agency to the 'Rose-calcio scale' absurdity of switching to Real Madrid for rational reasons. His positive, communitarian claim is that we are thrown into social traditions whose inherited values—like a team—make moral agency and action possible at all, a 'different kind of rationality' that flirts with relativism yet still needs an exit strategy for cultures that discriminate against women or torture children.

moral-relativism.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
moral-relativism.title: How Can I Compete with Geniusness
moral-relativism.relation: Timothy Dunn uses 'Patrick SmartPants', where a brain-coral transplant turns Patrick into a genius who abandons SpongeBob, to ask whether the happy ignoramus or the discontented genius lives better. After sketching a subjectivist defense of Patrick's choice to revert ('knowledge can never replace friendship'), the chapter tests Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism: since competent judges rank higher pleasures qualitatively above lower ones, Mill's dictum that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied condemns Patrick's destruction of his own higher capacities. Dunn then presses two objections — that people's actual lower-pleasure preferences may be genuine rather than socially produced, and that the capacity for higher pleasure seems worthless without its actual experience — leaving Mill's verdict in tension.

moral-relativism.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
moral-relativism.title: The Best Kind of Friend
moral-relativism.relation: Ruth Tallman tests Holmes and Watson against Aristotle's requirement in the Nicomachean Ethics that perfect friendship exists only between the 'alike in excellence': since the two live by irreconcilable moral codes (Holmes's cocaine and burglaries versus Watson's clean living and law-abidingness), Aristotelian moral naturalism denies they can be true friends at all, despite the raw panic in 'The Three Garridebs' proving mutual devotion. Recasting the pair as moral pluralists with different 'good for me's, she argues Holmes is actually the better friend, an 'integrity-promoting' friend who urges Watson to stay home from the Milverton burglary to honor Watson's own code, while the proselytizing Watson, who nags about cocaine yet tags along anyway, repeatedly violates his own integrity.

moral-relativism.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
moral-relativism.title: I’m in Need of Some Restraint
moral-relativism.relation: Tells how the Abraham and Isaac story introduced "redemption," a substitution rite that curbed the "pride of place" of first-borns while replacing human sacrifice — a transition the Egyptians and Greeks also made independently. Using Shirley Jackson's "The Lottery," the volunteering Druid victims and the martyr Perpetua, it argues any horror can be normalized by piety and tradition — Sarah Palin or Michele Bachmann would have defended first-born sacrifice in ancient Ur — and needles the reader with ritual chicken sacrifice versus KFC: "which of those two, in a just world, would really be more inhumane?"

moral-relativism.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within
moral-relativism.title: Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Grants that Larry looks like the Romantic ideal of the authentic self, Rousseau's amour de soi turned into candid self-expression, but argues his authenticity collapses into egoism: petty commandments about chicken skewers and beach jackets, one-strike firings like the toupee-wearing chef, and ceaseless sincerity tests. Through Sartre's categories Larry is bad faith in both directions, the 'cowardly bastard': he denies transcendence ('I can't help it') and hides behind fabricated personas, faking concern over a sick dog and exaggerating his Jewishness to the kidney consortium. Charles Taylor's The Ethics of Authenticity supplies the verdict that self-creation needs 'pre-existing horizons of significance,' so Larry's 'anything goes' authenticity is really moral relativism and justified self-interest, with Ayn Rand's virtue of selfishness as its unwanted philosophical ally. The chapter closes that only a relational authenticity, like the African ideal of ubuntu, could redeem Larry, and he lacks it, so 'maybe authenticity isn't for everyone.'

moral-relativism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
moral-relativism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.

moral-relativism.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
moral-relativism.title: The Devil and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Olli Pitkänen maps the Satanist spectrum beyond the Devil-worship of films like The Mother of Tears: LaVey's atheistic, morally subjectivist Church of Satan; the Nietzschean Übermensch cult of the Order of Nine Angles with its initiatory violence; the chaos-gnostic Temple of the Black Light (whose ideal, he says, is the Joker in The Dark Knight); and Finland's Star of Azazel, theistic Satanists whose theosophical moral realism makes Satan a presenter of choices rather than a willer of evil. On that last reading Vader destroying Palpatine and Sauron perishing with the One Ring show evil as human projection, and even Jesus counts as 'satanic' in the rebel-against-dogma sense.

moral-relativism.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
moral-relativism.title: Girls and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Ketcham sets Hannah B (Brooklyn) beside an imagined Hannah D (a Darfur village terrorized by the Janjaweed) to ask whether personal fulfillment depends on culture or on the individual. Rejecting relativism (which, per Alford, cannot even condemn suppression of belief), he turns to Rawls's Law of Peoples - five minimal human rights any well-ordered society must grant - and builds a thought experiment, 'Blandland,' a minimally compliant country where both Hannahs relocate. His conclusion: even Rawlsian minimum rights, under which life can remain Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short,' plus personal drive and the attitudes of others, jointly and indeterminately decide what either Hannah can become.

moral-relativism.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
moral-relativism.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Charlene Elsby asks what makes the McPoyles cross the line from offensive (like the Gang) into irredeemably creepy, working through their bathrobes, unibrows, incest, and constant milk drinking. Her answer runs through violated social convention: the creepy person is not merely making non-standard choices but seems unaware conventions exist at all, and Liam's 'It's society that has the problem' raises moral relativism only for the chapter to insist the creep reaction tracks something actually wrong, not just different. Adding the legacy of physiognomy (we judge character from appearance, and more harshly when the trait is controllable) and an inductive inference (everything the McPoyles do is creepy, so even the milk must be), creepiness emerges as an art of detection rather than a science: whether someone is creepy differs from whether they seem creepy.

moral-relativism.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
moral-relativism.title: 4. Lie or Die
moral-relativism.relation: Hawkes uses Rick's bar confrontation with Dave and Tony in 2.8 'Nebraska' to ask when lying is right, after defining lying through the Governor's white flag at the National Guard camp and Eugene's false cure claim. He rejects moral relativism - the Claimers' rules, Terminus's 'butcher or cattle', the Governor's 'we will do the only thing' - because it forbids criticizing rapists and cannibals and erases moral progress, then finds utilitarianism shaky given Eugene's unforeseen deadly consequences and Rick's refusal to hand Michonne to the Governor at 'Arrow on the Doorpost.' He defends a duty-based deontology in which the duty to protect the farm overrides the duty not to lie, and closes with Robert Kirkman's own lie about an alien invasion that got The Walking Dead published.

moral-relativism.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
moral-relativism.title: 12. Margaery for Queen!
moral-relativism.relation: Jones asks whether Margaery - who grooms Tommen, admits she was 'good at seeming good,' and may count as an abuser despite Westeros's norms - could still have been the best queen in the Seven Kingdoms. Against the prosecution's portrait of a cold egoist, he argues her charity to Flea Bottom's children shows a queen is good by what she does rather than why she did it, so selfish ambition welded to shrewdness can genuinely serve the common good. Comparing her with Ramsay (cruelty that provokes revolt) and Ned (benevolence without calculation that gets him killed), the chapter draws an implicitly Machiavellian conclusion - the people's best bet is hunger for power joined to the cunning to keep them onside - while doubting that cultural relativism can fully excuse her treatment of Tommen.

moral-relativism.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
moral-relativism.title: 12. Are We Really Sure They’re Wrong
moral-relativism.relation: Timothy Hsiao argues we cannot condemn the burning of the disabled or Smith's son's mandated euthanasia by appealing to Nazi values, since cultural relativism would make the Resistance the real wrongdoers; the horror we feel presupposes an objective natural law known to reason, the violation of which grounded the Nuremberg trials. From Augustine's 'an unjust law is no law at all,' the chapter then tests the Resistance's armed rebellion against the five just-war conditions — proper authority (the Resistance as agent of the moral law), just cause, reasonable chance of success (the newsreels as grounds for hope), proportionality, and last resort — and finds it justified.

moral-relativism.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
moral-relativism.title: 11. Fighting Ethical Relativism in Tales of Suspense
moral-relativism.relation: Reading Tales of Suspense, Pagnoni Berns and Veteri cast Iron Man as a man of every era - echoing LBJ's 'reason together', Cold War utilitarianism against Communism, playboy masculinity, and finally the Registration Act - which makes him a parrot of whatever relativism his age prefers. Captain America, literally frozen in time, holds Kant's categorical imperative: every life is an end in itself, so he saves Nazi prisoners in #71, trades his own life for a pilot in #61, and drinks possibly lethal serum without needing thanks, while Bucky's mediated, reward-seeking morality shows why ends corrupt moral worth. Because Cap's universal, ahistorical defense of human dignity holds from the 1940s to the 1960s and beyond, the authors rank him above the adaptable but context-bound Iron Man.

moral-relativism.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
moral-relativism.title: 5. Inside Gilead’s Misogynist Parlors
moral-relativism.relation: Hirschbein unravels the Genesis story of Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar as the script Gilead rereads to rationalize its 'misogynist parlors,' arguing that Gilead's exegesis is propaganda rather than scholarship—cherry-picking scripture that Nietzsche joked would appall the actual Jesus. He then spins the reader's moral compass: with Rorty's ironist he asks whether anyone initiated into Abraham's tribe or raised in Gilead can be blamed—are even Hitler and Commander Waterford products of their time?—and weighs Ofglen's suicide bombing of the Rachel and Leah Center against just war criteria of proportion, innocence, and chance of success. Finally, with Freud and Niebuhr, he suggests the Sons of Jacob built their surveillance state on a depraved view of human nature, so utopian schemes—Gilead included—are doomed from the founding.

moral-relativism.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
moral-relativism.title: 14. The Value of a Handmaid
moral-relativism.relation: Pérez assesses a Handmaid's value through Kant—Gilead gives women a price, not a dignity, so the Gilead–Mexico trade deal is human trafficking dressed as diplomacy—and through Marx's use value and exchange value, with fertility the commodity and Jezebels carrying both market and affective price. He adds Bourdieu's forms of capital to show Offred's social and resistant cultural capital against Janine's collapse, then weighs cultural relativism (via Renteln and Herodotus) before rejecting it for Gilead: its values were improvised and forced rather than naturally evolved, so the culture itself earns no pass. The Handmaids' refusal to stone Janine shows their collective worth: 'They should've never given us uniforms if they didn't want us to be an army.'

moral-relativism.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
moral-relativism.title: 4. Can We Do Enough Good
moral-relativism.relation: Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.

moral-relativism.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
moral-relativism.title: You Can Take the Man out of Cleveland . .
moral-relativism.relation: Da Silva and Found take Liz's stint as a Cleveland model in the episode 'Cleveland' as an entry into social constructivism: following Ian Hacking's account of socially constructed Xs and Marcia Eaton's socially constructed aesthetic response, taste is learned, culture-bound, and class-marked, so Jack's Manhattan standards condemn Liz's Burger King attire while Cleveland calls her a model. They then warn that aesthetic relativism ('you can't question taste') leaves no ground for condemning Tracy's solid gold boots or for resisting the powerful, since celebrities and the Black Crusaders have platforms that let them impose their standards. Searle's non-relativist account of social facts is floated as an escape route, and Liz's persistence as a New Yorker shows identity and values are constructed gradually through social belonging.

moral-relativism.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
moral-relativism.title: The Cosmic Divide
moral-relativism.relation: The chapter locates the real fan schism in worldview: the original series is Manichaean moral absolutism - Count Iblis and the Ships of Light wage a cosmic Light/Darkness war in which Evil is one force (Iblis sharing the Imperious Leader's voice) and humanity is the battleground - while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean relativism ('man is the measure'), where right depends entirely on context. Evidence: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of fuel reserves to find Starbuck; Leoben is airlocked after Starbuck's interrogation while Thorne is killed for torturing Athena; producer Eick even defends Caprica Six's killing of the baby as possibly a mercy. The two shows thus embody absolutist nostalgia for moral clarity versus post-9/11 moral ambiguity.

moral-relativism.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
moral-relativism.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: LoPresti uses 'This Week in God' segments (Ed Helms refereeing a Hindu-versus-Mayan 'faith-off', Colbert's roast line that all religions are infinite paths to accepting Jesus, Rob Corddry's purification rituals and God Exchange stock ticker) to lay out exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism as responses to religious diversity. Inclusivism like Colbert's 'anonymous Christian' logic is exposed as intellectual imperialism that erases genuinely distinct teachings such as the Buddhist non-self and impermanence, while the chapter defends a deep pluralism against the relativism that makes 'all religions equally true' meaningless. Its eulogy for the God Machine borrows Marx's view of religion as an instrument of mass control to explain why religious humor now survives only through a political lens.

moral-relativism.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
moral-relativism.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Through Daenerys's horror at her Dothraki wedding - public sex, lethal duels, and later the gang-rape of captives that Drogo calls 'the way of war' - the chapter distinguishes descriptive cultural relativism from normative moral relativism. The diversity of ethical codes in Westeros (crannogmen, wildlings, Craster) plus Cersei and Jaime's incest and the Targaryen brother-sister marriages show moral codes genuinely vary, and the audience's harsher judgment of Tyrion's whoring than of his siblings' incest illustrates our own culturally conditioned gut reactions. But the chapter concludes relativism must be rejected: no culture's say-so makes rape acceptable, while eating horse meat is fine and sibling incest depends on circumstances.

moral-relativism.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
moral-relativism.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Terjesen asks how Sinestro and Universo ever passed recruitment and answers that the Guardians' two-prong test of honesty and fearlessness reflects moral pluralism: universal rules kept deliberately thin so that different moral codes can coexist, which is why the vicious 'good bad man' Jack T. Chance keeps his ring on Hellhole. But honor, honesty, and justice are thick ethical concepts in Bernard Williams's sense, requiring cultural context to apply, so Laira's execution of a surrendered Amon Sur and the Guardians' own cover-ups (the Corpse, Kentor Omoto) cannot be settled by appealing to thin 'justice,' and the Alpha Lanterns' internal-affairs role cannot fix it. Moral particularism leaves the Corps with unresolvable disagreements about who the bad apples are.

moral-relativism.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
moral-relativism.title: NOTES
moral-relativism.relation: Taliaferro and Kastrul ask what the reader would do in the castaways' place, using Aristotle's view that character is a disposition to act under other conditions to assess Mr. Eko, Ben, Michael, Charlie, and Sawyer: people are not merely what they do but what they would do. Plato's Ring of Gyges, quoted at length, tests whether characters like Sun behave honestly only when watched. Against the idea that the island could reverse all values, they argue morality cannot be completely relative to context - invoking Chesterton's 'Thou shalt not steal' on the remotest star - and place Lost in the island-narrative tradition of the Odyssey and Robinson Crusoe as a story of the journey of the soul.

moral-relativism.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
moral-relativism.title: If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where
moral-relativism.relation: George Wrisley uses Lost as a testing ground against ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism: the disagreement over Sayid shooting young Ben (monster or innocent child?) motivates relativism, but the Argument from Disagreement fails for the same reason Locke and Mr. Eko's button dispute does not change what will actually happen if it goes unpushed. Simple subjectivism makes every judge infallible (the Man in Black could declare his murders right) and dissolves genuine disagreement between Jacob and his brother over killing their 'mother,' while cultural relativism makes the Dharma Initiative's torture of Sayid 'right' and would have ruled Martin Luther King Jr. wrong. He concludes that Lost's ambiguous cases - Michael's murder of Ana Lucia and Libby, Ben killing Jacob, Jack extorting Ben on the operating table - invite viewers to seek objective grounds Socratically, questioning their own moral judgments with further 'why's.

moral-relativism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
moral-relativism.title: Notes
moral-relativism.relation: David Kyle Johnson argues Kirk is a jerk for dismantling utopias—the machine-god Vaal in 'The Apple' and the spore colonists of Omicron Ceti III in 'This Side of Paradise'—whose members were happy, healthy, and arguably free. Taking up objections from the Mission Log podcast, he rebuts the 'stagnation' and 'drug' charges by testing the utopias against Aristotle's eudaimonia and Maslow's self-actualization, and exposes the appeal-to-nature fallacy behind 'artificial happiness'. Using Rousseau on primitive simplicity and Nozick's libertarian minimal state, he concludes that the real threat to freedom is Kirk himself (and a Federation that, as Eddington says, assimilates without telling you), and that at minimum cultural relativism forbids wrecking harmless societies.

moral-relativism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
moral-relativism.title: Notes
moral-relativism.relation: Victor Grech presents Klingons as a cultural pastiche—Mongol horde stereotypes, Japanese Bushido, Viking Valhalla, Shakespeare 'restored to the original Klingon'—whose 1500-year honor code and embrace of honorable death (Klag's dishonored father, Jadzia's rebuke of Kang) make them Nietzschean Ubermenschen who slew their own gods, echoing Nietzsche's 'God is dead'. The Kahless clone of 'Rightful Heir' ('perhaps the words are more important than the man') shows a messianism surviving deicide. He then reads Worf through Roland Barthes's 'Occidentalism' and one-way acculturation—Picard praising Worf's 'humanity' after 'Reunion'—while Azetbur's 'human rights' is racist jab in The Undiscovered Country and Trekkers' Klingon cosplay raise cultural relativism and appropriation.

moral-relativism.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
moral-relativism.title: Notes
moral-relativism.relation: Tests moral relativism against absolutism through Enterprise's "Cogenitor": Trip's liberation of the Vissian third-sex being - secretly scanning its brain, naming it Charles, teaching it to read - ends in its suicide, and the chapter asks whether Trip's judgments track rational moral truth or are Humean after-the-fact rationalizations of disgust, since on Hume's view reason is the slave of the passions and is/ought are separate. Kant's categorical imperative (the cogenitor used merely as a means of reproduction) and Aquinas's natural law are offered as absolutist resources on Trip's side, while Phlox voices a Benedict-style "morally good is just habitual" relativism and Archer concludes "we didn't come out here to play God", prefiguring the Prime Directive. The chapter lands on Mary Midgley's rejection of moral isolationism via her tsujigiri example and Quark's "we're better than you" speech to Sisko: cross-cultural judgment is possible, but only after understanding, and not on the first day of first contact.

moral-relativism.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
moral-relativism.title: Notes
moral-relativism.relation: LaRocca argues Boba Fett is best understood as an amoralist - neither a moral relativist nor an ethical egoist, but someone who has withdrawn from moral judgment altogether - reading his terse 'As you wish' to Vader and his insuring of Han's survival purely for payment as evidence. Through Michael Walzer's account of the soldier's constrained choice and the 'good mercenary' debate, he asks whether mercenary violence (Blackwater, private military contractors) really differs morally from a conscript's or clone's. The upshot is that Fett's grayness between Empire and Rebellion exposes amoralism as a surprisingly central part of political and military life.

moral-relativism.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
moral-relativism.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.

moral-relativism.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
moral-relativism.title: Notes
moral-relativism.relation: DeVan uses Rand's marriage to Aviendha, Elayne, and Min (and Jordan's own two-girlfriend anecdote) to survey ethical frameworks on polyamory, arguing the answer depends on which lens one uses. Sorting love into the Greek types (ludus, eros, mania, pragma, storge, philia, agape), he runs romantic, sexual, and marital polyamory through emotivism (Ayer), ethical egoism (Ayn Rand, the Forsaken), cultural relativism and social contract (Hobbes, the Aiel), natural law and Kantian duty (the Mahabharata's Draupadi, Genesis), divine command and religion (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), and consequentialism/utilitarianism, rights, and Aristotelian/virtue ethics, invoking Cadsuane's cattle analogy and Brad Wilcox's data favoring monogamy.

moral-relativism.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
moral-relativism.title: Silver or Steel?
moral-relativism.relation: Williams and Shump contrast Witcher 3's choice design with the illusory agency of immersive sims like BioShock, where the 'Would you kindly?' twist funnels players to one canonical good ending. In White Orchard's 'On Death's Bed' the witcher potion that saves Lena melts her mind, the succubus Salma in 'Deadly Delights' may be spared as a rational being who killed in self-defense, and Keira Metz's fate at Radovid's hands or Kaer Morhen topples dominoes that reach Lambert, so that good intentions yield random or grim outcomes. Drawing silver for monsters and steel for humans becomes the chapter's metaphor: every drawn sword is a classification that may condemn the wrong target, in a world where 'good' and 'bad' are relative points on an unpredictable spectrum.

moral-relativism.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
moral-relativism.title: Seventh Hole Cheating and Gamesmanship among Amateur and Professional Golfers
moral-relativism.relation: Lumpkin argues that amateur golfers routinely cheat while professionals do not, and dissects four rationalizations amateurs use: appeal to ignorance, appeal to popularity, appeal to tradition (Callahan's 'cheating culture'), and the belief that 'no one will ever know' — a golf-course version of Plato's Ring of Gyges where invisibility dissolves restraint. Drawing on Kohlberg's stages of moral development, she claims professionals reason at higher levels because officials, peers, and disqualification (e.g., J. P. Hayes) enforce the sport's social contract, whereas amateurs face no punishment. She concludes casual golfers would do better not to keep score than to keep a 'mythical' one, earning the right to score only once they follow the rules.

moral-relativism.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
moral-relativism.title: A Darker Shade Realism in Neo-Noir
moral-relativism.relation: Jason Holt argues that realism, especially about the role values play in people's lives, is the underappreciated essence of noir, offering a working definition of noir as 'stylized crime realism.' Surveying neo-noir detectives (Harper, Chinatown's Gittes), revamped femmes fatales who get away with it (Body Heat's Matty, The Last Seduction's Bridget), morally ambiguous protagonists (To Live and Die in L.A., Manhunter), and Lynch and Tarantino, he shows how the post-Production-Code freedom lets endings ring true to life by letting the guilty escape justice. He coins the 'normativistic fallacy' as the inverse of Moore's naturalistic fallacy: inferring what is from what ought to be, arguing that mainstream cinema's poetic justice commits it while neo-noir's downbeat endings correct it, fulfilling the realism latent in classic noir.

moral-relativism.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
moral-relativism.title: Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir
moral-relativism.relation: Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.

moral-relativism.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
moral-relativism.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
moral-relativism.relation: Rodriguez-Ruiz treats Ali and The Insider as dramatizing the methodology of philosophy, especially conceptual analysis and the politics of defining social concepts. Ali's challenges to 'patriotism,' 'freedom' and his slave name, and the manipulation of 'confidential,' 'addictive' and 'tortious interference' in The Insider, show how much rides on contested definitions. Against cultural relativism, he deploys James Rachels's Elements of Moral Philosophy (there are moral facts; some rules are needed for any society to exist) and discusses conceptual analysis (Jackson, Goldman) and Schiappa's 'how ought we use X,' leaving both heroes committed to independent thinking over consensus.

moral-relativism.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
moral-relativism.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
moral-relativism.relation: D'Aries and Hirsch read Paul Thomas Anderson's Hard Eight as a neo-noir moral inversion: the aging criminal Sydney seeks atonement not through religious penance but through selfless love, rescuing John and Clementine while removing the loathsome Jimmy (who knows Sydney killed John's father). They contrast him with Melville's Bob le flambeur and Besson's The Professional, where convention demands the criminal be punished. Sydney escapes formal justice but is sentenced to a 'prison without bars' of self-loathing (the bloodstained cuff), and the authors warn that such sympathy-for-the-devil inversions verge on nihilistic moral relativism.

moral-relativism.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
moral-relativism.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
moral-relativism.relation: Conard argues that Tarantino's postmodernism makes redemption impossible in Reservoir Dogs (and Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill). Using Danto on the 'end of art', Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives', and Rorty's contingent 'vocabularies', he shows the films embrace relativism about knowledge (rearranged chronology, unreliable perspectives) and about values. Mr. Orange plays Judas and Christ; the opening tipping argument exposes moral conventions as arbitrary, so becoming a 'real person' rather than a gangster is merely being a dork rather than cool. With no metanarrative to ground it, one way of life cannot be morally superior, so redemption fails.

moral-relativism.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
moral-relativism.title: Bamboozled Philosophy through Blackface
moral-relativism.relation: Flory argues Bamboozled deliberately makes its own audience laugh at Mantan's blackface coon routines to force self-reflection on how minstrel stereotypes still shape perceptions of African Americans. He reads Pierre Delacroix's shifting defenses of the show (free speech, art, 'get over slavery,' a simple-minded 'who is to judge' moral relativism) through Charles Mills's Racial Contract and 'epistemology of ignorance,' and his self-loathing through Fanon's struggle with racialization. Flory frames Lee as an Aristotelian gadfly: like Socrates, Lee arouses appropriately proportioned righteous anger (the Golden Mean) at injustice and goads viewers to philosophize, punishing Delacroix, Manray, and the Maumaus in a Manichaean moral structure to drive home minstrelsy's dehumanizing harm.

moral-relativism.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
moral-relativism.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
moral-relativism.relation: Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.

moral-relativism.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
moral-relativism.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of TV Noir
moral-relativism.relation: Sanders's introduction argues that TV noir is an autonomous art form in which film noir's themes are aufgehoben (Hegel's term: preserved and transcended, not negated), and that noir television dramatizes philosophical questions about alienation, relativism, freedom, and meaning. He surveys the volume's arguments: Fitzgibbons on Naked City's conflation of the normal with the moral, Skoble's counterexample of moral clarity in The Fugitive (Richard Kimble), Lee's morally ambiguous John Drake in Secret Agent, and his own readings of Miami Vice's 'sunshine noir' and Crockett's merger with his undercover persona Sonny Burnett. He frames Part 2 through Sartre and Camus, contrasting their call for engagement and defiance with classic noir's passive doomed protagonists (D.O.A.'s Frank Bigelow, The Prisoner's Number 6), and applies Camus's man of revolt to Jack Bauer in 24. He also raises standing objections: Nagel's ironic alternative to Camus's scorn, the incoherence of 'nothing matters' applied to Tony Soprano, and the Foucault/Lyotard-style postmodern critique of institutional power he finds in Crime Story.

moral-relativism.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
moral-relativism.title: Naked City: The Relativist Turn in TV Noir
moral-relativism.relation: Fitzgibbons argues that when The Naked City became the hour-long Naked City in 1960, TV noir underwent a 'relativist turn': episodes like 'Ooftus Goofus,' 'To Walk Like a Lion' (Arnold Platt's sympathetic embezzlement), and 'Memory of a Red Trolley Car' (Professor Johns, who refuses to save his own life) conflate the normal with the moral and leave viewers wondering whether conventionally wrong choices 'might not have been right in some way.' He traces this message to Ruth Benedict's cultural relativism, reconstructs her difference argument (from varying moral codes, as with Protagoras's 'man is the measure') and her conceptual argument (morality as socially approved habits), and shows both are invalid, the latter resting on the false assumption that 'morality' has one real definition. He then presses three objections to cultural relativism, including that its anti-ethnocentrism claim is a disguised absolute moral claim, making the position inconsistent, and that determining cultural membership collapses it into individual relativism, which licenses absurd conclusions like a moral right to rob and kill on Tuesdays.

moral-relativism.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
moral-relativism.title: White Nights of the Soul
moral-relativism.relation: Garcia reads Insomnia as the story of a cop who has lost himself and must choose between two doppelgangers: Walter Finch, the murderer who offers amoral 'partnership' and moral anti-realism ('that ultimate taboo? It doesn't exist outside our minds'), and rookie Ellie Burr, who embodies Dormer's better past as a conscientious policeman. Against Finch's 'moral math' and Dormer's own 'the end justifies the means' rationalizations, the chapter argues that the moral value of actions lies in intentions, motives, and character—Aquinas on what makes a killing an accident, Kant on being worthy of happiness rather than securing it. Dormer's sleeplessness becomes evidence of a conscience still alive, and his struggle figures what Kierkegaard calls purity of heart, willing one thing, with Socrates's refusal to escape in the Crito as the model of integrity. In dying to protect Ellie from losing her way, Dormer regains himself through commitment to another person, the Levinasian point that personhood is fulfilled only in and through other persons.

moral-relativism.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
moral-relativism.title: 18. Dissenting Opinions
moral-relativism.relation: Framing Kim and Jimmy's clashes as a problem in the epistemology of peer disagreement, the chapter asks whether learning an epistemic peer disagrees should make you suspend judgment (the conciliatory view) or stay steadfast, using a tip-calculation dispute and their office-versus-practice compromise. It argues moral disagreements differ because we rarely count someone who disagrees on one moral question as a genuine peer, and rejects 'no fact of the matter' relativism for implying slavery could be permissible. It then reads Kim's arc, including 'Wouldn't I?', as her moral beliefs genuinely shifting toward Jimmy's, complicated by self-interested and self-deceiving reasons for holding beliefs.

moral-relativism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
moral-relativism.title: How to do Philosophy
moral-relativism.relation: Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.

moral-relativism.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
moral-relativism.title: NOTES
moral-relativism.relation: Charles Taliaferro and Dan Kastrul argue, following Aristotle's dispositional account of character, that who the castaways are is a matter of what they would do under different conditions, illustrated by Mr. Eko's circumstance-driven violence and Ben Linus's shifting good-guy/bad-guy conduct. They deploy Plato's Myth of Gyges (the ring of invisibility) to test whether characters like Sun would act justly only when watched, and, against a completely reversed morality ('an island where skinning babies is good'), they argue via Chesterton that some overriding values are non-relative, so the show never fully reverses good and evil even amid its mysteries.

moral-relativism.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
moral-relativism.title: If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where
moral-relativism.relation: George Wrisley uses Lost's morally ambiguous choices to argue that ethical subjectivism and cultural relativism collapse under scrutiny. He tests them against Sayid's shooting of young Ben (which Kate sees as murdering a child), Michael's killing of Ana Lucia, and Jacob versus the Man in Black, showing that the Argument from Disagreement does not establish that moral truth is relative. He presses three fatal consequences—infallibility of the individual or culture, the impossibility of genuine disagreement between Jacob and the Man in Black, and no room for reform like Martin Luther King Jr.'s—while invoking Socrates' wisdom of knowing that one does not know as a model of tolerant objectivism.

moral-relativism.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
moral-relativism.title: From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere
moral-relativism.relation: Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.

moral-relativism.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy
moral-relativism.title: Chapter 1 The Conscience of Huckleberry Finn
