social-contract.relation: Littmann asks what a genuinely logical creature would do and grades the Cybermen against three accounts of reason: Hobbes's self-preservation and social contract, which the survival-focused Cybermen of 'The Tenth Planet' roughly satisfy but their later wars of conquest betray; Mill's utilitarianism, whose greatest-happiness principle, higher pleasures, liberty, and individuality condemn emotion-stripping, forced 'upgrades', and uniformity; and Hume's claim that reason alone motivates nothing, under which perfectly logical but emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing at all. The upshot is that Cyberman 'logic' is incoherent — no theory of reason makes them rational.

social-contract.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
social-contract.title: Spice as the Vehicle of Power
social-contract.relation: Reads the Duniverse as Hobbes's state of nature at galactic scale: Emperor, Landsraad houses, Guild, Bene Gesserit, and Tleilaxu are rationally self-preserving factions in a war of all against all over scarce spice, where 'justice' names only what enforcement power backs and life for the losers is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' Leto II is the Leviathan—a literal 'mortal God,' half sandworm—whose spice monopoly and fusion of political with spiritual authority impose a forced peace; his assassination then shows split authority re-igniting the conflict in the Scattering and the Honored Matres. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto's hoarding both illustrate that the power to destroy a thing is absolute control over it.

social-contract.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
social-contract.title: No Matter How You Flip the Patty . .
social-contract.relation: Michael Dodge asks whether Krabs may guard the Krabby Patty formula, sorting Bikini Bottom's property into collective, communal (Jellyfish Fields) and private, and deploying the tragedy of the commons — Krabs's jellyfish-squeezing factory in 'Jellyfish Hunter' — to show why shared resources get rationally overexploited. Hobbes grounds Krabs's right in sovereign enforcement (without the law, 'Pineapple Fever''s chalk-line household collapses into animals fighting over the fridge), Locke in labor-mixing, with Krabs's identity bound to his patties since 'Help Wanted', and Hume in conventions of justice born of selfishness and scarcity. All three support Krabs's legal and moral right to his secret recipe against Plankton.

social-contract.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
social-contract.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Jason Walker argues the zombie apocalypse is a Lockean rather than Hobbesian state of nature: rights to life, liberty, and property persist without government. Rick's 'I don't think those rules apply anymore' to Andrea over the mermaid necklace is justified by Locke's spoilage and 'enough and as good' provisos - the owner is almost certainly dead and the necklace would otherwise lie forever wasted - while Morgan's house-squatting, which protects the Thompsons' home, and Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo's nursing-home defenders show self-ownership and norms at work. The counter-cases, Chris's cannibal band ('a man's gotta eat') and the Governor, who treat persons as mere means, live out Hobbes's war of all against all and are destroyed by the Lockean right to punish that victims retain.

social-contract.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
social-contract.title: The Wire and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.

social-contract.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
social-contract.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Leslie Dale Feldman reads the 1968 film's blasted opening as Hobbes's state of nature - 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' - with the Lawgiver's 'Beware the beast Man' scroll echoing Hobbes's three causes of war (competition, fear, glory) and Plato's Ring of Gyges explaining why even the 'just' man acts rightly only under compulsion, both grounding the social contract's origin story. She then casts Dr. Zaius as Alexis de Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority - erasing Taylor's writing, lobotomizing Landon, and sealing Cornelius's cave 'to spare them all the care of thinking' - with Rousseau's man 'born free; and everywhere he is in chains' behind it. The chapter also traces Rod Serling's Twilight Zone fingerprints (nuclear-war twist endings like 'Time Enough at Last,' the cave of 'The Old Man in the Cave,' Adam-and-Eve survivor pairs, the beauty reversals of 'Eye of the Beholder') and reads Taylor and Nova's westward ride through Turner's frontier thesis and Kennedy's New Frontier, holding Serling's Hobbesian pessimism and his hope in tension.

social-contract.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
social-contract.title: Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Fitzpatrick uses the social contract tradition to explain Prohibition-era Atlantic City. Hobbes's state of nature fits the gang warfare left where no Leviathan is strong enough to enforce federal law against Nucky; Locke's fits a night-watchman government overreaching into Prohibition and thereby breaking the contract, as with Nucky's illegitimate protection 'taxes'; Rousseau's noble savage corrupted by commercial society fits the Klan's pleasure in cruelty and innocent Tommy set against scheming adults. Ethical egoism frames Nucky's framing of Hans Schroeder, consequentialism the Temperance Union's cost-benefit failure, and deontology Margaret's lying campaign speech, while Marx's and Mill's view that human nature is malleable explains the season-spanning transformation of Nucky from half-gangster into 'a gangster and a half.'

social-contract.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
social-contract.title: Homeland and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Roberto Sirvent and Ian Diorio ask what the state really asks soldiers to die for: not Hobbes-and-Locke's rational social contract, since we are Heideggerian thrown into the wreckage of democracy rather than a pure founding state, but a nation that makes itself sacred. MacIntyre's charge that killing for the nation-state is 'killing for the telephone company' frames the analysis of America's civil liturgies - oaths (semper fidelis), flag ritual mirrored eerily in Brody burying Jessica's thrown Quran, saints, martyrs, and Saul pitting belief in America against belief in Allah. Augustine's civitas dei names the result: America as chosen city of God, and Islam terrifies the West because its creed claims devotion above any national flag.

social-contract.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
social-contract.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Caballeros argues that political legitimacy in Ooo runs through parenthood: Princess Bubblegum rules the citizens she created ('You made me... you are my Glob'), the Ice King is redeemed when we learn Simon protected child Marceline, and the Flame King and Hunson Abadeer forfeit standing as fathers. Using Hobbes's view that a ruler is legitimate insofar as he protects his subjects, the chapter asks whether Bubblegum's protection-cum-manipulation—sabotaging Finn to let James die, jailing Tree Trunks—still counts, and it contrasts justified rebellion (Flame Princess deposing her father, Marceline resisting Abadeer) with Lumpy Space Princess's disastrous one. Good parenting, like good government, earns obedience; bad parenting loses the crown.

social-contract.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
social-contract.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.

social-contract.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
social-contract.title: 24. Who’s Duty to Whom
social-contract.relation: Dawson asks why the Doctor sides with humans and humanoids against rational non-humanoids, testing Kant first: a logic-grounded categorical morality can count the Daleks as immoral rather than amoral (universalized slavery is incoherent), but pure reason cannot motivate Daleks or the Master, and Kant's theory absurdly condemns the Doctor's lies and his theft of the TARDIS. Hobbesian psychological egoism and the social contract fare worse - the Daleks are no co-signatories, and self-sacrifices from Katarina to the Doctor's seemingly final years on Trenzalore resist the egoist's retelling - so the chapter lands with Hume: sympathy and benevolence found morality on feeling, which explains and partly excuses the Doctor's parochial partiality for beings who resemble him, making him 'at least half-Humean.'

social-contract.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
social-contract.title: 9. Anarchy, State, and Apocalypse
social-contract.relation: Da Silva and McKendry test the political legitimacy of four post-apocalyptic governance types: the Claimers' anarchy that collapses into Joe adjudicating 'claims', the Governor's and Rick's dictatorships ('This is not a democracy anymore!'), the prison Council's representative democracy with the three questions as a quasi-constitution, and Terminus's quasi-theocratic cannibal creed ('You're the butcher or you're the cattle'). Using Hobbes's state of nature and war of all against all, hypothetical social contract, and the twin tests of power and morality, they judge even the benevolent Rick-tatorship unjust because concentrated power is fallible and unaccountable. They conclude, with Churchill, that the Council's imperfect democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others.

social-contract.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
social-contract.title: 11. Have Fun Overthrowing This Evil Government!
social-contract.relation: Gibson reads Humperdinck's fabricated-pretext war against Guilder (framing Guilder for Buttercup's murder, with Vizzini's crew as private military contractors) through Just War Theory: it fails the jus ad bellum just-cause requirement built on Augustine and Aquinas, since the war would be retribution sparked by staged wrongdoing, and contractor motives of profit compound the violation. Michael Davis's critique of the ticking-time-bomb defense then shows that Rugen's torture of Westley is exactly the 'institution of torture' whose moral cost forbids ever licensing torture, since the torturer must be trained on victims first. Finally, even Hobbes's Leviathan - the most absolutist of social contract views - requires the sovereign to protect the people's safety and administer equal justice, so Humperdinck's record makes his rule illegitimate and the storming of the castle a justified insurrection.

social-contract.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
social-contract.title: 2. Sure We’re Criminals
social-contract.relation: Malloy asks whether the two law-breaking vigilantes are criminals and whether any duty to obey the law survives scrutiny. He runs consent theory through Superman surrendering in handcuffs in Man of Steel and the Red Son Superman's residence in the USSR, uses Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's security sovereign against Locke's natural-rights limits, deploys Hume against tacit consent (Batman would never leave Gotham even in No Man's Land), and dismantles gratitude theory (the Kents' adoption involved a sacrificial choice the law cannot make) and fair play (Nozick's Batman-lottery undercuts "I'm not wearing hockey pads"). He lands near Wolff-style philosophical anarchism: Superman's constrained lawbreaking endorses the law's legitimacy while Batman treats law as one more tool in his war, making him a force of chaos.

social-contract.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
social-contract.title: 10. Lord Vetinari’s Friendly Guide to Tyranny
social-contract.relation: Alloy stages the debate over Vetinari's legitimacy as letters to the Ankh-Morpork Times: a writer channeling Hobbes defends the contracted sovereign - a 'mortal god' who cannot commit crimes and secures freedom through security - while 'the late Jeremy Bentham' judges the Patrician by the greatest good of the greatest number yet would disenfranchise golems and the 'differently-alive' dead. The anarchist Wolff Paul Roberts rebuts both, denying any right to rule, rejecting tacit consent by residence, and holding up the free golems as models of uncoerced virtue, before a final letter defends Vetinari's limited, functional government. The frame - Vetinari quietly orchestrating the whole correspondence and planning Roberts's next letter - shows tyranny curating its own philosophical defense.

social-contract.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
social-contract.title: 12. The Law of Red Rising
social-contract.relation: Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.

social-contract.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
social-contract.title: 1 Introduction
social-contract.relation: Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.

social-contract.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
social-contract.title: 3 On the Origin of the Family
social-contract.relation: The chapter compares the liberal contract theorists with Engels (building on Morgan's Ancient Society) on the origin of the patriarchal monogamous family: Hobbes derives sovereign-husbanded 'little monarchies' from a state of nature in which women are men's equals, a derivation Susan Okin shows is contradictory; Locke grounds conjugal society in a voluntary compact with the husband as 'abler and stronger' last determiner, yet leaves women excluded from the social contract; Rousseau pairs passionate economic equality with some of the most sexist writing in Western thought, including fear of wives' sexual power in Emile. Against these static philosophies Engels gives a historical-materialist account in which the overthrow of mother right - the 'world historical defeat of the female sex' - followed from private property and inheritance, turning the bourgeois wife into a proletarian or prostitute while opening 'sex love' to the propertyless, and prescribing women's return to the labor force, socialized child-care, industrialized housework and easy divorce. John Stuart Mill's Subjection of Women appears as liberalism's one exception to its sexism, and a footnote sets Firestone's biological account of patriarchy against Engels's property account.

social-contract.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
social-contract.title: 4 On the Origin of the State
social-contract.relation: Opening with Newt Gingrich's complaint that students 'don't read enough Locke' and the Chinese premier's appeal to Rousseau, the chapter compares the three contract theorists' states of nature and purposes of government: Hobbes's war of every man against every man yielding an absolute sovereign with no separation of powers, Locke's peaceful nature in which mixing labor with land creates property and money then creates inequality, so that government's 'great and chief end' is protecting property through limited, separated powers and no food stamps, and Rousseau's compassionate natural humans corrupted when the first man enclosed land, so the state was founded on fraud and a general will that should 'force him to be free' and give people food stamps. Smith then reads the actual US founding as a chaste Lockean contract 'bastardized' on race and sex - the Declaration plagiarized from Locke, Abigail Adams's 'remember the ladies' laughed off, Dred Scott, with the 14th Amendment as the de-bastardizing 'Charter of Universal Freedom' - while Engels derives the state historically from the Iroquois and Greek gens, private property and class conflict. A final section documents white supremacy inside the tradition (Kant inventing the scientific concept of race, Hegel and Hume on Black inferiority), John Stuart Mill's 'Negro Question' as the tradition's decisive anti-racist break, Locke's own entanglements with the slave trade, and Marx's condemnation of slavery as super-exploitation.

social-contract.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
social-contract.title: 18. Red vs. Blue or Both Simply Leviathan Green
social-contract.relation: Smith reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes's Leviathan: unregulated superheroes live in a state of nature where life is violent and brutish (the Stamford explosion and Scarlet Witch's Lagos miscalculation as tipping points), and the Superhuman Registration Act is the social contract - a literal signed contract on Team Iron Man - offered as the way out. He then argues both leaders act as absolute sovereigns who never sought consent: Iron Man rules through the Illuminati, enforcement squads and the Negative Zone prison, Cap through an unofficial army bound by his own rules, as Moon Knight's tirade about their ego grudge match makes plain. The war is thus two Leviathans colliding and subjugating everyone else, resolved only when Iron Man's Leviathan wins and enforces registration.

social-contract.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
social-contract.title: 19. The Superhero Challenge to State Sovereignty
social-contract.relation: Ewing argues the Sokovia Accords are at bottom about state sovereignty: via Bodin's absolute sovereign, Hobbes's war of all against all and the Leviathan's monopoly on coercion, and Habermas's account of the modern territorial state's monopoly on legitimate violence, he shows that Avengers who ignore borders and cannot be countered (Thor, Hulk, Doctor Strange, Scarlet Witch) render the state's claim to sovereignty effectively meaningless - the US can only police rogue heroes by enlisting other heroes. Since states cannot guarantee enforcement and state power itself can turn predatory (HYDRA's infiltration of SHIELD, Nazi Germany, Cap's 'agendas change' warning), he concludes that neither unchecked heroes nor unchecked states should rule, and floats democratizing superpowers to restore the sovereignty of the populace.

social-contract.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
social-contract.title: 22. A New Civil War
social-contract.relation: Horn reads Marvel's Civil War as an allegory of post-9/11 America's Patriot Act debate over security versus liberty: Iron Man takes Hobbes's side, treating unregulated superhumans as the state of nature - a 'war of every man against every man' - that the Registration Act's social contract and punishment-backed rules must end, while Captain America takes Mill's On Liberty side, insisting full freedom for human nature must not be ceded to a government that will overreach, with Spider-Man torn between the two like the American citizen. Invoking Habermas's communicative action and deliberative democracy from Between Facts and Norms, he blames the two camps for talking past each other - Cap walling himself off while Tony keeps reaching out - and prescribes genuinely open dialogue as the only bridge that can marry security and liberty before the country devolves into its own civil war.

social-contract.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
social-contract.title: 16. He’s Ethickle Rick!!!
social-contract.relation: The chapter reads the Galactic Federation as Hobbes's Sovereign: Earth covenants in for security and gets an interplanetary TSA, pill-currency debt, and the surveillance droid Conroy, while the Citadel of Ricks tours Hobbes's three commonwealths in 'The Ricklantis Mixup', aristocratic Council, brief democracy, and Evil Morty's monarchy, where the Sovereign's rules cannot by definition be unjust. Against this, Rick embodies Hobbes's psychological egoism ('the object to every man is his own pleasure'), hiding his motives in the Riq IV hostage gambit and the Szechuan-sauce confession. Yet the chapter argues Rick's egoism is oddly ethical: in an infinite multiverse resources are not scarce, so refusing to surrender freedom to any Sovereign and competing for everything is the right way to live, with 'A Rickle in Time' and the self-sacrifice of 'The Wedding Squanchers' as its tested limits.

social-contract.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
social-contract.title: A Closer Look at Alice’s Trial
social-contract.relation: Argues Alice is right to attack the court of the King and Queen of Hearts because she never entered a social contract with Wonderland: unlike Socrates, who stayed in Athens and so had to abide by the verdict (Plato's Crito), Alice fell in involuntarily and is trying to leave. Dennis Knepp casts the Queen of Hearts as Hobbes's absolute sovereign whose public 'Off with their heads!' terrorizes the playing cards into obedience ('Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words'), while Locke's limited, consent-based government and Rawls's contractualism mark the better alternative the Hearts court fails to meet. Since Alice stands outside their covenant, she is her own more-than-a-mile-high Leviathan, rightly defending herself in the state of nature.

social-contract.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
social-contract.title: A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World
social-contract.relation: Lin argues the Bending World's supernatural inequality breaks Hobbes's condition that even the weakest can kill the strongest, the equality that motivates the social contract, so might-is-right is magnified: Ozai rules without bargaining while weak Earth Kings become Dai Li figureheads. Energybending's built-in 'moral self-destruct' needs no earthly accountability, resembling the divine right of kings rather than Arendt's insight that violence eradicates politics, and Aang wisely remains a passive guardian. The Avatar's reincarnation creates recurring power vacuums, and because bending is a non-redistributable endowment, the Equalist revolution haunts the Bending World like the specter of communism in the Communist Manifesto.

social-contract.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
social-contract.title: A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World
social-contract.relation: Lin uses Hobbes's observation that in our world the weakest can kill the strongest, grounding the social contract, to show what breaks when supernatural power is wildly unequal: Fire Lord Ozai need not bargain with generals as Earth Kings must with the Dai Li, and the eclipse is the only equalizer. Energybending gets a 'moral self-destruct' that no real technology has, making Aang an unaccountable guardian closer to the divine right of kings than to naturalist politics, though his refusal of rule keeps politics alive in Arendt's sense. Like Marx and Engels's specter of communism, the 'specter of Equalism' outlives Amon, because bending is a non-redistributable, lethal endowment, so democracy in Republic City is structurally haunted.

social-contract.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
social-contract.title: The Thin Veil
social-contract.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads the No Man's Land storyline, in which earthquake-isolated Gotham is carved into gang territories by Two-Face, Penguin, and the Joker, alongside Hurricane Katrina's flooding of New Orleans as twin real-and-fictional tests of Hobbes's state of nature and the social contract. He contrasts Jim Gordon's lawful, Machiavellian-seeming rebuilding of trust with Officer William Petit's slide into execution-style 'despotic' power, and highlights the pacifist witness of Father Christian and Dr. Leslie Thompkins against Hobbes's demand that churches defer to the sovereign. Batman's turn as a benevolent gang lord working to hand the city back to Gordon shows, for Patterson, that Batman's real enemy is anarchy itself.

social-contract.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
social-contract.title: Theorizing Government
social-contract.relation: Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive. Working from Max Weber's definition of the state as monopoly on legitimate violence, Hobbes's Leviathan, and Nietzsche's state as 'new idol,' he reads Year One's corrupt Commissioner Loeb, Year Two's self-appointed Reaper, Anarky's failed anarchist dystopia, Two-Face's broken faith in the law, and The Dark Knight Returns' state-loyal Superman and Commissioner Yindel. The Batman-Gordon partnership emerges as a precarious unofficial order in which Gordon tolerates the one exception to the state's monopoly on violence.

social-contract.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
social-contract.title: Walking the Tightrope
social-contract.relation: Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.

social-contract.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
social-contract.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: The Bocks test three answers to the good life against the show: Howard as hedonist (laser-obstacle-strip-chess, the 'whore of Omaha') read through Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, and Aristippus; ethical egoism via Glaucon's ring of Gyges and Howard's offer to Skype rather than visit the deported Raj; and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract read into Sheldon's roommate agreement, whose lack of a Hobbesian sovereign leaves 'I settle all ties' arbitrary and rule-following too thin for ethics. Aristotle's virtue and practical wisdom crown Leonard — the nucleus of the social group, as Amy says — as the closest thing to the phronimos. The gang's sabotage of Dennis Kim with a manufactured girlfriend closes the chapter by asking who really ruined whose life.

social-contract.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
social-contract.title: 8 T’Challa, the Revolutionary King Legitimation Crises in Wakanda
social-contract.relation: Porter uses Habermas's legitimation crisis to read Killmonger's reign: by governing flagrantly against Wakandan tradition — burning the Heart-Shaped Herb, waving off the unfinished challenge ritual with 'All that challenge shit is over with. I'm the king now' — he erodes not just his own standing but acceptance of kingship itself, moving Okoye from procedural objection to 'you are not fit to be a king.' He then argues the film inoculates monarchy against viewer critique through Shuri's permissible teasing and Wakanda's harmonizing of opposites, and shows that T'Challa's UN speech, matched line-by-line to Bossuet's defense of the divine right of kings, quietly reaches toward absolutism — leaving audiences cheering a hereditary, divinely sanctioned throne that Locke's consent of the governed would never legitimate in their own world.

social-contract.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
social-contract.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Torosyan argues The Daily Show models the critical thinking and good-faith civic discourse that real politics and TV news lack, reading John Oliver's 'Civil Disservice' interview with Froma Harrop and Stewart's clips of Rumsfeld contradicting himself on WMDs as exposing bullshit in Frankfurt's sense: assertion indifferent to truth. Stewart's reframing of William Bennett's gay-marriage talking points (is the debate about marriage or about who counts as human?) and his self-effacing interviews with Ramesh Ponnuru enact Rousseau's social-contract ideal of what news owes the public against Machiavellian ends-justify-means manipulation. Gadamer supplies the demand that Bennett question his own horizons, Nietzsche's Apollonian-Dionysian account of tragedy frames the show's satire, and the Tao Te Ching's 'let yourself be partial' governs the whole chapter.

social-contract.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
social-contract.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Vanderheiden treats America (The Book)'s textbook parody as serious democratic theory: its 'Democracy Inaction' diagnosis (a president chosen from a field of two, 99% incumbency, lobbyists as 'the white knights of democracy') tracks the thin versus thick democracy distinction and Benjamin Barber's deliberative democracy, with Putnam's social capital as the remedy for the satirized life cycle of national decline. The 'Dress the Supreme Court' gag, Senate color-by-numbers, and third-party graveyard expose representational exclusion, while the media chapter indicts conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role, invoking Mill's marketplace of ideas. The Earth (The Book) postscript notes that social contracts were historically written without the assent of the women and minorities they subjugated.

social-contract.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
social-contract.title: “Real Life Is Messy”
social-contract.relation: The chapter tests Zootopia's 'where anyone can be anything' against three ideals: the founding play's predator-prey war is a Hobbesian state of nature ('man is a wolf to man') pacified by social order; Judy's parking duty and Nick's 'you can only be what you are' expose how stereotyping confuses artificial barriers with real biological limits to self-determination; and the evolved end of predation frames a just multispecies society, read through Donaldson and Kymlicka's Zoopolis case for animal citizenship. Nussbaum's hint at 'the gradual supplanting of the natural by the just' is weighed against the dystopia of turning the wild into a world-sized zoo, leaving Zootopia aspirational rather than achieved.

social-contract.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
social-contract.title: “Look at This Stuff; Isn't It Neat ” disney and the Commodification of Political Values
social-contract.relation: Dale and Foy tour the parks' political philosophy: Cinderella's Castle looming over Liberty Square embodies the contradiction between princess hierarchy and Lockean self-government, since Locke's Second Treatise grounds rule in consent and majority will, forbids special rights for rulers, and justifies revolution — the very ideals the 'Declaration salad' celebrates under a monarchy's silhouette. The Epcot World Showcase, judged through Kymlicka, Benhabib, and Taylor's recognition-based multiculturalism, reduces eleven cultures to a consumable menu, so that per Barber's 'McWorld' Disney sells pre-packaged 'freedom' and 'multiculturalism' as spectator values that reinforce rather than transform.

social-contract.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
social-contract.title: Spice as the Vehicle of Power
social-contract.relation: Maps Hobbes's state of nature onto the Duniverse: the Emperor, Landsraad, Guild, Bene Gesserit and Tleilaxu are rational agents in a war of all against all over the scarce good of spice, where justice is meaningless until a supreme power enforces covenants. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto II's monopoly on a hoarded supply show how power over the resource itself becomes the trump card that forces peace, with the Fremen refusing to kill Stilgar illustrating the rational turn from mutual weakening to peace. Leto II, the half-sandworm 'mortal god' who fuses civil and spiritual sovereignty so that breaking law becomes sin, is presented as Hobbes's Leviathan, whose tyranny is 'quite literally, the best thing to happen to mankind.'

social-contract.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
social-contract.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Ted Henry Brown and Christie Maloyed stage the Enderverse as the international-relations debate between Hobbesian realism — Graff's 'if one of us has to be destroyed...' and the human-bugger Prisoner's Dilemma where the absence of communication forces mutual defection and war — and liberal institutionalism, which Peter's Locke and Valentine's Demosthenes argue out on Earth's nets. Machiavelli supplies Peter's theory of power: fortune opens the moment, virtù seizes it with 'the right words at the right time,' and force must back persuasion when belief fades, so that 'influence is power' and governing by persuasion beats fiat.

social-contract.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: John Irish reads the Amazon series' Vault 33 as Locke's Two Treatises staged and then betrayed: Overseer elections (Betty Pearson against Reg McPhee and Woody Thomas), town-council deliberation over captured Vault 32 raiders, and Lucy's 1950s-styled domesticity all mimic natural equality, consent of the governed, majority rule, and the preservation of property. Norm's discovery that every election is rigged in favor of cryo-preserved technocrats from Vault 31, that Lucy's marriage 'application' is engineered population control, and that Vault-Tec executives - including Lucy's mother Barb - voted to launch the Great War itself shows Locke's forms of consent, law, and rights preserved as empty ceremony. The chapter's argument is that Enlightenment liberalism stripped of transparency becomes authoritarian experiment management: consent becomes choreography in a commonwealth that is really a lab, right down to composting the raiders' bodies.

social-contract.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
social-contract.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Greg Littmann asks what sort of life is worth living by holding Final Fantasy protagonists and FFXI Online players up to three standards. Hobbes's egoism and defense of absolute monarchy condemn the altruistic, authority-defying heroes (AVALANCHE, the rebels of FFII and FFVI) while partly approving the gil-grubbing, rule-breaking FFXI player; Mill's utilitarianism praises the world-saving heroes but condemns grinding down beastmen and rates most gaming a lower pleasure; Aristotle's function argument and golden mean find heroes like Yuna immoderately self-sacrificial yet credit ordinary FFXI adventurers with genuinely virtuous moderation, helping others while keeping their own interests in view.

social-contract.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
social-contract.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Greg Littmann asks who should rule Westeros and answers with Hobbes's Leviathan: people act only from self-interest ('we are all Lord Littlefinger under the skin') and fight for gain, safety, and glory - the mountain clans, Robert's preemptive strike on Daenerys, Drogo's wars for pride - so without a sovereign life is a war of all against all, and only an absolute ruler makes oath-keeping self-interested. Mapping Hobbes's own civil war (the Stuarts onto the Targaryens), he argues that even Varys is right to serve 'the realm' and peace by betraying Ned, and that loyalty rightly transfers from Aerys to Robert to Joffrey because protection, not lineage or justice, is the point of the sovereign. He then criticizes Hobbes: Ned and Jon show people really do die for principle, and Mad King Aerys's overcentralized power left rebellion as the only remedy - the War of the Five Kings shows civil war's horror must be weighed against appeals to honor.

social-contract.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
social-contract.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: David Hahn contends Ned died because of his honor, not for it. Hobbes explains why: words bind no one without fear of enforcement - Cersei ripping up Robert's will ('Is this meant to be your shield, Lord Stark?') exposes Ned's belief that allegiance alone secures the King's Justice - and the Iron Throne itself is a Leviathan, forged by Aegon's dragons ending the state of nature, whose force rather than justice holds the peace. Machiavelli supplies the indictment of Ned's idealism: 'we who presume to rule must do vile things for the good of the realm,' so Ned's refusal to assassinate Daenerys, his merciful warning to Cersei, and backing the rightful but war-prone Stannis over Renly cost him his head and plunged the realm into civil war; the security of the state demanded exiling or killing the Lannisters and crowning Renly.

social-contract.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
social-contract.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Joffrey on the Iron Throne, immune from punishment for beheading Ned, is read as Glaucon's ring of Gyges made flesh: the chapter asks what reason he has to be moral when he can get away with everything, noting he lacks even Gyges's advantage of secrecy and is hated like the Mad King. Hobbes's social contract is considered and rejected as a motive for Joffrey - King's Landing is no Hobbesian community like the Night's Watch, and Joffrey does better free-riding on everyone else's morality. The Platonic answer carries the chapter: like Ned Stark, who refused the throne, lived honorably in Winterfell, and regretted trading his honor at Baelor, the just person with an ordered soul has the only genuine happiness, which Joffrey's desire-satisfying cruelty forfeits.

social-contract.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
social-contract.title: NOTES
social-contract.relation: Sharp argues that superpowered individuals break the equality assumption on which social contract theory rests: since Claire cannot be killed, D.L. can walk out of any jail, and Matt can sway juries, Hobbes's fear-of-death rationale for the contract seems not to apply to them. He then answers that the heroes remain effectively equal (Claire can still be killed by a wood splinter, Adam by decapitation) and shares Locke's and Rawls's reasons for contract, yet shows Rawls's difference principle would force the powered to serve society while the liberty principle forbids it, and that Sylar could not even be morally condemned under a pure Hobbesian reading. Cases like Claude's invisible petty theft (Glaucon's Ring of Gyges made real), the 'Five Years Gone' registered-superhumans future, and Linderman's plot to reunite society through the New York explosion lead to the conclusion that superpowers really would break society.

social-contract.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Casts Frank as the 'Foole' of Leviathan chapter 15 — the man who grants that covenants exist but thinks injustice can 'stand with reason' — and documents his befriend-then-betray pattern: Russo groomed for governor then gassed in his car, Zoe fed stories then pushed under a train, Walker befriended, helped and maneuvered into resigning, all to reap the contract's benefits while breaking it for 'the getting of a kingdom'. The chapter then defends Hobbes' reply via Kavka: the Foole's vainglory makes him overestimate his ability to deceive, and a detailed audit of Frank's two murders (fingerprints, witnesses, electronic traces, forensic evidence, alibis, high-stakes deception 'tells') shows them contingency-riddled and irrational. Even Frank's success is no defense — his presidency rests on others' errors and luck (Skorsy, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and above all Claire all remain loose ends), so he exemplifies the vainglorious Foole acting against the reason of his preservation rather than a rational violator of the social contract.

social-contract.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Courtland uses Hobbes's 'Foole' from Leviathan — who grants that covenants exist but insists injustice 'may sometimes stand with reason' — as the template for Frank, who enjoys the benefits of the social contract (security, cooperation, even Freddy's BBQ) while befriending and betraying Russo, Zoe, and Walker up to outright murder. Applying Hobbes's reply, the chapter audits both murders as contingency-ridden blunders — fingerprints, witnesses, cameras, forensic evidence, and the 'tells' of high-stakes deception — and diagnoses Frank's confidence as the vainglory behind Kavka's 'Foole's gold.' Even his success proves nothing: in the Latin Leviathan a fortunate outcome of reckless action is still imprudence, and his 'kingdom' rests on loose ends (Skorsky, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and Claire) that could bring the house of cards down.

social-contract.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Michels reads Frank as 'Hobbesian to the core' and democracy as 'the state of nature with elections': Walker, Matthews, and Vasquez show that elections elevate mediocrities, while Frank's America Works and his FEMA/Stafford Act end-run around Congress display the energetic sovereign for whom 'a tyrant is only a king disliked.' Hobbes's pleasure-pain psychology of appetite and aversion explains the cast — Frank's ribs, PlayStation, and pure taste for power; Russo's indiscriminate addictions; Doug's serial ones — while Hobbes's competition for gain, fear, and glory structures the Tusk money-versus-power war whose casualties include Freddy. With Hobbes's subordination of religion to civil power, Frank's crucifix-spitting 'I pray to myself, for myself' caps the case that truth only obstructs sovereignty, leaving Madison's 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' as the lone check.

social-contract.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
social-contract.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.

social-contract.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
social-contract.title: Selling Ol’ Shellhead
social-contract.relation: Malloy uses Spymaster's theft of Stark's armor designs in the Armor Wars and the U.S. government's legally valid appropriation of the technology after Tony announces 'I am Iron Man' to test two theories of property. Locke's natural-law view makes the designs an extension of Stark's laboring self — stealing them is like taking an arm — while Hume's social-contract view treats property as a useful convention whose violation makes the thief an enemy of society itself, and Rousseau supplies the cautionary image of the first man who fenced ground and said 'This is mine.' A closing thought experiment in which Tony sells Iron Man outright (like Siegel and Schuster selling Superman) argues that intellectual property can never be fully alienated: whoever wore the armor, Tony would still be Iron Man.

social-contract.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Skoble argues the Mad Max world is misread as anarchy: Immortan Joe, Aunty Entity, and Humungus are genuine rulers, so the Wasteland depicts tyrannical bad government, not 'no rulers'. Against Hobbes's claim that only fear of a sovereign produces order, he cites organically evolved order (medieval merchant law, the common law, private arbitration firms) and Locke's mere 'inconveniences' of statelessness to argue peaceful anarchism is possible and stable. Thunderdome's 'two men enter, one man leaves' shows the films' dispute resolution is power-based trial by combat, not the consent-based voluntary order anarchism envisions.

social-contract.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Spanakos and Drake argue that although the films look Hobbesian — life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' on roads without guardrails — rule in the Wasteland is never sustained by violence alone. Humungus needs the Toadie's epithets ('Lord Humungus... the Ayatollah of Rock and Rolla') and Immortan Joe rules through water rituals and the Valhalla myth that send War Boys kamakrazee willingly, believing they pursue their own glory. Drawing Weber's power/authority distinction, Arendt on power as people acting in concert, and above all Byung-Chul Han, they argue power takes its place 'in the soul of the other' through ritual, habit, and titles, turning into violence only when mediation fails.

social-contract.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Littmann treats Hobbes's Leviathan as a survival manual for post-apocalyptic Australia: the films illustrate his three causes of conflict — resource wars over guzzoline and water, preemptive strikes, and glory (the Nightrider's radio rant, Wez's stunts, the War Boys' 'Witness me!'). Bartertown's Thunderdome covenant and 'bust a deal, face the wheel' exemplify the social contract enforced by an absolute sovereign like Aunty Entity, while divided power (Master Blaster versus Aunty) courts civil war. He concludes Hobbes errs twice: Max's selfless acts (sparing Blaster, transfusing Furiosa) refute psychological egoism, and concentrating power in an Immortan Joe invites the very violence it fears — democracy removes leaders without blood.

social-contract.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
social-contract.title: NOTES
social-contract.relation: Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.

social-contract.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
social-contract.title: NOTES
social-contract.relation: Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.

social-contract.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
social-contract.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.

social-contract.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
social-contract.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
social-contract.relation: Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.

social-contract.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Alkema and Barkman put Q himself on trial, asking what justifies his judgment of humanity in 'Encounter at Farpoint' and Trelane's of Kirk in 'The Squire of Gothos'. Hobbes's Leviathan would license Q's might-makes-right sovereignty over a savage species, but Q lacks humanity's consent and cannot show he acts for future peace; Locke's natural law instead binds even nearly omnipotent beings, as Janeway's asylum ruling for the suicidal Quinn in 'Death Wish' demonstrates. Q's repeated self-sacrifice—in 'Deja Q' and the Continuum's civil war—reveals a conscience answerable to natural law rather than raw power.

social-contract.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Littmann shows Luke, Leia, and Han repeatedly put friends and family above the galaxy's freedom - Luke abandoning Dagobah for Bespin, the Jabba rescue, refusing to kill Vader - in the tradition of Homer's heroes, then submits them to Athenian scrutiny. Socrates's refusal to escape his Athens prison and his implicit just agreement with the city set civic duty over friendship; Plato would abolish the guardians' family and censor the Zeus-Kronos patricide myth yet approves of Luke sparing Vader; Aristotle prizes philia but holds citizens belong to the state. He concludes the philosophers mostly win: heroic loyalty is often moral failure, and good moral reasoning asks how many people an action affects, not just whom you love.

social-contract.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
social-contract.title: “Wherever I Go, He Goes”
social-contract.relation: Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.

social-contract.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_
social-contract.title: 2. Sure We’re Criminals
social-contract.relation: Alloy uses the problem of political obligation to split the heroes: against Plato's Crito, where Socrates refuses escape because even bad laws bind, Bruce Wayne simply flees arrest in Bruce Wayne: Murderer?/Fugitive, treating law as a tool of his war. He tests consent theory through Superman's chosen handcuffs in Man of Steel and Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's 'mortal god' versus Locke's natural-rights standard, lets Hume's objection sink tacit consent (Red Son Superman cannot really emigrate, and Batman would never leave Gotham), rejects gratitude theory via the Kents' adoption of Kal-El, and dismantles Batman's 'I'm not wearing hockey pads' defense with Nozick's Batman-lottery — concluding Superman's law-conforming restraint protects the public from him becoming Luthor's 'alien overlord', while answerable-to-no-one Batman remains a force of chaos.

social-contract.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
social-contract.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.

social-contract.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
social-contract.title: NOTES
social-contract.relation: Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.

social-contract.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
social-contract.title: NOTES
social-contract.relation: Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.

social-contract.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
social-contract.title: NOTES
social-contract.relation: Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.

social-contract.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
social-contract.title: “That Community’s a Lot More Wholesome and Functional than, Just for Example, Neptune Is”
social-contract.relation: Paul Hammond asks whether Veronica's habitual lawbreaking — switching the evidence tapes in the 'Pilot,' stealing Duncan's medical file, tricking Principal Van Clemmons — can be morally justified. He constructs a social-contract defense: Neptune's corrupt, class- and race-skewed sheriff's department under Don Lamb has failed to deliver the protection and justice that purchase citizens' obedience, releasing Veronica from her end of the bargain. Testing that defense against the Laws' speech in Plato's Crito (lawbreaking destroys the city; staying in Athens constitutes consent) and Kant's requirement that genuine law be universal, he concludes that where Neptune's civil law diverges from the moral law, Veronica's crimes can rise to a civil disobedience that is sometimes 'really just.'

social-contract.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
social-contract.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
social-contract.relation: Jason Walker pits Hobbes against Locke over whether Andrea may take the mermaid necklace when Rick says 'I don't think those rules apply anymore'. He reads the survivors' conduct—Andrea's single necklace under Locke's spoilage proviso, Morgan squatting in and fixing up the neighbors' house, Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo—as a Lockean state of nature where self-ownership and property rights persist without government, while Chris's cannibal band and the Governor embody the Hobbesian war of all against all, treating persons as mere means. The Lockean right to punish, exercised brutally by Grimes's group on Chris's hunters, vindicates rights even by Hobbes's own demand for enforcement.

social-contract.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
social-contract.title: Notes
social-contract.relation: Christensen and Holmes read the Third Age as Hobbes's state of nature, a postlapsarian chaos following the Breaking where Lews Therin's prideful attempt at purified sovereignty destroyed the Leviathan of the Age of Legends. They argue channeling the One Power is morally neutral power that only becomes sovereignty through practice, and that the Aes Sedai model Hobbesian order through their seven Ajah and, above all, the Three Oaths. Drawing heavily on Giorgio Agamben's Homo Sacer and The Sacrament of Language, they treat oaths and curses as the 'sacraments of power' founding sovereignty on the trustworthiness of the logos, using Moiraine's New Spring investiture to show how language itself binds and confers authority.

social-contract.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
social-contract.title: King Foltest, John Locke, and the Social Contract
social-contract.relation: Irish tests King Foltest's rule over Temeria against Locke's Two Treatises of Government: against Filmer's patriarchal divine right and Bodin's absolute sovereignty, Locke's political voluntarism holds that legitimate rule rests on the consent of free and equal subjects and exists to protect their lives, liberties, and property. Foltest's inherited throne lacks any social contract, and his edict protecting the striga Adda - the daughter born of his incest with his sister, who preys on Wyzim's citizens - breaches the Lockean sovereign trust. The Netflix 'Betrayer Moon' miners' uprising becomes a Lockean revolution: after 'a long train of abuses' the people may reclaim the sovereign power and even remove the king, so long as the new authority restores consent and the public good.

social-contract.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
social-contract.title: What Would Machiavelli Do
social-contract.relation: Reitsma treats the refereeless pickup game as a Lockean state of nature and asks how to beat the 'strategic ticky-tacker' who calls phantom fouls to win. He condemns first-strike cheating as wrong on Kantian grounds (the cheat 'makes an exception of himself') and by an ideal of Homeric athletic honor, then asks whether retaliatory ticky-tacking is justified. Reading Machiavelli's 'dirty hands' argument alongside Locke's claim that in a state of nature each person may punish transgressors, he concludes proportionate tit-for-tat cheating can make one a legitimate 'agent of justice' when no referee exists.

social-contract.book: 217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
social-contract.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
social-contract.relation: Flynn contends certain Westerns depict a 'law that stands behind the law' — a moral/natural law transcending and grounding the weak civil order — using High Noon, where Hadleyville proves unworthy of Kane's rectitude. High Plains Drifter evolves this into divine, supernatural retribution: the nameless Stranger, a pale-horse agent of apocalyptic justice, precisely punishes Lago for abetting the marshal Duncan's murder (whipping the whippers, renaming the town Hell). Flynn argues this vision is dangerous: by insulating justice from deliberation and depicting it as revelatory and divine, it derides the discursive, civil processes (Habermas-style communicative action) actually needed to make justice 'ours,' risking mere private vengeance — 'deserve's got nothin' to do with it.'

social-contract.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
social-contract.title: Justice, Power, and Love The Political Philosophy of Intolerable Cruelty
social-contract.relation: Biderman and Devlin trace Intolerable Cruelty through three theories of justice enacted by divorce attorney Miles Massey and femme fatale Marylin. 'Justice as power' is Thrasymachus's 'advantage of the stronger' and Machiavelli's might-makes-right, seen in Miles's courtroom war-room rhetoric and teeth imagery and in Marylin's plan to 'nail his ass' via marriage. 'Justice as compromise' is Hobbes's social contract escaping the state of nature, but the film shows the Massey pre-nup's signing and tearing to be merely a mask for power. When Miles and Marylin genuinely fall in love, their indifference to each other's wealth becomes a Rawlsian veil of ignorance and difference principle—justice as fairness—though the cynical Funniest Divorce Videos ending leaves that victory unguaranteed.

social-contract.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
social-contract.title: Ethics, Heart, and Violence in Miller’s Crossing
social-contract.relation: Herling reads Miller's Crossing through Hume's moral psychology of passion versus reason, arguing the film's dominant 'ethics' (voiced by Johnny Caspar) is Hobbes's social contract plus Thrasymachus's advantage-of-the-stronger and Plato's 'do good to friends, harm to enemies'—a relativism of power that Tom Reagan navigates by cool calculation. 'Heart,' the capacity for sympathetic attachment Hume makes the real basis of morality, keeps breaking through: Tom spares the pleading Bernie ('Look in your heart') at Miller's Crossing, and his loyalty to Leo secretly drives his 'plays.' But Bernie's betrayal, the surreal sympathy-crushing violence (the beatings, Leo's tommy-gun ballet, Caspar shooting the faceless Dane), and Leo and Verna's reunion steel Tom into lonely noir stoicism—'What heart?'—when he finally executes Bernie without mercy.

social-contract.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
social-contract.title: The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese
social-contract.relation: Skoble uses Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle to probe when vigilantism is justified, invoking Locke's claim that in civil society individuals delegate private vengeance to the state for objectivity. He argues Travis's rescue of the trapped child prostitute Iris is legitimate (the police won't help, she can't help herself) while his plan to assassinate Senator Palantine is madness, drawing the key line between correctly identifying a deserving target and mere perceived evil (contrasting Travis with Death Wish's Kersey, Batman, and Klan lynch mobs). He closes with Socrates' 'unexamined life' as the remedy: contemplating justice so we can confront real badness rather than turn away.

social-contract.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
social-contract.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
social-contract.relation: Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.

social-contract.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
social-contract.title: Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still
social-contract.relation: Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.

social-contract.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
social-contract.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
social-contract.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.

social-contract.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
social-contract.title: Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma
social-contract.relation: Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.

social-contract.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
social-contract.title: “Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature
social-contract.relation: Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.

social-contract.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
social-contract.title: Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West
social-contract.relation: Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.

social-contract.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
social-contract.title: “They Turned to a Man They Didn’t Fully Understand”
social-contract.relation: Foy and Dale argue that the Dark Knight trilogy endorses a conservative critique of liberal democracy: Batman taps every citizen's phone, tortures criminals, and kidnaps Lau from Hong Kong because Gotham's institutions cannot cope with a permanent state of crisis. Hume's conservatism—authority resting on habit and order rather than abstract rights and consent—explains Batman's defense of the existing order against Ra's al Ghul's razing of Gotham, while Schmitt's sovereign who declares the 'state of exception' frames Batman as the extra-legal protector who suspends rights during crisis (with Rachel's Caesar warning marking the danger). Against Locke's natural rights and Rawls's inviolability of the person, the Joker and Bane dramatize Strauss's twin fears that liberalism degenerates into nihilistic value-chaos or coercive revolutionary equality, and Burke's natural aristocracy of 'virtual representation' justifies relying on an unchosen elite hero. The trilogy's central puzzle is Batman's illiberal means—taking the blame for Dent's death to preserve the White Knight myth—dirtying his hands so that Gotham's official powers stay clean.

social-contract.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
social-contract.title: This Is the Age of Steel
social-contract.relation: Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.

social-contract.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
social-contract.title: 9. God the Programmer Is Dead
social-contract.relation: De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.

social-contract.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
social-contract.title: 13. Does God Have the Right to Destroy the Universe
social-contract.relation: Foresman asks whether Chuck has a negative right to destroy the multiverse, rejecting the question-begging 'God can do whatever God wants' and the bare creation/ownership argument (using the scrambled-eggs example) as insufficient. Drawing on Locke's Two Treatises—property arises from mixing labor, but even in the state of nature one may not destroy a creature except for a 'nobler use,' and hoarding beyond use is illegitimate—he concludes Chuck is a Lockean tyrant destroying universes he could simply recreate, so Sam and Dean's rebellion is justified.

social-contract.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
social-contract.title: 14. Revolting Punks
