On the dominant Western view - Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellect, Kantian dignity against Singer's speciesism challenge - walkers lack intelligence and so are not persons, so Morgan should shoot. They then argue walkers are metaphysically impossible beings, square-circles: dead tissue that somehow sees, smells, and runs down prey without functioning organs, energy intake, or the reanimated neocortex that movement and sensation require. Zombies fascinate because they are projections of our fears - dead yet moving, an afterlife of horror - a Hamlet-like caught-between-being-and-nonbeing.

personal-identity.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
personal-identity.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Dave Beisecker amplifies Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why would anyone enjoy watching, let alone compete for, AMC's 'stagger-on role' as a repulsive walker? Curiosity fails as an answer, since by Nagel's bat argument no amount of staggering around a set tells us what it is like to be a zombie - and since zombification destroys memory, desire, and self-concern, we would not survive it as persons in any interesting sense anyway. His solution is that zombies are the endearing losers and clowns of the undead world: playing one is a way to celebrate our inner awkward nerd and laugh at universal human ineptitude, which is exactly why Kirkman's shambling walkers, unlike fast zombies or glamorous vampires, invite impersonation.

personal-identity.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
personal-identity.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Silcox recalls his middle-school Paladin dying to eighty-three orcs while his friends held a memorial service, and asks whether grief for a player character is irrational. He tests Charles Taylor's narrative ethics—the thesis that we grasp our lives as unfolding stories—finding it challenged by Beckett's Godot, the novel-within-a-novel of Atonement, and Samantha Vice's warnings about story-shaped lives, and he notes leveling up and 4E's heroic PCs make characters story-like in ways ordinary lives are not. Ultimately PC death differs from real death because the campaign's story continues without the character, whereas death, as Nagel argues, cuts off our open-ended future; Silcox ends by recasting the self as a 'back-story' or metanarrative that enables storytelling, rejecting Descartes' claim that the power of imagination is inessential to our essence.

personal-identity.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
personal-identity.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Monica Evans argues that D&D is identity play in which players explore who they are through characters they create, perform and try to keep alive, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to ask whether a character re-rolled under a new edition, or replayed by another player, is still 'the same' character. She tests theories of the player-character bond (Gee's virtual, real and projective identities; Fine and Worch's 'identity bubble') on Wil Wheaton's Avenger Aeofel, whose in-character oath made Wheaton split the party and lose him rather than metagame. Bartle's four player types and the bulette-knowledge example show how each player manages the line between what they know and what their character knows, in a shared fiction where a glorious failure can be better than winning.

personal-identity.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
personal-identity.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Jeopardy! champion Ken Jennings argues that the silly answer-in-the-form-of-a-question conceit is the engine of the show's appeal, because it turns every topic, even Belgium, into a fractal of surprising factual connections rather than a dull definition. He defends the old-school internalization of facts in a Google age - champions are congenitally curious 'sponges' whose stored knowledge makes them better citizens and thinkers - and speculates that what we call the Self is largely the accumulation of facts in one's head. His philosophy of the show in a nutshell: do not just answer in the form of a question, live your life in the form of a question.

personal-identity.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
personal-identity.title: Psych and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.

personal-identity.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
personal-identity.title: Futurama and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Jenkins asks what makes Bender Bender when Leela still recognizes him as the walnut-panelled steam robot of 'Obsoletely Fabulous.' Scruffy's progressively repaired conference table stages the Ship of Theseus problem and the same body theory, while the Roboticon 'Soul Detector' (Fry sets it off, robots pass through) rules out Descartes' same soul theory for robots. Episodes from 'Anthology of Interest II' and 'The Honking' to 'The Prisoner of Benda' mind swap and Roberto's instant 1-X re-education support Locke's psychological continuity: Bender persists through an overlapping chain of memories and traits stored on his hard drive - 'Everything that is Bender is right here' - which is why an empathic, ascetic Bender ('The old Bender is gone') threatens his very identity.

personal-identity.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
personal-identity.title: Futurama and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Williams uses Hermes's slide from chest-harpoon to extendo-arm to Cylon eye to full robot body in 'The Six Million Dollar Mon' - until Zoidberg's 'Monster Mash' surgery restores his brain to Li'l Hermes - to ask what makes a person themselves under voluntary enhancement. The 'Ship of Planet Express' and the seven-year cell-replacement fact recast the Ship of Theseus, exposing our terror of upgrades as inconsistent with our constant physical change, while the therapeutic-versus-enhancement line (medical steroids vs doping, Aimee Mullins's blades) explains why Hermes's chosen upgrades disturb us. Cartesian interactionist dualism predicts Mecha-Hermes stays the same person, yet his personality shifts with his parts, so the chapter turns to physicalism and lands on functionalism: Hermes persists through each swap until the Roberto brain-chip replaces the brain that houses his memories and motivations.

personal-identity.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
personal-identity.title: Futurama and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Micic uses Fry's hundred-cups-of-coffee rescue in 'Three Hundred Big Boys' - a mysterious orange blur to onlookers while Fry calmly watches each cork pop - and the chronoton time skips of 'Time Keeps on Slippin'' as breaks in experience that Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit explains better than Descartes. Against the cogito's inference of a separate thinking 'I,' Hegel treats consciousness as the act of relating subject to object, whose ceaseless repetitions (here1, here2, here3...) we knit into the illusion of a unified self. The identical universes of 'The Late Philip J. Fry' (U1 = U2 = U3...) then model the same collapse of enumeration: the gaps in experience feel abnormal only because we never notice the constant gaps our own consciousness smooths over - including Nibbler's shadow in the pilot's cryogenics lab.

personal-identity.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
personal-identity.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Lopez uses the monster - 'one man made out of many' - to stress-test personal identity: brain-swap and amnesia-torture thought experiments first drive us to identify with our memories (the memory-based psychological criterion) and then, when Victor offers to wipe memory before the pain experiments, with our bodies, yielding inconsistent answers. The monster's own testimony - waking confused, prodding fire like an infant, acquiring language by eavesdropping on Safie's lessons, and building his values from scratch out of Paradise Lost and the cottagers - shows he is a genuinely new person rather than whoever once owned his corpse-parts, since we would not say a memory-wiped torture victim ceases to exist. He concludes the monster satisfies the five listed personhood criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness), with identity riding a continuing stream of consciousness running on a body that is, in the end, secondary 'hardware.'

personal-identity.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
personal-identity.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Michael Mendelson rereads James Whale's 1931 Frankenstein as a metaphysics of appearance versus reality: the seemingly monstrous creature killed Fritz only after Fritz tormented him with fire and the whip, killed Dr. Waldman while Waldman was trying to dissect him alive, and drowned Maria in innocent play, expecting her to float like the flowers they had been throwing. The 'criminal brain' was Fritz's accident and explains less than we assume, since the creature spares Henry's fiancée when she screams and faints. The real point is alterity: otherness is a relation, not a property, and individual and social identity are built by excluding an outside where monsters reside - so the horror was inside the well-ordered village all along, the monster is us, and we are its creators.

personal-identity.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
personal-identity.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: The chapter reads the show's storytelling as identity construction through Paul Ricoeur's narrative identity, built on Heidegger's insight that human being is fundamentally temporal: we live in memories and future possibilities, so 'damn you, past Ted!' collisions between selves are structural. Ricoeur's two times - linear cosmological time versus fragmented phenomenological time - explain the show's looped, goat-intruding storytelling, while Giddens's reflexive project of the self (dubbed 'reflexibility') and Turkle's new-media multiple windows explain our fragmented, self-designed identities. Goffman's dramaturgy completes the picture: Barney's womanizer persona is a Goffmanesque masquerade that collapses, the yips, when his first lover reveals the founding story was false.

personal-identity.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
personal-identity.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Nicolas Michaud argues that when you go extinct you do not come back, dismantling our three hopes: the soul, cloning, and an essential self. Cloning a T. rex yields a new individual 'Rex' with her own perspective, not the original; the soul cannot both be beyond science's reach and record memories and move bodies; and he deploys Gilbert Ryle's view that 'soul' is a language mistake - a mind is just what a functioning brain does, the way 'Jurassic Park' is just buildings, dinosaurs, staff, and money working together, ceasing when the functioning stops. A Hammond stripped by Alzheimer's and atom-replacement of every memory, trait, and particle still gets called John Hammond, so there is no essence over time: we already die constantly and never notice, which is why a second extinction holds no fresh terror.

personal-identity.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
personal-identity.title: The Devil and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether the Devil could actually get you by testing theories of the afterlife against Hamlet's ghost, Freddy Krueger, the possessions of The Exorcist and Evil Dead, Paranormal Activity, Dante's Inferno, Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, and Doom. Substance dualism cannot explain how a non-physical soul moves so much as a finger; the view that you are your body founders on recycled grave matter and the primacy of the brain; and if you are a program running on your brain, the Devil could torture infinite copies of you in Hell - even re-running you there from Heaven - unless duplication means neither copy is really you.

personal-identity.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
personal-identity.title: Homeland and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Jason Iuliano asks whether the Brody who lied to Helen Walker about Tom Walker's death is the same person as the one who beat Walker, and whether 2011 Brody is responsible for 2003 Brody's acts. He contrasts the biological criterion (same human animal), the psychological criterion of overlapping memories and intentions (so Brody remembering his family remains the same person), and the narrative identity theory Carrie invokes in 'Q&A' when she says Nazir pulled Brody apart and put him back together as someone else. A Carrie thought experiment about ECT outcomes and a Nazir mind-swap of Brody's and Walker's psychologies argue that only narrative coherence captures whom we should praise, blame, and anticipate surviving.

personal-identity.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
personal-identity.title: Homeland and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Laszlo Kajtar uses Brody's Complex PTSD - torture, forced killing of Walker, intrusive nightmares attacking Jessica - to test theories of personal identity. Animalism says Brody is the same biological organism before and after captivity, while the psychological approach, sourced in Locke's memory criterion, traces continuity of beliefs, desires, and intentions and finds it disrupted by trauma and Nazir's brainwashing, which filled the hole trauma left after Issa's death. Kajtar argues both miss the first-personal 'sense of self': like many PTSD sufferers, Brody feels he is not the person he was, and 'It's like she doesn't know who I actually am now' shows identity shattered from the inside.

personal-identity.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
personal-identity.title: Homeland and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Frank Scalambrino probes Carrie's 'personality paradox' through the 'You can't change your soul!' / 'Yes you can' exchange. Aristotle's Metaphysics offers one pole: only generation and corruption are substantial change, so Carrie persists essentially as human however her mania, job, and loves shift. Hume's rejoinder - sameness of kind is not given in sense experience but added by interpretation - opens the question of whether Carrie's identity is determined by intrinsic factors (love, soul, truth) or extrinsic ones (the CIA's rules, religious affiliation), with Saul representing extrinsic determination and Carrie privileging the intrinsic, while Brody's conversion shows a soul can change and re-order which factors govern a self.

personal-identity.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
personal-identity.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: The chapter asks whether Marceline has lost Simon Petrikov forever now that he is the Ice King, and tests every criterion of personal identity - body, memories, beliefs, personality, soul - finding each one either something that changes over time without ending a person (Finn survives losing his arm, Jake his fear of vampires) or something shared that then explains nothing. Borrowing Ryle's deflation of the soul as just the way the brain works - like Lemongrab renaming and remaking the Candy Kingdom, killing it without touching a single building - the author concludes Simon and the Ice King are two different people sharing one piece of machinery, like two operating systems on one computer. The dark payoff: bringing Simon back permanently would delete the Ice King, and by the same reasoning our own past selves are equally gone, a 'thousand deaths' a day that the chapter offers as Marceline's consolation, with Death's line 'you're gonna be the Ice King' as the haunting exception.

personal-identity.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
personal-identity.title: Dracula and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Richard Greene uses Dracula's transformations (man, bat, wolf, mist, and human-to-vampire) plus Vlad the Impaler's ordinary aging to pose the puzzle of persistence: the claims of consistency, change, and persistence cannot all be true together. He raises the justice objection to mereological essentialism (if any change made Vlad a new person, imprisoning him would punish someone else) and then tests endurantism (wholly present with time-indexed properties), perdurantism (temporal parts), and exdurantism (temporal counterparts) against the Count. He concludes endurantism best captures the intuition that one and the same guy was first human and later vampire.

personal-identity.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
personal-identity.title: 4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl
personal-identity.relation: Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.

personal-identity.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
personal-identity.title: 10. One Good, Solid Hope—the Impossible Girl
personal-identity.relation: Elsby and Luzecky ask what stays constant across Clara's echoes and argue traditional identity theories fail her: Locke's memory-continuity and same-life account cannot apply because no echo remembers the others, and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus—invoked by the Doctor's broom speech in 'Deep Breath'—rules out bodily continuity, since the echoes have different bodies and minds. Their positive view is that Clara is less a particular than a universal, a 'recipe' or species whose instances share an essence ('the soufflé isn't the soufflé; the soufflé is the recipe'), with the modern-day Clara 'real' as the origin of the echoes. That essence, shown in climbing the ladder to the clouds in 'The Snowmen,' facing the parasite-god with the most important leaf in human history in 'The Rings of Akhaten,' stepping into the Doctor's torn timeline in 'The Name of the Doctor,' and persuading the Time Lords in 'The Time of the Doctor,' is hope itself.

personal-identity.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
personal-identity.title: 21. Forgetting Is the Human Superpower
personal-identity.relation: Seymour reads the War-through-Eleventh Doctors through Freud's notion of Afterwardness (Nachtraeglichkeit) from Studies on Hysteria - memory is continually reforged as new information recontextualizes the past - so that learning Gallifrey was saved in 'The Day of the Doctor' changes not the Doctor but his memories of himself, turning penance into hope. She traces each Self constructed from Time War memory: Nine's guilt exploited by the Gelth and voiced in 'Boom Town' ('Only a killer would know that'), Ten's hubris once he forgets what he is capable of ('Time Lord Victorious' in 'The Waters of Mars'), and Eleven's danger when the memory fades and companions must remind him who he is ('A Town Called Mercy'). The chapter concludes the Doctor must keep the memory of his regret to keep being the Doctor - Clara's 'What you've always done. Be a doctor.'

personal-identity.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
personal-identity.title: 23. Failing and Forgiving in the Name of the Doctor
personal-identity.relation: Hoffman reads the Doctor's banishment of the War Doctor ('Doctor no more,' his actions 'not done in the name of the Doctor') as a failure of self-forgiveness driven by what Jeffrie Murphy calls the moral hatred of self and Robin Dillon the 'self-as-feared,' rather than mere guilt over the genocide of Gallifrey. Drawing on the self-forgiveness literature (Blustein, Griswold, Westlund), he argues that 'The Day of the Doctor' shows forgiveness neither excuses nor extinguishes blame: the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors forgive their past self by recognizing he shared their Doctorly motives and was forced into an impossible choice. Clara's outsider faith ('be a doctor') supplies the third-party affirmation that dissolves the identity-destroying dilemma and frees the Doctor to find the third option that saves Gallifrey.

personal-identity.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
personal-identity.title: 4. Nietzsche’s Faction Test
personal-identity.relation: Mallalieu uses Nietzsche's slave morality, will to power, and Ubermensch to read Roth's social experiment: Abnegation's foot-washing, guilt-driven selflessness is slave morality, Amity's drugged peace makes them willing slaves, and Peter - cruel, self-promoting, guilt-ridden - is the most Nietzschean character, whose memory wipe is an attempt to forget his way out of slave morality. Even the heroes turn out Nietzschean when Tris and Tobias dose the Bureau with memory serum, since Nietzsche holds that the old values must be forgotten before new ones can be created. But the chapter concludes the price is too high: losing your values along with your memories means losing your identity ('I would rather be dead than empty'), so Nietzsche's imagined experiment, played out through the Bureau's tools, would be a world good only for the strong and cruel.

personal-identity.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
personal-identity.title: 15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is
personal-identity.relation: David LaRocca tests Mr. Carson's claim that 'the business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' against the tradition of spatial memory metaphors and modern neuroscience. Downton itself becomes a memory palace - echoing Cicero, the Ad Herennium, and Augustine's 'court of memory' - whose characters defer endlessly to the past, while photographs (Tom with Sybil's image, Carson with Alice Neal's) act as sources and surrogates of memory in an age of acquisitional capitalism. Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research, Nicholas Carr's Nietzsche-typewriter anecdote, and Langdon Winner's point that technologies reshape life show memories are malleable rather than collectible possessions, undermining Carson's model and any fixed memory-based account of personal identity.

personal-identity.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
personal-identity.title: 12. They Just Want Me to Be Like Them
personal-identity.relation: Castro and Beisecker diagnose Lizzie's walker fixation as prolonged grief disorder: she displaces grief for her father onto the walker "Nick," denies final death ("They're just different"), and treats reanimation as a viable form of life she might join ("Maybe I should change"). They argue Carol's suppressive guardianship - the "look at the flowers" distraction and calling Lizzie weak and confused - aggravated the avoidance at the root of the disorder, so Lizzie's "transformation" of Mika was a misguided moral experiment rather than murder by a monster. The chapter contrasts Tyreese's affirming care ("You each do things your own way") as the guardianship that might have saved the girls, and notes Carol's refusal to let Lizzie reanimate denies her the dying-wish courtesy the group once granted Jim.

personal-identity.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
personal-identity.title: 14. Carol Didn’t Care
personal-identity.relation: Yuen grants that executing Lizzie was not wrong but argues Carol fell short of a moral ideal by ignoring Lizzie's preferences, deploying R.M. Hare's move from Bentham's happiness-maximizing classic utilitarianism to preference utilitarianism - illustrated by the group refusing to let Eugene test Aaron's water in "Them." Since Lizzie prefers a reanimating death ("She didn't hurt her brain"), a heart shot like the group's courtesy to Jim would have maximized preference satisfaction without endangering anyone. He answers the objections that Lizzie is a child and that walkers are mindless: her attempts to reason and her coherent post-apocalyptic values (like generational value shifts on homosexuality via Aaron and Eric) deserve respect, and whether a walker would still be Lizzie matters less than that the preference is hers now.

personal-identity.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
personal-identity.title: 15. My Zombie, My Self
personal-identity.relation: Greene asks what Walking Dead-type walkers are and answers with the Platonic method of definition learned from Socrates: place them in the genus undead (died but not at rest, neither alive nor dead) and differentiate them by differentia - corporeal, mindless, lacking superhuman or magical powers, still decomposing. Aristotle's hierarchy of life functions (nutrition, locomotion, reason) explains why walkers are not alive despite ambulating, and the standards of death (putrefaction, heart-lung, whole-brain, higher-brain) all certify that walkers are dead yet active. The chapter closes on personal identity - whether you survive becoming a zombie, as Carol's face at the barn and Carl's "she'll turn" about Lori presuppose - and admits the author chooses the self-interested reading that he could become his own zombie, for the sake of the scare.

personal-identity.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
personal-identity.title: 16. My Name Is—Hang on, What Was It Meant to Be Again Are You Sure Well, Okay Then . .
personal-identity.relation: Tim Jones argues the book is not really a love story but a warning about identity: against Descartes's transcendent self, the American pragmatists William James, Cooley, and Mead hold that the self is fluid and socially constituted, and Westley's serial reinvention (farm boy, Dread Pirate Roberts, Man in Black) - along with Mandy Patinkin's cathartic channeling of his father's death into Inigo - shows the freedom this mutability grants. The Goldman frame then exposes the danger: the fictionalized Goldman seizes Morgenstern's text, cuts its history, and rewrites it to his own ends, exactly as other people can seize our plastic identities and shape them for their interests rather than ours.

personal-identity.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
personal-identity.title: 12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld
personal-identity.relation: Pierce uses Moist von Lipwig's rehabilitation (Albert Spangler becomes Postmaster General), Cosmo Lavish's doomed project of literally becoming Vetinari, the Auditor Myria LeJean, Angua's transformations, the Librarian's orangutan body, Miss Level's two bodies, and duplicated Rincewind teleportation cases to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory theory, patched by Leibniz into psychological continuity, collapses into circularity under false-memory cases like a wizard implanting Teatime's murders in Rincewind's mind, while bodily and brain-continuity views founder on Igor part-swaps, splitting hemispheres, and identical-twin-style fission. Leibniz's own soul view and Reid's treatment of identity as a primitive, unanalyzable fact get their due, and Hume's skepticism about any continuing self marks the chapter's conclusion that every available view exacts a price.

personal-identity.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
personal-identity.title: 14. Being One’s Me (Witchy) Personal Identity on the Discworld
personal-identity.relation: The chapter reads Granny Weatherwax's analysis of Magrat—'you're your me'—through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, opening with Granny's broomstick, whose stick and bristles the dwarf engineers have replaced dozens of times yet which remains 'the same' broomstick, as a Theseus's-ship puzzle for witches. It stages Locke's view against the classic objections: Butler's circularity charge that memory presupposes identity, and fission worries raised by the duplicated Glods of Al-Ybi and by the mirror magic that splits Granny and Lilith among a billion reflections. Death's challenge to each witch to find 'the one that's real' in the mirror universe becomes the test case, and Granny's simply looking down at herself and saying 'This one' is offered as a vindication of a Butlerian, body-anchored and indefinable conception of personal identity.

personal-identity.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
personal-identity.title: 22. Cocking a Snook at Death, and Getting Away with It Does the Personification of Death Make It Less Scary
personal-identity.relation: Asking whether Pratchett's personified Death makes mortality less scary, the chapter reads Reaper Man's claim that belief created Death—the moment a living thing grasped non-existence, Death came into being—as a co-arising of dualistic concepts, and surveys psychopomps from Thanatos and Azrael to Yama and even modern assisted-dying organizations. Windle Poons's several kinds of death in Reaper Man ground the distinctions between animalistic, mindistic, and personistic death, showing that whether someone counts as dead can turn on which conception of the person is doing the counting. The closing meditation on Pratchett's own posterior cortical atrophy and the documentary Choosing to Die argues that conceptualizing death in advance—in living wills and bedside conversations with loved ones—is what lets us meet 'THERE'S JUST ME' a little less afraid.

personal-identity.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
personal-identity.title: 6. One Clone from Another
personal-identity.relation: Asks what metaphysically individuates one Leda clone from another, surveying the tradition: Aristotelian substances bearing properties, Plato's and Descartes's non-repeatable individual essences, Berkeley's and Hegel's soul-substances, Aquinas's matter-based view, Locke's memory-based personal identity (with its sleeping-copy and consciousness-download objections), and Hume's argument that substance is a meaningless idea. It then turns to the Buddhist framework — the Four Noble Truths, anatman (no eternal self), the five skandhas, and dependent origination, illustrated by Alison's soap-and-drug crates — before closing with Nishida Kitaro's logic of contradictory self-identity. Read through that lens, the clone dance party in Felix's loft shows each clone's moves are truly her own precisely because they incorporate and mirror her sisters': identity is relational, not intrinsic.

personal-identity.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
personal-identity.title: 7. I Am and Am Not You
personal-identity.relation: Reads the opening scene phenomenologically: when Sarah sees her face on Beth, her identity does not merely change genetically but unravels generatively, since her birth, ancestry, and place in world-history are all thrown into question. Using Husserl's lived-body (the absolute "here" of experience), his static/genetic/generative levels of analysis, the homeworld/alienworld distinction (Clone Club solidifies its identity against the Castor "brothers," until Helena cradles the dying Rudy), and Husserl's co-originality of I and world, the chapter presents identity as intersubjective, constituted by shared projects like Sarah's fight for Kira and the Clone Club's tribe-rituals. Kierkegaard's "life must be lived forwards but understood backwards" is broadened: to understand identity we must look before our own birth and beyond our death, into the lifeworld we inherit and pass on.

personal-identity.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
personal-identity.title: A Brief History of Cloning
personal-identity.relation: A history of cloning in science and popular culture, from Driesch's 1885 sea-urchin split and the tadpole nuclear-transfer work of Briggs, King, and Gurdon, through Rorvik's In His Image hoax, to Dolly, Polly, Ditto and Neti, and Mitalipov's human embryonic stem cells. On the fiction side it tracks how early stories (Sleeper, Four Sided Triangle, The World of Null-A, Invasion of the Body Snatchers) assumed a clone is literally the same person as the original, with the same age, memories, and desires — a metaphysical mistake, since a clone is a new person whose own experiences make her someone else — while later work (The Boys from Brazil, Jurassic Park, The Island, Never Let Me Go, Moon) got the science roughly right and moved on to the ethics, exactly where Orphan Black, with its careful Leda and Castor biology, lands.

personal-identity.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
personal-identity.title: A Farewell to David Bowie
personal-identity.relation: The editor's farewell argues that Bowie's greatness lay in relentless transformation joined to honesty: unlike acts from Kiss to Miley Cyrus whose theatrics are mere spectacle 'in an Aristotelian sense,' Bowie's characters (Ziggy, the Thin White Duke, simulating fellatio with Mick Ronson) opened a discussion of gender and 'the multiple ways of being in the world.' Tracing the career from parents' fear of rock through the Eno-shaped Berlin trilogy's symbolist minimalism and the despised continuity of 'Changes,' it reads The Next Day as a defacement of 'Heroes' and Blackstar as a Mapplethorpe-like series of self-portraits made while unflinchingly facing death.

personal-identity.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
personal-identity.title: 3. The Flux of It All
personal-identity.relation: Ammon asks whether anything persists beneath Bowie's serial personas, staging Parmenides's denial of change (with Zeno's paradoxes) and Descartes's melting wax against the Heraclitean flux of 'ch-ch-ch-changes.' Rejecting soul-substance views, he takes the empiricist line - Hume's introspection finds only particular perceptions, never a self - warns via the intentional fallacy (Manson's 'Helter Skelter,' Bloom's hawk) against letting Bowie's own pronouncements fix his songs' meanings, and tests 'meaning is use' on Bowie's calling rock stars fascists. Recurring undercurrents (dancing, apocalypse, distrust of authority) survive, but the conclusion is that Bowie's essence just is flux, 'the river we can't step into twice.'

personal-identity.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
personal-identity.title: 5. The One, the Only, Darrow
personal-identity.relation: Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.

personal-identity.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
personal-identity.title: 9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool
personal-identity.relation: Ben Fulman runs Deadpool's decapitations, the T-Ray personality split, and Evil Deadpool—his discarded body parts regenerating together in a dumpster—through the theories of personal identity: Locke's memory continuity, Reid's branching-memory 'Deadpool paradox', Chisholm's essential parts, the Ship of Theseus traced from Heraclitus to Plutarch, and later positions by Sider, Wiggins, Noonan, Grice, and Perry on overlapping memory chains and their circularity. Finding each account strained by Deadpool's cases, the chapter proposes that Deadpool stores his memories in the readers via the fourth wall. His identity over time is thus jointly sustained by the audience—a 'non-personal identity' that ends only when every reader has forgotten him.

personal-identity.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
personal-identity.title: Johnny—James—Buster—Jimmy—Jimi . . . How Many Jimis
personal-identity.relation: Editorial introduction tracing the successive identities of Johnny Allen Hendrix, James Marshall Hendrix, Jimmy James, and Jimi — from Seattle and the chitlin' circuit with the Isley Brothers and Little Richard to Chas Chandler's London — arguing there was no single Hendrix but a series of continual transformations. It dismisses a 'Hegelian unfolding of The Absolute' that would require true blues musicians to be born in the South, and speculates that the Jimi lost in 1970 was a would-be jazz-blues synthesizer, reading 'Rainy Day, Dream Away' and 'Still Raining, Still Dreaming' as evidence and invoking the rumored Miles Davis collaboration.

personal-identity.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
personal-identity.title: 12. The Broken Pieces of Yesterday’s Life
personal-identity.relation: Uses the flood of posthumous Hendrix releases — the dismal Lonnie Youngblood eight-track, 380-plus albums, the PPX litigations — to ask what we owe the dead and what access we may claim, weighing Kafka and Max Brod, Nietzsche's sister, Harper Lee's Go Set a Watchman, and Kundera's Mirek. It rejects the framing of conflicting rights: against the Cartesian picture of a hidden self the authors deploy Wittgenstein's beetle in the box — 'the human body is the best picture of the human soul' — to show that no one can fully control their public self, leaving only prudential discernment about which recordings should shape our image of the artist.

personal-identity.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
personal-identity.title: 1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession
personal-identity.relation: Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.

personal-identity.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
personal-identity.title: 3. My Sister, My Self
personal-identity.relation: Staged as a remembered backstage conversation among Elsa's freak show performers, the chapter has conjoined twins Bette and Dot work through the Ship of Theseus, the psychological-continuity theory of identity and its coma and false-memory counterexamples, Quine's claim that persons are only convenient posits rather than real entities, split-brain cases suggesting one body can host two minds, and fission worries about what would happen if they were separated - to ask whether they are one person or two, concluding it is a genuine paradox with no agreed answer.

personal-identity.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
personal-identity.title: 18. Thoughtcrime or Feelingcrime
personal-identity.relation: Alba Montes Sánchez argues that the real crime in Oceania is not thoughtcrime but 'feelingcrime': Winston lands in the Ministry of Love only once he falls in love, because beliefs alone do not motivate action while emotions and loves do — the problem of akrasia that puzzled Aristotle, since Winston carries his proof of Party lies for eleven years without acting. Using Harry Frankfurt's account of love as an involuntary, non-utilitarian, rigidly focused, self-affirming concern that organizes a person's priorities, she explains why Julia is irreplaceable and why Room 101 must destroy Winston's deepest allegiance rather than just his opinions. Surveying theories of individuality from Locke's memory to recognition and narrative, she concludes that a stubborn residue of selfhood survives in what we love — which is why Ingsoc must make war on love itself.

personal-identity.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
personal-identity.title: 7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me
personal-identity.relation: Lay tests Locke's memory theory against the series: Marsha in 'The After Hours' is only the mannequin-person again when she remembers being one, and David Gurney in 'Person or Persons Unknown' has lost his identity because his memories lack factivity — they correspond to no actual past. Reid's brave-officer chain and Parfit's psychological continuity from Reasons and Persons then let him handle the hard cases: Jana's fake 'memory tracks' in 'The Lateness of the Hour' can still constitute her identity as overlapping chains of mental states (severed by reprogramming into Nelda), while the post-Transformation girl of 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' has all of Marilyn's memories but not her beliefs, desires, or character — so Marilyn did not survive.

personal-identity.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
personal-identity.title: Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful
personal-identity.relation: Muntersbjorn argues that freedom comes in kinds and degrees and that selves are social fictions sustained by others, building on Annette Baier's claims that we are 'second persons' whose self-consciousness and freedom grow out of childhood interaction and mutual cross-examination. She reads the hosts' selective ignoring ('that doesn't look like anything to me') as Baier's dangerous art of self-deception, and contrasts Descartes' solitary introspection (hats and coats that may cover automata) and Russell's analogy-based answer to the problem of other minds with the hosts' deliberately scripted interpersonal checks that keep them from questioning their reality. Plato's Meno statues of Daedalus (opinion 'fastened up' into knowledge) frame hosts as property whose freedom is a matter of degree, and the chapter closes that if artificial beings are ever to become persons they must be treated as second persons first - the Golden Rule applied to the park.

personal-identity.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
personal-identity.title: Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve
personal-identity.relation: Trapero-Llobera reads Westworld as the culmination of Jonathan Nolan's Memento and Person of Interest projects, mapping seven nested 'observing systems' (Nolan, Sizemore, Stubbs and Elsie, Ford, the creators' personal stories, Maeve, and William as beta-tester) onto second-wave cybernetics (Foerster, Maturana, Varela, Hayles), where the observer participates in and constructs the observed world through feedback loops. She argues the show's hosts pass through Turing's imitation game (fake memories and personalities from textual repetition, as with Peter Abernathy's reveries), and that Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns convert prosthetic memory into experienced, autopoietic memory reconstructed in a 'Bergsonian' backward movement that gives them agency and purpose. William's two-timeline transformation into the Man in Black figures the 'semiosis of virtuality' - the hyperreal where original and copy are indistinguishable - ending in a collective bicameral mind in which everyone, audience included, inhabits the god-creator Ford's dream.

personal-identity.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
personal-identity.title: 1. The Genuine Article
personal-identity.relation: Written in the voice of a non-C-137 Rick, the chapter argues that whether the Beth at the end of 'The ABCs of Beth' is a clone doesn't matter, because our reverence for 'the genuine article' (like the original US Constitution) is romantic packaging, and a functional clone is as good as the original. It tests Robert Nozick's experience machine, whose three objections supposedly show we value genuine reality intrinsically, against Rick's pragmatism of believing what is useful, and reads 'The Wedding Squanchers' (Rick turning himself in to the Federation) as proof that his family is both instrumentally and intrinsically valuable to him. Your answer to the clone question, it concludes, is a Rorschach test revealing what you place intrinsic value on.

personal-identity.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
personal-identity.title: 2. The Unimportance of Identity When You Have a Portal Gun
personal-identity.relation: The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.

personal-identity.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch
personal-identity.title: 5. Who’d Rick Kill Or, Who Killed Rick
personal-identity.relation: Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.

personal-identity.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
personal-identity.title: 9. To Err Is Human, to Forget … Sublime
personal-identity.relation: Huntingford contrasts Stranger Things with its blueprint, Stephen King's It: where It forces the Losers Club back to the traumatic truth of childhood, the show traffics in 'false nostalgia,' vicarious nostalgia for an Eighties that only existed on screen, supported by Loftus's false-memory experiments (the impossible Bugs Bunny, Stewart's Root Beer) and Will's anniversary effect and El's mother's broken record of 'breathe, sunflower, rainbow... 450.' Against this malleability she sets Locke's memory theory of personal identity from the Essay and Sacks's 'lost mariner,' warning that nostalgic self-deception can rewrite the self, yet concluding, with It's own ending, that since we cannot survive some horrors, the comforting lie of misremembered childhood is what we tune in for.

personal-identity.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
personal-identity.title: 12. Who Is Will Byers
personal-identity.relation: Hammonds and Gordon use Mead's symbolic interactionism, in which the self emerges from interaction and stabilizes around 'identity anchors' others can expect, to unpack 'Zombie Boy': Mr. Clarke's Phineas Gage story frames Max's doubt that Will is still Will, Joyce's hovering and Will's fragile-child role co-constitute each other, and Will renegotiates a different identity with Jonathan ('Stop treating me like I'm gonna break'). During the Mind Flayer's possession, when Will screams that the creature is 'everywhere,' his family's stories of the toy truck and the crayon spaceship summon the kind, honest anchors of the old Will, showing identity as recognizable and stable yet ultimately negotiable, and that realizing and actualizing agency lets Will beat the role the monster assigned him.

personal-identity.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
personal-identity.title: 7. More Human than Humans
personal-identity.relation: Rob O'Connor reads replicants through N. Katherine Hayles's posthumanism — persons as amalgams of biological and informational-technological systems — arguing Rachael's procreation shows the posthuman body bypassing its designed limits, while Joi is a posthuman of the opposite construction, a hologram transcending her limits through emotion. Memory and experience, even implanted ones (Batty's 'tears in rain', Deckard's unicorn dream, K's wooden horse, 'all the best memories are hers'), supply the existential context that defines the posthuman self. K's epiphany before the giant Joi advertisement reveals he is a tool of the capitalist system, and his choice to die for the right cause is how he takes charge of his own identity.

personal-identity.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
personal-identity.title: 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here
personal-identity.relation: Tepley uses Eleanor waking in Michael's office to pose the problem of numerical personal identity: what makes the person in the chair the very same person who died seconds earlier on Earth? He eliminates the same-body theory, since bodies stay behind and lack spatiotemporal continuity, the same-mind theory of psychological continuity, which fails on the 802 reboots and implies the absurdity that two duplicates would both be Eleanor, and the same-soul theory, which offers no criteria for sameness. The 'Janet(s)' revelation that the humans are recomposed from 'essences' turns out to be Aristotelian-Thomistic hylomorphism, committing the show to a same-soul theory of identity it never defends.

personal-identity.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
personal-identity.title: 2. KISStory and Kulture of the Hottest Band in the World
personal-identity.relation: Historian and lifelong fan Matt Alschbach argues that the history of KISS is the history of its fans: his police-officer father taking him to the 1979 San Diego show, schoolyard debates over Alive! versus Alive II, rubbing pencil shadings over the Double Platinum gatefold to guess the band's faces, and strangers' comments on his KISS T-shirts all show the band forging identity and community. He recounts how Alive! rescued Casablanca Records, how the 1983 MTV unmasking and 1996 remasking reinvented the brand for new generations, and how the KISS KRUISE, $50,000 Vault Experience, and Rock & Brews extend its cultural reach. The chapter's claim is that KISS fandom supplies camaraderie, family bonds, and life-meaning across generations.

personal-identity.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
personal-identity.title: 6. The KISS Franchise
personal-identity.relation: Peter Finocchiaro takes Gene Simmons's and manager Doc McGhee's suggestions that KISS could become a franchise — new musicians stepping into the Demon and Starchild roles — and works out what band identity could mean. Using the Ship of Theseus, he distinguishes qualitative from numerical identity, invokes collective intentionality to explain how a band without a mind can perform intentional actions, and contrasts the 'originality connection' (being the actual founding members) with the 'continuity connection' (day-by-day chained succession), mirroring the bodily-versus-psychological debate about Gene Simmons's personal identity. His conclusion is that bands are governed by social rules fans collectively create — like the rules of basketball or musical genre — so in his imaginary two-KISS scenario, and for any future franchise, the fan base would decide which band is the real KISS rather than discovering a pre-existing fact.

personal-identity.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
personal-identity.title: Liz Lemon and High School The More Things Change, the More They Don’t
personal-identity.relation: Shores uses Jack's cookie jar collection and his fiftieth-birthday home movies in 'Apollo, Apollo', plus Liz's catastrophic high-school reunion in 'Reunion', to examine personal identity over time. Hume's bundle theory denies any self beyond a flux of perceptions, Whitehead offers three senses of a person over time, and Augustine locates past, present, and future in the mind as memory, sight, and expectation, which explains why Jack cannot recover his tenth-birthday joy by buying the Apollo Lunar Module toy yet feels 'like a kid' after laughing until he vomits. Ryle's 'elusiveness of I' and Rousseau on happiness as a fleeting state frame the conclusion that we continually reinterpret the past from the present, so the self is a stretched-out temporal continuity.

personal-identity.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
personal-identity.title: Introduction
personal-identity.relation: Frames the volume with Morpheus's red-pill speech in The Matrix, treating the rabbit-hole as our culture's portal of escape and asking how to make sense of what we find in Wonderland: hookah-smoking caterpillars, babies that turn into pigs, grins without cats, and trials where the sentence comes before the evidence. It takes Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the book's guiding question, tying knowledge of who we are and can become to memory of who we have been, and previews chapters on the feminist Alice, the Red Queen and nuclear strategy, mushroom trips, and the connection between Alice, procrastination, and the Spice Girls.

personal-identity.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
personal-identity.title: From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory
personal-identity.relation: Treats the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the classic memory-and-identity problem, rallying Plato's wax tablet and Meno doctrine that learning is recollection, Locke's memory criterion of the same person, and Diderot's dialogue on how without memory there would be no connected self. Tyler Shores reads Alice's botched recitations as Bergson's impersonal habit-memory swamping personal memory, her name-forgetting in the wood through Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations on the necessity of forgetting, the Red King's dream as Freud's alienated memory, and the White Queen's memory that 'works both ways' as a thought experiment tying memory, time, and self together.

personal-identity.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
personal-identity.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Sorts the Oscar/George Sr. twin confusion into the metaphysical, persistence, and evidential problems of personal identity, testing Aristotle's essential properties (why two actresses play one Marta, what makes each Richter brother distinct) and Descartes's immaterial soul (undermined by surrogate Larry, who stays Larry while Buster remotely operates him). Locke's memory criterion then explains why Oscar is not guilty of George's crimes and why Gob disowns what his forget-me-nows erased, before Thomas Reid's transitivity objection, staged through a lifetime of Gob's roofies, shows Locke committed to old Gob both being and not being young Gob.

personal-identity.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
personal-identity.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Uses the show's narrator and structure (the chain of contingencies costing Buster his hand, 'now that's how you narrate a story') to argue that we impose narrative on life to make it meaningful, starting from Aristotle's Poetics requirement of beginning, middle, and end. George Sr.'s endlessly reinterpreted J. Walter Weatherman lessons show storytelling as moral choice among possible versions of events, Nietzsche's advice to learn from artists commends styling one's own life aesthetically, and Kierkegaard's 'life must be understood backwards but lived forwards' explains both self-narration and the show's rewatchable 'call forwards', ending on narrative as the sense-making abstraction by which we know ourselves.

personal-identity.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
personal-identity.title: Opening Up Possibilities
personal-identity.relation: Argues, through Hilde Lindemann's relational account of personhood, that Zuko genuinely is all of the identities others hold him in (disappointing son, villain, ally) because being a person is a social practice of expression, recognition, and response. Aang's decision to hear Zuko out at the Western Air Temple, Iroh's stubborn refusal to accept Ozai's script for him (his anger itself recognizing Zuko as an agent capable of choosing otherwise), and Katara's historically-sensitive slow trust open up the possible future in which Zuko can become trustworthy, while the Earth Kingdom villagers' rejection of him in 'Zuko Alone' shows how weight of history and stereotype can shut possibility down. The chapter insists this is not letting wrongdoers off the hook: genuine apology, repair, and moral anger remain required (contrasting the Brock Turner case), but only a moral community that holds people in personhood makes redemption possible, so society should be arranged to give everyone the Iros and Aangs that Zuko was lucky to have.

personal-identity.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
personal-identity.title: Are you the Next Goliath
personal-identity.relation: Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.

personal-identity.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
personal-identity.title: Retelling Our Stories
personal-identity.relation: Milsky applies the narrative theory of personal identity drawn from Paul Ricoeur and Alasdair MacIntyre (we are the story we emplot about ourselves) to the two Sharons: Boomer's discovery that she is a sleeper Cylon is a 'factual disruption' of her self-story (she shoots Adama because her human narrative cannot cohere), while Athena's love for Helo is a 'disruption of belief' that rewrites her values about humans. He extends the analysis to humans: Starbuck's repressed childhood abuse, Roslin's Pythian-prophecy conversion, and Helo's love for a Cylon, plus Six expelling Athena and Tyrol refusing to acknowledge Boomer, show identity is also socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy. The chapter concludes disruptions are not identity-altering: like the Final Five in 'Crossroads, Part 2' (Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh, I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet'), integration and retelling preserve the continuity of self.

personal-identity.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
personal-identity.title: Frak-tured Finality
personal-identity.relation: Booth argues the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across media, so viewers must actively construct the story (which is why Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' only makes sense if you watched them), and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performative roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's wet-floor amnesia in 'Water,' and Hera's human-Cylon hybridity as postmodern identity-in-process. Against Baltar, who waits for D'Anna to assign him an identity, Tigh actively constructs his ('that's the man I want to be'), and the chapter ends suggesting viewers too become human-machine hybrids by constructing themselves from the show's fragments.

personal-identity.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
personal-identity.title: Who They Are or Who They Want to Be
personal-identity.relation: Harwood-Smith argues, against Descartes's pre-given 'I think therefore I am,' that Judith Butler's performativity explains the Cylons: Six is female because she performs femininity, no copy performs identically, and Cylon society fractures into hybrid identities with an 'embarrassed etc.' Sexual contact with humans is the catalyst that makes performance constitute reality, producing Athena's defection, Caprica Six's celebrity status, and D'Anna's religious fervor, while Cylons who never slept with humans stay apart. The same dynamic destabilizes humans who sleep with Cylons: Baltar's 'I must be a Cylon because I slept with one,' Tyrol's fear, and Helo's 'toaster lover' stigma, with Tigh's chosen stability ('that's the man I want to be') as the counterexample of performing who you want to be.

personal-identity.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
personal-identity.title: Into the Future
personal-identity.relation: Hanley dismantles the four alleged human-Cylon differences: humans are also 'made' (by God), contain non-organic parts, come as identical twins, and expect to survive death, so religious believers already believe they are Cylons. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), models Cylon resurrection as scanning-death-transmission-replication, and shows van Inwagen's replica-swap account of bodily resurrection faces the same worries about blank bodies and which body returns. Following Locke's consciousness criterion, that a soul independent of body and memory explains none of our identity judgments, he rejects karma-based reincarnation without memory, proposes a fission-style plot-fix for Athena's impossible memories of Tyrol, and ends with Cylons settling ancient Earth: 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'

personal-identity.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
personal-identity.title: “Your Flesh, Too, is Weak. But You Have… Potential”
personal-identity.relation: Mentyka maps the two antagonists of System Shock 2 onto the two classical criteria of personal identity: the parasitic Many, one flesh persisting through wildly different bodies, embody the bodily criterion, while the rogue AI SHODAN, pure data abandoning first Citadel then the Von Braun, embodies psychological continuity from Locke's memory theory. He runs the standard objections (Reid and Butler on memory's circularity, cell replacement, cybernetic implants, sleep and infancy) against both sides, then turns to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, only relations of degree, likening the reused 'Soldier #G65434-2' avatar to a person surviving through successors. The player character, physical like the Many yet armed with SHODAN's cybernetic knowledge, suggests identity needs both body and mind.

personal-identity.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
personal-identity.title: Taking the Leap (It’s Not Fair)
personal-identity.relation: Against the natural reading that Be Right Back fails because AshBot is a poor copy, the chapter argues that even a perfect duplicate, AshBot+, would not be Ash: like a perfect forgery of a twenty-dollar bill, it would share all intrinsic but none of Ash's relational properties (being Martha's beloved, the coming father of her child), which also exposes a fission paradox for psychological-continuity theories. Nozick's account of love as a 'we' — shared memory, autonomy, and well-being — explains why Martha cannot trade up or replace a dead partner without destroying the self constituted by the relationship. Parfit's view that only psychological continuity matters is then rejected: because Martha's relationship survives only if Ash does, survival itself matters, and Martha must mourn rather than cling to a specter.

personal-identity.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
personal-identity.title: Forget Cooper. Are We in a Simulation
personal-identity.relation: The chapter argues the horror of Playtest lies not in novelty but in immersion erasing the reality/fiction line: the rubber-hand and Muller-Lyer illusions, the paradox of fiction, and 'aliefs' show that knowing something is fake does not stop it feeling real, and for incorrigible experiences like pain the distinction collapses entirely. The AI's stripping of Cooper's memories and preferences is framed as loss of psychological continuity — a living death echoing his father's Alzheimer's — since with no memories Cooper cannot even answer who he is. The final move turns Bostrom's simulation argument on the viewer: because Cooper 'woke up' twice into deeper simulation and died 0.04 seconds in, we too may have no test that certifies we have ever left the simulation.

personal-identity.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
personal-identity.title: A Dilemma
personal-identity.relation: The chapter asks 'Is your cookie you?', running theories of personal identity through Black Mirror's copies: the soul theory surfaces when Clayton signs away his 'digital self'; Locke's memory theory implies Cookie-Greta is Greta - a reductio, since one person cannot be wholly in two places at once (the same problem for Ashley Too and the thousand Hang the DJ simulations) - and the perdurantist patch recasts Greta and her cookie as time-slices of one four-dimensional person. Physical theories (Olson's animalism, Unger's brain-essentialism) rule out survival by upload, so Yorkie dies when her body dies even though digital Yorkie continues in San Junipero; Parfit's no-self bundle view and the teletransporter case then dissolve the fear, since there is no ego to lose and ordinary survival is 'about as bad' as being destroyed and replaced by a replica. The upshot: the punishment and immortality plots (Joe's million-year Christmas loop, San Junipero) require cookies to be both conscious and psychologically connected in the right way, and the episodes' horror depends on leaving that genuinely uncertain.

personal-identity.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_
personal-identity.title: 14 The Afterlife of Erik Killmonger in African Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Paul Dottin argues that Black Panther lore inherited the racist 'Hamitic Hypothesis' (crediting Egypt rather than sub-Saharan Africa for Wakanda's civilization) and that Ta-Nehisi Coates and Ryan Coogler begin a Wiredu-style conceptual decolonization of it. Taking Killmonger's dying wish to be buried with the ancestors who jumped from slave ships literally, the chapter asks which African metaphysics could make his postmortem survival of substance, subjectivity, and setting rationally intelligible. It rejects Cartesian substance dualism (illustrated by T'Challa defeating the demon Mephisto only after trapping his spirit in a body) in favor of Wiredu's Akan quasi-physicalism and Adeofe's Yoruba theory of destiny (ipin) and inner head (ori-inu), then ranks Killmonger's afterlife options from limbo through the Ancestral Plane to deification as the ocean deity Olokun.

personal-identity.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
personal-identity.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
personal-identity.relation: James Bondarchuk tests purist principles about which line-ups are really Black Sabbath with thought experiments: the Ship of Theseus, from Plutarch plus Hobbes's reassembled planks, fits poorly because Geezer Butler is no plank, musicians contribute irreplaceable style, and "original members only" absurdly entails a Bieber piano-cover band would still be Sabbath, while the legal-ownership reading collapses once fans admit Bieber buying the name changes nothing. He concludes the whole "is it still Sabbath without Ozzy?" debate is not a metaphysical question with a fact of the matter but disguised aesthetic judgment, he remains a purist because Bill Ward's brooding drumming on "Black Sabbath" and "Hand of Doom" are integral to the Sabbath Sound, while conceding no objective answer exists.

personal-identity.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
personal-identity.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Wesley Cray distinguishes fragile line-ups from bands that persist through them and proposes three criteria for a band's identity over time, continuity (successive line-ups share at least one member, chaining across gaps), intention (the line-up directs its intentions toward being that band), and uniqueness (only one line-up per band at a time, as the Gorgoroth lawsuit shows). Applying them, Tony Iommi is Sabbath's only essential member since "Ozzy was fired" makes sense while "Tony was fired" would not, so most post-Ozzy line-ups really were Black Sabbath, though Seventh Star, Born Again, and Cross Purposes fail the intention criterion, and the 2006 Heaven and Hell reunion was Sabbath continuing under another name.

personal-identity.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
personal-identity.title: 15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is
personal-identity.relation: David LaRocca takes Mr. Carson's confession to Mrs. Hughes - 'The business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' - and asks whether memory really is a possession that can be collected. He traces the spatial metaphors Carson's view rests on: the classical memory palace of Cicero and the Ad Herennium, Augustine's 'huge court of memory' from the Confessions, and Downton itself as a haunted storehouse where photographs of the dead Sybil and Carson's lost Alice Neal keep trauma alive rather than heal it. Against this acquisitional model he sets contemporary neuroscience (Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research), which shows memories are rewritten rather than collected, undermining both Carson's nostalgia and the idea that personal identity is a fixed archive of the past.

personal-identity.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
personal-identity.title: Long-Term Identity
personal-identity.relation: Asks whether the final Duncan Idaho ghola, reawakened with the memories of all his serial ghola lives, is the same person as the original Idaho, testing physical continuity, Locke's memory criterion (Hayt before reawakening is not yet Idaho, which is why he dies again for House Atreides only after recovery), Parfit's psychological connectedness with its redescription of identity as mere survival, Schechtman's narrative self-constitution, and four-dimensionalist 'selfworms' with Gurney Halleck and Leto II as examples. It concludes that Herbert treats personal identity as something that shifts with technology and social recognition, so that the final Duncan's integration of five thousand years of lives is genuinely one person: same Duncans, same person.

personal-identity.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
personal-identity.title: Get Out of My Mind!
personal-identity.relation: Applies Locke's distinction between human animals and conscious, reflecting persons to the Duniverse, noting that the Bene Gesserit's 'we sift people to find the humans' gets Locke backwards. Jessica's Spice Agony extends her consciousness back to Raquella Berto-Anirul, which together with Reid's gallant-officer objection (recast as Gurney Halleck's fading memory of his sister's eyes) breaks the transitivity of Lockean identity, since Jessica-A and Raquella-C would have to be identical without sharing any memory. It closes by weighing psychological-continuity views against animalism and Dennett's self as a 'centre of narrative gravity', leaving puzzles like Alia the Abomination, who shares every memory with her mother.

personal-identity.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
personal-identity.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Silcox's fifth-level paladin died to eighty-three orcs and his middle-school friends held a funeral, and the chapter asks whether grief for a PC death is rational. Charles Taylor's narrative ethics — we grasp our lives as unfolding stories — would vindicate it, but objections from Beckett's Waiting for Godot and MacEwan's Atonement (via critic Samantha Vice) show stories can discourage seeing life as narrative, and the decisive asymmetry is Nagel's point about death: after the paladin falls the campaign story continues and the player can still watch it, whereas a person's own death forecloses any finding out how things turn out, a difference like February cold versus interstellar cold. He proposes instead that the self is a 'back-story' or metanarrative precondition of storytelling, closing against Descartes' Meditations claim that the power of imagination is 'in no way necessary' to his essence — take away someone's capacity for shared fiction entirely and nothing recognizable remains.

personal-identity.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
personal-identity.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Silcox and Cox read D&D modules as thought experiments in James Robert Brown's 'laboratory of the mind'. The Tomb of Horrors' four overlapping plane-shifted buildings restate Parfit's teletransporter puzzle — did the character who stepped through get annihilated, or is an exact copy walking around elsewhere, and does the answer differ for a Warforged or Tiefling? — while the Eberron setting's magically sentient Warforged run into Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': players cannot access Warforged experience and are really exploring what it is like for a human to suspend disbelief, like Greek actors donning masks. Mary Anne Warren's Space Traveler criteria for alien personhood collapse on contact with orcs who pass them yet eat you, and with the Flumph — lawful good, rational, but killed on sight by the authors' own party — showing personhood cannot be the only criterion for how to treat strangers; the closing twist is that philosophy contemplates scenarios sub specie aeternitatis while D&D forces immersion sub specie temporis, a habit of entertaining the impossible that is itself a philosophical virtue.

personal-identity.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
personal-identity.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Monica Evans asks what relationship holds between a player and a character, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to probe whether a character rebuilt under a new edition, recreated in Neverwinter Nights, or played in succession by two people is still the 'same' character. She applies James Paul Gee's three identities (virtual, real-world, projective) to Wil Wheaton playing Aeofel, whose in-character chase of Leer into an acid pit shows projective identity trumping good gameplay. Worch's 'identity bubble', Bartle's four player types, and the management of player versus character knowledge (the veteran whose wizard meets a bulette, the INT 7 barbarian Dak) frame D&D as a shared fiction in which players explore who they are or might be.

personal-identity.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
personal-identity.title: The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat
personal-identity.relation: Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.

personal-identity.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: David Lawrence opens with Fallout 4's 'Blind Betrayal', where Elder Maxson orders the player to execute Paladin Danse once his synth origin is revealed, and argues that moral status is a matter of capacities - sense of self, notion of past and future, values, life-plans, moral agency - drawing on Charles Taylor's concept of a person and narrative identity, not on biological substrate.
