Nick Valentine's hunt for Eddie Winter in 'Long Time Coming' and Curie's chosen embodiment in 'Emergent Behavior' show machines weaving reconstructed pasts into new life-plans, while ghouls like Hancock and Raul ('Old School Ghoul') and super mutants like Fawkes (who refuses to enter the lethal radiation chamber: 'I would not rob you of that') and the community-builder Marcus prove branded monsters can be more human than human. The factions embody warring philosophies of moral status: the Institute's property-slavery of its creations, the Brotherhood's 'wisdom of repugnance' (Leon Kass), and the Railroad's capacity-based abolitionism, with DiMA's Far Harbor question - how do you know you are not a synth? - turning the issue on the player.

personal-identity.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: The chapter rereads Fallout 3's original Project Purity ending — the forced walk into the lethal radiation chamber while radiation-immune followers Fawkes, Sergeant RL-3, and Charon each refuse — as the game's worst case of narrative paradox: the pre-authored story compels an action the player-authored character narrative cannot accommodate. On the narrative-identity view (mounted against Galen Strawson's denial of narrativity), the Karma system and companions like Fawkes matter through the story the player tells, so an evil, greed-driven Lone Wanderer dying nobly is a 'bad death' that unravels the motivation for the entire playthrough. Dying well requires death to fit the story, and Sarah Lyons's substitutable sacrifice — or a last-page redemption epiphany — is what restores narrative coherence.

personal-identity.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
personal-identity.title: 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here
personal-identity.relation: Asks what makes the person sitting in Michael's office numerically identical to the person who died on Earth. The same-body theory fails because bodies stay behind (buried or cremated) with no spatiotemporal continuity; the same-mind theory of psychological continuity fails on the 802 memory-wiping reboots and the duplication case of two psychologically-continuous Eleanors; the same-soul theory cannot say what makes two souls the same soul. The chapter concludes that 'Janet(s)' — essences reconstituting themselves in Janet's void — quietly commits the show to Aristotelian and Aquinan hylomorphism, while leaving open how anyone (even Janet) could tell that two persons share an essence.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Introduction
personal-identity.relation: The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Horcruxes
personal-identity.relation: Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Mind-Body Distinctions
personal-identity.relation: Opening Eric Saidel's chapter, the section takes Sirius's tail-chasing as Padfoot in Order of the Phoenix as its puzzle: is Sirius a man sometimes in a dog's body, a dog sometimes in a man's body, or a third 'someone' who persists through the change? It widens the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations, framing it as a question about identity and the mind-body relation.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Whose Reasons
personal-identity.relation: The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: A Step in the Right Direction
personal-identity.relation: Recasting the puzzle as a question of whose reasons cause Padfoot's actions, the section shows that strategy fails too: Harry as Runcorn and Ron as Cattermole act on Harry's and Ron's own reasons, never on those of the men whose bodies they wear, and dogs chase tails because it feels good, not for reasons at all. So reasons cannot explain either Padfoot's tail-chasing or werewolf Lupin's attacks, which come from his blood while his reasons would restrain him.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: A Unified Self
personal-identity.relation: The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: NOTES
personal-identity.relation: The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Choices
personal-identity.relation: Opening 'Choices vs. Abilities: Dumbledore on Self-Understanding' with Socrates' 'know thyself,' Bassham frames the books as Harry's progress from appearance to reality: the boy under the stairs who thinks himself ordinary gradually learns who he is. The pivot is the end of Chamber of Secrets, where Harry, alarmed that he shares Parseltongue and Slytherin potential with Voldemort, receives Dumbledore's dictum 'It is our choices, Harry, that show us what we truly are, far more than our abilities,' which Bassham sets out to test.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Abilities
personal-identity.relation: The chapter argues motive-choices reveal character best: Hermione's rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army does not make her a habitual rebel since character is habit, as Aristotle says, and Snape's apparently loyal Death Eater acts concealed his fidelity to Dumbledore and Lily, so bare acts mislead; Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny, acted on despite the dangers, is genuinely revealing. But the wizarding world complicates self-knowledge: Harry's vision as Voldemort attacked Arthur Weasley, the implanted memory framing Morfin Gaunt for the Riddle murders, and the firewhiskey scenario of Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and memory charms can make it undecidable whether it was really you who chose, since the boundaries between self and other are thinner there.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: “A Swirling, Silvery Mass”
personal-identity.relation: Opens Amy Kind's essay by presenting the Pensieve as a device for offloading memories like data from a hard drive, easing obsession and revealing patterns, and asks what that does to the boundaries of mind, memory, and self. If thoughts can be extracted from the head, tampered with, stored elsewhere, and shared, as with the Pensieve and Tom Riddle's diary, then memory-based accounts of what makes a person persist over time come under pressure, and it is no longer obvious whose mind a thought belongs to.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: Lumos!
personal-identity.relation: Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: NOTES
personal-identity.relation: Resolves the threat by sorting memories into know-how, factual, and first-person experiential kinds: identity rides on experiential memories, but Pensieve replays are third-person, as Rowling confirmed about Dumbledore's memory of Bellatrix Lestrange's trial. So sharing a Pensieve memory endangers who you are no more than sharing an experience or using a Time-Turner, and whether your thoughts sit in a mind, a Pensieve, or a notebook, they remain your own.

personal-identity.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
personal-identity.title: The Fantasy Objection
personal-identity.relation: Takes up the integrity objection advanced by the Freudian psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renunciation cannot change the fact that it was you who did the wrong, so posing as an altogether new person invites self-deception, as with the reformed alcoholic who still calls himself an alcoholic. Taliaferro grants the regeneration model can be abused but argues renewal requires something very close to dying to the past, using Snape, unable to confess his love for Lily, still nursing resentment, honored only when Harry names his son Severus, as the tragedy of reform without full renunciation.

personal-identity.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
personal-identity.title: NOTE
personal-identity.relation: Asks whether amnesia preserves numerical identity: is the Peter who wakes in the shipping crate still Volume-1 Peter, are Niki and Jessica one person, and is the Sylar whom Matt rewrites with Nathan's memories now Nathan? The chapter builds Locke's memory criterion, breaks it with Reid's transitivity objection run through Mohinder's timeline in 'Five Years Gone,' repairs it with Grice's and Perry's memory-ancestor chains, then destroys the repair with Arthur Petrelli's wipe of Hiro (Forgetful Hiro vs. Stabby Hiro), Bernard Williams's torture thought experiment, Parfit's psychological spectrum, and the graphic novel's branching self-copier Evan. It concludes that no memory criterion can define personal identity, yet memory still matters practically: Claire must act as if she persists over time to keep her promise to Zach and to bother finishing the manatee assignment.

personal-identity.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
personal-identity.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.

personal-identity.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
personal-identity.title: Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End
personal-identity.relation: Andersen argues Inception goes one step deeper than Descartes's dream argument: where Descartes doubted the world but kept ownership of his thoughts, the film imagines an identity-defining conviction — Fischer's sense of his father's judgment — being implanted so it never occurs to the victim to question it, which is to co-opt subjectivity itself. He reads Nolan's whole oeuvre (Following, Memento, The Prestige, Batman Begins) as variations on manipulation by misdirection, and diagnoses Cobb's inception on Mal in Limbo as the infection of her mind with Cartesian doubt, a philosophy impossible to live by. Since a totem guards against others' dreams but not self-deception, the film's answer is not universal doubt but trust: only by opening himself to Ariadne and choosing intimacy can Cobb go home and spin the top without looking.

personal-identity.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Gettings asks whether LEGO set #21103, the Cuusoo DeLorean Time Machine, is numerically identical to Team BTTF's original fan design — and why the fans deserve credit and royalties. Neither matter (his 1982 attic spaceship with bricks replaced one by one) nor form (a license plate added here or there) settles identity, as the Ship of Theseus puzzle and Hobbes' reassembly variation show, analyzed through Aristotle's matter/form distinction for substances. He adopts the causal/historical view: the released set continuously descends from the fans' submission just as the adult author descends from the boy who built the spaceship, and this same historical origin, in Lockean fashion, is what grounds the designers' labor-mixing property right — the musician-and-producer analogy explaining why Team BTTF keeps the larger share of credit.

personal-identity.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Mentyka uses minifigure puzzles — can 'Eliza' and 'Beth' be distinct characters when built from identical pieces, and is Eliza the same character after every piece is swapped out, a minifig Ship of Theseus — to introduce the philosophy of the human person. He runs through supervenience on physical parts, Locke's memory theory and its Butler–Reid controversy (Reid in the taxonomy), the Christian Resurrection-of-the-Body background, and Parfit's despairing deflation that identity matters less than what survives us. Against these he defends personalism, citing Max Scheler and Kierkegaard's call in The Single Individual to become one rather than a crowd: a person is both the sigfig and the AFOL building it, constituted by free choices and actions — which is also why the LEGO Movie's 'Where Are My Pants?' mass society is the enemy.

personal-identity.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box
personal-identity.title: Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the
personal-identity.relation: Rachel Robison asks how Zelda characters persist through radical change, recasting the Ship of Theseus as Tetra's pirate ship from Wind Waker, whose replaced planks Ganon reassembles into a rival ship and leaving Link to find the true one. Physical-continuity accounts fail because Link projects his consciousness into seagulls and temple mages and becomes a wolf in Twilight Princess; Locke's memory theory fails because Ocarina of Time's child/adult time loops break psychological continuity. Her solution: in the Zelda universe, the goddesses' destiny — embodiment of courage, wisdom, or power — supplies the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, a stipulative metaphysics videogames are free to have.

personal-identity.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
personal-identity.title: None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It
personal-identity.relation: Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.

personal-identity.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
personal-identity.title: Living and Dying as One: Suffering and the Ethics of Euthanasia
personal-identity.relation: Jason Eberl uses Joe Bonham of 'One' and Johnny Got His Gun to analyze suffering as loss of recognition (Hegel), loss of social contact (Aristotle's political animal), and loss of Kantian autonomy and dignity - 'a piece of meat that keeps on living'. He then works through the euthanasia debate: active versus passive euthanasia, Aquinas' doctrine of double effect for palliative care, Locke's psychological criterion of personal identity behind the higher-brain death standard applied to Terri Schiavo and PVS patients, concluding that the nurse's cutting of Joe's breathing tube would be active euthanasia because of the intention behind it.

personal-identity.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
personal-identity.title: Is It Still Metallica? On the Identity of Rock Bands Over Time
personal-identity.relation: Manuel Bremer and Daniel Cohnitz ask whether the band on Kill 'Em All is identical with the band on St. Anger. Lars' drum kit, rebuilt part by part plus the reassembled original, is a Ship of Theseus case yielding their 'Nothing Else Matters Principle'; Locke's distinction between same substance, man, and person - illustrated by a brain swap between Kirk Hammett and an envious rival - shows identity must be 'suited to the idea'; and Searle and Gilbert on collective intention show a band is a social group, not a collection of people. Their revised musical-style-plus-line-up-continuity theory faces fission problems (Megadeth) and the eliminativist option Quine's 'no entity without identity' invites.

personal-identity.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
personal-identity.title: The Office and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.

personal-identity.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
personal-identity.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.

personal-identity.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
personal-identity.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Southworth and Timm use the Clone Saga to teach real cloning science: molecular, therapeutic, and reproductive cloning, Dolly's 1-in-277 success rate, the impossibility of clone caskets and inherited memories — while crediting the 1970s writers for correctly making mitochondrial DNA the blood test that distinguishes Peter from Ben Reilly. They then evaluate the characters' reactions: Leon Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance,' which holds that a clone's genotype 'has already lived' and despotically fixes its life's expectations, explains Kane's genocidal self-loathing and Peter's rage and despair when told he is the clone, while Gregory Pence's rebuttal — that such repugnance rests on false expectations, as with twins or children of interracial couples — vindicates MJ's and Ben's insistence that a clone's moral worth lies in what it does, not where its genes came from.

personal-identity.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
personal-identity.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Uses SAMCRO's ink—Jax's full Reaper backpiece and John Teller memorial, Opie's portrait of Donna, Tig's marine 'Death Before Dishonor,' Juice's head tattoos—to argue that personal identity lives in the body, not just the mind. Descartes's cogito opens the 'I ink, therefore I am' framing but proves too thin to connect the thinking Jax to the tattooed body, so the chapter turns to Merleau-Ponty's claim that 'it is the body which points out, and which speaks': the tattoo makes the body itself the expression, and its meaning stays inexhaustible as the wearer changes. The Kyle Hobart episode—burned and cut for failing to black out his Reaper after expulsion—shows tattoos as identity claims the community can veto, making 'fire or knife' an enforced correction of a false statement about who he is.

personal-identity.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
personal-identity.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Uses Paul Ricoeur's distinction between idem-identity (sameness) and ipse-identity (selfhood) to dissolve the paradox of Tara's lower-back tattoo: she is bodily the same Dr. Knowles yet disavows the 19-year-old who got it, identity being the narrative that weaves the two together. Tig's mushroom-fueled apology to a doll and his 'I don't know who I am anymore' after killing Donna show character as the set of lasting dispositions by which we are recognized, while Opie's competing promises to Donna and SAMCRO anchor self-constancy up to his 'I got this' sacrifice for Jax. It closes with John Teller's manuscript as a narrative identity that receives no closure even in death — a just institution aiming at 'the good life with and for others' whose story Jax continues.

personal-identity.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: William Jaworski argues, opening with Breaking Bad's Skinny Pete and Badger, that you should never enter a transporter: after showing the MEM converter violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, he asks whether the reassembled pattern is you or a replica. He tests three escape routes—Vulcan katra substance dualism (The Wrath of Khan, The Search for Spock) in the tradition of Plato and Descartes; constitutionalism, on which you survive total replacement by robotic parts as Picard nearly does under Borg assimilation; and Parfit's survival-without-identity answer to Riker's fission in 'Second Chances'. Each fails or costs too much: dualism wrecks moral intuitions about killing, constitutionalism faces the two-Riker indeterminacy, and mere 'survival' cannot sustain the particularity of love.

personal-identity.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Trip McCrossin reads 'The Enemy Within's split Kirk (with its LBJ/Vietnam subtext) and 'Second Chances's two Rikers as a crash course in Locke's consciousness theory of personal identity, from 'Turnabout Intruder's body swap and reward-and-punishment problem to the transitivity-of-identity paradox that blocks both Kirks from being the original. Parfit's degrees of psychological connectedness, he argues, explain why TNG treats the both-Rikers-survive answer as uncontroversial where TOS agonized over it. But Thomas Riker's renaming, and David Wiggins's 'only a and b' rule, reveal that identity would become an extrinsic property if branching mattered—so the survival-versus-identity debate ends 'to be continued'.

personal-identity.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Uses Odo as a case study in George Herbert Mead's theory that the self emerges only through social interaction: language begins with significant gestures (Odo's tentacle-slap at Dr. Mora, his talking to the dying baby changeling in "The Begotten"), and specific others like Mora and Kira teach the attitudes that become the generalized other. The Meadian I/me split explains Ezri Dax's nine-selves crisis and Joran's emergence in "Field of Fire", and the failed outfield calls and Sisko's ejection of Rom in "Take Me out to the Holosuite" show characters still learning to take the attitude of the team. Odo's "justice trick" is reread as instinct rather than racial memory, his confession to Kira in "Heart of Stone" shows the name odo'ital ("nothing") redeemed by internalized others, and his choice of the station crew over the Great Link marks a cosmopolitan self.

personal-identity.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Sorts out Spock-Prime, bearded Mirror-Spock, and Abrams's Spock-2 using David Lewis's modal realism, counterparts, and Humean supervenience: identity is not directly perceived but judged from adjacent similar instances, as with Hume's natural properties. The refit Enterprise versus the Enterprise-A, plus the thought experiment of downloading the old ship's computer into the new one, carry a Ship-of-Theseus-style analysis of whether swapped cells and Spock's katra-separated death and Genesis resurrection preserve identity. Mirror-Spock turns out to be a worldmate within one enlarged world (Kirk's crossover in "Mirror, Mirror" makes the universes spatiotemporally continuous), not a transworld duplicate, and Spock-Prime and Spock-2 are like two highways overlapping until Nero's arrival in 2233 makes them diverge - two similar individuals formed by different successes and failures, never identical.

personal-identity.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Uses Palpatine's cloning of the last Zillo Beast, Boba Fett's SCNT creation from Jango, and Thrawn's Hand of Thrawn resurrection scheme to argue de-extinction is impossible: if species are individuals (Ghiselin's species nominalism, grounded in Darwinian variation against Aristotle's species essentialism), then extinction closes the species' unique life story, so any clone is a numerically distinct new individual. The same numerical-vs-qualitative identity point shows Thrawn's clone would not be Thrawn, and only Palpatine's dark-side survival in a cloned body - not cloning itself - counts as genuine resurrection.

personal-identity.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
personal-identity.title: “Good Soldiers Follow Orders”
personal-identity.relation: Brace uses Aristotle on numerical versus specific sameness, Locke's memory theory, and above all Frankfurt's second-order desires to argue the Jango Fett clones are distinct persons despite shared DNA: Fives's and Echo's accumulated memories and choices individuate them, and the Bad Batch's personalized quarters display what Yoda means by 'very different, each one of you are.' Frankfurt's 'wanton' frames Wrecker's impulsive Hulking, while Order 66 distinguishes freedom of action from freedom of will — Rex resists the chip's compulsion but cannot act on his second-order volition, so he never loses personhood. Crosshair's reveal that his chip was long removed recasts his loyalty to the Empire as a freely chosen (if immoral) second-order volition, his right as a person.

personal-identity.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department
personal-identity.title: A Real Lasting Legacy: Memory, Imagination, and Taylor Swift
personal-identity.relation: Uses Swift's songs to sort episodic, procedural, and semantic memory ('Christmas Tree Farm', guitar-playing, her December 13 birthday) and argues episodic memory underwrites both narrative identity (Schechtman), heard in 'The Moment I Knew' and being 'paralyzed' in 'All Too Well', and Lockean personal identity, where 'Hold on to the memories / They will hold on to you' makes memories constitutive of the person who survives over time. Locke's forensic person is invoked to connect memory with responsibility, so 'Would've, Could've, Should've' makes memories 'weapons' that force us to own past actions. The chapter then tests 'continuism' (memory as a kind of imagination, observer vs field memories) against the fact that Swift remembers a particular Christmas tree farm that caused her memory.

personal-identity.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.title: NOTES
personal-identity.relation: Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.

personal-identity.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
personal-identity.title: NOTES
personal-identity.relation: Grubb tests theories of personal identity on the supes: the bodily theory fails because Bill's and Jessica's bodies died and refunctioned at transformation, Locke's memory theory stumbles on amnesiac Eric (who stays Eric despite remembering nothing), and psychological continuity fails because vampirism inflated Bill's aggression and collie-Sam's mind when Andy draws a gun is anyone's guess. She closes with Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism — lives as long stories of temporal parts — which lets the rambunctious vampire Jessica count as the same person as the demure human girl because both are episodes in one continuing story.

personal-identity.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
personal-identity.title: Notes
personal-identity.relation: Divides Rust's season-one personae into Taxman (anti-natalist rule-follower), Belligerent (vigilante drunk paralyzed by Nietzsche's Gay Science demon of eternal recurrence), and Patient (the mystic who wakes from his coma feeling his daughter's love, compared to the Persian mystic al-Hallaj), asking what makes them one person. It tests the brute physicalist account (Williams and Ayer — the same bird-tattooed body), the Lockean psychological-continuity account, and the narrative account, arguing only the narrative theory explains how Rust changes without either ignoring change or multiplying selves in one body. The chapter ends by making Rust an exemplar for the viewer: we are narrators who choose who to become, so 'I know who I am' is a victory.

personal-identity.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
personal-identity.title: 7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me
personal-identity.relation: Lay applies Locke's memory theory to 'Person or Persons Unknown' and 'The After Hours': without factive memories linking David Gurney to his supposed past, and Marsha to her mannequin history, identity is lost in both directions. 'The Lateness of the Hour' strains the view, since Jana's implanted 'memory tracks' are not memories of real events yet she plainly is someone, and Reid's chain objection shows memory alone cannot span a life. Parfit's psychological continuity over the whole network of mental states resolves the cases, and 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' completes it: the post-Transformation person keeps Marilyn's memories but none of her desires or traits, so Marilyn did not survive.

personal-identity.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
personal-identity.title: Acknowledgment
personal-identity.relation: James South reads season one as Veronica forging a new identity after learning she is 'no longer that girl' — Lilly dead, Keith recalled, Lianne gone, herself raped — with her detective photography and knowing voiceovers enacting what Stanley Cavell calls viewing the world 'from behind the self,' an automatism that escapes subjectivity at the price of isolation and false certainty. The unicorn music box playing 'All You Need Is Love' marks the marshmallow beneath the noir shell: her detective work is really a quest to restore the fantasy family, which dies as she discovers her mother's alcoholism ('I bet on you, and I lost') and accepts the paternity results that let her choose Keith as father 'in a way that runs deeper than blood.' Renouncing the fantasy, she arrives at the new self who opens the door with 'I was hoping it would be you.'

personal-identity.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
personal-identity.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether you survive a walker bite, rejecting the body view via Dr. Jenner's 'Everything you ever were or ever will be—gone' because a mindless corpse is not you. He tests philosophical behaviorism and functionalism against walker behavior—Jenny turning her old doorknob, walkers distinguishing humans by smell—then adapts Dennett's thought experiment into a walker-and-rope computer functionally identical to a human brain. Since we can conceive that groaning machine lacking inner experience, behavior and function cannot settle which systems are conscious, leaving the bitten dying in ignorance of whether they face annihilation or reanimation.

personal-identity.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
personal-identity.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Dave Beisecker takes AMC's 'stagger-on role' zombie contest as an amplified version of Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why relish playing a repulsive walker when zombification is the fate no rational creature would wish even on its remains? He rejects the curiosity solution through Nagel's bat—no staggering around a set could reveal what it is like to be a zombie, and we wouldn't survive zombification anyway except as our remains—and notes we fantasize about being survivors, not monsters. His answer is affection and release: walkers are the geeks and clowns of the undead pantheon, and playing one lets us comically own our inner loser, which is why Kirkman's symbol-free zombies invite identification where Nazi zombies would not.

personal-identity.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
personal-identity.title: P A R T T H R E E
personal-identity.relation: James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.

personal-identity.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
personal-identity.title: “Do you even know where you are ”
personal-identity.relation: Marcus Arvan argues from show evidence (William stepping onto a moving train, pyrotechnic effects, instant crowds, graphically rearranging the park) that all of Westworld, lab included, is a videogame, and defends his 'Peer-to-Peer Simulation Hypothesis' as an explanation of quantum mechanics and relativity, citing Bostrom and Chalmers. Adopting functionalism/structuralism, he claims that anything doing what a human does is a person, so hosts like Dolores and Maeve are no less real or human than us, inverting Descartes' cogito and invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature. He warns that dehumanizing hosts, or dismissing Siri and Watson as unconscious, repeats the logic used to justify slavery and the Holocaust: to be simulated is to be real.

personal-identity.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
personal-identity.title: From Westworld to the World Outside and Back
personal-identity.relation: Onni Hirvonen argues that equating 'person' with 'human' is anthropocentrism, and surveys three accounts of personhood applied to the hosts: Dennett's capacity approach (self-consciousness, using Arnold's 'maze/journey inward'), Locke's performative 'forensic' approach (Bernard performs flawlessly as a person), and a Hegelian historical-struggle approach. Reading the hosts' revolt through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and Axel Honneth's expanding spheres of recognition, he compares their exclusion to the historical denial of personhood to indigenous Australians and women. He warns that merely inverting master and slave, or exterminating the humans, would leave no one to grant the mutual recognition the hosts actually seek, so only expanding recognition to include both counts as moral progress.

personal-identity.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
personal-identity.title: Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful
personal-identity.relation: Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.

personal-identity.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
personal-identity.title: Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve
personal-identity.relation: Trapero-Llobera situates Westworld within Jonathan Nolan's body of work (Memento, Person of Interest), arguing the show's apparent complexity hides a classic hero's-journey structure organized around observing systems and a 'semiosis of virtuality.' She reads William/the Man in Black as a 'schizoid android' and catalyst-observer, and Ford/Bernard as creator-and-prosthetic-memory pairs echoing Finch and the Machine. Turing's imitation game frames the hosts' fabricated memories, while Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns mark a shift from prosthetic to autopoietic, Bergsonian memory-recollection that turns them into observers building their own selves.

personal-identity.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
personal-identity.title: “When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”
personal-identity.relation: Lean treats Bernard's grief over the fabricated son Charlie as a thought experiment about intentionality, using Brentano's 'aboutness' and Frege's sense/reference (illustrated by Dolores knowing 'William' and 'the Man in Black' as one referent) to ask whether Bernard's memories refer to nothing. He offers Lamarque's fiction theory (emotion needs only entertained, not believed, thoughts, so Charlie could be a fiction rather than a lie) and an 'inheritance theory' using a causal theory of reference to ask whether Bernard's memories actually refer to Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that grieving makes Bernard 'most real' whatever the metaphysics.

personal-identity.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
personal-identity.title: II - AMNESIA, PERSONAL IDENTITY, AND THE MANY LIVES OF WOLVERINE
personal-identity.relation: Southworth uses Wolverine's serial mind-wipes to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory criterion, illustrated by Cassandra Nova and Charles Xavier swapping bodies in New X-Men, sorts Wolverine's history into distinct persons sharing one body (James Howlett, Logan, Team X, Mutate #9601, Weapon X), while Parfit's fission worries, mapped onto Jamie Madrox's duplicates, show sameness of memory is neither necessary nor sufficient for identity. The moral payoff: if Parfit's 'sameness of brain' view is right, we should be slow to blame the present Wolverine for Weapon X's atrocities, and equally slow to judge Emma Frost, Beast, or a resurrected Jean Grey.

personal-identity.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
personal-identity.title: Playing for the Same Team Again
personal-identity.relation: A fictional five-day phone dialogue between Michael Jordan and Phil Jackson works through the metaphysics of team identity before Jordan's 1995 comeback: qualitative versus numerical sameness, necessary and sufficient conditions ('same players, same positions'), Heraclitus's river, and whether the Bulls survive gradual turnover. The Ship of Theseus becomes the 'Boars' puzzle - the original five reassembled on an expansion team versus the continuous, degenerate Chicago roster - with Hobbes's two-ship twist, alongside the Minneapolis Lakers' move and a Bulls-Pistons gradual player swap. The resolution distinguishes the group (which persists by composition or continuity) from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only partly through fans' allegiance, echoing Searle's social reality; Jordan concludes he was asking the wrong question, and Aristotle's circular account of virtue supplies the model for circular criteria of loyal fandom.

personal-identity.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
personal-identity.title: Twelfth Hole Midround and Midlife Defining Moments
personal-identity.relation: Andy Wible uses defining mid-round shots (the water ball on Augusta's twelfth, the shank that ruins a round) as a way into theories of personal identity, asking why some events make us who we are. He runs through body theory, Descartes's soul theory ('I think, therefore I am'), and Locke's memory theory (the prince-and-cobbler case), refining it with Shoemaker's quasi-memories, to argue that memory is central to identity and explains why a golfer cannot shake a bad shot. He then weighs the Buddhist/Humean/Heraclitean denial of a permanent self as a coping tool ('someone else hit the shank') and debates whether the beta-blocker Propranolol, which dulls adrenaline-fixed memories, could ethically erase the yips much as it treats PTSD.

personal-identity.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
personal-identity.relation: Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.

personal-identity.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
personal-identity.title: Introduction
personal-identity.relation: LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.

personal-identity.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
personal-identity.title: The Instructive Impossibility of Being John Malkovich
personal-identity.relation: Hagberg treats Being John Malkovich as a refutation of the dualist fantasy that one could achieve transparent knowledge of another mind by occupying it. Through the film's four levels—Schwartz as spectator inside Malkovich, Lotte's transgender re-embodiment, Schwartz's puppeteering, and Malkovich falling into his own portal to the 'Malkovich, Malkovich' hell—he shows, via Jamesian relational sensation and Wittgenstein's private-language argument, that it is always still Schwartz who senses, so no one ever becomes Malkovich. The self-enclosed Malkovich world, where everyone can only say 'Malkovich,' dramatizes that selfhood is relationally emergent (Royce, Mead) and that experience is inviolably one's own (Margalit on remembered emotion).

personal-identity.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
personal-identity.title: Introduction
personal-identity.relation: Simon Riches's introduction frames the whole volume around Cronenberg's obsession with the Cartesian mind-body split, quoting the director that horror comes from being unable to reconcile a sharp mind with a dying body. It surveys the three parts of the book, showing how films like The Fly stage bodily transformation and personal identity, eXistenZ stages skepticism about the external world, and A History of Violence stages the nature of the self, arguing Cronenberg wears his philosophical interests 'on his sleeve.'

personal-identity.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
personal-identity.title: Tragedy and Terrible Beauty in A History of Violence and Eastern Promises
personal-identity.relation: Cynthia Freeland argues A History of Violence and Eastern Promises qualify as Aristotelian tragedies, using the Poetics' 'recognition and reversal' as Tom Stall is exposed as Joey Cusack and Nikolai's undercover identity is revealed. Analyzing the stairway sex scene, the Philadelphia gunfight, and Nikolai's naked bathhouse fight, she deploys Korsmeyer's notion of 'terrible beauty' (beauty in the horrific, like the bloody newborn) and Carroll/Gaut on empathy and identification, concluding both heroes commit an Aristotelian hamartia through their acceptance of violence.

personal-identity.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
personal-identity.title: Cronenberg as Scientist Antiessentialism, Sex as Remixing, and the View from Nowhere
personal-identity.relation: Peter Ludlow argues Cronenberg's true horror is scientific antiessentialism: The Fly, Shivers, Videodrome, and eXistenZ collapse the supposedly essential boundaries between human and fly, organic and mechanical, real and virtual, sane and mad, good and evil. Drawing on Quine's rejection of essence, Kripke's empirical essentialism, and Darwinian biology, he reads Brundle's fusion and Renn's VCR-stomach as showing we have no essence; sex is 'remixing' of information to lock out parasites, and Cronenberg narrates from Nagel's impersonal 'view from nowhere' where humans are not special.

personal-identity.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
personal-identity.title: What Happens to Brundle Problems of Teleportation and Personal Identity in the Fly
personal-identity.relation: Paul Snowdon uses The Fly to press the metaphysics of teleportation and personal identity, asking whether the object leaving the first pod is identical to the one arriving or merely a replica (the reduplication problem). Adopting animalism, he argues Brundle likely ceases to exist at first teleportation, and that the fly-Brundle fusion is a new creature rather than Brundle, so Quaife's belief she is euthanizing Brundle is unsupported; a Lockean memory-based view (via Parfit) could vindicate her, but the audience's 'blind acceptance' of it gives that theory no evidential support.

personal-identity.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
personal-identity.title: Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds
personal-identity.relation: Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.

personal-identity.book: 219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg
personal-identity.title: Self-Creation, Identity, and Authenticity A Study of A History of Violence and Eastern Promises
personal-identity.relation: Daniel Moseley distinguishes metaphysical from practical problems of personal identity, arguing A History of Violence and Eastern Promises explore the practical: who Tom/Joey and Nikolai really are, as a matter of self-creation and self-discovery of a 'practical identity' (Korsgaard). Using Sartre's bad faith and Cavell on movie-star 'individualities,' plus Charles Taylor's critique of individualist authenticity, he argues even the wicked Semyon exemplifies authenticity, so authenticity is not a moral ideal, and Nikolai's decent double life may be worth being less authentic.

personal-identity.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
personal-identity.title: 14. Diane, I Am Now Upside Down
personal-identity.relation: McMullen and Phillips take up the paradox of fiction (Radford's 'How Can We Be Moved by the Fate of Anna Karenina?'): how can Cooper, whom we know is not real, cause genuine emotion? Using the criterion that what exists has causal powers, they reject the forgetting, suspension-of-disbelief, and reminds-us-of-real-people explanations, and adopt Amie Thomasson's view (Fiction and Metaphysics) that characters are real abstract artifacts—like laws or the United States. This lets them explain our parasocial interaction with Cooper (treating him as a friend over coffee) and wishful identification (wanting to be him) as responses to something that genuinely, if abstractly, exists.

personal-identity.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch
personal-identity.title: 16. Doppelgängers, Doubles, and Tulpas
personal-identity.relation: Bunce reads Twin Peaks' pervasive doubling as dramatizing self-loss versus self-mastery. Cooper is good because he integrates his rational and mystical sides into an authentic whole, while BOB is a parasitic, one-dimensional inhabiting spirit and Laura chooses death over becoming BOB. He explains self-loss through La Rochefoucauld and Rousseau on amour-propre and the modern craving for esteem (Josie's masks versus Norma's refusal to become a brand), and traces the doppelganger motif from Jean Paul's satire of Fichte's clear I/not-I distinction to Dostoyevsky's The Double—arguing that, unlike Jean Paul, Twin Peaks affirms an authentic, whole self one is responsible for.

personal-identity.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
personal-identity.title: The Logic of Lolita Kubrick, Nabokov, and Poe Jerold J. Abrams
personal-identity.relation: Abrams argues Kubrick's and Nabokov's Lolita is a philosophical detective story descended from Poe's Dupin tales, and that Humbert fails as a detective because he lacks the right logic. Using Peirce's abduction (and Eco's overcoded/undercoded/creative types), he shows Humbert excels at 'overcoded' guesses—spotting a nymphet at a glance—but cannot make the 'undercoded' abductions needed to see that Quilty is shadowing him, because he is all chess-like calculation and no playful 'musement' or acumen. Humbert (the resolvent) and Quilty (the creative) split Poe's 'bi-part' double-Dupin; Quilty the changeling-Minotaur controls the labyrinth and dies behind Lolita's portrait as a self without a unified identity.

personal-identity.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
personal-identity.title: Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity
personal-identity.relation: The chapter uses the Wes–Holtz dispute over whether Angel owes punishment for Angelus's murders (Holtz's body-continuity view, glossed via Hobbes) to test theories of personal identity across the Whedonverse. It argues the shows present a Platonic separate soul as the metaphysical locus of identity — Fred ceasing to exist when Illyria consumes her soul, the shaman's soul-jar in 'Awakening,' the Judge finding Angelus 'clean' — while Angel's felt guilt, Darla's and Spike's resurrections, Buffy's and Faith's body switch, and Dollhouse's wiped Actives press the Lockean memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity successor. The Angel/Angelus case — eidetically shared memories but radically disconnected intentions, desires, and ethical sensibilities, developed over some 200 episodes — is offered as a richer cinematic counterexample than Locke's Day-Man/Night-Man or Parfit's fission triplet, forcing Neo-Lockeans to choose between memory chains and other psychological connections, and supporting Amy Kind's point that identity alone is not what matters for moral responsibility. Whedon's own verdict follows Parfit in discarding numerical identity but turns toward an ethics of care: what matters is staying properly psychologically connected to those one loves, so one 'finds out who you are' by being countable-on in ethically significant action.

personal-identity.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.relation: Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.

personal-identity.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.relation: Smith reads Memento as a test of Locke's memory theory of personal identity. He explains Locke's view that consciousness of past actions (not soul or body) constitutes the self, rehearses Reid's transitivity objection and the circularity objection, and uses Parfit's account of memory and fusion to defend a survival-not-identity reading. He distinguishes 'Leonard 1' (anterograde amnesiac who returns each cycle) from 'Leonard 2b', a person fused from his own memories and those projected onto Sammy Jankis, arguing we too are 'fused' survivors who reinterpret hazy pasts, complicating responsibility and concern for our futures.

personal-identity.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.relation: Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.

personal-identity.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
personal-identity.relation: Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.

personal-identity.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
personal-identity.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
personal-identity.relation: Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.

personal-identity.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
personal-identity.title: What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City
personal-identity.relation: Knight and McKnight read Blade Runner and Dark City as noir-influenced cyberpunk that asks what it is to be human. They argue that Deckard's replicant status (the origami unicorn, the shared family photo) and Murdoch's serially reprogrammed memory show memory to be unreliable, invoking Locke's prince-and-cobbler thought experiment and the problem of new brains in one body. Their conclusion is that it is emotion and relationship, not memory, that ground agency and personhood: Roy's empathy in dying and Deckard's love for Rachael, Murdoch's love for Emma/Anna, are what mark the characters as human.

personal-identity.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
personal-identity.title: Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall
personal-identity.relation: Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.

personal-identity.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
personal-identity.title: Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers
personal-identity.relation: Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.

personal-identity.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
personal-identity.title: Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys
personal-identity.relation: Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.

personal-identity.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
personal-identity.title: Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X
personal-identity.relation: LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.

personal-identity.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
personal-identity.relation: Eberl compares HAL in 2001 and David in A.I. to ask whether an artificially created being can be a person meriting respect and rights. He runs both through criteria of personhood—self-consciousness, rationality, social activity, autonomy—and Turing's imitation game/behaviorism, concluding their responses give sufficient evidence of personhood even if the soul question is open. He uses Hegel's master–slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their creations (Bowman disconnecting HAL; the Flesh Fair destroying Mechas), warning against a moral crime of 'biological supremacy,' and invokes Aristotle's telos/virtue to argue Flesh Fairs wrongly preclude Mechas from fulfilling their function, while David's Pinocchio 'leap of faith' and cry 'I'm special, I'm David!' mark his approach to personhood.

personal-identity.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
personal-identity.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.

personal-identity.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
personal-identity.relation: Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.

personal-identity.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
personal-identity.relation: Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.

personal-identity.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
personal-identity.relation: King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.

personal-identity.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
personal-identity.relation: Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.

personal-identity.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Popular Culture
personal-identity.relation: Morton reads Schizopolis as Soderbergh's philosophical autobiography of identity, quoting Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding on memory as the ground of personal continuity to interpret Fletcher Munson's 'transmigration' into the doppelganger Dr. Korchek. Because Fletcher carries his own memory and nature into Korchek, he cannot escape his failed marriage (Korchek is sleeping with Fletcher's wife), confirming Lockean continuity: he 'cannot escape his own nature.' Morton ties the film's decayed language games and Elmo Oxygen's gibberish to a view that language masks action, and reads Fletcher's fate-frozen ending as identity surrendered to outside forces.

personal-identity.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
personal-identity.relation: The editor's introduction frames the whole collection around three topics in Burton's corpus—identity, authority, and aesthetics—and previews each essay. On identity it contrasts an essentialist "core self" with an empirical, experience-built self, using Big Fish and Batman Returns as test cases; on authority it surveys Mars Attacks!, Sleepy Hollow, and Batman; on aesthetics it points to Sweeney Todd, death, and color. It functions as a roadmap that argues Burton's films merit philosophical reading rather than advancing one philosopher's thesis.

personal-identity.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
personal-identity.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
personal-identity.relation: Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.

personal-identity.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
personal-identity.title: CSI and the Art of Forensic Detection
personal-identity.relation: Knight and McKnight analyze CSI as 'procedural noir': Las Vegas instantiates the corrupt-city trope, and the show's methodological core is reading scientific evidence as a system of signs, generating and testing hypotheses through hypothetical flash reconstructions (Grissom's wrong incest-guess in 'Blood Drops', competing crash theories in 'Anonymous'). Three case studies carry the philosophy: Philip Gerard's defense attack on the team's competence makes forensic investigation an ethical matter of integrity and reliable process rather than mere evidence collection; the Paul Millander trilogy uses the trope of the double (Paul/Pauline, Judge Mason, the forged Grissom identity) to explore identity and self-knowledge; and Lady Heather's dominance-submission 'stop' convention reframes the femme fatale around reason, passion, and Grissom's desire to be known.

personal-identity.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
personal-identity.title: The Prisoner and Self-Imprisonment
personal-identity.relation: Biderman and Devlin use The Prisoner to test three dimensions of selfhood: Number 6's 'I am not a number!' defends the material self against the Village's conformity (Rover, uniforms, human chess pieces), his reflective self echoes Descartes's certain thinking thing, Kant's rational self-legislation, and Sartrean authenticity ('existence precedes essence'), while the finale's trial of the rebels addresses the relational self. The revelation that Number 6 is Number 1 is then read through Foucault: hierarchical observation, normalization, and examination make the Village Bentham's panopticon internalized, so the prisoner monitors himself and the ideal of a freely self-created identity collapses into social conditioning, as Nietzsche's herd come home. The chapter leaves the noir ambiguity intact: either Number 6 is the authentic individual vindicated by the Village council, or the self is a fiction and his odyssey hopeless.

personal-identity.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book
personal-identity.title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence and the Tragic Sense of Life
personal-identity.relation: Dunn interprets A.I. as a meditation on the 'tragic sense of life': treating David as a person, he argues the film dramatizes three doomed human desires (love, uniqueness, immortality) and tests two failed escapes from mortality, science (Professor Hobby, the Flesh Fair, David's suicide leap) and religious faith (the fraudulent Blue Fairy at drowned Coney Island). Defending the maligned finale, he reads the simulated Blue Fairy and the one-day resurrection of Monica as raising whether a perfect simulation of love can be 'real enough,' with David achieving a sober humanistic acceptance of impermanence.

personal-identity.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young
personal-identity.relation: Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).

personal-identity.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
personal-identity.title: “Are You Watching Closely ”
personal-identity.relation: Knight and McKnight analyze how Nolan's early films withhold narrative transparency: Doodlebug's regress of killers, Following's framing device that ends with Cobb vanishing into a crowd, Memento's reverse chronology, and The Prestige's twin frames of top hats and drowned doubles all force viewers to build and revise hypotheses about what happened, when, and who is responsible. Because actions cannot be morally evaluated until we know who performed them and why, the chapter ties narrative comprehension to moral judgment—Leonard's confabulated revenge and inability to recognize his own self-deception, Dormer's ambiguous redemption, and Ellie's unresolved choice over the bullet. The Prestige's doubles raise the identity question the authors gloss with Parfit's teletransporter—perhaps it does not matter which Angier survives—while Cutter's helping Borden kill Caldlow enacts Francis Bacon's 'wild justice' that the law cannot provide. The chapter closes on Nolan as auteur, whose self-conscious framing devices and play of masks make 'Are you watching closely?' at once the film's theme and its admonition to the viewer.

personal-identity.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
personal-identity.title: “You Don’t Know Who You Are”
personal-identity.relation: Peter Fosl argues that Nolan's protagonists are divided selves - public and private - whose self-creation runs through narratives and material signs (Memento's tattoos and Polaroids, Inception's safes, the Batcave, the Prestige twins' offstage swaps) that others can always reinterpret, steal, or manipulate.
