Following J.L. Austin on performative acts, he reads Following's Bill as losing authorship of his own story to Cobb's counter-narrative and Bruce Wayne as only ever performing roles written in advance, even at the Dark Knight ending's Florentine café. Augustine's memoria and Locke's memory-continuity ground the discussion of Leonard's broken self-knowledge ('You don't know who you are'), while Nietzsche on forgetting, Gadamer on the past's effective history, and Sartre on the dead as prey for the living frame how Leonard's forgotten past selves manipulate him into murdering Teddy and how Interstellar's Cooper reaches back through the Tesseract to alter his own past.

personal-identity.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
personal-identity.title: “Memory Man”
personal-identity.relation: David LaRocca reads Memento through Andy Clark and David Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis: Leonard's tattoos, Polaroids, and notecards just are his memory, doing exactly what Otto's notebook does in their original example - so that writing 'Don't believe his lies' on a Polaroid is literally modifying his mind and carries the moral significance of interfering with his person. Drawing on Liao and Sandberg's ethics of memory modification and Noël Carroll's account of the film's reverse-ordered narrative, the chapter argues Leonard remains a culpable moral agent in his lucid moments: he knowingly 'incepts' a false command into his own extended mind to preserve the avenging-husband narrative that constitutes his identity, becoming a serial killer. It closes on our epistemic and moral duty of cognitive fidelity - to build truthful narrative identities rather than lie to ourselves into murder.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: A Dead End
personal-identity.relation: Patrick Stokes uses the Doctor's regeneration and the multi-Doctor stories ("The Five Doctors," "The Caves of Androzani") to test theories of personal identity. He runs Locke's memory criterion against Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's Branch-Line teleportation case (a Gallifrey-to-Skaro replica), Nozick's Closest Continuer schema applied to the Valeyard, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity, showing each fails to explain regeneration. He gestures that identity may lie in a subjective self-appropriation, the Doctor taking ownership of his incarnations.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer
personal-identity.relation: Greg Littmann uses regeneration and dozens of Doctor Who transformations (doubles like the Abbot of Amboise, disembodied brains, transmats, Eldrad's body-hopping, Cassandra's possession) as hypotheticals to test criteria for personal identity. He shows bodily identity, spatiotemporal continuity of the body, the memory criterion (undercut by Donna and John Smith cases), and psychological/personality similarity each face counterexamples, deliberately leaving the question open so readers judge for themselves.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: What’s Persistence Without Identity
personal-identity.relation: Richard Hanley asks what counts as personal survival for a Time Lord, distinguishing body, mind, and soul theories. Using the Tenth Doctor's "every single cell" regeneration, the severed hand grown into a Doctor in "Journey's End," John Smith's Chameleon-Arch amnesia, and Jackson Lake's infostamp fugue, he argues bodily and soul continuity fail and defends a neo-Lockean mental-continuity criterion refined by Nozick's closest-continuer schema, concluding with Parfit that persistence may not be what matters in survival.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think
personal-identity.relation: David Kyle Johnson uses regeneration and the DoctorDonna to ask what makes the First and Tenth Doctor the same person. He debunks the Platonic/Cartesian soul via Phineas Gage and brain science, refutes Locke's memory criterion with Reid's transitivity and the amnesia/John Smith cases, questions Parfit's causal-chain view via the "Journey's End" meta-crisis, then argues persons are four-dimensional "time worms" (sets of stages) before pushing to the deflationary conclusion that, like a "heap," a person may not exist as a discrete entity at all.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too
personal-identity.relation: Bonnie Green and Chris Willmott use the Daleks' human-factor experiments ("The Evil of the Daleks," "Dalek," "Daleks in Manhattan") to lay out the philosophy-of-biology "species problem": are species natural kinds, individuals, or sets? They trace essentialism from an Aristotelian God-given essence through Darwin's overthrow of it to modern genetic essentialism (the humanizing Dalek DNA), then use the Dalek/Thal split to survey biological species concepts and monism versus pluralism. They close with personhood and Peter Singer's speciesism, asking whether human-Dalek Sec would deserve rights.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity
personal-identity.relation: Michael Hand uses the Doctor's regeneration to argue that life after death is logically possible. Because the First-through-Tenth Doctors are the same person despite total personality change (a dandy becoming a clown), identity is distinct from personality, so a god perfecting flawed Joe for heaven need not make him someone else. He then tests the replica theory against 'Journey's End' (the metacrisis Doctor) and 'Human Nature' (John Smith), concluding we favor bodily continuity, and endorses van Inwagen's 'divine cryonicist' solution to the unavailability-of-atoms problem, echoing the Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' praise of frozen humanity in 'The Ark in Space'.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: Love and Doctors
personal-identity.relation: Paul Dawson asks whether the Doctor dies when he regenerates by separating body, organism, and person. Using Kripke's rigid vs non-rigid designators he weighs whether 'the Doctor' names one individual or a role (the numbered Doctors, 'my replacements'), then applies Locke's memory criterion and Reid's transitivity objection, adopting Parfit's psychological-connectedness chain (via Sarah Jane's overlapping memories). He concludes the organism survives regeneration necessarily while the person survives only if psychological continuity holds, and argues the 'Journey's End' metacrisis Doctor Two is genuinely the person Rose loved through branching/fission.

personal-identity.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: One More Thing, Don’t Blink!
personal-identity.relation: Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.

personal-identity.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
personal-identity.title: 5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality
personal-identity.relation: Hellwig uses Dean's choice of Hell over Doc Benton's organ-replacement immortality in 'Time Is on My Side' to examine medical immortality. He pairs Dean's worry—that maiming and replacing your body makes you unrecognizably human—with Bernard Williams's Makropulos argument that immortality ends in categorical-desire-exhausting boredom, adding a third condition to Williams: a recognizably human life requires being able to self-identify with one's own body, illustrated by real disfigurement cases and Aubrey de Grey's biogerontology.

personal-identity.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
personal-identity.title: 14. Baby’s Identity
personal-identity.relation: Doll uses the Winchesters' Impala 'Baby'—repeatedly totaled and rebuilt from replaced parts—as a running Ship of Theseus (from Plutarch) to probe what makes an object or person the same over time. She tests Aristotle's four causes (favoring the formal cause) and Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism, both of which falter, then notes Supernatural's souls solve personal identity for the resurrected Winchesters and alternate-universe doubles; since soulless Baby has no such thread, her identity rests on the subjective, family meaning the Winchesters invest in her.

personal-identity.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
personal-identity.title: 9. The Seven P’s of Real Punk
personal-identity.relation: Prinz catalogs the poser tests - no newbies, scene participation, mall-bought clothes, taste tests, selling out, doctrinaire politics, pop punk - and argues punk is an identity, not a club: personal identity encompasses social identity, resisting narrative theories like Schechtman's that separate the personal from the social, a point his aesthetic-self survey (taste change feels like becoming a different person) confirms. This generates the Poser Paradox - everyone copies a role others created, so all punks are posers - which he escapes, or embraces, via Seven P's of subcultural capital (Priority, Pansophy, Preferences, Performance, Proficiency, Peril, Persistence), concluding with Poly Styrene that punks are genuine fakes.

personal-identity.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
personal-identity.title: 8. Self-Hatred as Identity
personal-identity.relation: Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.

personal-identity.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam
personal-identity.title: 10. Slippin’ Identity
personal-identity.relation: Šekrst uses Jimmy's many personas—Slippin' Jimmy, James McGill, Saul Goodman, Viktor St. Clair, Gene Takavic—to survey theories of personal identity. She shows psychological continuity (Locke's memory-based view) falters on sleep, comas, and Chuck's apparent dementia, and the brute-physical/bodily view falters on brain-transplant thought experiments and the Phineas Gage case ('no longer Gage'). She defends a narrativist account with a reality constraint: identity is the story one is disposed to tell about oneself, so Jimmy can disown Slippin' Jimmy and reidentify as Saul, and Gene can recall his Saul self—narrative being sufficient though perhaps not necessary for persistence, with others' stories contributing but the protagonist's being authoritative.

personal-identity.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
personal-identity.title: 19. Cleons and Cloning
personal-identity.relation: Heter examines the Cleon Dynasty's clones (Brothers Dawn, Day, Dusk) to ask what a clone actually is, rejecting definitions built on identity. He distinguishes numerical identity (the Mule just is Magnifico Giganticus) from qualitative identity (two copies of a book), then shows the Cleons fail to be qualitatively identical because of age, psychology, perceptual perspective, and even drifting genetics over time—so grounding cloning in shared qualitative/genetic identity yields the odd result that clones could gain or lose clone-status as their genes change. He instead proposes a causal definition: a clone is an organism whose genetic information results from an (imperfect) copying process originating in a donor, so Cleon I is not a clone but every later Cleon is.

personal-identity.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
personal-identity.title: Be Slow to Judge
personal-identity.relation: Southworth uses Wolverine and other X-Men to examine personal identity. Locke's memory criterion (illustrated by the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap and connected memories) implies that Wolverine's repeated amnesia makes him literally several successive persons until House of M restores all his memories. Jamie Madrox's up-to-100 duplicates function as a real-world version of Parfit's fission thought experiment, showing sameness of memory is insufficient for identity. Southworth applies Parfit's brain-based, seven-year view to Wolverine's constant healed head trauma and concludes we should be slow to judge characters as the 'same' culpable person.

personal-identity.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
personal-identity.title: “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”
personal-identity.relation: Littmann uses the Terminator films to ask whether machines can be persons. The Terminators clearly pass the Turing Test by convincingly passing for human, giving behavioral evidence that they think. Littmann then presses Searle's Chinese Room, reworked as a tiny non-English-speaking Austrian inside the T-101 reciting phonetic lines, to argue that behavior alone cannot prove genuine understanding or feeling. He concludes that the films' 'Terminator's-eye-view' shots, showing the world from the machine's perspective, are the strongest evidence that the machines are conscious and so may count as people surviving humanity's extinction.

personal-identity.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
personal-identity.title: None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It
personal-identity.relation: William J. Devlin applies David Lewis's distinction between external time and the traveler's personal time to Lost's season 5-6 time jumps, showing how Faraday's eternalist 'whatever happened, happened' (Chang's unbreakable rules) contrasts with the branching-universe model that Faraday later embraces with 'we're the variables.' Lewis's account resolves specific puzzles: why baby Miles and adult Miles can coexist without violating the indiscernibility of identicals, whether Faraday could kill his mother Eloise (the grandfather paradox), and the uncaused causal loop of the compass Locke and Richard pass between 1954 and 2007.

personal-identity.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
personal-identity.title: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
personal-identity.relation: Karavitis arranges thirteen Twilight Zone android/machine episodes on a moral spectrum from simple machines ('The Brain Center at Whipple's,' 'Steel') to indistinguishable androids ('The Lonely,' 'I Sing the Body Electric,' 'The Lateness of the Hour') to fully synthetic humans ('The Trade-Ins'). Using personhood, moral-agent/moral-patient distinctions, Aristotle's and Kant's views on animals, Singer and Regan on degrees not kinds, and Locke's memory theory of identity, he argues that if body-swapped Holts remain persons then scratch-built androids are persons too—so the destroyed androids were murdered, and evil is treating persons as disposable objects.

personal-identity.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
personal-identity.title: 7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me
personal-identity.relation: Lay contrasts Locke's memory theory of personal identity with Parfit's psychological-continuity view across several episodes. Locke's factive-memory account explains 'The After Hours' (Marsha the mannequin) and 'Person or Persons Unknown' (David Gurney's non-factive memories), but fails for 'The Lateness of the Hour' (android Jana has installed beliefs, not memories) and especially 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You,' where post-Transformation Marilyn keeps all her memories yet is a different person. Using a Reid-flavored chain of episodes, Lay argues Parfit gets it right: a whole overlapping network of mental states, not memory alone, individuates the self.

personal-identity.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
personal-identity.title: 10. Memories Are Made of This
personal-identity.relation: Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.

personal-identity.book: 264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy
personal-identity.title: Jane Austen and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Holdier asks how the many rival Elizabeth Bennets (Austen's, P.D. James's Death Comes to Pemberley, Grahame-Smith's zombie killer) can share an identity. He rejects the Cartesian cogito for ignoring circumstance and adopts Paul Ricoeur's ipse/idem distinction: the three Elizabeths may share the same ipse (moment-to-moment self and personality) while their different worlds produce distinct idem (narrative) identities. He then applies David Lewis's possible-world semantics and modal realism, arguing each Elizabeth is 'world-bound' and the others are her equally real 'counterparts,' sufficiently similar to be compared across worlds without being identical, so 'Elizabeth Bennet' can name both a single ipse and many idem narratives.

personal-identity.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
personal-identity.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
personal-identity.relation: Fink-Jensen, an anthropologist, uses narrative analysis and rites-of-passage theory (Van Gennep's separation/liminal/reincorporation stages) to examine how men construct the internal identity of 'father.' Drawing on interviews with first-time dads (Marc, Jim, Craig, Steve), she argues that because men lack the biological markers of pregnancy they feel alienated from the transition, and that Western 'couvade' activities – attending prenatal classes and appointments, hearing the heartbeat – plus telling birth stories function as rituals that cement fatherhood as an identity.

personal-identity.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
personal-identity.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
personal-identity.relation: Carreras, writing as a son, examines the ethical tension in the father-son relationship between using a father's inevitable influence and fostering the son's autonomy. Opening with Aristotle on parents loving children as 'something of himself,' he uses the case of Jerry (a lawyer) pressuring his son Jose (who loves 18th-century English literature) to argue for a 'foundational view' of autonomy – that the best life is one embraced 'from the inside,' likened to seeing without a value-blindfold – and advises fathers to ask 'Is this what he truly wants, or what I want?'

personal-identity.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.relation: Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.

personal-identity.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.relation: Kyle Fruh and Emily Thomas use tattoos to attack two questions of personal identity. Against Locke's dominant psychological (memory) account and for the unpopular somatic (bodily) account defended by Judith Thomson and Eric Olson, they argue the depth of people's attachment to their tattoos – individuating them or marking group membership – shows we identify with our bodies. On the 'Who am I?' question they argue tattoos have an 'anchoring effect' in narrative identity: permanent, irremovable ink (contrasted with new laser-removable ink, and with dehumanizing forced Auschwitz numbers) fixes a commitment 'come what may,' echoing Quine's phrase, so that 'when you get a tattoo, you tattoo you.'

personal-identity.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.relation: Rachel Falkenstern argues that although tattoos seem permanent, the embodied self is changing and finite, so tattoos are 'illusions of permanence.' Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology she dissolves the mind/body and self/tattoo boundary (we are our bodies, the world shapes us and we shape it); using the German aesthetic tradition from Kant to Hegel she reads a tattoo as a sensuous 'appearance of freedom' and links the Romantic notion of Bildung (self-formation) to choosing ink. She adds Foucault's aesthetic self-transformation and Shusterman's somaesthetics/Deweyan pragmatism to cast tattooing as reciprocal self-expression and self-creation that offers a glimpse of infinity within finitude.

personal-identity.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
personal-identity.relation: Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.

personal-identity.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
personal-identity.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
personal-identity.relation: Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.

personal-identity.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
personal-identity.title: The Vampire with a Soul Angel and the Quest for Identity
personal-identity.relation: Amy Kind uses Joss Whedon's Angel/Angelus to test theories of personal identity and moral responsibility. Body-swap episodes support the Lockean/Parfitian psychological (memory) theory over Olson's biological theory, and shared memories make Angel psychologically continuous with, hence identical to, Angelus. But Kind invokes Parfit's distinction between continuity and connectedness (with real cases like Katherine Power and Sara Jane Olson) to argue identity is not what matters: the ensouled Angel's radical break in psychological connectedness means he should not be held morally responsible for Angelus's atrocities. She closes with Mill that it is better to be Angel burdened by a soul than Angelus unburdened.

personal-identity.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
personal-identity.title: 4. Total Recall & The Sixth Day
personal-identity.relation: Rowlands treats Total Recall as a defence of the memory (psychological-continuity) theory of personal identity: erasing Quaid's memories and restoring Hauser's is an essential change that ends Quaid, so he fights for his existence. He works through and rejects the soul theory (dualism's problems) and body/brain theories via head-transplant and neuron-replacement thought experiments, distinguishing Aristotle's essential/accidental change and Heraclitus's river. The Sixth Day's cloning raises Parfit's fission/duplication problem: a double success cannot be a failure, driving him to abandon identity for a Heraclitean 'river of selves' bound by survival, not identity.

personal-identity.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
personal-identity.title: 9. Blade Runner
personal-identity.relation: Using Blade Runner's replicants ('I want more life, fucker!') and Roy's dying soliloquy, Rowlands asks how death can harm the one who dies. He states the Epicurean argument (while we live death is not yet; when dead there is no one to harm) and answers via harms of deprivation, illustrated by Tyrell's imagined brain damage. Drawing on Wittgenstein (death as the limit of life) and Heidegger's being-towards-death/being-towards-a-future, he distinguishes weak (non-conceptual) from strong (conceptual) possession of a future, arguing death harms more those with more invested. Linear time and the ultimate horizon of death are what let a life have meaning at all.

personal-identity.book: 298 - The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings
personal-identity.title: The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy
personal-identity.relation: Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.

personal-identity.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
personal-identity.title: Who is Who
personal-identity.relation: On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'

personal-identity.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
personal-identity.title: Be Slow to Judge
personal-identity.relation: Jason Southworth uses Wolverine's repeated memory erasures to test Locke's memory (and connected-memory) criterion of personal identity, arguing that on Locke's view a new 'person' inhabits Wolverine's body each time his memories are wiped, until House of M restores them all. He then deploys Jamie Madrox, whose duplicates share and re-merge memories yet act as distinct agents, as a real-comics version of Parfit's fission case, pushing Parfit's conclusion that identity requires physical (brain) continuity. Because Wolverine's healing factor constantly rebuilds his brain, the moral is to 'be slow to judge' whether a character is the same person who acted before.

personal-identity.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 5. Battlestar Galactica as Philosophy Breaking the Biopolitical Cycle
personal-identity.relation: Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.

personal-identity.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 18. Russian Doll as Philosophy Life Is Like a Box of Timelines
personal-identity.relation: The chapter treats Russian Doll's time loops (Season One) and time portals (Season Two) as vehicles for the metaphysics of time, comparing them to Groundhog Day and canvassing presentism, eternalism, and the growing-block theory. It argues the show is committed to a Parfit-style 'multiple timelines' solution to the problem of whether looped characters are numerically identical, and rejects a Berkeleyan idealist alternative. Its climax reads Nadia through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: unable to change significant past events, she becomes an 'absurd hero' who embraces her family and lot in life, smiling in the mirror, so Season Two's lesson (echoing Nietzsche's eternal recurrence) is that meaning comes from owning one's circumstances.

personal-identity.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 41. Blade Runner as Philosophy What Does It Mean to Be Human
personal-identity.relation: Shanahan argues Blade Runner is philosophical despite Ridley Scott's denial, using the replicants (Roy Batty, Rachael, Leon) as defamiliarizing 'mirrors' for the human condition. He shows the Nexus-6 replicants satisfy Descartes' two criteria for a thinking soul (linguistic flexibility, novel problem-solving) while human characters like Deckard prove as cold and empathy-deficient as the machines, collapsing the human/replicant distinction the Voight-Kampff test presumes. He then reads Rachael's implanted memories through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, Roy's 'tears in rain' death through Epicurean worries about finitude, and frames the whole via Plato's Cave line 'they are like us' — the replicants model our own concerns with memory, death, and the meaning of a temporally bounded life.

personal-identity.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 55. Avatar as Philosophy The Metaphysics of Switching Bodies
personal-identity.relation: Tepley asks whether Jake Sully's final body-switch with his avatar in Cameron's Avatar is metaphysically possible without brain transplant or souls. Using Locke's definition of a person and the transitivity of numerical identity, he shows animalism forbids body-switching, substance dualism (Descartes/Plato) is unavailable in the film's materialist world, and merely copying a brain pattern creates a duplicate, not the same person. His positive solution uses the constitution view (Aristotelian in origin) plus Clark's extended-mind idea to argue Jake literally extends into his avatar, then—via an analogy with split-brain corpus-callosum cases discussed by Nagel, Parfit, and van Inwagen—shrinks back so long as no second stream of consciousness forms, a model he extends to secular survival of death by mind-uploading.

personal-identity.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine
personal-identity.relation: Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

personal-identity.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
personal-identity.title: 85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality
personal-identity.relation: Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.

personal-identity.book: 310 - The Real Meaning of Doctor Who
personal-identity.title: 3. What Is Who
personal-identity.relation: The chapter runs the Doctor's regenerations and the 'Timeless Child' reveal through competing theories of personal identity: Plato's soul/Forms, Locke's memory continuity, and bodily continuity, all of which the Doctor's body-swaps and forgotten lifetimes defeat (the Twelfth Doctor's 'you are a broom' speech recasts the Ship of Theseus). It endorses an existentialist answer—personal identity is chosen and constantly 'becoming,' as the Thirteenth Doctor declares 'I know exactly who I am. I'm the Doctor'—and uses Sartre against Freud to explain how the Doctor and the Whovian fandom reconcile internal and external selves in a community of acceptance. It closes arguing that only an 'objective' immortality (memories preserved in the Matrix) survives death, not a subjective self.

aristotle-soul.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
aristotle-soul.title: Unknown
aristotle-soul.relation: Presents the life-source view held by some ancient Greek philosophers, on which the soul simply accounts for life itself, so that all living things, plants and animals alike, are ensouled. It applies the view to Rowling's world by noting that Blast-Ended Skrewts and even gillyweed would then have souls, though few philosophers today accept this conception.

aristotle-soul.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
aristotle-soul.title: “Luminous Beings Are We . . . Not This Crude Matter”
aristotle-soul.relation: Donnelly counter-reads The Empire Strikes Back against Aristotle's philosophical realism, in which nature is purposive, form and matter are inseparable, and each person is an irreplaceable primary substance. Lucas 'humanizes technology' - C-3PO reassembled like the Tin Woodsman, AT-ATs as beasts, Han slicing open the tauntaun with a sneer at its flesh, Luke admiring his new bionic hand - blurring Aristotle's art/nature distinction and reducing body to interchangeable machine parts, a Baconian will to power over nature that even Yoda's mind-over-matter training echoes (the chapter opens with Benjamin's remark that the copy eclipses the original). The result, he argues, is dehumanization: preferring the odorless tin heart to creaturely flesh trades the genuinely human for Gulliver's barn of horses.

aristotle-soul.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics
aristotle-soul.title: “Your Heavenly Father Feeds Them”
aristotle-soul.relation: Calef takes the Tides restaurant scene ('Who are you? What are you?') and Diogenes's plucked rooster versus Plato's 'featherless biped' as a springboard for testing every classic criterion of humanity against the film. Aristotle's rational soul fails because Mrs. Bundy's 'brain pans' reasoning is wrong and some humans cannot reason; Descartes's language test fails because the myna bird can learn to talk while horrified humans go mute; Rousseau's free will fails because the birds behave unpredictably and resist instinct while humans are trapped, caged, and herd-like; Aristotle's political animal and Hobbes's social contract fail because the town's hoods and lawbreakers contrast with birds that flock together across species. Even the appeal to God's favor turns dark, as the drunk quotes scripture while Revelation's birds gather for a supper of human flesh, leaving the film a mirror in which we must examine ourselves.

aristotle-soul.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
aristotle-soul.title: Transformers and Philosophy
aristotle-soul.relation: Spicher argues that when Bumblebee trades his beat-up 1976 Camaro for a shiny 2007 model only his appearance changes (an accidental change), never his identity, because transforming is part of a Transformer's essence like a human wearing a mask. Locke's memory continuity and Thomson's bodily criterion each fail - the embryo, coma, and corpse problems, plus the thought experiment of Megatron's memories transplanted into another body - so he defends an Aristotelian composite of form and matter in which the Spark is the soul-like form organizing the machine body, preserving identity through transformation as form guides matter toward actuality.

aristotle-soul.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
aristotle-soul.title: Transformers and Philosophy
aristotle-soul.relation: Eyestone argues Transformers are genuinely alive with souls by applying Aristotle's De Anima: self-motion, perception, and intellect fit Ratchet (who tells Buster 'I'm a machine, and I hear you!'), and even the troublesome nutritive faculty is secured, since Energon ingestion, agelessness, and building each other suit naturally immortal, semimortal beings whose reproduction resembles Primus's creation. He extends arete to machines - Megatron has the excellence of a military leader but not of a person, while Optimus's chosen, trained goodness (Grimlock's 'Autobot training,' the Aerialbots' decision in 'War Dawn') makes him virtuous - and answers his title question 'why not?', since Aristotle's mortal soul gives Transformers no worse a shot at heaven than we have.

aristotle-soul.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
aristotle-soul.title: Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood
aristotle-soul.relation: Rachel Robison asks why mythology — from Elizabeth Bathory's blood baths to Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, and True Blood's Sookie sensing and desiring Bill and then Eric — credits blood with immortality, youth, erotic compulsion, and shared knowledge, including the vampire's dark inversion of the Eucharist. Her answer runs through the history of philosophy and medicine: Aristotle, Empedocles, and Chrysippus located rationality in the heart and made blood its product, while Galen's humoral theory and bloodletting treated blood as the carrier of health, temperament, and identity — so blood naturally reads as the vehicle of personal identity, free will, and even knowledge, explaining how drinking it could transmit a maker's self to Sookie or Mina. She then asks whether the synthetic 'True Blood' of HBO's show could carry the same powers, concluding it works only if some property is shared with real blood or if the power attaches to the act of drinking what is taken as blood.

aristotle-soul.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
aristotle-soul.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
aristotle-soul.relation: A pub dialogue applies Aristotle's De Anima, where the soul is the first principle of living things, to cloning: since a living clone must have an emergent, unrepeatable soul, successfully cloning dinosaurs brings new life into existence, which is good, so cloning itself is ethical. It then argues that neither unguided natural selection nor a divine dragon-slayer who nonetheless allowed cloning technology gives us reason not to revive dinosaurs, against Malcolm's 'they had their shot'. But drawing on Plato's forms, it condemns Hammond for controlling rather than merely containing: the lysine contingency and enforced sterility leave the dinosaurs shadows of what they could be, denied their natural flourishing.

aristotle-soul.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
aristotle-soul.title: 15. My Zombie, My Self
aristotle-soul.relation: Greene asks what Walking Dead-type walkers are and answers with the Platonic method of definition learned from Socrates: place them in the genus undead (died but not at rest, neither alive nor dead) and differentiate them by differentia - corporeal, mindless, lacking superhuman or magical powers, still decomposing. Aristotle's hierarchy of life functions (nutrition, locomotion, reason) explains why walkers are not alive despite ambulating, and the standards of death (putrefaction, heart-lung, whole-brain, higher-brain) all certify that walkers are dead yet active. The chapter closes on personal identity - whether you survive becoming a zombie, as Carol's face at the barn and Carl's "she'll turn" about Lori presuppose - and admits the author chooses the self-interested reading that he could become his own zombie, for the sake of the scare.

aristotle-soul.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
aristotle-soul.title: 5. Other People’s Body Parts
aristotle-soul.relation: Explains Kyle Spencer's horror at the body Madison and Zoe assembled from other people's parts through the history of soul-body theories: Aristotle's De Anima account of the soul as the faculties of a living body (plus the Physiognomonics claim that small people have small minds - poor Ma Petite), Plato's Timaeus on body parts designed for philosophy and reincarnation into bodies fitted to one's vices, Avicenna's soul as a faculty-binding nexus that chooses its bodily vehicle like a vehicle serves its owner, and Merleau-Ponty's habitual body (the Axeman's axe as part of his body, phantom limbs), which best explains why walking around on someone else's legs 'has got to mess with you a little'.

aristotle-soul.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
aristotle-soul.title: 14. A Party to Celebrate the Personal
aristotle-soul.relation: Eric Mohr reads the 'Everybody's Special' week, Prince Tuesday shedding his royal cape because 'It's what's inside you that makes you special,' the plate factory that discards irregular plates, and King Friday's sameness mask-edict undone by Lady Elaine, as Max Scheler's personalism: persons are unique, unrepeatable 'individual value-essences' whose value only love discloses, which is why Corney's birthday party matters. Against the Aristotelian view that the soul is one universal form and our bodies merely individuate us, Scheler and Rogers hold the inner self is where difference deepens.

aristotle-soul.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
aristotle-soul.title: 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here
aristotle-soul.relation: Tepley uses Eleanor waking in Michael's office to pose the problem of numerical personal identity: what makes the person in the chair the very same person who died seconds earlier on Earth? He eliminates the same-body theory, since bodies stay behind and lack spatiotemporal continuity, the same-mind theory of psychological continuity, which fails on the 802 reboots and implies the absurdity that two duplicates would both be Eleanor, and the same-soul theory, which offers no criteria for sameness. The 'Janet(s)' revelation that the humans are recomposed from 'essences' turns out to be Aristotelian-Thomistic hylomorphism, committing the show to a same-soul theory of identity it never defends.

aristotle-soul.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
aristotle-soul.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
aristotle-soul.relation: Greg Littmann tests Sheldon's geek existence against Aristotle's ideal of living well: since humanity's distinctive function is reason (the DVD-player-and-screwdriver argument), a life devoted to thought like Sheldon's — down to his fantasy of being a thinking satellite in orbit — has genuine Aristotelian worth. The chapter argues Aristotle could even bless geek obsessions, because poetry explores universal hypotheticals (Terminator causal loops, Superman's laundry) and adventure fiction purges emotion much as tragedy's catharsis does. But Sheldon's arrogance ('Captain Arrogant'), rigid clinging to his spot on the couch, and selfishness toward Leonard and Howard would earn failing marks in virtue, so the modern geek gets a mixed yet partly vindicating report card.

aristotle-soul.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
aristotle-soul.title: Where Do We Go from Here
aristotle-soul.relation: Argues on Aristotelian–Thomist grounds that WALL-E and EVE cannot truly be intelligent: they are artificial because their formal cause lies outside them in the Buy n Large engineers' minds, whereas natural things like the captain, the cockroach, and the plant have intrinsic formal causes. Intelligence is the act of an intellectual soul — the formal cause of a living thing — so machines at best mimic WALL-E's grasp of spoon-ness, fork-ness, and spork-ness, as Kreeft's comparison of a computer to a library building that does not understand its books makes clear. The conclusion is that AI is qualitatively, not merely technologically, impossible, and Pixar's live-action cinematography is precisely what tricks us into taking the robots as real.

aristotle-soul.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness
aristotle-soul.title: The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat
aristotle-soul.relation: Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.

aristotle-soul.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
aristotle-soul.title: 12. How the Fork Did I Get Here
aristotle-soul.relation: Asks what makes the person sitting in Michael's office numerically identical to the person who died on Earth. The same-body theory fails because bodies stay behind (buried or cremated) with no spatiotemporal continuity; the same-mind theory of psychological continuity fails on the 802 memory-wiping reboots and the duplication case of two psychologically-continuous Eleanors; the same-soul theory cannot say what makes two souls the same soul. The chapter concludes that 'Janet(s)' — essences reconstituting themselves in Janet's void — quietly commits the show to Aristotelian and Aquinan hylomorphism, while leaving open how anyone (even Janet) could tell that two persons share an essence.

aristotle-soul.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
aristotle-soul.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
aristotle-soul.relation: Finkelman uses the Corps' strangest members, Mogo the sentient planet, Leezle Pon the smallpox virus, the billion-puffball Collective, and Dkrtzy RRR the mathematical equation, to run the philosophy-of-biology debate over what counts as an individual. Plato's 'carving nature at its joints' frames the question; Heraclitean flux and Parmenidean changelessness picture monism's extremes; Aristotle's substance and soul deny Mogo is a living individual since its ecosystems (the Resal) do not serve it as organs serve a body; Darwin's natural selection makes organisms the real units, with Sinestro's attacks a kind of artificial selection that adapted the Corps. Gene reductionism (George C. Williams and Dawkins) versus Gould's contextual pluralism then decides how to count one billion puffballs as one Lantern.

aristotle-soul.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
aristotle-soul.title: Notes
aristotle-soul.relation: Griem uses Perrin's telepathic bond with wolves, especially Hopper, to examine human-animal relationships and the assumed divide between human rationality and animal instinct. She traces the wolf's ambiguous image across Roman, Norse, Native American, and Christian traditions (Fenrir versus Geri and Freki; the Big Bad Wolf), and uses Plato's charioteer of the soul and Elyas's advice to control fear to frame the rational/emotional contrast. Citing cognition studies (Betty the tool-making crow) that suggest continuity between human and animal minds, she reads Perrin's fear of losing his humanity, his axe-versus-hammer struggle, and Hopper as anthropomorphized guardian animal in Tel'aran'rhiod to argue we should recognize animal rationality and embrace the beast within.

aristotle-soul.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
aristotle-soul.title: Notes
aristotle-soul.relation: Swanstrom and Fletcher analyze the saidin/saidar gender distinction through Aristotelian gender essentialism (men hot/active dominating saidin, women cool/passive surrendering to saidar) and hylomorphism. Using Balthamel's soul placed in a woman's body (Halima/Aran'gar) who still channels saidin, plus Avicenna's floating man and Descartes' dualism elevating soul to essence, they argue the soul, not the body, determines which half of the Power one touches, while Aquinas's soul-body union (needed by Birgitte and shown by the soulless Gray Men) preserves 'balance.' They then use hylomorphism to let showrunner Rafe Judkins strip gender essentialism yet keep saidin/saidar via 'Jain Doe': an ungendered soul leaning one way, correlated to sex only by biological population balance.

aristotle-soul.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
aristotle-soul.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
aristotle-soul.relation: Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.

aristotle-soul.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
aristotle-soul.title: 8. What Are You Hearing
aristotle-soul.relation: Wissner analyzes how the musical scores of dream/imagination episodes signal states of being, framing music through Plato (music as mimetic yet man-made and 'unreal,' functioning as image-evoking signs) and Aristotle (music forms images of character and, via ethos, can alter minds and moods). She shows how electronic instruments, reverberation, whole-tone and repeated melodies mark dream versus reality in 'Perchance to Dream,' 'A Stop at Willoughby,' 'Twenty-Two,' 'Shadow Play,' and 'The Midnight Sun,' arguing the scores answer whether characters are dreaming, awake, imagining, alive, or dead through contextual musical signs.

aristotle-soul.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
aristotle-soul.title: 3. Terminator I & II
aristotle-soul.relation: Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.

compatibilism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
compatibilism.title: A Rodent’s Destiny
compatibilism.relation: Takes Rowling's 2007 remark that there is 'no such thing as destiny' and maps the logical space it could occupy: compatibilist freedom within a predetermined course, libertarian freedom with a fixed future of true statements about what will happen, or an open future where claims about free choices are neither true nor false until made. The section asks whether Dumbledore means prophecies do not compel anyone or that their content is merely one of several possible futures.

compatibilism.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
compatibilism.title: Not His Mother’s Son
compatibilism.relation: Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.

compatibilism.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy
compatibilism.title: Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.

compatibilism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
compatibilism.title: Moral Autonomy
compatibilism.relation: Martin van Hees reads "Who Killed Davey Moore?" and "Ballad of Hollis Brown" as arguments that shared consent generates shared responsibility for tragedy even when fate makes the events inevitable - the referee, crowd, manager, and gambler all endorsed the fight, and we who tolerate poverty consent to the next Hollis Brown. He distinguishes a "limited optimistic view" (twisting fate by preventing particular tragedies) from the proclaimed inevitability of "The Times They Are A-Changin'" and the pessimism of "Blind Willie McTell," then defends compatibilism through Frankfurt's Jones/Black case: responsibility needs no alternative possibilities, only that one act from one's own will. Dylan's "moral autonomy" is taking a stance - singing the blues - inside a determined world.

compatibilism.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
compatibilism.title: Look Up, Look Up
compatibilism.relation: James Spiegel reads Dylan's God-haunted songwriting through philosophy of religion, sorting strong Augustinian-Aquinian providence ("Every Grain of Sand," "When He Returns") from the weak, risk-taking God of "Highway 61 Revisited" and "Joey." Dylan's moral judgmentalism combined with theological determinism makes him a compatibilist in Augustine's mold, while "Disease of Conceit" and "Pressing On" ("it run in my vein") press the compatibilist puzzle that Plantinga's libertarian power of contrary choice is meant to solve. Original sin becomes the "disease of conceit," and Socrates' Phaedo plus Kant's three postulates - God, freedom, immortality - ground Dylan's hope that "death is not the end," closing with Love and Theft's "Look up, look up."

compatibilism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
compatibilism.title: Introduction
compatibilism.relation: Frames Part III's metaphysics chapters. Lawrence's chapter uses The Matrix to survey dualism and the materialist theories of mind; Southworth's uses Wolverine's amnesia to test Locke's memory criterion and Jamie Madrox's duplicates for Parfit's view of identity; Pierce's asks whether Harry Potter's prophecies leave Harry free, probing compatibilism versus libertarian free will; and Littmann's asks whether Skynet's Terminators could be persons via a Terminator version of the Turing Test.

compatibilism.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
compatibilism.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
compatibilism.relation: Pierce asks what kind of prophecies Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are, starting from Aristotle's problem of future contingents and Alexander of Aphrodisias on self-fulfilling prophecy: Dumbledore's point that Voldemort's choice marked Harry shows the prophecy did not cause its own fulfillment. The Prisoner of Azkaban time travel — later Harry had always cast that Patronus — plus special relativity support a fixed future on which Rowling's denial of destiny amounts only to libertarian openness, and the chapter concludes that the wildly improbable luck fulfilling the prophecies (Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, the Sword of Gryffindor) makes best sense if some providential being is quietly guiding events.

compatibilism.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
compatibilism.title: “Just Like Mary Shelley, Just Like Frankenstein”
compatibilism.relation: Chuck Ward uses 'Mama Tried' (the meek family's rebel son doing life without parole) and the mysterious birthmark in 'Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodleloo' to ask whether character is fixed from birth, setting the songs' fatalism against Aristotle's account of character as habituated choice and Plato's claim that traits tend to be inherited. He surveys behavioral genetics, twin studies, The Bell Curve, and the supposed 'criminality gene' before arguing that genetic determinism is a mistaken reductionism: like the groovy atmosphere of a Dead show, which shapes the very individuals who produce it, complex systems admit top-down causation, so genes never act alone. The chapter's payoff is that the songs' studied ambiguity — mama tried, yet 'that leaves no one but me to blame' — shows art expressing, rather than resolving, the tension between free will and determinism.

compatibilism.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight
compatibilism.title: Sometimes We Live No Particular Way but Our Own
compatibilism.relation: Matthew Turner argues that a 'Playin' in the Band' jam — the band drifting from the tune into long collective improvisation and back — models a Stoic solution to free will shared by Epictetus, Spinoza, and Chuang Tzu: freedom is not uncaused choosing but responding well within constraints, so by the dichotomy of control there is no point resenting the band when it flubs a climax. Spinoza's definition of the free thing as one determined by its own nature, and Chuang Tzu's butcher who cuts oxen by spirit beyond skill, show the band letting the music 'play them' — Jerry's 'Tennessee Jed' riff never played the same way twice — as learned skill becomes second nature. Because the Dead jam within banks (keys, mutual listening, ability) yet generate something genuinely new and transcended every genre of 1960s music where the Monkees merely copied the Beatles, the Stoic attitude proves creative rather than quietist, an analogue for living freely within our own constraints.

compatibilism.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
compatibilism.title: Christmas in Jamaica
compatibilism.relation: David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.

compatibilism.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
compatibilism.title: Free to Be You and Me
compatibilism.relation: Bryan Barker reconciles Cylon programming and human 'destiny' with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's intelligible character: Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama under activation, Baltar's cowardly conversion to the Cylon God, Tigh's decision to stay at his post upon learning he is a Cylon, and Starbuck's flight into the storm in 'Maelstrom' all express innate, unchanging character rather than external compulsion. Even destiny, as in Leoben's prophecies to Starbuck, works like determinism unless reframed as character. On this view we are free because everything we do manifests who we immutably are, whether that character is programmed or born.

compatibilism.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
compatibilism.relation: Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.

compatibilism.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
compatibilism.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.

compatibilism.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
compatibilism.title: Almost Caught!
compatibilism.relation: Nicolas Michaud deploys Harry Frankfurt's attack on the principle that blame requires alternative possibilities: through a 'Dex kills Deb' case with a counterfactual intervener and a locked-steering-wheel driver, he shows one can be blameworthy despite having no choice, provided one acts because one wants to. Applied to Dexter, the question is which level of compulsion he has - and since he never truly restrains himself, never turns himself in, and his Season 2 relapse reads as empowerment rather than addiction, he seems to want to want to kill, so Frankfurt's verdict is guilt despite inevitability. The chapter closes with a fictional Princeton encounter where Dexter faces a dilemma - either his victims are blameless compulsives, making him a killer of innocents who violates Harry's Code, or wanting to kill makes them and him blameworthy - and Dexter's choice to kill Frankfurt himself proves he acts freely and is guilty.

compatibilism.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
compatibilism.title: Determinism’s Bounty on Free Will
compatibilism.relation: Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.

compatibilism.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
compatibilism.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Audits Walt's killings through Season Four - Emilio by phosphine gas in the RV, the captive Krazy-8, Jane left choking in 'Phoenix', the dealers he rams with the Aztec to save Jesse, ordering Jesse to shoot Gale, and the wheelchair bomb that kills Gus and Tyrus - grading each with Aristotle's criteria of capacity, motive, consequences, justification, and proximate cause. It argues self-defense excuses Emilio but dissolves for the imprisoned Krazy-8, that Walt actively created the danger he then refused to relieve when he let Jane die, and that special-relationship duties to Jesse plus a utilitarian ledger justify running down the dealers. Compatibilism is invoked to show guilt survives determinism, while the remote Wayfarer 515 crash is pinned mainly on Donald Margolis's own choices rather than on Walt.

compatibilism.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
compatibilism.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.

compatibilism.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
compatibilism.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.' Since deterministic causation and randomness exhaust the options, we are 'machines made of meat' wearing ice crowns inside our skulls, so deserved suffering makes no sense. The chapter concludes that just-deserts retribution (Princess Cookie's life sentence, America's prisons) should give way to deterrence, protection, and rehabilitation—freeing the Simon Petrikovs underneath.

compatibilism.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
compatibilism.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Miller argues from Jake's croak dream, the Cosmic Owl, and the Dungeon Train's future crystal that Ooo's future is real, visible, and changeable—hence a case of soft determinism: the dream of Jake dying in space is what caused Finn to accompany him and avert it, so the only being who could have intended the change, the Owl, is the sole certain free agent in Ooo. Every alternate Finn is missing his right arm—Shoko the thief, Farmworld Finn, pillow-world Finn, the Dungeon Train elder—hinting at an epic destiny, yet Finn altered the train future once he saw where it led Jake. The chapter closes on the open question of whether choosing one's fate differs from having it thrust on one, since every choice is caused by the past no one can change.

compatibilism.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
compatibilism.title: Dracula and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.

compatibilism.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
compatibilism.title: 7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change
compatibilism.relation: Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'

compatibilism.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
compatibilism.title: 10. We’re Not Free to Save Lee
compatibilism.relation: Bowman uses Telltale's Walking Dead videogame, where Lee always dies no matter what the player does, to stage the free will versus determinism debate. Laplace's demon grounds the determinist pole (the game's outcome is fixed like set particles), while Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith explain the player who says "I thought I could save both" at Hershel's farm rather than owning her choice. The chapter resolves the tension with fatalism or soft determinism - a compatibilist itinerary where Lee's death is a fixed benchmark but the player's choices in between define the character - and extends Bostrom's simulation hypothesis to ask whether we are Lee-like players inside someone else's game.

compatibilism.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
compatibilism.title: 18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld
compatibilism.relation: Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.

compatibilism.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
compatibilism.title: 16. Is Sarah Manning Responsible for What She Does
compatibilism.relation: Uses the genetically identical Leda clones against genetic determinism: Helena seems excused and Cosima responsible despite identical genes, so upbringing must explain the difference. But appealing to background triggers Galen Strawson's Basic Argument — no one is ultimately responsible for who they are, so no one is ultimately responsible for what they do — which the authors escape through Peter Strawson's reactive attitudes (our disgust at Helena softening to pity once her abuse is known, our judgment of Donnie shifting from malice to gullibility) and John Martin Fischer's two conditions: an agent is responsible when she is responsive to reasons that would move well-adjusted rational people and takes ownership of the psychology that produces her action. Helena's Prolethean programming exempts her; Cosima, Alison, and a marginally reformed Sarah remain responsible for what they do.

compatibilism.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
compatibilism.title: 9. Could the Axis Have Won the War
compatibilism.relation: Miguel Paley maps the three classic positions on metaphysical freedom onto the show: Frank the determinist (Laplace's demon; d'Holbach's claim, illustrated by the LSD interrogation, that the mind is as bound to causality as Connolly's falling body), Juliana the libertarian (Corliss Lamont's burden-of-proof argument, with Wegener's hesitation over the microfilm as deliberation a determined world would render pointless), and Tagomi the compatibilist (W.T. Stace's point that Juliana boards the bus freely though caused, while Frank is stripped by the Kempeitai unfreely though caused). Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' sums up compatibilism, and the chapter ends on what the answer means for holding Nazis responsible.

compatibilism.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
compatibilism.title: Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person
compatibilism.relation: The Azevedos contrast Maeve's awakening with Dolores's: Maeve becomes conscious not by recognizing a guiding voice as her own but through a change of heart on the escape train, after learning even her rebellion was scripted.
