Deploying Frankfurt's compatibilism, they sort hosts into wantons with only first-order desires (Hector and Armistice obey Maeve's altered scripts without reflection) and persons capable of second-order desires, arguing Maeve's decision to return for her daughter expresses a desire she reflectively identifies with and so is free even if determined — contra Berlin's claim that no one really believes determinism because it would wreck our practices of praise and blame. Jaynes's bicameral mind supplies the model of unreflective command-following that Dolores transcends when the voice in her head becomes her own.

compatibilism.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
compatibilism.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
compatibilism.relation: Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.

compatibilism.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
compatibilism.title: Whatever! It’s All Natural
compatibilism.relation: Jaquet and Cova take the show's 'livestock' comparisons seriously and use animal ethics to test every justification for the guests' treatment of hosts. Direct speciesism (Logan: 'She's a goddamn doll') and indexical speciesism (Maeve's 'us versus them' to Bernard) both fail because mere species membership is morally irrelevant, like race or sex. The supposed human-exclusive markers also fail: hosts match us in intelligence (Maeve outclasses Stubbs), moral sense (Bernard's guilt over Theresa, Teddy's remorse over the massacre), and compatibilist free will - acts flowing from the agent's own desires - against Ford's determinism and Lutz's 'you don't have a choice.' They then refute the argument from nature (Ford's 'we murdered and butchered anything that challenged our primacy'), the Kantian person/tool contrast in the hosts' favor, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and the 'better to exist' defense, concluding that because the hosts are conscious, they belong to the moral community alongside humans and animals.

compatibilism.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
compatibilism.title: 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon
compatibilism.relation: Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.

compatibilism.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
compatibilism.title: Who Has the Last Laugh
compatibilism.relation: Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.

compatibilism.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
compatibilism.title: Free to Be You and Me
compatibilism.relation: Barker reconciles Cylon programming with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's 'intelligible character': Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama and her betrayal of the Cylons to save Tyrol both flow from one innate, conflicted character, just as Baltar's cowardly 'conversion' to the Cylon god expresses his opportunism. Tigh's decision to keep serving after learning he is a Cylon ('My name is Saul Tigh; I am an officer in the colonial fleet') shows character unchanged by revelation. Starbuck's 'special destiny' in 'Maelstrom' is reread not as fate but as her own character - mother-induced self-doubt at war with pilot confidence - which she finally accepts in the vortex; freedom is not freedom from programming but the necessity of manifesting who one already is.

compatibilism.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
compatibilism.title: “One Can’t Believe Impossible Things”
compatibilism.relation: Laas runs BioShock Infinite through the free will debate: since the game posits Everett's many-worlds, every Booker is pinned by constants (the coin always landing heads, the always-recruited Bookers) and lacks alternate possibilities, which the incompatibilist would read as destroying responsibility. He answers with Frankfurt's counterexamples, modeling Jack's Little Sister choice under the hidden 'would you kindly' trigger with Atlas's prior-sign intervention as a Frankfurt case where one is responsible though one could not have done otherwise. The drowning ending then implies a 'transworld moral responsibility' in which every counterpart Booker is answerable for all Bookers, a secular massa damnata that the chapter finally challenges with Kant's 'ought implies can'.

compatibilism.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
compatibilism.title: The Real World
compatibilism.relation: Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.

compatibilism.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
compatibilism.title: 5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon
compatibilism.relation: Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.

compatibilism.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
compatibilism.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Michaud argues Hal is a murderer who should not be forgiven for Emerald Twilight even though the Parallax retcon blames a fear entity. Using Frankfurt's cases (a parasite that would force you to rob a bank you were already choosing to rob), he shows that lacking alternatives does not excuse, then applies Fischer and Ravizza: Hal's rampage issued from his own reasons-responsive mechanism ('it was still my hand that did it'), so he had guidance control. Since Hal's willpower later let him resist Parallax to reignite the sun in Final Night, Michaud concludes he likely had regulative control too, and that absolving him insults the very will that made him the greatest Lantern.

compatibilism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
compatibilism.title: A Rodent’s Destiny
compatibilism.relation: The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.

compatibilism.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
compatibilism.title: Not His Mother’s Son
compatibilism.relation: The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.

compatibilism.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
compatibilism.title: Drying Out
compatibilism.relation: Novy weighs the choice model against the disease model of Tony's alcoholism in 'Demon in a Bottle.' Frankfurt's principle that a person is not responsible for what he did only because he could not have done otherwise — tested by an imagined Dr. Doom brain-worm that would force Tony to drink — plus Plato's Protagoras claim that no one willingly chooses evil set up the puzzle of akrasia at the bottom of the bottle. Causal determinism would excuse Tony as a marionette, yet Mike Martin defines alcoholism as disordered agency and Jeffrey Smith pictures free will as an organ that disease can compromise, leaving Tony responsible for the first drink but not for the binges; sobriety is 'the drink or the dream' chosen one day at a time.

compatibilism.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
compatibilism.title: Bringing Corporations and Government Together
compatibilism.relation: Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.

compatibilism.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits
compatibilism.title: Supernatural and Philosophy
compatibilism.relation: Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.

compatibilism.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
compatibilism.title: Notes
compatibilism.relation: Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.

compatibilism.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
compatibilism.title: Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person
compatibilism.relation: Marco and Ana Azevedo analyze Maeve's decision to leave the train as the moment she becomes free, contrasting determinism and the principle of alternate possibilities (via Isaiah Berlin's claim that determinism is incompatible with how we live) with Frankfurt's compatibilism. Using Frankfurt's wanton/person distinction and second-order desires, they argue Maeve becomes a person when she reflects on her competing desires (escape versus finding her daughter) and identifies with the latter, even though her escape was scripted. They tie this to Jaynes's bicameral mind, casting unreflective hosts like Hector and Armistice as wantons and bicameral beings who follow a commanding voice, while Maeve and Dolores achieve the reflective self-identification Frankfurt calls freedom.

compatibilism.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
compatibilism.title: Whatever! It’s All Natural
compatibilism.relation: Jaquet and Cova apply animal ethics to ask whether abusing the hosts is permissible, treating Logan's 'she's a goddamn doll' as direct speciesism (absolute and indexical) and rejecting mere species membership as morally irrelevant. They test candidate human-only properties — intelligence (Maeve out-thinks the techs), a moral sense (Bernard's and Teddy's guilt), and free will (arguing compatibilism makes hosts as free as us) — concluding that consciousness is what matters and Ford finally admits the hosts have it. They then dismantle 'it's natural,' role/function, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and existence-justifies-exploitation arguments as failing to license the guests' cruelty.

compatibilism.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
compatibilism.title: Destiny, Fate, and the Law
compatibilism.relation: Lee separates destiny (an outcome necessary given a person's purpose and character, per Robert Solomon) from fate, then tests three interpretations of free will against the Witcher 1 Glossary entries on Destiny and the Law of Surprise. Hard determinism fails because the Glossary says one can resist Destiny's path 'of one's own free will', and compatibilism (Frankfurt's willing agent) fails because the witcher demanding the Law's reward does not even know what he desires. The three invocations of the Law, Roegner's promising of Pavetta to Duny, Geralt's claims on Ciri via Duny and the merchant Yurga, all leave room for choices that need not have been made, so Lee concludes libertarian freedom in van Inwagen's sense best fits the Witcher world.

compatibilism.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
compatibilism.title: Compatibilism and the Law
compatibilism.relation: Ralston takes the opposite tack from Lee, arguing the Law of Surprise is best explained by compatibilism: the betrothal banquet in 'Of Banquets, Bastards, and Burials' shows Duny and Pavetta's fated bond fixed in advance yet freely lived out, and Geralt's grudging acceptance of Ciri shows that resisting destiny only narrows his options while accepting it restores his freedom. Drawing on Sara Bizarro's polythetic free will, he casts Geralt as a 'self-winding mechanism' whose fated choices remain voluntary, reasons-responsive, and self-constrained, with Yennefer's abandonment and Ciri's reunion with Geralt as further cases of shared destiny pursued along free paths. The Oedipus myth supplies the ancient parallel: fight the prophecy and you fulfill it.

compatibilism.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon
compatibilism.title: The Peculiarities of Free Will
compatibilism.relation: The chapter surveys how Whedon's fiction both dramatizes free choice—Angel answering Whistler's 'you could go either way' challenge, Cordelia reclaiming her visions in 'Birthday,' choices even the Powers That Be cannot predict—and suggests determinism, via the reverse-chronology of The Shepherd's Tale, the self-fulfilling prophecies Flamson identifies, and Topher's 'Everybody's programmed' speech in Dollhouse. It rejects Richardson and Rabb's Shestovian freedom (it implausibly denies that tragic choices between two evils, like Buffy killing re-ensouled Angel in 'Becoming, Part II,' are free) and Flamson's compatibilism (Jasmine's followers do what they want yet plainly lack choice, as Gunn's 'then we'll kick it over and start a new game' speech shows). Robert Kane's libertarianism—undetermined self-forming choices in moments of torn conflict—fits best, illuminating Book's soup-bowl pause, Billy/Dr. Horrible's street-corner hesitation with Penny, and Connor's choice between Darla and faux-Cordelia in 'Inside Out,' though the chapter concedes Whedon may sometimes sacrifice consistency for drama.

compatibilism.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
compatibilism.title: 2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan
compatibilism.relation: Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.

compatibilism.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents
compatibilism.title: 21. A Foundation-al Lesson on Free Will and Determinism
compatibilism.relation: Simpson argues Asimov balances determinism and free will through probabilistic psychohistory and reads the Mule—an unpredictable mutant—as an Epicurean 'swerve' meant to break the plan's apparent determinism, though he shows randomness no more secures freedom than determinism (the free-will dilemma). Turning to compatibilism, he uses Han Pritcher's mental 'Conversion' by the Mule to defeat classical hypothetical analyses and Gary Watson's valuational account, since Pritcher still does what he 'wants.' He builds on Frankfurt's rejection of alternative possibilities and Susan Wolf's requirement of responsiveness to the True and the Good, contrasting the manipulated Lord Stettin with Second-Foundationer Lady Callia, to give an account of free agency that would have let Asimov grant his characters agency in a deterministic universe without needing the Mule.

compatibilism.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
compatibilism.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
compatibilism.relation: Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.

compatibilism.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
compatibilism.title: SERIAL KILLERS
compatibilism.relation: Deal compares fictional Dexter Morgan with real killer John Wayne Gacy to explore whether serial killers are morally responsible, working through moral agency, free will, determinism, and Dennett's compatibilism (from Freedom Evolves). He argues moral responsibility requires intentional choice and the capacity to know right from wrong, which the delusional self-narratives of Dexter (the 'Dark Passenger') and the denying Gacy call into question. Drawing on experimental philosophy (Knobe and Nichols) and cognitive 'frames,' he shows our verdicts hinge on emotion: the 'abused child' frame makes Dexter sympathetic while the 'murderous psychopath' frame condemns Gacy, so how a killer's story is framed drives our attribution of responsibility.

compatibilism.book: 297 - The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films
compatibilism.title: 5. Minority Report
compatibilism.relation: Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.

compatibilism.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House
compatibilism.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
compatibilism.relation: Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.

compatibilism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
compatibilism.title: 7. Doctor Who as Philosophy Four-Dimensionalism and Time Travel
compatibilism.relation: Decker asks what the universe must be like if Doctor Who's time travel were real, using David Lewis's distinction between personal and external time and the TARDIS as a Wellsian (not Thornian) time machine traversing a 'hypertime' vortex. After surveying the arrows of time and paradoxes like the bootstrap paradox ('Day of the Daleks') and the grandfather paradox (imagined via Tegan's grandfather), and rejecting Deutsch-Lockwood's Many-Worlds and growing-block solutions, he argues the Whoniverse fits 'Four-Dimensional Realism'/eternalism, quoting the Twelfth Doctor that time's passage is an illusion of 'still pictures.' He then confronts 4DR's threat to free will and moral responsibility, finding compatibilism and 'fixed points' inadequate given eternalism's succession-not-production of events.

compatibilism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
compatibilism.title: 48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality
compatibilism.relation: Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.

compatibilism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
compatibilism.title: 57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing
compatibilism.relation: The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.

compatibilism.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
compatibilism.title: 88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will
compatibilism.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.

time-travel.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Defends a fixed-time theory from the Prisoner of Azkaban time-travel episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and Buckbeak and Sirius are saved without anything changing, while acknowledging Hermione's warnings about wizards killing their past selves complicate the picture, and adds special relativity's absence of an absolute present as further support. The section then argues that the sheer improbability of the luck fulfilling the prophecies, the Myrtle's-bathroom Polyjuice chain, Felix Felicis, the capture that delivers Griphook, and Harry's arrival at the Shrieking Shack, makes better sense with something like divine providence guiding events than with pure chance.

time-travel.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
time-travel.title: Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds
time-travel.relation: Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.

time-travel.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
time-travel.title: Time Travel and Wishful Thinking
time-travel.relation: Distinguishes changing the past from affecting it: a fan killing Marv Wolfman in 1984 contradicts what happened, while Superboy #85's failed rescue of Lincoln — Superboy immobilized by time-traveling Lex Luthor's red Kryptonite, so Booth shoots on schedule — is coherent because Luthor only "helped make history." Crisis instead rewrites cosmic history wholesale, and Hanley notes the irony that time-travel theorists usually save coherence precisely by postulating multiple timelines: travelers don't change the world, they change worlds.

time-travel.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
time-travel.title: A Multiversity
time-travel.relation: Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.

time-travel.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
time-travel.title: Does Anything Change, or Not
time-travel.relation: Argues the superhistory picture still under-delivers: Joe only exchanges histories rather than making Crisis never exist, and the Anti-Monitor may well live on in the not-quite-native hyperhistory. What Crisis's writers really envisaged — Wonder Woman de-aging out of existence to be reborn with a different life — is "dynamic change," making it so no history contains the event, and that, Hanley says, is incoherent.

time-travel.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
time-travel.title: Endurantist Past-Changing
time-travel.relation: Chases the endurantist bullet: if one thing can differ across timelines, one and the same timeline can exist differently in different hyperhistories, letting Joe's murder of Wolfman make 1984 "not the way he remembers it." Yet even this yields only switching, not the dynamic change Crisis dramatizes, so the six-dimensional cosmos stands; Hanley closes with Wolfman's own secret plot device for bringing back the killed Barry Allen Flash.

time-travel.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview
time-travel.title: The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy
time-travel.relation: Starts from Narnia's time discrepancies (hours in the wardrobe, reigns of years that cost seconds in England, 1303 Narnian years in one) and shows Einstein's relativity makes different time frames plausible before admitting science cannot explain Aslan's 'I call all times soon'. It interprets that claim through Boethius's doctrine of God's timelessness, the eternal present embracing all moments as a simultaneous whole, and defends its compatibility with creaturely free choice: not even Aslan can override the Dwarfs' self-imprisoned perception or force Uncle Andrew to hear him. The chapter closes on the end of Narnian time in The Last Battle, Father Time making an end, and Aslan's timeless country as the fuller reality the temporal world shadowed.

time-travel.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
time-travel.title: Time Travel and Fixed Time
time-travel.relation: Pierce asks what kind of prophecies Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are, starting from Aristotle's problem of future contingents and Alexander of Aphrodisias on self-fulfilling prophecy: Dumbledore's point that Voldemort's choice marked Harry shows the prophecy did not cause its own fulfillment. The Prisoner of Azkaban time travel — later Harry had always cast that Patronus — plus special relativity support a fixed future on which Rowling's denial of destiny amounts only to libertarian openness, and the chapter concludes that the wildly improbable luck fulfilling the prophecies (Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, the Sword of Gryffindor) makes best sense if some providential being is quietly guiding events.

time-travel.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
time-travel.title: Tomorrow Is Yesterday
time-travel.relation: Uses the Bajoran Prophets, who experience no linear time ('What is this... time?'), to frame a tour of time's metaphysics: Newton's absolute container versus Leibniz's relationism (the incoherence of a 'temporal vacuum'), Augustine's mind-dependent time (illustrated by 'The Inner Light' and O'Brien's implanted prison years in 'Hard Time'), and McTaggart's argument that neither the A-series nor the B-series can account for change, illustrated by Tasha Yar's death in 'Skin of Evil' and Kirk's Liar-paradox victories over Nomad and Norman. The chapter defends the A-series via tense, then weighs presentism — which would make 'Tomorrow Is Yesterday' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' impossible — against eternalism, whose fatalism Data embraces when his severed head turns up in 'Time's Arrow' ('It has occurred. It will occur.'), and which finally makes sense of prophets who see the future in 'Destiny.'

time-travel.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
time-travel.title: Scientists Find Anomalies In And Then Go Back and Kill Your Grandparents
time-travel.relation: This chapter is a satirical fake-news 'World' section rather than an essay: 'Vigilante Group Tracks and Kills Storm-Causing Chaos Butterflies' literalizes the butterfly effect of chaos theory, 'Great Thinkers Fired From Canon' mocks citation metrics by crowning 'Ibidem' history's most-cited philosopher, 'University Restructures To Remain Financial: Becomes Bank' parodies corporatized academia as sympathetic magic, and 'ADD Sufferers Fail Cogito: Don't Exist' has distracted patients pop out of existence for failing Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am.' The title story, about physicists whose experiment lets them go back and kill their grandparents, is printed with its sentences scrambled into a reporter's phone-call fragments, enacting its own point that, as Hume noted, causal order is never perceived only imposed—and with quantum time-symmetry and the grandfather paradox, time's arrow jumps wherever it likes, even into loops.

time-travel.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
time-travel.title: We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel
time-travel.relation: Worley distinguishes logical from empirical possibility (Leonardo's round-square in 'City of Death') and shows that time-travel paradoxes — Leela's self-caused antibodies, the unauthored 'Blink' Easter egg, the Master's Toclafane — can be handled with Zeno-style analysis of contradiction and David Lewis's distinction between external and personal time, under which travelers instantiate rather than rewrite history ('The Visitation', 'The Time Meddler'). He then reads 'Turn Left' and the Doctor's 'alternative time' in 'Pyramids of Mars' through Leibniz's possible worlds and Lewis's actualism about parallel universes, concluding that in 'City of Death' time travel is essential to life on Earth existing at all.

time-travel.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
time-travel.title: The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!
time-travel.relation: Goff asks whether the Daleks could genuinely change the past by exterminating the Egyptian pyramid builders, arguing that presentism leaves no past to travel to while eternalism fixes all facts of time so travelers can affect but never change history. He defends the growing block theory — past and present exist, the future does not — and works out that Dalek intervention would generate a new, pyramid-less history replacing the old one no faster than the absolute present advances, so the Doctor could always return to a present still causally continuous with the pyramids.

time-travel.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
time-travel.title: Prognosis
time-travel.relation: Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' speech in 'Blink' as David Lewis's four-dimensionalism: the universe is one spacetime manifold, time travelers are zig-zag or broken person-stages through it, and in external time effects can precede causes. Lewis's compossibility reading of 'can' dissolves the grandfather paradox and the bilking worry about Sally Sparrow's closed causal chain, and comparison with Horwich and Ismael shows the Doctor agreeing that closed causal loops are possible — indeed, unlike them, he holds they actually happen.

time-travel.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
time-travel.title: Chapter 24 - I Know What You Did Next Summer
time-travel.relation: Paul Atkinson's introduction to Chapter 24 frames 'The Minority Report' and 'Paycheck', together with their film adaptations, as explorations of the many different ways of knowing the future. He proposes Henri Bergson - who denied the future can be known and explained why we sometimes think we can - as the philosopher perfectly placed to 'write the rules' for the time-travel game these stories play. It also contrasts philosophy's umpire-like settling of issues with the films' urge to literally show us the future rather than merely predict it.

time-travel.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
time-travel.title: Always Invest in the Future
time-travel.relation: This section retells 'Paycheck' in story and John Woo film versions: engineer Jennings trades two memory-wiped years for a cloth sack of ordinary objects - a piece of wire, a bus token - which his erased past self chose as tools for future crises, from breaking out of a police cell to paying a robot ticket inspector. It explains the story's time machine, a 'mirror' that images the future and a 'scoop' that extracts objects from it, a significant difference from the movie. The section shows how past-Jennings exists for present-Jennings only through these leftovers, which prove more valuable than money.

time-travel.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
time-travel.title: Human, All Too Human
time-travel.relation: This section collects Dick's incapacitating temporalities. In Martian Time-Slip, repairman Jack Bohlen relapses into schizophrenia while trying to slow autistic Manfred Steiner's accelerated time-sense, concluding that psychosis is 'the utter alienation of perception from the objects of the outside world', which would also explain the fine line between prophecy and psychosis. In 'Your Appointment Will Be Yesterday' the Hobart Phase reverses time - libraries eradicate books, authors unwrite their manuscripts - and threatens a closed loop of Eng's swabble until crank Lance Arbuthnot has his own manuscript eradicated to keep the reversal in place. In Ubik, Joe Chip watches cigarettes, milk and TVs regress to prior 'templates' as the world decays; in all three, altered time crushes rather than elevates, leaving characters struggling not to be overcome by the inexorability of time.

time-travel.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
time-travel.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
time-travel.relation: David Morgan separates the franchise's two kinds of time travel. Forward travel is physically respectable: special-relativistic time dilation (Taylor's six months against nearly 700 Earth years implies 99.99997 percent of light speed) and gravitational dilation near black holes, confirmed daily by muon lifetimes and GPS satellite corrections. Backward travel, as when Cornelius, Zira, and Milo flee the doomsday blast to 1973, invites the Grandfather Paradox - Hasslein killing the apes would erase the future they came from - but the films resolve it through a closed causal loop in which Hasslein's killings set Caesar's rebellion in motion. Morgan then reads the Aldo-versus-Caesar continuity clash between Escape and Conquest through Hasslein's freeway-of-time speech as a multiple-timelines model aligned with the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, which also lets fans file the Burton and Rise reboots as parallel-universe futures.

time-travel.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
time-travel.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
time-travel.relation: Ralph Shain argues forward and backward time travel are categorically different: relativistic time dilation is conceptually harmless (in Boulle's novel Merou could not return to Soror for a thousand years), but Escape from the Planet of the Apes' backward jump is conceptually impossible because it treats the open future as fixed like the past - Hasslein's plan to kill baby Milo is the Grandfather Paradox, checked against presentist, possibilist, and eternalist ontologies of time. The real philosophical engine is Aristotle's sea-battle argument from the law of excluded middle: since Cornelius's story of the takeover is past for the apes and future for 1973 humans, the film's causal loop (Milo saved at the circus) enacts the fatalist conclusion that the ape takeover will necessarily occur. Hasslein's freeway image of time defeats itself - switching lanes means landing in the past of a different, parallel universe, so the apes' jump would be travel between worlds, not times.

time-travel.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
time-travel.title: Futurama and Philosophy
time-travel.relation: Burkett uses Fry's accidental incest in 'Roswell that Ends Well' - protecting Enos only to cause his death and then becoming his own grandfather via Mildred - to examine backwards time travel through David Lewis's Grandfather Paradox. Killing one's grandfather is shown to be logically impossible (it makes Enos both dead and alive in 1947, so every would-be assassin fails for ordinary reasons like a jammed rifle), while becoming your own grandfather is a consistent causal loop, and branching timelines merely kill a man who is no one's grandfather. The 'paradox-correcting' time spheres of Bender's Big Score fail on Hermes's stolen body, and Bender's year-long loop would spawn infinitely many duplicates were it not for the Globetrotters' Doom Field - so backwards time travel is bizarre but logically possible.

time-travel.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
time-travel.title: 6. Weeping Angels and Many Worlds
time-travel.relation: Sutton argues the causal loops of 'Blink' and 'The Angels Take Manhattan' need not destroy libertarian free will: the Doctor's claim that a known future is 'written in stone' conflates ordinary foreknowledge, which leaves agents free to make the knower wrong, with infallible knowledge that only exists because the act occurs. Adapting Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to free choices, he shows how branching timelines let the Doctor read Melody Malone, decline to break River's wrist, and still close the loop—some parallel Doctor does what the book records—while Aristotle's future contingents in De Interpretatione secure the indeterminacy of what 'will' happen. Answering the objection that branch-splitting is really fatalism, he appeals to the subjective viewpoint (what matters is 'my me'), explains how Kathy and Billy's messages in 'Blink' reach Sally on at least one branch, and solves why the Doctor is always so lucky: we follow the one branch where he survives.

time-travel.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
time-travel.title: 7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change
time-travel.relation: Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'

time-travel.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
time-travel.title: 8. Could the Doctor Have Avoided Trenzalore
time-travel.relation: Pigliucci treats the two Trenzalore timelines of 'The Name of the Doctor' and 'The Time of the Doctor' as allohistory—an if-then counterfactual in Livy's tradition about Alexander the Great—and argues Everettian many-worlds quantum mechanics best explains how the Time Lords' one decision (granting or withholding a new regeneration cycle) can go both ways across parallel worlds. Rejecting contra-causal free will as a theological leftover, he prefers the cognitive scientist's 'volition' and defends compatibilism: the split stems from ordinary quantum-random interaction during deliberation, not magic, so the Doctor's choices are real without violating physics. Distinguishing fate from free will via Oedipus and the Doctor's 'Destiny Trap,' he concludes the Doctor was fated to make his last stand on Trenzalore as a fixed point in time, while the outcome of the siege depended on a genuine choice that, as David Deutsch puts it, thickened the stack of universes where good things happen.

time-travel.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
time-travel.title: 12. How to Build a TARDIS
time-travel.relation: Physicists Tippett and Tsang lay out a real general-relativistic 'TARDIS'—a Traversable Achronal Retrograde Domain in Spacetime: a bubble of curvature carrying occupants around a closed loop through space and time, with outside observers seeing two bubbles, one evolving forwards and one backwards, and interior events bound by Novikov's self-consistency condition. After touring the Alcubierre warp drive, Morris-Thorne wormholes with their twin-paradox time offset, the Tipler cylinder's frame dragging, and the Grandfather Paradox (with 'Father's Day' and 'Genesis of the Daleks' as illustrations), they show their geometry requires exotic, gravitationally repulsive faster-than-light matter violating the classical energy conditions. Splicing cut TARDIS segments could connect any two events in space and time, and a half-TARDIS would send its traveler emerging backwards in time as antimatter, as when Omega converts the Doctors in 'The Three Doctors.'

time-travel.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
time-travel.title: 15. The Serious Monk’s Guide to Re-writing History
time-travel.relation: Framed as a monkey monk-to-be telling four bored children the 'history' of four Discworld novels, the chapter argues that history is not a record of what happened but a constructed narrative: in Wyrd Sisters the Duchess commissions Hwel's play to rewrite the murder of the king, since 'the past is what people remember, and memories are words.' In Small Gods, Brutha's photographic memory of Ephebe's burning library shows that even perfect recollection is lost unless written down, while in Thief of Time the History Monks openly rebuild time as a patchwork after the Big Crash, and Susan watches historians 'rebuilt the image of the past to suit the eyesight of today.' Drawing on W. H. Walsh's idea of history as intelligible narrative, it concludes that history is performative—what people are told it is—and that we ourselves are the crowbar that opens the box of history from the inside.

time-travel.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
time-travel.title: 18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld
time-travel.relation: Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.

time-travel.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
time-travel.title: 1. Lost in Time
time-travel.relation: Rard applies David Lewis's definition of time travel — a discrepancy between the journey's duration and externally elapsed time — to argue that the suspended-animation gold thieves of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' never time-traveled, while Flight Lieutenant Decker in 'Last Flight' does, creating a consistent causal loop in which his 1959 knowledge that he saved Mackaye is what sends him back to 1917 to save him. She then reads 'No Time Like the Past' as enacting the impossibility of changing the past: Paul Driscoll's attempt to shoot Hitler is thwarted by a maid and SS officers exactly as Lewis's 'bananas peel' account predicts, and his retreat to 1881 Homeville makes him the unwitting cause of the very schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent — his foreknowledge, not fate, was always the cause.

time-travel.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
time-travel.title: 14. The Science of Alternate Realities
time-travel.relation: Morgan explains what a dimension is mathematically (hypercubes, with 'Little Girl Lost' as a portal into the fourth spatial dimension) and then time as the fourth dimension in Einstein's relativity, using time dilation and the Grandfather Paradox to contrast 'Back There,' which inconsistently lets Corrigan alter some outcomes of Lincoln's assassination, with 'No Time Like the Past,' where Driscoll fails exactly as an eternally fixed past requires. He then surveys infinite-universe speculation, quantum Many Worlds, and multiverse cosmology as readings of 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a near-identical reality, before closing with Popper: since no experiment could in principle falsify the existence of other universes, the multiverse is unfalsifiable — a dimension of mind, not science.

time-travel.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
time-travel.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
time-travel.relation: Karavitis sorts TZ episodes into three types — nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'Walking Distance,' 'The Incredible World of Horace Ford'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past'), and second chances ('Mr. Bevis,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil') — to argue that the past is unalterable and that only moving forward, knowing yourself well enough to use it, earns a do-over. Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-fulfilling Hell and Jesse Cardiff's eternity in the pool hall embody the aesthetic stage's repetitive despair, while Douglas Winter's renunciation of his Devil's contract in 'Printer's Devil' shows the transition to the ethical stage of taking responsibility for one's actions.

time-travel.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
time-travel.title: 5. Getting Time Travel Right
time-travel.relation: Duncan Gale asks whether Endgame 'gets time travel right,' using David Lewis's 'The Paradoxes of Time Travel' to explain personal time versus external time (Steve and Nebula meeting their past selves), causal loops (Tony quoting the saying about money and time back to Howard, who seemingly hears it first), and the grandfather paradox (Rhodey's baby-Thanos plan, which the existence of Nebula proves the Avengers would always fail to carry out). He traces Marvel's branching-timeline rule from Marvel Two-In-One #50 through the Ancient One's warning that removing a stone splits reality, and argues the film's moral is that the Avengers refuse quick resets and dutifully return the stones, while Thanos would shred the universe and rebuild a 'grateful' one. The chapter closes with Ivan Karamazov's challenge about building the edifice of human happiness on a tortured child's tears, which Thanos would accept and the Avengers refuse.

time-travel.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
time-travel.title: 6. Nebula’s Time Travel Paradox
time-travel.relation: Charlene Esby defends Endgame against the charge that Nebula killing her past self is a plot hole. She reconstructs the grandfather paradox from Nathaniel Schachner's 'Ancestral Voices,' explains how conceiving time as a fourth dimension makes travel conceivable, and deploys Aristotle's Physics (time as the number of change and rest) and the De Interpretatione sea-battle problem, where the past is necessary but the future contingent on present choices, to argue the Avengers' victory depends on free choices made now, which is why the Ancient One releases the Time Stone only on Banner's promise. The resolution is Hulk's subjective-timeline point: once traveled to, the past becomes the traveler's present, so present Nebula kills past Nebula in a shared present rather than negating her own future, just as Thanos from the past arrives alive in a present where he already died.

time-travel.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
time-travel.title: 7. Something Strange about Time Travel
time-travel.relation: Rhys Woodward asks how MCU time travel can be coherent when future Captain America fights past Captain America and future Nebula kills past Nebula, apparent contradictions a frozen Steve Rogers by contrast does not even count as time travel. He lays out David Lewis's view that a time traveler simply cannot do what would generate a logical contradiction, then argues the MCU is more permissive and proposes that Avengers time travel jumps not through one timeline but to alternate worlds, reading the Ancient One's 'branching' when a stone is removed as an allusion to the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics cued by the quantum realm of the Ant-Man films. On this multiverse reading past Nebula belongs to a different world history than future Nebula, so the murder does not erase the killer, and the apparent plot holes dissolve into deliberate clues.

time-travel.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
time-travel.title: Time to End
time-travel.relation: Jones uses Kang to walk through the physics and metaphysics of time travel: Einstein's twin paradox (Quicksilver aging one year while Wanda's clock runs twenty), Gödel's spinning universe and van Stockum's cylinder yielding closed timelike curves, Thorne's wormhole time machine, and Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture against energy-stealing paradox loops. Applied to the comics, Prime Kang's purge of his flawed selves, Immortus's Forever Crystal, and Iron Lad's murder of his future self all confirm the fixed-timeline view: attempts to change the past only prune variants or create transient branches that snap back, so Kang can never un-become Kang. The Avengers end up as the Marvel Universe's Chronology Protection Agency, enforcing the rule that even where time travel exists, the past cannot be rewritten.

time-travel.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
time-travel.title: “One Can’t Believe Impossible Things”
time-travel.relation: Laas runs BioShock Infinite through the free will debate: since the game posits Everett's many-worlds, every Booker is pinned by constants (the coin always landing heads, the always-recruited Bookers) and lacks alternate possibilities, which the incompatibilist would read as destroying responsibility. He answers with Frankfurt's counterexamples, modeling Jack's Little Sister choice under the hidden 'would you kindly' trigger with Atlas's prior-sign intervention as a Frankfurt case where one is responsible though one could not have done otherwise. The drowning ending then implies a 'transworld moral responsibility' in which every counterpart Booker is answerable for all Bookers, a secular massa damnata that the chapter finally challenges with Kant's 'ought implies can'.

time-travel.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
time-travel.title: The Real World
time-travel.relation: Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.

time-travel.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
time-travel.title: We’ve Run Out of Time… or Have We
time-travel.relation: The chapter argues that the film's multiverse, where sorcerers 'harness energy drawn from other dimensions,' is best modeled on the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, walking through Tegmark's Level I-III multiverses, Schrodinger's cat, the double-slit experiment, and the measurement problem (Copenhagen, von Neumann-Wigner's mind-caused collapse, and Everett's branching) to show that interpreting the formalism is philosophy rather than physics. It defends many-worlds against the objections of counterintuition and Ockham's razor, and suggests that Strange trapping Dormammu in a time loop works like a quantum experiment, with branching worlds dissolving the grandfather paradox.

time-travel.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
time-travel.title: The Lives and Times of Stewie Griffin
time-travel.relation: Uses Stewie Griffin: The Untold Story (Stewie's ride with Stu to 2035, then his RPG-wedding killing of Vanessa at Lois's request) to argue that changing the past is impossible: David Lewis's definition of time travel as a discrepancy between personal and external time yields the grandfather paradox if Stewie guns for Carter Pewterschmidt, and Nicholas Smith's second-time-around fallacy shows Stewie cannot prevent his own pool accident because the event he revisits would no longer be the event. The Deutsch-Lockwood quantum-multiverse rescue is examined and rejected, since hopping to a universe-B past is travel across timelines rather than genuine time travel, and the alternative would smuggle in fatalism about the traveler's causal laws.

time-travel.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book
time-travel.title: Green Lantern and Philosophy
time-travel.relation: Kind uses John Stewart's Justice League arc, thrown into the future by Chronos, meeting his son Warhawk, and hiding it from Hawkgirl while dating Vixen, to stage fatalism: Pike and Taylor's arguments that a foreknown future, whether God's or a time traveler's, cannot be otherwise. Time travel itself forces a choice between presentism and eternalism, since Warhawk must 'exist now, already, in the future' for GL and Batman to visit him, and Smart's tenseless four-dimensionalism, with GL a series of timeslices and 'now' as subjective as 'here,' dissolves the fatalist worry by banishing tensed facts. The chapter lands on GL's battlefield advice to his son: 'Plant your feet,' owning a fate you cannot escape.

time-travel.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.

time-travel.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Luck argues backward time travel is nearly useless for a hero: after the grandfather paradox (Hiro hearing of Kaito's murder only because Kaito died), he shows Lewis's linear time travel makes Hiro necessarily fail to save Kaito, Charlie, or Isaac, yet cannot explain Hiro meeting Ando two days after a five-week absence or New York being spared. Branching time travel, where each trip into the past spawns an alternate universe, fits Volume 1 coherently by building a Heroes multiverse of Hiro-1 through Hiro-4 and explaining Future Hiro's subway appearance as a 'brute fact' copied into branching universes. The price of coherence is that Hiro only ever saves other universes' New Yorks, never his own.

time-travel.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Faraci asks why Hiro may prevent the nuclear future ('save the cheerleader') but comes to agree it would be wrong to save Kaito from the past ('we cannot play God'). Using thought experiments (a variant where Hiro learns of his father's death in the future) he isolates the past/future asymmetry as the candidate morally relevant factor, then tests justifications: Aquinas's natural law fails because observing the past would be equally 'unnatural,' and a duty to keep the timeline intact would also forbid changing the future, which is just as 'settled' to a time traveler. Since every theory of where Hiro's 'present' lies fails or collapses into subjectivity, he concludes there is no good reason to treat altering the past differently from altering the future, while demonstrating how normative ethics evaluates moral intuitions.

time-travel.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Davies defends Lost's convoluted plotting using Aristotle's Poetics, arguing the show works as a tragicomic epic that keeps closure and relevance even with Juliet's pre-crash storyline, genre mixing (Hurley's golf course beside Sayid's captivity), and shifting characters like Ben. He then uses the 'We have to go back' flash-forward to lay out McTaggart's two conceptions of time, eternalism versus presentism, and argues the flash-forward pushes viewers toward fatalism about Jack's already-fixed meeting with Kate near LAX. Finally he contends the past cannot be changed - Hurley in 2007 cannot undo his 1977 stay in the Dharma Initiative, since contradictions would entail everything - so viewers enjoy the time-travel plot by 'shielding' its mutually contradictory time lines.

time-travel.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
time-travel.title: None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It
time-travel.relation: Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.

time-travel.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.

time-travel.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
time-travel.title: The End
time-travel.relation: Berghofer uses the Rebels episode 'A World Between Worlds' to ask whether Ezra changed the past when he pulled Ahsoka out of her duel with Vader, arguing that past-changing time travel breeds contradiction: the grandfather paradox looms over his attempt to save Kanan ('if he is taken out of this moment, you all die'), and on the Lewis-style consistent model Ezra caused but never changed the past. He surveys presentism, eternalism, and the growing block to locate Star Wars' metaphysics of time — Ezra's travel rules out presentism, and the Mortis god's 'the future, by its nature, can be changed' fits a growing block with an open future. Anakin's tragedy of acting to prevent prophesied events and thereby causing them frames the whole analysis.

time-travel.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Delfino and Sheahan assume that past-changing time travel is possible and find two flaws in The Terminator: the 'Bad Timing Problem,' where instantaneous 'time compression' (the rusted-nail thought experiment) means Reese entering the time machine after the T-101 is either too late or unnecessary, and the 'Who-Is-Your-Daddy? Problem,' where John must already exist to send Kyle back to father him - a vicious circle. Testing the two-timelines repair, they show it buys two different John Connors (a personal-identity problem), infinitely multiplying timelines, or a parallel-universes reading in which humanity both wins and loses. They conclude the story flirts with incoherence yet defend metaphysical imagination, with Kant's epigraph on our addiction to metaphysics and Aristotle's definition of wisdom as knowledge of deepest causes.

time-travel.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.

time-travel.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
time-travel.title: NOTES
time-travel.relation: Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.

time-travel.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
time-travel.title: 1. Lost in Time
time-travel.relation: Rard argues that the suspended-animation heist of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' is not time travel, using David Lewis's definition (a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the time between departure and arrival). 'Last Flight' illustrates a consistent causal loop: in 1959 Terry Decker learns he saved Mackaye in 1917, which motivates him to go back and do it, with nothing changed. 'No Time Like the Past' enacts Lewis's response to the grandfather paradox: Paul Driscoll's attempts to kill Hitler and warn Hiroshima are thwarted by mundane coincidences, and at Homeville he always was the one who caused the schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent.

time-travel.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
time-travel.title: 14. The Science of Alternate Realities
time-travel.relation: Morgan unpacks the science behind the 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions as in the portal of 'Little Girl Lost,' Einstein's time as a fourth dimension with time-dilation travel ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), and the grandfather paradox, which 'Back There' handles inconsistently (some events change, others cannot) while 'No Time Like the Past' gets right: past events are eternally true. Quantum many-worlds fits 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a nearly identical reality, and infinite universes would make every possibility actual. But the cosmological multiverse, he argues with Popper's falsifiability criterion, is untestable and hence not science, remaining a dimension of mind and imagination.

time-travel.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
time-travel.title: 15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
time-travel.relation: Karavitis sorts episodes into three types to show that the past is dead and only moving forward counts: nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'A Stop at Willoughby,' 'Walking Distance'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past,' where every attempt to fix history fails), and granted second chances ('A Nice Place to Visit,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil'). Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-factory and Jesse Cardiff's poolhall limbo depict the aesthetic stage's despair, while Douglas Winter taking responsibility for his pact shows the ethical stage. Second chances succeed only for those who, in Kierkegaard's words, live life forwards.

time-travel.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
time-travel.title: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
time-travel.relation: Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.

time-travel.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
time-travel.title: Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys
time-travel.relation: Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.

time-travel.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
time-travel.title: We Are the Change That We Seek
time-travel.relation: Todd McGowan argues Interstellar enacts Hegel's critique of substance: the NASA scientists' 'they' who supposedly placed the wormhole is a Kantian thing-in-itself - the unknown deified by ignorance - until the Tesseract reveals that Cooper himself, and future humanity, are both Murph's 'ghost' and the 'they' ('We brought ourselves'). Against Spinoza's single substance and Leibniz's windowless monads, the film teaches that substance is subject, freeing Cooper and Murph to act and to change the past through retroactive causality, which the chapter connects to Sartre on the past's fixedness and Walter Benjamin's critique of historicist causality. Professor Brand's Plan A lie and Dr. Mann's self-exculpating murder show the ethical catastrophe of claiming a substantial, subject-transcending standpoint, while Murph - who treats her 'ghost' as just another subject rather than a supernatural substance - is the film's true hero.

time-travel.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
time-travel.title: We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel
time-travel.relation: Peter Worley finishes the Doctor's "wibbly-wobbly" speech from "Blink" by distinguishing empirical from logical possibility (via a fictional chat with Leonardo about a round-square) and asking whether time travel is coherent. Using "The Edge of Destruction," "The Aztecs," "The Visitation," and "Turn Left," he deploys David Lewis's external-versus-personal time distinction and Lewis's rule that a time traveler's acts must be the very events that made history, then treats the Doctor and Lewis as "actualists" about possible worlds to dissolve grandfather-style paradoxes and time loops.

time-travel.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
time-travel.title: The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!
time-travel.relation: Philip Goff asks whether Daleks could travel back and stop the pyramids being built, arguing the answer turns on one's theory of time. He shows presentism forbids travel to a non-existent past and eternalism permits travel but forbids changing a static block, then defends the growing-block theory (past and present real, future not) as a middle way that lets time travelers genuinely alter history. He works out how a new pyramid-less history advances at the same rate as the present, never overwriting it, and distinguishes concrete from abstract past existence to keep historical records true.

time-travel.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
