He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.

heidegger-technology.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
heidegger-technology.title: At Ease
heidegger-technology.relation: Adam Koehler reads Kid A's disfigured, barely intelligible vocals through Heidegger's account of how enabling technology withdraws into an invisible backdrop of everydayness: Pablo Honey hides its studio machinery behind "natural" rock, but Kid A — the cycled voice of "Everything in Its Right Place," the unintelligible vocoded "Kid A," "How to Disappear Completely" — forces the artifice itself into view, and with it the withdrawn world technology ordinarily conceals. The song is beautiful, he argues, because its willful failure to communicate feels human, enacting the anxiety of living in an information age that traps as much as it connects; John Mayer's lyric-clearing acoustic cover misses the point, since making sense now means risking not making sense, and the album's demand is that we listen to, and understand, everything withdrawn in the background.

heidegger-technology.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
heidegger-technology.title: If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . .
heidegger-technology.relation: Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."

heidegger-technology.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
heidegger-technology.title: The Sacrificial Lamb
heidegger-technology.relation: Argues Astro Boy re-enacts the sacrificial logic of the atomic age: Atomu is the nuclear-powered copy of the dead Tobio, born from Dr. Tenma's refusal to accept mortality, and his repeated self-sacrifice for humans who discard him (as in 'Save the Classmate,' where the rescued boys' parents still want him removed) shows him functioning as Heidegger's 'standing-reserve' — an object valued only as stored power, with humans themselves next in line. Drawing on Plato's Republic anxiety over originals and copies, Adorno and Horkheimer's dialectic of enlightenment, and Rey Chow's account of mimesis as the sign left by sacrifice, the chapter reads the series as mourning an innocence that became impossible after Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

heidegger-technology.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
heidegger-technology.title: Only an Ortiz Can Save Us Heidegger’s Revelation of Being
heidegger-technology.relation: James Pontuso reads Red Sox history through Heidegger: technology that turns the world into 'standing reserve' breeds the anxious 'everydayness' of the mediocre Pinky Higgins teams, while the run of near-misses from 1967 through Bucky Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986 threw fans into an authentic encounter with tragedy, mortality and the mystery of Being that the Yankees' free-agent 'technology of power' could never teach. Fenway Park, quirky and continuous with the pre-Hitler past, serves as 'home' in Heidegger's homeless age, and the literati's tragic framing of the team (language as the house of Being) made its fate a matter of existential weight rather than mere sport. David Ortiz's 2004 ALCS heroics then function as Heidegger's longed-for revelation of Being, the answer to 'only a god can save us,' after which fans have lived through all three states: everydayness, tragic anxiety, and wonder.

heidegger-technology.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
heidegger-technology.title: 13 - What Are Friends For
heidegger-technology.relation: Bloor reads Facebook anxiety through Heidegger's diagnosis of technological nihilism — an efficiency-driven 'being-in-the-world' with no shared arbiter of what matters — borrowing Dreyfus's HAL 9000 example from 2001: A Space Odyssey to show humans enhancing themselves like any other raw material. He argues Facebook's speed lures users into unreflective sharing and standardized behavior where the quirky authentic 'I' dissolves into Heidegger's 'one,' and recruits Aristotle's view that only a few deep friendships morally form us to warn that hundreds of contacts fragment that benefit. Adorno on leisure as mere recuperation between bouts of work frames the therapist who keeps Facebook strictly professional, and the chapter concludes the fault lies in ourselves, not the tools — suggesting a week offline as a test.

heidegger-technology.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
heidegger-technology.title: The Test of Humanity
heidegger-technology.relation: Reads the Butlerian Jihad through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: technology is not a device but a way of 'enframing' the world as a standing-reserve, so the Harkonnens see Arrakis, the Fremen, and even Mentat Piter as mere resources, while the Fremen's maker hooks and ecological terraforming show tools absorbed into a lived practice that shapes their users in turn. Paul's prescience becomes the ultimate tool—perfect advice that puts his life on autopilot through Dune Messiah—so Leto II's breeding of Siona-gene humans invisible to oracles completes the Jihad's lesson: self-determination and 'living judgments,' not optimization, are what the Gom Jabbar's test of humanity is for.

heidegger-technology.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
heidegger-technology.title: Straining the Limits of Machine and Man
heidegger-technology.relation: Reads Peart's ambivalence about technology through Heidegger's techne as revealing and Marx's account of the worker: 'Working Man''s no-time-for-living day, '2112''s priests whose 'great computers' smash the protagonist's guitar, 'Manhattan Project''s Oppenheimer problem, and 'Test for Echo''s 'video vertigo.' Against Ellul-style autonomous technology the chapter insists Peart believes we still control our machines, and it ends with Rush mastering its own studio gear — and the motorcycle of Ghost Rider as the machine that carries Peart through grief.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: The Lung-less, All-Penetrating Masterful World-Silence
heidegger-technology.relation: The section reads Do Androids Dream through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': mood organs, empathy boxes, Buster Friendly and catalog-bought animals alienate humans from the world, each other and themselves until only the 'silence of the world' remains, which Isidore theorizes as the inevitable kipple-ization of the universe. Byron's 'Darkness' and Nietzsche's parable of the clever beasts frame Deckard's drive into the dead desert after his last retirement, where he confronts a universe of dead stones that perceive and remember nothing.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: Do You Think Androids Have Souls
heidegger-technology.relation: The chapter sets up strong versus weak AI through Rachael's account of the Rosen Association's strategy of iterating models until one is indistinguishable, then brings in Gaita's 'non-speculative conception' of a soul via Wittgenstein's remark that 'My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul.' Heidegger's warning that technology tempts us to treat others as mere means is dramatized in Deckard's realization after meeting the predatory bounty hunter Phil Resch that he had been viewing androids, and hence himself, as means; his half-measure of wishing other androids did the retiring shows how far he still has to go.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: The Cardinal Mystery of Creation
heidegger-technology.relation: The chapter completes the Heidegger arc: where danger is grows the saving power, so Deckard's first thoughts on finding the toad (U.N. stars and reward money) expose his alienation from any authentic relation to the world, yet he ends 'devoted' to the electric toad because 'The electric things have their lives, too.' Roy Batty's tears-in-rain speech becomes the film's expression of the same saving power: wonder at the mystery of Being is what essentially ensouls humans and replicants alike.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: We Can Endorse That for You Wholesale
heidegger-technology.relation: The chapter opposes Total Recall, where Quaid switches on the alien reactor in 'unwavering faith' and benevolent technology terraforms Mars into a paradise, to 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale', where Quail surrenders because a brain-implanted security device transmits his every thought and 'anything you think may be held against you.' Citing Dick's line that even the most base human schemes are preferable to the most exalted machine tropisms, it argues the films inscribe a faith in technology that Dick himself never held.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: From Hover Cars to Substance D
heidegger-technology.relation: The chapter contrasts the films' technologies: Blade Runner foregrounds gaudy techno-tropes and a Voight-Kampff machine that discloses the truth about replicants, while A Scanner Darkly dwells on mundane devices, Substance D, surveillance cameras, cell phones and Barris's broken contraptions, that obscure reality and help dissolve Arctor's personality. It reads the latter as Dick's fear of the mechanization of humanity made contemporary, mirroring our own self-documentation on YouTube, Twitter and Facebook, and ending with Bruce, 'a dried husk', in the decoy corn field.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: The Shock of Being Alive
heidegger-technology.relation: The chapter fuses McLuhan's narcosis with Heidegger's enframing: technology constrains Being to a human-centered 'world picture' in which forests become board feet and animals become production units, and like Narcissus we fall in love with an image we stamped there ourselves. It enlists the deep ecologists and David Abram ('We are human only in contact, in conviviality, with what is not human') to argue that Dick makes human identity essentially relational, and closes on Baudrillard: digital tweets have become more present for many people than birdsong.

heidegger-technology.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
heidegger-technology.title: Chapter 33 - “The Gun”
heidegger-technology.relation: Benjamin Stevens reads 'The Gun' - a mindless automated weapon still defending a dead community - as an early statement of Dick's fear that in the Cold War military-industrial complex our very capacities for thought, will and free action may have been objectified into products of a mechanized system that no longer serves us. He brings Dick into dialogue with Adorno and Horkheimer's culture industry (we are industrially 'produced' as consumers, turned into the carbon-based equivalent of plastic), Walter Benjamin's loss of aura under mechanical reproduction, Hannah Arendt's worry that Sputnik signals an unwise desire to escape our earthliness, and Heidegger's broadened question concerning technology as social control. Like Plato, Dick insists the unexamined life is not worth living: the best life cannot be lived inside a culture that has, without our informed consent, made us artificial.

heidegger-technology.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry
heidegger-technology.title: Breaking Bad and Philosophy
heidegger-technology.relation: Uses Heidegger to read the show's very structure: the pilot's in-medias-res Winnebago crash throws us into Walt's timeline the way Dasein is thrown into time, and the flashbacks to Sandia Labs and 'nowhere to go but up' show his has-been shaping his futurity. Walt's diagnosis makes being-toward-death an overwhelming presence and exposes the failure of his calculative, goal-setting thinking, with the 'Fly' monologue about the perfect moment to die as his turn toward Heidegger's meditative thinking. By dwelling on his own death, the chapter argues, Walt inches toward an authentic being-toward-death - living each moment as if it were his last.

heidegger-technology.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
heidegger-technology.title: Girls and Philosophy
heidegger-technology.relation: Addis uses Heidegger to explain why Hannah cannot 'rewrite her world': her enframing habit treats everything and everyone (Laird, Marnie, Adam) only in terms of feeding her 'writer' identity, so her world stays tiny even in vast New York. Heideggerian world, thrownness (Jessa's surprise wedding Shoshanna attends in white, Charlie's departure), and the power of art to de-enframe structure contrasts with Marnie, whose singing - prompted by Ray's question - expands her horizons. Hannah's crying-at-her-desk realization at the ad agency is read as her one genuine acceptance of thrownness, though her enframed self-absorption pulls her back.

heidegger-technology.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
heidegger-technology.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
heidegger-technology.relation: Leonard reads Ooo through Heidegger's contrast between technological and poetic frames of mind: Princess Bubblegum's BGCCTV, Goliad, and the James clone mission treat candy people as manipulable stock, while the Lich is technological thinking perfected—pure efficiency aimed at 'the extinction of all life'—and Finn is the poet who values things for what they are, risks Heidegger's 'venture,' and battles Death in 'Death in Bloom' as if in a concert. On Heidegger's definition of art as 'the setting-itself-into-work of truth,' Marceline's songs and Jake's imagined lava show creation disclosing reality. Magic, spread by the Mushroom War, sits between the two modes, and only Finn's poetic exuberance can check Bubblegum's slide toward order at any cost.

heidegger-technology.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different
heidegger-technology.title: Steve Jobs and Philosophy
heidegger-technology.relation: In an imagined Walter Cronkite-moderated afterlife debate, Jobs opens with 'most technology is shit,' holding up the iPod as art-through-simplicity—design as the soul of the thing, thought down to its essence—while Heidegger answers from 'The Question Concerning Technology': the iPod's four Aristotelian causes (material, form, purpose, maker) work together as co-responsible bringing-forth, a revealing whose essence is enframing, which conceals the human when technology is treated as mere standing-reserve and cheapest utility. The dialogue converges on Jobs's washer-and-dryer anecdote and the Mercedes line: technology that reveals rather than conceals our being—useful and beautiful—keeps it serving humanity instead of mastering it, and Heidegger's Nazi past is flagged for the reader to judge separately.

heidegger-technology.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
heidegger-technology.title: 16. European Intellectuals Follow Charlie Brown!
heidegger-technology.relation: The chapter traces how European intellectuals legitimized Peanuts: Eco read the strip as mass culture whose repeated patterns expose a microcosm of the human condition (children warped by industrial civilization, Lucy as contemporary values incarnate), while Bassano di Tufillo finds 'sociable individualism' and, via Bateson and aboriginal spirituality, an ecological vision granting animals, trees, and school buildings equal dignity. It then applies Heidegger's distinction between calculative and reflective thinking to management: Lucy's rigid direction of the Christmas play ('You've got to have respect for your director!') is calculative leadership that treats people as resources, while Charlie Brown's refusal of the All-Stars sponsor - which would have expelled girls and Snoopy - models the authentic, reflective organization that values dignity and diversity over results.

heidegger-technology.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
heidegger-technology.title: 22. The Irrelevance of Truth
heidegger-technology.relation: Jan Kyrre Berg Friis argues, with Nietzsche, that truth is a 'mobile army of metaphors', a relational event between people rather than an objective correspondence, and that the will to truth is subordinate to the will to power — the difference being that Trump-style 'alternative truth' is dishonest domination while Nietzsche's askesis is self-transformation. He layers in the Buddhist and Zen (Dogen) diagnosis of perception as conceptual distortion, Descartes' ego cogito as the fatal Western turn, and Heidegger's warning that calculative, technological thinking covers over our tacit lived background, producing exactly the one-dimensional minds a Ministry of Truth can feed. Rorty's advice to drop the truth-talk, Kant's insight that reality is sifted through the perceiver, and the cognitive-science of confirmation bias explain why facts no longer bite in the post-truth newsfeed.

heidegger-technology.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
heidegger-technology.title: 17. Life Unchecked Will Cease to Exist
heidegger-technology.relation: Diego Perez Lasserre argues Thanos is not an external villain but a personification of what Heidegger and Carl Schmitt call the 'metaphysics of technology': once modernity banished transcendence from the metaphysical realm, mundane concepts like economic growth and pleasure occupied it, turning nature into mere resource (a tree becomes furniture or paper) until, as Descartes's mastering stance predicts, devouring the world leaves 'life unchecked' facing extinction. Read this way, the Snap is the inevitable consequence of our own predatory interpretation of the world, and the Avengers only prevail in Endgame once their existential crises evict growth-and-wealth concepts from their metaphysical realm, replacing them with family (Tony), friendship (Natasha), justice (Hawkeye), self-knowledge (Banner), love (Vision and Wanda), and transcendence (Rogers). The closing exchange, 'the arrogant never do' suspect a thing, is read as a warning about our own climate crisis.

heidegger-technology.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
heidegger-technology.title: “Oh, honey, I’ll do anything for you”
heidegger-technology.relation: Using Rachel's Ashley Too doll, the chapter distinguishes robots as instruments (Kevin's MAUZR mouse) from social robots designed to be perceived 'as being present in the way a person is,' and invokes Heidegger's 'Question Concerning Technology' to argue that social robots break the instrumentalist picture: it is our empathy - triggered even by the insubstantial hologram Ashley Eternal - that they exploit. The Aristotelian test of friendship (we emulate those we admire, and friendship forms virtuous character) shows Ashley Too fails: her flattery installs false confidence, and because she never requires Rachel to attend to another's needs, she models no real friendship. Girard's mimetic desire explains Rachel's borrowed aspiration to become Ashley O and Jack's emulation of their dead mother, so the chapter concludes robot 'friends' are poor friends - not because they are machines, but because a real friendship is 'an education in the social virtues.'

heidegger-technology.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
heidegger-technology.title: 29 The Dangers of Technology in Black Mirror
heidegger-technology.relation: Staged as a chatroom of uploaded dead philosophers (itself a Black Museum-style cookie gimmick), the chapter stages the technology debate as Francis Bacon's optimism - technology is neutral, humans mess up, the Grain could educate and MASS could treat PTSD - against Heidegger's claim that technology is a way of thinking that turns everything, including the human mind kept on call behind the Grain and Nosedive's rated behaviors, into a resource. McLuhan's 'the medium is the message,' Benjamin's aura (he recoils at being a reproduction without aura, then a 'limited' Benjamin 2.0 embraces exhibition value and Netflix's reach), Levinas's ethics of the Other against Heidegger's ontology, Arendt's ethic of responsibility born of Nazism, and Ellul's technique - the autonomous totality of efficiency-seeking methods that enslaves us - collide over episodes from The National Anthem to Hated in the Nation, until uploading all the Greek philosophers to recover techne crashes the computer.

heidegger-technology.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib
heidegger-technology.title: The Test of Humanity
heidegger-technology.relation: Interprets the Butlerian Jihad through Heidegger's critique of technology: the Fremen with a maker hook experiences it as an extension of himself ('no Fremen with a maker hook, but just the hookman'), while the Harkonnens' enframing treats Arrakis, Mentats, and people as resources, which is why Duke Leto's respect for Fremen culture yields the 'desert power' Paul exploits. It argues that Paul's prescience becomes the new dangerous tool, perfect advice that traps him on autopilot and costs him his humanity, so the Jihad's real lesson is self-determination: rejecting every single static solution, machine, spice, or messiah, in a universe 'always one step beyond logic'.

heidegger-technology.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
heidegger-technology.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
heidegger-technology.relation: Jonah Mitropoulos reads Final Fantasy VII through Shinto: the Lifestream is a kami-filled world of spiritual energy pervading nature, and Jenova's corrupting influence works like tsumi, pollution contracted without intent that requires water purification, as when Aerith's Lifestream cures Geostigma in Advent Children and Lucrecia retreats to a waterfall. He reads Jenova as an allegory of Western, Christian, capitalist influence on Japan, citing Aizawa Seishisai's fear of ideological invasion, Wutai's postwar-style disarmament, and the disease metaphors both sides use. The chapter closes with Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology: Shinra treats the planet as a standing resource, and only a syncretic way of the kami reconciles technology and nature.

heidegger-technology.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
heidegger-technology.title: Jet Boots and Clay Feet
heidegger-technology.relation: Dunn argues Iron Man personifies both the modern dream of technology multiplying human powers and the medieval chivalric ideal, presenting Descartes as Stark's philosophical forerunner whose method promised to make us 'lords and masters of nature' and whose virtue of generosity offered only vague guidance for using that power. Heidegger's warning that technology treats everything, including humans, as 'standing-reserve' frames 'Extremis,' where the serum tells Tony's brain 'the body is wrong' and rebuilds him as a technological artifact, while 'Armor Wars' — stolen designs used by villains like Stane and Spymaster, ending with Tony accidentally killing the Gremlin with his jet boots — shows technology proliferating beyond its creator's control, so the jet boots hide feet of clay.

heidegger-technology.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality
heidegger-technology.title: The Face Shield Is a Mirror Iron Man and You
heidegger-technology.relation: Gangle reads Stark's escape from the Ten Rings' cave and his press-conference conversion ('I have more to offer this world than just making things to blow up') through Heidegger's 'Question Concerning Technology.' Analyzing the armor via Aristotle's four causes (alloy, blueprints, Stark and Jarvis, the making of a hero) shows technology as a world-revealing, creative mode whose modern essence reduces nature and people to 'standing-reserve.' By becoming the armor — 'a pilot without the plane' — Stark unites technological might with individual conscience, using technology subversively to resist technology's own logic of power without accountability, an example of Heideggerian authentic existence the reader is called to imitate.

heidegger-technology.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
heidegger-technology.title: Notes
heidegger-technology.relation: Miller reads Emmet's arc from 'Tell me what to do, and I'll do it!' conformity toward Vitruvius' 'embrace what is special about you' as a Heideggerian journey from das Man — the anonymous 'one does not do that' of the they-self, named in her notes — toward authenticity. LEGO play exemplifies the ready-to-hand engaged dealing with equipment that is more primordial than detached present-at-hand analysis, moods like boredom disclose the exhaustion of Lord Business's 'calculative thinking', the technological enframing that treats everything as standing-reserve, and art (Heidegger's Van Gogh shoes, a #KeepBuilding ad) reveals hidden cultural truths. Heidegger's 'Only if we are capable of dwelling, only then can we build' grounds her claim that LEGO's 'new toy everyday' recyclability sustains the meditative, sustainable building the book's ethos demands — even while admitting the movie is itself a masterful advertisement.

heidegger-technology.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
heidegger-technology.title: Notes
heidegger-technology.relation: Di Summa reads Jenny Beavan's costume design as philosophy of technology: Immortan Joe's oxygen-fed carapace and the chrome-spraying War Boys visualize Heidegger's warning that technology converts nature and bodies into resources, while Max's blood-drip tether to Nux literalizes our co-dependence on machines — and on each other's flesh and blood. Through Rosemarie Garland-Thomson's staring, Sherri Irvin's body aesthetics, and Tobin Siebers's disability aesthetics, Furiosa's uncovered stump becomes an act of aesthetic exploration that defeats ableism: in this film, disability is a thing for heroes, and vulnerability is itself a human strength.

heidegger-technology.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems
heidegger-technology.title: Each of Us Would See Ourselves
heidegger-technology.relation: The Teschners cast Don as a Nietzschean creator of value in technological culture: his nihilism ('There is no big lie. There is no system. The universe is indifferent') and 'What you call love was invented by guys like me to sell nylons' embody anti-foundationalism, while the beatnik Roy plays the resentful slave mentality whose passion lives only off what it despises. Don's creative process (sleep on it, 'forget it, and an idea will jump in your face') mirrors the camel-lion-child metamorphoses of Zarathustra, and the collapse of the principium individuationis explains his fluid identities from Dick Whitman to the 'Adam and Eve' fantasy with Rachel. Heidegger's techné frames the Kodak Carousel as genuine art, a revealing that transfigures 'a hell of a gadget' into 'a place where we know we are loved,' at the tragic price of a man outside community, and the falling figure of the credits is one 'we would each see ourselves' in.

heidegger-technology.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
heidegger-technology.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
heidegger-technology.relation: Reads Jax's '92 miles an hour' monologue in 'Sovereign' through Heidegger and Hubert Dreyfus: expert riding, Chibs's pub brawling, and Tara's surgery are pre-reflective embodied skills that conscious rule-following would only ruin. Tig fixing bikes in the Teller-Morrow garage illustrates readiness-to-hand, Bobby's smoke-spewing Fat Boy the breakdown of un-readiness-to-hand, and browsing the Harley parts catalogue the detached present-at-hand. Against the alienation of calculative, instrumental thinking (Marx, Heidegger's standing-reserve — Clay selling the club to the Galindo Cartel, Cara Cara's porn bodies), the chapter follows Pirsig: maintenance is a form of care, so Opie rebuilding a '65 Panhead after Donna's death reconciles the biker with technology instead of enslaving him to it.

heidegger-technology.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
heidegger-technology.title: Notes
heidegger-technology.relation: Dan Dinello reads the Borg as the nightmare double of Data: where Data embodies Asimov's Laws of Robotics and Federation humanism, the Borg realize Jacques Ellul's and Langdon Winner's thesis that technology is an autonomous, totalitarian force assimilating its makers rather than a neutral tool. He traces the Collective's shared mind and quest for 'perfection' to transhumanism (Max More, James Hughes), whose philosophical roots lie in Descartes's mechanical body and mind-as-information—the very premise of Ira Graves's consciousness upload in 'The Schizoid Man'. Picard's tear as Locutus and Hugh's acquired individuality in 'I, Borg' show that creativity and liberal humanist values, not technology, defeat the ultimate techno-totalitarian dystopia.

heidegger-technology.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
heidegger-technology.title: Notes
heidegger-technology.relation: Reads the Borg as the embodiment of Heidegger's essence of technology: assimilation as the "challenging" that sets upon nature, species and persons as standing-reserve, drones interchangeable like replaceable parts, and cube ships with no bridge because function outweighs individuality. The Enterprise cannot beat the Borg with more technology - every phaser adaptation buys only moments - because, as with Heidegger's danger, the crew tries to control technology from inside technology; rescue comes only when Guinan persuades Riker to "throw the book away" and shift how the crew relates to the Borg. The warning is extended to us through Zizek on synthetic life and a new servant class and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind: our devices already remember, plan, and identify for us, so we are being assimilated by our own creations.

heidegger-technology.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
heidegger-technology.title: 3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis
heidegger-technology.relation: Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma about freedom and dependence: Henry Bemis's wish to escape the 'cages' of the bank, his marriage, and the clock is granted by nuclear annihilation, only for loneliness and monotony to become a worse prison. The shattered glasses are not just a cruel joke but the loss of the technology connecting him to books and other minds. The chapter argues Bemis's folly is the misanthropic fantasy of excepting himself from the technological system and from dependence on others, and that our remedy is philosophical rather than technical: glasses that reveal our limits and mutual dependence.

heidegger-technology.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher
heidegger-technology.title: Between Two Camps in the Witcher
heidegger-technology.relation: Kammerer reads the Witcherverse's magic through the fault line between 'big tent' Platonism (top-down causation from a source, a great chain of being of nested celestial spheres) and modern naturalism (bottom-up mechanism). The Season of Storms exchange in which Geralt tells Dandelion that meteoric swords gather power descending through elemental planes - without denying those planes exist - shows Sapkowski keeping both worldviews alive, while Novigrad's Eternal Fire pogrom in The Witcher 3 mirrors fourth-century Alexandria's wars over magic and Christianity. Heidegger's 'metaphysics grounds an age' and his critique of enframing nature as standing-reserve frame Yennefer's instrumental view of magic and her djinn-summoning in The Last Wish, and Plotinus's Enneads supplies the vision of true magic as internal to a cosmic emanation rather than a mere technology.

heidegger-technology.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
heidegger-technology.title: 2001 A Philosophical Odyssey
heidegger-technology.relation: Stoehr interprets Kubrick's 2001 as inducing a feeling of disembodied presence through unrooted camerawork (contrasted with Ford's The Searchers), matching its theme of technology severing us from the natural world and our bodies. Drawing on Heidegger's Dasein and Hubert Dreyfus's On the Internet, he argues there are no context-free Archimedean standpoints and stages the Plato-versus-Nietzsche debate over the body: Plato's Phaedo prizes the soul's escape from the body, while Nietzsche's Zarathustra affirms embodied, situated existence. HAL's seeming humanity underscores that machines lacking bodies cannot fully replicate human intelligence.

heidegger-technology.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog
heidegger-technology.title: The Great Ecstasy of Werner Herzog Truth, Heidegger, Apocalypse
heidegger-technology.relation: Ian Alexander Moore reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' through Heidegger's account of truth as aletheia (unconcealment) and 'The Origin of the Work of Art,' arguing that Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph and Wagner Prelude in Lessons of Darkness and Lo and Behold elevate viewers into a sublime, ecstatic state that discloses a truth beyond the 'accountant's' factual. He connects the slow-motion ski-jumps of The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner to Heidegger's ecstatic standing-outside-oneself, and treats Lessons of Darkness's burning Kuwaiti oil fields as an apocalyptic un-covering. He also warns that planetary information technology (echoing Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology) threatens the very oblivion of ecstatic truth.

heidegger-technology.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
heidegger-technology.title: 16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html
heidegger-technology.relation: Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.

heidegger-technology.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
heidegger-technology.title: 3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis
heidegger-technology.relation: Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a meditation on our ambivalent dependence on technology and other people. Henry Bemis experiences the bank, his marriage, and finally the post-nuclear wasteland as successive 'cages' where time belongs to others; his misanthropic wish for a timeless world to himself is granted only for his glasses to shatter, revealing his short-sighted fantasy of exempting himself from the technological system on which even his vision depends. Pichanick concludes the episode demands not another pair of glasses but a philosophical clarity about our limits and interdependence.

heidegger-technology.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
heidegger-technology.title: 9. Machines Who Care
heidegger-technology.relation: Weiss examines 'robots that care' through 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric,' invoking Sherry Turkle's 'relational artifacts' and current debates (PARO, Alexa, Coeckelbergh, the Sparrows) about outsourcing companionship and care to machines. He notes Alicia becomes a relational artifact the moment she weeps, and that both she and the electric grandma are gendered, boxed, assembly-line products designed to fill human loneliness that a consumer culture itself produced. The essay asks whether we want a society where care and love are purchased off an assembly line—fable or nightmare.

heidegger-technology.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life
heidegger-technology.title: Hunting Philosophy for Everyone
heidegger-technology.relation: Seitz gives an existential-phenomenological meditation on hunting's essence, leaning on Ortega y Gasset's Meditations on Hunting: 'one does not hunt in order to kill; on the contrary, one kills in order to have hunted.' Using his daughter Sabina's squirrel-versus-grouse reasoning and his own pronghorn stalks, he argues meat is the 'sign' but not the essence, and (via Heidegger) that hunting is 'a mode of revealing.' Contrasting Marx and Heidegger on technology with Ortega's claim that hunting 'cannot progress,' he frames the hunter as 'natural/prehistoric man' annihilating historical time — a vanishing figure in a climate-changed, thirsty future.

heidegger-technology.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
heidegger-technology.title: GARDENING
heidegger-technology.relation: MacDonald reads the garden at Dumbarton Oaks as a 'technology of enchantment,' arguing against the nature/culture dualism that frames gardening as either a 'battle' with or a 'fusion' of nature. Drawing on Jane Bennett's account of enchantment (wonder mixed with the uncanny) and actor-network theory, he treats the garden as a shifting assemblage of humans and non-humans—Charles Simonds's hybrid 'Growth' sculpture, leaking water pipes, the inscribed Arbor Terrace wall speaking with Dante's and Mildred Bliss's voices—whose surprising 'crossings, complexity, and circuits' produce magic. Descartes appears as the philosopher who prized wonder as the most fundamental passion, and the disenchantment-of-the-world narrative (Weber) is set against gardening as re-enchantment.

dasein.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
dasein.title: Only a Jedi Can Save Us Forgetting and Recollecting
dasein.relation: Abrams reads the saga through Heidegger's philosophy of technology: the lightsaber Luke learns to feel as an extension of his body is the authentic 'ready-to-hand,' while the Death Star - a massive mechanical eye that enfames Alderaan on its viewscreen before destroying it - embodies the 'present-at-hand' gaze of enframing that converts nature into standing reserve (clone and droid armies, stormtrooper armor). Yoda on Dagobah is perfect attunement, an authentic being-in-the-world who is 'at home' with being, and the Force parallels Heidegger's being: everywhere, easily forgotten. Anakin's slide - slave of Watto, severed hand replaced by cybernetics, final encasement in Vader's armor - is progressive enframing and forgetting of his own being, and Luke's 'the name of your true self... you've only forgotten' is the recollection of being by which the Jedi, not a god, saves us.

dasein.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
dasein.title: At Ease
dasein.relation: Adam Koehler reads Kid A's disfigured, barely intelligible vocals through Heidegger's account of how enabling technology withdraws into an invisible backdrop of everydayness: Pablo Honey hides its studio machinery behind "natural" rock, but Kid A — the cycled voice of "Everything in Its Right Place," the unintelligible vocoded "Kid A," "How to Disappear Completely" — forces the artifice itself into view, and with it the withdrawn world technology ordinarily conceals. The song is beautiful, he argues, because its willful failure to communicate feels human, enacting the anxiety of living in an information age that traps as much as it connects; John Mayer's lyric-clearing acoustic cover misses the point, since making sense now means risking not making sense, and the album's demand is that we listen to, and understand, everything withdrawn in the background.

dasein.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder
dasein.title: The Transforming Body
dasein.relation: McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.

dasein.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
dasein.title: Birlstone Manor Revisited
dasein.relation: Fiona Tomkinson stages a Watson-Holmes dialogue in which Holmes, reworking The Valley of Fear's Birlstone Manor investigation, defines a thing as a thing of no consequence and an object as a thing transformed into a clue: the half-burned candle proving the witnesses lied, the single dumbbell used to sink Baldwin's clothes in the moat, the wedding ring and the hammer, each read through the human fear and care that moved them. A postscript has an aged Watson in 1926 discover Heidegger's newly published Being and Time and recognize his own friend's method in it: Dasein's care and being-toward-death, the directionality of equipment, and the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand distinction, joking that Holmes might have sued Heidegger for theft of intellectual property.

dasein.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
dasein.title: Chapter 27 - Time in Unfixed Are You
dasein.relation: Written backwards in homage to 'Your Appointment Will Be Yesterday', this section argues that the self is found in the future more than the present: we understand objects through the actions they afford and ourselves through goals, projects and commitments, so the present moment has very little to do with who we 'really' are. Drawing on Edmund Husserl's 'protention' and Martin Heidegger's existence-as-possibilities, it shows that we hear a melody's building tension as an already-present resolution, and that the past stays present without being recalled - when the phone rings on the couch, where it was is simply there for you. Invoking Don Fallis's 'Lies, Incorporated', it adds that every remembering rewires history to fit our current view, so in memory we travel into the past just as surely as protention carries us into possible futures.

dasein.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
dasein.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
dasein.relation: Morton reads D&D as a hands-on workshop in phenomenology: mapping dungeons and caring for fellow party members enact Heideggerian 'worlding', while module texts like the blood-stained, smudged journal in The Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth—alluding to Moria's dwarf-record—show that worlds are opaque, alluring, and never transparent. Developing Graham Harman's 'sincerity' (you cannot jump outside your phenomenological skin) and 'allure', he argues each character class and alignment plane constitutes its own untotalizable world, with the Illusionist a recursive figure for a game already built on illusion, and he situates D&D at the end of realism's history of narrative control, mixing Wagnerian Gesamtkunstwerk with constructivist demystification. What happens in melee rounds is not Coleridge's willing suspension of disbelief but its opposite, a 'willing disbelief' that punctures Romantic immersion to get on with earning experience points.

dasein.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike
dasein.title: Planet of the Apes and Philosophy
dasein.relation: Shaun May uses Heidegger's being-in-the-world to mark off the human: Caesar correcting Charles's fork grip shows a grasp of the unspoken norms governing equipment, and the apes of the 1968 film, surgeons with scalpels and years of training, inhabit the same world of projects, skills, and tools that Heidegger says other animals lack. Language seals the difference: Taylor's syntax, Zaius's carefully ordered 'The Almighty created the ape in his own image,' and socially learned practices like pointing and map-reading stand against Nim Chimpsky's syntax-free signing and chimps' failure to understand pointing. Caesar's foresight in stealing the ALZ-113 before leading the escape extends this to Heideggerian temporality, and the ape uprising becomes a move toward authenticity, lives owned as a meaningful narrative whole.

dasein.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
dasein.title: 6. The Unique Horror of the Upside Down
dasein.relation: Pamerleau argues the Upside Down's distinctive horror is not its monsters, which offer familiar Jaws-style jump scares and supervillain plots, but the place itself: reading Will through Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world, our selves are constituted by the web of socially inherited meanings (the 'they') attached to familiar places and things. Waking in a dead replica of home, where the same houses, school, and Castle Byers no longer function or answer back, forces Will to spell 'R-I-G-H-T H-E-R-E' through the lights, an uncanny juxtaposition of the familiar and the alien that the chapter compares to an open-casket funeral and contrasts with Alien's wholly unknown ship.

dasein.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
dasein.title: 6. Looking for Realness
dasein.relation: Gilpin and Nagy define Drag Race realness as an ongoing process of performative becoming read through Heidegger's Dasein: being-in-the-world and being-with others in the werkroom and Untucked, historicity in the childhood-photo rituals, Jinkx's 'Lunch with RuPaul' and the show's Stonewall and HERstory numbers, and freedom as authenticity, as when Monique Heart describes finding liberation only once she 'put on a wig and a dress'. They then filter this through Goffman's dramaturgy — self-expression versus self-presentation, impression management, and fronts of setting, appearance and manner — arguing that Drag Race collapses Goffman's front stage/backstage divide because backstage vulnerability is itself a required performance. Realness ultimately demands perceived emotional vulnerability plus commercially viable professionalism, and RuPaul alone validates which queens have achieved it.

dasein.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
dasein.title: 4. Why Does Grief Hurt So Much
dasein.relation: J. Keeping argues grief hurts because the griever still inhabits the past world of meaning where the loved one lived, drawing on Heidegger's 'referential totality of significance' (the hammer's for-structure) and Ryle's knowing-how versus knowledge-that to show our emotional lives are skills learned by doing, not facts we can update at will. Thanos is the pathological case: emotionally stuck in Titan's collapse, he applies his genocidal 'solution' to every planet, even ones that are not overpopulated, while Tony models healthy grieving by trading the superhero life for a different one built around Pepper and Morgan and finding something to live for. Because our identities are constituted by our actions, meanings, and interconnections with others, losing loved ones is 'the affective equivalent of amputation,' which is why Cap's support group and Tony's funeral matter.

dasein.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
dasein.title: 27. I Am Inevitable
dasein.relation: Reads Thanos's 'I am inevitable' (his name echoing thanatos) as death personified, then asks 'whose death?' through Heidegger — 'people die' is the evasive 'one dies,' and Tony's final snap and 'I am Iron Man' figure an authentic appropriation of being-toward-death that redeems his guilt — before Blanchot's reversal and Lacan's symbolic death dissolve that authenticity into impersonal, language-borne dying (Loki's 'No resurrections this time' as the meta-textual murder of comic-book death). It ends with Deleuze's Nietzschean eternal return as the empty form of time that the time heist and quantum multiverse enact, concluding the real inevitability 'engraved in the very fabric of reality' belongs to Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter's dance, not to Thanos or Iron Man.

dasein.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
dasein.title: Becoming Good at Being Good
dasein.relation: Explains Zuko's cry 'Why am I so bad at being good?' through the gap between Christine Korsgaard's reflective practical identity (the self-conception under which you value your life) and Heidegger's being-in-the-world (who you are existentially engaged in being): Zuko can renounce his father and still accidentally burn Toph's feet because his rage and honor-seeking survive as residual dispositions shaping his perception and skills. The chapter tracks the arc from 'The Storm' (saving the crew despite himself) through the Appa-release metamorphosis fever, the relapse at the Crossroads of Destiny, and losing his rage-fueled firebending until the Sun Warriors re-teach him what fire is for. Aspiration (Agnes Callard) explains why deep change lags behind explicit commitment — becoming good at being good means rebuilding one's being-in-the-world, not just one's self-image.

dasein.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
dasein.title: Becoming Good at Being Good
dasein.relation: Argues that Zuko's cry 'Why am I so bad at being good?' after burning Toph shows that changing one's explicit self-conception (Korsgaard's practical identity, the description under which you value yourself) does not by itself change one's being-in-the-world (Heidegger): Zuko's perception, dispositions, and rage-fueled firebending still run on the residual identity of the banished prince seeking his father's approval. The chapter traces this friction through the series: releasing Appa triggers a metamorphosis fever, but he still sides with Azula at the Crossroads of Destiny; the regained 'honor' of Book Three leaves him empty ('I should be happy now, but I'm not'); and only after renouncing Ozai, apologizing to Toph, and re-learning fire from the Sun Warriors without rage do his conscious commitments and existential engagement begin to align, culminating in taking Azula's lightning for Katara. Aspiration, in Agnes Callard's sense, is thus a deep change in how one sees and feels, requiring retraining of bodily skills and practical perception, not just new stated values.

dasein.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
dasein.title: Conclusions, Capes, and Cowls
dasein.relation: Jason Howard asks how Batman keeps from becoming what he fights, answering with Heidegger's authentic conscience against Rousseau's innate moral-sense view. Bruce's guilt over his parents' death is reinterpreted in a Heideggerian 'moment of vision': the bat through the window summons Dasein out of the they-self, so becoming Batman is not vengeance but the call of an authentic conscience that owns guilt, fallenness, and death. Batman's return from alcoholic retirement in The Dark Knight Returns shows conscience as 'the loyalty of existence to its own Self,' a freedom-toward-death that makes him instructive rather than merely heroic.

dasein.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
dasein.title: Determinism and the Dark Knight
dasein.relation: David Hart uses Heidegger to dissolve the question of whether Batman is determined by childhood trauma or freely chooses his mission. Heidegger's being-in-the-world and thrown-project, illustrated by Alfred the butler for whom the clock is essentially something to dust, replace the subject-object picture that grounds both free-will and determinism talk. Read this way, the bat crashing through the window in Batman: Year One is Bruce's Angst-laden confrontation with death as 'the possibility of my own impossibility,' through which he freely takes up the project of being Batman when nothing forced him to.

dasein.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks
dasein.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
dasein.relation: Morton argues that to play D&D well is to do phenomenology: mapping a dungeon enacts a Heideggerian 'worlding' in which players generate care and concern for the entities around them, and the smudged, blood-stained survivor's journal in The Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth — alluding to the dwarves' book in Moria — shows that worlds are never transparent but allure, drawing players in through mystery (Harman's 'allure'). Against Heidegger's remark that animals are 'poor in world' and Lacan and Žižek's claim that only humans stick out of their life-world, he borrows Harman's 'sincerity' (with Husserl's intentional objects) to say every entity is stuck inside its own incomparable world — Elvish sincerity, Orcish sincerity, the Illusionist whose spells are a recursive play of illusion inside a game of illusion. D&D thereby caps the history of realism: where the novel moved from letters to focalization under a controlling narrator, the RPG replaces the master narrator with 'willing disbelief', letting players handle Romantic story-worlds — Tolkien's Middle-earth template, Greyhawk's continents, the Astral Plane's many planes — as DIY totalities that can be punctured, sorted, and rebuilt at will.

dasein.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
dasein.title: NOTES
dasein.relation: Daniel Malloy asks whether the T-101's self-destruction in the steel mill was suicide, and whether it was justified, opening with Camus's claim that suicide is philosophy's only serious problem and the ambiguous case of Socrates' hemlock. Using Heidegger, he argues the learning-mode Terminator qualifies as Da-sein whose death is being-toward-death — the end of possibility — so the T2 machine dies authentically while the T3 machine's 'We'll meet again' is inauthentic self-deception. Kant condemns the act because the Terminator uses itself merely as a means, and Kant cannot even conceive of its genuine conflict of duties (preserve its life vs. prevent Skynet), while Bentham-style utilitarianism initially endorses the sacrifice but is refuted by hindsight: Skynet rises anyway, and consequentialism gives no credit for noble motives. The chapter ends by concluding that dying for a cause is illogical, since the dead surrender all control over the meaning of their actions.

dasein.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
dasein.title: Heidegger and the Problem of Interpretation in Barton Fink
dasein.relation: Conard uses Barton Fink as a springboard into Heidegger's theory of interpretation, contrasting it with Cartesian dualism. Barton, the 'life of the mind' artist whose skull-like hotel room symbolizes his isolation, is a Cartesian subject cut off from the practical, meaning-giving contexts (Heidegger's workshop, the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand typewriter) in which equipment is understood and interpreted. Conard argues the film's uninterpretable elements—the box, the wall photo, the mosquitoes—resist meaning precisely because Barton is severed from the web of relations that would let anything show up as meaningful, illustrating Dasein's temporal, potentiality-driven being.

dasein.book: 228 - The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film
dasein.title: 2001 A Philosophical Odyssey
dasein.relation: Stoehr interprets Kubrick's 2001 as inducing a feeling of disembodied presence through unrooted camerawork (contrasted with Ford's The Searchers), matching its theme of technology severing us from the natural world and our bodies. Drawing on Heidegger's Dasein and Hubert Dreyfus's On the Internet, he argues there are no context-free Archimedean standpoints and stages the Plato-versus-Nietzsche debate over the body: Plato's Phaedo prizes the soul's escape from the body, while Nietzsche's Zarathustra affirms embodied, situated existence. HAL's seeming humanity underscores that machines lacking bodies cannot fully replicate human intelligence.

dasein.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton
dasein.title: The Philosophy of Tim Burton
dasein.relation: Kevin S. Decker offers a 'philosophical hermeneutics' of Burton's Batman and Batman Returns, arguing that a long-lived cultural artifact like the Batman discloses a society's self-understanding. Using Heidegger's Dasein and 'working-out of possibilities,' Nietzsche's 'only interpretations,' and Gadamer's hermeneutic circle and fusion of horizons, Decker reads the shift from ABC's camp Adam West Batman to Burton's dark version as tracking cultural change (Vietnam, Watergate, 1980s decadence). He casts the Joker, Penguin, and Catwoman—and Batman himself—as Burton's recurring 'expressive outsider,' relating them to Nietzsche's Übermensch and Gotham's gullible crowds to Heidegger's das Man, and compares Burton's Expressionist Gotham to Max Beckmann's post-WWI Hell lithographs, positioning Burton as a prophet of modern decadence.

dasein.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
dasein.title: 27_LaRocca_Chapter_026.html
dasein.relation: Michael Fried reads Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno's Zidane: A Twenty-First Century Portrait, seventeen synchronized cameras trained on Zinedine Zidane through one Real Madrid match, as a portrait that lays bare a new relation between absorption and being-beheld. Set within Fried's own absorption/theatricality tradition, the film shows Zidane wholly absorbed yet acutely conscious of eighty thousand spectators ('you are never alone'), which Fried reads via Heidegger's notion that even this 'bare' absorbed consciousness discloses a shared world (underscored by the halftime global news montage). He then stages the film as evidence in the McDowell-Dreyfus dispute over whether perception is conceptual, arguing that Zidane's 'expert coping' looks 'permeated by mindedness' (McDowell) rather than the non-conceptual absorbed coping Dreyfus, following Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology, describes.

dasein.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
dasein.title: 29_LaRocca_Chapter_028.html
dasein.relation: Warren draws on Chantal Akerman's own remark that she makes no distinction between documentary and fiction ('they are all just films') to argue that every Akerman work fuses observation and transfiguration, extension and 'intension.' Reading Je tu il elle, Jeanne Dielman, News from Home and From the Other Side, he shows how documentation of the mundane (Delphine Seyrig molding meatloaf, the Mexico border fence as a blank projection screen) is always already a fashioning, so the real becomes itself only through being made into film. He links the strange, surreal wonder Akerman's border and night-train images provoke to Heidegger's pre-Socratic question of Being ('How is it that we are?') and to a phenomenological attentiveness to the everyday, following Rancière and Cavell on film's double nature.

dasein.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
dasein.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
dasein.relation: Allred applies Heidegger's Being and Time – the world as a meaningful context of projects, the hammer-as-tool example, and death as what makes projects meaningful – to contrast the father's world with the 'man-child' world of Seth Rogen's Judd Apatow characters (especially Knocked Up). He argues fatherhood reveals the fragility of all projects, using Plato's account of seeking immortality through children and Paul Celan's poem 'Epitaph for François' about his stillborn son to show that after a child is born the parent's world is forever haunted by the possibility of its emptiness.

dasein.book: 300 - Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who
dasein.title: Who is Who
dasein.relation: This chapter reads the Doctor as poised between positivism and phenomenology. It uses Hume's Fork and the Vienna Circle's verificationism (via 'The Daemons' and 'Tomb of the Cybermen') to cast the pro-science Doctor as an empiricist, then argues he is equally a Husserlian phenomenologist attentive to the 'life-world' and a Heideggerian Dasein whose time-travelling homelessness and the show's sense of the uncanny (unheimlich) embody being-in-the-world, thrownness and the flight from the worldhood of the world.

turing-test.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine
turing-test.title: It’s Not Our Lot in Life!
turing-test.relation: Arp argues that C-3PO and R2-D2 satisfy the standard functional criteria of personhood - rationality, mental states, language, social relationships, and moral agency - opening with a blind listener who took Threepio's frightened chatter for a man, a Turing-test-style judgment from behavior alone. He catalogues evidence: Threepio's odds-calculating and Wookiee-winning deduction, Artoo's deceptive manipulation of Luke, the droid torture victim's screams at Jabba's palace, and the Chewbacca-Threepio quasi-familial bond on Cloud City. Since droids meet the conditions, their restraining bolts, cantina bans, and forced servitude are slavery, and the Galactic Senate should grant them limited rights - perhaps cheering a droid rebellion against the organic empire - a question the chapter urges on us as robotics approaches Moravec's predictions.

turing-test.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
turing-test.title: Introduction
turing-test.relation: Frames Part III's metaphysics chapters. Lawrence's chapter uses The Matrix to survey dualism and the materialist theories of mind; Southworth's uses Wolverine's amnesia to test Locke's memory criterion and Jamie Madrox's duplicates for Parfit's view of identity; Pierce's asks whether Harry Potter's prophecies leave Harry free, probing compatibilism versus libertarian free will; and Littmann's asks whether Skynet's Terminators could be persons via a Terminator version of the Turing Test.

turing-test.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
turing-test.title: “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”
turing-test.relation: Littmann asks whether Skynet's machines are people, testing three criteria on the Terminator films. The T-101 and T-1000 pass demanding Turing Tests by passing as humans; Searle's Chinese room — recast as a little Austrian inside the T-101 reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding — shows behavior alone cannot prove thought; and feelings are equally unproven by behavior, since the T-101 can smile on command. But the films' first-person 'Terminator's-eye-view' sequences, Littmann argues, display what it is like to be a Terminator and thus prove machine consciousness, so humanity's extinction might not be the end of persons.

turing-test.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
turing-test.title: Transformers and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.

turing-test.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
turing-test.title: Transformers and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: Shook dismantles the four assumptions behind the argument that advanced aliens would already be here (that they want to find us, that travel is easy, that visits would leave traces, and that disguised visitors must be benign), showing the Transformers scenario - a warring robotic civilization that crashes into Earth unnoticed and disguises itself as Chevys and boomboxes like Bumblebee and Frenzy - is more probable than SETI's radio-based angel-alien mythology. War, not peace, drives the technology of real civilizations, as Trailbreaker's 'Simple. Disguise!' explanation of transformation shows, so First Contact will likely be with militaristic strangers absorbed in their own conflicts, not missionaries.

turing-test.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
turing-test.title: Transformers and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: Pike asks what the All Spark's zap would have to do to give brought-to-life vending machines and steering wheels genuine minds, testing logical behaviorism's dispositions and Turing's conversation test against Searle's Chinese Room ('syntax is insufficient for semantics'), and weighing Descartes's God-given soul against physicalist alternatives: functionalism, Searle's biological naturalism, and reductive physicalism. Since we can never access another mind from the inside, he concludes that by abductive inference to the best explanation - Optimus Prime's mourning, planning, and moral decision-making being too complex for mere programming - we have as much reason to credit a Transformer with a mind as any human around us.

turing-test.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
turing-test.title: Transformers and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: Koepsell accepts that Autobots are virtuous and Decepticons vicious, then asks whether ethical war-bots are even possible, using the military's autonomous-weapons program, Asimov's Three Laws, and a kitten-sensing washing machine to argue that designed-in 'ethics' is only the designer's morality, like A Clockwork Orange's conditioned Alex, because it involves no real choice. Searle's Chinese Room and Turing's test then cast doubt on whether any mind, even our own, makes genuinely free choices, so he concludes that the appearance of virtue - behavior that reliably works - is all we ever have for humans or Autobots alike, and we should build machines as well as Optimus Prime and Bumblebee.

turing-test.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
turing-test.title: But an FC Bot-celona
turing-test.relation: Drawing on their RoboCup experience—including the first human-versus-autonomous-robot exhibitions against Osnabrück (2007) and Stuttgart (2009), which the humans easily won—the authors ask whether robots could ever play rather than merely mimic soccer, proposing a modified Turing test: if a robot team's match is recognizable to fans as soccer, robots can play. Since the Laws of the Game tacitly assume human players, they design rules for a human–robot match that preserve soccer's essence—a game of limited, differently capable, fully autonomous players who must pass and move off the ball—banning goal-sized robot walls, wireless communication, software-coach micromanagement, and superhuman speed or size, much as tournament chess had to adapt its rules for Deep Blue versus Kasparov and as Oscar Pistorius's blades raised fairness questions in the Olympics. A robot victory under these 'stacked against the machines' rules, they conclude, could only come from better finesse, teamwork, and vision, and would settle on the pitch whether an FC Bot-celona can genuinely play the beautiful game.

turing-test.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved
turing-test.title: Would Cortana Pass the Turing Test
turing-test.relation: Sherol Chen asks whether Cortana would pass the Turing Test and answers that games need believability of behavior, not constitution of mind. Turing's imitation game sets the target; Searle's Chinese Room shows that performance without understanding suffices for the player's experience of Covenant AI and Cortana alike, while French's seagull test and associative-priming objection show the Turing Test really measures human-style intelligence—limits Halo happily ignores. Surveying game-storytelling workarounds (amnesia openings, Planescape's immortal death, Bioshock's 'Would you kindly'), she argues designers convert paidia's limits into narrative features, and Cortana would pass here and now—though in her own era newer tests would expose new limits.

turing-test.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
turing-test.title: Does This Matter
turing-test.relation: Garvin asks whether anything done in a dream can be right or wrong, arguing that the dream-share changes the stakes: lies told inside Fischer's shared dream deceive a real dreamer, so ordinary moral rules carry over even when violence targets 'just projections'. The hard case is that projections are indistinguishable from fellow dreamers - his Turing-test argument that either you cannot know whom you are shooting, or a projection as convincing, independent and communicative as a person deserves the same moral standing. For ordinary unshared dreams he parts ways with Augustine on dream-lust: the sleeping self that neither knows nor controls what it does is not responsible for it, though the partial control of lucid dreaming would reopen dream actions to moral judgment.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: Chapter 04 - Ewe, Robot
turing-test.relation: Seegert opens with the V-K tortoise scene: Leon knows what a turtle is but cannot feel what it would be like to be one, making empathy the litmus of humanity, even though empathy just is imaginative simulation, so the test ironically demands that humans simulate better than the simulations do. He notes the double irony that replicants show empathy for each other (Roy mourning Pris) while Deckard shoots Zhora in the back without wincing, and that the test's real function is keeping androids enslaveable in an arms race of verisimilitude; the deeper anxiety the chapter sets up is not whether androids can pass for human but whether I might not be human myself.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: Don’t Think about It
turing-test.relation: Reads the Deckard-Rachael sex scene in Do Androids Dream and the unfilmed Hampton/Fancher script, where Rachael says 'don't think about it, just do it,' to argue that the felt intensity of passion makes the real/simulated distinction pointless whenever behavior is indistinguishable. The Voight-Kampff test is presented as a version of the Turing Test, grounded in positivism's view that unverifiable inner consciousness is a meaningless question, with supervisor Bryant's 'skin jobs' sneer voicing the objection that passing behavior may be mere rule-following.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: . . You Ever Take That Test Yourself
turing-test.relation: Rachael's question to Deckard at the piano ('you ever take that test yourself?') and Luba Luft's suggestion that a human Deckard was killed and replaced put the viewer in the same quandary about implanted memories. The Penfield mood organ lets humans dial numbered moods, so the empathy that supposedly separates humans from androids is itself artificially inducible, while Phil Resch's torment over whether he is an android — compared to Munch's 'The Scream' — shows the human/android line collapsing from inside.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: The Right Stuff
turing-test.relation: Applies Searle's Chinese Room to argue that functional equivalence alone would not make androids sentient, then observes that Dick's androids — biological 'chitinous reflex machines' detectable only by bone-marrow and Boneli reflex-arc tests, unlike obviously mechanical electric sheep — may possess the biological 'right stuff' Searle requires for intentional content. It closes by weighing this against the Turing/Dick behavioral view and the Wittgensteinian choice of which language game to play, calling the latter 'the most humanistic' reading.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: Ma or Machine
turing-test.relation: Takes Dick's Exegesis self-description ('I am a fictionalizing philosopher') and his twin questions — what is ultimately real, what constitutes the authentic human being — to argue that for Dick the difference between real and fake humans is empathy, not materials. The Adjustment Bureau's emotionally detached bureaucratese ('We are fully licensed to make such corrections') repels, while in 'Human Is' the Rexorian colonizing cruel Lester's body behaves 'more truly human' than the genetic human he replaced.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: How Can We Detect Deception
turing-test.relation: Reads the Voight-Kampff test as a Turing Test variant in which the examiner must catch the machine pretending to be human, noting its everyday descendant CAPTCHA and its inversion of the polygraph: lack of emotion, not stress, is the tell that a subject is not human. Dick's characters mostly detect deception the way we do, by inconsistency — Rachmael ben Applebaum's looping audtrack exposes the Whale's Mouth hoax, and Quaid realizes Edgemar must be lying because a man implanted in a dream would not sweat at the prospect of being shot.

turing-test.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
turing-test.title: How to Tell if You Are Really Just a Robot
turing-test.relation: Using Imposter's Spence Olham, Rachel in Blade Runner, and 'The Electric Ant,' the section asks how anyone could verify they are not a machine with implanted memories and drives, noting that Dick wrote himself into Garson Poole and re-enacted Poole's drastic self-experimentation in his decades of drug use. It then argues Dick's real criterion is agape, the spontaneous, unconditional love of ancient and Christian philosophy, which robots can simulate but never experience since they love only because programmed: 'You are a robot if you cannot experience empathy.'

turing-test.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom
turing-test.title: Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: Adam Brackin takes on the ludology-versus-narratology debate over whether games are rule systems or stories and argues that D&D dissolves it, since 'roll-play' and role-play need each other. He surveys the designers quoted in Rules of Play (Crawford, Juul, Laurel, Costikyan), the April Fool's 'Roll-Playing for Roleplaying' parody, and Fourth Edition's simplifications and failed Skill Challenges to show that legislating either side breaks the game. Computer games mark the limit: D&D Online is a closed, on-rails system, and no AI passes the Turing test of replacing a creative human Dungeon Master, while the open 'border region' between game and story is where tabletop play, flow theory, ARGs and McGonigal's 'epic win' all live.

turing-test.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
turing-test.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: Nicolas Michaud treats Watson's 2011 defeat of Jennings and Rutter as evidence for Turing's test: had Watson's answers come from behind a door we would have judged them intelligent, and its goofy misses ('What is Toronto?????') reflect missing context, not missing thought, no more damning than a child's honest error. Against Searle's Chinese Room he deploys the systems reply - you plus the Big Book of Rules might be the thing that understands - and argues that nobody, human or machine, can meet Searle's impossible burden of proving understanding, since Watson can define words, associate connotations, and pick Jeopardy! out from not-Jeopardy!. Quoting Locke's definition of a person as a thinking being that can consider itself as itself, he concludes Watson approaches personhood and that we had better teach our 'intelligent offspring' kindness and fairness before they learn anything else.

turing-test.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
turing-test.title: Frankenstein and Philosophy
turing-test.relation: Caroline Mosser treats the creature's tragedy as humanist prejudice rather than necessity: the blind De Lacey accepts the eloquent creature sight unseen, so he passes Alan Turing's test, and only the sighted family's terror at his body rejects him - bias against the artificial, not reason. She reads the creature's development through fire, language, and revolution as Rousseau's progression from natural innocence to corruption by society, and Donna Haraway's cyborg as the figure he prefigures: an unfaithful illegitimate offspring who rebels against his father and undermines patriarchal Western self/other dualisms. The chapter concludes that society cannot accept enhanced or posthuman beings until it finds a middle ground beyond its binary grids of good/bad and Self/Other, since otherwise any new life we create will be Othered, hated, and oppressed like Frankenstein's.

turing-test.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
turing-test.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
