The resolution distinguishes the group (which persists by composition or continuity) from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only partly through fans' allegiance, echoing Searle's social reality; Jordan concludes he was asking the wrong question, and Aristotle's circular account of virtue supplies the model for circular criteria of loyal fandom.

heraclitean-flux.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
heraclitean-flux.title: No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western
heraclitean-flux.relation: Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'

heraclitean-flux.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
heraclitean-flux.title: “A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo
heraclitean-flux.relation: Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.

heraclitean-flux.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir
heraclitean-flux.title: Nietzsche and the Meaning and Definition of Noir
heraclitean-flux.relation: Mark Conard uses The Postman Always Rings Twice and Goodis's Night Squad to survey the failed attempts to define noir (genre, style, cycle, mood) and contrasts two theories of definition: Socrates/Plato's search for the essential form versus Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, in which no stable 'being' exists behind becoming and language falsifies a world in motion, making essences and definitions fictions ('I am afraid we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar'). He proposes that noir is best understood as an American artistic response to Nietzsche's death of God, the loss of transcendent meaning and value that produces noir's pessimism, alienation, and moral disorientation, citing Sam Spade shrugging off his partner's murder and Ole Andersen passively awaiting his killers. Ironically, the same flux that makes noir what it is (the death of God) is what makes noir impossible to define.

heraclitean-flux.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
heraclitean-flux.title: Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard
heraclitean-flux.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.

heraclitean-flux.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
heraclitean-flux.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
heraclitean-flux.relation: Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.

heraclitean-flux.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
heraclitean-flux.title: 25_LaRocca_Chapter_024.html
heraclitean-flux.relation: K. L. Evans argues that Adam McKay's The Big Short is fiction that nonetheless borrows documentary's assertive stance to make true claims about the 2008 subprime crisis and to insist ordinary viewers are smart enough to 'read the signs.' Using Aristotle on fiction (concerned with meaning not fact), Auerbach and the Heraclitean maxim that 'a man's character is his fate,' she distinguishes real people from 'characters' (living images) like the film's Michael Burry and Billy Beane, arguing that casting Brad Pitt signals the fictive stance. She invokes Deleuze's question about the 'mode of existence' of whoever pronounces a proposition to explain how the unreliable narrator Vennett can still narrate reliably, and how the film embeds indigestible factual 'markers' to refute the idea that the crisis was too complex to understand.

heraclitean-flux.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film
heraclitean-flux.title: 28_LaRocca_Chapter_027.html
heraclitean-flux.relation: Hagberg argues that Grant Gee's documentary Patience (After Sebald) achieves a truthful portrait of W. G. Sebald not by static correspondence but by enacting his shifting, connection-making sensibility, as displayed in The Rings of Saturn. He deploys Wittgenstein's remarks on aspect-perception and 'seeing-as' (the duck-rabbit, the 'lighting up of an aspect') to show that perception is always already inflected by imagination, memory and language-games, dismantling the empiricist picture of Locke, Hume and Berkeley in which brute sensation precedes reflection. Borges's 'The Garden of Forking Paths' and 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius' supply the model of a Heraclitean flux of forking, mind-dependent connections, and the film's darkroom-like fading images and layered soundtrack are read as mimetically faithful to how a human sensibility perceives and remembers.

heraclitean-flux.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
heraclitean-flux.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
heraclitean-flux.relation: Steven Horrobin sorts sailors into three kinds — the cultural-iconography poser, the racer chasing a land-based prize, and the 'sailor of the third kind' for whom the open-ended voyage is an end in itself — and argues the third lives 'in the shadow of Heraclitus.' Against the substantialist ontology of Parmenides and Democritus (persons and boats as fixed things), he defends a process view in which everything, like a wave, is a passing fluctuation of one universal substance; citing Spinoza, self-becoming is the super-process reflecting itself. He dissolves the Ship of Theseus paradox (and Parfit's parallel-ship version) by making identity the continuity of a process's function rather than fixed parts, arguing the violent, corroding life of a boat reveals the flux beneath apparently stable things.

heraclitean-flux.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
heraclitean-flux.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
heraclitean-flux.relation: Clancy Smith argues that a tattoo's ink is permanent but the memory it evokes is not, because the past no longer exists and recollection is always present and in flux (citing Heraclitus' river and William James on never-identical brain states). Using Augustine's 'present of things past' and Proust's Swann's Way, plus Dewey's immediate empiricism and Merleau-Ponty's critique of memory-as-projection, he contends that gazing at a tattoo (his 'Not Fade Away' epitaph tattoo, his friend Kalju's crossed-rifles, American History X's swastika) constructs a present meaning that tells us who we are now rather than recovering the past intact.

heraclitean-flux.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
heraclitean-flux.title: BLUES
heraclitean-flux.relation: Joel Rudinow stages a three-way internal dialogue ('Me,' 'Myself,' and 'I') debating whether the commercialized, white-inflected blues — the House of Blues chain, the Blues Brothers, Cyndi Lauper's Memphis Blues, Clapton's Cream 'Crossroads' — is still really the blues. 'I' introduces Heraclitus's doctrine that everything flows and you cannot step twice into the same river, using the Heraclitean flux of culture to argue the blues is a living, ever-changing tradition whose 'canon' cannot be pinned to a fixed time, place, or racial purity, dissolving the survive/thrive/arrive question into one about how a canon forms and evolves.

heraclitean-flux.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas
heraclitean-flux.title: DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
heraclitean-flux.relation: John Rowan and Patricia Hallen build an extended elevator metaphor for dating (Ann and Bob riding floors, pushing buttons to raise or lower intimacy, gravity pulling toward breakup) to capture Heraclitus's insight that a relationship is a reality in constant change, while invoking Plato to insist the conceptual reality of a relationship is as real as physical objects. They define dating as gauging the possibility of eventual commitment, cite Hume's canoe image for implicit communication of shared destination, and ground their strategies—be yourself, go slowly, communicate, befriend—in Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating honesty, courage, and loyalty as habits lying in the golden mean between deficiency and excess (e.g., the Look Who's Talking date who overshares is 'excessively honest').

memetics.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
memetics.title: The Scheme of the Meme
memetics.relation: Defining the meme via the OED and Richard Dawkins - a cultural element spread by imitation that mutates like a gene under selection - O'Neil explains why heroes transform: creators get new ideas, markets demand new stories, authors age, new writers arrive, popularity wanes, or an executive has a brainstorm. The evidence ranges over Superman escalating from leaping tall buildings to near-light speed, Batman morphing from 1930s gentleman crime-fighter to Adam West comedian to dark avenger, radio adding Jimmy Olsen and Kryptonite, the Hulk changing color, and Green Lantern changing identity from Alan Scott to Hal Jordan to Kyle Rayner. Gradual change feels organic; the returning fan simply finds the evolved meme unrecognizable.

memetics.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
memetics.title: Architecture and the Dream Machine
memetics.relation: Botz-Bornstein argues Inception presents dreams neither as separate worlds nor as Freudian symbols but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense: it synchronizes kicks, safe codes and the Piaf countdown like a computer coordinating contradictory layers of time. He links inception to Dawkins's meme theory, with the planted idea growing 'like a cancer' in Mal, and to the projections of Solaris, showing how the film unusually combines cognitive and psychoanalytic models in one vertical dream structure. Democritus's atomism frames Epstein's 'grains of reality' and the film's atomized media-images of the real world, while Benjamin and Baudrillard let him read Cobb's Limbo dystopia, Mombasa and Dubai's empty skyscrapers as an allegory of a globalized world of hackable neoliberal dream machines.

memetics.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
memetics.title: Jurassic Park and Philosophy
memetics.relation: Shea stages the Wu-Malcolm dispute through Hume's Dialogues: Jurassic Park is an 'intelligent design' so botched that, like Philo's world of needless suffering, it points to ignorant or malicious designers rather than a perfect God, undercutting Richard Owen-style design arguments. He then explains Hammond's folly with Darwinian natural selection and memetics, treating the dinosaur-theme-park as a meme that infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit, fame, and importance. Hammond's fatal errors were assuming evolution 'wants' humans to survive, that complexity means better adapted, and that he could outsmart selection, which the all-female raptors breeding and life 'finding a way' quickly refute.

memetics.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
memetics.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
memetics.relation: Peter Stone applies Dawkins's memetics and Dennett's Breaking the Spell to the rise of 'Hallelujah' from the troubled release of Various Positions to ubiquity via John Cale, Jeff Buckley, Shrek, and Rufus Wainwright. On Dennett's account religious memes thrive through hyperactive agency detection, doctrines rendered unfalsifiable and thus immune to evidence, and 'belief in belief' - and 'Hallelujah' is religiously ambiguous enough, from David and Bathsheba to Buckley's 'hallelujah of the orgasm,' to be as religious as any singer or congregation wants it to be, whether as Rabbi Kagan's hymn of the heretic or the Holy Trinity Church's 'Amazing Grace' lyric swap. Machiavelli's maxim that fortune governs half the outcome frames the song's lucky trajectory, and its carefully engineered ambiguity makes it a set of very 'happy memes' likely to keep replicating.

memetics.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
memetics.title: Architecture and the Dream Machine
memetics.relation: Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues that Inception presents dreams neither as divine messages nor as stylized fantasy but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense — a 'robot brain' whose synchronized kicks, Piaf countdown, and phone-number safes 'think' the different layers of time instead of reproducing a reality, with slow motion as cognition rather than dream-sign (against Bazin). He reads inception as Dawkins's meme theory given a psychoanalytic vertical dimension: the idea is implanted deep in the subconscious (Fischer's relation to his father), can grow autonomously 'like a cancer' as Mal's did, and subconscious projections converge 'like white blood cells' as in Solaris. The chapter then traces how the computer era — hypertext, Second Life, media-absorbed realities like Baudrillard's 9/11 — reshaped cinematic dreams and architecture, so that Ariadne's 'pure creation,' Cobb's Limbo dystopia, and Dubai's empty speculative towers all become the 'gilded dreamworlds' of an ephemeralized, hacker-ready built world — the dream machine as allegory of the globalized world, with atomized grains of reality echoing Democritus via Epstein and Benjamin's account of cinema bursting the prison of the everyday.

sartre-freedom.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
sartre-freedom.title: A Whole New World
sartre-freedom.relation: Watchmen forces the rethink wholesale by inventing a world where real people donned masks after Superman's 1938 debut, and its heroes are psychologically troubled - Rorschach, driven by the Kitty Genovese murder's thirty-eight silent witnesses, is ruthless yet sincerely committed to justice. Quoting Nietzsche's 'whoever fights monsters' aphorism, Skoble asks whether Rorschach or Batman became monsters, or whether the rest of us are the guilty bystanders; and since Rorschach shows the 'power' to fight crime is a matter of will and choice, Spider-Man's 'great power comes great responsibility' becomes a responsibility that falls on everyone.

sartre-freedom.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
sartre-freedom.title: The Sun Is Eclipsed by the Moon
sartre-freedom.relation: Randall Auxier uses Sartre's Psychology of Imagination to explain what 'Brain Damage' and 'Eclipse' do to a listener: auditory images live in time (unlike the spatial visual image of the prism cover), so Waters's repeated 'The lunatic is on the grass' and the anticipated drum entrances seize the will through repetition and the vortex of attention, while musicians themselves escape through an expanded 'now' — the trap-door in time Gilmour knows too well. Sartre's four positional acts of the image (positing the object as non-existent, absent, existing elsewhere, or neutral) are then worked through examples: imaging the contingently absent song, the superstition around imagining a beloved as dead (mode 1), and the neutral mode (4) that Pink Floyd favors over both benevolent and malevolent negations. The dark conclusion: music like Metallica at Guantanamo cancels the will, but Pink Floyd uses neutrality to show that in annihilating the world you destroy above all yourself and remain responsible for the choice — the sun eclipsed by the moon.

sartre-freedom.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth
sartre-freedom.title: Love Gone Good
sartre-freedom.relation: Johnson reads Cash as practicing "philosophy as a way of life" rather than theorizing: his love-gone-bad songs ("Cocaine Blues," "I shot a man in Reno," the addictions he chose) honor the descent into darkness, aligned with Socrates going down to Piraeus in the Republic, Nietzsche's Zarathustra descending into the depths, and biblical descents from Jacob at the Jabbok to Jonah to Christ, while his love-gone-good songs ("Daddy Sang Bass," "Man in Black") show the turn outward through which love interrupts darkness without erasing it. He frames this with Gabriel Marcel's "creative fidelity" (being at the disposal of others), Paul Tillich's courage to be, in which love is stronger than the nonbeing of death, and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism, where wanting my freedom obligates me to want everyone's. The Man in Black thus carries "a little darkness" on his back while insisting "all God's children ain't free," a lived, political-ethical philosophy rather than a doctrine.

sartre-freedom.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
sartre-freedom.title: The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities
sartre-freedom.relation: Cuddy asks how gamers relate to BSG videogame avatars — as an extension of the ego or a disposable other — using Freud's id/ego/superego to cast the avatar as a socially safe venue for reconciling forbidden desires (piloting a Cylon Raider) with the superego's demands. Against Rehak's claim that gamers simply drop the avatar when losing, he enlists Sartre: blaming the game or 'cheating' opponents is bad faith, a denial of the freedom to create one's own essence, with Lee's '33' debate about responsibility for the Olympic Carrier and Baltar's vacillation as in-show parallels. Sartre's facticity bounds the freedom — hard missions are fixed facts to deal with — so the gamer, like Adama's fleet, must take responsibility within limits.

sartre-freedom.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
sartre-freedom.title: Living with Our Choices
sartre-freedom.relation: Peters applies Sartre's occupied-France analysis from Existentialism Is a Humanism to 'The Resistance' webisodes: on New Caprica one can resist (Tyrol, Tigh), collaborate (Jammer joining the NCP), or do nothing (Duck staying home with Nora), each path a Sartrean project whose morality lies in choosing freely and living with the consequences. Jammer's execution for treason in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing after Nora's death dramatize the stakes — for Sartre, Duck's immorality lies in refusing to own the choice he made at the crossroads, and the Final Four revelation changes nothing since they chose as they believed themselves human. The chapter leaves open the Sartrean worry that wartime morality may simply be written by the winners.

sartre-freedom.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
sartre-freedom.title: Refereeing in the World
sartre-freedom.relation: Crowe uses Sartre to explain why refereeing is existentially anguished: in the moment of decision — Grosso's fall over Neill's outstretched legs at the 2006 World Cup — the referee is radically free and solely responsible, and that anguish drives the six familiar referee types into bad faith. The stickler hides behind the letter of Law 12 as Sartre's student hid behind ethical formulas, the ditherer repeats the woman who leaves her hand inert on her date's, the poseur and frustrated player over-act the café waiter's role, and the postman and tough guy play the 'champion of sincerity' who treats character as fixed. The ideal is the authentic referee 'refereeing in the world' — Collina disallowing his own awarded goal at San Siro and explaining why to Inter — who owns his contingency: 'This is what I have chosen.'

sartre-freedom.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
sartre-freedom.title: Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song
sartre-freedom.relation: Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.

sartre-freedom.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
sartre-freedom.title: Bad or Bad Faith
sartre-freedom.relation: Rebecca Steiner Goldner reads the show through Sartre's Being and Nothingness: Dexter's watching is the Look that crystallizes his victims into a fixed essence - Matt Chambers can never again reinvent himself in a new town - and the kill room stages the demanded shame and confession ('Look at what you did!'), echoing Sartre's caught peeping-Tom. She then argues Dexter's belief that he was born a killer, that his Dark Passenger leaves him no choice, is itself bad faith: existence precedes essence, and by Sartre's account even the reformed thief remains responsible for his past, as with Jeremy Downs and Dr. Meridian. We viewers root for Dexter because we see the freedom he denies - and love him because he never makes the authentic choice to abandon his murderous project.

sartre-freedom.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
sartre-freedom.title: What Does A Scanner See
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter answers Arctor's question with Sartre: the gambler cannot observe his way out of deciding again, because consciousness is a nothingness with no determinate essence to be observed, so a scanner used to find yourself 'sees nothing', and Fred watching his own footage is bad faith, hiding from freedom behind presumed facts about himself. Butler then flips the bleakness into Sartre's optimism, reading Dick's 'I myself, I am not a character in this novel: I am the novel' as the author freely remaking his life through the book, his first written without amphetamines, after the break-in he suspected he had staged himself.

sartre-freedom.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
sartre-freedom.title: Phil Chews the Fat
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter closes on VALIS's opening gambit, 'I am Horselover Fat, and I am writing this in the third person to gain much-needed objectivity', and Dick's proliferating self-theories (vitamin C overdose, alien telepathy, past lives, Gnostic revelation) across VALIS, Radio Free Albemuth and the Exegesis. Butler weighs the bad-faith reading, that Dick was nailing down a determinate identity to escape the responsibility to choose, against Dick's own android-human essays, in which the authentic human acts spontaneously and throws off masks, concluding that Dick's refusal to settle on any one theory of himself was his playful, Sartrean way of knowing he is not an android.

sartre-freedom.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
sartre-freedom.title: A Footloose Man
sartre-freedom.relation: Dick expounds Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism' through the essentialist picture — a God-given blueprint, like Keith's Bentley designed before manufacture — against Sartre's claim that we exist first and invent essences afterward, marriage and family included. Monogamy thus emerges as a human choice mandated by Western authority and imposed on conquered peoples, not an absolute ethic handed down from heaven, a freedom humans exercise even in dropping Deuteronomy's stoning rule. Keith, Mick and Simone discarded the inherited tradition of monogamy, while Charlie Watts chose to stick with it.

sartre-freedom.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
sartre-freedom.title: Get What You Need
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter closes by matching each man's relationship style to what he 'needs': Watts keeps the beat (literally knocking Jagger out for phoning 'Where's my drummer?'), Jagger gets serial seduction, Richards trades the Anita Pallenberg cauldron for Patti Hansen's steadying presence, while Sartre died in 1980 surrounded by quarreling lovers instead of family. Every arrangement, from an Okie widow's 'plate of shit you can deal with' to the Sartre-Beauvoir pact, involves trade-offs, and the existentialist lesson is that we remain responsible for whichever romantic path we choose. Heraclitus's dictum that life is tension, and Sartre's nausea at our own choices, frame both monogamy and the pact as equally legitimate gambits.

sartre-freedom.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
sartre-freedom.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Kempner reads The Walking Dead through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old value-system gone, survivors who cling to pre-made essence die — Hershel keeps his zombified son locked in the barn awaiting restoration, and Shane tries to steal Rick's old cop-and-husband identity rather than live his own existence. Rick's waking in the hospital is a rebirth: he first exists in the new world, then creates a way of being human, and his relapses into the sheriff uniform nearly get him killed. Carl shooting Shane to save his father completes the family's existential freedom (children are no longer 'innocent'), walkers — without will or choice — are the ultimate inauthentic beings, and the volume's tagline, 'forced to finally start living,' makes the zombie world a sternly optimistic humanist story.

sartre-freedom.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness
sartre-freedom.title: How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter uses Sartre to diagnose Barney's fixed persona of suits, womanizing, and Bro Code worship as bad faith: having freely chosen to become the suited businessman who stole Shannon, Barney now acts as if those are his only options, denying his radical freedom. Hardy maps Sartre's own examples onto the show - Wendy the Waitress play-acting a stereotypical waitress, the woman who ignores the knee-touch, Barney tuning out criticism with 'I'm awesome' - and reads emotions, via Sartre's Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, as magical transformations of the world like Marshall's 'best burger' quest and the Bob Barker paternity story. Barney's love for Robin and his secret reunion of Marshall and Lily are the moments he breaks out of bad faith and chooses freely against his persona.

sartre-freedom.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
sartre-freedom.title: The Devil and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Elizabeth Butterfield reads The Devil's Advocate through Sartre: Kevin Lomax's 'You set me up!' excuse - after defending the guilty Gettys and Cullen and abandoning MaryAnn - is textbook bad faith, a lie to himself about his own free choices. Milton the Devil plays existentialist, insisting 'I'm no puppeteer... I only set the stage. You pull your own strings,' until Kevin admits his vanity, his drive to win, motivated every choice. Radical freedom entails radical responsibility, and Kevin's final suicide is his last free act, chosen to keep coming out on top, while free will remains the one limit the Devil cannot breach.

sartre-freedom.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
sartre-freedom.title: Girls and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Crossley reads the millennials of Girls through Sartre's anguish: Hannah, cut off financially in the pilot, is 'condemned to be free' in a recession that owes her nothing, and Marnie's firing from the gallery ('I don't know what I want... I wish someone would tell me') confronts her with facticity and the terror of self-determination. Marnie's flight into wishing for a moral dictator and her later choice to sing map the bad faith/authenticity distinction, as does Hannah swapping her hoarder-story reading for a pretentious piece on death to please Ray. Even Jessa's total rejection of the 'supposed to's' is outed as its own bad faith, and the ad-agency arc shows twenty-first-century authenticity is inevitably compromised by the need to eat.

sartre-freedom.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
sartre-freedom.title: 11. Louis C.K.’s No-Bullshit Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Marie Snyder uses Sartre's existentialism to unpack Louis's Conan monologue about the 'forever empty': with God gone we are condemned to be free, thrown into a world with no ready-made purpose and alone with our choices - which explains both the cellphone distraction economy and the Live in Portland bit that 'even if you're with someone, you're alone.' Authenticity means ruthlessly honest self-awareness and owning every choice with no excuses - Sartre's waiter example, the claim that there is no cowardly temperament, and Louis's refusal to let 'a flaw in the human male' excuse the tits bit or porn masturbation. Since in choosing for ourselves we choose for all humanity, Snyder pairs Sartre's universalized responsibility with Louis's 'act in a way that, if everybody acted that way, things would work out,' and reads intimate others, as in the Sartre-Beauvoir open relationship, as mirrors that reflect us back to ourselves against the connectionless 'we're just cummers' porn culture. Bad faith - self-deception, distraction, blame - is the fallenness Louis keeps diagnosing in his audiences and confessing in himself.

sartre-freedom.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
sartre-freedom.title: 12. Confronting the “Forever Empty”
sartre-freedom.relation: Argues that Louis's 2013 Conan 'forever empty' confession—welcoming the sadness of listening to Bruce Springsteen alone in his car instead of texting—is an exemplary case of existentialist authenticity: Heideggerian anxiety discloses the nothingness beneath our projects, and Sartre's radical freedom, facticity, and bad faith explain why texting while driving and other distractions are escapes from self-creation. It then contrasts Eddie in Louie's 'Eddie' episode, whose suicide plan is a bad-faith loss of care and passion, with the 'Late Show' trilogy, where Janet exposes Louie's bad faith over the Letterman audition and he ends by shouting 'I did it!' at the Ed Sullivan Theater after Tardigan's scam.

sartre-freedom.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
sartre-freedom.title: 8. Laughing in the Face of the Absurd
sartre-freedom.relation: Argues that watching Beth die on the platform is Sarah's existential awakening — the absurd realization that "it is no longer true that everyone has their own face" — analyzed through Camus's absurd (the impossible and the contradictory), Sartre's nausea at inhuman humans, and Beauvoir's "subman" who never wakes from the mechanical life. Sarah must repeatedly witness "her own" death (Beth, Katja, Jennifer, the Helsinki clones), which robs death and life of settled meaning, yet she refuses nihilism: exercising the radical freedom Sartre says grounds all values, she fights Dyad on behalf of everyone's freedom, implicitly choosing it for all humanity. Like Camus's Sisyphus, whose rock is his thing, her struggle is her thing — and the Season Two clone dance party is her laughing in the face of the absurd.

sartre-freedom.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
sartre-freedom.title: 7. Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of a Warm Blanket
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter explains Linus's blanket via Winnicott's transitional objects, then argues the gang's wider habits - Great Pumpkin taboos, baseball fetishes and rituals - are 'magical thinking' that manufactures an illusion of control over an uncertain world. A middle section tours the mind-body problem (Hippocrates, Descartes's dualism and pineal gland, Huxley's epiphenomenalism, Searle's emergent consciousness) to ask who is really doing the reading. The fallacies section dissects Linus's unfalsifiable Pumpkin doctrine (post hoc after the taboo-breaking 'if') and Charlie's confirmation bias, before reframing his 'pantophobia' as Kierkegaardian angst and Sartrean nausea: with adults reduced to 'Mwaa mwaa mwaa,' the kids are condemned to be free.

sartre-freedom.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
sartre-freedom.title: 13. Weapon X Machina
sartre-freedom.relation: Cole Bowman argues Deadpool is the Marvel Universe's deus ex machina: phenomenologically alienated from a body he treats as a prop (cutting off his own hand to escape Colossus's manacle and flipping the silver behemoth the bird), he can step outside the causal chain the way Leibniz's Primary Truths says any genuinely free agent in a created order must. Sartre supplies the engine—radical freedom against determinism, with She-Hulk's shallow fourth-wall gags (killing the already-dead Porcupine) as bad faith by contrast and Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe as the extreme exercise of freedom against his creators and fans. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy account of the deus ex machina replacing metaphysical consolation frames this new kind of inside-the-story god, who complicates plots rather than conveniently fixing them.

sartre-freedom.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
sartre-freedom.title: 8. Facing Up to the Realities
sartre-freedom.relation: Argues that 'Machine Gun' and its Berkeley introduction ('people... fighting wars... within themselves, not facing up to the realities') make Hendrix an existentialist: since existence precedes essence, each of us lives multiple realities we must author responsibly. The lyric variants diagnose Sartrean bad faith twice over — 'evil man make me kill ya' is the helplessness that denies freedom, 'fight like a farmer' the blame that locates failure out there — before the reprise's acceptance ('let your bullets fly like rain') and free judgment ('I know all the time you're wrong') achieve authenticity amid the solo's sonic battlefield.

sartre-freedom.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
sartre-freedom.title: Conclusion An Infinity of Possibilities
sartre-freedom.relation: Engels reads William's transformation through Sartre's existential project: the white-hatted William and the black-hatted Man in Black are not a hidden true self finally revealed but two successive free choices of oneself, and the Man in Black's claim that the park showed him 'who he really is' is bad faith — a denial of his freedom that lets him absolve himself of cruelty, just as Ford's deathbed pivot cannot erase the facticity of his role in the hosts' suffering. Maeve's choice to leave the train is analyzed as her first self-chosen end and value judgment, suggesting a programmed android can begin constructing her own project despite Sartre's humanism. The open-ended finale — hosts free to fight back, the Man in Black smiling as he is shot — embodies Sartre's 'I am an infinity of possibilities' and the burden of being condemned to be free.

sartre-freedom.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
sartre-freedom.title: 20. Sympathy for the Existential Devils
sartre-freedom.relation: James McLachlan reads the films through Sartre: replicants are made like penknives, with an essence before existence, and their drama is going 'off baseline' — the freedom of nothingness by which Batty murders his maker-gods (Tyrell the Father, Chew and Sebastian the trinity) and K disobeys everyone. Sartre's Satan from his Baudelaire biography, Blake's Orc and the Marriage of Heaven and Hell's contraries, and the Great Chain of Being's contradiction between filling one's place and moral freedom frame Luv as a perfect penknife, a 'good angel' who fulfills her vocation, while Batty and K are redeemed by the love that breaks their programming. 'More human than human' turns out to mean: existence precedes essence.

sartre-freedom.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
sartre-freedom.title: 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
sartre-freedom.relation: Hubbard-Mattix frames the show's central paradox, each person is responsible for her choices yet those choices are formed by her relationships, as a collision between the existentialism of Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and the feminist idea of relational autonomy. Each character embodies a failure mode: Eleanor's futile rejection of social dependence, Chidi's evasion of accountability in bad faith, Tahani's destruction by living for others' approval, and Jason's unexamined loyalty to Pillboi, Donkey Doug, and the Jaguars. Their failures before Judge Gen teach the audience to choose relationships that enable growth while still owning one's choices.

sartre-freedom.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
sartre-freedom.title: Final Act
sartre-freedom.relation: Shaw argues everyone at 30 Rock performs a role that shields them from Sartrean radical freedom: Kenneth is Sartre's cafe waiter in bad faith, believing television is America's true art form and willing to 'die at my post' for NBC, while Jack psyches himself up with corporate slogans and Jenna's 'Black Tie' candor about marrying the last Hapsburg to be taken care of is the rare moment of good faith. Butler's gender performativity explains Jack's masculinity as a repeated script, from his Glengarry Glen Ross 'always be talking' allusion to Baldwin's brass-balls speech to his homosocial man-crushes on Don Geiss and Dick Cheney. Plato's wariness of imitation, Nietzsche on hypocrisy hardening into character, and Santayana's tragic mask frame the closing thought: the actors know they are performing, but the characters, like us, do not.

sartre-freedom.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
sartre-freedom.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Uses Sartre's cafe waiter, directly mirrored when Gob play-acts a waiter in 'S.O.B.s', to define bad faith as denying one's freedom by disappearing into roles: illusionist, Bluth Company president in George Sr.'s suit, 'any man' winning back Marta, Ward Cleaver father to Steve Holt (!). Distinguishing bad faith from impossible self-deception (beings-for-themselves have no pre-given essence), the chapter argues that even sincerity ('be yourself, Gob') is bad faith, and provocatively concludes Gob is happier and kinder to others in bad faith, reversing Socrates' 'know thyself'.

sartre-freedom.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
sartre-freedom.title: Living with Our Choices
sartre-freedom.relation: Peters reads 'The Resistance' webisodes through Sartre's occupied-France dilemma from Existentialism Is a Humanism (resist, collaborate, or do nothing, modeled on his student's choice between joining the Free French and caring for his mother): Tyrol joins the resistance for his family's future, Jammer joins the New Caprica Police to save lives and pays with execution by his former friends in 'Collaborators,' and Duck's choice to do nothing ends with wife Nora's death in the Temple massacre and his revenge suicide bombing. Since 'man is nothing other than what he makes of himself,' the chapter argues morality lies in the freedom to choose and in living with the consequences: Duck's refusal to accept his choice, not the choice itself, is the failure, and the Final Five revelation cannot retroactively alter choices made in good faith by Tigh, Tyrol, Anders and Foster. Which side holds the ethical high ground may simply be whichever side won and gets to write history.

sartre-freedom.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
sartre-freedom.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Baird contrasts Camus's absurdity — the divorce between man and world demanding 'lucid indifference' and an absurd art that refuses counterfeit meaning — with Sartre's, where the world's meanings are contingent human projections and freedom entails absolute responsibility (Being and Nothingness sits by the Dude's bed). He argues the film is Sartrean rather than Camusian: the Dude weaves random events (the peed-on rug, the ransom) into the interpretation 'Bunny kidnapped herself', holding it provisionally as one story among possible ones, while Walter never takes responsibility for his Corvette-swinging choices. The viewers, knowing all interpretations are groundless, watch the absurd from the front row.

sartre-freedom.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality
sartre-freedom.title: Black sabbath & philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Ken Pepper uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to explain how Tony Iommi's homemade plastic fingertips work: like the blind man's cane, they are incorporated into his body schema so that he perceives the fretboard through them, refuting the Cartesian "objective body" picture on which playing would be inner plans causing finger movements. On creative freedom, the chapter stages Merleau-Ponty against Sartre's radical freedom, Iommi did choose to relearn guitar after hearing two-fingered Django Reinhardt, and his restricted two-finger chords, lighter strings, and drop tunings birthed heavy metal, but Sartre is wrong that attitude alone transcends disability, since some possibilities (playing at all without the tips) were simply not live. Only Iommi, taking up the possibilities his body-in-his-situation afforded, could have invented metal.

sartre-freedom.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
sartre-freedom.title: “I Am Moana!”
sartre-freedom.relation: Stages Moana's dilemma between her father's Aristotelian essentialism — everything on Motunui has a fixed function, so Moana's essence as chief precedes her birth — and Sartre's existence precedes essence, with Heihei the unchanging chicken as a being whose essence really does precede existence. Tui embodies bad faith and the crowd (his own aborted voyage left him enforcing 'no one goes beyond the reef'), while Tala and then Moana live authentically through anguish, forlornness, and despair, until 'I am Moana!' marks her self-defined identity. Nietzsche's 'become who you are' and 'what does not destroy me makes me stronger' frame her resilience, which lets her free Maui ('Hook. No hook. I'm Maui.') and unmask Te Ka as Te Fiti whose stolen heart 'does not define you.'

sartre-freedom.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
sartre-freedom.title: Rafiki Holds the Mirror Up to Nature
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter reads The Lion King as a Disney retelling of Hamlet: Scar's murder of Mufasa parallels Claudius, and Simba's guilt-ridden exile acts out Hamlet's 'to be or not to be.' Timon and Pumbaa's 'hakuna matata' is Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage of pleasure without commitment, which Simba must leave for the ethical stage when Nala, Rafiki ('Whooo are you?'), and Mufasa's ghost demand he 'remember who you are.' Sartre's 'optimistic toughness' and Nietzsche's 'Become who you are' frame Simba's defiant 'I am' before the assembled Pride Lands as existential self-creation.

sartre-freedom.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge
sartre-freedom.title: The Existential Redefinition of Doctor Strange
sartre-freedom.relation: DiGeorgio traces Strange's 'existential conversion' from scientific nihilism ('matter and nothing more') through Sartrean bad faith — playing the brilliant surgeon while not really believing life meaningless, refusing the Ancient One's widened keyhole — to authenticity. His hesitation to stay and fight after killing a zealot, and the Ancient One's 'it's not about you,' set up his choice to defend humanity as Sartre's universal decree, choosing for all humankind in anguish and freedom. The endless time loop imposed on Dormammu is read as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence demanding total commitment to one's choices, so that by the end Strange lives existence-precedes-essence: what he does, not his 'brilliant surgeon' essence, defines him.

sartre-freedom.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter
sartre-freedom.title: Notes
sartre-freedom.relation: The chapter argues modding is the deepest freedom Bethesda-era Fallout offers: Sartre and Beauvoir's absolute freedom and facticity explain why vanilla players merely pick among given priorities while modders inject new meaning into the game, constrained but not determined by the Creation Engine. Spinoza's causal determinism becomes a model of 'immanent freedom' — just as Spinoza's agent is free by understanding their place in Nature's web of causes, the modder is free by grasping how they fit into the load orders, plugin files, and tools of the Creation Kit. Simone Weil's ideal of self-directed labor culminates the argument: Fallout: London's five-year, unpaid total conversion (the Atta-Boy, Churchill the bulldog, the punk-anarchist Pistols) embodies the convergence of thought and action that Moira Brown's line about putting broken glass back together captures.

sartre-freedom.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
sartre-freedom.title: 17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
sartre-freedom.relation: Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.

sartre-freedom.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic
sartre-freedom.title: Notes
sartre-freedom.relation: Contrasts Frank's ethical egoism with Beauvoir's existential ethics: Frank moves like an invisible Ring-of-Gyges wearer-murdering Zoe, reading everyone's self-interest-yet because he treats others purely as instruments his freedom is never 'prolonged through the freedom of others', and it fails in Season 3 when he miscalculates Jackie, Remy, and Claire. Claire's awakening through Michael Corrigan and her final walkout dramatize the Beauvoirian lesson that consciousness is freedom-as-nothingness whose values we remain collectively responsible for, not a license to will anything.

sartre-freedom.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
sartre-freedom.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Kempner reads the comic through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old world gone, survivors like Rick, Michonne, and Dale must create their own values, while characters who cling to pre-apocalypse essences (Hershel keeping his zombified son in the barn, Shane waiting for the government) bring death on themselves. Rick's hospital awakening is treated as an existential rebirth in which his cop uniform is an 'essence precedes existence' trap, and Carl shooting Shane (and later Ben in 'Fear the Hunters') shows children making free choices outside conventional morality. The chapter concludes the series is 'sternly optimistic' because total freedom, not zombification, is what defines the humans: 'in a world ruled by the dead, we are forced to finally start living.'

sartre-freedom.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
sartre-freedom.title: Conclusion An Infinity of Possibilities
sartre-freedom.relation: Kimberly Engels reads William's transformation into the Man in Black through Sartre's existential 'project': rather than discovering a pre-existing true self 'among the dead,' William's new situation in the park (loving and losing Dolores, killing the Confederados, Logan's betrayal) produces an existential rupture in which he chooses new ends, symbolized by trading the white hat for the black. She argues the Man in Black's claim to have 'found himself' is Sartrean bad faith, denying his freedom and facticity to evade responsibility for the harm he causes. Extending existentialism to androids, she reads Maeve's choice to leave the train and seek her daughter as her first freely formulated project, the start of her own 'infinity of possibilities.'

sartre-freedom.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
sartre-freedom.title: Eleventh Hole Philosophy in the Kingdom Golf, Mysticism, and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.relation: Mark Huston diagnoses why golf, more than baseball, gets mystical treatment in pop culture, using Michael Murphy's novel 'Golf in the Kingdom' (Shivas Irons, 'true gravity') and the film 'The Legend of Bagger Vance' (Junuh's 'authentic swing'). He plays William James's four marks of mysticism against Bertrand Russell's skeptical criteria, ties golf's appeal to individuality, contemplative time, nature (citing Emerson's 'transparent eye-ball') and Sartrean existential freedom, arguing that a golfer's freedom over whether to follow the rules mirrors Sartre's claim that in play man sets his own rules and must take responsibility. He reads Shivas Irons and Bagger Vance as Zen roshi figures using paradoxical, koan-like teaching to bring the student to a self-transforming 'authentic swing.'

sartre-freedom.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
sartre-freedom.title: Why Roger Federer Is the Best Or Is It McEnroe
sartre-freedom.relation: David Baggett asks who is the all-time best male tennis player and treats it as a genuine problem in metaphysics ('what is the case?') and epistemology ('how do we know it?'), surveying candidates from Tilden to Federer against ten criteria. He argues the sentence 'Federer is the all-time best' is vague, running the tennis-ball-losing-an-atom sorites through three theories of vagueness—fuzzy logic, supervaluationism, and Timothy Williamson's epistemicism, which he favors: there is a fact of the matter (God knows it) but our closeness-to-the-margin ignorance keeps us from knowing it. He uses Anselm's ontological argument and Guanilo's perfect-island reply to distinguish the all-time best from the best-possible player, and invokes Sartre's existentialist rejection of mere potentiality ('could've/should've') to insist he is asking who actually was best, not who might have been.

sartre-freedom.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams
sartre-freedom.title: Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw
sartre-freedom.relation: Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.

sartre-freedom.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
sartre-freedom.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
sartre-freedom.relation: Sanders's introductory survey frames Mann's cinema as suffused with existentialist themes—alienation, freedom, authenticity, and existential choice—citing Sartre's 'condemned to be free' as the key to protagonists like Thief's Frank and Heat's Neil McCauley, who choose personal truth over surrender. It maps the volume's essays: Nietzschean will to power in the crime films, Levinas's ethics of the Other in Thief and Collateral, and Lockean/Rousseauian visions of nature in The Last of the Mohicans. Mann's outsiders repeatedly face the fateful, doom-laden choices (McCauley abandoning Eady to kill Waingro) that define existential man.

sartre-freedom.book: 226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann
sartre-freedom.title: The Philosophy of Michael Mann
sartre-freedom.relation: Rybin links Mann's style-versus-substance debate to the existential self-definition of his characters, focusing on Public Enemies. Dillinger, who tells Billie 'the only thing that's important is where somebody's going,' is not yet an icon but is 'becoming Dillinger' as the film unfolds. In the penultimate scene, watching Clark Gable in Manhattan Melodrama—'die the way you lived, all of a sudden'—Dillinger achieves authentic self-definition by claiming the gangster myth as his own identity, a Warshovian 'experience of art'; Mann's editing collapses the space between Dillinger and the screen just before Dillinger is gunned down, the cost of authentic selfhood.

sartre-freedom.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
sartre-freedom.title: The Philosophy of Neo-Noir
sartre-freedom.relation: Barad uses Blade Runner to test what distinguishes humans from machines. Against Turing's claim that indistinguishable input-output makes a computer a mind, she deploys Sartre's dictum that in humans existence precedes essence while manufactured replicants (like a designed android) have essence first, so they can blame their maker. She reads the Voigt-Kampff empathy test through Sartrean forlornness and despair, and argues Roy Batty achieves authentic humanity when he kills Tyrell and freely chooses to save Deckard, becoming a life-giver rather than his programmed combat model.

sartre-freedom.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
sartre-freedom.title: The Prostitution Trap of Elite Sport in He Got Game
sartre-freedom.relation: Holt and Pitter argue that Lee's He Got Game exposes a 'prostitution trap' in which elite athletes, like literal prostitutes, become commodified bodies alienated from themselves. They read the parallel plots of star recruit Jesus Shuttlesworth, his father Jake pressured to broker a signing, and the prostitute Dakota as three versions of the same trap, invoking MacIntyre's internal-versus-external goods and Deci/Ryan's intrinsic-versus-extrinsic rewards to show how coercive money threatens Jesus's love of the game. Jesus escapes by exercising autonomy, negotiating on his own terms and skipping the press conference to reach an 'authentic realism.'

sartre-freedom.book: 231 - The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
sartre-freedom.title: The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick
sartre-freedom.relation: Shaw asks whether Kubrick's worldview is nihilistic by tracking the free-will-versus-determinism question across his films, arguing (against Vincent Canby) that A Clockwork Orange celebrates rather than condemns Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice: the state's Ludovico conditioning, which makes him retch at sex and violence, is more monstrous than Alex because it destroys the free will that grounds human meaning. Invoking Kevin Stoehr's distinction between Nietzsche's passive and active nihilism, Shaw claims Kubrick highlights the negative to point beyond it. He surveys the oeuvre—Dax, Bowman, Barry, Wendy, Joker, Bill Harford as choosing agents—and reads Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's Being and Nothingness on the contradiction of wanting the beloved's freely-given yet secure love.

sartre-freedom.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir
sartre-freedom.title: Noir et Blanc in Color: Existentialism and Miami Vice
sartre-freedom.relation: Sanders reads Miami Vice as existentialist 'sunshine noir,' where color and pastel locations carry noir alienation, and Crockett and Tubbs live rootless lives with shambles of romances and a culturally impoverished compass (Bolt, Buddy Holly, Buffett, Beckett, Betts). The episode 'No Exit' (Bruce Willis as arms dealer Tony Amato, whose wife Rita shoots him at the courthouse steps) is analyzed through Sartre's being-in-itself/being-for-itself conflict and 'hell is other people,' from which Danto says 'there is no exit.' 'Heart of Darkness' presents Ed O'Neill's undercover FBI agent Arthur Lawson, who prefers his Artie Rollins persona and hangs himself after debriefing, as a failure of authenticity and flight into bad faith that Crockett recognizes as his own peril as Sonny Burnett. Crockett's amnesia arc ('Mirror Image' through 'Redemption in Blood' and 'Bad Timing'), where he believes he is Burnett working for the Manolo organization, is resolved through Sartrean existential recognition and a freely chosen dangerous mission that restores his identity, since the Kierkegaardian leap of faith is unavailable in the show's secular world; Sanders also attacks Sartre's sanction of revolutionary violence in his preface to Fanon and Beauvoir's defense of Sade.

sartre-freedom.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
sartre-freedom.title: “Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler
sartre-freedom.relation: Kevin S. Decker argues the Doctor's morality is an "ethics of ambiguity" poised between Romanticism and existentialism, not any formula. Rejecting positivism, deontology, and utilitarianism as fits for the Doctor, he reads the Doctor's freedom, wandering, and rejection of Time Lord values through Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith (the student torn between mother and Free French) and Beauvoir's "adventurer" who confers value by choosing. The Romantic search for the infinite in small things and the Prometheus myth frame the Doctor as a liberating, self-defining moral exemplar.

sartre-freedom.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
sartre-freedom.title: 20. Punks Pissing People Off
sartre-freedom.relation: Juneko Robinson mixes memoir of circa-1980 anti-punk violence (routine beatings, the murder of Brian Deneke) with Sartrean existentialism to explain why punks 'pissed people off': punk's confrontational appearance exposed the contingency and hypocrisy of mainstream values, forcing others to take responsibility for them. Using Sartre's keyhole-peeper example from Being and Nothingness and No Exit's 'hell is other people', she argues that harassers lived in bad faith, dependent on how others see them, while punks were the witnesses who objectified the mainstream rather than the deviants being watched. Howard Becker's moral entrepreneurs explain the 'de-punking' panics and psychiatric commitments of kids who merely dressed weird, and Marmysz's 'nihilistic incongruity' shows punk converting society's hypocrisy into self-legislated virtue.

sartre-freedom.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
sartre-freedom.title: MOTHERHOOD
sartre-freedom.relation: Elizabeth Butterfield reads her exhausting early motherhood through Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex, arguing that 'the ideal mother,' like 'true womanhood,' is a social construction and that a mother is 'freedom in situation,' never a mother 'the way a stone is a stone.' She recasts Beauvoir's 'serious man' as the 'serious mother' who flees her freedom into the Motherhood Religion, and invokes Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and 'Hell is other people' (No Exit) to advocate the honest, self-aware 'genuine mother' over inauthentic self-sacrifice.

sartre-freedom.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
sartre-freedom.title: SERIAL KILLERS
sartre-freedom.relation: Dietrich and Hall explain why fictional serial killers (Hannibal, the Joker, Dexter, Grendel) allure us. Curiosity drives us to seek explanations for the mysterious, but the deeper pull comes from 'co-activation' of fear and pleasure inside a 'protective frame' (the screen or page) that strips away empathy for victims. They argue humans are rule-following creatures who must assert selfhood through rule-breaking to secure freedom, so the serial killer becomes an alluring avatar of ultimate freedom — the idea of the killer, safely framed, lets us test how thin the veneer of morality really is, as the Joker taunts.

sartre-freedom.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
sartre-freedom.title: 46. The Shawshank Redemption as Philosophy Freedom and Panopticism
sartre-freedom.relation: Hooke reads The Shawshank Redemption through two lenses. From Sartre he takes 'hell is other people' and the objectifying look from No Exit and Being and Nothingness — Shawshank's warden and 'sisters' embody a worldly hell of 'never' and 'always' — but argues Andy and Red's friendship, Andy's Mozart broadcast, and the hopeful ending invert Sartre, making freedom the shared warmth of friendship rather than the devouring gaze. From Foucault's Discipline and Punish he reads the prison's shift from spectacle to disciplinary surveillance and solitary confinement as panopticism, extending Foucault's insight that prisons, schools, and hospitals mirror one another (illustrated by his COVID-era campus). He closes with Nietzschean genealogy and redemption through laughter, joy, and giving.

sartre-freedom.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
sartre-freedom.title: 84. The Legend of Zelda Breath of the Wild as Philosophy Teaching the Player to Be Comfortable Being Alone
sartre-freedom.relation: Lay argues that Breath of the Wild teaches, chiefly through design rather than plot, that solitude is good for the player. He tests eternal return (the recurring Ganon-Zelda-Link cycle across the series), Sartrean absolute freedom and Kierkegaardian anxiety of choice (BotW's Korok-dung 'reward' and refusal to attach external meaning push players to make their own meaning), and Kierkegaard's inward 'repetition.' He lands on Mill's and Schopenhauer's defense of solitude-in-nature as self-actualizing rather than isolating, and reads sequence-breaking exploits as Marx-style spontaneous creative activity, concluding the game frames solitude as a path to eudaimonia and human flourishing.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
aquinas-double-effect.title: Galactus The Power and the Glory
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Galactus was designed to stand beyond good and evil, yet when the Watcher challenges him he cannot help moralizing, pleading that killing Earth's inhabitants is a merely foreseen and 'regrettable but unavoidable' side effect of his necessary feeding - a move the authors dissect as the same bad rationalization used by greedy executives and corrupt politicians, and one no cosmic being can escape needing. Only when the blind artist Alicia awakens the Surfer's buried compassion, and the Watcher brandishes the Ultimate Nullifier while pleading that humans carry 'the seed of grandeur', does Galactus spare Earth, hailing the 'glint of Glory' in mankind.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
aquinas-double-effect.title: The Finder of Lost Children
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Timothy Dean Roth reads Kill Bill as a modern Divine Comedy: Tarantino punishes by contrapasso like Dante—O-Ren dies by Japanese steel, Budd by snake, Elle by blindness, Bill by a broken heart—and both treat vengeance as a form of truth-telling and an act of love. Hattori Hanzo's warning that revenge 'is a forest' echoes Aristotle on how hard it is to set the limits of anger, while the stories-within-stories of orphaned Nikki and O-Ren enact the cycle of violence vengeance perpetuates. Against this, Aquinas's doctrine of double effect shows every one of the Bride's killings is defensive self-preservation, and the film ends where Jules's arc ends: in mercy, mutual forgiveness and a whispered 'thank you' of grace.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
aquinas-double-effect.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive' against Aquinas' Doctrine of Double Effect and Frankfurt's second-order intentions, arguing Ender's killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail double-effect proportionality because he intends excessive, fear-inducing harm to deter future attackers. He allows that Ender bears only partial responsibility for the xenocide since he could not know the 'simulation' was real, but concludes that, contrary to the Speakers for the Dead doctrine, Ender is not the blameless moral exemplar Card makes of him.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
aquinas-double-effect.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: James Cook grades the Third Invasion against the just war principles Ender was never taught: the war is preventive rather than genuinely preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq parallel), proper authority is compromised by deceiving the public, last resort fails since the hive-queen was trying to communicate, and non-combatant immunity condemns destroying the bugger homeworld. He stages Augustine's ban on killing in individual self-defense against Aquinas' permission of it, and uses Kant's humanity formula and Cicero's hostis/perduellis distinction to ask whether the buggers were ever treated as rational beings rather than mere threats.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
aquinas-double-effect.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Montoya tests Simon's choice to sacrifice his sanity by wearing the crown to save child Marceline against three ethical theories. Aquinas's doctrine of double effect clears him because the intended good (saving her life) outweighs the merely foreseen side effect (her tears, his possible future evils); Kant's categorical imperative rules out universalizing 'let children die to save myself,' since a world of universal using destroys the rule itself; and a fountain case where Finn must choose between world-saving plans and a drowning candy child separates act from rule utilitarianism, with rule utilitarianism preserving the duty to rescue. All three converge on the verdict that Simon, not Finn, is Ooo's greatest hero.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
aquinas-double-effect.title: Justified and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: The chapter assembles real contested self-defense cases beside Raylan's shooting of Tommy Bucks - the OK Corral and Wyatt Earp's far-from-clean vendetta ride, Curtis Reeves killing a texting moviegoer over thrown popcorn, George Zimmerman and Trayvon Martin, Ossian Sweet's mobbed house, Bernie Goetz's subway shooting, Gary Plauche executing his son's abuser on camera, and the Texas father who beat his daughter's rapist to death. Its philosophical machinery is Aquinas's principle of double effect from the Summa Theologica (self-defense may have two effects, saving one's life and slaying the aggressor, only the first intended), set against St. Augustine's condemnation of private self-defense as inordinate self-love. Florida's stand-your-ground law - where the dead man cannot tell his side - supplies the legal gray zone the show's title exploits.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
aquinas-double-effect.title: 14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
aquinas-double-effect.title: Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Bogaerts asks why every proactive superhero comes to grief: Nick Fury's unauthorized Secret War in Latveria, Tony Stark's exile of the Hulk and registration crusade, and the Illuminati's blunder all backfire (World War Hulk, the Skrull invasion), and Aquinas's doctrine of double effect—elaborated by Foot and Anscombe—cannot absolve them, since the foreseen harms were massive and disproportionate to the intended goods. Comics theory supplies the deeper cause: Reynolds's status quo defense and Jewett and Lawrence's American monomyth (via Campbell's hero's journey) make the superhero genre intrinsically reactive, guarding a paradise rather than remaking it, so heroes who 'move up into governance'—Thor as Lord of Earth, the Squadron Supreme's utopia—slide into supervillainy. Foot's act/omission distinction and the priority of negative over positive duties explain the trap, and why even Steve Rogers, as the new top cop, retreats to being Captain America again.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
aquinas-double-effect.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Lance Belluomini tests Card's creed that 'good or evil exist entirely in human motive, and not at all in the act' against Aquinas's Doctrine of Double Effect, finding that Ender's self-defense killings of Stilson and Bonzo fail the proportionality condition — he intended to 'win all the next fights' — so he bears moral responsibility despite his tears. After weighing Frankfurt's second-order intentions as a way to keep Ender a good person who did bad things, he concludes with Anscombe's 'double-think about double effect' that Ender is deceived about his own intentions and is no moral exemplar.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
aquinas-double-effect.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Air Force colonel James Cook walks the just war tradition through Ender's world: the Third Invasion is preventive rather than preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq war as the parallel), proper authority is undermined by the I.F.'s lies to its citizens, and last resort fails because the hive-queen was already trying to communicate with Ender. He contrasts Augustine's ban on killing in self-defense with Aquinas's permission, invokes Kant's formula of humanity for the buggers' rational nature and Cicero's hostis against dehumanizing enemies, and argues the I.F.'s failure to teach military ethics is itself part of the novel's tragedy.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
aquinas-double-effect.title: Living and Dying as One: Suffering and the Ethics of Euthanasia
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Jason Eberl uses Joe Bonham of 'One' and Johnny Got His Gun to analyze suffering as loss of recognition (Hegel), loss of social contact (Aristotle's political animal), and loss of Kantian autonomy and dignity - 'a piece of meat that keeps on living'. He then works through the euthanasia debate: active versus passive euthanasia, Aquinas' doctrine of double effect for palliative care, Locke's psychological criterion of personal identity behind the higher-brain death standard applied to Terri Schiavo and PVS patients, concluding that the nurse's cutting of Joe's breathing tube would be active euthanasia because of the intention behind it.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
aquinas-double-effect.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
aquinas-double-effect.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.

aquinas-double-effect.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
aquinas-double-effect.title: Notes
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Camosy takes up Randal's charge in Clerks that destroying Death Star II killed innocent independent contractors. Against utilitarian reasoning he deploys just war theory: terrorism is intentionally targeting innocents as a means, so Tarkin's destruction of Alderaan (and, he argues, Hiroshima) qualifies, while the Rebels, who would have been 'pleased' if the workers took the day off, do not. Since the crew was mostly conscripted clones and programmed droids with no moral responsibility, and destroying the station saved billions, the attack passes the proportionality test - an exercise in double-effect reasoning that asks fans to question the 'good guys lens.'

aquinas-double-effect.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
aquinas-double-effect.title: Notes
aquinas-double-effect.relation: Held examines the Tuatha'an Way of the Leaf as universal pacifism grounded not in religion, utility, or rights but in the metaphysical care of the self, echoing Gandhi's idea that violence taints the soul of the doer (shown by Adan exiling Lewin for rescuing raped girls and by Aram's tragic fall). He argues the Tinkers' pacifism, while idyllic, is untenable in a broken world: through Augustine's two cities, Aquinas's natural self-preservation and doctrine of double effect, and just war theory's jus ad bellum and jus in bello, he contends intentions matter and that no hero of WoT could be a pacifist, concluding the Tinkers free-ride parasitically on those who fight the Shadow and that their peace is not real peace but self-serving order-less quiet.

kingdom-of-ends.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
kingdom-of-ends.title: Power and Glory Tests of Virtue
kingdom-of-ends.relation: The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.

kingdom-of-ends.title: Check Out Time
