He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.

discipline.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
discipline.title: Prison Ghetto
discipline.relation: Kelly takes gangsta rap's payback attitude (50 Cent, Nas, Dr. Dre, OutKast) as the starting point for the philosophy of punishment: rappers doubt retribution because police, courts, and prisons lack legitimate authority over them - Public Enemy's "Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos" rejects the government's letter. Weighing Kantian and Nozickian retributivism against Bentham's consequentialist rationales, she argues desert, proportionality, and authority all fail in a racist system - racial profiling, the crack-versus-powder sentencing disparity, Wacquant's prison-ghetto thesis, Goodie Mob's "Cell Therapy", Dead Prez's "Behind Enemy Lines", KRS-One's officer-overseer analogy - leaving incapacitation as racialized social control rather than justice.

discipline.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
discipline.title: Urban Idiots Foucauldian and Pythonesque
discipline.relation: Using Foucault's Madness and Civilization, the chapter reads the Flying Circus sketch 'The Idiot in Society' and the 'Hermits' sketch as commentary on madness as a social construct that changes from the medieval tolerance of fools, through the Great Confinement, to modern psychiatric medicalization. Arthur Figgis, the village idiot, is nothing like Foucault's silenced asylum inmates: he speaks rationally to camera about the 'vital psycho-social service' idiots provide, deposits moss at the bank, and lectures in idiocy at the University of East Anglia — madmen who are integrated, have agency, and speak for themselves. The Pythons turn Foucault's picture upside down, since the visibly idiotic are socially integrated while the urban idiots in business suits are the ones confined behind asylum-like walls, and by making idiocy funny they restore the dialogue between reason and unreason that Foucault says the monologue of reason destroyed.

discipline.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
discipline.title: The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of
discipline.relation: Joan Grassbaugh Forry asks how conventional standards of beauty, femininity, and masculinity operate in the vampire aesthetic of Interview with the Vampire, Buffy, and Queen of the Damned. Using Foucault's figure of the soldier whose body is 'made' by discipline, and Bartky and Bordo's feminist extension of it to dieting, deportment, and ornamenting the female body, she argues vampires expose the ideology of natural beauty: they are youthful, elegant, and effortlessly beautiful - no gym, no reflection - so their beauty is pure naturalness with the discipline erased. Gender decides the payoff: ultra-feminine female vampires (Drusilla's dresses and tea parties, Akasha, childlike Claudia) are femmes fatales whose threat must be punished by death, ridicule, or infantilization, while feminized male protagonists (Louis, Angel, Spike painting his nails and watching Passions - the 'metrosexual') win audience identification and tragic dignity. Beauty, in short, is a shield for the male vampire and a death sentence for the female.

discipline.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!
discipline.title: Art, Madness, and Syd Barrett
discipline.relation: George Reisch reads The Wall through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: madness is not a brain lesion but a historical construction — Renaissance unreason, classical confinement, then Tuke's and Pinel's psychiatric regime in which the madman must know 'he is watched, judged, and condemned' until judgment is internalized — which explains why Pink imprisons himself brick by brick and asks at 'The Trial', 'Have I been guilty all this time?' The fascist worms and skinhead riots of 'Waiting for the Worms' are the same crusade for uniformity that drove Pink mad — Foucault's 'moral city' where 'virtue is an affair of the state' — so fascism and insanity are versions of each other, with Sartre's 'Hell is other people' from No Exit as the framing thought. Both the album ('Outside the Wall': 'the bleeding hearts and artists make their stand') and Foucault end by defending art as the last channel of unreason, and Reisch argues Syd Barrett's unanswerable absence was exactly that interrupting void powering 'Echoes', Dark Side, Wish You Were Here, and The Final Cut.

discipline.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
discipline.title: Progress Is a Myth that Truly Makes Life Worthwhile
discipline.relation: Garnar contrasts the material practice of collecting CDs -- shelving some 1,500-2,000 discs by genre, the Rachels' Egon Schiele packaging, and Humean associations binding particular discs to memories like buying blue hair dye the day he got New Order's Lowlife -- with the iPod-era 'iPhenomenon' of buying songs piecemeal from iTunes. Using William James's question 'How is the practice real?' he rejects the real/virtual split, and reads the freedom of iMedia as a corollary of Marx and Engels's 'single, unconscionable freedom -- Free Trade': the solipsistic consumer never confronts the artist the way the album as artifact (Coltrane's My Favorite Things ending, he realizes, had to end with 'But Not for Me') forces him to. The body supposedly made unnecessary by 'iLiving' remains, with Foucault, a site of discipline -- eating disorders, outsourced assembly labor, e-waste -- so he keeps his iPod but defends a plurality of media and calls progress a myth.

discipline.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
discipline.title: Become a Work of Art!
discipline.relation: Dumitrica reads iPod customization (skins, colors, playlists) as a Foucauldian technology of the self: identity is not a stable inner core but something continually made, as when a Facebook user who loses her 80G black iPod feels 'empty'. Against Foucault's examples of ancient care of the self and Christian confessional self-renunciation, she argues the iPod embodies the modern disciplinary self: we survey our playlists against what friends will think, dividing practices split iPod owners from users of 'lame MP3 or CD-players', and social-science-style lifestyle classifications (hip-hop vs heavy metal) shape our choices. The chapter ends by urging Foucault's aesthetic escape from pre-packaged lifestyle models — treat the self as a work of art, like the author sharing holiday photos with her father instead of plunging into a self-enclosed sonic bubble.

discipline.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
discipline.title: “Make It So”
discipline.relation: Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.

discipline.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
discipline.title: The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of
discipline.relation: Joan Grassbaugh Forry argues the 'vampire aesthetic' both enforces and destabilizes constructed norms of beauty and gender, reading vampire representation through Foucault's made soldier (the body produced by discipline rather than nature) and the Bartky-Bordo feminist analysis of disciplinary beauty practices. Vampires are effortlessly, youthfully beautiful — exempt from the dieting, grooming, and ornamentation that produce femininity — yet their beauty must appear natural, which is exactly the demand beauty culture makes of women; Queen Akasha, Drusilla, and child-vampire Claudia are ultra-feminine femmes fatale whose threat is neutralized by childlike femininity and punished by death or ridicule (Claudia ashes in the sunlight, Drusilla is made to look foolish), while the feminized male protagonists — Louis and Armand in Interview with the Vampire, Angel and nail-polishing, Passions-watching Spike in Buffy, Langella's elegant Dracula — turn beauty, taste, and expressed emotion into audience identification and beautiful martyrdom. The payoff: in the realm of the Undead the male vampire becomes a beautiful martyr while the female vampire becomes a disastrous woman we love to hate.

discipline.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness
discipline.title: The Moving Shadow of Truth
discipline.relation: Haffner and Vogel define martial arts by a Wittgensteinian family resemblance to combat and organize the promise of self-improvement as paired opposites, working them Hegelian dialectic style, granting some truth to each side. They ask whether training brings peace or violence (Hobbes's shield for a war of all against all and Freudian catharsis versus Aristotle's worry that habituated violence breeds violence), strength fantasies or Socratic humility about weakness (with Sun Tzu's know-your-enemy and Foucault on the teacher's gaze and dojo power games), Cartesian dualism versus embodiment, and appreciation of tradition versus its distortion. The lesson is that the martial path holds both light and shadow, and separating enlightenment from self-deception takes eternal vigilance.

discipline.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
discipline.title: The Dalek Within
discipline.relation: Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.

discipline.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
discipline.title: The Final Thrust to the Abdomen
discipline.relation: Eric Holmes argues that what we enjoy in Dexter is not killing but punishing, and reads the show through Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (with Hobbes and Locke on the right to punish): since the eighteenth century punishment has moved from public torture to the abstract, painless deprivation of liberty, and Dexter is a deliberate throwback to the older Sovereign. Every detail of the ritual is analyzed as torture designed to make the victim recognize he deserves it - displaying photos or the corpses of their victims (Mike Donovan), forced nudity and harsh light, and letting the punishment fit the crime (Trinity's own claw hammer, telling Miguel he killed Oscar). Dexter is 'the Sovereign we've been waiting for,' an unemotional agent of deserved pain that modern incarceration no longer provides.

discipline.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
discipline.title: Society’s a Bad Hit (If You’re Banging Up, Cranking, or Popping)
discipline.relation: This section argues A Scanner Darkly's primary philosophical contribution is the recognition that the fate of Dick's drug circle was social violence against those who did not fit in: dominant California normalizes the apathetic, slothful 'straights' of the Brown Bear Lodge while phone-tapping peace advocates, ransacking writers' homes, and hunting or abandoning drug users whose pain gets attributed to addiction rather than rejection. The Thelma Kornford mosquito-hawk episode, the deposition about color TVs, animals, and My Lai, and Donna's final 'It is easy to win' all expose how winning requires never choosing your own values.

discipline.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
discipline.title: The Wire and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Crosby takes Bunk's 'misdemeanor homicide' exchange about Marlo as the show's thesis that post-industrial capitalism makes human lives worth less, season by season devaluing beat cops, longshoremen, would-be reformers, the schoolkids of Season Four, and finally the journalists meant to sound the alarm. She deploys Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how institutions train docile participants and then require their regular sacrifice to keep operating, so that Simon's 'indifferent gods' of Greek tragedy are now postmodern institutions whose lightning bolts hit everyone in the 'hood. She ends with Camus's Sisyphus: Simon's call to commit to a righteous cause you probably will not win is the only response that offers human dignity, because 'this ain't Aruba... this America, man.'

discipline.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
discipline.title: The Wire and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Eckstrand uses Foucault to explain the show's central pattern that 'our thing is part of the big thing': power is exercised rather than possessed, flowing through networks in every direction, so even pawn Wallace can have kingpins, captains, and prosecutors running around after him, and McNulty's fake serial killer shows how the police-Sun-politics network can be worked from below. The stat game and standardized tests are Foucauldian power/knowledge, producing a truth ('shining up shit and calling it gold') that hides systemic crime and poverty while punishing truth-tellers like Daniels and reformers like Colvin and Freamon, and its three tools of discipline, hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and examination, are visible from Comstat and the project-class window to the grand jury that tames the dockworkers' union. Even reform becomes part of the machine it targets (Templeton's Pulitzer chase), so the best hope is the constant accumulation of small victories by those who keep fighting.

discipline.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
discipline.title: Futurama and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Onishi argues humor exposes cultural normalcy: Futurama transplants twenty-first-century prejudices into the future, where Leela's one eye still gets her mocked by the blind-and-deaf orphan Kirk ('The Cyber House Rules') and same-sex marriage is unremarkable while robosexual marriage is taboo ('Proposition Infinity,' a parody of California's Proposition 8). Leela's phaser-eye surgery and her self-loathing until 'Leela's Homeworld' reveals she is a mutant show standards of normalcy are cultural rather than natural, and are wielded oppressively. Drawing on Aristotle's habituation, Hume's habit, and Foucault's disciplinary production of subjects, the chapter uses Bender's change of heart after dating the Lucy Liu-bot head in 'I Dated a Robot' to argue habits change through meeting actual people rather than abstract 'ideas' of communities - which is how satire quietly extends what counts as normal.

discipline.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
discipline.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Chad Timm applies Foucault's disciplinary power to the International Fleet: Graff sorts monitored children like 'formless clay,' watches them through a Battle School Panopticon of head monitors and battleroom observation, and uses constant testing and the normalizing gaze to make Ender his own overseer and construct the identity of a commander. He closes by mapping the same sort-examine-discipline circuit onto standardized testing and Race to the Top, noting Ender's flicker of resistance when the children finally see through the adults' game.

discipline.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
discipline.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Stephenson and Waller start from disliking bland, marketable Piper and use Foucault's Discipline and Punish to argue that Litchfield is a microcosm of State power: arbitrary unwritten rules, counts, strip searches, and constant surveillance train prisoners into docile, compliant participants in capitalism, with specialist wardens, psychologists, and lawyers molding the abnormal into the normal. Prisoners specialize too (Red's kitchen, Nicky's ear, Vee's drugs) to survive, and specialization hides the surveillance. The show itself embodies the mechanism, making viewers aware they too live under the Panopticon, though deviants like Crazy Eyes and her standing pee keep open the possibility of refusing State values.

discipline.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life
discipline.title: 1. Drugging the Kids
discipline.relation: Seymour argues that the serums of Roth's world mirror the real-world medical control of young people: with no objective test, about 6.4 million American children are diagnosed with ADHD and medicated for diverging from adult-defined 'normal' behavior, just as Amity bakes peace serum into its bread and Dauntless uses simulation and truth serums on initiates. Tris's Divergence, and especially her failure to resist the peace serum because some part of her wanted to stop feeling, shows that the desire to conform is what makes chemical control work, while Tobias (re-running his own fear landscape) and Peter (erasing his own memory) model appropriating the serums as tools of self-control. Tris's resistance to the Bureau's memory serum then becomes a vicarious experience of power for young readers who face medication for their own 'divergence.'

discipline.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
discipline.title: 12. Only Deadpool Is Sane
discipline.relation: Chad William Timm argues Deadpool is not really insane but was made 'insane' by power: via Foucault's genealogy of madness, experts like Dr. Brighton (a robotic shell for Psycho Man) at Ravenscroft and Dr. Whitby at Crossmore, along with the courts that institutionalize him after the Hulk trial, run a knowledge/power nexus that labels, sorts, and disciplines him until he internalizes the madman identity ('I think I might actually be crazy'). Nineteenth-century psychiatry's invented link between crime and madness secured the experts' authority, and disciplinary power plus technologies of the self made Deadpool discipline himself. Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe's 'I can see through the bull##$%' and his fourth-wall awareness become resistance to these regimes of truth, and the chapter closes by turning Socrates's examined life on the reader: be careful whom you tell.

discipline.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
discipline.title: 6. Who Has the Power
discipline.relation: Samuelson uses Foucault to dismantle Phillip Price's creed of being 'the most powerful person in the room': power is not a possession but an operation. Elliot's men in black and the FBI's surveillance are disciplinary power - Bentham's panopticon realized in Allsafe's cube farm and the internet itself - while Angela's fight over the Washington Township leak is a struggle with biopower that no sovereign can be punished for, and Whiterose's knowledge is power-knowledge that operates anonymously no matter who holds it. If Foucault is right, Price, Mr. Robot, and Zheng are mere conduits, and no one will ever be the most powerful person in the room.

discipline.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
discipline.title: 10. Babies and Pleasures
discipline.relation: Wesch uses Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how ordinary women so quickly served Gilead: power is exercised rather than possessed, so Offred enjoying the Guardians' frustration, the 'Her fault!' Testifying, and the Particicution show everyone wielding whatever power is within reach. Gilead is a panopticon in Bentham's sense—the Eyes, paired shopping, 'Under His Eye'—where unverifiable surveillance makes citizens their own overseers, while biopower sorts desirable from undesirable populations, 'making live' fertile Handmaids (shatterproof glass against suicide) and letting Unwomen and unbabies die in the Colonies. Resistance is Foucauldian too: Offred's remembered food, Moira's bathroom gossip, and sex with Nick are the 'bodies and pleasures' that counterattack the deployment of sexuality.

discipline.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
discipline.title: 20. Under a Watchful Eye
discipline.relation: Timm gives a full Foucauldian reading: the Sons of Jacob's biblical 'knowledge' is a regime of truth produced by power (via the genealogical method Foucault took from Nietzsche), and Gilead rules less by sovereign violence (particicutions, the Wall) than by disciplinary power that defines, sorts, confines, and retrains—precisely the asylum-prison-school trajectory of Foucault's History of Madness and Discipline and Punish. The Red Center is that institution in miniature (Janine's 'Her fault, her fault'), the black vans with painted Eyes enact Bentham's Panopticon—power 'visible and unverifiable'—and biopower's medicalized control of women's reproductive bodies ties Gilead to Iowa's 2018 fetal heartbeat law. Offred's small refusals—her hidden name, the night that is 'mine,' the act of telling her tale—are the resistance Foucault always found inside disciplinary power.

discipline.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
discipline.title: 15. Abnormal Is the New Normal
discipline.relation: Berns, Foronda, and Zarate read the show anachronistically (via Didi-Huberman), arguing its millennial sensibilities deliberately clash with the 1980s setting to reveal that normalcy is a shifting social discourse rather than a natural fact: Joyce defends Will's possible sexuality like no 1980s mother would, Jonathan claims freakishness as a right, and audiences mourn plain, awkward Barb. Through Foucault's three figures from Abnormal, the monster (androgynous, tomboy-coded Eleven called 'freak'), the individual to be corrected (hippie Terry Ives, 'hysterical' Joyce, un-macho boys), and the masturbator (surveillance of the most intimate life), plus biopolitics and bullying as State-sanctioned discipline, they show the abnormal are the heroes: 'The X-Men are weirdos.'

discipline.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
discipline.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Chad Timm reads Battle School through Foucault's disciplinary power: monitors in the skull, sorting into armies, minute-by-minute schedules, and constant testing are the power/knowledge that constructs 'the soldier,' while the ever-possible observation of teachers and desks makes the school Bentham's Panopticon that trains students to police themselves. The proof of Ender's constructed identity is his singling out of Bean exactly as Graff singled him out on the shuttle, and Timm extends the lesson to standardized testing and Obama's 'Race to the Top.'

discipline.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords
discipline.title: Game of Thrones and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Applying Foucault's History of Madness, the chapter argues that sanity in Westeros is an act of naming by the powerful: Joffrey literally remakes the drunken Ser Dontos into a court fool, and 'Mad King' Aerys's brutality gets labeled madness while comparable violence by Jaime (throwing Bran from the window) and Robert (ordering Daenerys's assassination) counts as sane necessity. The power/knowledge nexus and the psychiatric fusion of crime with insanity explain how Robert's personal hatred of Rhaegar hides behind a medicalized diagnosis of Targaryen madness. The chapter then tracks Foucault's shift from sovereign to disciplinary power and technologies of the self: Dontos internalizes and performs his fool identity, Dany wonders 'perhaps I am mad' at Drogo's pyre, and Catelyn's freeing of Jaime is written off by Robb's bannermen as 'a mother's madness.'

discipline.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
discipline.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
discipline.relation: The chapter uses Foucault to explain how Salander could leave school without a certificate yet master Fermat-class mathematics: schools 'cut' students into fabricated 'human kinds'—the problem-solving child and the at-risk child (Popkewitz's alchemy)—and under No Child Left Behind that sorting licenses surveillance and discipline of everything an at-risk student does. Lisbeth's case shows the machinery: her correct answer marked wrong from the textbook key, her Rubik's-cube brilliance ignored, her 381 days strapped to a bed under Teleborian's silhouette-like gaze recasting Bentham's Panopticon, and her subsequent guardianship extending the watch over her money and behavior. Because power 'produces reality,' the at-risk label becomes self-fulfilling, and Lisbeth's refusal to be disciplined—her silence, tattoos, and asocial style—only supplies fresh evidence for the label.

discipline.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason
discipline.title: The Hunger Games and Philosophy
discipline.relation: Van Dyke uses Foucault's account of discipline and 'docile bodies' (with Susan Bordo's feminist elaboration) to explain how the Capitol rules: citizens satiated with abundance channel their hungers into fashion, body modification, and self-surveillance, and this self-focused discipline trains their attention away from the injustices that sustain them — which is how the genuinely affectionate prep team can weep over Katniss yet love the Games. She shows that District 13 disciplines just as totally through rigid schedules, rations, and punishment (the prep team chained for taking bread), so neither Snow's hidden indulgence nor Coin's overt regimentation leaves room for autonomy. Cinna's styling of Katniss demonstrates the alternative: body modification as internally generated self-expression and resistance that helps Katniss become the Mockingjay rather than a docile body.

discipline.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
discipline.title: Notes
discipline.relation: Meyer reads the franchise through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: Max's terror of becoming a 'terminal crazy' replays madness-as-contagion, the great confinement of the mad alongside rabid animals recurs in Max's leashing and Humungus 'unleash[ing] my dogs of war,' and delirium as one step out of reason's furrow frames Johnny the Boy's 'I was sick!' plea. Applying the M'Naghten cognitive test and the wild-beast standard to Johnny the Boy, Blaster, Wez, and Nux, he concludes most followers can still tell right from wrong and remain responsible. The ultimate blame therefore falls on the cult leaders — Toecutter, Humungus, and Immortan Joe — who manufacture and exploit a shared psychosis.

discipline.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery
discipline.title: Madness in the Mirror of Reason: Metallica and Foucault on Insanity and Confinement
discipline.relation: Brian Cameron reads 'Welcome Home (Sanitarium)' and 'Frayed Ends of Sanity' through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: the sanitarium is a total institution whose surveillance and power-knowledge produce docile bodies, confining madness as a threat to the rule of reason just as the seventeenth-century Hopital General confined the idle. Madness is not a mere disease but a socially defined deviance - and a form of rebellion against conformist society - whose violent 'cure' ('violent use brings violent plans') exacts an existential cost on the rebel, as 'The Unforgiven''s bitter old man shows.

discipline.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
discipline.title: Notes
discipline.relation: Reads Leia's gold-bikini captivity in Jabba's palace as an image of contemporary culture's fear of fat: Jabba, the rancor, and the Sarlaac personify uncontrolled appetite and Sartre's 'slimy' being-in-itself, while Leia's thin, disciplined body epitomizes the anorexic ideal. Drawing on Susan Bordo and Foucault's docile bodies, the chapter argues the scene chains women to a tyrannical ideal of slimness so that Leia herself becomes the oppressor, and closes with Sartre's point that consciousness depends on its body, so we should suspend the fear of flesh and embrace embodied life as the Force does.

discipline.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
discipline.title: Moral Autonomy
discipline.relation: Challans reads the clone army as a Foucauldian project of discipline: Kaminoan reconditioning, punishment of 'aberrance,' and the inhibitor chips produce the 'docile bodies' that made Order 66 executable, with Palpatine's propaganda framing the Jedi as traitors to supply its legitimacy. Milgram's obedience experiments explain why most clones became 'agentic' executioners, while the rare independence of Rex, Fives, and Tup in the Umbara arc — 'we are not a bunch of unthinking droids!' — shows how fragile moral autonomy is. He concludes that military competence itself requires independent judgment, as his Delta Force versus Rangers comparison after Mogadishu illustrates, making Rex the exemplar of the moral autonomy the chips were designed to destroy.

discipline.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way
discipline.title: “Wherever I Go, He Goes”
discipline.relation: Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.

discipline.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
discipline.title: She Got Game
discipline.relation: The Wallaces argue that both the detractors (Stacey Pressman's claim that women's basketball 'sucks') and the admirers (John Wooden's 'purest basketball' praise) judge the women's game by patriarchal standards drawn from the men's game. Using Sandra Bartky's feminist extension of Foucault, they show how the female body was disciplined under male surveillance - early rule changes split the court and banned stealing to protect 'femininity', while players deflected the 'Amazon' charge with beauty pageants, revealing uniforms, and the Playboy offer to Lisa Harrison. The modern WNBA of Lisa Leslie and Michelle Snow, who can dunk but choose team play, points to a new game that escapes the feminine/masculine dichotomy instead of measuring women against men.

discipline.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee
discipline.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
discipline.relation: Dale and Foy argue that across Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Hulk and Brokeback Mountain, Lee presents a pessimistic, Sartrean philosophy of identity in which authentic selves are irreconcilable with a hostile social world. They read Jen's caged gender rebellion and Jade Fox's rejection, Bruce's suppressed origins and rage-fueled transformation, and Ennis and Jack's concealed love as hidden identities that produce dislocation, deception and disorder. Invoking Kierkegaard and Heidegger's dasein on authenticity and Foucault's Discipline and Punish, they show society disciplining deviance so each hero is displaced or destroyed—Jack beaten to death like Matthew Shepard, the Hulk exiled to the Amazon.

discipline.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman
discipline.title: On Being John Malkovich and Not Being Yourself
discipline.relation: Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.

discipline.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
discipline.title: Monstrous motherhood
discipline.relation: The chapter argues that horror films about mothers are not static representations but Foucauldian sites where 'discourses of motherhood' are produced, policed and contested; using Foucault's account of bodies disciplined through power/knowledge, it treats films as cultural artefacts that both enforce and challenge norms of 'essential' and 'ideal' motherhood. It reworks Sarah Arnold's Lacanian 'Good Mother/Bad Mother' schema (the mother who sacrifices herself so the child enters the Symbolic and submits to the Law of the Father) alongside popularised Freudian mother-blame (the 'refrigerator mother', 'tell me about your mother') to read Psycho's Norma(n), the phallic mothers of The Killing Kind and The Brood, and the doomed single mothers of The Ring, Silent Hill and Triangle. It coins the 'monstrous-maternal' to argue that motherhood is framed as always-already monstrous because no woman can meet the impossible, shifting criteria of ideal motherhood, illustrated through Grace's Vivian/Madeline generational clash and Serial Mom's Beverly Sutphin.

discipline.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror
discipline.title: The ageing woman as (American) horror story
discipline.relation: The chapter theorises the 'abject barren body' — the menstruating, menopausal and post-menopausal woman — connecting menarche as an upswell of feminine power (Carrie's telekinesis, Ginger Snaps, The Witch's Thomasin) to menopause's cultural construction as loss and 'living decay'. Drawing on Mary Douglas and Kristeva on pollution and abjection, and on Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' and bodies defined by capacities rather than fixed being, it argues that the female reproductive body is more often barren than fecund and that this state is another generative modality, not an absence. It reads the Western biomedical pathologisation of menopause (Wilson's Feminine Forever, HRT) as a Foucauldian disciplinary discourse, then tracks older women through Sunset Boulevard's Norma Desmond, the hagsploitation cycle (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?, Strait-Jacket, Hush Hush Sweet Charlotte), and The Taking of Deborah Logan, concluding that Jessica Lange's American Horror Story roles offer the fullest, sexually frank rebuttal to the abjection and invisibility of the ageing woman.

discipline.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films
discipline.title: Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film
discipline.relation: Gooch argues that the post-2005 surveillance film cycle moves 'beyond panopticism': Foucault's disciplinary gaze gives way to Deleuze's 'societies of control,' and the surveiling gaze becomes direct domination and a form of biopolitical labor (Hardt and Negri) rather than an impersonal structure. He reads the prestige dramas (Redacted, Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs) as exposing the soldier's proletarianization and self-surveillance, and the thrillers/blockbusters (Déjà Vu, The Kingdom, Body of Lies, The Bourne Ultimatum, Eagle Eye, Burn after Reading) as staging a Marxist antagonism between living labor (the watching hero) and the fixed capital of surveillance technology. Using Deleuze's 'degraded time-image,' Kant's needed separation of subject and law, and Benjamin/Agamben's state of exception, he shows Eagle Eye inverting law and subject to justify preemptive war and turn biopolitical labor into the labor of subjection.

discipline.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western
discipline.title: Beating a Live Horse The Elevation and Degradation of Horses in Westerns
discipline.relation: Jennifer L. McMahon gives an existential account of Americans' ambivalence toward horses in westerns: because horses mirror human anxiety, herd-boundness, and the flight instinct that Sartre and Heidegger locate at the core of being, we transfer our self-loathing onto them and, driven by Nietzsche's will to power and Hegel's lord-and-bondsman struggle for recognition, we break them to prove our own mastery. Reading breaking scenes in All the Pretty Horses and The Horse Whisperer via Foucault's Discipline and Punish (the round pen as panopticon producing 'docile bodies'), she contrasts films like Hidalgo and The Electric Horseman that model Hegelian reciprocity, urging us to 'let go, turn in, and hook on' rather than dominate.

discipline.book: 244 - The Who and Philosophy
discipline.title: The Dalek Within
discipline.relation: Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.

discipline.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
discipline.title: Propaganda and Pedagogy for Apt Pupils
discipline.relation: Potter and Cobb read Apt Pupil—the blackmail-driven 'teaching' relationship between the boy Todd Bowden and the fugitive Nazi Kurt Dussander—to argue that all effective teaching is propaganda: persuasion by nonrational means (ethos and pathos beyond logos). They analyze the shifting teacher-student dynamic through Foucault's Power/Knowledge, showing power as a fluid relational 'order' rather than a possession, with Russell's definition of power and Nietzsche's Genealogy on the pleasures of subordination explaining Dussander's relief in obeying. Citing Bernays and Chomsky, they contend Todd and Dussander's oppressive, sadism-soaked curriculum merely strips the artifice from ordinary schooling, which has always been a system of control—culminating in Todd's transformation into a killer.

discipline.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy
discipline.title: The Shining ’s Overlook Hotel as Heterotopia
discipline.relation: Elizabeth Hornbeck analyzes King's Overlook Hotel through Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' arguing the hotel is a heterotopia—a socially produced space of crisis and deviance that juxtaposes and inverts normal relations, accumulating time as a 'chronic heterotopia' stuffed with its own ghosts and murders (Mrs. Massey, the Gradys, the 1921 photo). Cut off in winter, it strips away the norms of 'home' so Jack Torrance's inherited monsters (alcoholism, his father's abuse) can turn him from protector into a family-killer. She contrasts the maze-like Overlook with the panopticon of Grand Hotel and Bentham's surveillance-prison from Discipline and Punish, noting that King, unlike Foucault, treats transgression as horrific: the conservative horror genre restores the status quo only when Jack dies and the hotel burns.

discipline.book: 278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style
discipline.title: FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
discipline.relation: Collins analyzes paradigmatic Barbie play — dressing the doll and identifying with her as an idealized future self, from the 1959 TV ad to BarbieGirls.com — arguing it trains girls to define identity through fashionable bodily self-presentation for a male gaze (Brumberg's 'body project'). Using Sandra Bartky's feminist reworking of Foucault's *Discipline and Punish*, she treats beauty norms as a discipline producing 'docile bodies' whose self-surveillance internalizes a 'panoptical male connoisseur' (Bentham's Panopticon), offering cycles of pleasure and pain that bind women without any single sovereign to blame. Rather than banning Barbie (the failed 'Happy to be Me' doll), she proposes subversive play — Plump and Proud Barbie, Mursi lip-plate Barbie — as Heyes-style 'practices of freedom.'

discipline.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
discipline.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
discipline.relation: Hancuff and O'Connor read the song 'Santa Claus Is Coming to Town' and films like The Polar Express and Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town through Foucault's Discipline and Punish. Santa's all-seeing list-checking is a version of Bentham's Panopticon: children, watched but never seeing the watcher, internalize permanent visibility and discipline themselves. Invoking Foucault's Power/Knowledge and discursive practices, they argue the surveillance does not actually make children 'good for goodness' sake' – punishment is rarely delivered – but instead disciplines them into wish-lists and consumption, training them to be good consumers in late-capitalist culture, with Santa doubling as a corporate pitchman (Coke, Budweiser).

discipline.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
discipline.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
discipline.relation: Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.

discipline.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
discipline.title: Ideological Formations of the Nuclear Family in The Hills Have Eyes
discipline.relation: Lorena Russell reads both versions of The Hills Have Eyes through Althusser's Repressive vs. Ideological State Apparatuses (building on Gramsci's hegemony) and Foucault's account of power as multivalent with resistance internal to it, defending nuanced ideological criticism against Carroll's caricature. The films pit the 'normal' Carter family against the mutant/feral family produced by U.S. nuclear testing, using Clover's 'urbanoia' and class/Indian-exploitation guilt, Freudian repression, and the mannequin ghost town to expose 'family values' as constructed ideology. The Carters' descent into the mutants' own violence (Doug and Brenda 'butching up') destabilizes the bourgeois family rather than reaffirming it.

discipline.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
discipline.title: 46. The Shawshank Redemption as Philosophy Freedom and Panopticism
discipline.relation: Hooke reads The Shawshank Redemption through two lenses. From Sartre he takes 'hell is other people' and the objectifying look from No Exit and Being and Nothingness — Shawshank's warden and 'sisters' embody a worldly hell of 'never' and 'always' — but argues Andy and Red's friendship, Andy's Mozart broadcast, and the hopeful ending invert Sartre, making freedom the shared warmth of friendship rather than the devouring gaze. From Foucault's Discipline and Punish he reads the prison's shift from spectacle to disciplinary surveillance and solitary confinement as panopticism, extending Foucault's insight that prisons, schools, and hospitals mirror one another (illustrated by his COVID-era campus). He closes with Nietzschean genealogy and redemption through laughter, joy, and giving.

discipline.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
discipline.title: 81. Papers, Please as Philosophy Playing with the Relations between Politics and Morality
discipline.relation: Sievers argues that Papers, Please immerses the player as an immigration inspector in the totalitarian Arstotzka, where mechanically stamping 'approved'/'refused' and detaining Kolechians for bribes enacts Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, 'just following orders' functionary exemplified by Eichmann, who cannot think from another's standpoint. The paycheck-versus-family pressure and X-ray humiliation scenes show how fear and bureaucracy erase moral responsibility. Drawing on Butler's 'Can one lead a good life in a bad life?' and Foucault's biopower, she reads the visa candidates as 'precarious,' non-grievable lives whose worth the state allocates, and the game's Ezic resistance endings as showing how constrained moral resistance is under such a regime.

public-sphere.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason
public-sphere.title: After . . . Word!
public-sphere.relation: Marcyliena Morgan's afterword traces hip-hop battling to the philosophical houses and crews of Saturday kung-fu cinema (Wu-Tang's obsession included), reading hip hop's South Bronx birth through Victor Turner's ritual threshold state and defining "flow" as conscious movement within chaos to create balance and collective identity. The mantra represent-recognize-come correct, shout outs as a system of indexicality, and hip hop's counterpublic sphere function, she argues, to expose hegemony and contest Foucault's technologies of power - answering Cornel West's "ignoble paradox of modernity" - so that hip hop battles through the theoretical houses of Foucault, Bakhtin, Butler, Gramsci, and Habermas, where "there is no such thing as a dead philosopher - just one that has not been resurrected yet."

public-sphere.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
public-sphere.title: Unity in Diversity
public-sphere.relation: Lombardo asks whether the podcast, born as an unsanctioned side effect users reinvented out of the iPod (as hip hop reinvented the turntable before corporate co-option made it the hegemonic form), can be a public-sphere institution. Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.

public-sphere.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
public-sphere.title: 19 - facebook, Surveillance and Power
public-sphere.relation: Doyle and Fraser open with the Lady Shelley Sawers affair, in which Britain's new MI6 chief was exposed by his wife's public Facebook profile, to ask whether social networks democratize surveillance or perfect it. They read the CIA's social-media monitoring, the Chris Dreyfus promotion case, and Facebook's Beacon advertising scheme through Foucault — Bentham's Panopticon, the carceral continuum, regimes of truth, and the shift to statistically managing populations — arguing that narcissistic self-display makes people 'most controllable,' while Habermas's public sphere frames the hopeful side: Beacon's defeat by user protest, Glassdoor, and Iran's Twitter revolution as diffused power against the centralized state. Foucault's answer is neither utopia nor repression but an ethics of self-management for playing power games with minimum domination.

public-sphere.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_
public-sphere.title: 20 - Wall to Wall or Face to Face
public-sphere.relation: Bar-Tura, a Chicago Jewish social-justice organizer, evaluates Facebook by Habermas's ideal speech situation — equal chances to speak, initiate, and question, aimed at consensus — recounting how Jewish and Muslim teens scheduled to bowl together first met online and shed stereotypes by browsing each other's profiles. Yet face-to-face planning surfaced what wall-to-wall could not: the Shabbat timing question, and Muslim parents' unease about a north-side venue, which revealed socio-economic and racial divides rather than religious ones. Fixed, market-driven profile categories and the 'Daily Me' of niche idea consumption limit Facebook as a public sphere, so profiles must become people and the group must actually gather for social change.

public-sphere.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
public-sphere.title: History and Philosophy
public-sphere.relation: Imre reads Hungary's Aranycsapat as a political-philosophical event: Sebes's socialist 4–2–4 football was meant to prove that cooperative civil society could flourish under Stalinism, and the 6–3 demolition of England at Wembley, with its self-organizing positional play, became the sporting antithesis to Rákosi's regime — culminating in the 1956 Revolution that Arendt cited as a 'true' revolution of spontaneous councils. The 1954 final loss to West Germany (contrasted with Germany's own rebirth at Berne) entrenched a fatalism that history's organic 'grand narrative' and 'final synthesis' were against Hungary, helping destroy the civil-society possibility the team embodied and pushing Hungarians into anti-politics. His lesson: talent and beauty can be quashed by the contingency of history — igazság, truth-justice, never manifested, and soccer could not overcome history.

public-sphere.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
public-sphere.title: Chapter 16 - How Come You’re So Wrong, My Sweet Neo Con
public-sphere.relation: Joseph Foy introduces 'Sweet Neo Con' from A Bigger Bang (2005) as the Stones' most direct political statement — Jagger's blunt, non-metaphorical attack on Bush-era Christian hypocrisy, phony patriotism, and corporatist cronyism. Noting that the left (Michael Moore, Bill Moyers) cheered while the right (Matt Drudge) called it geriatric pandering, he argues both sides misread the song, which actually crystallizes the band's lifelong role in defining the public sphere.

public-sphere.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
public-sphere.title: No Place for a Street Fighting Man
public-sphere.relation: This section explains why the Stones seem apolitical beside Lennon's bed-ins and Dylan's protest songs: they rarely joined overt activism, and 'Street Fighting Man' remained only a hint. It then argues the judgment rests on too narrow a conception of the public sphere — the space connecting state and private life — because by legitimizing an anti-establishment counter-cultural identity and pushing rebellion into the mainstream (capped by the SS-uniform protest after Ed Sullivan censored 'Let's Spend the Night Together'), the Stones did political work without electoral politics.

public-sphere.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
public-sphere.title: Like a Rollin’ Stone
public-sphere.relation: Building the strong/weak publics distinction — rally-goers pursue decisions, concert-goers form identity — the section argues the Stones' influence runs through 'political socialization': prolonged emotional attachment to a rebellious worldview, from the tongue logo on dorm walls to 'Satisfaction's' indictment of mainstream media, gradually makes fans more distrustful of centralized power and state enforcement of cultural agendas. That slow identity shift, not candidate endorsement, is their politics.

public-sphere.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away
public-sphere.title: If You Turn Out Right, I’ll Eat My Hat Tonight
public-sphere.relation: The short closing section argues that in the mass-media age the line between political message and private life has dissolved: 'nearly all activities are now political', so sorting public-sphere discourse from private identity formation no longer tracks anything real. The Stones' covert 1960s rebellion and the overt 'Sweet Neo Con' are therefore one continuous project of resisting the single social mold neo-conservatives tried to impose — and Foy bets it will not be the last confrontation.

public-sphere.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal
public-sphere.title: Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy
public-sphere.relation: Sienkiewicz argues that Klosterman's LeBron James 'Decision' episode on Bill Simmons's B.S. Report modeled genuine public-sphere deliberation: where ESPN's Skip Bayless scored points over whether James looked remorseful, Klosterman proposed, via Tupac's 'Only God can judge me', that the televised announcement was a statement of confidence and a refusal to play the one-dimensional reality-TV role America demanded. The chapter lays out Habermas's eighteenth-century public sphere, its salons and 'public sphere of letters' where low-stakes aesthetic arguments (Mozart then, the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City now) train disinterested rational debate, and concedes Habermas's golden age is idealized historical fiction much like a Klosterman hyperthetical. Though Habermas blames commercial media for corroding rational discourse, Sienkiewicz contends that long-form podcasts like The B.S. Report and Contexts give Klosterman's pop-culture arguments the time and independence the old salons had, so arguing about Billy Joel or Ace Frehley strengthens rather than absolves democratic culture.

public-sphere.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question
public-sphere.title: Jeopardy! and Philosophy
public-sphere.relation: Joseph Foy argues Jeopardy! quietly serves democracy: the breadth of its categories rewards exactly the well-rounded, informed citizenry that theorists from Tocqueville to Delli Carpini and Keeter think self-government needs, and it answers Plato's Republic worry that ordinary people are unfit to rule by showing experts and stay-at-home parents alike fluent across the board. Because civic knowledge correlates with defending First Amendment freedoms, and because the show inserts the glorification of knowledge into the public sphere while bar-trivia gatherings build Putnam-style social capital, playing along at home rehearses the habits and virtues of democratic citizenship.

public-sphere.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile
public-sphere.title: 24. Post-Factual Democracy
public-sphere.relation: Hendricks and Vestergaard open with Trump's inauguration lies and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' to define post-factual democracy: a state in which opportune political narratives replace facts and evidence as the basis of debate, opinion formation and policymaking. Unlike Machiavelli, who taught that lies must at least be concealed, the post-factual politician pays no price for exposed falsehood once social media, the attention economy and populist us-versus-them narratives engineered for indignation and fear have stripped journalists and fact-checkers of authority — Arendt's remark that mass leaders show 'extreme contempt for facts as such' before fitting reality to their lies. Using Habermas's deliberative model and even minimal accountability theories of voting, they argue post-factuality destroys democratic legitimacy, and defend a 'factual democracy' that trusts science and journalism without becoming a technocracy — the real-world echo of the Party's command to reject the evidence of your eyes.

public-sphere.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
public-sphere.title: 21. Mister Rogers’s Lesson for Democracy
public-sphere.relation: Matthew Ussia maps the Trolley's transition between Rogers's house and the Neighborhood of Make-Believe onto Habermas's public sphere: the first-week crisis, Lady Elaine's rearranging of the neighborhood, King Friday's barbed-wire wall and 'Down with the Changes!,' Chef Brockett's humiliation, shows fear collapsing the space where a democracy works through conflict. Like Habermas, who feared television debates would hijack real public talk (and contra Sartre's 'Hell is other people'), Rogers used puppets to say the unsayable, modeling the deliberative space privatized modern life threatens to close.

public-sphere.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory
public-sphere.title: The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy
public-sphere.relation: Vanderheiden treats America (The Book)'s textbook parody as serious democratic theory: its 'Democracy Inaction' diagnosis (a president chosen from a field of two, 99% incumbency, lobbyists as 'the white knights of democracy') tracks the thin versus thick democracy distinction and Benjamin Barber's deliberative democracy, with Putnam's social capital as the remedy for the satirized life cycle of national decline. The 'Dress the Supreme Court' gag, Senate color-by-numbers, and third-party graveyard expose representational exclusion, while the media chapter indicts conglomeration for killing the press's watchdog role, invoking Mill's marketplace of ideas. The Earth (The Book) postscript notes that social contracts were historically written without the assent of the women and minorities they subjugated.

public-sphere.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire
public-sphere.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy
public-sphere.relation: The chapter reconstructs the real Swedish journalist behind Kalle Blomkvist: the 1950s reporter as the welfare state's mouthpiece alongside heroic police, the 1970s radical investigative journalist epitomized by Jan Guillou—whose exposure of the secret IB organization earned him a prison sentence and a revenge vindication, the direct template for Blomkvist—and the 1990s–2000s slide into 'sensation, scandal, and spectacle' around crime. It shows journalism decoupling from crime statistics—about a hundred killings a year in a country of 9.4 million, falling, yet alarmist coverage fueling tougher sentencing and the Nazi-rooted Sweden Democrats' entry into parliament—so the watchdog ideal of the muckraker who draws aside the veil on 'men who hate women and democracy' becomes a question: where have you gone, Kalle Blomkvist?

public-sphere.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades
public-sphere.title: A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics
public-sphere.relation: Sudnick and Garrett stage the Dewey-Lippmann debate through Weekend Update's citizen journalists: Drunk Uncle and Girl at Party exemplify Lippmann's propagandized pseudo-environments and echo chambers, while Stefon parodies the expert gatekeeper his technocratic 'machinery of knowledge' would install. Dewey's The Public and its Problems answers that democracy needs public education, a free and publicly funded press, and wide participation, with Point/Counterpoint and Cathy Ann's plea to log off and meet face-to-face as comic images of deliberative citizenship. The chapter ends with Dewey's hope that artists, from Opera Man to Sandler's Chanukah Song, are the real purveyors of news in a democracy consummated by artful communication.

public-sphere.book: 230 - The Philosophy of Spike Lee
public-sphere.title: (Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing
public-sphere.relation: Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.

public-sphere.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan
public-sphere.title: Plato, Habermas, and the Demonic Cobb
public-sphere.relation: Murphy treats Following as a provocation keyed to the copy of Plato's Republic glimpsed in The Blonde's apartment: Cobb, who slips unseen into houses and lives and reads people's 'boxes,' is the shepherd with the Ring of Gyges, able to act unjustly without ever facing detection. Against Glaucon's challenge the chapter weighs Socrates's answer that injustice enslaves and disorders the soul—but notes that Nolan shows Cobb victorious, a 'demonic' figure with all of Socrates's abilities and none of his love of justice, who drags Bill and The Blonde into a cave of illusion rather than out of one. Habermas supplies the modern retort: our rationality and sanity depend on the communicative action, truth, and fairness of a shared lifeworld, commitments a sociopathic loner like Cobb cannot renounce without taking refuge in mental illness, though the film never shows Cobb paying that price. Man of Steel's Clark Kent clutching the Republic while letting himself be bullied, and Jonathan Kent's fatal secrecy, become the counterimage of someone who consistently wills justice at personal cost, the closest Nolan comes to showing why justice is worth choosing.

public-sphere.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
public-sphere.title: 4. Punk as Praxis
public-sphere.relation: Smith argues punk's heart is neither a playlist nor an attitude but praxis in Aristotle's sense: autotelic, self-directed activity, which Heidegger read existentially as authentic existence and Arendt politicized as communicative action in a vibrant public sphere. Punk's 'no-saying' - to employment ('Career Opportunities'), commercialization ('EMI'), and entertainment - plus its affirmations of speaking in your own voice, forming bands and labels, and the fanzine/record-shop public sphere exemplify praxis, while post-punk's technical refinement around Factory Records and the Lesser Free Trade Hall gigs marks a shift from praxis back to Aristotle's poiesis.

public-sphere.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate
public-sphere.title: Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone
public-sphere.relation: Bar-Tura applies Habermas's Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere to argue coffeehouses once formed a genuine public sphere where private people 'bracketed' status under the force of the better argument — from the 1680–1730 'golden age' and Charles II's suppression proclamation to the Green Dragon and City Tavern that brewed the American Revolution and the India Coffeehouse of Lahore. He notes Nancy Fraser's feminist critique that these spheres excluded women, then argues today's chain 'coffee shops' (Oldenburg's 'third place' hollowed into laptop isolation) have become places of 'common solitude'; citing Arendt on power arising only when people act together and on thoughtlessness, he calls for reclaiming coffee-houses as sites of discussion and social change (Café Society, Discussions over Coffee).

moral-luck.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
moral-luck.title: The Mystery Solved
moral-luck.relation: Avery Kolers uses "Only a Pawn in Their Game" and its companion "Who Killed Davey Moore?" to argue that Dylan treats Byron de la Beckwith as a pawn: a poor white duped by divide-and-rule tactics, the psychological wage of whiteness, shame, and lynch-mob indoctrination into fearing a Hobbesian war of all against all. Against Aristotle's account of acting in ignorance, the chapter asks whether Beckwith's ignorance of his real enemies was culpable, concluding his bad moral luck (in Bernard Williams's sense) was manufactured by white supremacy and so reflects back on all white people. Dylan's refusal to name or voice Beckwith adopts Strawson-style objective attitudes, making blaming itself a political act aimed at the system rather than the shooter.

moral-luck.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust
moral-luck.title: The Golden Compass and Philosophy
moral-luck.relation: Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.

moral-luck.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations
moral-luck.title: If Only . .
moral-luck.relation: Bryan Pilkington applies Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel's analysis of moral luck, where factors outside an agent's control change how we evaluate the very same act, to Bill Buckner's Game Six error of 1986, alongside constructed cases of Jon Lester skipping the last page of his scouting sheet and a Fenway Franks truck driver who skips his brake check. Drawing on Nagel on negligence, Williams's notion of agent-regret (only Buckner, not Bob Stanley or Rich Gedman, can feel it), and a standard of reasonable expectation for a veteran first baseman, he concludes Buckner can rightly be blamed for the error and even for losing Game Six, though not for the World Series or for the cruel vilification he received. The chapter thus disciplines the fan's 'if only' blame game: a curse is never a satisfying target of blame, but neither is the situation instead of the person.

moral-luck.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
moral-luck.title: Luck as Anathema
moral-luck.relation: Eylon and Horowitz defend the maligned manager's excuse 'we outplayed them and were plain unlucky' by distinguishing genuine football luck from fluke-luck: unlike sprinting, where outrunning your opponent and finishing fourth is incoherent, football's rules constitute rather than merely measure the skill, and 'almosts'—Roritania City hitting the woodwork eight times while United's one sloppy shot goes in—show ability and success genuinely coming apart. The accusation that football rewards the undeserving then exposes the control condition of moral desert, illustrated by two assassins whose shots differ only by an intervening swallow and by a never-bribed referee who would have taken the money, so that the luck football manifestly displays infects morality and politics generally. Football is anathema to some fans precisely because, unlike life where luck also rules, it displays luck inside an activity explicitly designed to reward merit—yet the authors conclude that 'almosts' and the all-or-nothing scoring are also the source of the game's beauty, and nobody who loves it would have luck removed.

moral-luck.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
moral-luck.title: You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It
moral-luck.relation: Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.

moral-luck.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
moral-luck.title: Where the Bodies Lie
moral-luck.relation: Daniel P. Malloy uses Dexter to lay out the three kinds of moral luck introduced by Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel: constitutive luck (witnessing his mother's murder and being adopted by Harry, who taught him the Code instead of getting treatment, made Dexter a controlled killer while his brother Brian became 'an unchecked version' of the same child), situational luck (the choice between Brian and Debra in 'Born Free,' the forced kidnapping of Doakes), and resultant luck (Lila burning the shack with Doakes inside, and Dexter's mistaken kill of the innocent photographer Jonathan Farrow in 'Slack Tide,' which he meets with remorse and agent-regret). Against the thought that luck erases responsibility, Malloy argues that intentions remain fully ours, borrowing David Lewis's claim that attempted and successful murderers deserve identical punishment - so Dexter is answerable for every kill.

moral-luck.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
moral-luck.title: Homeland and Philosophy
moral-luck.relation: Dan Burkett defends Brody against blame for flipping the suicide-vest switch in 'Marine One' by arguing he was not free. On the desire-satisfaction view Brody freely avenge Issa, but via Locke's locked-room thought experiment (Carrie contentedly 'freely' staying in a house she cannot leave) the chapter motivates the libertarian requirement that one could have done otherwise, which Nazir's years of torture and brainwashing may have removed. The malfunctioning vest then raises moral luck - Brody is no better a person because the bomb failed - and since Dana's plea restricts his options just as coercively, the best defense grants Brody freedom throughout, making the switch blameworthy and his free choice to come home genuinely redemptive.

moral-luck.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
moral-luck.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
moral-luck.relation: McCrossin asks why Finn and Jake forgive Marceline although she tries to kill Jake, evicts them twice, drains Princess Bubblegum, and never shows remorse. Jake's change of heart ('my fear was based on ignorance') comes from witnessing her father Hunson Abadeer's cruelty and her abandoned childhood, so her bad acts flow from causes outside her control rather than pure choice. The chapter presses the remaining problem: we normally forgive the penitent offender, not the unrepentant one, and Marceline—unlike the moping vampires of Twilight, Underworld, and True Blood—never regrets, leaving readers to decide whether understanding without remorse can ground trust and friendship.

moral-luck.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes
moral-luck.title: Adventure Time and Philosophy
moral-luck.relation: Reading Finn's first season as a three-stage hero's journey - winning the Enchiridion on Mount Cragdor, being tested in 'Business Time', 'City of Thieves', 'Ocean of Fear' and 'Henchman', then doubly confirmed when Billy recognizes him - the chapter extracts a working handbook of heroism from his stumbles. Its lessons: heroism needs reason as much as courage (thinking through the gnome 'illusions', knocking himself unconscious to beat the Fear Feaster), plain luck plays a real and uneven part in saving Jake from the ogre, retribution should be temporary (the ogre's returned dollar), and heroes must check their sources (Penny's con). The deepest tension is that justice and compassion, instinct and reason, violence and non-violence must be perpetually balanced - Billy's nonviolent way becomes its own injustice when Finn medicates villagers without consent - so a real hero is simply someone who never stops trying to hold the balance.

moral-luck.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
moral-luck.title: Dracula and Philosophy
moral-luck.relation: Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.

moral-luck.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
moral-luck.title: 12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys
moral-luck.relation: Jones takes up the charge that loving Downton seduces viewers into admiring inequality, and answers that the Crawleys deserve our care because birth, not choice, gave them their position, so they should be judged only by what they do with it: Grantham paying for Mrs. Patmore's eye surgery, Violet throwing the flower contest after Isobel's challenge, the family gradually embracing Branson. He reads the show as a manifesto for social change through sympathetic contact between classes rather than Irish-style revolt - befriend the rich and their good nature will start to level the playing field. His own objection is that this makes change partly the responsibility of the less privileged, from Thomas being asked to soften Carson's homophobia to the poor being asked to be nice to the rich today.

moral-luck.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
moral-luck.title: 13. Time to Choose
moral-luck.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.

moral-luck.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
moral-luck.title: 24. The Fifty-Third Card
moral-luck.relation: Writing as the Joker playing 'the fifty-third card,' the chapter trashes both heroes at once: Superman is an attention-starved show-off who could save people invisibly but wants worship, and Batman is a billionaire who pours his fortune into toys and beatings while thousands of children die for want of the charity he could give. The real punchline is our hypocrisy: we are only as moral as our circumstances allow (born in the ghetto we would steal too), we mourn pets while eating smarter pigs and buying chocolate picked by child slaves, and in The Dark Knight's ferry scene everyone would really have pushed the button - since choosing not to help kills as surely as detonating, 'we kill every day.' The only honest hero would drop moral pretense, do what he genuinely thinks right, and remind us that under the skin we are all clowns laughing as the world burns.

moral-luck.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
moral-luck.title: 13. But Why Is Our World Better
moral-luck.relation: Tim Jones asks why Juliana and Tagomi are right to call the Allies-win world 'better' when our world also holds the Red Army's mass rapes in Berlin, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the Czech expulsions — a German widow or hibakusha who found Axis-victory reels could call them 'a better world' without being evil. His answer is a numbers-of-victims argument: Juliana's world duplicates our atrocities (the Heisenberg Device on Washington mirrors Hiroshima) and adds unique ones like the Nazi genocide in Africa, so our world is better for the most people — though its victims deserve the empathy and remembrance Obama showed at Hiroshima.

moral-luck.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
moral-luck.title: 14. Reel Lucky
moral-luck.relation: Elizabeth Rard uses Thomas Nagel's moral luck to show that Juliana's heroism and John Smith's Nazi career are largely products of circumstances beyond their control — Trudy's death in front of her, being born German twenty years before the war — while Frank's interrupted assassination of the Crown Prince shows luck intervening mid-action.
