Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.

camus-revolt.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
camus-revolt.title: How to Misunderstand Politics Completely
camus-revolt.relation: Melançon argues Radiohead's real politics lie not in the overt content of Hail to the Thief but in a Camusian movement from absurdity to revolt: 'Exit Music'''s violent shift from Romeo's tender 'you' to the distorted 'we hope that you choke' enacts revolt against imposed rules and wisdom, while the android of 'Fitter Happier' ('a pig in a cage on antibiotics') and the wished-for alien of 'Subterranean Homesick Alien' dramatize absurd life under others' dictates. Following The Myth of Sisyphus and The Rebel — 'I revolt, therefore we are' — he shows how the songs' 'I' becomes a collective 'we' ('Karma Police', 'Lucky', 'Dollars and Cents') whose revolt, like Sisyphus's conscious walk back down the mountain, affirms life without ever justifying murder. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of expression then explains why the songs are political anyway: artists express a still-unspoken 'fever' (it took years before 'Nude' could be said), creating a public and a common world — politics as unveiling rather than governing, down to 'Electioneering'''s admission that the band too campaigns for our vote.

camus-revolt.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
camus-revolt.title: A Large Rock Saved My Life
camus-revolt.relation: Lindsey Fiorelli reads OK Computer as Camus's absurd universe: "Subterranean Homesick Alien" and "Fitter Happier" portray a technological world drained of meaning, where to belong you must become a robotic "pig in a cage on antibiotics" and "Let Down" offers only the "emptiest of feelings." She stresses that Camus demands revolt, not escape — Sisyphus and Meursault embrace the absurd and thereby become happy — whereas Yorke's lyrics keep longing to flee (spaceships, growing wings, the resigned "No Surprises"). Yet the music itself embraces the technology the lyrics curse, and this, she concludes, is Radiohead's real Camusian move: like Camus writing novels about an alienating world, they carve Sisyphus's rock — modern technology, synthesizers and computers — into new and marvelous sounds, overcoming alienation by working within it.

camus-revolt.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective
camus-revolt.title: Mr. Monk Meets Alexander the Great
camus-revolt.relation: Wittkower argues that Monk's daily, unwinnable war on dirt and disorder is Camus's happy Sisyphus made concrete: Monk vacuums ceilings, touches lampposts, and solves murders knowing the dirt and the murderers will always return ('There's never hope... Hope. I hate hope's guts' in 'Mr. Monk Can't See a Thing'), yet he still finds enough satisfaction to take up the wipe again. Reading Ecclesiastes' vanity alongside the uncaring wasp of the opening, the chapter claims Monk shows us how to live wisely without resignation in an absurd world that does not care. He is paired with Diogenes the Cynic, whose barrel, raw onions, and midday lantern mirror Monk's pot-pie-Tuesdays and his refusal to overlook what everyone else ignores; like Diogenes telling Alexander the Great 'get out of my sun,' Monk lives by his own ideals no matter how society judges him. The essay closes that, like Camus addressing the Dominican monks, we should refuse to 'be reasonable' about evil and disorder and keep struggling without hope, wipe in hand.

camus-revolt.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now
camus-revolt.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
camus-revolt.relation: Rachel Robison-Greene reads the survivors through Camus: walkers are mere digger wasps, living tedious, meaningless loops without the consciousness that would make it agonizing, but the living - Morgan longing for the real Jenny back, Andrea losing Amy - face the absurd confrontation between human longing and an indifferent universe, just like Oran in Camus's The Plague. Of Camus's options, suicide (Jacqui and Dr. Jenner staying in the exploding CDC) and religion ('GOD FORGIVE US' on the farmhouse wall) are escapist, so she offers the absurd hero: Sisyphus with his rock, Rieux with his plague, matched by Rick hunting Atlanta for his family, Merle's self-preservation, and Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side. Against Nagel's ironic alternative, she argues we cheer Rick when he alone will shoot Sophia in Hershel's barn because his subjective commitments stay noble even with no objective meaning behind them.

camus-revolt.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man
camus-revolt.title: The Wire and Philosophy
camus-revolt.relation: Fagan traces the show's ubiquitous 'Game' to Heraclitus's fragment of Aion as a child moving game-pieces: the drug trade, police, docks, schools, and newsroom all have rules, fixed roles (D'Angelo's chess lecture where pawns get capped quick), winning reduced to stats, strife as justice, and cyclical recurrence with 'new dancers, new faces around the throne.' Bodie's dying rant that the game is rigged, the failed escapes of Wallace, D'Angelo, and Stringer's 'games beyond the game,' and even Omar's fatal loyalty to Butchie show that neither rule-following nor Omar-style code-breaking gets a piece off the board. Against critics who call the show nihilistic, he argues it rejects the Heraclitean picture through Camus's rebellion: Colvin, Bubbles, and Cutty fashion dignity by resisting the Game even though rebellion almost certainly fails.

camus-revolt.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
camus-revolt.title: 2. Maybe Jenner Was Right
camus-revolt.relation: Cowan uses Jenner's suicide in the exploding CDC (1.6 'TS-19') to pose Camus's question 'Why should I not commit suicide?', and rejects Jenner's despair the Camusian way: Michonne in 4.9 'After' - slaying her own walker look-alike and then her two pet walkers - is his Sisyphus in revolt, unlike Gareth, whose revolt lacks the respect for human dignity that makes Sisyphus happy. He then objects that Camus never explains why human life has intrinsic dignity in a godless universe, noting that Sartrean authenticity could equally license the Governor's Woodbury experiments or Gareth's cannibalism, and turns to Hershel's providential hope as the religious alternative. Following Plantinga, he argues belief in God can be properly basic through a sensus divinitatis - Hershel seeing God's hand in 2.4 'Cherokee Rose' and the tornado-spared barn of 5.10 'Them' - so if God exists, Jenner was not right.

camus-revolt.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
camus-revolt.title: 10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse
camus-revolt.relation: Heidi Samuelson argues Deadpool is Camus's absurd hero improved: his origin and his survival of impossible dismemberments embody the absurd as 'disproportion between intention and reality', and facing Camus's one real philosophical problem—suicide—he tries to die via the Hulk to join mistress Death yet must live on, rejecting both actual and 'philosophical' suicide (dogma). His mercenary sense of purpose, jokes in the face of oblivion, and compassion for Blind Al, Weasel, deaf Hawkeye, and Evan exemplify Camus's revolt, freedom, and passion. Sisyphus is the model: like him, Deadpool owns his rock—the healing factor and the killing—and is happy, laughing where Sisyphus is silent.

camus-revolt.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
camus-revolt.title: 9. A Human Fighting the Gods
camus-revolt.relation: Luzecky and Elsby argue gods cannot be heroes: Thor's strength, Hulk's rage and Tony's godlike intellect stand outside humanity, whereas Erskine's serum amplified Cap's nascent human goodness (as it exposed the Red Skull's badness), making him the best human rather than a superhuman. Reading Cap through Camus's absurd - the paradox of beings who strive for universality while stuck in particularity - they show him refusing both nihilistic reduction (Alexander Pierce's helicarriers in Winter Soldier) and Nietzsche's flight to 'other worlds' that hates this one. When Loki commands the crowd to kneel, the refusal Cap embodies is Sisyphus's defiant persistence, which is why he, and not the gods, is the Avengers' greatest hero.

camus-revolt.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
camus-revolt.title: 11. Dilbert’s Absurd World
camus-revolt.relation: Christian contrasts Camus's absurdity, the futile collision between our demand for meaning and a silent world whose only exits are suicide, a leap of faith, or Sisyphean revolt (an active defiance he takes partly from Nietzsche's rejection of resignation), with Adams's office absurdities. In Dilbert the absurd is contained and epistemic rather than pervasive and metaphysical: the battery-dead LED request, Dadaist mission statements, Catbert's evil HR policies, Wally's self-congratulatory Wally Reports, and Alice's harpoon all trace to people being idiots about different things, and could be fixed by honest credit and realizable plans. Dilbert's Business Dorky acceptance therefore looks Camusian but is not: it is recognition minus revolt, bewildered amusement where revolt and reform remain genuinely available.

camus-revolt.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
camus-revolt.title: One Must Imagine Ripley Happy
camus-revolt.relation: Reads Ripley-8 through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: discovering the room of failed clones confronts her with the absurd gap between her longing to be Ellen Ripley and the world's answer that she is lab-grown Number 8. Of Camus's three responses she refuses physical suicide (declining Call's knife - 'What makes you think I would let you do that?') and philosophical suicide (mocking the auton's programmed crossing herself in the chapel), instead living in revolt - 'I rebel--therefore we exist' - shared with Call, so that her serial extermination of Xenomorphs across four films becomes Sisyphean toil, and one must imagine Ripley happy.

camus-revolt.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
camus-revolt.title: The Big Lebowski and Philosophy
camus-revolt.relation: Brown and Fosl read the twin Lebowskis as America's post-1960s despair: the Big Lebowski is Kierkegaard's failed Caesar who despairs because he cannot rid himself of the self that did not become Caesar (a fake achiever living on an allowance), while the Dude is the failed leftist whose revolutions collapsed. Against nihilism Walter pulverizes with Nietzschean will, Kierkegaard prescribes the leap of faith, and Camus revolt — but the Dude offers a distinctly American answer, abiding repetition: rolling balls frame after frame like Camus's happy Sisyphus, repeating phrases and roles (Butlerian performativity) so that re-creating himself is his victory over meaninglessness, with No Country for Old Men as the dark twin where nihilism may be winning.

camus-revolt.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
camus-revolt.title: The Walking Dead and Philosophy
camus-revolt.relation: Rachel Robison-Greene applies Camus's absurdity to the series: walkers, like digger wasps, live meaningless loops without the self-reflective consciousness that 'poisons' experience, while survivors like Morgan longing for Jenny and Andrea for fishing trips with her father embody the clash between human longing and an indifferent universe, exactly as in Camus's The Plague at Oran. Suicide (Jacqui and Jenner as the CDC explodes) and religious consolation are escapist responses—the latter 'philosophical suicide'—so the authentic path is the absurd hero: Rick searching Atlanta for his family, Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side, the Vatos group caring for abandoned elders. Weighing Nagel's objection that absurdity arises from our clashing subjective and objective perspectives, she concludes we cheer Rick shooting Sophia in the barn because subjective commitment stays noble even where objective meaning is nowhere to be found.

camus-revolt.title: The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood
camus-revolt.relation: Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.

camus-revolt.title: The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent
camus-revolt.relation: Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.

camus-revolt.title: 24 and the Existential Man of Revolt
camus-revolt.relation: McMahon argues that 24 is genuine TV noir (crime focus, cynical tone, split screens, the femmes fatale Nina Myers and Sherry Palmer, Jack's heroin addiction as his internal demon) and that Jack Bauer is Camus's man of revolt. She lays out Camus's account of the absurd as the confrontation between our appetite for clarity and the world's unreasonable silence, rejects actual and 'philosophical suicide' as evasions, and maps Jack onto the man of revolt's defining traits: lucidity (his refusal to trust appearances, as when only he suspects President Logan of corruption and murder) and courage (risking nerve-gas exposure at CTU and entering the gas-plant fire). The terrorist threats Jack fights symbolize the absurd because their success, from Palmer's assassination to citywide nerve gas, would annihilate order and meaning themselves; as Camus's 'conqueror,' Jack employs violence reluctantly, without appetite for it, to establish non-violence, accepting a crushing fate without resignation.

camus-revolt.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
camus-revolt.title: 22. Punk Rock Saves Lives
camus-revolt.relation: R.W. Main argues punk saves lives by replacing the myth of purity - the ideal behind one-drop rules, eugenics, and moral exclusion - with a philosophy of filth that revalues the rejected and abject, letting the outcast reclaim agency. He stages Diogenes the Cynic's street-living, shameless filth as the original punk counterpoint to Plato's perfect Forms and philosopher-king (Plato the 'sell-out'), and enlists Nietzsche's claims that morality denies life while art saves it. Camus's Sisyphus closes the argument: punk's freedom is revolt, giving the gods the middle finger since 'there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn'; more concretely, punks save lives as anti-bullies, the 'Duncan Effect' of Some Kind of Wonderful and SHARPS skinheads protecting misfits.

camus-revolt.title: Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil
camus-revolt.relation: James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.

freud-civilization.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
freud-civilization.relation: Pratt reads the outlaw biker's FTW (Fuck the World) posture as pop-culture nihilism: Nietzsche's 'danger of dangers' and Camus's answer of scorn to an absurd universe ('there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn') are embodied by Brando's Johnny in The Wild One, Sonny Barger's Hells Angels, and the wanton Born to Lose club of The Born Losers, whose smashing matches Pisarev's Russian nihilism. He then shows how Willie G. Davidson's 1977 Low Rider and events like Daytona's Bike Week sanitized and marketed the rebellion, reducing skulls and DILLIGAF patches to ubiquitous fashion worth $340 million a week. Freud supplies the psychology: the superego keeps the rest of us tame, so we voyeuristically buy a tasteful version of outlaw freedom, even though pure nihilism, denying all truth, refutes even itself.

freud-civilization.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
freud-civilization.title: The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization
freud-civilization.relation: Simon Clark reads Romero's four Dead films through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the zombie is the return of the repressed, the ripped-out instinctual life of a civilization that demands work, and it multiplies exactly as humans (Stephen defending the mall, Ben fighting Mr. Cooper) lapse into unlawful self-gratification. The bite unites Eros and Thanatos - an erotic, engorged cannibalism that also regresses victims to rotting matter, which Clark glosses with Creed's vagina dentata. He then argues Day of the Dead's beach ending (John fishing, Sarah at peace) stages Marcuse's non-repressive civilization where work becomes play and liberated sexuality rejoins Eros, while Land of the Dead goes further: the evolved, tool-using zombies led by Big Daddy are the martyrs who actually found Marcuse's impossible pleasurable community, leaving living humans still fenced inside repression.

freud-civilization.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
freud-civilization.title: The Devil and Philosophy
freud-civilization.relation: Robert Arp's introduction opens with Halloween culture and his own seminarian past to ask whether belief in the Devil can survive scrutiny. He lays out a 'just deserts' argument - Hitler, Stalin, and Mao died unpunished while Job, Socrates, and Thomas More died unrewarded, so God, the Devil, Heaven, and Hell must exist to balance the scales - and then answers it with Freud's projection critique (religion as wishful thinking for comfort and moral control) and with the neuroscience tying the mind to a dying brain, which undermines the soul that Hell would punish. The chapter frames the whole book's project: testing devil-belief with arguments and evidence rather than taking it on authority.

freud-civilization.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
freud-civilization.title: Dracula and Philosophy
freud-civilization.relation: Pötzsch reads Dracula through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the Count fascinates because he lives out the aggression and sexual freedom civilization forces us to renounce, embodying the innate hostility in Freud's 'man is the wolf to man.' Freud's account - group power replacing individual might, 'love thy neighbor' as an impossible demand, the super-ego as an inner Van Helsing breeding guilt over forbidden impulses, with the id and ego mediating - is mapped onto Jonathan's 'wicked, burning desire' for the vampire women. The upshot: we resent culture because we traded happiness for security, yet living like Dracula would get our throats cut.

freud-civilization.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed
freud-civilization.title: It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy
freud-civilization.relation: Daniel Leonard takes CharDee MacDennis, the Gang's three-level drinking game, as an unconscious confession read through Freud's structural model. The 'Mind' level - grudge trivia like 'Denis is asshole. Why Charlie hate?' and drawing-guessing 'based solely on feel' - runs on the id and the pleasure principle; the 'Body' level of darts, kennels, and the no-cursing rule is restraint, properly the ego's job of deferring gratification (which only Dennis's manipulative D.E.N.N.I.S. System grotesquely exercises); and the 'Spirit' level of Emotional Battery and Public Humiliation externalizes the superego's guilt and ego-ideal, with Frank as the all-seeing punishing father. The Gang's psychology is backwards - their 'Mind' level tests exactly what is not conscious - and their over-strong superegos surface in rationalization and the Black Card's coin flip, while smashing the losers' idealized game pieces enacts a wishful symbolic patricide.

freud-civilization.title: 11. When Cruelty Is Not Enough
freud-civilization.relation: Conway argues the real horror of 1984 is not the torture chamber but O'Brien's worldmaking: he cultivated Winston and Julia's affair from lust into a hopeful little home precisely so that destroying it, and hope itself, the Party's true enemy, would be total. Against Rorty's influential reading of O'Brien as a torturer who breaks Winston for pleasure, Conway adds two amendments: Arendt's thoughtless technocrat, with O'Brien as an Eichmann figure whose Party affirms his competence and insulates him from rebuke, and Horkheimer and Adorno's warning that technical rationality has become a secular religion whose 'priests of power' sanctify cruelty. The result is a portrait of a warm-blooded, situationally sympathetic sadist who genuinely excels at building the selves and worlds he is then charged to dismantle.

freud-civilization.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
freud-civilization.title: NOTES
freud-civilization.relation: Hirschbein presents True Blood as a Freudian fable: vampires live the unrepressed id's Eros and Thanatos that civilization forces the rest of us to renounce, which is why they defeat all three sources of suffering (mortal bodies, nature, hostile neighbors) and why the show's convulsive sex and violence thrill us. Glamouring reproduces the posthypnotic suggestion that proved the unconscious to Freud, Sookie's mind-reading confirms his dark discoveries about our sexualized aggression, vampire myths work as projection screens for desires we disown, and Marcuse's complaint about 'genital tyranny' and sublimation frames Sookie's love as a near-realization of Freud's St. Francis ideal.

freud-civilization.book: 281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_
freud-civilization.title: Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone
freud-civilization.relation: Clack's 'Cannabis and the Human Condition' reads intoxication through Freud's Civilization and its Discontents, where drugs are the 'crudest but most effective' palliative against a life 'too hard for us,' tied to the pleasure principle and the Nirvana/death-instinct drive to discharge stimulus. He supplements Freud with Schopenhauer's pessimism — life oscillating between suffering and boredom — to add 'stimulus hunger' Freud ignored, arguing cannabis both dampens and stokes the 'fire in the brain' depending on THC potency (high vs. stoned). He concludes that, like religion, art and love, cannabis augments a bleak existence, so 'all cannabis use is medicinal.'

freud-civilization.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing
freud-civilization.title: SERIAL KILLERS
freud-civilization.relation: Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.

freud-civilization.book: 287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low
freud-civilization.title: BLUES
freud-civilization.relation: Ben and Owen Flanagan ask why people seek out 'anguished art,' comparing the blues to Aristotelian tragedy. They argue the blues protagonist, unlike the doomed tragic hero, survives — and his downfall comes from ordinary personal choices (wanderlust, whiskey, the wrong woman) rather than fated conflicts of duty, making imaginative identification easier for a plebeian audience. Aristotle's catharsis of pity and fear is broadened by Freud's account of sublimation and release of repressed sexual and aggressive drives; Robert Johnson's 'Love in Vain' and Muddy Waters' 'Five Long Years' are read as Sisyphean (Camus) images of loving and losing, so the blues offers beauty, release, and shared humanity by being more 'real' than happy pop.

standard-of-taste.title: Harley-Davidson and Philosophy
standard-of-taste.relation: Bourne argues that bikes like the Ducati 916 and Harley V-Rod are genuine works of art: Kantian disinterested attention is both possible and actual (he bought his Ducati Monster on styling alone), and Hume's standard of taste shows that judgments like calling a Honda Gold Wing elegant are answerable to criteria and informed comparison, so taste is not mere subjectivity. Against Wollheim he deploys Currie's account of the artwork as a type of action, so mass-produced instances are no obstacle, exactly as copies of Sartre's Nausea are the same novel; against Danto's aboutness requirement he claims motorcycles are about motorcycles, and should be evaluated like architecture, where function enters the aesthetic judgment. On Bauhaus principles the Ducati 916 expresses its own construction authentically while the V-Rod's styling compromises its ground clearance, which is what makes the Ducati, at least, high art.

standard-of-taste.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
standard-of-taste.title: 1. Arya Stark as a Rough Hero
standard-of-taste.relation: Dadlez asks whether Game of Thrones is morally defective for making audiences root for Arya Stark, a child murderer whose victims run from the insurance seller in Braavos to Walder Frey and his sons baked into a pie. Working through Hume's 'rough heroes' worry from 'Of the Standard of Taste' against Anne Eaton's 'robust immoralism' and the halo effect, she argues Martin's text never endorses Arya's killings but shows their cost to her - her suppression of doubt before the soup-shop assassination, her nightmare repetition of the names on her kill list, her reclaiming of 'Arya Stark of Winterfell' - so our investment is empathetic concern rather than corrupting approval, and the story is not ethically flawed.

standard-of-taste.title: 12. Putting the Fun Back in Non-refundable
standard-of-taste.relation: Defends Snatched against its 37 percent Rotten Tomatoes score by retracing art criticism from Plato's claim, grounded in his theory of copies and originals, that art is an inferior imitation of reality, to Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste', where value judgments track social values and refined experts may devalue works that offend their morals. Against moralistic critics, the chapter argues some art, like Guernica or 'Football Town Nights', exists to upset us. It then reads the film through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Emily's guilt-free firing scene and her cajoling her deflated mother toward Ecuador enact the refusal of socially manufactured guilt, putting the 'fun' back in non-refundable.

standard-of-taste.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough
standard-of-taste.title: Final Fantasy and Philosophy
standard-of-taste.relation: Alex Nuttall applies Hume's essay on the standard of taste to video games as art: beauty is not in objects (Sin's FFX rendering is just digital information) but in trained sentiment, yet quality differences are real, as the gap between Final Fantasy VII and the broken Superman 64 shows. Using the Malboro's Bad Breath as a metaphor for the confused, blinded, charmed state of novice judges, he lays out Hume's remedies of practice, repeated viewing, comparison, and reason against bias, and defends Hume against the circularity charge that good judges and masterpieces like FFVII define each other.

hume-miracles.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
hume-miracles.title: “Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism
hume-miracles.relation: Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.

hume-miracles.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
hume-miracles.title: The Epilogue A Question of Belief
hume-miracles.relation: Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'

hume-miracles.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
hume-miracles.title: What of Philosophical Relevance Is there in Tarantino’s Films
hume-miracles.relation: Bruce Russell argues that Tarantino's films share a pattern—a cruel man's life goes awry, violence erupts, and glimpses of compassion appear, like Mr. White comforting the shot Mr. Orange—but that fiction can raise philosophical questions without justifying general philosophical theses. He uses the Pulp Fiction exchange over the bullets that missed Jules and Vincent to raise Hume's problem of miracles (divine intervention versus a 'freak occurrence'), and applies the accounts of Mill, Gibbard, Hare and Hume to show that even Vincent's twisted code—balcony drops for foot massages, execution for keying a car—counts as having a morality. His conclusion: the films raise, but never answer in depth, the questions of what a miracle is and what it is to have a morality.

hume-miracles.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch
hume-miracles.title: Zed Is Dead
hume-miracles.relation: Keith Korcz applies Hume's 'Of Miracles' to Jules's survival of the hand cannon: a genuine miracle would suspend a law of nature, but as Vincent says, 'It's a freak, it happens'—and the testimony establishing laws of nature always outweighs miracle reports, while lucky coincidences (cats surviving four-story falls) are selectively reported. He answers objections from revised laws of nature (the 1919 eclipse confirming general relativity) and from prior belief in a miracle-working god, concluding with Hume that a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence. Jules's transformation is real, but would occur regardless of whether his belief in the miracle is true.

hume-miracles.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game
hume-miracles.title: Added Time
hume-miracles.relation: McDermid takes Maradona's cheeky 'a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God' claim literally and asks what would make either 1986 goal against England—the obvious handball or the Goal of the Century—a miracle, using Aquinas's definition of miracles as intentional divine acts beyond the order commonly observed in nature. He explores how God could intervene without breaking natural law, analogizing God to a goalkeeper exempt from the handball rule or a spectator outside the game: in a deterministic world He could only arrange initial conditions (a domino setup requiring fine-tuning at the Big Bang), while in an indeterministic quantum world He could load the chancy micro-events along Maradona's mazy, sensitively balanced run. Hume's empiricist argument against miracles then shows we could never be justified in believing either goal miraculous, since the mundane explanation—Maradona's cheek and skill, lapses of concentration, a missed handball call—always has the whole of past experience on its side.

hume-miracles.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
hume-miracles.title: The Epistemology of Deception
hume-miracles.relation: Shifts from the ethics of deception (Kant's near-absolute condemnation of lying versus Plato's morally justified governmental lies) to its epistemology, defining deception as intentionally causing a false belief. This definition explains why Cohaagen deceives Quaid, who falsely believes he is a construction worker, while Rekall cannot deceive the Quaid who really is a secret agent, and why the Zoner Cale merely misleads Spencer Olham in Impostor without deceiving him — with Hume's reasoning about miracle testimony modeling when to believe a probable deceiver.

hume-miracles.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
hume-miracles.title: The Devil and Philosophy
hume-miracles.relation: The Bocks use the courtroom frame of The Exorcism of Emily Rose to ask whether anyone could be justified in believing in demon possession, since the same seizures, polyglot voices, and levitations read differently under naturalism and supernaturalism. Kuhn's paradigms explain why neither worldview abandons ship at anomalies, and they weigh Wiebe's 'finite spirits as theoretical entities,' Hume's miracles argument (with Levine's Red Sea thought experiment as rebuttal), and the Cartesian ghost-in-the-machine premise that possession would require. Testing even a Men in Black alien hypothesis against the religiously specific phenomena, they conclude that a witnessed case like Emily's could rationally justify belief in possession.

hume-miracles.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
hume-miracles.title: 1. True Love and False Fronts
hume-miracles.relation: Fallis argues the movie is really about lying and duplicity, not true love: Humperdinck frames Guilder for Buttercup's abduction, the Dread Pirate Roberts is a serial persona, and even the heroes bluff their way into the castle. He treats this as 'adversarial epistemology,' showing that Descartes's malicious demon and Kant's argument that universalized lying is impossible only rule out extreme scenarios and cannot unmask mundane deceivers like Vizzini and Humperdinck (a point he sharpens with Parfit's objection that liars sometimes profitably tell the truth). What does real work are Hume's tools for evaluating testimony: Valerie catches Miracle Max lying about 'to blave' by asking what he has to gain, and Buttercup catches Humperdinck when his claim that every ship in the armada will accompany the honeymoon contradicts his promise of the four fastest ships.

hume-miracles.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
hume-miracles.title: 15. It Would Take a Miracle!
hume-miracles.relation: Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.

hume-miracles.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
hume-miracles.title: 11. The Truth about Lying
hume-miracles.relation: Fallis reads the series through the philosophy of testimony: TZ relentlessly punishes both truth-tellers (Bob Wilson's gremlin warning and nine more episodes) and liars ('Hocus-Pocus and Frisby,' 'The Four of Us Are Dying'), while Kant's letter on reticence suggests the untried third option of keeping quiet. On the receiving side, Hume's rules for discounting witnesses and his argument that one should never believe miracle reports explain why the crew disbelieves the gremlin and why 'Printer's Devil's' Devil reasons like Hume, Descartes' malicious demon returns in the disguised devils of 'The Hunt' and 'The Howling Man,' and the chapter ends endorsing Pascal's Wager: 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' argues we should believe even crazy, lying testimony just in case it is true.

hume-miracles.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way
hume-miracles.title: a14.xhtml
hume-miracles.relation: Stewart argues Middle-earth magic is rule-bound engineering rather than Hume's miracle as 'a violation of the laws of nature': spells fail, the Ring hides neither shadow nor wet footprints, and magic comes in strengths like gravity, so fear of Gandalf is fear of superior knowledge of nature's laws, not of lawlessness. The deeper point is Tolkien's linkage of magic with technology as the impatient will to make one's will effective quickly - Sauron is 'Lord of magic and machines', the Ring is the supreme technological artifact, Saruman's forged men and blast-fires embody domination - while elvish 'Art' is sub-creation and Beorn's communion with animals models harmony with nature. Like Thoreau pricing possessions in 'how much life' they cost, the chapter ends with Tolkien's warning that 'if a thing can be done, it should be done' is the great false assumption of our age.

hume-miracles.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!
hume-miracles.title: THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY
hume-miracles.relation: Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.

hume-miracles.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
hume-miracles.title: Notes
hume-miracles.relation: Asks whether Han Solo's 'hokey religions' dismissal of the Force is unreasonable given his evidence, answering no: Hume's argument against miracles explains why testimony of lightsaber tricks and mind tricks should not overturn Han's experience of consistent natural law, while Hume's problem of induction and custom/habit explain why both Han's 'luck' verdict and Obi-Wan's 'no such thing as luck' are habit-based generalizations. Peirce's fallibilism (backed by Putnam's 'fallibilism does not entail skepticism') lets Han and Obi-Wan each claim knowledge without certainty, echoing Obi-Wan's line that many truths depend greatly on our own point of view.

hume-miracles.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
hume-miracles.title: 11. The Truth about Lying
hume-miracles.relation: Fallis treats the Zone as a seminar in the philosophy of testimony: truth-tellers like Bob Wilson warning of a gremlin get dismissed as insane ('The Whole Truth' forces truth-telling as a curse), while convincing liars like Arch Hammer come to bad ends, so Kant's letter recommending reticence, saying true things but not the whole truth, looks like the best policy. On the receiving end, Descartes's malicious demon returns as aliens and devils ('To Serve Man,' 'The Howling Man,' 'Printer's Devil'), and Hume's advice to reject miracle-like testimony fails because in the Zone crazy stuff is often true. The chapter ends by endorsing Pascal's wager through 'The Big Tall Wish' and Jeff Myrtlebank's threat: believe the incredible witness just in case.

hume-miracles.book: 229 - The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes
hume-miracles.title: Eliminating the Impossible Sherlock Holmes and the Supernatural
hume-miracles.relation: Blanchette uses the Guy Ritchie film's Lord Blackwood 'resurrection' and 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' to ask whether a supernatural explanation is ever admissible. Drawing on Draper's definition of nature vs. the supernatural, Plantinga's natural-vs-logical necessity distinction, and Hume on miracles, he argues miracles are naturally impossible but not logically impossible unless nature is proven a closed system. He defends a truth-aimed methodology (pursue natural causes until the best explanation of failure is that none exists), showing Holmes rightly debunks both cases while thought experiments reveal conditions under which a supernatural verdict would become the rational inference.

hume-miracles.book: 261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone
hume-miracles.title: 11. The Truth about Lying
hume-miracles.relation: Fallis treats the Twilight Zone as a workbook in the philosophy of testimony (the ethics and epistemology of communication). Truth-tellers get dismissed as insane ('Nightmare at 20,000 Feet') while liars come to bad ends even when believed ('The Four of Us Are Dying'); Kant's reticence offers a third option to truth-telling and lying. On receiving testimony, he uses Hume on evaluating witnesses and disbelieving reports of miracles, then argues the show endorses Pascal's Wager—believe crazy testimony just in case—citing 'The Last Rites of Jeff Myrtlebank' and 'Mr. Garrity and the Graves,' plus Descartes's deceiving demon for the show's alien and devil deceivers.

hume-miracles.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
hume-miracles.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
hume-miracles.relation: Jurgensen and Southworth apply Hume's argument against miracles to the virgin birth, treating it as a claimed violation of the natural law that virgins do not conceive. They attack the credibility of the only witnesses, Matthew and Luke, noting their third-hand sources (Mark, Q, L/M), their contradiction over whether Mary and Joseph were married, and the mistranslation of Isaiah's ambiguous 'almah' as the Greek 'parthenos' (literal virgin). Invoking Hume's four defects of miracle testimony and his maxim that no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event, they conclude a rational person must reject the Christmas miracle.

hume-miracles.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
hume-miracles.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
hume-miracles.relation: Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.

hume-miracles.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
hume-miracles.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
hume-miracles.relation: Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.

hume-miracles.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom
hume-miracles.title: GARDENING
hume-miracles.relation: O'Brien reads Voltaire's closing injunction in Candide, 'we must cultivate our garden,' through David Hume to argue that gardening is therapy—a retreat from metaphysics and religion into the tranquility of common life. Hume rejects belief in miracles and religious 'enthusiasm' not by logic but by recalling everyday reasoning (a melon seed, not a miracle, explains melons in the greenhouse), and the gardener is the sophisticated artisan-reasoner attuned to nature's regularities. Gardening inculcates Humean virtues (industry, patience, balancing action, pleasure and indolence) and Haybron's attunement/engagement/endorsement, yielding Epicurean ataraxia; the Sisyphean gardener (Camus) fighting slugs, and Wittgenstein taking up gardening as a cure, illustrate the point.

hume-miracles.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
hume-miracles.title: 26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion
hume-miracles.relation: The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.

thomson-violinist.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
thomson-violinist.title: Suppose You Were Attached to a Dead Parrot The Role of Thought Experiments
thomson-violinist.relation: Takes the Argument Clinic sketch — Mr. Vibrating's pure contradiction versus the customer's demand for 'a connected series of statements intended to establish a proposition' — to argue that paying for good argument is not absurd, because only sustained argument with others gets most of us true beliefs about complex matters. It explains Rawls's method of reflective equilibrium (testing general principles against considered judgments about cases, illustrated by the author's Rimbaud/Rambo censorship blunder) and Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment, showing how such experiments force us to abandon groundless reasons: opponents of abortion who let the violinist go must find grounds other than the fetus's right to life. Good thought experiments, it closes, work like good Python sketches — the Dead Parrot sketch's internally logical absurdity — so a real argument clinic would serve a genuine social function, since interlocutors expose biases that solitary reflection cannot.

thomson-violinist.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
thomson-violinist.title: So, What Have Philosophers Ever Done for Us
thomson-violinist.relation: Taylor defends philosophy's bizarre examples against critics like Leon Kass by comparing them to Python's self-reflexive comedy: the 'Complaints' sketch's regress of complaints-about-complaints mirrors how thought experiments make us the audience of our own thinking, as with two coalmine trolley cases that pressure a simple 'minimize pain' utilitarianism toward rule utilitarianism. The 'Police Station' sketch, where it would be better if mad Angus's carnivorous-blancmange story were false, is itself a counterexample to 'always tell the police the truth', and 'The Visitors' stale three-year-old drink invitation undermines the claim that 'inviting in' a fetus creates duties, sharpening Thomson's violinist argument that a right to life does not include a right to another's body. Singer's drowning-child style example and Thomson's violinist show that far-fetched cases clarify practical issues like abortion and famine relief precisely by detaching them from clouding emotion, and the Life of Brian 'What have the Romans ever done for us?' scene supplies the answer: philosophers' examples clarify our views, test them, and are amusing.

thomson-violinist.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
thomson-violinist.title: 22. Lady Edith and the Trials of the Modern Woman
thomson-violinist.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Lady Edith's last-minute walk-out from the abortion clinic to stage the abortion debate: the classic anti-abortion syllogism, embryology's claim that 'Marigold once was an embryo,' and Mary Anne Warren's functional personhood criteria - echoed in Thomas's 'no bigger than a hamster' jab - which Tooley and Singer extend to infanticide on newborn George. Against the function view the chapter marshals the comatose Matthew and the sleeping Alfred, arguing that value lies in the kind of being one is, while size, development, environment, and dependency make no moral difference. It then adapts Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist as Edith hooked up to Dame Nellie Melba, but replies that abortion kills rather than unplugs and that the Law of Special Beneficence - Major Bryant's duty to Ethel's Charlie - obliges Edith toward her own child.

thomson-violinist.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
thomson-violinist.title: 22. Lady Edith and the Trials of the Modern Woman
thomson-violinist.relation: Gordon Hawkes uses Lady Edith's last-minute walk-out from the abortion clinic (4:7) to run the full philosophical abortion debate. He lays out the classic anti-abortion argument and the biological-continuity case that 'Marigold once was an embryo,' then presents Mary Anne Warren's functional personhood criteria, which - as with Singer and Tooley on infanticide - would deny rights even to newborn George, a consequence he rejects via the comatose Matthew and the sleeping Alfred's retained capacities. Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist argument is recast as Edith waking back-to-back with the ailing Dame Nellie Melba, and he answers it with the Law of Special Beneficence: if the feckless Major Bryant owes support to the child he never wanted, Edith owes at least as much to her own flesh and blood.

thomson-violinist.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom
thomson-violinist.title: MOTHERHOOD
thomson-violinist.relation: Bertha Alvarez Manninen reconciles her deepened respect for fetal life (after seeing her daughter on ultrasound) with a pro-choice stance by deploying Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment and the real McFall v. Shimp bodily-integrity ruling. She argues that even granting the fetus full personhood, no one's right to life entitles them to another's body, buttressing this with Kant's formula of humanity that a woman must not be reduced to a mere incubating means, and calls for American mizuko-kuyo-style grieving rituals so 'pro-choice' is not conflated with 'pro-abortion.'

bergson-laughter.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
bergson-laughter.title: Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)
bergson-laughter.relation: Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.

bergson-laughter.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
bergson-laughter.title: The Meta-Fear of Fear
bergson-laughter.relation: Noel Carroll traces Halloween's Undead imagery to the Celtic Samhain and its Catholic absorption into All Hallows' Eve, then asks the paradox: why do we take pleasure in images of the death that, as Heidegger says, is the deep source of Angst we spend our lives denying? He examines Ernest Jones's Freudian analysis - the vampire as wish-fulfillment disguising an incestuous desire, horror as the price the super-ego exacts - and rejects it as theoretically expensive, invoking the demand for simpler, more economical explanation. His own hypothesis is the 'meta-fear of fear': adolescent viewers (and aging ones) use horror films and the holiday's zombie costumes to test and master fear itself, with parody and Bergson's laughter as companion devices of emotional control - a folk remedy that needs no unconscious to work.

bergson-laughter.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead
bergson-laughter.title: The Meta-Fear of Fear
bergson-laughter.relation: Noël Carroll reconstructs Halloween's Undead iconography from the Celtic Samhain and Pope Gregory's absorption of it into All Hallows' Eve, then poses the paradox that people pay to be terrified by corpse imagery they would flee in a real morgue — odd, given Heidegger's point that the Angst of death is so deep we spend our lives denying it. He tests Ernest Jones's Freudian reading of the nightmare — the vampire revenant as a disguised, disavowed incest wish — and rejects it as a Rube-Goldberg apparatus requiring universal incestuous desire and the whole machinery of the unconscious, when sometimes a zombie is just a zombie and The Fog is simply frightening. His own hypothesis: horror films and Halloween give viewers, especially anxious adolescents, a controlled trial run of fear that eases the meta-fear of fear itself, with Bergson's 'anaesthesis of the heart' explaining why Halloween parody and laughter serve the same emotional-control function as the scares.

bergson-laughter.title: 13. Hangings, Shootings, and Other Funny Stuff in 1984
bergson-laughter.relation: Hietalahti combines Kierkegaard's thesis that the comic lies in contradiction, Plato's warning that laughter is malicious and must be chained by law, and Bergson's account of laughter as social punishment to explain Oceania's humor: the cinema audience laughs at refugees being machine-gunned, citizens clamor for public hangings, and the barroom joke about living in treetops humiliates the old man, because shared fear and hatred set the norms of what counts as funny. Doublethink explains why slogans like 'War is peace' provoke no laughter in Oceania, and the Ministry of Truth's amusement industry shows the Party deliberately weaponizes fun. The upshot is reflexive: Orwell indicts our own unexamined sense of humor, including the slogan that everything may be ridiculed, not merely Oceania's.

bergson-laughter.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
bergson-laughter.title: 4. Is It Immoral to Read Someone to Filth
bergson-laughter.relation: Birnie stages Alexis Michelle's hurt at the Season 9 body-shaming reads against Bianca Del Rio's 'rolodex of hate' to ask whether reading is immoral. He surveys the philosophical ethics of humor — Plato's Philebus on laughter as malicious delight in others' self-ignorance, Hobbes's 'sudden glory', Schopenhauer on why ridicule hurts, the Stoics' ideal of never laughing, Aristotle's eutrapelia as the golden mean between vulgar buffoon and boor, the Spencer–Freud relief theory, and Bergson's laughter as society's corrective — before endorsing the play theory: reads are consensual mock-aggression, verbal sport honed by marginalized black and Latinx ball culture. From this he derives three guidelines (play signals and consent, timing and audience given the show's younger mainstream viewers, openness to challenge) and concludes Katya's bus-stop read of Roxxxy was acceptable while stereotype reads need care.

bergson-laughter.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
bergson-laughter.title: 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny
bergson-laughter.relation: Pavelich asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny, answering with incongruity theory and Bergson's view of comedy as social punishment, seen in Tahani paired with a silent monk and Michael failing 802 reboots. The centerpiece is 'The Trolley Problem': Michael drops Chidi into Foot's thought experiment so Chidi becomes the instrument of his own agony, and by Bernard Williams's principle the real wrongdoer is Michael, who set up the situation. Eternal torture works as comedy only because everyday crappiness is watched on a twenty-two-minute scale, and Eleanor's forgiveness of Michael after seeing the tortures in Janet's VR makes her the show's real moral hero.

bergson-laughter.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
bergson-laughter.title: 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny
bergson-laughter.relation: Asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny and answers with incongruity theory (circus music under Michael's dejection; a comedy set in Hell) plus Bergson's view of comedy as social correction that deflates those who deserve it — Tahani's name-dropping, Michael failing 802 reboots. It centers on 'The Trolley Problem': Michael teleporting Chidi's ethics lesson into real runaway trolleys ('not real, but the pain is') is both incongruous humor and genuine torture, and invoking Bernard Williams shows the real wrongdoer is Michael, who rigged the situation, not Chidi who must choose. Eternal torture, it concludes, only works as endless low-grade everyday crappiness, which is comic in twenty-two-minute doses — and Eleanor's twice-given forgiveness of Michael, after seeing the centuries of torture in Janet's VR device, is the show's real moral marvel.

bergson-laughter.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life
bergson-laughter.title: The Office and Philosophy
bergson-laughter.relation: Against Hobbes's view that laughter expresses superiority and Bergson's that comedy humiliates the socially disruptive into conformity, argues that viewers of The Office feel humiliation 'by proxy': Michael Scott is immune to humiliation because his narcissism blocks the minimal condition for feeling it - recognizing he could do wrong (Prison Mike, his MLK name tag while stereotyping Kelly, reneging on the pledge to Oscar's nephew, Carol's rejection at Diwali). We blush, look away, and feel his shame in his place, which transforms neither Michael nor us but reaffirms our own decency, compassion, and grip on values like self-awareness - and the chapter answers the worry that this merely endorses 'Hollywood' values by noting the standards Michael violates (moral sight, honesty with oneself) cross value systems.

bergson-laughter.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry
bergson-laughter.title: Spider-Man and Philosophy
bergson-laughter.relation: Malloy asks why Spider-Man jokes while fighting for his life. After surveying the superiority theory (Plato, Hobbes's 'sudden glory'), Kant's incongruity theory, and Freud's relief theory, he adapts F. H. Buckley's moral-superiority account: Spidey's quips at the Vulture's boasting, Doc Ock's mercilessness, Kingpin's girth, and J. Jonah Jameson's sourness are moral corrections meant to goad their butts toward the virtues they lack. Aristotle's buffoon/wit distinction saves Spidey from vulgarity — he can be serious after Gwen Stacy's death — and his teasing of allies like the Thing and Captain America teaches social virtues, though the jokes rarely reform anyone.

bergson-laughter.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers
bergson-laughter.title: Philosophies of Comedy in O Brother, Where Art Thou
bergson-laughter.relation: McFarland explains the comedy of O Brother through Bergson's 'mechanical encrusted on the living' (the chain-gang pratfall where McGill forgets he is shackled, the toon-like plasticity of the escapees) and Kierkegaard's account of the comic as unresolved contradiction, like men bustling on a sinking ship. He argues the Klan-rally set piece refuses Jamesonian 'pastiche' by grounding its Wizard-of-Oz and Odyssey allusions in real historical guilt, forcing the postmodern aesthete-viewer, as in Kierkegaard's Either/Or, from the aesthetic to the ethical stage. The subverted ending—Penny rejecting the non-bona-fide ring—enacts Kierkegaard's view that marriage is comic because it 'binds' time and acknowledges contradiction rather than resolving it.

bergson-laughter.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bergson-laughter.title: 17. Last Week Tonight as Philosophy The Importance of Jokalism
bergson-laughter.relation: The chapter coins 'jokalism' to categorize Last Week Tonight with John Oliver as a new satire paradigm that fuses investigative journalism, fact-checking, and calls to action with comedy. It grounds this in the philosophy of humor—Plato's and Aristotle's suspicion of laughter and the 'superiority theory' running through Hobbes, Freud, and Bergson—and links satire to moral philosophy via the gap between ideal and actual politics. Using Oliver's segments on net neutrality, the death penalty, and the Equal Rights Amendment, it shows how the show builds a philosophical argument (problem, ideal, remedy) that provokes real-world change like the FCC website crash, arguing jokalism boosts critical thinking rather than mere infotainment.

bergson-laughter.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
bergson-laughter.title: 69. Larry David as Philosopher Interrogating Convention
bergson-laughter.relation: Carroll treats Curb Your Enthusiasm as a Kantian/Marxian 'critique'—an inquiry into the conditions of possibility—of everyday norms of civility, built on incongruity humor and Mary Douglas's theory of jokes as 'anti-rites.' Through episodes like the handicapped-stutterer, the new-house tour Larry refuses, the phone-call cutoff time, Ben Stiller's no-gifts party, and the buried five-wood, David shows that manners are non-necessary and arbitrary yet held in place only by intense (uncurbed) emotional 'enthusiasm,' epitomized by Susie Greene's operatic rage. Carroll answers the analytic skeptic by casting David's method as Socratic/maieutic (like Plato's Meno): the argument is completed in the reflective viewer's mind.

trolley-problem.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
trolley-problem.title: So, What Have Philosophers Ever Done for Us
trolley-problem.relation: Taylor defends philosophy's bizarre examples against critics like Leon Kass by comparing them to Python's self-reflexive comedy: the 'Complaints' sketch's regress of complaints-about-complaints mirrors how thought experiments make us the audience of our own thinking, as with two coalmine trolley cases that pressure a simple 'minimize pain' utilitarianism toward rule utilitarianism. The 'Police Station' sketch, where it would be better if mad Angus's carnivorous-blancmange story were false, is itself a counterexample to 'always tell the police the truth', and 'The Visitors' stale three-year-old drink invitation undermines the claim that 'inviting in' a fetus creates duties, sharpening Thomson's violinist argument that a right to life does not include a right to another's body. Singer's drowning-child style example and Thomson's violinist show that far-fetched cases clarify practical issues like abortion and famine relief precisely by detaching them from clouding emotion, and the Life of Brian 'What have the Romans ever done for us?' scene supplies the answer: philosophers' examples clarify our views, test them, and are amusing.

trolley-problem.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
trolley-problem.title: Introduction
trolley-problem.relation: Frames Part V's ethics chapters. Adams' chapter updates Plato's ring of Gyges for Heroes — with Claire's and Sylar's powers, why be moral? — answered by the properly ordered tripartite soul; McAleer's uses The Office to illustrate Aristotle's wit as a mean between buffoonery and boorishness; White's uses the Batman/Joker problem and a Bat-trolley version of Foot's case to argue deontologically that Batman need not kill the Joker; and Loftis' reads Watchmen's Ozymandias and Rorschach as a failed utilitarian and a failed deontologist, pointing to 'who watches the watchmen.'

trolley-problem.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating
trolley-problem.title: So, Case Closed – Right
trolley-problem.relation: White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.

trolley-problem.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
trolley-problem.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
trolley-problem.relation: Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. could only get a compassionate child to commit xenocide by presenting war as a game, a framing that neutralizes moral agency just as Milgram's shock experiments and the fake game show The Game of Death did. Using Sunzi's 'know your enemy' to frame the empathy paradox, Walzer's problem of dirty hands for Graff's lesser-evil choices, and Foot's trolley problem alongside drone 'Nintendo warfare' to show how distance makes killing easier, he concludes Ender was likely a willing pawn who let himself be deceived because he endorsed the war's survivalist goal.

trolley-problem.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
trolley-problem.title: 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny
trolley-problem.relation: Pavelich asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny, answering with incongruity theory and Bergson's view of comedy as social punishment, seen in Tahani paired with a silent monk and Michael failing 802 reboots. The centerpiece is 'The Trolley Problem': Michael drops Chidi into Foot's thought experiment so Chidi becomes the instrument of his own agony, and by Bernard Williams's principle the real wrongdoer is Michael, who set up the situation. Eternal torture works as comedy only because everyday crappiness is watched on a twenty-two-minute scale, and Eleanor's forgiveness of Michael after seeing the tortures in Janet's VR makes her the show's real moral hero.

trolley-problem.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
trolley-problem.title: 11. Those Agonizing Choices
trolley-problem.relation: Romanowski traces Chidi's indecision from the cowboy-boots lie through the rock-paper-scissors panic attack, arguing the show treats the agony of deciding as the universal human moral condition rather than a professor joke. 'The Trolley Problem' makes Foot's dilemma literal torture, and the show pointedly never gives the right answer, confirming Chidi's claim that there are no clean solutions to hard moral questions. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired particularism pitch in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' and Michael's 'I solved the Trolley Problem: you sacrifice yourself' moment, together with Chidi finally kissing Eleanor, show that acknowledging uncertainty is no excuse for inaction.

trolley-problem.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
trolley-problem.title: 14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors
trolley-problem.relation: Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man. Tahani's sixty billion dollars in charity earning no points, and Eleanor's fruitless 'What's My Motivation' blitz versus her costly confession, vindicate Kant's claim that only a good will gives actions moral worth, while Aristotle supplies the closing lesson that being good takes practice, not just study.

trolley-problem.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
trolley-problem.title: 10. Natasha, Gamora, and the Soul Stone
trolley-problem.relation: T.J. McSherry frames the two Vormir deaths as 'a futuristic, utilitarian trolley problem,' using Mill's greatest-happiness principle to argue Natasha's martyrdom was the more utilitarian choice (only the Avengers mourn her, while Clint's children need a father), even as Thanos's tossing of Gamora shows the same sacrifice-of-few arithmetic the Avengers rely on. Because the amoral Soul Stone rewards good and evil deaths identically, the chapter turns to Plato's Symposium, casting Red Skull as a Diotiman spirit-mediator of love and ranking each relationship on Diotima's ladder: Thanos is 'stuck at level one' in his stunted love for Gamora, kept alive only as a useful sacrifice, while Clint and Natasha's non-romantic love reaches level four through shared history, empathy, and their fight over who gets to die for the other.

trolley-problem.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
trolley-problem.title: 20. Thanos and the (Un)grateful Universe
trolley-problem.relation: Argues that Infinity War only has the structure of a superhero movie when told from Thanos's perspective, and that he passes a three-part 'superhero test' — beneficent goal (saving the universe from overpopulation), self-sacrifice (killing Gamora, destroying the stones, 'I lost more than you can know'), and willingness to make the tough decisions — while the Avengers fail it, staying split after Civil War and acting from selfish motives (Ant-Man wants Hope back, Black Widow says 'we owe it to everyone who's not in this room'). It then applies utilitarianism — Titan's collapse, Gamora's planet turned 'paradise,' the whales in the Hudson, the Snap as a trolley-problem lever Thanos alone will pull — to conclude Thanos is the true hero of the saga and the Avengers the unintended villains.

trolley-problem.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
trolley-problem.title: Not Bad, for a [Wo]man
trolley-problem.relation: Argues Ripley's crossed-heart promise to Newt shows partialist care rightly overriding impartial justice: Kant, Mill, and Rachels demand everyone count for one, but Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg and Noddings's carer-cared-for relation - completed in Newt's 'I knew you'd come' - explain why Ripley duct-tapes two guns together and descends into the hive. Her flexible, relational problem-solving (the lighter-sprinkler trick against the Facehuggers, learning the pulse rifle) beats Gorman's mission-first command, and the trolley-style arithmetic she rejects when the one on the tracks is her little girl is not a moral failing; even nuking the Queen's eggs raises Singer-style speciesism questions.

trolley-problem.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
trolley-problem.title: So, Case Closed-Right
trolley-problem.relation: Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.

trolley-problem.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down
trolley-problem.title: Ender’s Game and Philosophy
trolley-problem.relation: Matthew Brophy argues the I.F. neutralizes Ender's moral agency by masquerading xenocide as child's play: Rackham's paradox that total empathy with the buggers forbids killing them (Sunzi's 'know your enemy') is solved by deception, Walzer's problem of dirty hands is shifted from the child to the politicians, and Milgram-style game framing plus Foot's trolley-problem 'moral distance' show how killing grows easier at a console. Against the innocent-pawn reading, Brophy ends by suggesting Ender was a willing pawn who let himself be deceived in order to save humanity.

trolley-problem.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
trolley-problem.title: 2. How Can Torture Be This Funny
trolley-problem.relation: Asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny and answers with incongruity theory (circus music under Michael's dejection; a comedy set in Hell) plus Bergson's view of comedy as social correction that deflates those who deserve it — Tahani's name-dropping, Michael failing 802 reboots. It centers on 'The Trolley Problem': Michael teleporting Chidi's ethics lesson into real runaway trolleys ('not real, but the pain is') is both incongruous humor and genuine torture, and invoking Bernard Williams shows the real wrongdoer is Michael, who rigged the situation, not Chidi who must choose. Eternal torture, it concludes, only works as endless low-grade everyday crappiness, which is comic in twenty-two-minute doses — and Eleanor's twice-given forgiveness of Michael, after seeing the centuries of torture in Janet's VR device, is the show's real moral marvel.

trolley-problem.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
trolley-problem.title: 11. Those Agonizing Choices
trolley-problem.relation: Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.
