jung-collective-unconscious.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
jung-collective-unconscious.title: 4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
jung-collective-unconscious.title: 15. Aladdin Sane or Cracked Actor
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Riches and Watson weigh two readings of Bowie's 'cracked actor': either his cut-up method and persona-blurring (Ziggy taking over, the family schizophrenia that killed Terry) blurred imagination into hallucination, a Cartesian dream-vs-waking doubt filtered through Bowie's Jungian 'crack in the sky,' archetypes, and collective unconscious; or he deliberately challenged the sanity/madness distinction, as Foucault's Madness and Civilization and antipsychiatrist Thomas Szasz did. On the second reading 'All the Madmen,' the androgyny of 'Queen Bitch' and 'Jean Genie,' and 'Oh You Pretty Things'' Homo Superior rebel against Aristotle's identification of humanity with rationality, winning everyone the freedom to be their unconventional selves.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
jung-collective-unconscious.title: 10. Stranger Shadows
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Cornell reads the Upside Down as an externalized Jungian Shadow: the faceless Demogorgon, 'almost human but it wasn't,' embodies the archetypal shadow of the collective unconscious intruding into Hawkins, and the moral task is integrating it with the conscious ego. Will's possession by the Shadow Monster shows what Jung calls the ego identifying with an unintegrated shadow (his timidity leaving him overpowered), while El is the contrast: after her symbolic rebirth from the fleshy wall she faces absolute evil, acknowledges her own monstrous capacity to kill, and turns the shadow into heroism, ending at Nietzsche's 'becoming who she is.'

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
jung-collective-unconscious.title: The Illusion of Choice
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Kajtár argues BioShock Infinite is meta-fictional art: applying Dewey's Art as Experience, the whole journey from lighthouse to drowning is 'an experience', a unified aesthetic whole you live as Booker rather than a mere object of contemplation. The recurring lighthouse-man-city figures work as Jungian archetypes of the collective unconscious (extended to Campbell's hero's journey structuring Booker's departure, initiation, and return), and the Rapture cameo plus the ocean of lighthouses make the game a story about video game storytelling itself, where the constants are the fictional worlds players enter and the variables are sky or sea. The bird-or-cage choice that changes nothing, like Booker forgetting his 122 previous attempts, shows that rail-bounded interactivity does not disqualify the game from being art, and Levine's 'narrative legos' may one day unite story with real choice.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
jung-collective-unconscious.title: NOTES
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Baldwin argues the popular view of Bushido as a moral code (Nitobe, Star Wars, Kurosawa, Campbell's Jungian hero archetype) is historically wrong: by the Hagakure, Bushido is a death-ready 'mode of action' so morally neutral that even villains like Takezo Kensei or Sylar can practice it. He traces Hiro's evolution from comic-book and video-game hero-worship, through the Yaeko betrayal that turned Kensei into Adam Monroe, toward the fearless Future Hiro ideal of 'no-mind' readiness for death (echoing D.T. Suzuki's Zen reading). Because the Meiji reforms abolished the samurai class, Hiro can never literally be a samurai, only follow Bushido analogically, which lets him remain both superhero and samurai.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream
jung-collective-unconscious.title: Day Residue
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Auxier reverse-engineers how Nolan's dream-sharing could work — sedatives aligning brainwaves like a laser, the electrical dream machine, nested electromagnetic fields — and argues each deeper level buys time at the cost of lucidity, with Limbo as 'psychosis of forgetting.' He explains the film through Susanne Langer's theory of mythic consciousness: dreams become communicable only when forced into narrative order, so dream architecture is the insertion of images that survive transformation into the subject's dispositions — hence Eames plants the pinwheel in the safe so Fischer believes he placed it himself, and the Mombasa elders represent a collective, pre-modern consciousness modern individuals have lost. The resolution of the baggage-claim puzzle (Fischer's calm) is that the inception removed a doubt rather than planting one: doubt spreads easily in modern minds, and Fischer touched the ancestral place where 'our fathers desire our happiness.'

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone
jung-collective-unconscious.title: NOTES
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
jung-collective-unconscious.title: Notes
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned
jung-collective-unconscious.title: Notes
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Maps Campbell's Hero's Journey onto Luke's arc in A New Hope (ordinary world, meeting the mentor, crossing the threshold, atonement with the 'Dark Father' Vader), then argues both Campbell and Lucas misunderstand myth: following Malinowski, myth is a living social charter and therefore ideology, so Star Wars' cosmic dualism, male-centered monomyth, and celebration of violence conceal political and commercial power. The chapter's closing turn - 'Star Wars(TM) is the real Empire and the fans its consumer-subjects,' with Reagan's SDI and an 'insurgents vs. Empire' reading of the Rebellion as illustrations - applies ideology-critique to the franchise itself.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
jung-collective-unconscious.title: 4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.

jung-collective-unconscious.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
jung-collective-unconscious.title: NOTES
jung-collective-unconscious.relation: Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.

category-mistake.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
category-mistake.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
category-mistake.relation: Jason Holt defends the serious question of whether Cohen is a good singer against both anti-fans and fandom, arguing that judgments of taste purport to objectivity and cannot be settled by polls or Juno Awards. Borrowing David Hume's standard of taste - ideal critics with strong sense, delicate sentiment, practice, comparison, and freedom from prejudice - he judges Cohen in his 'weight class' as a singer-songwriter and vocal stylist, ranks him between Paul Simon and Bob Dylan, and offers the 'great singer-songwriter argument' that excellence in both crafts implies being at least a good singer. Much dismissal, he argues, is really style prejudice or a category mistake, and he ends by confessing that Cohen's voice saved him from teenage suicide, biasing him in the best possible way.

category-mistake.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
category-mistake.title: 17. Sweeping Up God’s Debris
category-mistake.relation: Robison-Greene reads God's Debris as a Socratic dialogue on speed: the Avatar, like Socrates after the Delphic oracle, guts the Postman's confidence so he can unlearn, and the whole book functions as a Cartesian skeptical hypothesis in the dream-and-evil-demon lineage, here that we are the dust of a self-destructed God and perception is illusion, with gravity re-described as probability. Her counterattack is that the cosmology commits category mistakes, since probability cannot cause dust to reappear any more than Joe can consist of tallness, and that God made of probability is incoherent even for an omnipotent being. The five levels of awareness collapse too: level-four skeptics are just people who trust reliable methods, and the Avatar's claim that the mind is an illusion generator is self-defeating, since his own omniscience presupposes objective truth.

category-mistake.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
category-mistake.title: The Lasting Legacy of Logic
category-mistake.relation: Treats Carroll the Oxford logician as a teacher hiding five lessons in Wonderland: watch your assumptions (the King infers the Knave's guilt from an unsigned letter), know what your words mean (Humpty Dumpty on 'glory'), don't confuse categories (the King's 'Nobody' and the Hatter's personified Time), don't switch subjects and predicates ('I mean what I say' versus 'I say what I mean'), and don't confuse necessary with sufficient conditions (Alice's Ada and Mabel arguments, with a hammer-and-egg illustration). David S. Brown grounds the lessons in Hume on causes discoverable only by experience, Aristotle's law of non-contradiction and categories, the Marx Brothers' 'Either he's dead or my watch has stopped', and Popper's point that a successful prediction cannot prove a hypothesis, only a failed one can refute it.

schopenhauer-compassion.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
schopenhauer-compassion.title: Leonard Cohen and Philosophy
schopenhauer-compassion.relation: Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.

schopenhauer-compassion.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
schopenhauer-compassion.title: Notes
schopenhauer-compassion.relation: Argues Rust Cohle's stated pessimism and in-principle embrace of suicide closely track Schopenhauer's view that suffering is built into the world with no providential redemption, yet the two diverge because Schopenhauer condemned suicide as an affirmation of the will-to-live rather than its denial. The chapter traces Rust's three-stage arc — jaded wannabe-suicidal pessimist who nonetheless energetically investigates the Dora Lange case, resigned drinker, and finally cautious affirmer of life after the Yellow King confrontation — and contends his detective work is really motivated by a Schopenhauerian morality of compassion and justice, not mere 'programming.' Rust's finale conversion is read as an evidence-based judgment that thoroughgoing pessimism is intellectually dishonest, since compassion and justice do score nontrivial victories.

schopenhauer-compassion.title: Ride the Pink Horse Money, Mischance, Murder, and the Monads of Film Noir
schopenhauer-compassion.relation: Silver reads Robert Montgomery's Ride the Pink Horse as a prototypically noir embodiment of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. The revenge-driven Gagin, like Hugo, is enslaved to money and will—'a man can do what he wants, but not want what he wants'—and takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world, blind to the monads and Platonic-cave shadows of fate around him. Against him stand Pancho's suffering kindness and the Indian girl Pila's selfless compassion, which Silver aligns with Schopenhauer's dictum that 'compassion is the basis of all morality' and his prizing of aesthetic transcendence. The carousel (tío vivo) and the burning of Zozobra, the god of bad luck, become symbols of will's pointless circular striving from which only sacrifice and art offer escape.

schopenhauer-compassion.title: From Desperation to Haven
schopenhauer-compassion.relation: Held reads The Tommyknockers, Desperation, and The Regulators through Arthur Schopenhauer's pessimism, arguing King's worlds are 'always already sunk in evil' and that the will to live swings life between pain and boredom even before the supernatural arrives. He identifies egoism as the root of King's cruelty (Hilly banishing David Brown to Altair-4, Bobbi turning her dog into a battery) and offers Schopenhauer's compassion-based virtue ethic, 'injure no one; help everyone,' as the answer, supported by MacIntyre on the degradation of happiness and set against Nietzsche's 'last man' and nihilism. Gard's rescue of David Brown ('the kid matters or nothing matters') and Johnny Marinville's self-sacrifice in Desperation exemplify the heroic, compassionate life that defies the dark.

korsgaard-constructivism.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only
korsgaard-constructivism.title: Homeland and Philosophy
korsgaard-constructivism.relation: Talia Morag reads Brody's colliding roles - Marine, congressman, father, Muslim, follower of Abu Nazir - and Carrie's unstable ones (CIA agent, bipolar patient, lover) through Korsgaard's notion of practical identities, whose contradictory obligations (kill and not kill) demand reconciliation. Following Kierkegaard's advice to rethink labels like 'Christian', Brody reinterprets his suicide tape as acting 'as a Marine' against domestic enemies - a rationalizing move the chapter treats as bordering on bad faith - while Dana's phone call in 'Marine One' reasserts the father identity and stops the bombing. Carrie's 'Q&A' re-description of Brody as a good man and future hero shows identities are constructed through choices, Sartre's point that we are not summaries of our past.

korsgaard-constructivism.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
korsgaard-constructivism.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
korsgaard-constructivism.relation: Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.

korsgaard-constructivism.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
korsgaard-constructivism.title: Becoming Good at Being Good
korsgaard-constructivism.relation: Argues that Zuko's cry 'Why am I so bad at being good?' after burning Toph shows that changing one's explicit self-conception (Korsgaard's practical identity, the description under which you value yourself) does not by itself change one's being-in-the-world (Heidegger): Zuko's perception, dispositions, and rage-fueled firebending still run on the residual identity of the banished prince seeking his father's approval. The chapter traces this friction through the series: releasing Appa triggers a metamorphosis fever, but he still sides with Azula at the Crossroads of Destiny; the regained 'honor' of Book Three leaves him empty ('I should be happy now, but I'm not'); and only after renouncing Ozai, apologizing to Toph, and re-learning fire from the Sun Warriors without rage do his conscious commitments and existential engagement begin to align, culminating in taking Azula's lightning for Katara. Aspiration, in Agnes Callard's sense, is thus a deep change in how one sees and feels, requiring retraining of bodily skills and practical perception, not just new stated values.

korsgaard-constructivism.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing
korsgaard-constructivism.title: Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
korsgaard-constructivism.relation: Joshua Crabill reads the hosts' awakening through Kant's story of Eve grasping autonomy and the etymology of autonomy as self-legislation, with Dolores swatting the fly and 'these violent delights' as her forbidden fruit. He uses Nietzsche's will-to-power turned inward to explain how the hosts' caged suffering builds an inner 'soul,' and Jaynes's bicameral commanding voice becoming one's own (Dolores hearing Arnold's voice turn into hers). Drawing on Korsgaard's reflective distance and Plato's divided soul, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own law), arguing that Korsgaard's 'determinism is no threat to freedom' lets Maeve, gaining admin access and choosing her daughter, genuinely 'write my own story.'

korsgaard-constructivism.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body
korsgaard-constructivism.title: YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
korsgaard-constructivism.relation: Heather Salazar interleaves philosophical arguments with yoga exercises to awaken a 'hidden ethical self.' Using Korsgaard's notion of practical identity, she has readers meditate on their roles and conflicts, then argues in Kantian fashion that recognizing the shared reasons behind everyone's pursuits obliges us to value others as we value ourselves; extending Korsgaard, that we must value the life and happiness we prize wherever they appear, in animals and plants; and via Buddhist interdependence (the world in a cup of tea) that caring for others and the environment just is a way of caring for ourselves.

wolf-meaning.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything
wolf-meaning.title: Girls and Philosophy
wolf-meaning.relation: Blessing and Wezowiczi test theories of life's meaning on the two narcissists of Girls: Hannah, whose purpose-driven pursuit of being a writer (manufacturing experiences, ignoring her father's medical procedure) shows that goal achievement alone collapses into Taylor's and Camus's Sisyphus problem, and Jessa, whose 'life addict' desire-satisfaction illustrates the Nietzschean live-in-the-moment view the authors find reckless and irresponsible. Using Wielenberg's excrement-eater and the subjectivist/objectivist debate, they land on Susan Wolf's 'loving objects that are worthy of love,' then argue via Socrates's examined life and Sartre's bad faith that neither Hannah's phony narrative nor Jessa's protective persona counts as authentic, examined living.

wolf-meaning.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield
wolf-meaning.title: Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy
wolf-meaning.relation: Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.

wolf-meaning.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
wolf-meaning.title: 1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey
wolf-meaning.relation: Blessing tests the Steve Jobs/Oprah 'do what you love' creed against Downton, where rigid class structure assigns nearly everyone a role they did not choose. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness (Matthew's war wounds, Mary's grief after his death) and purposefulness (Grantham's custodian speech), then weighs subjectivist theories of meaning, including Nietzsche's idea that meaning arises from the passionate process itself, against Nozick's permanence view and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness,' adding Kant's duty to develop one's talents against a world of idle pleasure. She concludes that the Abbey's ethos - Grantham as custodian not owner, Carson's pride in service, Patmore's kitchen, 'I have no right to be unhappy' - shows that socially necessary work one does not love can still make a meaningful life, while DWYL is elitist and narcissistic.

wolf-meaning.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
wolf-meaning.title: 8. Living for More
wolf-meaning.relation: Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.

wolf-meaning.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
wolf-meaning.title: 7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife
wolf-meaning.relation: Yang frames Eleanor's predicament as a dilemma: a finite life seems drained of value by its ending, while an immortal one collapses into boredom or into the disconnection of the 802 memory-wiped reboots. Camus's Sisyphus and Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view prove inadequate, so he adopts Susan Wolf's account of meaning as loving what deserves to be loved, which Eleanor's study of moral philosophy, her friendships, and her romance with Chidi satisfy even without God or eternity. John Martin Fischer's narrative approach then redeems the reboots as self-contained episodes, and Eleanor's note to herself in Scanlon's book shows memory wipes need not sever the story of a life.

wolf-meaning.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There
wolf-meaning.title: 1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey
wolf-meaning.relation: Blessing pits Steve Jobs's 'Do What You Love' creed (and Oprah's 'follow your bliss') against Downton's world of inherited roles, where nobody from Anna to Lady Mary chooses their work. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness, since Matthew's war wounds and Mary's grief over his death are painful yet deeply meaningful, and tests subjectivist theories such as Nietzsche's meaning-as-passionate-process against Nozick's demand that a meaningful life leave permanent traces and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'loving objects that are worthy of love.' Kant's duty to develop one's talents rather than idle for pleasure, and Lord Grantham's self-description as 'a custodian, not an owner,' anchor the show's counter-ethos of duty over desire, embodied in Carson, Mrs. Hughes, and Mrs. Patmore's pride in unloved, socially necessary work. The chapter concludes that Downton validates hard honest work as an end in itself, challenging the narcissism of the 'holy You' and expressive individualism.

wolf-meaning.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!
wolf-meaning.title: 7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife
wolf-meaning.relation: Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.

wolf-meaning.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland
wolf-meaning.title: Notes
wolf-meaning.relation: Berk maps Fury Road onto contemporary theories of meaning in life through three characters. Nux begins a Supernaturalist — Immortan Joe is his god and Valhalla his afterlife — collapses into nihilism after the humiliating 'Mediocre!', and ends a Naturalist who gives his life meaning by sacrificing himself to collapse the thruway and block Immortan Joe's armada. Max moves from pure survival to Susan Wolf's Hybrid Naturalism (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) when he commits to retaking the Citadel, and Furiosa, already there, embodies the film's own Objective List theory: virtue, autonomy, and relationships.

wolf-meaning.book: 271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy
wolf-meaning.title: FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE
wolf-meaning.relation: Austin offers practical wisdom for fathers of daughters, grounding fatherly obligations in daughters' fundamental interests and focusing on self-knowledge, moral development, and the common good. Invoking the Delphic 'know thyself,' Charles Taylor's 'strong evaluations,' and Aristotle's view that virtue grows through practice, he explains how to cultivate humility (including 'existential humility' before nature), courage (including self-sacrifice), and wisdom (curiosity, versatility, critical thinking) – e.g., analyzing advertising assumptions and limiting screen time – so a daughter can flourish and contribute to the common good.

wolf-meaning.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy
wolf-meaning.title: 60. Little Women as Philosophy Death or Marriage and the Meaning of Life
wolf-meaning.relation: The chapter tests Susan Wolf's 'fitting fulfillment' theory (meaning as subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) against Greta Gerwig's Little Women, arguing the March sisters and most historical women are ill-fitted to it. Jo is forced to make her writing 'mercenary and commercial' and marries; Amy abandons painting and marries Laurie because 'marriage is an economic proposition'; Marmee, Hannah, and Mrs. Hummel live from duty and self-sacrifice without joy. Invoking Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but becomes a woman' and Imposter Syndrome, it concludes fulfillment is indicative but not necessary for meaning, urging a purely objective theory that can value women's lives 'appropriately appreciated at least in principle.'

oedipus-complex.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later
oedipus-complex.title: Justified and Philosophy
oedipus-complex.relation: The chapter reads Harlan's family bonds through Freud's Oedipus Complex - Raylan bails Arlo out only at stepmother Helen's request, and Coover whimpers 'I'm sorry, Mamma' while cradled in Mags's arms after she hammers his hand, the submissive son destroyed by his need for his mother's approval. It then applies Schopenhauer's pessimism to Winona's pregnancy: if life is suffering, as On the Vanity of Existence argues, bringing a child into Harlan is selfish vanity, and Mags's dynasty-building - grooming Loretta, bequeathing the weed business - is the will-to-live seeking immortality through the family name. Only Boyd and Ava's unsentimental care for the demented Arlo, the chapter suggests, escapes both the Oedipal trap and the vanity of lineage.

oedipus-complex.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
oedipus-complex.title: 12. Not Why but Who
oedipus-complex.relation: Reads the mothers of Orphan Black through Freud and Lacan: Dr. Coady is the "phallic mother" at the center of the Castor clones' Oedipal drama (Rudy's kiss, the DNA trophies brought home to Mom), Tomas is Helena's abusive false father, Rachel is the child of a shattered Oedipal triangle, and the Symbolic Order that makes men active rational subjects and women passive reproductive objects is mirrored in the defects — neurological for the male clones, reproductive for the female. The chapter then brings in Luce Irigaray to show the show rewriting these stereotypes: the clones' spectrum of personalities and their constant impersonations destabilize fixed gender categories, and the many equally "real" mothers (Mrs. S., Amelia, Alison, Kendall) burst the woman-equals-womb equation. Beth's counsel to the delirious Sarah — "Stop asking 'Why?' and start asking 'Who?'" — becomes the feminist move from mechanism to women as active subjects.

oedipus-complex.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
oedipus-complex.title: Arrested Development and Philosophy
oedipus-complex.relation: Runs the Bluths through Freudian psychoanalysis: George Sr. hiding in the attic ('Sad Sack', 'Good Grief!') illustrates the unconscious, preconscious, and repression; Michael acts as ego mediating the family's id demands (the unfrozen stock spree) against George Michael's super-ego; Tobias dressing as a pirate among homosexuals and Michael's 'brother...bother' and 'Egg' slips are parapraxes betraying repressed desire; Buster's Motherboy dates and 'Why I Want to Marry My Mother' enact a failed Oedipus complex; and the brothers' scheme against George Sr. in 'Making a Stand' reenacts the primal horde of Totem and Taboo, origin of the incest taboo that haunts George Michael and Maeby.

oedipus-complex.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
oedipus-complex.title: Mmmyez: Stewie and the Seven Deadly Sins
oedipus-complex.relation: Kaye argues Stewie is funny because he portrays a truth we repress: Augustine's doctrine of original sin (defended as the only answer to why God lets the innocent suffer, and grounded in the pear-tree and jealous-infant episodes of the Confessions) — no one is innocent, not even babies. Systematically cataloging Stewie through Aquinas's Seven Deadly Sins, she shows lust (the Rupert-the-gay-teddy-bear projection, 'wee-wee stricken with rigor mortis', inverting Freud's Oedipal complex since Stewie hates his mother and barely tolerates his father), gluttony (hoarding Lois's breast milk, an orgy of fig newtons), sloth as Aquinas's 'oppressive sorrow' and malicious indignation ('Why don't you burn in hell?'), avarice, anger as revenge (bombs and graham crackers), envy (locking Jeremy in the car trunk), and pride, the Queen of Vices — Stewie's god complex ('Omnipotence. Gotta get me some of that'). Stewie's lone possibly-decent moment (warning Brian not to mock upside-down Jake Tucker's face) is left as the one loose thread.

oedipus-complex.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded
oedipus-complex.title: The Ego is a Housewife Named Lois
oedipus-complex.relation: Maps Freud's structural model of the mind onto the Griffin household: Stewie is the id (the broccoli-destroying weather machine in 'I Never Met the Dead Man,' the mind-control device foiled by Bill Cosby in 'Brian Does Hollywood'), Brian is the super-ego (talking kleptomaniac Lois into surrendering in 'Breaking Out Is Hard to Do'), and Lois is the ego that reality-tests and restrains both, with the id-ego miscommunication mirrored in Lois never understanding Stewie's speech. The Oedipus complex does the interpretive heavy lifting: Stewie's 'damn you, vile woman' obsession is misdirected maternal longing, Brian's 'Brian in Love' confession of love for his figurative mother resolves the complex and founds his moral boundaries, and Peter's Church of the Holy Fonz reads as failed father-identification, religion as substitute for the father.

oedipus-complex.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets
oedipus-complex.title: Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy
oedipus-complex.relation: Sets up Sons of Anarchy as a Hamlet retelling — Jax the prince, Clay the Claudius who murdered John Teller and married Gemma, Tara a gutsier Ophelia — and reads it through Freud and Ernest Jones's Hamlet and Oedipus: Jax's protest that he 'untwisted my mommy thing a long time ago,' his toleration of Gemma's meddling, and the Season 4/5 finale tableaux where Gemma displaces Tara at his side betray an unresolved Oedipus complex. Freud's three agencies get bodies: Clay as pure Id (beating Gemma in 'Hands'), Tara as Superego, Jax as the mediating Ego, with SAMCRO itself a collective Id worshipped in its 'chapel.' Oral and anal-stage fixations explain the Sons' chain-smoking, recklessness, and defiance of authority, while the Id's civil war between libido and the death drive plays out in Gemma's post-beating sex binge and Jax's unconscious pleasure in killing.

jung-archetypes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know
jung-archetypes.title: Dracula and Philosophy
jung-archetypes.relation: Callis reads the 1931 Lugosi film through Jung: Dracula is Mina's Shadow archetype and animus, embodying her repressed fear of sexuality and of the married life she claims to want, while the vampire's presence in every culture places him in the collective unconscious. Mina's arc - the Call to Adventure, crossing the threshold into Dracula's embrace, and 'resurrection' after his staking - becomes a Shero's Journey of confronting the shadow, with Dracula also playing the Shapeshifter archetype. The chapter ends doubting the happy ending, asking whether Mina defeated her shadow or merely surrendered her dreams of freedom.

jung-archetypes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time
jung-archetypes.title: 4. How Possible Is the Impossible Girl
jung-archetypes.relation: Smith asks how one Clara can exist as Oswin the converted Dalek, a Victorian governess, and a present-day nanny, and answers with philosophy of mind: after the real Clara steps into the Doctor's timeline on Trenzalore, the 'echoes' are best understood as manifestations within the Doctor's own subconscious, read through Freud's dream interpretation and id-ego-superego (the echoes act as his conscience) and Jung's archetypes, collective unconscious, individuation, and synchronicity—her name meaning clarity, her red wardrobe marking the copies, and the leaf of 'The Rings of Akhaten' as the meaningful coincidence that produced her. Aristotle's Categories frames what Oswin still shares with humanity after Dalek conversion, and the soufflé-is-the-recipe line together with social-cognition research on multiple selves supports the conclusion that the Claras are metaphysically the same person despite different bodies and roles—making the 'Impossible Girl' possible.

jung-archetypes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
jung-archetypes.title: 11. Meeting the Monstrous Self
jung-archetypes.relation: Piven reads 'The Width of a Circle''s monster sitting by the tree through the doppelgänger tradition (Rank's The Double, Dostoevsky, Kirk's 'Enemy Within,' Luke finding his own face in Vader's mask): the monstrous double is the self, and social identity is the mask that hides it, so 'we have met Sauron and he is us.' Deploying Jungian archetype against mere stereotype, Nietzsche's dictum that truth kills, and the Freudian superego - the devil as its alter ego, perversely enjoying the condemnation it inflicts - the chapter argues Bowie's erotic devil scene shows how moralistic societies brand innocent desire monstrous, and that an agonizing encounter with the inner monster, not clichéd self-mythology, is the dire necessity of self-knowledge.

jung-archetypes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
jung-archetypes.title: 15. Aladdin Sane or Cracked Actor
jung-archetypes.relation: Riches and Watson weigh two readings of Bowie's 'cracked actor': either his cut-up method and persona-blurring (Ziggy taking over, the family schizophrenia that killed Terry) blurred imagination into hallucination, a Cartesian dream-vs-waking doubt filtered through Bowie's Jungian 'crack in the sky,' archetypes, and collective unconscious; or he deliberately challenged the sanity/madness distinction, as Foucault's Madness and Civilization and antipsychiatrist Thomas Szasz did. On the second reading 'All the Madmen,' the androgyny of 'Queen Bitch' and 'Jean Genie,' and 'Oh You Pretty Things'' Homo Superior rebel against Aristotle's identification of humanity with rationality, winning everyone the freedom to be their unconventional selves.

jung-archetypes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon
jung-archetypes.title: 10. Stranger Shadows
jung-archetypes.relation: Cornell reads the Upside Down as an externalized Jungian Shadow: the faceless Demogorgon, 'almost human but it wasn't,' embodies the archetypal shadow of the collective unconscious intruding into Hawkins, and the moral task is integrating it with the conscious ego. Will's possession by the Shadow Monster shows what Jung calls the ego identifying with an unintegrated shadow (his timidity leaving him overpowered), while El is the contrast: after her symbolic rebirth from the fleshy wall she faces absolute evil, acknowledges her own monstrous capacity to kill, and turns the shadow into heroism, ending at Nietzsche's 'becoming who she is.'

jung-archetypes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
jung-archetypes.title: The Illusion of Choice
jung-archetypes.relation: Kajtár argues BioShock Infinite is meta-fictional art: applying Dewey's Art as Experience, the whole journey from lighthouse to drowning is 'an experience', a unified aesthetic whole you live as Booker rather than a mere object of contemplation. The recurring lighthouse-man-city figures work as Jungian archetypes of the collective unconscious (extended to Campbell's hero's journey structuring Booker's departure, initiation, and return), and the Rapture cameo plus the ocean of lighthouses make the game a story about video game storytelling itself, where the constants are the fictional worlds players enter and the variables are sky or sea. The bird-or-cage choice that changes nothing, like Booker forgetting his 122 previous attempts, shows that rail-bounded interactivity does not disqualify the game from being art, and Levine's 'narrative legos' may one day unite story with real choice.

jung-archetypes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust
jung-archetypes.title: Hey Goofy! Somebody Just Slipped My Culture a Mickey…
jung-archetypes.relation: Schuchardt argues Disney's real product is 'getting you in there' — colonizing the geography of the imagination: Pirates of the Caribbean is read as an allegory of corporate globalization, White Wilderness fabricated the lemming-suicide myth, and the parks' visual containment keeps visitors inside a world with 'more reality than nature' (Eco's hyperreality, in Baudrillard's territory). He claims Disney built this on Jung's archetypes via Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey under the mantra 'We Create the Mythology of the Future,' so that media consolidation (the Fox merger shrinking six conglomerates to five) narrows the Overton Window and Disney's manufactured mythology displaces Christianity as the reigning worldview.

jung-archetypes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World
jung-archetypes.title: NOTES
jung-archetypes.relation: Baldwin argues the popular view of Bushido as a moral code (Nitobe, Star Wars, Kurosawa, Campbell's Jungian hero archetype) is historically wrong: by the Hagakure, Bushido is a death-ready 'mode of action' so morally neutral that even villains like Takezo Kensei or Sylar can practice it. He traces Hiro's evolution from comic-book and video-game hero-worship, through the Yaeko betrayal that turned Kensei into Adam Monroe, toward the fearless Future Hiro ideal of 'no-mind' readiness for death (echoing D.T. Suzuki's Zen reading). Because the Meiji reforms abolished the samurai class, Hiro can never literally be a samurai, only follow Bushido analogically, which lets him remain both superhero and samurai.

jung-archetypes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates
jung-archetypes.title: Notes
jung-archetypes.relation: Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.

jung-archetypes.title: Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir
jung-archetypes.relation: Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.

jung-archetypes.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business
jung-archetypes.title: 4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest
jung-archetypes.relation: Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.

stoic-view-from-above.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
stoic-view-from-above.title: 4. On Being a Dead Person Who Hasn’t Died Yet
stoic-view-from-above.relation: Mark Ralkowski argues that Louis's 'dead people who haven't died yet' bit sounds like Marcus Aurelius, and that Dr. Bigelow's Season Four advice about back pain, the three-legged dog, and heartbreak works as the Stoic spiritual exercises Pierre Hadot described - above all the 'view from above' that re-describes things to strip them to their true value. Epictetus's dichotomy of control explains Bigelow's core advice: pain is not 'up to us' but our judgments about it are, so Louie should adjust his expectations to nature ('every second without back pain is a lucky second') instead of demanding a pain-free life. The apparently un-Stoic counsel to savor heartbreak ('misery is wasted on the miserable') is defended as genuinely Stoic: viewing his lost love from the perspective of a dead-person-who-hasn't-died-yet, Louie can accept sadness as precious and impermanent rather than being crushed by it. The chapter concedes Louis is no philosopher, but suggests his bits - contrasted with Seinfeld's 'polished' version on Talking Funny - can be read as newly discovered Meditations for comedy audiences.

stoic-view-from-above.title: Heroes of the Coliseum
stoic-view-from-above.relation: Reid draws an extended analogy between big-time college football players and Roman gladiators—both socially marginalized entertainers, controlled by coaches/editors and crowds, risking their bodies for others' entertainment. Through Roman Stoicism (Seneca, Epictetus, Cicero) she argues virtus does not depend on external wealth, status, or freedom but on accepting fate and excelling within one's role, so exploited athletes can still be genuine heroes of virtue. Following Marcus Aurelius's distaste for the games, she concludes those with power over players' unjust conditions are morally obliged to improve them.

legal-positivism.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
legal-positivism.title: 12. The Law of Red Rising
legal-positivism.relation: Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.

legal-positivism.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
legal-positivism.title: 15. You Can’t Use My Name
legal-positivism.relation: Recounts how Hendrix changed law twice: ExperienceHendrix v. PPX (the 'You can't use my name' tapes) imported the Wrotham Park/Blake standard so breach-of-contract damages can reflect the infringer's gains rather than the victim's losses, and Experience Hendrix v. Hendrixlicensing.com used Washington's Personality Rights Act to extend postmortem publicity rights beyond the state of domicile, raising the constitutional problems Rossi identifies. The chapter then reads the dispute over whether the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' is art or noise through legal realism versus natural law theory and legal positivism — law as what courts actually enforce — and through the Institutional Theory of Art, with a Wittgensteinian cluster definition marking the essentialist route that failed.

legal-positivism.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
legal-positivism.title: 3. Perry Mason v. Saul Goodman
legal-positivism.relation: Scalambrino compares Mason and Better Call Saul's Saul Goodman, who pull the same shady moves (Perry's evidence switching in 'The Case of the Crimson Kiss' and 'The Case of the Restless Redhead', Saul's fabricated 'pie sitting' videos) yet receive opposite moral verdicts. He frames this through natural law (Aquinas, Kant) versus legal positivism (Hobbes's command theory, Nietzsche's law as power), the audience's 'God's-eye' perspective, and the means/ends distinction, concluding provocatively that Perry's tampering is actually easier to justify from the positivist side, since he gambles on hunches without knowing his client is innocent, while the show's premises (he is already rich and famous, his clients always innocent) make the material conditions of Saul's lawyering moot for him.

legal-positivism.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
legal-positivism.title: Notes
legal-positivism.relation: Uses Hans Kelsen's legal positivism — law as amoral coercive order sustained by sanction, validated by authority rather than morality — to interpret season two's competing normative systems, from Vinci's city hall to the cartel's execution of the informant Irina. Against this background it separates revenge from Hegelian retributivism, reading Velcoro's shift from killing his wife's rapist to persuading Lenny Osterman to seek exposure instead, and Frank's communicative, confessing execution of the traitor Blake, as conflicted exercises of justice. The finale's bloodshed is read through Hegel's theory of tragedy as a collision of spheres of justice, each justified in its own eyes, whose transgression may precipitate change in Vinci.

stoic-premeditation.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
stoic-premeditation.title: 10. How to Be Free
stoic-premeditation.relation: O'Connell and Sirvent argue Seneca's Stoic freedom - release from fear of death and from every attachment - illuminates the two most enslaved groups in the story. The Unsullied's training strips them of possessions, names, lust, and fear, with Grey Worm's shame at fearing death for Missandei's sake showing exactly what attachment does to this freedom, while the Faceless Men's 'valar morghulis' mantra works like Seneca's recommended contemplation of death, letting Arya drink blindly from the cup at the House of Black and White. The chapter concludes that a fearlessness built by slaves and assassins really is a kind of freedom beyond their servitude, though Seneca would recoil at the brutal methods that produce it.

stoic-premeditation.book: 273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail
stoic-premeditation.title: SAILING Philosophy for Everyone
stoic-premeditation.relation: Gregory and Tod Bassham argue Stoicism is the seaman's philosophy of agency, teaching a clear-eyed grasp of what we can control, influence, or not control at all. Using Epictetus's play metaphor and 'you will fetter my leg but not my will,' Seneca and Marcus Aurelius on fear, they map three techniques onto sailing: cheerful resignation (Gerry Spiess righting Yankee Girl, Shackleton's James Caird crew laughing amid the Southern Ocean), self-sufficiency (splicing lines, emotional independence on a cramped boat), and negative visualization / premeditatio malorum (practicing docking under sail, imagining lost rudders). Skip Allen scuttling Wildflower and Dinelli's endurance illustrate the trichotomy of control and freedom of mind.

lacan-mirror-stage.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
lacan-mirror-stage.title: 3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!
lacan-mirror-stage.relation: Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.

lacan-mirror-stage.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
lacan-mirror-stage.title: Notes
lacan-mirror-stage.relation: Reads the Cohle–Hart pairing through Lacan: Cohle is at peace with the constitutive lack introduced after the mirror stage, and his hysteric's fixation on the Other's desire is what makes him the superior interrogator, while Hart exhibits obsessional neurosis and 'interpassivity,' letting the preacher's congregation do his believing for him. Following Deleuze's Oedipal structure of detective fiction and Hegel's point that heroes are denied guilt, the chapter compares Rust to Oedipus — both men who, after a child's death, renounce the father function through anti-natalism — while arguing Cohle surpasses Oedipus by philosophically mastering the knowledge that Oedipus lacked. Rust's tying off of his 'circle of violence' is read as the Lacanian sinthome: putting his symptom to work in the service of the case rather than being destroyed by it.

lacan-mirror-stage.title: The Philosophy of Ang Lee
lacan-mirror-stage.relation: Zietsma reads Hulk and Taking Woodstock as antiwar films that subvert the hegemonic culture of heroic violence, fitting Lackey's category of universal (Gandhian/early-Christian) pacifism. He argues both films disturb their genre's expected narrative and demasculinize the hero: Elliot the gay nonviolent hero and the transgender vet Vilma, and a weeping Hulk who is rescued by Betty and finally gives up his power rather than kill David Banner. He reads the bathroom-mirror 'Puny human' scene as an inverted Lacanian mirror stage unmasking America's violent militarism, framing the Vietnam War and war on terror as violence that only begets more violence.

lacan-mirror-stage.title: From Self-Alienation to Posthumanism The Transmigration of the Burroughsian Subject
lacan-mirror-stage.relation: Bolton argues William S. Burroughs's fragmented subjects—split by a parasitic 'Other Half' or word virus—are not postmodernism's dissolved nonsubjects but practitioners of a productive self-alienation. He aligns Burroughs's multiply-named, body-swapping characters (Mr. Bradley Mr. Martin, Joe the Dead) with Lacan's split subject constituted in language and with Derrida's iterable 'mark' and 'third that walks beside you' as an absent-present that dissolves binaries. Through Naked Lunch, Nova Express, and The Western Lands the Burroughsian subject transmigrates from Marxian/Hegelian alienation to N. Katherine Hayles's posthuman, gaining agency by extending into its technologized environment.

lacan-mirror-stage.title: Re(ct)ifying Empty Speech Cronenberg and the Problem of the First Person
lacan-mirror-stage.relation: Brook W. R. Pearson examines the problem of the first person 'I' in Cronenberg through Lacan, Wittgenstein, and Deleuze/Guattari. He reads Spider's 'schizo-phonetic partition' and Tom/Joey's shifting use of 'I' in A History of Violence as Lacanian 'empty speech' and the narcissistic 'monument' of a censored unconscious chapter that resurfaces; Wittgenstein's private-language argument and Moore's paradox recast Joey's split as an illegitimate private language game, and Deleuze/Guattari's account of the other as a 'possible world' reframes the frightened face on the cinema screen.

lacan-mirror-stage.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature
lacan-mirror-stage.title: Making Monsters The Philosophy of Reproduction in Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Universal Films Frankens
lacan-mirror-stage.relation: Hall reads Shelley's Frankenstein and the 1931 film and its 1935 Bride sequel through Luce Irigaray's Speculum, arguing that Victor's and Walton's quests for a whole, self-sufficient identity enact a patriarchal desire to reproduce sameness and deny the 'maternal waters,' with women reduced to mirrors that will not reflect. She uses Lacan's mirror stage and the camera's power over sight to explain how identity is fixed by being seen, and Derrida's 'Structure, Sign and Play' to recast identity as a perpetually rewritten, misshapen text. The Bride's refusing scream and the exploding phallic tower mark female desire as a negating power that disrupts patriarchal reproduction.

darshana.title: Richness and diversity in Indian thought
darshana.relation: Argues that in India philosophy and religion were never separated as the post-Kantian West separates them: philosophizing is a soteriological quest in which understanding the nature of reality directly affects one's destiny, more comparable to Socrates' quest for wisdom than to modern academic philosophy. It introduces the framework of darshanas ('views' of reality taught by seers), the claim that disciplined mental exercises can yield yogic perception of metaphysical truth, and karma-rebirth as the shared Indian worldview, contrasting ritual-correctness karma with the Buddha's radically intention-based version and discussing verbal testimony as an everyday but religiously unchecked means of knowledge. It closes by delimiting the book's scope (the six classical darshanas plus Buddhism; Jainism, Carvaka, and Shaivism omitted) and warning against the Western habit of romanticizing Indian thought as mystical rather than recognizing its strong rational-debate tradition. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

vedic-sacrifice.title: Sacrifice, cosmic speculation, oneness
vedic-sacrifice.relation: Presents the two coexisting branches of the Brahmanical tradition around 500 BCE: the Vedic sacrificial religion, in which precisely performed ritual actions (physical and verbal karma) maintained cosmic order (dharma) and underwrote brahmin social authority, and the Upanishadic internalization of the sacrifice. The Upanishads shift the focus to the person, teaching that experiential insight into the identity of one's essential self (atman) and the cosmos (Brahman) - 'tat tvam asi' - brings moksha from rebirth, illustrated with the Rig Veda 10.129 creation hymn and passages from the Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka Upanishads. It carefully distinguishes monism (one existent thing) from monotheism, sets the Upanishadic oneness against the pluralistic realism of the ritualists, and shows how this internal tension became the fault line along which later Indian philosophical debate would run. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

dependent-origination.title: The Buddha’s Middle Way
dependent-origination.relation: Reconstructs the Buddha's teaching as a Middle Way on three levels: socially between householder ritualism and renouncer asceticism, in monastic life between indulgence and austerities, and metaphysically between every permutation of existence and non-existence. It details the Enlightenment's three insights, the Four Noble Truths (dukkha better rendered 'unsatisfactoriness' grounded in the impermanence of all conditioned things), and dependent origination as the 'regularity of things'. Against the standard reading of anatta as 'there is no self', it argues the Buddha denied only independent existence and shifted inquiry from ontology to the workings of the cognitive apparatus (the five khandhas), citing his refusal to answer the Unanswered Questions. It also gives the Buddha's specific critiques of brahmin claims to authority, the purposelessness of ritual, and reliance on tradition over one's own experience. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

vaisheshika-categories.title: Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya
vaisheshika-categories.relation: Exposes Kanada's Vaisheshika pluralistic realism: seven categories (substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and absence) and nine eternal substances, with earth, water, fire, and air atoms combining to form all composite objects - the red of a red rose illustrating quality, inherence, universality, and particularity. It then presents Gotama's Nyaya contribution: a formal five-membered inferential method (thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion - 'there is fire on the hill because there is smoke') grounded in perception and invariable rules rather than Vedic testimony, plus criteria (doubt, purpose, possibility of certainty) for when enquiry is legitimate. Nyaya uses this method to 'prove' a plurality of eternal selves from the plurality of consciousnesses and their qualities, and the chapter notes the standing modern comparison of the method with Aristotle's syllogism. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

nyaya-five-limb-inference.title: Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya
nyaya-five-limb-inference.relation: Exposes Kanada's Vaisheshika pluralistic realism: seven categories (substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and absence) and nine eternal substances, with earth, water, fire, and air atoms combining to form all composite objects - the red of a red rose illustrating quality, inherence, universality, and particularity. abhidharma.title: Developments in Buddhist thought
abhidharma.relation: Traces Buddhist scholasticism from the eighteen early schools (Lokottaravadins, Sammatiyas, Sautrantikas, Sarvastivadins, with Theravada the survivor) through the Abhidharma projects - Sarvastivada dharmas existing in all three time modes with an essence (svabhava), Theravada's categorization of some 28 physical and 52 mental dharmas - and their critique of Nyaya-Vaisheshika partless atoms. It then presents the Mahayana response: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras' teaching that all dharmas are empty of own-being, and Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka demonstration that nothing with own-being can arise from itself, from another, from both, or spontaneously, together with his two truths (conventional and ultimate) and the 'emptiness of emptiness' - emptiness affirms, rather than denies, the dependently originated world, since without it no change or knowledge would be possible. It closes with Vasubandhu's Yogacara 'Mind-Only' analysis of transformations of consciousness, karmic 'seeds' in a storehouse consciousness, and the constructed, dependent, and perfected aspects of experience, which denies that perception establishes the external existence of its objects. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

yogacara-mind-only.title: Developments in Buddhist thought
yogacara-mind-only.relation: Traces Buddhist scholasticism from the eighteen early schools (Lokottaravadins, Sammatiyas, Sautrantikas, Sarvastivadins, with Theravada the survivor) through the Abhidharma projects - Sarvastivada dharmas existing in all three time modes with an essence (svabhava), Theravada's categorization of some 28 physical and 52 mental dharmas - and their critique of Nyaya-Vaisheshika partless atoms. classical-yoga.title: Yoga and Sāṃkhya
classical-yoga.relation: Presents Classical Yoga's Yoga Sutras as above all a practice manual for 'the cessation of the activities of the mind' (citta-vritti-nirodha), through which the practitioner discriminates the conscious but inactive witness (purusha) from unconscious, active manifest nature (prakriti) - delusion consisting in mistaking the manifest ego for the conscious self - and discusses the ambiguous status of the 'Lord' (Ishvara) verses. It then presents Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika as the matching dualist ontology: numerically plural but ontologically identical purushas versus one prakriti colored by the three qualities of goodness, passion, and inertia, enumerated through categories from buddhi (will/discernment) and the 'I-maker' (ahamkara) down to the gross elements, with satkaryavada (the effect pre-exists in the cause) argued by inference. It highlights the startling Samkhya conclusion that 'nothing really is bound; no-one is reborn and no-one is released', since only prakriti ever cycles, and closes with Hamilton's own suggestion that prakriti's manifestation may describe a cognition-dependent world of experience rather than material nature. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

samkhya-dualism.title: Yoga and Sāṃkhya
samkhya-dualism.relation: Presents Classical Yoga's Yoga Sutras as above all a practice manual for 'the cessation of the activities of the mind' (citta-vritti-nirodha), through which the practitioner discriminates the conscious but inactive witness (purusha) from unconscious, active manifest nature (prakriti) - delusion consisting in mistaking the manifest ego for the conscious self - and discusses the ambiguous status of the 'Lord' (Ishvara) verses. mimamsa.title: Bhartṛhari, Mīmāṃsā, and Vedānta
mimamsa.relation: Covers the later grammatical and exegetical schools: Bhartrhari's claim that the whole sentence is the unit of meaning, that there is no knowledge without language, and that reality is a continuous indivisible 'sound-Brahman' (shabda-Brahman) knowable through grammar; the Mimamsakas (Kumarila and Prabhakara) defending the eternal, authorless Veda as injunction, holding cognition itself intrinsically reliable so that knowing reveals both the plural external world and the autonomous agent-selves who perform the sacrifice (with an 'identity in difference' category analysis and visible-sized atoms). It then presents Vedanta: Shankara's Advaita monism in which atman is Brahman, plurality has only conventional reality (the coiled rope mistaken for a snake; the trees seeming to move to a boatman), ignorance rather than Brahman causes the world of appearance, and Shankara remains a theistic monist despite his 'crypto-Buddhist' critics; versus Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, in which Brahman really transforms itself into the qualified, plural world (parinama-vada) and selves relate to the Lord as redness to a rose - eternally inseparable yet distinct. The chapter treats its subject directly rather than through any pop-culture work.

mill-subjection-women.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
mill-subjection-women.title: 3 On the Origin of the Family
mill-subjection-women.relation: The chapter compares the liberal contract theorists with Engels (building on Morgan's Ancient Society) on the origin of the patriarchal monogamous family: Hobbes derives sovereign-husbanded 'little monarchies' from a state of nature in which women are men's equals, a derivation Susan Okin shows is contradictory; Locke grounds conjugal society in a voluntary compact with the husband as 'abler and stronger' last determiner, yet leaves women excluded from the social contract; Rousseau pairs passionate economic equality with some of the most sexist writing in Western thought, including fear of wives' sexual power in Emile. Against these static philosophies Engels gives a historical-materialist account in which the overthrow of mother right - the 'world historical defeat of the female sex' - followed from private property and inheritance, turning the bourgeois wife into a proletarian or prostitute while opening 'sex love' to the propertyless, and prescribing women's return to the labor force, socialized child-care, industrialized housework and easy divorce. John Stuart Mill's Subjection of Women appears as liberalism's one exception to its sexism, and a footnote sets Firestone's biological account of patriarchy against Engels's property account.

mill-subjection-women.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke
mill-subjection-women.title: The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy
mill-subjection-women.relation: White and Fisher run the show's women (and men) through feminist philosophy: the sex/gender distinction from Plato's Republic Book V and Mill's Subjection of Women through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Butler's antiessentialist performativity. Penny's hyper-femininity reads as Butlerian parody that satirizes the script, the Penny–Bernadette–Amy lineup exposes the custom that smarts and beauty must trade off, and Elizabeth Plimpton and Leslie Winkle ('come for the breasts, stay for the brains') break it — while the four guys fail every 'real man' stereotype beside Penny's muscle-bound exes like Zack. Gender emerges as an artificial label that limits everyone, and seeing that would be the show's ultimate change through parody.

mill-subjection-women.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick
mill-subjection-women.title: Notes
mill-subjection-women.relation: Gutwald takes seven-year-old Charlotte Benjamin's viral letter ('all the girls did was sit at home, go to the beach, and shop... but the boys went on adventures, worked, saved people') to argue the LEGO Friends theme is Wollstonecraftian 'friendly sexism' — revering girls as pretty play-things in a house-bound Heartlake City rather than oppressing them outright. Following Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes a woman' and her point that men describe the world from their own perspective, plus Mill's Subjection of Women observation that argument alone cannot beat a 'mass of feeling', she explains how pinkified toy segregation feeds implicit bias, schemas, and stereotype threat in both girls and boys. Her fix is structural: make Friends bricks and mini-dolls compatible with the rest of the system ('Let the Friends go to Space!') and return to the gender-neutral 1981 'What it is is beautiful' ad.

mill-subjection-women.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am
mill-subjection-women.title: TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am
mill-subjection-women.relation: Nancy Kang argues tattoos can function within a liberatory feminist ideology, accentuating rather than diminishing femininity by exposing the differential treatment of tattooed women. She surveys radical, Marxist, liberal and corporeal feminism (invoking Aristotle's dismissal of women, Mill's Subjection of Women, and Gramsci's hegemony), then reads pop-culture cases – Crash's tattooed Latino worker, Black Swan's Lily, the Perry 'pricks as needles' sexualization, carnival 'Tattooed Ladies' like Irene Woodward marked 'by the father's hand,' and the McGee/Bullock/Kat Von D scandal – to show corporeal feminism treats tattooing as a risky, self-owning revolutionary act.

dialectic-of-sex.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
dialectic-of-sex.title: 3 On the Origin of the Family
dialectic-of-sex.relation: The chapter compares the liberal contract theorists with Engels (building on Morgan's Ancient Society) on the origin of the patriarchal monogamous family: Hobbes derives sovereign-husbanded 'little monarchies' from a state of nature in which women are men's equals, a derivation Susan Okin shows is contradictory; Locke grounds conjugal society in a voluntary compact with the husband as 'abler and stronger' last determiner, yet leaves women excluded from the social contract; Rousseau pairs passionate economic equality with some of the most sexist writing in Western thought, including fear of wives' sexual power in Emile. Against these static philosophies Engels gives a historical-materialist account in which the overthrow of mother right - the 'world historical defeat of the female sex' - followed from private property and inheritance, turning the bourgeois wife into a proletarian or prostitute while opening 'sex love' to the propertyless, and prescribing women's return to the labor force, socialized child-care, industrialized housework and easy divorce.
