Against Finch's 'moral math' and Dormer's own 'the end justifies the means' rationalizations, the chapter argues that the moral value of actions lies in intentions, motives, and character—Aquinas on what makes a killing an accident, Kant on being worthy of happiness rather than securing it. Dormer's sleeplessness becomes evidence of a conscience still alive, and his struggle figures what Kierkegaard calls purity of heart, willing one thing, with Socrates's refusal to escape in the Crito as the model of integrity. In dying to protect Ellie from losing her way, Dormer regains himself through commitment to another person, the Levinasian point that personhood is fulfilled only in and through other persons.

iron-cage-rationalization.title: The Vale of Top Hats
iron-cage-rationalization.relation: Decker reads The Prestige's duplication as duplicity: the vale of top hats and the tank-preserved drowned doubles frame an argument that modern stage magic, and Nolan's filmmaking itself, run on the audience's willing self-deception—Robert-Houdin's 'clever man' who pays to be fooled and Nietzsche's artist 'accustomed to lying' meeting man's 'invincible inclination to allow himself to be deceived.' Weber's rationalization and the 'iron cage' supply the chapter's central allegory: Tesla's machine, unlike stage illusion, actually works, embodying a modernity of instrumental cost-benefit calculation in which progress demands ever-costlier sacrifice, making Borden the 'specialist without spirit' and Angier the 'sensualist without heart.' Benjamin's work of art in the age of mechanical reproduction dissolves the question of which Angier is the authentic original, since reproducibility abolishes authenticity and leaves Angier trading the intrinsic value of personhood for transcendence at the price of drowning himself nightly. Benjamin's dictum that every document of culture is also a document of barbarism ties the magicians' art, and Western technological progress from Edison's feuds to the coming World War, to its hidden human cost.

fabula-syuzhet.title: “Are You Watching Closely ”
fabula-syuzhet.relation: Knight and McKnight analyze how Nolan's early films withhold narrative transparency: Doodlebug's regress of killers, Following's framing device that ends with Cobb vanishing into a crowd, Memento's reverse chronology, and The Prestige's twin frames of top hats and drowned doubles all force viewers to build and revise hypotheses about what happened, when, and who is responsible. Because actions cannot be morally evaluated until we know who performed them and why, the chapter ties narrative comprehension to moral judgment—Leonard's confabulated revenge and inability to recognize his own self-deception, Dormer's ambiguous redemption, and Ellie's unresolved choice over the bullet. The Prestige's doubles raise the identity question the authors gloss with Parfit's teletransporter—perhaps it does not matter which Angier survives—while Cutter's helping Borden kill Caldlow enacts Francis Bacon's 'wild justice' that the law cannot provide. The chapter closes on Nolan as auteur, whose self-conscious framing devices and play of masks make 'Are you watching closely?' at once the film's theme and its admonition to the viewer.

plato-phaedrus-writing.title: Remembering, Reminding, and Forgetting with Leonard Shelby
plato-phaedrus-writing.relation: Dennis Knepp reads Leonard Shelby's Polaroids, notes, and tattoos through Charles Sanders Peirce's triadic semiotics, showing how each memento works at once as icon, index, and symbol (Firstness, Secondness, Thirdness), as when the Discount Inn photo resembles the motel, is causally produced by the camera pointed at it, and needs Leonard to interpret its written words. He then argues Memento is less a detective story than a fable of self-deception: the printed word's permanence lends Leonard's tattooed list of 'THE FACTS' an illusion of absolute authority, down to the fatal mis-tattoo of Teddy's license plate (SG137IU copied as SG1371U). The chapter ends by reading Plato's Phaedrus tale of Theuth and Thamus - writing as a potion for reminding, not remembering, that breeds only the appearance of wisdom - as an ancient diagnosis of how Leonard's external signs deceive him.

intellectual-virtues.title: Inception and Perception
intellectual-virtues.relation: Jamie Carlin Watson uses Inception's dream thieves to stage the dream argument for skepticism - from Socrates' puzzle to Theaetetus and Descartes's Meditations, with Sextus Empiricus's diversity-of-perception argument - and contends that totems cannot debunk it, since even Arthur's loaded die and Cobb's top cannot rule out being in your own dream, where your subconscious knows how the totem behaves. Against both believing as normal and Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment, the chapter turns to William James's will to believe (live versus dead hypotheses) and to intellectual virtues drawn from Zagzebski and Kornblith: beliefs can be valuable for reasons other than truth. The upshot is that Cobb, Arthur, and the twelve shared-dream sleepers in Yusuf's basement can believe well even if they cannot believe truly - which is why Cobb's walking away from the spinning top at the end can be read as believing carefully rather than certainly.

lacan-gaze.title: Engaging Otherness through Following
lacan-gaze.relation: Louis-Paul Willis reads Following as the prototype of Nolan's 'mind-tricking spectatorship,' where fragmented, multi-strand editing and staged details (the box of secrets, the hammer conversation, the near-identical glove shots) reveal to viewers that the film itself has taken their desire into account all along. Using Jacques Lacan's distinction between the look and the gaze, and the objet a as object-cause of desire, he argues that Bill's voyeuristic quest for the Other's hidden kernel - Cobb's 'everyone has a box' scene - is doomed because the voyeur becomes the viewed: the subject of the look becomes the object of the gaze, just as Bill the follower turns out to be the one followed and framed for murder. Bill's failure is thus the cinematic spectator's failure - there is no passive vantage point exempt from the Other's gaze.

hegel-substance-subject.title: We Are the Change That We Seek
hegel-substance-subject.relation: Todd McGowan argues Interstellar enacts Hegel's critique of substance: the NASA scientists' 'they' who supposedly placed the wormhole is a Kantian thing-in-itself - the unknown deified by ignorance - until the Tesseract reveals that Cooper himself, and future humanity, are both Murph's 'ghost' and the 'they' ('We brought ourselves'). Against Spinoza's single substance and Leibniz's windowless monads, the film teaches that substance is subject, freeing Cooper and Murph to act and to change the past through retroactive causality, which the chapter connects to Sartre on the past's fixedness and Walter Benjamin's critique of historicist causality. Professor Brand's Plan A lie and Dr. Mann's self-exculpating murder show the ethical catastrophe of claiming a substantial, subject-transcending standpoint, while Murph - who treats her 'ghost' as just another subject rather than a supernatural substance - is the film's true hero.

praxis-vs-poiesis.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
praxis-vs-poiesis.title: 4. Punk as Praxis
praxis-vs-poiesis.relation: Smith argues punk's heart is neither a playlist nor an attitude but praxis in Aristotle's sense: autotelic, self-directed activity, which Heidegger read existentially as authentic existence and Arendt politicized as communicative action in a vibrant public sphere. Punk's 'no-saying' - to employment ('Career Opportunities'), commercialization ('EMI'), and entertainment - plus its affirmations of speaking in your own voice, forming bands and labels, and the fanzine/record-shop public sphere exemplify praxis, while post-punk's technical refinement around Factory Records and the Lesser Free Trade Hall gigs marks a shift from praxis back to Aristotle's poiesis.

strong-vs-weak-nihilism.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
strong-vs-weak-nihilism.title: 6. When Punks Grow Up
strong-vs-weak-nihilism.relation: Meagher asks whether punks can mature, arguing via Sartre and Beauvoir that punk revolts against the 'spirit of seriousness' - the bad faith of treating values as externally imposed by God, law, or convention - and against the weak nihilism that merely abandons valuing after serious values fail. Following Devon Johnson's Black nihilism distinction, mature punk is strong nihilism: destroying decadent (Euromodern, colonial) values in order to create new ones, building scenes, labels, and institutions for future generations, fighting for others' freedom and decolonization as Arendtian politics, and - with Nietzsche's dead God and Crass's 1978 declaration - being willing to proclaim even punk itself dead.

three-metamorphoses.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
three-metamorphoses.title: 12. Early Punk and the Dionysian Lion-Child
three-metamorphoses.relation: Rentmeester reads early punk through Nietzsche's three metamorphoses of the spirit: the Sex Pistols' 'God Save the Queen' (the Thames boat arrest during the Silver Jubilee) is the lion destroying worn-out values, while the Stooges' 'I Wanna Be Your Dog' and Raw Power embody the child's sacred Yes, making punk a hybrid Dionysian lion-child. Punk is Dionysian rather than Apollonian - raw instinct over measured restraint, Iggy Pop's self-mutilation and the Gzowski interview - with 'camelistic' pop and soft rock critiqued via Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, and Sid Vicious's violence named as Freud's death drive.

politics-of-disaffection.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
politics-of-disaffection.title: 16. Punk Politics
politics-of-disaffection.relation: Prinz surveys punk's political paradox - anarchist punks from Crass and Rock Against Racism to straight edge versus the fascist flirtation of skinheads, the National Front, and Skrewdriver's 'White Power' - and tests four candidate unifiers (anti-authoritarianism, nihilism, individualism, and McLaren's politics of boredom), finding each one-sided. He proposes instead a politics of disaffection: alienation and negative affect toward the status quo that spans anarchist, Nazi, and apolitical punks alike, making punk a confrontational counterculture that says 'Fuck you' with a self-satisfied sneer, even if it never ended a war like the hippies claimed to.

bricolage.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
bricolage.title: 18. Wartime Propaganda as Punk Critique
bricolage.relation: Karen Fournier reads Julien Temple's 1979 film short Punk Can Take It as a bricolage of the 1940 wartime propaganda film London Can Take It!, hijacking its searchlights, steel helmets, and BBC announcer John Snagge's narration to recast the story as class warfare: the wartime 'people's army' produced a generation of working-class punks betrayed by postwar promises. Scenes like mannequins attacking a window dresser, tuxedoed Oxford-Cambridge types invading the pit, and a punk mob toppling a Johnny Rotten statue dramatize the real enemy: a corporate consumer culture that annexes the subculture and reduces it to mass-produced 'punk' products. The chapter argues that punk film, like Jamie Reid's safety-pinned Union Jack, turns the dominant culture's own tokens against it.

affect.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
affect.title: 19. Punk Consciousness and Class Consciousness
affect.relation: Tiffany Montoya reads punk lyrics and the DIY scene through Marx, Gramsci, and Lukacs, finding an emerging class consciousness in three stages: nihilistic discontent ('TV Party', 'Lost in the Supermarket'), systemic awareness of exploitation (Bad Religion's 'Suffer'), and full revolutionary consciousness with proletarian agency ('Class War', the Suicide Machines' 'Strike'). She shows how musical devices - Oi!-style gang vocals, work-song rhythms, the industrial drumming of Flogging Molly's 'The Power's Out' - create affective unity like military cadence, while mutual aid (Kropotkin) and do-it-yourself production make the scene a 'proletarian culture'. The chapter closes on Gramsci's warning that the capitalist state appropriates subversive culture (corporate festival sponsors, Hot Topic punk), asking whether punk will keep its vanguard or become 'rock for sustainable capitalism'.

labeling-theory.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
labeling-theory.title: 20. Punks Pissing People Off
labeling-theory.relation: Juneko Robinson mixes memoir of circa-1980 anti-punk violence (routine beatings, the murder of Brian Deneke) with Sartrean existentialism to explain why punks 'pissed people off': punk's confrontational appearance exposed the contingency and hypocrisy of mainstream values, forcing others to take responsibility for them. Using Sartre's keyhole-peeper example from Being and Nothingness and No Exit's 'hell is other people', she argues that harassers lived in bad faith, dependent on how others see them, while punks were the witnesses who objectified the mainstream rather than the deviants being watched. Howard Becker's moral entrepreneurs explain the 'de-punking' panics and psychiatric commitments of kids who merely dressed weird, and Marmysz's 'nihilistic incongruity' shows punk converting society's hypocrisy into self-legislated virtue.

matilda-effect.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
matilda-effect.title: 24. ReMENbering the Punk Movement
matilda-effect.relation: Georgina Mills argues that remembering punk through its men only - the British Library display naming the Sex Pistols, the Clash, and the Buzzcocks but no women - is more than the Matilda effect: it retroactively filters the whole movement through patriarchal norms. Using Iris Marion Young's concept of marginalization, she contends that as punk gained mainstream status the women who embodied its rebellion (the Slits banned from hotels on the White Riot tour, X-Ray Spex, Siouxsie) were pushed back to the margins of a movement they helped forge. Erasing them distorts punk itself, since women's twofold rebellion - against the establishment and against feminine compliance - and punk's DIY inclusivity were integral to it, as the misreading of Poly Styrene's 'Oh Bondage, Up Yours!' as mere shock shows.

paradox-of-tragedy.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
paradox-of-tragedy.title: 27. The Filth and the Fury
paradox-of-tragedy.relation: Greg Littmann asks why punk audiences enjoy songs wallowing in misery, boredom, anger, and disgust ('I Wanna Be Well', 'God Save the Queen', 'Bodies'), framing this as the old puzzle of dark art that extends from opera to Game of Thrones. Aristotle supplies the first answer: catharsis - purging pity and fear by feeling them, with Politics Book VIII adding that music relieves the pains of toil - explains why blasting angry punk vents frustration, especially at authority we cannot openly complain about. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' then proposes that artistic beauty converts subordinate negative emotions into intensified pleasure, but Littmann argues the conversion model is incomplete since lesser emotions do not always strengthen greater ones, concluding only that a love of dark punk is no sign of degeneracy.

value-pluralism.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
value-pluralism.title: 31. Out of Step with the World
value-pluralism.relation: Lustila and Olsthoorn ask what makes hardcore punk's cultural nonconformity ethically valuable, distinguishing it from Kantian autonomy (self-governance via Korsgaard) and Taylor-style authenticity using lyrics by Void, Negative Approach, and Burn. They offer two justifications: a contingent one, on which countercultures like vegan straight edge replace harmful mainstream norms (though hardline militancy fails the test), and a general one drawn from Mill's On Liberty - even the mere example of nonconformity, from punks and posers alike, enlarges the space of 'experiments of living' and pluralism everyone needs against the tyranny of majority opinion. Berlin's value pluralism backs the general value: countercultures are 'a wrench in the system' that multiplies the models of living available to all.

russells-teapot.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal
russells-teapot.title: Christmas Philosophy for Everyone
russells-teapot.relation: Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.

holes.name: Instrumental Rationality (means-end reasoning)
holes.what: Reasoning that evaluates an action solely by whether it is a reliable and feasible means to the agent's desired ends, independent of whether those ends or the act are moral.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire verdict on George's 'do the opposite' strategy is a decision-theoretic test of reliability and feasibility (minimal/medial/maximal rationality) that no existing slug covers.
holes.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Slovenian philosopher (b. 1949) fusing Marx, Hegel and Lacan; theorist of 'performative ideology' and cynical distance in The Sublime Object of Ideology.
holes.why: Chapter 20's framework is Žižek's account of ideology: we know the J. Peterman catalogue is fiction ('fetishists in practice, not in theory') yet it still regulates our buying.
holes.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst (1901-1981) of the Symbolic Order, the Imaginary, and the subject as lack ('reality is structured like a fiction').
holes.why: Chapter 20 grounds its claim that the self is an ideological fiction with nothing behind the mask in Lacan's Symbolic Order and the empty 'subject par excellence.'
holes.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

holes.name: Philosophy of Humor (the comic)
holes.what: Theories of what makes things funny - incongruity, superiority, relief - and the contrast between comedy and tragedy as ways of seeing.
holes.why: Chapter 21 advances its own humor theory - we laugh at the significance of the insignificant and cry at the insignificance of the significant - and the taxonomy has no humor or aesthetics-of-the-comic concept.
holes.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

holes.name: The Duty to Rescue (bad Samaritan laws)
holes.what: The claim that morality and law may require positive aid to those in peril (positive rights and easy rescues), not merely non-interference.
holes.why: Chapter 25's reading of the finale's Good Samaritan law turns on whether bystanders like the gang owe a duty of easy rescue, with supererogation vs the minimally decent Samaritan - no existing slug covers this.
holes.book: 001 - Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing

holes.name: Epistemic Contextualism
holes.what: The view that the standards governing knowledge attributions shift with context, so the skeptic's certainty requirement binds only in special philosophical settings.
holes.why: Chapter 17's main reply to the Matrix scenario is that Descartes's infallibility standard holds in the seminar but not in everyday life, where we genuinely know we are not dreaming.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Reductive Materialism (mind-brain identity)
holes.what: The view that mental states are identical with (reducible to) physical brain states, so experience is fully explainable in physical terms.
holes.why: Barwick's essay argues the whole premise of The Matrix presupposes Morpheus's reductive materialism ('real is simply electrical signals interpreted by your brain') and that this doctrine, once examined, makes the film's scenario impossible.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Eliminative Materialism
holes.what: The view that there are no mental states at all: folk-psychological talk of beliefs and experiences is a bankrupt framework to be eliminated in favor of neuroscience.
holes.why: Chapter 44 tests whether the film's authors might be eliminativists and argues the Matrix would be pointless if no experiences existed, forcing the essay toward the intentionality of consciousness instead.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Richard Taylor
holes.what: Twentieth-century American metaphysician whose work redefines fatalism as the thesis that whatever happens is unavoidable and links foreknowledge to the futility of deliberation.
holes.why: Chapter 50's account of the Oracle's fate is built directly on Taylor's quoted definition of fatalism, applied to the prophecies in The Matrix.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: The crisis condition in which life is seen as having no ultimate purpose, value, or meaning - for Nietzsche the aftermath of the death of God, to be passed through toward affirmation rather than dwelt in.
holes.why: Chapter 84 defines Hibbs's whole essay - The Matrix as a replay of Enlightenment-modernity debates that make liberal modernity 'a potential source of nihilism, a human existence void of any ultimate purpose' - and chapters 85-87 ask whether the film escapes it, but the taxonomy has no nihilism slug.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
holes.what: Russian novelist (1821-1881) whose Notes from Underground polemicizes against rationalist utopian socialism and defends irrational, spiteful free will against scientific determinism.
holes.why: Chapters 85-87 build their entire reading of The Matrix on Dostoevsky's underground man - the piano-key metaphor, hyperconscious paralysis, and reductio ad nihilum of Enlightenment social science - yet he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Religious Pluralism
holes.what: The family of views (extreme, fundamental-teachings, cafeteria, and Hick's transcendental pluralism) that many or all religions are equally valid routes to the same ultimate reality.
holes.why: Chapters 62-63 are devoted to defining four varieties of religious pluralism, testing the film's syncretic 'Neo-pluralism' against them, and answering pluralist objections to exclusivism; no taxonomy slug names this concept, and 'faith-vs-reason' only covers the justification side.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we have genuine emotional responses to characters and events we know do not exist, although emotion seemingly requires belief in the reality of its object.
holes.why: Chapter 94 states the paradox's three premises and canvasses solutions (Coleridge's suspension of disbelief, Walton's make-believe) as the engine of Worth's essay on why viewers of The Matrix respond to a world they know is staged; the taxonomy has no philosophy-of-art concept for it.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Frankfurt School critical theorist who co-authored the Dialectic of Enlightenment analysis of the culture industry as mass deception.
holes.why: Chapter 113 cites Horkheimer and Adorno's culture-industry essay to ask whether The Matrix is itself part of the capitalist dream-world it tells viewers to wake up from.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Guy Debord
holes.what: Situationist theorist whose The Society of the Spectacle holds that social life now presents itself as an immense accumulation of images.
holes.why: Chapter 116 quotes Debord's spectacle thesis as the frame for arguing that the Matrix is a media-saturated pseudo-world that improves on reality.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Slovenian philosopher fusing Lacanian psychoanalysis, Hegel and Marxism to analyze ideology in politics and popular culture.
holes.why: Chapters 119-126 are Žižek's essay reading the Matrix as the big Other, the two sides of perversion, and the screen of the Real.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst whose concepts of the big Other, the Real, alienation and jouissance reworked Freud through structural linguistics.
holes.why: Chapter 121 identifies the Matrix with Lacan's big Other and reads the desert of the real as the inconsistency the symbolic order conceals.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Claude Lévi-Strauss
holes.what: French structural anthropologist who analyzed symbolic systems, myth and kinship, including the Winnebago village drawings and the zero-institution.
holes.why: Chapter 123 builds its account of the Real as anamorphic distortion of a traumatic social antagonism on Lévi-Strauss's Winnebago example and zero-institution.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Nicolas Malebranche
holes.what: Cartesian occasionalist philosopher who held that God alone genuinely causes, coordinating relations between mind and body.
holes.why: Chapter 125 argues the Matrix is best modeled as Malebranche's occasionalist God, the third substance coordinating the virtual world with plugged-in bodies.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: Occasionalism
holes.what: The doctrine that created things have no genuine causal power; God coordinates mind-body and body-body events merely on the occasion of each.
holes.why: Chapter 125 uses occasionalism as the best conceptual apparatus for virtual reality, where the computer coordinates a player's intentions with simulated events.
holes.book: 003 - The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real

holes.name: The Banking Model of Education (critical pedagogy)
holes.what: Freire's critique of schooling as depositing information into passive students, reproducing control instead of liberation.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses the banking model as the modernist foil that Buffy's collaborative, inquiry-based knowledge-making in the library and 'Primeval' subverts.
holes.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed attacks authoritarian, dehumanizing education.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames its whole case for postmodern education beyond control through Freire's banking model versus dialogic, relational learning.
holes.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis, theorist of an unconscious whose desires are opaque rather than rationally explicable.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explains Willow's magic addiction and world-ending break through Freud's unconscious, pleasure principle, and 'enigmatic signifiers' (via Jonathan Lear).
holes.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Actions that are morally praiseworthy but not required, such that omitting them is not blameworthy.
holes.why: Chapter 21's second objection to virtue ethics is that Buffy's heroism is supererogatory, so ordinary people need not do what she would do.
holes.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale

holes.name: Fascism
holes.what: A mass political movement that seeks to renew the nation by forging a superior citizen in the crucible of war, celebrating combat, racial purity, spectacular heroism, and authority derived from an ancient order.
holes.why: Chapter 26's whole argument defines Buffy's slaying, demon racism, and ritual combat as proto-fascist and imagines 'brownskirts' death squads, but taxonomy.json has no fascism concept — Arendt's totalitarianism is a different frame the chapter never invokes.
holes.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose 1912 essay 'On the Universal Tendency to Debasement in the Sphere of Love' holds that affection and sexual desire are psychically incompatible (incest barrier, Oedipus complex, Madonna/whore split).
holes.why: Chapter 34's entire argument explains Buffy's popularity through Freud's debasement theory — Angel as forbidden object, Xander's overvaluation of Buffy, and the show's reinforcement of the forbiddenness of sex — and Freud appears nowhere in taxonomy.json.
holes.book: 004 - Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose 1927 essay 'Fetishism' explains desire fixated on a separated part-object as a defense against loss and the fear of the female.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its entire reading of the One Ring as a fetish object (and of Shelob as a vagina dentata) on Freud's theory of fetishism, and taxonomy has no Freud.
holes.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

holes.name: The Thing (Ding): 'Thinging gathers'
holes.what: Heidegger's account of the thing as a gathering that assembles people, world, and use - against treating objects as either fetishized commodities or inert matter.
holes.why: Chapter 14 leans on Heidegger's essay on the Thing ('Thinging gathers') to contrast Middle-earth's gift economy with the fetishized Ring, a concept distinct from his technology critique.
holes.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

holes.name: Evil as Privation of Good (privatio boni)
holes.what: Augustine's doctrine that evil has no independent existence but is a lack or corruption of good, as darkness is a lack of light.
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues at length that Tolkien's evil (Ringwraiths as nothingness, the Eye as 'a window into nothing') is precisely privation rather than a Manichean force - a specific concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

holes.name: Modernism
holes.what: The cultural-philosophical mood, crystallized after World War I, that old certainties and traditions are obsolete and the new is always better - 'all that is solid melts into air'.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, staging it in Saruman's and Denethor's despair and in the Ring's promise of remaking the world by power.
holes.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

holes.name: Dependent Origination (pratityasamutpada)
holes.what: The Buddhist doctrine that all things arise and exist only in mutual dependence, with no isolated, self-existing entities.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses dependent origination as the Buddhist parallel to the way Tolkien's peoples are shaped by and shape their environments, a canonical doctrine the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

holes.name: Eucatastrophe
holes.what: Tolkien's coinage for the sudden joyous 'turn' at the end of a true fairy tale - a miraculous, unmerited reprieve that gives a fleeting glimpse of Joy beyond the world's walls.
holes.why: Chapter 31 argues the whole trilogy is built as an epic fairy story whose Mount Doom ending is a eucatastrophe echoing Christian eschatological hope; no taxonomy concept covers it.
holes.book: 005 - The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All

holes.name: Gaston Bachelard
holes.what: French philosopher whose The Poetics of Space treats the home as 'our first universe', analyzing intimate space through a dialectic of shelter and threat.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of home plate, ballparks, and fan communities runs on Bachelard's dialectic of home and his 'well-determined centers of revery'.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: The Uncanny (unheimlich)
holes.what: Freud's notion of the terrifying that leads back to the long-familiar: the un-home-like that haunts the home.
holes.why: Chapter 10 explains why home plate feels both welcoming and threatening by applying the uncanny to batting and to scoring 'safe at home'.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: French theorist of sacrifice and language who defines sacrifice as an offering that creates Meaning for the Other and for the social group.
holes.why: Chapter 14 opens and structures its account of the sacrifice bunt on Kristeva's definition of sacrifice as a meaning-creating, community-forming offering.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Constitutive Rules (rules that define a game)
holes.what: Rules (Searle's 'X counts as Y in context C') that create the very activity they govern, as the rules of a game do, rather than regulating a pre-existing practice.
holes.why: Chapter 16 turns on rules that constitute baseball (players do not know them, they contradict each other), and chapters 19-20 ask when breaking them is cheating rather than strategy.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Ronald Dworkin
holes.what: Legal philosopher who held that law includes moral principles beyond its rules and that adjudication should interpret the practice in its best light ('law as integrity').
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Dworkin's integrity to justify MacPhail's pine-tar ruling, umpire Curry's 1887 call, and principled umpire discretion in hard cases.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Philosopher of language who analyzed performative utterances: uses of words (promising, 'I do', 'You're out') that bring facts into being.
holes.why: Chapter 17 analyzes umpire calls as performatives that also report witnessed events, which grounds when calls can be true or false and hence corrected.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: The Lusory Goal (Bernard Suits)
holes.what: Bernard Suits's account of games as attempting to win by overcoming voluntarily accepted obstacles (lusory goals) through limited means (lusory means).
holes.why: Chapter 17's 'first principle of games adjudication' is formulated in lusory-goal and lusory-means terms to decide hard umpiring cases.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: French political thinker whose Democracy in America praised democratic equality while warning of majority tyranny and democratic leveling into conformity.
holes.why: Chapter 22's thesis that dissenting Yankees are good for democracy is argued almost entirely through Tocqueville's analysis of majority rule and conformity.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Annette Baier
holes.what: Moral philosopher who argued that morality is grounded in trust and solidarity, modeled on a child's well-placed trust in her mother, rather than in abstract principles.
holes.why: Chapter 23 builds its account of baseball as a public moral community on Baier's claim that trust is where all our moral ladders begin.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Originator of the theory of evolution by natural selection, whose own account of human development (cultural rather than genetic evolution in The Descent of Man) diverged sharply from the 'Social Darwinism' built on his name.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues the Negro Leagues refuted Social Darwinism precisely by invoking Darwin's actual view that cultural, not genetic, development explains human achievement.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Bushido (the Way of the Warrior)
holes.what: The Japanese samurai ethical code stressing loyalty, self-denial, austerity, relentless training, and honor.
holes.why: Chapter 29's central question is whether Japanese baseball is genuinely shaped by Bushido's resolve and 'training of death' or whether that is an over-generalization about Japanese culture.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Games as Artificial Tests (lusory goals)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-sport view (associated with Bernard Suits) that games are rule-built artificial problems whose point is the mutual, appropriately difficult testing of skills.
holes.why: Chapter 34's verdict on the intentional walk rests entirely on whether walking Barry Bonds avoids the game's test or merely shifts it to other players.
holes.book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

holes.name: Sympathy for the Devil (moral allegiance to fictional villains)
holes.what: The puzzle in aesthetics of why audiences feel sympathy or pro-attitudes toward fictional characters whose real-world counterparts they would abhor, and whether that is morally dangerous.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is entirely structured around this puzzle - rejecting fascination, wish-fulfillment and identification explanations in favor of an 'alliance' theory - and no taxonomy concept covers audience response to immoral fiction.
holes.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

holes.name: Plato's Critique of Poetry (art, emotion and moral corruption)
holes.what: Plato's Republic X charge that dramatic poetry nourishes unruly emotions by getting audiences to sympathize with characters, thereby corrupting character and justifying the poets' exile.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its whole argument on Republic 605c-606d (quoted at length) and pairs it with Tolstoy's What Is Art?, but taxonomy has no Plato-aesthetics concept, only his ethics and metaphysics.
holes.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

holes.name: Tragedy and Catharsis (the Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's theory of tragedy: pity and fear, the hero 'in-between', tragic flaw (hamartia), reversal and recognition, and the catharsis of emotions.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues Tony Soprano is an Aristotelian tragic hero using these exact Poetics devices, and the taxonomy's Aristotle entries cover only his ethics, metaphysics and biology.
holes.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

holes.name: J.L. Austin (speech act theory)
holes.what: Oxford ordinary-language philosopher whose How to Do Things with Words founded speech act theory: performatives and the locution/illocution/perlocution distinction (developed on intention-recognition by P.F. Strawson).
holes.why: Chapter 29 is built entirely on Austin's framework, using it to decode mob orders, threats, oaths and Livia's manipulations, and taxonomy's philosophy-of-language entries (Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Quine, Kripke) do not include him.
holes.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

holes.name: Self-Knowledge (perceptual vs constitutive models; self-blindness)
holes.what: The epistemology of knowing one's own mind: whether self-knowledge works by inner sense (perceptual model) or is constitutive of mental states, whether it can be fallible, and Shoemaker's 'self-blindness' question.
holes.why: Chapter 30 ('Is Tony Soprano Self-Blind?') applies exactly this debate - Descartes's infallibility, the two models, brute error - to Tony's denial and self-misreading, and taxonomy lacks any self-knowledge slug.
holes.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

holes.name: Dante Alighieri
holes.what: Medieval poet-philosopher whose Divine Comedy, especially the Inferno, organizes sin into circles (incontinence, violence, fraud) and supplies a Christian moral geography of Hell.
holes.why: Chapter 32 uses Dante's Inferno as its entire framework - ranking the Sopranos cast into the circles, contrasting fraud with violence, and invoking Guido da Montefeltro - and taxonomy has no entry for Dante.
holes.book: 007 - The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

holes.name: Authorial Intention and the Intentional Fallacy
holes.what: The debate over whether an artist's actual intentions may settle or constrain the correct interpretation of a work (the 'intentional fallacy').
holes.why: Chapter 13 grounds its 'pragmatic optimism' reading in interpretive criteria — avoid biographical fallacy and eisegesis, and don't override Allen's own statements (against Sander Lee) without overwhelming argument.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist whose 'The Death of the Author' holds that a text's unity lies in its destination, not its origin — 'it is language which speaks, not the author'.
holes.why: Chapter 15 claims Allen's persona-filled prose exemplifies Barthes's theses and uses them to block biographical readings of Allen's stories and essays.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Wolfgang Iser
holes.what: Phenomenological literary theorist whose 'implied reader' actively fills a text's gaps and indeterminacies to compose the 'virtual text'.
holes.why: Chapter 15 applies Iser's gap-filling reader to Allen's non sequiturs, arguing that in Allen 'the gaps themselves are the meaning'.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Stanley Fish
holes.what: Literary and legal theorist who holds that 'interpretive communities' — shared reading strategies, not isolated texts or individuals — produce a work's meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 15's title concept is Fish's interpretive communities, used to explain which readers can 'get' Allen's allusions, genres, and Jewish humor.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Reader-Response Criticism
holes.what: Family of 1970s literary theories on which a work's meaning is produced in the act of reading, guided by the text but completed by readers.
holes.why: Chapter 15 uses reader-response theory to argue Allen's texts trap pretentious critics while still requiring readerly participation without runaway subjectivism.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Aesthetic Appreciation
holes.what: The philosophical account of what genuinely appreciating an artwork involves — here, a balanced engagement of intellect and emotion in which neither predominates.
holes.why: Chapter 16 builds a theory of aesthetic appreciation out of Allen's films, treating over-intellectualized and purely emotional responses as sham substitutes for it.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Incongruity Theory of Humor
holes.what: Schopenhauer's account of laughter as the sudden apprehension of an incongruity between a concept and the real object unexpectedly subsumed under it.
holes.why: Chapter 19 adopts this theory as its explanatory framework for how Annie Hall's jokes (subtitles, 'love fades', 'dynamite ham') deliver philosophical social analysis.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Postmodern Irony and the Great Divide
holes.what: The postmodern attitude (Eco, Huyssen) of consciously reworking the great models of high modernism with irony instead of naive sincerity, eroding the divide between high art and mass culture.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Allen's Bergman allusions in Another Woman and Deconstructing Harry as ironic 'recompositions' positioned between modernism and postmodernism via Huyssen's After the Great Divide and Eco's Barbara Cartland example, and no taxonomy slug covers allusion, irony, or the modernism/postmodernism debate in art.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Logical Positivism (verifiability theory of meaning)
holes.what: The Vienna Circle/Ayer doctrine that only tautologies and empirically verifiable statements are meaningful, dismissing ethics, religion, and metaphysics as nonsense.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds the character of Leopold Sturgis, the analytic philosopher whose empiricism underwrites the film's hedonism and whom Allen mocks, directly on Ayer's verifiability theory, which the taxonomy lacks despite having its critics.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Laughter and the Comic (Bergson)
holes.what: Bergson's theory that the comic arises from 'the mechanical encrusted upon the living' and that the comic person is invisible to himself while remaining visible to the world.
holes.why: Chapter 24 applies Bergson's Laughter to explain why Lester in Crimes and Misdemeanors is a comic character incapable of seeing his own defect, a philosophy-of-humor tool absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

holes.name: Alexander of Aphrodisias
holes.what: Second-century Aristotelian commentator whose On Fate argues against the view that prophecies like Apollo's to Laius cause the events they predict.
holes.why: Chapter 32 quotes Alexander at length to argue that Trelawney's prophecy revealed rather than caused Voldemort's choice of Harry, so the source of the argument needs its own slug.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Truth in Fiction
holes.what: The problem of what facts are true within a fictional world and what determines them - the text, readers, authorial intent, or genre conventions.
holes.why: Chapter 78 introduces Rowling's 'Dumbledore is gay' announcement as an instance of this problem, and Gendler's entire essay is organized around answering it.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Authorial Intent (intentionalism vs anti-intentionalism)
holes.what: The debate over whether an author's intentions fix a text's meaning or whether interpretation belongs to readers and public language (Wimsatt, Beardsley, Barthes vs Hirsch).
holes.why: Chapter 80 weighs anti-intentionalist critics against E. D. Hirsch's intentionalism to decide whether Rowling can settle what is true about Dumbledore after the series ends.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: German philosopher (1900-2002) of philosophical hermeneutics who held that all understanding proceeds from prejudgments and tradition.
holes.why: Chapter 96 (with 97 and 101) builds Garver's whole account of Dudley's and Harry's misreading and correction on Gadamer's notions of prejudgments and tradition.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Philosophical Hermeneutics (prejudgment and tradition)
holes.what: The theory that interpretation always starts from prejudgments shaped by personal and cultural memory, which understanding must expose to correction by what is interpreted.
holes.why: Chapters 96-102 apply this framework of prejudgments, tradition, and correction to how Dudley, Harry, and the reader come to know, and no taxonomy concept covers it.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: The Argument from Reason
holes.what: C. S. Lewis's argument (later reformulated by Alvin Plantinga) that if naturalism were true and thought a merely subjective event, reason could not reliably deliver truth, so rationality points to a rational ground beyond nature.
holes.why: Chapter 107 interprets Dumbledore's 'in your head but real' line through the Inklings' argument from reason as the explanation of why a mental experience can be genuinely real.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Logos (divine reason pervading reality)
holes.what: The doctrine, Greek and Stoic in origin and completed in John 1:1's identification of the logos with Christ, that a divine rational principle shapes and sustains the cosmos.
holes.why: Chapter 108 explains how human reason can be 'in the head' yet track reality by treating it as participation in this cosmic Logos, which Rowling hints at with the King's Cross setting.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Melanie Klein
holes.what: Psychoanalytic theorist whose integrity objection holds that mature moral reform must preserve continuity with the self that did the wrong rather than imagining rebirth as a new person.
holes.why: Chapter 134's central objection to the phoenix model of remorse-and-rebirth is Klein's insistence on identity over time, tested against Snape's failure to integrate his past.
holes.book: 009 - Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts

holes.name: Peter Abelard
holes.what: Twelfth-century philosopher-theologian whose Moral Influence Theory understands Christ's death as the supreme revelation of God's love that awakens love in the sinner and transforms them morally.
holes.why: Chapter 12 presents Abelard's view as one of the three atonement theories Gibson's film weaves together (embodied in the transformed Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, and the kneeling soldier) and defends it against the charge of neglecting objective guilt.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Personalism
holes.what: The view, developed by Boston personalists like Bowne and Brightman and shared by thinkers from Buber to Scheler, that persons as such possess intrinsic, irreducible value that must never be subordinated to abstract ideals or to single aspects of persons like happiness.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument, that Gibson's exclusive focus on the passion eclipses the whole person of Christ and risks relishing redemptive suffering, is explicitly grounded in the author's self-declared personalism.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of tragedy as arousing pity and fear in order to cleanse them, achieved through a plot in which a flawed hero (hamartia) falls from prosperity.
holes.why: Chapter 14 tests The Passion against catharsis and hamartia, shows a flawless Christ cannot make an Aristotelian tragedy, and only then defends its violence as the Kantian sublime instead.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Cinematic Verisimilitude
holes.what: The idea, associated with film theorist Andre Bazin, that photography's automatic, mind-independent recording of reality gives film unique credibility, which fictional narratives can exploit to pass as fact.
holes.why: Chapter 17 explains why Christian viewers take Gibson's slanted, Emmerich-based narrative as history: photographic realism transfers its evidential authority to the fiction, exactly as Griffith's Birth of a Nation did for the Klan.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Religious Mysticism
holes.what: The view, classically analyzed by William James, that a higher truth can be accessed through a painful inner journey culminating in a direct, short-lived, ineffable experience of God that defies rationality.
holes.why: Chapter 20's whole argument reads Gibson's suffering Jesus as a Jewish mystic in the line of Moses, Elijah, Daniel, the Kabbalah, and Hasidism, using James's four marks of mystical experience as its analytic tool.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Truth as Disclosure (aletheia)
holes.what: Heidegger's retrieval of the Greek aletheia: truth understood not as correspondence between proposition and fact but as uncovering or disclosing a new way for a world to show itself.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds its final answer to Pilate's question on aletheia, reading Jesus's 'I am the truth', the veritas anagram, and Claudia's dreams as disclosure rather than criteria-based truth.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The classic view that a proposition is true if and only if it matches the way things actually are.
holes.why: Chapter 22 applies it through Caiaphas's demand that Jesus come down from the cross as proof and The X-Files mantra 'the truth is out there', then objects that every verifying belief depends on further beliefs ad infinitum.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Coherence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The view that a proposition is true if and only if it coheres consistently with the body of propositions already known to be true.
holes.why: Chapter 22 maps Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction onto coherence and shows via Swinburne versus G.A. Wells, and George Costanza's fabrications, that coherence is necessary but not sufficient for truth.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Hermeneutics (interpretation of revelation)
holes.what: The theory of how texts — especially texts regarded as divine revelation — should be interpreted, weighing personal intuition, authority, the text itself, historical scholarship, and tradition.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire argument is that judging the film's fidelity to the Gospels requires a hermeneutics of Scripture on top of faith, and taxonomy has no concept for interpretation theory.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Divine Hiddenness (deus absconditus)
holes.what: The idea that God deliberately hides — Isaiah's 'God who hides himself' — so that people can freely choose or reject him rather than be coerced by overwhelming evidence of his presence.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its whole account of Christ's strategy and faith on the hidden God, and chapter 29 likewise treats God's elusiveness as the condition of genuinely knowing him.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Theories of Atonement (Christus Victor, Satisfaction, Moral Influence)
holes.what: Competing Christian accounts of how Christ's suffering and death reconciles humanity to God: conquest of the demonic (Christus victor), payment of the debt we owe God (Anselm's satisfaction), or a transforming moral example (Abelard).
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire reading of the film maps each pas de deux onto a different atonement theory, which no taxonomy concept covers.
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Christian Pacifism / Nonresistance
holes.what: The doctrine, drawn from Jesus's 'resist not evil' and 'turn the other cheek,' that followers should renounce violence and not resist evil, even at the cost of suffering.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is devoted to interpreting and defending Jesus's nonviolence, and taxonomy lacks any pacifism or nonviolence concept (ahimsa is Gandhi's distinct Hindu-derived doctrine).
holes.book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

holes.name: Holmes Rolston III
holes.what: Environmental philosopher who argues that organisms and ecosystems possess intrinsic (not merely instrumental) value and that value is holistic, embedded in the biotic community.
holes.why: Chapter 16 builds its entire reading of the 'living Force' and Jedi ecology on Rolston's intrinsic-value holism, citing his works more than any other thinker, and the existing land-ethic slug does not name its actual source.
holes.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine

holes.name: Leo Strauss
holes.what: Twentieth-century political philosopher who revived classical political rationalism and defended rule by a virtuous elite ('universal aristocracy') of those with insight into the highest good.
holes.why: Chapter 25 frames Anakin's 'someone wise' defense of benevolent dictatorship as Straussian, staging Strauss's elite rule against Dewey's democracy as a way of life as the chapter's central contrast.
holes.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: Victorian mathematician-philosopher whose 'Ethics of Belief' holds that 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.'
holes.why: Chapter 28's first half is structured around Clifford's evidentialism and shipowner parable as the position James's pragmatist faith must defeat, and no taxonomy slug covers the ethics of belief.
holes.book: 012 - Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine

holes.name: Carl Jung
holes.what: Swiss psychologist who posited universal inherited archetypes - symbols hardwired into the psyche that recur in dreams and myths.
holes.why: Chapter 22's first lens for explaining why superheroes persist unchanged in essence (Superman as Siegel's Samson-Hercules, the Flash as Mercury) is explicitly Jung's archetype theory, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Memetics (cultural evolution)
holes.what: Richard Dawkins' idea that cultural units ('memes') spread by imitation and mutate under selection pressures like genes.
holes.why: Chapter 23 explains the transformation of Batman, Superman, and the other heroes across eras and media entirely through Dawkins' meme concept, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Personalism
holes.what: A tradition (Borden Parker Bowne, Martin Buber) holding each person to be of fundamental, irreducible value that cannot be traded against aggregate goods.
holes.why: Chapter 43 argues superhero ethics in the Marvel Universe is personalism rather than utilitarianism, and that the heroes' personalism wins even Galactus over to the moral point of view.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: The Hero's Journey (monomyth)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's comparative-mythology framework: every hero cycles through departure, initiation, and return, transcending duality to singularity as a 'Master of Two Worlds'.
holes.why: Chapter 7 (ch45-ch48) reads Storm, Mystique, and Jean Grey primarily through Campbell's monomyth, which is the chapter's central analytic framework and absent from taxonomy.json.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
holes.what: Lawrence Kohlberg's three levels of moral reasoning: pre-conventional obedience, conventional conformity, and post-conventional principled justice.
holes.why: Chapters 46 and 48 grade Storm's and Jean Grey's moral growth against Kohlberg's levels before contrasting them with Gilligan's care ethics.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Moral Perfectionism
holes.what: A cluster of themes (found in Plato's Republic) holding that the self can and must keep becoming better, aided by exemplars and friends and threatened by conformity.
holes.why: Book Chapter 8 (ch50-ch52) is explicitly titled and structured around moral perfectionism as the theory illuminating Barbara Gordon's transformation from Batgirl to Oracle, and taxonomy.json lacks it.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Moral Perfectionism (the exemplar and the higher self)
holes.what: A moral viewpoint on which the ethical life is the quest to become a higher self, guided by exemplars who acknowledge and legitimate one's aspiration rather than dictate conformity.
holes.why: Chapters 53-55 read Batgirl: Year One and Oracle entirely through moral perfectionism (Nietzsche's 'Schopenhauer as Educator', Mill on individuality), a framework taxonomy lacks; ch53 introduces it via Barbara Gordon's quest for Batman's acknowledgment.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Wisdom (sophia, the larger picture)
holes.what: The classical ideal of wisdom: seeing the larger picture by training reason, through experience and meditative discipline, to master the pull of the senses and emotions on action.
holes.why: Book chapters 70-75 are all about the nature, training, and modern disappearance of wisdom (Solomon to Stoics); taxonomy has only Aristotle's narrower phronesis, not wisdom as such.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: The Double Danger (Works of Love)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's account of the moral/Christian life as a double struggle: inward against selfishness, and outward against a world that persecutes and ridicules genuine neighbor-love.
holes.why: Chapter 84 introduces the double danger from Works of Love and chapters 85-88 apply it to Spider-Man and the X-Men; no existing Kierkegaard slug covers neighbor-love or the double danger.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Actions that are praiseworthy to do but not wrong to omit — above and beyond what duty requires.
holes.why: Chapter 92 argues utilitarianism cannot accommodate supererogatory acts (Jean Grey's sacrifice) and chapter 93 concludes that being a superhero is precisely such a supererogatory choice; the concept is absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Eschatology (doctrine of last things)
holes.what: The branch of theology concerned with final things — death, judgment, the ultimate destiny of humanity and the cosmos.
holes.why: Chapter 16 (chs 103-109) argues that whether heroes like Superman are obliged to fight injustice depends on their eschatology, contrasting Christian theism's promised culmination with naturalism's 'unyielding despair'.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Evolutionary Ethics (morality as adaptive illusion)
holes.what: The Wilson-Ruse view that evolution has programmed us to feel moral obligation although ethics is an illusion 'fobbed off on us by our genes' with no external grounding.
holes.why: Chapter 106 uses this debunking account as the naturalist's main alternative to theistic moral grounding, and asks whether an illusory dagger still cuts once its illusoriness is seen.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Retroactive Continuity (retcon)
holes.what: The serial-fiction practice of later installments changing what is true of earlier ones ('corrections'), raising questions about truth and identity across a changing canon.
holes.why: Chapter 18 (chs 118-126) builds its entire DC Multiverse metaphysics on retcon 'corrections', from Watson's war wound to Crisis on Infinite Earths rewriting which universes ever existed.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Perdurantism vs Endurantism (how things persist through change)
holes.what: Two accounts of persistence: perdurantism treats persisting things as four-dimensional wholes with distinct temporal parts, while endurantism holds the whole thing is strictly identical and wholly present at each time it exists.
holes.why: Chapters 125-126 decide whether Superman-1 and Superman-2 are the same individual, and whether a timeline itself can change, by exactly this perdurantist/endurantist distinction.
holes.book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

holes.name: Self-Creation (giving style to one's character)
holes.what: Nietzsche's idea (Gay Science 290, developed by Nehamas) that the unity of the self is an achievement, not a given: one molds one's drives, strengths, and even weaknesses into a coherent artistic whole, making life a work of art.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire case for dieting as the art of living rests on 'giving style to one's character,' and no existing slug covers Nietzschean self-creation.
holes.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: Nietzsche's diagnosis that modern culture's values have become devalued and meaningless after the death of God, calling for a therapy of culture rather than new doctrines.
holes.why: Chapter 20 frames Atkins's alternative eating advice as an answer to 'nutritional nihilism' and builds its whole argument on Nietzsche's account of a culture in nihilistic crisis.
holes.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche

holes.name: Metabolic Rift
holes.what: Marx's term (revived by John Bellamy Foster) for the rupture capitalism drives between human production and natural nutrient cycles, e.g. soil fertility shipped to cities and lost as waste.
holes.why: Chapter 26 names Atkins the third metabolic rift — after industrial soil depletion and feedlot agriculture — to argue that atomizing food into nutrients deepens agriculture's break from ecological cycles.
holes.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher whose Distinction analyzes how 'taste' and habitus reproduce class distinctions through everyday cultural practices such as food.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Bourdieu's habitus and cultural capital to explain how Atkins moved 'white trash' foods like pork rinds into middle-class respectability.
holes.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst whose mirror stage and registers of the Imaginary, Symbolic, and Real explain how the ego is built from images and language, and what resists symbolization.
holes.why: Chapter 29's entire analysis of Atkins's body imagery, hunger, and carb-phobia is constructed from Lacan's mirror stage, ideal-ego, the Real, and his 'upholstery nails.'
holes.book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche

holes.name: The Primacy of Sound (vocative philosophy)
holes.what: The view that meaning and knowledge are grounded in the human voice and hearing rather than in sight or silent text.
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues Lewis makes sound the fundamental sense: Narnia is created by Aslan's song, evil begins with a bell and a spoken word, and truth is heard before it is seen.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Logical Positivism (verificationism)
holes.what: The doctrine, associated with A.J. Ayer, that only logically true or empirically verifiable statements are meaningful, making metaphysics and theology meaningless.
holes.why: Chapter 12 sets Lewis's voice-centered theory of truth against the logical positivism that dominated philosophy when he wrote the Chronicles.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Virtue Epistemology
holes.what: A theory of knowledge, launched by Ernest Sosa and developed by Lorraine Code, that defines justification through intellectual virtues such as valuing truth and knowing one's limits.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains why Uncle Andrew alone cannot hear the Talking Animals: he lacks the intellectual virtues a responsible seeker of knowledge needs.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Epistemology of Testimony
holes.what: The study of when a hearer is justified in believing a speaker's report, based on the speaker's reliability and the fit of the claim with background beliefs.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its whole argument from the Professor's defense of Lucy's wardrobe story and applies the resulting principles to reports of religious experience.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who argued that belief in God is an illusion born of infantile helplessness and the longing for a protecting father.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads the Green Witch's claim that the sun and Aslan are childish copies as a direct parallel to Freud's critique of religion, which the chapter then rebuts.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: The Genetic Fallacy
holes.what: The error of rejecting a belief as false solely because of its psychological or cultural origin.
holes.why: Chapter 15 answers the Freudian wish-fulfillment critique by naming the genetic fallacy: a belief's origin in desire does not show it is false.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Michael Polanyi
holes.what: Philosopher-scientist who argued that all knowing is a personal commitment guided by tacit knowledge: we know more than we can tell.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Polanyi's personal knowledge to interpret Lucy's unsharable certainty that she has seen Aslan and knows his face's intent.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Moral Imagination
holes.what: The capacity to see one's own values, choices, and life from fresh moral perspectives, a power that stories and literature exercise.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues the Chronicles work by moral imagination, moving readers through identification with Edmund's repentance, Lucy's tested faith, and Uncle Andrew's deformity of self-absorption.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: The Moral Imaginary
holes.what: The culturally transmitted stock of images, heroes, and monsters in a community's stories that shapes children's sense of good and evil.
holes.why: Chapter 24 asks whether Narnia's heroic and monstrous imagery breeds militarism and ethnocentrism in the young or, read closely, undermines them.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Scientism
holes.what: The view that only naturalistic science makes objective cognitive claims, relegating ethics and religion to subjective preference.
holes.why: Chapter 29 names scientism explicitly as the core of the modern secularism it critiques: Eustace's 'Experiment House' schooling and the Professor's 'why don't they teach logic' complaint turn on scientism's exclusion of religious and ethical answers from knowledge.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Religious Pluralism, Inclusivism and Exclusivism
holes.what: The debate over soteriology: whether all great religions save (pluralism), whether one religion is true but salvation is possible outside explicit membership (inclusivism), or whether explicit belonging is required (exclusivism).
holes.why: Chapter 33's entire argument is a fourfold classification of universal salvation, pluralism, inclusivism, and exclusivism applied to Emeth, Shasta, and Jill to show Lewis is an inclusivist; no existing taxonomy slug covers this debate.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: Ransom Theory of Atonement (Christus Victor)
holes.what: The early Christian view (Origen and the Greek fathers) that Christ's death is a ransom or exchange that liberates humanity from bondage to sin, Satan, and death, with evil defeated by its own devices.
holes.why: Chapter 34 argues Aslan's ransom of Edmund from the Witch's Deep Magic embodies the Ransom Theory and defends it against John Lucas's objections; the taxonomy has no atonement concept of any kind.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: The Argument from Reason
holes.what: Lewis's argument that naturalism is self-defeating because if all beliefs are produced by non-rational physical causes, rational inference, and hence belief in naturalism, cannot be trusted; sharpened by Anscombe's distinction between reasons and causes.
holes.why: Chapter 35 centers on the 1948 Lewis-Anscombe debate over this argument, its 1960 revision, and whether Narnia's Green Witch episode responds to it; 'faith-vs-reason' does not capture this specific argument.
holes.book: 015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview

holes.name: The Omnipotence Paradox
holes.what: The puzzle of whether an omnipotent being can do things like create a stone it cannot lift, standardly answered by restricting divine power to the logically possible.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument is built on this puzzle - the paradox of the blunt, the paradox of the glock, and Tupac's jailbreak paradox - which taxonomy lacks under Aquinas or otherwise.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: The Adaptive Unconscious
holes.what: The modern psychological picture of fast, automatic, goal-directed mental processing outside awareness - unlike Freud's repressive unconscious.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explicitly contrasts this 'new unconscious' with Freud's to explain why we are strangers to ourselves (misattributed arousal, implicit racism, facial misjudgment, wealth and happiness).
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation through art)
holes.what: Aristotle's view that art lets dangerous emotions be safely enjoyed and purged within a fictional realm kept apart from real life.
holes.why: Chapter 16 presents catharsis as the standard aesthetic solution to violent art that pragmatist rap aesthetics, insisting art is continuous with life, must reject.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: Race as Social Construction (critical racialism)
holes.what: The view that races are not natural kinds but groups created by assigning social meaning to bodies and ancestry, surviving the collapse of biological racialism.
holes.why: Chapter 19's three-step dismantling of racialist reasoning about who hip hop belongs to turns entirely on distinguishing classical from critical racialism, a concept taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: Jerrold Levinson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose intentionalist proposal holds that a work says what it would be reasonable to impute to its artist as a view significantly held and concerned to be conveyed.
holes.why: Chapter 23 adopts Levinson's proposal as its main analytical tool for deciding what Kelis, Lil' Kim, and Eminem's lyrics mean across insider and outsider audiences.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: Speech Acts (illocutionary acts)
holes.what: Austin's insight that words do things (marry, arrest, subordinate), extended by Rae Langton to the claim that authoritative pornography and speech can rank and subordinate women.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses illocutionary acts and Langton's authority conditions to argue that pimp rap may subordinate women more effectively than pornography can.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: The Use-Mention Distinction
holes.what: The philosophy-of-language distinction between using a word to refer to a person or group and merely mentioning the word itself.
holes.why: Chapter 25's defense of Chappelle's uses of 'bitch' and 'nigga' hinges on whether epithets are used of persons or mentioned, quoted, or reconstituted as endearments.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: Rectificatory Justice (reparations)
holes.what: The branch of justice concerned with remedying wrongdoing through punishment of perpetrators, compensation of victims, and apology.
holes.why: Chapter 30 is wholly organized around rectifying the injustices of slavery via compensation, apology, and 'forty acres and a mule' - a category it says Western justice theory has neglected.
holes.book: 016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason

holes.name: Benjamin's Philosophy of Language (naming and the creative word)
holes.what: Walter Benjamin's 1916 account ('On Language as Such and on the Language of Man') of language as the mental being of man, in which man's naming of things completes God's creation and the Fall degrades name into judgment.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire reading of "Man Gave Names to All the Animals" is built on this essay - naming as dominion and creation-completion, the snake and the nameless knowledge of good and evil - and taxonomy's only Benjamin concept (benjamin-aura) does not cover it.
holes.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)

holes.name: Moral Realism (objective moral law)
holes.what: The view that there are mind-independent moral facts and properties that make moral judgments objectively true or false.
holes.why: Chapter 23's central claim is that Dylan's moral judgments across decades presuppose an unchanging, objective moral order ("Dignity never been photographed"), and taxonomy contains only moral-relativism, its denial.
holes.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)

holes.name: Expression Theory of Art
holes.what: The theory (Wordsworth, Collingwood, Tolstoy) that artistry consists in expressing emotion, so that a work's value lies in the sincerity and depth of the feeling it makes conscious.
