holes.why: Chapter 25 applies expression theory at length to Greil Marcus's Self Portrait review and the two versions of Blood on the Tracks before rejecting it, and taxonomy has no philosophy-of-art concept for it.
holes.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)

holes.name: Formalism (classicist theory of art)
holes.what: The theory that an artwork's merit resides in its design, form, and pattern rather than in the artist's emotions, biography, or message.
holes.why: Chapter 25 uses formalism (Ricks's and Gray's praise of Dylan's verbal patterning versus his aesthetics of improvisatory imperfection) as the second of its three candidate theories of Dylan's artistry, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)

holes.name: The Ancient Quarrel between Philosophy and Poetry
holes.what: Plato's charge (Republic X) that poets trade in imitation and appetite rather than truth, and the running debate since over whether philosophy or poetry better discloses reality.
holes.why: Chapter 26's title argument - Plato's banishment of the poets, Boethius's Consolation, Nietzsche's ironism, and Dylan's anti-analytic remarks - is a direct engagement with this quarrel, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)

holes.name: Futurism (aesthetics of speed and the machine)
holes.what: Marinetti's 1909 avant-garde movement glorifying speed, machines, danger, and revolt as the beauty of modern life.
holes.why: Chapter 18 quotes the Futurist Manifesto at length and applies it as one of its three aesthetic lenses on the motorcycle's allure.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Institutional Theory of Art
holes.what: George Dickie's view that an artifact becomes art when the artworld confers that status on it, as a minister confers marriage.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses the theory to explain how the Guggenheim exhibit made motorcycles into art while searching other theories for why they deserved it.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: Nietzsche's 'danger of dangers': the collapse of all highest values, so that nothing is true and nothing has inherent value.
holes.why: Chapter 19 is built on nihilism as such, tracing it from Nietzsche and Camus to the outlaw biker's FTW attitude and its commercialization.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: The Standard of Taste (Hume)
holes.what: Hume's essay arguing aesthetic judgment is not mere subjective preference: informed, unprejudiced critics ground objective standards and genuine disagreement.
holes.why: Chapter 21 leans on it to show that calling a Honda Gold Wing elegant is criticizable and that bike aesthetics is not 'anything goes'.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Ontology of Art (type and token)
holes.what: The debate over what a multiple-instance artwork is, contrasting Wollheim's unique physical object with Currie's action-type account.
holes.why: Chapter 21 needs it to explain how a mass-produced Ducati 916 can be one artwork with many instances, like copies of a novel.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Object-Oriented Ontology (flat ontology)
holes.what: The view that all objects, human and inanimate, are equally real actors with no privileged human access to the world, rejecting Kant's human-world gap.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses Easy Rider's Harleys as autonomous heroes to argue exactly this anti-Kantian position, drawing on Whitehead and Latour.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Bruno Latour
holes.what: French philosopher of science and actor-network theory who treats humans and nonhumans as equal actors in networks.
holes.why: Chapter 23 names Latour (with Whitehead) as the exemplar of the new object-centered philosophy it endorses through Easy Rider.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Fetishism (Freudian)
holes.what: Freud's account of the fetish as an object endowed with power that wards off castration anxiety and manages sexual difference.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explains the black leather jacket as a Freudian fetish object of masculine power before turning to Marx's commodity fetishism.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Deployment of Sexuality
holes.what: Foucault's account, in The History of Sexuality, of how institutions incite, classify, and circulate sexual discourse as a technology of power.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire analysis of biker stereotypes (Motorcycle Syndrome, biker chicks, the police gauntlet) runs on this Foucauldian apparatus.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Qi (vital energy)
holes.what: The vital breath or energy flowing through heaven, earth, and the human body in Chinese cosmology, pairing with the five xing processes.
holes.why: Chapter 29 describes the accomplished rider blending with the four qi of heaven and five xing of earth to achieve harmony on the road.
holes.book: 018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle

holes.name: Incongruity Theory of Humor (comic vs horrific)
holes.what: The theory that comic amusement arises from perceived incongruity or category-violation, with Carroll's addition that horror requires disgust plus fear, so non-threatening violation yields laughter.
holes.why: Chapter 9's whole account of why Mr. Creosote's explosion is funny rather than horrific is built on this theory, and the taxonomy's only humor slug (bergson-laughter) is Bergson's specific theory, which the chapter never uses.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Reflective Equilibrium
holes.what: Rawls's method of testing general moral principles against considered judgments about particular cases and adjusting each against the other, ideally in conversation with others, until they cohere.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues the Argument Clinic sketch shows why this method — not mere contradiction — is how philosophical argument justifies moral beliefs, and no existing Rawls slug (veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) covers it.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Mindfulness (sati)
holes.what: The Buddhist discipline of focused, present-moment meditative awareness that cuts through distraction and craving.
holes.why: Chapter 14's title and conclusion ('Mind the Mindfulness') identify mindfulness as the positive alternative the film and the Buddha both offer to transcendentalism and distraction; the taxonomy has only Zen, not sati.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Karl Jaspers
holes.what: German existential philosopher who coined the 'Axial Age' (Achsenzeit), construing the last 2,500 years as the working-out of the world-religions' picture of life as a journey to transcendence.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its entire critique of The Meaning of Life around Jaspers's notion of 'axial' thinking — life as a journey to a destination — which Python's comedy supposedly reduces to absurdity, and no taxonomy entry covers him or the axial-age concept.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Madness as a Social Construct
holes.what: Foucault's thesis in Madness and Civilization that madness has no raw existence apart from a society's changing forms of tolerance, exclusion, confinement, and medicalization.
holes.why: Chapter 19 reads 'The Idiot in Society' entirely through this history of insanity, and the existing Foucault slugs (panopticon, power-knowledge, discipline) do not cover it.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Franz Kafka
holes.what: German-Czech writer of existentialist fiction whose worlds of bureaucratic insanity and irrational barriers trap ordinary people.
holes.why: Chapter 21 opens its existentialist case by reading the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches as Kafkaesque and comparing Gregor Samsa's train-catching worries to Python humor.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Saying vs Showing (Tractatus picture theory)
holes.what: Early Wittgenstein's view that propositions picture facts, that attempts to say what makes facts possible are nonsense, and that what cannot be said can only be shown.
holes.why: Chapter 22 diagnoses the 'Spectrum' sketch with this Tractatus doctrine and builds its self-refutation joke on the saying/showing ladder.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Rudolf Carnap
holes.what: Logical empiricist who diagnosed Heidegger's metaphysical sentences as nonsense and called metaphysicians 'musicians without musical ability'.
holes.why: Chapter 25 builds its thesis that philosophers are comedians without comic ability by revising Carnap's diagnosis of Heidegger.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Philosophical Nonsense (nonsense as a philosophical verdict)
holes.what: The early-analytic practice of diagnosing rival philosophy, especially metaphysics, as meaningless nonsense rather than false.
holes.why: Chapter 25's whole argument — that analytic philosophy is unconscious absurd comedy — is built on this nonsense-diagnosing tradition from Carnap to Wittgenstein's grammatical jokes.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Ordinary Language Philosophy
holes.what: The postwar British program (Wittgenstein, Ryle, Austin) that treats philosophical problems as confusions dissolved by analyzing everyday language use.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues the Bols, No Time to Lose, and Bruces sketches satirize this program, whose movement-level identity no existing slug captures.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Logical Positivism and the Verifiability Criterion
holes.what: The Vienna Circle's criterion that a statement is meaningful only if experience can verify it, famous for refuting itself and collapsing into semantic holism.
holes.why: Chapter 29's first theme is the positivist revolt against metaphysics and the self-refutation of the verifiability criterion that sets up the Dead Parrot and Black Knight clips.
holes.book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

holes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
holes.what: Russian novelist whose Notes from Underground and The Gambler are standardly treated as the overture to existentialism, defending the irrational, risk-embracing life against rational self-interest.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is built entirely on his two novellas and his roulette addiction, using them to argue that gambling is an existential activity beyond reason.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: American philosopher of language and mind whose interpretationism holds that attributing meanings, beliefs and thoughts to others requires assuming they share most of our beliefs (charity), with action a 'vector' of belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 17 applies Davidson's shared-belief thesis and vector model to explain how poker players attribute third- and fourth-order thoughts to opponents and why pros misread novices.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: The Principle of Charity (shared belief in interpretation)
holes.what: Davidson's demand that interpretation proceed by maximizing agreement, since identifying disagreement presupposes a background of largely shared true beliefs.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses it to show why Negreanu's bluff against Deeb needs a web of shared assumptions and why poker at its best forces deep agreement among strangers.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: Lewis's Principal Principle (chance as a guide to credence)
holes.what: David Lewis's norm that rational credence should defer to objective chance, challenged by Beebee and Papineau's relative probabilities computed only from what the agent knows.
holes.why: Chapter 19 evaluates four candidate probabilities for poker decisions against Lewis's principle and concludes only Beebee-Papineau relative probability is a usable guide at the table.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: Knowing How vs Knowing That
holes.what: Ryle's distinction from The Concept of Mind between propositional knowledge (knowing that) and skill as intelligent disposition (knowing how).
holes.why: Chapter 21 organizes all poker knowledge into these two Rylean categories, from internalized hand rankings to the dispositions that make a player fold bad hands.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: Belief versus Acceptance
holes.what: Jonathan Cohen's distinction between involuntary belief (a feeling that something is true) and the voluntary policy of accepting a proposition — acting as if it were true for practical purposes.
holes.why: Chapter 23 tests bluffing-as-acceptance against bluffing-as-lying and bluffing-as-bullshit, concluding good bluffing partly consists in acting as if one held a stronger hand.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: The Construction of Social Reality (institutional facts)
holes.what: Searle's account of how collective intentionality creates institutional facts — X counts as Y in context C — so games, money and law exist only by collective recognition.
holes.why: Chapter 25 uses Searle's social-objects method to define poker's necessary features and argue that online poker lacks the social institution that makes poker poker.
holes.book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

holes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
holes.what: Russian novelist-philosopher of existential Christianity whose underground man dramatizes self-despising despair and whose Father Zosima preaches faith confirmed by active love.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads 'Mysterious Ways' through Notes from Underground and grounds its account of faith's confirmation in Zosima's 'experience of active love' from The Brothers Karamazov; chapter 11 also counts Dostoevsky among the existential Christians alongside Pascal and Kierkegaard.
holes.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band

holes.name: Place, Home and Dwelling
holes.what: The account of how human lives are articulated through concrete places, with modernity diagnosed as homelessness - an inability to dwell (Heidegger's later thinking on place and dwelling).
holes.why: Chapter 13 is built entirely on this: The Joshua Tree as an album of place, home, belonging and loss, read through Heidegger on dwelling and Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', and no existing slug captures the philosophy of place itself.
holes.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Ordinary-language philosopher whose speech act theory (How to Do Things with Words) analyzes utterances as actions with locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary dimensions completed by cooperative audiences.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire explanation of U2's popular success - singing as an indirect illocutionary act that invites listeners to make songs relevant to their own lives - is constructed from Austin's distinctions, and Austin appears in the book's index as a principal figure.
holes.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation and purification)
holes.what: Aristotle's notion that tragedy and music work on the emotions of pity and fear, read by commentators either as medical purgation of excess feeling or as religious purification of the soul.
holes.why: Chapter 26 devotes a full section to the two scholarly readings of catharsis, mapping 'Exit' onto purgation and 'Until the End of the World' onto purification, and no existing slug covers it.
holes.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Twentieth-century Christian philosopher-apologist whose Abolition of Man argues that trained emotions, not syllogisms, are what make virtue psychologically possible.
holes.why: Chapter 26 takes its subtitle from The Abolition of Man and closes its Aristotelian case by quoting Lewis's claim that without the aid of trained emotions the intellect is powerless against the animal organism.
holes.book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band

holes.name: Natural Kinds vs Nominal Kinds
holes.what: The distinction between kinds whose membership is fixed by the world's own structure (water, electrons) and kinds unified only by our definitions and classificatory practices.
holes.why: Chapter 10's ontology of the Undead turns on arguing that vampires, zombies, and composite Undead form a merely nominal kind rather than a natural one, which grounds its claim that they share no deep unity.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: Malevolent Evil (non-instrumental desire to harm)
holes.what: A restrictive sense of evil defined by having and acting on non-instrumental motives to damage others' welfare, distinct from ordinary moral wrongdoing and from the Problem of Evil.
holes.why: Chapter 10 argues that zombies and most vampires lack exactly this motive structure and so are not evil, despite their horror-movie portrayal, making the concept the chapter's key analytical tool.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: The Amoral Psychopath (Cleckley)
holes.what: Hervey Cleckley's profile of the psychopath as cognitively normal but lacking basic empathic concern, and therefore amoral rather than immoral and not a fit target of blame.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Cleckley's case of Milt to draw the line between amoral creatures (Romero's zombies, Stoker's Dracula) that can be stopped but not blamed, and accountable ones (Coppola's Dracula, Louis, Lestat).
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Psychoanalytic theorist of abjection: the horrified fascination with bodily wastes, borders, and the corpse, which exposes death as already inside the self.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central explanation of vampire and corpse horror is Kristeva's concept of the abject, quoting her line that the corpse is 'the most sickening of wastes'.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's account of why revenants, dead bodies, and the return of the dead are the most potent uncanny figures, preserving primitive belief beneath a thin veneer.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses Freud's essay on the uncanny to argue that what horrifies us is not death but the returning dead, and reads Buffy's all-too-human killers as the uncanny in reverse.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: Eros and Civilization (non-repressive civilization)
holes.what: Marcuse's reworking of Freud holding that civilization, being historical, can evolve beyond repression once liberated sexuality rejoins Eros and labor becomes play.
holes.why: Chapter 25's whole argument is that Romero's zombies embody the return of the repressed and that Day of the Dead's beach ending and Land of the Dead's evolved zombies picture Marcuse's non-repressive civilization.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: Author of Democracy in America, who warned that democracy decays when individualism detaches citizens from one another and saw civic association as democracy's lifeblood.
holes.why: Chapter 26 measures Romero's communitarian heroes against Tocqueville's claim that Americans must join groups and connect across difference for democracy to survive.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: Humorism (the four humors)
holes.what: Ancient medical doctrine, systematized by Galen, that health and temperament depend on the balance of four bodily humors, with blood as the primary one.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses humorism and bloodletting to explain why legend credits blood with preserving youth, sustaining life, and carrying personal identity.
holes.book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

holes.name: Baron de Montesquieu
holes.what: French Enlightenment political philosopher whose The Spirit of the Laws (1748) argues that political liberty requires separating legislative, executive, and judicial powers so that power checks power.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire procedural answer to Bond's license to kill rests on Montesquieu's separation-of-powers doctrine as the check against abuse of executive power, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever

holes.name: Abduction (inference to the best explanation)
holes.what: Peirce's third mode of inference, alongside deduction and induction: reasoning from a surprising observation to the hypothesis that would best explain it - the logic of guessing and of detective work.
holes.why: Chapter 24's whole argument is that Bond's detective genius is Peirce's logic of abduction (including false and creative abductions and musement), and no existing taxonomy slug names the concept.
holes.book: 023 - James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever

holes.name: Rudolf Carnap
holes.what: Vienna Circle logical positivist who diagnosed metaphysical statements as meaningless pseudo-statements, most famously in his critique of Heidegger's 'Das Nichts selbst nichtet'.
holes.why: Chapter 8 presents Carnap's campaign against Heideggerian metaphysics as the twentieth century's high point of philosophy's anti-bullshit crusade.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Logical Positivism (the Vienna Circle)
holes.what: The Vienna Circle's program holding that meaningful statements are logical truths or empirically verifiable ones and that metaphysics is sophistry and illusion.
holes.why: Chapter 8 casts the Circle's 1929 'Scientific World-Conception' as the modern apotheosis of the Enlightenment fight against bullshit that Frankfurt continues.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Alfred Mele
holes.what: Philosopher who deflates self-deception, explaining it through motivated misinterpretation and selective evidence-gathering rather than an interpersonal deceiver-dupe model.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its case that bullshit can be unintentional directly on Mele's argument that self-deceivers mask evidence instead of playing deceiver and dupe at once.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: G.A. Cohen
holes.what: Political philosopher whose 'Deeper into Bullshit' replies to Frankfurt, defining bullshit by the unclarifiable unclarity of the product rather than the producer's indifference to truth.
holes.why: Chapter 14 stages the Frankfurt-Cohen debate, using Cohen's output-centered definition to explain unintentional bullshit that Frankfurt's process-centered account misses.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Bullshit as Unclarifiable Unclarity
holes.what: Cohen's output-centered definition of bullshit: discourse marked by an obscurity that cannot be clarified, whatever the speaker's state of mind.
holes.why: Chapter 15 needs it to classify alchemy and Althusserian prose as bullshit without accusing blameless method-users like Newton of intentional indifference to truth.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Pseudoscience (the demarcation problem)
holes.what: Claims that wear the trappings of science without its methods, raising the demarcation problem of separating genuine science from imitation science.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues the Intelligent Design movement is bullshit precisely because it disguises religious creationism in scientific-sounding concepts like 'irreducible complexity'.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Cognitive Bias (confirmation bias, framing effects)
holes.what: Systematic, built-in deviations from rational judgment, such as confirmation bias and framing effects, documented by cognitive and social psychology.
holes.why: Chapter 29 argues these architectural foibles of the mind explain why propaganda and bullshit take hold, from Iraq-war beliefs to information cocoons like Fox News.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Performative Utterances (speech acts)
holes.what: Speech acts (promises, pledges, commitments) in which saying the words itself performs the act, with distinct conditions for issuance and fulfillment.
holes.why: Chapter 46's key coinage 'performative bullshit' - commitments treated as fulfilled by their very issuance (video-store pledges, university mission statements) - presupposes exactly this speech-act machinery.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Ordinary-language philosopher who founded speech-act theory with the notion of performative utterances in How to Do Things with Words.
holes.why: Chapter 46 analyzes institutional 'performative bullshit' in explicitly performative terms - commitments issued versus fulfilled - whose framework Austin introduced.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: G.A. Cohen
holes.what: Marxist political philosopher whose essay 'Deeper into Bullshit' distinguishes product-based (structuralist) bullshit from Frankfurt's intention-based account and coins 'unclarifiable unclarity'.
holes.why: Chapters 48-63 and 77-81 of this unit are organized around Cohen's structuralist/intentionalist split, his OED-based two species, and his critique of Frankfurt's tactic/goal confusion.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Louis Althusser
holes.what: Structuralist Marxist theorist of ideological state apparatuses, interpellation, and overdetermination, whose 1960s French school exemplified academic obscurity for Cohen.
holes.why: Chapter 55 names the Althusserian school and its concepts of interpellation and overdetermination as the paradigm case of the academic bullshit Cohen became least tolerant of.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Rudolf Carnap
holes.what: Logical positivist whose 'Overcoming Metaphysics through the Logical Analysis of Language' diagnosed metaphysics as meaningless pseudo-sentences, targeting Heidegger's 'The nothing noths'.
holes.why: Chapters 61-63 build the unification of Frankfurt's and Cohen's bullshit directly on Carnap's teavy/toovy examples, his notion of pseudo-statements, and his diagnosis of metaphysics as disguised expression of a life-attitude.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Verificationism (the verifiability theory of meaning)
holes.what: The logical-positivist doctrine that a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified or deduced from other meaningful statements, rendering metaphysical and theological utterances pseudo-statements.
holes.why: Chapter 61 uses Carnap's verificationist test on 'teavy' and 'The nothing noths' as the precise forerunner of Cohen's unclarifiable-unclarity bullshit test.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Charles L. Stevenson
holes.what: American emotivist ethicist who coined 'persuasive definition' - redefining a term's descriptive meaning while preserving its emotive force - in Ethics and Language.
holes.why: Chapters 66-67 and 75-77 build their entire analysis of definitional bullshit, semantic negligence, and backfire on Stevenson's PD/PQD machinery.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Persuasive Definition
holes.what: A redefinition that changes a term's descriptive meaning (sense or reference) while covertly preserving its emotive force (tone), thereby smuggling in an argument as a definition.
holes.why: Chapters 66-77 analyze drunk-driver excuses, the No-True-Scotsman move, euphemism, the pornography and rape definitions, and even Frankfurt's own definition of 'bullshit' as instances of PD and its backfire.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: No True Scotsman Move
holes.what: The ad hoc rescue move (named by Antony Flew) of redefining a group term to exclude counterexamples, converting a falsifiable generalization into a vacuous necessary truth.
holes.why: Chapter 70's core example - Hamish MacTavish and his sugared porridge - is analyzed as high/low redefinition plus semantic negligence ending in Frankfurt-style bullshit.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: The Euphemism Treadmill
holes.what: The process, observed by Germaine Greer, by which euphemisms acquire the pejorative tone of the terms they replace and must be endlessly substituted for themselves.
holes.why: Chapter 74's whole argument is that tone-resetting euphemisms (from 'Eumenides' to politically correct and nukespeak coinages) backfire via this treadmill unless underlying attitudes genuinely change.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: The Demarcation Problem (pseudoscience)
holes.what: The problem of distinguishing science from pseudoscience by criteria beyond the sincerity or clarity of its practitioners, such as sensitivity to evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 81 argues astrology, chakra healing, and numerology are a third kind of bullshit - sincere and clear but evidence-insensitive - requiring exactly the demarcation account neither Frankfurt nor Cohen supplies.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: G.A. Cohen
holes.what: Analytic socialist philosopher whose essay 'Deeper into Bullshit' defined bullshit as unclarifiable unclarity and distinguished aim-bullshitters from disposition-bullshitters.
holes.why: Chapter 84 deploys Cohen's aim/disposition-bullshitter distinction to classify political bullshit, and chapters 86, 87 and 89 build on his content-based typology as the book's second pillar beside Frankfurt.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Peter Goldie
holes.what: Philosopher of emotion who argued that a person's life-narrative shapes and gives content to their emotional episodes and values.
holes.why: Chapter 90 builds its mechanism of political bullshit on Goldie's narrative theory of emotion, citing his work at nearly every step.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos)
holes.what: The art of persuasive speech and the discipline that studies how language moves audiences, systematized by Aristotle in his Rhetoric.
holes.why: Chapter 96 (and book chapter 15, 'Rhetoric Is Not Bullshit', chapters 96-99) is devoted to defending rhetoric from identification with bullshit, and the taxonomy has no rhetoric entry at all.
holes.book: 024 - Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: socially forbidden drives are repressed, and jokes — working like dreams — release repressed energy so it can be thought through (the talking cure).
holes.why: Chapter 9's closing section explains South Park's vulgarity as Freudian release — jokes break repression the way dreams do, the book's 'talking cure' for culture — and the taxonomy has no Freud entry.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: Informal Fallacies
holes.what: Named patterns of faulty reasoning — red herring, hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, ad hominem — in which the conclusion does not follow from the premises.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is an entire logic lesson built on South Park's Chewbacca Defense and other fallacy gags, and the taxonomy has no logic or fallacy concept at all.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: Victorian mathematician-philosopher who argued in 'The Ethics of Belief' that it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument — Stan Marsh versus psychics, cults, and Pascal's Wager — is Clifford's ethics of belief, and chapter 15 relies on his evidentialism too.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief (evidentialism)
holes.what: The doctrine that believing on insufficient evidence is morally wrong because beliefs guide action, harm others, and weaken the mind's powers of self-control and evidence-weighing.
holes.why: Chapters 13 and 15 both turn on evidentialism (against Pascal's Wager and for Clifford against James's will to believe), which no existing concept slug captures.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: Functionalism (philosophy of mind)
holes.what: The theory that mental states are functional input–process–output states realizable in any sufficiently organized system, biological or artificial.
holes.why: Chapter 17 argues functionalism is the theory of mind the Matrix films presuppose (sentient machines, Smith's seamless copy into Bane), against Searle's biological emergentism, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of religion whose soul-making theodicy holds that God allows moral and natural evil so that free creatures can develop virtuous character through responding to it.
holes.why: Chapter 22's culminating answer to Cartmanland's problem of evil — echoed by South Park's Jesus and reused at length in chapter 24 — is Hick's soul-making theodicy.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma and Tit-for-Tat
holes.what: A game-theory model in which each rational agent is better off defecting whatever the other does, though mutual cooperation beats mutual defection; the iterated version rewards the reciprocity strategy tit-for-tat.
holes.why: Chapter 39 uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and tit-for-tat to explain how the survivors on Lost generate trust and to recast the Hobbes-Locke disagreement about the state of nature.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: The Ticking Bomb Scenario
holes.what: A thought experiment, classically formulated by Henry Shue, asking whether torturing a captured terrorist who knows where a soon-to-detonate bomb is hidden can be morally justified.
holes.why: Chapter 41 organizes 24's entire depiction of Jack Bauer around the ticking bomb argument, dramatizing its utilitarian appeal while cataloguing why it fails in reality.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: The Social Construction of Race
holes.what: The view that races are not natural biological kinds but real social kinds, like money or political affiliations, constituted by collective classification and historical treatment.
holes.why: Chapter 42's core move is to reject biological race and argue that X-Men mutants could be racelike only as a socially constructed group, on the model of socially created kinds.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: Nishida Kitarō
holes.what: Founder of the Kyoto School (1870-1945) whose Zen-based philosophy of religion conceives God as Absolute Nothingness and uses kenosis (self-emptying) to join Buddhist emptiness with a personal, immanent divinity.
holes.why: Chapter 44 invokes Nishida's kenosis theology to reconcile the Cylons' monotheistic God of love with Buddhist emptiness and interdependent arising.
holes.book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who modeled the psyche as a conflict between instinctual drives (the id) and internalized social restraint (the superego), drives that repression can check but never eliminate.
holes.why: Chapter 8's reading of Sabotage rests on Freud: the aquarium's 'monsters from the Id' symbolize the chaotic drives Verloc fails to watch, grounding Hitchcock's anti-utopian claim that chaos cannot be planned out of the psyche.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Horrendous Evils
holes.what: Marilyn McCord Adams's term for evils of such grotesque disproportion and disorder that they threaten to destroy the positive meaning of the lives of both victim and perpetrator.
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues Psycho's shower murder and Norman's fate are horrendous evils, an aesthetic category of unfittingness that strengthens the logical problem of evil beyond what the generic problem-of-evil slug captures.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Knots (R.D. Laing)
holes.what: R.D. Laing's term for entangled binds in which acting on a motive brings, by a 'crazy' but inexorable logic, exactly the opposite of what one hoped for.
holes.why: Chapter 17's closing move names the Scottie-Judy relationship a knot: Judy's need to be loved makes her feed the projective fantasy that prevents Scottie from loving her, and the chapter title 'Knots' names this concept.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Logical Positivism (Vienna Circle)
holes.what: The Vienna Circle program (Carnap, Ayer) holding that science is the only proper model for philosophy and that only observation- and logic-anchored, verifiable claims are meaningful.
holes.why: Chapter 18's section 'Vertigo and the Vienna Circle' reads Scottie's fact-collecting, rule-deducing method as an implicit critique of positivism, which cannot accommodate the emotions and noncodifiable behavior that guide human minds.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher who argues the self is not a possession like a heart or liver but is constitutively formed through self-interpretation in ongoing dialogue with a community of others.
holes.why: Chapter 19 closes on Taylor's view that 'one cannot be a self on one's own,' using it to explain how Eve and the Kaplan role help make Thornhill into a new person.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Ethical Pluralism
holes.what: The view that people legitimately embrace the same goals and moral order for different and often conflicting reasons, so a community can act together while holding diverse conceptions of the good life.
holes.why: Chapter 22 explicitly defines and defends ethical pluralism as its thesis about Lifeboat: each survivor's different version of the Good is preserved, and the boat's collective action springs from converging moral outrage rather than shared doctrine.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Lifeboat Ethics (Hardin)
holes.what: Garrett Hardin's thought experiment picturing rich nations as passengers on a lifeboat who cannot take on more poor 'swimmers' without swamping everyone.
holes.why: Chapter 22 opens with and constantly returns to Hardin's essay, using the lifeboat scenario as a device that strips away politics and law to isolate ethical decision-making.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's theory that human motivation ascends a hierarchy from physiological and safety needs through love and esteem to self-actualization, with morality at the top.
holes.why: Chapter 22 devotes a full section to reading the Lifeboat survivors' descent to bare survival through the hierarchy, then argues Maslow 'loses the card game' because moral outrage overrides survival.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Aristotle's Poetics (mimesis and catharsis)
holes.what: Aristotle's defense of tragedy and imitation as natural, cathartic, and educational, imparting universal and necessary truths about human life.
holes.why: Chapter 24 needs the Poetics to stage Rear Window as adjudicating Plato's ban on imitative art against Aristotle's claim that drama cultivates moral insight - the film's epiphany about Jeff's neighbors is exactly the Aristotelian payoff.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: The category of acts that are good to perform but not wrong to omit, as when Jeff's intervention might be praiseworthy without being required.
holes.why: Chapter 25 needs the obligatory/supererogatory distinction to argue that once Jeff knows of Thorwald's crime, intervening is a genuine obligation rather than a merely heroic option.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Kinds of Probability (physical, statistical, evidential)
holes.what: The philosophical distinction between physical, statistical, and evidential probability - different senses in which an event can be improbable and different ways evidence supports a theory.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire analysis of Hitchcock plot twists and of Jeff-and-Doyle's evidence assessment in Rear Window turns on keeping these three kinds of improbability apart.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Intentionalism, New Criticism and Subjectivism (meaning in art)
holes.what: Competing theories of artistic interpretation holding that an artwork's meaning is fixed by the artist's intention, by the work itself, or by audience reception.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Hitchcock's cameos as its test case, arguing each of the three theories holds within its own domain and that no single source exhausts artistic meaning.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The puzzle of how we can know that other people have conscious minds rather than being unfeeling automata, given that we observe only their behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 30 offers Shadow of a Doubt as a counterexample to the Cartesian other-minds skepticism Descartes motivates with his hats-and-coats passage, with the two Charlies knowing each other's minds.
holes.book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

holes.name: Intellectual Property and Copyright
holes.what: The philosophical question of what intangible creations — ideas, performances, authored works — can be owned and controlled, and on what moral (rather than merely legal) basis.
holes.why: Chapter 12's whole argument about the Dead's taping ethos and the Archive.org dispute turns on whether a performance or an authored work is the kind of thing that can be owned at all.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: Leo Tolstoy
holes.what: Russian novelist and thinker whose 1898 treatise 'What Is Art?' defines art as the sincere communication of lived feeling that unites artist and audience in community, and rails against elitist high art.
holes.why: Chapter 16 is built entirely on Tolstoy's theory, arguing the Grateful Dead's music exemplifies his standard better than canonical works like Beethoven's Ninth.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: Infection Theory of Art (What Is Art?)
holes.what: Tolstoy's view that art transmits the artist's sincerely lived feeling to audiences — the stronger the infection, the better the art — with music the most universal and community-uniting of the arts.
holes.why: Chapter 16 applies this exact standard to Dead shows — joy and spiritual union infecting Deadheads past, present, and future — to rank the band above counterfeit mass entertainment.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher whose metaphysics holds that every actual occasion is self-creative and that the past enjoys 'objective immortality' — what has been done can never be undone, even by God.
holes.why: Chapter 19's resolution — that creative contribution and gratitude defeat death because even God cannot unmake your bass line — is drawn directly from Whitehead's process philosophy.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: George Santayana
holes.what: Spanish-American naturalist philosopher (1863–1952) who divided the one natural world into four realms of being — matter, essence, truth, and spirit.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues that 'Eyes of the World' is a direct lyrical statement of Santayana's ontology of psyche, spirit, and the spiritual life.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: The Four Realms of Being
holes.what: Santayana's division of reality into matter (inaccessible substance), essence (the forms and appearances consciousness directly knows), truth (the subset of true essences), and spirit (the light of awareness).
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the psyche–spirit distinction and spirit's contemplation of essences to interpret the 'Eyes of the World' chorus and the Dead show as Santayana's spiritual life.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: Error Theory (argument from queerness)
holes.what: Mackie's view that ordinary value judgments presuppose irreducible, objective value properties (queer entities) that do not exist, so all such judgments are systematically false projections of feeling.
holes.why: Chapter 27 tests Mackie's error theory, projection, and 'oughts by agreement' against Deadheads' disputes over whether the band's Space jams have real musical value.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: Decision Theory and Expected Value
holes.what: The framework for rational choice under uncertainty: assign probabilities and utilities to each outcome, compute every option's expected value, and choose the highest.
holes.why: Chapter 28 evaluates whether the sailor or soldier in 'Lady with a Fan' was wise through five expected-value calculations.
holes.book: 028 - The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

holes.name: Dante Alighieri
holes.what: Medieval poet whose Divine Comedy synthesizes Aquinas's ethics and whose principle of contrapasso makes each sinner's punishment embody the sin itself.
holes.why: Chapter 16's whole reading of Kill Bill maps the Bride's vengeance onto the Inferno's contrapasso and Dante's hellbound and purgatorial vengeful.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: Henri Bergson
holes.what: French philosopher of duration who distinguished lived, experienced time from spatialized clock time and analyzed cinema's mechanical illusion of movement.
holes.why: Chapter 20's account of why Pulp Fiction's out-of-sequence editing works rests on Bergson's clock time versus real time and his film-projector analysis.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: Poetics (imitation, catharsis, unity of action)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of tragic art: poetry imitates unified action, plots must hold together when rearranged, and audiences seek catharsis.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Pulp Fiction's time-twisting as Tarantino playing with the three unities and engineering catharsis, and its moral as Aristotle's incontinence.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma
holes.what: A game-theoretic situation in which each side's individually rational, self-interested choice leaves everyone worse off than mutual cooperation would.
holes.why: Chapter 22 defines Tarantino's standoffs as an 'ex-convict's dilemma' instance of the prisoner's dilemma and uses it to show group-rationality solutions fail.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis, which holds that childhood relations with parents form adult neuroses that must be worked through, famously via the Oedipus complex.
holes.why: Chapter 24 reads Kill Bill as Tarantino's Oedipal play and therapy session—killing the father, mother-lover reversal, neurosis—which is Freudian psychoanalysis, not any figure in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: Bushido (the way of the warrior)
holes.what: The Japanese samurai ethical code emphasizing loyalty, self-sacrifice, honor, and total service unto death to one's lord.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues Beatrix's revenge on Bill cannot be justified by Bushido because she violates her retainer duty by leaving her lord, who would then be justified in killing her.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: Nihilism (active and passive)
holes.what: Nietzsche's diagnosis that the collapse of religious meaning leaves life seemingly meaningless, borne passively (declining, inherited values) or overcome actively by creating new values.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads Vincent Vega as Nietzsche's passive nihilist who takes the world at face value, contrasted with Jules the value-creating free spirit.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: R.M. Hare
holes.what: Twentieth-century moral philosopher whose universal prescriptivism analyzes moral judgments as universal prescriptions rather than descriptions of properties.
holes.why: Chapter 9 uses Hare's universal prescriptivism, alongside the Mill–Gibbard and Hume accounts, to argue that even Vincent Vega makes genuine moral judgments and thus has a morality.
holes.book: 029 - Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch

holes.name: Rastafari (Babylon, I-tal, and Jah)
holes.what: A Jamaican religious movement grounded in the Old Testament that rejects 'Babylon' (white imperialist power structures) through natural living, ganja as sacrament, nyabinghi drumming, and 'soon come' time.
holes.why: Chapter 8 interprets the reggae Dub Side of the Moon, and Dark Side's money and time themes, entirely through Rasta reasoning, which no taxonomy concept covers.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Carl Jung
holes.what: Swiss psychologist whose theory of symbols, lucid dreaming, and the collective unconscious treats images and dreams as a conversation between the conscious and unconscious mind.
holes.why: Chapter 9 builds its reading of The Wall film on Jung's concepts of lucid dreaming and over-explicit versus genuinely symbolic imagery to explain how the movie works on its audience.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist whose monomyth of the Hero's Journey, departure, fulfillment, and return, describes the initiation structure of narratives across cultures.
holes.why: Chapter 9 superimposes Campbell's circular Hero's Journey on Aristotle's plot curve to model how the audience participates in The Wall and receives its meaning.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Carl Jung
holes.what: Swiss psychologist who proposed 'synchronicity,' an acausal connecting principle meant to explain meaningful coincidences.
holes.why: Chapter 11 examines and rejects Jung's synchronicity as one of the two main models for why the Dark Side of the Rainbow synchronization feels meaningful.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Apophenia (seeing patterns in randomness)
holes.what: The human tendency to perceive meaningful connections among unrelated phenomena, a term coined by psychologist Klaus Conrad and linked by Peter Brugger to creativity itself.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses apophenia, alongside Kuhnian pattern-recognition, as its psychological explanation of why the Dark Side of the Rainbow syncs are perceived without being designed.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Frankfurt School critical theorist whose Eclipse of Reason diagnoses modern thought as 'instrumental reason,' the application of self-interest to all situations for technical efficiency.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Horkheimer's instrumental reason and ideology critique, alongside Buber, to interpret the It-world of 'Welcome to the Machine,' work, and education.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Collective Intentionality (group agency)
holes.what: The thesis that groups can be agents with intentions, responsibility, and identity of their own, not reducible to the intentions of their individual members.
holes.why: Chapter 19 needs collective agency to explain how Pink Floyd can have a group legacy and why Waters's departure did not end the band.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Actual vs Hypothetical Intentionalism
holes.what: The debate in aesthetics over whether artworks should be interpreted and evaluated by their creators' actual intentions or by the hypothetical intentions of an idealized artist.
holes.why: Chapter 19 defends actual intentionalism (Hendrix's 'kiss the sky,' Waters's interviews) as the constraint on which albums genuinely count as Pink Floyd's work.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Non-Being (the path of Non-Being)
holes.what: The counterpart to Being — nothingness, privation, absence, and negation — whose status philosophers from Parmenides through Aristotle, Hegel, Marx, Sartre, and Heidegger contested.
holes.why: Chapter 22 organizes Pink Floyd's themes (alienation, Syd's absence, cosmic Angst) around this entire history of Non-Being, and the existing parmenidean-being slug covers only the Being side.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: Sartre's Theory of the Image (positional acts)
holes.what: Sartre's doctrine that an image is an act of consciousness which annihilates the perceptual world and posits its object as non-existent, absent, existing elsewhere, or neutral.
holes.why: Chapter 23 explains how 'Brain Damage' and 'Eclipse' work on the listener almost entirely through these four forms of the positional act, a doctrine the generic phenomenology slug does not capture.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: The History of Madness (unreason)
holes.what: Foucault's account of madness as historically constructed — Renaissance unreason, classical confinement, and the modern psychiatric regime that internalizes surveillance, guilt, and remorse.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads Pink's self-imprisonment, his guilt at 'The Trial', and Syd's artistic afterlife through this specific three-stage history, which power-knowledge and discipline only partially cover.
holes.book: 030 - Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist philosopher and social psychologist who held that the self arises socially, by taking the attitudes of others toward oneself.
holes.why: Chapter 8 quotes Mead's social theory of the self as its key philosophical support for the claim that Cash's socially manufactured persona became his authentic identity.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Narrative Identity (diachronic vs episodic selves)
holes.what: The debate over whether a person's self is constituted by a life-spanning narrative (diachronic self) or only by momentary experiences (episodic self).
holes.why: Chapter 9 organizes its entire reading of J.R. Cash around the diachronic/episodic distinction and proposes a third, not-fully-temporal self behind both.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who argues that many people (Episodics) do not experience themselves as temporally extended, and that chasing a grand life-narrative can be a danger.
holes.why: Chapter 9 explicitly uses Strawson's episodic view as one pole of the personal-identity debate it applies to Cash's contradictory selves.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Care Work (Love's Labor)
holes.what: Labor of caring for others, such as parenting, teaching, and nursing, that produces relationships and persons yet is typically unpaid or underpaid.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Eva Kittay's care work to bridge the intrinsic and extrinsic value of work and to frame the meaning-giving labor in Cash's songs.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Populism
holes.what: A political stance and rhetoric claiming to speak for the common people against elites, prizing straight talk and equal dignity while risking oversimplification and demagoguery.
holes.why: Chapter 13 is wholly organized around defining populism and asking whether Cash's anti-racist, pro-prisoner populism supports or corrodes democratic deliberation.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Gabriel Marcel
holes.what: French existentialist philosopher of participation, being-with-others, and 'creative fidelity' in love and commitment.
holes.why: Chapter 14 makes Marcel's 'creative fidelity' the organizing concept of Cash's 'love gone good': being at the disposal of and participating with others.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Appraisal vs Bestowal Theories of Love
holes.what: The debate over whether love responds to value already present in the beloved (appraisal) or confers value on the beloved (bestowal).
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its 'June Love' hybrid precisely to bridge the appraisal/bestowal dilemma it stages between Velleman and Irving Singer.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Situationism (situationist social psychology)
holes.what: The empirically supported thesis that human behavior is driven more by immediate situational factors than by stable character traits.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues from the dime, seminary, Milgram, and Stanford prison experiments that human nature is frail, grounding Cash's lessons of charity and avoiding bad situations.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Redemption (moral revaluation)
holes.what: The revaluation of a fallen person's worth through genuine transformation of character, typically requiring grace, hope, and recognition by others.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire argument is that Cash's music and life embody redemption, humility, hope, and the impossibility of redeeming oneself without others.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Inspired Anger
holes.what: Desire accompanied by pain and sorrow but without hope, for a justice, restitution, or restoration that can never be, directed creatively into art (built on Plato's Ion account of poetic inspiration as being possessed or blown away).
holes.why: Chapter 23's central, original category: Cash's 'Hurt' exemplifies this futile, mourning anger, which is distinct from Aristotle's justified anger and from no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Soul-Making Theodicy (John Hick)
holes.what: John Hick's answer to the problem of evil: God permits suffering because virtues like courage, fortitude, compassion, and temperance can only form in a world containing danger, pain, and deprivation.
holes.why: Chapter 27's whole argument tests whether suffering-driven character formation can justify God's permission of evil and concludes the theodicy is too weak on its own.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Privation Theory of Evil (privatio boni)
holes.what: Augustine's view that evil has no positive existence but is a corruption or falling-away from good, as darkness is merely the absence of light.
holes.why: Chapter 28 builds its Augustinian reading of Cash on this definition, contrasting it with monist and dualist accounts of the nature of evil, none of which taxonomy captures.
holes.book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

holes.name: Abraham Joshua Heschel
holes.what: Twentieth-century Jewish theologian who described the biblical prophets as people overwhelmed by God's pathos, conveying divine anguish at injustice rather than foretelling the future.
holes.why: Chapter 8 rests its entire test of whether Springsteen is a prophet on Heschel's distinction between poetic inspiration and prophetic revelation, his Jonah fable, and his account of lamentation.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German social theorist whose Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism traced modern capitalism to the religious valorization of worldly work.
holes.why: Chapter 9 tests Springsteen's songs of work against Weber's salvation-through-labor ethic as one of its three philosophical frames, alongside Marx and Arendt, invoking him repeatedly ('Weber would approve').
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Carl Schmitt
holes.what: German political theorist who defined the political as the friend–enemy distinction and defended sovereign rule through permanent states of emergency and homogeneous democracy.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses Schmitt's homogeneity-and-enemy model of democracy as the dark foil — echoed in multicultural identity politics — against which Dewey's diversity-managing democracy reads 'Born in the U.S.A.'
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Margaret Fuller
holes.what: American transcendentalist feminist who argued in Woman in the Nineteenth Century that men squander their freedom on appetite and domination and that women's full development would transform both sexes.
holes.why: Chapter 15 quotes Fuller's complaint about men's enslaving 'freedom' as evidence that the collateral damage of negative freedom falls on men as well as women.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
holes.what: Feminist social theorist who analyzed how male-built institutions — family, education, economy — systematically stunt women's development and damage men too.
holes.why: Chapter 15 relies on Gilman's account of socially constructed female dependence to explain why the heroines of 'Racing in the Street' and 'Fast Car' can first imagine freedom only through a man and his car.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Negative and Positive Freedom
holes.what: The distinction between freedom from external constraint (negative liberty) and freedom to realize one's capacities and become someone (positive liberty).
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire contrast between the male road-freedom of 'Racing in the Street' and the woman's freedom of 'Fast Car' is organized by this distinction, though it never names its canonical source.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Early modern Italian philosopher whose New Science holds that law, reason, and institutions arise from myth and imagination, grasped through 'imaginative universals' (archetypes) and memory rather than abstract reason.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Wendy, Peter Pan, and the city-as-altar as Vichian imaginative universals and casts Vico, not Descartes, as the victor in the war between imagination and reason.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Karl Jaspers
holes.what: German existentialist whose Existenz-philosophy analyzes 'ultimate situations' — death, suffering, struggle, guilt — as the limits of existence at which the self may leap in philosophic faith toward the unknowable Transcendent.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is structured entirely around Jaspers's boundary situations, using them to read Springsteen's songs of death, suffering, struggle, and guilt.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Mathematician-turned-metaphysician whose process philosophy holds that reality fundamentally consists of events rather than enduring objects, so events call for narrative rather than mere naming.
holes.why: Chapter 19 grounds its whole reading of 'Thunder Road' in Whitehead's event ontology — the screen door and Mary's dress as one event — making him the chapter's foundation.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Paul Ricoeur
holes.what: French hermeneutic phenomenologist who argued in Time and Narrative that selves discover and rewrite their identity through the stories they tell.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses Ricoeur's narrative identity to explain how 'Thunder Road' and the 1980 'Factory' performance retell and redeem the narrator's and listener's past.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: John J. McDermott
holes.what: 20th-century American philosopher of experience who built a 'metaphysics of transiency,' meliorism, and the 'Promethean self' out of James, Dewey and existentialism.
holes.why: Chapters 20 and 21 read 'Atlantic City' and 'Reason to Believe' almost entirely through McDermott's account of finitude, cutting and connecting relations, and hope without guarantees — a framework no existing taxonomy slug captures.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Poetics (mimesis and catharsis)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of art as imitation of universal human action, in which we delight because learning pleases and poetry is more philosophic than history.
holes.why: Chapter 27 grounds its explanation of why sad story-songs like 'The River' teach and please us in the Poetics' mimesis-and-learning thesis, which none of the existing Aristotle concepts covers.
holes.book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

holes.name: Narrative Identity (emplotment)
holes.what: Ricoeur and MacIntyre's theory that personal identity consists in the unified, emplotted story a person tells about their life, revisable in light of new facts.
holes.why: Chapter 9 builds its entire account of Boomer and Athena Sharon's identity crises on narrative identity, emplotment, and factual/belief disruptions, none of which taxonomy.json has a slug for.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway)
holes.what: Donna Haraway's hybrid human-machine figure whose breakdown of the human/animal, human/machine, and physical/non-physical boundaries makes identity itself hybrid and constructed.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses the cyborg to explain the humanoid Cylons and Hera as hybrids whose loyalties and identities must be actively constructed.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose structural model divides the psyche into id, ego, and superego, and whose 'family romance' describes the child's imaginative replacement of its parents.
holes.why: Chapter 11's first half explains the gamer-avatar bond as Freudian reconciliation of id and superego, and Freud's family romance also anchors the frameworks of chapters 12 and 15.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Double / Doppelgänger
holes.what: The gothic motif (theorized by Otto Rank) of a split second self — a corporeal Double or ghostly Doppelgänger — expressing anxiety about identity and the struggle between good and evil within.
holes.why: Chapter 12's whole framework reads Head Six and Head Baltar as Double and Doppelgänger tied to dissociative identity disorder, a concept taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Homi Bhabha
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist of ambivalence, mimicry ('almost the same, but not quite'), and hybridity between colonizer and colonized.
holes.why: Chapter 15 applies Bhabha's ambivalence and mimicry to explain why the humans can neither keep the Cylons other nor absorb Hera, the mixed child who menaces the colonial order.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Colonial Family Romance (métissage)
holes.what: Françoise Vergès's inversion of Freud's family romance: the colonizing 'parent' adopts colonized 'children' who must remain perpetually different and subordinate, with mixed-race offspring (métissage) as its site of fascination and anxiety.
holes.why: Chapter 15 structures its entire reading of human-Cylon relations, racial slurs, and Hera's threatened abortion around this romance and its collapse.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway)
holes.what: Donna Haraway's hybrid organism-machine figure, used in feminist theory to dissolve fixed categories of gender, race, and species.
holes.why: Chapter 17 opens by defining the Cylons through Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' before building its 'technoqueer' reading of Cylon reproduction on it.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway)
holes.what: The human-machine hybrid as a theoretical condition: per cyborg theory, humans are already cyborgs through vaccines, prosthetics, and medication.
holes.why: Chapter 18 ('I, Cyborg') argues humans are already cyborgs and the humanoid Cylons a further organic-technological integration, a framework taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Purity and Danger (dirt as matter out of place)
holes.what: Mary Douglas's anthropological account of how cultures use the body and notions of dirt and contamination to police social boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable bodies.
holes.why: Chapter 18 reads Cylon-contamination fears, segregation analogies, and Gina's torture as boundary-marking in Douglas's sense, with no matching taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: George Lakoff
holes.what: Cognitive linguist who maps political morality onto idealized Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models of the family as metaphors framing moral cognition.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Cain's Pegasus and Adama's Galactica in Razor as opposed Strict Father and Nurturant Parent families, with Kendra Shaw caught between the two models.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Wretched of the Earth (decolonizing violence)
holes.what: Fanon's account of colonial occupation as systematic violence and of anticolonial violence as the cleansing, self-creating force by which the colonized reclaim their humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 28 interprets the New Caprica insurgency's strikes and suicide bombings through exactly this framework, but taxonomy.json only carries Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Italian philosopher whose concept of 'bare life' names human existence stripped to mere biological survival, outside political meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Agamben's bare life to describe the fleet's existence in '33' as survival reduced to the brink of death between jumps.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Messianic 'To-Come' (democratie a venir)
holes.what: Derrida's notion of an unpredictable opening onto the future, a promise that is never present but structures hope and decision.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads the fleet's FTL jumps as metaphors for Derrida's messianic to-come, the sliver of hope between promise and danger.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who late in life posited the death instinct (Thanatos) warring against Eros, the life instinct.
holes.why: Chapter 37 makes Freud's death instinct the fulcrum of the series, reading Starbuck, Tigh and Baltar as fusing life and death drives.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Melanie Klein
holes.what: Psychoanalyst who placed infantile aggression and the projection/splitting of badness at the center of development, source of the paranoid position.
holes.why: Chapter 37's title concept is Klein's paranoid position, into which the whole human fleet is stuck after projecting its destructiveness onto the Cylons.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Death Instinct (Thanatos)
holes.what: Freud's unconscious drive toward quietude, inorganic rest and self-destruction, opposed to and fused with Eros.
holes.why: Chapter 37 analyzes Starbuck's self-sabotage, Tigh's drinking and the peaceful death-hallucinations as expressions of the death drive.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Paranoid Position
holes.what: Klein's early-infantile stance of projecting one's own aggression into others and remaining perpetually vigilant for its return.
holes.why: Chapter 37 argues humans project all evil onto the Cylons and must keep them in sight, leaving the fleet stuck in the paranoid position.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Mormon Theology (LDS metaphysics)
holes.what: Latter-day Saint metaphysics: Kolob, eternal progression toward godhood ('as man now is, God once was'), and absolute, inviolable moral agency.
holes.why: Chapter 40 argues the original BSG's ontology, Kobol, the Quorum of Twelve, sealing, deification and supreme free will, is built from Mormon theology.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian theorist of the dialogic: language and texts as many-voiced (heteroglossic, polyphonic) dialogues rather than single-authored utterances.
holes.why: Chapter 41's whole case that Moore's series is a 're-imagining' in dialogic parallel, not a GINO remake, rests on Bakhtin's theory.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Dialogism (polyphony, heteroglossia)
holes.what: Bakhtin's view that texts converse with past and future texts through many equally authoritative voices.
holes.why: Chapter 41 uses dialogism to describe how the two series, their religious and pseudo-archaeological sources, and fanfic talk to each other.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Manichaeism (Light versus Darkness)
holes.what: Mani's third-century dualist religion: a universe split between good Light and evil Darkness warring over humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 42 reads the original series' 'War of the Gods', Count Iblis versus the Beings of Light, as dramatized Manichaean moral absolutism.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Compulsory Heterosexuality
holes.what: Adrienne Rich's concept that heterosexuality is an imposed political institution enforced by social pressure, not a natural inevitability.
holes.why: Chapter 43 reads Starbuck's captivity as Leoben's simulated wife on New Caprica as a literalization of the feminist critique of compulsory heterosexuality.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: The Lilith Myth
holes.what: Jewish legend (Alphabet of Ben Sira, the Zohar) of Adam's first wife, created from the same earth as Adam, who left Eden and was later demonized as a child-stealing seductress.
holes.why: Chapter 44 maps Number Six and Sharon onto Eve and Lilith, arguing BSG lets the demonized first women of myth be redeemed.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Participatory Culture (textual poaching, fan fiction)
