holes.what: Henry Jenkins's account of fans who actively rewrite corporate-owned myths, creating value and community the originals lack.
holes.why: Chapter 45 is a fan story whose theme is whether fan fiction has value, pitting Jenkins against Adorno and Benjamin's culture-industry pessimism.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Coduction (Booth's ethical criticism)
holes.what: Wayne Booth's method of judging fiction ethically through sustained, informed, open-minded conversation among readers.
holes.why: Chapter 46 uses coduction to argue BSG is ethical because it invites open moral conversation, on suicide bombing and gay characters, instead of preaching.
holes.book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's account of concepts unified by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities rather than a common essence, as members of a family resemble one another in different ways.
holes.why: Chapter 8's central move is that Shuffle, Nano, Classic, and Touch share no 'iPodness' essence but only family resemblances, which language-games does not cover.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Actor-Network Theory (agency of objects)
holes.what: Latour and Law's theory that agency is distributed across networks of humans and non-human actants, so objects act on and shape human behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 8 uses ANT to argue the iPod tracks play counts, suggests purchases, and trains its user's gestures, so the device makes itself familiar to us.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who contrasted the pleasure principle (immediate gratification) with the reality principle (deferred gratification in light of the world's obstacles).
holes.why: Chapter 9 frames the iPod as wedged between the two principles, with the blobject expressing pleasure and the post-9/11, Iraq-war design climate the reality principle.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Georg Lukács
holes.what: Hungarian Marxist who developed Marx's fragmentary remarks into a full theory of reification and the 'phantom objectivity' of commodity relations.
holes.why: Chapter 11's account of the iPod world as a reified world -- and of modding as its limit case -- is built explicitly on Lukács rather than on Marx directly.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Reification (thingification)
holes.what: The process by which human relations take on the character of things while commodities acquire human, life-like qualities.
holes.why: Reification is the titled concept of chapter 11, which argues iPod users personify a commodity made by hidden workers; commodity-fetishism alone misses its objective/subjective structure.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Edward Said
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist whose Orientalism showed how the West constructs the Orient as an inferior, binary Other to justify and maintain dominance.
holes.why: Chapter 18's reading of the iPod as the white West's invisible standard is explicitly built on Said's Center/Margin and West/Other framework.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Whiteness as Invisible Default (whiteness studies)
holes.what: The critical-race thesis (Dyer, whiteness studies) that whiteness is an unmarked, universal standard by which everyone else is named, ranked, and found wanting.
holes.why: Chapter 18's core claim is that the iPod is whiteness's 'industry standard', dominant precisely because its whiteness goes unremarked; no existing slug covers whiteness studies.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist philosopher of technology whose cyborg hybridizes human and machine to unsettle essentialist identity categories.
holes.why: Chapter 19 reads Apple's silhouette ads as constructing a 'symbolic cyborgism' in which the iPod, not the face, defines the person.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Jean-Luc Nancy
holes.what: French philosopher whose The Inoperative Community argues community is never a lost organic whole nor a common identity, but an always-given 'being-with' in singular plurality that resists organization and politicization.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central claim — that iPod mobile clubbing is a genuine community without shared identity, and that the 'lost community' is a myth — is Nancy's doctrine outright, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: German hermeneutic philosopher whose Truth and Method and The Relevance of the Beautiful treat the artwork as play that draws spectators into its own realm and thereby gathers a community (the festival, the tennis crowd).
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses Gadamer's account of art creating its own community and leaving each participant a personal space as the bridge between iPod solitude and togetherness, and no taxonomy slug covers him.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Technologies of the Self (care of the self)
holes.what: Foucault's late-work concept for the practices (diet, writing, confession, meditation) through which individuals effect operations on their own bodies and souls so as to transform themselves toward happiness, purity, or wisdom.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies technologies of the self directly to the iPod — playlist-making and customization as self-formation, from ancient self-care to Christian confession to modern preference-lists — which the power-focused Foucault slugs do not capture.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Hans Magnus Enzensberger
holes.what: German essayist and media theorist whose 'Constituents of a Theory of the Media' (1970) lists the emancipatory potentials of new media: decentralized programming, each receiver a potential transmitter, mobilization, interaction, feedback, political learning, collective production, and self-organization.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire framework evaluates podcasting point-by-point against Enzensberger's eight criteria for an emancipatory socialist media, and no taxonomy philosopher or slug covers this media-emancipation theory.
holes.book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

holes.name: Cultural Literacy (E.D. Hirsch)
holes.what: E.D. Hirsch's thesis that reading and communication depend on shared background knowledge of a culture's vocabulary, allusions, and history rather than on content-free skills.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads 'Darmok' as dramatizing Hirsch's claim: Picard decodes Tamarian myth-speech only through shared stories like Gilgamesh, and the episode champions Great Books.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Classical Yoga (Patanjali's eight limbs)
holes.what: Patanjali's system of ethical restraints and observances, posture, breath control, and meditation culminating in the liberating oneness of samadhi.
holes.why: Chapter 9's core interpretive move maps Vulcan logic's three modes — formal, ethical, meditative — onto Patanjali's Yoga, reading Kolinahr and Spock's rebirth through samadhi and tantra.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: The Hedonistic Paradox
holes.what: The puzzle that pursuing pleasure for its own sake self-defeatingly yields pain, through frustration, mistaking pains for pleasures, or the boredom of getting everything wanted.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses the paradox to explain why the omnipotent, immortal Q — Quinn in 'Death Wish' above all — end up frustrated and miserable despite unlimited power.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Eugenics
holes.what: The program of improving the human gene pool by selective breeding or genetic intervention, historically coercive and state-driven, now debated as 'liberal eugenics'.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central cases — Khan's Augments, the Moab IV colony, prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis — are weighed against the history of eugenics from Plato to Buck v. Bell.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: The Right to an Open Future
holes.what: The principle (associated with Joel Feinberg) that parents and designers must preserve a child's future range of life choices rather than fix them in advance.
holes.why: Chapter 14 applies the concept to the Moab IV colonists, Worf and Alexander, the engineered Jem'Hadar, B'Elanna's baby, and Kass's argument against cloning.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Milton Friedman
holes.what: Economist whose stockholder theory holds that a corporation's only social responsibility is to maximize its owners' profits within the law.
holes.why: Chapter 17 structures its business-ethics debate around Friedman's stockholder theory opposed to stakeholder theory, voiced through Quark and Grand Nagus Zek.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Amartya Sen
holes.what: Nobel laureate economist-philosopher whose capability approach defines development as expanding the real freedoms people have reason to value, and poverty as capability deprivation.
holes.why: Chapter 17 closes by adopting Sen's capability approach to argue markets and greed are justified only as means to human welfare and freedom.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist philosopher of science whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' argues we are already cyborgs and that natural/artificial and similar dualisms underwrite domination.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses Haraway's cyborg to dissolve the human/machine boundary the Borg violate and to reach its conclusion that 'we are the Borg'.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Leon Kass
holes.what: Bioethicist who defends the 'wisdom of repugnance' — the view that repulsion at cloning or enhancement tracks real moral harm — and the treatment/enhancement distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 19 leans on Kass's repugnance principle to explain why the Borg disgust us, before arguing technology has already eroded that wisdom.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Positive and Negative Liberty
holes.what: Isaiah Berlin's distinction between freedom as non-interference (negative) and freedom as self-mastery enabled by resources and capacities (positive), with Taylor's reply that positive freedom 'by one's own lights' need not become tyranny.
holes.why: Chapter 20 leans on this debate to argue that the Federation supplies positive liberties — education, open debate, met basic needs — that Hegelian recognition requires beyond Locke-style negative liberty.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher who ranked 'major beauty' — harmony intensified by contrast and danger — above mere painlessness, seeing God's purpose as 'the evocation of intensities.'
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Whitehead's aesthetic theodicy to answer Hume: a holodeck-safe world without the mortality failsafe would lack the contrasts that make experience worth having.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Richard Swinburne
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of religion who defends theism probabilistically and argues that genuine responsibility for other beings is such a great good that it justifies a world containing evil.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Swinburne's responsibility theodicy to explain why Kirk leaves the Nexus: a simulated world offers pleasure but no real responsibility or chance to make a difference.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Philosopher of religion whose 'soul-making' theodicy holds that suffering and adversity are the environment in which immature beings develop moral character toward perfection.
holes.why: Chapter 21 applies Hick's soul-making theodicy to Q in 'Déjà Q,' whose pain-free omnipotence left him bratty until human hardship aboard the Enterprise taught him selflessness.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: The Differend (agonistics)
holes.what: Lyotard's notion of a dispute in which one party is stripped of the idiom needed to phrase its wrong, leaving a silence that the existing rules of the conflict cannot hear or remedy.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads the Bajor-Cardassia impasse in 'Duet' as a differend: the occupation's victims cannot phrase their loss in Cardassian, Federation, or Bajoran terms without distortion.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Presentism vs Eternalism
holes.what: Competing ontologies of time: only the present exists (presentism) versus the whole four-dimensional timeline being equally real (eternalism, the 'block universe').
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues presentism would make Star Trek time travel impossible and that eternalism best models the Prophets' atemporal outlook — though it carries fatalism, as Data's 'It has occurred. It will occur.' shows.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Functionalism (mind as software)
holes.what: Theory of mind identifying mental states with functional roles, so the mind is to the brain as a program is to hardware and could in principle run on a different substrate.
holes.why: Chapter 26 invokes functionalism to assess Star Trek's consciousness downloads — Korby, Ira Graves into Data, Juliana Tainer — asking whether the uploaded person is really you.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Eliminative Materialism
holes.what: The Churchland view that mature neuroscience will replace folk-psychological terms like belief, anger, and consciousness, revealing mental states as illusions of our outdated framework.
holes.why: Chapter 27 tests eliminative materialism (via Paul Churchland) as the scientific alternative to dualism for Data and McCoy before finding it unable to accommodate subjective experience.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Emergentism (mind as emergent property)
holes.what: The view that mind is a natural but irreducible, unpredictable property arising at thresholds of physical complexity, with novel causal powers over its material base.
holes.why: Chapter 27's title theory: emergentism is the proposed compromise keeping both mental causation and subjectivity while staying scientific, and the chapter worries it collapses into dualism in disguise.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: The Liar Paradox
holes.what: The self-referential sentence 'this sentence is not true,' which is true if and only if it is false — threatening the consistency of truth and, via the explosion problem, all of logic.
holes.why: Chapter 28's centerpiece: Kirk and Harry Mudd crash the android Norman with the Liar in 'I, Mudd,' exposing an inconsistency in the concept of truth beneath Vulcan's life of logic.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
holes.what: Gödel's proof that any consistent formal system able to express arithmetic contains truths — like a sentence saying of itself that it is unprovable — that the system can neither prove nor refute.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses the theorems, through the Lucas-Penrose anti-mechanist argument and Putnam's rebuttal, to ask whether minds outstrip computer programs like Landru.
holes.book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we feel genuine emotions (fear, grief, relief) toward characters and events we know do not exist.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is organized around explaining why players fear Gohma and grieve for Link's grandmother in Wind Waker despite knowing the game is not real, testing illusion, thought, and pretend theories against it.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Space of Flows vs Space of Places
holes.what: Manuel Castells's distinction between networked movement-space, where places are mere nodes in flows, and lived place-space with its own meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses this contrast to argue that the Ballad of Gales warp turns Wind Waker's sea into a space of flows, degrading environmental presence and the felt meaning of Hyrule's places.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Informal Fallacies and Critical Thinking
holes.what: The catalogue of everyday bad-reasoning patterns (hasty generalization, equivocation, false dilemma, ad hominem, slippery slope) and the standards of valid, sound argument used to expose them.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is a full lesson in argument analysis, diagnosing Zelda-community and real-world reasoning errors from 'all gamers are geeks' to videogame-violence panic, and taxonomy has no logic or fallacy concept.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Ludus and Paidia (modes of play)
holes.what: Roger Caillois's distinction between rule-bound, goal-directed play (ludus) and spontaneous, unstructured free play (paidia), adapted to games by Gonzalo Frasca.
holes.why: Chapter 16's entire argument about Link's forced morality and the player's glitch-hunting freedom is built on the ludus/paidia pair, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Bruno Latour
holes.what: Philosopher and sociologist of science who argued, in Laboratory Life with Steve Woolgar, that scientific facts and evidence are constructed through social practice, tools, and networks rather than discovered ready-made.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses Latour's framework as its backbone to show that Zelda fan timeline debates socially construct evidence and knowledge exactly the way laboratories do.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: The Hermeneutic Circle
holes.what: The idea that interpretation is circular: parts are understood through the whole and the whole through the parts, iteratively refined (Heidegger, Gadamer).
holes.why: Chapter 20 models how Zelda fans interpret the series, Ganon's recurrence making sense of Wind Waker's references, gossip stones pointing to the whole timeline, as exactly this circle.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Underdetermination of Theory by Evidence
holes.what: The thesis, rooted in Leibniz and later Quine-Duhem, that any finite body of evidence is compatible with infinitely many distinct theories, so evidence alone never fixes interpretation.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses underdetermination (via the y=2x guessing game) to show Zelda timeline data admit endless rival readings, which is why Ockham's razor and community standards of simplicity become necessary.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose essay Das Unheimliche (The Uncanny) analyzes the frightening as the familiar returned through repression.
holes.why: Chapter 22 devotes a full section to Majora's Mask's uncanny temporality, reading Link's Deku transformation and the hidden time songs through Freud's uncanny and its doubling repetitions.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: The Aesthetic Experience and the Art Status of Games
holes.what: The distinctive perceptual-emotional engagement with artworks, which some philosophers ground in objective properties of the object (Panofsky) or in rule-governed make-believe (Walton, Rosenstein).
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues Zelda is art because its make-believe viewing rules, translucence, and freeplay demand aesthetic experience; taxonomy has no philosophy-of-art concept besides Kant's aesthetics, which the chapter does not invoke.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst who modeled the psyche on dyadic relations of the ego to anchor-objects and on the subject's entry into the social symbolic order of language and culture.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses Lacan's dyad and social symbolic as its main framework: Link is the player's dyad, Hyrule the social symbolic, and the Triforce the triangle that ties them together.
holes.book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

holes.name: Race Feeling (races as vast families)
holes.what: Du Bois and Crummell's idea that races are 'vast families' bound by common history, impulses, and an inherited, quasi-sacred 'race feeling' that links individual self-realization to racial advancement.
holes.why: Chapter 12's central claim is that The Wiz stages Dorothy's cultivation of exactly this racial feeling—knowledge, feeling, courage, admittance—as a Black racial virtue, a concept no existing taxonomy slug (not even double-consciousness) captures.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: American philosopher (1895–1985) of mind, art, and symbolism who distinguished presentational (image-based) symbols from discursive (linguistic) thought and analyzed how dreams, fairy tales, and myths transform symbols.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds two of its three explanations of the Witch's melting—Oz as dream and Oz as fairytale—directly on Langer's quoted theory of symbols, and credits her (with Bergson) against the analytic tradition.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German idealist (1770–1854) whose philosophy of freedom, nature, and love treats God and self as developing through alienation and reconciliation rather than as static perfections.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is built entirely on Schelling's Of Human Freedom—quoting the Ungrund, the split of the groundless, and love as conscious unity—to read Dorothy's journey as a romantic eschatology.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Romantic Eschatology (Ungrund, alienation, conscious unity)
holes.what: Schelling's three-stage pattern of the journey: unconscious unity (the groundless Ungrund), fall into egoistic alienation, and return to unity through love that preserves real, limiting others.
holes.why: Chapter 18 maps each stage onto Dorothy's story—gray Kansas, the tornado and selfish quests, and the love-tinged homecoming—so the applied framework itself needs a slug distinct from Hegel's dialectic.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Eucatastrophe (the good catastrophe)
holes.what: Tolkien's term for the sudden, miraculous joyous turn at a story's climax that rescues the protagonists when their own efforts cannot—a glimpse of grace beyond tragedy.
holes.why: Chapter 19's pivot is that the film needs a eucatastrophic accident to defeat the Witch while Baum's book needs none, marking the difference between Old-World supernatural dependence and Baum's self-reliant optimism.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Appearance and Reality
holes.what: The classic distinction between how things seem to us and how they really are, and the question of whether appearances can be trusted to disclose reality.
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire reading of the green spectacles, the humbug Wizard, and Dorothy's maturation is organized around the appearance-reality distinction, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Repetition and Recollection
holes.what: Kierkegaard's pair from Repetition: recollection looks backward longingly at what is lost, while genuine repetition 'recollects forward,' re-appropriating life faithfully with a stable self amid change.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses exactly this pair to distinguish the various Dorothys' homecomings, recollecting old Kansas versus willing repetition with self-knowledge as in The Wiz, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we appear to have genuine emotions for characters we know do not exist, though caring about non-existent people seems impossible; theories include Currie's simulation and Walton's make-believe emotions.
holes.why: Chapter 27 must dissolve this paradox to justify asking whether Dorothy should have stayed in Oz, since wishing the best for a fictional girl has to make sense first.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Matriarchy Theory (Bachofen's Mutterrecht)
holes.what: Bachofen's theory that human culture originated in mother-right and evolved through Tellurian, lunar, Dionysian and Apollonian stages before patriarchy, carried forward by Harrison, Engels, Jung, and Gimbutas.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is built on this tradition, reading the Kumbric Witch, the Lurline cult, Mother Yackle, and the silver slippers as survivals of a declining matriarchy, and the chapter insists it is not feminist philosophy proper.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: The Axial Age
holes.what: The era of 'paradigmatic individuals' (Confucius, Laozi, Socrates, Buddha, Jesus) whose reforms moved religion from visible sun-cults toward universal, invisible ethical order.
holes.why: Chapter 33 presents Maguire's Oz as a thought experiment in history with no Axial Age, which lets matriarchal folk religion survive two extra millennia alongside an ineffectual Unionist monotheism.
holes.book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: French-Bulgarian psychoanalytic theorist whose The Powers of Horror (1980) introduced 'the abject' — what the clean subject expels (corpses, bodily fluids, the formless) — as a psychical and aesthetic category.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire reading of 'Creep', the Kid A artwork, and Radiohead's boundary-dissolving songs is built on Kristeva and her book, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: The Abject (abjection)
holes.what: Kristeva's notion of what is 'cast off' from the ordered world of subjects and objects — the bodily, formless, borderline — which simultaneously repels and fascinates, grounding an 'abject aesthetics'.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses abjection as the master aesthetic category for Radiohead's lyrics and imagery, and no existing slug (beautiful, sublime, authentic) covers it.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics and Politics that tragedy (and music) evokes pity and fear and then purges them, yielding tragedy's own proper pleasure.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains the pleasure of Radiohead's sad songs entirely through Aristotelian catharsis, which no existing Aristotle slug in the taxonomy names.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Ontology of Musical Works
holes.what: The debate over what kind of entity a musical work is — particular performances and scores (nominalism), a mental idea (idealism), or an abstract object like a number (realism).
holes.why: Chapter 10's core question 'What is music?' is exactly this ontology debate, tested on 'Like Spinning Plates' and 'Optimistic', for which the taxonomy has no concept.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Expression and the Action of Culture
holes.what: Merleau-Ponty's view that artists (and politicians) express a still-unspoken 'fever' of experience, creating works that summon a public and make the world common — an 'action of culture' distinct from governing.
holes.why: Chapter 21's second half rests on this Merleau-Ponty account of artistic expression and politics-as-unveiling, while the taxonomy's only Merleau-Ponty entry is embodiment, which the chapter does not use.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Ernst Bloch
holes.what: German Marxist philosopher of hope whose The Principle of Hope distinguishes 'abstract utopia' (the diffuse impulse that things could be different, found in daydreams and art) from 'concrete utopia' (informed, planned commitment to change).
holes.why: Chapter 22's entire argument that Hail to the Thief's dystopia is utopian thought rests on Bloch's abstract/concrete utopia distinction.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: American Marxist literary critic who argues in Archaeologies of the Future that after the collapse of concrete utopias, utopian thought survives as the contemplation of an impossible break from capitalism's eternal present, for which dystopias are as essential as utopias.
holes.why: Chapter 22 leans on Jameson's framework to explain how the album's imagined totalitarian world functions as hope and critique of the here and now.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Power vs Violence (natality)
holes.what: Arendt's distinction, in The Human Condition and On Violence, between power (people acting in concert, springing from plurality and the new beginnings of natality) and violence (instruments like weapons that counterfeit power and appear where power is in jeopardy).
holes.why: Chapter 23's whole reading of 'Just,' 'Sit Down. Stand Up.,' '2 + 2 = 5' and 'I Will' turns on this power/violence opposition and natality, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: French philosopher who ties philosophy to poetry as 'logical revolt' — thought pitted against the defective state of the world — and insists philosophy is part of the world rather than sovereign over it.
holes.why: Chapter 24 opens and closes with Badiou's philosophy-as-poetry-of-revolt as the frame for understanding Radiohead's project.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Madness and Unreason (History of Madness)
holes.what: Foucault's account of how the classical age of reason constituted 'unreason' — madness — as the excluded, inhuman remainder of rationality, thereafter feared as the other of humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses this exclusion of unreason to explain how the feared Other of Hail to the Thief (evil, the inhuman, the 'terrorist') is produced by reason itself.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: Heidegger's student whose Truth and Method develops 'historically effected consciousness': our awareness is determined by real past events, yet we can become conscious of this operativeness.
holes.why: Chapter 28's payoff for what 'Pyramid Song' makes audible is Gadamer's historically affected consciousness — life recognized as embedded in time.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: The Differend
holes.what: Lyotard's notion of the unstable state of language in which something that must be put into phrases cannot yet be, and literature or art bears witness to it by finding new idioms.
holes.why: Chapter 31 reads 'Everything in Its Right Place,' 'Kid A,' and 'Treefingers' specifically as bearing witness to the differend.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: Seduction (vs sex, desire, and production)
holes.what: Baudrillard's account (in Seduction) of seduction as an endless game of reversible signs, artifice, appearance and disappearance, Rules rather than Laws, that challenges the Enlightenment reduction of sex to biological desire and production.
holes.why: Chapter 33 applies seduction — aleatory suspension, the superficial abyss, trompe l'oeil, Rules vs Laws — to nearly every track on In Rainbows.
holes.book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

holes.name: The Moral Holiday
holes.what: William James's term (in Pragmatism) for a morally legitimate respite from care, worry, and moral struggle that renews us before we return to the fray.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is built entirely on the claim that Buffett's 'license to chill' is a Jamesian moral holiday — care-free but never care-less — and no existing taxonomy slug captures this specific concept.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Transformative Learning (the disorienting dilemma)
holes.what: Jack Mezirow's theory that a disorienting dilemma that unhinges core assumptions triggers disorientation, critical exploration of how those assumptions were formed, and re-orientation — a fundamental shift in how one makes meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 12 maps Buffett's life narrative onto Mezirow's four-stage transformative process (dilemma, disorientation, exploration, re-orientation), which is the chapter's entire analytic frame and is covered by no existing taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Bulgarian-French theorist who founded intertextuality theory: every text is a 'mosaic of quotations' reweaving pre-existing texts, so no author controls meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 16 defines Buffett's piracy and his being 'two hundred years too late' entirely through her intertextuality theory.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Intertextuality
holes.what: The doctrine that all writing, thinking, and selves are rearrangements of already-existing words and ideas rather than original creations.
holes.why: Chapter 16 needs it to turn Buffett's pirate into the ironic pirate whose self is stitched from borrowed cultural texts.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
holes.what: Pragmatist feminist (1860-1935) who argued that women's economic, physical, and mental dependence on men stunts the development of the whole species (Women and Economics, Herland).
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses her dependence and dress-reform critique as its main lens for judging the women in Buffett's songs and novels.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Josiah Royce
holes.what: American absolute idealist (1855-1916) whose philosophy of community holds that individuals find salvation only in Beloved Communities bound by shared memories and hopes.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Buffett's western songs and Rancho Deluxe as Roycean lessons about community and 'wise provincialism.'
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: The Philosophy of Community (Beloved Community)
holes.what: Royce's doctrine that humane societies arise only where individuals sacrifice selfish desires for the good of the whole.
holes.why: Chapter 22 applies it to 'Ringling, Ringling' and Rancho Deluxe to argue belonging, not rugged individualism, redeems Western boomtowns.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Neapolitan philosopher (1668-1744) whose New Science steers between Stoic fate and Epicurean chance by explaining events through natural causes, moral causes, and providence.
holes.why: Chapter 24's resolution of Buffett's fortune-versus-fate puzzle rests on Vico's triad and his notion of providence.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Providence
holes.what: Vico's idea that whatever is provided — the order of nature, formed character, and fortune's obstacles — can be turned to good ends, especially for others.
holes.why: Chapter 24 ends by defining contentment as gratitude for providence, the third term that reconciles Buffett's fate and fortune.
holes.book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

holes.name: Mind Uploading
holes.what: The proposed transfer or copying of a human mind from a biological brain onto a computer substrate, producing an uploaded, non-biological person.
holes.why: Chapter 9 claims advanced civilizations become robotic because the most adventurous members upload their minds into machine bodies, making all-robot starfaring colonies the likeliest source of Transformer-like visitors.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: The Fermi Paradox
holes.what: The tension between estimates that many extraterrestrial civilizations should exist and the complete absence of any observed evidence that they have visited or contacted Earth.
holes.why: Chapter 10's core argumentative move is refuting the four assumptions behind the 'if aliens existed they would already be here' reasoning, which is precisely the Fermi-paradox style argument the Transformers scenario escapes.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Representative Realism (indirect realism)
holes.what: The view that we perceive the external world only indirectly, through internal mental representations or sense data that mediate between mind and world.
holes.why: Chapter 14 organizes Sam's misperception of Bumblebee around the dispute between direct realism and this representative view, treating the Transformers' disguises as a sustained argument from illusion.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The skeptical puzzle that, since we only ever observe others' outward behavior, we can never verify that anyone or anything besides ourselves genuinely has a mind.
holes.why: Chapter 16's guiding question is whether we can ever know that Optimus Prime has a mind rather than merely acts as if he has one, which is the problem of other minds extended to machines.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Moral Personhood
holes.what: The cluster of capacities (rationality, mental states, language, social relationships, autonomous action) that qualify a being as a person who can be held morally responsible.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its entire case that Decepticons deserve blame and punishment on defining these personhood criteria and showing Transformers meet them despite metal bodies.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Empedocles
holes.what: Presocratic Greek philosopher (c. 492-432 BC) who saw Love and Strife as the two cosmic forces that respectively unite and separate the elements in an endless cycle.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Empedocles's Love-and-Strife cosmology as its first conception of love, mapping the generative Primus and the destructive Unicron onto its two poles.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, holding that rational self-interest is the only moral standard and that altruism is a disservice to both helper and helped.
holes.why: Chapter 23 stages Megatron as a Randian rational egoist whose 'You still fight for the weak; that is why you lose' is set directly against the Kantian duty of the Autobots.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Carl Jung
holes.what: Swiss psychologist and founder of analytical psychology who proposed a collective unconscious populated by universal archetypes shared across myths and cultures.
holes.why: Chapter 24 invokes Jung's universal archetypes (with C.S. Lewis and Joseph Campbell) to explain Optimus Prime as an archetypal noble leader and Christ-type whose mythic resonance outlasts mere toy marketing.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist whose 'hero with a thousand faces' monomyth describes the universal pattern of separation, trials, supernatural aid, and return found in hero legends worldwide.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues Optimus Prime is a classic hero by mapping his Orion Pax origin, betrayal by Megatron, and rebirth by Primus onto Campbell's four-stage hero's journey.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Fascism
holes.what: A militaristic political philosophy holding that a supreme leader must perpetually unify and mobilize the people for war, demanding absolute obedience, crushing dissent, and glorifying strength over the weak.
holes.why: Chapter 27 diagnoses Megatron's 'Peace through tyranny' and philosophy of Strength as fascism in the mold of Hitler and Mussolini, set against the Autobots' cooperative Community ideal.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics
holes.what: Isaac Asimov's fictional hierarchical robot code: a robot may not harm a human, must obey humans, and may protect itself, each rule subordinate to the previous.
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues the Three Laws are merely good design expressing the programmer's intentions, not machine morality, using the kitten-protecting washing machine and A Clockwork Orange's Alex as analogies.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: The Law of Association (comparative advantage)
holes.what: Ricardo's economic law, generalized by Mises, that even a party superior in every activity gains from specialization and trade, making cooperation mutually beneficial.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses the law - via a numeric example of Ratchet trading with a human mechanic - to argue that even all-superior alien robots have material reasons to trade with and respect humans rather than enslave them.
holes.book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind

holes.name: Truthiness
holes.what: Colbert's coinage for the feeling that something is true 'from the gut' - belief prized over facts and evidence - which this book analyzes as a distinct epistemic stance alongside lying and Frankfurtian bullshit.
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire argument is that truthiness is not the same as bullshit and deserves its own analysis, but no taxonomy slug names truthiness itself.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Paul Grice
holes.what: Philosopher of language whose cooperative principle and conversational maxims explain implicature - what speakers mean beyond what they literally say.
holes.why: Chapter 13 uses Grice's maxims as its central tool for decoding Colbert's coinages, jokes, and the title 'I Am America (And So Can You!)'.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Desiderius Erasmus
holes.what: Renaissance humanist whose Praise of Folly has the goddess Folly indict church and state, locating virtue and even Christ's saving work in playful foolishness.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads Colbert's fool persona as Erasmus's Folly speaking truth to power against America's Puritan hostility to play.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Play (paidia / eutrapelia)
holes.what: The tradition from Plato's Laws (humans as divine puppets who must learn to dance with the golden cord) and Heraclitus's 'child at play' to Aquinas's eutrapelia, treating play as essential to freedom, learning, and virtue rather than mere rest.
holes.why: Chapter 12's thesis is that the Report performs philosophy as play, siding with Plato and Heraclitus against Aristotle's disparagement of play.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Parrhesia (fearless speech)
holes.what: The ancient Greek practice, theorized by Foucault, of speaking the truth freely, critically, and at personal risk out of a duty of conscience.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central claim is that Colbert's WØRD segment is parrhesiastic critique of media and political orthodoxy.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Critical Thinking Dispositions
holes.what: The American Philosophical Association's seven habits of good thinkers - inquisitive, open-minded, truthseeking, systematic, analytical, judicious, and confident in reason.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is structured entirely around Colbert's character embodying the opposite of each of these dispositions.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Intuition and Self-Evidence
holes.what: The classical foundationalist idea that some truths (e.g. 'cruelty is wrong', Euclid's axioms) are known directly without inference, stopping the infinite regress of justification.
holes.why: Chapter 18 defends philosophical intuition as different in kind from Colbertian gut-truth, which is the pivot of its whole argument.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Jayarasi Bhatta
holes.what: Eighth-century Carvaka skeptic whose Lion of the Destruction of Principles argues that no definition of knowledge-terms can be made coherent, so epistemology itself is impossible.
holes.why: Chapter 16 presents Jayarasi alongside Nagarjuna as a pillar of Indian skepticism and imagines him dismissing Stephen's pronouncements as 'the gesticulations of a fool.'
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Aspect-Seeing (seeing-as / aspect-dawning)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's notion (the duck-rabbit) that one and the same object can be seen under different aspects, where what changes is our interpretation rather than the object.
holes.why: Chapter 21 defines humor itself as aspect-change, and the taxonomy has no slug for this central Wittgensteinian idea.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: the mind as id, ego and superego, with repression of unconscious desire and catharsis as therapeutic release.
holes.why: Chapter 22's whole reading of Colbert as America's id and the fundamentalist superego, whose irony works as catharsis, is Freudian, and Freud is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Psychoanalysis (id, ego, superego, repression)
holes.what: Freud's structural model of the psyche in which a healthy ego balances primal drives (id) against internalized moral authority (superego), with repression and catharsis governing the balance.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses id/ego/superego dynamics, repression, and catharsis to explain how Colbert's satire is psychologically therapeutic.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Irony (Socratic and Kierkegaardian)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's account of irony as earnestly saying what one does not mean — identifying with a view in order to outdo its enthusiasm and expose its emptiness.
holes.why: Chapter 22 grounds Colbert's method in long quotations from Kierkegaard's The Concept of Irony, for which the taxonomy has no slug.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Colorblind Racism (racial colorblindness)
holes.what: The ideology that justice means not seeing race at all, which in practice conflates racial equality with racial indifference and excuses ignoring racial disadvantage.
holes.why: Chapter 25 (with the chapter 28 Ishihara Race Test gag) builds its entire argument on the incoherence of Stephen's claim to be literally race-blind.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Linguistic License
holes.what: The permission, grounded in group membership or a personal relationship, to say things about a group that outsiders could not say without giving offense.
holes.why: Chapter 25 needs it to explain the 'black friend' bit, the Rosa Parks WØRD, and the N-word debate over who may say what.
holes.book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

holes.name: Reflective Equilibrium
holes.what: A method (devised by Nelson Goodman, popularized by John Rawls) that starts from considered judgments and adjusts principles and judgments against each other until they cohere.
holes.why: Chapter 7's 'Making the A-List' openly builds its ranking of great supervillains on this method, framing it as a villain's way to 'cheat' at evaluation instead of deriving criteria first.
holes.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

holes.name: Underdetermination of Theory by Data
holes.what: The thesis that empirical evidence never uniquely fixes a single theory, since incompatible alternatives can fit the same data equally well.
holes.why: Chapter 7's mad-science essay makes underdetermination the engine of its argument that theory choice necessarily smuggles in the scientist's values, and that denying this is precisely what makes science 'mad'.
holes.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

holes.name: Intellectualism vs Voluntarism (will and intellect)
holes.what: The medieval debate over whether the will must choose what the intellect presents as best (Aquinas's intellectualism) or can choose against that judgment (Ockham's voluntarism).
holes.why: Chapter 8's Magneto essay is constructed entirely on this debate, concluding the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment and so supervillains always act for what seems good to them.
holes.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

holes.name: Moral Nihilism / Error Theory
holes.what: The meta-ethical view, argued by J.L. Mackie via the 'argument from queerness', that there are no objective moral facts, so positive moral judgments are systematically in error.
holes.why: Chapter 8's meta-ethics essay gives nihilism equal billing with relativism and objectivism (testing it against Superman, the Red Skull, and moral disagreement), but the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

holes.name: Moral Community (moral agents and patients)
holes.what: The circle of beings owed moral consideration, divided into moral agents who can act morally and moral patients who can be affected morally, gated by criteria such as rationality.
holes.why: Chapter 10's X-Men essay defines mutant superiority by asking who belongs to the moral community and on what characteristics, a framing concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

holes.name: Omnipotence (and its paradoxes)
holes.what: The property of being all-powerful, classically probed by puzzles such as the stone too heavy to lift and whether the logically impossible falls within divine power.
holes.why: Chapter 11's opening essay is wholly an analysis of what limits an all-powerful being, applied to the Beyonder, Doctor Doom, and Galactus, and no taxonomy slug covers omnipotence.
holes.book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

holes.name: William Kingdon Clifford
holes.what: Victorian philosopher whose 'The Ethics of Belief' holds, via the shipowner thought experiment, that it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 14's verdict on Mrs. Coulter and on circumcision is built directly on Clifford's evidentialist principle and shipowner case.
holes.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

holes.name: The Liar Paradox
holes.what: The ancient puzzle of the Cretan who says all Cretans are liars: a self-referential statement that is true only if false.
holes.why: Chapter 16 explicitly uses the Liar Paradox to frame Lyra's claim that she is the best liar yet is not lying, and to model the trilogy's apparent turn against storytelling.
holes.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

holes.name: Ontology of Fictional Characters
holes.what: The branch of metaphysics asking what fictional beings are and what makes them the same character across tellings, media, and embodiments.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is organized entirely around the ontological status of Lyra, Pantalaimon, and the alethiometer as they move from page to audio, stage, film, game, and doll.
holes.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

holes.name: Panpsychism
holes.what: The view that consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality, so that nothing that exists is wholly 'dead matter.'
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues Pullman's cosmology of Dust, dæmons, specters, and a conscious Abyss is a panpsychist one, and lists fourteen kinds of conscious beings to make the case.
holes.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

holes.name: John Martin Fischer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who, with Mark Ravizza, grounds moral responsibility in guidance control, a reasons-responsive mechanism owned by the agent, rather than in the ability to do otherwise.
holes.why: Chapter 21 needs Fischer's guidance-control theory to argue Lyra can be a praiseworthy hero even though the prophecy forecloses her alternatives.
holes.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

holes.name: Fred Dretske
holes.what: Epistemologist known for the relevant-alternatives theory, on which a skeptical possibility defeats a knowledge claim only when it is relevant to the claim at issue.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds its defense of everyday knowledge, between Moore's common sense and Lewis's contextualism, on Dretske's relevant-alternatives approach.
holes.book: 043 - The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Eighteenth-century Irish philosopher whose A Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful roots the sublime in self-preservation, terror, and qualities like darkness, vastness, and loudness.
holes.why: Chapter 8's entire analysis of Zeppelin's sublimity—the concert roar, Bonham's drums, 'The Battle of Evermore'—is built on Burke's catalogue of sublime qualities.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Longinus
holes.what: Author (c. 1st century AD) of On the Sublime, which treats sublimity as inspired genius whose 'well-timed stroke scatters everything before it like a thunderbolt'.
holes.why: Chapter 8 has a full section using Longinus to explain Plant's flash-of-inspiration writing of 'Stairway to Heaven' and Page's solo as genius rather than recipe.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Emergence (collaborative emergence)
holes.what: The idea that group activity can produce novel, unpredictable properties not possessed by any individual component, as in improvised theater or band performance.
holes.why: Chapter 9's positive theory explains Led Zeppelin's creativity as collaborative emergence from the band's interaction, not from any individual genius.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Eduard Hanslick
holes.what: Nineteenth-century music critic whose On the Musically Beautiful argued that music's expressiveness lies in dynamically moving form and that the same music can suit opposite words.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central argument—that 'Stairway to Heaven' works with Gilligan's Island lyrics because words and music interact, and that Zeppelin transformed what it borrowed—rests on Hanslick's thought experiment and theory.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Mood (Stimmung / Befindlichkeit)
holes.what: Heidegger's notion that we are always already in some mood, which discloses the world as a whole in a particular affective light before any cognition.
holes.why: Chapter 11's thesis that there is a distinct, unnameable 'Zeppelin mood' articulated by the music—and its title concept of a 'Mood Mix'—is directly built on Heidegger's account of mood.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose theory of sexual development includes fetishism, castration anxiety, and the Oedipus complex.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies Freud's fetishism, castration complex, and oral/cannibalistic sexuality to explain Zeppelin's car, food, and body substitutions for the female figure in songs like 'Trampled Underfoot' and 'Custard Pie'.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Aleister Crowley
holes.what: Occultist (1875–1947) whose philosophy of Thelema—'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law', magick as will, and the True Will—made him 'the wickedest man in the world'.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is centrally about Crowley's influence on Jimmy Page (Boleskine Manor, the Zoso sigil, the Led Zeppelin III run-out groove) and evaluates Thelema's True Will philosophically.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: The Perennial Philosophy
holes.what: Aldous Huxley's term for the metaphysical core shared by all mystical religions: a Divine Ground, an eternal Self beyond the phenomenal ego, and union with the Ground as life's purpose.
holes.why: Chapter 14 frames Thelema as an instance of Huxley's perennial philosophy to explain Page's Hermetic quest for self-knowledge through music.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Ernst Cassirer
holes.what: Neo-Kantian philosopher (1874–1945) whose philosophy of symbolic forms treats myth and magic as fundamental modes of human thinking from which science and history develop.
holes.why: Chapter 15 states that most of its theory of magic and myth comes from Cassirer's books, using him as the respectable counterpart to Crowley.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Symbolic Forms (mythic consciousness)
holes.what: Cassirer's view that humans mediate the world through symbolic forms—myth, language, art, science—with mythic consciousness treating the world as wills and archetypal symbols.
holes.why: Chapter 15 uses symbols as repositories of stored will and mythic consciousness to explain why Plant's archetypal lyrics and the band's album art carry meaning across time.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Aggregates vs Conglomerates (Peter French)
holes.what: Peter French's distinction between groups defined merely by their membership (aggregates) and structured organizations with roles that survive member replacement (conglomerates).
holes.why: Gimbel needs this to argue Led Zeppelin is a conglomerate — role structure, not personnel, defines it — which is how Jason Bonham could fill his father's place while Plant remained irreplaceable; no existing slug covers collective or group identity.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Carl Jung
holes.what: Swiss founder of analytical psychology whose essay 'The Difference Between Eastern and Western Thinking' contrasts Western extroverted ego-consciousness with Eastern introverted dissolution of the self into the unconscious.
holes.why: Macan frames the East/West duality of 'Kashmir' (gnosis sought without, in the East) versus 'In the Light' (will and wisdom found within) through Jung's essay, making him the interpretive key to the chapter's final section.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: Surfaces, Flows and Repetition (Deleuze)
holes.what: Deleuze's 'surface philosophy': thought reoriented to pure immanence, where lived bodily flows with speeds, intensities and blockages, and repetition-with-difference, replace transcendent heights or hidden depths.
holes.why: Surber's answer to his title question is that Zeppelin is philosophical as Deleuzian surface art — the music syncs listeners' bodily flows ('Stairway''s growth, the live 'Dazed and Confused') — and the taxonomy's only Deleuze concept, the rhizome, does not cover this framework.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic category of overwhelming vastness, power or terror that attracts and overwhelms at once (Longinus, Burke, Kant), contrasted with the beautiful.
holes.why: Stone-Mediatore's list ranks ten Zeppelin songs — 'Stairway to Heaven' first — by how they exemplify Burke's, Kant's, and Longinus's theories of the sublime, a core aesthetics concept the taxonomy lacks outside Kant's taste-and-sublime entry.
holes.book: 044 - Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed

holes.name: The Magic Circle
holes.what: Huizinga's notion (developed by Salen and Zimmerman) that accepting a game's rules encloses a bounded space where special meanings hold absolutely.
holes.why: Chapter 12's five-step escape from nihilism turns on the player entering WoW's magic circle and then dissolving it.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: Johan Huizinga
holes.what: Dutch historian whose Homo Ludens defines play as a free, separate, rule-bound activity that generates culture.
holes.why: Chapter 19 traces Blizzard's consumer and troublemaker player models to Huizinga's Homo Ludens and opposes it with Homo poieticus.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: Donald Schön
holes.what: Design theorist whose 'reflection-in-action' holds that knowledge is generated in doing, iterating, and revising rather than applied from prior rational foundations.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Schön's reflective practitioner to read WoW class forums as genuine design practice where players co-construct knowledge.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist of the 'presentation of self' who analyzed everyday interaction as performance managed to keep one's 'face'.
holes.why: Chapter 24 builds its account of WoW role play as cathartic social performance directly on Goffman's performance and face-work concepts.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: Identity Tourism
holes.what: Lisa Nakamura's term for donning other-gender or other-race online personae as amusing prostheses supposedly without real-life consequences.
holes.why: Chapter 25 tests identity tourism through the author's months playing a female blood elf whom his guild took for a real woman.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: The Technological Singularity
holes.what: The hypothesized point at which artificial intelligence exceeds human intelligence and self-improves beyond prediction or control.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads all of Azeroth — its magic, gods, and perpetual war — as the remains of a society already past the Singularity.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: Dialetheism (True Contradictions)
holes.what: Graham Priest's thesis that some contradictions are really true, rejecting the Law of Non-Contradiction.
holes.why: Chapter 34 asks whether WoW's designers could program a true contradiction and tests it with Priest's 'Sylvan's Box'.
holes.book: 045 - World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King

holes.name: Graham Priest
holes.what: Contemporary logician and philosopher, the leading defender of dialetheism — the view that some contradictions are true.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire argument about Monk asserting 'he's the guy' despite impossible alibis is framed as a test of Priest's dialetheism versus the Law of Non-Contradiction, and taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Dialetheism (true contradictions)
holes.what: The thesis that some statements, such as the Liar Sentence, are both true and false at the same time, overriding the Law of Non-Contradiction.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is centrally about whether Monk's willingness to hold 'Wagner is guilty though he was in space' counts as tolerating a true contradiction, and no existing taxonomy slug covers non-contradiction or dialetheia.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Gaston Bachelard
holes.what: French philosopher of science and poetic imagination (1884-1962), known for epistemological breaks and psychoanalysis of the elements.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its account of Monk and House as truth-seekers punished for insight directly on Bachelard's 'Prometheus complex,' quoting The Psychoanalysis of Fire, and he is absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: The Prometheus Complex
holes.what: Bachelard's notion that the drive to know more than our fathers and teachers ('the Oedipus complex of intellectual life') is followed by punishment and suffering, like Prometheus chained for stealing fire.
holes.why: Chapter 20's central claim is that Monk and House exemplify this complex — blessed with insight and cursed for it — and no taxonomy slug captures the knowledge-punishment theme the chapter applies to the shows.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: The Reason vs Emotion Dichotomy
holes.what: The Western opposition of reason (masculine, public, objective) against emotion (feminine, private, disruptive), and the feminist critique that polarization of the two is a modern, gendered construction.
holes.why: Chapter 21 builds its entire reading of Monk and House on this dichotomy, with Stottlemeyer and Wilson as integrated countermodels, and no existing slug covers the emotion-reason relation itself.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Tractatus Picture Theory (the world as totality of facts)
holes.what: Early Wittgenstein's view that the world is the totality of facts rather than things, that true thoughts picture possible states of affairs in logical space, and that facts are contingent and logically independent.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses the Tractatus, not the later language-games, to model Monk's method as completing a total, true picture of the facts of his world.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Contemptus Mundi (medieval ascetic withdrawal from the world)
holes.what: The medieval monastic ideal of rejecting the corrupt, disordered world through ascetic withdrawal in order to pursue a higher truth.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues Monk's OCD-driven rejection of the dirty world is a secular contemptus mundi that enables his detached, backward-reasoning detection.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Liminality (the transitional stage between social roles)
holes.what: Van Gennep's and Turner's anthropological concept of the in-between stage in rites of passage, where a person belongs to no stable social category and gains marginal insight and danger.
holes.why: Chapter 25's core claim is that Monk's power comes from being stuck in the liminal stage between cop and civilian, mourner and mover-on, like the shaman.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Purity and Danger (dirt as matter out of place)
holes.what: Mary Douglas's anthropological theory that dirt is disorder, and that purity rituals create and reinforce the symbolic boundaries of a social order.
holes.why: Chapter 25 applies Douglas to read Monk's wipes and cleaning as a shamanic purification ritual that restores communal order, and his fear of dirt as sensitivity to disorder.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Skillful Means (upaya, the Bodhisattva's compassionate deception)
holes.what: The Mahayana doctrine that a Bodhisattva may use partial lies, tricks, and illusions tailored to each person's affinities to lead suffering beings toward awakening, as in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central section ('Mr. Monk Is a Liar') explains Vimalakirti, Shawn Spencer, and the show's own inconsistencies as skillful means used to awaken viewers.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Psychodynamic Therapy (making the unconscious conscious)
holes.what: The therapeutic method of bringing unconscious associations and repressed feelings into awareness so their emotional charge is lowered and new behavior becomes possible.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is a working demonstration of this method on Monk-as-'Andrew Mead', from his father-abandonment association to survivor's guilt over Trudy-like Terry.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist whose The Denial of Death argues that human culture, religion, and heroism are immortality projects built to deny the terror of death, and that we cope by narrowing awareness.
holes.why: Chapter 29 is organized around Becker: Monk is the born hyper-aware person who cannot practice the death-denial the rest of us learn, making him our jungle guide.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics that witnessing tragic drama purges emotions like pity, fear, and disgust from the spectator's soul, yielding relief and pleasure.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses catharsis to explain why viewers enjoy watching Monk confront the fears and horrors we normally train ourselves not to see.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis whose Beyond the Pleasure Principle introduces the repetition compulsion, trauma, cathexis, mourning, and the death drive.
holes.why: Chapter 30 is an extended Freudian reading of Monk built on Beyond the Pleasure Principle and the theory of mourning, and Freud is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: The Death Drive (Thanatos)
holes.what: Freud's postulated fundamental instinct to flee life's danger and uncertainty toward stability, quiescence, and the repetition of the same.
holes.why: Chapter 30 ('Mr. Monk and the Death Drive') identifies the death drive as the third and deepest source of Monk's compulsions, behind trauma-repetition and displacement.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Repetition Compulsion
holes.what: Freud's account, via the fort/da game and traumatic anxiety dreams, of the compulsion to repeat painful experiences in order to convert passivity into mastery and retroactive preparedness.
holes.why: Chapter 30's first half uses repetition compulsion to explain Monk's phobias, his fixation on nakedness after remembering his birth, and his dreams of returning to Trudy's murder.
holes.book: 046 - Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view that technology has so thoroughly altered bodies, cognition, and culture that we are already 'after the human' — cyborgs whose embodiment and mind extend into machines (Haraway, Hayles).
holes.why: Chapters 9, 11, and 13 organize their entire readings of Miyazaki, Ghost in the Shell, and Akira around the posthuman condition, but taxonomy has no concept slug for it (extended-mind and embodiment cover only parts).
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theor of science and technology whose 'A Manifesto for Cyborgs' casts the human-machine hybrid as a boundary-blurring figure with emancipatory, post-gender potential.
holes.why: Chapters 9 and 10 build directly on the Cyborg Manifesto — chapter 10 evaluates Gunslinger Girl's girl cyborgs entirely by whether they realize or betray Haraway's post-gender ideal — and she is absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Shinto and the Kami
holes.what: Japan's indigenous way of honoring kami (spirits in nature and ancestors), which Kasulis splits into an experiential 'existential' form and a prescribed, nationalist 'essentialist' (State Shinto) form.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads all of Spirited Away — torii, bathhouse purification, stolen names, nostalgia, the ever-present train — through the existential/essentialist Shinto distinction, which taxonomy's Eastern entries (Buddhism, Taoism, Zen) do not cover.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Religious Pluralism (vs exclusivism and inclusivism)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-religion problem of religious diversity: pluralists (Kant, Hick) treat religions as culturally varied, only equivocal responses to one ineffable Ultimate Reality, opposed by exclusivists and inclusivists who hold one religion propositionally true.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central framework is exactly this trichotomy, used to explain why anime blends Christianity with Shinto and Buddhism and renders doctrine 'inaccurately'; no existing slug (faith-vs-reason, kant-phenomena-noumena, moral-relativism) names the position.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Carl von Clausewitz
holes.what: Prussian military theorist whose On War treats war as an amoral force tending toward 'absolute war' yet always subordinate to the political goals that started it.
holes.why: Chapter 20's title argument is that Gundam's Zeon wars vindicate Clausewitz — war's gravity toward the absolute must be tethered to political aims, which Just War Theory operationalizes — and he is missing from taxonomy.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection models competition as open-ended selection with no fixed notion of the 'best' form of life.
holes.why: Chapter 22 structures its entire argument as Adam Smith's limited, humanity-bounded competition versus Darwin's unlimited evolutionary 'leveling up,' using Cell, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's hollowification as Darwinian cases.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Mimesis (art as imitation of life)
holes.what: The ancient concept of representation as imitation, whose Platonic critique (copies at removes from truth) and modern sacrificial reading (Rey Chow) treat the copy as bearing the marks of what it replaces.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central analytic tool is mimesis: Atomu is a robot copy of the dead Tobio whose imperfect imitation of the human both channels and exposes the violence of the atomic age, and no existing slug covers imitation-in-art.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Catharsis (purging of emotion through art)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics idea that sensational art cleanses spectators of pent-up emotions, safe-keeping them from acting those feelings out; the modern 'catharsis theory' of media violence descends from it.
holes.why: Chapter 29's core debate is whether hentai purges or feeds violent desire, staged explicitly as Aristotle's catharsis versus Plato's Republic alarm, with Feshbach, Berkowitz, and cultivation theory as modern heirs.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Arthur Koestler
holes.what: Essayist whose The Ghost in the Machine (1967) treats consciousness as emergent, pictures minds as 'holons' that preserve individuality within evolving wholes, and links self-transcendence to Eastern mysticism.
holes.why: Chapters 32 and 33 are built on Koestler: the manga's title comes from his book, the Major's merger with the Puppet Master illustrates his holon theory, and Oshii's Innocence is read as deliberately subverting him.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist of the cyborg whose 'A Cyborg Manifesto' treats the human–machine hybrid as breaking gender dualisms and rejecting both biological essentialism and goddess-nature feminism.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads Major Kusanagi as Haraway's post-gender cyborg enacted, quotes the Manifesto throughout, and names the film's forensic scientist after her; no taxonomy slug covers her.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Transhumanism and the Singularity
holes.what: The view that technology can and should carry human beings beyond biological limits, culminating in a Singularity where superhuman, self-evolving intelligence supersedes our species.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues the net-born Puppet Master dramatizes the Singularity (via Vinge and Kurzweil) and reads the film's ending as transhumanist techno-transcendence, a frame taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Anxiety (Angst)
holes.what: Heidegger's objectless state-of-mind in Being and Time in which the world feels unhomelike and the everydayness of 'the They' collapses, opening the choice of authentic existence.
holes.why: Chapter 34 explicitly develops Heidegger's Being-and-Time account of anxiety (not Kierkegaard's) to explain Shinji's screams and SEELE's leap into the Human Instrumentality Project.
holes.book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

holes.name: Nelson Goodman
holes.what: American philosopher (1906-1998) of the new riddle of induction, worldmaking, and the languages of art.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its entire 'blursed' argument on Goodman's grue paradox, entrenchment, and the claim that descriptions construct multiple worlds.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: The New Riddle of Induction (grue)
