holes.what: Goodman's puzzle that the same evidence confirms 'all emeralds are green' and 'all emeralds are grue,' so induction rests on entrenchment rather than evidence alone.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses grue to coin 'blursed,' showing that the evidence for the Curse equally supports a rival description under which 2004 retroactively reveals the team as blessed.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: Mysticism (knowledge by mystical intuition)
holes.what: The view that certainty and ultimate reality are grasped by direct intuition that transcends logic and even the law of non-contradiction.
holes.why: Chapter 25's stated thesis is that the Red Sox fan's epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics and philosophy of history are all 'Primitive Mysticism' that just knows and embraces paradox.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: Nihilism (the will to nothingness)
holes.what: Nietzsche's diagnosis that when the values that made suffering meaningful collapse, the will turns against itself and against existence.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues the 2004 championship removed the suffering that structured Red Sox fandom, producing exactly Nietzsche's will to nothingness among the fans.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: Richard Taylor
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher whose 'Good and Evil' argues the meaning of life lies in engagement in activity itself (his Sisyphus essay), against Schopenhauerian pessimism.
holes.why: Chapter 28 builds its middle innings on Taylor's reply to Schopenhauer—endless striving is the essence of a meaningful life—as the bridge to the Nietzschean ethics of challenge.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: The Disenchantment of the World
holes.what: Horkheimer and Adorno's thesis in Dialectic of Enlightenment that Enlightenment rationality reduces the world to calculable categories, dispelling myth and meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 32 quotes 'Enlightenment's program was the disenchantment of the world' to diagnose fans reducing Johnny Damon's entire career to the single concept 'traitor'.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: A. Bartlett Giamatti
holes.what: Yale Renaissance scholar, National League president and baseball commissioner (1938–1989) who wrote philosophical essays on baseball, leisure and American culture, including 'Take Time for Paradise'.
holes.why: Chapter 36 crowns him 'the Philosopher' and builds its account of Fenway's sacredness, winning as betterment, and circular time on quotations from 'Take Time for Paradise' and 'A Great and Glorious Game'.
holes.book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

holes.name: Natural and Nominal Kinds
holes.what: The distinction between kinds whose unity exists independently of us (water, electrons) and kinds unified only by our stipulations and classificatory practices.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central metaphysical claim is that the Undead form a nominal rather than natural kind, a motley assortment unified by our concept, which underwrites Vargas's argument that zombies, vampires, and composite Undead differ too much to share an evil nature.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: Malevolent Evil (non-instrumental desire to harm)
holes.what: Evil understood as acting on a non-instrumental desire to damage others' welfare, distinct from ordinary wrongdoing and explicitly distinguished from the theological problem of evil.
holes.why: Chapter 10 defines the evil traditionally ascribed to the Undead this way and then argues most Undead, above all zombies driven by instrumental hunger, lack the very motives required for it, so they are dangerous but not evil.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis, theorist of the repressed unconscious, whose account of the uncanny explains why the return of the familiar-as-dead terrifies us.
holes.why: Chapter 15 invokes Freud's theory of the uncanny to explain the horror of the slow zombie: the dead body's suppressed but familiar motion returning to us in disturbing, unbidden recurrence.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's class of the terrifying that leads back to something long familiar: repressed, once-comfortable material returning unbidden, epitomized by the return of the dead.
holes.why: Chapter 15's first half grounds the slow zombie's creeping horror in the uncanny, so that the later fast zombie can be measured as a break from uncanny repression into open social crisis.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: The Concept of Evil
holes.what: Analyses of evil as profoundly bad conduct or as acting from non-instrumental desires to harm others.
holes.why: Vargas's Undead-evil chapter turns entirely on the analysis of evil as a moral concept.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: Abjection (Kristeva)
holes.what: Julia Kristeva's notion of what simultaneously disgusts and fascinates because it blurs the self's boundaries, with the corpse as its ultimate embodiment.
holes.why: Chapter 24 explains the horror and fascination of vampires and demonized outsiders through the abjection of the corpse and the border-work of fear.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: the theory of instincts (Eros and Thanatos), repression, the superego, the uncanny, and civilization built on instinctual renunciation.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads Romero's zombies wholesale as Freud's return of the repressed, and chapters 24 and 28 rely on Freud's uncanny and Ernest Jones's Freudian nightmare analysis.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: Non-Repressive Civilization (Eros and Civilization)
holes.what: Marcuse's revision of Freud: a civilization in which liberated instincts are gratified rather than repressed, work transformed into play, and liberated sexuality reunited with Eros.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is built on this concept, reading Day of the Dead's beach ending and Land of the Dead's evolved zombies as Marcuse's non-repressive civilization realized.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: Author of Democracy in America, arguing democracy survives only through civic association and warning against individualism's detachment of citizens.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Tocqueville's civic-mindedness as the standard by which Romero's communitarian heroes (Ben, Riley, Big Daddy's zombies) are judged against individualists.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: The Meta-Fear of Fear (Carroll's horror theory)
holes.what: Noël Carroll's hypothesis that horror entertainment pleases by letting viewers safely test and master their own fear, easing the fear of being afraid.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire argument proposes this concept against the Freudian account to explain the pleasure of Halloween's Undead imagery and horror films.
holes.book: 049 - Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead

holes.name: The Echo Chamber / Daily Me
holes.what: Cass Sunstein's argument that personalized media let people hear only agreeing views, harming democratic deliberation and self-knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 7 uses Sunstein's Daily Me to frame the problem of intentional Facebook communities and the book's authenticity theme.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Contextual Privacy (contextual integrity)
holes.what: Privacy understood as respect for the implicit norms of distinct social contexts rather than as a simple public/private secrecy divide.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire argument is that Facebook users care about contextual privacy, not secrecy, and that Facebook as 'privacy virus' violates contextual integrity.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Convergence Culture (media convergence)
holes.what: The coming-together of content, computing, and communications, blurring personal communication and mass media addressed to nobody in particular.
holes.why: Chapter 11 analyzes Facebook precisely as the convergence of one-to-one messages and broadcasts, and its ethics follows from that blur.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: The Tetrad / Media Ecology (McLuhan)
holes.what: McLuhan's laws of media: every medium enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into something, and must be studied by form rather than content.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies the tetrad question-by-question to Facebook and completes a Facebook tetrad, so the concept itself is what the chapter teaches.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Politeness Theory (positive and negative politeness)
holes.what: Brown and Levinson's theory that interaction is organized around saving face via positive politeness (approach) and negative politeness (avoiding imposition).
holes.why: Chapter 13 structures its analysis of Facebook games like Mob Wars around positive and negative politeness and face-threatening acts.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Punctum and Studium (Barthes on photography)
holes.what: Barthes's Camera Lucida distinction between a photograph's general cultural interest (studium) and the piercing personal detail (punctum), together with the subject's 'air'.
holes.why: Chapter 15 argues Facebook profile pictures are all punctum and sorts them by Barthes's six photographic categories.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: The Online Disinhibition Effect
holes.what: John Suler's six factors (anonymity, invisibility, asynchronicity, solipsism, dissociation, minimized authority) that loosen restraint in online communication.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues Facebook eliminates all six disinhibiting factors, so that inhibition there prevents inauthentic 'fronting'.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: The Presentation of Self (Goffman's dramaturgy)
holes.what: Goffman's model of social life as theatrical performance in which actors manage impressions for different audiences.
holes.why: Chapter 18 applies Goffman's dramaturgical framework to Facebook profiles as stages for trying out and being held accountable for identities.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Raoul Vaneigem
holes.what: Situationist theorist whose The Revolution of Everyday Life urges creating 'situations' and reversing perspective to resist the spectacle.
holes.why: Chapter 19 draws its account of situations, derive, and playful resistance to Facebook as much from Vaneigem as from Debord.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Ciceronian Friendship (De Amicitia)
holes.what: Cicero's account of friendship as complete accord on all things human and divine, possible only among the good, and confined to a few.
holes.why: Chapter 21 builds its second half on Cicero's De Amicitia ('handmaid of virtue'), for which taxonomy has only the unrelated De Officiis duty slug.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Ivan Illich
holes.what: Catholic priest and radical social critic whose Tools for Conviviality (1973) attacked institutionalized modernization and defined 'convivial tools' that anyone can freely use for self-chosen ends.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is structured entirely as a test of Facebook against Illich's conviviality criteria, making him the chapter's central thinker and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Conviviality (convivial tools)
holes.what: Illich's ideal of autonomous, creative intercourse among persons, served by tools usable by anyone, for self-chosen purposes, without imposing obligations to use them.
holes.why: Chapter 25 judges Facebook by this standard — public self-censorship and disorienting information floods fail it — and no taxonomy slug names conviviality.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Excess of Seeing (Bakhtin)
holes.what: Bakhtin's claim that a viewer always sees more of a person than that person can see of themselves (their face, the world behind their back) and thereby 'consummates' or finishes them.
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses this concept as its title and organizing lens for how teachers view students' Facebook profiles, and no taxonomy concept captures it.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Natural Sympathy (Hume)
holes.what: Hume's 'disinterested sympathy': an innate fellow-feeling with human sentiment in general (theater, history, a well-contrived apartment) that gives pleasure and, when refined, grounds our moral standards.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire answer to the Facebook-skeptic is that status updates feed natural sympathy via 'ambient awareness,' and no taxonomy slug captures this Humean concept.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Ideal Speech Situation (Habermas)
holes.what: Habermas's regulative ideal of discourse in which all affected have equal chances to speak, initiate, question, and give reasons, oriented toward consensus.
holes.why: Chapter 32 evaluates Facebook organizing against this standard — distinct from the public sphere concept it draws on — so the chapter needs it as its own slug.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Playbour (digital/free labor)
holes.what: Unpaid user activity on commercial platforms — posting, tagging, translating, generating data trails — that functions as value-producing labor for platform owners.
holes.why: Chapter 33's thesis is that Facebook's play is 'interactivity labor' creating surplus value through attention, volunteer work, and data mining, and no taxonomy slug names the phenomenon.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Power as Acting in Concert (Arendt)
holes.what: Arendt's account of power as the human ability to act in concert — it exists only among people together in a public world, never as an individual possession.
holes.why: Chapter 33 defines power as 'the potential to act together' in public and measures Facebook's publics against it, but the taxonomy has no Arendt power concept.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Interpassivity (Žižek)
holes.what: Žižek's notion that a medium or object can undergo, enjoy, or believe on the subject's behalf (canned laughter, funeral weepers, the VCR), deferring the subject's own passivity.
holes.why: Chapter 35's whole argument is that the Facebook profile is an interpassive double that feels and believes for us, a concept absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

holes.name: Philosophy of Play and Games
holes.what: The philosophical analysis of what games are—constitutive rules, artificial obstacles, and the fiction that holds play at a distance from real life while re-enacting it.
holes.why: Chapter 10's thesis that football fascinates because it re-enacts the drama of life within a rule-bounded distance from reality is a philosophy-of-games argument no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Aesthetics of Sport
holes.what: The study of the aesthetic dimension of athletic play—grace, beauty, and style appreciated two-dimensionally alongside the result rather than reduced to it.
holes.why: Chapter 22's central claim that playing beautifully is morally better needs a concept for the aesthetic value of sporting play, which the taxonomy lacks outside Kant's specific doctrine of taste.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: Hermeneutic philosopher whose Truth and Method reads Kant's aesthetic disinterest as a 'methodological abstraction' and grounds judgment in shared, dialogical understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 25's account of Kant at the football ground leans on Gadamer's interpretation of disinterest and general validity to connect aesthetic judgment to public agreement among fans.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: To Kalon (the noble-and-beautiful)
holes.what: The ancient Greek ideal that an action or person can be at once aesthetically beautiful and morally noble—the 'beau geste'.
holes.why: Chapter 26 makes Kalon its positive ideal of honorable, beautiful football—De Rossi confessing his handball goal, opponents returning the ball to an injured player's team—and no existing slug captures this unity of beauty and nobility.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Collective Identity (us vs them)
holes.what: the formation of group identity through symbolic boundaries separating an 'us' from a 'them', giving members belonging and shared emotion.
holes.why: Chapter 30's whole analysis of derbies — Roma's coffin parade, the Old Firm, Fenerbahçe–Galatasaray — rests on derby fandom as collective identity built on belonging to one side and lasting aversion to the other.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Lynne Rudder Baker
holes.what: metaphysician whose 'constitution view' holds that an object (a statue, a dollar bill, a club) is constituted by, but not identical to, its material parts and can persist through their replacement.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses Baker's unity-without-identity theory as its solution to how Aston Villa remains the same club while owners, managers, players, and crest all change.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Mythistory (myth as social reality)
holes.what: the view, associated with William McNeill, that shared myths — whether or not factually true — are symbolic tools that constitute social reality and collective identity.
holes.why: Chapter 33's core claim is that football runs on myth — the Miracle of Berne, Athletic Bilbao's cantera, Barça's més que un club, the FC Start 'Death Match' — and cannot be understood through facts alone.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Dispositions and Mental Causation
holes.what: the analysis of mental states such as passion and belief as dispositions rather than occurrent events, and of the mind's causal efficacy in raising the probability of behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 34 explains Barcelona's 2008–09 treble by arguing Guardiola's passion is a disposition whose causal power, understood probabilistically, transformed an underachieving squad.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Constitutive and Regulative Rules
holes.what: Searle's distinction (Speech Acts) between rules that create the very activity they govern, like the Laws of the Game, and rules that merely regulate a pre-existing activity.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses the distinction to show football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements — hence Maradona's Hand of God stood — leaving a space filled only by ethics and fair play.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Nations and Nationalism
holes.what: theories of what constitutes a nation and a national character — shared culture, language, history, or (for Gellner) the organizational needs of industrial modernity.
holes.why: Chapter 36 asks who the Aranycsapat really played for and argues the 1954 World Cup loss and the 1956 Revolution forged and then shattered Hungarian national consciousness.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Theory of Metaphor
holes.what: the view that metaphors transfer meaning between 'spheres of discourse' via identity claims, letting one domain shape how another is understood.
holes.why: Chapter 37 explains how soccer clubs act as mirrors: Berlusconi builds a winning public persona by transferring AC Milan's victories to himself and severing its defeats, per the club-as-metaphor logic.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Fairness and Equal Claims
holes.what: the normative principle that a contest or distribution is fair when it gives due weight to all relevant claims — treating equals equally without requiring equal chances of winning.
holes.why: Chapter 41's defense of penalty shoot-outs turns on fairness: teams equally deserving after a draw may fairly be separated by an equal-chance procedure such as a lottery or shoot-out.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Petitionary Prayer and Divine Attributes
holes.what: the philosophical question whether an omniscient, perfectly just and good God could coherently answer petitions to secure particular worldly outcomes.
holes.why: Chapter 43 argues prayers for football victories are ineffectual because God's just nature cannot prefer teams, making the Fowl Man blame after Ghana's loss misplaced.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: philosopher of philosophical hermeneutics: understanding always proceeds from a historically situated 'horizon' of prejudices that fuses with the horizon of what is interpreted.
holes.why: Chapter 45 uses Gadamer's fusion of horizons to explain how football clichés enable, rather than block, understanding of the game.
holes.book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher whose causal theory of action explains intentional action as behavior caused by an intention, a combination of belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 9 frames the kendo no-mind puzzle with Davidson's account, asking how Takuan's thoughtless mushin action can still count as intentional.
holes.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

holes.name: Knowing How vs Knowing That
holes.what: The distinction between propositional knowledge (knowing that) and practical competence (knowing how), which need not manifest in actual ability to perform.
holes.why: Chapter 11's whole account of mastery rests on separating knowing-that, knowing-how and physical ability, none of which taxonomy currently has a slug for.
holes.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

holes.name: Care of the Self (practices of the self)
holes.what: Foucault's late ethical notion that self-transformation requires concrete techniques, 'practices of the self', through which one cultivates and governs oneself.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues karate liberates women as feminists precisely by supplying these practices of the self, a framework the existing Foucault slugs do not cover.
holes.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

holes.name: Henri Lefebvre
holes.what: French Marxist philosopher of everyday life whose The Production of Space shows how abstract spatial maps encode power and how people build resistant 'differential spaces'.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire analysis of the dojo as a created, resistant place is built on Lefebvre's production-of-space framework.
holes.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

holes.name: Epistemic Vices (vice epistemology)
holes.what: Character defects in the formation of belief, such as gullibility, closed-mindedness and misplaced deference, that reliably lead to false or unjustified beliefs.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues dojo culture breeds exactly these vices, from ki fantasies to blind deference to founders, and no existing slug names the notion of epistemic vice.
holes.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: German philosopher of philosophical hermeneutics who held that understanding always works within inherited traditions, interpreting rather than escaping them.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Gadamer to frame whether martial artists appreciate or distort the traditions that shape their identities.
holes.book: 053 - Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness

holes.name: Wishful Thinking (believing what you want to be true)
holes.what: Believing a proposition because one prefers, desires, or needs it to be true rather than because the evidence supports it.
holes.why: Chapter 7's entire argument coins the 'asschetic fallacy' to name the vice The Onion ridicules: people who exempt humans from evolution, buy fad diets, or trust breast implants because they want a flattering picture of reality.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Expressivism (non-cognitivism in metaethics)
holes.what: The metaethical view that moral claims express emotions or attitudes (or issue prescriptions) rather than stating truth-apt facts.
holes.why: Chapter 12 is built on expressivism—defended through Dan Savage's asshole-talk against moral objectivism, nihilism, subjectivism, and prescriptivism—and taxonomy has no slug for the view itself.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: A.J. Ayer
holes.what: British logical positivist whose emotivism treated moral statements as expressions of feeling, 'in a peculiar tone of horror,' rather than truth-apt propositions.
holes.why: Chapter 12 recruits Ayer as the classic authority for expressivism and extends his account of moral language to the language of assholery.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Legal Moralism (law enforcing shared morality)
holes.what: The view that the law may prohibit conduct because it is immoral or violates society's shared moral values, even when it is private, consensual, and harmless.
holes.why: Chapter 15's core is the Hart–Devlin debate over whether the ordinary man's disgust can justify criminalizing private homosexual acts, plus Feinberg's offense principle—none of which taxonomy's concepts cover.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: H.L.A. Hart
holes.what: Oxford legal philosopher who argued that a society's conventional morality, including popular disgust, cannot justify criminalizing private consensual conduct.
holes.why: Chapter 15's argument against Lord Devlin rests entirely on Hart's critique—that wicked shared values would equally license Nazi law, and that societies transform rather than disintegrate when their values change.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Queer Theory
holes.what: An analytical framework that dramatizes incoherencies in the supposedly stable relations between chromosomal sex, gender, and sexual desire, resisting fixed identity categories.
holes.why: Chapter 17 explicitly defines queer theory (via Jagose) and asks whether The Onion's fluid-sexuality stories are genuinely queer or just ambiguous, a framework taxonomy lacks despite having related Butler concepts.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Reductio ad Absurdum
holes.what: An argument that derives an absurd or untenable conclusion from a proposition in order to refute the proposition itself.
holes.why: Chapter 25 formalizes sarcastic Onion headlines (the RIAA suing radio, the teen-abstinence rally) as implicit reductio arguments and makes this the mechanism by which satire changes behavior.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Russell's Paradox
holes.what: The contradiction arising from considering the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, which is a member of itself if and only if it is not.
holes.why: Chapter 26 spends its central section explaining Russell's Paradox via Burger King Whopper sets as the target of Darrin's Heraclitean flux-based objection.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: William Clifford
holes.what: British mathematician-philosopher whose evidentialism holds it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence, because such beliefs can harm others.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Clifford's principle as the standing objection to religious faith and to James's will to believe, given religion's record of harm from the Crusades to 9/11.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The view that a belief or statement is true just in case it corresponds to an objective fact or state of affairs in the world.
holes.why: Chapter 29 frames traditional journalism's practice by this theory and contrasts it with the postmodern truth of Lyotard and Baudrillard that The Onion supposedly embodies.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: French Enlightenment satirist whose Candide ridicules Leibnizian optimism through Dr. Pangloss, ending with the counsel to cultivate our garden.
holes.why: Chapter 30 is titled 'Voltaire Lives' and reads The Onion's God stories as Candide's direct heirs in attacking theodicy as callous victim-blaming.
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The epistemological puzzle of how we can know that other beings have minds, or what they are thinking, since their thoughts are never directly observable.
holes.why: Chapter 32 explains every case of Onion satire taken literally as a failure of the analogical solution to the problem of other minds — deciding whether someone is 'just kidding.'
holes.book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

holes.name: The Growing Block Theory of Time
holes.what: The view that the past and present exist while the future does not, with reality growing as new events come into being.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues that only the growing block view (between presentism and eternalism) makes coherent sense of the Daleks traveling back and genuinely stopping the pyramids from being built.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: The Species Problem (essentialism, natural kinds)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology debate over what species are — essentialist natural kinds, individuals, or sets — and how their members are identified.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads the Daleks' human-factor and DNA experiments as species essentialism and weighs rival views of species before reaching its personhood and speciesism conclusion.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: The Indispensability Argument for Mathematical Platonism
holes.what: The Quinean argument that we should believe in whatever entities are indispensable to our best scientific theories, numbers included.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames the Carrionites, who do science with words instead of numbers, as a test of whether mathematics is dispensable to science and hence whether numbers exist.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Romanticism (imagination and the infinite in the finite)
holes.what: The movement holding that imagination, individual uniqueness, and the yearning for the infinite through small finite experiences matter more to a flourishing life than reason alone.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues the Doctor's ethics is half Romantic — Shelleyan imagination, Romantic-Gothic divided consciousness, finding the infinite in cups of tea — alongside its existentialist half.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Ludwig Feuerbach
holes.what: Nineteenth-century philosopher who argued that God and Christ are projections of humanity's own ideals, so theology is really anthropology.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire framing of the Doctor as a savior figure onto which Russell T Davies and viewers project human ideals explicitly rests on Feuerbach's projection theory, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: The view that life has no value or meaning of its own because value must come from something beyond life; Nietzsche's name for the devaluation of life that culminates in the will to nothingness.
holes.why: Chapter 31's core thesis is that the Master is Nietzsche's most advanced nihilist, willing universal destruction after seeing the end of the universe, against the Doctor's life-affirmation; taxonomy has death-of-god but no nihilism concept.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Noël Carroll
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose theory of art-horror defines monsters as scientifically inexplicable, category-violating beings that provoke both fear and disgust.
holes.why: Chapter 36 takes Carroll's fear-plus-disgust account of horror as its touchstone for explaining 'Blink' and revises it into fear plus impotence; he is central to the chapter and absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Early modern philosopher of history who held that myths originated as communal rituals channeling passion into social order, and that civilizations cycle into a 'barbarism of reflection' when reason dissolves those bonds.
holes.why: Chapter 42 uses Vico's philosophy of myth as its primary framework for reading 'The Daemons', 'Meglos' and 'Snakedance'; the author is a published Vico scholar and taxonomy has no Vico.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Frankfurt School critical theorist who co-authored Dialectic of Enlightenment, arguing that modern science is itself a myth in which mathematical procedure becomes the ritual of thought and enlightenment turns totalitarian.
holes.why: Chapter 42 leans on Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment for its claim that the Doctor's scientific 'laws of time' are self-imposed myths; taxonomy has Adorno but not his co-author.
holes.book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside

holes.name: Carl von Clausewitz
holes.what: Prussian officer whose On War treats war as a social activity and continuation of politics by other means, organized around the 'remarkable trinity' of people, military, and government.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is built entirely on Clausewitz's trinity, using it to analyze Duke Leto's Arrakis strategy and Muad'Dib's Fremen insurgency.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: The Remarkable Trinity (war as politics by other means)
holes.what: Clausewitz's account of war as a balanced social activity of popular passion, military chance and probability, and rational political purpose.
holes.why: Chapter 9 uses the trinity as its sole framework for reading the wars of Dune and their modern parallels in Afghanistan and Iraq.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
holes.what: French mathematician whose hypothetical 'Laplace's demon,' knowing all physical laws and the present state of the universe, could predict the entire future.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses Laplace's demon to model Paul's and Leto's prescience as deterministic prediction that threatens free will.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Richard Taylor
holes.what: Twentieth-century American metaphysician who defended fatalism, arguing that what happens happens inevitably through the causal efficacy of the past.
holes.why: Chapter 10 leans on Taylor's fatalism to argue that Paul's foresight makes his efforts to avert the jihad futile.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Communicative Action
holes.what: Habermas's notion of action oriented toward mutual understanding, contrasted with strategic goal-oriented action and treated as the basis of legitimate social order.
holes.why: Chapter 13's whole diagnosis is that Dune's rulers act only strategically, so their empires never achieve normative stability or democratic legitimacy.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Philosopher of religion whose 'soul-making' theodicy holds that hardship and evil are necessary conditions for moral and spiritual growth.
holes.why: Chapter 18 quotes Hick's Evil and the God of Love as the final word on how Dune's evil awakens the Fremen's goodness.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Marya Schechtman
holes.what: Philosopher whose narrative theory (The Constitution of Selves) defines personal identity as self-constitution through an intelligible life-story.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses Schechtman's narrative theory to explain why the final Duncan ghola can integrate his many past lives as his own.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: J. David Velleman
holes.what: Philosopher who holds that selves are characters in self-invented narratives: 'We invent ourselves . . . but we really are the characters whom we invent.'
holes.why: Chapter 20 invokes Velleman's narrative selfhood and the human impulse to self-consistency to explain the Duncan gholas' smooth integration of serial memories.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Narrative Identity (the self as story)
holes.what: The view that a person is constituted by organizing experiences into a coherent first-person narrative rather than by a brute identity relation.
holes.why: Chapter 20 needs narrative identity to treat the final Duncan's five thousand years of serial lives as one integrated self.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Eric Olson
holes.what: Philosopher of animalism: we are human animals and persist as long as our biological life continues, whether or not we remain conscious persons.
holes.why: Chapter 22 presents Olson's animalism as one of three futures for personal identity against Locke's psychological-continuity view.
holes.book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: American philosopher of mind and aesthetics (Feeling and Form) who holds that each art creates a 'semblance' of felt experience in a virtual space or time, and that mixed art forms obey a 'principle of assimilation'.
holes.why: Chapter 7 builds its entire account of Rush on Langer: lyrics are assimilated to music, music is 'virtualized time' creating the illusion of felt life, and processed live sounds are second-order virtualizations.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, a creed of rational self-interest and individualism conveyed through fiction such as The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged.
holes.why: Chapter 7 argues Peart's early lyrics ('Anthem', '2112') borrowed Rand's objectivism before he outgrew it, and dissects why Rand counts as a novelist with philosophical moments rather than a philosopher.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher of Distinction who argued that taste is class-coded: 'natural' early immersion in culture confers legitimacy and ease, while belated, studied learning bears a visible stigma.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses Bourdieu's distinction between natural and studied cultural learning to explain why critics stigmatize Rush's autodidact, note-perfect fans and why the band's studied virtuosity reads as class-marked.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Pure Language and the Task of the Translator
holes.what: Benjamin's view (in 'The Task of the Translator', not the aura essay) that translation is an echo called into the 'language forest' whose inevitable variations and errors release a 'pure language' beyond original and copy.
holes.why: Chapter 11 leans on this essay to defend imperfect Rush covers, live variations, and outright errors ('Turn the Page', the Feedback album) as completions of the work rather than corruptions of a Platonic original.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Habitus (structured dispositions)
holes.what: Bourdieu's notion that social practice is shaped by durable, embodied dispositions acquired through one's position in a field, giving actors 'relative autonomy' from external determination.
holes.why: Chapter 21 explicitly frames Rush's virtuosic absorption of 1980s music technology as the band's habitus, making it the chapter's concluding analytic concept.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Musical Meaning and Convention (text-painting, otherness)
holes.what: The view that music signifies through learned stylistic conventions and text-painting, so gestures like the tritone or 'exotic' scales carry meaning only for listeners competent in a tradition.
holes.why: Chapter 22's whole analysis of how Rush paints geography, outer space, and evil musically rests on this conventionalist account of musical meaning under the heading 'How Does Music Mean?'
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist of signs and pleasure whose late work analyzed desire, fragments, and the 'cruising' of texts by their readers.
holes.why: Chapter 24 explains the pleasure of Lee's voice and Peart's drums almost entirely through Barthes's writings on cruising, distraction, and the catch of sentences.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: The Pleasure of the Text (cruising)
holes.what: Barthes's idea that readers or listeners 'cruise' a text for fresh, repeatable moments of pleasure found in fragments, hooks, and productive distraction.
holes.why: Chapter 24 applies cruising to musical hooks, treating Peart's drumming as the distraction that carries listeners through Lee's much-criticized vocals in songs like 'Tom Sawyer.'
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Technological Determinism / Autonomous Technology
holes.what: The position (associated with Ellul, Mumford, and others) that technology develops by its own momentum, shapes society, and may escape human control altogether.
holes.why: Chapter 26 names technological determinism and 'Autonomous Technology' to frame 'Manhattan Project' and Feenberg's technocracy against Peart's belief that technology remains in our control.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-American novelist-philosopher whose Objectivism holds rational self-interest as the only moral life and champions laissez-faire capitalism and artistic integrity.
holes.why: Chapters 28 and 29 treat Peart's 'Anthem,' '2112,' and 'Something for Nothing' as Randian individualist libertarianism, with '2112' following her novella Anthem.
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: Friedrich Hayek
holes.what: Austrian economist-philosopher who argued that dispersed, tacit knowledge makes central planning impossible and that spontaneous order outperforms deliberate design.
holes.why: Chapter 28 reads 'Natural Science' and 'The Trees' as Hayekian warnings against scientism and imposed equality, citing The Constitution of Liberty and 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'
holes.book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

holes.name: The Spock Problem (emotions as value perceptions)
holes.what: Nozick's thought experiment asking why an emotionless but rational life like Spock's would be worse, answered by his claim that emotions are direct perceptions of value that create an internal replica of what we take pride in.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire argument about what Dexter's life lacks runs through Nozick's Spock Problem and the thesis that emotions let us feel rather than merely know value.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose philosophical anthropology defines the human as a 'self-interpreting animal' whose identity comes into being within inescapable frameworks of meaning and through recognition by others.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is built directly on Taylor's self-interpreting animal and inescapable frameworks to explain what remains human in Dexter.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The view (MacIntyre, Ricoeur, Taylor) that personal identity over time is constituted by the stories we tell about ourselves, narratives that interlock with and are answerable to others' accounts.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues Dexter's selfhood persists through flashbacks, voice-overs and blood slides as 'a story in search of a narrator', with MacIntyre's After Virtue quoted on narrative accountability.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist who argued that the fear of death is the mainspring of human activity and that culture and religion are death-denying immortality projects - the basis of Terror Management Theory.
holes.why: Chapter 17 leans on Becker's death-denial thesis and Terror Management research to explain Dexter's void and our own susceptibility to sanctioned killing.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Repetition Compulsion
holes.what: The psychoanalytic idea that we compulsively re-enact traumatic scenarios, attempting to master earlier helplessness by symbolically recreating and reversing it.
holes.why: Chapter 17's core claim is that each of Dexter's ritual kills restages and masters his mother's murder, transforming wretched victim into controlling executioner.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Bulgarian-French theorist whose Powers of Horror defines abjection - the recoil from what disturbs identity, system and order - with the corpse as its utmost form, 'death infecting life'.
holes.why: Chapter 18's entire reading of Dexter's kill scenes, the Skinner's victims and Rita's corpse turns on Kristeva's concept of abjection.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Abjection (the abject)
holes.what: Kristeva's term for the visceral, gagging rejection of what threatens the self's borders - filth, waste, the corpse - which both protects us from and exposes our fragile identity.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues the show's editing spares viewers abjection so we can identify with Dexter, until Rita's corpse in the bathtub forces it on Dexter and the audience.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Eighteenth-century Irish-British philosopher whose Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful made terror, darkness, power and vastness - experienced at a safe distance - the source of the sublime.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explains Dexter's appeal entirely through Burke's sublime, from the shipping-container flashbacks to Paul Bennett's skillet blow and Miguel's failed 'natural power'.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: The Sublime (terror at a distance)
holes.what: Burke's account of the delight blended with unease that we take in terror, astonishment, darkness, suddenness and power when danger presses from a certain distance.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues audiences find pleasure in Dexter's horror precisely as Burkean sublimity, a theory the taxonomy's Kant-centric aesthetics slug cannot capture.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Bulgarian-French theorist of abjection - that which disturbs identity, system, order (the corpse, bodily fluids).
holes.why: Anderson's Dexter chapter is built on abjection and the powers of horror.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Irish philosopher whose Enquiry defined the sublime as delighted terror, against beauty.
holes.why: Brace's Dexter aesthetics chapter is an application of Burke's sublime.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Bernard Mandeville
holes.what: Dutch-English author of The Fable of the Bees, notorious as the 'Man-Devil' for arguing that private vices are public benefits.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is substantially about Mandeville: it reads Harry's Code as his 'private vices, public benefits' principle, with Adam Smith's invisible hand as its respectable development.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Deployment of Alliance (vs. deployment of sexuality)
holes.what: Foucault's History of Sexuality term for the kinship apparatus of marriage, family and blood ties that binds individuals, intersecting with the deployment of sexuality in the family.
holes.why: Chapter 29 frames Dexter's whole Morgan-or-Moser choice - adopting Rita's family and killing blood-brother Brian - as an embrace of the deployment of alliance over the deployment of sexuality.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Whiteness (the invisible racial norm)
holes.what: Critical-whiteness studies (Richard Dyer): whiteness as a constructed, unmarked racial position that secures dominance by seeming to be nothing in particular.
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues the show's visual design and Dexter's characterization make this invisible whiteness visible and parody it, linking it to death and sexual dysfunction.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's five-tier model of human motivation: physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, and self-actualization.
holes.why: Chapter 31 maps Dexter's development across seasons 1-5 onto the hierarchy to answer whether a serial killer can be happy.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: Bad Conscience (the genealogy of guilt)
holes.what: Nietzsche's Genealogy account that civilization turned humanity's cruel instincts inward, producing guilt, debt, ancestor worship and ultimately the Christian God.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses this genealogy to explain Dexter's guiltlessness and his kinship with pre-moral men and Roman soldiers rather than modern Christians.
holes.book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter

holes.name: The Straw Man Fallacy
holes.what: An informal fallacy in which an opponent's position or a phenomenon is distorted into a weaker caricature that is then refuted.
holes.why: Chapter 8 argues Roger Ebert's verdict against videogames as art attacks a straw man, judging Halo from online clips without ever playing it.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Mimesis (imitation as playing pretend)
holes.what: Plato's notion of pretend-performance, attacked in Republic Book 10 as copying that shapes character for the worse, yet reclaimed in the Laws as the ideal city's own educational art.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument is that Halo is mimesis—epic pretend that trains players in nobility like Homeric epic trained Athenians—so no existing Plato slug covers its core concept.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Philosophy of Music (what makes sound music)
holes.what: The aesthetics question of what defines music—whether organized sound requires words, tonal centers, notation, or the Western concept of a musical 'work.'
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues Halo 2's linear scores sit uneasily with interactivity and resolves this only by expanding the very definition of music to include pitched, rhythmic sound effects.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: The Magic Circle of Play
holes.what: Johan Huizinga's idea from Homo Ludens that play occurs in a marked-off, rule-governed temporary world apart from ordinary life, like a temple or ritual space.
holes.why: Chapter 20 frames both religious apocalypse and the Halo universe as magic circles, and chapter 22 builds its play-as-escapism analysis on the same Huizinga passage.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Procedural Rhetoric
holes.what: Ian Bogost's term for how rule-based systems make arguments—the logics a program enforces define a 'possibility space' that persuades its users.
holes.why: Chapter 20 compares God's predetermined apocalyptic script to a game's procedural rhetoric, treating theology as the ultimate rule-based design.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst who divided the psyche into the real, imaginary, and symbolic orders and described the mirror stage as the ego's formation through identification with an image.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses the mirror stage and the ideal ego to explain players projecting themselves onto Master Chief's concealing mirrored helmet.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Carl Jung
holes.what: Swiss psychoanalyst whose collective unconscious generates archetypes—persona, anima/animus, self—that recur across myths, dreams, and literature.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Master Chief, Cortana, and the Covenant as Jungian archetypes mirroring the relationships of players' everyday lives.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Pierre Teilhard de Chardin
holes.what: Jesuit philosopher-paleontologist who envisioned evolution converging on the noosphere, a unified sphere of human consciousness drawn toward the Omega point.
holes.why: Chapter 22 invokes the noosphere—'the true ego grows in inverse proportion to egoism'—as the social antidote to the isolating individualism of Halo culture.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Game Theory (dominant strategies and free riders)
holes.what: The formal study of strategic choice, including dominant strategies that are best regardless of what an opponent does and the free-rider problems they create.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues camping is a dominant strategy in slayer matches that turns non-campers into exploited risk-takers, reframing the whole fairness debate about spawn camping.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Carl von Clausewitz
holes.what: Prussian officer and military theorist whose On War analyzes 'absolute war' as the reciprocal escalation of force, disarmament, and exertion between belligerents.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads the Rookie's ODST campaign as Clausewitzian absolute war blended with Ludendorff's total war, set against Master Chief's idealized Just War.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Aesthetic Self-Fashioning (care of the self)
holes.what: Foucault's late ethics in which individuals impose optional rules on themselves—ethical substance, mode of subjection, ethical work, telos—making life a work of art within power's constraints.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues expansive gameplay like Halo speed runs, Pacifist runs, and Zombie rules mirrors, enacts, or simulates exactly this practice of freedom, and no existing Foucault slug covers it.
holes.book: 059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism who defended rational self-interest and free-market capitalism, treating money as the tool of producers.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses Francisco d'Anconia's Atlas Shrugged money speech as the main defense of Mr. Krabs's pursuit of wealth before turning to Marx to condemn it.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: C. Wright Mills
holes.what: American sociologist who argued that a 'power elite' of corporate, political and military leaders manipulates democratic politics behind the scenes.
holes.why: Chapter 19 casts Mr. Krabs as the power elite rigging the Royal Krabby election, making popular voting a sham that serves elite interests.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: Dante Alighieri
holes.what: Medieval Christian poet-philosopher whose De Monarchia defends God-ordained monarchy and the ruler's need for both cardinal and theological virtues.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its entire evaluation of King Neptune's kingship, justice and the seven virtues on Dante's De Monarchia.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: The Tragedy of the Commons
holes.what: The dynamic in which individuals rationally overuse a shared resource until it is destroyed for everyone who depends on it.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses the near-extinction of Jellyfish Fields in 'Jellyfish Hunter' as its central argument for private property over communal commons.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who divided the mind into Id, Ego and Super-Ego and named the unconscious defense mechanisms (denial, repression, regression).
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads Patrick, SpongeBob and Squidward as Id, Ego and Super-Ego and analyzes the show's episodes entirely through Freudian defense mechanisms.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: Id, Ego and Super-Ego (structural model of the psyche)
holes.what: Freud's division of the mind into the instinctual Id, the reality-mediating Ego and the moralizing Super-Ego, managed by unconscious defense mechanisms.
holes.why: Chapter 25 casts the Conch Street trio in exactly these three roles to explain SpongeBob's denial and the comedy of inner conflict.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: Wonder and the Desire to Know
holes.what: The view that philosophy begins in wonder (Theaetetus), against Hobbes's account of curiosity as a 'lust of the mind' that can obsess its bearer.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads 'The Secret Box' entirely through the tension between wonder as philosophy's birth and curiosity as a morally dangerous lust.
holes.book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!

holes.name: Abduction (inference to the best explanation)
holes.what: Peirce's third mode of inference: reasoning backwards from surprising clues to explanatory hypotheses, later formalized as inference to the best explanation.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reconstruction of Holmes's method (echoed in chapters 16 and 25) turns on abduction, which the taxonomy lacks alongside deduction and induction.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Noel Carroll
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art and film whose The Philosophy of Horror defines horror through monsters that cross cultural categories and produce a compound of fear and disgust.
holes.why: Chapter 13 leans on Carroll's theory of horror to reclassify The Hound of the Baskervilles as gothic horror rather than detective fiction, and the taxonomy has no aesthetics-of-horror philosopher.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Immersion, Flow and Agency in Interactive Narrative
holes.what: The cluster of concepts (flow, immersion, agency, perceived affordance) from media philosophy and game studies explaining how audiences are absorbed in narratives and act within virtual environments.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues through exactly these concepts (Csikszentmihalyi's flow, Ryan's virtual reality, Murray's agency, Norman's affordance) that no one can be Holmes in fiction or in a video game.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Lying and Deception (epistemology of)
holes.what: The philosophical classification of deceptive practices, lying, misleading, false implicature, omission, bald-faced lies, self-deception, together with the moral and epistemological questions of when deception is wrong and how it is detected.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is a systematic taxonomy of deception across the Holmes canon that maps only partially onto existing slugs like deontology or Frankfurt's bullshit.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Rudolf Carnap
holes.what: Logical empiricist who argued that metaphysical statements are cognitively meaningless because they cannot be empirically verified.
holes.why: Chapter 25 closes by suggesting Holmes anticipated Carnap's dismissal of metaphysics, and the taxonomy has no logical-positivist philosopher.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Aestheticism (art for art's sake)
holes.what: The Victorian Aesthetic Movement's doctrine that beauty and refined perception are supreme values independent of morality or utility.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues Holmes is an aesthete in Walter Hamilton's and Oscar Wilde's sense, whose 'aesthetic sight' rather than deduction solves crimes.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Abduction (inference to the best explanation)
holes.what: Reasoning that invents explanatory hypotheses for surprising facts and selects among them, distinct from both deduction and induction.
holes.why: Chapter 27's core claim is that Holmes's 'deductions' are imaginative narrative hypotheses generated abductively and only later tested by elimination.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Hans Reichenbach
holes.what: Logical empiricist who gave induction a pragmatic justification: if any method predicts the future, induction works at least as well as that method.
holes.why: Chapter 32's Mycroft accepts Reichenbach's 'best bet' defense of induction instead of Sherlock's Popperian testing, which is the source of his superiority.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Profound Boredom (Langeweile)
holes.what: Heidegger's three forms of boredom — bored by, bored with, and profound boredom — as fundamental moods revealing beings as a whole.
holes.why: Chapter 35 explains Holmes's drug use, case selection, and even Moriarty's creation as responses to the three Heideggerian types of boredom.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: Marxist theorist of postmodernism as the cultural logic of late capitalism, emphasizing pastiche and the erosion of the high-culture/pop-culture divide.
holes.why: Chapter 39 quotes Jameson on the 'erosion' of high and low culture to argue BBC Sherlock is postmodern pastiche that re-weights Doyle's elements.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Pastiche (postmodern collage)
holes.what: The postmodern blending of sampled styles and texts into new works without parody's satirical edge, as in mash-ups and hip-hop sampling.
holes.why: Chapter 39's central claim is that Sherlock is a pastiche mixing 'A Study in Scarlet,' the game Heavy Rain, and TV-thriller codes into something new.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian theorist of the carnivalesque, grotesque realism, and folk laughter as unofficial forces that subvert official hierarchy.
holes.why: Chapter 44 argues Holmes reigns because he embodies Bakhtin's carnivalesque — fool-king, masks, and marketplace against the Queen's two bodies.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: The Carnivalesque
holes.what: Bakhtin's carnival spirit: laughter, disguise, and the crowning and uncrowning of kings that temporarily invert official hierarchies and liberate the body.
holes.why: Chapter 44 reads Holmes's disguises, jests, and self-crowning with Charles II's diadem in 'The Musgrave Ritual' as carnivalesque crowning and uncrowning.
holes.book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind

holes.name: Corporate Moral Personhood
holes.what: The question whether a corporation can be a bearer of moral rights and responsibilities - a moral person or agent - beyond its status as a legal fiction.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument is that Cobol, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow are moral persons because they have interests, rights, responsibilities and decision procedures, and no taxonomy slug covers corporate personhood or business ethics.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Milton Friedman
holes.what: Twentieth-century economist who argued that a corporation's only social responsibility is to maximize profits for its stockholders within the rules of the game.
holes.why: Chapter 13 stages whether Fischer-Morrow must break itself up as a choice between Friedman's shareholder-primacy doctrine and the view that a corporation owes duties to the moral community.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who treated dreams as the 'royal road to the unconscious', where forbidden wishes surface in disguised symbolic form, held back by the ego's censorship.
holes.why: Chapters 8, 17 and 18 all lean on Freud's unconscious-and-ego model of dreaming - as Hobson's foil, as the royal road that inception exploits, and as the sentinel that implanted symbols must sneak past - and taxonomy.json has no psychoanalysis entry.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: Philosopher of symbolism whose Philosophy in a New Key explains mythic consciousness: dreams become communicable myth only when transformed into narrative form.
holes.why: Chapter 18's account of dream architecture, lucid group dreaming and inception as untraceable symbol-transformation is explicitly built on Langer's theory.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Karl Jaspers
holes.what: Existential philosopher for whom being human means grasping our existence, with solitude revealing nothingness and the encounter with another person the way out of despair.
holes.why: Chapter 22 quotes Jaspers's Philosophy of Existence to frame Limbo as lonely, fragmentary nothingness and to make the encounter with another the film's way out of it.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Memetics (Dawkins's meme)
holes.what: Richard Dawkins's theory that culture replicates through memes (tunes, ideas, catch-phrases) passed from brain to brain by imitation, like genes in biology.
holes.why: Chapter 24 grounds inception itself in meme theory: the planted idea grows 'like a cancer' and can come to define or destroy the subject's world, as with Mal.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Cinema as a Thinking Machine (filmosophy)
holes.what: The film-theory view, from Jean Epstein's cinema as a 'robot brain' to Daniel Frampton's 'filmind', that film does not represent reality but itself thinks time and space.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central claim is that Inception is designed from the outset as a thinking machine that 'thinks' its dream levels, and no taxonomy slug covers film-thinking.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Time as the Number of Motion
holes.what: Aristotle's account of time as 'a number of change in respect of the before and after', an aspect of movement rather than an independent reality, with the now as its durationless boundary.
holes.why: Chapter 25 uses this theory, together with Aristotle's sleepers of Sardinia, to explain dream time dilation and the timeless 'eternal nows' of Limbo; no existing slug covers his philosophy of time.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who read dreams as the (often concealed) fulfillment of repressed desires, built by dream-work from the day's residues and marked by an uninterpretable 'navel'.
holes.why: Chapter 27 interprets the whole film as Cobb's single Freudian dream of mourning, complete with day residues from the airplane passengers and the dream's navel in the children.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst who held that the unconscious is structured like a language and that the neurotic subject does not desire what he wants nor want what he desires.
holes.why: Chapter 27's epigraph and framework are Lacanian: Cobb's desire/counter-desire split is the neurotic subject's structure, resolved only when it becomes a 'steady desire'.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Mourning and Melancholia
holes.what: Freud's distinction between the slow work of detaching from a lost loved one and melancholia, the self-enclosed inability to let the lost object go.
holes.why: Chapter 27 frames the entire plot as Cobb's impossible mourning of Mal, a melancholic life 'under the seal of death' that the dream finally lets him complete.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: The Life-World (Lebenswelt)
holes.what: Husserl's term for the pre-given, shared world of everyday waking experience that grounds all praxis and is the ultimate touchstone of meaningful experience.
holes.why: Chapter 28 quotes the Crisis on the life-world to argue that waking perception's shared dependability, not dreams full of mere 'shades' of people, is what Cobb's guilt finally returns him to.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Alfred Schutz
holes.what: Phenomenological sociologist who analyzed the paramount reality of everyday life, its multiple provinces of meaning with distinct 'cognitive styles', and in-order-to and because-of motives.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds its account of how Cobb deceives Fischer on Schutz's paramount reality and motive analysis, and Schutz appears nowhere in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Ultimate Concern (Tillich's definition of faith)
holes.what: Paul Tillich's account of faith as the state of being grasped by an ultimate concern, where treating preliminary concerns as ultimate constitutes idolatry.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses ultimate concern to diagnose Mal's locking away of her totem as idolatrous misplaced faith in the dream world, a different Tillich concept from the ground of being.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Building, Dwelling, Thinking (poetic dwelling)
holes.what: Heidegger's account that humans dwell poetically: building is a poetic act of creating and appropriating places, and the work of art originates from an unfathomable nothing.
holes.why: Chapter 30's whole argument casts the dream as a poetic dwelling built ex nihilo and Cobb's nightmare as the uninhabitable, and no existing Heidegger slug covers building and dwelling.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher for whom reality is change, understood through narratives co-ordinated in imagined spaces, with 'generic contrasts' as accretions of value and space as frozen time.
holes.why: Chapter 31 leans on Whitehead's process philosophy, generic contrasts, narrative and geometric space, to explain how the film's dream layers co-ordinate time, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For

holes.name: Raimond Gaita
holes.what: Australian philosopher who argues that 'human' is an irreducible moral concept and that in relating to others we have an attitude towards a soul, not an opinion that they have one.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its account of what makes us human on Gaita's irreducibility claim and his racist woman 'M' example, and chapter 19 reuses his 'non-speculative conception' of a soul.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Simone Weil
holes.what: French philosopher and mystic who held that there is an obligation toward every human being solely in virtue of their humanity, without any further condition.
holes.why: Chapter 17 quotes Weil's (written in occupied France) obligation-to-humanity thesis as the moral anchor for treating 'human' as irreducible.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: The Irreducibility of the Human
holes.what: The view that no list of capacities (rationality, agency, morality, love) captures what makes someone human; 'human' is a morally irreducible concept grounded in unconditional regard.
holes.why: It is chapter 17's central claim, applied to Isidore the chickenhead and to Deckard's refusal to label the retired androids, after chapter 16 has knocked down each candidate essence.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist who treated technologies as 'extensions of man' that captivate and numb their users, his diagnosis summed up as 'Narcissus as Narcosis'.
holes.why: Chapters 31-33 build their critique of the mood organ, empathy box and electric sheep directly on McLuhan's media-narcosis thesis.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Narcissus as Narcosis (technological self-enclosure)
holes.what: McLuhan's claim that technological extensions present our own reflection as an apparent other, numbing us to genuinely different beings.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses it to explain how androids, synthetic sheep and Mercer's empathy box mirror humanity back at itself while posing as others.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The problem that we have access only to others' behavior, never their subjective states, so we can never be certain that apparent others (human, android, or electric animal) have minds at all.
holes.why: Chapter 32 explicitly says Dick reconfigures this classic conundrum, extending the solipsistic worry so that even a 'real' sheep or desert toad may be a simulation.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Split-Brain: Two Minds in One Person
holes.what: The thesis, originating with A.L. Wigan and revived by neuroscientist Joseph Bogen, that each cerebral hemisphere supports a distinct mind, so one skull can house two selves.
holes.why: Chapter 36 grounds A Scanner Darkly's Fred/Bob split in Bogen's dual-brain research, quotations from which Dick embeds mid-dialogue in the novel.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Eugenics
holes.what: The deliberate control of human hereditary traits in a population through selective breeding or genetic intervention in pursuit of traits judged 'good'.
holes.why: Chapters 82-86 are built on Flow My Tears' engineered 'sixes' and Tidman's sterilization bill, and no existing taxonomy slug names eugenics itself rather than applied ethics in general.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view that 'human' is a narrow, essentialist notion being superseded, urging fluid redefinitions of the human, the natural, and the gendered (associated with Donna Haraway).
holes.why: Chapter 86 engages posthumanist theory as the contemporary philosophical counterpart to science fiction's next-step humanity and Dick's caution about it, and no taxonomy slug names it.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst who divided experience into the Imaginary, the Symbolic, and the unknowable Real, arguing ordinary 'reality' is a symbolic-imaginary construction.
holes.why: Chapters 96-98 interpret Dick's breakthroughs, Deckard's identity loss, and Ubik's regressions through Lacan's three registers and his slogan 'reality is not Real', which the taxonomy cannot tag.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: The Real (vs the Symbolic and the Imaginary)
holes.what: Lacan's order of what resists all symbolization and imagery, encountered only when the symbolic-imaginary construction of everyday reality breaks down.
holes.why: Chapters 96-98 use the Real as their central lens for Dick's collapsing realities, and neither skepticism nor any existing concept captures it.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Imre Lakatos
holes.what: Philosopher of science who refined Popper's falsificationism into the methodology of research programmes, distinguishing progressive from degenerating programmes kept alive by ad hoc modifications.
holes.why: Chapter 103's test for the irrationality of conspiracy theories rests directly on Lakatos's 'degenerating research program', a concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
