holes.why: Chapter 17 introduces Dick's 2-3-74 visions and the VALIS trilogy entirely through Gnostic texts and their imperfect-creator cosmology, but the taxonomy has no Gnosticism concept to map them onto.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: The section's entire exposition, Nag Hammadi, Sophia, Yaldabaoth, and gnosis as immediately certain hidden knowledge, is Gnostic doctrine for which the taxonomy has no slug.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: Syzygy, the paired-emanation doctrine used to explain Dick's twins motif and his dead sister, is specifically Gnostic and has no taxonomy equivalent.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: The section is a retelling of the Gnostic rewrite of Genesis from The Hypostasis of the Archons and On the Origin of the World, and no existing concept covers this myth.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Gnosticism (gnosis)
holes.what: An ancient religious movement, preserved in the Nag Hammadi library, teaching that the material world was made by an ignorant or malevolent demiurge and that salvation comes through gnosis, direct secret knowledge of our divine origin.
holes.why: The section's contrast between salvation by inner revelation and orthodox faith and sacrament, and the identification of VALIS with Yaldabaoth, are Gnostic themes without a taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Baron d'Holbach
holes.what: French Enlightenment atheist and hard determinist whose System of Nature argues that all human actions, like every natural event, are necessitated by prior causes, making free will an illusion.
holes.why: Chapter 145 quotes The System of Nature at length as the definitive statement that in a law-governed nature humans originate nothing, the exact position Quaid must confront.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose politics of recognition holds that identity is formed through social recognition and that dominant societies owe subcultures acknowledgment and affirmation of their worth.
holes.why: Chapter 149's argument that Arctor's friends fight for recognition, and that denying it is an egregious harm, is built directly on Taylor's recognition theory.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Douglas Husak
holes.what: American philosopher of law and drug policy who defends a moral right to use drugs and argues that criminalization cannot be justified by any standard rationale.
holes.why: Chapter 150 leans on Husak's critique of drug prohibition as cultural hegemony to answer the communitarian case for outlawing Arctor's subculture.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: The Possible and the Real
holes.what: Bergson's doctrine that possibilities are projected backward from the real and that prediction only closes gates on the impossible, since lived time is radically unforeseeable (imprevisible).
holes.why: Chapter 156 builds its whole Precrime analysis on this essay's gate metaphor and the possible/real distinction, for which bergson-duration alone is an inadequate fit.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Eternalism (vs growing block, presentism, branching futures)
holes.what: The ontology of time on which past, present and future events are all equally real, opposed to the growing block, presentist and tree-pruning models of temporal being.
holes.why: Chapter 169 is structured as a choice among exactly these four ontologies of time to argue that chance and freedom can coexist with eternalism in the one real world.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Norbert Wiener
holes.what: Mathematician who founded cybernetics, the science of communication and control via feedback in machines, animals and society.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire critique of 'Autofac' runs through Wiener's bombsight work, his definition of feedback, and The Human Use of Human Beings.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Cybernetics (feedback and control)
holes.what: The science of self-regulating systems in which machines and living things alike are governed by feedback loops of information and control.
holes.why: Chapter 28 applies cybernetic ideas of programmed, self-perpetuating control to the runaway automatic factories of 'Autofac', and no existing slug covers cybernetics.
holes.book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher of mind and art (Feeling and Form) who held that philosophers must know the arts from the inside, take artists as their teachers, and accept art's creation of illusory forms of feeling as irreducibly metaphorical.
holes.why: Auxier's entire chapter builds its method on Langer — her dicta frame section 12, her debate with Hegel drives section 19, and her notion of art as created illusion anchors sections 20-21.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Aestheticism (art for art's sake)
holes.what: The stance of drawing one's moral and religious values from the aesthetic realm, treating art and the artistic life as needing no justification beyond themselves.
holes.why: Section 16 explicitly defines the Stones and the pure bluesmen as 'aesthetes' whose values come from the aesthetic realm, the hinge between blues devotion and Warhol-era celebrity art.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Contemporary Slovenian Hegelian-Marxist philosopher whose book Violence (2008) distinguishes visible subjective violence from the objective violence embedded in language and economic systems.
holes.why: Surber's whole second chapter (sections 25-27) explains Altamont through Žižek's Violence, which he introduces as the modern breakthrough in the philosophy of violence.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Lacan's Three Orders (Imaginary, Symbolic, Real)
holes.what: Lacan's structural division of experience into the private Imaginary of images and memories, the public intersubjective Symbolic of language and codes, and the Real — the unsayable outside both that erupts at traumatic ruptures.
holes.why: Sections 25-27 classify the violences of fandom, Stones lyrics, and Altamont by mapping each onto the Imaginary, Symbolic, and Real, the chapter's central analytic tool.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Life as a Work of Art (giving style to one's character)
holes.what: Nietzsche's idea (Twilight of the Idols, The Gay Science) that one should survey one's strengths and weaknesses and fix them 'into an artistic plan,' so that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon.
holes.why: Chapters 34-36's entire reading of Jagger's two personas—artist and artwork at once—rests on this Nietzschean self-stylization, which no existing slug covers.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: White Mythology
holes.what: Derrida's notion that Western philosophy's abstract reason is a disguised metaphorics that whitens and universalizes its own European origins while effacing, marginalizing, and denying what it excludes.
holes.why: Chapter 45's thesis—that the Stones repudiated sunny pop's 'white mythology' by painting it black and returning to the blues—names and applies this concept throughout.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: The Metaphysics of Presence
holes.what: The Western privileging of what is present (being, light, the good) over what is absent, forgetting the conditions by which the present comes to be—Derrida's name for philosophy's heliotropic bias.
holes.why: Chapters 46-48 apply this doctrine explicitly, reading the Stones' shadows, darkness, and 'Paint It Black' as deconstruction of pop's privilege of light and presence.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Theoria (festival seeing and ekstasis)
holes.what: The ancient Greek practice of collective ritual seeing at Dionysian festivals—music and dancing that produced ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself' with a god's-eye look on the world—from which 'theatre' and abstract 'theory' both descend.
holes.why: Chapter 56's whole argument that Stones concerts are modern Dionysian theoria, making the band 'theorists' in the original Greek sense, is built directly on this unlisted concept.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Aristippus of Cyrene
holes.what: Founder of the Cyrenaics, the first systematic hedonists, who held immediate bodily pleasure—however unbecoming its cause—to be the good, with happiness merely a sum of particular pleasures.
holes.why: Chapter 59 reads 'Brown Sugar,' 'Out of Control,' and 'Monkey Man' as expressions of Aristippus's Cyrenaic 'simple hedonism,' which the following chapters contrast with Epicurean hedonism.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: The Hermeneutic Circle
holes.what: Heidegger's principle that interpretation always begins from a stockpile of prior assumptions and must circle back to revise them, with good interpretations converging on coherent understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 71 makes the hermeneutic circle (with Martin Eger's convergence test) the yardstick for whether readings of Guyville's song-by-song responses to Exile are trustworthy.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Imitation Theory of Art (mimesis)
holes.what: The Platonic-Aristotelian view that art works by imitation—artworks copy appearances, and knowing something means the mind containing a copy of its shape or harmonies.
holes.why: Chapter 78 argues critics dismissed Liz Phair's 'song-by-song response' because this inherited assumption equates inspiration with imitation, which her hermeneutic account of Guyville overturns.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher who saw reality as rhythmic bursts of energy and events rather than enduring substances.
holes.why: Chapter 85 introduces Whitehead's process philosophy as the framework for explaining the 'It' that lets the Stones channel energy, and he anchors all of Chapter 10.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Process Philosophy (concrescence)
holes.what: Whitehead's view that reality consists of rhythmic events or 'actual occasions' (datum, synthesis, satisfaction) rather than static things.
holes.why: Chapter 86 maps the Stones' rhythm section onto Whitehead's phases of concrescence to explain why the band rocks, the central argument of the whole unit.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Self-Creative Act
holes.what: Whitehead's notion of an act of experience that creates itself, not wholly explained by what came before or after it.
holes.why: Chapter 90 uses the self-creative act to explain how novel grooves are discovered and why they resist being named.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Thanatos (the Death Drive)
holes.what: Freud's concept of a death instinct or death wish operating beneath the life drives.
holes.why: Chapter 99 invokes thanatos to explain the 'little death' and the sacrifice of youth at the rhythmic heart of rock.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Cultural Appropriation
holes.what: The adoption of another culture's artistic forms by outsiders, contested over credit, exploitation and power.
holes.why: Chapter 109's central ethical question is whether white musicians like the Beatles and Stones wrongfully appropriated Black American music.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Complicity
holes.what: Accountability short of guilt for wrongdoing that one supports, enables, or fails to prevent, including collective complicity dispersed across millions of small contributions.
holes.why: All of Chapter 14 (ch122-129) is built on complicity as the concept 'between guilt and innocence', and taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.
holes.what: American jurist and legal pragmatist who defined law, from the 'bad man's' perspective, as a prediction of what the courts will in fact do.
holes.why: Ch133-134 explain Richards's Fordyce arrest and drunken trial through Holmes's prediction theory of law.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: John Austin
holes.what: Legal positivist who defined law as the command of a political superior imposing a duty, backed by a sanction for disobedience.
holes.why: Ch133 uses Austin's command theory as the positivist foil against which Holmes's bad-man realism is defended.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Legal Realism (law as prediction)
holes.what: The view that law is not a self-contained logical system of statutes but a prediction of judicial behavior, indeterminate and rooted in custom and social practice.
holes.why: Ch133-134 apply exactly this view to Richards's arrest, making the band's lawyer-and-judge antics the test case for what law is.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Allan Bloom
holes.what: Conservative philosopher who in The Closing of the American Mind attacked rock music and popular culture as debasing the young without authentic political content.
holes.why: Ch138 quotes Bloom's portrait of Jagger at length as the philosophical case that rock rebellion is merely commercial envy of money and fame.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Neo-conservatism
holes.what: Movement (Bell, Kristol) of disillusioned liberals willing to use state power to restore traditional order against 1960s liberalism, the counterculture, and bands like the Stones.
holes.why: Chapter 16 (ch135-140) frames 'Sweet Neo Con' and the band's whole political identity as a collision with neo-conservatism, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Mikhail Bulgakov
holes.what: Russian novelist whose The Master and Margarita stages a sympathetic, Augustinian Devil (Woland) working within God's plan in an atheistic Moscow.
holes.why: Chapter 19 (ch155-160) reads 'Sympathy for the Devil' as Jagger's response to Bulgakov's novel and its critique of Augustine's notion of evil.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: The Romantic Satan (the rebel Lucifer)
holes.what: The nineteenth-century Romantic idea of Lucifer as a heroic rebel against tyrannical authority — a symbol of creativity, energy and liberation rather than corruption.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire arc contrasts Augustine's Satan with the Romantic Lucifer the Stones embraced, a conception developed by Blake and Baudelaire that no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Allan Bloom
holes.what: Conservative political philosopher whose The Closing of the American Mind attacks rock music, calling Jagger a nihilist "demon" and "satyr" who legitimated drugs and thumbed his nose at moral and political law.
holes.why: The chapter quotes Bloom's indictment of Jagger at length as the leading intellectual voice of the anti-Stones moral panic, and the next section opens by dissecting Bloom's "morally offended viewpoint."
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Aleister Crowley
holes.what: Occultist "Great Beast 666" whose Thelemic law "Do What Thou Wilt" espoused a form of anarchism and whose Lucifer was the light-bearing god rather than Christianity's dark devil.
holes.why: The chapter makes Crowley, through Kenneth Anger, the source of the Stones' occult persona and of the Lucifer Rising project built around Jagger as a latter-day Lucifer.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: William Blake
holes.what: Romantic poet-painter whose Marriage of Heaven and Hell made the Devil a positive force of energy, emotion and creativity, and held that "the road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom."
holes.why: The chapter's "Flowers of Evil" section uses Blake's philosophy of energy and his attack on Augustine's Original Sin as the principal source of the Romantic evil the Stones channeled.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Charles Baudelaire
holes.what: French Romantic poet whose Flowers of Evil and "Litanies to Satan" found in Satan a symbol of political revolution and dark beauty, arguing that humans, not Satan, create hell on earth.
holes.why: The chapter reports Jagger's own admission that "Sympathy for the Devil" came from "an old idea of Baudelaire's," making him the song's acknowledged philosophical source.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French philosopher of excess who named humanity's surplus energy "the accursed share" and analyzed in clinical detail the proximity of eroticism, sacrifice and death.
holes.why: Chapter 22's account of the sex-and-death fusion in ancient ritual frenzy and in the Stones' debauchery rests directly on Bataille's "accursed share," which the chapter introduces by name.
holes.book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

holes.name: Intensive vs. Extensive Magnitude
holes.what: Kant's distinction between extensive magnitude, a whole whose parts add up to it exactly like a hundred pennies making a dollar, and intensive magnitude, a degree of reality that every real thing has and whose partial perspectives never exhaust the whole.
holes.why: Chapter 9 builds its entire reading of Klosterman's lists and the three-perspective Julia/Vance dialogue in Downtown Owl on this distinction, and no existing taxonomy concept covers it.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian thinker of dialogism and the carnivalesque: literature and popular festivities that suspend official hierarchies, crown and decrown kings, and celebrate low culture against official seriousness.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire framework reads Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs as carnivalesque literature, with Klosterman as the crowned and dethroned carnival king, and the taxonomy has no Bakhtin slug.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: The Carnivalesque
holes.what: Bakhtin's notion that carnival forms, in festivities or in literature, temporarily invert social hierarchies and mix high and low in a liberating celebration of the subversive.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies the carnivalesque to American Idol, Pamela Anderson, Saved by the Bell, and Klosterman's crowning as carnival king, and no existing concept slug fits this material.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: Hermeneutic philosopher of Truth and Method who held that all understanding proceeds from the interpreter's culturally inherited prejudices in an open dialogue with the text.
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire framework — sport as cultural text, Klosterman's prejudices, interpretations that shift yet can be definitively false — is Gadamer's hermeneutics applied to the '86 Celtics, soccer, and gridiron football.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Philosophical Hermeneutics
holes.what: The theory that meaning emerges from a fluid dialogue between interpreter and text, in which neither side is fixed and the text can challenge or resist its readings.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues Klosterman's soccer interpretation is an erroneous dialogue-thwarting reading while his football reading partly succeeds — a hermeneutic evaluation of pop-cultural interpretation.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist who founded media ecology, arguing media environments (the global village, hot and cool media, figure-ground) reshape perception and society.
holes.why: Chapter 25 claims Klosterman is a twenty-first-century McLuhan whose analyses of metal, Britney Spears, and laugh tracks borrow McLuhan's concepts without acknowledgment.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Media Ecology (the medium is the message)
holes.what: The study of whole media environments as systems that quietly structure human identity, culture, and experience, rather than evaluating individual media products.
holes.why: Chapter 25's thesis is that Klosterman is a (85 percent) media ecologist doing big-picture analysis of how radio, MTV, and magazines converge to reshape culture.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Otto Neurath
holes.what: Logical-empiricist philosopher of science who warned that 'pseudorationalism' misapplies rational frameworks beyond logic and mathematics, where they inevitably fail.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explains Klosterman's Jack-and-Jane breakup hypothetical as an instance of the pseudorationalism trap Neurath identified in ethical reasoning.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Pseudorationalism
holes.what: The false belief that messy human domains like ethics can be governed by objective rational rules, leading us to defend fabricated moral laws with endless ad hoc qualifications.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues everyone judging Jack and Jane is a pseudorationalist propping up a nonexistent cosmic rule against watching masturbation, instead of giving honest personal reasons.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Platonic Inspiration (the Ion's magnet)
holes.what: Plato's theory in the Ion that poetic creation is divine possession transmitted like magnetism down a chain — muse to poet to rhapsode to spectator — rather than a knowable craft.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses the magnet chain to ask whether Klosterman is an inspired artist or merely a powerful spectator-critic several links removed from the muse.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who theorized fantasy (day-dreaming) as wish-fulfillment that substitutes for ungratified desire from childhood onward.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses Freud's 'Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming' to argue pop-cultural fantasies (Lloyd Dobler, internet porn) are the condition that makes Klosterman's desires possible.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst whose dictum 'do not cede on your desire' and theory of constitutive lack frame desire as inherently unsatisfiable and self-reproducing.
holes.why: Chapter 30 reads Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' as a pseudo-Lacanian text in which satisfaction would only foreclose desire, making unfulfillment structural rather than accidental.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Slovenian philosopher-psychoanalyst who popularizes Lacan through pop culture, arguing the realization of desire coincides with its reproduction, not its fulfillment.
holes.why: Chapter 30 leans on Žižek's Looking Awry (the 'desire to desire,' fantasy staging desire as such) and his Star Wars Holiday Special example to gloss Klosterman's romantic failures.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Fantasy and Desire (psychoanalytic theory of desire)
holes.what: The psychoanalytic thesis that fantasy is the imagined scene which makes desire possible and keeps it circulating, while desire itself aims at recognition and is never fulfilled.
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues pop culture produces the fantasies that frame Klosterman's romantic appetites, and that his (and Billy Joel's) desire is really a desire to be recognized.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: John Calvin
holes.what: Reformation theologian whose doctrines of predestination, justification by faith alone, vocational calling, and unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest') defined Puritanism.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture (Left Behind, Kurt Warner, Jesus Camp) as Calvinist Puritanism, needing Calvin's election, calling, and truth-trumps-peace theology for the argument.
holes.book: 065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal

holes.name: Constant Conjunction (Hume on causation)
holes.what: Hume's view that we never observe causal power in nature, only repeated succession of events, with habit leading the mind to project causality onto constant conjunctions.
holes.why: Chapter 9's core move is reading Mr. Wednesday's con and its 'misdirection' as an engineered exploitation of exactly Humean constant conjunction, foiling a commonsense x-causes-y notion of causality.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Plato's Critique of Poetry (the quarrel with poetry)
holes.what: Plato's Republic charge that poets imitate appearances twice removed from truth, depict gods and heroes behaving shamefully, and nurture the appetites at reason's expense, warranting censorship.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is structured as Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under precisely this critique, answered later in the chapter by Aristotle's Poetics.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics doctrine that experiencing fear and pity for fictional characters purges those emotions from the audience, and that fiction shows universals, what could happen, better than history.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses catharsis to answer Plato: pity for Mad Sweeney's drunken breakdown purifies rather than corrupts the reader of American Gods.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Iris Murdoch
holes.what: Twentieth-century moral philosopher who held that moral life consists in a 'loving gaze' of just and loving attention to the individual reality of other people, preceding choice and rules.
holes.why: Chapter 15 makes Murdoch's loving gaze the mechanism by which Richard sees Door and incurs an obligation while the inattentive Jessica stays indifferent and invisible to need.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Moral Community and Moral Status
holes.what: The question of which beings count as full members of a community owed equal moral consideration, and what radical or partial exclusion from that community does to them.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads Neverwhere's magical invisibility as literal exclusion from the moral community, the analytic framework for its treatment of the homeless, slaves, and the dehumanized.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Amie Thomasson
holes.what: Contemporary metaphysician whose artifact theory holds that fictional characters are abstract artifacts, created by authors' intentional acts and dependent on them for existence.
holes.why: Chapter 24's positive solution for Gaiman's revised gods rests on Thomasson's Fiction and Metaphysics: characters like War are artifacts whose type can be retokened across authors.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Truth in Fiction
holes.what: David Lewis's 1978 analysis of what makes statements about fictional characters true or false, making the original author's pronouncements the arbiter of a character's properties.
holes.why: Chapter 24 frames the whole puzzle of Gaiman rewriting mythological characters via Lewis's truth-in-fiction, which seems to forbid John of Patmos's War becoming Good Omens' Scarlett.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Heterotopia (spaces of otherness)
holes.what: Foucault's notion of real 'counter-sites', cemeteries, ships, mirrors, that both represent and contest all the other spaces of a society at once.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explicitly cites Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces' to read The Graveyard Book's cemetery as a heterotopia, the uncanny in-between space where Bod alone can be at home.
holes.book: 066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

holes.name: Theory of Tragedy (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of tragedy in the Poetics: plot governed by reversal and recognition, the hero's hamartia (tragic flaw, often hubris), and the catharsis of pity and fear.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads Walter White as a Macbeth figure through Aristotle's reversal, hamartia/hubris, recognition, and catharsis, and no existing Aristotle slug covers the Poetics.
holes.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry

holes.name: Instrumental Rationality
holes.what: Reason used purely as a means-end tool for achieving goals, with no moral evaluation of the ends - the critical theorists' target in amoral, technocratic thinking.
holes.why: Chapter 20's central claim is that Gus Fring's corporate sociopathy is institutionalized instrumental rationality, a concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalytic theorist whose 'Real' names the unrepresentable kernel of trauma that irrupts into and reshapes our symbolically constructed reality.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire reading of Walt's cancer diagnosis, crimes, and lies as irruptions of the Real into his constructed reality is built on Lacan, who is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry

holes.name: Jacques Ellul
holes.what: French sociologist and philosopher of technology who argued that modern technology becomes an autonomous force subverting human purposes regardless of our intentions.
holes.why: Chapter 29 closes by invoking Ellul's autonomous technology to explain why Walt's meth enterprise, once embraced, cannot be made humane or undone.
holes.book: 067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry

holes.name: Functionalism (mental states as functional roles)
holes.what: The view that mental states are defined by their causal-functional role relating stimuli, other mental states, and behavior, rather than by what they are made of.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument about whether walkers are conscious runs through philosophical behaviorism and functionalism, and its walker-computer thought experiment is a functionalist scenario, but the taxonomy has no behaviorism or functionalism slug.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: The Paradox of Horror
holes.what: Noel Carroll's puzzle (The Philosophy of Horror, 1990) that audiences voluntarily seek out horror fiction whose monsters aim to produce fear and disgust, usually answered via curiosity, discovery, and the disclosure of the categorically interstitial.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames its whole question - why people compete for a 'stagger-on role' as a zombie - as an amplified version of Carroll's paradox, and the taxonomy has no aesthetics-of-horror concept to map it onto.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Noel Carroll
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose The Philosophy of Horror (1990) defines the horror genre by 'art-horror' monsters and the paradox of horror.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is built directly on Carroll's account of horror monsters and the paradox, naming him and his book as its theoretical foundation, but he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Political Realism (power over morality in statecraft)
holes.what: The tradition (Machiavelli, Morgenthau) holding that relations between states are governed by power, security, and survival rather than morality, that the worst state beats anarchy, and that a prince is better feared than loved.
holes.why: Chapter 24 evaluates Rick's prison, Woodbury, and Alexandria entirely through Realist state-formation theory (including second anarchy and war as state-builder), and no taxonomy slug captures Realism as such; machiavelli-ends only covers the ends-justify-means piece.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Facticity
holes.what: The given facts of one's situation and past (body, history, deeds), which freedom must own without being determined by them.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explicitly introduces facticity to read Rick's 'we became what we are' speech: denying one's past deeds or letting them dictate present behavior are both inauthentic.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Philosopher whose five criteria of personhood (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness) separate moral personhood from genetic humanity, and who holds that only beings capable of duties can hold rights.
holes.why: Chapter 30 builds its entire case that walkers lack moral rights on Warren's personhood criteria and her space-traveler thought experiment, but the taxonomy has no entry for her (only the ecofeminist Karen J. Warren).
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Personhood (vs genetic humanity)
holes.what: The criteria-based status of being a person owed moral consideration, distinct from merely being biologically human.
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues walkers fail every personhood criterion and so have no rights, and Hershel in the series claims walkers remain 'entitled to personhood' as sick people — a central concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Anti-Natalism
holes.what: The view that procreation is morally wrong because nonexistent children cannot suffer, while any child brought into existence certainly will face harm and death.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues Lori's pregnancy and Glenn and Maggie's wish for a baby are the worst thing survivors could do, recommending adoption of existing children instead — an anti-natalist argument the chapter applies but never names.
holes.book: 068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

holes.name: Incongruity Theory of Humor
holes.what: Kant's view that laughter arises when 'a tense expectation is transformed into nothing'—humor is the perception of an incongruity between expectation and outcome.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues incongruity is the only humor theory that covers every case, from Larry's panties to Krayzee-Eyez Killa's phone-book listing.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Relief Theory of Humor
holes.what: Spencer and Freud's account of laughter as the discharge of surplus psychic energy, whether from a situation suddenly revealed as unserious or from an expressed repressed desire.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses it to explain Curb's cringe-then-laughter structure and why fans laugh hardest at the rat-dog stomping scene.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Superiority Theory of Humor
holes.what: Hobbes's 'sudden glory': we laugh when we conceive some eminency in ourselves by comparison with the infirmity of others or our own former selves.
holes.why: Chapter 11 tests it on the long parade of Larry's social disasters and finds superiority neither necessary nor sufficient for humor.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Cultural Background Practices (the unknown known)
holes.what: Non-conceptual, embodied know-how about how one lives—tendencies, skills, and dispositions absorbed from a culture—that we know without knowing that we know it.
holes.why: Chapter 11's own thesis is that Larry's comedy exposes this 'unknown known' (tiptoeing at night, the stop and chat) and shows our social conventions are contingent.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German sociologist who traced the modern compulsion to work to the Calvinist doctrine of predestination and the worldly 'calling,' surviving secularization as capitalism's 'iron cage.'
holes.why: Chapter 14 frames its whole defense of Larry's idleness with Weber's Protestant ethic, quoting the 'ghost of dead religious beliefs' passage.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: The Protestant Work Ethic
holes.what: Weber's account of how duty in one's worldly calling became proof of election and then a surviving social norm that condemns idleness as a moral failing.
holes.why: Chapter 14 needs it to diagnose why Cheryl, Jeff, and Richard Lewis treat Larry's refusal to work as insanity or deviance.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Flanerie (the flaneur's idleness)
holes.what: Benjamin's figure of the urban stroller whose aimless, observant walking is a creative, productive form of active idleness against the demands of work.
holes.why: Chapter 14 casts Larry's sidewalk ambling and notebook jottings as flanerie, the second great 'idle pleasure' of his way of life.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Cheshire Calhoun
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose article 'The Virtue of Civility' analyzes the social functions and moral significance of civility.
holes.why: Chapter 15 says it is 'much indebted' to Calhoun for its defense of rules of civility against Larry's skeptical challenges.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Nihilism (the highest values devalue themselves)
holes.what: Nietzsche's diagnosis of a culture in which the highest values devalue themselves, so nothing matters more than anything else and moral talk survives as an empty shell.
holes.why: Chapter 17's thesis is that Curb depicts a humdrum, everyday nihilism—anonymous donors, terrorist warnings as leverage—where the good is hollowed out but its language still casts a spell.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Jewish Self-Hatred (the self-hating Jew)
holes.what: The charge, popularized by Theodor Lessing and Kurt Lewin, that a Jew has internalized the antisemitic stereotypes and worldview of the dominant culture.
holes.why: Chapter 18's guiding question is whether Larry's humor makes him a self-hating Jew or whether the show mocks that very idea.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: The Ethics of Laughter (the Just Joking Defense)
holes.what: Ronald de Sousa's rejection of the 'Just Joking Defense': laughter is voluntary enough that we are accountable for the jokes we make and at which we let ourselves laugh.
holes.why: Chapter 18 needs it to decide whether Larry's affirmative-action and religious jokes, and the audience's laughter at them, are morally wrong.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Use-Mention Distinction
holes.what: The semantic distinction between using a word with its usual meaning and merely mentioning the word itself as an object of quotation.
holes.why: Chapter 20 hinges on it: Larry only 'mentions' the n-word while quoting a racist, yet Dr. Page hears a use and shaves Jeff bald.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: L-Groups (Appiah's social identity labels)
holes.what: Appiah's account in The Ethics of Identity of identity labels (race, religion, baldness) that we stereotype, treat differentially, and internalize, and which deserve recognition and collective self-definition.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire 'Larry David Solution to Racial Difference,' including the bald-solidarity argument, is built on Appiah's L-group analysis.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: the Oedipal complex, id/ego/superego, neurotic anxiety, castration anxiety, and primary and secondary narcissism.
holes.why: Chapter 21 diagnoses Larry as a neurotic impotent and Jeff as a secondary narcissist using Freud's developmental categories; chapter 11 also uses his relief theory of humor.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Jessica Benjamin
holes.what: Psychoanalytic feminist theorist of mutual recognition between subjects (Like Subjects, Love Objects), developing Hegel's struggle for recognition.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Benjamin's account of mutual recognition as the standard by which Larry's and Jeff's masculinity pathologies are measured.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Michael S. Kimmel
holes.what: Sociologist of masculinity whose 'Masculinity as Homophobia' argues masculine ideals are policed by fear and judgment of other men ('the great secret of manhood: we are afraid of other men').
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Kimmel to explain how the expectations of masculine power produce Larry's neurotic impotence and Jeff's narcissism.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: The Impossible Gift (Derrida, Given Time)
holes.what: Derrida's argument that a true gift is impossible, since the moment a gift is recognized, reciprocated, or even known to the giver it enters an exchange that annuls it as a gift.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central framework: the shirt, freak book, pie, and bracelet all fail Derrida's test, showing no free gift can appear in Larry's world.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: The Gift (Mauss's gift economy)
holes.what: Marcel Mauss's account of gift exchange in archaic societies, where gifts are extensions of the giver that bind recipients and create obligations to give in return.
holes.why: Chapter 24 opens with Mauss to explain why gifts in Curb, like the $300 wine for Mel and Ed, always impose on the receiver and never come free.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose The Ethics of Authenticity defends authenticity as an ideal while warning that self-choosing requires 'horizons of significance' beyond the individual self.
holes.why: Chapter 27 leans on Taylor for its verdict that Larry's brand of authenticity is really egoistic moral relativism cut off from any background of things that matter.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Enthusiasm (enthusiasmos)
holes.what: The historical philosophical category running from divine possession and poetic inspiration (Plato) through religious fanaticism (Wesley, Shaftesbury, Locke, Hume) to Kant's aesthetic enthusiasm before the morally good.
holes.why: Chapter 29 is organized entirely around these senses of enthusiasm, asking which of them Larry displays and which the title's command tells us to curb.
holes.book: 069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within

holes.name: Catharsis (Poetics on tragedy and fiction)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics that tragedy purges pity and fear and that poetry, depicting what might be, is more philosophical than history.
holes.why: Chapter 9's central defense of D&D as worthwhile art runs through catharsis and the Poetics, which the taxonomy's other Aristotle slugs (eudaimonia, virtue ethics) do not cover.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: Contemporary French philosopher whose 'ethic of truths' holds that enforcing a single moral law or named Good generates evil as 'simulacrum' or 'disaster'.
holes.why: Chapter 12 relies on Badiou's ethic of truths for its main conclusion that Chaotic Good is a coherent position—pursuing good without accepting one universal moral law.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of narrative identity who holds that making sense of ourselves requires grasping our lives as unfolding stories oriented to the good.
holes.why: Chapter 13 takes Taylor's narrative ethics as its main interlocutor, testing it against D&D players' grief for dead characters before revising it into a 'back-story' view of the self.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle, rooted in Hume's Standard of Taste and developed by Walton and Gendler, that readers balk at imagining moral claims they believe false even inside fantastical fiction.
holes.why: Chapter 14 explains real-world anger at evil role-play via imaginative resistance, and Chapter 15 builds its defense of evil characters on dissolving that puzzle—no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Philosopher whose Space Traveler thought experiment asks how we could tell whether alien beings are persons with full moral rights (famous also for her abortion-era personhood criteria).
holes.why: Chapter 19 applies Warren's personhood criteria to orcs and the wrongly killed lawful-good Flumph to question when killing monsters is justified.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Art-Horror (Carroll's philosophy of horror)
holes.what: Noël Carroll's theory that horror fiction expresses the indescribable through monsters that are categorically impure, incomplete, or formless relative to the audience's conceptual scheme.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its entire account of why D&D's rule-based magic cannot model Lovecraftian unnatural magic on Carroll's art-horror apparatus, none of which the taxonomy captures.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Graham Harman
holes.what: Philosopher of Object-Oriented Ontology, holding that real objects are radically unknowable and that aesthetic 'allure' discloses their hidden reality.
holes.why: Chapter 21 develops its account of D&D worlds and character-class 'sincerities' directly from Harman's concepts of allure and sincerity.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Flat Ontology
holes.what: The view that all entities, human and nonhuman, living and nonliving, are equally substances endowed with powers (affects) and individuated by their history and capacities rather than by their current qualities.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads D&D's world of alliances, enchanted items and dice-driven encounters (Elric and Stormbringer, warriors in armor, ogre war bands) as an instance of Bryant's Deleuze-Latour flat ontology, for which the taxonomy has only the philosopher Deleuze and no concept.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we have genuine emotional responses to characters and events we know do not exist, since we neither react to what we merely pretend is real nor believe fictions are real.
holes.why: Chapter 25 states Radford's paradox and uses Walton's quasi-emotions answer to explain why players who know the campaign world is not real are nonetheless genuinely engrossed in their characters' fates.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that many concepts, notably 'game', have no common essence but are united by a criss-crossing network of overlapping similarities, like the shared features of a family.
holes.why: Chapter 25 applies family resemblance to decide whether D&D is a game, arguing it belongs to the family despite lacking central features such as winning and losing.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Kendall Walton
holes.what: American philosopher of art whose make-believe (prop) theory holds that paintings, novels and games are props that prescribe imaginings, within which propositions are fictional, that is, true in a fictional world.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is built on Walton's prop theory, treating D&D rules, dice, classes, character sheets, maps and miniatures as props prescribing imagination, and chapter 25 uses the same theory to answer the paradox of fiction.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Ludology vs Narratology Debate
holes.what: The game-studies debate over whether games should be understood primarily as rule-based systems (ludology) or as extensions of narrative and storytelling (narratology).
holes.why: Chapter 28 frames the whole role-play versus gameplay dispute through this debate and argues D&D's 'border region' fuses the two rather than choosing sides.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Metagaming (player vs character knowledge)
holes.what: The use of out-of-character player knowledge in play, together with the inversion of choice and chance between the player's perspective (dice rolls) and the character's perspective (race, background, abilities).
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses the gunpowder-crisis anecdote to show how metagaming can wreck or enrich a campaign, and how dice and character creation redistribute accountability between player and character.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: German philosopher of philosophical hermeneutics who analyzed understanding as an 'event' in which the interpreter's prejudices play an enabling role and interpreter and interpreted fuse their horizons.
holes.why: Chapter 31 develops its three models of knowing a D&D character (Collingwood's re-enactment, bracketing, fusion of horizons) directly from Gadamer's Truth and Method to reassess metagaming, and Gadamer is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom

holes.name: American Exceptionalism
holes.what: The belief that America possesses a unique character, mission, and set of values that set it apart from all other nations.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues Jeopardy!'s agonistic meritocracy, redemption arcs, physical buzzer tests, and middlebrow knowledge base are an index of distinctly American exceptionalist values, and no existing slug captures this thesis.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Ronald Dworkin
holes.what: Political philosopher who argued that meaningful equality requires equality of resources, not merely equal opportunity, so people can capitalize on opportunities and are responsible for their choices.
holes.why: Chapter 14 applies Dworkin's equality of resources to Jeopardy!, arguing identical rules are not enough if contestants lack the resources to compete, and no taxonomy slug covers him.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Will Kymlicka
holes.what: Political philosopher who argues justice requires protecting minority and national cultures, potentially through differentiated rights, so members can pursue their own conceptions of the good.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses Kymlicka's national-minority argument (and Quebec's Bill 101) to charge that Jeopardy!'s American-centric clue bank undermines equal respect for non-dominant cultures.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Bernard Suits
holes.what: Philosopher of games whose The Grasshopper defines gameplaying through prelusory goals, constitutive rules that introduce inefficiency, and the lusory attitude.
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire argument that Jeopardy! is a good game is built on Suits's definitions (prelusory goal, constitutive rules, lusory attitude), which the taxonomy lacks entirely.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Justified True Belief
holes.what: The classical analysis of propositional knowledge, from Plato's Theaetetus, as belief that is true and adequately justified.
holes.why: Chapters 16 and 20 both run their arguments through the JTB account (belief, truth, justification, and lucky true beliefs that are not knowledge), but the taxonomy contains only the Gettier problem, which presupposes it.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Bloom's Taxonomy of Learning Objectives
holes.what: A hierarchy of educational objectives running from recalling facts through comprehension, application, analysis, and synthesis to evaluation.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses Bloom's Taxonomy as its central yardstick, arguing Jeopardy! contestants operate only at the remembering level while real knowledge requires the evaluation level.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Maslow's Self-Actualization (hierarchy of needs, peak experience)
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's account of human motivation in which, once physiological, safety, belonging, and esteem needs are met, people instinctively strive to realize their fullest potential.
holes.why: Chapter 27 builds its whole philosophy of education on Maslow's self-actualization and peak experiences (applied to teachers), a framework the taxonomy lacks; its eudaimonia slug only loosely overlaps.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: F.H. Bradley
holes.what: British absolute idealist whose Appearance and Reality defended a single self-pervading Absolute Experience, and whose idealism was the target of Russell's and Moore's analytic revolt.
holes.why: Chapter 30's fictional Jeopardy! episode stars Bradley defending monism and the Absolute against Russell and Wittgenstein, but the taxonomy has no entry for him or British idealism.
holes.book: 072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German philosopher-sociologist whose rationalization thesis holds that modern life is dominated by bureaucratic institutions - formal rules, hierarchy, written records, and quantified measures - which trap people in the 'iron cage'.
holes.why: Chapter 18 explicitly builds its whole reading of The Wire's police department, drug crew, schools, and newsroom on Weber's thesis that bureaucracy is the hallmark of modern institutions, down to ending on the 'iron cage of futility and absurdity in modern institutional life', but no Weber slug exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Critical race theorist and founder of Critical Race Theory who argued that racism is a permanent feature of American society and that Black progress is perpetually subordinated to white self-interest.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explicitly builds its 'racial realist' critique of The Wire's class-based realism on Bell's permanence-of-racism thesis, and no taxonomy slug covers him.
holes.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

holes.name: Afro-pessimism
holes.what: The thesis (Frank Wilderson, Jared Sexton) that Blackness is positioned in modernity not as exploited labor but as the non-Human against which civil society defines itself, an antagonism no transfer of ownership or reorganization of existing categories can satisfy.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues, citing Wilderson, that Simon's categories of work and exploitation cannot account for the Black subject position in The Wire, which is exactly the Afro-pessimist claim.
holes.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

holes.name: The New Jim Crow
holes.what: Michelle Alexander's account of the War on Drugs and mass incarceration as a racialized caste system that permanently bars Black Americans from mainstream society and economy.
holes.why: Chapter 26 leans on Alexander's undercaste thesis to argue that the drug war continues Jim Crow by other means, something Simon's underclass framing erases.
holes.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed contrasts 'banking' education, which deposits inert content into students, with dialogical, liberatory education grounded in love, trust, and the experience of the oppressed.
holes.why: Chapter 33 evaluates Prezbo's classroom and Parenti's project class almost entirely through Freire's banking concept, alienating language, false generosity of paternalism, and dialogue, none of which the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

holes.name: Angela Y. Davis
holes.what: Philosopher and prison-abolitionist who argues that US punishment, from the Black Codes through today's carceral state, perpetuated slavery's master-slave relation by confining and brutalizing Black bodies deemed soulless and beyond reform.
holes.why: Chapter 36's core explanation of police brutality and the no-snitching code, the slave-master relationship and racialized bodily punishment, is taken directly from Davis's racialized punishment and prison abolition writings.
holes.book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The classic problem of how I can know that anyone besides myself has a mind, since I directly experience only my own.
holes.why: Chapter 11 stages exactly this problem in Zira's struggle to know that Taylor thinks while Dr. Zaius explains everything as 'a gift for mimicry,' but the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Mindreading / Theory of Mind (false belief)
holes.what: The capacity to attribute beliefs, desires, and intentions to others, master-tested by false-belief tasks and often taken to ground personhood.
holes.why: Chapter 13 settles whether apes are 'sneaky enough to be people' on whether they can mindread - attribute false beliefs per Hare, Call and Tomasello - and chapter 11's folk-psychology critique of mindreading uses the same concept, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Scientism (Science as Ideology)
holes.what: The dogmatic extension of scientific authority into a quasi-religious worldview that dismisses ethics and consciousness as meaningless or outside science's scope.
holes.why: Chapter 15's whole diagnosis is Rollin's 'scientific ideology' embodied in Dr. Zaius, Minister of Science and Chief Defender of the Faith, and the taxonomy has no scientism slug.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Logical Positivism (verifiability principle)
holes.what: The doctrine that a statement is meaningful only if it can in principle be verified (or falsified) by experience, banishing ethics and metaphysics as meaningless.
holes.why: Chapter 15 explains the verifiability criterion and applies it to the Hasslein Curve prediction versus 'there are intelligent beings in Heaven'; the existing 'falsification' slug is Popper's rival doctrine, not positivism.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: French political thinker whose Democracy in America warns that majority opinion becomes a 'tyranny' raising 'formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion.'
holes.why: Chapter 25 interprets Dr. Zaius's censorship, Landon's lobotomy, and 'what remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking?' through Tocqueville's tyranny of the majority, but the taxonomy has no slug for him.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of common descent and the branching evolutionary tree replaced linear, ranked pictures of the living world.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds its whole argument on Darwin's tree (against the Great Chain) to deny any pinnacle species and to place human nature in continuity with ape nature.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: The Great Chain of Being
holes.what: The pre-Darwinian idea, named by Lovejoy, that all living things are ranked on a single linear scale from simple to complex with rational humans at the top.
holes.why: Chapter 29 argues the Ape films assume this chain view of grades and that Darwinian tree thinking dissolves it, undercutting 'higher' and 'lower' species and species essences.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Semiotics (the theory of signs)
holes.what: The Peirce-Saussure theory that meaning is carried by signs whose content comes from convention, association, and interpretation rather than inherent properties.
holes.why: Chapter 33's core claim is that Goldsmith's score means nothing inherently and works only through learned sign-associations, an argument that needs the missing semiotics vocabulary.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalytic philosopher who rethought the self through the mirror stage, the imaginary-symbolic-real registers, and an unconscious structured like language.
holes.why: Chapter 35 reads Caesar's entire identity crisis through the mirror stage, the ideal-I, meconnaissance, and the three registers, none of which any existing taxonomy entry covers.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: The Mirror Stage
holes.what: Lacan's account of how the infant's jubilant identification with its mirror image founds an alienating ideal-I and a lifelong misrecognized sense of self.
holes.why: Chapter 35 applies the mirror stage directly to Caesar's reflections and to the human children he identifies with as the origin of his identity crisis.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Slavoj Zizek
holes.what: Lacanian-Marxist philosopher of ideology who analyzes how ideological fantasy structures social reality and how an Act can change the coordinates of the possible.
holes.why: Chapter 35 leans on Zizek's The Sublime Object of Ideology for ideological fantasy, the traumatic kernel of the real, and the Act that Caesar performs at the film's end.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Ideological Fantasy and the Act
holes.what: Zizek's notion that fantasy quilts social reality around a master signifier, hiding a traumatic lack, and that traversing the fantasy through an Act redefines one's identity.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses ideological fantasy to explain Caesar's new master signifier Freedom and his ape liberation, and the Act to read his final 'Caesar is home'.
holes.book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

holes.name: Informal Fallacies (red herring, ad hominem)
holes.what: Bad-reasoning patterns in which the premises seem relevant to the conclusion but are not, such as red herrings, ad hominem attacks, and inconsistencies.
holes.why: Chapter 9's whole case is that Shawn's psychic career is built on fallacies of relevance - red herring, ad hominem, and inconsistency - and taxonomy.json has no slug for fallacy theory.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Narratology (the philosophy of story structure)
holes.what: The study of how stories are structured and how narrative form produces its effect on an audience, as opposed to what a story says.
holes.why: Chapter 10 analyzes Psych purely through narratology - episode formula elements, the eidetic-memory sequence as structural pivot, and the projective illusion of the fourth wall.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Inference to the Best Explanation (abduction)
holes.what: Reasoning that selects, from competing hypotheses, the one that best explains the available evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 11 names IBE, alongside hypersensory perception, as the actual engine of Shawn's crime-solving and uses it to decide what each character should believe.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Thin-Slicing (rapid cognition)
holes.what: The ability to extract accurate patterns and judgments from very brief 'thin slices' of experience, as in gut instinct and snap judgment.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains Shawn's fake psychic successes as expert two-stage thin-slicing trained by Henry, drawing on Gladwell, Gottman, and Ekman.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Evidentialism
holes.what: The theory that a belief is justified only by the evidence the believer possesses, contrasted with reliabilism's truth-conduciveness standard.
holes.why: Chapter 14 gives evidentialism a full section and uses base rates and prior probabilities to show Shawn's hunches fail it, pairing it with the already-listed reliabilism.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Epistemology of Testimony
holes.what: The study of when we are justified in believing what others tell us, from Hume's demand for independent evidence to Reid's default trust.
holes.why: Chapter 20 frames the entire question of trusting Shawn's psychic claims as the philosophy of testimony, mapping Lassiter, McNab, and Juliet onto its competing theories.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: The Big Lie
holes.what: The principle, associated with Hitler and Goebbels, that a lie so colossal will be believed because no one would imagine anyone could distort the truth so infamously.
holes.why: Chapter 21's title thesis is that only the biggest possible lie - 'I am a psychic' - could save Shawn in the pilot, applying the big-lie principle and its reverse psychology directly to the show.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Reliability of Memory (false memories)
holes.what: The epistemological question of when memory counts as evidence, covering source confusion, suggestive questioning, and implanted or false memories.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues ordinary memory is only generally reliable - cataloguing source confusion, false memories, and suggestive questioning in Psych - so memory-based testimony needs physical corroboration.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: The Trickster Archetype
holes.what: A cross-cultural mythological figure who breaks rules, deceives, and disrupts established order, exposing conventions and opening new possibilities through mischief.
holes.why: Chapter 32's entire argument is that Shawn is a trickster - the fool who fools fools - and no taxonomy slug covers this mythological role.
holes.book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who modeled the mind as a battlefield of drives, famously dividing motivation into a life drive (Eros) and a death drive (Thanatos) alongside the id-ego-superego structure.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Colin Sweeney, Peter Florrick, and Louis Canning as psychoanalytic cases in which the death drive dominates the life drive, making Freud the chapter's central framework.
holes.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia

holes.name: The Death Drive (Thanatos)
holes.what: In Freud's drive theory, the destructive impulse toward aggression, distance, and death that in healthy people serves the life drive but in pathology dominates and directs it.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses the death drive to explain the show's everyday evil, from Sweeney's sadistic pleasure to Canning's self-attacking symptoms and Peter's paranoid barricade of protectors.
holes.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia

holes.name: Legal Realism
holes.what: The jurisprudential thesis that judges actually decide cases from personality, bias, mood, and politics rather than by logically deriving outcomes from legal rules.
holes.why: Chapter 17 tests legal realism against Judge Park's formalism, Judge Lessner's quirks, and Judge Baxter's kickbacks before turning to Hart's open texture and Dworkin's integrity theory.
holes.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia

holes.name: Partial Values (Slote)
holes.what: Michael Slote's paired values (tact and frankness, career and family) that cannot be possessed fully together, grounding his thesis that human perfection is impossible.
holes.why: Chapter 24 leans on Slote's partial values to argue Alicia can never perfectly combine career and family, so the good life is about balance rather than having it all.
holes.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia

holes.name: Epistemology of Testimony
holes.what: The branch of epistemology asking when believing someone on their word is justified, and whether speakers can have a right, or hearers a duty, to be believed.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues that positions of power - judge, jury, reader of Lambrose's book - carry role-dependent moral duties of presumptive belief, applied to Peter's lies and the Death Zone libel trial.
holes.book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: the id/ego/superego structural model, the Eros versus Thanatos contest, repression, the Oedipus complex, and civilization as built on renounced instinct.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads Van Alden's eruptions, the audience's identification with Nucky and Jimmy, and the Jimmy-Gillian incest as Oedipal primal-horde parricide entirely through Freud, but he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: Ethics of Docudrama (reel history vs real history)
holes.what: The applied-ethics question of when it is wrong to blend fact with fiction in historical drama that viewers may take as fact.
holes.why: Chapter 17 argues Boardwalk Empire's inaccuracies about Capone, McGarrigle, and Atlantic City's bloodless corruption unethically mislead viewers who 'learn' the false history, a gap the taxonomy's deception-free concept list does not cover.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: John Calvin
holes.what: Protestant reformer whose Institutes teach a radical doctrine of divine omnipotence: every event, including death, is determined by God's decree.
holes.why: Chapter 18 grounds Van Alden's strong providential theology in Calvin's determinism, quoting the Institutes directly to drive the problem of evil, yet Calvin is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: Doing vs Allowing Harm
holes.what: The debated doctrine, classically argued through active versus passive euthanasia, that actively causing a harm is morally worse than merely enabling or allowing it.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire assessment of Nucky's blame for Gillian's rape, and Jimmy's right to blame him, turns on whether enabling and failing to stop harm is as wrong as causing it, a distinction the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: The Ethics of Lying and Deception
holes.what: The moral analysis of lying: Kant's absolute ban, Grotius's life-saving exceptions, Bok on trust, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that are not intended to deceive.
holes.why: Chapter 20 is wholly devoted to which bootleggers' lies are wrong - altruistic lies, lies to the willing, lies to liars, bald-faced lies - and the taxonomy has no concept naming lying or deception.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: The Body Politic
holes.what: The ancient-to-early-modern metaphor of the state as a living organism whose ruler is the head and whose citizens are the parts, as in Seneca's De Clementia and Hobbes's Leviathan frontispiece.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Nucky's hygiene obsession, Prohibition's purity politics, and Nucky-as-king entirely through the body politic metaphor, which the taxonomy's political concepts do not include.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: Slavoj Zizek
holes.what: Continental philosopher whose Violence distinguishes visible subjective violence from objective violence - symbolic (language, racism) and systemic (the invisible coercion of capitalism).
holes.why: Chapter 29 is an extended application of Zizek's subjective/objective violence distinction to the show's gore and to Nucky's philanthropy-cum-racketeering, but Zizek is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed holds that true education requires dialogue among 'critical co-investigators' rather than one-way imposition.
holes.why: Chapter 30 leans on Freire's dialogue and problem-posing criteria to judge Nucky's, Chalky's, and Rothstein's storytelling as deficient pedagogy, but Freire is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book

holes.name: Isaiah Berlin
holes.what: Twentieth-century liberal philosopher famous for distinguishing positive and negative liberty.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is built entirely on Berlin's two-concepts-of-liberty framework, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: Positive and Negative Liberty
holes.what: Berlin's distinction between freedom as rational self-mastery and freedom from external interference.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses the distinction to diagnose Fry's Slurm addiction and human Bender's fatal indulgence as unfreedom despite no external constraint.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: Political Ecology
holes.what: The approach treating environmental crisis as inseparable from political-economic structures such as capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 11 applies Bryant and Bailey's political ecology to argue Futurama's trash-ball disaster is produced by capitalist consumption, not by insufficient recycling.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who explained perversion as symbolic escape from unconscious sexual anxiety.
holes.why: Chapter 14 leans on Freud's theory of perversion (with Stoller and McDougall) to read Zapp's fetishes, and taxonomy.json has no psychoanalytic thinker.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Philosopher of religion whose Irenaean 'soul-making' theodicy explains evil and God's hiddenness as conditions for moral development.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its entire answer to the problem of evil in 'Godfellas' on Hick's soul-making theodicy and epistemic distance, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: Soul-Making Theodicy
holes.what: The view that evil exists because the world is a vale of soul-making where free creatures develop, requiring God's epistemic distance.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies soul-making to argue Bender's divine meddling and God's light touch show why a good God permits evil.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: The Value of Fiction
holes.what: The question of how fiction relates to reality and what imaginative works can teach or accomplish in real life.
holes.why: Chapter 33's whole argument is that the line between Fry's fantasy and reality is porous and that fiction (the holophoner, Don Quixote) genuinely changes the real world, a theme taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: Unity of Consciousness
holes.what: Hegel's doctrine that consciousness just is the relating of subject and object, producing the illusion of a separate 'I'.
