holes.why: Chapter 34 uses this doctrine (rather than the dialectic) to dissolve Futurama's time skips and coffee-speed scenes into ordinary gaps of experience.
holes.book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement holding that we should use technology to overcome aging and death and transcend current human limits (de Grey, Max More, Bostrom, Harris).
holes.why: Chapter 10 stages its whole debate about radical life extension between Shelley's warning and transhumanists who call death the greatest of all evils, but the taxonomy has no transhumanism slug.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Liberal Eugenics
holes.what: The program of using genetic and reproductive technologies for parent-consumer-chosen human enhancement, which Habermas (The Future of Human Nature) argues undermines moral equality and autonomy by turning creation into manufacture.
holes.why: Chapter 11's core argument applies Habermas's critique of liberal eugenics to Venter's synthetic life and Victor's creation, and no existing slug names the doctrine.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Scientism (unlimited faith in science)
holes.what: The optimism that with enough time and resources science can control virtually every human adversity, including death itself.
holes.why: Chapter 13 identifies faith in unlimited scientific progress as the first of the three ingredients of the Frankenstein myth, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for it.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Conceptual Metaphor (source and target domains)
holes.what: The theory that metaphors map a familiar source domain onto a less-known target domain and shape how we see the world (unidirectionality; scientific metaphors like 'selfish gene' or 'world as machine').
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire evaluation of the 'Frankenfood' metaphor is conducted in this framework, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Human Enhancement
holes.what: Technologically improving human bodies and minds beyond medical treatment, up to conquering disease and death, by taking evolution into our own hands.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Victor as an enhancement pioneer and argues enhancement is not good in itself (the Midas problem); the generic applied-ethics slug does not name the concept.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose Basic Argument ('The Impossibility of Moral Responsibility') holds that no one can be morally responsible, since responsibility for actions would require responsibility for how one is, ad infinitum.
holes.why: Chapter 20's verdict that the monster is not responsible for his evil character rests on Strawson's impossibilism, and the taxonomy contains no Strawson.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's theory that human motivation climbs from basic physiological and safety needs through the 'love need' to higher needs like prestige and self-actualization.
holes.why: Chapter 22 explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a deprived 'love need', making the hierarchy load-bearing for its analysis of who is to blame.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development
holes.what: Jean Piaget's model of children's reasoning developing through the concrete operational (ages 7-11) and formal operational (adolescence onward) stages.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Piaget's stages to assess whether the monster had developed the mature reasoning needed for moral responsibility.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Diffusion of Responsibility
holes.what: The tendency of people in a chain of responsibility to feel and act less responsibly because each assumes someone else will intervene ('I didn't do it').
holes.why: Chapter 23's conclusion about killer robots and monsters is that blame spreads across many hands without diluting, and diffusion of responsibility is the named risk no taxonomy slug captures.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Physicalism
holes.what: The view that humans are entirely physical beings with no immaterial parts such as souls, mental life being wholly a matter of brain states.
holes.why: Chapter 25 frames the soul question as physicalism versus dualism, but the taxonomy offers only dualist slugs like cartesian-dualism.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Zygmunt Bauman
holes.what: Sociologist-philosopher of 'liquid modernity,' the light, individualized late modernity in which communal bonds dissolve and the foreigner or Other appears as a threat.
holes.why: Chapter 28 frames Victor's self-imposed isolation and our own networked detachment through Bauman's liquid modernity, and no existing slug covers him or it.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist of the cyborg, the hybrid of organism and machine that dissolves nature/culture and self/other boundaries and is 'exceedingly unfaithful' to its patriarchal origins.
holes.why: Chapter 30 devotes a section to reading Frankenstein's creature as Haraway's cyborg - an illegitimate offspring rebelling against the father - to undermine Western self/other ideology.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view that humanity should be understood, and may be remade, beyond traditional humanism, rejecting fixed natural/artificial and human/other boundaries (Pepperell's distinction between momentary consciousness and accumulated being).
holes.why: Chapter 30's central claim is that we may be ready to move beyond humanism and accept a 'new Frankenstein,' and the taxonomy has no posthumanist or transhumanist slug.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: William Godwin
holes.what: Radical British philosopher of political justice and human perfectibility, Mary Shelley's father, notorious for his attacks on marriage and the diminishment of family bonds.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads Frankenstein as Shelley's response to Godwin's utopian individualism, whose dreams of the perfectible man Victor embodies and the creature's fate tests.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's account of the frightening that emerges from the familiar and repressed (via Schelling: what ought to have remained hidden but has come to light), felt before whatever blurs living and dead, self and other.
holes.why: Chapter 35's middle section explains the creature's horror - human enough to resemble us, deformed enough to repel - through the uncanny, which no existing slug names.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Allen E. Buchanan
holes.what: Bioethicist who defends biomedical enhancement, arguing in Better than Human that evolution's haphazard course can be safely and beneficially improved upon.
holes.why: Chapter 38 stages the enhancement debate as Sandel's bioconservatism against Buchanan's bioprogressivism, and the taxonomy covers only the former.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: David Benatar
holes.what: Philosopher of anti-natalism who argues in Better Never to Have Been that coming into existence is always a serious harm.
holes.why: Chapter 39's argument that creating monsters or babies is wrong is explicitly informed by Benatar's book, including his diagnosis of pro-natal bias.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Anti-Natalism
holes.what: The view that it is wrong to bring new autonomous (or sentient) beings into existence, whether by procreation or by creation.
holes.why: Chapter 39 is built around defining and defending anti-natalism, applying it equally to conceiving children and to Frankenstein's act of creation.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: The Non-Identity Problem
holes.what: Parfit's puzzle that choices determining who will exist seem to wrong no existing, or even identical, future person, complicating duties to future people.
holes.why: Chapter 39 must answer it - via the case of Frankenstein activating a damaged brain rather than building a healthy one - for its claim that creating life wrongs the created.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: Enlightenment satirist-philosopher who, after the Lisbon earthquake, rejected optimistic theodicy (Candide) and held that morality demands we not pretend to make evil intelligible.
holes.why: Chapter 40 frames the monster's problem of evil through the Rousseau-Voltaire rivalry and Candide's 'tend to our garden,' yet Voltaire is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Susan Neiman
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who reads modernity itself as born from the Lisbon earthquake's destruction of theodicy, in the clash between Rousseau's and Voltaire's responses to evil.
holes.why: Chapter 40 explicitly adopts Neiman's account of the problem of evil as its central frame for reading the monster as a modern Job.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Colin McGinn
holes.what: Philosopher whose Ethics, Evil and Fiction connects moral evaluation to aesthetics, holding that virtue is beauty of soul and vice its ugliness (the aesthetic theory of virtue, G-beings and E-beings).
holes.why: Chapter 41's reading of Branagh's film as inverting our beauty-based moral judgments is built throughout on McGinn's aesthetic theory of virtue.
holes.book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue who attacked 'banking' education (teachers depositing knowledge into passive students) and proposed problem-posing dialogue as the practice of freedom.
holes.why: Chapter 7 evaluates Battle School through Freire's banking model and problem-posing pedagogy, and his teacher-domination critique explains Ender's sense of being 'someone's pawn'.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German Idealist whose Freedom essay treats evil as a real, positive principle (selfish 'contraction into the self') grounded in the dark ground of human nature, not mere absence of good.
holes.why: Chapter 8's entire account of Ender's moral development, Graff's sacrifice, and evil as an unavoidable possibility in all of us is built on Schelling's philosophy of freedom and evil.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: Game Theory
holes.what: The mathematical study of strategic interaction among players with payoff structures (zero-sum games, minimax, perfect vs imperfect information).
holes.why: Chapter 12 frames all of Ender's conflicts as games analyzed with von Neumann's minimax theorem, zero-sum structure, and information conditions, none of which the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: Walzer's dilemma that political leaders who do what necessity demands still do wrong, incurring moral guilt that no appeal to the lesser evil can wash away.
holes.why: Chapter 13 has a full section applying Walzer's dirty hands problem to the I.F.'s choice between xenocide and leaving humanity vulnerable, and to Ender's own self-deception.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: Bernard Suits
holes.what: Philosopher of games who defined game-playing as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles via prelusory goals, constitutive rules, lusory means, and the lusory attitude.
holes.why: Chapter 15's classification of the battleroom contests and the Giant's Drink as open or closed games rests entirely on Suits' four-component definition from The Grasshopper.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of mind and language who argued against the scheme/content dualism and for the principle of charity: interpretation requires assuming most of an speaker's beliefs are true and translatable.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is built on Davidson's 'On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme' - complete failure of translation, charity, and shared belief as the key to whether humans and buggers can understand each other.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: Game Theory
holes.what: The mathematical study of strategic interaction among players with payoff structures (zero-sum games, minimax, perfect vs imperfect information).
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses the Prisoner's Dilemma and Axelrod's shadow of the future to explain why humans and buggers defect into war when communication fails.
holes.book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of why we feel genuine emotions for characters and events we know do not exist.
holes.why: Chapter 8 distinguishes its 'Barney Paradox' of identifying with an immoral character from the classic paradox of fiction, which it explicitly names and builds on.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Cognitive Theory of Emotion
holes.what: The view that emotions are judgments or appraisals rather than mere bodily feelings, so they can be chosen and reshaped.
holes.why: Chapter 9 evaluates whether Barney can 'stop being sad and be awesome instead' by weighing somaticist (James), cognitivist (Sartre, Solomon), and embodied-appraisal (Prinz) theories of emotion, none of which the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Feminist Anti-Essentialism (non-essentialism)
holes.what: The view that women share no fixed set of defining traits and no single path a woman's life must take.
holes.why: Chapter 11 explicitly frames Robin's entire arc as a lesson in the non-essentialist feminism of Deborah Rhode and Drucilla Cornell, a doctrine no existing slug captures.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Truth in Fiction
holes.what: The question of which propositions are true within a fictional work, given explicit statements plus background beliefs and implication.
holes.why: Chapter 16 is wholly about deriving primary and derivative fictional truths in HIMYM, testing Lewis's pretense account and Currie's fictional narrator against the sub-versus-joint case.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Personal Autonomy
holes.what: Self-governance: setting one's own priorities and living by values that are genuinely one's own, historically withheld from women.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Robin as a feminist icon of autonomy, defining it through Marilyn Friedman and treating oppression as withheld autonomy; kant-autonomy (will autonomy) is a different concept.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Expected Utility Theory
holes.what: The theory that rational agents choose by maximizing probability-weighted satisfaction of their desires (expected utility).
holes.why: Chapter 22's whole analysis of Ted's Slutty Pumpkin vigil is an expected-utility calculation, and its conclusion about gut feelings is a critique of rational choice theory, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: Ricoeur's view that the self is constituted by the stories it tells about itself, unifying past, present, and future.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies Ricoeur's narrative identity to Ted's narration and the gang's storytelling; personal-identity alone misses the narrative-constitution thesis the chapter defends.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Law of Non-Contradiction
holes.what: Aristotle's principle that contradictory propositions cannot both be true at the same time and in the same sense.
holes.why: Chapter 27 quotes all three of Aristotle's formulations of the law and sets them, with Duns Scotus's explosion principle, against dialetheism to judge the possimpible; the taxonomy has no formal-logic concepts.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Dialetheism (true contradictions)
holes.what: Graham Priest's thesis that some contradictions are true, developed via paraconsistent logic to tame the principle of explosion.
holes.why: Chapter 27's positive argument uses Priest's dialetheism (In Contradiction, Beyond the Limits of Thought) to vindicate the possimpible; hegel-dialectic alone does not cover paraconsistent logic.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Graham Priest
holes.what: Contemporary logician and philosopher, leading proponent of dialetheism and paraconsistency.
holes.why: Chapter 27 stages Priest as Barney's wingman, drawing directly on In Contradiction and Beyond the Limits of Thought for the chapter's defense of true contradictions.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Duns Scotus
holes.what: Medieval philosopher-tradition associated with the principle of explosion (ex falso quodlibet).
holes.why: Chapter 27 features Duns Scotus as a character who derives anything whatsoever from Barney's possimpible contradiction via ex falso quodlibet, and the taxonomy lacks him entirely.
holes.book: 081 - How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness

holes.name: Memes (units of cultural inheritance)
holes.what: A meme is an idea or practice that replicates from mind to mind, allowing cultural change to be analyzed as an evolution parallel to genetic natural selection.
holes.why: Chapter 13's central explanation of why Hammond built the park is memetic: the dinosaur-theme-park meme infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit and fame.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: A movement seeking technologies that overcome fundamental human limitations, including aging and the enhancement of intellectual, physical, and psychological abilities toward a 'post-human'.
holes.why: Chapter 16 frames de-extinction and 'neo-dinosaurs' as continuous with transhumanist enhancement rather than as overreaching 'playing God'.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Hans Jonas
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of biology whose The Phenomenon of Life argues that after Darwin, conditions and environment, not changeless essence, explain what an organism is.
holes.why: Chapter 17's whole argument that genes are outdated Platonic forms and that gene banks cannot save species rests on Jonas's claim that 'conditions take the place of essence'.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Thorstein Veblen
holes.what: Economist and social critic whose Theory of the Leisure Class analyzes conspicuous consumption, buying expensive goods to signal status rather than for use.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses Veblen to decode Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, equating worth with price.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we genuinely feel emotions for characters and events we know do not exist, although we apparently only respond emotionally to what we believe is real.
holes.why: Chapter 20 is organized around this paradox to explain why movie dinosaurs frighten and thrill us although we know they are not real.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Philosopher who proposed five criteria of personhood (consciousness, reasoning, self-driven activity, communication, self-concepts) and argued that entities meeting most of them deserve respect.
holes.why: Chapter 25 runs its 'Dino Personhood Checklist' entirely through Warren's criteria to argue that velociraptors qualify as persons.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: The Reality of Fictional Entities
holes.what: Debates over the sense in which fictional characters and events exist or are real (Meinong, Walton's make-believe).
holes.why: Muniz's chapter claims screen dinosaurs are 'real' and needs the ontology-of-fiction vocabulary.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Obligations to Future Generations
holes.what: The view that present people owe enforceable duties to people who do not yet exist, because today's actions fix the world they are born into.
holes.why: Chapter 30's central proposal is Rupert Read's 'Guardians of the Future', a super jury vetoing laws that harm future people, and no existing slug covers duties to nonexistent generations.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: The Great Chain of Being
holes.what: The hierarchical scale of being running from God through angels, humans, animals, plants and minerals, placing humanity above nature and below the divine.
holes.why: Chapter 32 structures its whole argument around the rise and collapse of this hierarchy - from Plato through Genesis dominion and Descartes to Nietzsche's dead God - and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Hans Jonas
holes.what: German-Jewish philosopher (1903-1993) whose Imperative of Responsibility demands a new ethics for technological civilization: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.'
holes.why: Chapter 37 builds its entire argument on Jonas's responsibility ethics - his heuristics of fear, humility, and worst-case thinking diagnose Hammond's 'thintelligence' - yet he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

holes.name: Future Contingents (bivalence about the future)
holes.what: The question whether statements about future free actions are already true or false, tied to rejecting the law of bivalence for future-tense propositions.
holes.why: Chapter 14's first medieval solution has Aureoli deny that Jesus's prophecy about the Antichrist was true or false, and no taxonomy slug covers this logical doctrine.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German Idealist whose 1809 treatise on human freedom grounds evil in the self-asserting 'will of the basis' set against the will to love.
holes.why: Chapter 16's account of Satan as egoistic self-love that cannot endure the other, running from Bohme to Sartre, is built directly on Schelling's freedom essay.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Radical and Diabolical Evil (Kant)
holes.what: Kant's threefold distinction between ordinary frailty, radical evil (subordinating morality to self-love), and diabolical evil (doing evil for its own sake).
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire classification of Batman, Two-Face, and the Joker runs on this threefold division, which no existing taxonomy slug names.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Evil as Privation of Good
holes.what: Augustine's doctrine that evil is not a real positive force but a lack or corruption of good, as cold is the absence of heat.
holes.why: Chapter 35's contrast between Star Wars moral dualism and Augustinian monotheism rests entirely on the privation view of evil.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Sub-creation (Tolkien)
holes.what: Tolkien's idea that artistry is a subordinate making that rearranges created matter, distinct from true Creation and from dominating 'magic.'
holes.why: Chapter 37 explains Melkor's fall as the frustrated sub-creator who can only mimic and corrupt, never truly create, which is the chapter's central concept.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and novelist whose Screwtape Letters and The Problem of Pain argue the Devil exists and works by subverting human reason.
holes.why: Chapter 40's whole analysis of the Devil's tactics as logical fallacies is drawn from Lewis's Screwtape Letters, and Lewis is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and novelist whose Screwtape Letters and The Problem of Pain argue the Devil exists and works by subverting human reason.
holes.why: Chapter 41 reconstructs Lewis's argument from The Problem of Pain that either demons exist or God doesn't, and Lewis is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: The Free Will Defense
holes.what: The reply to the problem of evil that God permits evil because free agents, capable of love, must be able to choose wrongly.
holes.why: Chapter 41 extends the free will defense to natural evil by postulating demons as its free perpetrators, which is the chapter's core argument.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Immoralism in Aesthetics (moralism vs autonomism vs immoralism)
holes.what: The aesthetics debate over whether an artwork's immoral features count against, are irrelevant to, or can actually improve its artistic value.
holes.why: Chapter 46's whole argument is that Satanic metal's immorality (blasphemy, church burnings) can enhance its artistic value, a position taxonomy has no slug for.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation through tragedy)
holes.what: Aristotle's idea that watching tragedy lets an audience safely experience pity and fear and so purges those emotions.
holes.why: Chapter 48 uses catharsis as its second pillar for explaining why TV crime dramas like Criminal Minds and CSI entertain millions while feeling psychologically healthy.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Labor Theory of Value (use value and exchange value)
holes.what: Marx's Capital analysis that commodities have use value and labor-grounded exchange value, the basis of exploitation, prices, and monopoly power.
holes.why: Chapter 49's entire reading of the Faustian bargain treats the soul as a universal commodity with use and exchange value sold to a monopolist Devil, a framework taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Gloria Anzaldúa
holes.what: Chicana feminist theorist of the Borderlands who exposes binary identity as an oversimplification of lived experience and advocates a mestiza consciousness embracing ambiguity.
holes.why: Chapter 52 extends Beauvoir's Othering analysis of the woman-as-Devil trope with Anzaldúa's Borderlands and her critique of the gender dichotomy, but taxonomy has no entry for her.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Milan Kundera
holes.what: Novelist-essayist whose The Book of Laughter and Forgetting casts the Devil as meaninglessness set against the angels' excess of imposed meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 56 adopts Kundera's Devil-as-meaninglessness thesis as its entire framework and tests it against Iblis, the temptation of Jesus, and Lord of the Flies.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: The Diabolical Will
holes.what: Kant's notion of a will that does evil precisely because it is evil, which he held impossible for humans and proper to the Devil alone.
holes.why: Chapter 57's conclusion is that neither Machiavellian self-interest nor Schopenhauerian malice captures the Devil, whose evil requires Kant's diabolical will.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)
holes.what: French Enlightenment deist and satirist, author of Candide's attack on Leibnizian optimism and the quip that if God did not exist it would be necessary to invent Him.
holes.why: Chapter 62 is built entirely around evaluating Voltaire's claim that God and the Devil are socially necessary inventions, and taxonomy lacks any entry for him.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: Anton Szandor LaVey
holes.what: Founder of the Church of Satan (1966) whose Satanic Bible frames atheistic Satanism as carnal self-deification, self-controlled indulgence, and rational self-interest.
holes.why: Chapters 65, 69, 70, 72, and 73 debate LaVey's Satanism directly - its hedonism, its definition, its Epicurean debts - yet taxonomy has no slug for the philosopher at their center.
holes.book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game

holes.name: The Katechon (the restraining force)
holes.what: From 2 Thessalonians, the force that restrains the coming of the Antichrist and holds back the end of the world, later a key idea in political theology.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads the song 'The Future' as announcing that the katechon no longer works so the apocalyptic end has already arrived; no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Gnosticism
holes.what: A religious worldview in which the world is the flawed work of a lesser or malevolent demiurge and salvation comes through sparks of divine light escaping it.
holes.why: Chapter 14 asks 'Is Cohen a Gnostic?' and reads 'Anthem's' light getting in through the cracks as a Gnostic metaphor, a tradition the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Paul Grice
holes.what: Philosopher of language known for the conversational maxims and implicature, showing how context and speaker expectations generate meaning beyond the words uttered.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Grice's maxim of sincerity to explain why the 'golden voice' line of 'Tower of Song' is ironic in Cohen's mouth but a boast in Tom Jones's.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Conversational Implicature
holes.what: Meaning a speaker conveys by flouting conversational expectations rather than stating it outright, leaving hearers to work out what is meant.
holes.why: Chapter 17's core tool for explaining how covers change what a Cohen lyric communicates through persona, signature, and performance context.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Duende
holes.what: Lorca's 'black sounds': the dark, primordial emotional power that authentic art - flamenco deep song, the true love song - must channel, likened in the chapter to Nietzsche's Dionysian.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues Cohen's songs have duende, which is why they hearten rather than depress; no taxonomy slug covers this aesthetic concept.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Socratic Irony
holes.what: Ostentatious self-concealment in speech that makes hearers grasp the gap between words and intentions, analyzed by Kierkegaard in The Concept of Irony as a way of building personality and intimacy.
holes.why: Chapter 20's central claim is that Cohen seduces through Socratic irony; the taxonomy's elenchus and Socratic-ignorance slugs do not capture irony itself.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Empedocles
holes.what: Pre-Socratic thinker who explained the cosmos through an eternal cycle in which Love unites and Strife separates the elements.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the 'Empedocles effect' - the alternation of love and strife - as a central frame for the ambivalence of 'Hallelujah' and 'Suzanne.'
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Eugene Minkowski
holes.what: Phenomenological psychiatrist known for analyses of lived time and lived space, including auditory space as a dark, intimate space that envelops the self.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds its entire reading of Dear Heather around Minkowski's concepts of lived space and dark space, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Richard Dawkins
holes.what: Evolutionary theorist who introduced the 'meme' in The Selfish Gene: cultural units that replicate and compete for human attention the way genes compete in nature.
holes.why: Chapter 35 explains the spread of 'Hallelujah' through Dawkins's memetics; the taxonomy has Dennett but not Dawkins.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: Memetics (cultural evolution)
holes.what: The theory that cultural units - songs, theories, catchphrases - evolve by differential survival in human attention, as genes do in nature.
holes.why: Chapter 35's explanation of why 'Hallelujah' conquered popular culture is explicitly memetic; the taxonomy has no concept for cultural evolution.
holes.book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions

holes.name: The Four Loves (storge, eros, philia, agape)
holes.what: C.S. Lewis's four-fold Greek taxonomy of love: affection (storge), romantic desire (eros), friendship (philia), and sacrificial charity (agape).
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads every Homeland relationship as broken instances of these four loves, and the organizing framework (and C.S. Lewis) is absent from the taxonomy; philosophy-of-love alone does not capture it.
holes.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only

holes.name: The Myth of Religious Violence
holes.what: William Cavanaugh's thesis that the religious/secular violence distinction is a modern Western construction used to legitimize state violence as rational while deeming identical acts fanatical when religiously coded.
holes.why: Chapter 19 is built entirely on this critique to reread Homeland's terrorist/CIA double standards, and no taxonomy slug covers the religious-secular distinction or its politicized use.
holes.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only

holes.name: Political Dirty Hands
holes.what: Walzer's view that politicians sometimes must do what is genuinely wrong for good ends, accepting guilt rather than pretending the act becomes right.
holes.why: Chapter 20's climax frames Saul's and Carrie's deceit through the Dirty Hands tradition Walzer named in his 1973 article, and the taxonomy has Walzer but no dirty-hands concept.
holes.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only

holes.name: Abduction (Inference to the Best Explanation)
holes.what: Peirce's term for reasoning to the simplest hypothesis that best explains the observed facts.
holes.why: Chapter 25 makes inference to the best explanation - Dana's, Carrie's, and Lauder's unmasking of Brody - its central epistemological tool, credited to Peirce, but the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: Enlightenment satirist whose Candide mocked optimistic theodicy and who anchors the tradition that morality demands we NOT make evil intelligible.
holes.why: Chapter 28 structures the problem of evil around the Rousseau-versus-Voltaire dispute, using Voltaire's 'tend your garden' resignation as the pole Carrie's redemptive Rousseauian response rejects.
holes.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only

holes.name: Civil Religion
holes.what: The nation-state's self-presentation as sacred through rituals, oaths, flags, martyrs, and liturgies that claim ultimate devotion from citizens.
holes.why: Chapter 36 argues Homeland exposes American civil religion - the flag receiving worship owed to God - and no existing slug (closest: augustine-city-of-god) names this concept.
holes.book: 085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only

holes.name: Lacanian Desire (jouissance and objet a)
holes.what: Lacan's theory that desire is insatiable - a drive circling its object rather than reaching it, sustained by objet a as object-cause and jouissance beyond the pleasure principle.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire account of the Girls romance cycle rests on Lacan's theory of desire, which taxonomy.json's other Lacan slugs (mirror stage; the RSI registers) do not cover.
holes.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything

holes.name: Fashion Theory (clothes as sign system)
holes.what: The line of theory from Carlyle's Sartor Resartus through Barthes's fashion system and Veblen/Simmel's status signaling that treats clothing as a code expressing morality, sexuality, and social position.
holes.why: Chapter 28 interprets each Girls character's wardrobe entirely through these fashion theories, none of which taxonomy.json contains.
holes.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Psychoanalyst-philosopher of the 'new maladies of the soul': adolescent idealization of love, the need to believe, and the nihilistic 'kamikaze syndrome' when ideals fail.
holes.why: Chapter 30's reading of all four girls as Kristevan adolescents suffering for want of love is built on her Tales of Love, New Maladies of the Soul, and This Incredible Need to Believe, and she is absent from taxonomy.json.
holes.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything

holes.name: Paideia (Greek education of the soul)
holes.what: The classical Greek ideal of education as the formation of the whole person for life in the polis, debated by Plato and codified for the liberal arts by Isocrates.
holes.why: Chapter 31 evaluates the girls' liberal-arts education against paideia specifically, a concept taxonomy.json lacks despite its Plato and Aristotle entries.
holes.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything

holes.name: Agonism (affirmation of perpetual contest)
holes.what: The view (Honig, Mouffe) that conflict and contest are perpetual and valuable, demanding respect for worthy opponents rather than resolution or consensus.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses the agon to reinterpret the show's conflicts (the Beach House fight, MFA vs NYC) as worthy contest, and taxonomy.json has no slug for agonistic thought.
holes.book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we feel genuine emotions for characters we know do not exist, even though emotion seems to require believing its object is real.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is built entirely on this paradox (fear during 'Ocean of Fear', sadness for Marceline and Simon) and evaluates each of its three sentences, but the taxonomy has no slug for the philosophy of fiction or emotion.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Artemidorus of Ephesus
holes.what: Second-century Greek diviner whose Oneirocritica is the surviving ancient manual for interpreting dreams by the practical and moral consequences they foretell for the dreamer's station in life.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its entire reading of Finn's Flame Princess dream on Artemidorus's method - dreams reveal what is real and portend good or bad consequences - introduced through Foucault's Care of the Self.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Robert Pepperell
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of the posthuman who defines life as 'motivated meaning' and consciousness by observable attributes (thought, emotion, memory, awareness, intelligence, self-knowledge, sense of being) in varying densities rather than by biology.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses Pepperell's seven attributes of consciousness and his notion of motivated meaning as its main criteria for arguing that BMO is genuinely alive and conscious, and summarizes Turing through him.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Johan Huizinga
holes.what: Dutch cultural historian whose Homo Ludens argues that play is a separate, rule-bound 'presentation' that lies at the foundation of all human culture, including art, ritual and law.
holes.why: Chapter 30's opening argument that Adventure Time's stories are stories of play - separate from the serious world yet never pointless and always 'about' something - is built directly on Huizinga's theory of play.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Eugen Fink
holes.what: Twentieth-century phenomenologist (Husserl's student and assistant) who analyzed play as a purposeless activity with its own end, in which playthings acquire 'another, mysterious reality' and open whole imaginary play-worlds.
holes.why: Chapter 30's core apparatus - play as magic, BMO's chicken becoming the suspect Lorraine, playthings becoming dangerously real, and the pillow-fort play-world of 'Puhoy' - comes from Fink's philosophy of play.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Desiderius Erasmus
holes.what: Renaissance humanist who wrote the Enchiridion Militis Christiani (Handbook of the Christian Knight) and In Praise of Folly, redefining righteousness against corrupt churchly piety.
holes.why: Chapter 36 presents Erasmus's Christian-knight handbook, with its Folly-voiced critique of the powerful, as one of the four real-life enchiridions that teach Finn-and-Jake-style 'foolish' righteousness.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Christine de Pizan
holes.what: Medieval author commissioned by the French royal family to write The Book of Deeds of Arms and of Chivalry, a manual of warfare that also treats how leaders and heroes should behave, especially in defeat.
holes.why: Chapter 36 cites her book as a real-life Enchiridion for heroes - its advice to anticipate the unexpected and prepare for loss is applied directly to what Finn and Jake should learn before adventures.
holes.book: 087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that many concepts are united not by a common essence but by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, like the faces of one extended family.
holes.why: Chapter 9 uses family resemblance as its central tool to argue 'coolness' (Boyd Crowder) is a cluster concept that cannot be defined by a single essence, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Hegel's Rabble (Pauperismus)
holes.what: Hegel's account in the Philosophy of Right of an impoverished mass created by civil society that loses the sense of right, integrity, and honor that comes from supporting oneself by one's own work.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues coal capitalism created the Harlan rabble that produced Boyd Crowder, and no existing slug names this specific Hegelian concept.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Legal scholar and founder of Critical Race Theory, who argued that racism is ordinary, structural, and advances white material and psychic interests.
holes.why: Chapter 12 analyzes Justified's racial casting entirely through Bell's Critical Race Theory, but the taxonomy lists no CRT founder.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Interest Convergence
holes.what: Bell's thesis that reforms benefiting people of color occur only when they converge with the interests of white elite and working-class society, as in his reading of Brown v. Board of Education.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies interest convergence and the related CRT theses (ordinariness of racism, social construction, differential racialization) as its core analytic tools, none of which the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Ordinary-language philosopher who distinguished justifying an act from excusing it and founded speech-act theory (performative utterances, infelicities, misfires) in How to Do Things with Words.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire reading of 'He pulled first, I was justified', the rooftop dialogue, and Boyd's 'God made me do it' rests on Austin's justification/excuse distinction and performatives, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Edward Said
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist whose Orientalism showed how Western scholarship and media construct colonized peoples as exotic, savage Others to justify domination and exploitation.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds its whole 'Appalachianism' argument - hillbilly stereotypes justifying coal exploitation - on Said's account of othering, and he is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Orientalism (constructing the Other)
holes.what: Said's concept for discourses that represent a dominated people as exotic or savage Others, turning that 'knowledge' into justification for conquering and exploiting them.
holes.why: Chapter 22 transfers Orientalism to Appalachia (reality-TV hillbillies, Boyd's 'we are not your savages') and no taxonomy slug names the concept.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Friedrich Engels
holes.what: Marx's collaborator whose Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State ties monogamy, patriarchal inheritance, and prostitution to the rise of private property.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Engels's property-family thesis as its central lens on Mags, Ava, and the Harlan families, but the taxonomy lists Marx without Engels.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's theory that sons see their fathers as rivals for the mother's affection, and that this triangle shapes character and father-son conflict.
holes.why: Chapter 27 applies the Oedipus Complex by name to Raylan-Arlo and Coover-Mags (and chapter 25 reads the failed patriarchs through the Freudian father-son lens), but the taxonomy has no Freudian slug for it.
holes.book: 088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-born novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) of Objectivism, defending reason, rational egoism, and laissez-faire capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 12's case that counter-cultural individualism drives capitalism rests on Rand's 'creative mind' and her moral defense of capitalism in 'What Is Capitalism?'
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Personhood (moral personhood)
holes.what: The idea that rights and moral standing attach to cognitive and moral capacities rather than to species membership.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues Pixar trained Millennials to intuitively recognize personhood in non-humans (toys, robots, rats, monsters), a concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Creative Destruction
holes.what: Schumpeter's thesis that capitalist innovation incessantly destroys old industries and products from within as it creates new ones.
holes.why: Chapter 17 frames Jobs's Apple, like the automobile against the horse-and-carriage, as creative destruction in action—the driving force of capitalist progress.
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Objective Theory of Value
holes.what: Rand's view that value is neither intrinsic to things nor a subjective whim but an evaluation of the facts of reality by a rational mind in the context of a life.
holes.why: Chapter 18 answers the 'Jobs didn't invent anything' charge entirely through Rand's objective theory of value and its philosophically-versus-socially-objective distinction.
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally praiseworthy to perform but not blameworthy to omit—beyond the call of duty rather than required by it.
holes.why: Chapter 21 asks whether Jobs's sparse charity was a moral failing by testing whether charity is supererogatory, an imperfect Kantian duty, or obligatory under Singer.
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-born novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) of Objectivism, defending reason, rational egoism, and laissez-faire capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 23 evaluates Jobs's character through Rand's virtue of independence, her primacy-of-existence versus primacy-of-consciousness distinction, and Binswanger's Objectivist false-integration fallacy.
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Functionalism (philosophy of mind)
holes.what: The view that mental states are defined by the causal or computational role they play in a system rather than by their internal composition.
holes.why: Chapter 25 needs functionalism because List and Pettit's case that Apple literally thinks, forms intentions, and can be blamed rests on corporate decision structures instantiating functional minds.
holes.book: 089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

holes.name: Wesley Hohfeld
holes.what: Early twentieth-century American legal philosopher who analyzed legal and rule-governed relationships into eight jural elements: duty, claim, liberty, power, liability, immunity, and disability.
holes.why: Chapter 12's conclusion that Dracula's house-invitation rule and his dominance over brides, servants, and victims are best explained rests on Hohfeldian jural relations combined with natural law.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: John Martin Fischer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of free will who argues that 'guidance control' - acting from one's own reasons and desires even if only one path is available - is sufficient for moral responsibility.
holes.why: Chapter 18's case for holding Dracula blameworthy despite his cursed, conscienceless nature is built directly on Fischer's guidance-control account, which the chapter then argues fails for Dracula.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist and author of The Denial of Death (1973), which holds that human civilization is an 'immortality project' - a vast distraction and heroism system for evading the terror of our own deaths.
holes.why: Chapter 19's central reading of Dracula - as a story in which weak humans kill physical immortality to deny mortality and secure spiritual immortality - is explicitly grounded in Becker's death-denial theory.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Functionalism (multiple realizability of mind)
holes.what: The view that a mind is whatever performs the mental function, regardless of its physical substrate - so one and the same mind can be realized in wildly different bodies (against mind-brain identity theory).
holes.why: Chapter 21's core argument is that Dracula's mind remaining his own across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes brain-identity theory and is best captured by the functionalist 'same song, many formats' picture, which no existing taxonomy slug names.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Persistence Through Change (endurantism vs perdurantism)
holes.what: The debate over how objects persist through time: enduring wholly present at each moment, perduring as sums of temporal parts, or persisting via temporal counterparts.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is built entirely on this trilemma of consistency, change, and persistence and evaluates endurantism, perdurantism, and exdurantism against Dracula's shapeshifting, which the generic 'personal-identity' slug does not cover.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist whose 'death of the author' holds that a text's meaning is made by readers, not fixed by authorial intention.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explicitly invokes Barthes to argue that mechanically reproduced Dracula turns every reader into an author who decides what the novel says.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist whose monomyth, the Hero's Journey, describes the universal arc of the call to adventure, threshold crossing, ordeal, and return.
holes.why: Chapter 31 structures Mina's confrontation with Dracula as a 'Shero's Journey' using Campbell's Call to Adventure and the stages of the hero's transformation.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, which holds rational self-interest as the moral ideal and rejects obligation to the collective.
holes.why: Chapter 33 ventriloquizes Dracula's diary as a Randian defense of egoism and objective reality against Van Helsing's Marxist 'collective herd'.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, which holds rational self-interest as the moral ideal and rejects obligation to the collective.
holes.why: Chapter 36 stages Ayn Rand's fictional HUAC review decoding Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein as collectivist propaganda against capitalism.
holes.book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

holes.name: Homeric Heroic Ethics (kleos, time, arete)
holes.what: The value system of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey: competitive honor (time), glory (kleos), martial excellence, revenge, cunning, and loyalty to kin and comrades.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire argument maps the Gang's selfishness onto the heroic values of the Iliad and Odyssey, and the taxonomy has no slug for Homer's value system or the poet himself.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: Aristippus of Cyrene
holes.what: Socratic disciple and founder of the Cyrenaic school, the first egoistic hedonist, holding that present, bodily, personal pleasure is the only intrinsic good.
holes.why: Chapter 10 builds its entire reading of the Gang as hedonists around Aristippus and the Cyrenaics, who are absent from the taxonomy (which covers Epicurus but not Aristippus).
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: The Paradox of Hedonism
holes.what: The tendency of pleasure and happiness to elude those who pursue them directly, coming only as a by-product of aiming at other ends (Mill: ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so).
holes.why: Chapter 10 closes by diagnosing the Gang's failure through Mill's paradox of hedonism, a doctrine distinct from the Greatest Happiness Principle and named by no existing slug.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: John Duns Scotus
holes.what: Medieval Franciscan thinker (the Doctor Subtilis) who held that contingency holds at the very moment of action, reconciling God's immutable foreknowledge with a will that 'determines itself'.
holes.why: Chapter 11's account of free will, modality, and Charlie's beatification is built on Scotus's synchronic contingency, and the taxonomy has no Scotus slug.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: Peter John Olivi
holes.what: Thirteenth-century Franciscan whose censored writings defended the self-determining power of the will and described paired attitudes (zeal and mercy, glory and shame) held together by freedom.
holes.why: Chapter 11 draws both Olivi's theory of free will and his seven attitude pairs to explain how the Gang embodies contingency, and the taxonomy lacks him entirely.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: Creepiness
holes.what: An affective response of unease toward people who flout unspoken social conventions in ways that are ambiguous and unpredictable, leaving their intentions unreadable.
holes.why: Chapter 13 is explicitly about the essence of creepiness - violated convention, appearance, and unpredictability in the McPoyles - a concept absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: Sexual Consent
holes.what: Mutual, explicit agreement between fully-informed, competent moral agents, given beforehand in a context free of coercion or fear, without which sex is rape.
holes.why: Chapter 21 exists to define the necessary and sufficient conditions of sexual consent from the 'implication' scene, and no taxonomy slug covers consent or moral agency in this sense.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: Informal Fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, burden of proof)
holes.what: Recurring patterns of bad reasoning - attacking the arguer, appealing to authority, equivocation, arguing from ignorance, straw-manning - that make arguments defective independently of their form.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is a catalogue of the fallacies the Gang commits in the Cereal Defense trial, and the taxonomy contains no logic or fallacy slugs to map them to.
holes.book: 091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed

holes.name: Media Stereotypes (Lippmann's 'pictures in our heads')
holes.what: Walter Lippmann's account of stereotypes as overgeneralized mental representations of social groups that media reinforce when direct contact with the group is lacking.
holes.why: Carveth's critique of how Orange Is the New Black both advances and reproduces stereotypes of Black women on television is built directly on Lippmann's Public Opinion and subsequent content-analysis research.
holes.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

holes.name: White Privilege
holes.what: The unearned structural advantages white people receive in institutions and everyday interactions, typically invisible to those who hold them.
holes.why: The chapter's central argument is that Piper's whiteness buys Healy's favoritism, softer punishment, and narrative centrality while Black and Latina inmates' suffering goes unshown.
holes.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

holes.name: Manipulation (covert, non-rational influence)
holes.what: Influencing someone through covert or non-rational means (emotion, deception, exploited weaknesses) so they choose what they would not rationally endorse.
holes.why: Cherry's entire chapter defines and morally evaluates Vee's manipulation of the Litchfield inmates using McGinn, Barnhill, Noggle, and Stanley, and the taxonomy has no slug for manipulation itself.
holes.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

holes.name: Ideal vs Non-Ideal Theory
holes.what: The methodological debate over whether justice should be theorized for perfectly compliant conditions or built from actual unjust conditions, with critics arguing ideal theory conceals the perspective of the powerful.
holes.why: The chapter's core claim is that Rawls-style ideal theory is irrelevant in Litchfield and morality must start from the prisoners' real, non-ideal conditions.
holes.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

holes.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma
holes.what: A game-theory thought experiment in which each party's self-interested dominant strategy leaves both worse off than if they had cooperated.
holes.why: Greene's chapter is an extended exposition of the Prisoner's Dilemma and applies a variant to Piper and Alex's testimony decisions at Kubra's trial.
holes.book: 092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

holes.name: Philosophy of Television (medium theory)
holes.what: The philosophical study of television as a distinctive medium—its seriality, iterative evolution, liveness, and intimacy with its audience—and how the medium shapes the stories it carries.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues Doctor Who is a metaphor for television itself, built on the medium's junkyard origins, regeneration-as-recasting, and audience co-creation—a genuine topic no taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: Literary Alchemy (nigredo, albedo, rubedo)
holes.what: A symbolic framework descending from medieval and Renaissance alchemy in which writers depict a character's transformation through stages of dissolution (nigredo), purification (albedo), and rebirth (rubedo).
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire reading of 'Midnight' as the nigredo of the Tenth Doctor's death-and-rebirth arc depends on the concept of literary alchemy, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: John Corvino
holes.what: Contemporary American philosopher known for his defense of the morality of homosexual sex, especially the essay 'Why Shouldn't Tommy and Jim Have Sex?' and the book Same Sex.
holes.why: Chapter 31 builds its entire case for Doctor Who's same-sex and human-alien relationships on Corvino's systematic demolition of 'unnatural means immoral' arguments.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: Personal Autonomy
holes.what: The capacity for competent, free, well-reasoned self-governance that makes a being a responsible moral agent whose choices deserve respect.
holes.why: Chapter 31 makes autonomy the sole ground of sexual morality - consensual relationships between autonomous agents are permissible - and uses it to explain why the child Amelia's choice, manipulation, and coercion are wrong; the only existing slug, kant-autonomy, wrongly attributes the chapter's generic, non-Kantian notion to Kant.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: Mnemotechnics (memory burnt in by pain)
holes.what: Nietzsche's account in On the Genealogy of Morals II of how pain engraves promises and duties into memory, since only the strongest can remember by an act of pure will while others need 'that which never ceases to hurt.'
holes.why: Chapter 37 is built on mnemotechnics: the Doctor plants his painful loss in Amy's subconscious so that she can remember him back into existence, and no existing Nietzsche slug covers this Genealogy-II doctrine.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: J.R.R. Tolkien
holes.what: Fantasy author and philologist whose essay 'On Fairy-Stories' theorizes fairy tales as internally coherent secondary worlds that create 'secondary belief' and let readers 'recover' a clear view of reality.
holes.why: Chapter 37 relies on Tolkien's theory of fairy stories as its second pillar, explaining how the Doctor's bedtime story preserved him in Amy's memory and returned him to the universe.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: Self-Forgiveness
holes.what: Forgiving oneself for one's own wrongdoing, treated in the literature (Murphy, Dillon, Griswold, Westlund) as a distinct phenomenon with its own conditions, such as ending self-alienation without excusing the act.
holes.why: Chapter 38's central topic is specifically self-forgiveness - the Doctor forgiving his own past incarnation - which the generic forgiveness slug does not capture, and it engages a body of self-forgiveness literature the taxonomy lacks entirely.
holes.book: 093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: French Enlightenment satirist whose Candide, through Dr. Pangloss's 'best of all possible worlds,' ridicules optimistic attempts to rationalize suffering.
holes.why: Chapter 15 frames the modern problem of evil as a choice between Rousseau's demand to make evil intelligible and Voltaire's refusal, testing whether Tris is cast from Rousseau's mold or Voltaire's.
holes.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life

holes.name: Nicholas Wolterstorff
holes.what: Contemporary American philosopher of justice and religion who defends a rights-based theory of justice and recovers the Hebrew ideal of shalom as peace-through-justice.
holes.why: Chapter 16's entire argument that peace and justice are one - each person enjoying their rights - is built on Wolterstorff's trilogy (Until Justice and Peace Embrace, Justice: Rights and Wrongs, Justice in Love), which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life

holes.name: Alexander Meiklejohn
holes.what: Twentieth-century American educator-philosopher who defended an absolutist reading of the First Amendment as the guarantee that citizens remain sovereign in self-government.
holes.why: Chapter 20's closing argument for New Chicago's constitution rests on Meiklejohn's 1955 Senate testimony that political expression admits no abridgement, ending in his question of how the common good is determined.
holes.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life

holes.name: Virtue Epistemology
holes.what: The view that knowledge and justified belief depend on the intellectual virtues (courage, honesty, open-mindedness) of the knower, as in Linda Zagzebski's Virtues of the Mind.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central claim that the pursuit of knowledge is not morally neutral - you have to be good before you can be smart - is Zagzebski's and Montmarquet's virtue epistemology, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life

holes.name: Utopian Socialism (Owen and Fourier)
holes.what: Early nineteenth-century socialism (Robert Owen, Charles Fourier) holding that circumstances form character and that cooperation and fair contribution, not revolution, reform society.
holes.why: Chapter 11 identifies Branson's actual politics as Owen/Fourier-style utopian socialism and argues Robert's stewardship of the tenants approximates it, but taxonomy has only Marx and class struggle.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Noblesse Oblige
holes.what: The aristocratic doctrine that noble status carries binding obligations of service, protection, and care toward those of lower rank rather than mere entitlement.
holes.why: Chapter 11's central claim is that Robert's noblesse oblige - treating ownership as custodianship of tenants - is closer to socialism than Branson's professed politics, and no existing slug names the concept.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Georg Simmel
holes.what: German philosopher-sociologist (1858-1918) whose The Philosophy of Money argues that as money's role in a life grows, individuality and personal ties erode.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire reading of Matthew Crawley's corruption - principled lawyer turned money-driven suitor - rests on Simmel's thesis, and he is absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Nancy Sherman
holes.what: Contemporary virtue ethicist who argues manners give virtue its 'look and feel' - an 'aesthetic of character' that is part of virtue's substance, not mere adornment.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its claim that Downton's manners demonstrate and manifest moral character directly on Sherman's account, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Hierocles
holes.what: Stoic philosopher whose surviving fragment describes concentric circles of affinity, urging us to draw the outer circles inward and treat strangers as family.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Hierocles' circles as its Stoic account of how to treat others, set against Epictetus' role-based duties, and taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Inference to the Best Explanation (abduction)
holes.what: Peirce's third mode of inference, 'abduction': reasoning from a surprising fact to the hypothesis that would best explain it, evaluated for likeliness and loveliness (Lipton).
holes.why: Chapter 20 is wholly organized around this inference type, applying it to Vera's death, Edith's Swiss trip, and the Clarkson-Tapsell dispute, but taxonomy contains no slug for it.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Gaston Bachelard
holes.what: French philosopher (1884-1962) whose The Poetics of Space develops 'topophilia' - the intense love of place - through topoanalysis of intimate spaces, daydream, and the imagination.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is built entirely on Bachelard's topophilia, topoanalysis, and daydream theory to explain the show's appeal, and taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: The Art of Memory (memory palace)
holes.what: The classical mnemonic technique of storing memories in imagined places - palaces, courts, cabinets - from the Ad Herennium and Cicero through Augustine's 'court of memory.'
holes.why: Chapter 27 builds its reading of Carson's acquisitional model of memory around the memory-palace tradition and its spatial metaphors, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Philosophy of History (change and continuity)
holes.what: The branch of philosophy that studies patterns of change, continuity, and constancy in human history and how to distinguish them.
holes.why: Chapter 33 frames its whole account of the Great War's effect on Downton around change, continuity, and constancy as 'essential concepts for philosophers of history,' with no adequate taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Religious Language (analogy and the way of negation)
holes.what: The Thomist doctrine that human words apply to God neither univocally nor equivocally but analogically, supplemented by saying what God is not.
holes.why: Chapter 35's second half argues Downton's God-talk (Matthew's 'Our Father,' 'God is good' over Grigg's workhouse) works only through Aquinas's analogy and way of negation, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Pro-choice philosopher who distinguishes genetic humanity from moral personhood, defining persons by traits like consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness.
holes.why: Chapter 36's central pro-choice argument - personhood grounded in function rather than species membership - is Warren's, developed at length with no matching taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian thinker whose The Four Loves distinguishes affection (storge), friendship (philia), eros, and charity (agape).
holes.why: Chapter 37 organizes its entire analysis of Downton's relationships around Lewis's four-loves framework and agape as love that transcends justice, absent from taxonomy.json.
holes.book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Contemporary Italian philosopher of biopolitics, best known for Homo Sacer and the theory of the state of exception.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire argument is built on Agamben's sovereign/bare-life distinction, using it to explain how societies decide whose lives may be killed without crime or sacrifice, up to and including Lecter's victims.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Bare Life and Sovereignty (homo sacer)
holes.what: Agamben's paired concepts: bare life is life abandoned by political community, whose killing is neither crime nor sacrifice, and the sovereign is whoever decides which living beings count as bare life.
holes.why: Chapter 10 needs bare life/sovereignty to argue that Lecter's victims, slaughterhouse animals, condemned prisoners, and drone casualties all occupy the same killable status, and that the human/nonhuman line drawn by politics is never secure.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Aesthetic Distance (psychical distance)
holes.what: Edward Bullough's concept that aesthetic experience requires putting the object 'out of gear' with our practical needs and ends, striking a balance between over-distanced detachment and under-distanced immersion.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses aesthetic distance as its central analytic tool to test whether a psychopath like Lecter can have genuine aesthetic experience and to argue that appreciating homicidal art made of human bodies is necessarily over-distanced.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Agnotology (the study of ignorance)
holes.what: The study, developed by historian of science Robert Proctor, of how ignorance is actively produced and maintained - by secrecy, neglect, suppression, or strategic withholding - even when the knowledge is or was available.
holes.why: Chapter 20's organizing framework: Lecktor strategically manufactures ignorance in Will Graham, and the FBI and pop culture manufacture public ignorance about real serial murder and its forgotten 'less-dead' victims.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: French theorist of mimetic desire: we borrow our desires from models who become rivals, and the resulting reciprocal violence is resolved by scapegoating a victim.
holes.why: Chapter 23 structures its entire account of the Hannibal-Will rivalry (Alana as shared object, the Randall Tier killing, Mason Verger as scapegoat) on Girard's mimetic desire, mimetic violence and scapegoat mechanism.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Mimetic Desire and the Scapegoat Mechanism
holes.what: Desire imitated from a model who then becomes a rival, escalating into mimetic violence that ends when a scapegoat absorbs the community's conflict.
holes.why: Chapter 23 applies this sequence step by step to Will, Hannibal and Alana, and to Mason Verger's sacrificial death.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French philosopher of the 'accursed share' (the Necessary expenditure of surplus) and of transgression: taboos exist to be violated in ritual ways without being destroyed.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Hannibal's feasts as Bataille's display of social surplus and his cannibalism as transgression that heightens rather than abolishes the taboo on killing and corpse-violation.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Homosociality
holes.what: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's term for the non-sexual bonds of friendship, mentorship and rivalry between men that organize desire and power.
holes.why: Chapter 23's thesis is that Hannibal's 'rare gift' to Will is precisely such a homosocial bond, developed explicitly through Sedgwick's Between Men.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Empathy (Rogers' person-centered account)
holes.what: Carl Rogers' capacity to assume and communicate another person's internal frame of reference entirely without judgment, the foundation of client-centered therapy.
holes.why: Chapter 24 defines empathy through Rogers and argues that empathic contact with Hannibal destroys the empathizer's own moral perspective, as with Will and Dr. Du Maurier.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Aestheticism (art for art's sake)
holes.what: The stance that aesthetic value is sovereign: art and beauty are to be pursued for their own sake, independent of moral or intellectual value.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues Lecter is an aesthete par excellence who ranks the beautiful above the good, and that his art, cannibalism, murder and etiquette all flow from that ranking.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Noël Carroll
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose work on horror, humor and their shared incongruity structure is the reference point for philosophical discussion of the horror genre.
holes.why: Chapter 27 engages Carroll's claim that horror and humor are opposite mental states in order to argue that Lecter is funny and terrifying at the same time.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: The Incongruity Theory of Humor
holes.what: The view that we find funny what unites incongruous, incommensurable elements into a self-contradictory whole, as in the monster, the clown or the joke.
holes.why: Chapter 27 adopts incongruity theory as its first principle and applies it to Lecter's cannibal in-jokes such as 'I wouldn't do that to the food'.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Benedetto Croce
holes.what: Italian idealist whose expression theory of art replaces beauty with expression, admitting the ugly and terrible into the aesthetic.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Croce's expression-centered aesthetics, and his idea of reality as 'the aesthetic oneness of opposites', to classify Lecter's murder tableaux as art.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: David Novitz
holes.what: Philosopher of art who tied art to everyday life, holding that debates over art track society's changing values and that the arts are the skills by which we live.
holes.why: Chapter 28 needs Novitz to move beyond art-as-skill (Aristotle's techne) to the claim that murder is the skill by which Hannibal Lecter lives.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Noël Carroll
holes.what: Author of The Philosophy of Horror: the genre aims at fear and disgust directed at a threatening monster beyond current science, and our simultaneous attraction is the paradox of horror.
holes.why: Chapter 31 tests Lecter against Carroll's monster definition and paradox of horror, then argues he breaks both because he is a human, scientifically possible monster.
