holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Cynthia Freeland
holes.what: Philosopher of horror whose realist account defines the monster as any creature, however scientifically possible, that embodies social or moral perversion.
holes.why: Chapter 31 adopts Freeland's definition to explain why the human Lecter still counts as a monster and why his mythos deepens the paradox of horror.
holes.book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

holes.name: Philosophical Irony
holes.what: Saying the opposite of what one means or sustaining doubled meanings at once, used from Socrates to Kierkegaard as indirect communication and philosophical critique.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire method is reading the show's churches, signs, and 'Jesus' through irony as 'a doubleness of sense' (via Colebrook), a central lens taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More

holes.name: Jeff McMahan
holes.what: Contemporary just war theorist who rejects the moral symmetry of combatants, holding that unjust combatants act wrongly in killing even when excused by coercion or ignorance.
holes.why: Chapter 23's core is the Walzer-McMahan debate over whether soldiers on both sides of a war are equally justified in killing, and the taxonomy has only Walzer.
holes.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More

holes.name: Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
holes.what: Lawrence Kohlberg's theory that moral reasoning develops through six stages in three levels - pre-conventional (punishment and self-interest), conventional (conformity and law-and-order), and post-conventional (social contract and universal ethical principles).
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire analysis of Carol killing Lizzie, and its ranking of Carol above Rick, Hershel and Daryl, consists in placing the characters on Kohlberg's stages, and no existing taxonomy slug captures stage-based moral development.
holes.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's pyramid on which physiological and safety needs must be secured before belonging, esteem, and finally self-actualization become motivating.
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues that Walking Dead characters' moral stages track Maslow's tiers because survival needs are always at risk - Rick is stuck at safety, Daryl at esteem, and only self-actualized Carol reaches post-conventional morality.
holes.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More

holes.name: Preference Utilitarianism
holes.what: The utilitarian variant, associated with R.M. Hare and Peter Singer, on which right action maximizes the satisfaction of preferences rather than happiness or pleasure.
holes.why: Chapter 32's proposal that Carol should have shot Lizzie in the heart so she could reanimate rests entirely on counting Lizzie's preference to become a walker, something happiness-based classic utilitarianism (which the chapter contrasts via Bentham) cannot register.
holes.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More

holes.name: Goodman's New Riddle of Induction (grue)
holes.what: Nelson Goodman's puzzle that a predicate like 'grue' (green now, blue after a future date) fits all past evidence as well as 'green', showing induction needs an account of which predicates are projectible.
holes.why: Chapter 38's centerpiece pun is that the walker outbreak is literally 'gruesome': the dead rising is a grue-style future swing that no amount of past observation could have ruled out, as the cicada example makes vivid.
holes.book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More

holes.name: The Obligation of Promises
holes.what: The philosophical question of how promises create obligations, debated between conventionalist accounts (Rawls), expectationalist accounts, and self-respect based accounts (with Searle and Scanlon as key reference points).
holes.why: Chapter 13 is entirely about what makes promises binding - Westley's 'I will always come for you,' Humperdinck's broken vows, and Inigo's vow to his dead father - and the taxonomy has no concept covering promising.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Rhetoric of persuasion as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in each case, via the speaker's character (ethos), the audience's emotional state (pathos), and the argument itself (logos).
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire framework is Aristotle's Rhetoric applied to Westley's victories and Humperdinck's failures, but the taxonomy has no rhetoric concept for Aristotle.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Evidentialism (Clifford's rule)
holes.what: The view that belief is rational only when proportioned to evidence, crystallized in W.K. Clifford's 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.'
holes.why: Chapter 19 sets this evidentialist tradition (Descartes, Hume, Clifford) against hope-driven belief, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for the evidence-only side of the debate.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Honor Cultures
holes.what: The Nisbett-Cohen-Sommers distinction between lawless honor cultures, where personal retaliation for attacks on one's honor is a rational duty, and institutionalized cultures with state-administered justice.
holes.why: Chapter 21's defense of Inigo's revenge turns on Florin being an honor culture with no functional justice system, a framework the taxonomy does not cover.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Supererogation (acts beyond duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally praiseworthy and encouraged but not required, going above and beyond the call of duty.
holes.why: Chapter 24 proposes that Aristotle's virtues of friendliness and wittiness are supererogatory ideals rather than obligations, using supererogation as a load-bearing concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and novelist whose book Miracles defends supernaturalism, treating a miracle as God introducing a new element into the regular stream of nature rather than violating natural law.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire debate over Miracle Max's miracle pairs Hume's skepticism against Lewis's supernaturalism, and half its argument cannot be indexed without him.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Josiah Royce
holes.what: American idealist philosopher whose The Philosophy of Loyalty grounds the meaning of life in loyal service to freely chosen causes and in being 'loyal to loyalty itself'.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is built on Royce's philosophy of loyalty to explain the duelists' fair play, honor among thieves, lost causes, and why Westley's conduct satisfies though it is not precisely moral.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: The Philosophy of Loyalty
holes.what: Royce's view that a self comes into existence through willing, habitual service to a cause, that lost causes can be idealized into moral growth, and that loyalty itself deserves loyalty.
holes.why: Chapter 32 applies loyalty, loyalty's training through sport, and lost-cause idealization to Inigo, Fezzik, Westley, and Buttercup, and no existing taxonomy slug covers loyalty.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Principlism (Four Principles of Biomedical Ethics)
holes.what: Beauchamp and Childress's framework grounding medical ethics in four balancing principles: autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, and justice.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is structured entirely around applying the four principles to Miracle Max's treatment of Westley, and taxonomy has no slug for principlism or biomedical principles.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Comparative mythologist whose account of myth as the support of civilizations, moral orders, and cultural identity is the chapter's main authority.
holes.why: Chapter 37 quotes Campbell repeatedly to ground its claim that the Dread Pirate Roberts legend sustains Florinese cultural identity, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: Cultural Mythology (myth as social identity)
holes.what: The idea, developed by Joseph Campbell, Jerome Bruner, and Karen Armstrong, that shared myths supply a culture's identity, cohesion, and moral order and are updated rather than discarded.
holes.why: Chapter 37's central claim is that the Dread Pirate Roberts functions as the mythology of Florin's cultural identity, and no existing slug captures that concept.
holes.book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!

holes.name: The Principle of Plenitude
holes.what: The idea, traced by Arthur Lovejoy, that every genuine possibility must at some point be actualized.
holes.why: Chapter 20 explains Louis's 'no room for giant ants with top hats' punchline as an explicit rejection of this principle, and no existing taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: The Comic as Contradiction (irony vs comedy)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's view that the comic arises from the contradictions inherent in human existence, with irony merely spotting them and comedy living out their implications.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is framed by this thesis ('wherever there is contradiction the comical is present') and applies it to Louie throughout, but the taxonomy's Kierkegaard slugs cover only stages, despair, and anxiety.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: Explanatory Regress (explanation as answers to why-questions)
holes.what: The problem, starting from Hempel and Oppenheim's account of explanations as answers to why-questions, that every such answer itself invites a further why-question, ending only in brute facts or a 'Why not?'
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire reading of the 'Why?' routine is built on the explanatory regress and how Louis's 'eat your French fries' and 'Why not?' stop it, and the taxonomy has no slug for explanation, regress, or brute facts.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: Thomas Pogge
holes.what: Contemporary political philosopher who argues in World Poverty and Human Rights that the global institutional order (WTO, IMF, trade rules) actively and unjustly harms the world's poor, imposing duties on affluent participants.
holes.why: Chapter 32 devotes a full section to Pogge to argue that rich-world consumers are actively responsible for harm to the Global Poor, extending Singer's aid-based duty beyond mere donation.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: The Thought Experiment
holes.what: An imagined scenario (popularized by Ernst Mach, theorized by Tamar Gendler) that tests or reveals beliefs and reconfigures conceptual frames, producing an 'Aha' of understanding without a physical laboratory.
holes.why: Chapter 36's central claim is that Louis's bits (the white time machine, sitting in a chair in the sky) are playful thought experiments, a device the taxonomy nowhere names.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: White Privilege (identity privilege)
holes.what: Unearned social advantages granted by racial and other identities within a system that locks other groups out—Peggy McIntosh's 'invisible package of special provisions.'
holes.why: Chapter 38 is organized entirely around Louis's white-privilege bits, 'privileged deniers,' and Barbara Applebaum's white complicity, which intersectionality alone does not cover.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: Ferdinand de Saussure
holes.what: Swiss linguist (1857–1913) who founded structuralism with the theory of the arbitrary sign—signifier plus signified—undermining fixed foundations of meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 42's 'A Sign' section grounds Louis's street-sign and 'bag of dicks' bits in Saussure's arbitrariness of the sign, the basis on which it builds Derrida's deconstruction.
holes.book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored

holes.name: Natural Selection (survival of the fittest)
holes.what: Darwin's mechanism of evolution: heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction makes traits that fit an environment spread through a population.
holes.why: Chapter 12 measures Batman and Superman by fitness, adaptations, arms races, and biological altruism, and the taxonomy's social-darwinism slug covers only the ideology the chapter explicitly rejects, not the evolutionary framework it argues with.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Twentieth-century Christian writer and medievalist whose essay "The Necessity of Chivalry" defines the knightly ideal as holding ferocity and meekness together to the nth degree.
holes.why: Chapter 13 evaluates Batman and Superman's knighthood entirely through Lewis's chivalry essay, and no taxonomy philosopher covers him.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos (On Rhetoric)
holes.what: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion in On Rhetoric: appealing to the speaker's character, to the audience's emotions, and to logic and facts.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire argument ranks Batman and Superman as persuaders by how each balances the three modes, and no existing taxonomy slug names the rhetorical triad.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Actions that are praiseworthy to perform but not wrong to omit - the deeds of saints and heroes that go beyond obligation.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is built on supererogation from Urmson to Raz to decide whether Batman's risk-taking is heroic while Superman's rescues are mere duty, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Metabolic Rift
holes.what: Marx's term (revived by John Bellamy Foster) for the rupture capitalism tears in the material exchange between human society and nature - depleting soils and piling up waste faster than the earth can process it.
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire diagnosis of Batman's gadgets and Wayne Enterprises as an 'infinite environmental crisis' is built on the metabolic rift, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Mimesis and Catharsis (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of drama as imitation (mimesis) of human action that arouses pity and fear and purges them in catharsis.
holes.why: Chapter 17's whole argument is that Batman is a mimetic performance producing suspense and catharsis while Superman is transparent self-presentation, and the taxonomy has no Poetics slug.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: The category of acts that are praiseworthy and good yet beyond what morality obliges, introduced by J.O. Urmson's 'Saints and Heroes'.
holes.why: Chapter 18 turns on whether Superman's life-saving is obligatory or supererogatory and chapter 20 makes supererogation the test of true heroism, but no taxonomy slug names the concept.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Flow (optimal experience)
holes.what: Csikszentmihaly's state of optimal experience, reached when an activity's challenge is balanced with the doer's skill, between boredom and anxiety.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explains why Superman games fail and Batman games succeed entirely through keeping players in flow, which an overpowered hero destroys.
holes.book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

holes.name: Michael Huemer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose The Problem of Political Authority argues that the state has no special moral authority and defends philosophical anarchism.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Huemer's anarchism as the modern foil to Nozick's minimal state in reading the Nac Mac Feegle's contempt for all political authority.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian thinker whose Rabelais and His World theorizes carnival and the grotesque body as popular inversions of official high culture and social hierarchy.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Nanny Ogg, the Genua carnival, and Baron Saturday in Witches Abroad directly through Bakhtin's carnival/grotesque theory.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Michael Huemer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose The Problem of Political Authority argues that the state has no special moral authority and defends philosophical anarchism.
holes.why: Chapter 18 builds its section on Vimes's political realism - taxation as coercion, anti-utopianism, the psychology of submitting to authority - on Huemer's book.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Nelson Goodman
holes.what: Philosopher whose Languages of Art defines counterfeits as objects falsely purporting to have the requisite history of production, and inventor of the 'grue' paradox.
holes.why: Chapter 19 tests and revises Goodman's definition of the counterfeit to explain how Moist von Lipwig secures Ankh-Morpork's banknotes and stamps against forgery.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Institutional Facts (social reality)
holes.what: Searle's account of how collective agreement ('X counts as Y in context C') creates social realities such as money, borders, and games.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues paper currency works only because Moist cons Ankh-Morpork's merchants into collectively accepting slips of paper as money, which is Searle's institutional-fact machinery applied.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: The Situationist Challenge to Character
holes.what: The social-psychology-based thesis (associated with Harman and Doris) that behavior is driven by situational factors rather than stable character traits, undermining virtue ethics.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Rincewind cannot be a coward because the situationist challenge shows there are no character traits such as courage or cowardice to have.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Joseph Butler
holes.what: An eighteenth-century Anglican bishop who argued that consciousness of past actions merely reveals personal identity rather than constituting it, so identity is basic, indefinable, and presupposes the persistence of the person.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its reading of Granny Weatherwax's 'you're your me' and 'This one' around Butler's circularity objection to Locke's memory theory and his lack of worry about duplication cases.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: History as Narrative Construction
holes.what: The narrativist thesis (associated with philosophers of history like W. H. Walsh) that history is not the past itself but an intelligible narrative constructed by historians, so the past becomes what people are told it is.
holes.why: Chapter 15's central claim—that the Duchess rewrites history through Hwel's play and the History Monks patch time as 'a patchwork, really'—is exactly this narrativist thesis, for which the taxonomy has no slug.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: A Christian apologist whose moral argument holds that a universal Law of Human Nature, shared across cultures and felt even by unbelievers, is best explained by a divine moral lawgiver.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its whole account of Discworld sin on Lewis's natural-law moral argument, from shared intuitions about the enchanted wolf to the conclusion that God wrote the moral law into every creature.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Structures of Sin
holes.what: John Paul II's notion that personal sins consolidate into social structures that spread, become self-perpetuating, and make further sin easier, so evil becomes embedded in law and custom.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses the concept explicitly to read the Assassins' Guild, whose contract-sanctioned, tax-paying killing of the rich embodies sin sanctified by city law.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Eliminative Materialism
holes.what: The view that mature neuroscience will eliminate our commonsense folk-psychological entities—beliefs, desires, fears—leaving only brain processes as the whole story about the mind.
holes.why: Chapter 20 gives eliminative materialism its own section, explaining folk psychology through The Science of Discworld and setting it in the progression away from Descartes's dualism.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Functionalism (Philosophy of Mind)
holes.what: The theory that mental states should be defined by their functional roles, with the brain as hardware and the mind as software, rather than by what they are made of.
holes.why: Chapter 20 closes its survey of theories of consciousness with functionalism's computer metaphor and its identification with scientism, the claim that science alone explains the mind.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: Umwelt (Life World)
holes.what: Jakob von Uexküll's notion that each organism inhabits a species-specific perceptual world, a sensory island carved out of reality by what its body can detect and use.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire reading of Discworld creatures—the moth, the ambiguous puzuma, dromes, the re-annual plant—is organized around the Umwelt concept, for which no taxonomy slug exists.
holes.book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems

holes.name: The Non-Identity Problem (paradox of future individuals)
holes.what: Parfit's puzzle that an action shaping the exact conditions of someone's conception (like Sarah conceiving Kira young, or Neolution engineering doomed clones) cannot harm the person it produces, since a different choice would have produced a different person, even though it intuitively wrongs them.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is built entirely on this problem and its Implausible Conclusion, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German sociologist who held that the social sciences must interpret and understand human action from the inside (through motives) rather than predict it from the outside like natural science.
holes.why: Chapter 12 contrasts Mill's predictive model of the monitor experiment with Weber's interpretive paradigm, which frames the chapter's whole argument but is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Natality
holes.what: Arendt's notion that every human begins as a unique newcomer whose birth into a particular time, place, and circumstance grounds the capacity for new beginnings and authentic selfhood.
holes.why: Chapter 16's central claim is that cloning strips humans of natality the way mechanical reproduction stripped art of its aura, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for the concept.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Nishida Kitaro
holes.what: Japanese founder of the Kyoto School whose logic of basho and 'contradictory self-identity' (A is A only by being related to not-A) fuses Zen nothingness with Western metaphysics.
holes.why: Chapter 17's positive answer to what individuates one clone from another is Nishida's principle of contradictory self-identity applied to the clone dance party, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: The Epistemology of Peer Disagreement
holes.what: Contemporary epistemological debate over whether two epistemic peers who share all their evidence can rationally reach different conclusions, and what private evidence or starting points do to the puzzle.
holes.why: Chapter 22 exists to test exactly this debate — epistemic peers, shared evidence, private evidence — on the clones, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French feminist psychoanalytic philosopher who argues the Symbolic Order excludes women, and who rewrites the male philosophical canon through mimicry to open active roles for women as women.
holes.why: Chapter 25's positive framework is Irigaray's critique of the Symbolic/Imaginary divide and her rereading of motherhood in Orphan Black, but she is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: The Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's account of the child's libidinal attachment to the mother and rivalry with the father (transformed by Lacan into symbolic castration and entry into the Symbolic Order), central to psychosexual development.
holes.why: Half of chapter 25 analyzes Coady, Tomas, Rachel, and the Castor clones through the Oedipus complex, in Freud's and Lacan's versions, and no taxonomy slug names it.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Rosi Braidotti
holes.what: Contemporary posthumanist feminist philosopher whose work on nomadic subjects and the posthuman condition rethinks the human subject beyond the white male universal of European thought.
holes.why: Chapter 26 leans on Braidotti's The Posthuman and Nomadic Subjects to argue that only posthumanism lets a new, inclusive sisterhood return, and she is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view that biotechnology and biogenetic capitalism dissolve the fixed boundaries of the human, turning the body into a mix of organism and technoscience and freeing identity from given nature.
holes.why: Chapter 26 frames the clones as posthuman bodies whose condition enables the new sisterhood, and the taxonomy contains no posthumanism slug.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Philosopher whose Basic Argument holds that because we act from a psychology we did not ultimately choose, no one can be ultimately responsible for what they do.
holes.why: Chapter 30's middle section is built on Galen Strawson's Basic Argument, applied to why background-based excuses threaten all clone responsibility, and he is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: P.F. Strawson
holes.what: Philosopher who reframed moral responsibility around the reactive attitudes (resentment, gratitude, pity) we appropriately take toward one another rather than around metaphysical desert.
holes.why: Chapter 30's escape from the Basic Argument runs through P.F. Strawson's reactive attitudes — our shifting responses to Helena and Donnie — and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: John Martin Fischer
holes.what: Leading compatibilist whose account grounds moral responsibility in reasons-responsiveness and guidance control — acting through mechanisms that are responsive to reasons and one's own.
holes.why: Chapter 30's final answer to why Helena is exempt while Cosima is responsible is Fischer's two-condition account of reasons-responsiveness and ownership, and he is not in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA

holes.name: Iki (Japanese aesthetic of stylish chic)
holes.what: Shuzo Kuki's Japanese aesthetic ideal: cool, astringent chic that negates the 'sweet' (kitsch), expresses itself through the body, and stays a virtual possibility rather than an actuality.
holes.why: Chapter 2's central tool for explaining Bowie's 'kitsch-cool' body-stylization is Kuki's iki, for which the taxonomy has no slot.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Arthur Danto
holes.what: Twentieth-century analytic philosopher of art whose 'artworld' theory and 'end of art' thesis followed from Warhol's Brillo Box.
holes.why: Chapter 4 is built on Danto's philosophy of art (embodied meaning, the Art World, the end of art history), but he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: The End of Art (the Artworld)
holes.what: Danto's thesis that after Warhol's Brillo Box no style-lineage defines art; the Art World's theories decide what is art, and celebrity itself can be an art form.
holes.why: Chapter 4 explains Bowie's persona-as-performance-art and his rejection by the Art World entirely through this thesis.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Nonsense Literature and Artistic Value
holes.what: The philosophy-of-art question of how lyrics that avoid determinate meaning (nonsense in the line from Lear and Carroll to Bowie) can nonetheless have artistic value through mood and audience imagination.
holes.why: Chapter 5's entire argument is that Bowie's incomprehensible lyrics gain, not lose, artistic value by leaving interpretation to the listener.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Principle of Growth (impulses, desires, ambivalence)
holes.what: Russell's moral psychology from Principles of Social Reconstruction: an instinctive 'principle of growth' drives impulses and desires toward self-realization, inevitably tinged with ambivalence.
holes.why: Chapter 10 organizes all seven of Bowie's interpretations of death around this framework, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Denis Diderot
holes.what: Enlightenment philosopher whose dialogue Rameau's Nephew portrays Lui, the honest parasite and mask-wearing musician who owns the vices everyone hides.
holes.why: Chapter 13 draws its central comparison between Bowie and Lui, and Hegel's 'madness of the musician' is Hegel's reading of that dialogue.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Cynical Reason (the honest liar)
holes.what: Sloterdijk's account of modern cynicism: knowing, ironic participation in the corrupt system one condemns - being honest about one's own fakery.
holes.why: Chapter 13 uses cynical reason (via Sloterdijk and Sharon Stanley) to explain Bowie's postmodern persona-play as 'if you can't beat 'em, join 'em.'
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Capitalism and Schizophrenia (deterritorialization)
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus thesis that capitalist production itself generates schizophrenic flux - ceaseless decoding of desire, fads, and collapse of stable identity.
holes.why: Chapter 14 explains Bowie's persona-shifting as performance of capitalism's schizophrenic production, for which the existing 'rhizome' slug is inadequate.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Thomas Szasz
holes.what: Psychiatrist-philosopher of the antipsychiatry movement who argued mental illness is a myth by which psychiatry acts as an agent of social control.
holes.why: Chapter 15 quotes Szasz at length to pair his critique of psychiatric labeling with Bowie's 'All the Madmen' challenge to the sanity/madness line.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Madness and Civilization (the construction of madness)
holes.what: Foucault's account of how psychiatry's 'monologue of reason about madness' constituted madness as mental illness, breaking an earlier dialogue between madness and reason.
holes.why: Chapter 15 quotes Madness and Civilization directly to read Bowie as questioning the historically constructed sanity/madness distinction; power-knowledge alone does not capture it.
holes.book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose On the Origin of Species (1859) explains evolution through natural selection and contrasts it with man-made selective breeding.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire argument—that the Golds misapply natural selection, run the Institute as artificial selection, and are undone by the traits they bred into Reds—is built directly on Darwin's own distinctions and text.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Species Concepts (biological, phylogenetic, ecological)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology debate over what fixes a species—interbreeding (Mayr's Biological Species Concept), common descent, or adaptation to an ecological niche—replacing Aristotelian essentialism.
holes.why: Chapter 10 tests the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species against each of these three species concepts, none of which the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)
holes.what: French Enlightenment satirist whose Candide, through Dr. Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, argues morality demands we not pretend evil is intelligible.
holes.why: Chapter 12 stages Darrow's development as a move from the spirit of Voltaire (evil stays unintelligible) to the spirit of Rousseau, with Candide receiving extended treatment.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: Continental philosopher for whom love is one of four truth procedures: a contingent encounter that founds the 'Two scene' of seeing the world from the perspective of difference (In Praise of Love).
holes.why: Chapter 15's central claims—that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love and that Darrow and Mustang only become a couple at the trilogy's end—are argued entirely through Badiou's account of love.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Beauty as Harmoniousness (unity in variety)
holes.what: The classical tradition (Aristotle, Aquinas, Hutcheson) defining beauty as the appropriate, coherent ordering of an object's parts into a unified whole.
holes.why: Chapter 21 asks whether the Color society is beautiful precisely by applying this harmony definition of beauty, and the taxonomy has no concept for beauty or aesthetics generally.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Legal Positivism (law and morality separate)
holes.what: The view associated with Bentham, Austin, and H.L.A. Hart that a law's validity is one thing and its moral merit another: law is what is posited, with hard cases forming a penumbra.
holes.why: Chapter 22 weighs the Golds' legal order as valid positive law against natural law, and the taxonomy has no slug for legal positivism or the Hart-side of the debate.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: The Repugnant Conclusion (population ethics)
holes.what: Parfit's result that total utilitarianism favors a vast population of lives barely worth living over a smaller, happier one, with the mere addition paradox haunting average-utilitarian views.
holes.why: Chapter 24's argument about Mustang's obligations to future generations runs entirely through the Repugnant Conclusion and the mere addition paradox, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
holes.what: Civil-rights leader whose philosophy of agape, loving-forgiveness, and nonviolent resistance is set out in Stride Toward Freedom, Strength to Love, and The Trumpet of Conscience.
holes.why: Chapter 26 measures Darrow's violent Rising against King's nonviolent alternative, quoting King's accounts of agape, forgiveness, and the ends-preexistent-in-the-means throughout its second half.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: Transitional Justice
holes.what: The truth commissions, conditional amnesties, reparations, and dignified engagement by which societies move from large-scale atrocity to mutual cooperation instead of mass punishment.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues the post-Rising Society needs exactly a Truth and Reconciliation-style process for the Golds, and the taxonomy has no transitional-justice concept.
holes.book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

holes.name: The Standard of Taste (Rough Heroes)
holes.what: Hume's essay 'Of the Standard of Taste' arguing that art is judged by refined sentiment and that morally 'rough heroes' we plainly discover to be blameable cannot properly engage our imagination.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument over whether Game of Thrones is morally flawed for making the child-killer Arya lovable runs on Hume's standard of taste versus Anne Eaton's 'robust immoralism' and halo effect.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Tragic Conflict (the fragility of goodness)
holes.what: Nussbaum's idea, drawn from Greek tragedy, that luck can force a person to choose between two equally valid moral claims so that every option involves real loss and moral residue.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia, Stannis's parallel sacrifice of Shireen, and Aemon's honor-versus-love advice to Jon to argue that no prioritization of values can dissolve genuine tragic conflicts.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of how tragedy represents misfortune so audiences vent or purge emotions like pity and fear.
holes.why: Chapter 13 builds its account of why art rarely depicts sudden death, and how Game of Thrones represents life's fragility, on the Platonic-Aristotelian mimesis-and-catharsis framework.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Erich Fromm
holes.what: Humanistic psychoanalyst who located humanity's essence in its existential contradictions and held that the good life is 'affirmation of life' - love, growth, and principled disobedience to hollow authority.
holes.why: Chapter 14 frames Tyrion's humor and refusal to submit as Frommian life-affirmation against empty court ritual, citing Fromm by name as the chapter's central positive framework.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Voluntary, Involuntary and Mixed Actions
holes.what: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Book III distinction, used to judge blameworthiness: acts done under compulsion or duress are 'mixed' and can be pardonable or even praiseworthy when they choose the lesser evil for a noble end.
holes.why: Chapter 17's whole defense of Jaime's kingslaying rests on treating the regicide ordered under Aerys's duress as an Aristotelian mixed action rather than a voluntary crime.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: John Austin
holes.what: Nineteenth-century legal philosopher whose command theory defines law as the sovereign's command backed by the threat of force, the first scientific (positivist) theory of law.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Austin's command theory to give voice to Cersei's 'Power is power' and the three great men of Varys's riddle, before dismantling it.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: H.L.A. Hart
holes.what: Legal philosopher whose The Concept of Law replaced Austin's command theory, holding that law's authority rests on social acceptance of a rule of recognition rather than on coercive force.
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues through Hart's gunman/sovereign and obliged/obligated distinctions that the Lannisters are 'gunmen writ large' whose power, as Varys says, is only a trick, a shadow on the wall.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: The Westermarck Effect
holes.what: Edward Westermarck's hypothesis that living in close childhood intimacy produces a natural sexual aversion, explaining the incest taboo as an evolved instinct rather than repressed desire.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues Jaime and Cersei's relationship is written against Westermarck's evidence (primate studies, simpua marriages) and contrasts his natural-aversion account with Freud's Oedipal theory.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Filiation (legal parentage and legitimacy)
holes.what: The legal system determining who belongs to which family, conferring name, status, inheritance, and destiny on children and punishing those outside it.
holes.why: Chapter 29 argues the whole Game of Thrones social order runs on filiation - bastard names like Snow and Sand, Ramsay's legitimization, the Sand Snakes' freedom, and the defenselessness of the unfiliated all derive from it.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Moral vs Legal Consent
holes.what: Alan Wertheimer's distinction between sex that violates the law and sex that violates dignity or agency while remaining legal, including sex obtained by fraud or by disregard of the partner's status as a consenting subject.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses it to show that Drogo legally never raped Daenerys yet morally raped her, and to sort the Sansa-Ramsay and Cersei-Jaime cases into legal, moral, and reciprocal-subjectivity failures.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Susan Neiman
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose Evil in Modern Thought traces the problem of evil from its theological form to a secular one about virtue and happiness diverging, split between making evil intelligible and refusing to.
holes.why: Chapter 34 builds its whole contrast between Cersei's Sadean and Sansa's Kantian responses to suffering on Neiman's historical account of the problem of evil.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Empiricism (knowledge from observation and experiment)
holes.what: The view that sensory observation and practical experiment are the best sources of knowledge, contrasted with deference to textual authority, tradition, or occult secrecy.
holes.why: Chapter 39 argues Samwell Tarly's combination of field experience with dragonglass and rediscovered library knowledge makes him the empiricist who can start a Westerosi renaissance against the Maesters' monopoly.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Proper Functionalism (warrant)
holes.what: Plantinga's externalist theory of warrant: a belief is warranted when produced by truth-aimed cognitive faculties functioning properly in the environment for which they were designed.
holes.why: Chapter 40 defends Catelyn's trust in Brienne through proper functionalism, using the Labman replica and the Lord of Light's randomized design plan as its test cases.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who defends authenticity - being true to oneself - as a genuine ethical ideal forged in dialogue and relationships with others, despite its self-indulgent misuses.
holes.why: Chapter 47 explains Theon's collapse into Reek through Taylor's Ethics of Authenticity, arguing that identity is formed in relationships and that authenticity depends on virtue.
holes.book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die

holes.name: Anti-Psychiatry
holes.what: The movement (David Cooper, Thomas Szasz) criticizing psychiatry's coercive power relations, ineffective or harmful treatments, and unobjective, over-medicalized diagnoses.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is structured entirely around testing Lucy's booth against the anti-psychiatry movement's three criticisms; power-knowledge covers only the Foucauldian strand, not the Szasz-style institutional critique.
holes.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!

holes.name: The Nature of Faith (belief vs non-doxastic faith)
holes.what: The debate over whether faith is propositional belief held with near-certain conviction (Aquinas) or commitment that can persist without belief, acting in the face of doubt (Howard-Snyder).
holes.why: Chapter 25's whole argument is that Linus wrongly equates sincere faith with certain belief and that real faith is acting under doubt; faith-vs-reason does not capture this analysis of what faith is.
holes.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!

holes.name: Umberto Eco
holes.what: Italian semiotician and philosopher who analyzed mass culture ('apocalyptic' vs 'integrated' intellectuals) and hailed Peanuts as serious literature in his 1965 introduction to the magazine linus.
holes.why: Chapter 31's reading of the Peanuts microcosm and mass-culture meaning rests directly on Eco's Apocalittici e Integrati; culture-industry is adjacent but Eco's own framework is the load-bearing source.
holes.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!

holes.name: Transitional Object (Winnicott)
holes.what: Winnicott's intermediate area of experience (a blanket or toy) where the infant keeps inner and outer reality separate yet related, later diffusing into art, religion, and philosophy.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is built entirely on the claim that Linus's blanket is a transitional object enabling his philosophy and prophecy while blanket-less Charlie Brown is flooded by depression; no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!

holes.name: Amour Propre (pathological self-love)
holes.what: Rousseau's term for comparative, status-hungry self-love that seeks superiority over others, as opposed to healthy self-preservation (amour de soi).
holes.why: Chapter 12's central diagnosis of Deadpool as malignant narcissist rests on Rousseau's amour propre versus amour de soi distinction (alongside Freudian narcissism), and the taxonomy has no slug for either.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian philosopher of the carnivalesque: licensed bodily excess, grotesque humor, and inversion of hierarchies as subversive social release.
holes.why: Chapter 13 explains Deadpool's orifice jokes, grotesque masks, and boundary-overspill through Bakhtin's carnival excess (Rabelais and His World), a framework the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist of the 'hero's journey' (monomyth): a universal narrative arc in which the hero is transformed from self-centeredness into self-sacrifice through trials and revelations.
holes.why: Chapter 15 tests Deadpool's arc in 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly' entirely against Campbell's Hero of a Thousand Faces and The Power of Myth.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Skillful Means (upaya)
holes.what: The Buddhist principle that a normally wrong act, even killing, can be right when performed out of compassion to prevent greater harm.
holes.why: Chapter 16 justifies Deadpool's killing of the Hydra spy and the Niagara Bride contract through upaya, a concept the taxonomy lacks despite its karma and compassion slugs.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist of the 'hero's journey' (monomyth): a universal narrative arc in which the hero is transformed from self-centeredness into self-sacrifice through trials and revelations.
holes.why: Chapter 18 reads the Deadpool movie stage by stage through Campbell's monomyth (ordinary world, call, refusal, reward) before turning to MacIntyre and Kant.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Post-Heroic Warfare
holes.what: Edward Luttwak's thesis that modern technology (drones, standoff missiles) removes personal risk from combat, creating an unbridgeable gap between combatants and ending heroic warfare.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues Deadpool's healing factor is precisely such a technology, denying both him and everyone who fights him any chance to display courage.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Human Rights (Universal Declaration)
holes.what: The post-WWII doctrine that all humans possess inalienable rights by virtue of species membership, codified in the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
holes.why: Chapter 20 condemns Deadpool's genocide of the Marvel Universe by the Declaration's standard that every person's inherent dignity must be recognized and can be violated but never voided.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Law of Non-Contradiction
holes.what: The logical principle that nothing can both be and not be, or have and lack a property, in the same respect at the same time.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Deadpool Killustrated violates it - Ahab is killed by both the whale and Deadpool - and surveys what such impossible fictions mean for logic and imagination.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French theorist whose Theory of Religion defines religion as the search for lost intimacy recovered through sacrifice, violence, and sovereignty.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads Deadpool's killings as exactly the sacrificial violence that dissolves the profane world and opens onto sacred immanence in Bataille's sense.
holes.book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling

holes.name: Propaganda of the Deed
holes.what: The anarchist doctrine that shocking public acts, violent or not, serve as propaganda that wakes the masses from social slumber and forces society to change.
holes.why: Chapter 12 frames the entire 5/9 hack as propaganda of the deed, positioning fsociety between Berkman's violent anarchism and Gandhi's self-suffering.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Mimesis (art as imitation)
holes.what: Plato's doctrine that art imitates physical things, which themselves imitate the Forms, making art an imitation of an imitation - against Aristotle's defense of imitation as natural and instructive.
holes.why: Chapter 13's whole assessment of Elliot's imaginary friend, the Mr. Robot persona, and fsociety's masks turns on the Plato-Aristotle debate over mimesis.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Thomas More
holes.what: Author of Utopia (1516), whose character Hythloday argues that private property and money make justice impossible and imagines a commonwealth with no privacy.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Elliot's hacktivism and the case for tearing down the veil of privacy almost entirely through More's Utopia and its conspiracy of the rich.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Biopower
holes.what: Foucault's notion of modern power exercised over the life and bodies of populations through institutions and norms rather than by a sovereign's decree.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses biopower to explain why no one is punished for the Washington Township leak that killed Angela's mother.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Leon Trotsky
holes.what: Marxist revolutionary who argued in 'Their Morals and Ours' that revolutionary ends justify whatever means the class struggle requires.
holes.why: Chapter 20 stages the Dewey-Trotsky means-ends debate as the key test of whether Mr. Robot's hacktivism is justified.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Founder of modern conservatism who condemned the French Revolution, holding that society is an organism that must change only gradually through its traditions.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses Burke as the conservative condemnation against which Marx's and Nielsen's justifications of fsociety's revolution are tested.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Kai Nielsen
holes.what: Political philosopher who argues Marxist revolution is justified only when no other course of action could achieve the same end.
holes.why: Chapter 24 adopts Nielsen's no-recourse condition - confirmed by Angela's failed inside reform of E Corp - as the decisive justification of the 5/9 hack.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Whistleblowing
holes.what: An insider's report of an organization's illegal or immoral conduct to outside authorities or the public, with its attendant legal protections and social costs.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire explanation of why Angela abandons the Washington Township disclosure turns on the ethics and risks of whistleblowing.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: The Nomadic War-Machine
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's figure of an exterior, non-segmented collective defined by its capacity to betray the state's codes and interrupt capitalist flows.
holes.why: Chapter 28 models Elliot and fsociety as a nomadic war-machine whose revolution attacks limitation itself rather than any particular institution.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Corporate Personhood
holes.what: The legal doctrine treating corporations as persons bearing rights and liabilities even though they lack the intentionality and dignity of natural persons.
holes.why: Chapter 29's question of whether E Corp can be an evil or morally responsible person is exactly the problem of corporate personhood.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Deception and Keeping in the Dark
holes.what: Intentionally causing someone to have a false belief (deception) or to lack a true belief (keeping them in the dark), including the paradox of self-deception.
holes.why: Chapter 32 analyzes Mr. Robot's hacker war as applied epistemology built on defining deception versus keeping people in the dark.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Byung-Chul Han
holes.what: Korean-German philosopher of the transparency society, psycho-politics, and the burnout society, where power works through seduction and self-exploitation rather than repression.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Elliot, Tyrell, and Gideon as embodiments of Han's burnout society and its digital panopticon.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: The Fantastic (Todorov)
holes.what: Tzvetan Todorov's literary category of the unresolved hesitation between realistic and imaginary explanations of the events narrated.
holes.why: Chapter 35 argues the fantastic's ambiguity in Elliot's unreliable narration is precisely how Mr. Robot hooks its audience.
holes.book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist whose 'the medium is the message' holds that the form of a medium (print vs television), not its content, reshapes perception and society.
holes.why: Chapter 9's core apparatus is the print-to-television media shift drawn from McLuhan, Meyrowitz, and Postman, none of whom the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: The Counter-Monument
holes.what: A memorial strategy (often ephemeral, anti-monumental, dependent on circulation) that challenges official state memory by highlighting what permanent monuments fix and forget.
holes.why: Chapter 10 reads the clandestine Grasshopper newsreels and Tagomi and Juliana's exchanged flowers as counter-monuments against Nazi monumental history.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: Cruel Optimism
holes.what: Lauren Berlant's term for a relation in which the object you desire — usually 'the good life' — is itself an obstacle to your flourishing.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire diagnosis of John Smith's and Frank Frink's misery runs on Berlant's cruel optimism.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: Esoteric Writing (exoteric vs esoteric doctrine)
holes.what: The practice of concealing a radical or secret doctrine between the lines of a text, addressing different messages to different audiences.
holes.why: Chapter 16 follows Geoff Waite in reading Dick as an esoteric writer whose secret fascist philosophy hides beneath his popular surface texts.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: Limit Situations (Grenzsituationen)
holes.what: Karl Jaspers's boundary situations — death, guilt, suffering, conflict — that break ordinary cognition and can force a leap into a new mode of existence.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses Jaspers's limit situations to explain how the show's crises transform Tagomi and Juliana rather than merely confusing them.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: Cognitive Dissonance
holes.what: Leon Festinger's notion of the discomfort felt when actions or new information conflict with existing beliefs, resolved through external excuses or changed perceptions.
holes.why: Chapter 31 applies cognitive dissonance and its external/internal justifications to Frank, Joe, John Smith, and Tagomi's breakdowns.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: The Spirit of Abstraction
holes.what: Gabriel Marcel's term for granting an abstract category (race, nation, class) arbitrary primacy over concrete persons, turning people into non-persons.
holes.why: Chapter 33's whole account of Nazi anti-Semitism and American segregation is built on Marcel's spirit of abstraction.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: Posthumous Harm
holes.what: The thesis that events after a person's death can set back their interests or frustrate their desires, harming them though they no longer exist.
holes.why: Chapter 34's argument over whether Amazon harmed Philip K. Dick turns on this concept, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality

holes.name: The Sexual Contract
holes.what: Carole Pateman's thesis that the classic social contract presupposed a prior sexual contract subordinating women to men, which together with Charles Mills's racial contract forms the 'domination contract'.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire theoretical frame is Pateman's Sexual Contract joined to Mills's Racial Contract, and later chapters apply it to the marriage contract, but the taxonomy only contains the racial half of the pair.
holes.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German sociologist and founder of modern social science who defined power as the chance to realize one's will against resistance and analyzed class, status and party, charisma and legal-rational authority as the distributions of power.
holes.why: Chapter 10 states that its nine bases of power are 'an elaboration of Weber's ideas', and his definitions of power, charisma, authority and status carry the chapter's whole argument, yet he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed

holes.name: Reparations (rectificatory justice)
holes.what: The principle that victims of historical injustice and their descendants are owed compensation for wrongs such as slavery, segregation and neo-slavery.
holes.why: Chapter 16's concluding case for a 'Reparations Superfund' rests on the moral base of power and Bernard Boxill's Lockean inheritance argument, a conception of justice no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed

holes.name: Democratic Socialism / Social Democracy
holes.what: A regime keeping a regulated market economy but adding steep progressive taxation, strong unions and a universal welfare state, explicitly distinct from Marxist abolition of private property and central planning.
holes.why: Chapter 16's positive prescription - the Danish model of 'social democratic capitalism' as the realistic path to gender and racial equality in place of Marx's communism - names a distinct position with no taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of emotion through art)
holes.what: Aristotle's notion (Politics 8.7) that intense music and tragedy purge pity, fear, and frenzy, giving listeners harmless delight, pleasurable relief, and a more balanced state.
holes.why: Chapter 9's closing section argues Hendrix's 'Machine Gun' and tragic-hero persona deliver exactly this Aristotelian catharsis to his audience, but taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: The Hero's Journey (monomyth)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's three-stage myth pattern — separation, initiation, return — in which the hero leaves ordinary life, wins special knowledge and power, and brings a boon back to the world.
holes.why: Chapter 9 structures Hendrix's life and the 'Voodoo Chile' songs around this monomyth, casting him as a Prometheus who brings the fire of music back from his journeys.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Kant's Theory of Genius
holes.what: Kant's Critique of Judgment doctrine that genius is an inborn talent producing original, exemplary works which 'give the rule' to future art, without the genius being able to explain or teach how.
holes.why: Chapter 14's whole account of Jimi, Janis, and Jim runs on this doctrine — astonishment becoming admiration, the genius who cannot explain himself — which no existing slug covers.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Friedrich Kittler
holes.what: German media theorist (1943–2011) who held that media technologies are not mere tools but 'determine our situation,' as in Gramophone, Film, Typewriter.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Kittler's media theory to frame Hendrix's studio innovations, explicitly contrasting it with Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that concepts like 'game' have no necessary and sufficient conditions but are united by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues musical genres like rock are family-resemblance kinds, which is the backbone of its analysis of whether Jimi played rock.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Philosophy of Law (positivism, natural law, legal realism)
holes.what: Theories of what makes law law: posited by duly authorized legislatures (positivism), measured against moral or natural standards (natural law), or simply whatever courts enforce (American legal realism and Critical Legal Studies).
holes.why: Chapter 26 explains Hendrix's two law-changing cases through exactly this clash of jurisprudential theories, including Holmes's bad-man theory.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Institutional Theory of Art
holes.what: The view (associated with Danto and Dickie) that something is art when the art world — critics, museums, buyers and sellers — deems it so, rather than in virtue of intrinsic properties.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies this theory to decide whether Hendrix's Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' counts as art or mere noise.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Leo Tolstoy
holes.what: Russian novelist-thinker whose What Is Art? defines art as the infection of others by sincerely felt emotion, judged by particularity, clarity, and sincerity rather than beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 28 leans on Tolstoy's criteria to argue Hendrix's anthem is great art expressing 'bad feelings' about Vietnam, explicitly compared to Picasso's Guernica.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Chaos Theory and Emergence
holes.what: The study of non-linear dynamical systems where deterministic rules yield practical unpredictability (sensitive dependence, feedback loops) and order spontaneously self-organizes.
holes.why: Chapter 30 explains Hendrix's guitar feedback as an emergent, chaotic phenomenon and pits it against Laplacean predictability.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Pre-Socratic Element Theories (arche)
holes.what: The early Greek monists' search for a first principle (arche): Thales's water, Anaximander's quality-less apeiron, Anaximenes's condensing and rarefying air, and Empedocles's four elements driven by Love and Strife.
holes.why: Chapter 31 maps Hendrix's water, air, and fire imagery onto these theories — none of which except Heraclitus has a taxonomy slug — including Empedoclean Love and Strife.
holes.book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required

holes.name: Richard Taylor
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher whose Good and Evil argues that a life of repetitive toil, like Sisyphus's, is meaningful provided the agent embraces the task as its own end.
holes.why: Chapter 2's answer to the boredom of ghostly immortality in the Hotel Cortez rests on Taylor's Sisyphus argument alongside Bernard Williams's, and he is cited by name.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose Sources of the Self and A Secular Age describe the shift from porous selves in an enchanted, hierarchical cosmos to buffered selves in a disenchanted, mechanistic universe.
holes.why: Chapter 4 is built entirely on Taylor's framework - self-interpreting animals, attunement, enchanted and disenchanted worlds - to explain who survives an American Horror Story.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Porous and Buffered Selves
holes.what: Taylor's distinction between a self open to outside forces and independently meaningful reality (porous) and a self walled off inside a mind-imposed, disenchanted world (buffered).
holes.why: Chapter 4 uses the porous/buffered contrast to explain why believers in the supernatural survive haunted houses while disenchanted skeptics get gaslit, and why becoming porous again is costly.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Physiognomy
holes.what: The doctrine, reaching back to Greek medicine and the pseudo-Aristotelian Physiognomonics, that outward bodily features reveal moral character and inner faculties.
holes.why: Chapter 5 frames the whole body-soul question with physiognomy, using it to explain why Kyle rejects his reassembled body and to mock Aristotle's claim that small people have small minds.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Aristotle's Poetics (tragedy theory)
holes.what: Aristotle's theory of tragedy in the Poetics: mimesis of possible actions, the six formal elements, complete plots with reversal and recognition, hamartia, and the catharsis of fear and pity.
holes.why: Chapter 6's entire defense of Murder House and Asylum as great drama is a chapter-length application of the Poetics, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Alison Kafer
holes.what: Feminist disability scholar whose Feminist, Queer, Crip develops the political-relational model of disability and the politics of crip futurity against ableist assumptions about the future.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads Addy's and Beau Langdon's fates almost entirely through Kafer's critique of cure-only futures and her insistence that ableism, not disability, is the harm.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Eugenics
holes.what: The movement to improve the human gene pool by controlling reproduction, historically entwined with institutionalization, sterilization, and letting disabled infants die.
holes.why: Chapter 8 argues the modern horror genre was born from eugenic assumptions (The Black Stork, the Production Code) that Constance's treatment of her children reenacts.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Voodoo (Vodun / Vodou / New Orleans Voodoo)
holes.what: African-diaspora religious philosophy of Benin, Haiti, and Louisiana centered on serving the loa, spirit possession, ancestral connection, healing, and the crossing between the living and the dead.
holes.why: Chapter 9 explains Coven's Spirit Wars through Voodoo metaphysics - loa, possession, Papa Legba, zombies, and the gates of Guinee - none of which the taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist whose Stigma (1963) analyzes socially discrediting attributes, virtual versus actual social identity, and the management of spoiled identity.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of Freak Show - stigmatized performers, exploitation, and the show's own casting - is an application of Goffman's stigma theory.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Stigma (spoiled identity)
holes.what: An attribute that reduces its bearer in others' eyes from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one, spoiling social identity and limiting life chances.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses stigma's types (abominations of the body, blemishes of character, tribal stigma) to explain both the fictional freak show and the real one AHS mounts on television.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist whose The Denial of Death argues that human culture is an elaborate 'hero system' of symbolic immortality projects built to deny the terror of mortality.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Roanoke's cannibals, cultists, and reality-TV stars as Becker-style death deniers, and Becker anchors the chapter alongside Terror Management Theory.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Terror Management Theory (TMT)
holes.what: The experimental program (Greenberg, Pyszczynski, Solomon) built on Becker: mortality salience drives worldview defense, self-esteem striving, violence, and symbolic immortality projects.
holes.why: Chapter 16 cites TMT studies to explain Roanoke's murders, cults, and craving for screen time as defenses against the fear of death.
holes.book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally praiseworthy and good yet not obligatory - done above and beyond duty, like the Good Samaritan.
holes.why: Chapter 11's fifth attribute of heroism defines heroes as Extraordinary Samaritans whose saving acts are supererogatory, the criterion separating Wesley Autrey from Captain Sullenberger.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Patriotism (love of country vs nationalism)
holes.what: Civic love and loyalty to one's own nation and community, distinguished from nationalism and debated against cosmopolitanism.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its entire Cap-versus-Iron Man contrast on Scruton's, MacIntyre's and Nussbaum's accounts of patriotism against cosmopolitanism, a concept taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Stephen Darwall
holes.what: Contemporary ethicist known for distinguishing recognition respect (owed to persons as rational agents) from appraisal respect (owed for qualifying merits).
holes.why: Chapter 20's central claim - Cap gives recognition respect and trust while Iron Man gives only appraisal respect - is built directly on Darwall's two faces of respect.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Instrumental Reason (means-end thinking)
holes.what: Fixation on how to achieve goals at the expense of what is being done and why it matters, diagnosed by Adorno and Horkheimer in Dialectic of Enlightenment.
holes.why: Chapter 20 explains Iron Man's failures in Armor Wars and Civil War as instrumental reason eclipsing moral reason, a framework taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Technological Unemployment
holes.what: Job loss caused by automation and AI replacing workers faster than new jobs appear, with universal basic income proposed as a remedy.
holes.why: Chapter 22's core sections, via Martin Ford's Rise of the Robots, argue about displacement under the Fourth Industrial Revolution and the basic-income debate.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Russell's Paradox
holes.what: The set of all sets that do not contain themselves must contain itself if it does not, and vice versa, exposing a contradiction in naive set theory.
holes.why: Chapter 23 models the SHRA's no-win registration dilemma on Russell's paradox, which is why it is titled Iron Man Was Paradoxically Wrong.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: The Mythic Hero Archetype (gods and demigods as proto-superheroes)
holes.what: The Greco-Roman pattern of the craftsman-god (Hephaestus) and the demigod hero (Heracles) that modern superhero archetypes reprise.
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire mapping of Iron Man onto Hephaestus and Captain America onto Heracles rests on this mythic archetype, and taxonomy.json has no mythology or hero-archetype slug for it.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Trust (entrusting, vulnerability and self-trust)
holes.what: A freely given attitude of accepting vulnerability to another based on optimism about their intentions and competence, which cannot be coerced, guaranteed, or replaced by control.
holes.why: Chapter 27's whole argument that Cap's interactive trust beats Tony's objective control, plus its treatment of self-trust and earning trust back, is built on the philosophy of trust, for which the taxonomy has no slug.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: State Sovereignty (monopoly on legitimate violence)
holes.what: A state's supreme authority within its territory, centrally its relative monopoly over the legitimate use of coercive force.
holes.why: Chapter 30's central claim is that superpowered beings render state sovereignty meaningless, and no taxonomy slug names sovereignty itself as distinct from the social contract or the state of nature.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Henotheism (one supreme god among others)
holes.what: The worship of one supreme god that does not deny the possible existence of other, lesser gods.
holes.why: Chapter 31 needs henotheism to reconcile Captain America's 'There's only one God' with the real existence of Thor, Odin and the One-above-all in the Marvel universe, and the taxonomy offers no such concept.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Annihilation vs Attrition (Delbrück's taxonomy of strategy)
holes.what: Hans Delbrück's distinction between strategies that destroy the enemy's military capability in a decisive blow and strategies that grind down the enemy's will or capacity over time.
holes.why: Chapter 35 builds its entire contrast of Captain America as annihilation and Iron Man as technology-driven attrition on this strategic distinction, and the taxonomy has no slug for theories of warfare strategy.
holes.book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe

holes.name: Informal Fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, appeal to fear)
holes.what: Standard errors in reasoning, such as ad hominem, straw man, suppressed evidence, and appeals to fear or force, that persuade regardless of the truth of the conclusion.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is structured as a Party handbook teaching the strategic deployment of these exact fallacies to manufacture false beliefs and prevent thoughtcrime.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Neoliberalism
holes.what: The doctrine that human well-being is best advanced by liberating entrepreneurial freedoms within strong private property rights, free markets, and free trade, remaking the state on the model of the firm.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues that 1984's Doublethink and arbitrary bureaucratic power map onto neoliberal governance, from Chevron deference and whistleblower erosion to the Washington Consensus.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: The Right to Privacy
holes.what: The alleged moral right to control access to information about oneself, one's body, and one's personal space, defended via honor, self-ownership, or dignity.
holes.why: Chapter 18's entire assessment of mass surveillance turns on whether privacy is a right, an honor claim, or a dignity claim, and whether any of these can survive ubiquitous observation.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Philosophy of Sleep
holes.what: The view that sleep and dreaming are active modes of thinking in which the mind continues its own work rather than shutting off.
