holes.why: Chapter 20 argues the Party sleep-hacks Winston because sleep is a site of independent thought, and that our 24/7 devices impose a 'Newsleep' that erodes the reality-fantasy border.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: The Nonidentical (identity thinking)
holes.what: Adorno's concept of the unique, ungraspable other that escapes conceptual subsumption, which 'identity thinking' homogenizes; totalitarianism is identity thinking gone mad.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Julia's love, the ring-doves, and the body's mute protest as the nonidentical persisting inside Oceania's total identity thinking.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Dialectic of Enlightenment (domination of nature)
holes.what: Adorno and Horkheimer's thesis that enlightened reason's drive to subjugate nature within and without turns into instrumental domination, of which totalitarianism is the extreme consequence.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses this frame to read the Party's megalomaniac calculating rationality and its war on emotion, spontaneity, and nature as enlightenment's self-betrayal.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Orality and Literacy (media ecology)
holes.what: The media-ecology thesis (developed by Vilém Flusser, echoing Plato's Phaedrus critique of writing and Nyíri's reading of Wittgenstein) that linear writing creates logical, analytical, history-keeping thought, while orality favors repetition, memorization and chant.
holes.why: Chapter 29's core argument is that Oceania's telescreens force a reversion to orality while Winston's notebook keeps written, linear thought — and thus resistance — alive, a framework taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Scientism
holes.what: The fetishizing of narrow exact science, coupled with contempt for history, literature and other value-laden domains as not really knowledge at all.
holes.why: Chapter 32 argues (via Orwell on Syme, Bernal and the Lysenko affair) that scientism led scientists into political self-deception and helped totalitarianism replace genuine inquiry with pseudo-inquiry.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Speech Act Theory (performatives)
holes.what: J.L. Austin's theory (refined by John Searle) that utterances perform actions, analyzed into locution (what is said), illocution (what is intended) and perlocution (the effect).
holes.why: Chapter 33 uses speech act theory as its main lens on the Party's slogans, Syme's Newspeak, Julia's note and Twitter's mindcasting, but taxonomy.json has no speech-act slug and no J.L. Austin entry.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Principle of Non-Contradiction
holes.what: Aristotle's most certain principle: the same property cannot both belong and not belong to the same thing in the same respect at the same time (Metaphysics IV), earlier formulated in terms of opposites by Plato (Republic IV).
holes.why: Chapter 35 reads Newspeak's 'blackwhite', doublethink and Winston's finger-counting as the Party's systematic denial of non-contradiction, against the formulations of Plato, Aristotle and Avicenna; no logic slug exists in taxonomy.json.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Post-Factual Democracy (post-truth politics)
holes.what: A political condition in which opportune narratives and appeals to emotion replace facts and evidence as the basis of public debate, opinion formation and policymaking.
holes.why: Chapter 37 coins and diagnoses post-factual democracy (Trump's 'alternative facts', Brexit, fake news, the attention economy) as the real-world Ministry of Truth and argues it voids democratic legitimacy; taxonomy.json has no post-truth slug.
holes.book: 116 - 1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile

holes.name: Gorgias
holes.what: Sophist rhetorician whose Encomium of Helen likens persuasive speech to magic or drugs that rob listeners of free will.
holes.why: Chapter 9 builds its reading of Adams's Master Persuader hypothesis directly on Gorgias's claim that the right words reprogram an audience regardless of truth.
holes.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

holes.name: Sophistic Rhetoric (persuasion vs. truth)
holes.what: The Sophistic doctrine, opposed by Socrates in the Gorgias and Phaedrus, that persuasive power over an audience matters independently of truth and can be used for moral improvement or mere flattery.
holes.why: Chapter 9's whole framework is the Socratic-versus-Sophistic dichotomy about rhetoric, and taxonomy.json has only Protagoras's relativism, not the rhetoric-versus-truth debate this book turns on.
holes.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

holes.name: Confirmation Bias
holes.what: The unconscious tendency to seek and favor evidence that confirms one's existing beliefs while discounting disconfirming evidence.
holes.why: Chapters 17, 18, 27, and 28 all pivot on Adams's claim that bias is the human operating system, and the debate over whether that makes us irrational needs this concept, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

holes.name: Jason Brennan
holes.what: Contemporary political philosopher who defends epistocracy, restricting or weighting the vote to the competent (his hobbits, hooligans, and Vulcans typology).
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses Brennan's voter-licensing proposal as the modern heir to Plato's attack on rule by the ignorant, at comparable length to Plato and Mill themselves.
holes.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

holes.name: Ontology of Fictional Characters
holes.what: The debate over what fictional beings are: discovered possible worlds (possibilism), Meinongian nonexistent objects, or abstract artifacts created by authors (creationism).
holes.why: Chapter 24 exists to decide what Dogbert metaphysically is, and its possible-worlds machinery alone cannot capture the possibilism-Meinongianism-creationism dispute it surveys.
holes.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

holes.name: William Kingdon Clifford
holes.what: Victorian mathematician-philosopher whose ethics of belief holds it is always and everywhere wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 28 makes Clifford's epistemic responsibility the central standard by which Adams's climate-science pronouncements are judged irresponsible.
holes.book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality

holes.name: Scientism
holes.what: The fallacy of elevating science or scientific-sounding methods beyond what they can deliver, treating them as the only or guaranteed route to knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 11's central claim is that CSI-style forensics and TV procedurals commit scientism, which Cooper's unscientific methods expose; the chapter exists to apply this concept to crime-solving.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Madonna–Whore Complex
holes.what: Freud's diagnosis of men who split women into pure Madonnas they can love and debased whores they can desire, never both in one person.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument reads Laura Palmer's doubled identity, BOB's degradation, and the Fireman's idealization through this complex, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Incomplete Symbols (theory of descriptions)
holes.what: Russell's view that phrases like 'the present king of France' are meaningful without naming anything, acquiring complete meaning only in context.
holes.why: Chapter 17 models Lynch's ambiguous symbols (the traffic light, the foghorn, Harriet's line) as aesthetic versions of Russell's incomplete symbols.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: 20th-century American philosopher of mind and art who held that art creates virtual forms symbolic of feeling, with film presenting a dream-like 'virtual present.'
holes.why: Chapter 17 leans on Langer's Feeling and Form to explain why Twin Peaks' dream-logic imagery (especially Part 8) communicates feeling that explicit language cannot.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Roman Ingarden
holes.what: Polish phenomenologist who analyzed the artwork as a schematized structure of indeterminacies completed by the perceiver in a movement from potentiality to actuality.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Ingarden's schematization to explain why the Red Room dance scene needs the viewer's participation to become a work of art.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Estrangement Effect (Verfremdungseffekt)
holes.what: Brecht's theatrical technique of deliberately breaking the audience's immersion so viewers stay aware they are watching a constructed performance.
holes.why: Chapter 19 compares Twin Peaks' ambiguously diegetic music and self-aware melodrama to Brecht's estrangement effect as its main engine of audience discomfort.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: The Uncanny Valley
holes.what: The unease or revulsion triggered by figures that are almost but not quite human, falling short of engaging our empathy response.
holes.why: Chapter 19 extends the uncanny valley to behavior, arguing the townsfolk's slightly-off conduct and the Red Room entities place viewers between human and nonhuman.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Power-Over vs Power-To
holes.what: Feminist distinction between power as domination over other people and power as the ability to accomplish things through one's own capacities and resources.
holes.why: Chapter 22's whole argument sorts Josie's, Audrey's, Lana's, and Nadine's fates by whether they wield power-over or power-to, a distinction taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: The Angel in the House
holes.what: The Victorian ideal of the pure, selfless, domestic woman whose perfection is completed only by her death, as analyzed by Gilbert and Gubar's The Madwoman in the Attic.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues Laura Palmer is the Angel in the House reborn — valued most as a beautiful dying girl — and that the Bomb births a world built to destroy her.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Divine Madness (the manic art)
holes.what: Socrates' claim in the Phaedrus that madness sent by the gods — prophetic, poetic, erotic — is the channel of the greatest blessings and nobler than sober reason.
holes.why: Chapter 24 reads Cooper's dream-based detection as Socratic divine madness, with the show elevating madness over rationality as the road to truth.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Catharsis (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's notion from the Poetics that tragedy purges — or, on alternative readings, purifies and frees — the emotions spectators feel toward an artwork.
holes.why: Chapter 26 defines the viewer's release from the tyranny of rationality as a catharsis in exactly this Aristotelian sense, via Trela's reading of emotions purged of reality.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: Radford's puzzle of how we can feel genuine, rational emotions for characters we know do not exist.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is built on this paradox — why we love Cooper and hate James — and resolves it with Thomasson's abstract artifacts and parasocial-identification research.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Amie Thomasson
holes.what: Contemporary metaphysician who argues fictional characters exist as abstract artifacts created by authors and sustained by records of them.
holes.why: Chapter 27 adopts Thomasson's Fiction and Metaphysics as its resolution: Dale Cooper really exists as an abstract artifact, so our emotions toward him are rational.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Paul Ricoeur
holes.what: 20th-century French philosopher whose The Symbolism of Evil analyzes how evil is symbolized, notably as the defilement of the pure by something external.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Ricoeur's defilement symbolism to read the filthy-haired BOB, the soot-covered Woodsmen, and the frog-moth's contamination of the sleeping girl.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: François de La Rochefoucauld
holes.what: 17th-century French moralist whose maxims analyze amour-propre — self-love that breeds flattery, feigned virtue, and disguising oneself even to oneself.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses La Rochefoucauld's courtly amour-propre to explain Josie Packard's self-loss through dissimulation and Norma's refusal to feign virtue.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Jouissance (enjoyment beyond pleasure)
holes.what: Lacan's notion of an excessive enjoyment beyond mere pleasure, taken in what is missing or painful rather than in completion.
holes.why: Chapter 32 explains the cult pleasure of Twin Peaks' missing pieces — coffee without milk, the absent Laura, the Venere pudica — through jouissance as opposed to plaisir.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Pataphysics
holes.what: Alfred Jarry's 'science of imaginary solutions' that studies exceptions rather than general rules, superimposed on metaphysics as metaphysics is on physics.
holes.why: Chapter 33's whole reading treats Cooper's rock-throwing, tree-sniffing, and dream-clue methods as pataphysical imaginary solutions to the Laura Palmer case.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Gustav Fechner
holes.what: 19th-century German philosopher-psychologist who held a dual-aspect, animistic view of the world with a 'day view' and 'night view' of reality.
holes.why: Chapter 33 models Lynch's superimposed worlds — the Log Lady's animate log, glimpses of the Lodge — on Fechner's two-sided, ensouled universe.
holes.book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

holes.name: Guy Debord
holes.what: Situationist Marxist theorist of The Society of the Spectacle, in which social relations are replaced by relations mediated by images and commodities.
holes.why: Chapter 18 reads Inside Amy Schumer wholesale as an illustration of Debord's spectacle, from mediated romance to celebrity alienation, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist founder of symbolic interactionism who explained the self as socially formed through the interplay of the 'I' and the 'Me'.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses Mead's Mind, Self, and Society to explain how Schumer built her comic self through others' reactions, and he is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Hélène Cixous
holes.what: French feminist theorist of ecriture feminine whose 'The Laugh of the Medusa' calls on women to write their bodies and smash patriarchal truth with laughter.
holes.why: Chapter 24 frames Schumer's comedy as Cixous's Medusan laughter breaking up truth, quoting the essay throughout.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French feminist philosopher who reclaims mimesis as deliberately resubmitting women to sexist stereotypes in order to call the stereotypes themselves into question.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses Irigaray's strategic mimesis as the mechanism behind Schumer's stereotype-performing sketches like 'I'm So Bad'.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Sandra Bartky
holes.what: Feminist philosopher whose 'Fashion-Beauty Complex' analysis shows beauty norms functioning as disciplinary, capitalist oppression of women.
holes.why: Chapter 30's account of beauty oppression in I Feel Pretty is built directly on Bartky's Fashion-Beauty Complex.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Incongruity Theory of Comic Amusement
holes.what: Theory that laughter arises from perceived, non-threatening, non-cognitively-demanding violations of our expectations about how things are or should be.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues incongruity theory, not psychoanalysis, best explains the feminist subversion of decorum in Schumer's sketches.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Superiority Theory of Humor
holes.what: Theory that we laugh at a perceived butt of a joke from a position of felt superiority, giving laughter an element of cruelty.
holes.why: Chapter 10's question of whether the butt of Schumer's self-deprecating jokes is her or the shaming standard is framed entirely within superiority theory.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Relief Theory of Humor
holes.what: Freud's view that laughter discharges psychic energy otherwise spent repressing socially unacceptable feelings like anger, shame, and grief.
holes.why: Chapter 9 grounds Schumer's gallows humor and self-deprecation in Freud's relief theory, which the taxonomy lacks despite listing Freud.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Mimesis (imitation)
holes.what: Aristotle's notion of art and drama as imitation of nature and persons, reclaimed by Irigaray as strategic repetition of stereotypes to undermine them.
holes.why: Chapter 24 makes mimesis the key mechanism of Schumer's satire, running from Aristotle's Poetics to Irigaray's feminist rewriting.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Wabi-Sabi
holes.what: Japanese aesthetic ideal that finds serenity and beauty in imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness, exemplified by kintsugi's golden-repaired pottery.
holes.why: Chapter 12 lands its case for Schumer's self-acceptance on wabi-sabi and kintsugi as the alternative to Western perfectionism.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Bad Conscience (internalized guilt)
holes.what: Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals II account of guilt as socially inflicted pain turned inward, making people docile and easy to rule.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Snatched as enacting Nietzsche's claim that feeling bad is socially manufactured, a Genealogy thesis the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: The Standard of Taste (Hume)
holes.what: Hume's account of aesthetic value as socially determined, with refined judges as the informal standard, though moral sensibilities color their verdicts.
holes.why: Chapter 22 appeals to Hume's Standard of Taste to explain why critics punish Snatched for offending their morals.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Psychological Egoism
holes.what: Descriptive thesis that self-interest is the sole ultimate motivator of every human action, distinct from the ethical egoism the taxonomy records.
holes.why: Chapter 11 tests psychological egoism against Schumer's selfish characters and apparent altruists, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Implicit Bias
holes.what: Unconscious stereotypical attitudes that shape judgment without awareness but can be indirectly controlled by examining the stereotypes that feed them.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explains grape zones and rape-myth testimony as products of implicit bias and its debiasing strategies.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Rape Culture
holes.what: A social environment in which rape is endemic and normalized through stereotypes, excuses, and institutional failure to prosecute.
holes.why: Chapter 25 defines its grape zones as components of rape culture, and chapters 24 and 27 analyze Schumer sketches about it.
holes.book: 120 - Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!

holes.name: Surrealism (Breton)
holes.what: André Breton's movement defining art as psychic automatism — the imagination functioning free of rational control — seeking the point where the real and the imagined cease to be perceived as contradictions.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central thesis is that The Twilight Zone is a televised expression of surrealist philosophy, reading 'A World of His Own' as automatic writing and 'The Mirror' as Dalí's paranoiac-critical method.
holes.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's category of experience that is simultaneously strangely familiar and alien, provoked when repressed or rationality-bound material breaks loose.
holes.why: Chapter 10 argues the show's episodes (e.g. 'The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' 'A Stop at Willoughby') work precisely by provoking this uncanny experience in viewers — the affective signature of the Zone.
holes.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian philosopher and literary critic whose The Four Loves distinguishes charity, affection, friendship, and Eros, characterized by gift-love, need-love, and appreciative-love.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire analysis of whether Corry truly loves the robot Alicia is conducted through Lewis's four types and three qualities of love.
holes.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit

holes.name: Non-Place (Augé)
holes.what: Marc Augé's term for the anonymous transit spaces of supermodernity — roads, airports, hotels, malls — where neither singular identity nor genuine relations form.
holes.why: Chapter 24 reads the Zone's roads, ships, planes, hotel rooms, and malls as Augéan non-places that stage 1950s anonymity and identity crisis.
holes.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit

holes.name: Paul Churchland
holes.what: Philosopher of mind whose connectionism holds that cognition works through prototypes in massively parallel neural networks rather than sentence-like representations.
holes.why: Chapter 28 needs Churchland's prototypes and vector recategorization to explain the neural jolt of pleasure when a twist ending forces a story under a new prototype, as in 'To Serve Man.'
holes.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit

holes.name: The Society of the Spectacle
holes.what: Guy Debord's diagnosis that social relations in advanced capitalism are mediated by images, so that politics, authenticity, and even resistance become consumable spectacle.
holes.why: Chapter 33 applies Debord's spectacle to Black Mirror's 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits' to show image-politics turning totalitarianism into entertainment and rebellion into product.
holes.book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit

holes.name: Narrative Identity (life as narrative)
holes.what: The view that a self is constituted by the intelligible narrative it tells of its own life, subject to constraints of coherence (MacIntyre; Williams's critique; Schechtman).
holes.why: Chapter 4's whole frame — role-play as authoring a competing narrative of the self against MacIntyre's unity and Williams's constraints of coherence — depends on this concept, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Functionalism (being = structure and function)
holes.what: The view that what a thing is is fixed by its structure and what it does, so anything structured and functioning like a person is a person.
holes.why: Chapter 5's central claim that hosts are persons and that 'to be simulated is to be real' rests entirely on functionalism/structuralism, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: The Uncanny Valley
holes.what: Masahiro Mori's observation that humanlike robots gain our affinity up to a point, but near-human likeness with small flaws triggers sudden unease.
holes.why: Chapter 7 uses the uncanny valley to explain why the hosts' near-human appearance and movements turn revulsion into empathy and destabilize the human/robot boundary.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Narrative Identity (life as narrative)
holes.what: The view that a self is constituted by the self-told story of its actions, experiences, and psychological characteristics (Shoemaker, Schechtman).
holes.why: Chapter 8 explicitly conceptualizes Maeve's evolution in terms of narrative identity, cited to Shoemaker and Schechtman, as the ground of her personhood against her programmed narratives.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Eliminative Materialism (folk psychology is false)
holes.what: The Churchland-style doctrine that common-sense mental concepts like beliefs, desires, and the inner self are false theoretical posits that completed neuroscience will eliminate.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument reads Robert Ford's 'consciousness does not exist' as eliminative materialism shared with Paul Churchland (folk psychology) and Dennett, and taxonomy has no slug for this doctrine or for Paul Churchland.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Julian Jaynes
holes.what: Psychologist whose bicameral-mind theory holds that ancient humans obeyed hallucinated commands from one brain hemisphere until consciousness emerged as self-command.
holes.why: Chapter 15 devotes a section to Jaynes's theory, comparing bicameral beings to Frankfurt's wantons to explain Dolores's commanding voice and the episode title 'The Bicameral Mind.'
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Julian Jaynes
holes.what: Psychologist whose bicameral-mind theory holds that early humans heard stress-induced auditory commands ('to hear was to obey') before reflective consciousness arose.
holes.why: Chapter 16 threads Jaynes's theory through its account of the hosts' awakening — the commanding voice that becomes one's own — alongside Kant, Nietzsche, and Korsgaard.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Annette C. Baier
holes.what: Twentieth-century moral philosopher who argued that persons are 'second persons' - selves built through childhood relationships and mutual cross-examination - and analyzed trust and the 'vital but dangerous art' of selective attention and self-deception.
holes.why: Chapter 19 builds its entire account of host and human freedom on Baier's conjectures that self-conscious awareness comes from personal interaction and that personal freedom depends on others' willingness to challenge our self-deceptions.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: The Bicameral Mind (Jaynes)
holes.what: Julian Jaynes's theory that ancient minds operated in two chambers - hallucinated god-voices directing action - and that consciousness emerged when this broke down into introspective self-narration.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads Dolores's inner voice of Arnold and the hosts' split selves through the show's namesake bicameral-mind framework ('collective bicameral mind' as doppelganger), which no taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of how we can feel genuine emotions for characters we know do not exist, with Lamarque's answer that merely entertaining a thought, not believing it, suffices to move us.
holes.why: Chapter 22 rests its 'fiction theory' of Bernard's grief for his fabricated son on this philosophy-of-fiction debate, for which taxonomy has no entry at all.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Arthur Danto
holes.what: Philosopher of art whose Brillo Box argument holds that perceptually indiscernible objects can differ in art status only through theory and artworld context - the problem of 'indiscernibles'.
holes.why: Chapter 24's title argument uses Danto's indiscernibles to explain how hosts and guests (and art and entertainment) can be visually identical yet differ in status for autonomous viewers.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Avant-Garde and Kitsch
holes.what: Clement Greenberg's distinction between self-critical avant-garde art and standardized, consumer-pleasing kitsch that merely satisfies mass taste.
holes.why: Chapter 24 frames its central question - is Westworld self-referential art or 'meta-kitsch'? - through Greenberg's divide, which no existing taxonomy slug captures.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: The Naked and the Nude (aesthetics of nudity)
holes.what: Kenneth Clark's art-theoretical distinction between nakedness (the vulnerable, imperfect unclothed body) and the nude (the idealized body re-formed as art), extended by Berger's spectator gaze and Steinberg's incarnation symbolism.
holes.why: Chapter 25's three-part reading of Westworld's nudity (art form, male dominance, becoming human) is built directly on this framework, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: The purging of pity and fear that Aristotle says tragedy produces in its audience.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues Westworld works as a Greek tragedy whose catharsis comes from viewers' compassion for the hosts' suffering, a Poetics concept absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

holes.name: Social Cycle Theory
holes.what: The view, traced from Plato, Aristotle, and Sima Qian to modern sociologists, that political history repeats in cycles rather than progressing linearly.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire reading of Gilead as a credible near future rests on social cycles—Puritanism, purges, and child-seizures recur, and June repeats the former Offred's story.
holes.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

holes.name: Monumental History (use and abuse of history)
holes.what: Nietzsche's account of the dangerous, mythologizing use of the past to glorify a regime, contrasted with a critical use of history in the service of life.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads Gilead's and Ingsoc's rewritten Bibles and records as precisely Nietzschean monumentalism and contrasts it with the critical approach to history.
holes.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The theory that a belief or statement is true if and only if it corresponds to the way the world actually is.
holes.why: Chapter 14's case that Trump-era 'alternative facts' echo Gilead rests wholly on this theory: an alternative fact is a proposition that fails to correspond with reality.
holes.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

holes.name: Remix Culture (sampling and transformation)
holes.what: The theory, from remix studies, that all cultural production samples and transforms prior material, so no work is a pure original and no original exists to copy.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames Gilead as a restrictive remix of scripture and reads Offred's tale as an always-already-reconstructed remix, dissolving the question of Gilead's authenticity.
holes.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

holes.name: Biopower (making live and letting die)
holes.what: Foucault's notion of modern power over life: managing populations through birth, death, health, and reproduction, fostering some groups and letting others die.
holes.why: Chapter 22's core reading of Gilead—sorting desirable from undesirable populations, keeping fertile Handmaids alive, letting Unwomen and unbabies die—is biopower, which chapter 34 also applies to the medicalized control of women's bodies.
holes.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist and philosopher who analyzed power through forms of capital—economic, social, cultural, and resistant—rather than money alone.
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses Bourdieu's capitals to explain what value and power a Handmaid like Offred can hold when money is worthless and relationships and know-how are everything.
holes.book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: Marxist literary theorist who analyzed postmodernism as the cultural logic of late capitalism, marked by pastiche, the erasure of high/low art, and depthlessness.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire framework for reading Petty's music and persona as postmodern is built on Jameson's account of pastiche, commodified history, and 'free-floating' affect.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French philosopher of the 'general economy': excess energy that must be wasted, sacrifice, the accursed share, and the sacred/profane boundary of thinghood.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads Petty's videos 'Don't Come Around Here No More' and 'Mary Jane's Last Dance' entirely through Bataille's economy of waste, sacrifice and the creepy.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Matthew Ratcliffe
holes.what: Phenomenologist of mood and existential feelings who distinguishes everyday empathy from 'radical' empathy that refuses to presuppose a shared world.
holes.why: Chapter 16 leans on Ratcliffe's radical empathy and existential feelings to explain how the narrator of 'Insider' finally understands his beloved.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Authentic Love (Beauvoir)
holes.what: Beauvoir's ideal of love founded on the reciprocal recognition of each lover's freedom rather than fusion, delusion, or possession.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues 'Insider' charts a move from the lovers' mind-reading delusion toward exactly this Beauvoirian authentic love.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: The Arrogant Eye and the Loving Eye
holes.what: Frye's contrast between a presumptuous seeing that projects one's own mind onto others and a disciplined, self-knowing, loving attention.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Frye's arrogant/loving eye distinction, not her birdcage model, as the central tool for interpreting 'Insider'.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Susan McClary
holes.what: Feminist musicologist of the New Musicology who analyzes how music constructs gender through lyrics and composition (Feminine Endings).
holes.why: Chapter 17 explicitly adopts McClary's feminist music analysis as the framework for reading Petty's Greatest Hits catalog as feminist.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Ernst Cassirer
holes.what: Neo-Kantian philosopher of symbolic forms and humane humanism, Heidegger's opponent in the 1929 Davos debate.
holes.why: Chapter 21 stages Petty's 'change of heart' against the Cassirer-Heidegger Davos confrontation and holds up Cassirer's decency as the anti-asshole ideal.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Assholes: A Theory
holes.what: Aaron James's account of the asshole as someone who consciously and self-servingly exempts himself from rules he knows apply to everyone else.
holes.why: Chapter 21 builds its moral (try not to be an asshole) and its indictment of Heidegger directly on James's definition.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Objectivism vs Subjectivism about Value
holes.what: The debate over whether value (here, of music) consists only in listeners' subjective enjoyment or partly in mind-independent properties people can be mistaken about.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues Petty held a partially objectivist view of music's value, which grounds his ethical critique of profit-maximizing record companies.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: We-Mode and Shared Agency
holes.what: Theories (Tuomela, Bratman) of group agency, joint action, and collective commitment in which individuals act for group reasons rather than purely personal ones.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reinterprets Petty's legal battles with MCA as we-mode group action of the Heartbreakers rather than lone-hero individualism.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri
holes.what: Political theorists of Empire (2000) who analyze how global capitalist systems co-opt and absorb rebellion.
holes.why: Chapter 27 opens with Hardt and Negri's thesis that co-option (selling out), not failure, is the rebel's true opposite.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Josiah Royce
holes.what: American idealist philosopher of community and loyalty who held that genuine loyalty is to ideals and expresses itself as justice (The Philosophy of Loyalty, 1908).
holes.why: Chapter 28 grounds its account of Petty's misplaced-then-corrected Confederate loyalty in Royce's philosophy of loyalty.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: William K. Clifford
holes.what: Author of 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877), the evidentialist thesis that it is wrong always to believe anything on insufficient evidence, illustrated by the shipowner.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses Clifford's shipowner and ethics of belief as the core framework for Petty's 'Power Drunk' and 'Playing Dumb' critique of self-deception.
holes.book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

holes.name: Intrinsic vs Instrumental Value
holes.what: Something has intrinsic value when it is valued for what it is in itself, and instrumental value when valued only as a means to something else.
holes.why: Chapter 1 ('The Genuine Article') is organized entirely around whether genuine Beth, reality itself, and happiness are intrinsically or merely instrumentally valuable, and no taxonomy slug covers the distinction.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Underdetermination of Theory by Evidence
holes.what: A theory is underdetermined when the available evidence could equally well support rival theories, so no observation can decide between them.
holes.why: Chapter 3 makes the 'devastating' epistemological problem that every possible piece of evidence for the simulation hypothesis equally supports its denial the centerpiece of its skepticism.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Correspondence and Coherence Theories of Truth
holes.what: The correspondence theory says a claim is true when it matches an actual state of the world; the coherence theory says truth is consistency with all other true claims.
holes.why: Chapter 6 ('Truth in a Multiverse') builds its whole account of what makes claims true across timelines on this correspondence/coherence distinction, which taxonomy lacks, having only James's pragmatic truth.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Confirmation Bias and Dual-Process Thinking
holes.what: The tendency to seek and favor evidence confirming existing beliefs, driven by fast automatic System 1 thinking over slow deliberate System 2 reasoning (Kahneman, Wason).
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire analysis of the Headism religion in 'Get Schwifty' rests on illusory correlation, confirmation bias, and System 1/System 2 cognition, none of which taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Aquinas on Ignorance and Moral Responsibility
holes.what: Aquinas's distinction between concomitant, feigned or negligent, and consequent ignorance, which determines when ignorance excuses an action from moral responsibility.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses the three kinds of ignorance to decide whether Beth is morally responsible for shooting Mr. Poopybutthole, a doctrine taxonomy lacks among its Aquinas entries.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Supererogation (acts beyond duty)
holes.what: Supererogatory acts are praiseworthy deeds that go beyond moral obligation, so that declining them is not wrong, a category utilitarianism refuses to recognize.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire two-part debate over whether Jerry must give Shrimply Pibbles his penis, and by extension whether we must donate kidneys and blood, turns on the obligatory/supererogatory line.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Self-Respect (recognition vs appraisal; servility)
holes.what: Recognition self-respect is the regard owed to oneself as a rational autonomous agent, appraisal self-respect is earned for one's traits, and its absence is servility (Darwall, Hill).
holes.why: Chapter 14's diagnosis of Jerry, and its contrast with Rick's portal-assisted irresponsibility, is built on Darwall's two kinds of self-respect and Hill on servility, which kant-respect alone does not capture.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century novelist-philosopher whose Objectivism (rational egoism) holds rational self-interest as the highest virtue, rejecting altruism, collectivism, and mysticism.
holes.why: Chapter 18's entire thesis is that Rick is an Objectivist in Rand's sense, her 'ideal man', and taxonomy has no entry for Rand or Objectivism.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Max Stirner
holes.what: Nineteenth-century German egoist anarchist who held that only one's own interest and ability limit action, with egoists free to form loose unions of mutual need.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Stirner's individualist anarchism to distinguish the loner Rick from the Citadel of Ricks, which the chapter says Stirner's union of egoists actually describes.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: The Crowd Is Untruth (the public and leveling)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's critique of 'the public' as an abstraction in which the crowd becomes untruth, leveling individuals through envy, gossip, and passionless inaction.
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole reading of the Citadel of Ricks as envy, leveling, and passionlessness rests on this Kierkegaardian concept, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 125 - Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch

holes.name: Art-Horror (the paradox of horror)
holes.what: Noel Carroll's account of horror fiction: categorically transgressive, interstitial monsters produce art-horror through thought-based fear and disgust, and curiosity about them yields a paradoxical pleasure.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its entire explanation of the Demogorgon's appeal on Carroll's art-horror (with Kieran and Feagin on the grotesque), and chapters 16-17 reuse it; no taxonomy slug covers philosophy of horror.
holes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

holes.name: Terror Management (the denial of death)
holes.what: Ernest Becker's thesis that humans, uniquely aware of their mortality, build cultural and symbolic 'armor' (flags, religion, teams) to buffer the anxiety of death.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Becker's Denial of Death alongside Kierkegaard to explain why we seek out horror from a position of safety and why the Shadow Monster terrifies.
holes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

holes.name: The Demiurge (Gnosticism)
holes.what: A craftsman-creator entity, from Plato's Timaeus through Plotinus and the Gnostics, who fashions the material world as an imperfect copy of ultimate reality; for Sethian Gnostics an evil false god (Yaldabaoth).
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole reading of the Mind Flayer as ruler of the Upside Down works by comparing Plato's, Plotinus's, and the Sethian Gnostic versions of the Demiurge, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

holes.name: The Monster and the Abnormal (Abnormal lectures)
holes.what: Foucault's account of the juridico-natural monster (violating laws of nature and society) and the three figures, monster, individual to be corrected, masturbator, from which the modern 'abnormal' is produced via normalization.
holes.why: Chapter 24 defines every monster in the show through this framework, and no taxonomy slug captures Foucault's monster/abnormality analysis distinct from power-knowledge.
holes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist social philosopher whose symbolic interactionism holds that the self emerges from social interaction through shared symbols and stable 'identity anchors.'
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire account of Will Byers's identity before, during, and after Mind Flayer possession is built on Mead's symbolic interactionism, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

holes.name: The Monster and the Abnormal (Abnormal lectures)
holes.what: Foucault's account of the juridico-natural monster and the three figures (monster, individual to be corrected, masturbator) from which the modern 'abnormal' is produced through normalization and biopolitics.
holes.why: Chapter 29 structures its whole reading of freaks, tomboys, and 1980s normalcy around the three figures from Foucault's Abnormal, the same gap as chapter 24.
holes.book: 126 - Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon

holes.name: Art as Expression of Emotion (expression theory)
holes.what: The Croce-Collingwood-Langer view that art expresses and communicates emotion (creating a 'virtual' of space or time) rather than merely arousing it, enabling person-to-person understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 13's middle section rests on expression theory and Langer's 'virtual' to argue replicants' aesthetic-emotional acts prove personhood, which taxonomy's kant-aesthetics does not cover.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Hierocles
holes.what: Stoic philosopher (c. 2nd century AD) whose concentric circles describe oikeiosis, the expansion of self-concern from one's own body outward to family, community, and all rational beings.
holes.why: Chapter 14 structures its four-stage account of K becoming human entirely around Hierocles's circles and the Stoic doctrine of oikeiosis.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac
holes.what: Enlightenment empiricist whose living-statue thought experiment traces how touch alone generates awareness of one's body, external objects, and the self.
holes.why: Chapter 15 uses Condillac's statue (and Maine de Biran's revision of it) as the isolated-subject account of humanness that the film's relational, hands-and-touch answer refutes.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view (associated with N. Katherine Hayles) that persons are amalgams of biological and informational-technological components, so the human is not tied to the natural human body.
holes.why: Chapter 16's entire argument that replicants and Joi are 'posthuman' — bodies and identities built from bioengineering, artificial memory, and technology — rests on Hayles's posthumanist theory, absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Philosopher whose five-criteria functionalist test (consciousness, reason, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness) defines personhood independently of species membership.
holes.why: Chapter 17 measures Joi against Warren's five personhood criteria before mounting the Buddhist no-self challenge against them.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Doctrine of the Two Truths
holes.what: Nagarjuna's distinction between conventional truth (persons and objects usefully exist) and ultimate truth (nothing exists independently), allowing both levels to be true at once.
holes.why: Chapter 17 resolves whether Luv murdered Joi and who can be punished through the two truths, the chapter's explicitly named solution concept.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Picture Theory of Language
holes.what: The Tractatus view that language works by picturing possible states of affairs, which need not describe how things actually are.
holes.why: Chapter 23 explains Wallace's poetic, possibility-painting speech ('storm Eden and retake her') through Wittgenstein's picture theory, a different doctrine from taxonomy's later-Wittgenstein language-games.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: William Blake
holes.what: Poet-artist whose mythology of Orc, Lucifer, and the contraries pictures rebellion against God as the energetic source of freedom and creativity.
holes.why: Chapter 32 opens with Batty's misquoted Blake, reads Roy as Blake's Orc, and quotes The Marriage of Heaven and Hell to frame the films' angelic rebellion.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: The Great Chain of Being
holes.what: Hierarchical Christian cosmology ranking every being from God down to inert matter, each fulfilling the place and purpose assigned by its maker.
holes.why: Chapter 32 uses the Great Chain of Being's contradiction between ontological place and moral freedom to explain Wallace's angels and what it means to go off baseline.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Becoming-Woman (Deleuze and Guattari)
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's concept of the girl/woman as a destabilizing vacancy or universal other that transforms masculine binary structures — distinct from Beauvoir's account of becoming a woman.
holes.why: Chapter 36's whole reading of Joi, Luv, and Rachael is built on Deleuze and Guattari's becoming-woman; taxonomy's becoming-woman slug is Beauvoir's different feminist concept.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Friedrich Hayek
holes.what: Austrian liberal economist who argued markets aggregate dispersed knowledge better than planners and that state economic control slides into totalitarianism (The Road to Serfdom).
holes.why: Chapter 38 uses Hayek's three Road to Serfdom arguments to read stateless, corporate-dominated Los Angeles as the realized libertarian utopia.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Neo-Roman Liberty (freedom as non-dependence)
holes.what: The republican tradition (Roman law, Sidney, Machiavelli, recovered by Quentin Skinner) defining freedom as independence from another's will, not mere absence of interference.
holes.why: Chapter 38 needs neo-Roman liberty to explain Luv as a slave despite never being coerced — the blind spot it exposes in Nozick's and Berlin's negative liberty.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Mary Midgley
holes.what: Philosopher who grounded moral considerability in suffering, emotional fellowship, and minding what happens to one, rather than in species membership.
holes.why: Chapter 39 uses Midgley's three 'Persons and Nonpersons' criteria to argue that replicants and undocumented immigrants plainly qualify as persons.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Primordialism vs Constructivism (ethnic identity)
holes.what: Social-science debate over whether ethnic identity is a fixed inheritance by birth and nature or a fluid construct activated by social and political context.
holes.why: Chapter 40's analysis of replicants as an ethnic group and of K's identity shift rests entirely on the primordialism-constructivism framework.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Capitalist Realism
holes.what: Mark Fisher's claim that capitalism is widely held to be the only viable political-economic system, foreclosing the imagination of coherent alternatives.
holes.why: Chapter 41 argues 2049's dystopia cannot picture a post-capitalist future because capitalist realism has captured its imagination.
holes.book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World

holes.name: Wonder as the Beginning of Philosophy
holes.what: The feeling (thaumazein) with which philosophy begins, per Plato's Theaetetus and Aristotle's Metaphysics, a giddy yet quieting confrontation with the being of things.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire argument reads Mister Rogers's slow, silent show as the cultivated leisure in which this feeling of wonder, not mere curiosity, opens philosophy.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Mesmerism (animal magnetism)
holes.what: Franz Mesmer's theory of 'animal magnetism', debunked as science but surviving as hypnosis and the idea of magnetic personal charisma.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues Mister Rogers literally mesmerized children and Senator Pastore, tracing his hypnotic appeal from Mesmer through Freudian transference to screen charisma.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Pierre Hadot
holes.what: Historian of ancient philosophy who argued philosophy was originally a way of life, spiritual exercises aimed at inner transformation, not doctrine.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Hadot's 'philosophy as a way of life' as its central framework: Mister Rogers philosophizes as a communal way of life, not academic discourse.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Philosophy as a Way of Life
holes.what: Hadot's account of ancient philosophy as lived practice yielding peace of mind and inner freedom, in service of the human community.
holes.why: Chapter 12 needs it to claim Rogers's neighborhood is philosophy itself as lived practice rather than discourse about philosophy.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Philosophy for Children (P4C / community of inquiry)
holes.what: Lipman and Jackson's movement bringing philosophy into K-12 schooling through intellectually safe 'communities of inquiry'.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues Mister Rogers's show did on television exactly what p4c Hawaii does in classrooms, and the authors practice P4C themselves.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Maria Montessori
holes.what: Italian physician and educator whose 'planes of development' and 'prepared environment' treat education as an aid to the child's self-construction and the work of peace.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues the show is a Montessori prepared environment, with every transition and set detail developmentally aimed at peace through emotional growth.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Eugene Gendlin
holes.what: Philosopher-psychologist whose theory of 'experiencing' and symbolization (and the practice of Focusing) holds that naming felt meaning changes it.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds entirely on Gendlin's experiencing-and-symbols framework to explain how mentioning feelings makes them manageable.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Transitional Object (Winnicott)
holes.what: Winnicott's 'first not-me possession' (blanket, soft toy) that bridges the child's inner and outer reality and weans it from the caregiver.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues the Make-Believe puppets function as transitional objects and phenomena, which is why toddlers love them and Mister Rogers disappears behind them.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Parasocial Interaction
holes.what: Horton and Wohl's one-sided relationships in which audiences treat mediated television personas as friends and intimates.
holes.why: Chapter 20 needs it to explain how a child on a couch can genuinely befriend, imitate, and learn from Mister Rogers and his puppets through a screen.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: George Santayana
holes.what: American philosopher whose 'The Soul at Play' defends pretend play as a holiday in which the self's deepest truths surface.
holes.why: Chapter 21 leans on Santayana's play essays to argue that Rogers's make-believe uncovers reality better than plain empiricism.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: Pragmatist who held the self emerges socially by taking the perspectives of others, first in play.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Mead to explain how pretending to be teacher, mailman, or mommy in the show builds the child's individual self through perspective-taking.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Indirect Communication (pseudonyms)
holes.what: Kierkegaard and Hamann's method of writing through pseudonyms and fiction so readers must appropriate truth for themselves instead of being told.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues the Neighborhood of Make-Believe and Rogers's puppets are precisely this indirect communication, the puppets serving as his pseudonyms.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist philosopher of science whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' troubles the boundaries between human, animal, and machine.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the cyborg to argue the puppeteer is a human enhanced by the puppet, blurring exactly the boundaries the Anthropocene polices.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Timothy Morton
holes.what: Philosopher of ecology who calls for 'solidarity with nonhuman people', extending personhood and kinship beyond humankind.
holes.why: Chapter 23 cites Morton's Humankind to ground the claim that Rogers's puppets and animal neighbors make nonhuman persons part of the family.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The movement that dissolves humanist hierarchies by refusing the human/animal/object divide and the Western male center it secures.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues the show's toy credits, speaking Trolley, and Audrey Duck make it a posthumanist land where categories of human, animal, and thing blur.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Max Scheler
holes.what: Phenomenologist of values whose personalism holds each person is a unique, unrepeatable value-essence disclosed only in love.
holes.why: Chapter 26 reads 'you are special' as Scheler's personalism against Aristotle's shared rational essence, with King Friday's mask edict as the depersonalizing foil.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Personalism
holes.what: The ethical view that persons are valuable as unique, unrepeatable individuals rather than as rational agents or social role-bearers.
holes.why: Chapter 26 needs it to name the tradition (with its social corollary that community exists for persons, not vice versa) that Rogers's specialness message instantiates.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Carl Rogers
holes.what: Humanistic psychologist whose person-centered approach grounds growth in genuineness, acceptance, and empathic understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues Fred Rogers independently embodied Carl Rogers's three therapeutic conditions, making the show a growth climate for whole persons.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Unconditional Positive Regard
holes.what: Carl Rogers's principle of affirming a person and their feelings totally and without judgment, the precondition of psychological growth.
holes.why: Chapter 28 identifies it as the engine of 'I like you just the way you are'; chapter 16 likewise grounds the show's educational ethic in it.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Intrinsic vs Instrumental Value
holes.what: The distinction between what is good in itself, without qualification, and what is good only as a means to further ends.
holes.why: Chapter 31 defends 'you are special' as a claim of intrinsic worth against critics who read specialness as earned, extrinsic distinction.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: Enlightenment satirist whose Candide mocked Leibnizian optimism and held that evil is not to be rationalized but outlived by cultivating one's garden.
holes.why: Chapter 36 frames Mister Rogers's show as taking Rousseau's side against Voltaire on whether education must make evil intelligible.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: The Heinz Dilemma
holes.what: Kohlberg's thought experiment about stealing an unaffordable drug to save a dying spouse, used to stage his stages of moral reasoning.
holes.why: Chapter 37 recasts it with Henrietta Pussycat and X the Owl to contrast Gilligan's care-based response with Kohlberg's justice-based stages.
holes.book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: J.L. Austin, founder of speech act theory (How to Do Things with Words), showed that utterances like promising, ordering and apologizing perform actions rather than merely describe the world.
holes.why: Chapter 11 explicitly builds its analysis of reading and throwing shade on Austin's speech act theory — uptake, rules of successful performance, and perlocutionary effects — naming him alongside Searle as the framework's source.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Speech Act Theory (performative utterances)
holes.what: The theory that speaking is acting: utterances perform rule-governed acts (promising, ordering, pronouncing, insulting) whose success depends on uptake, speaker authority and context rather than literal meaning alone.
holes.why: Chapter 11's central project is defining reading and throwing shade as two speech acts philosophers have never analyzed, distinguishing them by uptake, at-issue content and intended perlocutionary effect.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Game Theory and Rational Choice
holes.what: The formal study of strategic decision-making that models situations like the Ultimatum Game and the Prisoner's Dilemma, defining rational action as maximization of expected utility.
holes.why: Chapter 12 models All Stars elimination politics as explicit games — utility maximization, the Ultimatum Game, a Trixie–Shangela Prisoner's Dilemma — to ask what a rational queen should do, and no taxonomy slug covers decision or game theory.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Play Theory of Humor
holes.what: The theory that humor is mock-aggression exercised in a safe, consensual, play-signaled setting — the verbal equivalent of sport or animal play-fighting.
holes.why: Chapter 13's moral verdict on reading rests on the play theory (Eastman onward): reads are permissible because play signals, consent and the reading/coming-for distinction keep them mock-aggression rather than real attack.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Erving Goffman, sociologist of everyday life who analyzed social interaction as theatrical performance: self-presentation, impression management, fronts, and the front stage/backstage divide.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Goffman's dramaturgy at length — self-expression versus self-presentation, the three components of fronts, and the collapse of backstage into front stage on Untucked — to explain how queens perform realness.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Mikhail Bakhtin, theorist of the carnivalesque and the grotesque (Rabelais and His World): an unofficial carnival time in which official hierarchies and binaries are suspended and transgression is celebrated through laughter.
holes.why: Chapter 18 gives Bakhtin his own section ('Bakhtin, Tops and Bottoms'), reading the Drag Race finale and drag itself as carnival time where the official world of rules and hierarchies death-drops.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist whose The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life analyzes all social interaction as theatrical performance with roles, scripts, fronts, and idealizations.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Goffman's performance and 'ideal type' framework as its main lens for reading 'Born Naked,' Snatch Game, and pageant-queen personae.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Revaluation of All Values (genealogy)
holes.what: Nietzsche's project in On the Genealogy of Morals of asking how values gained their worth through conflict, and of creating new values in their re-evaluation.
holes.why: Chapter 22 frames the entire C.U.N.T.-vs-A.S.S.E. value conflict of Drag Race through Nietzsche's revaluation and genealogical method, neither of which has a taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: What Is Art? (art status and the avant-garde)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-art debate over what makes something a work of art, from Danto's and Dickie's theories to Lopes's buck-passing theory and Walton's make-believe.
holes.why: Chapter 23's core question - whether a drag queen is a work of art and what the characteristic practice of her art form is - rests entirely on art-status theory the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Material Constitution (the statue and the clay)
holes.what: The metaphysical argument that a thing and its matter can coincide without being identical, as a statue depends on but is not the clay constituting it.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the statue-and-clay argument to show a drag queen survives losing every conventionally feminine attribute, so female impersonation is not essential to drag.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Erich Fromm
holes.what: Humanistic psychoanalyst and social philosopher whose The Art of Loving defines love as an active practice of care, responsibility, respect, and knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 25 builds its whole account of self-love before loving others on Fromm's four elements of love and his having-vs-being contrast.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Contemporary Italian philosopher of bio-politics and 'bare life' whose Nudities describes 'ethical spaces' for reflecting between performances.
holes.why: Chapter 26 borrows Agamben's 'ethical spaces' as its central framing for the privacy between personas that digital surveillance destroys.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Samuel von Pufendorf
holes.what: Seventeenth-century natural-law theorist of the duty of man and citizen, including duties owed to humanity at large.
holes.why: Chapter 26 rests its call to protect fellow humans from algorithmic surveillance on Pufendorf's 'benefits par excellence' duty to humanity.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Privacy and Surveillance
holes.what: The political problem of protecting self-generated identity and personal data from institutional, corporate, or algorithmic surveillance and profiling.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire argument is that blackbox data personas override self-identified identity and that Drag Race-style masking practices are needed to protect privacy.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Convergence Culture (participatory fandom)
holes.what: Media-theory account in which digital fan communities become subcultures of producers whose participation and content creation shape how shows operate.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explains Fire WERK With Me's memes and the Drag Race fandom's co-creation of the show through subculture and convergence-culture theory the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Meta-Reality and Media Meta-Commentary
holes.what: Roy Bhaskar and Jamie Morgan's notion of realities 'beyond reality as currently understood,' applied to television that comments on and parodies itself.
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses meta-reality and meta-commentary as its main analytic frame for Drag Race as a 'meta' show and its Twin Peaks meme crossover group.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement holding that death is a disease technology may eventually cure, making radical life extension and the abolition of death a goal.
holes.why: Chapter 28's closing section weighs the transhumanist demand to abolish death against a DragCon-eternity thought experiment showing endless life sours enjoyment.
holes.book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

holes.name: Bureaucracy as Rule by Nobody
holes.what: Arendt's account of bureaucracy as impersonal 'rule by Nobody', in which no one holds real authority or responsibility and everyone is deprived of the power to act.
holes.why: Chapter 11 reads the afterlife's point system as exactly such a bureaucracy, with Michael and Judge Gen shown to be powerless functionaries rather than rulers.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Meliorism
holes.what: James's view that the world is unfinished and that sustained human effort can genuinely improve it, which is what gives our actions moral worth.
holes.why: Chapter 13 uses meliorism's conditions, foreseeable consequences and no do-overs, to argue that the Soul Squad's afterlife growth earns no points and cannot matter morally.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Jonathan Dancy
holes.what: Contemporary moral philosopher best known for defending moral particularism, the view that there are no invariant moral principles.
holes.why: Chapter 21's climax has Eleanor cite Dancy by name to convert Chidi from Kantian rigidity so the group can lie its way through the Bad Place, and he is a contributor to the volume.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view that moral judgment must be made case by case from the specifics of a situation, without universal rules.
holes.why: Chapters 21 through 23 hinge on Eleanor's particularist defense of lying, which lets Chidi act at the moments his Kantian principles would paralyze him.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view that moral judgment must be made case by case from the specifics of a situation, without universal rules.
holes.why: Chapter 22 casts Eleanor's persuading Chidi to drop universal rules in the Bad Place as the key moment where praxis corrects theory.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view that moral judgment must be made case by case from the specifics of a situation, without universal rules.
holes.why: Chapter 23 presents Eleanor's movie-example pitch of Dancy's particularism as the turning point in Chidi's overcoming of his indecision.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Three Independent Factors in Morals
holes.what: Dewey's pluralist view that the Good (desire), the Right (duty and law), and the Virtuous (social praise and blame) are irreducible factors in moral experience.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Dewey's three factors to diagnose the shared flaw of the Big Three ethical theories and to explain Eleanor's third-option moral reasoning.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: Feminist view that persons and their choices are formed within social relationships rather than by atomistic, independent selves.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explicitly frames the show's paradox of individual accountability versus social dependence through the tradition of relational autonomy.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
holes.what: German pastor-theologian executed by the Nazis, known for 'religionless Christianity' and an ethics of responsibility to neighbors modeled on Christ.
holes.why: Chapter 33 devotes a full section to reading the Soul Squad's sacrificial love and Michael's conversion as Bonhoeffer-style religionless Christianity.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Nishkama Karma (desire-less action)
holes.what: Bhagavad Gita teaching that one must act without desire for the fruits of one's actions, since corrupt motivation voids an act's worth.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Eleanor's selfless departure and Janet's detachment as nishkama karma, the Gita's answer to the show's motivation problem.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Ethical Dualism (the good/evil binary)
holes.what: The view that good and bad are mutually exclusive categories into which persons and actions must be wholly sorted.
holes.why: Chapter 37 argues that moral growth, Jason's moral neutrality, and Michael's redemption all expose the Good Place/Bad Place dualism as false.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Somatic Marker Hypothesis
holes.what: Damasio's neuroscience claim that bodily 'gut feelings' built from social experience are essential shortcuts in moral reasoning rather than noise.
holes.why: Chapter 38 explains Chidi's stomachaches and his classroom-versus-real-life collapse through Damasio's somatic markers.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Contractualism (What We Owe to Each Other)
holes.what: T.M. Scanlon's view that an act is wrong if principles permitting it could be reasonably rejected by others affected.
holes.why: Chapter 38 reads Chidi's note-inscribed Scanlon book and the show's morality-is-other-people theme as contractualism in action.
holes.book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife

holes.name: Grievability (Butler)
holes.what: Judith Butler's notion from Precarious Life and Frames of War that lives become real and valuable to us insofar as they are grievable, while war and political violence produce 'ungrievable' lives we are prevented from mourning.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire reading of the Snap turns on Thanos making his victims ungrievable through scale and on Natasha retaining the capacity to grieve and act.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Knowledge-How vs Knowledge-That
holes.what: Gilbert Ryle's distinction between practical know-how (skills learned by doing, like hammering or feeling) and propositional knowledge-that, with know-how as more fundamental.
holes.why: Chapter 12 explains grief as retraining our affective know-how, since our emotional skills keep attuning us to a past world that no longer exists.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Infinitarian Paralysis
holes.what: Nick Bostrom's problem that in an infinite universe containing infinitely many good and bad lives, no action changes the total balance, leaving consequentialism unable to rank any action (closely tied to Hilbert's Hotel and Pascal's Mugging).
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues Tony Stark's consequentialism collapses in the infinite multiverse through this problem and its attempted cures (causal approach, expected value, infinity shades).
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Population Ethics
holes.what: The branch of value theory asking how many people should exist and how outcome value depends on population size, covering totalism, averagism, the person-affecting view, and Parfit's Repugnant Conclusion.
holes.why: Chapter 21 evaluates Thanos's Snap through exactly these rival theories and shows each one fails or backfires when applied to the Snap and its reversal.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Abduction (Inference to the Best Explanation)
holes.what: Charles Peirce's third mode of inference: reasoning from a surprising observation to the hypothesis that, if true, would best explain it, fallible yet central to science and everyday life.
holes.why: Chapter 23's whole analysis of Tony, War Machine, Cap-2012, the Ancient One, and Doctor Strange is built on abductive inferences, their fallibility, and how to choose the best explanation.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Bushido (the Way of the Warrior)
holes.what: The feudal Japanese samurai code, shaped by Buddhism, Shinto, and Confucianism and codified in texts like the Hagakure, that treats death as the measure of honor, discipline, and success.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads the whole Infinity War-Endgame arc through bushido's ichinen and shini-gurui, concluding that Thanos's resolve makes him the true samurai.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Theories of Humor (incongruity, superiority, relief)
holes.what: The three classic accounts of what makes things funny: incongruity (humor from violated expectations), superiority (laughter as sudden glory over others, Hobbes), and relief (laughter releasing psychic tension, Freud).
