holes.why: Chapter 26 applies all three theories to Loki, Thanos, and Thor respectively, and no existing taxonomy concept covers the philosophy of humor.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Carl Schmitt
holes.what: German political theorist (1888-1985) who argued that secular modernity never escapes metaphysics: mundane concepts like the nation, humanity, or economic growth simply take God's vacant place.
holes.why: Chapter 28 quotes Schmitt's Political Romanticism and Political Theology to explain how economic growth colonized the metaphysical realm and made Thanos 'inevitable'.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Aspect Perception (seeing-as)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's notion (Philosophical Investigations II) that one and the same object can be seen under multiple aspects — the duck-rabbit — so perception itself can shift ('now I can't unsee it') without the object changing.
holes.why: Chapter 35's entire diagnosis of Thanos is a failure of aspect perception — he never sees life under the 'existence of individuals' aspect — and taxonomy has no slug for seeing-as, only for Wittgenstein's language.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Martin Luther
holes.what: Reformation theologian whose distinction between God's 'left hand' (law, judgment, the alien work) and 'right hand' (grace, promise, the proper work) grounds his theology of the cross and the Heidelberg Disputation.
holes.why: Chapter 36's whole reading of the left- versus right-handed gauntlets, Thanos's 'inevitability' as law, and freedom as fulfilled promise is built directly on Luther's two-hands theology and Heidelberg Disputation theses.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Frankfurt School critical theorist whose The Eclipse of Reason distinguishes subjective reason (means–ends efficiency) from objective reason (ends valid in themselves) and warns that absolutized subjective reason enables technological barbarism.
holes.why: Chapter 37's central thesis that Thanos is 'mad because he is rational' — genocide as pure instrumental calculation unbound by objective ends — is Horkheimer's argument applied point by point.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Subjective vs Objective Reason
holes.what: Horkheimer's distinction between reason as mere instrument for efficiently reaching ends the subject simply chooses (subjective) and reason whose ends are recognized as valid independently of the will (objective).
holes.why: Chapter 37 argues Thanos's genocide is the absolutization of subjective reason — efficient means serving a self-chosen end with no objective limit — and contrasts it with Cap's refusal to trade Vision.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: The Tragedy of the Commons (carrying capacity)
holes.what: Garrett Hardin's argument that finite shared environments have a carrying capacity beyond which populations crash, so problems of shared resources admit no purely technical solution and require self-limitation.
holes.why: Chapter 38 uses Hardin's carrying-capacity logic (St. Matthew Island's reindeer, apex-predator self-limitation) to show why Thanos's one-time fifty-percent cull is a categorical error rather than a solution.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Maurice Blanchot
holes.what: French writer and thinker who reversed Heidegger's formula, conceiving death as 'the impossibility of possibility' — an impersonal dying (le mourir) that can never be appropriated or experienced as one's own.
holes.why: Chapter 39 pivots on Blanchot's reversal of being-toward-death: only I die for Heidegger, but Blanchot shows death can never be mine, opening the impersonal death that Lacan and Deleuze then develop.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Maurice Blondel
holes.what: French Catholic philosopher of action whose 1893 dissertation L'Action argues that human beings find meaning and fulfillment through willed action — the 'science of practice' — rather than through thought or scientific knowledge alone.
holes.why: Chapter 42's entire reading of Tony Stark — from Yinsen's challenge to the final snap as the 'synthesis of the self' — is an application of Blondel's primacy of action and his willed-will/willing-will dynamic.
holes.book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head

holes.name: Legal Positivism (law as posited command)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-law view that law's authority comes from being posited or commanded by a recognized power, with no necessary connection to morality.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire comparison of Mason and Saul Goodman hinges on the natural law versus legal positivism contrast, and only the natural-law half has a taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

holes.name: Reconstructive Memory (Loftus and eyewitness unreliability)
holes.what: The research finding that remembering rebuilds events with added information rather than replaying recordings, making eyewitness testimony systematically unreliable.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is built entirely on Loftus's memory research, flashbulb memories, and stress effects to undermine courtroom eyewitness identification, and no taxonomy concept covers the epistemology of memory or testimony.
holes.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

holes.name: Bayes's Theorem (conditional probability and evidence)
holes.what: The rule for transforming the probability of evidence given a hypothesis into the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence, via priors and likelihoods.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Bayes's Theorem as its sole analytical tool, modeling Mason's and the prosecution's reasoning over guilt and evidence in priors, likelihoods, and posteriors.
holes.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

holes.name: Alphonso Lingis
holes.what: American existential phenomenologist whose book Trust describes trust as a non-contractual break in the map of certainties and probabilities.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its account of the Perry-Della-Paul collaboration directly on Lingis's Trust, and the taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

holes.name: Catharsis and the Poetics of Tragedy
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of how tragedy builds and releases pity and fear through plot, reversal, discovery, and characters slightly better than the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 24 reads the whole Perry Mason formula as Aristotelian tragedy with the courtroom confession as the cathartic climax, but the taxonomy's Aristotle concepts stop at ethics and metaphysics.
holes.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

holes.name: Confession, Avowal and Veridiction (technologies of the self)
holes.what: Foucault's account of how the demand to tell the truth about oneself became central to law, penance, psychiatry, and the modern drama of criminal justice.
holes.why: Chapter 25 interprets the Mason confession scene through Wrong-Doing, Truth-Telling as a judicial drama of avowal and veridiction, and the taxonomy's Foucault slugs cover only surveillance, power/knowledge, and discipline.
holes.book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

holes.name: Anton LaVey
holes.what: Founder of LaVeyan Satanism and author of The Satanic Bible, which promotes self-indulgence, individual freedom, and life-affirmation rather than devil-worship.
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues KISS's values overlap with LaVey's actual Satanism while debunking the demonic stereotype attached to the band.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief (Clifford's evidentialism)
holes.what: W.K. Clifford's principle that it is wrong to believe or act on insufficient evidence, illustrated by the negligent shipowner thought experiment.
holes.why: Chapter 13 stages KISS's counter-evidence gamble on the Alive! live album against Clifford's demand for sufficient evidence before acting.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Collective Intentionality
holes.what: The idea that shared 'we-intentions' of individuals create social and institutional facts such as teams, money, and brands.
holes.why: Chapter 15 argues that what KISS does, and whether a franchise band of hired musicians would even count as KISS, rests on the collective intentions of members and fans.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Nicholas Wolterstorff
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose account of love distinguishes love as activity, as attachment, and as attraction (and whose memoir calls lives 'shot through with love').
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses Wolterstorff's three categories as the framework for sorting nearly every KISS song into kinds of love.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Aristippus of Cyrene
holes.what: Founder of the Cyrenaic school, holding immediate bodily pleasure to be the highest good, pursued with self-control and an alternation of work and play.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads KISS's sex songs and work-hard/play-hard ethos as a direct application of Aristippus's hedonism, including his cautions against overindulgence.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Obligations to Future Generations
holes.what: The question whether present people owe duties to preserve resources, places, culture, or experiences for people who do not yet exist.
holes.why: Chapter 23 builds and tests the Preservationist claim that the rights of future generations give Gene and Paul a duty to keep KISS performing.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian thinker whose theory of carnival holds that masking, laughter, and festivity suspend official hierarchies in an atmosphere of 'joyful relativity' that decrowns the serious.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reads KISS concerts, make-up transformations, and merchandise like the KISS Kondom and KISS Kasket as Bakhtinian carnival that lifts taboos on sex and death.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Bernard Lonergan
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose Insight names 'scotosis,' the intellectual blind spot that censors evidence against our entrenched interpretations.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Lonergan's scotosis to explain why each band member's memoir about recording 'Beth' suppresses inconvenient perspectives, alongside Sartre's bad faith.
holes.book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell

holes.name: Racialism (Appiah)
holes.what: The view, criticized by Appiah, that humanity divides into a small number of races whose members share fundamental, heritable physical, moral, intellectual, and cultural characteristics.
holes.why: Chapter 15's core argument that race is socially real but biologically spurious is built directly on Appiah's diagnosis of racialism, seen in Tracy's essentialist crisis over his DNA results.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Polymorphous Perversity
holes.what: Freud's view that infants possess undirected sexual drives in every direction, which culture and training then channel into specific adult orientations.
holes.why: Chapter 16's argument that sexual orientation is neither chosen nor innate but culturally trained rests on Freud's polymorphous-perversity picture of desire.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Colonization of the Lifeworld
holes.what: Habermas's thesis that bureaucratic 'systems organizations' (markets, administrations) increasingly invade and reorganize the shared cultural lifeworld, producing modernity's irrationalities.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses this Habermasian thesis as its central explanation of how managed-care bureaucracy and the market have distorted the social meaning of medicine and doctors like Dr. Spaceman.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Corporate Moral Personhood (CID structure)
holes.what: Peter French's thesis that corporations are moral persons because their corporate internal decision structure forms an intention-bearing, rational actor independent of any individual member.
holes.why: Chapter 20 leans on French's view to explain why GE functions identically with Don Geiss in a coma and why responsibility for corporate acts cannot be located in individual executives.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Corporate Moral Personhood (CID structure)
holes.what: Peter French's thesis that corporations are moral persons because their corporate internal decision structure forms an intention-bearing, rational actor independent of any individual member.
holes.why: Chapter 21 is built entirely on French's actorship and CID structure, from which it derives its provocative conclusion that corporations are our designed slaves.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian communitarian philosopher who argues that communities and the identities they supply are constitutive of the self, not optional attachments.
holes.why: Chapter 22 explicitly names Taylor as the communitarian source for its claim that communities make us who we are, the premise on which its reconciliation of Liz and Jack's philosophies turns.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: The Social Construction of X (Hacking)
holes.what: Ian Hacking's account of social-construction claims: X need not have existed or need not be as it is, because it is shaped by social practices rather than determined by nature.
holes.why: Chapter 26's whole argument that Liz is 'a model in Cleveland' and that taste is community-relative runs on Hacking's social constructivism and Eaton's construction of aesthetic response.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: Victorian philosopher famous for the ethics of belief: 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.'
holes.why: Chapter 27's conclusion that Tracy's unearned beliefs are not merely funny but immoral rests on Clifford's shipbuilder argument for evidential responsibility.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Knowledge as Justified True Belief
holes.what: The classical analysis of knowledge, from Plato's Theaetetus, as belief that is true and adequately justified, with true belief by accident insufficient for knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is organized entirely around this tripartite analysis, testing Tracy Jordan's claims for belief, truth, and justification in turn.
holes.book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There

holes.name: Organic Unity (Moore)
holes.what: Moore's Principia Ethica doctrine that the value of a whole need not equal the sum of the values of its parts.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses organic unity to explain how experiences bad in every moment (jam-yesterday-jam-tomorrow goods like jobs and parenting) can still be good 'on the whole', illustrated by bands like the Spice Girls.
holes.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of language and mind who denied that a language is a shared system of conventions and grounded communication in the charitable interpretation of speaker intentions.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is built entirely on Davidson's 'there is no such thing as a language' thesis, tested against Humpty Dumpty, 'uglification', and Wonderland malapropisms.
holes.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser

holes.name: Passing Theories (convention-free communication)
holes.what: Davidson's view that hearers improvise a 'passing theory' of each utterance's intended meaning, so shared rules are neither necessary nor sufficient for communication.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses it to explain how Alice understands 'curiouser and curiouser' and 'uglification' despite rule-breaking, while arguing the invention view cannot dispense with established meanings.
holes.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser

holes.name: Chronos and Aion (Deleuze's two readings of time)
holes.what: Deleuze's distinction in The Logic of Sense between Chronos, where only the present fills time, and Aion, where only an infinitely subdivided past-future exists and the present never arrives.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads the White Queen's 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' as aion: today never comes, it is always yesterday and tomorrow together.
holes.book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser

holes.name: Stakeholder Theory (vs. stockholder theory)
holes.what: The business-ethics debate between Friedman/Berle's view that a corporation's only duty is maximizing shareholder profit and Freeman's view that it owes moral consideration to everyone affected by its actions.
holes.why: Chapter 5's entire case that Weyland-Yutani wrongs its crews - Special Order 937, hidden mission risks, expendability - is built on running stockholder theory, libertarian contract theory, and stakeholder theory against each other.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: The Problem of Many Hands (corporate accountability)
holes.what: The difficulty of assigning moral responsibility for a large organization's harm when no single member controls or fully understands the whole, letting blame diffuse or settle on scapegoats.
holes.why: Chapter 7 devotes a central section to how Ash, Mother, and Burke embody Weyland-Yutani's deferral of accountability - each employee just follows orders, and the company sacrifices a scapegoat while keeping the profits.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: The End of History (Fukuyama)
holes.what: Fukuyama's thesis that liberal capitalist democracy is the endpoint of humanity's ideological evolution, so history 'ends' with no rival system left.
holes.why: Chapter 8's closing section argues the Alien saga's unreconstructed capitalist future vindicates Fukuyama's end of history against Marx's prediction of capitalism's collapse, making Marx's critique of alienation newly urgent.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Lawrence Kohlberg
holes.what: Psychologist whose six-stage theory of moral development culminates in post-conventional, impartial universal principles - the framework Gilligan critiqued as male-biased.
holes.why: Chapters 10 and 21 classify Ripley's quarantine refusal and her defense of killing the Alien3 specimen as Kohlberg-style post-conventional rule reasoning, the foil against which the care-ethics reading of her bond with Newt is measured.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Political Realism
holes.what: The view in international relations that power and survival, not moral principle, govern relations between states - Thucydides' 'the strong do what they will, the weak do what they must.'
holes.why: Chapter 12 frames Engineers, Xenomorphs, and humans as realist states and tests Ripley's orbital nuking plan against realism before turning to just war criteria, concluding her plan is vengeance masquerading as realism.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: H.P. Lovecraft
holes.what: American weird-fiction writer whose essays and letters articulate a philosophy of horror: fear of the unknown, cosmic fear at violations of natural law, strict realism in all else, and suggestion over explicit description.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues Alien is the best science-fiction horror film precisely because it executes Lovecraft's principles, from the alien's mysterious life cycle to mundane space-truckers and the disguised android Ash.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Cosmicism (cosmic horror)
holes.what: Lovecraft's doctrine that humanity is insignificant in an indifferent, Darwinian cosmos where human laws, morality, and meanings have no cosmic validity - the source of true horror.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses cosmic fear at violations of natural law as the master explanation of the Xenomorph's scariness: the creature is terrifying because nothing in nature as we know it can do what it does.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Noel Carroll
holes.what: Philosopher of art whose The Philosophy of Horror explains the genre via art-horror objects (fusion figures of categorically interpenetrating elements), disgust, and the paradox of fiction-induced fear.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is built entirely on extending Carroll's account of art-horror monsters to 'art-horror environments' like the acid-corroded Nostromo and the hive-colonized Hadley's Hope.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Art-Horror (fusion figures and the paradox of horror)
holes.what: Carroll's account of horror as the emotional response to monsters that violate our conceptual categories, disgusting yet fascinating, feared through empathetic identification with fictional characters.
holes.why: Chapter 17 needs the concept to explain the series' distinctive disgust and then argue that contaminated environments, not just fusion-figure monsters, do the horror work.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German Idealist whose Naturphilosophie grounds life in the 'duplicity' of conscious and unconscious productive activity, treating assimilation, excitability, sexuality, and contagion as intertwined.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Schelling's biology of contagion and his 'indifference' - the hidden identity of what fosters and what destroys freedom - to frame Ripley's suicide at the end of Alien3.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Alison Stone
holes.what: Contemporary feminist philosopher whose account of maternal subjectivity rethinks mother-child separation as embodied, affective, relational differentiation rather than violent break.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Ripley's mothering of Jonesy, Newt, and the Newborn - and her deaths and rebirths - entirely through Stone's maternal subjectivity and her critique of separation-based models.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Maternal Subjectivity
holes.what: The feminist-psychoanalytic idea that motherhood reshapes a woman's sense of self through embodied, relational experience, involving loss, repetition of her own daughterhood, and the problem of differentiation.
holes.why: Chapter 20's organizing concept: Ripley's relation to Jonesy, Newt, Mother, the Queen, and her own hybrid offspring is read as a case study in how mothering both constitutes and threatens the self.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Rape Culture
holes.what: The feminist analysis, coined by 1970s second-wave feminists, that society normalizes sexual violence against women and shifts blame to victims through everyday jokes, advice, and media tropes.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues the Alien films depict a twenty-second-century rape culture - Marines' banter, the prisoners' treatment of Ripley - and use equal-opportunity Facehugger violation to give male viewers a window into it.
holes.book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am

holes.name: Emotivism (boo/hurrah theory)
holes.what: A. J. Ayer's view that moral claims merely express emotional approval or disgust rather than state facts that could be proven.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses emotivism to read 'incest is wrong' as a 'Yuck!' before weighing it against Kass.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: The Wisdom of Repugnance (the yuck factor)
holes.what: Leon Kass's claim that visceral disgust is the emotional expression of deep moral wisdom that reason cannot fully articulate.
holes.why: Chapter 10's verdict on George Michael and Maeby turns on whether the yuck factor carries moral information.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: The Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's account of the boy's repressed desire for his mother and rivalry with the prohibitive father, extended in Totem and Taboo to the origin of the incest taboo.
holes.why: Chapter 11 diagnoses Buster's Motherboy devotion and Lucille Two romance as failed repression and reads the brothers' plots against George Sr. as the primal horde.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Shareholder vs Stakeholder Theories of Corporate Responsibility
holes.what: The business-ethics debate over whether a corporation's only duty is maximizing shareholder profit or whether it also owes duties to employees, customers, and communities.
holes.why: Chapter 15 measures the Bluth Company's 'Family First' practices against the shareholder model and Johnson & Johnson's stakeholder credo.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Speech Acts (performatives)
holes.what: J. L. Austin's theory that utterances like 'I do' or 'I apologize' perform actions rather than describe the world, succeeding only in the right context with the right speaker.
holes.why: Chapter 19 analyzes George Michael and Maeby's accidental wedding and Lucille's guilt-inducing 'I've been a horrible mother' as performatives.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Conversational Implicature (Grice's cooperative principle)
holes.what: H. P. Grice's account of how speakers communicate more than they literally say via the cooperative principle and the maxims of quantity, quality, manner, and relation.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explains Tobias's 'I just blue myself' double entendres and the 'fire... sale' audition through implicature rather than explicit meaning.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Political Obligation (why obey the state?)
holes.what: The question of what special duty citizens have to obey and support their state, answered by instrumental (public goods) or relational (shared bonds) theories.
holes.why: Chapter 27 needs political obligation to explain why George Sr.'s light treason is blameworthy beyond mere illegality.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Douglas's Theory of Jokes
holes.what: Mary Douglas's account of the joke as a symbolic pattern that momentarily deconstructs social hierarchy and gives the mind's monitoring system a holiday (building on Freud).
holes.why: Chapter 29's final section invokes Douglas to explain why the Bluths' contradictions are comic and why the joke is on Gob.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The view associated with Ricoeur and MacIntyre that a self constitutes itself by telling a unified, evolving story of its life.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses the show's narrator to argue we give ourselves identity and meaning through the stories we tell about ourselves.
holes.book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake

holes.name: Fazang
holes.what: Tang-dynasty Huayan Buddhist patriarch who illustrated the oneness of reality to Empress Wu Zetian through the metaphor of a golden lion statue.
holes.why: Chapter 8's account of ATLA's central theme of oneness is built on Fazang's 'Essay on the Golden Lion' and its claim that all things lack individual nature.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: The Chosen One Trope
holes.what: The fantasy narrative convention in which a pre-destined savior with innate powers, rather than collective struggle and learning, saves the world.
holes.why: Chapter 8's first argument is that ATLA subverts this trope: Aang's slow training, need for teachers, and dependence on Team Avatar replace passive salvation by an innate hero.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: V. F. Cordova
holes.what: Jicarilla Apache philosopher whose Native American metaphysics centers 'bounded space', the land base that shapes and obligates the people formed by it.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of the four nations, their benders, and their landscapes is organized around Cordova's concept of bounded space.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Indigenous Relationality
holes.what: The Indigenous ontological thesis that persons, land, animals, spirits, and ancestors are bound in relations of mutual responsibility and accountability to a specific place.
holes.why: Chapter 10 argues ATLA's bending, spirit world, Lion Turtle lore, and Order of the White Lotus express relationality and elder knowledge rather than Western power metaphysics.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Empedocles
holes.what: Presocratic who held that four ungenerated roots (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) are mixed and separated by the forces Love and Strife.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses Empedocles' four roots as the closest ancient analogue to ATLA's four bendable Elements and its question of whether they are fundamentally distinct.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Anaximander
holes.what: Presocratic who posited the apeiron, an unlimited undifferentiated origin from which the opposites generate and to which they return.
holes.why: Chapter 11 models ATLA's energy as Anaximander's apeiron, the single fundamental substance from which the four Elements might be generated.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Teotl (Nahua metaphysics)
holes.what: The Aztec (Nahua) doctrine that everything is fundamentally teotl, a single divine energy in constant motion and becoming.
holes.why: Chapter 11 compares the Sun Warriors' fire-as-life-energy to James Maffie's account of teotl to test whether ATLA's reality is one dynamic substance.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Qi (vital energy)
holes.what: The Chinese concept of a vital energy or life force flowing through bodies and the world, cultivated in practices like qigong.
holes.why: Chapter 11 identifies ATLA's bending energy and Guru Pathik's chakras with qi (and Hindu prana) to argue energy underlies the four Elements.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Abolitionism (prison and institution abolition)
holes.what: A theory of justice, built from Black radical thought, holding that unjust institutions are not buggy but essentially unjust and so must be abolished rather than reformed.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues ATLA itself offers an abolitionist account: the four nations, like prisons for prison abolitionists, are a rotten arrangement that must be abolished, not saved.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Denise Ferreira da Silva
holes.what: Contemporary theorist who critiques the modern 'grammar' of separability, determinacy, and sequentiality and proposes 'difference without separability'.
holes.why: Chapter 13 takes its central thesis, that the elements' and nations' differences need not ground separation, from her Black abolitionist critique of modern racializing thought.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Anishinaabe Worldview (manidoog and interconnectedness)
holes.what: The Ojibwe/Anishinaabe way of seeing in which manidoog (spirits) are as real as trees and valleys, creation is one interconnected whole, and the ultimate ground is mystery.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads ATLA's Water Tribe, Hei Bai, Tui and La, and the swamp's single living tree through Anishinaabe teachings the author received from his elders.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Yagyu Munenori
holes.what: Seventeenth-century Japanese sword master whose Heiho Kadensho teaches the distinction between the sword that takes life and the sword that gives life.
holes.why: Chapter 18's conclusion that bloodbending is morally neutral and intention-dependent rests on Munenori's katsujinken/satsujinken distinction.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Katsujinken (the life-giving sword)
holes.what: The martial-ethical ideal of using technique to suppress an opponent with minimal harm (the life-giving sword) rather than to dominate or kill (the life-taking sword).
holes.why: Chapter 18 applies this exact distinction to bloodbending: Hama's use takes life while Katara's restrained, compassionate use saves life.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Expected Utility Theory
holes.what: The standard philosophical theory of rational decision-making: an agent is rationally required to act when the expected value of acting exceeds that of not acting.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses expected utility theory (with a formal appendix) to prove that the villagers' red-shoes faith in Aunt Wu is rational, refuting Sokka's empiricism.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Joan Tronto
holes.what: Political philosopher who defines care as a species activity that maintains and repairs our world and distinguishes its phases: caring about, taking care of, and care-giving.
holes.why: Chapter 21 structures its entire analysis of Katara and the Gaang's politics around Tronto's definition and phases of care.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Native American Epistemology (ethical-epistemological maps)
holes.what: Indigenous approaches to knowledge that tie knowing to ethical attentiveness, community, place, ritual, dreams, and visions rather than individualist control.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads the Gaang's growth as building evolving ethical-epistemological maps in this tradition, against the Fire Nation's epistemology of control.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Roy Sorensen
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who introduced 'bald-faced lies', undisguised lies told without any intention to deceive the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central puzzle, the Dai Li's 'There is no war in Ba Sing Se', is analyzed as precisely Sorensen's bald-faced lies.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Counterstory (master narrative repair)
holes.what: Hilde Lindemann's notion that oppressive master narratives woven into a group's identity can be rooted out and replaced by stories depicting that group as morally worthy.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire argument is that Toph is a Proud Disabled Person counterstory to the Better-Off-Dead, Irrationally-and-Infectiously-Happy, and Supercrip master narratives, and the taxonomy has no slug for master narratives or counterstories.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Epistemology of Ignorance (willful ignorance)
holes.what: Charles Mills, Shannon Sullivan, and Jose Medina's account of how the privileged actively produce and maintain ignorance because knowing would cost them their advantage.
holes.why: Chapter 27 hinges on 'epistemic ignorance' — King Kuei's willful not-knowing of the war — which is a distinct concept from Fricker's epistemic injustice that the taxonomy already carries.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: False Dilemma and the Middle Way
holes.what: The informal fallacy of presenting two options as exhaustive, and the correlative practice of dissolving a conflict by rejecting both poles for a third way (the Buddha's middle way).
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues ATLA's deepest lesson — Bumi's neutral jing, Aang's energybending, Oma ending the village feud — is detecting and dissolving false alternatives, a concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Han Fei
holes.what: Qin-dynasty Legalist who held that human nature is bad and rulers need strict laws, censure, and terrifying sanctions rather than virtue.
holes.why: Chapter 30 quotes the Han Feizi throughout to read Ozai's scarring of Zuko, Azulon's death sentence, and the Fire Nation school system as Legalist statecraft.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Legalism (fajia)
holes.what: The Chinese school holding that social order comes from severe, clearly published laws and punishments rather than moral cultivation.
holes.why: Chapter 30 structures the whole Fire Nation (Ozai, Azula, the Fire Nation Oath, censure-based schooling) as Legalism set against Confucian ren, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Hilde Lindemann
holes.what: Feminist philosopher of narrative identity: persons are constituted by stories told by themselves and others, and are 'held in personhood' through others' recognition and response.
holes.why: Chapter 31's entire framework — connective tissue of narratives, holding in personhood, moral community — is Lindemann's, and she also anchors chapter 26's counterstory argument.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Holding in Personhood (relational identity)
holes.what: The social practice of treating someone as a person by recognizing and responding to their expressed inner life, which makes growth and redemption possible.
holes.why: Chapter 31 argues Aang's and Iroh's holding Zuko in personhood opens up his possible future, and no existing taxonomy slug captures this relational account of personhood.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: The Use of Uselessness
holes.what: Zhuangzi's doctrine that what is useless to rulers — the gnarled tree, the yak — escapes being cut down and lives out its years freely.
holes.why: Chapter 32 makes it one of Iroh's three Zhuangzian policies: conspicuous unusefulness (tea, Pai Sho, napping) keeps him at Zuko's side without becoming a tool of his quest.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Aspiration (the agency of becoming)
holes.what: Agnes Callard's notion of a deep, value-changing self-transformation that an agent can only achieve by aspirationally working at values she does not yet fully have.
holes.why: Chapter 33 frames Zuko's 'becoming good at being good' as aspiration, explaining why his explicit commitments outrun his recalcitrant dispositions, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: P.F. Strawson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher whose 'Freedom and Resentment' ties holding someone morally responsible to reactive attitudes such as resentment and moral anger.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Strawson's blame-as-moral-anger view as the foil that ATLA's anger-free strategies of responsibility (forgiveness, compassion, self-compassion) respond to.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Settler Colonialism (erasure of the native)
holes.what: Patrick Wolfe's account of a colonial structure that seeks to eliminate and replace Indigenous peoples and then erase them from the national origin story.
holes.why: Chapter 36's Fire Nation–United States comparison (manifest destiny, Sand Creek, Tuluwat, the appropriating Air Walkers) is built entirely on this erasure-and-replacement framework.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Pyotr Kropotkin
holes.what: Russian anarchist thinker who argued that cooperation (mutual aid), not competition, is the chief factor in evolutionary and social development.
holes.why: Chapter 37 grounds its claim that ATLA is full of unrecognized anarchists in Kropotkin's mutual-aid principle and cooperative view of human nature, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Mutual Aid
holes.what: The anarchist principle that people owe each other voluntary care and shared resources because humans are fundamentally cooperative rather than Competitive.
holes.why: Chapter 37 applies mutual aid to Team Avatar's division of labor, Senlin Village, disaster solidarity, and Iroh telling Toph there is nothing wrong with letting people help you.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Moral Dilemmas (non-negotiable duties)
holes.what: Situations where an agent faces two or more non-negotiable obligations that cannot all be met, so no choice avoids moral cost (Ross, Tessman, McConnell).
holes.why: Chapter 39 defines Aang's Dilemma through the negotiable/non-negotiable duty framework, and the taxonomy has no general moral-dilemma concept beyond the trolley problem.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Ogyen Trinley Dorje (17th Karmapa)
holes.what: Tibetan Buddhist leader whose book Interconnected argues that we are 'interdependent individuals' who grow only within webs of relationship and compassion.
holes.why: Chapter 40 reads Aang's isolation under an exalted title and his communal moral training entirely through the Karmapa's memoir-philosophy, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Dependent Origination (pratityasamutpada / interdependence)
holes.what: The core Buddhist teaching that all things and persons arise in mutual dependence, so nothing exists independently of its relations.
holes.why: Chapters 39 and 40 build Aang's widening compassion and his energybending victory on interconnection, but the taxonomy only has impermanence, non-self, and emptiness, not this doctrine.
holes.book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

holes.name: Indigenous Relationality (bounded space)
holes.what: Indigenous philosophical idea, developed by V.F. Cordova and Shawn Wilson, that persons, land, waters, animals, spirits, and generations are bound within a specific 'bounded space' by relations of knowledge and responsibility.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of the four nations, the Lion Turtle, and the Order of the White Lotus is built on bounded space and relationality, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: V.F. Cordova
holes.what: Jicarilla Apache philosopher (1937-2002) of Native American philosophy, known for the concept of 'bounded space' and relational personhood.
holes.why: Chapter 10's framework term 'bounded space,' and chapter 22's notion of cultural 'matrices,' are both Cordova's, and no Indigenous philosopher exists in taxonomy.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Empedocles
holes.what: Presocratic pluralist (c. 494-434 BC) who held the world is composed of four eternal 'roots' (earth, water, air, fire) moved by the forces Love and Strife.
holes.why: Chapter 11 treats Empedocles' four-root theory as the closest ancient analogue to ATLA's four bending Elements.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Anaximander
holes.what: Presocratic (c. 610-546 BC) who posited the apeiron, an unlimited indefinite source from which the opposed elements arise and to which they return.
holes.why: Chapter 11 models ATLA's energy as Anaximander's apeiron generating the four Elements, its leading monist hypothesis.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Teotl (Nahua metaphysics)
holes.what: Aztec/Nahua idea, systematized by James Maffie, that fundamentally everything is teotl, a single sacred energy in constant motion and becoming, tying sun, fire, and life together.
holes.why: Chapter 11 devotes a section to testing whether ATLA's inner-fire energy is like the Nahua teotl of the Sun Warriors' 'The Firebending Masters.'
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Abolitionism
holes.what: Theory of justice, rooted in Black radical thought (Angela Davis, Ruth Wilson Gilmore, Denise Ferreira da Silva), holding that certain institutions are irredeemable by design and must be abolished, not reformed.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues ATLA itself advances an abolitionist critique of the four nations via 'difference without separability,' a framework taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Power vs Violence (Arendt)
holes.what: Arendt's distinction that genuine political power is people acting in concert, while violence that imposes will by force circumvents and destroys politics.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses it to argue Ozai's comet-empowered Phoenix King rule is violence devoid of politics, and Aang's restraint as passive guardian opens space for politics.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Anishinaabe Worldview (manidoog and interconnectedness)
holes.what: Ojibwe/Anishinaabe understanding of creation as one interconnected whole populated by spirits (manidoog) and marked by mystery, with humans as dependents of the plant and animal beings.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Hei Bai, Tui and La, and Huu's swamp through Anishinaabe teachings of interconnectedness and spirits as ordinary residents of the world.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Yagyū Munenori
holes.what: Seventeenth-century Japanese swordsman-philosopher whose Heiho Kadensho distinguishes the sword that takes life (satsujinken) from the sword that gives life (katsujinken).
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Munenori's distinction to argue Hama's bloodbending takes life while Katara's saves it, so the technique itself is morally neutral.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Expected Utility Theory
holes.what: Decision theory on which an agent is rationally required to perform an action when its probability-weighted expected value exceeds that of the alternatives.
holes.why: Chapter 20's formal proof that Aunt Wu's red-shoes villager behaves rationally is an application of expected utility theory, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Native American Epistemology (ethical-epistemological maps)
holes.what: Indigenous approach to knowledge as holistic, communal, ethics-infused 'maps' built from all experience, including dreams, visions, ceremony, and elders, rather than from detached individual inquiry.
holes.why: Chapter 22's core machinery, from Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit to Burkhart's Coyote-versus-Thales contrast, is a Native epistemology taxonomy does not cover.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Bald-faced Lies (lying without intent to deceive)
holes.what: Roy Sorensen's undisguised lies, uttered openly with no intent to deceive the audience, typical of what oppressive states compel citizens to say, extended by Thomas Carson's warranting contexts.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central claim is that the Dai Li's 'There is no war in Ba Sing Se' is a bald-faced lie that standard deception-based definitions of lying cannot capture.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Narrative Identity (master narratives and counterstories)
holes.what: Hilde Lindemann's view that identities are woven from first- and third-person stories, damaged by oppressive master narratives, and repaired by counterstories that depict a person as morally worthy.
holes.why: Chapter 26's whole argument (Toph as a Proud Disabled Person counterstory rather than a Supercrip) and chapter 31's argument (Zuko's redemption through being held in personhood) both run on this framework, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Han Fei
holes.what: Chinese Legalist philosopher (c. 280-233 BC) who took from Xunzi that human nature is bad and argued order requires strict laws, censure, and severe punishments under an absolute sovereign.
holes.why: Chapter 30 reads Ozai's Fire Nation, from the agni kai punishment to the school oath and Azula's rule by fear, as Han Fei's Legalism in action, quoting the Han Feizi throughout.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Legalism (fa-jia)
holes.what: The classical Chinese school holding that people are selfish by nature, so social order comes from clear ranks, strict law, and harsh sanctions rather than virtue or ritual.
holes.why: Chapter 30 is organized as a battle between Confucianism and Legalism, and taxonomy.json has no slug for the Legalist side beyond the Xunzi tag it borrows.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Aspiration (the agency of becoming)
holes.what: Agnes Callard's notion of a deep, value-laden change in what a person values and who they are, pursued over time and characteristically marked by backsliding and confusion.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explains Zuko's 'Why am I so bad at being good?' through Callard's aspiration, and no existing taxonomy slug covers aspirational self-transformation.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Settler Colonialism (the logic of elimination)
holes.what: Patrick Wolfe's account of colonial regimes built on eliminating and replacing Indigenous peoples, sustained by narratives that erase the founding violence as inevitable or extinct.
holes.why: Chapter 36's comparison of Sozin's genocide of the Air Nomads with US manifest destiny, narrative erasure, and appropriation of sacred places is framed entirely by this concept, which no taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Pyotr Kropotkin
holes.what: Russian anarchist thinker (1842-1921) whose Mutual Aid argues that cooperation is an evolutionary tendency of human nature and the basis of a stateless ethics.
holes.why: Chapter 37 builds its account of Team Avatar's camp life and the villages of the four nations on Kropotkin's mutual aid, and taxonomy.json has an anarchism concept but no Kropotkin.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Noam Chomsky
holes.what: Linguist and anarchist thinker (b. 1928) who holds that any hierarchy or authoritarian institution bears the burden of justifying its own existence.
holes.why: Chapter 37 uses Chomsky's justified-hierarchies test as its main analytic tool, from the Toph-on-the-cliffside example to the Dai Li's unjustifyable secret police.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Ogyen Trinley Dorje (the 17th Karmapa)
holes.what: Contemporary Tibetan Buddhist leader whose book Interconnected develops an ethics of interdependence, compassion, self-control, and moral training within widening communities.
holes.why: Chapter 40 reads Aang's journey, the shared burden of exalted titles, and Zuko's repentance entirely through the Karmapa's Interconnected, a thinker absent from taxonomy.json.
holes.book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko

holes.name: Moral Exemplarism
holes.what: The view, revived by Linda Zagzebski from Aristotle's account of habituation, that we become good by imitating live moral exemplars rather than by rules or calculation.
holes.why: Chapter 10's whole argument—that Scott Lang deserves credit for Stature, Pym no blame for Ultron, and the Avengers themselves are exemplars for reformed villains—rests on this named concept, which the chapter introduces as the modern development of Aristotle.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: Metafiction (the metacomic)
holes.what: Fiction that self-consciously draws attention to its own status as artifact (Patricia Waugh), here extended to comics whose characters know they are drawn, printed, and read.
holes.why: Chapter 13 is built on this concept: She-Hulk's fourth-wall breaking, gutter-hopping, and the question whether her meta-awareness is delusion or superpower raise the problem of truth in metafiction, which taxonomy has no slug for.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: Sophistry (knack versus craft)
holes.what: The sophistic school of persuasive rhetoric that Socrates criticized as a mere 'knack' of flattery substituting for truth-directed craft, corrupting both person and polis.
holes.why: Chapter 14 explains Norman Osborn's media-staged rise and hollow institutions as exactly this knack-versus-craft failure from Plato's Gorgias; taxonomy's sophistic-relativism slug targets relativism, not rhetoric against truth.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: Joseph Butler
holes.what: Anglican bishop whose Fifteen Sermons (1726) treat resentment as a natural, self-protective passion whose excess must be overcome by forgiveness.
holes.why: Chapter 16's entire definition of forgiveness—relinquishing resentment without excusing or condoning—is built on Butler's sermons, which the chapter calls the accepted basis of contemporary forgiveness theory.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: John M. Doris
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose situationist critique (Lack of Character, 2002) uses social psychology to deny robust global character traits, allowing only local ones.
holes.why: Chapter 18 needs Doris as Aristotle's modern opponent: his 'local/regional traits' framework is what lets the chapter explain Hawkeye's successful redirection from villainy versus Quicksilver's backsliding.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: The American Monomyth
holes.what: Jewett and Lawrence's reworking of Campbell's hero's journey for American pop culture: a threatened paradise, failing institutions, a selfless superhero who redemptively restores the status quo and recedes.
holes.why: Chapter 22 leans on this concept (plus Reynolds's status-quo defense) to argue the superhero genre is structurally reactive, which is why proactive heroes like Fury and Stark are punished by their own narratives.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: The Great Chain of Being
holes.what: The hierarchical ordering of all beings from the eternal Creator down through increasingly contingent ranks, graded by power, longevity, and perfection.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explicitly builds a 'Marvel great chain of godhood'—One-Above-All, Living Tribunal, cosmic beings, elders, sky fathers, mortals—to reconcile Thor and Hercules with the Christian God, and taxonomy lacks this structural concept.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist whose The Four Loves distinguishes affection, friendship, Eros, and charity, each combining gift-love, need-love, and appreciative-love.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Lewis's four-loves framework as its primary analytical tool for deciding whether the Vision and the Scarlet Witch's marriage counts as love, and he appears nowhere in taxonomy.
holes.book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German sociologist and social theorist who defined the modern state as the institution that successfully claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its entire Batman-versus-the-state analysis on Weber's monopoly-of-legitimate-violence definition, explicitly contrasting it with Hobbes's Leviathan and Nietzsche's new idol.
holes.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that the things a general term applies to share no single common essence but are connected by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, like the members of a family.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central claim is that there are no necessary and sufficient conditions for being Batman and that 'Batman' is identified only through Wittgensteinian family resemblance, which the existing language-games slug does not name.
holes.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul

holes.name: Knight of Faith (vs knight of infinite resignation)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling distinction between the knight of infinite resignation, who renounces the finite for an eternal ideal, and the knight of faith, who by virtue of the absurd repossesses the ordinary through passionate devotion.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire argument is that Batman is a knight of infinite resignation while Alfred is the higher knight of faith, a distinction no existing Kierkegaard slug (leap of faith, despair, anxiety) captures.
holes.book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' uses the human-machine hybrid to dissolve the boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, and to rethink hybrid identity.
holes.why: Chapters 10 and 17 build their readings of the humanoid Cylons as hybrids directly on Haraway's cyborg, quoting the Manifesto.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: The Cyborg (human-machine hybridity)
holes.what: The cyborg is a being of mixed human and machine parts and, more broadly, a metaphor for existing between worlds such that all identity is hybrid.
holes.why: Chapter 10 applies cyborg hybridity to the Cylons and to viewers, and chapter 18 asks whether Cylons are super-cyborgs; no existing slug covers cyborgs.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Homi Bhabha
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist of colonial 'ambivalence' and 'mimicry': the colonized are urged to be 'almost the same, but not quite,' which destabilizes colonial authority.
holes.why: Chapter 15's analysis of human-Cylon race ambivalence quotes Bhabha's The Location of Culture throughout (ambivalence, mimicry as 'resemblance and menace').
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: The Colonial Family Romance
holes.what: Verges's postcolonial model (inverting Freud's family romance) in which the colonizing 'parent' binds colonized 'children' with benevolent ideology while policing racial difference, miscegenation and perpetual minority.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads the whole human-Cylon relationship (created Cylon 'children,' Hera's mixed blood, Roslin's maternal claim) as a colonial family romance.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Purity and Danger (body boundaries and contamination)
holes.what: Mary Douglas's account of 'dirt as matter out of place': bodies function as culturally invented boundaries, and feared contamination marks who counts as other.
holes.why: Chapter 18's core argument, that human/Cylon bodily boundaries and contamination fears are socially constructed, is built explicitly on Douglas's Purity and Danger.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: George Lakoff
holes.what: Cognitive linguist who argues moral and political reasoning is structured by unconscious metaphors, most famously the nation-as-family split into Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models.
holes.why: Chapter 23 maps Cain's Pegasus against Adama's Galactica entirely through Lakoff's two family models from Moral Politics.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Strict Father and Nurturant Parent Models
holes.what: Lakoff's pair of idealized family moralities (hierarchical obedience, punishment and self-reliance versus empathy, nurturance and open communication) that structure political worldviews.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the two models to explain Cain's kill-conditioning of Kendra, Adama's 'worthy of surviving' ethos, and Razor's political balance.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Italian philosopher best known for homo sacer and 'bare life' - human existence reduced to biological survival stripped of political meaning under sovereign power.
holes.why: Chapter 34 explicitly follows Agamben to describe the fleet in '33' as bare life suspended between two deaths, cut off from history and future.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Melanie Klein
holes.what: Psychoanalyst who placed the death instinct at the center of infant development, explaining anxiety through splitting, projection, and the paranoid position.
holes.why: Chapter 37 uses Klein's paranoid position and projection as its central lens: humans project aggression onto the Cylons and must stand perpetual watch for its return.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Mormon Theology (LDS cosmology)
holes.what: Latter-day Saint doctrines - Kolob, eternal progression, deification, uncreated matter, and absolute moral agency - teaching that humans may become as God is.
holes.why: Chapter 40 argues the original series' whole ontology (Kobol, Quorum of Twelve, sealing, the Beings of Light) is built from creator Glen Larson's Mormon theology.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian theorist of the dialogic: texts speak in polyphonic dialogue (heteroglossia) with other voices and texts rather than standing as single-authored works.
holes.why: Chapter 41 answers the 'GINO' charge with Bakhtin's dialogism, reading the re-imagined series as one polyphonic utterance in conversation with Mormon, mythic, and fan sources.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Mani
holes.what: Third-century Persian founder of Manichaeism, a dualist religion of perpetual war between the forces of Light and Darkness with humanity as the battleground.
holes.why: Chapter 42 reads the original series' moral absolutism - Count Iblis versus the Ships of Light - as Manichaean cosmology set against the remake's relativism.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Eve and Lilith Myths
holes.what: Genesis and rabbinic narratives (Zohar, Alphabet of Ben Sira) of the first women: Eve the transgressing mother of humanity and Lilith the demonized equal who refused subordination to Adam.
holes.why: Chapter 44 maps Cylons Six and Sharon onto Eve and Lilith in order to redeem both the demonized myths and the characters from misogynistic readings.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Coduction (ethical criticism of fiction)
holes.what: Wayne Booth's method of ethical criticism: validating one's judgment of a fiction by comparing reasons with other qualified readers in ongoing, open-minded conversation.
holes.why: Chapter 46 argues Battlestar is an ethical show because it invites coduction about abortion, torture, and suicide bombing rather than closing down discussion.
holes.book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

holes.name: Paul Ricoeur
holes.what: French philosopher who held that theodicies are a 'mad project' that fails before senseless suffering and that evil is best understood through the myths and symbols of cultures.
holes.why: Chapter 14 invokes Ricoeur to frame Sheldon's Star Trek and comic-book myths as symbolic frameworks through which he interprets Wil Wheaton's wrongdoing.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Scientism
holes.what: The view that science, especially fundamental physics, holds privileged epistemic authority over all other human endeavors and ways of knowing.
holes.why: Chapter 17 names and dismantles Sheldon's 'fundamentalist scientism,' the inverted-pyramid hierarchy of the sciences that licenses his contempt for engineering and the humanities.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Scientism
holes.what: The expansion of scientific explanation to every domain of knowledge, on the claim that only natural-science knowledge is really worth having.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire argument defines and criticizes the gang's scientistic worldview (the Wolowitz coefficient, the friendship algorithm) as the source of the show's humor.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Reductionism
holes.what: The Cartesian strategy of explaining complex wholes by dividing them into parts and building up from the simplest elements, often contrasted with emergent higher-level phenomena.
holes.why: Chapter 19 grounds scientism's appeal in Descartes's second and third principles of reduction and questions whether culture and subjective experience can be reduced to biology or C-fiber firings.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Many-Valued Logic
holes.what: Non-classical logics that admit truth-values between complete truth and complete falsity, so statements can be more or less true or false.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses many-valued logic to show how Raj can be right while Sheldon is not fully wrong, grounding degrees of truth against Sheldon's claim that wrongness admits no gradation.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher of language and mind who argued there is no such thing as radically different conceptual schemes and rejected an uninterpreted independent reality as a ground of truth.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central sections apply Davidson's 'On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme' to show Sheldon and Mary share one world, and his critique of metaphysical realism drives its tolerance argument.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Paul Grice
holes.what: Philosopher of language whose conversational maxims (for example, do not say what you believe to be false) ground implicature and the interpretation of sarcasm.
holes.why: Chapter 25's final definition of lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false rests on Grice's norms of conversation, which also explain why Sheldon misses sarcasm.
holes.book: 145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

holes.name: Kurt Gödel
holes.what: Austrian logician (1906–1978) who proved the completeness of first-order logic and then the incompleteness theorems.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire film analogy runs on Gödel: he is its central historical figure, from the Vienna completeness proof to the Königsberg announcement of undecidability.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
holes.what: Any consistent formal system expressing basic arithmetic contains true but unprovable statements, and cannot prove its own consistency.
holes.why: Chapter 10 maps the Dude's post-rug breakdown onto incompleteness and reads his new axiom 'the Dude abides' as the self-consistency claim the second theorem forbids.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: Josef Pieper
holes.what: Twentieth-century Thomist philosopher whose Leisure: The Basis of Culture defends contemplative leisure as essential to a fully human life.
holes.why: Chapter 12's final assessment of whether the Dude's abiding has merit rests on Pieper's concept of leisure, quoted at length alongside his Aquinas sources.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose diagnosis of modernity's malaises (disenchantment, disengagement, atomism) and ethics of authenticity criticize atomistic modern life.
holes.why: Chapter 20 structures its account of the Dude's nihilism-threatened world around Taylor's three malaises of modernity, quoting The Ethics of Authenticity and later essays throughout.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: Repetition (Gjentagelsen)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's forward-looking repetition: reinhabiting a choice or way of life so it is carried forward, inflected, and renewed, unlike backward-looking recollection.
holes.why: Chapter 22's central claim is that the Dude answers American nihilism through successful Kierkegaardian repetition — abidingly rolling frame after frame — a concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: Kierkegaardian Irony (indirect communication)
holes.what: Irony as indirect communication: saying something other than the literal message such that only the receiver's self-reflection can yield its truth.
holes.why: Chapter 25's whole analysis of Lebowski Fest Achievers is built on Kierkegaard's The Concept of Irony and indirect communication, not on any of his existing taxonomy concepts.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: Victorian mathematician-philosopher whose 1877 essay 'The Ethics of Belief' holds it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe on insufficient evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 29 is framed as a Clifford-versus-James debate over whether Walter was wrong to believe Bunny kidnapped herself, quoting Clifford's ship-owner case and evidentialism at length.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief
holes.what: The debate over whether believing without sufficient evidence is a moral wrong, and whether we can be responsible for — or choose — what we believe.
holes.why: Chapter 29 evaluates Walter's belief-forming practices entirely through the Clifford–James–Williams ethics-of-belief debate, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-American novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) whose Objectivism champions rational self-interest, laissez-faire capitalism, and art as a selective re-creation of reality; Andrew Ryan is her fictional male counterpart.
holes.why: Chapter 4's entire argument about Rapture as the fate of Galt's Atlantis, and the book's framing question of whether BioShock refutes Rand, turns on her biography, Atlas Shrugged, and her theory of art.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Objectivism (rational self-interest)
holes.what: Rand's philosophy that enlightened rational self-interest and unregulated capitalism are moral ideals, with 'parasites' who live off others as the enemy.
holes.why: Chapter 4 argues the game indicts not Objectivism itself but Ryan's failure to integrate emotion into it, and Ryan's ideology, propaganda, and 'sweat of his brow' speech in later chapters are all Objectivism in action.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Many-Worlds Interpretation (Everett)
holes.what: Hugh Everett III's reading of quantum mechanics on which the wave function never collapses and every measurement branches the universe into equally real parallel worlds.
holes.why: Chapter 9 treats BioShock Infinite's tears and constants-and-variables multiverse as Everett's many-worlds made real, which is what blocks alternate possibilities and generates the chapter's transworld moral responsibility thesis.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Frankfurt Cases (against alternate possibilities)
holes.what: Harry Frankfurt's counterexamples showing an agent can be morally responsible even when a counterfactual intervener would have made it impossible to do otherwise, refuting the Principle of Alternate Possibilities.
holes.why: Chapter 9's central move is modeling Jack's 'would you kindly' conditioning and the player's confined choices as a Frankfurt case with Atlas as the prior-sign intervener, so responsibility survives without alternative possibilities.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Carl Schmitt
holes.what: German political theorist (1888-1985) who grounded 'the political' in the friend-enemy distinction and defined the sovereign as 'he who decides on the exception'.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses Schmitt's concepts of political founding, antagonism, and sovereignty as its entire framework for analyzing Columbia's secession, its racism, the Vox Populi's tyranny, and the ending's elimination of DeWitt.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Human Enhancement (transhumanism vs bioconservatism)
holes.what: The bioethics debate over technologies that improve human bodies and minds beyond species-typical functioning, spanning therapy-versus-enhancement lines, transhumanist defenses, morphological freedom, and Habermas-style objections to designing children.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Plasmids and ADAM precisely as human enhancement technologies and stages the whole pro-and-con debate, including the enhancement arms race, designer children, and disability critiques of the 'normal functioning' ideal.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Philosophy of Beauty (beauty and morality)
holes.what: Classical and pragmatist accounts of beauty, from Plato's Symposium and Aristotle's order-and-symmetry to the question of whether aesthetic value shapes moral judgment.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads Dr. Steinman's surgical madness through Plato's and Aristotle's accounts of beauty and Dewey on aesthetic influence, arguing BioShock links beauty to goodness in ways players must learn to disentangle.
holes.book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

holes.name: Fiction as Philosophy (thought experiments)
holes.what: The thesis, developed by Thomas Wartenberg and others, that works of fiction and film can pose thought experiments, make arguments, and do philosophy in their own right.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central claim is that Black Mirror does philosophy the way Sartre's No Exit and utopian fictions from More to Bacon do — as thought experiment and social criticism rather than mere entertainment.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Seeing As (aspect perception)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's duck-rabbit notion that two people can have the same visual experience yet interpret, or 'see,' it as different things.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses 'seeing as' to explain why viewers, and the book's own authors, can legitimately interpret the same Black Mirror episode as making different philosophical points.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Byung-Chul Han
holes.what: Contemporary Korean-German philosopher whose The Transparency Society criticizes the modern imperative of visibility, surveillance, and self-exposure.
holes.why: Chapter 14 leans on Han's transparency society to argue that the Grain's total disclosure destroys the trust, secrecy, and freedom a society needs.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Social Trust (trust as complexity reduction)
holes.what: Niklas Luhmann's account of trust as the relational attitude that lets us act under uncertainty by reducing social complexity and anticipating the future.
holes.why: Chapter 14's core argument is that Grain-style total transparency erodes the interpersonal trust on which relationships, justice systems, and freedom all run.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Symbolic Capital (Bourdieu)
holes.what: Pierre Bourdieu's fourth form of capital: intangible prestige, honor, and social value that exists only through a society's recognition.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Nosedive's star ratings as a technology that makes each citizen's symbolic capital explicit and determines status and inequality.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: The Presentation of Self (impression management)
holes.what: Erving Goffman's dramaturgical account of social life as staged performance in which we manage impressions through roles, props, and masks.
holes.why: Chapters 14 and 22 both use Goffman's masks to explain how the Grain and Nosedive's ratings pressure people into performing themselves instead of living.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Dehumanization
holes.what: Conceiving of a group as less than human (vermin, monsters, disease), which dissolves the moral restraints that normally stop us from harming them.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues dehumanizing language and propaganda are our real-world MASS implant, enabling everything from the Holocaust to the Rwandan and Rohingya genocides.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: The Child's Right to an Open Future
holes.what: Joel Feinberg's idea that children hold rights in trust — to education, development, and a wide range of adult options — that parents must not foreclose.
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues Marie's Arkangel filtering violates Sara's right to an open future by stunting her autonomy, resilience, and capacity for empathy.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: The Attention Economy
