holes.what: An economic model (Herbert Simon) in which human attention is the scarce resource that platforms capture, optimize, and sell to advertisers - extended by Zuboff's surveillance capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 39's entire analysis of Smithereens runs on the attention economy and behavioral surplus, and no taxonomy slug covers platforms monetizing attention.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Gilbert Simondon
holes.what: French philosopher of technics who held that alienation arises from splitting culture from machines and that knowing our tools liberates us from the 'fetishism of the tool.'
holes.why: Chapter 39 rests its conclusion on Simondon's claim that machine-knowledge is the political answer to digital addiction, and taxonomy has no Simondon.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: Twentieth-century thinker of mimetic desire: we learn what to want by imitating models, which breeds rivalry with those near us.
holes.why: Chapter 40 uses Girard's mimetic desire (borrowed desire, models, external mediation) to explain Rachel's idolization of Ashley O, and taxonomy lacks Girard entirely.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Mimetic Desire
holes.what: Girard's thesis that desire is not spontaneous but copied from models, generating emulation, idol-following and rivalry.
holes.why: Chapter 40 applies mimetic desire directly to Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too's friendship and idol dynamics, and no existing slug covers imitation-based desire.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement to transcend human limits through technology - life extension, enhancement, and human-machine integration toward a posthuman state (homo technicus).
holes.why: Chapter 44 frames Be Right Back, San Junipero and the whole mortality debate through transhumanism (Kurzweil's three bridges vs Fukuyama's objection), which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist who argued 'the medium is the message': new technologies reshape human relations and perception regardless of their content.
holes.why: Chapter 47's uploaded McLuhan is a main interlocutor applying media ecology to the Grain, Black Mirror as art, and technology's dangers, with no taxonomy counterpart.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Jacques Ellul
holes.what: Philosopher of 'technique': the autonomous totality of efficiency-seeking methods that extends beyond machines and ends by enslaving human beings.
holes.why: Chapter 47 gives Ellul's technique a central, extended voice in its dialogue on technological domination, and taxonomy has neither Ellul nor the concept of technique.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Philosophy of Art (artistic value)
holes.what: The branch of aesthetics asking what makes something art and what gives it lasting value, e.g. Gardner/Goodman's criteria of interestingness, memorable form, and the invitation to revisit.
holes.why: Chapter 49's question of whether Black Mirror is lasting art is argued entirely through such criteria, and the taxonomy's only aesthetics slug is Kant's judgment of taste.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics
holes.what: Isaac Asimov's tiered rules constraining robot harm to humans, famous as a proposed safeguard against machine danger.
holes.why: Chapter 33 seriously engages the Three Laws as robot ethics for Metalhead's robo-dogs and explains why they fail, and taxonomy has no slug for them.
holes.book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Irish-British Whig statesman and philosopher (1729–1797), critic of the French Revolution who defended gradual, tradition-bound political change over rationally designed upheaval.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is built on Burke's Reflections-era argument that Wakanda's Challenge Day rituals and organic reform outperform Killmonger's rationally justified revolution.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Agnotology (cultivated ignorance)
holes.what: The study of ignorance as an actively constructed and maintained product, rather than a mere absence of knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 12 analyzes T'Chaka's concealment of N'Jobu's death and N'Jadaka's existence as ignorance deliberately manufactured to sustain Wakandan isolationism.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Ubuntu (I am because we are)
holes.what: Southern African ethical principle that persons are constituted through relations with others, grounding mutuality, hospitality, and recognition of shared humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues an isiXhosa-speaking Wakanda paradoxically lacks ubuntu, and that Etieyibo and Eze use it to ground a cosmopolitanism of shared humanity that Wakanda's isolationism betrays.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Pan-Africanism
holes.what: Movement holding that people of African descent share a common condition and should unite for liberation, from the 1900 Pan-African Conference through Du Bois, Garvey, and Nkrumah.
holes.why: Chapter 14 identifies Killmonger's plan to arm the diaspora as the violent wing of this tradition and measures it against T'Challa's institutional liberalism.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Liberal Internationalism and Collective Security
holes.what: International-relations doctrine that states should cooperate through institutions like the UN, with collective security deterring aggression and rights trumping national interest.
holes.why: Chapter 14 evaluates T'Challa's UN speech and Oakland outreach as exactly this doctrine, finding collective security impotent against the oppression Killmonger targets.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: The Civilizing Mission (moral defense of empire)
holes.what: The justification that conquest and rule over 'less enlightened' peoples benefits the conquered, from Rome's pacification through Kipling's white man's burden and Mill's trusteeship.
holes.why: Chapter 17 tests N'Jobu's and Killmonger's 'rule them all the right way' plan against exactly this imperial self-justification and its historical record of atrocity.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Legitimation Crisis
holes.what: Habermas's notion of a breakdown in the motivations and institutions that secure mass loyalty to a social order, leaving its norms unable to bind members.
holes.why: Chapter 18's central claim is that Killmonger's unkingly rule triggers precisely this crisis for Wakandan kingship itself, not just for his personal reign.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Divine Right of Kings
holes.what: Doctrine that monarchs derive authority directly from God rather than the people's consent, articulated by James VI and systematized by Bossuet.
holes.why: Chapter 18 maps T'Challa's UN speech proposition-by-proposition onto Bossuet's scriptural defense of absolutism, concluding Wakanda's king reaches toward divine-right rule.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Carol J. Adams
holes.what: Feminist-vegetarian critical theorist whose The Sexual Politics of Meat argues meat-eating symbolically reinforces patriarchal masculinity and the objectification of women and animals.
holes.why: Chapter 11 builds its entire reading of M'Baku's vegetarianism and Killmonger's hypermasculinity on Adams's meat-patriarchy framework.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Audre Lorde
holes.what: Black feminist poet and theorist of difference, interdependency, and the limits of using the master's tools against the master's house.
holes.why: Chapter 23 grounds its account of Wakandan women's womanist self-definition and solidarity across difference in Lorde's essays, quoted at length throughout.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Womanism (Alice Walker)
holes.what: Alice Walker's term for Black feminist consciousness — 'womanish,' audacious, committed to the survival and wholeness of an entire people — prioritizing communal over individual freedom.
holes.why: Chapter 23 applies Walker's four-part definition to Shuri, Okoye, and Nakia, arguing Wakandan women exemplify womanist rather than merely feminist philosophies.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Conceptual Decolonization
holes.what: Kwasi Wiredu's program of purging African philosophy of Western conceptual frameworks imposed during colonialism and renewing indigenous conceptual schemes.
holes.why: Chapter 25 frames Coates's and Coogler's re-Africanizing of Wakanda's pantheon and afterlife as exactly this project and uses it to expose the Hamitic Hypothesis lurking in Black Panther lore.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Quasi-Physicalism (Akan philosophy of mind)
holes.what: Wiredu and Safro Kwame's Akan theory that spiritual beings, if real, differ from humans by degree of physicality rather than by substance, rejecting the natural/supernatural dichotomy.
holes.why: Chapter 25 offers it as the African metaphysics that makes Killmonger's postmortem survival of substance and subjectivity rationally plausible where Cartesian dualism fails.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we have genuine, rational emotional responses to characters we know do not exist, although such emotions seem to require belief in their objects.
holes.why: Chapter 26 opens with it to explain why audiences genuinely weep for T'Challa and Wakanda, resolving it through the film's knowingly fictional representation of real racism.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement holding that humanity should use technology to transcend biological limits - defeating death, enhancing bodies and cognition, even morally enhancing ourselves.
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues its promises (Bostrom's Dragon Tyrant, moral bioenhancement) ring hollow for Black people while technologies embed anti-Blackness, and reads Wakanda as an Afrofuturist corrective.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Afrofuturism (and Africanfuturism)
holes.what: Art and speculation by people of African descent placing Black cultures in technologically advanced futures, recently distinguished by Nnedi Okorafor from the Africa-rooted Africanfuturism.
holes.why: Chapters 28-30 argue Wakanda's meaning depends on this genre: chapter 29 uses Afrofuturism to reframe vibranium as a thought experiment about harmonizing technology, nature, and culture.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Technological Instrumentalism and the Politics of Artifacts
holes.what: The debate over whether technologies are neutral means to independently chosen ends (instrumentalism) or themselves shape social and political life, exemplified by Langdon Winner's low-bridges case.
holes.why: Chapter 29 argues the film's instrumentalist framing of vibranium hides how technology co-constitutes Wakanda's culture, so exporting it could never be culturally neutral.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Paul Gilroy
holes.what: Contemporary race theorist whose The Black Atlantic frames diasporic Black identity as formed by exile, expropriation, and transatlantic movement rather than by any homeland.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses the Black Atlantic to explain Killmonger as an avatar of landless African American nationalism that Wakanda's rooted utopia excludes.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Cultural Property (nationalism vs internationalism)
holes.what: The debate over who owns cultural goods - the culture that produced them (cultural nationalism) or humanity at large (cultural internationalism) - central to museum repatriation disputes.
holes.why: Chapter 32 uses it to ask whether vibranium is Wakandan property or humanity's inheritance, mirroring the British museum's stolen Benin artifacts.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Audre Lorde
holes.what: Black lesbian feminist poet-theorist whose essay 'The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House' holds that an oppressive system's own instruments cannot end it.
holes.why: Chapter 34 structures its entire reading of Killmonger as a test of Lorde's thesis, asking whether the colonizer's weapons can ever liberate the colonized.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Coloniality of Power
holes.what: Anibal Quijano's concept that the racial classification invented to organize colonial labor extraction outlived formal colonialism as a durable global structure of domination, including neocolonialism.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses it to explain the global backdrop of Killmonger's revolution and to argue the film represses the colonial violence that alone makes its plot intelligible.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
holes.what: Civil Rights leader whose philosophy of nonviolent resistance and 'I Have a Dream' vision of interracial brotherhood anchored the mainstream American freedom struggle.
holes.why: Chapter 36 reads T'Challa's benevolence, mercy to M'Baku and Zemo, and UN 'one single tribe' speech as King's philosophy transposed into Wakanda.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Malcolm X (El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz)
holes.what: Black nationalist leader who defended self-defense 'by any means necessary' and, after his Mecca pilgrimage, moved toward a universal human brotherhood.
holes.why: Chapter 36 maps Killmonger onto Malcolm's militant rhetoric while stressing that Killmonger lacks Malcolm's intelligently directed extremism and later evolution.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: The Black Panther Party
holes.what: Oakland-based Black liberation organization (1966) whose Ten-Point Program joined armed self-defense against police brutality with community survival programs like free breakfast and health clinics.
holes.why: Chapter 37 reads N'Jobu's and Killmonger's Oakland radicalization and T'Challa's outreach center against the Party's history and its contested right to bear arms.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: State Monopoly on Legitimate Violence
holes.what: Max Weber's definition of the state as the institution successfully claiming the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
holes.why: Chapter 37 uses it to show why Black armed self-defense is recoded as aggression and why Killmonger, once legitimately king, turns Wakanda's legitimate violence toward revolution.
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Black (Africana) Existentialism
holes.what: A school (Paget Henry, Drucilla Cornell, Dwayne Tunstall) adapting phenomenology and existentialism to anti-Black racism, where the occasion for reflection is negrification rather than European reason's crisis.
holes.why: Chapter 38's reading of the museum scene and Killmonger's double-consciousness runs entirely through Africana phenomenology and Tunstall's 'ego displacement.'
holes.book: 149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_

holes.name: Eschatology (the Last Things)
holes.what: The branch of Christian theology concerning the last things: death, judgment, apocalypse, and deliverance, exemplified by the Book of Revelation.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument is that Black Sabbath's Satanic and apocalyptic lyrics are an eschatological imagination borrowing the literary devices of Revelation against the Cold War and Vietnam backdrop.
holes.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

holes.name: Philosophy of Music (convention vs natural expression)
holes.what: The debate over whether music's emotional meaning (joy, sadness, evil) is expressed naturally and universally or is a convention of a musical culture.
holes.why: Chapter 13 hinges on this dispute: McIver argues the devil's interval sounds evil only by Western convention, against Schopenhauer's claim that music directly expresses universal emotions.
holes.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of how tragedy purges the spectator's fear and pity through sympathetic engagement with horrific events.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central claim is that Sabbath's darkest songs ("Black Sabbath", "Iron Man", "Paranoid") work as catharsis exactly as Greek tragedy did, making the darkness essential to their artistic value.
holes.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that the instances of some concepts (like "game") share overlapping, criss-crossing traits with no single essence or set of necessary and sufficient conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues heavy metal is precisely such a concept, undefined by any stylistic conditions and united instead by resemblance to its prototype, Black Sabbath.
holes.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

holes.name: The Definition of Art (institutional and historical theories)
holes.what: The philosophical project of defining art, from imitation and expression theories through Danto/Dickie's artworld institutional theory to Levinson's historical definition.
holes.why: Chapter 19 tests each major theory of art against Sabbath and adopts Levinson's historical definition to validate the band's doom as art, and no philosophy-of-art concept exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

holes.name: Hasty Generalization (fallacy)
holes.what: The informal fallacy of concluding that all members of a group have a trait because one, a few, or even most observed instances do.
holes.why: Chapter 29's whole argument against the caveman stereotype of metalheads is that it commits this fallacy, and the taxonomy has no logic or fallacy concepts.
holes.book: 150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality

holes.name: Neil Postman
holes.what: Media ecologist and NYU professor whose Amusing Ourselves to Death argues television's entertainment bias turns news and public discourse into irrational, incoherent 'disinformation'.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire reading of The Daily Show (Crossfire, Cramer, Fox News Sunday, the Rally) is built on Postman's entertainment-bias thesis, which the chapter treats as the show's implicit philosophical ground.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Canadian communication theorist famous for 'the medium is the message', the claim that the form of a medium shapes what can be communicated, independently of its content.
holes.why: Chapter 9 presents Postman's thesis as a revision of McLuhan's slogan and illustrates it with his smoke-signals example, and the phrase recurs in chapters 13 and 20.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Truth in Fiction
holes.what: The question of how deliberately made-up but non-deceptive narratives can convey both particular facts and general truths, and how audiences distinguish the made-up from the asserted.
holes.why: Chapter 10's whole argument defines The Daily Show as fiction ('hilarious make-'em-ups') and explains how fake news can nonetheless be a genuine news source.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Horatian vs Juvenalian Satire
holes.what: The classical distinction between gentle, playful satire that treats vice as folly (Horace) and bitter, indignant invective that pays the world back with words (Juvenal).
holes.why: Chapter 11 assigns Colbert the Horatian and Stewart the Juvenalian ethos as the two poles of the Fifth Estate's satiric voice, and chapter 12 leans on Juvenal as well.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: The Fifth Estate
holes.what: A watchdog institution beyond the press, 'a watcher for the watchdogs', of bloggers, activists, artists and satirists who monitor the failing Fourth Estate.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is organized around the claim that The Daily Show supplies this emergent institution with an ethos rooted in Franklin-era fake news.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Aristophanes
holes.what: Athenian comic playwright (c. 446-386 BC) whose political comedies mocked demagogues like Cleon and whose Clouds caricatured Socrates as a charlatan.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Aristophanes as the founding case of political mockery and his Clouds as evidence of mockery's danger, and chapter 11 reads the Rally to Restore Sanity as Aristophanic comedy.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Parrhesia (fearless speech)
holes.what: The Greek term for frank, truth-telling speech offered at personal risk, which Diogenes called the most beautiful thing in the world.
holes.why: Chapter 17 casts the Cynics' parrhesia, and Stewart's satire by extension, as democratic shock therapy and the key instrument for 'defacing the currency' of corrupted convention.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Performing Marginality
holes.what: Joanne Gilbert's notion that women and minority comics turn their insider/outsider position at the margins into a subversive critique of the hegemonic mainstream ('judo rhetoric').
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses this frame to explain how Larry Wilmore's Senior Black Correspondent segments can say about race what white or mainstream pundits cannot.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Informal Fallacies
holes.what: Recurring error patterns in reasoning that appear correct: ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope, equivocation, and begging the question.
holes.why: Chapter 22 catalogs exactly these fallacies in political rhetoric as the primary target of The Daily Show's satire, and taxonomy.json has no logic or critical-thinking concept for them.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Reinhold Niebuhr
holes.what: Twentieth-century Christian realist who warned that believers treat God as 'the sanctifier of whatever we most fervently desire' and demanded humility about claims of divine sanction for political projects.
holes.why: Chapter 25 leans on Niebuhr's critique of religious pretension as its closing framework for Bachmann's, Robertson's, and Beck's certainty about the mind of God.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Religious Pluralism (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism)
holes.what: The three classic philosophical responses to religious diversity: exclusivism (only one religion is true), inclusivism (other faiths are anonymous versions of one's own), and pluralism (many traditions carry partial truths without collapsing into relativism).
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire analysis of the 'This Week in God' segments is organized around these three positions, which the taxonomy's religion domain lacks.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher whose metaphysics of universal flux, Creativity, and a persuasive Deity allows multiple genuine religious ultimates to underlie the world's diverse traditions.
holes.why: Chapter 26 invokes Whitehead's process metaphysics as the metaphysical platform that makes deep religious pluralism plausible and ends by endorsing his anti-dogmatic humility.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Separation of Church and State
holes.what: The constitutional principle, articulated in Jefferson's 'wall of separation' letter to the Danbury Baptists, that government may neither establish nor favor a religion nor impede its free exercise.
holes.why: Chapter 27's core argument is that courthouse nativities and public-school Christmas plays violate this wall, against originalist and David Barton-style objections.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Thomas Jefferson
holes.what: American Founder and radical anti-originalist who held that 'the earth belongs to the living' and urged each generation to refound its constitution rather than worship the Framers.
holes.why: Chapter 31's defense of living constitutionalism against Tea Party originalism is built around Jefferson's fake foreword to America (The Book), his letters to Madison and Kercheval, and Bleyer's use of him as 'anti-originalist par excellence'.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Speaker Meaning (Humpty Dumpty intentionalism)
holes.what: The view that a word means whatever its user intends it to mean, opposed to theories that ground word meaning in communal conventions of use and in dictionaries that merely report usage.
holes.why: Chapter 32 tests the Humpty Dumpty view, stipulation, dictionary regulation, and communal adoption against Colbert's and Stewart's neologisms, which are meaningful at first use.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Self-Deception and the Paradoxes of Irrationality
holes.what: Believing against evidence one recognizes as such, raising the static paradox (one person holding contradictory beliefs) and the dynamic paradox (knowingly deceiving oneself), classically solved by dividing the mind or by attention-directing.
holes.why: Chapter 33's account of truthiness as motivated irrationality is structured entirely around wishful thinking, self-deception, and how its two paradoxes might be resolved.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Truthiness (knowing with the gut)
holes.what: Colbert's coinage for the quality of preferring what one wishes or feels to be true over known facts, analyzable as motivated epistemic irrationality and, at its worst, subjectivism.
holes.why: Chapters 32 through 34 of this volume are built around the term and its epistemic dangers, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Friedrich Schlegel
holes.what: Early German Romantic who made irony central to philosophy, defining Socratic irony as 'the only involuntary and yet completely deliberate dissimulation' in which everything is playful and serious at once.
holes.why: Chapter 34 quotes Schlegel repeatedly as the source of the Romantic doctrine of existential irony that links Socrates to Colbert's persona.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: Rorty's Ironist and the Final Vocabulary
holes.what: Rorty's ideal of the liberal ironist, who has radical and continuing doubts about the final vocabulary she uses to justify her life, recognizes argument cannot settle those doubts, and treats her vocabulary as contingent rather than closer to reality.
holes.why: Chapter 34's central question, whether Colbert's persona is Rorty's ironist and whether truthiness betrays that ideal, is argued entirely through this framework, which the taxonomy's pragmatism concepts omit.
holes.book: 152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory

holes.name: J.L. Schellenberg
holes.what: Philosopher of religion whose argument from divine hiddenness claims a perfectly loving God would ensure that anyone open to a relationship could believe, so the existence of non-resistant non-believers is evidence there is no loving God.
holes.why: Chapter 13 is organized entirely as a rebuttal of Schellenberg's hiddenness argument, using Hidden Mickeys to challenge its first premise.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Divine Hiddenness
holes.what: The problem that God seems absent, silent, or non-existent even to willing believers, which Schellenberg turns into an argument against the existence of a perfectly loving God.
holes.why: Chapter 13's whole Hidden Mickeys analogy exists to show why God's traces can be ambiguous without contradicting perfect love.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: The feminist account that genuine autonomy is achieved only within networks of social relationship and dependence, not in spite of them.
holes.why: Chapter 16 contrasts traditional self-sufficiency with relational autonomy to explain why Dory thrives through supported interdependence while sidekicks like Dopey are defined by helpless dependence.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: The Beauty Myth
holes.what: Naomi Wolf's claim that socially constructed, media-driven beauty standards act as a punitive 'iron maiden' controlling women precisely as their social power grows.
holes.why: Chapter 17 applies Wolf's beauty myth to Ariel and Jasmine as princesses whose revealing design and unattainable body image police third-wave women.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Pope John Paul II
holes.what: Polish pope and phenomenologist whose 'theology of the body' and personalism defend marriage as a lifelong, exclusive mutual self-gift between persons made for communion.
holes.why: Chapter 18's Family Unity Model of marriage, parenthood, and the love-versus-use contrast (Quasimodo's 'Heaven's Light' against Frollo's 'Hellfire') is built directly on John Paul II's theology of the body.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: G.K. Chesterton
holes.what: English essayist and apologist whose philosophy of wonder, gratitude, and fairy tale treats astonishment at bare existence, and imagination that 'makes settled things strange,' as the heart of sanity.
holes.why: Chapter 22 diagnoses Mr. Banks entirely through Chesterton's Orthodoxy — the man who forgot who he is — and uses his nursery philosophy as the cure Mary Poppins delivers.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Jean-Luc Marion
holes.what: French phenomenologist whose Erotic Phenomenon analyzes love as the risky question 'Does anyone out there love me?' rather than an ego-certifying declaration.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire reading of Frozen — Anna's knocking, Hans's vanity, love overcoming fear — is built on Marion's philosophy of love.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Max Scheler
holes.what: German phenomenologist of value whose ethics holds that we first learn the good through moral exemplars rather than universal rules or consequences.
holes.why: Chapter 33's resolution — that clumsy, earnest Goofy teaches goodness as a moral exemplar — rests on Scheler after its Kantian and utilitarian readings fail.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Zoopolis (animal citizenship)
holes.what: Donaldson and Kymlicka's political theory of animal rights on which domesticated animals should be recognized as co-citizens of human communities.
holes.why: Chapter 36's second half reads Zootopia's multispecies society through Zoopolis's citizenship model rather than through classic animal-rights arguments.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: The Hero's Journey (monomyth)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's monomyth: the universal hero-adventure pattern built on Jungian archetypes that modern blockbusters follow.
holes.why: Chapter 39 claims Disney consciously constructs its mythology on Campbell's hero's journey ('We Create the Mythology of the Future'), and the taxonomy has only Jung's archetypes.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Vine Deloria Jr.
holes.what: Native American thinker for whom life is a sacred web of relationships in which the dead remain present and moral responsibility is shared by all beings.
holes.why: Chapter 40 uses Deloria's indigenous relationality as its main lens for the Circle of Life, Moana's grandmother, and Brother Bear's ancestral spirits.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Multiculturalism (politics of recognition)
holes.what: The view (Kymlicka, Taylor, Benhabib) that a just society must recognize and protect cultures on their own terms, not merely display them.
holes.why: Chapter 41 judges Epcot's World Showcase against multicultural recognition theory and finds a commodified counterfeit of it.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: McWorld
holes.what: Benjamin Barber's term for the homogenizing global commodity market that packages and sells culture in shallow form for consumption.
holes.why: Chapter 41's closing argument is that 'Disneyfication' sells political values like freedom and multiculturalism as McWorld-style commodities.
holes.book: 153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century Russian-American philosopher of Objectivism, an egoist ethics of rational self-interest and laissez-faire capitalism expressed in novels like The Fountainhead.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument frames Mordo's absolutism and Strange's choice through Rand's Objectivism, noting Steve Ditko's Rand-influenced creation of Doctor Strange.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Objectivism (A is A)
holes.what: Rand's philosophy built on three self-evident axioms — existence, consciousness, and identity (the Law of Identity, 'A is A') — with reason as man's means of survival.
holes.why: Chapter 12 tests each axiom against Wong's death-and-reanimation and Strange's multiverse of simultaneous realities, arguing the film breaks Rand's system from the inside.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Physicalism
holes.what: The metaphysical view that human persons are nothing over and above their working physical parts, with all mental facts explainable by physical (brain) facts.
holes.why: Chapter 14 casts Strange's 'we are made of matter and nothing more' creed as physicalism set against the Ancient One's substance dualism, with the astral-form scenes as its cinematic refutation.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Imre Lakatos
holes.what: Philosopher of science who judged research programs progressive or degenerating by whether modifications to the 'protective belt' around a theory's 'hard core' yield novel predictions.
holes.why: Chapter 18's closing section uses Lakatos's criterion as a third alternative to Kuhn and Feyerabend for deciding whether medicine and sorcery are rationally progressive.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Many-Worlds Interpretation and the Measurement Problem
holes.what: Everett's interpretation of quantum mechanics on which the wave function never collapses but branches at every quantum event into parallel worlds, central to the measurement problem.
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole argument is that the film's multiverse is a many-worlds multiverse, and taxonomy has no concept covering quantum-mechanics interpretations.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: Walzer's dilemma of the person in power who must violate moral principles to achieve a good end, leaving hands dirty even when the act is justified.
holes.why: Chapter 23 is organized around this problem, applying it to the Ancient One's dark magic, Kaecilius, and Strange's rule-breaking bargain with Dormammu.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Thomas E. Hill Jr.
holes.what: Contemporary Kantian philosopher known for 'Servility and Self-Respect,' which condemns servility as failing to assert one's equal dignity as a person.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central question—whether Wong's lifelong service is wrongful servility—is built directly on Hill's servility and self-respect argument.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Leo Tolstoy
holes.what: Russian novelist-thinker whose later Christian philosophy of nonresistance rejected all violence, state power, and property as sources of evil.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is built entirely around Tolstoy's Confession and his doctrine of nonviolence, yet he is absent from the taxonomy while his follower Gandhi is present.
holes.book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

holes.name: Noblesse Oblige
holes.what: The 'obligation of nobility': aristocratic status entails social responsibilities toward dependents, tenants, and community rather than mere entitlement.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues Robert Crawley's conservatism is best understood as noblesse oblige, and that treating ownership as duty to tenants brings his aristocratic code close to socialist ideals.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Utopian Socialism (Owen and Fourier)
holes.what: Early nineteenth-century socialism (Robert Owen, Charles Fourier) holding that character is formed by circumstances and that peaceful cooperation and fair contribution can reform society without revolution.
holes.why: Chapter 11 classifies Tom Branson's politics as Owen/Fourier-style utopian socialism rather than Marxism, and reads Robert's paternal estate management as unconsciously approximating those cooperative ideals.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Georg Simmel
holes.what: German sociologist-philosopher whose The Philosophy of Money argues that as money's role in a life grows, individuality and personal ties shrink and money's means become ends.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire reading of Matthew Crawley, his values eroding and his engagement to Mary driven by wealth, rests on Simmel's philosophy of money.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: The Morality of Manners
holes.what: The view (Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' Sarah Buss's reminders of respect, Hume's 'small morals') that etiquette and manners are part of moral virtue itself, expressing and cultivating respect rather than being mere convention.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is built on this concept, reading Matthew's, Branson's, Sir Richard's, and Violet's manners as demonstrations, cultivation, or counterfeiting of moral character.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Hierocles
holes.what: Little-known Stoic philosopher whose surviving fragment pictures the self at the center of concentric circles of affiliation that we should draw inward, treating strangers as family.
holes.why: Chapter 16 devotes its closing section to Hierocles's concentric circles as the Stoic answer to how Downton's residents should treat people across class lines.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Inference to the Best Explanation (abduction)
holes.what: Peirce's 'abduction': reasoning from a surprising fact to the hypothesis that would best explain it, judged by likeliness (evidential support) and loveliness (understanding provided), as developed by Peter Lipton.
holes.why: Chapter 20's whole analysis of the Clarkson-Tapsell dispute, Daisy's numerology, and Violet's statistical spin runs on inference to the best explanation, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Gaston Bachelard
holes.what: French philosopher whose The Poetics of Space offers a phenomenology of intimate spaces, arguing that houses, drawers, corners, and shells invite daydream (topoanalysis) and reveal topophilia, an intense love of place.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is built entirely on Bachelard's topophilia and topoanalysis to explain why the Downton opening credits make viewers feel at home.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: The Haptic (haptic space)
holes.what: Deleuze's concept of a cross-sensory response in which one sense, such as touch, is engaged by another, such as vision, creating immersive 'haptic space' in film and television.
holes.why: Chapter 25 repeatedly applies the haptic to Downton's opening shots, such as light flooding through shutters and lamplight, to explain how viewers are bodily drawn into the Abbey.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Personhood Criteria (Mary Anne Warren)
holes.what: Mary Anne Warren's five functional criteria - consciousness, reasoning, capacity to communicate, self-motivated activity, and self-awareness - that separate persons with moral rights from merely genetic human beings.
holes.why: Chapter 36's abortion debate over Lady Edith's pregnancy turns on Warren's person/human-being distinction, which grounds the pro-choice arguments the chapter examines and criticizes.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and philosopher whose The Four Loves distinguishes storge (affection), philia (friendship), eros, and agape (sacrificial love).
holes.why: Chapter 37's entire framework - grading Downton's relationships by the four loves and arguing agape perfects justice - is taken directly from Lewis, but no taxonomy slug exists for him.
holes.book: 155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There

holes.name: Carl von Clausewitz
holes.what: Prussian officer and war theorist whose On War treats war as a social activity and continuation of politics, balanced across a 'remarkable trinity' of people, military, and government.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is built entirely on Clausewitz's trinity, using it to analyze Duke Leto's Arrakis strategy, Muad'Dib's handling of the Stilgar succession, and modern irregular wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
holes.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib

holes.name: Communicative vs Strategic Action
holes.what: Habermas's distinction between action oriented to reaching mutual understanding with others and goal-oriented strategic action, with lasting social order possible only through the former.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues every Duniverse empire fails because its rule-making is purely strategic, lacking the communicative action and democratic legitimacy that create normative stability.
holes.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Philosopher of religion whose 'soul-making' theodicy in Evil and the God of Love holds that moral and spiritual growth comes only through response to real challenges, perils, and hardship.
holes.why: Chapter 18 closes by quoting Hick to explain how, in Lynch's Dune, good emerges as people respond to evil, the Fremen's goodness awakened by the struggle against Harkonnen oppression.
holes.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib

holes.name: Narrative Identity (self-constitution)
holes.what: The view (Schechtman, Velleman) that a self is constituted by an integrated, coherent first-person narrative of its life rather than by memory chains or bodily continuity alone.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses narrative theory to explain why the final Duncan Idaho ghola can integrate the memories of all his serial lives as one identity, 'It's like one lifetime'.
holes.book: 156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib

holes.name: Catharsis (purging emotion through tragedy)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics account on which experiencing tragedy purges the spectator's pity and fear, extended in this book to other emotions and media.
holes.why: Chapter 9's defense of D&D as worthwhile art leans on catharsis to explain how smacking imaginary goblins discharges real aggression and fear.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: French philosopher whose 'ethic of truths' argues that commitment to a single natural moral law produces evil, as a 'simulacrum' of the Good (Nazism) or a 'disaster' (wars for human rights).
holes.why: Chapter 12 invokes Badiou to ground Chaotic Good: one can pursue what one takes to be Good while refusing the authority of any single moral law.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of selfhood (Sources of the Self) who holds that identity requires an orientation to the good woven into one's life as an unfolding narrative.
holes.why: Chapter 13 quotes Taylor as the leading advocate of narrative ethics and tests his view against grief over a slain D&D character.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Narrative Identity (narrative ethics)
holes.what: The view that making sense of oneself as a persisting self requires grasping one's life as a story, and that fiction and life derive value in similar ways.
holes.why: Chapter 13 evaluates whether narrative ethics can rationalize a player's grief at PC death and replaces it with the self as 'back-story' or metanarrative.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle that readers readily imagine physical impossibilities but balk at imagining morally deviant worlds in which evil is right, discussed via Hume, Gendler, and Walton.
holes.why: Chapters 14 and 15 use imaginative resistance to explain why evil role-play can feel wrong, and whether players must be complicit in a character's wicked perspective.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Race Eliminativism vs Conservation
holes.what: The debate over whether, given that biology finds no human races, we should eliminate racial categories entirely or conserve them pragmatically for pride and solidarity.
holes.why: Chapter 16 frames the D&D elf-race stereotype problem through this exact debate, weighing Du Bois and Outlaw against Appiah's race-blind ideal.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Bioethicist whose Space Traveler thought experiment proposes criteria (religion, art, tool use, shelter) for when unfamiliar beings count as persons with full moral rights.
holes.why: Chapter 19 tests Warren's personhood criteria against orcs that pass them and the lawful-good Flumph killed on sight, concluding personhood cannot be the only moral criterion.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Art-Horror (the philosophy of horror)
holes.what: Noel Carroll's account of horror fiction as arousing art-horror through monsters that are categorically impossible, impure, or incomplete relative to our conceptual schemes, expressed by metonymy, massification, magnification, fission, and fusion.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its whole account of unnatural magic on Carroll's tropes and shows why D&D's mechanical spell rules make the inexpressible unplayable.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Graham Harman
holes.what: Object-oriented ontologist who holds that entities withdraw from all access, with 'allure' naming the aesthetic invitation into another object's reality and 'sincerity' our inescapable fusion with our own experienced objects.
holes.why: Chapter 21 borrows Harman's allure and sincerity to explain how D&D lets players handle the incomparable inner worlds of elves, orcs, paladins, and Illusionists.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Flat Ontology (object-oriented ontology)
holes.what: The view (Levi Bryant's onticology, kindred to object-oriented ontology and Deleuzo-Latourian assemblage theory) that all entities are active substances with virtual powers ('affects') whose qualities are variable local manifestations under local conditions, with no human privilege in the universe.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is an explicit exposition of this framework, using D&D substances, alliances, regimes of attraction and dice-driven chance to argue for it.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Levi Bryant
holes.what: Speculative realist philosopher and author of The Democracy of Objects, whose 'onticology' treats objects as powers that actualize differently in local manifestations and enter into transformative alliances.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is Bryant's own chapter expounding his ontology through D&D, and his technical vocabulary (virtual proper being, local manifestation, regime of attraction) has no taxonomy home.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's account (Philosophical Investigations) that the members of a concept like 'game' are united by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities rather than a single common essence.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central argument that D&D counts as a game, despite lacking winning and losing, is built directly on applying family resemblance to the concept of a game.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle (Colin Radford) that we have genuine emotional responses to characters we know do not exist, with Kendall Walton's make-believe theory of quasi-emotions and fictional truths as a leading solution.
holes.why: Chapter 25 devotes its second half to this paradox and Walton's answer to explain why players are emotionally gripped by D&D campaigns they know are not real.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Kendall Walton
holes.what: Philosopher of art whose make-believe theory of representation (Mimesis as Make-Believe) treats artworks as props that prescribe imaginings within fictional worlds.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is built entirely on Walton's prop theory, using it to explain D&D rules, dice, classes, character sheets and the claim that all games are art.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Make-Believe Theory of Representation (props)
holes.what: Kendall Walton's theory that representations are props prescribing specific imaginings, generating truths 'fictional' within a game of make-believe.
holes.why: Chapter 27 applies prop theory to every component of D&D (rules, dice, classes, attributes, modules, maps, miniatures) as its organizing framework.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Ludology vs Narratology
holes.what: The game-studies debate over whether games should be understood primarily as rule-based formal systems (ludology) or as extensions of narrative (narratology).
holes.why: Chapter 28 frames the whole role-play versus gameplay question through this divide and locates D&D's essence in the border region between the two camps.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Metagaming (player vs character knowledge)
holes.what: The use of out-of-character knowledge or game-level reasoning by players or DMs, and the craft of distinguishing and managing what players know versus what their characters know.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire account of the gunpowder crisis, fudged rolls, hero points and the choice-chance inversion rests on the concept of the metagame.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: R.G. Collingwood
holes.what: British idealist philosopher of history whose 're-enactment thesis' holds that historical understanding is re-thinking the thoughts of historical agents, later amended so the historian must also know that he is re-enacting.
holes.why: Chapter 31 builds its first two models of player-character understanding directly on Collingwood's re-enactment thesis as presented through Gadamer's Truth and Method.
holes.book: 157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue whose 'banking concept' critique of education and problem-posing dialogue treat learning as a practice of liberation from domination.
holes.why: Chapter 7 measures Battle School against Freire's banking model throughout and concludes Graff's teacher-dominated curriculum is exactly the domination-reproducing schooling Freire warned against.
holes.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German Idealist whose freedom treatise argues evil is a real, necessary 'contraction into the self' rooted in the dark ground of human nature, not a mere privation of good.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads Ender's violence, Graff's manipulation, and the novel's freedom-versus-fate theme almost entirely through Schelling's Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom.
holes.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down

holes.name: Game Theory (minimax, zero-sum games)
holes.what: The mathematical study of strategic choice among players, built on von Neumann's minimax theorem and ideas like zero-sum and imperfect-information games.
holes.why: Chapter 12 analyzes the battleroom and Ender's redefinition of the game through minimax and zero-sum reasoning, and chapter 27 reuses the Prisoner's Dilemma for the human-Formic war.
holes.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: Walzer's problem of whether political actors must sometimes commit moral wrongs, and still bear their stain, in order to avoid greater evils.
holes.why: Chapter 13 frames the I.F.'s war and its transfer of guilt onto child soldiers through Walzer's dirty-hands dilemma.
holes.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down

holes.name: Bernard Suits
holes.what: Philosopher of games who defined game-playing as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles via prelusory goals, constitutive rules, lusory means, and the lusory attitude.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its whole analysis of the battleroom and the Giant's Drink on Suits' definition and his open/closed game distinction.
holes.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of language and mind whose 'On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme' rejects radical incommensurability through translatability and the principle of charity.
holes.why: Chapter 17 explains the human-Formic wars as conceptual-scheme failure and casts Ender as the translator between schemes, relying on Davidson's arguments more than any other thinker.
holes.book: 158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down

holes.name: Pascal's Two Infinities (the disproportion of man)
holes.what: Pascal's Pensees meditation that man is 'a nothing compared to the infinite, a whole compared to the nothing', a middle point between the infinitely large and the infinitely small, terrified by infinite spaces whose ends and principles are hidden in impenetrable secrecy.
holes.why: Chapter 12 builds its reading of the show's infinite-space cinematography and Avasarala's Ring dilemma on extended quotations of this Pascal argument before turning to Kant's sublime as the answer, but the taxonomy contains no Pascal concept to express it.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: The Violence of Decolonization (Wretched of the Earth)
holes.what: Fanon's thesis in The Wretched of the Earth that decolonization is always a violent event and that anti-colonial violence is a 'cleansing force' which rids the colonized of their inferiority complex, shatters the colonial ontology, and creates new men.
holes.why: Chapter 23's central defense of Marco Inaros' asteroid attacks rests on this Wretched of the Earth account of violence and new humanism, which the existing black-skin-white-masks slug (the ontological color division) does not cover.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Patriotism vs Nationalism (Orwell's distinction)
holes.what: George Orwell's distinction between patriotism (defensive devotion to a place and way of life, forced on no one) and nationalism (obsessive identification that places the nation beyond good and evil in a quest for power).
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire reading of Drummer as patriot versus Marco Inaros as nationalist is built on this distinction and its three markers (obsession, instability, indifference to reality), which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Contemporary Italian philosopher whose Homo Sacer analyzes sovereignty through bare life and the state of exception.
holes.why: Chapter 25 uses his bios/zoē distinction as its central tool for reading Belters as lives the sovereign 'is permitted to kill without committing homicide'.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Bare Life (homo sacer, state of exception)
holes.what: Life excluded from the political and legal order, reduced to mere existence, that the sovereign may kill without committing homicide.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues Belters at Anderson Station, on Ilus/New Terra, and on Eros are repeatedly reduced to bare life by corporate and political sovereigns.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Biopolitics (power over life)
holes.what: Foucault's account of modern power that manages populations and decides whose life counts, blurring sovereignty across political, capitalist, and military actors.
holes.why: Chapter 25 frames the Anderson Station massacre and the Eros experiment through Foucault's Birth of Biopolitics and the fragmentation of sovereignty, themes taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Critical theorist who co-authored Dialectic of Enlightenment with Adorno, including the rereading of Odysseus and the Sirens as the first self-mastery in the domination of nature.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its portrait of Dresden, Mao, and Strickland as self-made monsters on Horkheimer and Adorno's Sirens episode and domination-of-nature thesis; Adorno is in taxonomy but Horkheimer is not.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Domination of Nature
holes.what: The Enlightenment dream (Bacon onward, reinterpreted by Horkheimer/Adorno and ecofeminists like Mies and Merchant) of boundless mastery over nature, which extends to the domination of women and the self.
holes.why: Chapter 26 reads Protogen's experiments and Marco's control of Naomi's reproduction through this thesis, and contrasts Holden's 'let grow and make grow' farm with it.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: The Anthropocene
holes.what: The proposed geological epoch in which human activity is the dominant force shaping Earth's climate and ecosystems, and the debates (anthropocentrism, Technozoic fixes, climate justice) around it.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is organized entirely around the Anthropocene — Earth's paved garden, Ganymede's cascade, Belter climate refugees — and taxonomy.json has no slug for it.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: The Frontier Myth and American Exceptionalism
holes.what: The destiny narrative casting space as a frontier to be conquered, importing American exceptionalist rhetoric into spaceflight culture (Kennedy, Mars Society, Zubrin).
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues the MCR's Martian exceptionalism is a direct import of this frontier rhetoric and that its unexamined metaphors block the MacIntyrean self-knowledge the chapter advocates.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Politics as Action: Making vs Doing
holes.what: Arendt's Human Condition distinction between making politics (strategic control of outcomes) and doing politics (speech and action that build a common world no one controls).
holes.why: Chapter 32's organizing argument is that Naomi's Ganymede rescue is doing politics balanced against Amos's and Melissa's making, a distinction taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Value Pluralism and Incommensurability
holes.what: The view that moral, epistemic, aesthetic, and prudential values are irreducible kinds sharing no common currency, whose conflicts may be dilemmas, matters of permissibility, or resolvable rankings.
holes.why: Chapter 34's entire argument about risky tradeoffs (Dresden, Cortázar, Volovodov, Okoye) rests on conflicts between incommensurable kinds of value, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Multiplicitous Subjectivity and World-Traveling
holes.what: Latina feminist phenomenology (Ortega, Lugones, Anzaldúa) of selves who inhabit several overlapping social worlds at once and travel between them, experiencing conflicting meanings simultaneously.
holes.why: Chapter 37 applies it directly to Naomi's life between Belter and Roci worlds, using Du Bois's double consciousness (which is in taxonomy) as its ancestor but lacking the central concept itself.
holes.book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

holes.name: Posthumous Harm and the Badness of Death
holes.what: The deprivationist debate over whether death, or events after it, can harm or benefit the person who died - Epicurean no-harm versus Feinberg and Pitcher's ante-mortem person.
holes.why: Chapter 9's whole argument about James's Project Purity sacrifice and the cannibalism of 'Blood Ties' turns on whether the dead can be harmed or wronged.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: David Benatar
holes.what: Contemporary South African philosopher and the leading defender of antinatalism (Better Never to Have Been).
holes.why: Chapter 10's Harm Argument against Lucy and Maximus having children is Benatar's asymmetry argument, which the chapter quotes at length and then rebuts.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Antinatalism (better never to have been)
holes.what: The view that bringing new persons into existence is morally wrong because existence guarantees serious harms that no benefiting can offset.
holes.why: Chapter 10 tests antinatalism against Fallout's wasteland to decide whether Lucy and Maximus may ethically reproduce.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The internalized, evolving life story integrating a reconstructed past and imagined future that gives a life unity and purpose (Charles Taylor, McAdams).
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses narrative identity as the criterion of personhood for Nick Valentine, Danse, Curie, Hancock, Raul, Fawkes, and Marcus.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist of science whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' treats the human-machine hybrid as a figure dissolving natural, technological, and social boundaries.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads the Pip-Boy and Fallout 4's Sole Survivor through Haraway's cyborg before contrasting it with Fallout's dystopian dependence on technology.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Transhumanism (human enhancement and post-humanity)
holes.what: The movement holding that humans should use technology to transcend biological limits, through enhancement now and post-human bodies or minds later.
holes.why: Chapter 15 argues the Fallout series is a transhumanist game whose gameplay both advocates enhancement and displays its risks.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Gloria Anzaldua
holes.what: Chicana theorist of the borderlands whose Nepantla (the in-between space) and mestiza consciousness describe identity forged in liminality.
holes.why: Chapter 16 maps the Sole Survivor's uncertain synth-or-human identity onto Anzaldua's Nepantlera to explain ethical action without a fixed identity.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Functionalism (philosophy of mind)
holes.what: The view that mental states are defined by their causal roles rather than their physical substrate, so minds are multiply realizable in silicon or flesh.
holes.why: Chapter 16's thesis is that the Railroad's pragmatist functionalism grounds synth personhood against Brotherhood dualism and Institute physicalism; chapter 17 develops it via Putnam's machine tables.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: The Uncanny Valley
holes.what: Masahiro Mori's observation that near-human artificial beings provoke revulsion as small imperfections make them eerie.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses the uncanny valley to explain why Gen-3 synths inspire suspicion rather than empathy in the Commonwealth.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: The Politics of Technology
holes.what: The thesis (Winner, Feenberg, Jasanoff, Ihde) that artifacts embody power and co-produce social order rather than serving as neutral tools.
holes.why: Chapter 21 needs it to show the Brotherhood's tech monopoly is political domination rather than neutral stewardship.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Political Socialization
holes.what: The lifelong process by which people acquire political beliefs and ideals of citizenship through family, school, media, and community.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues Little Lamplight's children are political agents who socialize each other into anti-Mungo citizenship.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: The Gamer's Dilemma
holes.what: Morgan Luck's puzzle that anyone who thinks simulating virtual murder is permissible lacks a principled reason to condemn simulating other virtual wrongs such as virtual child abuse.
holes.why: Chapter 28 builds its whole defense of Fallout's depiction of evil around this dilemma, concluding developers should depict whichever wrongs maximize simulated choice.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Kendall Walton
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose 'Categories of Art' holds that a work's aesthetic properties depend on the standard, variable, and contra-standard properties of the categories it belongs to.
holes.why: Chapter 31's entire account of Fallout's genre fusion and aesthetic risk is an application of Walton's category theory.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Categories of Art (standard, variable and contra-standard properties)
holes.what: Walton's framework on which artworks are judged relative to art categories whose standard properties qualify membership and whose contra-standard properties disqualify it.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses it to explain how Fallout can be simultaneously RPG, shooter, post-apocalyptic comedy, and why each added genre is an aesthetic gamble.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Simone Weil
holes.what: French philosopher and mystic who defined freedom as the convergence of thought and action, achieved above all through self-directed labor.
holes.why: Chapter 32 uses Weil's account of free creative labor to explain why the unpaid five-year Fallout: London mod is the fullest expression of freedom.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Francis Hutcheson
holes.what: Scottish Enlightenment philosopher who grounded beauty in an internal sense responding to 'uniformity amidst variety'.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Hutcheson's theory to explain the aesthetic pleasure of Fallout's orderly S.P.E.C.I.A.L. rules and gameplay 'crunch'.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Clive Bell
holes.what: Art critic and formalist who held that art's value lies in 'significant form' — arrangements of line and color that evoke a distinctive aesthetic emotion.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Bell's formalism to show Fallout 3's atomic-age style (Vault Boy, Pip-Boy green, western motifs) makes it a formally distinct artwork, not a reskinned Elder Scrolls game.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics account of tragedy arousing pity and fear in order to purge or perfect those emotions in the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 34 appeals to catharsis to explain how Fallout 3's dark themes deliver moral and emotional benefits.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Narrative Identity and Narrative Ethics
holes.what: The view that who we are and what we ought to do is grounded in the life-story we author from our interpreted past events.
holes.why: Chapter 35 argues Fallout 3's forced sacrificial ending is a bad death because it disrupts the player-authored character narrative that motivates play.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who argues 'against narrativity', denying that a good life requires understanding oneself as a continuous story.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses Strawson's skepticism about narrative identity as the main objection to its story-based account of RPG motivation.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist whose The Denial of Death holds that terror of mortality drives human striving and symbolic-immortality projects.
holes.why: Chapter 38 frames the appeal of post-apocalyptic fiction as a safe confrontation with the death-anxiety Becker described.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Humanist psychology's model on which physiological and safety needs must be met before belonging, esteem, and self-actualization become salient.
holes.why: Chapter 38 explains Fallout's appeal through characters' struggles to meet each level of the hierarchy in the wasteland.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: The Paradox of Tragedy (the attraction of dark art)
holes.what: The puzzle of why we enjoy depictions of suffering and horror in art that we would hate to experience in real life.
holes.why: Chapter 39 is organized around this puzzle — why players enjoy Fallout's hellish wasteland — and tests Aristotle's and Hume's solutions against it.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics account of tragedy arousing pity and fear to purge or perfect them in the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 39 tests katharsis as an explanation of why playing a horrific wasteland is fun and finds it wanting.
holes.book: 160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist and semiologist whose writerly/readerly distinction holds that readers actively produce a text's meaning from its signifiers.
holes.why: Chapter 8's entire argument is that FFVII is a Barthesian writerly text whose players produce the narrative by interpreting signifiers, and Barthes is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough

holes.name: The Writerly Text (semiology)
holes.what: Barthes's ideal of a text so rich in signifiers that its consumer must co-produce its meaning, contrasted with the closed readerly text.
holes.why: Chapter 8 applies exactly this distinction to FFVII's customizable characters and multiple entry points, and no existing slug covers semiology or reader-produced meaning.
holes.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough

holes.name: The Standard of Taste
holes.what: Hume's account of aesthetic judgment on which beauty lies in sentiment but the joint verdict of experienced, unbiased 'good judges' forms a genuine standard of artistic value.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is built entirely on applying this essay's good-judge criteria and the masterpiece circularity problem to judging video games as art, and the taxonomy has no Hume aesthetics slug.
holes.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough

holes.name: The Gaia Hypothesis
holes.what: Lovelock and Margulis's claim that Earth's biosphere is a self-regulating homeostatic system that maintains conditions favorable to life.
holes.why: Chapters 12 and 13 both organize their readings of the Lifestream and The Spirits Within around distinguishing Lovelock's Gaia from vitalist holism, and the taxonomy lacks any Gaia or ecology concept.
holes.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough

holes.name: Shinto (kami and tsumi)
holes.what: Japan's indigenous tradition in which kami, a spiritual presence pervading nature, and tsumi, pollution removed by purification rituals, shape an ecological 'orientation in living'.
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole reading of FFVII, the Lifestream as kami, Jenova as tsumi, and water purification rituals, rests on Shinto concepts the taxonomy lacks under eastern-world.
holes.book: 162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough

holes.name: Lying vs Other Deception
holes.what: The distinction between asserting something you believe false (lying) and misleading without asserting it, plus the debate over whether lying is morally worse than other deception.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument - Joffrey's lie, Ned's coerced confession, Cersei's unspoken incest, Mirri Maz Duur's implication - turns on this distinction, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords

holes.name: Personhood (person vs human being)
holes.what: The bioethics distinction between being biologically human and being a person with full moral standing, cashed out via consciousness, rationality, and self-awareness.
holes.why: Chapter 19 defends Daenerys's killing of Drogo on the ground that he is human but no longer a person (Tooley, Warren, Marquis, Singer), a concept the taxonomy lacks apart from Frankfurt's specific second-order-desires account.
holes.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords

holes.name: Physicalism
holes.what: The metaphysical thesis that everything that exists is physical and every feature of the world depends on the arrangement of physical stuff.
holes.why: Chapter 22 defines and defends physicalism, then uses Westeros's magic (wights, Daenerys's fire immunity) to ask whether souls could exist only by violating physical law.
holes.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords

holes.name: Gayatri Spivak
holes.what: Postcolonial feminist philosopher who argues that self-appointed saviors come to treat the people they help as permanently dependent and childlike, 'reproducing and consolidating feudalism.'
holes.why: Chapter 29 leans on Spivak's savior-becomes-oppressor argument as its central tool for showing how chivalric protection turns adult women into permanent, childlike wards.
holes.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords

holes.name: Game Theory
holes.what: The mathematical modeling of strategic interaction among rational agents, covering zero-sum and non-zero-sum games, incomplete information, repeated play, and backward (reverse) induction.
