holes.why: Chapter 33's entire reading - Catelyn's reverse induction that Bran was thrown, Tyrion converting his Eyrie trial into repeated games with Bronn and the mountain clans, and the 'I Cut, You Choose' fairness example - is an extended application of game theory, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist of the self whose Stigma and Asylums analyze how total institutions and discrediting labels produce 'spoiled identities' that eclipse the person behind them.
holes.why: Chapter 11 maps Salander's entire labeling saga—St. Stefan's admission rituals, Teleborian's casebook, the 'wise,' passing, and self-isolation—directly onto Goffman's stigma and asylum framework.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: Stigma and the Spoiled Identity
holes.what: Goffman's account of how a discrediting label (mental illness, criminal record) reduces 'a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one' and then governs every subsequent social encounter.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues the trilogy's real subject is not one wrongly labeled girl but labeling itself—the slippage from 'mentally ill' to violent and promiscuous that Salander's barbed-wire paper trail exemplifies.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: The McDonaldization of Society
holes.what: George Ritzer's Weberian thesis that fast-food principles—efficiency, calculability, predictability, control—colonize everyday life and breed irrationalities: homogenization, disenchantment, dehumanization.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses McDonaldization and 'Starbuckization' to explain what Salander's 7-Eleven pan pizzas and the characters' chain-café loneliness say about rationalized modern Sweden.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that complex concepts (games, numbers, literature) share no single essence but overlap and crisscross like the faces of a family.
holes.why: Chapter 20 proposes family resemblance as the only workable definition of 'literature' when deciding whether the Millennium Trilogy is popular fiction or literature.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of how we feel genuine emotions for characters we know do not exist, given that emotion normally requires belief in its object.
holes.why: Chapter 20 invokes the paradox and Coleridge's willing suspension of disbelief to explain readers' very real attachment to the invented, vulnerable Salander.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation or clarification)
holes.what: In the Poetics, the effect tragedy produces through pity and fear—traditionally a purging of those emotions, which Nussbaum rereads as their clarification or illumination.
holes.why: Chapter 21's whole argument is that we enjoy Larsson's men-who-hate-women violence because Salander's story cathartically clarifies our own pity and terror about rape, guardianship, and power.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: The Hacker Ethic
holes.what: The values Stephen Levy codified—unlimited access, information wants to be free, mistrust authority, judgment by skill alone—extended by Himanen and Wark into a playful, passion-driven information-age work ethic.
holes.why: Chapter 24 reads Salander's 'Salander's Principles,' Assange's WikiLeaks, and Blomkvist's journalism as embodiments of the hacker ethic in a free society.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: Jacques Rancière
holes.what: French philosopher who, in Disagreement, separates policing (the self-preserving administration of order) from politics (the contestation by the uncounted of who gets recognized).
holes.why: Chapter 25 leans on Rancière's policing/politics distinction to conclude that perpetual political contestation, not institutional housecleaning, is the real answer to the hidden Section.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: The Ethics and Epistemology of Gossip
holes.what: The debate (Bok, Code, Ayim, Portmann) over whether gossip is trivializing vice or a trust-based, knowledge-producing practice that can also police the powerful.
holes.why: Chapter 26 defends the trilogy's gossip networks—from Milton Security reports to Hacker Republic—as legitimate knowledge and underdog resistance rather than mere malicious talk.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: J.L. Austin
holes.what: Ordinary-language philosopher, founder of speech-act theory, whose 'A Plea for Excuses' distinguishes justifying conduct (showing it was right) from excusing it (denying full responsibility).
holes.why: Chapter 30 structures its entire verdict on Blomkvist's and Salander's lies and deceptions around Austin's justify-versus-excuse framework.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: The Ethics of Lying and Deception
holes.what: The branch of applied ethics asking when lying, misleading, and deception are justified, excusable, or always wrong (Kant's absolute ban versus casuistical defenses).
holes.why: Chapter 30 is devoted to whether Salander and Blomkvist may lie to and deceive 'bad people'—from the lottery trick to the Vanger cover-up and her trial testimony.
holes.book: 164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy - Everything Is Fire

holes.name: Rule by Nobody (bureaucracy)
holes.what: Arendt's account of bureaucracy as a system in which no one can be held responsible — 'rule by Nobody', the most tyrannical form since there is no one to answer — which deprives everyone of power and breeds violence as the only recourse.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument reads the afterlife's automatic point system, and Michael's and Gen's powerlessness before it, through this Arendtian concept.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Meliorism
holes.what: William James's doctrine that the world is unfinished and plastic, so individual and collective effort can genuinely improve it — with the added conditions that actions must have foreseeable consequences and be irreversible to carry moral worth.
holes.why: Chapter 13 uses James's meliorism and its two conditions to argue the humans' post-death growth earns no points, while Michael's irreversible sacrifices do.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Infinite Desert of Sin (why Hell is eternal)
holes.what: The Anselmian defense of eternal punishment: because God is an infinitely great being and every sin is against God, any wrongdoing, however small, deserves infinite punishment.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central question — whether Judge Gen can justly impose eternal torture — is structured around testing this doctrine and its three claims (INFINITE, SIN, GREATER).
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view, associated with Jonathan Dancy, that there are no invariant moral principles: what one ought to do is determined case by case by the morally relevant particulars of the situation.
holes.why: Chapters 21, 22, and 23 pivot on Eleanor citing Dancy's particularism to overturn Chidi's Kantian ban on lying so the Soul Squad can escape the Bad Place.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Jonathan Dancy
holes.what: Contemporary British moral philosopher, professor at the University of Texas at Austin, best known as the leading defender of moral particularism.
holes.why: The show's recurring 'movies vs. ER' argument is attributed to him by name, he authors chapter 36 of this very volume, and his particularism resolves the lying dilemma in chapters 21-23.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Contractualism (What We Owe to Each Other)
holes.what: T.M. Scanlon's view that an act is wrong if it would be disallowed by principles no one could reasonably reject, grounding morality in what we owe one another through our bonds with other people.
holes.why: The book on which Eleanor writes her note is the show's touchstone (chapters 23, 30, 38, 39 all lean on it), and Chidi's closing lecture — we choose to be good because of our bonds with others — is Scanlon's answer.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Omniscience (as a divine attribute)
holes.what: The doctrine that a perfect being knows all true propositions, traditionally counted among God's defining attributes and complicated by foreknowledge and by whether propositional knowledge exhausts understanding.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies the philosophical analysis of omniscience point by point to decide whether Janet is really all-knowing and what her gaps mean.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Three Independent Factors in Morals
holes.what: Dewey's essay arguing that the Good (desire), the Right (socially authorized demand), and the Virtuous (social praise and blame) are irreducible factors in moral experience, so genuine moral conflict and uncertainty are inescapable.
holes.why: Chapter 28's critique of the Big Three and its reading of Eleanor's 'option C' and the Medium Place as Deweyan reconciliation rest on this specific theory, not covered by the taxonomy's Dewey entries.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: The feminist idea that persons are socially constituted: autonomy is formed, exercised, and constrained through relationships with others rather than in spite of them.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explicitly names relational autonomy as one of the two traditions behind its paradox of individual accountability versus social dependence.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
holes.what: German Lutheran pastor-theologian executed by the Nazis in 1945, known for his prison-era 'religionless Christianity' and an ethics of responsibility modeled on Christ's example.
holes.why: Chapter 33 devotes a full section to reading Eleanor's repentance arc and Michael's self-sacrifice as Bonhoefferian responsible action, alongside Levinas.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Eschatology (doctrine of last things)
holes.what: The theological study of death, judgment, Heaven and Hell, and the final destiny of creation, including competing Christian accounts such as eternal conscious torment, universalism, and annihilationism.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues the show both critiques and imperfectly reproduces Christian eschatology, which is its central analytical frame.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Nishkama Karma (desire-less action)
holes.what: The Bhagavad Gita's teaching that one should perform one's duty without desire for the fruits of the action, since corrupt motivation strips an act of worth.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Eleanor's failed point-chasing and her selfless departure as exactly this Gita doctrine, the linchpin of its Hindu reading of the show.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Karma and Rebirth (Hindu)
holes.what: The Hindu doctrine, central to the Bhagavad Gita, that actions determine consequences across cycles of birth, death, and rebirth until self-realization frees one from the cycle.
holes.why: Chapter 34 maps the show's point system onto karma and the 802 reboots (Janet's included) onto rebirth; the taxonomy's only karma slug is Buddhist-attributed, which would misrepresent this explicitly Hindu chapter.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Somatic Marker Hypothesis
holes.what: Antonio Damasio's neuroscience thesis that bodily 'gut feelings' bias and prune decision options, making emotion integral to rational moral choice rather than its enemy.
holes.why: Chapter 38 explains Chidi's stomachaches through this hypothesis and uses it to attack the rationalist split between emotion and reasoning in traditional moral theory.
holes.book: 165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!

holes.name: Thick and Thin Ethical Concepts
holes.what: Williams's distinction between context-dependent value concepts like honor and honesty (thick) and context-free ones like right and just (thin).
holes.why: Chapter 13's account of why the Guardians cannot vet recruits or judge Laira rests entirely on honor and justice being thick concepts.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view, associated with Jonathan Dancy, that moral judgment proceeds from case-by-case perception of particulars rather than invariant principles.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues the Alpha Lanterns cannot supply context-free justice because no moral judgment avoids thick concepts.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Moral Pluralism
holes.what: The view that there are several valid conceptions of the good, positioned between relativism and absolutism.
holes.why: Chapter 13 defines the Guardians' recruitment policy as moral pluralism, explicitly distinguished in the text from the relativism the taxonomy names.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Hegel on Tragedy and Ethical Life (Sittlichkeit)
holes.what: Hegel's account of the tragic hero destroyed by one-sided individual moral conviction set against communal ethical life, yet aesthetically admirable.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads Hal, Sinestro, and Kyle entirely through this pattern; none of the existing Hegel slugs (dialectic, master-slave, Geist, history, recognition) covers it.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Guidance Control (Fischer and Ravizza)
holes.what: Fischer and Ravizza's compatibilist criterion of moral responsibility: ownership of one's action plus reasons-responsiveness, rather than the ability to do otherwise.
holes.why: Chapter 15's verdict that Hal is blameworthy under Parallax turns on guidance control versus regulative control; the generic compatibilism slug is too coarse.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Catharsis (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of tragedy arousing pity and fear in order to purge or refine those emotions in the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 19 needs it as Aristotle's half of the censorship debate against Plato's banishment of the poets, applied to the Comics Code and the O'Neil-Adams run.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: The feminist reworking of autonomy (Nedelsky, Mackenzie and Stoljar) on which relationships partly constitute the self rather than merely threatening self-determination.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues Kyle escapes Parallax only with Hal's help and that Corps life demands autonomy competency within unchosen relationships.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Irresolvable and Tragic Moral Dilemmas
holes.what: Situations (Hursthouse, building on Williams's Jim case) in which every available action violates a duty and leaves moral residue no matter what the agent does.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Soranik Natu's Hippocratic and Lantern oaths create exactly such an irresolvable dilemma; no existing slug names it.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Biological Individuality and the Superorganism
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology question of which levels of the living hierarchy (genes, organisms, species, superorganisms) count as real individuals.
holes.why: Chapter 27 runs this whole debate through Mogo, the Collective, and Leezle Pon, and the taxonomy has no philosophy-of-biology concept.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Peirce's Communal Mind
holes.what: Peirce's view that thought is a semiotic process not tied to any brain and that knowledge and truth are established only by an unlimited community of inquirers.
holes.why: Chapter 28 maps the Book of Oa and the Corps' shared ring knowledge onto it directly, and the existing Peirce slug (pragmatic method) does not cover it.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Impressions, Ideas and the Principles of Association
holes.what: Hume's empiricist theory that thinking copies sensory impressions into ideas and recombines them by contiguity, resemblance, and cause and effect.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explains Hal's boxing-glove constructs and Kyle's inventions entirely through this machinery, which no existing Hume slug covers.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Magic, Science and Religion (Mauss)
holes.what: Mauss's sociological demarcation of magic as private, rule-bound, and will-powered, against communal religion and open, collaborative science.
holes.why: Chapter 33 uses this triad, plus Clarke's three laws, to decide whether the Guardians are scientists or sorcerers; the taxonomy has nothing on the demarcation.
holes.book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

holes.name: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
holes.what: A prediction that helps bring about the very event it foretells through the response of those who hear it.
holes.why: Chapter 31 is built around whether Trelawney's prophecy was self-fulfilling through Voldemort's reaction to hearing it, a mechanism that the existing fate-vs-free-will slug (destiny and foreknowledge generally) does not capture.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Libertarian Free Will
holes.what: The view that free choices require genuinely open alternatives, the ability to have done otherwise, and so are incompatible with being determined.
holes.why: Chapter 33 defines libertarianism about freedom as the position that makes sense of Rowling's denial of destiny, and the love-potion chapters (48-49) lean on it, but the taxonomy only offers the generic free-will-determinism debate plus compatibilism.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Patriotism (special obligations to compatriots)
holes.what: The disposition to give preference to one's own country and compatriots, debated in political philosophy as a virtue, a vice, or a conditionally justified partiality.
holes.why: Chapter 58 opens a multi-chapter essay asking whether Gryffindor-style loyalty and civic patriotism are virtues or morally equivalent to Death Eater supremacy, a question no existing slug names directly.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Emma Goldman
holes.what: Lithuanian-born American anarchist activist and writer (1869-1940) who attacked patriotism as conceit and arrogance rooted in the accident of birthplace.
holes.why: Chapter 59 builds its case that patriotism is a vice chiefly on Goldman's argument that patriotism divides the globe into gated spots whose natives deem themselves superior.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Leo Tolstoy
holes.what: Russian novelist and Christian anarchist thinker (1828-1910) who defined patriotism as 'the desire for the exclusive good of one's own nation' and blamed it for producing war.
holes.why: Chapter 59 uses Tolstoy's definition of patriotism as the springboard for comparing patriotic preference to Voldemort's pureblood supremacy.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Jeremy Waldron
holes.what: Contemporary political philosopher who argues that cosmopolitan cultural hybridity, not rootedness in an ancestral community, is the appropriate response to the modern world.
holes.why: Chapter 65 quotes Waldron at length to set the cosmopolitan alternative to communitarianism and to read Harry's cross-cultural fluency as the books' model of flourishing.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Truth in Fiction
holes.what: The problem of what facts hold in a fictional world and what principles (explicit text, imports from reality, authorial intent, reader response, genre) generate truths beyond the sentences on the page.
holes.why: Chapter 78 introduces this problem to frame the dispute over whether Rowling's announcement makes 'Dumbledore is gay' true in the world of Harry Potter, and chapter 79 builds its primary-versus-secondary truth machinery on it.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: The Death of the Author (intentional fallacy)
holes.what: The anti-intentionalist thesis that an author cannot fix a text's meaning by declaration, because language is a social creation and readers' interpretations are not bound by post-hoc authorial statements.
holes.why: Chapter 80 stages this debate (Wimsatt, Beardsley, Gadamer, Barthes, Foucault, and Derrida against Hirsch's intentionalism) over whether Rowling can settle Dumbledore's sexuality by authorial fiat.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and Oxford Inkling whose argument from reason holds that if naturalism were true, rational thought could not reliably validate itself, so reason points to a cosmic Logos beyond materialism.
holes.why: Chapter 108 interprets Dumbledore's in-the-head-yet-real remark as Rowling's Inklings inheritance, building directly on Lewis's Barfield-inspired argument from reason and his claim that the whole universe is in the last resort mental.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: The Argument from Reason
holes.what: The claim that if naturalism were true, our reasoning would be nothing but non-rational causes, undermining reason's validity; hence rationality must participate in a rational order beyond nature.
holes.why: Chapter 108 uses this argument to explain how Harry's King's Cross experience can be both wholly inside his head and genuinely real, as an instance of reason participating in the divine Logos.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Melanie Klein
holes.what: Austrian-British psychoanalyst in the Freudian tradition who held that personal maturity requires keeping a solid commitment to being the self-same person who committed past wrongs.
holes.why: Chapter 134's integrity objection against the phoenix model of moral regeneration is explicitly advanced on Klein's authority: rebirth talk cannot erase the fact that it was you who did the wrong.
holes.book: 167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally praiseworthy but not required, going beyond what obligation demands.
holes.why: Chapter 10 concludes via Fishkin's objections that saving the world is supererogatory rather than obligatory, which is why the heroes could legitimately bill New York for their services.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Dennis F. Thompson
holes.what: Political ethicist whose Political Ethics and Public Office distributes blame for institutional wrongdoing to everyone who freely and knowingly contributes causally to a policy.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses Thompson's criterion as the decisive answer to which Company members are morally responsible for the bag-and-tag program and when whistle-blowing is warranted.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Epistemic Virtue and Responsibility
holes.what: Virtue epistemology: the truth-seeking traits (responsibility, impartiality, sobriety, courage) and duties governing what we are blameworthy for not knowing.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire verdict on Tim Kring rests on Montmarquet's four epistemic virtues, a framework the taxonomy lacks despite covering other epistemology.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Bushido (the way of the warrior)
holes.what: The samurai code, which the chapter via the Hagakure treats as a death-ready mode of action rather than a moral code.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is organized around whether Hiro genuinely follows historical Bushido, a central concept absent from the taxonomy's eastern-world entries.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Special Relativity (space-time)
holes.what: Einstein's theory that space and time coordinates are relative to the observer's inertial frame while the speed of light is constant for all observers, unifying them in a four-dimensional space-time continuum.
holes.why: Chapter 21's central section uses Minkowski diagrams, worldlines, and light cones to show that Hiro's teleportation and time travel would require breaking the speed of light.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Evolution by Natural Selection
holes.what: Darwin's theory that heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction fixes advantageous traits in populations over time, the core of modern evolutionary biology.
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues Dr. Suresh's 'evolutionary jump' of superpowered humans is scientifically impossible because fit mutations cannot arise and spread through the population in a few hundred years.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The classic problem of how we can know that beings who behave as we do actually have conscious minds rather than being mindless look-alikes.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues even Matt Parkman's telepathy cannot settle whether others have inner lives, and frames ordinary behavior-reading as 'mundane mind reading' justified only by pragmatic success.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Empathy (Einfühlung)
holes.what: The sharing or replication of another's feelings, running from Hume's sympathy to the phenomenological accounts of Scheler and Stein as the experience of foreign consciousness.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explains Peter Petrelli's empathic mimicry by testing rival theories of empathy — resonance, absorption, and duplication — and asks whether empathy can ground morality.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: The Ethics of Lying
holes.what: The debate over whether, when, and why deliberate deception is permissible, from Kant's absolute prohibition to Bok's presumption against lying and its public test of justification.
holes.why: Chapter 30's whole subject is when Heroes' heroes may lie, and its endorsed framework — Sissela Bok's presumption against lying — is a distinct position no existing taxonomy slug covers.
holes.book: 168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World

holes.name: Sub-creation (Tolkien's theory of art)
holes.what: Tolkien's view (in 'On Fairy-stories') that human artistic making is a subordinate imitation of divine creation, fashioning a Secondary World rather than seeking power over the primary one.
holes.why: Chapters 25 and 27 build their aesthetics on Tolkien's sub-creation - Aule making dwarves so others might enjoy the beauty of Ea, elvish magic as 'Art, not Power' - and no existing taxonomy concept covers it.
holes.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way

holes.name: The Philosophy of Play (Homo Ludens)
holes.what: The tradition (Schiller's play-drive, Huizinga's Homo ludens) holding that free play is constitutive of full humanity and the root of art, ritual and philosophy.
holes.why: Chapter 27 ('Hobbitus Ludens') is organized entirely around play and leisure as what completes humanity, and the taxonomy has no concept for play or leisure.
holes.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way

holes.name: Friedrich Schiller
holes.what: German idealist poet-philosopher whose Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man make the play-drive (Spieltrieb) what reconciles our natures and completes humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 27 quotes Schiller's play thesis ('man is only fully human when he plays') three times as its central philosophical framework.
holes.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of how we can have genuine, rational emotions (fear, pity) toward characters and events we know to be fictional.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is entirely structured around this named paradox as applied to pitying Bilbo and fearing Smaug, and the taxonomy has no concept for it.
holes.book: 169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way

holes.name: James M. Buchanan
holes.what: Nobel-winning economist and father of public choice theory who insisted politics be analyzed 'without romance', assuming self-interested politicians rather than romantic statesmen.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central positive argument is that Buchanan's demand to design institutions under the assumption that people like Frank Underwood run for Congress corrects Rawlsian ideal theory.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Public Choice Theory (politics without romance)
holes.what: The application of self-interest assumptions to politicians and voters, weighing government failures against market failures when designing institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 10 argues House of Cards vindicates public choice: SanCorp's rent-seeking, politicians' high discount rates, and Frank's self-dealing show why Rawls' strict-compliance ideal fails.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Max Scheler
holes.what: German phenomenologist of values who extended Nietzsche's ressentiment, diagnosing the modern industrial ethos as an engine of systematically repressed, spiteful emotion.
holes.why: Chapter 11 relies on Scheler's Ressentiment more than any other source to explain Claire's hatred of Gillian Cole, Adam Galloway and Michael Corrigan's unbending integrity.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Postmodernism (metafiction and self-referentiality)
holes.what: A movement rejecting Enlightenment faith in progress and objective representation, playing with irony, parody, and the collapse of the boundary between fiction and reality.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Frank's fourth-wall wave, his self-referential asides, and the show's flattening of affect at Zoe's death as postmodern techniques that seduce viewers into his nihilism.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: Walzer's problem that governing sometimes requires leaders to do what is morally wrong, so a good ruler must be capable of dirtying her hands yet reluctant to do so.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire argument tests whether Frank's willingness to order drone strikes and face down Petrov makes him fitter for office than Heather Dunbar.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Racial Capitalism
holes.what: The process (named by Nancy Leong) of deriving social and economic value from racial identity by commodifying it, so that nonwhiteness has value only insofar as it benefits white institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central claim is that Freddy Hayes's BBQ storyline sells blackness as 'authentic' spice for white consumption - an economy the chapter explicitly names racial capitalism.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Critical race theorist whose 'racial realism' holds that racism is a permanent feature of US society, so resistance should aim at defiant harassment of white supremacy rather than at achieving racial equity.
holes.why: Chapter 26 closes by adopting Bell's racial realism and his Biona MacDonald exemplar ('I live to harass white folks') as the stance from which its critique of Freddy's representation is made.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle (associated with Tamar Szabo Gendler) of why we refuse to imagine morally deviant claims as true within fiction - e.g. that a murder was noble - even though we can imagine dragons and unicorns with ease.
holes.why: Chapter 32 argues House of Cards, through Frank's fourth-wall asides and emotional seduction, deliberately dissolves the viewer's imaginative resistance to rooting for a double-murdering politician.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Bratman's Planning Theory of Intention
holes.what: Michael Bratman's anti-reductionist view that intentions are distinct plan-states - partial, consistency-demanding, commitment-bearing - that guide and coordinate action over time, against Davidson's reduction of intention to belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explains Frank's entire political scheming through the Davidson-Bratman debate over whether intentions are anything more than beliefs and desires.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Iris Murdoch
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher who argued that art fascinates by exploring 'the meaner, more peculiar aspects of our being,' leading audiences to relax their moral guard and become lazy sentimental spectators of fictional evil.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Murdoch to explain why viewers find Frank's fake eulogy, cruelty, and grave-urination entertaining rather than condemnable.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Truth as Disclosure (aletheia)
holes.what: Heidegger's account of truth as unconcealment or disclosure of being, rather than correspondence between statement and fact.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Frank's asides, eulogies, and maxims as plays of concealment and disclosure that make truth an event of being, its central Heideggerian move with no matching taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies

holes.name: Thrasymachus
holes.what: The Sophist in Book 1 of Plato's Republic who defines justice as 'the advantage of the stronger' and holds the unjust life preferable to the just.
holes.why: Chapter 7 reads Frank's cynical politics as Thrasymachus's challenge — his shepherd critique, his praise of injustice, and the tyrant as model politician structure the whole essay, not merely Plato's reply.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Public Choice Theory (politics without romance)
holes.what: The program, running from Hume's maxim that every man 'ought to be supposed a knave' to James Buchanan, of modeling politicians and voters as self-interested when designing political institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 10's positive proposal — design the ideal society assuming people like Frank run for office, countering rent-seeking and politicians' short-termism — is public-choice reasoning against Rawlsian ideal theory.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Max Scheler
holes.what: German phenomenologist who extended Nietzsche's account of ressentiment, locating its modern source in the industrial ethos of capitalism rather than Christianity.
holes.why: Chapter 11 analyzes Frank and especially Claire Underwood through Scheler's Ressentiment — the systematic repression of affects, value delusions, and the impulse to smash pedestals — more than through Nietzsche's own texts.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: The American Dream
holes.what: James Truslow Adams's ideal of a better and richer life open to everyone according to ability rather than birth, which Adams warned was decaying into mere materialism and means without ends.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues the show depicts the American dream perverted into power for its own sake, with Claire's ressentiment springing from the loftier values she sacrificed to it.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Postmodernism (metafiction and self-referentiality)
holes.what: The aesthetic-philosophical movement rejecting Enlightenment faith in progress, playing with fiction and reality through irony and parody — here metafiction, self-referentiality, and flattening of affect.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Frank's fourth-wall asides, his wave to the viewer, and Zoe's graphic death as postmodern techniques that implicate the audience in his nihilism.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: The Problem of Dirty Hands
holes.what: The problem, named from Sartre's play and formulated by Michael Walzer, that politicians sometimes must do what is genuinely wrong, and must then acknowledge guilt and accept public punishment.
holes.why: Chapter 17 judges whether Frank or Heather Dunbar is fit to rule precisely through Walzer's dirty-hands test, supreme emergency, and threshold deontology.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Racial Capitalism
holes.what: Nancy Leong's term for deriving social and economic value from racial identity by commodifying it, so that nonwhiteness is valued only insofar as it benefits white people and institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central claim is that Freddy Hayes's 'authentic' BBQ persona is exactly such a commodity, consumed by white viewers and discarded by Frank when its value drops.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Founder of critical race theory who defended 'racial realism', the view that racism is a permanent feature of US society, and urged defiance ('I live to harass white folks') over utopian hopes of racial equity.
holes.why: Chapter 26 closes by adopting Bell's racial realism as the stance of its own critique, refusing to hope the show's representation will ever interrupt white supremacy.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle (Tamar Szabo Gendler) of why audiences resist imagining morally deviant claims in fiction-such as a murder being 'noble'-even though they can imagine dragons and impossible worlds, explained as unwillingness rather than inability.
holes.why: Chapter 32 argues House of Cards produces a striking 'lack of imaginative resistance', seducing viewers through fourth-wall asides and emotional intimacy into rooting for Frank's murders.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Planning Theory of Intention
holes.what: Michael Bratman's view that intentions are distinct, commitment-involving plan-states (partial, consistency-demanding, control-enabling) that organize practical reasoning over time and are irreducible to belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is built on Bratman's antireductionism, using Frank's cross-temporal schemes and adjustable plans to show intentions doing work beliefs and desires cannot.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Iris Murdoch
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher who argued that art fascinates by exploring the 'meaner' aspects of our being, so that sympathizing with fictional characters relaxes the moral guard and weakens our better nature.
holes.why: Chapter 34 leans on Murdoch to explain why the Peachoid eulogy and the grave-urination scene entertain rather than appall us.
holes.book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

holes.name: Mimesis and Catharsis (art as imitation)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics doctrine that all art is imitation of human action, pleasurable because contemplating representations teaches us universal truths, with tragedy purging pity and fear (catharsis).
holes.why: Chapter 9's whole argument contrasts Peeta's life-affirming mimesis with the Capitol's perverse, catharsis-free spectacle, making mimesis the chapter's central concept and taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: De-creation (Rieff's deathworks)
holes.what: Phillip Rieff's diagnosis of modern art as 'de-creation': an anticulture's drive to violate and desecrate a society's sacred commanding truths instead of re-presenting them.
holes.why: Chapter 9 uses Rieff's de-creation to name what the Capitol's Remake Center and arena do to bodies and to the districts, linking freakish aesthetics to ethical abandon.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Schadenfreude (joy in another's suffering)
holes.what: Pleasure taken at another person's misfortune, condemned by Schopenhauer as the surest sign of a bad heart and by Kant as a diabolical vice, yet explained by Nietzsche through envy and status leveling.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is built entirely on Schadenfreude as the emotion that lets the Capitol audience enjoy children dying in the arena, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for it.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Dehumanization
holes.what: The process by which oppressors deny a group personhood or full humanity so that ordinary moral restraint against enjoying or inflicting their suffering is dissolved.
holes.why: Chapter 14's 'Savages' section makes dehumanization (Nazi propaganda, Capitol 'barbarian' rhetoric, the tribute-turned-mutt) the enabling mechanism of pleasurable cruelty.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Marcel Mauss
holes.what: French sociologist-anthropologist (1872-1950) whose The Gift argued that gift exchange in archaic societies creates binding obligations of reciprocity that hold communities together.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads Katniss's entire debt anxiety over Peeta's bread, Thresh's 'we're even,' and the Hob sponsors through Mauss's gift-exchange theory, and Mauss is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: The Gift Economy (reciprocity and invisible strings)
holes.what: The theory that gifts, unlike commodities, are never free: accepting one creates a social bond and an obligation to reciprocate, in goods, service, or loyalty.
holes.why: Chapter 15 applies this concept to nearly every relationship in the trilogy, from the bread that 'gave me hope' to loyalty in District 13, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist (1809-1882) whose theory of evolution by natural selection, and whose Descent of Man account of the moral sense evolving from animal social instincts, anchor the chapter.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is essentially an essay on Darwin: natural selection, fitness, group and kin selection, and the evolution of conscience explain the tributes' altruism, yet Darwin is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Personhood (criteria for moral personhood)
holes.what: The debate over which capacities, rationality, self-consciousness, autonomy, make a being a person and full member of the moral community, from Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature' to Locke's reflective thinking being.
holes.why: Chapter 18 applies personhood criteria to wolf-mutts with tribute DNA and to real human-animal chimeras to decide whether creating or weaponizing them violates moral rights, and taxonomy has no personhood slug.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Game Theory (prisoner's dilemma, tit-for-tat, Nash equilibrium)
holes.what: The mathematical analysis of strategic decision-making, including zero-sum games, the prisoner's dilemma, equilibrium points, and the tit-for-tat strategy in iterated play.
holes.why: Chapter 29 is built entirely on game theory — it models the tesserae odds, the Training Days subgame, and the arena as a tribute's dilemma, and no taxonomy slug covers strategic-choice modeling.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher whose concepts of economic, social, and cultural capital and of habitus explain how class power quietly reproduces itself through education and taste.
holes.why: Chapter 33's entire analysis of how Panem's schools keep the districts subordinate is built on Bourdieu's capital/habitus framework, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Thucydides
holes.what: Ancient Greek historian whose Melian Dialogue ('the strong do what they have the power to do') is the classic statement of political realism in interstate relations.
holes.why: Chapter 28 applies the Melian Dialogue directly to Capitol-district relations as its definition of political realism, and Thucydides has no taxonomy entry.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Carl von Clausewitz
holes.what: Prussian military theorist who defined war as 'a continuation of politics by other means,' framing war as an instrument of political goals.
holes.why: Chapter 28 opens with Clausewitz's definition and uses it to set up the instrumental view of war it evaluates against pacifism and the just-war tradition.
holes.book: 172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

holes.name: Activation-Synthesis Model of Dreaming
holes.what: J. Allan Hobson's theory that dreams are meaningless narratives the cortex fabricates to explain random brain-stem activation during REM sleep.
holes.why: Chapter 8's core argument that Inception's streamlined shared dreams are scientifically possible rests on criticizing this model and relocating dream generation to dopamine-driven cortical areas.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: B.F. Skinner
holes.what: American behaviorist who explained all behavior, including the feeling of choosing, as the product of conditioning and prior causes rather than free will.
holes.why: Chapter 12 cites Skinner's operant conditioning and closes with his confession that he never directed his own life to support its claim that conscious will is a post-hoc feeling.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Corporate Moral Personhood
holes.what: The question whether corporations count as moral persons bearing rights and responsibilities distinct from the humans who compose them.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues Inception's real agents are Cobol, Proclus Global and Fischer-Morrow, and builds a case that firms decide, hold rights and bear responsibility like persons.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: American philosopher whose Philosophy in a New Key explains mythic consciousness through symbolic transformation and the shaping of experience into narrative form.
holes.why: Chapter 18 builds its entire account of dream architecture, myth and inception on Langer's theory that dreams become communicable only when forced into narrative order.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Mythic Consciousness
holes.what: A shared, pre-modern form of consciousness in which experience is organized by living symbols and communal narrative rather than abstract signs.
holes.why: Chapter 18 reads the Mombasa dreamers, Fischer's militarized unconscious and the pinwheel inception through the contrast between mythic and modern 'civilized' consciousness.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Memetics (ideas as replicators)
holes.what: Richard Dawkins's theory that ideas (memes) replicate from brain to brain like genes, spreading through imitation and growing until they define or destroy a person's or culture's world.
holes.why: Chapter 24 states that the film's central idea of inception is inspired by meme theory — the planted seed of an idea grows in the subject's mind 'like a cancer' — making memetics the explicit cognitive-science anchor of the whole premise.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Film as a Thinking Machine (film-thinking)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-film theory (Jean Epstein's 'robot brain,' Daniel Frampton's 'filmind') that cinema does not reproduce reality but thinks it, producing logically structured dreamlike worlds and thinking time itself.
holes.why: Chapter 24's core claim is that Inception finally executes Epstein's prediction: Nolan does not stylize dreams, the film thinks them, synchronizing dream layers like a cognitive machine — a framework taxonomy lacks entirely.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Aristotle on Time (number of motion)
holes.what: Aristotle's definition of time as 'a number of change in respect of the before and after' — time is not an independent reality but an aspect of movement, known through perceiving change, with eternity as either endless succession or timelessness.
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire analysis of dream-time dilation, Limbo's two senses of eternity, and the mental versus physical 'now' is built directly on Aristotle's Physics definition of time, which taxonomy has no slug for.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Lacanian Desire (the neurotic's counter-desire)
holes.what: Lacan's doctrine that the neurotic subject does not want what he desires and does not desire what he wants, so that desire is structurally split against itself and mediated by lack.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads the whole film as the dream of a neurotic subject resolving the conflict between desire and counter-desire into a 'steady desire,' an analysis that rests on this Lacanian account of desire rather than on the mirror stage or the registers.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Mourning and Melancholia
holes.what: Freud's distinction between mourning, the gradual withdrawal of attachment from a lost beloved object, and melancholia, a self-enclosed state in which the loss is never worked through and life continues under the seal of death.
holes.why: Chapter 27 frames the entire film as Cobb's impossible mourning of Mal, contrasting completed mourning with the 'melancholic dullness' of his limbos, and taxonomy has no slug for this central Freudian distinction.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Alfred Schutz
holes.what: Austrian social phenomenologist (1899–1959) who analyzed the life-world's 'paramount reality' of everyday life, its multiple provinces of meaning with distinct cognitive styles, apperception, and 'in order to' and 'because of' motives.
holes.why: Chapter 29's whole first half — paramount reality, apperception via the coffee cup, provinces of meaning, and the motive analysis used to explain how Fischer is deceived in his dream — is Schutz's social phenomenology, and he is absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Poetic Dwelling (Building, Dwelling, Thinking)
holes.what: Heidegger's account that to dwell means to build one's place, that building is not mere architecture but poetic creation from an ungrounded origin, and that poetry is what first makes dwelling possible ('man dwells poetically').
holes.why: Chapter 30 is an extended application of Heidegger's dwelling essays — building and dwelling, the origin of the artwork, poetry as poiesis — to Inception's dream architecture and Cobb's uninhabitable nightmare, and no existing Heidegger slug covers it.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher (1861–1947) who analyzed change through narrative (algebraic) and spatial (geometric) order, treating space as 'frozen time' and understanding as achieved in 'generic contrasts' that accrete value.
holes.why: Chapter 31 calls Whitehead 'the Christopher Nolan of process philosophy' and uses his narrative-space method — with Bergson — to defend the film's dream-time physics and unlock the totem answer, but taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: The diagnosis that the collapse of God-grounded absolute values leaves life apparently meaningless — which Nietzsche warned against rather than endorsed.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames Raiders' Nazis and Belloq as failing through the wrong reaction to nihilism and Indy's improvised values as overcoming it, but taxonomy has no nihilism slug.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Gabriel Marcel
holes.what: French Christian existentialist (1889–1973) whose 'creative fidelity' analyzes commitment, availability ('être avec'), presence versus objectification, and openness to the sacred.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire reading of Indy's path home across all four films is built on Marcel's creative fidelity and 'being at home,' and Marcel is absent from taxonomy.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Methodological vs Metaphysical Naturalism
holes.what: The distinction between doing science while bracketing the supernatural (methodological naturalism) and denying that anything supernatural exists at all (metaphysical naturalism).
holes.why: Chapter 21 resolves Indy's 'fact, not truth' stance as methodological naturalism, its central interpretive distinction, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The view that a statement is true when it accurately describes how things actually are, facts being the features of reality that make statements true.
holes.why: Chapter 21's opening argument that 'archaeology seeks fact, not truth' is self-defeating rests entirely on this account of truth, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Agnosticism
holes.what: T. H. Huxley's position that reason and evidence do not suffice to justify either belief or disbelief in God, suspending judgment between theism and atheism.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Indy's surplus of confirming evidence for rival religions lands him in exactly this agnosticism ('There is always another explanation'), which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Comparative mythologist (1904–1987) who argued that cross-cultural myths share archetypes, notably the hero's journey, springing from primal human realities.
holes.why: Chapter 23 credits Campbell (Lucas's inspiration) for the cave-as-archetype frame and closes by saying Crusade deals with 'ideas percolating in the collective culture that Campbell described,' yet taxonomy lacks him.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Rudolf Otto
holes.what: German theologian whose The Idea of the Holy (1917) analyses religion's irreducibly nonrational core, the numinous (mysterium tremendum et fascinans).
holes.why: Chapter 26 reads the Ark's climactic scene in Raiders entirely through Otto's account of the holy, creature-feeling, and nonmoral divine wrath.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: The Numinous (mysterium tremendum)
holes.what: The nonrational experience of a terrifying yet fascinating divine presence, 'wrath' that is independent of the moral status of its target.
holes.why: Chapter 26's thesis is that the Ark kills according to numinous holiness rather than morality, so no existing ethics- or faith-centered slug fits.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Émile Durkheim
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher who defined religion through the categorical opposition between the sacred (set apart and forbidden) and the profane.
holes.why: Chapter 28's framework for why each artifact rewards reverence and kills violators is Durkheim's sacred/profane distinction from The Elementary Forms of Religious Life.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: The Sacred and the Profane
holes.what: The distinction between things protected by prohibitions and set apart (sacred) and the ordinary, touchable world (profane), whose violation draws sanction.
holes.why: Chapter 28 explains who survives and who dies at each object's hands (Ark, Sankara Stones, Grail) via violation or observance of the sacred–profane boundary.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Archaeological Ethics (stewardship and cultural property)
holes.what: The applied ethics of archaeology: stewardship of the archaeological record (Alison Wylie), looting, repatriation, museums, and cultural-property law such as the UNESCO 1970 convention.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is organized around stewardship, politicized archaeology, and competing cultural-property claims, none of which any existing slug covers.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian philosopher of language and the novel, known for dialogism and the chronotope — the fused time-space shape of a narrative discourse.
holes.why: Chapter 34's third pillar applies Bakhtin's 'adventure time' to explain the films' condensed, non-linear cinematic chronology.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Chronotope and Adventure Time
holes.what: Bakhtin's notion that genres fuse time and space, with 'adventure time' condensing or stretching hours while the world and heroes remain unchanged.
holes.why: Chapter 34 needs it to explain why Indiana Jones stays frozen outside ordinary time while Harrison Ford visibly ages.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Jenefer Robinson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of emotion whose Deeper than Reason explains how music arouses emotions, moods, and 'emotions of appreciation' through appraisal.
holes.why: Chapter 35's entire analysis of Williams's Indiana Jones cues is built on Robinson's theory of musical emotion.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Music and the Emotions
holes.what: The aesthetics-of-music question of how purely instrumental music arouses and expresses emotions, moods, and appreciation of beauty, and whether this matters to aesthetic value.
holes.why: Chapter 35 applies this debate to the Raiders March, Marion's Theme, and the Ark cue, and the taxonomy contains no music or aesthetics concept at all.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Carl von Clausewitz
holes.what: Prussian general whose On War defines war as a duel on a large scale and 'politics by other means,' the classic account of decisive battle and strategy.
holes.why: Chapter 36 frames Indy's entire fighting style in Clausewitzian terms of symmetric war, guerilla exhaustion, and the decisive blow.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Asymmetric Warfare
holes.what: Conflict in which a weaker party avoids the enemy's strength — through raids, ambushes, and raising the stakes — instead of seeking symmetric decisive battle, and the associated honor codes.
holes.why: Chapter 36 argues Indy is an asymmetric 'raider' rather than a soldier, and the taxonomy's only strategy slug (Sun Tzu's) is never used in the chapter.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Orientalism
holes.what: The Western style of representing Eastern societies as exotic, cruel, and irrational, legitimizing colonial domination (Edward Said, also Van Woerkens's 'colonial imaginings' of the Thuggee).
holes.why: Chapter 37's charge that Temple of Doom is an 'imperialist fantasy' making Hindus look like bloodthirsty barbarians is precisely an orientalism critique, with no existing slug to index it under.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The view that a statement is true just in case it corresponds to how reality is — 'to say of what is that it is, is true' (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1011b).
holes.why: Chapter 38's whole reconstruction and refutation of Indy's 'fact, not truth' lecture rests on Aristotle's correspondence account, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_

holes.name: Jacques Ellul
holes.what: French social theorist who argued the essence of technology is 'technique' — rationally arrived-at methods of absolute efficiency — not the machines that embody it.
holes.why: Chapter 8 uses Ellul's technique thesis to argue that the essence of Iron Man lies in know-how rather than hardware, setting up Descartes and Heidegger.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: The Precautionary Principle
holes.what: The decision principle that when potential harms are catastrophic enough they must be avoided regardless of probability, even when cost-benefit analysis favors proceeding.
holes.why: Chapter 10's whole argument over Iron Man-style battle suits turns on the dispute between cost-benefit analysis and this rival principle, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: T.M. Scanlon
holes.what: Contemporary contractualist moral philosopher whose account defines blameworthiness as acting on attitudes that impair a moral relationship, with blame properly directed by those close to the wrong.
holes.why: Chapter 12 leans on Scanlon's theory of blame to determine who may blame Tony for Stark Industries' weapons sales and what his atonement must involve.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: Tragic Moral Dilemmas
holes.what: Choice situations offering only terrible options in which no course of action lets the agent emerge with clean hands and unavoidable regret (Hursthouse).
holes.why: Chapter 13's defense of Tony's registration drive frames it throughout as a tragic dilemma of choosing the least bad option, a notion absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: Andrew Carnegie
holes.what: Gilded Age industrialist whose 'Gospel of Wealth' holds that the self-made rich should administer their surplus as trust funds for the common good rather than distribute it in small sums.
holes.why: Chapter 16 is structured as a sustained test of Carnegie's gospel against Tony Stark's stewardship of his wealth and armor technology, and the taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: José Ortega y Gasset
holes.what: Spanish philosopher who in Meditations on Quixote urged 'meditative' close reading of classic texts as the cure for a society's intellectual backwardness.
holes.why: Chapter 18 borrows Ortega's meditative reading method to argue that we call Stark a philosopher king only because we have lost the habit of reading deeply.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of action who argued akrasia is impossible because acting against one's best judgment requires having already revised that judgment.
holes.why: Chapter 22's analysis of Tony's drinking is framed as Davidson's 'How Is Weakness of Will Possible?' thesis answered by Searle's gaps, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: H. Richard Niebuhr
holes.what: Theologian who analyzed faith as trust and loyalty within communities oriented by a shared center of value.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Niebuhr's community-of-value and trust/loyalty framework to explain how the Avengers ground Tony's good life and how the sentient armor might join it.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: Karl Jaspers
holes.what: Existentialist philosopher who held that transcendent meaning shows itself only through 'ciphers' — cultural symbols that some perceive and others do not.
holes.why: Chapter 30's central claim that Iron Man is a cipher of transcendence, expressed through flight, false dichotomies, betrayal, and sacrifice, is Jaspers' concept outright.
holes.book: 175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality

holes.name: Formalism in Aesthetics
holes.what: The view that an artwork's (especially architecture's) aesthetic properties such as beauty arise from its internal formal properties — shape, color, arrangement — rather than from context, history, or function.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is a sustained defense of LEGO-based architectural formalism against contextualist and functional-beauty accounts, and taxonomy has no entry for formalism or aesthetics of form.
holes.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick

holes.name: Racial Constructivism (race as socially constructed)
holes.what: The view that race is a real but socially constructed category, constituted by social practices, conventions, and attitudes rather than by biology, and varying across contexts and times.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues the yellow minifigure's failed racial neutrality shows race is built from context-dependent conventions (black in New Orleans, white in Brazil), against biological essentialism and Appiah-style eliminativism; taxonomy lacks any philosophy-of-race constructivism entry.
holes.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick

holes.name: Personalism
holes.what: A philosophical movement (associated with Max Scheler, Emmanuel Mounier, and others) treating the human person — free, acting, and self-creating — as the central and measure-giving category of reality.
holes.why: Chapter 21's resolution of the minifig Ship-of-Theseus puzzle is explicitly personalist: identity rests on the agent's choices and actions, the person being both builder and built, and taxonomy has no personalism entry.
holes.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick

holes.name: Corporate Social Responsibility
holes.what: The thesis that companies bear moral duties beyond profit — to workers, communities, and the environment — and may properly be held to higher standards when they trade on an ethically positive image.
holes.why: Chapter 23 evaluates LEGO's Shell partnership, outsourcing layoffs, and supply-chain emissions against its wholesome brand image, asking whether profiting from an ethical image generates stricter moral obligations; taxonomy has no CSR or business-ethics concept.
holes.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick

holes.name: Modal Epistemology (knowledge of possibility and necessity)
holes.what: The study of how we know what could and must be — whether via imagination, conceiving, or theory-based extrapolation — and how much modal knowledge we actually have.
holes.why: Chapter 31 is an extended exercise in modal epistemology, testing whether imagination tells us what is buildable with LEGO and defending a theory-based epistemology of modality; taxonomy's closest slug, possible-worlds, is Lewis's metaphysics, not this epistemology.
holes.book: 178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of why we feel genuine emotions (fear, sorrow, joy) toward characters and events we know do not exist, given that emotions normally depend on belief.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is built on it: Wind Waker makes players fear Gohma and grieve Link's departure, and the chapter tests the illusion, thought, and pretend theories against the paradox before giving its multi-level-mind answer.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Kendall Walton
holes.what: Philosopher of art whose make-believe theory treats fictions as props that authorize games of make-believe, with fiction-directed feelings like Charles's movie slime terror counting as 'quasi-emotions'.
holes.why: Chapter 9 presents his pretend theory as the leading solution to the paradox of fiction, and chapter 25 builds its claim that Zelda is art on Walton's account of depiction as make-believe.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Informal Fallacies
holes.what: Recurring patterns of bad reasoning — hasty generalization, false dilemma, equivocation, ad hominem, slippery slope, and appeal to inappropriate authority.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire critical-thinking lesson through Zelda diagnoses each named fallacy in timeline arguments, gamer stereotypes, and videogame-violence debates.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Ludus and Paidia (modes of play)
holes.what: Roger Caillois's distinction between rule-bound, goal-directed play (ludus) and free, improvisational play (paidia), extended to videogames by Gonzalo Frasca's win-condition test.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses the distinction to split Zelda into the designed hero-game and player-made glitch play, which grounds its Nietzschean master/slave morality reading of players versus Link.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Bruno Latour
holes.what: Philosopher and sociologist of science who argued in Laboratory Life (with Steve Woolgar) that scientific facts and evidence are constructed socially within networks of actors, tools, and norms.
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole analysis of Zelda fan timeline debates uses Latour and Woolgar as its framework for how evidence gets negotiated and knowledge socially constructed.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Social Construction of Knowledge
holes.what: The view that knowledge and evidence are not passively received but actively negotiated into being by communities of practice, their shared norms and tools.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues that Zelda forum debates construct timeline knowledge socially — excluding the CD-i games by community norm — exactly as Latour says laboratories construct facts.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Underdetermination of Theory by Evidence
holes.what: The thesis that any finite body of evidence fits infinitely many incompatible theories, so evidence alone never forces a single interpretation.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses the curve-fitting game to show Zelda timeline evidence underdetermines interpretations, which is why fans must fall back on community-relative simplicity.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's notion that the frightening is the familiar made strange — the long-familiar returning through repression, marked by strange repetitions, doubles, and what should have stayed hidden.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Majora's Mask's looped time, Link's Deku Scrub transformation, and the hidden time songs as an 'uncanny temporality' drawn directly from Freud's essay.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Philosophy of Art (aesthetics)
holes.what: The field asking what makes something art — covering depiction, medium, style, aesthetic experience, and whether new forms like videogames can count as art.
holes.why: Chapter 25's argument that Zelda qualifies as art via make-believe, translucence, and freeplay needs the general art-status debate, which the taxonomy's Kant-specific aesthetics slug does not cover.
holes.book: 179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box

holes.name: Byung-Chul Han
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of power who argues power works by mediation, ritual, and habit — 'taking its place in the soul of the other' — and degenerates into violence only when unmediated.
holes.why: Chapter 2's conclusion explicitly rests on Han's What Is Power?: Immortan Joe's water rituals and Humungus's epithets show that 'power shines in its own absence.'
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: Sociologist who defined the state as the monopoly of legitimate coercion and distinguished mere power from authority grounded in legitimacy.
holes.why: Chapter 2 uses Weber's power/authority distinction to explain why Humungus needs the title 'Lord' and why a mugger's threat is power without authority.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: The Tragedy of the Commons
holes.what: Garrett Hardin's problem that individually rational overuse of unowned shared resources depletes them, extended into lifeboat ethics for allocating survival under scarcity.
holes.why: Chapter 4's title and core analysis read Bartertown's pig-shit economy, water rationing, and the spaceship-Earth model through the commons tragedy, peak oil, and lifeboat ethics, none of which taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist of The Hero with a Thousand Faces whose monomyth structures the hero's journey of departure, trials, apotheosis, and return.
holes.why: Chapter 6 measures Max against Campbell's hero's journey as its primary framework, concluding he fails the return-and-reintegration stage and is instead Camus's absurd hero.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Bodily Parthood (mereology of the body)
holes.what: The metaphysical question of what makes something a part of a human body, tested through criteria such as adhesion, bonding, life, function, and integration.
holes.why: Chapter 7's entire argument builds and tests five criteria of bodily parthood against Fury Road's muzzles, tattoos, blood bags, and prosthetic arms; taxonomy has no parthood or material-constitution concept.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Cary Wolfe
holes.what: Posthumanist theorist of the human/animal divide whose categories of humaninized and animalized humans track who is granted full human standing.
holes.why: Chapter 15 sorts the Citadel's population with Wolfe's humaninized/animalized distinction: Joe and his heirs at the top, Max the muzzled 'it' and the War Pups below.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Carol J. Adams
holes.what: Feminist-vegetarian theorist (The Sexual Politics of Meat) whose 'feminized protein' and animalized-women categories link misogyny with the exploitation of female animals.
holes.why: Chapter 15 applies Adams's categories to the Citadel's milking mothers and breeders, reading Mother's Milk as feminized protein produced by animalized women.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: The White Possessive Doctrine
holes.what: Aileen Moreton-Robinson's account of patriarchal white sovereignty as a possessive logic that naturalizes the nation and its stories as white property.
holes.why: Chapter 16 invokes the white possessive doctrine repeatedly to explain the all-white first two Mad Max films and to question whether Max's assumed authority rests on unmarked whiteness.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: The Poetics (catharsis)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics and Politics that arousing fear, pity, and anger in audiences purifies them (catharsis) and trains character through rhythm and melody.
holes.why: Chapter 18 applies catharsis and Politics Book 8 to explain why Junkie XL's Fury Road score benefits viewers by arousing and purging negative emotions.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: The Poetics (necessity and probability)
holes.what: Aristotle's demand that plot and character unfold by necessity or probability, with improbable wonders tolerated only when they buy emotional power.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies the Poetics probability standard to judge Fury Road's Namibian scenery and non-Australian accents as artistic faults, and to weigh the value of representation.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Bioconservatism vs Transhumanism
holes.what: The view (Leon Kass) that human nature and untouched nature carry an inherent dignity that enhancement technologies violate, opposed by transhumanists like Bostrom who see posthuman dignity as complementary.
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues the whole franchise stages the Kass–Bostrom debate — villains are machine-altered, the saved live green and unmodified — and taxonomy lacks any bioethics-of-enhancement concept.
holes.book: 180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland

holes.name: Aristotle's Poetics (tragedy, epic, and plot unity)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of tragedy and epic plot, including unity of action, closure, relevance, and rules about character, place, and time.
holes.why: Chapter 8's first half defends Lost's complicated storytelling by testing it against the Poetics' principles of closure, relevance, and unity, and the taxonomy has no concept covering narrative theory.
