holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Synchronicity (meaningful coincidence)
holes.what: Jung's principle that some coincidences are meaningful, acausal concurrences between inner psychic states and external events.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central analysis of Locke's walkabout and the castaways' intersections rests on Jung's theory of synchronicity, which the taxonomy lacks (only the collective unconscious is listed).
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma and Tit-for-Tat
holes.what: A game-theory model in which rational self-interest blocks cooperation, with tit-for-tat reciprocity as the winning strategy when the game is repeated.
holes.why: Chapter 18 explains how the castaways build trust from scratch and reframes the Hobbes-Locke disagreement through repeated prisoner's dilemmas resolved by tit-for-tat, a framework absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: The Tragedy of the Commons
holes.what: A situation in which individually rational use of a shared, dwindling resource destroys it, although collective restraint would preserve it for all.
holes.why: Chapter 18 analyzes the stolen drinking-water crisis on the beach as a tragedy of the commons requiring a rationing the survivors have no authority to enforce.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Carl Schmitt
holes.what: German jurist and Nazi-era political theorist whose Concept of the Political defines politics by the friend-enemy distinction and treats conflict as inescapable rather than soluble.
holes.why: Chapter 19 is built around Schmitt: it argues the survivors' relation to the Others embodies his friend-enemy logic rather than liberal consensus politics, and the taxonomy has no entry for him.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Louis Althusser
holes.what: Marxist philosopher who analyzed how ideology reproduces itself by interpellating individuals through repressive state apparatuses (force) and ideological state apparatuses (religion, school, family).
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire reading of Lost runs on Althusser's concepts of ideology, interpellation, and ISA/RSA, from Sawyer's fake heart-rate monitor to Claire drinking Locke's Kool-Aid.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Interpellation (being recruited into ideology)
holes.what: Althusser's account of how individuals are inducted into a belief system that they then take for granted as the truth without realizing they were recruited.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies interpellation to the survivors' fear of the Others, the button-pressing ritual in the Swan, and even the show's viewers.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Othering (the socially constructed Other)
holes.what: The construction of a group as fundamentally different and inferior across an us-versus-them divide, sustained by fear and marking the marker's power as the norm.
holes.why: Chapter 20 tracks how Lost builds the ideology of otherness around the Others - savage, animal, dehumanized - and then dismantles it as socially constructed when the boundary dissolves.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Filial Obligations (what grown children owe their parents)
holes.what: The debate over whether adult children owe their parents a debt for sacrifices and biology, or whether the ideal parent-child relationship is a friendship in which debts are out of place.
holes.why: Chapter 23 weighs Jane English's we-owe-our-parents-nothing friendship model against Sidgwick's and David Mellow's debt-of-gratitude accounts using Jack, Locke, Sawyer, and Miles.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: W.D. Ross
holes.what: British deontologist who held that morality consists of multiple self-evident prima facie duties whose relative weight must be sorted into an actual duty in each situation.
holes.why: Chapter 24 evaluates Michael's betrayal and attempted atonement entirely through Ross's framework of prima facie duties, actual duty, guilt, and moral risk.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Prima Facie Duties
holes.what: Ross's plural set of self-evident duties - fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, noninjury - that bind unless overridden by a more pressing duty in the situation.
holes.why: Chapter 24 sorts Michael's rescue of Walt against his duties to Jack, Kate, and Sawyer, asking whether his freighter espionage and saving Jin count as making amends.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and literary philosopher whose theory of myth as embodied meaning (rather than abstract allegory) underlies the Narnia chronicles.
holes.why: Chapter 27 reads Lost as Lewisian myth - Cuse and Lindelof's stated model - applying Lewis's myth-not-allegory view, his Narnia parallels, and his own atheist-to-faith journey mirrored in Jack.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: H. Richard Niebuhr
holes.what: Christian ethicist who saw faith as the center of value that organizes a life and revelation as an ongoing, communal reinterpretation of experience.
holes.why: Chapter 27 uses Niebuhr's Faith on Earth and The Meaning of Revelation to frame the survivors' move from suspicion to trust and their redemption within community.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Myth versus Allegory
holes.what: Lewis's view that fantasy worlds communicate theological meaning through the story itself, so the message cannot be dissected from the narrative as in coded allegory.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues Lost, like Narnia, is myth rather than allegory, so questions about the show's meaning must return to the episodes themselves rather than a decoded thesis.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Edward Said
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist whose Orientalism argued that Western representations of the 'Orient' construct a dehumanized Other to justify domination.
holes.why: Chapter 31 profiles Said as Sayid Jarrah's namesake and applies Orientalism to the audience's projection of savagery onto the Others and the terrorist labeling of Sayid.
holes.book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

holes.name: Standpoint Epistemology
holes.what: The view that some social positions (women, minorities, the young) grant privileged access to knowledge unavailable from dominant standpoints, so their testimony can justify beliefs others cannot get first-hand.
holes.why: Chapter 9's central tool: Don rejects Dr. Guttman's research and Pete's pro-Kennedy insight because 1960 Madison Avenue refuses to recognize women's and youth's standpoints as sources of justification, culminating in Peggy's Belle Jolie win.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Mimesis and Plato's Critique of Imitative Art
holes.what: Plato's Republic X charge that artistic imitation works on the passions prior to reason, cannot distinguish appearance from reality, and shapes the soul by habituating its audience's emotional responses.
holes.why: Chapter 10's whole argument, from viewers' reaction to Don's 'You're a whore' scene to Don's 'pictures where people appear to be in love,' turns on mimesis bypassing reason, a Plato topic the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: John Kenneth Galbraith
holes.what: Liberal economist (1908-2006) whose The Affluent Society argues advertising creates consumer desires, producing private wealth amid public squalor and a 'conventional wisdom' that desires originate with consumers.
holes.why: Chapter 11 reads Sterling Cooper's advertising (the Heineken campaign, the Cadillac picnic) through Galbraith's deep-self compatibilist account of manipulated, unfree consumer choice.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Milton Friedman
holes.what: Free-market economist (1912-2006) whose Capitalism and Freedom defends libertarian free will, advertising as information rather than desire-creation, and the market's power to erode discrimination.
holes.why: Chapter 11 sets Friedman against Galbraith as the other pole: Betty's Heineken purchase was free choice, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch illustrates Friedman's claim that bigotry costs businesses money.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Active Forgetting (the uses and disadvantages of history for life)
holes.what: Nietzsche's doctrine that forgetting is a positive strength: the past must serve life, rumination is a sickness, and strong natures 'have done' with their misdeeds and misfortunes with a single shrug.
holes.why: Chapter 13 organizes Pete (dyspeptic rumination), Peggy (willful forgetting of her pregnancy and baby), and Don (the dialectic of memory and forgetting) entirely around this concept, which no existing Nietzsche slug covers.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-American novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) whose Objectivism defends rational egoism, the virtues (honesty, independence, productiveness, pride), the second-hander versus independent creator, and a 'benevolent universe.'
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads Bert Cooper's Atlas Shrugged fandom, Don's identity theft as second-handedness, and the whole cast's inauthenticity through Objectivism; the taxonomy has no Rand entry.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: John Doris
holes.what: Contemporary moral philosopher (b. c. 1969) whose Lack of Character (2002) argues situationist social psychology undermines the existence of global virtuous or vicious character traits.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Doris's situationism (the dime-in-the-payphone study, local versus global traits) as the main modern challenge to judging whether Don Draper is a good or bad person.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Situationism (the critique of character)
holes.what: The thesis, drawn from social psychology, that small environmental factors predict behavior better than stable character traits, so people lack the global virtues and vices virtue ethics assumes.
holes.why: Chapter 21 applies situationism to explain Don's and Pete's circumstance-bound behavior (helping only when a dime is found; affairs only before weddings) before defending regional character traits against it.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Lawrence Kohlberg
holes.what: Moral psychologist (1927-1987) whose six-stage theory holds that moral development culminates in reasoning from universal principles of justice, a scheme built on studies of adolescent men.
holes.why: Chapter 24 measures Don's, Peggy's, and Joan's moral development on Kohlberg's scale as the foil to Gilligan's care ethics before ranking Aristotelian friendships.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Critical Race Theory (differential racialization)
holes.what: The framework (Delgado, Stefancic, Crenshaw and others) that race is a social construction sustained by power structures, including the differential racialization of minority groups to serve dominant interests.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explicitly analyzes Mad Men's black characters (Carla, Hollis, Sheila) through differential racialization and race as social construction, concepts the taxonomy's existing race and gender slugs do not cover.
holes.book: 182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems

holes.name: Moral Perception (moral blindness)
holes.what: The capacity to see the morally salient features of a concrete situation (associated with Iris Murdoch, John McDowell, Lawrence Blum); its failure is moral blindness.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central claim is that Michael Scott exhibits a distinct category of moral failure - moral blindness, beyond malice, akrasia, and ignorance - and chapter 19 reuses the notion, but taxonomy.json has no slug for it.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Self-Deception
holes.what: Believing a lie one tells oneself: knowing that p at one level while sincerely denying it at another, typically sustained by rationalization.
holes.why: Chapter 16 is an entire epistemology of self-deception applied to Pam's denial of her love for Jim, and taxonomy.json contains no such concept.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Self-Deception
holes.what: Believing a lie one tells oneself, raising the paradox of how deceiver and deceived can be the same person.
holes.why: The last third of chapter 17 analyzes the paradox of Dwight deceiving himself about his title, modeling it via a divided mind - a concept taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Positive Illusions
holes.what: Benign self-deceptive beliefs - overrating one's traits, control, and future - studied by psychologist Shelley Taylor as motivationally and emotionally beneficial.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Taylor's positive illusions to argue Michael's self-deception improves his moods, grounding its 'beneficial illusion problem' of authenticity versus happiness.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Fatal Strategy
holes.what: Baudrillard's notion that a system pushed to its limit reverses into its own destruction, with obesity, for example, as the fatal strategy of consumption.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Gareth Keenan as the embodiment of fatal strategy, a Baudrillard concept distinct from simulacra and the hyperreal that taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Stakeholder Theory
holes.what: The business-ethics view that a firm's decisions must weigh everyone affected by them - employees, customers, suppliers, the community - rather than only stockholder profit.
holes.why: Chapter 25 (and again chapter 29) is organized around weighing stakeholder theory against stockholder-first management at Dunder Mifflin, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Affirmative Action
holes.what: Preferential policies (quotas, set-asides, minority preference in hiring) designed to remedy the present effects of past discrimination.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire argument about whether affirmative action is justified, and whether education could replace it, turns on this concept, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Political Correctness (offensive speech)
holes.what: The debate over whether language and jokes that demean groups are wrong as disrespect for equality, and whether free speech or offense-avoidance should govern them.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is wholly about political (in)correctness in The Office - racist jokes, slurs, and porn at work - a topic with no matching taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Sexual Harassment
holes.what: Unwelcome sexual or gender-directed workplace conduct, analyzed either as wrongful communication violating privacy and autonomy or as discrimination that maintains women's subordination.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is entirely devoted to defining what makes Michael Scott a sexual harasser and why it is wrong, a concept absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Shareholder Primacy (Stockholder Theory)
holes.what: Milton Friedman's view that a manager's sole moral obligation is to spend stockholders' money maximizing profit, from which no unprofitable good deeds are required.
holes.why: Chapter 29 states and then attacks this stockholder argument before endorsing stakeholder amends for the watermark scandal; Friedman himself is also absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Moral Responsibility and Blameworthiness
holes.what: The conditions under which an agent deserves blame for an outcome - classically requiring intentional causation, here refined to failing a job duty that causally contributed to the harm.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds a criterion of blameworthiness to decide who should be fired for the watermark incident (Creed, Michael, Jan), a core ethics concept the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Natural Kinds
holes.what: The question of whether the world is objectively carved into kinds (water, leopards, species) that our terms track, or whether classification is a human convention imposed on unstructured reality.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is organized entirely around the natural-kinds debate introduced by Brent's Mr. Spock and dwarf/midget/elf classifications; no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Paraconsistent Logic (dialetheism)
holes.what: A non-classical logic that rejects the Law of Non-Contradiction and the Principle of Explosion, allowing rational reasoning from inconsistent premises (as in the lottery/redundancy paradox).
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues Gareth's 'Case of the Missing Tim' announcement is rational precisely because it reasons paraconsistently; the taxonomy has no logic concepts at all.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Graham Priest
holes.what: Contemporary logician (b. 1948) and leading champion of paraconsistency and dialetheism, author of 'The Logic of Paradox'.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explicitly follows the 'cause of paraconsistency' led most notably by Priest to defend Gareth's rationality.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist (1924-1974) whose The Denial of Death argues that terror of mortality secretly motivates all culture and human activity.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses Becker's death-denial thesis as its master framework for Michael's grief over Ed Truck, the bird funeral, and the rooftop stunt.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: The Denial of Death
holes.what: The repressive strategy of treating death as a mere fact of life that happens to others, through euphemism, ritual, and quests for symbolic immortality.
holes.why: Chapter 35 diagnoses every character - Michael above all - as denying death rather than confronting it, a concept distinct from Heidegger's being-toward-death and absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Mimesis (art as imitation)
holes.what: The theory that art imitates reality - for Plato twice removed from the Forms and knowledge-free, for Aristotle a natural instinct whose tragedy arouses pity and fear to produce catharsis.
holes.why: Chapter 36 runs from Baudrillard back through Plato's Ion and Aristotle's Poetics precisely to frame The Office as an imitation of Scranton, and the taxonomy has no mimesis or catharsis slug.
holes.book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

holes.name: Ethical Criticism of Art (autonomism vs moralism)
holes.what: The aesthetics debate over whether moral categories apply to artworks: radical autonomism (art is judged only aesthetically), radical moralism (moral value supersedes aesthetic value), and moderate moralism (both count).
holes.why: Chapter 9 structures its whole analysis of punching up vs punching down in SNL sketches on this trio of views, and no taxonomy slug covers ethical criticism of art.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: The Offense Principle (Feinberg)
holes.what: Feinberg's liberal principle that the state may restrict offensive (not merely harmful) conduct only when the offended person cannot voluntarily avoid the offense, the Volenti maxim.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses the offense principle to explain why SNL's offensive sketches stay permissible, since viewers can simply change the channel.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Aristophanes
holes.what: Athenian Old Comedy playwright (c. 449-386 BC) whose satirical plays, above all Clouds, ridiculed sophists, natural philosophers, and Socrates himself.
holes.why: Chapter 12 builds its satire-versus-smart-assery comparison on the Clouds and its caricature of Socrates, and chapter 14 reuses the same example of harmful caricature.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: The Principle of Charity
holes.what: The norm of interpreting an opponent's position in its strongest, most reasonable form before criticizing it.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues caricature and satire fail the principle of charity and proposes charitable restatement as the ideal of political debate.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Moral Grandstanding
holes.what: Warmke and Tosi's notion of using moral talk primarily to project one's own moral superiority, which fuels escalation, polarization, and devalued moral discourse.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies grandstanding to the Church Lady's Superior Dance and contrasts it with Sinead O'Connor's non-grandstanding protest.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Philosophy of Play (Homo Ludens)
holes.what: The theory (Huizinga, Suits, Pieper) that play is a free, intrinsically motivated activity outside ordinary life with its own rules, and that playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire reading of Wayne's World rests on play theory, from the magic circle to Wayne and Garth's word games, and no taxonomy slug covers it.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Liveness and the Ontology of Performance
holes.what: Performance theory (Sparshott, Thom, Davies, Auslander) asking what makes a performance live, what counts as viewing one, and how framing and technological mediation enter.
holes.why: Chapter 24 needs this apparatus to argue that SNL is live in real-time broadcast, that televised viewing counts, and that Kaufman's framed lip-synch is a genuine performance while Eminem's was a framing failure.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Theories of Humor and Laughter (play and relief theories)
holes.what: Classic accounts of why we laugh, such as Eastman's play theory (laughter as instinctive animal play) and Freud's relief theory (laughter as release of psychic tension).
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses play theory and relief theory to adjudicate between Norm Macdonald's involuntary-laughter ideal and NBC's applause-driven comedy, and taxonomy lacks any theory-of-humor slug.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Walter Lippmann
holes.what: American journalist and political theorist whose Public Opinion (1922) and The Phantom Public (1927) argued citizens navigate through distorted pseudo-environments and that democracy needs expert guidance.
holes.why: Chapter 27's Dewey-versus-Lippmann framing of Weekend Update's citizen journalists (Drunk Uncle, Girl at Party, Stefon) needs Lippmann as the expert-side pole of the debate.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Neil Postman
holes.what: Media ecologist whose Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985) argues television's entertainment bias turns news and public discourse into incoherent show business.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is organized entirely around Postman's 'Now...this' critique of TV news as exemplified by Weekend Update, and he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Canadian media theorist famous for 'the medium is the message,' the thesis that the form of a communication technology shapes its content and social effects.
holes.why: Chapter 28 grounds Postman's argument in McLuhan's thesis (and chapter 27 invokes his retribalization for echo chambers), so media ecology needs him in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Filial Obligations (what grown children owe their parents)
holes.what: The debate over special duties among family members: unconditional role-based obligation, reciprocity for benefits received, or Jane English's view that only affection, not debt, grounds family duties.
holes.why: Chapter 29 tests all three views of familial obligation against the Spade-Murphy feud, and taxonomy covers Confucian filiality but not this Western family-ethics debate.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: P.F. Strawson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher whose 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962) grounds moral responsibility in participant reactive attitudes rather than in desert or consequences.
holes.why: Chapter 33 culminates in Strawson's reactive-attitudes view to explain why SNL's lovably stupid characters escape blame, and he is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century novelist-philosopher whose Objectivism holds rational self-interest and voluntary trade, not sacrifice, as the moral ideal.
holes.why: Chapter 9 gives Objectivism a full section, arguing Spider-Man personifies the 'morality of sacrifice' Rand condemned and noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: Paul Kurtz
holes.what: Secular humanist philosopher who defined the good life as happiness through self-realization plus benevolence, fairness, and love, without religion.
holes.why: Chapter 9 opens with Kurtz's secular-humanist test of whether Peter Parker's life of enterprise, friendship, and hardship counts as happy.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: The Bad and the True Infinite
holes.what: Hegel's distinction between a 'bad infinity' of endless, never-completed progression and the 'true infinite' that is complete and self-related like a circle.
holes.why: Chapter 10 frames Peter's endless, unsatisfiable obligation as Hegel's bad infinity and contrasts it with the self-sufficient ethics of the true infinite.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: Supererogation
holes.what: Acts that are praiseworthy to perform but not blameworthy to omit — beyond the call of duty.
holes.why: Chapter 14 hinges on whether Spider-Man's rescues are obligatory duties or supererogatory acts, concluding failing to aid is a harm-causing omission and thus required.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: Transhumanism (human enhancement)
holes.what: The movement advocating the use of technology to expand human physical and cognitive capacities beyond biological limits.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire argument defends the ethics of making a Spider-Man against bio-conservative objections about playing God, equality, and human essence.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: Leon Kass
holes.what: Bioethicist whose 'wisdom of repugnance' holds cloning wrong because a clone's genotype 'has already lived,' despotically fixing the clone's life to another's expectations.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Kass's argument to explain Kane's self-loathing and Peter's despair at learning he may be the clone.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: Gregory Pence
holes.what: Bioethicist who defends cloning, arguing repugnance toward clones rests on false expectations, like prejudices against twins or mixed-race children.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Pence's rebuttal of Kass to vindicate MJ's and Ben's view that a clone's worth comes from its actions, not its genes.
holes.book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

holes.name: Loyalty (partiality to one's own)
holes.what: Devotion to particular persons or groups because they are one's own rather than because of their qualities, raising the problem of whether such partiality can be virtuous or must lead to wrongdoing.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is entirely organized around whether SAMCRO's loyalty—enforced by death for rats and extended even to Tig's disastrous revenge—can be a virtue, debating Royce, Oldenquist, Ladd, Hume, and Ewin on the topic.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Émile Durkheim
holes.what: French sociologist who redefined religion as a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things which unite into one moral community those who adhere to them.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire reading of SAMCRO as a community of faith—Opie's wake, the sacred Reaper logo, cuts, and chapel—is built explicitly on Durkheim's Elementary Forms of Religious Life.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: The Sacred and the Profane
holes.what: The distinction that religious communities set apart 'sacred' things—forbidden to the uninitiated—that embody the group's collective spirit and identity.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues SAMCRO's Reaper tattoo, cuts, clubhouse, and chapel are sacred objects whose policing (blacking out Clay's ink, fire or knife for Kyle Hobart) marks the community's boundaries.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Männerbund (hunting origin of religion)
holes.what: Walter Burkert's thesis that religion and ritual originated in all-male cooperative hunting bands that ritually re-enacted hunts and sublimated male aggression.
holes.why: Chapter 20's 'MC and MB' section uses the Männerbund to explain SAMCRO's male bonding, hierarchy, rivalries like Tig and Kozik, and the subordination of family to the club.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Paul Ricoeur
holes.what: French philosopher whose Oneself as Another distinguishes idem-identity (sameness) from ipse-identity (selfhood) and argues the self is constituted through narrative, character, and promise keeping.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire analysis of Tara's tattoo, Tig's breakdown, Opie's promises, and John Teller's legacy is built step by step on Ricoeur's theory of narrative identity.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The thesis that personal identity is constituted by the story a person weaves from sameness, selfhood, character, and promises, given an ethical aim of 'the good life with and for others.'
holes.why: Chapter 21's title is 'Narrative Identity in Charming' and every case in it (Tara, Tig, Opie, SAMCRO itself) is an instance of identity maintained through narrative.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Robert Pirsig
holes.what: American author of Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, who treats motorcycle maintenance as caring engagement with technology that overcomes alienation from the mechanical world.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is framed by Pirsig's book and resolves its argument with his claims that technology frightens because it feels like a 'death force' and that repair is a form of care.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Hubert Dreyfus
holes.what: Twentieth-century Heideggerian philosopher of mind who argued (with Stuart Dreyfus) that expert skill is pre-reflective, embodied know-how that cannot be captured by rules or AI representations.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Dreyfus's skill theory to explain why Jax's riding, Chibs's brawling, and Tara's surgery work best when conscious self-monitoring disappears.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Readiness-to-Hand (Zuhandenheit)
holes.what: Heidegger's analysis of equipment as-transparent-in-use (readiness-to-hand), conspicuous in malfunction (un-readiness-to-hand), or detachedly inspected (presence-at-hand).
holes.why: Chapter 22 organizes the biker's whole relation to the motorcycle around these three modes, from absorbed riding to the roadside breakdown to the parts catalogue.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: The Oedipus Complex
holes.what: Freud's account of the phallic-stage fixation in which a boy desires his mother and rivals his father, resolved by identification with the father, with lasting effects if unresolved.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central move, via Ernest Jones's Hamlet and Oedipus, is diagnosing Jax's bond with Gemma and rivalry with Clay as an unresolved Oedipus complex.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French feminist philosopher who argues patriarchal society devalues women, circulates them as commodities exchanged among men, and blocks women from speaking as independent subjects.
holes.why: Chapter 25 is a sustained application of Irigaray (This Sex Which Is Not One, Speculum of the Other Woman) to Gemma and Tara as 'old ladies' in a male-dominated club.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: The Public and Private Realms
holes.what: Arendt's distinction in The Human Condition between the public political realm where humans appear as truly human and the private domestic realm of necessity, labor, and the life process.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its 'feminine sphere versus masculine sphere' framing of SAMCRO directly on Arendt's public/private distinction and her worry about the collapsing 'social' realm.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Early modern Italian philosopher of history whose New Science holds that history moves in corsi and recorsi, decaying from imaginative founding through the 'barbarism of reflection' before re-founding.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Vico's cycle to explain SAMCRO's fall from J.T.'s imaginative 1967 founding into Clay's rational greed and the club's near-annihilation.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Homer
holes.what: Bronze Age Greek epic poet whose Iliad and Odyssey encode the archaic warrior ethos of honor, glory, loyalty, and revenge that later Greek moral philosophy defined itself against.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire argument maps SAMCRO's outlaw code point by point onto Homeric heroism, from Opie as the warrior to Odysseus's trickery and Achilles's revenge.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: Warrior Morality (Homeric honor culture)
holes.what: The pre-philosophical ethic of the Iliad and Odyssey in which a good life is measured by combat prowess, glory, loyalty to friends and family, ruthless victory, and revenge as duty.
holes.why: Chapter 30 identifies this warrior ethic as the value system SAMCRO shares with Homer's heroes, the foil against which Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle first reacted.
holes.book: 187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: English mathematician and philosopher (1845-1879) who argued it is 'wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence'.
holes.why: Chapter 8 ('Stan Marsh and the Ethics of Belief') is built on Clifford's principle, quoting it and applying it to Stan's debunking of psychics, cults, and unevidenced faith.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief (evidentialism)
holes.what: The doctrine that believing on insufficient evidence is itself an ethical wrong that weakens the mind, and that the burden of proof always lies with the person making the claim.
holes.why: Chapter 8 evaluates Stan's battles with John Edward, Scientology, and Mormonism by this evidential standard; existing slugs like philosophical-skepticism cover doubting, not the moral duty governing belief itself.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Ulrich Beck
holes.what: German sociologist-philosopher (1944-2015) of 'world risk society' and reflexive modernity: global, manufactured, unanticipatable risks that outstrip national concepts and control strategies.
holes.why: Chapter 9 reads 'Imaginationland' and the war on terror almost entirely through Beck's risk categories, citing him a dozen times as its theoretical backbone.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: World Risk Society
holes.what: Beck's thesis that modern risks are omnipresent, borderless, and 'not yet real', admitting only three responses—denial, apathy, and transformation into a 'cosmopolitan moment' of cooperation.
holes.why: Chapter 9 maps the Pentagon's 'nuke our imagination' panic onto denial, Cartman's Rambo individualism onto apathy, and Kyle and Butters' creativity onto Beck's transformative cosmopolitan response.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Informal Fallacies
holes.what: Named patterns of bad reasoning—hasty generalization, red herring, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, ad hominem—in which the conclusion is not supported by the premises.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is a catalog of exactly these fallacies illustrated by South Park episodes (the Chewbacca Defense, the 'Death' boycott, Barbrady's book ban), and the taxonomy lacks any logic or fallacy slug.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Inference to the Best Explanation (abduction)
holes.what: Reasoning that compares rival hypotheses by criteria of adequacy—fruitfulness, simplicity, conservatism, and scope—and accepts the most adequate one.
holes.why: Chapter 12's whole method for judging miracle claims against the embellishment hypothesis (and Stan and Kyle's 9/11 'raging clue') is abduction; the taxonomy has Popper and Kuhn but no slug for this core scientific method.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Religious Pluralism (vs exclusivism and inclusivism)
holes.what: Hick's position that the great religions are roughly on par as transformative responses to the divine, set against exclusivism (one religion alone is true) and Rahner's inclusivism ('anonymous Christians').
holes.why: Chapter 13 structures its entire reading of 'Super Best Friends' and 'Go God Go' around the pluralism-exclusivism-inclusivism triad, and the taxonomy has no slug for theories of religious diversity.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Thomas Jefferson
holes.what: American Founding Father and democratic theorist who grounded complete intellectual and religious liberty in natural right ('God hath created the mind free'), holding that truth prevails in free argument and debate.
holes.why: Chapter 20 devotes a full section to Jefferson's Virginia Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom as the American counterpart to Popper's open society, and the taxonomy lacks him entirely.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Labor Theory of Value
holes.what: The Marxist doctrine that a commodity's value is determined by the labor required to produce it, with labor-power itself priced at subsistence and subject to a 'historical and moral element'.
holes.why: Chapter 21's whole argument is that 'The Last of the Meheecans' shows racialization modifying the value of Mantequilla's labor-power — a central Marxian concept the taxonomy's other Marx slugs (alienation, fetishism, ideology) do not cover.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Libertarianism
holes.what: The political philosophy that individual liberty — in markets and in personal life alike — is primary and trumps state intervention, descended from Smith, the Austrian School (Mises, Hayek), and Rothbard.
holes.why: Chapters 25 through 27 argue South Park expresses Parker and Stone's self-identified libertarianism (free markets, anti-paternalism, self-ownership), yet the taxonomy has no libertarianism concept, only pieces like minimal-state or invisible-hand.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist philosopher and social psychologist who argued that the self emerges from the social process through 'taking the attitude of the other'.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its refutation of the libertarian 'omnicompetent individual' on Mead's intersubjectivity, using Randy's failure to see himself as Jimbo sees him in 'Medicinal Fried Chicken', and the taxonomy lacks Mead.
holes.book: 188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

holes.name: Josef Pieper
holes.what: Twentieth-century Thomist philosopher whose Leisure: The Basis of Culture argues that leisure and festivity—not mere work or pleasure—are the basis of contemplation and human flourishing.
holes.why: Chapter 8 is built entirely on Pieper's concept of leisure, applied to 'Shore Leave', the Omicron Ceti III spores, and Star Trek viewing itself as edifying play.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Moral Injury
holes.what: Nancy Sherman's notion that service members can be wounded in their moral identity—especially by shame—losing their sense of self rather than merely having done wrong.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses moral injury to explain Picard's Locutus guilt and shame in 'Family' and the captain's need to carry rather than erase guilt, regret, and remorse.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Self-Actualization (Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs)
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's account of the highest human need: fulfilling one's potential once biological, safety, and social needs are met.
holes.why: Chapter 12 tests whether Kirk's 'stagnation' complaints against the spore and Vaal utopias hold up by checking those societies against Maslow's criteria for self-actualization.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Positive vs Negative Peace
holes.what: Peace-studies distinction between negative peace (mere absence of violence) and positive peace (social conditions that let people fulfill their potential, making justice intrinsic to peace).
holes.why: Chapter 13 organizes its whole philosophy-of-peace reading of Trek around this distinction, applying positive peace to 'The Cloud Minders' and the Troglytes' 'right to the clouds'.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Cultural Appropriation and Acculturation
holes.what: The one-way imposition or adoption of a culture's practices outside their original context—acculturation for the assimilated minority, appropriation for the adopting majority.
holes.why: Chapter 15 uses Occidentalism, acculturation, and appropriation to analyze Worf's forced assimilation to Federation norms and Trekkers' adoption of Klingon language, ritual, and dress.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The techno-utopian program (Max More, James Hughes) of using genetic, cybernetic, and nanotechnological enhancement to surpass human limitations and become posthuman.
holes.why: Chapter 16's title thesis is that the Borg are transhumanists run amok: their pursuit of 'perfection' through assimilation mirrors and critiques real transhumanist enhancement goals.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Jacques Ellul
holes.what: French philosopher of technology who argued that 'technique' is an autonomous, self-augmenting reality that tolerates no outside judgment and is inherently totalitarian.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads the Borg primarily through Ellul's and Langdon Winner's claim that technology pursues its own course beyond human control, making the Collective technology itself.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: Feminist accounts (Mackenzie and Stoljar) holding that autonomy is enabled or suppressed by social relations rather than exercised by an isolated, self-sufficient individual.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses relational autonomy to argue Janeway's pleading with Kes supports rather than undermines her choice, and to ask whether the Borg Collective itself counts as autonomous.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Casuistry (case-based reasoning)
holes.what: A method of moral reasoning that works from paradigm cases and shared intuitions toward verdicts in new cases, rather than applying abstract theory top-down (Jonsen and Toulmin).
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues Star Trek is philosophy's great casuistic teacher: its episodes, from 'The Measure of a Man' to 'Nothing Human', are carefully staged case studies for viewers' intuitions.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Constitutionalism (persons constituted by bodies)
holes.what: Lynne Rudder Baker's view that a person and her body share all parts yet are distinct objects, the person being constituted by (not identical with) the body and surviving its gradual replacement.
holes.why: Chapter 23 gives constitutionalism a full section as the middle way between dualism and animalism for transporter survival, tested against Riker's fission in 'Second Chances'.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Annette Baier
holes.what: Contemporary feminist moral philosopher whose account of persons as "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood through long dependency, care, and mutual recognition anchors chapter 26's model of human nature.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central argument that Data, Seven of Nine, and the Doctor become persons through socialization is built directly on Baier's quoted account of personhood, and no existing slug covers it.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher whose metaphysics of actual occasions, organisms, and societies supplies chapter 30's entire framework for judging advanced life-forms.
holes.why: Chapter 30 is wholly built on Whitehead's philosophy of organism to argue the Q and Organians cannot be purely incorporeal, and the taxonomy has no process-philosophy entry.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Philosophy of Organism (process philosophy)
holes.what: Whitehead's view that reality consists of momentary experiential occasions with mental and physical poles organized into nested societies, where survival must balance creative intensity.
holes.why: Chapter 30 applies actual occasions, standing societies, and canalization to Organians, cloud-creatures, and the Q Continuum; nothing in the taxonomy captures process metaphysics.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Neera Badhwar
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of friendship whose paper "Why It Is Wrong to Be Always Guided by the Best: Consequentialism and Friendship" argues consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship.
holes.why: Chapter 31's core thesis - that Spock's consequentialism cannot accommodate Kirk's friendship - is Badhwar's argument, quoted extensively, and she is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist science-studies theorist whose 1985 "A Cyborg Manifesto" celebrates the human-machine hybrid as a way out of oppositional dualisms.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is framed entirely by Haraway's "I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess" against the Borg, and she is missing from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: The Cyborg (Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto)
holes.what: Haraway's figure of the human-machine hybrid as ontology and politics, dissolving boundaries between organism and machine and rejecting hierarchical binaries.
holes.why: Chapter 32 defends Borg values of heteronomy, collectivity, and simulation precisely through the cyborg concept; the generic feminism slug does not carry this specific machinery.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American social behaviorist whose theory of the socially emergent self (the I and the me, specific and generalized others, significant symbols and play) structures chapter 33.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is a sustained application of Mead's Mind, Self, and Society to Odo, and Mead does not appear in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: The Social Self (I and Me)
holes.what: Mead's account of the self as emerging from social interaction: the impulsive I responding to the internalized attitudes (the me) of specific and generalized others, learned through language and play.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explains Odo's personhood through the I/me distinction, gesture-language, and taking the attitude of the team; the generic personal-identity slug does not cover this developmental social theory.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Mary Midgley
holes.what: Twentieth-century British moral philosopher known for her critique of moral isolationism in "Trying Out One's New Sword".
holes.why: Chapter 34's resolution of the cogenitor dilemma rests on Midgley's anti-isolationism and her tsujigiri example, and she is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Moral Isolationism (judging other cultures)
holes.what: Midgley's target view that we cannot criticize cultures outside our own; she argues respect requires understanding, which makes informed cross-cultural judgment both possible and necessary.
holes.why: Chapter 34 applies this concept to Trip's judgment of Vissian cogenitor treatment and to Quark's cross-species critique, and no existing slug names the view being attacked.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Contemporary continental philosopher who extends Heideggerian worries about technology to synthetic life, ungoverned biogenetic research, and a new servant underclass.
holes.why: Chapter 35's concluding move - that the Borg warning has already arrived in synthetic biology and class division - is carried by Žižek's cited work, which the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Novalis
holes.what: German Romantic poet-philosopher (Friedrich von Hardenberg) who called for making the world Romantic - a qualitative raising of the ordinary to a higher power.
holes.why: Chapter 39 quotes Novalis's "the world must be made Romantic" as the key to Spock's taping of history and his Yesteryear self-rescue, and no Romantic figure exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Romanticism (the world must be made Romantic)
holes.what: The intellectual movement (c. 1770-1850) reacting against Enlightenment rationalization by treating imagination, nature, death, and irony as sources of meaning against nihilism.
holes.why: Chapter 39 explicitly reads "The City on the Edge of Forever" and "Yesteryear" through Romanticism, including the romantic focal point of history and beauty-in-death; the taxonomy has no Romanticism entry.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Secular Humanism
holes.what: The worldview centering human values and flourishing without recourse to a transcendent deity, here extended into Roddenberry's "humanist theology" of humanity's divine potential.
holes.why: Chapter 41's title concept is Star Trek's humanist theology - Roddenberry's atheism, the demand-for-worship test, and compassion as the divine attribute - and no taxonomy slug names humanism itself.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Secularization (religion and the public sphere)
holes.what: The political and social doctrine that public reason and government should operate independently of religious authority, balancing political democracy against civil liberties including freedom from religion.
holes.why: Chapter 42's moral arguments for a secular society (Picard refusing to be the Mintakans' god, Akorem's D'jarra theocracy) need this concept; democracy-theory alone misses the religion-in-politics dimension.
holes.book: 189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

holes.name: Thrasymachus
holes.what: Sophist in Plato's Republic who defines justice as the advantage of the stronger.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads the Sith Code and Sidious's 'I will make it legal' as Thrasymachus's might-makes-right set against Plato, but the taxonomy has no sophist-era thinker beyond Protagoras.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Moral Nihilism (there are no moral facts)
holes.what: The view that there are no objective moral facts; moral judgments are merely interpretations of phenomena.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is built on the claim that Palpatine teaches Anakin Nietzsche's moral nihilism and that the Iliad and Star Wars both reject it through compassion-based moral realism.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Mozi
holes.what: Warring States critic of Confucianism (c. 470-391 BCE) whose Mohism condemned offensive war and demanded impartial concern for the overall benefit of all.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads Jedi Master Kai Hudorra's withdrawal from the fight and his final sacrifice as Mohist, but the taxonomy's Chinese philosophy entries omit Mozi entirely.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Mandate of Heaven (tianming)
holes.what: The classical Chinese doctrine that Heaven grants rulers legitimacy through virtue (de) and withdraws it from bad rulers.
holes.why: Chapter 12 frames Palpatine's Empire against the Zhou dynasty's collapse through its opening section 'Heaven's Mandate Is Not Constant,' a concept absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Amoralism (withdrawal from moral judgment)
holes.what: The stance of acting outside moral categories altogether, distinct from both moral relativism and ethical egoism.
holes.why: Chapter 15's thesis is that Boba Fett is an amoralist rather than a relativist or egoist, and no taxonomy slug names amoralism itself.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Loyalty and Betrayal
holes.what: The debate over whether loyalty is a duty, a virtue, or a mere emotional connection, and what makes betrayal wrong.
holes.why: Chapter 21 is wholly organized around the moral value of loyalty (Royce, Fletcher, Keller) and the wrongness of betrayal, which no taxonomy concept covers.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Susan Bordo
holes.what: Contemporary feminist philosopher of the body who analyzes the cultural vilification of fat and the tyrannical 'anorexic aesthetic' of thinness as disciplines imposed on the female body.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explicitly builds its reading of Leia's captivity scene on Bordo's account of the fear of fat alongside Sartre and Foucault, but she has no slug in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German idealist whose freedom treatise treats evil as a real, dark 'ground' within the divine will that becomes evil when it asserts itself against the will of love.
holes.why: Chapter 28's positive answer to why the Force must have a dark side is essentially Schelling's dark-ground metaphysics, which no existing slug covers.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Panentheism
holes.what: The view that everything that exists is encompassed within one divine reality (Brahman, Dao, God, the Force) which nevertheless exceeds the world.
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues the Force is panentheistic and that this very doctrine creates the problem of how a good all-encompassing Force can contain or ground evil.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Enactivism
holes.what: 4E-cognition view (Varela, Thompson, Rosch) that perception, thought, and action form one enacted loop - mind is something you do, not a model built between perceiving and acting.
holes.why: Chapter 29 applies the enactivist perception-action loop to Jedi training and the flow of the Force; only Merleau-Ponty's embodiment is covered by the taxonomy.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Noam Chomsky
holes.what: Linguist-philosopher who holds that a genuine language requires syntax determined by a generative grammar.
holes.why: Chapter 33 uses Chomsky's structure-based criterion as the foil that rules Chewbacca's roars out of language before Wittgenstein's use-based answer brings them back in.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection makes heritable variation within species fundamental to biology.
holes.why: Chapter 34's argument that species essentialism is false, and hence that de-extinction is impossible, rests entirely on Darwinian natural selection.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: The Species Problem
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology puzzle of what individuates a species: fixed essential traits (Aristotelian essentialism) versus historical individuals defined by unique origins (Ghiselin's species nominalism).
holes.why: Chapter 34 is organized around this problem to argue that a cloned Zillo Beast could not resurrect the extinct species.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: The Monomyth (Hero's Journey)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's thesis, drawing on Jung, that all world mythologies share a single hero-quest structure of departure, initiation, and return.
holes.why: Chapter 36 maps Luke's arc onto the monomyth stage by stage and then criticizes it as ideology, and no taxonomy slug covers Campbell's framework.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we have genuine emotional responses to characters we know do not exist, given that rational emotion seems to require belief in really existing objects.
holes.why: Chapter 37 structures its entire analysis of grieving at Han's carbon-freezing around this paradox and the failure of the illusion, thought, and pretend theories.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist whose 'The Death of the Author' argues that a work's meaning is not fixed by authorial intention or biography.
holes.why: Chapter 39 leans on Barthes to argue that Lucasfilm cannot unilaterally dictate what counts as canonical Star Wars.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: The Death of the Author
holes.what: Barthes' thesis that interpretation should not privilege the author's intentions, since what readers bring to a text matters equally.
holes.why: Chapter 39 deploys this thesis against Lucasfilm's claim of near-total control over the Star Wars canon after the 2014 Expanded Universe reset.
holes.book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

holes.name: Noam Chomsky
holes.what: American linguist and political philosopher (b. 1928) known for his critique of state capitalism, neoliberalism, corporate power, and media propaganda, and for libertarian-socialist commitments to production for need rather than profit.
holes.why: Chapter 15 frames its whole reading of The Clone Wars — the Separatists' justified self-determination, the Halle Burtoni/Halliburton military-industrial parallel, and the Republic's democratic collapse — through Chomsky's analysis of inequality and democratic erosion, citing The Precipice throughout.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Institutional Theory of Art (the Artworld)
holes.what: The view that something is a work of art because the 'artworld' — artists, critics, curators, collectors, and appreciators — collectively confers that status on it, so nothing is intrinsically art.
holes.why: Chapter 19 runs Sabine's graffiti and the Syndulla Kalikori through representation, expression, and institutional theories of art, and Thrawn's collection shows the artworld's authority both making artworks and destroying them by removing them from context; taxonomy has no aesthetics concepts at all.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Cooperation with Evil (material and formal complicity)
holes.what: The Thomistic analysis of when contributing to another agent's wrongdoing makes one culpable, distinguishing formal from material, immediate from mediate, proximate from remote, and replaceable from necessary cooperation.
holes.why: Chapter 22's whole verdict on Galen Erso's Death Star work turns on these Thomistic complicity tools (via Flannery's Cooperation with Evil): his collusion is excused only because his material cooperation was mediate, remote, and non-necessary, a doctrine taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Legal Personhood
holes.what: The legal status of being a bearer of rights and duties rather than mere property, a category that legal systems apply independently of moral personhood.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues that sentient droids like L3-37 cannot be validly classified as property under a Kantian natural-law account and deserve legal personhood, citing real AI-inventorship and animal-personhood cases.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Ontology of Fictional Characters
holes.what: Theories of whether fictional characters genuinely exist and what makes two appearances of a character the same character (indiscernibility, authorial say-so, perspectival accounts).
holes.why: Chapter 29 tests identity-of-indiscernibles and say-so theories against the many Luke Skywalkers of canon, Legends, and fan fiction, concluding that character identity is perspectival.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Biopower
holes.what: Foucault's notion of modern power exercised over populations and life itself - managing birth, death, health, and biology - beyond sovereign and disciplinary power over individual bodies.
holes.why: Chapter 34 identifies the Client's and Dr. Pershing's experiments on Grogu and the Kaminoan cloning of Jango Fett as biopower, the third power form in its sovereign-disciplinary-biopower framework.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Colorism
holes.what: Preferential or prejudicial treatment of same-race people based on skin tone, privileging lighter skin over darker.
holes.why: Chapter 39 uses colorism to question why Finn and Jannah were cast as Black stormtroopers and why Finn's image was minimized in marketing, reading his treatment through skin-tone hierarchy.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Pacifism
holes.what: The view that violence and war are morally unjustified, in absolute, deontological, or consequentialist varieties, obligating nonviolent rather than passive action.
holes.why: Chapter 40 argues Luke Skywalker in The Last Jedi is a consequentialist pacifist whose Force projection on Crait is the paradigm of proactive nonviolent action, the chapter's central concept.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Forces of Becoming / Becoming-Other
holes.what: Deleuze's idea, built on Nietzsche's will to power, that bodies are bundles of competing forces whose power is to deform themselves and form new relations (becoming) rather than persist as fixed substances.
holes.why: Chapter 41 reads The Last Jedi's Luke as exercising a supreme becoming-other that overpowers even the Force, and distinguishes the noble will-to-become from the base will-to-dominate.
holes.book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection grounds the concepts of fitness, adaptation, and biological altruism.
holes.why: Chapter 12 ('Darwin in Metropolis') runs its entire Batman-vs-Superman comparison through Darwinian fitness, natural selection, and altruism, and Darwin is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Natural Selection and Fitness
holes.what: The evolutionary mechanism by which heritable traits aiding survival and reproduction spread, defining biological fitness and biological altruism.
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues Superman is the fitter and more effective 'Superhero' using natural selection, morphospace reasoning, and biological altruism, none of which taxonomy covers.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Twentieth-century literary scholar and Christian apologist whose essay 'The Necessity of Chivalry' analyzes the knight's double demand of fierceness and meekness.
holes.why: Chapter 13's whole comparison of Batman and Superman as chivalric knights is built on Lewis's account of knightly character as achieved art rather than nature.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: The Code of Chivalry
holes.what: The medieval knightly code pairing martial fierceness with meekness, courtesy, and restraint, treating knightly character as something achieved by art.
holes.why: Chapter 13 evaluates Superman and Batman against chivalry's double demand and crowns Superman the truer knight for his self-restraint.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos (modes of persuasion)
holes.what: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion in On Rhetoric: appeal to the speaker's character, to the audience's emotions, and to logic and facts.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire argument weighs Batman's pathos and logos against Superman's balanced ethos to decide which hero argues like a hero.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Good, praiseworthy actions that are not morally required — the deeds of saints and heroes, per Urmson and Raz.
holes.why: Chapter 18's core claim is that Batman's risky crime-fighting is supererogatory while Superman's rescues are merely required by his powers; taxonomy has no such concept.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The cultural and philosophical movement aiming to transcend the human condition through technology, genetic engineering, and enhancement.
holes.why: Chapter 22's central argument is that Superman, not Batman, is the proper goal of transhumanist self-improvement; taxonomy lacks the concept.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: The Metabolic Rift
holes.what: Marx's ecological idea, revived by John Bellamy Foster, that capitalist production ruptures the nutrient exchange between society and nature, accumulating waste faster than ecosystems can process it.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire Lois Lane–Batman dialogue charges the Bat-gear upgrade cycle and Wayne Enterprises with generating metabolic rifts of infinite consumption and waste.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Mimesis and Catharsis (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of drama as imitation (mimesis) of human action that arouses pity and fear (catharsis) in an audience.
holes.why: Chapter 29 defines Batman as mimesis—a theatrical mask whose staged death defeats Superman in The Dark Knight Returns—and taxonomy has no Poetics concept to map this to.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Umberto Eco
holes.what: Italian semiotician and novelist whose essay 'The Myth of Superman' argues comic-book commerce demands formulaic plots that keep Superman's world permanently unchanged.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses Eco's thesis to explain why Superman preserves the status quo while Batman actively tries to remake Gotham and can be imitated by successors.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Flow (optimal experience)
holes.what: Mihaly Csikszentmihaly's state of deep engagement that occurs when a challenge exactly matches a person's skill, between boredom and anxiety.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explains the absence of a good Superman video game through flow: an invincible hero can never be matched to player skill, unlike equipment-driven, trainable Batman.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally admirable but beyond obligation—good to perform though not wrong to omit.
holes.why: Chapter 32 builds its thesis that Batman is the more heroic on supererogation as the mark of heroism: Autrey's unobligated subway rescue is heroic, Sullenberger's trained duty is not, and Superman's near-obligatory guarding of Earth falls short.
holes.book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

holes.name: Reactive Attitudes (Freedom and Resentment)
holes.what: P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility, on which a being is a responsible member of the moral community just in case moral emotions like resentment and indignation are appropriate responses to it, as opposed to an objective attitude of management and control.
holes.why: Chapter 8's entire framework for deciding which monsters Sam and Dean may kill is Strawson's reactive attitudes, from soulless Sam to the 'moral monsters' of 'Bloodlust,' and neither the philosopher nor the concept exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

holes.name: Soul-Making Theodicy (Irenaean)
holes.what: John Hick's Irenaean theodicy, on which God allows evil and suffering because a world of adversity is a proving ground in which free but imperfect creatures forge virtuous, salvation-worthy souls.
holes.why: Chapter 19 devotes its final section to testing Hick's soul-making theodicy against Dean's world, arguing via the rugaru and the Winchesters' bloody moral growth that Supernatural contains far more suffering than soul-making could justify.
holes.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of religion (1922-2012), author of 'An Irenaean Theodicy' and the soul-making response to the evidential problem of evil.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explicitly cites and applies Hick's theodicy at length as the last defense of God against Dean's evidential argument, and Hick is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

holes.name: Naturalism (naturalistic explanation)
holes.what: The view that natural phenomena are explained by other natural phenomena via the senses and the scientific method, so that supernatural explanations are admitted, if at all, only where naturalistic ones fail.
holes.why: Chapter 25's whole project is to naturalize Supernatural, treating souls as genetic codes and deriving a phylogeny of demons, ghosts, and monsters from human origins, and the taxonomy has no naturalism slug under knowledge-science-reality.
holes.book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

holes.name: Ordo Amoris (the ordering of loves)
holes.what: Augustine's doctrine that character and happiness depend on loving things in their right order, with rightly ordered caritas opposed to disordered cupiditas.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire reading of Jamie, Dani Rojas, Rebecca, and Ted as father figure is built on Augustine's ordo amoris, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: Victorian mathematician-philosopher whose 'The Ethics of Belief' holds it is always wrong, everywhere, for anyone to believe anything on insufficient evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is structured as Clifford's evidentialism versus James's precursive faith, with Clifford's shipowner supplying the target thesis.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism who defended rational ethical egoism in The Fountainhead and 'The Virtue of Selfishness.'
holes.why: Chapter 12 argues Ted is an egoist by pairing Aristotle with Rand's Howard Roark, the hero of Ted's favorite book.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: The Middle Passage (Hollis)
holes.what: James Hollis's Jungian account of midlife, when the assumptions and provisional personality of life's first half collapse and one must choose an authentic second half.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads Ted's therapy arc with Dr. Sharon and his flight to and from London entirely through Hollis's Middle Passage framework.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Natural Goodness (Foot)
holes.what: Philippa Foot's view that moral evaluation rests on what is good for members of a natural kind, judged by their characteristic form of life.
holes.why: Chapter 16 grounds friendship's intrinsic value in Foot's Natural Goodness account of the human good, which taxonomy lists Foot only for the trolley problem.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian apologist and literary scholar whose The Four Loves analyzes affection and friendship as shared pursuit of a common good.
holes.why: Chapter 16 leans on The Four Loves to explain why self-gratifying characters like Jamie and Rebecca cannot have friends.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Patriarchal Masculinity (hooks)
holes.what: bell hooks's account of patriarchy as a dominance system that damages men too by demanding they suppress emotion and rule over the weak.
holes.why: Chapter 21's critique of Jamie, Rupert, Roy, and Nate runs entirely on hooks's patriarchal-masculinity framework from The Will to Change.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Kate Manne
holes.what: Feminist philosopher who defines misogyny as the enforcement mechanism policing women (and soft men) who challenge male entitlement.
holes.why: Chapter 21 applies Manne's Down Girl definition to George Cartrick's punditry and Rupert's public demeaning of Rebecca.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Sport as a Mutual Quest for Excellence (Simon)
holes.what: Robert Simon's philosophy-of-sport view that good competition is a cooperative 'mutual quest for excellence through challenge' where winning matters but respect for persons matters more.
holes.why: Chapter 22 resolves the Ted-versus-Beard dispute by adopting Simon's account as the 'New Lasso Way.'
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Philosophy of Music (arousal and mimesis)
holes.what: The aesthetics branch asking how music expresses and arouses emotion and can shape moral character, from Aristotle's Politics VIII through Schopenhauer to Robinson and Kivy.
holes.why: Chapter 24 needs it to explain how the show's score and soundtrack amplify each scene's emotion and warmth.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Voltaire
holes.what: Enlightenment satirist whose Candide ridicules Leibnizian philosophical optimism through Pangloss and ends in meliorism ('we must work our land').
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses Candide to expose the fatalism inside Ted's rom-communism before turning to Camus for the alternative.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: G.K. Chesterton
