holes.what: Edwardian essayist and Christian apologist who defended a paradoxical, evil-acknowledging philosophical optimism grounded in gratitude for Being.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues Ted's optimism is Chestertonian while lacking the theological foundation Chesterton insisted upon.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: The Holy Fool
holes.what: A literary-spiritual archetype of the naive-seeming outsider whose folly discloses deeper truth and heals others, from Don Quixote and The Idiot to Chesterton's Innocent Smith.
holes.why: Chapter 27 interprets Ted as a holy fool whose apparent incompetence reveals the true nature of sport, teamwork, and life.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: P.F. Strawson
holes.what: Author of 'Freedom and Resentment,' arguing reactive attitudes like anger and resentment are how we hold one another as members of the moral community.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explains why Nate is hurt by Roy's easy forgiveness through Strawson's reactive-attitudes thesis.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Eleonore Stump
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose Thomistic account treats forgiveness within a framework of love, distinct from (though ideally ending in) reconciliation.
holes.why: Chapter 32 uses Stump's framework to explain why forgiveness can be one-sided yet why Rupert's reconciliation is so difficult.
holes.book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch

holes.name: Functionalism (mind as computation)
holes.what: The view that mental states are defined by their functional or computational role rather than their physical substrate, so a mind can be realized in silicon as well as brain tissue.
holes.why: Chapter 11's central argument that humans are 'meat machines' continuous with Terminators rests on functionalism, applied through the Henrietta gradual brain-replacement thought experiment, and no existing slug covers it.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
holes.what: Lawrence Kohlberg's six-stage theory on which moral maturity consists in reasoning from abstract universal principles, tested with dilemmas such as the Heinz problem.
holes.why: Chapter 13 uses Kohlberg's stages and the Heinz dilemma to frame Sarah's principled killing of Dyson as the target of Gilligan's care-ethics critique, and no slug covers the stage theory itself.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: Twentieth-century French thinker whose Violence and the Sacred holds that violence leaves a contagious 'stain' on all who touch it and that societies purge it through purification rites and sacrifice.
holes.why: Chapter 14 builds its entire account of Sarah Connor's trauma, her failed reintegration into society, and warrior-purification rituals on Girard's stain framework.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Julien Offray de La Mettrie
holes.what: Eighteenth-century French materialist who in Man a Machine argued that humans are self-winding clocks, with no vital spark separating living from nonliving matter.
holes.why: Chapter 18 invokes La Mettrie's 'Mr. Machine' materialism alongside Turing to argue the self-terminating T-101 is a person and that machines may be evolution's next phase.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Deprivation Account of Death
holes.what: The view that death is bad for the victim because it deprives them of the future goods — experiences, projects, relationships — they would otherwise have had.
holes.why: Chapter 25 builds its answer to the Terminator's killing on Marquis's loss-of-future argument and Feldman's ante-mortem harm, for which no existing slug (only the rival Epicurean view is covered) exists.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Kairos (the opportune moment)
holes.what: The Greek concept of time as qualitative significance — the weighty, decisive right moment — contrasted with chronos, mere quantitative passage.
holes.why: Chapter 26 frames John Connor's Crystal Peak decision as a chairotic moment whose answer determines who he is, and the whole chapter is organized around this concept.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: H. Paul Grice
holes.what: Philosopher of language who distinguished sentence meaning from speaker's meaning and analyzed communication as inference (implicature) rather than encoding.
holes.why: Chapter 28's core claim is that the Terminator operates on the Code Model while humans follow Grice's Inferential Model, inferring speaker's meaning from context; Grice is also decisive in chapter 29.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Speaker's Meaning vs Sentence Meaning
holes.what: The Gricean distinction between what a sentence literally means and what a speaker means by uttering it on a particular occasion, recovered by inference from context.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses the distinction to explain why John's kidnapping cries and slang lessons baffle the code-bound T-101, and chapter 29 relies on it to deny that definite descriptions are ambiguous.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: P. F. Strawson
holes.what: Philosopher who argued against Russell that definite descriptions are referring expressions and that sentences are true or false only relative to a particular use.
holes.why: Chapter 29's first main section is built on Strawson's 'On Referring' objection that Kyle's 'The Terminator will kill you' genuinely refers to the machine at the door rather than quantifying.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Keith Donnellan
holes.what: Philosopher of language who distinguished the referential and attributive uses of definite descriptions.
holes.why: Chapter 29 applies Donnellan's distinction to Lieutenant Traxler's 'the phone book killer has no pity,' true either of whoever fits the description or of the particular Terminator the speaker has in mind.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Ned Block
holes.what: Philosopher of mind whose 'blockhead' thought experiment shows a machine with pre-stored answers to every question could behave intelligently without understanding anything.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses blockhead, alongside Searle's Chinese room, to explain the T-101's read-only canned responses and the T-1000's empty 'I know this hurts' as behavior without mental life.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Ada Lovelace
holes.what: Nineteenth-century pioneer of computing who held that machines cannot independently learn or originate anything; the Lovelace Test credits a machine with intelligence only when its output cannot be explained by its designer.
holes.why: Chapter 30's key evidence that the learning-mode T-101 has a mental life is that it passes the Lovelace Test — Skynet cannot explain or predict its novel, resistance-defeating behavior.
holes.book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Johan Huizinga
holes.what: Cultural historian whose Homo Ludens argues that play — voluntary, rule-bound activity within bounded spaces outside ordinary life — generates law, ritual, poetry, and social order itself.
holes.why: Chapter 10 builds its entire account of vampire mainstreaming as 'playing human' on Huizinga's play theory (boundaries like thresholds, rules like 'she's mine', goals, and the spoilsport who shatters the play-world), with Roger Caillois expanding the framework.
holes.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

holes.name: Chandran Kukathas
holes.what: Liberal theorist of the 'liberal archipelago' who holds that the liberal state should tolerate even illiberal, authoritarian subcommunities so long as membership remains exitable and no physical coercion is used.
holes.why: Chapter 14 tests vampire mainstreaming against Kukathas's toleration-based liberalism as the most permissive standard the feudal vampire hierarchy could hope to meet, and concludes the magister's coercive system fails even that test.
holes.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: Theorist of mimetic desire and the scapegoat mechanism, who argues that communities avert escalating internal violence by uniting against an innocent victim and that sacrificial religion grew out of this process.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads Maryann's Bon Temps, the Fellowship of the Sun's recruitment, and Godric's self-sacrifice almost entirely through Girard's mimetic rivalry, scapegoating, and sacrificial-religion theory, against Sookie's 'God forgives' alternative.
holes.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: Sociologist who diagnosed modernity as the 'disenchantment of the world' — the replacement of magical, religious, and purposive explanations by rationalized science and impersonal causation.
holes.why: Chapter 25 opens with Weber's disenchantment thesis to frame Sookie's scientific-naturalist discomfort with Bill's undead 'magic', and the chapter's arc is her existential re-enchantment through the heart's reasons.
holes.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

holes.name: Four-Dimensionalism (temporal parts)
holes.what: Theodore Sider's metaphysics of persistence on which persons are four-dimensional wholes composed of temporal parts, so the successive stages of a life compose one individual rather than being strictly identical.
holes.why: Chapter 27 ends by invoking Sider's 'life as a long story' of temporal parts to explain how Bill, Jessica, Sam, and Alcide remain the same individuals through drastic supernatural transformations that defeat bodily, memory, and psychological-continuity criteria.
holes.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

holes.name: Mozi
holes.what: Warring States critic of Confucianism who taught jian ai — impartial 'universal love' extended equally to all — against the graded, family-first affections the Confucians cultivate.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses Mozi's universal love as the counterpoint to Confucian family priority, reading Godric's all-embracing 'forgiveness is love' as universal care that must nevertheless first be learned through filial love.
holes.book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

holes.name: Cosmic Horror (Lovecraftian weird fiction)
holes.what: A horror mode associated with H. P. Lovecraft and Thomas Ligotti in which dread comes from discovering humanity's insignificance before indifferent forces that defeat the fixed laws of nature.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads Carcosa, the Yellow King, and Rust's pessimism as cosmic horror, and faults the finale for deflating the genre into ordinary crime.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Rationalism vs Empiricism
holes.what: The early-modern debate over whether knowledge and truth derive from reason alone (Descartes) or from sense experience (Hume).
holes.why: Chapter 10 frames Rust's pessimism as rationalist observation and deduction against Marty's emotion-driven worldview, and uses this debate to test whether pessimism is philosophy or personal temperament.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: David Benatar
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose Better Never to Have Been argues, via an asymmetry between pleasure and pain, that coming into existence is always a harm.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Benatar's asymmetry argument to reconstruct and defend Rust's anti-natalism, which series creator Nic Pizzolatto acknowledged as a source for the character.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Anti-natalism
holes.what: The view that procreation is morally wrong because bringing a sentient being into existence necessarily harms it.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reconstructs Rust's 'walk hand in hand into extinction' as a Benatar-style anti-natalist argument and asks whether it morally compels everyone to stop reproducing.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Slavoj Zizek
holes.what: Slovenian philosopher and Lacanian psychoanalyst known for ideology critique, analyses of capitalism and violence, and popular-culture films such as The Pervert's Guide to Ideology.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is built almost entirely on Zizek's Violence: Six Sideways Reflections, reading Vinci and season two through his account of ideology and systemic violence.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Subjective and Objective Violence
holes.what: Zizek's distinction between visible subjective violence (crime, terror, assault) and invisible objective violence — symbolic (language, domination) and systemic (the catastrophic side-effects of economic and political systems).
holes.why: Chapter 14 applies this typology to Vinci's corruption, Frank Semyon's collapse, and the 'we get the world we deserve' motif, arguing the show's visible violence is a symptom of systemic capitalist violence.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Hans Kelsen
holes.what: Austrian legal theorist whose Pure Theory of Law treats law as an amoral coercive order validated by authority and sustained by sanctions, divorcing law from justice.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Kelsen's concepts of delict, sanction, and indirect motivation to interpret season two's competing legal orders, from Vinci's city hall to the cartel.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Legal Positivism (law without morality)
holes.what: The theory that the validity of law rests on its enactment by a recognized authority, not on its moral merits.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Vinci's corrupt police, city administration, and organized crime as Kelsenian coercive orders to show why the protagonists must seek justice outside the law.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Self-Model Theory (neuro-nihilism)
holes.what: Thomas Metzinger's claim that the brain generates a conscious self-model, so no selves exist — only self-models that cannot be recognized as models — which Evan Thompson calls 'neuro-nihilism' and counters with an enactive view of the self as process.
holes.why: Chapter 18 identifies Rust's 'everybody is nobody' monologue with Metzinger's position and argues against this neuro-nihilism in favor of transcendence through love.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: Narrative Identity
holes.what: The view (associated with Marya Schechtman) that personal identity is constituted by a person's self-narrated life story rather than by bodily or psychological continuity alone.
holes.why: Chapter 19 defends the narrative account as the only theory that explains how the three Rusts (Taxman, Belligerent, Patient) can be phases of one person.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: The Noir Detective (hard-boiled fiction)
holes.what: The hard-boiled/noir tradition of detective fiction in which an investigator embedded in a corrupt city is an agent of action and equilibrium rather than of truth and ideal justice.
holes.why: Chapters 24 and 25 define True Detective as urban noir, contrasting the genre's cynical city with Plato's philosophy of the city and reading Cohle as the return of the noir hero.
holes.book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Christian philosopher and author of The Four Loves, which distinguishes charity, affection, friendship, and Eros.
holes.why: Chapter 5's entire analysis of whether Corry truly loves the robot Alicia is built on Lewis's four loves and their qualities of gift-, need-, and appreciative-love.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: The Four Loves (gift-love, need-love, appreciative-love)
holes.what: Lewis's taxonomy of love into charity, affection, friendship, and Eros, each manifesting gift-love, need-love, and appreciative-love.
holes.why: Chapter 5 applies this framework criterion by criterion to decide whether Corry's bond with Alicia is true love.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Mimesis (art and music as imitation)
holes.what: The Platonic-Aristotelian view that music and art are mimetic signs that imitate and arouse emotions without words.
holes.why: Chapter 8 explains Twilight Zone dream music through Plato's mimetic signs (Sophist, Laws) and Aristotle's ethos, and taxonomy lacks any concept for mimesis or philosophy of music.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Relational Artifacts (sociable robots)
holes.what: Machines (Sherry Turkle's term) that display behaviors making people feel they deal with sentient creatures that care, raising ethical questions about robot caregivers and companions.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is framed by this concept (Turkle, the Sparrows, Coeckelbergh) to evaluate Alicia and the electric grandma as care robots.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Marc Auge
holes.what: French anthropologist who coined 'non-place' and 'supermodernity' for anonymous transit spaces of the modern world.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Twilight Zone roads, planes, hotels, and malls as Auge's non-places of anonymity and identity crisis.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Non-Place (anthropology of supermodernity)
holes.what: Auge's term for spaces of transit (airports, roads, hotels, malls) that confer no identity or belonging, only fleeting contractual relations.
holes.why: Chapter 13's central thesis is that the Zone's emptiest episodes are staged in non-places where identity is stripped away.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Paul Churchland
holes.what: Philosopher of mind and neuroscience who defends connectionism: cognition via neural-network prototypes rather than sentence-like representations.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Churchland's connectionism and prototype theory to explain why grasping a twist ending delivers a pleasurable burst of insight.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Umberto Eco
holes.what: Italian philosopher and semiotician whose essay 'Ur-Fascism' lists fear of difference among fascism's defining traits.
holes.why: Chapter 20 cites Eco's Ur-Fascism to explain the forced sameness of the Transformation society in 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You.'
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Guy Debord
holes.what: Situationist theorist of 'the society of the spectacle,' in which authentic social life is replaced by images and representation.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Black Mirror's Waldo and Fifteen Million Merits through Debord's spectacle, where politics and even rebellion become images.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: The Society of the Spectacle
holes.what: Debord's diagnosis that modern social relations are mediated by images, so that politics, dissent, and authenticity are absorbed into spectacle and commodity.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues the Waldo candidacy and the commodified glass-shard protest exemplify totalitarian power operating purely as spectacle.
holes.book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher whose concepts of cultural capital and habitus explain how class-positioned dispositions reproduce social inequality.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses Bourdieu's cultural capital to explain why Wallace converts school, sport, and white friendships into mobility while Weevil stays trapped in Neptune's racial binary.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Cultural Capital
holes.what: Bourdieu's idea that habits, speech, tastes, and credentials function as a currency convertible into social standing and success.
holes.why: Chapter 11 needs it to analyze how Logan's mockery of Weevil's grammar and Wallace's 'colorblind' assimilation operate as moves in Neptune's racial and class economy.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Philip Zimbardo
holes.what: Psychologist whose 1971 Stanford prison experiment argued that bad situations and systems, not just bad apples, lead ordinary people to commit evil.
holes.why: Chapter 13 reads Dr. Kinny's Hearst mock-prison as 'SPE lite' and frames Neptune's corruption through Zimbardo's situationism before turning to Arendt.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Femme Fatale (and the Homme Fatal)
holes.what: The seductive, morally dangerous figure of film noir who promises love or redemption but draws the protagonist toward doom; Veronica Mars gender-flips her into Logan as the homme fatal.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central claim is that the show transposes noir's gender roles, making Logan the fatal figure whose 'epic love' promise Veronica must refuse to keep her detective independence.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: The Pure Past and Involuntary Memory
holes.what: Deleuze's view that the past exists in its own dimension of reality, accessed through voluntary recollection and Proustian involuntary memories whose scenes carry meanings they never had when lived.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads the show's soft-focus flashbacks and the song-triggered memories of Lilly as dramatizations of Deleuze's ontology of time.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Vengeance and Revenge
holes.what: The personal infliction of payback for perceived wrongs, contrasted with impartial justice; philosophers dispute whether getting even is a rational, dignity-restoring practice or a vice.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is devoted to evaluating Veronica's payback code through Socrates, Seneca, Nietzsche's creditor-debtor account, and Machiavelli on being feared rather than loved.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Trust (vs Mere Reliance)
holes.what: Relying on someone because of their commitments, so that violation is betrayal rather than mere disappointment; distinguished from prediction-based reliance on objects or habits.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues Veronica, by second nature and vocation, cannot extend this attitude to anyone — not Keith, Logan, or even Piz — at the cost of 'revealing trust' in her closest bonds.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: The Will to Truth (and Its Value)
holes.what: Nietzsche's problem from Beyond Good and Evil and The Gay Science: why do we want truth rather than untruth, uncertainty, or ignorance, and is 'truth at any price' a metaphysical faith?
holes.why: Chapter 25 tests the value of truth through Geena Stafford's firing, Mac's devastation at her adoption, and Veronica shredding her paternity results.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Inductive Reasoning (particulars to general)
holes.what: Inference from observed particular cases to a general or probable conclusion, yielding likelihood rather than the certainty of deduction.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explains Veronica's casework — Koontz's confession, the Mercer evidence, the chlamydia clue — as induction graded by probability, with Occam's razor as its pruning tool.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Inference to the Best Explanation
holes.what: The form of induction (developed by Peter Lipton) that treats the hypothesis best explaining the known facts — by consilience, simplicity, and completeness — as probably true.
holes.why: Chapter 27 analyzes Veronica's juryroom 'magic trick' and bus-crash solution as inference to the best explanation and asks whether the practice can be justified without circularity.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher whose The World Viewed treats photography and film as automatisms satisfying the human wish to escape subjectivity and view the world 'from behind the self.'
holes.why: Chapter 29 reads Veronica's surveillance photography, voiceovers, and isolation almost entirely through Cavell's account of photography and subjectivity.
holes.book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)

holes.name: Functionalism (mental states as functional roles)
holes.what: The view that a mental state is defined by its causal role linking stimuli, other mental states, and behavior rather than by what a system is made of.
holes.why: Chapter 13 applies behaviorism and functionalism to walkers and refutes them with a walker-computer thought experiment adapted from Dennett, so a slug for the theory under test is needed.
holes.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

holes.name: The Paradox of Horror
holes.what: Noel Carroll's puzzle of why audiences voluntarily seek out horror fiction whose monsters are engineered to provoke the negative emotions of fear and disgust.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames the desire to win a zombie extra role as an amplified paradox of horror and tests Carroll's curiosity-based solution before offering its own clownish-identification answer.
holes.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

holes.name: Political Realism (power over morality)
holes.what: The theory that states exist to escape anarchy, that power rather than morality governs relations between them, and that security justifies otherwise immoral rule.
holes.why: Chapter 24 judges Rick's prison, Woodbury, and Alexandria entirely by Realist criteria drawn from Machiavelli, Weber, and Morgenthau, and no existing slug covers that framework.
holes.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

holes.name: Facticity
holes.what: The existentialist term for the given facts of one's situation and past, which are part of the self but whose value and power the free individual chooses.
holes.why: Chapter 26 has a dedicated section on facticity to explain Rick's claim that 'We became what we are': the group must own its past violence without letting it trap them, and neither denying nor being determined by the past is inauthentic.
holes.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

holes.name: Personhood Criteria (Warren's five criteria)
holes.what: Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, capacity to communicate, self-awareness) for deciding which beings count as persons with moral rights.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire case that walkers have no duties and hence no rights rests on checking walkers against Warren's personhood criteria, and the taxonomy has no personhood-criteria entry.
holes.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

holes.name: Antinatalism
holes.what: The view that procreation is morally wrong because non-existent children cannot suffer and cannot consent, while existing children (e.g. orphans available for adoption) have prior claims on parental care.
holes.why: Chapter 33's central argument is that Glenn and Maggie act immorally by trying to conceive at the prison and that couples in our world should adopt rather than create children, an antinatalist case the taxonomy cannot tag.
holes.book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

holes.name: Monopoly on Legitimate Violence
holes.what: Max Weber's thesis that a state is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
holes.why: Chapter 6's Keene Act essay evaluates whether Rorschach's and Veidt's vigilantism, or state-employed heroes' coercion, can ever be legitimate, and that whole argument is framed by this Weberian criterion, which taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test

holes.name: Philosophy of Art (Aesthetics)
holes.what: The branch of philosophy that asks what art (and here literature) is and how classificatory categories like 'novel' or 'hybrid art form' apply to borderline works.
holes.why: Chapter 10's opening essay tests rival definitions of literature (Beardsley, Eagleton, Lamarque/Olsen, Hirsch) to decide whether Watchmen counts as a novel, and taxonomy has no aesthetics or definition-of-art slug beyond Kant's judgment of taste.
holes.book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test

holes.name: Annette C. Baier
holes.what: A 20th-century moral philosopher known for the idea that persons are 'second persons first' — selfhood is acquired through dependence on and cross-examination by other persons — and for her analysis of selective attention and self-deception.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire argument is built on Baier's conjectures about second persons and the 'dangerous art of ignoring,' and no taxonomy philosopher covers her account of interpersonally constituted selfhood.
holes.book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist whose essay 'The Death of the Author' argued that a work's meaning is made by readers, not fixed by authorial intent.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is built centrally on Barthes's death-of-the-author thesis (and its application to Jordan's literal death and Sanderson's completion), and no existing taxonomy philosopher or concept covers authorship or the death of the author.
holes.book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom

holes.name: Supererogation (Saints and Heroes)
holes.what: Acts that are morally good and praiseworthy but beyond duty - neither obligatory nor forbidden.
holes.why: Chapter 14 defines heroism through Urmson's supererogation, contrasting Sullenberger's trained obligation with Autrey's subway rescue and Wonder Woman's voluntary, unowed mission to Man's World.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: Slavoj Zizek
holes.what: Slovenian Lacanian social theorist of ideology, cynical reason, and the symptom/fetish distinction with fetishistic disavowal.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire reading of Final Crisis and Earth One runs on Zizek's apparatus, concluding Wonder Woman is the comic industry's fetish that disavows its misogyny.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: Amatonormativity
holes.what: Elizabeth Brake's term for the assumption that a central, exclusive romantic relationship is a universal goal everyone should pursue above friendship.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues DC's New 52 Superman-Wonder Woman romance erases a valuable cross-gender friendship under precisely this amatonormative assumption.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: Bushido (the way of the warrior)
holes.what: The samurai honor code - honor, courage, justice, loyalty, honesty, politeness, self-control, benevolence - codified for Western readers by Inazo Nitobe.
holes.why: Chapter 22's title argument is that Wonder Woman uniquely reconciles bushido's warrior virtues with feminist care ethics, and no existing slug names the code itself.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: The Ticking Bomb Scenario
holes.what: Henry Shue's thought experiment in which torturing a terrorist is the only way to learn the location of an imminent bomb, testing whether torture is ever permissible.
holes.why: Chapter 23 builds its case for legalized 'just torture' on Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations as ticking-bomb cases (Shue, Luban, Dershowitz), a dilemma the trolley-problem slug does not cover.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: Monique Wittig
holes.what: French feminist novelist and theorist who framed heterosexuality as a political contract ('the straight mind') and imagined women's revolutionary war in Les Guerrieres.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is explicitly built on Wittig: Themyscira's Amazons become her Guerrieres waging social and linguistic revolution against the heterosexual contract.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: Philosophy of Lying and Deception
holes.what: The analysis of what lying is - roughly asserting what one believes false in order to mislead - and why it is wrong.
holes.why: Chapter 30's core claim that the magic lasso necessarily prevents lying rests on a theory of deception as attempted domination of the hearer.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: The Liar Paradox
holes.what: The self-referential sentence 'This sentence is false,' true if and only if it is false, exposing incoherence in our ordinary concept of truth.
holes.why: Chapter 32 derives its 'Paradox of the Golden Lasso' as a Liar variant and uses revenge liars to argue our concept of truth needs philosophical repair.
holes.book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique

holes.name: Descriptive vs. Prescriptive Normality
holes.what: The distinction between 'normal' as a neutral statistical description and 'normal' as a prescriptive standard that things ought to meet, tied to society's handling of the abnormal.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire analysis of who would want the mutant cure turns on whether 'normal' describes or prescribes, and no taxonomy slug covers that distinction or the normality/abnormality theme.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Knowledge Is Power (Baconian science)
holes.what: Francis Bacon's doctrine that genuine knowledge is practical knowledge of nature's hidden causal mechanisms, valued for the power it gives us to improve human life.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Layla Miller's 'I know stuff' entirely through Bacon's identification of knowledge with power, which no existing concept slug captures.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Jose Ortega y Gasset
holes.what: Spanish existentialist philosopher who held that humans must make their own existence 'at every single moment,' constrained only by the past (History as a System).
holes.why: Chapter 17 applies Ortega's 'project,' 'substantial emigrant,' and 'man is what has happened to him' to Rachel Summers, the Scarlet Witch, and Kitty Pryde.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Metafiction (postmodern self-reference)
holes.what: The postmodern technique of a work drawing attention to its own fictionality and production, making its audience aware of its role in constructing the narrative.
holes.why: Chapter 19 argues Deadpool's knowledge that he is a comic character uses metafiction to raise ontological questions, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for postmodernism or metafiction.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Michael Ruse
holes.what: Philosopher of biology who defends evolutionary ethics, arguing moral norms are adaptive instincts and that objective morality is a useful illusion.
holes.why: Chapter 21's central foil is the 'Ruse-Magneto view' that morality is an evolved illusion, tested against Moore's naturalistic fallacy and Jean Grey's sacrifice.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Evolutionary Ethics
holes.what: The view that moral norms are products of natural selection, adaptive instincts like sympathy, rather than objective truths that can be grounded in nature.
holes.why: Chapter 21 is organized around whether evolution can ground ethics, from Magneto's fitness-based morality to Ruse's morality-as-illusion and Dennett's rule worship.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Ronald Dworkin
holes.what: Political philosopher whose 'Civil Disobedience and Nuclear Protest' distinguishes policy-based, justice-based, and integrity-based grounds for resisting state policy.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds its X-Men-versus-Brotherhood analysis on Dworkin's three-tier account of when resistance to the Mutant Registration Act and the cure is morally permissible.
holes.book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse

holes.name: Doxastic Voluntarism (deciding to believe)
holes.what: The thesis that we can choose what to believe; Bernard Williams's 'Deciding to Believe' argues against it because beliefs aim at truth, so a self-chosen belief would not be a belief.
holes.why: Chapter 27's core argument is that an underconfident shooter cannot simply choose to believe her next shot will go in, which is precisely the rejection of doxastic voluntarism.
holes.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint

holes.name: The Hot Hand Fallacy (misperception of randomness)
holes.what: The claim (Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky) that shooting streaks are ordinary chance runs and that players and fans misperceive patterns in random sequences.
holes.why: Chapter 28's skeptics ground their denial of hot hands in this fallacy claim, and Hales's entire chapter is a philosophical rebuttal of it.
holes.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint

holes.name: Institutional Facts (The Construction of Social Reality)
holes.what: Searle's account of facts that exist only through collective acceptance ('X counts as Y in context C'), such as money, presidencies, and teams.
holes.why: Chapter 30 resolves the same-team puzzle by separating the player group from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only relative to what the fans think.
holes.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint

holes.name: Constitutive Rules (rules that create the game)
holes.what: Rules that do not merely regulate a pre-existing activity but create the activity and its facts (points, strikes, goals), so that such facts exist only inside the rule system.
holes.why: Chapter 32's dispute over whether a waved-off basket 'really' scored turns on scoring facts being created by the rules and officials' awards rather than independently recorded.
holes.book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint

holes.name: Philosophy of Play
holes.what: The view, developed by Huizinga and Diane Ackerman among others, that play is a free, self-contained, intrinsically valuable activity outside ordinary utility that is constitutive of being human.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is centrally about play as an end in itself (Huizinga's three criteria, 'true play') and no existing taxonomy concept names play as such rather than eudaimonia or meaning.
holes.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links

holes.name: Game-Playing as Voluntary Overcoming of Unnecessary Obstacles
holes.what: Bernard Suits's definition of game-playing as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles, distinguishing pre-lusory goals from the lusory attitude that accepts constitutive rules.
holes.why: Chapter 20's whole argument is built on Suits's account (internal vs. external goals mirror his pre-lusory/lusory distinction), and the taxonomy has no concept or philosopher for the philosophy of games/sport.
holes.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links

holes.name: Mysticism
holes.what: The doctrine and study of direct, ineffable, unitive transcendent experience, marked by noetic quality, loss of ego, and timelessness (William James, Russell).
holes.why: Chapter 25 is centrally about mysticism as a category—defining its criteria via James and Russell and asking why golf attracts mystical representation—and the taxonomy has no concept for mysticism itself, only adjacent slugs like zen and neoplatonism.
holes.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links

holes.name: Multiple Realizability
holes.what: The thesis (from philosophy of mind) that one functional kind can be realized by many different physical substrates, so no single physical form is privileged.
holes.why: Chapter 30's core argument is that the optimal golf swing is 'multiply realizable'—the authors name and lean on the philosophy-of-mind concept directly—and the taxonomy has no concept slug for multiple realizability.
holes.book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links

holes.name: Constrained Maximization (constraint theory)
holes.what: Jon Elster's theory (from Ulysses and the Sirens) that self-imposed constraints, like Odysseus lashed to the mast, can enable and maximize otherwise impossible rational action.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire analysis of why Olympic boxing's constitutive rules succeed or fail is built on Elster's constrained maximization, and no taxonomy philosopher or concept captures it.
holes.book: 212 - The Olympics and Philosophy

holes.name: Playful World-Traveling and Loving Perception
holes.what: Maria Lugones's feminist idea that oppressed people resist injustice by playfully 'traveling' into others' worlds and adopting a loving, non-arrogant perception that sees them as fellow subjects.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire analysis of how Billie Jean King beat Riggs and later loved him is built on Lugones's world-traveling and loving perception, and no taxonomy philosopher or concept captures Lugones.
holes.book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: 18th-century philosopher whose Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and the Beautiful founded the aesthetic distinction between the terror-inducing sublime and the pleasure-giving beautiful.
holes.why: Chapters 9 and 12 build their whole reading of landscape and of Marianne's romantic sensibility on Burke's sublime/beautiful, which is the load-bearing philosophy rather than Kant's, yet Burke has no taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee

holes.name: The Sublime and the Beautiful
holes.what: Burke's paired aesthetic categories (the sublime as awe/terror, the beautiful as pleasing order), extended by Gilpin into the picturesque.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies this specific Burkean/Gilpin distinction to garden design and to the yin/yang of landscape; the only near slug, kant-aesthetics, ties the sublime to Kant, whom the chapter explicitly contrasts against Burke.
holes.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee

holes.name: Fang Dongmei (Thomé H. Fang)
holes.what: Twentieth-century Taiwanese neo-Confucian philosopher who synthesized Confucianism, Daoism and Whiteheadian/Bergsonian process thought into a metaphysics of 'comprehensive harmony' and 'creative creativity'.
holes.why: Chapter 15 leans heavily on Fang Dongmei's 'creative creativity' and comprehensive-harmony scheme to explain Wong Chia Chi's moral development, and no taxonomy philosopher covers this figure.
holes.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee

holes.name: Arnold Berleant
holes.what: Contemporary American aesthetician who founded environmental aesthetics on engaged, participatory sensory 'aisthesis', rejecting the disengaged-observer paradigm of fine-art appreciation.
holes.why: Chapter 15's whole first movement applies Berleant's engaged environmental aesthetics to Wong's shift from sight-only performer to whole-body participant, and the taxonomy has no philosopher or concept for it.
holes.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee

holes.name: Pacifism (universal / antiwar pacifism)
holes.what: The ethical position, with variants from universal (all violence is destructive) to antiwar pacifism (self-defense permitted, war not), that violence should be renounced as a path to redemption.
holes.why: Chapter 19's core thesis classifies Hulk and Taking Woodstock as Lackey's 'universal pacifism' and argues nonviolence is the only redemption; the taxonomy has ahimsa and just-war-theory but no general pacifism concept.
holes.book: 214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee

holes.name: Hélène Cixous
holes.what: French feminist philosopher whose 'The Laugh of the Medusa' theorizes 'écriture féminine,' women writing through the body.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire theoretical framework is Cixous's écriture féminine applied to di Prima; the taxonomy has no distinct slug for her or that concept.
holes.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view (after N. Katherine Hayles) that subjectivity extends beyond the bounded body into technologized environments via information feedback loops.
holes.why: Chapter 13's argument turns on Burroughs's subject 'transmigrating' into Hayles's posthuman; no existing concept slug captures posthuman/extended subjectivity distinctly.
holes.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats

holes.name: Postcolonialism / Orientalism
holes.what: The critical analysis of colonial power, Orientalist representation, and subaltern voice associated with Said, Spivak, and Bhabha.
holes.why: Chapter 15 frames Beat multiculturalism explicitly through Said's Orientalism, Spivak's subaltern, and Bhabha; the taxonomy has cosmopolitanism but no postcolonial/orientalism concept.
holes.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian literary theorist of dialogism, heteroglossia, and the carnivalesque.
holes.why: Chapter 19 reads Whitehead's film through Bakhtin's dialogic and carnivalesque alongside Deleuze; Bakhtin and those concepts have no taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats

holes.name: Murray Bookchin
holes.what: American libertarian-socialist thinker who founded social ecology, arguing ecological domination is rooted in social hierarchy.
holes.why: Chapter 26 stages Snyder between deep ecology and Bookchin's social ecology, quoting Bookchin's polemics at length, but the taxonomy has no Bookchin slug.
holes.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats

holes.name: Social Ecology
holes.what: The view that the ecological crisis stems from social hierarchy and domination among humans, so its solution must be social.
holes.why: The chapter's central axis is deep ecology vs. social ecology; 'deep-ecology' exists in the taxonomy but there is no matching slug for social ecology.
holes.book: 215 - The Philosophy of the Beats

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher of film, moral perfectionism, and the Hollywood comedy of remarriage, heir to Emerson and Wittgenstein.
holes.why: Chapters 15 and 16 (and the Introduction) are built on Cavell's moral perfectionism and his remarriage-comedy genre, which no existing taxonomy philosopher covers.
holes.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

holes.name: The Comedy of Remarriage
holes.what: Cavell's film genre in which an estranged couple journeys back together through conversation, self-transformation, and a 'green world' retreat.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind entirely as an instance and innovation of this specific genre, which has no taxonomy concept.
holes.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

holes.name: Fabulation (the writer as fabulator)
holes.what: Deleuze's notion of literature that invents rather than represents, opening onto the endless conditions of its own creation and confronting readers with the text as invention.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central claim about Adaptation — that Kaufman writes as a Deleuzian fabulator making something from nothing rather than imitating reality — has no matching taxonomy concept (rhizome does not fit).
holes.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

holes.name: Auteur Theory (and film authorship)
holes.what: Truffaut/Bazin debate over whether a film's director is its preeminent author, versus screenwriter-centered 'schreiber' accounts of film authorship.
holes.why: Chapter 13 turns on the auteur-vs-screenwriter dispute (Kaufman vs Clooney) to ask who authored Confessions of a Dangerous Mind, a film-authorship concept absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher known for work on film ontology, skepticism, and the acknowledgment of others.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its central argument on Cavell's claim that 'film is a moving image of skepticism' and his ontology of the moving image, but no matching philosopher slug exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

holes.name: Walker Percy
holes.what: American novelist and philosophical essayist who analyzed the self's placement in the world via immanence and transcendence in Lost in the Cosmos.
holes.why: Chapter 22 sets Percy's account of immanence/transcendence as the direct foil to Sartre and uses it to interpret every main character, but the taxonomy has no slug for Percy or his transcendence/immanence framework.
holes.book: 216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: 20th-century French theorist of mimetic (triangular) desire and the scapegoat mechanism, whose Deceit, Desire, and the Novel argues desire is copied from a mediating rival rather than spontaneous.
holes.why: Chapter 12 makes Girard's 'triangular desire' and the absent 'external mediating authority' the explicit engine of how Ray, Marty, and Visser go 'simple,' and no taxonomy philosopher or concept covers mimetic desire.
holes.book: 218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic experience of a greatness or power that exceeds the mind's capacity to measure or comprehend, provoking awe mixed with fear.
holes.why: Chapter 24 makes Kant's Sublime—the power behind BOB, the bomb, and garmonbozia that overwhelms reason—its central category, and chapter 17's treatment of the atomic-bomb sequence also leans on it; the taxonomy has kant-aesthetics (taste/judgment) but no dedicated Sublime slug.
holes.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch

holes.name: Romanticism
holes.what: The intellectual and artistic movement prizing wonder, imagination, perpetual becoming, and the artist's inner vision over rule-bound imitation and Enlightenment rationalism.
holes.why: Chapters 21 and 24 build their central arguments on Romanticism as a doctrine (Novalis, Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism, the mad poet, the Romantic hero), but the taxonomy has no concept slug for the movement itself, only individual figures and adjacent ideas.
holes.book: 220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: The loss of all objective value and meaning that follows the collapse of a binding moral framework such as Judeo-Christian religion.
holes.why: Chapter 17's central thesis is that Pulp Fiction is 'about American nihilism'; the taxonomy has 'death-of-god' but no slug for nihilism itself as the resulting condition.
holes.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir

holes.name: Tragedy and Catharsis
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics account of tragedy as a mimetic drama arousing pity and terror to effect a catharsis of those emotions.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire argument turns on whether films noirs meet Aristotle's formal criteria for tragedy and catharsis, and the taxonomy has no concept slug for tragedy, catharsis, or mimesis.
holes.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir

holes.name: Reinhold Niebuhr
holes.what: American Protestant theologian of Christian realism, author of Moral Man and Immoral Society and The Irony of American History.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Niebuhr's writings on original sin, the coercive role of force, and 'man's strength and weakness' as its primary interpretive lens for The Accused, but he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir

holes.name: Erich Fromm
holes.what: Frankfurt-school social psychologist and humanist, author of The Art of Loving and The Sane Society.
holes.why: Chapter 21 leans on Fromm's account of separateness as the source of anxiety and love as a 'decision' to explain Wilma's redemptive coupling, but the taxonomy lists no Fromm slug.
holes.book: 221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir

holes.name: Abjection (Powers of Horror)
holes.what: Kristeva's account of the abject, the jettisoned in-between that is neither subject nor object and threatens the boundaries of the clean, proper self.
holes.why: Chapter 7 builds gynaehorror directly on Kristeva's abjection (via Creed's monstrous-feminine) to explain the horror of the boundary-breaching reproductive body, but no philosopher or concept for it exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: The Monstrous-Feminine
holes.what: Barbara Creed's feminist-psychoanalytic figure of the gendered female monster (witch, monstrous womb, castrating femme castratrice) whose horror is bound to reproductive femininity.
holes.why: Creed's monstrous-feminine is the direct theoretical parent of the book's whole 'gynaehorror' concept in chapter 7, yet neither Creed nor this concept appears in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French post-structuralist feminist philosopher who argues woman is denied subjectivity and made the mirror/Other that props up the male subject and the masculine divine.
holes.why: Chapter 8's core reading of virginity (the virgin's exchange-value, the speculum, 'this sex which is not one') is built on Irigaray's Speculum of the Other Woman, but she is absent from the taxonomy's philosophers.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Compulsory Heterosexuality
holes.what: Adrienne Rich's thesis that heterosexuality is not innate but a socially and politically enforced institution that renders lesbian existence deviant or invisible.
holes.why: Chapter 8 closes its argument about heteronormative horror explicitly on Rich's compulsory heterosexuality and Wittig's heterosexual contract, and neither the concept nor these philosophers are in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Psychoanalytic feminist theorist of abjection, the maternal body, and the semiotic, whose Powers of Horror theorises birth as violent expulsion from maternal matter.
holes.why: Chapter 9 leans on Kristeva's Powers of Horror to analyse the pregnant/maternal abject body alongside Bakhtin's grotesque, but Kristeva is not among the taxonomy's philosophers.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist of technoscience whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' proposes the cyborg as a post-gender, boundary-confusing hybrid of organism and machine.
holes.why: Chapter 10's whole final argument about cyborg futures and reproductive technohorror is structured around Haraway's cyborg (and Braidotti's response to it), yet Haraway is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Rosi Braidotti
holes.what: Feminist philosopher of nomadic/posthuman subjectivity and materialist 'becoming' who links Haraway's cyborg to Deleuze's rhizome via sexual difference.
holes.why: Chapter 10 resolves its argument through Braidotti's metal-morphoses and embodied becoming as the productive alternative to erasing the female body, but Braidotti is not in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Abjection
holes.what: Kristeva's concept (from Powers of Horror) of the horror provoked by what must be expelled to maintain the clean and proper body and self, especially the maternal body.
holes.why: Chapter 11 grounds the monstrous-maternal partly in Kristeva's maternal-as-abject, and the taxonomy has no abjection concept and no Kristeva.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: The Monstrous-Feminine
holes.what: Barbara Creed's psychoanalytic-feminist account of how horror cinema constructs woman's sexual and reproductive difference as monstrous (womb, femme castratrice, archaic mother).
holes.why: Chapter 11's 'monstrous-maternal' is explicitly built as a revision of Creed's monstrous-feminine, which the taxonomy lacks entirely.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: The Abject Barren Body
holes.what: The author's framework linking menstruating, menopausal and post-menopausal female bodies as a non-reproductive yet generative modality that is culturally excluded and abjected.
holes.why: Chapter 12 is organised entirely around this coined concept of barren/menopausal abjection, for which the taxonomy offers no adequate slug.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: French psychoanalytic theorist whose Powers of Horror develops abjection, the semiotic, and the abject maternal body.
holes.why: Chapters 11 and 12 both rely substantively on Kristeva's abjection, but she is absent from the taxonomy's philosopher list.
holes.book: 222 - The Philosophy of Horror

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: Marxist literary and cultural theorist who analyzed postmodernism as the cultural logic of late capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire reading of The Shining is built on Jameson's account of the depthless postmodern present, pastiche, and the nostalgia film, and no taxonomy philosopher covers him.
holes.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams

holes.name: Pastiche and the Nostalgia Film
holes.what: Jameson's idea that late-capitalist art, lacking a living present, produces blank imitation of past styles, exemplified by the nostalgia film.
holes.why: Chapter 23 turns on this specific postmodern mechanism to explain The Shining's anti-nostalgia; the nearest taxonomy slug, simulacra, names a related but distinct Baudrillardian idea.
holes.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams

holes.name: Posthumanism and the Technological Singularity
holes.what: The idea, developed by Kurzweil and Moravec, that accelerating AI will produce superintelligent 'mind children' and transcend biological humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 27's whole forward-looking argument rests on Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's mind children as the real route to Kubrick's Star Child, which no existing taxonomy concept captures.
holes.book: 223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams

holes.name: Religious Non-Realism
holes.what: Hick's view that religious beliefs, myths, and rituals remain deeply significant and transformative even if the transcendent realities they posit do not exist—religion's value lies in its ethical and spiritual function rather than doctrinal truth.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire unifying reading of Shepherd Book, the Jaynestown statue, and 'Amends' turns on Hick's religious realism vs non-realism distinction, which no existing slug (e.g., religious-pluralism) captures.
holes.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon

holes.name: Robert Kane
holes.what: Contemporary libertarian on free will who locates genuinely free, morally responsible action in undetermined 'self-forming choices' made in moments of torn inner conflict.
holes.why: Chapter 10's resolution of the Whedonverse's paradoxical free-will portrayals rests entirely on Kane's libertarianism, and no existing slug covers libertarian free will or its leading defender.
holes.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon

holes.name: Stephen Mulhall
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose 'bold thesis' in On Film holds that some fictional narrative films are themselves philosophical exercises—'film as philosophizing' rather than mere illustration of philosophers' arguments.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is organized around Mulhall's bold thesis, Baggini's critique of it, and Mulhall's rejoinders, with Whedon's Angel as the confirming instance.
holes.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon

holes.name: Thomas E. Wartenberg
holes.what: Philosopher of film and author of Thinking on Screen, whose defense of film-as-philosophy rests on cinematic thought experiments and the counterexample/counterargument distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 12 is built around his debate with Bruce Russell — his imposition, explicitness, and generality objections taxonomy and his Matrix and Eternal Sunshine analyses structure the entire chapter and the book's later methodology.
holes.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon

holes.name: Bruce Russell
holes.what: Analytic philosopher who argues fictional narrative films can raise philosophical questions and provide counterexamples but cannot themselves present philosophically significant arguments.
holes.why: Chapter 12 is the record of his exchange with Wartenberg; his strictures on implicit argument and epistemic endorsement define the standard the book's Whedonverse readings must meet.
holes.book: 224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon

holes.name: Ludwig von Mises
holes.what: Austrian-school economist and libertarian social philosopher who theorized the entrepreneur as risk-bearing speculator and defended free markets against socialism.
holes.why: Chapter 19 builds its whole libertarian reading of The Aviator on Mises's Human Action account of the entrepreneur versus the manager, which no taxonomy philosopher covers (Adam Smith is used only for the invisible hand).
holes.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese

holes.name: The Entrepreneur (risk-bearing and market discovery)
holes.what: The libertarian/Austrian idea that the true entrepreneur profits by risking his own capital on an anticipation of future demand, a function distinct from mere management.
holes.why: The chapter's central applied concept—Hughes as visionary entrepreneur risking 'his own money'—has no taxonomy concept; invisible-hand captures only part of the argument.
holes.book: 225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese

holes.name: The Uncanny (das Unheimliche)
holes.what: Freud's account of the uncanny as a species of the familiar, rooted in repressed infantile fears (death, castration) and expressed through doubles and repetition.
holes.why: Chapter 18 builds its central reading of Chinatown's 'specific alienation' on Freud's essay on the uncanny and doppelgangers, which no existing Freud concept slug (unconscious, death-drive, civilization) captures.
holes.book: 227 - The Philosophy of Neo-Noir

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: American Marxist literary and cultural critic known for 'Reification and Utopia in Mass Culture,' postmodernism as the cultural logic of late capitalism, and reading mass-culture texts for their allegorical and utopian impulses.
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire reading of Ocean's Eleven is built on Jameson's concepts (the utopian figure of collectivity, the polysemous Jaws-shark, allegory/utopia, late capital), and no taxonomy philosopher captures this specific cultural-Marxist apparatus.
holes.book: 232 - The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: Nineteenth-century French political thinker whose Democracy in America analyzed American self-government, the citizens' 'art of association,' and the risk of a centralizing 'soft despotism.'
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument reads Mars Attacks! through Tocqueville's Democracy in America—the self-organizing power of ordinary Americans versus reliance on the federal government—and the taxonomy has no Tocqueville slug and no adequate substitute.
holes.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: 18th-century thinker whose 'Philosophical Enquiry' theorizes the sublime as awe born of terror-at-a-distance, opposed to beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire argument about 'Sweeney Todd' is built on Burke's aesthetics of the sublime, and no philosopher slug for Burke exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic experience of overwhelming awe blending pain, terror, and delight, set in opposition to beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 17 applies the sublime (and its tension with beauty) to Burton's urban 'Sweeney Todd' throughout, and the taxonomy has no concept slug for the sublime.
holes.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton

holes.name: The Fantastic (Todorov)
holes.what: Todorov's category naming the reader/viewer's sustained hesitation between a natural and a supernatural explanation, bordered by 'the uncanny' and 'the marvelous.'
holes.why: Chapter 18's reading of the Burton-Depp films rests entirely on Todorov's fantastic/uncanny/marvelous scheme, which the taxonomy lacks (Freud's uncanny slug is a different, psychoanalytic concept).
holes.book: 234 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton

holes.name: Paul Virilio
holes.what: French theorist of speed, technology and vision whose War and Cinema argues war is a 'logistics of perception' fusing the camera and the weapon.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire thesis about surveillance, eyeless vision and the fusion of sighting and triggering is built on Virilio, who has no philosopher slug in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films

holes.name: Societies of Control
holes.what: Deleuze's account of power in postmodernity as continuous, networked, short-term control mechanisms that supersede Foucault's enclosed disciplinary spaces.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues explicitly that war-surveillance film moves 'beyond panopticism' into Deleuzian control societies, a distinct concept the taxonomy lacks (it lists deleuze only with 'rhizome').
holes.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films

holes.name: Biopolitical Labor
holes.what: Hardt and Negri's term for hegemonic postmodern service work that produces knowledge, signs, affects and social relations rather than material commodities.
holes.why: Chapter 11's central analytic frame—the soldier/watcher as exploited biopolitical laborer against the fixed capital of surveillance—rests on this concept, which is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films

holes.name: Aspect Perception (seeing-as)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's concept from Philosophical Investigations II.xi of seeing one thing as another (the duck-rabbit), and the ethical articulation of experience it can involve.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument turns on aspect perception / 'seeing as' as an interpretive and ethical concept, which the taxonomy's Wittgenstein concepts (language-games, private-language) do not capture.
holes.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films

holes.name: Privileged Access (the perceptual model of self-knowledge)
holes.what: The view that a subject has direct, asymmetric introspective access to private inner mental states unavailable to others, modeling self-knowledge on inner perception.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central philosophical target is the 'privileged access' / perceptual model of self-knowledge that Apocalypse Now is read as dismantling, and no taxonomy concept names this doctrine of self-knowledge.
holes.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films

holes.name: Grievability / Frames of War
holes.what: Judith Butler's idea that normative frames determine whose lives are recognized as grievable and whose deaths are rendered ungrievable and thus outside the field of moral concern.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explicitly builds its critique of the 'ubiquitously absent enemy' on Butler's frames of war and ungrievable lives, and the taxonomy has no Butler concept beyond gender-performativity/heteronormativity.
holes.book: 236 - The Philosophy of War Films

holes.name: Spontaneous Order (kosmos vs taxis)
holes.what: Friedrich Hayek's idea that complex social orders (language, markets, custom) can be grown and self-generating rather than the product of deliberate design.
holes.why: Chapter 14's core argument distinguishes the farming villages' spontaneously evolved 'grown order' from the 'made order' of a battle plan, a Hayekian concept with no matching philosopher or concept slug in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western

holes.name: Tzvetan Todorov
holes.what: A structuralist literary theorist and philosopher whose The Conquest of America analyzes the self's encounter with the cultural Other, criticizing both the assimilation of difference and its translation into hierarchy.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire analytic frame is Todorov's typology of alterity (equality vs. difference, Columbus, Las Casas, Sepulveda), and no taxonomy philosopher supplies this theory of the Other.
holes.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western

holes.name: Alterity and the Encounter with the Other
holes.what: The problem of representing the cultural Other as simultaneously equal and different, rather than either assimilating it to the self or ranking it as inferior.
holes.why: The chapter argues that western films' Native Americans are egocentric projections that fail Todorov's demand to grant the Other both equality and difference; the taxonomy's 'levinas-face' concerns ethical obligation, not this representational politics of alterity.
holes.book: 237 - The Philosophy of the Western

holes.name: Cinematic Realism
holes.what: The aesthetic theory of what makes a film realistic—disguised representation, fidelity to reality, and the illusion that grounds emotional response—as developed by Bazin, Perkins, and Goodman.
holes.why: Chapter 21 is entirely about defining and defending cinematic realism as a philosophy-of-art thesis, and no existing taxonomy concept captures film/representational realism.
holes.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book

holes.name: Middle Knowledge (Molinism)
holes.what: Molina's doctrine that God (or any knower) can know the conditional future—what a free agent would freely choose in any fully specified circumstance—prior to and independent of that agent's actual choice.
holes.why: Chapter 23's central move is recasting the precogs' power as Molinist knowledge of the conditional future, and neither Molina nor middle knowledge exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book

holes.name: Luis de Molina
holes.what: 16th-century Spanish Jesuit whose Concordia (1588) introduced middle knowledge to reconcile divine providence and foreknowledge with human free will.
holes.why: Molina is the named philosophical anchor of chapter 23 ('Minority Report, Molinism...') and is used substantively, but he is absent from the taxonomy's philosopher list.
holes.book: 238 - Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book

holes.name: Aletheia (Truth as Unconcealment)
holes.what: Heidegger's conception of truth as a-letheia, an event of un-concealment or disclosure that precedes and grounds the correspondence theory of truth.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire argument turns on Heidegger's aletheia as the philosophical key to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and no taxonomy concept names truth-as-unconcealment (the existing Heidegger concepts cover authenticity, technology, das Man, being-toward-death, thrownness, Dasein, not aletheia).
holes.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog

holes.name: Siegfried Kracauer
holes.what: Weimar-era film theorist and Frankfurt-School-adjacent critic whose Theory of Film argues cinema 'redeems physical reality' by revealing the marvels of everyday life.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is a sustained Kracauerian reading of Herzog built almost entirely on Kracauer's film theory, but Kracauer appears nowhere in the taxonomy's philosopher list.
holes.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Co-founder of the Frankfurt School whose Eclipse of Reason and (with Adorno) Dialectic of Enlightenment critique instrumental reason, the concept of the 'fact,' and the administered world.
holes.why: Chapter 17 develops its critique of factual truth jointly through Horkheimer and Adorno, quoting Horkheimer extensively, yet only Adorno (and not Horkheimer) exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog

holes.name: Masculinism (glorification of manliness)
holes.what: The exaltation and promotion of traits traditionally subsumed under 'manliness' (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as heroic ideals, distinct from men's-rights masculism.
holes.why: Chapter 18's thesis is explicitly that Herzog holds a 'philosophy of masculinism,' and the taxonomy's gender concepts (gender-performativity, objectification, male-gaze, five-faces-oppression) name critiques of gendered power but not the affirmative glorification of masculinity the chapter analyzes.
holes.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog

holes.name: Kierkegaard on the Tragic (ancient vs. modern) and the Comic
holes.what: The aesthete 'A''s theory in Either/Or that tragedy requires an ambiguity between freedom/guilt and fate/suffering, and that a modern age of pure subjectivity collapses the tragic into the comic.
holes.why: Chapter 19's 'post-tragic aesthetic' rests specifically on Kierkegaard's theory of tragedy and the comic, which no existing Kierkegaard concept (leap-of-faith, stages, despair, anxiety, teleological suspension, subjective truth) captures.
holes.book: 239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog

holes.name: R.G. Collingwood
holes.what: Early 20th-century British idealist philosopher of art who distinguished genuine art (expression of emotion) from craft (producing a preconceived result).
holes.why: Chapter 10 leans heavily on Collingwood's art/craft distinction to explain why Crazy Horse's raw expression counts as art rather than crafted entertainment, and no taxonomy philosopher covers his aesthetics of expression.
holes.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy

holes.name: Sarah Lucia Hoagland
holes.what: Lesbian feminist philosopher whose Lesbian Ethics analyzes 'heterosexualism' as the structured balance of masculine predation and protection that de-skills and subordinates women.
holes.why: Chapter 17's entire analysis of Young's portrayal of women is built on Hoagland's concept of heterosexualism and femininity-as-subordination, which no existing taxonomy philosopher or concept adequately captures.
holes.book: 240 - Neil Young and Philosophy

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher of ordinary language, aesthetics and the ontology of film (The World Viewed), who held that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' presenting 'a world past.'
holes.why: Rothman's entire reading of Rouch's cine-trance rests on Cavell's ontology of film (the 'skin of the world,' the photographic object as subject), and Cavell is also the governing philosopher of chapters 12 and 15, yet no taxonomy slug names him.
holes.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film

holes.name: Aspect Perception (seeing-as)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's account of 'seeing-as' and the 'dawning of an aspect' (the duck-rabbit), in which perception is inseparably inflected by imagination, concepts and memory.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire argument that documentary portraiture is truthful turns on aspect-perception specifically, which is distinct from the existing 'language-games' slug and has no dedicated slug.
holes.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film

holes.name: The Film of Presumptive Assertion
holes.what: Noel Carroll's criterion that documentary is defined by the maker's categorical/assertoric intention that the film be taken as asserting something true about the actual world.
holes.why: Chapter 34 (and the volume's recurring frame) depends on this specific concept to explain why a hoax like I'm Still Here betrays documentary expectations; no taxonomy slug names it.
holes.book: 241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film

holes.name: Purity of Heart (willing one thing)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's ideal, from 'Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing,' of a will unified in the Good, with harmony and consistency across one's desires, choices, and actions, free of double-mindedness.
holes.why: Chapter 6's subtitle is 'the Struggle for Purity of Heart' and it reads Will Dormer's sleepless moral battle in Insomnia as exactly this Kierkegaardian fight against double-mindedness, with Finch embodying the adaptable double will.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Leo Strauss
holes.what: Twentieth-century political philosopher whose critique of liberalism warns that rights-based value pluralism decays into nihilistic relativism, while egalitarian revolutionary movements curdle into tyranny, and who read political order as founded on the friend-enemy distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 8 quotes Strauss's summary of Schmitt at length and structures its whole analysis of the Joker (nihilistic chaos) and Bane (coercive equality) around his two dangers of liberalism.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Rationalization and the Iron Cage (disenchantment)
holes.what: Weber's thesis that modern Western culture is dominated by instrumental, cost-benefit rationality which disenchants the world and locks it in an 'iron cage' of efficient, self-imposed institutions, producing 'specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart.'
holes.why: Chapter 9's central allegory reads Tesla's duplication machine and the magicians' economy of sacrifice as an embodiment of Weber's iron cage, but the taxonomy has no concept slug for rationalization, disenchantment, or the iron cage.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Fabula and Syuzhet (story vs. discourse)
holes.what: The Russian Formalist narratological distinction between the chronological order of the events narrated (fabula) and the order in which the narrative presents them (syuzhet).
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire analysis of Doodlebug, Following, Memento, and The Prestige rests on this distinction between story chronology and narrative presentation, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Plato's Critique of Writing (Phaedrus)
