holes.what: Socrates' tale of the god Theuth offering writing to King Thamus as a potion for memory, which Thamus rebrands a potion for reminding that breeds forgetfulness and only the appearance of wisdom.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses the Phaedrus critique of written signs to explain why Leonard's tattooed list of 'facts' gives him the illusion of knowledge while deceiving him.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Intellectual Virtues (virtue epistemology)
holes.what: Virtue epistemology treats believing well - attention to evidence, humility, trust, creativity - as valuable in ways that do not require one's beliefs to be true.
holes.why: Chapter 14's answer to what the dream thieves should believe rests on Zagzebski's and Kornblith's intellectual virtues: one can believe well even when the dream argument blocks believing truly.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: The Gaze and Objet a (Seminar XI)
holes.what: Lacan's account of the gaze as the point in the visual field from which the subject is looked at, producing a lack of mastery, with the objet a as the object-cause of desire.
holes.why: Chapter 18 reads Following's voyeurism and film spectatorship entirely through Lacan's gaze and objet a - the follower becoming the followed, the voyeur becoming the viewed.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Substance as Subject (absolute knowing)
holes.what: Hegel's thesis that what we take to be independent, self-subsistent substance is actually self-divided subjectivity, recognized in absolute knowing, which also frees the subject's act to work retroactively on the past.
holes.why: Chapter 19's central claim is that Interstellar stages this Hegelian doctrine - the alien 'they' revealed as future humanity - and no existing Hegel slug (dialectic, Geist, recognition) covers substance-as-subject or absolute knowing.
holes.book: 243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

holes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
holes.what: Nineteenth-century Russian novelist-philosopher of faith, free will, and moral responsibility to one's fellow man, especially in The Karamazov Brothers.
holes.why: Chapter 11 is built almost entirely on Dostoevsky's The Karamazov Brothers and Father Zossima's ethic of universal brotherly responsibility, with no adequate taxonomy philosopher covering him.
holes.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Comparative mythologist who formulated the monomyth or Hero's Journey in The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
holes.why: Chapter 12 applies Campbell's Hero's Journey / monomyth as its central structuring framework for the Winchesters' quest, and no taxonomy slug captures the monomyth (Jung's archetypes only partly overlap).
holes.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business

holes.name: The Monomyth (Hero's Journey)
holes.what: Campbell's cross-cultural narrative pattern in which a hero departs, is initiated through trials and a descent, and returns transformed.
holes.why: The chapter's core analysis maps Sam and Dean stage-by-stage onto the Hero's Journey (call to adventure, quest, descent, reward), which no existing concept slug represents.
holes.book: 247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business

holes.name: Praxis vs Poiesis (Aristotle)
holes.what: Aristotle's distinction between praxis (self-directed, autotelic action done for its own sake) and poiesis (production aimed at an external product), later read existentially by Heidegger and politically by Arendt.
holes.why: Chapter 13's whole argument defines punk as praxis and post-punk as a slide back into poiesis, and no existing taxonomy slug (e.g. practical wisdom or virtue ethics) captures this distinction.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Strong vs Weak Nihilism (Black Nihilism)
holes.what: The distinction (developed in analyses of Black nihilism) between weak nihilism, which denies the value of valuing altogether after traditional values collapse, and strong nihilism, which destroys decadent values in order to create new ones.
holes.why: Chapter 15's central claim that mature punk is strong nihilism - value-creation for a world of others' freedom - depends entirely on this weak/strong distinction, which the generic nihilism slug does not capture.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: The Three Metamorphoses of the Spirit (camel, lion, child)
holes.what: Nietzsche's schema in Thus Spoke Zarathustra of the spirit's transformations: the camel bears inherited 'thou shalt' values, the lion destroys them, and the child creates new values with a sacred Yes.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire reading of early punk as a hybrid 'Dionysian lion-child' is built on the camel-lion-child metamorphoses, and no existing Nietzsche slug (will to power, Übermensch) captures that schema.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Václav Havel
holes.what: Czech dissident playwright and later president whose political essays (especially 'The Power of the Powerless') analyze totalitarian ideology as ritual detached from reality and advocate 'living in truth' through parallel structures and civil society.
holes.why: Chapter 27 builds its account of punk political philosophy directly on Havel's writings - ideology as ritual, living in truth, the second culture - and narrates his route from the Plastic People's trial to Charter 77 and the Velvet Revolution.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: The Politics of Disaffection
holes.what: The thesis that a counterculture's politics is unified not by a positive ideological program but by shared alienation and negative affect (disaffection) toward prevailing norms, expectations, and power structures.
holes.why: Chapter 28 proposes this as the common denominator uniting anarchist, fascist, and apolitical punks after rejecting anti-authoritarianism, nihilism, individualism, and the politics of boredom, and no existing slug names it.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Self-Deception
holes.what: The paradoxical condition of being both the deceiver and the deceived, holding a false belief one is motivated not to recognize as false, via attention management, procrastination, perspective shifting, or rationalization.
holes.why: Chapter 20 is built entirely around self-deception as a distinct problem (Ten Elshof, Joseph Butler, Adam Smith) that the taxonomy has no dedicated slug for; Sartre's 'bad-faith' is only an approximate neighbor and no philosopher slug exists for Butler.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
holes.what: The reasoning error of letting unrecoverable past investments (money, time, effort) sway a forward-looking cost-benefit decision.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is built entirely around defining, illustrating, and partly rehabilitating the sunk cost fallacy, and no existing taxonomy concept names it.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: The Epistemology of Peer Disagreement
holes.what: The debate over whether learning that an epistemic peer disagrees with you should make you suspend judgment (conciliationism) or remain steadfast.
holes.why: Chapter 29's core apparatus is the conciliatory-versus-steadfast response to peer disagreement, a distinct social-epistemology topic absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: Contractualism
holes.what: Scanlon's view that an act is wrong if it is disallowed by principles no one could reasonably reject as a basis for general agreement.
holes.why: Chapter 31 makes Scanlonian contractualism one of its three co-equal moral theories (via Mike), but the taxonomy has slugs only for consequentialism and deontology.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: T.M. Scanlon
holes.what: Contemporary moral philosopher (b. 1940) who developed contractualism in 'What We Owe to Each Other.'
holes.why: Chapter 31 quotes and applies Scanlon's reasonable-rejection principle directly to Mike's contracts, yet Scanlon has no taxonomy philosopher slug.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: The Ethics of Promising
holes.what: The philosophical study of how promises create moral obligations, including whether immoral or illegal ('bad') promises bind.
holes.why: Chapters 34-35 are wholly about the obligation-generating force of promises and the paradox of bad promises, which no taxonomy concept captures.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: Paternalism
holes.what: Interfering with a competent person's choices against their will for their own supposed good.
holes.why: Chapter 36's central question is when paternalistic intervention in Chuck's healthcare is justified, a topic distinct from Berlin's liberty concept and unrepresented in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

holes.name: Paraconsistent Logic
holes.what: Non-classical logics in which the principles of non-contradiction and explosion do not hold in general, so a contradiction does not entail everything.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues at length that logicians revised classical logic to build paraconsistent systems and that these could be weaponized to justify Orwellian doublethink; no taxonomy concept covers this specific logical position.
holes.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents

holes.name: Longtermism
holes.what: The ethical view that positively influencing the long-term future—including vast numbers of far-future people—is a key moral priority, sometimes justifying present sacrifice.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explicitly frames Seldon as a possible 'long-termist' and evaluates the Seldon Plan against longtermism and its critics; the taxonomy has existential-risk but no concept for longtermism as a distinct ethical position.
holes.book: 253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents

holes.name: Fascism
holes.what: The interwar ultranationalist, anti-liberal, leader-and-state-worshipping political ideology of Mussolini and Hitler.
holes.why: The entire volume, and chapter 10's guiding question, is whether Nietzsche is the 'godfather of fascism'; the taxonomy has no fascism concept, only arendt-totalitarianism, which does not capture fascism specifically.
holes.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute

holes.name: Richard Wagner
holes.what: Composer and cultural ideologue (1813–1883) whose Das Judentum in der Musik and Bayreuth cult fused German nationalism, anti-Semitism, and aesthetics.
holes.why: Chapters 18 and 19 argue centrally that Wagner (not Nietzsche) was the real proto-fascist through whom Nietzsche's own positions are contrasted; the taxonomy has no slug for Wagner as a thinker/figure.
holes.book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute

holes.name: Pierre Bourdieu
holes.what: French sociologist-philosopher of taste whose Distinction argues aesthetic taste is a socially constructed marker of class reproduced through field, habitus, and cultural capital.
holes.why: Chapter 12 is built entirely on Bourdieu's field/habitus/cultural-capital analysis of Bourdain's taste, and chapter 9 also invokes his critique of taste; no existing taxonomy philosopher covers his sociology of taste.
holes.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic category, developed by Edmund Burke, in which vastness, danger, or terror produce awe and pleasure when experienced from safe (or psychical) distance, distinct from the beautiful.
holes.why: Chapter 11 leans heavily on Burke's and Bullough's sublime and psychical distance to explain the aesthetic appeal of dangerous/disgusting food; the taxonomy has no sublime concept and only a narrow Kantian-taste entry.
holes.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life

holes.name: The Abject
holes.what: Julia Kristeva's category for what fascinates and repels because it breaks down the boundary between self and other (corpses, wounds, bodily fluids), erupting the Real and reminding us of death.
holes.why: Chapter 11 devotes a section to Kristeva's abject to explain the allure of blood soup and mystery meat; no taxonomy philosopher or concept represents Kristeva or the abject.
holes.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life

holes.name: Society of the Spectacle
holes.what: Guy Debord's Situationist critique that in advanced capitalism authentic social life is replaced by its representation, and tourism is the consumption of the banal.
holes.why: Chapter 13 grounds Bourdain's traveler/tourist distinction in repeated quotation of Debord's Society of the Spectacle; the taxonomy has Baudrillard's simulacra but no Debord/spectacle entry for this specific critique of tourism as spectacle.
holes.book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life

holes.name: The Metaphysics of Race (biological vs. social race)
holes.what: The debate over whether race is a real biological kind, a socially constructed reality, or an illusion.
holes.why: Chapter 42 argues mutants are not a biological race but are 'racelike' as a social reality, and the taxonomy has specific race concepts (racial-contract, double-consciousness, intersectionality) but no general concept for the metaphysics/social-construction of race itself.
holes.book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today

holes.name: Louis Althusser
holes.what: Marxist philosopher who theorized ideology, interpellation, and the repressive vs ideological state apparatuses.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire argument runs on Althusser's concept of interpellation and the ISA/RSA distinction, and no taxonomy philosopher covers him.
holes.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

holes.name: Interpellation / Ideological Interpellation
holes.what: Althusser's process by which individuals are hailed into and constituted by an ideology they take for granted as natural truth.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies interpellation directly to the button-pushing survivors and to the socially constructed category of 'the Others,' and the taxonomy has no matching concept.
holes.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

holes.name: Jane English
holes.what: Contemporary moral philosopher known for the argument that grown children owe their parents nothing, since parental sacrifices create friendship rather than debt.
holes.why: Chapter 23 is built entirely on Jane English's 'What Do Grown Children Owe Their Parents?' thesis, and she is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

holes.name: W. D. Ross
holes.what: British ethicist who proposed a pluralist theory of self-evident prima facie duties balanced against one another to yield an actual duty.
holes.why: Chapter 24 evaluates Michael's betrayal solely through Ross's prima facie duties and 'actual duty,' and no taxonomy philosopher represents him.
holes.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

holes.name: Prima Facie Duties
holes.what: Ross's set of conditional moral duties (fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, noninjury) that can be overridden by weightier duties in a situation.
holes.why: The chapter's analysis of Michael turns on weighing prima facie duties to reach an actual duty, a concept the taxonomy lacks distinct from generic deontology.
holes.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

holes.name: H. Richard Niebuhr
holes.what: American Christian theologian and ethicist known for a relational, responsibility-centered account of faith and community.
holes.why: Chapter 27 pairs Niebuhr's relational theology with Levinas to explain redemption-in-community on Lost, and he is not in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons

holes.name: Neil Postman
holes.what: American media theorist whose Amusing Ourselves to Death argues that television's inherent bias turns all public discourse, even news, into entertainment.
holes.why: Chapter 9 is built entirely around Postman's thesis as the philosophical lens on Stewart's media critique, and no taxonomy philosopher captures his media-ecology argument.
holes.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News

holes.name: Neologism and Word-Coinage
holes.what: The philosophy-of-language question of how a newly coined term acquires genuine meaning and word-status, between individual intention and community/dictionary convention.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is entirely about how Daily Show/Colbert Report neologisms ('truthiness,' 'wikiality') become meaningful words, and the taxonomy has no concept for meaning-creation/neologization—language-games is only a loose stand-in.
holes.book: 260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News

holes.name: Arthur Danto
holes.what: Analytic philosopher of art who argued (via Warhol's Brillo Box) that artworks and mere real things can be perceptually identical, so art status depends on theory and history, culminating in his 'end of art' thesis.
holes.why: Chapter 27 devotes an entire section to Danto's historicist, essentialist philosophy of art to explain why Seuss's books count as art, and no aesthetics theorist of art fits any existing taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!

holes.name: The Definition of Art (aesthetic theory / institutional and historical theories)
holes.what: The philosophical project of stating necessary and sufficient conditions for something to be art, spanning Beardsley's aesthetic-experience definition and Danto's historical/essentialist account.
holes.why: Chapter 27's core argument turns on rival definitions of art (Beardsley vs. Danto), and the taxonomy has no philosophy-of-art or aesthetics concept to map this to.
holes.book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!

holes.name: Transhumanism vs Bioconservatism
holes.what: The debate over whether we should use biotechnology to enhance human capacities and defeat aging/death, opposed by bioconservatives who hold our limits are constitutive of our humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 6 is structured entirely around transhumanism (Bostrom, More) versus bioconservatism (Kass, McKibben, Fukuyama), and the taxonomy has no concept naming either the movement or the enhancement debate.
holes.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy

holes.name: Samsara (the cycle of death and rebirth)
holes.what: The Hindu cycle of death and rebirth from which a soul seeks liberation by working off accumulated karma across lives.
holes.why: Chapter 8 makes Roland's endlessly repeating quest an explicit figure for Hindu samsara alongside dharma, karma and samskara, but the taxonomy's only rebirth concept is buddhist-karma and has no Hindu samsara/samskara slug.
holes.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy

holes.name: The Paradox of Tragedy (pleasure in fictional suffering)
holes.what: The puzzle, framed by Aristotle's catharsis and Hume's 'Of Tragedy,' of why audiences take pleasure in fear, horror, and sorrow they would find painful in real life.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire defense of horror art turns on catharsis and Hume's paradox of tragedy, a distinct aesthetic problem the taxonomy has no concept for.
holes.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist and semiotician (1915-1980) best known for structuralist and post-structuralist criticism.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is built entirely on Barthes's essay 'The Death of the Author,' and no comparable literary-theory figure exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy

holes.name: The Death of the Author
holes.what: Barthes's thesis that a text's meaning is created by the reader rather than fixed by its author's intention, extending Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'intentional fallacy.'
holes.why: Chapter 15 applies this exact concept to The Shining and its adaptations; the taxonomy has no slug for authorship, intention, or reader-response theory.
holes.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy

holes.name: Middle Knowledge (scientia media / counterfactuals of freedom)
holes.what: Luis de Molina's doctrine that God (or a knower) can know true counterfactuals about what free agents would do, reconciling foreknowledge with freedom.
holes.why: Chapter 17's resolution of Johnny Smith's predictive knowledge depends specifically on Molinist middle knowledge, which the taxonomy does not cover (and Molina himself is absent).
holes.book: 263 - Stephen King and Philosophy

holes.name: Psychical Distance
holes.what: Edward Bullough's aesthetic principle that genuine aesthetic experience requires a filtered 'distance' balanced between practical under-distancing and abstract over-distancing.
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire argument turns on Bullough's psychical distance as the criterion of aesthetic experience, and the taxonomy has no aesthetics concept that captures it (kant-aesthetics is specifically Kant's judgment of taste and the sublime, which the chapter does not apply).
holes.book: 265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Italian philosopher of history whose New Science grounds knowledge of the human world in its historical development and tradition rather than in abstract reason.
holes.why: Chapter 1 relies on Vico's account of Roman dining and his claim that cooking marks the passage from nature to culture as its central interpretive framework, and Chapter 4 makes the 'Vichian' (tradition-based) versus 'Cartesian' (reason-based) epistemology of cookery the organizing contrast of the whole chapter.
holes.book: 268 - Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, and Be Merry

holes.name: Hume's Standard of Taste
holes.what: Hume's account, in 'Of the Standard of Taste,' that the joint verdict of qualified 'true judges' – marked by delicacy, practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice, and good sense – fixes a standard for aesthetic beauty.
holes.why: Chapter 7 is built entirely on this specific Humean doctrine (true judges, freedom from prejudice) to assess maternal perceptions of infant beauty, and the taxonomy has no aesthetics/taste concept attached to Hume.
holes.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom

holes.name: Intensive Mothering
holes.what: Sharon Hays's concept that contemporary Western culture demands mothers be selfless, child-centered, and make children their unconditional first priority above career or self.
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire analysis of celebrity-mom media rests on 'intensive mothering' as its organizing concept, and no existing taxonomy concept captures this distinct sociological-feminist idea.
holes.book: 272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom

holes.name: The Moral Argument for God's Existence
holes.what: The argument that objective/necessary moral truths and the binding force of moral obligation are best explained by, or require, the existence of God.
holes.why: Chapter 13's central dispute is Moreland's claim that necessary ethical truths ground better in theism than naturalism; the taxonomy has 'faith-vs-reason' and 'problem-of-evil' but no slug for God as the ground of morality.
holes.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate

holes.name: Dependent Arising (pratītyasamutpāda)
holes.what: The Buddhist doctrine that all phenomena arise and exist only interdependently, as empty nodes in a web of mutually conditioning causes, with no independent essence.
holes.why: Chapter 15 devotes extended analysis to dependent arising as distinct from and underpinning no-self and impermanence (the coffee cup as a web of physical, economic, and karmic conditions); the taxonomy lists non-self and emptiness but no slug for dependent arising itself.
holes.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate

holes.name: Interpretive Communities
holes.what: Stanley Fish's thesis that meaning and evaluation arise not from an object itself but from the shared assumptions and vocabulary of a community of readers/judges.
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire escape from taste relativism rests on Fish's interpretive communities of expert coffee cuppers, and the taxonomy has no philosopher for Fish nor a concept capturing this community-grounded theory of judgment.
holes.book: 274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate

holes.name: Fair Chase
holes.what: The hunting ethic requiring a balance that lets prey generally elude the hunter, with voluntary limits on technology and a duty of a clean, confident kill.
holes.why: Chapter 2 (Vitali) is centrally about redefining what makes fair chase 'fair' and no existing taxonomy concept (land-ethic, animal-rights, virtue-ethics) names this specific hunting-ethics doctrine that recurs across the volume.
holes.book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life

holes.name: Audre Lorde
holes.what: Black lesbian feminist poet-theorist whose essay 'Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power' theorizes the erotic as a deep source of female self-knowledge and power distinct from pornography.
holes.why: Chapter 10 (ch24) builds its whole positive account of what 'feels right' in porn on Lorde's erotic-as-power, but no Lorde slug exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

holes.name: The Erotic as Power
holes.what: Lorde's idea that the erotic is a disciplined internal resource and a form of empowering knowledge, sharply opposed to the sensation-without-feeling of pornography.
holes.why: Marinucci's argument turns on distinguishing empowering erotic experience from oppressive porn, a concept the taxonomy has no slug for (objectification and mackinnon-dominance capture only the critique side).
holes.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

holes.name: Denis Diderot
holes.what: French Enlightenment philosophe and Encyclopédie editor who also wrote erotic-philosophical fiction (Les Bijoux indiscrets, Supplément au voyage de Bougainville).
holes.why: Aberdein's central case for the philosophy/pornography synthesis rests on Diderot as a canonical Enlightenment philosopher writing porn, but the taxonomy lists no Diderot slug.
holes.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

holes.name: Aesthetic Value and Aesthetic Attention
holes.what: The theory of what gives an object artistic/aesthetic value and the mode of attention (opaque, formal) proper to appreciating art, distinct from other interests.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire argument turns on 'artistic interest' versus 'pornographic interest' and artistic value, a general aesthetics topic the taxonomy has no concept for (Kant's judgment-of-taste concept is narrower and unused here).
holes.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

holes.name: Aesthetic Disinterestedness / Psychical Distance
holes.what: The doctrine that genuine aesthetic experience requires disinterested contemplation of an object for its own sake, at a psychical 'distance' from desire (Schopenhauer, Bullough).
holes.why: Chapter 28 makes disinterestedness/psychical distance the very criterion separating fine art and erotica from pornography, but the taxonomy has no concept for aesthetic disinterestedness.
holes.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

holes.name: Jouissance
holes.what: The Lacanian/French-feminist notion of a radical, ego-shattering (coded feminine) pleasure distinct from ordinary comforting pleasure (plaisir).
holes.why: Chapter 34's core explanation of the male girl–girl porn consumer's pleasure is built on jouissance and its opposition to plaisir, a concept the taxonomy lacks despite listing Lacan.
holes.book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

holes.name: Religious Naturalism
holes.what: The view (developed by George Santayana and Steven Cahn) that religion's rituals, myths, and moral communities carry real human meaning without any commitment to supernatural entities.
holes.why: Chapter 30's whole argument that atheists can meaningfully celebrate Christmas rests on Santayana's religious naturalism, which no existing taxonomy concept captures.
holes.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal

holes.name: Fowler's Stages of Faith
holes.what: James Fowler's developmental-psychology model of faith unfolding through progressive stages (intuitive-projective, mythic-literal, synthetic-conventional, individuative-reflective, conjunctive, universalizing) across the lifespan.
holes.why: Chapter 31 is structured entirely around Fowler's Stages of Faith as the lens for its author's religious journey, and the taxonomy has no concept for lifespan faith development.
holes.book: 279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal

holes.name: Albert Schweitzer
holes.what: Theologian-philosopher whose 'reverence for life' ethic extends moral consideration to all living things, including plants.
holes.why: Chapter 13 builds its constructive plant-ethics argument directly on Schweitzer's reverence-for-life principle, which the taxonomy has no slug for.
holes.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom

holes.name: Plant Ethics / Moral Status of Plants
holes.what: The view that plants can be objects of moral consideration, possessing autonomy and interests warranting care and respect.
holes.why: Chapter 13's central thesis is the moral standing of plants specifically, which is distinct from animal-rights or generic anthropocentrism and has no dedicated taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom

holes.name: Actor-Network Theory / Assemblage
holes.what: The view (Latour, Callon, Law) that the world is made of heterogeneous networks of human and non-human actors whose agency is distributed and emergent, dissolving the nature/culture divide.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire re-description of the garden as a shifting assemblage of 'crossings, complexity, and circuits' rests on actor-network theory, which the taxonomy lacks any slug for.
holes.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom

holes.name: Aztec (Nahua) Animist Cosmology
holes.what: The Mesoamerican worldview in which organic and inorganic things share one vital spirit, so a mountain-and-water source becomes an altepetl embodying the city-state and cosmic order.
holes.why: Chapter 29 explains Texcotzingo entirely through Nahua animism and the altepetl concept, and the taxonomy has no Mesoamerican philosopher or concept to map it to.
holes.book: 280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyone - Cultivating Wisdom

holes.name: Evolutionary Explanation of Human Behavior
holes.what: The Darwinian, naturalistic strategy of explaining human traits, urges, and pleasures as inherited dispositions favored (or not selected out) by natural selection rather than by conscious purpose.
holes.why: Chapter 3 (Fitschen) is fundamentally an evolutionary explanation of why humans climb—arboreal dispositions carried forward, pleasures as adaptive—and the taxonomy has no Darwin/evolution philosopher or evolutionary-psychology concept to capture its central move.
holes.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

holes.name: Philosophy of Sport (value internal to athletic activity)
holes.what: The study of values internal to games and sports—style, difficulty, self-sufficiency, adventure—by which one athletic achievement is judged better or more admirable than another.
holes.why: Chapter 7 (Ebert and Robertson) argues self-sufficiency is a good-making value partly constitutive of mountaineering itself, an internal-to-sport value theory the taxonomy has no philosopher or concept for; the same gap recurs in Sailors' 'value of dangerous sport' (ch 6).
holes.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian communitarian philosopher known for The Ethics of Authenticity and the idea of a 'horizon of significance.'
holes.why: Chapter 23 relies substantially on Taylor's horizon of significance to correct Nietzsche and Mill, arguing self-creation gains meaning only in dialogue with community, but no Taylor slug exists in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

holes.name: The Sorites Paradox (the paradox of the heap)
holes.what: The ancient puzzle that removing one grain never turns a heap into a non-heap, exposing the problem of vague predicates.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central argument equates the free-rider problem with the sorites paradox and vagueness (via Galen's grains and cairn-building), and the taxonomy has no slug for the sorites paradox, vagueness, or the free-rider problem.
holes.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

holes.name: Peter Kropotkin
holes.what: Russian anarchist theorist whose Mutual Aid argued cooperation, not Social-Darwinist competition, drives human progress.
holes.why: Chapter 27 builds its gift-economy thesis directly on Kropotkin's Mutual Aid as the alternative to liberal self-interest, but the taxonomy has an 'anarchism' concept with no attached philosopher and no Kropotkin slug.
holes.book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist social psychologist who held the self is constructed through social interaction by 'taking the attitude of the other.'
holes.why: Chapter 28's constructive counter to Foucault's and Goldman's fatalism rests on Mead's creative social self, quoting Mind, Self and Society at length, and no taxonomy philosopher covers him.
holes.book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am

holes.name: Situationism (attribution bias)
holes.what: The view from social psychology and philosophy that seemingly trivial situational variables, not stable character, drive human judgment and behavior.
holes.why: Alfano's whole argument that Doug Clark's jury was swayed by disgust, gender bias, and media rests on situationism, which the taxonomy's 'moral-psychology' captures only loosely.
holes.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing

holes.name: Practical Moral Skepticism
holes.what: The doctrine that one may fully know what is good yet have no motivating reason to do it, distinct from epistemic doubt about moral knowledge.
holes.why: Howard explicitly organizes her historical survey of killers around 'practical moral skepticism' as a thesis about moral motivation, a specific position the taxonomy lacks.
holes.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing

holes.name: Communicative Rationality
holes.what: Habermas's notion of a reasoning oriented to mutual understanding through perspective-taking and reciprocity, contrasted with instrumental rationality.
holes.why: Keegan's entire diagnosis of Buffalo Bill's psychopathy is built on Habermas's communicative rationality as the deep-seated human trait whose loss produces psychopathy, and no taxonomy concept names it.
holes.book: 285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing

holes.name: The Rationality of Believing Yoga Theory
holes.what: The epistemological question of whether it can be reasonable, given modern science, to believe the ancient Indian theoretical apparatus of yoga (chakras, prana, kundalini, koshas).
holes.why: Chapter 16's entire argument is a testimony-based epistemology of belief in 'yoga theory' specifically; the taxonomy has general skepticism and Hume's induction but no concept for assessing the credibility of a superseded traditional theory against science.
holes.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body

holes.name: Samadhi / Yogic Union (purusha and prakriti)
holes.what: The yogic goal of union — the binding or integration of consciousness (purusha) with nature (prakriti), variously kaivalya, Vedantic realization, or Tantric Shiva-Shakti.
holes.why: Samadhi/yogic union is the organizing concept of chapters 8, 19, 21, and 32, but the taxonomy's Eastern concepts (atman-brahman, the-tao, buddhist-*) do not include the specifically yogic purusha–prakriti union or samadhi.
holes.book: 286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body

holes.name: Peter Abelard
holes.what: Twelfth-century medieval logician and ethicist who held that the morality of an act is determined by the agent's intention (consent) rather than the outward behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 23 rests its whole definition of a 'real date' on Abelard's intention-based ethics from his Ethics, and no existing taxonomy philosopher covers this intention-determines-the-act thesis.
holes.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas

holes.name: Johan Huizinga
holes.what: Dutch cultural historian and theorist of play whose Homo Ludens argues that culture arises in and through play, defining the 'magic circle' and the cheater/spoilsport distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire ludic analysis of dating and virtual worlds is built on Huizinga's theory of play, the magic circle, and spoilsports, and no existing taxonomy philosopher or concept captures the philosophy of play.
holes.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas

holes.name: Play and the Magic Circle
holes.what: Huizinga's account of play as a free, absorbing activity set apart in its own bounded time and space (the 'magic circle') with its own rules, distinct from ordinary serious life.
holes.why: Chapter 26 applies the magic circle and the play-spirit directly to the dating script and to Second Life, and the taxonomy has no concept for the philosophy of play or games.
holes.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas

holes.name: The Paradox of Choice (maximizers vs satisficers)
holes.what: Barry Schwartz's thesis that an overload of options tends to reduce satisfaction, distinguishing 'maximizers' who seek the absolute best from 'satisficers' content with the good enough.
holes.why: Chapter 31's central argument that abundant dating choice makes people unhappy maximizers is organized entirely around Schwartz's maximizer/satisficer distinction, which no existing taxonomy concept expresses.
holes.book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas

holes.name: Becoming and Deterritorialization
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's account of 'becoming' (becoming-animal, becoming-imperceptible) and lines of flight that dissolve fixed molar identities into molecular multiplicities.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire Deleuzean reading turns on becoming-shark, multiplicity, and lines of flight, which the taxonomy's only Deleuze slug (rhizome) does not adequately capture.
holes.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature

holes.name: Luce Irigaray
holes.what: French feminist philosopher and psychoanalyst whose Speculum of the Other Woman critiques the phallocentric, mirror-logic of Western philosophy and theorizes feminine multiplicity ('two lips').
holes.why: Chapter 20's reading of Frankenstein and reproduction is structured throughout by Irigaray's Speculum, but she has no slug in the taxonomy's philosopher list.
holes.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature

holes.name: Camp (Sontag's sensibility)
holes.what: Susan Sontag's aesthetic 'sensibility' that prizes artifice, exaggeration, theatricality and 'the good taste of bad taste,' seeing the world as Being-as-Playing-a-Role.
holes.why: Chapter 21's central argument sorts horror films by the camp sensibility from Sontag's 'Notes on Camp,' a concept the taxonomy has no adequate slug for (culture-industry covers only the Adorno/kitsch side).
holes.book: 289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature

holes.name: Montesquieu
holes.what: Enlightenment political theorist (1689-1755) known for the typology of republican, monarchical and despotic government and the separation of powers.
holes.why: Skilling's essay on The Good Government According to Tintin is built almost entirely on Montesquieu's classification of regimes and his 'power should be a check to power' doctrine, and the taxonomy has no matching philosopher slug.
holes.book: 301 - Comics as Philosophy

holes.name: Separation of Powers and Forms of Government
holes.what: Montesquieu's distinction between moderate governments (monarchy, republic) and despotism, and the division of state power into legislative, executive and judiciary branches that check one another.
holes.why: The Tintin essay applies this framework directly to Syldavia, Borduria and San Theodoros, and the taxonomy offers no concept for Montesquieu's regime typology or separation of powers.
holes.book: 301 - Comics as Philosophy

holes.name: Artistic Allusion
holes.what: An intended indirect reference from an alluding artwork to an identifiable source text that invites the audience to import associations, analyzed via Grice's conversational implicature and Austin's speech-act theory.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is entirely about artistic allusion in mass art (The Matrix/Sylvie and Bruno, Alien/Star Wars) and the taxonomy has no concept for allusion, implicature, or intentionalist interpretation.
holes.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture

holes.name: Emotional Identification vs. Sympathy in Fiction
holes.what: The philosophy-of-mind debate over how audiences relate emotionally to fictional characters—identification, simulation theory, sympathy as a pro-attitude, and mirror reflexes.
holes.why: Chapter 11's whole argument concerns the emotional bond between audiences and fictional characters, a topic the taxonomy's emotion/mind concepts do not cover.
holes.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture

holes.name: Spontaneous Order
holes.what: The idea, developed by Hayek from Smith and Darwin, that complex adaptive order can emerge from decentralized feedback without any central designer.
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire thesis reframes popular culture as Hayekian spontaneous order, a concept the taxonomy captures only obliquely through the Smith-specific 'invisible-hand'.
holes.book: 303 - Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture

holes.name: Informal Logic and Fallacies
holes.what: The study of argument structure (premises/conclusions, deductive vs. inductive, validity/soundness and strength/cogency) and of informal fallacies such as red herring, hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem.
holes.why: Chapter 2 is entirely a logic-and-fallacy lesson built on the Chewbacca Defense; the taxonomy has no concept covering argumentation or fallacies, so its central topic maps to nothing.
holes.book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House

holes.name: The Philosophy of Childhood (children as natural philosophers)
holes.what: The view, associated with Gareth Matthews, that childhood is itself a domain of philosophical inquiry and that young children spontaneously do genuine philosophy before it is schooled out of them.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire thesis is that Mister Rogers treated children as philosophers; no taxonomy slug names the philosophy of childhood or the child-as-philosopher claim it applies to the show.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Filial Obligation (what adult children owe their parents)
holes.what: The debated special moral obligations adult children may owe parents, and the candidate grounds for them — indebtedness, gratitude, biology, social role, or friendship.
holes.why: Chapter 13 (numbered 15) is built entirely around the ground of filial obligation and the 'Family First' motto; the taxonomy has friendship and gratitude fragments but no slug for filial/parental obligation itself.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Pacifism (the moral opposition to war)
holes.what: The family of positions morally opposing war, ranging from absolute pacifism to collectivist, pragmatic, and realist pacifism on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum.
holes.why: Chapter 14 (numbered 16) argues at length that the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist'; the taxonomy offers just-war-theory and ahimsa but no general slug for pacifism, which is the chapter's central classifying concept.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Colonialism / Coloniality
holes.what: The theory and practice of domination in which a foreign minority rules, exploits, and dehumanizes an indigenous or imported population, and the enduring 'colonial matrix of power' (coloniality) it leaves behind.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is entirely built on typologies of colonialism (settler, planter, extractive, postcolonial) and decolonization, which no existing taxonomy concept names—Fanon and Mills's racial contract cover pieces but not colonialism itself.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Superiority Theory of Humor
holes.what: The theory—traced from Plato and Aristotle through Hobbes—that laughter arises from a felt sense of triumph or superiority over others, one of the three main currents in the philosophy of humor alongside incongruity and release.
holes.why: Chapter 19's philosophical spine is the superiority theory of humor as the basis of satire; the taxonomy has only Bergson's specific 'laughter' entry and no general concept for humor/superiority theory.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: The view that life is meaningless and that no values, purposes, or actions carry ultimate significance.
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire thesis is that Rick & Morty presents and defends existential/cosmic nihilism, and the taxonomy has 'the-absurd' and 'meaning-of-life' but no slug for nihilism itself as the chapter's central concept.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief
holes.what: W.K. Clifford's principle that it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence, since beliefs guide action and endanger others.
holes.why: Chapter 31's central positive argument—that people must not accept religious views without good grounds—rests wholly on Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief,' which recurs and is also load-bearing in chapter 34, and no existing philosopher or concept slug covers Clifford.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Fascism
holes.what: A family of ultranationalist, authoritarian political ideologies exalting a leader-cult, in-group myth, and forcible suppression of opposition, defined by family resemblance rather than necessary-and-sufficient conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is entirely an argument that MAGA Trumpism is fascist and analyzes fascism's defining traits at length; the taxonomy has arendt-totalitarianism but no slug for fascism itself, which is the chapter's core concept.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Honor and Honor Codes
holes.what: A structured moral value in which a binding code, group affiliation, internalized self-worth, and a principle of (often disproportionate) redress define an agent's standing and identity.
holes.why: Chapter 39's entire philosophical analysis of The Godfather turns on a four-part account of personal honor as Don Vito's signature virtue, which no existing taxonomy concept (virtue-ethics, moral-psychology) captures specifically.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: A German Idealist who held that all reality manifests a will, and that the 'ground' of creative order is an ineradicable potential for disorder and a dark, passionate will that must be acknowledged rather than eliminated.
holes.why: Chapter 38 uses Schelling substantively to explain the ever-presence of the Force's dark side and why rightly-ordered love (not the elimination of darkness) achieves true balance for Rey and Ben; no German Idealist in the taxonomy covers this.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Philosophy of Humor and Laughter
holes.what: The philosophical study of humor and laughter as morally, existentially, and politically significant, including its liberating capacity for self-transcendence and resistance to oppression versus its reactionary reinforcement of the status quo.
holes.why: Chapter 43's central argument is that humor itself is a threefold tool of liberation (drawing on Critchley, Amir, Bussie, Eagleton), a distinct topic the taxonomy lacks; Freud's death-drive/unconscious slugs do not fit his essay on humor.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: The Constitution View (constitutionalism)
holes.what: The theory that a person is not identical to but is constituted by their body, as a statue is constituted by a lump of clay, allowing person and body to coincide yet differ in persistence conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 58's entire positive solution to how Jake switches bodies rests on constitutionalism (Baker, Shoemaker) as a named theory of persons distinct from animalism and dualism, and the taxonomy has no slug that captures the person/body constitution relation.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Animalism
holes.what: The view that we are numerically identical to our biological organisms (animals/bodies), defended by Eric Olson.
holes.why: Chapter 58 devotes a full section to animalism as the theory of persons that makes body-switching logically impossible, and it is treated as a distinct named position with no adequate existing slug (personal-identity is too generic to mark this specific thesis).
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Lying and Deception
holes.what: The applied-epistemology study of what lies and deception are and their varieties (spoken lies, keeping mum, concealing, showing the false vs. hiding the truth).
holes.why: Chapter 61 is centrally about the nature and taxonomy of lying/deception in Twain's Tom Sawyer, which the taxonomy has no concept slug for; frankfurt-bullshit and gettier-problem only touch adjacent ideas.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Philosophy of Humor
holes.what: Theories of what humor is and does, including relief theory, catharsis, self-deprecation, and comedy as cultural critique.
holes.why: Chapter 66's core subject is a philosophical critique of comedy and jokes themselves (relief humor, catharsis, self-deprecation), for which the taxonomy provides no dedicated concept slug.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Identification and Consubstantiality
holes.what: Kenneth Burke's rhetorical theory that persuasion works by making a speaker 'consubstantial' with the audience through shared symbols, bridging division into an 'acting-together.'
holes.why: Chapter 70 makes Burke's identification/consubstantiality and 'comic frame' the entire theoretical spine of its account of Maron's comedy-as-therapy, and the taxonomy has no philosopher or concept covering Burke or rhetorical identification.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Enrique Dussel
holes.what: Latin-American philosopher and founder of the philosophy of liberation, which theorizes thinking from the 'exteriority' of the oppressed periphery rather than the European center.
holes.why: Chapter 71 builds its central argument on Dussel's Philosophy of Liberation (barbarian philosophy, otherness, exteriority) alongside Marcuse, and the taxonomy contains no philosopher of liberation for the periphery.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: The Organic Intellectual
holes.what: Gramsci's figure who gains knowledge through the lived experience of a subaltern class and uses it to articulate that class's interests and challenge ruling-class hegemony.
holes.why: Chapter 72's whole thesis is that Pryor IS an organic intellectual; the taxonomy lists Gramsci only via 'hegemony,' with no slug for the organic-intellectual concept the chapter applies throughout.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Talmudic / Jewish Pluralist Epistemology
holes.what: A Jewish mode of knowing that accepts fixed commands (mitzvot) that are neither true nor false and generates wisdom through a multiplicity of contextual interpretations, dialogic rather than the unitary Hellenic-Christian search for one truth.
holes.why: Chapter 74's entire thesis is that Seinfeld's 'neo-Talmudic' comedy instantiates this distinctively Jewish epistemology, which no existing philosopher or concept slug in the taxonomy captures.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Philosophy of Humor
holes.what: The philosophical study of what jokes are and how comedy generates insight, e.g. incongruity and superiority theories of laughter.
holes.why: Chapters 74-79 all treat comedians as philosophers and lean on theories of how humor (incongruity, schema-shifting) produces wisdom, a recurring load-bearing topic the taxonomy lacks a slug for.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Color-Blind Racism
holes.what: Post-1960s racism (Bonilla-Silva) that minimizes systemic racism while stressing individual choice and responsibility, sustaining a 'white habitus' through coded cultural, not biological, explanations of inequality.
holes.why: Chapter 75 argues Chappelle's ethics of fairness and personal responsibility overlaps with color-blind racism, the analytic frame of the whole chapter, which has no taxonomy slug.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Habitus and Social Capital
holes.what: Bourdieu's account of the ingrained dispositions, tastes and social capital by which individuals reproduce and maintain their social class membership.
holes.why: Chapter 78 uses Bourdieu's habitus (and his Blackadder analysis) as the mechanism explaining why Fry's 'faint mockery' reinforces the class and institutions he mocks; neither Bourdieu nor habitus is in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Role Ethics (Teleological Particularism)
holes.what: The view that at least some moral obligations derive from the socially constructed roles an agent occupies (father, doctor, citizen), and that these role-based duties are relative to subject, time and culture rather than universal.
holes.why: Chapter 81's central thesis is the author's own 'teleological particularism,' a role-based ethics distinct from consequentialism, deontology, and moral particularism, for which the taxonomy offers no adequate slug.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic experience of pleasurable terror or awe before the vast, powerful or infinite, distinguished from beauty; developed by Burke (pain-based terror at a distance) and Kant (mathematical and dynamical sublime).
holes.why: Chapter 82 builds its analysis of Journey on the sublime as a category separate from beauty, drawing centrally on Burke, whom the taxonomy lacks, and on a sense of the sublime broader than the existing kant-aesthetics slug.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Transhumanism and Posthumanism
holes.what: The project (and debate over) using technology and enhancement to transcend normal biological limits of human body and mind, up to a posthuman state, weighing benefits against threats to identity, autonomy and human dignity.
holes.why: Chapter 84's whole subject is transhuman enhancement in Cyberpunk 2077 and the enhancement debate (Bostrom, Huxley, Kurzweil, Agar), a topic with no dedicated concept slug in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Simone Weil
holes.what: A French philosopher and Christian mystic (1909-1943) who analyzed power/force as a mutually damaging social relation and proposed universal obligations of compassion to meet the 'needs of the soul.'
holes.why: Chapter 84 uses Weil's critique of power and her mysticism of interpersonal obligation as one of the two thinkers grounding its final answer to transhuman corporatism, but Weil is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Structural Violence
holes.what: Johan Galtung's concept that unjust social structures inflict harm and unequal life chances without a direct physical perpetrator.
holes.why: Chapter 96's entire thesis is that From Hell connects physical violence to structural violence under patriarchy, and no taxonomy concept names this central idea.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Counterpart Theory
holes.what: David Lewis's view that a thing's modal properties are grounded in similar-but-nonidentical counterparts existing in other concrete possible worlds, not in transworld identity.
holes.why: Chapter 97 argues Deadpool's piles of distinct hero corpses can only be understood via Lewis's counterpart relation as a substitute for identity; possible-worlds alone does not capture the counterpart/transworld-identity distinction the chapter turns on.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: The Hero's Journey (Monomyth)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's archetypal narrative structure of departure, initiation, and return through which a hero is transformed.
holes.why: Chapter 99 structures its whole reading of Asterios Polyp around Campbell's monomyth (its 17 stages), an organizing framework with no counterpart in the taxonomy.
holes.book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

holes.name: Homosociality
holes.what: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's term for the social bonds between persons of the same sex, which she places on a continuum with homosexuality as forms of desire that structure male bonding and its exclusions.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire analysis of Some Kind of Monster - the Hetfield-Ulrich bond, the rivalry with Mustaine, the exclusion of women, and the policing of the homosocial/homosexual line - is built on this concept, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery

holes.name: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick
holes.what: American queer-theory and gender-studies theorist (1950-2009), author of Between Men and Epistemology of the Closet, who developed the concept of homosocial desire.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explicitly frames its reading of Metallica's male bonding with Sedgwick's account of the homosocial-homosexual continuum, and no taxonomy philosopher covers this framework.
holes.book: 183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash Course in Brain Surgery

holes.name: Allusion (intended reference beyond substitution)
holes.what: An intended reference that calls for associations going beyond mere substitution of a referent, rewarding recognition with aesthetic pleasure, intimacy, and community between author and audience.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is squarely about the aesthetics of allusion and carefully distinguishes allusion from parody, quotation, and 'accidental associations', but the taxonomy only offers popular-parody, which chapter 18 reserves for parody proper.
holes.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer

holes.name: Hypocrisy (not practicing what one preaches)
holes.what: The formal vice of acting in deliberate violation of the values one espouses tacitly or explicitly, distinguished from lying, weakness of will, and mere deception.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is wholly an analysis of hypocrisy as such - its definition, whether deception is essential (Wiggum's non-deceptive case), its distinction from integrity, and excusable or praiseworthy instances - and the taxonomy has only the generic moral-psychology bucket for it.
holes.book: 002 - The Simpsons and Philosophy - The D'oh! of Homer

holes.name: Darshana (philosophical 'view' or school)
holes.what: In the Indian tradition a darshana is a systematic 'view' of the truth about reality taught by a lineage of seers (rishis), combining ontology and epistemology with a soteriological practice aimed at liberation.
holes.why: Chapter 12 makes darshana the organizing framework of the entire Indian tradition (the six classical schools are all darshanas), and the book's structure is built around them, but taxonomy has no equivalent.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Vedic Sacrifice (yajna)
holes.what: The Brahmanical ritual religion in which brahmin priests, through precisely performed fire sacrifices with chanted Sanskrit formulas, maintained cosmic order (dharma) on behalf of society.
holes.why: Chapter 13's first half is an exposition of this sacrificial religion and its karma-as-ritual-action mechanics, which are the soil from which Indian philosophy grows, yet taxonomy covers no Vedic material.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Dependent Origination (pratityasamutpada)
holes.what: The Buddha's teaching that all phenomena arise in mutual dependence on conditions - 'when this is, that is' - so that nothing exists independently, underlying both impermanence and not-self.
holes.why: Chapter 14 presents dependent origination as the most radical of the Buddha's teachings and the key to the Middle Way, and chapter 17 builds Nagarjuna's entire emptiness doctrine on it, but taxonomy has no slug for it.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Panini
holes.what: Fourth-century BCE grammarian whose Astadhyayi, some 4000 rules, codified classical Sanskrit in one of the most sophisticated grammars in the history of linguistics.
holes.why: Chapter 15's whole defense of the Veda through language rests on Panini's grammar and the doctrine that ritually sounded Sanskrit is creatively efficacious; he is a central figure with no taxonomy presence.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Vaisheshika Categories (padartha)
holes.what: Kanada's pluralistic-realist ontology of seven categories - substance, quality, action, universality, particularity, inherence, and absence - with all substance reducible to nine eternal kinds including atoms.
holes.why: Chapter 16 is largely a detailed exposition of this categorial system, which supplied the ontology for the whole Nyaya-Vaisheshika school, and nothing in taxonomy covers it beyond the loose analogy of Greek atomism.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Nyaya Five-Membered Inference (anviksiki)
holes.what: The Nyaya school's formal logical method - thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion, as in 'there is fire on the hill because there is smoke' - grounded in perception and invariable concomitance.
holes.why: Chapter 16 presents this as the first formal philosophical method in India and the core of Nyaya's epistemology of pramanas; taxonomy has no entry for Indian logic.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Abhidharma (Buddhist dharma analysis)
holes.what: The scholastic Buddhist tradition of defining the teachings and categorizing all phenomena (dharmas) - e.g. Theravada's 80-odd kinds and Sarvastivada's time-transcending dharmas with own-being (svabhava).
holes.why: Chapter 17's first half is devoted to the Abhidharma schools and their reification of dharmas, which is precisely what Nagarjuna's emptiness critique targets; taxonomy lacks any coverage of it.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Yogacara 'Mind-Only' (cittamatra)
holes.what: The Buddhist school of Asanga and Vasubandhu analyzing experience as transformations of consciousness - karmic 'seeds' in a storehouse consciousness constructing the subject-object world, with constructed, dependent, and perfected aspects.
holes.why: Chapter 17 gives an extended account of this consciousness-only idealism as the alternative to Madhyamaka, and taxonomy has no slug for it or for Buddhist idealism generally.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Classical Yoga (Patanjali's Yoga Sutra)
holes.what: The darshana codified in the Yoga Sutras: a methodology for the cessation of the activities of the mind (citta-vritti-nirodha) that discriminates the conscious witness (purusha) from unconscious nature (prakriti).
holes.why: Chapter 18 is devoted to it and its companion Samkhya ontology, and taxonomy's only yoga-adjacent entries are unrelated; yoga as a philosophical system is entirely missing.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Samkhya Dualism (purusha and prakriti)
holes.what: The ontology of Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika: numerically plural, inactive, conscious purushas versus one eternal, active, unconscious prakriti manifest through the three gunas, with liberation as their discrimination.
holes.why: Chapter 18's second half expounds this dualism (including satkaryavada and the 'I-maker'), which is one of the six classical darshanas and the stated ontological partner of Classical Yoga; taxonomy has no entry.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Ramanuja
holes.what: Eleventh-century Vedantin of the Sri Vaishnava devotional tradition whose Vishishtadvaita ('qualified non-dualism') holds that Brahman really transforms into the qualified plural world and that selves are eternally inseparable from the Lord.
holes.why: Chapter 19 gives Ramanuja's system equal billing with Shankara's Advaita as the major Vedanta, noting it is more representative of ordinary Hindu belief, but taxonomy includes only Shankara.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: Mimamsa (Vedic exegesis)
holes.what: The darshana, from Jaimini through Kumarila and Prabhakara, defending the eternal authorless Veda as injunction, cognition as intrinsically self-validating, and a plural world of agent-selves who maintain dharma through sacrifice.
holes.why: Chapters 15 and 19 treat Mimamsa as the orthodox pole of Indian epistemology and ontology (word meaning guaranteeing existence, self-validating cognition), and taxonomy has no entry for this school or its epistemology.
holes.book: 110 - Hamilton and Philosophy - Revolutionary Thinking

holes.name: The Sorites Paradox (vagueness)
holes.what: The heap paradox: adding or removing single grains never seems to turn a non-heap into a heap, yet heaps exist, suggesting there is no sharp boundary for vague predicates.
holes.why: Chapter 7 deploys the pile/heap puzzle to argue there may be no objective criterion distinguishing 'real' from 'unreal' religions, leaving Fonzieism a borderline case.
holes.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded

holes.name: Maternal Thinking (Sara Ruddick)
holes.what: Sara Ruddick's account of mothering as an intellectual discipline responding to a child's demands for preservation, growth, and social acceptability, from which virtues like prudence, tolerance, and peacefulness are cultivated.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire framework — mothering as a discipline like math or science, with its own standards of truth and virtues — is Ruddick's theory, cited repeatedly, and no existing slug captures it.
holes.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded

holes.name: The Doctrine of Original Sin
holes.what: Augustine's doctrine that all humans are born with evil in their hearts, developed from the Confessions' pear-tree and jealous-infant observations and serving as an answer to why God lets the innocent suffer.
holes.why: Chapter 11's central thesis is that Stewie vindicates original sin — we laugh at the evil baby because it is true about all children — and taxonomy has Augustine's City of God, time, and divided will but not this doctrine.
holes.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded

holes.name: Arthur Danto
holes.what: American philosopher of art (1924-2013) who argued postmodern works like Warhol's Brillo Boxes deliberately defy traditional definitions of art and force the question 'What is art?'.
holes.why: Chapter 18's whole defense of Family Guy against the 'Simpsons did it!' rip-off charge rests on Danto's account of postmodern art as intentionally unfitting the representation, expression, and form theories; no existing taxonomy slug names him.
holes.book: 161 - Family Guy and Philosophy - A Cure for the Petarded

holes.name: Linda Zagzebski
holes.what: Contemporary virtue theorist whose exemplarist moral theory makes the emotion of admiration for exemplars the engine of moral development and self-improvement.
holes.why: Chapter 5's whole argument about whether and what to admire in Taylor Swift is built directly on Zagzebski's account of admiration, exemplars, and emulation.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Parasocial Relationships
holes.what: One-sided relationships in which a fan experiences intimacy with a celebrity who does not know them, structured by asymmetries of attention, communication, and knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 6 argues Swift's Easter eggs deliberately deepen exactly such parasocial bonds and analyzes their benefits (belonging) and limits (no identity dialogue) for fans.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Heather Widdows
holes.what: Philosopher who argues in Perfect Me that the contemporary beauty ideal (thin, firm, smooth, youthful) has become a global, overriding ethical demand governing self-worth.
holes.why: Chapter 7's analysis of Swift's fat-shaming, skinny-shaming, disordered eating, and the limits of individual resistance is organized entirely around Widdows's beauty-as-ethical-ideal framework.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Reputation (social epistemology of)
holes.what: A person's reputation is a shared group consensus about their character that is external to their control yet also an informational trace of their actions.
holes.why: Chapter 13's core claim is that Swift's reputation-era songs dramatize precisely this paradox: reputation is fake and out of her control, yet partly hers and genuinely informative.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Repetition and Difference
holes.what: Deleuze's thesis (building on Kierkegaard) that genuine repetition is not recurrence of an identical original but a forward movement that produces difference and newness.
holes.why: Chapter 16's argument that the Taylor's Versions are creative repetitions rather than subordinate copies rests entirely on this concept, which taxonomy.json lacks.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Archive Fever (le mal d'archive)
holes.what: Derrida's account of the compulsive desire to collect, organize, and conserve records against forgetting, with the archive as a living, never-finished site where remembering always entails forgetting.
holes.why: Chapter 18's entire framework is the 'archival art' of Swift's songwriting, read through Derrida's Archive Fever, Ricoeur's archival trace, Stuart Hall's living archive, and Halbwachs's collective memory, none of which taxonomy's existing slugs cover.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Paul Ricoeur
holes.what: French philosopher whose Oneself as Another grounds narrative identity in the tension between sameness (idem) and selfhood (ipse), making self-understanding interpretive.
holes.why: Chapter 19's core argument that Swift's rerecordings succeed through narrative identity is built directly on Ricoeur, and chapter 18 also uses his 'archival trace', yet he is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Michael Cholbi
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of grief who argues grieving transforms rather than ends our relationship with the dead, as reconstruction of the griever's practical identity yielding self-knowledge.
holes.why: Chapter 22's analysis of 'marjorie', 'Bigger Than the Whole Sky', and 'epiphany' is explicitly organized around Cholbi's Grief: A Philosophical Guide, including the collective-grief extension.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Philosophy of Grief
holes.what: The philosophical study of grief as a transformed continuing relation to the deceased, a process of rebuilding practical identity, and a source of self-knowledge, extended to collective grief.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is devoted to grief, and taxonomy has no grief concept (its emotion entries cover anger, humor, and love but not mourning).
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Affective Injustice
holes.what: Injustice done to someone in their capacity as an affective being (Whitney, Srinivasan): emotions denied proper uptake, or a forced choice between apt emotional responses to injustice and bettering one's situation.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues 'mad woman' depicts the transformation of women's anger into Madness as affective injustice, a concept adjacent to but distinct from Fricker's epistemic injustice.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Philosophy of Anger
holes.what: The theory of anger as a painful, pleasure-bearing response to perceived injustice carrying a desire for revenge (Aristotle's Rhetoric), including problems like Callard's eternal anger and the gendered politics of whose anger is permitted.
holes.why: Chapter 24 builds its account of female anger and 'Glitter Gel Pen Anger' on Aristotle's definition of anger and Agnes Callard's problem of eternal anger, which taxonomy lacks (ressentiment is a different concept).
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Feminist Standpoint Epistemology
holes.what: The view that knowledge is socially situated: one's social location shapes what one can know, and perspectives of marginalized groups can reveal truths masked by supposedly neutral 'objective' standpoints (Harding, Haslanger).
holes.why: Chapter 26's title and entire framework apply standpoint epistemology to the folklore love triangle, and no existing taxonomy slug covers situated knowledge or standpoint theory.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: Edith Stein
holes.what: Husserl's student and phenomenologist whose On the Problem of Empathy defines empathy as the perception of foreign subjects' experience, distinct from sympathy and inner imitation.
holes.why: Chapter 29's answer to how we know what Taylor Swift feels is built on Stein's empathy (against Lipps), making her the chapter's central philosopher though she is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 194 - Taylor Swift and Philosophy - Essays from the Tortured Philosophers Department

holes.name: W.D. Ross
holes.what: British deontologist who held that moral duties are 'prima facie' or conditional: real duties that can nonetheless be overridden by a stronger duty in particular circumstances.
holes.why: Chapter 5 leans on Ross's prima facie duties for its 'apparent dilemmas' side, arguing that one of Geralt's conflicting duties overrides the other once the relevant facts of Blaviken are known.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Peter Geach
holes.what: Catholic philosopher who argued that a rational or omnipotent God would never permit genuine moral dilemmas, since conflicting inescapable commands are incompatible with divine providence.
holes.why: Chapter 5 applies Geach's argument to the cursed Striga-Adda case to suggest the magic of the Witcher world is arranged so that a capable moral agent never faces a genuinely irresoluble dilemma.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Ethical Pragmatism
holes.what: Raff Donelson's view that moral decisions should be grounded in facts and shared community values open to justification, rather than in appeals to alleged moral truths.
holes.why: Chapter 6 uses Donelson's all-knowing Delphi thought experiment to cast Geralt's refusal of the lesser evil as ethical pragmatism: he deliberates on the facts against the Witcher's Code instead of following Stregobor's or Renfri's utilitarian principles.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: The Beauty Myth
holes.what: Naomi Wolf's thesis that socially imposed beauty standards work as a currency system that keeps male dominance intact, trapping women in a self-punishing 'Iron Maiden'.
holes.why: Chapter 14 interprets Yennefer's transformation and her pursuit of beauty as power through Wolf's Beauty Myth and Iron Maiden, showing her conforming to and being imprisoned by the standard at once.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Maternal Thinking
holes.what: Sara Ruddick's account of mothering as a practice of protection, nurturance, and training, a vocation rather than an identity that anyone, including men, can perform.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses Ruddick's maternal thinking to pinpoint when Yennefer (and even Geralt) genuinely becomes a mother to Ciri through sacrificial care rather than biology.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Reproductive Justice
holes.what: A feminist framework recognizing the social barriers that stop marginalized women from freely choosing to have or not have children, including coercive sterilization.
