holes.why: Chapter 15 evaluates Yennefer's sterilization at Aretuza as a reproductive-justice injustice that mirrors real-world coerced sterilizations of disabled, Roma, and Indigenous women.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Hélène Cixous
holes.what: French feminist theorist of écriture féminine who, in 'The Laugh of the Medusa', urged women to write their bodies and reclaim repressed female expression and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 16 frames Ciri's scream, her 'NO!', Calanthe's defiance, and the 'Medusa' figures of Renfri and Vereena entirely through Cixous's essay, which is the chapter's central framework.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Race as Social Construct
holes.what: The Critical Race Theory view (Omi and Winant's racial formation) that race is an unstable category created and transformed by political struggle and power, not a fixed biological kind.
holes.why: Chapter 18 applies this to the Continent, where racial lines are drawn by species, lineage, and political power rather than skin color, to explain anti-elven pogroms and the treatment of witchers.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Wrongful Discrimination
holes.what: The contemporary account (Lippert-Rasmussen, Hellman, Eidelson) of discrimination as unjustified worse treatment of a socially salient group, with demeaning further requiring a power asymmetry.
holes.why: Chapter 19 tests Geralt's everyday mistreatment against these criteria and concludes it is unjust wronging but not discrimination, since his taunters lack the power to subordinate him.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Ibram X. Kendi
holes.what: Contemporary historian and antiracism theorist who defines racism as rooted in racist policy and power, and holds that one is in each moment either being racist or being antiracist.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire framework - colorism, the 'drop rules,' dehumanization, and Ciri's antiracist choice - is built on Kendi's How to Be an Antiracist, and no existing taxonomy slug covers him.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Bronislaw Malinowski
holes.what: Anthropologist whose studies of Trobriand magic analyzed the spell as traditional words whose utterance generates and conveys a magical force (mana) toward an aim.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is organized around Malinowski's theory of verbal magic as the key to how Elder Speech spell-casting works, alongside Austin and Searle.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Speech Acts (performative utterances)
holes.what: The theory that some utterances (performatives and declaratives) do not describe the world but perform an act, changing the world by saying so under felicity conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 22's central claim is that Witcher spells are performative speech acts - Austin's performatives and Searle's declaratives - and the taxonomy has no concept slug for speech act theory.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Mimetic Desire
holes.what: Girard's thesis that desire is not spontaneous but copied from a model or mediator, so rivals imitating the same object escalate into mimetic rivalry and crisis.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explains the Pavetta betrothal brawl and the Novigrad witch hunts through mimetic desire and mimetic crisis, concepts the taxonomy lacks despite having Girard.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: The Scapegoat Mechanism
holes.what: Girard's account of how a crisis of all-against-all violence is resolved by unanimous violence against a marked victim, whose persecution reunites the community without solving its causes.
holes.why: Chapter 25's core argument is that the Eternal Fire's persecution of mages, elves, and witchers is Girardian scapegoating with the four stereotypes of persecution.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Becoming-Other (the Deleuzian sorcerer)
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's notion of mutation without preset outcome: the sorcerer as anomaly at the fringes who enters 'nuptials against nature' and cannot know in advance what they will become.
holes.why: Chapter 28 maps witchers, the Trial of Grasses, and the Law of Surprise onto Deleuze's sorcerer and becoming-other, a notion the taxonomy's 'rhizome' does not capture.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Reinhold Niebuhr
holes.what: Twentieth-century political theologian whose Christian realism (Moral Man and Immoral Society) holds that collective life can achieve only relative justice and lesser evils, never individual moral purity.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues against Geralt's 'Evil is evil' neutrality entirely through Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society; the taxonomy has only H. Richard Niebuhr, a different thinker.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Helene Cixous
holes.what: French feminist theorist of ecriture feminine who, in 'Sorties' and The Newly Born Woman, analyzes how women are frozen between the Medusa and the abyss in the patriarchal symbolic order.
holes.why: Chapter 35 draws equally on Cixous (with Kristeva) to read the striga and the bruxa as the monstrous feminine, and Cixous is absent from the taxonomy.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Axel Honneth
holes.what: Third-generation Frankfurt School theorist whose theory of recognition (self-confidence, self-respect, self-esteem, and antecedent recognition) derives from Hegel's forms of intersubjectivity.
holes.why: Chapter 36 explains moral monstrosity as losing antecedent recognition using Honneth's Struggle for Recognition and Reification as its main framework after Hegel himself.
holes.book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

holes.name: Graham Greene
holes.what: British Catholic novelist whose 'Greeneland' of pity, betrayal, and morally indifferent secular worlds shaped noir fiction and espionage literature, including The Ministry of Fear and The Third Man.
holes.why: Chapter 7's entire argument reads Secret Agent through Greene's films and his 'Greeneland' worldview, contrasting Drake with Bond and treating Greene's Catholic escape via a Kierkegaardian leap of faith.
holes.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir

holes.name: Ruth Benedict
holes.what: Anthropologist whose 'Anthropology and the Abnormal' (1934) argues that normality and morality are culturally defined, the classic statement of cultural relativism.
holes.why: Chapter 6's critique of Naked City's relativist turn is built around reconstructing and refuting Benedict's difference argument and conceptual argument for cultural relativism.
holes.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir

holes.name: Open Interpretation (multiple interpretability of art)
holes.what: The view that an artwork can legitimately admit multiple, mutually incompatible interpretations with no single closed best reading, and that this openness is aesthetically valuable.
holes.why: Chapter 20's central thesis is that Twin Peaks' metaphysical and interpretive openness (naturalistic vs supernaturalistic readings of BOB) is precisely what disqualifies it from noir while giving it its aesthetic piquancy, defended through the 'omissive' aesthetic; no existing taxonomy concept captures multiple interpretability itself.
holes.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir

holes.name: Thomas Paine
holes.what: Anglo-American revolutionary pamphleteer who argued in Common Sense and Rights of Man that government is a necessary evil distinct from society, and that civil rights rest on pre-existing natural rights.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses extended quotations from Paine's Common Sense and Rights of Man to anchor its Locke-style classical-liberal reading of The X-Files and Millennium, and the Millennium episode 'Collateral Damage' names its antigovernment radical after him.
holes.book: 235 - The Philosophy of TV Noir

holes.name: Bricolage
holes.what: Creating art by collaging found objects and borrowed fragments diverted from their original ends (Andre Breton's 'change of role'), so their juxtaposed meanings critique the source culture.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire reading of Julien Temple's Punk Can Take It rests on bricolage, defined via Breton and applied both to individual scenes and to the film's overall structure.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Georg Lukacs
holes.what: Marxist philosopher whose History and Class Consciousness develops reification and the proletariat's collective path to class consciousness.
holes.why: Chapter 31's three-stage account of punk class consciousness and its warning about losing revolutionary potential are built directly on Lukacs's theory.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Affect (affect theory)
holes.what: An externally induced intensity that shifts our experiential state and moves us to act, developed from Spinoza and Bergson through Deleuze to Massumi's affect theory.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses affect to explain how punk's tempo, dynamics, gang vocals, and work-song rhythms generate camaraderie and class agitation.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Labeling Theory and Moral Entrepreneurs
holes.what: Howard S. Becker's account of deviance as the product of rule-enforcers and moral entrepreneurs who label whole groups (rather than acts) as deviant.
holes.why: Chapter 33 uses Becker's moral entrepreneurs to explain the anti-punk moral panic, 'de-punking' programs, and psychiatric commitments of teens who merely dressed oddly.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: The Matilda Effect
holes.what: The systematic erasure or misattribution of women's contributions, which get credited to men instead (named by Margaret Rossiter after suffragist Matilda Gage).
holes.why: Chapter 37 argues the collective memory of London punk suffers a variant of the Matilda effect, with the Slits and X-Ray Spex written out of the movement's history.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Conviviality (Ivan Illich)
holes.what: Ivan Illich's ideal of tools and institutions that give people the power to shape their own lives and make things themselves, against dependence on corporate and state systems.
holes.why: Chapter 40 frames the Ramones' DIY ethic and Yee Loi's self-taught home recording with Illich's convivial tools as the alternative to institutional dependence.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: The Paradox of Tragedy (the puzzle of dark art)
holes.what: The puzzle of why audiences take pleasure in art that arouses disagreeable emotions like sorrow, terror, and anger, classically posed in Hume's 'Of Tragedy'.
holes.why: Chapter 41 is organized around this puzzle as applied to negative punk songs, testing Aristotelian catharsis and Hume's conversion account against it.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Francis Hutcheson
holes.what: Early modern philosopher of aesthetics who defined beauty as the pleasure we take in 'uniformity amongst variety' - order and complexity.
holes.why: Chapter 43 sets punk's simplicity and chaos against Hutcheson's account of absolute beauty as its principal formalist foil.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy

holes.name: Value Pluralism
holes.what: Isaiah Berlin's view that genuine human values are many, sometimes competing, and cannot all be realized within any single way of living.
holes.why: Chapter 46 grounds the general value of punk cultural nonconformity in Berlin's value pluralism: more countercultures mean more genuine values realized.
holes.book: 251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy
